Motivation: operators frequently pick conservative batching and quantization settings that leave money on the table. This PR introduces Cost Pilot, a runtime-driven suggester that analyzes recent request distributions and model family characteristics to propose safe batching defaults, KV/prefix cache presets, and quantization profiles (int8/4-bit recommendations) per-model. Goals: 1) provide non-invasive suggestions (opt-in) that reduce per-token cost while keeping p95 latency within SLO; 2) wire the suggester into the Console recommendations UI and the Optimize pipeline; 3) add a small, reproducible simulation harness for validating suggestion impact on unit economics.

What this PR contains: - A runtime telemetry consumer that computes a compact fingerprint of sequence length distribution, concurrency, and cache hit patterns; - Heuristics engine that maps fingerprints to suggested batching window, concurrency cap, cache presets, and quant profile; - Safe-apply mode that produces a rollout plan (canary -> ramp -> full) with expected cost delta and estimated latency impact; - Console API endpoint and a CLI helper (redwood optimize suggest) to preview and export suggestions; - Unit tests, simulation harness, and an integration test that runs the suggester on synthetic traffic.

Compatibility and rollout: suggestions are completely non-destructive by default. The Console exposes an \"Apply suggestion\" flow which either writes a canary policy (route-level override) or a full model config. We added feature flag optimize.cost_pilot.enabled to gate production rollout. Suggested values are conservative: initial quant recommendations keep a float fallback for catastrophic drift detection.

Checklist: - [x] Telemetry consumer and fingerprinting - [x] Heuristics core and quant profile mapper - [x] Suggestion export + CLI - [x] Console endpoint + minimal UI wiring (server-side only) - [x] Tests and simulation harness - [x] Documentation: docs/usage/cost-pilot.md - [x] Added Linear tickets where needed

Related: Linear: ENG-4829, ENG-4906, ENG-4932. A follow-up will add automatic A/B evaluation harness and a feedback loop to record production quality regressions for quant suggestions. See design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4829/cost-pilot-design (internal).
Diego Rios (reviewer): Please add a short note in the suggester docs about how we detect catastrophic quality regressions; otherwise LGTM.
Priya Gupta (author): Added a 'regression guard' section that explains float fallback and the p95 latency check, and linked the simulation results. PTAL.
Liam O'Connor (reviewer): Can we make the initial canary default to 2% traffic? Ops prefers 1% in prod. I think 2% is fine but call it out in rollout recommendations.
Priya Gupta (author): Updated the default canary to 1% and noted rationale in the docs; also added a CLI flag --canary-percent to override.
payload.title: cost-pilot: runtime-driven batching + quantization suggester

Context and motivation: We've seen multiple customer reports and fuzzing runs where malformed multipart payloads or mislabeled Content-Type headers caused the OpenAI-compat layer to accept binary blobs that later triggered model-serving failures or excessive memory copies. This PR introduces a light-weight preflight probing stage for tool/file attachments plus robust MIME fallback detection and additional safety checks to prevent streaming stalls and silent truncation.

Changes and high-level design: Adds an attachment preflight probe (default: first 8 KiB) that is used to: 1) heuristically detect Content-Type using internal sniffers and libmagic as a fallback, 2) compute a rolling SHA256 prefix used for early integrity checks during streaming ingestion, 3) validate that declared Content-Length (if present) matches the Summarized-Length we derive from chunked/form-data metadata. The preflight is non-blocking for small files and performed inline for larger streams with a configurable probe timeout (default 200ms) to avoid hurting latency SLOs.

Compatibility: The OpenAI compatibility layer maps incoming file param names and content-type hints into a normalized Attachment struct used by tool/function calls. To avoid breaking existing clients, we accept the legacy param names (file, files[], input_file) and normalize them. We add a new response error code 4227 (attachment_content_mismatch) when a detected/mapped MIME does not align with the declared mime and user-specified tool schema. Clients will see the new X-Redwood-File-Probe-Length response header when probing occurred.

Security and limits: Introduces hard limits per-attachment and per-request enforced at the compat layer and validated by the runtime: per-attachment soft limit 100MiB (policy warning), hard limit 512MiB (reject), per-request combined attachments 1GiB hard cap. Tool-level override supported for enterprise/private deployments via policy. Unknown/unsafe MIME types are rejected for tool invocations unless explicitly permitted via tool manifest.

Streaming stability improvements: Adds backpressure-aware buffering during preflight and stream commit phases, explicit Content-Length vs chunked consistency checks, and detection of truncated multipart boundaries (returning 400 with clear diagnostics). Also ensures we do not hold entire attachments in memory for tools that accept streaming processing — we wire probe metadata into the stream pipeline so downstream consumers get the probe head and then the rest of the body with minimal copying.

Tests and rollout: Unit tests for libmagic fallback and probe timeout behaviour, integration tests exercising OpenAI-compat parameter name permutations, and an end-to-end canary in perf-canary verifying no measurable latency regression on short text-only requests. Feature is behind a rollout flag (compat.attachment_preflight) and will be enabled for 10% of hosted API traffic after merge, then ramped based on telemetry.

Implementation notes (commits below) and files changed (high level) provide more context.

Risk and mitigation: The main risk is increased tail latency for attachment endpoints; mitigations: probe timeout, probe size tunables, and initial 10% rollout with close SLO monitoring. We also added a failing-fast mode for private installs to keep behaviour deterministic during upgrades.

See related work: ENG-4892 (mime sniffing library integration), ENG-4971 (compat layer file param mapping).
Jacob Lee: Good coverage. One question — why 8 KiB as the default probe size? Is this empirically derived?
Priya Raman: Chosen after running attachments corpus: 95% of MIME sniffing decisions stabilized within 6 KiB; 8 KiB gives headroom for multipart headers. Made configurable via probe_size_bytes.
Soraya Khan: Need to ensure we don't regress streaming memory. Please add perf histogram for peak mem during preflight processing.
Priya Raman: Added peak_mem metric and packed the preflight state machine so it can be zero-copy when libmagic not invoked.
Marco Villanueva: Approve after test for deprecated param input_file is added to integration suite.
Priya Raman: Added extra permutations to test_compat_file_params.py and a note in docs about legacy names.

Introduce a single release indexer and rollback manifest generator for the private-installer packaging pipeline. Motivation: current release metadata for private deployments is fragmented across per-arch Helm indexes, tarball lists, and ad-hoc rollback blobs which complicates automated upgrades and makes rollbacks error-prone. This PR adds a deterministic release-index.json format that aggregates artifacts (helm charts, installer tarballs, OCI blobs), provenance pointers (cosign signatures, sbom hashes, attestation references) and a compact rollback-manifests/ directory with incremental patches used by the installer to perform atomic rollbacks. Changes: - add cmd/release-indexer: builds release-index.json from CI artifacts, computes deterministic stable IDs, attaches provenance bundle references, and emits signed index + incremental patch files - add cmd/rollback-gen: produces rollback-manifests/<release>-<seq>.json that the installer uses to roll back a specific component set - update private-installer Helm chart values and templates to read release-index.json and prefer pinned artifact URLs when present - terraform/modules/s3-buckets: add new prefixing and lifecycle policy used to host both indexes and incremental patches - CI: new workflow .github/workflows/release-indexer.yml that runs indexer on build artifacts, cosigns the index, generates SBOM deltas, and publishes to release-buckets - docs: document index schema, upgrade flow, and rollback semantics - tests: unit tests for stable ID generation, e2e test that simulates an upgrade then verifies rollback-manifests apply cleanly Notes on implementation: the indexer computes stable IDs using a canonical JSON serialization and sha256 over (artifact URL, arch, variant, semantic version, builder-provenance). The rollback-gen ensures patches are idempotent by using a three-way diff against the previous index and emitting reverse-apply steps. Security: cosign signing and sigstore attestations are integrated in CI; the installer verifies signatures and rejects unsigned indexes unless an explicit permissive flag is enabled. Backwards compatibility: indexer emits a legacy-compatible shim for older installer releases that still read per-chart indexes. Migration plan: CI will publish both legacy files and the new index for two release cycles; a follow-up PR will flip the installer default to prefer the index. See linked Linear ENG-3482 for rollout milestones.
Morgan Lee: This looks promising. Two high-level asks: (1) show compatibility guarantees in the README (what older installers will accept) and (2) ensure indexer emits a stable canonical ordering to avoid churn in signatures.
Author (Aisha Kapoor): Added a compatibility section in docs/private-installer/release-index.md and implemented canonical JSON ordering using encoding/json with a deterministic key sort before hashing.
Diego Ramos: The Terraform change needs a short migration note for customers with cross-account replication. Please make sure the lifecycle policy doesn't inadvertently expire rollback patches.
Author (Aisha Kapoor): Updated terraform/modules/s3-bucket/main.tf to set a 90-day minimum for the rollback prefix and added outputs to opt-in to cross-account replication. Also added a test that verifies patches survive lifecycle prune.
Anya Patel: CI step 'sbom-delta' flaked in the first run; I see you added retries. Can we add a smoke assertion that the delta is non-empty for every meaningful change?
Author (Aisha Kapoor): Added assertion in ci/scripts/sbom-delta.sh to fail if delta is empty when version changes. Also added retries and exponential backoff for the upstream sbom generator.
Diego Ramos: Approved after Terraform migration note and lifecycle tweaks. Morgan + Anya approved once docs and flaky CI flakiness were addressed.
Repository automation: merge queued (squash) after passing checks.
Introduce deterministic release-index.json and rollback-manifests for private-installer; CI publishes signed indexes and incremental rollback patches. Backwards-compatible shim included; operators should read docs/private-installer/release-index.md for migration steps.
Rollout plan: publish index in parallel with legacy artifacts for two cycles before switching installer default.
Follow-up: small PR to flip installer default and add telemetry for index usage.
Support runbook added at docs/private-installer/rollback-runbook.md

Motivation: CI for private installer releases lacked a machine-readable release graph and a manifest-level validator that ties signed artifacts (images, helm charts, tf modules) back to the release manifest. This PR adds a release-graph generator and a manifest-validator stage to the private-installer CI pipeline to ensure provenance, enable safer upgrades/rollbacks, and block unsigned/unaligned manifests from publishing. Summary of changes: - new pipeline step 'build:release-graph' which produces a directed release graph (JSON) that maps artifacts -> helm chart values -> terraform module versions and includes cryptographic digests and SBOM references; graph is collated from build outputs and attestation metadata - new pipeline step 'validate:manifest' that consumes a release graph and enforces: cosign signature verification (keyless and KMS), SBOM presence, chart values checksum, and compatibility matrix checks for upgrades - small helper library under tools/release-graph that normalizes artifact metadata, computes canonical digests, and emits signatures-ready metadata for the signer job - Helm chart linting rules extended to emit a Helm manifest fingerprint (stable ordering) and surface mismatches between chart contents and release graph - Terraform module manifest extraction to include provider pins and a short policy check to prevent unsupported provider upgrades in the same release - CI orchestration changes: the validate step runs before artifact promotion and blocks publishing to the release bucket on failure - added an automated delta-rollback manifest generator which creates a minimal rollback plan from the release graph when a canary fails Why this is different: existing pipelines stamp artifacts and upload indexes, but we need a top-level release graph that can be consumed by Private control-plane for deterministic rollouts and by on-prem installers to reconcile manifests during upgrades. This PR focuses on making the release artifact a first-class, verifiable graph rather than loose indexes. Checklist: - [x] release-graph generator implemented - [x] manifest validator implemented and integrated into the CI workflow - [x] cosign verification (keyless and KMS) wired into validator - [x] Helm fingerprinting integrated - [x] Terraform module extraction implemented - [x] unit tests for tools/release-graph - [x] e2e run in staging that simulates signed artifact promotion - [x] added docs for ops on how to interpret the release graph Changes included (high level): tools/release-graph/* (new library and CLI), ci/pipeline/build-release-graph.yaml (new job), ci/pipeline/validate-manifest.yaml (new job), charts/private-installer/patches/manifest-fingerprint.yaml (helper), terraform/modules/release-metadata/README.md (docs), scripts/delta-rollback/gen-rollback.sh (new helper), tests/integration/release-graph-e2e (e2e harness). Testing and verification: - unit coverage for release-graph normalization functions - integration test that generates a release graph from staged artifacts, signs them with a test KMS key, then runs validator (CI job uses real cosign verification in staging) - staging rollout run that exercised the delta-rollback generator after a simulated canary failure - CI history shows two failed validator runs during early iteration (missing SBOMs) which were fixed by the chart/lint rule update Rollout plan: - merged to main and enabled in staging for one week; manual gating for production release (ops approval required) - enable automatic blocking on validator failures for subsequent releases; until then validator failures are opt-in via release-note flag Migration notes: - existing release index consumers must be updated to prefer release-graph.json; a small compatibility shim is provided under tools/release-graph/bin/compatify - operators must ensure cosign public key or KMS access is available in the Private control-plane to verify signatures Security considerations: - cosign key usage requires KMS scopes; the validator supports both keyless (OIDC) verification and KMS-backed verification; by default validator rejects unsigned artifacts - SBOM presence is mandatory for private installer releases; policy can be relaxed via a per-customer policy file if needed Documentation: - docs/private-installer/release-graph.md added explaining format and how to use the delta-rollback generator - ops playbook updated with steps to manually validate a release graph Known limitations & follow-ups: - release-graph currently serializes all digests in SHA256; we will add multi-algo support (ENG-6780 follow-up) - we do not yet have an automated remediation when validator fails (ENG-6723 will track a retry/auto-fix job) Related: ENG-6723 (release graph spec), ENG-6780 (multi-algo hashing), SUP-3048 (support ticket where customer asked for deterministic rollback plans).
Priya Nair: Please add a note about KMS key rotation impact on old releases; we shouldn't make old releases unverifiable.
Marcus Chen: Added rotation doc and compatibility shim for cached public keys. See tools/release-graph/compat.md
Sofia Alvarez: Validator should surface which rule failed in CI summary. Added structured failure reasons to job output.
Ethan Park: Confirmed that helm fingerprinting is order-stable across helm versions; added additional tests for templating edge cases.
Ops (comment): We need a small UX doc for operators to inspect release graphs; added docs/private-installer/release-graph.md
Add release graph generation and manifest-level validation to private-installer CI. This enforces signed artifacts, SBOM presence, and compatibility checks before promoting releases. Also introduces a delta-rollback manifest generator for safer rollbacks.
This PR intentionally keeps the release-graph format backward compatible via a small compat shim. Consumers are encouraged to migrate to release-graph.json.
Follow-ups tracked in ENG-6723 and ENG-6780.

Motivation: reduce peak GPU workspace while preserving latency SLOs across mixed-batch workloads. This PR introduces a kernel-aware workspace coalescer that performs late-binding of scratch buffers and compacts per-kernel temporary allocations into shared slabs, plus a KV hotset prioritization heuristic that biases in-memory KV shards toward recently accessed prefixes to avoid costly device-host swaps. The change set touches allocator, scheduler, and KV cache subsystems and includes: 1) a new KernelWorkspaceCoalescer that tracks kernel-level scratch footprints and coalesces compatible windows at submit time; 2) adaptive slab sizing triggered by observed sequence-length distribution and continuous-batching pressure; 3) a cooperative eviction policy for KV cache: hotset prioritization + deferred eviction for recently-inflight requests; 4) scheduler hints to prefer coalescing-friendly batching boundaries and to avoid mixing kernels with incompatible workspace shapes; 5) telemetry surfaces (histograms/counters) for workspace utilization, coalescing hit-rate, and KV hotset churn. Benchmark results (internal perf harness) show 18-28% reduction in peak workspace for decoder-heavy models, 10-15% lower tail latency under sustained concurrent streams, and KV swap reduction of ~4x for conversational workloads. Implementation notes: changes are mostly in C++ runtime with a thin Python test harness. Backwards compatibility: no API changes to runtime surface; behavior is behind runtime config flags (runtime.coalesce_workspace=true by default in staging). Checklist: [x] perf numbers added [x] unit + integration tests [x] docs for new config [x] rollout plan (canary + gradual enable), followups: refine eviction credit model and integrate with Dedicated autoscaler.
Asha Menon (2026-02-19): Can we avoid an extra allocation path for tiny kernels? Suggest a fastpath that reuses existing slab when footprint < 2KB.
Julian Park (2026-02-19): Added small-kernel fastpath and microbench in commit 9b2f4c1.
Diego Ruiz (2026-02-22): KV deferred-evict queue looks promising; need a safety valve if memory pressure spikes during GC-heavy workloads.
Julian Park (2026-02-23): Added eviction credits and emergency flush in e5d4a12.
Claire Zhang (2026-02-27): Tests look good; please add an observability dashboard snippet to help oncall interpret workspace-coalescer metrics.
Julian Park (2026-03-01): Dashboard snippet added to docs and screenshots to the PR description.
Runtime: lower GPU workspace usage and improved KV cache residency via kernel-aware workspace coalescing and KV hotset prioritization. Expect lower peak memory footprints and improved tail latency for decoder-dominant workloads. Configs: runtime.coalesce_workspace (bool), runtime.kv_hotset_window_ms (int).
payload.title: kernel-aware-workspace-coalescer-and-kv-hotset-prioritization

Motivation: New OpenAI Responses variants expose streaming fragmentation semantics, RNG/seed hints, and richer metadata that must be faithfully represented in Redwood's Responses compatibility layer. Without an adapter, hosted customers see reordering and truncated toolcall boundaries in streamed responses and cannot reproduce outputs when a seed is provided. This PR implements a protocol adapter that stabilizes fragment reassembly, preserves explicit tool/function-call boundary markers in the stream, and forwards RNG/seed hints plus metadata passthrough to the sampling layer. Design highlights: 1) Introduce lightweight fragment framing (frag_id, seq, final_flag) on the bridge to detect out-of-order chunks and perform deterministic reassembly with minimal buffering. 2) Emit and consume explicit toolcall boundary tokens at the adapter layer so function/tool callers receive well-formed call begin/end events even when the underlying runtime shards streams. 3) Map OpenAI-style "seed"/"deterministic" hint fields to an internal RNG-hint header and expose a seed proxy that pins sampling when requested for reproducible debug runs. 4) Preserve response-level metadata (request_id, model_attrs, user_metadata) by passthrough on the adapter and tag primary streaming frames with metadata headers so the console and observability pipelines retain attribution. 5) Fail-open fallback: when fragment integrity cannot be verified within a configurable timeout, the adapter falls back to per-chunk best-effort delivery and flags the event in logs/metrics. Implementation notes: Changes are concentrated in services/bridge/openai_adapter.go (adapter logic and framing), runtime/stream/framer.go (framing helpers), runtime/stream/reassembly.go (reassembly state machine), runtime/sampling/seed_proxy.go (seed handoff and validation), api/compat/responses_adapter_test.go (unit/integration tests), and docs/compat/openai-responses.md (compatibility guide). The adapter is feature-flagged under "openai_responses_adapter_v2" and gated behind a canary rollout. Tests and validation: added deterministic integration tests that replay recorded fragment orders, end-to-end tests against an OpenAI-compat harness, and a small perf canary to verify latency impact under 99th-percentile SLOs. Observability: new metrics added: adapter.frag_reassembly.latency_ms, adapter.frag_reassembly.reorders, adapter.toolcall.boundary_mismatches, and adapter.seed_forward.count. Rollout plan: 1) enable on internal canary; 2) run for 48h comparing toolcall event counts and reassembly metrics; 3) enable on hosted region eu-west-1 with gradual traffic ramp; 4) flip feature flag for Dedicated customers based on contracts. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] integration tests, [x] canary config, [x] docs updated, [x] rollout plan added. Impact: backward compatible for existing calls, minor latency increase in worst-case reassembly situations, improves streaming stability and deterministic reproduction for debugging. Related: ENG-3241 tracks the adapter work; SUP-9123 references a customer case where streamed toolcalls were split across fragments.
Compatibility adapter: stable streaming reassembly across Responses variants, explicit tool/function-call boundary markers, and passthrough of RNG/seed hints to Redwood sampling for deterministic debug runs. No API breaking changes.
Eliot Wong: Looks solid overall. Two asks: (1) tighten the reassembly buffer cap and expose as config; (2) add a small fuzz test that randomly reorders fragments to validate the state machine. Also please add a short migration note for Dedicated customers.
Marissa Cole (author): Addressed buffer cap and exposed via adapter.max_reassembly_buffer; added fuzz test suite under api/compat/fuzz_reassembly_test.go; added dedicated migration note in docs. PTAL.
Diego Alvarez: Approve after the perf numbers are posted from the canary run. Concern: seed passthrough must never override customer KMS restrictions; ensure validation rejects externally-supplied seeds if KMS-policy forbids it.
Marissa Cole (author): Added validation gate in runtime/sampling/seed_proxy.go that checks customer seed policy via authz call; updated tests to cover the restricted case.
Samir Patel: Left a nit on log level for boundary-mismatch (info -> warn) and a small comment about metric cardinality. Resolved by adjusting to warn only when mismatch rate > threshold.
7 commits: initial adapter scaffold and feature flag; framing helpers and proto changes; reassembly state machine with tests; seed proxy + sampling integration; toolcall boundary markers and console tagging; docs and compatibility guide; canary config and CI pipeline adjustments.
Squash and merge. Merge commit message: 'openai(compat): responses protocol adapter with stable fragment reassembly, toolcall boundaries, and seed handoff. Closes ENG-3241.'
payload.title: Responses protocol adapter: stable fragment reassembly, toolcall boundaries, and seed handoff for OpenAI compatibility

Motivation: Long-context workloads show fragmentation across microbatches that prevent effective dequant fusion and cause repeated dequant/rescale operations per token. This PR introduces a cross-batch dequant fusion pass plus an amortized per-token rescale step that cooperates with the KV cache and continuous batching coordinator to reduce redundant dequant work for INT8/FP8 mixed-precision serving.

Summary of changes: implemented a new CrossBatchDequanter that tracks compatible contiguous microbatch windows and emits a fused dequant operation for stacked tokens; added an AmortizedRescale operator that defers fine-grained scale adjustments until token groups exceed a stability threshold; extended the scheduler with a cross-batch affinity hint and modified the KV cache interface to expose per-layer scale metadata needed by the fused path. Also added kernel-level fastpaths for fused int8->fp16 conversion targeting long prefix reuse patterns.

Design notes: the fused path is opt-in behind a runtime feature flag (RUNTIME_FUSED_DEQUANT). When enabled the scheduler annotates queued requests with batch-affinity tags; CrossBatchDequanter periodically probes the queue to form mergeable windows constrained by latency SLO heuristics. AmortizedRescale computes a combined scale factor and only applies per-token micro-adjustments when the cumulative quantization error crosses a configurable threshold (defaults tuned from benchmarks). Compatibility: falls back to existing per-request dequant for heterogeneous model variants and when KV cache indicates incompatible scale signatures.

Benchmarks: microbench on p4d.24xlarge with a 16k context evaluation harness showed up to 22% throughput improvement and 18% average token-latency reduction on customer-like chat load (95th percentile latency remained within SLO). FP8/INT8 combined workloads saw better utilization due to fewer kernel launches and improved KV cache hit patterns. Detailed numbers included in /docs/perf/crossbatch-dequant-run-2026-02-20.md.

Testing: unit tests for CrossBatchDequanter and AmortizedRescale (kernel emulation mode), end-to-end CI smoke against the runtime with synthetic traffic, and a canary rollout configuration for Dedicated. Stress tests included kv-cache warm/cold cycles and continuous-batching scenarios. CI initially reported a flaky scheduler test (test_scheduler_affinity) which was fixed by adding a deterministic queue snapshot during window formation.

Rollout plan: behind feature flag, canary on dedicated pools with low-priority routing, opt-in for private deployments via config toggle. Observability: new metrics added (dequant_fused_windows, amortized_rescale_ops, per_layer_scale_mismatch) and alerting thresholds proposed in SLO dashboard PR.

Related: follows up on ENG-3962 and complements earlier kernel fusion work (see ENG-1538). Notable tradeoffs: slightly increased memory for temporary fused buffers; however the overall token compute/launch overhead drops substantially for long prefix reuse.

Files changed (high level): runtime/kernel/crossbatch_dequant.cc, runtime/kernel/crossbatch_dequant.h, runtime/kernel/fused_int8_fp16_path.cu, runtime/scheduler/crossbatch_coordinator.cpp, runtime/scheduler/crossbatch_coordinator.h, runtime/scheduler/affinity_hint.h, runtime/kv_cache/scale_metadata.h, runtime/kv_cache/scale_metadata.cpp, runtime/config/feature_flags.yaml, docs/perf/crossbatch-dequant-run-2026-02-20.md, tests/unit/test_crossbatch_dequant.cpp, tests/integration/test_amortized_rescale_endtoend.py and supporting mocks and CI scripts.

Commits: ["add cross-batch dequant core algorithm and API", "implement amortized per-token rescale operator", "scheduler: cross-batch affinity hint and coordinator loop", "kv_cache: expose per-layer scale metadata and compatibility checks", "kernel: fused int8->fp16 conversion fastpath (CUDA) with unit tests", "docs/perf: add benchmark run and interpretation notes", "tests: stabilize scheduler test by snapshotting queue during windowing"].

Review conversation (high level): reviewer Arjun Patel: "This is a promising direction — major nit: the window formation should account for heterogenous model variants to avoid incorrect fusion across layout changes." Author reply (Maya Chen): "Added compatibility probe and documented fallback semantics; windowing now checks per-layer signatures before merging." Reviewer Liam O'Connor: "Can we quantify memory overhead of fused buffers and add a guard to disable when memory pressure is high?" Author: "Added runtime guard and heuristic to revert to per-request dequant if free GPU memory < 6GB for the pool." Reviewer Sofia Martinez: "CI showed a flaky test — please stabilize." Author: "Fixed and added deterministic snapshot in the coordinator loop; CI green now."

Merge outcome: approved by reviewers after two iterations, CI green on final run, merged via squash.

Release notes: "Add experimental fused cross-batch dequant and amortized rescale path to improve INT8/FP8 mixed-precision throughput for long-context workloads; opt-in via RUNTIME_FUSED_DEQUANT flag. See perf docs for measured gains and rollout guidance."
Arjun Patel: The window formation should verify model layout signatures before fusing — otherwise risk wrong dequant semantics.
Maya Chen: Added signature probe and fallback path; updated tests and docs.
Liam O'Connor: Memory overhead concern for fused buffers; consider guard.
Maya Chen: Implemented memory-guard < 6GB threshold and a config knob.
Sofia Martinez: Flaky scheduler test observed on CI.
Maya Chen: Stabilized by queue snapshotting; re-ran CI.
Arjun Patel: LGTM after fixes.
Liam O'Connor: Approved.
Sofia Martinez: Approved.

Context and motivation: Our token-level cost and latency metrics have grown high-cardinality over the last year (per-route + per-model + variable token-length labels). This created two problems: Prometheus remote write ingestion costs spiked and some alert rules started firing noisy signals for low-traffic routes. This change introduces a deterministic bucketing strategy for token-level cost and a lightweight adaptive span sampling policy to keep tracing volume stable while increasing capture rate for error/slow paths. Goals: 1) Reduce metrics cardinality and long-term storage costs. 2) Keep token-level observability for SLOs and regression detection. 3) Reduce noisy alerts by moving to aggregated alerting and improved thresholds. 4) Maintain backwards compatibility for dashboards during a deprecation window.

Summary of changes: - Add token_cost_bucket metric label and a deterministic bucketer that maps raw per-request token cost to one of fixed buckets [0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500] micro-units. The runtime now emits token_cost_bucket and token_cost_estimate (capped float) while deprecating the previous free-form token_cost label. - Implement an adaptive span sampler: default sample_rate=0.01 (1%), errors and timeouts sample at min(10%, 10x base) and there's a short-term burst cap to avoid sudden spikes. Sampling decisions are deterministic per-request id to avoid partial traces. - Dashboard updates: Grafana panels replaced route-level noisy charts with aggregated service views; new panels show bucketed distribution and delta-to-baseline. - Alert tuning: switch token-cost SLO alerts from per-route P99 to service-level P99 with a 5% burn window; add a high-cardinality guard alert that triggers if unique label values exceed threshold. - Backwards compatibility: keep old metric token_cost_unbucketed exported for 30 days as a plain counter (no label cardinality growth) and add migration docs. - Tests: unit tests for bucketer edge cases, integration tests for exporter and sampling repeatability; CI runs include short perf bench to detect regression.

Commits (high-level): - 1f2a4d3: runtime: add token_cost bucketer and capped estimate export - 3c9b201: tracing: adaptive span sampler and deterministic decision - 7a8f33b: metrics/exporter: preserve legacy token_cost_unbucketed for deprecation - b2d1a9e: dashboards: grafana panels & migration script - 9d4c8f0: alerts: move token-cost alerts to service aggregation and add cardinality guard - f5e6a11: tests: unit and integration tests + perf smoke - c0d2b6a: docs: observability/token-cost-buckets.md and migration notes

Files touched (high-level): - redwood/observability/metrics/token_cost.go (bucketer + exporter) - redwood/observability/tracing/sampler.go (adaptive sampler) - redwood/observability/exporter/prometheus_exporter.go (label cardinality guards) - dashboards/grafana/token_cost_service_dashboard.json (new panels + migration notes) - docs/observability/token-cost-buckets.md - alerts/rules/token_cost_service_rules.yaml - tests/integration/test_token_cost_bucketing.go - tests/perf/smoke_token_cost_latency.sh - examples/observability/token-cost-demo.sh

Implementation notes and rationale: - Bucket boundaries are intentionally coarse (exponential-ish) to preserve signal for small-cost operations while collapsing long-tail expensive requests into manageable categories. payload.body:
Context and motivation: We observed repeated tail spikes in mixed workloads where a minority of long-sequence or KV-heavy requests would monopolize batching resources and push many small/kv-hit requests into long queue wait times. Previous approaches (simple priority buckets, deadline-based preemption) improved tails but produced oscillation and suboptimal kernel utilization on GPU (switching kernels frequently hurt throughput). This PR implements a cohort-oriented scheduling layer on top of the continuous batcher that: 1) groups requests into stable cohorts (short/normal/long sequences and kv-hit vs kv-miss), 2) assigns a weighted schedule that enforces proportional service to cohorts, and 3) biases kernel selection (kernel affinity) to reduce expensive kernel switches while still honoring fairness targets. Design summary: - Cohorting: requests are classified on enqueue into cohorts based on sequence_length quantiles and a KV-hit flag (fast path if cache hit). Cohort keys are compact (3 length buckets x 2 kv-hit = 6 cohorts). Cohorts are sticky for the lifecycle of a request. - Scheduling: per-cohort deficit counters implement a proportional deficit-round-robin with decay. Each scheduling tick selects batches from cohorts in order of deficit, but a soft cap prevents any cohort from consuming >X% of cycles for Y ms. - Kernel affinity: batches composed predominantly of short sequences prefer the int8 small-kernel path; long cohorts prefer the large-kernel fused path. The scheduler attempts to co-locate consecutive batches to the same kernel to reuse warmed kernels and reduce JIT/queue churn. - KV anti-starvation heuristics: kv-hit cohorts are given a small carry-forward credit and a short preemption window. If a cohort has seen repeated misses (i.e., been skipped >N times) the scheduler temporarily boosts its weight. Additionally, KV pinned entries get an aging score so that pinning does not permanently block eviction; very-old pins decay faster to avoid indefinite starvation of cache-backed requests. - Timeouts and preemption: soft-timeouts can preempt a batch that has not started execution after queueing for T_soft ms; preempted requests are requeued into the same cohort but receive a temporary priority bump to bound tail latency. Hard timeouts still exist for SLA enforcement. Implementation notes: - Changes live in runtime/batcher/cohort_scheduler.{cc,py} and runtime/kv/aging_cache.cc. - Minimal API surface: behavior is entirely internal to the batcher; no public API changes. - Added telemetry: cohort.dispatched_count, cohort.wait_ms_histogram, kernel.switches_per_minute, kv.pin_age_histogram. - Compatibility: new cohort mapping is feature-flagged via BATCHER_COHORTING=on; default is off for safe rollouts. Commit summary: - add cohorting classifier and unit tests - implement proportional deficit scheduler and soft caps - implement kernel affinity heuristics and kernel warm flags - add KV pin aging and anti-starve boost path - telemetry and dashboards - integration tests for mixed workloads - docs + rollout playbook High-level changed files (illustrative snippets): - runtime/batcher/cohort_scheduler.cc (new) - runtime/batcher/cohort_scheduler.h (new) - runtime/batcher/continuous_batcher.cc (modifications ~+130 lines) - runtime/kv/aging_cache.cc (modifications ~+85 lines) - runtime/metrics/cohort_metrics.cc (new) - infra/feature_flags/config.go (expose BATCHER_COHORTING) - tests/integration/cohort_mixed_workload.test (new) Example scheduler config (defaults in code): - cohort_buckets: ["short","normal","long"] - kv_hit_boost: 0.12 - soft_cap_pct: 0.45 - soft_timeout_ms: 25 - long_cohort_kernel: "fused-large" - short_cohort_kernel: "int8-small" Tests and validation: - Unit tests cover classifier boundaries, deficit counter wrap, and pin-aging behavior. - Integration harness simulated mixed workloads (70% short-kv-hit, 20% short-kv-miss, 10% long) across GPU types (A100, H100, and a CPU fallback). - Performance results (A100, 4x GPUs, steady-state synthetic):   - Baseline (no cohorting): p95=48ms p99=210ms throughput=1.00x cost-index=1.00   - Cohorting on (tuned defaults): p95=36ms p99=150ms throughput=0.99x cost-index=0.95   - Notes: p99 improvement is concentrated on mixed workloads; homogeneous long-only workloads see negligible change. Rollout and canary plan: - Feature-flag rollout in 3 phases: internal dev cluster -> 10% production w/ realtime telemetry -> gradual ramp to 100% if no regressions after 48h. - Canary health checks: cohort.wait_ms_histogram, kernel.switches_per_minute, p99 latency, error-rate. - Automated rollback triggers: p99 increase >10% or kernel.switches spike >3x. Review conversation (high level): - Evan: requested tighter bounds on soft_cap_pct and asked for thought-through defaults for small clusters. Response: added config override and conservative defaults; documented in rollout. - María: noted potential for oscillation when many cohorts are equal weight; I added exponential decay on deficit boosts to damp oscillation. - Calvin: asked for more telemetry around kernel switches; added kernel.switches_per_minute and single-run traces for first 10s. CI and flaky tests: - Initial CI run failed an integration test due to a race in requeue path; fixed by introducing a requeue backoff and re-ran CI. Final status: all checks passed. Performance experiments and regressions: - Microbench harness run for A100/H100/CPU showed kernel affinity reduced kernel-init jitter by ~20%. - Memory: no measurable increase in resident set; KV pin aging introduced small metadata overhead (~1.2% in cache footprint). Known limitations and TODOs: - Current cohorting uses static quantiles; future work (ENG-7928) will add adaptive cohort boundary tuning. - We do not yet auto-tune soft_cap_pct per-cluster; follow-up planned. - Edge case: pathological workloads that intentionally craft many very-large batches can still cause transient cache pressure; mitigation is documented in runbook. Related PRs and work items: - PR #47109 (kernel warm path improvements) - ENG-7928 (adaptive cohort boundaries) - ENG-7902 (kv-cache observability) Checklist: - [x] Unit tests added - [x] Integration tests added - [x] Telemetry and dashboards added - [x] Rollout plan documented - [x] Feature flagged - [x] Docs updated Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main on 2026-02-25 after approvals from reviewers and green CI.
Introduce cohort-based continuous batching with kernel affinity and KV anti-starvation heuristics. Reduces p99 tail by ~30% for mixed workloads; no API changes.

Motivation: customer signals and internal evals showed awkward ergonomics when callers needed to coordinate multiple tool calls in a single turn: racey injection of tool outputs into streaming chat responses, unclear retry semantics for parallel calls, and inconsistent behavior between Redwood SDKs and OpenAI function-call compat. This PR consolidates the server-side tool-invocation surface (ToolInvocation v2), introduces a ParallelToolRunner helper to express parallel or gated fanout, normalizes retry and idempotency behavior, and surfaces deterministic result-injection points for streaming responses. Key points: 1) API: new optional request fields: tool_calls (array of tool descriptors), parallel_mode ("concurrent"|"sequential"|"gated"), idempotency_key (string). These are backwards compatible: requests without tool_calls follow prior single-tool path. 2) Runtime: ParallelToolRunner executes tool workers with bounded concurrency, pluggable backpressure hooks, and exposes a merge strategy (first-complete, ordered, aggregated) so callers can choose deterministic injection semantics. 3) Streaming: added deterministic injection hooks that let the model stream partial text while tagged tool results are injected as structured events ("tool_result") rather than inlined text blobs; this reduces re-write churn and avoids mid-stream tokenization regressions. 4) OpenAI-compat: function-call -> tool mapping updated to keep previous function calling behavior by default but enables richer tool metadata (schemas and version tags) so existing clients remain compatible. 5) Retries: retry logic centralised into retry_helpers with per-tool idempotency checks and circuit-breaker guards; parallel retries are coordinated to avoid duplicate side effects by default. 6) SDKs: TypeScript and Python SDKs get ergonomic helpers: callToolsParallel(), callToolsSequence(), and tooling types for structured tool results. 7) Observability: new metrics and spans for tool_fanout.size, tool_fanout.latency_p50/p95, tool_injection.count, and a per-request tool_call.trace_id. 8) Rollout: feature-flagged on prod (runtime.feature.tool_invocation_v2) with a gradual ramp plan, canary on dedicated regions, and auto-fallback to legacy path on error. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-987) - [x] Runtime and API implementation - [x] SDK bindings for TS/Py - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Load/perf regressions within tolerance - [x] Docs/console exposés - [x] Migration guide and roll-out plan.

Maya: suggest tightening retry backoff for non-idempotent tools — adjusted to exponential backoff + explicit no-retry option for non-idempotent tool descriptor
Connor: request to add an integration test showing parallel tools with mixed success/failure — added integration-tests/tooling/parallel-calls.spec.ts to assert injection ordering and failure propagation
Introduce ToolInvocation v2 and ParallelToolRunner: better ergonomics for multi-tool flows, deterministic result injection for streaming responses, normalized retry/idempotency semantics, and OpenAI function-call compatibility improvements. SDKs updated for easier parallel/sequence calls.

Motivation: intermittent correctness regressions and rare kernel assertion OOMs during long-sequence continuous-batching workloads were being handled by an all-or-nothing safe-mode that fell back to FP32 CPU execution. That approach eliminated correctness incidents but caused large tail latency and cost spikes. This PR implements a hybrid fallback that trades small latency regressions for correctness while keeping most requests on the fast GPU path.

What this change does (single-line summary): Adds a gate that triggers a controlled fallback to compatible kernels (FP32 or CPU) when a set of runtime signals indicate likely correctness risk: KV cache checksum mismatch, kernel assert counter > threshold, or per-request token-level divergence above configured tolerance. The gate is conservative by default and behind a feature flag `hybrid_kernel_fallback` set to off in main; rollout configuration and safe defaults are included.

Key components in the diff (high-level):
- runtime/fallback/hybrid_gate.cc/h: new gate logic that aggregates signals, applies hysteresis and cooldown windows.
- runtime/kernels/kernel_selector.cc: exposes compatibility metadata and fallback candidates per model artifact.
- runtime/kv/consistency_checker.cc: lightweight KV prefix checksum hooks and sample counters.
- scheduler/continuous_batching_manager.cc: emits per-batch KV stability stats and integrates cooldown decisions.
- observability/metrics.yaml: new metrics: fallback_rate, kv_inconsistency_count, fallback_cooldown_seconds, fallback_latency_penalty.
- integration tests: tests/runtime/hybrid_fallback_integration_test.py: e2e scenarios with long sequences and simulated kernel asserts.
- docs/operational/fallbacks.md: rollout and runbook updates.

Commits (summary):
- 1/6 Add gate primitives and API for aggregated signals
- 2/6 Implement KV checksum sampler and lightweight counter
- 3/6 Hook gate into continuous batching manager and kernel selector
- 4/6 Add metrics and dashboards for visibility
- 5/6 E2E tests and deterministic replay harness
- 6/6 Docs and feature-flagging + rollout config

Testing and CI: Unit tests for gate logic and KV sampler were added. E2E integration tests were flaky at first due to nondeterministic replaying of kernel asserts; added deterministic random seeds and a 'test-only' bypass for timing. CI pipeline initially failed 2 runs on integration tests; failures traced to timing races in the test harness and fixed in commit 5. Final CI status: pass (build + unit + integration + lint).

Perf and correctness numbers from canary (10% traffic in staging for 48h):
- Correctness incident rate: down 93% (from 15 incidents to 1)
- Overall median latency: +0.8% (insignificant)
- 95th percentile latency: +8% (due to fallback tail) — mitigations: cooldown and batching-aware fallback reduce this in subsequent rollouts
- Token-level divergence (regression tests): eliminated for sampled workloads
- Unit-cost impact: +4% at 10% traffic; expected to be neutral at scale with further tuning of thresholds

Rollout plan: feature-flag off in main. Canary -> 10% for 48h (done) -> 50% for 72h (monitor fallback_rate and fallback_latency_penalty) -> 100% if no regression. Alert thresholds added: fallback_rate > 0.5% sustained triggers on-call, fallback_latency_penalty > 15% triggers rollback.

Back-and-forth in review (high level):
- Miguel Alvarez: requested stronger telemetry (per-model fallback_rate) and a new metric for 'fallback_reason' tag. Author: added per-model tags and expanded runbook.
- Sofia Chen: flagged potential double-accounting of KV checks when multiple batches mutate same KV; requested a cooldown hysteresis change from 30s->60s. Author: implemented 60s default but left param configurable.
- Derek Wong: requested an e2e test that simulates rapid switchback scenarios; author added an additional integration test and a 'no switchback' policy toggle.

Author notes and rationale: We prefer a conservative hybrid approach that preserves correctness without wholesale safe-mode fallbacks. The gate aggregates cheap signals that are already collected or cost <1% of request time. The tuning parameters (checksum sample rate, hysteresis windows, divergence tolerance) are exposed and documented. The default behavior offline is to be conservative; operators can enable a more aggressive mode for lower cost at their own risk.

Files changed count: 12. Notable small snippets included in runtime/kernels/kernel_selector.cc to avoid breaking ABI; kernel metadata additions are backward compatible. Integration tests added are deterministic and run in CI with fixed seeds.

Merge and deploy: Approved by reviewers after two rounds of changes. Merged via squash on 2026-02-22. Feature flagged off by default; ops aware via runbook and dashboard. Follow-ups: a follow-up PR will add automatic threshold tuning based on workload profiles (ENG-5410).

Related tickets: ENG-5321 (primary), ENG-5410 (follow-up auto-tuning), SUP-1983 (Customer-reported KV divergence incidents).
Introduces hybrid kernel fallback gating based on KV cache consistency and runtime error signals. Feature-flagged; rollout plan 10%->50%->100%. Adds observability metrics and alert thresholds.

Motivation: production model promotion needs deterministic, metric-driven promotion and a lightweight quarantine path for problematic variants without full rollback noise. This PR implements a thresholded shadow->canary promotion flow and a quarantine first-class primitive that isolates models showing drift or error spikes. Changes include: new rollout controller state machine, metric threshold DSL, quarantine API surface, deterministic warmup windows, and end-to-end integration with the observability stack and canary alerts. Design highlights: 1) Shadow priming stage: route mirrored traffic to candidate model while keeping responses hidden; automatic delta metrics (latency, token-err, perplexity, hallucination-score) computed over sampling windows. 2) Threshold evaluation: a compact DSL in rollout config allows percentage and absolute thresholds with lookback windows (e.g., latency_p95<120ms AND token_err_rate_delta<0.5%). 3) Canary promotion: automated gradual traffic bump with hold windows and automated rollback if thresholds violated. 4) Quarantine: when a threshold breach occurs during shadow or canary, the controller moves the variant to 'quarantined' state, which preserves logs, stops routing live traffic, and spins a lightweight readonly debug endpoint for replaying failing traces. 5) Safety: automatic cooldowns, explicit owner notifications, and a manual override to promote from quarantine after investigation. This description includes the user-visible rollout configuration changes and the operational playbook.

Add thresholded shadow-to-canary promotion flow and a quarantine lifecycle for model variants. Operators can now configure metric thresholds to trigger automated rollback and quarantine, inspect quarantined variants via console, and replay traces for debugging. Includes new rollout schema and example configs.
Unit tests cover DSL parsing and state transitions; integration tests exercise mirrored traffic, delta metrics, and quarantine transitions. E2E harness runs realistic traffic patterns to validate canary bumping and automated rollback. Introduce a predictive headroom scheduler that reserves and releases dedicated fleet capacity based on short-term traffic forecasts and tenant-level SLO intents. Motivation: current reactive autoscalers oscillate under bursty traffic and either overprovision (wasting committed capacity) or underprovision (breaching throughput SLAs). This PR implements an EWMA-based short window predictor augmented with anomaly suppression, a configurable confidence margin, and soft caps for burst-bank integration so tenants keep predictable burst behavior while preserving long-term utilization. Key user-visible behavior: new fleet config fields (prediction_window_seconds, confidence_margin_pct, warmup_duration_seconds, anomaly_backoff) and a per-tenant score that maps predicted QPS to an allocation delta. The scheduler integrates with existing burst token pool logic but prefers predictive headroom for gradual scale-up and falls back to immediate burst tokens only when prediction error is high. Also adds telemetry: predicted_vs_actual_qps histogram, headroom_reservations_gauge, and prediction_error_rate alert. Implementation notes: scheduler service running as part of fleet-controller selects scale actions every 5s by default; uses historical 60s sliding window for EWMA with optional ARIMA feature-flag for customers who opt in on Dedicated. The rollout is gated: config flag predictive_headroom.enabled default false; rollout plan includes Canary on two low-risk fleets, blue/green for Dedicated control plane, and a kill-switch that reverts to legacy autoscaler if error_rate > 5% for 10m. Includes unit and integration tests, new e2e perf canary scenario, and operator docs for tuning margins and warmup. Backwards compatibility: existing autoscaler configs remain valid; predictive configs are additive. See Linear ENG-6291 for acceptance criteria and metrics targets.

Ava Martinez: Added a note and micro-benchmarks in predictive_headroom.go comments and a small CPU budget check in the controller loop.
Priya Nair: Request change: tighten default confidence_margin_pct from 25 to 15 for lower-median tenants; updated defaults in helm values.
Marcus Bell: Approved after verifying telemetry metrics and canary results in staging. Left one optional nit about doc phrasing.
Merged after canary validation; no rollback needed. Enabled behind feature flag; dedicated customers must opt in. Canary showed 12% reduction in short-term overprovisioning on test fleets and maintained 99.9% throughput SLO during burst windows.
Introduce predictive headroom scheduler for Dedicated fleets (opt-in). Improves short-term provisioning accuracy to reduce wasted reserved capacity and maintains burst guarantees. Operator tuning guide added.

payload.body:
Motivation: Tool-calling surfaces at Redwood are increasingly parallel and streaming-first. We observed two classes of production failures: transient upstream tool timeouts that caused duplicate downstream side-effects when clients retried, and streaming stalls when concurrent tool return envelopes were merged into the chat stream. This PR introduces a lightweight "tool hydrator" that provides an idempotent result injection contract, cooperative backpressure hooks for streaming response pipelines, and an explicit retry policy surface compatible with our OpenAI-compat layer.

Summary: This change implements: 1) a tool hydration protocol that attaches an idempotency key and deterministic merge hints to tool responses so replays are safe; 2) backpressure-aware streaming merge that signals the runtime to slow or batch late tool insertions instead of blocking the token stream; 3) a retry/hedging policy expressed as headers/metadata so the front-end and OpenAI-compat middleware can make consistent retry decisions; 4) unit + integration tests exercising parallel tool calls with simulated latency spikes and flaky tool endpoints.

Design notes (high-level): The hydrator is a small middleware between the invocation layer and the response serializer. It stamps tool responses with: - idempotency_key: client-provided or generated at invocation time - merge_strategy: one of [append, replace-on-timestamp, replace-on-seq] - schema_hint: short structured-output hint to improve downstream parsing (e.g., json-schema-id) We enforce an at-most-once injection into the streaming response by checking the idempotency_key within the request's KV cache and writing a short hydrated pointer into the stream instead of re-emitting duplicate payloads. For long-running tool results we emit a placeholder token ("[[tool-pending:<id>]]") and later hydrate the placeholder when the result arrives; hydration applies the merge_strategy for deterministic placement.

Retry contract: Retries are permitted only when the tool call returned an explicit transient error marker (transient=true) or when the idempotency_key is present. If the tool returns "uncertain" we include a replay token and require the caller to call back with explicit confirmation. Backoff defaults are conservative (exponential with jitter, min 100ms) and are surfaced via headers so the OpenAI-compat adapter can translate them to Retry-After semantics where appropriate.

Compatibility and migration: Default behavior is backwards compatible; we only add optional metadata fields to tool responses. Existing clients that ignore these fields will continue to receive tool payloads, but will not benefit from idempotent replays or hydration placeholders. The OpenAI-compat middleware is updated to consume retry headers and to prefer merge_strategy when converting tool results into choices/attachments.

Testing: Added unit tests for hydrator logic, integration tests that run 3 concurrent tool calls with synthetic delays and validate no duplicate side-effects, and an end-to-end smoke test with the OpenAI-compat adapter ensuring streaming stability under backpressure.

Checklist: - [x] Hydrator middleware implementation - [x] Streaming merge hooks and placeholder tokens - [x] Retry headers and policy translation - [x] Unit & integration tests - [x] Docs: API contract comment added to /docs/internal/tool-calls.md

Related work: builds on previous work to stabilize tool fanout (see ENG-1807) and complements the KV cache improvements from ENG-1982.

Notes: This is intentionally conservative on schema and merge heuristics; future PRs can add richer structured-output negotiation and eval-driven merge selection.
4 commits: initial hydrator middleware + tests; streaming merge hooks; retry header translation for OpenAI-compat; docs and test flake fixes.
Diego Rivera: Left a few nits around error-edge handling in hydrator.go; please add a comment explaining why we choose replace-on-timestamp as the default.
Maya Chen: Responded — added comment and switched default to replace-on-seq after discussion; clarified why timestamp variant is kept for backwards compat tests.
Priya Nambiar: Requested an extra integration test that simulates a tool returning a partial stream and later completing; added test and it uncovered a race which was fixed.
Ethan Wells: Approved after CI green and flake fix; noted we should measure 99th percentile latency impact and file a follow-up if >5%
Features: Introduce tool hydrator middleware to enable idempotent tool result injections and placeholder hydration. Adds retry header surface for OpenAI-compat layer. Improvements: more resilient streaming merges under backpressure.
Migration: Backwards compatible; clients may opt-in to idempotency and merge strategies.

Motivation: different OpenAI-style models emit function/tool calling payloads with small shape and framing variations (partial JSON fragments in streaming, tool messages using either 'tool' or 'name', tool_choice semantics unclear when multiple tools are suggested). This PR adds a thin normalization layer in the OpenAI compatibility path that canonicalizes incoming tool invocation messages into a single ToolPayload shape and fixes streaming fragmentation so tool messages are emitted atomically to callers.

What this changes (summary):
- Introduce pkg/api/openai_compat/normalize.go: permissive mapper that accepts common variants ("tool" vs "name", nested "arguments" vs flat, content-type tags) and emits a canonical ToolPayload. The mapper records source-variant metadata for observability and fallback heuristics.
- Streaming framer changes in pkg/streaming/framer.go: coalesce partial events for tool messages until a complete JSON payload is available or a configured timeout elapses; emit a "tool_message.complete" framing event with an attached schema tag. This dramatically reduces truncated tool JSON seen by SDK consumers.
- Enforce tool_choice semantics in pkg/handlers/tool_invoke_handler.go and SDKs: the compatibility layer exposes a tool_choice policy flag (first|best|ensemble). Default is "first" to match historical behavior; an explicit "best" option selects the highest-scoring tool when model outputs include scores.
- Add a JSON schema mapper pkg/codec/json_schema_mapper.go that performs lightweight validation and auto-coercion for argument types (strings->json when appropriate).
- SDK updates (python/typescript) to expose normalized ToolPayload and a small helper to rehydrate tool messages into user-friendly shapes.
- Tests: new unit and integration tests to simulate fragmented streams, variant key names, and tool_choice permutations.
- Docs: docs/openai-compat.md describing the mapping, compatibility guarantees, and migration notes.

Compatibility notes and rollout: The normalization layer is additive and default-preserving: existing apps see the same shape unless they switch the tool_choice policy. Streaming behavior is improved so consumers who previously had to tolerate partial JSON will now get complete tool messages; there is a short grace period where both old and new framing are supported (compat-shims.yaml). Linear links: ENG-2345 (compatibility mapper), ENG-2390 (streaming framer). Support ticket SUP-411 reported truncated tool JSON in production and motivated the timeout tuning.

Checklist: 
- [x] Mapper and schema coercion implemented
- [x] Streaming framer + timeout and config knobs
- [x] SDK helpers and tests
- [x] Integration tests against streaming harness

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Some custom consumers relied on the previous raw stream shape. Mitigation: feature-flagged rollout, opt-out compat shim, and clear docs with migration examples.
- Risk: Over-eager coercion could change argument types. Mitigation: mapper records coercions and we log a warning metric; coercion can be disabled per-route.

Performance: CPU impact is negligible in microbenchmarks (<1% p50 on our serving harness) due to parsing being guarded by a cheap pre-check and short-circuit for well-formed messages. Memory overhead is a few allocations per tool message.

Links: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-2345/tool-payload-normalizer, https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-2390/streaming-framer
