Default behavior preserves existing shapes; see docs/openai-compat.md for migration steps.
payload.title: Normalize OpenAI-style tool invocation payloads and stabilize streaming tool-message framing

payload.body:
Motivation: clients integrating with OpenAI-style function/tool calling expect deterministic 'tool_choice' semantics and stable streaming handoffs when the assistant decides to invoke external tools. We observed multiple interoperability issues: (1) fragmented streaming messages lost tool selection context when the 'tool' metadata was embedded mid-stream, (2) schema mapping between OpenAI function objects and Redwood tool definitions produced loose/ambiguous typed outputs, and (3) fallbacks for partial/malformatted tool_choice messages were inconsistent across runtimes.

This PR implements a canonical 'tool_selector' envelope in the streaming protocol designed to be minimal and backwards-compatible. The envelope is emitted as a discrete framed event before tool invocation payloads; it contains a stable tool id, the resolved schema reference, and an explicit selection_reason (model_ranking | heuristic | user_request). When a client receives an early 'tool_selector' frame it can immediately prepare local tooling (e.g. open sockets, allocate cache partition) without waiting for the tool payload.

Key changes (summary): implements adapter and runtime plumbing to emit/consume the new envelope; adds deterministic mapping rules from OpenAI "function" schema to Redwood tool manifests (name, inputs.schema_v2, outputs.type_hints, required_fields); adds strict-mode toggle on the OpenAI compatibility adapter which rejects ambiguous tool_choice tokens instead of attempting best-effort mapping; updates streaming fragmentation boundaries so that partial JSON fragments don't change selector->payload association; extensive tests and new doc pages describing the behavior and migration.

Design notes: - Canonical envelope: {"type":"tool_selector","tool_id":"<id>","schema_ref":"<uri>","selection_reason":"..."} emitted as a single framed event in the stream. The framing ensures it won't be split across TCP buffers (runtime uses existing framed-message header). - Mapping rules: prefer explicit function.name -> tool_id; fall back to fuzzy matches derived from schema title and metadata. When multiple matches exist and strict_mode=true we return an ambiguity error to the client (400-level) so callers can disambiguate. - Streaming handoff: the runtime now pins the selector-to-stream id mapping for the lifetime of the invocation; subsequent fragments without a selector are attributed to the pinned tool until an explicit end_of_tool frame. - Backwards compatibility: when the upstream model sends the older 'tool_choice' token or in-stream text hint, the adapter performs the same mapping but emits a synthetic selector envelope before tool payload to make downstream processing uniform.

Testing and validation: unit tests for the mapping heuristics (tests/test_tool_mapping.py), integration tests that simulate fragmented streams (integration/streaming/test_tool_stream_fragments.py), and end-to-end compatibility tests against an OpenAI-compat client harness. CI showed a transient streaming e2e failure on the first run (flaky network ordering); reran and green. Performance impact: negligible (<1% latency) when selector envelope is emitted; small allocation decrease in runtimes that now reuse pinned metadata.

Migration: no action required for most customers. Opt-in strict_mode is exposed via the OpenAI adapter flag "compat_tool_strict=true" in the Redwood API shim. Customers who want to guarantee exact rejected/accepted mappings should enable strict mode and update their prompt/tool naming to match the canonical tool_id. See docs/openai-compat/tool-calling.md for examples and a migration checklist.

Rollout plan: staged rollout behind feature flag: start in canary for 24h, enable for 20% traffic for 72h, then 100% if no regressions. Observability: added per-invocation metric openai.compat.selector_emitted and mapping.ambiguity.rate and dashboards in Redwood Console.

Related: ENG-2241 (compatibility follow-up), SUP-897 (customer report about partial tool_choice streams).
Introduces a canonical streaming 'tool_selector' envelope and clearer mapping rules from OpenAI-style function/tool schemas to Redwood tool manifests. Improves robustness of tool_choice handling during fragmented streams and provides an opt-in strict compatibility mode. Backwards-compatible by default.
Liam O'Neill: Left a few inline nit comments on adapter.py; main question is whether selection_reason should be enum-validated at the transport layer (answered: yes, added validator)
Priya Raman: Asked for stricter schema validation on fallback mapping; implemented try/except and a metric for fallback_count
Evan Park: Approved after seeing fragmentation tests and ensuring no change to backward-compat paths
payload.title: OpenAI compatibility: canonical tool selector envelope and framed handoff semantics

payload.body:
Motivation: Dedicated fleets currently oscillate between reactive scaling and conservative stability for multi-tenant workloads. Small transient spikes cause unnecessary provisioning churn while long-term trend shifts are slow to converge. This PR introduces a multi-window autoscaler that balances short-term responsiveness with long-term stability via a dampening mechanism and per-tenant soft admission limits. Goals: 1) Reduce oscillation from microbursts while preserving fast recovery for genuine sustained demand; 2) Provide deterministic per-tenant throughput guarantees (soft limits) with graceful degradation under contention; 3) Surface new telemetry to evaluate headroom, utilization quantiles, and damping efficacy. Summary of changes: - New component src/autoscaler/multi_window_autoscaler.go: implements two-window controller (short window = 10s-30s, long window = 5m-15m) with configurable weighting and exponential dampening on scale decisions. - Admission refactor src/scheduler/soft_admission.go: introduces per-tenant soft-limits and a soft-deny path that enqueues requests into a priority-deferrable queue rather than hard rejecting. - Burst token bucket enhancer src/autoscaler/burst_banker.go: adds proportional decay to burst credits and a safety floor to prevent negative headroom. - Telemetry additions metrics/telemetry/tenant_util_quantiles.promql and metrics/telemetry/headroom_histogram.promql: emit p50/p90/p99 tenant utilization and headroom distribution, plus dampening events counter. - Policy config configs/dedicated/throughput_policy_v2.yaml: expose damping coefficients, multi-window parameters, and soft-limit tiers (gold/silver/bronze). - E2E tests tests/e2e/responsiveness_autoscale_test.py: synthetic workload harness that asserts stability under periodic microbursts and responsiveness on sustained ramps. - Docs docs/design/multi-window-autoscaler.md: design rationale, tuning guidance, and runbook entries for incident analysis. Backwards compatibility: The autoscaler is opt-in via the throughput_policy_v2.yaml feature flag; default behavior remains the existing single-window scaler until rollout is enabled for a fleet. Checklist: - [x] Implementation compiles and unit tests added - [x] E2E harness validates key scenarios (burst, ramp up/ramp down) - [x] Telemetry dashboards prototyped and prometheus queries added - [x] Feature flag gated for gradual rollout - [x] Docs and runbook updated for on-call teams Performance notes: In internal canary across two small fleets we observed a ~28% reduction in spurious scale-up events driven by short microbursts and a ~12% improvement in 99th percentile requester latency during burst windows due to smarter soft-admit behavior. Related: builds on ideas from ENG-531 (headroom observability) and ties into SUP-4521 (customer incident where oscillation caused cost spikes). Tuning knobs (high level): - short_window_seconds: responsiveness to immediate load - long_window_seconds: trend smoothing - dampening_alpha: exponential decay factor applied to successive scale decisions - soft_limit_tiers: per-tenant throughput floors and burst ceilings Rollout plan: 1) Enable on non-production dedicated fleets behind feature flag; 2) Monitor headroom/dampening events for 2 weeks; 3) Canary on low-traffic production fleets; 4) Gradual rollout with telemetry gating.
Arjun Patel: Can you explain why we chose exponential dampening instead of simple cooldown windows? I'm worried about long tails if alpha isn't tuned.
Maya Sutherland: Reply: Exponential dampening lets us reduce the effective weight of repeated scale actions without rigid cooldowns; it composes with the long window trend smoother to ensure we recover from real sustained demand. Added tuning guidance in the docs and a safety max-scale cap to avoid long-tail over-throttling.
Lina Gómez: Tests look good but I want to see an assertion for soft-admit fairness across tiers (gold shouldn't be starved by bursty bronze).
Maya Sutherland: Reply: Added fairness assertion to e2e harness and a proportional backfill path so gold tenants maintain minimum throughput when contention is present.
Tom Brewer: CI reported a flaky e2e on first run (race in queue draining). Please add a drain-wait and re-run.
Maya Sutherland: Reply: Fixed queue drain race and added deterministic seed in the synthetic generator. Reran CI and green.
Introduce an opt-in multi-window autoscaler for Dedicated fleets that reduces oscillation and improves responsiveness. Adds per-tenant soft admission limits, new telemetry for utilization quantiles and headroom, and configuration knobs for dampening and window sizes. Feature gated and safe to roll out gradually.
payload.title: Responsiveness-tiered dampening and multi-window autoscaler

payload.body:
Problem: Private/on-prem upgrades require a single, immutable snapshot of all artifacts (helm charts, installer images, terraform modules, SBOMs) so air-gapped clusters can perform deterministic upgrades and safe rollbacks. Today we rely on ad-hoc lists and ad-hoc signing which led to a rollback incident where a chart digest drifted between regions. Motivation: provide a reproducible, signed upgrade manifest that ties together all release artifacts and can be consumed by the installer and the TUF-backed artifact mirror used in air-gapped installs. What this PR does: 1) Adds a release manifest indexer pipeline job that collects build artifacts (image digests, Helm chart tarballs + .prov provenance files, terraform module lockfiles, and SBOM links), computes content-addressable digests, and produces a single compressed manifest bundle (upgrade-manifest-<version>.tar.gz). 2) Integrates cosign signing/verifying of both the bundle and individual entries, and stores cosign payloads alongside the manifest (enables key rotation audit). 3) Emits a TUF snapshot update: the pipeline stages the manifest into the TUF repo, creates consistent snapshot and timestamp metadata, and publishes the TUF metadata alongside the bundle for the air-gapped mirror. 4) Generates an upgrade-plan JSON (deterministic) that the installer uses for canary/cutover/rollback. The plan enumerates ordered steps with pre-check hashes and reversible actions. 5) Adds an installer-side manifest validator and rollback-checker that will verify signatures, validate chart provenance, and synthesize a rollback plan when a step fails. 6) CI: new integration tests that run an air-gapped simulation (local registry + mock TUF server) validating that the manifest can be applied and, on simulated failure, the rollback path is accepted. 7) Docs: docs/release/upgrade-manifests.md with consumption guidance for operator and platform teams. Checklist: - [x] manifest indexer job implementation and pipeline yaml - [x] cosign signing + verify step - [x] TUF snapshotting integration and publish stage - [x] installer manifest validator + rollback-checker - [x] helm chart provenance consumption (.prov files) - [x] terraform module lock digest collection - [x] integration tests for air-gapped apply/rollback - [x] documentation and runbook notes Rollout: merged to main and gated behind the existing release pipeline. The indexer job is feature-flagged for the next scheduled private-installer release so we can test mirrors without impacting hosted flows. Notes on security and keys: cosign keys are read from the secure KMS path referenced by the pipeline; TUF root delegation is unchanged but the snapshot/timestamp keys are managed in CI and rotated per the existing rotation playbook. Backwards compatibility: installers that do not yet opt-in will continue to accept the old manifest path; once operator teams switch to the new TUF-backed manifest endpoint they must point the installer config at the new index URL. Migration docs included. Why different from previous work: prior PRs focused on signing individual artifacts or rotating metadata; this change binds together the entire upgrade surface (helm + terraform + images + sbom + terraform locks) into a single signed, TUF-published manifest and adds concrete rollback automation consumed by the installer.
Arjun Patel: Can we avoid bundling full SBOMs into the manifest tarball? For air-gapped clusters we prefer SBOM references (S3 path) instead of embedding large files.
Maya Chen (author): Good point — indexer now stores SBOM references and a small SBOM index; full SBOMs remain in the release bucket. Updated pipeline accordingly.
Lina Gomez: Please add a unit test for the manifest validator when a chart digest doesn't match the .prov file.
Maya Chen: Added a failing-case unit test in installer/manifest/test_validator.go and a corresponding fixture.
Evan Park: CI integration flaked once on airgapped integration test (network timeout). Reran and all green. Also left a minor nits comment about log verbosity.
Arjun Patel: Approve after fixups. Leaving an approval comment.
Lina Gomez: Approved. Adding suggestion to follow up with runbook for emergency key rollforward.
- Introduce immutable upgrade manifest bundles for private installer releases.
- Add cosign-signed manifests and per-artifact provenance links.
- Publish manifest via TUF snapshot + timestamp for atomic, auditable air-gapped mirrors.
- Installer gains manifest validator and rollback-checker to automate safe rollbacks.
Feature-flagged: to enable, set installer.config.release_manifest.index_url to the new TUF endpoint and ensure KMS keys are available in CI. Operators should run the included mirror-validation script (tools/tuf/README.md) when seeding air-gapped mirrors.
payload.title: automated immutable upgrade manifests with helm provenance and TUF snapshotting

payload.body:
Context: We currently expose token-level cost and phase breakdown metrics, but teams still struggle to quickly identify SLO regressions caused by subtle per-token shifts across stages (tokenization, attention kernels, kv fetch, postprocessing). This PR introduces two complementary observability primitives: 1) token-ladder metrics — a compact, incremental per-token latency/cost series that shows delta contribution at each token position and stage; 2) cumulative-stitch rollups — lightweight cumulative aggregates that stitch token-ladder samples into session-level and route-level time-series for alerting and dashboards. Motivation: incident postmortems (ENG-2124) show long-tail SLO regressions where total latency increased without a clear single-stage spike. Token-ladder makes the per-token incremental contribution visible; cumulative-stitch provides an efficient rollup for long-term alerting without exploding cardinality. Changes: - New metrics: telemetry.token_ladder{tenant,route,model,stage,token_offset} (histogram), telemetry.cumulative_stitch{tenant,route,model,window} (sum/counter). - Sampling policy: token-ladder is sampled at 1:200 by default with deterministic seeding per invocation to preserve relative ordering across retries. - Aggregation: stitch rollups compute prefix sums over token-ladder for configurable windows (30s/5m/1h) and expose derived percentiles used by alerts. - Dashboard: added a Token Ladder panel (compact sparklines with stage stacks) and a Cumulative Stitch heatmap for routes. - Alerts: new alert rule slo.token_stitch_regression triggers when 95th percentile cumulative-stitch latency increases by >20% vs baseline over 6h with minimum sample floor. This PR includes an auto-mute for low-volume routes to reduce noise. Checklist: - [x] implement metric emission hooks in runtime stage manager - [x] implement sampling policy and deterministic seeding - [x] add stitch aggregation job with rollup retention - [x] create Grafana panels and dashboard JSON - [x] add alert and runbook - [x] unit tests for metric tagging and sampling - [x] integration sanity run on staging Testing: Unit + integration tests included. Staging playback ran a synthetic traffic mix (see commit msgs) and validated that token-ladder captures an introduced KV fetch jitter with the expected per-token delta at offsets 6..9. We also exercised the cumulative-stitch alert by simulating a controlled 25% increase in kernel latency; alert fired and auto-mute prevented noise for low-volume tenants. Rollout plan: - Feature gated behind observability.experimental.token_ladder flag - Enable for beta tenants for 2 weeks, monitor alert churn - Gradually enable default sampling for all hosted accounts after stabilization Release notes: - Added token-ladder and cumulative-stitch telemetry for improved per-token SLO root-cause analysis - New Grafana dashboard panels and an alert rule (slo.token_stitch_regression) - Experimental feature behind feature flag Backwards compatibility / cost: Default sampling keeps cardinality increases small. Stitch rollups are retained at coarse resolution to limit storage. Ops runbook summary included in repo/docs/observability/runbooks/token-ladder.md (linked).
Diego Ramos (2026-02-16): Nice work. A few asks: 1) please document the sampling seed determinism and how it behaves across retries/redirects; 2) consider lowering default sampling for extremely high-throughput models.
Asha Patel (2026-02-16): Responded: added seeding details in seeding_util.go comments and added a config override for per-model sampling rates. Also added a note in the runbook about retry semantics.
Maya Chen (2026-02-17): Question on alert noise — what's the expected false positive rate during model rollout windows? Can we auto-suppress around canary rollouts?
Asha Patel (2026-02-17): Answered: added auto-mute logic when Linear tag 'rollout=true' is present on routes; added sample floor requirement to alert to avoid triggering on very low volumes.
Diego Ramos (2026-02-18): Approved after minor nits fixed in dashboard legends and unit test flakiness addressed.

payload.body:
Motivation: Production workloads show wide variance in tenant access patterns: steady traffic tenants get large effective cache hit rates, while bursty tenants cause cache churn and tail latency spikes. This PR introduces a lightweight "cache ecology" controller that synthesizes per-tenant eviction and residency profiles from recent access histograms and a microburst fallback that temporarily reduces batch size and switches to microbatch-optimized execution paths when burst detection and KV-cache churn would otherwise violate latency SLOs.

What this changes: Adds an inference-side service and control loop that: 1) ingests tenant-level access metrics (prefix length, inter-arrival, hit/miss ratios) and produces a ranked set of eviction policies (LRU-variant, segmented-TTL, weighted-residency) and quantization rollback hints; 2) exposes a profile API used by the scheduler to apply tenant-scoped cache and batching overrides; 3) implements a fast-path microburst detector that toggles a microbatch executor and reduces prefetch aggressiveness for the affected tenant for a short cooldown window. The goal is to reduce cost from repeated cache thrashing while preserving 99.9th percentile latency by gracefully degrading to microbatches rather than dropping requests or causing large KV-cache recomputations.

Design notes: The controller runs in the serving plane with bounded CPU and memory budgets and uses exponentially-weighted histograms with a sliding window to avoid storing per-request traces. Profiles are versioned and lightweight (<=2KB). We intentionally keep the policy space small (4 eviction families x 3 residency levels) to limit combinatorial explosion and make rollout/safety analysis tractable. The microburst guard implements conservative heuristics first and records signals for later ML-based tuning.

Backward compatibility & safety: Default behavior is a no-op unless a tenant has opted into adaptive profiles. All profile changes are annotated with a safety score and a TTL; the scheduler rejects changes below a configurable safety threshold. We included a forced fallback toggle in the Console and a feature flag for private deployments. No model format changes.

Testing & benchmarks: Unit tests cover eviction generator math, profile serialization, and scheduler integration. Integration tests simulate interleaved steady and burst tenants using the perf-lab harness. On internal staging workloads, we observed: - 12% average token cost reduction across mixed workloads - 18% reduction in 99.9th percentile latency on bursty tenants (microburst path engaged) - negligible impact on steady tenants (sub-1% latency delta).

Rollout plan: Start with a small canary (5 tenants) + telemetry visibility (prefetch/miss-rate/latency per-tenant). If stable for 48h, extend to 20% of production traffic using a canary policy and auto-roll back on elevated P99 or miss rate regressions.

Migration steps: Console toggle and API allow opt-in; no mandatory migration. For Private installs, operators can enable the controller via the helm chart values (see docs change).

Related: ENG-2191 (workload telemetry), ENG-2210 (microburst execution paths).

Lena Park: Can you explain how profile churn cost is accounted for? Suggest adding a metric for profile churn and an opt-out TTL. (requested change)
Author (Ravi): Added profile_churn_total and churn_ttl configuration, added to controller.go and dashboard. Please re-review.
Diego Alvarez: Microburst detector thresholds look conservative; consider moving to a percentile-of-percentiles approach for noisy tenants. (comment)
Author (Ravi): Agreed. Adjusted detector to use 99th-percentile over the sliding window and added a noisy-tenant suppression flag. Kept default conservative for safety.
Priya Nair: Integration tests flaky on first run due to harness timing; reran CI and added small sleeps in test harness. Approving after CI green. (approved)
CI Bot: initial CI run failed lint on api proto formatting; fixed in second commit. All checks passed on re-run.
payload.title: tenant-aware cache-ecology + microburst fallback profiles

payload.body:
Motivation: multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads were seeing intermittent host stalls when KV cache prefetches and NCCL collectives contended for host resources. Existing scheduling overlapped collectives and compute but lacked a lightweight flow-control primitive to prevent head-of-line stalls and excessive kernel serialization. This PR introduces a credit-based pipelining layer for NCCL collectives and ties credits to KV-cache prefetch hooks so that expensive prefetches yield to in-flight collectives while preserving throughput.

Summary of changes: 1) credit_allocator: a new lock-free credit pool per TP group that tracks outstanding collective windows and grants up to N credits to launch interleaved kernels; 2) nccl_launcher: modified to consume/return credits and to attach a small metadata token to hostbuffers (hostbuf credit id) so host-side RPCs and prefetches can yield; 3) kv_cache_prefetch: integrates with the allocator to request and optionally defer prefetch work if credits are low; 4) kernel_interleaver: lightweight scheduler in the runtime that issues smaller micro-kernel launches (sub-chunked GEMM/softmax) when credits permit to improve overlap; 5) autotune: adds a conservative heuristics path that picks initial credit counts per model shape and per-cluster bandwidth tier; 6) metrics and tracing: new metrics tp.credit_grants, tp.credit_waits, tp.prefetch_yields and tracing tags to correlate stalls with credit starvation.

Benchmarks: ran canary suite on 8xA100 (NVLink) and 4xA40 (ethernet). Representative results vs main (median of 10 runs): - 8xA100 TP transformer-20b throughput +12% and 95th token latency -17% under mixed short/long sequences; - 4xA40 TP 7b pipeline saw 9% throughput improvement and p99 latency -14% for batched streaming workloads; - tail-case with pathological large KV prefetch previously causing 400ms host stalls now drops to <50ms and is handled by backpressure. Microbenchmarks show average NCCL host-buffer contention window reduced by ~65%.

Compatibility and rollout: change is behind feature flag REDWOOD_TP_CREDIT_PIPELINE and controlled by per-deployment config. Default disabled for older Dedicated clusters until a canary roll completes. No model format change. Autotune values are conservative to avoid regressions; customers can set explicit credit counts in route configs.

Testing: unit tests for allocator (race-free invariants), integration tests exercising interleaved launches with mocked NCCL, end-to-end perf canary on perf-canary infra, chaos test where KV prefetch threads are artificially delayed (passes). Added a regression test that injects credit starvation and asserts graceful defer of prefetch rather than host OOM.

Files changed (high level): runtime/tp/credit_allocator.cpp, runtime/tp/nccl_launcher.cpp, runtime/tp/kernel_interleaver.h, runtime/tp/kernel_interleaver.cpp, runtime/kv/kv_prefetcher.cpp, runtime/kv/kv_prefetcher.h, runtime/metrics/tp_metrics.cc, tools/autotune/tp_credit_tuner.py, tests/unit/test_credit_allocator.cpp, tests/integration/test_interleaving_e2e.py, docs/operations/credit_pipeline.md, examples/tuning/credit_examples.yaml, and minor changes to the canary deployment manifest and CI bench harness.

Implementation notes and rationale: credits are intentionally lightweight (16-bit counters) to avoid memory pressure and to be easy to serialize in hostbuf metadata. We chose an optimistic consume-return model instead of a token-queue to reduce host lock contention; fast-path avoids atomic ops for single-GPU launches. The interleaved micro-kernel launches split larger matmuls into contiguous sub-chunks aligned to cache lines to avoid additional memory traffic. The KV prefetcher now exposes a `try_prefetch_with_credit` API that either performs the prefetch or returns a suggested backoff window which runtime uses to schedule a deferred task.

Rollout plan: merge to main gated by perf canary and staged canary rollout to 10% of hosted clusters then to Dedicated alpha clusters. Feature flag default off for existing Dedicated customers until telemetry confirms stable tail latency.

Documentation: added ops doc with knobs and troubleshooting, and tuning examples for 4/8/16 GPU clusters explaining credit counts and expected behavior.

Known limitations: current autotune is conservative and may underutilize high-bandwidth topologies; future work will introduce dynamic credit adaptation based on live telemetry. Edge cases: on extreme heterogenous mixes the allocator may starve small collectives; mitigations include a prioritized credit queue (planned follow-up).

Checklist: - [x] unit tests - [x] integration tests - [x] perf canary runs - [x] docs updated - [x] feature flag added

Related: builds on ideas from ENG-987 experimental interleaver and references SUP-4421 customer incident where KV prefetches caused repeated host stalls.
Jonah Kim: Nice approach. Two asks: (1) can we expose a debug endpoint to snapshot credit state per-GPU for debugging, and (2) please document the heuristics used in autotune.
Aisha Patel: Added /_debug/tp/credits and expanded docs section with autotune heuristics (see docs/operations/credit_pipeline.md).
Miguel Santos: Observability additions look good. On the allocator: please ensure we don't introduce ABA by reusing small credit ids — prefer epoched ids or 32-bit tag.
Aisha Patel: Switched hostbuf token to 32-bit composed of credit_id:epoch to avoid ABA; updated tests accordingly.
Priya Rao: CI perf flakes earlier on ethernet cluster; after rerun numbers look acceptable. Approving pending a changelog entry.
Aisha Patel: Added changelog entry and release_notes; running a final perf canary on 4xA40.
Introduces credit-based NCCL pipelining and a KV-cache crediting mechanism to reduce host-side stalls and improve overlap between communication and compute for multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads. Backwards compatible; rollout behind env flag `REDWOOD_TP_CREDIT_PIPELINE`.
Feature gate REDWOOD_TP_CREDIT_PIPELINE. Default is OFF for Dedicated until canary window completes. Debug endpoints: /_debug/tp/credits and /_debug/tp/credit_metrics. If customers see regressions, disable feature and gather tp.credit_waits and tp.prefetch_yields metrics for triage.
payload.title: Credit-based NCCL pipelining + KV-cache crediting and interleaved kernel launches

payload.body:
Adds a lightweight inference health probe and a sampled kernel-queue explorer to improve incident triage and long-tail cost attribution. Motivation: recurring short-lived kernel queue stalls were noisy in SLO pages and made it hard to trace whether slow tails were caused by model-level token spikes, kernel contention, or tenant-induced backpressure. This PR introduces: 1) inference_health_probe: periodic synthetic pings that exercise a small, deterministic token path and emit a health metric (inference_probe_latency_ms) plus an opaque probe_id for trace linking; 2) sampled_kernel_queue_explorer: a new trace sampler that, when a probe or real invocation exceeds a kernel-queue latency threshold, captures a compact kernel-queue snapshot and stores a compacted span with queue_depth, head_kernel_id, and estimated_token_cost_hint; 3) dashboard panels: a compact 'Probe Pulse' timeseries, kernel-queue heatmap (bucketed by queue depth and model shard), and a 'Probe vs Real' latency scatter for quick triage; 4) runbook/playbook: an Observability Surge Playbook page with automated escalation steps and quick links to tenant-level cost and KV cache hit panels. Implementation notes: probe logic is opt-in per deployment via config.inference.probe.enabled (false by default) and probes are low-rate by design (0.1 rps per region) to avoid billing noise; the sampled kernel snapshots are stored in the observability compact store with a capped reservoir to limit cardinality. Backwards compatibility: no changes to public API surfaces. Checklist: [x] add probe runtime hooks, [x] add metric and span schema, [x] add dashboard panels, [x] add playbook and runbook links, [x] update docs and config reference, [x] add unit tests and e2e sampler smoke test. Related: ENG-6123 for incident RCA and OBS-47 for dashboard request. Expected rollout: feature gated for 2 weeks, enable for staging then incrementally to prod with guardrail on stored snapshot volume.
Ethan Park (reviewer): Can we avoid writing probe IDs to logs in plaintext? Suggest redacting before emit.
Priya Nandakumar (author): Good catch — switched to hash(probe_id) and updated telemetry docs to note non-identifying hash. Commits updated.
Marta Alvarez (reviewer): Dashboard looks good; add a per-model-shard breakdown and ensure color scale is log-friendly.

Motivation: We maintain three SDKs with slightly divergent credential/retry primitives and streaming ergonomics. That divergence causes repeated bug surface (auth token races, differing backoff defaults) and duplicated maintenance. This PR introduces a small, opinionated 'retry-adapter template' and a lightweight stream-surface shim implemented across the Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs to harmonize defaults and reduce duplicated logic.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a RetryAdapter template (config-driven) that normalizes backoff windows, jitter, and retryable-status heuristics across languages.
- Standardizes session lease/heartbeat hints exposed by streaming handles so consumers can implement warmup/prefetch logic consistently.
- Introduces a minimal, language-idiomatic stream-surface shim that maps the low-level event frames to a consistent async/pull model in each SDK (async iterators in Python/TS, channel-based iterator in Go).
- Moves credential rotation hooks into a single well-documented handshake lifecycle so the token refresh race window is reduced.
- Bumps package versions: python 0.23.0, typescript 3.2.0, go 1.6.0 (patch/minor as appropriate).

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc reviewed by SDK leads (referenced ENG-1129)
- [x] Unit tests added for each SDK's retry logic
- [x] Integration streaming tests exercising token rotation under load
- [x] Docs/changelog updated
- [x] Compatibility smoke tested (no breaking changes)

Commits summary:
- commit 1: introduce retry-adapter template + common docs (design rationale, config knobs)
- commit 2: python SDK: implement RetryAdapter, async iterator shim, unit tests, version bump
- commit 3: typescript SDK: implement RetryAdapter, pullstream facade, fix backpressure handling, version bump
- commit 4: go SDK: implement RetryAdapter, channel iterator, fix connector heartbeat deadlock discovered in tests
- commit 5: redwood core: expose lightweight session lifecycle hook for consumable heartbeats
- commit 6: docs: changelog entries and migration notes

Files/areas touched (high level):
- redwood-sdk-python/redwood/retry_adapter.py (new)
- redwood-sdk-python/redwood/stream/async_pull.py (shim)
- redwood-sdk-python/tests/test_retry_adapter.py
- redwood-sdk-typescript/src/retry/adapter.ts (new)
- redwood-sdk-typescript/src/stream/pullFacade.ts
- redwood-sdk-typescript/test/retry_adapter.spec.ts
- redwood-sdk-go/retry/adapter.go (new)
- redwood-sdk-go/stream/puller.go

Small illustrative snippet (TS adapter wiring):
const defaultConfig = { baseDelayMs: 50, maxDelayMs: 2000, jitter: 0.25, retries: 6 };
const adapter = new RetryAdapter(defaultConfig, tokenProvider);

Compatibility notes: The adapter uses conservative defaults designed to reduce spurious retries for streaming frames (especially 429/503). Applications that intentionally relied on a very small baseDelay should opt into a legacy profile via RetryAdapter.fromProfile('legacy').

Testing notes / CI flakiness: Third-party CI revealed an intermittent failure in the TS integration tests related to stream-backpressure under Node 18. Root cause: an edge case where a queued heartbeat could starve the user-data queue when the consumer used sync iterators. Fix: adjust pullFacade to prioritize data frames and add a microtask yield before applying heartbeat backpressure. The test was flaky locally but is stable post-fix.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Arjun Patel (reviewer): "Nice consolidation. Two asks: 1) add explicit metrics labels (retry_profile) to the SDK telemetry hooks; 2) call out migration steps for customers using custom retry loops."
- Marina Kline (author): "Added telemetry labels in commit 4, updated upgrade-guide with migration snippet and example backoff profiles."
- Lena Sørensen (reviewer): "Go change LGTM but please add a brief comment explaining the select loop ordering in puller.go — it avoids a deadlock we saw in integration tests."
- Marina: "Added a code comment and a small unit test that asserts ordering semantics."
- Diego Ramos (reviewer): "Can we avoid exposing the entire adapter config object in the top-level client surface? We should prefer builder helpers."
- Marina: "Agreed — introduced builders in Python/TS and helper constructors in Go; retained full config for advanced use only."

If you want to try the new behavior locally: see docs/sdk/upgrade-guide.md section "try the unified retry adapter" for quickstart snippets per-language.

Motivation: Dedicated fleets require predictable throughput guarantees while supporting short, high-priority bursts. Existing shared-burst/token-pool approaches lack per-tenant hierarchies and do not support explicit priority preemption between workloads. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: 1) a priority-aware scheduler for Dedicated serving nodes that implements weighted priority queues, inter-tenant fairness windows, and optional preemption for critical requests; and 2) a hierarchical burst-credit ledger that allocates, debits, and decays burst credits at both tenant and sub-tenant (team/route) levels so operators can define parent/child quotas and emergency reserve pools. Design summary: The scheduler maintains per-tenant queues with three priority tiers (critical, high, default) and weight buckets inside each tier. Requests are scored by (priority, age, weight) so urgent requests jump ahead only when credits permit; a pluggable preemption hook can evict low-priority queued executions when a critical request times out waiting. The ledger issues credits on a configurable cadence, supports token transfers between children and parents, and records a decay timeline to avoid permanent credit hoarding. Credits are persisted in the existing KV store with a lightweight migration that adds ledger entries under the dedicated/credits namespace. API and telemetry: Adds /v1/dedicated/credits endpoints to query balances, transfer credits, and inspect decay history. New metrics: dedicated.burst_credit_balance, dedicated.burst_credit_allocated, dedicated.preempt_count, scheduler.queue_depth_by_priority, scheduler.weighted_fair_utilization. Console: new CreditsOverview panel showing per-tenant balances, recent transfers, and predicted refill times. Config changes and migration: Adds new fields to dedicated_autoscaler.yaml: priority_scheduling.enabled (bool), ledger.hierarchy.enabled (bool), ledger.decay.window_seconds (int), ledger.default_refill_rate (tokens/sec), scheduler.preemption.enabled (bool), scheduler.max_preempt_percent (0-100). Migration path is provided in redwood/docs/ops/dedicated-migration.md and the migration_202603.go makes the ledger durable and backfills a conservative starting balance for existing tenants. Tests and CI: Unit tests cover scheduler scoring, edge cases around priority inversion, and race conditions; integration tests simulate hierarchical transfers and decay; perf sims approximate mixed workloads to validate impact on p99 latency. Initial CI run failed due to a data race in the ledger's in-memory cache; fixed by adding a mutex and a test that stresses concurrent transfers. Deployment plan and rollout: Feature behind dedicated.priority_scheduler feature flag; default OFF for existing clusters. Plan: 1) merge to main with migration but flag off, 2) deploy migration job during a maintenance window (recommended), 3) canary-enable for a small dedicated fleet, monitor dedicated.burst_credit_balance and preempt_count for anomalies, 4) progressively enable for more fleets and flip default to ON in a follow-up PR. Backwards compatibility: API adds endpoints and config keys but keeps previous token-pool behavior as a compatibility mode when ledger.hierarchy.enabled=false. Observability and alerts: Added alert if preempt_count spikes above configured threshold or if total allocated credits exceed safety cap for a fleet. Rollback: feature flag off reverts runtime behavior; migration is additive but includes a reversible backfill marker; instructions included in ops docs. Related: builds on ENG-4120 autoscaler telemetry work and complements SRE-241's per-fleet SLA tooling. See linked Linear tickets for perf targets and follow-ups.
Tomás Rivera: Overall design looks sound; two high-level asks: add formal proof/argument for starvation avoidance in the README, and ensure migration is reversible for at least 7 days. Also please benchmark p99 impact with mixed-tenant workloads.
Aisha Patel (author): Added an analysis section to redwood/serving/scheduler/README.md describing the fairness invariant and provided time-to-live markers for migration backfill so operators can revert allocations by deleting the backfill tag within 7 days.
Lena Cho: Found a race in ledger.go under concurrent transfer; CI caught it. After the mutex fix the integration tests look stable. Please add a unit that simulates N concurrent transfers to the same parent key.
Aisha Patel: Added stress test in dedicated_credit_ledger_test.go that runs 200 concurrent transfers and validates invariants; pushing updated commit.
Marcus Hall (SRE): Approve with comment: recommend an observability dashboard tile for total reserved vs used credits so on-call can quickly see if someone is draining a shared reserve. We added a dashboard yml and alerted on safety cap breach.
CI Bot: initial pipeline failed on race detector; subsequent run passed. Full e2e pipeline passed on second run.
Add priority scheduler and hierarchical burst-credit ledger for Dedicated fleets. New config flags: dedicated.priority_scheduling, ledger.hierarchy, scheduler.preemption. Migration job included; feature gated by feature flag. New metrics and console panel for credit visibility. See docs/ops/dedicated-migration.md for upgrade steps.
payload.title: Priority-based scheduler and hierarchical burst-credit ledger for Dedicated fleets

Motivation: Customers need safer, auditable ways to manage cost defaults (batching, cache hints, quant profiles) across tenants and deployments. Ad-hoc presets in code slow down ops and increase blast radius. This change introduces a declarative 'cost-manifest' format (YAML) plus a local CLI (econ-dryrun) that simulates unit economics, and a conservative rollout mechanism that can score tenants and gradually apply defaults with automated rollback on quality or cost regressions.

What this PR does (high-level):
- Add cost-manifests schema and parser in redwood/cost_manifests/ (supports batching.default_batch_shape, cache.kv_hint, quant.profile_name, target_unit_cost, safety_thresholds)
- Implement econ-dryrun CLI (tools/econ-dryrun) that: imports recent traces, simulates batching/cache/quant changes over a configurable horizon, and produces a per-tenant unit-econ PDF/JSON report and suggested rollback gates
- Add a conservative rollout controller in serving/runtime that: computes tenant scores (cold_ratio, qps_variance, embedding-heavy=false,sla_tier) and gradually applies manifest deltas with canary windows and automatic fallback when cost or eval metrics breach thresholds
- Wire manifest storage to the control plane with simple validation and dry-run endpoint for Console integration

Checklist: 
- [x] Schema defined with examples and unit tests
- [x] Baseline econ-sim harness and sample traces included
- [x] Runtime conservative rollout controller + simple in-memory simulated backend for tests
- [x] Console dry-run API path and docs page draft
- [x] Integration tests for rollout gating (flaky; retried once in CI)

Linear/Jira: ENG-2140 tracks the manifest schema and rollout controller. PM-721 covers the Console UX dry-run integration. SUP-4582 notes a customer ask that triggered this work.

Commits (summary):
- add: cost-manifests/schema.yaml and examples/tenant-defaults.yaml 
- feat: tools/econ-dryrun initial implementation (simulate traces -> unit-econ estimates)
- feat: runtime/rollout/conservative_controller.go (tenant scoring + canary windows)
- test: econ-sim unit/integration tests + sample traces in testdata/

Files changed (high-level):

- redwood/cost_manifests/parser.go (new): lightweight parser + validation errors mapped to user-facing messages
- tools/econ-dryrun/main.py (new): CLI with --input-trace, --horizon, --sim-steps flags and output report generation
- serving/runtime/rollout/conservative_controller.go (new): controller logic + unit tests
- serving/runtime/rollout/rollout_test.go (modified): add simulated network fixtures and tenant scoring tests
- docs/ops/cost-manifests.md (new): operator guide and examples

- testdata/traces/sample_prefill_trace.json (new): small trace used by econ-dryrun tests

Review thread (highlights):
- Evan Chen (2026-02-19): "Great direction. Two asks: 1) tighten validation so we never accept quant profiles without an explicit fallback; 2) add a synthetic load test in the integration matrix to catch canary flapping."
- Maya Patel (author) reply (2026-02-19): "Added explicit 'fallback_profile' required in schema; synthetic load test added (small). See commit 'schema: require fallback_profile' and 'ci: add canary synthetic load job'."
- Sofia Martinez (2026-02-21): "Can we ensure that dry-run outputs are deterministic across runs for the same seed? Right now stochastic sampling in econ-sim causes noisy recommendations."
- Maya reply (2026-02-21): "Econ-dryrun now accepts --seed flag; default seed fixed in CI runs. Added note in docs about stochastic components."

CI notes:

Lint, unit tests, and package builds passed on first run. Econ-dryrun's stochastic tests are run with a fixed seed during CI to keep results stable.

Performance considerations:

The runtime controller uses existing batching and cache APIs; the change is primarily orchestration with minimal per-request overhead. Benchmarks show <1% median latency impact in synthetic acceptance runs.

Testing & rollout plan:

Motivation: customers running Redwood in production want a single, auditable way to perform gradual model rollouts across hosted, dedicated, and private modes. Current practices spread logic across the control plane, SDKs, and ad-hoc scripts; that leads to inconsistent canaries, missing metrics for decisions, and slow emergency rollbacks. This PR introduces an orchestration agent (rollout-controller) that centralizes canary/A-B/shadow traffic policies, enforces safety checks, and wires automated rollback rules to eval and SLO signals.

What this change contains (high level):
- rollout-controller service: reconciles Rollout CRD-like objects stored in the control plane and drives traffic mutation via the routing layer. Supports canary steps, parallel A/B allocations, shadow mirroring, and scheduled rollouts.
- Policy engine: safety rules (latency regression thresholds, error-rate windows, quality regression tied to eval sets). Policies are pluggable and ship with default safe presets for low-latency, high-throughput workloads.
- Metrics & alert hooks: emits rollout-specific metrics (rollout_step_success, rollback_reason, canary_latency_delta_p50/p95, shadow_divergence_score) and creates tracing spans for each decision.
- Automated rollback: declarative rollback policies allow automatic revert on metric breaches, or escalate to manual approval if configured.
- Integration with Redwood Console: new rollout timelines and per-step graphs (docs in docs/rollouts.md).

Design summary: the controller stores a Rollout object (json schema stored in control plane) with steps. Each step can declare traffic_percentage, evaluation_queries, wait_duration, and rollback_policy. The controller reconciles desired vs actual traffic using existing routing APIs (no direct changes to router binary) so this is a control-plane-only change. To avoid noisy flaps, we implement hysteresis and rate-limited traffic changes.

Example Rollout JSON (illustrative, single-line in description): {"name":"model-embed-v2-rollout","target_model":"embed-v2","steps":[{"traffic":5,"wait":"15m","eval":"smoke-embed-set","rollback_on":["latency>+30%","quality<-2%"]},{"traffic":25,"wait":"30m"},{"traffic":100}]}

Implementation notes: initial reconciliation loop lives in cmd/rollout-controller/main.go, core logic in internal/rollout/controller.go, policy predicates in internal/rollout/policies.go, and metric/trace plumbing under internal/observability/rollout. No changes to model-serving runtime binaries were required; we reuse the routing API (control-plane call to /routing/v1/modify).

Testing and CI: unit tests included for policy predicates and decision paths; an end-to-end integration test simulates a canary with a synthetic latency regression to assert the controller triggers rollback. The pipeline initially failed a flaky e2e test (race on fake timers); fixed by moving to a deterministic clock abstraction. CI summary below.

Deployment plan: staged rollout of the rollout-controller itself via Dedicated Canary (replica-once) then full rollout. Default auto-rollback is enabled but opt-out via rollout.metadata. We will gate GA on 2 weeks of production telemetry with <1 incident over canaries and stable false-positive rate on rollback alerts.

Migration notes: existing ad-hoc rollout scripts will continue to work for 90 days; we will provide an import tool to convert them to Rollout objects recorded in the control plane.

Security/perm model: controller requires a new granular policy scope: routing.rollouts.{read,write,audit}. RBAC rules added to rbac-policy-bundle.

Related Linear/PM items: ENG-8421, ENG-8557 (rollback telemetry), PM-341.

Checklist: [x] design doc linked, [x] unit tests, [x] e2e test (flaky fixed), [x] docs updated (docs/rollouts.md), [x] console widgets wired (feature flag behind rollout-ui-alpha), [x] release notes

Notes on choices: chose control-plane-only approach to avoid per-runtime upgrade; this allows immediate safety patches and easier auditing. Hysteresis threshold is conservative by default to avoid oscillation.

Risk and mitigations: 1) Risk: controller mis-evaluates quality metrics due to noisy eval sets. Mitigation: rollouts can require multiple independent eval queries and configurable quorum. 2) Risk: runaway rollbacks during infra blips. Mitigation: the policy engine has debounce windows and requires sustained violations for automatic rollback.

CI timeline (single-line summary): first CI run failed on e2e flakiness; subsequent commits fixed deterministic clock and retriggered; final CI: all checks passed (unit, lint, e2e, integration).

Users impacted: platform engineers, release engineers, and SREs; no direct breaking API changes for customers.

Long description ends.
Nina Patel: Left a few nits on config validation. We should fail fast if a rollout is missing eval queries for canaries that are >10% traffic.
Jordan Lee (author): addressed in commit d4e5f6a — added validation and clear error messages. Also documented in docs/rollouts.md
Carlos Mendez: Concerned about cascading rollbacks when a downstream metrics pipeline lags. Suggest adding a lag-tolerance field. 
Jordan Lee: Added lag_tolerance setting with default 2m and unit tests to assert behavior (commit f7a8b9c).
Eve Sun: Approved after verifying e2e that automatic rollback triggers on sustained latency regression.
Adds rollout-controller: declarative canary/A-B/shadow rollouts with automated rollback policies and Observatory metrics; safe defaults for production; migration tool for ad-hoc rollouts; console timeline UI behind feature flag.
payload.title: Unified orchestration agent for model rollouts (canary, A/B, shadow) and automated rollback

Context and motivation:
Spot/preemptible GPU pools are an important cost lever for Dedicated, but unexpected evictions cause hard failures for low-latency tenant requests and undermine SLAs. Customers running mixed workloads (best-effort + reserved) need automated, predictable behavior when spot nodes are reclaimed. This PR implements a coordinated fallback allocator that: routes evicted requests to reserved capacity when available, applies tenant-priority windows to avoid noisy-neighbor amplification, and exposes eviction/fallback telemetry for capacity planning.

Design summary:
- New controller `spot_preempt_controller` watches node preemption/termination signals and actively reconciles in-flight KV-backed allocations.
- `spot_allocator` implements a best-effort handoff: it attempts to pre-book a reserved slot using a short-lived soft-reservation (10s default) before letting the request fail. If reserved capacity is fully saturated, the allocator applies tenant-priority rules (configurable weight + cooldown) to decide which requests to drain to lower-priority queues.
- To reduce thundering-herd behavior after mass preemptions, we add a randomized backoff window and per-tenant exponential cooldown (configurable).
- Telemetry: eviction_rate_per_pool, fallback_success_rate, soft_reservation_failures, tenant_fallback_count, preempt_latency_ms. These join existing capacity dashboards and a new Ops runbook.
- Feature-gated via config `spot_fallback.enabled` and orchestrator flag `--spot-fallback-mode=(dryrun|enabled)`. Dryrun mode emits telemetry and simulates state transitions without performing allocations.

What this PR changes (high-level):
- Adds new packages: pkg/allocator/spot_allocator.go, controllers/spot_preempt_controller.go, internal/telemetry/spot_metrics.go.
- Config updates: config/defaults.yaml introduces `spot_fallback` section; defaults keep the feature off.
- Docs: docs/ops/spot-instance-guidelines.md (runbook + recommended configs for Dedicated customers).
- Tests: unit tests for allocator logic and an e2e test injected into the perf-canary suite to validate behavior under synthetic preemption events.

Commits (summary):
- add spot allocator and controller scaffolding
- implement soft-reservation booking and preempt handoff
- add telemetry and Prometheus metrics + Grafana dashboard fragments
- integration tests and e2e scenario for mass-preemptions
- docs and config defaults + feature flag implementation
- followups: fix race in soft-reservation cancellation, tighten metrics labels to avoid cardinality blowup

Files changed (representative):
- pkg/allocator/spot_allocator.go (+512 additions)
- controllers/spot_preempt_controller.go (+340 additions)
- internal/telemetry/spot_metrics.go (+78 additions)
- config/defaults.yaml (+12 additions)
- docs/ops/spot-instance-guidelines.md (+220 additions)
- tests/e2e/spot-fallback.test.go (+80 additions)
- pkg/allocator/allocator_test.go (+142 additions)

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests cover the allocator decision matrix, soft-reservation lifecycle, and tenant-weight adjustments.
- Added deterministic mocks for node termination signals to keep unit tests stable.
- e2e test runs in perf-canary; the first CI run hit a known flaky timing issue in the perf harness (test exceeded default timeouts under shared CI load). I re-ran the suite with extended timeouts for the e2e job; subsequent run passed. CI status: all checks green after rerun.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Ravi Patel: "This looks solid; two asks: (1) add a feature flag so we can canary it per-cluster; (2) ensure metrics don't explode with tenant labels."
- Author (Ava): "Added `spot_fallback.enabled` config and consolidated tenant labels to `tenant_id` with an optional low-cardinality `tenant_tier` label. Also added a dryrun mode to vet behavior before enabling."
- Maya Thompson: "Can we make the soft-reservation TTL configurable and documented?"
- Author: "Exposed `soft_reservation_ttl_seconds` in config/defaults.yaml and documented the tradeoffs in the runbook."
- Noah Kim: "Edge-case: what happens when reserved capacity is in the middle of a rolling update? We need to avoid cascading drains."
- Author: "Added conservative detection for cluster maintenance windows (use `node.annotation/maintenance`) and introduced a maintenance grace window; allocator avoids fallback into nodes annotated as under-maintenance."
- Review outcome: approvals from Ravi and Maya after changes; Noah requested one follow-up to instrument a counter for cascade-avoidance which was added in a small follow-up commit.

Backward compatibility and rollout plan:
- Default is OFF. Ops can enable `spot_fallback.enabled=true` in a phased rollout: dryrun -> enabled in non-prod -> canary in one region -> broad rollout.
- No schema changes to persisted data; soft reservations live in ephemeral KV with TTL.

Operational considerations / Risks:
- Incorrect tenant weights could bias fallback toward high-paying tenants if misconfigured; default weights are conservative (uniform). Ops runbook includes tuning guidance.
- Metric cardinality kept low by limiting tenant labels and sampling high-cardinality metrics.
- Potential for transient latency spikes during large preemptions; mitigated by randomized backoff and pre-booking heuristic.

Follow-ups / TODOs:
- Add a cost-accounting pipeline to attribute spot savings vs fallback cost (ENG-1689).
- Add a migration to allow per-tenant default weights via the Console UI (product work).
- Run a week-long canary in `us-west-2` and collect fallback_success_rate and customer-visible error rates.

Merge details:
- Merged via squash on 2025-02-20 after approvals and a green CI (one rerun). Commit message summarizes design and links to ENG-1421.

Notes for reviewers/ops: the feature is fully gated; please use dryrun first and consult docs/ops/spot-instance-guidelines.md for parameter recommendations.
Introduce a coordinator for spot/evictable GPU pools: graceful fallback to reserved capacity, tenant-priority allocator, and eviction telemetry. Config is gated behind `spot_fallback.enabled`. Backwards compatible when feature flag is off.

payload.body:
Motivation: several customers expect exact /v1/chat.completions parameter semantics (role aliases, stop array semantics, logprobs mapping) while also relying on our streaming runtime. This PR implements a compatibility-layer negotiator that accepts various OpenAI-like input shapes and normalizes them into Redwood's internal request model. It also introduces a lightweight stream-heartbeat packet and a tool-call envelope to make function/tool handshake deterministic under backpressure.

What this PR does (single-change summary): normalize incoming /v1/chat params (role/name aliases, stop normalization, n/stream flags, logprobs, top_p/temperature fallbacks), add a 2s stream-heartbeat frame for long-running responses, and wrap tool/function call payloads in a compact structured envelope so downstream SDKs can parse function metadata even when a stream is interrupted.

Key behaviors and compatibility notes:
- Roles: accepts both "role":"assistant" and older shape "system/assistant/human" aliasing; normalizer maps common typos (e.g., "user": "human", "assistant_bot": "assistant").
- Stop tokens: supports string or array input; when array, we preserve order and dedupe adjacent duplicates; empty-stop (null/[]) semantics preserved per user request.
- n / best_of: maps legacy best_of -> n with deterministic selection; ensures deterministic seed behavior when present.
- logprobs: maps OpenAI-style logprobs response to Redwood's token-level scoring. When model doesn't expose precise logprobs, we synthesize approximate buckets and annotate as "approx_logprobs" to avoid breaking consumers.
- tool/function calls: when a tool call is emitted, we send a structured envelope event: {"envelope_type":"tool_call","tool_name":...,"metadata":...} as a single JSON line frame to keep tool metadata separate from streaming text deltas. SDKs are updated in separate PRs to consume this.
- Stream heartbeat: emits an empty control frame every 2s (configurable via RD_STREAM_HEARTBEAT_MS) to keep HTTP/HTTP2 intermediaries from timing out on long generations. Heartbeats are filtered by client SDKs; they are not surfaced as content tokens.

Design decisions: keep normalization non-destructive — if a user passes an explicit param (e.g., temperature=0.0), we do not override. Only missing or ambiguous fields are mapped. The negotiator lives at the API adapter boundary to avoid polluting internal runtime types. The structured envelope uses a "frame_type" field so future frames can be introduced without protocol churn.

Testing: unit tests for param mapping, integration tests hitting a local runtime binary, and a new flaky-tolerant streaming test that validates heartbeat preservation through proxies. CI required two reruns due to a known flake in the macOS test matrix; both reruns passed.

Migration and rollout: feature is behind an API-compat feature flag (openai_v1_compat = true) and will be enabled for a subset of accounts first. No breaking changes expected. Docs update included (docs/openai_v1_chat.md) with explicit examples of role aliasing and tool-call envelope parsing.

Motivation: production workloads hitting inference control-plane observed sustained CPU saturation in the request hotpath even when GPU utilization was moderate. Root causes traced to (1) cyclical memcpy/parse steps copying request buffers between IO thread, dispatcher, and worker threads; (2) a single global dispatch mutex that serialized fast-path requests during bursts; (3) synchronous KV cache lookups that blocked worker threads and caused head-of-line stalls; (4) thread pool oversubscription and excessive spinning for short critical sections. This PR implements a series of coordinated CPU-side optimizations aimed at reducing serialization and context-switching friction while preserving correctness and fallbacks.Key changes (single-line summary): unified per-core cooperative scheduler, zero-copy request header handoff, KV-cache prefetch + lock-free read-path, striped dispatch slots and seqlock fallback, adjusted default thread pool sizing and soft-yield policy.Implementation details: - Introduced a lightweight per-core work scheduler (runtime/scheduler.cc) that keeps a small fixed set of worker contexts pinned to a core group and uses a M:N cooperative yield policy for short tasks (<= 4ms). Heavy tasks are demoted to the existing worker pool. This reduces cross-core wakeups for common fast-path requests.- Reworked request handoff to use reference-counted buffer views instead of copying headers into an intermediate struct. New zero-copy types live in runtime/io/buffer_view.h and replace ~3 memcpy sites in the hotpath. The public surface retains the same request API; ownership rules are documented in comments and unit tests.- KV cache: added an optimistic lock-free fast-path using atomic version stamps and an immutable backing array for small entries (runtime/kv_cache_fastpath.cc). For misses, we continue with existing shard+mutex path and schedule a low-priority async fetch so worker threads aren't blocked.- Dispatch: replaced the single global dispatch mutex with striped dispatch slots keyed by request hash (8 stripes). Short critical sections use seqlock to provide lockless reads with a mutex fallback on detected races.- Threading: tuned the default worker pool down from NCPU*1.5 to NCPU+2 and added a soft-yield (sched_yield + short nanosleep) for brief spin-wait loops to avoid burning CPU during transient contention.- Added detailed documentation in docs/perf/cpu-hotpath.md describing tradeoffs and rollout plan.Benchmarks: - Synthetic qps test (100ms GPU latency emulation, 2k concurrent clients): 18% lower p95 latency on the hotpath and 24% reduction in CPU sys time. - Production-like trace replay (mixed short chat/long generation): sustained throughput increased 12% with 10-12% lower CPU utilization at 95th percentile request rate.Rollout plan and safety: - Feature gated behind a runtime flag (runtime.flags.use_unified_scheduler). Disabled by default on Dedicated nodes until we finish long-tail stability testing. - Added runtime telemetry hooks: per-stripe contended_count, zero_copy_fallbacks, kv_prefetch_misses.- Includes a canary + stage rollout script (deploy/canary_unified_scheduler.sh) that coordinates enabling the flag per-pool and collects perf counters for 48h before wider rollout.Testing and QA: - Unit tests covering buffer_view ownership rules and concurrent fast-path reads. - Integration tests that simulate KV miss fallback and verify no deadlocks. - Stress harness recorded in perf/bench/repro_unified_scheduler that reproduces an earlier incident (INC-1124) locally. - Load tests run on staging clusters for 72h.Observability and metrics added: runtime.dispatch.stripe_latency, runtime.scheduler.task_demotes, runtime.kv_fastpath.hits/misses, and a new trace span (scheduler.handoff).CI and infra: - New lint rule added to ensure buffer_view is not copied by value (static analyzer plugin). - Several existing flaky tests were stabilized by reducing shared global state and adding proper teardown.Notes on tradeoffs and limitations: - Zero-copy only applies to requests that fit header+small metadata into contiguous buffers; large attachment streaming still copies. - The cooperative scheduler is tuned for short CPU bursts; workloads dominated by long CPU preprocessing should still use the heavy worker pool. - There is a small additional memory overhead for the immutable KV backing arrays (~2% resident memory in our staging profiles).Checklist:
- [x] Benchmarks attached and reproducible
- [x] Feature-flagged and documented
- [x] Integration and unit tests added
- [x] Rollout script included
- [x] Observability addedCommits summary: - a1f3e2b: add unified per-core scheduler and task demotion APIs - b4d9c8e: introduce buffer_view zero-copy types and replace hotpath copies - c7a12f4: add kv cache optimistic fast-path and prefetcher - d0e3ff1: replace global dispatch mutex with striped slots + seqlock fallback - e21b7a9: thread pool sizing and soft-yield logic; tests and docs - f6c3b2a: add canary deployment script and telemetry hooks
Diego: Great direction. Please add a defensive assert in buffer_view to prevent accidental deep copy semantics. Also can we expose per-stripe counters to the console?
Author (Asha): Added debug-only assert and exported counters to telemetry. See docs/perf/cpu-hotpath.md for how to wire into Console.
Marta: Observed a small regression in long-running generator benchmarks in earlier iteration; how are you ensuring the cooperative scheduler doesn't starve long tasks?
Author (Asha): Scheduler demotes tasks > 4ms to the heavy pool; added integration test and a metric (task_demotes) so we can alert if demotion rate grows unexpectedly.
Elliot: CI initially failed with a race in kv_cache_fastpath tests; root cause was a missed fence. Fixed by adding atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst) on publish path.
Reviewer (Diego): Approving after fence fix.

Maintainer (release): Squash+merge after green CI.

Context: Private deployments require repeatable, auditable tenant bootstrapping and least-privilege RBAC bundles. Current manual steps for creating tenant roles, clusterbindings, and initial bootstrap permissions are error-prone during installs and upgrades. This PR automates policy bundle generation and safe application during both fresh installs and in-place upgrades for the Private installer (Helm + Terraform flow).

What this PR does: adds a terraform module to provision cluster-level bootstrap service accounts and a 'rbacctl' helper to generate and validate tenant-specific policy bundles; extends the Helm chart with templated ClusterRole/Role and ClusterRoleBinding/RoleBinding manifests that are gated behind a new chart value (rbac.automateBootstrap). Adds pre-install and post-upgrade Helm hook jobs to run validation and optionally apply bundles via the installer control-plane when running with --auto-apply. Includes a migration path for clusters with legacy role names and a rollback job that removes newly-created bindings if the install fails during the Helm post-install hook.

Key parts: terraform/modules/rbac-bootstrap - idempotent module that creates:
- bootstrap-sa (namespaced + cluster-scoped bindings required for early control-plane tasks)
- optional KMS key IAM grant (for Private entitlements) when kms.enabled = true

helm/redwood-private/templates/rbac-tenant-roles.yaml - parameterized templates for tenant roles with tenancy-scoped verbs; supports a tenancy.selector label to limit scope; supports generating both ClusterRole (for multi-tenant infra privileges) and Role (for tenant-scoped objects).

tools/rbacctl - new small CLI used by CI and the installer to:
- generate policy bundles in YAML from tenant manifest inputs
- run static validations (no wildcard verbs on storage, no cluster-admin grants without explicit approval flag)
- produce migration patches for legacy role name mappings

installer hooks - pre-install job validates the target cluster has required API versions and that the bootstrap SA exists. post-upgrade job applies bundles if --auto-apply is set and triggers a rollback job on failure.

Tests and validation: adds unit tests for rbacctl validations, helm template unit tests (helm-unittest), a new e2e scenario that exercises tenant isolation checks (runs in CI with a short cluster), and terraform integration smoke test for the bootstrap module.

Security / audit notes: all generated bundles include an annotation 'rbac.redwood.com/issued-by: installer' and a fingerprint hash that is checked by the validation step. Default behavior is dry-run; auto-apply requires the new config flag 'rbac.autoApply=true' and an explicit Linear approval (ENG-5891).

Migration & upgrade behavior: older clusters using legacy role names are detected by the pre-upgrade hook which emits migration patches (applied only if 'rbac.applyMigrations=true'). Rollback behavior is implemented as a Helm hook job that removes newly created cluster bindings and restores a marker ConfigMap to the prior state.

Usage notes (how operators run it):
- Fresh installs: helm install with --set rbac.automateBootstrap=true --set rbac.autoApply=false then review generated bundle at /var/lib/redwood/rbac-bundles/<cluster>-<ts>.yaml and apply with 'rbacctl apply' or via the console.
- Auto-apply installs: set rbac.autoApply=true and ensure terraform bootstrap module has created the bootstrap SA and the installer has KMS grant.

Checklist:
- [x] terraform module: idempotent bootstrap resources
- [x] helm templates: parameterized tenant roles + hooks
- [x] rbacctl: generate, validate, and apply paths
- [x] unit + helm template tests
- [x] e2e tenant-isolation smoke test (CI flakiness noted, retried)
- [x] security review items (SEC-214) addressed

Notes: this PR intentionally keeps auto-apply opt-in and preserves a dry-run-first UX to reduce blast radius. Documentation and console integration will follow in a companion PR that consumes the generated bundles for UI approval flow.

Aisha Khan: Added the explicit --force-admin check and enforcement of Linear key (ENG-5891) in validator; updated docs to show the approval flow.
Priya Desai: The Helm hook rollback looks good but can you avoid finalizers on the rollback ConfigMap to ensure it doesn't block deletions?
Aisha Khan: Removed finalizer and added an owner-ref pattern for the rollback marker to be cleaned up automatically; added an e2e assertion for marker removal.
Liam O'Connor: Terraform outputs look okay; add a comment about the required provider version (>=3.8.0) so operators don't hit upgrade surprises.
Aisha Khan: Added provider version pin and a short migration note in docs/operator/rbac-bootstrap.md.

Motivation: Long-lived and high-cardinality traces (very long token sequences, rare model paths, expensive fallbacks) are a dominant storage and query cost in our span store and make tail-latency debugging noisy. This PR implements a two-stage observability strategy: (1) microtrace rollups - compress long contiguous sequences of low-variance spans into a summarized microtrace that preserves aggregate timing, error counts, and representative exemplar spans; (2) reservoir histogram sampling for span durations and token-cost buckets so we keep high-fidelity distribution summaries without storing every sample.

Design summary: We add a rollup stage in the agent pipeline that identifies contiguous spans matching a heuristic (same route/model-instance, no error flags, contiguous token generation spans) and replaces them with a single summarized span that includes: count, total_duration_ms, p95_estimate_ms, exemplar_span_id, and a compact histogram key. For global metrics we emit reservoir-based histograms (bounded memory, sliding-window TTL) keyed by route/model/tenant that feed dashboards and alerts. The histogram implementation uses a fixed-size reservoir + decay window to ensure fresh tail visibility.

Compatibility and data model: Rollups are an additive transformation before storage and tag a span with label rollup.v=1. Existing consumers will see summarized spans alongside regular spans - we also keep one exemplar for each rollup so trace replays can expand the representative path for debugging. The new histogram keys are exported to the metrics pipeline under metrics.obs.rollup_hist.<aggregation> to avoid colliding with current metric names.

Operational plan: Default rollout to hosted and staging private deployments with config toggle redwood.obs.rollups.enabled=false. We will enable in small canaries for 48 hours and monitor: storage ingested size, query latencies for trace search, number of trace matches that include rollup spans, and user-facing debugging coverage (tracked via Linear ENG-2743).

Dashboards and alerts: New dashboards added: "Microtrace Rollup Overview" (storage delta, rollup ratio by route/model, exemplar coverage), "Reservoir Histogram Explorer" (approx distributions and tail percentiles), and a trace-search toggle to filter rollup vs full traces. Alerts adjusted: lowered noise on trace-store-queue-depth by 10% during rollout and added an alert when exemplar coverage < 99% for any high-SLA tenant.

Testing & validation: Unit tests for rollup heuristics and exemplar selection, load tests simulating 10k QPS long-sequence generation to validate memory bounds, and end-to-end test against local metrics pipeline. Manual verifications included sampling expanded exemplar traces and comparing end-to-end token-cost aggregates to ensure rollups do not alter billing math.

Checklist:
- [x] Implement rollup algorithm and exemplar retention
- [x] Add reservoir histogram implementation and exporter
- [x] Update dashboards and alert rules (Grafana + PagerDuty runbook draft)
- [x] Feature flag + canary rollout plan
- [x] Unit and integration tests

Related: touches on work in ENG-2817 (trace-query optimizations) and SUP-912 (support incident that exposed high-card span storms).
Arjun: The exemplar selection should prefer highest-latency child span — added a suggestion to prefer error-tagged spans; please add deterministic tie-breaker.
Maya: Implemented tie-breaker and added unit test. Also added a new sentinel label rollup.exemplar=true for easier query filtering.
Lena: Asked to validate that billing aggregates remain identical; provided load-test results showing <0.01% difference after rollups.
Carlos: CI flake on metrics exporter resolved by bumping protobuf package in requirements; reran CI.
Ops: Please update PagerDuty runbook with steps to temporarily disable rollups if we miss exemplars; added ops runbook file.
Arjun: Approving after minor doc fixes.
Lena: Approved
Introduce microtrace rollups to reduce span-store cardinality and reservoir histograms to preserve tail latency distribution with bounded memory. Opt-in via feature flag and rolled out via canary. Dashboards and alerts updated.

Motivation: private-installer releases were accumulating redundant artifacts and lacked machine-readable 'rollforward' metadata for fast upgrades in air-gapped installs. This PR introduces a pipeline and small runtime pieces to: 1) rotate old release artifacts (TTL-based, retention policy per-channel), 2) produce a compact rollforward manifest that describes upgrade-compatible artifact sequences, 3) integrate Helm chart checksum validation into release index generation, and 4) pin Terraform module references and embed provenance attestations so private customers can verify end-to-end integrity.

What this change does (high-level):
- New CI pipeline job 'installer-release-rotate' that runs nightly and performs TTL-based pruning of artifacts stored in release-bucket and artifact-catalog; supports dry-run and --apply modes.
- 'rollforward.json' manifest generator added to release indexer. Manifest includes ordered artifact IDs, required minimal delta patch, target helm checksums, and recommended rollback anchor.
- Integrates cosign signing step into the rotate pipeline for newly generated rollforward manifests and for Helm chart tarballs. Attestations (in-tree predicate) emitted to provenance/ folder.
- Adds a verifier CLI subcommand rw-release verify --manifest which validates signatures, compares Helm chart checksums, and checks SBOM hashes. This runs as part of e2e-installer job.
- Terraform module pinning: release pipeline now produces a terraform-modules.lock file with module source@version entries for the installer terraform modules to make upgrades deterministic.
- Fix: previous rollback implementation sometimes referenced stale index shards; the indexer rewrite ensures each shard has a canonical manifest and adds deterministic shard checksums to the ledger.

Checklist: - [x] Pipeline job added to CI config with toggle flags and required secrets. - [x] Indexer change tested locally against a synthetic bucket. - [x] cosign integration wired and documented. - [x] rw-release verify implemented and exercised in CI. - [x] Backwards-compatible: existing release indexes remain queryable; new rollforward manifests are optional for older installers.

Why this is safe: rotation runs in dry-run by default and requires a release engineer toggle to apply; signing steps reuse existing cosign keys and stick to current KMS practices. Rollforward manifests are additive; agents still can use old index flow.

Related: MAY help prevent incidents similar to SUP-122 that required manual artifact pruning and manual manifest stitching. See linked Linear ENG-4321 for rollforward format design notes.
Aisha Patel: Please add a short migration note for existing customers. How will older installers behave when rollforward.json exists?
Author (Liam): Added docs/private-installer/release-notes/rollforward.md explaining that rollforward is optional; installers older than 2024-11 will ignore it. Added a compatibility test in e2e-suite.
Miguel Ortega: The default rotation retention looks aggressive for enterprise customers; can we make the retention per-channel configurable from the console?
Author (Liam): Retention is now a pipeline variable and we added a channel-to-retention mapping in CI. Also documented the required RBAC to flip the apply toggle.
Dana Kim: Ran the e2e flow and cosign verification passed; one remaining nit: make the verifier exit code 2 for 'inconclusive' so that ops tooling can differentiate.
Author (Liam): Updated rw-release verify to return code 2 on inconclusive checks and added unit tests.
Additive: introduces rollforward.json in release indexes; optional for older installers.
New pipeline job 'installer-release-rotate' (nightly) with dry-run default; ops toggle required to apply.
rw-release verify: CLI helper to validate manifests, chart checksums, and signatures. Useful for air-gapped install verification.
Cosign keys reused from current release pipeline; new attestation predicate reviewed by security team.
Rotation requires vault-stored toggle; CI will fail fast if toggle secret is missing to avoid accidental deletion.
1) Run hack/simulate_release_bucket.sh to create a synthetic bucket with multiple channel artifacts.
2) Run ci/pipelines/installer-release-rotate.yml in dry-run mode: ./scripts/ci-run.sh installer-release-rotate --dry-run
3) Generate rollforward with tools/indexer/rollforward_generator locally and inspect rollforward.json for expected sequence.
4) Use rw-release verify --manifest rollforward.json to validate signatures and chart checksums.
5) Toggle apply in CI with appropriate secrets to run a real prune; validate ledger consistency with hashchain-check.
