Motivation: credential rotation and streaming reconnects are frequent sources of transient failures and operator complexity when customers run long-lived streams across multiple SDKs. This change introduces a small, cross-language "credential rotor" primitive plus a compact retry shim for streaming consumers to reduce windowed token thrashing and improve ergonomics for callers. The goal is backwards compatible: defaults are conservative and customers opt-in via SDK config or env var.

What I changed (summary):
- Added a credential-rotor interface and reference implementations in Python/TypeScript/Go that expose: lease acquisition, soft-commit, optimistic swap, and graceful fallback to previous token until drain.
- Implemented a lightweight streaming retry shim (PullStreamAdapter) that co-ordinates rotor handoffs, de-duplicates concurrent refreshes, and applies an exponential jittered backoff tuned for typical LLM token windows.
- Bumped SDK package versions and updated changelogs and migration notes.
- End-to-end tests that exercise rotation during streaming, race conditions, and cold-start behavior.
- Docs + short example snippets for each SDK showing opt-in config and recommended patterns.

Key design notes (single-line descriptions):
- Rotor leases default to 60s with a swap_threshold 0.35 (optimistic swap when 35% lease elapsed); configurable per-SDK.
- De-duplication uses an in-process singleflight per credential key; inter-process coordination is out of scope (recommended for Private deployments to use external KVS).
- The shim is intentionally minimal: it wraps existing stream consumption APIs and exposes a small callback for token refresh events so callers can plug their own telemetry.

Files touched (high-level):
- sdk/python/redwood/auth/rotor.py (new)
- sdk/python/redwood/stream/adapter.py (changes)
- sdk/typescript/src/auth/rotor.ts (new)
- sdk/typescript/src/stream/compact-shim.ts (new)
- sdk/go/auth/rotor.go (new)
- sdk/go/stream/shim.go (new)
- docs/sdk/rotor.md (new)
- tests/integ/rotor_streaming.py (new), rotor_streaming.ts, rotor_streaming_go.go

Checklist: implemented, tested, documented, bumped versions, and added migration notes.

Risks and mitigation:
- Risk: subtle races during parallel refresh; mitigations: singleflight per-key and unit tests that simulate concurrent refresh with mock time.
- Risk: customers relying on existing token lifecycle semantics might see different timing; mitigations: config opt-in and clear migration docs.

Related: references ENG-8240 (design doc), SUP-412 (customer incident that motivated this), and several cross-sdk streaming parity PRs.

Merge: squash-and-merge after approvals and CI green.
Adds a cross-SDK credential rotor and compact stream retry shim. SDKs: Py v2.3.0, TS v1.9.0, Go v1.6.0. Backward-compatible; recommends opt-in via config. Improved streaming reconnect reliability and reduced token refresh thundering by ~3x.
Arjun Gupta: overall good direction. Two asks: (1) can we reduce default lease to 45s? (2) please add a test that simulates concurrent refresh across 10 goroutines. 
Maya Liu: replied: reduced default to 60->50s after perf testing (noted in doc); added goroutine stress test and improved singleflight instrumentation.
Liang Zhao: please ensure TS public API surface stays tiny; drop helper that was exposing internal timer. 
Maya Liu: removed the helper and replaced with an opt-in diagnostics callback; updated changelog with migration guidance.
Priya Nair: CI flaked on go race detector initially; after fix tests pass locally and in CI. Approved.

Summary: Add a small, structured retry metadata header and an explicit idempotency-scoping mechanism to the OpenAI compatibility shim and streaming runtime so callers and downstream routers can make deterministic retry decisions for streamed tool/function calls. This clarifies Retry-After semantics and prevents idempotency key collisions across multiplexed streaming fragments.

Motivation: Customers observed inconsistent retry behavior for long-lived streamed tool calls (tool/function invocations) when proxies and CDNs normalized Retry-After or when clients used coarse idempotency keys across multiple logical tool invocations in the same session. The current behavior led to duplicate tool executions or silent rate limit loops for partial streams. This PR provides: 1) a compact structured header with deterministic retry window data, 2) an explicit idempotency_scope header to partition keys by logical call (stream, tool, function), and 3) mapping rules in the OpenAI shim to maintain backward compatibility with common OpenAI-style headers.

What this changes (high level):
- Adds X-Redwood-Retry-Meta: JSON-lite metadata for server hints (retry_window_ms, retry_type, token_cost_estimate) — consumers can use the numeric window instead of parsing Retry-After text.
- Supports Idempotency-Scope header to scope idempotency-key collisions (values: session, stream, invocation). When absent, behavior falls back to legacy single-key semantics.
- OpenAI shim maps OpenAI Retry-After to X-Redwood-Retry-Meta.retry_window_ms and emits structured error codes under error.type for consistent clients.
- Streaming runtime: when a stream contains multiple logical tool calls, runtime attaches scope-aware fragment IDs to idempotency resolution and stores KV-cache entries keyed by (idempotency_key, scope, fragment_index).
- Added server-side heuristics to avoid applying Retry-After from upstream proxies when noise is detected (e.g., 0/negative values, or >24h).

Files changed (high level):
- internal/openai_adapter/adapter.go: header parsing, mapping, and unit tests
- internal/openai_adapter/retry.go: structured retry metadata creation and mapping rules
- pkg/runtime/streaming/protocol.go: fragment metadata and idempotency scoping hooks
- pkg/api/headers.go: new canonical header constants and parsing helpers
- pkg/api/errors.go: new error.type values and mapping test fixtures
- sdk/python/redwood/openai_compat.py: compatibility shim emits new headers and preserves old ones
- test/integration/retry_metadata_test.go: integration scenarios with proxies and CDNs
- test/unit/idempotency_scope_test.go: unit tests for scoping logic
- docs/rate_limits.md: migration notes and examples
- charts/redwood/templates/config.yaml: opt-in feature flag for the structured headers

Commit summary: [3 commits]
- c1a2b3: add header constants, parsing helpers, and basic tests
- d4e5f6: implement structured retry metadata and OpenAI shim mapping
- f7g8h9: wire idempotency scope into streaming runtime and add integration tests

Compatibility and rollout:
- This change is behind an opt-in feature flag (api.structured_retry_headers). Default for hosted customers is disabled for 2 weeks while we monitor.
- The OpenAI shim continues to emit Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers for backwards compatibility. New consumers should prefer X-Redwood-Retry-Meta.
- Idempotency-Scope is additive; absence preserves legacy behavior. Customers using idempotency_key without scope will see no change unless they opt into scope enforcement.

Testing and QA:
- Unit tests cover header parsing, malformed metadata, and idempotency scoping logic (new test/unit files).
- Integration tests simulate a proxy that rewrites Retry-After and assert the runtime falls back to server-provided structured window when available.
- Performed manual canary on dedicated infra with sample workloads (chat-to-tool ping-pong) for 48 hours; no regression in p50 latency observed.

Rollout plan:
1) Deploy feature flag off to hosted for 48h while collecting metrics (error spikes, duplicate tool invocations).
2) Enable flag for 10% of traffic and monitor.
3) Expand to 100% after 7 days if metrics stable.

Migration notes for integrators:
- If you currently parse Retry-After text, migrate to parsing X-Redwood-Retry-Meta.retry_window_ms when available. Example header: X-Redwood-Retry-Meta: retry_window_ms=120000;retry_type=global;cost=15
- To partition idempotency keys across logical invocations, set Idempotency-Scope: invocation when issuing a stream-based tool call; server will use (idempotency_key, "invocation") as the backing key.

Security and privacy: No sensitive data exposed in headers. Structured retry metadata is intentionally small. We added validation to reject overly large header values to prevent amplification vectors.

Rollout observability: Added dashboard cards for structured-retry-metadata presence, idempotency-scope distribution, duplicate-tool-execution rate, and new error.type counts.

Release notes (user-facing): See release_notes field.

Example: header emitted by server: X-Redwood-Retry-Meta: retry_window_ms=60000;retry_type=soft;cost=3
OpenAI-compat example: server emits both Retry-After: 60 and X-Redwood-Retry-Meta: retry_window_ms=60000;retry_type=soft

Why this is different from previous work: Prior PRs standardized backoff envelopes and Retry-After text mapping. This PR focuses on a compact machine-friendly hint and explicit idempotency scoping for streamed/fragmented tool calls to eliminate collision classes that caused duplicate executions.

Notes: Tests initially flaked in integration CI due to recorded-proxy timestamps; fixed by tolerating small clock skew in test harness.

Acknowledgements: Diego (design review), Priya (runtime review), SRE on-call for integration infra help.

Diego Martinez: Can we avoid adding a second canonical header if we can make Retry-After numeric in the shim? Concern: intermediaries strip non-standard headers.
Ava Chen: We keep Retry-After for backwards compatibility; X-Redwood-Retry-Meta is intended for internal consumers and advanced clients. We emit both when feature flag enabled.
Priya Rao: Streaming runtime change looks good but please add an integration that simulates a stream with two tool invocations that share an idempotency_key to prove scoping prevents collisions.
Ava Chen: Added test/integration/retry_metadata_test.go that covers this scenario.
Ethan Park: CI failed on flakey recorded-proxy timestamps — suggest tolerating 500ms skew in harness.
Ava Chen: Updated test harness; re-ran CI and all checks passed.
Diego Martinez: Approve after addressing one nits in docs about header limits.
Ava Chen: Addressed; doc updated.
Add optional structured retry header (X-Redwood-Retry-Meta) and an Idempotency-Scope header to partition idempotency keys for streamed/tool calls. Default behavior unchanged; feature behind opt-in flag. Improves reliability for streamed tool/function invocations and clarifies retry semantics for clients.
payload.title: Structured retry metadata and scoped idempotency for streamed tool calls

payload.body:
Motivation: production telemetry and perf testing showed CPU-side contention on the global threadpool and high overhead in the synchronous request serialization path. Small, latency-sensitive requests were seeing p95/p99 blowups during load because a single global work queue and a serialize-on-hottpath design created head-of-line blocking. This PR introduces a sharded executor and offloads request serialization to a bounded background worker to reduce contention and free the hot path.
1) Sharded executor: new sharded_executor module implements N independent worker shards with per-shard run queues and optional CPU affinity. Shards are configurable via --executor-shards and default to number_of_cores/2. 2) Offload serialization: request->wire serialization (heavy protobuf/serde) is moved to offload_worker which uses lock-free SPSC queues to submit already-parsed work units to shards, removing per-request mutexes on the hot path. 3) Per-shard batcher: batching now happens inside each shard to allow smaller, more predictable batches based on latency budgets and sequence-length histograms. 4) KV cache fast-path: introduced a read-only lock-free fast-path for hot KV lookups using atomic pointers and epoch-based reclamation for writers; writes still synchronize but are uncommon. 5) Observability: added per-shard metrics (queue_length, avg_batch_size, worker_cpu_ms), new tracing spans for offload/serialize steps, and rollout docs. 6) Feature flag & rollout: runtime flag executor.shards and conservative rollout plan in docs. Results: internal perf lab shows median latency unchanged, p95 reduced by ~12%, p99 reduced by ~18% under synthetic mixed workloads, throughput improved ~22% when under sustained high QPS for small requests.
Unit tests: added coverage for sharded executor lifecycle and sharded batcher. Integration: end-to-end smoke with local GPU backend. Perf: microbench harness in serving/tests/perf runs nightly; this PR includes benchmark artifacts. CI summary: build: pass, unit-tests: pass, integration-smoke: pass, perf-smoke: pass (perf comparisons run in separate perf job, see ci/perf-runner.yml). One flaky integration run was re-run and resolved.
No breaking API changes. Default behavior preserves previous single-shard semantics when executor.shards=1. KV cache writer path unchanged except an additional memory barrier; we included a safety-mode flag kv.locked_write for customers to revert if needed. Rollout plan: stable->canary (5%)->regional (50%)->global with automatic rollback on CPU or latency regressions via the console alerting rules described in docs/ops/executor-rollout.md.
Shane O'Connor: Please add a stress test that simulates mixed small/large sequence lengths under spike conditions. Concerned about shard imbalance when single long sequence lands on one shard.
Priya Khatri: Added serving/tests/perf/sharded_executor_bench.cc to exercise imbalanced seq distribution and added skew mitigation policy (round-robin seed) in latest commit.
Liu Chen: KV fast-path looks promising but I want a formal memory-ordering justification and a leak test for epoch reclamation.
Priya Khatri: Pushed a design doc link and added leak detection unit test; explained memory ordering in comments in kv_cache_lockfree.rs. Will follow up with a short RFC.
Marcus Bryant: CI perf numbers look good; please ensure the rollout docs include steps to disable shard pinning on noisy multi-tenant hosts.
Priya Khatri: Updated docs/ops/executor-rollout.md with disabled pinning section and added console alert thresholds.
payload.title: sharded-executor: offload request serialization and reduce global threadpool contention

This PR adds an ergonomics layer for tool/function calling to support common production patterns: invoking multiple tools in a single call (sequential or parallel), injecting tool outputs into the model context in configurable ways, and specifying per-tool retry/timeout policies. Motivation: customers have been orchestrating chains in ad-hoc ways at the client layer which causes latency spikes, duplicated requests, and inconsistent streaming behaviour. This change centralizes orchestration in the server runtime, preserving streaming semantics while enabling safe parallelism and deterministic injection strategies. Summary of changes: 1) runtime: new ToolOrchestrator component that schedules and executes tools with concurrency limits, retry/backoff, and result-normalization; 2) API: OpenAI-compat additions to the call payload (tools[].parallel, tools[].retry_policy, tools[].injection) and a top-level tools_execution policy; 3) streaming: stable message envelope for tool events so client SDKs can surface partial tool outputs; 4) SDKs/docs: examples and migration notes. Backwards compatibility: default behavior preserves current single-tool sequential semantics when no parallel flags or orchestration options are provided. Tests: unit and integration tests added to validate concurrency, retry, and stream envelope ordering. See related Linear tasks ENG-1412, ENG-1429 and support ticket SUP-987 for customer repros.
Adds configurable multi-tool orchestration primitives: parallel execution flag, per-tool retry policies, and result injection strategies. Improves streaming stability for tool outputs and documents new OpenAI-compat API options.
Connor Liu: Nice overall shape. Two concerns: 1) we need deterministic stream ordering guarantees when tools run in parallel (clients rely on seq numbers), 2) double-injection edge case if a tool result is both streamed and then injected synchronously. Can you add a design note?
Maya Alvarez (author): Added explicit seq numbers to the streaming envelope and a 'finalized' flag. The orchestrator now enqueues 'injection' actions after finalization to avoid double-injection. See streaming_envelope.md and orchestrator comments.
Priya Nambiar: Retry semantics look good but need a max-total-time enforcement (cumulative across retries) or else model will wait forever. Also call out SLO impacts in the docs.
Maya Alvarez: Implemented retry_policy.max_total_ms and documented default = 3000ms. Orchestrator aborts remaining retries when total exceeds the limit and emits a tool.error event.
Ibrahim Saleh: Tests flaked when running integration with the shared test harness (race on orchestrator.cleanup). Suggest using per-test ephemeral tmpdir and deterministic clock for backoff. Also add an explicit shutdown hook to join pending threads.
Maya Alvarez: Fixed (deterministic clock injected into backoff util; orchestrator.shutdown joins executors). Re-ran flaky test locally and on CI.
Squash merged by Priya Nambiar after approvals. Merge commit message: 'Tool orchestrator: multi-tool parallelism, injection strategies, retries (ENG-1412)'. No migrations required; clients using vanilla single-tool payloads unaffected. Added migration note in docs.
payload.title: Tool orchestration: multi-tool parallel execution, result injection, and retry policies

Introduces a new CascadeStrand attention kernel with interleaved rotary rematerialization and scheduler hints to improve latency and throughput across mid-to-long sequence workloads. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via config flag. Recommended for quantized and mixed-precision workloads.
Summary: Implements the CascadeStrand attention kernel — a vectorized, strided-tiling attention path that interleaves rotary rematerialization with fused q/k/v transforms and a lightweight async-KV eviction hint for continuous-batching workloads. Motivation: latency and tail QPS for mid-long sequences (512-8192) showed uneven performance across our current kernel choices. Existing fused kernels excel at short sequences but suffer from memory blowups and KV contention on continuous-batching streams. CascadeStrand bridges the gap by: 1) tiling sequences into adaptive strands that preserve cache locality, 2) rematerializing rotary embeddings only at tile boundaries (reduces local memory and kernel register pressure), and 3) exposing scheduler hints so the continuous-batcher can pipeline strands across GPUs without blocking hot KV slots. High-level changes: - New kernel: src/runtime/attn/cascade_strand_kernel.cu (vectorized strided GEMM + tiled rotary remat loop). - Scheduler hooks: src/runtime/scheduler/strand_hints.{cpp,h} to propagate per-request strand granularity and preferred batch packing. - KV cache: kv_cache/async_eviction.h adds lightweight eviction hint metadata (not automatic eviction) used by dedicated and hosted modes. - Python bindings and opt-in flag: python/redwood/runtime/experimental.py to enable cascade-strand and runtime config keys. - Tests and benchmarks: tests/attn/cascade_strand_unit_test.py, bench/attn_cascade_stream.py. Commits (summary): - a1d3f7: initial cascade-strand kernel prototype and smoke tests. - b5f2c9: fused qkv transform and rotary remat loop, vectorized loads. - d2e8ab: scheduler hint APIs and continuous-batcher integration. - f7c3e1: microbenchmarks, regressions fixed, CI optimizations. Files touched (high-level): - src/runtime/attn/cascade_strand_kernel.cu - src/runtime/attn/kernel_utils.h - src/runtime/scheduler/strand_hints.cpp - src/runtime/scheduler/strand_hints.h - src/kv/kv_cache.cpp - src/kv/async_eviction.h - python/redwood/runtime/experimental.py - tests/attn/cascade_strand_unit_test.py - bench/attn_cascade_stream.py - docs/ops/cascade_strand.md - examples/serve/cascade_example.yaml - build/CMakeLists.txt Benchmarks: - Short seqs (<=128): ~+2% latency vs current fused path (within noise). - Medium seqs (512-2048): ~-22% median latency, -31% p95 compared to unified-fused kernel. - Long seqs (4096-8192): ~-14% median latency, p95 roughly parity but with 40% lower memory peaks on same batch sizes. - Throughput: up to +18% tokens/sec for continuous-batch microbench scenario (mixed lengths). Regression matrix: ran against models gpt-small/gpt-medium/llama-7B, FP16 and 8-bit postquant. No functional regressions found on unit tests; numerical deltas within acceptable tolerance. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag `enable_cascade_strand`. Canary rollout to dedicated clusters in eu-west-1, then opt-in for hosted customers with heavy mid-long workloads. Continuous-batcher will default to previous packing logic until the scheduler hint is enabled. Testing: - Unit tests added to validate rematerialization correctness and strand packing. - Stress test harness simulating long-lived streams with KV churn (bench/attn_cascade_stream.py). - CI: GPU integration tests (cuda-12.1) and macOS CPU smoke. Performance CI includes a new microbench with trending. Review conversation: "Sasha Kim (reviewer): Nice direction. Two asks: (1) can you reduce the register footprint by moving some accumulators to shared memory for older Ampere cards? (2) please add an explicit fallback path when rematerialization is disabled at runtime." "Author (Arjun): Addressed: moved accumulation into shared buffer for legacy SMs (commit d2e8ab) and added runtime check to fall back to unified-fused kernel if remat is disabled (commit f7c3e1)." "Leah Chen (reviewer): Bench numbers look promising. Can you add more deterministic unit tests around boundary tile sizes and odd-length sequences?" "Author: Added tests for tile boundary conditions and odd-length handling (tests/attn/cascade_strand_unit_test.py)." "Ravi Patel (approver): Approve after resolving CI flakiness on the bench runner." CI notes and reruns: initial GPU perf CI had noisy outliers; re-ran microbench with pinned allocation strategy and all checks passed. Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main by Leah Chen after approvals and a final perf smoke. Impact and next steps: - Ops: add `enable_cascade_strand` toggle in console feature flags and include metric dashboards to track latent KV eviction hints and strand packing efficiency. - Research: explore hybridizing with dynamic quantized GEMM paths to squeeze more throughput for 8-bit workloads. - Follow-ups: auto-eviction heuristics for KV (decoupled from this PR) and cross-GPU strand pipelining for multi-GPU per-request execution. Related: ENG-6421 (scheduler improvements), ENG-6533 (KV eviction telemetry). References: internal design doc https://linear.app/redwood/board/ENG-6421/cascade-strand-design, benchmark outputs in bench/outputs/cascade_2026-01.tar.gz.
payload.title: cascade-strand-attn-kernel-with-interleaved-rotary-rematerialization-and-continuous-batching-hints

Implements a kernel dispatch shadowing layer that pre-resolves quantized kernel choices, adds a KV-cache aware prefetcher optimized for prefix reuse, and a continuous-batcher token coalescer that reduces microbatch overhead for INT8/FP8 mixed execution paths. Target: production inference throughput and p99 latency on commodity GPUs while preserving existing correctness and rollout guardrails.
Context and motivation: production workloads show regressing tail latency when switching between INT8 and FP8 execution paths under mixed workloads (e.g., generated LLM chat plus short completion). Root cause analysis indicated three contributors: (1) runtime kernel selection costs under high-concurrency; (2) cold KV cache hot-swapping when execution path toggles; (3) microbatch fragmentation in the continuous-batcher that prevents token coalescence and increases kernel launch overhead. This PR introduces three coordinated components to address these issues: a) Shadowed Quant Dispatch: lightweight, lock-free layer that predicts and resolves the final quantized kernel (INT8 / FP8 / fallback) before the main scheduling phase and pins a kernel handle for the upcoming microbatch. It keeps a small MRU table keyed by (model-variant, seqlen-bucket, token-prefix-hash) to amortize selection cost and warm kernel caches. b) KV-prefetch heuristics: a backend prefetcher that observes prefix reuse across concurrent requests and schedules KV warm-loads to the device asynchronously. The prefetcher respects per-tenant isolation and backpressure quotas; it uses a sliding-window hit estimator to avoid noise. c) Continuous-batcher token coalescer: when continuous mode is enabled, the batcher merges small microbatches that share compatible KV windows into a single coalesced kernel invocation while preserving per-request KV offsets. Implementation notes: - New files added: runtime/quant/shadow_dispatch.{cc,h}, runtime/kv/prefetcher.{cc,h}, scheduler/continuous_coalescer.{cc,h}, unit tests and benchmarks under tests/quant_perf/. - Shadow dispatch is implemented as a header-only optimistic API used by the scheduler; it falls back to existing selection logic when prediction misses. - Prefetcher runs on a dedicated worker thread pool; runtime exposes a light-weight hint API (prefetch_hint(model, key, expected_seqlen)) that is best-effort and non-blocking. - Coalescer uses a KV-offset map to stitch KV segments; it encodes offsets in the kernel launch metadata to avoid copying. Checklist: - [x] Shadowed dispatch prototype + unit tests - [x] KV-prefetch heuristics + quota guards - [x] Continuous coalescer + integration tests - [x] Microbench harness for g4dn and a100 - [x] Feature flag gated (runtime.config.quant_shadowing = true) Compatibility and safety: feature is behind a runtime flag and off by default. All new paths have fallbacks to the previous stable code path. We added end-to-end correctness tests that validate token stream identity at the application level across mixed quant modes. Performance results (selected): - g4dn.xlarge: median token latency -12% (0.84x), p99 -18% (0.82x) for an ensemble of chat+completion workloads using INT8 primary with FP8 fallbacks. - a100: throughput +9% at 32 token sequences when quant_shadowing enabled. - KV-prefetch reduces cold-kv miss rate by 37% in replayed prefix-heavy traces. Observability and rollout: - Added tracing spans: quant.shadow.dispatch, kv.prefetch.hint, batch.coalesce.stitch - Added Prometheus counters/gauges: quant_shadow.predictions, kv_prefetch.hits, coalesce.merge_count - Runtime config keys: runtime.config.quant_shadowing, runtime.config.kv_prefetch_enabled, runtime.config.coalescer_enabled Rollout plan: enable flag in staging with 5% traffic, monitor quant_shadow.predictions and kv_prefetch.hits, then ramp to 50% with automated rollback on increased p99 or error-rate. Related work: follows on from ENG-8214 (quant kernel prefetching experiment) and complements ENG-9251 (continuous-batcher refactor). Commits: - 7 commits: initial shadow dispatch API, MRU table, prefetcher worker, coalescer stitcher, unit tests, integration tweaks, perf fixes. Merge outcome: squashed and merged after two approvals and green CI.
Miguel Torres: Nice direction, can you explain miss-handling? If shadow prediction is wrong do we incur double cost?
Asha Kumar: We designed shadow dispatch to be optimistic — on miss the scheduler falls back to the old selection logic; we measured miss double-cost < 2% of requests in traces. Added a follow-up to add telemetry for double-costs.
Priya Shah: Prefetch worker looks good but we need hard quota enforcement to prevent noisy tenants exhausting device memory.
Asha Kumar: Added per-tenant budget checks and a soft-degrade path that converts prefetch to low-priority copies; documented limits in runtime.config.
Ethan Li: Coalescer correctness seems subtle around KV window stitching for cross-request offsets. Please add an invariant test to ensure no KV overlap occurs.
Asha Kumar: Added invariants and randomized property-based tests (tests/integration/test_coalesce_end_to_end.py) and increased assertions under debug builds.
Priya Shah: CI microbench flaked once on a100 (memory pressure). Re-ran and it's green. Approving after logs added.
Miguel Torres: Approving. Left a minor comment about renaming a metric; addressed in follow-up commit.
payload.title: Shadowed quant dispatch, KV-prefetch heuristics, and continuous-batcher token coalescer for INT8/FP8 mixed paths

Motivation: customers using function/tool-calling and structured output have limited ability to correlate tool calls to per-route metrics, and streaming JSONL outputs lack stable tags for downstream log processors. This PR attaches per-route metric tags to function-call events, enriches JSONL streaming output with consistent telemetry headers, and adds trace propagation across the OpenAI-compat adapter layer. Changes aim to improve observability without changing public API semantics. Summary of changes: 1) Add per-route "route.tags" metadata to function-call events emitted by the gateway and runtime; 2) Emit a compact telemetry header ("rwid, srv, route, call_idx") at the start of streaming JSONL chunks to enable log reassembly; 3) Propagate distributed trace context and span IDs into function-call instrumentation and structured logs; 4) Update openai-compat adapter to translate OpenAI-style "request_id" into rwid and include route tags for compatibility; 5) Add unit and integration tests covering streaming reassembly and metric label cardinality limits; 6) Add doc comments and console notes for admins about limiting custom route tags. Checklist: - [x] Add telemetry header and tests - [x] Preserve streaming shape for openai-compat clients - [x] Ensure route tag cardinality cap (100) enforced - [x] Add end-to-end smoke test against mock tool runner - [x] Update docs and changelog Impact: no user-facing API change; observability improvements are additive. Rollout plan: feature gated behind experiment flag "obs.route_tags_tool_calls" for three days in canary, then staged rollout to 25% traffic, then full rollout assuming no regressions. Monitoring: added alerts for spike in unique route tags and increased rate of incomplete streams.
Jon Liu: Can you confirm the added telemetry header is at most 256 bytes to avoid proxy truncation?
Maya Patel: Confirmed, header is compacted and base64-encoded; tests include a 256-byte boundary case.
Sofia Ramirez: We should cap unique per-route tags to avoid high-cardinality metrics - where is that enforced?
Maya Patel: Cap enforced in runtime/instrumentation/serializer.go with a hard limit of 100 tags and metrics emitted when limit hit.
Evan Brooks: Integration tests flaked once on CI due to a timing window in the mock tool runner, please add retry/wait up to 500ms.
Maya Patel: Added small retry and fixed race; CI rerun included below.
Sofia Ramirez: Approving pending a short note in docs about tag cardinality and cost implications.
Sofia Ramirez: Approved after doc update.
Release-Manager (auto): No conflicts with main; merge allowed.
Add per-route telemetry tags for function/tool calls and compact streaming JSONL telemetry header (rwid, srv, route, call_idx). This improves ability to correlate tool calls with per-endpoint metrics and enables downstream log reassembly. Feature rolled out behind experiment flag obs.route_tags_tool_calls.

Background: production telemetry shows CPU-side tails driven by frequent short-lived IO wakeups and per-request serialization overhead (small payloads, many concurrent connections). Motivation: reduce syscall churn and cache thrash without changing existing external APIs. Change summary: introduce a configurable IO coalescer that groups pending socket/FD readiness into short (<500us) micro-batches processed by polymorphic workers, unify the per-request serialization path into a batched serializer that encodes multiple response frames in one pass, and add lightweight pacing to the worker pool so CPU pinning is optional. Design goals: (1) preserve latency SLOs for single-request fast paths, (2) reduce 95/99p CPU tail by avoiding repeated thread wake/sleep, (3) keep the change runtime-configurable and safe to roll back. What this PR does: 1) new module runner/scheduler/io_coalescer.rs that aggregates readiness events per-core and dispatches grouped events to polymorphic workers; 2) polymorphic worker pool (runner/scheduler/worker_pool.rs) that supports CPU-pinned and unpinned modes and can handle small burst windows; 3) batched serializer (runtime/serialization/batch_serializer.cpp) that takes vectorized response items and applies shared formatting/kernels once; 4) lightweight KV prefetch hints in runtime/kvcache/prefetcher.py to warm hot keys observed in batched requests; 5) a new runtime flag io.coalesce_workers (default: false for safety) and debug tracing; 6) benchmarks and perf harness changes under bench/perf/coalescer/*. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked in Linear ENG-2120 | - [x] unit + integration tests added | - [x] microbench harness and CI perf job updated | - [x] feature gated behind runtime flag | - [x] rollout plan with canary and metrics tracked Performance: end-to-end lab tests (nvme-backed VM, 32 vCPU, 8x A10 equivalent inference GPUs simulated) show: baseline 95th CPU-side request path latency 48ms -> 16-20ms with coalescer+batched-serializer enabled; p99 reduced 92ms -> 36ms; average CPU cycles/request reduced ~2.8x; observed 18% drop in token-level throughput at 1000 concurrent connections due to batching-induced micro-queueing in aggressive mode (mitigated by default conservative windows). Safety and compatibility: no external API changes, no model-serving kernel modifications; kvcache prefetch is best-effort. Rollout: staged enablement via feature flag; canary in us-west with 5% traffic for 24h, then 25%, then full. Revert: set io.coalesce_workers=false and redeploy; fallback safe-path keeps original serializer and worker semantics. Related: ENG-2187 (bench regression triage), SUP-4421 (customer report of tail CPU).
Initial design + benchmark posted by author. Avery asked for deterministic timers for coalescing window and a guard for high-load no-coalesce path; author added timer meters and a short-circuit fast-path. Morgan requested metrics for micro-batch size distribution and per-worker queue depth; added histograms and dashboards. Elena flagged potential interaction with existing affinity pinning; author added polymorphic worker modes and default unpinned rollout. CI perf job rerun once after minor allocator tweak; final approval from Avery and Morgan before merge.
Lab perf: 95p CPU-side latency 48ms -> 16-20ms; p99 92ms -> 36ms; average cycles/request ~2.8x improvement; small throughput tradeoff under aggressive batching (up to -18% at extreme concurrency); mitigations and conservative defaults included.
Disable runtime flag io.coalesce_workers and redeploy the control-plane config. If metrics do not recover within 15m, revert the release to previous image. All changes are gated so rollback does not require DB migration or data changes.
Introduce IO coalescer and batched serializer (opt-in). Reduces CPU-side tail latency; enable via runtime flag io.coalesce_workers. See perf notes for conservative defaults.
payload.title: Coalesce IO polymorphic workers and batched serialization to cut CPU tail latency

Motivation: We need a safe way to run shadow/mirroring experiments that exercise upstream model variants (or new runtime) without risking production availability. Existing mirror controllers at Redwood assume uniform mirroring ratios and a single global safety budget. This PR introduces a heterogeneous mirroring controller that: 1) allows multiple cohorts (user segments) to receive independently configurable mirror ratios, 2) applies a gradual-degradation safety policy that decays mirrored traffic automatically when signals indicate regression, and 3) exposes per-cohort failure budgets, throttles, and an explicit 'trial window' to limit blast radius.

Design summary: The controller implements an adaptive controller loop (mirroring_controller.go) that subscribes to: rollout config, cohort selectors, and metric signals (latency, error-rate, and quality-regression hooks). Key behaviors: - Mirror assignments are expressed as cohort-level weights (0.0-1.0). - A rolling evaluation window computes a combined "safety score" per cohort using configurable weights for latency, errors, and quality deltas. - When a safety score exceeds the configured threshold, the controller triggers gradual-degradation: a percent-decay policy that reduces mirrored traffic by a configurable step (default 30%) every evaluation period until the cohort returns to safe range or the trial window expires. - If degradation reaches floor (default 1%), the controller triggers an alert and can optionally unmirror the cohort. - The policy includes a recovery hysteresis to avoid flip-flop.

Configuration example (new API fields):
rollout: 
  mirror: 
    cohorts: 
      - name: "beta-users"
        selector: "region==eu and plan==beta"
        initial_ratio: 0.2
        failure_budget: 0.02
        safety_weights: { latency: 0.4, errors: 0.4, quality: 0.2 }
    gradual_degradation: 
      step: 0.3
      period_seconds: 300
      floor_ratio: 0.01
      evaluation_window: 900
      alert_on_floor: true

Operational notes: - This PR wires mirror telemetry into the Console (Traffic Mirror dashboard) with per-cohort charts and the aggregate safety-heat map. - We added a lightweight evaluation endpoint so SREs can simulate policy outcomes against historical traces. - Default behavior is conservative: if no cohort config exists, the controller behaves like the prior uniform mirror with an implicit low default ratio (0.01).

Testing and validation: Unit tests cover the safety-score computation, decay math, and hysteresis. Integration tests (e2e) simulate a three-cohort rollout exercising degrade/recover cycles; these live under e2e/test/traffic_mirror_integration.test.ts and are included in CI. Benchmarks show controller CPU overhead under 50ms per evaluation for up to 10k concurrent cohorts.

Backward compatibility & migration: API additions are additive; agents without cohort configs continue using platform defaults. We added a migration job to populate a conservative cohort for customers relying on global mirror fields.

Checklist: - [x] Implementation of controller loop and policy - [x] API and proto changes + model upgrades - [x] Console UI for cohort creation and charts - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Benchmarks and perf microprofile - [x] Documentation (docs/rollouts/traffic-mirroring.md)

Related: ENG-4382 implements the evaluation heuristics; ENG-4410 tracks Console UX work.
Introduces a traffic-mirroring controller that supports per-cohort heterogeneous mirroring ratios and an adaptive gradual-degradation safety policy; adds API fields and console UI; includes integration tests and observability; non-breaking for existing rollout configs.

Add API fields: rollout.proto + server-side parsing

Maya Patel (2024-11-06): Reply: added a paragraph in description and expanded unit tests to cover signal cardinality; failure_budget is normalized against request-rate-weighted error-rate (see mirroring_controller.go comments).
Sofia Ramos (2024-11-06): Minor: console chart labels need better tooltip contexts; in draft UI I saw raw counts without normalization.
Maya Patel (2024-11-07): Addressed: tooltips now show normalized rates and a small example in the doc. Also pinned the default floor_ratio to 0.01 to be explicit.

Motivation:
We have a long-running maintenance tax keeping tool versions synchronized across ~10 GitHub Actions workflows. Small version drift and inconsistent setup snippets caused multiple transient CI failures and made dependency updates error-prone. This PR centralizes toolchain configuration and replaces repeated setup logic with a single composite action (.github/actions/toolchain-setup) and a single source-of-truth config file (.github/toolchain.yml).

What this does (high-level):
- Adds .github/actions/toolchain-setup/action.yml: a composite action that installs Node, Python, Rust, and Java according to a common config file. It wraps setup-node/setup-python/actions-rs/setup-java and pins the recommended versions.
- Adds .github/toolchain.yml: canonical versions and OS-specific overrides (linux/macos).
- Updates CI workflows under .github/workflows/* to call the new composite action instead of repeating setup steps.
- Simplifies matrix definitions by referencing the centralized versions rather than hard-coded strings.
- Removes a few legacy one-off setup snippets that are no longer needed.

Checklist (author):
- [x] Add composite action and config file
- [x] Update CI workflows to use composite
- [x] Run full test matrix locally with act/emulation and on CI
- [x] Coordinate with SDK owners (TS/Python/Go) for any version bumps
- [x] Add brief docs in CONTRIBUTING.md pointing at .github/toolchain.yml

Detailed changes / commit summary:
- commit 1: Add toolchain config and composite helper (action.yml + README + tests)
- commit 2: Replace node/python setup in workflows with uses: ./.github/actions/toolchain-setup
- commit 3: Update workflow matrices to reference .github/toolchain.yml via env interpolation
- commit 4: Address reviewer nits, add fallback for runner OS that doesn't support prebuilt tool caches

Files changed (high-level):
- .github/actions/toolchain-setup/action.yml (new)
- .github/actions/toolchain-setup/README.md (new)
- .github/toolchain.yml (new)
- .github/workflows/ci.yaml (modified)
- .github/workflows/lint.yaml (modified)
- .github/workflows/integration-tests.yaml (modified)
- .github/workflows/release.yaml (modified)
Centralizes versions and toolchain setup used by GitHub workflows behind a single composite action; reduces per-workflow duplication and unifies node/python/rust/java versions. No runtime behavior changes expected for production services.
Riley Chen (review): Nice consolidation. Two asks: 1) add a matrix fallback when a runner doesn't have the cached toolchain; 2) ensure we still surface the individual version in workflow logs. 
Author reply: Added an explicit 'TOOLCHAIN_FALLBACK=true' env path and emit versions during setup. See last commit. 
Sofia Patel (review): Could we avoid introducing another action if maintainability becomes an issue? Suggest we make the composite intentionally small and well-documented. 
Author reply: Agreed — composite wraps existing community actions only and includes a README with upgrade guidance. 
Marta Lopez (approve): Tests ran green in staging; approving assuming no runtime changes.
payload.title: Centralize CI toolchain config and replace repeated setup steps with composite action

payload.body:
Motivation: We observed tail latency spikes and extra memory traffic when serving mixed-precision (INT8/FP8) workloads with prefix reuse. Root causes: (1) unnecessary materialization/dequant roundtrips for attention weight paths that are not used by the current request ordering, (2) imprecise per-head statistics collection for SmoothQuant that caused kernel divergence at scale, and (3) inconsistent KV routing when dequant fusion changes node layouts, which invalidates batching alignment heuristics.

This PR introduces an ordered dequant-bypass path that avoids dequantization and re-quantization for heads/blocks that are not referenced by the active request ordering, a SmoothStatCollector that computes activation scaling stats deterministically across batching boundaries, and a lightweight KV-consistent routing layer that pins fused-kernel variants to routing keys so continuous batching remains compatible with fusion-driven layout changes.

Summary of changes (single-line items):
- Add OrderedDequantBypass planner and runtime hooks to skip dequant on non-referenced heads.
- Implement SmoothStatCollector which aggregates per-channel activation scales using deterministic reduce ops and exposes stats to kernel selection.
- Introduce KVRoutingFingerprint to bind fused dequant kernels to routing keys used by the continuous batching router.
- Kernel change: fused_dequant_matmul_{int8,fp8}.cu updated to accept bypass flags and stat references.
- Runtime scheduler: update batching compatibility checks to consult KVRoutingFingerprint and ordered bypass masks.
- Add unit/integration tests and a perf microbenchmark harness.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc linked in Linear ENG-4821
- [x] Unit tests for planner and collector
- [x] Perf harness and baseline regression tests
- [x] Backwards-compatible: falls back to existing dequant path when feature flag off
- [x] QA on Dedicated staging with mixed small/large sequence workloads

Performance impact (end-to-end on our internal bert-like inference with 1-128 seq batch mix):
- 1.18x throughput increase on INT8 end-to-end path (p99 latency unchanged or improved)
- 12% average per-request memory traffic reduction in KV store windows due to bypassed materialization
- 7-9% lower latency tail in small-rt workloads (1-16 seq) when SmoothStatCollector is enabled
- Demonstrated no perf regression on FP8 float-ref path

Testing and CI: initial CI run had two flaky tests (perf/regression) failing on the runner; those were addressed by re-seeding the test harness and adding a small timing tolerance in test_assert_harness. Final CI: all checks pass (unit/integration/perf/e2e).

Backward compatibility and rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag `quant.ordered_dequant_bypass` and SmoothStatCollector behind `quant.smooth_stat_collect`. We will rollout as a staged canary: 5% -> 25% -> 100% on Dedicated clusters, with automated regression gates tied to the perf harness.

Related Linear/Jira: ENG-4821, ENG-4890; customer incident SUP-2219 triggered additional KV routing constraints.

Notes on implementation details: OrderedDequantBypass computes a per-request bitmask of referenced heads/blocks at pre-schedule time and attaches a compact 64-bit mask to the continuous-batch entry. The fused kernel accepts the mask and only materializes dequantized weights for set bits; non-materialized blocks are read via a fast-path that treats weights as quantized during matmul with calibrated scaling. SmoothStatCollector runs as a prewarm operator in the batch window that reduces activation max/mean stats with deterministic tree reduction to avoid non-determinism across batching orders. KVRoutingFingerprint derives a stable 128-bit fingerprint from the fused-kernel signature and the model's routing key; the router pins kernel variants to fingerprinted slots so existing batch aggregator assumptions remain valid.
Kunal Mehta (review): Nice work. Two questions: can we bound the worst-case CPU overhead of the SmoothStatCollector on tiny batches? Also please document the seed behavior in test harness so future flakes are easier to triage.
Aisha Patel (author): SmoothStatCollector runs on the batch leader only and uses SIMD-friendly reductions; measured CPU overhead < 2% in our microbench. Added comment + test that seeds the harness (see commit f12b3d0).
Liam O'Connor (review): I saw a small runtime issue when routing pinned kernel variants across regions due to signer differences. Can we ensure fingerprint generation is region-agnostic?
Aisha Patel (author): KVRoutingFingerprint uses model+kernel signature + normalized routing key; removed non-deterministic signer data. Added stable serialization step to ensure region-agnostic fingerprints.
Sofia Martinez (approval): Verified perf harness results; approve.
Added Ordered Dequant Bypass to reduce unnecessary dequantization for non-referenced heads, introduced SmoothStatCollector for deterministic SmoothQuant stats across batching boundaries, and added KVRoutingFingerprint to maintain batching compatibility with fused dequant kernels. Performance improvements for INT8 paths and reduced KV memory traffic. Feature gated and rolled out via canary.
This PR aims to be non-breaking: default flags are off until canary completes.
Follow-up tasks: ENG-4951 add metric for bypass hit-rate, ENG-4972 expand kernel unit coverage for exotic model layouts.
Bench harness and datasets used are checked into perf/benchmarks and are deterministic when run with --seed flag.
payload.title: Ordered Dequant Bypass, SmoothStat Collector, and KV-Consistent Routing for Quant Kernels

payload.body:
Motivation: transient kernel incompatibilities and scheduling pressure occasionally cause our fast (kernel-optimized) codepath to emit subtly different attention corner-cases compared to the stable slow path. This manifests as rare correctness drift under tight latency budgets when we aggressively favor the fast path. This PR introduces a low-overhead probe-and-validate gating mechanism plus a conservative "safe-mode" fallback to ensure correctness while preserving most of the fast-path win.

What this changes (summary):
- Fast-path probe: before switching a worker to a new fast kernel variant, the worker runs a tiny micro-benchmark (probe) that exercises attention edge-cases (short prefix, long memory, kv cache reuse) and computes a compact validation token (rolling hash + checksum) of the probe outputs.
- Lightweight consistency checks: the probe token is compared against an expected token for that kernel/model/seqconfig. Mismatches block the fast-path and create a diagnostic event.
- Safe-mode fallback: on mismatch or repeated probe failures the worker enters safe-mode: it routes requests to the stable slow kernel and uses a conservative precision profile (FP32/FP16 fallback sequence) to maximize parity. Safe-mode is scoped per-host and decays after a successful probe window.
- KV-cache-aware probing: probes are run both with empty and primed KV cache to catch cache-dependent divergences; we avoid draining real live KV entries by using a local ephemeral cache snapshot.
- Scheduling integration: scheduler adds a probe budget per epoch and prefers low-latency probes during low-util periods; probes are throttled to avoid affecting p99.
- Observability and rollback: new metrics (probe_success, probe_failure_reason, safe_mode_entries, safe_mode_duration) and a diagnostic payload attached to failure events; a quick flip flag inserted in config to disable probes or force safe-mode for emergency mitigation.

Checklist:
- [x] unit tests for probe harness and checksum comparison
- [x] integration tests exercising primed/unprimed KV paths
- [x] end-to-end canary on benchmark-lab with 3 models (gpt-small, gpt-medium, opt-6b)
- [x] dashboards for probe metrics and alerts on elevated failure rates
- [x] rollout plan and rollback flag in runtime config

Performance impact: canary results show median latency change +1% on typical sequences; tail impact negligible when probe budget is set to 1 probe per 10k requests per host. When fast-path is allowed, token throughput improved by 7-11% on our CPU+GPU mixed pools for served sequence-length distribution used in ENG-5421. Safe-mode incurs expected cost (2–3x token CPU work) but is scoped to affected hosts and decays quickly once a stable kernel/probe pair is validated.

Testing notes:
- benchmark-lab run id: bl-2025-11-26-ffprobe (attached metrics snapshot in PR artifacts)
- Integration harness includes a synthetic adversarial suite that ramps KV re-use patterns to surface cache-dependent bugs.

Compatibility and migration:
- Probe tokens are versioned by (model_hash, kernel_variant, seq_profile, probe_version). When loading older kernels that lack tokens the system treats them as probe-missing and will perform a full validation run the first time (safe-mode until validated).
- No model API changes. All config is behind runtime feature flag fastpath_probe_enabled (default ON in canary, default OFF in prod until we complete broader rollout).

Rollout plan:
1. Merge to main -> internal canary (benchmark-lab) for 48 hours.
2. Gradual rollout to Hosted low-traffic region (10% hosts) and monitor probe_failure_rate < 0.1%.
3. Expand to Dedicated pools, then set fastpath_probe_enabled ON for most fleets.
4. If probe failure spikes, flip fastpath_probe_enabled to OFF or force safe-mode (operator fix).

Notes on correctness tradeoffs: the design intentionally keeps probes compact to avoid p99 regressions; this means very rare divergence types might not be caught immediately and will surface as diagnostic events or user reports. The safe-mode provides a deterministic recovery path for these cases.

Related: references ENG-5421 (kernel stability), ENG-5490 (kv cache priming heuristics).
Miguel Ortega: Left a detailed comment about the potential for probe overhead to affect p99; suggested adding scheduler safeguards. Asha: added probe_budget and throttling in scheduler and re-ran canary.
Lena Park: Requested stronger telemetry around 'why' a probe failed (checksum vs. crash). Asha: split failure reasons and added probe_failure_reason label (checksum|crash|timeout|vc_mismatch).
Jordan Chen: Asked for safe-mode decay semantics. Asha: implemented exponential decay (success window of 5 consecutive probes to exit).
QA (automated): initial CI run showed one flaky integration test (kv-adversary) failing intermittently — test updated to be less timing-sensitive and re-run.
Introduce probe-based fastpath gating with lightweight validation tokens and a per-host safe-mode fallback. Adds probe metrics and a runtime flag to disable probes in emergencies. Improves fast-path safety with minimal median-latency impact; can be rolled back via config.
This PR intentionally keeps the probe payload minimal; future work (ENG-5602) will expand probe coverage if we can maintain the same budget constraints.
payload.title: probe-based fastpath gating with lightweight consistency checks and safe-mode fallback

payload.body: Motivation: bursts and short-lived spikes are still a major source of cost and poor p99 for Dedicated capacity customers. Current burst controls operate on instantaneous token pools and long-running warm pools cause steady cost overhead when used conservatively. This PR introduces a Temporal Credit Orchestrator (TCO) that schedules per-tenant credit allotments over configurable sliding windows, combined with a Deferred Warmup Controller that delays starting full warmlet allocation until a tenant's scheduled credit reaches a threshold. The design lets tenants accumulate credits during quiet periods and spend them predictably while avoiding aggressive always-on warm pools, reducing cost without degrading tail latency. Summary of changes: 1) runtime/scheduler: new package scheduler/temporal_credit_orchestrator.go that maintains per-tenant sliding-window credit balances with decay and explicit reservation APIs; 2) autoscaler: autoscaler/deferred_warmup_controller.go which watches TCO signals and ramps warmlet allocation only when scheduled credits exceed configurable warmup gates; 3) telemetry: telemetry/tenant_utilization_estimator.go that reports effective throughput and distinguishes warmup inflight from steady-state utilization; 4) config: api/configs/temporal_credits.yaml feature flag and default tuning profiles; 5) API/console: console: expose 'temporal credits' panel and warmup gate controls; 6) e2e and unit tests: tests/e2e/test_temporal_credits.py, tests/unit/test_orchestrator.py plus load harness scenarios; 7) docs: docs/design/temporal-credit-orchestrator.md and docs/ops/runbooks/warmup-guidance.md. Backwards compatibility: TCO is behind a feature flag (enable_temporal_credits) and defaults to off; the Deferred Warmup Controller is gated by 'deferred_warmup' flag and will not affect existing warm pools until enabled. Rollout plan: staged: enable feature flag in canary fleet for 48h with synthetic microburst replay, observe p99 and fleet cost, then incrementally widen to 10%/30%/100% of dedicated clusters. Metrics to watch: per-tenant consumed_credits/sec, scheduled_credit_balance, warmlet_start_rate, tenant_effective_utilization_5m, and p95/p99 latency. Why this is different: instead of only limiting instantaneous burst tokens we allow time-shifted credit scheduling and couple that to resource warmup decisions, which smooths both cost and tail latency. Related work: builds on ENG-309 (burst-token-pool refactor) and ENG-4201 (tenant budget advisor). This PR includes a light-weight simulation harness used for parameter tuning and reproducible tuning scripts in tools/sim/temporal_credit_simulator.go. Security and perf: no new user-facing auth surfaces. The orchestrator runs in control-plane and communicates with autoscaler over existing signed RPC channel; added unit tests for RBAC checks. Canary notes: initial canary ran with quotas lowered by 20% to surface regressions in fairness; we observed a 7% median cost reduction for a 2% p99 increase on one canary which prompted tweak to warmup gate thresholds and produced final numbers showing both p99 stable and 6% cost reduction. Deployment: merged to main and feature flags will be toggled via console.
payload.title: Temporal Credit Orchestrator and Deferred Warmup for Dedicated Fleets

This PR extends the model listing and capability endpoints to expose runtime hints (streaming stability hints, recommended kv-cache policies, batching/latency profiles), explicit compatibility flags for OpenAI-style features (function_calling, structured_output, streaming), and per-model pricing/limits metadata (tokens_per_second_estimate, max_context_tokens, soft_rate_limit, burst_capacity). Motivation: product teams need a single discovery API to make deterministic routing and graceful fallback decisions at runtime; SDKs and the OpenAI-compat shim need canonical fields to drive feature negotiation without brittle heuristics. The change includes: 1) schema additions to /v1/models and /v1/model-catalog with new flat fields; 2) a compatibility map that lists boolean flags and a deprecation & aliases map for older capabilities; 3) streaming stability hint tokens that indicate recommended chunking size and backoff policy; 4) pricing/limits fields surfaced for billing and client-side throttling; 5) an OpenAI compatibility layer update that maps Redwood capability names to OpenAI equivalents and exposes a single compatibility_score to help automated routing. Backwards compatibility: added fields are optional and default to safe values to avoid client breakage. See release_notes for migration guidance.
Added unit tests for serializer/deserialize, compatibility mapping tests, and integration test that exercises routing policy selection using new compatibility_score and streaming_hints. Load test validated tokens_per_second estimates under mixed batch sizes and reported within 10% of observed throughput.
Miguel Torres: Please add a short description for compatibility_score semantics and ensure it is unit-tested. Aisha Patel: Added tests and expanded docstring to clarify 0-100 scoring and that it's advisory only. Lena Chen: The streaming_hint backoff enum needs a default; suggest 'linear' with jitter. Aisha Patel: Default added and CI updated. Omar Hashim: Can we expose estimated tokens_per_second for both cpu and gpu? New fields: compatibility_flags (function_calling, structured_output, streaming), compatibility_score, streaming_hints (chunk_size, recommended_backoff), tokens_per_second_cpu/gpu, max_context_tokens, soft_rate_limit, burst_capacity. payload.body:
Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["\n\n", "\n\n\n"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust. - Response envelope parity: normalize streaming deltas to include a minimal structured 'choice' envelope (id, index, finish_reason) so downstream OpenAI-compat consumers don't need ad-hoc heuristics. - Tests & docs: add unit and integration tests for the normalizer, streaming handshake scenarios, and a new example in the docs showing a robust client reconnection strategy. Checklist: - [x] Parameter mapping implemented and unit-tested - [x] Streaming handshake and backpressure implemented with integration tests - [x] Role aliasing covered by parser tests - [x] Stop dedupe logic covered and fuzz-tested - [x] Sparse logprobs gating and tests - [x] Docs updated (compatibility section + example client) - [x] Runtime perf smoke tests run on canary cluster Notable design decisions: - We intentionally do not try to replicate obscure historical OpenAI quirks; instead the normalizer applies conservative, well-documented rules and exposes a strict compatibility flag for customers who really need historical behavior. - The streaming handshake is opt-out via a client header (X-Redwood-Compat: openai-v1) to avoid breaking existing non-OpenAI clients. - Sparse logprobs are computed on-demand and annotated in the response metadata to allow downstream billing/observability. Related: ENG-4321 (parameter normalization epic), SUP-2107 (customer-reported toolcall truncation).
Samir: Can you clarify how explicit null values are treated vs missing keys? There was a customer case where max_tokens=null meant 'use default' rather than '0'.
Author (Evelyn): Normalizer treats explicit null as 'unset' and falls back to model defaults; added a unit test for that scenario.
Asha: The backpressure header naming looks fine, but please add a short blurb in the docs about HTTP/1 clients where we emulate the behavior over SSE.
Author (Evelyn): Added docs section and an SSE emulation implementation for older clients.
Leo: Sparse logprobs look good; make sure we annotate toggles in telemetry so customers can track extra compute costs.
Author (Evelyn): Telemetry annotation added (adapter.openai_v1.sparse_logprobs=true) and documented cost footnote.
payload.title: chat v1: parameter normalizer, role aliasing, stop dedupe and streaming backpressure improvements for /v1/chat.completions parity

payload.body:
Motivation: production INT8/FP8 serving showed occasional latency spikes when long-lived KV caches and mixed-size sequences interacted with quantization metadata. These spikes occur when a hot prefix reuses KV state but downstream requantization happens at the full sequence boundary, causing a rare but visible token-jitter on P50/P95 for small requests. This PR implements two coordinated runtime features: 1) an adaptive per-token requantization pipeline that performs lightweight per-head rescaling only when KV-reuse heuristics indicate cross-batch scale drift, and 2) a KV-watermark mechanism to limit KV cache growth and trigger lightweight recompact/flush operations before kernels fall back to slow paths. Both features are opt-in runtime flags that default on for dedicated and hosted tiers after canary rollout.

What changed (high level):
- New kernel: runtime/quant/fused_dequant_attn_adaptive.cu — a fused dequant + attention path that accepts per-head scale vectors and a token-adaptive mask. Optimized memory layout reduces temporary allocations in the hot loop.
- Requant pipeline: runtime/quant/requant_controller.cc /.h — tracks per-key/value scale statistics, computes lightweight EMA of per-head scales, and emits per-request hints to the fused kernel. The controller falls back to legacy path if variance is high.
- KV-watermark: runtime/kv/kv_watermark.cc /.h — introduces low/ high watermarks for KV length per-shard; when high watermark is reached the shard runs an incremental recompact that preserves hot prefixes while trimming stale entries.
- Scheduler integration: scheduler/continuous_batcher.cc updated to surface KV hint metadata to the batcher so batches with similar KV fingerprints are coalesced, improving KV-cache hit locality.
- Metrics/tracing: observability/metrics/quant_metrics.cc adds per-request flags and histograms for "requant_taken", "kv_recompact_triggered" and distribution for the time spent in the adaptive kernel.
- Docs and flags: doc/runtime/quant.md and CLI flags for canary rollout, watermark thresholds, and controller aggressiveness.

Compatibility: The adaptive path is compatible with existing model formats and quantization metadata. We fall back to legacy dequant+attn kernels under three conditions: (1) requested model lacks per-head scale metadata, (2) controller variance exceeds configured threshold, (3) explicit compatibility flag off.

Checklist:
- [x] Kernel implementation and unit tests
- [x] Controller logic and integration tests
- [x] Scheduler coalescing for KV fingerprints
- [x] Canary rollout plan and migration docs
- [x] Perf benchmarks and guardrails
- [x] Metrics and alerts

Changes are scoped to serving runtime; no API surface changes to customer-facing Redwood API. Rollout: staged canary (5% hosted, select Dedicated pools), followed by incremental ramp to 100% if perf regressions are absent. Rollback is a single-flag flip or re-deploy of previous runtime which immediately disables adaptive controller and watermarking.

Motivation and technical notes:
- The controller computes per-head EMA of dequant multipliers on a per-key basis; when the EMA delta between the cached multiplier and incoming batch > threshold, the controller marks "requant_taken" for the request and emits a compact scale vector.
- The fused kernel applies per-head scale vectors in-register before matmul to avoid extra roundtrip memory writes; for FP8 paths we preserve exponent biasing when re-scaling.
- KV-watermark uses a two-phase background compaction to avoid blocking foreground inference; compaction is incremental and can be throttled by SLO-aware budget.

Benchmarks summary (internal perf lab, T4-like, seq_len distribution skewed to short sequences):
- Baseline (legacy dequant + attn): p50 token latency 6.8ms, p95 13.2ms, throughput 420 tokens/s
- With adaptive requant + watermark (canary config): p50 token latency 5.5ms (-19%), p95 10.8ms (-18%), throughput 485 tokens/s (+15%)
- Memory: average KV shard memory reduced ~8% after watermark compactions; worst-case memory tail improved ~24%.

Observed slight increase in CPU control-plane time (~2%) for the controller bookkeeping.

Risk analysis:
- Incorrect scale estimation could introduce quality regressions; mitigations: extensive evals included, controller defaults conservative EMA alpha and variance gates.
- Compaction during peak load could interfere with SLOs; mitigations: compaction budget and SLO-aware throttling.

Related work: follows design patterns from prior batching improvements (ENG-4327) and kernel vectorization efforts (ENG-3811).
Diego Navarro: Overall design looks good. Please add a scoped benchmark against p99 load to ensure compaction doesn't spike tail latencies.
Aisha Patel: Added p99 bench and SLO-throttling knobs; results in perf harness show negligible p99 regression with default throttling.
Priya Singh: Would like a signal when controller is frequently falling back; please emit a rate metric for fallbacks.
Aisha Patel: Added 'requant_fallback_rate' metric and alert runbook entry.
Evan Chen: Minor nit: kernel uses custom aligned allocator; ensure fallback path still uses standard allocator for portability.
Aisha Patel: Updated kernel to abstract allocator choice behind platform_alloc() helper; added test for fallback path.
QA: Found intermittent CI failure on integration test due to race in compaction; fixed with a lightweight shard mutex and retry backoff.
Performance: Introduces an adaptive requantization pipeline and KV-watermark compaction which together reduce p50 token latency by ~15-20% on INT8/FP8 workloads and improve throughput by ~10-20% in internal benchmarks. Operators: new runtime flags for enabling adaptive requant controller and KV-watermarks; defaults are off for customers not in canary. Backwards compatible: falls back to legacy dequant path when metadata missing or variance exceeds thresholds.
Canary rollout initiated after merge; monitoring dashboards (quant-adaptive) created in Grafana folder 'runtime/quant-adaptive' and alert 'QUANT_REQUANT_FALLBACK_RATE_HIGH' configured.
payload.title: Adaptive requantization pipeline and KV-watermarking for low-latency INT8/FP8 serving

payload.body:
Motivation: Streaming structured outputs that must satisfy grammar/CFG or regex constraints are fragile in two common scenarios: (1) tokenizers that split constraint boundaries across byte/word pieces (BPE, SentencePiece) cause frame breaks and invalid partial outputs during streaming, leading to downstream toolcall parsing failures; (2) combined constraint backends (CFG + regex) produce conflicting accept/reject decisions at stream boundaries when the serializer does eager framing. This PR introduces a "stream sanitizer" layer in the OpenAI-compat and runtime constraint pipeline to make streaming+constraints robust for tool/function-calling and structured output.

What this change does (single-pass summary):
- Adds a serializer+sanitizer component that sits between the constrained-decoder and the streaming encoder. The sanitizer buffers a minimal lookahead window (configurable per model/codec) to ensure emitted frames never split tokenizer atoms required by active constraints.
- Introduces a unified constraint-resolution pass: CFG rules and regex predicates are translated to a shared edge grammar that reports stable/unstable token prefixes rather than binary accept/reject on the fly. This avoids flip-flopping during streaming when partial tokens match multiple alternatives.
- Implements tokenizer-aware boundary heuristics for common tokenizers (gpt-bpe, spm, unigram): the sanitizer uses tokenizer metadata (token byte-length, continuation flags) to prefer emission only at safe split points or to add escape markers when necessary for OpenAI-compat streaming framing.
- Adds a fallback serializer that emits a safe "continuation marker" token sequence (configurable) when lookahead would exceed latency SLOs; consumer-side parsers (OpenAI-compat shim) know how to drop the marker and resume parsing. This reduces tail latency regressions while preserving correctness.
- Wire changes across modules: runtime constraint orchestrator, openai-compat streaming shim, console evens, and SDK streaming clients (TS) include decoder hints so clients can parse streamed structured outputs deterministically.

Why this is different from previous constraint fixes: earlier PRs fixed token-boundary heuristics or improved CFG backends in isolation. This PR focuses on the serialization boundary and the interoperability between grammar/reg-ex constraints and the byte/token framing used for streaming and toolcalls. It is intended to reduce production parsing incidents (see SUP-1337) and improve developer experience for function/tool-calling.

Testing and validation:
- End-to-end regression harness added for 5 representative models (gpt-bpe small/med, spm-legacy, spm-new, unigram) that runs 1200 streaming episodes with combinations of CFG-only, regex-only, and CFG+regex constraints. No parser failures observed in 100k streamed frames; baseline had ~0.8% parse failure for mixed constraints.
- Performance microbenchmarks: median additional latency per request +2.8ms for short responses (<64 tokens) and +0.9ms for long responses (>=512 tokens) with default lookahead=6. Cost/throughput impact measured on ded-cpu and ded-gpu pools; results acceptable for Dedicated customers and opt-in for Hosted.
- Unit tests: sanitizer heuristics, tokenizer metadata mapping, fallback marker round-trip, and OpenAI-compat client parsing updated. Integration tests added to redwood-e2e harness.

Operational notes and rollout:
- Feature gated behind runtime flag "stream_sanitizer_v1" and OpenAI-compat config "sanitize_streaming_frames". Default enabled for dedicated instances and opt-in for hosted.
- Console rollout plan: start with 5% of hosted traffic (non-prod) for 48 hours, track parser error rate and tail latency. See ENG-4821 for rollout checklist.

Backward compatibility: Client SDKs that do not understand the continuation marker will still receive valid text; the marker is chosen to be a rare, non-printing control sequence and sanitized by SDKs. However, the PR adds an opt-in compatibility header that SDKs should include to guarantee correct parsing; older SDKs will fall back to non-sanitized streaming behavior.

Files changed (high level): updated runtime/constraint orchestrator, openai-compat/streaming shim, redwood-sdk-typescript streaming client, e2e tests, docs/structured-output.md.

Merge outcome: squash-merged. Release notes appended.

Asha Patel: Nice design. Two main asks: (1) make lookahead window configurable per-model in addition to global, (2) add a CI job that runs the e2e harness on the smallest dedicated GPU to catch allocation regressions. Please address in follow-up or here.
Miguel Torres: Found a race in the pooled buffer deallocation when an error path triggers early. Suggested using a scoped buffer object. Also asked for more comments explaining the continuation marker contract so infra teams don't misinterpret as an escape sequence. Fixed in commit 7c9b3d0.
Evelyn Kim: Approved after small test additions. Left a nit about doc wording for SDK compat header.
Author reply: addressed Asha's per-model config request (added model_profiles table) and Miguel's buffer race; updated docs per Evelyn's nit.
Structured-output: added streaming sanitizer to prevent tokenizer-boundary and combined-constraint parsing failures. Default gated; opt-in for hosted. Improves tool/function-calling stability under constrained decoders. See docs/structured-output.md for migration steps and SDK updates.
Rollout using feature flag stream_sanitizer_v1; monitor parser_error_rate, stream_frame_retries, and p99 latency. If regressions, toggle off or reduce lookahead per model. See ENG-4821 for rollback steps.
