payload.body:
Context: Customers reported two related classes of failures for streaming API users that (1) received partial structured outputs when the client cancelled mid-toolcall and (2) retried/resumed streams that caused duplicate tool invocations or corrupted JSON blobs. Motivation: make client cancel/reconnect/resume semantics safer for structured output and tool/function calling while preserving low-latency behavior for simple text streams. Goals: (a) preserve toolcall boundary integrity — never invoke or commit a toolcall unless a durable boundary/safepoint is reached, (b) allow resumable progress checkpoints for long-lived streams so clients can resume from the last committed checkpoint without re-invoking tools, (c) provide a small handshake protocol extension for resume idempotency tokens and deadline negotiation so client+server can agree on how much work is durable after reconnects, and (d) maintain OpenAI-compat behavior for basic consumers.

This PR implements a runtime + protocol extension plus SDK glue to support "commit checkpoints" embedded in streaming frames. Checkpoints contain a short id (sha1 of recent output frame boundary), an idempotency token for pending toolcalls, and a monotonic progress cursor. Checkpoints are emitted at safe boundaries (end-of-json-object, end-of-toolcall-output, or configured chunk intervals). On client cancel, the server will: (1) attempt to emit a final checkpoint within the cancel grace window, (2) persist checkpoint metadata to the lease/stream metadata store, and (3) abort any uncommitted toolcalls. On client reconnect, clients present the last-known checkpoint id and resume token; the server reconciles and either resumes generation after the checkpoint or rejects resume if the checkpoint is unknown or expired. To avoid duplicate tool invocations we require toolcall boundary confirmation: tool providers must return a call-commit marker; until that marker is persisted the tool is treated as not-yet-committed and will not be replayed on resume.

Compatibility notes: The change is opt-in at the OpenAI compatibility layer via a new header X-Redwood-Resume: checkpoint-id=<id>;token=<tok>. Existing clients continue working unchanged. The Redwood Python and TypeScript SDKs get helpers to surface checkpointing and a small resume() helper that drives the handshake.

Design checklist:
- [x] Define checkpoint frame structure and schema-fingerprint approach (small, compact, stable)
- [x] Emit checkpoints at JSON/toolcall boundaries and on periodic intervals
- [x] Persist checkpoint metadata in stream lease store for 24h (configurable)
- [x] Require toolcall commit markers before commit; introduce transient toolcall state
- [x] Server-side resume handshake with token validation and deadline negotiation
- [x] SDK helpers (py/ts) + examples in quickstarts repo
- [x] E2E tests covering single-client cancel, reconnect+resume, and forced double-invoke prevention
- [x] Metric instrumentation for checkpoint emission rate, resume success rate, duplicate-invoke attempts

What changed (summary of commits):
- Implement stream checkpoint emitter and serializer in serving/runtime/streaming (checkpoint frames, small serializer)
- Add resume token negotiation endpoint and handshake logic in gateway/proxy
- Add transient toolcall state machine and commit-marker handling in runtime/tooling
- Add persistence glue for checkpoint metadata in lease-store with TTL
- SDK helpers and examples in redwood-sdk-python and redwood-sdk-typescript
- Add integration tests to eval-harness and redwood-quickstarts

Commits:
- "runtime: emit checkpoint frames at safe boundaries (checkpoint id + cursor + token)"
- "gateway: resume handshake endpoint and header parsing (X-Redwood-Resume)"
- "tooling: transient toolcall state and commit marker handling"
- "lease-store: persist checkpoint metadata with configurable ttl"
- "sdk(py/ts): helpers: StreamCheckpoint and Client.resume_from_checkpoint"
- "tests: e2e resume/cancel/duplicate-invoke prevention"

Files changed (high level):
- serving/runtime/streaming/checkpoint.go
- serving/runtime/streaming/checkpoint_serializer.go
- serving/tooling/toolcall_manager.go
- gateway/handlers/resume_handshake.go
- infra/lease_store/checkpoint_persistence.go
- sdk/python/redwood/streaming/checkpoint.py
- sdk/typescript/src/streaming/checkpoint.ts
- tests/integration/test_stream_resume.py
- quickstarts/streaming-resume/README.md

Review conversation (high-level excerpts):
- Ava Morgan (review): "Excellent approach keeping the checkpoint small. One concern: TTL=24h might be surprising for customers — recommend exposing as config per org."
- Author (Diego): "Agreed, exposed as org-level config with infra default 24h; added CLI flag for private deployments."
- Lina Chen (review): "What about streaming latency overhead? Can we guarantee no extra round-trip on hot path?"
- Author: "We only emit checkpoints at existing boundary points or on background intervals; path for plain text streaming unchanged. Added benchmarks showing <1% mean p99 increase in hot paths."
- Marcus Boyd (safety): "Tool commit marker requirement is good. Need audit events for uncommitted tool attempts — added."
- CI bot: "flake8/linters passed, integration tests initially flaky on env; reran and passed."

CI summary: all unit and integration tests passed after second run. Perf bench: micro-benchmark shows 0.6% p99 latency increase for streams with checkpointing enabled; streams without checkpointing unaffected.

Merge outcome: merged via squash. Merge commit message: "streaming: checkpointing + resume handshake to preserve toolcall boundaries and prevent duplicate tool invocations (ENG-1894)".

Operational notes for rollout:
- Default: feature gated off for legacy hosted customers. New API header enables behavior. Gradual rollout plan described in rollout/2026-03-stream-checkpoint-plan.md.
- Add migration docs for customers using custom tool providers (must return commit marker)
- Add console dashboard: checkpoint/resume metrics and duplicate-invoke alarms

Release notes:
- Added optional streaming checkpoints and resume handshake to prevent duplicate tool/function invocations on cancel+resume and to preserve structured output integrity across reconnects. Opt-in via X-Redwood-Resume header or SDK helpers. See quickstarts/streaming-resume for sample usage.

Breaking change: false

payload.body:
Context & motivation: Customers building complex tool-chains reported unpredictable latency and correctness when multiple tool calls run in parallel and mutate the prompt state. Existing 'inject-later' behavior caused nondeterminism when retries or out-of-order returns occurred. This PR adds a lightweight scheduler in the API surface and runtime to 1) allow callers to request a forked invocation context (snapshot of the model context) for parallel tool calls, 2) attach an idempotency_token to enforce at-most-once semantics and dedup retries, and 3) apply backpressure and per-model concurrency limits so heavyweight tools do not saturate a single model instance. Summary of changes: API additions: new optional invocation fields: "fork_context" (boolean), "injection_point" (string: "head"|"tail"|"named"), "idempotency_key" (string), "max_retries" (int, defaults to 2), and "merge_strategy" (string: "sequential"|"prioritized"|"overlay"). OpenAI-compat layer: function-calling signals are preserved; when fork_context is true we emit function_call events from the forked stream and map them back to the original chat in a deterministic way so existing OpenAI-compatible clients keep working. Runtime: new scheduler component that tracks per-model concurrency tokens, a small dedup-store (redis-backed with configurable TTL) for idempotency_key, and a result-merger that applies merge_strategy semantics with deterministic ordering. Reliability: backpressure uses token-bucket semantics with a low-latency fast-path; heavy tool calls can be prioritized or throttled based on new hints in the invocation metadata. Safety: injection points are validated server-side to avoid prompt-jumping attacks. Testing & perf: included unit tests for dedup and merge strategies, integration tests simulating parallel tool latency/partial failures, and a perf canary benchmark showing 18% tail-latency reduction for mixed tool workloads. Migration notes & compatibility: defaults preserve previous behavior when fork_context omitted; existing clients continue to work. For customers who rely on current nondeterministic injection ordering, opt-in to merge_strategy is required to get deterministic merging. Implementation notes: added scheduler at runtime/scheduler/*, idempotency store in runtime/dedup/*, API adapters in api/handlers/tool_invocation.go, OpenAI-compat mapping in api/adapters/compat_openai.go. CI & validation: initial CI run had lint and flaky integration failures which were fixed by retry hooks and an additional wait-for-service fixture. See commits below for incremental steps.
Introduces a tool-call scheduler with forked context support, idempotency tokens, and deterministic result injection. Adds new API fields for tool invocation ergonomics and improves stability under parallel tool workloads.
Evan Park (2024-09-19): Nice overall shape. Please add more unit tests around the overlay merge_strategy edge cases where keys collide.
Marika Chen (2024-09-20): Addressed and added tests for key collisions in test_merger_overlay_edgecases. Also added comments about deterministic ordering.
Sofia Ruiz (2024-09-22): Two nits: 1) validate idempotency_key length server-side, 2) document behavior when dedup store is unavailable. Please add both.
Marika Chen (2024-09-23): Added validation to api/handlers and a graceful-fallback path; documented fallback in docs/api/tool-invocation.md. Marking ready for re-review.
Kunal Mehta (2024-09-28): Integration flake repro steps look good. One concern about memory usage of snapshots under high concurrency; recommend an LRU window on snapshot store.
Marika Chen (2024-09-29): Implemented LRU eviction and added a metric (scheduler.snapshot_evictions) and a config knob (snapshot_store.max_entries).

payload.body:
Add a new Capacity Hedge Broker that centralizes decisions about how committed (reserved) capacity and opportunistic spare capacity are distributed across tenants. This broker enables proportional backfilling of idle slots while preserving per-tenant throughput guarantees and a bounded latency safety budget. Motivation: we've seen bursty tenancy cause long-tail latencies when opportunistic backfill aggressively preempts low-priority reservations. The broker implements (1) an occupancy partition model to split pool capacity into guaranteed, hedge, and opportunistic partitions, (2) proportional backfill logic that apportions opportunistic capacity by committed share plus recent utilization footprint, and (3) a soft-demotion penalty/decay so repeated preemption of a tenant reduces its opportunistic weight temporarily. This change touches the allocator, autoscaler decision path, and telemetry plumbing. It also adds unit and integration tests for backfill fairness and a small migration that initializes per-tenant hedge credits for existing reservations. The description below summarizes commits, files changed, review conversation, CI status, and merge details.
Introduce Capacity Hedge Broker (feature-flagged) to enable proportional backfilling and improved fairness; adds telemetry metrics for occupancy partition and backfill fairness. No customer-facing API changes. Rollout gating required: enable feature flag and run migration to seed hedge credits.
Run migrations/20260201_seed_hedge_credits.sql against control plane DB during maintenance window; enable feature-flag 'capacity_hedge_broker' in a canary region; monitor backfill_fairness_index and per-tenant latency percentile metrics before full roll-out.
1) Merge behind feature flag. 2) Run migration to seed hedge credits. 3) Canary-enable in us-west-2 for 48 hours. 4) Promote to remaining regions with automated health checks. 5) If fairness index regresses by >5% or 99th latency increases >10ms, rollback feature flag.
Risk: premature preemption could impact tail latency for critical tenants. Mitigation: broker enforces a locked latency safety budget per-tenant and uses a decay period for demotion weights; rollback via feature flag and migration can be reversed (credits are additive).
Benchmarks in lab show median throughput unchanged, opportunistic utilization increased by ~8% on low-util clusters, and 99th-percentile latency improved for best-effort tenants due to fewer repeated preemptions. See test matrix reference in PR comments.
Reviewers requested config-driven partitions, additional fairness tests, and telemetry tagging; author addressed all points. Performance signals in staging were positive. The PR was approved and merged via squash.
Diego Rivera (reviewer): Nice separation of concerns. Two asks: 1) can we simplify the occupancy partition constants as configurable knobs in config.yaml instead of hardcoded values? 2) please add a test simulating rapid repeated preemptions to validate the decay behavior.
Lina Park (author): Responding - moved partition constants to config and added decay_simulation_test in tests/integration. The test includes a ramped preemption pattern and asserts demotion weight never drops below configured floor.
Maya Chen (reviewer): Telemetry looks good but please add per-tenant tags to hedge_credit_gauge to allow filtering by organization. Also request an alert on unexpected negative hedge_credit deltas.
Lina Park (author): Added tenant_id tag to hedge_credit_gauge and a simple alert rule in ops/alerts.yaml recommending threshold-based alerting on negative deltas exceeding 5% of total credits.
Owen Blake (approver): Approving after the above fixes. Verified stage run and canary results. :thumbsup:
CI Bot: All checks green. Integration matrix completed on linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. e2e staging run green.
SRE should monitor metrics: telemetry.occupancy_partition.{guaranteed,hedge,opportunistic}, telemetry.backfill_fairness_index, telemetry.hedge_credit_gauge (per-tenant), allocator.preempt_events, and per-tenant p95/p99 latency. Default decay window is 10 minutes and can be tuned via config. If rollout shows increased eviction churn, flip feature flag off and notify infra oncall.
payload.title: Introduce Capacity Hedge Broker and Proportional Backfill Prioritizer

payload.body:
Motivation: Multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads suffer intermittent stalls when small, frequent sharded exchanges (AllToAll/Reduce) contend on NCCL progress and stream ownership. Prior fixes focused on batching or changing communicator scopes but did not address steady-state micro-stalls caused by repeated collective handoffs and kernel preemption. This PR implements a strided alltoall handoff primitive alongside a persistent-collective scheduler that pins short collective phases to dedicated CUDA streams and staggers their invocation windows to reduce NCCL reinitialization and cross-stream synchronization hotspots.

Design summary: - Introduced 'StridedAllToAll' which aggregates many small tensor slices into stride-aware segments before submitting a single NCCL alltoall operation when contiguous GPU peer layout allows it. This reduces NCCL invocation count while preserving latency for large slices. - Added a PersistentCollectiveScheduler that keeps a pool of long-lived CUDA streams and NCCL communicators per tensor-parallel group. Scheduler uses a lightweight token-based handoff to queue collective windows and enforces non-overlapping kickoffs for groups that previously collided. - KV cache integration: when serving with KV sharding, the scheduler coalesces KV fetches into the same strided segments when access locality is detected, enabling combined comm+KV windows. A small heuristics engine decides when to fall back to the prior path to avoid increased latency for skewed access patterns. - Backward compatible: default is opt-in via runtime config flags (runtime.experimental.strided_alltoall and runtime.scheduler.persistent_collectives). We keep previous scheduler as a fallback.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc referenced in PR body - [x] Unit tests for scheduler queueing and token handoff - [x] Microbenchmarks across 4xA100 and 8xA100 clusters - [x] KV cache interplay tests with synthetic access skew - [x] CI green and stress-run locally

Commits (high-level): - a1c9b6f Add StridedAllToAll primitive and unit tests - 7b4f2d3 PersistentCollectiveScheduler implementation and stream pool - e95d2b1 KV coalescing hooks and heuristics engine - 3f2b8a0 Integrate flags and runtime config parsing - 5c1d0ff Docs and quickstart for toggling during rollout

Files changed (high level): - rts/collectives/strided_alltoall.cpp/h - rts/scheduler/persistent_collective_scheduler.cpp/h - rts/kv/kv_coalesce.h - rts/config/runtime_flags.cpp - tests/collectives/strided_alltoall_test.cc - tests/scheduler/persistent_scheduler_smoke.cc - docs/rts/collectives.md - examples/bench/strided_alltoall_bench.py

Benchmark summary: - Baseline: 8xA100 TP=32, steady-state throughput 1200 tokens/s, 99th percentile token latency 58ms (small slice workload). - With StridedAllToAll + Persistent Scheduler: throughput increased to 1450 tokens/s (+20.8%), 99th percentile latency improved to 42ms (-27.6%), observed NCCL launch count reduced ~58% for the sampled timeframe. - KV-coalesced serving traces showed up to 18% additional reduction in p99 for mixed locality prompts. - Microbench stress tests (24-hour soak) show <0.1% increase in rare ordering regressions that are mitigated by a subsequent fallback path (enabled automatically under detected stalling).

Testing and CI: - CI: linux-build (pass), unit-tests (pass), integration-gpu (flaky -> rerun -> pass), lint (pass). - Added GPU-integration gating: a new job 'gpu-persistent-collectives' runs benchmarks on our perf-lab A100 pool during PR gating (was green).

Review thread (summary): - Michael Chen (reviewer): flagged potential deadlock if a scheduler token is lost during preemption; requested TTL and watchdog for tokens. - Author (Aisha): added a watchdog and re-queue path; added unit test to simulate scheduler preemption. - Sofia Martinez (reviewer): requested clearer metrics emitted for NCCL invocation rate; added telemetry counters (ncc_invoke_count, strided_merge_ops, scheduler_queue_depth). - Daniel Park (reviewer): suggested lowering default opt-in risk by shipping feature flags; PR implements flags and docs. - Security review (Ravi Patel): no new surface area; KV coalescing respects tenant boundaries and does not change key access privileges.

Risks and mitigations: - Risk: New scheduler may hide regressions that only appear under >32k token workloads. Mitigation: feature rolled out using canary gate in Redwood Console, with automatic rollback if token latency increases >10% across canary. - Risk: Interaction with third-party NCCL wrappers. Mitigation: compatibility pings and fallbacks to legacy communicator mode if handshake fails.

Release notes: - Add opt-in strided all-to-all aggregation and persistent collective scheduler to reduce NCCL invocation count and p99 latency for multi-GPU tensor-parallel serving. Configuration flags and runtime telemetry added.

Merge notes: Squash-merged into main after final CI gate and bench verification.

payload.body:
Motivation: teams keep re-implementing small credential handoffs and patterny async-iterable helpers across SDKs. This PR introduces a lightweight credential bridge (a small, zero-dependency runtime shim) plus a compact set of async pullstream helpers intended to be re-used by Python/TS/Go SDKs. Goals: 1) Reduce duplicated glue inside each SDK; 2) Provide a single, well-tested primitive for credential rotation + graceful stream restart; 3) Surface ergonomic helpers for common consumer patterns (buffered iteration, drain-with-timeout, checkpointing cursors). What this PR delivers (single-line list): - cred/bridge: portable credential exchange interface + in-memory lease cache - stream/pull: async pullstream helpers (prefetcher, checkpoint cursor, drainWithDeadline) - sdk-adapters: small adapters used by TS/Python SDKs (no runtime deps) - tests: focused unit tests and cross-language integration harnesses - docs: migration note + README with usage examples Checklist: - [x] interface design and tests - [x] local cross-sdk harness run (python, ts) - [x] API stability review with platform - [x] performance microbenchmarks and allocation profile - [x] doc snippets and migration guide Compatibility notes: no breaking API changes in public SDKs; SDK repos will adopt the bridge via small adapter PRs (follow-ups listed below). See linked Linear items for rollout plan and telemetry.

Added a repo-wide dependency-guard presubmit job and consolidated language lint/test scripts into tooling/scripts for consistent CI behavior. No runtime changes. Improves CI hygiene and reduces duplicated scripts.
Motivation: Over time we accumulated ad-hoc lint/test shell scripts across packages and multiple slightly-different GH Action job definitions. This made it hard to keep presubmit checks consistent and complicated adding a single dependency audit step across the mono-repo. This PR centralizes lint/test invocations into tooling/scripts (single entrypoints for node/python/go), removes duplicated GH Action fragments, and adds a dependency-guard presubmit workflow that performs license/dep-variance checks and blocks merges on suspicious changes.

What I changed: - Added tooling/scripts/{node,python,go}-check.sh wrapper scripts that normalize env, node/python versions, and exit codes. - Replaced in-repo ad-hoc npm/yarn calls with npm run tooling:check (node) or python -m tooling.check (python) where applicable. - Introduced .github/workflows/dependency-guard.yml: a lightweight presubmit job that runs dependency-guard (open-source wrapper with in-repo allowlist) plus a periodic audit schedule. - Consolidated existing lint/test GH Action fragments into .github/actions/standard-checks (composite action) and updated workflows to call it. - Removed duplicate scripts and updated README/tooling docs. - Small cleanup: fixed mismatched eslint configs, aligned jest thresholds, and added an ignore whitelist for legacy third-party transitive deps.

Rollout plan: Merge to main, watch the presubmit job for 48 hours; non-blocking periodic audit runs will surface transitive changes. Any blocked PRs can request the allowlist update via SUP-89.

Testing: Ran full suite on remote runner, fixed three flaky tests surfaced by standardized env. Dependency-guard was run against a historical baseline and the allowlist recorded in tooling/dep-allowlist.json.

Notes: This is intentionally conservative — dependency-guard is configured to block only high-severity or license violations by default; team can opt-in to stricter mode later. The composite action is lightweight to keep matrix times low.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Continuous-batching at high concurrency must balance per-request latency SLOs and batch efficiency. Previous batching relied on static coalesce windows and best-effort KV cache locality which led to intermittent p99 regressions under skewed KV access patterns. This PR implements a deadline-aware coalescing scheduler that adapts coalesce windows per-queue based on observed deadline pressure and explicitly preserves KV-cache affinity to avoid degrading the KV hit rate during aggressive coalescing.

Design summary: single-string overview of the approach so it appears as one continuous description. The scheduler introduces three cooperating mechanisms: (1) per-deadline micro-queues: requests are bucketed by remaining time-to-deadline into tight (<5ms), medium (5-25ms), and relaxed (>25ms) lanes to limit cross-impact slowdowns; (2) adaptive coalesce windows: each lane measures recent batching benefit (avg tokens/batch, head-of-line delay) and grows/shrinks its coalesce window using an additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease rule to chase throughput without violating SLOs; (3) KV-affinity preservation: each incoming request annotates the KV-keys it will access (best-effort) and the scheduler will attempt to coalesce requests that touch overlapping key sets into the same batch or hold back non-overlapping requests that would evict hot KV entries. We added soft pin reservations and a short-lived "affinity token" that biases batch composition without hard starvation.

Implementation notes: changes touch scheduler core (scheduler/coalesce.go), KV cache manager (kv/cache_affinity.go), metrics (observability/batching_metrics.prom), and e2e harness (bench/e2e_coalesce_test.go). The adaptive window uses a lightweight ring buffer estimator to track per-lane batch efficiency and a recent-deadline counter to trigger immediate flushes when a lane approaches SLO violation. KV-affinity is implemented as a compact bloom-filter hint per request (opaque to callers) to keep overhead minimal. We added unit tests for the ring estimator and integration tests that simulate heavy KV-skew and mixed workload latencies.

Benchmarks: microbench on a 8xA100 cluster with synthetic chat workload (80% short-turn, 20% long-turn) and KV-skew (top-20 keys hot): compared to main at time of PR the changes show: median latency +2% (tradeoff for throughput), p95 -8%, p99 -12%, sustained throughput +11% when coalescing windows adapt; KV hit-rate +6 percentage points in hot-key scenarios, which explains the tail latency improvement. Under uniform key access there is no regression in KV hit-rate.

Testing and CI: local unit test coverage added for estimator and KV hints. Integration bench harness included as a fast smoke test in CI; full cluster perf runs were done offline and results archived in the PR thread (link to internal benchmark page). CI initially failed on a race in the affinity token lifetime; fixed by moving token cleanup to the scheduler event loop and adding a deterministic clock in tests. Final CI status: pass.

Rollout and safety: feature gated behind a runtime flag (env REDWOOD_COALESCE_V2) and default-off for Dedicated customers until canary confirms improvements. Automatic fallback: when the adaptive window detects sustained SLO violations for a lane, it disables coalescing for that lane for a cooldown period. We also added tracing spans for diagnostics: scheduler.coalesce.window and scheduler.kv.affinity.

Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (ENG-9481) - [x] unit tests - [x] integration bench harness - [x] docs: console metrics added - [x] gated rollout flag - [x] changelog entry prepared

Related work: builds on ENG-8622 continuous-batching refactor and references prior fairness work but focuses on deadline-sensitive coalescing and KV-preservation rather than queue-prioritization.

Merge notes: squash merge. See commits summary below and the merge commit for attribution.
Improves tail latency and throughput by introducing deadline-aware coalescing windows; preserves KV cache hotness to avoid eviction-induced penalty. No API changes.
Arjun Patel: Overall nice approach. Please justify the bloom-filter false positive rate and cost in the design comments.
Maya Thompson: Reply: picked 1% target FP rate; added cost note and microbench showing <0.5% throughput overhead in the description.
Lena Ortiz: Left a few nits in coalesce_test.go about deterministic sleeps; prefer fake clock everywhere.
Maya Thompson: Addressed by replacing sleeps with fake clock; pushed fix in f1a6d33.
Samir Gupta: Approve after CI green; suggest we add a dashboard tile for per-lane missed-deadline counts in a follow-up.
Samir Gupta: Approved
payload.title: deadline-aware-coalescer: adaptive coalescing windows with KV-affinity preservation

Reduce CI runtime by ~35% by collapsing redundant matrix entries, batch similar unit/test jobs, and bump GH Actions and test-related deps. No behavior changes to runtime; tooling-only.
Summary: This PR reduces total CI runtime and maintenance surface by simplifying the GitHub Actions matrices, consolidating several nearly-identical jobs into grouped/parameterized steps, and updating a small set of Actions and test dependencies (actions/checkout, setup-go, node-version action, pytest and mocha dev deps).

Motivation: CI has been drifting toward long pipeline times because similar jobs were duplicated across multiple matrices (linux/python, linux/node, macos) and some jobs run end-to-end integration flows unnecessarily for lint-only changes. The infra team investigated and found typical pipeline wall-clock was ~42m; after these changes it's ~27m on average, with fewer queued runners and lower cost on self-hosted pools.

Changes included:
- Replace three per-OS, per-python-version matrices with a single cross-axis that only expands where tests actually vary (unit matrix now only varies python-version for packages that require it).
- Create a 'lint-and-fast-checks' composite step that runs once per push instead of per-matrix job.
- Collapse multiple unrelated e2e shims into a single parameterized job that accepts a 'profile' env var (smoke|full). Smoke runs by default; full runs are only triggered for nightly/release branches.
- Bump GH Actions versions: actions/checkout@v4 -> v4 (minor pinning), actions/setup-node pinned to v4.2.0, setup-go bumped to v4.3.1.
- Update test/dev deps where safe: pytest 7.x -> 7.3.x, pytest-cov bump, mocha 10.x -> 10.1.x; ran local test matrix to validate no behavioral regressions.
- Added repository-level caching for pip and npm artifacts using keyed caches to improve warm-run times.

Checklist:
- [x] Preserve test coverage and results for all affected jobs (unit, integration smoke, lint)
- [x] Verify PR builds on forks and main CI (self-hosted runners)
- [x] Document matrix changes in .github/ci/README.md
- [x] Run canary on release branch to ensure nightly full e2e still works

Motivation note: This is a toolchain/ops change only; no runtime code changes to the inference serving or API layers.

Commits (summary):
- refactor(ci): consolidate ci matrices and add composite lint step
- feat(ci): parameterized e2e job with smoke/full profiles
- chore(deps): bump actions/setup-node, setup-go, actions/cache keys
- chore(dev-deps): bump pytest/mocha minor versions and update lockfiles
- docs(ci): add CI README describing matrix decisions

Files touched (high-level):
- .github/workflows/ci.yml (matrix simplification, composite step references)
- .github/workflows/release.yml (ensure 'full' profile triggers on release)
- .github/workflows/nightly-e2e.yml (now uses parameterized job)
- .github/ci/README.md (new)
- scripts/ci/run_e2e.sh (parameterization and guard rails)
- tools/ci/cache-helpers.sh (cache key helpers)
- requirements-dev.txt, package.json (dev deps bumps)
- .github/actions/composite-lint/action.yml (new composite action wrapper)

Review conversation (high level):
- Evan Martinez: "Good reduction in job duplication. One request: make the lint composite opt-out for forks to avoid secrets leakage risk." -> Author reply: "Added skip-for-forks guard using github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork check; composite will run but skips steps that require secrets."
- Priya Nair: "Can we add a short README section explaining the 'smoke' vs 'full' triggers?" -> Author reply: "Done, added .github/ci/README.md with decision matrix and example triggers."
- Marco Rossi: "Observed a flaky integration that failed first CI run; was that caused by cache key change?" -> Author reply: "Tracked to a timing-dependent test (test_harness::wait_for_worker). I added a 50ms jitter in the smoke harness and marked the full integration to run on nightly; caches were rolled back for that job."

CI observations: First CI run failed one matrix entry (integration full) due to a flaky wait; reran single job and passed. Subsequent CI run on the PR passed all checks.

Performance: Measured median reduction ~35% wall-clock in CI, job-count reduced from 18 to 12 per push.

Rollout/Merge notes: Merged via squash to main after approvals from reviewers and green CI. No follow-up migrations required. If any repo in the monorepo experiences a new test failure that looks related, revert commit 3f7d9c2 (cache-key tweak) and open a follow-up to relax cache keying for that package.

Linear/Jira: ENG-4021 tracks the CI runtime reduction initiative; ENG-4039 tracks follow-ups to add more targeted cache keys and to roll the composite action into other repos.

Motivation: Customers running Dedicated pools asked for smoother capacity rebalancing when tenants change committed throughput and for a safe, observable path to drain nodes out of a fleet without disrupting tenant SLAs. This PR introduces a tenant-level shaping layer that (1) smooths abrupt throughput reductions, (2) packs tenants more efficiently across GPUs, and (3) adds a graceful decommissioning protocol (drain-probe + staged eviction) that maintains per-tenant throughput guarantees during node drain.

Design summary: The tenant shaper sits in the request router and enforces a short horizon rate profile per tenant derived from committed throughput, observed burst allowance, and recent token usage. It exposes a per-tenant 'shape window' that controls the steady-state token dispatch rate and a temporary 'elastic headroom' that can be borrowed/repaid. When a node is scheduled for decommission, a drain-probe step probes actual tail-latency and queue-utilization; if safe, the controller triggers staged cross-tenant placement moves with a backoff so SLOs degrade minimally.

What changed (high-level):
- Add router/tenant_shaper service with smoothing algorithm, borrowing accounting, and eviction hints.
- Controller flow: drain-probe -> placement plan -> staged-migrate + replicate-fallback.
- Scheduler updates: new allocation scorer that prefers packing affinity but respects tenant throughput SLOs.
- New Prometheus metrics and tracing spans for shaping decisions, probe outcomes, and migration progress.
- E2E and unit tests for borrowing/repayment, drain-probe gating, and metric rollup.

Compatibility and rollout: The default shaper is OFF for existing customers. A feature flag per-tenant enables it; rollout will start with internal Dedicated fleets and then opt-in customers. The drain protocol is backward-compatible: nodes without the controller will still be drainable via existing decommission paths.

Telemetry and alerting: Introduces tenant_shaper_effective_rate, tenant_shaper_borrowed_tokens, drain_probe_success, staged_migration_progress. Alerts suggested in release_notes.

Checklist:
- [x] Implementation and unit tests
- [x] Integration tests with small dedicated cluster harness
- [x] Observability: metrics + tracing
- [x] rollout feature flag + migration plan
- [x] Docs PR (separate) linked

Related: ENG-4821 implements the shaping algorithm; SUP-1219 is the customer support case that motivated staged migration.

Notes on behaviour and limits: Borrowed headroom is bounded to a tenant-configured percentage of committed throughput and is repaid within a configured window (default 10m). The shaping window defaults to 30s smoothing with exponential backoff for rapid spikes. The staged-migrate plan attempts to move one tenant at a time per affected node to avoid cascading bursts.

Testing notes: Ran the bench-harness with 3 workloads: interactive chat (low qps, bursty), embedding batch (steady high throughput), and mixed multi-tenant load. Observed 12-18% better packing efficiency vs baseline with no increase in 99th percentile latency during drains when shaper is enabled and tuned.

Rafael Ortiz: Overall this looks good — two requested changes: make the default borrow window configurable via CLI and add an integration smoke in the canary job.
Maya Chen: Thanks Rafael — added CLI flag and wired a quick smoke in canary harness. See commit f4e5d6a.
Priya Kapoor: The staged-migration backoff constants look conservative; can we make them adaptive based on current cluster utilization?
Maya Chen: Good point. I added a simple utilization multiplier (scheduler will multiply base backoff by 1 + util*0.5). We can iterate on this metric in a follow-up if needed.
Samir Patel: CI flake on windows build unrelated to this change (quota-test). Re-running checks.
CI Bot: All checks passed after re-run. Integration harness reported no regressions.
Added tenant-level shaping for smoother capacity changes, a graceful drain protocol (drain-probe + staged migration), new metrics for shaping and decommissioning, and a per-tenant feature flag to opt in. Recommended alerts: tenant_shaper_borrowed_tokens > 0 for >15m (investigate misconfig), drain_probe_failure rate > 5% over 10m.

Motivation: multiple customers reported edge cases where SDK token refreshers and secondary credential providers competed during fast stream reconnects, causing transient 401s and slow recovery. This PR introduces a lightweight, policy-driven credential failover mesh plus an async iterator pool for streaming SDKs (Python/TS/Go) to improve recovery determinism and consumer ergonomics.

What this PR does (single-line continuous description with sections): Adds a pluggable credential failover mesh that coordinates primary/secondary credential sources, a compact Retry/Circuit plugin to avoid thundering refresh storms, and an async iterator pool to reduce per-stream allocation and make backpressure handling consistent across SDKs; bumps Python, TypeScript, and Go SDK versions; updates docs and changelogs.

Key design points: the failover mesh is opt-in, configured via the SDK config object (failover_policy: prefer_primary|cascading|parallel_probe), exposes a simple lifecycle hook (onCredentialSwap) for observability, and ships with a safe default policy (cascading with jittered probe). The Retry/Circuit plugin is pluggable — customers can supply custom backoff windows or use the shipped adaptive preset. The iterator pool centralizes chunk buffering and allows iterative consumers to return handles for reuse, reducing GC pressure and smoothing memory spikes on high-concurrency streaming workloads.

Checklist: - [x] Implement mesh core (go/py/ts) - [x] Retry/Circuit plugin and presets - [x] Async iterator pool implementations for each SDK - [x] Cross-SDK integration tests (auth flakiness scenarios) - [x] Benchmarks for streaming memory/latency - [x] Docs + migration guide - [x] Version bumps and packaging

Compatibility & migration notes: Default behavior is backward-compatible. Existing code paths remain untouched unless users opt into the failover mesh or enable the iterator pool (config flags: enable_failover_mesh, enable_iterator_pool). The adaptive Retry preset is conservative; teams using custom retry profiles should validate in staging. Python: bump to 2.11.0 (minor API addition: SDKConfig.failover_policy, iterator_pool_size). TypeScript: bump to 1.14.0 (same API surface). Go: bump to v0.10.2 (constructor options added).

Files changed (high level): sdk/python/redwood/auth/failover_mesh.py (new), sdk/python/redwood/stream/iterator_pool.py (new), sdk/python/setup.py (version bump), sdk/ts/src/credential/mesh.ts (new), sdk/ts/src/stream/pool.ts (new), sdk/ts/package.json (version bump), sdk/go/cred/mesh.go (new), sdk/go/stream/pool.go (new), docs/sdks/failover-mesh.md (new), examples/streaming/failover-demo (new example), tests/integration/auth_replay (new scenarios), CI pipeline updates (.github/workflows/sdk-ci.yml).

Why not reuse previous session/lease shims: earlier session lease implementations were heavyweight and introduced new lifecycle semantics. The mesh is intentionally lightweight: it acts as an orchestrator for credential sources and retry policies rather than imposing a session store. This minimizes integration work for customers who only want safer refresh semantics.

Security & observability: mesh events emit non-sensitive telemetry via onCredentialSwap and onProbe (user-visible), and all network requests still pass through existing sanitized logging and KMS layers. We added unit tests to validate that credentials are never logged.

Related tickets: Linear ENG-2783, ENG-2790, and ENG-2815. Support follows SUP-2043 for a customer incident that motivated this work.

feat(stream): introduce async iterator pool and reusable chunk handles
refactor(sdk): extract retry/circuit plugin interface and presets

payload.body:
Context: In production workloads with long chat histories the KV cache dominates transient GPU workspace allocations and forces arena growth during batching spikes. Motivation: Reduce peak GPU footprint while preserving latency SLOs and steady-state throughput. Summary: Introduces a KV-prefetch hotset buffer and a sparse scratch allocator to avoid inflating the global arena during continuous batching. The hotset prefetcher tracks request-level KV hotness and pre-populates a compact per-device hotset capable of serving the majority of cache hits without expanding the scratch arena. The sparse scratch allocator exposes a lightweight free-list for short-lived activation fragments and returns large contiguous ranges back to the arena quickly, reducing fragmentation. Key changes: 1) runtime/kv: prefetch_hotset component with heuristics for prefix/predictive prefetch and bounded memory cap. 2) runtime/allocator: sparse_scratch_allocator that coexists with existing arena and supports deferred materialization for checkpointed activations. 3) scheduler: integrate prefetch decisions into continuous_batcher so requests in the same batch can share prefetched KV and avoid duplicate allocations. 4) observability: new metrics for kv_hotset_hit_ratio, scratch_frag_pct, and prefetch_evictions, plus a dashboard. Results: in internal LLaMA-2-13B quantized chat trace we saw peak GPU RSS drop ~18% (24.6GB -> 20.1GB), 95th latency unchanged within noise, throughput +3% under steady batching, and per-token cost reduction ~12%. Compatibility: falls back to existing arena+kv behavior when hotset cap is exceeded or prefetch disabled. Rollout: feature-flagged, opt-in per-customer; staged rollout with smoke tests and perf canary on dedicated pools. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] integration tests, [x] perf regression run, [x] docs, [x] observability. Related: ENG-863 describes requirements for KV costing and ENG-874 is follow-up for multi-GPU hotset federated eviction.
Ethan Park (2025-11-03): Nice decomposition. Two asks: add a stress test for prefetch backpressure and make hotset cap an explicit config parameter at runtime. Maya: added cap flag and stress test in continuous_batcher_test.cc (see commits).
Luca Moretti (2025-11-05): How does this interact with activation checkpointing and deferred materialization? Suggest adding a note in allocator to avoid double-free of deferred fragments. Maya: added guard and unit test covering checkpointed activations.
Aisha Rahman (2025-11-07): Observability looks good. Can we emit a synthetic prefetch in the perf harness to detect regressions? Maya: added benchmark variant that toggles prefetch and records hit ratio.
Merged via squash on 2025-11-10 by Aisha Rahman. Merge commit message: "kv-prefetch-aware-batching + sparse scratch allocator: reduce peak GPU memory and stabilize arena growth. Closes ENG-863."
Introduce KV prefetch hotset and sparse scratch allocator. Peak GPU memory reduced ~18% on targeted workloads. Feature is behind runtime feature flag 'kv_prefetch_hotset' and can be toggled per-deployment. No breaking changes expected; falls back to previous behavior when disabled.
Peak GPU RSS: -18% (24.6GB -> 20.1GB)
Steady-state throughput: +3%
P50 latency: +1% (within noise)
Per-token cost: -12% (measured on quantized LLaMA-2-13B trace)
Unit tests added for allocator and hotset eviction. Integration tests exercise prefetch across batch boundaries. Perf harness includes a regression profile comparing baseline vs prefetched runs. Benchmarks executed on dedicated gpu-canary pool; canary passed.
Risk: prefetch may increase memory if mis-tuned. Mitigation: hard cap config and auto-disable when prefetch_evictions spike.
Risk: interaction with multi-GPU kv sharding may cause duplicate prefetches. Mitigation: guarded sync path and eviction tokens to de-duplicate.
Risk: allocator fragmentation regressions. Mitigation: allocator exposes diagnostic metrics and fast fallback to global arena.
Feature is behind 'kv_prefetch_hotset' flag. Stage 1: internal canary on dedicated pool (5 servers) for 48h. Stage 2: opt-in customer beta with contractual workloads. Stage 3: gradual enable on non-sensitive hosted traffic with traffic steering and perf alarms. Full rollout requires KPI: kv_hotset_hit_ratio>0.6 and no latency SLO violations for 24h.

payload.body:
Motivation: private deployments require deterministic, auditable release artifacts and easy rollback semantics for on-prem/VPC installs. Existing release artifacts were ad-hoc: signed tarballs and a single index.json. That made reconciling upgrades with operator Terraform state awkward and increased risk during emergency rollbacks. This PR introduces a manifest orchestrator that (1) emits reproducible, content-addressed release manifests (build-trace bundles) combining artifact checksums, build metadata, dependency pins, and optional SBOM links, (2) produces an automated rollback bundle that includes a Terraform state snapshot reference and Helm chart patch diffs, and (3) wires these bundles into the CI/CD pipeline so every private-installer release includes a machine-readable rollback manifest alongside the signed artifacts. What changed: new tooling in /ci/release-orchestrator that generates a build-trace file per release (build-trace-{sha}.jsonl.gz), a delta-rollback bundle under releases/{version}/rollback.tar.gz and a canonical content-addressable index (cas-index.json) used by the installer and upgrade tool. The orchestrator integrates with the existing signing step (sigstore/cosign) and the artifact registry: after artifacts are built, ci/release-orchestrator computes canonical tarball digests (strip timestamps, normalize owner/mode), collects build metadata (builder image, git commit, build environment), queries Helm to produce a diff patch from target to previous release, snapshots terraform plan output and stores a short-lived snapshot pointer in the release metadata. The CI pipeline changes (github/workflows/release-orchestrator.yml) run the orchestrator in a gated job after image build and before publishing to the release bucket. The installer (private-installer/installer) now consumes cas-index.json to resolve artifacts by digest and validates the build-trace signature at deploy time when running with --verify-release. Rollback UX: operators can download releases/{version}/rollback.tar.gz which contains: helm-chart-patch.diff, terraform-state-snapshot-pointer, and a pre-signed rollback manifest that the installer understands. Motivation: Several customers and internal evals showed inconsistent behavior when the OpenAI-compat layer returned tool selection signals (e.g. 'tool_choice' with ambiguous metadata) across streaming and non-streaming modes. This caused duplicate tool invocations, incorrect schema inference, and brittle downstream tool routers in Redwood Dedicated/Private deployments.

This PR introduces a deterministic normalization step for the OpenAI invocation envelope, plus stream-resilient framing for tool/message fragments. The goal is to: 1) make the compatibility layer emit a single canonical selection signal for every invocation, 2) map OpenAI tool schemas into a stable internal schema with minimal changes for existing customers, and 3) make streaming fragments idempotent and re-assemblable at the service edge.

What changed (high level):
- New package: pkg/openai/normalize_invocation.go — normalizer that transforms incoming OpenAI-style responses into Redwood's canonical InvocationEnvelope. It collapses multiple tool signals into one selected_tool hint and preserves tool confidence/metadata in a stable metadata map.
- Tool schema mapper: pkg/tooling/tool_schema_mapper.go — conservative mapping rules for OpenAI 'parameters' -> Redwood typed schema, including type coercion rules and a small whitelist for nested objects.
- Streaming: server/streaming/frame_parser.go updated to add fragment IDs and checksum headers for tool/message fragments. Parser now supports out-of-order fragments and dedup by fragment id+checksum.
- API layer: server/api/openai_adapter.go updated to call the normalizer before routing to tool routing pipeline; updates to response shape sent back to clients to maintain OpenAI wire-compatibility while ensuring a single 'selected_tool' semantic in the internal router.
- Docs: docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md with migration notes and examples.

Compatibility notes:
- Outbound API responses remain OpenAI-compatible: we do not change the visible OpenAI fields returned to customers. Internally, however, the runtime will prefer the normalized 'selected_tool' hint to decide which tool to invoke. In the rare case of conflicting tool signals, the normalizer uses (in order): explicit_invocation field, highest-confidence tool_choice, then deterministic fallback to first available tool that matches schema.
- Customers who implemented custom tool routers based on raw tool_choice fragments should migrate to using the new normalized hint or consult the docs which show a 1-line change to switch to the normalized envelope.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit tests for mapping rules and type coercions included.
- Integration tests: simulated streaming sessions with fragmented tool metadata; verified idempotent assembler under network reorders.
- Canary rollout: staged to 10% of traffic for hosted API for 48 hours, then to Dedicated nodes behind a feature flag. Private installer includes an opt-in toggle for the first release cycle.

Migration steps for operators (short):
1) Review docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for the mapping table.
2) If you have custom routers, update to read the normalized 'selected_tool' header from the invocation payload.
3) Toggle feature flag if running Redwood Private/Dedicated during rollout.

Related work: links to internal Linear tasks ENG-7421 (tool-selection ambiguity), ENG-7553 (stream-fragment dedup).

Rationale for not changing public wire format: minimize breaking client changes while fixing internal flakiness in tool invocation semantics.

Release notes summary: Normalizes OpenAI invocation envelopes to ensure a single canonical tool-selection signal, improves streaming fragment resilience, and provides safe mapping rules for tool parameter schemas. Operators with custom routing should follow the migration guide in docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md.

Leo Carter (request changes): The mapping looks reasonable but I worry about nested parameter coercions. Can we add a strict-mode toggle for operators who want to reject coercions rather than coerce?
Asha Menon (author): Added a 'coercion_mode' config to tool_schema_mapper with 'permissive' and 'strict' options and documented it in the migration guide. Also added unit tests covering both modes.
Maya Singh (comment): CI initially failed on a flaky streaming test — I saw we added a small sleep in the assembler. Can we avoid sleeps and use deterministic signaling?
Asha Menon (author): Reworked assembler to use a fragment arrival map keyed by fragment-id+checksum and removed the sleep. Tests updated accordingly.
Rui Zhang (approved): Verified canary traces and the duplicated-tool incident no longer reproduces under the test harness. Approving for merge.
Normalize OpenAI invocation envelopes: canonical internal selection hint (selected_tool), stream fragment resilience (ids + checksum dedupe), and conservative tool parameter mapping with a strict/permissive toggle. No public wire-format breaking changes. Operators with custom routers should read docs/openai-compatibility/invocation-normalization.md for migration steps.

Add variance-aware autoscaler controller and per-tenant variance telemetry; improves stability under intermittent surge workloads and increases fairness of burst allocation.
Summary: Introduces a new variance-aware autoscaler that factors request-rate variance and burstiness into scale decisions and burst token allocation. This is targeted at intermittent-surge workloads (spiky, short-lived bursts from many tenants) where standard utilization-based autoscaling either overreacts or under-allocates burst capacity. Motivation: We observed several support incidents where tenants with highly variable arrival patterns caused oscillation in node counts and unfair consumption of burst tokens, degrading tail latency for other tenants. This change aims to reduce oscillation, make burst distribution fairer across tenants, and provide observability to tune policies. Key components: 1) controller/autoscaler/variance_controller.go: new controller that computes per-tenant mean and variance over a sliding window, derives an "effective demand" metric combining 95th percentile rate and variance penalty, and exposes decisions to the scaling plane; 2) pkg/scheduler/fair_burst_allocator.go: integrates variance metric into burst token allocation algorithm, preferring tenants with consistently high short-term variance to receive temporary soft credits while enforcing tenant-level fairness caps; 3) pkg/telemetry/metrics_exporter.go: new Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboard templates for per-tenant request variance, effective_demand, burst_credit_usage, and burst_credit_hitrate; 4) cmd/controller-manager/main.go: wires the new controller behind a feature flag (--enable-variance-autoscaler); 5) helm/charts/autoscaler/templates/: adds config options for sliding window length, variance weight, and maximum soft burst per-tenant. Design notes: - Effective demand = alpha * p95_rate + beta * sqrt(variance), where alpha and beta are tunable. Default alpha=1.0, beta=0.5. - Hysteresis and cooldown: dynamic cooldown scales with variance to avoid thrash: cooldown = base_cooldown + gamma * normalized_variance. - Burst fairness uses a time-decayed ledger so transient spikes don't permanently drain credits. Tests and CI: unit tests added for variance estimator, allocator fairness invariants, and edge cases (zero-traffic, constant traffic, synthetic heavy-tail spikes). Integration test added in perf-canary suite simulating 1k tenants with exponentially distributed spike arrivals to validate stability and tail latency. CI: all checks passed after two iterations (lint, unit, integration perf-lite). Rollout plan: gated behind --enable-variance-autoscaler and feature gate variance_autoscaler_v1. Step 1: deploy to canary clusters with default beta=0.5 and monitor metrics for 48h. Step 2: if tail latency improves and no regressions, enable in staging clusters. Step 3: gradual rollout to Dedicated fleet with telemetry-backed rollback triggers (burst_credit_hitrate drop or node oscillation rate > threshold). Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged when feature flag disabled. Migration: none. Observability and dashboards: new Grafana panels added (per-tenant variance heatmap, effective_demand distribution, burst_credit_consumption by tenant percentile). Performance impact: controller runs O(N) over active tenants; optimized with shard workers and sampling for large clusters. Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - We intentionally use sqrt(variance) to keep units closer to rate while still reflecting variability. - To limit overhead, high-cardinality tenant metrics are aggregated into percentiles by default; full per-tenant metrics are optional via config. - There is a small potential for temporary unfairness during burst draining windows; the time-decayed ledger mitigates this. Links: Related Linear tasks ENG-3492 (variance estimator), ENG-3620 (fair allocator integration). Related PRs: none.
Aisha Rahman (comment): Can you clarify how we tune beta for different fleet sizes? Author reply: Default beta=0.5 is conservative; added docs section outlining tuning guidance based on observed p95/variance ratios and a small script to compute suggested beta from telemetry.
Diego Morales (requested changes): The allocator loop has a potential O(M*N) path when reconciling many tenants; please add sharding and a cap. Author reply: Reworked allocator to use sharded workers and bounded queue, updated tests and added benchmark results to PR description.
Ethan Liu (approval): Reviewed the integration tests and perf numbers. Approve after CI green.
payload.title: variance-aware-autoscaler-and-intermittent-surge-fairness

Motivation: Several downstream apps reported awkward token migration when customers rotate credentials across services and observed subtle stream interruptions during credential refresh. This PR introduces a lightweight "trio" auth bridge and a small ergonomic surface that aligns refresh/backoff semantics across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs while preserving backwards compatibility. Scope: coordinated changes across SDK facades (py/ts/go) and the monorepo bridge layer. Goals: 1) Provide a single opt-in mode (auth.bridgeMode = "trio") that triggers coordinated token handoff and staged refresh to avoid mid-stream token holes. 2) Standardize backoff presets and named streaming presets (low-latency, balanced, throughput) exposed from SDKs. 3) Keep public SDK APIs stable: new fields are optional and default to previous behavior. 4) Bump SDK minor versions to signal ergonomics additions. High-level change summary: - Add a minimal bridge shim in /internal/cred/bridge that exposes a consistent handshake and lease lifecycle. - Expose bridgeMode and streamPreset in each SDK config struct/class with typed enums and docs. - Normalize retry/backoff presets and wire them into streaming adapters (pullstream/pushstream) to reduce duplicated logic across languages. - Add small compatibility adapters to ensure legacy token callbacks continue to work (fallthrough path). Implementation notes: - Python: new redwood_sdk.session.auth.TrioBridge (thin wrapper), added stream_preset enum + integration tests against local canary harness. - TypeScript: introduced AuthBridge class in src/auth/bridge.ts and updated PullStreamAdapter to accept preset hints for buffering/heartbeat. - Go: lightweight credential fanout adapter in stream/connector/bridge.go with unit tests and integration test against perf-canary. - Telemetry: emit a single metric per SDK when bridgeMode switches (redwood.sdk.bridge.switch) and a streaming preset tag on request metrics. - Tests: added unit tests for each SDK; e2e run in perf-canary validated no increased median latency for small-burst streams. Rollout plan: - Feature gated: bridgeMode disabled by default. - Dogfood rollout on staging with several infra customers for one week. - Monitor telemetry for error spikes and token-mismatch counts. Checklist: - [x] Add thin bridge and adapters in all three SDKs - [x] Expose enums and types with docs - [x] Add unit + e2e tests in each repo - [x] Update changelogs and bump SDK minor versions - [x] Add telemetry and alert for token-mismatch regressions Related: ENG-2345 (migration playbook), PM-987 (product spec).

Motivation: small-sequence, high-QPS workloads see disproportionate kernel-launch and scheduling overhead when using quantized execution paths (INT8/FP8 + smoothquant). This patch introduces a lightweight kernel coalescer and a KV-cache-aware scheduling policy to reduce per-request latency without sacrificing throughput. The change also fuses the dequantization step for smoothquant-adapted kernels when safe, reducing memory copies and extra kernel launches.

What changed: 1) kernel_coalescer: a runtime component that groups adjacent short kernels (typically per-head or per-MLU micro-op) at the launch layer into a single compound kernel invocation when the combined tensor shapes fit optimized microkernel tiling heuristics; 2) kv_aware_scheduler: scheduler scoring now includes a KV-warmth factor (cache hit rate + last-access recency) to prefer colocating requests that will reuse KV state on the same worker, reducing remote KV fetch latency; 3) dequant_fusion: added guarded fusion for smoothquant dequant->matmul->requant sequences for INT8/FP8 paths, with a verified fallback to existing separated path on mismatch; 4) continuous_batcher tweaks: token-aware microbatching with reduced padding amplification for mixed-length quantized requests; 5) telemetry & flags: feature flags to enable/disable coalescer and fusion per-customer, expanded histograms for kernel launch counts, per-request KV-warmth logging.

Compatibility & safety: Fusion is guarded by shape/scale checks and a per-model capability flag added to the model manifest. If runtime detects incompatible layout or scale drift (via a cheap sample check), it falls back to the original dequant path and emits a one-time regression telemetry event. The scheduler change is additive and can be toggled with the runtime.scheduling.kv_warmth weight. No changes were made to public APIs.

Benchmarks: microbenchmarks were run on p4d and A100 pools against a mix of short-sequence chat workloads (avg tokens/request 8), long-sequence generation (avg 512), and mixed-ratio traffic. Results: median p50 latency for INT8 short-sequence workloads improved 12% p50 and 9% p99; FP8 saw 8% p50 and 6% p99 improvements. End-to-end host CPU overhead reduced by 6% due to fewer kernel launches. Workload-specific caveats included a small throughput regression (1-2%) on extreme long-sequence-only synthetic cases when coalescer heuristics were enabled; heuristics default to conservative settings and can be tuned per deployment.

Testing: unit tests for kernel coalescer heuristics, scheduler scoring, and guarded fusion paths were added. Integration tests run in the perf-canary lab against the quant suite and KV cache stress harness. A small flake in dynamic-batcher was observed and rerun in CI.

Rollout plan: feature-flagged rollout starting with dedicated clusters and canary customers; monitor kernel.launches, kv.cache_hit_rate, latency.P50/P99, and dequant.fallback_rate. If dequant.fallback_rate > 0.5% for a model, automatically revert kernel fusion for that model.

Related: builds on prior work for batching and prefetch in ENG-1320 and smoothquant tuning in ENG-1182. Linked Linear tickets: ENG-1429 (coalescer), ENG-1473 (scheduler).
Introduces a kernel coalescer that reduces GPU kernel launch overhead for short token spans and a KV-cache-aware scheduler that prioritizes requests with warm KV state. Expect 8-18% median p50 latency improvement on small-sequence INT8 and FP8 workloads; no API changes.

Background & motivation: Over the last quarter we've seen a set of recurring issues in the OpenAI-compatibility surface when callers attach files or invoke tool/function calls with multipart/form-data payloads. Problems include: ambiguous or missing Content-Type headers causing incorrect handler routing, large attachments triggering unexpected memory pressure in the serving runtime during batching, and edge cases where chunked uploads are reassembled in ways that break tool-level parsing (e.g., JSON-in-attachment or newline-delimited tool payloads). This PR implements three coordinated defenses in the compat layer and serving runtime to improve safety and predictability for file/tool inputs while preserving backward compatibility for common OpenAI-style clients. Summary of changes and design: 1) Strict mime-context routing: the compat middleware now enforces route-level mime expectations. For public OpenAI compat endpoints we require an explicit Content-Type that maps to one of: multipart/form-data; application/json (for non-file payloads); or application/octet-stream (when signed by a client token permitting raw blobs). If Content-Type is missing or ambiguous we run a conservative content-sniff step limited to the first 512 bytes and only for Content-Type discovery, never as a fallback to change handler semantics. 2) Payload hysteresis thresholds: introduce soft/strict size thresholds per route and per-tool. Soft threshold generates structured warnings (x-compat-warning headers and telemetry) and suggests chunk-aligning; strict threshold rejects the request with 413 and a JSON payload describing recommended chunk size/token limits. Thresholds are configurable via compat config and default to conservative values that avoid common OOMs in continuous-batching. 3) Chunk-aligning and token-aware chunk policy: the client-facing middleware can suggest chunk boundaries aligned to token approximations for text-based attachments (json, ndjson, text/*) to help the runtime avoid mid-token splits that defeat KV-cache reuse and downstream tool parsers. The server also performs an optional reassembly that preserves original boundaries in metadata when trusted (private deployments), and otherwise enforces canonical chunking. 4) Per-tool payload throttling/backpressure: runtime scheduler gets a new light-weight quota for tool attachments expressed as token-equivalents and concurrent-attachment slots. When a high-throughput route would exceed configured attachment throughput we return 429 with Retry-After or enqueue with a short backoff, preventing head-of-line blocking for low-latency generation requests. 5) Compatibility behaviors: existing OpenAI-compat clients continue to work for the common cases; the compat middleware will emit compatibility warnings rather than hard errors for inputs that are within soft thresholds. We only reject at the strict threshold. Implementation notes: - New middleware: packages/compat/middleware/mime_router.go and mime_sniffer.go implement the routing/prioritization. - Runtime changes: runtime/scheduler/payload_throttle.go and runtime/batcher/chunk_align.go implement per-tool quotas and chunk-alignment heuristics. - Config: config/compat.yaml adds route-level soft/strict size thresholds and token-equiv heuristics. - Telemetry: observability/metrics/compat_metrics.go adds histograms and labels for: compat.mime.routed, compat.payload.rejected, compat.payload.warned, compat.attachment.throttled. - Docs & examples: docs/api/compatibility.md updated with the new header semantics and examples for JS/Python clients to perform chunk-aligning. - Tests: tests/integration/compat_uploads.test.ts (end-to-end), tests/unit/mime_router.test.go (unit), plus stress test harness changes under benchmark-lab/upload-stress to validate backpressure. Rollout plan: defaults are conservative and gated behind a feature flag compat.strict_mime_routing. We will flip the flag for hosted beta after an internal canary (perf-canary/compat-upload) validates no regressions on tail-latency and memory. Checklist: - [x] Middleware and runtime implementations - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Telemetry and dashboards (initial metrics) - [x] Docs for client chunking recommendations - [x] Config knobs and feature flag - [x] Backwards-compat smoke runs in perf-canary Known limitations and rationale: - Content-sniffing is limited and gated because blind sniffing can be surprising to clients; we only use it when Content-Type is absent and when it doesn't change handler semantics. - Token-estimate chunk alignment uses a heuristic (byte-to-token mapping) and is advisory for clients. Exact tokenization alignment requires client cooperation. - Some third-party clients that rely on missing Content-Type behavior may get warnings; the rollout will include a grace period. Security considerations: stricter Content-Type enforcement reduces attack surface (ambiguous multipart parsing) and prevents certain content smuggling patterns. Rejecting oversized attachments at the compat layer avoids downstream runtime memory exhaustion. Backwards compatibility: soft thresholds and warnings ensure existing clients continue to work while surface-area for breaking changes is minimized. See release_notes and merge details for timeline and opt-in instructions.

Motivation: Dedicated clusters suffer from tail latency and cost overhead due to cold-started worker processes and idle GPU spin-up. Static warm-pool sizes either waste capacity or fail to prevent bursts. This PR implements an adaptive warm-pool controller plus a cluster-level budget apportioner that distributes reserved idle capacity across clusters and tenants based on short-term demand signals and priority weights. Goals: 1) reduce tail latency for bursty workloads on Dedicated without large static reservations; 2) keep unit cost neutral by reclaiming idle warm capacity when not needed; 3) expose safe knobs for ops and allow gradual rollout via flags. Summary of changes: - controller/autoscaler: add AdaptiveWarmPoolController implementing proportional target sizing using short-term request rate, recent allocation utilization, and tenant priority score. - controller/apportioner: new ClusterBudgetApportioner that computes per-cluster warm allocations from a global warm budget with smoothing and minimum guarantees. - runtime: add warm-pool lifecycle management to node-agent to pre-warm containers and evict according to LRU+utilization heuristics. - metrics/logs: export warm_pool_target, warm_pool_allocated, warm_pool_utilization_pct, apportioner_score, apportioner_decisions for tracing. - docs/ops: operator guide for tuning warm thresholds and migration notes. - tests/sim: simulation harness and unit tests covering demand spikes, starvation scenarios, and rollback. Rollout plan and safety: default behavior remains off for existing clusters. New clusters created after the release will have the adaptive warm pool disabled by default; ops can enable per-cluster with a safety cap and gradual ramp (10% warm budget -> 50% over 24h). Controller includes backpressure to avoid over-provisioning when API server signals capacity pressure. Linked work: ENG-2147. Checklist: - [x] Controller implementation - [x] Apportioner algorithm and smoothing - [x] Simulation harness and unit tests - [x] Metrics and dashboards - [x] Documentation and ops guide - [x] Feature flag and rollout strategy
- Adds adaptive warm-pool sizing that reduces cold-start latency while improving GPU utilization across dedicated clusters.
- Introduces a cluster budget apportioner to allocate warm capacity among clusters/tenants based on recent demand and priority.
- New observability metrics: warm_pool_target, warm_pool_allocated, warm_pool_evictions, apportioner_score.
- Default configuration kept conservative; ops can opt-in and tune via runtime flags and Console UI.
2026-02-16 Sanjay Patel: Can you clarify the signals used for the proportional target? mixing rate and utilisation can be noisy; have you considered using P95 inter-arrival instead of raw rate?
2026-02-16 Maya Chen: We use a short exponential-weighted rate plus a utilization feedback term; P95 inter-arrival was evaluated in sim but was too reactive for multi-tenant noise. Adding EWMA gives smoother targets; details in comments in adaptive_warm_pool.go
2026-02-18 Liam O'Rourke: Tests look comprehensive. One nits: prefer context.Context to be threaded through apportioner APIs for future cancellation. Also please add a metric for 'warm_pool_evictions' so ops can detect thrash.
2026-02-19 Maya Chen: Good call on evictions metric; added it and threaded context through apportioner. Also added an integration test to assert eviction safety when global budget shrinks.
2026-02-20 Sanjay Patel: Default allocation looks a bit high for low-traffic clusters. Suggest default min-warm-per-cluster = 1 and a conservative global warm budget (5% of total nodes) for initial rollout.
2026-02-21 Maya Chen: Adjusted defaults to min-warm-per-cluster=1 and lowered default global warm_budget_pct to 5%. Documented rollout procedure and safe rollback steps in docs/ops/warm-pool.md
2026-02-25 CI: unit tests failed in simulator due to time-dependent race; rerun queued
2026-02-25 CI: rerun green after mocked time fix
2026-02-28 Evelyn Park: Approving on behalf of SRE; please squash commits and include a short migration note in release notes (ops will need to opt-in).

Motivation: We've seen intermittent long-tail latency that isn't captured well by existing per-request percentiles because cost is distributed across phases (ingest/queue, tokenizer, kv-lookup, decode, scheduling). This PR introduces per-token latency decomposition metrics, a waterfall dashboard, and log context propagation so on-callers can quickly correlate traces, logs, and metrics for a single long request.

Summary of changes: added a lightweight exporter that emits redwood.latency.decomp.{phase} (histograms and p50/p90/p99 counters) keyed by model, route, customer_tier, and token_bucket; propagated a stable token_span_id through the request path and enriched structured logs with it; added a Grafana waterfall dashboard for per-request breakdowns and a composite alert tuned to reduce noisy host-triggered incidents.

Checklist: [x] Add metrics and histograms to serving runtime (Go) [x] Propagate token_span_id in trace context (Python + Go) [x] Dashboard + example runbook [x] Integration tests that synthesize long-tail requests [x] Alert tuning and documentation link

Implementation notes: the exporter lives in platform/observability and exposes per-request rollups as histogram buckets (we chose expo-aligned buckets after benchmarking against production token distributions). For memory/speed reasons we compute the phase deltas in runtime hot-path and emit a small proto to the exporter. The token_span_id is derived deterministically from request_id + token_index (64-bit) to allow deterministic correlation without persisting state; it is attached to OpenTelemetry trace attributes and to our structured logs via the new propagator.

Backward compatibility and rollout: the metric names are additive (no renames). The propagator is a no-op unless the head_branch sets the feature flag in config (default off) and is guarded in code paths to ensure zero impact if not enabled. Rollout was performed as a canary: 5% traffic for 48h, then 25% for 24h, then full. We used the existing routing policy to fallback automatically to token_span_id-less logs if the propagator wasn't available.

Dashboard and alerting: added web/console/dashboards/latency-waterfall.json which contains a waterfall panel that assembles phase histograms for a single request using the token_span_id as join key. The SLO alert in slo/alerting/late_tail_rules.yaml uses a composite rule: it fires only when both (a) cluster-level tail latency p99 > threshold and (b) >10% of affected requests show decode-time > queue-time to reduce noisy host false positives. We also added a suppression rule for noisy hosts (nodes with known tracebacks) and tuned the Alertmanager grouping.

Testing: integration-tests/observability/test_latency_decomp.py adds synthetic traces that assert decomposition sums approximately to total latency, validates token_span_id appears in logs and traces, and checks the dashboard query can join metrics and logs for a single span. CI: two flakes were hit during first run (flaky histogram bucket assertion) and fixed by relaxing the test tolerance and improving retry logic.

Security/Privacy: token_span_id is not PII; it is an opaque numeric derived deterministically and logged only when feature flag enabled. Documentation: docs/observability/latency_decomp.md explains metric names, recommended dashboard queries, and a playbook for debugging long-tail incidents.

Rollout notes for on-call: the playbook highlights common patterns (kv-lookup spikes vs decode CPU saturation) and how to use the waterfall panel to triage. We also included an example alert edit to reduce noisy host signatures.

Links: Linear ENG-8421 (latency decomposition), support ticket SUP-3210 for customer incident referenced in motivation.
Miguel Torres (2026-02-13): Can we avoid extra allocations in hot-path when the feature flag is off? Aisha: the token_span_id path is guarded and allocation-free in the fast path; added benchmarks and micro-optimization to avoid allocs.
Rina Sato (2026-02-14): The histogram bucket choices look dense for short sequences — can we adopt adaptive buckets? Aisha: benchmarked adaptive buckets; chose expo-aligned as a better tradeoff for our token distribution. Added notes in docs.
Tom Becker (2026-02-15): Alert composite seems complex; will this increase MTTR? Aisha: composite reduces noisy host false positives by correlating decode-heavy requests; included simulated incident in test suite and updated playbook to guide responders.
Miguel (2026-02-16): CI flake on test_latency_decomp fixed, re-running.
CI bot (2026-02-16): E2E passed on rerun.
Tom Becker (2026-02-17): Approved after minor comment on dashboard formatting.
Aisha (2026-02-17): Squashed commits and updated changelog snippet.
Add per-token latency decomposition metrics and a waterfall dashboard; propagate token_span_id for log/trace correlation; introduce composite alert to reduce noisy-host false positives; docs and runbook added.
payload.title: latency-waterfall-and-log-context-correlation
