Context: OpenAI introduced a Responses v12 variant that exposes a client-facing deterministic seed and richer metadata attributes while slightly changing streaming chunk markers and tool-calling handshake timing. Customers using Redwood's OpenAI compatibility layer observed two issues: (1) client-supplied seeds were not consistently propagated through retries, cache hits, and internal fallback to smaller model variants, and (2) structured attributes in the v12 responses (attributes, tags, provenance) were being dropped or transformed during proxying. Motivation: ensure parity with OpenAI Responses v12 semantics so downstream apps (tool routers, evals, rerankers) see deterministic outputs and the same metadata attributes across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This PR implements a compatibility shim that (A) preserves the client seed (x-client-seed / request.seed) across the full request lifecycle including reconnects and retry resumes, (B) normalizes and forwards the v12 "attributes" map into Redwood's Response.Attributes field without flattening keys, (C) stabilizes streaming boundaries and reassembly logic to avoid duplicate tokens or missing tool-call markers when clients reconnect or when proxy re-streaming occurs, and (D) introduces a lightweight tool-handshake extension to the streaming protocol so tool availability signals arrive before tool calls in fragmented streams. Checklist: - [x] Propagate client seed into reroute/fallback paths and KV cache keys so cached responses respect determinism hints - [x] Add x-client-seed HTTP header and request.seed JSON support in OpenAI adapter - [x] Preserve attributes/tags/provenance as-is and add an attributes passthrough test-suite - [x] Rework streaming chunk reassembly to be idempotent for reconnects (sequence+fragment checks) - [x] Implement streaming preamble: TOOL_HANDSHAKE event emitted before first tool call fragment - [x] Add compatibility tests for Responses v12 examples and cross-variant fallbacks - [x] Update docs and API changelog notes for openai-compat v12 behavior and header guide Limitations / Notes: - This shim is conservative: when attribute keys conflict with Redwood internal keys we prefix incoming keys with "openai." to avoid accidental overwrites. - Determinism across quantized model fallbacks depends on identical sampling seeds; we surface warnings in the logs when fallback models are incompatible. - The handshake event is additive and ignored by older clients; the adapter will gracefully degrade if the client does not acknowledge the preamble.
3 commits: initial adapter shim and header plumbing; streaming reassembly + handshake implementation; tests, docs, and perf tuning. Key commit messages: (1) openai-adapter: forward x-client-seed and seed JSON field to routing layer; (2) streaming: idempotent chunk-reassembler + TOOL_HANDSHAKE preamble; (3) compat-tests: responses-v12 attribute passthrough and reconnect scenarios + docs update.
Marcus Nguyen: Can we be explicit about how seeds are mixed with per-model RNG offsets? If two models sample differently this could give surprising determinism claims.
Asha Patel: Good point. Added a warning in fallback_manager when a fallback model has an incompatible sampler; we also preserve the original seed and annotate the response with response.meta.openai.fallback_sampler_mismatch=true.
Lena Ortiz: Streaming reassembly looks solid but we need a tiny optimization for the seenFragments cache to avoid unbounded growth under high-QPS. Suggest LRU + TTL.
Asha Patel: Implemented LRU+TTL and added a stress test; notes added in streaming_reassembler.go. Benchmark shows <3% p99 latency impact under 500 QPS.
Diego Ramos: Request-level e2e test failing intermittently in CI (race on attributes map). Please run with -race and ensure map copies are made.
Asha Patel: Fixed by deep-cloning incoming attribute maps before cross-thread usage; reran CI -race locally before pushing.
Marcus Nguyen: Approved after fixes.
Lena Ortiz: Approved.
Diego Ramos: Approved and left minor nit for docs grammar which was addressed.
Compatibility: OpenAI Responses v12 - Redwood will now forward client-provided seeds via X-Client-Seed/request.seed and preserve v12 attributes/tags/provenance through the compatibility adapter. Streaming: improved reconnect resilience and TOOL_HANDSHAKE preamble to stabilize downstream toolcall ordering. Note: fallback to different sampler models may impact determinism; a warning flag is attached when sampler mismatch is detected.
payload.title: openai-compat: reconcile Responses v12 seed & metadata passthrough with streaming tool handshake

Motivation: We continue to see duplicated token refreshes and inconsistent retry behavior across SDKs during high-throughput streaming and batched workloads. This PR introduces a small, language-agnostic RetryPolicy compiler and a lightweight streaming progress envelope to bring parity and observability to Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. Goals: 1) Provide a declarative RetryPolicy format that compiles to runtime presets (hedged/hedged-with-backoff, fast-fail, conservative) so callers can pick documented semantics rather than hand-tuning numeric knobs. 2) Stabilize reauth handshake under stream reconnects to avoid thrash (single-flight refresh, backoff alignment). 3) Surface a StreamProgress envelope on async iterators/async generators that exposes token/offset hints and last-heartbeat timestamps for observability and more ergonomic client-side resumption. 4) Bump SDK versions and ship coordinated docs and examples.
Scope: - Add retry policy compiler modules and test vectors in each SDK.
- Add a small StreamProgress struct/type on iterator yields and a `with_progress` opt-in flag on streaming helpers.
- Centralize credential preflight and singleflight refresh in the shared auth shim used by all three SDKs (language-native implementations).
- Update README / migration guides and release notes.
Backwards compatibility: All new behavior is opt-in (new RetryPolicy config or with_progress flag). Existing defaults remain unchanged to avoid surprises in production.
payload.title: introduce-retrypolicy-compiler-and-stream-progress-unify-py-ts-go

payload.body:
Motivation: The KV cache has accumulated significant internal fragmentation on long-running hosts serving heterogeneous session lengths. Fragmentation increases memory footprint, triggers more frequent spillover/paging, and amplifies eviction churn under load. This PR introduces an alignment-aware allocation strategy plus a background segment coalescer and a threshold autotuner to reduce fragmentation and smooth spillover behaviour.

Summary of changes: 
- New alignment-aware slab allocator: buckets allocations to power-of-two alignment classes chosen to reduce wasted space for common KV sizes (8B, 32B, 128B, 512B, 2KB). The allocator records an "aligned_alloc_ratio" metric.
- Segment coalescer: background worker that merges adjacent free segments within a shard when fragmentation ratio exceeds a dynamic threshold. Coalescing is cooperative and throttled to avoid impacting serving latency (hot-path is lockless; coalescer uses try-lock ramps).
- Threshold autotuner: samples fragmentation, page-fault/spill events, and batch-insert rates to tune coalescing aggressiveness and per-bucket split thresholds at runtime. Tunable via feature flag and config knobs.
- Soft backpressure hook for continuous batching: large insert bursts now see soft delays coordinated with the allocator to avoid creating many tiny free segments that trigger immediate spillover under pressure. This integrates with the existing batching controller to apply token-level pacing.
- Telemetry & CI: new metrics and dashboard snippets; unit and stress tests added.

Why this is different from prior work: Prior PRs focused on eviction policies and spillback bisection. This change attacks the root cause: internal fragmentation and allocation alignment, reducing the amount of memory that must be reclaimed and therefore reducing eviction churn and paging.

Checklist: 
- [x] allocator implementation and unit tests
- [x] background coalescer + integration tests (simulated shard stress harness)
- [x] autotuner with conservative defaults and opt-out
- [x] metrics and console dashboard wires
- [x] canary rollout & feature flagging

Operational notes: The feature is gated behind the runtime flag "kv.align_coalesce_enabled" (default: false). We will enable it for perf-canary nodes for 48h, then a 10% production canary before full rollout. If regressions are observed, toggle the flag off — changes are additive and safe to revert at runtime.

Files changed count and size are moderate; this touches allocator, shard bookkeeping, and observability layers. Details in commits below.
1) allocator: add alignment-aware buckets and allocation helpers (meera/kv/allocator)
2) coalescer: background worker and heuristics + integration with shard free list
3) autotuner: sampling/decision loop and config binding
4) batching: soft backpressure hook and tests
5) metrics: add kv.aligned_alloc_ratio, kv.coalesce_ops, kv.soft_bp_events; dashboards
6) tests & docs: unit + stress tests, rollout docs and feature flagging
Sanjay Patel (2026-02-19): Nice direction. Two questions: what's the expected CPU overhead of the coalescer under steady state? And can the autotuner be bounded to avoid oscillation?
Meera Kline (2026-02-19): Coalescer is designed to be low-priority; in microbenchmarks we saw ~+2% CPU on median but no impact on p99 latency. Autotuner uses hysteresis and a dampening window (configurable) to avoid oscillation — added notes in doc.
Alex Morgan (2026-02-20): Tests look good; add a deterministic seed for the stress harness so flakiness is debuggable. Also please ensure metrics are tagged by shard and region.
Meera Kline (2026-02-20): Added deterministic seed to tests and per-shard tags to metrics. Updated tests and dashboard wiring.
Priya Desai (2026-02-22): Approve after CI rerun and a short perf summary in the PR body. Please include rollout steps in runbook.
Meera Kline (2026-02-22): Added perf summary and runbook section. Marking ready for merge.
Implements an alignment-aware allocator and background segment coalescer for the KV cache; reduces internal fragmentation and spill-triggered evictions. Feature gated behind kv.align_coalesce_enabled. See runbook for canary rollout.
Bench summary (perf-canary sim, 64-concurrency nginx-like workload):
- memory footprint: -9% (small-session heavy) to -14% (mixed workloads)
- eviction churn: -15% overall
- p50 token latency: ~0% change
- p99 token latency under heavy insert bursts: -8%
- CPU median: +2% (coalescer), peak unchanged
Notes: results vary by model and session distribution; autotuner defaults are conservative to prioritize p99 latency.
1) Enable kv.align_coalesce_enabled on perf-canary nodes (48h)
2) 10% production canary (72h) monitoring kv.frag_ratio, kv.soft_bp_events, p99 latency, and OOM/eviction rates
3) Gradual ramp to 100% if metrics stable; revert flag immediately if regressions observed
4) Post-rollout: ramp up coalescer aggressiveness via autotuner if frag_ratio stays > 0.25 for >24h
This PR intentionally keeps the hot-path allocation fast and lockless; heavy work is offloaded to the coalescer. The autotuner can be disabled by setting kv.align_coalesce_autotune=false for customers requiring deterministic allocation behaviour.
payload.title: Alignment-aware allocator and segment coalescer for KV cache

Motivation: Many production tenants see erratic micro-burst patterns where conservative batching settings either waste GPU cycles or cause tail-latency spikes. This PR introduces a lightweight 'mini-batcher guardian' runtime component that applies tenant-aware micro-batch shapes and a telemetry adapter that surfaces quantization sensitivity signals into our econ pipeline. It also adds a small CLI tool (quant-tuner) to synthesize candidate quant profiles from sampled workloads so tenants can safely evaluate compact quant profiles before rollout. Scope: runtime batching policy + guardian, telemetry bridge from runtime->econ service, quant-tuner CLI, docs and e2e smoke tests. Key behavior: - Mini-batcher guardian maintains per-tenant microburst counters and decides when to force smaller batch shapes for latency SLOs or larger shapes for cost SLOs. Decisions are policy-driven and respect tenant overrides. - Telemetry adapter exports a new signal stream: quant_sensitivity_{tenant,model,window} (estimated loss/cost delta for candidate quant tiers) and mini_batch_shape_{tenant,window}. These appear in the econ pipeline and console. - quant-tuner CLI can ingest replay/sampled traces and output N candidate quant profiles with safety estimates (expected token-cost delta, rank-regression estimate). Implementation notes: The guardian is intentionally minimal and runs as a hot-path filter inside the serving runtime; careful attention paid to allocation-free path for the common case. Quant-tuner is a standalone binary (go) that reuses model sampling and offline evaluator components. Backward compatibility: runtime flags default to off; admin-enabled per-cluster via feature flag enable_mini_guardian=true. Rollout plan: staged behind feature flag for 10 internal tenants -> 40 canaries -> global after 2 weeks of telemetry. Tests & results: microbench in perf-lab with sample multi-tenant chat workload (70/30 short/long tokens) shows median latency change: +0.6% (statistically neutral) and p95 latency down 4.1% for bursty tenants; token unit cost reduction ~7.8% for cost-optimized profiles when quant-tuner profiles used. Risks/mitigation: false-positive quant regressions — quant-tuner outputs conservative regression scores and PR includes automatic fallback to baseline model variant. What changed (high level): - runtime/mini_guardian.*: guardian logic and policy engine - runtime/batcher/*: new small batch shaper and containerized tests - telemetry/adapters/quant_telemetry.go: new adapter and export plumbing - tools/quant-tuner/: CLI, samplers, and offline evaluator - docs/ops/mini-guardian.md: rollout + feature flags - tests/e2e/mini_guardian_smoke_test.py: smoke + perf checks This description is a single continuous string and includes checklists, test summary and rollout notes.
Diego Martin (review): Could we add a short-circuit to avoid policy evaluation on low qps tenants? Perf-sensitive path needs zero allocs. -- requested change
Priya Kapoor (author): Added an allocation-free fast-path in runtime/mini_guardian.go and added microbench results (shape_manager_bench) to show <100ns median overhead for no-op path.
Aisha Thompson (review): Telemetry schema looks fine but please version the new signals to quant_v1 and add a migration note in telemetry/README.md. -- requested change
Priya Kapoor (author): version tag added (quant_v1) and README updated describing the ecollation in econ pipeline.
Lars Berg (review): quant-tuner outputs are promising; add a CI smoke check that runs quant-tuner against a tiny sample to prevent regressions in future changes. -- approved after change
CI Bot: smoke quant-tuner sample failed on first run (model artifact missing) — rerun triggered and passed.
- Add mini-batcher guardian to allow tenant-aware micro-batch shaping (feature-flag gated).
- Export quant sensitivity telemetry to econ pipeline (quant_v1 signals).
- Add quant-tuner CLI to generate candidate quant profiles from sampled traces (experimental).
- Minor docs and an e2e smoke test for guardian + quant flow.
Merged after requested changes were addressed. Rollout behind feature flag; initial internal canary scheduled.
Smoke tests included: unit tests, a quant-tuner sample run, and a perf-lab integration harness. Ops should enable feature flag and watch telemetry dashboard: quant_sensitivity_* and mini_batch_shape_* before broad rollout. If quant_sensitivity shows sustained negative regression >0.5% on eval set, auto-disable rollout for that tenant.
payload.title: mini-guardian: introduce mini-batcher guardian + quant telemetry adapter and CLI

Motivation: We have multiple incompatibilities between our internal streaming protocol and the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions streaming expectations that surface as flaky tool/function-calling handshakes, ambiguous stop-token semantics, and broken partial-logprob delivery for structured outputs. This PR: 1) introduces a lightweight 'framed JSON' envelope for every stream fragment (type + seq + payload) so consumers can reliably reassemble partial JSON structured outputs and function call metadata, 2) reconciles stop-token handling when callers provide an array of stop strings by prioritizing exact-token termination while preserving internal role-based stop heuristics, and 3) moves per-chunk logprob deltas into a dedicated metadata envelope so streaming parsers don't get malformed JSON when logprobs are emitted mid-response. Summary of changes: - runtime/stream/framer.go: new envelope encoder/decoder and heartbeat handling (adds sequence numbers, fragment_type field). - api/openai/v1_adapter.go: map OpenAI chat params -> internal request shape; implement stop-array reconciliation logic and add compatibility header opt-in for legacy behavior. - server/handler/chat_stream_handler.go: emit framed JSON chunks, ensure function-call partials include "fc_meta" header with call_id & arg_fragment indices, add backoff on transient write failures to reduce partial chunk loss. - sdk/ts/openai_compat.ts: client-side helpers to decode framed stream and rehydrate function-call arguments into a final call object. - docs/openai_compat.md: compatibility notes and migration guide. - tests/integration/chat_stream_stop_test.go: synthetic scenarios covering overlapping stops, multi-stop arrays, and streaming logprob envelopes. Backcompat and rollout: default behavior for new streams will be the framed JSON envelope. We add an opt-in header "X-Redwood-Compat: legacy-v1" to preserve the pre-existing newline-delimited protocol for older clients. This allows staged rollouts. Implementation details: - Framed JSON envelope schema (per-line): {"type":"chunk|meta|heartbeat|eof","seq":int,"payload":<object|string>} where payload for "chunk" contains {"role","content_fragment"} or for functioncall partials {"fc_meta": {"call_id","index"}, "args_fragment"}. - Stop reconciliation: when client supplies stop: [s1,s2,...] we perform longest-prefix match first, then exact token match, then fallback to role-based internal stops. We also expose an explicit boolean flag "openai_stop_strict" on the internal request if caller expects strict array semantics. - Logprobs: emitted as {"type":"meta","seq":N,"payload":{"event":"logprobs","deltas":{...}}} to avoid injecting numeric arrays into text fragments. Tests: unit tests for the framer encoder/decoder, integration tests that run a simulated slow backend to validate sequence reordering recovery and heartbeats, and CI flakiness checks. Migration notes for SDKs: TS SDK adds decodeFramedStream helper and examples in quickstarts. Rollout plan: feature gated behind feature flag "framed_stream_v1" for two weeks, then enabled by default with opt-out header. CI: some early runs failed due to race in framer when seq overflowed in the simulated test; fixed in commit "avoid seq reuse on late reconnect". Known limitations: this change increases request/response byte counts slightly due to framing fields; we mitigate with compact encoding (short keys) and optional compression in Dedicated. Related issues: SUP-4421 (customer reported malformed structured output on streaming), ENG-1327 (spec alignment work).
Add a framed JSON envelope for chat streaming to improve resilience and make /v1/chat compatible with structured outputs and function-call metadata. Stop-token reconciliation updated to align behavior with OpenAI stop arrays; logprobs moved to a separate metadata envelope during streaming. Backwards-compatible: legacy clients still supported by opt-in header. This PR adds an opt-in header "X-Redwood-Compat: legacy-v1" to preserve the pre-existing newline-delimited protocol for older clients and allow staged rollouts.
Evan Zhang (review): Can you add a short-lived feature flag to ease rollouts? Also we should measure token overhead impact in perf lab.
Author (Maya): Added feature flag 'framed_stream_v1' and included perf microbenchmarks in framer_test. See latest commit.
Priya Kulkarni (review): When function-call args come in fragments we need deterministic reassembly ordering; please add sequence indices for arg fragments and validate in tests.
Author (Maya): Added fc_meta.index and unit tests for out-of-order fragments. Also added a small backoff to the stream emitter to reduce writer contention.
Jordan Lee (approval): Approvals from infra and SDK sides. One minor nit about naming 'meta' vs 'control' but not blocking.
squash: framed JSON stream envelopes + stop reconciliation + function-call metadata passthrough\n\nIntroduces a resilient framed streaming protocol for /v1/chat parity, reconciles OpenAI-style stop arrays with internal heuristics, and delivers per-chunk logprob metadata in a separate envelope. Includes SDK helper and docs.
Default enablement two weeks after merge. Notify SDK owners to pick up new helper. Add migration blurb to 2025-11 release notes. Monitor SUP-4421 for regression.
payload.title: chat v1: introduce framed-JSON streaming envelopes, stop-token reconciliation, and function-call metadata passthrough for /v1/chat parity

Context: some production workloads (document-search chat and long-history assistants) show poor GPU utilization for large sequence lengths due to dense attention compute and memory-bound KV cache shuffles. This PR introduces a hybrid block-sparse attention microkernel plus a KV-shard scheduler that routes KV cache slices to co-located warps to reduce cross-SM memory traffic. The work also fuses the rotary/rope transform into the attention microkernel to avoid an extra memory pass. Design summary: - Block-sparse microkernel that partitions QKV into fixed-size blocks (64x64 / 128x128) and executes fused QK/softmax/V matmuls when dense blocks are present; falls back to a fast dense path for short sequences. - In-kernel rotary/rope application fused in-place into the Q/K compute to remove an additional kernel launch and memory write. Supports interleaved rotary for both single-head and multi-head layouts. - KV-shard scheduler in the runtime that pins KV shards by sequence-range and places requests with overlapping prefixes onto the same GPU stream/SM affinity group to maximize KV cache locality. - Continuous-batcher aware: kernel adds lightweight metadata to allow the batcher to coalesce blocks across requests with similar start offsets. Benchmarks (internal synthetic and canary on dedicated pool): - 2.2x throughput improvement for 8k context long-chat benchmark (N=32 concurrent streams) vs current main: 2.2x median throughput, 1.9x 95p. - 1.35x improvement on mixed short/long workload (50% <512, 50% 6k) in P99 latency under load. - CPU scheduling overhead increased by ~3% due to shard-placement bookkeeping; net cost justified by GPU gains. Checklist: - [x] Kernel implementation (CUDA) with unit-tested math kernels - [x] Runtime scheduler + fallback heuristics - [x] Integration tests against existing KV cache invariants - [x] Microbench harness + perf dashboards updated - [x] Canary rollout plan and abort thresholds documented Migration notes: - Feature is opt-in via runtime config 'attn.kernel=block_sparse' (default remains 'flash'). - For Dedicated customers, recommend enabling on a small percentage of nodes behind A/B rollout. - No model change required. Related: design doc at docs/design/attn/block_sparse_hybrid.md, perf dashboard run: perf/dashboards/block_sparse_oct2024.
Introduce an optional block-sparse attention kernel with fused rotary embeddings and a KV-shard-aware scheduler. Improves 90th percentile throughput on long-context chat workloads by up to 2.2x and reduces tail latency under contention. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via runtime config 'attn.kernel=block_sparse'.
Diego Alvarez: Initial pass looks good. Two questions: (1) can you explain the choice of block sizes and whether we expose that as a knob? (2) We need to ensure deterministic results for model evals when switching kernels.
Maya Chen: Reply: block sizes selected after sweep (64/128) — added config 'attn.block_size' with safe defaults and auto-tuner stub; deterministic numerics preserved by forcing same FP accumulation order in fused path (see block_sparse_kernel.h comments).
Priya Nair: Please add a fallback to dense path if block sparsity ratio < 10% to avoid worst-case regression on very dense attention patterns.
Maya Chen: Added heuristic and test (will fallback when sparsity < 12%).
Omar Hassan: CI flagged a flaky test in continuous_batcher; looks like a race on stream fences
Maya Chen: Fixed with explicit stream synch on the coalesce path and added stress test. Re-ran CI; all green.
Merged after addressing reviewer feedback and adding fallback heuristics. Canary ran for 48h on Dedicated pool with no regressions and a 1.9-2.2x sustained throughput improvement for targeted workloads. Rolled out as opt-in config with auto-rollback thresholds.
8k context, batch size 32: median throughput +2.2x, 95p +1.9x. Mixed workload P99 latency -26% under 75% load. Memory footprint: KV cache shard locality reduces global traffic by ~18% in canary traces.
payload.title: Block-sparse hybrid attention kernel with fused rotary and KV-shard scheduler

Context: We've observed inconsistent tail latency and suboptimal throughput for medium-length workloads (512-4096 tokens) when using the current FlashBridge tiled path combined with rotary/rope encoded models. This PR introduces a hierarchical tiled FlashBridge implementation with a lightweight rotary microfusion path plus a KV cache priority eviction policy to improve throughput, reduce memory churn, and stabilize p95/p99 latency under continuous batching.

Motivation: Production traffic analysis (see ENG-2431) showed that: 1) the monolithic tile scheduler was frequently creating imbalanced worklets causing warp underutilization, 2) rotary position application cost was duplicated across fused kernels/host-side code paths, and 3) KV cache eviction was agnostic to prefix reuse patterns which increased cache misses during conversational workloads.

What this PR does (high-level):
- Implements a hierarchical tiler: two-level tiling that first groups heads/rows by affinity then schedules micro-tiles to streaming CUDA kernels to increase occupancy and reduce warp divergence.
- Adds a rotary microfusion path: a thin fused kernel that applies rotary embeddings inline with q/k transform in the critical fastpath to avoid an extra transpose/scale roundtrip. The kernel is corner-case safe (falls back to existing path for unsupported dtype/seq_len).
- Introduces KV priority eviction: a hot-key heuristic that tags prefixes with recent reuse and evicts cold entries first; includes a compact LRU-ish ring for fast decisions under lock-free access.
- Continuous batching scheduler tweaks: adds a small bounded queue for microtiles to favor completing existing batches rather than starting new ones (reduces partial-batch penalties).
- Feature flags and graceful rollout: runtime flags (env + Console toggle) to enable hierarchical tiler, rotary microfusion, and KV-priority eviction independently. Canary rollout steps are documented.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Hierarchical tiler improves warp utilization but introduces slight bookkeeping overhead; we measured this overhead to be outweighed for typical conversational distributions (>64 tokens avg).
- Rotary microfusion limits: it only runs for fp16/amp-safe paths on GPUs with sm >= 80; for other configurations we fall back to the existing fused-attention pipeline to preserve correctness.
- KV priority eviction is heuristic-driven; we expose tuning knobs (decay window, tag weight) in the Console to adapt for different app access patterns.

Commits (summary):
- initial hierarchical-tiler prototype and tests
- add rotary-microfusion kernel and device tests
- implement lock-free kv-priority eviction ring and metrics
- scheduler: continuous-batching microqueue and backpressure fixes
- runtime flags, console controls, and rollout script
- perf regression tests and benchmark harness updates

Changed areas (high level):
- runtime/tiler/hier_tiler.cpp (new)
- runtime/tiler/include/hier_tiler.h (new)

Introduce a lightweight non-blocking session probe across Python/TS/Go SDKs; standardize stream iterator backpressure defaults and retry window names; bump SDK versions (py 1.8.0, ts 1.27.0, go 1.5.3).
Motivation: Teams observed sporadic mis-synced auth windows and surprising stream pause behavior when upgrading one SDK but not the others. This PR adds a tiny session-probe primitive (non-blocking background ping to validate active session/credentials), harmonizes a small set of ergonomics (stream iterator backpressure defaults, retry window names, and env var surface), and bumps SDK versions so downstream consumers get consistent behavior.

What changed (high level):

Summary: Add high-resolution in-process counters, frame-level tracing scopes and a lightweight Perfetto export hook to the runtime hot-path (continuous batching, scheduler, KV cache) to make microbench timelines reproducible and low-overhead for production-style runs. Motivation: existing NVTX-based instrumentation is useful for ad-hoc GPU traces but lacked fine-grained programmable counters and an easy path to generate deterministic traces for the microbench harness. This PR introduces per-thread frame counters, a compact ring-buffer event sink, and trace export that produces Perfetto-format JSON suitable for timeline viewers and long-running microbench ingestion. Design highlights: 1) hpc::FrameCounters: lock-free, per-core counters for category events (e.g., batch_start, batch_emit, kv_hit, kv_miss, schedule_wait). Counters are aggregate-friendly and exported as delta snapshots. 2) tracing::FrameScope: RAII-style scopes that annotate event boundaries and attach a small integer frame-id to both counters and the trace stream. Scopes are no-op when tracing disabled. 3) perfetto_exporter: modular sink that flushes the in-process ring buffer to a Perfetto-compatible JSON file; supports live stream-to-disk and postmortem dumps. 4) microbench CLI integration: bench/run_trace.sh driver that runs the existing batching microbench with tracing enabled, producing trace artifacts under artifacts/perf/ with metadata for the dashboard. 5) Runtime knobs: rtrace.enable, rtrace.sampling_interval_ms (for low-overhead mode), rtrace.max_events to bound memory. Backwards compatibility: NVTX emissions are preserved behind a feature flag; default remains the new compact exporter when the harness is used. Microbench runs were executed in CI perf job (separate job) that validates the exporter output schema and checks event continuity across frames. Manual validation: loaded generated traces into Perfetto UI and validated batch start/end pairing, KV hit/miss counts correlating with microbench config. Motivation: Streaming tool/function invocations from OpenAI-style clients sometimes emit partial fragments, non-conforming JSON, or out-of-band metadata. Upstream services expect a coherent tool invocation envelope, and our openai-compat layer needs to be resilient without requiring client changes. This PR introduces a lightweight runtime adapter ("Gatekeeper") that sits in the invoke path and performs three responsibilities in a backwards-compatible way: 1) resilient fragment coalescing and streaming admission control, 2) schema fallback and heuristic mapping for non-conforming tool payloads, and 3) structured-output annotations (schema_confidence, fragment_repaired) for downstream telemetry and gradual rollouts.

What this changes: The Gatekeeper adapts incoming streaming fragments into a consistent internal invoke envelope. It performs incremental validation: if fragments form valid JSON, pass-through is used; if fragments are invalid but repairable (common cases: trailing commas, isolated escaped newlines, missing closing brace), Gatekeeper attempts a deterministic repair and tags the envelope with schema_confidence and fragment_repaired=true. If a tool signature does not match any registered tool schema, Gatekeeper applies heuristic mapping rules (name alias table + type inference) and attaches a best_match_tool and confidence level. All repairs/mappings are recorded as events to observability and appear in trace spans. A feature flag toolcall_adapter_v2 controls rollout.

Compatibility & safety: No upstream API changes. Clients that already send well-formed tool calls are unchanged. The adapter rejects clearly invalid/ambiguous streams with a 400 and a structured error payload to keep behavior explicit for integrators. Repair heuristics are conservative and logged; a follow-up PR will add an operator console to flip strict mode per tenant.

Testing and verification: Unit tests cover edge fragments, near-miss JSON, alias resolution, and concurrent streaming sessions. End-to-end golden tests simulate chunked streams from the OpenAI SDKs and assert final invoke envelope parity with expected tool schema variants. CI includes a newly added flaky test harness that runs streaming scenarios under jitter.

Rollout plan: Enable toolcall_adapter_v2 as an opt-in feature for 10% of traffic in Dedicated, monitor metrics (toolcall.fragment_repaired, toolcall.schema_mismatch, toolcall.reject_rate, p95_infer_latency), then widen to 50% before global default. We will measure customer-facing error rate and a small latency delta due to admission processing; batching heuristics are preserved.

Notes: This PR also adds cross-cutting telemetry tags to help correlate repairs with prompt fingerprints and model variant. See docs/openai-toolcall-compat.md for operator-facing descriptions and migration guidance.
Riley: please document the exact repair rules and where we should stop trying to auto-fix (edge cases like ambiguous bracket counts). Also add a metric for repaired_count/attempted_count.
Maya (author): added detailed repair rules to docs and a gatekeeper.repair_attempts metric; left an owner TODO for the operator console work.
Samir: can we avoid copying large buffers for every fragment? Suggest switch to slice-backed buffers and limit max_buffer_size per session.
Maya: switched to slice-backed buffer and added a safeguard with max_buffer_size configured per tenant; tests updated.
Elena: tests look good but add a deterministic seed for jitter in e2e harness to reduce flakiness.
Maya: added deterministic jitter seed and re-ran e2e; CI green.
QA: flagged unexpected behavior when tool name matches multiple aliases; clarified fallback order and added an explicit tie-breaker rule.

Motivation: Our paged KV cache shows suboptimal reuse under high-concurrency multi-model workloads, and background reclamation contends on a single global allocator lock which amplifies tail latency. This PR introduces a bucketized slab sharding strategy plus a lightweight transactional pin API to group pin/unpin operations across request lifecycles and reduce global contention.
Summary of changes: 1) New bucketized slab allocator: splits the block arena into N runtime-controllable buckets driven by model-hint and size-class histograms; each bucket has its own freelist/eviction-heap and background reclaim worker to avoid hot global locks. 2) Transactional pin API: pins can be grouped into a short-lived transaction object that commits or aborts atomically, allowing the allocator to coalesce pin metadata updates and defer non-critical refcount churn. 3) Cross-bucket eviction hints: scheduler emits soft-affinity hints so long-lived KV entries are preferentially kept on the bucket matching their access pattern; eviction workers consult a small bloom+LRU sketch to prioritize candidates. 4) Adaptive reuse heuristics: block reuse now considers recent prefix-KV access and request latency SLOs to favor low-latency reuse versus aggressive compaction. 5) Observability: added per-bucket counters (allocs, evicts, contention-ms), per-transaction histograms, and a new dashboard panel. 6) Kernel/fastpath: optimized hot-copy path with 64B vectorized memcpy fallback using architecture-specific intrinsics for x86_64 and a plain memcpy for other arches.
Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (Linear ENG-2743) - [x] Unit tests for allocator and transaction commit/abort - [x] Integration test in perf-canary harness - [x] Benchmarks: end-to-end latency and throughput runs attached - [x] Observability dashboard config - [x] Docs update in redwood-docs describing transactional pin semantics

Files changed (high level): - src/kv/allocator/bucketed_allocator.{cc,h} - src/kv/allocator/transactional_pin.{cc,h} - src/kv/evict/evict_worker.cc - src/kv/fastpath/memcopy_optim.{cc} - tests/kv/allocator_tests.cc - perf/bench/kv_bucket_shard_bench.py - docs/kv/transactional_pin.md - observability/dashboards/kv_buckets.json

Author reply: added strong atomic commit with sequence tokens and unit tests covering concurrent commit/abort scenarios. - Priya Nair: Noted potential memory blowup if transaction abort path leaks temporary pins; requested a stress test. Author reply: implemented scoped-guard and added stress test with abort/no-op scenarios; CI stress run attached. - Evan Ortiz: Asked for perf numbers vs existing allocator under 4000 concurrent connections and mixed model load. Author reply: included perf-canary outputs showing 18% throughput uplift and 24% tail latency reduction p95->p99 compared to main under matched hardware.

Summary: Instrumentation and microbench additions to help diagnose layer-level kernel occupancy and batch-window interactions with KV-cache. This PR introduces a lightweight per-layer occupancy probe, a stamp-based KV-cache sampler ("kv-stamp profiler"), and an adaptive batch-window tracer that records contiguous request grouping behavior used by the continuous-batching scheduler. All probes are zero-cost when disabled and are guarded behind runtime flags and RBAC-controlled debug endpoints.

Motivation and context: We observed tail-latency regressions under mixed request shapes where a few large layers dominated GPU occupancy and caused scheduler-induced head-of-line blocking. Existing coarse counters were insufficient to map slowdowns to individual kernel launches or to correlate KV-cache reuse with batch-window size. This work aims to give engineers the tools to: (1) attribute occupancy regressions to specific model layers/kernels, (2) measure the effective batch-window (number of requests grouped per dispatch) over time, and (3) correlate KV-cache hit patterns with per-layer hot paths.

What changed (high level):
- runtime/probes/occupancy_probe.h/.cc: per-layer occupancy probe that hooks into kernel dispatch points and records occupancy (SM utilization estimate) + launch duration. Exports a compact proto-friendly record for tracing.
- runtime/probes/kv_stamp_profiler.h/.cc: stamp-based KV-cache sampler that attaches a short-lived token to requests and samples cache hits/misses across layers to compute reuse windows.
- runtime/scheduler/batch_window_tracer.cc: adaptive tracer that logs when the scheduler decides to flush a batch, capturing batch composition, sequence lengths, and KV stamps.
- tools/microbench/occupancy_benchdriver: small microbench harness to replay recorded traces at configurable QPS and report distribution of occupancy and batch-window sizes.
- observability/dashboards/occupancy-dashboard.json: Grafana panel definitions and Query Language (PromQL/SQL) mappings to visualize per-layer occupancy heatmap and KV reuse curves.
- controlplane: added debug endpoint /debug/probes to enable/disable probes and stream sampler snapshots (RBAC-protected).

Commits (summary):
- 9f3d2a8: add occupancy probe skeleton and proto definitions
- 1b4a7c2: implement kernel hookpoints and SM-util estimators
- 6c8ef91: add KV-stamp sampling and tag propagation through request context
- d4a11b3: integrate batch-window tracer into continuous batching scheduler
- aebb2f0: microbench harness + runner + synthetic workload generator
- be3c442: dashboards and CI runbook instructions
- c7f0d9a: tests, docs, and RBAC debug endpoint

Files changed (select highlights):
- runtime/probes/occupancy_probe.h (new)
- runtime/probes/occupancy_probe.cc (new)
- runtime/probes/kv_stamp_profiler.h (new)
- runtime/probes/kv_stamp_profiler.cc (new)
- runtime/scheduler/batch_window_tracer.cc (modified)
- tools/microbench/occupancy_benchdriver/main.cc (new)
- observability/dashboards/occupancy-dashboard.json (new)
- controlplane/http/debug_handlers.cc (modified)

Testing and results: Unit and integration tests were added for probe lifecycle and stamp propagation. Microbench harness reproduces a regression scenario: mixed traffic with occasional long sequences. Before instrumentation + adaptive tracer, under synthetic 500 qps workload with 5% long requests we observed 99th latency = 312 ms and visible spike in SM contention. After adapting scheduler thresholds (guided by the tracer insights) and enabling KV-stamp-aware coalescing, end-to-end 99th latency dropped to 245 ms (-21%), and average per-layer hotpath occupancy variance reduced by ~34% in the bench runs. Note: these numbers are from the microbench harness on a p4d instance; production effects would vary.

Backward compatibility and safety: All probes are opt-in via the /debug/probes endpoint and a runtime config flag (runtime.probes.enabled=false by default). The probe code avoids allocations on the hot path by using thread-local ring buffers and a lock-free aggregator. The control plane enforces that only users with the observability:admin role can toggle sampling.

Review conversation (selected excerpts):
- Jordan Lee (reviewer): "Nice work — this gives the visibility we needed. A couple of asks: (1) ensure SM-estimator doesn't allocate on every kernel path, (2) add a unit test for stamp propagation across async cuda streams."

- Priya Natarajan (reviewer): "Grafana panels look good, but let's avoid adding expensive dashboard queries to the default ingest. Recommend materializing a short-term rollup table in the observability pipeline."
- Maya Patel: "Agreed — changed dashboard to use pre-aggregated metrics (probe_occupancy_bucket) and added guidance in docs/observability/occupancy.md."
- Luis Gomez (reviewer & approver): "Approving after small nits. Please document RBAC access in the ops runbook."
- Ops comment (internal): "Temporarily disable probes in canary until we've validated throughput impact at production load."

CI summary: Initial CI run reported flaky unit on runtime/scheduler tests (timing-dependent) which was fixed by introducing a deterministic clock in the test harness. Full CI (build, unit, integration, lint) all passed on final run. Perf check (microbench pipeline) executed on the perf-lab pool; results above included.

Merge: Squash-merged into main on 2026-03-05 after approvals. Change is feature-flagged and shipped behind RBAC and runtime flag to minimize risk. The dashboards and docs are included in the same PR to make rollout and troubleshooting immediate.

Related work: complements earlier occupancy counters and tracing exports but focuses on correlating occupancy with KV-cache reuse and continuous-batching behavior. Distinct from prior NVTX/time-trace changes by providing a low-overhead sampled profiler and an adaptive tracer targeted at scheduler decision points.

Motivation: Reduce 95th/99th percentile token latency for INT8-heavy workloads while preserving deterministic fallback to FP8 and maintaining KV cache alignment for continuous batching. This PR introduces a tile-prefetch microkernel for int8 GEMM, an upstream dequant-fusion stage integrated into the runtime scheduler, and KV-cache alignment tweaks to avoid extra copies during continuous batching. Changes were iterated against the microbench harness and live canary traffic on a small dedicated pool. Summary of changes: 1) New microkernel redwood/runtime/kernel/int8_tile_prefetch.cpp and supporting headers. The kernel implements per-tile prefetch + intrinsics-friendly data layout for 8-bit matmuls with optional per-head requant hinting. 2) Scheduler integration redwood/runtime/scheduler/prefetch_tiler_scheduler.cc that exposes a tiler policy to the request router and merges the dequant fusion pass into the late scheduling stage so fused dequant+gemm can be scheduled on tile-prefetch capable devices. 3) KV cache alignment adjustments redwood/runtime/cache/kv_alignment.h and KV copy-path optimizations redwood/runtime/cache/kv_continuous_batch.cc to avoid unaligned writes that previously forced extra allocations at end-of-sequence. 4) A runtime config flag (runtime.config.quant.prefer_prefetch) and a safety gate that automatically falls back to the previous path when microkernel returns an unsupported status. 5) Bench harness updates and new unit/integration tests under redwood/tests/quant_perf and perf artifacts under redwood/benchmarks/ci. Benchmarks: On internal microbench suite with sequence lengths 128/256 and batch sizes 1-8 we saw median token latency drop 12%-20% and p99 drop 18%-26% for INT8 pipelines on A100-like devices when using the prefetch tiler; CPU-bound quant paths show no regression. KV continuous-batching scenarios improved throughput by up to 9% due to elimination of one copy per request. Compatibility and risk: The change introduces a non-default config flag and is guarded by hardware capability checks; default behavior unchanged until flag enabled on canary pools. The dequant fusion stage is conservative and preserves numerical equivalence within existing quantization tolerances. Rollout plan: enable on internal perf canary for 48h, monitor token-level latencies and quality metrics, then progressive rollout to dedicated pools. Related: touches scheduling, kernel, and cache subsystems; coordinate with infra and SRE for canary. See linked linear items for profiling runs and rollout checklist.
Reviewer Ethan: Can you add a guard for the microkernel on devices that expose reduced L1 bandwidth? Author: Added runtime capability probe and a fallback path; updated tests to simulate low L1. Reviewer María: Bench numbers look promising but please add accuracy regression tests for edge-case quant scaling. Author: Added quantized regression set and absolute-diff checks; numbers within expected tolerances. Reviewer Sven: CI showed a flaky scheduling test that timed out once. Author: Increased timeout and adjusted test to be deterministic; CI passed on rerun. CI notes: lint and unit tests passed on first run; a single flaky scheduling integration test failed and was rerun; all checks green after fixes.
Performance: Introduces optional INT8 tile-prefetch microkernel that reduces token latency and improves continuous-batching throughput when enabled; adds conservative dequant fusion into the scheduler to co-locate dequant+GEMM on prefetch-capable devices. Rollout: feature gated via runtime.config.quant.prefer_prefetch and rolled out gradually to canary pools. No behavioral breaking changes expected.

Context: Operator-level profiling in the last quarter showed sustained stalls on small-to-medium sequence lengths due to scatter/gather overheads and suboptimal KV warmup for bursty traffic. This PR introduces a new attention strategy (SlabConcatenate + FlashMixer microkernel) that reduces per-token overhead for heterogeneous sequence distributions and a lightweight async-KV coalescer that amortizes KV cache population across micro-batches. Motivation: 1) Reduce small-batch latency and increase throughput at mid-sequence lengths (256-2048) where customer workloads spend most of their tokens. 2) Retain deterministic rotary/rope semantics while enabling a fused concatenate path that avoids extra memcpy for tiled KV layouts. 3) Improve continuous batching horizon so runtime can opportunistically stretch batching without violating latency SLOs. What this change does: - Introduces FlashMixer microkernel: a variant of Flash-attention style tiling that mixes slab-concatenated Q/K/V regions to minimize memory fragmentation and enable a single fused rotary application pass. Optimized for 8-16 head widths on A100/RTX7x. - Adds SlabConcatenate path to the kernel selector with heuristics based on sequence length distribution and current batch skew metric. This path fuses concatenation, rotary application, and QK matmul into one kernel for contiguous slabs. - Implements Async KV Coalescer: a runtime stage that coalesces concurrent KV writes from overlapping micro-batches into a single GPU write and exposes a KV warmup metric. Coalescer has backpressure safety to avoid overpopulation for very long sequences. - Extends continuous batching horizon: runtime now computes an elastic horizon that trades a small p99 latency tail against higher throughput; this is governed by a new config: continuous_batching.max_horizon_ms and continuous_batching.tail_target_pct. - Preservation of model semantics: fused rotary/rope ops are designed to be numerically identical to the existing path (FP16 accumulation path validated). Testing & benchmarks: - Microbenchmarks (internal harness) show 9-14% throughput uplift and 6-10% median latency reduction at seq=512/1024 for T5-like models and ~12% on LLaMA-variant runs with head dim 64. - KV-heavy chat workload (continuous small messages) showed 18% cost improvement due to reduced redundant KV writes. - Extensive regression tests validate logits and sampling for baseline prompts and prompt sets in eval harness. Rollout plan: gated feature behind runtime flag slab_concat.enabled; rollout to canary clusters for 2 weeks; if no regressions, flip on in dedicated pools with auto-fallback to legacy path. Related: ENG-4821 (kv warmup telemetry), ENG-4899 (batching SLOs), SUP-3210 (customer-reported chat latency spike). Notes: this PR intentionally avoids global allocator changes and keeps the fused kernel opt-in. The body below includes a short appendix with file-level highlights and a summary of reviewer discussion and CI details.

Maya Chen (2025-11-20): Added coalescer_rejects metric and a tunable threshold; left default conservative (0.05).
Sofia Ramos (2025-11-24): The fused rotary pass looks good, but please add a unit test for odd head sizes and a numeric comparison at fp16 with huge batch sizes.
Maya Chen (2025-11-25): Added test and adjusted accumulation order to match baseline for odd head dims. Benchmark noise decreased.

Maya Chen (2025-11-29): Fixed linker issue in ops/Makefile and added a guard for quantized path to fallback to standard kernel (optional). CI green afterwards.
All CI checks passed after fix. Unit tests: 512/512. Integration tests: 98/98. Bench harness ran locally and in CI with smoke runs. Lint: pass. Built artifacts: linux-cuda12 (A100), linux-cuda11 (RTX series).
Introduces SlabConcatenate + FlashMixer fused attention kernel (opt-in). Adds Async KV Coalescer and continuous_batching horizon config. Expected throughput uplift 8-14% for mid-tail sequences and improved KV write efficiency for chat workloads. Rollout gated behind slab_concat.enabled.

Context: Multiple SDKs exposed slightly different streaming iterator ergonomics and credential refresh hooks which made cross-language examples and platform integrations brittle. This PR introduces a lightweight SessionDecorator abstraction and a small set of shared semantics (ResumeToken v2 + telemetry markers) to harmonize behavior across Python/TypeScript/Go. Goal: make stream consumers simpler to implement, provide a single place for automatic credential rotation and graceful resume, and add telemetry points to measure reauth/backpressure heuristics.

What this changes (high level):
- Add SessionDecorator (py/ts/go) that wraps an existing stream handle/iterator and: automatically refreshes credentials on auth failures, exposes a simple resume_token API, and emits telemetry events for: credential_refresh_attempt, credential_refresh_success, resume_attempt, resume_success, resume_fail.
- Introduce ResumeToken v2 semantics: small stable opaque token returned at stream checkpoints; safe to persist short-term for fast reconnection.
- Unify async iterator ergonomics: all SDKs now offer .stream() returning an async/pullable iterator with a single .resume(resume_token) helper. This removes previously divergent push/pull naming.
- Add backpressure hint optional argument (hint: "latency" | "throughput") to stream factory to allow runtime routing optimizations in Dedicated/Hosted.
- Deprecate older streamResume and token-swap callback signatures; provide compatibility shims for one release cycle.
- Bump SDK versions: python -> 0.42.0, typescript -> 1.12.0, go -> 1.7.3.
- Tests: unit coverage for decorator edge cases, integration tests exercising auth rotation against the dev auth-proxy, and cross-SDK interoperability smoke tests.

Implementation notes:
- Python: session_decorator.py implements an async generator wrapper that catches AuthExpired errors, triggers the provided credential_provider.refresh() and retries from a resume_token. Adds small coordination via an async Lock so concurrent reauth attempts coalesce.
- TypeScript: sessionDecorator.ts implements an async iterable class that mirrors the Python contract, exports a withSessionDecorator factory that preserves stream typing.
- Go: session_decorator.go adds a StreamDecorator type with Resume(ctx, token) and Start(ctx) iterator model; uses channels to translate push->pull where necessary.
- Telemetry: lightweight events emitted to existing "sdk.stream" namespace with fields: event_type, sdk_lang, duration_ms, error_class. These are instrumented behind a toggle so customers can opt into increased telemetry retention.

Checklist: [x] design doc (Linear ENG-2159) linked [x] unit tests added [x] e2e smoke tests added [x] docs updated in /docs/sdk/streams.md [x] version bumps for all three SDKs [x] feature flagged telemetry

Related: Linear ENG-2159, ENG-2164, support ticket SUP-4721. Docs: https://internal.redwood.ai/docs/sdk/streams#session-decorator (internal).

Noah Rivera: added microbenchmark in sdk/python/tests/bench_coalesce.py and documented results in PR description. Benchmark shows 95th percentile extra latency for coalesced refresh path < 6ms on CI baseline machines.
Eva Romero: asked to gate telemetry behind a feature flag; ensure that telemetry incurring no overhead when disabled.

Reviewers: approved (Asha, Liam, Eva) after last iteration.

Deprecated older streamResume callbacks — compatibility shims included. SDK versions bumped: py 0.42.0, ts 1.12.0, go 1.7.3. Feature-flagged telemetry for reauth/resume events.

Motivation: Several downstream partners expect a closer match to the OpenAI Responses surface, including variant response shapes, a deterministic seed/determinism flag, and request-level metadata passthrough that should round-trip into the returned response objects. This PR implements a compatibility layer and a guarded rollout that maps Redwood internal request fields to OpenAI-style Responses semantics while preserving our runtime invariants. High-level changes: 1) Responses variants: added an adapter that exposes the /v1/responses-like shapes (items, outputs, content blocks) and translates our streaming deltas into SSE-compatible delta chunks. The adapter supports both simple text responses and structured output blocks used by tool-calling. 2) Deterministic seed flag: introduced an optional query/body flag deterministic_seed and seed that signals repeatable sampling; this is translated into our sampling backend in a best-effort way (we document cases where exact determinism cannot be guaranteed, e.g., mixed-precision quantized kernels across GPUs). 3) Metadata passthrough: request.metadata is now propagated to response.metadata and preserved across retries and fallback model routing; audit logging records the original metadata for traceability. 4) Streaming stability improvements: hardened the chunk encoder, added rate-aware buffering to avoid partial JSON frames for structured outputs, and introduced backpressure knobs to reduce client-visible reorder under heavy batching. Implementation notes: - New package go/openai/compat/responses_adapter.go implements mapping logic and exposes a thin shim used by the OpenAI-compat HTTP handler. - Python and TypeScript SDK adapters updated to accept the new deterministic_seed/seed parameters and to surface response.metadata in typed objects. Files changed include unit and integration tests that validate deterministic runs across fixed RNG seeds and a compatibility test that replays a set of recorded OpenAI Responses fixtures. Rollout plan: feature is behind a feature-flag openai_responses_compat; start with internal customers set to opt-in, run A/B traffic for 48h, then enable by default if no regressions. Backwards compatibility: legacy OpenAI-compat endpoints continue to function; when deterministic_seed is absent we keep prior sampling behavior. Known limitations: exact bitwise reproducibility is not guaranteed across heterogeneous hardware; structured-tool step boundaries rely on the consumer respecting output markers. Checklist: implement adapter, wire SDK surfaces, add unit/integration tests, add docs snippet for determinism and metadata, gated rollout, monitor regressions.

Marta Li (2026-01-31): nits on naming: prefer deterministic_seed over seed to make intent explicit in payloads. Also requested an additional unit test for metadata passthrough when fallback routing occurs.
Aisha Patel (2026-02-01): Renamed fields in HTTP layer to deterministic_seed; updated sampler wiring and added fallback metadata test (integration/tests/openai_responses_fixtures/fallback_metadata_test.go).

See docs/openai-responses-compat.md for caveats and rollout plan.

Context: Customers reported rare nondeterministic tool selection during streamed OpenAI-compatible responses where the model returned multiple candidate tool choices split across streaming fragments. This caused downstream systems to sometimes pick different tools after reassembly. Motivation: make the OpenAI adapter produce deterministic, replay-safe tool_choice selection and deliver tool payloads with fragment-safe markers so reassembly cannot change choice. What this PR does: 1) Introduces a canonical serialization path for tool choice and tool descriptors: ToolDescriptor v2 with canonical field ordering and stable hashing. This prevents dict-order nondeterminism when computing tool signatures used by routable policies. 2) Adds lightweight per-chunk framing markers in the streaming envelope to ensure the boundary between a tool_choice event and its associated tool payload cannot be split by arbitrary chunking. The runtime now inserts an explicit "chunk_boundary_hint" token in the stream for cases where a tool_choice is immediately followed by a tool payload. 3) Augments the adapter mapping rules so vendor tool schemas (OpenAPI-like or freeform) are normalized into ToolDescriptor v2, including explicit parameter typing and a normalized examples array. 4) Implements deterministic tie-breaking heuristics for tool_choice when the model returns multiple candidates with equal score: prefer higher-explicit-priority annotation, then lexicographic tool-id, then stable-hash of canonical descriptor. 5) Adds compatibility layer to avoid changing external OpenAI-compatible JSON for customers relying on legacy frames: the adapter emits the new markers only when client indicates support via the X-Redwood-OpenAI-Compat header. 6) Tests + benchmarks: unit tests for serialization round-trip, end-to-end streaming tests that simulate fragment boundaries, and a lightweight perf benchmark demonstrating ~1% median token-latency regression on small cases but eliminating nondeterministic reassembly failures. Checklist: - [x] Spec: include canonicalization rules and framing E2E contract - [x] Implementation: adapter + runtime framing + policy tie-breaker - [x] Tests: serializer unit tests, streaming e2e harness, and regression alerts - [x] Docs: SDK typings update and migration notes - [x] Rollout plan: feature-flagged by default off, opt-in via header; staged rollout to dedicated customers Impact/risk: low functional change (opt-in), but careful rollout required for clients that parse raw stream fragments. Related: ENG-4871 (deterministic routing), ENG-4920 (stream reassembly incidents), SUP-1221 (support ticket about changing tool in flight).

feat(runtime): insert chunk_boundary_hint for tool payload transition
chore(tests): add streaming reassembly harness and unit tests
perf: add benchmark measuring token latency of additional framing markers
docs: add migration note and SDK typedefs for ToolDescriptor v2
Ivy Chen: Can you clarify why we need canonical JSON vs. protobuf? The team is concerned about adding yet another schema.
Maya Ortega: We considered protobuf but the OpenAI surface expects JSON and many clients reserialize; canonical JSON lets us interoperate without changing external shapes and avoids introducing a new wire format.
Lars Müller: The chunk_boundary_hint looks fine but will it increase stream size noticeably?
Maya Ortega: It adds a very small token in the stream only for boundary cases; benchmark shows <1% median token latency impact and negligible bandwidth increase on typical traffic.
Priya Natarajan: We should gate this behind the compat header for the first rollout to avoid surprising customers.
Maya Ortega: Agreed. Default behavior remains unchanged; header opt-in flips the adapter to emit framing markers and canonical descriptors.
Ivy Chen: Please add a real-world test using the mobile client chunker; it's been flaky before.
Maya Ortega: Added a mobile chunker simulation in the integration harness and ran it against two deduped agent scenarios; results included in CI.
Adds an opt-in OpenAI adapter feature that emits canonical tool descriptors and fragment-safe streaming markers to eliminate nondeterministic tool selection during fragmented streaming. Backwards-compatible and gated by X-Redwood-OpenAI-Compat header.
Feature is off by default. To enable for a customer, flip runtime feature flag 'openai_adapter.canonical_tool_choice' and instruct client to set X-Redwood-OpenAI-Compat: v2. Monitor streaming_reassembly_failures alert for first 48h.
1) Clients that parse raw framed fragments must opt-in after testing; 2) SDKs updated with ToolDescriptor v2 typedefs; 3) Operators can enable feature-flag per-customer in Console; 4) If issues, revert by disabling header or rolling back feature flag.
This PR intentionally minimizes surface area change by keeping external JSON stable unless the compat header is present. It centralizes tool normalization logic to make future policy work easier.

Motivation: large-sequence generation and long-lived KV/activation lifetimes cause volatile peak GPU working sets due to per-kernel scratch and activation retention. This PR adds two complementary runtime optimizations: (1) epochal activation spill: group model activations into 'epochs' based on layer/lifecycle analysis and allow cold epochs to be spilled to pinned host memory with fast async DMA and rehydration heuristics; (2) adaptive scratch packing: analyze per-kernel scratch lifetimes at compile-time and coalesce small, short-lived scratch allocations into packed buckets to reduce fragmentation and per-kernel workspace overhead. Design notes: - Epochal spill is conservative by default and gated under config.runtime.epochal_spill.enabled=false to avoid surprises in private/on-prem installs. Default: off for private, enabled for hosted canaries. - Spill policy uses a recency-and-cost score combining KV cache recency and estimated rehydrate cost; low-cost epochs are spilled first. - Scratch packing introduces a packing-bucket allocator layered on top of the existing arena. Buckets are keyed by alignment and expected lifetime class (short/medium/long). Packing is adaptive: the runtime observes allocation histograms over short windows and rebalances bucket sizes. - Continuous batching scheduler tweaks prioritize packing-favorable batch orderings and prefer lower inter-kernel scratch variance in a batch to reduce temporary high-water marks. - KV-cache eviction is augmented with a 'windowed hotset' score that biases eviction away from recently accessed token windows and layers with high reuse. Implementation summary: - runtime/arena/packed_allocator.{h,cc}: new bucketed allocator plus eviction hooks. - runtime/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cc: integrate packing hints and batch ordering heuristics. - runtime/kv/evict_policy.cc: windowed_hotset scorer and metrics. - runtime/activation/spill_manager.{h,cc}: epochal grouping, async spill/reload, warmup prefetch on predicted next-window accesses. - build targets and unit/perf tests added under test/runtime and perf/benchmarks/epochal_spill. Benchmarks (internal; averaged over 5 runs): - LLaMA-2-70B, seq=8192: peak GPU working set reduced by 22% (from 38.1GB -> 29.7GB); end-to-end latency change +3% p50, p99 +6% in worst case rehydrate path; throughput sustained within 2% of baseline for batch sizes >1. - GPT-like 13B, seq=4096: peak reduced 15%, latency impact <1.5%. Rollout: staged canary on dedicated pools with epochal_spill.enabled=true for low-util regions; monitor new metrics: runtime_epoch_spill_count, runtime_spill_latency_ms, gpu_peak_working_set_bytes, scratch_pack_ratio. Opt-out plan: config.runtime.epochal_spill.enabled=false or spill_threshold_bytes override. Backwards compatibility: no breaking API changes; all config flags are runtime-only. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (ENG-4821) - [x] unit tests for allocator and spill manager - [x] perf benchmarks and regression suite - [x] metrics and dashboards - [x] canary rollout plan - [x] docs/notes on tunables Changes are intentionally conservative in heuristics to limit regressions; trade-offs are documented in ENG-4821.

Aisha Patel (2026-01-28): Added config.runtime.spill_rehydrate_timeout_ms and the packing layer falls back to slab arenas when buckets are under pressure. Expanded tests to include synthetic fragmentation patterns (test/runtime/packed_allocator_test.cc).

Aisha Patel (2026-01-31): Fixed race by making free-list rebuild idempotent and added a deterministic stress harness. Reran CI; green.
Priya Nair (2026-02-01): Verified perf numbers on dedicated canary pool. Observed expected peak reduction but saw two regression traces where rehydrate overlapped with another large allocation and caused a transient OOM in an older driver. Recommendation: guard async spill with a runtime driver-quirks table. I'll approve after a guard is added.
Aisha Patel (2026-02-02): Added driver-quirks guard and fallback to immediate allocation path when pinned host DMA is unreliable. Addressed Priya's comment and squashed commits for merge.

Context and motivation:
This PR addresses a recurring class of incidents where aggressive fast-path kernel selection and lower-precision execution (fp16 / int8) produced rare but hard-to-detect correctness deviations for edge prompts. At the same time, customers expect throughput and lower cost. We need a runtime mechanism that lets us enable high-performance paths without risking silent correctness regressions in production.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a 'safelock' gating layer in the kernel selection path. The safelock prevents switching to a fast path unless a set of runtime validators pass (numerical consistency, kv-cache integrity checks, and recent success window).
- Introduces a precision toggle API (per-model, per-deployment) with three modes: strict (fp32 only), balanced (fp16 with strict validators), aggressive (fp16/int8 allowed once warmed).
- Adds a lightweight runtime validator harness: stochastic correctness probes run as background requests against canary inputs to compute divergence metrics (token-level mismatch rate, logit-delta distribution). Validators are cheap and attach metadata to requests that triggered path selection failures.
- Changes KV cache eviction policy to be conservative when cache-warmness is below threshold; combined with safelock it avoids invalidating cached KV frames that fast kernels rely on.
- Integrates safelock signals with the continuous-batching scheduler: until a deployment's validators reach a success threshold, scheduler prefers conservative batching and disables cross-model micro-batching that can expose interleaving bugs.
- Adds observability hooks: metrics (safelock.blocked_count, validator.mismatch_rate, precision.switch_count, kv.eviction_suppressed) and a dashboard stub.
- Adds a feature flag runtime.enable_safelock (default true for new deploys) and model config fields precision_mode and validator_policy.

Design notes and rationale:
- The safelock is intentionally conservative: it is designed to minimize customer-visible regressions at the cost of initial throughput until a model warms. We prefer false negatives (staying on slow path) over false positives (silent incorrect outputs).
- Validators are probabilistic and run only on a small fraction of traffic (configurable). We do not rely on end-user prompts alone; the system feeds a small canary corpus that includes known edge cases and adversarial tokens used in previous incidents.
- KV-cache eviction suppression is implemented as an additional guard in the eviction worker: if cache_warmness < 0.7 and safelock.enabled, eviction respects a soft TTL and only evicts when memory pressure exceeds a higher threshold. This prevents state churn that invalidates prefix caching assumptions used by some kernels.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(runtime): add safelock kernel gating and validator harness (A. Kumar)
- feat(config): model precision_mode and validator_policy proto + defaulting (A. Kumar)
- fix(kv): conservative eviction path and warmness estimator (R. Patel)
- perf(scheduler): integrate safelock signal into batching decisioning (L. O'Connor)
- test: end-to-end validator integration tests and canary job (E. Tan)
- docs: runtime safelock/precision-mode doc, migration notes (doc team)

Files touched (high-level):
- runtime/kernel_selector.cpp/h (safelock implementation, gating checks)
- runtime/precision_policy.proto (new model-level config)
- runtime/validator/ (background probe harness, small canary corpus)
- serving/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cpp (respect safelock signals)
- serving/kvcache/eviction_worker.cpp (suppressed eviction path)
- metrics/registry (new metrics added)
- tests/e2e/validators_integration_test.cc (new suite)
- docs/runtime/safelock.md (operator-facing guide and flags)

Small illustrative snippet included in the patch (non-executable):
"""
if (safelock.enabled() && !validators.passed_recently(dep)) {
  // force fallback to conservative kernel + fp32 path
  selectKernel = KernelSelector::conservative(model, seq_len);
} else {
  selectKernel = KernelSelector::fastpath(model, seq_len, precision_mode);
}
"""

Benchmarks / numbers:
- Baseline (main, before PR) on rtx-a100-80gb, long-tail tests: median latency 48ms, p99 180ms, throughput 2200 tok/s.
- With safelock enabled (default config) immediately after deploy: median latency +6% (51ms), throughput -8% (2024 tok/s) while validators warm.
- After 30m of live traffic and validator success: median latency +1% (48.5ms), throughput -2% (2160 tok/s).
- Aggressive mode (opt-in, warm): throughput +12% over baseline; we see a measurable cost win.
- We ran a correctness sweep against our regression corpus (n=1200 prompts) showing token-level mismatch reduced to <0.02% for balanced mode; in aggressive mode mismatch rises to ~0.6% on the corpus (expected, opt-in).

Testing and CI:
- Added unit + integration tests for validator harness and eviction behavior.
- Added synthetic stochastic tests that simulate rare floating-point edgecases.
- CI: initial pipeline had one flaky test (eviction_worker race) failing on Linux-asan; fixed in second commit. Final CI: all checks passed (build, unit, integration, perf-smoke).

Review discussion (highlights):
- Marco: "I like the safelock abstraction; can we ensure the validator corpus is editable by SREs without code changes?"
- Aisha: "Yes — validators read a canary file from /etc/redwood/validators/corpus.json and we added operator docs. SRE can update via configmap for k8s deploys."
- Eve: "Concerned about metric cardinality when we annotate every request with validator metadata."
- Aisha: "We emit aggregated counters and histograms; only a small sampling logs request-level debug traces behind a flag."
- Liam: "Scheduler changes look sane. Need additional canary rollout plan for enterprise customers with strict SLAs."
- Aisha: "Added rollout doc and an opt-out label on deployment config; default for existing deployments is unchanged (safe-mode learned)."

Edge cases / known tradeoffs:
- There is an initial throughput hit until validators warm. We mitigate by sampling only a small portion of traffic for validators and allowing manual warm-up (canary traffic injection).
- Aggressive precision_mode is opt-in; customers should enable only after verifying on internal test prompts. We include a CLI tool for running the validator corpus locally against a deployment.
- The KV eviction suppression increases memory use under some failure modes; we documented emergency knobs and introduced an automatic disable threshold if memory pressure remains high for 10s.

Migration / operator guidance:
- New deploys: safelock enabled by default. Operators can set runtime.enable_safelock=false to revert (not recommended).
- To opt into aggressive precision: update model config: precision_mode=aggressive and monitor validator.mismatch_rate.
- Dashboards: added a starter Grafana dashboard (docs link) and alerts for validator.mismatch_rate > 0.1% and safelock.blocked_count being unexpectedly high.

Backward compatibility:
- All config fields default to conservative behavior; no breaking changes. Models without precision_mode set continue to use fp32 until they pass validators.

Post-merge actions / follow-ups (linear):
- ENG-4983: add automated warmup job to inject synthetic canary traffic during deploy windows (follow-up).
- ENG-5122: add per-customer precision analytics and billing impact report.

Merge outcome:
- Final status: merged via squash. Branch merged to main after approvals from Marco, Eve, and Liam. CI green at merge.

If you want to test locally: run tools/runtime_cli --run-validators --config test/configs/precision_local.yaml against a dev deployment; run scripts/kv_warmup.sh to pre-fill the kvcache with the canary prefix set.

Thanks to Rohan Patel for eviction work, and the QA team for extended regression runs.

Patch size: moderate; favors safety and observability over aggressive micro-optimizations up front.

Added a runtime 'safelock' gating mechanism to avoid correctness regressions when enabling fast-path kernels and lower-precision execution. New precision toggle with runtime validators. KV-cache eviction made conservative under uncertain cache-warmness. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via config.

Motivation: Our current staged canary controller requires manual per-cohort tuning to hit statistical power and latency budgets for A/B experiments. This PR implements a Canary Sweep Controller that runs short, automated micro-experiments (sweeps) across traffic fractions to calibrate the optimal lift point for promotion or automatic rollback. The controller integrates with the rollout runtime, telemetry, and evaluation hooks to make closed-loop decisions while respecting latency SLOs and cost constraints. Design summary: 1) Sweep jobs: short-lived parallel trials at configured traffic fractions (e.g., 1%, 5%, 10%) with bootstrapped significance checks. 2) Calibration layer: computes an effect size estimate and traffic at which power >= configured threshold while staying within latency tail constraints. 3) Auto-attenuation: if sweep signals degraded latency or regression beyond thresholds, the controller reduces traffic and triggers snapshot rollback hooks. 4) A/B aware routing: integrates with the traffic router to allocate traffic slices for A/B experiments and report per-slice metrics. 5) Safety: requires at least two approved telemetry hooks and a soft holdpoint for staged rollouts; manual override supported. Checklist: - [x] Controller core + reconciler - [x] Sweep job CRD, CR controller wiring - [x] Integration with /rollout telemetry API and perf probes - [x] Canary-to-promote automation with canary snapshot creation - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Docs and playbook updates - [x] Demo script for internal testing Backwards compatibility: Existing Rollout CRs are unchanged; new fields are opt-in under rollout.spec.canarySweep. Migration: none required for current users; behavior inactive by default. Risks: sweep can increase short-term load; the controller enforces short time windows and rate limits. Rollout: gated behind feature flag rollout.canarySweep and enabled gradually for internal teams first.
Introduces canarySweep opt-in rollout capability: automated sweep calibration for A/B experiments, auto-attenuation when latency or quality regressions are detected, and new canary_sweep CRD. Enabled behind rollout.canarySweep feature flag. See docs/runbooks/canary-sweep-playbook.md for runbook and example rollout spec.
Jonah Li (reviewer): 'Nice shape. Can you clip the sweep duration to <= 90s to avoid tail amplification during high QPS? Also add a configurable safety backoff multiplier.'
Marta Ruiz (author): 'Good point — enforced 60s default, 90s max. Added safetyBackoff multiplier and validated in tests.'
Priya Menon (reviewer): 'Router changes look fine but please ensure AB slice labels are propagated to metrics tags; without that we can't join traces.'
Ethan Brooks (reviewer): 'Integration tests flaky in ephemeral CI; observed race in snapshot_manager cleanup — added a small delay and moved to idempotent cleanup.'
Priya Menon (approve): 'LGTM after minor telemetry tag fix.'
Jonah Li (approve): 'Approved.'
Ethan Brooks (approve): 'Approved — good to merge.'
- 7 commits total across feature branch
- Initial reconciler + CRD (mruiz): add canarySweep CRD and controller scaffolding
- Sweep job runner and bootstrap stats (jli): implement A/B sweep harness and baseline estimator
- Router integration (pmenon): extend traffic router to accept sweep slices
- Telemetry hooks (ebrooks): perf probe adapters and percentile checks
- Safety hooks and rollback orchestration (mruiz): snapshot + rollback playbook wiring
- Tests and docs (mruiz): unit/integration tests and README with example rollout spec
