Motivation: It has been difficult to correlate kernel-level hotspots with KV cache layout and continuous-batching backpressure events in production traces. This PR introduces three complementary low-overhead probes and a small microbench harness to make cause-and-effect visible during perf investigations and automated regressions. Summary of changes: (1) kernel-hotspot-tracer: lightweight sampling probe that annotates scheduler and CUDA kernel entry/exit with a compact hotspot identifier derived from callsite and op-type. Emits NVTX ranges when available and falls back to short tracepoints for environments without NVTX. Includes FLOPS-adjusted counters to avoid over-weighting long-running kernels. (2) kvcache-offset-histogram: on-KVcache-access histogram recording offset distribution and small-window reuse counts to detect pathological stride patterns introduced by certain tokenizers or model layouts. Buckets are power-of-two with a dense region for accesses under 1KB. Exported as Prometheus-friendly counters and optional trace annotations for correlation. (3) continuous-batch-pressure-probe: emits an instantaneous batch_pressure gauge when the batch queue begins to back up and a sampled per-window pressure histogram for debug builds. Hooks into the batching controller earlier in the pipeline to capture producer-side pressure and includes a token-rate estimator to reduce noise from transient spikes. (4) simple_seq_bench microbench: executable to exercise variable-length sequences, stridey KV access patterns, and kernel-heavy ops; emits a compact trace and histogram CSV for offline analysis and dashboard ingestion. Design: probes are guarded by feature flags and sample rate knobs with defaults off in release builds. Histogram storage is ring-buffer backed and uses per-worker aggregators to minimize atomics. NVTX ranges are used when available with a fallback so traces are consistent across environments. Rollout: feature-gated behind telemetry.feature_flags.kernel_hotspot and telemetry.feature_flags.kvcache_hist, default disabled. Canary rollout plan: 5 percent traffic for one week then expand if metrics are stable. Tests: unit tests for histogram bucketing and ring buffer safety, stress test for multi-producer writes, and a short GPU integration job that runs the microbench in CI. Backwards compatibility: non-breaking and opt-in. Follow-ups: small observability ingestion parser update (observability-pack) and a future probe for kernel memory-bandwidth when cupi integration is feasible.

Motivation: We observed cache-sensitive and sequence-length-dependent regressions when serving FP8/INT8 model variants on the high-throughput path. Two root causes surfaced in profiling: (1) redundant dequantization stubs inserted by the compiler leading to extra memory traffic across the KV cache boundary, and (2) suboptimal kernel selection for mixed FP8/INT8 attention matmuls at mid-sequence lengths, which increases both latency tail and per-token GPU utilization. This PR introduces an autotuned FP8 dequant rewrite pass (dequant-rewriter) plus a scheduler-aware kernel router that picks kernels based on runtime signals (sequence position, KV cache hit pattern, and batching profile).

Summary of changes:
- Implement dequant-rewriter: a graph-level pass that coalesces adjacent dequant ops, hoists dequantization out of hot KV cache paths when safe, and emits a fused "dequant+transpose" kernel where applicable. The pass supports conservative aliasing checks and a feature-flagged faster mode that assumes stable KV shapes in Dedicated deployments.
- FP8 autotuner: offline calibration tool and lightweight runtime probe that chooses between FP8-fused kernels, hybrid FP8/INT8 kernels, or fallback FP16 kernels per model and per-device. Tuner's decisions are persisted in model-serving metadata and can be overridden by rollout flags.
- Kernel router: scheduler integration that consumes continuous-batching statistics (batch size distribution, arrival jitter) and KV cache telemetry to choose kernel variants at request-time. Router minimizes kernel switches within a batch and prefers kernels that maintain low memory traffic across KV boundaries.
- Scheduler hints: expose a small set of hints (seq_pos_bucket, kv_hot_ratio, batch_shape_key) from the serving runtime to the kernel selector. These are lightweight scalar tags attached to batch descriptors.
- Tests and regressions: microbenchmarks for gbench and internal canary; unit tests for the dequant-rewriter; end-to-end perf test in the perf-canary workflow.
- Documentation: notes in docs/serving/quantization.md and a new troubleshooting section describing common FP8 failure modes and mitigation.

Design notes and rationale:
- We avoided aggressive whole-graph FP8 lowering because (a) some models use dynamic dispatch patterns incompatible with a single lowering, and (b) dequantization hoisting across KV cache write-back needs conservative checks to avoid stale keys. The rewriter therefore applies targeted fusion and hoisting, with a safe fallback to existing dequant ops when aliasing cannot be proven.
- Autotuner workflow: an offline pass analyzes representative prompts to build a candidate set. At runtime, a short probe (10s of warmup tokens) validates latency/throughput and writes a per-model best-variant tag. For private and dedicated tenants, the faster autotune mode is enabled by default; hosted tenants require opt-in.

Benchmarks (NVIDIA A100s, sequence mix representative of chat workloads):
- Baseline: mixed FP16 path (pre-change)
  - P50 latency: 86ms
  - P95 latency: 220ms
  - Tokens/sec: 35k
- Post-change (autotuned FP8-fused kernels + dequant-rewriter):
  - P50 latency: 72ms (16% reduction)
  - P95 latency: 165ms (25% reduction)
  - Tokens/sec: 45k (28% increase)
- For small-batch/high-jitter scenarios the kernel router avoided pathological kernel switches and reduced tail variance by ~30%.

Cost impact: in Dedicated benchmarks the improvements correspond to ~22% lower token-GPU-hours for the measured workload mix.

Rollout plan and safety:
- Feature-flagged under runtime.feature.fp8_autotune; default off for hosted mainline for 48h while we collect telemetry.
- Canary deployment to perf-canary and one Dedicated customer (internal) for 72h.
- Automatic rollback policy: if P99 latency increases by >10% or error rate increases by >0.5% over baseline within a 10m window, the rollout controller reverts to the previous kernel tag.

CI and validation:
- Unit and integration tests added under runtime/quant and serving/scheduler.
- Perf canary runs showed initial flakiness due to an aliasing edge-case; fixed by strengthening the alias analysis in the rewriter.
- CI: initial run failed one flaky test (serve_kv_integration_test) and was rerun: final CI passed.

Migration and compatibility notes:
- Models that embed custom kernels may require a one-line model metadata opt-in: "quant.auto_tune: true". We added a compatibility probe that logs recommended kernels without changing runtime behavior until opt-in.
- No API surface change to the Redwood public API.

Observability:
- New metrics: quant_kernel.variant_chosen, quant_autotune.probe_latency, quant_dequant.fused_ops.
- Traces: added tags for seq_pos_bucket and kernel_variant to GPU traces to make regressions easier to root-cause.

Related work: closes ENG-4231 (autotune baseline), progresses ENG-4278 (KV-aware scheduling).

Commits summary: see commits field below.

Files changed (high level): see changed_files field below.

Follow-ups:
- Add FP8 support to the GPU profiler export (ENG-4305).
- Expand autotune dataset to include longer-form decoding patterns.
- Evaluate similar rewriter for INT8-only models where dequantization churn is observed.

Ethan Park: Added conservative alias checks and a fast-path flag for Dedicated where we can assume stable shapes. See dequant_rewriter.h for the check and the feature flag backing.

Improves P50/P95 latency and tokens/sec for chat-like workloads. Ops: Feature-flagged rollout with automatic rollback conditions. Context: we see bursty fallback behavior in medium-length generative workloads where small timing variance in KV cache arrival and batching causes the serving runtime to flip into a conservative (alt-path) execution for a subset of requests, increasing tail latency and token-cost. Motivation: reduce unnecessary conservative fallbacks while preserving deterministic correctness for edge hardware-model combinations. This PR introduces a speculative-acceptance decision curve plus a KV coalescer holdback window: the runtime will tentatively accept speculative fast-exec decisions based on an adaptive confidence score; if downstream verifies a mismatch, requests are routed to the alt-path and a lightweight reconciliation is triggered. Design summary: 1) speculative acceptance module computes a confidence score from recent kernel success rates, sequence-length distribution, and observed KV arrival jitter. 2) KV coalescer holds short-lived writes (configurable, default 2ms) to give batching a chance without blocking correctness checks. 3) Numeric-mode guard (formerly "precision toggle" concept) exposes an explicit safe-mode flag that forces full-precision execution; otherwise speculative acceptance may opt for quant-mode kernels when confidence is high. 4) Metrics hooks record decisions, verified-mismatch counts, and reconciliation cost for offline tuning. Implementation notes: new modules added under runtime/scheduler (speculative_acceptance.rs) and runtime/kv (coalescer.rs, holdback_policy.rs). Small changes to quant dispatcher to surface the numeric-mode guard and ensure the reconciliation path replays a request with KV cache snapshot. Tests & validation: added deterministic unit tests for acceptance curve edge cases, integration tests that simulate KV jitter and ensure no silent correctness regression, and new loadtest scenarios that measured 18% reduction in fallback frequency on our medium-seq C4 workload with overall median latency impact under 1.5%. Rollout plan: staged rollout using A/B gating in Dedicated; feature gated behind runtime.experimental.speculative_acceptance with an initial 10% canary, monitor verified-mismatch, token-cost and p99 latency for 48 hours, then increment. Rollback: flip feature flag off; reconciliation path is synchronous-safe so turning off speculative acceptance guarantees identical behavior to pre-PR. Checklist: - [x] unit tests - [x] integration tests - [x] perf microbench harness - [x] observability dashboards and alerts - [x] docs update for ops (fallback behavior page).
Mateo Ruiz on 2026-02-16: High-level LGTM, please add a safety net metric for average reconciliation token cost so we can alert when cost increases. 
Aisha Patel on 2026-02-16: Added reconciled_token_cost gauge and wired to existing billing hooks in metrics; also added alert rule in dashboards. 
Jie Huang on 2026-02-17: Found a race in coalescer where a concurrent KV snapshot could be reclaimed; suggested weak ref -> upgrade to strong copy in the reconciliation hot path. 
Aisha Patel on 2026-02-17: Fixed by copying the snapshot during reconciliation; added unit test to assert snapshot lifetime. 
Priya Nair on 2026-02-18: Integration tests look good but saw a flaky failure on p99 under heavy load in CI reproducible locally; root cause was a non-deterministic timer resolution in holdback_policy. 
Aisha Patel on 2026-02-18: Rewrote holdback timer to use monotonic tick counter; re-ran CI and local loadtests. 
CI on 2026-02-19: initial CI run failed (integration timeout in speculative_acceptance_test) due to test timeout; author increased test timeout and refactored a long-running helper. 
CI on 2026-02-19: rerun passed (all checks green). 
Mateo Ruiz on 2026-02-19: Approved. 
Jie Huang on 2026-02-19: Approved with comment: consider adding a telemetry tag for model-variant to help per-model tuning later. 
Aisha Patel on 2026-02-19: Will follow up as a separate small PR to add model-variant tagging across acceptance metrics (ENG-901).
Introduces speculative acceptance decision curve and KV coalescer holdback to reduce unnecessary conservative fallbacks. Default is off behind runtime.experimental.speculative_acceptance. Expected impact: ~18% fewer fallbacks on medium sequence workloads; p99 latency unchanged for most workloads. Ops: new observability dashboard and reconciliation cost alert added.

Motivation: production workloads show that naive prefix caching + one-size quant profiles underperform across heterogeneous batches and multi-tenant GPUs. This PR introduces a Prefetch Negotiator service and a Compact Quant Advisor to automatically suggest conservative caching and quantization defaults per workload class. Goals: reduce token-cost by improving cache utility without increasing tail latency; provide compact quant profiles that retain quality for short/interactive sessions; make defaults consultable and overridable via runtime config. Changes: - New component: prefetch-negotiator (runtime service) that observes sequence-length distribution, KV cache hit patterns, and per-model latency budget and decides prefetch budget (KB per-request), eviction hints, and negotiation tags for routing. - Compact Quant Advisor: offline analyzer that profiles small prompt sets (warmup + edge cases) and synthesizes 2-3 compact quant profiles (e.g., 4-bit FP+per-channel scale, int8 hybrid) ranked by cost/quality score. - Policy glue: config layer to apply negotiated cache budgets and recommended quant profile to a model-variant at rollout time with canary gating. - Metrics and tracepoints: added prefetch_hit_ratio, prefetch_cost_estimate, quant_advisor_quality_delta, and a dashboard template. - CLI/tooling: `rwd cost-suggester prefetch --workload <yaml>` and `rwd quant-advisor profile <model> --samples <n>`. Implementation notes: Prefetch Negotiator runs as a sidecar in serving pods and emits signed negotiation tokens that the router honors; negotiation is optimistic and falls back to existing cache behaviour on mismatch. Compact Quant Advisor uses representative samples + accuracy hook to generate quality delta estimates; we avoid re-training and rely on calibrated post-quantization evaluation. Backwards compatibility: defaults are non-breaking; operators can opt-in via runtime flags. Testing: unit + integration with synthetic workloads that exercise bursty short-seq traffic and long-seq streams; manual QA on staging with a canary serving 5% traffic for a week. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Perf benchmark + dashboard - [x] Docs/CLI help - [x] Security review (KMS tokens usage) Rollout plan: initial rollout behind runtime feature flag, enable negotiator for low-latency tiers only (SLO <= 150ms) and enable quant advisor suggestions as non-binding recommendations for 2 weeks, then automatic apply with canary if cost savings exceed threshold and quality delta < 1.5%.
Asha Patel: Please add a safety timeout on the sidecar negotiation (avoid indefinite waits) - addressed in #3 commit and unit-tested.
Diego Martínez: Quant advisor quality delta estimation looks optimistic on tiny samples; request a 2nd metric to estimate sample representativeness - added rep_score in profiler.
Lena Kim: Can we gate negotiator to dedicated capacity only initially? Author: added a runtime flag and defaulted to 'tier: low-latency' in policy layer.
Infra CI: integration flake observed on gpu-setup step; rerun and updated test harness to preload drivers in staging images.
Adds a Prefetch Negotiator service and Compact Quant Advisor to suggest workload-aware caching and quantization defaults. Initial rollout behind a feature flag for low-latency tiers. Includes CLI tooling and dashboards.

payload.body:
Context: Previous multi-tool execution exposed two UX gaps: (1) nondeterministic ordering when multiple tool completions were injected into streaming responses which made downstream structured output assertions brittle, and (2) lack of coordinated backpressure/retry semantics meant slow external tools could either stall the whole response or lead to confusing partial injections. This PR implements a deterministic merge-and-inject pipeline, per-tool retry policies, and a backpressure gate that preserves tail-latency SLOs. Goals: 1) Deterministic injection order that can be aligned with function/tool call order or a stable priority key. 2) Per-tool idempotent retry with dedup keys and exponential backoff. 3) Optional backpressure gating so streaming tokens flush partial outputs when a tool is slow and then inject full results when available. Design decisions: - New execution primitive: ToolFanoutCoordinator which spawns tool workers, attaches sequence keys to each tool invocation, and produces ordered injection events. - Injection protocol: inject events are annotated with injection_index and injection_type (final|partial|fallback). Clients can opt into ordering_by_call_site vs ordering_by_priority. - Retries: retry semantics live in the coordinator; each tool has a retry policy (max_attempts, base_ms, idempotent boolean). Non-idempotent tools default to single attempt. Retries use a dedup token derived from request_id + tool_call_index to avoid double-application across restarts. - Backpressure gate: when a worker exceeds per-request latency budget, coordinator emits a "partial_injection" marker and continues streaming. When final tool response arrives coordinator emits replacement or append injection based on injection_type. - OpenAI compatibility layer: expanded function-calling shim to accept injection_index metadata and map it to function_call.result injection. Added translation layer so tools that respond as functions are compatible with existing SDK behavior. - Feature flag: guarded behind 'tool_fanout_v2' and an opt-in config on route-level. Implementation notes: - New files: runtime/coordination/tool_fanout_coordinator.{rs,py}, runtime/coordination/protocol.proto (protocol definitions), api/openai_compat/tool_injection_adapter.go, sdk/python/redwood/tools.py (helper surfaces), console/docs/tool-fanout.md. - Tests: unit tests for deterministic ordering, retries, and dedup token, integration tests simulating slow and failing tools, e2e streaming test to verify partial+final injection lifecycle. Checklist: - [x] Core coordinator implementation - [x] Backpressure gating - [x] Retry+dedup token - [x] OpenAI compatibility shim for function outputs - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Docs and SDK helper - [x] Benchmarks (latency profiles under 1-5 concurrent tools) Related: ENG-4521 (multi-tool UX), ENG-4607 (streaming stability), SUP-1182 (customer-reported flaky tool injections).
Improves multi-tool calling ergonomics: deterministic ordering for merged tool outputs, configurable per-tool retry/backoff, and an opt-in backpressure gate to preserve latency SLOs. No breaking change for default config; new flags behind feature flag 'tool_fanout_v2'.
Default behavior unchanged unless 'tool_fanout_v2' is enabled. Admins can opt into deterministic ordering and per-tool retries via route config. SDK helpers provide backward-compatible wrappers for common patterns.
Unit tests for coordinator state machine, property tests for dedup token uniqueness, integration harness with synthetic slow/failing tools, e2e streaming run against canary cluster. QA: run full streaming test matrix and perf canary with 1000 parallel sessions.
Benchmarked with 1-5 parallel tool calls; median token latency unchanged; 99th percentile increases by ~4% with gate disabled, and ~1.5% with gate enabled because of early partial flush. Cost impact negligible; batching unaffected.
Alice Chen: 'Coordinator looks good; please add more comments around state transitions and explain how partial vs final injection replaces vs appends in the streaming protocol.'
Jordan Li (author): 'Added explicit state diagram and inline comments in coordinator.rs; clarified replacement vs append semantics in protocol.proto and docs.'
Raj Patel: 'Can we avoid retrying non-idempotent tools by default? Also concerned about dedup token collision if request_id space is reused.'
Jordan Li: 'Non-idempotent tools default to max_attempts=1. Dedup token uses a 128-bit UUID derived from request_id + tool_index + request_nonce; added test to simulate request_id reuse across quick restarts.'
Priya Sinha: 'Integration tests look good; e2e streaming shows no regression in median latency but there is a 7% tail increase in the 99.9th percentile under 5 concurrent tools. Is that acceptable?'
Jordan Li: 'Measured with the backpressure gate off vs on. With gate enabled, tail latency regresses by ~2%. Included a config knob to trade latency for completeness; added docs describing recommended settings (routes with latency SLO < 200ms keep gate off and use async tool mode).'
integration-tests initially failed (flaky mock tool harness) at 2026-02-18; fixed harness race in tests, reran; all checks green by 2026-02-20
Feature behind flag. Recommend enabling for selective customers in canary with support present. Watch e2e streaming 99.9p and tool invocation error rates for first 48h after rollout.

payload.body:
Motivation: Quantized inference (INT8/FP8) at production scale is dominated by two things: kernel micro-inefficiencies when lanes compete for the dequant path, and wasted cycles waiting on KV cache tile loads that are not locality-aware. This PR introduces two cooperating runtime optimizations to address those hotspots: a cross-lane affinity mapper that pins logical KV ranges and compute lanes to consistent worker contexts, and a fused dequant prefetcher that stages dequantized tiles into a small software-managed staging buffer so kernels see warm data with reduced memory fanout.

High-level changes (single-string): Added an affinity mapping layer to the kernel runtime that emits lightweight hints to the scheduler (runtime/affinity/mapper.{cc,h}) and exposes a non-breaking opt-in flag (--quant-affinity=on). Implemented a fused dequant prefetch path in runtime/kernel/prefetcher_int8.cc that performs on-the-fly dequant + reorder into a contiguous staging slab sized per-GPU SM cluster. Updated the continuous-batching controller (runtime/scheduler/continuous_batching.rs) to honor affinity hints and prefer batching requests with matching KV affinity, reducing cross-warp memory pressure. Microkernel updates include a small API surface (runtime/kernel/tile_view.h) used by the prefetcher and int8 kernels to map staged tiles with zero-copy when supported.

Performance summary: On internal Llama-65B INT8 and FP8 quant profiles with 2k token windows and mixed request sizes, end-to-end P95 latency decreased by 8-12% and aggregate throughput improved by 16-22% on our CI GPU fleet (A100/A30 mixes). For KV-heavy chat workloads (prefix reuse > 75%) we observe up to 28% reduction in memory bandwidth utilization and 10-15% lower token cost due to fewer kernel stalls. Microbenchmarks included 1k/2k/4k token sweeps across batch sizes 1..32.

Compatibility and rollout: The changes are opt-in by default (quant-affinity=off). We ship with a canary rollout plan: enable on Dedicated dev pools for 48h, monitor token-level latency/CPU/GPU metrics and KV cache hit/miss ratios using Redwood Console dashboards, escalate if regression beyond 3% P95 or new OOMs are observed. No public API changes; SDKs unchanged.

Testing: Added unit tests for affinity mapping logic and prefetcher correctness (tests/affinity_mapper_test.cc, tests/prefetcher_int8_test.py). Added an end-to-end quant perf job to the CI benchmark matrix (benchmarks/quant_canary.yml). Ran extended stress on perf-canary cluster for 72h and validated rollback path.

Safety: Prefetcher includes a per-GPU budget and adaptive backoff; it will disable itself on sustained memory pressure or when kv-cache hit-rate drops below configured threshold. Affinity mapping falls back to existing scheduler behavior if hinting is unsupported or if head_branch config is absent.

Related work: This PR complements recent continuous-batching improvements and kv-cache routing changes (see ENG-1887 and PRs referenced in the linked linear items). It intentionally avoids modifying kernel numerical pathways — dequant semantics are unchanged and validated against float baselines. Refer to linked Linear tasks for rollout playbook and dashboards to watch.
Lina Gomez: Great direction — can we add a guard that disables affinity when cross-node KV replication is active? (requested change)
Maya Thompson: Added a guard that checks replication_mode; mapper now falls back to default when replication is async. See mapper.cc lines ~120-140.
Arjun Patel: Initial run showed a flaky perf test; looks like the staging slab sizing underestimated worst-case FP8 tile expansion. Suggest doubling max slab size with adaptive shrink. (requested change)
Maya Thompson: Implemented adaptive sizing with a cap controlled by runtime flag --prefetch-slab-max-mb; updated tests to exercise the cap.
Samir Kaur: Code looks safe; nvprof traces show reduced global loads per token. Approving once CI green. (approved)
CI Bot: perf/quant_bench infra failed on first run due to missing CUDA driver on runner; re-run succeeded. (info)
Add cross-lane affinity mapper and fused dequant prefetcher to reduce latency and improve throughput for INT8/FP8 quantized workloads. Opt-in via --quant-affinity flag. Can be enabled progressively via canary rollout.
If enabled in production, watch P95 latency, GPU memory pressure, and KV cache miss-rate. Fallback is automatic on OOM or sustained miss-rate regression; operator can toggle --quant-affinity off at runtime or use the rollout controls in Redwood Console.
P95 -8..-12% across A100/A30 fleet; throughput +16..+22% on representative llm-65b quant workloads; up to 28% memory-bandwidth reduction on KV-heavy traces. Test harness: 72h perf-canary sweep with batch sizes 1..32 and token lengths 1k/2k/4k.

Motivation: reduce end-to-end token latency for small-batch streaming workloads by minimizing memory traffic and branch mispredictions in the INT8/FP8 inference path. Summary: implement a compact hotpath that inlines dequantization into select attention and feed-forward microkernels, introduces a tiny relay stage to forward quantized metadata to the kernel without materializing dequant tensors, and hooks the KV-cache prefetcher to materialize only the currently needed KV window. Changes include a new IR pass (CompactDequantInline), kernel signatures that accept packed scale/zero-point hints, a lightweight per-stream relay buffer, and scheduler hints to keep hotpath lanes resident on the same worker thread. Testing: unit tests for the IR pass and kernel ABI changes; microbench harness comparing 1-8 token batch latencies across A100/RTX workloads; integration test exercising continuous batching with streaming TTFB targets. Rollout plan: default OFF; gated by the runtime config key runtime.hotpath.compact_dequant and opt-in on Dedicated for two weeks; canary traffic via rollout policy to 5% then 25% then 100%. Backwards compatibility: provides adapter when kernels are not available; falls back to existing dequant+kernel path. Checklist: - implement IR pass and codegen; - update kernel ABI and add validation tests; - update kv prefetch windowing; - add CI microbench step; - document runtime flag and rollout notes. Related: ENG-4872 (low-latency small-batch streaming), ENG-4901 (kv cache windowing improvements).
Jonas Park (review): Overall looks promising. Please add a safety net so the relay buffer cannot grow unbounded under pathological streaming clients.
Priya Reddy (reply): Added a bounded LRU-like eviction for relay entries and a per-stream max size config (runtime.hotpath.relay_max_entries).
Eleni Papadopoulos (review): The packed-metadata ABI is clever but needs a clear backwards compatibility test when older kernels are present on Dedicated nodes.
Priya Reddy (reply): Added an adapter layer and a unit test that simulates an older kernel returning EINVAL so runtime falls back to the legacy path; documented behavior in the ops doc.
Miguel Santana (review): Microbench artifacts show 8-12% p50 latency improvement on small batches; can we add a cost model note for token billing changes?
Priya Reddy (reply): Added a short note in docs/ops and a console flag to surface estimated token CPU/GPU savings for canary users.
Eleni Papadopoulos (approval): Approving pending CI-green and the relay bounds change.
CI (bot): One flaky test in bench microbench harness; reran and all green.
Local microbench (A100): 1-token batch p50 -12%, p95 -8%; 4-token batch p50 -9%; throughput unchanged for large batches. Memory traffic to global dequant buffers reduced by ~40% for hotpathed models.
Runtime: add compact dequant hotpath that inlines dequant into selected attention/FFN kernels to reduce memory traffic and p50/p95 latency for small-batch streaming workloads; gated behind runtime.hotpath.compact_dequant and off by default; KV cache prefetch windowing integrated to avoid unnecessary materialization; rollout controlled via canary.
Default disabled; to enable on Dedicated set runtime.hotpath.compact_dequant=true and configure runtime.hotpath.relay_max_entries; monitor runtime.hotpath.hotpath_lane_misses and kv.prefetch.materialization metrics. If unexpected fallbacks observed, check kernel ABI compatibility logs (hotpath.abadapter.warn).
This PR was driven by customer SUP-1198 where a payments product observed high TTFB for streaming completion endpoints; compact hotpath reduces tail latency without changing model outputs.

payload.body:
Problem: The OpenAI Responses API introduced a set of semantics (responses vs completions, explicit seed/determinism controls, and response-level metadata passthrough) that our OpenAI-compatibility layer did not fully honor. This caused incorrect caching behavior, sporadic nondeterministic results in determinism test suites, and loss of user-supplied metadata when proxying requests.

This PR implements end-to-end support for the new Responses API variants in the compatibility shim, including: mapping `responses.mode` to appropriate model routing, plumbing `seed` and `deterministic` flags through to our runtime so user-requested determinism is honored, and preserving arbitrary `metadata` objects from request -> internal request -> response. It also includes several small streaming stability fixes uncovered while testing long-running streaming responses (fragment reassembly and backpressure on partial tool calls).

What changed (high level):
- Add a Responses-compatible request parser that accepts both completions and responses shapes and normalizes to our internal request model.
- Expose `seed` and `deterministic` parameters in the OpenAI-compat layer and ensure those are communicated to the runtime scheduling/kernel selection codepath so quantization/batching heuristics avoid interfering with deterministic runs.
- Preserve `metadata` keys on the proxied request and include them verbatim on the returned response envelope; add whitelist-based passthrough config for enterprise users wanting stronger controls.
- Streaming fixes: ensure partial tool/function call events include metadata and stream markers in the same envelope to avoid reassembly ambiguity for clients. Add idempotent reassembly on the client-side helper we publish in the SDKs.
- Tests: add unit and integration tests for parse/serialize roundtrips, deterministic seeds, and an end-to-end streaming canary that exercises large payload streaming + metadata passthrough.

Checklist:
- [x] Compatibility parsing and normalization
- [x] Runtime flags plumbing (seed/deterministic)
- [x] Metadata passthrough + enterprise whitelist config
- [x] Streaming reassembly fixes and unit tests
- [x] Integration canary and e2e tests in eval-harness
- [x] Documentation snippets and migration notes in redwood-docs

Design notes and rationale:
- Determinism is best-effort across lower-level optimizations. We mark requests with determinism metadata and ensure the scheduler selects single-worker, non-batched execution when deterministic=true or seed is set. This increases latency/cost for those requests; documentation and telemetry flag these requests separately so customers can understand tradeoffs.
- Metadata passthrough is implemented as a minimal-copy envelope change at the compatibility shim boundary; we deliberately avoid schema enforcement in the shim and provide an enterprise toggle to enforce a server-side whitelist for regulated customers.
- Streaming: inconsistent partial envelopes were the main cause of reassembly bugs — we now include sequence numbers and a final=true marker for tool call closures; SDK helpers were adjusted accordingly.

Backward compatibility and migration: The shim accepts both old completions-style requests and the newer responses payloads. Most customers require no change. For deterministic workloads, customers should set `deterministic: true` or provide `seed` to get reproducible outputs; documentation link: https://docs.redwood.ai/openai-compat#responses-determinism

Rollout plan:
- Feature behind compat flag `openai_responses_v2` on the tenancy and account level.
- Canary rollout to 2% of traffic for 48 hours with synthetic prompts exercising streaming and deterministic paths.
- Monitor token-latency, deterministic-error-rate, and metadata-loss metrics in console.

Related: Linear ENG-4821, PM-219. See also the eval-harness PR that adds the deterministic test vectors.
Ethan Clarke: Please confirm scheduler behavior under heavy batching; deterministic requests should avoid batching — responded with scheduler unit that enforces single-worker mode when deterministic=true.
Lina Gomez: We need a feature flag so enterprise customers can opt out of metadata passthrough — added ops/feature_flags.yaml and enterprise whitelist config; see docs update.
Jordan Park: Streaming reassembly looked flaky in initial run — fixed race by adding sequence numbers and final marker; reran streaming canary and all passes.
Maya Singh (author): addressed comments, added additional integration tests, and updated docs with migration guidance.
OpenAI-compat: Adds support for Responses API variants including seed/deterministic flags and metadata passthrough. Deterministic requests will select single-worker, non-batched execution — may increase latency/cost. Feature is behind `openai_responses_v2` flag; see docs for migration steps.
payload.title: OpenAI-compat: Support Responses API variants + seed/determinism flags and metadata passthrough

payload.body:
Motivation: Our OpenAI compatibility layer currently exposes two pain points for customers using function/tool calling: 1) model-provided tool schemas don't map cleanly to Redwood internal tool descriptors (naming/param shapes), and 2) streaming tool invocations occasionally emit fragmented or partial tool messages over SSE which breaks downstream tool runners and observability. This PR implements a server-side schema normalization layer, a clearer tool_choice fallback heuristic, and a streaming envelope so tool messages are only emitted when complete.

What this changes (high level):
- Add a schema mapper that translates OpenAI-style 'functions' definitions into Redwood's internal tool descriptor format, with field aliasing, type coercion rules, and a validation step. The mapper supports a small rule set (rename map, required->optional normalization, array<->single coercion) and is extensible.
- Implement explicit tool_choice semantics: when a model returns an explicit tool selection we prefer it; when the model returns ambiguous 'tool' or partial name we run a deterministic resolver that prefers exact-name matches, then best fuzzy match, then a configured fallback tool (configurable per-tenant). This removes flakiness seen when models return partial names or alternate case.
- Streaming stability: updated stream_chunker to buffer tool invocation events and emit a single 'tool_invocation' envelope once the tool message is fully assembled. The envelope includes the normalized schema name and a checksum header to allow downstream deduplication. This prevents clients from receiving half-formed JSON that can break tool runners.

Motivation: our private-installer release pipeline did not have a compact, signed rollforward index optimized for long retention windows. This caused large manifest churn and slowed upgrades for air-gapped customers. It also wires the Terraform module for installer releases to stamp retention policies and exposes a Helm chart checksum annotation so operator upgrades are only triggered when the signed index changes. Motivation: Recent Responses API variants require stricter preservation of client-provided attributes (rng seeds, client metadata tags) and more robust streaming reassembly semantics when chunks are delivered out-of-order or partial. This PR implements a conservative stream-stabilizer state machine in the OpenAI-compat adapter, preserves and forwards client attribute headers into Responses vX framing, and tightens tool/function-call boundary markers to avoid misattribution during streaming reassembly. Goals: 1) Ensure rng/seed hints and opaque client metadata are present on the final assembled Response object and on any tool-call events emitted during streaming. 2) Make streaming tolerant to chunk loss and reordering by introducing sequence markers and a fallback reassembly path that requests a non-streaming re-fetch for the last-incomplete span. 3) Keep the compatibility layer backwards-compatible with existing vX-1 and vX behaviors; expose a toggle (compat.mode=stable-stream) for customers to opt into the stricter reassembly semantics. Summary of changes: - OpenAI adapter: add attributes header passthrough (x-rw-client-attrs/x-rw-rng-hint) and carry-through logic into response attributes. - Streaming reassembly: introduce StreamStabilizer with sequence markers, per-chunk checksum hint, and a compact reassembly buffer that triggers an inline re-fetch if a gap persists beyond a configurable window. - Tool/function call handling: emit explicit tool-call-start and tool-call-end markers in the chunk stream; attach preserved client attributes to tool-call events so downstream tooling receives the same metadata as final Responses objects. - SDKs: lightweight client header propagation helpers added to Python and TypeScript SDKs; example in examples/streams/toolcall-preserve.md. - Tests & CI: add deterministic replay tests for mixed-order chunk delivery and unit tests for attribute propagation. Backwards compatibility and rollout: default behavior remains conservative (existing flows unchanged). The new compat.mode flag is off by default; feature rollout to hosted begins with Canary and Dedicated beta. See release_notes field for user-facing changes and migration guidance.

Context and motivation: We observed frequent noisy canaries where short-lived anomalies caused either unnecessary rollbacks or prolonged manual interventions. This PR implements the "Canary Lifeline" controller: a probationary rollforward flow that allows a canary to progress under strict probation rules and applies a probabilistic rollback scorer when signals deteriorate. It reduces manual triage and allows safe, granular promotion of models in high-traffic environments. Design summary: The controller introduces two runtime primitives: (1) probationary windows that allow ephemeral metric volatility without immediate rollback, and (2) a probabilistic rollforward scorer that computes a confidence score for promoting or auto-reverting a canary based on multi-signal aggregation (latency P95, error-rate, model-quality delta, cost-per-token). Scoring is temporally weighted so recently improving signals are favored while persistent regressions escalate the rollback probability. Implementation highlights: - New controller: redwood/orchestrator/canary_lifeline.go implements the probation lifecycle (phases: seed, probation, verification, commit, rewind) and hooks into the existing rollout engine. - Probationary scoring engine: redwood/orchestrator/rollforward_scorer.go provides modular signal adapters and a configurable scoring policy (decay half-life, threshold bands, escalation multiplier). - API types: redwood/api/v1/rollout_types.go extends RolloutSpec with probationConfig and rollforwardPolicy fields. - Console: a small UI panel redwood/console/ui/rollouts/CanaryLifelinePanel.tsx surfaces score trajectories and suggests human action buttons (hold, promote, abort). - Tests and docs: integration tests under redwood/tests/integration/canary_lifeline_test.go plus a runbook at redwood/docs/runbooks/canary-lifeline.md. Backwards compatibility: Default behavior preserves existing rollout semantics when probationConfig is omitted. The controller is gated behind a feature flag rollout.control.canary_lifeline=false by default in config. Migration plan: - Canary Lifeline is off by default. - Early adopters can opt in per-namespace and pin policy parameters. - We'll run a staged internal rollout (dev -> staging -> controlled pilot) and monitor the new metrics introduced (probation_score, probation_duration_ms, rollforward_invocations). Testing and validation: Unit tests for scoring logic, simulated traffic harness for stochastic evaluation, and two integration smoke runs against the test cluster were added. CI: initial lint failure on TypeScript formatting fixed in follow-up commit; full pipeline green after rerun. Rollout/runbook: The docs include an operator playbook with recommended thresholds, synthetic smoke commands, and a retro-triage checklist for policy tuning. Observability: New metrics and tracing spans were added; the Console panel links to raw traces and the Eval set diff used for model-quality calculations. Risks and mitigations: - Risk: overly permissive probation could hide regressions. Mitigation: conservative default thresholds and a visible probation_score below 0.35 triggers auto-quarantine. - Risk: score drift due to noisy metrics. Mitigation: configurable decay and an anomaly-detection prefilter that gates signals. Related work and references: ENG-2439: probationary-rollforward-scorer (design); ENG-2501: rollout-metrics-unification. Files changed (high-level): see files_changed list for exact paths. Merge notes: squashed into main. Post-merge actions: schedule a six-week pilot with SLA-backed teams and create an alert for probation_score anomalies to the SRE rotations.
Owen Park: Nice separation of concerns. Two asks: (1) add a bounded memory queue for signal snapshots in the scorer to avoid unbounded allocations, (2) add a short note in the runbook about how to interpret low-confidence transient dips.
Author (Marina Kovács): Addressed — added a ring buffer abstraction and expanded the runbook section. See commit b9124f1 and runbook edits.
Diego Alvarez: Can we expose the probation_score series in the telemetry export? Ops needs it in Prometheus for alerting.
Author: Exposed probation_score and probation_duration_ms as Prometheus metrics and included an example alert rule in the docs.
Priya Ramanathan: LGTM after the CI flake fixed. Confirming the feature flag is off by default.
Maintainer (merge-bot): All checks passed; merging via squash.

payload.body:
Context: Our OpenAI-compat layer has had recurring issues when clients upload ambiguous or binary attachments without clear content-type or length headers. These cause parsing retries, confused streaming boundaries, and occasional function_call failures when tool runtimes receive corrupted payloads. This PR introduces two complementary protections: (1) deterministic media negotiation and normalization so the compat layer always annotates attachments with a canonical content-type + checksum; (2) per-file ingestion rate limits and adaptive chunk checks to prevent slow/bursty clients from overwhelming streaming parsers and downstream tool runtimes.

What this changes (high level):
- Compat layer now enforces an Accept/Content-Type negotiation step for incoming attachments. Preferred content-types for tool calls are application/json (pointer/meta), application/octet-stream (binary payloads), and multipart/form-data for multi-part uploads. Ambiguous cases (e.g. text/plain without charset for likely binary data) are rejected with a 400 and a clear error that lists accepted types.
- Attachments without a declared content-type will trigger a lightweight sniff: if first 512 bytes look like UTF-8 JSON/text we label application/json or text/plain; otherwise we label application/octet-stream. Sniffing is deterministic and logged for audits.
- Each file stream now carries an enforced per-file ingress rate limit (configurable per-customer and per-route). By default set to 4 MB/s for hosted API and 8 MB/s for Dedicated. Exceeding the rate returns a 429 with Retry-After and a hint header (X-File-Rate-Limit).
- For streaming uploads we added a small windowing protocol: the compat proxy tolerates out-of-order chunk arrival within a 500ms reorder window, but rejects incremental chunks that lack proper boundary markers when rate limits are tripped. This significantly reduces repeated partial-parsing in the serving runtime.
- For function/tool calls that reference files, we now require file metadata (content_type, size, sha256) in the function_call arguments. If missing, the compat layer computes sha256 and injects metadata before handing to the tool runtime. This prevents tool runtimes from having to re-read streams and reduces platform I/O.

Why this is safe and backward compatible:
- Well-formed clients that already send content-type and standard multipart/form-data will be unaffected.
- Clients that relied on opaque coercion of text/plain->binary will now get a clear error and guidance to set Content-Type or wrap the file as base64 in JSON. The error message includes a one-line migration hint to keep developer friction low.

Tests & validation included:
- Unit tests for negotiation logic, sniff heuristics, and sha256 injection.
- Integration tests that exercise multipart uploads, chunked transfer-encoding streams, and slow-client scenarios using our perf-canary harness.
- End-to-end tests: function_call with file refs across redwood (compat) -> runtime -> tool-invoker. Added a compatibility matrix test that runs against a matrix of SDK versions (python:1.x/2.x, ts:1.x) to ensure we don't regress client expectations.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implement negotiation + sniffing code in compat proxy
- [x] Add per-file rate-limiter middleware with config knobs on route/customer level
- [x] Compute and inject file metadata (sha256, content_type) for function_call refs
- [x] Add logging + audit events for sniffing decisions
- [x] Add unit/integration/e2e tests
- [x] Update docs/compat-guide (short migration blurb)

Related: ENG-2330 (rate limiting webhooks influenced design), PM-411 (docs/migration text), SUP-981 (customer incident that motivated stricter errors).
Adds stricter media-type negotiation in the OpenAI-compat layer for tool/file attachments, plus configurable per-file ingestion rate limits to protect streaming and tool-call stability. No breaking changes for well-formed clients; some malformed/ambiguous uploads will now be rejected instead of auto-coerced.
Ava Chen (reviewer): Please add a short migration note in docs/compatibility that callers should set Content-Type or base64-encode ambiguous files. Also call out default rate limits for Hosted vs Dedicated.
Rohan Patel (author): Added docs/compatibility/attachments.md and included default values in infra/config/defaults.yaml. I also added audit events when sniffing is used so we can count how often clients omit Content-Type.
Marta Novak (reviewer): Reasonable. Please add a unit test that specifically asserts that text/plain short snippets are not misclassified as binary when the first bytes are ASCII but content-length is > 1MB.

Rohan Patel (author): Added TestSniffLargeAsciiInBinary to services/compat/tests/sniff_test.go and updated the heuristics to consider size heuristics for ASCII-only streams. CI green after change.
Diego Alvarez (approver): Verified e2e with dedicated config. Metrics look stable and there is a small perf win from avoiding re-reads in runtime. Approving for squash-merge.

Add cross-repo artifact origin aggregation to release index used by private-installer; includes pipeline changes, index schema extension, signature/verification cross-checks, and docs for operator consumption.
Context and motivation: Private-installer releases consume artifacts produced by multiple build pipelines (core runtime, helm charts, terraform modules, third-party vendor artifacts). Existing release index entries pointed to single build blobs but lost origin metadata (repo/build-job/container image digest). This PR extends the release index generation to aggregate origin provenance across repos/pipelines so operators can inspect where each artifact came from and verify chain-of-custody at install time.

What this PR does: - Adds an `origins` aggregate block to the release index JSON that lists source repository, pipeline job id, build commit, and optional SBOM/cosign references per artifact. - Modifies the private-installer indexer job to query multiple artifact registries and cross-reference artifact digests to upstream build metadata (via the new origin-mapper service). - Adds origin-mapper microservice (lightweight Go lambda) that merges build metadata across internal buildkite/jenkins/job-run APIs and returns a normalized origin statement for an artifact digest. - Updates CI/CD pipelines: new step in release pipeline to call origin-mapper and attach signed origin blobs to TUF/manifest staging area. - Enhances verification: indexer validates cosign signatures on origin blobs (if present) and records signature verification result in the index. - Adds operator docs and an index API example in private-installer docs for auditors to query artifact origins during upgrades/rollbacks.

Checklist (implemented): - [x] Extend release index schema (index-schema/v2) with `origins` field and verification metadata - [x] Origin-mapper service implementation and unit tests - [x] Release pipeline changes (buildkite/jenkins) to emit origin blobs - [x] Indexer changes in private-installer repo to consume origin blobs - [x] Add integration test that replays multi-repo build metadata into staging index - [x] Docs: private-installer operator guide section on origin queries - [x] Security review: minimal privileges for origin-mapper to query job metadata APIs

Commits (high-level): - feat(indexer): add origin mapping hooks and schema v2 metadata - feat(origin-mapper): initial service with buildkite and jenkins adapters - ci(release): add origin-stage and sign-origin steps, upload to staging TUF area - docs(installer): add operator guide and example queries - test(integration): multi-repo origin aggregation smoke test - fix(ci): tolerate missing SBOM references for third-party mirrored artifacts

Files/areas changed (high-level): - private-installer/cmd/indexer: indexer changed to call origin-mapper and persist origins into index JSON - private-installer/internal/index/schema_v2.go: new schema and JSON marshaling changes - tools/origin-mapper/: new Go service and adapters for buildkite/jenkins - infra/ci/pipelines/release.yml: added origin-stage, sign-origin and upload steps - docs/private-installer/origins.md: operator documentation and API examples - charts/private-installer/values.yaml: small annotation for chart provenance - scripts/dev/replay-origins.sh: local dev helper to simulate upstream metadata

Review conversation (summary): - Lina: "Nice; can we guarantee origin-mapper rate limits won't blow up during a large release?" Author: "Origin-mapper queues queries and caches job metadata for 24h; added circuit-breaker and bulk query path. See origin-mapper/README for eviction rules." - Ethan: "Add tests for mirrored artifacts where upstream job metadata is absent." Author: "Added integration test that marks missing upstream metadata and attaches best-effort origin assertion with source:mirror and mirror-ref." - Zoe: "Signature verification path looks good, but require operator flag to enforce failed verification as hard-fail for critical releases." Author: "Added CLI flag `--enforce-origin-verification` to indexer and documented recommended usage in docs." - Security review (internal): "Ensure origin-mapper tokens scoped read-only and short lived." Author: "Confirmed; CI injects ephemeral tokens, and service uses read-only tokens with minimal TTL. Details in infra/ci/README-security.md."

CI summary: - Initial run: integration tests failed due to missing adapter for legacy Jenkins job API (fixed in second commit). - Second run: unit + integration + lint passed. - E2E staging run: origin blobs uploaded and cosign verification passed for signed artifacts; unsigned third-party artifacts recorded with `verified:false`. Final ci_status: pass.

Edge cases and limitations: - For artifacts mirrored from external vendors we may not retrieve upstream build job metadata; index will include `source: mirror` and a pointer to mirror provenance where available. - This PR does not change TUF signing policy; origin blobs themselves are uploaded to staging and signed with cosign in the release pipeline. TUF package signing remains the authoritative release signature. - Performance: origin-mapper adds an extra ~200-400ms per artifact during index generation in current staging; indexer runs concurrently and batching mitigates impact in typical releases.

Migration and rollout plan: - Index schema v2 is backward-compatible: indexer writes `schema_version: 2` and tooling falls back to v1 when v2 entry not present. - Rollout: release pipeline will emit v2 indexes to a staging bucket for two release cycles; operator tooling supports reading v1 and v2. - Post-merge action: update release-runbooks and notify SRE and compliance teams to start auditing origin queries on next private-installer release.

Merge outcome: Approved by Lina and Zoe after two rounds of review and tests; merged via squash on 2025-11-12.

Notes for future work: - Consider adding signed SBOM references into origin blobs for deeper attestation. - Explore offloading origin metadata to a dedicated provenance catalog service with search capabilities.

Background: Existing KV cache samplers capture coarse hit/miss and age distributions but miss short-lived reuse patterns and interleaved-key churn that drive worst-case tail latency. This PR introduces a low-overhead strided sampling approach that observes per-key delta reuse distances (kvdeltas) and aggregates them into compact histograms, plus a lightweight "mini-telemetry" export for microbench dashboards. Motivation: help ops and SREs detect pathological access patterns (stride patterns, near-term reuse storms) without enabling heavy kernel tracing. Key changes: 1) runtime/kvcache/strided_sampler.cc/h: new sampler implementing a cross-thread strided sampling scheme. The sampler chooses a small set of candidate slots per epoch and records per-sample kvdelta (number of requests since last touch) as a 16-bit delta to a ring buffer. Sampling is non-blocking, uses atomic 32-bit packs to reduce contention, and supports per-tenant sampling rates. 2) runtime/kvcache/kvcache_metrics.cpp: adds kvdelta histogram aggregation (log-buckets), windowed resets, and an on-demand flush API used by the mini-telemetry exporter. 3) tools/microbench/replay_harness: a tiny trace replayer that can inject synthetic stride patterns and measure observed kvdelta distributions; includes a new test trace format and conversion tool. 4) observability/exporters/mini_telemetry_exporter: CSV + speedscope-friendly timeline exporter that maps sampler ring samples into micro-frames (10ms buckets) and emits a compact JSON artifact that dashboards ingest. 5) console/dashboard/annotations: a new dashboard panel for KV delta heatmaps and an integration point for the mini telemetry artifacts. 6) added unit tests and a microbench scenario under perf/benchmarks/kvcache_strided_test.cc with baseline and stressed configurations. Runtime flags: --kvcache-stride-sample= (controls stride size), --kvcache-sample-rate=

(probability), --mini-telemetry-dir= (emit path). Backwards compatibility: sampler is opt-in (disabled by default); no user-visible API changes. Performance: microbench numbers included in this PR show median overhead <0.8% and p99 overhead <2.5% on a 512-concurrency Llama-like workload when enabled at recommended rates. The sampler exposed several previously hidden patterns in internal traces: short reuse storms and interleaved-key eviction cascades; these were used to inform a subsequent change (ENG-1902) to prefetch heuristics. Test plan: unit tests for ring buffer correctness and atomic packing; integration test running trace replayer with known patterns; perf microbench run with and without sampler demonstrating low overhead. Motivation: Current observability surfaces provide detailed per-request token cost and latency, but we lack a scalable, route-oriented rollup and an efficient way to correlate sampled KV-cache traces back to route-level cost attribution. This PR implements route rollups for token-level metrics, a lightweight attribution index that ties sampled KV/tracer spans to route keys, and a set of Grafana panels and alert rule improvements to reduce noisy alerts on long-tail routes.

Design summary: 
- Prometheus metric rollups: add prometheus metrics with suffixed _route_rollup that aggregate token_count, token_cost_usd, and tail_latency_ms by route and time window. Rollups are emitted at the collector sidecar and computed with series cardinality controls (hashed route buckets + tag cardinality caps).
- Attribution index: introduce an append-only, sharded in-memory index (observability/attribution_index) that stores a compact mapping from sampled trace_id -> {route_bucket, token_window_hash}. Span enrichment adds an index lookup id to tracer spans so sampled KV-cache traces can be resolved to route rollups without scanning logs. The index is ephemeral and bounded by memory and TTL to preserve privacy and performance.
- Tracing changes: add a small span attribute `obs.route_bucket` and `obs.attribution_id` for sampled KV/kv-cache spans. OTEL exporter includes these attributes and a small indexer process batches them to the attribution index.
- Dashboards & alerts: new Grafana dashboard `Route Rollups` with top-N route cost/latency panels, 95/99 percentile time-series per route bucket, and a heatmap for route cost concentration. Prometheus alert rules tuned to use percentile-based thresholds per route_bucket instead of a single global SLO, and with a noise suppression window for routes under 100 requests/min.

Backward compatibility and migration: instrumentation changes are additive. Rollups are opt-in via feature flag `obs.route_rollups.enabled` (off by default); tracing attributes are guarded by `obs.attribution.tracing` (default on for sampled traces). The attribution index runs in the observability sidecar by default but can be disabled for Private installs to avoid memory overhead.

Performance and safety: rollups reduce cardinality by hashing route names into 256 buckets by default; this value is configurable. Attribution index uses a fixed-size ring buffer per shard with LRU eviction to prevent unbounded growth. Benchmarks included show <2% CPU overhead on a 1000rps mixed workload with sampling_rate=0.02.

Files changed: Collector sidecar rollup emitter, OTEL span enricher, attribution index implementation, Grafana JSON dashboard, Prometheus alert rules, docs and migration notes, e2e tests and a small perf benchmark harness.

Checklist: 
- [x] Add collector-side rollup emitter
- [x] Add attribution index and span enrichment
- [x] Add Grafana dashboard and alert tuning
- [x] Add unit tests for index eviction behavior
- [x] Add e2e test that validates attribution lookup for sampled traces
- [x] Add migration docs and feature flags

Impact: When enabled, product teams will see aggregated per-route cost/latency insights with reduced cardinality, and SRE will be able to configure per-route alerts based on percentiles. Short-term risk: potential alerting blind spots if teams forget to enable rollups for newly added routes; mitigated by a dashboard flag that highlights routes without rollup coverage.

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps attribution metadata minimal to avoid PII leakage. The attribution_id is a salted hash and the index TTL defaults to 5 minutes. Ops can tune both via config. For Private deployments, ops can disable the attribution index or reduce sampling.

References: Linear ENG-7421, ENG-7540 for requirements; internal perf benchmark results attached in commits.

Diego Morales (2026-02-17): The attribution index eviction policy needs clearer invariants around TTL vs LRU. Marco: added unit tests and expanded comments in index.go; eviction uses TTL first then LRU within the TTL window.
Priya Patel (2026-02-18): Alert rule for tail_latency should include a suppression window for <100rpm routes. Marco: implemented suppression and added a dashboard panel that highlights suppressed routes.
Aisha Kaur (2026-02-19): Minor nits on PromQL in route_alerts.yaml. Marco: fixed and squashed into branch.
Diego Morales (2026-02-19): Approved after tests green.

Motivation: Multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads observed tail latency spikes when NCCL collectives contended with kernel launches and KV cache eviction/prefetch activity. This PR introduces an eviction-aware launch scheduler that coordinates kernel launches with the NCCL progress threads and KV cache prefetch/eviction signals to increase overlap and reduce stalls. Design: 1) Introduce a lightweight launch coordinator that tracks outstanding collective windows and delays non-critical kernel launches until a safe interleaving point; 2) Add a KV cache eviction hint API used by the runtime to mark soon-to-be-evicted KV ranges so prefetch can be prioritized before large collectives; 3) Extend the communication scheduler to stagger stream priorities and use a small local crediting mechanism to avoid single-stream saturation at the NIC/NCCL layer; 4) Add dynamic kernel batching window adjustment to expand batching when collectives are imminent and shrink when latency SLOs are tight. Implementation notes: Changes touch runtime/comm, runtime/scheduler, runtime/kvcache, and tests. New unit and integration tests validate ordering constraints and ensure no deadlocks. Microbenchmarks: On 8xA100 TP-16 experiments with seq_len=2048 and batch=4, end-to-end p99 latency improved 32% (from 278ms to 190ms) and throughput increased 12% under load. Tail KV eviction stalls decreased by ~60% in trace-driven replay. Rollout: feature-flag guarded, gated behind a runtime config (scheduler.eviction_aware=true). Checklist: implement coordinator, add KV hint API, update NCCL stream priority heuristics, add tests, add perf harness and dashboards, document feature in runtime/README. Related: addresses ENG-8843 and is complementary to earlier NCCL-throttler work.

Evan Zhang: Added coordination_delay_ms and added a fast-path that bypasses the coordinator for single-GPU / non-collective-only traces. Microbenchmarks show <0.5% overhead on single-GPU microbenchmarks.
Carlos Rivera: Request change: the KV hint API surface should accept opaque tokens instead of raw KV ranges to allow more flexible eviction strategies downstream.
Evan Zhang: Updated API to accept token handle and added mapping layer in kv_prefetcher. Left the old helper for backwards compatibility for one release.
Aisha Kumari: Could we add an opt-in telemetry event for cases where we delay a launch for >10ms? That will help debugging in prod.
Evan Zhang: Added telemetry event 'launch_delay_exceeded' and a sampling policy. Will watch during canary.
Priya Menon: Approving after CI flakes were resolved and perf dashboard linked.
Carlos Rivera: Approved. Verified p99 improvements on our internal 8x A100 job.
Release Manager: Merging after canary passed. Merge method: squash.
Introduce eviction-aware launch scheduler to improve overlap of NCCL collectives and kernel launches, add KV eviction hint API, staggered stream priorities, and dynamic batching window adjustments. Expected benefits: reduced p99 tail latency for multi-GPU TP workloads and fewer KV-eviction stalls. Feature behind runtime.scheduler.eviction_aware toggle.

OpenAI Responses v12 compatibility: preserve JSON Schema structured-output fields, forward deterministic seed hints and nested metadata, improve tool/function-call handshake for streaming, and harden chunk reassembly/backpressure. No user-facing breaking changes. Rollout as canary then global.
Context: Customers are adopting the newer OpenAI Responses variants that include explicit JSON Schema structured output and richer seed/determinism hints. Previous adapters dropped nested attribute namespaces and occasionally dropped tool-call 'handshake' signals under high-concurrency streaming, resulting in incorrect structured outputs and flaky tool invocations. This PR introduces an upgraded compatibility bridge for Responses v12 (and v12beta) to preserve and forward: 1) JSON Schema/structured-output envelope fields, 2) seed/determinism hints and rng annotations, and 3) nested metadata provenance (trace, source, request-id) through both streaming and final non-stream paths.

Motivation: keep downstream consumers (tooling, evals, observability) deterministic and compatible when switching to new OpenAI-style Responses while maintaining production-grade streaming stability.

Summary of changes:
- Bridge: add explicit mapping rules for Responses v12 structured fields -> redwood \"attributes\" envelope; preserve user-provided JSON Schema keys verbatim and expose schema validation errors as structured diagnostics.
- Tool handshake: implement a lightweight two-phase \"handshake\" in the tool-call path so tool endpoints receive a deterministic invocation token and declared schema before tokenized stream begins; handshake survives transient reconnects and uses the request-level seed for deterministic tool behaviour.
- Streaming stability: improve chunk reassembly by adding sequence checks and idempotent merge logic (handles partial bytes and out-of-order chunks from proxy layers). Add adaptive backpressure that signals upstream when KV cache warmup increases per-token latency.
- Metadata passthrough: threaded nested metadata (source.trace_id / source.span / provenance) through the bridge and keep the original namespaced keys on the Redwood side for observability and auditing.
- Tests: add unit tests for schema passthrough and handshake, integration tests that exercise streaming reconnects and tool replays, and e2e with the Python SDK sample that exercises function-calling.
- Docs: new compatibility doc outlining behavior and recommended rollout (canary 5% -> 25% -> 100%), and changelog entries for the API surface.

Checklist:
- [x] adapter mappings implemented
- [x] handshake protocol added and documented
- [x] streaming reassembly/backpressure fixed and load-tested
- [x] unit/integration/e2e tests included
- [x] CI green and canary rollout plan added

Performance notes: under synthetic bench this change added ~0.3ms median per-request overhead for handshake on streaming function calls but reduced 99th percentile errors for tool calls by ~87% on the canary fleet. Related: ENG-1428 (Responses v12 compatibility), SUP-88 (customer-reported flaky toolcall under streaming).

Maya Singh: Addressed — validation errors are returned with structured diagnostics RFC and unit tests added (tests/unit/responses_v12_mapper_test.go).
Zoe Martinez: Handshake looks good; my only concern is the performance impact at high qps. Can we gate handshake with a feature flag for the first canary?
Maya Singh: Added feature flag and config flag for enabling handshake per-model and per-route; updated canary plan in docs.

Fix: Streaming chunk reassembly and backpressure signaling to reduce toolcall flakiness.

Motivation: production customers see wide variance in per-request unit economics depending on payload distribution, prefix repetition and model quantization. Manual tuning (batch sizes, KV cache TTLs, quant profile selection) is error-prone and often reactive. This PR introduces a small, conservative automation that sets default heuristics for batching and KV-caching and provides a quantization prescreen that recommends model-quant pairs with estimated token-cost delta. The goal is safe, backwards-compatible defaults that reduce tail cost by targeting common patterns while providing operators a transparent simulation-backed recommendation before changes are applied.

Summary of changes: 
- Heuristic controller that computes per-route defaults based on sampled request histograms (payload length, prefix reuse, latency SLO). Defaults influence: continuous batching target size, batching latency cushion, KV cache TTL and prefix fingerprint sampling rate.
- Quantization prescreen runner: offline simulation harness that runs candidate quant settings (int8/int4/relaxed FP16) against a small corpus and emits an estimated quality delta + cost delta. Results are surfaced to the console and to the unit-econ dashboard.
- Unit-econ estimator integration: lightweight cost estimator that combines model latency profiles, batch size, and token estimates to show projected per-1M-token cost for recommended defaults.
- Safe rollout: new "safe-mode" flag prevents any automatic application of defaults in Dedicated/Private; defaults are suggestions unless operator flips the apply flag.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc + simulation plan (linked Linear ENG-4821)
- [x] Unit tests for controller heuristics and prescreen harness
- [x] Integration tests exercising sample route and reporting to the unit-econ estimator 
- [x] E2E smoke against real traffic replay in the benchmark-lab (no regressions)
- [x] Console UI hooks (backend only) for recommendations
- [x] Rollout plan + rollback path documented

Why this is conservative: defaults are computed from a 24h sampled histogram and bounded by policy caps; any recommendation labelled "apply-recommended" must be explicitly enabled per-organization. The prescreen reports an expected quality delta and includes a bootstrap validation step using customer-provided eval prompts if available.

Commit summary: 
- Add heuristic controller and sampling pipeline
- Add quant prescreen harness and simulation runner
- Integrate estimator with console recommendation API
- Add unit & integration tests; update observability events and metrics

Files changed (high level): 
- runtime/controller/unit_econ_heuristic.py (new) - core controller, sampling, default computation
- runtime/quant/prescreen_runner.py (new) - simulation harness for quant profiles
- runtime/estimator/cost_estimator.py (new) - unit-econ estimator and projection APIs
- console/api/recommendations.py - new endpoints for recommendations and prescreen results
- benchmark-lab/replays/unit_econ_smoke.json - sample traffic used in tests
- tests/unit/test_heuristics.py, tests/integration/test_prescreen_integration.py
- metrics/events.yaml - new observability events for recommendations and user actions

Testing and CI: ran full unit and integration suite on benchmark-lab; CI showed intermittent timeout in an unrelated flaky e2e (replayed and resolved). All required checks passed before merge. Performance validation: median downstream latency increased by <0.5ms for typical small-batch workloads; estimated per-1M-token cost decreased 4-12% for routes with >30% prefix reuse.

Rollout plan: stage behind feature flag in staging -> canary on 5% of traffic with recommendations shown but not applied -> operator review flow in Console -> 25% auto-apply (if explicit opt-in) -> full apply only after 14 days of monitoring. Rollback: flip feature flag or set safe-mode to true to revert defaults.

Related: references to prior cost automation PRs and research notes. Linear: ENG-4821 for design, ENG-4890 for prescreen evaluation.

Notes for reviewers: pay attention to sampling window sizing and policy cap logic in unit_econ_heuristic.py; the quant prescreen is intentionally conservative and uses a weighted quality metric, not raw perplexity. If you want to test locally, see instructions in runtime/quant/README.md included in changes.
Ethan Kline: Nice end-to-end. Two asks: (1) tighten the policy cap math so a single long-tail request doesn't blow up batch targets, and (2) add a small opt-out for private customers.

Feature gated behind 'unit_econ_recommendations' feature flag. To enable auto-apply for a workspace set 'apply_recommendations' in org config; otherwise recommendations are readonly. Safe-mode prevents auto-application in Dedicated/Private by default.

Improved attention throughput for long-context serving: new FlashAttention-v4 block fusion and rotary QKV interleaving reduce p99 token latency on GPU instances and lower token cost by up to 18% for chat workloads.
Motivation: reduce per-token overhead for long-sequence serving workloads and simplify fallback compatibility across attention variants. Summary: introduces an experimental FlashAttention-v4 block-fusion kernel plus a runtime transform that interleaves rotary-multiplied Q/K/V memory layout to reduce memory touches and improve vectorized loads; adds scheduler hints for continuous-batching to prefer low-latency batches for short requests and high-throughput packing for long requests. Changes include CUDA kernels, C++ runtime wiring, Python integration test updates, and perf harness additions. Design notes: the block-fusion kernel fuses QK compute, rotary application, and softmax scaling into a single fused path for blocks up to 128 tokens, falling back to the existing vectorized path for larger blocks; the QKV interleave transform reorders per-layer KV cache layout to an interleaved Q-K-V contiguous format which improves coalesced global loads on Ampere and Hopper architectures. Backwards compatibility: runtime supports a feature flag (attn.flashv4.enabled) and falls back to previous FlashAttention implementation when models are pinned or the kernel fails safety checks. Rollout plan: gate behind 10% canary on Dedicated, validate with the perf canary job, expand to 50% after 48h if error budget holds, then gradually enable by default. Checklist: [x] unit tests for kernel shaders; [x] integration tests for KV restore across warm restarts; [x] perf harness and baseline numbers added; [x] feature flag and metrics; [x] docs note in perf-tuning.md. Benchmarks (internal, p95/p99 token latency on g4dn equivalent): baseline FlashA-v3: p95=12.8ms, p99=25.3ms; this PR FlashA-v4 w/ interleave: p95=10.4ms (18.7% improvement), p99=20.9ms (17.4% improvement). Cost impact: synthetic request mix shows ~12-18% reduction in token GPU time. Risks and mitigations: fused kernel increases complexity and may surface numerical differences; added deterministic numeric tolerance checks and golden-output evals on a set of regression prompts. Related work: follows up on ENG-2972 (batching scheduler tweaks) and ENG-2150 (kv cache layout experiments).

Asha Patel: Added perf/bench/long_context_suite.py and a microbench driver for interleave in commit b2c4d55. Results included in PR description.
Evelyn Torres (request changes): Please add a safety check that falls back if NVCC computes divergent numerics on older drivers. Also noted missing CI coverage for restore on warm restart. 
Asha Patel: Implemented driver-version guard and golden-output warm-restore test in c3d8f11; CI now runs warm-restore on the smallest GPU target.
Samir Khanna: Approved after re-run of perf CI showed stable numbers and kernel memory usage within budget.

Motivation: Continuous batching improved throughput but exposed latency tail sensitivity under heterogeneous request mixes and long-lived KV cache hits. This PR introduces an adaptive scheduler layer that balances throughput and latency by applying fair queueing across priority lanes, a starvation detector that forces aging of stalled requests, and dynamic timeout windows for batch formation. Approach: 1) Add a lightweight multi-lane queue where requests are assigned a lane based on model variant, request size, and SLO tag; lane weights are tunable. 2) Implement priority aging: requests increment an urgency score while waiting; once score crosses a threshold they are promoted to a higher-service lane to prevent starvation. 3) Introduce adaptive batch-timeout calculation using recent interarrival statistics and per-lane latency SLOs; timeouts shorten for latency-sensitive lanes and lengthen for high-throughput lanes. 4) Starvation guard: per-queue watchdog that triggers a flush when the oldest request exceeds a configurable max-wait. 5) KV-cache-aware batching: prefer grouping requests with contiguous KV cache prefixes to reduce cache misses; integrates with existing cache index metadata. 6) Metrics and tracing hooks: new counters/gauges for lane sizes, promoted-count, starvation-flushes, timeout-adj-steps and histogram of batch formation delays. Backwards compatibility: Scheduler parameters default to previous single-queue behavior when feature flags disabled. Tests: unit tests for lane assignment, aging/promotion, timeout adaptation logic; integration tests exercising mixed-load scenarios and KV cache affinity. Benchmarks: On a mixed workload (70% short chat queries, 30% long-context summarization) we observe p50 latency unchanged, p95 reduced from 890ms to 560ms (35% improvement) for latency-sensitive lane and overall tokens/sec within 3% of prior baseline. Rollout: staged feature-flag rollout with Canary=10% -> 30% -> 100% with canary metrics smoke checks (p50/p95, error-rate, throughput) and auto-rollback on SLO regressions. Follow-ups: expose lane-weight tuning in console and provide a suggested tuning guide under redwood-docs.
Marco Li: Strong direction. Two concerns: how do we ensure cache-affinity grouping doesn't starve small latency-sensitive requests when a large batch could be formed? Please add explicit tests that simulate a persistent stream of cache-coherent large requests alongside sparse latency-sensitive ones.
Priya Desai (author): Good point — added the starvation guard and priority aging to address exactly that scenario and added an integration test 'scheduler_mixed_load_test.py' that models the behavior. See commits d4b2e99 and 9d6c1aa.
Eleanor Shaw: Need to be careful with the interarrival estimator — smoothing window must not be too large for bursty traffic. Suggest exposing smoothing factor as a tuning knob and defaulting to a shorter window for latency lanes.
Priya Desai (author): Exposed smoothing_factor in config and added docs recommending 50-200ms effective window for chat workloads.

Release Manager (automated): Verified migration safe and feature flag default off for tenants with strict SLOs.
Adaptive continuous-batching scheduler with fairness lanes, starvation prevention, and KV-cache-aware batching. Improves latency tail for mixed workloads while preserving throughput. Feature gated behind 'adaptive_scheduler' flag. See docs/scheduler_tuning.md for tuning guidance.
