Marco: Can you explain how QueueHorizon differs from the aging-token approach? I want to ensure we don't duplicate accounting.
Priya: QueueHorizon is a windowed admission frontier that prevents admitting requests whose expected service window exceeds a configurable horizon. It complements aging tokens by preventing the queue head from being dominated during short spikes; both mechanisms run together.
Yuna: We saw a small throughput regression in stress when backoff enabled at 5ms base. Can we expose a knob to tune aggressive vs conservative backoff?
Priya: Added config batcher.kv_probe.backoff_profile with presets (conservative, default, aggressive). Updated docs with recommended profiles for Dedicated vs Hosted.
Liam: The kernel selector hint looks good but needs a comment explaining safety for quantized kernels.
Priya: Added clarifying comment and unit tests for selector fallback to ensure quantized path unchanged if hint unsupported.
Tail P99 latency (mixed KV-heavy + short requests) reduced from 482ms -> 168ms in 95th-percentile scenarios (20k RPS mix), measured on c6g-large GPU cluster
Overall throughput impact: -2.3% at peak when using conservative backoff; aggressive profile recovers throughput with modest P99 tradeoff
KV-probe failures (timeouts) decreased by 68% due to staged backoff avoiding repeated immediate probes
End-to-end latency for short inference requests improved median by 12ms under bursty traffic due to horizon gating
Reviewers requested explicit tuning knobs and conservative defaults; we added three profiles, updated docs, and added e2e tests. CI flaked once on benchmark infra; rerun passed. After approvals from Marco and Yuna and a final security scan, we squashed and merged.
Added queue-horizon throttling to the continuous batcher to reduce tail latency under bursty mixed workloads
Introduced KV probe exponential backoff to reduce repeated KV pin contention and transient timeouts
New config knobs: batcher.queue_horizon.window_ms and batcher.kv_probe.backoff_profile (conservative|default|aggressive)
Metric changes: new telemetry 'batcher.queue_horizon_rejects' and 'kv_probe.backoff_count'
Canary rollout: 5% traffic for 24h, then 25% for 12h, 100% after 48h if no regressions. Monitoring: p99 latency, kv_probe.backoff_count, kernel-fallback-rate; automatic rollback on sustained p99 increase >20% or error spike.
Operators should monitor 'batcher.queue_horizon_rejects' and may select 'conservative' backoff for latency-sensitive Dedicated clusters. For priority-queue tenants, consider raising horizon_ms to prevent admission of long-context requests during bursts.
Unit coverage added for queue horizon math and backoff jitter. E2E YAML reproduces the mixed-workload scenario; benchmarks validated on staging GPU pool. Load test scripts included in tools/benchmarks.

Motivation: During several incidents we observed short-lived synthetic/noisy workloads (scheduled internal tests, tenant-side health checks, and 3rd-party probe traffic) causing transient eviction and headroom thrashing in Dedicated fleets. This PR adds two complementary controls: (1) a Synthetic Load Protector that tags and soft-throttles identified synthetic traffic to prevent it from consuming burst/headroom credits; (2) a Stable Headroom Allocation controller that smooths reservation adjustments using a percentile-based decay window to avoid oscillation when autoscaler signals spike.

What this PR does: adds request classification hooks, a synthetic-throttle policy and counter, a headroom allocator that computes reservation deltas using P90/P95 utilization baselines, and new telemetry to report per-tenant synthetic consumption and smoothed headroom allocations. Includes e2e canary rollout plan and migration notes.

Checklist:
- [x] classification + tagging for synthetic traffic (configurable by label and header)
- [x] soft-throttle policy with graceful fallback and tenant opt-out flag
- [x] headroom allocator with percentile decay window and hysteresis
- [x] metrics (synthetic_consumed_tokens, headroom_alloc_smoothed, allocation_delta_histogram)
- [x] unit + integration tests for race conditions and decay logic
- [x] canary rollout job definition and console dashboard tiles

Rollout plan: Deploy controller on dedicated fleet controllers in canary region (us-west-2) for 48h with a 2x synthetic-throttle default. Monitor allocation_delta_histogram and per-tenant SLO signals. If no regressions, expand to rest of dedicated pools over 3 days.

Design notes: Synthetic detection is rule-based and opt-in for now; rules are configurable via fleet policy CRD. Headroom allocator uses a sliding window histogram and applies a decay factor to previous reservation to compute new reservation = clamp(prev * (1 - decay) + forecast * decay, min_headroom, max_headroom). Forecast uses P90 of observed utilization in the window to be robust to short spikes.

Migration and compatibility: Default behavior is a no-op unless fleet policy enables it. Existing autoscaler and burst token pools are left intact; this controller only influences soft reservation deltas and synthetic-tagged requests are excluded from burst accounting when enabled.
Diego Alvarez: overall looks good, but please add a concurrency test for the allocator when multiple signals arrive simultaneously. See inline comment in allocator.go: handle potential double-update.
Maya Chen: added a new test allocator_concurrent_update_test and bump to use atomic patching of reservation; addressed race by introducing optimistic compare-and-swap in window_histogram.
Priya Nambiar: Can we avoid discounting short tenant-retries as synthetic? Suggest adding a minimum duration threshold to rule matching.
Maya Chen: implemented min_duration_ms and updated docs; default is 500ms to avoid classifying short retries.
Omar Patel (SRE): CI flaked on e2e in the first run (timeout in canary job). Re-run fixed it; please keep an eye on the canary timeout. Approved after green CI.
payload.title: Introduce synthetic-load-protector and stable-headroom-allocation to reduce noisy-neighbor regressions

Motivation: multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads show sporadic tail latency spikes when collectives are scheduled naively at layer boundaries. This PR introduces a wavefront-style collective scheduler that groups nearby collective ops into a compact execution wave and a compact_kernel_selector that prefers smaller, lower-latency kernels for short-sequence invocations. The goal is to reduce communication stalls, improve KV cache prefetch alignment with collectives, and give the runtime a low-overhead heuristic to pick kernels that minimize per-token latency for short and mixed-length batches. Work items: - implement wavefront scheduler with layer-aware grouping and interleaved compute/comm launch windows - add compact_kernel_selector with device-query and sequence-length histogram input - introduce a KV-shard prompter that prefetches KV shards for upcoming wavefronts (heuristic-based) - NCCL launch param autotuner that records performance fingerprints and falls back to conservative settings on regression - unit + integration tests and perf-canary workload validation Checklist: [x] scheduler core implementation and unit tests [x] kernel selector + device query [x] KV prefetch heuristic + metrics hooks [x] NCCL autotuner prototype [x] perf benchmarks against baseline [x] documentation and release note entry Context and motivation: customers running TP-4/8 models reported 10-30% 95/99 latency regressions after a recent batching change; root cause was misaligned collective launches interleaving with KV cache fills. This PR aims to reduce that variance without sacrificing throughput on large continuous-batching workloads.
+// wavefront_scheduler: group nearby collectives into a compact launch window
+void WavefrontScheduler::schedule_layer_group(...) { /* heuristics */ }
+// choose compact kernels for short sequences to reduce per-token overhead
+KernelProfile select_compact_kernel(const DeviceCaps& d, int seq_len) { ... }
+// KV prompter triggers async prefetch for shards that next wavefront will need
+kv_prompter->prime_shards(predicted_shard_list);

Motivation: provide a single policy layer that can express canary gradients, A/B splits, shadowing, and automated rollback triggers for model variant rollouts across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. This PR implements a policy-driven rollout engine and runtime hooks to route traffic incrementally, evaluate health metrics, and trigger automated rollback or promotion when thresholds are met.

What this change contains: checklist: [x] rollout policy DSL and parser; [x] runtime router integration (routing-by-policy); [x] metrics adapter to evaluate success criteria (latency, error-rate, quality-regression hooks); [x] shadow mode implementation (non-impacting mirrored requests); [x] A/B split support with weighted sampling; [x] automated rollback circuit with hysteresis and cooldown; [x] console integration for visualizing rollout state and editing policies; [x] e2e and unit tests with synthetic traffic scenarios.

Design notes: the policy DSL is deliberately conservative: it expresses a percentage gradient (start->target), evaluation windows, primary metrics with tolerated deltas, and fallback actions. Policies are evaluated by a lightweight controller: the controller emits routing directives to the router via an atomic config push (no hot-restart required). To avoid cross-tenant leakage the controller enforces model variant isolation and integrates with existing RBAC checks.

Rollout modes supported: 1) gradient canary (0->N% over time), 2) A/B experiments with deterministic assignment keys, 3) shadow/mirror traffic where responses are recorded and compared asynchronously, 4) manual promote/abort via console.

Safety: automated rollback is conservative — thresholds must be met for three consecutive windows and the controller requires a minimum sample size before taking action. A circuit-breaker prevents rapid flapping and records reasons in audit logs. Emergency abort can be triggered via API or console and will immediately revert routing directives.

Testing and validation: included e2e scenarios that run synthetic traffic mixes (latency skew, quality regressions simulated via metric stubs). We also added perf microbenchmarks ensuring router decision path adds <0.5ms p50 on our standard config.

Migration notes: existing rollouts configured with the older mirror/canary flags are automatically translated to the new policy model on startup with a one-time migration job. Admins can opt-out via the feature flag rollout.policy_migration=false.

Operational notes: rollout controller exposes metrics: rollout_progress, rollout_failure_count, rollback_count, policy_eval_latency_ms. Alerts recommended: rollout_failure_count > 0 for 5m and policy_eval_latency_ms > 250ms.

Related: ENG-7432 implements the policy DSL and engine; ENG-7500 wires the console UI and migration job.
Diego Morales (2026-02-20): Can we make the evaluation window configurable per-policy? Also flagging that the default sample-size threshold needs to be conservative; otherwise small tenants may flapping. Ava: made window configurable and increased default sample size to 500.
Priya Nair (2026-02-23): UX looks good. Two requests: 1) add an explicit 'dry-run' mode for A/B so results show in console without affecting production metrics, 2) ensure audit log includes the pre/post routing directive snapshot. Ava: added dry-run and expanded audit payloads.
Liam O'Connor (2026-02-28): Integration tests are solid but e2e occasionally failed on noisy CI; root cause was a test race in the migration job. Fixed by adding a leader-election short lease during migration and reworked tests to use deterministic ports. Tests green on rerun.
Introduce policy-driven rollouts: canary gradients, A/B splits, and shadowing with automated rollback. Includes migration tool for older canary/mirror configs and console support.
Impact: new metrics and audit logs added; default rollout policy conservative to avoid traffic churn.
Risk: misconfigured policies could route too much traffic to unstable variants. Mitigations: conservative defaults, minimum sample size, cooldown, manual abort and feature-flag to disable auto-migration. Admins should stage policies in dev before promoting to production.
payload.title: Policy-driven gradient rollouts and shadow/A-B traffic orchestration

payload.body:
Motivation: We need a low-overhead way to correlate scheduler decisions, KV-cache hot prefixes, and continuous-batching pressure in production-like workloads. Existing NVTX and perfetto exports are useful but either too heavy or too coarse for iterative scheduler tuning. This PR introduces a lightweight tracepoint sampler plus a compact microbench harness that reproduces batch-pressure scenarios seen in customer workloads.

What this PR does: 1) Introduces a TracepointSampler module (C++): periodic, low-payload tracepoints emitted around scheduler windowing and key KV-cache touchpoints. Sampling is rate-limited and context-tagged so it is safe to enable in Dedicated/Private pockets for short experiments. 2) Adds a BatchPressureMicrobench: a small harness that simulates mixed arrival patterns (burst+poisson), tracks batch fill/evict cycles, and reports per-step metrics (queue depth, avg-batch-size, scheduler-latency). 3) Adds a lightweight exporter template that converts sampler output to a compact CSV/JSON line format and a dashboard YAML for the perf observability stack. 4) Provides unit and integration tests for correctness and a CI bench job to run the microbench in controlled runners.

Design notes: - TracepointSampler emits an inline 64-bit tag plus epoch counter; it avoids heavy NVTX payloads to keep overhead < 0.2% in our microbench. - The sampler can be configured by percent-sampling or deterministic-epoch windows; configuration lives under runtime.conf under [tracepoint_sampler]. - The bench harness focuses on reproducing scheduler backpressure (when batches are delayed waiting for KV-cache or kernel queues). It is intentionally small so it can be run in CI and locally.

Benchmarks: Local runs on an r5-like simulated env show: - 0.12% median runtime overhead with sampler enabled at 1% sampling. - Microbench reproduces a clear inflection when batch-timeouts exceed 6ms and shows scheduler queue growth matching production traces. Included CSV outputs for two representative runs in bench/outputs/*.csv.

Testing & CI: - Added unit tests for sampler tagging and epoch wrap-around. - Added a bench CI job (ci/bench/bench-runner.yml) that executes microbench in a small container; results are archived as artifacts. CI initially failed due to a missing clock dependency in the test harness; fixed in second commit.

Migration / Rollout: This is a safe, opt-in instrumentation path. Default sampling is disabled in production configs. We recommend: 1) enable 0.1% sampling on a canary Dedicated node for 24 hours, 2) collect artifacts and load into the dashboard template, 3) iterate sampling/window params and run microbench locally to validate hypotheses.

Follow-ups: - Wire sampler output to the existing perf-trace ingestion pipeline (ENG-1185). - Add a lightweight JS/TS helper to download and visualise CSVs in the console (ENG-1190).

Related: builds on prior instrumentation work but intentionally avoids heavy NVTX payloads and Perfetto dependency so we can run in constrained CI nodes. See related PRs: ENG-93547-style batching probes and ENG-93421 (kv-cache sim) for context.
Adds a lightweight tracepoint sampler and a small microbenchmark that measures batch-pressure and scheduler stall contributions. Exposed a perf dashboard template for quick triage. No user-facing API changes.
Ben Ortiz (review): Can the sampler be further optimized to avoid atomic ops on the hot path? Suggested use of relaxed-atomics or sharded counters.
Aisha (reply): Switched to thread-local counters for the hot path and only use atomics on flush. Bench shows negligible change in overhead after update.
Sofia Müller (review): Dashboard YAML looks good but we should add a panel for 'avg-batch-wait-ms' and a simple alert for sustained queue growth.
Aisha (reply): Added panel and an example alert rule in the template; alert thresholds are conservative and documented.
Ethan Park (suggestion): Tests flaked on CI when container clock skewed. Consider using steady_clock mocks in tests.
Aisha (reply): Replaced system_clock usage with steady_clock for tests and added a clock mock helper in runtime/tests/utils/clock_mock.h
payload.title: Introduce lightweight tracepoint sampler and batch-pressure microbench for scheduler visibility

Motivation: Developers repeatedly hit vague runtime errors when streams failed (auth handshake, transient network) and had to implement ad-hoc parsing logic to decide whether to retry, resume, or surface an error. This PR introduces language-native typed error classes across the three SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go) and a unified ergonomic iterable reconnect API for stream consumers.

What this change does: 
- Introduces TypedError/StreamError subclasses with machine-friendly error_code, retriable, and suggestion fields across SDKs.
- Adds a new StreamIterable API (python: StreamIterable, ts: createStreamIterable, go: StreamIterator) that yields typed result objects and automatically attempts a single reconnect on retriable failures by default with backoff tuning. Reconnect behavior is configurable by the caller.
- Deprecates low-level sync callback hooks (on_chunk/on_error) in favor of async iterables/promises/iterators to improve ergonomics and parity.
- Adds structured telemetry hooks (opt-in) so apps can key metrics by error_code without brittle string matching.
- Small refactors: move common auth-retry utility into internal/sdk-common, update changelogs and bump SDK package versions.

Backward compatibility and migration: 
- Old callback APIs are still present but marked deprecated; they will emit one deprecation log per process and are scheduled for removal in the next major. Migration notes are added to each SDK CHANGELOG.
- Typed error shapes are additive; existing code catching broad exceptions will continue to work but can opt-in to typed handling for clearer logic.

Testing and rollout: 
- Unit tests added for typed error construction, serialization, and iterable reconnect edge cases. Integration tests simulate transient auth failures with a test double of the runtime.
- Canary rollout to Dedicated region us-west-2 for 72 hours before full merge.

Checklist: 
- [x] Python implementation and tests
- [x] TypeScript implementation and tests
- [x] Go implementation and tests
- [x] Changelogs and version bumps
- [x] Docs snippet in quickstarts repo pointing to new API example

References: Linear ENG-1987, SUP-402 (customer-facing incident), internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1987/stream-reconnect-typed-errors (internal link).
Ethan Park (request changes): The StreamIterable reconnect loop looks like it could retry non-idempotent streams when the model resumed in a different conversation state. Please add a guard for non-resumable streams or require explicit caller opt-in.
Anya Patel (reply): Added an explicit 'resumable' flag to the StreamIterable constructor and documented the caller opt-in behavior. Default remains conservative (single reconnect only for resumable streams).
Lina Gomez (nit): Could you flatten the error_code enum names for TS (avoid nested namespaces) and add a migration mapping in the changelog?
Anya Patel (reply): Flattened the enum, added mapping snippet to TYPESCRIPT changelog. Thanks for catching the nits.
Priya Varma (approve): Verified Python unit tests and manual smoke against canary dedicated cluster; LGTM after CI green.
Adds typed SDK error classes and a new ergonomic iterable reconnect API for streaming across Python/TS/Go SDKs; bump SDK versions: python 1.8.0, typescript 2.3.0, go v0.9.1.
payload.title: typed errors + ergonomic iterable reconnect API across SDKs

Introduces a reservoir-backed block allocator and a pin-coalescer that reduces KV cache churn and lowers tail latency. Backwards-compatible; enabled behind runtime flag by default for new clusters.
Motivation: Frequent small pin/unpin operations in our paged KV cache cause allocator metadata churn and increased eviction IO during high-concurrency workloads (continuation-heavy decoding). This PR introduces a lightweight reservoir-backed block allocator plus a pin-coalescer layer to reduce metadata updates and contention, and adds a kernel scheduling hint to prioritize hot pinned lanes. The design goals were: 1) reduce allocator metadata operations under bursty access patterns; 2) keep average allocation latency unchanged; 3) reduce eviction IO and tail latency for real serving workloads; 4) remain opt-in behind a runtime feature flag until bake.

Summary of changes:
- Implement ReservoirBlockAllocator: per-lane mini-pools that refill/return to a global reservoir to reduce global lock pressure. Allocation fast-path is lock-free for hot-path requests that can be satisfied from the lane reservoir; slow-path obtains from global reservoir with backoff and batching.
- Add PinCoalescer: when multiple adjacent small pins occur within a short epoch, coalesce them into a single metadata update to the block manager (reduces journal writes). Coalescer uses a bounded ring and epoch commit semantics to avoid long-lived pins.
- Kernel scheduling hint: the allocator exposes a hotness score for lanes (based on pin frequency); scheduler's priority queue (priority hints only) uses this to prefer pinned-hot lanes to avoid repeated cold fills.
- Tests & bench: microbench harness for continuous-batching-decoder scenarios, integration test to validate correctness under races, and a stress test to assert eviction stability under heavy pin churn.
- Operational: docs/allocator.md documents tunables and suggested defaults; a runtime flag enable_reservoir_allocator toggles behavior per-cluster.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(kv): add ReservoirBlockAllocator with per-lane reservoirs
- feat(kv): add PinCoalescer and epoch commit logic
- perf(kv): expose lane_hotness metric and scheduler hint integration
- test(kv): add reservoir and coalescer unit/integration tests
- bench: add continuous-batching decoder microbench and results harness
- fix(lint): address clippy warnings and unify error handling
- ci: update pipeline to add deterministic bench job for perf regressions

Files changed (high level):
- src/kv/block_allocator.rs (new core allocator implementation & comments)
- src/kv/pin_coalescer.rs (new coalescer with bounded ring buffer)
- runtime/scheduler/priority_queue.rs (hook to read lane_hotness hints)
- runtime/config/flags.rs (runtime flag enable_reservoir_allocator)
- tests/bench/reservoir_bench.rs (microbench harness)
- tests/integration/kv_eviction_stress.rs (race and eviction stability tests)
- docs/allocator.md (operational notes and defaults)

Microbenchmark results (CI deterministic bench run):
- Continuous-batching decoder (50 concurrent lanes, seq_len 256, batch target 8): p50 tokens/ms improved by ~12%, p95 reduced by ~18%, p99 reduced by ~22%
- Eviction IO: measured 18% fewer metadata writes in benchmark scenario; net IO decrease on SSD-backed cache nodes.
- CPU overhead: reservoir allocator adds ~1.2% steady-state CPU due to maintenance/refill; net throughput gains offset this in busy workloads.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Reservoir size per-lane is configurable; default chosen conservatively to avoid memory bloat on low-load nodes.
- Coalescer epoch is time-bounded (default 50ms) to avoid delaying pin visibility for readers. This introduces a tunable latency knob; defaults were validated on CI-benches and a small canary.
- Consistency model: pin coalescing does not change observable semantics (pins are still honored) — coalescing only batches metadata writes but commits them with epoch guarantees.
- Fallbacks: under memory pressure or if the reservoir empties, allocator falls back to global slow-path which preserves correctness.

Rollout plan: default enabled for new clusters; existing clusters can opt-in via console flag. We will roll canary to 5% traffic for 72h, monitor lane_hotness, eviction_write_rate, and p99 token latency before broad rollout.

Review conversation (selected threads): "Arjun Patel: Nice design. Two quick things: 1) can you add a safety check to ensure epochs don't starve readers? 2) what are memory bloat protections for misbehaving lanes?" "Author (Maya): Added epoch max-duration (50ms) and a max-reservoir-per-lane cap with eviction into global reservoir. Updated docs/allocator.md with recommended limits and rationale." "Sofia Liu: CI bench shows good wins but the priority hint coupling looked invasive. Please ensure scheduler fallback if hint source fails." "Author (Maya): Priority hint is advisory-only; scheduler still uses load-based fallback. Added comment and test to validate fallback behavior (priority_queue tests)." "Rajesh Nair: Found a race in coalescer commit path during stress run (two-epoch handoff)." "Author (Maya): Fixed with an atomic epoch swap + commit barrier; added reproducer test and stress-run in CI." "CI bot: Initial pipeline failed linter and flaky bench job timed out. Author pushed fix and retriggered. Final CI: all green including deterministic bench job." "SRE: Please add a dashboard for lane_hotness and eviction_write_rate before wide rollout." "Author: Dashboard tiles added to observability-pack; documented alert thresholds in docs/allocator.md."

CI summary: initial run had 1 lint failure and one flaky bench timeout; fixes were pushed and final run passed. Merge strategy: squash-and-merge after approvals and green CI. Impact statement: Expected to reduce tail latency and metadata IO in production serving workloads with heavy prefix reuse or continuous batching. No API changes to callers; feature is behind a runtime flag for safe rollouts.

Follow-ups:
- ENG-2280: add adaptive reservoir sizing based on observed hotset
- ENG-2335: explore coalescer persistence hints to further reduce journal writes
- Add canary monitoring playbook for eviction regressions (checklists updated in docs/allocator.md)
payload.title: Reservoir-backed block allocator and pin-coalescer to reduce KV cache churn

payload.body:
Motivation: Several production routes (chat-stream, tools/function_call, and OpenAI-compat proxying) have experienced intermittent stalls and truncated function_call payloads when large intermediate tool outputs are streamed in small chunks. Root cause summary: a) statically-sized streaming proxy flush thresholds and buffer headroom do not match per-route payload patterns; b) global payload size limit was too coarse (caused safe-failures for tool outputs but allowed oversized non-streamed requests); c) OpenAI compatibility shim assumed final-message framing which breaks when intermediate buffer flushes split function_call JSON tokens across frames.

What this PR does (summary): Adds a dynamic per-route payload limiter and adaptive streaming-proxy buffer tuning. The gateway now derives two parameters per route: effective_payload_limit (bytes) and buffer_flush_threshold (bytes). Derivation uses route metadata (route type: chat|tooling|embedding), model family hints, and historical size percentiles (configurable window). To preserve OpenAI compatibility we introduce a small "reassemble-on-boundary" shim that guarantees function_call JSON objects are not emitted mid-object across chunk boundaries when possible (best-effort with a soft timeout).

Key changes (high level): - gateway/routes/policy: new PolicyWeights to compute effective_payload_limit per-route and expose policy endpoint for manual overrides. - gateway/proxy/stream_buffer: adaptive buffer with three modes: passthrough (low-latency), accumulate (when API route signals structured-output), and reassemble (OpenAI function_call safety window). - gateway/openai/compat: added streaming-function-call-shim that watches for "function_call" object starts and attempts to flush complete tokens when buffer thresholds are hit. - metrics and observability: new metrics gateway.route.payload_limit_bytes and gateway.proxy.reassemble_invocations with tagging by route/model. - docs: gateway/operational.md updated with rollout and a knob to pin per-route limits. - tests: new integration streaming test covering fragmented function_call frames and a perf benchmark for latency/cost tradeoffs.

Behavioral notes / compatibility: - Default behavior is conservative: effective_payload_limit defaults to previous global limit, only routes with historical large-percentile traffic will increase limits. This avoids surprising regressions for customers who rely on strict per-request quotas. - OpenAI compatibility: shim is best-effort to avoid emitting function_call JSON mid-object. In extremely high-throughput scenarios, the shim will fallback to emitting partial frames with a diagnostic trace header; clients relying on precise framing should be advised to rehydrate frames. - Tooling: tool outputs larger than effective_payload_limit will be rejected with a 413-like structured error that includes guidance and a route-specific suggested limit. - Operators can set route annotations to force bypassing reassembly for ultra-low-latency workloads.

Testing and verification: Unit tests for buffer edge cases and policy computation. Integration tests simulate chunked streaming where function_call JSON is split across many small token frames. Canary rollout: feature gates enabled for 10% of traffic for 24 hours before ramping to 100% with metrics checks for increased tail latency and reassemble errors.

Benchmarks: Measured on staging with a mix of 50% chat-stream, 30% function_call, 20% tooling: - 95th percentile latency for chat-stream increased by +6ms on average when reassembly mode is active; - Tail error rate for truncated function_call decreased from 0.9% -> 0.02%; - Cost per token impact negligible (<0.5%) due to opportunistic passthrough mode.

Migration / rollout: - Default policies are backwards-compatible. - Operators with custom quotas should review new route-level settings; a migration script is provided to copy global quota -> per-route default. - Release notes include instructions for emergency rollback by setting gateway.feature.dynamic_payload_limits=false.

Notes for reviewers: Pay attention to race conditions in stream_buffer reassemble logic (I added a test that reproduces a previously observed race using channel-backed flushing). The reassembly shim has a configurable timeout (default 150ms) to avoid unbounded buffering under slow producers.

Hannah Li: Nice approach. Please call out the eventual consistency window for metrics used to compute percentiles (answer: 5m by default).
Miguel Santos: Added note and parameter default in policy.go and docs; also added test for stale percentile handling.
Dario Petrov: Concern about reassembly timeout value; can we make it route-configurable?
Miguel Santos: Made timeout configurable per-route via annotation; default kept at 150ms. Added e2e test to verify timeout backoff behavior.
Priya Natarajan: CI regression seen on flaky streaming test — looks intermittent on arm64 runners.
Miguel Santos: Disabled noisy test on arm64 and added ticket ENG-4509 to investigate runner variance.
Hannah Li: Approved after minor doc tweaks.
Dario Petrov: Approve (kept eye on backpressure integration).
- Gateway: added dynamic per-route payload limits and adaptive streaming proxy buffers.
- Gateway: added OpenAI function_call streaming shim (best-effort reassembly).
- Metrics: gateway.route.payload_limit_bytes and gateway.proxy.reassemble_invocations.
- Rollout: default off for 90% of traffic; can be enabled via feature flag and route annotations.
If you rely on strict global payload quotas, review per-route defaults after upgrade. Emergency rollback: set gateway.feature.dynamic_payload_limits=false and restart gateway-service. To opt a route into high-throughput passthrough mode add annotation gateway.payload_mode=passthrough.
payload.title: dynamic per-route payload limits + streaming proxy buffer tuning to stabilize function-calls and OpenAI-compatible chunking

Adds a pluggable attention adapter, runtime kernel probing, and a fused rope->rotary stitching path that yields latency improvements for mixed-length workloads. Backwards-compatible fallbacks retained.
Motivation: runtime needs to pick the best attention kernel variant for heterogeneous workloads without a heavy rollout. This PR introduces a pluggable attention adapter interface plus a small fused operator (rope->rotary stitch) and a kernel-probing harness so the scheduler can prefer the fused path when beneficial. The goal is lower p99 latency for mixed token lengths and more predictable tail-latency by moving compatibility checks out of the hot path.

What this does (high-level): - Introduce AttnAdapter interface to abstract kernel selection and probing. - Implement a CUDA probe kernel and lightweight C++ probe harness that records supported fused ops and numeric profiles. - Add a rope->rotary stitching fused op (rope_stitch) implemented with vectorized kernels for small rotary sizes. - Update the request router/scheduler to consult AttnAdapter decisions and prefer fused paths when they meet latency/cost heuristics. - Add deterministic unit and microbench tests, perf harness results, and docs for opt-in rollout.

Checklist: - [x] AttnAdapter API and unit tests - [x] probe kernel + safety timeouts - [x] rope_stitch operator (+ fallback) - [x] scheduler integration + policy toggle - [x] docs and perf notes - [x] benchmarks on Ampere and Hopper instances - [x] CI green after one rerun

Commits (summary): - Add AttnAdapter interface and base impl (adapter.py + adapter.h) - Kernel probe probe_kern.cu and C++ harness (probe_harness.cc) - Rope->rotary stitch operator (rope_stitch.cc / rope_stitch.cu) - Scheduler changes to consult adapter decisions (routing.py / scheduler.cc) - Tests and perf harness (tests/attn/test_probe.py, perf/attn_adapter_bench.py) - Docs (docs/perf/attn_adapter.md)

Files changed (high-level): redwood/serve/attn/adapter.py, redwood/serve/attn/adapter.h, redwood/serve/attn/probe_kern.cu, redwood/serve/attn/probe_harness.cc, redwood/serve/attn/rope_stitch.cc, redwood/serve/attn/rope_stitch.cu, redwood/serve/scheduler/routing.py, redwood/serve/scheduler/scheduler.cc, tests/attn/test_probe.py, perf/attn_adapter_bench.py, docs/perf/attn_adapter.md, setup/ci/attn-probe-matrix.yml

Review thread (highlights): Lina Gómez (reviewer): "Nice separation of concerns. Two asks: 1) add a deterministic seed and additional assertions in test_probe to avoid flakiness we saw in canary; 2) make the adapter fallback path explicitly opt-out via feature flag so we can A/B on Dedicated." Daniel Hsu (author): "Added deterministic RNG seed and strengthened assertions (tests updated). Feature toggle added: ATTN_ADAPTER_ROLLOUT env + runtime config; default off for Dedicated. See adapter.py lines ~120-145." Evan Park (reviewer): "Kernel probe harness looks solid; I'm concerned about the timeout semantics on extremely loaded hosts (we saw a 30ms probe stall last week). Can we bound probe to a pooled worker and fail-safe?" Daniel Hsu: "Probe now runs on a bounded worker thread with a 12ms soft timeout and a 50ms hard timeout; on timeout we log once per boot and mark fused ops as unavailable. This is documented in probe_harness.cc and in docs/perf/attn_adapter.md." Maya Singh (reviewer): "Perf numbers look promising; please add a perf dashboard link and note the GPU types where gains were measured." Daniel Hsu: "Added benchmark CSV and Grafana panel link to the docs; numbers: 6-12% p50 improvement, 8-18% p99 improvement on mixed-length chat workloads on A100/H100 with rope sizes <=64."

CI summary: - build: pass - unit-tests: pass (1 flaky kernel test required rerun) - lint: pass - integration-tests: pass - perf-microbench: pass (bench harness runs; recorded improvements) Note: initial CI run failed on a CUDA 11.7 build due to an ABI test; fixed by pinning a sub-dependency and reran — subsequent runs passed.

Performance notes: Benchmarks run with canonical chat workload (turn-taking messages with 8/32/512 histories). The adapter prefers fused rope_stitch for rotary dim <=64 and sequence lengths 256-2048 where the fused path reduces kernel launch overhead. Measured by perf harness: p50 improved 6-12%, p99 improved 8-18% depending on model and batch mix. Cost analysis: small increase in binary size (~120KB) and negligible runtime memory for probe tables; win is reduced token CPU/GPU cycles for short sequences.

Compatibility and rollout: Backwards-compatible. The fused rope_stitch has explicit fallback to per-layer rotary application when not available. A feature flag (ATTN_ADAPTER_ROLLOUT) controls automatic use; rollout plan recommends starting at 0% on Dedicated and 25% on Hosted with monitoring for regressed eval prompts.

Known limitations & follow-ups: - Current stitch operator targets rope sizes up to 128; follow-up work tracked in ENG-4993 to extend to larger rope shards and AVX2 fallbacks for CPU. - Add tighter perf regression alerts in the console (TODO tracked in ENG-5040). - Investigate micro-batching interactions with the adapter for very high throughput steady traffic (ENG-5072).

Merge: after reviewer approvals and CI green, merged via squash on 2026-02-25.

If you're validating locally: see docs/perf/attn_adapter.md for how to run the probe harness and perf scripts.

Motivation:
We frequently observe that promotes that look good on telemetry during a short canary window still cause edge-case regressions once given full traffic. This PR introduces two complementary primitives: (1) a traffic_escrow service that holds routing decisions and only releases commits once a rehearse pass and smoke policy succeed, and (2) a rehearse_proxy that can inject synthetic canary traffic and replay recorded request traces into candidate serving revisions without affecting production state.

Goals:
- Allow operators to stage promotes with a commit escrow lease that requires an endorsement from rehearse results before full cutover.
- Provide a reproducible, auditable rehearse run that exercises session affinity, header routing, and KV cache warmup without serving user writes to production.
- Reduce time-to-revert via an escrow ledger that records the include/exclude criteria, lease owner, and rehearse outcomes per promote.

What this PR contains (single-string description):
Implemented a TrafficEscrow controller, a RehearseProxy sidecar + router middleware, a small replay harness for synthetic canaries (replay driver + sampler), and related observability (metrics, traces, and a prometheus scrape target). Included an admin API to grant/revoke escrow leases and an operator CLI hook to trigger a rehearse run. The rehearsals are configurable with smoke policies and timeout/rollback thresholds.

Checklist:
- [x] TrafficEscrow controller + database-backed ledger (sqlite for dev, Postgres migration script included)
- [x] RehearseProxy middleware for routing and replay isolation
- [x] Replay driver and synthetic canary harness with pluggable samplers
- [x] Feature flag gating (rollout.traffic_escrow) and integration tests
- [x] Prometheus metrics + tracing spans for rehearse runs
- [x] Operator CLI commands and docs stub

High-level commits:
- commit 1: controller: add TrafficEscrow CRD and schema, controller reconciliation loop with lease lifecycle
- commit 2: middleware: rehearse proxy router and headers + session-affinity passthrough
- commit 3: replay: synthetic canary driver and reservoir sampler, smoke policy evaluator
- commit 4: telemetry: metrics, traces, and prometheus target
- commit 5: migrations: add escrow ledger table and migration script
- commit 6: tests: e2e rehearse integration tests + unit tests for policy evaluator

Changed files (high level):
- services/traffic-escrow/controller.go (new)
- services/traffic-escrow/ledger/migrations/0001_create_escrow_table.sql (new)
- services/traffic-escrow/api/escrow.proto (new)
- runtime/middleware/rehearse_proxy.go (new)
- runtime/replay/driver.go (new)
- runtime/replay/sampler.go (new)
- deploy/helm/templates/escrow-deployment.yaml (mod)
- observability/metrics/escrow_metrics.go (new)
- cli/ops/escrow_cli.go (new)
- docs/ops/traffic-escrow.md (new)
- tests/e2e/rehearse_integration_test.go (new)

Small illustrative snippet (rehearse proxy header handling):

func (rp *RehearseProxy) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if rp.isRehearseRun(r) {
        // tag and route to candidate revision; keep responses sandboxed
        r.Header.Set("X-Rehearse-Run", rp.currentLeaseID)
        rp.routeToCandidate(w, r)
        return
    }
    rp.routeNormal(w, r)
}

(Full diffs are intentionally small here; implementation files are focused and mostly additive.)

Operational notes:
- Default behavior is a no-op until rollout.traffic_escrow is enabled.
- The escrow ledger keeps soft TTLs for leases; expired leases auto-fail after the configured grace period.
- Rehearse runs can be run in parallel for non-overlapping cohorts; controller rejects overlapping leases by default to avoid double-warmup.

Review thread summary (single string):
See reviewers list for full thread. Key points from review: Liam asked for stronger invariants around overlapping leases; addressed by adding overlap detection in the controller and a unit test. Maya requested clearer observability for rehearse runs; added metrics and traces and a prometheus scrape target with labels rehearse_run and cohort_id. Diego recommended a Postgres migration rather than sqlite for staging; added migration and a readme about storage backends. CI flakes on the first run due to a timing issue in the replay sampler; fixed by adding deterministic seeding in tests.

Selected review comments and replies:
- Liam O'Connor (2026-02-16): "Controller needs deterministic behavior when two promotes touch the same cohort. How does reclamation work?"
  - Author reply (Priya): "Added overlap checks and a ReclaimLease method; controller now serializes conflicting lease requests and exposes a metric escrow_conflicts_total."

- Maya Li (2026-02-18): "Can we get a top-level metric that shows rehearse run pass/fail ratio over the last 24h?"
  - Author reply: "Added rehearse_run_result_total{outcome=\"pass\"|\"fail\"} and example dashboard panels in docs/ops."

- Diego Alvarez (2026-02-19): "DB choice: use Postgres in staging. Please include migration and docs."
  - Author reply: "Included migration script and a small switch in config to pick sqlite for dev, postgres for staging/prod."

CI and test summary:
- CI pipeline: unit (go test), linters (golangci-lint), integration (docker-compose rehearse harness), e2e (k8s kind).
- Run 1: unit/lint passed, integration timed out (race in replay sampler), rerun tests after deterministic seeding.
- Run 2: all checks passed.

Post-merge actions:
- Enable rollout.traffic_escrow behind a canary flag for SRE on a single cluster for two weeks (ENG-2401).
- Run a handful of rehearses using recorded traces to validate session-affinity and cache warmups.
- Add a small playbook to run a fast revert if rehearse failures exceed threshold.

Why this is different from existing rollout features:
This PR focuses on the concept of escrowed commits plus a rehearse proxy that allows routing and replay isolation so that candidate revisions can be exercised end-to-end without touching production state. Existing staged promote primitives at Redwood emphasize traffic phasing and shadowing; traffic escrow gives an operator-level commit gating primitive with a ledger and rehearsals that are auditable and replayable.

Risk assessment:
- Low to medium risk: mostly additive components behind feature flags. The largest surface is the rehearse proxy which touches routing; we've guarded it with feature flag gating and unit tests.

Notes for on-call and SRE:
- Metric to watch: escrow_conflicts_total, rehearse_run_result_total, rehearse_run_duration_seconds_bucket, rehearsal_sandbox_errors_total.
- CLI: redwood ops escrow grant --lease-id=<id> --cohort=<name> --owner=<user>

If any follow-ups are requested, they will be tracked in ENG-1024 and ENG-2401.
Adds a traffic escrow component and a rehearse-proxy to allow dry-run rehearsals of staged promotes. No API changes for external customers; operational feature behind feature flag. Improves safety for deferred promotes and reduces blast radius of bad promotes by enabling synthetic canary replays and commit-escrow leases.
Liam O'Connor: Controller needs deterministic behavior for overlapping leases; suggested serialization + metric for conflicts.
Maya Li: Request to add rehearse_run_result_total metric and dashboard panels.
Diego Alvarez: Use Postgres in staging; add migration and docs for storage backends.
SRE: Flag gating and rollout plan required before enabling in prod; recommended a canary cluster run.

payload.body:
Motivation: production streaming sessions occasionally become orphaned when clients disconnect without sending a cancel, leading to KV-cache leaks and inflated resource use. Additionally, OpenAI-compatible clients expect a predictable cancel semantics (immediate cancel + short resume window) which our existing session lifecycle did not guarantee under high load. This PR introduces (1) an eviction + reclaim TTL for idle/inactive sessions with a safe reclaim window and soft-cancel markers, (2) a client-side 'soft-cancel' window to allow reconnect+resume semantics compatible with OpenAI-style cancellations, and (3) a compatibility shim so function/tool-calling idempotency and structured-output flushes behave consistently during cancel/reclaim races. Design summary: - Session reclaim model: sessions are now tracked with two timeouts: idle_eviction_ms (short eviction signal used for routing decisions) and reclaim_ttl_ms (how long the session KV/cache is kept for potential resume). Evicted sessions move to 'reclaimable' state and are eligible for GC after reclaim_ttl_ms. - Soft-cancel safepoints: on receiving a client cancel, we mark the stream with a soft-cancel safepoint (soft_cancel_ts) and propagate a cancellable token to downstream toolcall execution. The server will still complete short-lived downstream calls within soft_cancel_window_ms before hard abort, enabling idempotent toolcalls and structured-output flushes. - Reconnect/resume behavior: clients that reconnect within reclaim_ttl_ms can reattach and continue if the server has not reclaimed the session; the API includes a new header X-Session-Reattach: <session-id> to attach. The OpenAI compatibility layer will translate openai-cancel into a soft-cancel followed by an expire timeline that matches expected behavior for existing clients. - Backpressure and fallback: if reclaim queues grow, an eviction prioritizer drops oldest reclaimable sessions first; we expose metrics to SRE to tune policies. - Safety & idempotency: function calls initiated before soft-cancel are annotated with a call_id and a finalizer hook; if reclaimed while a call is in-flight, the runtime will prefer replay semantics over duplicate execution when call_id is present. Files changed are intentionally concise: session lifecycle state machine, eviction queue implementation, header parsing in openai-adapter, and unit+integration tests. Rollout & feature flags: session.reclaim_ttl_ms and session.soft_cancel_window_ms are controlled by flags; default values are conservative (reclaim_ttl=5m, soft_cancel=3s) and will be ramped via canary (10% -> 50% -> 100%). Migration notes: operators should be aware of new memory metrics (session_reclaim_count, session_active_reclaimable) and may want to lower reclaim_ttl for low-memory clusters. Test plan: unit tests for state transitions, deterministic integration tests simulating disconnect + reconnect races, e2e with openai-adapter exercising toolcall idempotency and structured-output flush semantics. CI: full test-suite + a new stress job (streaming-orphan-stress) added to the pipeline. See linked linear items for performance targets and further instrumentation tasks.

Tomás Rivera: Concern about metrics cardinality for session_reclaim_count tags; suggest bucketing by reclaim_reason instead of session id.
Leah Kim: Switched to reason-bucketed metrics and added session_active_reclaimable gauge. See pkg/metrics changes.
Nora Singh: Please confirm that function-call replay won't silently execute non-idempotent side effects. We should document operator guidance.
Leah Kim: Documented operator guidance in docs/operational/session-reclaim.md and added an optional finalizer hook to assert idempotency before replay.

Motivation: We observe that one-size-fits-all defaults for batching, prefix caching, and quantization lead to suboptimal unit economics for many customers (small chat workloads and high-concurrency APIs). This PR seeds the platform with a compact set of workload-segment profiles and conservative defaults so new customers and freshly-provisioned routes get safer, cost-effective behavior out-of-the-box while still enabling advanced autotuners to adjust later.

What this PR does: Adds a workload-segmentation YAML that encodes three seed profiles (latency-sensitive, throughput-friendly, conservative-cost). Wires a lightweight selector into the defaults layer so newly created model routes get an initial configuration (batch, cache_ttl, quant_profile_hint) based on estimated 95th-percentile seq_len and QPS. Introduces a small runtime hook that logs the chosen profile (for observability) and a migration that backfills unset routes with the conservative-cost profile. Updates docs and console copy to explain rationale and how to override.

Key benefits: Faster time-to-good-unit-econ for new routes, fewer support tickets asking for manual tuning, clearer migration path from conservative defaults to autotuned profiles, and safer behavior in Dedicated/Private where surprise perf regressions are costly.

Risk and scope: Conservative seed profiles intentionally bias toward lower cost (slightly higher latency for long tail requests) to avoid over-provisioning. This is a config-and-docs-first change; no kernel/runtime algorithm changes. Feature gated behind a rollout flag (defaults.seedProfiles.enabled) and opt-out via route config.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for selector logic and YAML parsing added. Integration test simulates route creation with synthetic QPS/seq_len signatures and asserts expected default assignments. E2E perf runs on benchmark-lab show median token cost reduction of ~9% for newly created chat-like routes using the conservative profile. CI: all checks green after one flaky lint failure was fixed.

Rollout plan: feature flag enabled for staging immediately, gradual rollout to 10% of new hosted routes next week, 100% after telemetry and support signoff. Dedicated/Private customers will keep existing defaults unless operator flips the seedProfiles flag.

Files and high-level changes: See files_changed for details.

Related: ENG-6201 (seed profiles design), ENG-6217 (console copy and telemetry events).
Connor Lee: Nice move to default to conservative-cost for new routes. Two asks: add a short metric that counts how many routes have the seed defaults vs user-supplied defaults, and ensure the migration is idempotent for multi-region runs.
Author (Sofia): Added defaults.seed_assigned metric and made migration guarded by a safe idempotent WHERE clause; updated tests to validate metric emission.
Aisha Patel: Can we add a short note in the console explaining why latency-sensitive customers may want to opt into autotune? Also flagged a small nits in console copy.
Author (Sofia): Updated console copy and added an FAQ entry in docs/guides/seed-profiles.md.
Marta Ivanov: CI was failing on a lint rule; after fix I reran the benchmark job and the cost numbers look reasonable. Approve pending green CI.
CI Bot: All checks passed (unit, integration, lint, bench-smoke).
Introduce workload seed profiles and conservative defaults for new routes; feature gated and opt-out capable. Reduces unit token cost for chat-like routes by default; operators can opt into autotune for lower latency.

Context and motivation: Production latency spikes during long-tail generation workloads revealed two correlated contributors: (1) poorly observable prefetch scheduling behavior when multiple inflight requests cause competing KV cache prefetches, and (2) the overhead of dense NVTX instrumentation in high-throughput paths. This PR implements a lightweight, ticker-driven staged prefetch tracer and a shared KV cache sampling hook to make sampling cheaper and signal-rich for dashboarding and microbench collection. The feature is designed to be opt-in and safe for production rollout.

Goals: make it easy to: (a) sample prefetch decisions and cache evictions at low overhead, (b) correlate prefetch stages with kernel launch latency and queue depth without adding high-frequency NVTX ranges, and (c) export aggregated counters to existing perf dashboards and bench-lab harnesses for comparison across commits.

What changed (high-level): runtime/prefetch/staged_tracer.{cc,h} implements a ticker-based tracer that emits sparse NVTX ranges at stage boundaries and writes compact events into the ring buffer aggregator; runtime/kv/shared_sampler.{h,cc} adds a shared sampling hook with reservoir sampling and small histogram sketches; tools/benchlab/integrations/prefetch_microbench.py provides a microbench harness to replay scenarios; observability/exporters/perf_dashboard_adapter.go translates sketches into Prometheus-compatible histograms; configs/runtime_flags.yaml exposes feature flags.

Design notes and tradeoffs: sparse NVTX reduces instrumentation overhead by emitting ranges only on major stage transitions. The tracer uses a configurable tick (default 1ms) to batch events into the ring buffer and reduce contention. The shared sampler keeps a fixed-size reservoir per worker and merges reservoirs infrequently to bound memory and maintain sample quality. All features are gated behind runtime flags to retain backwards compatibility.

Benchmarks: benchlab scenarios (small-eval, long-gen, mixed-burst) on AWS p4d show a 3-7% p99 latency improvement for mixed-burst when replacing dense NVTX with staged tracer + sampler, and instrumentation CPU overhead dropped from ~2.1% to ~0.36% at default settings. Heavy-hitter sample coverage remained >90% at 1% sampling due to reservoir merge heuristics.

Testing and CI: unit tests cover reservoir merge and histogram sketch correctness; integration tests exercise benchlab replay against golden fixtures. Initial CI run hit a benchlab-smoke timeout due to an aggressive tick in CI containers; this was fixed by making the tick adaptive in container envs. Final CI status: all checks green.

Review highlights: Diego requested a tunable reservoir size; the author added runtime flag kvcache.reservoir_size with default 64. Mira asked about interaction with continuous batching; the tracer emits batch-level markers and per-sample IDs so dashboards can reconstruct lineage. Kofi approved after minor locking nits were addressed.

Follow-ups: wire sampler output into perf dashboard panels and add a prefetch heatmap; surface prefetch pressure to the dedicated scheduler; investigate adaptive sampling driven by observed variance.

Merge outcome: squashed and merged into main on 2026-02-25 after approvals and green CI. Bench artifacts stored under benchlab run id benchlab/2026-02-25/153567.
Added staged prefetch tracer and a configurable shared KV cache sampling hook for low-overhead production sampling; features are opt-in via runtime flags.

Motivation: Large, long-lived KV cache backends at heavy traffic reveal two correlated problems: (1) fragmentation of cached spans that prevents efficient reclamation of contiguous memory leading to frequent small spills to disk, and (2) static eviction scoring that does not adapt to shifting workload patterns (prefix-heavy vs tail-heavy access). This PR introduces a span-compaction-aware evictor and an online workload-feedback loop that biases eviction scoring to reduce fragmentation, reduce spillover churn, and improve tail latency under mixed workloads.

Design summary: single-threaded changes in eviction hot path are intentionally small; core behavior changes are: (A) SpanCompactor: a background compaction pass that opportunistically coalesces adjacent free spans when fragmentation crosses a tunable threshold, avoiding expensive full defrag during critical windows. Compaction is bounded by a budget (max_bytes per second and max_spans per cycle) and coordinated with the scheduler to avoid impacting per-request latency SLOs. (B) WorkloadFeedbackEvictor: eviction scoring extended with a short-term access histogram (micro-window) and a drift-corrected recency-weight, so frequently reaccessed small spans receive a temporary retention boost while cold large spans are prioritized for coalescing and eviction. (C) EarlySpillBackoff: when disk spill rates spike, policy throttles low-value evictions and increases compaction budget for short periods to reduce repeated spill-churn. (D) Telemetry: new metrics (kv.compaction.runs, kv.compaction.bytes_moved, kv.eviction.score_histogram, kv.spill.retries) and a diagnostic route to snapshot current span map for debugging.

Compatibility notes: all on-disk cache formats unchanged. Configuration knobs are behind a runtime flag feature.kv_span_compactor=false by default; rollouts can enable per-cluster. The compactor is safe on dedicated and private deployments; code paths include guardrails for air-gapped environments (no external calls).

Benchmarks: microbench harness runs with mix of synthetic workloads (50% small hot keys, 50% long-tail scans) measured on our perf lab NVMe+A100 nodes showed: median latency unchanged, p95 tail latency reduced 12% under mixed load, overall spillover events reduced 22%, and peak memory overhead improved by ~18% due to reduced fragmentation. End-to-end token-cost for a continuous-batching scenario with heavy KV cache reuse dropped ~6% after tuning. These numbers are reproducible with the included benchmark script in perf-canary/.

What changed (high level file areas): additions in runtime/kv/cache_compactor.{cc,h}, runtime/kv/evictor_feedback.{cc,h}, runtime/kv/metrics_registry.cc, runtime/scheduler/priority_hints.cc, config/defaults.yaml (new knobs), tests/kv/compactor_integration_test.cc, perf-canary/kv_fragmentation_bench.py, docs/observability/kv_compaction.md. Small public API additions: new config keys under kv.compaction.{enabled,bytes_per_sec,max_spans_cycle} and kv.eviction.feedback_window_ms.

Commit summary: - initial span compactor scaffolding and basic compaction loop - implement coalescing heuristics and budget framework - add workload-feedback histogram and merge into eviction scoring - integrate with scheduler via priority hints to pause compaction during high tail request load - metrics, tests, and perf harness - documentation and rollout guide - two follow-up fixes for race in compaction shutdown and test flakiness.

Files changed (high level): runtime/kv/cache_compactor.cc: new compaction loop and coalescer logic; runtime/kv/cache_compactor.h: interfaces and budget struct; runtime/kv/evictor_feedback.cc/.h: histogram and scoring integration; runtime/kv/kv_store.cc: hooks into eviction path and early-spill backoff; runtime/scheduler/priority_hints.cc: new pause/resume for background tasks; tests/kv/*: integration tests and race reproducer; perf-canary/*: reproducible benchmark scripts and configs; docs/observability/kv_compaction.md: telemetry and runbook.

Review conversation (high level): - Diego: requested clarifications on compaction budget interplay with autoscaler. Asha: added a scheduler hook so compaction budgets are halved when autoscaler signals high load; included unit tests. - Lina: flagged potential race on shutdown where compactor could touch freed spans; Asha: added a graceful checkpoint and a mutex/epoch guard and two tests that reproduce and verify fix. - Marcus: asked for more metrics around spill retries and a view into span histogram; Asha: added kv.spill.retries and an admin endpoint to snapshot span map. - Diego: ran perf lab numbers and asked for reproducibility artifacts; Asha: uploaded perf scripts and dockerfile for harness in perf-canary. Final approvals after minor test naming nits.

CI status: initial run failed on macOS lint (line-length in docs) and on a flaky integration test (compactor_shutdown_test). Fixes: docs lint fixed, added retry/timeout in test; subsequent CI run: all checks passed (build, unit, integration, perf-smoke).

Merging: squash-and-merge with a single commit message summarizing span compactor + feedback evictor; changelog entry added to release notes. Rollout plan: enable feature.kv_span_compactor in canary for 48h, monitor kv.compaction.* and kv.spill.* metrics for regressions, then widen to 10% then 50%.

Follow-ups (open todos): - autotune heuristics for feedback_window_ms per workload class (ENG-1987) - add a bounded multi-threaded compactor option for very large caches (future perf investigation) - integrate compaction budget signals with Dedicated autoscaler more tightly.

If you want to reproduce: see perf-canary/README.md for setup and perf-canary/kv_fragmentation_bench.py for the workloads used to generate bench numbers.

Asha Patel: Added scheduler hook to halve compaction budget on autoscaler high-load signals. See runtime/scheduler/priority_hints.cc and tests for behavior.
Lina Zhou: Found a race on shutdown where compactor touched freed spans in the store. Can we add an epoch or graceful drain?
Asha Patel: Added epoch guard and compactor checkpointing, plus an integration test that reproduces the previous flake.
Marcus Reed: Please expose spill retry metric and a snapshot endpoint for span map; helps debugging customer incidents.
Asha Patel: Added kv.spill.retries and admin span snapshot route under debug/admin/kv_span_map.

Motivation: under high-concurrency, the paged KV cache freelist would fragment after repeated allocations/frees of mixed-size blocks, increasing allocation latency and causing more frequent slow-path compaction. This PR adds an opportunistic freelist defragmenter that compacts adjacent free pages on free-paths and a lightweight hot-prefix selective pinning policy so frequently-accessed key prefixes avoid costly eviction. Goals: reduce p99 allocation latency, lower background compaction pressure, and improve tail latency for workloads with hot prefixes (chat sessions, long contexts).

Summary of changes:
- Opportunistic freelist defragmenter run inline on frees when a small threshold of contiguous free segments is observed (configurable).
- Compact-on-free path that coalesces adjacent free pages into larger blocks to improve reuse for larger token sequences.
- Adaptive reuse scoring: tracks short-term reuse frequency per page bucket and prefers reuse of high-score pages.
- Hot-prefix selective pinning: a small resident pin set for top-N hot key prefixes with LRU eviction; pins are persisted across ephemeral reconnects to stabilize performance.
- Scheduler hint: allocator exposes a gentle backpressure hint to the request scheduler when fragmentation crosses configured thresholds so the scheduler can delay batch growth and avoid thrashing.
- Tests and microbenchmarks: new unit tests for defragmenter invariants and a throughput/latency benchmark demonstrating behavior across workload mixes.

Compatibility: fully opt-in via runtime config flags (defaults are conservative).

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked in PR
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Microbenchmark
- [x] CI green after flake fix
- [x] Perf measurements attached

Related tickets: Linear ENG-4823 (KV fragmentation), ENG-4781 (hot-prefix regressions).

Added a read-only Rationale API for alert explanations and a lightweight token-penalty meter used by alert scoring. No customer-facing API changes. Backfilled dashboards and tuned a set of alert rules.
Context: On-call and SREs increasingly ask not just that an SLO is breached, but why — which token phases, model variants, or kernel queues contributed to the cost/latency signal. This PR implements a focused observability surface: (1) a read-only 'rationale' API that returns a concise, machine- and human-readable explanation for an alert window (token phase breakdowns, top-3 contributing callsites, and suggested mitigation), and (2) a new token-penalty meter used to weight samples for the alerting engine so that alerts reflect cost-incurring tokens rather than raw invocation counts. Motivation: reduce alert noise and speed up RCA by surface-level explainability without requiring deep trace pulls or heavy-weight queries. Summary of changes: - telemetry/service/rationale_api.py: new lightweight HTTP handler (read-only) that accepts alert_id/window and returns a compact rationale object (phase_summaries, contributors, suggested_fallbacks). Includes endpoint auth via existing service token. - telemetry/penalty/token_penalty.py: token-penalty meter implementation (pluggable strategy interface + default strategy combining token_cost, kernel_backpressure_factor, and kv_cache_miss_weight). - infra/alerts/alert_rules.yml: updated rule templates to call the penalty-weighted rate and include rationale links in alert messages. - console/dashboards/rationale-panel.json: added a small explainer panel and a sparkline that breaks tokens by phase for the selected window; the panel uses the rationale API for on-demand enrichment. - sdk-python/redwood/observability.py: thin client helper to call the rationale API and render results for internal CLI tooling and runbooks. - tests/*: unit tests for penalty scoring, rationale summarizer, and end-to-end smoke test that runs against the staging telemetry stack. - docs/observability/rationale-api.md: usage, examples, and recommended alert message templates. Migration/rollout plan: 1) Deploy rationale API behind a feature flag in staging and enable the console panel for internal users. 2) Use the penalty meter in a passive mode (adds a tag to alerts but doesn't change routing) for 48h to compare signal. 3) Flip penalty weighting into active alert scoring and watch SRE dashboards for false-negatives/positives. Monitoring and safeguards: - The rationale API is intentionally rate-limited and caches computed rationales for 15 minutes to avoid heavy query load. - Added a cost-safety circuit: if the rationale generation backend detects a query would scan >1M tokens, it returns a summarized fallback and records a telemetry event. - Penalty meter is configurable per-tenant and defaults to conservative weights (cost x1.0, backpressure x0.5, miss x1.2). Testing: - Unit tests: penalty math, serialization of rationale. - Integration: simulated alert windows with synthetic traces to validate the top-3 contributor extraction. - Load test: generated 500 concurrent rationale requests hitting cached vs. uncached paths; no P95 latency regression seen in staging. Rollback: feature flags and per-tenant gates allow immediate disable. Related work: ENG-4021 (alert explainability roadmap), ENG-4120 (token-cost-weighting for SLOs). Checklist: - [x] Implementation complete - [x] Unit & integration tests added - [x] Dashboard panel added - [x] Docs and runbook snippets - [x] Feature flags and conservative default weights - [x] Verified basic load behavior in staging

Liam O'Connor (approval): Verified integration test and staging load. Recommend squash+merge once CI passes.

Motivation: clients need richer filtering and billing metadata from the model listing endpoint to make routing and cost-aware decisions without extra calls. This PR introduces three orthogonal additions to the model directory API: 1) compatibility_scopes: coarse-grained flags that indicate if a model is compatible with OpenAI tools/fn-calling, streaming-first delivery, or embedding-only workloads. 2) streaming_ready_hints: lightweight per-model suggestions for preferred chunk sizes, max_chunk_latency_ms and recommended stream backpressure behavior to improve stability for clients using streaming. 3) billing_tiers: explicit fields describing unit pricing buckets and soft limits so SDKs and edge routers can surface cost estimates. To preserve backward compatibility we keep all new fields optional and documented in the OpenAPI spec. We also added a new query param scope_filter to allow server-side filtering by one or more compatibility scopes (e.g., ?scope_filter=streaming,openai_compat). Rollout: feature gated behind toggles; default off for older clients. payload.body:
Motivation: production tail cases show two distinct failure modes that create steep cost/latency tradeoffs: transient kernel OOMs or scheduling preemptions that could be recovered by a quick kernel retry, and mass KV-cache eviction storms triggered by synchronized long-context requests leading to repeated cold misses. This PR implements a tiered degradation strategy: 1) a lightweight "lazy kernel retry" fast-path that only re-invokes a compatible kernel on transient internal errors within the same request instead of immediately falling back to a lower-precision model; 2) an eviction throttler for the KV cache that rate-limits bulk eviction operations and staggers eviction windows to avoid concentrated cold-miss spikes. Changes are guarded by runtime flags and safe defaults so behavior is opt-in for Dedicated/Private until validated in canary. Checklist: [x] implement lazy kernel retry with backoff and probe; [x] add eviction throttler with per-pool tokens; [x] expose tuning knobs via config and Console; [x] add unit + integration tests; [x] benchmark end-to-end tail latency and token-cost impact; [x] doc changelog and rollout notes. Design notes: lazy kernel retry targets only errors marked as transient (OOM_HINT, SCHEDULE_PREEMPT, KERNEL_CRASH_TRANSIENT) and only retries kernels with identical numerical precision and compatible memory footprints; retry is limited to 1 attempt per request and uses a jittered 5-20ms scheduling slot to avoid thundering herd. If retry fails or kernel is incompatible, we fall back to the existing precision-degrade path. The KV eviction throttler introduces a token-bucket per-GPU-pool eviction gate; eviction requests consume tokens proportional to estimated bytes reclaimed; tokens replenish at a configurable rate. If tokens are exhausted, eviction requests are queued with exponential backoff and a lightweight admission check prevents eviction storms from queuing too many requests. Config knobs exposed: runtime.lazy_retry.enabled, runtime.lazy_retry.max_attempts, cache.eviction.token_rate, cache.eviction.bucket_size, cache.eviction.max_queue_ms. Backwards compatibility: disabled by default for hosted tier, enabled in canary nodes and Dedicated feature-flag. Performance: internal lab runs (BERT-like long-context workload + mixed chat) show 8-12% reduction in 95th/99th token latency in scenarios dominated by transient kernel failures, and 4-7% CPU/GPU token-cost improvement when eviction storms were previously causing repeated recomputation. Risk and safety: lazy retry can increase a small window of latency for requests that would have been better served by immediate precision downgrade; this is mitigated by the 1-attempt cap and conservative transient-error classification. The eviction throttler prevents cascading misses at the cost of delayed reclamation under memory pressure; we surface eviction pressure metrics to Console and add an emergency override that forces immediate eviction if realtime memory crosses a critical threshold. Testing: unit tests for retry decision logic and throttler token math, integration tests simulating kernel OOMs and synchronized full-length contexts, epidemiology-style load tests validating no increased burst error rates. Rollout: 1) canary on dedicated pool (5% traffic) with metrics dashboards added; 2) expand to low-latency customers after 2 weeks of stable metrics; 3) tenant opt-in for Hosted via Console toggle. Docs: added operational guidance and tuning suggestions in docs/ops/tiered_degradation.md. See release notes for user-visible flags and recommended values.
Diego Morales (review): Overall approach looks sensible. Main concern is ensuring we don't regress tail variance by adding retry jitter; can we add a metric exposing retry-induced latency to track regressions?
Author (Asha): Added retry.metrics.lazy_retry_latency histogram and a retry_reason tag. Also added an opt-out per-tenant flag so high-Latency-sensitive customers can disable retry at tenant-level.
Evelyn Chen (review): Eviction throttler makes sense, but token math needs to account for partial reclamation when pinned pages can't be evicted. Please ensure we don't silently starve eviction under memory pressure.
Author (Asha): Adjusted token consumption to be a lower-bound estimate and added an emergency override that bypasses the throttle if free-memory < 6% for the pool. Added tests simulating pinned pages where token consumption falls short.
Samir Gupta (approval): Verified integration test results and benchmark numbers vs baseline. Approve after CI green and docs updated.
Introduces a tiered degradation strategy that adds a conservative 'lazy kernel retry' for transient kernel failures and a KV cache eviction throttler to reduce cold-miss storms. Exposed runtime flags for tuning. Disabled by default on hosted; recommended canary rollout for Dedicated. See docs/ops/tiered_degradation.md for ops guidance.
Recommended conservative defaults: runtime.lazy_retry.enabled=true (canary), runtime.lazy_retry.max_attempts=1, cache.eviction.token_rate=5MB/s, cache.eviction.bucket_size=50MB, cache.eviction.max_queue_ms=5000. Monitor metrics: retry.metrics.lazy_retry_latency, cache.eviction.throttle_backpressure, cache.eviction.emergency_override_count.
Unit tests cover decision branches for transient errors and token math; integration tests simulate kernel OOM and coordinated long-context clients; stress runs in the benchmark lab show reduced 99th percentile latency in targeted failure modes. No increased error-rate observed in canary over 7 days.

Summary: This PR fixes several gaps in our OpenAI /v1/chat.completions compatibility layer: correct stop token behavior across batch and streaming paths, ensure logprobs alignment when truncation occurs, and make function_call handling deterministic in streaming mode. Motivation: Customers hit parity mismatches when migrating from OpenAI endpoints — stop tokens could be applied at a different stage than OpenAI (sometimes after logprobs), streaming could emit partial assistant messages then abruptly close causing downstream parsers to mis-handle function_call signals, and multi-choice streaming with n>1 had racey ordering. We need deterministic, documented parity so apps relying on OpenAI semantics behave the same on Redwood. Design and changes: 1) Stop semantics: unify stop handling to apply token/sequence truncation before final logprob computation and chunk emission. This mirrors OpenAI behavior: the stop token(s) are removed from the output text and any token-level probabilities associated with the stopped token are excluded from returned logprobs. Implementation: added a StopProcessor that runs as the final step of the decode pipeline; it signals stream close and adjusts cached KV/logprob windows. 2) Streaming stability: replace ad-hoc stream-close signaling with a two-phase shutdown: a FIN intent message followed by an ack window to ensure consumers see final function_call blocks. This fixes observed race where library consumers missed the trailing "function_call" object. 3) Function calling parity: ensure function_call:{"name":"auto"/"none"/"<name>"} mapping is preserved in streaming partial events; the assistant role tokens used to decide function invocation are buffered and emitted only when the call is complete or when a stop triggers an early flush. 4) Logprobs alignment: when trim/truncate occurs due to stop or max_tokens limits, we drop logprob entries for removed tokens and adjust token_index mapping fields to match OpenAI responses. 5) n>1 streaming ordering: guarantee deterministic choice ordering by tagging each choice stream with choice_index and holding interleaved chunks until sequence alignment is resolved by the router. 6) Backwards compatibility: introduced a feature flag redwood.openai.compat.strict_parity (default true) to gate exact behavior; non-strict mode retains prior Redwood semantics for customers who depend on them. Tests & CI: added unit tests for StopProcessor, streaming integration tests that spawn two simulated clients and assert final assembled messages match OpenAI reference traces, and e2e coverage for function_call streaming under early stop conditions. A flaky test (stream_close_race) was stabilized by increasing the ack window timeout and adding deterministic sleeps to the integration harness; CI now passes. Files changed (high level): - api/openai_compat/handler.py: added StopProcessor integration and feature-flag checks - serving/streaming/stream_manager.py: two-phase stream shutdown and choice_index tagging - serving/streaming/tests/test_stream_stop.py: new unit/integration tests - api/openai_compat/logprob_adjuster.py: normalize logprobs after truncation - sdk/ts/openai_compat_client.ts: client-side partial-event schema docs and example - docs/openai-compat.md: documented new strict_parity flag and migration notes - tests/integration/function_call_stop_repro.py: reproducer and e2e assertions Commits (summary): 1) add StopProcessor and tests 2) implement two-phase streaming shutdown + choice_index 3) logprob trimming/normalization and mapping fixes 4) add feature flag + docs 5) fix failing integration test and CI flakes 6) squash/final cleanup Review thread (summary): - Liam: requested additional unit tests around logprob mapping for multi-byte utf8 sequences. Author: added tests (serving/streaming/tests/test_logprob_utf8.py). - Diego: flagged potential perf regression from StopProcessor copying buffers; asked for microbenchmark. Author: added microbenchmark and optimized to use zero-copy views where possible. - Maya: asked to surface the strict_parity flag in the Console UI flags page; created DES ticket (DES-87). QA: Verified streaming stability against recorded OpenAI traces (chat_stop_variant_{a,b,c}) and confirmed parity for stop/logprobs/function_call sequences. Migration notes: Operators should be aware of the new redwood.openai.compat.strict_parity flag; default true, no customer action required. If a customer relied on Redwood's previous, slightly different behavior, they can flip the flag to false while they adapt. Breaking changes: none by default; changing the flag can change output text/logprob deltas so call out in release notes. Checklist: - [x] unit tests added - [x] integration tests added - [x] docs updated - [x] benchmark added - [x] QA signoff Links: Linear ENG-2048 (design), SUP-431 (customer report), docs https://internal.redwood/docs/openai-compat#stop-and-function-calling Notes: The description intentionally keeps details high-level; see code for exact edge case handling. This PR was squashed on merge and the final commit message summarizes the changes for release notes.

Anika: Added serving/streaming/tests/test_logprob_utf8.py that reproduces the UTF-8 case and asserts index mapping.
