Summary: Implement compatibility for the OpenAI Responses v13 semantics: propagate explicit seed/determinism hints and preserve per-token + per-segment structured attributes (metadata) end-to-end through Redwood's OpenAI bridge and streaming path. This PR focuses on three areas: 1) pass-through of the `seed`/`determinism` hint on both sync and streaming paths; 2) canonical mapping of Responses v13 structured attributes (attrs) into Redwood internal ResponseAttributes and back to downstream clients (OpenAI-compatible shape for function/tool call chunks); 3) streaming stability fixes for mixed chunks (text + tool call signals) to avoid reordering and partial-attribute drop during reassembly.

Motivation and context: Responses v13 introduces an expanded attributes envelope used by model tooling and evals teams to annotate segments with deterministic hints, provenance tags, and tooling handshake signals. Customers using Redwood's OpenAI-compat layer rely on exact propagation of these attributes for deterministic replay, offering strong guarantees for A/B and canary rollouts. Previously we preserved `seed` metadata in v11/12 adapters, but v13 adds nested structured attrs and a slight framing change for tool-call boundaries. Without correct passthrough, downstream SDKs and replay systems lose deterministic replay and function-handshake attributes, causing surprising behavior for customers using seed-based reruns or external tool orchestators.

What this PR changes (single-line checklist): - add request/response mapping for Responses v13 attributes -> Redwood ResponseAttributes -> OpenAI-compatible attribute passthrough; - wire `seed`/`determinism` on both REST and streaming code paths; - canonical mapping of Responses v13 structured attributes (attrs) into Redwood internal ResponseAttributes and back to downstream clients (OpenAI-compatible shape for function/tool call chunks); - streaming stability fixes for mixed chunks (text + tool call signals) to avoid reordering and partial-attribute drop during reassembly.

Implementation notes (high-level commits): commit 1: bridge: add v13 attribute serializer/deserializer and mapping table; commit 2: core/stream: change ReassemblyBuffer to attach attribute-frames and ensure monotonic attribute offsets; commit 3: api/compat: include seed header propagation for http/streaming requests and include fallback when absent; commit 4: tests: deterministic-replay integration test + new test vectors generated (golden files); commit 5: docs: add section "OpenAI Responses v13: seed & structured attrs passthrough".

Files changed (high-level): - src/compat/openai/v13_adapter.go (new mapping & serializer) - src/serving/stream/reassembly.go (stream/frame reassembly fixes) - src/serving/stream/stream_test.go (new integration vectors) - api/compat/http_adapter.go (seed passthrough on REST) - docs/openai/v13-compat.md (docs snippet) - testdata/responses-v13/* (golden chunk captures) - tools/generate_v13_vectors.py (helper used in tests) - go.mod / go.sum (minor deps)

Small illustrative snippet (v13 attr mapping):
 // v13 attr shape -> Redwood internal
 {"attrs": [{"k":"seed","v":12345},{"k":"provenance","v":"eval-run"}],"segment_type":"tool_call"}
 becomes
 ResponseAttributes{Seed:12345, Tags:["eval-run"], SegmentType:ToolCall}
 and when re-emitted to an OpenAI-compatible consumer we preserve the attrs envelope and add `redwood.bridge_id` tag.

Testing and QA: - unit tests for mapping both directions (v13 <-> internal) - integration test that opens a streaming connection, sends split tool-call chunks with interleaved attributes and asserts the reassembled final response keeps attribute boundaries and the seed value; uses recorded golden frames in testdata/responses-v13/ - smoke test with SDK: redwood-sdk-python example `examples/openai_v13_seed_demo.py` (added) - manual QA plan: exercise deterministic replay by re-sending request with seed and comparing token stream equality between two runs on same pinned model.

Backward compatibility: The adapter is additive: when v13 attrs are not present we default to current behavior. We preserve existing v11/v12 mappings via a compatibility shim. No customer-facing API changes except improved passthrough fidelity for v13 consumers.

Review notes and important tradeoffs: - We intentionally keep the mapping conservative: complex nested attr payloads are preserved as opaque kv lists instead of being normalized into typed fields beyond `seed` and `segment_type`. This avoids breaking future v13 evolution. - The streaming reassembly change attaches small attribute-metadata to chunk envelopes which increases envelope memory a small amount (benchmarked ~2% at 512-concurrency); we add an optimization flag to disable attribute retention if customers opt out for ultra-low memory environments.

Manual rollback plan: revert the v13 adapter and reassembly change together (single commit) and redeploy; the change is behind a feature flag in config (openai_v13_attrs_passthrough=true) to allow staged rollout.

Changelog entry (short): Add OpenAI Responses v13 seed and structured-attributes passthrough to the OpenAI compatibility bridge.

--- Review conversation (high level):
Ethan Liu (review): "Nice focused change. Two requests: 1) add a test for concurrent streaming where seed headers differ between sharded backends; 2) add a small benchmark for memory regression at 512 concurrency." 
Maya (author): "Added a concurrent streaming test and ran memory microbench; results included in the test output. I moved the attribute retention behind the feature flag to give ops a toggle." 
Sofia Romero (review): "Verified integration test locally. One nit: naming of ReassemblyBuffer.attachAttributes -> should read attachAttributeFrames for clarity." 
Maya: "Renamed in last commit." 
Daniel Kim (review): "Approvals pending CI green. Clarify logging level for dropped attrs when opt-out is enabled." 
Maya: "Set the log to debug and added a metric 'bridge.attrs.dropped' to observability pack (small spike metric)."

CI summary (timeline): - initial run (linux/go-test): fail (race detected in stream_test.go:122) - fix commit added synchronized queue -> re-run - second run: flaky lint on docs generation; docs lint fixed -> re-run - final run: all checks passing (unit, integration, lint, e2e smoke) - CI artifacts: testreport/html/index.html; perf/mem-bench/512-concurrency.csv attached.

Merge outcome: merged via squash-and-merge to main. Merge commit message preserved summary and Linear links. Feature gated on config flag `openai_v13_attrs_passthrough` and enabled for canary region us-east-1 for first 48h.

Post-merge actions: - monitor metric bridge.attrs.dropped and deterministic_replay.success_rate for 72h - coordinate with solutions-engineering to notify top 10 customers using seed-based reruns - cut a docs patch to stable site (scheduled next deploy)
payload.title: openai-bridge: v13 Responses compatibility - forward seed + structured attrs passthrough

payload.body:
Motivation: multi-tool patterns (parallel calls, fan-in injection) increased nondeterminism in how tool outputs were injected into the model prompt and streaming responses. This caused intermittent flakiness in structured outputs and made retries unsafe for side-effectful tools. This PR introduces a staged execution model and idempotent replay primitives to make multi-tool executions deterministic, safe to retry, and compatible with existing OpenAI-style function calling semantics.

What this changes (summary):
- Introduce a runtime 'staged' pipeline for tool calls: tools are scheduled into deterministic stages (prepare -> call -> collect -> inject) to guarantee a stable injection order across parallel executions.
- Add a gating/semaphore layer that limits in-flight tool calls per-request and enforces backpressure to protect downstream serving resources.
- Implement an idempotent replay token and deterministic result hash so retries can be replayed without duplicate side effects (requires tool adapter support).
- Update the OpenAI compatibility layer so function-call responses preserve staged injection metadata; no caller-facing API breaking changes — current behavior preserved unless staged mode is enabled.
- Add SDK shims (python/ts) that expose an opt-in 'staged' flag when calling tools or using run_tool_chain; adapters updated to support idempotent hooks.
- Improved telemetry: new metrics for stage latencies, semaphore contention, and replay counts.

Design notes:
- Determinism is achieved by assigning stable sort keys to tool requests (source order + tie-breaker) before parallel dispatch. We batch by stage so KV/cache insertion and prompt injection happen in a single deterministic pass.
- Replay token is generated from request id + stage metadata. Tool adapters must implement a replay check to short-circuit side effects; a fallback safe-execute path is provided for older adapters.
- Backpressure gating uses a leaky-bucket semaphore per-tenant that integrates with existing autoscaling hooks to avoid queuing storms during traffic spikes.

Testing and validation:

Motivation: Long-tail request patterns + heterogeneous KV cache hits were causing persistent queue skew across worker shards in the continuous batching scheduler. Small tenants and short sequences were starved behind heavy streaming requests that pinned KV caches, causing visible latency regressions for 95th/99th percentiles. This change introduces an adaptive slot rebalance controller that re-evaluates per-shard slot allocations on soft timeouts and when skew thresholds are exceeded.

Summary of changes: - Add a slot rebalance controller that computes a skew score across scheduling queues and issues low-cost token transfers between shards when imbalance is detected. - Integrate a short randomized graceful drain period to avoid coordinated preemption waves; this uses jittered timeouts and a small credit buffer to preserve KV pin locality where beneficial. - Introduce a lightweight probe sample that estimates per-tenant KV cache pressure and factors it into rebalance decisions (heuristic only; does not evict). - Tune default soft-timeout thresholds and make them configurable via scheduler config (continuous_batcher.rebalance.*). - Add observability: new metrics continuous_batcher.rebalance.skew_ratio, rebalance.attempts, rebalance.success_rate, and per-tenant probe_kv_pressure.

Design notes: - The rebalance controller is intentionally conservative: transfers only occur when skew_ratio > 1.8 or when a soft-timeout has fired 3x in a 30s sliding window. Transfers are limited to at most 10% of a shard's active slots per minute to avoid oscillation. - To reduce KV pin churn we prefer transferring slots associated with requests that have low KV residency (stateless/short sequences) first; longer lived KV-pinned sessions are avoided if probe_kv_pressure indicates high locality. - All heuristics are feature-gated behind continuous_batcher.rebalance.enabled and default to off for Dedicated customers unless explicitly enabled.

Backwards compatibility and rollout: - Default to off for existing clusters. - Feature flag gated + canary rollout via console (1% clusters -> 10% -> 50% -> global). - Includes automatic rollback hook if 95th latency increases by >10% or error-rate climbs >1% in canary buckets.

Benchmarks: - Synthetic mixed workload (70% short seq <64 tokens, 25% medium, 5% long streaming) on 8-shard cluster: 95th latency reduced 18%, 99th reduced 12%, tail throughput increased 6%. - KV-heavy skew scenario (two heavy tenants on shards 3/4): starvation events dropped from 23 to 3 per hour in load tests. Full benchmark logs attached in CI artifact.

What changed (high level file map): - scheduler/rebalance/controller.go (new): core rebalance logic and heuristics - scheduler/rebalance/probe.go (new): lightweight KV pressure probe - scheduler/batcher/continuous.go (modified): hook points for drain and token transfer - config/schema.yaml (modified): new rebalance config knobs - observability/metrics_registry.go (modified): metric registration - tests/scheduler/rebalance_test.go (new): unit tests for skew detection - e2e/perf/bench_rebalance.yaml (new): perf harness for canary

Commits (summary): - f3a9c7e: initial controller scaffolding and config knobs - b28d411: add probe, integrate with scheduler hooks - 7a5d2c4: add metrics and dashboard queries - e13b4d9: tests and benchmark harness - 4f11a21: benchmark tuning, flake fixes, docs - 9c0fef2: enable feature flag, canary rollout manifest

Review conversation (highlights): - Reviewer (Liam Carter): "Can we ensure transfers respect tenant isolation boundaries? Also please add a flag to disable KV-probe influence for enterprise customers who want strict locality." - Author reply (Asha Nair): "Added enterprise bypass flag continuous_batcher.rebalance.ignore_kv_probe and unit test to verify bypass path." - Reviewer (Marta Reyes): "Concern about oscillation under bursty traffic." - Author reply: "Added exponential backoff and an overall per-shard transfer cap (10%/min), included in design notes and unit tests." - Approvals: Liam Carter (approved), Marta Reyes (approved after adjustments), SRE rotation (auto-approve CI pass).

Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions surface expect a few nuanced behaviors (stop semantics, role-preserving role mapping, streaming logprob envelopes, and deterministic function_call hints). Our compatibility layer has historically handled these piecemeal; this change bundles a deterministic, well-tested mapping layer plus a streaming envelope that reduces parser churn for downstream SDKs.

What this PR does (high level): 1) Introduces a response-sculpting adapter that normalizes incoming v1 parameters (temperature/top_p/stop arrays/stop strings) into Redwood runtime configs, coalescing stop tokens with deduplication and priority ordering (explicit stop > system-supplied stop). 2) Adds a streaming logprob envelope: each delta event includes a compact logprob map when requested (logprobs mode) and a stable "terminate_reason" token on final events to remove ambiguity for partial consumers. 3) Preserves role metadata and adds role_alias resolution so tools that pass custom roles still receive canonical role labels in responses. 4) Extends function_call handling to surface both suggested and forced calls: when the model suggests a call we emit a standardized tool-call event; when callers force a function_call we validate against registered schemas and return an immediate structured output. 5) Implements conservative backpressure hooks in the stream coalescer to improve stability under bursty clients.

Compatibility notes: The adapter keeps backward-compatible defaults; previous consumers that do not request logprobs or function schemas should see no change. New behavior is opt-in via the v1 parameter mapping and an additional header (X-OpenAI-Compat: true) for private deployments that want explicit parity checks.

Testing and validation: Unit tests added for stop coalescing, role aliasing, function schema validation and negative cases. End-to-end tests simulate streaming clients (chunk reordering, reconnect resume) and assert final assembled events for both SDKs. Benchmarked against a production-like workload: median p99 tail latency increased by ~1ms in the worst case; CPU overhead on the agent path is <2% for common workloads.

Rollout plan: Feature gated behind openai_v1_compat flag. Canary on dedicated region us-west-2 for 48 hours with traffic mirroring; if stable, promote to main with a one-week monitoring window (alert on increased stream reconnects or event schema validation failures).

Related: ENG-1842 (param mapping), SUP-5523 (customer incident that exposed stop token mismatch).
Tomás Rivera: Important to ensure ordering for coalesced stops — what happens when a client supplies overlapping regex-based stops? Please add a test.
Asha Kapoor: Added deterministic precedence and a unit test for overlapping regex stops (stop_coalesce_test.go). Regex stops are treated as last-resort matches and are only applied when exact tokens don't trigger earlier stop rules.
Ling Chen: Streaming logprob envelope looks good but please document the size impact on the stream frame and add opt-out for clients concerned about bandwidth.
Asha Kapoor: Introduced a `logprobs=none|summary|full` mapping; default remains none. Documented bandwidth considerations in docs/openai_compat.md.
Noah Patel: Function schema validation makes sense; can we fail closed for invalid schemas or return a 4xx error to the caller?
Asha Kapoor: We return a 422 with a structured error payload and a telemetry event. This is covered in schema_validator.go and e2e tests.
CI: flaky test in e2e on reconnect simulated network delay — I retriggered and it passed on re-run.
Add OpenAI /v1 chat compatibility adapter: normalized params (stop coalescing & dedupe), streaming logprob envelope with terminate_reason, role alias resolution, and deterministic function_call schema validation. Opt-in via openai_v1_compat feature flag and X-OpenAI-Compat header.

Motivation: reduce tail latency and improve per-GPU throughput for common small-batch streaming workloads by separating concerns in the attention path. This PR decouples the fused QKV arithmetic from rotary/rope application and introduces a lightweight rope-swap stage plus a GPU-side KV prefetch streamer integrated with the continuous-batching scheduler. Rationale: tightly fused QKV+rotary kernels are fast on steady, large-batch workloads but cause memory layout churn and head-of-line blocking for bursty single-request streams and mixed sequence lengths. By splitting the fused kernel and moving rotary application to a deterministic post-QKV pass we can reuse packed QKV buffers across nearby requests and prefetch remote KV shards before decode starts. What this PR does: 1) Introduces a new tiled QKV kernel (FlashLoop wrapper) that focuses exclusively on Q/K/V matmuls and packing; it accepts an optional packed-output flag so the scheduler can keep buffers GPU-resident for a short window. 2) Adds a rope-swap stage (device and CPU fallbacks) that applies rotary/rope in-place or in a streaming chunked mode for very long sequences. 3) Implements a KV prefetch streamer in the continuous-batching scheduler that issues async copies for predicted hot KV shards while request tokens are being decoded; integrates with the existing cache eviction heuristics. 4) Adds runtime toggles and telemetry for the new stages (opt-in via config and feature flag for canary customers). Backwards compatibility: default behavior on main is unchanged until feature-flag rollout completes; new kernel is gated by runtime config so we can A/B or do canary rollouts. Testing: unit tests for kernel correctness (compare against fused QKV+rotary baseline), integration tests for scheduler prefetch logic, and microbench harness results included below. Benchmarks (A100, fp16, seq=1024 unless noted): - Small-batch streaming (batch=1, token-by-token): p50 latency down 7%, p95 down 14%, end-to-end throughput up 8-12% depending on model width. - Mixed-batch steady-state (batch 8-16): throughput neutral to +3% (depends on quantization path). - KV-heavy rerank workload (large cache churn): effective GPU utilization improved by ~15% due to prefetch overlap. - Worst-case long-seq (seq>8192): rope-swap chunked path shows 10% lower memory overhead vs fused kernel. CI notes: one flaky integration test (scheduler/eviction_test) failed on first run, was rerun and passed; no test regressions after fixes. Rollback plan: toggle feature-flag to false and revert canary pool; kernel code is additive and default path unchanged. Risks and mitigations: slight increase in code surface for kernel staging; mitigated by conservative defaults, telemetry, and canary rollout. Release notes: improved small-batch streaming latency and KV-heavy workload throughput via new split-QKV kernel and rope-swap prefetching. Additional context and links: Linear ENG-3789 for rollout plan, perf-canary dashboards attached in the PR comments.

Motivation: We have diverging streaming ergonomics across Python/TS/Go SDKs and subtle auth-retry edge cases that manifest as half-open streams or token race conditions during refresh. This PR unifies three areas: 1) a minimal, consistent 3-way auth handshake for stream starts and reconnects; 2) a small, opinionated consumer surface that makes backpressure and heartbeats explicit but ergonomic; 3) a single, test-backed retry policy and token-refresh hook that avoids duplicate requests during auth rotation.

Summary of changes (high level):
- Introduce a lightweight stream handshake: CLIENT_HELLO -> AUTH_OK -> SERVER_READY. Implemented in each SDK with shared semantics and compatibility fallbacks for older servers.
- Consumer ergonomics: new thin abstraction that replaces ad-hoc iterators/callbacks. Python exposes StreamConsumer (AsyncIterator + context manager) with buffer_size and heartbeat_ack semantics; TS exposes createStreamConsumer({onMessage, onComplete, bufferSize}) and an async iterable wrapper; Go exposes StreamReader(ctx) that implements io.Reader-like semantics for single-message reads and a Cancel() helper.
- Auth/retries: unified RetryWithAuthRefresh policy across SDKs. Retries are jittered exponential with token refresh hook invoked once per logical request; transparent idempotency guard added for non-idempotent unary calls.
- Backwards compatibility: consumers detect old handshake flows and fall back to legacy behavior for servers that do not return AUTH_OK. Migration warnings are surfaced at runtime (single warn log per process).
- Tests: added unit tests for handshake transitions and integration e2e stream tests in a local harness that simulates mid-stream token expiration.
- Version bumps: python 0.12.0, typescript 1.9.0, go 0.8.3.

Why this shape: the platform-level serving runtime already relies on explicit stream lifecycle events; exposing a small, consistent surface across SDKs reduces footguns (double-sends during reauth, leaked goroutines or pending async generators) and improves observability for consumers.

Migration notes:
- Python: replace raw async for msg in client.stream() with: async with client.stream_consumer() as c: async for msg in c: ...; short-lived code paths still supported but deprecated.
- TS: prefer createStreamConsumer over stream().iterator() when you need backpressure controls.
- Go: use NewStreamReader(ctx) to ensure reads cancel cleanly on token refresh.

Checklist: 
- [x] Cross-SDK API proposals agreed with SDK leads (Raj/Elena)
- [x] Unit + integration tests added
- [x] CI flake triaged and rerun (see CI summary)
- [x] Changelog & migration guide updated

Notes: this PR intentionally keeps signal surface minimal (3 flags + 2 callbacks) to avoid burdening consumers. See linked Linear ENG-2142 for design doc.
Raj: Can we avoid a second token refresh race if two concurrent streams call the hook? Suggest ensuring the hook is single-flight per token_id. Response: implemented singleflight guard in shared retry_policy with metrics (auth_refresh_locks).
Elena: TS consumer ergonomics look good but question on buffer default. Response: default buffer_size changed to 16 and documented rationale (latency vs memory).
Samir: Go Cancel() semantics — will it leak goroutines when Cancel is called mid-read? Response: added explicit test and closed goroutine via consistent context cancellation path; verified in go race run.
CI-bot: e2e streaming failed when simulating token expiry. Author: added extra wait/retry in harness and hardened backoff; reran and passed.
- SDKs: unify streaming handshake semantics across Python/TS/Go; introduce ergonomic StreamConsumer/StreamReader abstractions.
- Auth: single-flight token refresh hook and unified RetryWithAuthRefresh policy to avoid duplicate in-flight retries.
- Backwards compatibility: servers without AUTH_OK are supported with harmless warnings.
- Version bumps: python 0.12.0, typescript 1.9.0, go 0.8.3.
- Migration guidance added to docs/migration/streaming-migration.md

Motivation: Unreliable client networks and transient disconnects were causing noisy aborts and duplicate tool/function calls in the streaming OpenAI-compat layer. This PR introduces a first-class client-hiatus orchestration mechanism and a "soft-cancel" grace window so that short client disconnects do not immediately finalize sessions or replay tool calls. Design summary: (1) server-side ephemeral lease with configurable 'hiatus_ms' and 'grace_ms' to hold inflight sessions for a short period; (2) an explicit resume handshake: clients present a session token plus a monotonically increasing session-echo to safely rejoin and continue a stream; (3) soft-cancel semantics: when a client disconnects, the server marks a session as 'soft-cancelled' and continues producing a short terminal delta that allows downstream toolcall idempotency guards to commit safely, but it refrains from hard-finalizing model state until grace window expires; (4) lease refresh: long-running streams periodically refresh the ephemeral lease to avoid premature eviction; (5) backoff/jitter tuning: reconnect backoff uses capped exponential with randomized jitter to avoid thundering herd. Implementation notes: added a lightweight orchestrator (server/streaming/hiatus_orchestrator.go) that implements the lease state machine and exposes hooks for the adapter layer. The OpenAI-compat adapter (api/openai_adapter/stream_controller.py) was updated to (a) translate WebSocket disconnects into soft-cancel state, (b) accept resume() calls with session token and session-echo, and (c) enforce idempotent toolcall dedup keys derived from the session-echo + tool-call-id. SDK changes: python SDK exposes Stream.resume(session_token, echo_id) and a new Stream.hiatus_config to mirror server defaults. Console change: admin UI shows 'hiatus_age' and 'soft_cancel' metrics and a toggle for lowering the default grace window per-organization. Backwards compatibility: defaults preserve current behavior for most customers (default grace_ms=20000). Operators can lower to 0ms to restore immediate cancels. Testing: unit tests for state transitions, a deterministic integration harness that simulates network pauses, and end-to-end validations against the python SDK that assert no duplicate toolcall side-effects across reconnects. Rollout plan: feature flagged off by default; staged rollout to Canary (internal), then Dedicated customers with opt-in, then full enable. Metrics to monitor: session_reclaims, resume_success_rate, duplicate_toolcall_rate. Related work: follows ENG-5823 (stream durability) and ENG-5890 (openai-compat reconcilers).
Adds a configurable client-hiatus window and soft-cancel semantics for streaming sessions; introduces server-side lease refresh and reconnect orchestration. Backwards compatible by default; operators can tighten defaults via config.

Motivation: production streaming endpoints were brittle on client disconnects and did not provide a reliable resume or safe-cancel story for tool/function calling and structured output. This PR implements streaming lifecycle controls: (1) explicit client cancel semantics that let the server differentiate user-initiated cancel vs network disconnect; (2) short-term reconnect/resume support using resumable stream tokens and idempotency markers; (3) server-side idle and request timeouts with configurable policies and graceful flushing of function-calling state; (4) consistent OpenAI-compat streaming chunks and markers so existing clients see minimal behavior changes. Motivation: We observed customer incidents where short-lived client disconnects during multi-step function/tool-calling flows caused duplicate tool invocations or orphaned streaming sessions, leading to higher costs and inconsistent structured outputs. This PR introduces a server-side in-flight buffer and a short reconnect window with idempotency reconciliation to preserve end-to-end semantics while keeping latency and cost in check. Summary of changes: 1) Session manager: add a buffered-inflight queue that retains in-progress tool invocations for a configurable reconnect window (default 20s). Sessions now emit a compact session token (reconnect_token) on streaming start. 2) Tool invocation idempotency: introduce X-Tool-Invocation-Id header and runtime-side idempotency table so duplicate replays are deduplicated; tools should return idempotency-safe responses. 3) Reconnect/reconcile flow: upon client reconnect with reconnect_token, server attempts to reconcile buffered inflight work with the client's last-ack position, returning any accumulated partial structured output and the current tool invocation states. If the client reconnects after the window, buffered items are aborted with graceful teardown events. 4) Soft-cancel semantics: new soft-cancel signal allows clients to request an in-flight tool call be aborted only if it has not reached an irreversible side-effect point; otherwise the server completes the call and returns final structured output. 5) SDK/compat: TypeScript and Python SDKs added helper APIs to expose reconnect_token and soft-cancel semantics while preserving OpenAI-compatible streaming events (partial chunks, function_call start/finish events). 6) Observability: new metrics (session.reconnect_attempts, tool.invocation.dedup_hits, session.buffered_items) and traces to aid debugging. 7) Tests: unit tests for reconcile/timeout logic, integration tests simulating flaky client disconnects, and an e2e test that ensures no duplicate tool executions for retries. Checklist: - [x] API design reviewed for OpenAI compatibility - [x] Runtime changes gated behind feature flag streaming_reconnect_v2 - [x] SDK helpers implemented and docstrings added - [x] Metrics and tracing added - [x] Tests included and green on CI Design notes: reconnect_token is short-lived (default TTL 20s) to avoid long-lived server buffering. The buffered queue is size-capped per-session and uses LRU eviction for low-memory impact; overflow causes immediate abort with structured error to client. Soft-cancel is advisory to the runtime and will translate to an AbortableContext inside tool runners; tools can opt-in to fast abort or honor idempotency markers and complete. Compatibility: OpenAI-compatible streaming events are preserved: the server emits a function_call.start event when a tool is invoked, intermittent partial function_call.content chunks during streaming, and function_call.finish when completed; on reconnect the server will stream any missed chunks and then resume new output. CI notes: initial run flagged a flaky e2e test that relied on timing; test was stabilized by switching to event-based waits and re-run. Merge: squash-merged to main on 2026-03-03 after approvals. Impact: reduces duplicate tool calls in flaky network scenarios, gives SDKs a clear reconnect primitive, and improves observability for streaming interruptions. Runtime defaults keep memory/cost bounded and the feature is controlled by feature flags for gradual rollout.
Martin Li: Can we make the reconnect TTL configurable per-deployment? For high-throughput customers 20s may be too short.

Context: customer workloads and internal benchmarks showed inconsistent gains when enabling INT8/FP8 smoothquant paths alongside continuous batching and the KV cache. Two problems were apparent: (1) naive dequant->compute->requant ordering incurred extra per-token copies when requests in the same batch had different effective key/value prefix lengths, and (2) per-head scale mismatches in mixed-precision kernels produced small but measurable accuracy drift at tail latencies. Motivation: we need a single, production-safe change that improves end-to-end token throughput while preserving numeric fidelity and making the fused kernels robust to variable KV alignment and continuous batching semantics. Summary of changes: introduced an adaptive dequantization pipeline that defers full dequant work until per-batch KV alignment is known; implemented a batch-window coalescer that groups inflight requests into short windows (configurable default 4ms) to enable wider batching without violating latency SLOs; added a per-head scale correction step in the fused int8/fp8 kernels that compensates for quantization split across attention heads; changed kernel registration to prefer aligned fused kernels when a KV-alignment hint is present; added a runtime toggle `dequant.adaptive_pipeline` with three modes (off, conservative, adaptive). Performance: in production-like harnesses (GPT-2 XL / seq_len=1024, 8-GPU V100 cluster), adaptive mode shows median throughput +18% and p95 latency change within +3ms across steady-state traffic; single-GPU local perf tests for smaller models (LLaMA-7B) show +12% throughput and no regression in perplexity on standard eval sets. Correctness: we added deterministic unit tests that exercise misaligned KV scenarios and a regression suite validating output logits against baseline fp32 within epsilon=1e-3 for classification tasks. Rollout plan: flag gated behind `dequant.adaptive_pipeline` disabled by default; staged rollout to dedicated clusters for one week, then gradual Hosted rollout with canary percent increases; automatic fallback to legacy dequant path if error rates increase >0.5% or numeric regressions exceed threshold. Backwards compatibility: this change does not require model changes; it is safe for customers pinned to older model versions. Caveats: the adaptive pipeline adds a small CPU scheduling overhead (measured ~0.3ms per batch window), so for ultra-low-latency single-token workloads customers should keep the flag off. Notes: references to internal experiments and ticket INT-912 included.
Performance: ~15-22% throughput improvement on mixed INT8/FP8 workloads (varies by model and sequence length)
Feature: opt-in runtime flag `dequant.adaptive_pipeline=true` and new batch-window alignment for KV caches
Compatibility: fallbacks to previous dequant path when model geometry or hardware does not support fused kernels
Diego Morales: Please add a microbenchmark showing overhead of the batch-window coalescer on single-request tails. Author: added perf microbenchmark and results to bench/ with numbers in PR description.
Linus Cheng: Nit: prefer 'adaptive' naming where it represents actual runtime adaptation — can we make the conservative mode name clearer? Author: renamed modes to 'off','conservative','adaptive' and updated comments.
Sofia Kramer: The per-head scale correction is clever but needs a numerical stability proof. Author: added extra unit tests and a short comment explaining stable accumulation and guard rails for outliers.
Diego Morales: Approve after CI flake fixed.
Sofia Kramer: Approved.
payload.title: Adaptive dequantization pipeline and KV-aligned batching windowing for mixed-precision kernels

Context & motivation: We observed two production incidents where partially-failed shadow seeding left cohorts in a degraded equilibrium: shadow traffic was dropped mid-rehearsal due to transient infra pressure, but the orchestration state did not rewind cleanly, leaving requests routed to older variants or causing silent divergence during subsequent promotes. This PR introduces a 'resumable shadow skirting' pattern: instead of hard-aborting a shadow lane on transient degradation, we divert (skirt) a bounded fraction of traffic away, persist a checkpoint and a rehearsal reserve, and provide a rollback-oracle that can retroactively bisect and recommend an automated backout when fidelity regressions are detected.

Summary of changes: Added a skirt_controller that tracks per-cohort skirt state, durable checkpoints for KV cache and request fingerprints, and a rehearsal_reserve allocator that holds a small buffer of capacity for dry-run promotions. The rollback_oracle implements a two-stage heuristic: (1) fast-signal gating based on latency/error deltas and fidelity counters, (2) retrospective bisect that replays sampled shadow sessions against the baseline model to compute a divergence score. We also updated console UI to surface 'skirted' lanes and provide a manual rehearse/promote button. Tests include unit coverage for the controller state machine and an end-to-end integration that simulates transient infra pressure and validates correct resume semantics.

Checklist:
- [x] Controller state machine (idle -> skirting -> reserved -> resume/abort) with idempotent transitions
- [x] Durable checkpoints (write-once checkpoints + TTL eviction)
- [x] Rehearsal reserve allocator with strict capacity accounting
- [x] Rollback oracle prototype with telemetry hooks
- [x] Console surfaces and runbook links
- [x] Integration tests and CI workflow

Commits (high-level): a1f4e7b creates the controller and REST hooks; b2c9d33 implements the reserve allocator and checkpoint format (protobuf v2); c3d2a10 wires rollback heuristics and adds telemetry gates and alerts.

Changed areas (high-level description): The controller and allocator live in redwood/rollout and are language-mixed (Go controller, Rust allocator) — interface contract documented in rollouts/README. Telemetry rules were extended to include skirt_latency_p95 and skirt_divergence_count; console adds a new rollout-summary state and action. Tests added under redwood/tests/rollout to simulate skirting sequences. CI workflow updated to run the new integration test and a lightweight rehearsal smoke test in the merge pipeline.

Review conversation (condensed): 
- Asha Patel (reviewer): "Nice design — two questions: how do we bound cost of rehearsal reserve, and what guarantees exist for checkpoint TTL? Please add a guard for runaway reserves and mark checkpoint format as forward-compatible."
- Author (Marisol): "Added a global reserve_budget (configurable per-tenant) and TTL semantics; checkpoint format uses versioned protobuf with migration stubs. See b2c9d33 and docs/changes."
- Connor Liu: "Rollback-oracle looks promising; can we add a secondary safeguard so automated backouts require a severity threshold or a manual opt-in for enterprise tenants?"
- Author: "Oracle now exposes policy controls: auto_backout: (off|soft|strict) with default soft (2 independent signals + retrospective score). Documented in telemetry_rules.yaml and console UI."
- Diego Alvarez: "Integration test flake on CI — reproducer showed a race in controller transition. Confirmed and fixed with an explicit compare-and-swap in skirt_controller.go."
- Final: Approved by Asha, Connor; Diego requested final e2e run which passed.

CI summary: initial pipeline failed (flake in e2e, race condition). After fix, CI: build: pass, unit-tests: pass, rollout-integration: pass, lint: pass, e2e-smoke: pass. Rollout-e2e runs took ~7m on merge runner.

Backward compatibility & risk: No breaking API changes to public rollout API; internal contract added for checkpoint ABI (versioned). Risk area: increased complexity in controller state machine — mitigations: feature flagged off by default for existing tenants, opt-in via organization-level rollout policy, and an operator runbook added in docs.

Release notes: Adds 'resumable shadow skirting' to rollout features — allows orchestration to skirt traffic, reserve rehearsal capacity, and auto-detect + backout problematic model variants. Feature is behind a feature-flag and requires operator opt-in for auto-backout. See redwood/docs/rollouts/resumable_skirting.md for full guidance and runbook.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main by release-bot after approvals and green CI. Changelog updated. Follow-ups: ENG-3408 to expand rollback oracle to multi-metric causal scoring; ENG-3271 to add tenant billing telemetry for rehearsal reserves.
Docs: redwood/docs/rollouts/resumable_skirting.md added with operator runbook
Feature-flag: rollout.resumable_skirting disabled by default
Follow-up tickets: ENG-3408 (oracle improvements), ENG-3271 (billing metrics)
payload.title: Resumable shadow skirting with rollback oracle and rehearsal reserves

Motivation: customers are composing multiple tool calls in a single LLM turn and we see two recurring issues: (1) nondeterministic ordering when tooling schedules parallel executions, which complicates downstream result injection and rollout testing, and (2) duplicate side-effects when retries re-run non-idempotent tools. This PR introduces a lightweight protocol and runtime changes to make multi-tool/parallel tool calls safer and more ergonomic for SDK and OpenAI-compat surfaces. High-level changes: 1) call sequencing policy: callers can specify sequencing=\"ordered\"|\"unordered\"|\"optimistic\" per multi-call batch. Ordered preserves declared ordering and forces serial hydration into the model context; unordered allows best-effort parallel execution and merges results in a canonical deterministic merge order for injection; optimistic starts parallel execution but applies a deterministic commit phase that can drop duplicate results. 2) request fingerprinting + idempotency token: runtime attaches a fingerprint for each tool invocation (derived from tool name, stable args hash, and claimed idempotency token if provided). Retries consult the fingerprint to avoid re-executing side-effecting adapters when a duplicate result is available. 3) result hydration protocol v2: structured output is normalized into a compact envelope {\"tool\":...,\"seq\":...,\"schema_v\":2,\"payload\":...} and the SDK exposes an inject_results(context, envelope_list) helper that produces stable structured outputs for streaming and final responses. 4) backoff coordinator and per-tool retry policy: backoff is configurable by tool and by sequencing policy; optimistic mode uses conservative retry thresholds to minimize duplicate side-effects. 5) OpenAI compatibility: added an optional openai_compat flag that maps the new envelope to the legacy function call shape for older clients; streaming handshake updated so tool outputs are emitted as a single coherent chunk with an explicit tool-complete sentinel to avoid partial-state injection during streaming. Included changes: - runtime/tool_executor.py: sequencing policy implementation, fingerprinting, commit/rollback hooks - api/openai_compat/bridge.py: mapping envelope <-> function_call, optional feature gate - sdk/py/redwood/tools.py: inject_results helper + new call signature support - tests/test_tool_retries.py: unit tests for fingerprint dedupe + optimistic replay - docs/api/tool-calls.md: spec, sequencing examples, compatibility notes - console/rollouts/feature_flags.yaml: feature gate entry for optimistic sequencing Safety notes: optimistic mode is off by default for legacy customers; optimistic sequencing must be enabled via console flag or per-request header; non-idempotent tools should include an idempotency_token to get best-effort deduping. Performance: local benchmarks with typical 100rps multi-tool workloads show median latency delta +3.5% in ordered mode, -8% CPU by avoiding redundant executions in optimistic mode, and throughput +12% in unordered mode due to increased parallelism. Migration notes: existing clients continue to work; to opt into deterministic merging or optimistic retries, pass sequencing in the multi-call SDK helper or set openai_compat: false and use the new envelope-based streaming. Example (SDK pseudo): `redwood.multi_call([t1, t2], sequencing=\"optimistic\", idempotency_token=\"txn-123\")`
Liam Chen (requested changes 2026-02-19): Can we make the fingerprint algorithm stable across minor SDK versions? Recommend explicit version field in the fingerprint schema so we can rotate without invalidating dedupe. Also prefer using HMAC over plain SHA for the final token to avoid accidental leak of raw args.
Priya Singh (author reply 2026-02-20): Added version byte and switched to HMAC-SHA256 with a runtime signing key. See runtime/tool_executor.py line notes. Left a TODO to expose rotation tooling in a follow-up (ENG-2463).
Diego Marquez (comment 2026-02-21): Tests look good; one nit - the inject_results helper currently returns a list of envelopes. Can we provide an optional merge_strategy param for SDK consumers?
Priya Singh (reply 2026-02-21): Added merge_strategy parameter (`first_success`|`latest_ts`|`canonical_seq`) with default `canonical_seq`. Documented behavior in docs/api/tool-calls.md.
Anita Rao (approved 2026-02-23): Verified behavior against SUP-9821 reproduction steps. Approving; please ensure the feature gate is documented in the release notes.
Add call sequencing policy for multi-tool calls, result hydration protocol v2, idempotency fingerprinting to reduce duplicate side-effects, and an opt-in OpenAI compatibility bridge. Opt-in feature via console flag or per-request header. Impact: safer parallel tool execution and more deterministic injection into model context.
payload.title: Tool batching protocol and call-context migration for safer parallel calls

Motivation: Teams reported a recurring cold-start cost when the SDK rotated credentials under bursty streaming load. This PR introduces a small, transport-agnostic 'credential warmup adapter' that prefetches / primes credentials before the first heavy streaming usage and a light 'async iterator harmonizer' that normalizes buffer/backoff signals across Python/TS/Go SDKs. The goals are: (1) remove auth handshake stalls that surface as first-request tail latency, (2) provide a single opt-in knob for credential warmup and backpressure hints across SDKS, and (3) align telemetry labels so we can correlate warmup success with reduced token spend.

What this PR does (summary): single continuous description string covering change areas and checklist. - Add credential warmup adapter implementations in py/ts/go (small, opt-in component). - Introduce an 'iterator harmonizer' helper that standardizes pause/resume/backoff event contracts for async iterables/generators across languages. - Wire metrics (sdk.auth.warmup.*, sdk.iter.harmonizer.*) and a lightweight end-to-end smoke test per SDK. - Bump package minor versions: py 1.31.0, ts 1.28.3, go 1.9.2 to pick up shape changes in the iterator helpers. - Docs: add migration note, usage examples for enabling warmup and a troubleshooting FAQ. - Add changelog entries and compatibility note (non-breaking opt-in only).

Checklist: - [x] Implementation for Python - [x] Implementation for TypeScript - [x] Implementation for Go - [x] Unit tests for adapters - [x] SDK smoke e2e tests for warmup under mocked control plane - [x] Docs & changelog - [x] Version bumps and release notes

Notes: This is intentionally opt-in: default behavior unchanged. The adapter exposes a small interface (enable_warmup / warmup_timeout_ms / prefetch_count) documented per SDK. The harmonizer attempts to be conservative in producer/consumer semantics to avoid surprising changes to existing iterables. Backwards compatibility: no breaking API changes were introduced. Linked Linear items track telemetry dashboards and perf checklists.
Diego Morales: Nice cross-lang approach. Please add a small e2e that simulates a credential rotation during warmup and assert no resumed streams error out.
Maya Chen: Added e2e smoke harness in ci/e2e/warmup-smoke.yml and a simulated rotation test in sdk/python/tests/test_warmup.py (mock control plane).
Priya Nair: The TypeScript harmonizer changed the consumer pause signal semantics slightly. Can you add a migration note and a small example showing the old vs new pattern?
Maya Chen: Added docs/sdk/migration-warmup.md and an example in examples/warmup/ts; left the harmonizer conservative so existing pause()/resume() paths keep working.
Jonas Fischer: Observability: can we tag warmup attempts with the credential source (env/kms/assumerole) so we can filter dashboards?
Maya Chen: Added sdk.auth.warmup.credential_source label and incremented telemetry mapping.
- SDKs: Introduce optional credential warmup adapter to reduce first-request tail latency under credential rotation scenarios.
- SDKs: Add async iterator harmonizer that standardizes pause/resume/backoff signals across Python/TypeScript/Go.
- Telemetry: new metrics sdk.auth.warmup.* and sdk.iter.harmonizer.* and label sdk.auth.warmup.credential_source.
- Non-breaking, opt-in. See docs/sdk/warmup.md and migration notes for examples and knobs.
Recommend enabling the warmup adapter behind a feature flag for one week in canary customers. Monitor sdk.auth.warmup.success_rate and request tail p95 for first-token requests. No mandatory action for existing customers.

Motivation: Observability spend and storage growth have been driven by a small fraction of high-latency/long-token sessions. This PR introduces two complementary features to reduce O(1) trace storage costs while preserving signal for the heavy tail: 1) Stratified span sampling: deterministic, priority-aware sampling that keeps a bounded number of representative long spans per route and per time window; 2) Sharded cost histograms: per-model_shard token-cost and latency histograms to make unit economics visible across shards and to enable targeted tuning.

Summary of changes (high-level):
- Runtime: add a sampling controller that applies stratified reservoir sampling for spans. Sampling keys: (route_id, model_shard, latency_bucket). Retention priority influenced by span.duration, token_count, and error_flag. Configurable via feature flag and route-level overrides.
- Tracing: add new span tag `sample_priority` and `shard_hist_key`; emit sampled span-rate metadata to the tracing backend.
- Metrics: export sharded histograms for token-cost and per-token latency (HISTOGRAM_BUCKETS tuned to heavy-tail). Add derived metrics: shard_p50/p90/p99_token_cost and shard_token_cost_rate.
- Console/Dashboards: new "Sharded Cost" dashboard with small-multiples by model_shard and a long-tail resource usage panel. New alert rules that trigger on sustained shard_token_cost_rate increases (with dynamic baselining).
- Config: add `observability.sampling.stratified` config block and route-level annotations to opt in/out or set custom retention budgets.
- Tests: unit tests for sampling controller, e2e for metric emission, snapshot tests for dashboard JSON.

Commits (summary):
- 3f3b2a7: implement stratified reservoir sampler and runtime hook (runtime/sampling/*).
- 7b9d1c4: emit per-shard histograms and metrics export (observability/metrics/*).
- a1e4d2b: console/dashboard panels + alert tuning + docs (console/dashboards/*, docs/observability.md).

Files touched (high-level):
- runtime/sampling/controller.go (new)
- runtime/sampling/policy.go (new)
- tracing/exporters/zipkin_adapter.go (minor)
- observability/metrics/shard_histograms.go (new)
- console/dashboards/sharded_cost.json (new)
- platform/config/schema.yaml (updated)
- docs/observability.md (updated)
- tests/observability/sampling_test.go (new)

Checklist: 
- [x] Unit tests for sampler and metric tag propagation
- [x] Dashboard JSON included and smoke-tested in dev console
- [x] Docs updated with migration notes and knobs
- [x] Feature-flag gated; rollout plan added
- [x] QA: small production canary verified on `alpha` cluster for 72h

Rollout & migration notes: 
- This PR is feature-flag gated (observability.stratified_sampling.enabled=false by default). Admins can enable per-tenant or global.
- Backwards compatibility: sampled spans include a `legacy_sampled` flag while rolling out; metric keys use stable naming to avoid aliasing.
- Storage: default retention budget limits retained spans per (route, shard, hour) to 500 to prevent unbounded growth. Operators can increase budgets for debug modes.

Performance and cost impact: 
- In canary (alpha) we observed ~68% reduction in span writes from the heavy-tail cohort while retaining >92% of unique error signatures. Exported metric cardinality increased slightly due to per-shard histograms (+~6%), but overall storage cost decreased due to sampling.

Alerting changes: 
- Added `SLO-Observability-HighShardCost` which triggers when a shard_token_cost_rate rises >2x baseline for >10m. Baseline uses 90-day rolling median by default and can be tuned per-tenant.
- Reduced noisy pager churn by using a two-stage alert: brief warning (no page) then critical if sustained.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Luca Romero (review): "I like the stratified approach. A couple nits: ensure sampler determinism across restarts and add a CI test that validates bucket stability."
- Aisha (author): "Added deterministic RNG seeding and a snapshot test in tests/observability/sampling_test.go that verifies determinism across simulated restart cycles."
- Daniel Kim (review): "Dashboard looks good; suggest making histogram buckets slightly wider to reduce cardinality. Also note that per-shard metrics may produce heavy Prometheus label explosions for large shard counts."
- Aisha: "Widened buckets, added an aggregation metric `shard_token_cost_rate_agg` (rollup) and documented recommended max_shard_metrics in config. Ops approved for alpha canary."
- Priya Menon (approval): "Verified canary results and storage impact. Approving to merge when CI green."

CI history: initial run (unit + lint) failed due to flake in sampler test (race on RNG). Fixed in commit 3f3b2a7 -> rerun: all checks passed (unit, integration, lint, dashboard-lint). Post-merge quick-deploy tests passed on alpha.

Related work and references: ENG-9123 (obs cost reduction epic), RFC: /docs/rfcs/2026-01-stratified-sampling.md, convo in #infra-observability on 2026-02-10.

Merge: Squash and merge. Changelog entry autogenerated from release_notes. Feature flagged; disabled in main until org rollout window.

Notes for on-call and SRE: 
- If you see large gaps in traces for a route after enabling, check `observability.sampling.debug` route annotation; temporarily set to `retain_all` to capture a full traffic window.
- Use `console/dashboards/sharded_cost` to identify which model_shard is contributing to token-cost anomalies.

Overall this PR aims to reduce long-tail observability cost while preserving signal needed to debug latency and cost regressions per shard.
Introduces stratified span sampling with priority-based retention and per-model-shard token-cost histograms. Adds console dashboard panels and alert tuning knobs for long-tail request cost spikes.
payload.title: stratified-span-sampling-and-sharded-cost-histograms-for-heavy-tail-requests

Context: Private deployments need safer, tenant-scoped upgrade paths and unattended certificate bootstrapping for air-gapped clusters. This PR adds tenant-aware Helm hook templates and a lightweight cron-style cert-init job so on-prem installations can perform predictable canary upgrades and automated certificate rotation/bootstrap without operator intervention. It updates the values.schema.json to allow per-tenant hook config, introduces a new hooks/_tenant-hooks.tpl subtemplate used by all private subcharts, and adds a pre-upgrade canary weighting mechanism plus a post-failure rollback job. Motivation: current private installer upgrades operate cluster-wide and block on manual checks; tenants required a way to opt into staged rollouts and autonomous cert initialization for sealed-secret-based KMS setups. Changes: 1) values.schema.json: new properties "tenants" and "tenantHooks" with validation for per-namespace hook enablement and canaryWeight (0-100). 2) templates/hooks/_tenant-hooks.tpl: shared helper that renders pre-upgrade canary Job, post-upgrade rollback Job, and cert-init CronJob when enabled. 3) templates/webhook-deploy.yaml & templates/worker-deploy.yaml: minor annotations to opt into tenant hooks and to reference tenant-scoped serviceaccounts. 4) templates/preflight-configmap.yaml: move lightweight preflight checks for network/CNI to a configmap that's consumed by hook jobs. 5) chart/README.md: documented tenant-scoped upgrade flow and example values for multi-tenant clusters and air-gapped environments. Compatibility: default behavior is opt-out; existing values continue to work. Deployment notes: when enabling per-tenant hooks, administrators must create a Tenant CR (or map via values.tenants) with kube namespace mapping for the hooks to target. See examples in README.

d4e5f6a: add templates/hooks/_tenant-hooks.tpl to centralize hook rendering and tenant scoping
b7c8d9e: wire tenant annotations into webhook and worker deployments and make serviceAccount optional
e0f1a2b: add cert-init CronJob template and small utility script used in the job image (script only referenced)
f3a4b5c: update chart README with tenant upgrade guide and air-gap notes
c6d7e8f: add unit tests for values schema and helm template rendering in CI
Arjun: Can the canaryWeight be overridden per-deployment when tenants share the same cluster? Please ensure the validation prevents >100 values.
Author (Imani): Yes, schema enforces integer 0-100 and chart merges use priority: tenant-level -> global -> default.
Maeve: We should avoid creating RBAC privileges broader than the target namespace. Confirmed the hook renders namespaced rolebindings only.
Diego: CI helm-unittest failed once for missing default values; added test fixtures and re-ran. All green now.
Ops (post-merge): Remember to update private-installer to pass tenants map via --set when bootstrapping in air-gapped installs.
Added tenant-scoped Helm hooks and a CronJob-based cert-init for private deployments. New values.tenants and values.tenantHooks allow per-namespace canary rollouts (canaryWeight) and automated certificate bootstrap/rotation. Backwards compatible; opt-in.

Motivation: Provide a developer-facing structured response mode that 1) preserves streaming behavior for large responses, 2) surfaces deterministic schema validation error codes for programmatic handling, and 3) remains compatible with the OpenAI-style response_format and function/tool calling patterns. This PR introduces a 'structured_response_mode' enum (lenient|strict|best_effort), standardizes error codes emitted on schema validation failures, and modifies the streaming adapter to buffer and emit partial, reparsable fragments when strict mode cannot be satisfied. Key design goals: maintain low-latency streaming for large outputs, give callers machine-friendly error signals (e.g., ERR_SCHEMA_MISMATCH, ERR_REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING), and allow SDKs to opt into strict enforcement. Changes: - Add response_mode and schema negotiation handshake to inference API surface - Implement schema_validator with machine-readable error codes and short, stable messages - Extend openai_compat stream_adapter to support buffer preservation and rewind on schema fallback - Add python SDK helpers to choose behavior and translate error codes into exceptions/wrappers - Add integration tests for streaming + structured output + function calling - Update docs with migration guidance and examples Checklist: - [x] API definition + handshake implemented - [x] Runtime schema validator and error codes - [x] Streaming adapter buffer preservation implemented - [x] SDK gating + examples added - [x] Integration tests added and passing - [x] Docs updated How to test locally: run tests/integration/test_structured_output_streaming.py which spins a lightweight mock model and asserts streaming fragments are preserved when switching from strict to best_effort. Linear: ENG-1127 tracks runtime work; PM-341 covers product acceptance criteria. Related: builds on prior schema negotiation work (see PR 31206) but diverges by adding explicit error codes and a streaming buffer-preserve strategy.
Diego Marquez: Important improvement. Can we make the error code enum stable across releases? Also request small refactor in schema_validator to separate validation and message formatting.
Aisha Raman: Agreed on stable enum. Extracted ValidationResult -> crate schema_error_codes and added unit tests to lock codes. Refactor applied in commit 3b9a8ff.
Lena Hofstad: Streaming buffer preserve approach looks good but I'm concerned about memory growth for very long streams. Suggest a cap + eviction policy and a metric.
Aisha Raman: Added a soft cap and a metric (structured_output.replay_buffer_bytes) and evict-oldest policy; documented in observability changes. See commit a2d5e11.
Marcus Li: CI flaked on the integration test once (timeout). Reran CI. Tests passed on rerun. Please add a longer timeout to the flaky test.
Aisha Raman: Increased timeout and added retry hook in test harness. CI green on rerun.
Diego Marquez: Approving pending docs clarification on migration path for existing OpenAI-compatible clients.
Aisha Raman: Added migration section and examples in console/docs/structured-response-mode.md. Marking as ready.
Adds structured_response_mode (lenient|strict|best_effort) to the inference API; introduces stable schema validation error codes (ERR_SCHEMA_MISMATCH, ERR_REQUIRED_FIELD_MISSING, ERR_TYPE_MISMATCH); improves streaming adapter to preserve partial buffers and allow graceful fallback from strict to best_effort. SDKs updated to expose the toggle and translate codes into exceptions/wrappers. See docs/structured-response-mode.md for migration steps.

Background and motivation: Production workloads show variance in per-channel activation distributions across prompts and token positions which makes static requant scales suboptimal. We observed systematic p99 latency spikes when the runtime switched between hot and cold KV cache footprints under continuous-batching; these were exacerbated by small batching jitter when multiple streams aligned. This PR implements a dynamic per-channel requant stage combined with a KV-cache-aware scheduling hint and a jitter-resilient continuous-batching policy to smooth throughput while keeping low tail latency. Scope: 1) A lightweight per-channel scale estimator that runs on the microkernel hot path and updates requant multipliers at configurable amortization windows. 2) A cheap, lock-free KV cache sizing hint that the scheduler uses to avoid abrupt prefix evictions during batch coalescing. 3) A jitter-resilient continuous-batcher that introduces minimal, adaptive hold windows to align requests from high-variance sources without increasing median latency. 4) Microkernel changes to expose a fused transform that applies requant multipliers inline with dequant/attn input packing to eliminate an extra copy. Design highlights and tradeoffs: - Estimator runs every N tokens (configurable per model) and uses exponential moving moments to remain stable across bursts. The goal is to reduce per-token compute overhead to <0.5% while adapting scales within 5-10k tokens. - Scheduler hint is advisory: it tags requests with estimated KV working set delta. The placement layer still enforces hard SLOs; the hint avoids placing requests that would cause a working-set jump on the same GPU within a short window. - Batcher employs an adaptive jitter budget: it only delays the head of a queue by up to X ms if the expected throughput improvement outweighs the added latency; X decays if p99 latency rises. Benchmarks (representative): - OPT-13B, INT8 hybrid (smoothquant + per-channel dynamic re-quant): throughput +10.8% on steady-state mixed sized prompts, median latency +2% (due to micro-batching alignment), p99 latency -14% on tail-heavy traces. - Llama-2-7B FP8 fallback: end-to-end token cost reduced by ~7% due to fewer KV evictions and reduced memory copies. - End-to-end e2e test with 500 simulated concurrent streams: observed 8-12% lower GPU-side memcpy time and 6-9% better sustained throughput. Implementation notes: - Runtime changes: src/runtime/quant/dyn_requant.h/cpp, src/runtime/quant/microkernel_requant.s, src/runtime/scheduler/kv_hint_scheduler.cpp - Batcher: src/runtime/batching/jitter_batcher.cpp, with a new config block in configs/batching.yaml - Tests: tests/quant/test_dyn_requant.cc (unit), bench/latency/bench_kv_jitter.py (integration traces) - Docs: docs/perf/quantization.md updated with configuration knobs and suggested Linear tasks for tuning. Motivation: We observed a recurring CPU-side serialization hotspot in the request path when contention rises on the global serializer used to serialize request context, route lookups and KV-cache lookups. This PR replaces the single global serializer with per-shard asynchronous request queues, pushes KV-cache lookup heavyweight work off the network accept threads, and replaces strict thread pinning with lightweight affinity hints to reduce cross-core thrashing. Summary of changes: 1) Introduces RequestShard and ShardQueue: each shard has a lock-free MPSC queue that accepts lightweight request handles; workers pull requests and perform scheduling and kernel/eviction decisions. 2) Replaces global request serialization lock with per-request object sequencing and fence-free handoff via atomic states. 3) KV-cache fast path now does a batched probe step: on admission requests are grouped by shard, batched KV probes happen on local shard workers to exploit cache locality and reduce page faults. 4) Heavy synchronous operations (model weights load/quantize, cold KV misses) are offloaded to a background worker pool with backpressure tokens so latency-sensitive workers are never blocked. 5) Threading model tuned: removed strict cpu_set pinning in favor of affinity hints and a hop-count aware scheduling heuristic to prefer hot-shard locality without preventing OS migration. 6) Added observability: shard-level counters, per-step histograms (enqueue latency, queue-to-worker latency, kv-probe time), and a dashboard link. Performance impact: internal perf lab benchmarks for a mixed-inference workload with 32 concurrent clients show median tail savings: p50 latency -4.2%, p95 -9.6%, p99 -18.3% and sustained throughput +11% before hitting GPU saturation. CPU utilization traces show the global serialization spike eliminated and worker core CPU variance reduced by ~36%. Testing and validation: unit tests for ShardQueue and RequestShard ordering, integration tests that simulate KV-cache hot/cold ratios, and a rollout canary across 10% of dedicated capacity clusters passed with no increased error rate. Rollout plan: phased canary, observe shard-level metrics for 48 hours, then increment to 50% and full roll when no regressions. Related tickets: ENG-982 request path serialization, ENG-987 kv-cache eviction scheduling. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Perf benchmarks - [x] Observability panels updated - [x] Canary plan and rollback steps. Commits summary: see commits list below. Files touched: core/scheduler/shard_queue.rs, core/scheduler/mod.rs, core/kv/cache.rs, core/kv/eviction.rs, runtime/threading/affinity.rs, runtime/metrics/shard_metrics.rs, tests/integration/kv_shard_integration.rs, docs/observability/shard_dashboard.md. Merge outcome: squash merge into main with commit message that summarizes the shard queue and affinity hint changes. Notes for reviewers: pay attention to ordering guarantees in RequestShard, eviction interaction with batched probes, and backpressure token correctness for the background pool. If issues arise we can toggle the per-shard routing off via runtime flag.

Aisha Khan: Can we measure the impact of affinity hints in noisy multi-tenant nodes? response: added a noisy-node integration test and observed consistent improvements; documented in perf notes.
Liam O'Connor: Concern about eviction ordering when batching probes across shards, response: updated eviction logic to preserve per-request eviction-scoring timestamps and added an integration test to validate ordering.
Server runtime: Reduced CPU-side request serialization by replacing a global serializer with per-shard async queues. Improved tail latency and throughput under contention. Opt-in rollout behind runtime flag. Observability added for shard-level scheduling metrics.

Motivation: production traces from perf-canary and customer Dedicated clusters showed that a non-trivial fraction of tail latency and CPU utilization is spent on CPU-side request plumbing: JSON serialization/deserialization for control frames, shared thread-pool contention, and hotspots around KV cache lookup locks. This PR optimizes the request path to reduce overhead and contention without changing the public API. Summary of changes: 1) Introduce a compact binary frame for intra-service control messages to replace verbose JSON in hot code paths; frames are backward compatible and negotiated per-connection. 2) Replace the global thread-pool used for small async tasks with per-core worker pools pinned to CPU cores on Linux and macOS where supported; use an efficient MPMC handoff for cross-core work. 3) Change KV cache from a single sharded lock to per-shard lock-free read paths using sequence counters and an RCU-style updater to avoid short-lived lock contention during heavy read bursts. 4) Move metadata serialization off the hot path by preserializing common route headers and attaching by reference when request creation occurs. 5) Add a lightweight request-affinity scheduler that prefers placing related short-lived requests on the same core to improve KV cache locality and reduce cache misses. Testing and validation: unit and integration tests updated for frame negotiation and thread-pinning config. Added deterministic stress tests that simulate 5k concurrent small requests to validate no regressions in correctness. Perf results (perf-canary synthetic workload matching our microburst profile): median latency unchanged, p95 latency reduced by ~18-22% on typical CPU-heavy workloads, CPU sys usage down ~28% on 8-core instances in our lab, average throughput improved ~12% under load, and instance-level tail jitter reduced. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag "cpu_optimizations_v1" and enabled via a canary rollout to 5% of dedicated pools; observed metrics and rollback hooks added to console. Context: Streaming endpoints (SSE/WebSocket/progressive HTTP) need predictable auth semantics across preflight, initial handshake, and per-chunk delivery. Tool/function-calling and structured-output features rely on stable header propagation so downstream runtime routing and function authorization can reason about the request principal and scope. Previous inconsistencies caused 1) dropped project-scoped keys on CORS preflight + SSE upgrade, and 2) inability to validate per-chunk integrity for long-lived streams when using short-lived scoped tokens.

This PR unifies header handling across: the OpenAI-compat translation layer, streaming proxy, and the runtime auth middlewares. It introduces a backwards-compatible signed-chunk header and clarifies semantics for project/org-scoped tokens and nonce exchange.

What this PR changes (high level):
- Adds X-Redwood-Project and X-Redwood-Scope canonical propagation headers emitted by the compat layer when translating Authorization Bearer -> internal credential routing.
- Implements X-Redwood-Session-Nonce exchange header for browser flows. The server returns a short-lived nonce on successful preflight/handshake so clients can sign subsequent chunk frames.
- Adds chunk integrity header X-Redwood-Chunk-Sig (HMAC-SHA256 over chunk payload + sequence id) and validation in the streaming proxy. This supports long-lived SSE/WS streams without requiring reauth per message.
- Extends CORS preflight handling to explicitly allow Signed-Session and Chunk-Sig headers and exposes the Session-Nonce on responses. Policy: Access-Control-Allow-Headers includes Signed-Session, X-Redwood-Chunk-Sig, X-Redwood-Session-Nonce; Access-Control-Expose-Headers exposes X-Redwood-Session-Nonce.
- OpenAI-compat layer: when an Authorization: Bearer <token> is received, we attempt to resolve scope -> emit X-Redwood-Project & X-Redwood-Scope and a short-lived internal credential header (X-Redwood-Internal-Cred). Legacy clients without compatibility will continue to work (compat translations are opt-out via a header).
- Adds integration tests for SSE and WebSocket handshake flows, plus unit tests for signature verification edge cases (replay, out-of-order seq ids).

Notes on rollout and safety:
- Backwards compatible by default: clients that don't send Signed-Session or Chunk-Sig continue to function; only streams opt into stricter chunk validation when the server issues a Session-Nonce.
- Feature gate: compat_layer.header_translation can be toggled per-route (console + config flag) to assist staged migration and canary.
- Canary plan: enable for 5% of streaming traffic in prod for 48 hours, monitor error_rate/latency and chunk_signature_failures metric.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc reviewed by security and runtime teams
- [x] Unit tests for signature verification and header translation
- [x] Integration tests for SSE/WS preflight and handshake
- [x] OpenAI-compat translation implemented and feature-gated
- [x] SDK updates (JS + Python) with minimal client helpers (signChunk helper)
- [x] Docs updated (auth headers and CORS notes)

Risk: medium. Primary risk is accidental exposure of internal credential header; mitigated via strict translation rules, per-route feature gate, and scrub/strip logic at the public ingress layer.

- Add server-side rotation hints for Session-Nonce lifetimes (ENG-10010).

Motivation: customers want first-class JSON Schema-backed structured outputs that behave predictably in both streaming and non-streaming modes and interoperate with OpenAI-style response_format and function-calling expectations. This PR implements a server-side JSON Schema validation pipeline for response_format/schema, a configurable strict mode that returns structured validation errors, streaming-safe schema enforcement with graceful fallback, and compatibility hooks for the OpenAI compatibility layer. Changes are intended to be conservative: defaults preserve existing behavior; strict mode must be opted into via request params or headers.

Summary of changes:
- New response_format validation component wired into the request handler that validates model outputs against provided JSON Schemas (supports draft-07 and Draft 2019-09 subset used by common tooling).
- "strict" behavior: when enabled (x-redwood-strict-schema: true or response_format.mode=strict), the platform will reject or mark responses with structured error payloads on schema violations. The error payload follows a stable shape (error_type, path, message, suggestion) to be consumed by SDKs and client code.
- Streaming behavior: for streaming requests we perform incremental schema checks on partial JSON fragments and emit structured validation frames as part of the stream when irrecoverable violations are detected. To avoid noisy false positives we:
  * attempt incremental parse/recovery for common streaming patterns (chunked arrays, partial objects)
  * delay hard strict failures until a complete top-level object is assembled where possible
  * provide a per-request fallback policy (response_format.streaming_fallback=non_strict | strict_delayed | fail_immediate)
- OpenAI compatibility: the openai-compat layer now maps response_format to the OpenAI "response_format"/"function_call" semantics and ensures SDKs receive the same error shapes.
Function/tool-calling: if a schema is attached to a function return type, we validate the returned object before emitting a tool call to the client; in strict mode the tool call is blocked and a structured error is returned so callers can retry with corrected prompts.
- Error telemetry and observability: new metrics (schema.validation.total, schema.validation.failures, schema.validation.streaming_incidents) and traces for validation latency.
Docs: added migration notes and examples for Python/TS SDKs.
Backwards compatibility: default (no strict header/param) keeps previous permissive acceptance; streaming messages are unchanged by default except extra validation frame types when enabled.

Risk and mitigation: incremental parser improvements could surface edge-case regressions for badly-minted model output; mitigations include conservative delay of failures in streaming mode, feature flags for rollout, and a canary rollout to Dedicated clusters.

Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. Checklist: [x] unit tests for stream finalizer [x] integration test that simulates disconnect + resume [x] docs page and compatibility notes [x] change log entry. Related: ENG-1023 (stream lifecycle SLO), SUP-4572 (customer incident replicant).

Context: Continuous-batching latency spikes remain correlated with long-lived, low-KV-hit requests that accumulate in a single queue window and prevent small fast requests from being coalesced. Motivation: previous fixes (deadline steering, probe jitter) reduced some tail pain but left scenarios where a small number of KV-heavy requests would create a persistent backlog and cause cascading micro-timeouts in downstream queues. This PR introduces two coordinated strategies: 1) staggered window thresholds (per-priority, per-queue moving thresholds) that allow the batcher to open secondary ingestion windows when primary windows are clogged; 2) a lightweight KV-revival heuristic that performs a fast, opportunistic KV pre-warm for requests that are likely to unblock the cache and restore batching efficiency. The changes are safe-by-default, revertible, and covered by unit + perf tests.
