Motivation: intermittent warmup regressions with fragmented continuous-batching workloads and sparse KV-cache hits were causing spiky latency and rare capture-mismatch fallbacks during CUDA graph replay. This PR introduces a two-part approach: 1) staged capture priming — lightweight, incremental capture probes that prime kernels and the KV cache before committing a long-lived CUDA graph; and 2) kernel stitching — an optimizer that coalesces adjacent small kernels into a single capture-friendly kernel group to reduce capture fragmentation and decrease the number of graph replays. Implementation highlights: added a CapturePrimingCoordinator (runtime/cudagraph/capture_priming.h/.cpp) that runs ephemeral, non-blocking probe captures on a dedicated stream to warm up kernel kernels and populate KV cache entries associated with common prefixes; introduced a compact capture fingerprint (shape+op-hash) to detect safe stitching opportunities; implemented KernelStitcher to emit stitched launch plans when batch fragmentation would otherwise produce many tiny kernels; added a capture epoch counter and conservative fence semantics so probes cannot race with live replays; exposed a runtime flag redwood.cudagraph.priming_enabled and a knob priming_threshold to tune when staged priming triggers; telemetry: new metrics cudagraph.probe_count, cudagraph.stitched_kernels, cudagraph.priming_latency_ms, and cudagraph.replay_fallbacks. Fallbacks: when stitched kernel execution detects an unexpected shape mismatch we fall back to eager execution for that request and schedule a background recapture; capture mismatches are logged with a diagnostic sample id to aid triage. Tests: unit tests for fingerprinting and stitching, integration test that simulates fragmented continuous-batching with varying sequence lengths, and a stress job that ran 48h on staging GPUs. Results: in our internal perf lab, end-to-end p95 generation latency decreased by 6% on mixed-length workloads and cold-start replay fallback rate dropped from 4.2% to 0.3%; memory overhead from priming was <2% on average. Rollout plan: feature-gated off by default for Hosted; enable in Dedicated canaries with default priming_threshold=0.2; monitor cudagraph.replay_fallbacks and priming_latency_ms for 7 days before broad enabling. Related items: ENG-1124 (capture regressions triage), ENG-1199 (continuous batching frag tests).

Maya Chen (2026-02-20): Addressed hash determinism, added explicit sort for op-list before hashing, pushed fixup commit.

payload.body:
Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI Responses family expect stable streaming semantics, reliable tool/function call signal delivery, and preservation of determinism hints (seed/RNG) and user metadata when we bridge from our internal Responses v9-compatible runtime to the OpenAI API shape. This PR adds a resilience layer that: 1) performs backpressure-aware chunking and reassembly for streaming frames to avoid partial json/toolcall corruption on slow clients, 2) proxies a lightweight 'tool-signal' envelope so function/tool-calling boundaries are deterministic across retries and reconnections, and 3) forwards seed/determinism flags and a subset of user metadata transparently through the compatibility layer.

What this changes (summary): consistent chunk framing and reassembly on the server and client-facing bridge; explicit tool-signal envelope that annotates tool-call start/end + unique tool invocation id; passthrough of 'rng_seed' and 'deterministic' attributes from our Responses request model into the OpenAI-compatible response attributes; metadata routing (user-provided tags/trace id) added to response attributes and to audit logs so downstream services (console, evals) see the same identifiers.

Compatibility notes: We keep the OpenAI-compatible surface stable for existing callers. Default behavior is identical unless callers set determinism/seed or rely on streaming reconnects; in those cases the bridge guarantees idempotent framing (replay-safe chunk markers) and consistent toolcall reassembly. There are small opt-ins: the 'tool-signal' envelope is only applied when callers include a 'enable_tool_signal' flag (default true for our hosted API). For private deployments customers can opt-out via config.

Checklist:
- [x] Server-side chunking + reassembly implementation
- [x] Tool-signal envelope design + tests

payload.body:
Context: We need closer parity with OpenAI's /v1/chat.completions for customers migrating from OpenAI-style clients and for downstream SDKs that assume certain parameter behaviors. This PR harmonizes parameter semantics (temperature/top_p/stop/stream), stabilizes streaming framing for partial response reassembly, defines a compact envelope for tool/function call messages, and normalizes logprob/stop output to a single canonical schema so downstream evals and quality checks don't need special-case parsing.

Motivation: Previously, subtle mismatches in param coercion (e.g., falsy stop vs. explicit null), inconsistent handling of role aliases, and varying streaming frame shapes caused customer regressions during migration and brittle SDK logic. Additionally, toolcall outputs were emitted as ad-hoc fragments which complicated function routing in edge cases and retry scenarios.

What this PR does (summary):
- Canonicalizes chat params: explicit null vs omitted, numeric coercion for temperature and top_p, and whitelist/aliasing for role names (user/system/assistant/tool).
- Stabilizes stream framing: introduces a small frame header for every chunk that carries a sequence id, frame type (delta|tool|done|heartbeat), and optional json-mode marker; keeps backwards-compatible fallback parsing for old clients.
- Tool/function call envelope: emits a single well-formed tool-call event when a tool is invoked; the envelope contains tool_name, args (string|json), and optional provenance headers. This replaces earlier multi-chunk tool call patterns.
- Unified logprob schema: stop reasons, token logprobs, and token offsets are now embedded under response.logprobs with consistent keys: tokens, token_logprobs, token_offsets, stop_reason. Old fields are still emitted as deprecated aliases for one release.
- Response shaping: structured output for 'json_mode' requests is enforced: top-level message.content is either a plain string or a JSON-encoded object with content_type header. Streaming will emit partial JSON fragments under the same envelope type to aid reassembly.

Files changed (high level):
- runtime/streaming/frame_protocol.go (new framing + parser)
- runtime/streaming/frame_protocol_test.go (parser/unit tests covering reassembly & heartbeat)
- api/compat/chatv1/param_canonicalizer.go (param coercion and alias handling)
- api/compat/chatv1/response_normalizer.go (output shaping and logprob schema)
- api/compat/chatv1/toolcall_envelope.go (single-toolcall emitter)
- sdk/js/src/streaming/reader.ts (compat parsing of new frames, fallback to legacy)
- sdk/python/redwood/chatv1_client.py (parameter acceptance and docs)
- docs/openai_compat/chatv1_migration.md (migration notes and examples)
- tests/e2e/chatv1_migration_test.go (end-to-end scenarios)
- perf/canaries/chat_streaming_latency.yaml (adjusted canary config to account for header overhead)
- examples/chatv1-toolcall/ (updated sample showing tool envelope usage)

Commits (summary):
- 1a2b3c: introduce canonicalizer and initial unit tests
- 4d5e6f: implement framing protocol + parser and reassembly logic
- 7g8h9i: toolcall envelope emitter + SDK parsers for JS/Python
- a1b2c3: normalize logprob schema and add deprecation aliases
- d4e5f6: docs, migration guide and examples
- f7g8h9: canary/perf tweak and CI test adjustments

Review notes / decisions:
- We added a tiny header (3 fields) before payload to make reassembly deterministic under concurrent chunk streams. Hardware/throughput impact measured at +0.6% token overhead in our perf lab for small payloads, negligible at typical batch sizes.
- To preserve backwards compatibility, the JS and Python SDKs will continue to accept the legacy frame stream; new header-aware parsing is preferred when available (sdk negotiates by attempting header parse and falling back).
- The unified logprob schema intentionally groups stop reasons under response.logprobs.stop_reason to make automatic eval tooling easier. We emit deprecated fields response.tokens and response.token_logprobs for one release and will remove them after SDK upgrades are broadly available.

Testing performed:
- Unit tests for param canonicalization edge cases (empty lists, null vs omitted, role aliasing).
- Streaming reassembly fuzz tests that simulate interleaved tool-call and assistant frames.
- Integration tests: migration scenarios (OpenAI-like client sending top_p as string, stop as empty array, streaming toggled mid-request).
- Manual QA: ran example customers' prompts where older clients previously mis-merging tool outputs.

Backward compatibility & migration:
- Clients that upgrade SDKs gain new parsing and deprecation warnings.
- Servers using custom parser need to accept the small header; a fallback branch is documented in the migration guide.
- Operators can enable a compatibility flag in deploy config to allow legacy-only streaming for 30 days while dependent services upgrade.

Related work: ENG-1942 (param parity initiative), ENG-1978 (streaming reliability), SUP-889 (customer incident where stop arrays were ignored). This PR consolidates many smaller fixes into a cohesive interface to lower migration cost.

Release notes (short): Canonicalize v1/chat.completions params, stabilize streaming frames with a compact header for reliable reassembly, emit a single well-formed toolcall envelope for function calls, and normalize logprob/stop schema. SDKs updated (JS/Python) to parse the new frames and honor deprecation aliases.

Why this PR is different: Unlike previous incremental PRs that tackled parameter or streaming issues in isolation, this change intentionally coordinates runtime, API compat, SDKs, and docs so customer migrations are predictable and reversible. It prioritizes a single canonical output shape for logprobs and toolcalls to reduce downstream parsing complexity.

Merge outcome: squashed and merged after 2 approvals and one CI flake rerun.

Ethan Li: Overall looks great. Two questions: 1) Did you consider using varint encoding for the header to save bytes? 2) Can we avoid emitting deprecated aliases in perf path?
Neha Kapoor: Varint considered but added CPU/decode complexity; header is fixed 3-field little-endian for simplicity and deterministic parse. Deprecated aliases are not emitted on 'fast-path' quantized executor to keep perf stable.
Sofia Martinez: Please add migration snippet for top_p passed as string in docs (example client).
Neha Kapoor: Added example and unit tests covering top_p string coercion.
Oliver Chen: Unit tests flaked on CI once (streaming fuzz test). Is that stable now?
Neha Kapoor: Increased timeouts and added deterministic seeds; re-ran CI pipeline and all streaming tests passed.
QA (Priya Das): Verified end-to-end sample with external OpenAI-like client; toolcall reassembly and logprob shape validated.
Security (Rajiv Nair): Static review — no new surface, toolcall provenance headers must be treated as untrusted by consumers. Added note to docs.
SRE (Lena Hsu): Perf canary noted small latency increase; acceptable. Recommend monitoring 99th percentile for first week.
Product (Marta Kovacs): Approved for GA; migration docs clear enough for customers to act.
Canonicalize v1/chat.completions params and streaming framing; introduce single toolcall envelope; unified logprob/stop schema; SDK updates for JS/Python. Deprecated aliases emitted for one release.
Operators: enable"compat_streaming_v1" flag to continue serving legacy header-less frames during migration window. Monitor perf canary dashboard for +p95 latency regressions and disable legacy-only mode after clients upgrade.
API: chatv1 parameter canonicalization and streaming stability; toolcall envelope and unified logprob schema (sdk updates included).

payload.body: Motivation: large tensor-parallel workloads continue to see tail-latency and suboptimal bandwidth utilization on multi-socket multi-node clusters when model layer shapes vary. Existing static ring/allreduce placement and uniform chunking interact poorly with KV-cache prefetch windows and per-layer kernel performance characteristics. This PR introduces a hierarchical communication scheduler plus two complementary runtime optimizations: (1) layer-aware kernel selection that picks fused vs unfused kernels per-layer and preempts long-running kernels when small low-latency requests arrive, and (2) a KV-prefetch pipelining manager that overlaps eager shard transfers with compute at per-layer granularity. Summary of changes and goals: implement a two-level communicator partitioning (intra-socket local rings + inter-socket bridges) with adaptive chunk sizing based on recent per-link throughput; introduce a windowed send schedule that staggers chunk launches to avoid head-of-line blocking; add a layer profiler that collects microbenchmarks to choose attention/ffn kernels and a cooperative preemption path to yield GPU SMs for urgent batches; implement a prefetch manager that ties KV cache transfers to layer boundaries, supports speculative fetches for likely next prefixes, and a conservative eviction policy based on per-prefix hit probability. Checklist: - [x] scheduler core, communicator creation and runtime config - [x] adaptive chunking heuristics + runtime telemetry - [x] layer profiler and kernel selector - [x] cooperative preemption path and safe-fallback - [x] KV prefetch manager + eviction heuristics - [x] unit tests and integration perf harness - [x] documentation and runtime flags Design notes: hierarchical scheduler groups ranks by NIC topology to minimize cross-socket hops; per-channel token-bucket backpressure prevents a single large layer from starving others; adaptive chunk size uses an exponentially weighted moving average of recent allreduce bandwidth and latency to pick chunk sizes that maximize throughput while keeping per-chunk latency under the configured SLO. The layer-aware kernel selector stores choices keyed by (layer-id, seq-len, batch-size) and falls back to a cost model when unseen. Cooperative preemption exposes a short-latency interrupt path that runs a small handoff kernel to flush critical outputs and resume preempted work; this is gated behind a runtime flag and tested to avoid deadlocks. KV prefetch manager ties prefetch offsets to the model's layer order and allows speculative prefetch up to N layers ahead with a configurable byte cap; prefetches are demoted if they miss a hit threshold. Performance highlights (internal perf lab, p3dn-24 + 8xA100 config, tensor-parallel 8): - end-to-end throughput +18% on GPT-like 8B eval workload - 95th latency reduced from 340ms to 220ms for mixed short/long queries - KV cache hit-rate improved by 6 percentage points for conversational prefix workloads - network transmission tail reduced by 28% due to staggered chunk launches Testing and CI: included new unit tests for communicator construction, simulated perf harness tests for chunking heuristics, and end-to-end nightly perf job. One flaky test (integration/kv_prefetch_eviction) required two re-runs in CI and was stabilized with an extra timing fence. Deployment notes: runtime flags exposed under redwood.runtime.comm.* and redwood.runtime.kv_prefetch.*. Default rollout is gated behind a canary scoreboard in perf-canary and will be enabled for Dedicated pools after a 2-week canary with perf thresholds. Migration: no API changes; operators can tune chunk_size_policy and prefetch_max_layers. Rollback: feature guarded via runtime flags and can be turned off without model restarts. Files changed and rationale: net/comm/scheduler/hierarchical_scheduler.cc/hpp - core scheduling logic; net/comm/bridge_manager.cc - inter-socket bridge orchestration; runtime/kernel_selector.cpp - layer profiler and kernel selection; runtime/preemption/cooperative_path.cu - safe preemption handoff; runtime/kv_prefetch/manager.cc - prefetch pipeline and eviction; perf/harness/tp_hierarchical_bench.py - integration benchmark; docs/rtd/runtime_comm.md - design and tuning guide; tests/unit/* - new unit tests. Commits: - "proto: hierarchical scheduler initial scaffolding and communicator builder" - "perf: adaptive chunk size heuristics + EWMA bandwidth estimator" - "runtime: layer profiler and kernel selector with persistent cache" - "gpu: cooperative preemption handoff kernel and safety checks" - "kv: prefetch pipeline manager, eviction, and metrics" - "tests: unit and perf harness for TP hierarchical scheduling" Review summary and conversation: Reviewer Ariella Gomez: "Great decomposition; can we quantify additional CPU overhead from the layer profiler?" Author reply: "Profiler uses lightweight timers amortized across warmup steps; added microbenchmark showing ~1.6% CPU overhead on controller & explained in docs." Reviewer Samir Patel: "Concerned about deadlocks in preemption path when combined with persistent streams." Author reply: "Added additional fences and a stress test simulating preemption loops; updated cooperative_path.cu to assert safe state transitions." Reviewer Maya Hopkins (perf): "Adaptive chunking seems to favor smaller chunks on our 40GbE staging clusters; how does policy adapt on 100Gb?" Author reply: "EWMA learns the observed throughput and picks larger chunks on 100Gb links; added a regression test for link-speed emulation." CI summary: build/linux - pass, unit - pass, integration - pass (one flaky kv_prefetch_eviction re-run), perf-nightly - pass (canary report attached). Merge notes: squashed by Jinwoo Park, merge method squash, merge commit message references ENG-3289. Backports/Followups: a follow-up PR will add telemetry dashboards and a runtime knob for cooperative preemption aggressiveness. Release notes: "Introduce hierarchical communication scheduler to improve multi-socket TP bandwidth utilization, layer-aware kernel selection to reduce tail latency, and KV prefetch pipelining to raise effective cache hit rates. Default off for hosted customers; Enabled for Dedicated canaries and opt-in via runtime flags."

payload.body:
Added a latency-fence admission controller and a queue eviction policy for the continuous batcher to reduce tail latency regressions under high KV-pin contention. No API changes. Rollout gated behind feature flag.
Motivation: In production we observed recurring tail latency spikes when there is a mix of KV-heavy long-context requests and short low-cost requests. Existing continuous-batcher admission prioritizes throughput via coalescing which can let large KV-pin requests monopolize slots and cause starvation of short requests and SLO violations for p99. This PR introduces a lightweight runtime admission+eviction mechanism (latency-fence) that enforces a moving latency budget per scheduling horizon and allows preemptive eviction of low-priority queued items when predicted p99 would be violated.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a LatencyFence admission controller to the continuous batcher that maintains an exponential moving window of recently observed tail latencies (configurable percentile and decay). Incoming requests are classified by cost category (short/medium/kv-heavy) using existing runtime hints plus a small learned weight table. If admitting a request would push the predicted percentile above the configured fence, the controller will either: (a) reject/admit-to-fallback (for hosted paths), (b) mark for early eviction from the queue in favor of short requests, or (c) stall admission and trigger a fast-drain policy depending on the policy mode.
- Implements QueueEvictor which performs bounded, fairness-aware eviction during scheduling ticks. Eviction picks candidates by age/x-penalty and uses a per-queue debt token to prevent repeated eviction of the same tenant (debt tokens decay over time).
- Adds probabilistic KV-pin preemption: for requests that hold large KV pins but are stuck behind in waiting queues, the scheduler now opportunistically moves their KV pin into a compacted spill buffer (best-effort, does not alter model correctness) to allow serving of short requests first. This is guarded by config and telemetry to make it conservative.
- Adds a percentile-based timeout guard that will fast-fail queued requests older than N * EMWA(p99) to avoid queue buildup cascading into long tails. This is a soft fail when fallback is available; otherwise it extends the deadline with backpressure token.
- Exposes metrics (batcher.latency_fence.{admits,evictions,preemptions,fastfails}, batcher.eviction_age_dist) and a new per-route config flags in serving.yaml for experiment rollouts.
- Small kernel hint: when QueueEvictor triggers, it hints a short-lived kernel "kv_compact_hint" so the runtime selects a lower-latency kernel path for spill operations.

Files changed (high level):
- pkg/serving/batcher/latency_fence.go (new): core controller and config.
- pkg/serving/batcher/evictor.go (new): eviction selection and debt-token logic.
- pkg/serving/batcher/scheduler.go (modified): integrate admission checks and eviction hooks; add metrics emission.
- pkg/serving/kv/spill_buffer.go (modified): compact spill buffer implementation + kernel hint interface.
- pkg/serving/config/serving.yaml (modified): new per-route flags and defaults.
- internal/e2e/batcher_latency_test.go (new): deterministic scenarios for starvation and preemption.
- benchmarks/batcher/bench_latency_fence.go (new): microbench and p99-oriented bench harness.
- docs/observability/batcher_metrics.md (modified): documentation for new metrics.

Commits (summary):
- 8c7d3a2 add LatencyFence controller and basic EMWA p99 store
- 1b9e5f4 implement QueueEvictor and debt tokens with tests
- f204b11 hook admission checks into scheduler tick and add metrics
- a64f3d0 add KV spill buffer compact path + kernel hint API
- d1b4e9c add e2e tests and bench harness; docs for metrics
- c3b2a76 tweak thresholds after perf run, add feature flag gating

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- This PR is intentionally conservative: evictions are bounded and debt tokens are used to avoid oscillation and tenant starvation. We prefer fast-fail + fallback over hard eviction when fallback model variants exist.
- The EMWA p99 prediction is lightweight and tuned for responsiveness rather than absolute accuracy; it worked well in lab workloads and reduced p99 in our canary by ~18-22% in mixed KV/short workload at 95th percentile load.
- Probabilistic KV-pin preemption is best-effort: it can reduce per-token CPU by moving pinned KV segments into compact buffers, but we do not change model outputs. This avoids complexity of reloading weights.

Benchmarks:
- microbench (bench_latency_fence) shows p95/p99 improvements in mixed workload (25% p95, 18% p99) at target throughput with config fence=95, decay=0.2.
- End-to-end canary (10% of traffic for two hours) against main reduced observed p99 tail spikes from 340ms->270ms and reduced queued request count by ~30%.

Tests:
- unit: evictor selection, debt token decay, EMWA updates.
- integration: scheduler admission flows, kernel-hint path executed when spill takes place.
- e2e deterministic test that simulates KV-heavy tenant plus bursty short requests to validate fairness and that debt tokens prevent livelock.

Observability and rollout plan:
- Feature gated behind serving.yaml: routes can opt-in to "latency_fence: enabled|experiment|disabled". Default is disabled.
- Metrics added to Console dashboards and Alert rule for spike in batcher.latency_fence.evictions or fastfails.
- Rollout plan: enable for internal canary tenants (dedicated capacity) -> 5% hosted traffic -> 25% -> wider. Watch p99, evictions, preemptions, and errors.

Backward compatibility: No public API changes. Configs default to off. If teams enable the feature they should verify fallbacks are available for critical routes.

Reviewer discussion (highlights):
- Diego Alvarez: "Nice focused work. Need to ensure debt token rate is safe under tenants doing repeated short bursts. Please add amortized tests."
  - Author: "Added debt-token amortized decay test and extended e2e to simulate oscillating tenants."
- Carmen Liu: "Concerned about false positives from EMWA p99 on cold starts. Can we add a startup grace period?"
  - Author: "Added startup grace flag (default 60s) and unit tests covering it."
- Maya Kapoor: "Can we gate kernel hint behind runtime capability detection? Not all runtimes support the kv_compact_hint."
  - Author: "Added capability probe at scheduler init and no-op fallback when unsupported."

CI summary:
- unit: pass (ran on linux/amd64 and linux/arm64)
- integration: pass (flaky test patched during review and re-run)
- e2e: pass (deterministic harness)
- bench: bench job completed; artifacts uploaded with latency histograms.

Merge notes:
- Merge method: squash
- Changelog: included under release_notes above.
- Post-merge: enable feature-flag in staging for a 24h soak and add dashboard panels for the new metrics. We will coordinate with SRE to set preliminary alerts.

Potential follow-ups (next PRs):
- refine admission prediction with small online learner per-route
- make eviction policy aware of route SLAs to support strict tenant-level SLOs
- explore kernel-level optimizations to speed spill compaction paths further

Contact: @asha (author) for rollout coordination and benchmarks.

payload.body:
Context: Teams repeatedly ask for sensible defaults for batching, cache TTLs and quantization when onboarding models to Redwood. Currently defaults live in multiple places and require manual tuning with evals and internal heuristics. Goal: ship a small, auditable suggestion system that observes recent workload signals and proposes conservative default profiles for batching.window_ms, batch_size caps, prefix/KV cache TTLs, and quantization presets. The suggester is opt-in by default and produces human-readable suggestions surfaced in the Console and via a new API endpoint.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight offline heuristic engine (defaults-suggester) that consumes short-term aggregated telemetry (per-route QPS, median latency, 50/95/99 latency quantiles, token length distribution) and maps to a ranked set of suggested profiles. 2) Introduces a new API: POST /optimize/v1/suggestions which returns JSON suggestions with confidence scores and an explanation string. 3) Wire up Console: a Suggestions panel on per-route settings with an Apply & Preview flow that shows estimated unit-cost delta and latency impact. 4) Add a gated runtime flag so the runtime can accept a profile payload for immediate application (useful for Dedicated/Private workflows). 5) Provide a small set of canonical profiles (conservative, balanced, aggressive) for batching and quantization, plus TTL presets for prefix/KV caches. 6) Add end-to-end test coverage and benchmark harness runs comparing before/after for representative traffic shapes.

Design notes and trade-offs: - The engine intentionally errs conservative: suggestions will never increase batch window beyond a route-level safety cap derived from SLA settings. - Quantization suggestions prefer per-model family presets (e.g., OPT/GPT-like) and include fallbacks; we do not auto-apply quantization in-host, suggestions only. - Telemetry ingestion is opt-in; customers can disable telemetry for suggestions in account settings. For Private installs the suggester can be run locally against their telemetry export. - Suggestions include an estimated unit-cost delta computed from our unit-econ model; we expose the formula in the Console and include the prompt/eval link so teams can validate quality impact.

Files touched: runtime/batching/suggester.go, optimize/suggester/service.go, api/handlers/suggestions.go, console/src/routes/RouteSuggestionsPanel.tsx, console/src/api/suggestionsClient.ts, docs/operations/defaults-suggester.md, config/profiles/default-profiles.yaml, tests/e2e/suggestions_flow.test.ts, bench/harness/suggester_traffic_shapes.yaml, telemetry/migrations/add_suggester_event.sql, scripts/ci/bench-suggester.sh

Testing: - Unit tests for mapping heuristics and profile ranking. - E2E test simulating three traffic shapes (short chat, assistant longform, embeddings micro-bursts). - Benchmarks: microbenchmark harness run on a c6g-xlarge-equivalent cluster with representative models showed median latency change within +3% for conservative profiles and unit-cost reduction up to 24% for balanced profiles on nuclear workloads. Results attached to the CI artifact and linked in the console patch notes.

Rollout plan: feature gated. Step 1: merge behind feature flag and enable suggestions only for internal org and canary customers. Step 2: collect feedback for 2 weeks. Step 3: enable Console UI for self-serve with telemetry opt-in prompt on first usage. Step 4: document caveats and add guided eval for teams that accept aggressive quantization suggestions.

Open questions / TODOs: - Add an explicit opt-out banner in Console per compliance request (tracked in ENG-7922). - Provide an exportable CSV of suggestion history for audit. - Consider a future ML-backed suggestion engine once we have more signal.

References: Linear items ENG-7842, ENG-7901. Internal benchmark dashboards: /dash/bench/suggester/33219.

This description is intentionally high-level; see docs/operations/defaults-suggester.md for the full spec and the API contract.
Marco Ruiz: Nice end-to-end. Two quick questions: 1) telemetry sensitivity — what fields are we exporting? 2) safety cap logic: please clarify how SLA caps are enforced so we don't regress p99 for high-priority routes.
Asha Patel (reply): Telemetry is aggregated and windowed, we only ingest per-route QPS/latency quantiles and token length histograms. No raw prompts or user identifiers. SLA caps are derived from route.metadata.sla_ms if present else global-default-sla; batch window is min(suggested, sla_safe_window). Added comments and unit tests (see runtime/batching/suggester_test.go).
Priya Nair: Benchmarks look promising. Can we add a small canary that surfaces the suggested unit-cost delta in Console before apply? UX should show the estimate and a confidence score.
Asha Patel (reply): Added preview UI and the confidence score from the ranking function. Preview includes a cost/latency estimate computed from the unit-econ model. Updated Console tests accordingly.
Daniel Kim: Please add a feature flag to avoid automatic runtime exposure in Dedicated until security signoff. Also add a telemetry opt-in toggle on account-level configs.
Asha Patel (reply): Added runtime.gated.features.suggester boolean guard and account.suggestions.telemetry_opt_in. Documented both in the runbook.
Introduce a conservative, opt-in defaults suggester that recommends batching and cache TTL profiles plus quantization presets. Suggestions are surfaced in Console with cost/latency estimates and are gated behind account-level telemetry opt-in. Useful for teams who want quick, audited starting points for unit-econ driven tuning.
Enable feature flag runtime.gated.features.suggester=false by default in main cloud. For canary orgs set to true via admin console. Ensure bench artifacts are uploaded to /artifacts/bench/suggester/33219 before enabling wide rollout.

Reduced peak GPU transient workspace up to 28% on long-context workloads via spanwise trimming and kernel padding heuristic; improves continuous-batching tail latency and reduces KV-cache eviction pressure.
Motivation: long-context generation and mixed-length continuous batching cause transient workspace blowups in the serving runtime. This PR introduces a spanwise scratch trimming pass plus a kernel-padding optimizer that cooperates with the scheduler and KV-cache pipeline to reduce peak ephemeral allocations without regressing throughput. High level: 1) Spanwise trimming: we analyze activation lifetimes at the operator-span level and release non-essential scratch segments earlier when safe (configurable slack). 2) Kernel-padding optimizer: a lightweight heuristic that chooses per-kernel padded workspace sizes to avoid pathological oversubscription from worst-case kernel footprints while still benefiting from vectorized kernels. 3) Scheduler hooks: new stride-aware scheduling hints let the batch coalescer and kernel launcher align padded sizes and avoid tail allocations. 4) KV-cache cooperation: a small API to allow the KV manager to proactively compact hot segments when a trimming window is entered. 5) Ops and ABI: additions are backwards-compatible; new options are gated behind runtime flags. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (internal/ENG-9341) - [x] unit tests for trimming heuristics - [x] integration test with continuous-batcher - [x] perf benches across long/short context mixes - [x] canary rollout plan and rollback flag Implementation notes: trimming introduces a conservative default slack of 8 tokens and is enabled for models with >8 layers by default; kernel-padding optimizer uses historical kernel footprint histograms collected during warmup to pick 75th-percentile padded sizes. Behavioural guarantees: no activation correctness changes; trimming only affects ephemeral scratch, not persistent checkpoints. Observability: added metrics runtime.scratch.trimmed_bytes, runtime.kernel.pad_factor, runtime.kv.compactions_triggered and traces for trimming windows. Rollout: feature is behind runtime flag redwood.runtime.span_trim_enable and will be enabled in Dedicated canaries for 48h before global rollout. Related: this complements ENG-9143 (arena tuning) and ENG-9410 (continuous batching improvements). Links: design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-9341/spanwise-scratch-trimming; canary run notes: internal/perf/canary-2024-11-10. Why different from previous work: instead of coarse arena-level free coalescing we operate at operator-span granularity and coordinate padded kernel sizing with the scheduler to avoid reintroducing fragmentation. CI: initial CI run failed on an unrelated Python lint in infra; fix was applied and CI green on rerun. Merge notes: squash merge after approvals; no migration scripts required.
Aisha Khan: Nice direction; can you clarify how trimming interacts with checkpointing? Are we at risk of evicting live activation slices?
Priya Nair: Trimming only targets scratch buffers allocated by kernels (transient workspaces). Persistent activation checkpoints are untouched. We added assertions in debug builds to ensure no overlap with checkpoint allocations.
Marco Li: CI flaky in integration test on GPU memory error during initial run; looks like a race in KV compactor. Can you add a backoff?
Priya Nair: Added a linear backoff and a retry in kv_compactor; updated tests to surface retries deterministically. Reran canary and memory error did not reproduce.
Daniel Reiser: Request changes on observable labels — prefer runtime.kernel.pad_factor -> runtime.kernel.pad_ratio for consistency across metrics
Priya Nair: Renamed metric in latest commit and updated dashboards in docs link.
payload.title: Spanwise scratch trimming and kernel-padding optimizer to reduce transient GPU workspace

Motivation: The monolithic bash pipelines under .github/workflows and scripts/legacy-ci.sh have become brittle and hard to iterate on across services. This PR modernizes the pipeline by introducing reusable GitHub composite actions, a plugin hook system for per-repo policy, and a small cross-platform ci-toolbox binary to compute robust cache keys and talk to the remote cache store. Scope: 1) Add .github/actions/checkout-composite, test-shard-composite, lint-runner-composite. 2) Replace repo-level shell orchestration with composite action calls and a dynamic matrix generator (tools/ci/matrix-gen.js). 3) Remove scripts/legacy-ci.sh and in-repo Docker-in-Docker usage; use buildah/kind where needed. 4) Add ci-toolbox (tools/ci-toolbox/main.go) used by composite actions for cache keying and fast retries. 5) Add .github/ci-config.yml with opt-in staged rollout flags for teams to adopt incrementally. Checklist: - [x] Add composite actions and document inputs/outputs - [x] Implement matrix generator and update matrix shapes - [x] Port lint/test usages to new composites - [x] Add ci-toolbox with basic cache key and remote fetch - [x] Add integration CI job that runs composites end-to-end on a canary subset - [x] Remove legacy script invocations and update README-ci.md Migration notes: The new composites are backward-compatible by default and live alongside legacy workflows during a 2-week canary. Owners can enable ci-config.yml flags to opt into new flows. Rollback is as simple as switching the workflow reference back to legacy scripts if an issue is detected. Risks and mitigations: Cache-key changes may cause cache misses on first runs; ci-toolbox includes a dry-run mode to preview keys. Matrix reshaping can increase pipeline concurrency; we added a default concurrency limit and a dynamic shard sizing heuristic. Future work: Add telemetry hooks to Redwood Console for per-route CI latency and cost, and introduce a GH App to enforce team opt-ins.
Diego Ramos: Nice move away from brittle bash. Please add a unit test for matrix-gen edge cases.
Asha Mehta: Added unit tests for empty-service-lists and large-shard heuristics in commit 4.
Maya Chen: We need an opt-out flag for repos that still depend on Docker-in-Docker; can you add an explicit allow-dind: true in ci-config.yml?
Asha Mehta: ci-config.yml now supports allow_dind and a canary_percentage. Default is false.
Evan Liu: CI runs flaked once on macOS runners in step 'install-tools' — reworked tool install order and pinned go:1.20 image in composite; reran and green.
Maya Chen: Approving pending green CI and docs update.
Diego Ramos: Approved. Squash-merge when ready.
Internal: Replace legacy bash CI with composable GitHub composite actions and a lightweight ci-toolbox binary. No user-facing behavior changes.
7 commits: initial composite action skeleton, matrix generator, ci-toolbox CLI and unit tests, workflows switched to composites for core services, removed legacy scripts, docs and README updates, pinned minimal action SHAs.

Motivation: customers increasingly chain multiple tool calls per turn and want lower tail latency by running compatible tools in parallel, plus predictable result injection and idempotent retries. This PR introduces a server-side concurrent tool runner, extends the OpenAI-compatible function_call surface to allow explicit parallel calls and tool-result references, and updates SDK helpers and streaming merge semantics to keep the API stable for existing clients. Summary of changes: 1) runtime: add services/inference/tool_runner/concurrent_runner with a pluggable execution strategy (sequential | parallel | hybrid), a run_id-based idempotency layer for retries, and deterministic merge ordering for structured output injection. 2) api/openai-compat: extend function_call payload with optional keys: "parallel_calls" (array of tool names), "tool_result_refs" (map-like list of result identifiers), and "injection_policy" (deterministic | merge_stream | attach_raw). The compat layer translates these into internal execution plans and exposes merged streaming boundaries to callers. 3) streaming: improve chunk merging to reduce interleaving artifacts when multiple tool streams are active; add a small backpressure window to avoid head-of-line blocking in multi-tool flows. 4) SDKs: python & typescript helpers to create and await parallel tool futures, helpers to submit a single composite call that the server will execute in parallel when possible, and a deterministic merge utility for client-side local execution. 5) docs & tests: update openapi spec, add e2e test harness that exercises parallel function calls, and add unit tests covering retry idempotency and injection ordering. Backwards compatibility: default behavior remains sequential tool execution; the new keys are opt-in. Also preserved the original function_call semantics for single-tool usage to avoid breaking existing OpenAI-compatible clients. Rationale: moving parallelism into the platform lets us optimize batching and GPU utilization while keeping SDK ergonomics simple; adding run_id/idempotency reduces duplicate side-effects for retried calls. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag concurrent_tool_runner.enabled. Initially enabled in staging and can be opt-in per-tenant via config; will be enabled by default after 2 weeks of telemetry. Related: linked_linear ENG-4123 ENG-4181. Notes: this PR intentionally avoids introducing a new RPC surface; changes are translations within the compat layer and runtime to minimize client churn.
Diego Morales: please add a feature flag and tenant opt-in controls before merging. Ava Chen: added concurrent_tool_runner.enabled and tenant config path; also documented the default rollout plan. Priya Nair: can we guarantee no increased memory spikes when parallelizing lots of small tools? Ava Chen: added a bounded worker pool with per-request concurrency cap and tests simulating 100 small-tool parallel requests. Liam O'Connor: nit on naming: 'tool_result_refs' is awkward; suggest 'tool_output_keys'. Ava Chen: kept both keys in translator for compatibility and added alias mapping in docs. Diego Morales: approve after CI green. Priya Nair: approve after addressing backpressure tuning. Merge performed via squash once staging telemetry validated behavior.
Added server-side concurrent tool runner (opt-in). Extended OpenAI-compatible function_call payload to support parallel_calls and tool result references. SDK helpers for parallel tool orchestration (Python & TypeScript). Streaming merge improvements to reduce interleaving when multiple tool streams are active.
payload.title: concurrent-tool-runner: parallel tool invocation + OpenAI function_call compatibility updates

Motivation: Production workloads with mixed INT8/FP8 layers pay a high cost on repeated dequant/requant cycles and small-prefix KV cache lookups. This PR implements two orthogonal optimizations: (1) a 'scale-reservoir' that maintains compact shared per-layer scale state and serves micro-requantized buffers to downstream kernels, avoiding full dequant paths for short-lived tensors, and (2) a vectorized INT8 compatibility shim that allows FP8 kernels to accept requantized INT8 input without a heavyweight convert. Additionally, we add a KV coalescer in the cache layer to merge adjacent small prefix lookups into fewer GPU uploads and a scheduler hook so the continuous-batcher prefers reservoir-warm slices when possible. Key user-visible outcomes: (a) lower per-token GPU compute when hybrid-precision models are used, (b) fewer GPU memory transfers for KV-prefetch patterns common to chat-like workloads, and (c) safe rollback via a feature flag and a canary rollout path. Changes: new runtime/kernels/int8_shim.cpp/h — vectorized shim and dispatch paths; runtime/scheduler/reservoir_scheduler.cpp/h — scheduler scoring, reservoir lifecycle; runtime/cache/kv_coalescer.cpp/h — prefix coalescing logic and metrics; runtime/loader/quant_hints.cc — model loader exposes per-layer scale hint metadata; runtime/tests/bench_int8_shim.py and runtime/tests/test_kv_coalescer.cc — unit and microbench harnesses; docs/perf/benchmarks/int8_reservoir.md — reproducible commands and plotting. Benchmarks: microbench on A100 and H100 with batch sizes and sequence lengths representative of customer chat workloads (seq_len=16 and seq_len=96) show 12-18% median throughput uplift and 6-9% reduction in p99 latency for the INT8/FP8 mixed model we used as a proxy. End-to-end token-cost simulation on Dedicated workloads indicates a ~10% token compute cost reduction under the tested profile. Compatibility and safety: feature gated by runtime flag REDWOOD_INT8_RESERVOIR; shim only enabled when model metadata includes 'quant_scale_hint'. KV coalescer has heuristic thresholds and a CI test asserting no semantic change in prefix lookups. Rollout: canary on 5% Dedicated capacity for 72 hours, expand to 25% then full rollout if regression-free. See linked Linear ENG-4721 for rollout playbook. Checklist: implement kernels and scheduler hooks, add unit and perf tests, document benchmark steps, add feature flag, run security review for new allocation path.
Introduces an adaptive scale-reservoir and an INT8->FP8 compatibility shim plus a KV cache coalescer. Improves hybrid-precision throughput and reduces p99 latency for short- and medium-context workloads. No API changes; rollout as canary to Dedicated tier then staged to Hosted.
Ethan Walker: Nice separation of concerns between reservoir and scheduler. Can you add a regression unit that validates no semantic changes for KV prefix ordering?
Maya Rodriguez: Added test_kv_coalescer.cc with randomized prefix sequences and a deterministic reference runner; results included in bench harness.
Priya Nair: The shim is clever but please add a microbenchmark showing overhead of the shim when disabled vs enabled to ensure we don't regress FP-only paths.
Maya Rodriguez: Added bench that toggles the feature flag; FP-only paths show <0.7% variance (within noise), details in docs/perf/benchmarks/int8_reservoir.md.
Jonah Lee: Confirmed concurrency safety around reservoir eviction under high batch pressure; requested a small fix for the atomic fence in dispatch.
Maya Rodriguez: Pushed fix for memory fence and added comment explaining the ordering requirement.
Ethan Walker: LGTM after CI green and docs updated.
payload.title: Adaptive scale-reservoir + vectorized INT8 shim with KV coalescer for hybrid-precision paths

Motivation: observed high peak GPU workspace usage for mixed-sequence inference (short+long requests) and multi-query fanout workloads. Existing arena tuning + static activation checkpointing provided good average memory savings but left headroom in two patterns: (1) transient scratch buffer spikes from kernels that allocate per-op temp buffers, and (2) suboptimal kernel choices when the operator fanout (key/value heads * queries) changes runtime characteristics. This PR implements two complimentary mechanisms to reduce peak workspace: 1) dynamic scratch reuse: a runtime scratch allocator that tracks short-lived temp regions by lifetime buckets and reuses buffers across operators within the same execution frame, avoiding repeated allocations and reducing fragmentation; 2) fanout-aware kernel selection: extend the kernel-selector to consider request fanout and KV cache reshaping costs when choosing between tiled/packed attention kernels and the low-memory fused attention kernels.

Summary of changes: implemented a lightweight scratch manager in runtime/scratch_manager.{cpp,h} with a lock-free free-list per-sizeclass and lifetime-tagging. Hooked the scratch allocation path into the kernel interface and modified critical kernels (attention, rotary, layernorm) to request scratch via the manager. Added a fanout heuristic in runtime/kernel_selector.cpp that uses observed Q*K fanout counters (collected per-model) to pick kernels that trade compute for lower transient memory. Added a compatibility path so that models pinned to older kernel profiles will continue to run the legacy selector. Integrated unit and microbenchmarks under benchmark-lab/ with a new benchmark script fanout_memory_profile.py and an end-to-end e2e memory test that simulates interleaved short/long requests.

Performance results: on A100-40GB with GPT-2 style model (1B params) and mixed workload (50% seq_len=32, 50% seq_len=1024) peak workspace dropped from 16.8GB to 12.1GB (~28% reduction). For high-fanout Q=16 tests the transient peak reduced by ~34% when the fanout-aware kernel was selected. End-to-end latency impact: median latency for long requests increased ~2.3% in a worst-case knob-on scenario where the low-memory kernel is used; this is within the SLA tradeoff and we expose a config flag to prefer latency vs memory at policy-level.

Compatibility and rollout strategy: feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled=false by default in this PR; we plan a phased rollout: enable on non-production clusters for 2 weeks, then opt-in for Dedicated clusters with memory pressure, finally flip default after one week of metrics monitoring. Kernel selection heuristic is additive and can be disabled with runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic=false. Added telemetry metrics: runtime.scratch_reuse.alloc_reuse_ratio, kernel_selector.fanout_decision_count and memory.scratch_peak_by_model.

Testing: added unit tests for scratch manager lifecycle and size-class reuse; added integration tests that assert no OOM on synthetic high-fanout scenarios; ran infra e2e-bench and observed stable results. CI: linux-unit-tests, cuda-smoke, and e2e-bench run green in the final run. Created a small fuzz harness to ensure lifetime tagging prevents use-after-free across frames.

Backward compatibility: no breaking API changes; the kernel interface signature extended with an optional scratch_token but remains backward-compatible with default nullptr behavior. Documentation: runtime/README.md updated with configuration knobs, and redwood-docs/ops/gpu-memory-tuning.md includes recommended settings for Dedicated customers.

Notes: this PR intentionally avoids changing global arena sizing heuristics in this iteration — that will be a follow-up to measure impact of scratch reuse on arena fragmentation (ENG-1919). Also, we identified a secondary opportunity to compress KV cache layout when fanout>8; tracked separately under ENG-1875.
Alex Ortega: Nit - please add a short note on concurrency model for the free-lists. Also, can we expose a knob to limit max per-frame scratch?
Maya Chen (author): Added concurrency notes in scratch_manager.h and exposed runtime.scratch_reuse.max_frame_scratch (default large).
Priya Nair: Verified benchmarks locally on p4d; I saw similar 26-30% peak reduction. One request: add a test ensuring legacy kernel path still used when model pinned.
Maya Chen (author): Added model-pinned test and compatibility checks in kernel_selector.
Samir Patel: Approved after CI green. Left a follow-up to audit arena metrics (ENG-1919).
Reduced peak GPU workspace by ~28% for mixed short/long workloads via dynamic scratch buffer reuse.
Added fanout-aware kernel selection which reduces transient memory for high-query fanout workloads.
Exposed runtime knobs to tune memory vs latency tradeoffs: runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled and runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic.
payload.title: dynamic-scratch-reuse-and-fanout-aware-kernel-selection-to-reduce-peak-gpu-workspace

payload.body:
Motivation: Multi-GPU tensor-parallel workloads suffer from suboptimal collective placement and small-KV churn when requests are micro-batched across heterogeneous racks. This PR implements three coordinated runtime optimizations to improve throughput and tail latency: (1) topology-aware peer balancing: build NVLink/NIC-aware ring/graph membership using a lightweight port-speed probe so collectives prefer intra-node/NVLink lanes and minimize cross-node hops, and dynamically rebalance peer pairs when per-step bandwidth estimates indicate hotlinks; (2) async kernel dispatch: move per-layer kernel launch to a dispatch thread pair that annotates CUDA streams with priority and orders kernels for overlap with NCCL comms, and add a non-blocking enqueue-locality check so compute work can start as soon as required dependencies are queued; (3) KV-cache coalescing at the request router: group concurrent small KV reads into coalesced bulk fetches and fold redundant cache population work to reduce memory traffic and small-launch overheads. Design notes: peer selection runs at model load and is re-evaluated when topology events are seen (PCIe/NVLink health changes, new GPUs added). Peer balancing uses a lightweight EWMA of measured pairwise bandwidths to pick an alternating pairing sequence for each micro-batch window. Async dispatch uses two prioritized CUDA streams per device (compute_high, compute_low) plus a comm stream; we rely on CUDA stream priorities instead of artificial host sleeps which reduces scheduling jitter. KV coalescer is conservatively enabled behind the feature flag tp_topo_pb and has a max-coalesce window (configurable) to avoid added latency for single-request critical paths. Implementation summary: runtime/scheduler: add TopologyProbe and PeerBalancer modules, extend DeviceResources to expose stream priorities; runtime/comm: new TopoRingBuilder that prefers NVLink edges, updates NCCL unique IDs to include pairing hints; runtime/dispatch: KernelDispatcher refactor, introduce DispatchFence for dependency tracking and switch to cudaLaunchKernelAsync for fused kernels; router/kv_cache: RequestCoalescer layer with in-process batching and de-duplication. Compatibility and safety: fallbacks to previous ring builder when topology probe fails or when running on unsupported drivers; coalescer has a conservative timeout and a per-model opt-out. Tests and validation: microbenchmarks using benchmark-lab show 18-25% throughput improvement on 8xA100 NVLink topology for half-precision decode workloads with 2048 seq; 95th percentile tail latency reduced by ~14-20% for 8k token streams when KV coalescing is enabled. Perf canary across 3 dedicated clusters showed stable error rates and no observable degradation in output quality. Rollout plan: feature-flagged in main, staged canary to dedicated-qa, then incremental ramp to production Dedicated pools over 72 hours with monitoring on NCCL error counters, GPU PCIe errors, end-to-end latency SLOs. Observability: emit metrics peer_balance/pair_changes, topo_probe/latency_ms, kvcoalesce/coalesce_rate, dispatcher/stream_stall_ms, and add tracing spans for coalescer windows. Documentation: updated runtime/README and redwood-docs/perf for recommended config knobs. CI and perf runs: included unit tests for peer balancer invariants and integration tests in perf-harness. This change is primarily internal runtime improvements; no user API changes expected.
Improves multi-GPU tensor-parallel throughput and tail latency by introducing topology-aware peer selection, dynamic peer balancing, asynchronous kernel dispatch with stream priorities, and KV-cache request coalescing. No API changes. Rollout gated behind feature flag 'tp_topo_pb'.
Ethan Park: Can you describe failure modes when NVLink bandwidth is asymmetric? Recommended adding an EWMA and a cooldown window.
Lina Ortega: Responded that EWMA already in PeerBalancer and added cooldown; included comment in code and unit tests to validate cooldown behavior.
Priya Nair: Suggests adding a config toggle to limit coalesce window for low-latency flows; asked for a perf run showing single-request latency impact.
Lina Ortega: Added per-model opt-out and microbench that shows median single-request latency increase <1ms with coalesce window set to 2ms.
Lucas Meyer: Code review: requestCoalescer locking looks fine but suggest avoiding blocking on IO thread; recommended converting the final flush to a thread-pool callback.
Lina Ortega: Implemented thread-pool flush and re-ran CI; updated tests.
payload.title: Topology-aware peer balancing, async kernel dispatch, and KV-cache coalescing

payload.body:
Motivation: we observe persistent tail latency regressions in mixed workloads where KV-heavy requests hold pins and block continuously batched windows. Previous fixes (cohorting, timeout guards) reduced some cases but left intermittent starvation when request sizes and arrival patterns create long-lived head-of-queue holds. This PR implements a lightweight ticket+lease scheme for the continuous batcher that enforces bounded queue-hold time, improves dequeue fairness across request classes, and enables controlled lease extension for low-latency short workloads.

Design summary: single-threaded ticket assignment per incoming request, short lease token assigned at enqueue, scheduler uses ticket age and lease state to decide coalescing vs. early-dequeue; a skew-aware penalty function gradually deprioritizes requests that repeatedly requeue due to KV pin conflicts; support for an optional per-model lease-duration override; metrics and traces for ticket lifecycle. No API surface changes.

Checklist: 
- [x] design doc linked (ENG-5173)
- [x] unit tests covering ticket lifecycle and penalty decay
- [x] integration test with simulated KV-pin contention
- [x] bench suite run against internal mixed workload harness
- [x] docs: brief explainer in serving/README.md

Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag `continuous_batcher.ticket_lease_enabled` (off by default for dedicated early customers). Start with 10% canary on redwood-hosted inference for internal testing, observe tail p99/P95 and KV lock-duration metrics for two weeks, then progressive ramp if stable.

Behavioral notes: 
- Normal short text-only requests get short default leases (8ms) and are favored for coalescing.
- KV-heavy requests receive initial short lease but may request a single lease-extension via a lightweight handshake; extensions are rate-limited per-client to avoid head-of-line monopolization.
- Requests that hit their max-retry penalty window are evicted into a separate slow-path queue that gets scheduled at fixed small intervals to guarantee forward progress (prevents starvation).

Benchmarks (mixed workload synthesizer): 
- 95th latency on mixed KV-heavy test: improved from 142ms -> 116ms (18% reduction)
- 99th latency: improved from 312ms -> 256ms (18% reduction)
- Overall throughput under nominal load: +6% due to reduced queuing hold time
- Microbench: ticket allocation overhead ~0.6us per request in hot paths (measured on c6g-gpu infra).

Compatibility and safety: the scheme is conservative by default (short leases, single extension). Configurable knobs documented in serving/configuration.md. No model-format changes. Fallback: when disabled, scheduler reverts to previous coalescer behavior.

Related work: references prior PRs on fairness and timeout guards (see ENG-4211, PRs in 60000-65000 range).

Notes: this PR focuses on scheduler heuristics and bookkeeping; a follow-up will expose telemetry-driven auto-tuning of lease durations and penalty backoff constants.
Jonas Müller: Can we avoid a global allocator if the ticketing state becomes a contention point at high ingress? Suggest sharding tickets per worker. — Requested changes
Aisha Patel: Implemented a per-worker local ticket cache to amortize allocation; added bench comparing central vs sharded allocator (see commit b7c3d44). — Reply
Priya Desai: Need a graceful fallback path when rate-limited lease extension is exhausted to avoid client-visible errors. Suggest documented retry guidance. — Comment
Aisha Patel: Added slow-path queue with deterministic scheduling and documented retry guidance; added integration test that asserts forward progress under heavy KV contention. — Reply
Marcus Rivera: Bench numbers look promising. Please add metric tags to distinguish tickets created with extension vs without for slice analysis. — Comment
Aisha Patel: Added ticket_extension tag and ensured metrics emitted; updated telemetry dashboard snapshot in docs. — Reply
CI bot: bench job initially failed on first run due to harness seed nondeterminism. Re-ran after fixing seed; subsequent runs passed.
Improves continuous batcher fairness and reduces tail latency for KV-heavy mixed workloads via a ticket+lease queueing scheme. Feature behind a runtime flag; disabled by default for safety. See serving/configuration.md for knobs.
payload.title: ticket-lease-queueing-scheme to reduce KV-heavy starvation in continuous batcher

Context: In high-concurrency mixed workloads we observed correlated slot reclamations and KV cache warmups causing transient starvation and p95 latency spikes. This PR implements two complementary runtime controls: (1) jittered slot reassignment to spread slot release/reassignment events across short randomized windows (configurable), and (2) a KV-warmup throttler that staggers cold-KV prefetches and enforces a soft admission budget per-slot to avoid simultaneous heavy prefetches. Changes: Implements a new scheduler helper (jitter_reassign) which inserts small randomized offsets before slot handoff and coordinates with the slot allocator to avoid churn; implements kv_warmup_throttle which tracks per-model warmup tokens and decays budgets based on successful cache hits; exposes scheduler.tuning.jitter_ms and kv.warmup.budget_rate config knobs; updates continuous_batcher admission path to consult warmup budget before immediate prefetch; adds lightweight metrics (jitter.delay_ms distribution, kv.warmup.throttle_rejections) and dashboard panels. Commits: "add jittered slot reassignment helper"; "implement kv warmup token bucket and decay"; "plumb knobs through config and expose metrics"; "perf tests and bench harness for mixed workloads". Changed files (high-level): runtime/scheduler/jitter_reassign.go; runtime/scheduler/slot_allocator.go (small API); runtime/kv/warmup_throttle.go; runtime/batcher/continuous_batcher.go (admission path); metrics/registry.go (new metrics); docs/benchmarks/jitter_warmup_readme.md; tests/perf/test_jittered_reassign.py; tests/unit/test_kv_warmup_throttle.go; ci/workflows/perf.yml. Motivation: Previous approaches (hard timeouts and global cooldowns) either caused head-of-line blocking or were too coarse-grained for multi-tenant bursts. The jittered reassignment spreads out reassignments to reduce synchronized pressure on the slot allocator and downstream kernel selection; warmup throttling prevents cache stampedes and reduces wasted kernel invocations. Performance: On internal perf harness using a 64-GPU cluster and mixed 75% short, 25% long requests we saw median latency change ~+2ms, p95 reduced ~18%, p99 reduced ~10%, and KV cache miss storms reduced by ~42% in burst scenarios. CPU/GPU utilization improved: fewer small kernel startups and more sustained larger kernels resulting in 6% lower cost/throughput token. Testing: unit tests for token decay and edge cases; perf tests covering staggered bursts, tenant fairness, and long-tail KV loads; load test in staging with warmup budget default of 10 tokens/sec. CI: initial perf run showed a flaky bench; reran perf pipeline with increased harness stabilization and all checks passed. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind runtime.scheduler.jittered_reassign (default enabled for dedicated clusters, opt-in for hosted at 10% rollout), staged ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automated rollback on regression signals (p95 increase >5% or error rates >0.1%). Backout: config toggle and immediate revert PR prepared if needed. Related: references ENG-4219 for prioritized scheduling work, ENG-4291 for KV cache prefetch follow-up. Checklist: design doc attached in Linear; unit tests added; perf benchmark included; docs updated.
Introduces jittered slot reassignment to reduce synchronized preemption, adds KV-warmup throttling to avoid cache stampedes, and exposes two new tuning knobs for batcher schedulers. Improves p95 latency under mixed workloads and prevents starvation observed in multi-tenant bursts.
Ethan Clarke: Can you explain why a randomized jitter is better than exponentially backoffed retries for reassignment?
Priya Natarajan (reply): Jitter reduces synchronized events across slots; exponential backoff pushes responsibility to requesters and can still cause correlated retries across tenants. We benchmarked both and jitter had lower p95 in mixed bursts.
Maya Rios: Please add a test for the warmup token decay edge case where decay interval is extended by scheduler stall.
Priya Natarajan (reply): Added test_kv_warmup_throttle.go covering stall+decay scenario and updated comments to document expected behavior.
Liam Zhang: Suggest exposing metrics with rate-normalized panels to make alerting simpler.
Priya Natarajan (reply): Updated metrics/registry.go to publish per-minute normalized counters and added dashboard panels.
payload.title: scheduler: jittered slot reassignment and KV-warmup throttling

Motivation: Downstream customers reported two classes of incompatibilities when proxying OpenAI-style function/tool calls through Redwood: (1) nondeterministic 'tool_choice' semantics under temperature/sampling when multiple compatible tools exist, and (2) fragmented streaming messages for long, structured tool outputs that break standard JSON schema validators. This PR implements a compatibility layer that (a) introduces an arbitration step to normalize tool_choice semantics to deterministic, policy-driven selection while preserving sampling behavior when explicitly requested, and (b) replaces the previous naive streaming envelope with a FragmentedMessageSerializer that emits framed, schema-aware fragments plus finalization markers to safely reconstruct structured outputs on clients that expect either OpenAI streaming frames or Redwood framed envelopes.

Summary of changes: single-continuous description of the work below.

Design highlights:
- Arbitration: add invoke_arbitrator that sits before tool invocation. By default it deterministically selects the highest-priority tool based on model-intent matching and explicit tool annotations (preferred, fallback). If the original request included sampling semantics (temperature > 0 and top_k/top_p present) the arbitrator emits a selection token in the streaming path instead of forcing a fully deterministic pick; clients can opt-in to either strict-deterministic or permissive-sampling modes via the new 'invoke_selection_mode' parameter (values: "deterministic", "sample-allow").
- Serializer: FragmentedMessageSerializer splits structured outputs (large JSON blobs or newline-delimited JSON) into schema-bound fragments. Each fragment includes a compact header: {fragment_id, seq, total_estimate, schema_tag}. A finalization frame contains the canonical schema_hash and a CRC of the reconstructed payload to aid client-side validation. Serializer supports both OpenAI-style data: and tool invocation frames and Redwood's internal framed envelope; we map between them based on client compatibility hints.
- Backwards compatibility: default behavior matches previous Redwood semantics for existing clients. OpenAI-compat clients (detected via Accept-Compat header or compatibility flag in request) receive framing that mirrors OpenAI streaming boundaries while preserving the fragment headers in a hidden metadata channel (x-rw-frag) so proxies can reconstruct.
- Runtime: minimal overhead assigned to fast-path: small, in-place headerization for fragments and a predict-first-run policy that avoids recomputing model->tool match scores where a cached profile exists.

Testing & rollout plan:
- Added unit tests for arbitration deterministic vs sampling modes (tests/api/test_invoke_arbitrator.py).
- Integration tests cover streaming reconstruction under simulated network reordering, truncated frames, and client-side schema validation failures (tests/integration/test_fragmented_stream_roundtrip.py).
- E2E perf microbenchmarks show median added overhead < 1ms per fragment for typical 8k-token outputs on GPU nodes; regression tests added to perf-canary harness.
- Rollout: enable on staging for 48h behind feature flag rw:openai-invoke-compat, then ramp to 10% production, monitor tool-invoke error rate and invocation latency percentiles.

Why this is different from prior work:
- We explicitly separate selection policy (arbitration) from execution: previously selection was implicit in the sampling loop and hard to reproduce. The arbitration API is pluggable for future rules (cost-aware, region-aware, ML-based selector) without changing streaming framing.
- The serializer provides a formalized fragment header and finalization CRC which prevents silent schema corruption that customers reported during ephemeral reconnects.

Risks / mitigations:
- Clients that depend on raw token streams might need minor updates: mitigated by dual-path framing and automatic downgrading to legacy stream for clients that pass no-compat headers.
- Edge-case: model-initiated tool handoffs (multi-tool chains) require arbitration to be reentrant. We added reentrant-safe locks and idempotency keys to prevent duplicated invocations.

Checklist:
- [x] implement arbitration logic and serializer
- [x] unit + integration tests
- [x] docs (redwood-docs/compatibility/invoke.md) updated with selection_mode and fragment schema
- [x] perf canary
- [x] feature flag gated rollout plan

Notes: the description above is the single string for the PR body. See commits for more granular step notes.
Marcus: Can the arbitration step be configured per-route via console? Response (Sasha): yes — added route-level config and Console UI hooks; Lina: serializer header size might add overhead in small fragments, can we compress header? Response: switched to 8-byte compact header and delta-encoded seq which reduced header overhead by ~36%; Evan: tests look good but add a case for truncated finalization CRC fail -> added test and handling to emit explicit 'schema_mismatch' exit frame before connection close.

Motivation: Customers were seeing indeterminate behavior when clients disconnected mid-stream (mobile network flaps, proxy resets) and then reconnected: generated tokens could be duplicated or lost, function-calling side effects were inconsistently applied, and OpenAI-compat clients received confusing error payloads. This PR introduces a pragmatic, opt-in streaming lifecycle handshake and cancellation safeguards to make disconnect/reconnect/resume behavior deterministic and backwards-compatible.

Summary of changes: Adds a resume handshake token, server-side grace-window and per-stream timeout semantics, improved mapping for OpenAI-compat abort/cancel errors, and safe function-calling guarantees when clients reconnect. Includes runtime changes, adapter mapping, SDK surface notes, tests, and docs.

Design goals and constraints: 1) Backwards-compatible by default: existing clients continue working with current semantics; new handshake is enabled via header or query param. 2) Deterministic retries/resume: resumed streams should continue from the last acknowledged token, never re-execute completed function calls. 3) Minimal latency impact for non-resuming clients: default flow retains current fast-path. 4) Observable: metrics for resume attempts, aborted-inflight, and resume success rate.

Protocol and API changes (high level): - New optional outbound header: X-Resume-Token: client-supplied token used to correlate a resumed stream with a recent disconnected stream. Servers issue a Resume-Offer frame at disconnect that contains a server-side resume token and last-ack offset. - New request query param: resume_window_ms (default 30000) controls how long the server will honor resume attempts for a given stream id. - New server timeout param: stream_idle_timeout_ms (default 60000) to bound resource retention post-disconnect. - New SSE/Chunk frames: RESUME_OFFER, RESUME_ACCEPT, RESUME_REJECT, HEARTBEAT to coordinate state. (When using HTTP/2 gRPC-like streaming the frames are translated into control messages.)

Server behavior and safety: - On client disconnect, the runtime records the last-confirmed token offset and issues a RESUME_OFFER when it is safe to resume (i.e., KV cache intact). The offer includes a server_resume_token and last_ack_position. - The server holds execution state for resume_window_ms. If a new connection presents X-Resume-Token matching a live server_resume_token and offset <= last_ack_position + hysteresis, the server responds with RESUME_ACCEPT and resumes token emission from next position. - To avoid double-execution of function/tool calls, function-call side effects are only marked committed after the client acknowledges receipt of a special CALL_CONFIRM frame. During resume, the runtime consults the call ledger and will not re-run committed calls; in-flight calls that did not reach CALL_CONFIRM will be retried once with idempotency keys. - If the resume fails (mismatch token or expired window), the server returns RESUME_REJECT and the client may reopen a fresh stream; server enforces server-side backpressure and cold-start fallback to alternate model variants if capacity is constrained.

OpenAI compatibility adapter changes: - Map native abort/disconnect reasons to OpenAI-compat error semantics: aborted-by-client => code: 499/cancelled with message "Client cancelled stream"; server-timeout => 503 with body matching OpenAI shape. - For streaming-chat endpoints, the adapter now honors X-Resume-Token and includes resume metadata in the chunked response for OpenAI-compat clients that opt-in via header "X-OpenAI-Resume: 1". This preserves OpenAI-compatible behavior while enabling deterministic resume. - Function-calling: adapter uses the new CALL_CONFIRM frame to report that a function invocation payload has been delivered; only then will OpenAI-compatible /responses include function result committed state.

Compatibility and opt-in rollout: - Feature is guarded under feature flag streaming-lifecycle-v2. Default off for all existing accounts; enabled on canary accounts and progressively rolled to larger tenants. - SDKs (Python/TS) will include helpers to manage resume tokens and heartbeat handling. Docs include migration notes and an example for mobile reconnect patterns.

Testing and observability: - Unit + integration tests that simulate flapping connections, mid-call disconnects, duplicate resume attempts, and expired resume windows. - Added e2e tests for OpenAI-compat streaming in CI matrix. - New metrics: streaming.resume_attempts, streaming.resume_success, streaming.resume_rejections, streaming.inflight_call_retries. Added tracing spans for handshake phases: handshake.offer, handshake.accept, handshake.reject, handshake.timeout.

Migration checklist: - [x] Implement server-side resume token store and eviction. - [x] Add SDK helpers and docs. - [x] Add OpenAI-compat adapter mapping and tests. - [x] Add metrics and tracing. - [x] Canaries in prod and rollout automation.

Risks and mitigations: - Risk: state retention increases memory footprint on high-concurrency workloads. Mitigation: server enforces stream_idle_timeout_ms and per-tenant limits; resume_window_ms default is conservative. - Risk: tool/function idempotency edge cases. Mitigation: explicit CALL_CONFIRM semantics and idempotency keys; we test common patterns and add telemetry for uncommitted calls.

Rollout plan: Canary on 3 customers and internal staging for 48 hours; measure resume_success and in-flight_call_retries; open rollout gradually, disabling on SLO breach.

This description is intentionally dense; see changed files for implementation details and inline comments.
Tomás Nguyen: Overall approach looks good. A few clarifying questions: 1) How do we prevent resume tokens from being reused by malicious clients? 2) Can we tighten the default resume_window_ms for free-tier tenants?
Asha Patel: Answers: 1) Resume tokens are cryptographically signed and bound to tenant+stream id; we also rotate and revoke tokens on explicit stream termination. 2) Yes, we added per-tenant overrides and free-tier defaults to 15s to limit retention (see runtime/streaming/handshake.go).
Maya Reddy: We need more unit tests around function-call idempotency when network fails between CALL_CONFIRM and ACK. Also please add a metric for uncommitted_call_retries.
Asha Patel: Added tests in handshake_test.go and adapter tests; added streaming.uncommitted_call_retries metric. Also added explicit lint justification for the new control frame names.
Ben Carlson: CI flakes on the OpenAI-compat e2e in the first run, re-ran and it passed. Approving once CI is green.
Optional streaming resume handshake: opt-in via X-Resume-Token or resume_window_ms. Improves determinism for reconnects and adds safer function-call semantics during reconnects. Backwards compatible by default. See docs/streaming-lifecycle-handshake.md for migration steps.
