Motivation: Streaming inference workloads showed uneven latency tails when mixing quantized kernels and fp32 fallbacks during dynamic batching. This PR implements a lightweight 'rendezvous' handoff between INT8-optimized kernels and fallback execution paths, combined with a KV-aware scheduler that aligns continuous-batching windows with KV cache affinity so that prefetched KV state is reused more deterministically. Summary of changes: 1) new kernel handoff protocol in the runtime that exposes a minimal ABI for passing KV affinity metadata, 2) scheduler additions to track per-request KV fingerprints and form rendezvous groups that prefer homogenous quantization paths, 3) minor changes to the kernel loader to surface throughput/latency profiles for runtime routing decisions, 4) e2e perf tests and a calibration script that collects sequence length and KV hit statistics. Checklist: - [x] Design doc and microbenchmark results included - [x] Unit tests for handoff logic - [x] Integration perf harness and recording - [x] CI passing on main matrix - [x] Backcompat: handoff is opt-in behind runtime flag for now Implementation notes: The handoff protocol is intentionally minimal: it passes a tokenized KV fingerprint string, a preferred quantization tag (int8/fp8/fp32), and a micro-decision hint (prefer_low_latency / prefer_throughput). Runtime uses this to deterministically route a request through the same kernel group for the duration of a batch or to fall back if capacity isn't available. The KV-aware scheduler keeps a small LRU of recent KV fingerprints per worker and biases rendezvous group formation to avoid mixing high-mismatch requests into the same continuous-batch, which previously caused repeated KV reloads and higher latency variance. Performance summary: On our internal LAMBDA-small benchmark with mixed sequence lengths, steady-state throughput is flat but p95 latency improves by 18% and token compute drops by ~12% on average when the feature flag is enabled. For large-sequence tails the scheduler reduces KV reloads by ~30%. Commits: single squash for merge. See commits list for atomic changes. High-level changed files: runtime/kernel_handoff.cpp runtime/kernel_handoff.h runtime/kernel_interface_v2.h scheduler/kv_rendezvous_scheduler.cpp scheduler/kv_affinity.h scheduler/continuous_batcher.cpp runtime/loader/kernel_loader.cpp tests/perf/bench_int8_streaming.py tests/unit/test_kernel_handoff.py docs/rfc/int8-smoothscale-rendezvous.md build/CMakeLists.txt Why this is safe: The new handoff is behind a runtime flag and defaults to disabled. Kernel ABI changes are additive; older kernels are untouched. The scheduler is additive and conservative: it only biases group formation, never rejects requests. Rollout plan: enable flag for canary pool, run perf harness for 48h, gradually expand to 50% of serving capacity, monitor p95/p99 and KV miss rates. Related PRs and background: This builds on telemetry collected by ENG-1423 and the kernel profiling work in ENG-1487. It is complementary to other quantization-path work but focuses on runtime routing and KV cache alignment rather than new quant kernels.
Diego Alvarez: The rendezvous idea looks promising. Can we ensure the fingerprint is compact and won't add overhead to hot-paths? Please add microbenchmarks for encoding/decoding the fingerprint.
Maya Chen: Added compact varint-based encoding; microbenchmarks are in tests/perf/bench_int8_streaming.py with allocation numbers. Encoding cost is <0.5% of token compute on our microbench.
Priya Raman: Scheduler biasing needs to be cautious about overheavy skew in multi-tenant pools. Suggest a tunable threshold and fallthrough to default policy.
Maya Chen: Added tunable thresholds and documented safe defaults in the RFC. Scheduler falls back to round-robin if a rendezvous would starve capacity.
Samir Patel: Did you validate fallback behavior when an INT8 kernel is busy but fp32 is free? Need predictable degradation path.
Maya Chen: Yes, runtime will prefer same-path rendezvous for the batch build but will fall back to the fastest available compatible kernel; tests added to validate this path.
Priya Raman: CI perf flaky on one run. Please re-run perf job before merge.
Maya Chen: Re-ran perf suite; results stable. CI now green.
Diego Alvarez: Approving with two nits in comments (inline).

Motivation: our monolithic build graph and full-pipeline CI runs slow iteration and increase cost for PRs that touch a small subset of services. This PR separates the internal build dependency graph from CI orchestration, introduces per-package incremental checkpointing for test artifacts, and wires a lightweight detection layer to only run downstream stages when inputs changed. Goals: reduce PR feedback loop, lower CI minutes for typical infra/SDK changes, and make release hooks deterministic for incremental releases. What I changed (high level): decoupled core build graph (tools/build/graph.py) into an explicit dependency manifest and runtime loader; added incremental checkpoint producer/consumer (tools/build/checkpoint.py + scripts/ci/checkpoint-restore.sh); implemented a CI policy layer (ci/policies/detect-changes.py) that computes minimal stage sets; updated GitHub Actions workflows to support staged checkpoints and conditional jobs; documented the policy and rollback steps in docs/ci/README.md.

Implementation notes: the build graph is now a JSON manifest generated at build-time (tools/build/manifest_writer) and consumed by the CI runtime to compute subgraphs; checkpointing serializes test results and selected artifacts (hash keyed) to a short-lived S3-compatible store used by runners; restoration is best-effort and fails safe (if a checkpoint is missing we fall back to full stage). The CI policy uses a fast file-globbing change classifier with a small mapping table (repo paths -> stage names) and a conservative fallback to full CI for PRs with broad touches. Rollout plan: land behind feature flag (env CI_USE_CHECKPOINTS), run on canary repo subset for 48 hours, monitor false negatives (missed changes) and CI flakiness, then enable by default. Checklist: - [x] implement manifest writer and loader - [x] add checkpoint producer and consumer - [x] integrate with GitHub Actions and add conditional job gates - [x] document behavior and rollback steps - [x] smoke at scale on canary repos - [x] add metrics (ci.checkpoint.hit/miss, ci.stage.count) Additional context: this change is part of ENG-3176 to reduce median CI time for SDK/infra PRs by 40%. A separate follow-up will expose checkpoint telemetry in the Console and add heuristics to re-run flaky stages automatically.

Summary: Add a Cost Rules Engine that automatically recommends and applies batching and KV-cache defaults per model and workload profile, exposes quantization profile hints for safe auto-application, and introduces a unit-economics estimator in the console and CLI. Motivation: customers routinely ask for hands-off cost tuning; operational teams want reproducible, audited defaults that reduce per-token costs without surprising latency regressions. This PR bundles runtime heuristics, a small rules DSL, console UI plumbing, and an opt-in rollout for auto-quantization. What changed (high level): - new runtime module redwood/serving/cost_rules.py with rules evaluation, telemetry hooks, and safe-apply gates - batcher tuning extension that selects default batch sizes based on latency SLOs and sequence-length histograms - KV cache policy defaults and prefix cache eligibility heuristics - quantization profiling pipeline (offline profiler + runtime hinting) and a safe auto-apply policy with rollback - console/CLI cost estimator showing projected per-token unit economics with suggested knobs - integration tests, docs, and an opt-in feature flag + audit logs Rollout plan: default rules are disabled by default for existing tenants. We enable the rules engine for internal canaries and add a gradual opt-in toggle in the console. Quantization auto-apply is gated behind a policy that requires: a) offline eval against golden prompt set, b) latency/regression guardrails, and c) explicit tenant opt-in. Checklist: - [x] implement rule evaluator and runtime hooks - [x] expose console estimator and API endpoints - [x] add offline quant profile pipeline and safe-apply path - [x] add unit + integration tests - [x] add docs and release notes - [x] add audit events and rollout flag Notes on safety: the rules engine never mutates a serving model binary directly; it returns a recommended configuration which a controlled subsystem applies with canarying and audits. The PR includes a conservative default profile that favors latency SLOs for small-sequence chat workloads and cost for high-throughput embedding workloads. Related: ENG-3412 (cost-automation epic), ENG-3470 (quantization-safety), SUP-1298 (customer support case motivating default cache rules).

Context and motivation: Responses v5 introduced a small-but-important set of fields commonly used by customers migrating from OpenAI: a top-level `seed_hint` / `deterministic` pair for repeatability, and a `metadata` object that must be passed through verbatim into the final tool/function call payload and the recorded response for auditability. Our hosted API previously supported older 'seed' semantics (internal deterministic RNG flag) and ad-hoc metadata propagation for a subset of tool calls. This PR adds a compatibility shim so v5 OpenAI-style requests are honored without requiring changes to the runtime kernel.
Adds OpenAI Responses v5 compatibility shim: maps seed_hint/deterministic to runtime seed_id, ensures deterministic requests are batched separately, preserves top-level metadata into tool/function call payloads and audit logs. Includes SDK Python wrapper and migration docs. Backwards compatible with existing OpenAI/Redwood requests.
Operational notes: 1) Deterministic requests are isolated at batching boundary — expect slightly higher per-token cost for deterministic-heavy traffic because of reduced batching efficiency. 2) Metadata is stored verbatim for audit; large metadata blobs (>32KB) are rejected with a 400 and guidance to use object storage references. 3) SDK and examples updated; customers migrating should test critical prompt sets with the Responses v5 flag and verify seed-based repeats in staging before enabling in prod.
Unit tests added for mapping and batch segmentation. Integration matrix covers streaming reassembly, concurrency with mixed deterministic flags, and metadata passthrough for function/tool calls. Manual QA ran end-to-end with a sample tool that returns structured JSON and verified schema integrity after passthrough.

Author (Priya): Seed_hint is materialized as a per-request seed_id and we add it to the batching key. Batches will be segmented by seed_id so deterministic requests are never co-batched with others; documented in runtime/streaming/reassembly.go. See new unit test 'BatchSegmentationBySeed' added in mapping_test.go.
Maya: Test flakiness observed in reassembly test on CI (timeout). Suggest reducing timeout and adding a backoff retry for streaming chunk ordering guarantees.
Author (Priya): Reduced test timeouts and added a deterministic scheduler stub for the integration test to eliminate CI timing flakiness. Also added an explicit assertion on chunk sequence numbers.
Jordan: SDK change looks good. Please include a short example in docs showing how metadata is surfaced in function/tool outputs (audit use-case).
Author (Priya): Added docs/migration/openai_v5_migration.md with an example mapping metadata->client_metadata and a note about audit logging retention.
This change is intentionally implemented as a compatibility layer in services/openai-compat to keep the core runtime stable. Future work (ENG-4250) will consolidate seeding APIs and expose a first-class deterministic mode in the public Redwood API.

Context: tensor-parallel workloads at longer sequence lengths saw pronounced tail latency and KV-cache stalls when single large allgather operations saturated NCCL and serialized with compute. This PR introduces two coordinated changes: 1) a lazy allgather splitter that slices large allgathers into subwindows sized by runtime sequence-length histograms and active KV entries, enabling earlier progressive availability of KV shards to compute lanes; 2) a priority NCCL stream allocator and scheduler that pins small/latency-sensitive chunks to high-priority comm streams while routing bulk aggregation to background streams. Motivation: reduce head-of-line blocking, increase overlap between comm and compute, and reduce NCCL stream stalls on multi-node, multi-GPU clusters. Design summary: lazy splitter observes per-request prefix lengths and dynamic KV usage; it produces ordered chunk descriptors dispatched as separate NCCL allgather ops. A lightweight combinator ensures correct reassembly for downstream KV cache refill without changing model-level semantics. The priority stream allocator exposes a stream affinity table (per-GPU) and a heuristic to prefer mapping small-first chunks to priority streams that have lower expected queuing delay. The scheduler change in runtime/scheduler injects boundaries to interleave compute slices with pending comms based on a predictive cost model calibrated by microbenchmarks. Implementation notes: changes span runtime/tp/allgather_splitter.* (C++), runtime/scheduler/priority_stream_scheduler.* (C++), runtime/nccl/stream_pool.cc (affinity and priority support), serving/flags/config.proto (new runtime flags), tests/bench/tp_allgather_bench.py (microbench harness), and docs/perf/lazy-allgather.md. Backwards compatibility: default is off for private deployments; hosted will enable flag behind a gradual rollout gate after cluster verification. Testing: unit tests for splitter ordering and reassembly, synthetic microbenchmarks on 8xA100 and 4xH100 clusters, integration runs with real workloads used in ENG-3124. Results: 12-18% steady-state throughput increase on small-batch long-seq TP configs, 1.4x reduction in 95th percentile latency during KV cache warmup phases, and 35% fewer NCCL stream stalls observed in trace captures. Checklist: - [x] microbenchmarks and traces - [x] unit and integration tests - [x] docs and rollout notes - [x] feature flag gating - [x] reviewers and perf signoff
Introduce lazy allgather splitter and NCCL priority stream assignment to improve multi-GPU tensor-parallel throughput and reduce tail latency; default scheduler heuristic updated; opt-in via runtime flag rtp.lazy_allgather=true.

Sofia Alvarez: Benchmarks look good; request that we add a regression unit that simulates bursty small-sequence workloads to ensure priority streams don't starve background collectives.
Maya Patel: Added synthetic burst test and updated scheduler to degrade priority allocation under sustained background load.

Motivation: users operating MQA models (qwen/mistral variants) observed throughput regressions on multi-head GPUs when token distributions are highly skewed by a few hot tokens. Root cause analysis showed head-wise tensor packing triggered suboptimal kernel selection and oversized KV-cache snapshots for LLaMA-style rotary/stride variants, increasing memory movement and serialization overhead. This PR introduces two complementary runtime optimizations: 1) Per-head tiling hints that allow the scheduler to choose head-local tile sizes based on observed head activation sparsity, enabling smaller kernels for skewed heads while keeping dense heads on high-throughput kernels; 2) KV-windowed routing which maintains a tunable sliding window for KV snapshot materialization per-request-group to avoid full-KV snapshots on short-context bursts and to prefer compact delta snapshots when sequence growth is small. Design notes: the changes are runtime-only and behind two feature flags (runtime.per_head_tiling, runtime.kv_windowing_delta). Per-head tiling computes head occupancy histograms over an adaptive epoch and surfaces a hint enum (COMPACT|BALANCED|THROUGHPUT) to the kernel selector. KV-windowed routing tracks per-route recent max-prefix-length and uses a small LRU-indexed ring buffer to store recent KV deltas; routing prefers delta materialization if predicted extra-memory-copy cost is less than the kernel startup amortized cost. Tests and validation: microbenchmarks across LLaMA-2-13B, Mistral-7B-Instruct and Qwen-14B-MQA with synthetic skewed prompts, real-chat replay workloads and end-to-end Redwood-hosted API workloads. Observed results: 8-18% median p99 generation latency reduction on skewed tails, 12-22% per-token throughput improvement for short-burst conversational workloads, and peak GPU memory reduction up to 9% on MQA variants. Rollout plan: feature flags default-off for 1 week of dogfooding, then opt-in on Canary, followed by controlled ramp to GA with telemetry gated thresholds. Backwards compatibility: no model format changes and kernel fallbacks for unknown hint values. See linked Linear tickets for further follow-ups and benchmarking tasks.

Motivation: Production teams increasingly ask for safe, explainable defaults for batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles tuned to their unit-econ targets. Manual tuning is slow and error-prone; naive defaults either leave money on the table or cause latency regressions. This PR introduces the 'Batch-Cache Policy Synthesizer' — a small service and integration that synthesizes conservative, runbook-driven defaults and optional suggestions for aggressive cost-saving profiles, backed by workload traces and unit-econ objectives.

What this changes:
- New service: internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer that consumes sampled request traces, cost/latency SLO goals, and historical model perf profiles to output a ranked set of policy candidates (batching window, max batch size, prefix cache TTL, kv-cache-hotlist-size, quantization profile id).
- CLI: tools/cost-synthesizer/bin/rcs (runbook-config-synth) for operators to generate profiles locally from a trace file and preview expected token-cost and p50/p95 latency deltas.
- API: /v1/internal/policy_synthesizer/generate (protected) to request on-demand policy suggestions for a customer or model route.
- Redwood Console integration: Add a lightweight Recommendations drawer that surfaces the top-3 candidates along with estimated saving, expected latency impact, and confidence score.
- Safeguards: Every suggestion includes a conservative fallback policy and an automatic canary rollout plan (10% traffic -> 50% -> 100%) with automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions.
- Tests: unit tests for candidate scoring, integration tests for the CLI path, and e2e smoke that runs a small synthetic trace through the service and validates metrics emitted to metrics.redwood (new metric: optimizer.synthesized_policy.{applied,rolled_back}).

Design notes (short):
- Scoring model: multi-objective heuristic that combines estimated per-token cost delta, expected p95 latency delta (from per-op instrumentation), and an uncertainty penalty derived from sample size. Operators can pick a unit-econ target multiplier (e.g., 0.8x cost target) and the synthesizer returns candidates that meet the target while keeping p95 within a user-configured latency window.
- Quant profiles: the synthesizer references the model-registry quant profiles and recommends the lightest quant that has a validated quality delta < configured threshold (default 1% BLEU/ROUGE-style surrogate). If no profile passes, quant recommendations are omitted.
- Safety floor: all policies include a required minimal TTL and max_batch safeguards to avoid excessive batching for latency-sensitive routes.

Files changed (high level):
- internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer/service.go (core synthesizer)
- internal/optimizer/policy_synthesizer/score.go (scoring heuristics + unit-econ logic)
- tools/cost-synthesizer/cli.go (trace -> suggestion path)
- api/internal_routes.go (new internal endpoint + auth guard)
- console/src/components/RecommendationsDrawer.tsx (UI surface)
- docs/operator/runbooks/policy-synthesizer.md (runbook + rollout playbook)
- tests/integration/synth_cli_test.go
- tests/e2e/synth_smoke_test.yaml

Short commit summary: 
- feat(synthesizer): initial synthesizer and scoring heuristics
- feat(cli): rcs tool and local trace parsing
- feat(api): internal endpoint and auth scope
- feat(console): recommendations drawer and telemetry hooks
- test: integration + e2e smoke coverage and CI job
- docs: runbook and operator guidance

Backwards compatibility: The synthesizer produces policy JSON that is fully compatible with the existing /configs/policy schema. There are no default changes to runtime behavior unless an operator explicitly applies a synthesized policy or accepts a Console recommendation.

Rollout plan: Merge to main -> feature flag guarded release for 48h to internal canary orgs -> open beta for customers with opt-in flag in Console -> enable for customer accounts with automated guardrails after 30 days if telemetry shows safe behavior.

Notes on CI: Initial CI run showed a flaky timing-dependent test in synth_cli_test.go (race with metrics exporter). I added a deterministic fake exporter and re-ran. The final CI run passed: all unit, integration, and e2e smoke checks green.

Sofia Martinez: We use bootstrap sampling on trace segments; explained in score.go comments and added a unit test. Uncertainty is expressed as a multiplicative penalty on cost savings.

Context and motivation: Customers using the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat.completions adapter reported intermittent loss of final token logprobs and mismatches when mixing legacy stop arrays with structured tool-calls. Motivation: We need automated, repeatable canaries that detect latency/throughput regressions before full rollouts and block unsafe deployments. This PR adds a continuous regression-detector pipeline and a rollout-guard CI job that integrates with our protected-branch rules.

What this does: Adds a perf-canary runner, a CI job (ci/perf-canary.yml), infra hooks for the rollout-guard, and a small dashboard + docs. The canary runs a short synthetic workload against candidate builds, compares summary statistics (p50/p95/throughput) to a rolling baseline, and fails the check if a statistically significant regression or >X% cost-latency tradeoff is detected. The check can block merges (protected branch) or trigger automatic rollback during automated deploys.

Design highlights: Uses a lightweight, reproducible harness (tools/perf-canary/runner.py) that: generates representative request traces (sampling distributions derived from production traces), warms caches (KV prefix warmup), and runs multiple iterations to estimate p50/p95 and throughput. Baselines are pulled from our TSDB (Prometheus) using a 7-day rolling window and a median+MAD-based baseline with configurable sensitivity. Statistical test is bootstrapped percentile comparison with configurable alpha; thresholds and sample sizes are configurable via ci/perf-canary.yml and infra/rollouts/guard.tf.

Rollout guard behavior: When the canary job runs as part of a release pipeline it emits a GitHub check with structured metadata (baseline-id, metrics, delta-percent, p-value). If the job fails, the rollout-guard marks the deployment as blocked and creates a Linear ticket (automated) with the top failing metrics and traces. For PR-triggered runs the job posts a summary comment and a compact artifact with trace snippets.

Testing & rollout: Local dev: python -m tools.perf_canary.runner --local-mock to run against a mock model serving fixture. Staging: the pipeline will run against the staging fleet for 24 hours to collect baselines; then will be enabled as a required check on release branches. Rollout plan: opt-in for 2 weeks for canary-as-check, then flip to required on main for release tags.

Motivation: Customers reported two classes of production instability when using long lived streaming sessions through the OpenAI compatibility adapter: abrupt disconnections leaving incomplete tool/function calls, and client-driven cancel semantics that produced ambiguous server state. This PR adds an explicit session negotiation + termination contract, explicit client cancel tokens, and robust server-side idle/active timeouts to make streams deterministic and resumable where possible. Changeset summary: 1) Protocol: introduce optional Stream-Session header with a server-issued session_id and resume_token. Clients may present resume_token within 30s to pick up an in-flight stream. 2) Cancel semantics: adds a client-cancel event ("CANCEL_TOKEN" frame) that reliably marks in-progress function/tool calls as cancelled; server responds with an acknowledgement frame before stopping the stream. 3) EOF and structured output: add an explicit EOF control frame ("STREAM_EOF") and a small framing extension for structured output chunks so tooling functions can be reassembled deterministically after reconnects. 4) Timeouts: server now enforces two timeout tiers: active_token_timeout (max time waiting for client ACK during a tool call) and session_idle_timeout (max idle time before session eviction). Defaults were chosen to be conservative (active 45s, idle 120s) with config overrides per deployment tier. 5) OpenAI-compat adapter: preserve existing OpenAI-compatible chunked data shape but add a top-level meta chunk that contains session_id/resume_token when available so existing SDKs remain compatible while opt-in resume semantics are supported. 6) SDK updates: exposed session resume API in JS/TS and Python SDKs plus a cancel() convenience. 7) Tests & observability: added unit and integration tests covering reconnect resume in the happy path and simulated partial tool execution aborts; added per-session metrics (session_start, session_resume, session_eof, session_eviction) and tracing baggage to link function calls across reconnects. Checklist: - [x] Protocol design doc (linked internal spec) - [x] Implementation in service runtime - [x] Adapter mapping for OpenAI-compat - [x] SDK surface for resume/cancel - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Add metrics and alerts Rollout: staged behind feature flag streaming_resume in main and enabled for canary customers first. Backwards compatibility: adapter returns resume metadata only when the client and server advertise support through headers; non-upgraded clients continue to receive standard chunked responses with no behavioral change. Related linear: ENG-1124 (streaming stability spike), ENG-1190 (tool-call idempotency).
Diego: Please clarify how call_id maps to tool invocation retries; requested deterministic call_id generation for idempotent retries. Author: added call_id field in the framing and deterministic generation based on request nonce and sequence number.
Maya: Add observability hooks to distinguish EOF vs eviction. Author: added session_eof/session_eviction metrics and trace tags; updated observability doc.
Samir: Concerned about default timeouts being too low for slow external tools. Author: exposed config overrides per deployment and added a canary config with longer defaults for tool-heavy customers.
QA: Found a race in test harness where resume_token expiry path sometimes caused double-finalize; added a test harness sleep and extra guard to ensure single finalize. After fixes, QA approved the integration tests.
Lead Eng (Samir): Approved and requested squash merge after CI green.
Improved streaming session resilience: server-issued session_id and resume tokens enable reconnect-and-resume for short disconnects; explicit client cancel frame and server ack to make tool/function call cancellation deterministic; new STREAM_EOF control frame for reliable structured output termination; server-side active and idle timeouts configurable per deployment; SDK updates (JS/TS/Python) expose resume and cancel helpers; enabled behind feature flag streaming_resume. No breaking changes for older clients.

Context and motivation: Customers frequently surface two pain points when composing LLM responses with external tools: 1) streaming instability when tool results and model tokens interleave mid-stream, and 2) duplicate side-effects from naive retry semantics for parallel tool calls. This PR introduces a unified 'Tool Caller' API and a delayed-commit retry strategy to address both issues in a developer-friendly, OpenAI-compatible surface. Design summary: The Tool Caller provides a single entrypoint for: a) orchestrating ordered or parallel tool invocations with deterministic merge semantics, b) registering streaming checkpoints so the model can safely stream partial token output without observing incomplete tool side-effects, and c) delayed-commit retries that only expose tool results to the model after idempotency checks pass. Streaming stability is handled via per-tool stream checkpoints plus a small bounded rebuffer window to preserve low-latency streaming while avoiding mid-stream observable state changes. The retry model uses idempotency tokens and a delayed commit phase: tool runs return provisional results that are not yet injected into the model stream; on success and idempotency confirmation we atomically commit the result into the model's context. Implementation highlights: server/api/tool_caller.py defines the ToolCaller class and public HTTP/SDK surface. server/streaming/stream_manager.py implements streaming checkpoints, rebuffer window, and backpressure integration. server/runtime/tool_dispatcher.cpp contains the low-level executor changes for parallel task orchestration and idempotency hooks. SDK shims (sdk/python/redwood/tools.py and sdk/typescript/src/tool-client.ts) expose the new call signature while preserving the old openai-compatible helpers via a compatibility layer. Observability: introduced tool_caller_latency and tool_commit_success metrics and added a small dashboard tile. Tests: new integration test (tests/integration/tool_composition_test.py) covers ordered, parallel, failure+retry, and streaming-snapshot scenarios. CI: added a targeted e2e workflow ci/workflows/tool-e2e.yml. Migration notes: The compatibility layer keeps old helper names; consumers that depended on streaming-mid-tool injections should migrate to the new two-phase commit injection model. See docs/migration/tool-caller-migration.md for a step-by-step guide and sample code. Rollout plan: feature-gate the new API for hosted and dedicated deployments for four weeks, shadow traffic for two days, then enable for 10% of main traffic for a week before full ramp. Monitoring will focus on commit latency, duplicate-effect rate, and streaming rebuffer tail latency. Backout plan: revert feature flag and disable delayed commits; hotfix branch created if we see increased error budgets. Benchmarks: internal perf runs show median end-to-end latency increase of ~6ms for single-tool calls due to idempotency checks, but multi-tool parallel calls saw a 22% reduction in observed duplicate side-effects and a 12% improvement in 99th percentile streaming stability in our multiplexing demo. Checklist: - [x] API spec and SDK shims implemented - [x] Observability added - [x] Integration tests added - [x] Migration guide written - [x] Benchmarks and rollout plan documented QA and verification steps: run example-apps/multiplexing-demo against local stack, validate no duplicate side-effects for simulated retries, run tool-composition integration test under stress, verify CI e2e pass. Security review: idempotency tokens are scoped per-customer and rotated via KMS; we added a short section in docs on token lifecycle. Known limitations: long-running tools that stream their own state must adopt the provisional-result pattern; we added examples in the migration doc. Relationship to other work: builds on ENG-2191 (tool orchestration primitives) and complements ENG-2248 (streaming stability improvements).
Adds a unified Tool Caller API that offers deterministic semantics for multi-tool and parallel tool invocations, streaming stability fixes, and a delayed-commit idempotent retry strategy to reduce duplicate side effects.

Motivation: reduce token latency and increase throughput for medium-to-long context workloads by shipping a new set of attention kernels and a couple runtime scheduling tweaks. This PR introduces two FlashAttention variants (memory-optimized and fused-qkv path), a fused rotary/rope pre-rotation step, and scheduler-side heuristics that improve continuous batching and KV cache locality. It also contains microbenchmarks, CI hooks, and a migration note for custom kernel fallbacks. Changes include kernel sources, host-side glue, scheduler policy, and perf harnesses. Checklist: [x] flash variants implemented and unit-tested [x] fused qkv and rotary op added [x] continuous batcher heuristics updated [x] KV prefix cache integration with kernel fast-path [x] benchmarks added [x] documentation and migration notes added. Summary of changes and rationale: we observed recurring tail latency spikes for long conversations due to inefficient rotary application and extra memory copies in QKV paths. The memory-optimized Flash variant reduces intermediate allocations by streaming rotary application into fused matmul kernels. The fused-qkv path removes a roundtrip copy for QKV interleaving when model layout is compatible. Scheduler improvements bias batch formation to keep high prefix-reuse requests together and to avoid splitting high-KV-hit requests across GPU lanes. This reduces KV cache churn and improves effective throughput for chat workloads. Compatibility: kernels have runtime probes and fall back to previous CUDA kernels if compute capability or workspace is incompatible. Documentation in docs/perf/attn-kernels.md explains runtime flags and a new REDWOOD_ATTN_KERNEL env var for operators. Testing and benching: microbench harness (benchmarks/attn_latency.yaml) reproduces production-like distributions (50/30/20 split for small/medium/long contexts). End-to-end perf runs were executed on dedicated CI runners with A100/80GB and RTX6000 pools. Observed improvements (median across 5 runs): - LLaMA-2-13B, seq=512: p50 latency down 27% (from 112ms to 82ms), throughput up 1.8x for streaming-batched workloads. - Llama-2-7B, seq=2048: p95 latency down 34% and 2.1x throughput in high-KV-reuse scenarios due to reduced cache churn. - Memory working set reduced by ~18% on average for long-context workloads. Runtime regression guard: perf-evals are included in CI and a canary rollout config is added in the console so we can route 5% traffic to the new kernels for a week before full rollout. Rollout plan included. Migration notes: customers with custom CUDA kernels should set REDWOOD_ATTN_KERNEL=legacy to disable new paths. Related: SUP-4412 (support ticket with a customer workload that motivated isolated KV churn investigation).

LLaMA-2-7B seq2048: p95 1.2s -> 0.79s (34% reduction), throughput 2.1x in high-KV-reuse profile
Memory working set: -18% on A100-80GB for long sequences

End-to-end cost estimate: ~22% token-cost reduction for chat-like workloads when running on dedicated capacity

Risk: perf regressions under rare batch shapes; Mitigation: perf-gating CI and initial 5% canary rollout with monitoring and automatic rollback policy
Performance: upgraded attention kernels with fused-qkv and fused-rotary paths, new FlashAttention memory-optimized variant, and scheduler heuristics to improve KV cache locality and continuous batching. Expected to reduce latency and token cost for conversational workloads. Config: REDWOOD_ATTN_KERNEL to toggle operator path.

Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions. Related items: Linear ENG-2728 (multipart uploader stability), PM-146 (OpenAI compat feature parity).
Liam Chen: key question — do we need to special-case application/pdf? many partners send PDFs as application/pdf; current whitelist would block it. Suggest adding application/pdf or making whitelist configurable per-tenant.
Aisha Patel: replied — agreed, added application/pdf to tenant_whitelist in config and made default conservative. Added test case + note in docs explaining why binary blobs should be limited.
Ravi Singh: please ensure the validator surfaces clear errors for multipart boundary parsing failures; I saw a flaky crash in an initial run.
Aisha Patel: replied — parser now catches malformed boundary exceptions and returns a 400 with error.type=malformed_multipart and includes low-signal debug id for tracing; updated tests.
Sofia Alvarez: approved — addressed my comments about metrics naming and added a suggestion to include counter tags for tenant_id and route_id.
CI Bot: integration-tests failed on first run due to test harness timeout; rerun completed successfully.
QA: noted an edge case where client SDK retries might double-submit large files; added a recommendation in docs and an optional idempotency header support in adapter.
Added multipart/form-data support on OpenAI-compat API paths with strict content-type validation and configurable per-file and per-request size limits. Default limits: 10MiB per file, 50MiB per request. Feature is behind a feature flag and can be enabled per-tenant. See docs/openai-compat/multipart.md for migration steps.

Motivation: long-tail inference workloads (mixed sequence lengths and multi-tenant bursts) expose inefficiencies in a single-kernel dispatch strategy and occasionally trigger noisy KV cache pressure. This PR implements an adaptive kernel selector that chooses between two optimized attention kernels at runtime (small-seq fastpath + wide-seq streaming fastpath), introduces a small fused rotary-reshape CUDA kernel to remove redundant transposes when rotary embeddings are used, and adds a lightweight KV reservation mechanism to reduce eviction churn under bursty continuous-batching.

What this PR does (high level):
- Runtime kernel selector: heuristics based on sequence length, batch shape distribution, and available SM occupancy to pick best kernel per request group. Selector lives in serving/runtime/attn/kernel_selector.cpp and exposes a stable decision API so other schedulers can consult it.
- Fused rotary-reshape: new CUDA kernel fused_rotary_reshape.cu removes an intermediate permute and reduces memory traffic for rotary-enabled models (~1.6x reduction in transient mem ops on long sequences). Hooked into the kernel code path when rotary flags are detected.
- KV reservation: add kv_reservation.h/.cpp that lets the continuous batcher reserve a bounded KV budget for in-flight canary/cold requests so we avoid evicting hot prefixes during transient spikes. Implemented conservative default: 8% reservation per model instance, configurable in runtime config.
- Batching/backpressure tweaks: continuous_batcher now exposes a backpressure token check and will fall back to the small-seq kernel earlier to meet p95 latency SLOs for short requests.

Checklist: 
- [x] Kernel selector implementation + unit tests
- [x] CUDA fused rotary-reshape implementation + correctness tests
- [x] KV reservation mechanism + e2e smoke test
- [x] Bench harness changes and new benchmarks
- [x] Docs: perf rationale and flags in docs/perf/attn_kernels.md

Performance summary (bench running on p4d-like staging infra, mixed workload):
- End-to-end token throughput +13-17% on 2048-8192 seq mix for a 16-GPU pool when selector chooses wide-seq kernel.
- Memory transient traffic reduced ~1.6x for rotary models when fused kernel engaged.
- p95 latency for short seq requests unchanged (<2% regressions in noise runs).
- KV eviction events under bursty load reduced ~45% in microbench.

Compatibility and rollout: changes are backward-compatible. Selector defaults to conservative thresholds and can be disabled with runtime flag REDWOOD_ATTN_KERNEL_SELECTOR=off. Fused rotary kernel used only when model metadata reports rotary format. KV reservation is conservative and tunable. Rollout plan: gradual canary (10% traffic) for 48h then 50% -> 100% after monitoring.

Related: ENG-4412 (kernel selection), ENG-4475 (kv-cache hardening), small followups to SDKs will land separately to expose config flags.

Merge notes: squash merge after final perf sign-off.

Priya Shah: Please add a flag to force the legacy single-kernel behavior for emergency rollbacks. Also add a short comment about the decision boundary rationale.
Evan Grant: Added REDWOOD_ATTN_KERNEL_SELECTOR flag and expanded doc comments in kernel_selector.h explaining heuristics. Commented on the empirical boundary and included caveats.
Daniel Kim: Fused rotary kernel looks good. Need to ensure alignment assumptions are documented; add a CI test for 16-bit edge-case where padding != 0.
Evan Grant: Added alignment checks and a unit test for 16-bit padding scenarios. Confirmed with CUDA team that warp-aligned loads are safe here.
Miguel Alvarez: KV reservation defaults look conservative. Suggest exposing a per-model override in model config for enterprise tenants. Also ask to include counters for reservation hits/misses in observability.
Evan Grant: Exposed model-level reservation param and added two counters (kv_reserve_hits, kv_reserve_evictions) to runtime metrics. Documented in attn_kernels.md.
Priya Shah: Verified perf numbers on staging. Approving pending green CI.
Daniel Kim: Approved. Left a small nit on doc wording.
CI Bot: All checks passed. Safe to merge when approvers are present.
Release Manager: Please schedule a canary rollout and watch kv_reserve_evictions metric for 24h post-deploy.
Adaptive attention kernel selection and fused rotary reshape reduce transient memory traffic and improve throughput for long-sequence rotary models. KV reservation reduces eviction churn during bursts. Enablement is opt-out via REDWOOD_ATTN_KERNEL_SELECTOR flag.

Summary: Introduces a configurable tool result merge policy and a per-invocation exponential backoff/retry budget aimed at improving ergonomics and determinism for parallel/multi-tool calls. Motivation: the previous default (inject-first-returned) caused nondeterministic structured-output injection when multiple tools returned overlapping JSON fragments or produced idempotent but out-of-order updates. This led to subtle regressions in downstream parsers and customer incidents (SUP-9021). Design: add three merge strategies: first_wins (legacy), last_wins, and merge_patch (depth-aware JSON/struct merge that preserves keyed identities and deduplicates array items when an id key is present). Merge order is deterministic by explicit priority then monotonic timestamp. Implement a per-call RetryPolicy that exposes base_delay_ms, factor, max_attempts, max_delay_ms, jitter_pct and an overall retry_budget_ms to avoid retry storms that starve streaming tokens. The runtime applies exponential backoff with jitter and a budget check before scheduling retries; when budget is exhausted we surface a partial-injection event and optionally trigger a fallback model or canned response based on caller policy. API surface: ToolInvocationOptions gains result_merge_policy and retry_policy fields. OpenAI compatibility: map legacy tool_call behavior to result_merge_policy=first_wins by default and emit a single deprecation notice per workspace when user libraries request explicit tool_call hints. SDKs: TS/Python/Go helpers to opt-in and a migration linter rule that flags ambiguous tool call patterns. Rollout: default behavior remains first_wins to preserve backwards compatibility; merge_patch is enabled behind a gate and will be rolled out to 10% traffic for initial experiments. Observability: new metrics added tool_result_merge.policy{policy} count, tool_result_merge.conflicts, tool_result_merge.resolved_by and retry metrics retries_per_invocation and retry_budget_exhausted. Dashboards updated under "Tooling / Result Merge" to show conflicts over time and the fraction of calls that used merge_patch. Testing: unit tests for conflict resolution, array deduping, id-key heuristics and integration tests that simulate 3 parallel tool calls with conflicting ids and transient failures. Performance: microbenchmarks show a median 7-12% extra CPU latency on 3-way merges with merge_patch but end-user parser error rate drops by 18-42% depending on workload. Backwards compatibility: no breaking change by default; customers can opt into alternate policies per-route or globally. Docs: added migration guide and examples showing how to express merge policies for common tooling patterns. CI/QA: initial CI run failed lint and a flaky time-sensitive test; fixed by mocking monotonic clock and adding unit test coverage for jitter. Merge and deployment: feature-flagged implementation, gradual ramp to 100% after 2-week smoke window, emergency kill switch in Console. Related work: ties to ENG-2431 and earlier speculative affinity work; addresses SUP-9021 incident. See commits for implementation details and changed files for exact locations of changes.
Eleni Strauss: This looks very helpful. Two asks before approving: 1) can we avoid copying large JSON blobs when doing merge_patch? 2) add metric for bytes_copied_by_merge. Priya Kulkarni: switched to in-place shallow diffs where possible; added bytes_copied_by_merge metric and tests for large payloads.
Marcus Li: The merge_patch name is slightly ambiguous. Can we document the semantics explicitly and add a deterministic tie-breaker for identical priorities? Also please ensure this does not change KV cache keys' semantics. Priya Kulkarni: added explicit priority then timestamp tie-breaker and updated KV cache key tests to assert no change in behavior.
Jonah Rivera: Request to add a visible retry_budget_exhausted alert and an emergency kill-switch in Console. Also asked for an example showing how to opt-out per-route. Priya Kulkarni: added alert to SLO dashboard and a Console toggle; included route-level opt-out example in migration doc.
Add configurable tool result merge policies and per-invocation exponential backoff for parallel tool calls. Default behavior unchanged; opt-in merge_patch provides deterministic depth-aware JSON merging and deduplication by id keys. New metrics and dashboard panels for policy usage and conflict resolution. SDKs include helpers and a linter to assist migration.
This PR is intentionally conservative: default is legacy behavior to avoid breaking users. The implementation is feature-flagged and rollout is gradual. We measured correctness improvements in end-to-end parser tests which motivated prioritizing this change over low-latency micro-optimizations. The team will follow up with a smaller perf-optimization PR that trades some CPU for lower median latency when merge_patch is used.

Motivation: Dedicated fleets need predictable committed throughput but also the ability to absorb short bursts without manual capacity changes. Current autoscaler reacts too quickly to transient load spikes which either overprovisions or throttles latency-sensitive requests. This PR introduces three coordinated changes: (1) a fleet-level burst token pool that allows short lived over-commit up to a configurable budget, (2) smoothing for the autoscaler using an adaptive EWMA to reduce oscillations, and (3) extended utilization reporting and Prometheus metrics so SRE and customers can observe token consumption and true GPU utilization.  Design summary: - Burst token pool: each fleet now maintains a token pool measured in 'tokens' where 1 token ~= 1 request-second at fleet target concurrency. Tokens are refilled at the committed rate and can be consumed when instantaneous load exceeds committed capacity. There are global and per-tenant caps and an eviction policy to avoid token hoarding. Config knobs include --burst-pool-size, --burst-refill-rate, and --burst-per-customer-limit. - Autoscaler smoothing: replace the previous simple moving average with an adaptive EWMA that weights recent samples by variance; this avoids jumping the target replica count when a short spike occurs. New flag: --autoscaler-smoothing-window-ms and --autoscaler-variance-threshold. - Utilization reporting: new Prometheus metrics: redwood_fleet_utilization, redwood_fleet_burst_tokens_total, redwood_fleet_burst_tokens_consumed, redwood_burst_token_evictions, and per-gpu redwood_gpu_active_pct. Metrics include labels for fleet_id, region, and model_family.  Implementation notes: - services/fleet-manager/burst_pool.go: core token pool, refill loop, and eviction. - services/fleet-manager/autoscaler.go: EWMA estimator and integration with scale decision path. - pkg/metrics/registry.go and integrations/prometheus: register new metrics and add dashboards. - cmd/agent: add agent-side accounting to enforce per-customer burst-per-worker limits and to forward token consumption events. - infra/helm: expose new environment variables and defaults for Dedicated customers. - docs/dedicated/autoscaling.md: operational guide, migration steps, knob descriptions, and recommended SLOs.  Migration and rollout: Default behavior preserves existing capacity semantics (burst pool disabled by default for existing fleets). New dedicated customers created after this deploy have a small default burst pool enabled (configurable by account). Rollout plan: canary at 5% fleets for two days, then 50% for one week, then full rollout. Customers can opt-in early via fleet annotation. Operators must run scripts/migrate_burst_tokens.sh to seed historical usage if they want non-empty pools for existing fleets.  Backwards compatibility and safety: - If burst pool is disabled, autoscaler behaves exactly as before. - Token consumption cannot reduce committed throughput; only extends short bursts. - Eviction prevents low-priority or idle tenants from starving active ones — policy documented in docs.  Testing: - unit tests for token accounting and EWMA estimator. - integration e2e test tests/e2e/fleet_burst_test.go simulates step load and validates no oscillation and controlled token use. - load test in benchmark-lab showed 8-12% reduction in 95th percentile latency under bursty workloads with <3% steady-state cost increase.  Observability and alerts: added recommended Grafana panels and Prometheus alert rules (alerts if burst_tokens_consumed > 80% for >10m). Also added runbook entries.  Related work and references: ENG-3127 (autoscaler stability epic), SRE-88 (incident follow-up for over-scaling).
Daniel Kim: Can you clarify the semantics of token refill when a fleet is scaled down? Is the pool preserved or zeroed? (asked 2026-02-06)
Asha Menon: Answer: pool is preserved up to a tombstone window; documented and added test to cover pool retention across scale-to-zero. (2026-02-07)
Priya Sharma: How do we ensure multi-tenant fairness when one tenant floods with requests? Need clearer eviction policy. (2026-02-08)
Asha Menon: Added per-customer limits and eviction policy doc with deterministic LRU+priority buckets; also added unit test for eviction. (2026-02-10)
Ethan Brooks: Nit: move default flags to infra/helm values and ensure secrets/operators can override. Also CI flake on e2e/fleet_burst_test.go — looks timing sensitive. (2026-02-12)
Asha Menon: Moved flags and hardened test timing by using deterministic clock in tests; CI rerun passed. (2026-02-13)
Priya Sharma: Approve after docs update and runbook included. (2026-02-15)
Daniel Kim: Approved and squashed merge on green. (2026-02-16)
Introduce fleet burst token pool (off by default), autoscaler smoothing (configurable), and new utilization metrics. Operators can opt-in and follow docs/dedicated/autoscaling.md for migration. Customers see improved tail latency under bursty traffic with minimal steady-state cost impact.

payload.body:
Motivation: For the quantized inference stack we've been shipping two main bottlenecks: (1) the dequantization+matmul fusion path for INT8 kernels introduces extra memory traffic and kernel launches at each attention and FFN block; (2) SmoothQuant scaling interacts poorly with our scheduler and continuous-batching heuristics, causing variable p99 regressions under mixed-sequence workloads. This PR introduces three coordinated changes: 1) a fused dequantize+gemm kernel that accepts packed INT8 weights and produces FP16 accumulation with optional requantization hooks; 2) a scheduling tweak that biases smoothquant scaling application to the slower stage of the pipeline and batches compatible sequence shapes together more aggressively; 3) a lightweight KV-cache-aware fast path that skips per-step dequant for cached KV blocks and reuses FP16 cached keys when the model quantization profile allows it.
High-level summary of changes: - Implement fused_int8_dequant_gemm CUDA kernel with vectorized loads, int8->fp16 accumulation, and single-kernel scale+bias application; exposed via runtime/kernel_registry. - Add quant_profile metadata to model descriptors to select the optimal kernel variant at load time (INT8_PACKED, FP8_DYNAMIC, FP16_FALLBACK). - Scheduler: introduce SequenceShapeAffinity rule to group similar-length requests for continuous batching; add SmoothQuantWindow heuristic to only apply per-layer scaling on first N tokens of a request when streaming is enabled. - KV cache: store an optional FP16 shadow of int8-packed KV blocks for reuse; add LRU soft cap and transparent eviction. - Telemetry: new perf counters (kernel_time_fused_int8, kv_shadow_hit, smoothquant_applied) and unit tests.
Performance numbers (microbench on T4 and A10G; averaged across 50k requests of mixed lengths 16/128/512): - Baseline (old INT8 path): p50 12.8ms p95 38.2ms p99 78.5ms throughput 22 toks/s - This PR (fused + scheduling + kv-shadow): p50 11.4ms p95 29.6ms p99 49.3ms throughput 28 toks/s - Relative: p99 reduced ~37%, throughput +27%, token GPU time reduced ~18%.
Safety and compatibility: default model load remains unchanged; INT8 packed models must declare quant_profile or fallback to old path. This avoids accidental perf regressions for older deployments.
Checklist: - [x] Kernel implementation + unit tests - [x] Scheduler heuristics and e2e perf harness - [x] KV-shadow LRU + eviction tests - [x] Telemetry and console dashboard metric wiring - [x] Backwards-compatible model descriptor changes - [x] Integration smoke runs on Dedicated cluster
Implementation notes: commits include a sequence of focused patches (see commits field). The fused kernel uses 128-bit vector loads and tail-handling similar to other fused kernels in kernels/cuda/; we add a small inline assembly path for faster requant when supported by arch. The scheduler change is additive: SequenceShapeAffinity is a soft hint; it will not prevent immediate dispatch when latency SLO is tight. KV-shadow stores fp16 only when the quant_profile allows dequant-lossless shadowing.
Files changed (high-level): - runtime/kernel_registry.py: register fused_int8_dequant_gemm - kernels/cuda/fused_int8_dequant_gemm.cu: new kernel implementation and tests - runtime/scheduler/affinity.py: SequenceShapeAffinity and SmoothQuantWindow heuristics - runtime/kv_cache/kv_shadow.py: FP16 shadow store, eviction policy - model/quant_profiles.py: quant_profile schema and loaders - telemetry/metrics.py: new counters and tagging - tests/perf/test_quant_kernels.py: microbench harness and assertions - docs/quantization.md: updated guidance and model packaging notes
Commits (summary): - a1c3f8a: initial fused kernel prototype and unit tests - b4d2e10: vectorization, tail handling, and arch-specific paths - c7f9b01: expose kernel via kernel_registry and add quant_profile selector - d2a8f44: implement SequenceShapeAffinity scheduler rule and tests - e5b1c3f: KV-shadow store with LRU and eviction unit tests - f1039d7: telemetry counters and console dashboard wires - f8b6a22: perf tuning, CI fixes, and documentation
Update/Review conversation (selected): - Priya Natarajan (reviewer): "Great direction. My main concern is memory overhead for the FP16 KV shadow under high-concurrency. Can we bound memory and prioritize eviction for older sequences?" Author reply (Ethan): "Answered: KV-shadow uses an LRU soft cap with eviction triggered at 0.6*mem_limit and immediate reclamation to 0.8*mem_limit to avoid thrashing; added bench in tests to ensure p99 doesn't regress under pressure." - Liam O'Connor: "Kernel looks good; please add more comments around the arch-specific asm path and a fallback when not supported." Author: "Added comments and a runtime is_x86_avx512 check; fallback to scalar path included." - Sara Kim: "How does this interact with canary rollout? We need a safe toggle in runtime to opt-out quickly." Author: "Added runtime feature flag runtime.flags.quant_fused_enabled and a per-deployment override exposed to Dedicated/Private configs; tests added."
CI checks summary: - linux-build: pass - unit-tests: pass - perf-regression: pass (bench run) - flake8/lint: pass - integration-smoke(dedicated): pass
Merge outcome: merged via squash on 2026-03-05 by Ethan Zhao; merge commit f9c2d11. Post-merge actions: - Backfill quant_profile to community model registry (docs/quantization.md has migration steps) - Dashboard alert to watch kernel_time_fused_int8 p99 for next 72 hours - Coordinate with Customer Success for a small set of Dedicated customers to enable feature flag during next maintenance window.
Performance: Improved INT8/FP8 dequant fusion paths and scheduling; lower p99 latency on common seq-len workloads; no API changes.

Why: We need a single decision plane that can reliably coordinate rollback actions across canary, A/B, and shadow lanes while preserving observability and auditability. Existing scripts and heuristics were duplicated across promotors, leading to inconsistent rollback timing and missing correlated telemetry. What: Adds a lightweight "Rollback Broker" service and a Promoter shim that performs a handshake with rollout lanes to decide deterministic rollback, backoff, or staged drain. The Broker exposes an opinionated policy adapter that can evaluate: - multi-metric gates (latency/err/quality) - cohort-level cooldowns and credits - synthetic smoke / canary dry-run scoring - audit ledger for replayable decisions How: - New controller: rollout/rollback_broker_controller.go implementing the broker state machine - Promoter shim: promoter/handshake_shim.go to unify canary, AB, and shadow promoters behind a single API - Policy DSL: policy/rollback_policy_v1.yaml and runtime adapter - Ledger: telemetry/rollback_ledger (append-only protobuf records) - E2E harness: tests/e2e/rollback_broker_smoke_test.go - Telemetry: metrics, traces, and events (console integration) Compatibility: The broker is opt-in via cluster rollout config; default remains original promoters. Rollback behavior can be toggled per-rollout and per-cohort. Checklist: - [x] Controller and promoter shim implemented - [x] Policy adapter + default policy shipped - [x] Ledger + protobuf schema added - [x] Unit tests for policy evaluation - [x] E2E smoke for canary + shadow handshake - [x] Console eventing + dashboard links - [x] Documentation and runbook draft - [x] Feature flag gating in operator config Notes: - Policy is intentionally conservative by default (prefer staged drain over immediate abort) - Ledger events are stored in telemetry bucket and can be replayed for incident analysis - This PR includes migration code to annotate in-flight rollouts so operator can pick correct decision path Related: ENG-2148 (unify promoter interfaces), SUP-4312 (customer incident: inconsistent canary rollback), ENG-2179 (telemetry ledger design)
Arjun Patel: Nit - please split the large policy YAML into smaller docs/examples; also add a short example in the operator config. (resolved)
Lina Ortega: Concern - ledger could grow quickly; can we add TTL/archive policy and clarify retention in docs? (author replied: ledger is append-only; retention/plumb to telemetry lifecycle added in docs and operator flags)
Daniel Ruiz: Suggestion - when broker declines immediate abort, emit an 'escalation' event so SREs get a paging hint; added console event integration. (accepted)
CI Bot: e2e-rollback failed on first run due to test flake (timeout). Reran and passed.

Motivation: production workloads show wide variance in sequence lengths and per-request priorities; static ring scheduling leaves high-priority short requests waiting behind long-running shards, and KV-cache prefetches for upcoming tokens are not coordinated with cross-GPU NIC timelines. This PR introduces an adaptive ring scheduler that dynamically reorders tensor-parallel collectives to maximize overlap of communication and compute across heterogeneous micro-batches and integrates a priority-aware KV prefetch queue to reduce tail latency. Summary of changes: 1) scheduler/adaptive_ring_scheduler: new C++ core that monitors per-peer bandwidth/latency, outstanding micro-batch sizes, and request priority tags and emits an ordered sequence of collective operations that maximizes comm/compute overlap; 2) comm/nccl_tuning: add prioritized stream allocation and backlog-aware concurrency limits exposed as runtime knobs; 3) kv/prefetcher: implement priority prefetch queue with soft-deadline semantics and early-retry on slower peers; 4) kernels/allreduce_fused.cu: introduce an optional fused allreduce+scale kernel used when the scheduler selects aggregation-first ordering to reduce PCIe hops; 5) batching/hetero_packing: smarter micro-batch packing to reduce padding when pairing long and short sequences; 6) tracing/metrics: new metrics for prefetch hit rate, scheduler reorder rate, and per-request overlap efficiency; 7) tests/perf: new benchmark harness that reproduces mixed-length, mixed-priority workloads. Backwards compatibility: defaults maintain previous ordering unless admin enables adaptive scheduler in runtime config (runtime.config.enable_adaptive_scheduler=true). Checklist: - [x] design doc and perf plan (docs/design/adaptive_ring.md) - [x] unit tests for scheduler decision logic - [x] integration tests against NCCL multi-node CI - [x] benchmarks measuring 99th percentile latency improvements - [x] feature flag gating for gradual rollout Performance results: on our internal 8xA100 cluster with mixed-length synthetic traffic (50% short 64 tokens, 50% long 2048 tokens) and a 30% high-priority request subset, we measured: - 95th p99 latency reduced from 48ms to 30ms for high-priority requests (37% improvement) - aggregate token throughput improved 12% due to reduced wasted padding and better overlap - KV prefetch hit rate improved from 67% to 89% for prioritized requests Risk and mitigations: scheduler makes heuristic decisions that could cause starvation of low-priority work under extreme load; mitigated by a tunable fairness window and a cap on priority reorders (runtime knobs added). The fused kernel is optional and guarded by a runtime capability check. Deployment plan: behind feature flag and gated per-customer; rollout to dedicated clusters with canary traffic, monitor prefetch hit rate and p99 latency, and enable auto-fallback to legacy ring ordering on regression. Related: ENG-4897 (scheduler roadmap), ENG-4912 (KV cache improvements), SUP-2101 (customer incident that triggered this work).
Evan Park: Nice design. Question: how do you prevent priority inversion when many high-priority short requests stream in?
Priya Sharma: We cap reorders per fairness window; default window is 100ms and cap=4 reorders per window. Added config knobs and unit tests for starvation scenarios.
Lina Gomez: Can the fused kernel be toggled at runtime? What about driver compatibility?
Priya Sharma: Yes behind runtime capability check and a flag runtime.kernels.enable_fused_allreduce; the build includes a fallback; added a CI matrix job for driver combinations.
Marcus Chen: CI showed flakiness on one NCCL test in the first run; reran and added a retry/backoff in the test harness. Verified stability in subsequent runs.
Add adaptive ring scheduler with prioritized KV prefetching and optional fused allreduce kernel. Improves p99 latency for prioritized short requests in mixed workloads and increases overall throughput by reducing padding and improving comm/compute overlap. Feature is disabled by default and gated by runtime config.
payload.title: Adaptive ring scheduler for heterogeneous batching with priority KV prefetch

payload.body:
Motivation: improve robustness of browser streaming when using project/org credentials and cookies while standardizing header semantics for scoped ephemeral tokens and request signing. Previously we had multiple ad-hoc behaviors across the compatibility layer that caused intermittent streaming disconnects, CORS header leaks, and ambiguity between Authorization and project-scoped keys. This PR introduces a signed session nonce header, clarifies header precedence, updates the OpenAI-compat mapping for legacy Authorization patterns, and hardens CORS handling for streaming endpoints.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a new header X-RW-Session-Signature (signed nonce) produced by the control plane during session start and validated by streaming workers to prevent mid-stream credential swaps and replay in browsers. Signature uses the existing request-signing key family; implementation reuses canonicalization code but adds streaming pseudo-headers to the signature payload.
- Introduces a clear precedence rule: if X-Project-Key or X-Org-Key is present it wins over Authorization bearer tokens for project-scoped access; scoped ephemeral tokens (claim: "scoped_session") still take precedence when TTL is present. The new precedence table is documented in the header semantics section.
- OpenAI compatibility: we now accept Authorization: Bearer <project_id>:<key> and map it to internal X-Project-Key so legacy clients work without changing their auth flow. This mapping is recorded in audit logs with a masked key.
- Cookie+Streaming fixes: for browser streaming with cookies we now emit Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-RW-Session-Signature,X-RW-Session-Nonce and set SameSite=None on the signed cookie for cross-site clients. The TS SDK streaming helper was updated to set fetch mode 'cors' and credentials 'include' in the example to demonstrate correct behavior.
- Request-signing normalization: lower-case header names for canonical form and include the :method and :path pseudo-headers for signature stability across proxies. This reduces false-negative signature rejections seen when requests transit edge proxies that reorder header casing.
- Telemetry and metrics: new metric rw.streaming.auth.signature_validation{result=ok|fail} and an alert that fires if signature_fail rate > 0.5% for >10m on any region.
- Tests and CI: adds unit tests for nonce validation, E2E that exercises cookie+streaming in a headless browser environment (flaky test isolated and retried in CI), and OpenAI-compat header mapping tests.

Files changed (high level): control-plane/session/controller.go, runtime/streaming/conn_auth.go, runtime/streaming/nonce_validation.go, api/middleware/auth_headers.go, sdk/ts/streaming-client.ts (example), docs/specs/auth-header-semantics.md, docs/compat/openai-auth.md, infra/monitoring/alerts.yaml, tests/e2e/streaming-cookie.spec.ts, tests/unit/signing_normalization_test.go, pkg/audit/audit_logger.go, pkg/http/cors.go

Compatibility notes: The new X-RW-Session-Signature header is additive and will not break existing clients that do not use browser cookie streaming. The Authorization -> X-Project-Key mapping preserves backward compatibility for legacy clients; however operators should rotate keys that use the legacy Authorization format and migrate to explicit X-Project-Key or scoped ephemeral tokens for improved isolation.

Rollout plan: feature gate the signed-nonce validation on runtime nodes for the first week in the canary region (us-west-2) with a soft-fail mode (log & metric but allow) and then flip to hard-fail after metrics look clean. The PR includes the soft-fail toggle and a migration guide in docs/specs/auth-header-semantics.md.

Testing notes: Local unit tests + mocked streaming worker validation; CI initially hit a flaky headless-browser streaming test (see CI section below) which was isolated by increasing the socket timeout in the test harness and adding an explicit wait for the initial signature to arrive. After the fix CI passed on rerun.

Followups:
- ENG-4631: add a short-lived rotation endpoint for session signing keys and wire into the control plane UI.
- PM-1102: update SDK quickstarts to prefer scoped ephemeral tokens for browser examples.

Review conversation summary: See review_threads array for full comments. In short: reviewer asked for additional SameSite/secure cookie tests and audit log masking; I added tests and ensured keys are masked in logs. Reviewer requested to move the signature canonicalization helper out of runtime/streaming into pkg/signing for reuse; refactor done. Final approval granted after E2E flakiness fix and a quick perf check which showed <1% extra CPU on the streaming path.
Ethan Blake (2026-02-11): Please add SameSite and Secure cookie tests for the new session cookie; browsers differ in default behavior. Action: added tests and updated cookie helper.
Marta Ruiz (2026-02-13): Can we keep legacy Authorization mapping behind an opt-in flag? Concerned about audit noise. Response: mapping is enabled by default but we mask keys in audit logs and emit metrics; we added a config toggle for enterprises that want to opt out.
Zhiwei Chen (2026-02-16): Move canonicalization helper out of runtime package to pkg/signing to avoid duplication. Action: refactor done; updated imports.
Ethan Blake (2026-02-18): E2E flaky failure observed in CI; request increasing test harness timeout. Action: increased socket timeout and added explicit wait for initial signature; CI rerun passed.
Marta Ruiz (2026-02-19): Approve after fixes + doc updates.
Stabilize browser streaming authentication: adds X-RW-Session-Signature for signed nonces, clarifies header precedence (X-Project-Key > Authorization unless scoped token present), OpenAI-compat mapping for legacy Authorization tokens, CORS exposure for session headers, and improvements to canonicalization for request signing. Includes soft-fail rollout toggle and metrics/alerts for signature validation.

Adds a lightweight cross-layer profiling pipeline: a CUPTI-based GPU kernel timing module that records per-kernel start/end timestamps with correlation IDs, an eBPF user-space probe set that samples host-side scheduling and queue-depth at request boundaries, a small CLI microbench (rtbench) to run deterministic microbench sweeps and emit heatmaps, and a Prometheus collector + Grafana dashboard JSON to visualize kernel latency heatmaps and host/GPU correlation metrics. Motivation: existing coarse-span timing hides per-kernel variability that drives our scheduler and batching heuristics; this PR enables precise, low-overhead signals for model-specific kernel cost models and SLA debugging. The description below is a single continuous string and includes motivations, compatibility notes, and rollout guidance. Compatibility: CUPTI build is optional and gated by a runtime flag; eBPF probes require Linux 5.x kernels and CAP_SYS_ADMIN during install for the collector service. Rollout plan: gated behind an opt-in telemetry feature flag for 2 weeks, then enabled in staging, then can be flipped for Dedicated customers. Related work: follows up on ENG-7621 (batching heuristics) and pairs with the microbench harness added in ENG-8124. Caveats: CUPTI introduces a small (0.2-1%) overhead on very small sequences in some microbench cases; tests and thresholds are in the telemetry README.
Ben Harper: Please add unit coverage for the label normalization logic in kernel_collector.go. Also, can the correlation id use a stable 64-bit hash?
Alyssa Cortez: Added unit tests in kernel_collector_test.go and switched to xxhash64 for the correlation id in the second commit
Mina Patel: eBPF scripts look good but add a failure-safe path when CAP_SYS_ADMIN is missing; we can't make install fatal for non-admin nodes
Alyssa Cortez: eBPF install now logs a warning and gracefully disables probes when capabilities are missing; added docs in ops runbook
Luis Ortega: Small nit: rename rtbench output --format=json to --output-format json (consistency with other tools)
Alyssa Cortez: renaming done in final commits
