Background: Different SDKs implemented retry/backoff semantics and stream restart heuristics inconsistently, which caused customer-facing flakiness for long-lived streaming sessions and opaque retry behavior under auth window expiry. This PR introduces a cross-language "retry-timeline" contract plus a small, ergonomic stream adaptor that standardizes reconnect/backoff and unblocks the last mile of parity for Py/TS/Go.

What changed (summary): 1) Introduced a common retry-timeline configuration (max_total_duration, initial_backoff_ms, max_backoff_ms, backoff_multiplier, jitter_window_ms) surfaced in each SDK with sane defaults and explicit override. 2) Added a lightweight stream adaptor (StreamResumeAdapter) that centralizes heartbeat handling, credential-refresh hooks, and resume-vs-restart policy decisions. 3) Plumbed telemetry hooks: retry_reason, attempt_index, total_backoff_ms to existing SDK telemetry so platform teams can tie regressions to config changes. 4) Minor API ergonomic additions: Python async iterator helper (.aiter_with_retries()), TypeScript AsyncGenerator wrapper (.withRetryTimeline()), Go StreamHandle.Resume(ctx) convenience. 5) Version bumps for each SDK and unit/integration test matrices updated.

Commits (high level): - decouple: add retry-timeline interface and default implementation across sdk packages - feat(py): aiter_with_retries helper + tests - feat(ts): withRetryTimeline wrapper + examples - feat(go): StreamResumeAdapter + Resume helper - chore: telemetry tags and metrics mapping - test: long-run streaming integration tests (loopback harness) - ci: matrix updates and cross-sdk lint fixes

Files touched (high level): - sdk/common/retry_timeline.proto (contract + docs) - sdk/python/redwood/retry_timeline.py - sdk/python/redwood/stream_adaptor.py - sdk/typescript/src/stream/withRetryTimeline.ts - sdk/go/stream/resume_adapter.go - sdk/*/tests/integration/long_stream_reconnect_test.* - docs/sdk/retry-timeline.md - examples/multi-sdk/stream-reconnect/*

Small illustrative snippet (TypeScript wrapper):
const wrapped = client.stream.open(...).withRetryTimeline({ max_total_duration: 120000, initial_backoff_ms: 100, backoff_multiplier: 2.0 });

Testing and CI: Ran unit tests across all three SDKs and an end-to-end looping harness that simulates auth expiry mid-stream. CI initially failed on TS linter (import ordering) and Go vet on a nil-check; both fixes were added in follow-up commits and CI passed on the final squash. Matrix includes node 16/18, python 3.9/3.10, go 1.20/1.21.

Review highlights / conversation: - Diego Ramirez (reviewer): "Strong +1 for centralizing the timeline — please ensure default values are conservative for high-latency regions." Author: "Defaults chosen after running the loopback against us-west and eu-west latency profiles; documented in retry-timeline.md." - Sofia Chen: "TS ergonomics look good, but add an example with function-calling/resumable tool streams." Author: "Added examples/multi-sdk/stream-reconnect/ts-function-calling.md and accompanying test harness." - Arjun Mehta: "Go Resume helper is convenient but may hide context cancellation semantics; add doc note." Author: "Added doc note and small API comment recommending explicit ctx wiring for callers who expect immediate cancellation." - Diego: "Telemetry tags should be present on all retry exits (success/failed); otherwise we won't be able to attribute regressions." Author: "Added retry_reason and total_backoff_ms tags to post-mortem telemetry path." Review status: approvals from Diego & Sofia; Arjun requested one doc tweak which was addressed.

Backward compatibility and rollout plan: No breaking changes to public surface—new helpers are additive and defaults preserve prior behavior (max_total_duration default is very large). For conservative rollout we gated the TypeScript wrapper behind a feature flag in the hosted SDK registry for two weeks while collecting telemetry. We rolled SDK versions: python 3.8.10, typescript 1.6.2, go v1.5.1. Customers on Dedicated can opt-in to the stricter timeline via console toggle; Private installs receive documentation to manually enable the adaptor.

Why this is unique: Rather than adding language-specific heuristics we define an explicit timeline contract that SDKs implement uniformly; the stream adaptor is intentionally small (thin policy layer) to minimize surface area and improve debuggability.

Follow-ups and TODOs: - ENG-4275: Add example configurations tuned for mobile vs server workloads (tracked). - ENG-4382: Produce benchmark doc showing cost/latency tradeoffs of different timeline settings. - Roll forward the feature flag after 2-week telemetry validation and publish migration notes.

Merge: Squash merged to main after approvals and successful CI.

CI summary: All checks passed on green build (unit + integration + cross-sdk lint).

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps credential plumbing abstract (delegate to SDK credential providers) to remain compatible with existing delegated auth flows. If downstream teams need a deeper integration (e.g., credential prefetch for long streams) we'll follow up with an opt-in extension rather than changing defaults.
Small breaking-surface avoided; SDKs receive ergonomic retry-timeline config and a lightweight stream adaptor for parity. Patch releases: py 3.8.9 -> 3.8.10, ts 1.6.1 -> 1.6.2, go v1.5.0 -> v1.5.1.

payload.body:
Context: long-tail token cost and multi-stage latency spikes frequently surface only when a request traverses several model-serving stages (tokenization, encoder, decode, fallback). Existing alerts were per-route and per-quantile but lacked a compact way to group requests by 'stage footprint' and automatically route alerting weight to the stage(s) most likely responsible. Motivation: reduce alert noise and accelerate RCA by grouping invocations into stage-aware cohorts and deriving a route x stage alert matrix that attributes SLO violations to the most likely pipeline stage. What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight token_stage_cohort service that computes a deterministic cohort key per invocation based on stage-level metrics (token counts per stage, kv-cache hit pattern, decode-batch size) and stores short-lived cohort aggregates. 2) Introduces an alert route-matrix generator that consumes cohort rollups and emits alert bindings which bias escalation to the top-k stages for that route. 3) Adds a new dashboard focused on cohort drift, stage heatmaps, and per-cohort cost/latency breakdown to help oncall quickly validate root cause hypotheses. 4) Wires the generator into the existing alerting pipeline with a safe canary rollout and automatic quiet-window attenuation to avoid regressing noise. Compatibility and rollout: service defaults to read-only mode until flagged by a feature flag; alert generation starts cross-account in a low-sensitivity mode (only P90/P99) and is then ramped after 72h of monitoring. Testing: unit and integration tests added; ran a 48h synthetic replay against production-like traces (see test run in CI). Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Dashboard panels - [x] Docs for oncall and runbook - [x] Feature-flagged rollout Plan for operators: deploy to staging -> enable feature flag -> monitor cohort drift and false-positive rate -> bump sensitivity -> full rollout. Links: Linear ENG-1248 (cohorting design) and PM-432 (dashboard spec).
Diego: Can cohort keys be stable across model version rollouts? Added suggestion to include model-version hash in key derivation. Response: we now namespace cohort keys with model-major-version and include fallback mapping in cohort_store.proto.
Priya: Alert noise risk—please limit initial sensitivity and provide quiet-window behavior. Response: implemented quiet-window attenuation and low-sensitivity defaults; documented in docs/observability/token-cohorting.md.
Liam: test coverage looks good but add an e2e replay with partial KV-cache misses. Response: added synthetic KV miss replay in tests/integration/test_cohorting_flow.py and CI run shows stable results.

payload.body:
Context: Cross-SDK follow-up to earlier session/lease work — introduces an "auth tactician" component that centralizes token TTL awareness and a small prefetch policy to avoid tail latency for streamed pull/push APIs. Motivation: customers saw intermittent ~200-400ms spikes when long-running streams triggered last-second token refreshes; retry/backoff logic masked this but increased request churn and observable noise. Goal: reduce tail latency by proactively warming credentials within a TTL window, provide a small, well-documented opt-in prefetch policy across Python/TS/Go SDKs, and clean up PullStream ergonomics so the language SDKs expose a common surface for cancellable/asynchronous consumption. What I changed: 1) auth/tactician: new minimal stateful component (Python: redwood_sdk.session.tactician, TS: auth/tactician.ts, Go: session/tactician.go) that tracks token TTLs, schedules a single prefetch per session when TTL < configured window, and exposes hooks for the SDK session factories to opt into warm-up; 2) prefetch policy: defaults to disabled for backwards compatibility, opt-in via SDK session config as prefetch_window_ms and prefetch_enabled; adds telemetry events (tactician.prefetch.scheduled, tactician.prefetch.success, tactician.prefetch.error); 3) PullStream refactor: unified pullstream interface name changes (Python: PullAsync -> PullStreamAsync, TS: PullStream class tidy, Go: PullIterator improvements) and clarified cancellation semantics in all three SDKs; 4) retries interplay: small change to retry predicate so a refresh in-flight counts as a non-retryable transient state for a single attempt to avoid double-refresh races; 5) docs and examples: migration guide, prefetch demo, and updated version notes for Python/TS/Go SDK releases. Compatibility notes: all changes are opt-in and default behavior is preserved; SDK minor bumps included to expose the new options (py 2.7.0, ts 1.18.0, go 1.5.0). Testing: unit tests around tactician scheduling and backoff, integration tests that run a long-lived PullStream while forcing token TTL expiry, and end-to-end scenario against a staging control-plane that simulates delayed token issuance. Rollout plan: feature flagged server-side and SDK flags default off; enable in canary customers after 2 weeks smoke. Checklist: [x] add tactician implementations across three SDKs [x] add telemetry and docs [x] add integration tests [x] add version bumps and changelogs [x] run cross-SDK regression job
Aisha: +1 on overall approach; can we keep prefetch disabled by default? Also request clearer metric names for integration with Console. Ethan: Prefetch default is false; added telemetry prefixes tactician.prefetch.* and included mapping in docs. Luca: I think the TS PullStream rename might be breaking for some consumers; would prefer an alias export to maintain ergonomics. Ethan: Added export alias PullAsync -> PullStream in TS package entrypoint to preserve import paths. Riley: go iterator change looks good but please add comment about thread-safety of the tactician scheduling state. Ethan: Added sync.Mutex guard and a unit test simulating concurrent Close/Refresh. Aisha: CI flaked once on the e2e test due to timeouts. Ethan: increased test timeout and added retry logic in the harness; reran CI. Final: approvals from Aisha and Luca; Riley left an approving comment after the mutex test landed.
Added an opt-in auth 'tactician' that can prefetch credentials shortly before expiry to reduce stream-tail latency. New SDK config: prefetch_enabled (bool), prefetch_window_ms (int). PullStream naming unified across SDKs; TS maintains backward-compatible exports. Minor SDK bumps: py 2.7.0, ts 1.18.0, go 1.5.0.
This change is behind SDK and server-side feature flags. Do not enable globally until smoke tests for canary customers pass. Coordinate coordinated release: publish SDKs (py/ts/go) in same day and update Console mapping for tactician telemetry.
publish python wheel, npm publish typescript package, go module tag, update SDK samples repo, enable flag for 5% canary, monitor tactician.prefetch.* metrics for error rates
Unit coverage: tactician scheduling, retry predicate interaction, pullstream cancellation; Integration: simulated TTL expiry while a long-lived stream is open; End-to-end: validated streaming latency tail reduction in staging with prefetch_enabled=true (median tail reduced from 320ms to 60ms in controlled run).
CI: lint/format OK; unit tests PASS; integration tests flaky first run (timeout) then PASS after timeout bump; e2e staging puzzle: one run had 502 from staging auth service simulated delay, rerun passed.

Motivation: previous function-calling / tool-calling ergonomics made multi-tool flows brittle in the face of partial failures, streaming tool outputs, and heterogeneous retry requirements. This PR introduces the Toolchain Conductor API and runtime changes to make multi-tool orchestration explicit, safer, and simpler for SDK consumers while improving streaming stability and OpenAI-compat structured-output behavior.

What changed (high level):
- New top-level 'toolchain' field in the API surface that lets callers declare a directed sequence/graph of tool invocations and per-tool execution policies (parallelizable, ordered-inject, idempotency-token, retry-policy).
- Explicit 'inject_policy' semantics for how tool results are merged back into the LLM input: append-only buffer, deterministic slot injection (index by tool name), and optional merge hooks for user-supplied merge functions.
- Streaming improvements: tools now emit chunked 'partial_result' events with stable markers; the runtime buffers/flushes partials per client backpressure window to avoid garbled interleaving in streamed chat responses.
- Retry ergonomics: per-tool idempotency tokens and 'retry-hints' (max_attempts, backoff_strategy, retry_on_partial) allow safe retries without double-injecting results or re-running non-idempotent side effects. The conductor coordinates token usage and mirrors idempotency onto downstream tool invocations.
- Parallel execution: 'concurrency_hint' allows the runtime to safely execute independent tools in parallel with an ordering-affinity map to preserve deterministic injection when required. The conductor produces a canonical merge order for cases where results are required in the prompt.
- OpenAI compatibility: function-calling framing updated to support nested structured outputs produced by ensembles of tools; the compat layer maps conductor outputs into the old function-calling response shape and emits a new 'toolchain_metadata' field describing per-tool statuses for consumers that opt-in.
- Observability: added per-tool metrics (latency_p50/p95, injection_failures, retry_count), conductor-level tracing spans, and new dashboard panels.
- Tests & docs: integration tests for partial-stream recovery, idempotent retry flows, and examples in SDKs plus updated API reference.

Why this is safer: callers can opt into strict injection ordering, idempotency enforcement, and per-tool retry controls which prevents subtle duplication bugs (e.g., re-invoking a billing API or re-applying a mutation). The explicit conductor model also makes reasoning about streaming boundaries and backpressure easier for client implementers.

Backward compat: default runtime behavior preserves prior semantics for simple single-tool calls; the new toolchain surface is opt-in. OpenAI-compat responses remain available but with additional metadata when the conductor is used.

Next steps: small follow-ups to expose a higher-level SDK builder (ToolchainBuilder) and an admin flag to enable strict deterministic injection across replicas (ENG-7510).
Diego Martinez (review): Overall looks good — can you clarify failure semantics when a tool returns a partial result and then errors?
Ava Lin (author): we introduced 'partial_result' + terminal 'error' event; the conductor will surface the partial and then emit a failure status for that tool. Retry policy 'retry_on_partial' controls if we re-run from the last safe boundary.
Samiya Khan (request_changes): we need stronger guarantees that retries won't double-inject. Can you show where we dedupe injects?
Ava Lin: added idempotency token propagation and an inject ledger in injector.go with tests demonstrating dedupe across retries. See new unit test 'test_injector_dedupe'.
Tom Becker (comment): please ensure this doesn't regress streaming throughput; consider a non-blocking flush path for large partial streams.
Ava Lin: added non-blocking flush that stream-queues large partials and defers injection ordering decisions to the conductor's merge step; added perf test simulating 100 concurrent partial streams.
Added a new opt-in Toolchain Conductor API for multi-tool orchestration: per-tool retry policies, idempotency tokens, deterministic injection options, streaming partial_result semantics, and improved OpenAI-compat structured output mapping. Default single-tool behavior unchanged.
This is opt-in. SDKs (Python/TS) expose ToolchainBuilder examples in docs/api/toolchain.md. Admins who want strict deterministic injection across replicas should follow ENG-7510 for enabling the cluster-wide flag.
Manual QA performed for: partial stream recovery, retry-on-partial flows, parallel execution deadlocks. Added integration tests that run in CI.
payload.title: Toolchain Conductor: API for multi-tool orchestration, injection semantics, and retry ergonomics

Motivation: Multiple SDKs had slightly divergent retry presets and streaming ergonomics that made cross-language feature parity and user documentation inconsistent. This PR consolidates retry presets into a compact, documented set, surfaces a slim streaming facade that is consistent across Python/TypeScript/Go, and adds a credential resilience layer that falls back to configured providers before surfacing errors. Scope: changes are limited to SDK surface layers and small supporting machinery in the SDK packages; runtime platform code is untouched. Key changes include: 1) introduce 'compact' and 'latency-optimized' retry presets with a tiny DSL and mapped defaults in each SDK; 2) implement a thin PullStream / PushStream facade with identical semantics in py/ts/go, including an explicit 'resumeFromCheckpoint' hint and cancellation token hooks; 3) add CredentialMediator that accepts ordered providers and performs soft-fallbacks with telemetry hooks; 4) bump SDK versions: python 2.8.0, typescript 1.17.0, go 1.12.0 and update changelogs; 5) small doc updates and example apps to demonstrate multi-SDK parity. Safety: added test harnesses to exercise retry windows and streaming resume under controlled flakiness. Backwards compatibility: existing constructors are preserved with deprecation warnings for the legacy retry config. Why here: making parity changes in the monorepo ensures we can ship aligned docs and examples at the same time.
Marcus Liu: Nice consolidation. Two asks: add explicit note in CHANGELOG about deprecated legacy_retry_config and include an example showing how to migrate. Also please add a small e2e that simulates transient auth failures.
Elena Park: Thanks Marcus, added migration snippet in python/typescript changelogs and a flaky auth test harness under tests/e2e/auth_flaky_sim. Will push shortly.
Priya Singh: The TS PullStream surface looks good but the cancellation semantics need to be deterministic across Node and browser. Can we make cancel() idempotent and document event ordering?
Elena Park: Made cancel() idempotent and added explicit ordering in docs/sdk/streaming.md. Added unit tests covering double-cancel.
Diego Marquez: CI showed intermittent race in Go stream resume; narrowing goroutine handoff and adding small sleep in test fixed it. Consider revisiting production backpressure semantics later.
Elena Park: Acknowledged. Left TODO in code and filed ENG-9611 to follow up on streaming backpressure semantics in runtime.
Small ergonomics and parity changes across Python/TS/Go SDKs: consolidated retry presets, lightweight streaming surface for pull/push streams, credential fallback mediator and version bumps for all SDKs.

Problem and motivation: customers and SREs have been asking for more granular visibility into per-request cost and latency drivers. Current dashboards show per-request latency and token counts but do not attribute cost or latency to KV-cache behavior (cache hits vs misses) or to token class (prompt vs completion vs system). This makes it hard to tune batching, caching, and quantization tradeoffs or to investigate incidents where cost spikes without obvious throughput increases. This PR introduces schema-level metrics and tagging that let us break down latency and cost by: model, region, kv_cache_hit (true/false), token_type (prompt|completion|system), billing_tier, and request_route. It also adds a set of dashboards and alert adjustments to reduce noisy paging from transient KV misses. Summary of changes: 1) Runtime telemetry: emit two new counter/histogram families: redwood.kv_cache.requests_total{kv_cache_hit=(true|false)} and redwood.request.latency_ms_bucketed with an additional label kv_cache_hit and token_type. 2) Cost tagging: attach estimated token cost label redwood.cost.estimate_usd_per_request (sampled histogram) and redwood.cost.token_usd with labels token_type and model_variant to all generation responses. 3) SDK and API: minor header change so SDKs propagate trace + cost tags end-to-end for hosted and dedicated modes. 4) Dashboards: Grafana dashboard added for KV cache KPI panel, token-cost heatmap by model and region, and a new slow-path investigation panel that slices latencies by kv_cache_hit and token_type. 5) Alerts: tuned the token-cost anomaly alert to use median-of-5m with suppression for short-lived KV miss bursts; added a new alert for sustained KV miss rate > 5% over 10m (ENG-4872). 6) Tests and CI: unit and integration tests for metric labels, and a small e2e smoke harness that verifies the histogram buckets remain stable under high-load synthetic runs. Rollout plan: staged rollout via runtime feature flag enable-kv-cost-metrics: start in staging (2/18), canine lab (perf-canary) for 48h, then 10% prod traffic for 24h, then 100% with a follow-up rollout to add quantization-specific tags if no regressions on cost telemetry (ETA +7 days). Backward compatibility: metrics are additive and default to label kv_cache_hit=unknown in older binaries; no API surface break. Links: Linear ENG-4872, docs PR referencing dashboard JSON (internal link: https://internal.redwood/grafana/dash/kv-cache-kpis). Checklist: - [x] Runtime metric instrumentation added - [x] SDK propagation tested - [x] Grafana panels and JSON exported - [x] Alerts tuned and false-positive tests added - [x] Smoke test in perf-canary: passed
Liam: Can we avoid cardinality explosion with token_type label? Consider sampling for high-volume endpoints.
Author reply (Maya): We sample token-level cost histograms at 1/10 for high-throughput models and emit full counts for slow-path models. Added sampling config to histogram_buckets.yaml.
Priya: Graph looks noisy for some regions; we should add per-region rollup option.
Author reply: Added region rollup and minimal retention note to dashboard JSON; left per-region view as opt-in.
Diego: CI flake on the smoke harness; re-run fixed it. Approved after green CI.
Adds KV-cache hit/miss metrics and token-level cost labels to runtime telemetry. New Grafana dashboards for KV cache KPIs and token cost heatmap. Alert tuning to suppress transient KV-miss noise and a new sustained-kv-miss alert. Backwards compatible; metrics are additive.
Ops: enable feature flag enable-kv-cost-metrics in staging first. Watch metric redwood.kv_cache.requests_total and redwood.request.latency_ms_bucketed; suppression policy lives in infra/alerts/alert-rules.yaml. If token-cost histograms cause ingestion pressure, set sampling.rate.high_throughput_models=10 in runtime config.

Fix: stabilize CUDA graph capture/replay warmup heuristics to prevent replay mismatches and improve steady-state latency for variable-length workloads. No API changes.
Context: A production regression was observed when enabling CUDA graph capture + replay for some multi-batched chat workloads. The replay path was failing or producing higher latency for requests that grew the KV cache or had variable sequence-length distributions. Root cause: the warmup capture phase recorded a single representative shape in many cases; shape-guarding logic that we added earlier was too strict in some paths and too permissive in others, causing either replay mismatches or never capturing beneficial graphs.

This PR introduces a conservative, multi-shape warmup and relaxed equivalence classes for shape guards so that captured graphs better cover the real workload distribution. Key changes: consolidated warmup runner to capture N representative shapes (small/median/max sequence buckets), add KV-capacity-aware guards (bucket by kv_slots_used range), and a replay fallback that automatically falls back to non-graph execution on mismatch and triggers a background recapture with the observed shape. Also includes metrics and traces to detect capture thrash.

Summary of changes (single continuous description): Implemented WarmupShapeSampler and integrated into cuda/graph_manager; extended shape guard policy to include kv_slot buckets and to allow compatible padding/stride differences; updated kernel selector to accept relaxed dim matches for common batched kernels; added a short-circuit replay fallback path that retries without replay if a shape mismatch is detected and enqueues an async recapture job; added unit + integration tests, stress test harness updates, and a perf benchmark that reproduces the original regression.

Why this approach: Capturing multiple representative shapes reduces replay misses while keeping capture overhead bounded. Bucketing by KV occupancy is important because KV cache growth changes internal tensor sizes even when sequence length appears constant. A lightweight fallback prevents 5xx/incorrect outputs and improves reliability during warmup under load.

Testing and verification: Local and CI runs include the new integration suite. We added flaky-tolerant checks in the GPU test job and re-ran kernel correctness tests across different batch/seq combinations. Perf run: steady-state p95 token-latency improved by 6-12% on the benchmark harness compared to the prior graph-replay implementation for mixed-length chat traces. No observed correctness regressions in the unit/integration matrix.

Operational notes: This change adds a small runtime config (env vars) to adjust warmup capture count and kv-bucket boundaries. Defaults tuned to avoid extra capture overhead for low-throughput customers. We added a metric "cuda_graph.capture_recaptures" and an alert rule template for capture thrash.

Checklist:
- [x] Implement warmup multi-shape sampler and KV bucket guards
- [x] Add replay fallback and async recapture job
- [x] Kernel selector relaxations and unit tests
- [x] Integration tests + perf harness reproducer
- [x] Update docs/changelog and add observability hooks

Files changed (high level): runtime/cuda/graph_manager.py, runtime/cuda/shape_guards.py, runtime/scheduler/continuous_batcher.py, runtime/kv_cache/kv_store.py, tests/integration/test_cuda_graph_replay.py, tests/perf/bench_graph_warmup.py, docs/CHANGELOG.md
Arjun Patel: Could you explain the boundary choices for kv-slot buckets? I'm worried about an edge-case where small changes flip the bucket frequently.
Sofia Martinez: Good point — I've added hysteresis to bucket transitions (10% headroom) in shape_guards and documented it in comments. This prevents frequent recapture for small incremental KV growth.
Maya Li: The replay fallback looks good, but can you ensure that we don't double-enqueue recapture jobs under high contention?
Sofia Martinez: Added a dedupe token in the recapture queue; jobs within 500ms for the same model+shape are coalesced. See runtime/cuda/graph_manager.py:recapture_queue logic.
Connor Hughes: CI GPU job failed once on kernel correctness; re-ran and it passed. Approving once green.
Arjun Patel: Approved after addressing kv-bucket hysteresis and dedupe-token.

Motivation: Continuous batching currently balances throughput vs tail latency by using hard deadlines and coarse fairness buckets. In mixed workloads (small chat turns interleaved with long KV-pinned generations) small requests see 95/99th tail spikes when batch slots are consumed by long-running work. This PR implements a soft slot reservation scheme with decay and age-weighting to reduce tail latency without starving heavy flows.

What this change does: Adds a lightweight reservation allocator that maintains ephemeral slot credits per request class (class determined by token-boundary hints + KV pin flag). Credits are granted based on recent service rate and a configurable reservation window and then decay exponentially if unused. Reservations are "soft": they bias the batch selection algorithm (probabilistic weight addition) rather than forcibly preempting existing work. To guard against starvation the scheduler applies an age-weighted fairness boost which increases priority of waiting requests over time and a fast-reclaim timer that recovers unused reservations from stalled owners after a short threshold.

Key knobs and defaults: feature flag: scheduler.enable_soft_reservations (default false) reservation_window_ms: 50 (rolling window for granting) reservation_decay_half_life_ms: 200 reclaim_threshold_ms: 150 age_boost_rate: 0.01 per 10ms max_soft_fraction: 0.25 (max fraction of batch slots influenced by reservations) preemption_safe_mode: when true, reservations never preempt already-started kernels; default true.

Telemetry and observability: new metrics: scheduler.soft_reservations_granted_total, scheduler.soft_reservations_reclaimed_total, scheduler.age_boost_factor, scheduler.reservation_usage_ratio. Added per-class latency histograms and a dedicated dashboard wiring in perf/soft-reservations.

Behavior under load: In synthetic mixed workload perf-canary runs we observed: small requests (<=64 tokens) 95th latency reduced from 122ms -> 68ms (~44% improvement) at 85% aggregate capacity; 99th reduced from 310ms -> 148ms. End-to-end throughput changed by -1.6% in a KV-heavy saturated synthetic (worst-case), but improvement for latency-sensitive classes was measured without tail amplification.

Testing and validation: unit tests for allocator and decay model added (tests/scheduler/reservation_test.go), integration tests in the continuous-batcher harness and a canary config under pkg/bench/perf_canary/elastic_reservations.yaml. We ran a 48-hour perf canary across two clusters (canary-1: small-L, canary-2: mixed-KV) to detect regressions; Canary metrics are linked in the internal dashboard (ENG-4689).

Compatibility and rollout: The feature is behind scheduler.enable_soft_reservations and off by default for no-risk installs. Rollout plan: (1) enable in perf CI and canaries, (2) enable for a subset of tenants via console feature flag for 1 week, (3) staged ramp across Dedicated pools, (4) enable-by-default after metrics stabilization. Emergency kill-switch available via scheduler.feature_toggle.

Risk and mitigations: There is a small throughput regression in synthetic KV-saturated tails; mitigations include lowering max_soft_fraction and enabling preemption_safe_mode. The implementation avoids kernel-level preemption (no in-flight kernel termination) to prevent instability on CUDA/ROCm paths.

Notes for reviewers: focus review on correctness of reclaim logic (pkg/scheduler/slot_reservations.go), interactions with KV pin prioritization (pkg/kv/cache_manager.go hooks), and telemetry labels for per-class histograms. The implementation takes care to remain lock-light and uses atomic counters to avoid contention hotspots.

Related: builds on prior work (ENG-4412 queue-horizon experiments) but differs by using probabilistic weighting and timed decay rather than strict slot leases.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc updated (docs/perf/soft_reservations.md) - [x] Unit tests added - [x] Perf canary run completed - [x] Observability wired - [x] Feature flag gated - [x] Docs and release notes prepared

Merge strategy: squash merge into main after two approvals and green CI.
Introduce a tunable soft slot reservation mechanism for the continuous batcher that reduces tail latency for small/latency-sensitive requests while preventing starvation of large/kv-heavy requests. Default off behind feature flag; safe rollout is recommended.
Ethan Cho: High level LGTM. Please add a comment explaining the reclaim_threshold rationale and add an integ test that simulates a stalled holder.
Marisol Vega: Added reclaim threshold comments and a synthetic stalled-holder test (reservation_test.go::TestReclaimStalledHolder). Also included histograms for reclaimed vs used counts.
Priya Nair: Could we avoid an allocation hot-path in allocator.giveCredits()? Looks like a slice growth in tight loops.
Marisol Vega: Good catch — changed to pre-allocated ring buffer for per-class windows, pushed a fix in c1a4fe7 -> 4f9b2d1.
Gareth Mills: Observability looks good. One nit: metric labels should not include raw tenant IDs; changed to tenant_shard label.
Also, CI lint failed initially (gofmt) — please run gofmt across scheduler pkg.
Marisol Vega: Ran gofmt and fixed lint; CI rerun passed. Addressed metric label nit by using tenant_shard.

Motivation:
We need reproducible, auditable release artifacts for Private deployments (VPC/on-prem installer). This PR wires up automated attestation and notarization into the existing release pipelines so that Helm charts, Terraform modules, and the on-prem installer tarballs are (1) reproducibly built, (2) cryptographically attested for build provenance, and (3) notarized with a timestamped signature stored alongside release manifests.

What this changes (summary):
- Adds a CI pipeline that produces deterministic build artifacts, generates SBOMs, and emits in-toto attestations for: Helm chart bundle, terraform modules, and the private-installer tarball.
- Integrates a notarization step that signs artifacts using a hardware-backed key (KMS/HSM integration stubbed for e2e; sees scripts/notarize.sh).
- Enhances release manifest generator to include provenance links (attestation uri, sbom uri, signature digest) and to publish a compact release-manifest.json to the releases bucket.
- Updates Helm chart metadata (Chart.yaml) with immutable digest fields and chart provenance annotations consumed by the installer.
- Terraform module releases now include a module_manifest.json with module version, provider pinning, and attestation reference.
- Adds a rollback-safe release marker: when a bad release is detected we can toggle 'active_release' in the manifest which the installer reads for safe rollback.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- We use in-toto attestations (simple layout) instead of full SLSA pipeline enforcement for now to reduce blast radius and unblock ops. Future work will add stricter SLSA levels.
- Notarization uses an HSM-backed signing flow where the key material is kept in KMS. For CI we use a test key; the pipeline includes a gate to require a production KMS binding for production releases.
- Deterministic builds: we pin builder images and canonicalize timestamps when generating tarballs and charts to minimize non-determinism. This increases build complexity but is necessary for reproducible provenance.

Files touched (high level):
- installer/helm/private-installer/Chart.yaml (add provenance annotations)
- installer/helm/private-installer/values.schema.json (validation for manifest-driven upgrades)
- installer/ci/release/provenance-pipeline.yaml (new)
- build/pipelines/attest-notarize.yaml (new)
- scripts/release/notarize.sh (sign + publish signatures)
- terraform/modules/private-network/module_manifest.json (generated)
- terraform/modules/registry/Makefile (release step integration)
- installer/release/release-manifest-generator.go (adds provenance fields)
- docs/private-deploy/release-provenance.md (docs)

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for release-manifest-generator added (installer/release/release-manifest-generator_test.go).
- CI integration job runs attestation pipeline with test key and verifies signature and SBOM content.
- Manual: produced a candidate release (v0.17.3-rc) in staging, verified installer applies the chart with provenance annotation and that the rollback marker toggles as expected.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge into main behind feature flag (env var ENABLE_NOTARIZE=true) so production releases are opt-in.
2) Run several canary releases to staging for internal clusters.
3) Once validated, flip feature flag for official private-installer release pipeline.

Checklist:
- [x] deterministic build artifacts for helm/tf/installer tarball
- [x] produce SBOMs and in-toto attestations
- [x] notarization + signature publishing script
- [x] release-manifest generator writes provenance references
- [x] basic docs + runbook

Related Linear/Jira:
ENG-4721 (release automation: provenance), ENG-4892 (installer rollback markers), SUP-302 (customer request for signed artifacts).

Notes for reviewers:
- The KMS/HSM integration is intentionally abstracted and gated; see scripts/release/notarize.sh for the test-key path and build/pipelines/attest-notarize.yaml for gating logic.
- The Helm digest annotations are consumed by the installer; ensure the chart linter and Helm repo index generation are unaffected.

Priya Kapoor: Please confirm that the production KMS key ID is required before flipping the feature flag (I see a gate but want explicit enforcement).
Author (Ananya Rao): The pipeline will error out at notarize step if PROD_KMS_KEY is unset; added an explicit check and a helpful failure message.
Miguel Santos: We should add a small e2e that validates rollback marker behavior — added a test that flips active_release in staging.
Oliver Chen: nit: tighten chart annotation key namespace (we use 'redwood.io/provenance' now). Updated Chart.yaml accordingly.
Added automated attestation and notarization for private-installer artifacts (Helm charts, Terraform modules, installer tarballs). Release manifests now include provenance references (attestation URI, SBOM URI, signature digest). Notarization gated behind KMS binding; feature-flag rollout planned.

payload.body:
Motivation: We see recurring high tail latency events where requests take a 'slowpath' through the runtime (kernel stalls, queue backpressure, or unexpected KV cache miss sequences) that aren't visible in coarse per-route percentiles. This PR adds a lightweight slowpath capture pipeline and a targeted hot-prompt sampler to help diagnose and correlate these events to prompt shape, tenant behavior, and kernel-level signals. Design: 1) slowpath_detector: in the serving runtime we add a low-overhead detector that marks invocations as slowpath when GPU queue wait > 25ms or stage stall > configured threshold. 2) structured capture: when an invocation is marked and a probabilistic sampler fires we emit a compact JSON trace with prompt fingerprint, stage timings, kernel tags, model_variant, small token-cost sketch (count & sketch digest), and a redacted prompt signature. 3) hot-prompt sampler: a frequency-based detector that promotes a fingerprint to "hot" when it appears > X times in Y minutes; while hot it collects higher-fidelity captures (including appendix token-level timing for first N tokens) behind a configurable cap to bound cost. 4) dashboards and alerts: add a new "Inference Slowpath Radar" dashboard (heatmap of slowpath density by model/region, prompt-cohort table, recent hot fingerprints) and an alert rule "hotprompt_surveillance" that fires when a hot fingerprint causes > P99 latency regressions across tenants; the alert includes dynamic cooldown and an adaptive sampling cap so we do not overload telemetry. Implementation notes: the detector emits to the existing telemetry ingestion with a new metric family slowpath.marker and a compact trace envelope slowpath.capture.v1. The hot-prompt sampler maintains an in-memory LRU frequency table with spill to Redis for Durable mode in Dedicated/Private deployments. Backwards compatibility: all captures are privacy-first: prompt bodies are hashed and redacted by default; telemetry consumers opt-in to higher fidelity. Tests: unit and integration tests for detector thresholds, sampler rate limits, redis spill behavior, and the dashboard JSON schema validator. Docs: includes operator guidance for tuning thresholds and cost caps and a migration note for Dedicated customers. Checklist: - [x] runtime detector implemented and benchmarked for <0.5% median CPU overhead - [x] structured capture schema and ingestion mapping added - [x] hot-prompt frequency algorithm with configurable caps - [x] dashboards and alert rule added and validated in staging - [x] unit + integration tests - [x] operator docs and runbook entries - [x] performance bench for worst-case sampling cost Rollout plan: feature is gated behind an observability flag (sdk flag + server-side gate). We will enable slowpath.marker export in staging for 48 hours, run the dashboard with synthetic slowpath injections, then enable hot-prompt promotions at 10% of production traffic for two weeks before increasing. Problem: Streaming endpoints and the OpenAI-compat layer accepted mixed content payloads inconsistently which led to silent truncation and misrouting of tool/file attachments, and unclear behavior when callers combined streaming with multipart uploads. This PR: 1) Adds a rigorous multipart/form-data validation layer for streaming and non-streaming endpoints that enforces Content-Type and boundary checks, rejects ambiguous content types, and returns clear 4xx errors with machine-readable error codes. 2) Implements per-file and per-request limits for tool/file attachments (configurable via service-level flags and per-customer overrides) with graceful backpressure for streaming uploads. 3) Fixes streaming stability issues for chunked multipart bodies by introducing a streaming parser that can handle interleaved event frames and large binary parts without buffering the whole part in memory. 4) Extends the OpenAI compatibility shim so that tool calling semantics match expected types when files are present (file->tool reference translation, and deterministic multipart ordering). 5) Adds E2E tests for Python/TS SDKs, unit tests for the parser, integration tests exercising the compatibility layer, and examples in quickstarts and docs. Migration notes: Clients that previously relied on loosely typed content-types (e.g., sending application/json with a binary body) will now receive 400 errors and should switch to multipart/form-data or application/octet-stream. Motivation: we need a single control-plane primitive to express multi-stage canaries, A/B experiments, and shadowing with explicit intent detection and deterministic fallback decisions. This PR introduces a RolloutDecisionGraph CRD plus a controller that composes routing edges driven by observed intents (latency_regression, semantic_drift, cost_spike) and metric decay windows to avoid flip-flop rollbacks. The decision graph lets operators declare intents, weighted edges, safety gates, and fallback chains in one compact spec, and the controller translates nodes into traffic policies that work across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Key behaviors: 1) intent detectors consume the existing observability stream (latency p95, failed-response-rate, eval-score-delta) and emit typed intents with confidence scores, 2) edges have conditions with decay windows so transient spikes do not immediately trigger rollbacks, 3) fallback chains support graceful degradation strategies (mirror->canary->full, canary->reduce-weight->quarantine) and automatic remediation hooks that call existing SRE runbooks, 4) graph evaluation is deterministic and versioned so rollouts are auditable and reproducible. Backwards compatibility: existing rollout CRDs and traffic-split configs are supported; the controller will upgrade legacy configs into a single-node graph unless an explicit RolloutDecisionGraph is provided. Testing and results: integration tests were run against the perf-canary harness with synthetic latency drift and drift-injection experiments; median time-to-detect reduced by 18% for semantic drift scenarios and automatic rollback TP improved 24% versus the previous thresholded approach. Migration: operator-facing docs include a conversion tool `rwdctl rollout convert` and examples for common patterns (canary mesh, multi-model A/B, shadow quarantine). Security & safety: graph evaluation runs in the control plane with strict RBAC and audit events emitted per decision. Implementation details: CRD schema (apiextensions v1), controller uses a two-stage reconcile (evaluate intents -> compute graph decision -> push traffic policy to router), includes a small interpreter for expressions used in conditions (safe subset of CEL). Monitoring: new metrics rollout_graph_evaluations_total, rollout_graph_decisions{outcome}, rollout_graph_fallbacks_total and traces linked to trace-id for each decision. Migration plan and rollout: staged rollout of the controller to Dedicated pools then Hosted; feature gate rollout_graph_v2 can be toggled per-tenant. See linked Linear tasks for adoption plan. This description is intentionally compact but complete and references the changed files and tests below.
Jonas: Overall design looks good, but we need stronger guarantees around evaluation determinism across controller restarts; please add a seeded evaluation step and record seed in audit events. Aisha: added deterministic seed persisted to the RolloutDecisionGraph status and included seed in trace metadata. Marta: request to simplify CEL usage to a safe subset to avoid runtime panics in the control plane; suggested explicit whitelist of functions. Aisha: restricted interpreter to the documented subset and added unit tests. Ethan: noted we should expose a per-tenant feature flag; added feature gate rollout_graph_v2 and documented how to toggle. Jonas: approve after minor docs nits. CI flake on integration test re-run was resolved by increasing test harness timeout and pinning synthetic workload timing. Motivation: Customers observed client disconnects that left server-side streaming state in a limbo where tool-calls were retried and KV-cache backfills were skipped, causing higher token costs and functional duplication. This PR introduces a 'silence probe' reconciliation path, a reconnect probe that attempts lightweight session health checks on client reconnects, an explicit cancel-deadline enforcement for in-flight tool/function calls, and safer backfill semantics when reconnect resumes. Summary of changes: 1) server: add silence-probe detection that marks streams as 'candidate-orphan' after configurable idle windows and enqueues a lightweight snapshot probe before evicting; 2) reconnect: on new client handshake include reconnect-probe phase which validates KV-cache continuity and replays missing prefix tokens if safe; 3) cancel-deadline: tool invocation subsystem now tracks cancel deadlines separately from client websocket state and enforces idempotent abort semantics with explicit response code for clients; 4) backfill behavior: when resuming, we prefer prefix-reconciliation over blind backfill and record a short reconciliation trace to observability; 5) OpenAI-compat: adapter layer now maps the reconnect-probe handshake into a 409/202-style flow when applicable and preserves function-call idempotency tokens. Implementation notes: code changes touch the session manager, rpc/stream controller, toolcall executor, and the OpenAI compatibility adapter. Default timeouts are conservative (idle->candidate-orphan = 45s, probe timeout = 5s, cancel-deadline grace = 2s) with knobs exposed in config. Tests: added unit tests for probe state transitions, e2e integration test that simulates abrupt client disconnect and reconnect with toolcalls, and property tests for idempotent abort on repeated cancel signals. Safety: probe performs non-destructive validation only and will not execute user-visible toolcalls during reconciliation. Rollout plan: feature gated via runtime flag 'streaming.silence_probe_v1' with spreadsheet of customers to flip; metrics added: stream.probe.started, stream.probe.success, stream.resume.reconciled, toolcall.abort.forced; alerting suggested on probe.failures > 1% over 10m. Backwards compatibility: existing client behavior unchanged unless server flag enabled. Related: follows ENG-4821 and references earlier streaming incident INT-998. Breaking change: none. See release_notes for end-user impact.
Marcus: requested tighter metrics granularity around probe latency and suggested a separate probe_failure tag for tenant-scoped indexing. Elena: found a race in session eviction path when probe returns while eviction is already scheduled; asked for a test and small lock refactor. Samir: asked for clearer mapping of reconnect flow in OpenAI-compat adapter and an explicit 409 vs 202 decision table. Author replies: added metric 'stream.probe.latency_ms' and split probe_failure tenant tag, refactored eviction locking to use session-level RW mutex and added unit test, documented decision table in adapters/openai/handshake.go and docs/streaming-silence-probe.md. Approval: Marcus approved after metrics change. Elena approved after lock fix. Samir approved after docs update.
Feature gated streaming silence-probe and reconnect probe which improves resilience after abrupt client disconnects. Adds cancel-deadline enforcement for toolcalls to avoid duplicated side effects. No behavioral changes until the runtime flag is enabled.

Context: Multi-tool call patterns at scale expose a tradeoff between per-request latency and downstream execution overhead when we naively fan out tool invocations. Customers reported jitter in streaming handshakes when several tool results were injected concurrently (see ENG-8921). Motivation: Smooth out spikes from parallel tool warmups and avoid duplicate retries while preserving deterministic injection order (for structured output consumers and OpenAI tool-calling compatibility). This PR implements a lightweight coalescing invoker that introduces a configurable grace period (default 10ms) to allow closely timed tool calls from the same top-level request to batch their execution, plus deterministic merge points for tool-result injection and a coordinated retry protocol that reduces duplicate tool executions. Key changes and design: 1) Grace-window coalescer (api/invoker/coalescer.py): collects tool call intents for a single request context for up to grace_period_ms before dispatching a prioritized execution set. Grace window is short (default 10ms) to keep tail latency bounded; tunable via request-level config. 2) Deterministic mergepoints (runtime/invoker/mergepoint.go): tool results are assigned stable sequence slots at dispatch time so downstream structured output assembly is order-deterministic even if tools finish out-of-order. This preserves existing structured-output expectations and OpenAI function-call ordering semantics. 3) Coordinated retry token (protocol/invoker_retry.proto + runtime): introduces a small idempotency token coupled with a coordinator lease to avoid concurrent retries launching duplicate side effects when multiple workers observe timeouts. Token acquisition is optimistic; fallback retry uses backoff and escalates to a single-quorum retry owner. 4) Streaming handshake stabilizations (api/gateways/openai_compat_stream.go): when streaming a response that will include tool-result injections, the gateway now waits for mergepoint assignment and streams slot-wrapped fragments to clients. We added a lightweight client-side marker in TS SDK so OpenAI-compat clients can present partial structured frames while preserving tool-call streaming expectations. 5) SDK ergonomic surface updates (redwood-sdk-typescript/src/tool-coalesce.ts): a new helper wraps parallel tool calls in a coalesce() helper so application code can opt into the grace-window behavior explicitly (default opt-out). 6) Tests and telemetry: integration tests added for high-concurrency tool scenarios, unit tests for mergepoint sequencing, and new metrics (invoker.coalesce.window_ms, invoker.mergepoint.latency, invoker.retry.quorum_falls) for Console dashboards. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is opt-out via the coalesce helper; internal routing will enable coalescing for customer-tiered policies where cost/perf tradeoffs favor batching (Dedicated plans). For users relying on immediate dispatch, new request flag coalesce=false bypasses the grace window. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag 'invoker_coalesce_v1'. Start with internal dogfood and canary on perf-canary cluster for 48 hours, then staged enablement on 10% of hosted traffic. Monitoring and observability: dashboards added to the 'invoker' tab in Redwood Console to track coalesce rate, average delay introduced, and any observed regression in percentiles for end-to-end token latency. Risks and mitigations: - Small added latency due to the grace window; mitigated by short default and per-request override. - Complex retry semantics could hide transient failures; mitigated by alerts for quorum_falls and automatic disabling if threshold crossed. Test plan: - unit tests for coalescer (edge cases: zero grace, long tail arrivals) - integration tests simulating 200 concurrent tool calls per request - streaming handshake tests with OpenAI-compat client simulation - load test comparing cost/requests before/after merge. Documentation: docs/api/tool-coalescing.md and an SDK example added in redwood-quickstarts/tool-coalescing-example. Related: builds on earlier tooling around deterministic injection and complements ENG-9047 (structured output regressions), ENG-8921 (streaming jitter incident).
Ravi Patel: Nice direction. A few questions about the retry quorum---can we avoid a blocker where the quorum holder dies before finishing and leaves a duplicate side-effect?
Ava Martinez: We added a short-lived lease with automatic failover; the coordinator will escalate to a quorum-based owner after lease expiry. Added tests to simulate owner crash (see test_invoker_coalesce.py).
Lin Chen: For OpenAI streaming compatibility, are clients expected to upgrade SDK? What's the plan if they don't?
Ava Martinez: Streaming format remains backward compatible. The SDK helper gives better ergonomic surface but gateway emits slot-wrapped fragments that degrade gracefully: older clients will receive plain text stream with injected payloads; new clients get structured frames. Documented in docs/api/tool-coalescing.md.
Marta Kowalska: Performance numbers? I want to make sure P99 doesn't regress for chat workloads.
Ava Martinez: Added perf-canary results in the PR: median increased by 2ms, P95 by 6ms, P99 unchanged within noise. Included flags to disable per-request. See telemetry/dashboards/invoker_coalesce.json.
Ravi Patel: Suggest tightening default grace window to 5ms for hosted tier to be conservative.
Ava Martinez: Reduced default to 10ms for Dedicated and 5ms for Hosted in subsequent commit and added runtime policy to override.
Introduces an opt-in coalescing invoker that batches closely timed tool calls using a short grace window to reduce duplicate warmups and stabilize streaming handshakes. Adds deterministic mergepoints for ordered tool-result injection and a coordinated retry token to minimize duplicate side-effects. Opt-in via SDK helper or request flag; gated rollout.

Summary: Add a compatibility layer for the incoming Responses v8 variant that preserves deterministic hints (seed/rng flags), forwards client metadata tags intact, and stabilizes streaming chunk boundaries for tool/function call reassembly. This PR centralizes the mapping logic so that other adapters (SDKs, private installer) can reuse the same translation rules. Motivation: Customers are adopting the new Responses v8 semantics (explicit seed + context-tag fields). Without a consistent mapping we see reproducibility regressions and toolcall reassembly bugs in streaming. This change reduces conversion drift and eliminates a class of flakiness observed in production canaries.

What this changes (high-level):
- Add responses-v8 adapter in pkg/openai/compat that maps v8 flags to internal RNG hints (seed-channel + deterministic-level).
- Preserve top-level client metadata (user_metadata, context_tags, annotations) through the bridge so downstream services (audit, metrics, autoroller) see the original attributes.
- Stabilize stream framing: introduce a framing anchor that pins toolcall boundary metadata on chunk edges to ensure assembled tool/function calls are not split incorrectly during resumptions or partial reconnects.
- Transparent fallbacks: if the client supplies both legacy "seed" and the new "determinism" object, prefer determinism but log the divergence for telemetry.
- Tests: unit, integration, and a new lightweight end-to-end canary to validate reassembly across connection restarts.

Design details: the compatibility layer lives under pkg/openai/compat/responses_v8_bridge.go and exposes a single function TranslateResponsesV8(reqBytes) -> InternalRequest. Key translation rules: map v8.seed -> rng_hint.seed (string), v8.determinism.level -> rng_hint.level (enum: none|soft|hard), context_tags -> request.metadata.context_tags (preserve order), user_metadata -> request.metadata.user_metadata, and structured_output.schema -> enforcement hints on the generator pipeline. For streaming, the assembler will now attach an "anchor-id" to the last chunk of a logical frame, and the reassembler reconciles chunks using anchor-id + sequence numbers to avoid mis-association when a client reconnects mid-stream.

- [x] Add translation layer and unit tests
- [x] Wire metadata passthrough to audit and console plumbing
- [x] Streaming framing anchor + reassembly tests

Motivation: INT8 inference for large decoder models showed suboptimal memory layout overhead and extra dequant steps when combined with smoothquant-style per-channel scaling. This PR introduces a weight prepack path and a small kernel-lane allocator that lets the runtime fuse smoothquant dequantization into the kernel dispatch without materializing intermediate dequant tensors. Goals: 1) lower wall-clock latency for first-token and steady-state by removing memory-bound dequant copies, 2) reduce peak GPU memory for multi-tenant workloads by prepacking int8 weights in a compact layout and sharing lane metadata across batches, 3) keep compatibility with existing KV cache and continuous-batching pipelines. What changed (high-level): - New weight prepack module (src/runtime/kernel/int8_weight_prepack.cc/h) that produces a packed INT8 layout with per-channel scale/zero-point metadata optimized for our vectorized GEMM kernels. - Kernel adapter hooks (src/runtime/kernel/kernel_adapter.cc) to accept packed weights and apply smoothquant per-channel scaling on-the-fly inside the GEMM launcher when the model has smoothquant metadata. - Kernel lane allocator (src/runtime/scheduler/lane_allocator.cc/h) that assigns model weight lanes to worker threads/GPU streams so packed weights can be reused across microbatches without copying. - KV cache coordinator updates (src/runtime/scheduler/kv_cache_coordinator.cc) to pin KV cache blocks to the same lane affinity when the request uses pinned weights, avoiding cross-lane synchronization. - A shortfall fallback: when model uses dynamic shape patterns incompatible with lane reuse, runtime falls back to previous dequant-copy path automatically. Performance: microbenchmarks on a 32B decoder model (batch sizes 1..8, seq len 1..1024) show median token latency improvement of 9-16% at steady state and 18-28% for first-token latency on Ampere A100, with peak memory reduction of ~12% at high concurrency. Compatibility/risks: The change touches low-level kernel dispatch. We limited the surface by gating packed-weight paths behind a model feature flag and added runtime checks for per-channel metadata version. Rolling plan: staged canary rollout on Dedicated pools with a 2-hour canary window, monitor latency, token error-rate regressions, and memory counters. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for weight prepack and kernel adapter - [x] Integration test exercising smoothquant models through hosted API - [x] Performance bench scripts added - [x] Migration doc and feature flag gating - [x] Observability: added counters for lane cache hits/misses, packed-weight size. Related: ENG-3421 (quant kernel latency), ENG-3498 (kv cache affinity).
Marcus Li: Overall this looks solid; can you add a short docstring describing the layout produced by the prepack method? I had to trace through the code to confirm alignment guarantees.
Anika Rao: Added header docstrings and a diagram in prepack_smoothquant_notes.md per Marcus' request.
Diego Torres: The lane allocator is clever. Concern: potential starvation if many small requests contend for lanes. Suggest adding a fairness counter or aging policy.
Anika Rao: Added simple LRU aging policy and a unit test to simulate heavy small-request contention; PTAL.
Priya Nair (SRE): We need an observability signal for fallback-to-copy rate; ops will want to alert if it spikes after rollout.
Anika Rao: Added metrics runtime.quant.packed_weight_fallback_count and added to Console dashboards as part of the rollout task.
Marcus Li: CI failure on clang-format fixed in latest commit; approving pending perf numbers in canary.
Diego Torres: Verified no regression on tokenization edge-case tests; merging after canary.

Motivation: customer workloads with highly skewed request sizes (short chat messages interleaved with long context generations) were exposing p95/p99 latency spikes despite aggressive batching. Investigation showed two contributing factors: (1) the scheduler was coalescing tokens without awareness of prefix-hotness leading to oversized batches that pushed some requests into longer KV read paths, and (2) KV cache cold-misses for recently-used key ranges created stalls while the decoder waited on memory transfer.

This PR introduces two complementary runtime improvements to reduce tail latency and improve throughput: (A) a token-aware continuous batching scheduler (CompactScheduler) that maintains small fast-path batches for low-token requests while opportunistically coalescing larger requests, and (B) a shadow-KV prefetcher that tracks recent token window footprints and proactively stages KV shards into GPU-local memory for predicted next-chunk accesses. Together these reduce p95 by ~28% and p99 by ~41% on mixed chat/long-gen workloads in our internal canary.

What changed (high level):
- runtime/scheduling/compact_scheduler.{cc,h}: new scheduler implementing a token-aware policy with exponential backoff thresholds and a quick-path queue for <=8-token requests.
- runtime/kv/shadow_prefetch.{cc,h}: new lightweight prefetcher that observes KV index access traces and issues low-priority memcpy streams to warm caches. Prefetch policy is adaptive and throttles based on GPU memory pressure.
- runtime/attn/kernel_glue.cc: small refactor to expose a prefetch hook and a compact-batch fast path in the attention dispatch.
- runtime/attn/compact_attention.cu: new compact attention kernel optimized for small batch sizes and short sequences; uses fused rotary application inline with q/k computation to avoid extra memops. Kernel is mixed-precision friendly and contains guards for nvcc compute capability fallbacks.
- tests/perf/bench_compact_scheduler.py and bench/fixtures: new benchmarks and dataset to reproduce mixed short/long patterns.
- docs/perf/compact-scheduler.md: operational notes and recommended config knobs for Dedicated pools.

Checklist: 
- [x] Scheduler algorithm implemented with unit tests
- [x] Kernel integrated and smoke-tested on Ampere+ and Hopper GPUs
- [x] Prefetcher respects mem pressure and does not OOM in stress tests
- [x] Microbenchmarks and end-to-end canary run included

Benchmarks (canary, perf lab, NVIDIA A100, single-GPU):
- Mixed chat (80% <=8 tokens, 20% long gens): p50: 6.2ms (baseline 6.5ms), p95: 24.1ms (baseline 33.6ms), p99: 46.3ms (baseline 78.5ms)
- Long-only (seq_len=1024): throughput up 7% (tokens/sec) compared to baseline fused-attn path due to better kernel selection heuristics.
- GPU utilization: average utilization stable; memory copy overlap increased by ~12% due to low-priority prefetch streams.

Compatibility and safety:
- Prefetcher is opt-in via runtime config (redwood.runtime.shadow_prefetch = true) and off by default for Private deployments.
- CompactScheduler is behind a rollout flag; default behavior unchanged for existing clusters.
- No public API changes.

Follow-ups:
- Integrate with SmartRouting to use tenant-level workload profiles to further tune thresholds (ENG-4870).
- Explore combining shadow prefetcher with KV shard placement metadata to pre-stage only colocated shards.

References: Linear ENG-4721 (attn tail latency), bench/issue-312 memory-overlap investigation.

Maya Chen (author): Added prefetch.hit_ratio gauge and a stress test that toggles mem pressure (tests/perf/prefetch_mem_pressure_test.py).

Maya Chen (author): Added compile-time fallback and runtime check; CI run re-verified on sm_70 and sm_80 images.
Liam O'Connor: Approving pending CI — small nit: document the rollout flag in the release notes.

Motivation: We continue to see noisy tail latency alerts driven by high-cardinality context joins and duplicated context keys emitted from the serving runtime. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) an invocation-context denormalizer that produces a compact, canonical invocation record (reduces cardinality and deduplicates context blobs), and 2) a latency-signal attenuator that downweights highly noisy token-phase signals before they feed into alert windows and SLO rollups. Goals are to reduce alert fatigue, improve SLO signal-to-noise, and make downstream aggregation cheaper.

What this changes (high level):
- New ingestion pipeline stage (denormalizer) that consumes span/context messages and emits canonical invocation objects with stable keys and sampled context anchors. Configurable retention of full context blobs for 1% of invocations for debugging.
- Attenuator service applied as a deterministic pre-aggregation transform: computes a noise score per token-phase stream and applies weight clipping + hysteresis to reduce transient spikes affecting percentile-based SLOs.
- New dashboard: Obs/Invocations/Denorm & Attenuated-Latency summarizing pre/post attenuation p50/p95/p99, noise score histogram, and cost impact estimate.
- Small SDK/ingest changes: telemetry protobuf version bump, compatibility shim in event-forwarder.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc (ENG-5182) reviewed by SRE and telemetry.
- [x] Integration tests for denormalizer canonicalization.
- [x] E2E latency pipeline test with synthetic noisy traces.
- [x] Dashboard panels and runbook entry added.
- [x] Feature gated and rollout plan prepared (start at 1% tenants, ramp to 20% after 72h).

Risk and mitigation: Denormalizer changes keys used by some downstream consumers. To avoid breakage we emit both legacy and canonical keys for 7 days and provide a consumer migration lint. The attenuator is opt-in per-tenant via config; default rollout starts in observability staging.

Operational notes: The attenuator computes a "noise_score" (0-1) using inter-arrival variance and token-phase entropy; values >0.7 are clipped progressively. Config knobs: noise_window_ms, clip_threshold, hysteresis_ms. Rolling metrics available under telemetry.invocation.denorm.* and telemetry.invocation.attenuator.*.

Related: ENG-5223 (dashboard and SLO tuning), incident INC-2026-02 (noisy token-phase SLOs).

Maya Patel (author): Added test vectors in denorm.proto and a cross-SDK reference implementation in sdk/telemetry/compat_shim.go. Bumped default clip_threshold to 0.75 and made it tenant-configurable. Updated tests.

Maya Patel (author): Added p95 delta panel and rollout annotations. Added runbook steps to dashboards/README.md.

Adds a denormalized invocation context stream, a lightweight attenuation layer for noisy latency signals, and a dashboard for fast-path detection. Backwards compatible consumer APIs. No customer-facing API changes.

Reduced GPU peak workspace by up to 28% on long-context models via adaptive scratch allocator and deferred activation checkpoint scheduling. No API changes. Rollout: opt-in via runtime flag 'adaptive_scratch=on' followed by gradual default enablement after smoke validation.
Motivation: GPU workspace (scratch) and activation memory are significant cost drivers for long-context generation and multi-tenant Dedicated pools. Previous changes (arena tuning, static checkpointing) helped but left headroom for per-request adaptation and better interaction with KV cache and continuous batching. This PR implements two coordinated changes: 1) An adaptive scratch allocator that shrinks kernel scratch reservations on hot paths using real allocation traces and a light-weight eviction policy; 2) A deferred activation checkpoint scheduler that opportunistically delays checkpoint insertion until after the kernel selection pass when sequence-to-sequence and KV cache usage are known. Design summary: The adaptive scratch allocator records per-model per-kernel high-water marks over rolling windows and exposes a soft cap that kernels consult at selection time; if the soft cap would be exceeded we attempt two actions: pick a lower-scratch kernel variant or apply a temporary micro-batch split. The deferred checkpoint scheduler moves most activation checkpointing decisions out of the eager graph transform and into the runtime scheduling stage so decisions can use real batch sizes, kv-cache presence, and current scratch headroom. This reduces over-checkpointing on requests that will hit the KV cache and reduces worst-case workspace pressure. Implementation notes: - runtime/inference/scratch_allocator.cpp: new AdaptiveScratchManager, hot-path lock-free counters, bounded trace buffer. - runtime/inference/checkpoint_scheduler.cpp: new DeferredCheckpointPlanner, heuristics to trade memory vs. compute (default: aim for <=15% additional compute). - runtime/kernels/kernel_selector.cpp: kernel variants now expose 'scratch_estimate' and 'checkpoint_safe' metadata; selection integrates with AdaptiveScratchManager. - runtime/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cc: minor changes to expose batching window to planner. - tests/perf/scratch_memory_bench.py: synthetic long-context scenarios across models (gpt-style, encoder-decoder) and KV cache toggles. - docs/ops/scratch-tuning.md: operational guidance and rollout recipe. Tests and results: microbenchmarks show peak GPU workspace reduction of 18-28% across 4 tested models at 32k context; tail latency impact is +4% median, +9% 95th when the allocator picks lower-scratch kernels; overall token throughput for large batches unchanged within noise. KV cache interplay: requests with warm KV cache see much larger benefits because deferred checkpointing avoids storing activations that are unnecessary for cached steps. Safety/rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag 'adaptive_scratch' and 'deferred_ckpt' (both default off). We added a gradual rollout plan: enable in Canary region, observe memory headroom and OOMs for 72h, then opt-in to Dedicated pools with autoscaler guards. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] perf scripts, [x] docs updated, [x] rollout plan, [x] security review (no secrets). Backwards compatibility: none; internal only. Related: ENG-3245 (workspace reductions initiative), ENG-3299 (kv-cache improvement spike).
Diego Ramos: This looks promising. Can you add a safety circuit for cases where the allocator oscillates and causes repeated micro-batch splits? Suggest a backoff cooldown per-model.
Maya Lin: Added a cooldown mechanism (AdaptiveScratchManager::cooldown_ms) and tested with aggressive allocation spikes. Benchmarks included in bench_results/2026-02-20.
Lucas Nguyen: The deferred checkpointing change is invasive. How does this interact with tiled-kv cache eviction? Please outline any assumptions about KV lifecycle.
Maya Lin: Deferred planner consults KVCache::is_warmed(request_id) during planning. If KV lifecycle indicates eviction in same window, we conservatively keep checkpoints. Documented in scratch-tuning.md.
Serena Park: CI failed on linux-gpu-lint initially, some style fixes needed in scratch_allocator.h.
Maya Lin: Fixed style nits and added clang-format CI enforcement for runtime/* files.
Merged to main after two rounds of review and CI stabilization. Feature gates left off by default; ops will enable in canary on 2026-02-25. No regressions observed in e2e smoke tests; memory headroom improved on Dedicated canary by ~22% on average.

Motivation: production traffic showed two related failure modes for long-lived streaming sessions: (1) transient host-level stalls cause long tail reconnects that then overwhelm downstream model capacity during bursts, and (2) aggressive client-side aborts lead to lost tool invocations and inconsistent outputs when servers enforce a hard immediate cancel. This PR introduces an adaptive reconnect hedging probe plus a configurable client-abort window with soft-abort semantics to reduce both overloading and spurious tool call duplication while preserving OpenAI-compat streaming semantics.

What this changes: adds a backpressure-aware hedging probe that issues a parallel light reconnect attempt when server-side processing latency crosses a workload-adaptive threshold; introduces a soft-abort window on the server that accepts a short grace period after a client cancel to complete idempotent tool calls and to produce a deterministic final token; surfaces two new API-facing config knobs (stream.reconnect_hedging.enabled, stream.client_abort_window_ms) exposed via the OpenAI-compat adapter with sane defaults and canary gating.

Compatibility and rollouts: default behavior mirrors current semantics (hedging disabled, abort_window_ms=0) until feature-flagged for canary cohort; OpenAI compatibility adapter preserves event ordering and will emit an explicit event type "hedge_probe" on the wire for observability consumers. No breaking changes for existing SDKs.

Testing and validation: unit tests for hedging probe scheduling and probe cancellation; integration flake tests that simulate stall->hedge->failover scenarios; long-running soak test at 10% canary on dedicated infra for 48h. Benchmarks show a 22% reduction in 99.9th percentile session reconnection latency under synthetic stall injections and a ~2% median increase in extraneous probe traffic which is controlled by adaptive thresholds.

Metrics and observability: new metrics: stream.hedge.probes_issued, stream.hedge.probe_success_rate, stream.abort.soft_window_accepts, stream.abort.soft_window_rejects. Added dashboard tile and alert: HedgeProbeFailureRate > 1% for 5m.

Related work: follows design notes in Linear ENG-1871 and references prior server-lease work (ENG-1369) for session fencing. Linked support ticket SUP-8122 for a customer incident that motivated larger abort window experimentation.

Rollout plan: merge to main, with a behind-flag canary (10% traffic -> 50% -> 100%) over two weeks. Monitor hedging probe success rate and tool duplication counters before enabling wider abort window (>250ms).
Carlos Mendes (requested changes): Can we make the default abort_window_ms 0 to avoid surprising customers? Also request an explicit note in the docs about idempotency guarantees for tool calls.
Marina Geller (author reply): I changed the default to 0 and added a section in docs/streaming-lifecycle.md outlining idempotency expectations and recommended customer configuration. Also added a feature-flag gating plan to rollout notes.
Aisha Patel (nit): Please add more logging when a hedge probe is cancelled due to successful primary progress; that's useful for our trace correlation dashboards.
Marina Geller (author reply): Added probe_cancel logging with trace_id and probe_latency fields; updated tests to assert logging emitted.
Evan Liu (approved): Verified integration test harness reproduces stall scenario and sees expected hedging behavior. Metrics emitted as described. Approving for merge after CI green.
Adds adaptive reconnect hedging probes and a configurable client abort soft-window to reduce spurious reconnect storms and preserve deterministic tool finalization. Backwards-compatible and disabled by default.
