Motivation and summary: This PR implements a dedicated parameter translation layer in the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions compatibility adapter and adds a lightweight tool-capability negotiation handshake for function/tool calling. Our goal is to reduce edge-case mismatches between client v1 params and Redwood's internal runtime while improving streaming resilience when tool calls are present. Context: customers have hit subtle regressions when mixing stop arrays, logprobs requests, and function/tool calls across streaming and non-streaming paths. Previously we tried to fold fixes into the stream coordinator; this approach centralizes translation rules and capability negotiation to make behavior deterministic and easier to test. What this PR does (high level): - Add a v1->internal param translation module that: maps role conventions (role aliases/namespaces), normalizes stop semantics (string vs array vs null), and synthesizes logprob requests into internal token-level profiling hooks without enabling expensive backprop-like work paths. - Introduce a tool-capability negotiator: during stream handshake we emit a concise capability token that advertises whether the server can perform structured tool calls in-stream (framed tool output) vs deferred tool-resolution. Clients that lack parity fall back to non-streamed tool call semantics. - Streaming stability changes: fragment coalescing window expanded for fragments that contain a tool invocation token; added a 100ms minimum inter-fragment delay on tool fragments to avoid parser races in clients that buffer up to N fragments. - Structured output: introduce an optional v1 flag `structured_response=true` (back-ported via translation) that generates a framed JSON envelope for tool outputs and assistant final messages, preserving both role metadata and function-call metadata in a single `envelope` object. - Stop/logprob harmonization: implement a normalization pass that: removes duplicate stop tokens, ensures stop precedence with function-call terminators, and emits a per-response `logprob_summary` when clients request `logprobs` while streaming (we avoid full token-by-token logprob streaming to control overhead). - Backwards compat notes: translation layer is conservative—if an unknown or conflicting param is provided we log a compat warning and fall back to historical behavior. Tests and coverage: included unit tests for role aliasing, stop array coalescing, capability negotiation handshake, and an integration test that runs the streaming handshake + function call against a mock tool. Checklist: - [x] Parameter translation module implemented with feature flag (off by default in non-v1 flows) - [x] Tool-capability negotiator added to stream handshake - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Docs inline comments and a short note to the compatibility guide - [x] Benchmarked: small regression (<1% latency p95) on standard load - [x] E2E validation against OpenAI-compat test vectors Caveats and follow-ups: - The structured_response flag is experimental; we will gate it by a flag until we verify interop with beta SDKs. - We observed a flaky test in the first CI run related to websocket teardown; fixed by adding a bounded close timeout and a retry in the mock harness. Related Linear items and followups: ENG-2419 (v1 compat parameter gaps), ENG-2475 (streaming functioncall parser hardening), ENG-2631 (structured output evaluation). Links: Linear/ENG-2419, RFC:docs/rfcs/v1-param-translation.md
Priya Singh: Can we avoid enabling structured_response by default? Suggest gate behind feature flag. (addressed)
Diego Alvarez: The logprob_summary approach looks good, but add a size limit to prevent huge payloads in chat-heavy workloads. (added 2KB cap)
Tom Bennett: Streaming fragmentation change may impact client SDKs that assume minimal latency; added note to compat guide and increase coalescing tests. (ack)
Maya Patel: Reply - feature flag preserved, added size cap and docs. Also added integration test exercising SDK-side reconnects.

Motivation: reduce end-to-end token latency and improve throughput for causal generation on Ampere+ GPUs by combining a FlashAttention v3-style fused attention kernel with an in-kernel rotary/rope application and a KV-cache-aware scheduling path. This PR introduces a new kernel that applies rotary embeddings and key/value interleaving inside the attention compute to eliminate separate transforms and extra device-to-device memory ops. It also adds a lightweight scheduler that prefers in-place KV layouts for streaming workloads and steps down to the v2 codepath for compatibility on unsupported hardware.

What changed (high level): fused attention kernel (flashattn_v3.cu) that: 1) applies rotary/rope rotations inside the per-head attention compute; 2) performs QKV projection packing and interleaves KV to match the KV-cache layout used by the runtime; 3) reduces kernel launches by merging scale, softmax + dropout + output matmul into a single fused pipeline for causal workloads. Added a kv-aware scheduler that selects the in-kernel-interleave path when streaming token rate and sequence patterns indicate benefit. Added fallbacks and runtime feature detection (compute capability, shared memory limits) so existing deployments remain functional when hardware does not support the new kernel.

Benchmarks: Microbenchmarks run on p4d/p3 and A100 infra. Representative improvements observed on language-modeling workloads (causal decode, batch size 1, short prompt expansions): p50 latency -18% to -27% (depending on seq_len), throughput (tokens/sec) +12% to +24% for short/medium contexts. For longer context (>=4096) p95 latency improvements were smaller (5-10%) due to memory-bound stages, but kernel-level GPU SM utilization improved by ~22%. Perf test harness added under tests/bench to reproduce these numbers and a CI perf check that validates no regressions vs a baseline (reference v2) within noise.

Compatibility and rollout: No API or wire-level change. The new kernel is optional and selected by runtime heuristics. We added a feature flag REDWOOD_USE_FLASHATTN_V3 to force the new path for testing. On merge the plan is a staged canary: 5% of hosted inference traffic -> 25% -> full, plus Dedicated canaries on reserve clusters. Observability: new tracing spans for kernel selection and KV-cache hit ratio, and dashboard updates in docs/perf/flashattn_v3.md. Fallthrough path keeps previous behavior to avoid regressions.

Checklist: implementations, unit and integration tests, bench harness, docs, canary plan, release notes drafted. Related Linear tasks: ENG-4257 (kernel integration), ENG-4312 (scheduler heuristics).
Liam: Can we guarantee numerical equivalence for rotary application? Request unit tests to compare against v2 for several dtypes and sequence lengths.
Author (Maya): Added test_rotary_fuse.py with deterministic inputs and float32/float16 checks; differences within eps for float16 confirmed. Added doc comment about fp16 rounding behavior.
Sofia: Concern about shared memory footprint on 80GB A100 vs 40GB variants. Suggest runtime detection and fallback. 
Author: Implemented compute-cap detection; kernel chooses smaller tile sizes when shared mem is constrained and falls back to v2 if limits exceeded.
Devon: CI perf check failed initially on cuda-nightly due to ABI mismatch with a helper macro. Fixed by removing inline asm and adding compatibility shim. Reran CI, all green.
Performance: Added optional FlashAttention-v3 fused kernel that applies rotary embeddings in-kernel and interleaves KV for streaming workloads; reduces kernel launches and improves token throughput by ~12-24% on Ampere-class GPUs. Safety: runtime feature detection and fallback to v2 ensure no behavior changes on unsupported hardware.
Canary plan: enable REDWOOD_USE_FLASHATTN_V3 for 5% hosted traffic; monitor p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU SM util, kv_cache_hit_ratio. Rollback plan: flip feature flag to false to resume v2 path.

Context: Customers using the OpenAI /v1/chat.completions compatibility layer reported subtle divergences in streamed payloads when tool calls and stop tokens interacted with role aliasing. Motivation: Align the stream framing, stop sentinel priority, and logprob damping so that downstream OpenAI-compatible clients see deterministic stop behavior and compact JSON payloads without duplicating role metadata. This PR implements a consensus policy that (1) coalesces adjacent empty role tokens emitted during stream stitching, (2) applies a stop-priority resolver that prefers explicit stop-array hits over heuristic token-level stop scoring, and (3) slims response envelopes by removing duplicated role/name fields in fragmented frames while preserving a final full-message envelope. Changes: runtime: stop_priority_resolver added with deterministic comparator for stop-array vs token-logprob; stream-coalescer: merges adjacent delta frames that only contain role/name to a single header frame; envelope-slimmer: drops redundant role/name on intermediate fragments, re-inserts on final flush; compatibility: chatv1 adapter mapping tweaked to prefer explicit stop matches when stop array present; tests: added regression tests for streaming a tool call followed immediately by a stop token; docs: updated API compatibility notes and streaming framing appendix. Motivation: short-sequence INT8 workloads (chat snippets, low-context queries) were showing suboptimal vector unit utilization and extra memory traffic due to per-token misalignment and an extra dequant/rescale op introduced by the smoothquant-style preprocessing. This PR introduces a per-token "token-lane coalescer" tiling strategy together with a fused lightweight lane re-scaler ("smoothscale") that folds into the dequant path to eliminate an intermediate kernel launch. The work targets the runtime kernel layer and scheduler hints so the continuous batching subsystem can coalesce token lanes before packing, and the KV packer aligns INT8 KV blocks to 128B boundaries to avoid unaligned device loads. Key outcomes: +18% steady-state throughput on A100 for short (<=64) sequences on our internal int8-Llama-like model, 6–12% reduction in tail latency P95, and peak memory bandwidth savings that reduce overall token cost. Approach: 1) Add token-lane tiler kernel that groups tokens across requests into per-lane chunks to improve SIMD utilization; 2) Implement smoothscale fusion inside the int8 dequant kernel (single combined pass) rather than a separate op; 3) Update kv_packer to emit aligned strides and expose an alignment-aware load codepath in the int8 kernels; 4) Add scheduler hints to continuous_batcher so batcher prefers coalescing lanes when sequence histogram indicates many short requests; 5) Provide runtime feature flag and canary rollout path for Dedicated clusters. Compatibility: runtime exposes both legacy and fused paths behind a dynamic feature flag; fallback to legacy path if kernel not available or alignment mismatch occurs. Tests & safety: unit tests for numerical equivalence within epsilon on validation prompt sets, perf benchmarks in CI (short/medium/long histograms), and a staged canary rollout (10% capacity) before full merge. Related Linear tasks: ENG-4821, ENG-4867. Checklist: [x] kernel implementation [x] scheduler hint [x] kv packer alignment [x] tests & perf harness [x] docs note [x] canary rollout plan. Links: design doc (internal): /docs/design/int8-token-lane-coalescer.md, perf run: internal.perf/243501, linear: ENG-4821.
Jordan Kim (review): please add counters for coalesced lanes and a metric for alignment misses; also verify fp8 reference results remain within tolerance.
Priya Nair (author): added lane_coalesce_count and kv_alignment_miss counters, and extended numeric tests against fp8 reference with 1e-4 tolerance.
Lina Ortega (review): observed a 3% regression for medium sequences in one perf run — can you add a scheduler threshold to avoid coalescing when median seq > 128?
Priya Nair (author): added median-based threshold heuristic to continuous_batcher; updated perf harness and re-ran benchmarks.
Ethan Zhao (approval): verified canary perf dashboards, CI green; approves and recommends squash-merge once final CI completes.
Short sequences (<=64 tokens): +18% throughput, P95 latency -8ms; Medium (65-256): neutral to +2% depending on histogram; Long (>256): no change. Memory bandwidth reduced by ~9% on observed kernels. CI perf runs attached: internal.perf/243501/results.json
Feature gated; canary to 10% of Dedicated capacity for 48h with perf and correctness guardrails; if stable, increase to 50% for 72h then full enable. Automatic rollback if numerical regression >1e-3 or throughput regression >3% on canary traces.
Performance: ~+18% throughput for INT8 short-sequence workloads; rollout controlled by runtime feature flag; no public API change; recommend canary before Dedicated-wide enable.
This PR was intentionally conservative about FP8 path interaction — the fused kernel supports a flag-driven scale-flow compatible with both INT8 and FP8 microkernels. Future work: investigate cross-request KV packing to further reduce loads for microbatching scenarios.

payload.body:
Motivation: We have multiple downstream needs that couldn't be satisfied by the legacy model capability schema: (1) lightweight, per-request runtime hints that the routing layer and serving runtime can use without deserializing the full model profile; (2) a transparent metering knob for tool/function calling (customers asked for per-invocation crediting separate from token billing); and (3) richer guidance for streaming fallbacks so clients can degrade more gracefully when a model variant switches to a lower-throughput tier. This PR introduces three related surfaces: capability_headers, function_call_credit, and streaming_degradation_policy, alongside an OpenAI-compatible shim that surfaces structured-output hints in /v1/models list responses.

Summary of changes (high level):
- API: Add optional capability_headers map to /v1/models and /v1/models/:id responses. These are short key/value runtime hints intended for fast routing decisions (examples: "supports_prefix_cache": "true", "max_prefetch_tokens": "256").
- Catalog schema: Deprecate legacy capability_schema.v1 (kept as legacy_capabilities for migration) and introduce capability_schema.v2 that references compact headers + full capability document. Migration docs added.
- Billing: Introduce function_call_credit as a first-class optional numeric field on model profiles and endpoints. This allows the billing system to attribute cost for tool/function call ops independently; SDKs and console will display credits usage.
- Streaming: Add streaming_degradation_policy on model profiles to expose a list of ordered fallbacks and suggested partial-output tokens thresholds (helps clients decide when to switch to a summarized streaming path). Also include preferred_prefetch_hint to suggest prefix caching window.
- OpenAI compat: Update the /v1/models listing returned by the OpenAI-compat shim to include capability_headers and structured_output_hints under the "capabilities" umbrella so downstream OpenAI-compatible clients can discover behavior without touching Redwood-specific endpoints.
- Docs & SDK: Docs page describing migration, examples for reading capability_headers and consuming streaming_degradation_policy; Python and TypeScript SDK surfaces to parse new fields.

Commits (summary):
- commit 1: api: extend model list + get handlers to populate capability_headers and streaming_degradation_policy (handlers and serializers)
- commit 2: catalog: add models_v2 schema, migration script to copy legacy_capabilities into full_profile and generate default headers
- commit 3: billing: record function_call_credit into usage events and expose in billing UI (console changes)
- commit 4: sdk/docs: parse helpers and docs for migration and examples

Files changed (representative):
- src/api/handlers/models_list.go (updated serializer and OpenAI-compat shim)
- src/catalog/schemas/models_v2.json (new compact schema)
- tools/migrations/migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go (migration script)
- services/billing/credits.go (add function_call_credit aggregation)
- console/src/components/model/ModelDetails.tsx (show capability headers and credits)
- sdk/python/redwood/models.py (new fields + helper parser)
- docs/migrations/capability_headers_migration.md (migration and rollback guide)

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests: added for serializer and parser behavior (capability_headers omitted vs present), billing aggregation tests for function_call_credit.
- Integration: end-to-end test in perf-canary that validates streaming_degradation_policy is honored by the router under simulated capacity pressure; canary shows no increase in 95p latency on main model variants.
- Backwards compatibility: /v1/models still returns legacy_capabilities field for consumers that haven't migrated; the OpenAI-compat shim prefers capability_headers but will fall back to legacy_capabilities when capability_headers is absent.

Migration strategy & rollout:
- Stage 1 (canary): populate capability_headers from existing full capabilities via migration script; run canary for 2 days to ensure no regression in routing or billing.
- Stage 2 (gradual): expose new headers to 20% of API responses; monitor routing decisions and SDK parsing errors.
- Stage 3 (opt-in enforcement): allow customers to opt-in to strict schema validation via a console toggle (default off).
- Final: Deprecate legacy schema via announcement; grace period until 2026-06-01, after which legacy_capabilities may be removed for new write operations.

Review conversation (condensed):
- Owen Park: "Large change — please ensure migration script is idempotent and add a safety flag so we can revert on dataset problems." — Author: "Migration is idempotent; added --dry-run and --cutover flags in migrate_capabilities_v1_to_v2.go; documented in migration md."
- Lina Gomez: "Need to ensure function_call_credit can't be negative and that default is 0 where absent; also clarify how it interacts with token billing." — Author: "Validation added; billing pipeline will emit both tokens and function_call_credit events. Release notes updated to clarify pricing semantics."
- Harriet Zhao: "Does the streaming_degradation_policy open us up to oscillation if multiple routers act on hints?" — Author: "Router change includes a small randomized jitter and a dead-time to prevent oscillation; added comment in routing code and unit test."
- QA (Slack): reported one flaky test in console snapshot related to ModelDetails layout — fixed by stabilizing test data ordering in the SDK.

CI summary: initial run had lint warnings (long line in models_list.go) and one flaky integration test; both addressed in follow-up commits. Final status: all checks passed (unit, lint, integration, e2e canary). Performance canary showed stable tail latency; billing integration tests validated function_call_credit emitted for simulated tool calls.

Rollout notes for operators:
- The migration tool writes a migration_log to S3; if any migration errors occur, the --rollback flag will reverse schema updates made to the catalog DB.
- Feature gate: runtime.capability_headers (default: enabled for all API nodes in next release). If issues appear, ops can disable gate per region to return legacy behavior immediately.

Decision rationale and follow-ups:
- We intentionally kept capability_headers compact and stringly-typed to avoid heavyweight schema churn; full capabilities remain available for deep inspection and compatibility with existing tooling.
- Follow-ups: ENG-2639 to add UI visualization for streaming_degradation_policy, ENG-2670 to instrument per-function-call credit telemetry in the billing dashboard, and ENG-2692 to add a half-life cache invalidation for capability_headers to support fast rollbacks.

Merge outcome: Squash merge by Lina Gomez on 2026-02-19 after approvals from all reviewers and green CI. Release note entry drafted and scheduled for the 2026-02 minor release.
Add new capability header fields (capability_headers) and introduce function_call_credit metric for per-call accounting; deprecate legacy capability schema v1 with migration path; add streaming degradation policy and prefetch hint support. Non-breaking for read-only clients; write-migration recommended before 2026-06-01.

Motivation: private-installer releases need reproducible, auditable bundle indices and the ability to rotate signed metadata without causing client churn. This PR introduces a TUF-inspired rotation step in the CI build pipeline and a release-bundle orchestrator that assembles, signs, and publishes deltas and full bundles for VPC/on-prem installers.

What this changes: adds a new pipeline stage (bundle-orchestrator) that: 1) collects artifacts from build stages (helm charts, terraform modules, installer images), 2) generates a versioned release-bundle manifest, 3) publishes a TUF-style metadata tree and timestamp file, 4) rotates signing keys via cosign/HSM hooks, and 5) publishes a signed index and per-arch delta packages for faster upgrades. The orchestrator is configurable by env and supports dry-run, fast-forward-only, and emergency-rollback modes.

Key design notes: we adopted a minimal TUF-like metadata structure (root, targets, snapshot, timestamp) to avoid introducing a full TUF dependency in the installer; metadata is canonical JSON with deterministic sorting. Signing is pluggable: by default the pipeline uses cosign with keyless ephemeral annotations for PRs and KMS-backed keys for release branches. A lightweight provenance record (SBOM link + build-info) is attached to each target entry.

Checklist/QA: - [x] unit tests for metadata canonicalization - [x] integration tests for cosign sign/verify using test KMS - [x] e2e pipeline run on staging publishing a full bundle and delta - [x] upgrade test from 1.8.x -> 1.9.x using delta packages - [x] rollback test using timestamp truncation

Rollout plan: land to main behind feature flag CI_BUNDLE_ORCHESTRATOR=enabled. Run 3 weekly canary releases to staging, monitor installer clients for metadata fetch and verify latencies. After stable canaries, enable on release branch and perform signed release.

Rollback plan: orchestrator publishes incremental timestamped manifests. To roll back, operator may set ORCHESTRATOR_ROLLBACK_TO=<timestamp> which truncates timestamp and snapshot to a previous signed state; the pipeline validates metadata chain before publishing. In emergency the service supports publishing an emergency root rotation with operator approval.

Related: ENG-4128 (bundle rotation), ENG-4187 (installer upgrade reliability), SUP-1223 (customer report: failed private upgrades), docs PR will follow to document operator commands and KMS setup.
Ben Carlson: Can we gate the root rotation behind the KMS approval flow? I want explicit operator ack before publishing. Author: added ORCHESTRATOR_FORCE_ROOT_ROTATION env and added audit log entry; kept manual switch for release branches.
Isabel Wu: The canonicalization needs deterministic ordering across go versions. Are we pinning encoding? Author: using go-jsoncanonical (vendor) and added tests across 1.19/1.20 CI matrix.
Diego Marquez: Delta publishing looks good but add verification step on consumer side; otherwise a corrupt delta could break upgrades. Author: added post-publish verification job and consumer verify script to charts.
CI Bot: pipeline passed on staging run #42 with cosign signatures validated.
Security Reviewer: confirm cosign key rotation docs and KMS IAM policy samples added. Author: pushed docs/operator/release-orchestrator.md and samples/iam-policy.json in a follow-up commit.
Adds a TUF-style metadata orchestration stage to the private-installer CI that enables signed bundle rotation, delta publishing for faster upgrades, and operator-controlled rollback. Defaults to disabled; operators must enable via CI_BUNDLE_ORCHESTRATOR. See docs/operator/release-orchestrator.md for setup and KMS guidance.
Squash-merged after 2 approvals. Staging canary run successful; no regressions observed in installer metadata fetch paths.
create docs PR to expand KMS examples and RBAC
announce in #release-automation and schedule operator training
add telemetry for metadata fetch latencies and cosign verification failures
This PR intentionally avoids pulling in the full TUF Go library to keep the installer's runtime footprint small; we implement a compatible metadata layout sufficient for index rotation and verification. Future follow-ups may migrate to a full TUF implementation if needed.

Motivation: production workloads show a 6-12% token throughput regression on long-context LLMs when enabling smoothquant+int8 fallback paths with KV cache misses. This PR introduces a hierarchical dequant adapter and a KV-prefetch adapter that together reduce dequant overhead and friction with continuous batching and token coalescing.
Goals: 1) reduce per-token dequant/copy overhead when parts of the KV cache are warm; 2) make dequant fusion decisions hierarchical (layer+head) to avoid over-dequantizing for short-lived keys; 3) integrate a lightweight prefetch adapter that warms hot-key ranges ahead of predicted token sequences; 4) keep changes backward-compatible and gated behind a runtime flag.
Summary of changes: - runtime/dequant: add HierarchicalDequantAdapter that tracks dequantization heat per-layer and per-head, allowing selective in-place requant/dequant where kernel-safe. When severity is low, the adapter defers full float32 dequant until the KV window crosses a threshold. - runtime/kv: add KVPrefetchAdapter which subscribes to the continuous-batcher affinity hints and issues speculative prefetches for likely-to-be-requested KV windows; includes a small LRU predictor for token prefix patterns. - scheduler: continuous batcher now emits affinity hints (soft, weighted) to the KVPrefetchAdapter; affinity windowing tuned to prefer low-latency microbatches. - kernels: introduce two small microkernel entrypoints under runtime/kernels/quant: fast_path_requant_inplace (INT8) and safe_path_dequant (FP16-aware), and a planner to choose between them using adapter signals. - telemetry: new metrics (dequant.defer.count, kv.prefetch.success_rate, batch.affinity.match_rate) and two new debug traces for heatmap visualization. - config: runtime flag runtime.experiments.hierarchical_dequant and safe defaults off for hosted customers; enabled by default on internal nightly clusters.
Backwards compatibility and rollout: This change is behind a feature flag and includes runtime fallbacks to the existing dequant path. We opted for a conservative rollout: alpha->canary->general based on kv.prefetch.success_rate and downstream latency SLOs.
Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for adapter logic and kernel decision planner - [x] E2E perf harness against canary models (gpt-large) - [x] Metrics and dashboards updated - [x] Docs note in the runtime ops guide
Key results from local e2e runs: - End-to-end token throughput +9.7% on long-context (8k) runs with moderate KV locality - Median p99 latency reduced by 5ms in microbatch-heavy traces - Prefetch hit rate averaged 78% when affinity hints were stable - No measurable regression on short-context (<512) runs
Implementation notes and rationale: - Hierarchical dequant: previous boolean per-layer dequant switches were too coarse. We observed cases where heads in the same layer had differing reuse patterns; per-head heuristics capture this and allow reuse of requantized tensors. - Prefetch policy: predictor is intentionally tiny - a 512-entry circular LRU keyed by prefix fingerprint - to keep memory + compute overhead negligible. We found a heavier model caused more harm than benefit in mixed workloads. - Kernel selection: added microkernel entrypoints rather than overhauling existing kernels to reduce risk and simplify rollback. The planner invokes the fast_path_requant_inplace only if adapters report heat > threshold and batch size >= batch threshold.
Commits summary: - a9b3f6f Add HierarchicalDequantAdapter and adapter API hooks - 1c4d8b2 Implement KVPrefetchAdapter and LRU prefix predictor - 5e2a41c Add kernel fast_path_requant_inplace and safe_path_dequant entrypoints - d77f9a1 Integrate affinity hints in continuous batcher and wire adapters - 9f83c10 Add metrics, dashboards config and feature flag gating - f2b7e33 Tests: adapter unit tests and perf harness job config
Changed areas (high level): - runtime/dequant/hierarchical_adapter.{cc,h} - runtime/kv/kv_prefetch_adapter.{cc,h} - runtime/kernels/quant/fast_path_requant.cu - runtime/kernels/quant/safe_path_dequant.cu - runtime/scheduler/continuous_batcher.cc (affinity hints) - runtime/telemetry/metrics_registry.cc (new metrics) - tools/perf/harnesss/canary_config.yaml - docs/runtime/flags.md (feature flag docs)
Review conversation: Reviewer Marcus Hall: "Nice reduction in churn. Two asks: (1) can the hierarchical heat table be bounded memory-wise? (2) please add a safety net when prefetch queue stalls." Author (Priya): "Heat table uses a small 64-entry per-layer ring with decayed counters; I'll add more comments and a defensive backpressure check for the prefetch queue." Reviewer Lena Cho: "Kernel chooser looks sound but add a tracing span around the decision and the adapter signals for easier postmortems." Author: "Added trace spans and included metrics for decision counts." Reviewer Benito Cruz: "CI flaked on the nightly fp8 allocator test; is that related?" Author: "Unrelated; CI job had an upstream allocator race. I re-ran the job and it passed. I also added a short retry in the test harness to prevent flakes."
CI summary: - build: pass - unit-tests: pass - integration-tests: flaky -> rerun -> pass - perf-harness: pass (baseline comparison recorded) - lint: pass - security-scan: pass
The integration-tests initially failed on allocator races in unrelated tests; rerun succeeded.
Perf impact: internal canary runs show throughput improvement of +6 to +12% depending on workload locality. The prefetched warmups reduce cold-KV penalty for long sequences.
Rollout plan: - enable on nightly clusters for 48h - enable on alpha (internal) with runtime flag enabled by default for internal accounts - monitor kv.prefetch.success_rate and latency SLOs for two weeks - gradual canary in hosted clusters, roll back if kv.prefetch.success_rate < 60% or 99th percentile latency regress > 5%
Release notes: "Introduce a hierarchical dequant adapter and lightweight KV prefetching to reduce dequant overhead and improve token throughput for long-context workloads. Disabled by default for hosted customers; opt-in via runtime.experiments.hierarchical_dequant."
Merge strategy: squash and merge into main.
Follow-up work: - experiments to tune head-level heat decay schedules - A/B test on fp8-safe_path to explore more opportunistic FP8 use - dashboards to correlate prefix fingerprints with prefetch success rate

payload.body:
Motivation: continuous_batcher suffered from micro-slot fragmentation under bursty, small-request workloads. Small requests frequently became isolated slots and prevented efficient KV cache pin warmups; combined with sharp credit decay this produced starvation for medium-size requests and higher P99 tail. Our goal was to reduce fragmentation without increasing average latency or violating SLOs. Solution summary: introduce a lightweight 'slot coalescence bank' (coalesce_bank) that temporarily accepts sub-threshold partial slots for short adaptive windows, re-emit them as consolidated slots when either (a) enough compatible slots arrive, (b) a jittered soft-timeout expires, or (c) a precedence credit threshold is hit. Key elements: 1) coalesce_bank: a bounded per-worker ring that indexes partial slots by locality keys (KV pin fingerprint + model variant) and arrival age; entries are mergeable when combined token count < target_batch_size*1.2 and model/kernel affinity matches. 2) smoothing of admission credits: credit decay function replaced with a two-stage exponential->linear decay to avoid abrupt de-prioritization after transient bursts. 3) jittered adaptive soft-timeouts: soft timeouts are jittered per-coalesce key using a hash-based offset to avoid synchronized flush storms. 4) KV pin-awareness: when pins are present, bank holds higher-priority merges for a slightly longer hold window to improve cache warmup benefit. 5) safety knobs: feature-flag gating, bounded memory accounting, and a fast-path bypass for hard-deadline requests (deadline flag present). Implementation notes: changes are localized to continuous_batcher/scheduler.go and a new continuous_batcher/coalesce_bank.go with 280 lines of implementation and unit tests; runtime/kv_cache/pinning.go updated to expose a non-blocking hint API; metrics and tracing hooks added to metrics/batcher_metrics.go and tracing/span_tags.go; a perf harness and benchmark slot_coalesce_benchmark.go added under perf/bench. Observability: new metrics coalesce.bank.size, coalesce.bank.merge_count, coalesce.bank.expire_flush_count, admission.credit_smoothness_ratio. Benchmarks and results: controlled perf lab (8xA100 nodes) using mixed small/medium chat workload. Compared to main baseline: - 12% P99 reduction on total request latency for mixed burst workloads - 9% median latency improvement for microburst scenarios - 18% throughput improvement at same tail latency target (SLO: P99 < 220ms) - KV pin hit-rate improved by +7 percentage points during warmup phases. Safety and regressions: initial canary revealed a race in coalesce_bank eviction path (fixed in follow-up commit by adding cooperative backoff and a CAS-protected index). Load tests at scale (staging cluster) show no change to memory P95 and acceptable additional metric cardinality. Testing: unit tests for merge semantics and edge cases; deterministic fuzz tests for timeout jitter; integration canary against dedicated pool; end-to-end perf harness. Rollout plan: behind feature flag 'coalesce_bank_v1' with staged rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 75% -> 100% per-region with automated rollback on >5% P99 regression or >1% request error increase. Documentation: docs/cookbook/slot_coalescence.md added with explanation of flags and tuning knobs. Checklist: - [x] design doc + perf plan referenced in ENG-2984 - [x] unit + fuzz tests - [x] staging canary run - [x] metrics + alerts updated - [x] feature flag gating - [x] rollback plan

2026-02-16 Ava Martinez: Added perf harness commit; results summarized in description.
2026-02-17 Priya Desai: Can the coalesce bank cause head-of-line blocking for large requests? We should ensure bypass path exists.
2026-02-17 Ava Martinez: Bypass hard-deadline and large-request fast-path implemented; added unit test.
2026-02-18 Liam OConnor: I saw a flake in "EvictionPathRaceTest" during CI, looks like a double-free in eviction callback.
2026-02-19 Ava Martinez: Root cause was non-atomic index rotation; added CAS and cooperative backoff, updated tests.
2026-02-20 Jonah Kim: Metrics look good. One nit: reduce cardinality of coalesce key label, use coarse fingerprint.
2026-02-21 Ava Martinez: Switched to 64-bit coarse fingerprint.

Introduce 'slot coalescence bank' to group sub-threshold micro-batches, smoothing admission credits and jittered soft-timeouts. Improves tail latency and throughput with safe rollback and feature flag.
Feature-flagged improvement to continuous batching that coalesces sub-threshold slots to reduce fragmentation and improve KV cache warmup; contains safeguards for deadlines and bounded memory. Follow-up work: explore adaptive bank sizing (ENG-3021) and kernel-specific affinity hints.

payload.body:
Motivation: Long-context workloads (>=16k tokens) dominate several customer workloads. Existing FlashAttention and separate QK/KV kernels yield suboptimal memory traffic when serving long sequences with continuous batching and active KV caching. This PR introduces an adaptive kernel strategy that fuses QK compute and KV accumulation paths where beneficial, plus a lightweight KV prefetcher and a rotary-interleave layout to reduce memory bandwidth and kernel launch overhead. Design: 1) New fused kernels (CUDA) that compute QK scores and simultaneously write/aggregate KV fragments for future decode steps. These kernels are selected when sequence-length, batch composition, and kv cache hit heuristics indicate net win. 2) Adaptive kernel dispatcher: runtime heuristics (histogram of seq lengths, batch fill factor, GPU occupancy) choose between FlashAttention variants, fused QK-KV path, or the legacy split kernels. 3) KV prefetcher: background thread schedules small prefetches of cache pages for the most likely next-tokens based on route-level bandit policy, reducing tail latency on cache-miss heavy workloads. 4) Rotary interleave: reorganizes rotary embeddings in-memory to make fused kernels use contiguous loads for q/k/v, reducing strided accesses on long context. Implementation notes: - CUDA kernels implemented in runtime/attention with careful register/block tuning for Ampere/Blackwell GPUs. - Dispatcher lives in runtime/attention/kernel_dispatcher.cc and exposes a policy hook for testing via env vars. - Continuous batcher updated to expose batch shape histograms and to annotate requests with expected next-token probabilities (used by prefetcher). - Small pinned-memory prefetch buffer added to runtime/kv_cache, with heuristics to avoid polluting hot-cache entries. Tests & validation: microbenchmarks (tests/benchmarks/attn_long_context.py) show median throughput gain of 18% on 32k-context benchmarks vs previous flash-attn-only baseline, p50 decode latency reduced 12% for batched streaming, and token-cost reduction of ~9% under production-like mixes due to fewer kernel launches and lower GPU memory traffic. We ran full GPU integration tests, perf canary, and private deployment smoke tests. Rollout plan: feature gated behind env REDWOOD_FEATURE_ADAPTIVE_FUSE and opt-in in Dedicated as default off for first 2 weeks. Safety: we added deterministic fallbacks and correctness unit tests comparing fused outputs to reference split-kernel outputs for a variety of dtype/seq-length/model-size combinations. Backwards compatibility: no API changes. See release_notes for user-visible improvements.
Ethan Park: Can we get deterministic unit tests that cover rotary offsets and half-precision edge cases? Maya Chen: Added tests in tests/unit/test_fused_vs_split.py that compare fp16/fp32 outputs and several rotary offset patterns across seq lengths up to 32k. Also added a CI perf gate that runs a reduced microbenchmark on each PR. Sofia Ruiz: Concerned about polluting the KV cache with speculative prefetches for low-probability tokens. How do we avoid regressions for small batch sizes? Maya Chen: Prefetcher uses a conservative bandit with decay and an LRU guard; for small batches (<4) prefetching is disabled. We also added telemetry to monitor prefetch hit/miss ratios and an env flag REDWOOD_PREFETCH_ENABLE to turn this off. Liam O'Connor: Any impact on memory footprint for multi-tenant Dedicated? Maya Chen: Pinned buffer defaults to 32MB per GPU and is configurable by deployment; we added a guard to cap total pinned usage to 1% of GPU memory by default. QA: Found a race in the dispatcher when batch histogram updates happen concurrently — fixed in commit f90c2e1 and added a mutex around histogram writes. Post-merge: ops will run a canary for two days on a small fleet before enabling the feature by default for internal staging.
Improves long-context inference throughput and latency by introducing an adaptive fused QK-KV kernel path, KV prefetching, and memory-layout optimizations for rotary embeddings. Gains: ~18% throughput on 32k-context benchmarks, ~12% p50 decode latency reduction, ~9% token-cost reduction in mixed workloads. Feature is behind REDWOOD_FEATURE_ADAPTIVE_FUSE and off by default for Dedicated; safe rollout planned.

Background: On clusters with heterogeneous interconnects (mixed NVLink/NIC link speeds and asymmetrical topologies) we observed recurring NCCL stalls and bandwidth oscillation under TP workloads. This manifested as throughput variance across microbatches and elevated p99 tail latency for short-running inference requests. Motivation: previous fixes focused on static stream priorities or rigid batching heuristics which either underutilize good links or exacerbate stalls on slow links. This PR implements an adaptive link-rate smoothing layer and NCCL pacing integration to harmonize collective launches with per-peer link conditions and the runtime scheduler. Key changes and approach: 1) Link-rate estimator: continuous lightweight probe that measures effective per-peer bandwidth and short-term variability; estimator lives in scheduler/peer-rate-estimator and exports a smoothed rate with decay/window parameters tuned for inference workloads. 2) NCCL pacing adaptor: introduces optional pacing tokens in the comm adapter to space collective launches when peer variability is high; pacing is conservative by default and disabled for uniformly fast topologies. 3) Slack windows & micro-shear prevention: scheduler now computes a small slack window for kernel dispatch to absorb jittered arrival times from peers and aligns kernel launches with KV-cache prefetch completion when available. 4) KV cache alignment hook: prefetch manager negotiates a preferred alignment point with the scheduler for batched requests so comm-heavy windows avoid blocking on cache population. 5) Telemetry & guardrails: new metrics (peer_effective_bw, nccl_pacing_suppressed, pacing_tokens_issued) and a dynamic safety threshold that disables pacing if aggregate throughput would drop. Performance: in lab runs (8-node, mixed NVLink + EDR InfiniBand topology) typical large-TP workloads gained 12-18% sustained throughput and p99 latency improved by ~25% for short requests; NCCL stall events as recorded by tracers dropped ~60%. Testing and validation: - microbench suite: tp_collectives_bench extended with hetero-link scenarios - end-to-end canary: perf-canary harness with 10% traffic for 48h - unit + integration: scheduler, comm adapter, kv prefetch mocks - stress: ramp tests up to 200 concurrent sessions Rollout plan: canary 10% on dedicated clusters for 48h -> 50% -> global. Operator flags: pacing enabled=false by default for existing clusters; enabled=true for targeted clusters requires no code rollback. Risk and mitigation: conservative defaults, auto-disable if pacing causes throughput regression, and manual opt-out available via runtime flags. Related work: this complements prior comm scheduling efforts (see ENG-6123 family) and is intended to pair with future topology-aware kernel selectors. Notes: preserves existing public API surface; only runtime internals and ops docs are updated.
Ethan Wu: Can you explain how the probe traffic avoids perturbing production workloads? We should bound probe sample size.
Author (Priya): Probe uses a low-rate in-band estimator with adaptive throttling; added explicit bound and backoff to avoid congestion (see peer_rate_estimator.cc).
Marisol Ortega: Approve with one nit: prefer metric name 'peer_effective_bw_bytes' for clarity.
Author (Priya): Renamed metric and updated dashboards.
Dmitri Petrov: Requested change: make pacing opt-out dynamic via operator API (not just startup flag).
Author (Priya): Added runtime flag and operator endpoint; documented behaviour and rollout safety checks.
Introduce adaptive NCCL pacing and link-rate smoothing to reduce comm stalls on heterogeneous interconnects; opt-in via runtime flag. Improves throughput and tail latency on mixed-topology TP clusters.
Default behavior unchanged; to enable: set runtime.pacing.enabled=true on staging cluster. Monitor metrics 'nccl_pacing_suppressed' and 'peer_effective_bw' during rollout.
Deploy canary config to 3 dedicated clusters, update perf dashboards, schedule follow-up to evaluate interactions with kernel-selector heuristics (ENG-7392).
payload.title: Adaptive link-rate smoothing and NCCL pacing for heterogeneous interconnects

payload.body:
Motivation: Clients need richer signals from the model index to make routing and UI decisions without probing instances. This change adds explicit capability flags and lightweight stability/practical hints for streaming and function/tool calling so SDKs, the console, and routing logic can choose conservative defaults and present correct UI affordances. Summary of changes: 1) API: extended /v1/models and protobuf schema with optional fields: supports_streaming (bool), streaming_recommendations (object encoded as JSON string with keys recommended_chunk_size, max_concurrent_streams, graceful_close_delay_ms), supports_function_calls (bool), function_call_schema_hint (string, compact JSON Schema or type hint), openai_compatibility_level (enum: none/basic/compat), pricing_per_1k_tokens (string, e.g. "0.004USD"), max_context_tokens (int as string). Fields are optional and default to conservative values when absent. 2) Runtime: compatibility shim updated to map OpenAI-style function-calling metadata into function_call_schema_hint so the SDK OpenAI-compat layer can automatically populate function signatures for client-side validation. 3) SDKs & Docs: updated TypeScript and Python SDK types and the model index docs page with examples and migration notes. 4) Tests: added e2e surface tests for model listing, unit tests for mapping logic, and flaky-test guard for streaming backpressure behavior. Implementation notes: - server/api/models.go: adds new fields to model listing serialization, uses best-effort probes to populate streaming_recommendations from runtime profile metadata. - api/proto/models.proto: schema bump (v1->v1+), maintains backwards-compat. - runtime/compat/mapping.go: logic to synthesize function_call_schema_hint from model metadata and to set openai_compatibility_level. - docs/api/model-index.md: exhaustive examples including the new streaming_recommendations payload. Motivation: Customers are using multi-tool call graphs (chain-of-tools + parallel tool fans) and need safer, more ergonomic ways to hydrate tool outputs back into downstream tool inputs while preserving deterministic structured output shapes. This PR adds an async hydration layer on the tool invocation path, a deterministic merging strategy for structured results (JSON schema merging + conflict resolution policy), and robust retry/backoff semantics for tools invoked in parallel. Goals: 1) Make multi-tool flows less error-prone for app developers; 2) Reduce silent races when parallel tool calls return at different times; 3) Keep OpenAI-compatibility for function/tool calling while exposing more explicit ergonomics for engineering teams.
Improves tool-calling ergonomics: introduces async result hydration for multi-tool graphs, deterministic merge strategy for structured outputs, and exponential backoff/retry plumbing for parallel tool invocations. Backward-compatible with existing OpenAI-style function-calling semantics.
Implementation details: the async hydration layer attaches a hydration token to each tool invocation; results are streamed back into a per-request ledger, which the merger consumes when either all expected results arrive or a soft timeout triggers. Retry semantics: parallel fanouts use exponential backoff with jitter and a shared circuit-breaker per tool type to avoid thundering herds. OpenAI compatibility: preserved function-calling signature; hydrateToolResults returns outputs in both OpenAI-style 'arguments' and Redwood's structured result wrapper. Backwards compatibility: default merge policy is 'prefer-schema' which preserves stable behavior for existing customers while surfacing conflicts to the application via telemetry and structured error payloads.
For most customers: no action required. To opt into experimental stricter merging, set config 'tool.merge.policy=strict-error' in console or private config. SDKs: new helper hydrateToolResults() available in TS SDK; Python SDK shim to follow in subsequent PR. Note: if you rely on non-deterministic merge behavior, test with the new harness first.
Marco Nguyen: 'Nice work — important for reliability. Two asks: add a canary metric and make the default merge policy explicit in config.'
Aisha (author): 'Added metrics and default set to prefer-schema; documented in api doc and config.'
Elena Ruiz: 'Please add a short integration test that simulates partial failures from a parallel fanout and ensures deterministic output across reruns.'
Aisha: 'Added hydration.test.ts with a deterministic replay harness; CI covers it.'
Devon Clarke: 'Consider reducing any global locks in the executor; we should prefer per-request state to avoid throughput regressions.'
Aisha: 'Reworked executor to use per-invocation promise groups; microbenchmarks show no throughput regression.'
Approvals: Marco approved after metric addition; Elena approved after tests; Devon approved after lock removal and perf checks.

Merged to main via squash on 2024-11-20. Post-merge: rolled out to canary cluster (redwood-canary-2) with a 2-hour observation window; collected metrics showed a 12% reduction in downstream error rates for multi-tool flows and no latency regressions at p95. Feature flag `tool.hydration.v1` enabled by default for hosted API users; documented opt-out in private deployments.

Adds low-overhead CPU/GPU sync latency probe, a waterfall timeline exporter consumable by perf dashboards, and a small microbench harness for synthetic kernel scheduling scenarios. No API changes.
Motivation: We see intermittent end-to-end spikes where CPU scheduling waits for GPU-side work (kernel enqueue vs. completion) and our existing NVTX ranges + counters were insufficient to correlate fine-grained CPU->GPU handoffs. This PR introduces a low-overhead 'cpu_gpu_sync' probe that timestamps enqueue, launch_ack, and completion acknowledgment points (with a path for optional NVTX annotation), plus a compact waterfall JSON exporter that groups per-request CPU and GPU segments for visualizing interleaving across worker threads and CUDA streams.

What this change does: - Adds runtime/instr/cpu_gpu_sync.{h,cc} implementing a tiny ring buffer sampler (lock-free, pre-allocated) keyed by request id and epoch. The probe is enabled via runtime flags and is optimized for hot paths (fast-path inlined timestamp + tag write). - Adds scheduler hooks (runtime/scheduler/sync_hooks.cc) to record enqueue->dispatch->completion edges. Hooks are fenced to avoid instrumentation during shutdown. - Adds exporter: tools/perf/exporters/waterfall_exporter.cc which reads the ring buffer and emits a compact per-request waterfall JSON (versions v1/v2) suitable for ingestion by our perf dashboard and ad-hoc analysis (speedscope + chrome-trace compatible fragments). - Adds microbench: infra/microbench/cpu_gpu_sync_bench.{cc,py} with small scenarios (single-threaded burst, multi-threaded small batches, and KV-cache primed paths) that exercise enqueue latency and observe tail behavior. - Adds lightweight counters: runtime/instr/counters.h with per-thread occupancy counters and a cumulative sync-wait histogram (HDR-like buckets, but stored as flat counts to avoid dynamic allocations). - Adds docs: docs/perf/instrumentation/cpu_gpu_sync.md with enabling flags and examples of waterfall output.

Checklist: [x] unit tests for ring buffer safety (sanity) [x] microbench harness and CI smoke [x] perf exporter small integration test [x] docs and runbook entry for how to use waterfall traces for RCA

Commits: ["introduce cpu_gpu_sync probe and ring buffer (Priya Menon)", "hook scheduler enqueue/complete paths (Priya Menon)", "waterfall exporter and v1 schema (Evan Zhao)", "microbench harness and basic scenarios (Priya Menon)", "add counters and small unit tests (María Torres)", "docs and examples (Priya Menon)"]

Files changed (high level): ["runtime/instr/cpu_gpu_sync.h", "runtime/instr/cpu_gpu_sync.cc", "runtime/instr/counters.h", "runtime/scheduler/sync_hooks.cc", "tools/perf/exporters/waterfall_exporter.cc", "infra/microbench/cpu_gpu_sync_bench.cc", "infra/microbench/run_bench.py", "docs/perf/instrumentation/cpu_gpu_sync.md", "tests/instr/test_ringbuffer.cc", "tools/ci/bench-smoke.yml", "third_party/speedscope/README.md", "BUILD.bazel"]

Small illustrative snippet (in description form): ``// fast path: record enqueue timestamp
inline void record_enqueue(uint64_t req_id) { if (!enabled) return; auto t = clock::now_ns(); rb_.write(req_id, TAG_ENQUEUE, t); }``

Testing and results: - CI: bench-smoke pipeline runs the microbench scenarios; results embedded as artifacts (waterfall JSON + simple CSV summary). - Local perf runs (NVIDIA A100, sequence_len=1024 synthetic) show the exporter can capture sub-200us host->device handoff variance on steady-state but reveals outlier clusters when scheduler batching increases queue depth. - Overhead measured: typical per-request instrumentation adds ~120ns on the hot path when NVTX is disabled, ~450ns when NVTX annotation path is taken. We added a runtime knob to turn NVTX tagging on only for debug captures.

Backward compatibility and safety: The ring buffer defaults to 0 (disabled) in prod; enabling requires an env flag or console toggle. The implementation avoids allocations on hot path and uses per-thread pre-allocated buffers to bound tail latency. Exporter reads buffers with a simple epoch gating to avoid partial records.

Follow-ups: - Add a dashboard ingest pipeline to aggregate waterfall traces by request template (ENG-9310) - Add a condensed per-route tail report that summarizes sync-wait percentiles - Consider an optional lightweight on-host correlator that tags traces with syscall-level latencies for deeper RCA

Motivation: Customers are building multi-tool workflows where the model fan-outs tool calls in parallel and expects a single, deterministic structured injection back into the next model turn. We observed two classes of problems in production: (1) non-deterministic ordering and partial/overlapping streamed tool outputs which break structured output parsing, and (2) retry storms and duplicated results when a subset of parallel tool calls fail transiently. This PR introduces a reconciliation layer and retry choreography to make parallel tool-calling ergonomics reliable and OpenAI-compat friendly.

What this PR does (high-level): Adds a Reconciler component that: 1) accepts concurrent tool responses (streamed or final) and materializes a canonical merged representation; 2) enforces deterministic injection ordering via a reconcile_id and explicit injection_strategy; 3) implements per-tool retry/backoff and a short-circuit policy for "first-success" strategies to reduce tail latency and cost. On the API surface we add opt-in request flags for OpenAI-compat requests: "reconcile_id", "injection_strategy" (values: "merge", "first-success", "serial"), and "max_retries_per_tool". SDK helpers expose an ergonomic call_tools(...) helper that returns the reconciled structured output and metadata for diagnostics.

Key design points: - Deterministic ordering: callers can opt to preserve the generation order with "serial" or allow a merge strategy that combines outputs by semantic slot. Reconciler uses a stable slot ordering derived from the call graph to avoid flakiness. - Streaming stability: partial streamed chunks from tools are buffered and reassembled in a small in-memory window (configurable via reconcile_window_ms) before they are forwarded as a single atomic injection event to the language model. This prevents the model from seeing interleaved partial payloads. - Retry choreography: per-tool backoff is jittered and bounded; the reconciler tracks idempotency keys provided by tools to dedupe retries. For "first-success" strategy we short-circuit remaining tools once a minimum-success threshold is reached. - OpenAI compatibility: function-calling style metadata is preserved; reconciled outputs are emitted as valid function-call payloads (name + arguments) so existing OpenAI-compat clients can consume results without extra parsing changes. - Observability: events, per-tool latencies, retry counts, and reconciliation decisions are emitted to existing traces/metrics. We added tracing tags reconcile_id and injection_strategy.

API changes and backwards compatibility: - New optional fields on the inference request JSON: "reconcile_id" (string), "injection_strategy" (string), "max_retries_per_tool" (int), "reconcile_window_ms" (int). Defaults maintain current behavior (no reconciliation; naive injection) so this is opt-in and non-breaking. - SDK helpers: python and typescript convenience functions wrap the new fields and handle streaming reassembly. Existing SDK call sites that don't opt in see no change.

Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - Reconciler lives in runtime/reconciler.py and sits between the tool-runner and the streaming response multiplexer. It maintains an ephemeral in-memory buffer keyed by reconcile_id; for large outputs we spill to disk using the existing chunk-store utility to avoid OOM. - To avoid increased tail latency we aggressively favor optimistic short-circuits under "first-success" and expose per-request thresholds. - We added integration tests that replay production failures (partial stream cuts, duplicated tool callbacks) to assert deterministic reconciled outputs.

Benchmarks: microbenchmarks on a 4xA100 stack show median additional latency of ~4ms for reconciliation in the common case (small tool outputs) and 95th percentile increase of ~12-18ms when buffering larger streamed payloads. Cost/regressions: we observed negligible tokenization overhead; the main cost is slightly increased CPU for reassembly under heavy fan-out which is bounded by a configurable concurrency limit.

Rollout plan: - Feature gated behind runtime flag reconcile.enabled=false by default. - Canary rollout to 10% of hosted traffic with a revert window of 48 hours. - SDK release (python/ts) coordinated: minor semver bump with new helper exposed. - Docs/compat: update OpenAI-compat page with examples showing function-call style reconciled results and migration notes.

Testing: Unit tests for reconciler logic, end-to-end integration tests that validate deterministic injection and retry backoff behavior, and performance runbooks added to benchmarks/. CI: added a new workflow to exercise long-lived streaming reconnection scenarios.

Notes for reviewers: focus on idempotency/dedupe correctness (reconciler/keys), spike protection under many concurrent reconcile_ids, and the SDK ergonomics (is call_tools intuitive?). Also validate the OpenAI-compat output shape in docs/openai_compat/tool-calling.md.

Related: ENG-9876 (design), SUP-2219 (customer incident), ENG-10012 (retry policy work).

Author (Aisha Khan): We derive the stable slot order from the call graph emitted with the request (tools are assigned deterministic indices). Retries are keyed to the original slot index so dedupe is deterministic.
Ravi Singh: Need circuit-breaker so a misbehaving tool doesn't drag reconciler memory. Also prefer upper bounds on in-flight reconcile_ids.

Introduces a compatibility shim and runtime fixes to support an evolving Responses v3 streaming envelope used by OpenAI-compatible clients. This PR addresses three user-visible classes of issues observed under load: (1) fragmented streaming frames that split UTF-8 token boundaries or split function_call tool frames which caused out-of-order assembly, (2) loss or mutation of function_call intent during gateway->router->worker handoffs and cross-region fallbacks, and (3) client-specified seed/determinism flags and arbitrary response-level metadata not being forwarded into the serving pipeline or audit rows. The implementation normalizes incoming v3 envelopes into a compact internal event model, provides a deterministic reassembly algorithm that stitches partial byte sequences and tool frames, serializes function_call intent into the routing context to survive asynchronous queuing and fallbacks, and attaches client seed and metadata to the request context and audit enrichment. The feature is behind a runtime flag openai_responses_v3_compat and gated by an explicit client-version header so that older traffic is unaffected. Rollout plan: dark-launch 10% traffic, staging dogfood with end-to-end tracing, canary ramp to 50% then promote after 48 hours of stability. Includes unit/fuzz tests for reassembly invariants, an integration fallback scenario to validate header preservation, SDK adapters in TypeScript/Python, CI pipeline additions, and docs for SDK consumers and operator flags.

Priya Raman: added tests/integration/test_resp_v3_fallback_preserve_headers.py and fixed a race by serializing context before enqueueing to the router.

This PR wires a CI pipeline that builds release artifacts for the private-installer chart and associated Terraform modules, produces SLSA-style provenance attestations, signs artifacts with cosign (KMS-backed keys), uploads signed bundles to a staging bucket, and emits a chained release manifest that references digested artifacts and attestation records.

Introduce a reservoir-based per-tenant quota allocator with leaky-bucket style recovery and eviction-safety. Adds metrics and migration guidance. Backwards compatible with current token pools.
Context: Dedicated clusters sometimes see oscillatory tenant throughput after hard evictions or burst draining: tenants either starve for a long tail or spike immediately when capacity frees up. This PR implements a reservoir-based quota allocator that smooths tenant replenishment and prevents transient takeover while preserving burstability.

What this implements: a tenant 'reservoir' (soft budget) that is consumed by requests. The reservoir refills at a configurable leak rate (tokens/sec) computed from a tiered policy: base_rate (guaranteed throughput), adaptive_boost (short-term refill after sustained idleness) and cooldown_decay (prevents aggressive refills after eviction). Replenishment is computed as a convolution over a short moving window of measured served tokens, resulting in a gentle recovery curve rather than an instantaneous refill.

Key features and rationale: 1) Smooth recovery curve: avoids sudden token floods after preemption or cold-start; improves tail latency for co-tenants. 2) Eviction-safety: when a tenant is preempted, reservoir recovery follows a delayed ramp (configurable) to avoid immediate reconsumption of freed capacity. 3) Compatibility: the allocator sits as an optional policy in the Dedicated scheduler and falls back to existing percent-based quotas when disabled. 4) Observability: exposes reservoir_fill, reservoir_drain, refill_rate, and overdraw events with histograms for recovery time. 5) Admin controls: per-tenant profiles (steady_rate, burst_cap, recovery_delay, cooldown_mult) and a cluster-wide override for emergencies.

Design notes: reservoirs are represented as a floating point budget tracked in the scheduler; requests check budget before admission. Overdraws are allowed up to a small safety cap (configurable) and are penalized by lengthening the cooldown. The replenishment formula is intentionally conservative (90th percentile pacing) to prioritize SLO stability over aggressive utilization. We also added a short-term credits buffer to allow headroom for in-flight KV-cache misses without immediate throttle.

Testing and validation: unit tests for refill math and edge cases (eviction+immediate traffic) included. Integration (e2e) tests simulate a 3-tenant dedicated cluster with one tenant evicted mid-run and verify no more than 10% cross-tenant tail latency degradation. Perf runs on staging show a 12% reduction in 99p latency for co-tenants in eviction scenarios and negligible steady-state throughput loss (~0.8% median).

Migration plan: feature-flag rollout (off by default). Stage 1: enable in canary clusters for 48h, collect metrics and alarms. Stage 2: opt-in for customers on Dedicated beta. Stage 3: default enable after two weeks of stable signals. We included a toggle to map existing token-pool quotas to initial reservoir levels to avoid surprise changes.

Checklist: - [x] Core allocator implementation - [x] Config schema and defaults - [x] Metrics + dashboards - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Docs/ops runbook - [x] Feature flag gating

Risks and mitigations: incorrect refill tuning could reduce utilization — we default to conservative rates and provide easy overrides. Eviction edge cases were stress-tested; added telemetry to detect recovery stalls.

Files of interest (summary): see files_changed for details.

Notes for reviewers: focus on refill math in pkg/autoscaler/reservoir.go and on the eviction handoff path in internal/scheduler/alloc.go. Metrics naming follows the new observability conventions and is backwards compatible with dashboards in observability/metrics.

Liam Becker (2025-02-13): Can we get a clearer justification for the default cooldown_mult=1.5? Suggest adding a short doc explaining the numeric choice and sensitivity tests.
Aisha Patel (2025-02-13): Added sensitivity tests and a section in docs/ops/reservoir-quotas.md explaining experiments. Default chosen to limit immediate reconsumption while allowing quick steady-state recovery.

Motivation:
We need a deterministic way to hold, inspect, and safely rewind model rollout traffic for live canaries and A/B experiments without losing session-affinity or producing silent regressions. Current pause mechanics are ad-hoc (manual scaling, pod cordon) and opaque in telemetry which makes post-hoc root cause and safe rewind labor-intensive.

What this PR does (summary):
- Introduces a Pausepoint state machine inside the orchestrator that exposes explicit holdpoints for staged rollouts. Holdpoints can be triggered by policy (telemetry gates) or manually from the Console.
- Implements a Cohort Quarantine controller that isolates affected user slices when a holdpoint is entered; quarantined cohorts are routed to a shadow or golden variant, and traffic is stamped for replay.
- Adds Transparent Rewind: deterministic session-preserving replay of quarantined traffic against previous model snapshots with side-by-side scoring so operators can compare deltas before committing an automatic revert.
- Expands telemetry: every pausepoint decision now emits a decision_reason tag, cohort_id, and a deterministic trace id that ties replay sessions to original requests.
- Includes operator runbook and console UI for inspecting pausepoint state, kicking off a rewind, or escalating to manual rollback.

Design notes:
- Pausepoint lifecycle: OPEN -> HOLDING -> QUARANTINED -> REPLAYING -> RESOLVED (COMMIT/REVERT). Transitions are guarded by timeouts and safety tokens so long-running holds can be auto-escalated.
- Quarantine semantics: quarantined cohorts are isolated at routing layer; their requests are mirrored to both candidate and golden models. Mirrors are rate-limited and tagged for replay capture.
- Rewind integrity: replay is performed preserving session cookies and KV cache pointers when available; where exact replay is impossible (external side-effects) we mark the trace as non-deterministic and exclude it from automatic revert decisions.

Checklist:
- [x] Pausepoint state machine + controller implementation
- [x] Cohort quarantine routing + mirror capture
- [x] Deterministic replay harness for transparent rewind
- [x] Telemetry tags and Console UI for pausepoint inspection
- [x] Integration tests covering holdpoint flow and replay verification
- [x] Runbook and operator playbook for incident handling

Backward compatibility:
- Pausepoints are opt-in via a new CRD (Pausepoint) and a feature flag. Default behavior for existing rollouts is unchanged.

Risks and mitigations:
- Increased memory footprint for mirrored requests: mitigated with streaming mirrors and configurable retention TTLs.
- Replay non-determinism could produce spurious signals: we surface non-deterministic flags and exclude affected traces from automated scoring.

How to test locally:
1) bootstrap local orchestrator with feature flag enabled (scripts/local_replay_fixture.sh)
2) create a Pausepoint CR using examples/rollouts/cohort_quarantine.yml
3) trigger a canary and send test traffic; use Console PausepointPanel to enter HOLD state
4) initiate Replay and watch telemetry spans emitted to local Jaeger

Related work and tickets: ENG-3245 (pausepoint design), ENG-3310 (transparent rewind prototype), SUP-4421 (customer incident: noisy canary requiring manual quarantine)

Notes on scope: This change focuses on rollout control-plane and routing glue; it does not attempt to modify model runtime kernels or KV cache serialization across versions — those are future follow-ups (linked in design doc).


Jordan Blake: Nice decomposition; two questions: how do we guarantee session-affinity during replay when candidates change network endpoints? Suggest adding a sticky session token in the routing layer.
Author (Aisha Noor): Agree — added sticky session token logic and tests (see pausepoint_controller.go commit).
Ravi Kapoor: CI showed a flaky test on first run. I retriggered and it passed. Also: please add a TTL knob to the cohort quarantine list to prevent indefinite quarantine.
Author (Aisha Noor): Added quarantine_ttl to CRD and defaulted to 30m in helm chart. Updated runbook to warn operators about long quarantines.
Priya Singh: Telemetry looks good, but for privacy we should redact PII before storing replay payloads. Add a pipeline step to scrub headers.
Author (Aisha Noor): Added header-scrub hook in scripts/local_replay_fixture.sh and marked non-deterministic traces when scrub removes key fields.

Motivation: In production we observed tail-latency spikes and near-starvation of small non-KV requests when KV-heavy requests dominated continuous-batching queues. This PR introduces a dynamic deprioritization policy that detects long-running KV-dominant queues and reweights request admission and scheduling to reduce starvation while preserving batch efficiency. Approach: add token-based aging for fairness, per-queue KV-pressure heuristics, transient deprioritization buckets for KV-heavy groups, and a kernel-hint flag to prefer low-overhead kernels for short requests. Also introduce a soft release policy in the KV pin manager to proactively free pinned cache entries when a queue is deprioritized. Implementation highlights: 1) scheduler/continuous_scheduler: new "deprioritize_score" computed from recent kv_ratio, avg_service_time, and age, used to adjust admission priority and timeouts; 2) scheduler/aging_token: lightweight token bucket that guarantees forward progress for aged requests; 3) kernel/kernel_selector: expose "prefer_small_request_kernels" hint; 4) kv_cache/pin_manager: add background eviction signal when deprioritization fires to avoid long-term pin accumulation; 5) observability: new metrics (scheduler.deprioritize_events, scheduler.kv_pressure_ratio, scheduler.age_starved_count) and dashboards; 6) tests: synthetic kv-heavy and mixed workloads included in perf harness. Results: in lab kv-dominant 75/25 mix, p95 latency for non-KV small requests dropped 18% and p99 dropped 23% with <5% throughput loss for KV throughput; reduction in observed starvation incidents from 14/day to 1/day in canary. Rollout plan: gated rollout via feature flag with 1%, 10%, 100% progression and realtime metrics alerts. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] perf tests, [x] e2e smoke, [x] observability, [x] docs, [x] migration guidance. Related: ENG-1298 (scheduling fairness), ENG-1303 (kv pin release).
Ava Patel: Nice approach. Two concerns: how do we avoid oscillation where deprioritized queues reappear and then flip-flop? Can we add hysteresis?
Marisol Vega: Added hysteresis window and decay factor to deprioritize_score; documented behavior in code comments and tests.
Jared Nguyen: Kernel hint is neat; please ensure it's opt-in per deployment. Also run the matrix with large-sequence workloads.
Marisol Vega: Kernel hint behind feature flag and empirically tested with seq_len 512/1024; no regression observed.
Ethan Cho: Suggest adding an integration test that simulates pin saturation and ensures the soft release reduces pin count.
Marisol Vega: Added an integration test (tests/integ/pin_release_saturation.py) and a CI perf job to run it on schedule.
Ava Patel: Approving after addressing oscillation and integration test.
Jared Nguyen: Approved.
Ethan Cho: Approved with no further comments.

Motivation: Add first-class support for a strict JSON Schema style 'response_format' that can be validated synchronously or during streaming, and ensure OpenAI compatibility layer maps its 'response_format' and 'schema' usage into our runtime behavior. This PR introduces a 'strict' validation mode that rejects outputs that do not conform and produces clear, machine-readable error messages for callers. It also adds incremental/streaming validation so that long-running generation can be validated as tokens arrive and early failures can be surfaced to clients.

What changed (summary): implemented a response_format parser that accepts 'json_schema' payloads and a 'strict' flag; added streaming validator that emits validation events on the stream (prefix event type: validation_error / validation_warning); updated the OpenAI compatibility shim to translate OpenAI-style 'response_format' and 'schema' into our internal representation; added runtime guards so fallbacks to permissive mode are available via policy for backward compatibility; extended API docs and SDK examples to show the new flags.

Key behaviors: in strict mode the runtime will attempt to fully validate the completed JSON object against the schema; if validation fails the request returns a structured 400-level error with a short machine code (e.g. VALIDATION_ERROR_SCHEMA_MISMATCH) and a human message that includes the top 3 violations. When streaming, partial validation runs on complete JSON fragments; streaming validation failures are emitted inline as 'validation_error' events and, if strict mode is enabled, the stream is closed with a trailing error event. The OpenAI compat layer accepts both top-level 'response_format' and the legacy 'schema' key and preserves the strictness flag (openai: "response_format": {"type":"json_schema","strict":true}).

Compatibility: default behavior remains permissive unless the caller sets strict mode. For customers relying on older OpenAI-compatible behaviors we added a rollout toggle (policy: openai_compat.strict_response_format=false) that keeps the legacy permissive semantics. We added a migration note in docs for Dedicated/Private admins.

Testing and rollout: unit tests cover schema parsing, validator edge cases, and error formatting. Integration tests exercise streaming validation with large token sequences and function-calling scenarios. We staged the change behind a feature flag and ran a canary on 5% of traffic for 48h before enabling broadly.

Docs: API reference updated with examples for strict mode, streaming validation event types, and sample SDK usage.

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps the validation engine pluggable; future work will add optional remediation suggestions (e.g., 'coerce_number') and richer error paths for tool-calling workflows.
Liam Ortega: Requesting clarification on the streaming semantics: when exactly do we emit validation_warning vs validation_error? Please add a compact state machine comment in stream_validator.go.
Author (Priya Nair): Added state machine comment and unit tests for boundary chunking in stream_validator.go. validation_warning is emitted for recoverable/formatting issues that do not break the final schema; validation_error is emitted for violations that would make final validation fail under strict mode.
Mina Chen: Found an edge case where function-calling outputs (tool responses) may include top-level non-JSON tokens (e.g., plain text). We should ensure tool output is passed through permissive parsing unless the tool contract specifies JSON. Recommend updating the docstring and adding a test.
Author: Added guard and test to ensure tool outputs are treated as permissive by default; added docstring to function-calling plumbing.
Carlos Duarte: CI flaked once on e2e streaming run; re-ran and all checks are green. LGTM after minor comment fixes.
Mina Chen: Approved.
Liam Ortega: Approved and merging via squash once canary validated.

Motivation: tenant allocation and throttling heuristics have produced oscillatory behavior in multi-tenant fleets where sudden short-lived spikes cause aggressive scaling followed by underutilized capacity. This PR introduces two coordinated mechanisms: (1) a Tenant Throttle Lattice - a multi-dimensional, soft-throttle lattice that composes concurrency, route-level rate, and ephemeral throughput bands to provide smooth, priority-aware degradation; (2) a Utilization Sentinel - a composite telemetry signal that fuses GPU occupancy, KV-cache hit-rate, queue latency P95, and model step time into a single utilization score used by autoscalers and the operator console. Goals: reduce autoscaler churn on short spikes, add an explicit soft-floor for high-priority tenants, and surface a more robust utilization signal that prevents misattribution of load. Changes are scoped to the autoscaler, runtime metrics exporter, controller config, and observability dashboards. Checklist: - [x] Implement lattice data model and enforcement layer - [x] Emit sentinel metrics and register Prometheus counters/histograms - [x] Backfill unit tests for lattice transitions and sentinel smoothing - [x] Add e2e load test harness with synthetic tenant traffic patterns - [x] Docs: configuration guide and console dashboard snippets - [x] Canary rollout plan and operator feature flag (runtime.enableThrottleLattice) Backwards compatibility: lattice is behind a feature flag and defaults to off for existing Dedicated clusters. Sentinel metrics are additive and do not change existing metric names; new composite metrics prefixed with rwd_sentinel_ are introduced. Rollout: feature-flag canary to 10% of Dedicated fleets for 48 hours with fast rollback. Migration notes: operators should validate sentinel.calibration_window and tenant.priority_tiers in config before enabling.
