payload.body:
Context: We continue to see intermittent starvation of short, high-priority sequences when continuous-batcher queues are dominated by long, KV-heavy sessions. Previous fixes (fairness timeouts, weighted queues) mitigated some cases but left pathological scenarios where a small number of sessions could hold batch slots for hundreds of ms due to large KV pin counts and unpredictable model kernel <-> sequence interplay.
Motivation: reduce end-to-end tail latency and avoid manual operator interventions (burst drains) while preserving batching efficiency for large requests.
Summary of changes: 1) Sliding-service-window aging: instead of a single fixed 'age' counter per request, each queue maintains a sliding time window (configurable, default 40ms) that computes per-session effective age weighted by service time. Sessions that have accumulated service time beyond a per-window threshold are bumped in effective priority to prevent starvation. 2) Local KV-pin heuristic: requests that pin > X KV entries (configurable default 64) are marked as 'kv-heavy' and receive a soft backoff in admission (they can still batch but will be lowered in priority unless their effective age signals starvation). 3) Adaptive admission timeout: a per-batch adaptive timeout that shortens when queue depth is below target, and lengthens under sustained throughput pressure to preserve batching efficiency. 4) Conservative early-release: when a batch contains a mix of kv-heavy and small requests, small requests can be early-released after partial execution (prefix completion) to reduce tail for short queries.
Design notes: - All heuristics are local to the scheduler instance to avoid cross-node coordination overhead. - Parameters (window_ms, kv_pin_threshold, service_threshold, min/max_admission_ms) are exposed as runtime-config flags and a new SchedulerConfig proto. - Safety: early-release occurs only when model supports prefix-safe yields (flagged per-model), otherwise the request stays in the batch. - Telemetry: new metrics added: scheduler.window_age_ms, scheduler.kv_heavy_admissions, scheduler.early_releases, scheduler.starvation_promotions.
Benchmarks: - Testbed: 8xA100 staging cluster, mixed workload: 80% short (<=64 tokens, no KV pin), 20% long (>=1024 tokens, kv-pin mean 96). - Baseline: main@2026-01-01. - Results (median / p95 / p99 for short requests): Baseline: 18ms / 142ms / 320ms. This PR: 16ms / 111ms / 248ms (~22% improvement at p95). KV-heavy tails unchanged or slightly worse by ~4% p99 in extreme overload, tradeoff justified by overall user impact.
Reduce starvation in continuous batching: introduce sliding-service-window aging policy and local KV-pin heuristic. Improves 95th percentile latency for mixed KV-heavy workloads by ~22% in our staging tests.
Diego: Can we make window_ms configurable per-deployment? Asha: yes, exposed via SchedulerConfig and runtime flags; default 40ms; will add docs
Claire: Concern about early-release and hallucination risk for structured outputs. Asha: early-release gated by model.capabilities.prefix_safe; added unit tests and model metadata check
Evan: Observability looks limited for kv-heavy counts over time. Asha: added scheduler.kv_heavy_admissions metric and a trace tag kv_pin_count on admission events
payload.title: Sliding-window aging + KV-pin heuristic to reduce continuous-batcher starvation

payload.body:
Motivation: We observed repeated CPU-side stalls on the request hot path under mixed workloads (short chat completions vs long generation). Root causes identified: 1) synchronous KV cache lookups and repeated syscall boundaries when requests hit cold prefixes; 2) aggressive thread-to-core pinning causing poor work-stealing and imbalanced queues during bursty traffic; 3) small, eager batching stalls while waiting for a strict batch size.

This PR introduces three coordinated runtime changes aimed at reducing per-request CPU latency and increasing sustained throughput without changing model kernels: 1) lightweight per-worker KV prefetch that issues asynchronous read-ahead for likely KV keys for requests in the ready queue (uses existing cache backend interface; prefetch is best-effort and does not change correctness); 2) a "burst scheduler" that allows short-lived requests to bypass strict batch-size gating and create micro-batches while longer requests are routed to slower path or cooperative workers; 3) relaxed thread affinity: we convert hard O(1) thread-to-core pinning in the CPU workerpool to soft affinity hints and enable work stealing across neighbouring NUMA domains when local queues exceed threshold.

Implementation notes: all changes are opt-in via runtime config flags under "runtime.experimental": kv_prefetch=true, burst_scheduler=enabled, soft_affinity=true. Prefetch is implemented as a non-blocking task scheduled on the worker's I/O executor and returns a lightweight future; if the prefetch misses or is in-flight, the request continues using the original lookup path so no correctness regressions. The scheduler change leverages the existing request classification pipeline (light vs heavy heuristics by token-budget and model-profile) to route to either micro-batcher or standard continuous-batcher. Micro-batches have a small token/time budget (configurable) and are flushed sooner to reduce latency tail.

Performance: on our internal chat workload (50% short completions, 50% long continuations) with 8 x A100 nodes: - median CPU request latency reduced 14% on p95 across hosts; - end-to-end throughput improved 11% measured at same p95 latency target; - KV cache hit-rate on first lookup improved ~6% due to prefetch, reducing remote reads. When soft_affinity=false and prefetch enabled, we saw no improvements—this confirms the scheduler+affinity changes are synergistic. Microbenchmarks attached in CI artifacts show the prefetch path adds ~120ns overhead on hot-path enqueues when miss rate is low.

Testing and rollout: unit tests for prefetch logic and scheduler were added. Integration tests simulate bursts and confirm no deadlocks or resource leaks. Canary rollout plan: enable flags on a small Dedicated pool, monitor CPU p95, KV remote-read rate, dispatcher queue lengths and revert if observations exceed thresholds.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc: internal RFC linked in Linear ENG-12892
- [x] Unit + integration tests added
- [x] Benchmarks and perf regression guardrails
- [x] Opt-in flags behind runtime config
- [x] Observability hooks: new metrics (kv_prefetch.requests, kv_prefetch.hits, scheduler.microbatch.count)

Notes: this PR purposefully avoids kernel-level changes (no model operator modifications) to keep the blast radius small. Future follow-ups: adaptive prefetch heuristics based on prefix reuse rates; expose micro-batch budgeting in the console for fine-grained tuning.

Marco Ruiz: Can we make prefetch opt-out per-tenant? Some enterprise customers prefer strict I/O determinism.
Aisha Patel: Yes, added runtime flag and per-tenant override in config; default off for Private until validated.
Emily Chen: Concerned about extra memory pressure from in-flight prefetches under very high concurrency.
Aisha Patel: Prefetch is gated by a concurrency cap per-worker and global in-flight metric; added tests for cap enforcement.
Jared O'Neill: The soft affinity change worries me for NUMA heavy workloads — any regressions seen there?
Aisha Patel: We added NUMA-aware stealing thresholds and a stress test; performance on our NUMA synthetic was flat to +3%.
Marco Ruiz: Approved after CI green and perf numbers validated on canary.
Introduce opt-in KV prefetch and burst scheduler to reduce CPU-side latency and improve throughput for mixed short/long workloads; disabled by default for Private installs. Observability: kv_prefetch.* and scheduler.microbatch.* metrics added.

payload.body:
Summary: Adds an "invocation-bridge" pipeline component that stitches sampled traces, compacted structured log bundles, and token-level cost rollups into a small footprint index and a compact cost heatmap dashboard. Motivation: long-tail cost & debugging is dominated by a small fraction of invocations where context and prefetching patterns matter; existing rollups either lost context or were too large to query interactively. This PR introduces a lightweight joiner that keeps a bounded set of context anchors per invocation and exposes a compact heatmap view for per-route token-cost vs latency slices.

What this changes (single continuous description): The PR adds a new background worker (invocation-bridge) that consumes sampled traces and structured log bundles, attaches up to N context anchors (prompt prefix signature, KV-prefetch hint, first-k tokens fingerprint) and writes a compact invocation index and a small per-invocation token-cost histogram. On the query surface we add a new dashboard panel (Compact Cost Heatmap) that allows slicing by route, model variant, and prefetch hint label. The change also introduces: 1) a small on-disk serialization format for context bundles (compact protobuf v2) used by the bridge, 2) a KV-prefetch signal extractor that tags invocations when prefetch calls were observed, 3) two new metrics (invocation.bridge.latency_ms and invocation.bridge.join_rate) and two tracing tags (bridge.context_count, bridge-prefetch).

Design notes and tradeoffs: The bridge intentionally keeps per-invocation state bounded (configurable default anchors=4) to avoid explosion in storage and index cardinality. We opted for a compact histogram (8 fixed buckets, 4-bit counts) to keep payloads small and make heatmap rollups cheap. The sampling strategy is layered: input traces are sampled by the existing adaptive sampler; the bridge then applies a deterministic shingle-based sampling to ensure coverage of long-tail prompt patterns. We prioritized read/query performance for the dashboard over storing full logs; full log lookup remains available via an index pointer.

Checklist:
- [x] Bridge worker implementation and tests (invocation_bridge/*)
- [x] Compact context proto and serializers
- [x] Extractor for KV-prefetch and prompt-fingerprint
- [x] Migration that backfills for last 30 days (limited to traces sampled)
- [x] Dashboard JSON + per-route slice queries
- [x] CI and e2e smoke tests
- [x] Documentation notes (observability/bridge.md)

Rollout plan: feature gate off by default for existing clusters. Admins can enable via telemetry.feature.invocation_bridge=true. We will run the bridge in a canary mode for 48h in staging and then enable for 10% of production traffic for two weeks (monitor invocation.bridge.join_rate, new metric error rate, and SLO delta). Backfill job is optional and rate-limited (configurable) to prevent overload.

Migration notes: No breaking schema changes. The bridge writes new compact artifacts under telemetry/invocation_bridge/{tenant}/{date}/. The backfill job is idempotent. If feature is disabled, dashboards will gracefully hide panels.

Security & privacy: Context bundles are stripped of PII by the existing log-sanitizer step; we added an extra scrub stage for any key/value pairs in prefetched objects. Artifacts written are ACL'd to tenant storage and follow current retention policies.

Observability additions: metrics: invocation.bridge.latency_ms, invocation.bridge.join_rate, invocation.bridge.backfill_progress. Logs: invocation_bridge.INFO events for join start/finish and failure reasons. Traces: added bridge.* span names and tags described above. Dashboards: dashboards/compact_cost_heatmap.json (panel, query templates, drilldowns to invocation detail).

Performance: Local benchmarks show bridge adds ~1.1% CPU and ~100ms background processing per sampled trace at default anchors=4. Storage overhead estimated at ~3% increase for sampled trace artifacts (configurable via anchors and histogram density).

Related work: complements existing prefix-warmup traces and token-cost rollups (see ENG-4012). This is intentionally compact to serve interactive SRE workflows without full trace rehydration.
Evan Park: Nice incremental design. Two asks: (1) make anchors configurable per-tenant (not just cluster) and (2) add a short-circuit when no prefetch signals are present to avoid unnecessary writes.
Maya Chen (author): Added per-tenant override via tenant.config.telemetry.invocation_bridge. Added prefetch short-circuit; updated tests to cover both paths.
Sophie Rivera: Dashboard looks useful. Request: default time-range should be 6h and add a route-level color scale that is consistent across time windows. Also flagged a query that could scan full index; recommend adding a tenant+date prefix filter.
Maya Chen (author): Updated dashboard JSON to default to 6h and added stable color scale. Added tenant+date prefix in queries and included a note in docs about cost of wider time range.
Arjun Patel: Found a flake in test_worker where a timing assumption made the test brittle. Suggested using a fake clock.
Maya Chen (author): Reworked tests to use the test clock harness; CI flake resolved.
SRE Review (automated): Confirmed the backfill job's throttling knobs and monitoring targets.
Adds an opt-in 'invocation-bridge' telemetry worker that produces compact context bundles and a compact cost heatmap dashboard for interactive debugging of long-tail expensive invocations. Feature is feature-gated and disabled by default. Backfill available but rate-limited.
Enable with telemetry.feature.invocation_bridge=true. Monitor: invocation.bridge.join_rate, invocation.bridge.latency_ms, bridge.backfill_progress. Backfill is optional and should be run during low-traffic windows. See docs/observability/bridge.md for runbook.

Motivation: reduce per-token unit cost for mixed-latency workloads while preserving p99 latency SLOs by combining an empirical cost-SLO prober, a cold-cache prefetcher for KV-heavy prompts, and a split-batcher that dynamically decides between size- and latency-optimized microbatches. This PR wires a lightweight probing loop into the runtime optimizer, exposes safe default profiles, and adds metrics and canary flags. Changes are designed to be opt-in via config flags and non-breaking for existing deployments. Checklist: [x] implement prober loop and SDK flags; [x] add cold prefetch hook and cache TTL tuning; [x] add split-batcher with heuristics for long and short sequences; [x] add unit tests and integration canary; [x] add docs snippet and console feature flag. Impact: expected unit cost reduction for conversational workloads with 1-2 sentence prompts (10-25%) and for long-context retrieval scenarios (5-15%) at minimal p99 regressions under typical load. See linked Linear tasks for rollout plan and dashboard updates.

Priya Shah: Concern about cold prefetch causing extra egress for private deployments - author: added a toggle to disable prefetch for private installs and added KMS-tagged opt-out in config; noted in docs.

Introduce cost-SLO prober (opt-in) with cold-cache prefetch and a split-batcher that chooses size- or latency-optimized microbatches; metrics and console flags added; recommended canary before global enable.

payload.body:
Motivation: Private deployments require tighter isolation between GPU node pools, network configuration, and Terraform state to support per-customer upgrades, safe rollbacks, and parallel apply workflows. Currently we keep a single, monolithic state per-cluster which causes long locks during upgrades and makes targeted rollbacks risky. This PR refactors the Terraform layout and introduces two new reusable modules (gpu_node_pool and iam_instance_profile), moves to a split-state layout, and wires minimal networking changes required for customer VPC topologies.

What this PR does (summary):
- Extract modules/gpu_node_pool: encapsulates node pool sizing, autoscaling policies, GPU taints, node-affinity labels, and kubelet config overrides.
- Add modules/iam_instance_profile: creates least-privilege instance roles and instance profiles for GPU nodes (SSM, CloudWatch, limited S3 for telemetry upload), with an optional external id for cross-account/private setups.
- Update modules/networking to support per-nodepool route tables and optional private subnet tagging for on-prem-style NAT routing.
- Move remote state to env-scoped backends with an additional nodepool-scoped backend option. Defaults keep backward compatibility by mapping old backend when migrating.
- Add scripts/migrate-state.sh: automated helpers to split state via terraform state mv, with dry-run mode and logging.
- Add example private/gpu-cluster.tf and testing harness to run a zero-downtime canary apply against staging.

Why this layout: The split-state approach reduces contention for long-running operations (e.g., draining/replacing GPU pools), enables targeted rollouts (canary one nodepool), and makes incremental restores/rollbacks possible by isolating state for critical components. The IAM module centralizes least-privilege concerns for audits and future RBAC automation.

Migration notes (high-level):
1) Run terraform init against the existing env backend and review current state.
2) Use scripts/migrate-state.sh --dry-run to get a mapping plan; confirm the plan in Linear ENG-1274.
3) For each nodepool to split out: terraform state mv <old_resource> <new_module_address> and verify with terraform plan.
4) Apply nodepool backends independently. For customers with strict change windows, plan/approve each nodepool apply.

Rollback guidance: Keep old backend snapshots (we retain S3 versioning and a timestamped lock) and use terraform state mv to recompose the original state if a rollback is needed. The script includes an --undo mapping file.

Testing performed:
- Staging deployment (private-eu-stg) exercised a full canary: created a new GPU node pool (nvidia-a100) with taints and node-affinity for inference workload; drained one old nodepool and validated k8s pod disruption budgets and service availability.
- IAM role checks: Verified instance profile attaches only required policies (CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy, SSMManagedInstanceCore + scoped S3 putObject to telemetry bucket).
- CI: terraform init/validate/plan/fmt/lint passed after one fmt fix; e2e canary apply executed against staging and smoke tests passed.

Checklist (author):
- [x] Module extraction and unit tests for tf modules
- [x] Migration script with dry-run and logging
- [x] Example for customer-private VPC topology
- [x] Security review: least-privilege IAM defaults
- [x] Performance test: reduced plan lock contention in staging

Notes and tradeoffs:
- This introduces more Terraform state files to manage; operational complexity increases but enables parallelism and safer rollouts. We provide automation to mitigate human error.
- Nodepool-level state means cross-resource references must use data sources or remote_state outputs; we add output contracts in modules to make this explicit.

Related: ENG-1274 (split TF state for private), ENG-1389 (gpu autoscale improvements).
Introduce modular GPU node pools and IAM instance profile modules for Private deployments. Add a split backend/state layout per-environment and per-nodepool to improve parallelism and reduce plan conflicts. Provide migration helper and rollback guidance. No user-facing API changes; infra-only.
Anita Rao (2026-02-23): Can you justify exposing external_id in the IAM module? We need it for cross-account installs but must ensure it's optional and never required by default.
Priya Malhotra (2026-02-23): Good catch — external_id is optional and documented. Default is null; module will only create a condition when set. Added tests to verify behavior.
Liam Chen (2026-02-25): Request changes: the node affinity logic needs an explicit topologyKey for multi-az clusters, and please add acceptance checks for scheduling (PDB respects during drain).
Priya Malhotra (2026-02-26): Addressed: added topology_key var with default "topology.kubernetes.io/zone" and added a staging acceptance test that simulates drain and validates PDB and readiness gates.
Marcus Vega (2026-03-01): Approved after LGTMs and CI green. Verified that the state migration script has a dry-run and undo path.

Summary: Introduces a smoothing layer in the Dedicated Autoscaler and a lightweight backpressure signal propagated from the gateway to fleet controllers. This reduces autoscaler thrash on spiky traffic and gives gateways a controlled way to shed load gracefully against per-pool soft capacity and throughput guarantees.

Motivation: Customers on Dedicated have reported oscillations when short bursts cross autoscaler thresholds and then recede; this leads to unnecessary GPU spin-ups and billing variance, as well as transient error spikes. The gateway currently responds with 429s or fallback heuristics; we need a first-class, observable mechanism that cooperates with autoscaling and preserves headroom for SLA-critical requests.

Changes in this PR:
- Autoscaler: add Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing of utilization and request rate with configurable half-life per-pool. New config fields: smoothing_window_ms, smoothing_alpha (derived).
- Soft capacity & grace tokens: each pool now tracks a small ephemeral token bucket (grace_tokens) to allow short bursts without triggering scale-up, decaying over time and replenished by underutilization.
- Gateway backpressure: add a new X-Redwood-Backpressure header and a compact gRPC/backchannel (gateway->controller) event to advertise desired ingress rate reductions per-route when pool smoothed_utilization > threshold.
- Controller/gateway handshake: gateway subscribes to per-pool backpressure_quota updates; controllers include backpressure_rate in scheduling decisions and expose metrics.
- Telemetry: new metrics smoothed_utilization, grace_tokens_available, backpressure_rate, backpressure_rejections. Add Prometheus labels for pool_id, model_id, and region.
- API schema: extend dedicated pool spec with smoothing and backpressure knobs; added validation and defaults.
- Console/docs: admin UI now surfaces smoothing window and current backpressure state with guidance.
- Tests: unit tests for smoothing math, integration e2e that injects burst traffic and asserts reduced scale-up churn and controlled 429 behavior.

Checklist:
- [x] Design review with SRE and Runtime teams (ENG-2147)
- [x] Unit tests for smoothing and token bucket
- [x] Integration e2e simulating bursty traffic
- [x] Telemetry dashboards updated
- [x] Migration notes and rollout plan
- [x] Backwards-compatible API schema changes (defaults safe)

Implementation notes:
- EMA parameters chosen to have ~30s half-life by default; pools serving low-latency workloads can set shorter windows.
- Grace tokens default to 2 tokens per pool; a token represents ~1s worth of headroom at pool's nominal throughput.
- Backpressure is advisory: scheduler will attempt to respect backpressure_rate before rejecting; only when backpressure persists will the gateway return 429s.
- To avoid unsafe throttling loops, backpressure updates include a monotonic seq and TTL.

Breaking changes: none expected; all new fields are optional with safe defaults.

Rollout plan: staged rollout: 1) feature gated off by default; 2) enable on Canary Dedicated clusters for 48h; 3) enable for opt-in customers with console toggle; 4) enable by default after 2 weeks of stable metrics.

Migration: API customers can ignore new fields; operators upgrading on-prem should ensure controllers and gateway are updated together.

Testing:
- Unit and integration tests added under tests/e2e/dedicated_smoothing_test.go
- Load test harness reproduces 1-2 minute burst profiles and asserts scale-up events reduced by >=50% while 95th-p99 latency impact <5% in our baseline.

Commits (high level):
- 0f9a8b2: controller: add smoothing math and metrics
- 1b3d2c4: gateway: backpressure header + backchannel client
- 8a7f6e1: api: add dedicated pool schema changes + validation
- c3e4d5b: telemetry: register new metrics and dashboards
- d4f2a9f: console: show per-pool smoothing/backpressure state
- f5b6c7d: tests: unit + e2e harness for burst scenarios

Files changed (high level):
- controller/autoscaler/smoothing.go: implement EMA and smoothing helpers (approx. 220 LOC)
- pkg/allocator/soft_capacity.go: grace tokens and soft capacity decisions
- gateway/backpressure/handler.go: header parsing and backchannel emitter
- api/config/v1/dedicated_pool.yaml: schema additions and docs
- telemetry/metrics_registry.go: new metric registration
- console/src/pages/pool/BackpressureCard.tsx: UI surface
- tests/e2e/dedicated_smoothing_test.go: load test harness
- helm/charts/redwood/templates/pool-config.yaml: default knobs
- ops/rollout/2026-03-dedicated-smoothing.md: rollout instructions

Small illustrative snippets:
- smoothing.go (EMA core): "smoothed = alpha*instant + (1-alpha)*smoothed"
- handler.go (gateway header): "if hdr := req.Header.Get(\"X-Redwood-Backpressure\"); hdr != \"\" { parseAndApply(hdr) }"

CI and checks:
- CI: go build, unit tests, linters (golangci), frontend unit tests
- e2e pipeline run on canary (k8s)
- Initial CI run: failed flakiness in e2e; reran and passed on second attempt.

Review thread summary:
- Marco Alvarez (SRE): requested clearer backpressure-to-scheduler contract and TTL handling. Response: added monotonic seq + TTL and explicit scheduler fallback behavior (controller will not reduce scheduling below 50% of nominal unless pool explicitly marked best-effort).
- Leah Kim (Runtime): asked for benchmark numbers for default EMA half-life; Response: added results from synthetic bursts showing 60% reduction in scale-ups with 30s half-life.
- Owen Patel (Security): requested audit logging for backpressure events; Response: added structured audit logs under telemetry/backpressure_events.
- Reviewer approvals: Marco Alvarez approved after TTL addition; Leah Kim approved after benchmark numbers; Owen Patel approved after audit logs.

Merge and post-merge actions:
- Merge method: squash and merge
- Post-merge: created a follow-up issue to add gauntlet tests against real customer workloads (ENG-2210)
- Updated canary dashboards and set alert: DedicatedPool.SmoothedUtilization > 95% for 5m -> page oncall

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: misconfigured smoothing window could delay needed scale-ups -> mitigation: default conservative half-life and admin override to disable smoothing per pool.
- Risk: backpressure loops between gateway and controller -> mitigation: monotonic seq + TTL + min-scheduling floor.

Release notes: "Improves autoscaler stability by smoothing utilization signals and introduces an advisory backpressure mechanism from gateway to controllers to reduce churn on short bursts. Operators: feature is opt-in and has safe defaults; see admin docs for tuning guidance."

CI status: pass

Motivation: teams have asked for a promote flow that lets us seed real traffic via shadowing, then progressively promote (hedged) traffic with the ability to pause/resume and an automated scheduled rollback if safety gates fail. This PR implements a resumable shadow-promote runtime + operator playbook: 1) a shadow seeding controller that can persist a partial promote state (so promotes survive controller restarts), 2) hedged-traffic routing policy that splits live traffic into primary/candidate lanes with configurable hedges and quorum logic, 3) scheduled rollback window support (timeboxed automatic backout if metrics diverge), and 4) telemetry snapshotting at each holdpoint (prefix KV, sample smoke traces, eval set gating). The description below is intentionally linear but the implementation is modular. Changes: - runtime/controller: new shadow_promote controller (resumable state persisted to rollout-store) and hedged router policy (quorum thresholds, hedge_ratio, max_inflight) - api: rollout API extension rollout.spec.promote.strategy = {type: "hedged", hedgeRatio, resumeTokenTTL, scheduledRollback: {enabled, windowMinutes}} - operator/playbooks: add playbook (docs/playbooks/shadow-promote.md) with step-by-step commands to inspect resume tokens, force-finish, or abort promote - telemetry: snapshots recorded to telemetry-store at each holdpoint + smoke-set eval hook; added new metrics: rollout.resume_count, rollout.hedge_confidence, rollout.rollback_trigger_reason - tests: unit tests for state persistence, e2e scenario that simulates controller crash & resume and a scheduled rollback firing Checklist: [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-2129) [x] unit tests [x] e2e smoke scenario [x] migration path for existing rollout CRDs [x] playbook and quickstart Example config (inline): rollout.spec.promote = {"type":"hedged","hedgeRatio":0.15,"holdpoints":["initial-smoke","telemetry-stable"],"resumeTokenTTL":3600,"scheduledRollback":{"enabled":true,"windowMinutes":30}} Backwards compatibility: default promote behavior unchanged unless strategy=hedged. Rollout store schema change is additive; migration applied via migration/20260214-add-resume-token.sql Note: description compressed into a single paragraph per repo conventions.
Adds a resumable shadow-to-canary promotion flow with hedged traffic routing and an optional scheduled rollback window; includes playbook and telemetry snapshots for safe promotes.
Maya Kline: Nice end-to-end, but can we avoid a global lock when persisting resume tokens? This will block high-concurrency promotes.
Author (Arjun): Switched to per-rollout lease and sharded store in a follow-up commit (see a1b2c3 -> l4m5n6). Removed global lock and added tests.
Lena Ortiz: The hedged router needs a clearer tie-breaker when quorum is ambiguous (e.g., 50/50). Recommend deterministic tie-breaker based on latency favoring primary.
Author (Arjun): Added hedge_confidence metric and deterministic tie-breaker (latency_pref) with feature flag for teams to opt-out.
Tomás Ruiz: CI flaked on e2e once; reran and passed. Approve after addressing small comments on telemetry retention defaults.
Author (Arjun): Lowered default telemetry snapshot retention to 7 days and added CLI to export snapshots for longer-term SLO debugging. Marking as ready to merge.
Step 1: apply migration migration/20260214-add-resume-token.sql Step 2: deploy controllers (kubectl apply -f deployment/shadow-promote-controller.yaml) Step 3: to kick off hedged promote, POST rollout with strategy=hedged. Inspect resume token: redwoodctl rollout resume-token get <rollout-id>. To force-complete: redwoodctl rollout promote finalize <token>. To abort: redwoodctl rollout promote abort <token>. Scheduled rollback: controller will emit rollout.rollback_triggered metric and perform traffic reversion; operator can disable scheduledRollback in rollout spec to prevent automatic backout.

Introduce Priority Lease Oracle for bounded ephemeral reservations; adds per-lease utilization telemetry and a degradation fence to preserve throughput guarantees under high contention. Includes operator docs and console visualization for lease heatmaps.
Motivation: Provide a middle-ground between instantaneous burst tokens and long-term reservations so low-latency tenants can opt into short-lived bounded reservations that are proactively reclaimed or hardened into commitments when load patterns justify it. This reduces tail throttling and makes autoscaler decisions more stable in mixed workloads. What this PR does: 1) Implements a Priority Lease Oracle component that issues timeboxed 'leases' with configurable size, priority, and soft-to-hard threshold logic; 2) Adds a degradation fence mechanism that prevents aggressive lease hardening when global headroom is below configured SLO thresholds; 3) Emits new telemetry streams for per-lease utilization, lease churn, and lease-to-commitment conversion rate for downstream costing and alerting; 4) Exposes a concise operator API and console view to visualize active leases and recent conversions. Design summary: The oracle receives lease requests from the admission layer. Each lease is evaluated against a local headroom estimator and a global threshold oracle which linearizes recent utilization and predicted short-term capacity. Leases are granted as bounded credits with an expiry and a softThreshold value. If utilization for a tenant consistently exceeds softThreshold over an observation window and global headroom is sufficient, the oracle upgrades the lease to a short-term commitment (hardening) and notifies the autoscaler and billing pipeline. If global headroom is low, the degradation fence triggers conservative backoff and emits a lease-defer event so clients fall back to pre-configured lower-priority paths. Rollback plan: The controller supports feature-flag gating via config priorityLease.enabled=false. Rolling back sets the gate to false and drains active leases over their TTL. Also a 'revert-lease-oracle' runbook is included in docs. Testing and validation: Unit tests for oracle heuristics and conversion logic; integration test that simulates mixed-tenancy bursts and validates that tail latency stays within SLO and that upgrade/downgrade paths are exercised; e2e canary run on a dedicated pool with synthetic bursts. CI: initial lint and unit failures fixed in subsequent commit; final run green. Observability: New metrics prefixed redwood.leases.{granted,converted,expired,rejected,utilization_p75,utilization_p95}; lease events are exported to eventbus with tags for tenant_id, priority, origin. Console: adds Lease Heatmap panel and a Lease Audit table under Dedicated -> Pools. Backwards compatibility: Leasing is opt-in and does not change default admission behavior. Security: tenant-scoped leases only; audit logs retained for 90 days. Related work: follows ideas from ENG-1429 proactive reservations and borrows telemetry hooks added in ENG-1487. Linear ticket SUP-9087 captured a customer incident where rapid short bursts caused repeated rejections; this PR implements a mitigation path. Checklist: - [x] PriorityLeaseController implementation - [x] Threshold oracle and degradation fence - [x] Telemetry and event exports - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Console panels and docs - [x] Runbook and rollback steps Performance notes: In perf canary, enabling leases at 10% of pool capacity reduced tail 99.9th latency by ~18% for bursty tenants while increasing short-term committed capacity by ~4% during conversion windows. Cost impact: conversions are charged through existing commitment billing path; default lease TTLs are conservative to avoid billing surprises. Operator config: new config section 'priority_lease' with fields max_lease_per_tenant, default_ttl_ms, soft_to_hard_window_ms, degradation_fence_threshold_pct. API surface: POST /pools/{id}/leases to request a lease; GET /pools/{id}/leases for active leases; admin endpoints to adjust thresholds. Docs: added RFC and operator guide under docs/dedicated/priority-leases.md. Known limitations: rare oscillation observed in synthetic workloads with extreme oscillatory load; mitigations included extra hysteresis and a conversion cooldown. Future work: predictive conversion using short-horizon forecasting and economy-aware lease sizing.
Marco Li: Left a couple of nit comments on naming and suggested moving the softThreshold into a typed struct for clarity.
Samira Noor: Asked for more detail on how billing signals are emitted; author replied with follow-up commit that adds tags to the commit-notification event.
Jared Kim: Requested a safety test that simulates global headroom collapse. Added integration test 'LeaseDegradeSafety' to address this and updated test matrix.
QA: Verified canary results and asked for clearer console hints on lease TTL units; updated UI tooltip text in console commit.
payload.title: priority-lease-oracle: proactive bounded reservations and degradation fence

Motivation: recent incidents showed increased p99 latency spikes when the runtime switched kernels aggressively for short sequences and simultaneously attempted speculative KV prefetching. This PR introduces an adaptive kernel selection policy plus a controlled prefetch degradation path that trades a small amount of throughput for deterministic correctness and lower tail latency under mixed workloads.

What this does (single-string description): Adds a KernelSelector that scores candidate kernels by estimated latency, numerical-safety score, and cache-friendliness; introduces a fallback budget token that bounds how often the fast path can be taken per model+device pair; implements a PrefetchDegradationPolicy that steps down speculative KV prefetch aggressiveness when p95/p99 latency or error-rate thresholds are exceeded; exposes a runtime flag --safe-mode to force conservative kernel and disable micro-prefetch heuristics for regulated workloads. The change coordinates with the continuous-batching layer to emit per-batch scoring metadata so the scheduler can avoid mixing high-risk fastpath batches with conservative ones.

Commits summary: compact, focused commits: 1) kernel selector core + scoring table (kernel_selector.rs, kernel_profiles.json), 2) fallback budget token implementation and metrics, 3) kv prefetch policy and prewarm adjustments (kv/prefetch.rs), 4) scheduler integration (scheduler/batch_manager.rs), 5) unit + microbench + e2e regression tests, 6) docs and changelog.

Files (high-level): runtime/kernel_selector.rs, runtime/kernel_profiles.json, scheduler/batch_manager.rs, kv/prefetch.rs, kv/cache_metrics.rs, serving/continuous_batching.rs, tests/perf/test_kernel_selector.py, tests/e2e/prefetch_degradation.yaml, docs/runtime/fallbacks.md, .github/workflows/perf.yml. Small illustrative snippets are included in the diff where helpful (see kernel selection scoring in runtime/kernel_selector.rs and the degradation thresholds in kv/prefetch.rs).

Performance notes: microbenchmarks on our internal perf-lab (A100 and T4 pools): adaptive selector reduces bad-kernel mispicks by 62% on mixed-length traces; p99 CPU-side tail reduced 18% on A100 with minimal p50 impact. Prefetch degradation cut memory thrash in KV-heavy workloads and removed a class of correctness-sensitive race where prefetch + rapid cache eviction led to stale KV lookups; we instrumented and validated by adding deterministic KV roundtrip tests.

Safety/correctness: numeric-safety score favours kernels with proven fp16/quantized stability for the model; the fallback budget ensures we do not silently oscillate between kernels (avoids thrash). The --safe-mode flag forces: 1) kernel policy to 'conservative', 2) prefetch disabled, 3) strict KV validation on every cache hit (adds latency but improves determinism). Documentation in docs/runtime/fallbacks.md explains when to use safe-mode (regulated/enterprise customers, incident mitigation).

Testing: added unit tests for kernel scoring edge cases, microbench harness to simulate mixed sequence-length streams, and an end-to-end scenario that reproduced the original incident locally. CI matrix covers x86 A100/T4 runners; a flaky perf test (tests/perf/test_batching_latency.py) initially failed and was rerun once. All checks passed on final run: build, lint, unit, microbench, and e2e regression.

Review thread (condensed into single string):
- Ava Chen (review): "Can we add a telemetric signal for fallback-budget depletion? Want to ensure operators see throttling events."
- Leah (author): "Added metrics: runtime.fallback_budget.used and runtime.fallback_budget.reset_count; documented in metrics.md."
- Miguel Torres (review): "Concerned about memory overhead of prefetch accounting on large-model KV, suggest bounded history window."
- Leah: "Implemented ring-buffer accounting with configurable window; default 128 entries, configurable via env VAR."
- Priya Nair (review): "Please justify safe-mode defaults and add opt-in threshold tuning."
- Leah: "Added configuration docs and conservative defaults that mirror existing SLA targets; included a small utility to translate latency SLOs to prefetch thresholds."
- Final: Approvals from Ava and Priya after addressing comments; Miguel requested a follow-up for telemetry retention, tracked in ENG-4210.

CI summary: build ✓, lint ✓, unit tests ✓, microbench ✓, e2e regression ✓ (one flaky perf test rerun). Post-merge: perf dashboards updated automatically via perf-lab webhook to include runtime.fallback_budget.* metrics.

Release notes: "runtime: add adaptive kernel selection and KV prefetch degradation policy to reduce tail latency and provide a --safe-mode for deterministic deployments. See docs/runtime/fallbacks.md for configuration and operational guidance."

Merge: Squash-merged to main after approvals and CI green. Follow-ups: ENG-4210 (telemetry retention), ENG-4299 (experiment: dynamic fallback budget tuning via RL controller).

payload.body:
Context: Customers and downstream SDKs expect parity with OpenAI's /v1/chat.completions semantics for param names, role preservation, stop and logprob behavior, and the shape/handshake of streaming function/tool call envelopes. This PR aims to close several incompatibilities observed during the recent migration pilots: (1) inconsistent acceptance/aliasing of v1 params (temperature, top_p, n, stop variants), (2) loss or collapse of role/metadata on fragments when streaming tools/function outputs, (3) ambiguity in stop token handling when multiple stop sources are present, and (4) intermittent stream framing failures under backpressure that broke tool-handshake/hand-off in high-throughput scenarios.
Summary of changes: 1) Param normalization layer: added a single translation table and coercion pass in the openai_compat adapter to accept common v1 aliases (eg: "temperature" | "temp", "top_p" | "topP"), coerce numeric types and validate mutually-exclusive configs (n + stream combos guarded). 2) Role & metadata preservation: stream fragments now attach an immutable role_id header and compact role metadata blob that survives chunking; role metadata is re-stitched at the stream coalescer to produce consistent role fields in framed JSON envelope. 3) Stop/logprob semantics unification: introduced stop-source weighting in the scorer so when multiple stop signals arrive (model-level EOS, user-supplied stop array, tool-inserted sentinel) we deterministically prioritize and emit a single canonical stop event and a best-effort logprob envelope describing the reason. 4) Tool/function handshake stabilization: implemented a two-phase handshake on stream start (capability advertisement + tool schema confirmation) and graceful fallback to framed-tool-text mode when the client does not accept rich tool envelopes. 5) Stream framing & backpressure fixes: improved coordinator's chunking heuristics, added heartbeat keepalive and an adaptive retry/backoff for transient write errors to avoid tearing stream boundaries. 6) SDK adapters and docs: small SDK compatibility helpers (Python and TS) plus an expanded docs note describing the framing envelope and expected client behavior.
Testing & CI: unit tests added for parameter aliasing, stop arbitration cases, and tool handshake state machine. Integration: end-to-end streaming tests with the python SDK and a lightweight Go client reproduced earlier flakes and are now stable on CI after two retries. A flaky harness test (tests/integration/test_streaming_high_load.py) required a test timeout bump and a small harness sleep to avoid racy client shutdown; we captured this as a test-only change.
Rollout plan: staged rollout behind feature-flag (openai_compat.v1_parity) — enabled for internal smoke and 10% of prod traffic for two days, then ramp to 100% if no regressions.
Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged unless the feature flag is enabled; clients using raw v1-like params will now be accepted and normalized (no API key or auth change).
Todo/Follow-ups: publish a small migration note to customers using custom stream parsers (ENG-4900), add observability for stop-source frequencies (ENG-4912), and run a perf canary for peak-traffic streaming.
Checklist: - [x] Param normalization implementation - [x] Role metadata persistence across fragments - [x] Deterministic stop/logprob arbitration - [x] Tool handshake fallback mode - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Docs update Related Linear: ENG-4821 (openai v1 parity), ENG-4837 (stream stability), ENG-4900 (customer migration)
Alexei Dobry: Please add a short explainer for the stop-source priority table and why tool-originated sentinels should be lower priority than model-eos. Also prefer a deterministic tie-breaker instead of random selection.
Priya Kapoor: Added a deterministic priority map (model_eos > user_stop > tool_sentinel) and documented tie-break behavior in code comments and openai_compat.md.
Samara Liu: The two-phase handshake looks fine but can we avoid an extra roundtrip for clients that already advertise accepted_envelopes? Consider piggybacking on the initial capability advertisement.
Priya Kapoor: Good suggestion — initial capability advert now includes accepted_envelopes and we short-circuit confirmation for known-legacy clients. Kept fallback for unknown clients.
Diego Marin: Noticed a potential race in fragment coalescer when a heartbeat triggers a flush concurrently with a tool handoff. Added a mutex and a unit test reproducer.
Priya Kapoor: Fixed with mutex and added test; also added a small explanatory comment in fragment_coalescer around concurrency model.
OpenAI /v1/chat.completions parity: parameter normalization and stronger stream/tool handshake. No breaking changes expected; improved streaming resilience and clearer stop/logprob semantics for compatibility with downstream clients.
Feature gated. When enabled the adapter will accept v1-style param names and emit a consistent framed JSON envelope for tool outputs; clients that relied on ad-hoc stream framing should read docs/openai_compat.md before upgrading.
1) Flip feature flag in helm values for staging. 2) Run smoke suite against python SDK. 3) Monitor stop_source metrics and stream error rate for 48h.
- Very large role metadata blobs are truncated to 8KB to avoid excessive memory churn; this may affect unusual custom metadata. - Some third-party parsers that split purely on newline boundaries will need minor updates to handle the framing envelope.
payload.title: parity-layer: unify chatv1 params, stabilize tool handshake and framed response envelope

payload.body:
Motivation: Dedicated clusters occasionally hit simultaneous microburst demand across AZs, which caused asymmetric eviction and poor tenant fairness when one cluster absorbed spillover while others throttled aggressively. This PR implements an Intercluster Slack Orchestrator (ISO) and a complementary Spillover Throttler (ST) to coordinate transient slack pooling, improve cross-cluster fairness, and surface utilization signals for billing and SLOs. Design summary: ISO maintains soft "slabs" of capacity that can be loaned across clusters for short windows; slabs are tracked per-tenant and per-priority window, and reclaimed with non-blocking backpressure signals. ST applies a graceful spillover policy that converts sudden overcommit into prioritized, time-decayed throttles rather than immediate drops, enabling downstream retries to succeed without wide-scale evictions. Implementation notes: adds slab allocator module, spillover controller, tenant-level lease bookkeeping, delta-based telemetry hooks, and new prometheus metrics (redwood_iso_loaned_slabs_total, redwood_st_active_spillovers, redwood_tenant_spill_latency_p50/p95). Rollout and safety: feature gated behind runtime.featureFlags.interclusterSlack; default off for Dedicated until feature flag is enabled for select tenants. Includes canary rollout plan: 5% of Dedicated clusters -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%, with automated rollback if tenant_throttle_rate > 2% or p95-latency regression > 10% over baseline for 30m. Related work: builds on ENG-3421 (telemetry standardization) and ENG-3490 (tenant throttle interfaces). Checklist: [x] slab allocator algorithms implemented and covered by unit tests, [x] integration test harness for 2-cluster failover scenarios, [x] e2e perf job added to benchmark-lab with synthetic microbursts, [x] docs updated in redwood-docs/observability about new metrics, [x] rollout playbook added to runbooks/runbooks/intercluster-slack.md. Backwards compatibility: API surface is internal to runtime; no breaking API changes to customer-facing endpoints. Observability: added dashboards and alert rules in observability-pack to track spillover ratio and cross-cluster fairness index. Summary: improves tenant fairness during short bursts, reduces noisy evictions, and provides actionable telemetry for capacity planning.
Liam Chen: Can you clarify the slab lifetime and reclamation guarantees? If a slab is loaned and the donor cluster suddenly regains load, how do we prioritize reclaim vs. fairness?
Anya Patel: Slab lifetime defaults to 90s; reclamation is best-effort preemption with exponential backoff for borrowers. Donor reclaim requests carry a priority tag; ST will convert low-priority loans into decayed throttles first. I added a paragraph in slab_allocator.go and unit tests that simulate donor bounce scenarios.

Anya Patel: Added a benchmark-lab job 'microburst-canary' and an e2e assertion in integration harness. Results attached to PR comment (raw metrics).

Marcos Rivera: Approving after small comment on doc phrasing; thanks.

Add per-token-phase latency/cost quantiles, KV-hit annotated traces, and SLO attenuation to reduce alert noise from cold-start phases.
Summary: Add a new observability surface that breaks down inference invocations into token phases (client prefix, prompt, generation, post-process) and emits per-phase token-level quantiles and cost attribution. Introduces an SLO attenuation mechanism for alerts that downweights known noisy phases (startup/cold-cache) and reduces duplicate alert churn for long-tail tenants. Motivation: long-tail SLO noise is dominated by a small number of high-cost but low-frequency cold-start invocations and post-processing spikes. By segmenting token latency/cost into phases and attenuating alerts from noisy phases, we can improve signal-to-noise for on-call and reduce pager fatigue. [x] Add e2e smoke test in perf-canary to validate attenuation reduces alert rate under synthetic coldstart workload Changes (high-level): - runtime/telemetry/token_phase_instrumentation.go: new phase boundaries + helpers to emit per-phase histograms and labels - d1f4a22 Add dashboard panels and dashboard JSON - e8a3f67 Add attenuation rule and tests - f1c2e30 Fix flaky integration test on CI Changed files (selected snippets): - runtime/telemetry/token_phase_instrumentation.go (new): emits histograms named redwood_token_latency_phase_seconds{phase="generation|prompt|prefix|post"} and labels tenant/model/region - Two asks: 1) please add an explicit metric documenting the percent of total token cost attributed to each phase so ops can create budget views; 2) clarify attenuation behavior when multiple phases are noisy." - Aisha (author): "Added redwood_token_cost_phase_fraction gauge and expanded attenuation_rule.yaml explanation to prefer attributing to the heaviest-cost phase and only attenuate if phase_fraction > 0.6. Summary: This PR collapses multiple serializing codepaths into a compact zero-copy serializer and replaces static pinned worker pools with an adaptive eventloop pool that dynamically balances affinity and batching pressure. Motivation: we observed two CPU-side bottlenecks under mixed workloads: excessive memcpy/encoding churn in the request serializer and coarse-grained thread pinning that amplified latencies when concurrent request shapes changed. Those interactions prevented the KV cache prefetch hints and continuous batching heuristic from realizing throughput gains. Goal: reduce per-request CPU overhead, preserve cache locality where helpful, and allow batching heuristics to scale without manual thread pin fiddling. Changes made: 1) Introduced compact_serializer: a unified serializer layer that emits zero-copy message frames for common request shapes and falls back to full encoding for edge cases. The serializer integrates with the KV cache layer to annotate frames with prefetch keys so the runtime can start KV lookups while the request is still being assembled. 2) Replaced the fixed-size pinned worker pools with adaptive_eventloop_pool: each event loop now starts with a light-weight io/compute split and can grow/shrink workers per numa-domain based on observed queue depth, latency SLO pressure, and batch formation rate. The pool avoids premature pinning; threads are opportunistically pinned only when sustained CPU affinity advantages are measured. 3) Decoupled serialization from response assembly: serialization tasks are now scheduled onto a small, low-latency serializer ring and can be executed inline for tiny requests to avoid enqueue/dequeue overhead. Larger requests use the ring to amortize copies. 4) KV cache hints and prefetch integration: serializer emits prefetch hints and an opt-in fast-path that requests KV lookups at frame creation time. We added a prefetch budget to avoid thundering when many frames are created. 5) Continuous batching improvements: made batch formation aware of the adaptive pool so that in high-concurrency scenarios batch timers are relaxed when threads are saturated, and in low-concurrency scenarios timers are tightened to reduce tail latency. 6) Kernel selection advisory tweak: the runtime now feeds short-lived request size histograms into the kernel selector to prefer lower-overhead kernels for sub-256 token runs. Testing and validation: microbenchmarks across representative workloads (token lengths 8, 64, 512; batch sizes 1..64) show median CPU-per-request reduction of 22% and end-to-end throughput improvements of 12-18% depending on model and hardware. p99 latency improved by 10-30% in mixed traffic scenarios that previously showed high variance due to thread migration. Load tests on dedicated pools with NUMA enabled confirm no regressions in long-running stability. Rollout plan: feature gated by opt-in config runtime.flags.compact_serializer and runtime.flags.adaptive_eventloop. We will enable behind a canary on 10% of inbound traffic for 48 hours and monitor p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel selection changes, batch size distribution, KV hit/prefetch ratios, and CPU usage per-core. Backwards compatibility: no API changes. The serializer keeps the wire format identical; fallbacks ensure edge cases behave as before. Notes about safety: added safeguards to avoid unbounded prefetching and to revert thread pinning when it increases tail latency. Observability: new metrics added - serializer.frames_zero_copy, serializer.inline_hits, eventloop.pool_size, eventloop.pin_rate, kv.prefetch_attempts, kv.prefetch_evictions. Follow-ups: plan to wire these into the Console rollout charts and add a regression eval for small-request regressions in the eval-harness.
Reduced CPU path overhead for small/medium requests: compact serializer + adaptive eventloop pool yield improved throughput and lower p99 latency. No API changes.
Alejandro: Can we avoid allocating the frame metadata on the hot path? Maya: Yes, replaced it with an inline tag for the common case; fallback uses heap metadata.
Priya: The adaptive pool seems to oscillate on the second load pattern. Please add hysteresis. Maya: Added 250ms stabilization window and unit tests to prove no oscillation.
Samir: Request to add a safety cap to KV prefetch budget to avoid thundering during spikes. Implemented with per-node budget and integrated into metrics.
Alejandro: Approved after CI green and perf numbers verified on benchmark-lab.

Motivation: quantized inference on bursty, short-sequence traffic suffers from repeated dequant/requant work and KV-cache churn when continuous-batching mixes tokens from different requests. This PR implements a lightweight ‘stash-and-merge’ prefix reuse mechanism combined with per-layer scale pooling and a delayed-dequant commit to reduce redundant dequant ops during windowed KV reuse. Summary of changes: 1) Add a KV prefix stash that keeps lightweight compressed representations of recently evicted KV windows to allow immediate rehydration without full dequantization when the runtime detects high prefix reuse probability. 2) Introduce per-layer scale pooling metadata produced at model load time (scale_pool.json blobs) so INT8/FP8 layers share quantization scaling when safe, reducing per-token recompute of rescale factors in the fast path. 3) Implement a delayed-dequant commit point in the continuous-batching pipeline: dequant work is staged and only committed for tokens that are about to be shipped to the network or to layers that require full-precision inputs, enabling amortized dequant when tokens are later merged from stash. 4) Kernel/runtime: small refactor of int8_microkernel and fp8_fuse paths to expose a dequant hint API and a compact in-memory stash format. 5) Heuristics: per-customer and per-route knobs (default-on for hosted) to control stash size, stash TTL, and the confidence threshold for reuse. 6) Extensive test harness and benchmarks (bench/stash_merge/) covering end-to-end latency, p50/p95/p99, and memory overhead. Performance: in internal benchmarks on a 48GB A100 pool with a real-world bursty chat workload, we observe 18-32% improvement in token throughput for short sequences (1-32 tokens) at p95 tail latency kept within 5% of baseline. Memory overhead for stash (default config) is ~3-6% at 500 qps; CPU amortization reduces per-token dequant CPU by ~27%. Backwards compatibility: stash format is versioned; when disabled by config the runtime falls back to current KV eviction+rehydration path. Rollout plan: feature-flagged rollout to canary hosts (10%) for two weeks, metrics guarded (token throughput, dequant CPU, KV rehydrate latency), followed by progressive ramp to 100% with an automatic rollback if p95 latency regresses >10%. Security & privacy: stash entries are kept in-process and respect existing KMS/encryption boundaries in private deployments; no new network surface added. Risks & mitigations: potential correctness edge-cases for poorly calibrated per-layer pools—added regression suite with golden prompt sets and a validation job that compares outputs against baseline float32 to detect regressions >0.5% token-level divergence. Related work: builds on prior KV-windowing, dequant-fusion and hybrid-quant scheduling efforts (see ENG-281, ENG-303). Implementation notes: added config flags: runtime.kv.stash_enabled, runtime.kv.stash_ttl_ms, quant.scale_pool_path, runtime.dequant.delayed_commit_threshold. Documentation & examples: updated docs/ops/kv-stash.md and examples/quickstarts/stash_tuning.ipynb. Owner: Asha Ramesh. Impact: notable improvement for chat/assistant workloads where prefix reuse is common, minimal risk to long-sequence throughput.
Miguel Ortega: overall this looks promising. Can you clarify memory accounting for stash entries under low-memory nodes? I’d prefer an LRU with strict budget enforcement.
Asha Ramesh: added strict budget enforcement and low-memory fallback to immediate eviction; updated tests to simulate OOM conditions.
Priya Patel: CI showed a flaky test in bench harness on p95 measurement after the first commit; re-run and ensure determinism.
Asha Ramesh: fixed timing nondeterminism by seeding the harness RNG and added retries in CI job; re-ran benchmarks and attached stable numbers.
Ethan Liu: can we expose a diagnostic metric for stash hit-rate per-route and integrate into console? Also add a SLO guard to prevent stash-induced p99 regressions.
Asha Ramesh: added runtime.metrics.kv_stash_hit_rate and a p99 guard metric; console dashboard patch will follow in a separate PR (docs ticket ENG-3622).
merged via squash and merge by Miguel Ortega (approved) on 2026-02-02. Commit message consolidated; CI green at merge time. Release notes: Adds KV prefix stash and delayed-dequant commit to reduce redundant dequant work; improves short-sequence token throughput by up to 32% under bursty traffic. Config flags available to opt out.
Adds KV prefix stash (stash-and-merge) and delayed-dequant commit to amortize dequantCost in mixed-precision paths; default-on for hosted; knobs available for tuning; benchmarks show 18-32% throughput win for short sequences.

Motivation: Tensor-parallel inference on multi-GPU clusters showed recurring idle periods where ranks blocked waiting on collectives. This PR introduces a pipelined scheduling approach and NCCL/CUDA-level tuning to increase overlap between communication and compute, reduce tail latency, and improve throughput for long sequences and high-token-rate workloads.

Summary of changes: added a pipelined microbatch scheduler that staggers microbatches across TP ranks, introduced per-layer non-blocking collectives on dedicated CUDA streams with explicit stream synchronization points, optimized host-pinned buffer allocation for NCCL rendezvous, and refined KV-cache sharding to reduce cross-rank fanout during KV fetch. Also added heuristics to dynamically choose microbatch size and number of in-flight pipeline stages based on runtime latency samples.

Compatibility and safety: changes are gated behind a runtime flag (TP_PIPELINED_COLLECTIVES=true) and default to previous behavior. The merge includes feature gates, extensive logging, a perf benchmark harness, and a rollback env var to disable pipelining cluster-wide. No API surface changes.

Testing and validation: unit tests for scheduler invariants, integration tests for correctness under synthetic workloads, and perf runs on 8xA100 instances. Benchmarks are included in perf/tp_overlap_bench. See benchmark_results field for measured gains.

Runtime knobs added (config keys): runtime.tp.pipelined_collectives, runtime.tp.max_inflight_stages, runtime.tp.nccl_stream_count, runtime.tp.dynamic_microbatching.

Deployment notes: flip the runtime flag in canary first (10%), monitor token-level latency p95 and per-rank GPU utilization; fallback to TP_PIPELINED_COLLECTIVES=false if error rates or p95 regressions >10% observed.
Diego Ramos: Nice work — the per-layer stream model looks promising. Two asks: (1) ensure fallback path avoids deadlocks if NCCL returns an error mid-stage, (2) clarify memory accounting for pinned buffers.
Asha Menon (author): Addressed both — added a retry+abort policy in nccl_transport.cu and incorporated pinned buffer accounting into the allocator; expanded logs to emit pool usage metrics.
Priya Kapoor: Can we make dynamic_microbatching opt-in per-model? Ops teams prefer conservative defaults. Also observed a 2% increase in CPU usage on the controller during our canary; is that expected?
Asha Menon: dynamic_microbatching is behind runtime.tp.dynamic_microbatching (default false). Increased controller CPU is from additional telemetry; added sampling reduction and optimized the stats aggregation loop to bring it back in line.
Jun Park: test flakiness near network partitions — would like an automated chaos test.
Asha Menon: added a simple network-partition integration test that simulates delayed collectives and verifies recovery via the retry path.
Improves multi-GPU tensor-parallel throughput and latency by pipelining microbatches and overlapping collectives with compute. Adds runtime flags to enable/disable pipelined collectives and dynamic microbatching. Includes perf harness and rollout guidance.
8xA100 synthetic long-seq (seq_len=4096, batch=4): throughput +1.31x, p95 latency -14%
8xA100 steady-token-rate test: sustained throughput +1.22x, GPU utilization increased from 62%->88%
Small-batch microbench (batch=1, seq=512): latency stable within +/-3% (no regression)
Canary 10% for 24h -> 50% for 6h -> full rollout. Monitor p95 token latency, per-rank GPU util, error-rate. Rollback by setting TP_PIPELINED_COLLECTIVES=false on controller or using the scripts/deploy/enable_tp_pipelining.sh to toggle off.
Unit tests cover scheduler invariants and stream ordering. Integration tests validate correctness of allreduce/concat paths under normal and partitioned networks. Perf harness run nightly against a dedicated perf-lab pool; observed stable telemetry and improved GPU utilization.

This PR adds a new opinionated quickstart that demonstrates a production-oriented RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) deployment pattern using a lightweight k8s sidecar retriever combined with a typed tool-contract approach for tool-calling. Goals: 1) provide an approachable example for teams that want to separate retrieval from model execution without running an external managed vector DB; 2) show how to declare explicit JSON schemas for tools and use the Typescript/py SDK helpers to validate contracts at runtime; 3) include a local retriever emulator that runs as a sidecar in the pod so the quickstart is fully runnable on a developer laptop or in a CI test cluster. The quickstart includes: - A README-guided walk-through that covers architecture, deployment steps (kubectl / kind / k3d), and troubleshooting. - A small Python microservice (fastapi) that hosts the app logic and uses the Redwood SDK to call the hosted API or a local Private deployment via env configs. - A Go-based sidecar retriever that emulates a vector DB (in-memory) and exposes a simple HTTP search API with configurable latency profiles for testing SLOs and cache behavior. - Typed tool contracts (JSON Schema and TypeScript types) for two tools: 'document_fetch' and 'source_extractor'. The SDK examples show schema validations, error handling, and graceful fallback to a cached result. - GitHub Actions CI workflow that runs lint, unit tests, and a kind-based end-to-end smoke test. - Example alerting rules and SLO snippets for the Redwood Console based on token cost and tail latency. Why this is different from existing quickstarts: most RAG examples target hosted vector services or focus on agent/single-process orchestrators. This quickstart is intentionally ops-oriented: it teaches patterns for sidecar retrieval, typed tool contracts, and localizable emulation of production latency profiles so platform and infra teams can iterate without incurring DB costs. Checklist:
- [x] Add starter code for python app and go sidecar
- [x] Add README and architecture diagram (SVG)
- [x] Add types and schema examples
- [x] Add CI workflow and smoke test
- [x] Add console SLO examples
Notes: The retriever emulator is explicitly not intended for production persistence. It is annotated in the README with migration guidance to a cloud vector DB or Redwood Dedicated-backed persistent retriever. Related Linear: ENG-4821 tracks the sidecar pattern validation, PM-129 requested the typed contracts feature.
Elliot Park: Nice pattern. Can we avoid a hard-coded port for the sidecar? Suggest making it configurable via env with default 8081.
Aisha Malik: Good catch, made port configurable and added an env var example in the README.
Maya Chen: For the typed contracts, please add an example of a partial failure where the retriever returns schema-mismatched results and the SDK handles it gracefully.
Aisha Malik: Added a test case and a sample 'on_schema_mismatch' handler section in the README.
Diego Alvarez: The GH Actions kind cluster times out intermittently; set action to use smaller images and increase retries instead of long sleeps.
Aisha Malik: Tweaked the workflow to retry kubeadm steps and reduced image size; re-ran CI.
Adds a Kubernetes sidecar RAG starter demonstrating typed tool contracts, a local retriever emulator, and a CI smoke test. Useful as an ops-oriented example for separation of retrieval and model execution.

Summary: Adds a tokenwise scale-lowering compiler pass and a ring-buffer collation stage in the runtime to reduce per-token quant/dequant churn and to coalesce KV cache writes from continuous-batching. Motivation: some workloads with short prefixes and frequent small continuations were suffering from per-token scale conversions and tight kernel launches that prevented microbatch coalescing on INT8 and FP8 execution paths. This PR targets the hot path by lowering scale operations earlier and grouping adjacent KV writes into a ring-backed collator so the GPU-side kernel sees larger contiguous work items without changing model numerics.

What changed (high-level):
- New compiler pass runtime/quant/scale_lowering.cc that detects consecutive token-scale operations and emits a lowered tokenwise scale applied as a fused kernel input where safe. The pass is careful to preserve per-head scaling semantics and falls back to explicit dequant when quantization boundaries are ambiguous.
- Ring-buffer collation runtime/scheduler/ring_collator.cc which accumulates KV cache writes from the continuous-batching queue and emits coalesced write batches to the kernel backend. Collation is implemented lock-free per-GPU-stream and supports configurable watermark/latency tradeoffs.
- Cache eviction hook runtime/cache/evictor.h to ensure collated segments respect existing per-shard eviction windows and do not hold stale KV pointers across rollouts.
- Microbench harness bench/quant/token_collation_bench.py and a small integration test tests/quant/scale_lowering_test.cc that validate numerical parity against the baseline within tolerated quantization noise.
- Docs: docs/perf/quant-collation.md describing knobs, feature flags, and recommended settings for Dedicated and Private deployments.

Commits (summary):
- feat(quant): introduce tokenwise scale-lowering pass (Marina Alvarez)
- perf(scheduler): add ring buffer collator and watermark policy (Marina Alvarez)
- fix(tests): stabilize scale-lowering unit tests and edge-case fallbacks (Marina Alvarez)
- bench: add token collation microbench and CI benchmark job (Marina Alvarez)
- docs: usage and rollout guide for quant collation (Marina Alvarez)

Files touched (representative):
- runtime/quant/scale_lowering.cc, runtime/quant/scale_lowering.h
- runtime/scheduler/ring_collator.cc, runtime/scheduler/ring_collator.h
- runtime/cache/evictor.h
- bench/quant/token_collation_bench.py
- tests/quant/scale_lowering_test.cc
- docs/perf/quant-collation.md

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Numeric safety: the scale-lowering pass applies a conservative analysis to ensure per-head and per-token scale semantics are preserved. Where the analysis is inconclusive (eg. custom layer-scale hooks or non-standard quant tables), the pass emits an explicit dequant/requant path to preserve correctness. The feature is gated by runtime.quant.scale_lowering and runtime.quant.enable_collation flags.
- Latency vs throughput: ring collator uses a watermark delay (default 1.5ms) to collect contiguous KV writes; on low-concurrency workloads customers can reduce or disable collation to prioritize single-request latency.
- Memory: ring-buffer allocates an ephemeral per-stream buffer sized by max_batch_tokens which defaults to 8k tokens per GPU. This is configurable and documented.

Benchmarks:
- Microbench on A100 (seq_len 2048, batch 8, generation 128): throughput +15% for INT8 end-to-end token/s compared to baseline quant path; median tail latency (p95) increased <2% with default watermark.
- Real workload sim (chat-like prefixes with many small continuations): median tokens/sec +18% and average GPU kernel launches reduced by ~22%. Detailed bench outputs attached in PR artifacts.

Review conversation (high level):
- Daniel Kim (review): "Nice win. Can you add a small test covering per-head scales and the mixed-precision fallback? Also please verify this doesn't regress KV streaming on Dedicated low-memory instances."
- Author reply: "Added per-head unit test and an explicit Dedicated config run in CI. Evictor hook added to avoid stale pointer windows."
- Sofia Nguyen (review): "Please document the feature flags and safe rollout steps; add a metrics counter for collated_batches and collated_tokens."
- Author reply: "Docs added and two counters (quant.collation.batches, quant.collation.tokens) exposed to console and Prometheus."
- Ethan Park (approval): "Bench numbers look solid; tests are green. Recommend squash-merge after CI smoke passes."

CI and validation:
- Unit tests: pass
- Integration (scale path): pass
- Bench job: artifacts show throughput improvements; bench job marked as informational in CI (not gating).
- Lint/format: pass

Rollout plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag off by default.
2) Canary on small Dedicated pool (internal tag: canary-quant-collation) with metrics for collated_batches and kernel_launch_count.
3) Gradual ramp with health checks for tail latency and model-quality regressions (Linear ENG-9273 monitors).

Related: Linear ENG-9273 (quant perf initiative), ENG-9410 (kv cache coherency), SUP-1891 (customer report of small-continuation latency).

Notes for maintainers:
- If future work expands the pass to span inter-layer fusions, ensure the analysis preserves custom kernel hooks (eg. fused FusedFFN variants).
- The ring collator intentionally avoids reordering across tokens belonging to different request IDs; do not change that invariant without consensus.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged after green CI and two approvals.

If you want to test locally: see docs/perf/quant-collation.md and run bench/quant/token_collation_bench.py with --gpu-streams and --watermark-ms to reproduce microbench numbers. 
- Introduces a tokenwise scale-lowering pass for INT8/FP8 execution paths that reduces transient requant/dequant overheads by ~12-18% on common LLM workloads.
- Adds a ring-buffer collation layer for KV-cache request slices that coalesces contiguous token writes and reduces kernel launch stalls.
- Backward-compatible: no API surface changes; runtime behavior gated behind feature flag runtime.quant.scale_lowering (off by default).

payload.body:
Summary: This PR implements an execution planner (opPlanner) that consolidates token-aware scheduling decisions for quantized execution and adds a compact dequant adapter to reduce memory bandwidth when materializing per-head dequant scales during KV access.

Motivation: We observed a ~10-18% latency tail increase on inference traces with highly variable prefix lengths (chat workloads) due to frequent kernel rebinds and repeated per-token dequantization of KV slices. The execution planner centralizes kernel selection and microbatch coalescing decisions so we can: 1) avoid unnecessary kernel swaps between INT8 and FP8 execution paths, 2) perform token-aware microbatching (coalesce short requests without increasing worst-case p99), and 3) opportunistically reuse dequantized KV tiles across nearby requests.

Key changes (implementation):
- runtime/op_planner/: new planner that consumes request metadata (sequence length, preferred precision, routing hints) and emits an execution plan (kernel sequence, batch boundaries, cache reuse hints). The planner is intentionally lightweight and deterministic.
- runtime/kv/compact_dequant_adapter.cc/.h: implements a contiguous short-lived dequant buffer format for KV tiles (packed per-head) and a fast path that returns zero-copy views when the backend supports in-place requantization.
- runtime/scheduler/token_coalescer: token-aware microbatch coalescer that groups short sequences up to a configurable token_budget without violating per-request latency SLO.
- runtime/kernels/int8_fp8_router: refactor to accept planner directives (prefer_packed_dequant, pipeline_stage) rather than making per-call heuristics.
- tests/e2e/quant_scheduling: added synthetic traces (mixed chat, streaming) to validate fallbacks, drift metrics, and throughput comparisons.

Behavioral notes:
- New planner adds a small scheduling decision cost (~100ns/request) but reduces kernel boundary crossings by ~45% on our workloads.
- Compact dequant adapter reduces memory traffic on KV reads by up to 28% (measured on A10 tests) and shows a 6-12% end-to-end token throughput gain for chat workloads that frequently hit regional KV reuse.
- FP8 fallback profile: planner can downgrade to FP8 when batch composition indicates reduced head-wise variance; this is a conservative fallback and requires explicit policy in model profile.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc (Linear ENG-1248) linked
- [x] Unit + integration tests
- [x] E2E benchmarks added
- [x] Perf regression guardrails updated
- [x] SRE signoff on rollout strategy

Commits (high-level):
- a1b3e5d: add op_planner interface and typedefs
- bd72f6c: implement compact_dequant_adapter and unit tests
- c3d9f2a: token_coalescer + integration with request router
- e6f4a1b: refactor kernel router to accept planner hints
- f98a2b0: e2e traces + perf harness updates

Changed areas / files (high level):
- runtime/op_planner/{planner.cc,planner.h}
- runtime/kv/compact_dequant_adapter.{cc,h}
- runtime/scheduler/token_coalescer.{cc,h}
- runtime/kernels/int8_fp8_router.{cc,py}
- tests/e2e/quant_scheduling/{mixed_chat.yaml,run.sh}
- docs/ops/quant-deploy.md (rollout notes)

Small illustrative snippet (planner directive example): "// planner output: {batch_end: 128, pipeline_stage: 'int8-main', prefer_packed_dequant: true}"

Review conversation (condensed into single thread):
- Miguel Santos (requested changes 2026-02-21): "Can we avoid introducing a new planner API surface that duplicates existing scheduler logic? Please sketch migration path and ensure we don't regress dedicated capacity flow."
- Asha Menon (author reply 2026-02-22): "Planned migration: op_planner is a thin layer that currently delegates to the old heuristics for Dedicated. We'll keep a feature flag and run against Dedicated smoke tests; the planner only becomes authoritative after a canary window. Added tests to assert identical decisions for dedicated ./config/dedicated_mode=true."
- Priya Rao (comment 2026-02-24): "Bench numbers look good, but please add a synthetic with heavy KV churn and one with nearly zero reuse to validate worst-case."
- Asha Menon (author reply 2026-02-25): "Added two e2e traces per request type and added guardrail metrics for KV-churn p99. Also instrumented planner decision latency."
- Jordan Kim (approved 2026-02-28): "Approach looks reasonable; compact_dequant_adapter is neat and the allocator is safe on our backends. Approving for merge once CI green."

CI and gating:
- CI: linters + unit tests + integration tests passed.
- Perf job: ran mixed_chat on A10/4xGPU with committed harness; throughput improved 9.8% median and 7.3% p99 improvement over baseline.
- A flakey GPU test failed initially (cuda-allocator-timeout) and was rerun; final run green.

Rollout plan:

- Canary 5% traffic on main for 48h with perf/latency alarms.
- If regressions within 48h, auto-fallback to legacy heuristics.

Merge outcome: squashed and merged to main (squash commit: "quant: add execution planner + compact dequant adapter (ENG-1248)").

Notes for ops:

Follow-ups (next steps):

- Add more aggressive FP8 autotuner based on live head-variance signals.
- Add telemetry to track planner-induced kernel-switch reductions per model.
Improves INT8/FP8 serving throughput by introducing an execution planner that reduces kernel switch overhead and a compact dequant adapter that lowers memory traffic for KV-heavy workloads. No API changes.
