payload.body:
Context and motivation: production inference for quantized transformer models revealed two recurring hotspots: (1) scatter in kernel entrypoints when lanes have mixed quant formats (INT8 vs FP8) causing suboptimal vectorization and register pressure, and (2) KV-cache hits that still triggered a partial dequantize path because of legacy prefix handling. This PR implements a packed-lane fusion approach for Q/K/V and attention kernels plus a lightweight KV fastpath that avoids dequantizing cached keys under compatible quantization metadata.

What this PR does (high level): packed-lane fusion: introduces a small buffer-format and tiled iterator that packs lanes of compatible quant types into contiguous microtiles before calling a single vectorized microkernel. The microkernel is agnostic to whether input tiles are INT8 or FP8; it expects a per-lane scale table and emits a compact requantized output. This reduces branches at the kernel boundary and enables wider SIMD usage across mixed-precision model snapshots. KV fastpath: adds a compatibility check to the KV cache lookup pipeline. When a cached entry has identical quant metadata and contiguous layout, we return a pointer to the packed tile and skip the dequant->requant transform on the hot path. The fastpath is opt-in via a new model-config flag `kv.packed_fastpath=true` and protected behind a feature flag with rollout gating.

Key changes (files/modules): sources changed include runtime/submitter/continuous_batcher.cc (scheduling hooks to detect prefix reuse), runtime/kvcache/packed_cache.{cc,h} (cache metadata + packed tile allocator), kernels/quant_microkernel_vnni.S (vectorized kernel entry that consumes packed tiles), runtime/exec/kernel_dispatcher.cc (packed-lane dispatch path), and python/tests/regression/test_quant_kv_fastpath.py (behavioral tests). Several small config and CI test updates were added for stress runs.

Commits summary: - feat: packed-lane tile iterator and allocator - feat: quant microkernel (VNNI-optimized) with per-lane scale table - perf: KV cache fastpath and metadata checks - test: end-to-end regression + microbench harness - docs: rollout and feature-flag notes

Microbench results (CI perf harness): int8-legacy baseline (64 batch, 32 tokens): 1.00x throughput; packed-lane + fastpath: 1.34x throughput, 12% lower p95 latency on short contexts (<=16) due to avoided dequantize; mixed-int8/fp8 snapshots saw 1.18x improvement (reduced kernel entry overhead). Memory impact: packed tiles increase transient memory by ~6% but reduce copy-related allocations on hot paths.

Compatibility and rollout: new model-config flag `kv.packed_fastpath` defaults to false. Operators can enable per-deployment via runtime config. We ship with a safe fallback: if metadata mismatch is detected or the packed allocator cannot satisfy alignment, we fall back to the existing dequant path. The change is backwards-compatible with on-disk cache files: on startup we scan cache entries and mark which ones are eligible for fastpath.

Review highlights and decisions: - Diego requested an explicit invariants doc for per-lane scale tables; added comments and a short design note under docs/design/quant-packed-lane.md. - Priya asked to keep the fallback cheap; introduced a one-shot check and moved heavy consistency checks to background validation to avoid tail latency. - Sam asked about GPU scheduling interactions; added a dispatcher hint so CUDA/hip backends can prefer aligned buffers for packed tiles (no functional change).

Testing and CI: unit tests for allocator, microkernel correctness (bit-exact requant thresholds for fixed seeds), and regression tests for KV cache semantics were added. CI runs included microbench stress on a dedicated perf runner; initial flaky failure in the NV kernel checksum test was fixed by tightening rounding behavior in the microkernel. Final CI status: pass (linux-AMD64, linux-CUDA smoke, python-integration).

Security and observability: added a perf metric `kv.fastpath_hits` and `kv.fastpath_misses` and exposed a small debug endpoint to enumerate cached entries eligible for fastpath. No sensitive data is added to logs.

Docs and release notes: brief rollout instructions and the flag description were added to docs/ops/feature_flags.md and docs/perf/quant_optimizations.md.

Merge and follow-ups: merged with squash on 2026-03-02 after approvals. Follow-up work tracked in ENG-11002: improve cross-GPU pinned allocator for packed tiles, and ENG-11014: extend fastpath to multi-head grouped layouts.

Notes for maintainers: keep an eye on p95 latency in the first week after rollout for models with high prefix reuse and heterogeneous quant snapshots. If regressions occur, disable `kv.packed_fastpath` and collect the `kv.fastpath_*` metrics for triage.
Diego Martinez: Can you add explicit invariants for per-lane scale table layout and ABI? Please add a short design doc.
Avery Chen: Added docs/design/quant-packed-lane.md and comments in packed_cache.h. Invariants: 16-byte alignment, scale table entries per 32 lanes.
Priya Nair: Ensure fallback is cheap — don't run heavy checks on hot path.
Avery Chen: Moved deep validation to background thread and kept single-shot metadata compare on hot path.
Sam O'Neill: How does this interact with multi-GPU allocator? Potential misalignment on some backends.
Avery Chen: Added dispatch hint and follow-up ENG-11002 to address cross-GPU pinned alloc.
CI Bot: NV kernel checksum flaky on first run — see build log artifacts.
Improves quantized inference throughput for mixed INT8/FP8 models by packing compatible lanes and avoiding unnecessary dequant on KV cache hits. Opt-in via kv.packed_fastpath; safe fallback to legacy path. Metrics: kv.fastpath_hits / kv.fastpath_misses.
payload.title: Packed quantized lane fusion and KV fastpath for transformer kernels

payload.body:
Motivation: incidents in the last quarter showed that single-metric rollback (typically error-rate) was too coarse for several classes of regressions: subtle semantic regressions that didn't immediately spike errors but harmed downstream quality, and transient infra-induced latency spikes that recovered quickly but caused noisy rollbacks. This PR introduces a stage-partitioned rollback policy that evaluates multiple signals (latency p90, request error rate, end-to-end QA eval score) per traffic partition (cohorts: paid/free, beta/opt-in) and triggers automated mitigations with cooldowns, quarantines, and optional human-in-the-loop escalation.

What this changes (high level):
- New RolloutPolicy CRD extension: "stagePartitions" field lets operators declare per-stage partitions with metric guards and weighted thresholds.
- Multi-metric evaluator: configurable rule engine that combines metrics with logical gates (AND/OR) and supports hysteresis windows to avoid flapping.
- Partition-aware automatic actions: graceful rollback to prior model variant, divert partition to a warm fallback model, or transition partition to shadow mode for traffic capture and replay.
- Quarantine and replay support: when a partition is quarantined an audit event and traffic capture snapshot are created for offline investigation and automated replay testing.
- Console + alerting hooks: new UI widgets to visualize partition-level metrics and an opt-in policy simulator in Console for dry-run validation.

Implementation notes:
- Controller changes: rollout-controller has a new stage-partition reconciliation loop that evaluates metric windows (default 10m primary window with 3m sampling stride). We added per-partition state persisted in the rollout status to track cooldowns, consecutive breaches, and last-action timestamps.
- Metrics ingestion: extended the metrics adapter to fetch model-level latency/e2e QA scores from Observability (Prometheus for latency, internal eval-store API for QA scores). Aggregation uses a sliding window reservoir to avoid bias when partitions have low qps.
- Safety: all automatic actions are gated by a feature flag (rollout.partitioned.auto_mitigate) and require a minimum sample count; actions emit structured audit logs and create a rollback runbook link.
- Backwards compatibility: existing RolloutPolicy schemas remain valid; controllers treat old policies as single-partition defaults.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for evaluator logic and CRD parsing (added ~40 tests).
- Integration tests: simulated canary runs against the perf-canary harness with synthetic regressions (semantic degradation and latency bursts).
- Load test: 1k rps sustained on perf-lab to validate aggregation when partitions have skewed traffic.
- Staging rollout: dry-run enabled on staging for 48h; we used the Console policy simulator to validate thresholds and observed no false positives.

Rollout plan:
1) Deploy to staging with feature flag off.
2) Enable dry-run for a subset of rollouts (no actions) and validate metric collection for 24h.
3) Canary in prod: apply to low-risk customers (opt-in beta cohort) with auto-mitigate disabled for 72h.
4) Gradual enable of auto_mitigate: 1% -> 5% -> 20% of eligible rollouts over a week.

Operational notes for on-call:
- When a partition mitigation occurs, a PagerDuty incident is created for SEV-3 by default; SEV-2 if mitigations affect >10% of paid traffic.
- Runbook included at: https://linear.app/ENG-3120/runbooks/partitioned-rollback (linked in audit entry).

Related tickets: ENG-3120, ENG-3299, PM-2042.

Checklist: [x] CRD schema bump documented; [x] unit + integration tests; [x] Console changes behind feature flag; [x] migration notes added to docs; [x] security review completed.

Notes on differences from prior approaches: this PR focuses on guardrails at the traffic partition level (not only at global rollout level). It reduces noisy global rollbacks by isolating mitigations to the affected cohorts and enabling controlled replay to validate quality regressions before a full rollback.

Diego Marquez: Can we tolerate partitions with very low QPS? The sliding-window reservoir addresses bias but add a minimum-sample check to avoid noisy decisions — addressed in multimetric.go (added minSamples config).
Lina Zhou: Add explicit audit events for every automatic action so security/compliance can trace mitigations. — added structured audit log events and a link to the replay snapshot in the status.
Tom Higgs: Suggest exposing an "opt-out" label for customers who prefer manual rollouts. — added an optOut label check in reconciliation and documented in examples.
Aisha Patel (author): Thanks all — addressed comments and updated tests. Ready for final review.

Motivation: production LLM streams occasionally deliver partial or fragmented tool schema information which causes incorrect tool_choice decisions, duplicate tool invocations, or hard failures when the compatibility adapter expects an exact schema match. This PR implements a soft-schema affinity layer that assigns confidence scores to candidate tools based on partial schema intersection, argument name proximity, prior message context (prefix/KV cache signals), and streaming continuity heuristics; it also adds a fragment-repair handler that coalesces broken JSON or framed tool-invoke payloads across stream chunks into a normalized invoke envelope. The OpenAI compatibility adapter is updated to prefer soft-bound tool variants when confidence exceeds a configurable threshold and to fall back to the existing deterministic router for exact matches. A route-level feature flag "soft_bind" (default: false) allows staged rollout for Dedicated/Private customers. Changes include: server/openai_compat/soft_schema_bind.py: affinity matcher and scoring; server/streaming/recovery_handler.rs: fragment coalescer and continuity token heuristics; sdk/python/redwood/openai_compat.py: opt-in soft_bind per-route and telemetry hooks; docs/openai-tooling.md: migration and behavior notes; tests/integration/test_toolcall_fallback.py: cross-chunk fragment tests; ci/pipelines/compat.yml: rerun-on-flaky integration tolerance. Checklist: [x] design doc linked to Linear ENG-4321; [x] unit tests; [x] integration tests covering cross-chunk fragments; [x] perf benchmarks (p99 within target); [x] docs and migration notes; [x] feature flag gating for gradual rollout. Migration notes: default behavior remains unchanged; enable soft_bind to reduce false-negative tool routing and to decrease spurious tool errors observed in streaming scenarios. Backwards compatibility: preserved; no public API schema changes. Performance: microbenchmarks show ~1.8% median latency regression under synthetic high-fragmentation load while reducing fallback tool invocations by ~12%. Risk: low-to-moderate due to concurrency in the recovery handler; addressed with stress tests and a short TTL on repair buffers. Related work and references: ENG-4321, PM-118, SUP-9988 (customer report).
Jonah Lee: overall approach looks good; please add a couple more unit tests for ambiguous-attribute scoring; also ensure metrics emitted at each decision point.
Maya Patel: added two more unit tests for attribute collision cases and wired decision metrics (affinity_score and decision_source) into telemetry.
Priya Desai: can we toggle soft_bind per-route in the console? If not, add a rollout plan.
Maya Patel: added a console-facing flag to the route config (console PR will follow), included rollout plan in docs; default remains disabled.
Samir Gupta: ran stress tests across Dedicated cluster; observed one panicked case which I reproduced — fixed by adding a repair-buffer TTL and stronger locking in recovery_handler.rs; verified with 10k simulated fragments.
Add opt-in 'soft_bind' mode for OpenAI-compatible tool calls that improves robustness to fragmented or partial schema payloads by scoring candidates and repairing stream fragments; enabled via route config; default off.

payload.body:
Motivation: On mixed-precision fleets we observe sporadic tail-latency spikes when the serving runtime switches between INT8 and FP8 kernels under pressure. Root causes include coarse-grained fallback logic (per-device) and KV-cache prefetches that assume a single precision for the entire microbatch. This PR introduces two cooperating components: (1) a HeterogeneousQuantFallbackCoordinator that reasons about per-request and per-layer precision compatibility and orchestrates graceful handoffs between quantized kernels (INT8/FP8) and the full-precision path; and (2) a KVPrefetchAdapter that annotates KV prefetch windows with precision hints and aligns cache warming to the coordinator's decisions.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a coordinator service inside the runtime scheduler that keeps lightweight, epoched precision-maps for active model versions and routes requests to the most compatible kernel path while minimizing kernel switch overhead.
- KVPrefetchAdapter propagates precision hints into the KV cache warming pipeline so that prefetched KV entries use the quantization layout expected by the chosen kernel or include a small inline dequantization token when mixed precision is unavoidable.
- Introduces a small lock-free per-GPU staging structure used by the coordinator to avoid global scheduler locks during precision transitions.
- Adds metrics and tracing hooks (precision.route, precision.transition_ms, kv.prefetch_mode) so we can observe fallback frequency and prefetch mismatches.
- Includes unit tests and microbenchmarks (CPU/CUDA) and a perf harness to reproduce the tail-latency scenarios.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- The coordinator chooses per-request precision by combining: request-level hints (from model config or client headers), per-layer compatibility scoring (fast heuristics computed from kernel profiles), and recent observed quantization success rate. This avoids gratuitous fallbacks for requests that can run entirely in INT8.
- We did not implement model-rewrite to stitch different precision layers into a single fused kernel (out of scope for this PR). Instead we focus on runtime orchestration and cheap data-path transforms.
- The KVPrefetchAdapter supports three modes: exact-layout (prefetch using kernel's preferred layout), dequant-inline (prefetch with small dequant tokens appended), and universal (store in a neutral layout and convert on load). The adapter selects mode based on memory pressure and observed conversion cost.

Testing and results summary:
- microbench/perf/hetero_quant_bench reports: average latency unchanged, P99 improved by ~12% on a mixed INT8/FP8 workload compared to naive device-level fallback, and token throughput improved ~6% under 75% quantizable workload.
- CI runs: linux-build: pass; cuda-tests: initially flaky (race in coordinator startup), fixed and re-run: pass; lint: pass; benchmarks: included baseline.

Backwards compatibility: Coordinator integrates behind an opt-in runtime flag (--hetero-quant-fallback=on). Default behavior is unchanged unless the flag is enabled. KV adapter is gated behind a config flag and defaults to universal mode for older deployments.

Follow-ups:
- Expand kernel-side fast-paths to accept pre-converted KV layouts to further reduce dequant overhead.
- Add a sampling-based evaluator to surface which layers would most benefit from static model rewrites.

References: Linear ENG-7421 for the incident ticket and ENG-7523 for the follow-up performance work; SUP-1982 captured customer repro traces.
Ethan Morales (2026-02-22): Can you explain how the epoched precision-map avoids stale decisions when models are rolled out quickly? Suggest adding a TTL and metrics for decision staleness.
Priya Shah (2026-02-22): Added TTL and a precision.map.stale counter, and documented the tradeoffs (PR updated).
Wei Zhang (2026-02-24): I saw a small memory regression in the bench run. Is the staging buffer size configurable? We should bound it based on GPUs and model context length.
Priya Shah (2026-02-24): Made the staging buffer tunable via runtime config and added a safeguard to cap entries per-GPU. Bench results re-run and mem regression resolved.
Lucas Carter (2026-02-26): CI showed a sporadic crash on coordinator init under heavy concurrency. Looks like a startup race with the epoch counter. Please harden initialization and add a test that spawns many concurrent routers.
Priya Shah (2026-02-27): Fixed the race (commit g9d2a44), added the concurrent init test; CI green after rerun.
Introduce opt-in heterogeneous quantization fallback coordinator and KV prefetch adapter to reduce tail latencies on mixed-precision fleets; enable via --hetero-quant-fallback flag.

Context and motivation: Production customers reported gaps in correlating streaming responses with backend routing metadata and third-party traces. This PR introduces per-route metric tagging for the streaming pipeline and carries HTTP/KV baggage through the OpenAI-compat shim into internal tracing spans so logs, metrics, and traces can be joined reliably. Changes: 1) route-tagging: attach route_id and route_variant as metric tags on the per-request metrics emitted by the streaming frontier and the response aggregator; 2) baggage propagation: read request-level baggage keys (x-rw-request-id, x-rw-route, custom kv) from the compatibility layer and map them to span tags using the observability contrib helper; 3) structured audit lines: augment JSON access-log entries with route, shim_mode, and trace_id for easier ingestion into ELK/structured sinks; 4) backwards-safe: the compatibility layer falls back to existing request-id header when baggage absent. Commits (high-level): - initial: add route_tag plumbing in streaming frontier and aggregator - followup: map baggage keys into opentracing span tags with unit tests - fix: handle nil baggage map on legacy requests - tests: add integration test exercising streaming + shim + trace correlation - docs: console docs for per-route metrics and an example Kibana query Changed files (high level): - inference/streaming/frontier.go (add tags to metrics emit path) - inference/streaming/aggregator.go (preserve route tag in aggregation counters) - api/openai_compat/shim.go (read baggage and inject into context spans) - observability/tracing/propagator.go (new helper to convert baggage->tags) - logging/json_access.go (augment access log payload) - docs/observability/streaming-route-metrics.md (how to use and example queries) Small illustrative snippet: emitMetrics("tokens_emitted_total", count, map[string]string{"route_id": routeID, "route_variant": rv}) Review conversation summary: - Diego: requested explicit unit tests for nil-baggage and for duplicate header precedence. Author: added tests and updated patch. - Lina: asked to ensure tags are bounded (max length) to avoid metrics cardinality explosion; author added sanitizer and documented limits. - Marco: requested a migration note for Dedicated customers running older private agents; author added a migration section to docs and an opt-out flag in the shim. Integration bench: smoke-tested on staging with canary traffic (5%) for 48 hours; metrics emitted as expected and traces correlate across OpenTelemetry backend. Risk and rollback: feature guarded behind feature-flag "obs.per_route_tags" and the shim flag "compat.inject_baggage" so we can revert without code rollback. Related: touches streaming, api-compat, and tracing subsystems; follow-up items include adding route-level SLO dashboards and enabling route tag dimensions in sampling rules. 
Adds per-route metric tags and propagates KV baggage into span tags for better correlation across streaming and non-streaming paths. No public API breaking changes.

payload.body:
Motivation: We continue to see tail latency regressions in mixed-precision kernels when models with large kv-cache footprints are routed through the 'fast' execution path. This PR introduces a lightweight compatibility shim and a per-request 'precision hint' header that lets the router/scheduler choose a conservative execution mode for requests that prioritize correctness over absolute token throughput.

What this PR does (single-string description): Adds a kernel-compat shim layer in the runtime that detects binary incompatibility or quantization sensitivity for a model+request combination and exposes a low-overhead boolean that the scheduler uses to avoid aggressive fusion/quantization fast-paths; implements an opt-in HTTP header (X-Redwood-Precision-Hint: prefer-correct | prefer-fast | neutral) and SDK flags that map to the same hint; extends continuous-batching logic to respect per-request hints by routing hinted requests to a separate lightweight queue that favors conservative kernels and smaller batch coalescing; introduces a KV-cache safety check that prevents prefix-optimized eviction heuristics from running for hinted requests; updates the metrics to surface how many requests used the compatibility shim and the delta in p50/p95 latency and token cost; includes tests and performance microbenchmarks.

Design notes and trade-offs: The shim is intentionally minimal: it does not change model weights or quantize on the fly. Instead it flips kernel-selection heuristics (no aggressive fused attention kernels, prefer fp16-safe paths, disable some prefetch transforms) and reduces batch coalescing windows to reduce peak memory pressure on hinted requests. This increases per-token cost but avoids correctness edge-cases introduced by certain fused kernels (observed in edge-case tests with malformed KV cache shapes). We chose a header + SDK-first API because it is the least invasive while enabling customers and platform teams to opt-in per-call.

Migration and rollout: The feature is behind a server-side flag (runtime.enable_precision_hint_shim). Default is off for all clusters; enabled in staging during canary; default for some internal teams with model reg tests. Rollout plan attached in the checklist.

Checklist: - [x] shim implementation and unit tests - [x] SDK header plumbing (python + ts) - [x] scheduler queue change and e2e tests - [x] add metrics and dashboard panels - [x] perf microbenchmarks (attached) - [x] rollout gating flag and docs

Related: Linear: ENG-4280, ENG-4297. Incident: SUP-1223 (customer reported hallucination/regression after aggressive kernel upgrade). More context: see internal doc https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4280/precision-hint-design (internal link).

Notes for reviewers: focus on runtime/shim correctness (no changed behavior for default-off), scheduler behavior (deadlocks or starvation between two queues), and SDK ergonomics. The PR intentionally avoids changing model catalog metadata until we validate metrics from canary.

Release notes: Adds an opt-in per-request precision hint header and a runtime compatibility shim to favor correctness over fused-kernel throughput.

Lina Gomez: Left a comment on runtime/compat/shim.go - can we make the detection deterministic across restarts? Reply: Ethan Park: shim maintains a strict serialization of detection state; added a small on-disk marker and unit test. 
Marcus Patel: Scheduler change looks OK but I'm worried about hinted-queue starvation under heavy hinted load. Reply: Ethan Park: added metrics and a low-priority backpressure channel which will allow hinted queue to borrow capacity from default when overall latency SLOs are in danger.
Ava Chen: SDK surface is slightly wordy; can we provide helper enum docs? Reply: Ethan Park: simplified the TS/PY helpers and updated api/headers.md with examples.
QA Bot: e2e hinted_queue_test failing intermittently on CI. Reply: Ethan Park: fixed a race in the test harness; re-ran CI and tests passed.

Motivation and summary:

We observed that single-threshold batching (max-batch-size only) can yield large cost variance across mixed workloads: small short requests suffer latency when waiting for large batch thresholds, but lowering thresholds increases per-token cost under high QPS. This PR introduces a small, operationally conservative stepped batching policy that trades off a couple of microseconds of scheduling overhead for much more stable unit economics across variable request size/QPS.

What this PR does (single-string summary):
- Implement 'stepped' batching policy in the serving runtime: the scheduler can be configured with an ordered list of candidate batch sizes (e.g., [1, 4, 16]) and per-step latency bounds. The runtime opportunistically serves smaller batches when latency SLOs are tight and ramps to larger steps when throughput allows.
- Add a `quant-safety` static linter that inspects quantization profiles and model graph ops to catch unsafe combinations (e.g., per-channel quant on ops we don't support in the CUDA/XT kernels, or FP16-only fused ops missing fallback). The linter emits warnings and suggested safe profiles.
- Add 'unit-econ smoke tests' to the CI: lightweight workload simulator that runs short generation workloads across a small matrix of batch sizes, quant profiles, and cache settings, and verifies cost-per-token regressions are within expected bands. Smoke tests run in ~8 minutes and gate regressions for perf/infra changes.

Implementation notes and commits (high-level):
- commit 1: runtime: stepped batcher core + scheduler hooks (api contract unchanged; new config block under route->batching)
- commit 2: runtime: careful backpressure handling and metrics (per-step latency histograms, step_transition_counter)
- commit 3: tooling: quant-safety linter as a CLI subcommand and CI check (bin/quant-linter)
- commit 4: tests: unit-econ smoke test harness + CI job + small golden baselines (ci/smoke/unit-econ/)

Files touched (high level):
- services/serve/scheduler/stepped_batcher.rs (new)
- services/serve/config/batching.yaml (docs + examples updated)
- runtime/metrics/registry.rs (added step-level metrics)
- tools/quant-linter/main.go (new)
- tools/quant-linter/rules/*.go (rules for op compatibility and fallbacks)
- ci/smoke/unit-econ/run_smoke.py (new harness)
- ci/.github/workflows/unit-econ-smoke.yml (CI job)
- sdk/python/examples/bench/stepped_batch_example.py (example config)
- docs/observability/batching.md (explain metrics and when to use stepped batching)
- tests/integration/serve/stepped_batcher_endtoend.test (integration test)

Small config example included in docs (snippet):

  batching:
    strategy: stepped
    steps:
      - size: 1
        max_latency_ms: 20
      - size: 4
        max_latency_ms: 50
      - size: 16
        max_latency_ms: 200

Notes on design choices: we intentionally keep the default step set conservative (1,4,16) to avoid surprising throughput regressions for large sustained QPS. The scheduler uses a tiny state machine to avoid flip-flopping between steps: a step transition requires a short stabilization window (configurable, default 50ms).

Quant-safety linter details:
- Static analysis of exported model graph + quant profile.
- Rules added: unsupported op-quant combos, precision funnel points (places where FP32->INT8 may lose critical dynamic range), and kernel mismatch with our CUDA kernels.
- Linter outputs machine-readable JSON and human-friendly summaries used by CI to annotate PRs. Example output: "WARN: op=matmul, quant=per_channel_int8 -> kernel_fallback_needed"

Unit-econ smoke tests:
- Simulate 1m equivalent tokens split across generated short (avg 12 tokens) and long (avg 160 tokens) requests to mimic chat + summarization mixes.
- Measure median latency, p95, and cost_per_1000_tokens. Failures trigger an artifact dump with token/time traces to help reproduce locally.

Review conversation (high-level transcript):
- Miguel: "Nice approach. Can we make the step list hierarchical per-route? Some customers want different steps for embeddings vs generation."
- Author (Asha): "Yes — config supports per-route batching blocks. Examples added to docs and example config file."
- Jade: "Quant-linter looks solid; add an allowlist for customers with known model exceptions."
- Author: "Added allowlist file support and tests for the allowlist behavior (tools/quant-linter/allowlist_test.go)."
- Evan: "CI time looks okay, but make sure smoke tests don't flake on low-QPS CI runners."
- Author: "Added retry + seeding and reduced variance; smoke runs ~8 minutes on our CI images."
- Miguel (approval): "Approve after green CI and one more perf run on canary infra."

CI summary: initial run had one transient failure in smoke tests on ubuntu-latest runner due to clock skew; rerun succeeded. All checks now green.

Backward compatibility and rollout:
- No breaking API changes. The batching config is additive; if customers omit strategy, existing behavior (legacy max-batch-size) remains.
- Enabled stepped batching only when explicitly configured. We plan to roll out conservative defaults in the Dedicated face as an opt-in for early customers.

Testing and perf numbers (representative):
- Mixed workload (40% short, 60% long) on g4dn.xlarge: median latency improved ~6% vs single-threshold tuned for throughput and cost-per-token reduced ~12% compared to always-on small-batch strategy. p95 latency was within the configured budgets for the step set above.

Follow-ups and todos (post-merge):
- ENG-2101: automatic step-suggestor that profiles live traffic and proposes step tuples per-route.
- Add telemetry to Redwood Console to visualize step transition heatmaps per-route.
- Expand quant-linter rules to cover model conversion tooling and add auto-fix suggestions where safe.

Merge details:
- Merge method: squash and merge.
- Final merge commit: "squash: stepped batching + quant-linter + unit-econ CI (Asha Patel)"

If you want to run locally: see sdk/python/examples/bench/stepped_batch_example.py and tools/quant-linter/README.md for quickstart.

Adds a stepped batching policy with conservative defaults, a static quantization-safety linter to catch incompatible quant profiles, and a new suite of unit-econ smoke tests for CI. No user-facing API changes; operational defaults improved.
This PR bundles runtime, tools, and CI changes to keep the feature integrated end-to-end. Kept scope tight to make reviewable while providing clear follow-ups for automatic tuning and Console UX.

Context: teams routinely hit regressions where aggressive microbatching or permissive quant presets reduce cost but cause tail latency or quality issues in mixed workloads. This PR introduces a lightweight runtime guardrail layer that estimates per-request marginal token cost and enforces conservative defaults for microbatching and compact quant profiles by default. Motivation: provide an opt-out, observable set of defaults that protect SLAs while still enabling meaningful unit-econ wins for typical web-scale inference traffic. Changes in this PR: 1) runtime/scheduler: add MicrobatchPolicy that chooses per-route microbatch ceilings based on recent token-cost distribution and a simple short-window SLO classifier; 2) optimize/cost_estimator: introduce estimator that computes a marginal-cost-per-token delta for quant profiles and batching modes (approximate, fast, cache-friendly); 3) config/defaults: add cost_guardrails.v1 containing default target_tradeoff (safety-first), max_microbatch_tokens, compact_quant_safety_margin and rollout flags; 4) CLI/console: surface a new page and CLI flags to preview expected cost/latency impact before enabling a profile; 5) e2e tests + smoke: add workload fixtures that simulate mixed short/long sequence workloads and validate no >2x tail latency regression; 6) docs: add a guide and recommended on-ramp for converting existing autoscale/batching configs to the new guarded presets. Implementation notes: MicrobatchPolicy uses a rolling 2-minute window (configurable) of (tokens, latency, success) samples to estimate a safety-bound microbatch_token_limit = max(16, median_tokens * safety_multiplier) subject to an absolute ceiling. The cost_estimator is intentionally conservative: it weights observed runtime token cost with quantized-mode delta calibrated from offline kernel benchmarks and per-instance throughput counters. Defaults: target_tradeoff="safety", safety_multiplier=1.1, max_microbatch_tokens=1024, compact_quant_safety_margin=0.07. Backwards compatibility: the guardrails are opt-out by route via config.allow_guardrails=false. Rollout plan: feature-flagged on staging for 48h, then 10% production canary for 72h, then gradual 100% if no regressions. Metrics & alerts: new metrics redwood.costguard.microbatch_ceiling, redwood.costguard.violations, redwood.costest.estimated_delta; alert if costguard.violations > 0.5% of traffic for 1h or if p99 latency regresses > 15% vs baseline. Testing: unit tests for policy math, mocked estimator harness, end-to-end smoke tests with perf lab harness; manual benching on small GPU pool included in PR. Docs & examples: updated quickstarts to include recommended presets for chat vs completion routes. Security & compliance: no secrets changes. Known limitations: the estimator does not currently account for multi-tenant interference; follow-up ENG ticket upserts detection and tenancy-aware calibration. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked - [x] unit + e2e tests - [x] docs - [x] canary/rollback plan - [x] metrics and alerts - [x] performance smoke in perf-lab
Ethan Liu: please add a short explanation for safety_multiplier and why 1.1 is chosen. Maya: added comment and linked bench numbers used to calibrate 1.1. Sofia Martinez: Can we surface an opt-out per-route in the console? Maya: yes, added route-level toggle and CLI flag --allow-guardrails=false, updated docs. Bernard O'Neill: CI failed once on the perf smoke due to flakiness in the fixture; reran and added small backoff in test harness. Ethan: suggest adding an integration test that simulates quant mode toggles; Maya: added additional e2e test and updated commits. Sofia: approved after docs tweaks. Bernard: approved. Merge hold lifted after successful 10% canary run and no alert triggers.
Introduce opt-out runtime guardrails for microbatching and compact quant profiles that provide conservative defaults to protect latency SLAs while enabling cost reductions. New metrics and console previews added. Rollout under feature flag.
Enable feature flag cost_guardrails_enabled=false by default in existing clusters. During canary set to true for 10% of traffic using rollout controller. Watch redwood.costguard.violations and redwood.costest.estimated_delta. Rollback by toggling flag or reverting to previous scheduler (main).

Motivation: multiple SDKs had divergent retry logic for ephemeral streaming requests which led to inconsistent user experiences and repeated ad-hoc fixes. This PR introduces a compact RetryAdapter library (golang + shared interface used by each SDK), exposes lightweight typed stream iterators in Python/TypeScript/Go to reduce boilerplate when consuming server-sent events, and pins the SDK packages to v1.6.0-alpha for a controlled rollout. Summary of changes (single-string description): add internal/retry adapter with configurable policy (max_attempts, base_backoff_ms, jitter, idempotency header support) and a small circuit-breaker for repeated 429/503; python: add redwood.sdk.streams.TextStream and StreamEvent typing, expose .events() async iterator and convenience .read_text() for single-message flows; typescript: add StreamEvent<T> and createStreamIterator() helper returning AsyncIterable<StreamEvent<T>>; go: add stream.IterEvent typed channel helper and NewRetryAdapter constructor used by client.StreamStart; common: update proto/stream.proto to add optional start_idempotency_key (backwards compatible), bump docs and examples; test: add unit and e2e checks covering idempotent restart, jitter distribution, and typed iterator ergonomics. Testing and rollout: CI initially failed on a flaky python streaming test, rerun fixed; canary rollout of pinned SDKs to internal prod team for 48h before wide release. Backwards compatibility: streaming start adds an optional header/field; SDK helpers are additive and do not require callers to change. Checklist: [x] unit tests added for retry adapter and iterators; [x] integration test for transient 503->recover; [x] docs updated; [x] linear tickets referenced (ENG-4127, ENG-4139).

payload.body:
Motivation: our current INT8/FP8 inference paths show good throughput on long sequences but suffer p95 latency regressions under mixed request sizes due to suboptimal kernel layouts and missing prefetch across fused dequant->matmul->requant sequences. This PR implements a fused kernel tiling and software prefetch strategy across quantized paths to reduce memory stalls, aligns KV-cache allocations to tile boundaries, and adds a small micro-batching optimization for continuous-batching workloads.

What this change does (high level): 1) Introduces a tiled fused kernel that performs dequant->matmul->requant in a single pass for INT8 and FP8 variants when the model layout matches (GEMM-friendly dims). 2) Adds a lightweight software prefetch schedule that issues prefetches for next tiles and KV cache slices to hide DRAM latency. 3) Aligns KV cache page allocations to tile boundaries and exposes a runtime hint in the scheduler to prefer tile-aligned KV slices for continuous batching. 4) Adds a small micro-batching path (batch sub-slices of size 2..8) for low-latency steady-state streaming that keeps latency SLOs while enabling efficient vectorized kernels. 5) Adds compatibility shims so fallback (dequant-fusion disabled) still uses the existing kernels.

Implementation notes: - New files: serve/runtime/kernels/quant_tiled_fused.cc/.h implement fused kernels with explicit tiling and pointer-aliasing checks. - CPU and GPU prefetch helpers implemented behind runtime toggles: serve/runtime/kernels/prefetch.h (CPU), cuda/quant_prefetch.cu (GPU). - KV cache allocator now exposes allocate_aligned(size_t bytes, size_t tile_bytes) and is used by the scheduler when tile hints present. - Scheduler: serve/scheduler/tiling_scheduler.cpp adds a heuristic to pick tile-aligned backends and to split continuous-batching windows into micro-slices. - New perf harness bench/bench_quant_tiling.py (microbench) and tests/perf/test_quant_paths.py.

Backward compatibility: the runtime uses a conservative autotune: fused-tiling enabled only when model metadata indicates contiguous attention heads and when quant config is compatible. Runtime flag: REDWOOD_QUANT_TILE_AUTO=true (default). If the fused path fails runtime checks it falls back gracefully to the existing dequant->matmul path. No API changes.

Testing & validation: - Unit tests: kernels correctness validated against dequant->matmul reference on a matrix of sizes covering 8..4096 and different head counts. - Integration tests: end-to-end inference with streaming enabled, verifying outputs within tolerance (L2 < 1e-3 for FP8, < 1e-2 for INT8 where applicable). - Smoke tests on Dedicated with mixed traffic replay (see ci logs). - Benchmarks: see performance_summary field.

Rollout: rolled out behind a feature flag and staged by model: default off for non-curated models; enabled for selected internal verified models. Observability hooks added to Console to show whether tiled fused kernels are in use per-request.

Caveats & known issues: - On very short sequences (<32) the micro-batching overhead can increase CPU time; scheduler disables micro-slices for seq_len<32 by default. - Some older GPU drivers showed prefetch instruction stalls on very large tile sizes; conservative tile defaults chosen and an env var REDWOOD_QUANT_TILE_MAX_BYTES to override for experimentation.

Checklist: - [x] Design review (ENG-5423) - [x] Benchmarks added - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Docs (release notes) - [x] Feature flag protected

Microbench (Xeon + A100 baseline=existing dequant->matmul path): INT8 fused tiled kernel shows 1.85x median throughput improvement and 22% p95 latency reduction for seq_len=512..2048 on encoder-only layers. FP8 fused path shows 1.4x throughput and 18% p95 p95 reduction. Continuous-batching with micro-slices reduces p95 by additional 8-12% in streaming workloads while increasing steady-state CPU by ~6%. End-to-end customer traces with tiled kernels reduced tail latency spikes related to KV fetch by ~35%. Memory working set reduced by ~10% due to in-place fusion and reduced temporary buffers.
Jared Huang: Can you add a microbenchmark comparing fused vs fallback on the 8-head 2048 length case? Also verify memory correctness with misaligned KV slices.
Aisha Patel: Added bench_quant_tiling.py and included the 8-head 2048 case; KV allocator now clamps and reports misalignment to logs (see last commit).
Lena Moretti: Please ensure autotune won't flip on for unknown models; suggested default off and opt-in via metadata.
Aisha Patel: Autotune default is conservative; only curated models enabled by metadata + flag. Added explicit unit test for metadata gating.
Calvin Brooks: CI flaky on CUDA prefetch kernel (timeout). Re-run required.
Aisha Patel: Fixed a race in the CUDA prefetch stream and split the test to avoid long single-run time. Re-ran CI and green.
Introduce fused tiled quantized kernels (INT8/FP8) with software prefetch and KV-cache tile alignment. Improves p95 latency and throughput for compatible models; enabled behind feature flag and model metadata. See docs/release/notes-quant-tiling.md for details and tunables.
Ops: feature flag REDWOOD_QUANT_TILE_AUTO controls autotune; REDWOOD_QUANT_TILE_MAX_BYTES overrides max tile size. Added Console metric tiled_kernel_in_use (bool) and tiled_kernel_latency_breakdown. Watch for increased CPU on micro-batching; default heuristics disable micro-slicing for seq_len<32.

Motivation: production traces and microbenchmarks showed significant CPU-side tail latency attributed to expensive thread pin/unpin sequences and repeated small serializations of request headers when forming continuous batches. This PR introduces two complementary optimizations: 1) a dynamic NUMA-aware threadpool that probes topology at startup and maintains pliable worker groups to avoid frequent expensive task pinning/unpin operations and to reduce cross-node memory traffic; 2) a bulk request serializer that coalesces header/metadata encoding for small contiguous requests into a zero-copy-friendly header slab when safe, falling back to the original path for incompatible payloads. Changes are targeted at the runtime hotpath and designed to be opt-in via runtime flags to simplify rollout. Checklist: - [x] add NUMA probe and topology-aware worker groups - [x] implement dynamic worker affinity policy with low-overhead heuristics - [x] implement bulk-serializer with zero-copy slab and safe fallback - [x] add kvcache hinting to avoid serialized work for cached prefixes - [x] microbench harness + performance tests - [x] e2e smoke tests on dedicated hardware Motivation, design and tradeoffs are inlined in docs/runtime/numa-bulk-serializer.md. Rollout plan: behind feature flag 'runtime.dynamic_numa_bulk_serializer'; staged A/B on canary fleet; fall back to previous threadpool on degraded metrics. Impact summary: p50 generation latency decreased 6-12% across mid-to-long sequences in our internal bench, CPU syscalls related to sched_setaffinity reduced by ~82% on noisy NUMA nodes under bursty load, and end-to-end tail latency (p99) improved by up to 18ms in heavy continuous-batching scenarios. Compatibility: no changes to API surface. The feature is disabled by default. Related work: follows observations from ENG-14522 and complements existing batching work in ENG-14971.
Diego Ramirez (reviewer): Nice direction. Please justify why dynamic affinity is preferred over static pin maps in the design doc. Consider fallback when numa info is inconsistent across kernels.
Priya Nair (author): Added section in docs/runtime/numa-bulk-serializer.md explaining decision; dynamic affinity avoids expensive remap operations at runtime and can react to hot-node pressure.
Marta Kline (reviewer): Bulk serializer looks good but edgecases around encrypted payloads need explicit checks. Also, can you avoid allocations in the hotpath?
Priya Nair (author): Bulk-serializer uses a preallocated slab per-worker and validates 'is_contiguous' and 'not_encrypted' flags before coalescing; added unit tests and comments.
Liam O'Connor (reviewer): CI failure on macOS build (clang) — thread APIs used are Linux-specific. Can we gate the probe to only POSIX platforms with sched support?
Priya Nair (author): Gated probe behind #ifdef and added a noop fallback path for macOS and musl; test matrix updated.
Marta Kline (reviewer): Left a few small nits around comments and naming; approve after those are fixed.
Diego Ramirez (reviewer): Verified perf numbers on canary cluster and approve.
Repo Maintainer (merge): squashed and merged after approvals.

Motivation: Customers with mixed workloads see suboptimal unit economics because static batching and cache defaults don't adapt to per-workload token distributions and model memory footprints. This PR implements a lightweight workload profiler, a cache-prefetch component, and a resource-aware quantization scheduler to reduce per-token cost while preserving tail-latency SLOs.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a runtime workload fingerprinting agent that collects sequence length histograms, KV cache hit patterns, and transient concurrency spikes. The agent emits compact fingerprints once per minute for each model/route.
- Introduces a prefetcher that uses recent fingerprints to warm prefix/KV caches on cold-starty traffic patterns (short bursty queries that reuse prefixes). Prefetching is conservative by default and includes budget controls per-tenant.
- Implements a quantization scheduler that recommends per-model quant profiles (fp16, int8, mixed) based on memory headroom and observed latency sensitivity. Scheduler exposes a safe margin and cost/latency delta estimates.
- Exposes a new diagnostics endpoint and Console dashboard hooks to visualize model heatmaps, predicted cost delta, and prefetch budgets.

Design notes:
- Prefetch decisions are deterministic and weighted by an exponential moving average of prefix reuse probability; we avoid aggressive prefetch on low-score models.
- The quant scheduler simulates a latency/VRAM curve using offline microbenchmarks and live traces; recommendations are conservative (default margin +15% latency buffer).
- All components run in the serving control plane and are opt-in by route via a new config block (route.optimizations). This preserves per-customer control and avoids surprise behavior for managed Dedicated/Private installs.

Introduce a staged precision degradation mechanism that probes lower-precision kernels (INT8/FP16) speculatively while keeping a correctness rollback window to ensure no silent regressions. This PR implements a speculative kernel prober that runs a lightweight probe alongside the production high-precision path for a configurable fraction of requests, a rollback handshake that compares summary metrics/digests rather than full outputs to avoid token-level cost, and a non-blocking fallback handshake for continuous batching and KV cache coherence. Motivation: customers have asked for lower per-token cost but we must avoid silent quality regressions or KV cache inconsistencies when toggling precision at runtime. The change aims to make the fast/int8 path safe-by-default while preserving latency SLOs and cache correctness across batch boundaries. Key behaviors: 1) Speculative prober runs in parallel only for requests matching the probe filter (traffic percentage + bucketed prompt shapes). 2) Probe produces a short statistical digest (token n-gram hashes + top-k distribution sketch) that is compared against the high-precision digest inside a micro-rollback window (first N tokens or until a configured stability metric). 3) If the digest divergence exceeds the threshold, we mark the kernel as "candidate-untrusted" and route similar shaped requests to safe-mode for a cooldown period. 4) For continuous batching, we avoid blocking the batch while waiting for probe comparison by attaching a deferred reconciliation step that can still trigger a model-level rollback and evict/repair KV cache entries if divergence is detected post-facto. 5) Added observability hooks and a rollout safe-guard so operators can ramp probe fraction and thresholds. This PR is focused on runtime orchestration and correctness plumbing; kernel implementations for specific backends are mocked behind the KernelProbe interface and exercised via integration tests. Checklist: [x] kernel prober control plane and config knobs [x] digest generation and comparator [x] non-blocking rollback/reconciliation flow [x] metrics + tracing for probe outcomes [x] integration tests for batching + KV coherence [x] docs update and rollout guide in runtime/ops/PROBING.md
Liam Chen: Overall this looks promising. My main concern is the cost of running probes in parallel for long contexts — can we bound memory/dedicated device usage?
Author (Maya): We cap speculative probes to a small in-process worker pool by default and the prober emits an early-abort if sequence length or token cost exceeds thresholds. Config knobs exposed so ops can set device affinity if desired.

Author (Maya): Switched comparator to a smoothed KL with heavy tail clamping; added a tunable divergence threshold and unit tests demonstrating stability.
Vikram Singh: How do we guarantee KV cache coherence if reconciliation runs after batches commit? Potential stale pointer issues.
Author (Maya): We implemented a conservative repair path: reconciliation can mark keys as 'repaired' and schedule eviction+refetch for affected request IDs; we also added an opt-in strict-mode which blocks commit until probe comparison completes for high-SLA buckets.

Author (Maya): Fixed race and added deterministic seeding for the mock kernels; re-ran CI and confirmed green.
Sophie Ramos: Approve after a small nit on comments in batcher.go.
Vikram Singh: Approve, would like telemetry dashboard follow-up (ticket linked).

Motivation: continuous-batching in the serving runtime currently groups requests by simple seqlen buckets (power-of-two or fixed ranges). These approaches either over-pad short requests or create too many small batches for long tails, harming throughput and cost. This PR introduces a quantile-driven partitioner that composes batches based on observed sequence-length quantiles per lane/hw-class, combined with an online cost heuristic to minimize padding overhead while respecting latency SLOs.

Design summary: compute lightweight seqlen quantiles over a sliding window per routing lane (e.g. model+device family+priority). Partition incoming requests into quantile bins (Q0..Qk) where k is auto-selected by the estimator to tradeoff batch fill vs queueing delay. At batch flush time the partitioner composes batches by greedily filling each quantile bin up to a kernel-friendly size, but with a kernel-aware cap (knowing which kernel/quantization mode will be used for that seqlen range) so we avoid mixing seqlens that force slow kernels. The system integrates with KV-cache affinity: requests hitting the same cached KV segment are preferred to be co-batched when beneficial; if co-batching would incur excessive padding the affinity is relaxed.

Key algorithmic points: 1) Quantile estimator uses reservoir sampling + fixed-size histogram to remain memory-bounded in high QPS. 2) Auto-k selection uses an AIC-like penalty for partition count to avoid overfitting rare tails. 3) Cost model is additive: token_cost(seq_len) + queue_cost(wait_ms) + kernel_penalty(seqlen_mix). Kernel_penalty is a small precomputed table derived from microbenchmarks (shipping in this PR). 4) Backpressure signals (overall queue depth and model pool utilization) dynamically reduce k to coarsen bins under load.

Why different from existing bucketing: instead of fixed boundaries, quantile bins adapt to workload shifts (e.g., carrier burst of long transcripts) and remove manual tuning per-customer. This complements, not replaces, existing seqlen-bucketing and stride-based batching: it will fall back to coarse buckets if quantiles are unstable.

Benchmarks: microbench on dedicated c5-like and p4d-like nodes with a Llama-2-70b-like trace: median padding tokens reduced by 28% vs current fixed bucketing; P50 latency unchanged, P95 latency improved by 6% on high-mix traces, and per-token GPU time decreased by 12% on average. End-to-end cost modeling on a productionish trace (60M reqs/day synthetic mix) yields estimated 9-14% cost savings depending on kernel choices. More details in notes_on_benchmarks below.

Implementation notes: new files added under src/runtime/batching/* and src/runtime/metrics/*, a small kernel_penalty table generated from scripts in tools/bench/kernel_costs/, and unit + integration tests under tests/batching/. The partitioner is feature-flagged behind FLAG_QUANTILE_PARTITIONER and gated on canary rollout.

Testing & rollout: local unit/integration coverage included, deterministic sim harness reproduced in CI with synthetic traces. Canary rollout plan: 1) enable on 5% of Hosted API traffic for a low-priority model family for 48h, monitor padding_tokens_ratio and latency SLOs; 2) expand to Dedicated pools with canary nodes, 3) global enable for compatible model families. Rollout controlled via Redwood Console flag and canary policy.

Related work: references ENG-8943 (cost-savings initiative), earlier experiments in ENG-7811 (stride-aware batching), and design notes in docs/runbook/batching-heuristics.md.

Checklist: 
- [x] benchmarked on representative traces
- [x] unit & integration tests
- [x] feature flag + canary rollout path
- [x] reviewer approvals

Impact: estimated cost reduction for mixed-seqlen workloads, improved tail latency consistency, and less manual tuning for customers with variable seqlen distributions.
Microbench: Llama-like trace, p95 improvement 6%, padding tokens -28%. Cost model: 9-14% token-cost reduction depending on model/kernel. Bench harness and raw outputs under tools/bench/quantile_results/*.csv
Unit tests for estimator and composer; integration sim reproduces synthetic traffic mixes; smoke canary on dedicated pool; monitor metrics: partitioner.quantile_stability, batching.padding_tokens_ratio, latency.p95, gpu_utilization.
Sofia Patel: Nice work — can you explain how this interacts with continuous batching time-based flush? I worry about increased jitter.
Author (Priya): The partitioner is orthogonal to time-based flush. We maintain per-quantile timers; we queue until either count cap or timer fires. Under high jitter we coarsen bins via backpressure to reduce timer skew.
Ethan Moore: Please add safety to avoid co-batching requests with incompatible KV-cache versions — we shouldn't degrade cache hit isolation.
Author (Priya): Added compatibility check and explicit affinity relaxation policy; see partition_composer.rs change.
Introduce quantile-driven batch partitioner (opt-in). Reduces padding for mixed-seqlen workloads and improves P95 latency in experiments. Feature flagged and rolled out via canary.

Motivation: Dedicated fleets occasionally face head-of-line coldstarts when multiple tenants burst concurrently. Large tenants can monopolize ephemeral warm pools and push small/interactive tenants into high-latency cold starts. This PR introduces two coordinated features: 1) Ephemeral warmlets: very short-lived, lightweight prewarmed worker slots that are proactively created when a tenant's recent short-tail qps increases beyond a threshold; warmlets are tracked per-tenant and recycled aggressively to avoid long-term capacity drift. 2) Tenant fairshare deprioritization window: a short, configurable window (default 45s) applied after a tenant consumes its short-term warmlet allotment; during the window the tenant remains available but is deprioritized for ephemeral prewarming to protect interactive SLA of other tenants. Both features are safety-gated behind the new runtime flag --enable-ephemeral-warmlets and default to disabled for existing Dedicated clusters. Key changes: autoscaler: new warmlet allocator and scoring policy, integration tests for scoring fairness; runtime: warmlet lifecycle manager, metrics and eviction policy; scheduler: updated placement hints to prefer warmlets for interactive routes; telemetry: new metrics warmlet_reuse_rate, tenant_deprioritize_count, warmlet_eviction_latency, plus a combined utilreporter gauge warmlet_headroom_ratio. Rollout plan: opt-in config for dedicated pools, gradual ramp via canary config targeting 5% → 25% → 100% of fleets, monitor warmlet_reuse_rate and 99th pct tail-latency for interactive tenants, automatic rollback if warmlet_reuse_rate < 12% after 30 minutes. Checklist: [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-8701) [x] unit and integration tests [x] canary config and console flags [x] metrics + dashboards [x] documentation update in /docs/ops/dedicated-warmlets.md [x] migration plan and safety gate docs.
Reviewer: Diego Alvarez — The allocator logic looks reasonable but I'm worried about churn on small clusters. Please add an integration test that simulates 200 tenants with bursty traffic and assert no more than 15% additional pod churn.
Author (Maya): Added integration test warmlet_end_to_end_test.go that replays traffic patterns; results included in CI run.
Reviewer: Sasha Patel — Can we make the deprioritization window tenant-configurable per-account? Some customers want tighter behavior. Also ensure this doesn't bypass per-tenant committed capacity.
Author: Window is configurable via dedicated_config->ephemeral_warmlet_window_secs and we explicitly honor tenant reservation before any warmlet allocation; added a unit test for reservation precedence.
Reviewer: Amir Hussein — Lint flagged a couple of race conditions in the allocator; uncommented locking around lastUse tracking and added comment about lock ordering. Also validate metrics tags for tenant_id.
Author: Addressed and added race-test harness; updated telemetry tags to include safe truncated tenant hash.
Approvals: Diego approved (LGTM), Sasha approved with comment addressed, Amir gave final approval after race fixes.
Merge: merged by squash after CI green and canary configs added.
Introduces ephemeral warmlets (opt-in) to reduce short-tail coldstart latency and a tenant deprioritization window to protect interactive SLAs. Feature is behind a runtime flag and disabled by default for existing Dedicated clusters. Metrics added: warmlet_reuse_rate, tenant_deprioritize_count, warmlet_eviction_latency. See docs/ops/dedicated-warmlets.md for configuration and rollout guidance.

Context: onboarding tenants for Dedicated/Private often requires manual tuning of batch/cache defaults and quantization profiles. Teams repeatedly ask for safe, opinionated defaults that reduce cost without degrading tail accuracy. This PR introduces a lightweight "Lean Onramp Wizard" (CLI + Console hooks) that autogenerates tenant-prefill presets and runs a quantization validator simulation before recommending profiles. Motivation: reduce time-to-value for SRE/Customer Engineering during onboarding, and avoid regressions when we suggest aggressive int8/4-bit variants. Changes in this PR: 1) new CLI command `redwood onramp init --tenant <id>` that collects a small sample workload, runs a fast profiler, and emits a tenant-prefill preset (batch shapes, cache TTLs, per-route prefill thresholds) 2) quantization-validator: a local dry-run harness that applies candidate quant profiles (FP16, int8, int4 approximations) against a held-out prompt set and reports a small set of unit-econ metrics (mean latency, 90/95 latency, token cost delta, end-to-end quality delta) and a pass/fail verdict against tenant SLA thresholds 3) telemetry tagging: onramp presets emit structured telemetry with tags pref:tenant_onramp=v1, sample_hash and validation results for auditability 4) Console integration: an endpoint and UI payload (console API) that allows Customer Success to preview presets and force-apply with an approval workflow 5) safety gate: an opt-in conservative mode that will only recommend quant profiles if quality delta <= 0.6% (configurable) Rollout plan: feature gated behind `onramp:enabled` FF. Default behavior is read-only (no automatic live application) until ramped. Implementation notes: the CLI is implemented as a thin wrapper around an existing profiling library to avoid duplication. The quant-validator uses a lightweight sampling evaluator (200 prompts by default) and an embedding-based semantic similarity check + token-level diff heuristics to approximate quality regressions; exact evals are deferred to larger runs. Checklist: - [x] CLI plumbing and command docs - [x] quant-validator core harness + smoke tests - [x] telemetry tagging and Console preview API - [x] unit tests for serializer and CLI flags - [x] e2e smoke run against a synthetic tenant workload Manual testing: ran the onramp workflow against internal sandbox tenant `dev-tenant-12`; results: recommended batch size 8, prefill_ttl=30s, recommended quant profile: int8-stable with predicted token-cost -26% and quality delta +0.1% (pass). Related: ENG-3421 (onramp UX), ENG-3599 (quant-safety).
Marco Silva (reviewer): Nice approach. A few questions: how do we ensure the sample is representative and not adversarial? Can we expose the sample size and seed to CEs?
Arielle Chen (author): Answer: CLI exposes --sample-size and --seed flags. Default sample_size=200 chosen from production-like traces (prior work with profiler). We added a sample_hash telemetry field so support can reproduce the exact sample.
Rhea Nambiar (reviewer): The quant-validator's similarity heuristic seems conservative; can we add a second metric based on logprob deltas?
Arielle Chen (author): Good suggestion — added a token-logprob-delta check as a secondary signal in validator, and tuned thresholds to avoid false positives on stable int8 profiles.
Tomás Ortega (reviewer): CI flaked once on the e2e smoke due to model availability. Suggest we mock network calls in unit tests and limit e2e to nightly for now.
Arielle Chen (author): Implemented a retry wrapper and a mock mode; updated CI job to run smoke in the "onramp-test" stage (non-blocking) and kept unit tests fast.
Marco Silva (reviewer): Approve after minor doc clarifications.
Rhea Nambiar (reviewer): Approve.
- Add 'redwood onramp init' to generate tenant-prefill presets and a quantization validation report.
- Console preview + approval workflow for safe application of presets.
- Telemetry tags for auditability of onramp runs.
Note: feature gated (onramp:enabled=false by default); visible to CEs after enabling.
This PR intentionally keeps validator conservative; the goal is first to reduce operational toil. Future work: integrate with the larger eval harness for full-quality regression checks, and add auto-rollout with canary traffic split when a tenant opts-in.

Improve installer release manifest generation: rotate artifact-level annotations for provenance, add environment-tagged manifest fragments for safer rollbacks, and bump Helm chart schema for v0.18.0. No user-facing breaking changes.
Motivation: our private-installer release pipeline currently stamps artifact provenance in a single monolithic annotations blob which makes incremental rollforward/rollback brittle in air-gapped environments. This PR splits per-artifact annotation blobs, rotates annotation keys for KMS-backed signing metadata, and introduces a small manifest fragment assembler that produces environment-tagged release manifests (e.g. vpc-staging, onprem-aws, onprem-baremetal).

Summary of changes: consolidated signing metadata serializer into scripts/signing/annotation_rotator.py; added a manifest fragment assembler at ci/release/manifest_fragments.go that merges signed shards into environment-specific release manifests; bumped helm/redwood-installer/Chart.yaml to apiVersion v2 and updated values schema for chart hooks used by upgrade/rollback; added Terraform module output to terraform/modules/installer/outputs.tf for release_manifest_ref to ease automation; added docs/docs/releases/manifest-rotation.md with operational runbook.

Why this is different: instead of rotating a single index, we now maintain per-artifact annotation files alongside the release index so the installer can apply or rollback individual components without re-signing unrelated artifacts. The annotation_rotator supports retention windows and key version tags so KMS/COSIGN rotations are decoupled from manifest assembly.

Testing: unit tests for annotation serializer and assembler integrated into CI; end-to-end pipeline run in staging created env-specific manifests and performed a dry-run install using the private-installer image. Verified artifact apply/rollback by toggling a single service manifest. See CI logs linked below.

Rollout plan: merge to main; the release job will publish a v0.18.0-installer candidate to the internal bucket and publish environment-tagged manifests. Staged rollout to vpc-staging for 48h, then to onprem-aws. If anything fails, the manifest assembler supports a --rebuild=false mode to re-use last consistent fragments and we can perform immediate rollback by selecting the previous fragment tag.

Notes: this PR touches signing utilities and release assembly; ops must have KMS key version available in staging before the next roll. Linear ENG-1972 contains the automated optional fallback to previous-key when cosign verification fails.

Small illustrative snippet (annotation_rotator usage):
  $ python3 scripts/signing/annotation_rotator.py --key-version v2 --source-bucket releases/staging/2025-11-03 --out-prefix fragments/vpc-staging

Files of interest (high-level): ci/release/manifest_fragments.go, scripts/signing/annotation_rotator.py, helm/redwood-installer/Chart.yaml, terraform/modules/installer/outputs.tf, docs/releases/manifest-rotation.md

Evan Cho: Can we guarantee idempotency when multiple runners try to rotate the same artifact? Added suggestion to add a 'lease' in the bucket writer.
Author (Maya Patel): Implemented a simple compare-and-write with object preconditions; added tests to cover concurrent rotate attempts.
Priya Singh: Need clearer failure handling for cosign verify failures during assemble. Recommend a flag to opt into 'best-effort' vs 'strict' modes.
Author (Maya Patel): Added --strict-verify flag to manifest assembler; default remains strict in CI and best-effort for manual runs.
Carlos Méndez: Confirm terraform output doesn't leak any secrets and that the output is stable across plan/apply cycles. Looks good after minor doc clarifications.

Summary: Introduces a neon-orchestrated hybrid attention path that combines a lightweight FlashAttention-style fast path with a tiled microkernel fallback. The patch adds a tiler that decides at runtime between (1) the optimized Flash micro-path for dense short sequences and (2) a new neon-prefetch tiled kernel for long contexts and odd sequence-lengths. Additionally this PR implements a lazy-KV streaming integration: instead of allocating/evicting large KV pages eagerly, the runtime streams KV slabs on demand and performs background prefetch with priority hints from the batcher. Motivation: our production traces show two dominant sources of per-token latency and cost: kernel selection overhead for mixed-length workloads and expensive full-KV swaps on long-context workloads. The hybrid path reduces kernel dispatch overhead and keeps the fast Flash path density benefits while the tiler maintains throughput on longer sequences. Design notes: - Kernel Tiler: a lightweight heuristic that computes tile sizes based on seq_len, k/v cache hits, and device utilization. Tiler exposes hints to the scheduler (tile_size, prefetch_priority, use_flash_path). - Flash micro-path: minimal changes to the existing Flash bridge to support neon-friendly memory layout and allow partial-row processing for non-4x head dims. - Neon tiled kernel: a new microkernel optimized for moderate tile sizes (32..256) with streaming prefetch and FP16 accumulation; includes an in-kernel rotary index remap to avoid extra memory passes. - Lazy-KV streaming: KV is broken into logically contiguous slabs. When a request needs a slab not present, we schedule an async prefetch and continue with partial KV (best-effort) to maintain tail latency. Background prefetching uses LRU+priority hints from the tiler. - Scheduler integration: continuous-batcher emits per-request hints (hot_token_prefix, expected_future_tokens) so the runtime favors coalescing requests that share KV slabs. - Fallback semantics: graceful fallback to the tiled kernel if flash_path fails or when the tiler estimates minimal benefit. Implementation touches: serving/runtime/tiler/* (core tiler & heuristics), serving/runtime/kvcache/streamer.* (lazy slab manager + prefetch worker), serving/runtime/kernels/neon_tiled_attn.* (new kernel), serving/runtime/kernels/flash_bridge adjustments, tests/perf/bench_attn_tiler.py, docs/attn_tiler.md. Testing & benchmarks: - Microbenchmarks across sequence lengths 8..16384, heads 8..64, model dims 1024..6144. - Canary on dedicated pools (pool-attn-4g). Results (canary): p50 latency -6%, p95 latency -12% on mixed-length workloads (avg seq ~512), throughput +18% on long-context workloads, token-cost -9% (due to fewer KV churns). Rollout plan: canary to 5% dedicated capacity for 48h, monitor tail latency, KV cache miss rate, memory OOMs. If no regressions, gradual increase over 7 days. Migration notes: no API changes. Config flags: runtime.tiler.enabled (default: true), kvcache.lazy_streaming (default: false) — kvcache.lazy_streaming off by default during initial rollout. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-1842) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf harness runs - [x] Canary plan - [x] Docs update - [x] Security review (no new surface) Known limitations: streaming introduces additional background IO which can increase memory churn under extreme concurrency; tiler heuristics are intentionally conservative and will be tuned as we gather telemetry. Backwards compatibility: existing model pins and rollouts remain unaffected.
Maya Singh: Nice approach. Can you add a short unit test that simulates partial-KV availability so we exercise the partial-forward path?
Evan Chen: Added a test in tests/unit/partial_kv_sim.cc and a perf harness scenario to the bench suite. Also added metrics 'kvcache.partial_forward_count'
Liam O'Rourke: Two nits: (1) rename prefetch_priority -> slab_priority (2) add a short comment on why rotary remap is in-kernel. Otherwise LGTM.
Evan Chen: Renamed per request and expanded the kernel comment to explain avoiding extra memcpy during remap.
Ravi Iyer: Observability: add an exported trace span around tiler decisions and the async prefetch edge. Please ensure spans include tile_size and slab_id.
Evan Chen: Added spans and unit tests for trace fields. Verified with local Jaeger that spans are emitted.
Maya Singh: Approving after CI pass.
Liam O'Rourke: Approved. Good microbench wins are convincing.
Introduce neon-orchestrated hybrid attention tiler and lazy-KV streaming: reduces p95 latency on mixed workloads and improves throughput for long-context models. Config flags introduced: runtime.tiler.enabled, kvcache.lazy_streaming. Backwards-compatible.

Context: production workloads with mixed sequence distributions (chat plus long-context retrieval) expose two friction points: 1) inefficient prefetch and reservation of KV cache leading to intermittent tail latency spikes when new contexts miss the fastpath, and 2) overhead from rotary/rope coordinate recomputation across fused attention paths. This PR introduces a coordinated change to the attention runtime: a two-tier prefetch scheduler and a lightweight rotary-offset-squeeze transform that reduces per-token rotary arithmetic when possible. The changes are designed to be backward-compatible with existing model configs and to be toggled via config flags for staged rollout.

What this PR does (high level): implement a prefetch scheduler that maintains priority lanes (latency-sensitive, throughput, and background fill) and an adaptive reservation window for KV cache; introduce a rotary-offset-squeeze transform operator that detects contiguous rotary offsets and emits a compact representation for the fastpath fused-attention kernels; add kernel hooks so the runtime can switch between 'squeezed-rotary' and standard rotary at the model-layer granularity.

Technical details: the prefetch scheduler runs in the request router before request batching and performs lightweight sequence-length prediction and cache-residency estimation; based on policy it either: a) place request in low-latency lane and pre-allocate a small KV reservation, b) schedule into batcher with optimistic prefetch, or c) mark as background for rehydrate-only scenarios. Reservation bookkeeping uses an LRU-informed window and exposes metrics for predicted vs actual hit rates. The rotary-offset-squeeze transform identifies when rotary index offsets increase monotonically within a tile and encodes the base offset plus stride, enabling the fused-attn kernel to apply a single vectorized rotary instead of repeated scalar ops.

Compatibility and rollout: default behavior is unchanged. New behavior is gated by two server-side config flags: runtime.attn.prefetch_enabled and runtime.attn.rotary_squeeze_enabled. The PR includes config migration docs and a canary rollout plan: 5% traffic -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with metrics monitored (p95 latency, KV hit rate delta, token/sec).

Benchmarks: measured on p4d-like machines with mixes representative of product workloads (50% chat seq<=128, 35% seq 256-512, 15% long seq 1024+). Observed median improvements after enabling both features: throughput +1.18x at seq512 under sustained load; p95 latency reduced by 17% for latency lane requests at small batch sizes (<=4); average GPU memory overhead for KV reservations reduced by ~9% due to tighter reservation windows; rotary arithmetic reduced by ~22% in fused-kernel fastpath, measured as FLOP-equivalent reduction. Microbenchmarks: fused-attn kernel with squeezed rotary shows a 9-14% speedup depending on head count and dtype (fp16/tf32).

Tests and CI: unit tests for scheduler state machine and rotary encoder edge cases; integration tests that run a synthetic workload harness against the local runtime with and without the flags; perf CI job included a 30-min soak run on perf-lab cluster (initial run flaky due to a race in reservation bookkeeping; fixed in second commit). All CI checks passed on merge.

Files of note changed: runtime/attn/prefetch_scheduler.py, runtime/attn/rotary_squeeze.cu, runtime/attn/kv_reservation.cc, runtime/attn/kernel_hooks.h, tests/attn/test_prefetch_scheduler.py, benchmarks/attn/prefetch_soak.yaml, docs/ops/rotary_squeeze.md.

Follow-ups: 1) extend reservation estimator with per-customer heuristics (ENG-4187), 2) add telemetry-derived automated lane assignment to replace simple heuristics, 3) explore further fusion opportunities combining KV eviction hints with rotary squeeze encoding.

Summary: this change reduces tail latency variance and CPU/GPU cost in mixed workloads with a conservative, feature-flagged rollout and clear telemetry.

Aisha Patel: Please add a short blurb in the runtime docs about how rotary_squeeze interacts with model quantization — I want to avoid surprises when models switch to int8.
Jordan Kim: Added docs/ops/rotary_squeeze.md and a note about quantization; the kernel emits a fallback scalar path for int8 where the squeeze is not safe.
Carlos Mendez: Nice work — can you clarify how reservation window growth behaves under bursty traffic? I want to ensure we don't over-allocate on transient spikes.
Jordan Kim: Reservation window uses exponential backoff with a max cap and decays after stable low-miss periods; added unit tests for burst scenario.
Linnea Berg: Perf numbers look promising; please include a canary plan and alert thresholds in release notes.
Jordan Kim: Canary plan added to description and release notes; alerts wired to p95 > baseline*1.15 and KV miss delta > 5%
Introduce prefetch scheduler with priority lanes and rotary-offset-squeeze transform. Performance improvements for mixed-length workloads: ~1.18x throughput at seq512 and reduced p95 latency for latency-sensitive requests. Flagged rollout: runtime.attn.prefetch_enabled=false, runtime.attn.rotary_squeeze_enabled=false by default. See docs/ops/rotary_squeeze.md for details and quantization considerations.
