Context: small, high-QPS microbatches and continuous batching expose a pathological pattern in tensor-parallel workflows where frequent KV cache evictions and many small all-reduce/NCCL calls dominate CPU/GPU scheduling overhead and NCCL latency.
Motivation: reduce the number of fine-grained collectives without compromising worst-case latency or cache correctness. This PR implements a lease-based KV windowing mechanism coupled with a windowed all-reduce coalescer and targeted NCCL burst/coalesce tuning.
Design summary: 1) KV Lease Manager: new lease semantics for KV entries used by continuing prefix/cache windows. A lease gives the runtime a bounded period (configurable default 8ms) during which an entry is eligible for delayed eviction to allow cross-microbatch coalescing. Leases are lightweight and per-peer (not global) to preserve correctness for partial shard eviction.
2) Windowed AllReduce Coalescer: the TP collective path buffers small tensor collectives that are marked coalescible into a single batched all-reduce according to a window (max_count=4, max_wait=6ms). Windows are sized by token-size heuristics and KV lease membership; the algorithm guarantees deterministic ordering and fallback to immediate dispatch if window thresholds are exceeded.
3) NCCL burst/coalescing knobs: a small set of NCCL params and stream scheduling adjustments (burst_coalesce=true, async_stream_batch=2) that increase the effective coalescing of adjacent launches while keeping occupancy constraints. These knobs are guarded behind runtime detection and can be disabled per-cluster.
4) Scheduler integration: the launch scheduler is extended to be window-aware: it pre-reserves streams and defers kernel launch until window closure for coalescible tensors. This includes safety gates for latency-sensitive requests (pin request tag to bypass).
Benchmarks (8xA100, 16 TP ranks, small sequence length 32, real prompt mix):
- Median token tail latency reduced by 18% (from 42.5ms -> 34.9ms) for the small-seq microbatch workload.
- Aggregate throughput improved by 27% for 32-token steady-state streams.
- NCCL call count reduced by 42% for the workload mix; average NCCL call size increased ~2.4x.
- KV eviction churn decreased 60% due to leases, reducing memory churn and CPU GC spikes.
Implementation notes:
- New files: src/runtime/tp/collectives/windowed_allreduce.cpp/.h, src/runtime/kv/lease_manager.cpp/.h, src/runtime/scheduler/window_coordinator.cpp/.h, src/runtime/nccl/nccl_tuner.cpp (tuning knobs), integration stubs in continuous_batcher.cc.
- Exposed two runtime knobs: redwood.runtime.kv_lease_ms and redwood.runtime.tp_window_ms; both default conservative values.
- Backwards-compatible: if leases/windowing disabled, behavior is identical to prior code path.
- Tests: added unit tests and a micro-benchmark harness under benchmarks/perf/windowed_allreduce_bench.py.
Checklist:
- [x] Design doc (docs/rfcs/lease-kv-windowing.md)
- [x] Unit tests for lease semantics and coalescer
- [x] Integration perf harness and baseline numbers
- [x] Runtime knobs & gating
- [x] CI green
- [x] Benchmarks added and reviewed
Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: increased worst-case latency for extremely latency-sensitive single-request flows. Mitigation: pinning tag bypasses windowing; window defaults are conservative and subject to rollout.
- Risk: interactions with Dedicated autoscaler jitter. Mitigation: disabled by default on Dedicated until canary complete.
Rollout plan: staged canary on internal perf cluster -> 10% customer canary with metrics tracking (KV eviction rate, NCCL call count, token latency) -> global release.
Related work: builds on prior comm-coalescing work (see ENG-2237) and NCCL pacing experiments in nccl_tuner. This PR is intentionally conservative with defaults to avoid user-facing latency regressions.
Arjun Patel (2026-02-16): Nice approach. Two asks: (1) a unit test that verifies lease expiry under jitter, (2) add a metric for "window_coalesced_calls" so we can track adoption over time.

Introduce a lightweight kernel lifecycle sampler and dashboard annotation hooks to improve visibility into per-kernel latency, queueing, and KV-cache interaction in the serving runtime. Motivation: production incidents in Oct/Nov showed transient latency spikes correlated with long tail kernel scheduling and cache thrash; existing NVTX ranges were useful but lacked compact per-kernel occupancy histograms and cross-request tag continuity. This PR adds: 1) a thread-local kernel lifecycle sampler that records kernel enqueue/start/complete timestamps with a compact ring buffer; 2) per-kernel occupancy counters exposed as exponentially-bucketed HDR-style histograms; 3) a small annotation API to emit short-lived dashboard events (start/stop markers) that are mapped to Grafana variables in the observability-pack; 4) KV-cache probe points to record soft-hit vs hard-miss latencies and a per-request hit-sequence fingerprint to aid regression triage; 5) lightweight continuous-batching probes that capture batch size distributions and per-batch scheduling delays. Implementation is runtime-only and conditioned behind a runtime flag (--enable-runtime-sampler) so cost-free when disabled. The description below documents usage, compatibility, and verification steps. Usage: enable flag on dedicated/private and hosted dev clusters; sampler outputs to /var/run/redwood/sampler.sock (unix socket) and integrates with existing observability-exporter via a new microprofile exporter that ships small JSON/line proto events. Backwards compatibility: the API is additive and feature-flag guarded; NVTX integration remains unchanged but now the sampler enriches NVTX ranges with kernel IDs for easier aggregation. Testing: unit tests for ring buffer semantics, integration test against perf-canary harness, and microbench added for 50/95/99 latency regression checks. Linked work: ENG-3284 (runtime observability), ENG-3340 (scheduling regressions).
Asha: requested lowering syscall frequency and exposing an opt-in exporter; Miguel: asked for clearer semantics around ringbuffer overflow and suggested HDR bucketing; Claire: asked for a smaller surface area for hosted runtime and added flag gating. Author replies: implemented batching of exporter writes, added overflow drop counter with sampling, and moved default to disabled. Follow-up: add rollout notes to Dedicated runbook. Final: approved after microbench shows 0.5% median wall-time overhead in non-production sample and clear improvements in 99th percentile scheduling latency on perf-canary.
Add runtime kernel lifecycle sampler and dashboard annotations (experimental, disabled by default); exposes KV-cache hit/miss probes; adds microbench for batch scheduling; configuration behind --enable-runtime-sampler flag; recommended for Debug/Canary deployments;
perf-canary baseline: 99p scheduling delay = 42ms
perf-canary with sampler: 99p scheduling delay = 28ms (after tuning scheduler knobs)
microbench overhead: median +0.5%, p99 +1.2% when sampler enabled
Unit tests: sampler ring buffer semantics and HDR helper; Integration: perf-canary runs with CI gating; E2E: deployed on internal dedicated cluster with flag enabled and exercised via continuous-batching workload; CI pipeline added to run microbench and report regression diffs.
Sampler writes to unix socket and exporter batches events; when enabling at scale, set exporter batch_size to >=128 and sampling_rate to 0.01 to bound metric cardinality. Add grafana dashboard variable sampler_scope to filter annotations per deployment. Follow rollout plan in docs/observability/runtime-sampler.md.

Motivation: Clients using the OpenAI-compat layer and our public model listing need a single, predictable surface to discover per-model capabilities (streaming stability, function/tool-calling support, structured-output specializations) and unit economics (pricing per token, soft/hard limits and concurrency). This PR extends the model catalog API and internal catalog objects to include capability and pricing metadata, plus server-side filters that power the console and SDKs.

Summary of changes: added explicit capability flags (openai_compat, supports_streaming_stable, supports_function_calling, structured_output_profiles) to the model listing; exposed priced_units and limits metadata (cost_per_input_token, cost_per_output_token, max_tokens_per_request, recommended_concurrency, rate_limit_tier). Implemented new query params for the GET /v1/models endpoint to filter by capability, max_estimated_cost_per_k, min_stability_score, region, and quantization support. Updated the OpenAI compatibility layer to prefer models with openai_compat=true for compatibility endpoints and to fall back predictably to compatible variants when a requested capability is not available. Added docs, SDK bindings, and tests.

Why this is safe: fields are additive. No breaking schema changes for existing consumers. Default behavior for compatibility endpoints is unchanged unless clients explicitly query the new fields or filtering. We included a migration path for older model entries missing cost metadata (defaults used and surfaced as "unknown").

API additions (examples):
- GET /v1/models?capability=function_calling&region=us-east-1&max_estimated_cost_per_k=0.50 -> returns models that advertise function calling and whose cost_per_1k_tokens <= 0.50.
- New model-listing response includes keys: capabilities (list), pricing (object), limits (object), compatibility_flags (list). Example snippet in response body (condensed for PR):
  "models": [{"id": "redwood-slim-1b", "capabilities": ["embeddings","streaming"], "pricing": {"cost_per_input_token": "0.00005", "cost_per_output_token": "0.00006", "currency": "USD"}, "limits": {"max_tokens": "4096", "recommended_concurrency": "4"}, "compatibility_flags": ["openai_compat"]}]

Implementation notes:
- internal/catalog/store: extended ModelRecord with flattened string lists for capabilities and compatibility_flags; pricing/limits stored as strings to avoid schema churn in metadata blobs.
- api/handlers/models: added parsing for new query params and server-side filter combinators; implemented pagination and estimation of cost-per-request for the max_estimated_cost_per_k filter.
- openai-compat layer: updated selection logic to prefer exact capability matches, then compatibility-flagged fallbacks, then nearest-latency alternative. This avoids regression for streaming clients while giving a predictable fallback path.
- SDK updates: python and ts SDKs gain ModelCatalog.list_models() optional filters.
- docs: new reference doc with examples and migration guidance.

Testing: Added unit tests for filter logic, integration tests exercising the openai-compat routing, and a small perf smoke to ensure the filter path does not add >1ms median overhead. CI initially caught a flaky kv-cache test unrelated to the change; rerun resolved it.

Rollout plan: Feature is behind a feature flag (model_catalog_capabilities_v2) and enabled for internal and canary tenants first. Console uses the new fields only when the flag is on. After 2 weeks of canary telemetry (stability and no client errors), we will flip default and update external SDK releases.

Related: ENG-4821 (catalog UX for capability discovery), SUP-188 (customer reported mismatch between advertised function calling and actual routing), docs PR will follow to expand examples.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the filter combinator correctness (api/handlers/models/filter.go), openai-compat selection priority (pkg/openai/selector.go) and the SDK bindings. The JSON snippet above is illustrative; exact field names are in the updated API doc file.
Ava Chen: Could we keep pricing fields optional in the public response if unknown? Some older models don't have pricing metadata. Maya Patel: Yes — we return 'unknown' strings for cost fields when missing and documented in migration notes.
Diego Martinez: The selector changes look good; can we add a tie-breaker by recommended_concurrency? PRiya Nair: Added tie-breaker using recommended_concurrency then latency; updated tests.
Liam O'Connor: Integration tests look flaky locally for one case — fails when the canary tenant doesn't have any openai_compat models. Maya Patel: Added a canary fixture in the test harness; reran.
Ava Chen: Approved after addressing docs and ensuring feature flag gating is in place.
Expose model capabilities and pricing in the model listing. New filters for capability, region, quantization, and estimated cost per 1k tokens. Additive API change; default behavior unchanged. Clients should opt into new fields via filters or SDK updates.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Long-sequence generation workloads (4k+ tokens) observed tail latency spikes under mixed-service traffic. Existing blockwise kernels and single-shard KV cache placement cause uneven GPU utilization and hot spots in the scheduler. This PR introduces a new attention kernel (lane-fusion) that fuses QK/KV micro-ops across contiguous head lanes, combined with a KV striping policy to distribute persistent KV shards across GPU slabs, and an async continuous-batcher that performs non-blocking windowed assembly of request batches.

Design summary: lane-fusion kernel consolidates the inner QK and value gather into a single CUDA path when sequence layouts align (most common in long, steady-generation workloads). KV striping maps persistent KV cache entries into N logical stripes per GPU slab to avoid single-slab hot allocation and to allow concurrent prefetch/eviction streams. The async continuous-batcher runs as a lightweight coroutine loop in the serving thread pool and exposes an adaptive window controlled by observed p95 latency — the window grows under low-latency headroom and shrinks on SLO pressure.

What changed (high level): commits: - Add lane-fusion attention CUDA kernel with fallback paths for misaligned sequences. - Implement KV stripe_manager with placement heuristics and async prefetcher/evictor. - Add async_continuous_batcher (Rust) with configuration knobs and integration with smart-routing. - Bench harness and perf tests for long-sequence steady-state and mixed-concurrency profiles. - Docs and runtime flags for opt-in and telemetry.

Checklist: - [x] Kernel correctness tests (unit and fuzz) - [x] Microbenchmarks for QK and gather paths - [x] End-to-end RLHF-style generation bench - [x] CI builds and GPU smoke tests - [x] Telemetry: added per-stripe allocation metrics and batcher window gauge

Benchmarks (CI harness on p4d.24xlarge, 32-batch concurrency mixed with 80% short/20% long requests): - Baseline (prior main): p50=18ms, p95=143ms, p99=212ms, throughput=1.0x - This PR (lane-fusion + striping + async batcher): p50=15ms, p95=118ms, p99=173ms, throughput=1.18x. Improvements are most pronounced on steady long-sequence tails.

Operational notes: the new KV striping is opt-in (runtime flag: --kv-striping=enabled, stripes=4). Lane-fusion requires models with contiguous head memory layout; runtime performs a capability check and falls back automatically to existing fused kernels otherwise. Async batcher is enabled by default in this branch but gated behind an internal feature flag until we validate in staging.

Testing and rollout plan: staged rollout: enable in perf-canary cluster (50% traffic) for two days, collect stripe allocation heatmaps and batcher window metrics, then enable for Dedicated pools with controlled capacity. Telemetry dashboards added under Redwood Console -> Runtime -> LaneFusion: per-model p99, stripe-utilization, batcher-window.

Known limitations: - Small-sequence workloads (<=128 tokens) see negligible benefit; batcher may slightly increase median under high burst traffic until adaptive window converges. - Striping increases meta-memory overhead (small constant per-stripe).

Related: ENG-3172 (scheduler improvements), ENG-3320 (kv eviction policies).
Reduced p99 per-token latency by ~18% for long-sequence (>4k) generation; added lane-fusion attention kernel, KV striping policy, and an asynchronous continuous-batcher with adaptive windowing. Backwards-compatible API. Opt-in via runtime flags.
Liam O'Connor: Can we add a compatibility check so lane-fusion doesn't get selected for legacy models?
Maya Chen: Added capability probe in runtime/attn/select_path.cc and fallback coverage in unit tests (see commit a3f9bf0).
Priya Desai: The stripe_manager looks good, but can eviction be prioritized for low-hit stripes?
Maya Chen: Yes — stripe_manager exposes a priority hint; default policy is LRU-per-stripe, I added an API to inject custom priorities for canary experiments.
Marco Bell: Microbench shows a regression for batch size=1 on short sequences; is that expected?
Maya Chen: Expected. Async batcher has an initial windowing warm-up; we added a fast-path bypass for batch_size==1 in this patch to limit regressions.
Aisha Rahman: CI GPU smoke failed once due to a flaky memcpy path, fixed in e9b1c2f, re-ran and all checks passed.
Liam O'Connor: Approving after telemetry and docs updated.
Priya Desai: Approved.

payload.body:
Adds an adaptive slot reservation coordinator to the continuous batcher to reduce KV-pin starvation and improve fairness across latency-sensitive and throughput-sensitive workloads. No API surface changes.
Summary: Implement an adaptive slot reservation coordinator for the continuous batching scheduler to address observed starvation of small, latency-sensitive requests when KV-heavy long sequences dominate the batcher. Motivation: Recent production traces and perf canaries showed tail-latency regressions for short-chat requests during KV-intensive traffic bursts. Existing fairness gating was coarse-grained and could not account for KV pin density or request age. This PR introduces a lightweight coordinator that reserves and dynamically reassigns 'execution slots' inside the batcher pool based on multi-factor scoring (request_age, kv_pin_density, estimated_token_cost, and priority_tier). The design favors low-latency requests without creating hard capacity islands and supports graceful soft-preemption when long-running batches exceed soft timeouts. What changed (commits): 1) c1a4d9b initial coordinator implementation: scheduler/slot_coordinator.{cc,h}, continuous_batcher_adaptor.{cc} hooks, metrics and config knobs. 2) 2f9b55e performance fixes: reduce atomic contention, use per-worker minibuckets, optimize kernel selection hints to avoid repeated lookups. 3) 8e7d120 tests and docs: end-to-end unit/integration tests, benchmarking harness script, docs/operations/slot-coordinator.md. Motivation and design highlights: - Adaptive scoring: each queued request exposes metadata (kv_pin_estimate, sequence_len_estimate, arrival_ts, customer_tier). Coordinator computes a score that biases selection towards low-age/low-kv requests when tail latency SLOs are at risk, otherwise relaxes toward throughput maximization. - Soft reservation with decay: slots are soft-reserved for latency-sensitive classes but decay over time (configurable half-life) to prevent permanent partitioning. - Soft preemption: if a running batch exceeds the soft_timeout threshold and there are pending high-priority small requests, the coordinator flags the running batch for early flush (flush of partial tokens + safe KV cache preservation) and reclaims one slot. This uses cooperative preemption to avoid evicting KV pins unsafely. - KV-awareness: the coordinator reads kv_pin_density metrics from the per-request admission token and reduces scheduling preference for requests that would pin a large fraction of K/V cache until a cooldown is observed. - Low overhead: implemented with lock-free rings and per-worker minibuckets; adds amortized ~0.5% CPU on steady state in microbenchmarks. Files changed (high-level): - runtime/scheduler/slot_coordinator.cc/h - runtime/scheduler/continuous_batcher_adaptor.cc - runtime/kv_cache/kv_pin_metrics.cc/h - runtime/config/slot_coordinator_config.yaml - tests/scheduler/slot_coordinator_unit_test.cc - tests/integration/slot_coordinator_e2e.sh - docs/operations/slot-coordinator.md - bench/perf/slot-coordinator-bench.py - examples/slot-coordinator-configs/local.yaml - CI: .github/workflows/slot-coordinator.yml (adds targeted perf jobs) Testing and results: - Unit tests: new coverage for scoring logic and decay semantics. - Integration: stress runs with mixed workloads show 35-60% reduction in P95 latency for short requests under KV-heavy background load, with <3% throughput regression on long sequence workloads. - Canary perf runs on staging TV showed stable KV cache hit ratios and reduced tail spikes. CI and review timeline: - Initial CI run: failed one flaky test: tests/integration/heavy_kv_emulation (timeout). - Rerun CI after adding a small test timeout increase and improved test harness determinism; subsequent run passed full matrix. Review comments and responses (excerpted): - Thomas: "Can we avoid adding global coordinator state that serializes admission?" Author: "Coordinator is sharded per worker with a light aggregation layer; code and comments updated to clarify no central lock is used." - Elena: "What guarantees do we have for KV cache consistency if we preempt a batch?" Author: "Added a safe-eviction path: we preserve KV pins for partial sequences and attach a reclamation token; documented in runtime/kv_cache/README and tested in e2e." - Marco: "Add observability: per-slot occupancy and preemption counters." Author: "Added metrics: scheduler.slot_reserved_count, scheduler.slot_preemptions_total, scheduler.score_distribution{quantiles}." - QA: "Repro scenario for flaky test included; added histogram seeding to reduce nondeterminism." Merge and rollout plan: - PR merged via squash on 2026-02-22 after approvals from Thomas and Elena. - Feature gated behind runtime.feature_slots_v1 toggle; rollout plan: enable in Canary region for 48 hours, monitor P95/P99, KV hit ratio, and per-slot preemption counters; then progressively roll to production. Backwards compatibility and impact: - No changes to public API. - Configurable toggle and knobs allow safe rollback. - Documentation added under docs/operations with tuning recommendations and suggested knobs for tenants with heavy KV workloads. Notes for on-call: - Alert to create: Increase in scheduler.slot_preemptions_total without corresponding decrease in scheduler.latency_p95 suggests coordinator is not effective and should be disabled. - If unexpected KV cache churn appears, disable feature toggle and consult runtime/kv_cache owner. Related work and references: - ENG-3842 design doc link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-3842/slot-reservation-coordinator-design - Related PRs: follow-up will integrate prioritized batching with dedicated GPU pools (planned ENG-3999). Why this is unique: Instead of simple age-based or token-bucket heuristics this PR combines KV-awareness, decaying soft reservations, and cooperative soft-preemption to reduce starvation without hard partitioning. It also emphasizes low overhead and safe KV cache semantics.

Motivation: We have accumulated several ad-hoc code paths to support INT8 and FP8 inference (smoothquant transforms, dequant fusion, and microkernel variants) which complicate scheduling, KV-cache alignment, and continuous batching. This PR introduces a modest orchestration layer (quantized-path-orchestrator) that: 1) makes explicit path selection rules for INT8 vs FP8 vs full-precision based on model metadata and runtime signals; 2) merges the dequant-fusion decision logic into the scheduler so fused dequant can be applied when it yields end-to-end token-cost wins; 3) aligns KV-cache slot allocation across quantized variants to avoid cache fragmentation and redundant copies; and 4) plugs path-aware continuous-batching heuristics so batch formation respects quantization boundary constraints. Summary of changes: consolidated path routing tables under runtime/quantized/orchestrator; added a small policy DSL to encode compatibility (e.g., supports_smoothquant, requires_dequant_fusion, kv_alignment_hint); extended the runtime scheduler to query the orchestrator when deciding batching windows and token coalescing; added fast-paths in the int8 microkernel launcher to accept fused-dequant buffers to avoid extra memcpy; added unit and e2e perf tests and a canary rollout gated by a feature flag. Design goals: reduce duplicated branch logic across kernels, avoid KV-cache churn when mixing variants, preserve latency SLOs while improving throughput and token-cost. Known constraints: full FP8 support requires newer cuDNN kernels on some clouds; the orchestrator has a conservative default policy (prefer older stable path) that can be overridden via route policy. Checklist: - [x] Design doc and microbenchmarks attached - [x] New scheduler hooks implemented - [x] Kernel fast-path to accept fused buffers - [x] KV-cache alignment logic added - [x] Unit tests and perf harness updates - [x] Canary feature flag and rollout plan Tests & perf: Microbenchmarks on c7g-like instances (internal lab) show throughput improvements of 1.25–1.32x for common 8k-context chat workloads when choosing INT8 fused-dequant path vs previous dynamic path selection; p95 latency reduced by ~12–20% for batched inference where dequant fusion avoided an extra memcpy; token-cost reduction observed ~10–14% across our internal benchmarks due to better batching affinity. Rollout plan: staged canary to 5% dedicated pools for 48h, validate cost and error budgets, promote to 25% then full release. Backout: feature flag and a per-route override allow immediate fallback to previous routing logic. Migration: no user-visible API changes; admin-only feature-flag defaults to off for cross-region private installs. Security/compatibility: no new network surfaces; user data stays in-process. Implementation notes: the orchestrator is intentionally tiny (~420 LOC of runtime glue); heavy lifting remains in kernel implementations. See release_notes below for selected callouts.
Marcus Liu: Overall this is a great consolidation. Please add a short note in orchestrator.py that explains the safe default policy for older hardware. Resolved by adding explicit default policy in commit b3e9f12.
Rina Patel: Can you add a regression test that mixes FP8 and INT8 requests in a single continuous-batch window? Added tests/quant_path_tests.py scenario 4 in f8e7b55.
Diego Alvarez: Concern about KV-cache memory spikes after rollout. We added a conservative per-pool KV soft-cap and telemetry to watch for OOM signals; will monitor on canary.
runtime: added quantized-path-orchestrator to unify INT8/FP8 routing and dequant-fusion decisions. Improves throughput and reduces latency for quantized workloads; rollout is canary-gated. No API changes. Admins can toggle via feature flag 'quant_orchestrator'.
payload.title: quantized-path-orchestrator: unify INT8/FP8 smoothquant + dequant-fusion scheduling

payload.body:
Motivation: Improve end-to-end throughput and p99 tail latency for INT8/FP8 inference paths without regressing quality. We observed that dequant->transpose->attention kernels were paying repeated per-token memory operations and poor packing across micro-batches, especially for short sequence workloads. This PR introduces an "attention funnelizer" kernel stage that fuses the dequant/scale step with q/k/v layout transforms and a small prefetch path, plus a lightweight requant scheduling layer that informs the runtime how to group micro-batches for vectorized microkernel execution. The continuous-batcher improvements ensure the runtime can maintain tight SLOs while enabling larger, opportunistic coalescing for throughput.

Changes in this PR: single-string description with checklist and notes: - implement AttnFunnelizer microkernel: fuse dequant+multiply-by-scale + q/k/v transpose + optional per-head requant hint. - add RequantScheduler policy hook to the continuous batching pipeline to produce aligned microbatch windows for INT8/FP8 kernels. - KV cache alignment changes to maintain zero-copy when AttnFunnelizer is used and ensure cache offsets remain 64-byte aligned across versions. - runtime config: new kernel_hint.attn_funnelizer.enabled and kernel_hint.requant.pack_size tunables exposed to Redwood Console. - tests and perf harness updates: microbench driver, integration perf test for 8x short-seq workloads. - docs: brief runtime/ops note and FAQ entry.

Why this is different: existing dequant fusion efforts focused on per-layer fusion; this work targets the attention path specifically and the interaction with continuous batching. Instead of collapsing many ops inside the backward-compatible attention kernel, the funnelizer produces a packed attention-ready buffer which downstream kernels can consume with minimal memory traffic and predictable alignment. The requant scheduling layer is runtime-only and does not change model exports.

Benchmarks (internal perf harness, A100, FP16 baseline vs INT8/FP8 variants): - INT8 + AttnFunnelizer + RequantScheduler: +18% median throughput, +12% 95th percentile throughput; p99 latency reduced by 8% in continuous-batching mode for short sequences (<=64). - FP8 with funnelizer: +10% throughput vs previous FP8 path, p99 -5%. - Memory traffic on the attention hotpath reduced ~22% measured by nvprof counters.

Compatibility and rollout: non-breaking for models that do not enable the kernel_hint flags. Default is off for public hosted rollout; enabled for dedicated clusters behind a feature flag. Provides safe fallback to the legacy dequant path if the kernel is not available or alignment constraints fail.

Checklist: - [x] Kernel microbench and functional tests - [x] Integration perf harness updates - [x] CI passing (flake run after addressing a clang-tidy complaint) - [x] Console config & docs - [x] Release notes entry

Notes and follow-ups: - Follow-up PR to add a lightweight auto-tuner that chooses pack_size based on observed sequence distribution (linked ENG-2114). - Investigate combining with per-head requant multipliers upstream in the model loader (design doc sketch linked).
Arjun: Nice work — can you add a short note on numerical equivalence tests for per-head scaling? I want to ensure we don't drift when requant hints are used.
Author (Lena): Added additional regression tests comparing baseline and funnelized outputs with multiple seeds. See tests/unit/test_attn_funnelizer.cpp.
Sofia: CI flake — one of the perf scripts assumed /tmp permissions. Pls make harness tolerant to env differences.
Author (Lena): Fixed harness to use mkdtemp and added CI job env normalization.
payload.title: Attention funnelizer + requant scheduling + continuous-batcher for improved quantized kernel throughput

payload.body:
Motivation: The OpenAI Responses variants that customers adopt increasingly rely on explicit determinism/seed directives and lightweight structured-output annotations passed through the HTTP layer. Without preserving those hints across our OpenAI-compat adapter we observed divergences between direct upstream behavior and Redwood-hosted responses in customer compatibility testing (see ENG-4821). This PR implements two coordinated changes in the adapter and runtime surface to improve compatibility and reduce customer surprises: 1) deterministic/seed propagation: accept and translate OpenAI-style determinism flags (seed, deterministic, x-seed) present as either JSON fields in the Responses body or as HTTP headers, and persist them through the routing, reassembly, and streaming layers so that streaming reassembly uses the same determinism hint used by the model selection logic; 2) structured-output annotations: accept structured output schema hints (openai_schema, schema_hint, or x-output-schema) and surface them to the structured-output postprocessor and the tool-call router. Implementation summary: - HTTP adapter: new header handling for X-OpenAI-Seed, X-OpenAI-Deterministic and X-OpenAI-Output-Schema; these are normalized to internal headers X-Redwood-Seed and X-Redwood-Output-Schema during internal RPCs so that downstream components see a consistent key. - Payload parsing: Responses-compatible body parsing now reads top-level "determinism" and "seed" keys in addition to existing generation params and merges them with header values (headers take precedence). - Streaming reassembly: streaming reassembly now attaches a deterministic-context token to each stream chunk and includes seed metadata in the final reassembly envelope so consumers and logs can assert determinism and replay. This prevents a class of flaky stream reorder bugs seen during canary. - Tool/function calling: the toolcall envelope now carries the propagated schema hint on the function metadata so third-party tool runners can perform schema-aware validation/dispatch. - Backwards compatibility: adapter will ignore unknown header keys and continues to accept legacy openai-style body shapes; a compatibility shim maps older "seed_hint" fields to the new internal header where detected. - Tests and validations: unit tests for adapter parsing, integration tests exercising streaming reassembly with seeded responses, and an end-to-end canary against a mocked OpenAI-responses backend were added. Checklist: - [x] Add header normalization in adapter layer - [x] Merge seed into routing decisions (with tests) - [x] Attach seed/annotations to streaming reassembly envelope - [x] Surface schema hint to toolcall metadata - [x] Add integration tests and canary job - [x] Update docs/compat notes (short note in docs site) Related: ENG-4821 (compat issues during customer test runs), ENG-4835 (structured output rollout plan). Breaking change: none; feature is opt-in via header/body keys. Rollout plan: feature gated behind a config flag responses.adapter.enable_seed_passthrough (default off). We enabled the flag in the dedicated canary namespaces and verified downstream regression metrics before merging.
Ethan Park (reviewer): Can you confirm headers take precedence over body-level seed when both are present? The compatibility matrix in ENG-4821 assumes header-first behavior.
Maya Chen (author): Yes — updated adapter/parse.go: headers override body keys. Added explicit unit tests to cover both orders.
Priya Nair (reviewer): Suggest adding a short-lived metric that counts how often seed is provided via header vs body so we can monitor usage post-rollout.
Maya Chen (author): Added seed_source metric and emitted tags (header|body|none); seen in canary results. PTAL.
Luca Romano (approver): Integration looks good. I ran the canary against the mocked backend and confirmed identical token stream orders with seed set. Approving for merge.
CI Bot: All checks passed. canary/responses_seed_canary completed with 0 failures.
Adapter: preserve and propagate Responses determinism/seed directives and structured-output hints. Opt-in via responses.adapter.enable_seed_passthrough; enables more reliable compatibility with OpenAI Responses variants and allows schema-aware tool dispatch.
payload.title: responses-adapter: propagate determinism/seed headers and structured-output annotations

payload.body:
Motivation: customers continue to see two pain points when using `response_format` / JSON schema based outputs in streaming mode: 1) partial or malformed streaming chunks trigger tool/function calls prematurely (tool invocation tokens embedded in broken structures), and 2) streaming parsers drop the response when final validation fails without useful, actionable feedback. This PR introduces a small behavioral surface and runtime fencing to address both issues while preserving OpenAI-compat expectations.

What this PR does (high level):
- Introduces a response contract "fencing" layer that defers tool/function invocation until the runtime has validated (heuristically) that the streamed JSON structure contains a syntactically plausible tool_call envelope. This prevents accidental tool activations from transient stream fragments.
- Adds a partial-stream validation pass that runs continuously on the stream buffer and emits non-fatal validation annotations to the SDK and console (validation.hints). Final strict validation still runs at completion and can be configured to be lenient or strict via the new `contract_mode` flag (`lenient|strict|diagnose`).
- Maps new validation and fencing error codes to existing OpenAI-compat error categories so downstream clients (and our OpenAI shim) can continue handling errors in existing flows. See mapping table in docs/openai-compat.md.
- Exposes a `contract_mode` top-level request param. Default behavior remains backward-compatible: if a request includes `response_format` but no `contract_mode`, behavior matches existing runtime (best-effort schema hints, tool calls allowed on first well-formed envelope). Explicit `contract_mode=strict` enforces final-schema acceptance before triggering tool calls and will turn final-validation failures into structured 4xx-style responses. `contract_mode=diagnose` retains behavior plus emits a diagnostic stream of validation hints (non-fatal) to simplify prompt tuning.

Design notes and choices:
- Fencing is implemented as a lightweight state machine inside the streaming runtime: states = {"collecting", "envelope_seen", "fenced"}. The runtime will only transition to `fenced` (and permit tool dispatch) after a syntactic envelope (closing braces/brackets) plus a small set of semantic predicates (presence of required keys like "name" and "arguments" for tool_call) are observed in the buffered stream. This is intentionally conservative to avoid false positives.
- Partial validation uses an incremental JSON/JSON-schema validator (streaming validator) with a capped lookback window to maintain latency. Hints are batched and emitted as a separate `validation.hints` stream event that the SDK surfaces (or logs) but does not interrupt generation.
- To preserve OpenAI-compatibility we maintain the existing `response_format` param shape and add `contract_mode` as an opt-in enhancement. The OpenAI shim translates legacy `format` and `response_format` combinations to `contract_mode=lenient` by default.

Files changed (high level):
- api/server/streaming_contracts.py (new): fencing state machine and streaming validator glue
- api/handlers/respond_v2.py: accept and route contract_mode; minor routing changes for shim compatibility
- sdk/python/redwood/client.py: new streaming hooks for validation.hints events and `contract_mode` helper in request builder
- docs/openai-compat.md: compatibility notes, mapping table for error codes, migration guidance
- tests/test_stream_validation.py (new): end-to-end streaming tests covering fence transitions and hint emission
- examples/structured_tool_calls/contract_mode_demo.ipynb: demonstration notebook for users
- scripts/perf/measure_stream_latency.sh: updated to include fencing enabled/disabled runs

Commits summary:
- feat(streaming): add streaming validator and incremental schema hints (D. Chen)
- feat(api): integrate contract_mode and fencing in respond_v2 (D. Chen)
- feat(sdk): surface validation.hints in python SDK (A. Miller)
- docs: add openai mapping + migration guide (P. Nair)
- test: add fence state e2e tests and CI matrix (S. Gupta)
- perf: add perf script to compare latency with fencing enabled (D. Chen)

Review conversation (high level snippets):
- Elliot Ramos: "This looks good overall. My only concern is the conservative fence delaying legitimate tool calls in low-latency agents (e.g., 50ms budgets). Can we expose a heuristic flag to relax the fence for low-latency routes?"
- Daria Chen: "Yes — added `fence_aggressiveness` route config (0..3). Default 1 (moderate). We keep it off for `contract_mode=lenient`. Added tests for aggressiveness values 0 and 3."
- Priya Nair: "Docs mapping table is helpful. Please add one migration example showing the shim behavior for existing users relying on immediate tool dispatch."
- Daria Chen: "Added example in docs and an example notebook; clarified SDK behavior (hints arrive as an async event, not as exception)."
- Samir Gupta: "CI flake on test_stream_validation — re-run once with more generous timeouts. Also confirm that memory growth stays bounded with the lookback window."
- Daria Chen: "Adjusted timeouts and added an LRU-like cap on the validator buffer; CI passed on re-run."

CI and release notes:
- CI: all checks passing on main matrix. One flaky test fixed. Additional perf runs show median latency increase of ~6ms with fence_aggressiveness=1; teams can opt out for latency-sensitive routes.
- Release notes: "Add contract_mode request flag to control streaming schema validation and tool-call fencing. New SDK hook `validation.hints` streams diagnostic validation messages; see migration notes in docs/openai-compat.md."

Testing and rollout plan:
- Canary rollout to 10% of hosted traffic for two days with contract_mode=diagnose enabled for internal integration tests. Monitor tool invocation rate (should not increase) and validation.hints volumes.
- If metrics are stable, flip default to include `contract_mode=diagnose` for new response_format requests for 30% traffic. Strict remains opt-in.
- Hotfix path: route-level config allows immediate disabling of fencing for customers who need original behavior.

Rollback plan: automated toggle to disable fencing at route/provisioning layer; immediate fallback to legacy parser if memory or latency regressions exceed thresholds.

Elliot Ramos: request a heuristic flag for low-latency routes
Priya Nair: add migration example and clarify SDK behavior
Samir Gupta: re-run flaky test and verify memory bounds
Daria Chen: added fence_aggressiveness and updated docs/tests as requested
Introduce `contract_mode` (lenient|strict|diagnose) to control streaming schema validation and tool-call fencing; SDKs receive `validation.hints` stream events; new route config `fence_aggressiveness` to tune fencing heuristics. Backward compatible by default.
Existing clients get legacy behavior by default. To opt into the new behavior, include contract_mode in requests or set route default. The OpenAI shim maps legacy formats to contract_mode=lenient. See docs/openai-compat.md for examples.
Fencing reduces risk of accidental tool invocation from malformed streams. No new credentials introduced. Ensure policy checks still run at dispatch time. Auditing events include fence decisions for post-incident analysis.

Context and motivation: We frequently see transient spikes in latency or throughput that correlate with small cohort shifts (time-of-day, client mix) and cause the canary system to prematurely pause or rollback rollouts. This PR implements two related mechanisms: (1) Cohort-progression Smoother, a lightweight temporal smoothing and cohort-weighted aggregation that stabilizes short-lived fluctuations while preserving sensitivity to sustained regressions; and (2) Stable-Cutover Gate, a rollout guard that enforces stricter progression criteria (longer observation windows, higher confidence thresholds, and adaptive rollback budgets) when the signal shows high entropy or cohort churn.

Design summary: The smoother maintains per-cohort rolling quantiles for latency and throughput and computes a cohesion score that down-weights cohorts whose metrics deviate transiently from the overall trend. The gate consumes cohesion + uncertainty metrics and adjusts the canary progression state machine: when cohesion is low the gate lengthens stage durations, requires multi-cohort agreement for cutover, and limits step size. When cohesion returns, the gate automatically shortens windows. This is intentionally additive: it plugs into the existing canary evaluator pipeline (probe scheduler -> metric aggregator -> decision engine) and exposes knobs for SLO-weighted sensitivity.

Key changes (high-level files):
- pkg/canary/smoother.go: new cohort smoothing and cohesion scoring logic (with package-level unit tests).
- pkg/canary/gate.go: stable-cutover gate implemented with state transitions and metrics export.
- pkg/canary/config.yaml: runtime knobs for window sizes, decay factors, cohesion thresholds.
- internal/probes/scheduler.lua: probe scheduling adjustments to ensure cohort-balanced sampling.
- test/e2e/cohort_rollout_test.go: synthetic traffic harness to validate behavior under cohort churn.
- docs/perf/canary-smoother.md: design doc and operator guidance.
- ci/metrics-checks.yml: new CI scenario to run the e2e under varied traffic shapes.

Commits:
- 7a3b1f2 Add initial smoother implementation and unit tests
- c4d2e9a Integrate cohesion score into aggregator pipeline
- ef52b67 Add stable-cutover gate and state machine tests
- 490b1bc Hook up metrics and dashboards for cohesion/entropy
- 1d2f3a4 Add e2e harness and CI job for synthetic cohort churn
- a7c12de Fix flake in probe scheduler under heavy parallelism

Testing and validation: Unit tests cover the smoother math (decay, weight update, quantile maintenance) and gate transitions. The e2e harness runs multiple traffic shapes (single-cohort, two-cohort alternating, bursty churn) and asserts that: (a) short transient spikes do not trigger immediate rollback, (b) sustained degradation within a majority cohort still triggers rollback within configured budget, and (c) gate enforces extended observation windows when cohort entropy > threshold. CI includes a reproducible synthetic run; flakiness was iterated down from 12% to <2% in multiple re-runs.

Operational notes and rollout plan:
- Feature flag: canary.cohort_smoother.enabled default=false.
- Gradual rollout: enable in staging, then enable for a small subset of internal traffic, then opt-in by customer for dedicated runs.
- Metrics to monitor: cohort_cohesion_score, cohort_entropy, smoother_effective_window_ms, gate_state, canary_stage_duration. Dashboards added under perf/canary/smoother.
- Rollback: immediate opt-out via feature flag or set cohesion_threshold=0 to bypass the smoother.

Backward compatibility and safety: Implementation is additive and disabled by default. Config knobs allow operators to tune aggressiveness. No public API changes.

Review conversation (highlights):

  - Daniel Park (author): "Addressed: switched to t-digest for quantiles and capped retention per-cohort with eviction TTL. See pkg/canary/smoother.go commit 7a3b1f2 and comment in config.yaml explaining max_cohorts."
- Luis Gomez [comment]: "Gate looks good but we should expose an emergency bypass for SRE to expedite cutovers during incidents."
  - Daniel Park: "Added gate.bypass_token env var and documented emergency checklist in docs/perf/canary-smoother.md. Also added audit metric gate_bypass_used{true|false}."
- Samantha Ye [approval after fixes]: "Tests look solid and e2e harness reproduces expected behavior for the scenarios I asked for. Approving."

Merge outcome: Merged via squash on 2026-03-02 after approvals from Aisha and Samantha and green CI. Post-merge: created dashboards and an alert that fires when cohort_entropy rises above configured threshold for more than 10 minutes.

- Ops playbook update: include synthetic run for each major release to confirm smoother stability.

Notes for reviewers: This PR focuses on reducing false positives from short-lived cohort noise while keeping harshness for genuine regressions. The cohesion concept is lightweight and intentionally conservative; downstream default parameters are set to avoid masking real issues. If we see missed regressions in canary history, we can incrementally lower decay factors but will prefer adjusting per-product SLO weights.
Adds a cohort-aware smoothing layer that reduces false-positive canary regressions during phased rollouts and a stable-cutover gate that enforces conservative progression when signal volatility is high.

Motivation: Recent rollouts showed transient baseline shifts across regions and tenant cohorts that caused noisy canary signals and premature rollbacks. This PR adds a federated signal normalizer to reduce cohort-level baseline variance and a granular cutover policy to enforce phased traffic migration with rollback budget accounting.

What this changes: Implements a normalization stage that consumes per-cohort latency and throughput fingerprints, fits a lightweight robust linear transform (median-based) per-slice, and exposes a normalized delta used by the canary evaluator. Adds a new CutoverPolicy primitive that accepts traffic tiers, staged percentages, cooldown windows, and a rollback-credit budget. The canary orchestrator now uses normalized metrics to compute regression scores and consults the CutoverPolicy before advancing traffic.

Design notes: The federated normalizer operates at two time resolutions: fast (1m) and slow (1h) rolling windows. Each cohort contributes a sketch (p50/p90/p99, qps) to the aggregator; the transform is computed using a robust estimator to avoid being dominated by bursts. The normalized delta is the difference between candidate and baseline after applying cohort transforms and a global shrinkage factor to control sensitivity. CutoverPolicy enforces minimum-successful-probe-counts per stage, consumes rollback-credit on failed stages, and supports emergency-abort hooks.

Backward compatibility: New behavior is gated behind a config flag perf.canary.federated_normalizer=false by default in existing deployments. The CutoverPolicy is available to rollout plans but does not replace existing simple cutover configs.

Testing: Unit tests for transform math and edge cases (empty cohorts, zero traffic) included. Integration harness added that replays historical traffic traces (prod replay + synthetic drift) to validate reduced false-positive rate. End-to-end canary sim shows a 42% reduction in noisy rollbacks on our historical dataset.

Migration & rollout: Feature flagged. Plan: enable in canary lab for two weeks on non-critical namespaces, then enable for low-traffic customers, monitor stability dashboards and rollback budget consumption metrics.

- [x] Unit tests

Motivation: We need a lightweight, opinionated curator that generates cost-aware defaults for new deployments and suggests tiered profiles (budget/standard/premium) for batching, cache presize, and quantization level. This PR adds a heuristic bundler that composes small, explainable profile templates and a curator CLI that can scaffold and shadow-evaluate them against a sampled workload. Goals: 1) reduce time-to-safe-defaults for teams onboarding Dedicated/Private deployments; 2) provide measurable unit-econ deltas between tiers; 3) make profile suggestions auditable and reversible.

What this PR does: single-string summary of changes below. Implement a profile curator service (library + CLI) that: - generates tiered templates for batching+cache+quant (three budgets: low/medium/high) - adds an Orchestrator hook to run shadow evaluations and collect token-level cost deltas - ships a compact format for 'profile bundles' (YAML) that can be stored with model metadata - introduces a 'heuristic bundler' which assembles presets from simple rules (e.g. frequent short requests => aggressive batching + small cache; long-form completions => conservative batching + higher-precision quant) - surfaces an explainability payload (why X preset chosen) for auditability - wires up conservative rollout: newly generated defaults are suggested in the Console but not applied until accepted.

Testing & validation: - unit tests for bundler rules and profile serialization - integration test that runs the CLI scaffold against a synthetic workload and asserts cost, latency, and quality thresholds - shadow evaluation harness that runs candidate profiles against live traffic (sampled) and records token economics without affecting production flows - comparative evals against current defaults to produce delta report.

Rollback & safety: - Bundles are non-destructive; Console interaction required for activation. - All curated profiles include a safe-fallback mapping (model-variant + region) to prevent capacity regressions. - Added telemetry to detect quality regressions (prompt sets, BLEU-like metrics for targeted workloads) and automatic revert suggestion.

Upgrade notes: This PR introduces a new dependency (pyyaml-light) for parsing profile bundles in the curator CLI and a small runtime hook in the serving runtime for shadow evaluations. See release notes below.

Related work: ENG-8321 (profile curator epic), ENG-8390 (shadow eval infra).

Motivation: Recent canary runs showed recurrent false-positive tail-latency alerts during short traffic spikes, and we observed noisy variance for small-batch inference workloads. This PR introduces a two-part defense: 1) a lightweight temporal signal smoother that reduces high-frequency noise in per-route latency fingerprints while preserving changepoints, and 2) a traffic-granularity guard that slices canary evaluations by traffic orthogonals (route, payload-size bucket, and client tier) and gates rollouts when small, concentrated cohorts drive apparent regressions.

Goals: reduce alert churn, avoid unnecessary rollbacks for bursty micro-cohorts, and improve detection power for sustained regressions. This is intended as a conservative enhancement — default behavior is opt-in per-alert and the rollout guard has configurable thresholds and cooldown periods.

What changed (high-level): - Add exponential moving quantile smoother (EQS) and heteroskedasticity-aware window sizing to the canary metric stream processor. EQS adapts window length based on recent variance estimates so long-lived trends are preserved but transient spikes are suppressed. - Add traffic-granularity slicing to the canary evaluator. Evaluations now compute cohort-level fingerprints for route/payload_size/client_tier and will only escalate if either (a) a majority-weighted cohort shows sustained degradation, or (b) a global signal exceeds a tunable severity threshold. - New staged-fallback policy: on cohort-only degradation, the orchestrator applies a soft cork (reduce canary traffic by N%) and schedules a strengthened probe set; on global degradation the system triggers standard rollback. - Exposed config knobs in canary config and Redwood Console: smoothing_alpha, variance_thresholds, cohort_min_samples, staged_cork_percentage, staged_cork_cooldown. - Unit + perf tests and a small runbook for oncall to interpret cohort-level alerts.

Context: Global canary signals routinely miss short-lived, cohort-specific surges that cause tail latency regressions for a subset of traffic (e.g. tenants, regions, or new client SDK versions). These transient bursts can evade aggregate detectors and lead to customer-facing regressions during staged rollouts.

Motivation: We need a lightweight detector that attributes short-lived latency shifts to traffic cohorts, correlates surge fingerprints with tail-percentile shifts, and enforces a conservative throttle/rollback budget so rollouts stay safe without over-triggering on noisy signals.

What this PR does: Adds a cross-cohort surge fingerprinter plus a throttle orchestrator that integrates into the existing canary pipeline. The fingerprinter builds a compact, time-windowed sketch for each cohort (traffic key) and produces a normalized "surge signature" vector. The orchestrator computes similarity between new and baseline signatures, correlates with percentile shifts (p50/p95/p99), and applies an adaptive probe-throttle or rollback-credit policy. The feature is behind the existing canary feature-flag and defaults to off for user-triggered rollouts.

Implementation notes: - Cross-cohort fingerprinter implemented in perf-canary/detectors/fingerprinter.go using a sliding window Count-Min + truncated histogram sketch to keep memory bounded. - Surge similarity uses cosine distance with decay-weighted recent windows to prefer sustained divergence. - Orchestrator (perf-canary/orchestrator/throttle_orchestrator.py) exposes three policy knobs: sensitivity, stability-window, and rollback-credit-rate. - Metrics: new labels/metrics prefixed with pc_cohort_ (pc_cohort_surge_score, pc_cohort_similarity, pc_cohort_throttle_actions). - Integrations: hooks added to canary-evaluator to provide cohort-aware gating and to the rollout controller to consume throttle decisions.

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for fingerprinter accuracy and memory bound checks. - Integration tests using the synthetic-traffic-replay harness to simulate skewed cohort bursts and verify correct gating. - Benchmarks: microbenchmark shows ~1.8% median CPU increase and <4ms p99 additional latency on the detector path for typical traffic shapes; acceptable for Dedicated and Hosted with feature-flag toggled.

Checklist: [x] Design doc linked (ENG-2145) [x] Unit tests [x] Integration e2e test in perf lab [x] Metrics + dashboards updated [x] Feature-flag gating [x] Backwards-compatible changes only

Backward compatibility / migration: All changes are behind a feature flag. Fingerprinter state stored in ephemeral in-memory stores with an optional Redis-backed persistence (opt-in in config). No schema migrations.

Risks and mitigations: Memory growth for extreme cardinality cohorts mitigated by per-customer caps and a global eviction policy. False positives reduced by requiring both surge similarity and percentile correlation before throttle/rollback credit application.

Related: ENG-2145 (design), ENG-2199 (test harness), SUP-4123 (customer incident that motivated this work).

payload.body:
Motivation: transient, periodic interference (GC sweeps, noisy neighbors, periodic telemetry jobs) has caused low-amplitude latency regressions that percentile-only detectors occasionally miss and that can trigger noisy rollbacks. This PR introduces a new detector that analyzes latency time-series in the frequency domain and fuses spectral residual signals with existing percentile drift metrics to produce a more stable canary signal. Design summary: 1) Windowed FFT transform of per-request p95/p99 time series over short sliding windows (configurable); 2) Compute spectral residual energy in targeted bands (e.g., 0.5-5s cycles) and normalize by traffic power to be traffic-aware; 3) Produce a residuals_score time series and combine with percentile delta via a probabilistic fusion step (logistic weight based on signal SNR); 4) Graceful Threshold Adapter: thresholds are scaled by a lightweight traffic intensity estimator and by recent variance to avoid over-reacting to cold-start or low-sample windows; 5) Rollout guard: when residuals_score exceeds adaptive threshold for N consecutive windows we pause canary traffic and open an investigation alert with suggested probes. Implementation notes: detector implemented in perf-canary/src/detectors/freq_residuals.py using numpy/scipy primitives with a fallback optimized CFFI path for high-throughput hosts; fusion and threshold adapter live in perf-canary/src/eval/fusion.py; added PromQL metric exporters and Grafana panel JSON for visibility under observability/canaries/freq-residuals-panel.json. Tests and validation: unit tests cover spectral normalization, SNR-based weighting, and adapter scaling (perf-canary/tests/test_freq_residuals.py); integration canary harness added to perf-canary/integration/canary-sim that replays synthetic traffic with injected periodic noise to validate true/false-positive curves; load impact: CPU microbenchmarks show ~2% extra CPU on probe workers, latency overhead negligible. Rollout plan: feature flag behind perf.canary.freq_residuals.enabled; start with passive mode (score logged but not gating) for 48h in perf environment, promote to active gating on a small percentage of canaries, then global default after two weeks if false-positive rate < 1% and detection recall improves. Related work: builds on ENG-2480 (spectral baseline) and complements existing percentile-aware detectors in this codebase. Backwards compatibility: detector registers as optional evaluation plugin; default off for existing canaries. Metrics to watch: residuals_score, fused_canary_signal, false_positive_rate, mean_time-to-pause, CPU impact. Operational playbook: added runbook section pointing to runbooks/canaries/freq-residuals-runbook.md with RCA steps and suggested probes. This PR includes code, tests, panels, and runbook entries. Context: We need safer canary strategies for stateful LLM sessions (chat-like flows) where splitting by user ID can still surface regressions tied to session affinity or state. Current canaries either shadow (no user-visible change) or static canary cohorts that remain pinned to a subset of traffic, which delays discovery of issues that only appear when canary runs across many different session histories. This PR introduces an autonomous 'roving canary' controller that incrementally and deterministically moves canary assignment across session shards while preserving session consistency for active sessions. It also adds a lightweight replay/playback hook that captures minimal session context for deterministic repro on the canary model when a telemetry alert fires. Motivation: reduce time-to-detect for regressions that only manifest across varied session histories; enable post-failure deterministic playback for faster RCA. What changed (high level): 1) New roving controller that implements timebox-driven shard rotation and ensures in-flight sessions remain pinned until completion; 2) Session-affinity table and graceful handoff code to avoid mid-session model flips; 3) Deterministic playback library that captures nonce-limited KV cache and prompt slices for safe replay in a sandboxed execution path; 4) Console UI hooks and rollout graphing to visualize roving sweep progress; 5) E2E tests and loadbench scenarios for mixed session-length distributions. Rollout plan: staged merge to main, enable behind feature flag rollout.roving_canary=false by default, smoke rollout to internal org with 1% of traffic, then enable 5%, 20% progressing via automatic health gates. On alert, controller automatically pauses and schedules playback jobs for recent sessions from the roving windows. Backwards compatibility: controller degrades to static cohort assignment if the session-affinity store is unavailable. Safety: we enforce a max-sessions-in-flight threshold and a kill-switch that immediately collapses roving back into stable cohort. Related work: builds on ENG-2029 (canary orchestration) and ENG-2058 (session affinity API). Checklist: - [x] Controller implementation + unit tests - [x] Playback capture library + sandboxed runner - [x] Console visualization and metrics - [x] Loadbench scenarios - [x] Documentation and runbook entries - [x] Feature flag gated and documented Known limitations: playback currently supports only deterministic prefix capture (no external tool integrations yet); migration path for very long-lived sessions requires reconfiguration of the max-inflight window. Release notes: see field below.
Aaron Patel (2026-02-12): Can you elaborate on the security model for saved playback artifacts? Response: Playback artifacts are nonce-signed, encrypted at rest with customer KMS in Private deployments; in hosted, artifacts live in a short-lived encryption key and auto-expire after 72 hours.
Sophie Nguyen (2026-02-13): I'm concerned about mid-session latency spikes when reassigning shards. Response: We added a in-flight session threshold and handoff path so active sessions are never moved until completion; rotation only affects new sessions post-tick.
Kofi Mensah (2026-02-15): Tests look good, but add a regression test for long-lived sessions. Author reply (2026-02-16): Added a long-lived session e2e case and a soak job in loadbench, see tests/e2e/roving_sweep_spec.go.

Admins should read docs/runbooks/roving_canary.md before enabling; playback artifacts expire automatically and are encrypted in hosted runs.

Motivation: existing canary detectors focus on population-level metrics (p50/p95) which miss phase-aligned regressions that only affect specific request clusters. This PR implements a latency-affinity probe and a traffic seam that (1) groups requests by lightweight affinity keys, (2) maintains EWMA-backed quantile sketches per affinity bucket, (3) computes a correlation score to identify phase-correlated increases in tail latency, and (4) ties this signal to the rollout guard to automatically throttle or pause canaries when correlated degradation is observed.

What this change contains (high-level):
- latency_affinity_probe: new probe module that extracts a 4-part affinity key (route, prompt-length-bin, recent-kv-hash-prefix, model-variant) and assigns traffic into buckets.
- affinity_quantiles: sketching + EWMA layer that maintains p50/p95/p99 over a 2m sliding horizon with half-life tuning to respond to short-lived spikes but ignore micro-noise.
- correlation_scoring: computes Spearman rank correlation and a weighted percentile divergence score across synchronous buckets to detect phase-alignment.
- traffic_seam_controller: rollout guard integration that clamps canary weight, puts the canary into "seamed" mode (traffic diverted to a shadowed pool), and emits reasons for operator visibility.
- dashboards/alerts: Grafana panels and Alertmanager rules for affinity churn, seam activation, and top offending affinity buckets.
- canary-simulator tests: synthetic workloads to validate sensitivity/precision trade-offs and false-positive rate at 0.6% target.

Checklist: 
- [x] Probe + controller implementation
- [x] Unit tests for affinity extraction and quantile sketches
- [x] Integration tests using canary-simulator (deterministic scenarios)
- [x] E2E smoke in staging with real traffic shadowing for 24h
- [x] Docs (guide + config reference)
- [x] Observability (metrics, traces, dashboards)

Performance and safety notes:
- The affinity key is intentionally compact (4 fields, hashed) to keep memory footprint low. In our staging run with 2M requests/day we observed ~12k active buckets and ~0.6% increase in runtime CPU during probe sampling.
- Default sensitivity is conservative: we require correlation_score >= 0.7 and sustained percentile delta (p95 delta > 35ms for 3 consecutive 10s windows) before the seam triggers. These thresholds are configurable per-service.

Why it's different from previous detectors:
- This detector specifically targets phase-correlated regressions (e.g., specific prompt templates, transient upstream service outages that affect a subset of requests, or cache warmup patterns) that do not materially change aggregate p95 immediately.
- Instead of only comparing canary vs baseline aggregates, we look for synchronous divergence across affinity buckets to reduce false positives driven by traffic composition shifts.

Testing summary: 
- Unit: 45 tests added, coverage +3.2% for probe package.
- Integration: canary-simulator scenarios included: 'phase_spike', 'mixed_payload_regression', 'noisy_background' — the detector correctly identified phase_spike and remained silent on noisy_background.
- Staging: deployed with canary weight 5% on redwood-service-beta for 24h, seam remained idle; synthetic phase spike injected at hour 3 activated seam and rollback path as expected.

Migration and config:
- Feature gated behind perf.affinity_probe.enabled=false by default; rollout plan: enable in staging for 2 weeks, tune thresholds, enable in production for low-traffic services first.

Related work and docs: linear/ENG-7123 contains the design doc and decision log. Short guide added to docs/canaries/affinity-probe.md and sample config in examples/canary-configs/affinity.yaml.

Commits (summary): see commits list below for granular messages.
New affinity-based canary detector: groups traffic by request affinity and detects phase-correlated tail-latency regressions. Adds a traffic seam mechanism to safely pause or reduce canary weights when correlated regressions are detected.

Samir Patel: Added de-duplication heuristics: the seam now prefers signals with higher per-bucket sustained divergence and will de-dupe if kv-warmup tag is set in trace/span. Also added an opt-out config for services that already run kv-warmup detectors.

Introduces a rolling resilience-curve canary that detects gradual, sustained degradations and a tiered fallback policy (soft fallback -> model variant -> rate fallthrough) to limit blast radius during rollouts.
Motivation: We observed slow, multi-hour regressions that did not trigger existing spike-focused detectors; this PR adds a time-weighted 'resilience curve' canary that measures cumulative degradation slope across cohorts and triggers tiered safeguards. High level: 1) rolling resilience curve evaluator that computes a decay-weighted degradation area under curve (AUC) for latency and error rate across multiple cohort slices (region, client-class, route). 2) temporal quorum voting: requires consensus from multiple independent cohorts before a hard fallback. 3) tiered fallback policy: soft fallback (traffic shaping + alert only), model-variant fallback (route to a lower-cost stable variant), and rate fallthrough (graceful request shedding with progressive SLAs). 4) adaptive probe scheduling that increases probe frequency for cohorts showing rising AUC and backs off when stabilized. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-18721) - [x] unit + integration tests - [x] e2e smoke in perf lab - [x] docs added under docs/perf - [x] fallthrough behavior validated with canary simulator Implementation notes: The resilience curve is implemented in canary/engine/resilience_curve.py with an efficient incremental aggregator and configurable half-life. Voting is implemented as a quorum module that accepts weighted cohort votes. Fallbacks are implemented in alerts/rollout_guard.go and routing/soft_fallback.rs. This PR also adds a canary simulator harness and two smoke tests. Related: builds on prior probe-scheduling work (ENG-17234). Risk/rollback: feature gated behind canary.v2 flag; rollout guard defaults to soft mode until explicitly enabled in the console. Testing: see test/integration/resilience_smoke_test.py and perf-canary lab run id perf-lab-20260212-07. Merge notes: squash-merged to main after addressing review comments and CI fixes.

Motivation: long-tail token cost and latency noise make it hard to correlate bursts to kernel warmup, prefix vs completion cost, and scheduling contention. This PR introduces two complementary observability primitives: (1) an Invoke Slice Sampler that slices invocations into time-aligned 'slices' to preserve bursty token-attribution while dramatically reducing cardinality and storage cost; and (2) a Token Cascade Explainer that attributes per-token cost/latency to a small set of causal contributors (prefix KV hits/misses, kernel warmup penalty, batching wait, and I/O stalls) and exposes an explainer panel in the console. Summary of changes: - New sampler: telemetry/ingest/slice_sampler.go adds a deterministic slice keyed by (tenant, route, invocation_bucket) and emits sampled span anchors plus compact slice digests. Sampler is opt-in via telemetry.config.slice_sampling.enabled=false|true. - Token cascade: pkg/observability/token_cascade.go implements cascade attribution heuristics that correlate per-token timing with kernel occupancy metadata and KV cache events; exposes cascade tags on spans (cascade.stage and cascade.score). - Dashboards: dashboards/invocation_cascade_explainer.json adds a new panel with per-slice token waterfall, kernel warmup heatmap, and slice-level cost breakdown (prefix vs completion vs kernel). - Ingest/transform: telemetry/transform/slice_hydrator.go and telemetry/transform/cascade_enricher.go perform lightweight join of sampled anchors to full spans to produce rollups. - Docs & examples: docs/observability/token-cascade.md and examples/observability/quickstart-slice.sh. - Tests: tests/e2e/observability/synthetic_slice_test.py adds deterministic workload that reproduces warmup-burst patterns and validates attribution. Design notes and rollout: the slice sampler reduces telemetry volume by ~12x on our internal bursty trace workloads; we configured a conservative default sampling rate of 1/100 slices per tenant but added adaptive rate increases for tenants with high SLO sensitivity. The cascade explainer is purely additive instrumentation and will appear as optional panels; it does not change any runtime decision logic. Backwards compatibility: existing span shapes and tags remain unchanged unless telemetry.config.cascade_enrichment.enabled=true. Rollout plan: feature flag gated, staged rollout over 2 weeks: opt-in in staging, 10% of production tenants, 50% after stability checks, full rollout. Testing: unit tests for sampler determinism, integration tests for hydration path, and e2e synthetic replay. Checklist: - [x] implement sampler and hydrator - [x] add cascade attribution heuristics - [x] new dashboard panels and docs - [x] synthetic e2e tests - [x] feature-flag gating and config defaults Performance notes: measured ~0.8ms median overhead added to ingest path when enrichment enabled (95th percentile spikes at 5ms during backfill). Storage cost impact: with default sampling we saw ~12x reduction in sampled-span volume on internal traces, with cascade rollups adding ~3% storage. Related: ENG-6591 (observability long-tail), SUP-4121 (customer-reported burst attribution request).
Ava Chen (reviewer): Nice separation between sampling and enrichment — can we make the slice key stable across language SDKs? Suggest exporting the hash function spec in telemetry/hash_spec.md.

Context and motivation: We frequently see noisy short traffic bursts during canary evaluations that inflate variance and cause spurious rollback decisions. Previous guard logic operated on fixed windows which either missed regressions in low-traffic periods or overreacted to transient spikes. This PR implements an episode-driven orchestration layer which: 1) identifies contiguous "episodes" of traffic based on request inter-arrival time and per-route signal consistency; 2) aggregates statistics inside episodes for robust percentile estimates; and 3) applies a rate-cap-based fallback when episode-based routing would otherwise increase upstream concurrency beyond safe thresholds.

Design summary: The new EpisodeOrchestrator component lives in perf-canary/orchestrator and integrates with the existing probe scheduler. Episodes are detected by a lightweight state machine (idle -> collecting -> quiesce) using a tunable inter-arrival threshold and minimum episode size. Statistical aggregation supports weighted quantile merging so short episodes do not dominate long ones. The rate-cap fallback is a conservative gate: when projected cutover QPS would exceed configured rate caps for the target pool, traffic is throttled and progressively ramped using a token-bucket-like controller with backoff.

What this PR changes: Adds orchestrator core, exposes policy knobs in canary policy schema, updates the probe scheduler to request episode boundaries (so probes can be correlated to episodes), extends the evaluation engine to compute episode-aware baselines, and wireframes a simple dashboard tile in the Console for episode health and projected cutover QPS. Includes unit tests, integration test scenarios, and a small synthetic load harness used in local verification.

Checklist:
- [x] Episode detection algorithm implemented and unit-tested
- [x] Weighted-merge quantile estimator added
- [x] Rate-cap fallback controller implemented with canary policy override
- [x] Integration tests covering: low-traffic, bursty-traffic, and sustained load cutover
- [x] Console tile and metrics exported (episode_count, episode_duration_p95, projected_cutover_qps)
- [x] Documentation page added to perf-canary/docs describing policy knobs and recommended defaults

Testing and validation: Local synthetic runs using the attached harness demonstrated reduced false-positive rollback events in the bursty-traffic scenario (historical test set: false positives reduced from 6/10 to 1/10). Integration test suite includes a seeded seed-traffic generator and deterministic randomization so CI can reproduce episodes. CI initially flagged a flaky integration that depended on real-time timers; I replaced timer sleeps with a virtual clock in tests which resolved flakiness.

Operational considerations and rollout plan: The feature is behind a canary policy feature flag (episode_orchestrator: enabled=false by default). We will roll out to canary namespace batches: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with the rate-cap fallback enabled for the first two phases to avoid unexpected concurrency increases. We recommend enabling on low-traffic routes first and monitoring the new episode metrics for at least 48 hours.

Related work: builds on probe correlation hooks added in ENG-1443 and complements the traffic curation probe work. Linear tickets: ENG-1895 (feature), ENG-1950 (dashboard).
Introduce an episode-driven canary orchestrator that groups short-lived traffic episodes for more stable statistical comparisons; add a rate-cap fallback to avoid overload during spiky cutovers. Backwards compatible; configurable via canary policy flags.
