Background: Optimize now requires quality gates before applying cost-saving config diffs (batching/cache/quantization). We’ve had a near-miss during beta where enforcement drifted between services (Optimize apply endpoint blocked correctly, rollout promotion didn’t). This PR adds a dedicated perf-canary stage that continuously verifies gate enforcement semantics end-to-end against a controlled staging route, and alerts on regressions.

What this adds:
- New canary stage: `quality_gate_enforcement`
  - Executes an end-to-end scenario against staging Optimize + eval-harness + rollout-controller API surface.
  - Validates enforcement at the apply boundary (blocked when gate != PASSED) and at promotion boundary (canary promotion blocked on failed gate).
- A small, deterministic test fixture:
  - Uses a dedicated canary account + route (non-production) and a synthetic config diff that is expected to FAIL the gate (known-bad quant profile on long-context prompts).
  - Uses a separate config diff that is expected to PASS smoke gates (benign batching window tweak) to ensure the stage itself isn’t only testing the fail path.
- Result reporting:
  - Emits `perf_canary_stage_result{stage="quality_gate_enforcement"}` and per-assertion tags (apply_blocked, promotion_blocked, pass_path_ok).
  - Posts a structured summary to #eng-sre-canaries when failures persist > 2 runs, with links to gate run ids and artifacts.

Behavior / Failure modes:
- Stage is non-flaky by design: retries only on 5xx/timeouts; no retries on assertion failures.
- Hard timeout: 12m for the stage (to avoid blocking the entire canary suite). If evals exceed budget we treat as failure and page as SLO regression (this catches the "gates blocking rollouts too long" class of issues).
- Guardrails: stage aborts early if canary environment is not "staging" or if the route/account id doesn’t match the allowlist.

Rollout:
- Enabled in staging canary pipeline immediately.
- For prod canary pipeline, staged behind `CANARY_ENABLE_QUALITY_GATE_STAGE=true` (default off) so SRE can enable after one week of stable staging signal.

Notes:
- This PR does not change gating logic; it only validates existing behavior and surfaces regressions earlier.
- Related: ENG-3928 (rollout controller respects gate), ENG-3926 (metrics), ENG-3931 (required checks).

Screenshots/Artifacts:
- Example success run output is included in the PR comments (log excerpt + metric names).
Allison Grant: Metrics look good, but can we avoid high-cardinality tags (gate_run_id) on the main counter? Suggest logging gate_run_id and keeping metrics low-cardinality.
Connor O'Brien: Good call. Updated to emit gate_run_id only in logs + Slack payload; metrics now only tag stage/assertion/result/region.
Sean Gallagher: I’m worried about flakiness if the stage depends on a real eval run every time. Can we make the PASS path a smoke gate only (small prompt subset) and require eval runtime budget checks?
Connor O'Brien: Updated PASS path to use smoke-gate-only recommendation type; also added explicit budget assertion (fail if eval > 8m).
Sahana Iyer: Please add a guard to prevent this from ever running outside staging unless explicitly enabled. We’ve had canary fixtures leak into prod before.
Connor O'Brien: Added env allowlist + required flag `CANARY_ENABLE_QUALITY_GATE_STAGE=true` for prod pipeline; also fails closed if env cannot be verified.
Chloe Martin: On the promotion-blocked assertion: ensure we’re checking the denial reason code, not string matching. The rollout controller has structured errors.
Connor O'Brien: Switched to structured `denial_reason_code == QUALITY_GATE_NOT_PASSED`; added unit test for error parsing.
Sean Gallagher: Can we link the oncall runbook in the Slack message? Also add a dedupe window so we don’t spam when staging is degraded.
Connor O'Brien: Added runbook link to docs section and Slack payload; dedupe window set to 60 minutes per stage+region.
Added a new perf-canary pipeline stage that continuously verifies Optimize quality gate enforcement (apply blocked unless PASSED; canary promotion blocked on failure) and alerts SRE on regressions. Staging enabled by default; prod gated behind feature flag.

payload.body:
Context: recent rollout exposed intermittent capture thrashing where repeated CUDA-graph capture attempts fail or regress tail latency when traffic has high variance in sequence length. Root cause analysis highlighted two contributing factors: (1) aggressive immediate recapture attempts cause kernel selection oscillation and eviction of warmed KV cache, (2) priming/warmup logic relied on fixed-size priming batches that misaligned with real request length distributions, producing noisy kernel choices. Motivation: avoid full rollback recaptures and reduce warmup flaps by introducing coordinated backpressure for replay attempts and a probe-driven priming stage that aligns KV priming window to workload shape distribution. Summary of changes:
- Introduce a ReplayThrottler in the runtime scheduler that serializes capture attempts per-GPU with exponential backoff and priority slots for already-warmed kernels. The throttler provides a low-overhead consensus (token) to capture drivers so they do not concurrently evict each other.
- Add ProbePriming: lightweight probe requests sent to the capture coordinator to estimate the active sequence-length histogram before running a full priming/capture. ProbePriming adapts probe batch sizes and target sequence lengths based on recent seen distributions and CPU-side sampling to avoid over- or under-priming.
- Implement ResumableCapture: allow an interrupted capture/replay sequence to resume from last-known safe checkpoint (kernel mapping + KV-alignment token) instead of reverting and replaying priming from scratch. This reduces wasted kernel captures on transient failures.
- KV-alignment windows: record KV cache footprints during probes and use soft-shape-alignment guards that are tolerant within a configurable window (default +/- 8 tokens) to reduce false-positive shape mismatches that previously forced recapture.
- Metrics and tracing: new metrics (replay_throttler_backoffs, probe_priming_success, resumable_capture_restarts) and trace spans to help correlate capture activity with tail-latency spikes.
- Tests and canary: unit tests for throttler logic and priming heuristics; an integration canary that runs continuous-batch and burst workloads on a dedicated perf pool.
Checklist: [x] Design doc linked (ENG-4897) [x] Unit tests added [x] Integration canary completed [x] Backwards-compatible defaults (throttler enabled, conservative windows) [x] Rollback plan: disable throttler or set windows=0 when needed
Impact/risk: changes are opt-in per-deployment via runtime flags; default is conservative to avoid sudden behavior changes. The throttler can increase capture latency for extremely rare long-running captures but reduces oscillation and overall failed recaptures; default parameters tuned against historical traces.
Testing:
- Microbenchmarks: synthetic steady-state and burst tests (see notes_on_benchmarks)
- Canary: 48-hour canary on group-perf-us-west with mixed seq-length traffic; no regression in 95/99/99.9 latencies observed; capture failure rate dropped.
Rollout: staged to main, then to dedicated pools over 2 weeks, with toggles to disable probe priming or resumable capture if incompatibilities observed.
Related: follows up on ENG-4520 and complements previous capture-stability work; not a functional replacement for shape-guard tightening.
Docs: added internal runtime flags docs and console observability mapping.

payload.body:
Context: As part of standing up Runtime LTS, we’re using perf-canary to gate patch releases with a small set of canonical workloads. During the 1.18 LTS pilot we saw a few cases where p95 latency regressed in ways that were operationally meaningful (tail spikes / backpressure) but didn’t trip the existing thresholds because they were tuned for mainline signal rather than “slower-change” LTS expectations.

This PR tightens p95 regression thresholds for the LTS gate and adds explicit documentation for the exception/waiver flow that Release Managers can use when benchmarks are noisy (runner contention, transient GPU clocking variance) or when a known/acceptable tradeoff is made (e.g., deliberate throughput vs tail trade).

What changed (high level): 1) LTS-specific thresholds: reduce allowed p95 latency regression from 5% -> 3% on the canonical LTS benchmark set; keep p50 at 2% (unchanged) and tighten throughput regression from -4% -> -3% for the same set. 2) Add a minimum sample-count rule for p95 comparisons (avoid false positives on short runs): require >= 20k tokens per scenario before gating is evaluated; otherwise mark as “insufficient data” and require rerun. 3) Add a documented waiver workflow: a single, auditable “perf-waiver” artifact linked in the PR / release issue, requiring approvals from Perf Owner + SRE + Release Eng lead, with time-bounded validity (per patch only) and mandatory rerun on dedicated runners if the initial run was on shared capacity.

Why: LTS customers are more sensitive to tail latency regressions because they tend to run closer to reserved capacity and use stricter SLOs; we want the default gate to be conservative. The waiver process is to keep us pragmatic when the measurement system is noisy—without silently weakening gates.

Risk: Tightening gates will increase failures/flake until we reduce runner contention (tracked in INT-3368). This PR mitigates with (a) sample-count rule, (b) rerun guidance, and (c) explicit waiver process rather than ad-hoc “LGTM, ship it” decisions.

Rollout: Enabled only for LTS release-branch workflows (release/* and runtime-*-lts) and leaves main branch thresholds unchanged.

Test plan: ran CI unit tests; validated config parsing; dry-ran the LTS workflow against an existing baseline artifact; verified the waiver template renders and is attached to the GitHub Action summary.

Refs: ENG-4825 (Integrate perf-canary gates into LTS release), ENG-4821 (Runtime LTS initiative), INT-3368 (benchmark runner capacity).
Marcus Reed (Perf test suite owner): The 3% p95 limit feels right for LTS, but we should be explicit about what metric we compare (p95 end-to-end vs model-only). Can you clarify in docs? Also, sample count: is 20k tokens enough for the long-context scenario?

Jonas Weber (author): Good call. The gate compares end-to-end request latency p95 as emitted by the benchmark harness (includes queueing + runtime). I’ll add a note in docs/lts/gates.md. Re: 20k tokens—this is per scenario per variant; for long-context we typically hit ~60–120k tokens/run, so we should be safe. The rule is mainly preventing short “smoke” runs from tripping p95.

Claire Dubois (Benchmark methodology): +1 to explicit metric definition. I’m slightly worried about flake on shared runners with 3%. Can the waiver doc require rerun on dedicated runner capacity before waiver is granted?

Jonas Weber (author): Yes—updated waiver doc: if the run was on shared capacity or if the variance indicator > 1.5%, rerun on dedicated runner is mandatory before waiver can be approved.

Allison Grant (Observability/perf signals): Waiver workflow needs an audit trail for release managers. Can we make the action upload a waiver form (even if empty) so the release PR has a consistent artifact name?

Jonas Weber (author): Implemented: the action always publishes a “perf-waiver.md” artifact stub. If waiver requested, it must be filled and re-uploaded (or attached in the release PR) with approvals.

Connor O'Brien (Release Eng lead): Please align terminology with runtime LTS runbook: “waiver” vs “exception”. We’ve been using “waiver” in runbooks. Also, ensure this only applies to LTS release workflows.

Jonas Weber (author): Renamed docs and action summary to “waiver”. Confirmed the workflow applies lts_profile only for release/* and *-lts branches. Mainline continues to use default_profile.

Marcus Reed: Docs update looks good. One more request: add a reminder that repeated waivers for the same scenario should open an infra ticket (runner contention) or a runtime ticket (real regression). Not a blocker but useful.

Jonas Weber (author): Added a “When waivers repeat” section linking to INT-3368 and suggesting filing a runtime perf regression ticket if the same benchmark regresses twice.

Approvals: Marcus Reed approved; Claire Dubois approved; Allison Grant approved; Connor O'Brien approved.
LTS perf gates now enforce stricter p95 latency and throughput regression thresholds.
Release managers have a documented, auditable waiver workflow for noisy benchmark results.
Added minimum sample-count requirements to reduce false-positive p95 regressions.
payload.title: Tighten p95 regression thresholds for Runtime LTS gates + document waiver workflow

payload.body:
Motivation: Current benchmark runners focus on steady-state token mixes and burst profiles but miss workload patterns where the token density drifts gradually within a session (temporal sparsity). These drift patterns expose different kernel hotpaths (KV cache fragmentation, token packing overhead, and scheduler idle->busy transitions) and cause energy/latency tradeoffs that our standard benches do not reveal. This PR introduces a new workload runner and reporting pipeline that (1) synthesizes controlled temporal sparsity (tilt) across sessions, (2) collects per-kernel energy and latency signals, and (3) produces compact differential reports suitable for regression detection and onboarding new kernel optimizations. Features: - Tilt scheduler: config-driven ramp functions (linear, exponential, sinusoidal) that vary tokens-per-request and sequence length over epochs to simulate drifting usage. - Energy probe shim: optional integration with existing telemetry agents to capture power samples (GPU socket/SM counters, PCIe power when available) and correlate to token boundaries. - Latency tilt reporter: output format includes epoch-level p50/p95/p99, energy-per-token, and kernel attribution (top-3 kernels by CPU/GPU time). - Regression pipeline: small utility to diff two runs and highlight energy/latency deltas and per-kernel attribution changes; emits a markdown summary for PRs. - CI integration: lightweight smoke test and a reproducible synthetic scenario for nightly bench runs. How to run locally: bench-run --runner temporal-tilt --config bench/configs/tilt/sine-tilt.yaml --seed 42 --telemetry=energy:local This will run a short synthetic session and write a report to out/tilt-run-<ts>.json. Design notes: - Avoids intrusive changes to existing runtime; probes attach via the bench telemetry interface so they are no-ops if telemetry is disabled. - The energy probe supports a pluggable backend (mock, nvidia-smi, linux-powercap). - The tilt scheduler is deterministic given a seed and series of epoch rate fixtures to enable CI reproducibility. Motivation/context links: Linear ENG-5123 (workload characterization), ENG-5431 (kernel attribution POC). Checklist: - [x] runner scaffolded and config schema - [x] energy probe with mock backend - [x] basic integration tests - [x] diff/report utility - [x] docs and quickstart - [x] CI smoke job added Risks and limitations: - Energy telemetry accuracy depends on host permissions and hardware; mock backend is provided for determinism. - Not intended as full power modeling; intended for comparative regressions and attribution. Recommended follow-ups: - Add an extended script for multi-GPU cross-model comparisons. - Combine with long-horizon session replayer in benchmark-lab to validate warm cache steady-state interactions.
Jun Park: Can we avoid polling nvidia-smi in the hot path? Suggest adding sampling buffer and separate writer thread.
Ava Martinez: Addressed - energy probe now samples on a separate goroutine and writes to a ring buffer. Added tests for sampling behavior.
Maya Singh: Tests look good, but add a short explainer in docs about interpreting energy-per-token when sequence lengths vary.
Ava Martinez: Added section to docs clarifying normalization strategy (energy/token vs energy/seq-token) and example calculations.
Leo Becker: Approve after CI green and minor comment fixed (typo in docs).
Automation Bot: unit tests rerun succeeded - marking CI green.
Introduce temporal sparsity (tilt) workload runner and energy-latency tilt reports. Enables detection of energy regressions and kernel attribution across drifting token-density workloads. Noted as non-breaking; opt-in via runner flag.
payload.title: Temporal sparsity prober and energy-latency tilt runner

payload.body:
Summary: This PR adds a new perf-canary scenario that generates bursty, highly-variable request load (concurrency ramp + prompt-length ramp) against Hosted API routes to validate overload protection behavior. The goal is to ensure we see explicit overload responses (429/503 w/ stable error codes + Retry-After) and graceful degradation instead of tail-latency blowups/timeouts during bursts.

Context: As part of the Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding reliability program (ENG-4821), we need a repeatable canary that exercises the failure mode we see in real incidents: fast concurrency spikes plus long prompts causing prefill pressure and queue backlogs. We previously only had steady-state throughput scenarios, which are not good at catching retry storms/timeouts. This scenario is intended to be used in dark launch + regional canary gates.

What’s included: 1) New scenario: burst_overload_ramp. Phases: (a) Warm-up steady load, (b) Concurrency ramp 50 -> 600 over ~6 minutes with jittered arrival, (c) Prompt length ramp (p50 ~600 toks, p95 ~6k toks) while holding concurrency high, (d) Recovery ramp-down to verify breaker close and latency returns. Routes: /v1/chat/completions (streaming ON + OFF variants) and /v1/completions (non-stream) behind a single scenario config switch. Models: configurable, defaulting to the primary hosted chat model and a fallback-eligible model pair when enabled. Regions: parameterized (default us-east) for canary rollouts.

2) Assertions/health checks: - Latency SLO guard: p95 and p99 tracked per-phase; scenario fails if p99 latency exceeds threshold for >N consecutive windows while shed rate remains low (signals we are timing out rather than shedding). - Timeout/transport errors: hard fail if client-side timeouts or connection resets exceed a small budget, since overload should be expressed as an explicit error response. - Overload response contract: when we get 429/503, validate JSON payload contains (a) stable overload error code, (b) request/correlation ID, and (c) recommended retry guidance. Validate Retry-After header is present for overload responses (warn -> fail in phase C if missing). - Retry-storm avoidance: scenario client respects Retry-After and applies exponential backoff + jitter for idempotent retries only; by default, we do not retry streaming requests.

3) Metrics export: - Adds a scenario-local summary of: overload_rate, breaker_open_rate (derived from response codes/payload), timeout_rate, and per-phase latency deltas. - Writes a small JSON summary artifact consumed by the canary runner so SRE can gate rollouts on the key numbers without spelunking logs.

4) Docs: - Adds a short README snippet for running locally and recommended flags for canary environments (region/model overrides, max_rps guardrails, and how to disable retries for incident simulations).

Implementation details: - Workload generation uses our existing arrival scheduler but adds: (a) phase-aware target concurrency, (b) per-request prompt size distribution (log-normal-ish) to mimic real prompt variance, and (c) optional streaming mode toggle. - Response validation looks for overload error codes in the JSON body (string match for now) and validates Retry-After parsing. This is intentionally strict to catch regressions like “429 without header” seen in SUP-2860 and “503 without code” which leads to ambiguous client behavior. - Kept dimensions low to avoid high-cardinality metrics. Scenario emits only per-phase aggregates plus a small set of tagged counters (region, route, streaming=true/false).

Files changed (high level): - scenarios/burst_overload_ramp.yaml (new) - scenarios/burst_overload_ramp.streaming.yaml (new) - runner/scenario_loader.go (add schema fields: phases, prompt_profile, streaming toggle) - workload/prompt_profile.go (new: prompt length distribution helpers) - validation/overload_contract.go (new: Retry-After + error payload checks) - cmd/perf-canary/README.md (updated) - tests/overload_contract_test.go (new)

How to run: - Local quick run (safe): perf-canary run --scenario burst_overload_ramp --duration 12m --region us-east --max-rps 120 --dry-run=false - Streaming variant: perf-canary run --scenario burst_overload_ramp.streaming --duration 12m --region us-east - Suggested canary gate: run in canary env with a capped max-rps and compare (timeout_rate + p99) against baseline; overload_rate is expected to increase during peak phases.

Risk/rollout: This only affects perf-canary. The default scenario set is unchanged; the new scenario must be explicitly invoked. We keep conservative defaults (max_rps cap, no retries for streaming) to prevent accidental pressure on prod.

Checklist: - [x] Scenario config reviewed with SRE (Rafael) - [x] Retry/backoff behavior respects Retry-After - [x] Fails on timeouts/connection errors beyond budget - [x] CI green - [x] Added unit tests for Retry-After parsing and payload requirements

Review notes: Rafael Mendes: “Can we make the failure mode explicit? I want the scenario to fail if timeouts rise but shed stays near zero (meaning breaker isn’t firing). Also please ensure we don’t retry streaming; it masks the issue and is not what customers do.” Christine Wong: “Done. Added a guardrail: if p99 spikes + timeout_rate > 0.5% in phase B/C while overload_rate < 0.2%, we fail with a message pointing to the likely regression (breaker not opening / admission not shedding). Also disabled retries for streaming by default; non-stream retries are capped and honor Retry-After.” Aisha Bello: “Please keep summary dimensions minimal; we’ve had cardinality blowups when scenarios emit per-prompt-length tags.” Christine Wong: “Ack. Only emits per-phase aggregates and route/streaming booleans; prompt lengths are only reported as histogram buckets locally in the JSON artifact (not as tagged metrics).” Sofia Ivanova: “Prompt length ramp: can you align to the runtime team’s expectation (long prefill is the pain point). Also, would be great if we track a prefill-like marker even client-side.” Christine Wong: “Adjusted prompt distribution so p95 is long enough to hit prefill pressure and added a client-side ‘time_to_first_token’ measurement for streaming; included in the summary artifact for phase C.”

CI: - build: pass - unit-tests: pass - lint: pass - integration smoke (staging endpoint): pass

Merge: Squash merged to main.

Follow-ups: - Add optional dependency brownout phase (simulate downstream latency) as part of game day scripts (ENG-4830). - Once ADR-014 error payload is fully rolled out, tighten payload validation from string match -> structured schema validation.
payload.title: Add burst traffic scenario to validate overload shedding vs timeouts

payload.body:
This PR adds first-class benchmarking workflows intended for Runtime LTS + release branches and produces a gateable summary artifact that Release Eng can use during patch week. Motivation: today we run perf-canary ad-hoc and interpret results manually. For LTS we need something repeatable: (1) a reusable workflow that can be invoked from the runtime release branch CI, (2) a deterministic set of benchmark suites + hardware matrix, and (3) a single "pass/fail + deltas" artifact that is easy to review and attach to go/no-go. What ships here: new GitHub Actions workflows in perf-canary that support workflow_call + workflow_dispatch, a small gate-evaluator that compares results against a pinned baseline, and a renderer that emits both machine-readable JSON and human-readable Markdown. The gate logic is intentionally conservative and does not set final thresholds in this PR (that is handled in a follow-up tuning PR); here we focus on artifact shape + integration points. Release managers will be able to grab the artifact from the run, link it in Slack/Confluence, and attach it to the release PR checklist. Example artifact names: gate-summary.json (for automation) and gate-summary.md (for humans).
Jonas Weber (review): The artifact format looks good. Two asks: (1) ensure the gate evaluator fails the job when required suites are missing (we’ve had partial uploads), and (2) please include baseline commit SHA in the summary so it’s auditable for LTS.
Marcus Reed (author): Good call. Added schema validation + explicit "required_suites" list and wired missing suite to hard fail. Also included baseline_ref_resolved (full SHA) in both gate-summary.json and gate-summary.md.
Claire Dubois (review): Can we make the GPU matrix explicit and not rely on defaults? Release week we’ll want A100-80GB + H100-80GB as separate lines, and we should record runner type + driver/cuda versions in the summary.
Marcus Reed (author): Updated workflow inputs so callers must specify gpu_matrix, and added runner metadata capture (nvidia-smi, driver, cuda, container image digest) into the summary. The metadata lives under a "provenance" section in markdown and as flat keys in JSON.
Allison Grant (review): From an SRE perspective, we need a clear rerun story when runners are contended. Can we mark the summary with a "noisy run" flag when we detect high variance between repeated subruns?
Marcus Reed (author): Implemented a basic variance check for the throughput sweep subruns and a noisy_run=true marker when coefficient of variation exceeds a small threshold. It doesn’t fail the gate by itself; it’s informational until thresholds are finalized in ENG-4825 follow-ups.
Connor O'Brien (review): Please align naming with the release checklist: artifact should be called lts-gate-summary.* not gate-summary.* to avoid confusion when multiple artifacts are attached. Also ensure workflow_call outputs include an artifact URL we can paste into the release PR.
Marcus Reed (author): Renamed artifacts to lts-gate-summary.json/md and added a step that prints the Actions run URL + artifact name in the job summary. workflow_call now exposes outputs: gate_status, summary_artifact_name, run_url.
Jonas Weber (approve): Looks ready. Let’s keep thresholds out of this PR; follow-up PR can tighten p95 regressions once we’ve validated stability on real runners.
Connor O'Brien (approve): Approved. This unblocks wiring perf-canary into the runtime LTS patch runbook.
Merged via squash. Release managers can now run perf-canary against a runtime release branch ref and receive a single lts-gate-summary artifact with baseline SHA, deltas, provenance, and a gate pass/fail status suitable for LTS patch go/no-go.
Internal: perf-canary now supports release-branch/LTS gating workflows with a standardized summary artifact (JSON + Markdown).
payload.title: Add LTS/release-branch benchmark workflows and gate summary artifact

payload.body:
Summary: This adds a new synthetic canary test that exercises Redwood’s graceful degradation behavior (fallback model and/or fallback region) and emits low-cardinality signals that map directly to incident taxonomy categories (Routing/Fallback misbehavior, Capacity/Fleet shortage, Control plane/routing config). Motivation: Recent incidents and taxonomy workshops highlighted that we don’t currently have a reliable, continuous signal that the “degrade gracefully” path is actually working end-to-end (router decision -> fallback selection -> request succeeds -> correct fallback_reason emitted). This canary is intentionally not a throughput/perf benchmark; it is a correctness + reliability smoke test with a small number of requests on a fixed cadence. What it does: (1) Sends a small chat completion request using a policy that prefers a primary model/region, but is allowed to fall back to a designated compatible model and a designated secondary region. (2) Validates that the response is successful and that the response metadata includes a structured fallback_reason when a fallback occurs (or explicitly indicates no fallback when not needed). (3) Publishes Prometheus metrics and structured logs that can be used in incident tooling/dashboards without exploding label cardinality. Key signals emitted: - perf_canary_degradation_success{tier="hosted",path="model"|"region"|"none"} - perf_canary_degradation_latency_ms_bucket{tier="hosted",path=...} - perf_canary_degradation_fallback_reason{tier="hosted",reason="capacity"|"health"|"policy"|"timeout"|"unknown"} (allowlist only; unknown is a single bucket) - perf_canary_degradation_expected_fallback_mismatch_total{tier="hosted",expected="model"|"region",observed=...} Mapping notes (incident taxonomy): - Sustained failures in this canary are an early warning for Routing/Fallback misbehavior vs Capacity shortage. The metric split (reason allowlist) is aligned with the router fallback_reason enums added in redwood, and is intended to support ENG-4824 taxonomy instrumentation. Rollout/ops: - Default: enabled in prod canary clusters at 1 req/min per region pair, small payload (<= 128 output tokens). - Alerting thresholds are intentionally conservative (multi-window, minimum burn) to avoid paging on transient blips; see follow-up in observability-pack. - Credentials: uses existing perf-canary service account and a dedicated routing policy ID restricted to canary traffic. Testing: - Unit tests for metadata parsing + allowlist mapping. - Integration test runs in CI against mock router endpoint. Notes: No customer-facing change. This is internal telemetry only.
The canary intentionally uses a fixed allowlist of fallback_reason values (capacity, health, policy, timeout, unknown). Any new enum values from redwood are mapped to unknown until explicitly approved (cardinality guardrail).
The test supports three expected paths: none (no fallback), model (fallback model in same region), region (fallback region). The policy config selects which path we expect per environment run.
Mismatch detection is tolerant of cases where no fallback occurs because primary is healthy; the mismatch counter only increments when the config explicitly forces a fallback scenario (via policy) and the observed metadata disagrees.
When fallback_reason is missing from response metadata, the test logs a structured event with observed fields to help debugging. This is treated as a soft failure in staging and a hard failure in prod (configurable).
Mina Haddad (Routing): Can we confirm the request actually hits the router path where fallback_reason is set? If this goes through any direct model pinning we’ll get false confidence.
Sergio Costa (Author): Good call. Updated config to use routing policy ID (no direct model pin). Added validation that response includes routing_decision_id and selected_model/selected_region fields; otherwise test fails with explicit error.
Allison Grant (Observability): Please do not emit raw model IDs or region pairs as labels. That will blow up cardinality. Keep path and reason only; anything else should be in logs.
Sergio Costa (Author): Done. Removed model/region labels; now only {tier, path} and {tier, reason}. Added structured log fields for selected_model and selected_region for debugging.
Aisha Bello (SLO/SLA): Add guidance for how this ties into incident taxonomy dashboards. Also, what’s the expected alert behavior?
Sergio Costa (Author): Added docs/runbooks/degradation-path-canary.md with suggested panels (success rate + mismatch + reason mix). Alerts are out of scope here, but I added recommended thresholds and noted we’ll wire them in observability-pack.
Rafael Mendes (SRE): This should map cleanly to ENG-4824/4828. Please add a short section explaining the taxonomy mapping and what ICs should do when it fires.
Sergio Costa (Author): Added “Taxonomy mapping + IC actions” section in the runbook, including quick decision points (capacity vs routing vs control plane) and links to the routing/fleet dashboards.
Mina Haddad (Routing): One more: ensure we don’t accidentally trigger large cross-region egress costs or load. Can you cap request rate and payload size explicitly?
Sergio Costa (Author): Added hard caps: max 1 req/min per configured pair, max_output_tokens=128, timeout=8s. Also added a CI guard to prevent increasing cadence without approval.
Internal: Added degradation-path synthetic canary to validate model/region fallback correctness and emit taxonomy-aligned signals for dashboards/incident classification.
payload.title: Add synthetic canary for graceful degradation path (model/region fallback)

Introduce an ensemble-based anomaly detector for the perf canary pipeline and a conservative 'stability window' rollout guard. Motivation: recent incidents showed single-signal detectors (p95 latency only) lead to noisy blocks and false rollbacks when environmental noise (network jitter, transient region effects) spikes briefly. The new detector aggregates three orthogonal signals (latency distribution shift, p95 variance across regions, and network jitter proxy) using a lightweight ensemble scoring (EWMA + Bayesian vote). To reduce reactive churn we require a configurable stability window (default: 5m sustained score > threshold) before the guard blocks or triggers rollback. This PR includes the detector runtime, controller integration, guard wiring in the canary orchestration, dashboards, synthetic probe changes, unit/integration tests, and a migration plan with staged rollout. The description below summarizes design, implementation, testing, and rollout notes.
Anika: Can you clarify how the weights are derived for the ensemble? Recommendation: default to 0.5 latency / 0.3 variance / 0.2 jitter and expose in config. Also request tests around weight edge cases.
Riley: Responded that weights are currently empirically tuned from last 90 days of canary history; exposed as runtime config and added unit tests. Will add a Linear task for long-term automated tuning.
Mateo: Noted potential alert fatigue: suggest an 'escalation window' separate from stability window so short blocks open paged-only after longer sustained failures. Requested docs explaining oncall flow.
Riley: Added escalation window config and updated runbook with oncall flow. Also added a non-paging severity for transient blocks under 15m.
Jules: Verified code style, asked for additional type hints in Python and a short note on cost impact. Approved after CI green and docs updated.
CI: Build passed; e2e had two flakes initially but rerun passed. Tests show ~0.3s extra CPU time in synthetic probe worker under heavy load; considered acceptable.
Squash-merged after resolving review comments and adding runbook. CI green on final run; small test flakes were stabilized by adding deterministic seeds to the harness.
Adds an ensemble anomaly detector combining latency shifts, cross-region p95 variance, and a network jitter proxy; introduces a configurable 'stability window' (default 5 minutes) to require sustained signal before blocking a rollout; new dashboards and runbook included. Default guard is enabled for internal perf canaries; admins can tune weights and windows via perf-canary/config/guards.yaml.
payload.title: Ensemble anomaly detector + stability-window rollout guard for canaries

payload.body:
Context and motivation: We frequently see gradual-performance degradations that slip past point-estimate canaries because the signal is distributed across multiple traffic phases and timescales. This PR introduces a multiscale fingerprint quarantine guard that: (1) builds phase-aware traffic fingerprints at multiple temporal granularities, (2) detects divergence across scales using a robust similarity metric, and (3) applies progressive quarantine controls that throttle or isolate suspect traffic slices during rollouts.

Design summary: The guard computes per-route phase fingerprints (startup, steady-state, tail) using stratified quantile histograms for latency and throughput features. Fingerprints are kept at 5s, 1m, and 15m aggregation windows and compared to a rolling baseline using cosine similarity + Kullback-Leibler smoothing for distribution drift. When sustained divergence is detected at the mid and long scales but not at the finest scale (indicating slow drift rather than transient spikes), the guard triggers a progressive quarantine: first divert 10% of canary traffic to a spectator pool, then pause new canaries for the route and escalate to automatic rollback if divergence exceeds thresholds for 30m.

What this changes: - New guard implementation and registration (canary/guards/multiscale_quarantine_guard.py) - Telemetry: adds multiscale_fingerprint.* metrics and event annotation (metrics/telemetry_schema.yaml) - Canary evaluator integration points and config knobs for thresholds and quarantine policies (canary/configs/multiscale_guard.yaml) - Unit + integration tests and a small synthetic traffic generator used for local validation (tests/perf/multiscale_guard_test.py, tests/perf/synthetic_traffic.py)

Testing and validation: Local unit tests, integration tests against the perf-canary harness, and a staging week-long replay of 72 hours of production traces with injected slow drift patterns. We observed earlier detection (median lead time +18 minutes) compared to baseline percentile-only canaries and zero false positives on the replay dataset. CI runs: full test matrix and telemetry linting passed on the final push.

Rollout plan: Feature flag behind canary.guard.multiscale_quarantine. Start with shadow mode for two weeks on <staging> then enable soft quarantine for low-risk routes (10% traffic diversion) and expand to more aggressive policies only after SRE sign-off. The PR includes doc notes and an ops runbook (docs/ops/multiscale_quarantine_runbook.md) describing thresholds, troubleshooting queries, and rollback steps.

Checklist (author): [x] unit tests added [x] integration test harness replayed [x] telemetry schema updated [x] docs & runbook added [x] SRE consult performed
Ethan Brooks: Good overall. Two items: clarify how we avoid reacting to seasonal traffic shifts; add a short note about probe sampling bias.
Author (Anika): Added a short-term seasonal adjustment using a weighted baseline and documented sampling assumptions in the runbook.
Li Wei: Can we make thresholds per-route configurable and bounded by org policy? Also suggest we emit a structured event when quarantine activates.
Author (Anika): thresholds are config-driven; added schema limits and implemented structured quarantine events (multiscale_quarantine.trigger) in telemetry.
Priya Kapoor: Tests look good; please ensure we have an SLO-blindness test (that we don't inadvertently break SLO calc paths).
Author (Anika): added an SLO path integration test to ensure SLO metrics continue to be computed for quarantined traffic.
Adds a multiscale fingerprint quarantine guard to canary evaluator. Detects gradual distributional regressions across multiple time scales and applies progressive quarantine controls to protect production traffic. Feature gated behind canary.guard.multiscale_quarantine.
Runbook available at docs/ops/multiscale_quarantine_runbook.md. Key dashboards: multiscale_fingerprint.similarity, multiscale_quarantine.active_routes, multiscale_quarantine.divergence_seconds. Default soft quarantine diverts 10% traffic and is reversible via feature flag.
payload.title: Add multiscale fingerprint quarantine guard for gradual regressions

payload.body:
Context: We regularly observe tail-latency regressions that are not correlated with aggregate p95/p99 shifts but instead manifest as short-lived, high-intensity concurrency hotspots (e.g. sudden affinity to a small subset of routes, backend shard hotness, or scheduler alignment effects). These regressions frequently evade existing canary detectors which rely on aggregated distributions and throughput-weighted signals, resulting in either missed regressions or noisy false positives.

This change introduces two complementary pieces:
1) Concurrency Heatmap Prober — a lightweight continuous probe that builds a temporal heatmap of concurrency by traffic key (route/service/shard tag). The probe tracks short-window occupancy and concentration metrics (entropy, top-k mass, burstiness index) and exposes a probabilistic risk score for hotspot-driven tail events.
2) Gradual Pause Rollout Gate — a rollout guard that uses the heatmap risk score to apply a controlled, staged pause to canary traffic (not a hard rollback). Instead of flipping from go -> rollback, the gate reduces canary traffic in configurable micro-steps while continuing targeted probes to validate whether the hotspot dissipates. This reduces churn and gives the scheduler/time-based factors a chance to stabilize.

Design highlights and motivation: The heatmap uses reservoir sampling per traffic key with time-decayed counts; this allows bounded memory with recency bias. We compute entropy and top-3 mass and combine them into a single risk score using a small probabilistic model (logistic blending with configurable thresholds). The Gradual Pause Gate consumes that score and performs staged traffic corking with exponential backoff windows. This approach is intentionally orthogonal to existing percentile-based detectors so the system can reason about regressions caused by concentrated concurrency vs. global latency shifts.

Compatibility and safety: All toggles live behind runtime feature flags and a canary-policy predicate. Default behavior is off. When enabled, the gate defaults to conservative thresholds (first stage: 25% traffic reduction, probe budget 5% of normal requests) and never pauses traffic below a minimum availability floor. The change contains multiple safe-guards: minimum probe sampling, circuit-breaker on probe flakiness, and telemetry rollbacks if probe success rate drops.

What I changed (high-level):
- pkg/canary/probers/heatmap_prober.go — core heatmap logic, reservoir sampling, risk scoring
- pkg/canary/gates/gradual_pause_gate.go — rollout gate implementation and state machine
- pkg/canary/config/defaults.yaml — new config knobs for heatmap bins, smoothing, pause stages
- pkg/telemetry/metrics.go — new metrics (concurrency_heat_entropy, concurrency_top_mass, heatmap_risk_score, gradual_pause_stage)
- internal/e2e/canary_heatmap_test.go — integration tests with synthetic hotspot loads
- dashboards/canary_heatmap.json — Grafana dashboard focused on probe visualization
- docs/operations/canary_heatmap.md — operator guide, tuning advice and runbook

Testing and QA: unit tests for reservoir logic, property tests for decay behavior, and an e2e harness that simulates skewed traffic (100x intensity on 2 of 1k keys) to validate detection and staged pause. Added load profiles to perf-lab and ran a 24-hour soak with randomized scheduler alignments to ensure no stability regressions. We also exercised the circuit-breaker by forcing probe failures to validate safe rollback behavior.

Rollout plan: Merge to main behind feature flag. Stage rollout to staging clusters with gradual rollout (10% accounts) for 48h, then increase to 50% if no incident. If the gate triggers >3 times in 24h for the same service, ops alert routes to SRE for manual triage.

Open questions / TODOs: bind heatmap keys to richer runtime labels (per-customer affinity) — future follow-up (ENG-9739). Consider adding a hierarchical heatmap that aggregates by service -> route -> host for faster triage.

Added comments and a config knob for the cap."\nAisha Rao (2026-01-27): "Please add an explainer in the docs for ops to tune pause-stage sizes. Also added minimum availability floor so no rollout can reduce service below 50% by default."\nMiguel Hernandez (2026-01-29): "Integration test flake: the e2e harness sometimes fails when scheduler alignment happens; can we make the probe timing jittered to avoid deterministic race?"\nSamira Patel (2026-01-30): "Adjusted the probe schedule to add randomized jitter and re-ran the suite. CI rerun passed locally. Added the note to the test to avoid future flakes."\nEvan Liu (2026-02-01): "Approve after CI green and a quick prow job review. Context: We continue to see short-lived latency regressions that correlate strongly with transient GPU/host memory pressure during warmup and during certain batched workloads. Existing canary detectors focused on latency/throughput signals can overreact (false positives) or underreact (missed degradations) when memory pressure is the root cause. This PR introduces two complementary components: 1) a lightweight Memory Probe that samples per-host GPU/OS memory utilization distributions and computes short-window entropy and tail co-moments with latency; 2) a Rollback Sentry that fuses the memory signal with existing canary scorecards to produce a risk score used by the rollout controller to throttle or stop canary ramps. Design summary: - Memory Probe: continuous sampling (1s aggregated) of resident GPU memory, allocator fragmentation metric, and RSS for the inference process. Computes 95/99 percentiles, short-window skew, and an entropy-like measure that detects unexpected dispersion in memory usage across hosts. - Correlation layer: streaming correlation (Spearman, robust to outliers) between memory 95/99 percentiles and tail latency (p95/p99). Correlations maintained as exponentially weighted moving estimates to react quickly but avoid single-spike sensitivity. - Rollback Sentry: takes inputs from the canary evaluator (latency deltas, throughput deltas, error rates) and memory-correlation outputs to compute a single 0-100 risk score. Rules: if risk >= 70 -> immediate canary pause and automatic rollback candidate; if risk in 50-70 -> throttle ramp and require manual ACK; risk < 50 -> normal rollout. The sentry also factors in traffic-weighted amplification to reduce noisy signals from low-volume slices. Motivation: By adding memory-awareness we reduce both false-positive rollbacks triggered by transient GC/allocator events and false-negatives where latency regressions are caused by memory saturation rather than model-level regressions. Checklist: - [x] Memory Probe implementation and unit tests - [x] Streaming correlation module and integration tests - [x] Rollout Sentry scoring logic and policy configuration - [x] E2E synthetic workload tests (bursty batch, warmup scenarios) - [x] Dashboard panels and alerts for memory-correlation heatmap - [x] Documentation and operator runbook - [x] Canary experiment in perf-canary staging cluster Testing and validation: Ran staged canary on perf-canary/staging across three workload shapes (steady small-batch, bursty batch, mixed latency-sensitive). Observed a 38% reduction in unnecessary rollback events in synthetic warmup tests and correct blocking of a memory-induced p99 regression in one injected fault run. CI: unit and integration suites passed, one flaky host-level metric test stabilized by increasing aggregation window. Rollout plan: - Roll out to canary evaluator in staging for 48 hours - Gradual opt-in for new canaries (default off for legacy rollout jobs) - Monitor heatmap and false-positive rate for two weeks before defaulting to on. Configuration: all thresholds and weights are feature-flagged and tunable via canary policy YAML. Operator note: if your environment has external memory reclamation hooks (custom allocators) set memory_probe.skip_low_level=true to avoid noisy fragmentation signals.
Adds a memory-aware graceful throttle probe and an adaptive rollback sentry for canary evaluations. Improves resilience against memory-induced latency spikes by scoring rollback risk and pausing traffic ramps when memory pressure correlates with tail latency degradation.

Maya Chen: Thresholds are conservative and feature-flagged. We derived them from 120 synthetic runs across 6 host types; added a config map so SREs can tune per-region.
Priya Rao: Please add a safety valve that ignores memory signals for very low traffic slices to avoid overfitting to noise.
Maya Chen: Added traffic-weighted amplification and a skip_low_volume flag; updated tests to cover that case.
Diego Martinez: CI flake in integration test — looks like metric ingestion race. Recommend increasing aggregation window to 1s for the sampler.
Maya Chen: Increased aggregation window and added retry logic; re-ran CI and green.

Context: We need a safer path for promoting shadow traffic to a canary that preserves session affinity and lets operators 'rewind' a partially promoted commit without a full rollback blast.
This PR introduces a rewindable canary lane that (1) supports session-affine traffic handover, (2) records compact model snapshot diffs to enable sub-minute rewinds, and (3) ties promotion gates to telemetry anchors (latency P95, error-rate, hallucination-rate) with configurable tolerances.
Motivations: nightly model churn and multi-variant A/B tests often surface regressions only after partial promotion and with session-affine state; current rollbacks are coarse-grained and can cause user-visible flips.
Design summary:
- New controller RewindableSwapController orchestrates staged promotions in small session-slice increments (configurable slice_size) and records an immutable promotion journal in object storage.
- Each promotion step emits a telemetry anchor snapshot (p95, error_rate, hallucination_rate, embedding-drift) and stores the snapshot alongside the snapshot-diff reference.
- Rewind operation replays the journal in reverse: it applies compact diffs to the serving plane and gracefully drains newly routed sessions.
- Session stickiness is preserved by a session-token mapping table; we add an optional session-migrate policy to migrate active sessions without a hard cutover.
- Safety gates are policy-driven: anchors must be within thresholds (defaults: p95 +10%, error_rate +0.5pp, hallucination_rate +1pp) for promotion to proceed.
- Developer ergonomics: CLI and Console integration for a one-click "rewind to N" with a preview of telemetry deltas.
What changed (high-level files):
- services/rollout-controller/controllers/rewindable_swap.py (controller + reconciliation loop)
- services/rollout-controller/api/v1alpha/rewindable_swap.proto (CRD/API)
- services/telemetry/anchors/anchor_probe.go (anchor snapshot and evaluation)
- docs/runbooks/release/rewindable-canary-playbook.md (operator playbook)
- console/components/canary/rewind-preview.tsx (UI preview)
- integration-tests/test_rewindable_canary.py (end-to-end tests)
Checklist:
- [x] Controller reconciliation and leader-election tested
- [x] Telemetry anchoring integrated with existing metrics pipeline
- [x] Integration tests covering promote/partial-promote/rewind
- [x] Console and CLI hooks included
- [x] Docs and runbook with step-by-step rewind guidance
Rollout plan: We will feature-flag the controller (feature.rewindable_canary = false by default). Deploy to staging for 48h, run synthetic smoke for 6 hours, then enable in canary region for a small internal cohort (1% sessions) before wider rollout.
Migration notes: Backwards compatible with existing Swap controller. If feature flag is disabled, behavior falls back to current atomic-swap.
Security: Journal objects are written to customer-specified object stores with ACLs; we reuse existing KMS envelope encryption.
Testing: Unit tests for diff application and rewind logic, integration tests that use a local object-store stub and simulated sessions, and end-to-end smoke in staging.
The CI pipeline initially failed on lint (prettier/flake8 infra) and a flaky telemetry assertion; both were addressed in followup commits and pipeline passed. See commits & conversation for details.

Motivation: Our existing canary guard triggers on simple aggregated latency/throughput thresholds which produces noisy full rollbacks for short, high-request-rate transients. This PR introduces a rate-weighted anomaly detector that scores canaries by combining latency, error-rate, and request rate into a single anomaly score and a soft-rollback traffic policy that reduces rather than immediately cancels traffic for marginal regressions.

What this changes (high level):
- New detector implementation (pkg/detectors/rate_detector.go) that computes a rate-weighted z-score across configured metrics and emits a single 'anomaly_score' for a canary window. The detector supports dynamic windows: short (30s) and steady (5m) and does a weighted blend.
- Controller integration (cmd/canary/controller.go) to consume anomaly scores and map them to actions: continue, reduce-traffic, rollback. The default mapping is: score<1.5 continue, 1.5<=score<2.5 -> reduce traffic by 30%, score>=2.5 -> full rollback. Thresholds are configurable per deployment.
- Soft-rollback policy (pkg/rollout/soft_rollback.go): orchestrates a staged traffic reduction with cooldowns, and a path to automatic recovery (gradual ramp-back) if metrics stabilize. Works with existing traffic-shift primitives.
- Metrics and telemetry: adds canary.anomaly_score gauge, canary.soft_rollback_events counter, and rollout.action_reason tag to existing rollout metrics.
- e2e scenarios and CI harness updates (e2e/perf/canary_rate_qa.yaml, tests/perf/canary_rate_detector_test.go) covering bursty QPS, sustained degradation, and noisy spikes.
- Docs and Helm chart updates (docs/operational/perf-canaries.md, charts/perf-canary/values.yaml).

Small illustrative snippet (from pkg/detectors/rate_detector.go):
func Score(window MetricsWindow) float64 {
    // compute z for latency and error rate, weight by request_rate
    lz := zscore(window.latency, baseline.latency)
    ez := zscore(window.error_rate, baseline.error_rate)
    weight := 1 + math.Log(1+window.request_rate) * cfg.RateWeight
    return (lz*cfg.LatencyWeight + ez*cfg.ErrorWeight) * weight
}

Testing and CI: Unit tests added for detector math and policy mapping. e2e job simulates QPS bursts; CI job was flaky initially due to a timing assumption in the e2e harness which I fixed by aligning time window boundaries. Full CI matrix passed on final run (lint, unit, integration, e2e).

Rollout plan: Feature is behind a canary feature flag (perf_rate_detector) and off by default. We'll enable in the perf-canary staging environment for 48h, evaluate anomaly_score distribution via the new dashboard panel, then enable soft-rollback policy for 10% traffic across a small set of non-critical services before wider rollout. Linear tickets ENG-3321 and SRE-119 track staging and rollouts.

Backward compatibility: Detector is opt-in and does not change existing threshold-based guards until the feature flag is enabled. Config schema additions are additive.

Files changed (high-level):
- pkg/detectors/rate_detector.go
- cmd/canary/controller.go
- pkg/rollout/soft_rollback.go
- e2e/perf/canary_rate_qa.yaml
- docs/operational/perf-canaries.md
- charts/perf-canary/values.yaml

Notes: This PR focuses on reducing noisy full rollbacks and catching regressions that correlate with request rate. It intentionally keeps the mapping from score->action conservative; operations can tune weights and thresholds per-service.
Liam O'Connor: Can we make the rate-weighting function robust to synthetic traffic spikes caused by healthchecks?
Maya Chen: Added a filter to ignore known healthcheck user agents and also added an optional per-service min_request_rate config to avoid over-weighting tiny services.
Priya Iyer: The soft-rollback feels useful but could leave services in a degraded steady state. How do we ensure recovery?
Maya Chen: Soft-rollback has a cooldown and a two-tier ramp-back if metrics are stable for the cooldown window; added tests and a dashboard alert that flags prolonged soft-rollback states for SRE review.
Diego Martinez: How does this interact with multi-variant rollouts?
Maya Chen: Controller applies soft-rollback per-variant; if a variant is reduced below 5% traffic the fallback variant path is triggered. Documented in the rollout policy comments.
Priya Iyer: CI flakiness was fixed in the last commit, verified e2e run passed. Approving after green CI.
Maya Chen: Addressed comments and squashed commits for merge.
Adds a rate-aware anomaly detector for performance canaries and a configurable soft-rollback traffic policy. Improves detection precision for short, high-throughput bursts and reduces noisy full rollbacks during transient spikes.

Motivation: Recent incidents showed rapid traffic bursts could trigger aggressive rollouts and cascade retries that look like regressions even when the candidate is healthy. This PR introduces a phase-aware canary pauser and a lightweight backpressure detector to differentiate transient traffic spikes and system backpressure from genuine model performance regressions, and to automatically pause or throttle the canary traffic in a controlled way. High-level changes: 1) Phase-aware Canary Pauser: adds a new canary state machine with phases (probe, monitor, steady) and allows short, policy-driven pauses between phases when signal quality is low. Pauses are stratified by traffic slice (user-agent, route, priority bucket) to avoid global halts. 2) Backpressure Detector: implements a probabilistic backpressure signal derived from queue length, worker saturation, and 95/99 tail latency joint probability; it exposes a short-lived backpressure score used to trigger graduated throttles and prefer-fallback routing. 3) Safe fallback policy: integrates with routing to shift a small percentage of traffic to a lower-capacity model variant or regional pool instead of full rollback when backpressure is detected. 4) Observability and alerting: adds per-phase metrics, backpressure score histogram, and a dashboard with example alert thresholds and runbook links. 5) Tests and canary harness changes: synthetic load tests and a deterministic simulator for phase transitions. Rollout plan: merge to main behind feature flag perf.phase_pauser=true; gradually enable for internal perf-canaries first, monitor metrics for two weeks, then baseline external canaries. Checklist: [x] unit and integration tests, [x] end-to-end simulator test, [x] dashboard and alert panels, [x] feature flag gating, [x] docs updates in perf playbook. Commits summary: (1) add phase state machine and pauser logic, (2) implement backpressure score calculator and probe hooks, (3) routing integration and safe-fallback policy, (4) synthetic load scenarios and simulator, (5) dashboards and alert rules, (6) tests and CI tweaks. Impact: aims to reduce false-positive canary rollbacks by avoiding hasty rollbacks during traffic spikes and to protect underlying serving fleet from overload. Related: ENG-3421 adds the canary lifecycle API used here, SUP-9082 covers a customer incident that motivated early backpressure metrics.
Ben Turner (2026-02-10): Overall approach looks sound. Question: how do we avoid oscillation between pause and resume in noisy slices? Suggest adding a hysteresis timer and minimum phase dwell time.
Aisha Kumar (2026-02-11): Reply: added minimum_dwell_ms and exponential backoff on consecutive pauses, see phase_pauser.py lines 142-180 in this PR.
Camille Ortiz (2026-02-12): Can we surface the backpressure score in tracing for sampled requests so SRE can correlate traces?
Aisha Kumar (2026-02-12): Added span tag 'canary.backpressure_score' and instrumented in probe path.
Diego Morales (2026-02-13): CI flakes on integration timing in the synthetic simulator; bumping timeouts fixed it. Approved after green CI.
Introduce phase-aware canary pauser and backpressure detector to reduce false-positive rollbacks during traffic spikes. Feature gated. See docs/perf/playbook_canary_pauser.md for usage and configuration.

payload.body:
Summary: Add a new Harmonic Ensemble Deconvolver (HED) component to the perf-canary pipeline. HED fuses three orthogonal detectors (spectral drift, temporal-windowed percentile shifts, and traffic-shape-conditioned residuals) and applies a lightweight deconvolution step to separate short-lived noise harmonics (traffic burst and probe artifacts) from persistent regressions. The goal is to reduce false-positive canary alerts while preserving sensitivity to real throughput/latency regressions and to provide a tenant-aware fallback that keeps rollouts moving during noisy traffic windows.

Motivation and context: Over the last 6 months we observed a ~18% false-positive rate in canary alerts for tail-latency regressions that correlate with short-lived client-side spikes and synthetic-probe alignment issues. Existing single-signal detectors either overreact to traffic harmonics or under-detect gradual degradations. HED addresses both by: 1) deconvolving periodic noise components using a compact harmonic filter; 2) combining detectors in an ensemble using a weighted consensus that is calibrated per-tenant and per-route; 3) exposing a controlled fallback policy that temporarily softens cutover thresholds (graceful corking) while creating a prioritized re-probing schedule.

What this PR changes:
- New component: perf_canary/detectors/harmonic_ensemble.py implementing the harmonic decomposition, consensus logic, and per-tenant weighting lookup.
- Integration: pipeline stages updated to call HED between metric-aggregation and canary-evaluator. This includes a new API hook canary.pipeline.deconvolve(metrics, tenant_id).
- Rollout guard extension: add a tenant-aware fallback policy that reduces new traffic weight if HED reports high harmonic-contamination but low consensus severity. Fallback is configurable via canary policies: .fallback.window_seconds and .fallback.max_soft_percentage.
- Telemetry: new metrics hed.harmonic_contamination_ratio, hed.consensus_score, hed.deconvolved_latency_p90 and corresponding tracing spans for attribution.
- Tests: unit tests for harmonic decomposition, ensemble weighting, and an end-to-end integration test using historical traffic replayer; added canary harness fixtures to simulate tenant-specific noise.
- Documentation: docs/perf-canary/HED-design.md and short guide in docs/operator/runbooks/canary-fallbacks.md.

Design highlights and tradeoffs:
- The harmonic filter is intentionally low-compute (FFT over rolling window with fixed N=128) so it can run in the pipeline without requiring additional workers. We avoid full spectral-learning to keep memory bounded.
- Ensemble weights are initialized from historical baseline and are updated weekly by a background calibrator job (not in this PR). The PR includes the hooks for weight refresh.
- Fallback policy is conservative: it only decreases route cutover weight up to a configurable soft percentage and requires HED to report contamination for at least two consecutive evaluation windows to take effect. This prevents oscillation during multi-minute traffic shifts.

Testing and results:
- Unit: 26 new unit tests, coverage +2.1% for perf-canary package.
- Integration: ran the synthetic traffic replay for 48 hours on staging (traffic mix A/B/C) and ran 72-hour historical backfills across 12 tenants. Results: false-positive alerts reduced by 45% (relative) for tail-latency regressions attributed to short-lived bursts; true positive detection latency for sustained degradations improved by 30% (median). No measurable adverse impact on throughput or CPU on canary pipeline workers (avg +3% CPU, p95 unchanged).
- Chaos test: injected client-side bursts and probe misalignment for two tenants; HED prevented unnecessary rollback in both cases and re-scheduled probes which discovered the regressions as persistent and then triggered normal rollback after 8-12 minutes.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implementation of HED algorithm and ensemble consensus.
- [x] Pipeline integration and API hook.
- [x] Unit & integration tests.
- [x] Metrics/tracing instrumentation.
- [x] Documentation and runbook updates.
- [x] Reviewed and approved by perf and sre.

Backward compatibility and rollout plan:
- HED is gated behind a config flag canary.features.harmonic_ensemble=false by default. We will enable it for a small subset of tenants on staging for 48h, then enable on 10% of traffic on lower prod and monitor hed.consensus_score and alert rates for 72h before full rollout.
- No breaking changes: the canary evaluator API remains stable; the deconvolution step is additive.

Risks and mitigation: 
- Risk: under-detection if ensemble weights are miscalibrated for a tenant. Mitigation: fallback policy is conservative and background calibrator will tune weights; ops can revert via feature flag.
- Risk: increased CPU on pipeline workers. Mitigation: harmonic filter uses tuned N=128 and early-exit heuristics; metrics added to watch CPU and queue length.

Related work: This complements the temporal-windowed and percentile-weighted detectors introduced earlier (see ENG-1553 and PRs in this repo). It is intentionally orthogonal to the latency-cliff detector; HED reduces noise that often causes spurious cliff detections.

How to review: Focus on detector correctness (harmonic_ensemble.py), unit tests in tests/perf_canary/test_harmonic_ensemble.py, and the limited API changes in pipeline.py. Trace examples and graphs are in docs/perf-canary/HED-examples.png.

Ethan Morris (reviewer): Overall looks good. Two asks: (1) show a simple example of the harmonic spectrum in the docs so ops can understand contamination; (2) add a short-circuit to skip deconvolution when traffic volume < min_samples.
Maya Chen (author): Added spectrum example and implemented min_samples short-circuit (defaults to 64). Updated docs and tests accordingly.
Sana Iqbal (reviewer): Can you add a small note on how this interacts with replayer-derived baselines? I want to ensure weekly calibrator won't diverge.
Maya Chen: Added paragraph in HED-design.md describing calibrator constraints and conservative learning rate; left the calibrator job disabled until we have 2 weeks of production HED telemetry.
Leo Park (approver): Approved after verifying end-to-end integration test and staging replay metrics. CI flakiness noted earlier was rerun and green.
payload.title: Introduce harmonic ensemble deconvolver and tenant-aware fallback for perf canaries

Motivation: We observed several transient throughput bursts in production where existing canary probes either (a) over-injected traffic and amplified noise (causing false positives), or (b) used coarse fixed-window decay which reacted too slowly to quick phase-shifts. This PR adds two complementary safeguards: 1) a hopwise-decay probe scheduler that decomposes probing windows into hop segments with exponentially decayed weights to prioritize recent samples while retaining historical context; 2) a traffic-tempering rollout guard that dynamically limits probe injection and rate of traffic increase based on short-term volatility metrics.
Ravi Patel: Nice design. Can we get a short worked example in docs that shows parameter tuning for a 10%-burst traffic pattern?
Ava Martinez: Added a worked example in docs/traffic-tempering.md and an example config under examples/
Sofia Liu: There was a flaky test run (TestHopwiseDecayStability) in CI — I saw an intermittent 1ms timing drift. Please add tolerances.
Ava Martinez: Increased tolerance and added deterministic seed for timing-based test; re-ran CI.
Jonah Kim: Guard integration looks good. One request: when tempering kicks in, emit a high-signal metric (canary.tempering.active) to make alerting simpler.
Ava Martinez: Emit canary.tempering.active with boolean dimension and added docs for alerting rule.

Add hopwise-decay probe scheduler and traffic-tempering rollout guard (opt-in). Improves resilience to short-lived bursts and reduces false-positive canary rollbacks. See perf-canary/docs/traffic-tempering.md for tuning guidance.

payload.body:
Summary: Introduces a traffic sharder for synthetic benchmark runners that can partition generated requests across multiple runner instances (shards) and a latency-path linker reporter that correlates end-to-end latency across shard boundaries. Motivation: Existing runners model single-process hotspots and interleaved sequences but do not easily emulate cross-runner contention and backpressure that customers see with multi-pod deployments. This makes it hard to reproduce p95/p99 regressions caused by shard-local queuing and cross-shard coordination. Solution: Add a pluggable sharder component that sits in the workload generator and shards traffic according to configurable policies (hash-by-session, round-robin windowed, adaptive hotset split). Each request is stamped with a lightweight correlation id and a path tag so the latency-path linker can stitch traces across shards and produce per-path p50/p95/p99 deltas as well as a per-shard affinity heatmap export. Implementation notes: Python prototype for the sharder lives in runners/sharder.py and provides a local simulation harness; the latency-path linker reporter is implemented in Go to integrate with existing reporter pipelines and emits a compact CSV and Prometheus-friendly metrics via shard_affinity_exporter.py. We also added a small C++ worker hotpath fix for multi-threaded enqueue semantics in shard_worker_impl.cc and a convenience CLI + Dockerfile to run a small multi-shard cluster locally. Tests and verification: integration test simulates 3 shard topologies and asserts deterministic trace stitching and bucketed latency deltas (tests/integration/test_cross_shard_replay.py). Performance runs were executed in the perf pipeline (ci/perf-pipeline-config.yaml) with a synthetic workload manifest (benchmarks/manifests/cross-shard-sim.yaml). Results: baseline run (3 shards, hash-by-session) shows expected p95 uplift of ~18% when hotset affinity is enabled vs evenly distributed baseline; exporter produces per-shard heatmap and CSV with path-linked histograms. Commits: initial + linker + exporter + tuning + race fix + docs. Review conversation summary: Reviewer Anika requested CLI knobs for shard window size and a short reproducible example; addressed in commit 4 and added examples/cross_shard_quickstart.md. Liam pointed out a potential memory growth in the correlation map; fixed by using a bounded LRU in shard_affinity_exporter.py and added tests. Context: We observed repeated reopen/reclose oscillation during multi-tenant regional pressure events. Root cause analysis pointed to interleaved circuit transitions and simultaneous tenant-level SLO relaxations that caused cascading reassignment of requests and KV-drain churn. This PR introduces two pieces: (1) an intersectional SLO holdoff matrix that enforces a short, configurable holdoff when multiple SLO signals converge for the same tenant/route, preventing aggressive successive concessions; (2) an atomic circuit sequencer in the control plane that ensures circuit state transitions (open -> probing -> closed) for a given region/zone are applied serially with a bounded window to prevent flip-flop storms. The changes are intentionally conservative and feature-flagged behind `slo_holdoff_v2` and `atomic_circuit_sequencer`. payload.body:
Motivation: We continue to see transient tail regressions during small traffic bursts that cause binary rollback decisions in the canary orchestrator. Those rollbacks are noisy for low-risk regressions and make gradual rollouts brittle for multi-tenant workloads. This PR introduces two complementary controls: (1) a quantile-slice hedger that evaluates distributional drift across time-sliced quantiles and emits a graded instability score, and (2) a stochastic cutover circuit that converts high-frequency binary cutovers into probabilistic, smoothed attenuation actions (traffic attenuation / short-circuiting) to avoid synchronized rollbacks across cohorts.

Summary of changes: implemented a new hedger component in the perf-canary evaluator, wire-up to the canary orchestrator for soft attenuation actions, added end-to-end tests and synthetic scenarios, and added dashboards and runbook guidance. The approach focuses on reducing false-positive full rollbacks while still surfacing sustained regressions for human review.

Design highlights: 
- Quantile-slice hedger: splits recent request latency samples into N temporal slices (configurable, default 5) and computes target quantiles (p50/p90/p95/p99) per slice. The hedger computes inter-slice deltas and a weighted entropy score that downweights short-lived spikes and upweights persistent shifts. Output is a normalized instability score [0,1] and an ordinal severity (ok/warn/degrade).
- Stochastic cutover circuit: when instability enters warn/degrade, instead of immediate rollback we apply a probabilistic attenuation policy: a percentage of traffic is diverted to a fallback model or throttled for short randomized windows. The circuit uses a low-disruption schedule (Poisson-based jitter + exponential backoff on repeated hits) so multiple tenants or regions don't cut over synchronously.
- Integration: instability score is exposed to the canary orchestrator as part of the evaluation result. Orchestrator mapping now supports action types: none, attenuation, canary-pause, full-rollback. Default policy for warn => attenuation; degrade => attenuation + notify.

Testing & validation: 
- Unit tests for hedger scoring math and entropy weighting.
- Synthetic integration tests that replay production-ish traffic traces with injected transient and sustained regressions to verify attenuation triggers vs rollback triggers.
- End-to-end smoke tests to validate orchestration actions and that traffic is routed correctly under attenuation.
- CI flaky test re-run: one integration test failed on first run (timing-dependent), re-run passed. Full pipeline green on final commit.

Operational notes: 
- New config flags added (perf_canary.hedger.slice_count, perf_canary.hedger.quantiles, perf_canary.circuit.base_attenuation_pct). Defaults are conservative and backwards compatible.
- Added a new dashboard tab `Hedger / Cutover` showing per-cohort instability score, recent slice quantiles heatmap, and attenuation action history.
- Runbook updated with guidance: for persistent degrade (instability > 0.6 for 10m) teams should follow the existing rollback playbook. Soft attenuation is intended as a transient mitigation.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implementation and unit tests
- [x] Integration tests (synthetic scenarios)
- [x] Dashboard and runbook updates
- [x] Feature flagged behind perf_canary.hedger.enabled (off in prod by default)

Risk / mitigation: 
- Risk: attenuation could mask real regressions. Mitigation: attenuation is accompanied by persistent telemetry and alerts; the hedger severity escalates to degrade for sustained issues.
- Risk: added compute overhead from quantile slicing. Mitigation: sampling rate and slice_count are configurable; hedger runs in a separate lightweight evaluation worker to avoid blocking the primary pipeline.

Merge outcome: squashed and merged once reviewers ran the integration harness in staging and CI was green.

Related work: references ENG-1947 for rollouts reliability story and ENG-1952 for attenuation policy spec.

Notes for reviewers: look for correctness in entropy weighting and the attenuation scheduling; pay attention to the test that re-ran in CI (integration/synthetic/cutover_schedule_test) and comment if the jitter constants need tuning.
Samir Patel (2024-11-05): Nice concise design. One ask: please document why we choose Poisson jitter for attenuation windows vs uniform jitter. Also add a small benchmark for hedger CPU overhead.
Maya Chen (2024-11-06): replied: Poisson jitter chosen to reduce chance of simultaneous alignment across cohorts; added micro-benchmark (hedger_benchmark) and documented reasoning in hedger.md.
Olivia Hart (2024-11-08): requested change: make default slice_count configurable via env var and lower default to 5. Verified in staging with sample traces.
Maya Chen (2024-11-09): addressed and pushed change, updated tests and CI config.

Context & motivation: We frequently see noisy regressions blocked by the gap between synthetic probes and actual production traffic shapes. This PR adds a traffic replica simulator that can replay sampled production slices into a canary instance (isolated test replicas) so detectors evaluate real-world query shapes, KV cache warmup, and user session patterns. It pairs that simulator with a human-friendly rollback playbook that consolidates detector outputs into a prioritized remediation checklist and recommended automated actions (circuit, throttle, fallback model, or immediate rollback).

What this PR delivers (high-level): 1) A lightweight traffic replica runtime (perf_canary/simulator) that consumes sampled request traces (ndjson) and replays them with configurable concurrency/temporal scaling and header-preserving semantics. 2) Integration hooks from existing canary detectors to the simulator so we can run offline and live replays as part of evaluation pipelines. 3) A rollback playbook (docs/playbooks/rollback.md) with templated pager messages, escalation steps, and automated rollback recipes that can be executed from the Console or via the CLI. 4) End-to-end unit and integration tests and a small infra change to grant the canary agent permissions for ephemeral replay resources.
