Context and motivation: This PR adds a lightweight, browser-first visual RAG flow designer aimed at product and developer teams who want to prototype retrieval-augmented generation pipelines and tool-calling interactions without spinning up a backend. The goal is to lower the barrier for experimentation: users can wire up a retriever, sketch prompt templates, attach simple tool stubs, and run end-to-end examples using a local LLM shim or Redwood hosted endpoints.

What this delivers: a new examples workspace (examples/visual-rag-workbench) with a React-based flow canvas, a minimal local shim (node) that emulates token streaming and function/tool call hooks, TypeScript SDK sample that demonstrates structured output + tool invocation, documentation pages in docs/rag/visual-workbench.md, and a short video/screenshot asset. The workbench emphasizes discoverability and repeatability: built-in prompt presets, a small set of example retrievers (memory, simple vector store backed by in-memory embeddings), and test prompts for regression checks.

Highlights: - Visual editor with nodes for retriever, prompt template, LLM, and tool. Nodes expose minimal config properties; the editor serializes to a JSON flow spec compatible with the TypeScript SDK runner. - TypeScript SDK example (packages/sdk-typescript/examples/visual-workbench.ts) showing how to load a flow spec, run a session against hosted or local runtime, and handle function/tool calls with typed inputs/outputs. - Local shim (examples/visual-rag-workbench/shim) that can be started with npm run dev and optionally points at Redwood hosted endpoints via env vars. The shim supports streaming and simulated latency to test UX under different SLOs. - Docs page with step-by-step quickstart, troubleshooting, and guidance on moving from prototype to a Dedicated deployment.

Checklist (what I changed and why): - New example project: examples/visual-rag-workbench (frontend + shim + sample data) - TypeScript SDK sample: packages/sdk-typescript/examples/visual-workbench.ts - Documentation: docs/rag/visual-workbench.md - Static assets: site/static/img/visual-workbench.png, site/static/video/visual-workbench-demo.mp4 (trimmed) - CI: added a playground workflow that boots the shim and runs smoke tests against the example (ci/workflows/playground-visual-workbench.yml) - Tests: integration smoke tests under examples/visual-rag-workbench/test/smoke that validate the flow serialization, tool call stub, and streaming token handling.

Compatibility & security notes: The shim intentionally runs in unprivileged mode and never persists customer secrets. Examples default to a sandboxed in-memory vector store. We added a doc subsection on how to swap the shim to call Redwood hosted endpoints with saved credentials (do not check in). The work intentionally does not change any runtime or production code paths.

How to try locally: 1) cd examples/visual-rag-workbench/frontend && npm install && npm run dev 2) cd ../shim && npm install && REDWOOD_API_KEY=... npm run dev 3) Open http://localhost:3000 and select the local runtime in the top-right. A set of sample flows and prompt presets are available. The README contains a one-line command to seed the sample index.

Testing & CI: The PR includes a lightweight CI job that launches the shim in a container, runs the smoke suite, and verifies the TypeScript example can run against the local endpoint. CI occasionally timed out on the first run due to test port collisions; I added a random port fallback and reran.

Related: ENG-4987 (prototype funding), DES-872 (UX validation), PM-324 (roadmap item for quickstarts).

Motivation: We observe periodic QoS regressions when tenant-specific batch caching config falls back too eagerly to compact quantized models during capacity pressure. This PR introduces a decision-layer (BatchCacheFallbackAdvisor) that uses short-window telemetry and a conservative unit-econ score to recommend safe fallback actions and quantization tiers per-tenant.

Summary of changes: introduces a lightweight advisor library, a CLI dry-run mode, a telemetry gating flag, and a small set of heuristics to avoid aggressive fallback that increases latency or harms output quality. This is intended as an intermediate safety net while we iterate on the full policy compiler.

What it does (high level):
- Adds pkg/econ/advisor: decision logic that computes a fallback recommendation for batch-cache eviction and quantization tier selection given recent latency, error-rate, and token-cost signals.
- Provides a tenant-scoped scoring function that balances unit-econ (tokens/second cost) and latency SLO risk.
- Exposes a new CLI: econctl suggest --tenant <id> --dry-run that returns recommended actions without applying them.
- Adds a telemetry gating toggle (enabled by default for canary) that prevents rollout unless we see stable metrics for 30m.
- Adds end-to-end smoke tests and a deterministic simulator for reviewer replay.

Checklist: [x] design doc linked inline, [x] unit tests added, [x] e2e smoke added, [x] docs updated, [x] telemetry dashboards updated, [x] canary gating enabled by default.

Backward compat: No changes to public API. The advisor is opt-in for existing tenant policies; the default behavior for tenants without explicit use remains unchanged. The CLI is purely additive.

Rollout plan: Merge to main, enable canary for 10% of tenants for 48h, monitor the prefilling/latency dashboards and the unit-econ score. If regressions appear, the advisor can be disabled with econ.advisor.enabled=false at runtime and queued for hotfix.

Related: ENG-4921 (safety gating), ENG-5012 (unit-econ telemetry).
Marco Chen: Can the advisor be configured to prefer low-latency fallback over cost savings for a tenant? Response: yes — added tenant-level override (prefer_latency bool) and documented precedence in policy_integration.go.
Leah Ortiz: e2e flakiness observed in CI, test seeds are non-deterministic. Author: fixed — deterministic seed added to simulator and test, and added a retry harness in CI for the smoke job.
Samir Gupta: Please add metrics for advisor decisions so we can audit why a fallback was chosen. Author: added advisor.decision_reason and advisor.score telemetry counters and updated dashboards.
Marco Chen: Suggest adding a kill-switch via feature flag for rapid rollback. Author: added econ.advisor.enabled gate; default true only for canary.
Leah Ortiz: small nits on docs wording and example outputs. Author: addressed and pushed doc edits.
Introduce a conservative BatchCacheFallbackAdvisor to provide tenant-scoped safe fallback recommendations and quant-tier heuristics; adds econctl dry-run; telemetry gating and advisor decision metrics for auditing. Rollout is canary-gated.
If tenant latency SLOs spike after rollout, toggle econ.advisor.enabled=false and open an incident with ENG-4921 tagged. Advisor emits advisor.decision_reason telemetry; use prefilling and unit-econ dashboards to troubleshoot.

Summary: Adds a small, focused example set and docs demonstrating best practices for tool-calling external connectors (HTTP APIs, webhooks, and database adaptors) from RAG agents and tool-calling flows. The goal is to give engineers a reference for safe external I/O: retries with jittered backoff, idempotency tokens, short-circuiting on known transient errors, authentication patterns (token rotation + KMS/HSM hints), and a lightweight local emulator for offline testing.

Motivation and context: We've seen multiple customer support threads and internal runbooks where integrations with downstream APIs cause silent duplicates, unbounded retries, or leakage of credentials during local development (see ENG-2345). This PR collects a minimal, copy-pasteable sample set plus docs to reduce integration time and avoid common pitfalls. It also feeds a quickstart entry on the docs site so users can find the pattern when wiring tool-calling into their agent.

What this PR includes (high-level):
- End-to-end examples: TypeScript and Python connector stubs showing authenticated calls, exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency header support, and circuit-breaker heuristics.
- Quickstart: docs/quickstart that walks from "hello connector" to running an agent that calls a mock external service.
- Local emulator: a tiny bash+node emulator for CI and local dev to simulate transient failures, 429 throttles, and slow responses.
- Tests: a basic integration smoke workflow (GitHub Actions) and a local script to exercise retry scenarios.
- Docs: two new docs pages added to redwood-docs (reference + tutorial) and the example README linking to the quickstart and emulator.

Commit summary:
- 0f3a9c2: initial skeleton of connectors example and README
- a1b7d55: add TypeScript example and devcontainer for quickstart dev loop
- d4c120b: add Python example and idempotency helper; add docs pages
- e2b44f6: add emulator script and GitHub Actions smoke workflow; wire quickstart link in docs nav

Files changed (high-level):
- redwood-examples/connectors/*: new example library and README + devcontainer
- redwood-docs/reference/tool-calling/connectors.md: new reference describing connector API patterns and recommended headers
- redwood-docs/tutorials/tool-calling-reliability.md: tutorial with stepwise instructions and sample prompts
- .github/workflows/connectors-smoke.yml: lightweight CI to run emulator + sample script

Notes on design decisions:
- Examples are intentionally minimal and opinionated: using explicit idempotency tokens (Idempotency-Key header) rather than opaque dedupe inside the agent. This maps well to common third-party APIs and avoids coupling agent internals to downstream semantics.
- Backoff uses decorrelated jitter (referenced in tutorial) with a configurable max attempts guard inside the connector helper.
- Auth examples show short-lived tokens and a rotation-ready placeholder that references KMS but does not require a KMS integration to run the quickstart emulator.

Testing and CI:
- CI: the new connectors-smoke workflow spins up the emulator container and runs the TypeScript sample end-to-end, asserting no duplicate invocations after simulated retries. The CI currently runs on PR and merges only after green checks.
- Local testing: devcontainer and integration_emulator.sh provide a reproducible dev loop that simulates 429/500/timeout behaviour.

Review conversation (excerpt):
- Samir Patel (reviewer): "Nice focused example. A couple of asks: 1) can we make the default retry attempts lower in CI to avoid long runs? 2) include a short note about when NOT to retry (e.g. 4xx with application-level errors)."
- Priya Nair (author): "Reply: lowered CI attempts to 3 and added explicit logic to opt-out retries for 4xx except 429. Added a paragraph and code comment on rationale."
- Diego Martinez (reviewer): "Can you add a short snippet for webhook signature verification? I often see customers miss this in quickstarts."
- Priya Nair: "Added a webhook_signature.md snippet and referenced it from the reference doc. Kept signature examples generic (HMAC) to avoid tying to a specific provider."
- Ava Chen (reviewer, docs): "Docs look good; small nit on naming (connector vs adapter). Suggested renaming one header for clarity."
- Priya Nair: "Applied rename and updated cross-references."
- CI: initial run failed due to flaky emulator start timing; fixed by adding a readiness probe in emulator and re-run succeeded.

Merge strategy: squash merge. The branch was squashed into a single commit at merge time and merged to main after approvals (2 approvals).

Backwards compatibility and risk: This change is purely additive: examples and docs only. No runtime or API surface changes to the platform. Marked breaking_change: false.

Follow-ups (recommended):
- Add a compact checklist in the console docs when teams enable tool-calling in prod: auth posture, rate limit policies, cost accounting per-tool.
- Expand emulator to simulate per-tenant quotas for future Dedicated/Private testing (follow-up ENG ticket created).

How to try locally (quickstart excerpt):
1) git clone && cd redwood-examples/connectors
2) ./integration_emulator.sh start (spins up local mock)
3) in another shell: devcontainer or npm run start:ts or python examples/connector_examples.py --target http://localhost:8081
4) Observe logs; run integration_emulator.sh simulate-throttle to test 429 backoff

If you want to review the implementation details, the docs page includes code excerpts and a suggested audit log pattern for connector invocations to help SRE and security teams reason about retries and duplicate suppression.

TL;DR: small, practical example set + docs that reduce the time-to-safe-integration for tool-calling external APIs.

Motivation: debugging RAG sessions and reproducing regressions is hard when tool calls, retrieval snapshots, and model nondeterminism are involved. This PR introduces a lightweight deterministic replay workbench and a compact session snapshot format (.ragsnap) that records retrieval results, tool-call logs, prompt scaffolding, model RNG seeds, and a minimal KV-cache fingerprint so teams can reliably replay and debug RAG runs locally or in a CI-backed replay runner. Summary of changes: 1) CLI: rag-snap record/replay commands to capture a live session from the local dev proxy and to replay it deterministically; 2) Replayer UI: a tiny single-page workbench that can load .ragsnap files and step through the session (prompt -> retrieval -> tool -> model tokens) with a timeline and inline diffs; 3) Example templates: two RAG templates (agent+tool-calling and plain retriever+generator) with annotated checkpoints and a sample session recorded against the sample index; 4) Telemetry hooks: optional linkage to Redwood Console snapshot IDs so telemetry traces can point to a replayable artifact; 5) Tests: smoke playback unit tests and an integration e2e that runs a recorded session headless in CI. Rationale: small, reproducible artifacts that include retrieval snapshots and deterministic seeds make root-cause analysis for hallucinations, regressions after kernel changes, and batching-induced behavior much faster. Migration notes: the new .ragsnap format is opt-in and lives in examples/recordings; it does not change any public API surfaces. Checklist: - [x] Implement CLI recorder + replayer - [x] Add SPA replayer UI and timeline view - [x] Add two annotated RAG templates with authoring notes - [x] Add tests and CI job (replay-smoke) - [x] Docsite page that explains how to record/replay and interpret snapshots - [x] Add telemetry links to console snapshots Files of interest and short explanation: examples/replay/sample-session.ragsnap captures a small user session against the sample index (used by the e2e); src/playground/replayer/* contains the UI and a compact playback engine; examples/templates/deterministic-agent.yaml and examples/templates/deterministic-retriever.yaml are the annotated quickstarts. Related: this complements ENG-1223 (replayable telemetry) and follows design notes in PM-452. Known limitations: large indices are not captured (we snapshot top-k retrieval results only), some external tool side effects are stubbed during record/replay (we capture tool outputs instead), and the current KV-cache fingerprint is minimal (future PR will include full token-level cache dumps for deep debugging).
Asha Patel (2026-02-20): Nice iteration; can you add a short note in the workbench UI indicating which parts are stubbed (retrieval vs external tool outputs)?
Sofia Nguyen (2026-02-20): Response: added a 'replay fidelity' banner to the UI and an inline tooltip that lists what was snapshot vs what is stubbed.

Sofia Nguyen (2026-02-22): Addressed: added --tolerance and exit codes, tightened timing by driving playback off explicit event timestamps; pushed fix (commit c4d9a22).

payload.body:
## Context
We need a reliable, repeatable live-demo artifact that SEs can run (and re-run) in the demo tenant without hand-editing prompts or copy/pasting curl commands. This PR adds a small "Sales Demo App" that showcases: (1) chat completions w/ streaming, (2) structured output (JSON schema) and validation, (3) tool calling, and (4) retry + basic failure-mode handling so we can keep a demo moving.

This is intended to back the "Core API demo" scenario in the demo tenant: a single command runs the same scripted flow, and we can show the expected outputs in the UI/terminal to make regressions obvious.

## What’s included
- New demo app under `apps/sales-demo/` (TypeScript + Node) with a minimal web UI and a CLI scenario runner.
- Scenario runner (`pnpm demo:run --scenario <name>`) that executes a deterministic sequence:
  - Streaming chat completion (token streaming to terminal + optional SSE to UI)
  - Tool call: `lookup_order_status(order_id)` (local stub, deterministic)
  - Tool call: `get_weather(city)` (local stub, deterministic)
  - Structured output: returns a JSON object conforming to a provided schema (validated at runtime)
- "Golden" expected outputs captured per scenario (stable snapshots) + a `--update-goldens` mode for controlled refresh.
- Small set of scenarios mapped to the standard talk track:
  - `01-core-chat-streaming`
  - `02-tool-calling-order-lookup`
  - `03-structured-output-triage-json`
  - `04-retries-and-timeouts` (simulates transient 5xx + reconnect; does not rely on real outages)
- Configuration for demo stability:
  - Supports pinning `REDWOOD_DEMO_MODEL` and `REDWOOD_DEMO_MODEL_VERSION` (defaults align with the demo tenant pinned route name, not a moving catalog alias)
  - Single place to set `REDWOOD_API_KEY`, `REDWOOD_BASE_URL`, `REDWOOD_PROJECT_ID`
- Guardrails:
  - Refuses to run if pointed at a non-demo base URL unless `ALLOW_NON_DEMO=1` is explicitly set.
  - Redacts API keys from logs.

## Why native SDK vs OpenAI-compatible endpoint
We use the native Redwood SDK client here to avoid drift in parameter naming and to make it easier to highlight Redwood-only features (structured output helpers + tool call ergonomics). The CLI exposes an `--openai-compat` flag as a follow-up idea, but it is not implemented in this PR to keep scope tight.

## File/area summary
- `apps/sales-demo/`
  - `src/server.ts`: minimal web server + SSE streaming bridge
  - `src/scenarios/*.ts`: scenario scripts (single responsibility, deterministic)
  - `src/tools/*.ts`: tool definitions and stubs (order lookup, weather)
  - `src/structured/schema.ts`: JSON schema + runtime validator
  - `src/redwood/client.ts`: SDK client wrapper + retries/backoff
  - `src/goldens/*.jsonl`: expected outputs (line-delimited JSON events)
- `apps/sales-demo/README.md`: run instructions + talk-track mapping
- Root changes:
  - `pnpm-workspace.yaml`: add the app to workspace
  - `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: run lint/typecheck/unit tests for the new app

## How to run (SE quick path)
1) `pnpm i`
2) `cd apps/sales-demo`
3) `export REDWOOD_API_KEY=...` (scoped demo key)
4) `export REDWOOD_BASE_URL=https://api.demo.redwoodinference.com` (demo env)
5) `pnpm demo:run --scenario 01-core-chat-streaming`

## Determinism notes
- We set `temperature=0` and fixed `seed` where supported.
- Prompts are designed to be stable and avoid long-form free generation.
- Golden outputs assert on structure (event types + required fields + schema validity). We do NOT assert exact token-by-token text for streaming events to avoid flakiness.

## Tests
- Unit tests for:
  - Structured output validation
  - Tool call dispatch (ensures tool args match expected schema)
  - Retry/backoff behavior (fake timers)
- CI: `pnpm -C apps/sales-demo lint && pnpm -C apps/sales-demo test && pnpm -C apps/sales-demo typecheck`

## Screenshots / demo notes
No screenshots in this PR. The UI is intentionally minimal; primary demo path is CLI + optional browser view for exec-friendly viewing.

## Follow-ups
- Add a small "scenario index" page with one-click run + copy-to-clipboard outputs.
- Add optional OpenAI-compatible transport mode for customers who want drop-in testing.
- Wire this into the demo tenant reset to automatically run 1-2 scenarios and populate Console traces.

Examples repo only; no product release notes.

Motivation: Teams repeatedly ask for a low-friction way to author and iterate on RAG agent tool-calling flows locally without spinning up the full infra or writing lots of boilerplate. Summary of changes: 1) new example 'vscode-rag-authoring' extension that provides commands: 'RAG: Start Local Sandbox', 'RAG: Run Step', 'RAG: Replay Session' and an inline lint panel with rules for malformed tool schemas and mismatched tool-call signatures; 2) presets under redwood-quickstarts/rag-presets/ — streaming-min-latency, batch-cost-optimized, and dev-prototyping which wire up example prompts, a lightweight local vector store mock, and eval harness snippets; 3) docs and quickstart page updates in redwood-examples/docs/rag-authoring-presets.md with screenshots and a troubleshooting section; 4) test harness updates (playwright smoke + unit tests) and CI integration. Implementation notes: - The VSCode extension is implemented as a thin shim that talks to the existing local sandbox runner in examples/sandbox via HTTP on a random ephemeral port. It intentionally avoids shipping heavy native dependencies; the local runner remains the single source of truth for sandbox behavior. - Lint rules are small JSON-schema-based checks with a few JS helper rules (tool-signature checks, required-example prompts, detection of immediate-looping action patterns). They run in the extension and as a CLI check (npm run rag-lint). - Presets are authored as plain YAML files and include a small metadata block that the extension reads to populate the preset picker. Motivation: teams building RAG systems often need to iterate on indexes continuously as new documents arrive (changefeeds, user uploads, streaming sources). Existing quickstarts demonstrate one-off ingestion into a vector DB but lack a small, repeatable CLI and notebook workflow for incremental indexing, local testing, and schema drift debugging. This PR introduces a lightweight CLI tool, a set of incremental-index notebook templates (Python) and a complementary TypeScript example that integrates the CLI with a running agent for tool-calling and reindex-on-demand. The goal is to provide a minimal, production-adjacent pattern for: 1) running idempotent upserts into an index, 2) emitting compact diff telemetry for indexing jobs, and 3) safe rollbacks when embeddings or encoding pipelines change. What this PR contains: - lightweight CLI: tools/incremental_index_cli.py (Python), minimal flags for --source, --batch-size, --dry-run, --checkpoint-file, and --embed-model to make it easy to script in CI and notebooks - notebook templates: notebooks/incremental_index_playbook.ipynb (annotated tutorial for data scientists showing incremental runs, checkpoint inspection, and KV cache warmup) - TypeScript example: examples/ts-incremental-watcher/ that listens for file additions and hits the CLI using child_process and demonstrates tool-calling from an agent to trigger upstream reindex and patching metadata - docs page: docs/quickstarts/incremental-indexing.md with interactive steps, recommended runtimes, and observability knobs (how to expose token-level cost in console, suggested canary prompts) - tests and smoke harness: tests/integration/test_incremental_index.sh and a small fixture data set under examples/fixtures/ - README changes and local-run scripts for CI and dev loop Checklist: - [x] CLI implementation and argument parsing - [x] Notebook template with explanatory narrative - [x] TypeScript watcher example and README - [x] Docs page and quickstart sidebar link - [x] Basic integration smoke test - [x] Added Linear links and changelog blurb Notes on design decisions: - The CLI uses a compact checkpoint file (JSONL with last-processed id and cursor token) to keep the implementation filesystem-first and runnable in air-gapped installs (aligns with Redwood Private needs). - We intentionally avoid introducing a new DB dependency; the examples work with in-memory sqlite for the notebook and provide guidance for Milvus/Weaviate/Redis in the docs. - The TS watcher intentionally shells out to the CLI to show how teams can decouple the indexing control plane from the embedding workers (mirrors some production patterns). Related: ENG-1120 (batching improvements) and ENG-1299 (observability probes).

Motivation: teams repeatedly ask for a lightweight, replayable local playground to iterate on retrieval-augmented generation prompts, tool-calling behavior, and agent orchestration without spinning up full infra. This PR introduces `rag-sim`, an interactive CLI 'simulation shell' that lets authors run stepwise scenarios, inject fake tool responses, snapshot sessions, and export deterministic seeds for CI/eval pipelines.

What this PR does: adds a small TypeScript CLI shim and example playbooks that emulate the Redwood runtime semantics (context window simulation, KV cache warmup stub, and streaming output). The shell supports step, run, rewind, and patch commands so developers can test partial tool failures and fallback logic quickly. Sessions can be exported as JSON or a compact replay script that our e2e harness can consume. The goal is low-friction iteration for authoring and regression tests; this is intended as examples/dev tooling only (not for production serving).

Checklist:
- [x] Implement CLI core loop and command parser
- [x] Add tool stub interface and example tool responses
- [x] Add three authored playbooks demonstrating common failure modes (retrieval miss, tool timeout, malformed tool output)
- [x] Documentation quickstart under docs/quickstarts/rag-sim-shell.md with screenshots and step-by-step commands
- [x] Unit tests for CLI command parsing and replay export
- [x] CI workflow to run smoke replay scenarios on PRs

Usage (short): `npx @redwood/rag-sim playbooks/example-localsearch.yml --export session1.json` then `npx @redwood/rag-sim replay session1.json --stepwise`. The README includes more examples and a sample Linear link for the test scenarios.

Commits summary: three commits - initial CLI scaffold and parser; add tool-stubs + three example playbooks; docs, tests, and CI workflow. See changed files below.

Why this is different: instead of a full SDK change, this is a focused dev-oriented sandbox that mimics runtime decision points (cache hits, batching signals, and tool fallbacks) so prompt authors and solutions engineers can iterate without heavy infra. It also provides deterministic exports to improve flaky-eval reproducibility.

Risks and mitigation: the CLI vends no production credentials and uses only local stubs by default. We added linting, typechecks, and a small smoke CI to catch regressions.

Related: ENG-3421 (authoring ergonomics), PM-58 (playbook templates).
Add `rag-sim` interactive CLI for stepwise RAG authoring and local debugging; includes examples, docs, and CI smoke tests.
Diego Alvarez: Nice idea — can we make the export schema stable (versioned) so CI won't break?
Maya Chen (author reply): Export includes a top-level `version` field; updated exporter and bumped tests to validate version header.
Priya Natarajan: Should we warn users when a playbook references a model key that might require hosted credentials?
Maya Chen (author reply): The CLI now emits a clear warning and refuses to forward requests; playbooks in examples use stubbed model configs only.
Jonah Park: lgtm pending small nits (typo in README and missing test for rewind command)
Maya Chen (author reply): Fixed README typos and added a unit test for rewind; reran CI.
Run `npm ci && npm run build` then execute `npx @redwood/rag-sim --help`; run `npx @redwood/rag-sim playbooks/example-tool-timeout.yml --stepwise` to reproduce the timeout scenario. CI smoke workflow path: .github/workflows/rag-sim-smoke.yml.

payload.body:
Motivation: provide a compact, developer-friendly CLI sandbox for rapid RAG experimentation that emphasizes stepwise debugging and minimal production friction. This PR introduces miniRAG: a zero-config CLI that wires a lightweight local indexer, a mock retriever, and a typesafe tool-stub system to demonstrate tool-calling workflows and telemetry capture probes. The target audience is product engineers and SDK consumers who want a reproducible, local-first RAG loop with clear debugging hooks.

What this PR delivers (high level):
- A CLI scaffold (bin/minirag) with subcommands: init, ingest, query, replay, and probe.
- Typesafe tool stubs (TS + Go examples) showing how to declare tool interfaces and wire results into prompts safely.
- Capture probes: a small telemetry format and runtime hooks that record prefix cache hits, retriever latencies, and model token counts to JSONL for later inspection.
- A minimal local indexer based on sqlite and a fast in-memory vector shim for demos.
- Integration tests (smoke and stepwise debug tests) and a CI workflow for the example.
- Docs and a short quickstart page on the docs site (docs/site/minirag.md) with copy-paste commands.

Why this is different: unlike our full RAG quickstarts that focus on web SDKs or devcontainers, miniRAG is intentionally CLI-first and minimal: it should run with Node 18 (or Go toolchain), no Docker required, and be useful for rapid iteration in CI or local scripts. The emphasis on capture probes is to make it easier to teach and debug production regressions by recording compact, structured traces tied to specific queries.

Compatibility and constraints:
- Works with Redwood local dev API or the hosted API (env var switch).
- Typesafe stubs compile in TS projects that use our SDK types; the Go example is intentionally small and uses explicit interfaces rather than codegen.
- Not intended for production scale; indexer is ephemeral for demos.

Runbook (how to try locally):
1) git clone && cd redwood-examples/minirag-cli
2) npm ci && npm run build (or go build for the Go sample)
3) ./bin/minirag init --example-samples
4) ./bin/minirag ingest ./examples/sample-docs --index sqlite://./data/minirag.db
5) ./bin/minirag query "Explain token routing in Redwood" --probe out/probes.jsonl
6) ./bin/minirag replay out/probes.jsonl --stepwise (replays per-probe with timings)

Testing and CI: the PR adds an integration test that runs the CLI in a temporary directory and validates that probes include expected fields. CI workflow runs lint, unit tests, integration smoke, and a quick e2e that uses the hosted API with a mocked key.

Docs and teaching notes: the docs/site/minirag.md contains a 5-minute walkthrough, a troubleshooting section for common environment issues, and a short section on how to convert probe output into a CSV for quick analysis.

Checklist:
- [x] CLI scaffold and commands implemented
- [x] Typesafe TS tool stubs + Go tool example
- [x] Capture probe runtime + JSONL spec
- [x] Smoke integration tests and CI workflow
- [x] Quickstart docs and troubleshooting
- [x] Demo scripts for local replay

Related work: ties to ENG-4821 (debuggable RAG prototypes) and a small intersection with the telemetry team for the probe format. This is purposely conservative in the telemetry surface; probes capture only non-sensitive operational metadata by default.

Notes for reviewers: focus on ergonomics of the CLI commands, the clarity of the probe format (docs included), and the tightness of the types in the TS tool stubs. The Go example is intentionally explicit to avoid heavy dependencies. If approved we'll follow up with a short blog-style tutorial and a lightweight Playground integration that reuses the probe format.
Liam O'Connor: Nice focused example. Can we make the probe format backwards-compatible with the existing telemetry proto? I don't want a proliferation of ad hoc formats.
Maya Chen: Good point — probe format is intentionally orthogonal and documented; added a migration section in docs/site/minirag.md recommending a small adapter script. Also added a reference to the telemetry proto in the header comments.
Priya Sinha: Integration test flaked once in CI; could you add a retry for the network call in the e2e?
Maya Chen: Added a small retry and a shorter timeout; test is now deterministic in local runs and CI.

Summary: This PR adds a small, opinionated Go quickstart that demonstrates building a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) micro-playground using the Go SDK, typed tool contracts, and a local dev runner with built-in telemetry probes. Motivation: we have many TS/Python examples; several customers and internal SDK advocates asked for a concise Go-first example that focuses on: 1) typed tool calling with contract validation, 2) a minimal local runner for fast feedback loops (no cloud infra required), and 3) lightweight telemetry hooks that show what to surface in Redwood Console. What changed (high level): - new example: examples/go/rag-playground/ containing README, main.go, tool_contracts.go, dev-runner (small binary stub), and sample dataset - docs: docs/examples/go-rag-quickstart.md added to the docs site tree - tests: integration smoke test that runs the dev-runner against a seeded in-memory index - CI: workflow updated to run Go example smoke tests on linux-amd64 Scope & trade-offs: This example intentionally keeps things small: it uses a tiny in-memory vector store and a mock tool (webhook echo) rather than production connectors. The goal is developer onboarding rather than production readiness. Checklist: - [x] Add example code + README with step-by-step local run instructions - [x] Add typed tool contract definitions and contract linter config - [x] Add smoke test and CI job - [x] Add docs site page and quickstart guide - [x] Add telemetry probe examples and wiring Usage: See examples/go/rag-playground/README.md for step-by-step instructions. Typical flow: 1) go run ./examples/go/rag-playground/main.go --local-index 2) open the dev-runner web UI at http://localhost:8080 to send prompts and inspect prefix cache / telemetry 3) use ./scripts/seed-index to load sample docs Commits (summary): - init: add go module and example scaffold - feature: main runner and typed tool contracts - test: add smoke tests and fixtures - docs: add quickstart page and images - ci: add workflow for go-examples Smoke test notes: The smoke test instantiates the dev-runner with a deterministic seed and asserts that: - a simple query returns 3 retrieval hits - the tool call mock responds with a 200 echo - telemetry events (request.start, retrieval.complete, generation.complete) are emitted to a local file sink (used by the smoke test) Local development steps (condensed): 1) Install Go 1.21+ 2) cd examples/go/rag-playground && go run ./main.go --dev 3) In another terminal run: curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/query -d '{"q":"what is redwood inference"}' Example snippet (from main.go): "// small example: create client and run a retrieval-augmented prompt
client := redwood.NewClient(os.Getenv(\"REDWOOD_API_KEY\"))
resp, _ := client.Generate(ctx, &redwood.GenerateRequest{Model: \"rw-compact-1\", Prompt: prompt})
fmt.Println(resp.Text)" Related: ENG-1042 (Go SDK ergonomics) and internal examples backlog. Migration/rollout: This is additive. No infra changes required. Follow-ups: - Add an example showing dedicated/private deployment wiring - Expand the dev-runner to optionally persist telemetry to a mock console - Add interactive web UI for tool-call inspection
Add a compact Go RAG playground that demonstrates Go SDK usage, typed tool contracts, local telemetry probes, and an offline dev runner for iterative debugging.

Marta Kozlowski (author): Good call — switched to a build target and removed prebuilt binary artifact; updated README.
Asha Patel (reviewer): Typedefs in tool_contracts.go look great. One nit: add an example of how to handle contract validation errors in the README.
Marta Kozlowski (author): Added a short FAQ section showing contract validation handling and best-practice suggestion to retry with a cleaned payload.

Motivation: Provide a compact, platform-agnostic quickstart that demonstrates how to bind external tools into RAG-style agents across Node, Go, and a lightweight WASM runner. This playground helps engineers validate tool contracts quickly and iteratively without setting up complex infra. What this PR adds: a self-contained playground under quickstarts/cross-toolbinding with three language adapters (ts, go, wasm), a small contract verifier that runs schema checks against tool responses, telemetry probe hooks that emit compact spans/events for the Redwood Console, and lightweight e2e smoke scripts. Checklist: 1) Add docs and README with quickstart instructions; 2) Provide typed contract schema + verifier binary and npm package wrapper; 3) Add CI smoke job that runs language adapters and verifier in CI; 4) Add example prompt sets and sample index for a toy corpus. Usage summary: checkout, cd quickstarts/cross-toolbinding, run ./scripts/bootstrap.sh to install local adapters, then run npm run dev:ts or go run ./adapters/go/main.go or ./wasm/runner to see tool-calling flow; the verifier will produce a compact contract report in logs. Links: Linear ENG-1287; Support ticket SUP-2211 for telemetry expectations. Notes: the playground is intentionally small (no production infra); telemetry hooks use the console-instrumentation shim with opt-in env var REDWOOD_TELEMETRY=1.
Add new cross-platform quickstart that demonstrates typed tool bindings, live contract verification, telemetry probes, and example integrations for Node/Go/TS. No breaking changes.
Local smoke: ./scripts/bootstrap.sh; npm run dev:ts; go run ./adapters/go/main.go; ./verifier/bin/verifier --schema=verifier/schema/tool.json --input=sample_response.json; CI smoke job replicates these steps in a containerized environment

payload.body:
## Summary
This refactors the existing RAG example to align with the new Quickstart template retriever abstraction and error handling patterns. Goal is to keep examples and templates consistent so users don’t learn one-off patterns from the examples.

Key changes:
- Introduce `Retriever` interface usage in the example (mirrors template `retriever` contract)
- Replace ad-hoc exceptions with standardized error types + taxonomy mapping
- Normalize “empty retrieval” behavior (don’t silently answer without sources unless explicitly configured)
- Add minimal tracing/log conventions (request id passthrough + span names) so troubleshooting matches docs

## Motivation / Context
Templates are shipping a shared retriever interface + error taxonomy. The current RAG example has:
- Tight coupling to a specific vector store implementation
- Inconsistent failure modes (empty results returns 200 with hallucinated answer)
- Non-standard logging and no correlation id propagation

This PR updates the example so it stays in lockstep with template conventions.

## Design notes
### Retriever contract
The example now depends on a small interface:
- `retrieve(query, *, top_k, filters) -> List[RetrievedChunk]`
- `RetrievedChunk` includes `text`, `source_id`, `score`, and optional `metadata`

Vector store specifics live behind an adapter.

### Error handling
The example now uses a template-style taxonomy:
- `RetrievalConfigError` (misconfiguration / missing index)
- `RetrievalTimeoutError`
- `RetrievalEmptyResultError`
- `RetrievalBackendError` (unexpected vector store failure)

User-facing behavior:
- Empty retrieval returns a structured error by default with a “how to fix” hint
- Optional `ALLOW_EMPTY_RETRIEVAL=true` keeps prior behavior for folks demoing quickly

### Observability
Adds:
- Span `rag.retrieve` with attributes: `rag.top_k`, `rag.filter_applied` (boolean), `rag.result_count`
- Log fields: `redwood.request_id` (if present), `rag.query_hash` (no raw query)

## Implementation
Commits:
- `c1a0d7b` examples/rag: add retriever interface adapter scaffolding
- `5e3b2c1` examples/rag: switch query path to use retriever + chunk normalization
- `df2129e` examples/rag: add standardized errors + empty result behavior
- `aa8bd41` examples/rag: add basic tracing/log fields and redaction guard
- `b4a81f3` docs: update README and troubleshooting section

Changed areas (high-level):
- `examples/rag/`:
  - `retriever.py` / `retriever.ts` adapter wiring (depending on example flavor)
  - `rag_pipeline.*` updated to call `retriever.retrieve(...)`
  - error mapping + user-facing messages
- `examples/rag/README.md` updated to match template language and troubleshooting

Illustrative snippet (Python):

Old:
- Call vector store client directly in pipeline; empty results fall through.

New:
- `chunks = retriever.retrieve(query, top_k=top_k, filters=filters)`
- `if not chunks and not allow_empty: raise RetrievalEmptyResultError("No relevant chunks found", hint="Run ingest step or verify INDEX_PATH")`

## Test plan
- `make lint` / `make typecheck`
- `pytest -k rag` (covers empty retrieval + backend error mapping)
- Manual:
  - Run ingest
  - Query known doc
  - Query nonsense string (validate empty retrieval error)

## Screenshots / Output
- Included updated terminal output in README showing empty retrieval error text and remediation.

## Follow-ups
- Once templates land TS retriever adapters, we should port the TS example fully to the shared package instead of duplicating helper types here.

Refs:
- Linear: ENG-4182 (RAG+agent template), ENG-4187 (config schema/validation)
- Related: redwood-quickstarts PR-105 (retriever interface + adapters)
- RAG example now uses the same Retriever abstraction as the Quickstart templates
- Standardized error taxonomy + user-facing messages for common retrieval failures
- Added basic instrumentation hooks (spans + log fields) consistent with template conventions
Monica Patel (review): This looks aligned with the template contract. Two asks: (1) please ensure we never log raw user queries; (2) can we make empty retrieval behavior explicit in README so users don’t think it’s a model failure.

Sabrina James (author): Good call. I swapped raw query logging to `rag.query_hash` and added a note in README under Troubleshooting + an env var section for `ALLOW_EMPTY_RETRIEVAL`.

Allison Grant (review): For spans, `rag.result_count` is fine, but please avoid any per-document IDs as span attributes (cardinality). Also, can you rename span to `rag.retrieval` to match convention used in the templates?

Sabrina James (author): Updated: span is now `rag.retrieval`, removed `source_id` attribute entirely, and kept only booleans + counts.

Wei Chen (review): README wording: can we match the docs phrasing (“retrieval returned 0 chunks”) and link to the ingest step earlier? Also add a short section on what to do when `INDEX_PATH` is missing.

Sabrina James (author): Updated README to match phrasing and moved ingest instructions up. Added a dedicated troubleshooting bullet for missing index.

Monica Patel (approval): LGTM after latest push. Thanks for keeping behavior compatible via the env flag.

Allison Grant (approval): Approved. Attributes look safe now.

Wei Chen (approval): Approved.

Motivation: Mobile-first teams frequently ask for a compact, battery-friendly reference for building retrieval-augmented agents on Android/iOS using Kotlin Multiplatform. This PR adds a small set of opinionated examples and an accompanying docs quickstart that demonstrate: 1) performing client-side retrieval with an incremental index, 2) calling external tools (calendar, web-search shim) via a lightweight tool-calling adapter over WebSocket, 3) streaming and resumable responses (partial-response resume), and 4) offline-first UX patterns (local cache + optimistic UI).

What this PR includes (single continuous description): Adds a Kotlin Multiplatform mobile sample (android/ios targets) named "mobile-rag-lite" that contains a compact runtime binding to the Redwood API, a Ktor-based WebSocket tool-bridge shim (server example), and a Quickstart doc under docs/quickstarts/mobile-rag-lite.md. The quickstart walks through creating an incremental vector index using the embedded store, wiring the client to call the Redwood hosted API, and wiring tool-calls (calendar and http-search) that are proxied through a tiny Node/Ktor shim for demo purposes. The example emphasizes low-power batching, token-aware timeouts, and fallback policies for flaky networks.

Checklist: - [x] Kotlin Multiplatform sample scaffold (android + ios simulator) - [x] Compact SDK binding (Kotlin) that mirrors Redwood client call patterns - [x] Tool-calling adapter sample (WebSocket + HTTP bridge) - [x] Quickstart docs + runbook for CI smoke tests - [x] Unit tests for adapter and index helpers - [x] Telemetry hooks example (metric counters + session traces) - [x] Licence and README updated

Commit summary: "Initial kotlin multiplatform scaffold and samples" (adds the project structure and core bindings), "Add ws tool-bridge and demo server" (Ktor and Node examples used for local dev), "Quickstart docs and runbook" (docs + CI smoke definitions), "Fix telemetry and timeouts based on review feedback".

Changed areas (high level): - mobile-rag-lite/ (new KMM project with sample app, README and tests) - tools/ws-tool-bridge/ (Ktor server + minimal Node shim for quickstart) - docs/quickstarts/mobile-rag-lite.md (step-by-step quickstart) - docs/snippets/kotlin-bindings.md (API snippets and usage patterns) - .github/workflows/mobile-smoke.yml (CI smoke runner that uses Android emulator and iOS simulator stubs) - samples/testdata/inc-index/ (small seed corpus and test prompts) - license/ NOTICE updates

Small illustrative snippet (inlined for reviewers): "// client: perform incremental index upsert
val idx = LocalIndex.open(context)
idx.upsert("doc-1", text = "Release notes for Q1")
val emb = redwoodClient.embeddings.embedText("user query")
val hits = idx.search(emb, topK = 4)
val prompt = PromptBuilder.withContext(hits).withUser("What changed in Q1?")
redwoodClient.chat.stream(prompt, onDelta = { delta -> render(delta) })"

Review conversation (summary as a single continuous string): Reviewer Ethan Ross: "Nice compact layout — main ask is to make the tool bridge auth optional and document the security caveats. Also please avoid shipping demo API keys in the repo." Author reply (Priya): "Updated to require a local .env for demo keys and added a clear SECURITY.md section in the tool-bridge explaining KMS/HSM options for Private deployments. Removed all placeholder keys." Reviewer Marina Kovács: "Please add a short paragraph in the quickstart about batching and token-based timeouts for mobile networks." Author reply: "Added a dedicated section 'Mobile batching and timeouts' with recommended defaults and links to Optimize tooling." Reviewer Jonah Li: "CI flakes on emulator boot seen in run 2, can we shorten emulator setup and run a headless smoke mode?" Author reply: "Added emulator warmup in workflow and a headless smoke path; tests moved to parallel jobs to reduce timeouts." Ethan follow-up: "Approved after the docs and security notes landed."

CI summary and checks: - unit-tests (Kotlin): pass - lint (ktlint + detekt): pass - docs-spellcheck: pass - smoke-mobile (emulator): pass after wobble fix - e2e-sample-toolbridge: flaky-> rerun-> pass

Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main once reviewers approved and CI green. Release notes: "Add Kotlin mobile RAG quickstart and tool-calling adapter (mobile-rag-lite). Includes KMM sample app, WS tool bridge demo, and quickstart docs describing offline-first indexing and tool-calling patterns."

How to run locally (condensed): 1) cd mobile-rag-lite && ./gradlew :app:installDebug to launch Android sample (or use ios simulator target). 2) Start tools/ws-tool-bridge with LOCAL_DEMO_KEYS set and run npm run dev in node-shim for the HTTP tool proxies. 3) Follow docs/quickstarts/mobile-rag-lite.md for stepwise guide including index seeding and telemetry toggles.

Notes for maintainers: The Kotlin binding is intentionally compact and mirrors the JS/TS SDK ergonomics — keep parity but prefer idiomatic KMP naming. Telemetry hooks are pluggable via a MetricsAdapter interface. This PR purposely avoids shipping production auth for the bridge and documents recommended production deployments (Private controller + KMS).
Ethan Ross: Make tool bridge auth optional and document security caveats; do not commit demo keys.
Priya Patel: Removed placeholder keys and added SECURITY.md and env requirement for local demos.
Marina Kovács: Add mobile batching and token timeout guidance in quickstart.
Priya Patel: Added 'Mobile batching and timeouts' section with defaults and monitoring pointers.
Jonah Li: CI emulator flake; suggest headless smoke mode and faster warmup.
Priya Patel: Implemented headless smoke path and emulator warmup job; tests split to parallel jobs.
Add lightweight Kotlin Multiplatform mobile RAG quickstart (mobile-rag-lite) with a compact tool-calling adapter and quickstart docs. Useful for teams prototyping mobile agents and offline-first UX patterns.
This is intended as a reference implementation — keep the bridge intentionally minimal. Security doc outlines production hardening; please review the SECURITY.md section in tools/ws-tool-bridge. Perf knobs for mobile batching live in shared/config/NetworkConfig.kt.

Motivation: Dedicated customers need a predictable minimum throughput commitment even under transient overloads without sacrificing overall cluster efficiency. This PR introduces the Throughput Safeguard Controller (TSC) plus a throttle-orchestration layer that coordinates soft-throttles, capacity reclaims, and short-term headroom loans across fleet partitions. Design summary: TSC maintains per-tenant SLA windows (configurable percentiles and durations) and computes a minimal commit rate that must be enforced by request routers. Throttle-orchestration is an async coordinator that applies soft-throttles first, then issues temporary headroom loans from warm pools, and finally triggers proportional reclaimed tokens from low-util tenants when outages are imminent. Implementation notes: adds a new controller pkg/controller/safeguard with a reconciler loop, protobuf for the SafeguardPolicy CRD, scheduler hooks into pkg/routing to enforce policy tokens, new telemetry metrics (safeguard_committed_rps, safeguard_throttle_events_total, safeguard_loaned_tokens), and a fair reclaim algorithm implemented in pkg/fleet/reclaimer.go. Config knobs: policy.percentile, policy.window_seconds, policy.min_commit_rps, policy.max_loan_duration_ms, reclaim_threshold_percent. Migration: default policies are disabled; operators can enable per-tenant via Console or CLI. Rollout: feature-flag gated, will be enabled for 10% of Dedicated clusters for canary then ramp. Tests: unit tests for controller logic, integration tests that simulate overloads and assert commit guarantees, stress benchmark added to benchmark-lab harness. Related: Linear ENG-1980, ENG-2034. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Telemetry dashboards added - [x] Docs and Console knobs - [x] Feature flag gating - [x] Manual canary plan
Arjun Patel: Can we avoid global locks in the reconciler? Please see inline suggestion to use tenant-scoped caches.
Maya Chen: Switched to tenant-scoped caches in latest commit b8e2d4f, added metrics to show reconciliation latency.
Sofia Rivera: Telemetry looks good, can we add a histogram for loan duration?
Maya Chen: Added safeguard_loan_duration_ms histogram and dashboard tile.
Liam O'Connor: Integration test flaked once on CI due to timing, recommend adding a retry with backoff in the test harness.
Maya Chen: Added retry/backoff and increased timeouts, CI run green.

Motivation: teams building RAG flows need a reproducible way to evaluate telemetry signal fidelity (token-level traces, tool-call boundaries, index access markers) against ingestion cost and query latency. This PR adds a compact "playground" that demonstrates three telemetry fidelity presets (minimal, standard, verbose), a fidelity matrix document describing recommended signals and retention, and small adapter shims to wire the playground into TS and Python quickstarts.

What I changed: added a telemetry fidelity matrix doc under examples/playground/telemetry, a headless playground runner that spins up a local RAG sandbox with an instrumented proxy, TypeScript and Python adapter examples with run.sh and README snippets, and a small smoke CI job that validates telemetry events are emitted for each preset. The playground intentionally keeps dependencies minimal and uses an in-memory index for quick iteration.

Checklist: - [x] Add fidelity matrix and guidance docs - [x] Add playground runner and adapters (TS + Python) - [x] Add smoke CI job and fixture data - [x] Add examples to docs navigation (redwood-docs PR link in comments) - [x] Unit tests for telemetry probe helpers

How to use (quick): 1) cd examples/playground/telemetry 2) ./run_playground.sh --preset=standard 3) open http://localhost:3456/playground to run scripted scenarios or use the CLI runner: ./playground_cli.py --scenario=tool-fallback 4) Inspect emitted events in ./telemetry/out/{preset}.json or stream to a local endpoint.

Why this is unique: many existing quickstarts show RAG tool-calling and authoring; we lacked a small reproducible harness for telemetry cost/benefit experiments. This playground is intentionally opinionated: it captures a minimal set of signals by default and provides clear knobs to increase fidelity so engineers can reason about token-level costs vs. observability.

Related: Linear ENG-2143 (telemetry presets research), ENG-2209 (playground CI). Also references a companion docs PR on redwood-docs to add a short authoring guide and a telemetry best-practices sidebar (link posted in reviewer comments).
Added a new RAG telemetry fidelity matrix and a small playground with adapters for TypeScript and Python. This introduces telemetry presets and sample probes to help teams tune metrics cost vs. signal tradeoffs without instrumenting production workloads.
Liam Chen (reviewer): Nice work, Maya. Can you reduce the default verbose preset retention window? Token traces balloon quickly and can confuse new users.
Maya Ortega (author): Good point, reduced verbose preset retention from 7d to 24h and added a note in the fidelity matrix about cost impact.
Anika Rao (reviewer): The TS adapter uses a small local WebSocket shim. Please add an example of streaming telemetry events in the README.
Maya Ortega (author): Added a streaming example and a small helper script to convert events to CSV for quick inspection.
Diego Martinez (reviewer): CI job failed on first run due to flaky test 'test_probe_backpressure' — looks like a timing assumption in the test. Please add retries or use a deterministic fixture.
Maya Ortega (author): Reworked the test to use deterministic fixtures and exponential backoff; re-ran CI and it passed.

Motivation: Engineers authoring RAG agents and tool contracts often iterate between schema changes, example steps, and end-to-end smoke tests. This PR introduces a compact, local-first playground that 1) previews typed tool contracts (JSON Schema + human-readable contract view), 2) synthesizes step templates from a contract (CLI + UI), and 3) provides a tiny devserver and VS Code snippet pack so authors can iterate without needing the full dev stack. The goal is to reduce authoring feedback loops and contract drift between examples, docs, and runtime stubs. What this PR adds: - a new example workspace at redwood-examples/step-synthesizer-playground with multiple sample tool contracts and canonical step templates - a CLI binary scripts/rw-synth that generates step skeletons from contract metadata and can emit VS Code snippets and inline test harnesses - a lightweight devserver (playground/server.js) that renders a contract-preview UI, allows one-click synthesis of example steps, and validates structured-output roundtrips against the contract schema - VS Code extension snippets at redwood-examples/.vscode/snippets/step-synth.code-snippets and a README authoring guide at redwood-examples/step-synthesizer/README.md - unit smoke tests that run the synth pipeline and validate the generated snippets against a small lint rule set (tests/synth.test.js) Usage examples: - Synthesize into an examples folder: ./scripts/rw-synth synth --input examples/contracts/payment.json --out examples/steps/payment --format vscode - Run devserver: cd redwood-examples/step-synthesizer-playground && node server.js && open http://localhost:3002 - VS Code: install snippets by copying .vscode/snippets/step-synth.code-snippets into your workspace and trigger with prefix "rwd-step" Checklist: - [x] Contract preview UI for JSON Schema + human summary - [x] CLI synth commands and --dry-run - [x] VS Code snippet generator - [x] Smoke tests and CI jobs - [x] Docs/README with quickstart and troubleshooting Notes on design decisions: - The contract preview intentionally renders a simplified human summary (field descriptions, required/optional, example values) instead of a full JSON Schema editor to keep the surface area small for the initial release. - The synth CLI emits conservative step skeletons (comments and minimal I/O scaffolding) so generated code is safe to paste and iterate on. - We intentionally avoid adding runtime dependencies on the redwood core runtime; this stays fully in examples to keep the onboarding friction low. Related work: Links to internal Linear items: ENG-1423 (authoring feedback loop), PM-98 (docs quickstart uplift). Also references to the authoring UX spike in ENG-1399. CI notes: initial CI run failed due to a flaky snapshot in synth.test.js; fixed by normalizing timestamps in generated snippets. Merge strategy: squash. Backwards compatibility: no breaking changes to runtime APIs; this is examples-only and docs-facing.
Diego: Nice UX on the preview page. Two small asks: make required fields visually distinct and add a link to the contract JSON. Author: added a subtle red badge for required fields and an inline toggle to view raw JSON.
Priya: Can the CLI emit .md quickstart snippets for README? Author: added --format md which emits a minimal markdown snippet and added a section to README.
Lucia: test flake observed on CI (timestamps). Author: normalized timestamps in stub generation and added a deterministic fixture for CI. CI green after change.
Adds an examples-first authoring playground for tool contracts and step synthesis. Includes rw-synth CLI, a contract-preview devserver, VS Code snippets, and smoke tests. This is docs/examples only and does not change runtime behavior.

Context: teams frequently request small, composable agent examples they can embed in feature branches and workshops without the overhead of full RAG stacks. Motivation: provide a compact set of agent patterns (synchronous tool-calls, deferred tool batching, structured-output contracts) plus a short runbook that explains when to choose each pattern and a minimal telemetry preset for fast diagnostics. What this PR does: 1) adds a compact workshop under examples/agent-patterns that contains three runnable agent templates (sync-toolflow, batch-tool-conductor, contract-first-parser) with README-driven exercises; 2) provides a runbook (docs/quickstarts/agent-patterns-runbook.md) that maps real product scenarios to patterns, includes cost/latency tradeoffs and quick checklist for production hardening; 3) introduces a tiny telemetry preset and example probes (telemetry/presets/compact-agent.json and telemetry/probes/sample-probes.js) so engineers get actionable traces and token-cost breakdowns during the workshop; 4) updates the devcontainer and CI smoke job to support the lightweight workshop. Checklist: - [x] Add runnable templates with minimal dependencies and step-by-step README - [x] Add runbook with decision matrix and rollback guidance - [x] Add telemetry presets and example probes - [x] Add tests and smoke CI job for the workshop - [x] Get approvals from docs and examples reviewers Not included in this PR: full-scale eval harness, language translations and multi-region deployment guides (follow-ups tracked in ENG-9142). Links: Linear: ENG-9142. Support ticket: SUP-987.
Adds a compact workshop and runbook for agent patterns: lightweight tool-calling templates, structured-output validation examples, and telemetry presets for quick RAG experimentation.
Asha Mehta: This looks great as a lightweight on-ramp. Two questions: can the batch conductor be run locally without queue infra?
Riley Chen: Yes — the batch conductor uses an in-process scheduler with a mock queue adapter; the README explains how to swap to SQS/Kafka in prod.
Samir Patel: Suggest adding a short section in the runbook about fallback strategies when tool latency spikes (circuit breaker + repeatable ephemeral retries).
Riley Chen: Added a 'tool resilience' subsection and a minimal sample circuit-breaker config per your suggestion.
Claire Nguyen: The structured-output linter is important — can we include an example failed contract and a sample debug trace?
Riley Chen: Included a failing contract sample in contract-parser/tests/fixtures and added a sample trace in telemetry/probes.
Asha Mehta: CI flaked on the first run (docker network timeouts) but rerun passed. Approving now.
Samir Patel: Approved after the circuit-breaker add.

Motivation: Provide a lightweight, local-first RAG authoring playground that lets engineers iterate on retrieval strategies and prompt variants without requiring cloud credentials or a remote index. This quickstart is aimed at product/infra engineers who want deterministic, reproducible authoring flows: live indexing, offline similarity search (annoy/nmslib fallback), deterministic prompt evaluation harness, and live validation assertions against a small corpus.

What this PR adds (single continuous description): Adds a new example project under examples/local-authoring-sandbox. The sandbox contains: 1) devcontainer and docker-compose for a reproducible local environment (Redis-based KV shim, local Annoy index builder, a tiny HTTP shim that emulates Redwood streaming responses), 2) an authoring CLI (authorctl) that scaffolds documents, builds indices, runs example prompts and records structured predictions, 3) a validate-playground web app (Svelte) which runs a suite of prompt+retrieval test cases and displays token-level traces and similarity diagnostics, 4) a set of canonical prompt test cases and a baseline evaluation harness that records output diffs for regression detection. The README includes a step-by-step quickstart and troubleshooting notes for common local pitfalls (port collisions, index memory tuning).

Files & code highlights: - examples/local-authoring-sandbox/devcontainer.json and Dockerfiles for a reproducible dev environment. - examples/local-authoring-sandbox/authorctl: small Python CLI (click) that exposes `init`, `index`, `run`, and `record` commands; index command supports ANN (annoy) and brute-force fallback; run supports deterministic RNG and tokenization stubs for reproducible traces. - examples/local-authoring-sandbox/validate-playground: Svelte app that consumes recorded runs and displays: retrieval hit table, prompt transformations, and a playback of generated token traces. - docs/snippets/local-authoring-guides.md: new quickstart doc included in the docs site navigation. - small shim server examples/local-authoring-sandbox/shim_server: a tiny fastapi app that returns mock streaming chunks to validate client-side streaming logic locally.

Checklist (author): - [x] Add example repo skeleton + devcontainer - [x] Implement authorctl index/run/record - [x] Add validate-playground UI + test cases - [x] Add docs quickstart and troubleshooting - [x] Add unit tests for authorctl key codepaths - [x] Add CI job (examples-ci) to smoke the devcontainer build and run basic `authorctl index` command.

Usage summary: - git clone && open in VS Code devcontainer OR docker-compose up - authorctl init --corpus sample_data/ - authorctl index --method annoy --params "n_trees=8" - authorctl run --case example_1 --deterministic true - open validate-playground at http://localhost:3000 to inspect retrieval and traces

Compatibility notes: This example intentionally avoids requiring Redwood API keys. It includes a small adapter to plug into Redwood SDK stubs so teams can switch to real inference with a single config change. The example also demonstrates model variant fallback by simulating two model profiles in the shim server.

Security and privacy: The sandbox stores all data locally. The README warns about copying production PII into the sample corpus and suggests redaction scripts included under examples/local-authoring-sandbox/scripts/redact_sample.sh.

Why different from existing RAG quickstarts: Existing quickstarts focus on cloud-backed indices or fully managed pipelines; this PR emphasizes a local-first iterative loop (authoring + live validation) to shorten the feedback loop for prompt engineering and retrieval ranking experiments.

Migration/rollback: Deleting the examples/local-authoring-sandbox directory reverts all changes. The examples CI job is isolated and will be removed with the directory on rollback.

Miguel Santos: Nice work — the devcontainer makes local testing frictionless. Left a comment about exposing only one port in docker-compose to avoid collisions.
Aisha Kapoor (author): Thanks — fixed compose ports and added a note in the README about common port ranges.
Priya Menon: Could we add a short section showing how to toggle the shim to call a real Redwood hosted endpoint? Requesting a small example config (done in docs/snippets/local-authoring-guides.md).
Jordan Lee: Unit tests look good. One flake in CI on macOS runner during `authorctl index` — I reran and it passed. Consider reducing default annoy trees for low-memory dev machines (updated CLI default to 4).
Add local-first RAG Authoring Sandbox: reproducible devcontainer, authoring CLI, offline index builder (annoy fallback), validate-playground UI, and docs quickstart for local prompt/retrieval iteration.

Motivation: Developers building RAG pipelines and agent tool-calling workflows often need a lightweight way to iterate locally without spinning up external tool services (search, TTS, function mocks) or hooking in production telemetry. This PR adds a compact, single-file tool-simulator and a small telemetry probe that emits realistic, structured traces/metrics into the local Redwood Console dev mode. The goal is to make hands-on examples faster to run in workshops and CI, reduce onboarding friction, and provide stable inputs for quickstart-driven evals.

What this PR introduces (high level):
- compact-tool-sim/: a tiny HTTP-based tool simulator (Node + single-file Python starter) that exposes three test endpoints: /search, /summarize, /math. Each endpoint simulates latency profiles and deterministic output so prompts and evals are reproducible.
- telemetry-probe/: a minimal probe that can be run alongside the simulator; it emits span traces, token-level metrics, and custom events to the local dev console or stdout in a Redwood Console-friendly JSON envelope.
- examples/rag-playground/README.md: a guided quickstart that wires the Redwood SDK (TS + Python snippets) to the simulator and probe; includes prompts, a small test corpus, and a smoke-test harness.
- devcontainer and makefile targets to let contributors run the full playground with one command.

Files changed: compact-tool-sim/node/server.js, compact-tool-sim/python/sim.py, telemetry-probe/probe.js, examples/rag-playground/README.md, examples/rag-playground/devcontainer.json, examples/rag-playground/Makefile, examples/rag-playground/sample-index.jsonl, docs/quickstarts/rag-playground-compact.md, CI/workflows/rag-playground-smoke.yml.

Design notes and tradeoffs: The simulator intentionally keeps behavior deterministic (seeded RNG) to make automated scenario assertions reliable. Latency shaping is configurable with environment variables so tests can simulate cold/warm cache characteristics without complex infra. The telemetry probe emits compact envelopes (no PII) and provides an opt-in mode to forward to an HTTP endpoint matching Redwood Console local ingestion for easy demoing. We avoided introducing new third-party deps except small, well-maintained test helpers to keep the example lightweight.

Testing and validation: Unit-level tests included for simulator response shapes and the smoke harness. Manual validation steps are in the README and CI is wired to run the smoke workflow which spins the simulator, runs the quickstart script, and asserts a handful of output invariants (tool outputs present, telemetry envelopes emitted, and SDK call counts).

How to use locally (summary):
1) git clone && cd examples/rag-playground && make dev
2) Open the dev console (http://localhost:3000) or review stdout to confirm probe envelopes
3) Run the sample notebook or the TS/py quickstart; sample prompts are under sample-index.jsonl

Checklist: 
- [x] Example code (TS + Py)
- [x] README quickstart and smoke CI
- [x] Devcontainer and make targets
- [x] Minimal telemetry probe with local console compatibility
- [x] Deterministic simulator outputs for reliable tests

Related work: This is complementary to the heavier RAG harness in examples/rag-testbench. It is intended as a minimal onboarding path for workshops and dev playgrounds (linked Linear ENG-4729). The docs page references the longer testbench for users who need richer data and multi-tool orchestration.

Release notes: added a compact RAG playground for local development and telemetry-enabled simulator for quicker iterations and demos.

Migration notes: No runtime changes to Redwood backends. This is examples-only and opt-in by contributors.

Miguel Ortega (reviewer): Nice small surface — can you make the telemetry envelope schema explicit in the README? also suggest adding an env var to toggle deterministic mode.
Aisha Patel (author): Added envelope schema section to README and TELEMETRY_SCHEMA.md; simulator now accepts RAG_SIM_DETERMINISTIC=1 (default).
Harper Lin (reviewer): CI flaky on first run — we hit a 30s timeout during server startup. Recommend increasing wait/retry and adding a health-check endpoint.
Aisha Patel (author): Increased CI wait/retries and added /health endpoint; reran CI. All green.
Samir Rao (reviewer): Documentation nit — include license header in Python shim and call out no-PII guarantee.
Aisha Patel (author): Added license header and explicit no-PII note in README and probe output.
payload.title: Introduce compact RAG tool-simulator and telemetry probe playground
