Enhances presubmit routing, adds a lightweight dependency curation probe, and migrates lint entrypoint to a typed action. No API changes. Improves CI feedback speed for small changes and reduces noise from infra churn.
Context: Our presubmit lanes were noisy and slow for small edits due to monolithic lint/test runners and indiscriminate dep-checking. This PR splits the presubmit topology into a fast 'prober' path (quick syntactic and dependency-smoke checks) and a fullpath that runs on targeted changes. Motivation: reduce feedback latency for engineering workflows, lower CI cost for trivial PRs, and introduce an automated dep-curation probe that surfaces transitive-package churn earlier. Scope: implements a lightweight presubmit-prober composite action (TS), a dependency-curation job that computes a shallow dependency index and flags newly-visible transitive changes, migrates the legacy bash lint entrypoint to a typed TS action for deterministic inputs, and adds a small smoke-suite and gate to ensure we do not regress coverage. Checklist: - [x] Add presubmit-prober composite action and action.yml - [x] Implement dependency-curation job and heuristics - [x] Migrate lint entrypoint to typed TS action with integration tests - [x] Wire staged lanes (fastpath/probe -> fullpath) with annotation and stage labels - [x] Update docs and CONTRIBUTING.md to explain new lanes - [x] Add telemetry events (ci.probe.start/ci.probe.result) Implementation notes: The prober action is written in TypeScript for hermetic parsing and stable input validation; it runs a quick eslint --print-config check, a staged unit-test snapshot run (focused by TEST_PATTERN env), and a lightweight 'dep-index' that inspects package-lock/yarn.lock metadata to build a changed-deps delta. The dependency-curation job runs only on package.json/lockfile changes or when the prober reports 'dep_delta > 0'. To keep changes minimal, the fullpath still reuses existing test matrix and cache layers. Files changed (high level): - .github/actions/presubmit-prober/* (new TS action, tests) - .github/workflows/presubmit.yml (split lanes, stage annotations) - .github/workflows/dependency-curation.yml (new job) - infra/ci/lint-entrypoint.ts (replaces scripts/lint-entrypoint.sh) - ci/smoke/probe-smoke.test.ts - docs/ci/presubmit.md - package.json, yarn.lock (action deps) Security and perf considerations: The TS action runs under the existing GitHub runner permissions and does not access secrets beyond the default GITHUB_TOKEN; dependency-curation is read-only. Performance: fastpath median runtime reduced from ~7m to ~45s on trivial edits. Review conversation highlights: Marco Li: "Looks great — a few nits on action inputs and log verbosity. Can we make TEST_PATTERN opt-in via workflow input?" Author (Aisha): "Good call — made TEST_PATTERN optional with sensible default. Also added telemetry to help tune defaults." Diane Park: "I want clearer failure-level mapping (probe vs full). Please add an explicit status annotation when probe fails non-blocking vs blocking." Author: "Added annotations and a 'probe.severity' output to control lane behavior; documented in CONTRIBUTING.md." Ethan Ross (approval): "Approach clears flakiness observed in infra runs; approving pending CI." CI: initial run had lint flake in typed action build (node14->node16 mismatch); fixed by pinning setup-node to 3.x and rerunning. Final CI: pass on all jobs including smoke and matrix. Merge: squashed and merged to main with commit b6f3a1d. Impact: reduces premerge churn for small PRs, surfaces transitive dependency changes earlier, and paves the way for future presubmit routing experiments (dynamic probe thresholds). Rollout plan: feature gated via repo-level boolean ci.prober.enabled (default true for core/* paths, false for legacy infra/*); telemetry will be observed for two weeks before promoting probe to default for all paths. Known limitations: dep-curation heuristics are conservative and may produce false positives for workspace rearrangements; we will tune with ENG-4410 telemetry. Related work: builds on earlier dep-provenance efforts (ENG-3301) and presubmit-slicing prototype (ENG-4182).
payload.title: Rework presubmit signature routing and introduce dependency curation probe

payload.body:
Context and motivation: In production traffic we observed a class of failures where SSE event payloads containing JSON arrays/objects were reconstructed with bytes crossing event boundaries after aggressive non-blocking flushes and transport-layer coalescing. Symptoms included partial JSON tokens stitched across different events, function-call sentinel loss, and occasional parser hangs when clients streamed small fragments rapidly. This surfaced most often in OpenAI-compat streaming paths where clients rely on strict event boundaries for function/tool calling and structured output.

Summary of change: This PR introduces a layered approach to prevent cross-event byte-run and to make fragment reassembly deterministic across languages and runtimes. Key elements: 1) transport_shim: a non-invasive normalization layer that ensures writes emit an explicit short boundary marker ("␞") when a write is split by the runtime without changing wire protocol semantics unless the client opts in; 2) streamer.go: coalesce logic updated to avoid merging trailing whitespace or delimiter bytes from one event into the next; 3) parser.py: state machine hardened to treat the explicit boundary marker and sequence headers as strong reassembly hints and to avoid greedy joining of partial JSON tokens; 4) opt-in seq+checksum header: X-RW-SSE-FRAG-V1 allows clients to request per-event sequence numbers and a lightweight checksum to assist in replay/resume scenarios (compat flag, default off); 5) tests: replay-based integration test and fuzz harness for high-frequency tiny fragments; 6) docs: added migration notes and best-practices for clients.

Checklist: - [x] Reproduceable regression test added (integrationtests/sse_replay_test.py) - [x] Parser unit tests covering partial token sequences - [x] Fuzz harness for small fragment workloads - [x] Backwards-compatible by default (compat header opt-in) - [x] Benchmarked for perf regressions (no observable latency increase under representative workloads) - [x] Docs/migration notes updated

Implementation notes: - The boundary marker chosen (U+241E RECORD SEPARATOR visual) is deliberately unlikely to appear in model output and is stripped by the parser when present; transport_shim only emits the marker when a write is sliced by the runtime; clients that enable X-RW-SSE-FRAG-V1 get sequence headers (rw-frag-seq) and a 32-bit Adler-style checksum to validate reassembly. - Parser behavior: when a sequence header is present, events are validated and a small reassembly window is used to reject out-of-order fragments rather than silently merge them. When header absent, parser preserves previous relaxed behavior but will no longer greedily concatenate trailing bytes that look like partial JSON tokens across event boundaries. - Performance: microbenchmarks showed <1% median latency impact and no cost to aggregate throughput; the normalization step is O(1) per sliced write.

Compatibility and rollout: - Default behavior unchanged for existing clients. - Sequence+checksum is behind opt-in header; we will enable the header for Redwood-owned clients in a canary channel and monitor telemetry (SSE-reconstruct-failures metric). - Plan to enable the boundary marker unconditionally in the transport in a delayed rollout if no adverse effects are observed.

Testing and validation: - Added deterministic replay test that replays recorded tiny-fragment sequences captured from production load; validated parser produces identical event stream before and after changes when header absent, and tolerantly correct when header present. - Added fuzz harness that generates write-slice patterns and verifies JSON integrity, sentinel placement, and function-call boundary preservation. - CI: flaky integration test retried once, then passed; all checks green.

Related tickets: ENG-2345, ENG-2410, SUP-9876.

Notes for reviewers: focus on parser state transitions in parser.py (comments call out the key FSM changes) and on the transport_shim heuristic for when to emit the boundary marker; both are intentionally conservative to avoid breaking existing clients. The seq+checksum code path is isolated and guarded by the opt-in header for safe rollout.

Release notes: Fixes rare SSE streaming reconstruction bugs under high-frequency tiny-fragment workloads that could cause partial JSON tokens to cross event boundaries; adds an opt-in per-event sequence/checksum mechanism to improve replay/resume robustness.
Ethan Rivera: Good breakdown — I want to see a comment in transport_shim explaining why we chose U+241E vs double-newline. Also add a unit test for the streamer coalescing edge-case.
Maya Patel (author): Added comment and test; updated transport_shim.go with explicit rationale and link to docs/compat/sse-framing.md
Linh Tran: Parser changes look sensible. Question: should we treat checksum validation failures as soft-fail or hard-fail?
Maya Patel (author): Opted for soft-fail with metric emission on first failure and hard-fail only when header indicates strict mode. Documented in compat note.
Carlos Gomez: Integration tests reproduced the original bug locally and now pass. Approving after minor nitfix on logging verbosity.
Fix: SSE framing normalization to avoid partial-JSON crossing event boundaries; opt-in per-event seq+checksum for improved replay/resume robustness.
Canary rollout planned: enable header for internal customers next week, monitor SSE-reconstruct-failures and sse-frag-checksum-fail metrics.
None required for existing clients. Optional: enable X-RW-SSE-FRAG-V1 for improved replay guarantees. See docs/compat/sse-framing.md for details.
// Python client opt-in example
headers = {
  'Accept': 'text/event-stream',
  'X-RW-SSE-FRAG-V1': '1'
}
# client will receive rw-frag-seq and optional checksum per event when enabled
payload.title: Normalize SSE fragment timing and non-blocking event framing

Adds a minimal 'Chefplate' RAG playbook with a local runner, TypeScript bindings, and telemetry probes for iterative authoring.
Motivation: Create a compact, opinionated RAG playbook template for fast local iteration and authoring. 'Chefplate' is a tiny scaffolding that demonstrates: 1) end-to-end local runs against a seeded index, 2) typesafe tool bindings and TS-friendly playbook schemas, and 3) low-friction telemetry probes to make regressions visible during prompt edits. This targets developer experience engineers and product teams who want a reproducible local authoring loop before onboarding to production Redwood pipelines.

What this PR contains (single continuous description):
- Checklist: [x] minimal playbook schema (YAML + TS types), [x] local-runner (node) with hot-reload dev loop, [x] seeded example index + indexer script, [x] telemetry probes and example dashboards (DevConsole snippet), [x] docs page and quickstart README, [x] CI smoke job + unit tests, [x] small e2e scenario.

High-level commits:
- commit 1: create chefplate template layout and README with usage instructions and example prompts
- commit 2: add local-runner implementation (node/ts), lightweight in-memory vector store shim, and hot-reload dev session loop
- commit 3: add typescript bindings and generated types for playbook schemas; add example tools (http-fetch, file-store)
- commit 4: add seeded-index generator script and small sample data set (~60 documents) for repeatable local plays
- commit 5: add telemetry probes and opt-out flag; add DevConsole snippet to docs
- commit 6: CI workflow and smoke e2e; fix linting issues reported by CI and rerun tests

Changed areas (high level):
- examples/chefplate/README.md - new quickstart and recipes
- examples/chefplate/playbook.yaml - opinionated minimal RAG playbook
- examples/chefplate/src/runner/local-runner.ts - local Node runner with hot-reload loop
- examples/chefplate/src/tools/http-fetch.ts - example tool shim and types
- examples/chefplate/src/indexer/seed-data.ts - small index generator
- examples/chefplate/src/types/playbook.d.ts - generated TS types for playbook schema
- docs/playbooks/chefplate.md - docs site quickstart and DevConsole snippet
- ci/workflows/chefplate-ci.yml - small CI to validate smoke e2e and linting

Review conversation snapshot:
- Diego Ramirez (reviewer): "Nice minimal surface. Two asks: (1) add a telemetry opt-out env var so customers can run offline, (2) reduce sample dataset to <100 docs for CI speed."
- Avery Chen (author): "Added TELEMETRY_OFF env and reduced seed data to 60 docs; also added note in README about offline usage."
- Samira Patel (reviewer): "Runner looks good. Could we split hot-reload into a 'dev' flag to keep the example runner simple for CI? Also asked for a short command example for Windows users."
- Avery Chen: "Splitted flag and added explicit powershell commands to README. Addressed lint nit where promises were not awaited."
- Lena Fischer (approver): "Confirming QA smoke pass on macOS and linux. Approving for merge after squash."

CI and test notes:
- First CI run: lint failed (prettier/tsc), fixed in commit 6.
- Subsequent CI run: unit tests and smoke e2e passed. Rerun required for flaky network mock, fixed with deterministic mock and retry wrapper. Final status: pass.

How to try locally (short):
1) git clone && cd examples/chefplate
2) yarn && yarn seed:index (creates local/seed.json)
3) yarn dev:runner --playbook playbook.yaml --dev (hot-reload)
4) open the built DevConsole snippet or hit /metrics to see telemetry probes (TELEMETRY_OFF=1 disables payloads)

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- The in-memory vector shim in local-runner intentionally mirrors production calls but does not depend on external stores to keep onboarding friction low. It's not for scale.
- Type generation is intentionally minimal to keep examples approachable; a full codegen pipeline is left to a follow-up task (ENG-3421 follow-ups).

Security and compliance:
- The example includes a telemetry opt-out and avoids shipping any real PII data. Seed data is synthetic.

Merge outcome: Squash merged to main on 2026-03-05 by Lena Fischer (squash merge). Merge commit: 7a3b9f8c0e2d2c8a1f6a4d9b.

Related items: Linear ENG-3421 tracked the follow-ups for full codegen and CI expansion. PM-1101 captured the product acceptance criteria. Support ticket SUP-88 requested an on-prem friendly quickstart; chefplate addresses that by documenting TELEMETRY_OFF and offline runner notes.

Notes for maintainers:
- If you update playbook schema, regenerate types using scripts/generate-types.sh in examples/chefplate.
- Keep the seeded dataset light to avoid long CI times.

This PR aims to be a small, self-contained pattern that teams can fork to prototype RAG flows locally before migrating to Redwood Dedicated or Private deployments.
payload.title: introduce-chefplate-rag-playbook-local-runner-and-type-bindings

Motivation: Teams building multi-step conversational agents often need a lightweight playground to design, stub, and evaluate decision-graph based toolflows (branching tool calls) without committing a full orchestrator. This PR introduces a self-contained example and quickstart that demonstrates a Decision Graph approach to RAG-driven conversations: explicit nodes, conditional edges, and deterministic tool stubs to make stepwise testing and telemetry trivial. Summary: Adds a new 'decision-graph' playground under examples/decision-graph-stubber with: (1) a compact YAML graph schema, (2) a NodeRunner shim that performs local tool stubbing and deterministic KV cache seeding, (3) a browser-playground HTML that visualizes execution paths and telemetry markers, (4) a step-by-step quickstart doc that shows integrating the graph with Redwood streaming and structured output. What this is not: not a replacement for the full orchestrator or production workflows. This playground is explicitly for design iteration, authoring, and deterministic e2e tests. Checklist: - [x] Add YAML schema, parser, and validation tests - [x] Implement NodeRunner stub harness and deterministic tool responses - [x] Add browser visualization for decision paths and event timeline - [x] Quickstart doc with runnable local scenario and telemetry probes - [x] CI smoke test (headless run of a canonical graph) Usage (short): 1) cd examples/decision-graph-stubber 2) yarn install && yarn start:dev 3) open http://localhost:8080/playground.html to author a graph, press Run, and inspect the step timeline 4) Run yarn smoke to execute canonical scenarios and verify telemetry markers Why this is useful: - Designers can enumerate branching conditions in YAML and simulate noisy retrievals - Engineers can stub external tools (search, DB, webhook) with deterministic payloads for stable unit/e2e assertion - Product managers can capture canonical decision-paths as test fixtures for regressions Related work: inspired by node-based authoring in the RAG playbook and the decision DAG experiments in ENG-7891. Also references the session-replay patterns added in PRs that introduced stepwise tracing. API/contract notes: The NodeRunner exposes a small adapter surface (startNode, callTool, emitEvent) documented in examples/decision-graph-stubber/README.md; the playground demonstrates how this adapter maps to Redwood streaming APIs and structured output validators. Motivation: shipping high-quality RAG features depends on authoring ergonomics and quick iteration loops. This PR introduces the "Retrieval Authoring Studio" (a light browser extension + example toolkit) to make it fast for engineers and content authors to capture snippets, construct retrieval + prompt templates, and validate structured outputs before committing configs to production. The extension is intentionally offline-first and privacy-conscious: embeddings can be produced via a local embedding shim, or proxied to Redwood with explicit key input. Key pieces: 1) browser extension that captures page fragments, normalizes text, attaches metadata (source URL, DOM selector), and stores packs locally; 2) a small Node-based example helper (examples/ra-studio/node-helper) that shows how to: create an index, run similarity search, and call Redwood's hosted or dedicated inference endpoints with a template; 3) authoring UI examples (examples/ra-studio/ui) that demonstrate structured-output validation hooks and streaming previews; 4) docs updates (docs/ra-studio) with step-by-step authoring walkthroughs and a troubleshooting section for common embedding/encoding mismatches; 5) a minimal telemetry shim (opt-in) that emits anonymized event summaries for feature usage and authoring regressions so teams can iterate on templates. Checklist: - [x] Extension captures fragments, stores packs, and exposes export/import JSON. - [x] Node helper implements index and simple async re-ranker example. - [x] UI examples include structured-output validation and test fixtures. - [x] Docs site pages added with screenshots and a quick smoke-run. - [x] CI smoke test that runs the node-helper against a local vector store emulator. Security/privacy notes: extension never ships keys; users must paste an API key for temporary testing or use the local embedding shim. Telemetry is opt-in only; events are coarse (counts, latencies, anonymized templates) and documented in docs/ra-studio/telemetry.md. Testing: unit tests added for text normalization, a small E2E smoke job runs the node helper with the emulator in CI. Rollout: merged to main; we will soft-launch examples on the examples portal and monitor opt-in telemetry (if any) for early adopter feedback. Related: ENG-2041 tracks adding richer template assertions, PM-78 is the product brief for authoring workflows.

Context and motivation:
This PR introduces a small, focused playbook and example runtime for teams that want policy-driven scheduling for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) across heterogeneous serving backends (hosted, dedicated, and edge workers). Many customers have similar patterns: retrieval latency varies by index shard and region, and downstream token cost / latency targets vary by route. Rather than bake one scheduler into the runtime, this playbook provides a reference scheduler and tiny worker shims that demonstrate: policy configuration, per-request routing heuristics, KV-cache-aware batching, and graceful fallback to local or compact models when backlog is high.

What's included (high level):
- docs/playbooks/rag-scheduler.md: playbook describing scheduler concepts, JSON/YAML policy examples, and rollout guidance.
- examples/rag-scheduler/ts-quickstart/: a TypeScript quickstart that wires a simple policy to the Redwood API and a stubbed retriever.
- examples/rag-scheduler/worker/go-worker/: a minimal Go worker that accepts scheduled tasks, demonstrates batched KV-cache reuse, and emits compact traces (zipkin-compatible).
- ci/workflows/rag-scheduler.yml: lightweight CI smoke that installs deps and runs the quickstart script.
- telemetry/presets/rag-scheduler-presets.json: suggested metric names and dashboards for the Console.
- tests/integration/rag-scheduler-smoke.test.ts: local smoke test that starts the quickstart and ensures a request path goes through scheduler -> retriever -> worker.

Description of changes / commits (summary):
- commit 1: add initial playbook doc and policy examples (docs/playbooks/rag-scheduler.md)
- commit 2: add TS quickstart and sample policy loader (examples/rag-scheduler/ts-quickstart/*)
- commit 3: add Go worker shim and small contract test (examples/rag-scheduler/worker/go-worker/*, tests/integration/*)
- commit 4: CI workflow and telemetry presets + minor docs tweaks

Files changed (high level):
- docs/playbooks/rag-scheduler.md (new)
- examples/rag-scheduler/ts-quickstart/index.ts (new)
- examples/rag-scheduler/ts-quickstart/policy.example.json (new)
- examples/rag-scheduler/worker/go-worker/main.go (new)
- examples/rag-scheduler/worker/go-worker/README.md (new)
- ci/workflows/rag-scheduler.yml (new)
- telemetry/presets/rag-scheduler-presets.json (new)
- tests/integration/rag-scheduler-smoke.test.ts (new)

Small illustrative snippet (policy loader):
const policy = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(process.env.POLICY_PATH || './policy.example.json', 'utf8'))
// policy: { priorities: ["region","latency"], fallbacks: { "highLoad": "compact-model" } }

Review conversation (highlights):
- Ravi Patel (reviewer): "Nice focused playbook. Two quick asks: add a default TTL to the local KV cache sample and make the policy example explicit about 'maxConcurrentPerWorker' so teams aren't surprised by default behavior."
- Ava (author): "Added TTL and explict maxConcurrentPerWorker in policy.example.json; added comments in the TS quickstart about tuning for Dedicated vs Hosted."
- Lina Chen (reviewer): "CI failed on first run due to an integration test flakiness; can we make the test resilient to port contention? Also add a short section in the playbook about telemetry keys so Console dashboards can be imported."
- Ava (author): "Updated test to use a random local port and added telemetry preset file. Re-ran CI; all green."
- Marcus Cole (approver): "Approving — I like the clear rollout guidance and the smoke test. The Go worker is intentionally minimal which is good for teams to extend."

CI and validation notes:
- First run: Node linted and tests; integration smoke failed intermittently due to fixed port assumption (flaky).
- Fix applied: test updated to acquire a free port before starting quickstart; CI re-run passed (checks: lint, build, test, smoke).
- Telemetry preset validated locally in Console dev environment.

Backward compatibility and stability:
- No breaking changes to Redwood APIs. This PR is examples + docs + a lightweight worker shim. Marked breaking_change=false.

How to try locally (short):
1) cd examples/rag-scheduler/ts-quickstart && npm install
2) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=... && export POLICY_PATH=./policy.example.json
3) npm run start:quickstart  # starts a tiny scheduler proxy that routes to the Go worker
4) npm run smoke  # runs the local smoke test that exercises the full flow

Merge outcome:
- Merged by: Marcus Cole (squash and merge)
- Merge method: squash

Notes for maintainers and next steps:
- This playbook is intentionally small; follow-ups could include: a Python worker sample, a more complete policy editor in the Console, and an end-to-end demo that includes Dedicated capacity fallbacks.
- Suggested tracking linear tickets: ENG-2451 (scheduler enhancements), PM-612 (console policy editor).

Related: ENG-2103 (prior work on KV cache hints), SUP-1023 (customer request for region-aware routing).
Adds a configurable scheduler playbook for RAG deployments plus lightweight TypeScript and Go worker samples. Enables policy-driven routing for retrieval, batching and edge worker assignment.

Context: Engineers and docs users asked for a compact, stepwise authoring experience that teaches RAG authoring idioms while providing runnable stubs. This PR adds a lightweight 'Authoring Wizard' playbook (stepwise scenarios, inline assertions) and a set of small execution stubs and typed bindings so users can run and extend the examples locally. Motivation: accelerate onboarding for new users, provide a reproducible smoke CI path for RAG templates, and surface telemetry probes so platform teams can show realistic traces. What this PR does: - New playbook: examples/authoring-wizard/playbook.yaml with three guided scenarios (index->retrieve->tool-call->finalize). The playbook supports a replay mode for deterministic e2e authoring. - Tool stubs: small TypeScript tool adapters in examples/authoring-wizard/tools/ (http_stub.ts, db_stub.ts, file_tool.ts) showing safe failure modes and structured responses. - Typed bindings: examples/authoring-wizard/bindings.ts with example TypeScript types for tool outputs and tool-caller helpers. - Dev environment: a devcontainer and a small local-runner script so you can run the playbook locally with one command. - Docs: docs/site/rag/authoring-wizard.md with a short tutorial, expected outputs, and troubleshooting tips. - Telemetry probes: examples/authoring-wizard/telemetry/probes.toml that maps probe names used in the playbook to recommended dashboard panels. - CI: ci/workflows/rag-smoke.yml runs a fast smoke invocation of the playbook against the stubs (intended to catch regressions in runtime and example API surfaces). The playbook intentionally keeps external I/O minimal so the smoke CI is stable and fast. Related: Linear ENG-7821 tracks follow-ups (editor integration and more assertions). SUP-1187 documents a support case that motivated the improved troubleshooting section. Implementation details and design choices: - Plays are authored as short YAML steps with explicit 'inputs', 'tool_call', and 'assertions' nodes to make expectations machine-checkable. - Tools return structured JSON with an envelope {status, output, diagnostics} so examples can demonstrate graceful degradation. - Typed bindings are intentionally small (50–100 LOC) to act as a template for consuming applications. - Telemetry probes are lightweight tags emitted by the playbook runner; the probes.toml maps to example panels in the docs. Motivation: Debugging complex RAG tool-call topologies and KV-cache interactions is time consuming; engineers frequently need to reproduce a failing session end-to-end, visualize tool dependencies, and assert intermediate tool outputs. This PR introduces two complementary developer-facing tools: 1) a dependency-graph workbench (web-based static demo + local electrum-style bundle) that renders tool-call DAGs, cache hit/miss annotations, and per-node timing/profile overlays; 2) a session-playback CLI that can ingest recorded traces (redwood .rtrace format) and replay requests against local stubs or live endpoints with deterministic seeding, producing trace diffs and step assertions. The change also adds three new RAG example templates (parallel-fanout-agent, sequential-kv-proxy-agent, and conditional-router-agent) and a docs quickstart page under Developer Workbench. Summary of commits: commit 1: scaffold dependency-graph renderer and sample corpus (workbench/web + static JSON serializer); commit 2: implement session-playback CLI (play, diff, assert subcommands), deterministic seeding and stub adapters; commit 3: add example templates and typesafe tool-binding stubs (TS + Python); commit 4: docs, templates, and CI smoke tests for playback. Changed areas (high-level): - workbench/web/: new static demo and renderer (D3-based minimal graph layout) and sample corpora; - tools/playback/: Rust-based CLI entrypoint with a thin TS shim for local stubs; - examples/templates/: three RAG templates (parallel-fanout, sequential-kv-proxy, conditional-router); - docs/devworkbench.md: new quickstart and debugging walkthrough; - tests/ci/playback-smoke/: e2e smoke harness and assertions; - telemetry/probes/: small probe to export trace fragments to .rtrace. Testing notes: added unit tests for deterministic seeding, CI includes an e2e smoke job that runs the playback CLI against local stubs. One playback test was flaky on first CI run due to a race in stub startup; fixed with a 200ms backoff retry and re-ran. Review thread highlights: Kai: "Nice ergonomic tooling — two asks: document the rtrace schema and add a small JSON schema for quick validation; also can we ensure playback exits non-zero on assertion failure?"; Marisol: "Added rtrace-schema.json in telemetry/probes and updated CLI to return non-zero on assert failures; expanded docs to show example error codes."; Elena: "Renderer is great, but layout needs stable node ids for animation between runs — suggest using deterministic hashing of tool name + invocation index."; Marisol: "Switched layout to use MurmurHash-based ids; added tests to ensure stability across equivalent traces."; Dante: "CI flake fixed; approve after cleanup of a stray console.log."; Marisol: "Removed leftover console.log and squashed commits for merge." CI and merge: initial CI run showed one flaky playback-smoke test (playback-stub-liveness) which failed; rerun passed. Post-merge actions: create follow-up ENG task to add a VSCode devtool for rendering inline graphs (ENG-3029) and a perf baseline for graph render latency. Docs site update: docs/devworkbench.md added with step-by-step quickstart, example traces, and a short troubleshooting table. UX note: the workbench is intentionally shipped as a read-only static bundle in this PR (no backend) to avoid onboarding friction; a future PR will add live websocket annotations for dedicated/private deployments. Merge outcome: merged to main via squash, changelog entry added in docs/changelog.md.
New developer workbench: dependency-graph visualizer and a session-playback CLI to reproduce and assert RAG execution flows locally; docs page and quickstart added; non-breaking example tooling improvements.

Summary: Adds a compact, 'kitchen-sink' RAG playground that demonstrates a production-oriented developer loop: local incremental indexing, a minimal TypeScript frontend, a lightweight in-memory retriever, and Rust-compiled WASM shims that simulate external tools (search, calculator, image-metadata). This is an opinionated quickstart to help engineers prototype tool-calling agents and offline-first RAG workflows without heavy infra.

Motivation and context: Engineers repeatedly ask for a single, small-scale example that stitches several platform features together: streaming, tool-calling, structured outputs, and an offline-friendly indexer that can run in a dev container. Existing examples are either single-focus (only tool-calling or only indexing) or require cloud services. This PR provides a local-first bundle that mirrors how customers compose these building blocks in Redwood deployments and ties into the docs site quickstart. Linked Linear tickets: ENG-9401 (playground blueprint), PM-2103 (docs quickstart).

What this PR contains (high level):
- A compact TypeScript playground UI (playground/ts-app) with a minimal chat panel, streaming stub, and structured output validator. The UI runs a dev server and includes seeded prompts and step-by-step onboarding.
- A local incremental indexer (playground/indexer) that produces small L2 JSON indexes optimized for the included examples; supports incremental adds and simple vector similarity via cosine using precomputed embeddings (mocked in dev mode).
- Rust tool shims compiled to WASM (playground/tools/wasm): calculator, web-search-stub, and image-metadata-extractor. The shims expose deterministic interfaces for tool-calling tests and can run in Node and browser via WASM-bindgen.
- Example agent harness (playground/agent) that wires Redwood TS SDK calls to the UI, demonstrates function calling, structured output parsing, and a replayable session recorder for e2e developer assertions.
- Docs site update (docs/quickstarts/rag-kitchen-sink.md) with stepwise instructions, architecture diagram, and troubleshooting tips.

Commits:
- 1f3b9c2: initial playground scaffold: TS app + indexer + README + basic wiring
- c9d4b11: add Rust tool shims, wasm build scripts, and CI wasm test shim
- 3a7f2aa: agent harness + recorder, structured-output validator, replay fixtures
- e1b0f07: docs quickstart and troubleshooting, example prompts, license header fixes

Files touched (high level):
- playground/ts-app/src/* (UI and streaming client)
- playground/indexer/* (indexer CLI and sample dataset)
- playground/tools/wasm/* (Rust crates, build.rs, wasm-bindgen glue)

- docs/quickstarts/rag-kitchen-sink.md
- scripts/ci-wasm-test.sh, .github/workflows/playground-ci.yml (small CI workflow)

Testing and CI:
- Added a lightweight GitHub Actions workflow that runs: cargo test (wasm build check), node unit tests for the TS harness, and a smoke e2e that runs the replay harness in headless mode. The initial CI run had a flaky wasm bindgen network step; I added a retry and local artifact caching. After the retry the full CI passed on this branch. ci_status shows pass.

Review notes and decisions:
- Security: Rust WASM shims are intentionally deterministic and sandboxed; they do not perform outbound network calls in dev mode (web-search-stub returns seeded fixtures). This keeps the quickstart safe for offline or air-gapped demos.
- Mocking vs real embeddings: To make the quickstart fast and deterministic, embeddings are mocked with seeded vectors by default but the indexer includes an optional flag to call a real embedding provider for advanced users. This is documented.
- Size: The goal was to keep the bundle small (< 15MB compressed when built) so it can run in a devcontainer. Binary artifacts are not checked in; CI builds wasm artifacts on demand.

Review conversation (high level timeline):
- Amina Desai (reviewer): "Love the end-to-end story. Two asks: (1) add a short smoke test that validates a tool call chain in the replay harness, (2) clarify offline security assumptions in the README."
- Marcus Nguyen (author): "Added smoke test (playground/agent/tests/replay-smoke.spec.ts) and expanded README to call out offline defaults and embed flag. PTAL."
- Rory Patel (reviewer): "WASM packaging looks good; one nit on CI: use actions/cache for cargo registry to speed subsequent runs."
- Marcus Nguyen: "Switched CI to use actions/cache and added a short note in docs about caching strategy for local dev."
- Elena Ortiz (approver): "Docs are clear and the example is compact enough for the quickstarts section. Approved."

Edge cases and known limitations:
- The web-search-stub intentionally returns limited results; it is not intended as a production search integration. Customers should wire a real search tool for high-fidelity retrieval.
- The mocked embeddings trade fidelity for deterministic tests. The indexer supports a flag (--real-embed) to opt into real embeddings which requires API keys (described in docs).
- WASM performance in the browser is intentionally unoptimized; the example targets developer ergonomics, not production latency.

Merge and rollout:
- Merged via squash on 2026-02-02 by Amina Desai.
- Docs site quickstart added to the next docs release; docs/quickstarts/rag-kitchen-sink.md includes migration notes for existing quickstarts.

How to try locally (short):
1) git clone && cd playground/ts-app
2) ./scripts/dev-setup.sh (installs npm, builds wasm shims)
3) npm run dev (open http://localhost:5173)
4) run the replay harness: node playground/agent/replay.js --fixture=fixtures/basic-flow.json

If anything breaks: see docs/quickstarts/rag-kitchen-sink.md troubleshooting. Special thanks to Amina, Rory, and Elena for the reviews.

Motivation: provide a reference implementation for teams that want to run multi-stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows at scale using AWS Step Functions (Express) orchestrator backed by CDK. Many customers ask how to compose retrieval, chunking, model calls, and external tool invocation with deterministic retries, observability, and low orchestration cost — this example demonstrates a pragmatic pattern using a lightweight state machine and Redwood SDK calls from Lambda tasks.

What this PR contains: a self-contained examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/ directory with: CDK app (TypeScript) that provisions an Express Step Function, Lambda task handlers (Node.js) that call Redwood via the SDK for retrieval and generation steps, a small DynamoDB-backed vector cache example, an EventBridge + WebSocket stub for streaming partial outputs back to a dev client, sample IAM least-privilege policies, and a README with local dev and deploy instructions. The example favors clarity and ops-readiness over production hardening; we document trade-offs.

Key design decisions and trade-offs: single-step model invocation is wrapped in a Lambda to keep StepFn debugability and retries simple; long-running model streaming is simulated with short-lived step functions + EventBridge because Express StepFn has 5-minute limits — we call out options (Activity workers, SQS+Fargate) for production. We show how to pin model versions and configure fallback model routing (via environment variables) to mirror Redwood routing policies.

Local dev quickstart (excerpt):
  1) yarn install && cd examples/rag-stepfn-cdk && yarn bootstrap
  2) cp .env.example .env and set REDWOOD_API_KEY, AWS creds, and LOCAL_VECTOR_DIR
  3) yarn start:local (runs SAM local for Lambdas + StepFn local runner shim)
  4) curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/start -d '{"query":"What is Redwood Inference?"}' to exercise the pipeline

Included files (high level): examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/README.md, examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/cdk/bin/app.ts, examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/cdk/lib/stepfn-stack.ts, examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/lambdas/retriever/index.ts, examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/lambdas/generator/index.ts, examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/lambdas/stream-proxy/index.ts, examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/templates/stepfn-definition.json, examples/rag-stepfn-cdk/test/integration.sh

Testing notes: unit tests added for the Lambda handlers (jest) and a lightweight integration script that runs against local SAM. CI is configured to run the TypeScript build, lint, and unit tests in the repository examples job. We intentionally do not run full CDK deploys in CI to avoid creating infra in CI, but CDK synth is executed for smoke validation.

Security and least-privilege: example IAM policies are scoped to the example resources and documented in README. We surface common hardening recommendations (KMS for secrets, private VPC endpoints for DynamoDB, restrict StepFn execution role to specific ARNs).

Docs and dev experience: README contains architecture diagram (ASCII), sequence of traceable event IDs for tracing, and a troubleshooting section with common error messages from the Redwood SDK (auth, rate-limits, model-not-found). We also include a short recipe for switching the Lambda generator to call Redwood Dedicated endpoints (env var REDWOOD_ENDPOINT).

Checklist: 
  - [x] Add CDK stack and minimal IAM
  - [x] Add Lambda handlers and local runner shim
  - [x] Add README with quickstart and architecture notes
  - [x] Add unit tests and CI synth/lint/build steps

Related work and tracking: references Linear ENG-4123 for multi-step orchestration patterns and DOCS-88 for examples consolidation. This is a self-contained example and does not change Redwood SDK behavior.

Migration notes: this is an additive examples folder; no breaking changes. See release notes below for where to find the example in the docs site tree.

If reviewers prefer a different streaming approach (activities vs EventBridge) I can follow up with an alternate branch and a short doc linking pros/cons.

Adds an interactive RAG sandbox demonstrating batched tool-calls, streaming tool output examples, and a notebook-playground with smoke tests. No breaking API changes.
Motivation: provide a compact, opinionated example that demonstrates how to safely batch tool-calls in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) flows on Redwood, while preserving streaming responsiveness and predictable unit economics. This sandbox is intended for engineers evaluating batching trade-offs (latency vs cost), authoring tool contracts, and validating streaming partial results inside notebooks.

This PR introduces: 1) a sandbox runner that executes RAG sessions with configurable batch windows and a mock tool registry that supports both sync and streaming tool protocols; 2) a Jupyter/Colab-friendly notebook that walks through the lifecycle (index -> query -> tool-call batching -> streaming aggregation -> result normalization); 3) TypeScript and Python example bindings for the sandbox runner so teams can copy/paste into their projects; 4) a minimal e2e smoke harness that runs the sandbox locally in CI; 5) docs and a short tutorial in the examples README describing when to use batching and common pitfalls.

Checklist:
- [x] Add sandbox runner and tool registry (ts/python)
- [x] Notebook walkthrough with stepwise assertions
- [x] Samples showing batched vs unbatched metrics (latency/cost)
- [x] CI smoke test that verifies no regressions in sandbox runner
- [x] Docs and README + quickstart command
- [x] Code comments and lightweight diagrams in README

Testing notes: CI runs the smoke harness that starts a lightweight mocked Redis cache and spawns the sandbox with three simulated tool providers (fast, slow-stream, batched-worker). The harness asserts that: 1) batched requests reduce total token count to simulated model backend by >=12% in the example workload; 2) streaming tools surface partial payloads within 300ms after tool-worker emits first chunk; 3) fallbacks to unbatched path occur cleanly if the batch window is exceeded. CI initially flaked on the streaming integration due to timing assumptions (see review comments), fixed by increasing mock tool backpressure timeouts and adding jitter-resilient assertions.

Usage: 'examples/rag-batched-sandbox/README.md' contains quickstart commands; the notebook lives at 'examples/rag-batched-sandbox/notebooks/batched_tool_demo.ipynb'. The TypeScript sample is 'examples/rag-batched-sandbox/ts-client' and Python sample is 'examples/rag-batched-sandbox/py-client'.

Notes on design decisions: the sandbox opts for an explicit batch window (configurable in ms) instead of implicit rate heuristics to keep the example easy to reason about. Tool-call bundling is demonstrated using a deterministic keying scheme (by tool and input-shard) to make it straightforward to map batched responses back to original requests. The streaming tool adapter uses chunked JSON-lines over a small websocket shim to remain implementation-agnostic for both hosted and private deployments.

Related work: this ties to ENG-2146 (inference batching policy RFC) and the 'streaming partial results' doc in the runtime folder.
Diego Marquez: Please add a short note about how the batch window interacts with the runtime's prefix caching; otherwise looks good.
Priya Anand: Suggest extracting the deterministic keying logic into a small util with unit tests to avoid duplication in ts/py clients.
Elliot Chan: CI flaked on streaming assertions — increased timeouts locally helped. Can we make assertions tolerant to jitter?
Sofia Park (author): responded with patch to add caching note, extracted keying util, and adjusted CI harness to use exponential backoff in assertions.

Motivation: onboarding teams building RAG-powered agents often need a realistic local environment that exercises tool-calling, external webhooks, and telemetry hooks without needing a production backend. This quickstart provides a lightweight sandbox: a local webhook simulator, a pluggable tool adapter for Node and Python, an interactive debugger UI for stepping through agent decisions, and Redwood Console telemetry wiring examples.

What this PR adds (high level):
- quickstarts/rag-webhook-sandbox/: a self-contained playground with an Express-based webhook simulator (TypeScript) and a small Python tool adapter to demonstrate cross-language tooling.
- debug/ui/: minimal Electron-based interactive debugger that attaches to the local runner, displays decision traces, KV cache snapshots, and allows replaying single-turn interactions.
- devcontainer.json + .github/workflows/quickstart-smoke.yml to let contributors run the sandbox in Codespaces or CI and validate the smoke tests.
- docs: README with step-by-step runbook, example telemetry dashboards JSON for Redwood Console, and migration notes for existing RAG quickstarts.

Key features and rationale:
- Webhook simulator reproduces common failure modes (slow responses, transient 500s, JSON schema drift) so developers can build robust tool-call error handling and fallback policies.
- Instrumentation hooks export structured events compatible with Redwood Console: prompt tokens, model name, tool call metadata, webhook latency, and sandbox trace IDs. That makes it easy to wire the quickstart into per-route dashboards.
- Interactive debugger focuses on reproducibility: snapshot/restore of KV cache, replay deterministic seed for stochastic models, and step-through of the agent’s tool resolution logic. This is intentionally minimal (no heavy UI) to keep the surface area small while proving the UX.

Checklist: 
- [x] Add TypeScript webhook simulator and example payloads
- [x] Add Python adapter demonstrating tool invocation and error handling
- [x] Add debugger UI and CLI to attach/detach traces
- [x] Add devcontainer configuration and README runbook
- [x] Add CI smoke test workflow that runs an end-to-end scenario

How to run locally (short):
1) cd quickstarts/rag-webhook-sandbox && pnpm install && pnpm run start:simulator
2) In another shell run the local runner: pnpm run start:runner (or python -m quickstart_adapter.app for Python adapter)
3) Open debug/ui (npm install && npm run start) to attach to the running trace id printed by the runner.

Compatibility and upgrade notes:
- No breaking changes to existing quickstarts. The telemetry events are additive; their schema is documented in the README.
- The debugger uses the same agent instrumentation interfaces already present in the SDK; only examples are added.

Testing: CI contains a quickstart-smoke job that boots the simulator and runner and performs three scripted interactions (success, webhook 500->retry, slow response timeout), asserting the runner recovers and emits expected telemetry events.

Related work: Builds on ideas from ENG-2248 (RAG dev feedback loop) and the local replay work in PM-431.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the telemetry schema consistency, the small surface area of the debugger, and the smoke test determinism. For any suggestions to expand the simulator failure modes, prefer adding them as follow-ups to keep this PR reviewable.

Ethan Morales (review): Nice focused scope — left two nits around telemetry field names and a suggestion to normalize trace_id -> sandbox_trace_id. Please address in a follow-up if you prefer a smaller merge.

Context: Customers running the Private (on-prem / air-gapped) installer reported two recurring requirements: (1) the ability to verify vendor bundles with cryptographic signatures before install to satisfy security/compliance policies, and (2) out-of-the-box runtime artifacts that match Ubuntu 20.04 LTS (focal) node images used by several enterprise customers. This PR implements signed offline bundles plus vendored .deb runtime packages and adds installer-side verification + a documented key rotation flow.

Summary of changes: add GPG signing workflow for generated airgap bundles, include a minimal set of Ubuntu Focal .deb runtime artifacts (glibc/backports + kernel-headers pinned), verify signatures during preflight, extend the installer CLI to accept a --trusted-keys path or use the built-in bundle keyring, and add a rollback-safe unpack path when signature checks fail. Also includes documentation for operators (key rotation, emergency revoke) and CI coverage for signature verification.

Checklist:
- [x] Add signing key generation and verification helpers
- [x] Vendor focal runtime .deb artifacts and metadata in slim bundle variant
- [x] Installer preflight verifies signature and package checksums
- [x] CLI flag --trusted-keys and key rotation docs
- [x] Integration test that exercises an unsigned-bundle failure and a successful signed-bundle path
- [x] Release notes and upgrade guidance

Why this approach: Signing bundles gives a minimal, auditable trust boundary for air-gapped installs without requiring an external KMS. Vendor .deb artifacts for focal are limited to runtime packages that customers commonly lock on (libc, udev, iproute2) to reduce drift between the runtime the installer configures and customer node OS. The verification happens pre-extract so we avoid partially-applied installs and preserve rollback semantics.

Related: builds on some prework in ENG-8320 (airgap bundle refactor), and addresses SUP-1286 customer asks about offline verification.
James Kline: Please expand the docs section with specific guidance for rotating keys in an unattended environment. Also confirm that the keyring format is compatible with upstream apt-key deprecation.
Aditi Shah: replied: added key-rotation steps and switched to 'trusted.gpg.d' style keyring for compatibility; documented migration from apt-key in docs/airgap/signing-keys.md.
Sofia Martinez: Can we limit the focal package set further? shipping fewer packages reduces bundle size. Suggest dropping kernel-headers unless strictly required.
Aditi Shah: replied: reduced the set to only libc6, libssl, iproute2, udev, and busybox for init helpers; kept kernel-headers out of the slim bundle and documented the rationale.
Ravi Patel: integration test flake on CI referencing a timeout — looks like the e2e runner had network hiccup when downloading test fixtures; will re-run CI after addressing retry in test harness.
James Kline: APPROVED after comments addressed. Will squash-merge once e2e stability confirmed.
- Added cryptographic signing for airgap/offline bundles. Installer now verifies bundle signatures and checksums before extraction.
- Vendor-matched runtime packages for Ubuntu 20.04 (focal) included in slim bundle variant to reduce OS drift for customers on focal.
- New CLI flag --trusted-keys and operator docs for key rotation and emergency revoke.

Operator guidance: existing airgap bundles are still supported. To use signing, generate or import a signing key and populate --trusted-keys before running install. See docs/airgap/signing-keys.md for command examples. No automatic migration is performed; operators must coordinate key rollout across nodes.
This PR touches offline bundles and the slim runtime set. Validate installation on Ubuntu 20.04 testbeds and ensure the signed-bundle verification is part of the release smoke test. Coordinate with the SRE team before enabling signed-bundle enforcement by default.

payload.body: Context: Customers deploying Redwood Private in regulated regions require a deployment-side guard that enforces data residency policies and proves KMS key origins to downstream audit systems. This PR introduces a lightweight residency-gate middleware and a KMS-origin attestation flow integrated into the private installer. Motivation: existing region-pin checks lived only at the control plane and were bypassable during air-gap installs; we need an installer-time and runtime assertion that 1) inbound tenant configs are residency-compliant, 2) customer CMKs are bound to an allowed region, and 3) every installation emits a signed audit envelope asserting key provenance for later verification. Changes: implemented residency_gate middleware (pkg/middleware/residency_gate.go) that validates tenant metadata against installer-configured geozones and rejects non-compliant onboarding attempts; added envelope_signer (pkg/audit/envelope_signer.go) to produce RFC-compliant signed audit envelopes containing: tenancy id, key ARN/alias, key region, installer fingerprint, and timestamp; templated KMS attestation artifacts for the installer (cmd/installer/templates/kms-attest.yaml) so on-prem installers can perform a signed attestation step with local KMS or HSM; added helm values file (deploy/helm/values-residency.yaml) to enable residency-mode toggles and key scoping policies; included an integration test harness (test/integration/residency_gate_test.go) exercising permitted and blocked flows; migration helper (scripts/migrate/kek_rebind.sh) to assist operators re-binding tenant KEKs to region-scoped CMKs during residency enablement. Security considerations: signer uses customer-managed KEK when available; fallback to installer-scoped ephemeral KEK is explicitly logged as lower-trust and requires operator acknowledgement; all audit envelopes are hashed and stored in the installer audit log with transparent headers for downstream forwarders. Backwards compatibility: residency gate is opt-in via helm value residency.enabled=false by default; enabling flips admission behavior and will reject previously-allowed non-compliant tenant records until migration script is run. Testing: unit tests for middleware and signer, integration test matrix across three geozones and local KMS emulator, and an end-to-end smoke run in CI. CI: initial run showed a flaky integration test (timing-sensitive KMS emulator); fixed by adding a readiness probe and reran — CI passed. Rollout plan: merge to main behind feature flag; coordinate a staged rollout with installed customers via cherrypick channel; recommend operators run scripts/migrate/kek_rebind.sh in a maintenance window; record attested envelopes to customer-provided audit storage if configured. Related: references ENG-1452 for policy model and SEC-2021 for audit envelope format. Checklist: [x] design doc linked [x] unit tests [x] integration tests [x] docs (docs/security/residency-gate.md) [x] migration helper [x] security review. Reviewer notes and thread summary: Aisha: requested clearer failure modes in middleware (replies: added explicit error codes and operator guidance in docs and tests); Dmitri: asked to make envelope format compatible with existing audit-forwarder schema (replies: added normalization layer in envelope_signer and example forwarder mapping in docs); Marta: asked for a non-ephemeral fallback warning in the installer UI and a prominent helm value description (replies: added helm value notes and UI warning stub). Merge: squashed and merged after approvals. Release notes: "Installer: opt-in residency-gate middleware and KMS origin attestation; installer now supports signed audit envelopes for key provenance. See docs/security/residency-gate.md for migration steps." Breaking change: false

payload.body:
Motivation: private on‑prem/VPC upgrades require greater atomicity and preflight validation to avoid partial rollouts and long rollback windows. This PR introduces a small release staging layer, Helm preflight hooks (pre-install/pre-upgrade/validate), and a compact compression/packing step for release manifests and provenance files so that the installer can stage an entire release snapshot atomically and validate it before switching the live release pointer. Design summary: 1) release-stager: an ephemeral staging area in S3/GCS with an atomic 'active' pointer object; publish pipeline uploads a packed, signed archive and a JSON index; after successful post-signature validations the pipeline atomically swaps a symlink-style object (bucket key replace) to make the new release active; 2) manifest packing: index_pack.go creates deterministic tar stream, zstd compresses blobs with level 3 for speed, and the pack includes SHA256 provenance metadata for each entry to simplify verification during installs; 3) Helm preflight hooks: small Helm hooks run before install/upgrade to validate node resources, image accessibility, KMS availability, and required CRDs; failures are surfaced early and abort the Helm transaction; 4) installer/rollback: upgrade tool gains a two-phase apply with an automatic dry-run validation and a deterministic rollback plan derived from the staged index so rollbacks are fast and do not rely on ad-hoc heuristics. CI changes: new pipeline job ci/pipelines/release-stager.yml validates packing/compression, runs signature verification, and performs a smoke deploy to minikube in under 6 minutes. Security: signing routine ensures reproducible tar order before cosign signing and inserts a small attestation with build-info and builder git-ref. Backwards compatibility: published archives include both packed zstd artifact and legacy uncompressed blobs to allow older private-installer clients to continue fetching if necessary; rollout plan includes a two-week dual-read window before deprecating legacy path. Testing: unit tests for packer and signature validator, integration tests for staged swap and Helm preflight, and manual canary in a staging VPC. Rollout: merge -> pipeline produces staged artifact -> run canary promotion job -> after 24h and monitoring approval, auto-swap active pointer for production. See release_notes for more details and migration steps.
Diego Ramirez: Great direction — two questions: (1) how do we guarantee the atomic swap across S3/GCS and avoid partial reads during swap? (2) can we keep a short-lived dual-read window by default?
Asha Patel: Response: swap implemented by an object-replace with versioned buckets and a linearizable head object; we add a small retry backoff (100ms) during installs to handle eventual consistency edge-cases. Dual-read window set to 48h by default configurable via TF module.
Sophie Nguyen: Can we validate KMS availability earlier? Helm hook runs a KMS health-check and fails fast; added unit tests for simulating KMS timeout.
Evelyn Clark: Nit: packer code needs a deterministic file ordering comment and a test. Addressed in commit 'test(pack): add deterministic-order test'
Diego Ramirez: CI failure on first run (integration timeout) — re-run fixed it and logs show transient minikube image pull issue. Verified in subsequent run. Approved after green CI.
Pipeline: release-stager (pack -> sign -> verify) passed; e2e minikube smoke test passed; linters passed. First CI run timed out on minikube image pull, rerun was green.
- Introduces atomic release staging: publishes a packed, signed artifact and atomically swaps the active release pointer in object storage.
- Adds deterministic packing and zstd compression for release manifests and provenance, reducing release size and improving upload latency.
- Adds Helm preflight hooks (pre-install, pre-upgrade) to validate cluster preconditions and abort unsafe rollouts.
- Upgrade tool now generates a deterministic rollback plan from staged indexes to make rollbacks reliable and fast.
- Backwards compatibility: staged artifacts include legacy uncompressed blobs for a configurable dual-read window.
- CI: new release-stager pipeline with minikube smoke test and signature validation.
Unit: packer deterministic order, zstd roundtrip, signature verify. Integration: staged swap + Helm preflight on minikube. Manual: canary promoted to staging VPC and monitored for 48 hours before prod promotion.
1) Operators: update terraform module for release bucket to enable versioning and object-lock suggested setting. 2) If you run on very old installer clients: keep legacy-read enabled (env RELEASE_LEGACY_READ=true) until clients are upgraded. 3) To opt into atomic swap immediately, set release_stager_enabled = true in tf module and run apply. 4) To roll back a staged release: use tools/upgrade/plan_and_rollback --release <name> --rollback-to <timestamp> which calculates deterministic steps from the packed index.
This PR is intentionally conservative about compression level to prioritize install speed on constrained customer networks. We plan to introduce optional higher compression for air-gapped distribution in a follow-up change.
If a production install reports 'manifest-signature-mismatch' after promotion, fall back to previous active pointer (stager.undo_swap) and open SUP ticket; artifacts remain in the staging bucket for forensic analysis.
installer: atomic release staging, deterministic manifest packing, Helm preflight hooks, and deterministic rollback plans (Asha Patel)
payload.title: atomic release staging, Helm preflight hooks, and compressed release manifests for safer private-installer rollouts

payload.body:
Motivation: Private/on-prem customers running air-gapped or tightly controlled environments need deterministic upgrade outcomes. Two common failure modes we've seen in incidents are (1) unintended Terraform resource churn during apply and (2) missing chart artifacts or image references in airgapped clusters. This PR introduces three coordinated pieces: a Terraform plan guard (installer/terraform/modules/plan_guard) that enforces an allowlist and diff threshold before apply; a Helm airgap shim (installer/helm/airgap-shim) that stages and validates all chart assets and image digests ahead of rolling upgrades; and a migration simulator tool (installer/tools/migration_simulator) that can run DB/KV schema migrations in dry-run mode against a snapshot to detect incompatible changes before an in-place upgrade. Summary of changes: - installer/terraform/modules/plan_guard: new module that wraps terraform plan/apply with a preflight validator (configurable thresholds, allow/deny rules, and auto-approve gating). - installer/helm/airgap-shim: small utility and chart hooks to bundle required tarballs and image digests, validate registry replacement maps, and produce a signed asset manifest for offline clusters. - installer/tools/migration_simulator: Go binary that can replay migration SQL/transform logic against a detached DB snapshot and emit a regression report with row-level checks and schema diffs. - installer/docs/upgrade-playbook.md: updated step-by-step including how to run the plan guard, use the airgap shim, run the migration simulator, and perform the orchestrated rollback if needed. - ci: added tests for plan_guard logic and a unit test harness for migration simulator using SQLite snapshots. Backwards compatibility: Plan guard is opt-in via a top-level flag in the Terraform root (guard_enabled = false by default) so existing automation is unaffected. The Helm shim is additive; it exposes an alternate release flow for airgapped installs. Migration simulator does not change runtime migration code; it is strictly a preflight tool. Testing and verification: - Local integration tested against a reproducible example cluster and a synthetic DB snapshot (see installer/examples/airgap-smoke). - Terraform plan guard tested with scenarios: benign diff, resource rename, and unexpected deletion; guard thresholds behaved as expected, blocking destroy-heavy plans. - Helm shim validated on an offline KIND cluster (chart assets served from local registry) and through OCI tarball manifests. - CI: unit tests and a small integration job passed on re-run; one flaky test in early runs (migration_simulator/sql_parser_test) was stabilized by simplifying the parser and adding a fixture. Rollback/runbook: The playbook documents a staged rollback orchestrator that leverages the plan guard's dry-run mode to detect residual drift and the airgap shim's manifest to re-seed missing artifacts. Steps include: 1) mark tenant for maintenance (installer/scripts/quarantine.sh), 2) snapshot current DB and object storage, 3) run migration simulator to verify revert path, 4) apply rollback release using Helm shim with signed manifest, 5) validate with smoke prompts and metrics. Security notes: Signed manifests use the existing KMS/HSM integration; the migration simulator never ships snapshots off-cluster unless explicitly exported by an operator. Known limitations: - Simulator currently supports primary Postgres schemas and a subset of KV transforms; complex stored procedures are not simulated. - Plan guard thresholds require tuning per customer workload. See upgrade-playbook for mitigation. Links: Linear ENG-2124 for the feature epic; a follow-up is tracked under INF-403 to add Postgres stored procedure simulation.
Add an optional pre-upgrade Terraform plan guard that blocks apply when drift or unexpected resource churn is detected; introduce a Helm 'airgap shim' that stages chart artifacts for disconnected clusters; include a local migration simulator that runs schema migrations in dry-run mode against an exported DB snapshot; provide an updated upgrade playbook documenting safe dice-roll rollback steps and verification commands.

Aisha Khan: Yes — added resource_level_thresholds and documented examples in plan_guard/README.
Samir Patel: Migration simulator is a great safety net. Can we add an explicit disclaimer about not running simulator in production DBs?
Aisha Khan: Added warning in simulator README and playbook; emphasized operator-only execution and snapshot requirement.
Miguel Ortega: CI flaked on sql parser; pushed a fix and re-run. Approving post-fix.
Priya Nair: Approve after docs update.
Miguel Ortega: Merged via squash after approvals.

Motivation: Current on-prem Terraform stack couples GPU node pools, IAM roles, and TF state layout into a single module which makes incremental upgrades and region/VPC splits brittle for customers. This PR separates concerns so operators can manage GPU pools, service IAM bindings, and backend state allocations independently, and adds a migration helper for existing installs. Summary of changes: - Introduce modules/private/gpu-pool: standalone GPU node pool module with explicit taint/affinity inputs and optional preemptible support. - Introduce modules/private/iam-bindings: declarative role attachment per-service-account instead of implicit role provisioning. - Change state layout: split tfstate per-vpc and per-gpu-subpool; moved bucket keys and lock prefixes to a configurable namespace. - Add tools/tfstate-migrator: small Go utility + Make target to perform in-place state moves and reparenting for customers upgrading from <1.4. - Update examples/private-onprem/ to show new module composition and a migration guide. - Add acceptance tests and CI tf-plan coverage for multi-vpc and single-vpc layouts. Checklist: [x] design doc linked in ENG-9123 [x] module unit tests [x] tf validate and plan coverage [x] migration helper smoke-tested in internal cluster [ ] docs/examples: one remaining snippet to be polished before full docs site update (follow-up). Testing notes: Local tf plan applied against mocked backend, migrator ran against snapshot state (see tools/tests/migrator_integration.log). CI run initially failed lint due to naming collisions in example vars, fixed in commit 6b3f9c. Risk & rollout: This is a user-facing change to state layout and requires operators to run the migrator for existing installs. New installs are unaffected by default if you leave state_namespace unset. I marked this as a breaking_change because rolling upgrades without running the migrator will lead to duplicate state files and lock contention. Migration plan is detailed in release_notes and migration_steps below. Commits summary: - Add standalone gpu-pool module and tests (morgan/feat/gpu-pool) - Extract iam-bindings from core module and add policy table (morgan/refactor/iam) - Introduce tfstate namespace and migrator utility (morgan/tool/tfstate-migrator) - Update example compositions and CI pipelines (morgan/chore/examples) - Fix lint and variable names (morgan/fix/lint) Review highlights: - Diego: requested clearer variable names and explicit migration opt-in flag; added opt-in flag migrated=true. - Priya: asked for RBAC least-privilege checks; added IAM policy JSON and tests. - Avery: flagged possible race on state lock; migrator now takes a lock/coordination flow and prints rollback hints. Merge notes: Squash-merged after CI passed and a quick production smoke on an internal staging cluster. See merged_at for timestamp.
Diego Marquez: Please add a migration opt-in flag and document the operator workflow.
Morgan Lee: Added 'migration.do_migrate' boolean and updated README with step-by-step. Also added dry-run mode to migrator.
Priya Narayanan: Can the IAM policies be scoped more narrowly? Suggested changes to remove broad storage admin binding.
Morgan Lee: Scoped down storage access to only the tfstate bucket prefix and added a dedicated reader role for monitoring.
Avery Singh: Noted potential lock contention during parallel migrator runs; added a locking annotation and coordination recommendation.
Avery Singh: Approved after we added lock/rollback guidance.
1) Read the release_notes and ensure operator has service account with tfstate-migrator role (see modules/private/iam-bindings/README.md).
2) Run tools/tfstate-migrator --dry-run against current remote state to enumerate moves and conflicts.
3) Run migrator with --do-migrate while holding maintenance window, it will take a lock on the backend and reparent state keys.
4) Apply updated terraform composition that references new modules and set state_namespace to the new value.
5) Verify resources in target TF state and run terraform plan in CI to ensure no diffs remain.
Private installer: decouple GPU nodepool, IAM bindings, and terraform state layout into discrete modules. New flag 'migration.do_migrate' and tools/tfstate-migrator included to assist upgrades. Existing installs must follow migration_steps to avoid duplicate state and lock contention. New installs are opt-in and backwards compatible when state_namespace is unset.
Added integration test that runs migrator against synthetic state, added dry-run mode, and documented operator rollback steps.
Follow-up PR planned to update docs site snippets and add a guided migration playbook for SRE onboarding. Also will add an automated migration job to the installer for enterprise customers.

Motivation: customers running on-prem developer clusters requested an officially supported microk8s air-gapped installer path. This PR introduces a microk8s-targeted offline bundle, a delta-based patcher to dramatically reduce archive size for incremental updates, Terraform/provider fixes to surface registry mirror and snap-specific hooks, and Helm chart adjustments so the runtime works consistently with microk8s networking and CRI defaults. Work includes: 1) new bundle layout under installer/airgap/bundles/microk8s with slim OCI layers and explicit snap hooks, 2) a delta_patcher service that computes binary deltas between bundle versions and an unpack-time apply step to keep download footprint small, 3) Terraform module changes to support microk8s node labeling, registry mirror variables, and a provider shim for the installer to write local registries, 4) Helm chart compatibility bits (service type normalization, tolerations, and adjusted readiness probes), 5) installer preflight checks that detect microk8s channel, snap versions, and available disk space, 6) test harness updates and CI job matrix expansion to include microk8s (snap) smoke tests. Checklist: - [x] bundle creation and signing - [x] delta patcher implementation and unit tests - [x] Terraform module updates and docs - [x] e2e smoke tests on microk8s-ubuntu and microk8s-coreos - [x] QA signoff and staged rollout plan.
Adds official microk8s air-gapped bundle and Terraform/provider compatibility; reduces offline bundle size via delta patching; installer now performs microk8s-specific preflight checks.

Motivation: Provide an idempotent, label-driven reconciliation engine that automates VPC peering, subnet ownership assignments, conditional security group attachments, and Route53 private DNS policy wiring for control plane private deployments. Many installers required manual peering and ad-hoc route updates during multi-account and multi-AZ rollouts; this PR introduces a declarative label surface (subnet:role=controlplane|egress|workload and subnet:owner=region/zone/team) and a controller that creates deterministic peering attachments, route propagation, and DNS forwarding records with safe rollback hooks. High-level changes: 1) Terraform module updates to network module to accept subnet labels and to expose peering resource metadata for external controllers; 2) New lightweight reconciler binary (installer/reconciler) that reads desired subnet labels from TF state or cluster config and performs peering/route53 actions via AWS APIs with exponential backoff and state checkpoints; 3) Helm chart changes to controlplane to add DNS glue environment and a readiness probe that verifies private-hosted-zone delegation before advertising endpoints; 4) Upgrade/rollback tooling: terraform plan integration with --dry-run reconciliation mode, a staged canary rollout for peering attachments, and a 'peering-safeclean' command that performs non-destructive teardown and verifies route/classic-record removal; 5) Acceptance and e2e smoke tests that simulate cross-account peering and conditional sg injection. The description below summarizes design, commits, files touched, testing, rollout and rollback instructions, and outstanding follow-ups. Checklist: [x] Add subnet label TF variables and outputs [x] Implement reconciler CLI + unit tests [x] Helm chart: add dnsGlue config + probe [x] Add smoke/e2e tests in perf-canary harness [x] Document runbook and rollback steps [x] CI passing on integration runner. Commits summary: feat(tf): add subnet labels and peering metadata outputs; feat(reconciler): initial controller + checkpointing; fix(reconciler): backoff & idempotency on duplicate attachments; feat(helm): dns-glue env + readiness probe; test(e2e): add cross-account peering smoke; docs: runbook and upgrade notes. Files changed (high level): installer/terraform/modules/network/variables.tf, installer/terraform/modules/network/outputs.tf, installer/terraform/modules/network/peering.tf, installer/reconciler/main.go, installer/reconciler/checkpoint.go, installer/reconciler/aws_client.go, installer/helm/charts/controlplane/values.yaml, installer/helm/charts/controlplane/templates/dns-glue-configmap.yaml, installer/helm/charts/controlplane/templates/readiness-probe.yaml, tests/perf-canary/e2e/peering_smoke_test.go, docs/runbooks/private-controlplane-peering.md, scripts/peering-safeclean.sh, ci/integration/reconciler_integration.yml. Testing performed: unit tests for reconciler (covering duplicate-peering, transient API failures), integration job against a long-running dev AWS account (peering create/accept/route-sync), Helm chart acceptance where readiness probe blocks traffic until DNS glue is present, and an e2e smoke that validated Route53 resolver rules in a shared-hosted-zone configuration. Rollout plan: 1) Deploy TF changes with --target module.network and capture outputs; 2) Run reconciler in --dry-run mode to assert intended peering actions; 3) Rollout reconciler as pre-deploy job to create peering attachments; 4) Deploy controlplane Helm chart (first canary AZ, then global) and validate readiness; 5) Promote reconciler to 'managed' mode to perform route and DNS record updates. Rollback plan: reconciler supports --reconcile-mode=dry|apply|revert; to revert, run --reconcile-mode=revert which performs non-destructive withdrawal of routes and peering attachments while preserving checkpoints to avoid accidently removing shared resources. Security notes: peers are created with restricted security groups and a deterministic tag format (redwood:peering=<cluster>-<env>) so automated cleanup and billing attribution works. Migration notes: Existing installs without subnet labels are supported via a discovery mode (reconciler infers role by CIDR -> az mapping) but will log a migration suggestion to add labels. Outstanding follow-ups: add GCP/Azure provider adapters (tracked ENG-1903), expand RBAC around reconciler KMS usage, and add more granular CircuitBreaker controls in the reconciler to avoid mass-peering during region faults. Merge rationale: validated in integration, adds safe rollback paths and non-breaking terraform outputs; decided to squash merge to keep tf history compact.
Marcus Liu: Can the reconciler avoid creating peering across accounts that are in a billing relationship edge-case? Please add a guard and a dry-run abort on suspicious cross-account pairings.
Author (Ananya Rao): Added a preflight guard that checks allowed-account-list, and reconciler now emits a high-severity log and requires --force to proceed if accounts are not in allowlist.
Helen Park: Helm readiness probe looks good, but add a tolerance for eventual DNS propagation delays (60s -> 300s).
Author (Ananya Rao): Increased probe timeout to 300s and added a toggleable environment variable 'DNS_PROBE_TIMEOUT' to values.yaml.
Add label-driven subnet peering automation and DNS policy engine. Terraform exposes new subnet label inputs and peering metadata outputs. New reconciler binary performs idempotent peering, route and private-hosted-zone wiring with dry-run and revert modes. Helm controlplane chart gets DNS glue and readiness probe. Rollback-safe with 'revert' reconcile mode and peering-safeclean helper.
