Motivation and summary: This PR adds a migration rehearsal workflow that lets operators run a dry-run upgrade (including Helm hooks and DB schema migrations) against a shadow tenant environment and produces a tenant-impact score to prioritize rollouts. The goal is to reduce surprise rollbacks by surfacing: migration duration estimates, number of affected tenant tables, potential restore time, and a deterministic checksum timeline for assets created/removed during migration. The feature is intended for Private deployments (VPC and on-prem) where operators want an automated dry-run path that mirrors a real upgrade without touching live tenant data.

What this PR delivers (high level):
- rwi-migrate-rehearse: a CLI subcommand (installer/tools/migrate_rehearse.sh + Go binary shim) that orchestrates Terraform plan, Helm dry-run with hooks executed in a 'rehearsal' namespace, and a mocked-schema-migration runner that records operations to a migration journal.
- Tenant impact scoring service (installer/pkg/migration/impact): computes a score based on (estimated downtime, number of DB migrations, blob store deltas, rollback complexity). Output is a top-level human-readable report and machine-readable JSON artifact stored in the installer-state bucket.
- Helm chart changes: pre-upgrade hook job (templates/hooks/preflight-migration-job.yaml) capable of running migration rehearsals; hook tolerations and resource limits are conservative to avoid impacting control-plane nodes.
- Terraform changes: redwood_private_installer migration module now emits migration_plan_id and plan_summary outputs; adds a lifecycle rule to preserve rehearsal artifacts for 72 hours.
- Add-on helpers: migration-plan-diff utility that compares rehearsal journal to the current cluster state and surfaces unsafe file/secret modifications.

Checklist (manual run notes):
- [x] Add CLI glue and unit tests for tenant-impact scoring
- [x] Helm hook templates and e2e helm-dry-run integration test
- [x] Terraform outputs + docs for operators
- [x] CI e2e scenario added to perf-canary to exercise a rehearsal run

Testing and e2e: Rehearsal runs are covered by: (1) unit tests for scoring logic (pkg/migration/impact/*_test.go), (2) an integration fixture in tests/e2e/rehearse that spins up kind clusters and applies helm dry-run with the preflight job, and (3) a lightweight end-to-end canary job in deployment pipeline that validates artifact upload and plan_summary parsing. CI showed intermittent helm dry-run flakiness on older k8s versions; CI re-run passed (see ci section).

Backward compatibility and safety: This change is opt-in. Operators must enable rehearsal by setting installer.config.enableMigrationRehearsal=true in their values; by default the feature is off. Rehearsal artifacts are namespaced and use mocked migration runners unless operators opt into a read-only dry-run against a copy of tenant DB. No live tenant writes occur during default rehearsals.

Operational playbook (short):
1) terraform apply with migration module enabled (will create migration_plan_id output).
2) run rwi migrate rehearse --plan-id=<id> --tenant-sample=10 (creates artifacts under installer-state/<plan-id>/).
3) review migration-report.json and tenant-impact.json, act on high-impact tenants first, schedule canary/partial rollout.

Related work and links: Linear ENG-4201 (migration safety roadmap), ENG-4203 (rehearsal MVP). Follow-up items: automatic canary rollout integration (next PR), tighter credential scoping for rehearsal jobs.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the scoring heuristics (pkg/migration/impact/score.go), the Helm hook behavior during dry-run (templates/hooks/), and Terraform outputs (terraform/modules/migration/outputs.tf). The rehearsal uses a short-lived service account; make sure RBAC changes look reasonable.

Maya Chen (author): Replied that the scoring defaults to ignoring comment-only migrations; added unit tests and a whitelist config (pkg/migration/impact/config.go).
Priya Rao: Asked for an explicit RBAC review; flagged the preflight job ServiceAccount permissions for closer scrutiny.
Maya Chen: Reduced privileges on the rehearsal ServiceAccount and added an integration test that asserts no write verbs are allowed. Added documentation about operator approval required for enabling read-only DB dry-run.
Owen Li: Noted terraform state retention window; requested we keep rehearsal artifacts for 72 hours instead of 7 to allow postmortem analysis. Adjusted lifecycle rule accordingly.
Introduce optional migration rehearsal workflow and tenant-impact scoring. Adds CLI hook, Helm preflight job, Terraform outputs, and e2e tests. Opt-in feature for Private deployments to reduce rollback risk.
See docs/operator/migration_rehearsal.md for full runbook. Short path: terraform apply -> rwi migrate rehearse --plan-id=<id> --tenant-sample=10 -> review installer-state/<plan-id>/migration-report.json

Motivation: private deployments frequently require tenant-scoped GPU nodepools where the node identity and subnet selection are decoupled from the monolithic installer TF modules. This PR introduces two small, composable Terraform modules: (1) gpu_nodepool_identity_wrapper — a lightweight IAM/instance-profile wrapper that centralizes nodepool identity configuration (assume-role for workload operator, instance profile creation, and optional KMS encryption bindings), and (2) subnet_resolver — a deterministic subnet selection helper that locates matching subnets by tags, AZ affinity, and available IP capacity. Both are aimed at reducing per-tenant duplication in tfstate and making upgrades/rollbacks safer by confining state to narrower keys. For customers who want to migrate state into tenant-scoped tfstate prefixes we provide scripts/tfstate-prefix-transformer.sh with usage examples. Motivation: Reduce airgap bundle size and speed up node bootstrap on minimal distros by generating a sparse OCI lockfile and supporting unprivileged runtime bootstrapping. This PR implements a compact OCI index generator that computes a delta-aware manifest (sparse lockfile) so on-prem registries only need to store referenced layer blobs, and adds an opt-in unprivileged runtime bootstrapping path for systems without systemd or where installers run as a non-root operator. The change touches three areas: (1) mirroring pipeline: new mirroring script and Terraform module extensions to publish sparse lockfiles and sign them; (2) bootstrap runtime: a new runit/runc shim and containerd prefetch hook that runs under a control-plane service account to pull minimal images during node init; (3) upgrade and rollback hooks: an atomic apply flow that uses filesystem snapshots (zfs/btrfs fallback) to enable fast rollback when partial image syncs occur. Backwards compatibility: mirror registry still supports full bundles, nodes that don't opt into the sparse flow continue to use existing OCI manifests. Security: lockfiles are signed with GPG/KMS and verified by the bootstrapper; unprivileged pull uses a gated helper that only has pull scope. Includes docs and e2e tests. Testing: local mirror e2e with k3s and microk8s, upgrade/rollback smoke tests on a 3-node airgapped cluster. See linked Linear for rollout plan.

Author: added 'bootstrap.unprivileged.enabled' toggle and defaulted to false. Jared: Concern about ZFS-only rollback; added btrfs fallback and an explicit safety check in the hook. Diego: CI flake on macOS runner unrelated to PR; reran tests. Priya: Approved after adding brief runbook section. Jared: LGTM — merging once CI is green.

payload.body:
Problem: On private (VPC/on-prem) deployments we rotate KMS/HSM wrapping keys regularly. Existing sealed-secrets assets in clusters and stored backups are not automatically re-encrypted when a new KMS wrapping key is promoted, which causes unnecessary manual work during key rollovers and can lead to brief service disruptions during operator-driven rotations. Motivation: Automate safe re-encryption of SealedSecrets and provide a Terraform/Helm friendly hook so rotations can be coordinated from the control plane without human intervention. This PR introduces two pieces: 1) a lightweight controller 'sealedsecret-reconciler' that watches SealedSecret and Secret pairs and re-encrypts sealed payloads with the currently-active KMS key. 2) A 'kms-delegate-rotation-hook' Terraform module and Helm post-upgrade Job template that invokes the KMS rotation sequence and kicks the reconciler to perform staged rewrapping. Implementation highlights: - sealedsecret-reconciler: Go controller (controller-runtime) running as an opt-in Deployment in the private-installer chart. It observes a cluster-level ConfigMap containing the active-wrapping-key metadata and runs rewrap operations against SealedSecrets in a namespace-safe, rate-limited fashion. Rewraps are idempotent and include a short TTL on per-secret lock annotations to avoid thundering herds. - kms-delegate-rotation-hook: Terraform module (modules/kms_rotation_trigger) which emits a rotation token into the installer control plane (sealed in Vault or sent to the delegated KMS operator). The Helm chart includes a templated Job that, when triggered, posts a rotation event to the controller's endpoint and monitors progress via CR status. - Rollout safety: Controller performs a 3-stage rewrap (namespace batches -> 10% concurrency -> full) configurable via values.yaml. It respects bypass labels (redwood.io/skip-rewrap) and namespace allowlists. - Failure modes: On transient KMS errors the controller retries with exponential backoff and emits Prometheus metrics and events. If a rewrap set fails beyond retry limits, the controller marks a RotationStatus CR and creates a diagnostics Secret with a compact failure report. - Backups: As part of the hook we emit a pre-rotation sealed backup to a user-configurable Bucket/Vault path; post-rotation we create a verification manifest that lists rewrap checksums. - Security and audit: All rewrap operations are logged to the cluster audit log and to the installer control plane audit sink (when configured) including key fingerprint and operator identity. We never persist plaintext secrets outside ephemeral containers. - Testing: unit tests for controller logic and integration harness using KinD + Vault emulator. End-to-end smoke tests were added to the installer's CI pipeline (post-deploy rotations against a test KMS) and are gated behind the 'rotation' CI profile. Checklist: - [x] controller core, RBAC, and Helm hooks - [x] Terraform module + examples in examples/tf/kms-rotation - [x] integration tests (KinD + Vault) - [x] metrics, events, and audit logging - [x] docs (UPGRADING_ROTATIONS.md and chart README) - [x] staged rollout config and bypass labels Migration notes: - Default behavior is disabled. Operators must opt in via values: sealedsecretReconciler.enabled = true and provide delegateKMS config. - When enabled, the reconciler will only act on SealedSecrets created after the configured cutoff timestamp unless the operator explicitly triggers a full rewrap. Follow-ups (future PRs): - Add HSM PKCS#11 provider plugin for in-cluster operations (planned ENG-4279) - Automated validation against existing encrypted backups (UX improvements) - A CRD-driven UI in Console to visualize rotation progress Related: ENG-3321 (rotation playbook), SRE-198 (incident from manual rewrap).

Context: Private upgrades were relying on tribal knowledge for preflight checks and rollback readiness. Motivation: automate multi-AZ switchover for Private deployments and encode DR runbooks as code so runbooks are executable, testable, and versioned. This PR adds first-class support for mirroring Debian (apt) and RHEL/CentOS-style (yum/dnf) package repositories as part of the air-gapped installer bundles and introduces an image-manifest indexing step that powers the offline Helm chart index and the installer preflight verification. Motivation: customers in regulated environments commonly request reproducible on-prem bundles where OS/package artifacts are mirrored alongside container images; previously we only produced OCI tarballs and a simple image list which was error-prone for apt/yum pipelines. Changes: 1) new mirror tooling under install/packaging that builds a minimal apt repo (Packages.gz + Release + GPG signing hooks) and a yum repo layout with repomd.xml generation; 2) an image-manifest/index generator that emits a single index JSON connecting package artifacts, image tarballs, and Helm chart archives; 3) offline Helm chart modifications to read the generated index and resolve image references using mirror prefixes; 4) Terraform module inputs to configure mirror prefixes, preseed signing keys, and S3/HTTP storage backends for bundle hosting; 5) a new upgrade/rollback helper script (scripts/upgrade/rollback-airgap.sh) that validates the index, verifies checksums/signatures, and supports staged rollbacks by restoring prior index snapshots; 6) docs for maintainers and a new integration smoke test for mirrored bundles. Implementation notes: the apt/yum mirroring code is intentionally lightweight (no external apt-mirror deps) and designed to run inside our airgap-bundler container; we generate deterministic manifests with content-addressed filenames to make delta uploads easier; GPG signing is optional and controlled via terraform variable mirror_signing_key; Helm offline chart support uses a small pre-render hook to rewrite image refs at install-time when a mirror prefix is provided. Backward compatibility and upgrades: index format is versioned (index_version: "v1"); the installer supports legacy bundles by falling back to legacy-image-list.json when index v1 is absent; upgrade script migrates existing bundle layout to the new index and snapshots previous layout for rollback. Testing and validation: added unit tests for index generation, integration test that builds a tiny apt repo and validates apt-get update inside a container, and a CI job that runs a full bundle build on a smaller sample to exercise Terraform variables. Security: keys are never baked into bundles; the default flow uses a separate key export step and the installer reads from a provided key file during signing. Linear tickets and risk: ties to ENG-2248 for index spec and INF-331 for terraform inputs. This is scoped to the private-installer repo and should not affect hosted runtime. Merge notes: squash-merged; follow-up tasks include adding SUSE/zypper support in a subsequent PR and upstreaming the index schema to the model-registry for cross-product compatibility.

Context and motivation:

Customers running Redwood Private on on-prem and air-gapped clusters reported long first-request latencies when nodes needed to pull large model images during upgrades or initial installs (ENG-2145). In addition, tenant-init and migration jobs sometimes compete for resources during upgrades, causing transient pod evictions and partial rollouts. This PR introduces two related improvements aimed at hardening installs and upgrades for private deployments: (1) per-hook capacity profiles (values schema + templating helpers) so chart consumers can declare concurrent worker limits and probe thresholds for init/hook pods, and (2) an optional on-prem image pre-warm DaemonSet that proactively pulls configured images before they are required by runtime pods.

Summary of changes:
- Add values.schema.json entries for .hookProfiles and .onPremPrewarm with validation and examples.
- New chart helper templates (templates/_hook-capacity.tpl, templates/_prewarm-helpers.tpl) to render resource and affinity overrides and a stable graceful-shutdown annotation consumed by hooks.
- Add templates/prewarm-daemonset.yaml: conditional DaemonSet that runs as a low-priority, node-local image puller and exposes metrics for progress. The DaemonSet is optional and disabled by default.
- Add templates/hook-postinstall-stager.yaml: lightweight PostInstall Job wrapper that respects capacity profile settings and emits a readiness marker to coordinate rollout waves.
- Update NOTES.txt to surface pre-warm status and next steps for operators.

Checklist:
- [x] values schema coverage for new keys
- [x] Unit tests for helper templates (helm template smoke)
- [x] Small integration smoke run in CI (helm template + kubeval)
- [x] Docs: add brief usage note to chart README (screenshot/examples deferred to follow-up)

Commits (high-level):
- a1b2c3d: add values.schema.json entries and README example for hookProfiles and onPremPrewarm
- d4e5f6g: implement prewarm DaemonSet template + RBAC and serviceaccount glue
- h7i8j9k: add helper templates and postinstall stager job; update NOTES and tests

Files changed (high level):
- values.schema.json (modified) -- add validation blocks for .hookProfiles and .onPremPrewarm

payload.body:
Summary: This PR adds a safe, deterministic “admin bootstrap” path for RBAC v2 in Redwood Private installs to prevent lockout under deny-by-default. On first install/upgrade (when RBAC v2 is enabled), the installer will create an initial role binding granting a built-in admin role to a customer-specified subject (email or IdP group). This also documents the recommended approach for mapping IdP groups (SAML/OIDC) to Redwood roles in Private.

Context / Motivation: As we roll RBAC v2 into Private, new clusters can end up with RBAC enforcement enabled before any role bindings exist, resulting in a hard lockout where no identity has permissions to create the first role binding. Hosted/Dedicated can rely on internal provisioning workflows; Private needs an install-time “seed” that is explicit, auditable, and easy for customers to configure. This PR implements the minimum bootstrap mechanism (one initial binding + recovery tooling) and ties it to policy bundle versions so that it remains consistent across upgrades.

What’s included:
- Installer config/values to specify a bootstrap admin identity:
  - `rbacV2.bootstrapAdmin.email` (single user email)
  - OR `rbacV2.bootstrapAdmin.idpGroup` (IdP group string as emitted in claims)
  - Mutually exclusive; installer fails fast if both are set.
- Install/upgrade hook that (idempotently) creates:
  - RoleBinding: `bootstrap-admin` scoped to the org created by the installer (and cluster scope where required for installer-only operations)
  - Role: `org_admin` (reference to built-in template from the policy bundle; no ad-hoc permission list in installer)
  - Annotation: `rbac.redwood.ai/bootstrap=true` and `rbac.redwood.ai/policyBundleVersion=<version>` on the binding for evidence/debug.
- Explicit behavior gating:
  - No-op unless `RBAC_V2_ENABLED=true` (or Helm equivalent `rbacV2.enabled: true`).
  - If RBAC v2 is enabled but no bootstrap subject is provided, installer prints a blocking error with next steps (including recovery command) rather than proceeding.
- Recovery / break-fix command:
  - Adds `rwctl rbac bootstrap-admin --email <user>` and `rwctl rbac bootstrap-admin --idp-group <group>`.
  - Requires local cluster admin kubeconfig (i.e., this is a cluster-operator action) and emits an audit event `rbac.bootstrap_admin_binding.created`.
- Docs:
  - Adds a Private guide section: “Mapping IdP groups to Redwood RBAC roles” with examples for Okta (SAML), Azure AD (OIDC), and generic OIDC.
  - Documents recommended separation of duties: use a group-based binding for day-to-day admin, and keep a small break-glass user separate.

Implementation notes:
- Uses Control Plane RBAC v2 APIs when available; falls back to writing the RoleBinding CRD directly if the Control Plane is not yet reachable during install. Both paths converge on the same schema and labels.
- Idempotency: binding create is upsert-like. If the binding exists, installer verifies the subject and role match the requested config; if they differ, installer fails with a clear message to avoid silently escalating or breaking access.
- Scoping: bootstrap binding is created at org scope; additionally, for installer-required cluster-level operations (e.g., registering the cluster, health checks), a minimal `private_cluster_operator` role binding is created only when `rbacV2.bootstrapAdmin.includeClusterOps=true` is set. Default is false.
- Audit: for both installer and `rwctl` flows, we emit an audit log event containing subject type (user vs group), subject identifier, role template name, scope, and policy bundle version.

Config examples (Helm values):
- Email bootstrap:
  - `rbacV2.enabled: true`
  - `rbacV2.bootstrapAdmin.email: "security-admin@customer.com"`
- Group bootstrap:
  - `rbacV2.enabled: true`
  - `rbacV2.bootstrapAdmin.idpGroup: "Redwood-Org-Admins"`

Docs excerpt: For OIDC, ensure your IdP includes groups in the ID token or userinfo response and that the claim name configured in Redwood matches. Example: `oidc.groupClaim: "groups"` and then bind `rbacV2.bootstrapAdmin.idpGroup` to a string present in that claim.

Testing:
- Added an integration test that brings up a minimal Private control plane with RBAC v2 enabled and asserts:
  - Bootstrap RoleBinding is created.
  - A user with matching email can call `/v1/orgs/{id}/roles:list` (sanity check).
  - A non-matching identity receives `PERMISSION_DENIED`.
- Added unit tests for config validation, idempotent upsert behavior, and Control Plane unavailable fallback path.

Operational considerations:
- Upgrade path: If upgrading an existing cluster to RBAC v2, bootstrap binding is only created if no admin bindings exist (to avoid changing existing customer setups). Installer logs whether it created or skipped bootstrap.
- Evidence: The binding annotations and audit event are intended to be attachable in SOC2 evidence packets for “authorized administrators provisioned via documented process”.

Related:
- Linear: ENG-18410 (Private installer admin bootstrap), ENG-18388 (feature-flag rollout)
- Follow-up (not included): Add Console copy linking to Private docs for group claim troubleshooting; tracked in DES-927.

Checklist:
- [x] Idempotent bootstrap binding creation
- [x] Fast-fail on misconfiguration (both email and group)
- [x] Audit event emitted
- [x] Docs for IdP group mapping (SAML/OIDC)
- [x] Integration tests for fresh install
Marcus Lin: Please ensure we never proceed with RBAC v2 enabled and no bootstrap binding (deny-by-default lockout). Also need an auditable marker on the bootstrap binding and an audit event for evidence.
Benji Okafor: Agreed. Added blocking validation + annotations `rbac.redwood.ai/bootstrap=true` and policy bundle version, and emitted `rbac.bootstrap_admin_binding.created` from both installer and rwctl paths. Pushed 2 more commits.
Kaitlyn Nguyen: For OIDC group mapping, customers will be confused about claim names vs group values. Can we add a doc example showing the `groupClaim` setting and what group strings look like?
Benji Okafor: Added OIDC section with Okta + Azure AD examples and explicit note about claim name matching, plus troubleshooting commands to inspect token claims.
Ines Carvalho: Scope question: Do we need cluster-scope permissions for the bootstrap user? I’d prefer least privilege by default.
Benji Okafor: Default remains org-admin only; cluster ops binding is opt-in via `includeClusterOps`. Installer logs which scopes were created.
Vivek Kulkarni: For pilot customers, we should recommend group-based bootstrap (not a single person). Also call out a break-glass user separately.
Benji Okafor: Added docs guidance: primary admin via group binding + separate break-glass user. Also clarified that bootstrap binding can be rotated by creating a new binding and deleting the bootstrap one.

Motivation: Customers deploying on bare-metal and EFI-only nodes reported intermittent failures during initial local OCI registry seeding and node preflight in air-gapped sites. This PR introduces a focused end-to-end implementation: 1) a small, deterministic OCI vendor indexer that produces per-distro granular manifests (so installations only pull necessary artifacts for a given distro/arch), 2) a registry-seed job that supports EFI-only boot paths and ensures images required by kubelet and the runtime are pre-provisioned, and 3) a safer upgrade model that favors atomic rollforward deltas and a promotion hook instead of in-place rollbacks to reduce boot-time drift in constrained environments. Changes are implemented across Terraform modules (registry mirror + seeding IAM/ACLs), Helm charts (chart hooks and tolerations for bare-metal init jobs), and the installer preflight/upgrade orchestration. Checklist: - [x] Add per-distro OCI indexing and lockfile generation - [x] Terraform: new module registry-mirror/v1 with OCI seed job IAM and minimal subnet examples - [x] Helm: offline-seed job as Job + pre-install hook with hostPath for EFI artifacts, affinity rules for bare-metal - [x] Installer: preflight verifies EFI bootloader artifacts and pin TLS cert thumbprints for registry seeds - [x] Tests: e2e on kubeadm (bare-metal lab) and k3s single-node air-gapped simulate. Backwards compatibility: indexer emits an OCI lockfile compatible with our existing sealed-bundle seeding flow; the Terraform module is additive and guarded behind a feature flag. Rollforward strategy: instead of attempting a full rollback in air-gapped sites where image churn is constrained, the promote hook applies an atomic delta bundle with explicit retention rules; operators can still trigger a manual rollback but the default path minimizes partial-state failure. Related: references PR #427501 (seed minimal vendor), #51203 (signed bundles) and design doc ENG-6890-oci-indexing (internal).
Arjun Patel: Please split the large main.go into indexer + util packages; testability is hard otherwise.
Maya Chen: Split applied in commit c3d6a9f; indexer/utils separated and unit tests added.
Lena Morales: Can we avoid hostPath usage where possible? HostPath is required here to stage EFI blobs for grub-install on some vendor images; added tight path + doc note.
Samir Gupta: Terraform plan shows IAM role created with broad perms; tightened to s3:GetObject and ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability in b2e5d7a.
Ops: e2e run failed first run due to missing mtls cert; fixed by pinning thumbprints in d4f7b1e and rerun CI which passed.
Kubeadm bare-metal lab: seeded local OCI mirror via registry-mirror module, validated kubelet pulled vendor images from mirror without internet access.
K3s airgap simulation: single-node install with minimal lockfile validated drift-free promotion behavior across 2 upgrades.
Cross-arch: indexer exercised for amd64 and aarch64 lockfile outputs; small delta observed for initramfs artifacts and handled by manifest filter.
Adds distro-granular OCI indexer and a registry-mirror Terraform module to support EFI-only bare-metal seeding; Helm chart adds offline-seed job and installer preflight includes EFI artifact checks and TLS thumbprint pinning. Upgrade model updated to prefer atomic rollforward promotion for air-gapped sites.
Design rationale: we observed multiple partial-install failures where installers attempted to download unnecessary initramfs/kernel variants; the new indexer narrows the set to distro+arch+kernel flavor which reduces mirror size and speeds seeding. The rollforward approach reduces manual rollback churn for operators in disconnected environments. Operational playbook and runbook snippets added to docs/installer/offline-seeding.md.
payload.title: Bare-metal EFI registry seeding and distro-granular OCI indexer with safe rollforward upgrades

Motivation: Private deployments need stronger guarantees around restore correctness and safe downgrade/rollback behavior. Operators and installers must be able to verify a candidate restore will succeed before switching traffic or completing an upgrade. This PR adds a lightweight runtime "restore validation prober" that performs idempotent, incremental dry-run restores against a quarantined namespace and surfaces deterministic compatibility failures, plus a version compatibility adapter that maps cluster operator and helm chart versions to a validated restore strategy.

Summary of changes: added a controller-based prober that spins up a namespaced restore sandbox, replays logical WAL/checkpoints (or S3 snapshots in air-gapped mode), validates schema migrations via a read-only migration runner, and emits a RestoreValidation CRD with outcome and deterministic failure codes. The prober is tolerant to partial restores and supports incremental resume/retry with locked checkpoints. A new compatibility adapter translates operator/CRD/helm release versions into a prober runbook (preflight steps, allowed downgrade gaps, migration shim selection). Helm chart changes add pre-upgrade hooks and a restore-sanitizer Job template; Terraform module updates expose new variables for snapshot retention and restore-test toggles.

Why this is different: previous work focused on backups, checksums, and manual rollout guardrails. This PR automates preflight validation of restores and encodes version-aware runbooks to avoid unsafe downgrades. It supports both VPC and on-prem installer modes and includes an air-gap-friendly S3 replay path.

Checklist: - [x] Add RestoreValidation CRD and controller - [x] Helm: add templates for restore-sanitizer job & pre-upgrade hook - [x] Terraform: expose backup module flags to run prober in CI - [x] Add migration runner for read-only schema validation - [x] Wire audit events to operator logs + console metrics - [x] Add unit + e2e tests against a local Kind cluster and an air-gapped smoke harness

Testing & verification: CI runs unit tests and a fast Kind e2e that exercises a full backup -> incremental restore -> prober validation cycle. On merge, we executed a canary on a dedicated QA cluster where the prober detected a misordered migration in legacy tenant DBs and blocked the final promote step, demonstrating intended behavior.

Rollout plan: merge to main, create a canary release against the dedicated QA private deployment, monitor restore_validation metrics and the console gating badge. If metrics stable for 48h, promote to staged rollout for customer clusters.

Rollback plan: prober writes an idempotent checkpoint and a restore-token to S3/KV. If the post-upgrade prober fails in production, operator will automatically mark the release as unsafe and initiate an orchestrated rollback using the checkpoint and documented restore commands (included in release_notes).

Related: ENG-1984 (restore validation runbook), SUP-9012 (support case that motivated prober), ENG-2012 (helm preflight hooks RFC).
Carlos Diaz (2025-01-11): Left a few nit comments on checkpoint naming and CRD fields. Can we guarantee idempotency across restarts?
Priya Menon (2025-01-11): Reply: Checkpoint IDs are content-addressed and include timestamp+snapshot-hash; prober resumes by checking completed checkpoints before replaying. Added a unit test to exercise controller restarts.
Yuki Tanaka (2025-01-13): Request changes: migration_runner should not apply migrations in any mode; only validate. Also asked to add RBAC for the prober service account.
Priya Menon (2025-01-14): Addressed: migration_runner is now read-only; added RBAC manifest and tests for least-privilege access.
Marta Kowalski (2025-01-16): Approved after e2e logs looked good and a successful QA canary. Left a follow-up to add a throttling backoff for large tenant restores.
Add RestoreValidation CRD and a preflight restore validation prober that can be used to verify upgrades and rollbacks. Helm charts include a new pre-upgrade sanitizer job. Terraform backup module exposes flags to run validation in CI. No breaking changes to existing backups; enables safer rollouts for private deployments.
Merged to main via squash. Canaries started on 2025-01-18; QA canary detected a legacy migration issue which blocked promotion until a migration shim was applied.

Summary: This PR introduces three coordinated Terraform modules and operational docs to support tenancy-bounded GPU pools, IAM sharding, and VPC segmentation for Redwood Private installations. Motivation: Private installs supporting multiple tenants have faced scaling limits and operational blast radius when GPU pools, IAM roles, and tfstate were global. This patch reduces cross-tenant coupling by enabling per-tenant GPU nodepools, tenant-scoped IAM role shards, and optional VPC network segmentation while keeping a migration path from the existing global layout. Changeset: 1) module/tenant-gpu-pool: new module to provision GPU nodepools scoped to a tenant identifier. Supports node taints/affinity, taints-per-profile mappings, and nodepool lifecycle policies. 2) module/iam-shard: decomposes previously-global instance roles into tenant-scoped IAM shards; includes minimal cross-tenant read-only roles for operator visibility. 3) module/vpc-segment: optional VPC segmentation helpers and route table templates to create tenant-isolated subnets and peering hooks for shared services. 4) state/layout: introduces per-tenant tfstate backends with a small migrator CLI (bin/tfstate-migrate.sh) and examples for locking and state naming conventions. 5) docs/migration.md: end-to-end operator guide for migrating from global state to per-tenant state with throttled rollout and rollback instructions. Compatibility: The modules are opt-in via feature flags in the installer config (installer.tfvars) so existing single-tenant installs are unchanged until operators enable tenancy mode. Migration plan: provide operator with a dry-run mode; run migrator for one tenant at a time; validate resources in a canary tenant and confirm monitoring/alerts before continuing. Rollout steps are included in docs/migration.md. Testing: added unit TF tests (kitchen/inspec-like harness) for module inputs and a small e2e run against a lightweight test VPC for GPU allocation behavior. CI: terraform fmt, validate, plan-for-check, and a batched apply smoke test in sandbox. Performance: GPU pool provisioning retains existing autoscaler hooks; no runtime-serving changes. Security: IAM shards follow least-privilege patterns and add a tenant-management role used by the installer controller; cross-tenant operator visibility is limited to a read-only audit role. Developer notes: the modules are parameterized to support both cloud and on-prem node discovery (kubelet registration or static node lists). Related: follows work called out in ENG-1289 and ties into the Dedicated autoscaler work. Checklist: [x] module unit tests added; [x] migration docs written; [x] e2e smoke; [x] CI green. Migration caveats: existing automation that assumes global role names must be updated; sample compatibility aliases are provided to ease transition.
Adds modular Terraform for tenancy-bounded GPU nodepools, IAM sharding for least-privilege per-tenant roles, and optional VPC segmentation. Includes a migration helper for consolidating state into per-tenant tfstate backends. No user-visible API changes; operators should follow the migration steps in the PR description.
Rafael Ortiz (reviewer): Can we keep the old global role names as aliases around for 90 days to give automation time to switch?
Maya Chen (author): Added scripts/compatibility/role-aliases.tf that creates aliases for the previous role ARNs when feature flag 'enable_tenancy' is true. Documented the deprecation timeline.
Priya Nayar (reviewer): The migrator seems destructive if run without locking; can we add a dry-run and an explicit lock-check?
Maya Chen (author): Migrator updated to verify backend lock support and added --dry-run which produces a plan artifact. Also added retries and exponential backoff for state copy operations.
Samir Patel (reviewer): E2E smoke failed on first run due to subnet CIDR overlap in our sandbox; please guard peering creation with a cidr-check.
Maya Chen (author): Added cidr_overlap_precheck to vpc-segment and CI now runs the check before attempting peering.

Motivation: private deployments require tighter control over which VPCs and subnets can reach the private control plane. Existing private-installer allowed broad endpoint access and relied on coarse subnet placement for upgrades which made safe rollouts cumbersome. This PR introduces two complementary changes: (1) explicit private endpoint authorization via security-tagged security groups and endpoint policies so cross-account and cross-VPC peering can be granted programmatically; (2) deterministic subnet stitching and a maintenance-subnet handoff mechanism that lets the installer move controlplane workloads between subnets during upgrades with a safe drain/rollback path.

Summary of changes: - Terraform: add module terraform/modules/controlplane/endpoint_authorization that creates aws_vpc_endpoint_service_permissions, aws_vpc_endpoint_policy (when using Privatelink), and helper IAM role for cross-account acceptance. Introduces a security tag scheme (redwood:cp-access=[env,owner]) used to label SGs. - Terraform: add terraform/modules/controlplane/subnet_stitching which provisions maintenance subnets and a lifecycle policy that annotates previous subnets for rollback window. - Helm chart: update charts/private-installer/templates/controlplane-deployment.yaml to support an init container that verifies endpoint reachability and marks readiness only after the stitching handoff completes. - Installer CLI: add commands bin/rwpi subnet stitch --from <subnet-id> --to <subnet-id> and bin/rwpi endpoint authorize --peer-account <acct-id> which call the underlying Terraform controller and wait for acceptance. - Tests: integration harness updates under test/e2e/privatelink and new unit tests for the Terraform plan diffs. - Docs: docs/private-installer/endpoint-auth.md and docs/private-installer/subnet-stitching.md with operation runbooks and rollback steps.

Checklist (included in description as a single string): - [x] Terraform module implemented and unit tested - [x] Helm chart changes with health-probe integration - [x] Installer CLI commands with feature flags behind "stitching" opt-in - [x] E2E test added to nightly suite - [x] Security review: SG tagging and IAM bounded to required actions - [x] Internal docs and runbooks added

Why this is safe: endpoint authorization is opt-in and gated behind a new Boolean var controlplane.endpoint_authorization_enabled (default: false). Subnet stitching requires explicit staging labels on subnets and the installer will refuse to stitch unless both sides have matching stitch:allow tags. The Terraform plan includes a TTL annotation for rollback (stitching.rollback_ttl_days) so stale handoffs are automatically considered unsafe and must be explicitly overridden.

Migration notes: operators upgrading from older installer versions will see a no-op unless they enable endpoint_authorization_enabled and provision maintenance subnets. The included docs have a step-by-step guide for enabling the feature in production clusters, including sample Linear/Jira tracking templates for cross-account acceptance flows.

Commits summary: see commits field for high-level commits.

Related: builds on prior work for maintenance subnets (ENG-3621) and cross-account peering automation (SUP-872).
Liam Chen (2024-10-21): Initial review - good direction. Please tighten IAM policies in endpoint_authorization/main.tf; least privilege only for 'ec2:AcceptVpcEndpointConnections' and reference the exact service principals. Also add a comment explaining cross-account acceptance flow for Operators.
Maya Patel (2024-10-22): Addressed IAM scope; replaced broad role with inline policy and added doc section describing acceptance flow. PTAL.
Sofia Alvarez (2024-10-24): Found a timing flake in e2e where the init container marks ready before route table propagation completes. Suggested adding explicit RT propagation check and a configurable backoff.
Maya Patel (2024-10-25): Added RT propagation probe and backoff with exponential retry. Pushed commit e3c9ab4.
Rajesh Iyer (2024-10-28): Security review - SG tagging scheme looks reasonable. Please ensure tags are applied in terraform plan for existing SGs (migration step). Also request a unit test validating tag immutability on critical SGs.
Maya Patel (2024-10-29): Added plan-only migration module and a unit test that asserts the tag application path. CI initially failed on linter for a gofmt issue; fixed and re-ran.
Liam Chen (2024-10-31): Approve after small nit on CLI help text. Confirmed e2e passed in nightly.

Add opt-in control plane private endpoint authorization and deterministic subnet stitching to enable safe in-place upgrades and cross-account endpoint acceptance. Admins must opt into 'endpoint_authorization_enabled' and follow the new runbooks for cross-account flows.
Operations: enable feature behind feature flag; provision maintenance subnets with stitch:allow tags; follow docs/private-installer/subnet-stitching.md for a staged rollout. If rollback is required, use bin/rwpi subnet stitch --rollback-window <days> to revert within configured TTL.

Summary: Implements a cross-account route ownership model for private control plane VPCs and an automated DNS handoff path that propagates service-records to authorized consumer accounts. Motivations: customers deploying Redwood Private across multiple AWS accounts were manually synchronizing route table updates and forwarding DNS records; this caused operational toil during upgrades and periodic incidents where the control plane lost egress visibility. This PR automates assignment of route ownership via tags, introduces a cross-account role assumption flow, and wires a new 'dns-handoff' Terraform module and a lightweight reconciliation Lambda to propagate Route53 Resolver rules and service-records.

What it does (high level):
- Terraform: new module modules/vpc/route_ownership that tags route tables and creates an IAM role and policy for named-account takeover.
- Terraform: new module modules/dns/dns_handoff that creates Route53 Resolver endpoints, resolver rules with target IPs for consumer accounts, and SSM parameters to share metadata.
- Installer orchestration: the private-installer boot sequence now calls the handoff job as part of the post-controlplane step when `enable_cross_account_handoff=true`.
- Reconciliation: added a small Lambda (go) that runs under a cross-account role to synchronize service A records and conditional forwarder rules; runs as AWS EventBridge scheduled job and on-demand via the installer.
- Backwards compatibility: feature guarded; existing deployments opt-in. Migration helper `rwictl migrate-route-ownership` maps legacy route tags and performs a dry-run before committing.

Checklist: [x] Terraform module implemented and unit-tested with terratest harness; [x] Installer hook and CLI migration command; [x] IAM least-privilege review completed; [x] E2E smoke test against a 2-account sandbox; [x] Docs and upgrade notes added to private-installer/README.md.

Commits (high level):

Motivation: Private installs frequently hit contention on GPU nodepools when multiple tenants request capacity simultaneously and when tfstate boundaries are too coarse for safe incremental upgrades. This PR introduces two complementary Terraform modules plus orchestration helpers: a lease-aware GPU lifecycle module that manages tenant-scoped ephemeral leases (allocation, drain, reprovision) and a network segmentation module that creates per-tenant subnet slices and route policies with deterministic allocation. Design highlights: the GPU lease module exposes a lightweight lease resource, associated IAM roles for ephemeral node provisioning, and a small lifecycle controller hook (stateless) that coordinates lease handoff via a shared tfstate-compatible index. The networking module provides deterministic /28 slice allocation per-tenant with optional NAT egress per-slice, tag-based route propagation, and explicit peering rules for cross-tenant control plane connectivity. State layout and migration: to avoid monolithic tfstate edits the PR adds a state-proxy migrator script that can split a large cluster state into three bounded statefiles (cluster-core, tenant-leases, tenant-network) and includes a dry-run mode plus idempotent checkpointing so we can roll back. Rollout plan: staged deploy using canary tenant leases, verify drain/reprovision flows in a dev cluster, run migrator dry-run, then migrate one tenant at a time with observability hooks. Backwards compatibility: new modules default to opt-in via top-level variables; existing private-installer manifests will continue to apply unchanged unless maintainers switch to lease-aware modules. Testing: unit terraform tests + integration test harness that simulates 50 concurrent lease requests and verifies no more than configured pool size are active, plus e2e on a pre-prod VPC. Migration notes: operators must run the included migrator and validate tenant-network CIDRs; the PR documents a safe rollback path that moves resources back to the original cluster-core statefile if a post-migration validation fails. See related Linear items ENG-8543 and INFRA-121 for product context.
Jared Thompson (review): Can you expand on how the lease index is coordinated to avoid split-brain if two operators run the migrator concurrently?
Maya Singh (author): The migrator uses a checkpoint file and an acquire/release lock in the cluster-core statefile via a small lock resource; the PR adds a retry-and-backoff loop and a manual override flag. I documented the sequence in the migration guide.
Evelyn Park (review): IAM roles look broad in the first commit. We should scope the ephemeral node role to only the actions required for node provisioning and tagging. Also prefer separate service account per-tenant in GCP plans.
Maya Singh (author): Updated iam policy and split service account creation per-tenant. Permissions are narrowed to actions: compute.instances.create, compute.instances.delete, compute.instances.setTags, and iam.serviceAccounts.actAs. See updated variables.tf for kubelet identity mapping.
Carlos Mendes (review): CI flake on integration harness observed timeouts when simulating 50 concurrent lease claims. Are timeouts adjustable?
Maya Singh (author): Increased harness timeouts and added exponential backoff on the test harness to reduce transient failures. CI re-run passed.
Add lease-aware GPU lifecycle Terraform module (opt-in) to provide tenant-scoped ephemeral GPU leases and safe drain/reprovision flows.
Add deterministic network segmentation module for per-tenant subnet slices and route policies.
Add state-proxy-migrator utility to split monolithic tfstate into bounded statefiles with dry-run and rollback support.
Migration guide and rollback checklist included in docs/private-installer/gpu-lease-migration.md.
Before switching production manifests to use the new modules run the migrator in dry-run mode and validate the checkpointed mappings. The migrator produces a mapping file that must be inspected; see docs/private-installer/gpu-lease-migration.md for the rollback procedure.
Integration test simulating 50 concurrent lease requests completed in CI with 0 over-allocations. E2E smoke on preprod verified node drain, ephemeral reprovision, and network slice isolation with tagged routes.
ENG-8543: add observability alerts for lease contention and migrator failures
INFRA-121: add automated canary rollout script to promote tenant-by-tenant migration
Refactor: consider moving lease controller hook into a small controller binary instead of helm init script

Motivation: on-prem/private installs run across a wide variety of Kubernetes distro variants (kubeadm, k3s, rke2, bottlerocket variants) and customers in air-gapped environments need the installer to reliably apply a compatible CNI stack from a vendored bundle. This PR introduces a lightweight distro-agnostic CNI transformer and an offline metadata index that lets the installer pick and patch the correct CNI manifests at install time without pulling anything from the public internet.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds installer/pkg/transformer: a small binary that consumes vendored CNI manifest templates and applies distro-specific transform rules (serviceAccount, hostPort vs hostNetwork, crd ordering shims).
- Adds an offline metadata index (assets/offline-index.yaml) that lists vendored image digests, helm/manifest mapping, and per-distro transform rules (k3s, rke2, kubeadm). The index is generated by scripts/generate-offline-index.sh and consumed by the transformer.
- Extends the Helm chart (charts/installer) to accept pre-seeded CRDs and provide a cniMode override (managed | vendor | passthrough).
- Terraform module changes (terraform/modules/airgap): expose var.cni_mode and a preseed_assets S3/OCI var so customers can point to their seeded registry.
- Adds e2e test vectors for k3s and rke2 that run the transformer against vendored bundles (test/airgap/e2e-cni.sh).
- Improves checksumming and OCI mirror index generation to ensure deterministic offline artifacts (scripts/offline-index-checksum).

Files of interest (summary):
- installer/pkg/transformer/transformer.go (core transformer logic)
- assets/offline-index.yaml (generated index sample)
- scripts/generate-offline-index.sh (index generator)
- charts/installer/values.yaml (new cniMode controls)
- terraform/modules/airgap/main.tf (expose cni vars)
- docs/offline-cni.md (design + upgrade notes)

Checklist: 
- [x] Transformer binary + unit tests
- [x] Offline index generation script + sample index
- [x] Helm chart cniMode and CRD preseed support
- [x] Terraform variable surfaces and example usage
- [x] Minimal docs and upgrade notes
- [x] E2E smoke test for k3s/rke2 paths

Why this approach: shipping a small transform step keeps the vendored bundles smaller (no multiple distro-specific copies) while giving a deterministic, auditable way to adapt manifests to cluster distro constraints at install time. The index file is intentionally compact (image digests + transform rule refs) to make offline seeding and verification straightforward.

Backward compatibility and upgrade path: default behavior remains cniMode=managed (current behavior). When a customer opts into cniMode=vendor, the installer will read the offline index and run the transformer. Documents in docs/offline-cni.md describe how to upgrade a cluster to use vendor mode and provide a rollback procedure (installer rollback hook will revert transformed manifests and resume managed CNI).

Summary: Add a Crossplane-backed provisioning flow and a TLS orchestration component that coordinates HSM/KMS key lifecycle events with Helm/Terraform upgrades for private deployments.
Motivation: customers asked for an automated path to provision cloud-backed KMS instances (and on-prem HSM proxies) using Crossplane so the Private Installer can own end-to-end lifecycle for tenant keys during cluster bootstrapping and upgrades. This also reduces manual steps during TLS certificate rotations and prevents drift between sealed-secrets/Vault state and KMS key metadata.
Design: 1) crossplane/controller: new CRD 'KMSProvision' that maps to provider resources (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or an HSM-proxy Deployment); 2) provisioning module: terraform shim and new Crossplane composition templates shipped in helm chart's templates/crossplane/; 3) tls-orchestrator daemonset: a small controller that watches KMSProvision and Secret resources, coordinates staged key rotation (create new key, copy metadata, re-encrypt sealed secrets, rollout server certs), and emits progress metrics; 4) upgrade hooks: helm pre-upgrade/post-upgrade hooks talk to the orchestrator to ensure staged rollback-safe rotations; 5) installer flag: --enable-crossplane-kms and --crossplane-namespace to opt in.
Upgrade/rollback: orchestrator implements a three-phase rotation (provision -> mirror -> switch) with safe rollback markers written to a ClusterConfig CR. If a helm upgrade fails, the orchestrator halts switch phase and leaves old keys active; an automated rollback script reverts sealed-secret rewrites.
Security: all Crossplane compositions created with least-privilege roles; orchestrator talks to KMS with short-lived certs issued by cluster CA; HSM proxy path supports PKCS#11 or gRPC plugin.
Testing: unit tests for controller logic, e2e test harness that runs a mini Crossplane control plane in-kind, and upgrade-scenario integration tests against the private installer testbeds. Backwards compatibility: opt-in only, existing clusters unaffected unless flagged.
Rollout plan: feature gated in installer 1.18.2, developer preview in sandbox clusters, followed by canary on two customer VPCs.
Related work: ENG-5732 (crossplane provisioning), ENG-5789 (tls-orchestrator design).

Motivation: On private deployments customers require automated, auditable rotation of key encryption keys (KEKs) used to envelope-encrypt SealedSecrets and other installer-managed secrets while preserving the ability to roll back upgrades safely. This PR introduces a small on-cluster controller (kms-guardian) plus Helm upgrade hooks and a Terraform module bump to automate HSM-backed KEK rotation and safe sealed-secrets snapshotting. Summary of changes: 1) New component: kms-guardian operator (controller + CRD). Responsible for scheduling KEK rotations, orchestrating HSM key wrap/unwrap (PKCS#11 compatible), and writing rotation events to the installer's audit log. Operator supports dry-run and a "fastpath" test mode for SoftHSM in CI. 2) Helm chart changes: a post-upgrade hook creates an atomic snapshot of sealed-secrets (namespaced) into an S3-compatible bucket using an envelope encryption KEK pulled from the HSM. A pre-rollback hook validates that the snapshot decrypts with the previous KEK and aborts rollback if validation fails. Hooks are idempotent and expose TTL labels for retention. 3) Terraform module bump: terraform/modules/kms provider bumped to v2.4.0 with new resources for HSM policy statements and a new output to supply KEK metadata to the installer. 4) Installer bootstrap updates: bootstrap flow now includes an HSM policy verification step and optional SoftHSM fallback for dev/on-prem installs. 5) CI and tests: added e2e/upgrade-rollback tests that exercise rotation during a simulated upgrade and confirm rollback safety. Added a SoftHSM matrix to the e2e pipeline for validation. Checklist: - [x] Implement kms-guardian controller and CRD - [x] Add Helm post-upgrade and pre-rollback hooks - [x] Terraform module bump and documentation - [x] e2e upgrade/rollback tests and CI matrix - [x] Add audit log events and metrics (prometheus counters per rotation) - [x] Docs: README for operator and runbook for rotation/incident response How it works (high level): kms-guardian calls into the HSM via the PKCS#11 shim to create a new KEK version, then re-encrypts a per-namespace envelope key used to encrypt SealedSecrets payloads. The Helm post-upgrade hook runs an idempotent snapshot job that collects SealedSecrets CRs, encrypts the snapshot with the current KEK (HSM-wrapped), and uploads to customer-configured object storage. On rotate, kms-guardian coordinates a multi-step handoff: generate new KEK -> use HSM to wrap new KEK with HSM master -> update metadata and push new encrypted envelope keys -> signal readiness -> Helm hooks run validation where necessary. Rollback safety: pre-rollback hook decrypts a tiny marker payload from the snapshot using the previous KEK; if decryption fails the rollback is blocked and operators are alerted. Security considerations: operator never exports raw KEK material; all wrapping/unwrapping happens inside HSM or SoftHSM. Audit events include rotation initiator, rotation version, and thumbprints. Backwards compatibility: optional feature flag `installer.kmsGuardian.enabled`; default is off for older installs. Testing: added unit tests for the operator's state machine and integration tests that run against SoftHSM in the CI matrix. Also added a local-mode script for customers to validate HSM connectivity in air-gapped installs. Related: references ENG-9213 for product requirement and SEC-377 for threat-model signoff. Notes: this is intentionally conservative in scope — operator handles KEK lifecycle and orchestrates snapshot/validation but does not migrate application-level keys (outside installer-managed sealed-secrets). Future work: automate HSM failover integration and a CLI for manual rotation.
Adds KMS Guardian operator for HSM-backed key lifecycle, Helm upgrade hooks to snapshot and rotate sealed-secrets backups (envelope encrypted with KEK), and bumps terraform/modules/kms to v2.4.0. Includes e2e upgrade/rollback tests and SoftHSM CI job.
Marcus Keller: Can we avoid doing any raw key material movement in the operator? Ensure everything goes through the PKCS#11 interface.
Asha Patel (author): Confirmed, operator uses PKCS#11 wrapper; added unit tests that assert no plaintext KEK is ever persisted.
Yuki Tanaka: Need a clear failure mode if HSM is unavailable mid-rotation. Also ensure metrics expose rotation latency.
Asha Patel (author): Added graceful abort path and prometheus metrics (kms_rotation_attempts_total, kms_rotation_failures_total). Updated runbook with recovery steps.
Sofia Ramirez: Terraform module bump affects on-prem upgrade docs — please add migration notes.
Asha Patel (author): Added migration notes to terraform/modules/kms/README.md and installer docs.
Ops: CI e2e flaky on SoftHSM in macOS runners — changed to linux-only matrix.

payload.body:
Motivation: Private control planes in multi-tenant customer VPCs frequently require more deterministic subnet allocation and carefully managed egress policies. Current installer behavior leaves control-plane ENIs spread across broad subnet pools which makes lifecycle operations (upgrade, rollback, tear-down) error-prone and forces customers to maintain large, permissive security groups and complex DNS conditional-forwarding rules. This PR introduces three coordinated features to address these problems: 1) immutable subnet-tenancy slices for the control plane so instances can be pinned to stable CIDR ranges per AZ and tenant lifetime; 2) an egress-policy lifecycle model driven by prefix-lists and managed terraform resources so we can roll egress changes with a clear create-or-replace semantics (reduces SG churn); and 3) a lightweight "dns-janitor" daemon and Helm chart that mirrors resolver records into a read-only in-VPC resolver endpoint to replace brittle cross-account Route53 forwarding during upgrades and rollback.

What this PR does (summary):
- Terraform: adds modules/pp-controlplane/subnet_tenancy module that allocates deterministic subnet slices (configurable slice_size and tenancy_tags) and exposes outputs for ENI placement helpers.
- Terraform: new prefix-list based egress_policies module with lifecycle = replace semantics and explicit apply-time change detection to avoid transient allow windows.
- Helm/Installer: introduces helm/redwood-private/dns-janitor chart (small Go binary container) and installer hooks to deploy a read-only resolver that mirrors a subset of control-plane DNS records to customer VPC via resolver endpoints. The Janitor uses read-only Route53 API credentials scoped to list/get and incremental delta sync.
- Installer orchestration: upgrade and rollback hooks updated to (a) quiesce egress policy changes, (b) pin/evict control-plane instances from affected subnet slices, (c) ensure DNS-janitor is deployed before changing control-plane endpoints.
- Tests: a new integration test that simulates rolling updates with induced subnet-roll disruption and verifies no transient egress hole and DNS continuity.

Design notes and tradeoffs: immutable subnet slices simplify lifecycle reasoning at the cost of slightly more complex CIDR planning for the customer. We expose parameters to keep default behavior identical to previous releases unless the tenant opts-in (opt-in flag: controlplane.subnetTenancy.enabled). Egress prefix-lists reduce security-group explosion but require customers to accept prefix-list objects (documented in upgrade notes). DNS-janitor intentionally avoids write access into customer Route53 zones; it only publishes a per-customer read-only resolver endpoint to avoid cross-account write requirements.

Testing done: local terraform plan/apply against a test account, helm lint + chart smoke, end-to-end upgrade integration (simulated in CI), manual cross-account validation with partner infra team. See commit log for specifics.

Rollback strategy: installer now performs a three-phase topology switch: prepare (deploy janitor + new prefix-list staging), migrate (pin and migrate instances), finalize (remove staging artifacts). Rollback reverses finalize/migrate while keeping janitor in place to maintain DNS continuity.

Checklist:
- [x] Terraform module implemented and unit-tested
- [x] Helm chart for dns-janitor with chart tests
- [x] Installer orchestration hooks updated and tested
- [x] Integration test validating egress continuity and DNS behavior
- [x] Docs: upgrade notes and opt-in instructions included in README

Related: ENG-3242 (design doc), INF-88 (customer request), SUP-4123 (support case), see internal doc link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-3242/control-plane-subnet-tenancy
Ravi Patel: We need a migration plan for customers already using custom prefix lists — can we include an import helper?
Maya Lindgren (author): Added an import helper script and documented the import flow in installer/README-upgrades.md (see commit f4a3b2c).
Elena Gomez: helm chart looks good but image security scan flags got a medium severity package — prefer Alpine 3.19. I also requested a podSecurityContext.
Maya Lindgren (author): Switched base image to alpine:3.19 and added podSecurityContext, pushed fix in commit 3f1e6b7. Re-ran chart tests locally; CI updated.
Tomás Alvarez: Integration test flaked two runs due to rate limits on Route53 in the test account, added retries; approved after re-run.
Ravi Patel: Approved — left a minor nit about output naming (suggest consistent prefix).

payload.body:
Problem: Private deployments performing in-place schema changes or operator-driven upgrades can race (multiple CI/CD runs, manual operator actions, or automated patchers) which leads to partially-applied migrations and mismatched tenant state. We need a robust guard that: 1) prevents concurrent migrations across controller replicas and automation runs, 2) provides an operator-level pause to quiesce requests for targeted tenants during a migration window, and 3) verifies that pre-upgrade backups are intact and restorable before allowing schema application.

This PR introduces a consensus-backed migration lock (based on the cluster's etcd/consensus layer where available, falling back to a tenant-scoped leader election CRD) and an operator pauser that quiesces inbound tenant traffic during schema transforms. It also wires a preflight backup verifier that computes and records checksum manifests for logical PostgreSQL dumps before migrations proceed. The goal is safe in-place schema transforms with deterministic, reversible steps and clear operator controls.

Changes: single continuous description of what was done (checklist): 
- implement a MigrationLock CRD and controller that acquires a cluster-scoped consensus lease with retry/backoff and TTL metadata
- add a TenantQuiesce subcontroller that annotates ingress proxies (helm chart hook) and toggles a feature-flag on the operator to pause new requests for a tenant during the migration window
- add a migration preflight command to the installer CLI: `installer migrate --tenant <id> --dry-run/--apply --backup-checksum <auto|path>`
- wire automatic logical backup creation (pg_dump) into the migrate flow and record checksum + object path in BackupManifest CRD
- add a `migration.dry_run=true` path that executes schema transformations in a sandbox (helm test job) and reports a rollout readiness score
- introduce terraform module inputs for `migration_lock_ttl` and `operator_pause_grace_seconds` and document defaults
- Helm chart: add pre-upgrade hook that waits for MigrationLock and runs the backup verifier, and a post-failure hook that triggers an automatic unlock with a diagnostic bundle
- add metrics (migration_lock_acquired_total, backup_verification_status) and tracing spans for the lock lifecycle
- tests: unit tests for lock backoff, e2e test using a two-controller race scenario, and a restore smoke test that validates checksum match after a simulated restore

Commits: [summaries] 
- feat(migration): add MigrationLock CRD + controller with TTL and renewals
- feat(operator): add TenantQuiesce controller and operator pause flag
- feat(installer): add `migrate` CLI flow, backup verifier and checksum manifest wiring
- feat(helm): helm hooks for pre-upgrade backup-check and post-failure diagnostics
- tf(migration): terraform inputs and docs for migration lock config
- test(e2e): race-condition e2e harness and restore smoke test
- chore: docs and README updates for private-installer migration flow

Files changed (high level):
- chart/private-installer/templates/hooks/pre-upgrade-backup-check.yaml (new helm pre-upgrade hook that blocks until backup verification passes)
- api/v1/migrationlock_types.go, controllers/migrationlock_controller.go (CRD + controller)
- controllers/tenantquiesce_controller.go (operator-pauser logic)
- cli/installer/cmd/migrate.go (installer migrate CLI + flags)
- docs/migration-runbook.md (runbook for operators + rollback steps)
- terraform/modules/installer/variables.tf (migration_lock_ttl, operator_pause_grace_seconds)
- tests/e2e/migration_race_test.go, tests/e2e/restore_smoke_test.go

Migration flow and rollback plan (operator runbook summary):
1) Run `installer migrate --tenant T123 --dry-run` to exercise the dry-run path. The dry-run creates a namespaced sandbox job in the cluster and reports schema diffs and a readiness score.
2) Create a pre-upgrade backup via `installer migrate --tenant T123 --run-backup` (this is automatic if `--run-backup` not suppressed). The BackupManifest CRD will contain checksum and signed metadata (GPG optional).
3) Acquire the MigrationLock (controller will attempt consensus lease). If lock acquisition fails, operator may retry or abort; UI surfaces owner and TTL.
4) Operator toggles TenantQuiesce; ingress will start returning 503 for new session requests for the target tenant while allowing inflight requests to drain within `operator_pause_grace_seconds`.
5) Apply schema transforms. The helm pre-upgrade hook ensures the backup-check passed before hitting migrations.
6) On success, release MigrationLock and unquiesce the tenant.
7) On failure or timeout, the post-failure hook collects diagnostics, performs an automatic unlock (with TTL), and can optionally trigger a restore job using the BackupManifest. The runbook includes steps for manual failback when automatic restore is insufficient.

Testing and verification notes: 
- e2e race test simulates two parallel migrators and asserts that only one succeeds and the other receives a clear backoff error + owner metadata.
- restore_smoke_test verifies that BackupManifest checksum can be fetched and used to validate a restored dump; smoke test runs pg_restore in a sandbox and compares row counts for a sample table.
- Unit tests cover TTL expiry, renewals, and operator pause grace period.
- CI: initial runs failed on a flaky race in the e2e harness (timing assumptions around controller leader election). I adjusted the harness backoff and added a deterministic latch; rerun passed (CI status: pass).

Review conversation (summary):

Context: Support escalations for Private upgrades getting stuck at migrations are taking too long to triage because we’re missing a consistent artifact set and the installer’s failure output doesn’t guide the operator to the right next step. This PR adds a first-class diagnostics bundle and improves upgrade/migrations failure hints so Support/SRE/Platform can move from “stuck” -> “actionable” quickly. Ties to SUP-1845 and ENG-4828.

What’s included:
- New command: `redwood-private-installer diagnostics bundle --reason upgrade --output <path>`
  - Produces a single `.tar.gz` with a predictable directory structure.
  - Explicitly avoids collecting secrets (no K8s Secrets, no env dumps from pods). Basic redaction is applied to common token patterns in logs.
  - Includes a `MANIFEST.txt` with versions and timestamps to make email/Slack handoffs easier.
- Upgrade/migrations aware collection:
  - Installer logs for the attempted run (including last ~5k lines, plus full file if available).
  - Kubernetes resources relevant to the upgrade path (namespace-scoped):
    - `kubectl get pods,deploy,sts,job,cronjob -o wide`
    - `kubectl describe` for the migrations Job (if present) and any CrashLooping pods.
    - `kubectl logs` for migrations job pods (current + previous when supported).
    - Recent namespace events (last 2h) and warnings.
  - Helm status/history for the control plane release when deployed via Helm (non-fatal if not present).
  - Node pressure summary (disk/mem) from `kubectl describe node` (capped to the node(s) hosting control plane pods; best-effort).
- Clearer failure hints:
  - If the upgrade appears stuck at migrations (job running > threshold or repeated restarts), print a “What to check next” section with the exact commands to run and what output to attach.
  - Detect common classes of failures and emit targeted hints:
    - Image pull errors -> check registry reachability / pull secret configuration.
    - RBAC forbidden errors -> verify the installer service account cluster role binding.
    - Postgres connectivity / auth failures -> verify DB endpoint reachability and credentials rotation timing.
    - Schema lock / long-running migration -> provide guidance on collecting DB lock diagnostics (without exposing credentials) and when to escalate.
  - All hints include a “When to escalate” line that points Support to include the diagnostics bundle and reference SUP key(s).

Why this design:
- Support needs a single artifact they can request that doesn’t require live debugging on a customer cluster.
- The bundle format is stable so macros and KB articles can be copy/paste-ready.
- We intentionally do not attempt to auto-remediate. We only collect and guide to avoid surprising changes in regulated environments.

How to test:
- `make test` (unit tests for bundling/redaction + hint classification)
- Manual:
  - Run `diagnostics bundle` on a healthy cluster (should succeed and include expected files).
  - Simulate a failing migrations job (bad DB host) and confirm installer emits hint + bundle includes job logs/events.

Follow-ups (out of scope for this PR):
- Add a Support-facing doc page that mirrors the required artifacts + “stuck migrations” checklist (handled in ENG-4828 rollup).
- Add optional `--since` for events/logs window control (defaults are chosen to keep bundles reasonably sized).
Private installer: adds a support-friendly diagnostics bundle for upgrade failures (esp. stuck migrations) and improves error messaging with actionable hints and required artifacts list.
Sean Gallagher: Can we ensure we’re not collecting anything that could contain secrets (env vars, kube secrets, etc.)? Also, please add a one-liner that Support can paste into a ticket to request this bundle.
Ethan Park: Confirmed: no Secrets API calls, no env dumps. Added explicit allowlist collectors and a MANIFEST disclaimer. Also added a short macro-friendly snippet in CLI help output: `Please run: redwood-private-installer diagnostics bundle --reason upgrade --output ./redwood-diag.tar.gz`.
Naomi Feldman: Redaction looks helpful but regex-based redaction can be brittle. Can we keep the bundle internal-only unless customer explicitly approves sharing? Also cap file sizes.
Ethan Park: Added hard caps (default 5k lines per log stream + max 20MB per file) and a banner in the command output: “Bundle may contain sensitive operational details; share only via approved secure channel.” The installer already uses the Support portal upload flow; this aligns with that process.
Priya Natarajan: Great direction. Two asks: (1) include the installer version + git SHA in the manifest, (2) add detection for CrashLoopBackOff on the migrations job and print a hint.
Ethan Park: Done. Manifest now includes installer version + build SHA + timestamp. Added CrashLoopBackOff classification with guidance to include `kubectl describe pod` and previous logs.
Rafael Mendes: Suggest including a minimal node pressure snapshot. We see disk pressure causing opaque failures during upgrades.
Ethan Park: Added best-effort node describe for nodes hosting control plane pods, truncated to pressure + conditions sections to avoid huge output.
If customer reports upgrade stuck at migrations, request diagnostics bundle and attach to SUP ticket: `redwood-private-installer diagnostics bundle --reason upgrade --output redwood-diag.tar.gz`.
Bundle is namespace-scoped and best-effort; if RBAC prevents collection, the tool will still produce a partial bundle and note missing collectors in MANIFEST.txt.
Escalation-ready artifacts: diagnostics bundle + approximate start time of upgrade attempt + installer version from MANIFEST.txt.
payload.title: Add upgrade diagnostics bundle + failure hints for stuck migrations

This PR introduces a 'rotation-simulator' lightweight tool and Helm/Terraform changes to enable safe, observable dry-run rotations of TLS keys and KMS/HSM key promotions for private deployments. Motivation: customers and internal SREs need a way to validate complex cross-resource rotations (Vault sealed secrets, KMS key promotion, intermediate CA swaps) without touching live secrets or changing traffic routing. The simulator runs in a controlled namespace and exercises the same sequence of calls the installer will perform during an actual rotation: generate new keys, publish to Vault with sealed secret templates, update Helm chart hooks for canary certs, run Terraform plan/apply on a staging state, and validate identity checks. Key features: 1) rotation-simulator binary that can be run locally or in CI and supports `--dry-run`, `--inject-failure=step_name`, and `--compare-only` modes so teams can inject failures and verify rollback paths; 2) Helm chart additions include a pre-upgrade hook and a post-upgrade validation job that coordinates with the simulator using a lightweight CRD-compatible lock file; 3) Terraform module idempotency fixes and a staged-promote resource that records tombstone metadata to make rollbacks deterministic; 4) new e2e pipeline definitions that exercise the simulator against a mocked HSM endpoint and a Vault dev server inside KinD; 5) documentation and a playbook that explains verification steps, expected logs, and metrics to monitor during a dry run. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is opt-in via values.yaml toggles (rotationSimulator.enabled=false, terraform_module.kms_dry_run=true). We added feature gates so existing Private installations are unaffected unless operators enable the workflow. Security considerations: simulator never exports cleartext private key material to logs or external storage. It interacts with KMS/HSM using wrapped keys and simulates key handles when running against the mock HSM. We also added checks to require an operator-approved Linear ticket in metadata for any non-dry-run migration. Testing: unit tests for the simulator binary, a small integration harness used in CI that spins up Vault and a mock HSM, and a full e2e run that executes the dry-run path and asserts no network-facing changes were made. See docs/upgrade/rotation-dry-run-playbook.md for the operator checklist and known limitations. This PR includes implementation, tests, docs, and Terraform schema changes. See release notes below for the operator-facing summary.
Three logical commits: initial simulator scaffolding and CLI; Helm hook templates + values schema and chart tests; Terraform module idempotency and staged-promote resource + integration test harness. Minor followups: adjust RBAC for the validation job and tighten logs to avoid secret material.
Reviewer Omar: 'Great idea, this will save a lot of incident risk. Please add a quick note in the README about when to use `--inject-failure` vs `--compare-only`.' Author Maya: 'Done, expanded README examples to include a typical CI snippet and a failure injection matrix.' Reviewer Elena: 'CI flaked on the first run due to KinD resource limits; can we add retry logic to the e2e job and a smaller test profile?' Author Maya: 'Added retries and a light profile for PR runs while keeping the full profile for nightly e2e.' Reviewer Luis: 'Terraform plan output parsing seemed brittle; prefer using a dedicated `staged_promote` output instead of grepping logs.' Author Maya: 'Reworked the module to expose an explicit JSON output and updated the harness to consume it.' Final approvals: Omar and Elena approved after followups. Luis approved after the module change. All threads resolved before merge.
Added rotation-simulator tool and safe dry-run workflow for KMS/HSM and TLS rotations. Operators can perform a non-destructive dry run that validates Helm hooks, Vault interactions, and Terraform state changes before promoting keys. Opt-in via values.rotationSimulator.enabled=false and terraform_module.kms_dry_run=true. Includes e2e harness and operator playbook.
