Motivation: Customers running Redwood Private in fully air-gapped datacenters reported two recurring issues: 1) inconsistent CNI installs when kernels differ from our build matrix, and 2) manual, error-prone steps to seed private OCI/Helm registries. This PR introduces an end-to-end offline-friendly flow: packaged, precompiled BPF-CNI kernel module bundles for common enterprise kernels plus a new OCI-Helm seeder sidecar utility that can be run from the airgap bootstrap container to atomically seed registries and charts. Summary of changes: packaged kernel module artifacts per distro (ubuntu20/22, rhel8/9, rocky, almalinux) with vmlinuz/headers checksums; an installer hook that probes target nodes and selects the closest-compatible module bundle; an offline Helm OCI seeder that pulls from provided artifact tarballs and imports images/charts into the local registry with optional signature verification; terraform module updates to create a registry seed job and a registry credential secret; Helm chart tweaks to surface device-mapper and module-loader knobs; and tests and preflight checks added to the installer preflight. Design notes: To avoid kernel compilation in customer environments we ship prebuilt, signed .ko bundles plus a fingerprint manifest. The installer probes uname -r and glibc/kernel headers and performs a checksum-based compatibility match; if no exact match exists, it falls back to a closest ABI-compatible bundle and inserts a graceful warning in the console output and audit log. The OCI seeder uses an idempotent import layer: tarball->verify->import->promote so retries are safe. Security: all bundles and helm charts are signed with our airgap signing key and verified locally before install; signature failure aborts the seeding step and surfaces a clear remediation path. Migration and rollout: added a canary flag in the installer config (installer.canary.offline_module_loader=true) to enable gradual rollout on Dedicated/Private installs. For major customer migrations we provide a helper script that collects /lib/modules and system info to help produce a custom bundle. Testing: added unit tests for the module selector logic, integration test harness that runs the seeder against a local registry in CI (recorded in ci/seeder-e2e), and manual validation on Ubuntu 20.04 kernel variants. CI run notes: initial CI run failed linter on variable naming in terraform module; fixed in second commit and all checks passed. Backwards compatibility: the default remains the previous build-from-source flow unless the canary flag is set. Documentation: added docs/private/offline-seeding.md and a troubleshooting section for kernel mismatches. Rollout plan: merge to main, cut a 0.31.0-alpha private-installer image with seeder sidecar, enable canary for internal staging clusters, gather telemetry on module fallback events before broad rollout. Related: ENG-12458 tracks broader vendor bundle matrix expansion.
Adds support for precompiled BPF CNI bundles and a new offline Helm OCI seeder; improves airgap installer device/kernel compatibility and adds signed bundle verification
Priya Kapoor: Please add a clear audit log entry when the installer falls back to a non-exact kernel bundle. We need this for support triage.
Mateo Alvarez: Added an audit log line and included it in the doc troubleshooting steps (see docs/private/offline-seeding.md). Also added a telemetry tag 'module_fallback' to the installer heartbeats.
Ethan Ross: Terraform change looks good but we should add an expiration TTL on the registry seed job to avoid orphaned jobs.
Mateo Alvarez: Added ttl_seconds_after_finished to the Job spec and moved credentials to a k8s secret with limited RBAC scope.
Lena Müller: One security question: where is the signing key stored for airgap customers? We need to document the rotation pattern.
Mateo Alvarez: Documented recommended customer flow: use their KMS to sign bundles or request a signed bundle from Redwood; rotation guidance added in docs and an 'unbind' helper to revoke a bundle.

Motivation: Reduce offline bundle size for constrained on-prem installs and make distro-specific packaging pluggable. Many customers run in air-gapped environments with strict image quotas (edge appliances, gov clouds). The existing full-vendor bundle duplicates many distro artifacts and pulls in unnecessary CNI/kernel modules; this causes large transfers and slower upgrades. This PR introduces a compact vendor lockfile format + a selective distro packaging pipeline and installer hooks that validate signatures during install/upgrade.
Summary of changes:
- Add a compact OCI lockfile generator that emits minimal index records for required runtime images and optional distro components (kernels, initramfs, cni).
- Implement a packaging pipeline that produces two artifact classes: core-runtime bundle (required) and distro-adapter bundles (optional per distro).
- Add installer-side controller hooks to fetch and validate the compact lockfile, reconcile installed adapters, and apply atomic delta updates (delta snapshots) for adapters only.
- Add package signing verification during preflight and rollback validation to prevent unsigned state after failed upgrades.
- Provide Terraform modules and Helm chart knobs to select which distro adapters are included at bundle creation time.
Checklist:
- [x] generator CLI and YAML/JSON lockfile schema
- [x] packaging pipeline (core + adapters)
- [x] installer controller hooks + preflight checks
- [x] Terraform/Helm knobs and example user flow
- [x] tests: unit tests for lockfile generator, e2e for adapter install path (simulated airgap)
- [x] release notes and upgrade notes
Commits (high-level): 1) add compact lockfile schema and CLI (mgen/lockfile v0.1) 2) packaging pipeline: adapter splitter and manifest builder 3) installer: adapter controller + preflight signature check 4) terraform: module vars + examples 5) helm: chart values and conditional templates 6) tests and CI glue 7) docs and release notes
Changes (files and high-level diffs):
- cmd/mgen/lockfile.go (+420 additions): new CLI to generate compact lockfiles from an OCI index and optional distro manifest.
- build/packager/adapter_splitter.py (+310): splitting logic to create core vs adapter bundles and compute delta snapshots.
- installer/controllers/adapter_controller.go (+560): reconcile loop to apply adapter bundles when present; preflight signature verification hook.
- charts/installer/templates/adapter-hook.yaml (+80): Helm hooks to enable/disable adapter reconciliation.
- terraform/modules/airgap_bundle/variables.tf (+40) and examples/complete-compact.tf (+70): knobs for selecting adapters and signing keys.
- docs/airgap/compact-lockfile.md (+210): guide and migration steps.
- test/e2e/airgap_adapter_install_test.go (+120): simulated offline test using local registry and signed bundles.
Review conversation (selected excerpts):
- Reviewer: "Adapter controller looks good but need stronger idempotency guarantees when a partial delta fails during apply."
- Author: "Agree; added a transactional marker in the controller state to avoid double-apply and added roll-forward logic during reconcile."
- Reviewer: "Can we avoid duplicating kernel modules across adapters?"
- Author: "Adapter splitter now deduplicates by content-hash and writes shared blobs into core-runtime bundle; documented in compact-lockfile.md."
- Reviewer: "Terraform examples need a note about passing KMS signing key ARNs for airgapped environments."
- Author: "Added example and notes; we recommend pre-provisioned KMS keys and offline-signed manifests for fully airgapped sites."
CI status: initial run failed on linter (helm templates flagged), fixed in commit 4, tests: unit tests pass, e2e flaky on CI due to local registry timing -> added retry and increased timeouts; final CI status: pass (all checks green, e2e retried once).
Performance notes: compact bundles reduced total artifact size by ~38% on our baseline (k3s+almalinux+flatcar) in the test harness; installer adapter apply latency for a single adapter ~28s (cold) vs 12s (warm) with shared blobs in core bundle.
Migration notes and user impact:
- Upgrade path: existing full bundles can be converted into compact bundles using the mgen CLI (documented). The installer will accept both formats during a grace period.
- Rollbacks: rollback now validates signatures of the rollback snapshot; unsigned rollback attempts are rejected and leave the cluster in the pre-upgrade state.
- Backwards compatibility: the compact lockfile schema is additive; older installers ignore adapter fields but will still be able to apply core runtime.
Release notes:
- Add compact vendor lockfile and selective distro adapter packaging to reduce airgap bundle size and enable faster adapter-only upgrades.
- New terraform/helm knobs for adapter selection and signing.
- Installer now verifies package signatures preflight and during rollback.
Testing performed: unit tests, integration (packaging pipeline), e2e simulated airgap adapter install, manual validation of signed bundles with KMS-signed manifests.
Related Linear/Jira: ENG-4281, ENG-4310, PM-2093.
Breaking change: false.
Files changed count: 12. Additions: 834. Deletions: 412.
Merge: squashed after tests passed; merged to main on 2026-02-21.

payload.body:
Motivation: Private control plane deployments have diverse networking topologies (shared transit gateways, multiple VPCs per AZ, on-prem VPNs). Customers asked for an optional, declarative way to wire Route53 conditional forwarding to resolver endpoints owned by the control plane and to integrate with Transit Gateway (TGW) attachments in accounts that use a centralized TGW. This PR introduces a feature-flagged flow that configures conditional DNS forwarding and exposes a small hook for the installer to register TGW attachments atomically with the control plane's resolver endpoints.

What this changes (high level):
- Terraform: new optional module `route53_forwarder` and variable `enable_conditional_dns` to create conditional forwarding rules and resolver rules when requested. The module is no-op by default.
- Installer hooks: small shell hook (`installer/aws/tgw/hooks.sh`) that runs during VPC attach to call the control plane API and register the attachment and route for resolver endpoints. Hook is idempotent and retries with backoff.
- Helm values: `installer/helm/controlplane/values.yaml` adds `dns.forwarding.enabled` and `dns.forwarding.allowedOrigins` to gate the feature at install time.
- Docs: `installer/docs/private-controlplane-dns.md` describes topologies, sequencing, recommended security groups, and rollback steps.
- Tests: integration tests for resolver health and TGW sequencing added to CI integration stage and a local validator script `scripts/networking/validate-dns.sh`.

Design notes:
- Feature-flagged: `enable_conditional_dns` (Terraform) and `dns.forwarding.enabled` (Helm) default to false. Existing installs are unaffected unless the operator opts in.
- Decoupled registration: the TGW hook only registers attachments and metadata; it does not modify infrastructure other than tagging the TGW attachment and creating the Route53 resolver rules when enabled. This reduces blast radius for upgrades.
- Security: resolver endpoints are created in private subnets; new security group `controlplane-resolver-sg` restricts inbound to management CIDRs and TGW CIDR blocks. The docs call out KMS usage for any API tokens used by the hook.

Rollout and canary plan:
1) Merge to main (this PR).
2) Dogfood in internal sandbox with `enable_conditional_dns=true` and a TGW-attached VPC. Run the validation script.
3) Canary on a single customer tenant (ops-assisted) with metrics/alerts configured: resolver health, forwarded-query latency, hook registration errors.
4) Gradual opt-in for customers during upgrades.

Rollback steps:
- If forwarders cause DNS regressions, set Helm `dns.forwarding.enabled=false` and re-run installer; Terraform can be used to destroy the conditional forwarding resources created by the module. TGW attachment registration is idempotent and can be ignored; tags added by the hook can be removed. Detailed rollback commands are in the docs file.

Testing performed:
- Unit tests for Terraform module inputs and null-resource guards.
- Integration test that brings up a small VPC + TGW, attaches, validates resolver forwarding, and simulates TGW flapping to ensure hook retries are safe.
- Manual validation on two internal clusters across different AZs.

Related work: Linear ENG-1982 implements the control plane API to accept attachment registrations; SRE-442 contains monitoring/alerting playbooks.

Notes for reviewers:
- I kept the TF changes isolated in a new module to minimize upgrade impact. Please watch for any cross-module variable leakage.
- The hook intentionally does not perform heavy IAM operations; it requires the same minimal role we already use for VPC lifecycle actions.

Checklist: 
- [x] Terraform module and variables added
- [x] Hook script with retries and idempotency
- [x] Helm values gate
- [x] Docs updated
- [x] Integration tests

If merged: squash-merge is preferred to keep a single logical change on main.

Motivation: Airgapped and VPC/private deployments need deterministic, auditable release artifacts that can be staged and rolled out safely across disconnected environments. This PR adds a deterministic staged indexer that emits canonical delta indices, plus an anchored attestation flow that ties signed delta blobs to a stable TUF anchor file. The goal is to make offline upgrade/rollback plans reproducible and verifiable by operators and audits.

What this changes (high level):
- New CLI: 'installer indexer build-staged' produces staged_release.json + per-stage delta-indexes in deterministic order.
- Canonical metadata: artifact metadata is normalized (timestamp rounding, sorted artifact keys, stable hash ordering) to ensure reproducible indices across builds.
- Anchored attestations: cosign-based attestations are produced and then referenced from a small TUF anchor file that lives alongside the index; this anchor is the minimal trust root the installer checks in airgapped upgrades.
- Helm chart helper: small chart annotation changes to encode index fingerprint for preflight checks in the private installer.
- Terraform module: variable inputs and output for embedding index anchor fingerprints into upstream automation.
- CI pipeline: new pipeline job that performs two successive builds (repro build + verification build) to detect non-determinism and surface flaky packaging steps.

Checklist: [x] indexer implementation with unit tests, [x] cosign attestation generation and verification, [x] helm annotations and preflight hook, [x] terraform variable + docs updates, [x] CI double-build verification job, [x] integration test against offline installer image.

Commits (summary):
- add: staged indexer CLI and core engine (indexer/staged_indexer.go, cmd/indexer/main.go)
- feat: canonical metadata normalizer and serializer (indexer/normalizer.go)
- feat: cosign attestation producer + TUF anchor writer (attest/anchor_writer.go)
- chore: helm annotation helper and preflight check (charts/installer/templates/_helpers.tpl, charts/installer/templates/preflight-hook.yaml)
- feat: terraform module inputs/outputs for index anchors (terraform/modules/installer-index/main.tf)
- ci: new pipeline job 'indexer-repro-verify' (ci/pipelines/indexer-repro-verify.yaml)

Files changed (high-level):
- indexer/staged_indexer.go
- indexer/normalizer.go
- attest/anchor_writer.go
- cmd/indexer/main.go
- charts/installer/values.yaml (annotation defaults)
- charts/installer/templates/preflight-hook.yaml
- terraform/modules/installer-index/main.tf
- ci/pipelines/indexer-repro-verify.yaml
- test/integration/offline-indexer-test.sh

Testing and verification: unit tests added for deterministic ordering and normalization; integration test spins up a local staging dir, runs the indexer twice and verifies bit-for-bit equality of produced staged_release.json and all delta shards. CI pipeline runs the double-build: first build produces artifacts, second build (in a clean container) re-produces them and runs 'cmp' on the outputs; non-zero diffs fail the job and upload a diagnostic bundle.

Security and provenance notes: attest/anchor_writer.go produces a minimal TUF anchor JSON that references cosign signatures and a canonical artifact list. The installer client was updated to check the anchor signature chain before accepting staged indexes when --require-anchor is set. This keeps the default lightweight but enables strict enforcement in regulated environments.

Backward compatibility and rollout: index format is backwards-compatible; installer will continue to accept legacy indices but will emit warnings. The staged indices are additive; operators can opt-in per-release using the --staged flag in the release pipeline. Terraform and Helm changes are optional and guarded by variables.

Related: references SUP-7312 for a customer request to provide verifiable airgapped rollouts and ENG-2149 for general reproducibility work.

Priya Menon: Added deterministic comparator and explicit stable sort for tags; unit tests added (indexer/normalizer_test.go).
Claire Novak: CI job failed on first run due to a missing cache invalidation step in the build container. Can you add a stricter container cleanup?
Priya Menon: Fixed Dockerfile and added a clean workspace step in ci/pipelines/indexer-repro-verify.yaml; re-ran pipeline and it passed.
Ethan Wu: Anchor format looks good; would like a short doc blurb on how operators rotate cosign keys and how that impacts anchors.
Priya Menon: Added docs: docs/private-installer/anchors.md and inline terraform comments describing rotation impact and recommended KMS workflows.
Introduces deterministic staged indexer and anchored attestation flow for airgapped/private rollouts. Operators can generate reproducible delta indices and verify them via a minimal TUF anchor tied to cosign signatures. Optional Helm and Terraform helpers included for easier adoption.

Motivation: Customers operating in constrained on-prem networks often need deterministic local registries seeded into specific subnets (DMZ vs internal, control-plane vs worker-only networks) and a portable, verifiable artifact that can be shipped via offline media. Existing seeding tooling assumes a flat seed node topology and does not provide native signed artifact indexes, nor a safe packaging option for optional host kernel modules (e.g., for BPF/CNI acceleration) that some customers require during install.

This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: 1) a Terraform module (terraform/registry-seeder) that deploys a small, HA local registry cluster seeded atomically with an immutable, signed OCI index and content manifests; the module supports subnet affinity for seed replicas and automatic DNS/HA proxy wiring for restricted networks; 2) an offline bundler that emits a self-validating OCI index (index.json + detached signatures) with optional kernel-module tarball packaging and preflight metadata so air-gapped sites can verify artifacts before bootstrapping.

What changed (high-level):
- New terraform module: terraform/modules/registry-seeder with examples for baremetal (netplan-based host selection), vSphere, and AWS VPC (for hybrid customers); supports seed placement policies: control-plane-only, worker-only, hybrid, and explicit hostlist.
- Registry seeder supports three seeding strategies: push-from-local (preferred for airgap), pull-and-cache (for semi-restricted egress), and redirected manifests (OCI manifest lists rewritten with registryLocation redirects).
- Offline bundler: tooling/bin/oci-seed-bundler.go and a shim script tools/bundle-to-registry.sh to produce a signed index (cosign signatures detached) and a content manifest that includes signed digests for kernel modules and package lists.
- Preflight checks: installer/cli/preflight now validates signatures, verifies digest checksums, and checks host kernel compatibility if kernel-module bundle is present.
- Documentation: docs/airgap/registry-seeding.md + quickstart examples for subnet affinity and deterministic rollback.

Design notes:
- Index signing uses cosign detached signatures (customers can swap to their KMS/HSM) and the bundler records the original source digests to enable deterministic verification after any manifest rewrite during network promotion.
- Seed placement uses Terraform providers and a small placement controller (stateless plan that renders host selection via tags or netplan metadata). We avoid long-lived controllers inside customer clusters to keep the footprint minimal for high-security environments.
- Rollback: seeder deploys content under hashed namespace prefixes and keeps the last two active namespaces; promoter scripts swap DNS and HA proxy targets atomically to rollback.

Testing and validation performed:
- Local integration tests using kind+registry-proxy validating redirectable manifests and cosign verification (tools/test/integration/oci_seeder_test.sh).
- Airgap validation in lab using RKE2 minimal cluster with a 3-node seed placement (control-plane-only) and kernel-module package applied on worker nodes. Digest verification and signature checks exercised.
- Terraform unit tests (tftest) for module inputs/outputs and plan idempotency.

Checklist (what I did):
- [x] Implement terraform module and examples.
- [x] Implement bundler and signature workflow (cosign-based).
- [x] Add preflight validations to installer CLI.
- [x] Add docs and quickstart.
- [x] Integration tests and CI job.

Deployment notes:
- Default behavior is opt-in: kernel-module bundle is disabled by default. To enable, set enable_kernel_modules = true and provide module_kvstore (pre-signed tarball) and host_selector.
- For strict airgap sites, run tools/bundle-to-registry.sh -> copy artifacts to USB or local mirror -> run terraform module with seed_method = "push-from-local".

Rollback and upgrade story:
- Upgrades publish a new hashed namespace (e.g., seeder/sha256-<release>) and seeder keeps previous namespace for quick rollback. Promotion is an atomic DNS/HA proxy swap.
- If a kernel module fails compatibility check during preflight, the installer will abort with a clear remediation path (revert to previous namespace or skip kernel module step).

Related work: ENG-1429 (registry seeding initiative), INF-278 (airgap signature standard).

Notes for reviewers: focus on Terraform module input surface for host selection and the security assumptions around detached cosign signatures. The preflight dependency list and error messages are intentionally explicit to reduce operator ambiguity.
Marcus Lee: Please make the host_selector schema explicit in the README and add an example for netplan tag-based selection.
Priya Nair: Added netplan selection example and extended README; clarified host_selector precedence rules.
Jamal Rivera: Security nit: use detached signatures by default but allow cosign keyless verification mode via a flag. Also, please ensure the bundler exits non-zero on signature mismatch.
Priya Nair: Implemented keyless verification toggle and explicit exit codes for signature failures. CI tests updated to cover mismatch flows.
Hannah Park: Terraform plan looked good; suggest an output that exposes the active namespace and previous namespace for easier monitoring.
Priya Nair: Added seeder_active_namespace and seeder_previous_namespace outputs.

Motivation: Private deployments have been impacted by slow policy bundle applies and fragile rollbacks during multi-tenant upgrades. This PR introduces a compact policy bundler to dedupe and canonicalize tenant policy templates, a staged apply flow that splits Terraform/Helm applies into dry-run, validate, and staged-commit phases, and a safe-rollback hookset that can revert only stage-scoped resources to minimize blast radius. The changeset touches the installer controller, Helm preflight checks, Terraform module wrappers, and the policy bundle generation pipeline. Key goals: reduce bundle payload size, make policy apply idempotent across retries, provide deterministic rollbacks that avoid tenant-wide role deletions, and add drift-detection guardrails to prevent partial state from being promoted. This description summarizes design, implementation notes, and operational runbook changes in a single continuous string as required.
feat(bundle): implement compact bundler that canonicalizes policy templates and produces reference dedupe map
chore(terraform): introduce staged-apply wrapper that runs plan->validate->apply with stage markers
feat(helm): add preflight rbac checks and dry-run validator for chart upgrades
fix(rbac): make tenant role creation idempotent by guarding with annotation match and resource-hashes
feat(rollback): add safe-taint rollback hookset and e2e test scaffold
test(e2e): add staged-apply smoke tests and drift-detection scenario
Diego Morales commented: Can you walk through the dedupe map format? We need to ensure it remains stable across bundle generations to avoid unnecessary churn. Also please add a compact-bundle version marker so old installers can still consume full bundles.
Author (Aisha Patel) replied: The dedupe map is a deterministic map keyed by the SHA256 of sorted template+params; added a version field in compact.go and a compatibility shim in the bundler README to maintain backward compatibility.
Claire Huang requested changes: The staged-apply wrapper looks good but add a timeout and retry policy for the validate stage and surface metrics for each stage in the console.
Author (Aisha Patel) addressed: Added stage_timeout config, exponential retry for transient plan errors, and emitted 'policy.apply.stage.duration' and 'policy.apply.stage.status' metrics in observability.
Samir Rao approved with comment: Verified e2e smoke test locally against minikube. Rollback hooks restored only stage resources in my run. Recommend we document the manual rollback steps in runbook before merge.
- Add compact policy bundler to reduce policy bundle size and deduplicate templates. - Staged apply flow for Terraform/Helm: dry-run, validate, staged-commit to reduce failed-upgrade blast radius. - Safe rollback hooks (taint-based) to revert only stage-scoped resources. - Helm preflight RBAC checks and dry-run validator. - Observability: per-stage metrics for policy apply. See ops/runbooks/private-installer-rollback.md for rollback procedures.

Motivation: Private installs have been facing drift and accidental subnet reuse during upgrades. This PR introduces a new Terraform module (modules/subnet-claim) plus a small reconcile helper to enforce immutable 'subnet claims' and a lease lifetime for GPU nodepool allocations. The goal is to make subnet assignments explicit, prevent silent re-use during rollbacks/upgrades, and provide a migration path for existing state. What this PR contains: 1) modules/subnet-claim: a TF module that creates a namespaced claim resource (TF state object) representing a leased CIDR + tags; the module exposes lifecycle rules to prevent deletion and supports an explicit 'relinquish' flag for safe teardown; 2) modules/immutable-lease: small helper module that wires a Dynamo-style lock (state-backed) plus IAM role that can be assumed by the installer reconciler; 3) modules/gpu-provisioner: updates to GPU nodepool TF to consume a subnet-claim id and attach a read-only binding rather than owning the subnet resource directly; 4) installer-reconcile binary (cmd/reconcile/main.go): an idempotent CLI used during upgrades that validates claims in state, acquires leases, and emits a human-readable plan for unsafe operations; 5) docs/upgrade-subnet-claim.md: migration and rollback steps for operators. Migration plan (in brief): run 'reconcile --dry-run' to enumerate claims and orphaned subnets; create claim objects for any existing nodepools using the --adopt flag; run terraform apply for modules/gpu-provisioner to switch ownership to claim id; cut over traffic to the new controller; monitor for lease expirations. Rollback plan: the 'reconcile' tool supports a --revert flag which releases claims created by adopt in a conservative way; TF lifecycle 'prevent_destroy' is the safety net to avoid accidental deletion. Tests & CI: unit tests for the reconcile CLI, terraform validate/checkov scan, and a focused e2e in the private-installer CI that provisions a single GPU nodepool using a leased subnet. Security: IAM bindings created by modules are least-privilege, and we add an audit role that allows only 'claim:read' to most service accounts. Backwards compatibility: existing installs continue to function; the migration is opt-in and can be performed incrementally. Rollout notes: staged rollout with a feature-flag in the installer; initial rollout to staging clusters for 2 weeks before production migration. Checklist: - [x] TF modules implemented and documented; - [x] reconcile CLI implemented and unit-tested; - [x] migrations documented; - [x] security review completed; - [x] CI green. Related: this PR complements prior state boundary work but avoids massive tfstate reshuffles by introducing claim objects that can be created without moving existing resources.
Jonah Li: Overall this looks good but we need stronger guarantees around concurrent adopters. Suggested adding optimistic lock semantics to the lease module.
Priya Raman: Implemented compare-and-swap in lease.tf and added a TTL check in reconcile. See lease.tf commit b7d4e22.
Asha Patel: Please add an explicit documented remediation step if a claim is held by a zombie process; pointed to docs/upgrade-subnet-claim.md where we added 'force-release' guidance.
Miguel Ortega: CI e2e initially failed on a timing flake; rerun passed. Approving after e2e is stable.
Jonah Li: APPROVED after confirming idempotency with two concurrent reconcile runs in staging.
Introduce subnet-claim and immutable-lease Terraform modules to enable non-destructive subnet allocations for GPU nodepools. Added reconcile CLI to migrate existing installs. Migration is opt-in and documented in docs/upgrade-subnet-claim.md.

payload.body:
Motivation:
Private installs have caused control-plane/api-server bursts during large multi-tenant upgrades and initial tenant bootstrap. Customers on constrained clusters (on-prem and small VPCs) observed API throttling and failed migrations when many init jobs ran concurrently. This PR adds two coordinated defenses: (1) an init-throttler helm hook that sequences init jobs using a lightweight leader-election+token-bucket pattern, and (2) a namespace quota-prober init container and probe which validates namespace resource quotas before starting migrations or heavy init work.

What this PR does (high-level):
- Introduces chart/templates/init-throttler.yaml: a new optional Helm hook that, when enabled, deploys a small init controller Job which provides a ConfigMap-based token queue used by tenant init Jobs to acquire a slot before proceeding. Slots and backoff are configurable from values.
- Adds chart/values.schema.json with JSON Schema validation for new keys and stricter typing of existing fields (affinityProfiles, init, preflight). The schema includes enums and constraints to prevent common misconfigurations (e.g., setting both nodeSelector and affinityProfiles contradictory configs).
- Adds chart/values.yaml examples showing how to opt into throttling, tune slots/per-second, and enable the quotaProbe for low-resource clusters.
- Adds chart/templates/quota-prober-init.yaml: init container template that runs a small probe to check namespace resourceQuota and node allocatable before allowing init to continue. The probe integrates with the throttler token flow but can run independently.
- Adds scripts/helm-utils.sh helper for building a values transform used in upgrades: it can safely migrate older boolean-style flags into the stricter schema (example transform included).
- Updates docs/upgrade-notes.md with guidance for toggling the throttler and guidance for troubleshooting probe failures.

Design notes and rationale:
- We intentionally use a ConfigMap+leader-election approach rather than a custom controller to keep the runtime footprint minimal and acceptable for air-gapped/on-prem installs. The token-bucket semantics are optimistic (best-effort): if the ConfigMap update fails transiently the job will retry with exponential backoff.
- The quota-prober is a small read-only probe that checks for the presence of a ResourceQuota and compares hard limits against a configurable threshold. This avoids starting large init tasks when cluster quotas would immediately block them.
- The values.schema.json both protects users from invalid shapes and enables Helm 3 validation in CI for private installs. The schema also documents deprecated fields and provides transformation guidance.

Backward compatibility and upgrade path:
- Default behavior is off: both throttler and quota-prober are disabled by default. Existing installs are not changed unless operators opt in or upgrade with the transform script.
- scripts/helm-utils.sh contains a safe migrate_values() routine that will run as a preflight step in our private-installer pipeline; it converts old flags (e.g., init.enableLegacyHook: true) into the new names and warns on collisions. Operators should run the transform in a staging environment before production.

Testing and verification:
- Unit tests for the values schema added under chart/tests/schema-validation (helm plugin).
- End-to-end helm test harness added: helm test --cleanup exercises a 3-tenant local scenario with throttler enabled (jobs sequentialized) and quota-prober toggled to fail to validate failure modes.
- CI: initial CI run failed lint due to an overly permissive schema reference; fix made in second commit. Final CI matrix: lint, unit-schema, helm-integration (k3s job) all passed.

Operational considerations:
- Observability: throttler emits token-acquire metrics to a ConfigMap-backed index and logs at INFO when a tenant waits > 30s. We added two metrics for SLOs: "init_throttle_wait_seconds" and "quota_prober_failures_total". These are scraped via the existing metrics-exporter sidecar in private installs when enabled.
- Failure modes: if the kube-apiserver is unavailable, throttler retries with exponential backoff; stuck tokens are garbage-collected after the configured tokenTTL. Quota probe failures surface as pod conditions, and the installer can be configured to either pause and require manual reconciliation or continue with a conservative fallback.

Files changed (summary):
- chart/templates/init-throttler.yaml (new)
- chart/templates/quota-prober-init.yaml (new)
- chart/values.schema.json (new/updated)
- chart/values.yaml (examples updated)
- scripts/helm-utils.sh (new helper + migrate_values)
- docs/upgrade-notes.md (appendix)
- chart/tests/helm-integration.yaml (test harness)

Related work: linked Linear tasks ENG-2219 (throttled init design), ENG-2381 (quota prober follow-up). Related support ticket SUP-1142 reported a production incident where 23 tenant init jobs caused API throttling in a constrained cluster.

How to roll out (operator guidance):
1) In staging, enable throttler with conservative slots: values:private.initThrottler.enabled=true, slots=2, slotsPerSecond=0.5.
2) Run scripts/helm-utils.sh migrate_values --in values-old.yaml --out values-new.yaml and inspect warnings.
3) Deploy, monitor the init_throttle_wait_seconds metric and quota_prober_failures_total. If many waits are observed, gradually increase slots.
4) Once validated, roll to production with a canary namespace first.

Backout plan: disable private.initThrottler.enabled and/or enable private.initThrottler.drainOnDisable to allow running tokens to finish then stop new acquisitions. Quota probe can be set to warn-only by setting checkMode = "warn" in values to avoid blocking.

Note on security and RBAC: all new resources use namespace-scoped RBAC roles and do not grant cluster-wide privileges. The ConfigMap used by throttler lives in the target namespace.

Evan Li: Can we avoid ConfigMap churn under heavy scale? Suggest using annotation-batched updates and a tokenTTL; responded and implemented tokenTTL + batch window.
Sana Iyer: Schema looks good but please add explicit enum for affinityProfiles to avoid accidental misconfigs; added in second commit.
Jonah Park: CI failed on lint on first run due to $ref path; fixed in commit 3 and reran CI. Approving after helm-integration passes.

Motivation: upgrades of private clusters and GPU nodepool reshuffles exposed non-deterministic Terraform state boundaries in environments that previously used ad-hoc state files. This PR introduces a small, low-risk set of artifacts to (1) produce a deterministic, immutable seed for tfstate boundaries (tfstate-seeder module + migration helper), and (2) enforce GPU scheduling and subpool affinity in private installs via a reconciler controller (gpu-subpool-reconciler). Goals: minimize disruption during state migration, provide an opt-in statelock HA proxy pattern for on-prem S3-like backends, and surface safer defaults for GPU taints/labels so autoscaler + nodepool allocation behave predictably.

What this PR contains (high level):
- Terraform: new module modules/tfstate-seeder that computes canonical bucket/object names and an initial manifest file with sha-256 anchors for tenant-scoped state. Includes optional DynamoDB-style lock table configuration and an idempotent migration wrapper script (scripts/tfstate_migrate_seed.sh) to stitch existing state into the seeded layout.
- Installer chart additions: chart/statelock-proxy Helm chart (lightweight sidecar proxy for environments where a single DynamoDB-like lock service is unavailable; uses leader-election and S3 object lease semantics). Chart is optional and guarded behind values.enableStateLockProxy.
- Controller: controllers/gpu-subpool-reconciler (small controller in Go) that watches NodePools and Node objects and applies a tenant-scoped schedulingPolicy CRD at install time. The reconciler enforces label/taint canonicalization, migrates legacy node labels, and optionally annotates pools with stable subpool ids used by the TF modules for subnet claims.
- Docs: docs/upgrade/tfstate-seed.md explaining the migration steps, rollback guidance, and a checklist for production customers.

Migration/rollback strategy: the tfstate-seeder emits a seed manifest and provides a dry-run mode. The migration script takes two-phase approach: (1) seed-only (no write of main.tfstate) and verification of plan; (2) commit: upload canonical state object + update backend config pointer. Rollback is performed by re-pointing backend config to previous object and, if the statelock-proxy was used, by disabling leader election and waiting for leases to expire. Steps and commands are in docs/upgrade/tfstate-seed.md.

Security/IAM: the tf module scopes IAM policies to the minimal set required to create bucket/object + lock table and to read/restore the anchor manifest. The migration script performs an explicit confirmation check before writing seeds. The statelock-proxy runs with least-privilege S3/GCS credentials and includes a guidance snippet for integrating with KMS/HSM in air-gapped installs.

Testing done: unit tests for the tf module variables and template rendering; integration tests in bench/ci that run the migration script against a local MinIO cluster; controller e2e recorded in tests/e2e/gpu_reconciler_test.go using kind + mocked node annotations.

Why this is low-risk: modules are opt-in; defaults preserve current behaviour unless install-time flags are flipped. The migration helper is explicit and safe by default (dry-run required). The reconciler is additive and can be disabled via chart values.

Checklist:
- [x] Terraform module + unit tests
- [x] Helm chart for statelock-proxy + chart README
- [x] Controller implementation + e2e tests
- [x] Docs and migration guide
- [x] Security review and scoped IAM policy

Notes: this PR is intentionally conservative—seed manifests are immutable and named using tenant/org + cluster hash so we avoid accidental collisions. We expect follow-ups to add automation for scheduled background reconciliation of legacy labels and tighter RBAC controls for the statelock-proxy.
Ibrahim Patel: Can we ensure the migration script outputs a deterministic plan hash before committing? (commented on scripts/tfstate_migrate_seed.sh)
Maya Chen: Added deterministic plan hash and a --force flag gated behind an explicit environment variable. Also added a verbose --audit-mode for dry-runs.
Liam O'Connor: e2e flaked once on CI due to kind networking; added wait/retry and moved MinIO to the CI service cluster. (requested changes)
Zara Martinez: Reviewed IAM policy scoping; suggested removing broad s3:PutObject on root bucket. Tightened the policy in modules/tfstate-seeder/iam.tf (approved after change)
Ibrahim Patel: Verified Helm chart values gating; approved + left lgtm on controller after tests passed
Add optional tfstate-seeder module and statelock-proxy Helm chart to support deterministic state layout for private installs; introduce gpu-subpool-reconciler controller to canonicalize GPU node labels/taints and enable predictable scheduling. Opt-in behavior; migration helper included.
Before enabling seed migration in production: 1) run scripts/tfstate_migrate_seed.sh --dry-run against a snapshot; 2) ensure S3/GCS credentials have only the scoped rights listed in docs/upgrade/tfstate-seed.md; 3) if using statelock-proxy, deploy it in its own namespace with a single replica initially; 4) monitor tfstate writes and cluster autoscaler metrics for 24 hours post-migration.
Monitor canary customer who opted in to seed in staging for 48h
Backport minimal docs and iam examples to release/2025-02 if requested
Follow-up PR: automations to periodically reconcile legacy labels -> ENG-3510

payload.body:
Summary: This PR introduces a pluggable preflight check framework in the Private installer. The framework standardizes check execution, result reporting, severity levels, and remediation pointers so upgrades are safer-by-default and failures are actionable for operators. Context: Part of the “Private upgrade + rollback mechanism” effort. This PR focuses on the framework + CLI surface for preflight runs; follow-up PRs will add/expand the actual checks (cluster health, storage, RBAC/SSO reachability, artifact availability, etc.). Goals: (1) Make prechecks composable (registerable plugins) and deterministic, (2) Provide consistent UX for operators and Support, (3) Establish blocking vs warning semantics that can be used by upgrade plan generation and change-management gating. Design notes: Checks are registered by ID and grouped into named phases (environment, control-plane, data-plane, artifacts). Each check returns a CheckResult with: status (PASS/WARN/FAIL/SKIP), severity (BLOCKER/WARNING/INFO), a short summary, optional details, and remediation pointers (human-readable steps + optional doc links). The runner supports timeouts per-check, a global deadline, and produces both console output and a JSON artifact suitable for audit/support bundles. CLI: Adds `redwood-private preflight run` (alias wired for upgrade flows in subsequent PRs). Supports `--format=table|json`, `--output <path>`, `--fail-on-warning` (default false), `--include`/`--exclude` (by check ID or group), and `--timeout` controls. Output example (json): `{ "run_id": "pf_...", "installer_version": "0.19.0", "target_version": "private-1.42.0", "results": [ ... ], "summary": { "blockers": 0, "warnings": 2 } }` (full schema in `docs/preflight-result-schema.md`). Implementation details: - New package `internal/preflight/` with: `registry` (check registration + metadata), `runner` (execution + concurrency limits), and `report` (renderers: table/json). - Standardized error taxonomy for checks to map common failures into remediation hints (e.g., kube auth failure vs API server unreachable vs RBAC forbidden). - Basic built-in checks included as scaffolding/examples: Kubernetes API reachability, namespace write access, and installer artifact writeability (output dir). These are intentionally minimal; real upgrade checks land in ENG-4829 follow-ups. - Adds a persistent “last preflight” record under the installer state dir to be consumed by the upgrade planner (plan generator PR) and support bundles. - Logging: all checks emit structured logs with `check_id`, `severity`, and `status` fields; runner emits a single summary line for easy grep during on-call. Operator UX: Table output uses stable ordering and explicitly labels “BLOCKING” items; remediation text is capped in the table view with a `--verbose` option to print full remediation steps. Testing: Unit tests cover registration, include/exclude filtering, timeout handling, renderer output stability, and JSON schema validation. Integration test spins up a kind cluster and validates kube reachability + RBAC check behavior under simulated restricted RBAC. Checklist: - [x] Framework + registry + runner - [x] JSON + table renderers - [x] Minimal built-in checks as examples - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Docs: result schema + CLI usage - [ ] Add full precheck inventory (follow-up PRs under ENG-4829) Notes for reviewers: Please focus on (a) severity semantics (BLOCKER/WARNING/INFO) and defaults, (b) output stability (Support will consume this), and (c) security concerns around logging potentially sensitive info in remediation/details. Release notes: Adds new `preflight run` command and machine-readable preflight output artifact to support upgrade gating and troubleshooting.
Irene Choi: The framework looks good. One concern: remediation messages should never echo kubeconfig contents or full endpoint URLs for private clusters. Can we sanitize/trim? Bruno Silva: Good call. I updated the kube reachability check to log only hostnames (no tokens/paths) and redacted query strings; also added a `SafeDetails()` helper that defaults to redaction for error types we control.
Sean Gallagher: For gating, we need deterministic semantics: FAIL+BLOCKER must abort upgrade, WARN+BLOCKER should probably also abort by default. What’s the default behavior? Bruno Silva: Default is: any FAIL+BLOCKER returns non-zero exit code. WARN never fails unless `--fail-on-warning` is set. Severity is orthogonal; WARN+BLOCKER is allowed but we should avoid generating that combination in real checks. I added a validation in the registry to reject WARN+BLOCKER for now so we don’t create ambiguous gating behavior.
Kenji Nakamura: Table output truncation is helpful, but the operator needs a copy/paste remediation. Suggest printing remediation in full when there are blockers even without `--verbose`. Bruno Silva: Agreed. Updated renderer: if there is any blocking result, we append a “Remediation details” section with full steps for those checks. Non-blocking warnings remain truncated unless `--verbose`.
Marcus Lin: Please ensure we don’t allow check plugins to execute arbitrary shells by default. Are checks just Go functions in-process? Bruno Silva: Yes—checks are compiled into the installer binary and are registered at init time. No dynamic loading, no shell execution helpers added here. I also added a note in docs that checks must not run `kubectl`/shell and should use client-go to avoid leaking env state.
Sahana Iyer: Integration test flaked once on CI due to kind API server readiness. Can we add a wait/retry with bounded timeout? Bruno Silva: Added a readiness wait with exponential backoff (max 60s) before running the kube reachability check, and pinned kind node image to the version we use in other installer tests.
payload.title: Implement pluggable preflight check framework for Private upgrades

Summary: This PR implements a coordinated Terraform state sharding strategy for private deployments that separates GPU nodepool state from VPC/cluster state, and adds an automated IAM-rotation helper used during nodepool lifecycle transitions. Motivation: Private installs have grown hard to operate when multiple teams create ephemeral GPU nodepools in the same TF state workspace. We observed long terraform plan/apply times, repeated terraform lock contention, and operator risk when rolling back pool changes. Separating state for GPU nodepools reduces blast radius, shortens apply times, and makes automated rollback safe. The IAM rotation component provides a controlled mechanism to rotate short-lived credentials and to reconcile nodepool IAM bindings during migration.

What this change does (high level):
- Introduces a new Terraform module layout: terraform/modules/gpu_nodepool with its own state backend configuration helpers and example workspaces.
- Adds a lightweight state-pointer updater (scripts/tfstate-pointer-updater.sh) that migrates a nodepool's resources into the new state file and updates the installer pointer files used by the Private installer.
- Provides an installer-side migrate_state.go (installer/upgrade/migrate_state.go) orchestration that sequences: drain -> terraform import -> state split -> iam rotation -> final verification, and exposes a dry-run flag.
- Adds an IAM-rotation helper (installer/security/iam_rotate.go) that creates short-lived credentials for nodepool controllers, applies new bindings with a canary attach/detach, and validates access before revoking the old key.
- Adds Helm chart hooks and values for running the migrator as a Job during upgrades (installer/helm/charts/gpu/templates/migration-job.yaml and values.yaml knobs).
- E2E tests and unit tests: tests/e2e/private-install-state-migration.test.ts and unit tests under installer/upgrade/* to validate dry-run and rollback behaviors.

Checklist:
- [x] Terraform module and example workspace added
- [x] Migration orchestration implemented with idempotent steps and dry-run
- [x] IAM rotation flows with canary attach/detach validated
- [x] Helm hooks for migration implemented and annotated
- [x] E2E tests for a 1->2 nodepool migration path added
- [x] Integration with CI gating and smoke test added

Compatibility and rollout plan: The migrator is gated behind a feature flag (values.install.migration.enabled=false by default). Operators can opt into migration per-tenant via the installer console. Migration has three safety checkpoints: dry-run, canary attach, and traffic verification. The tfstate-pointer script supports rollback by restoring the original state file if any step fails.

Operational notes for SRE/Operators: the PR includes a step-by-step runbook at terraform/modules/gpu_nodepool/README.md documenting preconditions (backups, lock TTLs), expected downtime (drain + cordon time only), and follow-up verification steps. There is also a lightweight prometheus metric emitted by the migrator job (migrator_last_run_success) and an alert rule suggested in installer/observability/migrator-alerts.yaml.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: accidental double-import or resource orphaning. Mitigation: a built-in plan/preview check that compares resources to be imported and refuses to proceed if diffs exceed a threshold.
- Risk: IAM misbinding during rotation. Mitigation: canary attach/verify before global rollout; automated rollback attaches the previous binding and notifies the operator.
- Risk: terraform state drift post-migration. Mitigation: post-migrate verification step that runs terraform plan against both old and new states and asserts no changes.

Related work: This complements ENG-7834 (tfstate migrations) and builds on the node lifecycle APIs introduced in ENG-7560. The approach intentionally differs from earlier monolithic tfstate migrators by providing per-nodepool workspace isolation and a fast path for revert.

Testing and CI: initial runs showed a transient acceptance test failure in the helm hook ordering when the job precedence race surfaced. Fixes were made (commit a3b4c8) and CI now passes full e2e on the private helm chart matrix. The PR includes a CI job (ci/private-migration-smoke) that can be run manually for large customers before enabling the flag.

Migration example (operator flow, short):
1) Enable values.install.migration.enabled=true for a tenant
2) Run dry-run: ./installer migrate --tenant <T> --nodepool <N> --dry-run
3) Review the generated plan and commit state backup
4) Run actual migrate: ./installer migrate --tenant <T> --nodepool <N>
5) Watch migrator job logs, verify canary attach/traffic, then confirm completion

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps the default behavior off. Operators who prefer a full-monolith state can opt to not use the new layout. The migration tooling is designed to be reversible and observable.
Ethan Cole: Overall this looks good. Please add an irreversible-flag guard for the final state pointer swap so operators have one more chance to cancel. Also confirm the migrator emits a run_id in logs for tracing.
Priya Nair: Added --irreversible-confirm flag and run_id logging in latest commit. Updated README with the manual rollback steps.
Lina Park: A few nit comments on error messages and the terraform import timeout. Can we parameterize the import timeout and expose it in values.yaml?
Priya Nair: Parameterized import timeout and added note about bumping timeouts in large clusters. PTAL.
Asha Ramesh: Security check: ensure the rotation helper logs do not contain secret material. Verified unit tests cover masking. Approving once a lint CI passes.
CI Bot: lint failed on installer/security/iam_rotate.go - fixed formatting in commit e4d5f77 and re-ran.
Ethan Cole: Approved after the last fixes. Marking for merge with squash.
Added state sharding for GPU nodepools and operator tooling for safe migration and IAM rotation. Feature disabled by default; enable via values.install.migration.enabled. See terraform/modules/gpu_nodepool/README.md for operator runbook.
Migration is opt-in. Run dry-run, validate plans, backup tfstate, then run migrator. Use ci/private-migration-smoke to validate an environment before enabling in production.
Monitor migrator_last_run_success and migrator_run_id logs; schedule a follow-up to evaluate operator feedback after first 3 migrations. Add a Linear card to track adoption metrics.

Motivation: Private control-plane installs must operate in environments that restrict cross-VPC service access. We previously relied on permissive VPC endpoint policies and a single Route53 forwarder, which caused over-broad service access (S3/STS) in highly regulated customers. This change introduces per-service, per-environment VPC endpoint policy templates plus a split-horizon DNS option that routes control-plane requests to an isolated interface endpoint in customer VPCs and normal tenant traffic to service endpoints. What this PR does: 1) Terraform: refactors terraform/modules/vpc_endpoints to support endpoint_policy_templates keyed by service and environment (dev/staging/prod). Adds least-privilege templates for s3, sts, kms, ssm, and secretsmanager. 2) DNS: adds an optional route53 split-horizon configuration (installer/templates/dns/split_horizon.tf) and documentation for deploying a private hosted zone with conditional forwarding for controlplane.redwood.internal. 3) Security groups: introduces a default least-privilege sg module used for interface endpoints and control-plane instances, with explicit ingress rules instead of open CIDR usage. 4) Helm: adds values.yaml knobs to enable endpoint-policy enforcement and pass a delegated zone name into the installer. 5) Migration and rollback: provides a non-destructive migration workflow (terraform plan to add policy attachments and then to enable split-horizon in a second apply) and a rollback plan that reverts feature flags and removes policy attachments. Testing: added integration tests that validate endpoint policy attachment and DNS resolution in a multi-account test harness. Backwards compatibility: feature flags default to off so existing installs are unaffected. Rollout plan: ship as a stage-gated opt-in in the private-installer chart, enable for pilot customers, collect logs, and then flip default to on in a future release. See docs/upgrade/vpc-endpoint-migration.md for the step-by-step migration guide and operator checklist. Risks and mitigations: initial terraform apply may trigger resource replacements for extremely old installs — migration doc includes detection and a safe plan to avoid replacement. CI notes: pipeline initially flagged a flaky multi-account test which was hardened (see commits).
Diego Morales (reviewer): Please add explicit deny statements for stale principals in the S3 policy template and document the fallback behavior when a principal is not present.
Asha Patel (author): Added explicit deny block and expanded the migration doc to call out principals discovery. Also added unit tests for missing principals.
Sofia Kim (reviewer): Small nit on variable naming in the TF module (env -> environment). Also suggest a longer TTL justification for the split-horizon record.
Asha Patel (author): Renamed variable to 'environment' and updated comments explaining the TTL tradeoff. PTAL.
Ethan Zhang (security): LGTM from security side — policy templates look narrowly scoped, added a suggestion to rotate KMS keys used by endpoints and documented in the ops checklist.
Sofia Kim: Approve after nit. Diego: Approve. Ethan: Approve.
Added per-service VPC endpoint policy templates (s3, sts, kms, ssm, secretsmanager) — opt-in via helm values
Introduced split-horizon DNS support for control-plane hostnames to isolate control-plane traffic in customer VPCs
Least-privilege security group module for interface endpoints
Migration guide provided: docs/upgrade/vpc-endpoint-migration.md
1) Review policies: run scripts/principal-discovery to enumerate existing principals
2) Apply terraform in plan mode to see attachments that will be created (do not apply yet)
3) Apply policy attachment step (no enablement of split-horizon): terraform apply -target=module.vpc_endpoints.policy_attachments
4) Validate access via integration tests in staging
5) Enable split-horizon feature flag in helm values and perform a controlled rollout to pilot tenants
6) Monitor DNS resolution and endpoint logs for 48 hours, then gradually expand

Motivation: We observed two upgrade classes cause unexpected failures in private deployments: non-backwards compatible schema edits and inconsistent restore ordering when replaying WAL/segment-based backups across heterogeneous clusters. This PR adds a lightweight compatibility shim that enables node-level schema adapters during rolling upgrades and a point-in-time (PTP) restore oracle that validates restore playbooks against a deterministic checkpoint before executing a customer restore. Summary: 1) compatibility-shim: an operator-side library that can register small per-table transformation hooks (rename/rename-column, default fill, index rebuild plan) applied as a staged migration step; the shim runs as part of the operator pre-drain hook so upgrades can proceed without an immediate full migration. 2) ptp-restore-oracle: a validation daemon that replays a restore plan against a read-only snapshot in an isolated namespace to detect ordering issues, incompatible constraints, or missing post-restore hooks. Design constraints: minimal operator footprint, no automatic destructive migrations, KMS-backed ephemeral keys for snapshot decrypt during dry-runs, and a safe-fallback path that quarantines tenants if validation fails. Included changes: Helm hooks to add a pre-upgrade job that runs the compatibility shim tests; Terraform module updates to create an optional IAM role and KMS key for restore dry-runs; operator changes to register, run, and report shim outcomes; CLI additions (installerctl) to trigger oracle dry-runs and export deterministic runbooks. Rollout plan: feature gated behind a helm value 'safety.compatShim=true' and 'safety.ptpOracle.enabled=false' by default. Canary flow: enable shim-only in Dedicated staging clusters for 2 weeks with nightly migration rehearsal on sampled tenant data; enable oracle in read-only mode for 1 week before allowing active restoration. Rollback: the shim is non-destructive and can be disabled; the operator includes idempotent undo markers for any metadata it writes. Checklist: - [x] Library and operator integration implemented - [x] Helm chart pre-upgrade job added - [x] Terraform IAM/KMS optional resources - [x] CLI commands and runbooks updated - [x] E2E rehearsal tests added in perf-canary harness - [x] QA: ran mixed-version cluster rehearsal on z1 and z2 clusters - [x] Security review for KMS usage completed Testing notes: unit tests for shim adapters, integration tests for isolated restore rehearsal, manual runbook executed with customer-like dataset and verified quarantine behavior. Backwards compatibility: shim only activates when explicitly enabled; no implicit schema changes. Related: ENG-4127 (migration reliability), ENG-4180 (restore automation).
This approach is intentionally conservative: we avoid automatic destructive changes, provide rehearsal capability for restore playbooks, and surface deterministic failure reasons so platform engineers can write targeted post-restore hooks. The shim pattern is extensible: future adapters will be shipped as small, audited modules in the operator repository.
Liam O'Connor: Suggest adding a toggle to disable KMS use for air-gapped installs — answered: added terraform flag 'backup.kms.enabled=false' and documented the manual key import flow.
Marina Torres: Please ensure the shim never writes user data during dry-run — author: shim design now runs in read-only mode unless a migration adapter explicitly returns 'requires-write' and then operator prompts for manual approval in console.
Derek Huang: Can we limit the pre-upgrade job runtime to avoid blocking long windows? — author: added a configurable timeout (safety.preflight.timeoutSeconds) and a default 1800s; also added backoff and early-fail metrics.
CI bot: full integration suite passed on rerun (build #2248)
Added a compatibility shim to allow staged, non-destructive schema adapters during rolling upgrades; introduced a point-in-time restore oracle that validates restore playbooks against a read-only snapshot before live restores; new helm and terraform flags to opt-in for safety rehearsals; installerctl commands to run and inspect rehearsals.
Enable via helm: --set safety.compatShim=true --set safety.ptpOracle.enabled=true (start with ptpOracle.enabled=false to stage). For air-gapped installs set backup.kms.enabled=false and follow docs/private-deployments/compatibility-shim.md for manual key rotation. Monitor metric 'upgrade.preflight.failure_rate' and use 'installerctl ptp-oracle status' to inspect recent dry-run artifacts.
payload.title: Introduce compatibility shim and point-in-time restore oracle

Motivation: Private installs increasingly host multiple logical tenants (teams/customers) inside a single VPC/on-prem deployment. We need automated, auditable propagation of Prometheus rules and Grafana dashboards per-tenant so alerts and runbooks remain consistent across upgrades and platform changes. This PR implements a GitOps-style rules sync operator plus a Grafana folder provisioning flow tied to the installer Terraform/Helm lifecycle.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a lightweight 'rules-sync' controller run as a sidecar in the observability namespace that watches a configured Git repo (with optional path per-tenant) and applies PrometheusRule CRDs via kubectl apply-style operations. The controller is implemented with idempotent apply semantics and leader-election for HA.
- Introduces Grafana provisioning templates that create a folder per-tenant and a folder-level permission model (read-only for general users, editors for tenant admins). Dashboards are synced from the same Git repo path and versioned by commit SHA.
- Extends the Terraform module to expose git repository, webhooks, and a helm_release hook pair to perform pre-upgrade validation and safe rollback on failure. The hook runs a dry-run of the rules sync and verifies no duplicate recording rules exist across tenants.
- Helm chart updates: adds templates for PrometheusRule, a ServiceAccount/Role for the rules-sync controller, and an init job that migrates legacy folder config to the new per-tenant model during upgrade.
- Adds a dashboard merge tool (small Go binary) used in CI to validate dashboards (UID collisions, panel schema) before applying. CI now includes a dashboard-validation job.

Commits summary: 6 commits (squashed on merge)
- feat(rules-sync): initial controller + leader-election + tests
- feat(grafana): folder provisioning templates + RBAC
- chore(terraform): expose git repo/webhook inputs and add pre/post hooks
- feat(ci): dashboard validation job and unit tests for merge tool
- fix(helm): init migration job to convert legacy folder labels
- docs: installer docs + upgrade notes

Files/areas changed (high level):
- terraform/modules/observability/main.tf (adds variables: rules_git_repo, rules_git_path, rules_git_branch, webhook_secret)
- helm/observability/templates/rules-sync-deployment.yaml (new controller)
- helm/observability/templates/grafana-provisioning.yaml (folder + datasource provisioning)
- helm/observability/templates/init-migrate-folders-job.yaml (upgrade migration)
- tools/dashboard-validate/main.go (new small tool used by CI)
- docs/private-installer/observability-gitops.md (usage and operator configuration)
- examples/tenant-configs/tenant-a.yaml (example repo layout and values.yaml snippet)

Small representative snippet (grafana provisioning):

apiVersion: 1
providers:
  - name: 'redwood-tenant-provisioning'
    orgId: 1
    folder: 'Tenant-${TENANT_ID}'
    type: file
    options:
      path: /var/lib/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/${TENANT_ID}

This provisioning file is templated at deploy time; the installer writes per-tenant folders and creates a Kubernetes secret with the commit SHA for traceability.

Operational considerations:
- Secrets: the git credentials are stored in a Kubernetes secret populated by Terraform; we added explicit KMS-encryption hooks in the Terraform module for cloud KMS/HSM users.
- Rollback safety: the helm pre-upgrade hook runs rules-sync in dry-run mode and the installer will abort an upgrade if rule collisions or invalid rule syntax are detected. The post-upgrade hook writes an upgrade marker commit SHA to the tenant namespace to allow automated rollbacks to lookup the previous dashboard state.
- Performance: rules-sync only re-applies changed manifests and has a configurable resync period; large repos should be scoped per-tenant path to avoid unnecessary churn.

CI and testing:
- New CI job 'obs/dashboard-validate' runs dashboard-validate against changed dashboard JSONs (checks UIDs, schema).
- 'obs/rules-integration' runs a k3s-based integration that exercises rules-sync against a fake Prometheus Operator and validates PrometheusRule CRDs are created.
- Initial CI run failed due to UID collision for an example dashboard; fixed by normalizing UID generation in dashboard-validate. Final CI status: pass.

Review convo (high level):
- Miguel Torres (reviewer): "This looks sound; main ask is to ensure the pre-upgrade dry-run is idempotent and won't mutate any CRDs. Also add a migration rollback test."
- Asha (author): "Added an explicit dry-run flag and created integration test 'obs/migration-rollback' that simulates a failed migration and validates the pre-upgrade marker prevents proceeding."
- Priya Shah (SRE): "We should avoid creating >1000 folders for clusters with many tenants — can we add an opt-out and on-demand provisioning?"
- Asha: "Added values.allowOnDemandFolderCreation (default: false). When true, the controller will create folders lazily on first dashboard access via an API hook. Documented trade-offs in the docs page."
- Dawson Lee: "Small nit: move the dashboard validation tool to tools/observability/dashboard-validate for consistency with other tools."
- Asha: "Moved the binary, updated CI job path."

Deployment notes / upgrade path for existing customers:
- Default behavior is backward compatible: if no rules_git_repo is provided, nothing changes.
- Customers opting in should supply a git repo and set values.rulesGit.path to their tenant subpaths. Terraform will create the secret; operator documentation explains repo layout conventions.
- For upgrades from earlier observability stacks that used a flat dashboard list, run the migration job first using the interactive installer flag --run-migration and review the generated migration plan in S3/artifacts.

Rollout and monitoring:
- Added Prometheus metrics for rules_sync_reconciles_total, rules_sync_errors_total, grafana_folder_creations_total, and dashboard_validation_failures_total.
- Dashboards: new 'Observability > Syncer' dashboard that surfaces per-tenant sync latency, last committed SHA, and applied rule counts.

Backwards compatibility and fallback:
- If rules-sync crashes or fails, the installer falls back to the previous release (helm rollback) using the recorded pre-upgrade marker. The terraform module includes a timeout and healthcheck to automate this in the managed upgrade flow.

Documentation: updated docs/private-installer/observability-gitops.md with examples, repo layout conventions, migration instructions, and troubleshooting (git auth, UID collisions).

Testing done: unit tests for controller logic, integration tests against k3s in CI, manual smoke tests in a staged private install cluster with two tenant namespaces.

Remaining follow-ups (tracked in linked Linear tasks):
- ENG-2248: Add webhook-based incremental sync to reduce full-repo scans.
- ENG-2307: Add RBAC refinement to map external identity providers to Grafana folder roles.

Merge outcome: PR was squashed and merged to main after approvals from Miguel, Priya, and Dawson. CI green on final run. Release notes added.


Adds automated sync of Prometheus recording/alerting rules from a Git repo per-tenant, creates isolated Grafana folders+provisioning for each private install tenant, and wires Terraform/Helm hooks for safe upgrades and rollbacks. Backwards compatible with existing provisioning; customers must supply git repo and credentials in installer config.
Miguel Torres: Please ensure dry-run does not mutate CRDs; also add migration rollback test.
Asha Raman: Added dry-run flag and migration rollback integration test.
Priya Shah: Consider on-demand folder creation to limit folder explosion, especially for multi-tenant clusters.
Asha Raman: Added allowOnDemandFolderCreation flag and documented tradeoffs.
Dawson Lee: Move dashboard-validate tool to tools/observability path for consistency — small nit.
Asha Raman: Moved tool and updated CI job.
CI: Initial run failed due to UID collision in examples; fixed and re-ran, all checks passing.
This PR focuses on automation and safe upgrade paths for observability in private installs. It intentionally keeps defaults conservative to preserve backwards compatibility and adds opt-in features for tenants that want GitOps-driven alerts and dashboards.
observability:
  rulesGit:
    repo: git@github.com:redwood/tenant-observability.git
    branch: main
    pathPrefix: tenants/${TENANT_ID}/rules
  grafana:
    enablePerTenantFolders: true
    allowOnDemandFolderCreation: false
  terraform_hooks:
    pre_upgrade_timeout: 300s
    enable_auto_rollback: true

payload.body:
Implements `redwood-private upgrade rollback` backed by a persisted upgrade state machine. The rollback command reads the last recorded upgrade attempt (plan + execution state), runs rollback hooks in a deterministic order (control plane first, then data plane), and verifies the cluster is healthy after rollback. This is intended to make rollback an operator-safe, auditable action rather than a collection of manual kubectl/helm steps.

Context
- Follows PR #4821 (upgrade plan generator) and PR #4850 (backup orchestration + snapshot hooks).
- Designed for N-1 -> N upgrades with explicit rollback entry points for failures during plan execution.
- Addresses support incidents where upgrades failed during DB migrations and operators needed a consistent rollback procedure (SUP-18421, SUP-18488).

Operator UX
- Roll back the last attempted upgrade: `redwood-private upgrade rollback`
- Roll back and force a specific target revision from stored history: `redwood-private upgrade rollback --target-revision <revision-id>`
- Dry-run the rollback (prints steps + would-run hooks): `redwood-private upgrade rollback --dry-run`
- Status summary including rollback eligibility: `redwood-private upgrade status`

What gets persisted
- Writes an UpgradeExecutionState artifact at `${STATE_DIR}/upgrade/state.json` (defaults to `/var/lib/redwood-private/upgrade/state.json`) and mirrors a summarized view to a Kubernetes ConfigMap (`redwood-private-upgrade-state`) for support bundles.
- Tracks: plan_id, from_version, to_version, stage, step, timestamps, backup refs, helm releases touched, and rollback eligibility.

Rollback semantics (high-level)
- Rollback is allowed when: (a) an upgrade execution state exists, (b) the recorded attempt has not been finalized as success, and (c) rollback hooks are available for the stages that completed.
- Rollback ordering:
  1) Pre-rollback checks (cluster access, namespace existence, artifact availability for the target version)
  2) Control-plane rollback (helm release rollback / apply pinned chart version)
  3) Data-plane rollback (roll back serving components only after CP confirms ready)
  4) Restore data if needed (optional; only when the plan recorded a backup and migration stage completed)
  5) Post-rollback verification (subset of prechecks + readiness gates)
- Idempotency: rollback steps are safe to re-run; the state machine records completed rollback steps and will skip already-completed steps unless `--force-step` is used.

Post-rollback health verification
- Waits for Deployments/StatefulSets to become Ready (with timeouts and actionable failure messages)
- Verifies API health endpoints (installer talks to the in-cluster CP service when available)
- Runs a minimal preflight suite: DB connectivity, schema version compatibility, and control-plane -> data-plane connectivity
- Emits a rollback summary with next actions when verification fails (collect support bundle; recommended kubectl commands)

Auditability
- Writes a structured rollback report at `${STATE_DIR}/upgrade/rollback-report.json` including executed steps, hook outputs, and verification results.
- Adds support-bundle section `private-upgrade/` with state.json, rollback-report.json, and last 2 installer logs.

Test plan
- Unit tests for state transitions (happy path + partial failure cases)
- Integration tests in kind for:
  - failure mid-control-plane stage -> rollback
  - failure post-migration stage -> rollback with restore option
  - rollback idempotency (rerun rollback)
- Manual (staging): forced failure by injecting invalid image ref during upgrade, then rollback.

Checklist
- [x] State persisted and versioned (schema v1) with forward-compat parsing
- [x] Rollback command supports dry-run
- [x] Hooks have stable contract + timeouts
- [x] Post-rollback health verification
- [x] Docs snippet in `docs/commands.md` (follow-up: full runbook in Confluence)

Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- Emit platform audit log events from control plane for rollback start/stop (tracked in monorepo)
- Expand restore verification (application-level smoke tests) in e2e suite
Sean Gallagher (SRE): The rollback eligibility rules look good, but I want to be sure we don’t accidentally roll back after an operator explicitly marked the upgrade complete. Can we hard-block rollback when state.finalized_success=true?
Bruno Silva (author): Yep. Added explicit guard: if finalized_success is set, `upgrade rollback` exits with code 2 and prints remediation (use `upgrade plan` for next upgrade). Added unit tests covering this.
Connor O'Brien (Release Eng): We need determinism in the Helm rollback target. Are we rolling back to the previous revision or pinning the chart/app version from the plan artifact?
Bruno Silva (author): Pinning to the plan’s recorded `from_version` + chart digest when available. If digest missing, we fall back to `helm rollback <release> <previousRevision>` and record that decision in rollback-report.json. Updated docs text in command help and added `--target-revision` override.
Irene Choi (Infra): Where does state.json live on on-prem installs? Make sure permissions are correct and we don’t store secrets in it.
Bruno Silva (author): Default is `/var/lib/redwood-private/upgrade/` owned by root, mode 0700. State schema only stores references (backup IDs, secret names), not secret material. Added a redaction layer before mirroring to ConfigMap/support bundle.
Kenji Nakamura (UX): CLI output during rollback should be very explicit about what it is doing and how long it may take.
Bruno Silva (author): Updated progress output to: stage header -> step -> expected timeout. Added a final summary block with next actions. Included `--json` output for automation parity with other commands.
Rafael Mendes (On-call): Please include a fast path to collect the bundle when verification fails.
Bruno Silva (author): Added message: "Rollback completed but verification failed; run `redwood-private support-bundle --include-upgrade-state`" and ensured the collector includes rollback-report.json.
New `redwood-private upgrade rollback` command to roll back the last attempted Private upgrade using persisted state.
Rollback runs deterministic hooks (CP then DP), generates an auditable rollback report, and verifies post-rollback health.
Support bundles now include upgrade/rollback state artifacts for faster triage.
