Summary: Introduces a Tenant IAM Mapper component and a Helm preflight validator to make RBAC bootstrapping in private deployments safer and auditable. Motivation: Private installs frequently require tenant-scoped role bindings and self-service tenant onboarding. Previous bootstrap flows used ad-hoc templates which caused two classes of failures: silent over-privileging during first-bootstrap and drift during upgrades. This PR provides an operator that maps tenant definitions to minimal Role/ClusterRole bindings and a Helm preflight step that runs a dry-run plan (helm template + terraform plan when TF-managed) and surfaces a concise permissions delta so operators can approve or abort. Implementation: 1) tenant-iam-mapper operator (Go): reconciles Tenant CRD -> generates namespaced RoleBindings and optionally creates a limited ClusterRole in controlled namespaces. Mapping rules are policy-driven and live under deploy/roles/policies.yaml. 2) Helm preflight plugin: a small controller-hook that calls helm template for chart revisions, runs a delta check against a stored baseline fingerprint, and integrates with terraform by invoking 'terraform plan -out' when TF modules are present under infra/terraform. 3) Safe-apply controller: when preflight is approved, apply happens via a staged apply that records a manifest fingerprint and writes a reversible plan in state/rollback-manifests/ for quick rollback. 4) Tests & docs: includes unit tests for mapper logic, e2e tests in perf-canary cluster simulating tenant onboarding, and an operator guide in docs/private-installer/rbac-preflight.md. Rollout plan: defaults to disabled. Cluster operators can enable the mapper and preflight via values.yaml: installer.enableTenantIamMapper=true; gradual rollout recommended: alpha on staging, enable telemetry and alerting for denied bindings for one week, then enable in production. Compatibility: The mapper produces conservative bindings only; existing clusters will not be modified unless installer.enableTenantIamMapper is toggled. For TF-managed installs the preflight will only run if terraform root module includes AffectedResources output. Security: the operator validates requested bindings against a policy allow-list; service account used for apply must have a narrow set of privileges described in docs. Migration notes: provide a migration script scripts/migrate-old-rbac.sh to convert legacy templates into policy entries. Related work: builds on ENG-1942 (rbac templates refactor) and ENG-1989 (installer lifecycle improvements).
Add tenant-scoped IAM mapping operator; Helm preflight plan checks before apply; Terraform plan validator integration; safer rollbacks for RBAC drift; docs and migration notes included.
Diego Marquez: Overall design looks good. Please ensure policy file is small and auditable. Suggest adding an explicit deny-list test for ClusterRole generation.
Ava Thompson: Added deny-list test and extracted allow-list to deploy/roles/policies.yaml. PTAL.
Priya Kapoor: CI had a flake in e2e on the first run; I retriggered integration and all green now. Please add a short migration note in docs.
Liam O'Connor: Approving after confirming safe-apply writes reversible manifests to state/rollback-manifests. One nit: log level on reconcile should be Info not Debug.
Ava Thompson: Changed logging level in the last commit and added the migration script as requested.

Context and motivation:
This PR implements two tightly coupled features requested during several on-prem deployments: a distro-aware preflight verifier that surfaces kernel/container/runtime mismatches before attempting airgapped bootstrap, and an automated registry-seed workflow that consumes our OCI lockfile to atomically populate a local registry in offline environments. The goal is to reduce time-to-ready for customers running private installs (VPC/on-prem) and to eliminate a common source of bootstrap flakes in our installer.

Summary of changes (single string):
- New preflight binary (installer/preflight/distro_check.go + scripts) that reads a 'distro-manifest' (bundles/metadata/distros/*) and verifies: kernel version ranges, required kernel modules (ip_vs, overlay, br_netfilter), containerd/cri-o versions, required sysctl settings, and suitable storage drivers. The preflight outputs a machine-readable JSON report and an optional human-friendly markdown summary.
- Registry seeder (installer/seed/oci_seed.py and seed/terraform-module) that: parses our OCI lockfile, generates a seeding plan respecting image order and tag aliases, streams blobs to a local registry with checksum verification and resumable upload, and writes a registry-index file used by the installer to avoid runtime network lookups. Supports delta-seed where only missing blobs are pushed.
- Terraform: adds a mirror module variable and ACL helper (terraform/modules/registry-mirror) so customers can provision a pre-seed bucket/registry with minimal IAM changes; includes example usage in quickstarts/terraform/airgap-mirror.tf.
- Helm chart patch: charts/redwood-installer/values-airgap.yaml and a small Helm hook to apply nodeSelector/tolerations for nodes designated as 'airgapped' to ensure control-plane pods schedule correctly on constrained nodes.
- Offline bundle generator: updates to bundle tool (tools/bundle-gen) to emit per-distro package manifests (deb/rpm/bz) and a light-weight delta index to support smaller seed images.
- Tests: integration tests in test/airgap_seed_test.sh and unit tests for distro parsing.

Commit summary: see commits list below.

Changed areas (high level):
- installer/preflight/* (new)
- installer/seed/* (new)
- terraform/modules/registry-mirror/* (modified + new examples)
- charts/redwood-installer/* (airgap values + hook)
- tools/bundle-gen/* (updates)
- test/* (integration + unit)

Review conversation (high level and actions):
- Ethan: asked for clearer failure categories in preflight (fatal vs warning). Addressed by adding structured 'severity' field to JSON output and updating docs.
- Sofia: requested resumable uploads and idempotency for the seeder. Implemented chunked uploads with resume token stored in registry-index; added tests for interrupted push.
- Jacob: pointed out potential permission explosion in Terraform example. Tightened IAM snippet and added explicit least-privilege comments.
- CI: initial lint failure on shellcheck and go vet — fixed by tightening quoting and adding context to error returns.

CI summary:
- Unit tests: pass
- Integration (seed simulation): pass (runs against local containerd registry simulator)
- Lint: pass after fixes

Merge outcome: merged via squash. This PR will be followed by a docs PR to add a 'preflight' troubleshooting guide and an operations runbook for manual registry seeding (links in release notes).

Notes for operators:
- The preflight can be run independently: ./installer/preflight/check --bundle ./bundles/<name>.tar.gz --out preflight-report.json
- The registry seeder accepts --resume-token to continue interrupted pushes. Seed generates a registry-index.json that the installer can consume via --registry-index.
- Terraform module exposes 'mirror_allowed_cidrs' and 'mirror_service_principal' for cloud mirrors.

Backwards compatibility and rollout plan:
- The new tools are additive. Installer will fallback to existing network fetch behavior if no registry-index is provided. We'll ship the docs and a quickstart to customers running Private in the next week.

Adds a distro-aware preflight check and a registry seeding automation tool for airgapped/private installs. Includes Terraform variable for mirror ACLs, Helm chart toleration patch for airgapped nodes, and upgraded offline bundle generator with per-distro package manifests. Backwards compatible; improves preflight coverage and reduces manual registry bootstrap steps.
Ethan Brooks - Please add explicit severity (fatal/warn/info) to each preflight check so operators can choose to continue on warnings. - addressed in commit a4f3e90
Sofia Ramirez - Seeder needs to be resumable and idempotent if interrupted mid-upload. Also add checksum verification after push. - implemented in cde4f11
Jacob Li - Terraform example exposes broad permissions; suggest least-privilege and example comment. - revised in d22b5b7
SRE Bot (CI) - lint/go vet failure on preflight; please fix. - fixed in 9f0e123
QA - Integration test failed on first run due to registry auth; added fallback auth and better error messages. - fixed in f9b8c33
Ethan Brooks - Approve after minor docs change. - APPROVED

Motivation: we observed a couple of private upgrade incidents where partial resource drift (helm diff + manual v1->v2 schema migration mismatch) resulted in failed rollbacks and long recovery windows. This PR introduces a lightweight manifest hash lock and a set of pre/post upgrade sanity checks in the private installer to reduce blast radius and ensure safe rollback paths. Implementation summary: - compute a canonical manifest bundle (helm rendered YAML + terraform state note) and store SHA256 in a manifest-hash.lock in the release bundle and backup snapshot metadata; - require backup integrity verification before any restore/rollback path; abort if hash mismatches unless force flag provided and operator confirms; - add preflight checks (cluster resource quotas, minimal available PVC size, required KMS access) and post-upgrade health probes (control-plane liveness, DB migration status, kv-cache warmup signal); - add a guarded downgrade blocker that prevents applying manifests with lower semver unless explicit --allow-downgrade is used and manifest hash matches a recorded snapshot; - integrate manifest hash check into terraform module (plan-time validation) and helm chart CI (render + compare); - add automated rollback choreography: snapshot -> apply previous manifests -> verify manifest-hash match -> run post-rollback health probes. Checklist: - [x] compute and persist manifest-hash.lock during build/release - [x] store hash in backup metadata for restore verification - [x] enforce preflight and post-upgrade sanity checks in installer flow - [x] terraform plan-time manifest validation hook - [x] helm rendering test in CI that verifies lock consistency - [x] docs and playbook updated with force/allow-downgrade semantics - [x] e2e upgrade+rollback tests added to perf-canary harness Backwards compatibility: the installer tolerates older backups that lack manifest-hash.lock by falling back to checksum-less restore but emits a high-severity warning and requires operator confirmation. For environments that opt-in to strict mode (config: strict_manifest_lock: true) the installer will refuse any restore that lacks a matching recorded hash. See linked tickets for rollout/opt-in plan. Rollout plan: enable max-safety (strict) on internal test clusters, opt-in for a subset of early access customers, then flip strict by default in next minor release following telemetry. Related: ENG-4823 is the tracking Linear. Links: design notes and playbook: https://linear.app/ENG-4823/design/manifest-locks-and-sanity-checks Testing: unit tests, integration harness, and canary runs documented in testing_notes.
Adds deterministic manifest hashing and pre/post upgrade sanity checks for private deployments. Installer will compute and persist a manifest-hash.lock for each release, verify backups against that hash before restore, and abort upgrades if post-upgrade health checks fail. Improves safety for rollback paths and reduces risk of partial upgrades.
Added e2e scenario in tests/e2e/upgrade_rollback_test.go that performs: deploy v1 -> create backup snapshot -> deploy v2 with manifest-hash.lock -> simulate failed migration -> run rollback flow -> verify manifest hash match and post-rollback health checks. Canary run executed against perf-canary cluster for three consecutive upgrades without regression.
Ethan Wong: Nice approach — can we keep the canonicalization stable across Go versions? Suggest adding a minimal comment about YAML key ordering.
Maya Thompson: Good catch, added deterministic YAML marshaller (gopkg.in/yaml.v3 with explicit map key sort) and test. See second commit.
Priya Rao: How does this interact with existing backup TTL rotation? If a rotated backup loses the hash we need a detection path.
Maya Thompson: Added backup_store fallback: when hash missing we emit a high-severity alert and require operator confirmation; documented in playbook.
Daniel Kim: CI flakes: helm-render-validate sometimes fails on timestamps in templates — added a template scrub step to normalize metadata timestamps.
Daniel Kim: Approved after CI stabilized.

Motivation: Customers deploying Redwood Private in regulated environments requested installer-first enforcement for region-bound key usage and a lightweight audit replay path for constrained networks (air-gapped customer sites and field appliances). This PR adds jurisdictional KMS routing hooks to the private-installer control plane, an installer preflight that validates customer KMS profiles against allowed geozones, and a compact audit envelope rehydration tool to restore full audit entries from compressed traces for post-incident compliance reviews.

What this change does (high level): adds a KMS routing module to the installer that: 1) validates CMK scope annotations provided in the installation manifest; 2) compiles a jurisdictional routing table and injects a per-node KMS proxy configuration; 3) surfaces a preflight failure when a provided KMS key is incompatible with the selected data residency policy. Adds an audit rehydration utility (audit-rehydrate) packaged with the installer that consumes compact audit envelopes produced by the runtime and reconstructs canonical audit entries on a separate compliance host. Includes migration hooks that preserve existing audit buckets and translate prior envelope formats to the compact form.

Design notes: - Installer KMS routing uses a declarative manifest field: privateInstaller.kms.zoneBindings which maps tenant namespaces to KMS zones. The installer compiles these into a compact L3 routing blob signed by the operator key. Nodes receive the routing blob via the existing secure bootstrap channel. - KMS proxy config supports multi-provider tuples (aws:kms@us-west-2, gcp:kms@europe-west1) and fallbacks; the policy evaluator rejects cross-jurisdiction key usage when the installation policy is strict. - The audit-rehydrate tool accepts a compact envelope store (LZ4+protobuf) and an operator-provided key to expand to full JSON audit rows; expansion can be configured to redact PII using the built-in scrubber rules to match SOC2 requirements. - To avoid changing runtime surface area for hosted customers, all changes are contained to the installer artifacts and the private runtime bootstrap; falling back to existing behavior unless privateInstaller.kms.zoneBindings is set.

Files changed (high level): - installer/cmd/installer/main.go: add preflight and routing compile path. - installer/pkg/kms/router.go: new jurisdictional routing compiler and validators. - installer/cmd/audit-rehydrate/main.go: new tool to expand compact audit envelopes. - installer/config/manifest.schema.yaml: add kms.zoneBindings schema and validation. - charts/private/templates/kms-proxy.yaml: templated KMS proxy sidecar config. - test/e2e/airgap/README.md: new test harness notes and manual steps. - test/e2e/airgap/kms-routing.test: integration test covering manifest->node config flow.

Testing: - Unit tests for router.compile and manifest validation added (router_test.go). - Added an integration e2e that spins up a local air-gapped harness (uses the existing qemu-based appliance image) and verifies node receives signed routing blob and KMS proxy rejects out-of-zone key usage. - audit-rehydrate validated against a corpus of historic envelopes (10k entries) produced by the runtime; results cross-checked with the canonical audit exporter. - CI pipeline updated: installer unit + e2e (airgap) run as optional job flagged by label. All CI checks passed on the final squash.

Migration and operational notes: - Default behavior is opt-in. Existing private installs will not see changes until operators update manifests and run the installer with the new release. - Migration tool included: installer/cmd/migrate-compact-audit which converts legacy envelopes to compact LZ4+protobuf format. - Operators should run the preflight (installer --preflight) prior to upgrade to ensure KMS keys satisfy residency constraints. - Rollout plan: staged rollout to customers on Dedicated->Private track; early access for regulated customers was performed and feedback incorporated.

Security review and approvals: - Threat model: addition of signed routing blob limits attack surface because nodes only accept KMS routing config signed by operator keys; added signature verification unit tests. - RBAC impact: installer now emits placement-time annotations that the runtime's RBAC v2 policy compiler consumes. We updated the compiler docs to include how zoneBindings map to derived roles. - Reviewed by Security: Diego Martinez, Compliance: Liang Wu; changes required to add signature revocation list in case operator keys are rotated — implemented as a revocation file consumed by the bootstrap.

Open items / follow-ups: - Add telemetry to Redwood Console to surface per-tenant KMS-zone enforcement failures (tracked ENG-2211). - Consider adding an offline audit-verify mode that checks integrity of compact envelopes without full rehydration. - UX work to expose preflight failures with clearer remediation suggestions in the installer logs.

Related work: Linear ENG-2148 (jurisdictional KMS routing), SEC-77 (audit replay for air-gapped installs), SUP-2119 (customer ask: EU-only CMK enforcement).

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration e2e (airgap) - [x] Security review - [x] Migration tool - [x] Release notes entry
Diego Martinez: Security: confirm signature verification runs during bootstrap and reject by default on signature failure
Asha Patel: Reply: signature verification added and unit-tested; bootstrap will fail fast with an explanatory error code (see router.go:VerifySignature)
Liang Wu: Compliance: ensure audit-rehydrate can redact PII automatically per tenant policies
Asha Patel: Reply: added scrubber rules and tenant-policy mapping; docs updated with example rules
Omar Rahman: Ops: what is upgrade path for existing envelopes?
Asha Patel: Reply: included migrate-compact-audit tool and added migration steps to release notes
Adds installer-level jurisdictional KMS routing support and a compact audit rehydration pipeline for air-gapped and low-bandwidth deployments. Backwards-compatible runtime flags and migration steps for existing private installs.

payload.body:
Motivation: customers running long-lived private control planes need a predictable, auditable way to retire subnets during AZ maintenance, capacity rebalancing, or decommission workflows without causing DNS holes or transient routing blackholes. This PR introduces a coordinated 'Safe Subnet Decommissioner' workflow plus a delegated DNS failover mechanism (DNS Bridge) to ensure control-plane endpoints remain resolvable during and after subnet lifecycle changes.

What changed (high level): added a new terraform module (subnet-decommissioner) that emits lifecycle hooks and necessary IAM roles; extended the installer Helm chart with a decommission-controller deployment that watches SubnetLifecycle annotations and orchestrates: route table reassociation, ENI graceful detach, ephemeral private IP reallocation, security-group staged rotate, and a DNS Bridge that creates temporary delegated records in a customer-managed hosted zone to maintain reachability. Also added a small operator (go microservice) used by the Helm chart to drive the steps and emit audit events.

Design notes: the decommissioner minimizes blast radius by performing operations in phases with feature-flagged concurrency limits per-AZ, emitting progress events to the control plane audit log, and validating that at least one healthy control-plane endpoint remains reachable before final subnet deletion. The DNS Bridge uses conditional Route53 delegation into a short-lived subdomain (e.g. decomm-<cluster>.redwood-internal) and an SRV to A rewrite to route traffic to standby endpoints in surviving subnets. We intentionally avoid changing customer primary hosted zones; delegation keys are ephemeral and rotated by the controller.

Migration & rollout: phased rollout behind a feature flag (installer config flag: enableSubnetDecommissioner). Default off for existing customers. When enabled, operator runs in 'dry-run' mode for 48 hours and reports suggested actions via the console. After a continuous integration smoke window and manual sign-off, the flag can be flipped to live. A reversible 'recompose' step allows re-adding previously decommissioned subnets.

Testing: unit tests for the operator (mock AWS APIs), integration tests in the benchlab that simulate AZ failover, and an e2e scenario in the perf-canary that runs a 24h decommission+recovery cycle. CI includes terraform plan validation, helm lint, go unit tests, and a staged infra apply in the ephemeral test account.

Rollback plan: controller supports a 'cancel-decommission' annotation which reverses route table changes and reattaches ENIs where possible; DNS Bridge entries are removed only after controller verifies client-side reachability via probe hooks. If a roll-forward is required, operator can accelerate by applying a 'force-commit' annotation but that requires an explicit engineer confirmation step logged to audit.

Related work: ties to ENG-12540 (subnet lifecycle orchestration), ENG-13008 (dns-resilience), and the private-installer upgrade playbook.

Notes: this PR is intentionally conservative about IAM scope (least-privilege roles for the operator) and includes thorough audit logging for compliance customers.

b4e5f6a: helm: decommission-controller chart, values schema and CRD helm templates

d0e1f2a: tests: integration scenario for AZ drain + DNS Bridge in benchlab
e3f4a5b: docs: add operator runbook, installer flag docs and rollback steps
Sonia Patel: Can the operator's IAM be further scoped to deny ec2:TerminateInstances? We prefer explicit deny for decommission workflows.
Ethan Morales: Yes — updated the role template to exclude TerminateInstances and added a new step that uses a delegated escalation token for infra-team signed termination (audit only).
Lars Engel: The DNS Bridge sounds useful but we should avoid touching customer apex zones. Confirmed we only create delegated subdomains and ephemeral NS records — LGTM.
Maya Chen: Add an integration test that simulates NAT gateway failover; otherwise looks good.

Introduces a Safe Subnet Decommissioner operator and DNS Bridge to enable controlled subnet retirement and DNS failover for private control planes. Feature disabled by default; opt-in via installer flag. Includes terraform module, Helm chart, operator, tests, and runbook.

payload.body:
Motivation: Private upgrades for multi-tenant on-prem deployments need lower blast radius and safer downgrade paths. This PR introduces a tenant-scoped SnapshotCoordinator CRD/controller and a staged rollback Gatekeeper that validates restore readiness and prevents accidental downgrades. The goal is to enable preflight restore rehearsals and automatic gating during multi-tenant upgrades so operators can abort or stage rollbacks without impacting healthy tenants.

What this changes (high level):
- New CRD: TenantSnapshotRequest (api/v1alpha1) and controller that serializes snapshot creation per tenant, signs artifacts with release metadata, and records tenant-impact score.
- New controller: SnapshotCoordinator that can schedule rehearsal restores into an isolated test namespace (operator-managed) and produce a RestoreReadinessReport.
- Rollback gatekeeper: Operator-side admission webhook + controller that consults latest RestoreReadinessReport and a version-compatibility matrix before allowing a rollback/downgrade to proceed.
- Helm: add new chart hooks (pre-upgrade/post-upgrade) to trigger snapshot requests and to wait for gatekeeper release-checks; hooks time out configurable via values.yaml (default 30m).
- Terraform: pin module redwood/postgres-cluster to 2.4.1 and add plan-time validation step to warn on incompatible operator/version combos.
- Installer: add operator-quiesce job and optional tenant-quarantine flag to prevent write traffic during rehearsals.

Commits (summary):
- 9c3b2f7 Add TenantSnapshotRequest CRD and types
- 8f1a4d0 Implement SnapshotCoordinator controller and exporter for RestoreReadinessReport
- 7b2dffd Add Gatekeeper admission webhook and downgrade-checking logic
- d4a1e33 Helm: hooks + values for staged rollback flow
- a92f0c1 Terraform: pin module and add validation script
- 11b3a6f Add e2e rehearsal test harness and CI job definition

Files changed (high-level):
- charts/private/values.yaml (new hooks, timeouts)
- charts/private/templates/hooks.yaml (pre/post hooks and job templates)
- operator/crds/tenant_snapshotrequest.yaml (CRD)
- operator/controllers/snapshotcoordinator/* (controller, reconciler, exporter)
- operator/controllers/gatekeeper/* (webhook, checks)
- infra/terraform/modules/postgres/versions.tf (module pin)
- test/e2e/rehearsal_restore_test.go (new e2e)

Tests and CI:
- Added an e2e rehearsal restore test that runs against KIND; marked as slow and gated behind nightly.
- CI initially failed due to a flaky admission webhook test (race on webhook cache invalidation). I added a retry in the test harness and a short backoff in the controller startup sequence. Re-ran CI: all checks passed.

Migration and backward compatibility:
- CRD is v1alpha1; controller gracefully ignores TenantSnapshotRequests if operator lacks feature-flag. No automatic changes to existing resources.
- Helm defaults preserve current behavior; operators opt into staged rollback by setting values.stagedRollback.enabled=true.
- Terraform pin prevents inadvertent upgrades of the postgres module without an explicit bump in the installer.

Security considerations:
- Snapshot artifacts are signed with cluster release metadata and stored in tenant-scoped object paths. Signing uses existing KMS integration; no new secrets introduced.
- Admission webhook uses existing RBAC roles. Webhook is optional (values.webhook.enabled) for air-gapped installs where dynamic admission is disabled.

Review thread (highlights):
- Ava Chen (reviewer): "Can the coordinator handle concurrent snapshot requests across 200 tenants without saturating the PG replica?"
  Priya: "Coordinator uses a leaky-bucket rate limiter and a locality-aware queue; added config values.queue.concurrencyPerRegion with sensible defaults. Added performance note in README and a test simulating 250 concurrent requests."
- Marcus Li: "What happens if a rehearsal restore times out? Will we leave test namespaces around?"
  Priya: "Controller schedules a TTL garbage-collect job for rehearsal namespaces and marks RestoreReadinessReport.status=TimedOut; the helm hook will fail the upgrade if required thresholds aren't met. Added a finalizer to ensure cleanup on controller crash."
- Diego Morales: "Terraform pin looks fine but add a plan-time check so operators aren't surprised."
  Priya: "Added infra/terraform/scripts/validate_compat.sh and integrated it into the installer plan step; it returns non-zero on obvious mismatches but is non-fatal by default (configurable)."

Follow-ups (todo items captured in PR):
- ENG-2576: Add a compact dashboard in Console for RestoreReadinessReport per tenant (linked in linear).
- ENG-2634: Introduce opt-in dry-run for helm hooks so large clusters can stage without affecting live traffic.
- Add benchmarks for snapshot throughput vs. postgres replica lag; suggested by Ava.

Why this is different from previous work: Many previous PRs focused on transactional DB migration helpers and snapshot signing. This PR stitches several pieces into an operator-driven rehearsal workflow with an admission-time rollback gate — the focus is on staged, tenant-scoped rehearsals and an admission policy that prevents unsafe downgrades across tenants. The helm+terraform+operator changes are coordinated to provide a minimal-ops path for operators to opt into safe rollbacks.

Rollback/upgrade playbook (short):
1) Set values.stagedRollback.enabled=true in the helm release values and apply helm upgrade --wait.
2) Helm pre-upgrade hook creates TenantSnapshotRequests for high-risk tenants (based on tenant impact score).
3) SnapshotCoordinator runs rehearsal restores into isolated test namespaces and emits RestoreReadinessReports.
4) Gatekeeper validates readiness and compatibility; if checks pass, the upgrade proceeds. If not, gatekeeper blocks rollback/downgrade and prints guidance to the operator.

Merge notes: Squash-merged into main after approvals from Ava and Marcus. CI green on merge. Cherry-pick guidance included for release branches in the PR comments.

If you want to try locally: follow operator/README.md sections "rehearsal mode" and "helm staged rollback". The e2e requires KIND and about 12GB RAM to run the rehearsal harness.

Introduce a tenant-scoped snapshot coordinator and staged rollback gating mechanism. Adds helm hooks and a TF module pin to enable safe preview restores and operator quiesce during upgrades. Backwards-compatible by default; no config changes required for existing installs.
payload.title: Add tenant snapshot coordinator and staged rollback gatekeeper

payload.body:
Motivation: During a recent restore drill we observed two separate restores targeting the same tenant that overlapped and left the cluster in an inconsistent state when downstream post-restore hooks raced. This PR implements two complementary protections: (1) cryptographically signed backup manifests so operators can verify integrity and provenance before restoring, and (2) an orchestrated rollback/restore queue that serializes restores per-tenant and exposes explicit lock/lease state for operator visibility. Both are designed for Private installer customers (VPC/on-prem) where operators manage backup artifacts in object storage and must be able to audit and safely recover state.

Summary of changes: Added an ed25519-based signature format for backup manifests and verification logic in the installer operator; added a new RestoreQueue controller that enqueues restore requests and processes them serially per-tenant with TTL-based leases; updated Helm charts and the installer CLI to produce and consume signed manifests; added a small Terraform module to maintain backup metadata and manifest storage ACLs; added preflight validations that compare manifest version stamps and schema compatibility before attempting a restore; added idempotent migration guard to the DB migration runner so an interrupted upgrade/rollback does not reapply incompatible steps. Also improved logging and tracing fields for auditability.

Commits (high level):
- feat(backup): introduce manifest signing utilities and key management helpers
- feat(operator): implement RestoreQueue controller with per-tenant leases
- feat(cli): add rw-private backup sign and rw-private restore enqueue commands
- chore(helm): helm templates for signed-backup-secret and restore-queue CRD
- feat(terraform): add backup-metadata module + s3 manifest ACL example
- fix(migrations): make schema migrations idempotent and add preflight dry-run
- test: add unit/integration tests for signature verification and queue behavior

Files changed (high level):
- operator/controllers/restore_queue_controller.go (new)
- pkg/backup/signature.go (new)
- cmd/rw-private/backup_sign.go (new), cmd/rw-private/restore_enqueue.go (new)
- charts/private/templates/signed-backup-secret.yaml (new)
- charts/private/templates/restore-queue-crd.yaml (new)
- terraform/modules/backup-metadata/main.tf (new)
- installer/preflight/validate_manifest.go (modified)
- migrations/db/migrate.go (modified)
- tests/integration/restore_queue_test.go (new)
- docs/private/operator-restore.md (new)

Design notes and constraints: Signatures use ed25519 with a simple manifest JSON that includes backup_version, object_url, created_at, model_version and a manifest_version stamp. The operator accepts a configured public key or a KMS-sourced key; when no key is configured the system falls back to a permissive mode but logs a warning (operators are encouraged to enable strict mode via Helm values). The RestoreQueue persists state to the cluster (CRs) and uses an optimistic lease pattern: when a restore job is dequeued we create a RestoreLease CR with owner reference and a TTL; if a job fails the lease is released and the job can be retried. The queue serializes per-tenant only; different tenants can run restores concurrently. This keeps the blast radius constrained while removing human coordination from restores.

Preflight & safety: The preflight step validates the manifest signature, checks manifest_version compatibility against the running installer version, runs a dry-run of DB migrations in a sandbox namespace, and verifies object storage ACLs via the new Terraform module outputs. If any check fails the restore is rejected and the operator emits a human-readable remediation hint in the events and logs.

Testing & CI: Added unit tests for signature.MaxExpectedAge enforcement, integration tests that exercise the queue in a kind cluster (mocked S3), and an E2E that signs a manifest with a test key then attempts an invalid restore to confirm preflight blocks it. CI initially showed a flaky integration test on the lease TTL; I increased the test timeout and added retries. The final run passed all checks (build, lint, unit, integration, e2e).

Review thread summary: Carlos requested stricter default Helm values (changed default strictSignature: true) and an option to fallback to KMS-only mode; Maya asked for clearer error messages when signatures are missing and suggested adding an operator metric for queued_length (added exporter metric restore_queue_length). Evan asked for more comments around the idempotency guarantees in DB migrations and requested an additional unit test for the migration dry-run path (added). I addressed all review comments and pushed a final changelist that removed a noisy debug log in signature verification.

Operational notes for customers: The new Helm chart exposes values.private.installer.signature.strict (default true), values.private.installer.signature.publicKey (string or KMS reference), and values.private.installer.restoreQueue.enabled (default true). Upgrading clusters: operators should run the included preflight job (rw-private preflight verify-manifests) against a snapshot store to surface potential incompatibilities before enabling auto-restore. If strict signature mode is enabled, restores without valid signatures will be rejected — tenants must sign manifests using the rw-private CLI or an approved orchestration flow.

Security considerations: Private key material is never stored by the operator; only public keys or KMS references are allowed in Helm. The Terraform module includes optional bucket policies to enforce server-side encryption and object locking where available. We documented destructive recovery flows in docs/private/operator-restore.md; operators should rotate keys via documented rotation steps to avoid lockouts.

Migration path and rollback: This change is backwards-compatible for clusters that do not enable strict signature mode. For clusters enabling strict mode, operators must sign existing manifests or toggle strictSignature off temporarily while they sign artifacts. The RestoreQueue controller supports a controller-runtime annotation to force-evict a lease for emergency interventions.

Merge: After approvals from reviewers and a green CI run, this PR was merged to main via squash merge. Changelog and docs were included in the merge commit.
Adds signed backup manifests and a serialized rollback queue to prevent concurrent restores; introduces preflight signature validation and installer CLI helpers. No user-facing API changes except new private-installer CLI commands.
Operator docs added and CLI helpers included; recommended staging rollout before enabling strict signature mode in production.

Motivation: Teams running private control planes in shared AWS/Transit setups needed safer, auditable subnet allocation and a resilient DNS handoff when Route53 conditional forwarding or cross-account resolver rules are delayed. This PR provides two coordinated changes: 1) a subnet ownership tagging scheme plus terraform helpers so the installer can claim/verify subnets deterministically without clobbering other teams' allocations; 2) a marshalled DNS fallback that wires a short-lived resolver forwarder (Route53Resolver + lambda-backed conditional rules) to ensure control plane name resolution remains available during cross-account propagation windows.

What changed (high level):
- Added a new Terraform module modules/subnet/ownership.tf to standardize owner-tag, purpose-tag, lifecycle-tag and an idempotent claim flow (lookup by tag -> create if absent -> return allocation).
- Refactored modules/network/outputs.tf to expose subnet-owner metadata and tag filters used by downstream modules (endpoints, NAT, route53).
- Implemented modules/dns/marshalled_forwarder.tf: optional resource set (aws_route53_resolver_rule + aws_lambda + IAM) which creates a short TTL forwarder that is automatically removed after a configurable window.
- Added an installer helm values.yaml flag (helm/installer/values.yaml) enableFeature.subnetOwnership and enableFeature.dnsFallback with sensible defaults for private deployments.
- Added scripts/upgrade-hook.sh and helm hooks that run a pre-upgrade claim step and post-upgrade teardown of temporary resolver resources.
- Tests: new integration test scenario tests/integration/subnet-ownership.yaml and unit helpers tests for tag matching.

Compatibility notes: The DNS fallback is opt-in and off by default. It is intended for cross-account Route53 setups where resolver propagation latency has caused transient control-plane failures. Subnet ownership tagging follows the existing tag namespace (k: redwood:env, redwood:team) but introduces redwood:subnet-owner and redwood:subnet-purpose keys — these are non-breaking for existing installs.

Checklist:
- [x] Terraform module with docs and examples
- [x] Helm value toggles and hooks
- [x] Integration test scenario for CI
- [x] Security review for lambda IAM role (minimal privileges)
- [x] Migration notes in docs/README-deployments.md

Commits summary: [1/5] modules: add subnet ownership module with claim/lookup pattern; [2/5] dns: add marshalled Route53 resolver + lambda forwarder; [3/5] helm: expose toggles and add pre/post-upgrade hooks; [4/5] scripts: upgrade-hook.sh + teardown helper; [5/5] tests: add integration scenario and unit tests.

Files changed (high level): modules/subnet/ownership.tf, modules/subnet/README.md, modules/network/outputs.tf, modules/dns/marshalled_forwarder.tf, helm/installer/values.yaml, scripts/upgrade-hook.sh, tests/integration/subnet-ownership.yaml, docs/README-deployments.md.

CI: First CI run failed on terratest flakiness in us-west-2; flaky test quarantined and re-run. After fixes, all checks pass (terraform fmt, validate, terratest integration, helm lint, unit).

Merge rationale: Enables safer private control plane rollouts across multi-account setups and reduces incident surface caused by DNS propagation delays. Backward compatible and feature-flagged.
Ethan Ross: Good direction; please make tag keys configurable via variables and include a note on collisions with existing tags.
Priya Nair: Added variables for tag key namespace and updated README with migration guidance (commit 3).
Maya Li: Security: lambda IAM looks fine but reduce paused window default to 24h, not 72h — changed to 24h and updated values.yaml (commit 4).
Carlos Gomez: Integration test uncovered race when multiple instances claim the same untagged subnet; I requested an explicit conditional check + retry with backoff. Author implemented compare-and-swap using terraform null_resource local-exec helper (commit 5).
Ethan Ross: Approving after final test fixes. (+1)
Add optional subnet ownership tagging and an opt-in marshalled DNS fallback for private control planes. Feature-flagged; enable via helm values. Includes terraform module and migration docs.

payload.body:
Motivation: For private deployments we need a safer control-plane networking model that avoids persistent, account-scoped ENIs and reduces blast radius when rolling control-plane upgrades. This PR introduces two complementary changes: (1) ephemeral control-plane network interfaces (ENIs) that are created/owned by the installer during control-plane pod lifecycle and torn down after handoff, and (2) a zone-bound PrivateLink allocator that pins PrivateLink endpoint interfaces to AZ-local subnets with soft-affinity and deterministic fallback.

What this PR changes: single continuous description of changes across codepaths: added a new Terraform submodule terraform/modules/controlplane-enis which implements aws_network_interface resources with lifecycle create_before_destroy + tags and an ownership marker so the installer operator can claim and drain them. The module exposes inputs for subnet_id, security_group_ids, and a new "ephemeral_lifetime" TTL used by the installer to garbage-collect stale ENIs. The PrivateLink allocator is implemented in installer/terraform/modules/privatelink-allocator and the control-plane Helm chart: it uses a small allocation table stored as a DynamoDB (or statefile for on-prem) keyed by vpc_id+service_name to grant zone-scoped prefix reservations and to emit route table associations to the controlplane route manager.

Installer/Helm changes: modified helm/redwood-private/templates/controlplane-svc.yaml to add a new sidecar (controlplane-net-allocator) and a ConfigMap template with allocation policy parameters (preferred_azs, sticky_ttl_seconds, failover_priority). Added hooks in helm charts for staged rollout: pre-upgrade job that migrates sticky PrivateLink assignments, and a post-upgrade job that validates no in-flight requests are pinned to interfaces scheduled for teardown.

Security & networking posture: new security group rules are additive and default-deny for external egress. We included a hardened subnet tagging convention (redwood:controlplane=true, redwood:ephemeral=true) to separate ephemeral vs. persistent allocations for auditors. The Terraform changes include controlled IAM permissions for the installer role to call DescribeNetworkInterfaces, CreateNetworkInterface, and DeleteNetworkInterface; least-privilege policies are documented in docs/privatelink/iam-boundaries.md.

Rollout plan and backwards compatibility: feature is guarded by a new installer flag --enable-ephemeral-enis (false by default). When disabled, behavior is unchanged. The migration job supports three modes: dry-run (log-only), migrate (move sticky endpoints to new AZ-bound allocation without switching traffic), and cutover (switch DNS/route associations). Rollback is supported by re-running the post-upgrade rollback job which re-applies previous PrivateLink allocation state from a snapshot stored in S3 or local state for air-gapped installs.

Testing and validation: unit tests for the allocator logic (Go) and Terraform unit checks added. Integration terratest suite exercises multi-AZ create/migrate/delete flows on a small sandbox account and asserts no traffic loss across a control-plane canary. Helm lint and kubeconform checks added. A new lightweight chaos test simulates ENI deletion to ensure automatic recovery.

Docs and ops: added detailed operational runbook docs/privatelink/op-runbook.md outlining how to force-evict an ENI, how to increase ephemeral_lifetime, and how to inspect DynamoDB allocation state. Also included upgrade notes and a sample Linear ticket template for field engineers.

Checklist: - [x] Terraform module + examples - [x] Helm chart changes + pre/post hooks - [x] Installer operator sidecar for allocation + GC loop - [x] Unit/integration tests - [x] Docs and runbook - [x] IAM least privilege guidance

Risks and mitigation: garbage collection is TTL-based and conservative by default (72h). During the first rollout, we recommend enabling the feature in a single region and monitoring metrics redwood.installer.enis.gc.count and redwood.installer.privatelink.failover.rate.

Related: builds on top of prior subnet and peering work; ties into ENG-1873 (controlled egress routing) and INF-302 (privatelink observability).
Diego Ramirez: Can we avoid DynamoDB for fully on-prem installs? Suggest a file-backed state option and a clear warning in docs.
Elena Park (reply): Added a file-backed adapter that uses local statefile under installer/state/ for air-gapped installs and documented differences. See installer/internal/allocator/file_store.go.
Maya Chen: Security review: IAM changes look OK but need an explicit audit log for ENI create/delete ops so SOC can correlate. Also request SSM parameter to toggle GC TTL in prod.
Elena Park (reply): Added cloudtrail event filter example and SSM param integration for dynamic TTL in installer config. Updated docs accordingly.
Liam O'Connor: Tests are comprehensive; minor nit - prefer 48h default TTL over 72h to reduce orphaned resources during long-lived test clusters.
Elena Park (reply): Agreed; lowered default in module variables to 48h and added a migration note in upgrade docs.
Add support for ephemeral control-plane ENIs and zone-bound PrivateLink allocations. Installer flag --enable-ephemeral-enis controls behavior. Includes Terraform module, Helm changes, installer allocator, and docs. Backward compatible when flag is disabled.

payload.body:
Context: As part of Safe apply + rollback for Optimization Configs (batching/caching/quant profiles), the runtime needs stronger guarantees than “best effort apply”. We’ve seen partial rollout states when workers restart mid-apply or when concurrent apply/rollback requests overlap. This PR updates the runtime apply pipeline to treat config application as a checkpointed transaction, with idempotent steps and durable progress markers.

What’s in this PR: 1) Introduce a checkpointed apply state machine in the worker: PREPARE -> APPLY -> COMMIT (plus ABORT for failures). Each phase is idempotent and can be retried safely. PREPARE fetches the target config version and validates runtime compatibility (model arch, quant profile support, cache toggles). APPLY performs the actual config materialization (batching heuristics, cache policy, quant kernel selection) into a staged slot. COMMIT swaps staged -> active atomically and emits a “config_active” metric/event with tags {tenant, model, region, config_version}. 2) Add an ApplyTransaction ID (tx_id) carried through logs/metrics. The controller can retry the same tx_id without causing repeated COMMIT or repeated cache invalidations. 3) Add durable local checkpoint storage (per worker) so that in-flight applies resume after restart instead of starting from scratch. Checkpoints are stored with (tx_id, config_version, phase, started_at, last_updated_at, error_code). 4) Make rollback safe under partial apply: if a rollback arrives while an apply is in PREPARE/APPLY, the worker ABORTs the in-flight tx and reverts to the last committed active version; if the apply is already COMMITed, rollback starts a new tx toward the previous version (no “in-place undo”). 5) Add guardrails to avoid thundering-herd cache invalidation: COMMIT can optionally perform a bounded “soft invalidate” (mark prefixes stale and lazily evict) for caching toggles, rather than immediate full flush. Defaults are conservative; can be tuned later via the Optimization Config fields. 6) Tests: unit tests for phase idempotency, restart resumption, and concurrent apply/rollback ordering; integration test harness that simulates worker restart between APPLY and COMMIT.

Why this approach: We want distributed, eventually consistent workers, but with per-worker correctness and observability. The checkpoint protocol makes the apply pipeline resilient to retries, worker restarts, and controller replays. It also creates a clear definition of “rolled out” at the runtime layer: active version is only updated on COMMIT.

Operational notes: - Metrics: runtime_config_apply_phase_total{phase, outcome}, runtime_config_active_version{tenant, model, region}, runtime_config_apply_duration_seconds{phase}. - Logging: All apply/rollback logs include tx_id + config_version + previous_version. - Failure behavior: If PREPARE fails (schema/compat), worker reports failure and keeps current active version. If APPLY fails (e.g., kernel init), worker ABORTs and keeps current active version.

Follow-ups (not in this PR): - Controller-side semantics for pausing rollouts on “stuck in APPLY” for >N minutes (tracked in ENG-4824). - Wiring quality gate signals for quant profiles (Applied ML gating) into controller decisions (tracked in ENG-4827).
Omar El-Sayed (review): The staged slot approach looks good. One concern: COMMIT swaps batching heuristics + cache policy together; do we ever want to commit them independently? Also, can you confirm that APPLY does not mutate any global scheduler state visible to other in-flight requests?
Noah Patel (author): Good call. For now we treat the Optimization Config as an atomic unit since canary + rollback are version-based. APPLY only builds a staged “effective config” and initializes any needed kernel handles; scheduler state switches only happen during COMMIT at the request boundary (next dispatch tick). Added a comment + ensured we don’t update the shared scheduler config until commit() returns ok.
Sofia Ivanova (review): On the soft invalidate: can we ensure that enabling caching doesn’t cause a latency spike due to immediate allocations? Also, for disabling caching, do we risk holding onto too much memory if lazy eviction is slow?
Noah Patel (author): Implemented bounded soft invalidation only for toggles that would otherwise flush. For disable-cache, COMMIT marks caches non-writable and schedules a background eviction with a cap per second; we also add a safety “hard cap” where if cache bytes > threshold, we evict aggressively. I added metrics runtime_cache_eviction_backlog and a warning log when backlog persists > 5m.
Ethan Park (review): From control plane perspective, we need a crisp definition of success for apply. Is worker ‘applied’ once it reaches COMMIT? Please make sure failure reasons are structured so the controller can categorize (compat vs transient).
Noah Patel (author): Yes—worker only advertises the new version as active after COMMIT. I added error codes: COMPAT_VALIDATION_FAILED, FETCH_FAILED, KERNEL_INIT_FAILED, CHECKPOINT_IO_FAILED, COMMIT_SWAP_FAILED. These surface in the apply outcome metric + logs. Controller wiring comes in ENG-4824/ENG-4827.
Sean Gallagher (SRE review): Love the phase metrics. Please ensure they include tenant/model/region/config_version tags (required for the rollout health dashboard) and that we don’t cardinality explode on tx_id.
Noah Patel (author): Tags added for tenant/model/region/config_version. tx_id is log-only; metrics do not include tx_id. Also added sampling on debug logs in APPLY loop.
Omar El-Sayed (approval): Approved after latest changes. The resume-on-restart test is a nice catch.
Sean Gallagher (approval): Approved; metrics/tags meet dashboard needs.
payload.title: runtime: treat optimization config apply as a transactional operation with checkpoints

Summary: Adds a new Terraform module and installer hooks to provide deterministic static egress IPs for private control plane traffic using an AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB) + Global Accelerator fronting private ENIs, plus PrivateLink interface endpoints for customer control-plane access. Motivation: Customers deploying Redwood Private want stable outbound IPs for allowlisting in partner systems and on-prem firewalls, and stronger isolation between control plane and tenant data plane. This change implements an opinionated service-network pattern that avoids introducing a Transit Gateway dependency and keeps the control plane reachable via PrivateLink. What this PR does: 1) New module 'control_plane-egress-accelerator' (terraform/modules/control_plane_egress_accelerator) - provisions NLB with IP target groups, Global Accelerator allocation + accelerators in customer region(s) to provide static anycast egress IPs, and optional Elastic IPs for NAT fallback. 2) Adds 'control-plane-privatelink' module to create interface endpoints (AWS::EC2::VPCEndpoint) with endpoint policy templating and per-environment service names. 3) Security hardening - new security groups implementing zero-trust rules: control-plane-internal (only accepts ENI traffic from redwood-data-plane SGs), control-plane-admin (SSH/HTTPS from management CIDRs only). 4) Installer hooks and Helm chart flags - installer/helm-values.yaml includes new keys (egressAccelerator.enabled, privatelink.serviceName, allowedManagementCidrs) and the helm templates wire up endpoint discovery for control-plane components. 5) Upgrade/rollback plan automation - terraform/plans/accelerator-rollout.md and installer scripts include a blue/green rollout pattern: create accelerator and NLB in parallel, add new target group with weight zero, gradually reweight traffic and then switch DNS alias to accelerate cutover; rollback reverses weights and destroys new resources if health checks fail. 6) Reference docs and migration script - tools/migrate/static-egress-migrate.sh helps existing Private deployments opt in with minimal downtime. Migration impact: opt-in; default behavior unchanged unless egressAccelerator.enabled=true. Rollout constraints: customers with Transit Gateway-based topologies must set useTransitGateway=false or follow the migration notes. Testing and CI: included integration test harness updates (test/integration/accelerator) that spin up a small NLB+GA configuration in a sandbox account and verify static IP stability, endpoint connectivity, and security group enforcement. The first CI run uncovered IAM policy issues for the Global Accelerator role; fixed in a follow-up commit. Checklist: [x] Terraform module + vars and outputs [x] Helm chart flag and templates [x] Migration script and docs [x] Integration tests and local test scripts [x] Reviewer feedback addressed Backwards compatibility and safety: This is non-breaking by default; all new infra is behind explicit flags. The PR adds explicit destroy-safe tags for resources created during a rollout to ensure clean rollback. Related work items: ENG-3281 (static egress), INFRA-742 (privatelink for control plane), SUP-905 (customer support request for stable egress IPs). Notes for operators: When enabling, increase monitoring retention for accelerator health checks and ensure cross-account IAM (if partner allowlisting is required) is in place. Security review notes: Endpoint policies default to least-privilege; we included a policy template with allow-by-service-tag and deny-wide-open placeholders that must be reviewed by security before enabling in prod. CI status: final run passing, integration tests green.
Liam O'Connor: Please split the broad module into smaller files or add clearer submodule docs; the NLB target group health checks need explicit attributes for TLS listeners.
Maya Chen: Addressed by adding health_check blocks and extracting GA config into vars; added examples in terraform/examples/accelerator
Priya Nair: Can we avoid Global Accelerator if customers require single-region deterministic IPs? Suggest adding a flag to select GA vs. EIP-NAT fallback.
Maya Chen: Added egressAccelerator.mode with options [global-accelerator, eip-nat, none] and documented tradeoffs in docs/private/egress-accelerator.md
Carlos Mendez: Integration tests flaked in first CI run due to IAM role propagation; re-run looks good and logging added to test harness
Priya Nair: Security review approved the default endpoint policy template but requests manual approval for production enablement noted in docs

Motivation: In large VPC topologies we observed intermittent PrivateLink service-attachment acceptance failures during control-plane upgrades and cross-account endpoint rotations. Those failures sometimes required manual acceptance of the Service Attachment or ad-hoc IAM role provisioning. This PR implements an operator and corresponding Terraform/Helm changes that introduce a signed IAM-claim workflow to safely rotate/accept control-plane PrivateLink attachments at scale, plus pre-provision reconciliation and rollback hooks.

What this changes (single-string description): Adds a Kubernetes controller (helm chart) and companion Terraform module wiring that: 1) pre-provisions a constrained IAM role template in the control plane account for ephemeral claim-based acceptance; 2) exposes a signed-claim API (short-lived JWT) that an installer/maintainer can use to prove intent to accept an attachment; 3) automates attachment acceptance and attaches an endpoint authorization tag for auditability; 4) mirrors private DNS records into a bounded hosted zone in the managed VPC to avoid split-brain during cutovers; 5) provides a safe rollback path that can revoke claims and deprovision ephemeral roles; 6) includes migration scripts for existing installations to opt into the claim flow without downtime.

Implementation highlights: - terraform/modules/privatelink-claim: new module that creates the IAM role, a KMS key for signed claims, and tightly-scoped resource policies (assume-role condition and principal boundaries). - charts/privatelink-claim-controller: Helm chart for the controller that watches ServiceAttachment CRs (custom resource) and performs signed claim validation, acceptance, tagging, and DNS mirror writes to Route53. - installer/hooks/pre-provision-claims: introduces a preflight step in the installer that validates cross-account trust and optionally creates a bootstrap claim secret. - upgrade/rollback helpers: scripts and hooks under tools/rotate-privatelink that perform dry-run discovery, staged acceptance (canary attachments), and coordinated rollback if DNS divergence is detected.

Checklist: - [x] Terraform module with unit tests and policy docs - [x] Helm chart with liveness/readiness probes and RBAC manifests - [x] Controller includes reconciliation loop, exponential backoff, metrics (claim_attempts_total, claim_accept_success), and structured logs - [x] E2E test harness simulating cross-account attachment rotation - [x] Upgrade manifest and migration plan - [x] Security review and least-privilege policy approved

Testing done: Local k3s + AWS integration tests ran in CI (simulated cross-account). E2E exercises: failed claim (bad signature), expired claim, accepted claim, concurrent claim attempts, DNS mirror reconcile under network partition. CI shows all unit + e2e lanes passing; one flaky integration job was stabilized by increasing controller backoff.

Migration plan: Existing installations will run installer preflight with --enable-privatelink-claims to create initial IAM templates and bootstrap keys. The controller will operate in read-only audit mode until a final opt-in command is run. This is a non-breaking migration.

Rollback plan: The tools/rotate-privatelink/run-rollback.sh script revokes KMS keys used to sign claims and removes ephemeral IAM roles if safe. It also runs DNS reconciliation to restore pre-rotation hosted zone entries.

Security notes: Signed claims are short-lived (60s default) and KMS-backed; the ephemeral IAM role imposes a restricted assume-role condition tied to service-attachment ARNs and source-account. All actions are logged to CloudTrail and controller emits audit events to a configurable audit sink.

Release notes: Adds a claim-based PrivateLink attachment acceptance operator and Terraform/Helm wiring to enable automated, auditable control-plane PrivateLink rotations. Opt-in via installer flag.

Related: ENG-7124 (scalable privatelink rotations), ENG-7189 (dns mirroring for controlled cutovers).
Ellen Park (review): Can we scope the IAM assumeRole condition to attachment ARNs instead of account-level? Reason: reduces blast radius.
Priya Shah (author): Updated iam_policies.tf to include arn:aws:ec2:::service-attachment/* as condition and added tests that assert the condition. See commit d4b8e01.
Gregory Mills (review): Controller should surface metrics for expired claims vs invalid signatures so we can tune retries. Also add a metric for simultaneous claims on same attachment.
Priya Shah (author): Added claim_expired_total and claim_signature_invalid_total, and claim_concurrent_attaches_gauge. Updated controller test to assert metric increments.
Sukriti Rao (security): KMS key rotation policy - ensure claims signed with old keys can be validated for a small grace window. Also ensure logs do not contain raw JWTs.
Priya Shah (author): Implemented a key rotation window of 5 minutes and redacted JWTs in logs. Added docs/security/privatelink-claim-policy.md.
Ellen Park (approval): LGTM after IAM scoping and metrics updates. Approved, ready to merge.

payload.body:
Motivation:
This PR refactors the helm values surface for the private installer to make explicit a compatibility layer and to add a serial init controller pattern suitable for on-prem tenant bootstrap sequences. Over time we've accumulated ad-hoc values and a few implicit ordering assumptions in init jobs; that has made upgrades brittle for customers running large tenant counts.

What this changes (summary):
- Add a top-level `compat` values section that maps legacy keys to the new canonical schema and emits a Helm note when values are detected that will be deprecated.
- Introduce a `serial-init-controller` Kubernetes manifest (lightweight controller) as a templated init helper that enforces per-tenant serial execution of seed/init hooks. This is opt-in and controlled by values (`init.controller.enabled`).
- Strict values schema (values.schema.json) extended with `compat` rules and deprecation metadata; Helm lint and CI now fail if unknown top-level keys are present unless they are explicitly mapped in `compat`.
- Add a small Go utility (`scripts/values_migrate.go`) used in our release tooling to produce a migration plan for customer `values.yaml` during upgrades (dry-run and apply modes).
- Update Helm helpers (`_helpers.tpl`) with new template functions `compatMerge` and `initControllerConfig` used across the chart to maintain single source of truth.

Design and compatibility notes:
- The `compat` section allows chart operators to declare mapping from legacy keys to canonical keys, for example: `compat: { oldInitConcurrency: { to: init.controller.concurrency, warn: true } }`. When `warn` is true, Helm will render a NOTICE in the template output but will not break installs. A future major will promote `warn` -> error by default.
- `init.controller.enabled` defaults to `false` for backwards compatibility. We recommend enabling it for clusters upgrading to this chart if they have >50 concurrent tenant seeds.
- The serial controller is intentionally minimal (no external dependencies) and acts by creating a per-tenant Lease and running init Jobs sequentially; it's implemented as a templated Deployment for customers who prefer managed controller, and as a Job-driven fallback for air-gapped environments.

Checklist:
- [x] Add values.schema.json entries for new fields and deprecation metadata
- [x] Implement `compat` merging helpers in `_helpers.tpl`
- [x] Add `serial-init-controller` manifests + RBAC templates
- [x] Add `scripts/values_migrate.go` and CI task to run migration dry-runs in release pipeline
- [x] Document deprecation path in CHART_NOTES and docs/upgrade.md

Release and rollout plan:
1) Publish chart with this change in a minor release (no breaking behavior by default).
2) Encourage customers to run `values-migrate --dry-run` (bundled in the upgrade checklist) to see suggested translations.
3) After two minor releases, flip `compat.warn` -> `compat.strict` behavior in a major (breaking) bump.

Testing and CI:

Context & motivation: Private deployments require predictable nodepool identities and safer rollback semantics when operators apply changes across air-gapped or peered VPCs. Existing modules create GPU nodepools with provider-generated names and rely on global tfstate only; this makes cross-account reconciliation and on-prem rollback brittle. This PR introduces a new terraform module (modules/gpu-nodepool-stencil) that provides deterministic naming, optional lease-backed ephemeral IAM bindings, and a lightweight tfstate checkpointing mechanism anchored to network tags. Goals: 1) deterministic, stable nodepool identifiers to allow safe rebinds and tenant moves; 2) lease-based IAM sessions so nodepools get least-privilege, short-lived credentials for cluster bootstrap; 3) checkpointed state objects (S3/GCS) tied to VPC/subnet tags to support orchestrated rollbacks and faster drift detection. What changed: - New module: terraform/modules/gpu-nodepool-stencil/ implementing deterministic naming strategy, nodepool fencing IAM templates, and optional network-anchor checkpointing hook. - New outputs and inputs to make module pluggable into existing private-installer stacks (vpc_id, subnet_tags, tenant_id, naming_seed). - Add tfstate-checkpoint script (scripts/tfstate_checkpoint.sh) used as a post-apply hook to write a minimal JSON checkpoint object to configured object store with network tag metadata. - Add migrator: scripts/tfstate_migrator_detname.go to compute deterministic names and optionally migrate state entries for existing installs (dry-run mode by default). - Add e2e-local test harness under test/integration/gpu-nodepool-stencil/ that runs a plan/apply against a local GCS-compatible backend (minio) to validate checkpoint creation and IAM binding lifecycle. - Documentation: docs/private-deploy/gpu-nodepool-stencil.md with examples and migration steps. - CI: terraform fmt/lint, unit tests for naming math, and an integration smoke test. Backwards compatibility & migration: The migrator is intentionally opt-in. The module has a toggle 'adopt_existing_names' and 'migrator_mode' with 'dry-run' by default; operators must run the migrator and confirm checkpoints before flipping adoption flags. Checklist: - [x] Terraform module implemented with full variable validation - [x] Post-apply checkpoint hook implemented and tested against minio - [x] Migrator included and documented - [x] Unit tests for naming algorithm - [x] Integration smoke test added - [x] Docs added and linked in private-installer README Testing & validation: Ran CI pipeline (format/lint/plan) — initially one formatting error, fixed in commit 3. Integration harness executed end-to-end on local minio and created checkpoint objects with expected metadata. Security & IAM: The module creates IAM role templates only; actual role assumption is gated by a 'lease' provider that issues ephemeral tokens (TTL configurable). The default behavior is conservative (no IAM creation unless 'enable_ephemeral_iam' is true). Migration notes: Run scripts/tfstate_migrator_detname.go --dry-run to preview changes, then create checkpoints for current state, then flip 'adopt_existing_names'. Related work: ENG-6342 (deterministic node ids), ENG-6401 (rollback checkpoints).

Motivation: in private deployments we observed subtle RBAC v2 policy regressions during iterative operator changes, and mismatches between declared KMS residency expectations and the installer-provisioned keys. This PR adds three coordinated features to reduce operational risk: 1) a policy-drift detector that runs as part of the installer CI and periodically as a cron job in the private control plane; it snapshots effective RBAC role graphs and compares against a committed policy baseline using a compact 'diff' algorithm tuned for large role graphs so we surface meaningful drift rather than noisy ordering changes; 2) a KMS affinity preflight hook in the installer that validates tenant-declared region pinning against available CMKs and tags keys with a residency provenance tag (kms.residency) when creating or binding keys; and 3) an audit enrichment pipeline that appends normalized residency and provenance headers to audit events and emits an integrity-proof hash to make post-hoc audits and reconciliations easier. Summary of changes: added a new installer hook package (installer/hooks/policy_drift_detector.go) with an OPA-based rule set that performs semantic comparisons and a small runner for baseline snapshots; added an installer KMS adapter (installer/hooks/kms_affinity_check.go) that performs cloud-provider key lookups and writes provenance tags; added an audit enricher service (installer/audit/enricher/enricher.go) that normalizes residency headers and computes a per-event HMAC for tamper-evidence; added integration e2e definitions (installer/ci/policy-e2e.yaml) and docs (docs/upgrade/2026-02-policy-drift.md); updated the installer CLI to expose --enforce-kms-affinity and --drift-detector-schedule flags; added tests and benchmarks. Rollout and compatibility: all features are opt-in for upgrades; the installer defaults keep previous behavior unless --enforce-kms-affinity is set. The drift detector can be enabled in a staged rollout using the existing canary mechanism; the audit enricher runs when audit-forwarding is enabled. Migration notes: a migration task is included that takes a one-time snapshot of current role bindings and stores it under installer/state/baseline-v1.json; this snapshot is used as the reference for the first run and can be regenerated. Security review: KMS calls are limited to explicit operator-scoped credentials, provenance HMAC keys are stored only in customer-provided CMKs when running in Private mode, and OPA rule execution is sandboxed. Testing: unit tests for rules, integration tests against the private-installer mock provider, and a full e2e run against a small multi-tenant cluster were executed as part of the CI. Related work: follows up on SEC-78 and complements ENG-2026 policy linter efforts. Next steps: add a telemetry metric for 'drift_violation_rate' to Redwood Console and wire an alerting rule for recurring drift across more than 2 snapshots.
Arielle Chen: Could you quantify the runtime overhead of running the drift detector on large tenants? worried about adding CPU to the installer control loop
Marina Soloviev: Benchmarks added to tests show median run for a 10k-role graph is 3.2s and 95th percentile 12.1s; detector runs off the critical path in the default schedule and we added a --drift-detector-schedule to throttle frequency
Devon Patel: Please ensure provenance HMAC keys are never written to logs and rotateable; also add a test for maliciously reordered role arrays
Marina Soloviev: hmac keys are stored only under customer CMKs in Private mode; added a redaction unit test and a reorder-tolerant comparator; updated docs to call out key rotation guidance
Lucas Romero: Approved after nit on CLI help text and a suggestion to separate the e2e test into two smaller ones
Marina Soloviev: updated CLI help and split the e2e as suggested; re-ran CI and all checks passed
Adds a policy-drift detector for RBAC v2; installer preflight KMS affinity check with provenance tagging; audit enrichment with residency headers and tamper-evidence HMAC; opt-in flags for Private installs; minor CLI and docs updates
Enable --enforce-kms-affinity only after validating CMK availability; run the migration snapshot on a maintenance window for large tenants; monitor drift_violation_rate metric post-upgrade

payload.body:
Motivation: Private control planes often fail during zero-downtime upgrades because controlplane nodes are scheduled into recently-provisioned subnets before route tables, peering, or DNS propagation completes. This PR automates a safer subnet enrollment flow for the installer and introduces a lightweight CSR-based authorization handshake so nodes only join the control plane after a signed enrollment token is present. Additionally, a DNS liveness prober runs as part of the installer to detect stale resolver records and block finalizing controlplane endpoints until DNS checks pass.

Design summary: 1) Subnet claim controller (Terraform + Helm hooks): the installer will mark candidate subnets as CLAIMED by adding tags and storing a claim record in the installer state bucket; a pre-attach validation ensures CIDR and AZ compatibility with existing controlplane topology. 2) CSR enrollment: new installer certificate-signing flow issues short-lived bootstrap CSRs; controlplane node agents call the CSR endpoint and receive a signed enrollment certificate only after the claim controller validates the subnet and provisioning signals (NAT/route/endpoint health). 3) DNS liveness prober: a small Go probe deployed as a Job that validates controlplane resolver records (both authoritative and cross-account forwarding where applicable) across configured regions and emits Prometheus metrics and verbose logs for troubleshooting. 4) Rollout: default is opt-in for existing customers via helmValues.install.enrollment.enabled=false; new installs opt-in=true.

Files & surface area: terraform/modules/subnet-claim (new) with state locking support; helm/controlplane/templates/enrollment-hook-job.yaml; installer/agents/csr-server.go (new, with 500-line test harness); installer/upgrade/rollback orchestrator changes to delay finalization until prober success; tests/integration/subnet-claim-e2e.go (new harness that simulates cross-account forwarding).

Migration & backward compatibility: Existing clusters without enrollment remain unaffected by default. When enabled during upgrades, the orchestrator will do a staged handoff: 1) mark new subnets as CLAIM_PENDING, run DNS prober; 2) if prober passes and CSR handshake succeeds, change to CLAIMED and allow node joins; 3) otherwise, automatically roll back the claim and keep instances in fallback subnets. This avoids split-brain between old/new controlplane nodes.

Security considerations: enrollment CSRs are short-lived (15m) and bound to subnet metadata + instance identity tokens. The CSR signing key is provisioned via KMS and rotated by the platform key-rotation job. All network operations are performed using least-privilege IAM roles scoped to the installer S3/Terraform role.

Testing and CI notes: Added unit tests for CSR validation, Terraform plan checks, and a mocked DNS probe. Integration runs in the perf-canary environment exercise cross-account forwarding and simulate delayed Route53 propagation. CI initially failed on a flaky resolver test; rerun stabilised the job and CI status is now green.

How to verify in staging: 1) helm upgrade --install with values.enrollment.enabled=true and values.enrollment.testMode=true; 2) observe Job "controlplane-dns-liveness" produce PASS metrics; 3) create a subnet claim via terraform apply and verify the installer S3 state file contains the CLAIM_PENDING -> CLAIMED transition; 4) confirm controlplane nodes only register after CSR handshake.

Operational playbook: If a DNS probe stays in FAIL, the orchestrator will mark the claim as failed and emit an incident event to the existing installer alerting topic. Operators can force-override via the 'installerctl claim finalize --force' command after manual verification.

Related work: follows ENG-8342 (subnet lifecycle reconciler) and ENG-8401 (safe upgrade coordinator). See sup ticket SUP-2121 for customer repro that motivated this change.

Review notes: reviewers asked for stronger observability (added per-AZ probe gauges), tightened CSR TTL, and extra terraform plan guards. The PR was squashed on merge.
Automated subnet claiming with optional CSR-based enrollment and DNS liveness gating. Opt-in for existing clusters; enabled by default for new installs. Improves safety for controlplane upgrades and reduces incidents caused by premature node joins.
