Motivation: Customers operating in fully isolated air-gapped environments requested a simpler, auditable mechanism to compose and promote runtime bundles atomically and to perform deterministic rollbacks without relying on external registries. This PR introduces a bundled-dependency index (compact YAML/JSON manifest) that enumerates component images, checksums and version constraints, plus a lightweight promote/rollback controller that performs atomic bundle activation on the target cluster.

What this change does: adds a new 'bundled-index' manifest format and generator (cli: rhub-bundle index), implements a PromoteController that validates bundle checksums, prefetches sealed credentials to a local sealedsecret store, and swaps runtime configmaps/helm releases in a single transaction with a promote annotation. If a promote fails, the controller runs the rollback path using the last-known-good index entry. The terraform module that seeds a local OCI mirror has been extended with a 'seed_policy' flag to allow optional ACL scoping and pre-seeding verification hooks. Finally, Helm chart and values schema changes allow operator-driven promotes (chart values.promote.enabled).

Backward compatibility and upgrade notes: existing airgap users are not forced to change; the bundle index generator is additive. Upgrades: operator will not auto-promote without explicit annotation; cluster administrators must run `rhub bundle index --manifest` and `kubectl apply` the bundle or use the new `rhub promote` helper. We include a migration script (tools/migrate/legacy-to-index.sh) that converts older sealed-bundle layouts into the new indexed format.

Checklist:
- [x] Bundle index generator (CLI) implemented
- [x] PromoteController with atomic swap + rollback path implemented
- [x] Helm chart values and RBAC for controller added
- [x] Terraform module extension for registry seeding and ACLs
- [x] Documentation updates and example playbook (docs/airgap/promote-playbook.md)
- [x] Integration tests: local mirror + promote/rollback scenario

Testing performed: unit tests for index parsing and checksum validation, e2e on KIND with a seeded OCI registry (simulated offline mirror), manual test of promote followed by induced failure to validate rollback path. Performance: index parsing and manifest apply are sub-second for typical bundle sizes (~200 artifacts); promote controller performs batch secret prefetch with backoff to avoid saturating local registry.

Security notes: the promote flow ensures signed index files (ed25519) are verified against a configured key in the installer KMS path. Sealed credential fetching respects RBAC and logs access via audit events. The migration script warns if unsealed secrets are found.

Limitations and future work: current promote controller assumes manifests fit in a single ConfigMap/Secret (we will add multi-chunk support in follow-up). We also plan to expose atomic promote as a Helm hook to integrate with operator-managed releases.

Links: linear: ENG-9274, docs: ./docs/airgap/promote-playbook.md, terraform module: ./terraform/oci-seed, cli: ./cmd/rhub-bundle
- Add bundled dependency index manifest for offline installs
- Introduce atomic promote controller to enable zero-downtime bundle switch and deterministic rollback
- Terraform module tweaks for registry seeding and ACLs
Rafael Jimenez: Overall design looks solid. Can we have a clear failure-mode diagram in the docs? Also please gate the controller RBAC more narrowly (namespace-scoped) — avoid cluster-admin.
Author reply: Added namespace-scoped RBAC and a failure-mode appendix in docs (see docs/airgap/appendix-failures.md).
Priya Sharma: The migration script touches secrets; can we add a dry-run mode and stronger warnings?
Author reply: Added --dry-run to the migration script and an explicit checklist in the playbook.
Liam O'Connor: CI flaky on e2e when registry seeding is slow; suggest increasing backoff and adding idempotency in seeding step.
Author reply: Increased backoff, made seeding idempotent and added retries to e2e test harness.

Motivation: long-running init jobs in private installs were failing on transient network errors or node reboots, leaving tenant installs partially seeded and causing confusing rollback behavior. This PR adds a resumable init worker pattern and proactive network validation probes so installs can self-heal and upgrades can resume without manual intervention. Design summary: 1) Init resumer controller: a lightweight templated Job + sidecar pattern that persists step-state into a ConfigMap named redwood-init-resume-{{ .Release.Namespace }} and respects an exponential backoff TTL. Jobs include a compact resume protocol that reads the last successful step id and resumes from the next checkpoint. 2) Hook-level resume flag: values.private.init.resume.enabled and values.private.init.resume.ttlSeconds allow operators to opt-in and tune retention. 3) Network preflight probe: a templated preflight Job and probe helper that performs normalization checks (DNS resolution for control-plane endpoints, TCP connect to customer gateway IPs/CIDRs, cloud metadata reachability for onprem) and writes a structured result to a preflight ConfigMap used by the installer to gate long-running init jobs. 4) Template helpers: helpers added for templating lock ConfigMap names, backoff annotations, and idempotent job command wrappers. 5) Upgrade path: upgrade and rollback tooling will now detect resume-enabled releases and, if a previous init job failed, will schedule a fast-retry resume job instead of a full reinstall. Backwards compatibility: resume feature is opt-in and disabled by default; when disabled, behavior is identical to current hooks. Migration: operators can opt-in by setting values.private.init.resume.enabled=true and optionally configure values.private.init.networkPreflight.{enabled,targets,timeout}. Security considerations: ConfigMaps used for resume metadata are cluster-scoped within the namespace and do not contain secrets; we added RBAC rules scoped to the release ServiceAccount. Testing: included unit tests for template rendering and a small integration harness that simulates a transient network failure and demonstrates resume across a node reboot. Rollout plan: feature will be behind the values flag for one release and monitored via a new alert redwood.install.resume-failures in the SLO toolkit. See release_notes below for operator steps and caveats.
Arjun: The backoff TTL default seems aggressive for air-gapped installs, can we make it longer by default? Author: Raised default to 86400s and added values.private.init.resume.ttlSeconds for tuning.
Lisa: Need to ensure resume ConfigMap can't be abused to inject commands. Author: The resume payload is a small JSON with step ids and checksums, we validated we never store scripts or commands. Added a schema validator in the resumer sidecar.
Tomas: Helm template lint failed on indentation for _helpers.tpl, please run helm template lint locally. Author: Fixed indentation and added unit test to cover helper rendering.
CI: integration e2e failed on first run due to flakey cloud metadata access, reran and all checks passed.
- Added opt-in resumable init worker pattern to reduce manual intervention after transient failures. Enable with values.private.init.resume.enabled=true.
- Added network preflight checks customizable via values.private.init.networkPreflight.targets and timeout.
- No breaking changes when disabled. Operators should test resume in a staging environment before enabling in production.
Enable with helm upgrade --set private.init.resume.enabled=true --set private.init.networkPreflight.enabled=true. Recommended to start with ttlSeconds=86400 and targets set to control-plane IPs and gateway CIDRs. Watch alert redwood.install.resume-failures and preflight metrics under installer.preflight.*.
payload.title: Resumable init workers and proactive network validation probes

Summary: This PR adds a small domain-specific orchestrator DSL inside the Helm templates to sequence tenant-scoped init Jobs, plus an optional preflight image verification job that validates images against a provided manifest or mirror. Motivation: private/on-prem installs in air-gapped environments require deterministic init sequencing and a way to verify that required container images are present in an offline mirror. The current hook model requires manual orchestration; this change centralizes policy and makes init phases declarative and auditable.

Checklist:
- [x] Add values.schema for new keys (initOrchestrator, airgapVerification)
- [x] Implement templates: _helpers.tpl, init-orchestrator-job.yaml, preflight-image-check.yaml, annotations and RBAC snippets
- [x] Add example values: tests/values-airgap.yaml and examples/airgap/README.md
- [x] Unit Helm template tests for sequencing and conditional rendering
- [x] Document runtime behavior in docs/private-installer.md

What changed (high level):
- charts/redwood-private-installer/templates/init-orchestrator-job.yaml: New templated Job that is rendered when .Values.initOrchestrator.enabled is true. The template accepts a small DSL: waves -> stages -> tasks. Waves are serialized with an ordinal and respect tenant-scoped concurrency and leader-election annotations. The Job uses a small init controller image (configurable) that interprets the DSL and executes defined sub-jobs via Kubernetes Job API.
- charts/redwood-private-installer/values.schema.json: Added schema for initOrchestrator and airgapVerification sections, with validation for required fields in airgap mode (manifestChecksum or mirrorRegistry).
- charts/redwood-private-installer/templates/_helpers.tpl: New helper functions to render DSL JSON blobs and stable names for orchestrated Jobs and to emit safe annotations for audit logs.
- charts/redwood-private-installer/templates/preflight-image-check.yaml: Optional preflight Job that validates the presence and digest of images against a provided image-manifest ConfigMap or offline registry credentials. Runs before orchestrator waves when enabled.
- charts/redwood-private-installer/NOTES.txt: Updated to explain airgap flow and fail-open vs. fail-closed behavior.
- charts/redwood-private-installer/README.md and docs/private-installer.md: Documentation for configuring orchestrator DSL, timeouts, and recommended mirror layouts.
- tests/values-airgap.yaml and tests/template-tests/init-orchestrator-test.yaml: Examples and assertions covering the main branching behaviors.

Commits (summary):
- 1f3a2d2 Add initial orchestrator DSL templates and helpers
- b4c8d9f Add preflight image verification job and schema validations
- 9e7f4a1 Wire up values and add example airgap values file
- 3c2b8f7 Add unit template tests and CI pipeline step for airgap tests
- 5a1b0e3 Fix: parameterize backoff policy and expose leader-election annotation

Design notes and rationale:
- Orchestrator DSL is intentionally minimal (waves->stages->tasks) so the template stays readable and control plane logic remains in a tiny, audited init-controller container instead of complex Helm hooks. This reduces Helm lifecycle surprises while enabling deterministic ordering across tenants.
- The preflight image verification supports two modes: manifest (ConfigMap with image:digest entries) and mirror-check (attempts registry pull using provided credentials). In air-gapped installs, operators can supply a manifest, and the Job will gate the install if essential images are missing unless allowMissingImages=true is set.
- Concurrency: .Values.initOrchestrator.maxConcurrentWaves can be scoped per-tenant (we emit tenant labels) so platform operators can limit parallel seed jobs.

Review conversation (high level, single continuous narrative):
- Evelyn Park: "Can we make the backoff policy configurable per-wave rather than global? Some tenants have slow seed tasks."
- Author (Anya): "Good point — initial patch had a global setting. Updated to allow per-wave backoff and a sane global default; added schema and tests."
- Marcus Li: "Security: the preflight job touches registry credentials. Please ensure we don't log secrets and add a note about using projected service account tokens or KMS for credentials."
- Author: "Agreed. The Job uses a Kubernetes Secret volume mounted as a file; I added log redaction in the init-controller and documentation recommending projected service account tokens for short-lived credentials. Also added an RBAC snippet restricting the init-controller to Job/ConfigMap access only."
- Ravi Sharma: "Nit: helper names collide with existing prefix. Rename orchestration helpers to 'rpOrch' to avoid collisions."
- Author: "Renamed helper functions and updated templates accordingly."
- Evelyn Park (approval): "Approach looks good, tests exercise the main paths. Approving pending CI green."

CI and verification:
- Pipeline: linters -> helm unit tests -> template-tests (airgap) -> integration smoke on k3s runner. First run had one flake in integration (timeout on k3s job startup). Re-ran the integration stage; all checks passed. Final status: pass.

Backward compatibility and migration:
- This change is additive. initOrchestrator is disabled by default. Existing installs are unaffected unless operators opt-in. Schema additions are backward compatible with previous values files.

Manual test scenarios performed by author:
- Airgapped install using tests/values-airgap.yaml with manifest mode and mirror mode against local registry mirror.
- Non-airgap install with orchestrator enabled and multiple tenant labels to validate per-tenant concurrency gating.
- Simulated missing image in manifest to verify fail-open vs fail-closed behavior.

Follow-ups & TODOs (tracked in Linear):
- ENG-1987: add an optional controller mode to run the orchestrator as a Deployment instead of a Job for very large clusters (future work).
- ENG-2032: extend preflight checks to validate OCI signatures and attestations.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main after CLA and DCO checks. Changelog entry included in release notes.

Files changed (illustrative snippets):
- templates/init-orchestrator-job.yaml (new): renders when .Values.initOrchestrator.enabled == true and consumes .Values.initOrchestrator.dsl. Job is annotated with "rp.redwood.com/init-wave": "{{ .wave }}" to help tracing.
- templates/preflight-image-check.yaml (new): conditional on .Values.airgapVerification.enabled; mounts secret 'airgap-registry-credentials' when provided.
- values.schema.json (modified): new definitions for initOrchestrator and airgapVerification with enum validations and regex for image digests.

If you want to test locally: helm template ./charts/redwood-private-installer -f tests/values-airgap.yaml --set initOrchestrator.enabled=true | less

Notes: This PR purposefully keeps the orchestrator controller image minimal. The controller intentionally performs no destructive actions other than creating Jobs; all real changes are surfaced as Jobs/ConfigMaps so operators can audit them easily. The preflight job does not retry image pulls by default in manifest mode (it verifies digests), but mirror-check can be configured for retries.

Contact: @anya for follow-ups and rollout guidance.
Adds an init orchestrator DSL for sequencing Helm hook Jobs and a preflight image verification step for air-gapped/private installs. Backoff and concurrency are configurable; includes values.schema updates and example airgap values file.

Motivation: Private control plane deployments in multi-AZ customer VPCs occasionally surface drift where subnets lack the expected 'redwood:controlplane' AZ tags or the stub private hosted zone (split-horizon) is not provisioned to route control-plane traffic to the local AZ endpoint. This causes cross-AZ hairpinning and latency spikes when the control plane routes to a different AZ. This PR automates detection and safe remediation for those gaps during installer runs and enables a guarded bootstrap path for creating per-AZ stub zones and minimal route table associations when requested. What this changes: 1) terraform/installer: subnet-allocator module now writes/reads the new tag set redwood:cp-role, redwood:cp-az and a tagredwood:cp-enforced timestamp; an idempotent reconciler ensures missing tags are added without reassigning IPs. 2) dns/bootstrap: introduces a templated bootstrap worker (stubzone_bootstrap.sh) that creates private hosted zones with split-horizon delegations and associates them to target VPCs per-AZ if feature flag is enabled. 3) helm/patch: private-controlplane chart gains values.controlPlane.bootstrapStubZone=false by default and a jobs.cron job for emergency rehydration. 4) scripts/rollback: adds restore-subnet-tags.sh that safely reverses only tags the installer added within last 24h to support rollback. 5) tests: integration tests that simulate a two-AZ VPC with missing tags and validate no IP reassignments and correct route propagation. Backwards compatibility: New behavior is off by default and uses conservative IAM principals that only allow hosted-zone and tagging operations when explicitly enabled. Rollout plan: merge to main, ship as feature-flagged installer release; stage in canary customers with 1% enabling bootstrapStubZone; monitor routing latencies and the 'cp_tag_enforcement' metric exposed in console. Rollback plan: set bootstrapStubZone=false and run restore-subnet-tags.sh if a rehydration caused unforeseen issues. Checklist: [x] terraform module unit tests updated [x] integration tests added [x] docs updated with operator guide [x] feature gated in helm values [x] IAM policies scoped and documented Testing performed: local dry-run against a sandbox AWS account, integration tests in CI (mocked Route53), and a small canary deploy to staging where tags were rehydrated without IP churn. Related: ENG-2439 (subnet reconciliation), ENG-2491 (dns stub-zone design).
Adds AZ-aware subnet tagging, idempotent stub-zone bootstrap for split-horizon DNS, and optional ephemeral endpoint failover. Backwards compatible with existing control plane allocations.
Liam O'Neill: Requested tightening of IAM policies for Route53 changes and added a note to docs about propagation delays. Aisha: Addressed in commit 'fix: scope stubzone IAM to customer-hostedzone-ops role' and added docs note. Marta Silva: Asked for explicit idempotency tests for route table associations to ensure no unintended detach/attach operations; added integration test and documented the invariants in the reconciler. Ethan Zhao: Approved after CI green and a successful staging canary. Final: LGTM from all reviewers.

Summary: Introduces an OCI catalog manifest and a small CLI ('mirrorctl') to build/verifiy an air-gapped registry mirror and perform checksum-verified, atomic bundle applies. Motivation: customers in regulated environments need deterministic offline bundles with end-to-end integrity validation and safe rollback hooks; existing airgap tooling lacked a machine-readable image catalog and lacked an atomic apply that can be rolled back cleanly. Changes: 1) installer/mirrorctl: new lightweight binary and subcommands (index, mirror, verify, apply, rollback) that produce and consume a catalog.json containing image refs, digests, and file checksums; 2) pkg/installer/atomic_apply: new apply engine that validates image digests against catalog, stages bundle metadata, and performs Helm upgrades with --atomic semantics plus preflight checksum gating; 3) terraform/modules/registry-replication: optional module to create registry replication manifests and S3/GCS index storage used by mirrorctl; 4) helm/redwood/templates: values schema extended to accept imageDigestMapping and bundleMetadata entries; 5) distro-support/rocky: packaging and node-init snippets to support Rocky Linux 9 images (sysctl tuning and containerd config) for customers using Rocky in air-gapped datacenters. Backwards compatibility: existing slim bundle format remains supported; mirrorctl can import older index formats and will generate catalog.json when mirroring. Security: manifests are signed using the existing bundle signing key (cosign) and mirrorctl verifies signatures prior to apply. Testing: unit tests added for checksum verification and staged apply/rollback simulation; end-to-end tests added under tests/airgap/e2e that run a local registry mirror in CI and exercise the apply/rollback flow. Rollout: feature gated behind installer CLI flag --enable-oci-catalog and disabled by default for current customers; documentation added. Related: ENG-3245 (airgap catalog), ENG-3310 (rollback guarantees); SUP-7892 documents a customer issue that motivated checksum gating.
Tomás Rivera: Please add a short explanation of why we need checksums in addition to image digests. Also add a unit test that simulates a mismatched checksum during apply.
Nora Singh: Added explanation in docs and unit test in tests/atomic/checksum_test.go that intentionally injects a corrupted file to ensure apply aborts. PTAL.
Priya Nair: Can mirrorctl import older slim index formats? We should provide a migration helper for customers with existing mirrors.
Nora Singh: mirrorctl migrate-import command added; doc section explains behavior and that migrating will regenerate catalog.json with digests and file checksums.
Evan Chen: Minor: prefer deterministic JSON ordering for catalog.json to avoid flaky checksum behavior when re-generating. Suggest using a canonical marshaller.
Nora Singh: Switched to canonical JSON marshaller, added tests to assert stable output. All good from my side.
Tomás Rivera: CI showed an intermittent failure on e2e run due to port conflict; I re-ran the job and it passed. Approving.
Adds mirrorctl and OCI catalog manifest support for air-gapped installer; supports checksum-verified atomic bundle apply and rollback; optional Terraform module for registry replication; Rocky Linux node-init snippets for on-prem customers. Feature is behind an opt-in flag. (ENG-3245, ENG-3310).
Enable with --enable-oci-catalog on installer; to mirror an airgap bundle: run mirrorctl index --source <bundle> --out catalog.json; mirrorctl mirror --catalog catalog.json --target-registry <registry>; verify with mirrorctl verify --catalog catalog.json --registry <registry>; apply with installer apply --catalog catalog.json --atomic. For rollback use mirrorctl rollback --catalog <catalog.json> --target-registry <registry>. See docs/operator/airgap-mirroring.md for full steps.
Security review completed: cosign-based signing enforced by default for catalog.json; mirrorctl refuses to apply unsigned or tampered catalogs unless --insecure-allow-unsigned is explicitly provided and logged.
Existing slim bundles can be migrated by running mirrorctl migrate-import --bundle <bundle.tar.gz> which will emit a catalog.json and optional registry mirror plan. Documented caveats for incremental mirrors in docs/operator/airgap-mirroring.md.
payload.title: Add OCI catalog mirroring with checksum-verified atomic bundle apply; Rocky Linux node base support

payload.body:
Context: Private deployments in multi-AZ environments need predictable egress IPs for allowlisting and per-AZ capacity isolation. The current installer uses a single shared NAT layer which makes IP allowlisting brittle and complicates egress budgeting across availability zones. This PR introduces zone-aware NAT gateway provisioning with deterministic allocation from configurable EIP pools and tightens control-plane security groups for the control-plane-to-worker and control-plane-egress flows.

What this PR does (summary): adds a new terraform module and variables to allocate per-az NAT gateways backed by pre-allocated EIP pools; introduces an optional deterministic allocation map so customers can pin EIPs to AZs; updates Helm templates used by the private control plane to surface NAT/EIP configuration and new annotations for kube-proxy egress routing; hardens default security-group rules by converting wide 0.0.0.0/0 control-plane egress to scoped destination CIDRs and explicit port lists; provides an opt-out flag for customers who prefer a single shared egress or who manage NAT externally.

Key implementation notes: deterministic_eip_map (map string->list) is a user-provided mapping of AZ->EIP list used in the tf module; when not provided, the module will allocate from an EIP pool per-AZ with deterministic naming so re-runs are idempotent. NAT Gateway resources are created per-AZ with route table attachments isolated to control-plane subnets only. Security-group changes are additive by default (creates redwood-controlplane-tight and migrates rules gradually). The module exports a small status object (id list) via Terraform outputs used by the Helm chart templates.

Compatibility and rollout: this change is non-breaking by default. The migration path for existing clusters is a two-step upgrade: 1) enable the module in dry-run mode to generate recommended eip allocations and preview Terraform plan; 2) switch on create_nat_per_az=true and apply. A migration helper script (scripts/migrate-egress.sh) is included to validate connectivity, rotate NAT attachments, and perform rollback if healthchecks fail. The opt-out flag (controlplane.egress.use_shared_nat=false by default for upgrades) lets operators defer migration.

Testing: Terraform unit runs were executed against a local terraform-compliance harness and integration tests were run in the benchmark-lab AWS account with a 3-AZ topology. Smoke tests include IP allowlist verification for a sample webhook (external firewall), e2e service-to-internet flows, and failover tests where a single AZ NAT is destroyed to validate fallback to neighboring AZ NATs if enabled. CI summary below.

Rollout notes for SRE and customer-ops: 1) For customers with static allowlist requirements we recommend providing deterministic_eip_map during install. 2) For existing clusters on older installer versions, follow the migrate-egress.sh workflow and schedule a maintenance window to apply Terraform state changes to route tables. 3) If using marketplace images with strict IP ACLs coordinate with network teams to pre-provision EIPs.

Related: builds on work from ENG-4020 (subnet allocation) and complements INF-71 (privatelink egress proxy).
Liam Chen: Can we make the default behavior opt-in for new installs? I don't want surprises for single-AZ customers.
Maya Rodriguez: Default for new installs is per-az NAT true; I added 'create_nat_per_az' and documented the opt-out flag. For single-AZ installs the module short-circuits to single NAT so behavior is safe.
Sofia Kaplan: Security changes look good but we need a short window of overlap where both SGs exist to avoid breaking existing control plane connections.
Maya Rodriguez: Added sg migration plan and a tf resource 'redwood_controlplane_sg_migration' as a no-op resource that operators can plan/apply before switching rules. See security/sg-migrations/README.
Ravi Desai: Tested migration script in benchmark-lab. Recommend adding a metric for nat_gw_active_count to observability-pack.
Maya Rodriguez: Added metric export and a dashboard JSON in observability-pack under separate PR (linked).
Sofia Kaplan: Approving pending one small comment on variable naming consistency.
Maya Rodriguez: Addressed naming comment and squashed commits. Ready to merge.
Add optional per-AZ NAT gateways with configurable EIP pools for predictable egress IPs; introduce deterministic_eip_map for pinning EIPs to AZs; tighten control-plane security groups and provide a migration helper script. Non-breaking by default; follow migration guide for existing clusters.
1) Review example.tfvars and generate deterministic_eip_map if allowlisting is required. 2) Run scripts/migrate-egress.sh in a staging environment. 3) Apply Terraform plan during maintenance window. 4) Validate external webhook connectivity and monitor nat_gw_active_count metric.
This PR requires AWS account permissions to allocate EIPs and create NAT gateways. Customers using BYO-NAT should set controlplane.egress.use_shared_nat=true and skip providing deterministic_eip_map.
payload.title: Zone-aware egress NAT with assigned EIP pools and security-group hardening

payload.body: Context: customers running Private deployments reported rare failures when performing multi-stage upgrades where component inter-dependencies (schema, config, seed data) required coordinated rollbacks. Motivation: provide a safe, testable staged rollback path that understands service dependency ordering and preserves tenant-visible seeded state so that partial rollbacks do not leave the cluster in an inconsistent or unbootable condition. What this PR does: 1) Introduces a reversible dependency graph used by the installer to compute rollback stages; edges cover DB migrations, config map velocity, helm chart ordering, and tenant seed/data artifacts. 2) Adds ‘seed-preserve’ mode: when enabled, pre-rollback hooks snapshot tenant-seeded objects (application-level seeds and lightweight KV entries) into encrypted, versioned manifests stored in object storage with a TTL and rotation policy. 3) Implements a staged rollback executor that runs rollback stages in reverse topological order with signal checkpoints so operators can pause between stages and run integration smoke tests. 4) Adds a cli subcommand “installer rollback-plan --dry-run” that emits a human-readable plan and an operator-safe JSON plan; the JSON includes per-stage healthchecks and required preconditions. 5) Adds automatic downgrade guard checks that prevent application binary downgrades if schema compatibility checks fail; these checks are pluggable to allow product teams to opt-in. 6) Adds telemetry events and RBAC-scoped audit logs for each rollback stage and seed snapshot operation. Checklist: [x] design doc linked (Linear: ENG-2345) [x] unit tests for plan generator and serializer [x] integration test harness for staged executor using local Vagrant cluster [x] end-to-end dry-run validated against a sample two-tenant cluster [x] documented operational playbook and CLI usage (docs/installer/rollback.md) Testing notes: dry-run and encrypted snapshot creation were exercised against a local postgres instance and minio; tests include simulated partial failure (post-stage failure) and observed automatic resume/retry behavior. Compatibility: default behavior is opt-out; installer flags preserved for existing installs. Rollout plan: feature behind feature flag enabled by default for new private installs, and behind opt-in for existing customers; will be gated by a 2-week beta with selected customers. Rollback plan: staged executor supports resume-from-stage and manual abort; seed-preserve manifests can be used to restore tenant seeds if automated rollback cannot complete. Related work: complements earlier safe-rollback and migration-preview tooling. Security: snapshots are encrypted with customer-provided KMS keys when available; rotation TTL of 30 days by default. Limitations: not targeted at large binary data restores (those remain outside scope); heavy tenant-count clusters may need longer pause windows. Migration path: installer will validate cluster state and optionally recommend a canary rollback before full rollback. Links: design doc https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-2345, sample plan output in PR files. Commit summary: a) add dependency-graph package and graph serialization; b) implement plan generator and JSON emitter; c) implement staged executor with pause/resume; d) seed snapshotter and encryption layer; e) CLI flags and documentation; f) integration tests and telemetry hooks; g) unit tests and mocks. Files changed (high level): installer/cmd/rollback.go; installer/pkg/depgraph/* (new); installer/pkg/seedshot/* (new); installer/pkg/executor/staged.go; docs/installer/rollback.md; charts/redwood/values.rollback.yaml; scripts/e2e/rollback-smoke.sh; proto/installer/audit.proto; Makefile updates. Review conversation summary: initial review requested a smaller default TTL and clearer UI for pause/resume. Connor: "Please make TTL configurable and ensure KMS fallback behavior is explicit in logs." Author: "Made TTL configurable via --snapshot-ttl and added KMS fallback log lines; tests updated." Mateo: "Executor should surface stage-level metrics for SLOs." Author: "Added basic counters and trace spans; will iterate on dashboards in a follow-up." Sana: "Does this change the default behavior for existing installs?" Author: "No, default opt-out for upgrades; new installs get opt-in true but flagged in release notes." CI: pipeline ran unit, lint, and integration jobs; one flaky e2e job failed initially and was re-run; final CI green. Merge outcome: squash-merged to main after approvals and green CI. Release notes: "Added staged rollback support with dependency-aware execution and optional seed-state preservation. New CLI tools: installer rollback-plan and installer rollback --resume. Snapshots are encrypted with KMS when configured. Opt-in for existing clusters."
payload.title: staged-rollback-with-dependency-graph-and-state-seed-preservation

payload.body:
Motivation: Private deployments require repeatable, auditable automation for key management and TLS lifecycle to meet compliance and uptime SLAs. This PR adds an end-to-end installer path that provisions customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM), integrates HashiCorp Vault as an optional transit layer, and automates TLS certificate issuance and rotation via cert-manager + sealed-secrets.

Summary of changes: Adds Terraform modules, Helm chart updates, and installer hooks so the operator can opt into: (1) provisioning an envelope encryption key in cloud KMS or configuring PKCS#11-backed HSM; (2) wiring that key to a Vault Transit backend (optional) for centralized signing/encryption; (3) configuring the sealed-secrets controller to use an external key provider; (4) automating certificate issuance and zero-downtime rotation for internal mTLS via cert-manager and Kubernetes deployment rolling semantics. The installer now accepts a single high-level config block: "kms_provider" with choices [aws_kms, gcp_kms, azure_keyvault, pkcs11_hsm, vault_transit]. The implementation uses envelope encryption for persistent secrets and short-lived signing keys for TLS.

What this PR touches (high level): Terraform: modules/tls_kms (new), modules/hsm_connector (new). Helm: charts/sealed-secrets/values.yaml, charts/redwood-core/values.yaml (cert-manager config), charts/installer/templates/hooks.yaml (pre/post-install hooks for key bootstrap). Installer CLI: cmd/install/main.go (new flags), pkg/installer/provisioning.go (k6 logic). Docs: docs/private/kms-and-tls.md and migration notes.

Design notes: - Default behavior remains unchanged for users who do not opt in. - When kms_provider=vault_transit we do not provision cloud KMS keys; instead we create a Vault role/secret-engine and store envelope keys in Vault with a TTL. Vault integration is pluggable: the installer writes a minimal policy and a long-lived management token into the control plane secrets that only the provisioner uses. - For HSMs we added a small PKCS#11 shim container that mounts credentials and exposes a gRPC adapter to the sealed-secrets controller. This keeps dependencies out of the controller binary. - Seal/unseal: existing sealed-secrets flow is preserved but the controller key is now optionally provided by the external KMS/HSM. We also add migration tooling that re-encrypts existing SealedSecrets with the new key in a deterministic, batched process to avoid cluster-wide restarts. - TLS rotation: cert-manager issues new certificates with overlapping validity and the rollout controller triggers a rolling restart of pods annotated with redwood.com/auto-rotate=true. We implement a two-phase rotation (prep + cutover) to ensure no simultaneous certificate expiry.

Security and compliance: - All provisioning calls are logged to the auditor (installer emits linear IDs and request IDs). - KMS keys are created with constrained key policies (minimum principals) and key-rotation metadata. - Secrets at rest remain envelope-encrypted; the private key material for TLS is never written to plain files on disk by the installer. - For HSM-backed setups we document FIPS and PCI considerations in docs.

Testing performed: - End-to-end in staging using AWS KMS + Vault Transit: created key, validated envelope encryption for persistent secrets, rotated controller key and observed zero-downtime SealedSecrets decryption. - HSM flow tested against SoftHSM and a PKCS#11 mock for functional parity. - Cert rotation exercised with canary clusters (50% rollout) and synthetic traffic to validate no TLS hiccups. - Unit tests: new installer package coverage 78%. Integration tests: terraform apply/destroy in CI smoke job.

Rollout plan: 1) Merge in main. 2) Publish new installer release candidate and smoke in internal staging. 3) Enable opt-in in a pilot customer cluster (support + SE present). 4) Promote to GA config once pilot confirms.

Rollback plan: the installer writes a migration log and a reversible mapping of old->new secret envelopes. If any issues occur we run the included migrate/revert tool to rewrap secrets with the previous key and restart sealed-secrets controller with previous config. HSM migrations are flagged as non-automatic (operator must confirm rollback).

Notes and caveats: - Vault integration requires network access and a managed auth path; we provide a bootstrap token but recommend switching to AppRole or IAM-based auth post-install. - PKCS#11 HSM setups require operator intervention for initial module installation and PKCS#11 library path; we document steps but cannot automate hardware plug-in. - This PR intentionally avoids changing the default key provider to avoid surprising existing customers.

Checklist: - [x] Terraform modules - [x] Helm chart changes - [x] Installer CLI flags and docs - [x] Migration tooling and tests - [x] E2E validation in staging

References: Linear ENG-3279 for automation spec; SEC-410 for security review.
Arjun Patel (2026-02-19): Please add smoke tests for AWS KMS + Vault; also expand token handling doc. - Addressed in latest commit, added smoke job.
Sophie Martinez (2026-02-21): Can we avoid storing long-lived Vault tokens unencrypted in secrets? Suggest using short-lived AppRole credentials. - Reply (Maya): Installer now supports AppRole hookup as optional post-install step; bootstrap token is marked expiring and logged for rotation.
Liam O'Neill (2026-02-23): HSM PKCS#11 shim looks good but add metrics for adapter health. - Added adapter_liveness and adapter_error_count metrics in shim container.
SRE Bot CI (2026-02-24): integration/terraform apply failed on SoftHSM instance intermittently. - Investigation: race condition in SoftHSM import; fixed with retry/backoff in installer provisioning code.
Automated support for customer-managed KMS/HSM, optional Vault Transit integration, and cert-manager-based TLS rotation for Private installer. Includes Terraform modules and Helm chart integration. Opt-in only; no default changes.
Medium: introduces new external dependencies (Vault, HSM). Defaults unchanged and feature is opt-in; migration tooling reduces blast radius. Recommend pilot rollout before customer enablement.
payload.title: Automated KMS/Vault + TLS certificate rotation and secrets automation for Private installer

Implements the end-to-end restore path for Redwood Private in the installer CLI. This adds a new `restore apply` command that: (1) performs strict preflight checks (cluster connectivity, namespace/CRD readiness, version compatibility, storage backend access, and integrity checks on the backup artifact), (2) restores control-plane state in a deterministic order (cluster prerequisites, control-plane chart values/config, DB restore, then service rollout), and (3) runs post-restore health checks and emits a validation report that Support/SRE can use for escalation. The goal is to make restores repeatable, safer to run under time pressure, and easier to debug when something goes wrong. Restore ordering is intentionally conservative to avoid the on-prem issues we saw in SUP-18477 (missing CRDs/incorrect bootstrap order). Security note: we do not restore secret material from backups; we restore secret references and validate that required KMS/external secret providers are reachable. The report includes sanitized environment details (versions, timestamps, artifact IDs), step-by-step results, and pointers to relevant logs. Usage examples: `private-installer restore apply --artifact s3://<bucket>/backups/<id> --namespace redwood-private --report /tmp/restore-report.json` and `private-installer restore apply --artifact ./backup.tgz.enc --offline --validate-only`.
- Private installer: introduce `restore apply` with deterministic ordering, guardrails, and a support-ready validation report. - Adds optional `--validate-only` mode and clearer failure categorization (preflight/artifact/restore/validation).
Ethan Park: The ordering looks good, but we need a hard stop if CRDs aren’t present. We cannot attempt to apply the control-plane chart before CRDs exist (this is what bit us on-prem). Also please ensure we fail fast with an actionable message (which CRD group/version is missing). Benji Okafor: Agreed—added a CRD preflight step that checks the required GVKs and prints the exact missing resources. Also added `--skip-crd-check` (hidden) for internal dev only; default is strict. Sean Gallagher: Can we make sure the report is something Support can ask customers to upload without leaking secrets? Also: step timings and error categories are key. Benji Okafor: Implemented redaction for env vars/flags that may contain tokens; report includes timings per step and `error_category` (preflight | artifact | restore | validation). Added `--report-redact-level=strict` defaulting to strict. Hanae Suzuki: Please confirm we never write decrypted artifact contents to disk in a temp dir by default. On air-gapped/offline this becomes a footgun. Also how do we handle KMS unavailability during restore? Benji Okafor: Updated decrypt path to stream to the restore consumer; temp files are only used if `--workdir` is set explicitly. For KMS: preflight checks reachability and key access; if KMS is down we fail before touching cluster state. Connor O'Brien: This should produce a stable artifact ID and include installer version/backup format version in the report. Also ensure exit codes are consistent for automation. Benji Okafor: Added `artifact_id`, `backup_format_version`, `installer_version`, and standardized exit codes (2=preflight, 3=artifact, 4=restore, 5=validation). Fatima Noor: On-prem edge case: missing CRDs after a cluster rebuild is common; the runbook expects the installer to provide a clear remediation step. Benji Okafor: Added remediation hints to the CRD check output and linked to the internal runbook section in the CLI message. Final review: Ethan approved after CRD check and exit code cleanup; Sean approved after report redaction review; Hanae approved after streaming decrypt change.
payload.title: Add `restore apply` workflow with preflight checks and post-restore validation report

payload.body:
Motivation: customers running Private deployments asked for a reproducible, observable DR drill workflow that can be executed in a dry-run mode, exercised in CI, and fully rolled back automatically. This PR implements a telemetry-first DR harness and end-to-end canary failover automation plus a set of rollback playbooks as code.

What this changes (high level):
- Terraform: new module terraform/modules/dr_canary that provisions an isolated canary VPC/subnet + Kubernetes namespace + service account and exposes a lightweight canary agent (dr-canary) with ingress disabled by default. The module includes tagging and IAM policy templates for pre-authorized failover.
- Helm: updates to private-installer Helm chart to add lifecycle hooks (preFailover/postFailover), a helmValues.toggle.drDryRun boolean, and templates for dr-coordinator CronJob and dr-hook sidecar.
- Installer: private-installer binary gains a --dr-dry-run flag that simulates node evacuation and resource reallocation without touching production IPs; it also emits structured telemetry events to the telemetry endpoint.
- Telemetry harness: a new observability stack snapshot (prometheus rules, grafana dashboard, loki queries) under ops/dr-harness that captures failover latency, endpoint convergence, DB replica promotion events, and KV-cache warmup metrics.
- Rollback playbooks: ansible/playbooks/dr_rollback.yml and scripts/rollback-checker.sh implement the documented rollback semantics (detection, traffic cut, state verification, and rehydrate cache).
- Tests and CI: added a lightweight e2e workflow .github/workflows/dr-canary.yml that runs the terraform module in an ephemeral environment (using aws-account-test creds), executes the dr-canary scenario in dry-run and active modes, and validates telemetry assertions.

Why this is structured this way: the design separates provisioning (terraform) from control-plane actions (helm + installer) and from verification/telemetry (prometheus/grafana + CI). Dry-run mode allows teams to validate behavior without service disruption; the telemetry-first approach makes regressions visible in dashboards/alerts.

Rollout plan: 
1) Merge feature behind feature flag (helmValues.toggle.drEnabled=false by default).
2) Enable the dr-canary terraform module in staging tenants; run CI job and post dashboards to a shared SLO board.
3) Gradually enable drEnabled in canary tenants and run weekly DR drills.

Rollback and remediation: the ansible playbook supports two modes: automated (best-effort) and manual (guided). The rollback-checker.sh will produce a JSON report consumed by the installer to either abort or proceed with rehydrate. Included explicit guard rails to avoid automated traffic cuts unless both health-checks and telemetry predicates fail.

Files changed summary (high level): terraform/modules/dr_canary (new module), charts/private-installer/templates/dr-coordinator.yaml (new), charts/private-installer/values.yaml (patch), cmd/private-installer/main.go (dr-dry-run flag + telemetry emit), ops/dr-harness/prometheus.rules.yaml (new), ops/dr-harness/grafana/dr_dashboard.json (new), ansible/playbooks/dr_rollback.yml (new), scripts/rollback-checker.sh (new), .github/workflows/dr-canary.yml (new), docs/runbooks/dr-drill-runbook.md (new).

Quick usage (example): 
1) Add module to tf root: module "dr_canary" { source = "./modules/dr_canary" env = "staging" }
2) helm upgrade private-installer --set toggle.drDryRun=true -f values-dr-staging.yaml
3) ./private-installer --dr-dry-run run --script=ops/dr-harness/simulate-failover.json

Small snippet: helm values example to enable dry-run mode: 
{
  drEnabled: false,
  drDryRun: true,
  drCoordinator: { schedule: "@hourly" }
}

Security and safety considerations: dry-run avoids BGP/real IP reassignments and uses a canary VPC with isolated IAM. Rollback playbooks require a signed runbook token and are gated by RBAC checks in the installer.

Motivation: Private (VPC/on-prem) customers suffered two recent upgrade incidents where partial schema migrations plus out-of-band config rollbacks left clusters in a state that prevented safe downgrades. This PR adds two coordinated mechanisms to reduce blast radius and enable safe rollback when upgrades fail: (1) a lightweight downgrade-anchor metadata layer that records reversible anchors for critical migrations, and (2) a transactional migration stager operator that stages, validates, and checkpoints schema changes before they are promoted to production state.

What this changes (high level): the migration stager introduces a staging queue and preflight pipeline that runs per-tenant dry-runs, creates atomic backup checkpoints (S3/GCS or local filesystem depending on installer config), and only promotes migrations after a compatibility probe passes. The downgrade-anchor records a small, immutable metadata row per migration (anchor_id, upstream_version, checksum, rollback_script_ref) and a compatibility hint that lets the installer generate an automated rollback path when feasible. The installer CLI and terraform preflight module are extended to perform anchor verification and to refuse plans that would remove anchor-protected artifacts without an explicit release step. Helm charts include new pre-install/post-upgrade hooks that create/verify checkpoints and export anchor metadata to the operator.

Why this is different: existing guardrails focus on backups and runbook-driven rollbacks; this change creates an in-band, machine-verifiable anchor and a staging operator to reduce human error and enable safe automated rollbacks for a larger class of migrations (DDL with forward/backward compatible patterns). The design intentionally keeps the anchor compact and reversible where possible; irreversibly destructive migrations still require an explicit admin acknowledgment.

Compatibility notes: default behavior is opt-in via the installer values (private.migration.enableStager = true, private.migration.enforceAnchors = "warn"|"enforce"). For air-gapped installs, anchors are persisted to the on-disk backup directory and verified via the operator's checksum store. The change does not force any model or runtime changes for hosted customers.

Testing and rollout: unit tests for stager state machine, integration tests that run staged migrations against a local postgres instance with tenant sharding enabled, and an e2e canary test that verifies anchor-based rollback works with helm canary releases. We staged the rollout in three phases: opt-in tests, default-on for patch releases, and enforce mode 2 weeks later.

Operational runbook summary (short): 1) Run installer plan; 2) Run `installer migrate plan --staged` to generate staged plan and anchors; 3) Trigger promote once preflight passes; 4) If promote fails, run `installer migrate rollback --anchor <id>` which will attempt automated rollback using the stored rollback_script_ref and the backup checkpoint.

Related: SUP-5121 (customer incident), ENG-2893 design doc, ENG-2948 telemetry integration.
Hannah Kim: Please add metrics to track staged vs promoted migrations and a histogram for promote latency. Also add an owner field to anchors so we can identify who initiated a stale anchor.

Ravi Patel: Preflight now emits clear actionable errors and references installer docs section.

Adds a migration stager operator and a compact downgrade-anchor metadata layer. Provides staged dry-run, checkpointing, and automated rollback hooks for private installs. Opt-in by default; operator must be enabled via installer values. See docs/private/migrations.md for runbook and examples.

This PR introduces a controlled partial-restore flow and a tenant-quarantine mode to reduce blast radius when rolling back or restoring subsets of a Private deployment. Motivation: larger clusters with multi-tenant namespaces sometimes only need a targeted restore (single tenant, small time window) but existing restore tooling required full-cluster restores or manual fencing. This change adds: 1) a partial restore controller that accepts a tenant selector and a point-in-time snapshot reference, performs namespace-scoped restore of resources and PVCs, and wires into existing restore verification hooks; 2) a tenant-quarantine mode that temporarily isolates restored tenant namespaces from inbound routing and cross-tenant scheduling until integrity checks pass; 3) a helm chart patch set to expose the new controller and quarantine feature gates; 4) terraform module updates to make snapshot references and quarantine toggles configurable for private installs; 5) migration helpers to pin compatible operator/controller versions during restore to avoid schema drift. The design prioritizes safe automated restores: the controller stages resources in an isolated namespace, replays PV binds with transactional checks, runs schema compatibility checks against the target operator image, and only flips network policies when health checks and sample evals succeed. Rollback/upgrade considerations: the controller records an idempotent restore plan and a reversible quarantine marker so operators can abort or re-run without leaving dangling networking rules. Security: restored secrets are re-encrypted with cluster KMS keys when the cluster key differs from snapshot keys. Testing: unit tests for controller logic, integration tests on KIND and an internal on-prem harness with mocked blockstore snapshots, and a validation e2e that runs sanity traffic through the quarantine gate. Rollout: feature is gated off by default; enable via Helm values.quarantine.enabled and terraform variables. Docs: added an operations playbook for partial restores, runbook steps for aborting, and example terraform snippets. Backwards compatibility: existing full-restore paths are unchanged. This PR is intended to reduce restore time, lower blast radius for tenant-scoped incidents, and provide safer automated rollback paths for Private deployments.

Priya Nambiar: Can we make the quarantine timeout configurable and add metrics for quarantine duration? Added values.quarantine.timeout_seconds and metrics.quarantine_duration_seconds in controller.
Liam O'Connor: Terraform changes need a migration note for existing installs that pin module versions - added a release note and a sample plan that uses 'terraform state replace-provider' guidance.
CI Bot: e2e failed on first run due to timing of readiness probe; retried and passed after adjusting probe and test wait strategy.
Carlos Ruiz: Approving after quick follow-up verifying secret re-encryption behavior on a key-rotation scenario.
Priya Nambiar: Left a minor nit on helm README formatting; resolved in final commit.
Add partial restore controller and tenant-quarantine mode: allow namespace-scoped restores from snapshots, isolate restored tenants until health checks pass, configurable via Helm and Terraform. Includes migration guidance for terraform state and notes on KMS re-encryption.
Enable behind feature gate: values.quarantine.enabled=true. For large clusters prefer snapshot subsetters and pre-warming PVCs. Abort flow: call restorecontroller abort API with plan id; controller will rollback staged resources and clear quarantine marker.
Unit tests: pass. Integration: ran against internal on-prem harness with blockstore emulator. E2E: validated quarantine gating prevents ingress during restore and releases after health checks. Observed one intermittent readiness timing issue fixed in follow-up commit.
Feature gated, non-breaking by default. Operators should test restores in a staging cluster before enabling in production.

Motivation: Past upgrades have exposed two recurring problems for private deployments: accidental downgrades (operator error or rollback scripts that do not account for schema/feature flags) and inconsistent backup formats across installer versions which makes restores brittle. This PR introduces a lightweight downgrade-blocker in the installer, pins on-disk backup metadata to a stable v2 format, and adds a deterministic restore test to the CI matrix.

Summary of changes: Added a check in the private installer that refuses to apply a release with an older semantic version if that release would require a schema downgrade; the check is driven by a new release-metadata.json (version + schema_version + migration_path). Implemented a stable on-disk backup v2 format (single tar.gz with manifests/etcd-snapshots/secrets.enc and a compact manifest.json) and utilities to produce/consume it. Introduced an idempotent schema-migration runner with pre/post hooks and automatic dry-run mode. Hooked backup/restore smoke into CI to validate cross-version restores (main->v1.3 pin and back). Updated terraform and helm manifests to pin provider/module versions used by the installer so backups produced during restore tests are reproducible.

What this change does (concrete): 1) installer/upgrade/downgrade_blocker.go: adds logic that compares incoming release metadata to cluster state and rejects operations that would lower schema_version or remove required migrations. 2) installer/backup/format/v2_spec.md + tools/backup/create_v2_backup.go + tools/backup/restore_v2.go: define and implement the v2 backup format, including an encrypted secrets container compatible with KMS/HSM integration. 3) installer/migrations/runner.go: idempotent migrations with a dry-run flag and a deterministic lock file to prevent concurrent migration runs. 4) terraform/modules/version_pins.tf and charts/private/values.yaml: version pins for terraform providers and helm images used by the private installer. 5) ci/restore-e2e.yml: new CI matrix job which takes a v1.2 backup and attempts to restore it onto this branch and then back to v1.2 to validate downgrade guard behavior.

Testing performed: unit tests for migration runner (mocks for DB state), integration restore e2e that runs in GH Actions using a small ephemeral K3s cluster and mocked KMS provider, manual end-to-end restore/upgrade tests against a local vm cluster. All CI jobs passing in the PR run after a transient failure in the first integration run (flaky network to GH container registry) which was rerun.

Rollout plan: merge to main, cut v1.3.0-rc with the metadata file included. Default installer behavior remains conservative: the downgrade-blocker is enabled by default but can be temporarily relaxed with a documented admin flag --allow-downgrade-forced (requires explicit acceptance in audit logs). We will roll out the change to Dedicated customers on a staged schedule and provide a migration guide.

Rollback plan: installer will refuse to downgrade automatically; to recover a cluster that must be moved back to an older release we provide a controlled path: 1) take a v2 backup, 2) use a provided compatibility tool to map schema changes (installer/migrations/compatibility_mapper.go), 3) run restore with --force-downgrade (requires operator approval and generates a mandatory audit bundle). The force path is intentionally manual and logged.

Security notes: secrets in backups are encrypted using envelope encryption; restore tooling integrates with KMS via the existing KMS adapter. The downgrade blocker adds an operator-visible audit event.

Related: ENG-1182 (upgrade reliability), PM-431 (customer ask: guaranteed restore across minor versions).

Checklist: [x] migration runner unit tests, [x] backup/restore e2e, [x] helm/terraform pinning, [x] docs and upgrade guide, [x] audit events for forced-downgrade.

Maya K. Patel: Added a deterministic migration lock file and a leader-check path; documented the invariant in runner.go comments.
SRE (CI): initial integration job failed on network to GHCR; reran and all checks passed.
Installer: refuse schema-downgrades by default; introduce on-disk backup v2 format for consistent restore compatibility; idempotent migration runner with dry-run mode; provider/module version pinning for reproducible restores.
After merging, notify Dedicated customers of the stricter downgrade guard. Backups created by v1.2 older installers will continue to be restored via the provided v1->v2 shim for the next three minor releases. If a customer truly needs to force a downgrade, follow the documented forced-downgrade path and collect the audit bundle.

Summary: Adds an interactive migration pauser controller and a cluster compatibility checker used by the private installer preflight to prevent unsafe upgrades or downgrades. Motivation: we observed two incidents where a schema migration applied during a cluster upgrade caused tenant-level restore failures during rollbacks. This PR introduces runtime protections and deterministic checks that reduce blast radius for in-place upgrades and make automated/machine-driven restores safer.

What this PR does (single-flow): 1) Introduces a lightweight controller (installer/migrationpauser) that can insert a per-upgrade pause point. The controller exposes a CRD MigrationPause that operators can create to halt the installer rollout between helm upgrade hooks and final migration application. Pause points are idempotent and time-limited by default (72h) so a forgotten pause does not block indefinitely. 2) Adds a cluster compatibility checker (cmd/preflight) invoked by the installer and the Terraform module as an optional preflight step. The checker performs: Helm values compatibility checks, a dry-run of kube manifests in a sandbox namespace, and a schema migration dry-run against a read-replica using pg_dump/pg_restore --schema-only mode to detect incompatible DDL (example: dropped columns used by older server components). 3) Adds a restore-verify helm hook that captures restore artifacts and performs an automated verification on a small sample dataset (post-upgrade cannot proceed unless sample restore passes or operator overrides). 4) Adds a version-lockfile (installer/version-lock.yaml) emitted by the build and consumed by the installer to pin chart / module / image checksums used in the upgrade path to make downgrade detection deterministic. 5) Terraform changes add a data source that validates backup object-store URIs and a new module output that surfaces last-successful-snapshot metadata for use in rollout playbooks.

Files touched at a high level: - charts/redwood-private/templates/migration-pause-crd.yaml - charts/redwood-private/templates/restore-verify-hook.yaml - terraform/modules/installer/main.tf - terraform/modules/installer/outputs.tf - cmd/preflight/main.go - cmd/preflight/checker/compatibility.go - tools/backup/verify.go - installer/version-lock.yaml - docs/operational/upgrade-playbook.md - e2e/tests/upgrade_pause_test.go - tests/fixtures/sample_restore.sql - scripts/ci/run-preflight.sh

Testing and verification: Unit tests added for the Compatibility checker (checker unit suite). Integration smoke e2e added to run in CI staging: the test creates a sandbox namespace, applies a canary upgrade with MigrationPause CRD, exercises backup/restore sample verify, and validates that the installer respects the pause until the restore-verify step succeeds. CI: initial run had a flaky e2e due to timing in the fake-pg replica; flake fixed by retry/backoff in e2e harness. Final CI status: pass.

Migration/rollback story and operator experience: - Normal upgrade: installer runs preflight -> compatibility check passes -> helm upgrade runs -> migrations applied -> restore-verify hook executes -> finalization. - If compatibility check fails: installer aborts early and prints remediation hints and a generated remediation.yml with suggested steps. - If restore-verify fails during upgrade: rollout pauses and sets MigrationPause. Operator receives a short checklist via console/CLI with commands to collect debug artifacts and to trigger manual rollback or accept risk and continue. - For rollback safety: version-lockfile prevents accidental reapplication of mismatched charts/images; restore verification ensures backups are restorable before finalizing.

Checklist (what I did): - [x] Implement MigrationPause CRD and controller with default TTL and idempotency. - [x] Implement compatibility checker with Helm dry-run and schema dry-run. - [x] Add restore-verify helm hook and sample verification logic. - [x] Hook Terraform module to surface last-successful-snapshot metadata. - [x] Emit and consume version-lockfile during installer flow. - [x] Unit tests + e2e integration test in staging. - [x] Docs: upgrade-playbook and operator runbook.

Rollout plan: merge to main, ship alpha toggle (installer flag --enable-migration-pauser default false) for one week to low-traffic customers, exercise with Dedicated staging clusters, then flip default to enabled after validating no false-positives for two weekly upgrades.

Risks and mitigations: - False positives in schema dry-run: addressed by limiting to schema-only dry-run and sampling key tables; operators can opt out per-tenant. - Added complexity to installer flow: we gate the feature behind a flag and default TTL to avoid deadlocks. - Restore-verify runtime cost: verification works on a sample dataset by default; full restores still possible via manual path.

Related: ENG-8421 (upgrade incidents), ENG-9145 (restore resilience), SUP-3317 (customer report).
Aditi Rao: Please add an e2e for the case where the compatibility checker returns a false-positive; how can an operator override safely?
Author (Marisol): Added an operator override flag --force-continue with explicit interactive confirmation and an audit log entry. Also added an example remediation.yml describing safe follow-ups.
Benji Kim: The helm hook looks good but we should ensure post-install hooks don't extend PVC lifetime unexpectedly. Can we scope restore-verify to ephemeral PVCs?
Author: restore-verify uses ephemeral PVCs bound to the sandbox namespace and cleans up with finalizer; added a unit test to assert cleanup.
Lars Engel: Approve after minor docs clarification on TTL semantics.
Aditi Rao: Approve.
CI: one flaky e2e initially failed (timeout against fake-pg replica), retried and passed. All checks green. 
Adds installer safeguards for in-place migrations: MigrationPause CRD (operator pause points), compatibility preflight checker (helm + schema dry-run), restore-verify helm hook, and version-lockfile support. Feature gated behind --enable-migration-pauser. Recommended to enable in staging first.
If an upgrade is paused with MigrationPause set, do not manually delete the CRD until backups are validated. Use 'redwood-installer preflight --remediation <remediation.yml>' to get suggested steps. Contact Delivery if restore-verify indicates missing snapshots.

Motivation: Customers deploying Redwood Private across multiple AWS accounts often need Transit Gateway (TGW) attachments for cross-account control plane connectivity and a way to scope private DNS resolution to the control plane without exposing zones broadly. This PR automates TGW attachment creation and tidy delegation of a control-plane-scoped Private Hosted Zone via Route 53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints. It also tightens the security group model for control-plane endpoints to default-deny and only allow explicit CIDR/account attachments. Changes summary: 1) New Terraform module modules/networking/tgw/ that encapsulates TGW creation, cross-account attachment role document, and a lifecycle mode that supports create-only (for air-gapped upgrades) or reconcile. 2) Installer top-level deployment wiring to optionally enable tgw_attachments with a mapping of account IDs and attachmentopts. 3) Route53 automation: modules/dns/delegation.tf creates a control-plane PHZ with conditional delegation records, plus resolver rules and endpoint resources that are tied to the TGW attachment's route propagation. 4) Security: modules/sg/controlplane_sg.tf converts existing broad endpoint SGs into a least-privilege set with explicit ingress lists generated from the attachment map, and adds automated rotation hooks for SG references used by the control plane. 5) Helm chart values: values-private.yaml adds feature flags to toggle tgw and resolver automation per-environment. 6) Migration helper script scripts/terraform/migrate-tgw-attachments.sh to import existing TGW attachments and reconcile state with minimal downtime. Testing and validation: Unit-tested the TF modules with local terratest mocks, end-to-end validation in a staging account that simulates cross-account attach (recorded runbook attached). CI: plan/apply guard rails included; CI runs terraform fmt, validate and a mocked plan diff; end-to-end apply validated against a dedicated staging sandbox. Rollout plan: feature is behind the installer flag "enable_cross_account_tgw" and disabled by default; staged rollout recommended for customers with cross-account networking requisites. Rollback: the modules include an explicit variable to turn the lifecycle into "delete_on_disable" false by default; to rollback, flip the flag and run the provided migrate-tgw-attachments.sh to detach with tracked state. Security notes: cross-account IAM role created by the module is narrowly scoped to AttachVpc and RejectTransitGatewayVpcAttachment resources and requires an explicit acceptance token from the owner account. Related work: builds on ENG-988 and the private deployment DNS hardening initiative.
Arjun Patel: Please make the TGW attachment lifecycle idempotent for partial applies and add a note about transient route propagation delays.
Maya Chen: Added a retry loop in the attach helper and documented propagation caveats in README-ops.md.
Zoë Martínez: The resolver endpoint creation needs a deterministic name to avoid drift, suggested using a hash of account+region.
Maya Chen: Updated delegation.tf to compute a stable name and added terratest assertion for name stability.
Ethan Brooks: Confirmed that the IAM role only permits Attach/Accept and added an explicit deny for DeleteTransitGateway to be extra safe.
Maya Chen: Added the deny statement and an integration test that asserts missing permissions fail the attach step with clear diagnostics.
Feature: Optional automation to create cross-account Transit Gateway attachments and scoped control-plane private DNS delegation. Notes: Disabled by default, requires cross-account IAM cooperation and network routing review before enabling.

Context: Several on-prem / air-gapped Private installs reported Grafana coming up without any Redwood dashboards after install/upgrade because the offline bundle did not include the minimum-pack dashboard JSONs and Prometheus rules (SUP-49210, Slack thread: airgap-bundle-missing-grafana-dashboards). This PR updates the air-gap bundle build so the observability artifacts are shipped as first-class, versioned bundle contents. What changed: (1) add observability artifacts to the airgap bundle payload: Grafana dashboard bundle (runtime + control plane), Prometheus alerting/recording rules, and default log collector configs; (2) update the bundle manifest schema usage to explicitly list these artifacts under the 'artifacts' section with stable filenames and SHA256s; (3) wire extraction/install into post-unpack steps so upgrades can safely rehydrate dashboards/rules without requiring outbound fetches; (4) add a lightweight validation step in the bundle build pipeline to fail if any referenced observability artifact path is missing. Notes/constraints: No customer data is embedded; artifacts are static JSON/YAML shipped with the installer. This does not enable/disable observability components by default; it only ensures the offline bundle contains the required files when customers enable the minimum pack via Helm values. Backward compatibility: Existing bundle consumers continue to work; new manifest entries are additive. Follow-ups: noise tuning and runbook links live in the observability-pack rules PRs; this PR only handles packaging and offline delivery.
Fatima Noor (review): Can we confirm the bundle build does not attempt to fetch dashboards from the internet at build time? Air-gapped customers won’t have that option and our internal build sometimes runs in restricted networks too.
Connor O'Brien (author): Yep — all files are sourced from the repo under packaging/airgap/artifacts/observability. The build script only copies local files + computes sha256. I added a CI assertion to fail if any path is missing so we don’t silently produce an incomplete bundle.
Chloe Martin (review): Dashboard filenames: please keep them stable and versioned; Grafana provisioning can be sensitive if we rename on upgrades. Suggest prefixing with private-min-pack-v1-*.json and keeping a top-level index file optional.
Connor O'Brien (author): Done. Renamed to private-min-pack-v1-runtime.json, private-min-pack-v1-control-plane.json, and private-min-pack-v1-infra.json. Also updated the manifest entries so the artifact IDs are stable even if we add more dashboards later.
Kevin Osei (review - security): Log configs: please double-check we’re not shipping example configs that encourage logging request payloads by default. Also ensure the manifest doesn’t include anything that looks like a secret (tokens, endpoints).
Connor O'Brien (author): Good catch. The shipped collector config is the baseline redaction-safe config (no body logging; includes request_id and hashed tenant_id only). No endpoints/tokens in the repo artifacts — sinks are documented as placeholders only. Updated docs to explicitly call out that secrets must be provided via Kubernetes Secrets.
Rafael Mendes (review - SRE): Can we add a simple post-unpack check that surfaces a clear error if dashboards are missing? This would have saved us time in SUP-49210.
Connor O'Brien (author): Added installer/post_install/validate_bundle_contents.sh and wired it into the airgap smoke test. It fails fast with a list of missing artifact paths and points to the on-prem runbook section.
Diego Santos (review): Upgrade behavior: we should avoid overwriting customer-modified dashboards if they’ve edited them in-cluster. Are we writing into a separate directory that Helm picks up, vs pushing directly into Grafana via API?
Connor O'Brien (author): We only extract into the installer’s shared artifacts directory (used by Helm chart provisioning). We’re not pushing to Grafana APIs. Customer customization in-cluster remains their responsibility; our extracted bundle is treated as immutable inputs to provisioning.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Customers running private control planes in multi-AZ deployments asked for a safer, auditable path to rotate control-plane subnets and move PrivateLink/ENI endpoints with minimal per-request disruption. Existing approaches either required full cutovers (causing short traffic spikes) or manual operator steps that were error-prone. This change implements a label-driven subnet swap flow plus a conditional endpoint sticky-routing mechanism that keeps active control-plane connections pinned to existing endpoints while new allocations warm up, and only shifts DNS TTLs after healthy probes pass.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a label-based subnet claim mechanism in the Terraform modules: controlplane_subnet.claim_label and controlplane_subnet.swap_marker. Allows the installer to mark a new subnet as candidate and then flip ownership with a controlled window.
- Implements an endpoint sticky-router sidecar in the private controlplane Helm chart (kube-controller extension) that pins in-flight client sessions to the existing PrivateLink/ENI endpoint during rollout, falling back to the new endpoint only after graceful drain.
- Introduces a DNS migration helper: a small orchestration job (helm hook + installer runner) that performs health probes, reduces DNS TTL, and atomically updates Route53/Cloud DNS records only when probes succeed. Supports conditional TTL rollback on probe failures.
- Exposes installer flags for staged rollouts: --staged-subnet-swap, --endpoint-sticky-duration, --dns-conditional-migrate. These default to safe conservative values.
- Adds end-to-end acceptance tests and a canary job in CI that simulates a swap (with mocked ENI endpoints) to validate orchestration and failure recovery paths.

Design notes and constraints:
- The label-driven swap keeps resource names stable (no recreation of core control-plane instances) so customers with strict IP allowlists or external firewall mappings experience minimal churn.
- Sticky routing intentionally pins high-latency/long-lived requests to the old endpoint for up to endpoint-sticky-duration to avoid mid-request failures; short requests are routed according to policy to maximize cutover speed.
- DNS migration lowering TTL is best-effort; in some cross-account setups the authoritative DNS changes may be delayed. The job logs detailed diffs and writes a rollback marker if the migration does not meet the configured health thresholds within the timeout.

Checklist (implemented):
- [x] Terraform module: controlplane_subnet claims and swap_marker support
- [x] Helm chart: endpoint-sticky-router sidecar + configmaps
- [x] Installer CLI flags and validation logic
- [x] DNS migration orchestration job + rollback marker
- [x] CI acceptance test and canary workflow updates
- [x] Docs: installer README and upgrade notes

Commits (high level):
- feat(tf): add label_claim and swap_marker to controlplane subnet module
- feat(helm): add endpoint-sticky-router sidecar and config flags
- feat(installer): expose --staged-subnet-swap, validation, and rollout controller
- feat(dns): implement conditional-dns-migrate job and rollback marker logic
- test(ci): add canary acceptance job for staged swap scenario
- docs: describe rollout steps and recovery procedures

Files/areas changed (high-level):
- terraform/modules/controlplane_subnet/main.tf (add claim_label var, lifecycle guards)
- terraform/modules/controlplane_subnet/outputs.tf (swap_marker output)
- helm/controlplane/templates/sticky-router.yaml (new sidecar + service account)
- helm/controlplane/values.yaml (endpointSticky config)
- installer/cmd/rollout/swap.go (rollout controller and flags parsing)
- installer/internal/route53/migrator.go (conditional TTL migration + rollback)
- ci/workflows/canary-staged-swap.yml (canary test)
- test/acceptance/staged_swap_test.go (integration simulation)
- docs/installer/staged-subnet-swap.md (user-facing instructions)

Review conversation (highlights):
- Diego Alvarez (review): "This looks promising. Two safety asks: 1) can we gate the default behavior behind an explicit feature flag in releases, and 2) ensure IAM for the DNS migrator is least-privilege and auditable?"
- Author reply: "Added installer flags (disabled by default) and tightened IAM policy to only put-get-change records on the target hosted zone; also added CloudTrail note in docs."
- Mei Lin (review): "The sticky-router sidecar needs resource limits and health endpoints so kube can kill/restart it safely."
- Author reply: "Added resource requests/limits and a /healthz probe; updated Helm values to tune them."
- Omar Haddad (approval): "Verified test harness can simulate partial failures; LGTM after minor nits fixed."

- Integration canary: ran in CI with a mocked ENI endpoint cluster; highlighted one race where swap_marker wasn't set before DNS change — fixed by introducing a barrier step in swap.go
- Lint: terraform fmt/tflint, go vet, helm lint — all pass on final run

Rollout and migration instructions (for release / ops):
1) Enable feature with installer flag --staged-subnet-swap=true in a single region.
2) Provision candidate subnet (installer will label it with claim_label).
3) Wait for health checks and warm-up period.
4) Trigger swap controller (installer exposes a staged-swap subcommand).
5) Endpoint sticky-router will keep in-flight sessions bound; DNS migrator will lower TTL and run probes.
6) On successful probes, DNS migrator updates records and writes swap_marker to confirm completion.
7) If probes fail, migrator increases TTL back and the swap is aborted with rollback marker written; operator may investigate logs and retry.

Known limitations and future work:
- Cross-account DNS where RecordSet changes are proxied require separate delegation hooks; we added a TODO to support delegated-write flows.
- Multi-region simultaneous swaps are not supported in this PR; follow-up will add a global orchestration coordinator.
