Motivation: private control planes frequently suffer from stale or colliding subnet allocations and orphaned cross-account peering attachments after interrupted upgrades. This PR implements a subnet lifecycle manager and an automated peering cleanup + DNS propagation helper to make VPC provisioning and upgrades more resilient. Scope: terraform refactor + new module (controlplane/subnet-lifecycle), a small helm values change to surface the control-plane DNS config to the installer, a new reconciler job (gauntlet) run via the installer to garbage-collect stale VPC peering and push conditional Route53 delegation records for cross-account control plane discovery. Changes are backwards-compatible for existing installs; the reconciler can be enabled via helm/tf boolean and defaults to disabled in older clusters. Checklist: - [x] Terraform module and examples added - [x] End-to-end plan for safe rollout on existing customers (blue/green-style secondary subnets) - [x] Integration tests for peering cleanup in perf-canary - [x] Helm chart value + docs - [x] Smoke tested in staging with a multi-account setup Summary of behavior: - Subnet lifecycle module: provides deterministic tagging and an idempotent claim model for control plane subnets. When enabled the module will claim available subnets by tag, annotate Terraform state with claim metadata, and, when a reclaim is needed, create a replacement subnet before removing the old one to avoid downtime. - Peering cleanup reconciler: scans AWS for VPC peering connections tagged for 'redwood-controlplane', detects attachments that are in FAILED or DELETING states for >24h, and safely removes stale peering objects after validating that no active routes reference them. The reconciler also optionally reconciles route table propagation in cross-account setups via SSM-triggered cross-account lambda. - DNS propagation helper: when peering is created the installer now emits a controlled Route53 NS delegation template and can optionally create conditional forwarding via Route53 Resolver rules for cross-account lookup. The helper uses Alias records for the control-plane LB to avoid chasing IPs across peering. Rollout notes: - Default is disabled for existing installations. To enable, flip installer helm value controlPlane.subnetLifecycle.enabled or set terraform variable control_plane_subnet_lifecycle = true and run the 'subnet-claim' plan. - For CIDR rotation/upgrades, the module supports create-before-destroy with a transient attachment window. Operators should follow the included RUNBOOK for blue/green swap and DNS cutover. Related work: ties to ENG-1427 (subnet allocation hygiene) and SRE-88 (peering reliability incidents).
Liam Chen (review): The create_before_destroy in subnet resource looks good but we need to ensure route table reassociation is handled atomically. Please add unit tests for the reassociation path.
Aisha Thompson (author): Added a helper in aws/route53_helper.go to re-attach routes and updated integration test to cover reassociation.
Sofia Patel (security): Verify IAM least-privilege for the reconciler lambda. Can we avoid any wildcard iam:PassRole?
Aisha Thompson (author): Reconciler uses narrowly-scoped cross-account role ARNs passed in via terraform outputs; removed PassRole usage and documented the required policy in README.
Diego Morales (approver): Verified staging run against a 3-account setup; peering cleanup removed 2 stale attachments and did not touch active routes. Approved for merge.
Squash commit message: feat(installer): subnet lifecycle manager + peering cleanup + DNS propagation helper — 18 files changed, tested in staging. Manual roll-forward performed on 2026-02-21.
Added an optional subnet lifecycle manager that enables safe CIDR rotation and deterministic subnet claims. Added a reconciler that garbage-collects stale VPC peering attachments and a DNS propagation helper to automate conditional delegation for cross-account control planes. Feature is opt-in and disabled by default for existing installations.
Set helm value controlPlane.subnetLifecycle.enabled=true and run 'terraform apply' for the subnet-lifecycle module. Follow runbook to create transient secondary subnets, wait for traffic mirroring to steady-state, then perform DNS cutover. For peering cleanup enable reconciler only after confirming routes have stabilized.
Disable the reconciler and set terraform var control_plane_subnet_lifecycle=false. If a subnet was replaced, revert by runbook steps: reassign routes from the replacement back to the original and delete the replacement subnet. Contact SRE if the reconciler already cleaned up peers; we provide an audit log and reversible terraform plan in the runbook.
payload.title: Control plane subnet lifecycle manager + automated peering cleanup and DNS propagation

payload.body: Context: Customers running Redwood Private require stronger guarantees that customer-managed keys (CMKs) used during bootstrap are not accidentally re-scoped and that installer operations leave an immutable audit trail. This PR adds a KMS Escrow Assertion Validator to the private installer, hardens audit capture during bootstrap/migrations, and provides a non-disruptive migration path for existing installs. Motivation: recent customer reviews and an internal compliance audit highlighted two gaps: (1) the installer accepted KMS key ARNs/identifiers without validating provider assertions (origin, region, attributes), and (2) audit envelopes created during bootstrap could be mutated by post-install tooling. This PR addresses both issues to reduce blast radius and to meet SOC-like requirements for signed, append-only audit artifacts. Changes (high level): added a standalone validator component (installer/pkg/kms/validator.go) which verifies signed escrow assertions (provider fingerprint, region pin, tenant binding, timestamp, and nonce) against a configurable trust bundle; introduced an audit envelope signer and immutability flag (installer/pkg/audit/envelope.go) to ensure bootstrapping events are wrapped, signed (HSM/KMS), and stored append-only; extended the installer config schema and helm templates to accept trust bundles and audit retention policies; added a migration tool (installer/cmd/migrate-kms-assertions) that can scan existing installs and emit remediation suggestions without changing live resources by default. Checklist: - [x] assertion validator implementation + unit tests - [x] audit envelope signer + integration test harness - [x] helm values + docs updates - [x] migration tool + dry-run mode - [x] end-to-end smoke on GKE/AKS - [x] security review and threat model updated Commits summary: 1) initial validator scaffold and trust bundle parsing; 2) implement signature verification + region/tenant checks; 3) audit envelope signer + append-only writer; 4) helm/values + schema bump; 5) migration tool and dry-run; 6) tests, docs and bugfixes. Files changed (representative): installer/pkg/kms/validator.go, installer/pkg/kms/validator_test.go, installer/pkg/audit/envelope.go, installer/cmd/migrate-kms-assertions/main.go, charts/private-installer/values.yaml, charts/private-installer/templates/configmap.yaml, docs/private-installer/kms-escrow.md, scripts/e2e/smoke-kms-assertions.sh, scripts/ci/validation.yml, scripts/ci/integration-kms.yml, tools/trustbundle/generate.go, Makefile. Tests and CI: all CI pipelines passed on final run (unit, integration, e2e smoke). One flaky integration job (integration-kms) failed on first run due to ephemeral GKE quota; rerun passed. Security review: threat-model updated; recommended runtime KMS binding added to doc. Migration path and rollout notes: migration tool defaults to dry-run and emits remediation steps; operator must run with --apply to perform non-reversible changes. For installs that opt into enforcement mode (helm value kube.kms.enforceEscrow=true) the validator gates installer success and will fail fast on mismatch. Backwards compatibility: default install remains permissive (validator logs warnings) unless enforcement flag enabled. Rollout plan: soft rollout to internal staging by 2025-11-10, gradual enablement on customer canaries, disable enforcement by default for first two weeks while we gather telemetry. Rollback: helm can be used to disable enforcement flag; audit envelopes already written are append-only and preserved. Review conversation highlights: - Liam: "Overall looks good. Please add a test that simulates a wrong-provider assertion and ensure the migration tool reports it without applying changes." - Author: "Added validator_test.go with bad-assertion case and updated migration dry-run output to include remediation hints." - Sofia: "Need to ensure we surface a clear error message for ops when enforcement is enabled; current error string is too low-level." - Author: "Reworked error messages and added a grooming doc (docs/private-installer/kms-escrow.md#errors)." - Rohan: "Can we sign envelopes with either customer CMK or operator KMS?" - Author: "Yes — added selector logic and documented the trust model; default is operator-signed envelopes, customer CMK optional if provided and permitted by policy." Approvals and merge: after addressing comments the PR received approvals from all reviewers on 2025-11-18. CI green, security review completed; merged via squash on 2025-11-20. Release notes: "private-installer: add optional KMS assertion validator and signed, append-only audit envelopes for bootstrap; migration tool available in dry-run. Enforcement is opt-in via helm values (no behavior changes by default)." Impact and follow-ups: - Ops: recommend internal runbook update and canary enablement checklist in runbooks/ - SRE: add metric kms_validator.reject_count and audit.envelope.sign_latency to platform dashboards - Product: notify customers in security bulletin and provide migration guidance. Misc: no breaking API changes to installed services; installing with enforcement=true can fail boot if assertions are invalid (documented).
payload.title: Introduce KMS escrow assertion validator and audit hardening for private installs

Adds a centralized log shipping option (promtail -> S3 -> loki indexer) as an optional subchart to the private-installer Helm bundle, a terraform module to provision long-term object storage and Grafana workspace configuration, and a one-shot dashboard migration utility that performs a schema-safe migration of existing Grafana dashboards during upgrades. Motivation: customers deploying Private need a reliable, upgrade-safe path to connect cluster logs and persisted dashboards into the observability stack without manual intervention. This PR implements the Helm templates and values schema, the Terraform module that creates an S3-compatible bucket with lifecycle rules and IAM policy, a k8s Job-based migration runner that performs dashboard diffs and backouts, unit and e2e tests for the chart and migration tool, and documentation + an upgrade checklist. The description below summarizes commits, changed areas, CI outcomes, and review thread.
Customers requested minimal-ops observability onboarding for Private installs that survives upgrades and keeps dashboards consistent. Prior manual steps were error-prone during rolling upgrades and large dashboard diffs caused outages. This PR reduces operational burden by automating provisioning, safe migration, and providing rollback tooling.
- Optional Helm subchart for cluster log shipping (promtail -> S3 -> loki compatible indexer). - Terraform module to provision S3-compatible storage and Grafana workspace config. - Dashboard migration utility: dry-run, apply, and safe-backout modes. - Upgrade checklist and examples for Private deploys. - e2e tests for end-to-end validation.
Local chart unit tests via helm-unittest and schema validation added. e2e tests run in CI against a KinD cluster with mocked S3 gateway. Migration runner covered by integration test that exercises dry-run and apply paths.
Luis: Please ensure IAM policy generated by terraform restricts PUT only to the migration prefix and adds lifecycle rules to prevent infinite retention. Response: Updated module to accept prefix and lifecycle block, added example usage.
Priya: How will the migration handle dashboard UID changes and panel id collisions? Response: Migration runner computes a diff and will write to a backup namespace before applying; a --dry-run mode included and a safe-backout script is provided.
Owen: CI timeout on e2e test due to slow container startup. Response: increased pod readiness timeout and added retry logic to test harness; re-ran CI and all checks passed.
payload.title: add-central-log-shipper-and-dashboard-migration-tooling-for-private-installs

Motivation: customers deploying the private control plane have asked for deterministic, AZ-aware outbound egress controls, safer peering lifecycle handling across accounts, and explicit DNS forwarding validation so upgrades don't silently break service discovery. This PR adds stateful security-group templates for control-plane instances and pods (per-AZ naming and tags), introduces installer-managed peering lifecycle hooks to avoid stale peer routes during rolling upgrades, and adds a DNS TTL sanity check/opt-in forwarding policy. What changed: 1) terraform/modules/controlplane: new module 'sg_templates' that generates stateful SGs with deterministic names, per-az egress ip-pools annotation support, and KMS-encrypted tag metadata. 2) installer/hooks/peering-lifecycle: a small shell+py hook that runs after VPC create to accept peering across accounts when cross-account role is provided, and that performs safe teardown ordering during destroy. 3) helm/controlplane/values.yaml: new values.controlPlane.egress.policy and values.controlPlane.egress.azIpPools to enable AZ isolated egress. 4) terraform/roles: optional cross-account role and readme describing minimal IAM. 5) infra/route-policy: small module to toggle route propagation and attach deterministic route tables to controlplane subnets. 6) docs/upgrade-playbook.md: rollout guidance, canary checklist, and rollback steps. Checklist: [x] Terraform validate and fmt [x] Unit tests for hook scripts [x] Integration smoke test against minimal private deployment [x] Docs updated Release plan: merge to main, cut a private-installer release, stage to qa cluster with --set controlPlane.egress.policy=az-isolated then promote to staging. Backout: change policy to 'shared' and run peering teardown hook which will unroll routes in reverse-order. Usage notes: by default new behavior is opt-in via helm values.controlPlane.egress.policy, existing deployments continue unchanged until operator flips the flag. The peering accepter requires a cross-account role ARN in terraform/roles/README when peering across org boundaries. Quick example snippet: terraform module "controlplane" { source = "./modules/controlplane" control_plane_subnets = var.control_plane_subnets egress_policy = "az-isolated" peering_accepter_role_arn = var.peer_accepter_role_arn }
Diego Morales: Can we avoid hardcoding port ranges in the sg template? Please add a variable with sane defaults.
Asha Patel: Updated to expose egress_port_ranges with defaults; added unit tests to cover overrides.
Liam O'Connor: The peering hook looks good but we should make acceptance idempotent if retries happen during network flakiness.
Asha Patel: Hook is now idempotent and records accepter request IDs in state bucket; added retry with backoff.
Diego Morales: One minor nit on variable naming; otherwise approving pending CI.
CI: terraform-validate passed, unit-tests passed, integ smoke failed on first run (flaky e2e), rerun succeeded.
Liam O'Connor: Approved.

payload.body:
Motivation: Private deployments require reproducible, auditable TLS certificate rotation with least-privilege key usage. Operators currently perform manual cert updates using ad-hoc scripts; this creates downtime risk and audit gaps. This PR implements an automated rotation pipeline that ties together Kubernetes SealedSecrets, HashiCorp Vault (transit & PKI), and cloud KMS envelope keys, plus Terraform modules and Helm hooks to orchestrate upgrades and safe rollbacks.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a new Terraform submodule `secret-rotation` to provision KMS keys, Vault policies, and an auxiliary state bucket/lock for rotation metadata.
- Adds a Helm chart patch and lifecycle hooks for the installer that bootstrap sealed secrets and a rotation controller on upgrade-install.
- Introduces a rotation controller (lightweight Go binary) that: obtains new certs from Vault PKI, envelopes private keys with cloud KMS, seals resulting Kubernetes Secret using SealedSecrets controller, applies to cluster, and monitors readiness before switching ingresses.
- Migration tool: a one-shot job to convert existing unsealed TLS Secrets into SealedSecrets while recording previous keys for safe rollback.
- E2E harness updates: rotation acceptance test and canary rollout scenario in the perf-canary suite.

Checklist: 
- [x] Terraform plan + apply tested against staging account (uses mock KMS in CI)
- [x] Helm chart dry-run and post-install hook tested in KIND cluster
- [x] Migration job tested against staging clusters with old certs
- [x] RBAC tightened for controller (Minimal roles for writing SealedSecret and reading KMS/Vault)
- [x] Audit logs wire-up: Vault audit + KMS key use events documented

Design notes: 
- SealedSecrets are used as the canonical persisted resource; the rotation controller seals new keys and never stores unencrypted private keys in cluster state. 
- Vault PKI is the CA; the controller requests issuance and relies on Vault TTL/renewal endpoints. Private key material is envelope-encrypted with cloud KMS (envelope keys are managed by Terraform-created KMS keys). 
- Terraform module creates: KMS key (with rotation enabled), Vault policy for the controller, and a small S3/GCS bucket to hold rotation metadata (last-rotated, previous-key-id) with object-level ACLs.
- Helm hooks: pre-upgrade installs the migration job (if needed) and post-upgrade triggers the controller canary rollout for cert swap. Hooks are idempotent and have deadlines to avoid blocking installs.

Rollback & safety: 
- Every rotation stores the previous sealed secret and KMS ciphertext id in rotation metadata. The controller exposes an endpoint to initiate a rollback which re-applies the previous SealedSecret and swaps ingress TLS atomically.
- Canary flow: controller rotates a single ingress (or a percentage via weighted ingress) first, waits for health checks, then proceeds. Failures auto-revert using stored metadata.

Testing: 
- Added unit tests for envelope encryption and SealedSecrets pack/unpack. 
- New e2e test exercises full path: issue cert -> controller seals -> apply -> readiness -> rotate back.

Related: Linear ENG-3145, SRE-212; Support ticket SUP-1122 for customer migration request.

Notes on deployment: Run `terraform apply` for `secret-rotation` first, then upgrade installer chart with `--set rotation.enabled=true`. See notes_for_ops field for step-by-step.

This description contains the full set of changes, migration steps, and rollback procedures.

Miguel Ortiz: Requested change - ensure previous key material is retained in an immutable store and not garbage-collected immediately; add TTL-based GC with operator override.
Priya Nair: Reply - added rotation metadata bucket and GC policy in Terraform; operator override endpoint included in controller (see controller/ops.go).
Emily Chen: Comment - suggestion to split KMS provisioning into separate apply step for infra-only customers; implemented via optional module flag and documented deploy ordering.
Samir Patel: Approve with comment - please add one more e2e for cross-region KMS latency; filed follow-up ENG-3210.
Emily Chen: Approval - verified RBAC and Vault policy least-privilege in staging cluster; ready to merge.
Automated TLS certificate rotation for private installs: introduces a rotation controller that integrates Vault PKI, cloud KMS envelope encryption, SealedSecrets, Terraform modules for infra, and Helm hooks for safe upgrades. Includes migration tooling and rollback safety. Non-breaking; opt-in via rotation.enabled=true.
1) Apply terraform: cd terraform/modules/secret-rotation && terraform init && terraform apply -auto-approve
2) Upgrade installer Helm chart with: helm upgrade --install redwood-installer ./helm/installer -f values.yaml --set rotation.enabled=true
3) Monitor canary: controller exposes /health and /rotation-status; wait for canary success before full rollout.
4) To rollback a failed rotation: curl -XPOST -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://controller.example.internal/rollback?ingress=<name> -- the controller will re-apply stored sealed secret and swap ingress certs.
5) Ops should confirm KMS key policies and Vault audit are present; see docs/ops/rotation-runbook.md for troubleshooting.
payload.title: Automate TLS cert rotation via SealedSecrets + Vault + KMS; Helm & Terraform changes

payload.body:
Context: Private deployments require predictable, auditable upgrades. Operators need a way to validate schema migrations and backups before cutting over, and a robust automated path to roll back when an upgrade introduces incompatibilities. This PR introduces three coordinated safety primitives: 1) a migration dry-run mode that executes migrations against an ephemeral clone of state and produces a deterministic migration report; 2) Helm lifecycle hooks and installer-managed markers that enable atomic rollback paths if post-upgrade health checks fail; and 3) pre-upgrade backup capture and checksum verification integrated into the installer and the Terraform preflight. Goals: reduce upgrade-induced incidents, provide an operator-friendly verification step, and make automated rollback safe and auditable. What I changed (high level): - installer/commands: add `redwoodctl upgrade --dry-run` which 1) snapshots volumes (PVC or local) into a temporary clone, 2) spins up a migration sandbox using the same chart values but isolated k8s namespace, 3) runs the DB and index schema migrations against the clone, and 4) returns a migration report (SQL changes, estimated row touch, affected indices). - helm charts: add pre-upgrade hook templates (pre-upgrade-job, post-upgrade-validation) plus a rollback marker secret that the installer monitors. Charts include a new values flag `migrations.rollbackGuard.enabled`. - terraform modules: add an explicit state-lock-and-validate step for private deployments (Terraform run will now create a managed lock resource and run `terraform plan` with a validation pass against a cloned infra state when `upgrade_dry_run=true`). - backup/restore: the installer now captures a compressed backup and computes a SHA256 checksum; the dry-run compares checksum after clone/restore to confirm fidelity. - health checks and rollback: if the post-upgrade validation job fails, the installer will automatically trigger the Helm rollback and initiate a verified restore from the pre-upgrade backup. A failure path includes detailed logs and a fail-open option for emergency manual intervention. Checklist (implemented): [x] redwoodctl dry-run command and CLI UX [x] sandbox namespace orchestration + cleanup [x] Helm pre/post hooks and rollback marker secret [x] Backup capture (PVC snapshot or file-level tar) + SHA256 verification [x] Terraform validation + state lock resource [x] Integration test harness for dry-run path [x] Documentation for operators and runbooks How to exercise locally: 1) Build the installer binary: make build-installer 2) Create a development cluster and deploy a representative private deployment (see docs/quickstart-dev.md) 3) Run `redwoodctl upgrade --target-version vX.Y.Z --dry-run` 4) Inspect the generated report at /tmp/redwood-upgrade-report-<ts>.json and verify checksums 5) Try a simulated failing validation by toggling `migrations.postUpgradeValidation.failOn=true` in the chart values to force a rollback Notes on safety and design choices: - The dry-run uses an isolated namespace and ephemeral PVCs so production workloads are not affected. - We rely on storage provider snapshot semantics when available, otherwise we fall back to file-level tar+rsync. - Migration dry-run is intended to be deterministic; it records SQL statements and row counts observed in the sandbox, but operators should still run smoke tests against application behavior. - Automatic rollback is conservative: we only rollback if the validation job exits non-zero and the rollback marker secret has not been manually cleared. - Terraform changes are additive and introduce a managed lock resource; no mutable provider behavior is required. Risks and mitigations: - Long-running dry-runs may increase I/O load on shared storage: dry-run can be scoped to specific services via flags. - Storage providers without snapshot support will have slower clone times: documented fallback and operator warnings added. - False positives in validation: validation job logs are retained for 7 days and include re-run commands to reproduce the failure. Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main behind feature flag default-off 2) Dogfood on internal staging private cluster for 2 weeks 3) Gradual opt-in for customer upgrades via support-assisted channels 4) Promote to default for all private deployments after 30 days and no regression incidents Metrics to monitor post-release: - % of upgrades that used dry-run mode - Frequency of automatic rollbacks and root cause categorization - Time for dry-run + sandbox cleanup - Backup verification failure rate Related work: ENG-2178 (schema-versioning), infra/terraform#402 (state-lock work), docs/ops-runbooks#39 (runbook additions).
Diego Morales: Please add a short timeout and retry policy for the validation job; long waits in CI caused flaky failures. (addressed)
Lina Chen: Can we make the checksum algorithm configurable? In air-gapped installs some customers have policy requirements. (we added a config and default to sha256)
Owen Baker: Confirmed terraform changes do not require provider upgrades; ran module tests against 0.15 and 0.16 (LGTM)
Aisha Patel (author): replied to Diego with an additional retry loop and an exponential backoff; replied to Lina with docs for configuring checksum algorithm in values and terraform variables.
Added `redwoodctl upgrade --dry-run` to validate migrations and backups before production cutover.
Installer will capture a pre-upgrade backup and verify checksum before performing upgrade; automatic rollback on validation failure is now supported (opt-in behind chart flag).
Terraform modules include an optional managed state lock and plan validation step for safer upgrades.
payload.title: Add migration dry-run, atomic rollback hooks, and pre-upgrade backup verification

payload.body:
Adds vendor partitioning and distro-specific preflight profiles. Operators can opt into partitioned bundles to reduce airgap bundle sizes and speed up upgrades. Includes helm/terraform helpers and rollback safety checks.
Motivation: air-gapped/private installs at large customers continue to balloon in size because vendor bundles include all distro overlays and optional modules. This PR introduces 'vendor partitioning' — a deterministic layout that splits an offline bundle into: base-runtime, distro-overlay/<distro>, optional-modules/<name>. Partitioning reduces snapshot sizes and allows targeted delta application during upgrades.

What this PR does (single-string summary):
- Adds a partitioner that computes a deterministic, signed index for offline bundles (ordering + checksums).
- Introduces distro-aware preflight profiles that run lightweight probes and kernel/config checks before applying an overlay. Profiles are authored as small YAMLs under installer/preflight/profiles/*.
- Adds an atomic delta-applier that applies partitions in a safe order with checkpoints and idempotent rollback markers.
- Helm chart changes: offline preflight Job, a new hook for staged overlay apply, and a post-install verification hook.
- Terraform module updates: registry seeding helpers (local registry init), a new variable to control partitioned-seeding, and provider validation.
- Rollback tooling: partial-rollback controller that can revert only the last applied partition when a failure is detected, preserving previously applied overlays.

Checklist (for reviewers and operators):
- [x] Unit tests for partitioner checksum and ordering logic.
- [x] End-to-end airgap integration test that seeds a local registry and validates staged apply/rollback.
- [x] Terraform validate + plan tests for the registry module.
- [x] Manual smoke on k3s and RKE2 (see test notes).

Migration notes: existing sealed bundles remain compatible. Operators that opt into partitioning will need to re-generate the offline bundle with `installer tools bundle partition --profile <profile-name>`; the CLI supports a `--compat` flag to emit a single combined bundle for older toolchains. The preflight profiles are additive and won't run unless referenced in the install configuration.

Security notes: the partition index is signed with the existing bundle signing key (same key family used for full-bundles). We added signature verification to the apply path and fail-safe behavior that prevents partial applies if the signature verification fails. Audit logs emit partition-level events for traceability.

Related: ENG-1423 (bundle size reductions), ENG-1429 (safe upgrades), SUP-620 (customer incident that motivated partial rollback).

Backwards compatibility: no breaking API changes to the installer control plane. Helm values add an opt-in `partitioning.enabled` boolean. Default remains false to avoid surprising existing customers.
To opt-in: regenerate bundles with `installer tools bundle partition --profile rke2 --sign-key /path/to/key` and set helm value `partitioning.enabled=true`. Motivation: customers running fully air-gapped Private deployments reported two recurring pain points: (1) manual kubelet/node provisioning steps that vary by distro, and (2) brittle offline registry mirroring that broke during incremental upgrades. This PR delivers: 1) a cross-distro kubelet provisioning helper that generates systemd unit snippets + containerd mirror configs from the airgap catalog and injects them into the node bootstrap bundle; 2) an OCI registry mirror manifest generator that produces deterministic image manifest lists and mirror index files so mirror replication can be validated offline; 3) a reproducible delta-bundle generator that emits compact binary diffs between runtime release bundles to reduce s3/usb transfer sizes and speed upgrades in low-bandwidth datacenters; 4) an upgrade/rollback hook that stages kubelet config changes and can atomically swap systemd unit drop-ins to avoid mid-upgrade kubelet restarts. Changes are guarded behind the new installer flag --airgap-kubelet-mirror. Backwards compatibility: installers that don't enable the flag see no change in bundle layout. Safety: all generated artifacts are signed with the installer GPG key and the installer now emits a verification manifest with sha256 sums of each artifact. Checklist: - [x] unit tests for manifest generator - [x] integration smoke test with k3s and rke2 bundles - [x] installer e2e in airgapped CI matrix - [x] upgrade/rollback scenario tested on VM lab. Known limitations: kubelet helper currently supports systemd-based distros (Ubuntu/Fedora/RHEL/CentOS/Alma) and containerd; non-systemd distros will fallback to a documented manual step. See ENG-4783 for next steps (non-systemd support, Windows nodes). Deployment notes: operators must add the generated mirror index to their private registry seed; rollback is automatic only if the generated delta patch applies cleanly. Links: runway doc https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4783/airgap-kubelet-mirroring, internal S3 bucket path s3://airgap-builds/delta/2024-10-12/.
Ethan Park: The deterministic ordering in mirror-index looks good, but can you add an explicit 'build_epoch' field so downstream validators can detect reproducible builds?
Maya Chen (author): Added build_epoch as an int64 to mirror_index and updated verification manifest; kept timestamp truncation to seconds to avoid drift during replication.

Motivation: Private deployments need a safer, operator-driven way to perform schema migrations and rollbacks across multi-tenant clusters. Previous upgrades occasionally left clusters in a state where a naive downgrade could break tenant DB schemas or leave a partial logical replication setup. This PR introduces (1) an interactive safepoint API exposed by the operator to mark tenant migration safepoints, (2) a rollback-fence that prevents downgrades when incompatible schema delta exists, and (3) a set of Helm and Terraform guard checks to ensure plan/upgrade parity before applying changes.

Summary of changes (single-line): interactive safepoint operator API, rollback-fence enforcement, helm preflight hook to quiesce workloads, timeline-aware postgres snapshotter and restore verifier, terraform state version gate.

Checklist (for merge):
- [x] Operator: add Safepoint CRD + controller to record migration checkpoints and upstream WAL position
- [x] Installer: implement rollback-fence logic that reads last safepoint and schema-compat index
- [x] Helm chart: add pre-upgrade hook that quiesces user-facing processes and snapshots logical replication slots
- [x] Terraform: add plan-time check that validates cluster manifest hash and fails apply if state version mismatches
- [x] E2E: add integration test that performs upgrade -> set safepoint -> simulate downgrade attempt -> assert fence blocks downgrade
- [x] Docs: write runbook for interactive safepoint operations and emergency rollback flow

Detailed description: The operator now exposes a new CRD called RedwoodMigrationSafepoint which operators (or the CLI) can create to mark a tenant-aware migration checkpoint. Each safepoint records a cluster-scoped manifest hash, postgres timeline ID, LSN, and an optional human message. The safepoint is written atomically and also persisted to the installer metadata store. During upgrades, the operator will record an automatic pre-migration safepoint (when enabled) and annotate it into the release metadata. The rollback-fence consults the latest safepoint and a lightweight schema-compatibility index (stored as a manifest label) before permitting any Helm/Terraform-driven downgrade. If the fence detects a schema delta that cannot be auto-downgraded, it rejects the operation with an actionable error and links to the runbook.

Helm changes: added hooks/ pre-upgrade-job.yaml which calls operator apis: operatorctl quiesce --release <release> --timeout 5m and operatorctl snapshot --tenant <tenant> to produce a consistent logical snapshot. Hook is non-blocking by default but can be forced via values: preflight.quiesce=true. Also added post-rollback-validation hook that waits for WAL replay and checksum verification.

Terraform changes: new module variable manifest_lock_hash and pre-apply validation that calls the installer API for expected state. A sentinel file is written to the cluster object store as a short-lived plan-lease; terraform apply will fail if another active plan-lease exists or if the manifest hash differs. This prevents divergent state.apply sequences across CI and manual runs.

Postgres snapshotter & restore: add timeline-aware logical snapshotter which captures timeline ID and LSN alongside snapshot tarball. Restore verifier replays WAL up to the LSN and then runs a fast integrity check (row counts + schema checksums) for configured critical tables. The restore path includes a --dry-verify mode for customers to run a low-risk restore verification before committing.

Runbook & UX: documented operator CLI verbs: safepoint create/list/delete, operatorctl fence-status, operatorctl force-unlock (requires 2 approvals). The runbook includes step-by-step rollback example: create safepoint -> take snapshot -> attempt downgrade (blocked) -> follow remediation steps (roll-forward migration, rollback gate rescue).

Commits (high-level):
- Add RedwoodMigrationSafepoint CRD and controller scaffolding
- Implement safepoint persistence and manifest-hash annotation
- Add rollback-fence service and API endpoints
- Helm: pre-upgrade quiesce hook + post-rollback verifier
- Terraform: plan-lease & manifest-hash preflight check
- Postgres: timeline-aware snapshotter and WAL replay verifier
- Tests: e2e upgrade/downgrade integration and unit tests for fence logic

Changed areas (representative files):
- operator/api/v1alpha1/migration_safepoint.go
- operator/controllers/safepoint_controller.go
- installer/services/rollback_fence.go
- helm/redwood/templates/hooks/pre-upgrade-quiesce-job.yaml
- helm/redwood/templates/hooks/post-rollback-verify-job.yaml
- terraform/modules/cluster/main.tf (plan-lease check helper)
Luis Martinez (reviewer): Can the safepoint be auto-rotated to avoid unbounded metadata growth? Suggest TTL with a configurable retention policy.
Author (Anjali): Added retention config with default 90 days and an operator GC job. See safepoint_retention_days in values.schema.json
Priya Natarajan (reviewer): The terraform plan-lease is great — what happens on CI flakes where a lease is left behind? Need a reclaim path.
Author (Anjali): Implemented a reclaim API that requires two operator approvers to force-reclaim a stale lease; documented in the runbook and protected behind RBAC. Tests added.
Ethan Zhao (reviewer): Postgres restore verifier is expensive for large tables — can we provide a fast checksum sample mode?
Author (Anjali): Added --verify-sample-percent (default 1%) to verifier and a config to whitelist critical tables for full checks. See docs.
CI Bot: Integration tests passed on run #3 (flaky network retry), all checks green.
Luis Martinez: Approving with comments. Priya: LGTM. Ethan: Approve.
Adds operator-backed migration safepoints and a rollback fence to prevent unsafe downgrades. Includes Helm pre-upgrade quiesce hooks, timeline-aware Postgres snapshotter and restore verifier, and Terraform plan-lease guard. Provides runbook and CLI verbs for interactive safepoint management.
If a customer is blocked by the rollback-fence, follow runbook: 1) request safepoint export (operatorctl safepoint list), 2) validate snapshot integrity via dry-verify, 3) either roll-forward the migration or request a two-approver force-unlock. Support should record manifest_hash and safepoint LSN when filing SUP tickets.

Motivation: private installs observed significant Prometheus downtime during control-plane upgrades in customers with large TSDBs. Existing solutions (full snapshot + restore or blue/green shims) are heavy and error-prone in air-gapped environments. This PR introduces an incremental snapshot-and-restore flow for Prometheus plus Helm prechecks to avoid stateful data-loss and reduce manual intervention.

What this PR does: Adds a small controller (implemented as a Kubernetes Job + helper scripts deployed via Helm hooks) to take incremental TSDB snapshots before an upgrade, push artifacts to the configured object store (S3/GCS-compatible or local blob store), and perform a validated restore to a warm replica if the primary fails during the upgrade. Introduces a Helm precheck job that runs before observable upgrades to validate storage access, retention settings, WAL size heuristics, and available disk. Adds a terraform variable and installer flag (observability.incremental_prom_snapshot = true) to enable the flow for customers who opt-in.

High level components changed: 1) Helm charts: new charts/observability/operators/prom-snap-operator with preinstall/postupgrade hooks; 2) Installer: terraform/modules/observability/main.tf adds blobstore credentials and lifecycle-managed bucket creation when available; 3) Documentation: docs/observability/upgrade-playbooks.md with step-by-step runbooks and failure modes; 4) CI: test/integration/observability/upgrade-sim.sh to validate snapshot/restore in CI; 5) RBAC: minimal serviceaccount/rolebinding for operator jobs.

Design notes: - Incremental snapshots rely on Prometheus TSDB snapshot plus WAL segment copy for faster restores. We prefer incremental when bucket storage and retention are configured. - The operator is intentionally transient: it runs as a Job and cleans up snapshots > configurable retention. No long-lived controller required to keep the installer footprint small. - Helm prechecks fail fast (non-blocking when flag disabled). For air-gapped installs the precheck also validates local blobstore endpoints and certificate trust.

Backwards compatibility & opt-in: The flow is opt-in and defaults to false. Without the flag, installer behavior is unchanged. The Helm charts include templates that are no-ops unless the flag is set.

Testing performed: - Local integration: simulated 3-node Prometheus cluster; performed incremental snapshots and validated WAL re-attach and TSDB consistency after restore. - CI: added upgrade-sim.sh that runs in k8s-in-docker runner to exercise prechecks and snapshot/restore. - Tested with a mocked S3 endpoint to ensure airgapped TLS behavior is respected.

Operational runbook summary (also in docs): 1) Enable flag and run terraform apply. 2) Initiate upgrade; Helm precheck runs automatically. 3) If precheck passes, snapshot job runs and uploads incremental artifacts. 4) During upgrade, if the primary becomes unhealthy, operator triggers restore to warm replica. 5) After rollout, snapshots older than retention are garbage-collected.

Security considerations: credentials for blobstore are provisioned via installer secrets and never logged. Jobs run with minimal RBAC. Snapshots are encrypted at rest when the target supports server-side encryption.

Why this is unique: focuses on incremental (not full) snapshots, minimal transient operator, and explicit Helm precheck integration to reduce upgrade blast radius for private clusters where manual operator interventions are hard.

Checklist:
- [x] Helm templates and hooks
- [x] Terraform module opt-in flag and minimal bucket provisioning
- [x] Integration tests and CI job
- [x] Runbook + docs
- [x] Security review (credential handling, RBAC)

Add an incremental Prometheus snapshot & restore operator plus a Helm preflight check for observability components to reduce downtime during private-cluster upgrades. Backward compatible; optional feature gated behind installer flag.
Ethan Blake: Please split the precheck into a small script and move heavy validation to optional mode; installer runs must stay fast.
Priya Sharma: Done. Precheck now has a fast 'core' mode that runs by default and a deferred 'deep' check you can enable separately. I split the script under charts/observability/precheck/ and added a timeout to the helm hook.
Marta Lindqvist: How do we handle partial uploads if connection drops? We need idempotency or resume support.
Priya Sharma: The upload uses an idempotent artifact key (cluster/tsdb/incremental/<snapshot-id>). A partial multipart upload is aborted and retried by the job; we added exponential backoff and a final integrity check (size + md5).
Tao Chen: CI flaked once on restore; I saw a race between job cleanup and restore attach.
Priya Sharma: Fixed by adding a lock file and a small wait loop in the restore script; retest shows stable behavior. Added an integration test to reproduce the race in CI.
Ethan Blake: Approving after minor nit fixes were applied.
Marta Lindqvist: Approved (tested locally with mocked S3).
Tao Chen: Approved and verified helm hook ordering is correct for upgrades.

payload.body:
Motivation: Restores in private deployments occasionally collide with tenant activities (cron jobs, operator reconciliation) which can corrupt state if multiple restore attempts overlap. We need a low-friction guard that: (1) prevents concurrent restores inside the same tenant namespace, (2) makes restore operators idempotent so retries are safe, and (3) exposes short-lived fencing state for operator visibility and automation.

Summary: This PR introduces a namespace-level fencing CR annotation + a small lock controller used by the installer/restore controller. It also adds idempotency helpers for the restore flow (idempotency key generation, checkpoint markers, and safe-apply helpers). Helm chart changes wire the controller as a sidecar for the restore job; Terraform outputs include a new IAM role grant used for optional external locker backends.

What changed (high level):
- installer/restore/idempotency.go: helper functions to create idempotency keys, write idempotency checkpoints to S3-compatible object store, and verify replayability.
- controllers/namespace-fence/fence-controller.go: small controller that sets/clears the annotation and exposes fence status via a status subresource.
- helm/private/templates/restore-job.yaml: add fence sidecar container and env flags to enable idempotency checkpoints.
- docs/private/restore-runbook.md: updated runbook with new operator signals and step-by-step recovery flow.
- terraform/modules/installer/outputs.tf: export optional role/account for external lock plugins.
- e2e/tests/restore_fence_test.go: new tests that validate single-namespace fences and concurrent restore retry semantics.

Backwards compatibility: The fence is opt-in by default (installer flag enableNamespaceFence=false). When enabled the restore controller will acquire a fence annotation and fail fast if the namespace is already fenced. Operators upgrading from earlier releases without the flag will not change behavior.

Testing performed: unit tests for idempotency helpers (local mock S3), controller unit tests (fake client), and e2e that runs two parallel restores and verifies the second waits and then picks up the idempotency checkpoint rather than reapplying partial state. CI: all checks passed, including helm lint, go vet, unit tests and e2e smoke (see CI summary below).

Upgrade & rollback notes: Administrators can enable the fence feature via installer flag or Helm value. During rollback to older installer, fence annotations are tolerated (controller will be missing) — the runbook documents safe removal: clear fence annotations and delete any in-flight checkpoint objects. If a restore fails mid-flight, operator can re-run with the same idempotency key (exposed in restore controller logs) to resume.

Operational considerations: we added a short TTL (default 30m) for fences so a stuck controller won't lock namespaces indefinitely; long-running restores should extend the fence. The PR includes Prometheus metrics for fence_acquire_total and fence_held_seconds for alerting.

Related: ENG-9142 for orchestration cadence, SUP-7782 for incident notes where overlap caused data churn.

Checklist:
- [x] unit tests added
- [x] e2e test for concurrent restores
- [x] helm chart entries and linting
- [x] docs updated (runbook)
- [x] release notes entry

Liu Chen (requested changes): Please add a short TTL and a metric for fence duration — otherwise operators can be left with lingering fences. Refer to our SLO playbook for alert thresholds.
Author (Asha Mehta): Added TTL config and fence_held_seconds metric in follow-up commit d1c8a9e. PTAL.
Tomás Rivera (approved): Verified e2e reproduces prior failure modes and validated that the second restore resumes from checkpointed state.
Priya Kapoor (approved): Helm changes look good; confirmed values default to disabled so upgrade is non-disruptive.
Add optional namespace fencing for private restores to prevent concurrent restores from colliding.
Introduce idempotency helpers to allow safe restore retries and resume semantics.
Expose fence metrics for alerting and a short default TTL to avoid stuck locks.

payload.body:
Problem: Customers operating air-gapped / restricted VPC Private deployments need a safe, auditable path to swap the cluster KMS key material to an externally-managed HSM/KMS without downtime. Existing rotation approaches require cluster-wide restarts or manual Vault rewraps. This PR introduces a 'sideload proxy' pattern plus staged SealedSecrets switchover to enable an out-of-band key promotion with deterministic rollback.
Design summary: The sideload proxy accepts encrypted key material from an out-of-band operator (on-prem HSM or cloud KMS) over a mutually authenticated channel. The proxy performs envelope unwrap using the target KMS and exposes a read-only KMS binding to in-cluster components for a configurable grace window. The staged switchover uses SealedSecrets 'double-reencrypt' pattern: 1) create new sealed secrets using the new KMS key material in a 'shadow' namespace, 2) run health probes against the shadow-backed workloads, 3) flip annotation 'sealedsecrets.redwood.ai/active-sideload' which triggers controller to atomically switch mounts/config maps to new secrets, 4) keep the old key material pinned for a configurable rollback window. Safety features: opt-in annotation, 120s confirmation window, audit events logged to Vault/HSM audit backend, enforced HSM key policy check, and terraform null_resource preflight validations. Migration path: terraform plan will create binding resources and register a migration job; operator runs 'make migrate-kms --dry-run' to validate; when ready, set helm values.sideloadProxy.enabled=true and annotate namespace with 'sealedsecrets.redwood.ai/prepare-switchover=true' to stage. Docs and runbook included.
Add: KMS sideload proxy controller to enable out-of-band KMS key promotion; Add: Helm chart flags (sideloadProxy.enabled, switchover.dryRun) and SealedSecrets staged-switchover job; Add: Terraform kms-migration module with safe rollback hooks. Note: default behavior is disabled; operator must opt-in via Helm values and resource annotations.
Unit tests for controller logic and mock KMS were added. Integration e2e covers full migration (dry-run, stage, activate, rollback). Local manual validation steps included in docs. CI matrix runs with and without sealed-secrets-controller v0.19+.
Risk: accidental promotion or partial swap leading to drift. Mitigation: opt-in annotation, 2-minute confirmation window, audit logs, compatibility tests, and an automated rollback command. Risk: timing/flaky e2e on low-RPS clusters; mitigation: controller retries and readiness probe tuning.
Operators must ensure HSM/KMS endpoint certs are trusted by the sideload proxy; if using cloud KMS, ensure service account has 'decrypt' and 'wrapKey' permissions. The terraform module creates an IAM binding which must be pre-approved in restricted environments.
Marco: asked for a stronger safety guard around the 'activate' path to avoid accidental promotion (requested an opt-in annotation and a 2-minute confirmation window). Priya: implemented the annotation and added controller-level deterministic timers + audit event emission. Evelyn: requested clearer rollback docs and a scripted rollback target in the terraform module; added terraform null_resource hooks and a documented dry-run mode. Samir: raised question about sealedsecrets controller compatibility; added an adapter test and compatibility matrix. CI: initial integration e2e failed due to timing flakiness in the job; increased readiness probes and added retry logic, reran and all checks passed. Final signoffs from Marco and Evelyn with "approved with comments" and Samir gave an explicit LGTM.
payload.title: Introduce KMS sideload proxy and staged SealedSecrets switchover

Motivation: Private deployments need predictable, auditable updates and safe rollback paths for clusters that cannot reach our hosted control plane. This PR adds a compact delta artifact signing flow and an automated rollback-plan generator that: 1) produces per-release delta bundles (tar.gz deltas + provenance metadata), 2) signs delta manifests with our KMS-backed signing key, 3) generates a machine-readable rollback plan (instructions + required artifacts) for every release bundle, and 4) exposes Terraform-friendly outputs so on-prem upgrade orchestrators can fetch verified deltas and apply rollbacks without live API access. This is intended to reduce bandwidth for upgrades, accelerate patch creation, and give operators clear, auditable rollback instructions.
5 commits: (1) build: add delta bundler and provenance schema; (2) security: integrate KMS signing helper and rotation hooks; (3) tooling: rollback-plan generator and YAML schema; (4) terraform: exports to module outputs + example usage; (5) tests: add CI validations and e2e smoke for apply/rollback flow.

- installer/pkg/provenance/schema/v1.proto (new) -- compact provenance schema for deltas
- installer/pkg/signer/kms_helper.go (modified) -- new SignDelta function and key rotation hook
- installer/tools/rollbackplan/generator.py (new) -- creates rollback-plan.yaml for a given release bundle
- helm-charts/redwood-private/values-rollback.yaml (new example) -- integrates rollback plan reference

- ci/release/delta_pipeline.yml (modified) -- new pipeline stage for delta bundles, signing, and plan publish
- tests/e2e/priv-installer/delta_apply_test.sh (new) -- smoke apply/rollback verification
- docs/priv-installer/release-deltas.md (new) -- operator guide for applying deltas and rollbacks

Ava Martinez: Updated proto and added a version field, kept backward compat.
Maya Singh: Question about KMS permission model; can the signer run as a short-lived task?
Ava Martinez: Yes — added rotation hooks and IAM role example in docs; changed signer to use STS-assumed credentials with limited lifetime.
Liam O'Connor: CI flake on e2e script, suggested mocking remote artifact registry for unit tests.
Ava Martinez: Added mocked registry tests and re-ran CI.

Maya Singh: Approved.

Maintainer (Cecilia Hart): Squash-merged after CI green and 2 approvers.
- Added delta artifacts: smaller patches for private-installer upgrades.
- Signed delta manifests (KMS-backed).
- Automatic rollback-plan generator that produces a machine-readable YAML plan per release.
- Terraform module outputs for delta/rollback URLs to integrate with on-prem orchestrators.
- New CI pipeline stage to build, sign, and publish delta bundles.
Unit tests: signer, proto serialization, generator logic. Integration: mocked registry tests for publish/verify. E2E smoke: KinD cluster apply and stepwise rollback using generated rollback-plan.yaml. Manual validation steps included in docs/priv-installer/release-deltas.md.
Operator flow (summary): 1) Download release bundle + delta_manifest.json and rollback-plan.yaml from the artifact registry URL exported by Terraform. 2) Verify signatures with provided public key (cosign or built-in verifier). 3) Apply delta in 'staged' mode and run health probes. 4) If probe fails, run rollback-plan steps in order (plan includes exact artifact URLs and preflight commands). 5) For emergency offline rollback, apply artifacts from signed offline mirror following the same verification steps.
Risk: operators may accidentally apply an incompatible delta. Mitigation: delta bundler emits a compatibility matrix and verifier refuses mismatched release_version or incompatible-kernel markers; CI also runs cross-version smoke tests. Risk: signing key compromise. Mitigation: rotation hooks, limited-scope signer role, and short-lived credentials documented.

Motivation and summary: This PR enhances the private installer airgap tooling to support atomic registry synchronization semantics and adds first-class output for Flatcar Container Linux and k3OS targets. Customers running immutable-rootfs distributions and appliance-like nodes have been running into partial-pull failures and excessive disk usage during large bundle installs. The new atomic registry-sync produces a transactionally-applied set of image layers and metadata on the mirror registry so installs either complete successfully or leave the mirror unchanged.

What changed: - New binary 'airgap-regsync' (go) which performs: pull -> verify -> push to mirror -> commit marker. It uses a two-phase commit marker file in the mirror registry metadata namespace to ensure consumers only see completed syncs. - Image set minimizer: computes the minimal image layer subset needed for a requested release (uses manifest diffing across stable/runtime images) to drastically shrink bundle size for constrained networks. - OS-specific manifests: templates and hooks for Flatcar and k3OS that handle overlayfs/immutable root constraints, systemd unit changes, and container runtime config adjustments (containerd snapshotter flags). - Terraform module updates: redwood-terraform/mirror now exposes variables for commit-marker TTL, blob GC window, and registry object prefixes so infra teams can configure multi-repo mirrors. - Installer preflight checks: ensures enough image cache space, verifies kernel cmdline flags required by k3OS/Flatcar, and validates that the target mirror implements blob range requests (for partial layer resume). - Rollback safety: the installer will roll back mirror pointer on failed post-install hooks and will trigger GC-unpublished for orphan layer cleanup.

Context: Private deployments need safer upgrade paths that work in air-gapped environments and with operator-managed Terraform state. This PR adds an offline migration planner (CLI) and a Terraform state verification step to the installer to reduce rollback blast radius and make post-upgrade verification deterministic. Motivation: Operators have asked for a reproducible, reviewable migration plan that can be generated without cluster access (for change boards) plus a verification step that validates the target infrastructure state matches the expected release manifest before the helm release proceeds. Summary of changes (high level): 1) migration/planner: new CLI tool 'rwi-migrate-plan' that produces a compact plan artifact (JSON + SHA256) describing upgrade steps, DB migration sequence, expected CRD/CR changes, and a dry-run summary. The planner can run against manifests only (offline) or against a live cluster. 2) installer/terraform: terraform verify hook added that compares remote terraform state (when reachable) or local plan file against the release lockfile; it fails-fast on drift > 0.1% of resources (configurable). 3) helm: pre-upgrade hook to store a 'release-lock' ConfigMap with release hash and allowed-rollback flag; operator flows set allowed-rollback=false by default for major schema changes. 4) migrations: migration manifests now include a step-level 'check' command and an idempotency token so retries are safe. 5) tests: added unit tests for planner serialization and an integration smoke test that validates a blueprint upgrade from v1.4.3 -> v1.5.0 in CI Docker environment. Checklist: - [x] CLI planner implementation and help docs - [x] Terraform verify module + config flag - [x] Helm release-lock pre-upgrade hook - [x] Migration step idempotency tokens - [x] Unit tests and lightweight CI integration - [x] Linear references and internal docs Updates/commits (summary): - commit 1: add migration planner binary + docs + example plan export - commit 2: terraform: add verify module, config option 'terraform_verify_threshold' - commit 3: helm: release-lock ConfigMap and pre-upgrade hook, update templates - commit 4: installer: wire up planner as optional preflight step and add CLI flags - commit 5: tests: add planner unit tests and integration smoke harness Files changed (high level): - migration/planner/* (new files): main.go, plan.go, serializer.go, README.md - installer/cmd/preflight.go: call planner when --dry-plan specified - terraform/modules/verify/main.tf: new module for state comparison - helm/charts/redwood/templates/release-lock-configmap.yaml: new template - charts/templates/hooks/pre-upgrade-release-lock.yaml: new hook - migrations/*.yaml: added 'idempotency_token' and 'check' fields - test/integration/smoke/blueprint-upgrade.sh: new CI smoke script Example snippet (planner export skeleton): '{"plan_version":"1","steps":[{"id":"db-001","kind":"migration","desc":"add index to kv_store","checksum":"sha256:...","check":"/bin/psql -c \"SELECT 1\""}]}' Review conversation (high level): - Reviewer Kenji Matsuo: requested clearer failure messaging when terraform state endpoint times out; asked for a knob to opt out of remote state checks in air-gapped installs. - Author (Aisha): added --skip-remote-state and improved logs per request; updated docs to emphasize offline plan workflow. - Reviewer Marta Lopez: asked for an explicit note on how release-lock interacts with automatic rollbacks; author clarified that override requires an operator flag and audit entry. - Review turns: 3 rounds; final approvals from Kenji and Marta. Motivation and summary: We have recurring incident post-upgrade where partially-applied helm/manifest sequences combined with out-of-order DB migrations lead to transient data/state mismatches and manual rollbacks. This PR introduces two complementary automation pieces that reduce human error and make upgrade/restore operations more deterministic for Private deployments: 1) an 'atomic release sequencer' binary (and Helm wrapper) that orchestrates small, ordered release changes with transactional checkpoints, and 2) a 'restore verifier' that runs post-restore sanity checks (CR status, schema fingerprints, KV-store checksums, and a small application-level probe) before marking the restore as complete.

What changed (high level): - New cli/tool: installer-sequencer (Go) that wraps helm upgrade/install and enforces a sequenced apply model. It records checkpoints to a namespace-scoped ConfigMap (immutable checkpoint IDs) and supports a --dry-run-preserve flag to stage operations into an ephemeral namespace for validation. - Helm chart changes: small hooks and a lightweight post-install probe container added to redwood-core chart; added labels/annotations used by the sequencer to detect release phases. - Restore verifier: a new step in the installer restore flow that validates: (a) DB migration versions match expected schema fingerprint, (b) critical CRDs are in Ready state, (c) sample inference request returns expected 200 + schema shape, (d) blobstore checksum matches pre-backup manifest. Failing checks halt finalization and emit diagnostics. - Schema migration dry-run mode: migration runner can execute in a transactionally-isolated ephemeral DB (when available) and produce a migration report used by the verifier. - Operational docs: runbook + example commands added to docs/installer/restore-verifier.md. - Tests: unit tests for sequencer state machine and integration tests exercising restore verifier against a small on-cluster dev DB.

Files changed (high level): - cmd/installer-sequencer/main.go (new) - internal/sequencer/state.go (new) - charts/redwood-core/templates/probe-job.yaml (modified) - charts/redwood-core/values.yaml (modified) - installer/restore/verifier.go (new) - installer/restore/fixtures/expected-schema.json (new) - docs/installer/restore-verifier.md (new) - test/integration/restore-verifier/* (new tests) plus small build/test infra changes to CI matrix.

Commit summary (single-line per commit): - 1a2d3f: add sequencer CLI scaffold and basic state machine; - 2b3c4d: implement checkpoint persistence and rollback hooks; - 3c4d5e: wire sequencer into helm wrapper and add feature flag; - 4d5e6f: add restore verifier core checks and report format; - 5e6f7a: chart probe/job and values; - 6f7a8b: integration tests + docs and CI matrix update.

Testing and CI: - Local unit coverage added for sequencer state transitions. - Integration job runs in the GH actions matrix using k3s (fast) to validate restore verifier end-to-end. - One flaky e2e run was observed on CI (race on the probe job pod readiness); flakiness mitigated by a small readiness-wait loop and the check re-run (see commit 6f7a8b). Final CI status: all checks green on the merged commit.

Security/upgrade considerations: - The sequencer persists immutable checkpoint IDs; the ConfigMap used is namespaced and read-only to non-installer service accounts. We added RBAC entries for the sequencer service account; review recommended. - Restore verifier requires read access to Secrets/ConfigMaps containing migration fingerprints; access is limited and scoped.

Migration/runbook (short): - Opt-in via installer flag --use-atomic-sequencer (defaults to off for now). - To perform a safe upgrade: 1) installer-sequencer stage --release redwood-core --version vX.Y.Z --dry-run-preserve (validate ephemeral run output). 2) If dry-run OK, installer-sequencer apply --release redwood-core --version vX.Y.Z. 3) On failure, sequencer will attempt deterministic rollback to last checkpoint (logs to /var/log/installer-sequencer.log). - For restore: installer restore --backup-id id1234 (when sequencer enabled, restore verifier runs automatically and will fail the restore if invariants not met). Docs include remediation steps and commands to extract diagnostics.

Review thread highlights: - Liam: asked for stronger invariants for schema fingerprinting (we now compute a normalized column/type fingerprint and include migration runner report). - Sofia: requested RBAC audit and minimal SA rights, addressed in commit 3c4d5e and documented. - Arjun: asked for a non-destructive dry-run for customers without ephemeral DB; we added a conservative checksum-based dry-run path that verifies schema compatibility without applying migrations.

Release/rollout plan: - Feature is behind a flag for now. We plan a gradual opt-in for customers doing Private upgrades; the default will remain as-is until we've exercised it with a small group. - Follow-up items tracked in ENG-4890: add grafana dashboards for sequencer checkpoint latencies and a telemetry ping on sequencer outcome (success/failure/rollback).

Why this is different from previous work: Existing upgrade safety PRs focused on transactional DB migrations or backup format. This PR focuses on treating the full release as an ordered, checkpointed sequence and pairing that with a stronger post-restore verification step and a migration dry-run mode—reducing manual intervention surface area for on-prem operators.

Notes: - Maintainers: please pay attention to the small Helm hook added (probe-job). It should be tolerant to cluster-level scheduling delays. - Tests added are intentionally conservative; we want to catch ordering races early.

Merge info: Squash merge performed. Merge commit message: "installer: atomic release sequencer + restore verifier (ENG-4821)".
Adds an "atomic release sequencer" wrapper for helm upgrades, a post-restore verifier that runs cluster invariants and lightweight API probes, and a schema-migration dry-run mode for on-prem installs. No behavioral changes to default upgrade from an operator's perspective; opt-in behind feature flag.
Opt-in feature flag --use-atomic-sequencer. ConfigMap checkpoints live in namespace <release>-installer-checkpoints. RBAC changes in charts/redwood-core/templates/rbac.yaml. See docs/installer/restore-verifier.md for runbook.

Motivation: Customers running Redwood Private in multi-AZ environments have asked for a repeatable, auditable failback path after a region/availability-zone incident. This PR implements an end-to-end automation suite: cross-AZ snapshot orchestration, idempotent restore jobs wired into the Helm charts, and runnable runbooks-as-code so operators can perform restore drills with minimal manual steps.

What this PR does (high level):
- Terraform: new module terraform/modules/dr-orchestration that provisions S3-compatible snapshot buckets, lifecycle rules, and IAM roles for cross-AZ snapshot ingestion (supports AWS/GCS-compatible endpoints).
- Helm: updates to charts/redwood-private-installer to add a dr-controller (lightweight k8s controller) and preStop/backup hooks; introduces a Job template templates/dr-restore-job.yaml for orchestrated restores.
- Runbooks-as-code: docs/runbooks/orchestrated-failback-playbook.md plus a small CLI wrapper scripts/dr/run_restore_playbook.sh that invokes the Helm job and monitors progress via the controller API.
- Utility: scripts/dr/snapshot-syncer.go (small binary) that safely copies snapshots between object stores and verifies checksums; used by the Terraform-provisioned CronJob for scheduled replication.
- Tests: integration/e2e/dr_restore_test.go adds a synthetic outage + restore flow that validates PV reattachment, KV cache warmup, and service ingress readiness.

Commits (summary):
- Add terraform module for cross-AZ snapshotting and IAM roles (Asha Menon)
- Helm: add dr-controller manifests and dr-restore-job template (Asha Menon)

Related work: ENG-9124 tracks the orchestration controller workstream; ENG-9198 tracks internal runbook standardization. This PR implements the first deployable unit of both.

Context: This PR adds an experimental scheduler that preferentially routes short-sequence requests to a low-latency path optimized for quantized kernels. Motivation: many interactive workloads (chat boxes, search snippets) have short generation lengths where kernel launch and scheduling overheads dominate. This experiment attempts to reduce median and tail latency by introducing a lightweight fast-quant execution path and a request classifier that routes <128-token sequences to the fast path when feature flag is enabled.

What this contains: single continuous description string. Implementation details: new scheduler module (runtime/fast_quant_scheduler.py), a small request classifier that uses token-length + model-profile heuristics, lightweight kernel selection hints for the runtime, and a toggleable config flag (runtime.features.fast_quant_scheduler=true). Benchmarks are included in the PR body.

Benchmarks: microbenchmarks on p4d-8x using the bert-600 and opt-125m variants show median token latency improvement of ~18-22% for sequences <=64 tokens, p95 improvement of ~12%. End-to-end chat simulation with gallery prompts shows ~14% median latency win and negligible quality regressions on sampled outputs.

Safety and risk: this is an experiment. Fast path uses a more aggressive quantized kernel which may yield slightly different float outputs; we recommend enabling only for non-critical customers while we run regression suites. The scheduler is feature-flag guarded and defaults to off. We added a rollout plan in the checklist.

How to test locally: run `pytest tests/runtime/test_fast_quant_scheduler.py` and `scripts/bench/compare_latency.sh --model opt-125m --seq 32,64 --runs 1000`. There is also a small CLI `tools/ff_scheduler_ctl.py` to toggle the flag on local dev clusters.

Notes: this PR is intentionally self-contained with clear toggles and metrics so it can be A/Bed and iterated quickly.

Avery Patel: Added perf/alerts/fast_quant_quality.rule and a dashboard link in the benchmark doc.

Avery Patel: classifier is purely token-length + model-profile for now; added a safeguard that routes to main path if queue latency exceeds threshold. See runtime/fast_quant_scheduler.py line 84.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Streaming TTFB spikes in mixed workloads remain a top customer pain point. Existing flush cadence + backpressure heuristics are reactive and cause microbursts when kernels are scheduled separately for adjacent microbatches. This PR introduces two complementary runtime changes: 1) an anticipatory kernel merge pass that detects adjacent microbatches with compatible kernel requirements and fuses their launch to avoid redundant kernel setup/teardown; and 2) an eager-output-drain path that proactively flushes already-computed tokens when downstream credit is likely to be available, reducing head-of-line latency for streaming consumers. Both changes are designed to be conservative by default and toggled under runtime flags for gradual rollout. Summary of changes:
- runtime/scheduler: add KernelMergePlanner which inspects next-N microbatches (configurable window) and proposes merge candidates when kernel config, device affinity, and memory footprint are compatible; new heuristics weigh predicted latency savings vs. extra queueing.
- runtime/launcher: implement fused kernel launch path with minimal synchronization and a fallback to existing per-microbatch launches.
- runtime/emitter: add EagerDrainController that monitors credit trends and preemptively emits completed token ranges; integrates with existing backpressure signals to avoid violating SLOs.
- runtime/kv_cache: prefetch alignment hints are emitted when kernels are merged so KV warmup can be shared between merged microbatches.
- runtime/metrics: new histograms for fused-kernel-duration, eager-drain-saved-ttfb, and merge-decision-rejection-reasons.
- tests/perf: new microbench harness replicating mixed small/large sequence workloads and a canary profile used to autotune the merge window.
- docs: runtime tuning guide section and examples for feature flags.
Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests for KernelMergePlanner heuristics
- [x] Integration test for fused launch path
- [x] Perf regression guard rails and CI microbench
- [x] Docs and runtime flag coverage
- [x] Manual canary run in staging
Observability notes: New metrics and logs are gated behind a runtime flag and emitted at low cardinality. Merge decisions are sampled (1%) in production to limit overhead; sampled traces include microbatch metadata and reasoning for auditability. Performance summary (staging canary):
- Mixed workload (60% short streams, 40% long streams) saw median streaming first-byte latency reduced by ~22% and P95 reduced by ~18% across a fleet of p3-equivalent instances.
- Tail reduction for interleaved small requests improved by ~28% due to reduced kernel churn.
- Cost per token is roughly neutral (slight improvement for workloads with >15% mergeable microbatches)
Safety and rollout plan:
- Feature flags: runtime.flag.enable_kernel_merge, runtime.flag.eager_output_drain, runtime.flag.merge_window_size. Default: disabled in production; enabled in canary for 2 weeks with sampling.
- Automatic rollback: if average P95 increases >5% over baseline for 30min, flag auto-disable.
- Gradual ramp: canary -> 10% of traffic -> 50% -> 100% with health gating after each step.
Backwards compatibility: no public API changes; internal event shapes in traces extended (backfilled by versioning).
Potential risks: over-aggressive merging can increase latency for long-running streams if merge buffering waits too long; we mitigate with a max-wait heuristic and preference for low-queue-time merges. CI/Codestate: One flaky test (emitter/credit-siphon-spec) required a test timeout bump and was rerun, all checks passed on the final commit. Please see commits for details and the canary report attached.
Diego Martinez: Nice direction. Two asks: (1) please add a safety net that prevents merging when a microbatch has an active long-running KV rewarm; (2) add telemetry for "merge wait time" so we can detect excessive buffering.

Motivation: Mobile and edge customers reported sporadic higher tail latency when streams attempted to refresh credentials mid-request and when the SDK aggressively prefetched credentials. This PR unifies a light-weight credential stitching path across Go/TS/Python SDKs, introduces an opt-in streaming throttle hint header to smoother backpressure, and bumps SDK minor versions to pick up the ergonomics surface changes. Changes are intentionally conservative and backwards-compatible: old SessionBuilder APIs are shimmed to the new SessionFactory with deprecation warnings; the runtime path only uses credential stitching when REDWOOD_SDK_CRED_STITCH=enabled to avoid cross-product surprises. Implementation summary: 1) Credential stitcher: introduces a small coordinator that attempts local stitch of a short-lived lease token into an existing session without forcing a full reauth round-trip; this reduces windowed auth churn for high-throughput stream bursts. 2) Streaming throttle hints: SDKs now accept a numeric "x-redwood-throttle-hint" header from the server; the client will adjust prefetch and batching aggressiveness when present. 3) Ergonomic API polish: consolidated SessionFactory across languages, added WithThrottleHints and WithCredStitch options, and improved error messages for failed reauth attempts. 4) Safety: added runtime opt-out via env var and a toggle in client options for teams who prefer current behavior. Migration notes: rename SessionBuilder->SessionFactory in new examples (old symbol still exported with deprecation notice), to pick up the stitch behavior set REDWOOD_SDK_CRED_STITCH=enabled or call client.WithCredStitch(true). Testing: unit tests for stitch success/failure, integration tests to validate header propagation, e2e on a local canary service that simulates credential churn. Checklist: [x] design doc linked in ENG-1987 [x] unit + integration tests [x] multi-SDK version bumps and changelogs updated [x] docs samples updated [x] performance microbenchmark attached
Asha: Can the stitcher fall back safely to a full reauth if stitching fails? (answered) - Priya: yes, stitcher returns ErrStitchFailed and the session layer performs a normal refresh as fallback.
Diego: Please add metrics for stitch attempts and stitch failures (requested) - Priya: added metrics stitch.attempts and stitch.failures and included in integration tests.
Claire: The deprecation notice for SessionBuilder should be visible in both runtime logs and docs (requested) - Priya: updated docs, examples, and logger to emit one-time deprecation warning at startup.
Mason: CI flaked on integration test twice, suggest retry wrapper (comment) - Priya: wrapped the canary test with a 3x retry and added jitter to token churn simulator to reduce deterministic timing races.
SDK minor bumps: Go v1.5.0, Python 0.9.3, TypeScript 1.6.2
Introduce optional credential stitching to reduce auth churn during stream bursts (opt-in via env or client option)
Add server-driven streaming throttle hint header (x-redwood-throttle-hint) to allow client-side backpressure tuning
SessionBuilder deprecated in favor of SessionFactory; shim remains for backward compatibility
