Motivation: streaming responses in production exhibited high 95/99th token latency under common microburst traffic. Root causes identified: (1) token generation loop used blocking flush cadence that batched too aggressively for low-latency clients, (2) backpressure from synchronous KV cache writes and global locks, and (3) kernel scheduling favored throughput over rapid token dispatch. This PR reworks the token loop to be event-driven with adaptive flush cadence, adds non-blocking async KV cache writes with lock striping, and introduces a fast-path scheduler for streaming sessions. Changes are gated behind feature flag `streaming-low-latency` and rolled out as a canary on the perf-canary cluster before wider rollout. Checklist: - [x] Profiling and root cause writeup attached - [x] Token loop rewrite + unit tests - [x] Async KV cache + integration tests - [x] Scheduler fast-path + e2e canary run - [x] Documentation: runtime tuning guide updated - [x] Feature flag and rollout plan described in PR body What changed (high level): - Token loop: converted from synchronous loop that flushed after accumulating N tokens or T ms to an event-driven loop that flushes immediately when forward pass completes and adaptively relaxes batching for longer sequences. Introduced a minimum flush cadence default of 12ms (previously effectively 50-100ms under microburst batching) and a jittered backoff to avoid synchronized flush storms. - Backpressure/backoff: replaced global request queue backpressure with per-session credit buckets so a slow client doesn't stall unrelated sessions. Token emission now respects a per-session soft-rate and hard-rate fallback. - KV cache: writes are now async and use lock striping per-key-shard; synchronous fence at end-of-stream only when necessary. Reads keep existing consistency model; we prefetch adjacent KV shards when sequence length grows to reduce miss penalty. - Scheduler: added a low-latency fast-path that prioritizes streaming sessions with small outstanding batch sizes and pins them to warm kernels; throughput scheduling unchanged for bulk inference. - Kernel/kernels selection: added a micro-batch kernel path that targets single-token forward when sequence window is small, reducing kernel invocation overhead. - Observability: new metrics (stream.flush_latency_ms, stream.flush_count, stream.backpressure_sessions) and dashboards added; traces include token loop stalls. Testing and results: - Unit and integration test suites updated; new harness for simulated slow clients. - Canary run (perf-canary cluster) across 200 concurrent streaming sessions with mix of short/long sequences. Results vs main baseline: median token-to-token latency: -12.5% (from 8.0ms to 7.0ms), p50 latency -12.5%; p95 token latency: -28% (from 34ms to 24.5ms); p99 token latency: -32% (from 92ms to 62.5ms). End-to-end streaming tail (95th percentile response time for 128-token responses) improved ~18%. Cost impact: slight increase in GPU kernels invoked (micro-batch path) but offset by reduced prefix replays and improved batching heuristics; net token cost estimated to be within +/-1% in our workload mix. Rollout plan: enable `streaming-low-latency` for internal canaries -> stage in one region -> monitor stream metrics and error budget for 72h -> gradual ramp to 100% if stable. If regressions seen, rollback to main via feature flag. Backwards compatibility: no API-level changes; default behavior unchanged unless feature flag is enabled. Notes on potential regressions: throughput-sensitive batch jobs could see small throughput regression; operator docs updated with knob guidance to disable fast-path for throughput-critical queues. Related: ENG-7421 (token loop redesign), ENG-7589 (kv cache async writes).
Ethan Li: Overall this looks great; can you quantify memory overhead for async KV writes?
Anya Kapoor: Async writes keep an upper bound of 8MB per shard; added tests for memory caps and metrics (kv.async_write_buffer_bytes)
Priya Desai: Concern about jitter causing token storms at high concurrency. Any mitigation?
Anya Kapoor: Added jittered backoff and per-session credit buckets; canary showed no synchronized flush spikes in traces
Marcus Chen: Approved after nits. Please add runtime knob to force old behavior per-queue
Anya Kapoor: Added queue-level config `enable_stream_fastpath` and documented rollback steps
CI: flaky test 'streaming_slow_client_test::reconnect' failed on first run; rerun passed
Streaming token generation: reduced tail token latency by up to ~32% p99 with an opt-in low-latency mode; added tuning docs and new metrics. Rollout gated behind feature flag.
Canary: p50 token latency -12.5%, p95 -28%, p99 -32%; end-to-end 95th response latency improved ~18%; minimal cost delta (~+/-1%) on our mixes.
payload.title: Rework streaming token loop and flush cadence to reduce tail latency

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Customers integrating long-lived streaming workflows reported two recurring issues: (1) first-request auth latency spikes when SDK fetches fresh delegated credentials on warmup, and (2) minor API surface mismatches between Go/TS/Py stream iterables caused duplicated reconnection logic in client apps. This PR introduces a credential seeding helper and a compact stream-compat shim in the Go SDK, plus coordinated documentation and minor version bumps to align ergonomics across languages.

Goals: reduce warmup auth latency for bursty workloads, provide a small compatibility layer so apps sharing cross-language examples can reuse the same reconnection patterns, and add a few retry/telemetry presets that match runtime routing expectations.

What changed (high level):

Motivation: Teams using the Go SDK reported friction composing credential fallback logic with streaming consumers and applying retry presets tuned for low-latency token refresh windows. This PR introduces a small orchestration layer (credential-orchestra) plus a compact set of stream helper utilities and typed retry presets to make common patterns ergonomic and cross-compatible with the polyglot SDKs. Summary of changes: - credential/orchestra: a lightweight coordinator that accepts multiple credential providers (primary, fallback, refresh) and exposes a single Resolve(ctx) API which returns a stable credential handle plus TTL metadata used by stream heartbeats. The orchestra is pluggable and does not change existing provider interfaces. - stream/helpers: utilities to create cancelable, checkpoint-aware stream consumers (PullStreamContext, StreamWithLease) that automatically wire credential refresh signals from the orchestra. Includes a small graceful-resume helper used by long-lived chat sessions. - retry/presets: typed retry profiles (LowLatencyShortWindow, Balanced, Throughput) as Go structs and builder helpers; presets map to backoff/jitter/timeout shapes used by transport-layer calls and stream reconnect logic. - API polish: minor renames to stream factory constructors to reduce ceremony (OpenStream -> NewStream or NewCancelableStream depending on signature); preserved backward-compatible wrappers for older names. - docs and examples: added a new example showing how to compose CredentialOrchestra with a multi-provider configuration and a stream consumer that survives transient auth failures. Implementation notes: - CredentialOrchestra keeps internal lease metadata and exposes events via a simple channel; it never performs network I/O itself, it coordinates provider lifecycles and schedules preemptive refresh callbacks. - Stream helpers subscribe to orchestra events and trigger a soft reconnect when the inside-of-window TTL falls below a threshold; reconnects use the provided typed retry presets to avoid aggressive retries under bursty load. - Retry presets are intentionally conservative by default and overridable; they are annotated so TypeScript/Python teams can mirror the shapes easily in a follow-up. Testing and validation: - Unit tests added for orchestra lifecycle, provider selection ordering, and TTL propagation. - Integration test in the e2e harness that simulates a rotating token endpoint and asserts stream continuity across multiple refresh cycles. - Manual smoke tests with the internal Perf Lab (short chat sessions, high QPS token churn) confirm latency tail improvements when using LowLatencyShortWindow preset. Rollout plan: - This PR is merged into main behind a feature flag (sdk.go.cred_orchestra.enabled=true by default for SDK v1.8.0). - Coordinate with Python/TS SDK maintainers to land counterpart helpers (follow-ups tracked in ENG-2543). - Monitoring: added telemetry hooks to count orchestration-promoted reconnects and measure mean time-to-refresh; dashboards will be created in observability-pack after merge. Known limitations & follow-ups: - CredentialOrchestra currently assumes providers expose TTL metadata; for older providers a shim adapter is required (tracked in SDK-198). - There is a documented follow-up to add an in-memory shared lease cache for multi-process hosters (performance win, tracked in ENG-2627). - TypeScript and Python presets will be added in separate PRs to maintain cross-SDK parity. Backward compatibility: - No breaking changes to public interfaces; renamed constructors have compatibility wrappers that log deprecation warnings for one major release. - Consumers that opted into the new orchestration behavior will see improved stream resilience and slightly different retry timing. Context/related work: mirrors conversations from ENG-2543 and SUP-417 where enterprise customers highlighted token churn when using short-lived delegated credentials in dedicated/private deployments. This PR aims to give SDK users an explicit, observable building block to handle that case without requiring bespoke app logic.
Anika Rao: Left a couple of inline suggestions about locking in orchestra.go — prefer a read-mostly locker for TTL reads.
Evelyn Park: Addressed the locker comments, simplified the lifecycle state machine, added tests for concurrent Resolve calls.
Diego Morales: Question on the default preset values — suggested reducing maxDelay in LowLatencyShortWindow to 300ms; updated in second commit.
Samir Gupta: Approved after CI green and perf lab smoke validated behavior on t4g. Medium: please add a note to the release notes about deprecation wrappers.
QA: Noted a flaky integration test (auth churn test) and required one rerun; reran CI and all checks passed.
Doc reviewer (Maya Chen): Added a small example snippet to the docs to show wiring with Kubernetes KMS provider.
Evelyn Park: Added follow-up tickets for shared cache (ENG-2627) and cross-SDK presets parity (ENG-2701).
payload.title: Introduce credential-orchestra, stream helpers, and polished retry presets for Go SDK

Summary: Introduces a light-weight regional "surge absorber" component plus a transparent fallback proxy to reduce cascading circuit flips during short-term capacity spikes. Motivation: We observed two incidents where transient egress pressure in a single region caused rapid circuit state churn and tenant-level mass fallbacks, worsening latency and causing client retries. This PR adds a mitigation that throttles and absorbs brief surges at the routing layer and routes affected requests to a transparent fallback proxy that can serve compatible model variants or alternate capacity tiers.

What changed (high level): - Add an in-router surge-absorber with a token-bucket window and soft-queue to smooth very short spikes (<= 2s). - Introduce transparent-fallback-proxy service that can forward requests to lower-cost compatible variants or regional peers without exposing fallback routing to callers. - Telemetry: new metrics (surge_absorbed_count, fallback_proxy_forward_rate, fallback_latency_ms_p50/p95) and trace tags added to trace the absorber decision path. - Policy: new JSON policy entries enabling per-tenant and per-route softness thresholds (defaults conservative). - Tests: unit + integration harness with synthetic spike replay and a small chaos script.

Behavioral notes: The absorber is conservative by default: it will only buffer up to 100 requests and hold them for up to 2s before allowing fallback. The transparent fallback proxy supports header-based routing so downstream services can still observe original request metadata. No customer-visible API changes.

Rollout plan: 1) Feature-disabled on main; enabled behind feature flag ff.regional_surge_absorber for 10% of traffic in us-west-2 for the first 24h. 2) Observe metrics and error budgets; expand to 50% if p95 latency and SLOs are stable. 3) Ramp globally after 72h with an automatic rollback script if surge_absorbed_count > threshold and fallback latency > 2x baseline.

Testing: Unit tests added for token-bucket math, queue eviction and fallback decision. Integration tests added to perf-canary suite — synthetic sinusoidal spike, and a realistic client-retry pattern. Local annotation harness verifies trace tags are present. CI initially flaked on an e2e due to a timeout in the mock peer; rerun succeeded.

Migration and compatibility: Policy file format extended with a backward compatible optional "soft_window_ms" and "soft_queue_size". Existing policies remain valid. Operators can pre-seed preferred fallback model variants via the operator console.

Risk and fallback: Low to medium. The absorber is opt-in; a buggy path would at worst route to the fallback proxy which currently mirrors the original routing logic. A fast rollback toggle and a region-level circuit unbind are provided.

Related: ENG-4021 (incident postmortem), ENG-4187 (regional routing policy work).
Luca Romero: Positive direction. Please ensure the token-bucket is monotonically monotone across multi-threaded fetches — saw a race in the first commit.
Maya Patel: Fixed race in commit 'chore: atomic window refactor' and added unit that failed previously; pushed update.
Priya Singh: Can you add a metric for 'fallback_proxy_forward_rate' with tags for tenant and route? We'll need it for incident dashboards.
Maya Patel: Added metric and dashboard YAML; included tenant+route tags. Also added an alert threshold suggestion in the docs.
Aaron Chen: Integration test looks good but e2e occasionally times out in CI; recommend increasing mock-peer timeout to 10s in the harness.
Maya Patel: Increased timeout and re-ran CI; all checks green.
Priya Singh: Approved after minor telemetry naming nits.
Luca Romero: Approved — good to squash and merge once canary config is set.
Adds a per-region surge absorber and a transparent fallback proxy to reduce cascading circuit flips during short spikes. Feature gated and opt-in; operators should follow the rollout playbook in docs/operators/regional-surge-absorber.md.

## Context Redwood Console route-level experiments (A/B/n) uses deterministic assignment based on a stickiness key and returns assignment metadata via response headers. Beta customers and Support reported confusion about how to pass the key and how to confirm which variant a request hit (see SUP-24877, INT-1193). This PR updates the Python SDK to (1) let callers provide a stable stickiness key in a standard way, (2) surface experiment/variant headers on responses, and (3) add opt-in troubleshooting logs that are safe by default. ## What changed - Add `experiment_sticky_key` (and alias `sticky_key`) optional argument to `Client.chat.completions.create(...)`, `Client.responses.create(...)`, and the generic request wrapper. The SDK maps this to request header `X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key`. - Parse and expose response headers: `X-Redwood-Experiment-Id`, `X-Redwood-Experiment-Variant`, `X-Redwood-Route-Id`, `X-Redwood-Experiment-Config-Version`. These are available via `response.experiment` and `response.headers` (raw) without changing existing payload models. - Add a minimal debug logger gated by `REDWOOD_SDK_DEBUG_EXPERIMENTS=1` (or `client_options.debug_experiments=True`). Logs include which stickiness key source was used (explicit arg vs derived), which headers were emitted, and whether the request used streaming/retry paths. By design, we do NOT log the full stickiness key by default; we log a short hash prefix for correlation and a "low entropy" warning when the key looks accidental (e.g., missing/empty/"unknown"). - Streaming: ensure assignment headers are captured on the initial HTTP response and persisted through stream iteration so callers can still inspect `assigned_variant` even if they only consume tokens. - Retries: make sure the retry wrapper preserves `X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key` and does not drop the request-id/experiment headers when constructing the retry request. - Docs/examples: update README snippets to show best practice (use a stable user_id / customer_id, not request_id). Add a short troubleshooting section: "Why do I see skew?" and "Where do I find the assigned variant?". ## Example ```py from redwood import Client client = Client(api_key=os.environ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"]) resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="redwood/llama-3.1-70b-instruct", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the following..."}], experiment_sticky_key=user.id, ) print(resp.experiment.experiment_id, resp.experiment.variant_id) # Always available: print(resp.headers.get("x-redwood-experiment-variant")) ``` ## Notes / design decisions - Header naming matches platform ADR/OTel conventions and the Console docs: we normalize access in Python (case-insensitive) but preserve the raw header map. - We intentionally avoid introducing a hard dependency on Console/experiment service types in the SDK; this remains a thin header feature. - Debug logging is opt-in and redaction-first (hash prefix only). ## Testing - Unit tests for header injection + parsing. - Integration-ish tests using `responses` to simulate streaming responses with headers. - Regression test for retry wrapper preserving experiment headers. ## Rollout - Safe to ship as patch/minor; no API removals. - Docs change should reduce Support churn around "missing variant headers" and "how to verify assignment". Related: ENG-9032 docs guide and the examples app update in redwood-examples.
Jordan Lee: Can we align the header name with the policy engine? We use `X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key` and return `X-Redwood-Experiment-Variant` (string). Also: please confirm we don't ever default to request_id as sticky key.
Dylan Brooks: Updated to `X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key` and removed the earlier fallback-to-request-id idea. If callers don't pass a key, we omit the header and emit a debug warning (opt-in).
Logan Wright: For debugging, can we include a correlation-safe identifier? We need to help Support without leaking user identifiers.
Dylan Brooks: Added `sticky_key_hash_prefix` (first 8 chars of sha256) in debug logs only; raw key never logged unless `REDWOOD_SDK_DEBUG_EXPERIMENTS=unsafe` (not documented).
Kaitlyn Nguyen: Any auth/RBAC implications? Make sure we don't expose internal debug endpoints or privileged headers.
Dylan Brooks: No debug endpoints added. Only reads standard assignment headers already returned to customers. No additional scopes.
Caleb Johnson: Streaming header behavior: headers are present only on the initial response, not per chunk. Ensure the SDK stores them before yielding tokens.
Dylan Brooks: Fixed in `Stream.__enter__` to capture headers and attach to the stream response wrapper; added a test that consumes only the iterator and then reads `stream.experiment`.
payload.title: Add route experiment header support + troubleshooting logging

Motivation: customers asked for a lightweight, local-first tool to surface unit-economics signals for Redwood-hosted workloads and to export quantization profile suggestions from observed inference traces. This PR adds a small CLI (redwood-econ) and SDK helpers to produce tenant-level CSV heatmaps, sample-weighted unit-cost estimates, and an opinionated exporter for quant-presets (candidate quantization/bitwidth recommendations) so downstream ops teams can run audits and seed Dedicated/Private defaults.

What this PR delivers: 1) python/redwood/econ/reporter.py: core reporter that ingests request/trace samples and produces per-tenant unit-econ CSV and JSON summaries; supports prefix aggregation, warm/cold split, and per-model shape buckets. 2) python/redwood/econ/quant_export.py: exporter that synthesizes quant-presets from token-cost curves and per-shape loss estimates; includes conservative fallback rules and a compact YAML output compatible with on-prem deploy tooling. 3) CLI entrypoint (bin/redwood-econ) to run local dry-runs, simulate tenant rollups, and export artifacts. 4) integration tests and fixtures (tests/test_econ_reporter.py, tests/fixtures/*) and minimal docs (docs/econ-reporter.md) with examples and recommended thresholds.

Design notes: the reporter is intentionally sync-first and memory-bounded (streaming aggregator) to be runnable in dev environments. Quant exporter applies a three-stage filter: safety thresholds, sample-weighted cost delta, and a stability window to avoid noisy recommendations. We avoided changing runtime codepaths to reduce risk; SDK helpers are pure computation and optional.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for aggregator and exporter logic - [x] CLI basic e2e smoke - [x] Docs and examples - [x] Telemetry hooks (opt-in) - [x] Manual smoke on staging with a tenant snapshot (ENG-3421)

Usage: redwood-econ summarize --input traces.ndjson --tenant tenant_123 --out tenant_123_econ.csv
redwood-econ export-quant --input traces.ndjson --out quant-presets/tenant_123.yaml

Compatibility and rollout: Non-breaking. The CLI and SDK live in the python package; no API surface change for hosted inference. We will ship as a minor SDK release and recommend ops teams run the CLI against 24-72h trace slices to seed quant-presets.

Related: ENG-3421 (unit-econ UX), ENG-3495 (quant export safety rules).
Aisha Patel (reviewer): Nice direction — can we tank the memory usage on pathological tenants? Suggest switching the in-memory shape-bucket map to an LRU capped at 10k keys or streaming to disk after threshold. Also request a small sample of a produced quant YAML in the PR body.
Author (Marina): Addressed — switched to a capped LRU map with a configurable cap via env var REDWOOD_ECON_BUCKET_CAP. Added an example quant YAML (docs/econ-reporter.md). Updated tests to cover boundary evictions.
Liam Chen (reviewer): Tests look good. Two small nits: prefer explicit decimal formatting for cost deltas and add an opt-out flag for telemetry hooks for compliance customers.
Author (Marina): Added cost formatting and --no-telemetry flag to CLI; updated docs and changelog note.
Ruben Alvarez (approver): Ran a staged dry-run against a 48h snapshot from staging-qa. Output looks reasonable; quant presets were conservative and matched our heuristic baseline. Approving for merge after CI passes.
Added a lightweight SDK CLI (redwood-econ) to generate tenant unit-economics reports and export candidate quantization presets. Useful for ops and cost-analysis workflows; non-breaking SDK addition. See docs/econ-reporter.md for examples and recommended thresholds.

Context: SUP-4821. Some customers store the Redwood API key in secrets managers or copy/paste flows that include a trailing newline. The Python SDK previously used .strip() on the key, which can remove leading/trailing whitespace unexpectedly and cause auth failures when keys are not exactly preserved. Changes: normalize by rstrip("\r\n") only; add a warning if whitespace is detected; add unit tests for newline and carriage-return cases; update docs string in README. Release: v0.9.4.
Connor OBrien: Does this break anyone who intentionally had spaces?
Ethan Park: We only remove trailing CR/LF now; if someone had leading spaces it would have failed anyway; we emit a warning when whitespace is present.
Aisha Rahman: +1, matches what we saw with Kiteframe. Please add note in release notes.
Ethan Park: Added.
payload.title: Avoid stripping API keys; only remove trailing CR/LF

payload.body:
Context: Runtime is shipping tiered workload-aware batching defaults (fast / standard / cost-efficient). Customers need an SDK-level way to explicitly pick a tier (or keep server defaults) without reaching into manual batching knobs. This PR adds an optional `batching_tier` parameter across request surfaces and sends it as an HTTP header for the control plane/runtime to interpret.

What’s in this PR: 1) Client option: add `batching_tier: Optional[str]` (and typed Literal where available) on generation endpoints (chat + completions + embeddings where applicable, though runtime will ignore for non-generation). 2) Transport: serialize `batching_tier` into header `X-Redwood-Batching-Tier` with wire values: `fast`, `standard`, `cost-efficient`. 3) Validation: reject invalid values client-side with a clear error message; allow None/unspecified. Also normalize `cost_efficient` -> `cost-efficient` for ergonomics (accept both on input, always send `cost-efficient`). 4) Docs: add usage examples and a short FAQ note explaining that tier selection affects scheduling/batching behavior only (no change to logging/retention). 5) Changelog: add an entry under Unreleased.

Why header vs body: We already use headers for request-level policy hints (e.g., tracing/debug flags). Keeping this as a header avoids changes to multiple request schemas and makes it easy to apply consistently across endpoints.

Backwards compatibility: Default remains unchanged. If `batching_tier` is not set, the SDK sends nothing and the service selects the default tier per route/model policy.

Example:
- Python: `client.chat.completions.create(model="redwood/llama-3.1-70b", messages=[...], batching_tier="fast")`
- Wire header: `X-Redwood-Batching-Tier: fast`

Notes / follow-ups: - We intentionally do not expose manual batching knobs in the SDK in this PR; tier selection is the supported surface. - Dedicated override precedence is handled server-side (customer override > route policy > tier default); this PR just passes the requested tier.

Testing: - Unit tests for validation + normalization. - VCR-style integration test verifies header is present. - Lint + mypy.

Release note (SDK): Add `batching_tier` parameter to select workload-aware batching tier (fast/standard/cost-efficient).
Henry Cho (review): Can we avoid accepting arbitrary strings? Prefer a typed enum/Literal to reduce support issues. Also please clarify docs that choosing a tier is a latency/cost trade-off and not an SLA guarantee.

Wei Chen (author): Added `BatchingTier = Literal["fast","standard","cost-efficient"]` plus input normalization for `cost_efficient` (common python style). Invalid values now raise `ValueError` with the allowed set. Updated docs language to avoid SLA wording.

Jordan Lee (review): Header name/value: runtime expects `X-Redwood-Batching-Tier` and value `cost-efficient` (hyphen). Please ensure we always send hyphenated form even if user passes underscore.

Wei Chen (author): Implemented normalization: accept `cost_efficient`/`cost-efficient`, always serialize as `cost-efficient`. Added tests asserting exact header values.

Allison Grant (review): Minor: please add a note that tier selection is included as a label in some metrics/traces server-side; SDK shouldn’t promise visibility. Also consider whether high-cardinality concerns apply.

Wei Chen (author): Added a short note: “tier may appear in server-side telemetry” without promising a specific dashboard view. No client-side cardinality changes.

Henry Cho (final): Looks good. Thanks for keeping this backwards compatible and consistent with the TS SDK plan. Approved.

Merge: Squash merged.
payload.title: Add batching_tier request option (header) for workload-aware batching defaults

Context: Teams reported subtle production flakes where long-running streaming sessions would deadlock while the SDK attempted token refresh near connection shutdown. Root cause: mismatched defaults across languages (py: grace=5s, ts: grace=2s, go: none) combined with non-deterministic drain logic in the stream consumer. Motivation: provide predictable, cross-language semantics for credential grace windows and give app authors explicit, ergonomic controls for draining streaming responses. What this PR does: 1) introduce a unified config property 'session_grace_ms' (default 5000) surface on all SDK clients; SDKs continue to accept language-idiomatic names but map to the canonical value in shared test fixtures. 2) add 'stream_drain_timeout_ms' with a default of 3000 to guard shutdown path; streaming helpers now expose drain_until_eof(timeout_ms) convenience methods on Python/TS and DrainWithContext(ctx, timeoutMs) on Go. 3) refactor token refresh handshake to be cancelable and cooperative with drain: refresh now registers a short-lived lease and yields shutdown precedence to drain paths. 4) add cross-sdk integration tests that simulate concurrent refresh and EOF arrival, and a stress test harness that reproduces the original deadlock pattern. 5) bump package versions: python 1.9.0, typescript 2.6.1, go 1.4.0 (minor/patch bumps only). Checklist: - [x] design doc (ENG-1842) and UX doc reviewed - [x] unit tests added for all three SDKs - [x] crosslang integration test added to perf lab - [x] reviewed and approved by SDK leads - [x] release notes drafted Testing and CI: initial CI run showed a flaky TS streaming test (stream-drain-signal) — reproduced locally, fixed race by moving the drain signal to the top-level loop and adding a short backoff in the TS connector. All CI checks green on rerun. Migration notes: default values are conservative; existing callers should be unaffected. If teams relied on the previous lower grace intervals, they can set session_grace_ms explicitly. Operational notes: this change reduces rare stalled streams at the cost of a modestly longer shutdown window in some workloads; metrics added to the Console: sdk.session.grace_ms_applied and sdk.stream.drain_timeout_ms_applied. Rollout plan: quick canary to ~10% of hosted SDK traffic for 48h, then gradual increase. If we see an uptick in shutdown latency beyond expectations, we will roll back and revert to per-sdk defaults while we iterate. Related: SUP-4021 (customer incident), ENG-1842 design doc.
Aligned session grace/reauth defaults across Python/TS/Go SDKs, added ergonomic stream drain helpers, fixed an edge case that could cause stalled drains when token refresh overlaps generation. Minor version bumps for all SDKs.
Omar Reyes: Can you explain why 5s was chosen as the default? Is it empirically driven?
Ava Chen: Chose 5s after running the stress harness under realistic network jitter; it covered 99.7% of reproductions while keeping shutdown latency acceptable. Added note in UX doc.
Nina Patel: TS test was flaky in CI — I see you added the backoff, please add a short comment explaining the tradeoff so it's not removed by future authors.
Ava Chen: Added inline comment and extracted backoff as 'drainYieldBackoffMs' constant with a unit test asserting > 95% success over 500 runs.
Soren Li: Approve after the changelog bump. Observability: can we emit a metric when refresh yields to drain?
Ava Chen: Added metric sdk.refresh.yield_to_drain with counts and labels (sdk_lang, client_id).

Summary: Adds a lightweight RAG Debug Annotator tool and a Snippet Suggester quickstart to help engineers iteratively debug retrieval+generation failures. Motivation: debugging RAG sessions is time-consuming because errors can live in retrieval, prompt engineering, tool calls, or model fallbacks. This PR provides an opinionated developer workflow: capture a session trace, annotate tokens and retrieval hits inline, and surface suggested prompt/snippet rewrites to improve grounding and tool invocation reliability. What this PR includes: - A minimal web-based annotator (React) that loads a session trace JSON and overlays: token-level highlights, retrieval hit provenance links, and tool-call traces. - A Snippet Suggester engine (TS + Python examples) that generates small prompt edits and candidate tool wrappers based on heuristics and eval traces (prefix length, hallucination markers, and failing tool sigs). - Quickstarts: TypeScript quickstart with devcontainer and local runner, Python quickstart (async worker) showing how to attach the annotator to live sessions. - Docs: new devguide page with step-by-step troubleshooting recipes, metrics to watch (prefix coverage, retrieval recall, prompt entropy), and recommended guardrails for canarying prompt rewrites. - Tests: unit tests for the suggester heuristics and e2e smoke for the annotator renderer. - Telemetry: optional debug-only traces emitted as a compact trace.json format and small additions to the console's sample traces examples. Why this is useful: developers can reproduce a failing RAG session locally, iterate on targeted prompt edits suggested by the suggester, and validate fixes with the same trace format used in production. Checklist: - [x] Annotator UI implemented and wired to local trace loader - [x] Snippet Suggester: TS implementation + Python reference wrapper - [x] Quickstart README & devcontainer added - [x] Docs page with recipes and example traces - [x] Unit and e2e tests added to harness - [x] CI linting and typechecks passing

Commit summary: - feat(annotator): initial React app and trace viewer

## Summary
This adds first-class Python SDK helpers for the Safe Apply + Rollback project so operators and customer admins can (1) query which Optimization Config version is currently active for a given deployment/scope and (2) pin a deployment to a specific config version (with optional validation-only mode).

These helpers wrap the control plane APIs introduced in the platform work (Optimization Config Service) and standardize:
- request/response models (including scope fields)
- error handling for common authz/RBAC failures
- safe defaults (read-only methods require no additional permissions; pin requires explicit role)

## Motivation
Support and on-call workflows need a consistent way to answer "what optimization config is active right now?" and to execute a controlled rollback/pin without spelunking through raw endpoints. This is also needed for Private / Dedicated automation (Terraform/installer aside) where Python scripts are used to coordinate changes.

## API (new)
### Client helpers
- `client.optimization_configs.get_active_version(...)`
  - Returns the active config version for a given `deployment_id` and optional scope filters.
  - Intended for debugging, audit correlation, and post-change verification.

- `client.optimization_configs.pin_version(...)`
  - Pins a deployment to a specific `config_version_id`.
  - Supports `dry_run=True` to validate permissions and scope compatibility without applying.
  - Returns an operation payload (request id, effective scope, and the pinned version).

### Data models
- `OptimizationConfigScope` (tenant/model/region)
- `OptimizationConfigVersionSummary` (id, created_at, created_by, state)
- `OptimizationConfigPinResult` (deployment_id, pinned_version_id, effective_scope, request_id)

## Notes on permissions / RBAC
- `get_active_version` surfaces permission errors as `RedwoodPermissionError` with the server-provided `required_permission` when present.
- `pin_version` requires the new "optimization change operator" permission on the target scope. The SDK adds a short troubleshooting hint in the exception message (e.g., "Ask an org admin to grant optimization_config:apply").

## Implementation details
- Adds `OptimizationConfigsAPI` module under the client with clear docstrings and type hints.
- Uses existing request plumbing (no new HTTP stack).
- Both helpers accept `idempotency_key` and forward it to the API via `Idempotency-Key` header.
- Normalizes config version identifiers to string and validates non-empty.

## Example
```py
from redwood import Redwood

rw = Redwood(api_key=os.environ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"])

active = rw.optimization_configs.get_active_version(
    deployment_id="dep_7f8c...",
    scope={"model": "llama-3.1-70b", "region": "us-east-1"},
)
print(active.id)

# Pin (used for rollback/pinning during incident response)
rw.optimization_configs.pin_version(
    deployment_id="dep_7f8c...",
    config_version_id="ocv_20260122_0012",
    scope={"model": "llama-3.1-70b", "region": "us-east-1"},
    idempotency_key="rollback-2026-01-22-sev2",
)
```

## Testing
- Unit tests added for:
  - happy path parsing for `get_active_version`
  - pin request shape + idempotency header propagation
  - RBAC denied responses (403) -> `RedwoodPermissionError`
  - invalid inputs (empty deployment_id/version_id)
- Tests use `responses` to mock control plane endpoints.

## Backwards compatibility
No breaking changes. New methods only. No existing names changed.

## Release notes
- Python SDK: add Optimization Config version helpers (`get_active_version`, `pin_version`) for Safe Apply/Rollback workflows.

---
### PR checklist
- [x] Added unit tests
- [x] Added/updated docs and examples
- [x] Ran `make lint` and `make test`
- [x] Added changelog entry

### Screenshots / output
N/A (SDK-only change).
Benji Okafor: Can we align naming with control plane docs? They call this "active_version" vs "current". Also please ensure scope fields match tenant/model/region exactly.
Felix Schneider (author): Updated method name to `get_active_version` and introduced `OptimizationConfigScope` with tenant/model/region. Added validation for unknown keys in the scope dict.
Jordan Lee: For RBAC denied, can we surface the required permission if the server includes it? This will reduce INT-3390 style tickets.
Felix Schneider (author): Added parsing for `required_permission` when present and included it in `RedwoodPermissionError`. Also added a short hint string for pin failures.
Ethan Park: Pin endpoint supports idempotency keys; can we plumb that through? Also please add a dry-run option so operators can validate without changing state.
Felix Schneider (author): Added `idempotency_key` param and forwarded header. Added `dry_run=True` which sets `validate_only` on the request. Added tests for both.
Chloe Martin: Docs request: please include a snippet that prints the active version and shows how to pin during rollback. Also ensure this doesn’t collide with existing `deployments.pin_*` naming.
Felix Schneider (author): Added docs page + snippet and confirmed no collision. This lives under `optimization_configs` namespace.
Benji Okafor: LGTM after the scope validation tweak.
Ethan Park: Approved.
Jordan Lee: Approved.

Context: As part of the cross-language SDK parity initiative, we need a single timeout model that behaves predictably across Python/TS/Go and can be mapped cleanly onto each language's underlying HTTP client. We also have multiple support reports (notably SUP-29410) that Python streaming appears to ignore configured timeouts, plus internal feedback that timeouts are hard to reason about because we currently treat a single float as "some" timeout without clarifying whether it is connect vs read vs overall. What this PR does: Implements the v1 timeout model for the Python SDK with explicit connect/read/overall semantics, and maps those to httpx.Timeout consistently for both streaming and non-streaming requests. Adds migration notes and tests to lock behavior and prevent regression. Behavior / API changes: 1) Adds a new Timeouts type (redwood.timeouts.Timeouts) with fields connect_s, read_s, overall_s. The SDK accepts this via Client(timeouts=Timeouts(...)) and request overrides (e.g. client.chat.completions.create(..., timeouts=...)). 2) Maintains backwards compatibility for Client(timeout=...) but deprecates it (warning) and defines a stable mapping: timeout=<float> is treated as overall_s. connect_s/read_s use defaults unless explicitly set. 3) Streaming: read timeout is still honored for idle reads (i.e., if the stream stalls and no bytes are received within read_s, we raise RedwoodTimeoutError). overall_s caps total request wall time including streaming. 4) Request cancellation via context manager / generator close now reliably aborts the underlying httpx request and stops background reads (important for avoiding hung sockets). Defaults (aligned with ADR-sdk-timeout-model): connect_s=10, read_s=60, overall_s=300. Note: these are intentionally conservative for non-streaming; streaming callers are expected to set read_s higher if they expect long gaps between events (docs follow-up in ENG-5128). Error typing: Introduces RedwoodTimeoutError (subclass of RedwoodAPIError) surfaced consistently with request_id when available. Implementation notes: - Centralized timeout resolution in _client.py so precedence is: per-request override > Client.timeouts > deprecated Client.timeout > env var REDWOOD_TIMEOUT_S (deprecated) > default. - Uses httpx.Timeout(connect=..., read=..., write=..., pool=...) with write/pool derived from connect_s unless explicitly overridden internally; overall_s is implemented via httpx's "timeout" plus an explicit wall-clock deadline enforced in our request wrapper to avoid edge cases where streaming iterators can outlive a request timeout. - Adds a small helper (timeouts.py) that clamps/validates values (non-negative, overall >= max(connect, read) if all present), and normalizes ints/floats. Tests: - Unit tests for resolution/precedence (client vs request override, env var fallback, deprecated alias mapping). - Integration-ish tests with MockTransport to simulate: connect timeout, read stall on streaming, overall deadline exceeded mid-stream. - Golden assertions for exception shape (type, message, retryable=false, request_id present when response headers include x-request-id). Migration notes included below and in docstrings. Migration notes (tl;dr): Existing code using Client(timeout=30) still works, but will emit a DeprecationWarning; update to Client(timeouts=Timeouts(overall_s=30)) or set granular values. If you were relying on the old behavior where streaming could run indefinitely despite timeout configuration, you may now see RedwoodTimeoutError unless you increase read_s/overall_s for streaming workloads.
Ibrahim Khan: Can we make sure the precedence order matches the draft standard? Specifically per-request > client > env > default, and the deprecated alias shouldn't override explicit granular values. Also please confirm what we do if overall < read. Sabrina James (author): Updated resolve_timeouts() to follow per-request > Client.timeouts > deprecated Client.timeout > env var > default. Added validation: if overall_s is set and (connect_s/read_s) are set, we raise ValueError when overall_s < max(connect_s, read_s) to avoid silent surprises. For backward compat when only overall_s is set, we keep defaults for connect/read. Allison Grant: Please avoid writing our own timer loops if httpx already enforces total timeout; timer loops can be flaky under event loop scheduling. Also, we need the error shape to include timeout_ms and request_id where possible for parity with ENG-5129. Sabrina James (author): Agreed. We still use httpx.Timeout for connect/read/pool/write. The extra overall deadline enforcement is only applied around streaming iteration because we saw cases where the initial response was within timeout but iteration could run indefinitely; the wrapper enforces a wall-clock deadline and cancels the response stream on expiry. Added fields on RedwoodTimeoutError: timeout_ms and phase (connect/read/overall). Request_id is pulled from headers when available (x-request-id) and from JSON error bodies when present. Owen Phillips: The SUP-29410 repro was "timeout not honored on streaming". Can we add a regression test that simulates a stream that emits one chunk then stalls, and assert we error out with a typed exception that includes request_id? Sabrina James (author): Added tests/test_streaming_timeouts.py::test_stream_read_timeout_on_stall and ::test_stream_overall_timeout_mid_stream. Both use MockTransport and a fake byte iterator; we attach x-request-id and assert it propagates into RedwoodTimeoutError. Ibrahim Khan: One more: DeprecationWarning should be quiet by default in normal runs; but we should document it and add a single warning on client init, not per-request. Sabrina James (author): Updated to warn once on Client construction when timeout= is passed. No per-request warnings. Ibrahim approved. Allison approved after confirming error fields and defaults. Owen approved after verifying SUP repro passes locally.
Python SDK: Added Timeouts(connect_s, read_s, overall_s) and standardized timeout behavior across streaming and non-streaming requests.
Client(timeout=...) remains supported but is deprecated; use Client(timeouts=Timeouts(...)) instead.
Streaming now honors read and overall timeouts consistently; stalled streams will raise RedwoodTimeoutError with request_id when available.

This PR introduces two collaborating pieces to improve SRE signal quality and operator ergonomics: (1) an Invocation Chronicle Diff panel and associated API that surfaces compact deltas between invocation snapshots (prefix/response/token-phase deltas, KV-cache hits, kernel queueing deltas) so on-call can quickly see what changed between a baseline and a problematic invocation; and (2) a Precision Alert Harmonizer service that applies deterministic post-processing to alert triggers to reduce noisy churning from long-tail token-phase variance. Motivation: frequent noisy alerts during mid-latency spikes were caused by subtle differences in invocation shape (e.g., prompt length shifts, KV-prefetch miss patterns) that current SLO rules treated as separate incidents. Operators spend time triaging obvious diff-only regressions. Goals: - Provide a compact, queryable 'diff' for a sampled invocation pair that highlights phase-level token cost/latency deltas and related log excerpts - Reduce alert churn by applying phase-aware smoothing and deterministic deduplication across similar diffs - Expose toggles for SRE/tenant teams to opt into conservative or aggressive harmonization modes Design summary: - Invocation Chronicle Diff: new API endpoint /v1/observability/chronicle-diff that takes two invocation ids and returns a compact delta summary (token-phase delta, KV hit delta, kernel-queue delta, top-3 divergent spans, sample log excerpts). We return a small fingerprint hash for grouping similar diffs. The UI panel calls this endpoint for two selected snapshots and renders a three-column diff: baseline, delta, head. - Precision Alert Harmonizer: lightweight stateless service in observability plane; subscribes to alert events, retrieves invocation digests for the samples attached to the alert, computes the chronicle diff fingerprint and consults a deployable policy table (tiered by tenant and route). If the diff fingerprint matches a recent resolved fingerprint within a short window, the harmonizer will suppress duplicate alerts or annotate the alert with suggested remediation and noise-score. Operators can tune suppression window and strictness per-tenant. Non-goals: this change does not alter primary SLO calculations; it only annotates or suppresses downstream alert delivery. Checklist: - [x] API + backend for chronicle-diff - [x] UI panel in Console (Observability -> Invocation) - [x] Harmonizer service with demo policy table - [x] Unit + integration tests and smoke harness - [x] Feature flag: observability.chronicle_diff.enabled, observability.alert_harmonizer.mode Rollout plan: feature behind flags. Stage 1: enable chronicle-diff read-only in dev and staging consoles. Stage 2: enable harmonizer in passive mode (annotate-only) for a small set of tenants. Stage 3: enable suppressions for tenant opt-in only, monitor false-suppression rate for 2 weeks. Backout: flip observability.alert_harmonizer.mode to off. Related: ENG-4221 (alert-churn RCA), ENG-4304 (invocation-snapshot-indexing). Testing: added table-driven tests for fingerprint stability, integration tests exercising suppression policy, and a small replay-run against 48 hours of synthetic invocation traces to validate false-suppression < 0.5%. Performance: chronicle-diff compute is optimized to run on compact invocation digests; typical latency < 25ms for snapshots in the 1-10k token range. Security and privacy: diffs only include sampled log excerpts and are sanitized via existing log redaction pipeline. No new PII fields are persisted. Monitoring: new metrics added: observability.chronicle_diff.requests, observability.chronicle_diff.errors, observability.harmonizer.suppression_rate, observability.harmonizer.false_suppression_estimate. Dashboards: added a small harmonizer summary dashboard and a chronicle-diff explorer panel. See changed files for specifics.
Diego Ramos: Can we guarantee fingerprint stability across minor digest schema changes? If not, add versioning to the fingerprinting algorithm.
Priya Nambiar (reply): Added algorithm version field to the fingerprint payload and a unit test that verifies stability across benign schema additions. See chronicle_diff.go lines 112-136.
Maya Chen: The panel looks good; suggest adding a hover tooltip that links to the matching suppression history for the fingerprint.
Priya Nambiar (reply): Added tooltip and a 'recent matches' drawer in the UI that queries /v1/observability/chronicle-diff/matches.
Liam O'Connor: CI flake observed in integration test. The replay harness occasionally times out on large replays. Can we cap synthetic trace size in CI?
Priya Nambiar (reply): Lowered replay size for CI and added retry logic; flagged the larger replay for nightly runs.
Diego Ramos: Please add a metric for suppressed_alerts_count per tenant so product can measure impact.
Priya Nambiar (reply): Added observability.harmonizer.suppressed_alerts.total (tagged by tenant_id).
Maya Chen: Approve after addressing the CI timeout and fingerprint versioning.
Added Invocation Chronicle Diff API and Console panel for compact invocation deltas; introduced Precision Alert Harmonizer to reduce noisy alert churn with tenant-scoped policies. Feature is behind feature flags: observability.chronicle_diff.enabled and observability.alert_harmonizer.mode. Default mode: off. Admins can opt-in per tenant.
When enabling suppression mode start in annotate-only mode. Watch observability.harmonizer.false_suppression_estimate and observability.harmonizer.suppressed_alerts.total for unexpected suppression. Backout by toggling observability.alert_harmonizer.mode=off.
Enable observability.chronicle_diff.enabled in staging
Open Console -> Observability -> Invocation, pick two invocation snapshots and verify diff renders
Enable harmonizer in annotate-only mode for tenant test-tenant-123 and trigger known noisy pattern; verify alert annotated but still delivered
Enable suppression mode for test-tenant-123 and verify duplicate alerts are suppressed within configured window

Summary: This PR integrates the shared SDK parity conformance harness into redwood-sdk-go and adds the initial fixture set covering: (1) retryable HTTP responses (429/5xx) including Retry-After parsing, (2) network/transient transport failures, and (3) streaming interruptions (server FIN mid-event / partial chunk) with consistent typed error shape and request_id propagation. Motivation: During the SDK parity initiative, we’ve repeatedly found cross-language drift in edge-case behavior (esp. Retry-After handling and streaming disconnect surfacing). The goal of this harness is to make the Go SDK run the same behavioral tests as Python/TS so we can catch mismatches in CI before release. Scope/details: - Adds an internal conformance runner that spins up an httptest.Server and replays scripted responses from fixtures under testdata/conformance/fixtures/*.json. - Adds a deterministic fake clock + backoff recorder so tests assert retry timing windows (vs exact sleeps). - Adds fixtures for: * 429 with Retry-After (seconds) and Retry-After (HTTP-date) * 500/502/503 retry behavior (bounded attempts, jitter window) * transport errors (dial tcp refused, context deadline exceeded, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF) classification as retryable vs terminal * streaming disconnects: mid-event EOF, truncated JSON payload, and proxy-like half-close behavior (client sees io.EOF while parsing SSE/data lines). - Plumbs request_id capture from response headers into the harness assertions (aligns with INT-1182 request_id visibility). What this PR does NOT do: - Does not change default retry/backoff settings (handled in PR #612) - Does not change public error types (handled in PR #624); this harness simply asserts current taxonomy stays aligned with the standard - Does not add any telemetry/logging (tracked separately in ENG-5129) Implementation notes: - The harness uses a Scenario file format shared across SDKs conceptually, but implemented in Go as a small parser over JSON fixtures with strict validation. - Streaming tests use chunked transfer encoding and a controllable writer that can: flush partial frames, close mid-write, and optionally omit the final '\n\n' SSE delimiter to simulate proxy truncation. - Retry tests do not sleep; they intercept the backoff function via an injected BackoffStrategy interface in internal/testutil and record requested delays; assertions check delay grows exponentially and stays within jitter bounds, and that Retry-After overrides computed backoff when present. CI: - Adds a new GitHub Actions job 'go-conformance' that runs 'go test ./... -run Conformance' on pull requests and main. - The job is marked required for merge (per ENG-5127). Testing: - go test ./... -run Conformance - go test ./... (full suite) - Validated locally that the 429 Retry-After (HTTP-date) fixture reproduces SUP-29477’s historical bug (previous code ignored date format; now asserted in tests; implementation already fixed in #612). Follow-ups: - Extend fixture coverage to include: 409 idempotency guidance (non-retryable), 408/499 semantics, and streaming cancellation (client-initiated) vs disconnect (server/proxy). - Once Python/TS runners are fully wired, we should align fixture names/IDs 1:1 and publish a small README in the shared conformance plan repo. Screenshots/logs: Example assertion output when Retry-After is not respected: "expected first retry delay to be derived from Retry-After=2s, got 400ms" (see ConformanceRetry429RetryAfterSeconds). Example assertion output when stream disconnect does not surface request_id: "expected error.request_id != ''" (see ConformanceStreamDisconnectMidEventEOF).
Go SDK: adds cross-language conformance tests for retry/backoff (429/5xx + Retry-After), network error classification, and streaming interruption error surfaces. No customer-facing API changes; test-only + internal harness.
Ibrahim Khan (requested changes, 2026-02-12): "Nice. Two asks: (1) make sure we test Retry-After in both delta-seconds and HTTP-date formats; (2) avoid real time.Sleep in conformance tests so CI is stable." Mateusz Zielinski (reply): "Done. Added retry_429_retry_after_http_date.json and switched runner to inject FakeClock + BackoffRecorder; assertions now check computed delays without sleeping." Allison Grant (comment, 2026-02-13): "Can we assert jitter bounds instead of exact backoff? We should allow small variance across implementations." Mateusz Zielinski: "Yep; assertions now check delay within [base*(1-jitter), base*(1+jitter)] and only enforce monotonic growth + max cap." Sahana Iyer (comment, 2026-02-14): "CI: please split required job so conformance can be re-run quickly; also ensure it runs on forks without secrets." Mateusz Zielinski: "Updated workflow to add a dedicated go-conformance job with no secrets; uses standard go tooling only." Monica Patel (approval, 2026-02-18): "Ship it. This is exactly the gate we need before we flip defaults and message customers."
Initial run failed due to flaky timing assertion (used time.Sleep). Updated harness to record backoff requests (no sleeping). Final status: pass. Checks: lint-go (pass), unit-tests (pass), go-conformance (pass), govulncheck (pass).

Summary: This PR introduces a lightweight credential-metrics bridge and language-native typed stream handles for Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. The bridge surfaces token lifecycle events (refresh, failure, fallback) and retry/backoff transitions as low-overhead telemetry counters/tags. The typed stream handles provide a small ergonomic API that wraps the underlying streaming protocol with explicit lifecycle hooks (on_start, on_resume, on_error, on_close) and safe typed envelopes to reduce buffer copies and improve cross-language parity.

Motivation: Teams have asked for better observability into credential churn and retry behavior without having to instrument service code. Streaming ergonomics between SDKs have drifted: the TS/Go shapes exposed a few helpers that Python lacked, and Python had a more heavyweight iterator model that caused extra buffering. This change aims to: 1) provide consistent telemetry (counts + last-event tags) for credential operations across SDKs, 2) unify streaming ergonomics (typed handles and lifecycle hooks), and 3) make a small performance win by avoiding an extra frame copy on chunk assembly.

High-level changes: - Add credential_metrics module that emits: credential.refresh.count, credential.refresh.duration_ms.p95, credential.refresh.failures, credential.refresh.fallbacks, stream.resume.count. Metrics are emitted via existing telemetry hooks (no new exporter required). - Introduce typed stream handles in each SDK with the same public surface: start(options), next(), resume(), close(), and lifecycle callbacks. Implementations translate to native async iterables / async generators / channels idiomatically per language. - Hook credential events into the SDK retry machinery so retry/backoff transitions increment a metric and attach a last-event tag for quick query. - Minimal public API additions: a new optional SDK config key: credential_telemetry: { enabled: boolean, namespace: string } (default off). - Add examples and docs and bump SDK patch versions.

Files touched (high level): see changed_files. Tests: added unit tests for credential event emission in each SDK and integration smoke tests for typed stream handles across a local test harness. CI: one flaky TypeScript test (stream-heartbeat.spec) failed on the first run due to timing; was retried and passed. All other suites green.

Commits summary: - c8f3a1d: Add credential metrics bridge (py/ts/go) and wire into retry paths. - b4ef9a2: Implement typed stream handle for Python and TS; add examples. - 9d2b7c1: Go typed handle + perf tweak to chunk assembly; tests and docs.

Review conversation (abridged): - Lena Ortiz: "Can we keep the default disabled for telemetry and document the cost/volume tradeoff?" -> Author: "Yes — credential_telemetry defaults to false; updated docs and examples to show enabling and query examples." - Graham McKee: "The typed handle API looks good, but can we reduce allocations in the Python iterator when resuming?" -> Author: "Addressed in second commit: use memoryview-backed buffer slices and preallocate a small chunk pool; added test asserting zero extra copy on resume path." - Sophie Laurent: "Please add a note to the changelog about the TS test flakiness and the retry on CI." -> Author: "Done; CI note added and flaky test marked with ephemeral tag while we evaluate upstream timing variance"

Performance notes: Microbenchmarks show ~8-12% lower median memory allocation per stream in Python when using the typed handle vs old iterator for 2KB chunk workloads. TS and Go saw negligible CPU change, and Go saw ~6% lower heap churn due to avoiding an intermediate buffer during chunk concat.

Backward compatibility: All changes are additive. credential_telemetry is opt-in. Typed stream handles are provided alongside existing streaming helpers and can be adopted incrementally. No breaking changes to existing calls.

Release plan: - Bump Python SDK to 2.6.0, TS SDK to 1.12.0, Go SDK to 1.5.3. - Publish docs/metrics.md with examples and recommended Grafana/PromQL snippets. - Announce in SDK changelog and suggest opt-in rollout.

Merge: Squashed and merged after approvals; merge commit includes a short migration note and links to the Linear tasks.
Adds a credential telemetry bridge and typed streaming handles across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs; improves retry telemetry, reduces stream memory copies, and bumps SDK patch versions.
Monitor credential.refresh.* cardinality in staging when teams opt-in
Observe TS stream-heartbeat flakiness root cause (timing window) and consider increasing CI harness timeouts
Consider an opt-out sampling mode if telemetry shows high cardinality across many service tokens

Added delegated refresh scheduler for long-running streams; introduced async stream shim to smooth cross-SDK parity; bumped python SDK to 0.10.2. No public API breaking changes expected.
Context and motivation: Long-running streaming consumers observed periodic tail-latency spikes when the token refresh path attempted synchronous refreshes while the stream loop held internal locks. This PR introduces a delegated refresh scheduler that decouples credential renewal from the hot path and an async stream shim that provides a lighter-weight async iterator façade for common consumer patterns. The goal is to reduce streaming tail-latency, make token lifecycle behavior observable, and align ergonomics across Python/TS/Go SDKs without changing the core streaming protocol semantics.

What this PR does (single-pass summary):
- Adds a DelegatedRefreshScheduler that runs refreshes on a bounded background worker pool and surfaces a small async-ready lease object to stream sessions.
- Replaces the previous synchronous token refresh path in the streaming client with a non-blocking handoff to the scheduler and a best-effort prefetch for hot sessions.
- Introduces AsyncStreamShim: a compact async iterator wrapper that preserves current message envelopes but yields a simpler consume()/aiter() pattern used in most example apps.
- Exports a lightweight telemetry hook for credential handoffs so ops can wire up metrics (refresh latency, queue depth, failures).
- Adds cross-language interop tests that validate session behavior when the server returns a 401 during an active stream.

Motivation: Intermittent streaming interruptions in long-lived streams were traced to tightly-coupled token refresh windows and aggressive client-side retry gates. Teams asked for an ergonomic primitive that: 1) makes token lifetime management explicit to SDK consumers, 2) lets SDKs pre-emptively acquire/renew short-lived leases used for streaming sessions, and 3) tunes retry windows automatically based on lease health and observed stream heartbeat.

This PR introduces a lightweight 'CredentialLease' primitive in the Python SDK, an adaptive retry optimizer that consults lease health to scale retry backoff ceilings, and harmonizes top-level config key names with companion PRs in the TypeScript and Go SDKs (see linked PRs). The change is intended to be opt-in: defaults preserve current behaviour.

What this PR does (summary):
- Add credentials/lease.py: CredentialLease, LeaseManager, TTL jittering, prefetch policy, and metrics hooks.
- Add retry/optimizer.py: AdaptiveRetryOptimizer which adjusts retry windows based on lease state and streaming heartbeat.
- API ergonomics: expose 'lease' argument on StreamingClient and add convenience 'with_lease' context manager.
- Cross-SDK parity: rename config keys to `lease_ttl`, `lease_prefetch_margin`, and `retry_ceiling_ms` to match TS/Go (backwards-compatible aliases preserved).
- Tests: unit tests for lease lifecycle, integration mock for streaming with simulated token rotation, and e2e smoke for retry elasticity.
- Docs: updated SDK reference and quickstart snippet demonstrating a streaming consumer using a CredentialLease.
- Changelog and version bump to 1.29.0.dev -> will be released as 1.29.0.

Python SDK: Usage API now exposes billed token counts and cache hit attribution (when available) to match invoice/usage exports. No breaking changes; new fields are optional and default to None when not returned by the API.
Context: As part of the metering hardening workstream, the Usage API is being extended to include fields that distinguish billed vs raw tokens, and to attribute cache hits where applicable. Finance/RevOps and customers have asked for a consistent way to reconcile invoice line items with usage exports, particularly around retries/fallback, caching, and token counting semantics. This PR updates the Python SDK usage client and response models to surface these new fields so customers can self-serve reconciliation and internal analytics. What changed: (1) Added optional response fields to usage records: billed_prompt_tokens, billed_completion_tokens, billed_total_tokens, and cache_hit (bool) + cache_hit_tokens (int, optional). (2) Updated the usage client to pass through the fields without forcing schema validation failures on older servers (gracefully handles missing fields). (3) Added docstrings + README snippet describing the difference between raw tokens and billed tokens, including how to treat None values during rollout. (4) Added unit tests using recorded fixtures for both pre-field and post-field payloads. (5) Added a short migration note for customers parsing usage exports into typed dataclasses/Pydantic models. Notes/semantics: billed_* fields are what Redwood uses for pricing and invoicing for Hosted API. raw token fields (prompt_tokens/completion_tokens/total_tokens) remain the underlying model tokenization counts, but may not reflect billing adjustments due to caching and platform behavior. cache_hit indicates the request was served partially or fully from cache; when present, cache_hit_tokens represents the tokens not executed on GPU (for attribution/analytics) and should not be assumed equal to a discount unless contractually specified. Rollout: Backend is shipping fields behind a gradual rollout; SDK must tolerate missing fields. This PR intentionally does not rename existing fields to avoid breaking changes. Related: redwood/pr-27485 (Expose cache-hit and billed token fields in usage API).
Nadia Rahman (review): Can we confirm naming matches the API fields exactly? We should avoid the SDK inventing its own names unless we document mapping. Also, for cache attribution: should cache_hit_tokens be optional even when cache_hit=true? Monica Patel (author): Yep — aligned with the backend response naming (snake_case). cache_hit_tokens stays Optional[int]; during rollout the backend can emit cache_hit without tokens for some models/regions until backfill completes. Added docstring + tests to cover cache_hit=true, cache_hit_tokens=None. Chris Osei (review): Please add a small migration note for customers who deserialize usage records into strict schemas; this will help CS/Sales when customers compare invoice vs usage exports. Monica Patel (author): Added a section to docs/usage.md and a snippet in README: 'If you use strict parsing, allow unknown fields or update your schema to include the optional billed_* fields.' Allison Grant (review): I’d prefer a single billed_tokens field but I understand backend is splitting by prompt/completion. Can we also include billed_total_tokens for convenience? Monica Patel (author): Added billed_total_tokens to the model and wired it through. Also updated the example to compute totals defensively if the server only returns prompt/completion in early rollout. Nadia Rahman (follow-up): Tests look good. One more thing: ensure we don’t treat missing billed_* as 0; None is important for rollout. Monica Patel (author): Updated parsing defaults to None; tests assert None when absent. Approvals: Nadia Rahman approved. Chris Osei approved. Allison Grant approved.

Context: Hosted data residency enforcement returns a deterministic error when a request would violate the org/project/API-key region policy (see ADR-022 + gateway work in ENG-4833). Today the Python SDK surfaces this as a generic APIError, which makes it hard for customers to catch and handle (e.g. prompt the admin to update allowed regions) and for support to quickly pull request traces.

What this PR does: Adds a dedicated exception type, ResidencyPolicyViolationError, and maps residency enforcement responses into it. The exception exposes (a) error_code (machine readable), (b) request_id (for support + audit correlation), and (c) help_url (docs link for remediation). The rest of the response payload is still preserved on the base error for debugging.

Behavior: - If the API returns HTTP 409 with error.code matching residency enforcement (e.g. RESIDENCY_POLICY_VIOLATION), raise ResidencyPolicyViolationError. - For all other errors, keep existing behavior (APIError subclasses like RateLimitError, AuthError, etc.). - For streaming: the exception is raised when the initial response is an error; mid-stream transport failures remain unchanged.

Why 409: Aligns with the public error contract for policy blocks (conflict with configured policy) and matches the gateway rollout.

Testing: Added unit tests for mapping and for preserving request_id/help_url. Also added a small integration-style fixture to ensure unknown codes do not get misclassified.

Docs: This PR does not update public docs; it only changes the SDK surface. A separate docs PR will reference the new exception in the Python examples.

Checklist: - [x] Linked to PM-1490 acceptance criteria (machine readable error + actionable guidance) - [x] Added tests - [x] No breaking change (new exception is a subclass of APIError) - [x] Backwards compatible parsing (help_url is optional; request_id may be absent on older gateways)

Motivation: Improve cross-SDK ergonomics for credential rotation and controlled shutdown/drain of streaming consumers. Some customers observed stale credentials during rapid rotation and difficulty draining long-lived async iterators when changing auth providers. This PR introduces a flushable SessionBridge (flush()/notifyDrain()) and an opt-in SSE/Chunked streaming header to surface stream lifecycle notifications to proxies and middleware. It also synchronizes SDK package versions to v2.3.0 for Py/TS/Go to reduce interop surprises.

Summary of changes (single-line continuous body with short sections):
- Add SessionBridge.flush() API: callers can force credential rotation and begin a coordinated drain window; underlying sessions emit a DRain-Start event to registered iterators.
- Add SessionBridge.notifyDrain(reason) for graceful shutdown hints from host processes (used in Private installer and Dedicated autoscaler hooks).
- Streaming headers: introduce X-Redwood-Stream-Notify and X-Redwood-Stream-Seq for SSE and chunked responses to help middleware detect stream progress and finalization. Header is opt-in via client config (streamNotify: true).
- SDK ergonomics: Python async iterator gains .flushable() helper that registers with SessionBridge; TypeScript async generator gets .drain() shim; Go iterator Add Drainable interface.
- Backoff/defaults: reduce default reauth jitter window to 10s -> 6s for common mobile/edge reconnections; documented rationales in comments.
- Tests: unit + integration tests added for cross-sdk drain signal, header propagation, and credential rotation race.
- Docs: quickstart snippet and upgrade note added to SDK CHANGELOGs and consolidated in redwood-docs/upgrade-auth.md link included.

Summary: Adds golden transcript tests for streaming tool-calling in the Python SDK to lock down the canonical event model used across docs/examples. These tests validate (a) partial tool-call argument deltas, (b) correct final tool-call assembly, (c) tool-result message injection, and (d) error branches for truncated/disconnected streams. Motivation: We’ve seen repeated regressions and user confusion around partial tool-call args mid-stream (see SUP-18421). The examples refresh work requires stable, cross-language behavior; these tests provide a guardrail and a source of truth for fixture payload shape. What’s included: - New pytest suite that replays recorded streaming event sequences (“golden transcripts”) through the same consumer logic used by examples. - Fixtures that cover: single tool call, parallel tool calls (multiple tool_call_ids), and an interrupted stream where tool args arrive in multiple chunks. - Output normalization to prevent flakes: strips request_id, timestamps, and nondeterministic IDs; stable ordering for parallel tool call assembly; and line-ending normalization for CI parity. - Developer workflow for updating fixtures: set UPDATE_GOLDENS=1 to regenerate transcripts locally (documented below). CI notes: Golden tests intentionally avoid live API calls. We record fixtures once and then replay them. This keeps CI reliable and removes dependency on model variability. There is still a small risk of flake if JSON key ordering changes in serialization; the normalizer now canonicalizes JSON before comparison. How to run: - pytest -k golden_streaming_tool_calls - To update fixtures: UPDATE_GOLDENS=1 pytest -k golden_streaming_tool_calls Notes / gotchas: - These tests assert payload-shape and assembly semantics, not model content quality. - The fixtures include partial args segments to mirror real-world streaming behavior; do not “simplify” them into one chunk, otherwise we regress the exact failure mode we’re guarding. - If the event model changes, please coordinate with ENG-4826 (docs) and the TS/Go fixtures to keep parity.
Ibrahim Khan: The fixture approach looks good. Two asks: (1) ensure we normalize tool_call_id only when it’s clearly nondeterministic; we still want to assert that the same id is used across deltas within a call. (2) Add one case that includes partial JSON args that only become valid at the end (mirrors SUP-18421).
Sabrina James (author): Updated normalizer to preserve per-call tool_call_id consistency (we only strip request_id / timestamps / trace ids). Added tool_calls_partial_args.jsonl fixture where args are invalid JSON until the last delta and we assert assembly results in valid JSON.
Sahana Iyer: CI flake risk: are we relying on dict ordering for JSON comparisons? We’ve had cross-platform diffs on this before. Recommend canonicalization + stable dumps.
Sabrina James (author): Good catch. Added canonical_json() that sorts keys and removes whitespace for comparisons. Also normalized \r\n to \n when reading fixtures.
Brian Murphy: Please add a brief comment in the test explaining that we’re validating event semantics (ordering + assembly) rather than model output. Otherwise future readers will try to “fix” the fixture content.
Sabrina James (author): Added comments + expanded tests/golden/README.md to clarify intent and update procedure.
Monica Patel: Approving contingent on one more thing: add a marker so these can be run separately (fast) and don’t slow down the full suite too much.
Sabrina James (author): Added pytest -m golden marker and wired into CI under unit-tests; it’s ~0.6s locally.
Ibrahim Khan: LGTM. This unblocks ENG-4823/ENG-4826 parity work.
Monica Patel: Approved.
Sahana Iyer: Approved.

Motivation: Dedicated fleet autoscaling observed short-term oscillations when reservation adjustments and burst allocations reacted to raw utilization spikes. This caused repeated micro-resizes and transient headroom churn that bumped 95th percentile tail latency under sustained bursty traffic.

This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: (1) a Commitment Gradient Mediator that blends reservation deltas using a tunable multi-window gradient (fast/medium/slow) to avoid aggressive reservation flips; (2) a Utilization Signal Normalizer that attenuates short-lived util spikes and exposes a stabilized percentile-based utilization signal to the autoscaler and billing telemetry.

Highlights (single continuous description):
- Adds a GradientMediator component inside pkg/autoscaler that computes a smoothed reservation delta using weighted gradients across 3 windows (10s, 60s, 5m) and a configurable momentum term. The mediator enforces a commit rate cap and a minimum hold window to avoid churn.
- Introduces telemetry/reservations/normalizer.go: performs per-tenant utilization normalization, switching between low-pass filtering and robust-percentile gating when signal variance exceeds threshold. Emits util_normalizer.{raw,smoothed,pct_var} metrics for debugging and downstream gating.
- Integrates mediator outputs with existing dedicated allocation controller: decisions now require both mediator-consensus and health-check-stable before adjusting GKE/instancegroup reservations.
- Backfills unit + e2e coverage: autoscaler/mediator_test.go (unit), e2e/dedicated-mediator-smoke.yaml (integration test harness using synthetic spike generator).
- Adds a lightweight canary for 10% of tenants behind a feature flag to monitor impact before global rollout.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc (docs/design/commitment-gradient.md) reviewed by SRE and Autoscale WG
- [x] Unit tests added and passing
- [x] Integration smoke test validated in perf-lab cluster (5 runs)
- [x] Telemetry dashboard prototype created (dashboards/dedicated/commitment-gradient.json)
- [x] Feature-flag gating and rollout plan included

Operational impact: In our perf-lab runs the mediator reduced reservation oscillation events by ~68% and lowered headroom churn (measured as reservation toggles per-minute) from median 0.9 -> 0.13 for synthetic mixed workloads. Observed 95th latency improved ~12% for bursty scenarios during the canary window.

Compatibility and rollout: Default behavior is opt-in via feature flag. We will enable the 10% canary for 48 hours, evaluate stability, then bump gradually. No breaking changes to RPC/schemas.

Related: ENG-4432 (autoscaler stability), ENG-4510 (dedicated billing signals).
Miguel Alvarez (2025-11-13): Nice approach. Two asks: (1) make the gradient windows configurable via deployment config; (2) add a kill-switch metric if mediator starts rejecting all adjustments.
Aisha Nair (2025-11-13): Added config plumbing and emitted mediator.rejection_count metric. See commits a8d7e04 and b5a77c2.
Priya Desai (2025-11-15): Can we add a short-circuit path when underlying infra reports degraded capacity so we don't block emergency scale-ups?
Aisha Nair (2025-11-16): Implemented infra health short-circuit with a 30s bypass; documented behavior and added unit tests.
Connor Li (2025-11-17): Tests look good. One nit: tighten logging level for mediator debug logs in production.
Aisha Nair (2025-11-18): Switched debug -> trace behind feature flag. Ready for merge.
Introduce Commitment Gradient Mediator to reduce reservation oscillations and Utilization Signal Normalizer for stable autoscaler inputs. Opt-in via feature flag; initial canary at 10% tenants. Improves stability and reduces headroom churn for bursty workloads.
