Motivation: customers see uneven tail latency when client-side prefetch and retry heuristics diverge across language SDKs. This PR implements a syncable prefetch strategy and a set of compact retry presets (latency-aware, throughput-lean, conservative) and introduces a lightweight Python stream facade to match ergonomics shipped in the TS/Go SDKs. It unifies telemetry labels for credential prefetch events so server-side correlators can reason about client-driven prefetch, and surfaces a small opt-in API (Stream.prefetch_policy) for teams that want deterministic warmup behavior. Changes include API surface parity, new retry presets wired into the session factory, unit + integration tests for prefetch behavior, and docs/examples. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-1428) - [x] proto/contract reviewed with SDK leads - [x] unit tests (prefetch, retry logic, stream iteration) - [x] e2e simulated burst tests in CI - [x] docs + example notebook - [x] version bump to 1.14.0 Release notes: Adds opt-in Stream.prefetch_policy and three retry presets for client-side ergonomics; aligns Python SDK stream semantics with TS/Go for credential prefetch and retry metrics. See linked Linear tickets for rollout plan. No behavioral change unless opted in. Rollout: feature gated behind SDK config defaulting to previous behavior; will flip after monitoring window. Related: SUP ticket SUP-7721 covers a customer incident that motivated exposing prefetch telemetry. Notes: kept implementation compact to avoid increasing import surface; uses existing session cache and background refresh worker with a configurable jitter schedule.
Diego Martinez: Important perf question — the background refresh worker uses a single thread per process; will that saturate in high-concurrency server apps? Suggest making the worker pool size configurable. Reply (Aisha): Agreed; exposed SDK config 'prefetch.worker_pool' with default 1 and doc note explaining tradeoffs.
Renee Cho: Can we avoid importing heavy deps in streaming.__init__ to keep cold-start smaller? Suggest lazy import of the retry registry. Reply (Aisha): Moved registry init to lazy loader inside session_factory to avoid import-time cost.
Liam O'Connor: Tests flaked in CI on first run (integration prefetch burst); appears to be timing sensitive. Action: add deterministic jitter seed and a 50ms slack in the assertion. Reply (Aisha): Added deterministic seeding in tests and a short slack; re-ran CI and passes.

payload.body:
Context
We have multiple reports of streaming requests terminating mid-response (corp proxies, flaky networks, server FIN mid-chunk). Today the iterator tends to surface a generic httpx/requests exception (or StopIteration) without (a) request_id, (b) a typed error class to allow customer handling, or (c) any access to partial output that was already received. This is also blocking cross-language parity work where TS/Go are converging on explicit disconnect taxonomy.

What this PR does
- Introduces a typed exception for streaming disconnects: StreamDisconnectedError (subclass of RedwoodAPIError) that carries request_id, status_code (when known), retryable flag, and partial_response (accumulated text + token/event counts).
- Makes streaming partial output semantics explicit:
  - The streaming iterator yields events as they arrive.
  - If the underlying connection terminates unexpectedly after at least one event has been yielded, we raise StreamDisconnectedError.
  - The exception includes partial_response so callers can decide whether to keep partial output, show it with a warning, or attempt a new request.
  - We do NOT auto-retry streaming (by design) to avoid duplicating side effects / billing ambiguity.
- Improves request_id capture and propagation:
  - Prefer x-redwood-request-id (and x-request-id fallback) from the initial response headers.
  - If headers are unavailable (some proxy modes), attempt to parse request_id from the first SSE event metadata when present.
  - Ensure StreamDisconnectedError.request_id is populated whenever we can recover it.
- Documents retry guidance for streaming in the Python README + docstrings:
  - Safe retry only before any tokens/events were received.
  - After first token, retry is application-dependent; recommend idempotency keys where applicable and logging request_id.
- Adds tests for mid-stream disconnects + proxy-buffered disconnect behavior using a deterministic streaming test server and a socket-level “cut connection mid-event” helper.

Why this aligns with the SDK parity standard
- Error taxonomy: provides typed error with request_id and retryable signal.
- Streaming semantics: consistent with conservative retry stance agreed in parity RFC (no implicit retries for streaming; surface partial output + guidance).

Implementation notes
- Added redwood.errors.StreamDisconnectedError + StreamingPartialResponse dataclass.
- Updated ChatCompletionStream (and legacy generate_stream) to accumulate partial text and event_count.
- Normalizes low-level exceptions (httpx.ReadError, httpcore.RemoteProtocolError, requests.exceptions.ChunkedEncodingError) into StreamDisconnectedError when they occur after streaming has started.
- Handles the “disconnect before first event” case as a regular transport error (still retryable via non-streaming retry middleware if enabled).

Backward compatibility
- No changes to successful streaming output.
- Behavior change: instead of occasionally returning silently / raising a generic network exception, callers will now reliably receive StreamDisconnectedError for mid-stream termination. This is intentionally more actionable.

Screenshots / examples
Python example:
try:
    stream = client.chat.completions.stream(model="redwood/verified-7b", messages=[...])
    for event in stream:
        ...
except StreamDisconnectedError as e:
    logger.warning("stream disconnected", extra={"request_id": e.request_id, "partial_len": len(e.partial_response.text), "events": e.partial_response.event_count})
    # retry guidance: only retry automatically if e.partial_response.event_count == 0

Testing
- Added unit tests for:
  - disconnect after N events -> raises StreamDisconnectedError w/ partial_response
  - disconnect before first event -> bubbles as transport error (retryable via normal policy)
  - request_id extraction from headers
  - request_id extraction from SSE metadata fallback
  - error redaction: ensure API key never appears in exception repr

Release note
Python SDK streaming now raises StreamDisconnectedError (includes request_id + partial output) when a stream terminates unexpectedly. Streaming is not automatically retried; docs include recommended retry patterns.
Ibrahim Khan (review): Can we make the retry guidance explicit in the exception itself (retryable flag semantics)? Specifically: retryable=true if we never emitted an event, otherwise false. Also, please make sure request_id is pulled from x-redwood-request-id first (parity standard).
Sabrina James (author): Updated. StreamDisconnectedError.retryable is now computed based on whether any streaming events were yielded. Also adjusted request id precedence: x-redwood-request-id -> x-request-id -> SSE metadata fallback. Added tests.
Allison Grant (review): Please ensure we capture enough fields for debugging/telemetry: request_id, disconnect_reason (best-effort), retry_count (should be 0 for streaming), timeout_ms (if available). Even if we can’t emit telemetry yet, the error should expose these. Also check that repr/str does not include raw headers.
Sabrina James (author): Added disconnect_reason (enum-ish string: remote_closed|protocol_error|read_timeout|unknown) and set retry_count=0 for StreamDisconnectedError. Timeout_ms is plumbed when the underlying client provides it (httpx timeout config). Confirmed error string does not log headers; tests added for redaction.
Owen Phillips (review): This resolves SUP-29410? The customer repro was “timeout ignored while streaming” and then a hard hang. Do we now reliably cancel/raise when read timeout is hit?
Sabrina James (author): Yes—read timeouts now map to StreamDisconnectedError(disconnect_reason=read_timeout) once streaming has started; prior behavior sometimes bubbled as httpx.ReadTimeout without request_id. For the hang case, the iterator now checks for keepalive timeouts and raises after the configured read timeout. Added fixture that simulates proxy buffering to confirm we don’t spin indefinitely.
Dana Lo (review): TS/Go are using partial_output fields named partial_text and event_count. Any chance we match names to keep parity docs simpler?
Sabrina James (author): Kept Python idioms but aligned field names in the public surface: partial_response.text + partial_response.event_count. Docs now show the equivalent names per language; we can revisit if we want strict naming parity at the exception field level.
Streaming: raise StreamDisconnectedError on mid-stream termination (includes request_id, disconnect_reason, and partial_response).
Docs: clarify that streaming is not auto-retried; provide safe retry guidance (only auto-retry before first event).

payload.body:
## Context
Quickstart Templates (Python + TS) are shipping with opinionated safe defaults for timeouts/retries/backoff and streaming robustness. The Python SDK currently relies on httpx defaults and a light wrapper; this causes template-generated apps to behave differently than our guidance (esp. behind proxies / transient network failures) and makes support troubleshooting inconsistent.

This PR standardizes default timeouts and retry policy in the Python SDK to match the v1 template safe defaults, adds documentation, and adds tests to prevent regressions.

Linked: ENG-4187 (shared config schema/validation), ENG-4186 (streaming stability smoke tests), PM-914 (safe defaults policy)

## What changed
### 1) New default timeouts
Adds a structured `RequestTimeouts` config with different defaults for streaming vs non-streaming calls.

Defaults (unless overridden by user):
- Non-streaming requests:
  - connect: 5s
  - read: 60s
  - write: 60s
  - pool: 5s
- Streaming requests:
  - connect: 5s
  - read: None (do not apply a per-read timeout to the stream body once established)
  - write: 60s
  - pool: 5s
  - initial_response_timeout: 30s (new; time to first byte / first SSE event)

Rationale: many user reports are “streaming disconnects / hangs” behind corporate proxies. Applying a read timeout to an established SSE stream creates false-positive timeouts during normal pauses; we instead enforce an initial response timeout and rely on connection lifecycle errors thereafter.

### 2) Standard retry policy + backoff
Adds a `RetryPolicy` config and standardizes behavior across endpoints.

Defaults:
- max_retries: 2
- backoff: exponential w/ jitter
  - base: 250ms
  - max: 4s
  - jitter: full jitter
- retryable conditions:
  - transport errors (connect errors, timeouts before response headers)
  - HTTP status codes: 408, 429, 500-599
- respect `Retry-After` header for 429 (seconds or HTTP date)
- non-retryable (explicit): 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 (and any response where a body has already been consumed)

Safety note (non-idempotent POSTs): we only retry when we can be confident the request was not processed (e.g., connection error before response headers). For streaming, we will not retry after receiving any bytes/events to avoid duplicate generations.

### 3) Clearer streaming retry semantics
- Streaming generator now tracks whether any SSE events have been yielded.
- If a disconnect happens before the first event, we may retry per policy.
- If a disconnect happens after the first event, we raise a `StreamingInterruptedError` with guidance to users (and include request id when present).

### 4) Docs + examples
- New doc page: `docs/usage/timeouts-and-retries.md`
- Updates to quickstart docs to describe:
  - default timeouts
  - default retries
  - how to disable retries (`RetryPolicy(max_retries=0)`)
  - how to tighten cost controls (lower `initial_response_timeout`, max_retries, and downstream app-level time budget)

### 5) Tests
Adds unit tests for:
- retry classification (status codes, transport errors)
- backoff and Retry-After parsing
- timeout wiring for streaming vs non-streaming
- streaming retry safety (no retry after first yielded event)

## Example usage
```py
from redwood_sdk import RedwoodClient
from redwood_sdk.config import RequestTimeouts, RetryPolicy

client = RedwoodClient(
    api_key=os.environ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"],
    timeouts=RequestTimeouts(
        non_streaming_read=30.0,
        streaming_initial_response=20.0,
    ),
    retries=RetryPolicy(max_retries=1),
)
```

## Migration / compatibility
- This is not intended to be breaking, but behavior will change for users previously relying on implicit “no retry” behavior.
- Users who need strict at-most-once semantics can set `max_retries=0`.
- Users who already pass an httpx client can still do so; we document how SDK timeouts interact (SDK config wins unless user opts out).

## Reviewer notes / discussion highlights
- Monica Patel (DevEx): requested that defaults exactly match template guidance and that docs mention how CLI `doctor` checks relate to timeouts/retries. Updated docs with a section “Troubleshooting: 429s and streaming disconnects” and linked to template troubleshooting language.
- Christine Wong (SRE): asked for explicit guardrails around streaming retries and clarification that we do not retry after partial streams. Added `StreamingInterruptedError` and tests covering “retry only before first event.”
- Brian Murphy (API ergonomics): flagged that gateway returns `Retry-After` in seconds and sometimes as date depending on upstream; added robust parsing and unit tests.
- Kaitlyn Nguyen (Security/auth): asked that auth failures (401/403) never retry and that error messages do not echo API keys. Confirmed non-retryable list and verified redaction in error formatting.

## CI
- ✅ lint
- ✅ unit tests
- ✅ mypy
- Initial failure: `test_streaming_retry_safety` flaked due to timing assumptions in a mocked async iterator; fixed by making the mock deterministic and re-ran CI.

## Checklist
- [x] Defaults align with template safe defaults (PM-914)
- [x] Streaming behavior safe (no duplicate generations after partial output)
- [x] Docs updated and linked from quickstart
- [x] Unit tests added

Merge: Squash merged to `main`.

Python SDK examples now include route-level quantization profile enablement (opt-in) and a verification pattern using debug resolution metadata.
Context: The Quantization Profile Library is opt-in and enabled at the route level via `quantization_profile_ref`. We’ve had repeated questions from design partners on (a) what the Python SDK call should look like for setting the route config and (b) how to confirm the profile actually applied (vs. policy fallback to baseline). This PR updates the Python SDK examples/snippets to show a full end-to-end flow: create/update a route with `quantization_profile_ref`, send a request through that route, and verify resolution by enabling debug metadata and checking the resolved `quant_profile_id`/outcome. What’s included: (1) New example: `examples/routes/enable_quantization_profile.py` showing `routes.update(...)` with `quantization_profile_ref="qpl:<model_id>:recommended"` and basic guardrails (try/except for incompatibility). (2) Added snippet to README + docs section clarifying semantics: `"default"` preserves baseline behavior; `"qpl:*"` is opt-in and may fallback if incompatible. (3) Verification guidance: enable debug resolution metadata and check `response.debug.route_resolution.quantization` fields (applied/fallback/disabled) plus the `quant_profile_id` when present. (4) Minor SDK typing/docstring updates in the `RouteUpdate` model to cross-link the feature and error behavior. Notes: This does not change any API surface area; it only updates examples + documentation to match control-plane behavior and the current debug payload shape from `redwood` PRs in the main repo. Follow-ups: once Console changelog + audit events are fully GA, we can add a docs link for “who changed what” and recommend correlating via request_id + audit logs.
Example (new):

route = client.routes.update(
    route_id="rt_123",
    model="llama-3.1-70b-instruct",
    quantization_profile_ref="qpl:llama-3.1-70b-instruct:recommended",
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    route_id=route.id,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize: ..."}],
    max_tokens=128,
    request_options={"include_debug": True},
)

q = getattr(resp, "debug", None)
if q and q.get("route_resolution"):
    quant = q["route_resolution"].get("quantization")
    # quant = {"outcome": "applied"|"fallback"|"disabled", "quant_profile_id": "qp_...", "reason": "..."}
    print("quant outcome:", quant)

Monica Patel: The example is great, but please avoid implying we’ll always return a quant_profile_id. When we fallback or when debug is off, it won’t be present. Can you update the snippet to show conditional checks and mention `include_debug` explicitly? Ibrahim Khan (author): Updated example to guard on debug presence and to print outcome + reason when fallback occurs. Also added a short note that without debug metadata you should rely on platform dashboards/audit logs for confirmation. Chloe Martin: The error handling text should match what the control plane returns for incompatibility. We’re using `incompatible_quantization_profile` with a remediation message (e.g., unsupported GPU class / max context). Can you update the docs copy to reflect that and not mention HTTP 409 specifically? Ibrahim Khan: Adjusted wording to avoid hardcoding status codes; example catches `RedwoodAPIError` and prints `e.code` + `e.message`. Alex Martinez: Please add a short callout in README: default behavior unchanged when field is unset or set to `default`, and this is opt-in per route (not tenant-global). Ibrahim Khan: Added callout under Routes -> Advanced configuration, plus link to the public docs PR for quantization profiles. Monica Patel: Approved after last pass. Chloe Martin: Approved.

Motivation: Prompt-set regressions are noisy — some regressions are low-impact (minor phrasing differences) while others are high-severity (safety or major quality drop). Existing CI gates treat all failures equally, producing noisy alerts and hard-to-interpret failures. This PR introduces a severity-calibrated probe that fuses multiple eval metrics into a single ordinal severity score, and wires a prioritized failover CI hook that uses that score to decide whether to soft-fail, block, or recommend an automatic failover to a designated fallback model or route.

What this changes (high level): commit 1 adds the probe implementation and a lightweight aggregator that accepts multiple metric adapters (accuracy delta, semantic-similarity drift, latency-penalty, toxicity spike). commit 2 implements a CI hook integration that runs the probe as part of nightly and pre-merge smoke checks and emits an actionable severity score and suggested failover policy. commit 3 adds unit and integration tests, calibration fixtures, docs and an example cohort.

Files touched (illustrative): src/probes/severity_probe.py — core probe and fusion logic; src/metrics/adapters/fusion.py — adapters and weight config; integrations/ci/severity_hook.yaml — CI hook definition and gating thresholds; tests/test_severity_probe.py — unit tests and edge cases; docs/guides/severity-probe.md — usage and calibration guide; examples/cohorts/priority_cohorts.json — sample cohorts used in nightly runs.

Key behavior details: the probe computes per-cohort metric deltas against a rolling baseline, normalizes each signal into a 0-1 impact score, and then applies a severity weight schedule to produce a 0-100 severity integer. Operators can configure three threshold bands: advisory (20), enforced-soft-fail (50), hard-block/auto-failover (80). The CI hook produces a structured summary and an ordered list of failover actions (recommendation -> canary route -> full route) along with confidence. The hook integrates with existing rollback/playbook workflows so that teams can opt into fully-automated failovers or manual review.

Small example (pseudo): 
probe.evaluate(cohort, baseline) -> {"severity": 67, "signals": {"quality_delta": 0.42, "toxicity_spike": 0.14, "latency_penalty": 0.11}, "recommended_action": "canary-route:fallback-v2"}

Tests and CI: first CI run revealed a flaky integration test for the baseline fetcher (transient network dependency). I converted the fetcher to a test-injected supplier and added a local baseline fixture; rerun passed. CI matrix summary: unit (pass), integration (pass after rerun), linter (pass), smoke (pass). There is a follow-up TODO to add a short-lived mock baseline service for deterministic test runs (ENG-832).

Review notes / conversation summary:

Summary: Implements the cross-language retry policy standard for the Python SDK: retry on 429 + transient 5xx + selected network/transport errors, exponential backoff with jitter, and proper Retry-After parsing (seconds and HTTP-date formats). Exposes configuration knobs on the client so customers can tune or disable behavior. Context: This is part of the SDK parity initiative (ENG-5120) to eliminate "works in TS but not in Python" inconsistencies, reduce support cases around intermittent 429/5xx/timeouts, and align SDK behavior with platform signals (Retry-After, request_id). Behavior (defaults): max_attempts=4 total (1 initial + up to 3 retries); retryable HTTP status codes: 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 (and 408 when the server responds with it); non-retryable: all other 4xx (e.g., 400/401/403/404/409/422) to avoid duplicate side-effects and billing confusion; retryable network errors: connect errors, DNS resolution errors, connection resets, TLS handshake errors, and read timeouts raised by the underlying HTTP client; backoff: exponential starting at 0.5s, capped at 8s, using jitter (full jitter by default) to reduce herd behavior; Retry-After: if present on a retryable response (notably 429), we honor it as the minimum delay, clamped to max_backoff to avoid extremely long sleeps in client code. Retry-After parsing details: supports integer seconds ("Retry-After: 5") and HTTP-date (RFC 7231 style). If the date is in the past or unparseable, we fall back to computed backoff. Config surface (new/standardized): ClientOptions: max_attempts (int), max_retries (int alias; deprecated warning if both set and disagree), initial_backoff (seconds), max_backoff (seconds), jitter ("full" | "none"), retry_on_status (list override), respect_retry_after (bool, default true). Request-level override: per-request options allow disabling retries (retries=0) for non-idempotent calls or workflows where the caller already handles retries. Notes on streaming: this PR does NOT add automatic retries for streaming responses. Streaming retries remain opt-in and should be implemented at the application layer with idempotency guidance (tracked separately); the retry middleware explicitly bypasses streaming iterators to avoid duplicating partial outputs. Implementation overview: Added a RetryPolicy abstraction used by both sync and async clients; implemented RetryAfterParser that accepts seconds or HTTP-date and returns a delay; integrated policy into the HTTP transport wrapper to centralize decision logic (status/network classification, sleep, attempt counting); ensured we propagate request_id into raised errors (when present) so callers can correlate retries with server logs; added unit tests using mocked responses and transport exceptions; updated docstrings and examples for configuration knobs and safe defaults. Files/areas changed (high level): redwood/_http/retry.py (new RetryPolicy + backoff), redwood/_http/transport.py (wiring), redwood/_client.py (options plumbed), redwood/errors.py (ensure request_id survives wrapping), tests/test_retry_policy.py, tests/test_retry_after.py, tests/test_transport_retries.py, docsstrings in client options and README snippets. Illustrative snippet (Python): options = RedwoodOptions(api_key=..., max_attempts=6, initial_backoff=0.25, max_backoff=10.0, respect_retry_after=True); client = Redwood(options=options) // client.chat.completions.create(...). Alternatively per-request: client.chat.completions.create(..., request_options={"max_attempts": 1}) to disable retries. Why these defaults: SRE guidance was to avoid retry storms under elevated 429s; honoring Retry-After and adding jitter is critical for protecting the gateway and improving tail latency. We intentionally do not retry 400-series validation errors to avoid duplicate actions and billing disputes (see SUP-29438). Testing: Unit tests cover: 429 with Retry-After seconds; 429 with Retry-After HTTP-date; malformed Retry-After; Retry-After in the past; 500/502/503/504 backoff increments and jitter; non-retryable 400 does not retry; transport exceptions (connect/reset/read timeout) retry; max_attempts respected; sleep is not invoked when retries disabled; streaming path bypasses retry wrapper. Rollout/compat: This changes default behavior for some callers who previously observed fewer retries (or immediate retries). Knobs are exposed; we also log a warning if legacy option names are used. Docs/migration notes will be updated in a separate docs PR for the cross-language parity release. Review notes: Ibrahim requested we clamp Retry-After to max_backoff (done) and ensure HTTP-date parsing uses timezone-aware values (done). Allison requested full-jitter by default and to document attempt counts (done). Marcus requested that we never log api_key values and that error messages mention configuration without printing secrets (no secrets logged; confirmed). Review conversation (highlights): Monica Patel: "Can we ensure Retry-After date parsing handles proxies that send RFC1123 with GMT?" Sabrina: "Yes, using email.utils.parsedate_to_datetime + UTC normalization; added tests." Ibrahim Khan: "Please avoid retrying 409s; TS had a bug retrying 400/409 and it caused duplicate side-effect concerns." Sabrina: "Confirmed: only 408/429 and 5xx per standard; added explicit test for 409." Allison Grant: "Default max_attempts=4 (3 retries) seems right; add jitter to reduce synchronization." Sabrina: "Implemented full-jitter; added note in docstring." CI: Initial run failed on lint (unused import in retry.py) and a flaky timing assertion in one test; fixed by mocking sleep and asserting call count/delays deterministically. Final checks: python-unit-tests (pass), lint (pass), typecheck (pass), packaging (pass). Merge: Squash merged into main; follow-up tickets: add conformance fixtures runner integration (ENG-5127) and update docs/migration notes (ENG-5128).
Python SDK now uses standardized retry defaults (429/5xx + network errors) with exponential backoff + jitter and respects Retry-After when present. New knobs: max_retries/max_attempts, backoff tuning, and a switch to disable Retry-After honoring. No API surface redesign; behavioral change is limited to defaults and is configurable.
payload.title: Standardize retry/backoff behavior + Retry-After handling (SDK parity v1)

Context: Customers have reported intermittent spikes in tail latency during auth refresh windows and long-running streaming sessions. This PR introduces (1) adaptive backoff profiles that automatically select conservative/optimistic retry windows based on recent error patterns and request criticality, (2) a streaming heartbeat auto-pause/resume mechanism to reduce noisy client-side reconnects during transient network blips, and (3) a cross-SDK delegated-auth failover that allows SDKs to transparently fall back to a delegated credential chain when primary token refresh fails. Motivation: improve end-to-end streaming stability and reduce cost from unnecessary retries while keeping SDK ergonomics consistent across Python/TypeScript/Go. Summary of changes: - Core: new backoff profile registry and runtime selector added to SDK core; backoff profiles are declarative and ship with three presets (conservative, balanced, aggressive) plus a telemetry-driven adaptive selector. - Streaming: introduce heartbeat auto-pause in streaming client: when transient connectivity or CPU stalls are detected the stream enters a soft-paused state (sends lightweight probe pings) and resumes automatically with a resume token to avoid full reconnect. - Auth: implement delegated-auth failover: SDKs attempt delegated credential chain (process-shared refresh, external credential provider hooks) when primary token exchange returns a 401/403 pattern indicating downstream auth service unavailability; this is pluggable and disabled by default. - Cross-SDK parity: behavioral parity tests and examples added for py/ts/go; unified configuration surface (ClientOptions.backoffProfile/backoffAdaptive/streamHeartbeat/windowMs/authFailover) to keep ergonomics aligned. - Telemetry: new metrics (sdk.backoff.profile_chosen, sdk.stream.pause_count, sdk.auth.failover_trigger) and logs at INFO/DEBUG for decision points. - Docs & changelogs: per-SDK changelog entries and updated quickstart snippet in docs/sdk-auth.md. Checklist: - [x] Design reviewed by ENG-2201 stakeholders; - [x] Unit tests for backoff selector (py/ts/go); - [x] Integration test harness: simulated 401 storm to validate auth failover; - [x] E2E stream stability test with network flakiness scenario; - [x] Telemetry events emitted and validated in local dev; - [x] Docs and changelog updated; - [x] Version bumps: py sdk -> 2.14.0, ts sdk -> 1.27.0, go sdk -> v1.5.4

Motivation: Tensor-parallel (TP) workloads with many small key-value lookups suffer measurable cross-node latency when communicating per-token KV slices via NCCL collectives, especially on 8+ node clusters with small per-request payloads. This PR introduces an optional NVSHMEM-backed shared slab for hot KV pages and a staged allreduce bridge that (1) reduces host-to-device handshake overhead for small shards, (2) lets nodes perform lock-free reads from a shared slab where hardware permits, and (3) performs a lightweight staged allreduce that only moves compacted/compressible chunks when full reduce semantics are not required immediately.

Design: - NVSHMEM shared-slab allocator: a contiguous slab region that holds hot KV pages in compressed (LZ4-lite) form. Slab metadata lives in a small NVSHMEM-resident header that uses sequence counters for wait-free handoff. - Read path: TP runtime probes NVSHMEM first for a KV slice; on hit it decompresses in-place and populates per-GPU cache lines without a full NCCL rendezvous. On miss, normal NCCL allgather/allreduce path executes. - Staged allreduce bridge: for gradient-less KV reads (inference-only), we use a size/entropy heuristic to decide between immediate NCCL allreduce for large/opaque shards vs. staged bridge for small/compressible shards. The staged bridge performs peer-to-peer NVSHMEM copy followed by a light aggregate step that uses an ephemeral CUDA kernel to merge chunked deltas. - Fallbacks: - If NVSHMEM is unsupported (older CUDA/driver) the runtime falls back to NCCL-only path. - If slab pressure is high, eviction demotes to NCCL path.

Implementation notes: - New components: src/runtime/collectives/nvshmem_bridge.cpp, src/runtime/kv/kvcache_shared_slab.{h,cpp}, src/runtime/kv/slab_eviction_policy.cpp - Heuristics tuned: compression threshold, chunk size (defaults: 32KB chunks, 12% entropy threshold), spin/timeout on NVSHMEM header prior to fallback. - Safety: sequence counters + epoch tags to ensure readers never see torn compressed headers; unit tests simulate concurrent reads/writes and NVSHMEM driver restarts.

Tests and CI: - Unit tests: tests/unit/test_shared_slab_eviction.cpp, tests/unit/test_nvshmem_header_consistency.cpp - Integration: tests/integration/test_nvshmem_kvcache.py runs a 4-node TP scenario in CI emulation (GHA job with loopback NVSHMEM sim) - Benchmarks: scripts/benchmarks/nvshmem_runner.py and perf results included under perf/nvshmem/ - CI: initial flake on Ubuntu-latest GPU job due to driver mismatch; pinned to CUDA 12.3 runner and rerun.

Performance: - 8x16-GPU TP cluster synthetic small-token stream: median per-token latency reduced 18% (from 12.3ms -> 10.1ms) and p99 reduced 22%. - End-to-end RLHF-ish chat eval (multi-turn, cache-friendly prompts): throughput improvement 14% and 11% lower inter-node bandwidth egress due to compression-aware chunking. - Microbenchmarks show NVSHMEM-hit latency for a 16KB shard ~40-60us vs NCCL-based gather ~210-260us.

Risks & mitigations: - NVSHMEM availability: guarded behind config flag and runtime autodetect. - Correctness: thorough deterministic tests and eviction/invalidation hooks; added a debug dump to verify slab contents post-merge. - Observability: added metrics (kvcache.nvshmem.hits, kvcache.nvshmem.evictions, kvcache.staged_bridge.count) and tracing spans for slab probes and staged merges.

Release notes: - Experimental NVSHMEM-backed shared KV slab and staged allreduce bridge to reduce TP inference latency for small shards. Opt-in behind --enable-nvshmem-kvcache flag.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc (docs/arch/collectives.md) - [x] Implementation - [x] Unit & integration tests - [x] Perf harness and baseline numbers - [x] Metrics and tracing changes - [x] Feature flag + fallback path

Ravi Menon: Added tombstone epoch and reclamation window (30s default) and a debug flag to force immediate reclamation for test harness.
Miguel Torres: The entropy threshold seems aggressive for some LLM datasets; can we expose it as a per-model knob and document safe defaults?
Ravi Menon: Exposed kvcache.compression.entropy_threshold and documented it in docs/arch/collectives.md. Benchmarks updated to show sensitivity sweep.
Lena Wong: CI emulation looks good. Please ensure the fallback path is exercised in our nightly matrix for older drivers.
Ravi Menon: Added nightly job entry 'compat-legacy-driver' that runs NCCL-only path to keep coverage.
Asha Patel: Approved after addressing the tombstone/reclamation window and metrics additions.
Miguel Torres: Approved.
Lena Wong: Approved.
Experimental: NVSHMEM-backed shared KV slab + staged allreduce bridge to reduce inter-node KV latency for tensor-parallel inference. Opt-in via --enable-nvshmem-kvcache. Falls back to NCCL when unsupported.
8x16 TP small-shard latency: median -18% p99 -22%; RLHF-chat throughput +14%; network egress -11% on small-shard workloads.

Summary: Adds customer/operator-facing documentation for key rotation in Redwood Private/Dedicated contexts, plus an audit-friendly evidence checklist that maps cleanly to common SOC2/ISO narratives. This PR is intended to reduce back-and-forth during enterprise security reviews by making our rotation steps and evidence artifacts explicit and repeatable.

Context / why: Regulated customers (and prospects) are asking for (a) a clear rotation procedure (including rollback criteria) and (b) the exact evidence they can expect to produce/receive (who approved, what changed, when it happened, what logs prove it). This doc set aligns with the ongoing KMS hardening effort and the rotation strategy in ADR-008.

What’s included: 1) New page: “Key rotation procedure (KMS envelope encryption)” covering prerequisites, roles/responsibilities (Customer vs Redwood), staged rollout, dual-read window, cutover, verification, and rollback. 2) New page: “Rotation evidence checklist” that can be used as a runbook attachment and as audit evidence. Includes templates for a rotation log entry, required screenshots/exports, and pointers to audit log event types. 3) Updates to navigation + cross-links from the Private KMS Operator Guide and Security FAQ sections to reduce discoverability issues.

Audience: Private operators, SRE/on-call, Security/GRC reviewers, Sales/SE support during enterprise security reviews.

Notes on scope: This is documentation-only and does not introduce new technical behavior. It references implementation behavior that is landing in the core repo (dual-read support, audit log events, healthchecks). Where behavior differs between Hosted vs Private, we call it out explicitly.

References: - ADR-008 (Key rotation strategy: dual-read window + cutover criteria) - Linear: ENG-4826 (evidence artifacts), PM-913 (customer expectations), ENG-4821 (initiative epic) - Support: SUP-19405 (customer evidence request / cutover questions)

Content highlights (key decisions captured in docs): - Rotation cadence: documented as customer-driven (typical quarterly/annual), with Redwood providing a repeatable procedure + evidence artifacts; the doc avoids committing to a universal cadence but includes guidance and defaults used in regulated deployments. - Dual-read / dual-decrypt window: documented as the recommended approach to avoid hard cutovers; includes a minimum observation window and explicit cutover criteria (error-rate and decrypt-mismatch signals). - Rollback: explicitly documented; includes triggers (e.g., elevated KMS errors, decrypt mismatches) and the fastest safe rollback path (toggle to prior key version + keep dual-read during investigation). - Evidence: checklist enumerates approvals, change tickets, timestamps, config diffs, audit log exports, and validation outputs from installer preflight (Private).

Screenshots/examples: Redacted examples are included (ARNs, tenant IDs, regions). Please flag anything that looks too close to production formatting.

Test plan: - Local docs build: `pnpm install && pnpm build` - Link check: `pnpm lint:links` - Preview reviewed in Netlify: see CI checks.

Checklist: - [x] Reviewed with Security (terminology + evidence expectations) - [x] Reviewed with SRE (rollback triggers + operational steps) - [x] Reviewed with Product (customer-facing positioning) - [x] Added cross-links from Private KMS operator guide - [x] Added “last reviewed” footer + owners for ongoing maintenance

Follow-ups (not in this PR): - Once PR redwood/pr-18541 lands, update evidence page to include final audit log event names/fields (placeholders included). - Once dashboards ship (observability-pack/pr-844), add a “Verification dashboards” subsection with canonical panel links per environment.
Elliot Price (Docs) 2025-11-09: The structure reads well. Two requests: (1) move “Evidence checklist” earlier in the page so operators see it before step-by-step; (2) add a small “Who does what” table (Customer vs Redwood vs Joint) to reduce ambiguity in Private deployments.

Kira Thompson (author) 2025-11-09: Done. Evidence checklist is now linked at the top and the responsibilities table is added under “Prereqs and ownership”.

Marcus Lin (Security Eng) 2025-11-10: Please tighten language around ‘fallback’ during KMS outage so it doesn’t imply we can decrypt without KMS. We can degrade availability and preserve correctness, but we should not suggest bypassing KMS. Also, add a note that key disable/delete is treated as an incident and requires Security escalation.

Kira Thompson 2025-11-10: Updated. The outage section now states: no bypass; behavior is fail-closed for decrypt, with bounded retries/circuit breaker to avoid storms. Added escalation note for key disable/delete.

Olga Petrov (Compliance) 2025-11-11: Evidence checklist looks good. Can we explicitly call out acceptable substitutes when a customer cannot share screenshots (e.g., export from SIEM / audit-log-exporter)? Also add a “Retention” line for what we recommend customers retain.

Kira Thompson 2025-11-11: Added “acceptable substitutes” under each evidence row + a retention recommendation section. Kept it phrased as guidance, not policy.

Add a stepcontrolled RAG playbook and TypeScript tool-negotiation sample to demonstrate deterministic step boundaries and structured tool selection for reproducible RAG workflows.
Provide a composable quickstart that reduces cognitive load for teams wanting deterministic, auditable RAG flows with clear telemetry and evaluation hooks.
Introduce a lightweight scenario-driven RAG playbook (stepcontrolled flow) and TypeScript agent samples demonstrating tool-negotiation patterns. Useful for quickstarts, authoring labs, and reproducible e2e tests.
Context: Teams building RAG-enabled agents often need examples that show predictable control over step execution, structured clarification turns, and graceful tool fallback. This PR introduces a compact 'stepcontrolled' playbook pattern and accompanying TypeScript agent examples that demonstrate a negotiation-style tool-calling protocol (tool-negotiation) for multi-tool workflows.

Motivation: Existing quickstarts show tool-calling and retrieval, but they assume either fully-committed tool selection or free-form agent decisions. For production workflows (customer-facing assistants, regulated decision flows), we need deterministic step boundaries and explicit negotiation signals so downstream systems can assert invariants and instrument SLAs. The new materials lower onboarding time for teams that want reproducible stepwise debugging and telemetry hooks.

What this PR adds: (single continuous description) - docs/rag/stepcontrolled-playbook.md: narrative and reference for the stepcontrolled pattern, state model, and telemetry hooks (prefix, step tokens, assertion points). - examples/agents/ts/tool-negotiation-sample/: a minimal TypeScript agent shim that performs retrieval, proposes candidate tools, negotiates a single tool selection via a structured clarification turn, and executes with retries and fallback. - examples/agents/ts/tool-negotiation-sample/README.md: quickstart and local run instructions (devcontainer + env example). - static/images/stepcontrolled-lifecycle.svg: architecture diagram showing sequencing, KV cache checkpoints, and telemetry probes. - docs/snippets/stepcontrolled-eval.yaml: an example evaluation scenario (step assertions) for the harness. - site config update to add new quickstart tile and SEO metadata.

Checklist: - [x] Author docs and examples - [x] Add unit smoke for TS example (local run) - [x] Lint docs (mkdocs) - [x] Add schematic evaluation snippet - [x] Add telemetry probe points to diagram

Notes and links: - Linear: ENG-6124 for design and ENG-6125 for the TS shim implementation. - Local reproduction: follow README in the TS sample; it spins a local mini-index and an in-memory tool stub. - This PR is intentionally small in runtime scope but aims to be a composable pattern for larger authoring kits.

Files changed are small and targeted; no runtime library changes are included in this PR. For adoption guidance, see the final section in docs/rag/stepcontrolled-playbook.md.

Context
We need consistent, queryable analytics for the public benchmark landing page + interactive table so Marketing Ops can report on benchmark launch KPIs (engagement → signup/demo) and Sales can see top-of-funnel intent signals. This PR adds client-side instrumentation for the key interactions called out in PM-826.

What this PR does
- Adds a small benchmark-specific event schema (packages/analytics/src/events/benchmark.ts) and emits events from the benchmark page UI.
- Emits events for:
  - Filter changes (model, region, context length bucket)
  - Metric toggle changes (latency/$ vs p95 latency vs $/1M tokens)
  - Export clicks (CSV, JSON)
  - CTA clicks (Start free trial, Request demo, Dedicated sizing)
- Normalizes payload fields so downstream dashboards don’t require bespoke parsing.
- Includes basic payload validation + unit tests to prevent accidental breaking changes.

Event names + payloads
All events are emitted via the existing `track()` client wrapper and include the common context (session_id, page_path, referrer, utm_* where present).

1) benchmark_filter_change
- model: string | null
- region: string | null
- context_length_bucket: one of ["<=2k", "2k-8k", ">8k"] | null
- metric: one of ["latency_per_dollar", "p95_latency_ms", "cost_per_1m_tokens"]

2) benchmark_metric_toggle
- from_metric: string
- to_metric: string

3) benchmark_export_click
- export_format: one of ["csv", "json"]

4) benchmark_cta_click
- cta: one of ["start_trial", "request_demo", "dedicated_sizing"]
- destination: string (relative URL)
- placement: one of ["hero", "sticky", "below_table"]

Implementation notes
- We debounce filter-change emissions by 250ms so quick successive toggles don’t generate a burst of events.

- We gate tracking behind `PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ENABLED` and no-op in local dev unless explicitly enabled.
- Export events fire on user click (not on file download completion). CSV/JSON generation is client-side; there’s no server callback to measure completion reliably.

Testing

  2) Change model + region filters → see benchmark_filter_change with expected payloads
  3) Toggle metric → benchmark_metric_toggle
  4) Export CSV/JSON → benchmark_export_click
  5) Click each CTA → benchmark_cta_click

Motivation: We observed repeated narrow-window capacity cliffs when fleet decommits (especially spot preemptions and aggressive autoscaler decommits) coincide with tenant bursts. Existing warm-pool logic reacts too late and the Dedicated scheduler can experience transient throughput loss and higher tail latency. This PR introduces two complementary components: (1) a reservation slack hedger that tracks per-pool and per-tenant decommit risk and computes a small proactive buffer (slack hedge) to keep a minimal prebaked warmlet pool; (2) a warmlet pre-bake provisioner that pre-provisions short-lived, pre-bound warmlets that are non-billable until attached, and which are safe to preempt when actual demand materializes.

Summary of changes: adds a hedger controller that computes an EWMA-based decommit-rate and a zone-aware slack ratio; integrates hedger signals into the provisioning planner; implements warmlet pre-bake lifecycle and a minimal runtime integration so runtime will attach warmlets with KV cache warmup hints. Exposes telemetry: slack_hedge_ratio, warmlet_prebake_count, warmlet_prebake_reap_rate, decommit_ewma_1m. Adds unit + integration tests and a migration note for dedicated capacity configs.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked (Linear ENG-3120)
- [x] Unit tests for hedger logic
- [x] Integration test simulating spot preemptions and tenant bursts
- [x] Telemetry dashboards updated (Grafana/telemetry config)
- [x] Migration: default slack_hedge_ratio set to 0.02 (2%) for existing pools

Commits: ["hedger: initial EWMA decommit estimator and config (ae4f3c)", "planner: consume hedger signal and reserve buffer slots (b1c2d7)", "warmlet: pre-bake lifecycle and GC safety (d9e1a5)", "telemetry: expose hedger and pre-bake metrics (f3b2c1)", "tests: integration scenario for preempt+burst (c7a9b0)"]

Files changed (high level): ["pkg/autoscaler/hedger.go", "pkg/provision/warmlet_prebake.go", "pkg/planner/reservation_planner.go", "telemetry/metrics_registry.go", "integrations/tests/prebake_decommit_scenario.yaml", "docs/dedicated/migrations/slack-hedger.md", "pkg/autoscaler/hedger_test.go"]

Small representative snippet (from hedger.go): "func computeSlack(decommitEWMA float64, targetSLO float64) float64 {\n    base := math.Min(0.05, decommitEWMA*1.2) // conservative cap at 5%\n    return math.Max(0.0, base - (targetSLO * 0.1))\n}\n" — the implementation is in the repo; snippet above is illustrative.

Testing and CI: initial CI run failed integration due to timing flake in prebake GC; fixed by adding jitter and stronger timeouts. Final pipeline: build: pass, unit tests: pass, integration: pass, lint: pass. Deployment plan: gradual rollout behind feature flag (provisioner.enabled=false by default). We will enable on a small dedicated pool subset in canary, watch slack_hedge_ratio and warmlet_prebake_reap_rate for GC pressure.

Rollout and safety: hedger computes conservative default slack (2%) and will never allocate beyond a configurable hard cap per-pool. Prebaked warmlets are preemptible and tracked separately from regular reservations to avoid billing surprises. If the hedger detects sustained low utilization, it scales prebakes to zero automatically.
New hedger controller (pkg/autoscaler/hedger.go) computes per-pool decommit EWMA and outputs slack_hedge_ratio
Reservation planner consumes slack signal and reserves buffer slots in reservation_planner.go
Warmlet prebake lifecycle implemented (pkg/provision/warmlet_prebake.go) with safe GC and preemption semantics
Telemetry metrics and dashboards added (telemetry/metrics_registry.go, docs)
Integration tests simulating spot preemptions and sustained bursts added
Arjun Patel (reviewer): Nice approach. Question: what unit is decommitEWMA in? seconds? fraction? Please clarify and add bounds checking so it can't produce NaN.
Maya Chen (author): decommitEWMA is a fraction (decommits per slot per minute normalized). Updated comments and added NaN guard in computeSlack; added unit tests that exercise zero and extremely high decommit rates.
Sofia Rivera (reviewer): Integration test was flaky; observed prebake GC race where a warmlet was double-reaped when a preempt and GC coincided. Can we add a CAS guard or move to optimistic locking?
Maya Chen (author): Switched GC to use staged state transitions with CAS and added random backoff jitter. Integration test updated to surface race deterministically; CI green now.

Maya Chen (author): Added Grafana alert in docs/migrations and wiring to existing alerting team.
Introduce reservation slack hedger and optional warmlet pre-bake provisioner. Default hedger slack set to 2% per-pool. Feature gated; enable via provisioner.enabled and hedger.* configs. Improves resilience to sudden decommits and reduces transient throughput loss.
Feature rolled out behind feature flag. Default behavior for existing customers is unchanged. Ops runbook added to docs/dedicated/runbooks/prebake-hedger.md explaining knobs, observed metrics, and rollback steps.

Small ergonomic API changes to the TS streaming client, parity fixes for credential throttling across Go/Python SDKs, and default retry-window tuning. No breaking changes for existing call sites.
Summary: This PR harmonizes a lightweight credential-throttle (reauth backoff) across the TypeScript, Go, and Python SDKs and adds a compact streaming resilience surface to the TS SDK so calling code can opt into connection-level fallbacks without pulling in heavyweight session machinery. Motivation: In high-concurrency server scenarios we observed auth storms where token refreshes triggered reconnect cascades; the goal here is an ergonomic default that reduces thundering reauths and provides parity for streaming ergonomics across SDKs.

What changed (high level):
- TypeScript: introduced StreamController API (opt-in) that centralizes reconnect/backoff + graceful resume. Exposes .pause(), .resume(), .on('fallback', cb).
- Cross-SDK: added credential-throttle window config (default 10s) to prevent concurrent refresh attempts for the same credential id. Implemented in TS and mirrored in Go/Py helpers.
- Retry tuning: default backoff profiles tightened for small-token workloads (reduce tail latency under steady load).
- Tests & docs: unit + integration tests for throttle behavior; updated SDK changelogs and a short migration note.

Checklist: [x] design doc linked (ENG-2029) [x] unit tests added [x] integration smoke test against the canary runtime [x] docs/migration note [x] changelog entry

Commits (summary):
- a7f3b22 add StreamController: compact API for pause/resume and fallback hook; initial tests
- c1d9f88 implement credential-throttle and backoff profiles; cross-sdk spec updates
- e3b9a07 docs: migration note, changelog, and test flakiness fixes

Files changed (high level):
- packages/sdk-ts/src/stream/controller.ts (new) -- 120 LOC core controller with internal state machine
- packages/sdk-ts/src/stream/index.ts (expose new API surface)
- packages/sdk-ts/tests/stream/credential-throttle.test.ts (new)
- packages/common/auth/credential_throttle.ts (shared spec + TS impl)
- packages/sdk-go/internal/cred/throttle.go (mirror implementation)
- packages/sdk-python/redwood/cred/throttle.py (mirror implementation)
- docs/sdk/migration/ts-stream-controller.md (migration notes)
- examples/ts/stream-resume-sample.ts (usage snippet)

Small TS usage example (illustrative):
const controller = client.streamController({ credentialId: 'svc-12', throttleWindowMs: 10000 });
const s = controller.openChat({ model: 'redwood-compact' });
s.on('fallback', (meta) => console.warn('fallback to polling', meta));
await s.start();
// caller can pause/resume during backoffs

Review conversation (high level and truncated):
- Sofia Martinez (reviewer): "Nice compact surface. Please prefer explicit naming for the 'fallback' event payload and document lifecycle edge cases (server-initiated close vs network blip). Also suggest adding a short integration test that simulates concurrent refreshes."
- Arjun (author): "Addressed: renamed payload to { reason, previousState }, added integration test that spawns 8 concurrent clients sharing a credential id; added comments explaining server-initiated close semantics."
- Lukas Weber (reviewer): "LGTM modulo a small comment on the backoff constants; prefer exponential capped at 5s for initial window."
- Arjun: "Adjusted profile to cap at 5s per Lukas + updated changelog to call out the tuning."
- Maya Chen (approver): Approved after CI green and integration run stable.

CI and checks:
- lint (TS): pass
- unit tests (TS): pass
- integration tests (TS-canary): initially one flaky failure (stream-resume-sample) -> rerun -> pass
- go unit tests (cred throttle): pass
- python unit tests (cred throttle): pass
- cross-sdk smoke: pass

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: callers relying on undocumented streaming internals might behave differently if they depend on implicit reconnect semantics. Mitigation: StreamController is opt-in; default client behavior unchanged. Added migration doc and examples.
- Risk: throttle misconfiguration could delay legitimate refreshes. Mitigation: default window conservative (10s) and opt-out via config.

Merge strategy: squash and merge. Reasoning: small set of cohesive commits; simplifies git history.

Post-merge actions:
- cut minor patch on TS SDK (v1.7.3) with migration note (handled by release pipeline)
- announce in #sdk-updates with example snippet and recommended config for high-concurrency servers

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps the TS API minimal — the goal is parity-level ergonomics without pushing session lease semantics into the default surface. Follow-ups planned to: (1) expose metrics hooks for throttling events, (2) add a lightweight CLI diagnostic for credential storms, (3) measure real-world impact on Dedicated capacity customers.

Add a fractional session replay wizard to docs: interactive playground + example sessions. Enables engineers to replay segments of RAG conversations for deterministic debugging, reproduce model/tool interactions, and attach telemetry slices. No breaking changes; opt-in feature behind docs playground flag.
Motivation: debugging RAG flows is often noisy — developers asked for a way to replay narrow time windows of an agent/session (a few turns, or a particular tool call) without rerunning upstream index/ingest or exposing full production traces. This PR introduces a fractional session replay wizard in the docs playground: a small web UI + backend helper that can load a saved session, let users select a fractional time range or token window, and step through generation + tool calls with deterministic inputs.

What this PR contains (high-level):
- docs/playground guide: new page explaining the replay wizard UX and best practices, with screenshots and annotated flow.
- interactive playground: embeds a JS replay player that fetches trimmed session JSON and drives a stepper UI.
- examples: three sample RAG sessions (simple Q/A, multi-tool booking flow, and a failure reproduction).
- SDK integration example (TypeScript): shows how to produce a session envelope that the replay player consumes.
- telemetry hooks: small metrics emitted for replay start/stop, fraction selected, and tool-call replayed counts.
- tests: headless puppeteer test that runs the player in CI and asserts deterministic outputs for the provided sample session.

Checklist:
- [x] Add docs page and frontmatter with redirect to playground
- [x] Add replay player JS + minimal CSS and accessibility labels
- [x] Add three example session JSON files
- [x] Add TS SDK example + README snippet
- [x] Add telemetry config for replay metrics
- [x] Add integration test and CI job entry
- [x] Add release note entry in changelog

How it works (short):
1) A session JSON is a simple envelope: metadata, turn list, tools invoked (with deterministic tool inputs/outputs), and model seeds.
2) The replay wizard accepts a fractional range (e.g., 0.22-0.37 of the session timeline) or absolute turn indices.
3) The replay player trims the envelope server-side (so we only transfer the slice) and then replays deterministically in the browser by feeding each step to the local stepper runtime. For tool calls, the player can either show recorded outputs or re-invoke them via a sandboxed stub if the developer opts-in.

Backward compatibility / rollout:
- The feature is opt-in in the docs playground via a "replayEnabled" flag. No runtime changes required for hosted inference. The SDK example shows how to annotate sessions but does not modify existing production telemetry.

Testing & QA notes:
- Added puppeteer integration test that loads the player, selects the fractional slice for the multi-tool sample, and asserts the UI step output matches expected recorded outputs.
- Manual QA: cross-browser smoke for Chrome/Edge and keyboard-only navigation for accessibility.

Links and references:
- Example sessions stored under examples/rag/replays/
- Docs preview: https://docs.redwood.com/rag/playground/replay-wizard (internal preview)
- Linear: ENG-2149 (design + prototype), PM-1884 (product acceptance)

Known limitations:
- Replay currently supports only sessions produced by the new session envelope schema (SDK example included). Older session formats will require a lightweight migration script (tracked in follow-up).
- Tool re-invocation in sandbox mode is limited to stubbed adapters (do not use with live production tool endpoints).

Merge notes: squash-merged to main. The feature is gated behind the docs playground flag; marketing will be notified before public posts.

Introduces a latency-aware reservation hedger that proactively adjusts tenant commitments to preserve p99 latency SLOs and a utilization harvest agent that emits sampled, windowed metrics for downstream billing and autoscaler decisions.
Context: customers on Dedicated have reported p99 latency regressions during mid-size surges even when overall utilization looked healthy. Root cause: reservation allocation was blind to tail-latency pressure and the autoscaler reacted too late, causing cascading warm-pool exhaustion. This change introduces two cooperating components: 1) LatencyBackedReservationHedger (controller) that watches p50/p90/p99 latency windows and temporarily reduces soft commitments for low-priority tenants and 2) UtilizationHarvestAgent which produces windowed, TTLed utilization fingerprints (per-tenant, per-pool) consumed by the hedger and billing. Goals: prevent latency regressions, reduce recovery churn, and provide stable telemetry for autoscaler decisions. Design highlights: - hedger observes latency histograms (10s/60s/5m windows), converts to an urgency score, and applies soft commitment deltas respecting tenant SLAs and policy guardrails; - harvest agent emits compact HDR sketches and delta snapshots at configurable cadence and supports sampled export to remote telemetry backends; - both components are non-blocking and configuration-driven with safe defaults; - added e2e and unit tests; - backward compatible: feature gated by a config flag and safe by default. Checklist: [x] design doc linked (linear ENG-2891) [x] unit tests for hedger and harvest agent [x] integration test that simulates surge and verifies p99 bound [x] docs/ops updated with tuning guidance [x] feature gate + rollout plan [ ] dark launch to 20% of dedicated clusters (follow-up).

Motivation: Private deployments have accumulated ad-hoc GPU nodepool and IAM wiring across clusters. This PR factorizes GPU nodepool definitions into a tenant-scoped module (gpu_nodepool/namespace) and adds a composable cross-account IAM bindings module that centralizes principals for KMS/HSM and bastion access. It also formalizes a state layout (state_schema_version = "v2") to make per-environment, per-cluster, per-tenant state prefixes explicit and provides a small tfstate-migrator helper to move state without manual terraform state mv invocations.

Scope: single PR touching Terraform modules only (no application code). Changes target private deployment workflows used by the installer and by on-prem operator teams. The change set includes module API changes, docs, examples, and an opinionated migrator script to ease rollout.

Checklist:
- [x] Factorize gpu_nodepool into modules/gpu-nodepool/tenant_namespace (variables: tenant_id, env, cluster, gpu_profile)
- [x] Introduce modules/iam/cross-account-bindings with configurable principals and binding types (kms, hsm, bastion, service-account)
- [x] Add state schema variable state_schema_version and backend_prefix helper (default: v2)
- [x] Provide scripts/tfstate-migrator (Go binary) and state/migrations/README.md with migration plan
- [x] Update examples/private-deploy/* and add example for tenant layout
- [x] Run unit/integration terraform fmt/lint and a gated e2e that provisions a tiny private cluster in our test account

Compatibility and upgrade path:
- This is backwards-compatible at runtime but will require operators to run the migrator when switching to state_schema_version=v2. The migrator supports a dry-run mode and will generate the required terraform state mv commands for manual review.
- Variable rename notes: previous top-level gpu_pool_name becomes scoped as tenant_gpu_pool_name; mappings updated in examples. A short conversion table is in docs/upgrade-notes.md.

Migration steps (operator-facing):
1) Checkout branch and run make migrator-build to produce scripts/tfstate-migrator
2) ./tfstate-migrator --from-prefix="envs/old-layout" --to-prefix="envs/v2/clusterX/tenantY" --dry-run > planned-moves.txt
3) Review planned-moves.txt, then re-run without --dry-run to apply (or apply individual terraform state mv commands)
4) Update terraform backend config to set state_schema_version = "v2" and apply module changes

Testing and validation:
- Added unit tests that validate module variable schemas and local values (tests/terraform-unit)
- CI pipeline: terraform fmt -> tflint -> terraform init/validate -> gated e2e that runs the migrator in dry-run mode and creates a short-lived test instance (tests/e2e/private-cluster-alloc.yaml)

Rollout considerations:
- Staged rollout recommended: pick one non-production environment, run migrator, validate state, then proceed to prod clusters.
- The cross-account IAM bindings module intentionally separates the target principal list from binding creation to avoid accidental privilege escalation; reviewers should validate principal lists before apply.

Related work: ENG-5121 (tenant isolation for GPU pools), ENG-5248 (state hygiene and tfstate tooling).

Notes: This PR intentionally does not change RBAC policies beyond what's necessary for binding creation. A follow-up will land a Helm tweak in the private-installer to consume tenant-scoped names from the new module outputs.
Introduce tenant-scoped GPU nodepool module and a reusable cross-account IAM bindings module; add state schema v2 and a tfstate migrator helper. Upgrade notes included — operators must run migrator before applying new modules. No runtime behavior changes expected but terraform var names changed for tenant scoping.

## Summary
This PR introduces a new **Quickstart Templates** section in the docs IA and updates navigation to make templates discoverable from the main sidebar and from relevant SDK pages.

Primary goal: reduce “where do I start?” friction by giving users a single place to find template options (RAG + agents first), and a clear path to either (a) use GitHub template repos directly or (b) use the template CLI.

## Motivation / context
DevEx is shipping production-minded quickstart templates (safe defaults, streaming robustness, observability hooks). The docs currently surface examples and SDK guides, but there is no dedicated landing area for templates, and no consistent navigation route from SDK pages.

This PR is the docs-side IA plumbing to support:
- A top-level landing page for templates
- A small set of child pages (initially stubbed/linked) that will be filled in by follow-up PRs
- A canonical link to the `redwood-quickstarts` repo and CLI installation instructions

Context: The original runtime PR (redwood#44782) introduced an ergonomic multi-tool execution surface with deterministic tool result injection, per-tool retry policies, streaming markers, and an OpenAI compatibility shim. Since that merge, the runtime implementation and SDK helpers have had a small round of follow-up adjustments (naming and defaults) that left the docs in the monorepo slightly stale for customers reading the docs site. This PR updates the docs site to reflect the current shipped surface while preserving notes about legacy/compat behavior.

What changed in the documented API: 1) Mode naming: docs now describe the primary parallel mode as mode="parallel" (with deterministic injection) and call out that mode="parallel-safe" remains accepted as a legacy alias in 1.14.x for compatibility; 2) Header naming for the OpenAI shim: docs now recommend header "X-Redwood-Tool-Execution: parallel" and note the previous header "X-Redwood-Tool-Exec" as deprecated but still recognized; 3) Streaming event schema: docs now show the normalized SSE/JSON event envelope where the event type field is "type" with values tool_start/tool_delta/tool_end/injection_point (the runtime renamed tool_chunk -> tool_delta); 4) Concurrency defaults: docs now reflect the runtime default orchestrator concurrency of 8 workers (previously 4) and document ORCHESTRATOR_CONCURRENCY as the override, including guidance for private deployments.

Updated examples (docs-only): The request envelope examples remain centered on the top-level tool_execution field and deterministic injection, but the snippet is updated to avoid implying that clients must set inject_results explicitly. Example shown in docs: {"input":"Translate and summarize","tool_execution":{"mode":"parallel","tools":[{"name":"translate","idempotency_key":"tx-123","retry":{"max_attempts":2,"backoff_ms":200},"stream":true},{"name":"summarize","retry":{"max_attempts":1}}]}}. The docs also add a small mapping table for OpenAI-style function_call payloads explaining how tool_call_id maps into Redwood tool identifiers and how ordering is stabilized.

Idempotency and retries clarification: The docs now state that idempotency_key is required only when a tool is declared side-effectful (side_effects=true) and retries are enabled (max_attempts > 1), matching current validator behavior; purely read-only tools may omit idempotency_key even when retries are enabled. The docs also clarify that the server may downgrade parallel execution to sequential when it detects ambiguous side effects or missing idempotency, and that this downgrade is surfaced via a response field in the tool execution summary (documented here; no code changes in this repo).

Migration notes: Added a short section "Upgrading from early-access docs" describing the deprecated mode/header names, and explicitly noting that older clients that send mode="parallel-safe" and/or header "X-Redwood-Tool-Exec" will continue to work during 1.14.x but are planned for removal in a future major release.

Testing/CI: Docs build and link checks pass; updated snippets are validated by the docs-site JSON snippet linter. No runtime code changes included.

Follow-ups: A separate runtime PR will add a dedicated response schema reference page (generated OpenAPI) so the event examples stay in sync automatically; tracked in ENG-6014.
Docs refresh for multi-tool execution: updates examples to match current runtime behavior (mode name, header name, event schema), clarifies idempotency requirements for side-effectful tools, and documents default concurrency change (4 -> 8) plus env var override. No product behavior changes introduced by this PR; docs only.
Priya Kapoor: Please make it explicit which names are deprecated vs current (mode + header) and add a one-line timeline for removal.
Maya Chen (author): Added a "Deprecated" callout box for mode="parallel-safe" and header "X-Redwood-Tool-Exec" and noted "supported throughout 1.14.x; removal no earlier than 1.16".
Alejandro Ruiz: The idempotency rule here contradicts the original PR text (it used to require idempotency_key for any side-effectful tool). Can we confirm current behavior and cite it accurately?
Maya Chen (author): Confirmed in runtime validator: idempotency_key is required when side_effects=true AND retries enabled; updated wording and added an example of server downgrade to sequential when missing.
Nina Patel: The streaming event example should show the exact field names clients should key off of; avoid prose-only descriptions.
Maya Chen (author): Added a concrete JSONL snippet with fields: type, tool_name, tool_call_id, seq, timestamp, and payload.

## Summary
This updates our tool calling documentation to match the canonical cross-SDK semantics (as implemented in the refreshed examples) and adds a “Known pitfalls” section based on recent support + SE feedback.

Primary goals:
- Reduce copy/paste failures from outdated payload shapes.
- Make streaming + tool calls understandable across languages (esp. partial args + final assembly).
- Set expectations around parallel tool calls and safe handling of tool results.
- Point readers to runnable, maintained examples.

## What changed
- Rewrote the Tool calling guide to:
  - Use consistent terms: “tool definition”, “tool call”, “tool arguments”, “tool result message”.
  - Show the recommended message loop: user -> assistant (tool calls) -> tool result messages -> assistant (final).
  - Clarify when to validate arguments (before executing tools) and how to surface validation errors back to the model.
- Added a new “Known pitfalls (read this if things look flaky)” section covering:
  1) Partial tool arguments while streaming
     - Tool args may arrive as incremental deltas; do **not** JSON-parse until you have the final assembled args.
     - Recommendation: buffer tool_call.arguments text by tool_call_id, parse on completion, validate schema, then execute.
     - Explicit callout linked to SUP-18421 (truncated args mid-stream) and the workaround pattern.
  2) Parallel tool calls
     - Multiple tool calls can be requested in a single assistant turn; examples show iterating all tool calls and returning tool results for each.
     - Guidance: preserve tool_call_id, return results as separate tool messages, and avoid interleaving tool output with assistant text.
  3) Type/shape mismatches across languages
     - Added a short “shape” section explaining the stable fields we document and where SDKs differ in naming/typing.
     - Callout to SUP-18452 (TS type mismatch) and the updated TS example.
  4) Retry and failure handling
     - Guidance on tool execution failures (timeouts, non-200s): return a structured error payload as tool result, then allow the model to retry or choose a fallback.
     - Warning: do not silently drop tool failures; it produces confusing assistant behavior.
- Linked runnable examples:
  - Added “Try it now” links to redwood-examples streaming+tools sample (PR: redwood-examples#311) and referenced the quickstart template refresh (redwood-quickstarts#204) as a full app.
  - Added a short “Expected console output” block so readers know what success looks like.

## Files / pages touched (high level)
- docs/guides/tool-calling.mdx (major rewrite)
- docs/guides/streaming.mdx (small x-link + note about partial tool args)
- docs/reference/api/chat.mdx (terminology alignment + link to guide)
- docs/partials/known-pitfalls-tool-calling.mdx (new)
- sidebars + nav (moved tool calling to sit next to streaming + structured output)

## Screenshots
- N/A (content-only). Code tabs were verified manually.

## Test plan
- `pnpm install && pnpm build` (passes)
- `pnpm lint` (passes)
- `pnpm test:links` (passes)
- Manual:
  - Verified code tabs render for Python/TypeScript/Go and copy button works.
  - Clicked all new outbound links (examples + quickstarts) and ensured correct anchors.

## Notes for reviewers
- This PR intentionally avoids introducing new API semantics. It documents the canonical pattern already agreed in DevEx and implemented in the SDK/example refresh.
- If any page suggests we guarantee valid JSON in streamed tool arguments, please flag—this is explicitly not guaranteed.

## Review conversation highlights
- Elliot Price: Requested we move “Known pitfalls” higher on the page and add a one-sentence warning about parsing partial JSON during streaming. (Done)
- Ibrahim Khan: Asked for explicit guidance on buffering args by tool_call_id and parsing only on completion to prevent truncated-args bugs. (Added + linked SUP-18421)
- Brian Murphy: Requested a short, concrete parallel-tool example and clarification that tool results must be separate tool messages, not assistant text. (Added)
- Dana Lo: Requested TS wording change from “function call” to “tool call” and a note about runtime validation even with static types. (Updated)

- link-check

Motivation: Customers running multi-tenant workloads asked for stronger cross-tenant audit correlation for incident investigations while still preserving tenant isolation guarantees. Separately, operator teams want an auditable KMS escrow path to support emergency decrypt workflows for regulated customers. This PR delivers a small, backwards-compatible RBACv2 stabilization pass plus a new audit correlator service and a lightweight KMS escrow attestation flow.

What this PR does: - Adds an audit correlator that augments existing audit events with stable correlation keys (hashed claim fingerprints + region pin) to make multi-service traces joinable without leaking tenant-identifying metadata. The correlator lives as a library and an optional sidecar to keep runtime opt-in. - Introduces a KMS escrow attestor component that records escrow requests to the audit log, ties them to an operator attestation token, and attaches sealed metadata so downstream auditors can validate the request timeline. No plaintext key material is stored. - Stabilizes several RBACv2 decision code paths: reduces decision cache jitter (deterministic key ordering), adds stricter deny-before-allow evaluation for operator-scoped bindings, and hardens temporal grants evaluation to respect region pinning flags. - Adds operator-facing docs and runbook (docs/operator/escrow-and-correlation.md) describing escalation, attestation token minting, and how audit proofs are validated during postmortems.

Implementation notes: - The correlator computes correlation_key = HMAC_SHA256(service_claims_fingerprint || region_pin || correlation_salt_v1) and emits correlation_key as an opaque hex string in audit metadata (field audit.corr_key). This design intentionally avoids tenant IDs or other PII. - KMS escrow attestor integrates with existing kms/allocator package via a new EscrowManager interface; the implementation only records a sealed envelope (kms.escrow.envelope_ref) in the audit log and submits a verified attestation record to the compliance indexer. - RBACv2: decision engine changes are limited to four functions in pkg/authz/rbacv2/engine.go and the in-memory cache eviction policy; the public API surface is unchanged. All new feature flags are behind feature gates: feature.audit_correlator and feature.kms_escrow.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for correlator hashing and envelope sealing - [x] Integration test that exercises a simulated operator escrow request and verifies audit envelope contents - [x] RBACv2 deterministic ordering tests - [x] Documentation and runbook added - [x] Feature gates added and defaulted to off for Dedicated and Private by config

Rollout plan: - Merge to main in squash, enable feature flags in canary clusters for a week, run the escrow e2e with compliance team, then enable correlation-only in hosted read-only telemetry pipelines, and only enable full escrow in Dedicated/Private with an operator onboarding checklist.

Backwards compatibility: Correlation key is optional metadata; existing consumers ignore unknown audit fields. Escrow attestation is guarded by feature gate and a tenant-level allowlist; no customer KMS operations change unless explicitly opted in via the operator runbook.

Security considerations: - Correlator design is reviewed with privacy and SRE: it never emits tenant identifiers and correlation_salt_v1 is derived per-deployment and rotated quarterly. - Escrow requests mandate operator attestation (MFA-backed) and are rate-limited; audit envelopes are signed with the service signing key. - RBAC changes intentionally shift deny-evaluation earlier; tests and a brief canary were run to ensure no regressions in common flows.

Follow-ups (future PRs planned): - telemetry consumer to index correlation_key for faster cross-service queries - administrative UI for escrow request lifecycle (approval/deny) - automated audit proof replay tool to validate escrow envelopes during DR scenarios

Related work: Linear: ENG-2104 (audit-correlator), SEC-987 (escrow-attestation); references: docs/arch/audit-design.md and pkg/kms/README.md.
