Summary: This PR updates internal and external documentation to reflect Redwood’s tiered reliability commitments for Hosted (shared) vs Dedicated (reserved capacity) and the associated error budget policy. It explains (a) canonical SLIs and SLO targets at a high level, (b) how to interpret error budget status in Console and what it means operationally, and (c) escalation expectations and what data is required for support/SRE triage. Motivation: We’ve had repeated customer escalations around latency spikes and 5xx/stream disconnects during burst traffic, plus confusion about what counts against SLOs (client aborts, invalid requests, rate-limits, fallback/retries). This PR consolidates and standardizes wording across docs site pages used by CS/SE and customers. Scope: Hosted + Dedicated only; Private is mentioned as future work and explicitly out-of-scope for enforcement in this phase. Contents included in this PR: Tiered SLO overview page with definitions (SLI vs SLO vs SLA), tier scope, and in-scope endpoints (chat/completions, embeddings, streaming). Error budget explainer page: reporting window, what “budget remaining” means, burn-rate alerting concept (multi-window), and common misunderstandings (e.g., a short spike can be OK if it doesn’t materially burn budget). Streaming reliability section: what counts as a streaming failure, how we distinguish server disconnects vs client aborts, and how retries/fallback are accounted for. Escalation guide: for Hosted vs Dedicated, expected response path, when an event becomes an incident, and the required intake fields (timestamps, region, model, request IDs, and whether it was streaming). Console guidance: where to find the SLO dashboards, how to filter by tier/region, and how to interpret annotations (deploys/incidents). Non-goals: This PR does not change SLO targets themselves, does not publish contractual SLA language, and does not add new product UI—only docs updates and alignment. Notes on terminology: We intentionally use “SLOs (internal)” vs “SLAs (contractual)” and call out that exclusions may differ between internal measurement and contract language. Where possible, we reference the source-of-truth internal policy pages and keep the external pages focused on customer comprehension. Checklist: [x] Hosted vs Dedicated definitions reviewed by PM Hosted + PM Dedicated; [x] Streaming failure accounting reviewed by SRE; [x] CS escalation path reviewed by CS leadership; [x] Links to runbooks/status comms policy added for internal readers; [x] Added examples and ‘what to send Support’ snippet for common cases (latency spikes, elevated 5xx, stream disconnects).
From site/docs/reliability/streaming-reliability.mdx: "We classify streaming as unsuccessful when the server terminates the stream with an error (5xx) or the connection drops before a terminal event is sent. Client-initiated aborts (client closes connection) do not count against SLOs when reliably detected via gateway abort signals."
From site/docs/reliability/error-budgets/index.mdx: "Error budget is the allowed unreliability over the rolling window. A transient spike may page on burn-rate, but only sustained burn consumes budget materially. When budget is exhausted for a tier/region, non-emergency releases may be frozen until mitigations restore budget trajectory."
From site/docs/support/escalations/_intake-template.mdx: "Required: UTC timestamps, region, tier (Hosted/Dedicated), endpoint (chat/completions/embeddings), model, streaming yes/no, 3–5 request IDs, and whether retries/fallback were enabled."
Aisha Bello (SRE) 2026-02-13: The streaming section is close, but please be explicit about what we do with 499s and client disconnects. We should avoid implying we always detect client aborts perfectly—word it as 'when reliably detected' and point to request IDs for ambiguous cases.
Elliot Price (author) 2026-02-13: Good call. Updated wording to 'when reliably detected via gateway abort signals' and added a note that ambiguous disconnects should be escalated with request IDs so SRE can classify using traces.
Nikhil Sharma (PM Hosted) 2026-02-14: For Hosted, can we avoid listing hard numbers for latency SLOs here? I’d prefer the external doc to describe measurement and expectations, and link to the Console dashboard, otherwise we’ll have to keep this perfectly in sync with internal targets.
Elliot Price (author) 2026-02-14: Adjusted: removed explicit percentile targets from external page; kept them in internal-only docs (linked) and described 'tiered latency percentiles' at a conceptual level. External page now focuses on how to interpret dashboard + what we do during incidents.
Lauren Bishop (PM Dedicated) 2026-02-14: Dedicated customers will ask 'is fallback allowed' and 'does fallback count as success'. We need a crisp statement: fallback may occur to maintain availability, but latency may be impacted; SLI accounting is based on what the customer sees at the API boundary.
Elliot Price (author) 2026-02-15: Added a 'Routing/fallback and SLI accounting' section: success/latency are measured end-to-end at the API boundary; internal retries/fallback do not get special treatment, and the customer-visible outcome is what counts.
Jasmine Liu (VP CS) 2026-02-15: Escalation expectations look good, but add a clear split: Dedicated escalations route to Enterprise on-call and can trigger tier-specific incident comms; Hosted uses standard support SLAs unless there’s broad impact.
Elliot Price (author) 2026-02-15: Added tier-specific routing language and a short table: 'Who to contact / what happens next'. Also linked internal status/comms guidelines for CS/SE.
Sean Gallagher (Dir SRE) 2026-02-16: Please add a paragraph about burn-rate alerts vs incidents. Customers will see 'budget is burning' in conversation and assume outage. We need a definition: burn-rate = early warning; incident = declared based on impact thresholds and duration.
Elliot Price (author) 2026-02-16: Added 'Burn-rate alerts are internal early-warning signals' section + example scenarios. Also added wording to avoid overpromising comms for brief burns that auto-mitigate.
Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering) 2026-02-16: Minor: ensure we have a single canonical link we can send to customers asking 'how do you measure reliability'. Right now there are three pages.
Elliot Price (author) 2026-02-16: Added a short 'Start here' block on tiered SLO landing page and ensured the support/escalation page references it as the canonical entry point.

Context: Teams building retrieval-augmented generation pipelines asked for a concise, modular playbook that shows iterative authoring patterns, versioned prompt sets, and a lightweight 'tool-factory' sandbox for creating and testing tool-call stubs locally without spinning up full backend services. Motivation: reduce onboarding friction for product and infra engineers by providing a single-playbook flow that demonstrates best practices for incremental indexing, structured output checks, telemetry probes, and safe tool-calling patterns. What this PR changes: 1) Adds a modular playbook page that walks through stages: project bootstrap, index strategy, prompt families and canary evaluations, stepwise debugging with replayable traces, and rollout guidance for canary->gradual->global; 2) Adds a sandboxed tool-factory guide and sample stubs in TypeScript that run as an in-process mock server and a CLI to bind tools to an agent persona; 3) Adds diagrams and an SVG flow that can be embedded in the docs site; 4) Adds a small quickstart script that creates a seeded local index, runs the agent against a canned dataset, and emits structured evaluation artifacts for comparison. Implementation notes: This is docs-only with code samples under docs/authoring-studio/examples and a tiny shell helper under docs/snippets; samples are intentionally small and non-production to avoid accidental reuse as operational code. The playbook emphasizes incremental evaluation: seed->simulate->assert->rollout. Checklist: - [x] Playbook draft written and reviewed by product - [x] Tool-factory sample implements two example tools (search-stub, calculator-stub) and includes interface docs - [x] Quickstart script tested locally on macOS and Linux WSL - [x] Accessibility pass on new diagrams - [x] CI docs lint passing Commits: 4 commits: initial playbook scaffold and outline; add tool-factory TypeScript stubs and README; add quickstart script, diagrams and examples; docs polish and typo fixes. This PR is intentionally conservative: examples are sandboxed and non-networked by default to avoid exposing credentials or running services in CI.

Summary: This PR updates public documentation to introduce Redwood’s workload-aware batching defaults and the three customer-facing latency SLO tiers: fast, standard, and cost-efficient. It explains what each tier optimizes for, how Redwood selects a profile, how to choose a tier per route/use case, and how to override defaults (Hosted API request-level, route-level policy, Dedicated tenant/cluster override). It also adds a troubleshooting checklist focused on common post-migration issues (tail latency spikes, streaming jitter, throughput vs latency trade-offs, and override precedence confusion). Motivation: We’re rolling out tiered batching defaults in runtime 1.22; customers need a clear mental model and concrete examples so they can adopt defaults safely without accidentally degrading streaming UX or overpaying for throughput. Scope of docs changes: Adds a new conceptual page “Batching tiers (SLO defaults)” under Performance → Inference tuning; Updates API reference to document `batching_tier` parameter and the corresponding request header; Updates Python/TypeScript examples to show tier selection for chat (streaming) vs batch summarization; Adds “How defaults are chosen” section with high-level signals (prompt length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming, concurrency) and an explicit note that Redwood does not do per-tenant real-time autotuning in this release; Adds FAQ: what happens if you don’t pick a tier (answer: standard by default, unless your route policy pins a tier); Adds Dedicated-specific notes on override precedence and where to view the effective tier in Console; Adds troubleshooting checklist and a short decision tree for latency vs cost issues. Key guidance included: Tier definitions (customer-facing): fast: prioritizes tail latency protection for interactive experiences and streaming; standard: balanced defaults for mixed workloads; cost-efficient: prioritizes throughput/$ per token with higher batching aggressiveness while maintaining published targets under typical loads. How to choose: fast for streaming chat endpoints, agent loops, user-facing autocomplete; standard for most APIs and mixed usage; cost-efficient for offline/batch jobs (summarization pipelines, embeddings at scale, rerank batches) and non-interactive endpoints. Overrides: Hosted API: per request via SDK parameter `batching_tier="fast"|"standard"|"cost_efficient"` (and header `X-Redwood-Batching-Tier` for raw REST callers); Route-level: policy config in Console/route configuration (documented as recommended for consistency and auditability); Dedicated: tenant/cluster override (documented precedence: customer override > route policy > platform default). Troubleshooting: If p99 increases after switching to fast: verify endpoint is actually set to fast (effective tier), check concurrent requests per route, ensure streaming is enabled for UI, and consider reducing concurrent tool calls or switching heavy routes to standard. If streaming feels “bursty”: confirm you’re using streaming responses end-to-end, and understand that tier selection affects queuing/batching but not token content; if UI jitter persists, fast tier is recommended and you may need to lower client-side chunk aggregation. If cost-efficient causes queueing: move interactive routes back to standard/fast, or apply cost-efficient only to batch routes; if you need both, split routes or create two policies pointing at the same model with different tiers. If overrides don’t seem to apply: check precedence (Dedicated override vs route policy), and confirm you’re not mixing request-level tier with a pinned route policy (docs now call out the behavior explicitly). Notes/limitations called out: Tiers are SLO defaults, not a guarantee for all workloads; workloads with extreme prompt lengths or highly bursty concurrency may still need route-level tuning or capacity adjustments; Tier selection does not change logging/retention or data handling; it only affects runtime scheduling/batching behavior; In overload, Redwood may apply backpressure and/or degrade gracefully; docs reference standard retry/timeout guidance rather than exposing internal modes. Rollout coordination: Copy aligns with Hosted API messaging and runtime rollout. Console screenshots are intentionally minimal in this PR (design is still landing), but we added textual pointers to where users can view ‘effective tier’ and ‘why this profile’. Related work: Runtime tiered defaults (runtime 1.22) and SDK parameter support are being shipped in parallel; this PR links to the example snippets that match the upcoming SDK releases. Testing: `docs:build` and `docs:linkcheck` passing; ran `npm test` for docs site; verified code samples compile (TypeScript) and run (Python) against current SDK APIs on main.
Elliot Price (review): Please avoid wording that implies a hard guarantee; recommend “targets” and “designed to meet” rather than “will meet.” Also add a short “what happens if I don’t pick a tier” FAQ.
Wei Chen (author): Updated tier language to “targets”/“designed to meet published latency targets” and added FAQ clarifying default is standard unless pinned by route policy. Pushed commit `docs(troubleshooting): add default behavior FAQ`.
Henry Cho (review): The parameter naming needs to match SDKs. Are we standardizing on `cost_efficient` in APIs but “cost-efficient” in UI copy? Please ensure the doc shows both and mentions accepted aliases (if any).
Wei Chen (author): Updated API reference to show `cost_efficient` value and the docs copy uses “cost-efficient” in prose. Added note: “SDKs accept `cost_efficient`; Console shows ‘cost-efficient’.” No aliases documented beyond header name.
Lauren Bishop (review): Dedicated section needs a clear precedence example. Customers keep mixing tenant override and per-request tier and then assuming per-request wins.
Wei Chen (author): Added a dedicated callout box: “Precedence: Dedicated override > route policy > request-level.” Included an example table with three scenarios and the effective tier.
Aisha Bello (review): Troubleshooting checklist should include what metrics to look at in Console (p95/p99, queue depth, batch size). Keep it high-level but actionable.
Wei Chen (author): Added “What to check” bullets: latency percentiles by route, queueing indicators, and batch size distribution. Avoided internal metric names; kept it Console-facing.
Sofia Ivanova (review): In the “How defaults are chosen” section, please explicitly state the selection considers streaming vs non-streaming and prompt length distribution (already in design), but don’t over-specify the scheduler knobs.
Wei Chen (author): Done—added a short paragraph on inputs/signals and removed the earlier mention of specific wait budgets/max batch tokens.
payload.title: Docs: explain batching SLO tiers (fast/standard/cost-efficient), defaults, overrides, and troubleshooting

Motivation: Our single-path CI (monolithic lint -> unit -> integration -> release smoke) has grown slow and brittle. Developers hit 10+ minute feedback loops for trivial lint or dependency changes, and dependency churn has caused transient infra failures that block work. This PR introduces a lightweight CI operator gate and sharded fast-feedback lanes to reduce iteration time while preserving safety for release branches.

What this PR does (high-level): - Add a small, idempotent CI operator job (scripts/ci/operator_gate.py + action) that validates dependency snapshots, checks action SHAs, and gates heavy pipelines on a preflight pass. The operator also tags PRs with "fastpath-eligible" when only safe files change. - Split the default workflow into three lanes: fastpath (lint + unit tests + dep-scan, targeted), runtime-sharded integration (integration tests split by runtime: runtime/cpu, runtime/gpu, runtime/quant), and full-nightly (heavy e2e and long-running sanity). Fastpath runs in <6m for most changes. - Move lint to a hermetic container image (tools/lint-runner) to reduce flakiness from host variations and cached node_modules. - Introduce a dependency-snapshot manifest (build/dep-snapshot.yaml) and an action that verifies package-lock / yarn.lock / go.sum consistency against the snapshot on PRs touching dependency files. - Pin a small set of composite actions and add an action-sha verifier to CI operator to reduce surprising upstream action changes. - Add small UX: GitHub PR comment bot summarizing which lane ran, and clear rerun instructions for flaky integration shards.

Why this is different from prior CI refactors: Rather than stitching more steps into the same monolith, this change introduces an operator/gate coupled with explicit fast/slow lanes and a small amount of metadata on PRs to decide routing. The aim is to cut developer wait time for ordinary changes while keeping a conservative path to catch regressions for releases.

Commits (summary): - commit 1: add ci operator script, basic verification and labeling - commit 2: split workflows into .github/workflows/ci-fastpath.yml and ci-sharded-integration.yml - commit 3: add tools/lint-runner Dockerfile and hermetic lint entrypoint - commit 4: dependency snapshot manifest and lockfile verifier action - commit 5: pin composite actions and add action-sha-verifier - commit 6: PR comment reporter and docs updates in docs/ci/fast-feedback.md

Files changed (high level examples): - .github/workflows/ci-fastpath.yml (new) - .github/workflows/ci-sharded-integration.yml (new) - .github/workflows/ci-nightly.yml (tweaks) - .github/actions/operator/entrypoint.sh (new small wrapper) - scripts/ci/operator_gate.py (new) - tools/lint-runner/Dockerfile (+entrypoint.sh) - build/dep-snapshot.yaml (new manifest) - docs/ci/fast-feedback.md (new doc) - package.json / go.mod touched in a couple of microservices (to update lock verification flow)

Testing and CI behavior: Initial run: fastpath showed ~40% reduction in median feedback time. On the first CI run, dep-scan failed due to two packages missing a checksum in our snapshot; fixed in commit 4. Integration shards were flaky on the first run (gpu shard timed out); added a retry wrapper and lowered parallelism for the GPU shard which stabilized subsequent runs. CI check matrix summary: - fastpath (lint, unit, dep-scan): pass - integration-shards (cpu, gpu, quant): cpu: pass, gpu: flaky->pass after retries, quant: pass - nightly/long-e2e: unchanged and scheduled - action-sha-verifier: flagged two out-of-date composite actions (pinned them).

Review conversation (abridged, included in the PR body for audit): - Arjun Rao (reviewer): "High-level: love the operator approach. Two asks: 1) can we document the exact criteria for fastpath-eligible files? 2) the operator scripts should be idempotent and not race the label bot." - Maya (author): "Answered: added explicit path patterns in docs/ci/fast-feedback.md and added a tiny ledger file in /tmp on the action runner to avoid duplicate labeling." - Lena Ortiz: "Can you make lint-runner image smaller? The current image is ~600MB; suggested drop build tools and use multi-stage." - Maya: "Addressed via a multi-stage Dockerfile and alpine-based final image, now ~160MB." - Tomás Delgado: "Integration shards look good; please add an alerting threshold for shard flakiness so we can detect regressions." - Maya: "Added a metric export to the console agent for shard-failure-rate (metrics/ci/shard_failure_rate) and configured an alert in SLO tooling (slo/alerts)." - CI bot: initially failed dep-scan -> author fixed and pushed commit, CI retried and passed; reviewers re-approved.

Release notes (user-facing): "Developer CI: reduced median PR feedback time by introducing a fastpath CI lane and an operator gate that validates dependency snapshots and action SHAs. Lint runs use a hermetic runner; integration tests are sharded per runtime. No behavioural changes to production code."

Backwards compatibility and risks: - This is a CI infra change only; does not change runtime or model-serving code. - Risk: new operator adds another moving piece; mitigations: operator logic is intentionally tiny, runs as a read-only verifier for main branches until a 2-week burn-in where it will be allowed to gate by label. - Risk: sharded integrations may hide cross-shard interactions; mitigations: keep nightly full-e2e and add a post-merge job that runs a compact cross-shard smoke set for merged PRs.

Follow-ups (small): - Add a dashboard showing fastpath vs slowpath throughput and median feedback time (ENG-2312). - Migrate a few more repos (redwood-sdk-python, redwood-examples) to the same operator pattern in a follow-up.

Related work: ENG-2241 (CI workstream), ENG-2312 (fast-feedback metrics), and previous CI hygiene PRs that pinned action SHA lists.

Merge: Squash-and-merge after final approvals.

Arjun Rao: please document fastpath file criteria — added docs/ci/fast-feedback.md
Lena Ortiz: reduce lint-runner image size — switched to multi-stage alpine image
Tomás Delgado: add shard flakiness alert — added metric export and SLO alert rule
CI Bot: initial dep-scan failed due to missing checksum; addressed in commit 4; rerun passed
Hotfix risk: operator initially runs as advisory for 2 weeks before full gating
Fastpath eligibility: changes limited to docs, frontend CSS, single-service non-dep files, and tests (pattern list in docs)

This PR publishes the customer-facing Release Notes taxonomy/style guide for model/version changes and adds concrete examples to reduce ambiguity around breaking vs non-breaking changes. This is intended to be the canonical reference for (a) Redwood Docs writers editing generated notes, (b) engineers authoring metadata change summaries, and (c) PM/Support reviewing public wording. The guide is aligned with the changelog generator categories and explicitly calls out redaction rules (public vs internal) so we don’t repeat the incident where incomplete/internal notes were briefly published. Scope: docs-only content and IA updates; no generator code changes in this PR. Includes: category definitions (Security / Breaking / Deprecation / Quality / Performance / Bugfix), severity language guidance, “what changed/why/risk/rollback” structure, and a breaking-change decision tree focused on API/contract compatibility (tokenizer, structured output schema, tool calling behavior, safety filters, prompt-format expectations). Also includes a set of example release notes for common events: version promotion, tokenizer bump, quantization profile change, runtime requirement change, rollout rollback, and deprecation announcement. Follow-ups: (1) link this guide directly from the release note preview artifact output (redwood PR-18452), (2) add a short checklist to the reviewer template in redwood-model-registry. Screenshots: not applicable (content-only).
Elliot Price (review): Can we be explicit that “Performance” claims must be phrased as relative/typical and not guarantee numbers unless backed by published benchmark methodology? Also please add an example of acceptable wording vs unacceptable marketing language.
Wei Chen (author): Added a subsection under Performance: “allowed phrasing” + “not allowed”. Also added an example note that says “typical latency improved in our internal eval harness” and explicitly calls out that results vary by prompt/sequence length.
Marissa Cole (review): Breaking-change definition needs to match what Console will surface. Specifically, if a model’s tool-calling schema tightens validation (e.g., enum restriction), that is breaking even if the endpoint is the same. Add that example + mention rollback guidance requirement.
Wei Chen (author): Added a breaking example under Structured Output / Tool Calling and updated the template section to require a “Rollback / mitigation” line for Breaking + Deprecation categories.
Connor O'Brien (review): Please add a checklist we can link in review flows: category chosen, severity chosen, “what changed/why/risk/rollback”, redaction verified. Also please mention that notes are generated from metadata/events and editors should avoid inventing details not present in the artifact.
Wei Chen (author): Added a short “Reviewer checklist” section and an “Editing generated notes” section that explicitly discourages adding details not present in the generator artifact; editors can clarify language but shouldn’t introduce new claims.
Naomi Feldman (security review): Good start. Add a clear list of prohibited content examples: internal incident IDs, specific customer names/accounts, internal-only metrics thresholds, vendor/hardware SKUs when it could reveal deployment topology. Also note that security-related changes must not imply exploitability details unless cleared.
Wei Chen (author): Added “Do not include” bullets + example redactions. Added note: Security category wording should be high-level unless Security approves expanded disclosure.
Kira Thompson (review): For Private customers, the ‘version’ they see may be an upgrade bundle. Can we add one example showing how we phrase notes that map to a bundle and mention that rollout timing differs by deployment mode?
Wei Chen (author): Added an example under Rollback/Upgrade: “Private bundle 2025.10.2 includes model X promotion…” and a line in the guide: “Availability and rollout timing may differ across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.”
Elliot Price (final): Approved. Please ensure PR-9312 references this guide from the landing page.
Wei Chen (author): Done in this PR by adding cross-links from release-notes/index.md.
Docs: New Release Notes Style Guide with categories, severity language, and breaking-change rules
Docs: Added example release notes for common model/version change events
Docs: Added redaction guidance for public vs internal change details

Context: Lifecycle growth experiments sprint is rolling out onboarding email v2 + in-console nudges. Our current Hosted API quickstart path doesn’t match the new CTAs (email + console) and we’re seeing confusion around “where do I create an API key?” and “what’s the fastest first request?”. This PR updates the onboarding docs so the docs, lifecycle emails, and console nudges all point to the same activation steps.

What changed: (1) Reworked Hosted API quickstart landing page to an explicit checklist: Create API key (Console) → Make first request (copy/paste snippet) → Enable streaming → View usage dashboard. (2) Added dedicated “First successful request” section with minimal curl + SDK examples aligned with the email CTA. (3) Updated internal links to console pages used by nudges (API keys, usage) so the docs match the console surface. (4) Added UTM-safe guidance for lifecycle CTAs (docs links do not hardcode campaign UTMs; emails can append UTMs). (5) Clarified common failure modes (“missing/invalid API key”, “403 due to org role”, “no tokens counted yet”) and point to the appropriate troubleshooting page.

Why: Reduce time-to-first-token (TTFT) and reduce early dropoff between signup → API key → first request. Also ensures messaging consistency with Soojin’s approved onboarding guidelines (latency/cost/reliability framing).

Notes/guardrails: No pricing language changes. No change to tracking pixels or retargeting tags. All outbound links remain first-party; lifecycle UTMs are appended by the email system.

Screenshots: N/A (docs-only).

Test plan: (a) Preview docs build locally, (b) validate all links (including /console deep links) and ensure no broken anchors, (c) run markdown lint.

Context: INT-3321 reported that the language code tabs on the Streaming guide stopped switching content (clicking "Python"/"TypeScript"/"Go" updated the tab UI but the code blocks did not change). This started after the recent CodeTabs refactor that moved tab state into a shared hook and introduced per-page persisted language preference.

Root cause: the tab selector was reading the selected tab value from localStorage (e.g. "typescript") while the rendered tab list used display labels (e.g. "TypeScript") and a different `data-tab` attribute. After hydration, the hook would treat the stored value as invalid, fall back to default, and then subsequent clicks only updated the tab header state (not the underlying code block visibility), because the querySelector used the wrong attribute.

Fix: normalize to a single canonical key (`python` | `typescript` | `go`) across: (1) the tab button `value`, (2) code block `data-language`, and (3) persisted localStorage key. Also ensure the DOM update runs after hydration and targets only the nearest CodeTabs container so multiple tab groups on a page don’t interfere.

What changed:
- CodeTabs now uses `value` keys and renders `data-language` consistently.
- `usePreferredLanguage()` sanitizes localStorage values (unknown/legacy values -> default).
- CodeBlock wrapper applies an explicit `data-language` on the outer container (not the inner pre), which fixes selector brittleness across MDX transformations.
- Added a Playwright regression test that loads the Streaming guide and asserts tab switching actually changes the visible code content.

Before/after screenshots:
- Before (broken): docs/_screenshots/INT-3321-before.png
- After (fixed): docs/_screenshots/INT-3321-after.png

Test plan:
- Local: `pnpm install && pnpm dev` then open /guides/streaming and click language tabs; verify code content switches and the copy button copies the visible tab content.
- Persistence: select Go tab, refresh page, confirm Go remains selected.
- Multiple groups: verify tab switching in one group does not change other groups on the page.
- E2E: `pnpm test:e2e tests/code-tabs.spec.ts`.

Notes:
- This PR is intentionally scoped to the selector/state mismatch + regression coverage. It does not change the docs content or example text beyond ensuring tab keys match the conventions we use in the updated streaming/tool calling guides.
Elliot Price: Confirmed repro matches INT-3321 and asked to ensure multiple tab groups on one page don’t conflict. Wei Chen: Scoped DOM updates to the closest `.rw-code-tabs` container and added a test case with two groups.

Kira Thompson: Requested alignment with docs terminology: use lowercase keys internally but preserve display labels (“TypeScript”, “Python”, “Go”). Wei Chen: Kept display labels as-is; only internal `value` keys are normalized.

Sahana Iyer: Asked for a regression test to prevent reintroducing the selector mismatch during future MDX/theme changes. Wei Chen: Added Playwright spec asserting visibility toggles and copy-button correctness for the active tab.

Brian Murphy: Sanity check that this doesn’t change example semantics for streaming/tool calling docs refresh. Wei Chen: No content changes; purely UI plumbing + selector stability.

Approvals: Elliot Price, Sahana Iyer. Merged after green CI.
Docs site: fixed language code-tab selector regression on Streaming guide and other tabbed code blocks; added e2e coverage to prevent recurrence.

Added a new `docs/contrib` section with contribution-ready RAG playbook templates, a community playbook index, and a lightweight test harness for template validation. No runtime or API changes.
Context & motivation: external contributors frequently open PRs adding RAG playbooks and agent examples, but onboarding and review are slow because (1) there is no standardized template for playbooks, (2) examples often omit structured-output contracts and test harnesses, and (3) docs lack a discoverable index for community-contributed templates. This PR introduces a contrib playbook index and a set of contributor-facing templates and validation helpers to reduce review friction and improve quality for community-submitted RAG artifacts.

What this change does: adds a new `docs/contrib/` section and example assets under `examples/rag/contrib-templates/`. Key contents: * docs/contrib/README.md — overview and contribution guide tailored to RAG templates (how to write a playbook, required metadata, linting rules). * docs/contrib/playbook-index.md — searchable index of contributed playbooks with metadata schema and tagging guidance. * examples/rag/contrib-templates/stepwise-playbook-template.yaml — a canonical stepwise RAG playbook (tool binding examples, timebox annotations, telemetry probes). * examples/rag/contrib-templates/contracted-agent-example.ts — small TS agent stub with structured-output schema and inline tests. * tools/rag-template-validator/ — lightweight node-based harness that validates front-matter, structured-output contracts, and runs local smoke interactions against the Redwood test shim. * docs/snippets/structured-output-linter.md — docs describing how to opt-in to structured output linting and add CI checks.

Commits (high-level): * 3d4b9e4 — initial scaffold: add docs/contrib README and index page + placeholder metadata schema * 8c2a1b7 — add stepwise-playbook-template.yaml and agent stub example * b5f7c12 — integrate rag-template-validator with README usage and add small test fixtures * d1aef45 — apply feedback: clearer metadata fields, examples for telemetry probes, tidy copy + unit tests for validator harness

Files changed (high level): * docs/contrib/README.md (new) * docs/contrib/playbook-index.md (new) * docs/snippets/structured-output-linter.md (new) * examples/rag/contrib-templates/stepwise-playbook-template.yaml (new) * examples/rag/contrib-templates/contracted-agent-example.ts (new) * tools/rag-template-validator/package.json, index.ts, tests/* (new) * website/sidebar.json (updated to expose contrib section) * .github/workflows/rag-template-ci.yml (new lightweight CI job that runs validator on PRs under examples/rag/contrib-templates)

Small illustrative excerpt (playbook front-matter): "---
title: 'Customer-support RAG playbook (stepwise)'
tags: ['support','faq','agent']
author: '{{contributor_name}}'
outputs:
  - name: resolution_summary
    type: structured
    schema: '{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"summary\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"ticket_id\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}'
---\"

Review conversation summary: * Ethan Morgan (reviewer): "Love the validator harness. Please add a short migration note in the playbook-index for existing examples we already host." — addressed in d1aef45 with an added paragraph in playbook-index.md. * Lena Cho: "Can you provide a TypeScript example showing function/tool-calling with explicit output contracts?" — added contracted-agent-example.ts and inline comments, responded in the PR thread. * Marco Ruiz: requested a smaller CI job matrix to keep exec time low; updated .github workflow to run the validator first and only run smoke interactions on label 'run-smoke'. * Reviewer approvals: Ethan approved after changes, Lena approved with minor comments left as TODOs.

CI summary: * Lint: pass * Docsite build: pass * rag-template-validator tests: initially one flaky fixture failing (smoke-interaction), re-ran and fixed race condition in tests — final status: pass * GitHub Actions: new workflow rag-template-ci triggered on examples/rag/contrib-templates changes; validated on this branch.

Security & compliance: No secrets or infra changes. The validator runs only local mock interactions against the Redwood test shim; it does not call any external hosted model endpoints by default. Contributors can opt into live-run smoke tests via explicit label, which is documented.

Backward compatibility & migration: Non-breaking. Existing docs and examples remain untouched; website sidebar is updated to surface the contrib index. We include a short migration note for maintainers to tag older community playbooks with metadata fields required by the validator.

How to test locally: 1) bootstrap node dependencies under tools/rag-template-validator 2) run `npm run test` to validate fixtures 3) run `node index.js validate examples/rag/contrib-templates/stepwise-playbook-template.yaml` for a quick lint + contract check 4) optionally add label `run-smoke` to trigger the mock-interaction smoke runner in CI (documented in docs/contrib/README.md).

Follow-ups & future work: * Add quickstart that converts an existing example into the new front-matter format (LOW priority). * Integrate the validator as an opt-in GitHub App so maintainers can enforce the schema automatically.

Merge outcome: merged via squash by Evelyn Brooks on 2026-02-18 after final approvals. Thank you to everyone who reviewed and contributed test fixtures and copy edits.

Summary: This PR refreshes the public-ish Usage & Billing FAQ to align with current platform behavior and the ongoing metering hardening work. Primary goals are (a) reduce invoice disputes by being explicit about definitions (raw vs billed tokens), (b) set expectations around caching and retries/fallbacks, and (c) document the dispute/credits process in a way that matches Finance/Legal policy.

Context: We’ve had multiple support threads where invoice token counts did not match what customers inferred from client-side tokenizers or from older doc language, plus confusion around streaming disconnects and retry behavior. In parallel, Engineering is rolling out metering fixes (idempotency/dedupe, cache-hit attribution, OpenAI-compat alignment) behind shadow-billing. This doc update is meant to be stable and accurate both before and after the meter fixes, while clearly calling out what can change.

What changed (high level): 1) Added an explicit “Raw tokens vs billed tokens” section with definitions and examples. 2) Clarified caching semantics: cache hits can reduce billed tokens; customers will see cache hit attribution in usage where available. 3) Clarified retries/fallbacks: Redwood does not intentionally double-bill retries; how we dedupe is described at a behavior level (not implementation details). 4) Streaming: added guidance on partial generations, disconnects, and what counts as “generated” for billing; wording avoids promising per-chunk determinism and focuses on billed token reporting as source of truth. 5) Dispute process: added a plain-language dispute window and required artifacts (request IDs, date range, export) and linked to support escalation path; explicitly states that credits/refunds are reviewed case-by-case under contract terms.

Notes on wording choices: This PR intentionally avoids tying the definition of billed tokens to a specific tokenizer library name/version. Instead, it defines billed tokens as “the token counts reported by Redwood in usage exports/console for a request” and explains that these are computed server-side using the model’s tokenization rules and Redwood’s billing attribution rules (e.g., caching). Legal asked that we avoid language that can be read as a guarantee that ‘client token counts = invoice token counts.’

Follow-ups (out of scope): a) Once ENG exposes billed_tokens + cache_hit fields broadly in the customer usage API, we should add a screenshot + API example (blocked on rollout). b) Add a dedicated page for ‘Usage exports & timezone behavior’ once the export TZ fix lands; for now this PR adds a short note and points customers to UTC as the canonical boundary.

Internal references: Meter fixes / fields referenced in copy are being implemented in other repos (redwood PRs and SDK PRs). This PR is purely documentation and does not change billing behavior.
docs: rewrite Usage & Billing FAQ structure and add glossary for token terms
docs: add caching + retries + streaming clarifications and examples
docs: add dispute process section + links to support and usage exports
docs: polish language per Legal review (avoid absolute guarantees; clarify definitions)
docs: add changelog note and redirect from legacy FAQ anchors
Soojin Lee (Product Marketing): The new ‘billed tokens’ definition reads a bit defensive. Can we add a short paragraph framing this as ‘for fairness and predictability, we show billed tokens per request’ and then give a concrete example? (Also would be good to mention cache hits can reduce billed tokens.)
Elliot Price (Author): Updated the intro paragraph and added a worked example under ‘Raw vs billed’ showing prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, billed_tokens with a cache-hit note. Also added a one-liner that the Console/usage export is the canonical record for billing.
Michael Grant (Legal): Two tweaks: (1) remove “we will not bill for failed retries” — too absolute; instead say we aim to avoid double-billing and investigate anomalies. (2) Dispute language: use ‘within the dispute window specified in your Order Form’ rather than stating a universal number of days.
Elliot Price (Author): Done. Replaced the absolute statement with behavior-level wording + ‘contact Support with request IDs’. Updated dispute section to reference Order Form/MSA terms and kept a generic ‘promptly’ suggestion. Added an explicit ‘contract governs’ sentence.
Nadia Rahman (Telemetry): In the streaming section, the line ‘we bill only for tokens delivered to the client’ is not always true if the connection drops after generation but before all chunks are delivered. Suggest we say we bill based on server-side generated tokens for the request, as reported in usage, and note that disconnects can lead to fewer tokens received than generated.
Elliot Price (Author): Adjusted streaming section accordingly and added a short FAQ entry: ‘Why did I receive fewer tokens than billed_tokens?’ with disconnect explanation + recommendation to use request_id for debugging.
Monica Patel (SDK): Please avoid implying the SDK retries are always enabled. Different clients can configure retries. Also, add that idempotency keys are recommended for safe client retries.
Elliot Price (Author): Updated retry section to note retries may be performed by client, gateway, or server depending on configuration and failure type, and added a small best-practice callout: set idempotency_key for safe client-side retries.
Chris Osei (Product Ops): Can we add a caveat for experiments / changing meters? Something like ‘if we update how usage is displayed, we’ll communicate and preserve auditability.’
Elliot Price (Author): Added a short ‘Meter and reporting changes’ note: we may add fields/clarify attribution; invoices are based on the billing ledger; usage exports are for transparency and reconciliation; material changes follow change-control.
Docs: Clarified billed token definitions and how caching impacts billed usage.
Docs: Expanded guidance on retries, streaming disconnects, and request ID-based reconciliation.
Docs: Documented dispute/credits workflow and linked to usage export guidance.

Context: teams onboarding new models lacked a compact, consistent summary to include in release notes and product changelogs. The registry stores fragmented telemetry and perf stamps which made generating human-friendly excerpts brittle. This PR introduces a stable intake context-hash (a deterministic fingerprint of the intake bundle) and an automated, size-constrained release-excerpt generator that produces short prose suitable for release notes and the model catalog. Motivation: reduce manual edit cycles, improve provenance, and make small release blurbs deterministic across rollouts. What changed: - Add intake context-hash generator (sha256 over normalized manifest + sampling seed + perf-stamps) and persist as model.metadata.context_hash - Add compact release-excerpt service (server + CLI preview) that consumes the context_hash and telemetry tokens to synthesize a 240-char excerpt and a 1-line blurb. - Backfill migration: script to compute context_hash for existing models and flag models where telemetry is insufficient. - Catalog UI hook: preview endpoint to render generated excerpt and allow curator overrides. - Tests + static typing and small performance optimizations to generator path. Migration risk: low; generator is additive and curator override is always available. Rollout: staged - compute hashes in background, enable excerpt generation for new onboardings immediately, enable catalog preview in beta for internal curators, then opt-in for public release notes. Related: ENG-2147 (catalog UX for model blurbs), SUP-7721 (support ticket requesting consistent release snippets). Checklist: [x] unit tests for hash, generator; [x] end-to-end smoke in dev cluster; [x] migration script with dry-run. Documentation: added README and CLI usage examples in docs/onboard/excerpts.md.
Introduce deterministic intake context-hash and an automated compact release-excerpt generator. Adds migration job to compute hashes for existing models and a catalog preview for curators. No breaking changes. Admins can opt-out of auto-generated blurbs.
Unit tests cover hash calculation, generator fallbacks, and CLI. Integration smoke tested against dev registry with synthetic telemetry. Migration dry-run validated on a 1k-model sample and exposes metrics: backfill_time_per_model: ~120ms (median).
Adds a one-time backfill job (registry/onboard/migration_backfill.py) - runs as background low-priority task. Dry-run flag available and recommended before full backfill. Backfill writes context_hash to model.metadata.context_hash and marks model.metadata.context_hash_version=1.
1) Deploy service and schema bump to main. 2) Run migration in dry-run for 48h and review metrics. 3) Run controlled backfill (staged by creation_date). 4) Enable catalog preview for internal curators. 5) After 2 weeks opt-in for auto-release-excerpts in public catalog.
Monitor metrics excerpt.generator.latency and backfill.queue.length. Canary on small subset of catalog entries first. Provide override endpoint for curators at /api/catalog/models/:id/excerpt-override.
Adds preview button on model detail page and a small editable textarea with generated excerpt and 'apply' toggle. UI is behind feature flag 'catalog_excerpts_preview'.
Evan Chu: Can you clarify the exact inputs to the context_hash and how we prevent drift?
Maya Ortiz: Context_hash is computed from a normalized manifest JSON (sorted keys, trimmed whitespace), the intake sampling seed, and a stable fingerprint of attached perf-stamps. We include versioned hashing code so past hashes are reproducible.
Priya Raman: The generator occasionally produced slightly awkward prose in edge cases. Can we add a fallback templated blurb?
Maya Ortiz: Added deterministic template fallback for cases where telemetry tokens are below threshold; documented examples in docs.
Lars Becker: Migration load—will backfill job saturate DB?
Maya Ortiz: Backfill runs as a low-priority background job with concurrency controls and a dry-run mode; added metrics and a cancellation toggle.
Evan Chu: Approving after nit on CLI help text fixed.
Priya Raman: Approved.
Status: Squash-merge after green CI and migration dry-run in staging.

Summary: This PR adds first-class AWS and GCP Marketplace onboarding docs to reduce time-to-first-token for marketplace buyers and to unblock partner submission requirements. It introduces a Marketplace onboarding landing page, provider-specific step-by-step guides (Subscribe → Entitlement → Provision org → Create API key → First request), and an entitlement troubleshooting page with concrete error states and recommended next actions. It also links to the Marketplace Security Documentation Pack and clarifies which security artifacts are public vs available on request.

Motivation / context: Marketplace buyers are procurement-led and frequently get stuck during entitlement propagation and org linking. Partner feedback requested clearer customer-facing steps and explicit guidance for common failure modes (e.g., existing orgs, multi-subscription, delayed entitlement sync). This doc set is intended to pair with the console marketplace entrypoint (ENG-22112) and entitlement verification endpoint work (ENG-22110) by documenting the same error codes/UX copy.

What’s included: (1) New docs IA for Marketplace onboarding under /docs/marketplace/ with a landing page that routes customers by provider and deployment type (Hosted/Dedicated/Private). (2) AWS Marketplace guide covering subscription, private offers vs public offers, entitlement timing expectations, how to find product code / account identifiers needed for support, and first-call examples. (3) GCP Marketplace guide covering subscription, billing account prerequisites, procurement approvals, and first-call examples. (4) Troubleshooting: a dedicated Entitlements & provisioning troubleshooting page with a table mapping common errors (ENTITLEMENT_NOT_FOUND, ENTITLEMENT_PENDING, ORG_ALREADY_LINKED, SUBSCRIPTION_MISMATCH, REGION_NOT_AVAILABLE) to remediation steps, including when to wait vs when to contact support and what data to provide. (5) Security: links to the Marketplace Security Documentation Pack index and a short ‘Security & compliance for marketplace buyers’ section with safe wording (no over-claims), plus notes on audit logs and retention controls.

Out of scope: Pricing details beyond high-level SKU descriptions (handled in the pricing/packaging pages update PR). No changes to console UX or backend entitlement logic.

Notes for partner submission: Final URLs introduced in this PR are stable and intended to be used in AWS/GCP marketplace listing fields. If redirects/vanity URLs are needed for older links, we should track separately (see INT-771).

QA: Ran local docs build, link checker, and spell/markdown lint. Verified nav placement and breadcrumbs. Confirmed that security links do not expose gated evidence directly and instead route to the security pack overview with ‘contact us’/‘on request’ language for reports.

Screenshots: Not included in this PR; screenshots will land once Design finalizes the capture set (DES-913).
Elliot Price (Docs): Requested tightening the information architecture to keep Marketplace docs under a single /marketplace prefix and avoid duplicating content across AWS/GCP pages. Suggested extracting shared sections (definitions, first request, org linking) into partials to reduce drift. Author update: extracted shared partials and replaced duplicated blocks.

Naomi Feldman (Security/Compliance): Asked to avoid implying “SOC 2 certified” language and to ensure claims are aligned with the security packet wording (e.g., ‘SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA/on request’). Requested clarifying shared responsibility and not listing specific retention periods as hard guarantees without referencing configuration. Author update: replaced language with approved phrasing, added shared responsibility callout, and moved retention specifics to a ‘see security packet’ link.

Marcus Lin (Security Eng): Pointed out that entitlement troubleshooting should not instruct customers to paste raw tokens/logs into support tickets. Requested guidance to share request IDs and timestamps instead. Author update: updated support escalation section to request request_id, org_id, cloud account ID, subscription ID, and timestamps; added explicit ‘do not share prompts/keys’ note.

Ben Carter (Growth): Requested explicit ‘How long does provisioning take?’ expectations and a prominent ‘What to do if you’re stuck’ box above the fold to reduce drop-offs. Author update: added entitlement timing partial and a troubleshooting CTA box on both AWS/GCP pages.

Alex Martinez (DevEx): Requested linking this doc set from the Quickstart entrypoint and ensuring the first request examples use the marketplace-safe base URL and include environment variables. Author update: updated snippets and added a shared marketplace links snippet for consistency.

Final review: All reviewers approved after wording and IA changes; CI green; merged via squash.
Docs: Added AWS/GCP Marketplace onboarding guides, entitlement troubleshooting, and links to the Marketplace Security Documentation Pack to reduce marketplace buyer friction.

Context: The Confluence playbook "Docs site content staging and canary publishing playbook" is now out of date. Since the Feb game-day we changed (a) staging to PR Preview Environments, (b) canary routing from edge rules to the docs-router service, and (c) our acceptance thresholds and smoke suite ownership. This PR refreshes the playbook in-repo and adds a small "runbook" appendix for the oncall. Goal: reduce rollback latency and eliminate ambiguity about which commands/URLs are current. Summary of updates (what changed vs the old playbook): 1) Environments: Staging is no longer a single long-lived site. We now use per-PR preview envs. The shared environment is "preprod" (formerly called staging) and is only used for final integration checks. URLs now: - PR Preview: https://pr-<number>.preview.docs.redwood.com (created automatically on PRs) - Preprod: https://preprod.docs.redwood.com - Prod: https://docs.redwood.com 2) Canary routing: We no longer use ad-hoc CDN edge rules. Traffic shifting is done via docs-router (Envoy) weights and a cookie override for debugging. Canary commands updated to the new deploy wrapper (docsctl) and router config. 3) Acceptance criteria: Tightened thresholds based on incident review: - Server 5xx for canary cohort must be < 0.05% (was 0.1%) over the 30 min window - Client JS exception rate delta must be < 10% (was 20%) - p95 render time delta must be < 10% (was 15%) - Added explicit "broken anchors / sidebar nav" check in CI 4) Canary ramp schedule: Standardized to 1% -> 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with specific dwell times, and an optional "internal-only" ramp via the employee login gate for large rewrites. 5) Rollback: Rollback now uses pinned content artifact IDs rather than "previous-stable" (which was ambiguous after the artifact retention change). Added explicit command to fetch the last good artifact and a note about router weights during rollback. 6) Smoke tests: Split into "fast" (CI) and "live" (preprod/prod) and clarified owners. Motivation: production inference traces show significant pad amplification when many short requests (seqlen <= 16) occupy their own slots. Traditional bucketing reduces that but still leaves sub-slot wasted token capacity and causes extra KV cache entries and kernel launch overhead. This change implements SeqFusion: a slot-concatenation packing heuristic that coalesces multiple short sequences into a single execution slot while preserving per-request KV isolation and stream-level latency SLOs.

Design summary: SeqFusion creates 'micro-cohorts' of short requests that are concatenated into a single padded buffer up to a per-slot soft-capacity (configurable, defaults to 512 tokens). The runtime treats the fused slot as a single sequence for kernel execution but maintains a mapping table to demultiplex outputs back to original requests. To keep latency bounded we: (1) enforce a jitter-aware hold window (default 12ms) before fusion, (2) prioritize unfused long sequences to avoid head-of-line blocking, and (3) fall back to standard bucketing for edge cases (very high entropy length distributions). Key implementation points: kernel alignment pads the fused sequence to nearest vector-width boundary to retain efficient GEMM paths; KV cache entries are stored per-original-request but preallocated in a contiguous memory slab for the fused slot to improve cacheline locality; the scheduler updates slot accounting to include fused-count heuristics so autoscaler sees realistic effective throughput.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc linked (Linear ENG-7862)
- [x] End-to-end unit tests for fusion/unfuse paths
- [x] Perf microbench harness + mixed-length trace runs
- [x] KV cache unit tests for isolation/eviction correctness
- [x] CI GPU + CPU integration runs
- [x] Observability: new per-slot 'fused_count' metric and pad_amp reduction metric

Commits (high-level):
- feat(core/scheduler): add seqfusion slot allocator and hold window timer
- feat(runtime/exec): fused-slot execution path + demux output writer
- perf(kernels): align fused buffers to 32-byte vector lanes; update attention kernel invocation
- feat(kv): contiguous-slab allocation + per-request meta index for fused slots
- test: harness for mixed-length trace; add regression tests for eviction correctness
- docs: explain SeqFusion config and safety knobs

Files changed (high level):
- core/scheduler/slot_allocator.rs (new fusion policy + heuristics)
- runtime/exec/fused_slot.rs (core fused execution path)
- runtime/kv/slab_allocator.rs (contiguous slab for fused slots)
- kernels/launch/config.rs (alignment adjustments)
- tests/perf/mixed_length_trace.rs (new harness)
- docs/ops/seqfusion.md (operational guidance)

Small illustrative snippet (runtime/exec/fused_slot.rs):
- before: launch_kernel(&slot.buffer, seq_len, kv_refs)
- after: launch_kernel(&fused.buffer, fused_len, fused_kv_refs) // demux metadata used after write-back

Review conversation (selected):
- Jared Lin (review): "I like the approach — two concerns: 1) the hold-window might increase P99 for short requests under heavy load, and 2) memory accounting for fused slabs needs to be hedged against OOM bursts. Can you add a safety valve to disable fusion when mem pressure is high?"
- Marina (author): "Added auto-disable when overall slab usage > 78% and a per-node backpressure metric exposing 'fusion_disabled_by_mem'. Also tightened hold-window to be jitter-aware (exp backoff) to limit p99 regressions; added tests."
- Priya Raman (review): "Verified on perf harness: mixed-length trace (80% seqlen<=16) shows token/sec +19% and pad tokens -28% with tail latency within SLOs. Please add an observability note to the ops doc."
- Owen Castillo (approve): "Looks good; small nit on naming (fused_count -> fused_slot_count) addressed in follow-up commit."

CI summary: initial run failed lint on naming conventions; fixed. GPU perf suite (r18) shows +12% throughput overall and better kernel occupancy on short-seq workloads. Regression tests for KV eviction pass. All green on second run.

Safety and rollback: SeqFusion is feature-flagged (runtime config: "seqfusion.enabled") and defaulted ON for mixed-length queue profiles only. Added runtime metric "fusion_disabled_by_mem" and an operator-facing runtime toggle in the console; rollback route: set seqfusion.enabled=false and drain node, revert head_branch if incidents persist.

Merge: squash and merge; changelog entry added under runtime/perf. Merge method: squash/merge.

Introduce SeqFusion slot-concatenation packing: reduces average padding tokens by ~28% for mixed-length workloads. Backwards-compatible; runtime auto-enables under heuristics. Improvements to KV cache routing and kernel alignment.
Mixed-length perf harness (trace: 120k requests; 80% seqlen<=16, 20% seqlen>128): avg throughput +19% token/sec, pad-token reduction -28%, p95 latency change +1.8ms (within SLO), p99 unchanged. Kernel occupancy improved on short sequences (measured via occupancy sampler).
Enable seqfusion for queues with median seqlen <= 24. If fusion_disabled_by_mem > 0.05 for >5m, investigate slab fragmentation and consider raising slab-capacity or disabling fusion on the node. Observe fused_slot_count and pad_amplification metrics after enabling.
Feature-flagged, memory auto-disable, hold-window adaptivity, fallback to existing bucketing, additional e2e tests added.
This change is complementary to existing bucketing strategies: SeqFusion targets many small concurrent requests without increasing inter-request padding. It intentionally keeps KV entries per-request to simplify security/audit boundaries while co-locating memory to improve locality.
Jared Lin: I like the approach — two concerns: 1) the hold-window might increase P99 for short requests under heavy load, and 2) memory accounting for fused slabs needs to be hedged against OOM bursts. Can you add a safety valve to disable fusion when mem pressure is high?
Marina Velasquez: Added auto-disable when overall slab usage > 78% and a per-node backpressure metric exposing 'fusion_disabled_by_mem'. Also tightened hold-window to be jitter-aware (exp backoff) to limit p99 regressions; added tests.
Priya Raman: Verified on perf harness: mixed-length trace (80% seqlen<=16) shows token/sec +19% and pad tokens -28% with tail latency within SLOs. Please add an observability note to the ops doc.
Owen Castillo: Looks good; small nit on naming (fused_count -> fused_slot_count) addressed in follow-up commit.
payload.title: SeqFusion: slot-concatenation dynamic packing to minimize padding amplification

Adds a lightweight stepwise debugger and inline-assertion harness to the RAG quickstarts and SDK examples. Motivation: teams repeatedly asked for a deterministic, reproducible way to step through retrieval+agent decisions during authoring and CI (see ENG-9123). This PR introduces: 1) a docs walkthrough (docs/rag/stepwise-debugger.md) that explains the mental model and recommended invariants for RAG debugging; 2) two minimal example toolkits (Python + TypeScript) that wire the debugger into the SDKs and surface per-step traces, token-level latencies, and assertion hooks; 3) an inline-assertion DSL that lets authors codify expected retrieval hits and tool-call side effects for regression tests; 4) a local-playground recipe for the docs site that lets authors run stepwise sessions in the browser via the devcontainer. Key goals: make step-by-step traces first-class, enable small automated regression checks in CI, keep the examples compact and copy-paste friendly. Changes include small SDK helpers (non-breaking) and docs-only site config. Motivation: provide a lightweight, self-contained browser quickstart that demonstrates a minimal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) flow without requiring a backend. Many customers prototype knowledge features in the browser and run into pitfalls around blocking main-thread embedding computation and large synchronous index loads. This PR adds a walkthrough and an opinionated example that uses a Web Worker to compute embeddings, a tiny on-disk JSONL index (vector_index.jsonl) for demo corpora, and the Redwood SDK client in a restricted browser environment.

What changed (high level): the PR adds a step-by-step guide (docs/guides/browser-rag-webworker-quickstart.md), a runnable example (examples/browser-rag/) with a minimal HTML UI, a Web Worker implementation for async embedding generation (worker/embeddings_worker.ts compiled to embeddings_worker.js), a small sample vector index (worker/vector_index.jsonl) and a telemetry snippet to show how to capture latency and token usage from the browser. The example intentionally relies on in-browser approximate nearest neighbor search (brute-force L2 for the small demo index) and documents how to replace it with a WASM ANN library for larger corpora.

Checklist: - [x] Guide with prerequisites and security considerations (CORS, CSP, local file sizes). - [x] Example project with step-by-step run instructions. - [x] Web Worker-based embedder and graceful fallback to remote embedding API. - [x] Telemetry example that reports token/latency metrics to a configured endpoint (opt-in). - [x] Docs site navigation entry. - [x] Smoke tested on Chrome (desktop) and Firefox.

How to run locally (short): 1) cd examples/browser-rag 2) npm ci && npm run build 3) npx http-server -c-1 ./ (or open index.html via local dev server) 4) Open Developer Tools -> Network and Console. The README has troubleshooting hints for CSP and local file sizes.

Testing and QA notes: small automated smoke job added to the docs pipeline triggers a static render and link-check. A manual preview was created in our docs preview environment to validate images and the interactive UI. We exercised the fallback path where the Web Worker cannot compute embeddings (Safari private mode) and verified the UI surfaces the remote-embed option.

Security note: the example ships a tiny sample index and documents that production datasets should never be embedded client-side. The telemetry snippet is opt-in and respects a user toggle; no secrets are embedded in the example.

Related: links to ENG-1947 (internal spec), DOCS-332 (content plan). This is intentionally self-contained so customers can fork the example and swap the index for a backend call or a WASM ANN library.

Merge: squash-merged after reviewers approved and CI green.
Ethan Cole (request changes): The worker fallback path should be more explicit in the guide; unclear what happens on Safari iOS. Please add a short note and a test scenario.
Priya Sinha (author reply): Added Safari notes and a documented fallback test (see README steps). The worker now returns a structured error that the UI surfaces to the user.
Marta Ruiz (suggestion): Telemetry opt-in toggle looks good; can we add a one-line example showing how to attach a Datadog/OTLP endpoint?
Priya Sinha (author reply): Added telemetry-config.yaml and a short paragraph that shows how to wire OTLP collectors; the example keeps defaults off.
Jun Park (approved): Verified example builds and smoke tests pass in preview. UX of the policy/csp doc looks clear. Approving.
Introduce a browser-focused RAG quickstart demonstrating an offline index and Web Worker-based embedder; no breaking API changes.

Summary: Add 'SimLab' quickstart for developers to author, run, and iterate on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) scenarios locally with minimal setup. The quickstart focuses on fast feedback loops: scenario step assertions, lightweight telemetry probes (latency, token cost, assertion pass rate), and a compact runner that can replay synthetic user sessions for testing and evals. Motivation: teams repeatedly ask for a minimal example that bridges docs and examples — not a full authoring studio but richer than a single README. This PR introduces a single opinionated, reproducible sandbox that can be used for authoring, CI smoke checks, and onboarding.

What this includes (single-line summary): docs/quickstarts/simlab/README.md, example corpora, prebuilt telemetry probes, a local sim runner (node + python shims), structured-output assertion examples, and CI smoke manifest.

Checklist:
- [x] Quickstart narrative and step-by-step README
- [x] Compact starter corpus and index script
- [x] Local sim runner with configurable concurrency and seedable randomness
- [x] Telemetry probe harness (latency, token-cost, assertion pass rates)
- [x] CI smoke job example (docs smoke) and link-checker integration
- [x] Example prompts + structured-output lint examples
- [ ] Integration with the authoring web UI (follow-up: ENG-2346)

Compatibility notes: the runner targets the Redwood API but falls back to a local mock shim (for offline demos). The telemetry probes emit JSONL telemetry suitable for ingestion into the console or for local analysis via simlab/telemetry/parse.py.

How to try locally (abridged):
1) cd docs/quickstarts/simlab
2) ./bootstrap.sh  # installs minimal node/python deps, creates test-index
3) ./run-sim --scenario sample-ticket --replay 5 --concurrency 1
4) ./telemetry/collect.sh  # runs built-in probes and prints pass/fail summary

Design decisions (brief):
- Keep API surface intentionally small: single README, one run script, and a telem probe harness so teams can copy the pattern into CI.
- Use JSONL for telemetry to avoid schema coupling; telemetry/parse.py contains a small mapping to convert to the Console ingest format for deeper analysis.
- Make prompts and assertions explicit (assertion files live under scenarios/ and are YAML-like) so regressions are actionable.

Related: ENG-2345 (SimLab spec), PM-98 (onboarding improvements), SUP-421 (customer ask for local scenario replay), docs: #authoring-playbooks
Added SimLab quickstart: a lightweight authoring + telemetry playground for RAG scenarios. Includes local-run scripts, example prompts, and built-in probes for latency/cost assertions.

Context: Dedicated staged rollouts need deterministic, auditable stage-by-stage promotion and a safe abort path. This PR implements the action endpoints on the dedicated-pool-rollouts service, wires audit event emission, and adds correctness guardrails (idempotency keys + optimistic concurrency) to make promotion safe under retries and operator concurrency.

What’s included: (1) New actions: POST /v1/dedicated_pools/{pool_id}/rollout_plans/{plan_id}:promote and POST /v1/dedicated_pools/{pool_id}/rollout_plans/{plan_id}:abort. (2) Deterministic state transitions + validation: only RUNNING|HELD plans can be promoted; only RUNNING|HELD can be aborted; COMPLETED/ABORTED are terminal. Promotion increments stage_index (monotonic), records promoted_at, and snapshots gate evaluation summary at time of action. Abort transitions to ABORTED and reverts active stage routing intent to the last known-good baseline (control plane intent only; data plane applies via existing reconciler). (3) Audit events: emits dedicated_rollout.promote and dedicated_rollout.abort via the central audit pipeline; payload includes actor, pool_id, rollout_plan_id, previous_stage, new_stage, reason (required), request_id, idempotency_key, and concurrency token. (4) Idempotency: supports Idempotency-Key header (and x-redwood-idempotency-key alias for legacy clients) for promote/abort; stores action result keyed by (rollout_plan_id, action_type, idempotency_key) with a 24h TTL; repeated requests return the original response with a 200 and an Idempotency-Replayed: true header. (5) Optimistic concurrency: supports If-Match: W/"rollout-plan-rev:{n}" (preferred) and request body field expected_revision (compat); mismatches return 409 Conflict with the current revision and a human-readable message to prevent double-promote under retries or two operators clicking promote.

API/behavior details: Promote requires reason in the request body; it returns the updated rollout plan resource (including stage_index and revision) plus action metadata (action_id, replayed flag). Abort requires reason and optional abort_mode (best_effort|strict); strict will fail closed if the plan is not reconcilable (e.g., missing baseline config), best_effort will still mark ABORTED and rely on operator follow-up; default is strict for now (per SRE/security review).

Testing: Added unit tests for state transitions, idempotency replay, and revision conflicts; added an integration-style test using the in-memory DB harness to cover promote->promote (replay) and promote->abort interactions. Manual testing in dev: exercised endpoints via adminctl against a test Dedicated pool, verified audit events show up in audit-viewer with required fields.

Notes: This PR intentionally does not implement force-promote/hold; those are tracked separately and require explicit admin-only RBAC and additional audit constraints. Gate evaluation is read-only here; this PR only snapshots the gate summary into the audit event and rollout action record.
Control plane now supports explicit promote/abort actions for DedicatedPoolRolloutPlan with auditable, idempotent semantics.
Audit events emitted for rollout actions (create/update already existed; this adds promote/abort + override scaffolding).
Ethan Park: Can we ensure promote is monotonic even under concurrent requests? I’m worried about two promotes landing at once and skipping stages.
Benji Okafor (author): Added If-Match support + revision increments on each action. The repo update is conditional on revision; the second request will get 409 with current revision. Also added an idempotency store so retries don’t double-promote.
Jordan Lee: For determinism/auditability, the audit event needs the exact stage definitions (or at least stage_id + config hash) at time of promotion. Otherwise later edits to the plan could confuse reconstruction.
Benji Okafor (author): Good call. I added stage_id and stage_config_digest to the promote/abort audit payload. Full stage JSON felt too large for SIEM; digest should be enough to correlate with the plan revision.
Kaitlyn Nguyen: Please confirm RBAC: who can abort vs promote? Also reason should be required for both actions for compliance.
Benji Okafor (author): Promote/abort require dedicated.rollouts.write on the pool. Reason is now required (non-empty) in both handlers; validated server-side and surfaced in audit payload. Added tests.
Rafael Mendes: Abort semantics: strict default is good, but what happens to routing intent? Is there a chance we keep sending traffic to a broken stage if abort fails strict due to missing baseline?
Benji Okafor (author): Strict abort failing means we don’t change state; operator sees 422 with remediation steps. Best_effort is available but not default. Also added metric + log when abort fails due to missing baseline, so oncall can page the owning team.
Chloe Martin: Console backend wants stable error shapes for 409 and idempotency replay. Can we standardize on a machine-readable error code and include current_revision?
Benji Okafor (author): Updated error responses to include code (REVISION_CONFLICT / IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSE_MISMATCH) and current_revision. Also returning Idempotency-Replayed header for replays; body includes replayed boolean.
Merged into main via squash on 2025-02-24 after approvals (Platform + Security + SRE). Follow-ups filed: (1) add force-promote/hold admin actions with stricter RBAC + warnings, (2) wire policy-engine gate snapshot into action response for Console evidence view, (3) tighten abort_mode defaults once baseline reconciliation is fully enforced.

Motivation: customers asked for smaller, repeatable authoring artifacts that capture stable checkpoints for RAG authoring workflows and enable telemetry-driven regressions during prompt/index changes. This PR adds a compact 'checkpoint' template format, new telemetry-guided assertion examples, and an embedded authoring devcontainer/watch-mode recipe so engineers can iterate locally against seeded indexes. What this includes: 1) new compact checkpoint schema and examples (YAML+JSON) that capture prompt seeds, index snapshot pointers, and golden-response assertions; 2) a telemetry-guided assertions guide that maps telemetry signals (token-latency, rerank-quality, recall-window) to test thresholds and suggested remediation; 3) two new runnable samples: typescript/mini-agent and python/authoring-worker that demonstrate checkpoint-driven test runs and automatic rollback hooks; 4) a minimal devcontainer and a lightweight file-watcher that automatically runs the checkpoint harness on file changes; 5) an authoring VS Code extension manifest (samples only) that surfaces checkpoint failures inline and links to telemetry dashboards. Checklist: - [x] Add checkpoint schema and examples - [x] Add step-by-step guide for telemetry assertions - [x] Add TS and Python samples with README how-to - [x] Add devcontainer + watch-mode recipe - [x] Add tests for the harness smoke flow - [x] Docs lint and build passed How to validate: follow the README in docs/rag-authoring/checkpoints to run the devcontainer, create a checkpoint, and run `python harness.py --checkpoint ./samples/checkpoints/minimal.yaml`. Context and motivation: Our full-lint and dependency-update pipeline has become a major contributor to PR feedback latency and noisy failures when transitive deps churn. This PR introduces two orthogonal changes aimed at improving developer feedback velocity and making dep updates observable and easy to triage: 1) staged lint lanes: a lightweight 'quick-lint' lane that runs on every push to give sub-2m feedback (fast checks, staged ESLint + python-flake8 subset, path-aware), and a deeper 'full-lint' lane that runs in pre-merge or nightly jobs; 2) dep-rotation CLI and CI integration: a small CLI (tools/dep-rotator) that performs bounded dependency rotation trials in an ephemeral job to detect incompatibilities earlier and produce a concise compatibility report. Design goals: reduce noisy failures on main CI, surface dep incompatibilities as targeted failures, remove unnecessary wall-clock time on common PRs, and provide an automated path to rotate minor/patch deps with safe gating. Summary of changes: added ci/actions/staged-lint.yml and ci/actions/quick-lint-composite action; added tools/dep-rotator (Go binary wrapper + integration tests); added a new presubmit job matrix that prefers quick-lint for small changes via path-filtering and schedules full-lint only for broad changes; introduced dep-rotation workflow ci/workflows/dep-rotation.yml which can be triggered manually, on schedule, or by linked Linear ticket; updated docs/developer/ci.md with rollout notes and opt-out flags; minor refactor of existing ci/scripts/run-lint.sh to make it composable. Checklist: implementation done; unit + integration tests added for dep-rotator; staging deploy of CI YAML validated in feature repo; reviewers: please validate job timeout and cache key behavior; rollout: staged rollout to 'fast-feedback' lane for 72 hours, monitor flaky-lint alerts and presubmit latency. Migration notes: no API or runtime breaking changes; teams that relied on always-running full-lint on push should update CI expectations or set the LINT_ALWAYS_FULL=true env in project config; containers caching keys unchanged except for quick-lint which uses a separate cache prefix. Metrics to watch post-merge: median presubmit latency, percentage of presubmits that short-circuit to quick-lint, dep-rotation report failures per week, flaky-lint alert rate. Related: ENG-4821 defined the fast-feedback SLA; ENG-4980 tracked dep-rotation requirements.
feat(ci): add quick-lint composite action | feat(cli): add dep-rotator cmd + integration tests | refactor(ci): split presubmit matrix and add path-aware filter | docs: ci.md rollout and opt-out instructions | ci: wire dep-rotation workflow and permissions
Sven: Please add an opt-out flag for monorepo components that still require full-lint on push; Maya: added LINT_ALWAYS_FULL support and documented it; Rita: observed flaky test in dep-rotator integration on x86-2024 image, requested increased timeout and improved retry logic; Maya: bump timeout to 8m, add one retry for network pulls, integration test adjusted; Liam: requested more explicit cache-key separation to avoid polluting full-lint cache; Maya: switched quick-lint cache prefix and added expirations; Rita: approved after retries fixed; Sven: approved after opt-out added; Liam: approved after cache change; CI: green on final run; author squashed commits and added release notes; final merge approved by all reviewers.
- Introduces quick-lint presubmit lane to speed up common PR feedback; can be disabled per-project via LINT_ALWAYS_FULL=true. - Adds dep-rotator CLI and a scheduled/manual dep-rotation workflow to proactively detect dependency incompatibilities. - Refactors presubmit matrix to be path-aware reducing average CI wall time.
