Motivation: onboarding workflows currently accept free-form metadata which makes downstream changelog automation brittle and prevents signing/credentialing of intake payloads. This PR introduces an intake credential orchestrator that issues and validates short-lived, signed onboarding credentials; it also introduces a privacy-aware sampled affinity heatmap exporter that produces small, anonymized artifacts used by changelog generation and release teasers.

What this change does: adds a credential minting & verification layer for model intake, wires a new CLI hook (intakectl export-heatmap) and server-side exporter to produce epoched heatmaps from sampled telemetry, and integrates the artifacts into the changelog-autodraft pipeline so release notes can include small, privacy-safe perf snapshots. The orchestrator supports both local keypairs (dev) and integration with the KMS-backed signer used by Private deployments.

Design notes: the credential contract is intentionally minimal: a scoped nonce, model_id, sanitized sample hash, and a short TTL (1h) to limit replay risk. The heatmap exporter runs sampling hooks that respect the onboard metadata_keeplist and applies differential-privacy noise (configurable epsilon) before emitting compact PNG + JSON metadata that changelog-generator consumes. Exporter outputs go to the existing release-briefs bucket with a new prefix to avoid cross-contamination.

Testing and migration: added unit + integration tests that exercise KMS signer (mocked) and local dev signer, sampling rate governor, and the changelog-autodraft end-to-end flow. Migration: existing intakes without credentials are accepted with a deprecation warning for 30 days; a Linear task will track rollout.

Security & privacy: credentials are signed and short-lived to reduce attack surface. Samples are sanitized and no raw prompts or model outputs are included in export artifacts. Reviewed with security: SUP-321 documented the threat model and allowed config.

Notes for reviewers: focus review on credential boundary checks (src/onboard/credential_orchestrator.py), sample sanitizer (exporters/heatmap_exporter.py), and the new intakectl CLI entry. The changelog integration is small glue (hooks/changelog-sampler.yaml) but important for automation completeness.
2025-07-09 Lydia Chen: Overall design looks good. Please ensure TTLs are configurable per-tenant; we don't want a hard 1h for all customers.
2025-07-09 Asha Patel: Reply: made TTL configurable via onboarding profile; default remains 1h. Added unit test to cover override case.
2025-07-10 Evan Park: Concern about sample leakage — can we assert no raw tokens are included in artifacts? Suggest adding sanitizer unit tests.
2025-07-10 Asha Patel: Reply: added sanitizer tests and an explicit assertion to strip 'prompt'/'output' keys from any sample metadata before export.
2025-07-11 Marta Kaczmarek: Small nit: the KMS signer mock is verbose; simplified to a helper fixture. Also left one styling comment in credential_orchestrator.py.
2025-07-12 Asha Patel: Addressed styling and replaced the mock with the shared kms_test_fixture. Re-ran CI; all green.
Add: intake credential orchestrator (short-lived signed onboarding credentials) and sample affinity heatmap exporter. Changelog automation can now include small, privacy-safe perf heatmaps for release briefs. Migration: legacy intakes accepted for 30 days with deprecation warning.
Operator must add KMS signer ARN to infra secrets for Private deployments; devs can use local keypair via ONBOARD_SIGNER_MODE=local. New S3 prefix 'release-briefs/heatmaps/' will be used by exporter. Monitor exporter failure metric exporter.heatmap_exporter.failures.
Smoke: run intakectl create + mint credential + validate
Heatmap: run intakectl export-heatmap against sample dataset, assert PNG + metadata emitted
Changelog: trigger changelog-autodraft pipeline and confirm heatmap inclusion in draft

Context and motivation: This PR adds a compact, interactive RAG 'Contract Playground' and a short TypeScript workshop for developers who want to author retrieval-augmented agents with explicit tool contracts and accessible authoring flows. The goal is to provide a low-friction onboarding path (live sandbox + step assertions) that demonstrates contract-first tool binding, structured output validation, and keyboard/screen-reader friendly examples.

What changed (high level): Added a docs playground page under /playgrounds/contract-playground with an embedded TS runner, a minimal mock indexer backend used by the smoke CI, an example contracts schema, and updated authoring-studio accessibility styles. Also included a small authoring checklist and a stepwise assertion snippet for unit-style prompt tests.

Why now: Several customers requested clearer examples for tool contracts and deterministic assertions during rollouts. Internal feedback from Solutions and Docs indicated the authoring UX was a barrier when using keyboard-only flows. This PR addresses both areas and ties the example into the platform's structured-output linting guide.

Motivation: teams building retrieval-augmented workflows repeatedly ask for concise authoring guidance and a lightweight in-doc walkthrough they can fork into their apps. Context: We’re standardizing the Redwood sales demo environment (demo tenant) and need one canonical, internal guide that SEs/AEs can follow without tribal knowledge. This PR adds an internal “Sales Demo Guide (v1)” with a 30-min run-of-show, prep checklist, tenant reset/healthcheck steps, and a “backup mode” section for when live steps fail (quota/model/dashboard/auth issues). The guide links out to the Confluence runbooks and the demo deck/talk track, and is written to be resilient to product UI drift by emphasizing stable URLs/commands and expected outcomes rather than pixel-perfect click paths. Scope: docs only (no product changes). Security note: guide is internal-only and explicitly states that demo data must remain synthetic; includes safe-sharing rules (no exporting audit logs; no copy/pasting API keys into shared docs; do not grant external access to demo org).
Title: Sales Demo Guide (Internal) — v1
Audience: Sales Engineering + AEs (pilot); internal-only
Owner: Elliot Price (Docs) | Technical owner: Markus Klein
Last updated: 2025-11-20

Purpose
This page is the canonical guide for running a consistent Redwood Inference demo using the demo tenant. It is optimized for reliability: it includes a default 30-minute flow, optional branches (Hosted vs Dedicated-style controls vs Private/VPC narrative), and a “backup mode” plan when live steps fail.

What this guide covers
- Pre-demo checklist: tenant health, keys, dashboards, model pins
- Live demo run-of-show (30 minutes) with AE↔SE handoffs
- Exact API calls for: streaming chat, structured output, tool calling, retries
- Console tour: cost/latency breakdowns, errors, rollouts (safe synthetic workload)
- Reliability story: fallback routing + graceful degradation (what to show vs what to say)
- Backup mode: screenshots/recordings + canned outputs + “how to recover in 60 seconds”
- Troubleshooting: 429s, empty dashboards, auth/RBAC, region/streaming issues
- Security and sharing rules (synthetic-only, least privilege, recording guidance)

What this guide does NOT cover
- Customer POC onboarding (separate process; do not reuse demo tenant)
- Deep performance tuning beyond the scripted toggles
- Any non-synthetic dataset usage

Single source of truth (link hub)
- Demo deck (canonical): Confluence → Sales enablement → Pitch decks → “Redwood demo deck v1”
- Talk track script: Confluence → Positioning & messaging → “Demo talk track v1”
- Runbook: Demo tenant reset: Confluence → Eng Platform → Runbooks → “Demo tenant reset runbook”
- Provisioning overview: Confluence → Eng Platform → How-tos → “Demo tenant provisioning overview”
- Demo environment SLOs: Confluence → Eng SRE → SLO and error budgets → “Demo environment SLOs”
- Capacity/quotas runbook: Confluence → Eng Infra → Runbooks → “Demo capacity and quotas”

Pre-demo checklist (T-15 minutes)
1) Confirm you have the correct scoped demo API key
- Use only keys issued for the demo org/project.
- Do not paste keys into shared docs/slides.
- If you suspect a key was shared, rotate (see reset runbook).

2) Run the demo tenant healthcheck
- Goal: verify quota headroom, model pin availability, dashboard ingestion, and that reset is not running.
- Expected: PASS across: auth, quota, model availability, console ingestion freshness.

3) Verify Console dashboards are populated (synthetic traffic)
- Check time range (last 60 minutes).
- Ensure you are looking at the correct demo project.
- If graphs are empty, start the synthetic traffic generator job (see troubleshooting).

4) Confirm model pins for the demo routes
- Demo routes must remain pinned to known-good model versions.
- If a model is unavailable in-region, follow the fallback policy; do not “pick a random model” live.

5) Open backup assets
- Have the backup screenshots folder open.
- Have the 2–3 minute backup recording ready.
- Have the canned outputs file ready for structured output + tool calling.

30-minute default run-of-show
Minute 0–3 (AE)
- Set context: “We help you ship LLM inference with predictable latency/cost/reliability across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.”
- Ask 1–2 discovery questions: latency SLOs, cost sensitivity, security constraints (VPC/on-prem), regions.

Minute 3–12 (SE) — Core API demo (streaming + structured output + tool calling)
- Show streaming chat completion: emphasize low-latency token streaming and retry behavior.
- Show structured output: “We can enforce JSON schema so downstream code doesn’t break.”
- Show tool calling: “Model calls a tool; we execute; we return result; model finalizes.”
- If customer is sensitive to compatibility: mention SDKs + OpenAI-compatible endpoint as options.

Minute 12–20 (SE) — Production economics + observability
- Toggle batching/caching preset to illustrate latency vs cost tradeoff.
- Open Console: token-level cost and latency breakdown, per-route dashboard.
- Show error analysis panel with synthetic errors (safe to demo).

Minute 20–25 (SE) — Reliability (fallback routing / graceful degradation)
- Explain: routing policy chooses region/model variant based on latency/capacity.
- Show a controlled “degraded” scenario: route fails over to compatible variant; app stays online.
- Emphasize: for demos we use a safe fallback policy aligned to pinned model families.

Minute 25–30 (AE)
- Summarize outcomes: predictable serving economics + unified operations across deployment modes.
- Next step options: POC plan (eval prompts, throughput targets), security review call, Dedicated sizing.

Backup mode (use when live steps are brittle)
Trigger conditions
- You hit 429 throttling during the live call.
- Console dashboards are empty and won’t populate quickly.
- Auth/RBAC blocks access to the demo org/project.
- A pinned model is temporarily unavailable in the chosen region.

Backup mode path A: “Screenshots-only Console tour” (fastest)
- Switch to annotated screenshots (rollouts view, cost breakdown, error analysis).
- Narrate “what you would see live” and the outcome, not the internal implementation.
- Do not claim the screenshot is from the customer’s environment.

Backup mode path B: “Recorded demo clip (2–3 min) + live Q&A”
- Play the clip for: streaming + structured output + tool calling.
- Continue with Q&A and architecture slides.

Backup mode path C: “Canned outputs + explain API contract”
- Paste pre-generated JSON outputs for structured output + tool calling.
- Emphasize: contract stability, schema guarantees, retries.

Troubleshooting quick references
- 429 / throttling: reduce parallelism; confirm quota; switch to hosted region with headroom; follow capacity/quotas runbook.
- Empty dashboards: verify time range and project selection; start synthetic traffic generator; check ingestion freshness; see SUP-4189 notes.
- RBAC/access issue: confirm you’re in the correct IdP role mapping; follow INT-993 guidance; do not request admin role as a workaround.
- Streaming disconnect in a region: switch region; avoid repeated retries live; use backup mode clip; log incident for follow-up.

Security and sharing rules (demo environment)
- Synthetic-only: never use customer data, even “sanitized.”
- Least privilege: use scoped keys; rotate if exposure is suspected.
- Recordings/screensharing: avoid showing API keys, internal tenant IDs, or unredacted audit logs.
- External access: do not grant prospects access to the demo tenant. Use a separate POC tenant when approved.

Appendix: SDK snippets
- Python: streaming + retries + tool calling (stable snippet)
- TypeScript: streaming + structured output validation

Notes for maintainers
- Keep this guide stable across UI churn by linking to durable runbooks and by referencing expected outcomes.
- If a live step fails more than twice in a week, update backup mode guidance and file an issue against the product/runbook.


Soojin Lee (PMM): Can we avoid the term “Optimize” in the guide? Field feedback is that it confuses customers. Suggest: “cost/performance controls” or “serving optimization toolkit.”
Elliot Price (author): Done—updated all headings to “Cost & performance controls” and added a one-line glossary entry mapping it back to product naming when needed.
Markus Klein (SE): Please make the healthcheck step explicit (command/URL + what PASS means). Also add a note: don’t improvise model selection if pinned model is down—use the fallback policy or backup mode.
Elliot Price (author): Added explicit healthcheck instructions (kept generic, links to runbook for exact command). Added callout box in model pins section + backup mode trigger condition.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Backup mode is good, but add a guardrail: if dashboards are empty, first check time range and project selection before running the traffic job (we’ve had false alarms). Also link SLO page for expected ingestion freshness.
Elliot Price (author): Added “check time range + project selection” as step 1 and linked demo SLOs page under dashboard freshness.
Alex Martinez (DevEx): Snippets should pin SDK versions and avoid experimental flags. Also suggest including both native Redwood SDK and OpenAI-compatible example, but keep one as primary.
Elliot Price (author): Updated snippet pages to pin versions and marked OpenAI-compatible example as optional appendix; primary path remains native Redwood SDK.
Dylan Brooks (Console): For the Console tour, please avoid referencing the flaky “rollouts” sub-tab name; it’s being renamed. Better: “Deployments → Rollouts (A/B)” and mention it may appear as “Experiments” in some builds.
Elliot Price (author): Adjusted wording to be outcome-based and added a note about possible label changes.

Introduces an elasticity guardrail controller that enforces tenant elasticity caps and a background utilization sampler for percentile telemetry. Improves stability under tenant surges and provides per-tenant utilization histograms for SLO tuning.
Motivation: tenants with bursty traffic occasionally trigger aggressive autoscaling which leads to noisy neighbor effects and uneven performance across the fleet. This PR adds an "elasticity guardrail" that limits short-term elasticity across dedicated pools while preserving throughput guarantees for steady-state load. It also introduces a lightweight utilization sampler that emits per-tenant p50/p90/p99 utilization estimates to drive better autoscaler decisions.

What this changes: the new controller maintains a per-tenant ephemeral credit bank (elasticity credits) that accrues slowly under steady usage and decays over time. Rapid ramp-ups consume credits from a local surge buffer; when credits deplete the admission layer enforces a soft throttle that prefers degraded-but-safe execution paths (lower-concurrency slots, model-variant fallbacks, or queued tokens) before requesting cluster-wide provisioning. The utilization sampler collects rolling sampled histograms and reports percentiles to the control plane at 10s granularity.

Design details: credit accrual rate is configurable via the pool config (fields: elasticity.credit_rate, elasticity.max_bank, elasticity.decay_tau). Consumption is measured in concurrency-seconds to align with tenant throughput billing. Admission policy is a prioritized set of fallbacks: 1) reduce concurrency reservation, 2) use quantized model variant, 3) queue request with capped wait. The guardrail is independent of reserved capacity so steady commitments are unaffected.

Testing & validation: unit tests for credit arithmetic, integration tests that exercise admission fallbacks, and a synthetic loadbench that runs 24-hour replay traces from a large tenant. Locally reproduced the production incident (SUP-1128) and verified that the guardrail reduced noisy neighbor evictions by ~78% in the trace. Microbenchmarks: median latency unchanged, p99 latency decreased by ~3.2% for the fleet under mixed workloads; service-level cost impact was a ~7% decrease in emergency provisioning events.

Checklist:
- [x] Controller implementation and reconciliation loop
- [x] Admission layer hooks and prioritized fallback paths
- [x] Telemetry sampler and export mapping
- [x] Config knobs and K8s CRD fields documented
- [x] Unit + integration tests
- [x] Loadbench simulation and perf summary attached

Rollback plan: the guardrail is feature-flagged and controlled by a cluster feature toggle (feature.elasticity_guardrail). Rolling the flag to OFF disables both admission enforcement and credit accounting. CRD additions are additive and safe to remove if needed.

Related work: follows on from ENG-5432 which defined the admission fallback matrix. Complements existing reservation and warm-pool controllers but is intentionally conservative (no automatic capacity pre-provisioning).

Notes for reviewers: focus on correctness of credit decay math, admission ordering semantics, and tagging of telemetry metrics to avoid high-cardinality explosions. The sampler intentionally bins tenants into cohort buckets for histograms to limit metric cardinality.

Motivation: We see persistent alert noise and high trace volume from bursty endpoints where short token microbursts (many tokens emitted in <200ms windows) trigger per-token SLO alerts and create heavy tracing load. This PR adds a lightweight token-pacing metric family and a deferred-span-hydration flow to reduce noise and trace storage while preserving investigative fidelity. What changed: 1) Telemetry: added token_pacing.{count,rate,percentile} meters at the invocation level to capture tokens/sec over short sliding windows (50ms, 200ms, 1s) plus a microburst boolean indicator. 2) Tracing: introduced deferred span hydration in the tracing pipeline: initial invocation traces are emitted as compact anchors with minimal attributes; full span bodies are stored in a short-lived side-store and only hydrated for sampled investigations, anomaly-triggered lookups, or on-demand by the console. 3) Dashboard: new dashboard token-pacing-overview with cohorted microburst heatmap, per-route pacing percentiles, and a compact hydration hit/miss chart. 4) Alerts: added an alert tuning recipe that uses paced-rate instead of raw token count for noisy routes and applies a transient-suppression backoff to reduce repeated firing for bursty traffic. 5) Docs & SDK: docs/observability/token-pacing.md and SDK helpers for clients to emit pacing hints. Rollout plan: feature gated by telemetry.feature.token_pacing; start as opt-in for Canary tenants for 48h, then progressive rollout with 10/30/100% tenant sampling over two weeks. Testing: unit tests for pacing calculators, end-to-end against the ingest pipeline with synthetic microbursts (see tests/integration/token_pacing_test.py), and load tests showing 4-10x reduction in hydrated-span write volume for bursty routes. Backwards compatibility: on by feature flag; default behavior unchanged. Related work: follow-ups expected to integrate token-pacing into adaptive batching and to extend hydration search APIs for on-demand debugging. Checklist: - [x] Telemetry collectors implemented - [x] Tracing pipeline deferred store + hydrator - [x] Dashboard panels and templates - [x] Alert recipe and runbook updates - [x] Integration + load tests - [x] Docs for operators and SDK hints
Maya Chen (reviewer): Nice approach, can you justify the chosen window sizes and how they interplay with batching?
Ava Martinez (author): windows chosen after load benching on bursty demo traffic; 50ms to catch microbursts, 200ms to align with typical batching thresholds, 1s for route-level pacing. Added comments in code and the doc with bench results.
Dmitri Karpov (reviewer): Concern about the hydrator side-store availability in Private installs — how do we fail gracefully?
Ava Martinez: hydrator side-store is optional; if unavailable we fallback to full-span write in the main pipeline and emit a telemetry tag (hydration_fallback=true). Added config path and migration steps to docs.
Maya Chen: CI lint flagged a styling issue in pacing_window.py; please run black/format.
Ava Martinez: fixed formatting and added unit tests for edge cases.
payload.title: Introduce token-pacing meters and deferred-span hydration for noisy endpoints

This PR adds internal (public-ish) documentation pages for the Hardware Tuning Profiles pack (H100/B200/L40S) covering: what profiles are, how profile selection works, what “expected behavior” means, safe operating envelopes, common failure modes, and oncall/operator troubleshooting steps. Motivation: we have multiple workstreams landing schema/loader/presets and perf-canary gates; docs need to ship alongside so SRE/CS/field and customers on Private have a single reference for (a) how to reason about profile-enabled rollouts and (b) how to safely override / rollback when something looks off.

Key goals in this doc set: (1) Be explicit about scope: “expected behavior” is guidance based on benchmark methodology, not a contractual guarantee. (2) Make selection + override order legible (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private). (3) Provide troubleshooting playbooks (tail latency regression, OOM/fragmentation on L40S, ambiguous GPU SKU detection, multi-GPU/MIG notes) with concrete toggles and what to check in dashboards/logs. (4) Link out to the authoritative artifacts (ADR, schema doc, workload matrix, perf-canary gates, known issues).

What’s included:
- Overview page: Why profiles exist, what changes when enabled, and how we roll them out safely.
- Profile selection + override order: runtime auto-detection, compatibility checks, and precedence rules; how to confirm the selected profile.
- “Expected behavior” pages per SKU (H100/L40S/B200): workload assumptions, throughput vs tail-latency tradeoffs, and when NOT to use the tuned mode.
- Troubleshooting guide: symptom -> likely cause -> verification steps -> mitigations/rollback.
- FAQ for Support/Solutions: what’s safe to change, what requires Eng involvement, and how to collect a minimal triage bundle.

Not included:
- Any changes to runtime behavior itself (this is docs-only), and no new external/marketing site content. This is intended for internal docs + Private operator reference.

Rollout note: this will be linked from the runtime release notes and from the rollout runbook. Wording has been reviewed to avoid overpromising; we consistently use “expected behavior”, “typical”, and “observed in benchmark suite” with explicit workload envelopes and caveats.
Kira Thompson: Troubleshooting section is strong. Please add a single “Oncall quick start” at the top with 5 steps max and links to the detailed sections. Also add explicit rollback criteria language and where to record the decision.
Elliot Price (author): Added “Oncall quick start” block + a rollback criteria callout; linked to rollout runbook and incident template. Also added a note: capture pool/region, selected profile metric, and effective config dump before rollback to help root-cause.
Neha Kapoor: Wording needs to be careful: don’t imply SLO guarantees. Replace “will improve” with “typically improves” and add a disclaimer that perf varies by workload and capacity conditions.
Elliot Price (author): Updated language across all expected behavior pages; added a consistent disclaimer section and changed headings from “Performance improvements” to “Typical deltas (benchmark suite)”.
Claire Dubois: In the workload envelope sections, please name the workload matrix dimensions we actually test (seq buckets, concurrency, streaming vs non-streaming). Also link the methodology page rather than paraphrasing too much.
Elliot Price (author): Added explicit bullets for seq length buckets + concurrency levels, and added a single canonical link for methodology/workload matrix to reduce drift.
Hiro Tanaka: H100 page: add a “when not to use throughput-first mode” example (short prompts + high request rate can hurt streaming p95). Also call out that kernel selection is seq-len bucketed and that anomalies should be validated against bucket distribution.
Elliot Price (author): Added the example and a “validate your bucket mix” section with suggested metrics to check (prompt tokens histogram, decode length histogram, streaming duration).
Sofia Ivanova: Scheduler section should mention fairness/backpressure knobs at a conceptual level but avoid listing every internal knob name (those are in schema docs and change). Suggest: describe modes and observable symptoms, and link to schema reference for exact keys.
Elliot Price (author): Reworked scheduler section to be mode-oriented; removed unstable key names; added link to schema reference and updated troubleshooting mapping to symptoms rather than knobs.
Marissa Cole: Add a short section on customer-facing communication: how Support should describe changes when a customer sees different latency after a rollout.
Elliot Price (author): Added “Support comms guidance” in FAQ with approved phrasing and escalation triggers (include p95 delta threshold, error rate changes, OOM/retry spikes).
Paula Mendes: Please add a note in the perf-canary linkage about noise/flakiness and that only gated metrics should block rollouts; others are “investigate”.
Elliot Price (author): Added a “Gates vs signals” callout and consistent wording: gates block promotion; signals create a ticket for investigation.
Internal docs: Added Hardware Tuning Profiles documentation (usage, selection/overrides, per-SKU expected behavior, troubleshooting + oncall quick start). Linked from runtime rollout guidance to reduce misconfiguration and speed up triage.

Introduce a distributed headroom oracle and an occupancy signal bridge that combine cluster-level occupancy signals into tenant-level headroom estimates. Adds new telemetry metrics and a rollout plan for Dedicated clusters.
Motivation: Dedicated fleets currently rely on local per-node util signals and a single autoscaler view which can cause oscillation when tenants burst across many nodes. This PR implements a distributed headroom oracle plus an occupancy-signal-bridge that aggregates spatial occupancy, produces smoothed tenant headroom estimates, and exposes percentile-backed guarantees that the autoscaler can use to make less reactive scaling decisions.

What this PR does (single continuous description): Adds a signal-bridge binary (occupancy-bridge) that subscribes to node occupancy streams, computes per-cluster occupancy distribution sketches, and publishes compact occupancy digests to the headroom-oracle service. Implements headroom-oracle which merges occupancy digests with tenant reservation ledgers, tenant-weighted priority slices, and recent request latency percentiles to output a headroom time series per tenant. The autoscaler (scale-controller) is extended to optionally consume the headroom oracle time series and apply a convex-safety buffer function (configurable) before proposing capacity moves.

Key behaviors and guarantees: - The oracle provides a 5/50/95 percentile headroom estimate per tenant for N=1/5/15 minute horizons. - The occupancy-bridge uses spatial smoothing across rack and AZ boundaries to avoid single-node noise. - The autoscaler uses a configurable convex safety buffer (default: 1.25x on short horizons, taper to 1.05x on long horizons) to avoid oscillation. - When oracle signals are unavailable, autoscaler falls back to the legacy occupancy estimator and emits a telemetry flag.

Files changed (high-level): - cmd/occupancy-bridge/main.go: new binary that ingests node occupancy (gRPC) and publishes TiKV-like digests (compact histograms). - services/headroom-oracle/service.go: merge logic, percentiles, and storage of short-window time-series. - controllers/scale-controller/autoscale_policy.go: optional oracle consumer and convex buffer application. - telemetry/metrics_registry.go: new metrics and tags. - integration tests: autoscaler/oracle_integration_test.go and e2e/occupancy_bridge_smoke_test.go. - docs/ops/dedicated-oracle.md: operator runbook and troubleshooting.

Commits (summary): [1] add occupancy-bridge skeleton + ingestion proto and histogram digest; [2] implement digest merge and sketch serializer; [3] headroom-oracle merge logic, percentile exports, unit tests; [4] autoscaler: oracle-mode, convex buffer impl, unit tests; [5] telemetry and dashboards; [6] integration tests and docs; [7] bugfix: ensure backward-compat on legacy estimator fallback; [8] minor lint/test fixes.

Testing and benchmarks: - Unit tests added for digest merge and percentile correctness. - Integration test runs (CI) simulate 100 tenants over a 3-AZ cluster with synthetic bursts; observed 42% reduction in scale-up churn and 18% lower cost over a 30-minute sustained burst compared to baseline autoscaler in canary env. - Load profile script included at tools/bench/oracle_load_simulator.py used to validate scaling decisions locally.

Telemetry and observability: New metrics: - redwood.headroom_oracle.headroom_estimate{tenant_id,percentile,window} - redwood.occupancy_bridge.digest_publish_latency_ms - redwood.autoscaler.oracle_mode_decisions - redwood.autoscaler.safety_buffer_applied
Dashboards: ops/dedicated/headroom-oracle (new) and autoscaler/oracle-mode (update). Logs: structured events emitted when fallback triggers.

Operator migration and rollout: - Phase 1 (canary): enable occupancy-bridge and oracle-mode on one dedicated fleet with low-risk tenants (internal). - Phase 2 (staged): enable on additional fleets behind a feature flag; monitor redwood.autoscaler.oracle_mode_decisions and headroom_estimate percentiles. - Rollback: flip feature flag to false; bridge publishes expiry tombstones so oracle can trim stale digests.

Security/Cost: occupancy-bridge transmits compact digests only; no raw request payloads leave nodes. Added RBAC role cluster:occupancy-bridge-reader. Estimated additional cost: small (proxy and bridge CPU), measured at ~2% higher control-plane CPU for canary fleet.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-3247)
- [x] Unit and integration tests added
- [x] Benchmarks run and attached
- [x] Operator runbook included
- [x] Telemetry and dashboards wired

Notes: This design intentionally separates the noisy node-level stream (occupancy-bridge) from the decision service (headroom-oracle) to make the oracle easier to reason about and easier to simulate. Future work: add a per-tenant explain API and a confidence score that the UI can surface.
Marco Alvarez (2026-01-25): Please add a short section in the runbook about how stale digests are handled. Also prefer streaming gRPC with backpressure rather than polling. Aisha: added tombstone logic and switched to gRPC stream in commit 2b3c4d5.
Sven Bergström (2026-01-28): The convex buffer function looks promising but the default multiplier seems aggressive for large tenants. Can we make it tenant-size aware? Aisha: implemented tenant-weighted tapering in autoscaler commit 4d5e6f7 and added unit tests.
Priya Desai (2026-01-30): CI flaked on the integration test (timeout). Can you increase test timeouts and add a retry in the simulator harness? Aisha: bumped timeouts and added deterministic seed to simulator; re-ran CI.
Marco Alvarez (2026-02-03): LGTM after addressing comments. Approving.

Context and motivation: Continuous batching has improved throughput but we still observe rare long-tail request starvation when a small set of high-cost KV-heavy requests monopolize the in-memory slot pool. Existing priority escalations were too aggressive (starving background classes) or too static (unable to react to transient spikes). This PR implements a slotted priority-decayer allocator that gives short, reclaimable "slots" to higher-priority requests while decaying their effective priority over time so that long-running or repeated high-cost requests gracefully yield to waiting lower-priority traffic. The goal is to reduce observed 99.9th latency tail without regressing median throughput.

Summary of changes (single-string commit summary):
- Add SlotAllocator and PriorityDecayer components to runtime scheduler.
- Implement jittered slot timeouts and backoff to avoid synchronized evictions.
- Add per-tenant max-wait heuristics and a soft preemption path for pinned KV cache entries.
- Introduce metrics and tracing points for slot acquisition/release and starvation events.
- Tweak kernel hinting to prefer fused kernels for short-sequence KV-heavy microbatches.
- Tests: unit & integration tests for fairness, starvation scenarios, and a small load test harness.

Commits (high level):
1) feat(scheduler): initial slotted allocator implementation (slot_allocator.rs + interfaces) — Maya
2) perf(scheduler): add priority decayer logic + jittered timeouts — Maya
3) feat(kv): soft-unpin hook and TTL for pinned KV entries (kv_cache.rs) — Maya
4) test(scheduler): add starvation regression tests and load harness — Maya
5) docs: add design note and observability docs for allocator behavior — Maya
6) fix(tests): flake in scheduler_timeout_test caught and addressed — Maya

Files changed (high-level, illustrative):
- runtime/scheduler/slot_allocator.rs
- runtime/scheduler/priority_decayer.rs
- runtime/scheduler/mod.rs (wiring & interfaces)
- runtime/kv/kv_cache.rs (soft-unpin, pin_ttl)
- runtime/telemetry/metrics.rs (new metrics)
- runtime/tests/allocator_starvation_test.rs
- examples/benchmarks/continuous_batcher_starve_sim.rs
- docs/design/slot_allocator.md
- docs/observability/slot_metrics.md

Small illustrative snippets (kept minimal):
- slot timeout jittering: "let timeout = base_timeout + rng.sample(jitter); // prevents herd eviction"
- decayer update: "priority = priority * exp(-decay_rate * held_slots)"

Design notes and rationale: The slotted model treats the continuous batcher pool as a set of reclaimable slots rather than exclusive worker tokens. When a request acquires a slot it is given a soft TTL. High-priority requests receive shorter but immediate slots; if they retain the slot beyond the TTL their effective priority is decayed so queued lower-priority requests eventually get scheduled. This prevents pathological starvation where a few expensive requests keep re-occupying slots. Jittered TTLs ensure evictions are spread to avoid synchronized thundering-herd re-requests. The allocator also exposes a soft preemption hook: when a tenant exceeds max-wait for a request class, the scheduler may trigger soft-unpin on heavily pinned KV entries, allowing progress for waiting traffic at the cost of cache churn — this is controlled by tenant-configurable heuristics.

Observability and metrics: Added metrics:
- scheduler.slot_acquire_total
- scheduler.slot_release_total
- scheduler.slot_evicted_jittered_total
- scheduler.priority_decay_events
- scheduler.tenant_max_wait_exceeded
Tracing spans added for allocation lifecycle and soft-unpin windows. Design doc and observability pages added in docs/ to help SRE tune decay_rate, base_timeout, and jitter width per workload.

Testing and CI: Initial CI run failed on scheduler_timeout_test due to a race in the test harness (timing assumptions vs jitter). Fixed by making the test assert ranges rather than absolute timings and adding a retry harness for flaky timing. Comprehensive unit tests added for decayer math, integration tests simulate mixed KV-light and KV-heavy load with per-tenant QoS and assert no starvation for 30s windows in the harness. Local perf tests show 15-22% reduction in 99.9th latency for our KV-heavy synthetic workload with <3% median throughput regression in the tightest configs.

Review conversation (condensed into a single string):
- Arjun Patel (reviewer): "Nice approach — treated slots as reclaimable is a good mental model. Two asks: add a feature flag and ensure decay parameters are tenant-configurable via runtime config. Also please add a microbenchmark for the decayer math to prove negligible CPU overhead." 
- Maya Chen (author): "Added feature flag (experimental.slotted_allocator) and made decay_rate / base_timeout tenant overridable; added microbenchmark in runtime/bench/decayer_bench.rs." 
- Liam O'Connor (reviewer): "Concern about KV soft-unpin causing cache churn on hot slots — can we gate on pin_count > threshold and add a cooldown to avoid repeated churn?" 
- Maya Chen: "Added a cooldown window and pin_count threshold check; documented tradeoffs in docs/design/slot_allocator.md." 
- Sofia Martinez (SRE reviewer): "Metrics look good. Please ensure the slot eviction metric is tagged with tenant_id and model to help debugging." 
- Maya Chen: "Added tenant/model tags to eviction and max_wait metrics."
- Arjun Patel: "Approving pending small nit on a log line formatting (fixed)."
- Merge: "squash and merge" after CI green.

CI matrix summary: unit tests (linux) = pass, integration (kitchen) = pass, lint (clippy/format) = pass, perf smoke = pass. One rerun after the timing flake; all checks green on final.

Backward compatibility and rollout plan: This feature is behind an experimental feature-flag. Default disabled on main. Rollout plan:
1) Canary (10% of traffic) with feature flag enabled and elevated observability (1h window) — monitor slot_evicted_jittered_total and tenant_max_wait_exceeded.
2) If stable at canary, enable for more tenants and reduce decay aggressiveness for latency-sensitive customers.
3) For Dedicated/Private customers requiring stability, this stays opt-in until verified.

Follow-ups: (a) Auto-tune decay_rate based on observed retry/backoff patterns (ENG-8489), (b) tighter kernel hinting integration to preferentially route short-seq KV-heavy microbatches to the fused kernel path (performance win observed in local bench).

Notes: No breaking API changes. Configurable knobs added to runtime config are documented; defaults are conservative. The merged patch increases code paths in scheduler but keeps previous behavior by default when the feature flag is off.
payload.title: Slotted priority decayer: slot allocator for continuous batching to reduce starvation

payload.body:
Summary: This PR adds a lightweight heuristic release annotator plus an associated profile curation workflow to help automate changelog blurbs and surface actionable profile deltas during model onboarding. The annotator synthesizes short, structured release notes from differences between successive model profiles (performance, latency distributions, and qualitative eval metrics), and attaches provenance anchors so downstream releases can be traced back to source artifacts.

Motivation: The registry holds many onboarding artifacts but developers still write release notes manually. We want consistent, machine-assisted release summaries that highlight material changes (perf regressions, size/quantization changes, new tokenization artifacts) and suggest rollout guidance.

Goals:
- Produce concise 1-3 sentence changelog blurbs per variant.
- Surface top 3 metric deltas with suggested actions (e.g., "consider enabling cache", "promote quantized candidate for cost-sensitive routes").
- Stamp provenance anchors (profile-hash, fingerprint, dataset-seed) so releases are auditable.
- Keep onboarding optional and incremental: users opt-in via onboarding config or CLI flag.

Implementation details:
- annotator/engine: Python microservice integrated into the onboard pipeline (registry/onboard/annotator.py). It consumes two profile JSONs (baseline, candidate) and produces an annotation object serialized as a compact blurb and list of gist-like notes. Heuristics include weighted scoring across metrics: latency p95, mean tokens/sec, normalized quality delta (we use the existing eval harness scores), model size (MB), and quantization flag. Each metric is assigned a tunable weight with defaults chosen from historical onboarding deltas.
- provenance anchors: we generate a deterministic fingerprint using model hash + dataset-seed + profiler-version (new CLI flag --profiling-seed). The fingerprint is stored in profile metadata as anchor:v1:<hex>.
- blurb synthesis: short sentences built from templated fragments with a beam of variants; we score candidates by clarity and conciseness heuristics and pick the top-ranked blurb. Example output: "Candidate variant 't1-7b-q4' reduces endpoint cost by ~28% (est.) with a 4% mean quality delta on deveval; recommend canary with caching enabled."
- profile curation workflow: a new workflow in registry/pipelines/curation.yaml that runs annotator, produces a curated_release.json, and pushes an automated change-note draft to Linear when configured.
- CLI: onboard-cli gains flags --profiling-seed and --annotate-release (boolean) to produce deterministic anchors and automatic drafts.
- Safety heuristics: annotations include conservative gating rules: if quality delta < -2% or latency regressions > 30% we mark annotation as "requires-review" and do not auto-post.

Tests and CI:
- Unit tests added for metric weighting and blurb templates (tests/test_annotator.py).
- Integration test that runs a small candidate/baseline pair and asserts the annotated gist matches golden fixtures (tests/fixtures/*).
- CI initially failed lint on a docstring; fixed and reran. All checks now green.

Review thread summary:
- Ava: requested stronger justification for default metric weights and asked for a way to override via org config. Response: added registry/config/annotator_defaults.toml and docs in redwood-model-registry/docs/annotator.md describing weight overrides per-tenant.
- Diego: asked to avoid auto-posting to Linear by default. Response: changed default to opt-out and added clear consent checks; documented the behavior.
- Emily: requested an audit log entry for every generated blurb. Response: added audit emit in the pipeline and a short retention note in docs.

Commits:
- c1a4f2d: add annotator core, blurb templates and scoring harness
- b9e7d3a: introduce provenance fingerprint generator and CLI flag --profiling-seed
- 4f2b6e1: pipeline: add curation workflow and Linear draft hook (opt-in)
- 77d9a11: tests and fixtures for annotator; golden fixture updates
- 8bb3e4c: docs, config defaults, and audit log emit
- faf5b12: fix linting and CI flakes

Changed files (high level):
- registry/onboard/annotator.py (new)
- registry/cli/onboard.py (CLI flags)
- registry/pipelines/curation.yaml (workflow)
- registry/config/annotator_defaults.toml (defaults)
- registry/docs/annotator.md (doc)
- tests/test_annotator.py, tests/fixtures/*
- registry/hooks/linear_draft.py (opt-in hook)

Rollout plan:
- Stage 1 (canary): enable annotator for internal onboarding only; keep Linear hook off.
- Stage 2 (customer opt-in): surface annotator in the Console onboarding flow and allow org-level defaults.
- Stage 3 (optional auto-post): allow teams to opt into automatic Linear drafts.

Migration notes:
- No breaking changes. Profiles gain two optional fields: provenance_anchor and curated_blurb. Existing tooling ignores them if absent.
- For deterministic fingerprints, teams should pass --profiling-seed or set a value in onboarding config.

Observability & monitoring:
- Added metrics: annotator.calls, annotator.duration_ms, annotator.decisions.* (counts of "auto-post", "requires-review").
- Added an alert (low volume after rollout) to detect if annotation success drops below 90%.

Security & privacy:
- The annotator never uploads raw datasets; it consumes aggregated profile metrics only. The Linear hook only posts draft text and the provenance anchor; secrets are masked.

Why this is different: prior PRs focused on changelog extraction from release streams or heavy-weight curated bundles. This PR intentionally targets the onboarding path, produces compact, actionable blurbs, and is designed to be conservative and opt-in.

Future work:
- Integrate with release note composer in Console to allow editing generated blurbs.
- Add a model-specific learned scoring model (replace heuristics) once we collect 1000+ annotated deltas.

Merge outcome: squash merge to main after approvals from Ava and Diego. Changelog automated entry created in CHANGELOG-curation.md.
Ava Patel: Can we expose the metric weights per-org? Some teams weight latency much higher than quality.
Sasha Nguyen: Added annotator_defaults.toml and docs; weights are overridable via org config and Console settings (docs updated).
Diego Ramirez: Do NOT auto-post to Linear by default. We need explicit consent.
Sasha Nguyen: Switched Linear hook to opt-in; default remains off and pipeline will only create local draft files unless configured.
Emily Chen: Add an audit log entry when a blurb is generated so SRE/Compliance can trace back communications.
Sasha Nguyen: Added registry/audit emit path and a short retention policy note in docs.
Adds a heuristic release annotator and profile curation workflow: generates concise changelog blurbs from profile deltas, tags variant provenance anchors, and exposes CLI flags for deterministic profiling seeds. Backwards compatible; opt-in via onboarding config.

Motivation: v3 of the public response envelope introduces a stricter typed 'envelope' for streaming events and tool call payloads. Several downstream SDKs and customers are on older streaming parsers and will break if we flip the rollout flag with the new envelope shape. This PR implements an adaptive "schema negotiator" middleware in the OpenAI-compat proxy that can: 1) honor an opt-in Prefer-Schema header (e.g. Prefer-Schema: v3-alpha or Prefer-Schema: v1), 2) automatically coerce v3 envelopes back to v1-compatible streaming fragments when the client signals legacy parsing, and 3) provide a server-side fallback mode that injects minimal compatibility events when tool/function call streaming transitions fail. The negotiator is intentionally conservative: it only performs lossy coercion when the request explicitly opts into compatibility or when the request comes from a legacy-sdk user-agent whitelist.

Implementation summary:
- new middleware at proxy/routing layer (compat/negotiator.go) that parses headers and attaches a negotiation context to the request
- header rules: Prefer-Schema, X-RW-Schema-Coerce (true|false), X-RW-Compat-Mode (strict|compat-auto|force)
- streaming path: a streaming translator that maps v3 envelope frames to v1 frames and emits legacy-style "delta" tool call markers; when translation would lose structured metadata we include an inline "compat-meta" event so clients can surface a deprecation notice
- non-streaming responses: best-effort schema downcast with a deterministic field mapping preserved in compat/mapping.json
- rollout plan: start with opt-in header behavior behind a feature flag, enable user-agent whitelist for nightly SDK builds, then gate automatic coercion under Canary stage for 48 hours before broader rollout

Backwards-compat considerations and migration notes:
- This shim is not intended as a long-term substitute for SDK updates; it is explicitly lossy for certain typed fields (tool metadata timestamps, internal trace ids) and those losses are documented here.
- Customers must be encouraged to adopt Prefer-Schema: v3 once they upgrade SDKs. We emit a persistent deprecation log entry per-client to the audit sink (audit/compat-events) to surface long-lived consumers still relying on the shim

Testing and validation:
- unit tests for header parsing and mapping tables
- e2e streaming tests with the internal streaming harness (bench/stream-compat-harness) simulating slow parsers and reconnects
- integration tests exercising tool-calls across the compat layer and verifying that the coerced stream is parseable by legacy SDK parsers
- load-test that validates latency impact (<2% p50 increase) and resource overhead

Rollout checklist (in-code):
- feature flag gate introduced and default = off
- audit log emitted on any coerced response
- metric compat.coercion.count and compat.coercion.lossy_count
- canary config for region us-west-2 and dedicated customers only
- SDK owners notified (ts/python/go)

Implementation notes and files changed are listed below. Please review the header naming, the translation mapping, and the Canary scope.
Liam Chen (reviewer): Please avoid adding new global headers if we can reuse Prefer-* patterns; can we use Prefer-Schema instead of X-RW-Schema-Coerce?
Asha Patel (author): Great call, kept Prefer-Schema and added X-RW-Schema-Coerce as explicit override for partner contracts. Updated docs to clarify precedence.
Mariana Ortiz (reviewer): The compat-meta event is fine but include a compact reason code so telemetry can aggregate; also please add a feature-flag metric.
Asha Patel (author): Added compat.coercion.reason_code and increment on lossy transforms. Also added feature flag metrics and updated tests.
Derek Hughes (approver): Verified e2e harness; latency delta looks acceptable. Approving with the canary restriction in place.
Added an adaptive schema negotiator shim that can coerce v3 streaming envelopes to v1-compatible streaming fragments behind an opt-in header and canary rollout. Not a permanent compatibility layer — customers should upgrade SDKs to v3 to receive typed streaming events. Metrics: compat.coercion.count, compat.coercion.lossy_count, compat.coercion.reason_code.

payload.body:
Adds internal entitlement verification APIs for AWS/GCP marketplace subscriptions, including stable error codes for console onboarding and integration tests. No customer-facing API changes.
Context: Marketplace onboarding currently relies on the entitlement sync job eventually populating our Entitlements table. Console has no reliable way to distinguish “still propagating” vs “invalid subscription” vs “already linked to a different org”, leading to confusing retries and support escalations (see SUP-4821).

This PR adds first-class entitlement verification endpoints (AWS + GCP) and a typed error-code contract that the console onboarding flow can consume.

What’s included: (1) New endpoints (internal) - POST /v1/marketplace/entitlements:verify - POST /v1/marketplace/entitlements:link (used after verify succeeds) - GET /v1/marketplace/entitlements/{entitlement_id} (debug/CS tooling, RBAC-gated). All endpoints are behind the internal API gateway and require an authenticated Redwood session + org context; no raw cloud credentials are accepted.

(2) Provider normalization: The request accepts provider=aws|gcp and a provider-specific “registration payload” captured by console during marketplace subscription confirmation. We normalize that into a single internal identifier: marketplace_entitlement_key (e.g., aws:customerIdentifier:<id> or gcp:procurementAccount:<id>). We store the normalized key and a hash of the raw payload (for dedupe/traceability) but do not persist the full raw payload.

(3) Error code contract for onboarding: The response includes a stable machine-readable error_code and a short user_message for console display. Codes implemented in this PR: - INVALID_PROVIDER (400) - INVALID_REGISTRATION_PAYLOAD (400) - UNAUTHENTICATED (401) - FORBIDDEN (403) - ENTITLEMENT_NOT_FOUND (404) - ENTITLEMENT_PENDING (202) (subscription exists but not yet visible to Redwood / sync has not ingested) - ENTITLEMENT_ORG_MISMATCH (409) (entitlement is already linked to a different org) - ENTITLEMENT_ALREADY_LINKED (409) (same org tries to link again) - ENTITLEMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE (503) (provider API timeout/5xx; should retry) - ENTITLEMENT_STALE (202) (entitlement exists but last_verified_at is stale; refresh queued) - RATE_LIMITED (429).

(4) Refresh behavior: verify attempts a fast-path DB lookup. If not found or stale, we enqueue an on-demand refresh job (bounded, deduped by entitlement key) and return ENTITLEMENT_PENDING or ENTITLEMENT_STALE with retry_after_seconds. This avoids synchronous dependency on AWS/GCP APIs during onboarding, while still improving perceived reliability.

(5) Audit + observability: - Adds audit log events: marketplace.entitlement.verify and marketplace.entitlement.link (includes org_id, provider, entitlement_key prefix, request_id) - Adds metrics: marketplace_entitlement_verify_total{provider,result}, marketplace_entitlement_verify_latency_ms, marketplace_entitlement_refresh_enqueued_total - Adds structured logs with request_id and marketplace_provider.

(6) Integration tests + docs: - Integration tests cover: pending->success path, org mismatch, already linked idempotency, stale refresh enqueue, provider unavailable mapping - Updates OpenAPI spec and internal API docs page used by Console + DevEx - Adds minimal examples for console: verify then link.

Security notes: - The verify/link endpoints are not exposed in the public Redwood API; they are internal control-plane endpoints used by the console onboarding flow. - Registration payload validation is strict and provider-specific; we redact payloads from logs by default. - Entitlement keys are partially masked in logs/audit trails.

Rollout plan: - Merge behind feature flag: marketplace_entitlement_verification_v1 - Console will start consuming error codes after DES-912/ENG-22112 lands; until then endpoints are safe/no-op for existing flows - After rollout, we can tune retry messaging and remove legacy console polling behavior.

Checklist: - [x] API endpoints implemented with RBAC + input validation - [x] Stable error codes documented and added to OpenAPI - [x] Integration tests (happy + edge cases) - [x] Metrics + audit logs - [x] Backfill migration not required (uses existing Entitlements table, adds columns nullable)

Follow-ups (out of scope): - Admin/CS endpoint to manually trigger a provider refresh for a specific entitlement key - Add telemetry event mapping in console (ENG-22114) - Tie verify/link results into onboarding funnel dashboard (Ben’s baseline doc).
Chloe Martin (review): Can we make sure the console never has to parse provider-specific shapes? It should be error_code + next_step only. Also please confirm which statuses we should treat as retryable.
Ethan Park (author): Yep. Console contract is provider-agnostic: {status, error_code?, user_message?, retry_after_seconds?, entitlement_id?}. Retryable: ENTITLEMENT_PENDING, ENTITLEMENT_STALE, ENTITLEMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE, RATE_LIMITED. I added a table to docs/internal/api/marketplace-entitlements.md and updated OpenAPI examples.
Cole Summers (review): How does this interact with metering dimensions? Linking must not create multiple active entitlements for a single org+provider.
Ethan Park (author): link is idempotent on (org_id, provider, entitlement_key). If the entitlement is already linked to the same org, returns ENTITLEMENT_ALREADY_LINKED (409) with the existing entitlement_id. If linked to a different org, ENTITLEMENT_ORG_MISMATCH. No changes to metering here; this only establishes the entitlement<->org relationship used later by the billing pipeline.
Marcus Lin (review): Please ensure we’re not logging raw registration payloads, and that audit events don’t include customer identifiers in full.
Ethan Park (author): Done. Added redaction helpers; logs only include entitlement_key prefix + hash. Audit event stores provider + org_id + request_id; entitlement_key is masked to first 6 chars + suffix.
Nadia Rahman (review): Integration test flaked once on job queue timing in CI. Can we make it deterministic?
Ethan Park (author): Fixed by injecting a fake clock + asserting enqueue call rather than waiting for job execution. Reran CI: green.
Priya Natarajan (approval): Looks good. Ship behind flag and coordinate console adoption.
Alex Martinez (approval): Docs updates are clear; examples match what we need for onboarding guides.
payload.title: Marketplace: entitlement verification endpoints + onboarding error codes

payload.body:
## Summary This PR adds a docs build step that consumes generated changelog artifacts (from the model registry/control plane changelog generator) and renders versioned, customer-visible model release note pages in the docs site. It also produces an RSS feed and a machine-readable JSON feed for programmatic consumption. The goal is to make model/version promotions visible and consistent (Hosted/Dedicated/Private where applicable) while keeping internal-only details redacted and enforcing the taxonomy/style constraints defined for customer notes. ## Why We currently have model/version changes scattered across internal release processes and ad-hoc docs updates, which has led to customers seeing “silent” model updates and inconsistent guidance on what changed / what to do. This PR is one leg of the end-to-end pipeline: (1) metadata change events => (2) changelog generator artifact => (3) docs build consumes artifact => (4) published release notes pages and feeds. ## What’s included - Adds `scripts/release-notes/ingestChangelogArtifacts.ts` which downloads/reads changelog artifacts (local path in CI; optional remote URL via env var for preview builds), validates against `publicChangelogArtifact.schema.json`, and writes a normalized `generated/release-notes/models/*.json` index used by the site. - Adds page generation for: `/release-notes/models/:modelSlug/:version` (versioned page) and `/release-notes/models/:modelSlug` (model landing page with version timeline + filters). - Adds feed generation: `public/release-notes/models/rss.xml` and `public/release-notes/models/feed.json`. - Adds guardrails: fails build if any entry is marked `visibility=internal` or includes internal-only fields (defense-in-depth; the generator already filters, but docs should not trust inputs). - Adds canonical URLs + stable IDs for feed items (`modelSlug@semver` + published timestamp) to avoid duplication across builds. - Adds minimal “rollout context” rendering: when a note includes public rollout info (e.g., Hosted first, Dedicated next), the page displays it, but does not render account-specific targeting, regions, or internal policy rules. - Adds partial backfill support: can ingest a small set of historical artifacts to seed the index (no attempt to rewrite legacy freeform release notes). ## Non-goals - Customer notification subscriptions (email/webhook). - Rendering any private/embargoed changes. - Surfacing internal audit or SIEM export details (those remain in Console/Admin + audit logs). ## Implementation notes - Artifact format: expects the v1 public artifact output from the changelog generator (see `redwood` PR-18441 and `redwood-model-registry` PR-18421). We validate the artifact schema + enforce redaction checks. - Sorting: versions are sorted by `published_at` primarily; semver is used as a tie-breaker. - Feeds: RSS is “last 50 items” (configurable); JSON feed includes the same window. - SEO: adds `noindex` for drafts/preview builds; production build only publishes the generated pages. - Failure modes: build fails fast with a concise error message showing the offending entry ID and the field that violates public policy (e.g., `internal_notes`, `incident_id`, `customer_name`). ## Testing - Unit tests for ingestion + schema validation + redaction enforcement. - Snapshot tests for RSS and JSON feed outputs. - Local verification via `pnpm release-notes:mock` (creates a mock artifact in `./fixtures/changelog/`) and `pnpm dev` to confirm routing and page rendering. ## Rollout plan - Behind `PUBLIC_MODEL_RELEASE_NOTES=1` flag for staging. - After generator artifacts are available for at least one model family, we will enable in prod and add a top-level nav link (separate PR to avoid coupling IA changes). ## Screenshots/Examples (text) - Example URL: `/release-notes/models/llama-3-1-instruct/3.1.2` - Feed URL: `/release-notes/models/rss.xml` and `/release-notes/models/feed.json`
Elliot Price: Can we guarantee we never publish internal-only fields even if the generator regresses? Also please add a human-friendly build error to help docs oncall triage.
Wei Chen (author): Added explicit denylist checks + schema validation in docs build. Error now prints entry ID + field name + remediation hint ("re-run generator with public filtering; check ENG-9825 redaction rules").
Kira Thompson: Private customers will ask whether these notes match upgrade bundles. Can we render “availability by deployment” clearly but without overpromising timelines?
Wei Chen (author): Rendered `availability` section only when present in public artifact and kept language factual ("Available in Hosted" / "Planned for Dedicated" if provided). No dates unless artifact includes an explicit public date.
Jada Williams: Please ensure stable IDs for feed entries; we had dupes previously when ordering changed. Also watch out for semver parsing with model variants like `-q4_k_m` suffixes.
Wei Chen (author): Feed IDs now use `model_slug + version + published_at` and we normalize version display separately from route param. Added tests covering variant suffixes and non-strict semver (we fallback to lexical + published_at).
Connor O'Brien: CI: I want this to run in preview builds but not block unrelated doc-only edits when PUBLIC_MODEL_RELEASE_NOTES=0. Also add an explicit artifact freshness warning if source is missing.
Wei Chen (author): Workflow now runs ingestion only when flag is enabled (staging/prod). For preview builds, it uses fixtures unless `CHANGELOG_ARTIFACT_URL` is set. If missing in prod/staging, build fails with a clear message and points to the producing job.
Elliot Price: Approved after the redaction tests landed.
Docs site can now publish per-model, per-version release notes from generated changelog artifacts.
Added public RSS and JSON feeds for model release notes.
Build-time validation prevents internal-only fields from being published.
Docs build enforces public-only schema + explicit denylist checks to prevent leakage of internal notes, customer identifiers, incident references, or rollout policy internals. Production build fails closed if a violating field is detected.
Add top-level nav entry and docs IA updates (tracked in PM-412 follow-up).
Coordinate enablement timing with changelog artifact production in `redwood` (ENG-9823) and CI preview checks (ENG-9826).
Add a small curated backfill set once final taxonomy/style guide lands (see PR-9320).
payload.title: Generate public model release notes pages from changelog artifacts (plus RSS/JSON feeds)

This PR introduces a standardized, public-facing post-incident summary format and two example summaries, aligned with the internal Confluence template used by SRE/Comms Leads as part of the Status Page Transparency Upgrades initiative. Motivation: customers have asked for consistent, quickly publishable summaries with clear impact/timeline/prevention detail (ref SUP-28502 and recent status accuracy escalations), and our existing docs do not define what a “post-incident summary” contains or what we will/won’t include for sensitive incidents (Dedicated/Private). Summary of changes: (1) Add a new docs page defining the post-incident summary structure (Impact, Timeline, Root cause class, Mitigation, Prevention/Follow-ups, Where to get help) with explicit confidentiality guidance; (2) Add example summaries that demonstrate appropriate level of detail (no customer identifiers, no capacity specifics, no exploit-level info) and consistent phrasing across incident phases; (3) Update the status page docs index and cross-link from the incident communications guidance so Support can point customers to a stable reference; (4) Add wording notes for Dedicated/Private incidents: what may be published publicly vs when we will publish a “limited summary” and where customer-specific detail will live (support ticket / CSM follow-up). Non-goals: changing the actual status page UI, automating summary generation, or committing to new SLAs/TTFU targets in public docs. Rollout plan: publish docs concurrently with the internal training rollout (PM-620) and keep examples as living references; legal/security reviewed language for safe defaults. Screenshots: N/A (text-only).
Excerpt added to docs/status/post-incident-summaries.md: “We aim to publish a post-incident summary once service is stable and the initial cause/mitigation is understood. Summaries are written to be useful for engineering teams operating production workloads, without disclosing customer-identifying details, sensitive security information, or capacity/architecture specifics that could increase risk. If an incident affects Dedicated or Private deployments, we may publish a limited public summary and provide additional context directly to affected customers via Support/CS.”
Wei Chen (comment): Suggest tightening the “Root cause” section to “Root cause class” to avoid over-promising certainty in early summaries; also add one sentence explicitly stating that numbers may be approximate initially.
Elliot Price (reply): Good call. Updated headings to “Root cause class” and added a note in Timeline/Impact that metrics may be refined as analysis completes.
Kira Thompson (comment): Dedicated/Private language needs to be clearer: we should not imply per-customer status visibility on the public page. Recommend adding “customer-specific impacts are communicated directly” and remove any mention of “tenant-level components.”
Elliot Price (reply): Agreed. Removed tenant-level phrasing and added “customer-specific impacts are communicated directly via Support/CS channels.”
Dev Patel (comment): Please add a short section “How to reference this summary in a support ticket” + link to status page and incident ID conventions so agents can macro it consistently.
Elliot Price (reply): Added a “Where to get help” line that calls out including request IDs + region + timeframe, and ensured the examples include an incident identifier format agents can copy.
Naomi Feldman (comment): Security note: avoid listing exact WAF rules, exploit details, or vendor advisories until cleared. The examples are fine; just add a single explicit bullet to the “Do not include” list.
Elliot Price (reply): Added bullet under “Do not include” to cover exploit-level details and unreviewed vendor/security advisories.
Michael Grant (comment): Legal: remove ‘we will’ commitments around timing; use ‘we aim’ / ‘when feasible’ and avoid implied SLA language.
Elliot Price (reply): Updated timing language throughout to “aim” and “when feasible,” removed any numeric time commitments, and aligned wording with PM-612 policy.
Paula Mendes (approval): Looks aligned with the internal template and tone guidance; examples are strong. Approved after latest copy edits.
Public docs now include a standardized post-incident summary format and examples, aligned with internal incident comms templates; includes guidance on sensitive details and Dedicated/Private handling.
payload.title: Add public post-incident summary format + examples (aligned with internal template)

Summary: Adds an 'econ-runner' CLI and an anticipatory batch catalog that synthesizes per-tenant batching/caching defaults and candidate quantization profiles based on recent traffic signals and unit-econ targets. Motivation: customers with spiky but predictable patterns (scheduled reports, nightly batch jobs, and periodic tenant ramps) need safer automated defaults for batching, prefetching, and quantization that reduce unit cost without risking tail latency regressions. This PR introduces a production-safe, tenant-aware pipeline that (1) samples recent traffic patterns, (2) simulates batch/cache/quant trade-offs locally using the existing cost simulator, and (3) provisions suggested defaults that can be applied as tenant profiles or validated via canary routes. Design: - econ-runner CLI (Go) orchestrates sampling, local sim, and profile output; supports dry-run and apply modes. - anticipatory_batch_catalog: stores candidate batch sizes, KV cache TTL heuristics, and quant profiles ranked by expected tokens-per-dollar and P95 latency impact. - integration with telemetry: cost signal collector exports a recent window (30d) of token distributions and sequence lengths; runner uses this to seed sims. - runtime adjustments: lightweight admission filter in the scheduler consults tenant profile when routing to prefer compact profiles under cost targets; fallback to standard profile on SLA pressure. Migration and safety: default mode is dry-run. The apply step creates tenant-scoped proposal objects in the control plane (not auto-applied) unless --auto-apply is set and the tenant has opted-in. We added a conservative guard: only profiles with simulated P95 < baseline + 10ms and estimated unit-cost delta > 3% are proposed for apply. Testing and validation: unit tests for sim harness, integration tests against local runtime mock, end-to-end smoke with a synthetic tenant workload, and a benchmark sweep covering small/medium/large sequence lengths. Rollout plan: feature gate behind internal flag; start with opt-in beta tenants; monitor cost delta and latency SLOs; auto-revert if regressions observed. Checklist: - [x] econ-runner CLI and docs - [x] anticipatory batch catalog proto and persistence - [x] simulation harness wiring and test coverage - [x] safe-apply guardrails and opt-in path - [x] console doc and short how-to - [x] perf bench run and telemetry dashboards updated Notes: This PR prioritizes conservative defaults — it is intentionally restrictive to avoid surprise regressions. Future follow-ups: continuous learning loop (automatic proposals after N successful applies), and a UI flow in Console for reviewing proposals.
Marcus Nguyen: Please ensure the sim harness uses the same kernel/quant code paths as production. If we diverge we get optimistic cost estimates.
Author (Lena Ortiz): Updated the harness to invoke the runtime kernel selector in 'sim-mode' and added a smoke test that compares sim output to a 1k-sample production replay.
Aria Cho: I think the guard threshold for P95 is tight; can we make it tenant-configurable and default to 10ms? Also add an early-exit if the workload has >80% short sequences (no batching benefit).
Author: Added tenant-configurable guard and early-exit heuristic; documented behaviour in the guide.
Samir Patel: CI flake on the integration suite (random timeout). Suggest increasing test timeout and marking unstable test as flaky with retry.
Author: Added retry wrapper and increased timeout; reran CI.
Introduces econ-runner CLI and anticipatory batch catalog. Admins can generate tenant-specific batching, cache, and quantization proposals based on historical signals. Safe-apply requires opt-in; proposals can be reviewed in Console. Expect conservative cost savings (see perf summary).

Summary: Align Private (VPC + on-prem/air-gapped) upgrade/rollback documentation with the new installer workflow: plan -> prechecks -> backup -> apply -> verify -> rollback (if needed). This updates the operator-facing steps, introduces troubleshooting playbooks for common precheck and upgrade failures, and clarifies rollback guarantees/limitations (esp. around schema migrations and partial rollouts). Motivation: Support escalations and design partner feedback indicated the previous docs were ambiguous about (a) which checks are blocking vs warning, (b) what gets backed up and how to validate restore readiness, and (c) when rollback is safe vs when manual intervention is required. This PR is the docs companion to private-installer changes (upgrade plan generator, preflight framework, backup orchestrator, rollback state machine) and Helm ordering changes (control plane before data plane). Audience/visibility: Internal runbooks + external-ish docs pages that are shared with Private customers under guidance. What changed (high level): 1) Rewrote the main upgrade procedure to use new commands and phase naming: Generate plan, Run prechecks, Create backup, Apply upgrade (control plane then data plane), Post-upgrade verification, Capture artifacts/support bundle. 2) Added a troubleshooting index for: precheck failures (storage headroom, DB connectivity, OIDC reachability, TLS/DNS), migration lock timeouts, stuck Helm hooks/jobs, artifact/bundle verification errors for air-gapped upgrades, and rollback failures. 3) Added explicit rollback guidance: rollback entry points, expected time, health checks, and a decision tree for 'rollback vs fix-forward' based on stage. 4) Updated on-prem/air-gapped section with offline bundle verification expectations (checksums/signatures), mirror endpoints, and common operator mistakes. 5) Added an 'Upgrade artifacts for auditability' section describing what the installer persists (plan JSON, precheck results, backup IDs, execution log, audit events) and what to attach to support tickets. Notes: This PR intentionally does not introduce net-new policy; it documents the gating/checklist already being formalized elsewhere. Where behavior is still being finalized, wording is 'as of Private installer >= 1.9.0' and points to release notes. Checklist: - [x] Steps match installer CLI (plan/apply/rollback) - [x] Troubleshooting covers top 5 support cases (SUP-18421, SUP-18488, SUP-18510, SUP-18577) - [x] On-prem/air-gapped guidance includes bundle verification and offline registries - [x] Security reviewed language around backups/secrets (no plaintext exports, KMS/HSM expectations) - [x] Link check + docs build + Vale pass
Kira Thompson (requested changes): The procedure still mentions the old 'upgrade run' command in two places; please replace with plan/apply and ensure rollback references the stored upgrade state path. Also add a short 'what success looks like' section with concrete verification commands. Elliot Price (author): Fixed the remaining 'upgrade run' references, added a 'Success criteria' block under Post-upgrade verification (pods ready, API /healthz, control plane connectivity, sample inference request), and clarified the default state directory plus flag overrides. Connor O'Brien: Please call out that upgrades are supported N-1 -> N for GA, and that skipping minors is 'unsupported unless explicitly approved'. Also add a sentence about upgrade windows and release gating. Elliot Price: Added 'Supported upgrade paths' section and pointed to the release gating page; included language that multi-hop is not automated in v1. Rafael Mendes: Troubleshooting for migration lock timeouts should include the mitigation we used in staging (check for long-running transactions + retry after backoff), and the strong warning about not deleting migration jobs blindly. Elliot Price: Added a dedicated 'Migration lock timeout' page with safe mitigations and a 'do not' list. Fatima Noor: Air-gapped docs should include the exact failure mode we see: checksum mismatch due to proxy rewriting or partial downloads; and instructions to re-verify with sha256sum and re-sync bundle. Elliot Price: Added that scenario + remediation, plus a note about using the provided manifest file as the source of truth. Naomi Feldman (security): Please ensure we do not imply secrets are exported during backup; keep the language at 'references/handles' + KMS expectations. Elliot Price: Updated backup language to avoid suggesting plaintext secret export; added a short callout that secrets remain in K8s/secret store and backups capture refs/config + DB snapshots only. Approvals: Kira Thompson (approved), Connor O'Brien (approved), Rafael Mendes (approved), Fatima Noor (approved), Naomi Feldman (approved).
Docs-only: Updated Redwood Private upgrade/rollback procedures to match new installer workflow; added troubleshooting for prechecks/migrations/artifacts; clarified supported upgrade paths (N-1 -> N) and rollback constraints.
payload.title: Update Private upgrade docs: new installer commands, troubleshooting, rollback guidance
