Title: Docs: add observability hooks reference for quickstart templates

Context
We’re shipping production-minded RAG + agent quickstart templates that emit standardized OpenTelemetry signals plus Redwood-specific conventions. Support/SRE feedback has been consistent: we need a canonical reference page (1) defining the required spans/attributes/metrics/log fields, and (2) mapping those to Redwood Console dashboards so users can verify instrumentation quickly and understand what they’re looking at.

What this PR does
- Adds a new docs reference page: "Observability hooks (reference)" for Quickstart Templates.
- Documents required spans + span attributes (including what is REQUIRED vs RECOMMENDED).
- Documents required metrics (names, types, units, and allowed dimensions) and includes a “cardinality guardrails” section aligned with Observability/SRE guidance.
- Adds a “Mapping to Redwood Console” section that calls out which dashboards/panels use which signals (Templates Overview, RAG Latency Breakdown, Tool Failures, Retrieval Quality, Token Economics).
- Adds a small “How to validate locally” checklist (view trace tree, confirm metrics are flowing, confirm request-id correlation).

Non-goals
- This does not introduce new instrumentation in templates/SDKs; it’s documentation only.
- This does not document every possible OTel semantic convention; we focus on the minimum set needed to make templates supportable and dashboards functional.

Docs IA / links
- Linked from the Quickstart Templates landing page and the RAG+Agent walkthrough.
- Cross-linked from the Troubleshooting page ("No traces in Console?" and "Missing tool spans?").

New/updated content (high level)
1) Tracing
- Required span hierarchy (expected parent/child relationships):
  - http.server (or equivalent framework span)
    - redwood.llm.request
      - redwood.rag.retrieve (optional for non-RAG)
      - redwood.agent.iteration (0..N)
        - redwood.tool.<tool_name> (0..N)
- Required span attributes (REQUIRED):
  - redwood.request_id (from API response header when available; used for support correlation)
  - llm.system = "redwood" (or llm.provider = "redwood"; chosen term documented for consistency)
  - llm.model (pinned model identifier)
  - llm.operation ("chat" | "responses" | "embeddings" | "rerank")
  - http.response.status_code (for the client call span)
  - error.type (normalized error taxonomy keys)
- Recommended attributes (RECOMMENDED) with cardinality cautions:
  - redwood.deployment_mode ("hosted" | "dedicated" | "private")
  - redwood.region
  - redwood.template.name / redwood.template.version (for template-originated traffic tagging)
  - tool.name (low-cardinality) and tool.result (DO NOT log raw output)
- Redaction rules:
  - Explicitly prohibit recording prompt/user content as span attributes.
  - Recommend hashing document IDs if they must be included.
  - Provide examples of safe logging fields.

2) Metrics
- Required metrics (names, types, and units):
  - redwood.llm.latency_ms (histogram)
  - redwood.llm.tokens.input (counter)
  - redwood.llm.tokens.output (counter)
  - redwood.llm.requests (counter)
  - redwood.llm.errors (counter)
  - redwood.rag.retrieval.latency_ms (histogram)
  - redwood.rag.retrieval.results_count (histogram)
  - redwood.tool.calls (counter)
  - redwood.tool.errors (counter)
- Required metric dimensions (allowed list):
  - llm.model, llm.operation, redwood.template.name, redwood.template.version
- Forbidden/high-risk dimensions (explicit):
  - user_id, session_id, request_id, full URL paths, document titles, arbitrary tool args

3) Logs
- Minimal structured log fields to align with support workflows:
  - level, message, timestamp
  - redwood.request_id
  - error.type, error.message (redacted)
  - llm.model, llm.operation
  - tool.name (if relevant)

4) Mapping to Redwood Console
- Dashboard: Templates Overview
  - Uses redwood.template.name/version + redwood.llm.requests + redwood.llm.latency_ms
- Dashboard: Token Economics
  - Uses redwood.llm.tokens.input/output + latency histograms for cost/latency analysis
- Dashboard: Tool Failures
  - Uses redwood.tool.errors + tool spans with error.type/tool.name
- Dashboard: RAG Latency Breakdown
  - Uses redwood.rag.retrieval.latency_ms span timing + llm request span timing

Why this matters
- Reduces "is it instrumented correctly?" support load.
- Makes template dashboards immediately actionable.
- Prevents accidental high-cardinality tags and prompt/PII leakage.

Implementation notes
- Content is aligned with internal standards discussed with Allison/Logan (span naming + attribute set) and SRE feedback (cardinality guardrails, redaction language).
- Added a small admonition block where we previously saw proxy issues with opt-in telemetry headers; the reference clarifies that template tagging is optional and must not include user data.

Screenshots
- N/A (docs-only). Included example trace tree and metric table inline.

Testing
- `pnpm lint`
- `pnpm test:links`
- `pnpm build`

Follow-ups
- After merge, we should link this page from the SDK instrumentation guide (Wei is tracking separately) and ensure the observability pack dashboard names match the final docs strings.


Commits
1) docs(quickstarts): add observability hooks reference page
2) docs(quickstarts): link reference from templates landing + walkthrough
3) docs(observability): add metric tables + cardinality guidance

Motivation: Teams asked for a small, opinionated playground that demonstrates progressive RAG patterns (single-shot retrieval, multi-step tool calling, and live telemetry hooks) without pulling the entire examples repo. This PR adds a lightweight 'scenario lab' in the docs site plus a compact 'snippet garden' that collects bite-sized code samples for tool-binding and telemetry instrumentation.

What this contains: - A scenario-lab guide (docs/rag/scenario-lab/index.md) with three curated scenarios: 'Search + Update', 'Form-filling with tool calls', and 'Fallback to backup model'. Each scenario includes expected prompts, sample prompts, and a deterministic verification checklist for evals. - Snippet garden (docs/snippets/snippet-garden.md) with 10 runnable snippets: 4 TypeScript, 3 Python, 2 shell examples, and an OpenAPI mock for tool stubs. Snippets emphasize safe tool-call shapes, input sanitization, and streaming-handling best practices. - Small examples folder (examples/rag/snippets/*) with a compact TS and Python binding that mirror the snippets; intentionally minimal dependencies so they can be copied into customer sandboxes. - Updated docs site config and a basic static flow diagram (docs/images/flow-diagram.svg) for the scenario-lab visual. - CI: lightweight doc linting and link checks were added to scripts/ci/validate-docs.yml to ensure snippets build in the docs runner.

Why this approach: prior quickstarts were full-stack and useful but heavy for first-time readers. The scenario-lab is designed to be a shorter intermediate step: reproducible, reviewable (can be used in quality gates), and easy to port into a codebase or a Playbook. The snippet-garden aims to centralize tiny best-practice examples so engineers don't copy entire quickstarts for a one-off pattern.

Testing and verification: - Manual walkthrough of each scenario using the local mkdocs preview. - Ran the new docs CI (link checks + snippet extraction) on the branch. - Smoke-tested TS and Python snippets against the open-source shim in examples/rag/snippets. - Verified all links and images render correctly in the built site.

Checklist: - [x] Add scenario-lab content and visuals - [x] Extract snippets into a single docs page - [x] Add minimal runnable examples (TS/Python) - [x] Add doc CI linting for snippet extraction - [x] Add Linear tickets and link SUP ticket for a known telemetry gap

Notes/Limitations: - These snippets intentionally avoid advanced stateful session code; stateful session patterns will be covered in a separate playbook. - Telemetry hooks in snippets are illustrative; production telemetry should use the full Redwood Console SDK.

Related: ENG-3281 (scenario templates), PM-421 (docs priority). For follow-ups: add runnable Docker devcontainer for each snippet and add a 'migration' page that maps snippet patterns to full quickstarts.

Goal: publish marketplace-friendly, customer-facing security docs that AWS/GCP reviewers and enterprise buyers can use without opening a ticket, while keeping claims accurate and consistent with our SOC 2/ISO-aligned controls. This PR adds (1) a Marketplace Security Overview page with a simple system/data-flow narrative and clear shared responsibility boundaries, and (2) a buyer-focused FAQ that answers common procurement/security questions (encryption, audit logs, retention, residency, incident response, support SLAs, and how to request evidence).

Key points / decisions (per Security & GRC review): we avoid absolute language like "we never store prompts" and instead document our default handling + configurable controls; we call out that some security evidence (SOC 2 Type II report, pen test summary) is available under NDA / upon request; we do not claim certifications we do not hold; we state encryption practices at a level appropriate for public docs (in transit + at rest, KMS options for Private) without disclosing sensitive implementation details.

Content added:
- /security/marketplace/overview: scope, deployment modes (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and how security responsibilities differ, high-level data flow, encryption overview, identity/access, logging/audit, retention/residency, subprocessors pointers, and evidence request path.
- /security/marketplace/faq: short Q&A for procurement-led buyers, including marketplace subscription->entitlement->org provisioning expectations and who to contact when entitlement propagation is delayed.

Follow-ups (out of scope here): add diagrams once Design finalizes the screenshot/diagram pack (DES-913), and align FAQ wording with the final marketplace listing FAQ blocks once PMM locks copy for AWS/GCP submission.
- New public docs pages: Marketplace Security Overview + Marketplace Buyer FAQ
- Wording aligned to Security/GRC guidance (no over-claims; clear shared responsibility)
- Links to gated evidence request flow (SOC 2 report, pen test summary) for procurement

This PR adds the initial customer-facing documentation for Route experiments (route-level A/B/n testing) in Redwood Console Rollouts. It focuses on: (1) what route experiments are and when to use them, (2) how deterministic assignment works and how to choose/pass a stickiness key to avoid skew, (3) how to interpret the built-in metrics (latency/cost/error/throughput + optional quality signals) and guardrails in Console, and (4) troubleshooting common beta issues (missing attribution on streaming retries, propagation lag/stale results, skew when sticky key is low entropy). The guide is intentionally light on statistical significance claims; it documents basic deltas and guardrail thresholds only (per GA scope). It also documents headers and SDK helpers surfaced during beta so users can self-debug variant assignment. Includes updates to the navigation, terminology glossary, and a small FAQ entry on audit logs and RBAC. Related: ENG-9032 (docs), PM-482 (GA requirements). Also reworked Guardrails to describe default soft-stop + notification and that some orgs can enable automatic stop with admin controls; removed internal flag names."

Summary: This PR publishes initial external documentation for the Retention controls + compliance reporting pack workstream. It adds a retention controls overview (supported data classes, tier defaults, and how to configure), documents limitations and operational semantics (TTL vs purge, change history, verification), and updates the Security FAQ with customer-ready answers for security questionnaires.

Motivation: Enterprise security reviews (Dedicated/Private) are consistently asking for (a) configurable retention by data class and (b) a standardized evidence package for audit logs + retention configuration. Prior docs were a mix of internal Confluence and ad-hoc SE answers; this makes the baseline story consistent and reduces back-and-forth.

What’s included:
- New docs page: “Retention controls” covering supported data classes (request/response logs where enabled, audit logs, traces/metrics retention, and artifacts where applicable), what Redwood does by default by deployment tier, and how customers change retention (Console + API + Terraform for Private where supported).
- New docs page: “Retention controls limitations & semantics” clarifying: TTL enforcement is asynchronous; deletes are idempotent; retention controls apply to stored telemetry/logging data (not model weights); and short retention may reduce debugging history unless a documented break-glass exception is approved.
- Updated Security FAQ entries: “Do you support configurable retention?”, “Can you provide an audit log export?”, “What is included in the compliance reporting pack?”, “How do you handle legal hold / incident holds?”
- New section: “Requesting the compliance reporting pack” describing how to request the baseline package (via Support ticket or AE/SE), expected content (audit-log coverage summary, retention configuration export, data residency/region summary, RBAC/access report, evidence checklist), and typical turnaround for a specified time window.

Notes / wording constraints:
- Avoids making certification claims (no “SOC 2 certified” language); uses “aligned to SOC 2 / ISO-style controls” and “customer evidence pack” phrasing.
- Legal hold wording intentionally scoped: describes the concept and that holds are tracked/audited, but does not publish internal approval matrix details.
- Includes explicit caveats for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (e.g., some stores may be customer-managed in Private; retention enforcement depends on configured backing services and installed purge jobs).

Follow-ups (not in scope for this PR):
- Add screenshot annotations once the Console retention settings page is GA.
- Add a dedicated “Report pack format/versioning” page once the export format ADR lands in public docs.

Review checklist:
- [x] Security reviewed customer-facing terminology (audit logs vs request logs)
- [x] GRC reviewed evidence pack section headings
- [x] CS validated request flow and expectations
- [x] Docs build/link check green
Naomi Feldman (2025-02-25): Please add an explicit statement that retention controls apply to stored telemetry/log data and not to model weights, and clarify Hosted vs Dedicated differences for request/response logs (since logging can be disabled).
Elliot Price (2025-02-25): Added a “Scope” callout in the overview + a Hosted/Dedicated/Private table noting request/response logs are only retained when enabled by tenant logging settings.
Marcus Lin (2025-02-26): Watch the phrasing on legal hold. Don’t publish the internal approval matrix; keep it high-level and emphasize auditability. Also: avoid “purge is immediate” language.
Elliot Price (2025-02-26): Updated language to “asynchronous deletion” and “time-bounded enforcement”; replaced legal-hold section with a brief explanation that holds are tracked and audited and may override deletion within permitted policy boundaries.
Olga Petrov (2025-02-27): The compliance pack section should match the baseline contents we’ve been using in reviews: include retention configuration export, audit-log coverage summary, data residency summary, RBAC/access control report, and an evidence checklist. Also add a short note on specifying the desired time window for exports.
Elliot Price (2025-02-27): Aligned the bullet list, added a “What we need from you” subsection (tenant/org, region(s), time window, and point of contact).
Rachel Kim (2025-02-28): Request flow: please route self-serve customers to Support first and enterprise customers via AE/SE is fine. Also add an expectation on turnaround time (e.g., 3–5 business days) with caveat depending on scope.
Elliot Price (2025-02-28): Added a request options table (Support vs AE/SE) and a typical timeline statement + caveat for multi-region / long time windows.
Kira Thompson (2025-03-01): Nit: there’s a claim that reports are available “on-demand.” We should say “available upon request” until the generator service is GA. Also a couple of broken anchors in the sidebar.

Context: We’re seeing a consistent cluster of onboarding tickets and quickstart drop-off related to API key setup (wrong key, key copied with whitespace, env var not loaded in shell/CI, using the wrong header). This PR tightens the API key + environment variable docs to be more explicit and adds a troubleshooting section focused on the most common 401/403 patterns (mapped to Support macros). This is a prerequisite for the Console onboarding checklist deep links so the checklist step can send users to a single canonical page. Changes: (1) Clarify ‘Create an API key’ flow with explicit callouts about key visibility (shown once), key naming, and least-privilege guidance where applicable. (2) Standardize on REDWOOD_API_KEY as the canonical env var name across docs and quickstarts; include a compatibility note for OPENAI_API_KEY only in the OpenAI-compat docs (not on the core API key page). (3) Add copy/paste-safe examples for Bash/Zsh/Fish, PowerShell, Docker, GitHub Actions, and Vercel/Render style secret config; include a quick verification snippet that prints the presence (not the value) and then performs a minimal /v1/models request. (4) Add a dedicated “Troubleshooting 401/403” section with a decision tree: 401 invalid_api_key vs 401 missing_authorization_header vs 403 key_revoked/disabled vs 403 project_not_allowed vs 403 org_policy; includes how to rotate keys and what to send Support (request-id + timestamp + region) without sharing the key. (5) Tighten language around common gotchas: ‘export REDWOOD_API_KEY=…’ must be in the same shell session, no quotes that get included in value, avoid trailing newline when copying from password managers, and ensure the key belongs to the same workspace/project as the Console UI you’re using. (6) Update redirects and cross-links from quickstarts so “Set your API key” points here rather than multiple legacy pages. Notes: No product behavior changes; doc-only. This is intentionally opinionated about env var naming to reduce mismatch across examples and telemetry attribution (checklist funnel). Follow-ups: we should update older blog/README references to OPENAI_API_KEY separately (tracked in ENG-5831 subtask).
Elliot Price (review): Can we avoid having both REDWOOD_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY on the same page? We’ve been trying to keep the core path clean for hosted users.
Wei Chen (author): Yep — I moved OPENAI_API_KEY references to the OpenAI-compat doc only and added a short note + link from the main page (“Using OpenAI-compatible clients?”). Core page now only uses REDWOOD_API_KEY.
Dev Patel (review): Troubleshooting section is great. Can you add a very explicit callout that users should not paste the key value into tickets, and tell them what metadata to provide instead (request-id, approximate time, region)?
Wei Chen (author): Added an info box in the troubleshooting page and mirrored the same language on the API key page. Also included an example of what to send Support.
Kaitlyn Nguyen (review): For the 403 cases, let’s be careful about implying “scope” if we don’t expose per-scope keys to all tenants yet. Suggest wording like “key disabled / workspace policy / project restrictions”. Also: can we mention that API keys are workspace-bound and that switching workspaces in Console is a common source of confusion?
Wei Chen (author): Updated the 403 copy to avoid “scope” language and added a “workspace mismatch” bullet with a screenshot alt-text reference (no image in repo) and precise Console steps (“check workspace selector in top-left”).
Priya Shah (review): In SUP-18421 we saw users include quotes: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="rk_...". That’s fine in bash, but some copy/paste ends up including smart quotes from docs. Please ensure we use plain quotes or avoid quotes entirely.
Wei Chen (author): Examples now avoid quotes entirely unless necessary; where we do show quotes (PowerShell), it’s plain ASCII. Also added a note about smart quotes when copying from rich text.
Elliot Price (final review): Looks good. Please add one more verification snippet that checks the env var is set without echoing it (we’ve had people paste screenshots).
Wei Chen (author): Added `python -c` and `node -e` one-liners that only print “set/not set”, plus a curl call that returns HTTP status + request-id header.
Elliot Price (approval): Approved.

Motivation: With the provision-to-ready automation rollout, we need a single, up-to-date internal operator guide that explains (a) what each readiness state means, (b) what to do when nodes are stuck or failing validations, and (c) where to look first (dashboards/logs/runbooks) without rediscovering tribal knowledge in Slack threads. This PR updates the internal docs to match ADR-017 readiness semantics and the current control-plane/Fleet Readiness Service behavior, and standardizes remediation guidance (drain/quarantine/reimage order) to reduce risk during on-call.

Summary of changes: Adds an operator-focused "Provision-to-ready operations" page that describes the canonical states (Allocated/Provisioning/Validating/Ready/Quarantined), the authoritative signals for transitions (agent heartbeat + validation artifacts + control-plane writes), and practical triage flows for common failures (kubelet join, driver parity, GPU health, NCCL smoke test, perf canary). Adds a "stuck in Validating" decision tree with time-based thresholds and clear ownership boundaries (Infra/Fleet vs Platform vs SRE). Links the docs to the current dashboards and runbooks, and includes a quickstart section for internal console usage (filters, drill-down, and where to find failure reasons/artifacts). Also documents the image channel rollout + rollback basics (candidate/stable), including the audit event trail for channel changes.

Notable clarifications: (1) Quarantine is a safety state used when failures repeat or indicate hardware/network fabric issues; it is not a generic catch-all for "slow provisioning". (2) Reimage is the preferred first-line remediation for image/driver drift failures; quarantine is preferred for GPU health or NCCL/fabric failures after retry policy is exhausted. (3) Do not manually set readiness state except via the approved operator workflow; state changes are audited.

Docs links added/updated in this PR: Provision-to-ready failures triage runbook; SLO/time-to-ready page; dashboard catalog; gameday plan; ADR-017 reference; Fleet Readiness Service API overview.

Rollout note: These docs assume the staged rollout feature flag is enabled only for us-east A100 pools; wording is careful to avoid implying global availability. References SUP-28433 for the "stuck in Validating" support pattern and INT-1042 for dashboard access/least-privilege.

Screenshots: Included updated internal console screenshots (redacted pool IDs) showing readiness state filters and failure reason drill-down.

Testing: Ran docs build locally and link checker; CI includes markdown lint + internal link validation.
Vanessa Ortiz (Infra/Fleet): "This is close. Two asks: (1) please make the remediation order explicit (drain -> quarantine -> reimage) and include the safe exceptions, and (2) the NCCL smoke test section should mention the known flake mode + when to re-run vs quarantine." Author (Talia Benson): "Updated remediation sections with a numbered flow, plus added a callout box for NCCL flake mitigation and the retry/backoff pointer. Also added the 'do not quarantine for slow provisioning' warning." Vanessa Ortiz: "Looks good now. +1."

Aisha Bello (SRE): "Can you add the actual SLI/SLO names we page on, and a link to the dashboard panel for P95 time-to-ready? Also, the 'page vs ticket' guidance should match our rollout tuning (ticket for elevated failure rate unless >X% for 15m)." Author: "Added the metric names used in alerts (time_to_ready_seconds p50/p95 + step_failure_rate) and linked to the dashboard section; updated guidance to match the initial tuning notes."

Ethan Park (Platform): "Minor: In the readiness semantics, please align wording with ADR-017: control plane stores current state; events/validation artifacts are attached but not event-sourced. Also clarify who can mutate state (service accounts vs operator overrides)." Author: "Aligned language, added an 'Authoritative state' paragraph, and added a table for read vs write permissions + audit expectations."

Connor O'Brien (Release Eng): "Please add a short section on rollout comms: where the go/no-go checklist lives and who signs off." Author: "Added a 'Staged rollout' section with checklist link and sign-offs; noted kill switch behavior." 

Fiona McCarthy (SecOps): "Thanks for calling out audit. Please add a line that image channel changes must be done via the approved workflow and are logged; no manual edits in Terraform state." Author: "Added explicit guidance and linked the audit events page."

Approvals: Vanessa Ortiz approved; Aisha Bello approved; Ethan Park approved; Connor O'Brien approved; Fiona McCarthy approved.

Motivation: customers building long-running RAG workflows asked for better authoring ergonomics when iterating on multi-step playbooks. This PR adds a first-class docs guide and matching example code for: 1) checkpointing RAG playbook state (so authors can persist and resume sessions safely), and 2) exporting and importing authoring snippets (compact, portable JSON/YAML bundles) for sharing and CI-driven regression tests.

What this PR includes: an author-oriented narrative + quickstart that walks through: creating a checkpoint-aware playbook, running an interactive session in the local devcontainer, exporting snippets after each step, and importing them into a fresh session. The guide highlights best practices for telemetry (what to sample), privacy knobs (PII redaction examples), and recommended contract tests to prevent regressions. Also included are two runnable example artifacts (TypeScript and a tiny Node CLI) and a small docs-site component for embedding a live snippet runner sandbox.

Why unique: previous quickstarts focused on single-run examples; this guide targets iteration workflows and reproducible authoring, with explicit snippet export/import semantics and telemetry suggestions. The examples are intentionally compact so they can be dropped into existing developer sandboxes or CI.

Checklist: - [x] Add docs page: docs/playbooks/interactive-checkpoints.md - [x] Add example TS snippet exporter: examples/snippets/exporter.ts - [x] Add playground runner component: docs-site/components/snippet-runner.mdx - [x] Add devcontainer quickstart for local testing: quickstarts/interactive-playbook/devcontainer.json - [x] Add unit smoke tests for exporter CLI - [x] Run linter/docs build and fix issues

Notes: this PR is docs-first: none of the runtime surface changes are required to author or run the examples. Implementations use existing Redwood SDK APIs (no breaking surface changes). The telemetry recommendations reference existing console features and the Optimize toolkit suggestions.

Usage summary (authoring flow): 1) Start quickstart devcontainer 2) Run `yarn start:playbook` to open the interactive runner 3) Exercise steps and use the "Export Snippet" button to create a portable YAML bundle 4) Rehydrate in a fresh session with the CLI `redwood-snippet import bundle.yml` 5) Use the included smoke tests to assert output stability

Summary: Consolidates three previously divergent auth helper implementations into a small set of credential pipelines (preset, delegator, and fallback) and introduces a lightweight StreamOperator abstraction that sits between SDK transport and user async iterables. Motivation: Multiple SDKs kept reimplementing the same credential chaining and streaming glue which made parity, testing, and telemetry difficult. This PR centralizes the auth flow patterns and standardizes the stream handoff surface so SDKs have a consistent developer experience while allowing transport-specific optimizations.

Changes (high-level):
- Introduce credential pipeline presets (Preset, Delegator, Fallback) with a common semantic contract across Py/TS/Go. Presets encapsulate TTL, prefetch, and backoff hints.
- Add StreamOperator (lightweight) that: normalizes chunk envelopes, handles graceful pause/resume hooks, exposes a small backpressure hint API, and integrates with credential lifecycle events for preemptive refresh.
- SDK updates: Python adapter (redwood-sdk-python) exposes CredentialPreset and StreamOperator classes; TypeScript adds equivalent types and generator helpers; Go adds thin interfaces and a small concrete shim for iterator adapters.
- Retry ergonomics: new default retry profile bundles for streaming (latency-aware) and auth-fallthrough profile.
- Telemetry: emit credential pipeline events (prefetch, swap, fallback) and stream operator metrics (paused_duration, resume_count) to existing SDK telemetry hooks.
- Tests: integration matrix that exercises preset combinations and stream operator pause/resume across transports (http/ websocket).

Commits (summary):
- 9 commits, squashed on merge. Key commits: initial crosslang design and interfaces; python implementation + tests; ts implementation + typings; go shim and examples; telemetry hooks; docs and examples; CI fixes.

Files (representative):
- sdk/python/redwood/auth/presets.py (new)
- sdk/python/redwood/stream/operator.py (new)
- sdk/python/tests/test_stream_operator_integration.py (new)
- sdk/typescript/src/auth/presets.ts (new)
- sdk/typescript/src/stream/operator.ts (new)
- sdk/go/credential/preset.go (new)
- sdk/go/stream/operator_shim.go (new)
- docs/sdk/streaming-operators.md (new)
- examples/multi-sdk/credential-pipeline-demo/* (added small demos)

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc linked and reviewed (ENG-9142)
- [x] Implementations in Python/TS/Go
- [x] Unit + integration tests
- [x] Telemetry hooks wired
- [x] Examples and docs updated
- [x] Version bumps and changelogs updated

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- The StreamOperator deliberately stays minimal (only pause/resume/backpressure hint and lifecycle callbacks) to avoid locking SDKs into an opinionated runtime. We avoided adding batching semantics here because batching is runtime-specific and should remain in the serving-layer.
- CredentialPresets are intentionally lightweight descriptors (TTL, prefetch boolean, fallback order) not executors; actual execution is in each SDK's credential adapter so customers can plug KMS/HSM logic.

Review thread (selected):
- Dylan Price (review): "Overall direction looks solid. Two asks: 1) clarify interactions between StreamOperator.pause() and transport-level read loops to avoid deadlock; 2) ensure telemetry tags include preset name for downstream aggregation."
- Priya (author): "Added clarifying comments and updated operator.pause() docstring to mention non-blocking semantics and expectation that callers call resume(). Telemetry tags now include preset_name and chain_id."
- Maya Chen (review): "TS typings look good. Suggest renaming 'delegator' to 'cascade' in TS to match internal naming."
- Priya: "Renamed TS symbol to CascadePreset; kept python/go name 'Delegator' to avoid larger refactors in other packages in this PR. Filed follow-up ENG-9201 to align names across repo."
- Arjun Rao (review): "Go shim needs an explicit noop implementation for old iterators to avoid nil pointer panics in older Go SDK users."
- Priya: "Added shim with fallback noop that logs debug event when old iterator is used; added test covering nil shim case."

CI and iteration: 
- Initial CI run: build failures in ts unit tests due to a timing-dependent generator test flake; python lint flagged a stray TODO in presets.py.
- Follow-up: tightened TS test to reduce timing assumptions (use deterministic test clock), removed TODO and addressed linter comments. Final CI: all checks pass (unit, integration, linters).

Backward compatibility: 
- Exposed types are additive; no existing public method signatures were removed. We bumped minor versions for each SDK (Python 1.9.0, TypeScript 2.3.1, Go 1.8.4) to reflect added features. Migration doc added at docs/sdk/upgrade-1.9.0.md.

Telemetry & observability: 
- Added new events: credential.pipeline.prefetch, credential.pipeline.swap, stream.operator.paused_duration_ms, stream.operator.resume_count. These plug into current SDK telemetry sinks and are opt-in via existing telemetry flags.

Follow-ups (post-merge):
- ENG-9201: name normalization across SDKs (Delegator -> Cascade)
- ENG-9302: evaluate adding optional batching helper in StreamOperator for dedicated environments
- ENG-9344: expose higher-level retry composer for auth fallthrough scenarios

Merge outcome: Merged via squash after approvals from Dylan and Maya. Merge commit message summarized design, tests, and version bumps. CI green at merge time.

Notes for release engineer: bump SDK packages and publish new changelogs. Python wheel: update setup.cfg extras to include new telemetry events. TypeScript: publish v2.3.1 and update package readme examples. Go: tag v1.8.4 and run module tidy.

Contact: Priya Sharma (author) for follow-ups and to coordinate the naming sweep (ENG-9201).

Summary: Introduces a new CLI tool (redwood econ-orchestrator) and an accompanying workload stitcher pipeline to automate tenant-level batching, cache presets, and quantization profile recommendations. Motivation: customers repeatedly ask for a safe, reproducible way to generate defaults that balance latency SLOs and unit economics without manual trial-and-error. This change packages our simulation + telemetry heuristics into a developer-friendly CLI, supports presets-as-code output, and wires a safety gate that prevents aggressive profiles from being auto-applied. Key features: - redwood econ-orchestrator CLI: local dry-run mode, tenant mode (pulls anonymized telemetry snapshot), and export mode (profiles as YAML). - Workload stitcher: synthesizes realistic batch/sequence-length traces by combining sampled production requests, synthetic tail-length injections, and configurable burst patterns for stress testing. - Econ engine: unit-econ calculator that simulates per-token cost, estimated GPU seconds, and predicted p50/p95 latency under different batch/cache/quant combinations. Produces ranked candidate profiles. - Safety/guardrails: conservative candidate scorer, rollback hints, and a quarantine policy for any profile that increases 95th percentile latency by more than configured threshold. - Profiles-as-code export: YAML artifacts include batching shape, cache TTL hints, quantization target (bits, calibration dataset tag), and human-readable notes. - Integration points: CLI can call the new /internal/econ/simulate endpoint (server-side) or run fully offline using historic telemetry exports. Context: We’ve had multiple user reports + internal reviews pointing out that the Streaming guide and the tabbed code examples drifted over time across languages (different event names, different assembly rules, and inconsistent error handling). This PR refreshes the Streaming guide content and updates the tabbed code blocks so Python/TypeScript/Go all reflect the same canonical mental model. Primary goals: (1) a single consistent pattern for consuming streaming events, (2) consistent guidance on assembling the final message from deltas, (3) clear handling of disconnects/errors, and (4) link hygiene while we migrate pages.

What changed:
- Streaming guide restructure:
  - Added an explicit “event loop mental model” section up front (iterate events, switch on event.type, accumulate deltas, finalize on message_end).
  - Added a “final message assembly” section that explains exactly what to append (content deltas) vs what to treat as metadata.
  - Added an “error + retry” section that calls out disconnects and safe re-request patterns.
  - Added a short “structured output while streaming” callout: do not parse partial JSON until final; validate then retry if invalid.
- Code tabs parity:
  - Python/TS/Go tabs now mirror each other in structure and naming (same section ordering, same event-handling branches, same logging guidance).
  - Removed older snippet variations that implied you’ll always get a complete tool-call args blob in a single event.
  - Added minimal comments that explain why partial tool-call arguments happen and what to do (buffer until tool_call_end / message_end).

Introduce an adaptive provisioning pacer that smooths autoscaler decisions across dedicated fleets by applying a gamma-weighted pacing window to reservation and burst allocations. Motivation: recent incidents showed repeated oscillation when tens of tenants simultaneously ramp causing flapping autoscaler decisions and transient SLA slippage. This PR implements a pacing layer between the decision engine and provisioner so that scale up/down intents are rate-limited with stateful momentum, tenant-level dampening, and configurable burst forgiveness. The change touches three areas: 1) decision smoothing: a new Pacer module that consumes scale intents and emits paced deltas using a configurable half-life and gamma decay parameter; 2) budget and burst integration: pacer respects per-tenant guaranteed throughput envelopes and optional ephemeral burst credits; it can defer non-critical adjustments to preserve headroom; 3) instrumentation and alerting: adds metrics for pacer_active, pacer_output_delta, pacer_rejections, and tenant_pacer_latency plus dashboards and an alert when pacing causes more than 3 consecutive deferred scale operations. Includes unit tests for edge-cases, an integration test that replays historical incident traces, and a canary job for dedicated clusters. Backwards compatible: pacer is off by default and enabled through the autoscaler.policy.pacer config. See linked Linear items for rollout plan and experiment gating.
Liam O'Connor: Can we avoid tenant starvation when multiple pacer defers pile up? Please add a fairness check.
Maya Chen: Added a fairness window and unit tests for starvation scenarios (see pacer_test.go). Also clarified behavior in docs.
Priya Singh: Integration test showed a small memory spike in the canary job — can we cap in-memory intent queue and persist overflow to the redis-backed queue?
Maya Chen: Implemented bounded queue with persistent spillover; reran canary and memory stayed stable.
Rafael Torres: Metrics look good but add an SLI that ties pacer-induced deferrals to SLO degradation so we can auto-disable if needed.
Maya Chen: Added tenant_pacer_deferral_ratio SLI and an emergency disable flag controlled via autoscaler.policy.pacer.enabled=false.
Adaptive provisioning pacer: opt-in pacing layer to smooth dedicated cluster autoscaler actions, reduce oscillation, and integrate tenant burst budgets. Config via autoscaler.policy.pacer (half_life, gamma, max_queue_size, enable_spillover). Observability: new pacer metrics and dashboards. Rollout: canary in dedicated clusters followed by gradual enablement per-tenant.
Canary deployed to two dedicated clusters in us-west-2 for 72h. Feature gate off by default. Rollout plan in ENG-3421: enable for low-risk tenants (10%) for 24h then ramp based on pacer_deferral_ratio SLI.
Create runtime-gate in Console to toggle pacer per-tenant; add regression alert to SRE runbook; schedule 1-week telemetry review in ENG-3499.
This work is a direct mitigation for SUP-1182 where a spike in background batch workloads caused repeated scale flaps and SLA degradation for interactive tenants. The pacer prevents rapid oscillation by enforcing momentum and honoring guaranteed envelopes.
The gamma decay algorithm uses a configurable decay coefficient to weight recent intents more heavily while still preserving a tail for older requests. This choice gives predictable smoothing for bursty traffic patterns compared to simple exponential smoothing used previously. Benchmarks in perf/bench/pacer show 12-18% reduction in scale operations and a 35% decrease in transient SLA errors under synthetic multi-tenant replay workloads.

Adds runtime enforcement for KMS encryption-context assertions and a backwards-compatible audit envelope v2. No customer action required; opt-in rollout described in notes.
Motivation: customers require stronger guarantees that encrypted payloads include tenant and region assertions in the KMS encryption context and that audit logs carry verifiable provenance. This PR adds an encryption-context-validation middleware in the serving runtime and introduces audit-envelope-v2 (schema + signer) with optional replay-protection markers. Changes include: 1) runtime/security/encryption_context_validator.go: middleware that verifies required keys (tenant_id, km_region, request_id) are present and match token claims; 2) audit/envelope/v2.proto + envelope signer: new schema and signer that embeds a provenance digest and optional region pin; 3) rbac/policy/translator: map existing RBAC v2 role attributes to encryption-context permissions so service roles can be granted 'kms:assert' scoped by geozone; 4) integrations/kms/mock_kms_test.go + e2e tests in test/e2e/audit_kms_endtoend_test.go covering happy path, missing keys, and replay detection; 5) docs/security/data-residency-and-kms.md with rollout guidance and migration steps; 6) helm/values.yaml flag enableAuditV2 and runtime config enableEncryptionContextValidation; 7) minor SDK surface: python client adds headers for explicit encryption-context. Migration plan: feature gated behind runtime flag and helm toggle; default rollout to a pilot org group for 2 weeks then gradual ramp; audit v2 is backwards compatible (consumers can still parse v1); when enableAuditV2=true the platform emits v2 envelopes alongside v1 for 30 days. Motivation: streamline how Helm values and templating drive init/rollback hooks for the Redwood Private installer so operators have a single, well-documented surface for preflight/init tasks, graceful rollbacks, and upgrade-time migrations. This PR consolidates multiple values blocks scattered across charts into a central values.schema.yaml, introduces a small templating helper for hook annotations, and swaps the previous ad-hoc initJob to an operator-friendly initHook Job that is idempotent and respects .Values.lifecycle.preInstall.enabled. Key goals: 1) avoid behavior drift between on-prem and VPC deployments, 2) make rollback actions declarative and reversible, 3) give clear defaults while allowing site-specific overrides for network/KMS/db checks. Changes include: values schema refactor, new _helpers.tpl for hook annotations and timestamps, initHook job templated with wait semantics, a post-install hook for KV pre-warm and cache priming, and documented upgrade notes for v1.2 -> v1.3. Checklist: - [x] values.schema.yaml added and referenced by Chart.yaml - [x] templates/_helpers.tpl with hook helpers - [x] templates/init-hook-job.yaml (idempotent, retries) - [x] templates/rollback-hook-job.yaml (safeguarded) - [x] unit tests for values validation and template rendering - [x] integration smoke test in chart CI - [x] docs/PRIVATE-HELM.md updated with examples and rollbacks How to review: focus on values schema (types and required flags), hook TTL/cleanup behavior, and safety of rollback job (it must NOT delete user data). This PR is intentionally conservative: default preInstall.enabled is false for existing clusters, and migration logic in chart helpers checks for legacy values to preserve behavior. Linear: ENG-1234 implements the lifecycle contract; SUP-987 documents a support escalations case that prompted clearer hooks.
- Consolidated private Helm values into values.schema.yaml for clearer validation and backwards compatibility.
- Added templated init-hook and rollback-hook jobs (disabled by default) to support safer installs and rollbacks.
- Introduced hook helper templates to centralize annotations and cleanup behavior.
- Docs: PRIVATE-HELM.md with upgrade/rollback examples and troubleshooting steps.
Upgrade notes: After upgrading the chart operators should: 1) audit values against new values.schema.yaml (helm get values | helm diff if available), 2) set .Values.lifecycle.preInstall.enabled=false for a canary rollout, 3) if using legacy initJob, set .Values.legacyInit.enableMigration=true to run automatic conversion. Rollback behavior: rollback-hook runs only when .Values.lifecycle.rollback.enabled=true and requires annotation 'redwood.io/allow-rollback: "true"' to execute destructive cleanup. KMS & VPC note: KMS checks in init-hook are no-op unless .Values.kms.enabled=true (safe default).
Rollback and init hooks are non-destructive by default. Destructive cleanup paths require an explicit annotation and dryRun=false. Hook containers run as non-root and read-only filesystem where possible; reviewers should double-check any image updates for CVE exposure.

Title: Multi-locale Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) quickstart and internationalization (i18n) evaluation playbook.

Summary: This PR introduces a focused quickstart and evaluation playbook for teams building RAG experiences that support multiple locales (languages, scripts, and regional variants). It includes two example integrations (TypeScript and Python), a per-locale embedding guidance section, a small set of curated locale test datasets for evaluation, docs site navigation updates, troubleshooting notes for tokenization/encoding edge cases, and a lightweight harness to measure retrieval + generation quality per locale. The goal is to reduce time-to-value for customers who need multilingual RAG with production-grade evaluation and practical guidance on commons issues (e.g., punctuation differences, right-to-left languages, and tokenizer idiosyncrasies).

Motivation & context: We get frequent requests from platform customers and partners about language coverage and correctness for non-English workloads. Existing quickstarts focus on English-first flows. This PR addresses gaps identified in ENG-2143 and recent partner feedback (SUP-452) by providing: (1) example code that demonstrates locale-aware indexing and prompt scaffolding, (2) eval playbooks for measuring per-locale precision and hallucination rates, (3) recipes for embedding model selection and normalization per script, and (4) how-to for fallback routing and translation proxies.

Checklist:
- [x] Add TypeScript quickstart: examples/i18n-quickstart/ts/{app,docs}.
- [x] Add Python quickstart: examples/i18n-quickstart/py/{worker,notebook}.
- [x] Add i18n evaluation playbook: docs/guides/i18n-evals.md.
- [x] Add sample locale datasets (small): data/i18n-samples/{ja,ar,es,ru,hi}.jsonl.
- [x] Update docs site nav and quickstart index.
- [x] Add tests for locale-aware tokenizer smoke checks (CI).
- [x] Add migration notes and troubleshooting doc.

Commits (high level):
- c1a2b3: scaffold i18n quickstart structure and README for TS example.
- d4e5f6: implement Python worker example and notebook showing end-to-end indexing+query.
- a7b8c9: add i18n evaluation playbook and small sample datasets, with expected metrics baseline.
- e0f1g2: docs site navigation and search indexing updated to include i18n guide.
- h3i4j5: add CI smoke tests for tokenizer/encoding and small test harness to run evals in GH Actions.

Files changed (high level):
- examples/i18n-quickstart/ts/README.md (new): step-by-step quickstart for TS, highlights locale-aware prompt templates, and demonstrates embeddings normalization pipeline.
- examples/i18n-quickstart/ts/sample-app.ts (new): minimal server that indexes locale-specific docs and performs RAG queries with per-locale prompt templates.
- examples/i18n-quickstart/py/worker.py (new): background indexer showing language detection, normalizer, and embedding model selection.
- examples/i18n-quickstart/py/notebook.ipynb (new): walkthrough for local experimentation and eval plotting.
- docs/guides/i18n-evals.md (new): playbook describing metrics (locale-precision, subset-ROUGE, hallucination-rate), test composition, and how to interpret regressions.
- docs/quickstarts/index.md (updated): added link to the new quickstart and short blurb on language coverage.
- data/i18n-samples/{ja.jsonl,ar.jsonl,es.jsonl,ru.jsonl,hi.jsonl} (new): small curated retrieval prompts and gold answers per locale for smoke evaluation.
- .github/workflows/i18n-smoke.yml (new): CI job to run lightweight tokenizer/eval checks on PRs touching i18n files.
- tests/tokenizer_smoke_test.py (new): language tokenization sanity checks.
- docs/troubleshooting/i18n.md (new): common pitfalls and how to troubleshoot tokenization mismatches and embedding drift.

Notes on implementation details and choices:
- Embedding normalization: examples recommend normalizing punctuation (NFKC) and mapping full-width/half-width characters for East Asian scripts before indexing. The playbook explains when to apply model-based translation vs. embedding translation.
- Tokenization edge cases: documents include a short matrix highlighting tokenization differences and approximate token cost implications for common languages.
- Locale routing: sample-app.ts includes a small strategy function to route requests to regionally-optimized model variants and to fallback to translation proxies when retrieval quality is low.
- Evaluation harness: docs/guides/i18n-evals.md contains a recommended baseline for acceptance (per-locale precision >= 0.75 on curated set) and instructions to add more locale data to CI for enterprise customers.

Review conversation (condensed):
- Jordan Lee (reviewer): "Nice to see datasets included — can we keep the sample corpora deliberately small to avoid licensing issues? Also add a note about character normalization in the quickstart."
- Priya (author): "Yes — all samples are synthetic or public-domain; I added the normalization section and an explicit note about dataset provenance in the README."
- Mateo Alvarez (reviewer): "The playbook metrics look good, but suggest adding a short script to compute hallucination-rate automatically. Otherwise teams will interpret metrics differently."
- Priya: "Added scripts/eval/hallucination_checker.py and documented how it works and its failure modes."
- Sofia Chen (reviewer): "CI job failed first run due to flaky tokenizer expectation on macOS runners — we should pin the environment."
- Priya: "Refactored the smoke test to avoid platform-specific byte encoding assumptions and added GH Actions matrix to pin python 3.10 linux runner."
- Jordan Lee: "Approved after the CI rerun. Good to merge with squash."

CI and validation: The PR triggered a new GH Actions job (i18n-smoke) which initially failed due to platform encoding assumptions; after the fix all checks passed. The final CI status is: pass (unit + smoke + lint). A subset of the eval scripts are intentionally light so they run quickly in PRs; the full playbook recommends running the larger suite in nightly pipelines.

Backward compatibility and migration: This change is additive (docs and examples only). No runtime or API surface changes. Marking as non-breaking.

Testing notes: Included a few deterministic smoke tests and an example notebook with reproducible plots showing per-locale retrieval precision and a notebook section for manual qualitative checks. The sample datasets are intentionally small (~50 examples per locale) and are meant as templates for teams to expand.

Merge outcome: Squash and merge to main on 2026-03-02 after approvals. Release notes and docs redirects have been queued for the next docs site build.

Follow-ups (suggested):
- Add end-to-end performance notes for multilingual tokenization and cost implications (ENG follow-up ticket suggested).
- Expand datasets for additional locales (Vietnamese, Thai) and add RTL visual test harnesses for UI teams.
- Consider a small partner-facing workshop to validate recommendations on real-world corpora.

If anything needs to be reverted quickly: the PR is docs/examples only; revert would remove quickstart and playbook from the site and example manifests.

Contact: Priya Natarajan (author) for follow-up; Mateo Alvarez for eval playbook questions.

Context
Private deployments now support versioned Optimization Configs with safe apply + one-click rollback in Console. Private operators requested an equivalent workflow when Console access is unavailable (break-glass) or when rolling back during cluster/network issues.

This PR adds an operator-friendly rollback command to the `redwood-private-installer` CLI. The workflow is designed to be safe by default (explicit scope + confirmation), idempotent (retries won’t wedge state), and observable (structured logs + correlation IDs).

What’s in this PR
- New CLI command: `rwpi optimize-config rollback`
  - Rolls back the active Optimization Config version for a given scope by calling the Private control plane rollback API.
  - Supports explicit targeting:
    - `--tenant <tenant_slug>` (required)
    - `--model <model_id>` (optional; defaults to tenant-wide if omitted)
    - `--region <region>` (optional; defaults to installation region if omitted)
    - `--to-version <version_id>` (required)
  - Safety guardrails:
    - `--dry-run` prints the computed blast radius and the current/target versions without executing.
    - `--require-active-version` (default true) prevents rollback if the installer cannot confirm the currently active version.
    - Interactive confirmation with “type-to-confirm” using a deterministic confirmation string: `ROLLBACK <tenant>/<model-or-*>/<region-or-*> to <version>`.
    - Optional `--force` to bypass confirmation for automation (still logs a warning).
  - Emits a generated `change_request_id` (UUID) included in installer logs and passed through as an HTTP header for control plane/audit correlation.

- Preflight + verification
  - Preflight checks:
    - Installer can reach the control plane endpoint and is authenticated.
    - Target version exists and is compatible with the requested scope.
    - RBAC check: operator token must have the rollback permission.
  - Post-action verification:
    - Polls the control plane “active version” endpoint until it reports the target version or timeout.
    - Prints clear next steps when verification fails (includes curl commands and where to look in control plane logs).

- Installer state tracking (for safer operator workflows)
  - Records the last observed active version per scope in the installer state file to make it easier to revert during repeated incidents.
  - Does not attempt to be the source of truth; it is only used to improve operator UX (the control plane remains authoritative).

- Documentation
  - Adds `docs/operator/optimization-config-rollback.md`:
    - Example rollbacks
    - What “rolled back” means in Private (control plane pointer update + rollout controller applies to workers)
    - Common failure modes (RBAC denied, scope mismatch, verification timeout)

Example
- Dry run:
  `rwpi optimize-config rollback --tenant acme --model llama-3-70b --region us-east-1 --to-version ocv_01J0Z9... --dry-run`
- Execute:
  `rwpi optimize-config rollback --tenant acme --model llama-3-70b --region us-east-1 --to-version ocv_01J0Z9...`

Changed areas (high level)
- cmd/rwpi: command registration + flags
- internal/controlplane: API client additions:
  - GET active optimization config version (for verification)
  - POST rollback (with `change_request_id` propagation)
- internal/operator: confirmation + blast-radius formatting helpers
- docs: operator guide
- tests: unit tests + lightweight kind smoke test

Notes / design choices
- This PR intentionally does not implement fully automatic rollback loops. The command requires explicit target version and an operator confirmation by default.
- Verification polling defaults to 90s with exponential backoff; can be overridden via `--verify-timeout`.
- If the control plane rollback returns success but verification can’t confirm, the command exits non-zero to encourage explicit operator follow-up.

Rollout plan
- Internal use first (Redwood SRE + Private deployments on-call) during gamedays.
- Publish to Private operator docs after GA feature flag is enabled in Private control plane.

Follow-ups
- Add optional integration to annotate the customer’s Prometheus (if present) with rollback events.
- Support reading candidate rollback targets from the control plane version history to reduce manual copy/paste of version IDs.

Refs
- Linear: ENG-4829 (Private deployments sync + rollback), ENG-4825 (rollback endpoint)
- Related (monorepo): runtime rollback race fix in redwood/pr-20111
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Can we make sure this fails safe if the installer can’t confirm the currently active version? During incidents we’ve seen partially degraded control plane endpoints and I don’t want operators rolling back blind.

Vivek Kulkarni (author): Added `--require-active-version` default true. If we can’t read active version, we abort unless `--force` is provided. Also `--dry-run` now prints a warning when the active version is unknown.
Marcus Lin (Security): Please confirm the rollback call is authorized via the same RBAC permission as Console rollback, and that we don’t log bearer tokens in debug output.

Vivek Kulkarni (author): Confirmed RBAC uses `optimization_config.rollback` on the control plane side; installer just surfaces 403 with a clear message. Also scrubbed Authorization headers from debug logs and added a unit test for the logger redaction helper.
Ethan Park (Control Plane): For verification, please hit the active-version endpoint rather than reading k8s objects directly. The rollout controller is authoritative and we need to keep the client contract stable.

Vivek Kulkarni (author): Updated implementation to use `GET /v1/optimization-config/active` (scoped), no direct k8s reads. Removed the earlier ConfigMap fallback.
Connor O'Brien (Release Eng): Any backward-compat concerns if the control plane doesn’t have the new endpoint yet?

Vivek Kulkarni (author): The command checks endpoint availability and returns a friendly error instructing to upgrade control plane first. The rest of the installer is unaffected; no behavior changes unless the command is invoked.
Kira Thompson (Tech Writing): Doc request: include a short section on how to find valid version IDs + an example of tenant-wide rollback.

Vivek Kulkarni (author): Added a section pointing operators to the control plane `/versions` endpoint and included a tenant-wide rollback example (model omitted).

Context: The presubmit pipeline has accreted a tangled set of concerns: language-aware lint runners, telemetry shims, toolcache priming, and a fragile release hook. This PR decomposes the presubmit 'origami' (folded biz-logic inside the monolithic runner) into composable adapters and adds a deterministic 'release-handshake'—a lightweight protocol between presubmit and the release orchestrator to reduce flakey merges during release windows. Motivation: Reduce presubmit maintenance surface, speed up fastpath green merges, and provide a visible, auditable gate for release merges. Design summary: 1) Split presubmit into three adapters: lint-adapter (language plugins), toolcache-adapter (lazy priming and cache hints), telemetry-adapter (uniform metrics and provenance stamps). 2) Introduce release-handshake: a small state machine and annotated commit-status that the release orchestrator listens to; presubmit will mark candidates as READY_FOR_RELEASE only when the selected smoke-suites pass and release-prober acknowledged. 3) Add an opt-in fallback that allows non-release branches to follow previous fastpath behavior. Checklist: - [x] extract lint plugin registry and wire to adapter interface; - [x] implement toolcache hint emitter and lazy priming flag; - [x] introduce telemetry envelope (trace-id + presubmit-phase) and route to ci-metrics; - [x] implement release-handshake state transitions and annotated status context; - [x] add unit tests for adapter plumbing and handshake FSM; - [x] update docs (CONTRIBUTING.md presubmit section) and release runbook; - [x] coordinate with Release team for rollout. Rollout plan: feature-flagged on presubmit (flag off by default), enable in Canary repos for 48h, switch to broad rollout when handshake has 12h of stable traffic. Related: ENG-3120 for presubmit rearchitecture; ENG-3199 for release reliability.
Luis: Please add explicit backoff for the handshake re-try loop; observed some tight retries in local run. Priya: Added exponential backoff with jitter in handshake.go and added unit test for retry window. Ethan: Approve after minor nits on telemetry labels. Aisha: Request change – split the status context key to avoid colliding with external bots. Priya: Updated status key to redwood/release-handshake and added compatibility shim for older listeners. Final: Approved by Ethan and Luis; Aisha gave final thumbs-up after shim verification.
3 commits: 1) refactor: extract adapter interfaces and lint-adapter (Priya M.); 2) feat: add toolcache-adapter and telemetry envelope (Priya M.); 3) feat: implement release-handshake FSM + status context and tests (follow-up commit)
Introduce modular presubmit adapters (lint/toolcache/telemetry) and a feature-flagged release-handshake protocol to reduce release-window flakiness; no behavioral change by default until feature flag is enabled; rollout notes in docs/CONTRIBUTING.md under 'Presubmit & Release'

Summary
Adds first-pass public documentation for RBAC v2 across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. This PR introduces: (1) a conceptual overview of RBAC v2 primitives (permissions, roles, bindings, scopes), (2) a permission catalog reference page (with naming conventions and deprecation/versioning notes), (3) built-in role templates with recommended assignments, and (4) migration notes from RBAC v1/coarse roles including dual-read behavior and troubleshooting for permission denied.

Motivation / context
Enterprise customers (Dedicated + Private) are asking for least-privilege guidance and auditability artifacts. Support/Solutions also need a stable reference for: “what does this permission do?”, “which role should I assign?”, and “why am I denied?”. The docs in this PR align to the RBAC v2 enforcement + audit decision logging work landing in platform services.

What’s included
- New docs page: /security/rbac-v2/overview
  - Definitions: Permission, Role, Role Binding, Subject (user/service principal), Scope (org/project/environment/cluster)
  - Enforcement model: deny-by-default, gateway + service checks, consistent 403 semantics
  - Auditability: authz decision context fields (subject/action/resource scope/policy version/decision/denial reason)
- New docs page: /security/rbac-v2/permissions
  - Permission string format + namespacing (redwood.<domain>.<resource>.<action>)
  - Stability + deprecation policy (no silent semantic changes; documented replacements)
  - “Sensitive operations” callouts (key rotation, secret operations, role changes, routing policy edits, audit export)
- New docs page: /security/rbac-v2/role-templates
  - Built-in templates (Org Admin, Security Admin, Billing Admin, Read-only Auditor, Deployment Operator)
  - Guidance for separation of duties (Security Admin ≠ Billing Admin by default)
  - Scope examples for Dedicated/Private (cluster-scoped operator; environment-scoped auditor)
- New docs page: /security/rbac-v2/migration
  - Dual-read/feature flag rollout explanation
  - Expected behavior during transition (v1 roles mapped to v2 templates; denies surfaced with reason codes)
  - Troubleshooting: interpreting denial reason codes; when to escalate; how to request temporary elevation

Non-goals
- This does not document a customer-exposed policy language/ABAC.
- This does not publish internal-only permissions or break-glass runbooks in full; we link to a high-level “Emergency access” section and keep operational steps internal.

Notable details / decisions
- Permission catalog is presented as a curated reference with examples + categories rather than a full dump of every internal action. The page includes a “How to find the exact permission” section pointing to Console Permission Viewer (coming soon) and API error details when debug headers are enabled for admins.
- Migration page explicitly calls out that some previously implicit capabilities may require explicit grants under v2 (deny-by-default).

Screenshots
- N/A (text-only docs). I verified local rendering and navigation.

Checklist
- [x] Content reviewed with Security Eng + PM
- [x] Link checker passes (no broken internal anchors)
- [x] Adds redirect stubs for old RBAC v1 doc URLs
- [x] Notes on audit log fields match current schema naming

Follow-ups
- Add a generated “permissions table” section once the permission registry stabilizes (to avoid churn). Proposed approach: nightly job to export a versioned markdown artifact from the registry used by services.
- Add Console screenshots for role editor and permission viewer once DES-914 lands in product UI.
Naomi Feldman (PM) — Requested changes: The migration page should be explicit that v2 is deny-by-default and can surface new 403s if customers relied on implicit org-admin powers from legacy roles. Also add a short section on how Support should ask for the denial reason code and request ID.

Elliot Price — Updated migration doc with a “What changes under deny-by-default” section and added a Troubleshooting checklist (request id + denial reason code + scope). Also clarified that legacy role mappings are transitional.

Marcus Lin (Security Eng) — Requested changes: Please avoid publishing internal break-glass procedure details. High-level guidance is fine, but the approval workflow and alerting channels should remain internal.

Elliot Price — Done. Replaced detailed steps with a short “Emergency access” overview and a note that Redwood Support/SecOps coordinate break-glass on request for enterprise contracts.

Kaitlyn Nguyen (Platform) — Comment: Permission format example should match the registry naming (domain/resource/action) and avoid implying version suffixes in the string. Deprecation guidance should reference documented replacements.

Elliot Price — Adjusted examples and added a note that versioning is handled via compatibility guarantees + documented deprecation, not embedded in the permission string.

Tessa Morgan (UX) — Comment: In the troubleshooting section, recommend user-facing copy that doesn’t reveal sensitive authorization details by default, but points admins to debug headers / Console Permission Viewer.

Elliot Price — Updated troubleshooting copy to emphasize least information by default; admin debug path called out separately.

Jordan Lee (Policy) — Approval: Content aligns with current evaluation model and denial reason code strategy.

Final review — Naomi Feldman approved after rewording the “role templates” section to emphasize separation of duties and recommended defaults for regulated orgs.
Docs: Published RBAC v2 overview, permission reference, role templates, and migration guidance for enterprise customers (Hosted/Dedicated/Private).

Context: Over the last month multiple presubmit flakes were traced to partial dependency rotations and large toolchain bootstraps that race on networked artifact stores. This PR introduces two related mitigations: (1) a dependency rollback actuator that can detect a failing presubmit cohort after a dep rotation and automatically pin the presubmit runner to the last-known-good dependency snapshot, and (2) a lightweight build adapter that replaces the legacy monolithic bootstrap path for presubmit lanes with a thin, cache-first initializer to dramatically reduce I/O and start time. Motivation: reduce noisy presubmit failures during large dependency updates, speed feedback loops for engineers, and lower CI egress/IO costs. Summary of changes: - infra/ci/rollback/actuator.go: new actuator and reconciliation loop, with backoff and safe-mode toggle. - infra/ci/rollback/README.md: operational runbook and commands for manual rollback+inspect. - infra/ci/build_adapter/adapter.py: lightweight adapter with two-stage cache warm path. - ci/workflows/presubmit.yml: wiring to call adapter for targeted lanes and a feature flag gate for actuator. - scripts/dep-snapshot-tool: helper to create and list snapshots used by actuator. - internal/telemetry/ci_metrics: added counters for rollback events and adapter warm hits. - tests/ci_simulation_test.go: simulation harness for rotating deps and validating actuator behavior. Commits: 1) add rollback actuator and snapshot CLI 2) implement lightweight adapter and wire presubmit lanes 3) add telemetry and tests 4) docs/runbook and minor refactors Review checklist (what I validated): - Unit tests added for actuator reconciliation and adapter warm path - Integration simulation validates rollback triggers on 2 consecutive cohort failures - Manual smoke: exercised on staging org with a synthetic dep rotation, verified automatic pin and then unpin after snapshot promotion - Load: validated adapter reduces presubmit bootstrap median by ~48% on our internal sample workloads Rollout plan: feature-flag gated on presubmit; staged enablement across teams (platform -> core-services -> rest) over a week; actuator starts in "observe" mode, then "enforce" after 48h stable. Backports: small backport requested for the release/* branch for customers pinned to older presubmit infra (ENG-2147). Risk and mitigations: actuator holds a safe-mode toggle, exponential backoff to avoid oscillation, and a manual override in runbook. The adapter adds a compatibility shim for runners that still expect the old bootstrap format. Operational notes: see infra/ci/rollback/README.md for runbook and alert tuning. Motivation: CI for prompt-set regressions currently treats all failing prompts as equal which causes noisy hard-blocks for low-impact regressions and noisy signal for triage. This PR introduces a severity-weighted failure classifier (SVFC) that: 1) assigns a contextual severity score to individual prompt-set failures (low/medium/high based on topicality, token-impact, downstream metric delta and historical flakiness), 2) aggregates a severity-adjusted regression rate metric used in CI decisions, and 3) plugs into a progressive CI attenuator that can soften CI enforcement for low-severity regressions while keeping high-severity failures blocking. What changed: added a new classifier and supporting feature flags, an integration point in the CI eval hook that emits a severity breakdown annotation on PRs, a new evaluation metric severityAdjustedRegressionRate surfaced in test reports and dashboards, CI policy configuration with default thresholds (low=0.05, medium=0.02, high=0.005 fraction), a small sample prompt-sensitivity dataset for unit/regression tests, and docs on how teams can tune attenuation behavior per repo or per prompt-cohort. Design considerations and tradeoffs: classifier uses a compact heuristic model (logistic blend of token-level delta, semantic-change score, and historical flakiness) to keep latency minimal; full ML-backed models are out of scope for this change but can be layered later. The progressive attenuator implements a leaky-quarantine pattern: low-severity failing prompts are flagged and counted towards a quarantined bucket that will delay block escalations for a configurable grace window, while medium/high severity still trigger quicker review. Backwards compatibility: feature gated off by default; default policy is conservative (blocks on medium+ by default) so existing CI behavior is preserved until teams opt-in. Related: ENG-4289 (ev-harness quality gates), SUP-3412 (support ticket on noisy prompt CI blocks).

Motivation: Intermittent multi-turn regressions have surfaced where small prompt edits cascade down generation chains and amplify hallucination rates across prompt-sets. This PR introduces a probabilistic "prompt-cascade detector" that flags PRs where a proposed prompt change is likely to produce cascading failures across related prompts. The detector is intended as a 'soft-block' CI hook: it fails PR checks with a descriptive report but does not auto-revert. The goal is to give reviewers and engineers early, prioritized signal for high-risk prompt edits without creating a hard gate that blocks rapid iteration. What this PR does: 1) Adds a new detector module that computes a cascade-risk score using a lightweight Bayesian model combining: semantic drift (embedding cosine shift between baseline and candidate prompts), structural sensitivity (token-level delta and prompt-template branching factor), and cross-example amplification (a small simulated replay that measures disagreement amplification across a sampled cohort). 2) Integrates the detector as a CI plugin (ci/hooks/prompt_cascade_check.py) that runs in PR checks and emits a score + recommended actions. 3) Adds a dashboard-friendly JSON report format and an automated issue suggestion when score > high threshold (creates text to prefill a Linear issue). 4) Adds unit and integration tests and a short docs page outlining thresholds and how reviewers should interpret the signal. Non-goals: This is not a replacement for full regression evals or human review; the model is calibrated to minimize false positives and surface high-confidence cascade patterns. Score interpretation: - score < 0.15: low risk, pass quietly. - 0.15 <= score < 0.45: caution, report added to PR checks. - score >= 0.45: high-risk, CI soft-block — check cannot be merged without explaining mitigation in PR description, but maintainers can override. Implementation notes: The core detector is in src/eval_harness/detectors/prompt_cascade.py and exposes a single function `compute_cascade_score(candidate_prompt, baseline_prompts, sampling_config)` that returns a numeric probability and a short explanation list. The CI hook wraps that and calls a small 10-sample simulated replay using mocked model responses via our existing eval-mock harness to keep runtime under 30s in CI. Config: A new config block in eval-config/ci_hooks.yml allows teams to tune thresholds per repo. Backwards compatibility: Existing CI only sees a new optional check; default behavior is opt-in per repo via config. Privacy: All in-PR prompt text remains in PR context; no external telemetry is sent by default. Checklist: - [x] Detector implementation - [x] CI hook integration - [x] Unit tests and integration smoke - [x] Docs and threshold guidance - [x] Linear auto-suggest template Included artifacts: short JSON report schema, example Linear text, and guidance in docs/ci/prompt-cascade.md. Risks and mitigation: We tuned the Bayesian prior conservatively to limit noisy soft-blocks; added an allowlist for known benign prompt scaffolding patterns. Future work: tie the detector to the eval-harness historical registry to perform per-prompt historical variance priors and surface more actionable diffs. See also ENG-4721 for follow-up metrics telemetry and ENG-4789 for per-team thresholding.
Ethan Kim (reviewer): Nice approach. Two requests before approving: (1) make sure the mocked replay uses deterministic seeds so CI is stable; (2) add a short opt-out annotation for PRs that are just docs/example prompt tweaks.

Summary: Introduces a CI adapter that attaches sample-weighted local explainers to smokecheck/regression failures and prioritizes flaky/impactful prompt-sets for triage. Motivation: Our smokechecks surface frequent failures but lack a quick signal for which prompts contribute most to downstream quality risk. This PR augments the eval pipeline with a lightweight explainer that estimates per-sample influence (counterfactual token-saliency proxy + Monte Carlo perturbation aggregate) and a prioritizer that surfaces the top-K prompt-sets by weighted-impact score. The feature operates in two modes: offline (during nightly backfills) and fast-path in CI (on triggered regression failures) with a bounded runtime budget. Changes: - New CI adapter: eval_harness/ci/adapters/sample_weighted_explainer.py (core logic + config) - Hook integration: eval_harness/ci/hooks/impact_prioritizer_hook.py (attaches to smokecheck job) - Small metrics: eval_harness/metrics/impact_metrics.py (sample_weighted_impact, top_k_coverage) - Tests: tests/ci/test_explainer_fastpath.py and tests/metrics/test_impact_metrics.py - Docs: docs/ci/quality_gates.md (added a short section describing the adapter and how to tune budgets) - Config: ci/default_hooks.yaml updated to include prioritizer with conservative defaults Compatibility: The adapter is opt-in in CI via an env flag EVAL_EXPLAINER_ENABLED and bounded by MAX_EXPLAINER_SECONDS. Default run in PR CI is disabled; enabled in nightly/regression pipelines and for manual triage runs. Performance: Fast-path mode samples N=32 perturbed completions and uses token-saliency heuristics to approximate influence; wall-time budget for fast-path is 6s per prompt-set in CI. Motivation doc and microbenchmarks in the PR description show median extra CI time of ~1.8s per failure when fast-path is enabled, and ~18s in nightly full-mode. Safety and cost: explainers do not store model outputs beyond ephemeral evaluation logs and respect data retention policies. There are knobs for on/off, sample size, and a fallback to a cheap heuristic when budget is exceeded. Related: Linked to ENG-2097 (priority triage for prompt regressions) and ENG-2275 (smokecheck failure taxonomy); follows design notes in docs/ci/arch/impact-triage.md.

Motivation: existing CI gates are brittle for prompt sets with heterogeneous lengths, multi-turn contexts and low-frequency anchors which lead to noisy false positives. This PR introduces a hierarchical fidelity oracle that fuses multiple evaluation signals (semantic similarity, role-aware turn consistency, token-level saliency, and anchor stability) across temporal cohorts and prompt granularity, and exposes a non-blocking CI adapter that surfaces soft-fail quality regressions with prioritized remediation suggestions. Core behaviors: 1) compute per-prompt multi-signal fidelity vectors, 2) aggregate per-cohort with recency-aware weighting and uncertainty calibration, 3) emit composite fidelity score and explainability hints (top contributing tokens and failing turns), 4) provide a non-blocking CI decision path which fails only on high-confidence regressions and otherwise annotates PRs with risk tiers and suggested rerun probes. This change contains: implementation of scorer and adapter, integration tests, docs and an example anchor manifest.
