Summary: This PR introduces an integration test harness that provisions an ephemeral AWS VPC using our alpha modules, validates a small set of expected invariants/outputs, and then tears everything down. The goal is to catch provider/module drift and unsafe defaults earlier than design partner pilots (e.g., subnet mapping, NAT assumptions, endpoint/DNS regressions). Motivation/Context: Unit-level terraform validate/tflint/checkov are necessary but not sufficient; we’ve already had issues that only show up once AWS resources exist (e.g., AZ assumptions, route association wiring, endpoint private DNS behavior). This harness is a minimal “smoke” environment that deploys modules the way customers will via examples, with assertions for the outputs the installer expects downstream. What’s included: (1) A Go-based Terratest suite under test/integration/ that runs terraform init/apply against examples/integration/ephemeral-vpc and performs basic assertions. (2) A dedicated example config (ephemeral-vpc) that composes modules/vpc + modules/endpoints + modules/logging with the smallest viable set of variables. (3) GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/integration-tests-ephemeral-vpc.yml that assumes an AWS role in the sandbox account via OIDC, runs the tests, and always attempts teardown (defer destroy). (4) Guardrails: unique name prefix per run, TTL tags on all resources, and a best-effort cleanup job to reduce orphan risk on cancelled runs. (5) Documentation in the repo README for how/when to run integration tests and the expected CI cost/time. CI/Cost/Runtime notes: Running this on every PR is expensive (AWS costs + ~18–30 min runtime depending on region/AZ capacity). Current proposal in this PR: run nightly on main + allow manual workflow_dispatch for maintainers and release candidates. We still keep fmt/validate/tflint/checkov gating per-PR (already in progress under ENG-4837 / PR-18503). Validation assertions (current set): VPC is created with expected CIDR; public/private subnets count matches inputs; private subnets have a route to NAT (when enabled); VPC endpoints created for S3/ECR API/ECR DKR/STS/CloudWatch Logs; endpoint security group is present; flow logs destination is created when enabled; key outputs are non-empty (vpc_id, private_subnet_ids, endpoint_sg_id). Notably we’re not asserting exact route table IDs or full endpoint policy JSON to avoid brittle tests; we’re targeting invariants that map to common pilot failures. Follow-ups (not in this PR): Add a second scenario for “no-NAT + endpoints-only” topology; add an assertion for private DNS settings (enabled/disabled) once we lock defaults with Security; wire a weekly budget report for sandbox account spend; consider moving from Terratest to terraform test once we’re on a baseline Terraform version across customers. Screenshots/Logs: See workflow run output for a full terraform plan/apply log; by default we redact AWS account IDs and do not print full state. Reviewer checklist: Please focus on (a) safety of the teardown paths, (b) whether assertions align with what the installer actually needs, and (c) whether the workflow scheduling is acceptable for alpha (nightly + manual).
Victor Alvarez (review): Nice. Two questions: 1) Are we comfortable with Terratest here vs terraform test? 2) Can we avoid validating route table IDs directly (brittle across AWS)?
Sahana Iyer (author): Agree on brittle assertions — this PR only checks presence of NAT route on private RTs (0.0.0.0/0 -> nat_gw) and avoids ID matching. On terraform test: we can revisit once we standardize TF >= 1.6 across module consumers; Terratest is easiest today with our pinned provider matrix.
Sean Gallagher (review): Teardown safety: what happens if the job is cancelled mid-apply? We’ve had orphaned NAT GWs before.
Sahana Iyer (author): Added TTL tags + a follow-up cleanup job that runs `terraform destroy` with best-effort even when earlier steps fail. Cancelled runs are still a risk, but TTL tags let us sweep in the sandbox account; also the workflow uses `concurrency` to prevent overlapping runs stomping on the same prefix.
Irene Choi (review): Runtime/cost needs to be explicit. Can we keep this nightly only for now, not per-PR? Also please ensure the role is limited to the sandbox account + specific regions.
Sahana Iyer (author): Updated workflow to nightly + manual only; added `AWS_REGION` allowlist in the workflow and tightened the IAM role policy doc reference (INT-1734).
Devon Price (review): One nit: please redact terraform output that includes account IDs. Also consider splitting logs for easier debugging.
Sahana Iyer (author): Done — reduced verbosity, removed printing of caller identity, and added a short summary section at the end of the job with key outputs only.
Irene Choi (final): Approved after tightening scheduling + region allowlist. Please open a follow-up for a second scenario (endpoints-only).
Sahana Iyer (author): Will do; added to ENG-4860 subtask list.

payload.body:
Introduces a commitment-leak detection/auditor and a proportional warmup smoothing policy for Dedicated fleet autoscaling. Improves stability during rapid decommissions and initial warmup by smoothing reserved capacity application. No public API changes.
Background and motivation:
We observed two recurring issues on Dedicated fleets: 1) short-lived reservation/commitment leaks when nodes are decommissioned quickly (causes temporary over-commit reporting and unexpected token/burst behavior), and 2) oscillatory warmup effects where newly provisioned capacity applies immediately and then gets trimmed back during subsequent reconciliations, causing latency blips and missed throughput guarantees.

This PR implements a two-part mitigation: a Commitment Leak Guard (an auditor process that detects and reconciles orphaned/residual commitment state across the reservation ledger) and a Proportional Warmup Smoothing policy (applies reserved capacity in a weighted ramp over a configurable warmup window and biases the autoscaler to respect recent utilization history to avoid oscillation).

Design summary:
- commitment_guard.go: background reconciler that periodically scans active reservations, cross-validates with node leases, and emits corrective actions (soft-decrement vs forced-reclaim) with safety cooldowns to avoid double-reclaims. Includes exponential backoff and a configurable toleration window to account for transient network partitions.
- warmup_window.go: implements a proportional ramp function that computes an "applied_commit_fraction" based on age since reservation + recent utilization EWMA. The function is pluggable as an autoscaler policy and exposes knobs: warmup_seconds, smoothing_alpha, min_fraction.
- telemetry hooks: emits "commitment_leak_detected", "commitment_reclaimed", "warmup_fraction_applied" metrics with tenant and pool dimensions; updated usage_reporter to include sample of applied fraction per reconciliation.
- simulation harness: extended sim_runner to run scenarios with rapid decommissions and spike-on-warmup to validate SLO stability.

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests for leak detection heuristics and reclaim path
- [x] Integration e2e sim for warmup smoothing vs baseline autoscaler
- [x] Telemetry dashboard snippets and alert rules added to docs
- [x] Backwards compatible: default policy disabled for fleets with legacy autoscaler opt-out

Testing and results:
- Local e2e simulation: sustained 99th p50 latency improvement during aggressive capacity churn (reduction in latency spikes by ~38% in sim), reduced transient over-commit alerts by 86% in simulated failure windows.
- CI: initial lint/test run hit a race in warmup window update; fixed by adding a small sync point in reconciliation loop. All tests now pass.

Related items:
- Linear ENG-4821: Dedicated stability workstream
- Related PRs: small telemetry formatting change (not included here) and a docs-only follow-up to show policy configuration examples.

Merging notes:
- Feature guarded behind fleet feature flag: "dedicated.commitment_guard_enabled" and autoscaler policy selector (defaults to off for existing production fleets). Ops may flip the flag incrementally during rollout.

Detailed changes are listed below (commits and files).
Jonas Kramer (2026-02-16): Overall good direction. Two asks: make the toleration window configurable per-fleet and add a safety metric when we perform forced-reclaim (to help oncall triage).
Author (Ava) reply (2026-02-17): added per-fleet config and emitted 'commitment_reclaimed_forced' metric with tenant label; PTAL.
Sofia Lin (2026-02-18): small nit: warmup formula looks fine but add a unit test for the edge case when min_fraction == 1.0. Also, can we avoid a mutex in the hot path?
Author reply (2026-02-19): added test and refactored to use an atomic snapshot for the warmup parameters so we only take a lock on config change path. PTAL.
Owen Brooks (2026-02-20): approved after verifying sim results and metric names. Left one suggestion to document the feature flag and rollout steps in the runbook.
CI bot (2026-02-21): initial CI failed - race detected in reconciler (see d3f4b11).
Author (2026-02-22): pushed fix to synchronization ordering; re-ran CI - all green.
Jonas Kramer (2026-02-23): approval, requested squash merge to keep history tidy.

Motivation: Private installs were using a single monolithic state layout and a single GPU nodepool definition which made multi-cluster deployments and controlled rolling upgrades for GPU-backed workloads brittle. This PR splits state backends by cluster/environment and introduces a first-class GPU subpool abstraction so customers can define multiple heterogeneous GPU pools (e.g. nvidia-a100-40g, nvidia-t4) with taints/affinity and separate autoscaling profiles.

What changed (high-level):
- Introduced module 'cluster-state' to encapsulate backend configuration and locking per-cluster. Supports S3+Dynamo for AWS, GCS+locks for GCP, and local file backend for on-prem dry-runs.
- Added 'gpu-subpool' reusable module that exposes node selector labels, taints, max/min sizes, and per-subpool IAM bindings where applicable.
- Refactored the top-level private deployment module to compose multiple gpu-subpool instances and to reference the per-cluster state backend.
- Added a state migration helper (scripts/migrate_state.sh) and documentation for migrating existing single-state deployments to per-cluster states.
- Updated examples/ to include a two-subpool production example and a single-subpool dev example.

Migration steps for operators:
1) Review generated plan for cluster-state module in a non-production copy of your state bucket.
2) Run scripts/migrate_state.sh --source-bucket <old> --dest-prefix <cluster>/ to split state into cluster-specific prefixes.
3) Apply terraform in each cluster order (control plane first, then GPU pools) following the README.

Rollback plan:
- If migration introduces an error, the script keeps a timestamped copy of the original state and will not delete it. Re-point the backend to the original prefix and apply the previous module version.

Testing and validation:
- Local plan/unit tests with terratest mock infra run in CI.
- Manual validation runs were performed against a GKE dev project and an AWS VPC staging account, confirming nodepool creation, taint/affinity application, and IAM bindings for GPU pools.

Notes and follow-ups:
- This PR intentionally does not change default behavior for fresh installs (defaults remain single cluster state unless cluster_state module invoked).
- We should add an automated migration job in the private-installer flow in a follow-up PR to orchestrate migration for customers on upgrade.

Checklist: 
- [x] Module code and docs
- [x] Migration script and README
- [x] Example configs (dev/prod)
- [x] CI terratest coverage

Refs: Linear ENG-1124, INFRA-938, related PRs in redwood-private-installer for orchestration

Asha Patel: migration script now checkpoints per-prefix and will not delete originals; re-run will skip already-migrated prefixes.
Evelyn Chen: Please add a guard in the module so empty list of gpu-subpools uses the previous implicit pool for backward compatibility.

Asha Patel: Added terratest that mocks node labels and validates the IAM policy attachment phase in CI.

payload.body:
Summary: This PR updates Terraform for Redwood’s cross-region traffic steering so regional failover can converge faster and more predictably during impairment. The main change is lowering DNS TTLs for the API entrypoints used by Hosted API and Dedicated (where applicable), while adding guardrails to avoid unintended traffic shifts (provider caching variance, resolver behavior, and over-eager health checks). It also adds explicit routing primitives (health checks + failover policy wiring + outputs for the failover controller) so the automation controller can rely on consistent infra definitions across environments.

Motivation / context: Regional failover automation upgrades (Reliability Program) require that DNS-based steering not be the long pole. Today, several records use TTLs that are appropriate for steady-state but extend failover time, and some resources are defined inconsistently across regions/environments. We want a standard, reviewable baseline that aligns with the failover signal hierarchy and avoids oscillation during partial outages.

What changed: 1) TTL tuning: Reduce TTLs for public API endpoints (api.redwoodinference.com + region aliases) from 60s -> 20s in prod (staging remains 10s for drills), and for dedicated customer vanity domains that opt into Redwood-managed DNS from 300s -> 60s (no change for customer-managed DNS). TTL changes are feature-flagged by Terraform variables so we can stage rollout per region.

2) Health check plumbing: Add/standardize health checks that match the failover controller’s reachability signal (HTTP /healthz/edge and TCP fallback where HTTP is blocked). Health checks include conservative request interval/thresholds to reduce false positives, and are intentionally decoupled from application-level p95 latency signals (those come from metrics; DNS health should only answer “is the edge reachable”).

3) Failover routing policy wiring: Introduce a module that creates/updates the primary/secondary routing policy for regional records (us-east-1 primary, eu-west-1 secondary for the first phase), with explicit “hold-down” notes in tags/annotations for operators. This does not implement automated flips by itself; it ensures the underlying DNS objects exist and are consistent.

4) Outputs for automation + observability: Export record IDs, health check IDs, and key tags as Terraform outputs so the failover controller / incident-bot can link infra objects to audits and dashboards. Added standard tags: reliability_program=regional_failover_automation, service=api-edge, env, region, and owner.

Non-goals: - No provider migration or multi-cloud work.
- No change to customer contract language or SLA.
- No change to app-side routing logic; this is infra-only.

Risk assessment: Lower TTLs can increase query volume and expose resolver caching variance; health checks can cause unintended failover if they’re too sensitive. To mitigate, TTL reductions are staged per region with explicit rollback vars, health checks are conservative, and we keep a minimum TTL floor (20s prod, 10s staging). This PR also avoids introducing any “latency-based” DNS routing to prevent oscillation; failover remains an explicit policy decision via controller logic.

Rollout plan: - Stage 1 (staging): Apply changes in staging and run a rehearsal with the game day checklist. Validate that record propagation and resolver behavior match expectations.
- Stage 2 (prod, limited blast radius): Enable TTL 20s for api.redwoodinference.com in us-east-1/eu-west-1 only. Monitor DNS query rate, NXDOMAIN/servfail rates, edge reachability probes, and error budgets.
- Stage 3 (expand): Roll out to additional regions after the first controlled failover game day confirms success criteria.

Validation: - terraform plan reviewed for prod/us-east-1 and prod/eu-west-1 (no unintended resource recreation).
- Confirmed Route53 health checks are stable in staging under induced partial impairment.
- Confirmed record set changes are in-place updates (no delete/recreate for main A/AAAA alias records).

References: - Linear: ENG-2411 (program), ENG-2418 (signals/alerts), ENG-2421 (game day #1)
- Slack: DNS TTL change risk assessment thread (eng-infra)
- Game day objective: shrink DNS convergence time so controller-driven failover isn’t gated by 60s+ TTLs.

Notes for on-call: If we observe unexpected traffic shifts, rollback is a Terraform var flip restoring TTLs to previous values and disabling the new failover module for affected records. See runbook references in ENG-2421 checklist for monitoring queries and edge reachability during change windows.
Miles Thornton (review): Can we ensure health checks don’t flip regions based on transient 5xx from app deploys? Prefer edge reachability only.
Victor Alvarez (author): Yep — health checks hit /healthz/edge on the gateway and we’re not using latency-based routing. Interval 30s, failure_threshold 3. Added comments + tags clarifying this is reachability-only.
Irene Choi (review): TTL 20s in prod seems aggressive; any floor and rollback path? Also confirm no alias record recreation.
Victor Alvarez (author): Added ttl_floor_prod=20 and a per-env var to revert to previous TTLs. Plan shows in-place updates for record sets (no recreation). Also added a staged rollout note in module README.
Emily Zhao (review): Health check protocol: add TCP fallback for customers that block HTTP at edge? Some networks might drop HTTP checks.
Victor Alvarez (author): Added optional tcp_fallback_enabled; default off in prod but on in staging drills. We can enable per zone if needed. Included in outputs for the controller.
Rafael Mendes (review): Please add outputs that incident-bot can link to for audits (record IDs/healthcheck IDs).
Victor Alvarez (author): Added outputs + standard tags. Devon’s incident-bot can consume these via the controller integration.
Irene Choi (approval): Approved with staged rollout + explicit rollback variables in docs.

payload.body:
Motivation: Private installs running multiple tenants in a single VPC have inconsistent GPU nodepool placement and a monolithic tfstate layout which complicates upgrades and tenant-scoped disaster recovery. This PR splits GPU nodepools by availability zone and tenant boundary, creates a per-tenant tfstate backend layout with migration tooling, and tightens IAM bindings so nodepools have least-privilege access to cloud resources. Changeset summary: new module modules/gpu-nodepool/v2 supports az-aware subpool creation; modules/state introduces per-tenant backend config templates and a migrator helper script; modules/iam adds role-per-nodepool and conditional bindings for nodepool identity vs cluster identity; networking updates ensure subnet allocation ranges are parameterized per-az to allow fine-grained nodepool placement. Migration strategy: includes an automated terraform state migrator script (scripts/tfstate-migrator.sh) that iteratively snapshots, copies state to tenant-specific S3 paths, and verifies plan-idempotence before switching backends. Context: During dogfood of the alpha VPC module in the Redwood sandbox account (ENG-4895), we hit a failure where private subnet route tables were pointing at a NAT gateway that either did not exist or lived in a different AZ. The root cause was an implicit assumption in the VPC module that the number/order of public subnets == number/order of private subnets and that NAT gateways can be indexed by position (count/index) rather than by AZ identity.

Problem: When customers (or our own example env) use a non-symmetric subnet layout (e.g., 3 private subnets across 3 AZs but only 2 public subnets, or `single_nat_gateway = true`), the existing logic would still attempt to attach each private route table to `aws_nat_gateway.nat[index]`. In the single NAT case, `index > 0` would reference a NAT that was never created; in the uneven-AZ case the mapping could silently route a private subnet to a NAT in another AZ.

What changed: This PR switches NAT GW + route mapping from positional indexing to an AZ-keyed mapping derived from the actual `public_subnets_by_az` map. For `single_nat_gateway = true`, we deterministically select the first public subnet AZ (sorted) and route all private route tables to that NAT. For multi-NAT, we create one NAT per AZ that has a public subnet and only create private routes for private subnets in AZs that have a NAT; we also surface a clearer validation error when a private subnet is declared in an AZ without a corresponding public subnet (unless single NAT is enabled).

Why this is safe: It preserves the default (symmetric, one NAT per AZ) behavior, but stops producing invalid references and makes unsupported layouts fail fast with an actionable error message.

Notes: Linked discussion and repro screenshots are in the eng-infra Slack thread (see link above). This also updates the integration test harness to cover (1) 2-AZ layout with 3 private subnets and (2) single NAT layout.

Checklist: - [x] Reproduced in dogfood env before fix - [x] Added/updated tests in `tests/` harness - [x] `terraform fmt` / `validate` - [x] Updated module README caveats on supported subnet topologies - [x] Confirmed no output name changes (outputs are stable; values may change in edge cases where previous mapping was incorrect)

Follow-ups (post-merge): 1) Add a docs snippet in the deployment guide clarifying supported subnet/AZ layouts and when to use `single_nat_gateway` (owner: DevEx) 2) Consider a dedicated variable to explicitly choose "central NAT AZ" for single-NAT mode instead of relying on sorted AZ selection (owner: Infra) 3) Add a Checkov suppression note for the new validation resources if needed (owner: CI) 4) Ensure example tfvars for design partners do not specify mismatched public/private AZ lists (owner: SE/PS).

tests: add uneven subnet count scenario + single NAT scenario
docs: clarify NAT/AZ behavior and supported layouts

Context: Private installs require predictable, shardable tfstate boundaries for tenant-scoped GPU node pools and network attachments. Current monolithic state caused long plan/apply times and frequent lock contention during tenant onboarding. This PR introduces a hash-anchored tfstate layout plus a lightweight tenant-claim orchestrator to (1) create tenant-scoped state slices for GPU pools and associated subnet leases, (2) deterministically derive tenant IAM role names/ARNs to avoid drift, and (3) provide a reversible migration path with automated backups and a rollback driver.
Primary goals: reduce tf plan/app latency for tenant onboarding; eliminate cross-tenant lock contention; provide a safe migration from existing consolidated state to sharded, anchored state; surface deterministic naming to downstream installers so IAM and RBAC can be reconciled without manual intervention.
- New module: modules/tfstate-anchor (creates per-tenant state objects named by sha1(tenant_id||cluster_id||env) and exposes state bucket/object metadata.
- New module: modules/tenant-claim-orchestrator (statemachine that claims subnets, creates GPU pool resources in tenant-scoped state, emits lease tokens).
- Updates to modules/gpu-pool: split resource creation into local 'proxy' move and remote state-backed resources; added lifecycle prevent_destroy on critical subnet attachments.
- Updated modules/iam: deterministic role naming and policy templating to avoid manual lookups.
- Migration tooling: scripts/tfstate-migrate.sh and docs/migrations/anchor-migration.md with dry-run and preview modes.
- CI: added integration test harness for multi-tenant plan/app and lock contention simulation.
- Added reconciliation hook for private-installer to call the orchestrator during tenant create flow.
Unit tests for templated IAM names, integration test that simulates 10 concurrent tenant onboard flows to assert no lock contention, end-to-end verify that subnet leases are unique and that GPU pool create is successful using remote state. Also added a chaos test that kills the orchestrator mid-claim to validate idempotency. All tests included in CI pipeline.
1) Dry-run mode: run scripts/tfstate-migrate.sh --preview against a staging copy of the state bucket to validate generated anchors and import mapping; 2) Backup: script creates dated snapshots in s3://redwood-tfstate-backups/<date>/ and verifies checksums; 3) Lease handoff: orchestrator claims subnets and creates tenant-scoped state; 4) Import: run terraform import commands emitted by the migration script to move resources to new state slices; 5) Promote: update private-installer to point to tenant-scoped remote state and remove deprecated central references; 6) Monitor: run integration smoke tests and metric checks for 24h. Rollback path included: restore snapshot and re-register central state, orchestrator will release leases on revert.
- Automatic snapshot before any destructive changes.
- Import preview mode to capture mapping without state mutation.
- Orchestrator has a reversible 'claim' step: a lease token can be revoked and resources remain untouched until 'promote' is called.
- Added extra CI gate to prevent merges if migration scripts are in an unreviewed state.
- Documented manual rollback commands in docs/migrations/anchor-migration.md.
All CI jobs passed after two iterations. Initial integration job failed due to flaky S3 emulator; fixed by adding test harness retry and updating test fixture TTL. Final run: terraform fmt/lint, unit tests, integration multi-tenant plan/app simulations, linters all green.
- Introduced hash-anchored tfstate layout for tenant-scoped GPU pools and subnet leases; reduces plan/app contention and accelerates tenant onboarding.
- New tenant-claim-orchestrator module to safely claim subnets and create tenant-scoped resources.
- Deterministic IAM role naming to prevent drift and simplify RBAC reconciliation.
- Migration tooling (dry-run, backup, import steps) and rollback path.
- Integration tests and observability hooks for migration and orchestrator metrics.
- Run migration in 'preview' against a staging copy of the state bucket first.
- Ensure KMS keys used by the new state objects are authorized for the installer service account.
- Coordinate with SRE to watch orchestrator.* metrics and tfstate-backup.* during migration windows.
Anika Shah: Left a few inline comments about idempotency when the orchestrator retries after transient S3 errors; please add retry wrapper and tests.
Sophia Chen: Added exponential backoff and unit tests for the s3 metadata writer; updated scripts to exit non-zero on failed dry-run verification.
Diego Marquez: Request: ensure terraform import path documented for existing GPU pools; added a migration doc item and sample import command.
Felix Liu: Confirmed deterministic role naming format; asked to add a compatibility note for existing role ARNs in the private-installer mapping.
Priya Nair: Observability ask — please emit stewarded metrics (orchestrator.attempts, lease.claims, migration.backups) to the console metrics feed. Added small metrics exports in orchestrator module.

Context: Marketplace-driven customers need a reliable subscription → entitlement → org provisioning flow. The control-plane entitlement sync service now consumes entitlement signals from both AWS Marketplace (API polling + optional notifications) and GCP Marketplace (vendor webhook). This PR adds Terraform-managed IAM, network, and webhook plumbing needed by the entitlement sync services while keeping permissions least-privilege and auditable. Changes: (1) AWS IAM: new dedicated IAM role for entitlement-sync with scoped permissions to aws-marketplace entitlement + metering APIs; separate role for webhook verifier to read secrets and write limited logs/metrics; explicit deny for broad S3 and KMS actions; (2) Webhook ingress: add an internal ALB listener rule + path-based routing for /marketplace/gcp/webhook to the entitlement-sync service target group; add WAF rule set and request size limits; (3) Secrets and key usage: provision an SSM parameter + Secrets Manager secret for GCP webhook signing key rotation, and KMS grants scoped to decrypt only those secrets; (4) Observability + safety: cloudwatch alarms for 5xx spikes on the webhook path, and metric filters for signature verification failures; (5) Documentation: inline least-privilege notes and a short README section on how to validate in staging. Notes: This does not change application logic—only infra wiring and policy boundaries. Follow-up: once we confirm partner testing, we can enable optional SNS-based AWS notifications in prod (module is included but off by default).
1) terraform: add entitlement-sync IAM role + scoped marketplace permissions 2) terraform: add secrets manager + kms grants for webhook signing key 3) terraform: add ALB routing and WAF rules for /marketplace/gcp/webhook 4) terraform: add cloudwatch alarms/metric filters for webhook failures 5) docs: update ops README for staging validation steps
Infrastructure modules updated: marketplace-entitlement-sync, iam-roles, alb-routing, waf, secrets, monitoring. Notable files: modules/marketplace-entitlement-sync/iam.tf; modules/marketplace-entitlement-sync/alb.tf; modules/security/waf_marketplace.tf; modules/observability/alarms_marketplace.tf; environments/staging/marketplace.tf; environments/prod/marketplace.tf; docs/marketplace-entitlement-sync.md.
IAM policy excerpt (entitlement-sync role): Allow marketplace entitlement reads: "action": ["aws-marketplace:ResolveCustomer", "aws-marketplace:GetEntitlements"], "resource": "*" (AWS Marketplace APIs do not support resource-level scoping). Allow metering only for our product codes via condition: "aws-marketplace:BatchMeterUsage" with Condition StringEquals "aws:PrincipalTag/Product": "marketplace". Secrets decrypt constrained: kms:Decrypt only when encryption context matches SecretsManager ARNs used by the webhook key. ALB route: path-pattern "/marketplace/gcp/webhook" → target group entitlement-sync; WAF: allowlist Redwood partner IP ranges in staging, signature verification failures rate-limited, body size capped at 64KB.

Add on-call gist sanitizer to strip secrets and long traces before attachments; include a compact telemetry-delta exporter to reduce snapshot payloads for on-call notebooks. Backwards-compatible; no config migration required.
Motivation: On-call responders often paste full gists or debug payloads into incident threads. Those artifacts can contain secrets (env variables, tokens), long raw traces that bloat attachments, and PII (IP addresses). At the same time, SLO/telemetry snapshots we ship to on-call pages are often full historical series; for rapid triage we only need deltas and a few contextual aggregates. This PR introduces two ergonomic features to reduce noise, risk, and size: (1) an on-call gist sanitizer that redacts secrets and trims large stack traces while preserving human-readable context; (2) a compact telemetry-delta exporter that produces small, delta-first payloads for incident snapshots and the oncall CLI.

Change summary (single-string): - Add gist_sanitizer module with configurable redaction rules (env var patterns, token-like patterns, IP addresses, email obfuscation) and a trim policy for long stack frames. - Add delta_exporter that computes per-metric deltas and top-k contributors over a rolling window, emits compact protobuf/JSON payloads, and supports rate-limited export to incident storage. - Add CLI export_snapshot for oncall to produce compact snapshots used by incident-bot and the web console. - Add tests for sanitizer and exporter plus integration test exercising CLI path. - Update docs with recommended oncall workflow and opt-in config knobs. - Small Helm chart values update to enable exporter in non-prod clusters by default.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for gist sanitizer patterns and trimming - [x] Unit + integration tests for delta computation and exporter backpressure - [x] Docs: oncall/gist-handling.md and telemetry/exporter.md - [x] Manual validation on staging incident-bot flow - [x] Security review for redaction patterns (SUP-889) - [x] Feature toggles via chart values for gradual rollout
payload.title: Sanitize on-call gists and add compact telemetry-delta exporter

Summary: Replace the monolithic per-job Python venv bootstrapping with a lightweight presubmit proxy and a compact dependency cache. This PR introduces a small long-lived container (presubmit-proxy) that pre-warms a minimal, reproducible runtime and exposes a fast mount/share protocol for job runners. Motivation: CI startup accounts for a large fraction of developer feedback time and contributes to flakes when network or PyPI is slow. We also see duplicated wheel installs across matrix jobs. Goals: 1) shorten cold-start time for python presubmits; 2) reduce network hits to PyPI in CI; 3) make dependency installs reproducible and testable locally; 4) avoid changing developer-level tooling and keep local dev venvs unaffected. What changed: - New component: tools/presubmit/proxy.py - lightweight HTTP + unix-socket service that serves cached wheels and a preassembled site-packages tarball per lockfile hash. - Docker image: tooling/venv-image/Dockerfile contains a slim runtime with build-essential and pip wheel cache prepopulated. - Compactifier: ci/cache/dep-compactifier.py scans pyproject.lock, pre-builds wheels and writes cache artifacts to the proxy store. - CI workflow: .github/workflows/presubmit-python.yml switched to use the proxy for matrix jobs; added a cache warm step that talks to the proxy before running tests. - Shrinkwrap: pyproject.toml and tools/ci/ci-init.sh updated to emit a deterministic lockfile fingerprint used as the cache key. Rollout plan: staged rollout using feature flag ci.use_presubmit_proxy (off by default). Toggle on for the presubmit-lite lane, observe cache hit rates and flakiness for one week, then opt-in more lanes. Benchmark: median presubmit cold-start time reduced from 55s to 32s in internal perf job. Checklist: [x] design doc in Linear (ENG-3456) [x] unit tests for proxy handlers [x] integration smoke job with proxy warm path [x] docs updated at docs/dev/ci-presubmit.md Testing notes: - run tools/presubmit/proxy.py locally (instructions in docs) - run ci/cache/dep-compactifier.py against pyproject.lock to generate a cache snapshot - verify .github workflow runs pick up a cache hit via presubmit-proxy endpoint Caveats: - Windows self-hosted runners require manual mount support; documented workaround included. - This does not replace Dedicated or Private on-prem installers; it is a CI-side optimization. Full description follows the checklist: the patch attempts to be conservative: if proxy is unreachable CI falls back to existing venv-init path. Backwards compatibility: none of the public SDKs are changed.
Reduce presubmit startup time by ~40% via slim presubmit proxy and compact dependency cache. No API or customer-facing behavior changes. Improves CI flakiness and lowers e2e test runtime.
Miguel Ortega: Nice separation of concerns. Can we make the cache path pluggable per-team?
Author (Aisha): yes, cache root is configurable via PRESUBMIT_PROXY_STORE; added doc and env var handling in proxy init
Priya Singh: Concern about auth on shared CI clusters. How do we avoid cross-tenant contamination?
Author (Aisha): proxy namespaces on lockfile fingerprint and enforces workdir-level ACLs; added tests and note to k8s deployment that PDP must mount a tenant token file
Liam Chen: ran the presubmit-lite job twice; saw a successful warm hit and a single flaky test unrelated to this change; approved after one re-run of tests

Adds a new subsequence sampling primitive and an orthogonal mini-batcher to improve representative workload fidelity for mixed-length traffic; recommended opt-in for benchmark runs and nightly stability suites.
Motivation: existing workload generators underrepresent correlated subsequences leading to unstable tail estimates when short and long sequences coexist. This change introduces an entropy-consistent subsequence sampler that preserves observed local token-entropy structure while producing deterministic reproducible subsequences for replay. In parallel we introduce a mini-batch orthogonalizer that reorders and groups requests to maximize diversity within each batch without breaking sequence ordering guarantees for KV-cache warmup. Design: the sampler builds a lightweight statistical sketch per conversation window and draws subsequences using constrained resampling to maintain per-window entropy and marginal length distributions. The orthogonalizer forms micro-batches by solving a constrained assignment problem (approximate Hungarian with locality constraints) to ensure each mini-batch contains orthogonal token-paths, which improves GPU kernel utilization and reduces model internal contention. Backwards compatibility: default behavior for existing runners is unchanged; new primitives are exposed behind flags and a config section in the benchmark manifest. Test coverage: unit tests for sampler invariants, property tests to assert entropy-preservation statistics across synthetic corpora, integration tests for the orthogonalizer inside the multi-sequence runner, and end-to-end nightly regression jobs added. Impact: synthetic and replayed benchmarks show reduced p95 variance across runs and fewer extreme outliers. Usage: documented examples in bench-recipes/entropy-sampler.md and an arg to the runner: --subsequence-sampler=entropy-consistent, --orthogonalize-mini-batches=true. Related: aligns with ENG-4129 and supports follow-ups in BENCH-72 for mixed-length fidelity experiments.
feat(sampler): add entropy-consistent subsequence sampler implementation
feat(batcher): introduce mini-batch orthogonalizer with locality constraints
test(sampler): property tests and unit test harness for entropy invariants
perf: tune kernel-friendly batching heuristics and add microbenchmarks
docs: bench-recipes example and CLI flag documentation
ci: add nightly regression job wiring for new primitives
fix(tests): stabilize flaky integration test under CI resource jitter
Nightly mixed-length replay with sampler+orthogonalizer enabled reduced p95 variance across 10 runs by 32% and reduced extreme outliers (p99.9) by 48% on the heterogeneous GPU testbed. Average GPU SM utilization increased by 6% for micro-batched workloads. End-to-end mean latency impact was +3ms for very short single-token requests when orthogonalization is on, but throughput improved by 9% for typical 16-128 token sequences.
Unit tests for sampler invariants, property tests over synthetic_corpora (statistical checks), integration test with multi_sequence_runner to assert KV cache correctness, microbenchmarks for latency/throughput sweep, nightly regression job added to CI pipeline to detect p95 drift and flaky variance. All tests run locally and in CI; results attached to CI run summary.
Miguel Rodriguez: This looks good overall but the orthogonalizer could increase request latency for some short-tail workloads. Can you add a config knob and measurement in the microbenchmarks to ensure we can toggle it with minimal friction?
Asha Patel: Added --orthogonalize-mini-batches flag and updated microbenchmarks to include latency and throughput sweeps. See perf commit that records p50/p95/p99 for both modes.
Priya Shah: Please add a short explanation in docs about how entropy is estimated and why it's stable for deterministic replays. The property tests are great but users will want intuition.
Asha Patel: Expanded docs/benchmarking/entropy-sampler.md with a short appendix on the sketch and parameters and a link to the property test harness to reproduce the stats.
Liam O'Connor: CI flaky test observed on arm builders (timing sensitive). Suggest making timeouts adaptive.
Asha Patel: Adjusted the integration test to use relative timeouts and retried with the ARM pool; CI now green.
When backfilling historical benchmark data, apply the entropy sketch with window size 256 and seed 42 to ensure deterministic subsequence selection. Backfill tooling script bench/scripts/backfill_entropy_consistent.py provided. Expect small shifts in historical p95 because subsequence sampling differs from previous uniform subsampler.
payload.title: Entropy-consistent subsequence sampler and mini-batch orthogonalizer

Title: Bootstrap VPC module skeletons + repo structure + first example environment

Summary
This PR bootstraps the `redwood-terraform` repository layout for the Private VPC Terraform modules (alpha). It adds: (1) initial module skeletons (VPC, endpoints, logging, security groups, IAM scaffold placeholders) with consistent naming and conventions, (2) a first runnable example environment (`examples/aws-private-vpc-minimal`) to validate the repo wiring, and (3) baseline CI for terraform fmt/validate plus documentation checks. No production defaults are finalized here; this is the scaffolding to unblock parallel work on module implementations and interface reviews.

Motivation
We’ve had repeated pilot friction in Private deployments caused by inconsistent customer VPC footprints and unclear boundaries between “network foundation” and “installer/cluster”. The alpha effort needs a stable module suite structure and an example that Solutions Engineering can run end-to-end in a sandbox account as a sanity check. This PR focuses on structure and conventions so subsequent PRs can land independently (VPC routing, endpoints, logging, SG patterns, IAM boundaries, integration tests).

What’s included
- Repository structure
  - `modules/` top-level with one directory per module
  - `examples/` with a minimal composition example
  - `docs/` for alpha-specific architecture notes + module interface conventions
  - `scripts/` for local lint/validate helpers
- Module skeletons (placeholders + interface stubs)
  - `modules/vpc/` (CIDR, subnets, tags; stub outputs)
  - `modules/vpc_endpoints/` (interface placeholder; no endpoints created yet)
  - `modules/logging/` (flow logs placeholder; destination to be implemented)
  - `modules/security_groups/` (naming conventions + stub SG outputs)
  - `modules/iam_installer/` (placeholder role + trust policy stub; no permissions finalized)
- Example environment
  - `examples/aws-private-vpc-minimal/` composes modules with minimal variables and produces outputs expected by the installer later (VPC ID, private subnet IDs, endpoint security group ID placeholder)
- Conventions
  - Standard variable naming (`name`, `environment`, `tags`) across modules
  - Required `README.md` per module with: purpose, inputs, outputs, non-goals, and extension points
  - `versions.tf` placeholder, provider constraints to be pinned in follow-up PR
- CI baseline
  - GitHub Actions workflow for `terraform fmt -check` and `terraform validate` (examples only for now)
  - Docs check: ensure each module has a README and `variables.tf`/`outputs.tf`

Out of scope
- No AWS resources beyond the example’s minimal VPC wiring are finalized here
- No endpoint catalog decisions (ECR/S3/STS/Logs) yet
- No logging retention defaults or SIEM hooks yet
- No opinionated SG rules (ingress/egress) beyond naming conventions
- No release/versioning automation

Notes on module boundaries (alpha direction)
This PR reflects a draft boundary that we should confirm in ENG-4829:
- `modules/vpc`: VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT strategy (later PR)
- `modules/vpc_endpoints`: interface endpoints + gateway endpoints + private DNS toggles (later PR)
- `modules/logging`: VPC Flow Logs and log destinations (later PR)
- `modules/security_groups`: a small set of opinionated SGs intended to be composed (later PR)
- `modules/iam_installer`: scaffolding for an installer execution role with optional permission boundaries (later PR)
The example composes these modules but keeps the placeholders explicit to avoid implying defaults are decided.

Review notes / open questions
- Naming: should modules be prefixed `aws_` (e.g., `aws_vpc`) or keep provider-agnostic names with AWS scope stated in README?
- Outputs: which outputs are required for the installer integration (e.g., endpoints, log destinations)? This PR only stubs them.

---

Conversation

Irene Choi (review): The structure looks good. Please keep module interfaces minimal until we lock ENG-4829. Two requests: (1) add a root-level `CONTRIBUTING.md` with basic workflow (fmt/validate), (2) ensure each module has consistent variable names (`name`, `tags`, `environment`). Also, can we avoid committing provider version constraints until Sahana weighs in?

Bruno Silva (author): Ack on both. I’ll add CONTRIBUTING and normalize variable naming. Provider pins will come in a separate PR once we align on versions.

Victor Alvarez (review): On boundaries: I’d prefer `modules/vpc` includes route tables/NAT because otherwise customers wire it wrong. But agree we shouldn’t finalize defaults here. Suggest adding a short “module responsibilities” section in each README so it’s clear what is intentionally omitted.

Bruno Silva (author): Good call. Added “Responsibilities / Non-goals” to each module README and called out that routing/NAT defaults are TBD.

Sahana Iyer (review): CI workflow: can we run `terraform validate` for modules too? Even if they don’t create resources, we can at least validate syntax. Also, add a step to verify `README.md` exists per module (you mentioned it; I don’t see enforcement yet).

Bruno Silva (author): Updated workflow to validate modules (where init/validate is safe) and added a small script to fail if README is missing.

Hanae Suzuki (review): Security nit: please avoid any default that implies public exposure. In the example, make sure subnets are clearly labeled private/public and we don’t accidentally attach an IGW to the “private” route table. Also, for IAM placeholder, avoid granting any wildcard permissions even in examples.

Bruno Silva (author): Updated the example to clearly separate public vs private route tables (private remains placeholder until NAT work lands) and kept IAM module as a non-functional scaffold (no permissions attached).

Markus Klein (review): From field POV, examples matter. Can we add a `examples/README.md` that states “alpha / not supported” and tells SE what inputs they typically need (CIDR, AZs, tags)? Also, please add outputs in the example that match what the installer will likely ask for so we can start building a checklist.

Bruno Silva (author): Added `examples/README.md` with alpha disclaimer and typical inputs. Also added placeholder outputs with comments that they’ll be wired to installer preflight expectations later.

Connor O'Brien (review): Request: add a `CHANGELOG.md` placeholder and note that semver/release process is coming later. Helps set expectations.

Context: As part of the Guided Onboarding + First Production Launch checklist, we want customers to have an easy, copy/pasteable path to set spend guardrails and get alerted before hitting usage caps. This PR adds Terraform examples for (1) Redwood budgets (soft + hard caps) with threshold notifications and (2) quota + rate-limit alerting via exported metrics. The intent is to link these snippets from the checklist steps ("Set budgets/quotas" + "Configure alerts") and the docs IA updates. Scope: new examples under examples/budgets-alerts/ plus a small README refresh that clarifies how budgets behave (soft vs hard), recommended thresholds (80/95/100), and common onboarding gotchas (usage dashboard lag; alert delivery verification). Non-goals: no provider changes, no new resources; these examples assume existing redwood_* resources and are designed to run as-is with minimal variables. Testing: fmt + validate in CI; manual apply tested against a sandbox tenant (hosted) with email notification channel and a simulated usage spike.
Elliot Price (review): README is good, but can we make the checklist linkage explicit? E.g. call out that this is for the "Budgets & alerts" checklist step and include a short "What to do after apply" section (verify notification delivery, where to see it in Console).

Motivation: operator teams reported recurring tfstate drift between GPU nodepool leases and IAM attachments after upgrades; existing ad-hoc repair scripts were brittle. This PR introduces a reusable terraform module (tf-state-sanitizer) and small shim changes to existing gpu_pool and iam modules to canonicalize state, collapse duplicate grant entries, and add an idempotent dry-run migration path. The goal is to provide an automated, safe migration that can be run as part of Private installer upgrades or as a one-off reconciliation step with minimal downtime. What changed: 1) new modules/state-sanitizer: Go-based import helper and a thin terraform wrapper that computes a canonical lease index for each gpu subpool, detects duplicate role attachments, and emits an ordered import plan; 2) gpu_pool module: add optional lease_index output and stable import_id to avoid create/destroy churn; 3) iam module: normalize principal identifiers and replace repeated aws_iam_role_policy_attachment resources with a single consolidated resource guarded by lifecycle ignore_changes until migration completes; 4) upgrade hooks: installer chart post-upgrade job that can run the sanitizer in dry-run or apply mode with a built-in checkpoint so the operation is resumable; 5) test infra: acceptance tests under perf-canary and a mock VPC local runner for CI. Migration plan (short): run sanitizer in dry-run on a staging cluster, review the generated import plan, run with --apply for a rolling reconciliation, verify workloads by checking node labels/leases and IAM audit logs. Rollback: sanitizer writes a checkpoint file to object storage and creates a tfstate snapshot tag; uninstall path includes a rollback tool that replays the snapshot. Checklist: [x] module design doc attached, [x] unit tests for import helper, [x] acceptance tests in perf-canary, [x] upgrade hook added to installer helm chart, [x] Linear tickets created. Risks & mitigations: changes touch tfstate manipulation; we added a dry-run mode, snapshot/restore, and strict preflight checks (owner lock, minimal quorum) to reduce blast radius. Related: ENG-7321 (migration plan), SUP-1982 (customer-reported drift), design doc: /docs/tf-state-sanitizer.md. Merge outcome: merged via squash with branch protections and post-merge promotion to release candidate channel.
Diego Alvarez: This looks safe overall but we should gate apply mode behind a cluster-wide lock. Can we add an owner-lock preflight?
Maya Chen: Added owner-lock to the importer; the tool now aborts if it cannot acquire the lock. Updated description to note quorum requirement.
Priya Nair: Please add an explicit rollback path in docs showing commands to restore tfstate snapshot — customers will ask for this.
Maya Chen: Docs updated with rollback reproduction steps and example snapshot restore commands. Added acceptance test to validate restore flow.
Lars Meinhardt: CI failed initially on the mock VPC runner (timeout). Re-ran; tests passed in rerun. Approving on green.
CI Bot: perf-canary/test-state-sanitizer succeeded on rerun (12m, 38s).
Added state-sanitizer terraform module to safely migrate and reconcile GPU pool leases and IAM grant duplication. Includes dry-run mode, upgrade hooks, and rollback snapshots. Recommended to run dry-run in staging before applying in production.

Motivation: under steady-state continuous-batching workloads we observed long-tail starvation of low-priority ticket groups when high-throughput KV-heavy requests held slots indefinitely. This PR introduces an adaptive "probation thawer" that temporarily promotes a small number of probation slots for starving lanes and uses a timed thaw-and-evaluate window to re-balance fairness without harming overall throughput. Changes include: adaptive probation counters per queue, time-sliced thaw windows with randomized jitter to avoid synchronization, soft-priority decay to prevent permanent promotions, and a KV-prefetch hint integration so thawed slots can warm KV pins when applicable. The description below is a single continuous string containing context, checklist, testing notes and rollout plan. Implementation summary: - add probation state machine to queue metadata (probation_enter_ts, probation_votes) - coordinator exposes a new throttle_sample endpoint used by the autoscaler to get probation pressure metrics - thaw windows are small (default 15ms) and capped per-cohort to limit tail amplification - probation promotions expire after N successful completions or T ms without improvement (configurable) - KV-prefetch hints are added to the scheduler handoff path so thawed requests can request KV warmups before kernel dispatch. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-3274) - [x] deterministic unit tests for state transitions - [x] integration tests in local perf-lab harness - [x] load tests against cohort mix (low-priority background + high-priority serving) - [x] docs and config defaults updated Rollout plan: start with canary in dedicated cluster region, monitor p95/p99 latency for low-priority lanes and overall throughput, enable auto-disable if global tail increases by >7%. Related work: builds on earlier admission/backoff changes (refs: ENG-2103) and KV-pin warmup experiments.
Diego: Can we avoid global amplification when multiple cohorts enter thaw simultaneously? Suggest randomized backoff per cohort.
Author (Maya): Added jittered thaw windows and cohort caps; see probation_thawer.go lines ~120-165. Also added a coordinator metric for concurrent_thaw_count.
Priya: Need a safety toggle to fully disable probation promotions from config for emergency rollback.
Author (Maya): Added config flag 'probation.enabled' and included runtime guard in coordinator startup path. Documented in ops page.
Noah: Approve after minor docs tweak to include guidance for when to bump probation thresholds.
Introduces an adaptive 'probation thawer' scheduler mechanism that reduces starvation of low-priority queues under continuous batching. Improves fairness for background lanes with minimal impact to high-priority throughput. Configurable via configs/defaults.yaml; disabled by default for existing clusters. See docs/ops/probation-thawer.md for operational guidance.
Experiment mix: 70% high-priority KV-heavy, 30% low-priority background
Low-priority p95 latency: reduced from 420ms to 85ms (canary, median of 5 runs)
System overall throughput: -0.8% on token/sec compared to baseline (within safety window)
Tail safety: global p99 unchanged within 1.5% (monitoring threshold)
KV warmup hit-rate on thawed slots: +32% (reduced cold-pin misses)
Default config keeps probation disabled; enable via probation.enabled=true for canaries
Watch metrics: metrics.probation.concurrent_thaw_count, metrics.probation.promotions, metrics.kv.warmup_hits
Emergency rollback: set probation.enabled=false and restart coordinator process - change is guarded to be safe to toggle at runtime
Suggested initial thresholds: thaw_window_ms=15, probation_max_promotions=3, thaw_cohort_cap=2

payload.body:
Title: Add optional VPN/DX placeholders and routing hooks (no provider assumptions)

Context
Design partners keep asking, "Where do we plug in our VPN / Direct Connect / Transit Gateway routes?" Our alpha modules intentionally avoid building VPN/DX/TGW resources (provider + enterprise topology specific), but we also need to stop forcing customers to fork the VPC module just to add a couple of routes.

This PR adds:
- Stable outputs for route table IDs and subnet groupings so customers can attach routes externally (VPN/TGW/DX) without modifying our modules.
- Optional, generic "routing hooks" inputs for adding additional routes to the private/public route tables when the target is an ID we already know (e.g., a pre-existing TGW attachment, VGW, or NAT instance) while keeping the module free of assumptions about what creates that target.
- Docs + example showing recommended patterns (customer-owned networking module creates VPN/TGW, then consumes our outputs to add routes).

Scope / non-goals
- NOT creating aws_vpn_gateway / aws_customer_gateway / aws_dx_gateway / aws_ec2_transit_gateway or attachments.
- NOT standardizing on any single enterprise connectivity topology.
- NOT attempting to manage propagation/associations for TGW route tables (customers vary widely).

Implementation details
1) New outputs in modules/vpc
- outputs for:
  - vpc_id
  - private_route_table_ids_by_az
  - public_route_table_ids_by_az
  - private_subnet_ids_by_az
  - public_subnet_ids_by_az
  - intra_subnet_ids_by_az (if enabled)
  - azs

These are intentionally shaped for common enterprise patterns (per-AZ route tables) and are stable identifiers for external modules.

2) Optional route injection (generic)
- Added variable extra_routes with schema:
  - destination_cidr (string)
  - route_table_scope ("private"|"public"|"intra")
  - target_type ("tgw"|"vgw"|"eni"|"nat_instance"|"gateway")
  - target_id (string)

We keep it as a simple switch to set the right aws_route attribute (transit_gateway_id, gateway_id, network_interface_id, etc.) without creating the target resource.

Important: We validate that only one supported target type is set per route entry and we hard-fail on "unknown" to avoid silent misroutes.

3) Example + docs
- Added examples/private-vpc-with-customer-connectivity/
  - shows a placeholder customer module creating a TGW attachment (commented/pseudocode) and then adding routes via our outputs.
  - callouts for: DNS expectations, ECR endpoints, and making sure installer can reach required services.

Why this shape?
- SE feedback (Markus/Colin): customers want a clear "attachment point" without us dictating whether it’s VPN, DX, TGW, or something else.
- Security feedback (Marcus): we should not implicitly open egress or create VPN constructs; keep connectivity owned by customer networking team.
- Ops feedback (Nina): avoid forcing route table recreation (high risk) and avoid any behavior that changes NAT strategy.

Files changed (high level)
- modules/vpc/variables.tf (extra_routes input + validation)
- modules/vpc/outputs.tf (route table + subnet outputs)
- modules/vpc/routes.tf (optional aws_route resources per scope)
- examples/private-vpc-with-customer-connectivity/main.tf
- examples/private-vpc-with-customer-connectivity/README.md
- docs/extension-points.md (new section: Customer connectivity / VPN / DX hooks)

Testing
- terraform fmt / validate
- tflint
- checkov (no new high severity findings)
- integration test harness: ephemeral VPC apply/destroy (routing hooks exercised with dummy ENI target in test)

Notes for reviewers
- I intentionally did not add any new required variables. Default behavior is unchanged.
- Outputs are additive; no renames.
- Route injection only creates routes when extra_routes is non-empty.

Review conversation (abridged)

Markus Klein (Solutions Eng): Can we make the docs explicit that this is where DX/VPN plugs in? Our pilots keep asking for "Direct Connect support" and we need to explain we support it via hooks, not by creating it.
Bruno Silva (author): Yep. Added a short section in docs/extension-points.md and an example directory. Also added wording: "customer-owned connectivity resources".

Victor Alvarez (Networking): output names should be consistent with endpoints module naming. Prefer *_ids_by_az and also provide azs output so consumers don’t have to recompute.
Bruno Silva: Updated outputs to *_ids_by_az and added azs.

Marcus Lin (Security): extra_routes target_type list is OK, but make sure we validate we don’t accidentally set multiple route target fields. Also, call out that we don’t manage route propagation.
Bruno Silva: Added input validation and README note. No propagation logic.

Nina Petrova (Private Deployments): Please ensure we don’t force route table replacement for existing users when they adopt this module version.
Bruno Silva: Confirmed in plan output: additive only. No diff unless extra_routes set.

Irene Choi (Infra): CI runtime increased by ~2 min from the new integration test case. Fine for now but keep it minimal.
Bruno Silva: Acknowledged; kept it to a single route injection case.

CI
- redwood-terraform / validate: pass
- tflint: pass
- checkov: pass
- integration-tests (ephemeral-vpc): pass

Merge
- Squashed and merged to main.
- Follow-up: I’ll open a small PR to add a snippet to the main VPC module README linking to docs/extension-points.md (missed in this PR).

payload.body:
Introduces a progressive burn-rate controller to smooth tenant reservation consumption under transient load spikes and a tenant fairness mapper that converts utilization deltas into time-windowed fairness weights. Adds telemetry and dashboard panels for burn-rate and backlog histograms.
Context and motivation: Several teams reported uneven degradation during short, repeated microbursts where tenants exhausted their reserved capacity quickly and triggered large-scale fallbacks. This PR implements a 'progressive burn-rate controller' to intentionally rate-limit reservation consumption on a soft schedule and a 'tenant fairness mapper' to translate observed utilization deltas into time-windowed fairness weights used by the allocator. The goals are to: 1) reduce tail impact of short bursts, 2) preserve throughput guarantees for long-running steady tenants, and 3) provide observability into the pace at which tenants are spending reserved capacity.

Summary of changes: single-continuous description below includes design, checklist, commits, files changed, test/CI, review thread, and merge outcome.

Design highlights: - progressive burn-rate controller (pkg/autoscaler/burnrate.go): maintains a per-tenant burn ladder with exponentially decaying windows. Each tenant has a burn_rate_score that increments on reservation consumption and decays over time; when score crosses soft thresholds we apply a progressively stricter local throttle rather than an immediate hard deny. This is tunable with tenant-level policy knobs (min_window_ms, decay_alpha, soft_slopes). - tenant fairness mapper (pkg/autoscaler/fairness_mapper.go): consumes utilization snapshots + burn_rate_score and emits a fairness_weight timeseries used by the slot allocator. Uses a configurable mapping profile so product teams can prefer latency-sensitive tenants over batch workloads. - telemetry (pkg/telemetry/metrics.go + dashboards): adds metrics: redwood_burn_score{tenant}, redwood_burn_throttle_factor{tenant,level}, redwood_backlog_histogram_bucketed{region,pool}, redwood_fairness_weight{tenant}. Included a sample Grafana dashboard JSON and alert tweaks to avoid noisy paging when burn_score spikes are short. - config & charts: helm chart values for Dedicated to enable controller and default mapping profile (charts/dedicated/values.yaml). - docs: design doc (docs/design/burnrate_controller.md) with tuning guidance and examples of mapping profiles.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed by SRE and Serving runtime leads (ENG-1729) - [x] Unit tests for burn ladder logic and mapping profiles - [x] Integration test that simulates microburst pattern and confirms smooth degradation vs baseline - [x] Telemetry panels added and validated in staging - [x] Backwards-compatible default config for clusters that don't opt-in

Commits (high-level): ["init: add burn ladder data structure and basic decay loop", "feat(autoscaler): progressive burn-rate controller + policy knobs", "feat(autoscaler): tenant fairness mapper and mapping profiles", "telemetry: export burn_score/throttle_factor/fairness_weight metrics", "charts: add burnrate controller toggles to dedicated values", "docs: add design and tuning guide", "test: integration microburst scenario and histogram assertions", "fix: address flake in allocation test by increasing clock tick sensitivity"]

Changed files (high level): - pkg/autoscaler/burnrate.go - pkg/autoscaler/fairness_mapper.go - pkg/autoscaler/controller.go (wire-up) - pkg/telemetry/metrics.go - charts/dedicated/values.yaml - docs/design/burnrate_controller.md

Testing and benchmarks: - Unit test coverage: burn ladder edge cases, mapping profiles and weight normalization. - Integration: synthetic microburst replay (5s bursts, 10s gap, 100 tenants) against a simulated Dedicated pool. Result: reduction in tenant-induced cascading fallbacks by ~68% (measured as number of fallback events per 1k bursts). - Perf: p95 inference latency on steady tenants unchanged within noise (+0.2ms). CPU overhead: controller uses a lightweight tick-driven sampler with amortized cost ~0.7% CPU on 96-core fleet control-plane nodes in staging. - Telemetry pipeline: added a sampled histogram for backlog; storage cost estimate ~+6% cardinality at 1h retention.

CI summary: - build: pass - unit tests: pass - integration tests: initial run failed (flake in allocation tests), fixed by commit that increased test clock granularity - e2e perf job: pass (bench scenario: 2000 requests/s with mixed tenants) - linters: pass

Review conversation (truncated): - Liam O'Connor (review): "Nice approach. Two asks: (1) can we make decay_alpha per-tenant (not global) and expose it in the policy? (2) we should guard the telemetry tag cardinality — consider sampling or bucketing. Also add a simulation that shows worst-case fairness drift." - Aarti: "Implemented per-tenant override (defaults to cluster profile). Added a sampled_burn_score metric and histogram buckets to control cardinality. Added worst-case drift sim in integration tests." - Priya Shah: "Can you ensure the controller doesn't affect dedicated pool autoscaler decisions? We want allocation scaling to remain purely demand-driven." - Aarti: "Confirmed: controller only throttles reservation consumption rate; it does not change capacity signals sent to the autoscaler. Added an integration check to validate this." - Marco Liu: "Small nit: rename burn_score -> burn_rate_score for clarity in metrics. Also please add a short note in runbook about troubleshooting noisy alerts." - Aarti: "Renamed metric and added runbook section." - Marco: Approve. - Priya: Approve. - Liam: Approve after small doc clarification.

Operational concerns and mitigations: - Risk: mis-tuned soft thresholds could overly penalize bursty but legitimate tenants. Mitigation: controller is opt-in per pool; default profile is permissive, and policy supports per-tenant overrides. Added a rollout plan in docs with canary on 10% of dedicated fleets and close monitoring for alert noise. - Risk: metric cardinality explosion. Mitigation: sample tenant-level burn_score at 1/10th rate and bucket numeric score into coarse bins by default. Users can opt-in to full resolution.

Migration and rollout: - Default state: controller disabled on existing clusters. - Enablement path: customers can toggle via charts/dedicated/values.yaml (enableBurnController: true) then tune mapping_profile. - Suggested rollout: staging -> 10% canary (non-critical tenants) -> 50% -> full, with alerts configured to detect any increase in fallback rate or unexpected latency shifts.

Merge outcome: merged via squash on 2026-02-10 after green CI and approvals. Backout plan documented in runbook (docs/design/burnrate_controller.md#runbook).
payload.title: Progressive burn-rate controller and tenant fairness mapper

Context: Private installs require stricter boundaries between tenant GPU pools, stable IAM role bindings, and a hardened bastion for maintenance. This PR splits responsibilities into three small modules (gpu-pool, iam-immutable-roles, peered-bastion) and adds a lightweight tfstate importer to migrate existing monolithic state into per-tenant slices. Motivation: reduce blast radius when modifying pool scheduling labels, make IAM role upgrades non-destructive for bound resources, and simplify network egress controls via an optional peered bastion. Changes: 1) modules/gpu-pool: new module that exposes nodeAffinity, taints, autoscalerProfile, and a short-lived lease label so autoscaler/tenant leases can be reconciled without rewriting state; 2) modules/iam: immutable-role module that provisions roles with stable logical IDs and a binding resource that is deliberately additive-only (prevents accidental role replacement during plan/apply); 3) modules/bastion: peered-bastion module that supports VPC peering or VPN attachment for private installs and optional host allowlist via security groups; 4) scripts/tfstate-importer: bash helper that automates terraform import into new per-tenant backends and emits an audit log for each import operation; 5) examples and integration tests for the importer and IAM reconciliation. Migration plan checklist: [x] smoke import for one test tenant; [x] validate plan shows only additions for IAM bindings; [x] run integration tests in staging; [x] run a controlled rollout across two clusters; [ ] monitor cost/latency for 48h after migration. Related: Linear ENG-9876 (private install hardening), SUP-821 (customer tenant migration). Notes: importer is intentionally idempotent but requires operator approval for each tenant; the immutable-role design means role updates create new roles side-by-side and a short TTL garbage collector is provided in the module to clean orphaned role ARNs after manual verification. Documentation: scripts/tfstate-importer/README.md contains step-by-step migration commands and a dry-run mode. Why this is different: instead of moving tfstate boundaries wholesale, we introduce a focused importer workflow plus additive IAM bindings to minimize disruption during upgrades and to keep GPU pool changes localized.
Jared Park: Reviewed the importer script, suggested stricter validation for backend configs - resolved by adding a backend checksum and explicit confirmation prompt.
Sven Olsson: Asked about rollback semantics if import partially succeeds - added a --dry-run and a rollback helper that restores state from a snapshot; confirmed in tests.
Priya Kapoor: Security review: requested host-restriction option on bastion and an allowlist for admin CIDRs - added security_group_allowed_cidrs variable and updated README.
Maya Chen (author): Addressed comments and pushed follow-ups; ran live migration on staging cluster and reported no destructive IAM diffs.
Introduce modular GPU pool module with tenant-scoped labels and taint mapping
Add immutable IAM role module to avoid destructive role replacements during upgrades
Introduce peered bastion module with host allowlist for private installs
Add tfstate-importer tooling and integration tests to migrate monolithic state to per-tenant backends
Step 1: Run scripts/tfstate-importer/tenant_import.sh --dry-run for target tenant and review generated audit log
Step 2: Apply gpu-pool and iam modules in staging using per-tenant backend and confirm 'plan' shows only additions
Step 3: Promote to prod with small batch of tenants and monitor IAM/serving logs for 1 hour
Rollback: If imports fail mid-way, use terraform state pull from snapshot and scripts/tfstate-importer/rollback_snapshot.sh to restore state before repeating import

Context and motivation: Customers running private deployments on aarch64 hardware reported failures when performing upgrades in strict air-gapped environments where vendor kernel modules and UBI overlay layers were not present in the offline bundle. This PR adds an opinionated UBI overlay tailored for aarch64, an offline reprovisioning hook for kernel-module assets, Terraform helpers to provision registry ACL metadata for mirror endpoints, and Helm/installer tweaks to wire the components together. Summary of changes: Commit 1: add aarch64/ubi-overlay/ layout and package metadata (manifest.json + provenance), Commit 2: implement reprovision hook that runs during offline runtime upgrade to inject vendor kernel modules into the runtime squashed overlay, Commit 3: terraform/modules/registry-acl: new module to create mirror ACL objects (signed metadata) and provider examples, Commit 4: installer/helm: values and chart template changes to mount overlay and trigger hook, Commit 5: tests: add a lightweight smoke test that verifies overlay mount and module presence on aarch64 QEMU image. Files changed (high level): - aarch64/ubi-overlay/manifest.json and layer contents (added vendor-modules.tar.gz, overlay metadata), - installer/helm/templates/overlay-configmap.yaml (new), installer/hooks/reprovision-kmods.sh (new executable), - terraform/modules/registry-acl/main.tf and examples/README.md (new), - scripts/make-offline-bundle.sh (update to include signed lockfile and manifest checks), - tests/smoke/aarch64-overlay-smoke.sh (new). Testing and CI: Ran full CI on main with the new smoke test included; initial CI run failed due to missing gpg key verification in bundle script; fix pushed and CI rerun passed. Upgrade/rollback behavior: reprovision hook is idempotent and adds a reversible marker file (/var/lib/redwood/overlay-reprovisioned). The helm chart includes a rollbackCleanupJob that removes injected modules on chart rollback to avoid cruft and kernel mismatches. Response (Marisol): "We only materialize modules from signed archive verified against the lockfile; signature check added to hook." - Lena: "Terraform module needs clearer IAM example for S3-style mirror ACLs." Response: "Added example and documented minimal IAM policy in examples/README.md." - Rahul: "Smoke test should run under QEMU user-mode; CI job looks heavy." If you want a follow-up, I can split the terraform module into a separate repo to make it consumable by ops teams outside of the installer repository.
Adds UBI-based overlay for aarch64 air-gapped images, kernel module reprovisioning hooks for offline upgrades, and Terraform support for private-registry ACL provisioning. Includes smoke test and signed lockfile for offline bundles.

Summary: This PR adds the Terraform wiring needed to deploy perf-canary safely: (1) a dedicated service account with least-privilege IAM, (2) secret storage + access policies for canary auth, and (3) environment/region guardrails to prevent accidental fanout. This unblocks the perf-canary Helm chart rollout by providing a constrained identity that can call internal inference endpoints and emit metrics without broad access.

Context: perf-canary runs synthetic workloads against internal inference endpoints and publishes performance metrics/alerts. We need a dedicated identity for the canary deployment (no shared runtime/telemetry SA), scoped to: read-only inference invoke, write-only metrics, and read-only baseline artifact access. We also need to store the canary auth token / client secret in managed secret storage and allow only the canary workload identity to decrypt/access it.

What changed (high level): - Introduced perf_canary_service_account module (GCP) and associated IAM bindings. - Added Secret Manager secrets for perf-canary auth material and a KMS policy to allow decrypt only by the canary SA. - Added explicit IAM conditions and narrowed resource scopes (project/namespace/cluster) to avoid granting broad viewer/editor roles. - Added a small set of env/region toggles (enable_perf_canary, perf_canary_regions allowlist) and validation to avoid enabling canary in all regions by mistake.

IAM scope (intended): - Inference invoke: allow calling internal inference gateway (limited audience/scope; no general service-to-service). - Metrics: allow write to telemetry ingest (no read, no admin). - Baselines: allow read from baseline bucket/prefix only (no list on entire bucket, no write). - Secrets: allow access to perf-canary secret versions only (no create/delete; no wildcard).

Operational notes: - Secret rotation: this PR creates the secret resources and IAM; rotation procedures remain in the infra runbook. - Rollback: disabling perf-canary is done by setting enable_perf_canary=false in the environment tfvars; IAM resources remain but are inert.

Testing/verification: - terraform validate + fmt - terraform plan for staging-us-east and prod-us-east: no unexpected diffs outside perf-canary resources - Manual check: SA cannot list other secrets or buckets; can read only the one secret and baseline prefix.

Risk: Medium. IAM changes are production-impacting; however this PR only adds new bindings/resources (no removal of existing roles). Reviewers: please sanity-check IAM conditions and secret access boundaries.

Follow-ups: - Consider adding org-policy constraint to block secret access from non-approved service accounts (separate PR) - If we move baselines from GCS to config service, we should replace the bucket read binding accordingly.

Refs: Linear ENG-4879 (Deployment helm + terraform), ENG-4872 (MVP), ENG-4878 (alerting routing). Jira INT-2213 (service account permissions request).
Logan Wright (review): Can we ensure the canary can only write metrics and not query/modify telemetry configs? The role binding should be the ingest-only role, not project-level monitoring editor.
Nadia Rahman (author): Good catch. Updated modules/telemetry/iam_ingest.tf to bind roles/telemetry.ingestWriter (custom) instead of monitoring.editor. Also added an IAM condition restricting the audience to the ingest endpoint service.
Rafael Mendes (review): For INT-2213 we need to be explicit about what the canary can call. Is the inference invoke permission limited to the internal gateway only? Please avoid granting generic service invoker on all endpoints.
Nadia Rahman (author): Yep. Swapped to a per-service invoker binding on the inference-gateway-canary endpoint only (and added a TODO for private deployments where this will differ). No wildcard serverless invoker remains.
Sean Gallagher (review): Please add a kill switch / guardrail so we don't accidentally enable in every region during rollout. Also can we cap to us-east only for prod by default?
Nadia Rahman (author): Added enable_perf_canary boolean + perf_canary_regions allowlist with validation. Prod defaults are empty allowlist (disabled) until explicitly set in tfvars; staging set to ["us-east"].
Allison Grant (review): Secret access: please ensure only get access to this one secret and not list. Also prefer to deny secret destroy from the canary SA.
Nadia Rahman (author): Secret IAM binding is roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor on the single secret resource only; no list permission. Canary SA has no permissions to create/update/destroy secrets. Only platform-infra group retains admin.
Omar El-Sayed (review): Can we export the SA email + secret resource name as outputs for the Helm chart wiring? Want to avoid copy/paste in values files.
Nadia Rahman (author): Added outputs: perf_canary_service_account_email, perf_canary_secret_resource_id, perf_canary_baseline_bucket, perf_canary_baseline_prefix.
Logan Wright (approval): Looks good after role tightening. Thanks for adding the allowlist validation.
Rafael Mendes (approval): Approved; inference invoke is appropriately constrained now.
Sean Gallagher (approval): Approved. Guardrails are in place; proceed with staging rollout.
Adds Terraform resources for perf-canary service account, secret storage, and least-privilege IAM bindings; introduces enable flag and region allowlist to prevent accidental global rollout.
