Motivation: Customers deploying Redwood Private in stricter regulated environments requested a smaller Ubuntu-based runtime bundle (22.04) optimized for constrained air-gapped environments and an improved, modular vendor indexer that supports incremental delta snapshots. This PR introduces a slim Ubuntu 22.04 runtime bundle profile, refactors the offline image index format to be modular (index shards + manifest), and updates the Terraform registry-replication module to optionally use the new index format for faster syncs and reduced bandwidth.

Summary of changes: added ubuntu-22.04-slim runtime bundle (compressed tar.gz, stripped docs, minimal kernel modules), implemented index-shard format v1 for the airgap indexer (index-manifest.json + shard-<n>.json), added dedupe layer to offline image packaging, updated Helm chart to expose registry-proxy.enabled and mirror.oci settings, extended the installer "airgap-apply" flow to accept --index-shard flag and to perform atomic apply using snapshot fencing. Terraform: added optional parameter "use_index_shards" and optimized S3 upload concurrency for large delta snapshots. Rollback/upgrade: introduced preflight checks and a new rollback hook that validates bundle signature before applying a rollback.

How to test locally: follow docs/airgap/ubuntu-22.04/README.md (included). Example: ./bin/airgap-tool build --profile ubuntu-22.04-slim --index-shard-size 200MB && ./bin/airgap-tool pack --output /tmp/airgap-slim.tar.gz. Deploy to a k3s lab cluster with registry-mirror enabled and run ./scripts/e2e/airgap-sync.sh. CI includes an airgap-registry-indexer-e2e job that exercises shard creation and registry replication.

Upgrade notes: upgrade path is backwards compatible. Default behaviour remains the monolithic index unless --use-index_shards=true is set. For customers using the Dedicated registry replication Terraform module, enabling shards can reduce peak bandwidth but requires the newer airgap-tool >= 0.28.0. Please follow the migration checklist in docs/airgap/migration.md.

Checklist: - [x] Add ubuntu-22.04-slim bundle recipe and packaging pipeline - [x] Implement index-shard manifest and shard creation tools - [x] Helm changes for registry-proxy and mirror settings - [x] Terraform module parameter and docs - [x] E2E test for shard-based replication - [x] Package signing and verification step added

Related work: builds on prior airgap improvements (see SUP-1337 and ENG-6120) and complements the offline delta snapshot work in ENG-5830.

Notes: kept the new index format intentionally simple (manifest + shards) so on-prem mirrored registries can stream shards sequentially and resume. The packaging script also deduplicates blobs across bundles which reduced typical bundle size by ~12% in our benchmark sample.
Miguel Torres (2026-02-27): Can you add a switch to disable shard-based restore for customers who can't stream?
Asha Kapoor (2026-02-27): Added --disable-shard-restore flag to airgap-apply and documented it in migration.md
Dana Li (2026-02-28): Terraform change looks good but please add an acceptance test for S3 uploads (low-risk).
Asha Kapoor (2026-02-28): Added acceptance test harness and marked it slow in CI, gated by env var.
Evan Schultz (2026-02-29): e2e was flaky initially; observed race in shard_writer when parallelizing writes. Please confirm fix.
Asha Kapoor (2026-03-01): Fixed race by moving shard write queue into a single writer goroutine and added a stress test. CI rerun passed.
Miguel Torres (2026-03-01): Approved after CI green and docs updated.
Release Manager (2026-03-01): Merged via squash-merge.
Add a new Ubuntu 22.04 slim airgap bundle profile, modular index shard format for faster incremental syncs, Helm support for registry-proxy and OCI mirror settings, Terraform registry-replica improvements, and new rollback signature verification hook.
Operators enabling shard-based replication should ensure airgap-tool >= 0.28.0 and set S3 endpoint lifecycle rules to keep shard manifests for the expected window. If using on-prem S3-compatible storage, enable range requests for shard downloads.

Title: Stratum Rotor: staged promotion engine with cohort-aware holdpoints and rollback playbook

Summary: Adds a new promotion engine (stratum_rotor) to the rollout subsystem that schedules phased promotions across stratified cohorts (strata). The engine emphasizes deterministic snapshot commits, cohort-aware holdpoints, and an entropy-based stall detector to prevent blind ramping. It also wires a new rollback playbook that integrates offline replay checks and reversible snapshot commits. This PR touches operator, controller, docs, and integration tests.

Motivation and context: We frequently see regressions during aggressive canaries where session stickiness and bursty traffic cause nondeterministic regressions. Current controllers either rely on naive percentage ramps or expensive bisects. Stratum Rotor provides a middle path: staggered strata promotion with session-fencing and silent-window rehearse for low-risk validation, plus an automated rollback advisor when fidelity regressions cross thresholds. Related Linear: ENG-3214, ENG-3491.

What I changed (high level):
- rollout/stratum_rotor.py: core engine implementing strata queues, snapshot commit/abort API, entropy stall detector, and holdpoint logic.
- operator/controllers/promote_controller.go: integrate stratum rotor as an alternate promotion strategy and add license to select strategy via rollout spec.
- docs/rollouts/stratum-rotor.md: architecture, knobs, and recommended release playbook.
- tests/integration/test_stratum_rotor.py: synthetic traffic scenarios (session-coherent, burst, slow-degrade).
- helm/values-rollout.yaml: feature flag and defaults.
- telemetry/metrics.yaml: new metrics (rotor.strata_promote_count, rotor.holdpoint_trigger, rotor.entropy_score, rotor.rollback_advisor_recommend).

Representative commits (squashed on merge):
- 3b6f9a2: initial stratum rotor engine & unit harness
- a47d2c1: integrate engine into operator promote controller; add rollout.strategy.type selector
- 9f2e1b4: add entropy stall detector and silent-window rehearse logic
- 7c5b22f: add offline replay hook & rollback-advisor wiring
- d91e3a0: integration tests + charts + docs

Files changed (illustrative snippets):
- rollout/stratum_rotor.py (new):
  - queue model: strata = [S0, S1, ...] with per-stratum window and session token map
  - commit API: commit_snapshot(snapshot_id) -> atomic on leader, returns checkpoint token
- operator/controllers/promote_controller.go: added switch { case "stratum-rotor": controller = NewStratumRotor(...) }
- docs/rollouts/stratum-rotor.md: contains step-by-step canary template and rollback playbook

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests: full coverage for rotor queueing and commit/abort paths.
- Integration: test suite simulating session-coherent traffic and bursty error injection. One flaky integration (test_replay_race) failed on first CI run; re-ran and passed. CI checks: build, unit, integration, lint, helm-lint (all green on final run).

Review conversation (high level):
- Arjun Patel (code review): "Mechanics look solid. Concern: commit_snapshot is leader-only but we may try leader failover mid-commit. Add idempotency and upgrade tests."
- Maya Chen (author): "Added commit_idempotency checks and leader-failover integration tests in 7c5b22f."
- Sofia Martinez (sre): "Can we expose rotor.entropy_score and add alert guidance?"
- Maya Chen: "Added telemetry and alert guidance docs; default thresholds conservative."
- Ethan Liu (perf): "Batching within strata may increase tail; add a max-batch-latency knob."
- Maya Chen: "Added config knob and documented the tradeoff."
- Final approval: Arjun Patel (approved), Sofia Martinez (approved), Ethan Liu (approved).

Operational playbook (short):
1) Start with rollout.spec.strategy: { type: "stratum-rotor", strata: 4, session_fence: true, silent_window: 60s }
2) Monitor rotor.entropy_score and per-strata error rates; holdpoints will pause promotion automatically if entropy_score > 0.7 or error delta > 1.5x baseline.
3) If holdpoint triggered, the rollback advisor will suggest either: (a) rollback last committed snapshot, or (b) replay sampled traffic to the previous snapshot in offline dry-run.
4) Use "redwoodctl rollout snapshot-rewind <id>" to perform an immediate revert if advisor recommends.

Rollback playbook highlights: reversible snapshot commits are stored in the rollout ledger; aborting a commit triggers a coordinated session drain for the target stratum then swaps checkpoint tokens. Offline replay harness runs against sampled requests captured during silent-window and returns a paired diff report.

Backward compatibility: The new strategy is opt-in via rollout.spec.strategy.type and defaults to existing behavior if not set. No public SDK/API changes.

Performance implications: Small additional memory for per-session fencing maps. We measured median latency impact <0.3ms in internal perf lab with 3 strata; tail under control with max-batch-latency knob. See benchmark-lab notes in the PR.

Follow-ups (future work):
- ENG-3602: cross-region strata affinity to minimize cross-AZ session drift.
- ENG-3710: adaptive strata sizing based on traffic entropy.

Merge: Squash merge performed by Arjun Patel on 2026-02-24. Commit summary: "Add Stratum Rotor staged promotion engine with holdpoints, entropy detector, and rollback playbook (ENG-3214, ENG-3491)". CI green at merge time.

Notes: Drafted with reproducible test seeds to reduce flakiness. Operators and SREs have been notified and a runbook entry added to docs/rollouts/stratum-rotor.md.

Introduce 'Stratum Rotor' rollout engine: deterministic snapshot commits, cohort-aware holdpoints, entropy-based stall detection, session-fenced promotions, and an automated rollback playbook. Backwards compatible; no public API changes.
payload.title: Stratum Rotor: staged promotion engine with cohort-aware holdpoints and rollback playbook

Summary:
This PR introduces a set of Terraform module and state-layout changes to support edge/on-prem Private deployments where GPU nodepools are created and managed by tenant-bound controllers. The goal is to reduce blast radius during changes, enable safe per-edge tfstate checkpoints, and tighten IAM scopes for GPU attach/detach and subnet claims.

Motivation and context:
- Operators deploying Redwood Private into edge racks requested stronger isolation between tenant-managed GPU attachments and cluster-wide networking resources to avoid a single tfstate mutation impacting unrelated tenants.
- Existing monolithic tfstate for private clusters makes upgrades and rollbacks risky in environments with intermittent connectivity and manual approvals.
- Security review flagged overly-broad instance profile/POLICY attachments used by the GPU lifecycle controller; we need narrower IAM roles scoped by edge region and lease ID.

What changed (high level):
1) New modules added under modules/edge:
   - modules/edge/tfstate-anchor: helper that creates a namespaced backend key prefix and optional checksum tag for migration tooling.
   - modules/edge/edge-gpu-attach: idempotent GPU attach/detach resources, uses a delegated role and does not mutate cluster-level subnets.
   - modules/edge/iam-edge-lease: template for per-lease IAM role with assume-role conditions and minimum necessary permissions.
   - modules/edge/network-attachment-shard: lightweight network attachment resources that only hold minimal mapping data and DNS records.
2) Refactor of top-level private deployment layout to place edge attachments under their own tfstate prefixes (configurable by var.edge_tfstate_prefix).
3) Migration shim: scripts/migrate-edge-state.sh and a small terraform provider wrapper to create an initial anchor file and copy state entries into the new prefix with checksums.
4) Helm values: small values.yaml tweak to point the GPU lifecycle controller to the delegated role ARN and to a /metrics endpoint used by the migration job.

Design notes and constraints:
- The tfstate-anchor module purposely keeps state keys tiny and deterministic; it stores a single metadata key per edge that the migrator uses to validate copy/rename operations.
- The iam-edge-lease module restricts permissions to ec2:AttachVolume, ec2:DetachVolume, ec2:DescribeInstances, and iam:PassRole for a single role name pattern; it also scopes by aws:ResourceTag/edge-lease-id when available.
- Network-attachment-shard avoids creating or deleting VPCs: it only creates small route53 records and an attachment mapping resource consumed by the controller.
- The migration script is opinionated: it will transact copies into the new prefix and then mark the anchor as migrated. It can be NO-OPed with --dry-run.

Rollback and upgrade plan:
- We added a migration guard which requires that a successful plan and apply are recorded in the anchor metadata before the controller starts using the new state prefix.
- On failure, the controller retains the old state key and we include a revert path in scripts/migrate-edge-state.sh that will re-copy the original keys back.

Testing and validation performed:
- Unit-style validation: terraform validate on all modules and fmt/lint fixes.
- Integration: ran the migration in a staging edge cluster with three tenant leases, validated controller reconciliations, and simulated a failover where control plane connectivity dropped and came back.
- Security: verified IAM role policies in a dry-run account and ensured no wildcard resource ARNs beyond the necessary instance profiles.
- Performance: confirmed that moving to smaller per-lease state prefixes reduces plan time by ~28% in a 1200-resource state snapshot.

Commits included (summary):
- 1) add edge tfstate-anchor and helper scripts (migrate-edge-state.sh, README)
- 2) introduce edge-gpu-attach, iam-edge-lease, network-attachment-shard modules and document expected usage
- 3) refactor root private layout to accept var.edge_tfstate_prefix and wire delegated role ARNs into values.yaml and examples
- 4) tests: add local integration harness script and add CI lint rule exceptions for the migration scripts

Files changed (high-level):
- modules/edge/tfstate-anchor/main.tf, outputs.tf, README.md
- modules/edge/edge-gpu-attach/{main.tf,variables.tf,iam.tpl}
- modules/edge/iam-edge-lease/{policy.json.tpl,main.tf}
- modules/edge/network-attachment-shard/{main.tf,outputs.tf}
- examples/private/edge-deploy/values.yaml (helm values reference)
- scripts/migrate-edge-state.sh (bash, idempotent)
- README-private-edge.md (migration and rollout documentation)
- tests/integration/edge-migration-ci.yml (CI harness changes)

Small illustrative snippet (edge-gpu-attach/main.tf):
resource "aws_iam_role" "edge_lease_role" {
  name = format("redwood-edge-lease-%s-%s", var.edge_id, var.lease_id)
  assume_role_policy = data.template_file.assume_role.rendered
  tags = { "edge-lease-id" = var.lease_id }
}

Review conversation (abridged into this single body string):
- Liam O'Connor: "Great direction. Two asks: 1) can we avoid any drift windows where both tfstate prefixes are writable? 2) add a rollout checklist for support to follow during live migrations."
- Priya (author): "Answer: migration is copy-only until the anchor is flipped; copy uses object-level checksum verification to avoid partial moves. Added a rollout checklist to README-private-edge.md and a dry-run flag to the script."
- Diego Morales: "IAM template looks good but please run tfsec/opa scans; also consider limiting iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs instead of pattern where reachable."
- Priya: "Addressed: tightened PassRole to specific naming pattern and added tfsec suppressions where the provider forces dynamic names; added CI step to run tfsec on modules/edge."
- Zara Patel: "Minor: docs should call out expected RBAC for the controller pod; otherwise LGTM."
- Final: Approved by reviewers after the tfsec fix and doc addition.

CI and checks:
- terraform fmt/lint: pass
- unit-validate: pass
- tfsec security scan: initially failed (rule AWS018 - iam_passrole_wildcard) on commit 2, fixed in commit 3, rerun passed
- integration/edge-migration-ci: pass (ran a small staging migration)

Release notes (for operators):
- Introduces per-edge tfstate prefixing and new edge modules for GPU attachments and IAM lease roles.
- Migration tooling included; operators must run scripts/migrate-edge-state.sh per edge before upgrading controllers to v1.7.0.

Why this is different from earlier state refactors:
- Prior PRs reorganized large tfstate boundaries for multi-tenant clouds; this PR targets low-connectivity edge/on-prem installations and introduces a small-footprint anchor + copy-based migrator that is safe for manually operated environments.

Merge outcome:
- Squash-merged to main once CI green and approvals obtained. The migration guide and scripts were included in the merge commit.

Followups planned:
- Add a controller-side feature flag to allow automatic switching to the new state prefix after a configurable grace period (ENG-2189).
- Add metrics to track migration success/failure per-edge (ENG-2201).

If you need to reproduce the migration in staging: see README-private-edge.md -> "Migration quickstart" which lists required IAM, S3 backend access, and the dry-run command.
payload.title: Isolate edge-onprem TFState for GPU attachments and narrow IAM scopes

Motivation: Private installs running GPU workloads have produced recurring terraform drift between per-tenant GPU nodepool resources and the central tfstate when clusters are upgraded or when operator-managed labels change. This PR introduces a new gpu_nodepool module built for drift resilience and a lightweight tfstate overlay pattern to isolate tenant-scoped transient resources during rolling upgrades.

What this does (single-line summary): Adds a drift-resistant modules/gpu_nodepool with guarded lifecycle rules, introduces modules/tfstate_overlay for non-destructive overlay state attachments, and templates IAM role bindings to reduce manual reconciliation.

Key changes and rationale:
- New module modules/gpu_nodepool: encapsulates nodepool creation, taint/label reconciliation, and a controlled replacement flow (pre-drain hook + nodegroup swap). Uses lifecycle.prevent_destroy guards on cloud resources that are sensitive to accidental deletes and exposes a replace_strategy variable to opt into safe replace behavior during major upgrades.
- New module modules/tfstate_overlay: implements an optional overlay state mechanism (concatenate state views) so tenant-scoped transient resources (e.g., ephemeral GPU leases, per-tenant NAT allocations) can be kept in an overlay state rather than the canonical cluster tfstate. This limits lock contention and reduces blast radius when rolling back or migrating.
- IAM templating in modules/iam/role_templates.tf: converts several hand-maintained role bindings into parameterized templates to ensure stable role identity between installs and to make drift detection faithful (role ARNs are stable across migration).
- scripts/tfstate-migrate.sh: a migration helper that creates a reversible snapshot and performs a non-blocking copy of selected resources to an overlay state backend. Includes dry-run and rollback modes.
- docs/examples/private/overlay-migration.md: documents step-by-step migration and rollback for on-prem customers with constrained maintenance windows.

Backward compatibility and safety: All changes opt-in by default. The new overlay is disabled unless tfstate_overlay.enabled = true in the root module. Lifecycle.prevent_destroy guards can be relaxed with a flag for operators that prefer destructive redeploys. The migration script is provided for manual, audited migrations.

Testing done: unit Terraform plan tests (mock backends), end-to-end on a staging cluster with a simulated tenant eviction and rollback, and k8s node drain simulation for replacement flow. Linter/format fixed on second commit.

Checklist:
- [x] Module implementation
- [x] Unit plan tests
- [x] e2e staging validation
- [x] Documentation and migration guide
- [x] CI green after lint fix

Related: ENG-10123 (tenant rollout reliability), ENG-10345 (tfstate scale improvements).
Diego: Can we avoid lifecycle.prevent_destroy on the autoscaler role? That broke a previous restore in INT-742. Suggested making it opt-in via variable.
Priya: Reworked to make prevent_destroy gated behind variable and added migration smoke test to ensure restore path works.
Lila: Please add explicit plan diffs in the docs for the overlay switch — operators need to know what to expect during cutover.
Priya: Added examples/overlay-migration.md with concise plan diffs and rollback commands.
Owen: CI failed on tfsec in the first run (hard-coded ARN). After templating roles, tfsec warnings resolved.
Priya: Verified tfsec and added an explicit test in tests/terraform/plans to assert no hard-coded ARNs remain.
Initial gpu_nodepool module and basic tests
Add tfstate_overlay module and migration script
IAM role templating and unit test fixes
Address linter errors reported in CI, format and docs updates
Add e2e regression test and README examples
Introduces a new gpu_nodepool TF module with guarded lifecycle and an optional tfstate overlay mechanism for tenant-scoped transient resources. Includes IAM role templating and a reversible tfstate migration helper. Opt-in via tfstate_overlay.enabled=false by default.

Motivation: private deployments increasingly need to reorganize tfstate across VPC and tenant boundaries when customers add dedicated GPU subnets or migrate tenant networks. Existing migrations are ad-hoc, risky, and require long maintenance windows. This PR introduces a new, opt-in Terraform module (modules/state-stitcher) plus companion TF fragments for nodepool subnet affinity to enable safe, incremental state stitching and an automated migration helper script.

What this PR does (single-line overview): adds a state-stitcher TF module to perform controlled tfstate concatenation/relocation, implements tenant-scoped GPU nodepool -> subnet affinity constructs, provides an idempotent migration helper (scripts/state_migrate.sh), and documents upgrade and rollback procedures for the private installer.

Details: The state-stitcher module exposes an explicit mapping of source tfstates + resource selectors to a target consolidated state. It uses remote state read-only snapshots, verifies resource identity (name/labels/resource_id), and generates a migration plan file that the helper script uses to perform a staged import and state push. For GPU nodepools we add variables and lifecycle rules to bind nodepool resources to tenant_subnet claims so node allocation respects tenancy and AZ affinity.

Migration path: 1) Run terraform plan with modules/state-stitcher in dry-run to produce a migration plan file; 2) Run scripts/state_migrate.sh --dry-run to validate; 3) Run migration with snapshots + automatic rollback point (creates tfstate backup in a customer-specified backend or S3); 4) Smoke test using tests/e2e/private-upgrade-smoke.yaml; 5) Promote to main. The helper supports --rollback-on-failure and will attempt to revert any applied imports if downstream checks fail.

Compatibility and safety: This is opt-in (module not included by default in private-installer charts). The module is compatible with existing module inputs (vpc_id, tenant_id, remote_state_backend). Extensive validation is included: resource identity checks, label/tag assertions, and a pre-migration diff summary. We added unit tests for the module and an e2e smoke for the upgrade path.

Why this is different from previous TF refactors: Instead of just moving tfstate boundaries, this PR provides a declarative, verifiable stitching mechanism with a repeatable helper and documented rollback. It targets GPU tenancy problems specifically (nodepool drift where GPUs were scheduled to shared subnets), and introduces subnet affinity variables and taint-safe lifecycle to reduce migration blast radius.
Marco: Can you walk through the invariants the stitcher checks before performing imports? Aisha: The helper enumerates resource IDs from the source snapshot and checks name + tag patterns and an optional owner label; if any mismatch is found it refuses to continue unless --force is supplied and explicit allow-list is given. Nina: Please add an example showing a two-stage migrate for cross-account tfstate. Aisha: Added example.tfvars and an example in the README. Evan: CI e2e flakes on first run; looks like timing with remote state locking. Aisha: added a sleep + lock-check step in state_migrate.sh and retried CI. Marco: Recommend adding a safety backup step to push snapshots to a separate bucket before imports. Aisha: implemented backup routine and exposed backup_backend optional var. Nina: Approved after docs update. Evan: Approved after adding retry and better logging. CI: first run failed (linting on shellcheck), fixed script to satisfy shellcheck, second run all checks passed. Merge: squash and merge with a short commit message.
Adds 'state-stitcher' Terraform module and GPU nodepool subnet affinity helpers. Includes migration helper script with dry-run and rollback support, e2e upgrade smoke tests, and documentation. Opt-in and non-breaking by default.
medium - touches tfstate; mitigations: dry-run, automated snapshot backups, preflight validators, and rollback option in helper script.
Unit tests for selector logic (tests/unit/test_state_stitcher.tf), shellcheck and shfmt fixes for scripts, ci e2e upgrade smoke validated cluster after migration (nodes with GPUs launched into claimed subnets).
If a customer reports nodepool allocation failures after migration, check the migration plan logs in artifacts (ci/e2e-upgrade), verify tfstate backup exists in the configured backup backend, and run scripts/state_migrate.sh --rollback <plan>. For partial failures inspect logs/lock files in remote state and contact infra oncall.
This PR should be applied to release branches only after running the migration dry-run against a staging snapshot. Do not enable for customers with custom state backends unless backup_backend is configured.
payload.title: Introduce state-stitcher TF module and GPU nodepool subnet affinity

Title: Add VPC Flow Logs defaults + configurable log destinations (CloudWatch/S3)

Context
We’ve had repeated pilot friction around “are we capturing network telemetry by default, and where does it go?” For Redwood Private VPC deployments we want sane, audit-friendly defaults while still letting customers route logs to their own sinks (CloudWatch or S3 today; SIEM forwarding remains out-of-scope for these modules).

This PR introduces a new flow logs submodule and wires it into the example envs:
- Default-on VPC Flow Logs for the created VPC
- Destination options: CloudWatch Logs or S3 (customer-owned bucket supported)
- Explicit retention/lifecycle inputs with conservative defaults and clear cost/audit trade-offs

What changed
1) New module: modules/flow-logs
- Creates aws_flow_log for the VPC
- Supports traffic_type = ALL by default (input override allowed)
- Destination selection:
  - cloudwatch: creates/uses a CloudWatch Log Group + IAM role for vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com
  - s3: writes to S3 bucket ARN (either module-managed or customer-provided)
- Default format uses the AWS recommended extended fields (includes: account-id, vpc-id, subnet-id, instance-id, interface-id, srcaddr/dstaddr, srcport/dstport, protocol, tcp-flags, packets/bytes, start/end, action, log-status)

2) Retention/lifecycle defaults + inputs
- CloudWatch retention default set to 90 days (var.flow_logs_cloudwatch_retention_days) to meet common audit expectations; customers can increase/decrease.
- S3 lifecycle default set to 365 days (var.flow_logs_s3_expiration_days) when using module-managed bucket; if customer supplies their own bucket, lifecycle is not mutated.
- Both destinations support optional KMS encryption:
  - CloudWatch: kms_key_id on the log group
  - S3: bucket SSE-KMS when module manages the bucket; customer buckets are assumed to be already compliant

3) Example updates
- examples/alpha/private-vpc now enables flow logs by default and demonstrates both destination types via commented tfvars blocks.

4) Docs
- README updates for flow logs behavior, destination trade-offs, and “customer-owned bucket” expectations (encryption, access logs, lifecycle handled by customer).

Key implementation notes
- We deliberately do not create CloudWatch subscription filters / SIEM forwarding here. The module outputs log_group_name/log_group_arn (CloudWatch) or bucket_arn/prefix (S3) so customers can attach their own forwarding pipelines.
- For S3 destination we include an optional log_prefix to keep multi-env buckets tidy.
- For CloudWatch destination we create a least-privilege IAM role allowing only logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents to the specific log group.

Illustrative snippet (module interface)
- enable_flow_logs (bool, default true)
- flow_logs_destination (string: "cloudwatch"|"s3", default "cloudwatch")
- flow_logs_cloudwatch_retention_days (number, default 90)
- flow_logs_s3_bucket_arn (string, optional; if set, module will not create bucket)
- flow_logs_s3_expiration_days (number, default 365; only applies to module-managed bucket)
- flow_logs_kms_key_id (string, optional)

Review discussion highlights
- Kevin Osei (Security): requested we avoid silently writing logs into a Redwood-managed bucket by default; agreed. Default destination remains CloudWatch (customer account) and any S3 bucket is explicitly customer-owned unless they opt into module-managed bucket creation.
- Allison Grant (Observability): asked that we use traffic_type=ALL by default and include log-status/action fields to ease troubleshooting. Incorporated.
- Marcus Lin (Security Eng): requested KMS hooks for both CloudWatch and S3 paths and a clear doc note that customer-owned buckets must enforce encryption + least-privilege bucket policy. Added.
- Irene Choi (Infra): raised cost concerns about CloudWatch retention defaults. We kept default at 90 days to align with typical audit requirements for regulated pilots; customers can set lower values, and docs call out expected cost drivers.

CI
- terraform fmt/validate: pass
- tflint: pass
- checkov: pass (initial failure on S3 bucket public access block in the module-managed bucket path; fixed by adding PublicAccessBlock + explicit bucket ownership controls)
- integration tests: skipped (not yet wired for this module in ENG-4860 harness; follow-up ticket to extend ephemeral VPC test to assert flow log resource creation)

Files/areas changed (high level)
- modules/flow-logs/* (new)
- modules/vpc/outputs.tf (expose vpc_id for flow logs wiring in examples)
- examples/alpha/private-vpc/* (enable + tfvars documentation)
- docs/README.md (new section: Flow Logs)

Merge
- Merged via squash to main.

Follow-ups
- ENG-4860: extend ephemeral integration test to assert flow logs creation and destination-specific outputs
- Add optional CloudWatch log group name override (if customers want to centralize logs) after first design partner feedback

Internal: Terraform modules now support region/GPU-type rollout gating with safe defaults (only us-east + A100 enabled) for the provision-to-ready staged rollout.
Title: Add staged rollout variables by region (default: us-east + A100 only)

Context
As part of the provision-to-ready automation staged rollout (ENG-4829), we need Terraform defaults that prevent accidental enablement outside the initial canary scope. The control-plane/orchestrator feature flag can block later in the flow, but we want the IaC layer to enforce guardrails earlier by constraining which regions and GPU SKUs can be provisioned with the new pipeline hooks.

What this PR does
- Introduces module-level rollout gating variables keyed by region and GPU type.
- Defaults the rollout to us-east + A100 only (safe-by-default for week 4 canary).
- Adds consistent outputs that the provisioning orchestrator uses to determine whether a pool is eligible for staged provisioning.
- Updates validation to fail fast on invalid combinations (e.g., unknown region keys, empty allowlists when rollout is enabled).

Changes (high level)
- new variables:
  - staged_rollout_enabled (bool, default: true)
  - staged_rollout_allowed_regions (set(string), default: ["us-east-1"])
  - staged_rollout_allowed_gpu_types (set(string), default: ["a100"])
  - staged_rollout_mode (string, default: "allowlist")
- new locals:
  - effective_rollout_enabled = staged_rollout_enabled && contains(allowed_regions, var.region) && contains(allowed_gpu_types, lower(var.gpu_type))
- new outputs:
  - rollout_eligible (bool)
  - rollout_reason (string; empty when eligible)
- module wiring:
  - dedicated-pool module now passes rollout vars to submodules that emit tags/outputs consumed by the provisioning automation.

Files / modules touched
- modules/dedicated_pool/variables.tf
- modules/dedicated_pool/outputs.tf
- modules/dedicated_pool/main.tf
- modules/fleet_tags/main.tf
- envs/prod/us-east/dedicated/*.tfvars (example)
- docs/dedicated/rollouts.md

Plan output examples
Example A: us-east-1 + A100 (expected eligible)
- Input:
  - region = "us-east-1"
  - gpu_type = "a100"
- Output:
  - rollout_eligible = true
  - rollout_reason = ""
- Tags:
  - redwood:provisioning_rollout = "enabled"

Example B: us-west-2 + A100 (expected blocked by default)
- Input:
  - region = "us-west-2"
  - gpu_type = "a100"
- Output:
  - rollout_eligible = false
  - rollout_reason = "region_not_allowed(us-west-2)"
- Tags:
  - redwood:provisioning_rollout = "disabled"

Example C: us-east-1 + H100 (expected blocked by default)
- Input:
  - region = "us-east-1"
  - gpu_type = "h100"
- Output:
  - rollout_eligible = false
  - rollout_reason = "gpu_type_not_allowed(h100)"

Notes
- The allowlists are intentionally conservative and can be expanded by explicit env tfvars as we move to the next region/SKU.
- This is meant to complement (not replace) the control-plane feature flag / kill switch.

Testing
- terraform fmt / validate
- terraform plan (sample envs)
- added minimal unit-style checks via variable validation blocks (ensures non-empty allowlists in allowlist mode)

Rollout / Ops
- For the first staged rollout, no env overrides are required because defaults already scope to us-east-1 + A100.
- To expand rollout, update env tfvars:
  - staged_rollout_allowed_regions = ["us-east-1", "eu-west-1"]
  - staged_rollout_allowed_gpu_types = ["a100", "h100"]

Checklist
- [x] Safe defaults (constrained rollout)
- [x] Outputs documented for orchestrator consumers
- [x] Plan examples included
- [x] Reviewed with Fleet/Release for rollout sequencing

Review conversation (highlights)
Vanessa Ortiz: Can we ensure the default behavior is restrictive even if someone forgets to pass gpu_type in a module call?
Keiko Yamamoto (author): Yes — gpu_type is already required in dedicated_pool, and I added validation to error if it’s empty/unknown. Also lower() normalization ensures "A100" vs "a100" doesn’t bypass allowlist checks.

Connor O'Brien: Please add a short docs section that explains how this interacts with the control-plane feature flag so release comms don’t overpromise.
Keiko Yamamoto: Added docs/dedicated/rollouts.md with a note: Terraform gating prevents accidental provisioning; control-plane kill switch remains authoritative for runtime behavior.

Nina Petrova: Suggest making rollout_reason stable strings (no freeform) so tooling can key off it.
Keiko Yamamoto: Updated rollout_reason to use stable enums: region_not_allowed(<region>) and gpu_type_not_allowed(<type>) only.

Harish Reddy: Any risk this blocks emergency capacity adds during an incident?
Keiko Yamamoto: Defaults are restrictive, but capacity ops can override allowlists in tfvars with explicit change review. Also, setting staged_rollout_enabled=false preserves previous behavior for emergency cases.

CI
- terraform-lint: pass
- terraform-validate: pass
- docs-check: pass

Merge
Squash merged after approvals; no follow-up changes required for ENG-4829 beyond env-specific overrides as we expand rollout scope.

Motivation: In high-concurrency production traffic we observed occasional starvation of medium-latency requests by very high-parallel KV-heavy tails. This PR introduces a backpressure-aware queue manager and a priority-smoothing policy that reduces starvation risk while preserving batching efficiency. Summary of changes: 1) Introduced a per-queue token regulator that tracks effective inflight weight using a fast-exponentially-weighted moving average (EWMA) of active tokens; queues that exceed a configurable soft-budget accrue backpressure and are temporarily deprioritized for new batch assembly. 2) Added an age-based smoothing factor so items that waited beyond an age threshold get boosted into the next batch (prevents indefinite postponement). 3) Implemented an in-flight KV pin hint: when a request includes heavy KV usage we mark the KV pages as "pinned_hint" for the batch window so subsequent small requests are preferentially scheduled onto different workers (reduces head-of-line blocking). 4) Adaptive tail timeout extension: head-of-line requests that are close to finishing their kv-cache priming can request a micro-extension (configurable up to 30ms) to avoid aborting batches and regressing throughput. 5) Telemetry: new metrics for queue_backpressure_score, queue_age_boosts, kv_pin_conflicts and micro_timeout_extensions to make tuning observable.
Design notes: - The backpressure regulator is lightweight and lock-free in the hot path: it uses per-core counters with periodic aggregation to avoid contention. - Priority smoothing uses a compact two-bin aging counter (fast and slow age buckets) to keep memory overhead low. - The KV pin hint is advisory only; actual KV memory pinning remains managed by the cache; the hint simply influences scheduling to avoid co-locating heavy KV loads.
Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for regulator math and aging boost rules - [x] Integration test in benchmark-lab with mixed KV-heavy and KV-light workloads - [x] CI perf benchmark before/after (95th/99th/mean) - [x] Docs: scheduler tuning guide updated with new knobs - [x] Observability: dashboards and alert rules added
Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind runtime.scheduler.v2 and enabled in Canary pool for 72h before account-wide rollout. Observability thresholds set to detect increased p95 or reduction in throughput and to automatically rollback.
Impact: In internal Canary runs with a 70/30 mix (kv-heavy/kv-light) we saw 8% median latency improvement for kv-light requests, 14% improvement in 99th percentile completion time for mixed workloads, and no measurable loss in aggregate token throughput. Related: ENG-4821 (kv-tail incident post-mortem), ENG-4890 (scheduler tuning spike).
Comment (Miguel): Can we avoid adding a global lock when aggregating per-core counters? Author reply: aggregation is done on a timer and uses atomic add/cas; no global mutex. Comment (Lena): The micro-extension sounds risky for latency SLOs. Author reply: ext is bounded and only applied when the request is already primed; we rolled it out to Canary and observed fewer aborts. Request (Ravi): Add an e2e test that mixes 1k concurrent small requests with 100 long KV requests. Author: added integration in benchmarks and documented results.
Added backpressure-aware queue manager and priority smoothing to reduce starvation of medium-latency requests in mixed KV workloads. New tuning knobs: runtime.scheduler.v2.backpressure_alpha, runtime.scheduler.v2.age_threshold_ms, runtime.scheduler.v2.micro_timeout_ms. Metrics added: scheduler.queue_backpressure_score, scheduler.queue_age_boosts, kv.kv_pin_conflicts.
payload.title: backpressure-aware-queue-manager-and-priority-smoothing-for-continuous-batching

payload.body:
Background and motivation:
This PR introduces two small, composable terraform modules to reduce operational risk during Private installations that use GPU node pools and sharded tfstate layouts. We've seen recurring incidents where control-plane drift or partial apply failures during nodepool upgrades required manual state surgeries (ENG-4821). The goal is to provide a repeatable, automated safety net: ephemeral backups of nodepool metadata and a lightweight tfstate anchoring helper that produces a signed checkpoint file distributed to the ops bucket.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds modules/gpu_ephemeral_backup: an opt-in module that creates a snapshot of the nodepool control metadata, saves kubelet/CRI config snippets, and records a lightweight manifest (node labels, taints, instance-ids) to the configured artifacts bucket. Designed for very short retention (24–72h) to minimize storage and compliance exposure.
- Adds modules/tfstate_anchor: helper that, when invoked, creates a signed checkpoint object (HMAC using a KMS key) that includes the backend state version and a checksum of critical tf resources; intended as a checkpoint for emergency rollbacks and as a hook for the tfstate-migrator workflow.
- Wire-up examples in examples/private/gpu-upgrade-safety which demonstrate using both modules around a nodepool upgrade plan (pre-apply snapshot, post-apply anchor).
- Tests and CI: adds terratest-style integration snippets and unit validation via tflint/tfsec CI gates.

Why this is different from existing state helpers: 
- Lightweight: we do not duplicate full tfstate snapshots (those are expensive/slow). Instead we capture a minimal, verifiable checkpoint that is sufficient to detect drift and reconstruct resource pointers for the tfstate reconciler.
- Kubernetes-aware: the backup manifest captures node-level Kubernetes metadata necessary to reattach pods/stateful-resources to replacement nodes.
- Designed for Private: integrates with our private artifacts bucket patterns, KMS key usage, and tenancy-scoped IAM roles.

Files changed (high-level):
- modules/gpu_ephemeral_backup/main.tf (new)
- modules/gpu_ephemeral_backup/outputs.tf (new)
- modules/gpu_ephemeral_backup/variables.tf (new)
- modules/tfstate_anchor/main.tf (new)
- modules/tfstate_anchor/README.md (new)
- examples/private/gpu-upgrade-safety/README.md (new)
- examples/private/gpu-upgrade-safety/main.tf (new)
- ci/terraform/lint.yml (updated to run tflint on new modules)
- tests/integration/gpu_ephemeral_backup_test.go (new terratest stub)

Commits (high-level):
1) init: add gpu_ephemeral_backup module skeleton and basic manifest writer
2) anchor: implement tfstate_anchor with KMS-signed checkpoint generation and helper outputs
3) examples & docs: add example deployment and README guidance for upgrade hooks
4) ci & tests: add tflint/tfsec CI changes and a terratest stub; fix lint issues raised during CI

Design notes and implementation details:
- The ephemeral backup module is intentionally small: it runs a single provider-backed data collection step that queries cloud provider instance metadata and the kube API (via optional provider credentials) and marshals a manifest object to an artifacts bucket. It exposes a short-lived pre-signed URL and a retention TTL.
- The tfstate_anchor module computes a canonical digest (sorted keys) of the supplied critical resources (map input) and writes a JSON checkpoint to the artifacts bucket. A KMS HMAC key (or HSM-backed symmetric key) is used to sign the payload; signature and signer metadata are included in outputs. Consumers (tfstate-migrator, upgrade-runner) can validate anchors before performing destructive operations.
- Both modules are usage-optional and can be wired into existing plan/apply pipelines in private deployments. We do not alter any existing core tfstate backends by default.

Security and compliance considerations:
- Checkpoints contain metadata but do NOT include full credentials or secrets. Any optional kube API access is performed via the provided role/credentials; default behavior is metadata-only.
- Artifacts bucket ACLs follow existing private deploy patterns; the module requires a kms_key resource ARN and a role that can sign/verify.
- Retention defaults to 24 hours but is configurable to meet customer compliance needs.

Testing and validation performed:
- Local terratest run against a small dev project (mocked provider) validated manifest shape and signature validation flow.
- CI added tflint rules and tfsec suppressions with justifications in README.
- Manual validation with the tfstate-migrator dev harness: created anchor -> deliberately induced partial apply -> run migrator validation -> verified anchor prevented unsafe rollback without explicit acknowledge.

Migration/upgrade path and rollback plan:
- This is opt-in. Existing Private installs will not be affected unless the module is included in their private deployment stacks.
- Recommended rollout: include gpu_ephemeral_backup and tfstate_anchor in canary tenant stacks for one week; validate creation of artifacts and signature verification; then expand to remaining tenants.
- In case of problems the modules can be removed without impacting core state backends; artifacts are purely supplemental.

Review thread (summary):
- Ava Chen: asked for stronger validation on the manifest schema and a unit test for missing fields; requested the retention default be 24h instead of 7d for security.
- Author reply: added a JSON schema validation, added test cases, and updated default retention to 24h (see commit 3).
- Diego Morales: asked for explicit IAM permission docs and a suggestion to avoid broad storage ACLs.
- Author reply: added IAM role policy snippet in README and switched to bucket-level objects with signer-only put permissions.
- Liam O'Connor: ran a small integration using the private installer dev cluster and requested a minor rename of output keys for consistency; author updated outputs in commit 4.
- Final: reviewers approved and requested small followup to add production terratest scenarios later.

CI history and resolution:
- Initial pipeline: tflint reported two stylistic issues and tfsec flagged an allowed IAM pattern; CI failed on first run.
- Fixes: corrected tflint warnings, added tfsec suppressions with rationale, updated lint workflow. Final CI green on run #3.

Operational notes for SREs/Field engineers:
- When enabling the modules in a tenant, ensure the artifacts bucket uses lifecycle rules and that KMS keys are rotated per org policy.
- The anchor verification command (scripts/verify_anchor.sh) is included in the examples directory; use it to validate anchors before applying rollbacks.

Follow-ups (future work):
- Add a small operator runbook to automatically reconcile artifacts cleanup post-upgrade.
- Integrate anchor validation as a pre-check in the private-installer upgrade controller.
- Expand terratest coverage to a production-like environment and add a scheduled job that validates anchor creation.

TL;DR: Adds two opt-in terraform helpers to make GPU nodepool upgrades and tfstate-boundary migrations safer by providing short-lived backups and cryptographically-signed checkpoint anchors. Opt-in, backwards-compatible, and CI-tested.

Add new terraform module 'gpu_ephemeral_backup' for short-lived snapshot/restore hooks during nodepool upgrades; add 'tfstate_anchor' helper to create cryptographically-signed state checkpoints for safer rollbacks. No user-facing API changes; opt-in via module inclusion.
payload.title: Introduce GPU ephemeral backup tfmodule and tfstate anchoring helper

payload.body:
Context: Solutions Engineering has repeatedly asked for a concrete starting point for VPC module inputs during design partner pilots. This PR adds sanitized example tfvars for two representative regulated-enterprise topologies (strict egress + endpoints-heavy; and hybrid connectivity placeholder) along with a short walkthrough that explains what to change vs what should remain as-is. The goal is to reduce back-and-forth during discovery/pilot kickoff and to encode Redwood-validated defaults without leaking customer-identifying details. Safety note: examples intentionally avoid customer names, account IDs, on-prem IP ranges, IAM ARNs, domain names, and any internal hostnames; all values are either generic placeholders or clearly marked as "REPLACE_ME". Includes a reviewer discussion on what is acceptable to ship in-repo for alpha and guidance on how to share these examples externally (copy/paste into customer repo, do not link to internal paths).
Markus Klein (SE): This is exactly what we need for kickoff. Request: add a clear section on what we can safely share with customers vs internal-only notes. Also rename "acme"/"northstar" to something generic in paths; we should not have customer identifiers in the repo even if sanitized.
Bruno Silva (author): +1. I’ll switch to design-partner-1/2 directories, remove any lingering names, and add a "Sharing guidance" section that says to copy into the customer repo and never ask them to reference our internal examples directly.
Hanae Suzuki (Security): Please confirm there are no real account IDs, real domains, or real on-prem CIDRs. Also watch out for leaked internal hostnames in comments. Suggest adding an automated grep in CI for common patterns (12-digit ids, .corp, etc.).
Bruno Silva (author): Agreed. Added scripts/redaction_scan.sh and wired it into the workflow. Also replaced the last remaining sample ARN with "REPLACE_ME". No domains included; Route53 private hosted zone is referenced as a generic variable only.
Victor Alvarez (Networking): On endpoints, please include both ecr.api and ecr.dkr and call out private DNS behavior explicitly in the walkthrough. Missing that is a common failure mode (see SUP-28411).
Bruno Silva (author): Updated design-partner-1 example to include both endpoints and added a troubleshooting note in the walkthrough: if image pulls fail, check ECR endpoints + private DNS enabled.
Irene Choi (Infra): CI: checkov is currently running across the whole repo; examples can cause noise. Can we scope checkov to modules/ and leave examples as non-blocking?
Bruno Silva (author): Done. Workflow now runs checkov required on modules/* and non-blocking on examples/*, but still blocks on redaction scan.

Motivation: prompt sets used in downstream products occasionally contain edge cases that only surface under contextual adversarial pressure such as injected session tokens, role-swapped histories, or subtle suffix manipulations. These failures can be noisy and produce a high false-positive rate when treated as hard CI failures. This PR introduces a context-aware red-team prober that synthesizes adversarial variants by combining prompt templates with recent session context snippets and a small corpus of adversarial transforms, plus a prioritized soft-fail CI adapter that converts noisy probe failures into graded alerts based on impact scoring and prompt criticality. What this change includes: 1) a prober engine (eval_harness.probers.context_redteam) that generates deterministic adversarial variants using a seeded transformer of template rules and history snippets so runs are reproducible; 2) a scoring pipeline that computes per-probe metrics including token-level hallucination-rate, policy-safety score, confusion-index, and a composite impact score used by the adapter; 3) a prioritized prompt map (config/priority_map.yaml) that marks high-value prompts to escalate to hard failures while routing lower-priority probes through a soft-fail attenuation path; 4) a small deterministic replay harness so individual probe failures can be re-run locally for debugging; 5) CI integration (.github/workflows/nightly-eval.yml) that schedules a staged run: fast smoke probes on PRs and full red-team sweep nightly; 6) telemetry hooks to expose new eval metrics in the console and to allow alerting thresholds. Rationale: by combining contextual sampling and priority-aware failure handling we get earlier detection of impactful regressions while keeping PR feedback signal-to-noise acceptable. Safety/permissions: the prober runs only in gated CI contexts by default and uses a sandboxed replay harness; no production data is stored by the prober. Backwards compatibility: default config keeps existing CI paths unchanged and enables the adapter only for teams opt-in in eval config. Testing: unit tests cover probe generation, scoring, and adapter decision logic; lightweight integration tests run in CI. Rollout: feature-flag gated and rolled out to nightly by default with a two-week observation window before enabling hard failures for high-priority prompts. See linked linear items for rollout checklist and metrics thresholds.
Adds context-aware adversarial probing to nightly evals, metric integrations for hallucination and policy-safety, and a soft-fail adapter for prioritized prompts.

Add prioritized soft-fail adapter, impact scoring, and priority map config
Integrate hallucination-rate and policy-safety metrics into eval pipeline
Add replay harness and unit tests for prober and adapter logic
CI: add nightly-eval workflow and PR-level smoke probe job
Address review feedback: optimize probe generation performance and reduce memory footprint

Context: Private deployments have started seeing occasional tfstate divergence when a parallel apply overlaps subnet and GPU nodepool changes. This caused transient resource duplication and occasional evictions in large clusters. This PR introduces two complementary Terraform modules and operational tooling: a tfstate-consistency-signer (lightweight helper that writes a signed checkpoint blob to a central state bucket after coordinated applies) and a rolling-gpu-pool-migrator (controller-like module that emits an ordered plan to rotate GPU nodepools across AZs with minimal disruption).

What this PR does:
- New module: modules/tfstate-consistency-signer
  - Generates a signed metadata file (s3/gs) that includes apply-id, timestamp, and checksum of the state file.
  - Integrates with existing state backend configuration via optional provider hooks; does NOT replace backend.
  - Includes an optional pre-apply validation step (terraform null_resource + local-exec) to fail fast if signatures mismatch.
- New module: modules/rolling-gpu-pool-migrator
  - Accepts current nodepool map, target nodepool spec, and a rotation window policy.
  - Produces a plan file (JSON) listing atomic steps (drain -> cordon -> create -> attach -> validate -> destroy) that operators can review.
  - Supports canary rotation and health-check gating (kube-probe based) for on-prem and VPC installs.
- Changes to examples/ and docs/ showing upgrade workflow and recommended Linear ticket template.

Migration plan (operators):
1) Deploy tfstate-consistency-signer as an opt-in module referencing existing state bucket.
2) Run a single coordinated apply (signer will write checkpoint blob). Verify signed checksum in bucket and compare to current state.
3) Enable rolling-gpu-pool-migrator in dry-run to emit plan and review.
4) Execute rotation with canary=1, monitor console dashboards, then increase batch size.

Rollback and safety:
- All changes are additive; signer is opt-in and migrator supports dry-run.
- In case of partial rotation failure, migrator emits rollback steps and preserves the old nodepool for fast reattach.
- The pre-apply signer validation will block automated CI applies if detected checksum mismatch, reducing merge-time conflicts.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for signer HMAC generation and plan serializer (modules/tests)
- Integration tests using minikube + local S3 mock to verify plan execution and node drain/reattach flows (ci/integration)
- Load tests on staging clusters to simulate concurrent terraform applies and verify signer prevents divergent state

Related work: ENG-2211 (state incident post-release), ENG-2247 (gpu-allocator drift detector), SUP-1198 (customer report for on-prem eviction during upgrade).

Checklist:
- [x] modules implemented
- [x] docs and examples updated
- [x] tests added and passing in CI
- [x] migration and rollback guidance included

Notes: This PR purposely keeps the signer as a small helper (no secret management baked-in beyond HMAC key); we'll follow up with KMS/HSM integration and a controller-based signer if adoption metrics justify it.
- Added tfstate-consistency-signer module to certify state snapshots.
- Added rolling GPU pool migrator module to move workloads with zero-downtime.
- Backwards-compatible; no action required for most customers. See migration notes.
Daniel Kim: Nice approach—can you clarify the HMAC key rotation story? If the key rotates, how do we validate older checkpoints? Author reply: The signer writes key_id along with HMAC and we keep a key history map in the state bucket. Rotation is handled by adding new key entries; the validation code accepts previous keys for N days (configurable), docs updated.
Sofia Martinez: Migrator plan appears to assume that CSI volumes can be reattached quickly. On some on-prem infra that is not true. Suggest adding configurable drain timeout and force-retire flags. Author reply: Added drain_timeout and force_retire variables; default conservative values included and documented.
Liam O'Connor: CI integration failed on first run due to localstack S3 pathing. Request: add retry logic and clearer errors. Author reply: Fixed localstack path handling and added exponential backoff for uploads.
QA Bot: Integration tests passed in dry-run but failed in execution for a specific scenario where node labels didn't match filter. Author reply: Updated migrator filters to accept label selectors and fallback to taints when labels missing; added test coverage.

Context
Provision-to-ready automation needs a stable contract from IaC so the orchestrator can reliably discover: (a) which nodes belong to which dedicated pool, (b) what image channel/version the pool is pinned to, and (c) which regions/pool types have provisioning automation enabled. Today we have a mix of ad-hoc tags and inconsistent outputs across modules, which has made early rollout debugging slower than it needs to be (see SUP-28411 for the most recent "where did these nodes come from" escalation).

What this PR changes
1) Standardizes tags on dedicated GPU pools
- Adds a required baseline set of tags to the dedicated pool and node group resources:
  - redwood:fleet_pool_id (string)
  - redwood:fleet_pool_type (= "dedicated")
  - redwood:region (e.g. "us-east-1")
  - redwood:image_channel ("candidate" | "stable")
  - redwood:image_version (optional, when pinned)
  - redwood:provisioning_hooks_enabled ("true" | "false")
- Tags are applied to the backing ASG/instance template resources where supported so downstream discovery (agent + control plane) can use a single lookup path.

2) Adds outputs consumed by the provisioning orchestrator
- Exposes consistent module outputs:
  - pool_id
  - pool_region
  - image_channel
  - image_version
  - provisioning_hooks_enabled
- These outputs are intended to be wired into the fleet provisioning orchestrator config and the readiness service registration step.

3) Guardrails for required variables (fail fast)
- Adds validation/preconditions so plans fail early if:
  - pool_id is empty
  - region is unset/invalid
  - image_channel is not one of {candidate, stable}
  - provisioning hooks are enabled but image_channel is unset
- Keeps defaults non-disruptive: provisioning hooks remain opt-in via enable_provisioning_hooks (default false). Existing dedicated pools should see tag-only changes unless explicitly opting into hooks.

Notes / design choices
- Tag names intentionally do not include per-node identifiers (avoids metric/tag cardinality explosions downstream).
- We keep the tag namespace as redwood:* to match internal conventions and allow filtering/permissions rules in cloud consoles.
- image_version is optional to support channel-following pools (candidate/stable) without forcing a pin; orchestrator can treat (channel, version?) as the image selector.

Testing
- terraform fmt
- terraform validate
- tflint
- terratest: modules/dedicated_pool (basic plan/apply in ephemeral env)

Rollout
- Safe to merge: tags are additive. Outputs are additive.
- Teams enabling hooks should do so behind the existing region/pool feature flags in the provisioning automation rollout plan. Follow-up wiring will happen in control-plane/orchestrator PRs.

Checklist
- [x] Tags applied at the correct resource level (ASG/launch template where possible)
- [x] Outputs documented in modules/README
- [x] Validations don’t break existing callers (defaults preserved)
- [x] Reviewed with Fleet + Release Eng

Follow-ups
- Wire module outputs into orchestrator config generation (ENG-4822/ENG-4829)
- Update dashboards to rely on standardized tags for pool grouping once rollout expands beyond us-east A100
- Dedicated pool modules now emit standardized tags and outputs used by provision-to-ready automation (pool id, region, image channel/version). - Guardrails added to fail fast when required variables are unset or invalid (prevents silent drift and post-provision surprises).
Vanessa Ortiz: Can we make sure tags land on the instance template/ASG, not just the EKS nodegroup wrapper? The validation agent does cloud-side discovery early in bring-up.
Keiko Yamamoto: Good call. Updated gpu_node_group module to propagate tags to launch template and ASG tags (where supported). Added terratest assertions for both paths.
Jamal Pierce: pool_id needs to be stable and match what capacity planning uses. Can we keep the tag key name aligned with the readiness service fields? (fleet_pool_id vs pool_id)
Keiko Yamamoto: Renamed to redwood:fleet_pool_id for the tag and kept output as pool_id. Added a short note in README mapping tag->output->readiness field.
Sahana Iyer: Please keep enable_provisioning_hooks default false; we can’t risk enabling hooks broadly before the image pipeline is fully staged.
Keiko Yamamoto: Confirmed. Default remains false and the validation only triggers when explicitly enabled.
Fiona McCarthy: Any tags exposing customer identifiers? Also, ensure we’re not outputting anything that should be treated as secret.
Keiko Yamamoto: No customer identifiers added. pool_id is an internal UUID-like identifier; no secrets in outputs. Added a comment to avoid embedding customer names in pool_id values.

Motivation: Private deployments increasingly require per-tenant isolation for GPU capacity and state. Current Terraform layout stores shared pools and global TFState keys which makes per-tenant imports and rolling updates risky and noisy. This PR adds tenant-scoped GPU lease modules, a state-concatenation keying pattern, and a state migrator script to safely split existing global state without downtime.

What this PR introduces (high level): 1) module/tenant-gpu-lease: a new TF module that provisions a lightweight lease controller, dedicated nodepool shims, and IAM bindings scoped to a tenant identifier. The lease controller is implemented as a CRD-enabled bootstrap (cloud-init + systemd unit) that marks capacity as "leased" in a DynamoDB-style lock table (provider-agnostic key-value table resource). 2) state_key concatenation: we introduce a consistent state key pattern tfstate/<env>/<tenant>/<component> so each tenant's GPU/nodepool lifecycle is decoupled from the global compute state. 3) lock sharding and migrator: a small Go migrator (scripts/tfstate-migrator.go) that runs in dry-run mode to map existing resources into tenant states and orchestrates remote state copies with lock handoff to avoid double-apply. 4) IAM least-privilege templates: new iam/nodepool-role module with narrower permissions for node bootstrap and HSM/KMS envelope unwrap permissions. 5) Networking isolation helpers: per-tenant subnet route table attachments, optional VPC peering keys and route selectors to support on-prem isolation. 6) upgrade/rollback plan and docs: scripts/upgrade-plan.md and rollback instructions for safe rerolls.

Why this is different than previous refactors: instead of splitting nodepools by AZ or GPU label, this change focuses on tenant scoping and introducing a composable state keying pattern that can be adopted incrementally per-tenant. The migrator provides a safe migration path with a native dry-run and reconciliation loop.

Compatibility and rollout: The modules are opt-in. Existing deployments remain unchanged unless the env-level config toggles tenant_mode = true and maps tenant IDs. The migrator supports partial migration: you can pick a single tenant and move its compute resources to a new state key. The plan supports automatic fallback: if post-migration smoke tests fail, the migrator can reverse the operation and rehydrate the original state.

Testing and CI: terratest suite added for module/tenant-gpu-lease which runs with a local emulator for the key-value lock table and a mocked cloud provider for nodepool APIs. CI initially failed because of fmt/validate issues; those were fixed in followup commits. The PR passed the full pipeline and a manual canary in staging with a single-tenant migration.

Files touched (high level): module/tenant-gpu-lease/*, module/iam/nodepool-role/*, scripts/tfstate-migrator.go, scripts/upgrade-plan.md, examples/tenant-migration/{main.tf,vars.tf}, charts/installer/values-tenant.yaml, docs/private/tenant-state-concat.md

Release notes: Adds opt-in tenant-scoped GPU lease modules and a safe TFState migrator for per-tenant state decomposition. This enables isolated upgrades and per-tenant capacity billing.

Checklist: - [x] design doc linked - docs/private/tenant-state-concat.md - [x] unit + terratest added - module tests and CI - [x] migration tool with dry-run - scripts/tfstate-migrator.go - [x] rollout + rollback docs - scripts/upgrade-plan.md
Connor Patel: Can we avoid adding any provider-specific DynamoDB resources in the module? Suggest abstracting the lock-table interface so customers can choose native cloud TTL tables or our existing k/v service.
Maya Chen (author): Good point — converted lock table to a provider-agnostic 'kv_table' abstraction and added adapters for aws_dynamodb_table and a local file-backed stub used by tests.
Elena Rivera: The IAM template looks ok but we need to ensure the role cannot assume broad compute permissions. Please restrict iam:List* actions and add a comment explaining the minimal set used for node bootstrap.
Maya Chen (author): tightened policy and added explanatory comments with least-privilege rationale. Also added an integration unit test that verifies no wildcard in actions.
Samir Gupta: The migrator is powerful; include explicit user prompts and dry-run as default to reduce accidental runs. Also add telemetry metrics for migration duration and failure rates.
Maya Chen (author): made dry-run default and added optional --apply flag. Added Prometheus metrics export hooks and documented them in scripts/upgrade-plan.md.

Context: As part of the SIEM-ready audit export beta, enterprise onboarding needs a consistent IaC story for provisioning destination-side infra and handing Redwood a least-privilege credential reference (vs pasting secrets into Console). This PR adds a small set of Terraform modules and examples to configure audit export destinations for S3 delivery, Splunk HEC, and Datadog Logs intake, including opinionated secret storage (AWS Secrets Manager / SSM) and outputs that match the control-plane export config API fields. Scope: (1) modules/audit_export_destination_s3 for S3 bucket prefix layout + optional SSE-KMS + cross-account assume-role policy snippet; (2) modules/audit_export_destination_splunk_hec for storing HEC token as a secret and generating a Redwood destination payload (endpoint/index/source/sourcetype); (3) modules/audit_export_destination_datadog_logs for storing API key as a secret and generating a Redwood destination payload (site/endpoint + tags). Each module outputs a "destination_spec_json" string suitable for pasting into Redwood Console or piping into the control-plane API, and emits a "secret_ref" (ARN or SSM parameter name) instead of the secret value. Security notes: outputs are marked sensitive where appropriate; IAM policies default to least privilege; KMS key is optional but strongly recommended; we document egress allowlist requirements and explicitly avoid supporting arbitrary HTTP sinks in beta. This PR is targeted at Solutions Engineering / Customer Success doing enterprise onboarding for the beta cohort; it’s feature-flagged on the Redwood side and does not by itself enable exports.
PR Title: Add Terraform resources/modules for SIEM audit export destinations (S3, Splunk HEC, Datadog) + secret references

Summary
- Adds three new modules to help enterprise customers provision destination-side resources and pass Redwood a secret reference (not raw credentials).
- Includes examples for common beta onboarding paths, including S3 cross-account + SSE-KMS.
- Updates root README with a new "SIEM audit export beta" section and links to examples.

Motivation
Enterprise onboarding for the SIEM-ready audit export beta needs an IaC-friendly way to:
1) create/configure destination infrastructure (especially S3 delivery),
2) store destination credentials safely (Splunk HEC token / Datadog API key) without pasting into the UI, and
3) produce a destination config payload that matches Redwood’s control-plane API.

What’s included
1) modules/audit_export_destination_s3
- Provisions (or references) an S3 bucket and configures a prefix for audit export objects.
- Optional SSE-KMS support (recommended); example includes CMK and least-privilege PutObject to prefix.
- Optional cross-account assume-role trust policy with external_id support.
- Outputs: destination_spec_json (string), plus IAM snippets/role ARN outputs needed by Redwood-side adapter.

2) modules/audit_export_destination_splunk_hec
- Stores HEC token in AWS Secrets Manager (or SSM Parameter Store) and outputs a secret_ref.
- Outputs destination_spec_json with endpoint/index/source/sourcetype, plus secret_ref.*.
- Notes on HEC rate limiting and recommended batching defaults (informational).

3) modules/audit_export_destination_datadog_logs
- Stores Datadog API key as secret and outputs secret_ref only.
- Outputs destination_spec_json with site/endpoint and tag defaults for audit categories.

Non-goals / clarifications
- This does not enable exports by itself. Exports remain gated by Redwood feature flags + tenant allowlist (ENG-5184).
- Filters/backfill windows/rollout policies are configured in Redwood Console / control-plane API, not Terraform.
- Beta only: no support for arbitrary HTTP sinks or Private/on-prem patterns in this repo (documented elsewhere).

Security considerations
- No module outputs raw secret material. Outputs are restricted to secret references (ARN/parameter name).
- S3 permissions default to least privilege and can be scoped to prefix.
- KMS usage is strongly recommended; module supports KMS key ARN input.
- Cross-account role trust policy includes optional external_id.

How to use
- See examples/audit-export/README.md for copy/paste snippets. Each example prints a destination_spec_json you can paste into Redwood Console (Audit Export Settings) or use in the control-plane export config API.

Testing
- terraform fmt/validate across modules and examples
- tflint
- checkov policy checks

Rollout
- Intended for SE/CS onboarding of beta customers. Coordinate enablement via internal runbook/INT-9012 and confirm tenant allowlist is set before expecting events to flow.

Refs
- Linear: ENG-5144, ENG-5151, ENG-5156, ENG-5184
- Beta readiness: PM-858

Benji Okafor (review): The destination_spec_json output is super helpful. Can we align field names to match the control-plane API exactly (destination.type, destination.config.*, secret_ref.*), so SEs don’t need to translate? Also, please call out that filters/backfill are configured in Redwood, not in these modules.
Diego Santos (author): Updated outputs to mirror the API naming (type/config/secret_ref) and expanded examples/README to clarify that filters/backfill are configured in Console/API. Also added a note that the modules only cover destination-side provisioning + secret reference creation.
Hanae Suzuki (review): Please ensure we never output the Splunk HEC token / Datadog API key as a plain-text output. Even with `sensitive = true`, it shows up in state and can leak in logs. Recommend taking token/key as input, storing it in Secrets Manager, and only outputting the secret ARN/parameter name. Also add guidance on rotation (update secret value; Redwood reads via secret_ref).
Diego Santos (author): Confirmed: we only output secret ARN/SSM parameter name. No module returns secret values. Added rotation guidance + clarified state implications in module READMEs.
Kevin Osei (review): For S3: default to SSE-S3 is fine, but for regulated customers we should recommend SSE-KMS with customer-managed key. Default remains minimal to avoid breaking existing setups, but README strongly recommends KMS for enterprise.
Connor O'Brien (review): Rollout note: please reference the beta feature flag + tenant allowlist (ENG-5184). Even though this is terraform, Support needs to know this doesn’t enable export automatically. Also please add a quick "paste into Console" snippet in examples.
Diego Santos (author): Added explicit callout to tenant allowlist / feature flag gating + a "Console paste" snippet in examples/README. Linked INT-9012 for internal enablement workflow.

Motivation: We have multiple FlashAttention variants and several ad-hoc fused ops (rotary, rope) which complicate kernel selection and prevents smooth rollouts. This PR introduces a small compatibility layer (FlashBridge) that normalizes QKV layout and exposes a single fused rotary/rope operator so the runtime can pick the best back-end without per-model branching. It also adjusts the continuous-batching scheduler to expose a tunable adaptive window and integrates a lightweight KV-cache prefetch heuristic that reduces cold-KV misses for long-lived chat sessions. Changes are backward compatible and gated behind runtime flags (runtime.attn.flashbridge_enabled, runtime.scheduler.adaptive_window_ms, runtime.kv.prefetch_enabled). What this PR does: 1) Adds FlashBridge abstraction (C++): a thin shim that translates internal tensors to the memory/stride expectations of multiple FlashAttention implementations (FlashA V3, FlashA-lite, FuseX). 2) Implements a combined fused_rotary_rope operator (CUDA + CPU fallback) that performs rotary embedding application and rope swapping/interleave in a single kernel to reduce memory traffic. 3) Scheduler updates: adaptive continuous-batching window (ms-based), and a hot-key preservation policy that avoids coalescing requests with sticky KV sessions. 4) KV cache: prefetch heuristic that warms likely next-blocks for recurring chat sessions; configurable TTL. 5) Telemetry: new micro-metrics for kernel selection, per-model flashbridge fallbacks, and prefetch hit-rate. 6) Tests and perf harness: unit tests, integration smoke, and perf bench scripts. Checklist: - [x] Core abstraction implemented - [x] Fused operator implemented with CPU fallback - [x] Scheduler and kv-prefetch wired into runtime - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Benchmarks show net improvement - [x] Docs updated (internal perf guide). Links: design doc (internal): https://linear.app/redwood/board/ENG-1273/flashbridge-design, benchmark scripts: tests/perf/bench_attn.py. Rollout plan: feature gated, staged canary (10% traffic) then global rollout after 48h of no regression on p99 latency and error-rate.
Avery Chen: overall design looks good. Please add a runtime flag to disable prefetch per-deployment (answered: added runtime.kv.prefetch_enabled).
Samir Patel: can you add microbench (seq512, seq2048) with both flash variants? (answered: added bench_attn.py variations and attached CSV).
Lena Koskinen: nit: document CPU fallback perf expectations in docs (answered: updated docs/perf/attention-upgrade.md).
Avery Chen: the kernel can be memory-bound for seq<=64, add an early-path to skip fuse (answered: added heuristic in kernel_selector.cc to prefer plain attn for very short sequences).
Samir Patel: CI flaked on e2e once, re-run passed (CI note).
Merged by Avery Chen via squash; merge commit contains summarized changes and references ENG-1273. Canary rollout started after merge as described in the PR. No hotfixes required during canary window.
Introduce FlashBridge (kernel abstraction) and a fused_rotary_rope operator to reduce memory copies and memory-bound stalls; adaptive continuous batching window and KV prefetch heuristic to improve throughput and p99 latency for long-lived chat sessions. Feature gated behind runtime flags. Expect ~12-28% token/s increase depending on sequence length and model; p99 latency reduction ~18% for seq512 in our bench harness.

Introduce a credential fallthrough chain and per-language ergonomic adapters for streaming clients, add unified backoff preset profiles and telemetry tags, and bump Python/TS/Go SDK versions. Motivation: teams repeatedly implement custom credential cascades and slightly different streaming ergonomics across languages; this PR centralizes the policy, provides idiomatic adapters for each SDK, and ships tested backoff presets so production apps can pick sensible defaults. Changes include a new CredFallthrough interface, language adapters (py: CredentialChain, ts: CredComposer, go: CascadeProvider), a StreamBackoffProfile enum shared by all SDKs, streaming hook for graceful reconnects and telemetry labels for credential sources. Also includes migration shims and deprecation warnings so existing callers continue to work. See release notes and migration guidance.

Recommended migration: adopt CredentialChain when you rely on multiple token sources (env, file cache, delegated token server). See docs/guides/migration/credential-fallthrough.md for examples per language.
