Motivation: existing synthetic workload runners focus on fixed sequence-length distributions or simple bimodal mixes. Real traffic often exhibits abrupt shifts in token-length distribution (for example, a UI change that causes prompts to include an extra context block) which can amplify tail latency due to cache fragmentation and kernel scheduling. This PR introduces a small, configurable suite that emulates sequence-length transitions and a lightweight detector that flags 'tail amplification' events during benchmark runs.

What this PR adds (high level): 1) seqlen_emulator: a runner that generates workload traces with controlled Markov-style sequence-length transitions (configurable transition matrix, dwell time, burstiness). 2) tail_amplification_detector: streaming detector that computes amplification ratio (p99_after / p99_before) and issues annotated events for the reporting pipeline. 3) integration harness: glue to run the emulator against existing perf-canary clusters and produce JSONL time-series for the reporting pipeline. 4) docs and example profiles.

Checklist: [x] emulator core + config schema, [x] detector + unit tests, [x] integration harness and example Linear job, [x] perf CI workflow that can replay saved traces against baseline, [x] docs.

Why different: unlike sequence-mix synthetic runners this tool models transitions (the temporal dimension of distribution change) and explicitly measures amplification of tail quantiles rather than just absolute p99. This helps identify scenarios where short bursts of longer sequences cause disproportionate cost/latency impact.

Related: ENG-7342 (perf-signal-detection), ENG-7561 (benchmark-suite-refactor). Also links to internal doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-7342/seqlen-transition-emulator (internal).
Marcus Li: please ensure the emulator can run deterministically for CI comparisons — request added seeded_sampler (addressed in d12a8c4)
Ritu Sharma: detector window length needs to be configurable and documented; suggested default values — added window param + docs update
Daniel Park: memory usage looked high when replaying multi-hour traces; optimize by streaming JSONL and reusing buffers (addressed in d12a8c4)
Author (Aisha): responded to all comments, added unit tests covering determinism and a small nightly replay job to validate detectors against stored traces
Adds a benchmark lab tool that emulates temporal transitions in sequence-length distributions and a detector that quantifies tail amplification; includes example profiles and CI replay workflow to compare amplification ratios against baseline. Useful for identifying bursty prompt changes that disproportionately affect p95/p99 latency.
New emulator + detector to surface amplification-of-tail events caused by rapid sequence-length distribution changes; integrated into perf CI with example traces.
payload.title: Introduce sequence-length-transition-emulator and tail-amplification detector

payload.body:
Context: Long-tail latency spikes in steady-state runs were traced to nondeterministic warmup phases where sequence primer ordering and random trace replay caused noisy p95/p99 shifts. This PR introduces a deterministic warmup replayer plus a multi-sequence primer that lets workload runners reliably prime KV caches, prefix caches, and attention cache states for repeatable steady-state benchmarking. Motivation: Reduce noise in regression signals from warmup variance and make perf baselines reproducible across runs and CI shards. Goal is not to micro-optimize runtime, but to provide a reproducible priming path and a light-weight validation harness that guarantees same sequence ordering and timing semantics across hosts. Changes: - New bench/runner/deterministic_replayer.py: replay engine that accepts normalized traces and deterministic timing profiles. - New bench/runner/multi_sequence_primer.py: orchestrates interleaved sequences, supports prefix merging and synthetic token insertion for realistic priming. - bench/configs/deterministic_warmup.yaml: configuration presets (short/medium/long) used by CI and local profiling. - bench/utils/trace_normalizer.py: converts collected traces into canonical forms (canonical tokenization, anonymization of IDs, consistent timestamp deltas). - tests/integration/test_primer_replayer.py: integration coverage for determinism assertions across 3 seeds and 2 host types. - ci/workflows/bench.yml: adds a deterministic bench job that runs the warmup-only profile on PRs labeled "benchmark". Implementation notes: - Determinism is enforced by a combination of normalized traces and fixed rng seeds; we avoid global state where possible and expose a ReplayContext object to the runner. - The replayer can run in two modes: strict (asserts identical sequence of emitted tokens) and tolerant (allows whitespace/tokenizer variants but asserts same token ids after normalization). - The primer supports interleaving policy strategies (round-robin, weighted) to simulate multiplexed tenant scenarios. Performance impact: baseline warmup-only runs show p95 reduction variance from ±9.8% to ±2.1% over 20 repeated runs (local VM), and end-to-end benchmark CI runs show improved stability of baseline metrics (p95 confidence interval width reduced by ~3.6x). Checklist: - [x] Design doc walkthrough with ENG-7122 stakeholders - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] CI job added and green - [x] Benchmarks added to baseline runbook - [x] Release notes drafted How to exercise locally: 1) python -m bench.runner.deterministic_replayer --config bench/configs/deterministic_warmup.yaml --trace samples/short_coldstart.trace 2) python -m bench.runner.multi_sequence_primer --mode strict --policy round-robin --runs 20 Notes and limitations: - This does not change serving runtime batching logic; it's purely a workload/priming harness. - Determinism guarantees apply only after trace normalization; traces collected from different tokenizer versions must be normalized first. - The replayer is intentionally lightweight; future work (ENG-7210) will add a golden-trace repository and artifact signing. Commits summary: see commits list for short descriptions. Merge: squash and merge to main after 2 approvals.
Owen Chen: Can we avoid importing global RNG state in the replayer? Looks like ReplayContext seeds a global in one path. -- reviewed inline and requested small refactor.
Priya Desai: Good catch — refactored to thread-local RNG inside ReplayContext, added explicit seed argument and enforced no global uses. See commit b4d9e21.
Marceline Ortiz: Tests look good; can we add a short CI gate that only runs the warmup profile so perf PRs don't need full E2E every time?
Priya Desai: Added ci/workflows/bench.yml with a lightweight warmup-only job triggered for 'benchmark' label. Kept E2E optional to avoid CI cost.
Noah Kaplan: Confirmed p95 variance improvement on my local GCP worker (n1-standard-8) — approving.
Merged by Marceline Ortiz via squash on 2026-02-18. Squash commit: 'deterministic warmup: primer + replayer (ENG-7122)'. Merge rationale: improves stability of perf baselines and reduces CI noise; low risk to serving runtime. Backcompat: none (benchmark-only).
Add deterministic warmup replayer and multi-sequence primer to benchmark lab. Improves reproducibility of steady-state perf runs and reduces warmup variance when comparing baselines. How to use: bench/runner docs and configs included.
payload.title: Multi-sequence primer and deterministic warmup replayer

payload.body:
Motivation: existing workload runners exercise steady-state and bursty traffic but do not mimic slow, thermal-like drift and micro-jitter observed on GPU fleets during long runs. This causes noise in p95/p99 profiling baselines and makes regression detection brittle. This PR introduces a phase-aware sequence thermostat workload and a sparse-signal denoiser + windowed hotspot reconciler so profiling baselines are resilient to thermal drift and measurement noise. Changes include: 1) bench/runners/phase_thermostat.py: a new workload runner that emits sequences with controlled inter-request drift, frequency-domain jitter, and epochal thermal profiles (configurable ramp, hold, cool). 2) bench/telemetry/denoiser.py: a lightweight filtering stage that removes high-frequency sampling noise and reconstructs per-kernel time series using median-window and spectral thresholding heuristics. 3) bench/reporters/window_reconciler.py: merges overlapping hotspot windows across epochs to produce stable per-kernel baselines and highlights persistent regressions. 4) perf/artifacts/phase_baselines/: new baseline outputs (flamegraphs, kernel-sample histograms, PSD plots) with metadata. 5) tests/integration/test_phase_thermostat.py and tests/unit/test_denoiser.py: coverage for runner and denoiser edges. 6) CI: add perf-sim job that runs a short synthetic epoch on PRs to validate non-regression of the denoiser. Commits and files changed listed below. Rationale: by simulating slow drift + micro-jitter we can detect regressions that only manifest under thermal conditions (e.g., scheduler backpressure, small kernel regressions amplified under slow-down). The denoiser reconciles noisy samples so alerts are driven by meaningful signals, lowering false positives in the benchmark pipeline. Backwards compatibility: runner and denoiser are opt-in via benchmark configs; default global pipelines unchanged. Rollout: merge to main, land behind a feature flag, enable perf-sim CI for benchmark-lab. Linked linear tickets: ENG-1423 (phase-aware runner), ENG-1560 (denoiser & reconciler), SUP-418 (customer-reported noise during nightly profiling).
Add phase-aware workload runner and signal-denoising pipeline to improve stability of kernel-level profiling under thermal/jittered conditions.
Evan Liu (2024-11-05): Nice direction. A few requests: make the default jitter parameters conservative and add a short mode for CI so PRs don't run long. Also ensure the runner respects --seed for deterministic traces.
Marisol Ortega (2024-11-05): Addressed: added --ci-mode flag that short-circuits epochs to 10s and added deterministic seed handling. Updated tests to assert determinism.
Priya Singh (2024-11-06): Suggest moving spectral-threshold constants to config with clear docstrings; otherwise approve pending small nit on logging verbosity.
Marisol Ortega (2024-11-06): Moved constants to bench/config/thermostat.yaml, reduced telemetry log level for noisy samplers.
Connor Blake (2024-11-07): Verified perf-sim job runs on my branch and baseline outputs match expectations. Approving for merge.
CI Bot (2024-11-07): perf-sim: pass; unit-tests: pass; integration-load: pass; lint: pass
payload.title: Phase-aware sequence thermostat and sparse-signal denoiser for drift-resilient profiling

payload.body:
Context: we need a stable, machine-readable way to express non-breaking and breaking changes to model variants (performance profile deltas, tokenizer changes, major architecture changes) so consumers and automated release tooling can make safe rollouts and generate accurate changelogs. This PR introduces two related pieces: 1) a lightweight semantic versioning policy for model variants (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) with concrete rules for when to bump each part; 2) an immutable profile-stamp concept (profile_id + profile_checksum + semver) stored on each variant that ties a specific performance profile snapshot to a variant. Motivation: current onboarding churn makes it hard to determine whether a variant update is backwards compatible for embedding/serving contracts or is purely a profile calibration. The semver + stamp allow automated changelog generation, safer routing fallbacks, and deterministic comparisons during canaries. What this PR does: - Adds variant.semver (string) and variant.profile_stamp (string) to the registry API and DB schema, with a migration and backfill that tries to infer a sensible PATCH bump for historical variants. - Implements stamp generation code that computes a canonical profile checksum from the eval profile JSON and combines it with the semver into a single stamp like "v1.2.3+ps.9f2a1b". - Exposes CLI helpers: `model-registry stamp generate <variant>` and `model-registry stamp validate <variant>` to help validators and onboarding scripts. - Adds docs (docs/model-semver.md) with explicit rules and examples and a migration guide for operators. - Adds integration tests for stamp generation, validation, and registry lookup semantics. - Adds a small compatibility shim in the serving routing layer to prefer exact profile_stamp matches for pinned deployments and fall back by semver rules otherwise. Checklist: [x] RFC/spec in code comments and docs [x] DB migration script + safe backfill strategy [x] API + proto changes and backward compatibility notes [x] CLI tooling [x] Unit + integration tests [x] Docs and migration guide [x] Feature-flag gated rollout (default disabled for Private installs) Commits summary: see commits list above. Files changed: high-level files enumerated above; migrations/20260115_add_variant_semver.sql contains the backfill logic (non-destructive: adds columns nullable then populates). Backfill approach: infer semver from existing release notes and timestamps where possible; when ambiguous default to 0.0.PATCH with a generated stamp to avoid false major/minor bumps. Review thread summary: - Marek: asked for explicit rules for what triggers MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH and requested unit tests that simulate tokenizer changes vs profile-only changes. - Aisha: added a deterministic tokenizer-change detector heuristics and tests in test/integration/stamp_backfill_test.go; clarified MAJOR rule in docs with examples. - Kimberly: flagged that the proto change could break older SDKs; requested compatibility note and version negotiation. - Aisha: added compatibility shim and updated api migration notes; SDK teams will be notified separately for a minor SDK bump. - Luis: requested the backfill be reversible; added migration that keeps an audit table with prior values to support rollback for Private installs. CI: initial run showed a docs lint failure and an intermittent integration timeout; fixed both by reformatting docs and adding retry logic to the backfill test. Final CI: all checks passed (unit, integration, lint). Merge notes: squashed and merged to main on 2026-01-22 via squash merge; release will be gated behind the feature flag and accompany a model-registry minor release. Impact and follow-ups: - RK: release notes generator now consumes profile_stamp to produce per-variant changelogs. - SDK teams: coordinate minor version bump to surface semver fields. - Ops: run backfill in staging and approve before enabling feature flag in production. Related work: ENG-7923 (onboard automation), ENG-7987 (changelog tooling), PM-451 (product requirements).
Introduce semantic versioning guidelines for model variants and an immutable profile-stamp attached to variant metadata. Adds DB migration, API fields, CLI utilities, docs and tests. No runtime breaking changes; rollout gated via feature flag.
payload.title: Semver guidelines and profile-stamp for model variants

payload.body:
Motivation: We frequently see tail latency regressions that only appear for particular sequence-length distributions. Existing workload runners produce aggregate token-level metrics but do not attribute variance to model kernels or layers. This PR adds a 'kernel-variance prober' that runs focused microbenchmarks across sequence length windows and collects fine-grained per-kernel timing and variance profiles so we can prioritize kernel/graph-level optimizations and targeted quantization tradeoffs. Change summary: - New binary tools/bench/prober/kernel_variance_prober.py: orchestrates probing campaigns across sequence-length buckets, random seeds, and batch shapes; supports warmup/steady-state detection and adaptive sampling. - Benchmark harness extensions bench/harness/sequence_sampler.py: sequence-length aware samplers and an API to plug sampling policies into existing runners. - Profiling exporter bench/reporters/kernel_variance_reporter.go: aggregates raw kernel timing logs into per-layer heatmaps and high-variance segment reports; outputs ndjson for downstream ingestion. - Integration test bench/tests/test_kernel_variance_endtoend.py: small runtime smoke verifying consistent profiling across CPU/GPU backends. - CI job .github/workflows/benchmark-prober.yml: a lightweight workflow that runs the prober in a constrained emulation mode for PRs to prevent regression in core loops. Why this is different: instead of only measuring latency or throughput aggregates, the prober attributes variance to kernel implementations (attention, rotary, layernorm, matmul) and to sequence-length regions which helps routing, batching and kernel-selection decisions in the serving runtime. Usage notes: the prober can be invoked locally with `tools/prober/run_prober --profile-config examples/probes/length_scan.yaml`; output is an ndjson stream consumable by the reporting pipeline. Backwards compatibility: no runtime or serving changes; this is a benchmark-only change. Rollout plan: land as experimental tooling behind a feature flag; run nightly full-resolution campaigns for critical models and surface regressions in the benchmark dashboard.
Priya Desai: Why use a fixed bucket width for sequence lengths? Suggest exposing a percentile-based bucket option to handle long-tail requests.
Tomás Ortega: Reply: added percentile-based bucketing and an adaptive mode that switches based on observed distribution (see sequence_sampler changes).
Ethan Park: CI shows a sporadic flake on the GPU smoke test (test_kernel_variance_endtoend.py::test_profile_consistency). Can we add retry logic or increase warmup?
Tomás Ortega: Reply: increased warmup and added deterministic RNG seed for the smoke CI; moved flaky path behind --ci-emulation flag. Reran CI and green.
Marta Kovacs: Suggest clarifying NDJSON schema in reporter docs and adding an example of how to import into the dashboard ingestion pipeline.
Tomás Ortega: Reply: added docs/bench/kernel-variance-prober.md with schema and ingestion steps.

Motivation: intermittent microbursts and KV-cache invalidation were causing non-deterministic p95 regressions in our seq-mix benchmarks. This PR introduces a new benchmark harness, the Interleaved Sequence Fuzz Runner, that generates correlated interleaved request sequences with configurable sample weights and interleaving patterns, plus a lightweight KV-cache checkpointing layer to exercise cache hits/misses deterministically with replay. Design: the runner composes three primitives: a sequence fuzzer (pattern generator with Markov-backed probability matrices), an interleaver (controls request interleaving and overlap window), and a sampler that attaches weights to sequences to reproduce real-world token distribution skew. The KV-cache checkpointing records and replays KV cache state at configurable checkpoints so we can deterministically reproduce cache-dependent tail latency. Implementation: new binary 'seq-fuzz-runner' under tools/bench, modular Go code with an external JSON workload spec (examples/seq-fuzz-specs/), and a small Python reporting adaptor that converts run traces into the benchmark-lab event schema. This PR includes: - deterministic checkpoint format (binary v1) and migration shim - sample-weighted scheduler that supports per-sequence and per-token weights - interleaving modes: round-robin, burst, poisson-mix - an end-to-end example and README with tuning knobs and cost/perf tradeoffs - integration with existing runner harness and the aggregate reporter API See linked Linear tickets ENG-1492 and ENG-1510 for acceptance criteria. For reproducibility, add --seed flag and deterministic KV checkpointing. Related: this ties into the profiling baselines work for stable-region detection. Performance summary from local runs: median p95 improved in synthetic replay by 0-2ms under light load; under heavy interleaving we observe increased dispatch jitter which our scheduler telemetry now captures (new metrics: seq_fuzz.interleave_jitter_seconds, seq_fuzz.kvcache_hit_ratio).

This PR introduces the 'Heterogeneous Momentum Load Weaver' (weaver) and a complementary 'Flakemap' exporter for the benchmark-lab. Motivation: existing runners synthesize steady and bursty traffic well but do not model temporal autocorrelation (momentum) across session cohorts or expose kernel-conditional flaky behaviour in a compact visualization. The weaver generates multi-tenant, multi-model traffic with tunable momentum parameters per cohort, allowing experiments that interpolate between purely IID request streams and long-memory traffic bursts. The Flakemap exporter generates a kernel-aware instability map that correlates intermittent error spikes and elevated tail latencies with the serving kernel and sequence-length buckets, helping debug regressions introduced by kernel selection or quantization profiles. Key changes: 1) benchlab/weaver/weaver.py: new weaver core that composes cohort definitions, momentum kernels, and inter-cohort correlations; supports seedable RNGs for deterministic replay. 2) benchlab/exporters/flakemap.py: exporter that consumes telemetry summaries and emits tiled SVG/JSON flakemaps and a minimal CSV breakdown for downstream analysis. 3) benchlab/configs/weaver_presets.yaml: several curated workload presets (low momentum, bursty momentum, long-tail-primed) used by CI and local profiling. 4) tests/test_weaver_end2end.py: end-to-end harness that validates determinism, basic throughput envelopes and verifies flakemap output invariants. 5) docs/bench/weaver.md: usage recipes, suggested L0/L1 workloads for kernel attribution, and integration notes to the baseline regression pipeline. Design notes and distinguishing behavior: the weaver exposes two momentum primitives: persistent momentum (cohort-level drift where the recent request rate biases the near future) and sticky primer (where priming sequences cause repeated cache-favorable paths). Both primitives are parameterized so teams can stress different warmup and KV cache behaviors. The Flakemap exporter produces a compact view that aligns time-slices, kernel versions, and sequence-length strata to reveal correlated anomalies. Compatibility: the tool integrates with existing benchlab telemetry; outputs are compatible with the benchmark-lab trace-summary v2 schema and can be pushed to the existing reporting S3 bucket or local artifacts folder. Tests and validation: included unit tests for stochastic invariants, a small smoke harness that runs on Github Actions using a reduced synthetic model to validate CI, and a sampling job that generated a 1k-run sample set used in local perf review. Performance impact: minimal on the benchlab harness itself (the weaver is a generator, not a serving path); CI runs were kept light by default and full fidelity presets are gated behind an environment variable. How to use: install benchlab via dev-env, run benchlab-weaver --preset=burst-momentum --duration=10m --out=artifacts/ then use benchlab-flakemap --input=artifacts/summary.json --out=artifacts/flakemap.svg. Rollout plan: land PR in main behind feature flag set to false by default, enable for perf engineers and SRE on-demand, add canary job to nightly to ensure no regression in p95/p99 variance. Backwards compatibility: no changes to existing runners or playback formats unless the flakemap CSV output is explicitly consumed. Related items: ENG-2121 (design + evaluation plan), ENG-2987 (CI integration for nightly coverage).

Motivation: Long-tail cost and latency events are often seeded by poor KV-cache priming and temporal clustering of rare long responses. This PR adds a compact "stochastic temporal surgeon" runner that synthesizes skewed-length session traces and a cost-aware prefill synthesizer that tries different prefill budgets to measure KV-cache efficacy vs. token-cost tradeoffs.

What this PR contains: - New runner `temporal_surgeon` that emits session traces with controllable long-tail injection (frequency, amplitude, burst-width) and optional per-session primer sequences. - Cost-aware prefill component (harness + Python evaluation) that experiments with prefix budgets and reports token-cost vs P95 latency and quality deltas. - Compact reporting pipeline that produces a Phase Alignment Heatmap (compact NDJSON) mapping token-phase occupancy to kernel-level hotpoints for quick triage. - CI integration: lightweight end-to-end smoke tests and a resource-limited integration test for the runner so it can be exercised on CI without large infra.

Why unique: unlike previous burst/replayer tools, this focuses on (1) surgical long-tail insertion at epoch boundaries, (2) coupling cost-models into prefill strategy permutation testing, and (3) a small, human-readably compact heatmap format intended for rapid on-call inspection and automated alerting.

Usage: see README at benchmark-lab/runners/temporal_surgeon/README.md for example CLI invocations and sample config YML. Typical invocation: `bl-runner temporal-surgeon --seed 42 --longtail-rate 0.02 --burst-width 8 --prefill-budget 32`

Notes: this is intentionally small-footprint; the runtime runner is written in Rust with a thin Python harness for result aggregation and cost-model sweeps. The PR includes benchmark vectors used in our internal perf-suite and a short tutorial notebook for exploratory analysis.

Context and motivation: As we onboard more open and proprietary model variants, cross-model interference and tokenization differences are recurring blind spots when we compare latency and quality across workloads. This PR adds two companion tools: a multi-model concurrency matrix generator that synthesizes cross-traffic scenarios and a tokenization-fidelity reporter that quantifies variance introduced by different tokenizers across model families. || Summary of changes: 1) new CLI matrix_generator that builds traffic matrices from a config specifying model mixes, sequence-length distributions, and concurrency envelopes; 2) sampling engine that produces deterministic epochal workloads with priority-prefetch hints for KV-cache priming; 3) tokenization_fidelity reporter that runs a set of prompts through multiple tokenizer implementations, computes per-token alignment and split variance, and serializes compact differential reports for downstream dashboards; 4) small baseline dataset and example notebook; 5) CI perf-e2e pipeline step that takes a snapshot and uploads flamegraphs. || Commits: (see commits list). || Files changed (high level): added generator and sampler python modules, new reporter and serializer, tests, CI perf job, docs and example notebook. || Testing and CI: Local unit test coverage > 92% for new modules; integrated end-to-end perf job included in this PR. Context: We regularly see long tail latency correlated with inefficient prefetch and kernel hotpath contention in multi-tenant inference runs. This PR introduces two pieces: 1) a Prefetch Trajectory Synthesizer (PTS) — a workload generator that emits synthetic request sequences with parameterized prefetch patterns and correlated KV-cache warmup behavior; 2) a Hardware-Annotated Flamegrid Reporter (HAFR) — a reporting backend that merges kernel-level telemetry (sched, cycles, L2 misses) and eBPF-marked span timing into a tiled flamegrid visualization.
Motivation: existing workload runners exercise request shape and sequence length distributions but do not surface prefetch timing dynamics or attribute kernel-level hotspots across sequences. PTS lets us systematically explore prefetch timing (lead/lag), batch coalescing, and KV cache priming strategies. HAFR lets perf engineers and runtime authors see which kernel or driver path is responsible for flame hotspots and how they align to sequence positions and batch boundaries.
Summary of changes: - New workload generator binary bench/pts/pts_runner (go) with a config-driven DSL for trajectory parameters (lead_ms, jitter_pct, kv_primer_fraction, primer_strategy). - Integrations so PTS can be launched from the e2e bench harness and recorded as a named traffic profile. - New reporter backend bench/reporters/flamegrid_hardware which consumes trace spans + kernel counters exported by our eBPF collector and outputs an annotated JSON+SVG package. - Lightweight aggregation service bench/reporters/annotator which correlates per-request spans with kernel slices by matching pids/timestamps and a small fuzzy-window alignment. - Test harness updates to run PTS profiles in the multi-node simulator and emit HAFR artifacts into the artifacts bucket for historical comparison.
Checklist: - [x] PTS runner basic API and config parsing - [x] PTS integration with bench harness and simulator - [x] eBPF marker consumption and alignment logic - [x] Flamegrid renderer (SVG + compact JSON) - [x] Unit tests for alignment heuristics - [x] End-to-end smoke runs and baseline artifact generation - [x] Documentation: bench/pts/README.md and bench/reporters/README.md
How to exercise locally: - make bench-pts-run PROFILE=trajectory_small - collects systrace + eBPF counters into tmp/artifacts/ - benchctl compare --left baseline/2025-11-01 --right tmp/artifacts/
Key design notes: - PTS generates deterministic pseudo-random sequences when a seed is provided so diffs are reproducible. - Alignment between spans and kernel slices uses a 5ms default fuzzy window but exposes configuration per-run to account for clock skew across nodes. - To keep the reporter lightweight we do coarse-grained kernel attribution (hot kernel symbol or driver path) rather than full-stack unwinding; this keeps CPU overhead under 3% in our smoke runs.
Performance and findings: - Synthetic runs with PTS profile 'lead_heavy' reproduced a previously-observed p99 amplification where late prefetch (lead_ms < 2ms) caused +18% p99 tail due to small-batch kernel context churn. - Using PTS to test an altered batching policy reduced p95 by 9% and p99 by 12% in the single-GPU microcluster when combined with a 4ms aggressive primer window. - HAFR artifacts made it trivial to see that a particular driver path (nvml power read) correlated with micro-bursts; this surfaced a driver polling behavior we adjusted in the runtime.
Backwards compatibility: the reporter outputs the same compact flame JSON schema we already use; the annotated fields are optional so older visualization tools ignore them.
Security considerations: the eBPF collector needs root to capture kernel counters; the reporter runs as part of in-house CI-only bench agents — no customer data is shipped.
Related linear: ENG-9145 (prefetch study), ENG-9201 (reporting enhancements).
Release notes: ["Introduce Prefetch Trajectory Synthesizer (PTS) to generate prefetch-aware benchmark workloads.", "Add Hardware-Annotated Flamegrid Reporter (HAFR) to correlate kernel telemetry with span timing.", "New bench artifacts available under artifacts/prefetch_trajectory/* for historical comparison."]

Motivation: Multi-arm experiments and noisy traffic patterns made our rigid canary lanes brittle for long-running A/B tests. Liquid staging introduces flexible staging lanes that dynamically allocate traffic across arms using a safety-aware scheduler and provides deterministic rollback snapshots. This PR implements the protocol, the scheduler, runtime hooks, a console surface, and end-to-end tests.

What it does: Liquid staging creates ephemeral 'lanes' that can absorb shadow traffic, warm KV caches, and run gradual ramping across multiple arms simultaneously. A central rollback scheduler tracks per-lane safety signals (latency, error-rate, key-quality metrics) and computes rollback watermarks; when thresholds are breached a coordinated rollback snapshot is applied to affected lanes. The scheduler also supports holdpoints for manual verification and automatic fallthrough to a fallback variant.

Design notes: Uses a two-phase commit-like staging handshake: (1) recruit: create lane, attach shadow stream, start warmup; (2) flow: start phased traffic allocation with smoothing windows; (3) commit: promote lane, drain older lanes. Rollback snapshots are lightweight meta snapshots (routing + pinned model version + KV-clear flags) to guarantee deterministic reversion. Metrics gating is pluggable via policy DSL (policy.v1) and integrates with existing SLO gates.

Files changed: runtime scheduler, rollout controller, API surface (rollouts.v1), console UX, docs, helm values, and new e2e harness.

Testing: unit tests for scheduling heuristics, integration tests simulating multi-arm traffic bursts, and a staging replay harness used to validate rollback determinism. CI had one flaky integration test (staging_replay_test) which required a retry; subsequent rerun passed.

Migration/compatibility: Backwards compatible with existing canary APIs. New features are opt-in via rolloutStrategy: "liquid". If not set, controllers behave as before.

Motivation: reproducing long-tail latency behavior in the wild has been difficult because traces alone don't capture prefetch/priming behavior and cross-frontend priority shifts. This PR introduces an epochal prefetch replayer that replays historical sessions in time-epochs while simulating prefetch priming, background eviction, and prioritized request redistribution across simulated frontends. The goal is to produce repeatable, high-fidelity tail events for regression testing and to surface actionable knobs (prefetch window, eviction resilience, priority redistribution) for the serving runtime and Dedicated autoscaler.

What this change does: 1) Adds a replay engine that groups trace events into epochs (time windows) and runs each epoch with configurable prefetch phases where KV cache priming requests are issued prior to main traffic. Prefetches can be prioritized by key hotness and sequence position. 2) Adds a priority redistributor that simulates cross-front-end weight shifts (e.g., when routing policies change or a host becomes saturated) and injects gradual traffic shifts during an epoch to recreate redistributive tail amplification. 3) Adds a reporter that emits epoch-level snapshots (p50/p95/p99/p999 latency histograms), per-kernel flamepoint markers, prefix-KV hit/miss time series, and a compact recommendation blob with suggested prefetch window sizes and batching thresholds. 4) Provides a small Dockerized harness and example configs for running deterministically in CI or locally.

Why this is unique: existing runners focus on synthetic mixes or sequence-phase fuzzers; this PR emphasizes temporal cohesion (epoch boundaries), explicit prefetch simulation, and redistribution dynamics that we observed in production incidents where tail events correlated with rapid route weight changes. The tool is intended to sit alongside other benchmark-lab runners as an integration-level stress test for the serving runtime and caching strategies.

Checklist (intent-to-merge): - [x] Implementation: replay engine, redistributor, reporter - [x] Unit tests for epoch boundary correctness and prefetch ordering - [x] Integration smoke that runs a 3-epoch replay in CI container - [x] Documentation: bench/README.md and example configs - [x] Performance sanity: reproducible p99 regression on synthetic incident trace

How to run (short): docker build -t epoch-replayer . && docker run --rm -v $PWD/examples:/work/examples epoch-replayer --config /work/examples/prefetch-config.yaml --epochs 3 --seed 42

Related work and references: ENG-4267 (incident triage: redistributive tail amplification), ENG-4299 (kvcache eviction profiling). See bench/configs/prefetch-config.yaml for parameterization.

Test plan and observed numbers: CI runs the smoke replay (3 epochs, 10k sessions) in ~8m on a ci-large runner. Local runs with a synthetic incident trace reproduced a 35% increase in p99 when prefetch window was disabled vs enabled (prefetch window = 200ms used in recommendation). The reporter includes raw histograms and a compact CSV meant for downstream ingestion into the telemetry pipeline.

Rollback/compat: purely additive under bench/; no runtime changes. If the tool causes flakiness in CI the revert is trivial (revert this PR).

Files touched (high-level): bench/replayer/epochal_replayer.go, bench/replayer/prefetch_scheduler.go, bench/reporter/epoch_reporter.py, bench/configs/prefetch-config.yaml, Dockerfile.bench, bench/tests/test_epoch_replayer.go, bench/README.md

Motivation: Cold-starts and short-context sessions continue to dominate tail latency in our production traces. Existing warmup priming is static and either over-primes (wasting tokens) or under-primes (leaving kernels cold). This PR introduces a hybrid warmup orchestrator that combines a short lived aggressive primer for the first few requests and a decaying primer estimator that gradually reduces primer tokens as sequence history accrues. Design: 1) hybrid_warmup.py implements the orchestrator and a configurable schedule engine, supporting exponential and linear decay profiles; 2) a small estimator component computes an initial primer length based on recent session entropy and model tokenization characteristics; 3) primer caches are stored in a lightweight LRU keyed by session fingerprint with explicit TTLs to avoid warmup amplification; 4) a new decay_profile_reporter exports per-session warmup token counts, p95 latency delta vs baseline, and primer hit/miss ratios to the bench telemetry pipeline. Tests: unit tests for decay math and estimator heuristics, integration smoke in the bench harness against a 2-model local stack, and a deterministic replay test that asserts no worse than 3% regression on median latency for long sessions. Rollout plan: staged Canary via the perf-canary harness with traffic split 0.5/5/20/100 and automatic rollback on latency regression >5% at p95. Context and motivation: Microbench reporters in benchmark-lab currently emit per-sample traces and event-aligned latency points which are powerful but expensive to store/aggregate for long-running experiments. This PR introduces a 'latency-slab-stitcher' stage that composes contiguous microbench segments into time-aligned 'slabs' and applies a lightweight hotpath annotator that attributes slab-level latency spikes to kernel groups (hotcalls) using sampled stack markers. The goal is to reduce storage, produce stable slab-level p95/p99 curves for long runs, and provide a practical bridge between microbench traces and high-level flame/hotpath reporting. Design summary: - Slabs are fixed-duration windows (configurable, default 1s) annotated with aggregated token counts, request counts, p50/p95/p99, and an entropy score. - Stitcher accepts both real-time stream input (Kafka / kinesis ingest adapters) and offline segment lists (local JSONL). - Hotpath annotator samples kernel tags emitted by the runtime and maintains frequency-weighted attribution per slab, producing a compact hotpath summary for each slab. - Output is compatible with existing compact-telemetry-parquet exporter and the new slab-metrics API in the observability-pack. Checklist: - [x] implement slab windowing and merge semantics - [x] add hotpath annotator and attribution heuristics - [x] streaming and offline ingest adapters - [x] unit tests for aggregation invariants - [x] end-to-end integration test with compact exporter - [x] docs: README and quickstart snippet Usage notes and how to run locally: - Quickstart: tools/slab-stitch/README.md contains a docker-compose harness that spins up a local kafka and a sample microbench generator. - Command: ./bin/slab-stitch --input sample-segments.jsonl --window 1000 --output slabs.jsonl - To run as a streaming pipeline, use tools/slab-stitch/deploy/kinesis.yaml and set KINESIS_STREAM env var. Backward compatibility: the stitcher emits the same metric names used by legacy reporters plus a new 'slab.hotpath' namespace. Existing dashboards will display slab-level aggregated time series automatically when the slab exporter is wired. Two requests: (1) make slab windowing deterministic for edge-aligned timestamps (documented), and (2) consider a simple top-k threshold for hotpath so low-noise noise doesn't appear in dashboards." - Author (Aisha): "Agreed on determinism; added a timestamp-normalize step and documented it in windower.rs. For hotpath, implemented top-k with a configurable min-weight threshold; default filters noise while preserving regressions." - Owen Grant (reviewer): "Can we add a small benchmark targeting overhead of annotator at 10k req/s? We should ensure stitcher doesn't become a bottleneck." - Author: "Added microbench harness under tests/perf/slab_annotator_bench.rs and included CI smoke job with 10k req/s run (short) to validate overhead." - Ravi Menon (approver): "LGTM after resolving one nit about log level and adding a changelog entry." - Author: "Addressed nits, updated changelog." Motivation: Current benchmark runners assume stationary arrival processes (Poisson / constant QPS) which under-represent real production patterns (startup ramps, diurnal drift, heavy-tailed burst windows, and sporadic degradations). This PR introduces a configurable nonstationary load pacer plus a boundary-aware sampler to ensure representative tail coverage, and a compact quantile-drift reporter for automated regression detection.

What this changes: - New pacer module (bench/pacers/nonstationary_pacer.py) that synthesizes time-varying arrival rates via piecewise-defined functions (ramps, sinusoids, burst impulses, step changes) and supports a user-specified schedule file. The pacer exposes deterministic seeds, repeatable epoching, and optional jitter models to exercise scheduler jitter in the runtime. - Boundary-aware sampler (bench/samplers/boundary_sampler.py) which prioritizes generating traces that hit sequence-length boundaries, KV cache cold boundaries, and precise token-offset windows. It implements adaptive oversampling for rare boundary events while keeping global QPS budget intact. - Quantile drift reporter (bench/reporters/quantile_drift_reporter.py) that collects sliding-window quantiles (p50/p90/p95/p99) per-cohort and emits a compact drift histogram plus a CSV/JSON payload suitable for downstream aggregation. The reporter computes Wasserstein distance and an asymmetric drift score to prioritize regressions that affect tails more than medians. - Integration harness updates: runner config schema extended (bench/configs/nonstationary_examples.yaml), CI workload profile (ci/bench_profiles/ci_nonstationary.yaml) and a lightweight end-to-end integration test that runs a 30s diurnal+burst scenario on a small local runner to validate determinism.

Checklist: - [x] Core pacer implementation with API and unit tests - [x] Sampler implementation with focused unit tests for boundary coverage - [x] Quantile drift reporter with unit tests and example outputs - [x] Integration test + CI profile - [x] Docs: short README with usage examples and config reference

Compatibility notes: The pacer is additive — existing stationary profiles remain supported. Default behavior without a schedule file is backward-compatible (falls back to constant QPS). No runtime API changes to serving binaries; all changes live in the benchmark-lab harness.

Performance notes: On local CI profile (30s diurnal + burst) the end-to-end harness added ~0.8s of overhead per 60s window due to extra sampling bookkeeping; this is acceptable for offline benchmark runs and the reporter is low-overhead (sub-1% CPU in our microbench runs).

Related work: ENG-4123 (represent real-world arrival patterns), ENG-4189 (improve tail coverage), SUP-2241 (support ticket requesting diurnal scenario for a customer incident).

How to run: see bench/README.md -> Section "Nonstationary pacer" for a full invocation; quick start: python -m bench.runner --profile ci_nonstationary.yaml --seed 42.

Notes on determinism and seeding: The pacer accepts a global seed that deterministically generates the schedule + jitter stream. The integration test asserts byte-for-byte identical sequence IDs and timestamp offsets when run with the same seed and host time zone.

Risks and follow-ups: - We added more knobs which can be misused; documented recommended presets for CI vs. long-running fidelity tests. - Follow-ups: add a Flink-based aggregator for large-scale runs (ENG-4216).
Evan Park (reviewer): Can we guarantee determinism across platforms? timezone / clock differences have bitten us before.
Maya Chen (author): The pacer uses monotonic offsets and serializes event timestamps relative to epoch-0 in the harness; we added a deterministic timezone-agnostic checkpoint in the integration test. See test_nonstationary_pacer.py for the assertion.
Diego Valdez (reviewer): Metric names look fine but please use canonical prefix bench.quantile_drift.* to avoid collisions with runtime metrics.
Maya Chen (author): Updated metric prefix and added a small mapping function in reporter; pushed fix (de4f219).
Ruth Almeida (reviewer): The oversampling factor could blow up overall token budget if misconfigured — can we cap it?
Maya Chen (author): Added a configurable max_oversample parameter and a hard cap in the sampler to ensure global QPS budget is respected. Added tests verifying the cap behaviour.

Motivation: We have observed intermittent small regressions when model-serving uses aggressive token interleaving combined with dynamic kernel selection under transient GPU contention. These regressions are low-frequency in perf runs and difficult to reproduce with existing drivers. This PR introduces two pieces: 1) a token-interleaving fidelity validator (ti-validator) that replays representative interleaved request streams against a golden model execution trace and flags divergence in token timing/ordering and soft-quality regressions; 2) a GPU-throttle simulator that injects controlled, time-bound reductions in available streaming multiprocessors / simulated clock to exercise scheduling pathologies. The overall goal is to make low-rate correctness/latency anomalies reproducible in CI and local experiments. Changes in this PR: - new bin/ti-validator: a reproducible runner that accepts recorded request traces (jsonl) and a golden token trace, outputs per-step divergence metrics and a small ASCII timeline for quick triage; - new bench/sim/gpu_throttle: small simulator that integrates with the lab harness and toggles simulated capacity windows and per-kernel latency multipliers; - telemetry hooks: per-step tags emitted to the lab metrics pipeline (labels: ti_run_id, throttle_profile, seed); - CI test: a deterministic unit test that runs the ti-validator on a micro-trace and expects zero divergence; - docs: README + usage examples and a short guide for adding new throttle profiles. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked in Linear ENG-9102; - [x] unit + integration tests; - [x] telemetry + tagging; - [x] basic docs and quickstart; - [x] bench harness integration. Commits: ["Initial ti-validator binary and core replay loop (maya/ti-validator)", "Add gpu_throttle simulator and throttle profiles (maya/gpu-sim)", "Telemetry tags + metric adapters (maya/telemetry)", "Tests and docs; fix flakiness in timeline assert (maya/fixes)"] Changed areas (high-level): - bin/ti-validator.py: core replay and divergence heuristics - bench/sim/gpu_throttle.py: capacity windowing and kernel slowdown hooks - lab/harness/injectors.py: small adapter to enable throttle profiles in CI runs - telemetry/adapters/bench_metrics.py: emit tags and counters - tests/ti_validator_test.py: deterministic microtrace test - docs/benchmark-lab/ti-validator.md: usage and adding profiles Review conversation summary: "Arjun: Please add a safety cap on total simulated slowdown; observed a local run stall at 10x slowdown. Response (Maya): Added a global cap and an exponential backoff for the simulator; updated tests to validate no stall. Lina: Can we make the validator tolerant to benign non-determinism (timing jitter) by using a configurable epsilon and sample window? Response (Maya): Added windowed matching with configurable epsilon and documented default thresholds; left a flag --strict for deep debugging. Benji: Telemetry tags look good, but please ensure sensitive payloads are never emitted. Response (Maya): Validator only emits token ids/hashes and timing deltas; added a scrubber and documented privacy bounds. CI notes: Initial run showed one flaky integration test that timed out under simulated throttle; test timeout increased and harness made deterministic by pinning rng seed. Final CI: all checks passed (unit, lint, integration, bench-smoke). Merge: squash-merged into main after approvals from Arjun and Lina. Risk assessment: Low-medium. This is test/harness code only but touches telemetry and the harness adapter; careful when enabling throttle profiles in production-like experiments. How to use: 1) capture trace with bench/recorder; 2) run bin/ti-validator --trace mytrace.jsonl --golden golden.tokens --throttle low_latency_profile; 3) inspect divergence report and timeline.
Adds a token-interleaving fidelity validator and a lightweight GPU throttle simulator used by the benchmark lab to validate correctness/reliability of batching + interleaving under transient GPU contention. No user-facing API changes.

Motivation: Our existing benchmark harness runs monolithic saturation ramps that obscure transient hotpath contention and cross-model interference. This PR adds a token-cascade stager: a lightweight runner that issues staged token batches that intentionally vary prefix overlap, interleaving, and KV-cache priming to reveal cascade saturation behavior at sub-second granularity. It also includes a saturation-curve emulator that synthesizes throughput/latency curves for a model+kernel configuration by replaying staged cohorts across concurrency buckets. This helps diagnostics for scheduling, kernel hint selection, and batching heuristics. Changes: - New runner: benchmark/token_cascade_stager.py (config-driven; YAML templates for stage definitions) - Emulator: bench/saturation_curve_emulator.go (parallel probes, per-stage warmup, statistical aggregator) - Reporter: tools/cascade_reporter.ts (CSV + compact JSONL outputs; adds stage metadata and kernel hints) - Test harness updates: bench/harness/runner_integration_test.py and bench/harness/testdata/cascade_examples.yaml - Minor runtime hook: runtime/hints/kern_hint_registry.cc to accept optional stage-derived affinity hints - CI: new perf job config .github/workflows/perf-cascade.yml Checklist: - [x] Stage definition format documented in bench/README.md - [x] Unit tests for YAML parser and reporter - [x] Integration sanity run on small cluster - [x] Perf run with baseline (main) and new runner for comparison Performance notes: Initial runs on c6g-style GPU cluster (8 nodes) produced clear S-curve saturation where models with large KV footprints switch to degraded tail latency at 65-70% token throughput; the cascade stager exposes a microburst window where batching improves p95 but increases p99 for some kernels. See reporter outputs attached as artifacts in CI. Backwards compatibility: Runner is opt-in, harness defaults unchanged. Linear/Jira: ENG-5483 primary ticket, SUP-2241 reproducer. Risks and mitigations: Synthetic stage patterns may not reflect production prompt distribution; we included templating and a corpus of real prefixes to minimize divergence. Follow-ups: integrate stage-derived kernel hints with the scheduler scoring function (ENG-5591).

Introduce a new composite session synthesizer that generates realistic, correlated multi-session workloads and an accompanying low-overhead kernel-sampling probe for fine-grained per-kernel latency attribution. Motivation: existing synthetic runners produced independent requests which under-represented burst coupling and payload-correlated cache effects observed in production request traces. This change provides: 1) a client-side session graph model (user/session/action) that emits sequences with configurable interleaving, payload-size correlation, and sequence-length distributions; 2) a payload correlator that ties input payload templates to expected tokenization/seq-length distributions so benchmarks reflect real token mixes; 3) a kernel-sampling probe that periodically samples active kernel execution timings (aggregate histogramed) with <2% overhead in our microbench harness; 4) a reporter that produces per-run artifacts (sequence-mix.json, kernel-sample.csv, session-latency-breakdown.csv) for downstream analysis and flamepoint visualization. The description below covers design choices, how to run locally and in CI, and a short compatibility note. Design highlights: use streaming priming to warm KV cache for long-running sessions, synthetic user graph allows hotspot routing to simulate tenant-localized traffic, and the kernel sampler hooks into the existing runtime tracer with a bounded sampler to avoid perturbing tail latency. Backwards compatibility: the new runner is opt-in under bench manifests; existing suites are unaffected. Checklist: [x] tests and integration harness added  [x] docs snippet in README.md  [x] perf baseline recorded and attached  [x] initial CI matrix passed  Related Linear: ENG-1874, ENG-2359. Related PRs: benchmark-lab/pr-43910 (session-primer), perf-canary/pr-731 (canary integration).

Context: The new Cost Model what-if endpoint is intentionally flexible (batching/caching/quantization knobs) and will be called by Optimize (interactive) and potentially Console (hot paths). In early staging tests and after SUP-31877 triage, we saw two failure modes: (1) callers passing extreme parameter values (e.g., batch size 4096, cache warm-rate > 1.0) leading to unrealistic savings outputs, and (2) expensive computations when callers submit high-cardinality workload summaries (large histograms / too many route keys) that can blow our latency budget and increase tail p95s. This PR adds explicit policy guardrails at the API boundary so the service is safe-by-default, deterministic, and bounded. Summary of changes: (A) Introduce a centralized PolicyGuardrails layer for what-if requests that validates and clamps input ranges (where clamping is explicitly allowed) and rejects invalid/unsafe requests with clear error codes. (B) Enforce request bounds for cardinality: max number of workload segments, max histogram buckets, max distinct route/model keys, and max scenario count per request. (C) Add a compute budget heuristic: estimate worst-case complexity from the request and reject if above threshold (protects CPU and avoids unbounded fanout to model catalog/telemetry lookups). (D) Add an allowlist for parameterized what-if dimensions in v1 (batching, prefix-cache, kv-cache, quant profile change) and explicitly reject unknown/experimental dimensions unless the caller is in an internal allowlist (feature flag + service-to-service identity). (E) Standardize error responses for guardrail failures: HTTP 400 with error_code=CM_GUARDRAIL_* for caller-correctable issues; HTTP 403 for forbidden dimensions/tenancy; HTTP 429 for rate-limit triggers; and a consistent message + remediation hints so Optimize can surface actionable UI text. Guardrails (v1): - scenario_count: max 10 scenarios per request; - workload_segments: max 25 segments (Optimize currently uses <= 8); - histogram buckets: max 32 buckets for seq_len distribution and max 32 for output_len distribution; - route/model keys: max 50 distinct keys; - batch_size_target: [1, 256] (reject outside); - microbatch_size_target: [1, 64]; - cache_hit_rate: [0.0, 1.0] (reject outside; no clamping); - cache_warm_rate: [0.0, 1.0] (reject outside; note: renamed internally to warm_rate to avoid ambiguity); - quantization_profile_id: must exist in model catalog and must be compatible with base model; - overhead_allocation_policy: must be one of {request_attributable_only, blended_cluster_overhead}; - max_estimated_compute_units: 1.0 (internal scale); reject above threshold. Observability: adds metrics cost_model.whatif.guardrail_reject_total{reason=...} and cost_model.whatif.request_shape{segments=...,buckets=...,scenarios=...} to support tuning. Also adds structured log fields guardrail_reason and request_shape_summary for incident triage. Tests: unit tests for validation + error mapping; golden tests ensuring deterministic output and stable error codes; load-test fixture ensuring guardrails prevent worst-case request shapes from entering compute. Notes: This PR intentionally rejects requests rather than silently clamping in most cases, to avoid producing misleading ROI estimates. The only clamping performed is for missing optional fields that have safe defaults (e.g., absent cache_hit_rate defaults to observed baseline). Follow-ups: (1) coordinate with Optimize to align UI input widgets with these ranges and surface error_code messages; (2) document guardrails in internal docs; (3) revisit limits after we collect two weeks of production telemetry on request shapes and latency.
Jonas Weber: Can we avoid clamping at all? It’s dangerous for ROI calculations. Also please ensure we can represent uncertainty later without widening the request shape. Ethan Park: Agreed. The only clamping left is for missing optional baseline fields (safe defaults). Out-of-range values will be rejected with CM_GUARDRAIL_RANGE and a remediation message. Aditya Rao: Optimize uses cache warm-rate in the UI right now. We need a clear contract for warm_rate vs hit_rate, otherwise support issues repeat (SUP-31877). Ethan Park: Added explicit fields warm_rate and hit_rate with bounds [0,1], and updated error messages to call out both. Also rejecting if both are provided but inconsistent with baseline_mode=observed. Sofia Ivanova: The batch_size upper bound of 256 seems low for some offline throughput sweeps, but probably correct for interactive what-if. Can we make it policy-driven per caller? Ethan Park: Implemented per-caller override behind internal allowlist (service identity + flag). Default remains 256 for safety. Rafael Mendes: Please add metrics for rejections and a dashboard-friendly reason label. Also ensure this doesn’t turn into a 5xx for bad input. Ethan Park: Added guardrail_reject_total{reason} and mapped all validation failures to 400 with stable error_code. Allison Grant: Error codes should be stable and documented; also ensure determinism (same input => same error). Ethan Park: Added error catalog in schema package and golden tests asserting exact error_code strings. Requested changes (round 1): tighten defaults, add tests for worst-case request shape, and include allowlist behavior. Addressed in commits 4-6. Approvals: Jonas, Sofia, Rafael, Allison, Aditya.

Motivation: We frequently observe latent degradation in per-token latency and memory usage when serving requests that span several thousand tokens (long-horizon dialogs or document completions). Existing benchmarks cover steady-state short- and mid-length sequences but do not reproduce interaction patterns that cause kernel backpressure, KV cache churn, or tail amplification. This PR introduces a new long-horizon sequence emulator (LHSE) and an accompanying spectral tail mapper reporter to expose frequency-domain signatures of tail events across kernels and micro-batching slots. The change is intended for the benchmark lab: a representative workload runner that exercises realistic tokenizer splits, interleaved priming and streaming steps, and session-level warmup behavior; plus a reporting pipeline that correlates latency quantiles with kernel-level sampling spectra so SRE and runtime teams can triage long-tail regressions. Changes: added runner binary and harness, new protobuf for long-horizon workload definitions, a lightweight sampler that can capture per-step telemetry, a spectral mapper module that consumes telemetry and produces per-kernel spectrograms and tail attribution summaries, e2e benchmark and unit tests, and CI matrix entries. Notable constraints: runner has a configurable memory ceiling and synthetic priming modes; the spectral mapper is offline-only (we convert to streaming in a follow-up). Backwards compatibility: no changes to existing short/mid-length benchmarks or CI presets. How to use: ./bin/lhse --config examples/long_horizon/demo.yaml to run locally; report generation: ./tools/spectral-mapper --input traces/*.ndjson --out reports/spectral-<ts>.json. Benchmarks and sample reports included in /benchmarks/long_horizon/samples. Summary of results: on a 48GB A100 instance with sequence horizon 4096 and microbatch 8 the runner produces a p95 of 74ms and a p99 of 210ms in our simulated mixed-dialog workload; spectral mapper highlights recurring kernel hotbands at attention and kvcache eviction windows. Related work: ENG-4123 (long-tail regression story), ENG-4970 (kvcache lifecycle tuning).
Representative run (A100-48GB, microbatch=8, horizon=4096): p50=22ms, p90=58ms, p95=74ms, p99=210ms. Spectral mapper indicates periodic spikes aligned with attention recompute windows and KV cache eviction; recommends exploring staggered KV checkpointing and slot-aware prefetching.
Diego Marquez: Nice approach; can you add a flag to throttle token emit rate to simulate slower clients?
Author (Aisha Khan): Added --token-rate flag in second commit; default preserves prior behavior.
Priya Patel: spectral-mapper dependency on scipy might be heavy for CI — consider optional install or wheel caching.
Author (Aisha Khan): moved scipy import to optional extras and added minimal fallback (FFT from numpy) for CI runs.
Jonah Li: tests look good; I want an example of a failing trace to exercise the mapper end-to-end.
Author (Aisha Khan): included a synthetic failure trace in samples and a short note in the README.
Adds long-horizon sequence emulator and offline spectral tail mapper for long-tail analysis. Provides new benchmark runner and reporting pipeline under benchmarks/long_horizon. No API or runtime-breaking changes. Suggested follow-ups: streaming mapper and KV prefetch probe (ENG-5241).

## Summary
This PR adds first-class mixed-workload benchmark scenarios to benchmark-lab and a standardized report generator that highlights p95 deltas vs a baseline run.

These scenarios are intended to reproduce the head-of-line blocking patterns we see under mixed prompt-length distributions (short chat prompts interleaved with long-context prompts) and to provide a stable measurement harness for the Serving Runtime scheduler prototype.

## What’s included
- New scenarios:
  - `mixed_80_20`: 80% short / 20% long requests
  - `mixed_50_50`: 50% short / 50% long requests
  - `mixed_long_spike`: time-varying mix with a "long" spike window to emulate bursty long-context traffic
- Deterministic request mix generation (seeded) so repeated runs are comparable.
- Standardized mixed-workload report:
  - Computes p50/p95 for end-to-end latency and TTFT (if enabled in the driver)
  - Computes throughput deltas
  - Emits a concise markdown summary and a machine-readable JSON artifact for downstream tooling (perf-canary / dashboards)

## Scenario definitions (high-level)
Short vs long is defined by prompt/context set selection; the scenario runner does not infer lengths from the model.
- Short set: chat-like prompts (low prefill cost, small context)
- Long set: long-context prompts (high prefill cost, larger context)

`mixed_long_spike` parameters (defaults):
- Warmup: 60s, steady state short-heavy
- Spike: 30s, long-heavy
- Cooldown: 60s, returns to steady state
All windows maintain constant RPS (the only change is class composition).

## Reporting
New report generator produces:
- `mixed_workload_summary.md` (human-readable)
- `mixed_workload_summary.json` (for automation)

Delta computation is run-to-run, keyed by metric name and scenario name:
- Baseline: `--baseline-run <artifact_path>`
- Candidate: current run

Example output excerpt (markdown):
- mixed_80_20
  - p95 e2e latency: 1820ms -> 1410ms (-22.5%)
  - p95 TTFT: 410ms -> 365ms (-11.0%)
  - throughput: 92 tok/s -> 91 tok/s (-1.1%)

## CLI usage
- Run a mixed scenario:
  - `bench run --scenario mixed_80_20 --model llama-3-70b --hardware h100 --duration 180s`
- Generate delta report vs baseline artifacts:
  - `bench report mixed --baseline-run artifacts/baseline/ --candidate-run artifacts/candidate/`

## Changed areas
- `scenarios/mixed_workload/*.yaml`: scenario definitions + window schedule for long_spike
- `drivers/request_mix.py`: seeded mix generator + time-window override support
- `reporting/mixed_workload_report.py`: computes deltas and writes MD/JSON
- `reporting/schema/*.json`: adds `mixed_workload_summary` schema version `v1`
- `docs/scenarios.md`: documents the new scenarios and knobs

## Small illustrative snippet
Added scenario config shape (YAML):
- name: mixed_80_20
  mix:
    short_weight: 0.8
    long_weight: 0.2
  seed: 1337
  duration_s: 180

## Test plan
- Local:
  - Ran `mixed_80_20` and `mixed_50_50` against dev runtime endpoint with fixed seed; verified stable class counts and report generation.
  - Validated JSON schema against sample artifact.
- CI:
  - Unit tests for mix generator and delta computation.
  - Lint/type checks.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- Perf-canary job wiring (tracked in ENG-2456) will consume `mixed_workload_summary.json` and alert on p95 regression thresholds.
- Add trace replay-backed scenario (non-synthetic) once anonymized distribution bins are finalized.

## Links
- Linear: ENG-2449 (add mixed workload benchmarks), ENG-2417 (initiative)
- Related runtime work: scheduler prototype PRs in `redwood` (classification + two-queue dispatch)

---

### Commits (summary)
1. Add mixed workload scenario YAMLs + long_spike schedule
2. Seeded request mix generator + time-window override
3. Mixed workload report generator (MD/JSON) + schema
4. Docs + examples
5. Tests + CI wiring tweaks

### Review conversation (highlights)
**Lena Fischer:** Can we guarantee determinism across python versions / platforms? Also want to ensure we don’t accidentally change RPS while changing the mix.

**Rina Kobayashi (author):** Updated mix generation to use `random.Random(seed)` locally (no global RNG) and added an assertion that total request rate remains constant per window; only class selection changes.

**Claire Dubois:** Please document what "short" and "long" mean in terms of the prompt sets. Also add a note about why we’re not using SRPT in the harness (we’re measuring scheduler policies, not simulating them here).

Motivation: We need an automated harness that stresses mixed-precision and integer-backed kernels across sequence length distributions representative of production workloads. The goal is to (1) exercise quantized code paths (q4/q8/mixed) at varying batch/seq mixes, (2) surface per-kernel latency and memory regressions, and (3) export a compact occupancy-slab histogram that ties kernel hotness to slab allocation dynamics. This PR introduces two cooperating components: a) hybrid-quant-kernel-stress-runner: a reproducible workload runner that can spawn controlled surge patterns, probe kernel fallbacks, and record per-token breakdowns; b) occupancy-slab-reporter: a reporter that consumes runner traces and emits per-epoch slab occupancy histograms, per-kernel invocation counters, and a compact CSV summary for downstream dashboards. Description of changes (high level): - New runner binary under cmd/stress-runner that supports flags for --quant-mode (fp16|q4|q8|mixed), --seq-mix (json spec), --surge-interval, --concurrency, --kv-prefill-ratio and outputs protobuf traces + compressed trace tarball. - New reporter under tools/occupancy that ingests trace tarballs and emits: slab_occupancy_<epoch>.jsonl (newline-delimited), kernel_invocation_<epoch>.csv and a small per-run summary YAML. - Small additions to benchmark lab plumbing: CI job to run a smoke stress-runner with a toy model, a trace sanitizer utility to remove secrets and nondeterministic timestamps, and a kube job manifest example for running the harness in-cluster. Why this is different: Existing runners in the lab exercise sequence variety and batching logic, but none systematically target quantized kernel fidelity and the allocator slab dynamics that impact memory amplification and OOM-proneness when integer kernels thumbnail memory layout. Checklist: - [x] Implemented runner and reporter binaries - [x] Added unit tests for trace sanitizer and CSV exporter - [x] Added lightweight end-to-end smoke job in CI - [x] Added Linear tickets for follow-ups (ENG-1289, ENG-1342) - [x] Documented flags and output format in README under benchmark-lab/ops/README.md Usage notes: The runner supports a compact sequence-mix language: e.g. --seq-mix='[{"p":0.6,"len":32},{"p":0.3,"len":128},{"p":0.1,"len":512}]' and a quant-mode of "mixed" which will randomly choose q4/q8/fp16 kernels according to --quant-mix-probs. Example command used in internal experiments: ./stress-runner --quant-mode=mixed --quant-mix-probs='[0.5,0.3,0.2]' --seq-mix='[{"p":0.7,"len":64},{"p":0.3,"len":256}]' --concurrency=48 --surge-interval=120s. Key findings from local runs: - On a 16GB A100-like dev instance, mixed quant run (q4/q8/fp16) reduced total resident set by ~38% vs pure fp16 but exhibited a 10-14% p95 latency regression when sequence-length 256 portions spiked and triggered kernel fallbacks. - Occupancy slab reporter shows a long tail of 8KB slabs retained during q8-paths, indicating an allocator fragmentation pattern that amplifies peak RSS during surge tails. These are preliminary and captured in artifacts/bench-742018/2025-11-10/. Output artifacts: compressed traces, csvs, and a small flame snapshot (flamegraph.svg) are attached in CI artifacts for the smoke run. Backwards compat: Runner defaults to fp16 and reproduces existing bench harness behavior when quant-mode=fp16. Follow-ups (non-blocking): add automatic canary for kernel fallback threshold (ENG-1342), integrate CSV output into the perf dashboard, and extend reporter to emit a per-model CDF export for storage.

Motivation: We frequently see paired microburst patterns in customer workloads (short spike, short quiet, second spike) that standard single-burst profilers miss. This PR adds a new workload runner (Spike-Twin) that synthesizes paired-spike sessions with configurable separation and jitter, plus an epochal trace exporter/aggregator that builds per-epoch kernel-level flame profiles and emits anchored traces for downstream anomaly detection. The goal is to provide a representative runner for paired-burst scenarios and a reporting pipeline that makes cross-run comparisons simple. What this change includes: 1) spike-twin runner implemented in Go with sequence primer support, session jitter and warmup modes; 2) epochal-flame-aggregator Python pipeline that ingests raw perf traces, aligns them into fixed-length epochs, computes per-kernel token cost and p99 latencies, and generates a compact flame snapshot for each epoch; 3) new fixture profiles and a deterministic RNG seed option to make CI runs reproducible; 4) integration tests that validate alignment across noisy runs and check for regression in per-epoch tail latency; 5) docs and a short how-to for adding new paired-burst profiles. Motivation: We observed recurring short-duration concurrency spikes during seq-heavy workloads that were not captured cleanly by the existing flamepoint exporter. This PR introduces a lightweight 'seqburst consolidator' runner plus an occupancy timeline visualizer so we can (1) compress and annotate bursty sequences into coherent events, (2) attribute kernel occupancy and memory pressure across the burst lifetime, and (3) export compact timelines compatible with the lab's timeline UI.

What this implements: - A new runner: bench/seqburst/consolidator that takes raw session traces and consolidates adjacent short sequences into 'bursts' using a configurable time-gap and token-threshold heuristic. The output is a compact JSON event stream with per-burst metadata (primer-length, peak-concurrency, slot-occupancy, kv-checkpointed). - Occupancy timeline visualizer: tools/visualizers/occupancy_timeline.py renders burst events into an interactive HTML + SVG timeline suitable for manual inspection and inclusion in run artifacts. It highlights per-kernel occupancy bands and overlays memory pressure markers. - Flamegraph annotator: exporters/flame_annotator adds burst tags to existing per-kernel flame outputs so flamegraphs can be correlated back to bursts. - Integration glue: a new ingest path from consolidator -> aggregator that reduces artifact size by ~6x for highly bursty traces.

Design notes and tradeoffs: - The consolidator is intentionally lossy: it collapses micro-events to reduce downstream storage and highlight clinically relevant bursts. We preserve sample pointers so raw traces can be rehydrated when necessary. - Heuristics are tunable via config/seqburst.yaml (gap_ms, min_tokens, max_burst_duration_ms). Default values chosen after exploratory runs on production-like traces. - Visualizer is dependency-light (only uses d3 v7 and a tiny css bundle) to keep artifacts self-contained.

Testing and validation performed: - Unit tests covering burst detection edge cases (wraparound, nested bursts, extreme primer lengths). - E2E benchmark on a node with mixed sequence lengths (profile corpus: long-tail-2025). Compared baseline exporter vs consolidator path on the same traces: artifacts size reduced 5.8x and mean inspection time dropped by 72%. - Perf regression guard rails: added an automated smoke run in CI that runs the consolidator on a small sample trace and asserts output invariants (non-overlapping bursts, valid timestamps).

Checklist: - [x] Bench runner implemented and unit-tested. - [x] Visualizer + HTML artifact generation. - [x] Exporter annotated flames. - [x] CI smoke test and sample fixture added. - [x] Documentation: README with how-to, config knobs, and recommended workflows.

How to run locally: 1) python -m bench.seqburst.consolidator --input sample_traces/long-tail-2025.ndjson --output /tmp/bursts.ndjson 2) python tools/visualizers/occupancy_timeline.py /tmp/bursts.ndjson --out /tmp/occupancy_timeline.html 3) Open the HTML in a browser for interactive inspection.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the consolidator heuristics (bench/seqburst/consolidator.py) and the invariants asserted in tests/test_seqburst.py. The visualizer is intentionally minimal; UX improvements can be a follow-up (ENG-6899).

payload.body:
Motivation: We need a production-representative chat streaming workload for the Q1 2026 perf baseline & suite. Existing harness coverage is request/response (non-streaming) only, which under-measures scheduling + queueing dynamics and makes TTFT/TPOT comparisons noisy across client implementations.

What this adds: (1) A chat streaming workload generator (server SSE / chunked streaming) with configurable request-mix, sequence-length bins, and streaming cadence; (2) a concurrency ramp runner (warmup + stepped load) to mimic bursty traffic and reduce variance; (3) standardized baseline outputs for TTFT + TPOT with explicit measurement boundaries (client-side network excluded as much as practical).

Key behaviors: Request mix is modeled as weighted "cohorts" (e.g., short prompt + short decode, short prompt + long decode, medium prompt + medium decode) with configurable distributions. Concurrency ramps from N0 -> N1 -> ... with per-step dwell time, plus a warmup phase that primes model weights and KV allocations without counting metrics. Streaming pacing is implemented as a token-consumption loop that intentionally reads from the stream as fast as possible (to avoid client backpressure becoming the bottleneck). We also capture a separate "client_read_lag_ms" diagnostic to detect accidental client throttling.

Metrics: We compute TTFT as time from request send -> first token/chunk observed by client (first content token, not headers). TPOT is computed as (time from first token -> last token) / (num_tokens_after_first) and exported along with total tokens, completion time, and basic HTTP error classification. Output is emitted as JSONL (one line per request) plus an aggregated summary JSON with p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT, and throughput (req/s and output_tokens/s). The summary file is shaped to be ingested by the baseline dashboards and aligns with ADR-0172 metrics naming (full manifest wiring comes in PR-21432).

How to run: `bench run chat_streaming --endpoint $URL --model llama-3.1-70b --region us-east --mix mixes/chat_streaming_v1.json --ramp ramps/step_10min.json --seed 42 --out out/2026-01-05/`.

Notable implementation details: The generator supports both OpenAI-compatible chat completions streaming and Redwood API streaming, controlled via a `protocol` flag. We use a monotonic clock source for timing and include per-request attempt IDs for correlation with server traces. Error handling distinguishes connect timeouts, first-byte timeouts, mid-stream disconnects, and server 429/5xx to help triage overload vs regressions.

Testing: Adds unit tests for distribution sampling and pacing edge cases (empty stream, immediate EOS, chunk coalescing) and a small integration test that replays a canned streaming trace to verify TTFT/TPOT computations are stable.

Follow-ups: (a) Replace the temporary summary schema with the canonical run manifest + results format once PR-21432 lands; (b) add long-prefill workload (ENG-4824) and embeddings mode (ENG-4825); (c) wire the ramp runner into perf-canary nightly after threshold calibration (ENG-4828).
