Context and motivation: We need a focused microburst workload that reliably triggers short, high-concurrency token bursts to exercise scheduling and per-kernel tail behaviors observed in customer traces. This PR adds 'echo-prober', a compact runner that issues short, repeated primers and randomized echo sequences to reproduce microburst hotspots, and a new 'kernel_snapshot' reporter that captures lightweight per-kernel samples (stack traces + perf counters) and symbolicates them before exporting to the existing reporting pipeline.

What this PR does (high level): Adds a deterministic microburst workload runner, sampling buffer with edge-aware flush semantics, symbolization hooks that integrate with the symbol cache, an NDJSON exporter adapter for the reporting pipeline, and documentation + CI config to run the new suite in the benchmark lab integration job. The runner emphasizes low-noise collection (short-lived primers, coordinated warmup) so we can isolate kernel-level hotspots without long-run noise.

Checklist: [x] runner implementation and CLI flags for concurrency/epoch length/primer, [x] sampling buffer and flush-on-idle/rate-limit, [x] symbolization integration with symbol-cache service, [x] exporter adapter to pipeline (ndjson), [x] unit tests for buffer and symbolizer, [x] docs and example workload config, [x] CI integration for nightly baseline.

Commits summary: See commit messages above. Notable changes include addition of sample_buffer.go that implements a ring buffer with lock-free snapshots and a bounded background flusher, and reporter.go that collects kernel sample events and batches them into ndjson records with metadata (runner id, epoch, wall time). The symbolizer_test adds a small synthetic vmlinux symbol table to validate symbolication under high submit rates.

Files changed (high level): bench/runners/echo_prober/* — runner and config; bench/reporters/kernel_snapshot/* — main capture and exporter adapter; bench/pipeline/exporters/ndjson_exporter.go — small helper to normalize records; bench/utils/* — new sample buffer and tests; docs/benchmark-lab/echo-prober.md — how-to and analysis notes; scripts/ci/benchmark-lab-integration.yaml — adds nightly job tie-in.

Testing and CI: Local unit tests for buffer and reporter added and passing. Integration CI initially failed on the benchmark-lab-integration job due to an intermittent timeout when symbolizer fetched an external symbol-cache in the sandbox; resolved by adding a short local symbol cache fallback and making symbol fetches optional in test mode. Final CI run shows all checks passing: unit, linters, race-detector, and benchmark-lab-integration (nightly scheduling enabled).

Review conversation (summary):

- Author reply: Added sample_buffer_test to explicitly exercise concurrent flush and graceful shutdown; documented invariants in code comments.

- Author reply: Added config flag 'symbolize=false' for long runs and an adaptive backoff for symbol fetches; documented behavior in echo-prober.md.
- Luca Romano: Suggested improving the NDJSON exporter schema to include runner metadata and epoch tagging; also requested a small change to exporter error handling to avoid halting pipeline on single failed record.
- Author reply: Updated exporter_adapter to include runner_id and epoch fields and to log and continue on record-level failures.

CI artifacts include a nightly baseline artifact produced by the new runner (ndjson) which will seed the profiling dashboard.

We plan to add a lightweight aggregation view in the reporting pipeline to surface most-common kernel frames within 72 hours of nightly runs.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main after approvals. No breaking changes.

payload.body:
Motivation: Long-duration benchmark runs in Benchmark Lab are noisy and expensive to store because we capture full-event traces and per-sample payloads for every iteration. Two common pain points: (1) realistic warm-cache steady-state is expensive to reach deterministically across different sequence-length mixes; (2) raw telemetry volume for long runs (multi-hour stress / soak) is large, which slows downstream analysis and inflates storage costs.

Design & changes: Introduce a timebox seeder (timebox-seeder) that drives a configurable, bounded priming stage prior to each measurement epoch. The seeder supports: target distributions (seq-length, token-priming prefixes, model-mix), controlled eviction pressure knobs, and deterministic seeding modes (seed schedules can be reused across runs for reproducibility). Parallel to the seeder, add a hierarchical telemetry compactifier (rollup-telemetry) which consumes sample-level events and emits multiresolution rollups: fixed-window histograms for latency/queueing, sparse top-k hotpath counts (kernel and code-path labels), and a compact KV-cache delta summary. Rollups are time-aligned to the benchmark epochs and include provenance tags so downstream reporters can reconstruct coarse timelines for debugging.

API & operator UX: New CLI targets: `benchctl seed --profile <yaml>` and `benchctl rollup --out <path>`. We also added two YAML profiles under bench/configs/profiles/ to demonstrate common web-chat and search-like mixes. The default CI benchmark workflow now runs a 2-minute timebox seed before each steady-state sampling window. The new rollup files are gzipped ndjson, with one record per rollup-epoch.

Results: On the representative multi-model chat workload (mix: 0.7 single-turn short, 0.3 multi-turn long) we observed: - telemetry footprint reduction: ~40x (raw events -> rollups) for a 2h soak; - steady-state p95 latency stability improved across repeated runs (stdev reduced by ~18%) because the timebox seeder produces consistent cache state; - wall-clock time to reach measurable steady-state reduced by 30% in our lab when using a 2-minute timebox profile vs no explicit seeding.

Backward compatibility: Rollup outputs are additive; we kept the raw capture path behind a flag so existing analysis pipelines continue to work. The seeder can be disabled per-run. No changes to existing benchmark schema were required.

Operational notes: Rollup writer includes a size threshold which auto-rotates files when the gzipped rollup file exceeds the configured limit (default 64MB). We added a lightweight sanity-checker binary that validates rollup provenance and TTL.

Why this is different from previous work: This PR focuses on two pragmatic operational bottlenecks: deterministic warm-cache priming in a timeboxed, reproducible way (as opposed to ad-hoc long warmups), and reducing telemetry storage/ingest costs for long soak/soak-like workloads while preserving actionable signals for regressions and hotspots.

Link to related Linear items: ENG-2384 (timebox seeding design), ENG-2401 (rollup format and storage savings).
Adds a timeboxed seeding harness and a multiresolution telemetry rollup writer. Improves long-run telemetry footprint and produces more realistic warm-cache steady-state profiles.
3 commits: (1) initial timebox-seeder implementation with profile loader and CLI; (2) rollup-telemetry writer + ndjson gzip serializer; (3) CI workflow updates, profiles, and tests. Each commit includes unit tests and small integration harnesses that run in the bench CI pool.

Motivation: Existing workload runners sample request shapes uniformly or by hand-curated mixes which misses temporal correlations (sequence length bursts, conversational rollups) observed in customer telemetry. This PR adds a sequenced traffic synthesizer and a profile-guided baseline collector to produce representative, reproducible workloads for latency and KV cache profiling.

What this PR does (single-string summary):
- Introduces `temporal_correlated_runner.py`: a new workload runner that replays synthetic sessions with configurable sequence-length autocorrelation and inter-request timing distributions. Supports seedable RNG for repeatable runs.
- Adds `profiles/guided_sampler.py`: profile-guided input sampler that consumes production histograms (token count, prompt prefixes, user-session lengths) and generates weighted samples to exercise long-tail and bursty patterns.
- Adds `profiles/baselines/*`: stored canonical baselines (JSON) for short/medium/long conversational workloads and a README describing how to generate/validate them.
- Adds `reporters/provenance_delta.py`: an enrichment layer for the existing reporter pipeline that annotates aggregated deltas with profile provenance and sample counts to help root-cause SLO regressions.
- Small test harness and CI workflow updates: unit tests for sampler, an integration test that runs a short synthetic replay in the benchmark container, and a flakiness guard for timing-dependent tests.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Temporal correlation model: an AR(1)-like mechanism was chosen (configurable rho) instead of full HMM to keep generation cheap and interpretable. This is sufficient to reproduce burstiness seen in telemetry while keeping runtime overhead low.
- Profile-guided sampling prioritizes tail coverage: sampler supports a "tail_weight" parameter which increases sampling probability for rare long sequences to ensure regressions are caught early. This increases average test cost but improves regression sensitivity.
- Determinism: the runner exposes a `--seed` flag and dumps RNG state to the run metadata to make replays reproducible.

Testing and results summary:
- Unit tests: 18 new tests covering sampler distribution, RNG determinism, and provenance annotations.
- Integration run: a short run (1000 simulated tokens across mixed sessions) executed on CI container showed negligible added overhead to runner startup (<40ms) and produced expected delta annotations.
- Local perf run (nvme rig): using the new runner with baseline profile `baselines/conv-long.json` surfaced a 7.2% median tail latency increase on a quantized model variant; this surfaced a batching/KV-cache regression that the runtime team fixed in a follow-up.

Add a focused benchmark that exercises the interaction between nonblocking I/O (async client libraries) and our prefetching heuristics, plus a lightweight kernel-saturation mapper that samples kernel occupancy during runs. Motivation: several internal investigations (ENG-2897) showed amplified tail latency when prefetch policies and nonblocking request patterns intersected under high concurrency. This PR delivers: 1) a new runner (benchmarks/io_prefetch/nbio_replay.py) that can replay real session traces with configurable async client concurrency, socket batching windows, and prefetch policy toggles, 2) an epochal kernel sampler (reporters/kernel_saturation_mapper.go) that attaches to running instances to sample per-kernel occupancy and queueing metrics every 50ms, 3) a small operator to correlate kernel saturation with batch sizes and latency histograms (tools/analysis/prefetch_correlation.py), 4) test harness changes to add a dedicated perf CI job (ci/perf/nbio-prefetch.yaml) that runs the benchmark in a reproducible dockerized environment. The description below contains the checklist and usage notes. Checklist: - [x] implement runner + mapper - [x] add unit tests for runner input parsing (benchmarks/io_prefetch/tests) - [x] add integration test that runs a short replay on CI (ci/perf/nbio-prefetch.yaml) - [x] document config knobs and expected outputs (docs/benchmark-lab/nbio-prefetch.md) - [x] add example visualizer script (tools/analysis/prefetch_correlation.py) Usage: run `python nbio_replay.py --trace traces/session_2025-10-01.json --concurrency 128 --prefetch=adaptive --sample-kernel=unix:/tmp/ksock` to execute a 5-minute smoke run that emits CSVs consumed by the mapper. Motivation: Synthetic workload runners at the benchmark lab have historically focused on either purely stochastic mixes or long-running steady-state traces. Teams asked for a compact, configurable runner that can express temporally varying mixes (ramp/hold/spike patterns) with guarantees about tail behaviour so that profiling baselines are repeatable. This PR introduces the Temporal Mix Sculptor: a workload generator that composes named phases (delay, ramp, hold, burst, decay) into a timeline and emits request sequences with controllable concurrency, sequence length mix, and token distributions.

Key features implemented: bounded-tail oscillation detector (BTOD) — a lightweight online detector that flags microburst oscillations and produces an oscillation_score per epoch (0..1) so that downstream reports can disambiguate pathological tail events from steady-state variance; epochal histogram summarizer — compact per-epoch histograms (fixed 256 buckets) using reservoir+count-min sketch hybrid to bound memory for long runs; temporal policy DSL — a small declarative YAML schema to describe multi-phase mixes and deterministic seeds for reproducible runs; per-request trace IDs and KV-cache priming options so runs can model warm/cold starts.

Why this matters: several recent perf investigations required isolating oscillatory tail events from steady high-p95s when validating kernel changes. The BTOD score is intended to be surfaced as a top-level dimension in reports (oscillation: true/false and score) and to drive automatic run reclassification in the reporting pipeline. The smaller histograms enable nightlies to retain useful distributional information without exploding storage costs.

Commits summary: single-squash merge with a sequence of focused commits during review: initial scaffold and DSL, core runner loop and phase engine, BTOD algorithm and tests, histogram summarizer and exporter, telemetry/trace id plumbing, unit/integration tests and small CI fixes.

Backward compatibility and safety: Runner defaults to the existing 'steady' profile unless a temporal policy is supplied. The histogram exporter adds a new compact endpoint but does not remove or change any existing exports. No breaking changes to public interfaces.

Release notes: Adds a new Temporal Mix Sculptor workload generator (benchmark-lab) with oscillation detection and compact histogram exports to improve regression triage for tail events.

Motivation: We lack a focused micro-benchmark that correlates mixed-precision quantization thresholds with sustained throughput and real GPU memory fragmentation under long-lived multi-tenant sequences. Teams tuning quantization profiles (FP16/INT8/quant-aware blocks) have seen throughput wins in short runs, but in production the allocator fragmentation and long tail of priming tokens degrades sustained throughput and increases OOM risk. This PR adds a reproducible test harness and a visual heatmap reporter to make that interaction measurable.

What this PR adds: mp-quant-frag-bench (new CLI + python runner) that: 1) runs configurable mixed-precision thresholds across model submodules; 2) emits an allocator-level fragmentation metric FFR (Free Fragmentation Ratio = largest_free_block / total_free); 3) simulates mixed tenant workloads by parameterized interleaving of short/long sequences and context-cuts; 4) produces machine-readable outputs (ndjson) and an HTML heatmap + SVG that maps sequence position vs FFR and throughput.

Key implementation notes: - Benchmark harness lives under bench/mp_quant_frag/ with runner.py, driver_config.yaml, and a lightweight C extension that samples CUDA allocator free lists (best-effort; falls back to NVTX-only on unsupported drivers). - Added a warmup strategy that mirrors production prefix priming so quantization warmup effects are captured. - Introduces a small estimator for quantization-induced kernel eviction pressure to correlate with fragmentation spikes. - Added a reporter that aggregates runs into a delta heatmap and a per-bucket p95/p99 throughput table consumed by the perf dashboard.

Checklist: - [x] Basic harness + CLI - [x] Unit tests for config parsing and reporter aggregation - [x] Perf run on dev cluster (A100-40GB) - [x] Heatmap generation and HTML artifact upload step - [x] Documentation snippet in bench/README.md

Small illustrative diff (reporter header): --- reporter.py +++ reporter.py @@ def compute_ffr(heap_snapshot): -    # placeholder implementation +    # compute largest contiguous free block and total free to form FFR +    largest = _find_largest_free_block(heap_snapshot) +    total_free = sum(region[1] for region in heap_snapshot if region[0] == 'free') +    return largest / max(1, total_free)

Two asks: (1) make FFR computation robust when total_free is very small and annotate when sampling is best-effort; (2) add a smoke test that runs the HTML reporter headlessly so we catch regressions." Introduce a rampdown-mode traffic generator and a per-cohort stability reporter. Adds a new CLI entrypoint `benchctl rampdown` and a JSON/CSV exporter for cohort stability metrics. No breaking API changes.
Motivation: We observed that long-running steady-state benchmarks mask subtle cohort-level regressions that only surface when traffic intensity tapers. This PR introduces a lightweight rampdown traffic generator and an accompanying per-cohort stability reporter to capture those regressions. Goals: 1) Provide a deterministic rampdown waveform for synthetic runs; 2) Emit per-cohort stability metrics (p50/p95/p99 drift, sequence churn, primer-hit-rate) after each phase; 3) Produce compact, operator-friendly exports for downstream heatmap and anomaly pipelines. What changed: - New CLI command benchctl rampdown --duration --cohorts-file --decay-profile that builds a traffic schedule which linearly or exponentially decays concurrency and token rate across a run. - A scheduler module that pins seeds for deterministic sampling and supports cohort-weight annealing to preserve relative proportions during decay. - A per-cohort stability reporter that aggregates sequence-level deltas, KV-cache warmup fidelity, and token churn into a single JSON line per cohort and a CSV summary for quick ingestion. - Small test harness additions and a lightweight example workload in examples/rampdown/README.md. Compatibility: The generator plugs into existing runners via the standard runner.LifecycleAPI; no changes required for consumers beyond opting in. Usage: benchctl rampdown --duration 30m --cohorts-file cohorts.yaml --decay-profile linear --export ./out/rampdown.json Testing and perf: Local CI includes unit tests for scheduler determinism and a microbenchmark comparing steady vs rampdown runs on a small model. On our staging cluster the same workload showed a 1.3% higher p95 variance across cohorts during rampdown, which aligns with manual investigation. Adds a new deterministic workload runner that produces reproducible session trajectories and on-demand warmup checkpoints; no API breaking changes.
Motivation: tail latency investigations for long-lived conversational workloads were hard to reproduce — transient priming paths and nondeterministic warmup order meant we could not reliably recreate the same KV cache state. This PR introduces a stateful trajectory sequencer runner that (1) deterministically schedules multi-turn sessions with configurable affinity and drift, (2) records compact warmup checkpoints (KV priming snapshots) and (3) provides a deterministic replay mode that applies checkpoints to reproduce tail events.

What I changed: single PR that implements the runner, checkpoint serialization, a small deterministic scheduler, and a reporting exporter that annotates traces with checkpoint IDs and session-affinity buckets. The runner supports: per-session seed, length distribution profiles, interleaving policies (round-robin, affinity-weighted, random-with-seed), and explicit checkpoint injection points. Checkpoints are small JSON blobs of token prefixes + KV metadata (non-sensitive) and an index file that maps checkpoint -> model-compatibility hints.

Why this matters: teams can now write golden reproducer harnesses for slow tails, instrument the warmup path, and share checkpoints between benchmark runs to compare kernel-level profiles with identical initial states. This reduces flakiness in perf regression triage and speeds up root cause analysis for divergence between model variants.

Testing and validation: unit tests added for scheduler determinism, checkpoint roundtrip, and export format. End-to-end synthetic runs on the benchmark cluster show p95/p99 stability when replaying the same checkpoint across 10 repeated runs: p95 variance < 2%, p99 variance < 5% (baseline without checkpointing had p99 variance ~18%). CI includes an integration job that runs a short deterministic scenario against a small local runtime container; flaky latency-test failed on first CI run due to a timing race and passed on retry.

How to use: util/bench/seq_runner --profile conversational_long --seed 42 --checkpoint-out=checkpoints/run-20260214.zip to record; util/bench/seq_runner --replay-checkpoint=checkpoints/run-20260214.zip --profile conversational_long --verify to run replay mode and emit a reproducible trace. Documentation updated in docs/benchmarking/seq-runner.md with example workflows and recommended profiles.

Migration/compatibility: no changes to public API surfaces used by customers. Checkpoint files are schema-versioned, and the runner will refuse to apply checkpoints incompatible with the target model (safety guard).
Reproducer run (n=10) against local single-GPU runtime with model-x-quant: baseline replay disabled: p95 mean 78ms (var 1.8%), p99 mean 220ms (var 18%); with checkpoint replay enabled: p95 mean 76ms (var 1.2%), p99 mean 205ms (var 4.6%). Token throughput difference negligible (<1.5%).

Elena: Scheduler determinism looks good; please add a small fuzz test for seed collisions. — Author: added seed-collision test and fixed deterministic RNG seeding.
Tao: The reporter emits checkpoint IDs but not model hints; can we annotate compatibility info? — Author: added model-compatibility hint into checkpoint index and annotation in traces.

payload.body:
Motivation: tenant-level allocation hotspots and micro-fragmentation cause frequent small evictions and suboptimal slab utilization under mixed workloads (short-chat QPS + long-generation tails). This PR introduces a three-part memory-management strategy to reduce fragmentation, smooth eviction storms, and avoid synchronous spill-related latency spikes. Design: 1) Strided Evictor: an eviction selection strategy that walks slab memory in deterministic strides (configurable stride size) to avoid localized hot-slot thrashing. The evictor biases by age + recency but enforces stride gaps to distribute evictions across segments, reducing contiguous free-run fragmentation. 2) Adaptive Vacancy Smoothing: a background compaction-friendly pass that opportunistically migrates cold entries into coalesced runs to create larger contiguous free regions for future large allocations. It uses a sampled heatmap per slab class and applies a moving-average vacancy threshold to decide migration windows. Smoothing runs are throttled by CPU/IO headroom heuristics to ensure steady-state costs remain negligible. 3) Async Spill Controller: when memory pressure is sustained and vacancy smoothing cannot make enough room, we initiate asynchronous, rate-limited spill-to-disk for selected cold ranges rather than immediate eviction. The controller coordinates with the KV spill subsystem to batch spill jobs and backpressure upstream allocation loops so we avoid synchronous eviction stalls. Implementation highlights: - New kv/evict/strided_evictor.cc/.h implementing configurable stride, eviction policy hooks, and unit-tested determinism. - Vacancy smoother implemented as kv/maintenance/vacancy_smoother.{cc,h} with a lightweight sampling heatmap and pluggable cost model. - Async spill controller in kv/spill/async_controller.{cc,h} with a spill job queue, backpressure tokens, and integration points for disk spill workers. - Runtime knobs exposed via config schema: kv.eviction.stride_size, kv.smoother.enabled/interval/cpu_limit, kv.spill.async_threshold/batch_size. - Bench harness and microbenchmarks added under benchmark/kv to reproduce fragmentation regressions. Tests & validation: unit tests for deterministic eviction, integration tests for smoother throttling, and end-to-end perf runs in benchmark-lab pipeline. Motivation: performance regressions are brittle when synthetic workload shapes diverge from production distributions. This PR introduces a workload fidelity scaler and an accompanying regression harness that can morph baseline workload traces to target fidelity envelopes and run deterministic golden-run comparisons. Summary: adds a fidelity scaler module that applies stretch/compression, sequence-length mixing, token-velocity perturbation, and concurrency jitter models to archived trace inputs, plus a harness that runs multiple seeded replays, captures per-step latency/p99/p50 and KV-cache hit statistics, and outputs a compact regression report suitable for automated triage. This is intended to reduce noisy flaky regressions by enabling tuned synthetic runs that better approximate customer traffic shapes. Key behaviors: (1) fidelity profiles are declared as YAML with named envelopes (low-latency-mobile, bursty-ad, long-context-retrieval) and can be composed at runtime; (2) the scaler supports deterministic RNG seeds for reproducible golden runs; (3) harness integrates with perf-db to store run artifacts and with the reporting pipeline to emit a delta-summary JSON. Backwards compatibility: existing canonical trace formats are accepted and unchanged; new optional metadata fields are namespaced under "fidelity.v1". Test plan: added unit tests for scaling transforms, integration test that replays a 10k-step trace under three fidelity profiles and verifies metrics within expected bands, and an end-to-end costume nightly job that runs on perf-canary. Rollout: feature gated behind benchmark_lab.fidelity_scaler flag; default off for all CI lanes. Related: ENG-1089 (reduce noise in e2e perf signal).

Motivation: our existing benchmark runners focus on either long-horizon sequences or short-burst traffic; they do not faithfully reproduce real production mixes where clients interleave short prompts, mid-length context completions, and occasional long document generations within the same session. This PR adds a new 'seq-mosaic' workload runner that synthesizes a realistic per-session mosaic of sequence lengths and token distributions and couples it with an Affinity Heatmap Serializer that produces compact per-kernel 'richness' telemetry suitable for offline analysis. Design summary: 1) session generator: builds sessions from configurable distributions (short/mid/long proportions, inter-arrival jitter, user intent switch probability); 2) primer manager: issues deterministic priming sequences with probabilistic dropout to emulate KV-cache churn; 3) affinity-aware scheduler: emits labels for token spans denoting likely kernel hotpaths (soft affinity) for downstream attribution; 4) heatmap serializer: encodes per-batch/kernel coverage and token-density histograms into a compact ND-JSON-friendly blob with versioning. Context: We need a lightweight, repeatable way to estimate per-kernel energy cost on the benchmark cluster to inform batching and kernel-selection heuristics. Motivation: latency and token-cost are well-covered by existing suites, but energy (and its correlation with kernel shapes and microbatch sizes) is under-instrumented. This PR introduces a microbenchmark harness that runs narrow, deterministic instruction sequences across kernels to produce a compact per-kernel energy estimator and a small trace sink for downstream aggregation. Design summary: 1) microbench/energy_harness: a deterministic runner that (a) pins to a single GPU, (b) runs repeated micro-kernels with controlled occupancy and sequence length, and (c) collects hardware energy counters via RAPL/NVIDIA DCGM when available. 2) telemetry/compact_sink: a minimal NDJSON trace sink that encodes per-sample energy, latency, kernel-id, and a lightweight checksum; records are deliberately compact (fields are short keys, delta-encoded timestamps) to reduce storage and transfer cost. 3) analysis/estimator: a small script that fits a simple linear+interaction model between measured energy and instruction mix / kernel footprint; produces per-kernel coefficients consumed by autoscaler and kernel-selector prototypes. Implementation notes: no changes to runtime kernels; all collection happens from user-space counters and a short runtime shim that triggers warmup and steady-state windows. The harness supports a calibration mode that runs power-taxonomized sequences to compensate for baseline drift. Testing and results: synthetic run on a p4d-small cluster with 12 repetitions produced coefficient variance <4% for long-running kernels and ~8-12% for ultra-short kernels; end-to-end noise reduction by the calibration step improved stability by ~30% (see attached sample reports in commits). CI: unit tests for parsing and NDJSON format, an integration test that runs a mocked counter provider, and a lightweight smoke-run on a single CPU runner. Backwards compatibility: the compact sink is opt-in via config and does not affect existing telemetry pipelines. Release impact: none to API; this is a benchmarking infra feature. Related work: ties to ENG-1324 (autoscaler cost model) and ENG-1409 (kernel-selection heuristics). Checklist: - [x] harness implemented - [x] sink format defined and schema tested - [x] estimator script + simple eval harness - [x] docs and README - [x] reviewer feedback addressed

Title: Add quant profile rollback benchmarks (latency + quality) and CI artifact export

Context
We’ve had a few regressions during quant profile experiments where we needed to confirm that a rollback actually restores baseline behavior (both performance and quality) before unpausing a rollout. This PR adds first-class benchmark scenarios to benchmark-lab that (1) compare two quant profile versions head-to-head and (2) validate that a rollback from candidate -> baseline produces results within defined tolerances.

What’s in this PR
- New benchmark suite: quant_profile_rollback
  - Runs A/B comparisons for two quant profile versions (e.g., qp_v12 vs qp_v11) on the same prompt distribution and concurrency.
  - Runs an explicit rollback scenario: baseline -> candidate -> baseline, ensuring the second baseline run matches the first baseline run (within noise thresholds).
- Metrics captured
  - Perf: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, tokens/sec, time-to-first-token, GPU util (if exported by runner), request 5xx rate.
  - Quality: task-level aggregate metrics from the eval harness output (pass@1 / exact match where applicable), plus a lightweight “output drift” metric (normalized Levenshtein distance over a fixed deterministic subset) to detect surprising changes that still pass task thresholds.
- Artifacts
  - Emits a single JSON summary artifact suitable for safe-apply gates: artifacts/quant_profile_rollback_summary.json.
  - Includes tags for tenant/model/region/config_version when provided (for parity with the rollout health dashboard annotations).
- CI integration
  - Adds a CPU-only “smoke” mode for PR validation (schema + harness wiring + artifact format).
  - Keeps the full GPU run behind the existing nightly / on-demand workflow (no new default GPU CI spend).

How it works
- The suite takes two quant profiles and a model target:
  - --baseline-profile (required)
  - --candidate-profile (required)
  - --model (default: rw/llama-3.1-8b-instruct)
- It executes three phases in order:
  1) baseline: run prompts, record perf + quality, save output fingerprints for deterministic subset
  2) candidate: same workload, record deltas vs baseline
  3) rollback_to_baseline: re-run baseline profile and compare against phase (1)
- Pass/fail logic is intentionally conservative and mirrors the gating ADR direction:
  - rollback baseline perf must be within +3% p95 and +5% p99 latency vs initial baseline (configurable)
  - rollback baseline quality must be within 0.2% absolute of initial baseline on aggregate metric (configurable)
  - output drift on deterministic subset must not exceed threshold (defaults tuned to avoid flaking)

Usage
- Local (requires access to benchmark runner + dataset):
  - ./bench run quant_profile_rollback --model rw/llama-3.1-8b-instruct --baseline-profile qp_v11 --candidate-profile qp_v12 --concurrency 32 --prompt-set prompts/quant_canary_v3.jsonl
- CI (smoke):
  - .github/workflows/bench-smoke.yml runs with --smoke and validates summary artifact schema.
- Nightly/on-demand GPU:
  - .github/workflows/bench-quant-rollback.yml

Files / areas changed (high level)
- benches/quant_profile_rollback/*: new scenario + runners
- harness/quality/*: adapter for pulling aggregate metrics + deterministic subset drift calculation
- tools/artifacts/export_summary.py: JSON summary writer shared with other suites
- .github/workflows/bench-smoke.yml: schema smoke
- .github/workflows/bench-quant-rollback.yml: nightly/on-demand GPU execution
- docs/benchmarks/quant_profile_rollback.md: how to run + interpret output

Illustrative summary JSON (excerpt)
{
  "suite": "quant_profile_rollback",
  "model": "rw/llama-3.1-8b-instruct",
  "baseline_profile": "qp_v11",
  "candidate_profile": "qp_v12",
  "baseline": {"p95_ms": 182.4, "p99_ms": 311.7, "quality": 0.8421},
  "candidate": {"p95_ms": 175.1, "p99_ms": 298.2, "quality": 0.8416},
  "rollback_to_baseline": {"p95_ms": 183.6, "p99_ms": 314.1, "quality": 0.8420},
  "gates": {"rollback_perf_ok": true, "rollback_quality_ok": true, "drift_ok": true}
}

Notes / limitations
- This does not attempt to prove kernel-level cache invalidation correctness. It is an end-to-end benchmark meant to catch “mixed state” issues and obvious regressions after profile swaps.
- The drift metric is only evaluated on a deterministic subset (fixed seed, temp=0, top_p=1) to keep noise low.

Review discussion (summary)
- Jonas Weber: Requested that quality gate be absolute-delta, not relative, and that we record the exact eval harness version/hash in the summary.
  - Arjun Desai: Updated gates to absolute delta, added harness_git_sha in artifact metadata.
- Sana Farid: Flagged potential flake from small sample size on the deterministic subset; suggested increasing subset from 64 -> 128 and adding a minimum token count.
  - Arjun Desai: Bumped subset to 128, added min_total_tokens guard; smoke mode uses a smaller subset but only validates schema.
- Noah Patel: Asked whether rollback run should warm up separately to avoid cold-start skew.
  - Arjun Desai: Added warmup_requests per phase (default 20) and excluded warmup from metrics.
- Sean Gallagher: Asked for clear “operator reading” in docs and a single red/green output line suitable for runbooks.
  - Arjun Desai: Added docs section “What to look at during rollback” and an explicit SUMMARY: PASS/FAIL line.

CI
- bench-smoke (ubuntu-latest): PASS
- lint/format: PASS
- unit tests (harness + artifact schema): PASS
- bench-quant-rollback (on-demand GPU): PASS (attached artifact)

Merge
Squash merged. Follow-up: wire this artifact into perf-canary gate publishing (tracked separately under rollout controller integration work).
Adds benchmark scenarios that compare quantization profile versions and validate that rollback restores baseline latency/quality within tolerance; publishes a single JSON summary artifact for gate evaluation.

Introduce an adaptive seed scheduler and a hash-partitioned replay mapper to improve deterministic multi-worker replay fidelity and reduce sampling noise across GPUs. Motivation: current replay runner distributes traces unevenly under heterogeneous GPU pools and suffers from high quantile jitter when short tail bursts dominate a single worker. This PR implements: 1) Seed scheduler: online estimator that assigns synthetic seed traffic probabilities per epoch to reach target p95/p99 variance budgets without manual tuning. 2) Hash-partitioned replay mapper: deterministic split of sessions across workers by a configurable stable hash on session_id+seed, ensuring worker-local k/v cache priming and reproducible hotpath placement. 3) Epochal sample condenser: lightweight aggregator that merges micro-segments within an epoch to reduce noise from sub-100ms bursts while preserving peak events for tail analysis. 4) Tracer integration: emit kernel-boundary timestamps (cuda kernel start/stop markers) alongside throughput samples so we can align host-side latency with kernel-level activity. 5) Reporting: new cycle-aligned quantile aggregator and gpu-fidelity-normalization step added to the report pipeline to surface per-GPU variance and enable cross-cluster comparisons. Implementation notes: CLI flags for --adaptive-seeds and --hash-partitioning added to benchmark-runner; config schema extended under bench.replay.{scheduler,partitioner} with sane defaults; small refactor of runner/core to expose deterministic sharding hooks. Tests: synthetic multi-gpu CI job (bench/replay-integration) added; unit tests for scheduler estimator and mapper. Checklist: - [x] Feature implementation - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration job - [x] Docs (bench README) - [x] Perf baseline run included

Ethan Liu: Can you add a short synthetic run demonstrating reduced p99 jitter across a 4-GPU pool? The integration job should include an assertion on p99 variance for regression prevention.
Priya Menon (author): Added a versioned hash salt and included a bench/replay/p99-variance.test in the CI job. Integrated a short synthetic run summary in the PR description.
Mina Patel: Tracer payload looks fine; ensure payload size is bounded to avoid high cardinality in traces. Consider sampling kernel markers at 1 in N for very high-throughput runs.
Priya Menon: Bounded the tracer marker batch to 128 per request and made sampling configurable via bench.tracing.sample_rate.
Jordan Reyes: Approving after CI pass and the additional synthetic assertion.
Added adaptive seed scheduling and deterministic hash-partitioned replay mapper to improve multi-worker replay stability and reduce p99/p99.9 jitter. New reporting metrics: cycle-aligned quantiles and per-GPU fidelity normalization. Opt-in via --adaptive-seeds and --hash-partitioning; no breaking changes to existing configs.
Baseline run attached: 4xA100 heterogeneous sim, 1M sessions replay, adaptive seeds enabled. Result: p99 variance down 42% vs control, median throughput stable, slight 3% CPU overhead for scheduler bookkeeping. Full logs uploaded to internal benchmarking bucket.
Low. Deterministic hash partitioning changes only replay distribution; production serving unaffected. Tracer markers are size-bounded and disabled by default. Scheduler is opt-in to avoid behavior drift in existing benchmark suites.
Tooling change only. Users of bench/replay who opt-in will get more stable quantiles and reproducible multi-worker replays. No runtime behavior change for hosted inference.
This PR paved the way for follow-ups: adaptive cross-model seeding (ENG-2301) and autoscaling-aware partitioners that respect hot spot locality.

Motivation: Our existing benchmark lab lacked a lightweight multi-tenant workload runner and an automated pipeline to turn collected CPU/GPU profiles into consumable performance reports. Motivation: intermittent microbursts and KV-cache churn are causing reproducible but low-frequency slowpaths that our current session replayers smooth over. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: a windowed primer sampler (a runner that replays realistic request windows with configurable sliding/overlap semantics and deterministic seeding) and a slowpath signal annotator (a reporter that enriches traces with per-kernel invocation metadata and a synthesized 'slowpath_score'). Goals: 1) make small, transient slowpath regressions visible in aggregated bench runs; 2) provide actionable annotations linking tail latency spikes to kernel-level events and cache-priming status. Summary of changes: implemented windowed_sampler.py (new runner with YAML-driven profiles and seed control), added slowpath_annotator.go (exporter that consumes bench traces and emits annotated CSV/Parquet summaries plus a compact JSON summary used by downstream dashboards), added deterministic primer harness to utils/primer.py, extended CI bench matrix to include a 'windowed' workload permutation, added unit+integration tests and a lightweight fixture dataset under testdata/windowed-primer. Context/links: Related internal investigation ENG-3456 (kernel-slew tail events); proto spec for annotator: docs/bench/slowpath-annotator.md. Usage notes: runner supports run-length, window-size, overlap, primer_strategy (none|kv|kv-full), and seed parameters. Annotator outputs per-window metrics: p50/p95/p99, slowpath_count, avg_kernel_dur_ms, primer_hit_rate, slowpath_score (0..1). Summary: Adds a compact 'anchor runner' binary and a delta telemetry fuser utility. The goal is to provide a low-overhead, source-of-truth anchor run that produces compact, mergeable telemetry artifacts suitable for fast regression diffing and long-term storage. Motivation: our current full-profile runs are expensive to store and slow to diff for routine CI catches. This PR introduces a smaller canonical run and a post-processor (delta fuser) that merges per-run deltas into a single compact timeline for downstream change detection.

Design & implementation: 1) compact-anchor-runner: a thin runner executable (go) that replays a representative session mix (token-level sampler + context primer) with deterministic RNG seeding and limited instrumentation. It emits a compact protobuf-lite payload containing: sequence IDs, key kernel-time-annotated spans, p50/p95/p99 microbuckets, and a minimal KV-cache hit map. The payload intentionally omits large token traces and full heap snapshots to keep size < 80KB per run. 2) delta-telemetry-fuser: a python utility that takes multiple compact payloads and produces a fused delta file containing per-cohort summaries and a delta-of-quantiles record optimized for git-friendly diffs. The fuser attaches run-metadata (commit, model, hw-tag) and computes signed checksums to aid reproducibility. 3) reporting pipeline integration: CI step 'anchor-diff' added to the lightweight benchmark pipeline which runs the anchor-runner on a small litmus set, pushes artifacts to the artifact store, and then triggers the fuser to produce a delta artifact consumed by our perf-notifier.

Checklist: - [x] compact runner binary and tests - [x] fuser utility and unit tests - [x] CI integration in lightweight bench workflow - [x] metrics mapping and schema docs - [x] smoke run against staging cluster - [x] reviewer approvals

Files changed (high level): - cmd/compact-anchor-runner/main.go (new) - bench/anchor/primer_sets/short_mix.yaml (new) - bench/anchor/runner_test.go (new) - tools/delta_fuser/fuser.py (new) - tools/delta_fuser/schema.md (new) - ci/workflows/light-bench-anchor.yml (modified) - reporters/anchor-uploader/manifest.go (modified) - docs/bench/compact-anchor.md (new)

Compatibility & migration notes: The compact payload uses a new top-level "anchor_v1" schema that coexists with our existing full-profile outputs. Downstream consumers (perf-notifier and storage indexer) are updated in this PR to accept the new schema. No changes required to existing long-run datasets.

Testing & results: We ran the anchor runner across three representative commits against the p4-staging cluster (same seed). End-to-end CI runtime for the anchor workflow: ~6m (median) vs full profile ~42m. Typical artifact sizes: 48-76KB. Early sensitivity: anchor diffs caught a 6% p95 regression in a small scheduling tweak (reproduced in full-run) with negligible noise after 10 runs.

Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main and enable 'anchor-diff' on the lightweight bench schedule. 2) Monitor false-positive rate for 2 weeks, collect sample diffs. 3) If noise > 10% for a given model cohort, widen primer set and increase sampling.

Follow-ups (tracked in ENG-1107): - add optional micro flamepoint markers to the compact payload for hotspot triage - hook fuser output into automated regression labeling and Slack perf channel - experiment with delta compression for multi-run longitudinal stores

References: Linear tickets ENG-1024, ENG-1107. Related docs: docs/bench/compact-anchor.md. CI runs and artifacts: link to artifact index will be posted in the perf-notifier thread after merge.

Context: Marketing site + interactive benchmark table needs a stable, versioned export of benchmark results that can be ingested by the web build pipeline and served via the results service (ENG-18566). This PR adds an export step that materializes benchmark outputs into (1) a canonical JSON bundle and (2) a CSV for quick inspection / spreadsheet workflows. Both artifacts are versioned, have an explicit schema version, and include a machine-readable changelog so the docs/web layer can safely detect and adapt to changes.

What’s included: - New exporter module (export/public_artifacts) that takes validated run aggregates and emits:   - artifacts/public/v1/results.json (canonical)   - artifacts/public/v1/results.csv (flat, human-friendly)   - artifacts/public/v1/changelog.json (schema + field-level changes)   - artifacts/public/v1/manifest.json (build metadata: git sha, created_at, prompt_set, regions, models, filters) - Schema versioning:   - schema_version follows semver and is embedded in every exported file header/metadata.   - Current version: 1.0.0 - JSON schema file added (schemas/public_results.schema.json) for internal validation + downstream contract tests. - Stable ordering and determinism: exporter sorts rows by (model_id, region, workload_id, context_bucket) and emits canonical JSON with stable key ordering to reduce diff noise in PRs and caching layers. - Backfill-friendly: exporter supports including a "dataset_id" and "run_group_id" so we can publish multiple refreshes without clobbering prior runs. - CLI changes: benchmark-lab runner adds --export-public-artifacts and --public-artifacts-dir flags; default path is ./artifacts/public/v1. - Tests: unit tests for schema compliance, CSV column consistency, and changelog generation; golden-file snapshot tests for results.json and results.csv. - Docs: README section on "Public artifacts" including intended consumers (docs site, marketing site, results service) and guidance for bumping schema_version.

Non-goals / guardrails: - No changes to how metrics are computed (latency/$ normalization stays in PR-4821). This is only an export + contract layer. - No PII / sensitive IDs are included; this PR intentionally only exports aggregated results and high-level config descriptors. (Redaction enforcement is handled separately; see follow-up PR-4873.)

Consumer contract (high level): - results.json includes: schema_version, dataset_id, generated_at, dimensions (model/region/workload/context_bucket), metrics (p50/p95 latency_ms, throughput_toks_per_s, cost_per_1m_tokens_usd, latency_per_dollar), and method flags (streaming=false for this dataset, caching_policy_id, batching_policy_id). - results.csv is a 1-row-per-dimension record intended for quick charting; it shares metric names with results.json where possible.

Rollout plan: - Land exporter behind the CLI flag; CI will run exports on the small smoke dataset. - Web team (Felix) will consume artifacts from a pinned schema_version and fail fast if schema_version mismatches expected major version. - Once docs site wiring is merged, we will enable exports in the full region sweep pipeline.

Risks: - Schema churn during methodology tweaks. Mitigation: semver schema_version + changelog.json + downstream contract tests. - Size of JSON bundle if we add too many slices. Mitigation: exporter supports filtering dimensions and splitting outputs per region/model in a follow-up if needed.
Felix Schneider (review): Can we guarantee backwards compatibility for the web table? I need a clear contract for column names and a way to detect a breaking change without parsing the whole file.

Rina Kobayashi (author): Added schema_version at top-level for JSON and as a commented header line for CSV ("# schema_version=1.0.0"). Also added changelog.json + a contract test that asserts the CSV header matches the schema.

Mei Lin (review): Please ensure determinism—row ordering and float formatting. Otherwise we’ll get noisy diffs and flaky cache behavior.

Rina: Updated exporter to sort by (model_id, region_id, workload_id, context_bucket) and format floats with fixed precision (latency_ms: 3 decimals, cost_usd: 6 decimals, throughput: 4 decimals). Added golden snapshots and made tests tolerant only within those formatting rules.

Nadia Rahman (review): For latency_per_dollar, can we document the exact unit? People will interpret it differently (ms per $ vs seconds per $). Also make sure we don’t rename existing metric keys without a major bump.

Rina: Documented units in README and in schema field descriptions: latency_per_dollar_ms_per_usd. Kept key name "latency_per_dollar" for continuity, but added "latency_per_dollar_unit" in manifest.json for explicitness. Also added a schema bump policy section (major bump on rename/remove).

Logan Wright (review): Please add a manifest field for git_sha and runner_version. Web ingestion needs build provenance.

Rina: Added git_sha, runner_version, and prompt_set_id to manifest.json. Also included generated_at (UTC ISO-8601) across artifacts.

Elliot Price (review): Can we add a short "How to bump schema_version" checklist? This will be referenced by docs/PMM.

Rina: Added README checklist + changelog.json format spec (fields: from_version, to_version, breaking, changes[]).

Final approvals: Felix ✅, Mei ✅, Nadia ✅, Logan ✅, Elliot ✅
Benchmark pipeline can now export versioned public artifacts (results.json/results.csv) with schema_version, manifest, and changelog to support the interactive benchmark web page ingestion.

Motivation: We lack a compact, deterministic benchmark fixture that reproduces common short-sequence hotpaths (latency-sensitive generations of length 8-64 tokens) while being cheap to run in CI and on local dev machines. Current suites are heavyweight and noisy; this PR introduces a curated mini corpus plus an experimental sparse CPU probe reporter that samples kernel-level wall-clock for a small set of annotated hotspots. The goal is faster benches that still exercise scheduling, KV-cache priming, and transient batch assembly so we can catch regressions early.

What this PR contains (high-level):
- mini_bench_corpus/: a compact set (12 sessions) of synthetic and real prompt traces sampled from production anonymized logs, normalized for determinism (fixed tokenization seeds, pinned random seeds, and controlled primer lengths).
- runner/mini_runner.py: lightweight harness that spins up the same runtime used by larger benches but with strict timing windows and a deterministic sampler to remove non-deterministic jitter.
- reporters/sparse_cpu_probe.py: an opt-in reporter that attaches a short-lived wall-clock probe to specific runtime phases (tokenize, model_dispatch, kv_priming, generate_step) and emits per-phase histograms only when the probe triggers (1% sampling by default). Designed to avoid adding noise to general benches.
- ci/mini-bench-workflow.yaml: a small GitHub Actions workflow that runs the corpus on PRs with a ~6 minute budget; it compares p50/p95 against a baseline artifact and fails on regressions above threshold.

Design and rationale:
Determinism: each trace is annotated with a seed and a deterministic tokenization path; the runner enforces identical preconditions (no background threads, CPU governor hint) so runs are repeatable within CI environment variance bounds.
Sparse probing: instead of instrumenting every run, the reporter samples a tiny fraction and attaches a reproducible trace ID so if we see a regressed sample we can re-run the same trace at higher fidelity. This keeps overall noise low and avoids skewing aggregate numbers.
Compatibility: The code uses existing bench harness interfaces (Runner and Reporter base classes) so it's a non-invasive addition and can be toggled from larger suites.

Commits (summary):
- Add mini corpus with 12 session JSONs and deterministic token metadata.
- Implement mini_runner harness with deterministic scheduler and CLI flags (--seed, --reps, --noisy=false).
- Add sparse_cpu_probe reporter that uses perf_event_open fallback to a tight wall-clock sampler when perf unavailable.
- CI workflow to run the mini suite on PRs and store artifact diffs.
- Tests for determinism (unit test asserts repeatable token sequences across runs) and integration test for reporter output schema.

Files changed (top-level):
- benchmark-lab/mini_bench_corpus/ (12 files added)
- benchmark-lab/runner/mini_runner.py (+450 lines)
- benchmark-lab/reporters/sparse_cpu_probe.py (+180 lines)
- benchmark-lab/tests/test_mini_determinism.py (+120 lines)
- benchmark-lab/ci/mini-bench-workflow.yaml (+60 lines)
- docs/bench.md (small addition linking the mini suite)
- README updates to document how to reproduce sampled failures locally

Testing and CI:
- Local unit tests added (pytest). Determinism test asserts identical token hashes across 3 runs with different wall-time but identical seeds.
- Integration regression check runs three repeated executions and computes p50/p95; CI workflow uploads an artifact 'mini-bench-baseline' on the first green run and compares subsequent runs to it.
- GitHub Actions matrix contains: ubuntu-latest (cpu-only), and an optional docker GPU job (manual).
- CI results: first run succeeded, a flaky timer test failed on second run due to CI jitter and was fixed by tighter sleep calibration; final CI status: pass.

Review thread (highlights):
- Mariana Lopez: "Nice small suite — can we reduce the default sampling from 1% to 0.5% to further lower overhead in cross-repo CI?"
- Riley Chen (author): "I tried 0.5% in an earlier iteration and saw loss of signal for 1-2 regressions; leaving at 1% for now but made sampling a CLI/config flag and added documentation on how to lower it per workflow."
- Ethan Park: "Can the reporter fall back gracefully when perf_event_open is not permitted in constrained runners? Also please ensure the reporter doesn't change scheduling affinity."
- Riley Chen: "Added fallback to monotonic wall-clock read with tighter sampling window; reporter only reads timestamps and never sets affinity. Added an integration test to validate behavior on restricted containers."
- Nora Singh: "Tests look good, but add a badge and baseline artifact upload so we can track long-term drift."
- Riley Chen: "Added artifact upload and a short section in docs/bench.md recommending baseline refresh cadence (monthly or after major compiler/toolchain upgrades)."

Performance & safety notes:
- This suite is explicitly not intended for capacity planning; it's a fast signal suite to detect regressions in hotpaths. For throughput/occupancy capacity planning, continue using the larger multi-stage suites.
- Reporter uses sampling with minimal overhead (<0.5% observed in local microbench runs).

How to reproduce a sampled failure locally:
1) Use runner/mini_runner.py --seed <trace-seed> --reps 10 --reporter sparse_cpu_probe --trace-id <id>
2) If the reporter indicated a regression sample, pass --high-fidelity to re-run that trace with full instrumentation and KV-cache warmup.

Follow-ups/TODOs:
- Add automated upload of sample traces to the artifact store for easier bisecting. (ENG-2178)
- Wire a dashboard in Redwood Console that surfaces mini-bench p50/p95 trends over time. (ENG-2104)
- Experiment with adaptive sampling rates tied to observed variance.

Merge notes:
- Squash-merged to main after final approval from Mariana and Ethan. Release notes added to the repo changelog. No configuration defaults were changed for existing suites.
Adds a small deterministic benchmark corpus and a low-overhead sparse CPU probe reporter for microprofile comparisons. No user-facing API changes.

payload.body:
Title: Add time-to-ready SLI calculation (provisioning -> Ready) from event timestamps

Context
We’re rolling out provision-to-ready automation for Dedicated pools, and we need a canonical SLI for “time-to-ready” that is consistent across regions/GPU types and robust to retries/quarantine. This PR adds an SLI calculator in slo-toolkit that derives duration from the event stream produced by the provisioning orchestrator and fleet readiness service.

What this PR does
- Introduces a new SLI: time_to_ready_seconds (aka provision_to_ready_seconds) computed per node instance based on event timestamps.
- Uses event timestamps rather than scrape-time to avoid skew and to survive delayed ingestion.
- Defines the start and end markers as:
  - start: first Observed(Allocated) or ProvisioningStarted event for a node (prefers Allocated when present)
  - end: first Ready event (terminal Ready transition) for that node’s “bring-up attempt”
- Adds normalization logic to handle out-of-order events, duplicates, and multiple attempts.
- Adds guardrails so quarantined nodes do not silently poison the SLI distribution (we record as outcome=quarantined and exclude from success SLI, but still emit a separate failure duration).
- Adds unit tests and golden fixtures covering edge cases observed during baseline measurement.

SLI definition details (aligned with ENG-4821)
- SLI name: provision_to_ready_time
- Measure: (ready_ts - allocated_ts) in seconds
- Population: nodes in Dedicated and shared fleets that emit readiness events (pool_type tag)
- Success criteria: node reaches Ready within SLO window (SLO enforcement lives elsewhere; this PR only computes the raw duration distribution + outcomes)
- Outcome tags:
  - outcome=ready (terminal success)
  - outcome=quarantined (terminal failure)
  - outcome=unknown (insufficient data; excluded from SLI)

Implementation notes
- Added EventWindowResolver to group events into a single bring-up attempt. Rules:
  - Prefer the earliest allocated/provisioning_start timestamp as start.
  - If a node emits multiple allocated/provisioning_start events, treat them as retries within the same attempt unless a ReimageRequested or NodeReplaced event is present (then start a new attempt window).
  - If Ready occurs before start due to out-of-order ingestion, clamp by sorting on event_ts; if still inconsistent, mark unknown and emit a debug counter.
- Added dedupe by (node_id, event_type, event_ts) with a small tolerance window to avoid double-counting when the same state transition is re-emitted.
- Clock skew handling: if ready_ts - start_ts < -30s, mark outcome=unknown and increment provision_to_ready_clock_skew_total.

New metrics emitted by slo-toolkit
- slo_provision_to_ready_seconds (histogram; tags: region, gpu_type, pool_type, image_channel, outcome)
- slo_provision_to_ready_computed_total (counter; tags: outcome)
- slo_provision_to_ready_unknown_total (counter; tags: reason=missing_start|missing_ready|clock_skew|invalid_sequence)

Files changed (high level)
- pkg/slis/provision_to_ready.go: new SLI computation + windowing/dedupe
- pkg/slis/provision_to_ready_test.go: unit tests for edge cases
- pkg/events/schema.go: adds a small set of event types used to split attempts (ReimageRequested/NodeReplaced)
- pkg/export/prometheus.go: registers histogram + counters
- configs/slis.yaml: wires SLI into the default SLO bundle
- testdata/fixtures/provision_to_ready/*.jsonl: event stream fixtures from staged rollout simulations

Tests added / edge cases covered
- Missing Allocated but has ProvisioningStarted -> uses ProvisioningStarted as start.
- Duplicate Ready events -> only first terminal Ready ends the window.
- Out-of-order ingestion -> sorts by event_ts and validates sequence.
- Ready emitted, then Quarantined (should be impossible) -> treated as invalid_sequence (unknown) and flagged.
- Quarantined without Ready -> produces outcome=quarantined duration using quarantine_ts as terminal end.
- ReimageRequested mid-stream -> splits into a new attempt; only the successful attempt contributes to outcome=ready.

Rollout / compatibility
- Backwards compatible: no changes to existing SLIs.
- The new SLI is off by default unless included in the deployed slis.yaml bundle; this PR adds it to the default bundle in this repo, but production enablement is controlled in the deployment pipeline.

Follow-ups
- Once the control-plane readiness service is authoritative everywhere, we should remove fallback reliance on ProvisioningStarted for start_ts (kept for now to avoid gaps during staged rollout).
- Consider adding an explicit attempt_id emitted by the orchestrator; would simplify window splitting.

Release notes (internal)
- Adds time-to-ready SLI computation for provision-to-ready automation dashboards and alerting.

Links
- Linear: ENG-4821
- Related rollout work: provision-to-ready automation sprint

Checklist
- [x] Unit tests for resolver/windowing
- [x] Prometheus metric registration + naming review
- [x] Fixture coverage for out-of-order / duplicate events
- [x] Docs in configs/slis.yaml updated

PR conversation (abridged)
- Aisha Bello: “Can we ensure quarantined nodes don’t show up in the ‘success’ histogram? We need a separate view for failure duration.”
  - Miles Thornton: “Yes—added outcome tag and excluded outcome!=ready from success SLI aggregation; still emitting histogram with outcome label for analysis.”
- Allison Grant: “Please avoid high-cardinality labels (node_id). Also, image_version might be too granular vs image_channel.”
  - Miles Thornton: “Confirmed: no node_id labels. Switched to image_channel; image_version remains available via logs but not as a metric tag.”
- Rafael Mendes: “What’s our stance on clock skew? We saw some negative durations in baseline.”
  - Miles Thornton: “Added -30s tolerance; anything beyond that is unknown and increments a skew counter so we can quantify.”
- Sergio Costa: “Can we add a fixture for ‘Ready then Quarantined’ to ensure we detect invalid sequences?”
  - Miles Thornton: “Added invalid_sequence test and counter.”

CI
- unit-tests: pass
- lint: pass
- go-test-race: pass
- build: pass

Merge
Squash merged by Miles Thornton on 2025-10-14.

Context and motivation: Production latency variability on heterogeneous sequence mixes shows recurring short-lived hotsets (small subset of prompt templates that dominate tail latency for minutes). Existing phase-agnostic samplers under-sample these short-lived regimes, so our regressions miss real-world tail behavior. This PR adds a lightweight 'phasebound primer' that detects epochal hotset shifts and maintains an adaptive hotset reservoir used to bias sampling for profiling and offline attributions. It also introduces a per-epoch kernel sampler that captures kernel-level hotpath attributions with prior-weighted sampling to stabilize estimates when hotsets are small.

What this PR does (summary): - Add adaptive hotset reservoir that tracks token/sequence signatures with time-decayed counts and an eviction policy tuned to short epochs. - Add per-epoch kernel sampler that ties sampled requests to kernel execution traces and aggregates per-kernel latency deltas across epochs. - Introduce a compact delta-exporter (ndjson) that emits per-epoch hotset summaries and kernel attribution records for downstream reporting pipelines (compatible with the existing telemetry ingestion). - Tests and benchmarks: unit tests for reservoir logic, integration harness that runs mixed-seq synthetic workload for 4 hours and produces p50/p95/p99 deltas vs baseline. - Observability: new metrics (hotset_size, reservoir_evictions, kernel_sample_rate, epoch_variance) and a dashboard json under docs/dashboards/phasebound-hotset.json.

Key results (from local benchmark lab runs): - Mixed-sequence synthetic workload (bimodal lengths 64/2048, 60/40 split) - Phasebound sampler increases hotset-capture recall from 0.42 to 0.86 for short-lived bursts (<= 5 minutes) - End-to-end p95 latency reduction in profiling runs: median 12% reduction vs prior sampler (profiling budget matched) - Estimated token-cost impact for profiling: 8% lower sampling cost to reach same attribution confidence compared to uniform sampling.

Commits (high-level): - 0a3b9f1: initial phasebound primer skeleton and interface - 5e7d2b4: reservoir core: time-decay counters, LRU eviction with reservoir caps - f2c1e88: per-epoch kernel sampler and trace attachment - a9d4c6f: delta-exporter ndjson schema + ingestion compatibility layer - 7f1b2a0: unit and integration tests + synthetic workload runner - c12b3d7: docs: dashboard + howto for running the new harness - 3d9f7e4: CI: flaky test stabilization and retry logic for histogram assertions

Files changed (high level): - src/samplers/phasebound_primer.py - src/samplers/reservoir.py - src/samplers/kernel_sampler.py - tools/bench/harness/phasebound_harness.py - tools/bench/reports/delta_exporter.py - test/samplers/test_reservoir.py - test/integration/test_phasebound_end2end.py - docs/dashboards/phasebound-hotset.json - .github/workflows/bench-ci.yml

Design notes and heuristics: - Reservoir uses a two-tiered structure: a small high-fidelity tier for very frequent signatures and an exploration tier for new arrivals; time-decay tunable ensures short hot bursts are retained long enough for a full epoch. - Kernel sampler applies a Bayesian prior (small pseudocount) per-kernel to avoid overfitting on single-sample spikes; priors are configurable per-deployment class. - Exporter emits compact ndjson records: epoch_id, hotset_hash, top_k_signatures, kernel_attributions (kernel_name, delta_ms, sample_weight). The schema is intentionally flat to integrate with the pipeline's mapreduce-style aggregators.

Review conversation (highlights): - Diego Rivera (review): "Nice modularization. Reservoir eviction needs a configurable upper bound per-tenant; can we avoid a global default that might OOM in extreme multi-tenant runs?" - Author (Maya): "Added per-tenant cap with a default safe-guard and documented the knob. See reservoir.py:TenantReservoirConfig." - Anika Bose (review): "Can you add integration smoke to the bench CI so we don't regress the exporter format? Also a note on ndjson schema versioning." - Author: "Added a smoke job in bench-ci and bump exporter to schema v1 with forward-compatible fields." - Liam O'Connor (approval): "R+ with minor nits; left one comment about metric naming." - Final author reply: "Addressed metric rename and added unit test for metric exposition."

CI and flaky behavior: - bench-ci pipeline: 3 runs during review. First run failed due to an unrelated histogram assertion (test_hist_aggregator) that times out under constrained runners; added retry+backoff and test isolation. Second run passed locally; third run on CI passed all jobs. Overall CI status: pass.

Rollout and migration notes: - Feature gated behind runtime flag sampler.phasebound.enabled (off by default for Dedicated until validated). - Backwards compatible: when disabled, sampler falls back to previous uniform/phase-agnostic sampler. - Telemetry consumers should be prepared for exporter schema v1; ingestion pipeline will ignore unknown fields.

Follow-ups and open items: - ENG-8891: instrument per-tenant memory accounting under high-multitenancy (tracked separately). - Measure end-to-end production impact under trace-sampled live traffic (we expect similar improvements but need to validate on live burst shapes). - Consider a lightweight on-device variant for constrained profiler agents.

Merge outcome: Squash merge to main; final merge commit: squash-33177-phasebound (author: Maya Chen). Changelog entry added.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration harness - [x] Benchmarks and summary - [x] Docs + dashboard - [x] CI green

If you want to run the harness locally: tools/bench/harness/README.md includes step-by-step; a typical run: python -m tools.bench.harness.phasebound_harness --duration 240 --save /tmp/phasebound_run.ndjson

Introduce a phase-aware primer that builds an adaptive hotset reservoir and a per-epoch kernel sampler. Improves p95 on mixed-seq workloads and provides a compact delta export for downstream attribution pipelines.

payload.body:
Motivation: production traces show that short, high-intensity bursts (token surge windows) often dominate tail latency and cost but are poorly represented by existing sequence-mix samplers. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: (1) Adaptive Timeline Fragmenter (ATF) — an instrumentation-aware runner that slices long sessions into context-coherent fragments while preserving KV-cache continuity for warmup analysis, and (2) Burst Convolution Reporter — a reporter that identifies burst windows and computes convolution-style burst metrics (burst-width distribution, intra-burst p50/p95/p99, inter-burst spacing histogram, and aggregate burst-shaped cost modeling).

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a timeline fragmenter runner that can emit fragments with overlap and metadata tags to preserve warmup semantics for the serving runtime. Fragmenter supports several heuristics: energy-based (token entropy spike), fixed-time sliding window, and adaptive density thresholding.
- Implements burst detection and a burst-convolution aggregation pipeline that computes per-fragment and cohort-level burst metrics with optional symbolication hooks for prompt templates.
- Integrates new reporters into the existing bench harness and a lightweight visualization export (ndjson + small HTML viewer) for manual inspection.
- Adds end-to-end tests validating fragment warmup preservation and a synthetic workload generator that can inject controlled bursts for CI/benchmark regression tests.

Design notes / tradeoffs:
- The fragmenter emits fragments with an overlap window to preserve KV-cache warmup; overlap defaults to 64 tokens but is configurable per-profile. This trades some measurement duplication for more realistic latency during warmup-sensitive workflows.
- Burst convolution uses a sliding aggregation kernel; kernel width is configurable and documented. We intentionally avoid global normalization across sessions to keep cohort comparisons stable when input lengths vary.
- Memory overhead is small: fragment metadata is lightweight and the reporter streams aggregates to avoid holding full traces in memory.

Checklist:
- [x] Timeline fragmenter implementation
- [x] Burst detection and convolution reporter
- [x] Integration with bench harness config and example profiles
- [x] Unit + integration tests for fragment warmup semantics
- [x] Basic ndjson export and small visualization viewer (dev only)
- [x] Docs: bench/README and timeline-fragmenter.md

How to run locally:
1. Build the bench binary: make bench
2. Run the synthetic burst generator: ./bin/bench --profile profiles/synthetic_burst.json --mode generate --out /tmp/bursts.ndjson
3. Run fragmenter + reporter: ./bin/bench --runner fragmenter --profile profiles/timeline_fragmenter.json --input /tmp/bursts.ndjson --report out/burst_report.ndjson
4. Open dev viewer: scripts/viewer.sh out/burst_report.ndjson

Related: Linear ENG-3124 (profiling high-intensity bursts), BENCH-58 (bench reporting backlog). This PR is intended to be the baseline for follow-ups that will: (a) add automated regression thresholds for burst-shaped regressions, and (b) plug these metrics into the console alerting pipeline.

Notes on CI: initial run failed due to an ordering race in TestFragmentWarmup; added a coordination barrier and re-ran. All tests pass on linux amd64 and macos-latest.

Merge strategy: squash merge; keep commits focused and preserved in the squash message for auditability.
Victor Huang: Naming nit — 'convolution' sounds heavy; are we sure we don't want 'convolver' or 'burst-aggregator'?
Maya Patel: I chose 'convolution' to emphasize the sliding-kernel aggregation semantics; can rename later if tooling prefers shorter terms.
Victor Huang: OK, fine; please add a short comment in reporter.py explaining kernel semantics.
Maya Patel: Done in latest commit.
Sofia Rivera: Can you add a small test ensuring overlap window actually preserves warmup latency?
Maya Patel: Added TestFragmentWarmup which failed initially due to ordering; fixed with a barrier and re-recorded expected warmup timeline.
Liam O'Connor: CI green, small doc nit (typo in timeline-fragmenter.md) — resolved. Approving.
Liam O'Connor: Approved.
Merge-bot: Merged by Maya Patel via squash on 2025-01-22.
Adds adaptive timeline fragmenter runner and burst-convolution reporter. New metrics: burst-width distribution, intra-burst p95/p99, inter-burst spacing histogram. Includes synthetic burst generator and example profiles for regression tests.

payload.body:
Motivation: reproduce and measure prefetch behavior deterministically across CI and local runs to triage kernel-affinity regressions affecting p95/p99 tails. This PR adds a lightweight prefetch orchestrator that deterministically schedules primer requests and a reproducible hotpath recorder that emits a compact seed+trace artifact usable by the benchmark harness to replay identical scheduling and kernel affinity sequences. Changes include a seedable scheduler, durable prefetch plan serialization, a deterministic randomizer for primer selection, and a compact binary trace schema with an optional JSON fallback. The goal is to enable: 1) stable perf baselines for nightly/regression suites, 2) root-cause analysis of kernel-affinity induced tail-latency spikes, 3) a reproducible on-demand replay mode that can be shipped to infra for postmortems. Compatibility: default behavior is opt-in for existing runners; no change to current nightly flows unless enable_prefetch_orchestrator=true in benchmark config. See linked Linear items for rollout plan and integration tests.
5 commits: initial deterministic scheduler impl; add seed serialization and loader; introduce hotpath recorder and compact trace writer; integrate orchestrator into seq-replayer runner with opt-in flag; add unit+integration tests and docs updates.
Ava: Overall looks good — can we make the seed format forward compatible? suggested tagging with schema version (resolved in second commit).
Jacob: Found a flaky assertion in test_prefetch_repro.py on mac runner; added a tolerance and moved test to linux-only in CI matrix (author replied: added a log and tightened cleanup to avoid residual timers).
Sana: Question about CPU pinning interactions: requested a small doc note and a unit test simulating co-located workloads (author: added doc paragraph and synthetic co-located test).
Marcus: Approved after CI green and small nits addressed (rename variable, add type hints).
Adds an opt-in deterministic prefetch orchestrator and a reproducible hotpath recorder for benchmark replaying and root-cause analysis. Nightly baselines can opt-in to produce seed+trace artifacts for reproducible tail investigations.
Initial CI run failed due to platform-specific timer flakiness; rerun with linux-only integration and stabilized cleanup. Opt-in flag prevents user-facing behavior changes. The compact_trace.proto is intentionally minimal to keep artifacts small and fast to ship.

payload.body:
Motivation: existing workload runners cover independent request streams (single-sequence throughput, sequence-mix) but do not model correlated cross-stream load spikes that occur in production (e.g., user action fanout, background sync overlapping with foreground traffic). This PR introduces a correlated-load generator harness plus an end-to-end telemetry export pipeline to capture cross-stream latency, queue-growth, and synchronization metrics so that downstream analysis and reporting can reason about tail behavior caused by inter-stream contention. Key deliverables: 1) bench/correlated_runner.py - a new runner that models N interdependent streams with configurable correlation matrices, jitter, and fanout; 2) telemetry/otel_exporter.py - lightweight OTel exporter that emits per-request attributes, cross-stream correlation IDs, and histogram buckets; 3) reporting/cross_stream_reporter.py - post-run aggregator that computes cross_stream_p50/p95/p99, queue_peak_avg, backlog_area (integral of queue length over time), and produces CSV + NDJSON outputs for the existing reporting pipeline; 4) integration test harness (tests/integration/test_correlated_end_to_end.py) that runs the runner against the model stub and asserts telemetry invariants; 5) CI workflow update to run the correlated workload in a short smoke mode on PRs. Design notes: the runner uses event-driven scheduling (asyncio) with a central correlation controller that injects synthetic causality between streams; correlation is parameterized as a matrix of probabilities (float in [0,1]) that governs whether an event in stream A triggers related events in stream B within a time window. Telemetry uses OpenTelemetry traces + custom metric instruments; to avoid high cardinality, correlation IDs are hashed to a bounded dimension and we export representative sample traces at a 1/100 sampling rate in CI mode. Backwards compatibility: the runner is opt-in for the lab (not enabled by default), uses existing bench runner interfaces, and integrates with current reporting consumers. Checklist: [x] add correlated runner and unit tests; [x] add OTel exporter with config; [x] add reporting aggregator and CSV/NDJSON writer; [x] add integration smoke test; [x] update CI workflow; [x] document config knobs (README). Known limitations and future work: higher-fidelity user models (session state), long-running persistence of correlation IDs to simulate multi-minute flows, and a telemetry ingest sidecar for high-throughput on-prem runs. Impact: enables reproducible stress tests for cross-stream tail behavior and provides structured outputs for the dashboarding team to add cross-stream charts.

Ethan Walker: Can the runner blow up memory if correlation fanout is high? Suggest add a hard cap on queued derived events and emit backlog alerts so the reporter can detect overloads.
Daniel Chen: Implemented queue cap (configurable) and backlog_area metric. Added an integration assertion that backlog_area stays below a threshold in smoke mode. Also added a unit test for queue cap behaviour.
Lena Fischer: Minor: prefer snake_case in metric names and include unit labels (ms) for latency histograms. Also asked to include a short example in docs showing how to reproduce a 5-stream correlated spike.
Daniel Chen: Updated metric names to cross_stream_p95_ms, cross_stream_p99_ms, and included example run command in docs/bench/correlated.md.
Add correlated workload runner and end-to-end telemetry exporter for cross-stream tail analysis. Includes reporting aggregator and CI smoke tests. This enables reproducible correlated spike tests and CSV/NDJSON outputs for dashboards.

Backward compatibility: default behavior unchanged for existing runners; correlated runner is opt-in.
Follow-ups: add a Jupyter notebook that visualizes backlog_area over time and integrate with perf-canary dashboards.
