Motivation: We need representative, phase-aware burst workloads that reflect realistic nonuniform arrival patterns (bursts separated by variable quiescent intervals) and a lightweight metric to surface kernel-level contention during those bursts. Existing replay harnesses assume uniform inter-arrival times or fixed burst sizes which under-estimate micro-congestion observed in production. This PR introduces a sequenced burst replayer (Poisson-modulated bursts with deterministic priming options) and a compact kernel congestion index (cong_idx) scorer that runs on sampled telemetry to highlight contention hotspots across kernels and sequence phases.

Summary of changes: Adds a new benchmark runner bin/seq-burst-replayer, a telemetry processor that synthesizes a congestion index per kernel and per sequence-phase, a small aggregation/reporting pipeline that emits per-cohort cong_idx time-series and a dashboard-ready CSV exporter. The replay mode supports: deterministic priming, poisson-modulated inter-burst intervals, configurable tail-edge jitter, and optional KV-cache priming window alignment. The cong_idx is computed from a small set of signals (stream stall time, kernel queuing wait, memory-copy overlap, and active SM utilization delta) and normalized per-GPU so it can be compared across instance types.

Why it's different: Instead of only measuring p95/p99 under static bursts, this runner emphasizes phase transitions and computes a single interpretable congestion score to help devs triage whether tail spikes are due to scheduling contention or model-side compute variance. The exporter is intentionally compact (CSV + JSON summary) to be easy to pull into existing profiling dashboards.

How to run (examples):
  ./bin/seq-burst-replayer --spec specs/nonuniform-poisson.yaml --duration 3600 --kv-prime=200 --out ./runs/seqrun-20251103
  python tools/congidx/processor.py --input ./runs/seqrun-20251103/telemetry.ldjson --output ./runs/seqrun-20251103/cong_report.csv --window 5s

Checklist: [x] Implements runner + telemetry processor [x] Unit tests for cong_idx normalization [x] Small end-to-end smoke benchmark in CI [x] Documentation in docs/bench/sequenced-burst.md [x] No user-facing API changes

Observed results (example): On an NVIDIA A10G test cluster with default batching and KV priming=200, a representative two-phase workload shows: baseline replay (old runner) p95 token-latency = 312ms, new sequenced runner p95 = 278ms after applying adaptive priming and pre-warm. Cong_idx highlights kernel:matmul_fp16 as the top contributor during the second-phase tail with cong_idx=0.67 (normalized). These numbers are illustrative and vary by model and batch mixing.

Notes on design: cong_idx is intentionally heuristic and lightweight — it is not a replacement for full perf traces. It is intended as a high-signal alert to focus investigative profiling runs (flamegraphs, nsight). Scale implications: processor runs in <1/10 real-time for 1h of telemetry on a 4-core profiling host.

Related: ENG-4729 (burst-workload coverage), ENG-4791 (telemetry compacting), SUP-2217 (customer-reported tail under nonuniform traffic).

Aisha Patel (author): cong_idx normalizes against a per-GPU baseline collected during warmup; tests added to validate insensitivity across 50-200Hz sampling. CSV now includes gpu_model and driver_version columns.

Aisha Patel: Added the e2e assertion to ci/workflows/perf-smoke.yaml and a toleration flag to avoid flakiness on ephemeral infra.

Motivation: We need a lightweight runner that produces compact, timestamped snapshots of inference traffic across multiple sequence-length cohorts so that downstream reporters can stitch quantile curves across windows. Existing runners either emit full traces (too heavy) or only cumulative metrics (too coarse). This PR introduces 'SeqShot', a snapshot runner that samples short, aligned time-slices across cohorts, and a 'quantile-stitching' reporter that merges per-window histograms into a smooth composite latency quantile curve suitable for regression diffing and visualization.

What this changes (single continuous body): Adds a new bench harness (SeqShot) that performs synchronized short-lived probes across specified cohort buckets (seq-length, payload size, model variant). Snapshots include per-request metadata (cohort id, seed, trace-id), latency histograms, and optional kernel-level tags. The reporter consumes snapshot batches and performs an overlap-aware stitching algorithm that glues adjacent window histograms using weighted interpolation to produce a global quantile curve resilient to out-of-order snapshots and transient spikes.

Checklist: - [x] Implement SeqShot runner with seeding and deterministic replay mode - [x] Implement quantile-stitching reporter with configurable overlap factor - [x] Add unit tests for stitching logic and histogram merge edge cases - [x] Add end-to-end integration test that runs SeqShot against the local micro-bench env - [x] Benchmarked on a microburst and steady-state scenario, results attached in artifacts - [x] Updated README and runner docs

Context and motivation: We observed persistent tail variance during multi-sequence warmups in the continuous-batcher experiments: single-primer warmup often left shard-local KV caches out of phase, producing amplified p95/p99 variability when sequences cross shard boundaries. This PR implements a hierarchical warmup synchronizer (the 'Phase Coupler') to coordinate warmup primers across node-local and cluster-level layers, and adds a phase-aware profiler serializer and a token-pathline reporter to make per-token warmup progress observable for benchmark analysis.

What this PR does (single continuous description): - Adds a hierarchical warmup synchronizer that runs at two levels: node-local primer orchestration and cluster-phase coupling. The coordinator exposes deterministic phase epochs so primers on different GPUs/instances align their KV cache priming windows. - Introduces phase markers in the profiling pipeline and a compact phase-aware serializer (protobuf + delta-encoded token timestamps) so phase boundaries are not lost in aggregation. - Implements a token pathline reporter that reconstructs per-request token-level warmup contribution (which tokens populated KV slabs, which primers were used) and exports CSVs and compressed parquet-like blobs for offline analysis. - Adds tests: unit tests for scheduler state machine, integration tests simulating multi-shard warmup with synthetic traffic, and an end-to-end benchmark job that demonstrates reduced tail variance in a controlled scenario. - Modifies the benchmark harness to optionally enable phase coupling via a toggle flag (enabled=false by default for backward compatibility). - Documentation: README describing tuning knobs and a short howto for analyzing token pathline outputs with the bench visualizer.

Checklist: - [x] Design review with infra and runtime (ENG-2142) - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration warmup simulation - [x] End-to-end benchmark job + baseline comparison - [x] Documentation snippet and chart example - [x] CI green (after lint fix)

Commits (high level): - f2a1c9e: introduce phase-coupler core scheduler, state machine, and API stubs - 6b3d2a4: implement node-local primer coordinator and RPC shims - ab7c48d: add profiling phase markers and serializer proto definitions - 9e4d0f1: token pathline reporter (CSV + compressed blob writer) - 4b5e2c7: harness integration: toggles, flags, and e2e scenario - c2d7a88: tests and deterministic seed harness for CI - 8f9b33a: docs and bench visualizer example - 0a1b2c3: lint fix and CI configuration updates

Files changed (high level): - scheduler/phase_coupler.py (new) - scheduler/README.md (new design doc + knobs) - runtime/primer_coordinator.cc (updates to RPC handler) - profiling/phase_serializer.proto (new) - profiling/phase_serializer.go (new: serializer + tests) - reporters/token_pathline_reporter.go (new) - bench/harness/phase_coupler_job.yaml (new benchmark job) - bench/harness/tests/test_phase_alignment.py (new) - docs/bench-setup/phase-coupling.md (new) - ci/flakeignore (updated) - Makefile (targets for generating serializer bindings) - go.mod/go.sum updates

Why now: This provides an internal capability to deterministically prime KV caches across heterogeneous warmup primers and reduces spurious regression noise in tail latency benchmarks. It is intended to make our benchmark baselines more reproducible across CI runs and lab clusters.

Testing notes and results: The e2e bench job compares baseline (no coupling) vs enabled coupling on a 4-node cluster with mixed sequence lengths. Key results from local lab run (attached to the benchmark run artifact): baseline p95 = 312ms, baseline p99 = 680ms; with phase coupling p95 = 254ms (-19%), p99 = 498ms (-27%). End-to-end test included deterministic RNG seeds to remove sampling variance; see bench/harness/artifacts/phase-coupler-run-2026-02-28.tar.gz for traces.

Backward compatibility and rollout: Coupling is opt-in via the bench harness flag bench_phase_coupler_enabled (default false). We will roll out to nightly benchmarks for two weeks before enabling by default for regression runs. No customer-facing API change.

Observability: Adds two new metric families: bench.warmup.phase_epoch (gauge) and bench.warmup.token_primed_total (counter). Token pathline outputs include mapping to primer worker IDs and KV slab ids for root cause attribution.

Risks and mitigation: The synchronizer introduces extra coordination RPCs; for production runtime we keep this disabled by default and use it only within benchmark lab clusters. The serializer uses delta-encoding; if a bug corrupts phase markers it only affects offline analysis, not runtime serving.

Related work: builds on earlier primer orchestration efforts (ENG-1789) and denoiser tracing (ENG-1905).

Merge notes: Squash-merged after CI green and approvals.

Introduces a hierarchical warmup synchronizer and a phase-aware profiling serializer plus a token pathline reporter. Intended for benchmark lab use: no runtime API changes for customers; internal telemetry and perf tests benefit.

Maya Patel: Good question — the coupler uses epoch leases and a sliding acceptance window; if a node misses an epoch we mark it as 'lagging' and allow shadow priming for up to 3 epochs before forcing catch-up. Added details in scheduler/README.md.
Lina Chen: Tests look solid. I asked for a small unit test covering delta-encoding edge-case (zero-length deltas).
Maya Patel: Added test for zero-length deltas in profiling/phase_serializer_test.go. CI triggered.
Omar Farouk: CI initially failed lint on scheduler/phase_coupler.py (unused import). Once fixed, re-run passed. Approving now.
Jorge Ramirez: Approved after confirming metrics names and tags; note: consider a future opt-in for production-scale runs.

Context: Multiple SDK teams asked for a lighter-weight streaming bridge that standardizes auth preset selection, improves retry ergonomics, and tightens iterator ergonomics across Python/TypeScript/Go. Motivation: Reduce duplicated auth selection logic in customer code, make streaming resume/heartbeat interactions predictable across SDKs, and align minor API ergonomics so feature parity is easier to maintain. Summary of changes (high level): 1) Introduced "compact auth presets" library (internal/auth/presets.go + sdks/* glue) that codifies three supported auth profiles: direct-token, delegated-refresh, and prefetched-lease. 2) Added a small streaming-bridge shim (sdks/typescript/src/stream/bridge.ts, sdks/python/redwood/_stream_bridge.py, sdks/go/stream/bridge.go) that normalizes resume tokens and exposes a tiny ergonomic async iterator / generator surface for pull/push streams. 3) Reworked retry configuration shape to use RetryProfile (a compact declaration that ships with SDK defaults) and added back-compat adapters to accept the previous backoff shape. 4) Tightened iterator behavior: iterators now expose an isPaused() hint and a graceful close() that flushes pending resume state. 5) Added telemetry hooks for reauth attempts (telemetry keys: sdk.auth.reauth_attempt, sdk.auth.fallback_used) and added unit/integration tests around heartbeat/reauth races. 6) Version bumps: python-sdk -> 1.31.0, typescript-sdk -> 1.28.5, go-sdk -> 1.9.2. Compatibility notes: This is intentionally non-breaking for typical consumers. The old retry config is still accepted via an adapter layer; however, a handful of minor optional parameter names were renamed for clarity in TS (maxRetryWindow -> retryWindowMs) and an alias is preserved during the transition. Migration notes: If you supply custom retry config structs, update to RetryProfile or rely on the adapter. If you previously relied on internal resume token shapes, switch to passing the resume token string or use the bridge's resumeHint accessor. Tests and QA: Added 48 new unit tests across sdks/python and sdks/typescript, and 6 small integration harness scenarios that run against the local streaming canary in CI. Manual verification included cross-language smoke (py->ts->go examples) and a short soak on the perf-canary cluster for 4 hours. Docs: Added upgrade guidance at docs/upgrade-sdks.md and small usage examples in examples/streaming. Why this is unique: Instead of pushing language-specific divergent ergonomics, the PR creates a compact, opinionated bridge and small public primitives that are identical in behavior across languages, making future parity work incremental. Related work: builds on ENG-2120 (stream resume spec) and complements ENG-3373 (retry-presets RFC).
Daniel Ortiz: Please justify why we chose three presets instead of keeping the larger matrix; note that customers often have hybrid flows. Author reply: Short answer - we want an opinionated surface to reduce error modes; the presets are extensible and a 'custom' preset path is available. Marta Li: Can we preserve the old retry config names for one release to make migration easier? Response: Yes, adapter added and test coverage included. Rohit Anand: Small nit - rename maxRetryWindow to retryWindowMs in TS to clarify units. Author: Implemented and added alias; tests updated. Daniel Ortiz: Approve after green CI. Marta Li: Approve. Rohit Anand: Approve. Merge: squash and merge after release checklist completed.
- Introduce compact auth presets and a small streaming bridge to unify resume/reauth behavior across SDKs. - Add RetryProfile as the recommended retry config shape; adapter for legacy shapes included. - Expose ergonomic iterator helpers: isPaused() and close() to flush resume state. - Add telemetry for auth reattempts and fallback usage. - SDK version bumps: python 1.31.0, typescript 1.28.5, go 1.9.2.

Adds a new benchmark harness that simulates interleaved priming/cohort access patterns to exercise KV-cache reuse and memory churn across GPUs, paired with a lightweight snapshot "tee" that captures per-epoch memory liveness metadata to an external object store for offline analysis. Motivation: we observed production tail regressions correlated with nonuniform priming across tenant cohorts; existing runners either target pure single-stream warmup or broad-stroke mixed loads but don't capture liveness metadata needed to diagnose persistent allocation hotspots. This PR introduces an extensible simulator, a memory-snapshot tee, new microbenchmarks and a reporting pipeline that produces compact epochal liveness histograms and object-store artifacts for flamegraph correlation. The description below lists commits, changed areas, CI summary, review thread highlights and perf baseline, and notes about rollout and follow-ups.

Motivation: existing workload runners sample sequences uniformly and fail to capture phase-skew behaviors observed in customer traffic (e.g., bursts of long sequences interleaved with many short ones). This PR adds a phase-stratified workload generator (seqblast) that explicitly models sequence-length phases and produces deterministic, seedable workloads suitable for profiling and regression comparisons. The change also includes a lightweight "stitch" reporter that correlates per-token latency deltas with kernel selection boundaries so we can attribute tail spikes to specific execution kernels or cache effects.
Changes: - bench/runners/seqblast_runner.go: new Go runner implementing configurable phase distributions, phase-duration schedules, and weighted sequence priming to emulate KV-cache warmup/decay patterns. Supports deterministic seed, per-phase warmup windows, and per-sequence metadata tags. - bench/reporters/stitch_reporter.py: Python reporter that ingests runner traces and runtime kernel telemetry, stitches token-level timing across phase boundaries, and emits a compact CSV plus JSON summary for downstream visualization. - configs/profiles/seqblast_profile.yaml: example profiles for short-burst, long-tail, and mixed-phase workloads used by CI and perf lab. - tests/bench/seqblast_integ.test: integration harness that runs seqblast against a local perf-canary endpoint and asserts steady-state token rates and KV cache hit behavior. - docs/benchmarking/seqblast.md: design notes, recommended profile parameters, and examples for reproducing customer-like phase-skew traffic.

Motivation: Long-tail burst patterns in customer traffic cause noisy p95/p99 regressions in our inference profiling. Existing workload synthesizers either amplify bursts unrealistically or smooth them with heuristics that lose temporal locality. This PR introduces a deterministic long-tail burst smoother that preserves session-level locality while reducing artificial kernel coalescing, plus a compact trace serializer to reduce reporter storage overhead for high-resolution runs.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a new workload synthesizer (long_tail_smoother) that post-processes generated request streams and applies epoch-aware smoothing rules. The smoother uses a tunable 'burst_decay' kernel and epoch-resampling to maintain representative hot-paths while reducing microburst noise for stable baselines. 2) Implements a compact trace serializer (compact_trace_serializer) in Go that writes deduplicated event frames and an index table for fast downstream aggregation. The serializer targets our reporter pipeline and reduces disk usage by ~4x for high-frequency traces. 3) Integrates both pieces into the experiment harness and adds per-run metrics for 'smoothed_burst_ratio', 'residual_kv_hits', and 'trace_compaction_ratio'. 4) Adds unit and integration tests and updates the benchmark dashboard query templates.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked in ENG-4621 - [x] Unit tests for smoother edge cases - [x] Integration test exercising serializer in a 1k-request short-run - [x] CI linting and type checks - [x] Dashboard query updates and example run artifacts attached

Performance notes: In local and CI perf runs we see median throughput within 2% of the original generator, p95 reduced in noisy microburst scenarios by 18-27% (depending on sequence mix), and trace storage reduced by 3.6-4.5x. These numbers are in the PR run artifacts (perf/artifacts/77421).

Compatibility and rollout: The smoother is opt-in via harness flags (--smoother=long_tail, --burst-decay=0.75) so it will not affect existing baselines until we flip the default in a follow-up. Serializer is backward-compatible with the reporter pipeline; the legacy JSON trace writer remains available behind a flag.

Notes for reviewers: Pay attention to metric names and label cardinality; the serializer deduplicates frames based on a 128-bit hash, we need to be sure collision risk is acceptable for production-size runs. The PR intentionally keeps the hash seed configurable for replay determinism.

Release notes: Added an opt-in long-tail burst smoother for workload generation and a compact trace serializer to reduce reporter storage and speed up downstream aggregation.

Introduce a new benchmark harness that composes cross-model primer weaving with a stochastic kernel-saturation emulator to better surface multi-model contention and warmup hysteresis. Motivation: existing runners exercise single-model hotpaths and do not simulate realistic cross-model primer interleaving seen in production where multiple model families share GPU pools. This PR implements a PrimerWeaver orchestrator that synthesizes interleaved primer sequences across 2-6 model variants with configurable affinity and overlap, a SaturationEmulator that models kernel queueing and thermal backpressure via a saturation_index metric, and exporters that produce per-epoch quantiles, occupancy histograms, and a compact flame snapshot compatible with the perf-lab visualization pipeline. The design focuses on deterministic repeatability (seeded sampler), lightweight state checkpoints for kvcache priming, and an opt-in fidelity mode that trades sampling fidelity for throughput in CI smoke runs. Includes a small set of canonical workload manifests and a migration note for existing benchmark scripts.

3) export occupancy histograms and compact flame snapshots
4) add manifests for cross-model seed scenarios and CI smoke profile

payload.body:
Motivation: Production latency regressions at p95/p99 sometimes coincide with rapid context switches between short sequences (e.g. webhooks + chat) where the KV cache thrashes in micro-batches. We needed a lightweight runner that can emulate context-switch frequency and a sampler that reports batched KV-cache eviction/hit trajectories so we can correlate kernel scheduling with cache resilience. This PR introduces: 1) seqswitch: a compact simulator for sequence context switching and micro-batching. It can replay a hybrid workload composed of long conversational sequences and short stateless calls, injecting configurable switch intervals and coalescing patterns. 2) batched-kvcache-sampler: a probe that runs alongside workloads to sample KV cache state in batch boundaries; it produces time-series of per-key residency and eviction counts and a derived "cache resilience" curve (how quickly a key is re-primed after eviction under given concurrency). 3) quantile-resilience-reporter: a reporting pipeline that merges latency quantiles with cache-resilience traces and emits a delta report keyed by phase and kernel family. Design notes: - The emulator targets low overhead: it is implemented as a Rust microservice (bench/seqswitch) that instructs the existing workload runner to vary sequence boundaries and injection timing rather than forking full additional VM workloads. This keeps experiments reproducible and cheap. - The sampler instruments the runtime's kvcache metrics via a lightweight sampling API (bench/samplers/batched_kvcache). It performs synchronized snapshots at batch commit boundaries to avoid tainting latency numbers. - Reporting: new exporter (bench/reporters/quantile_resilience) takes: latency_histogram, kvcache_snapshots, kernel_tags and produces CSV + JSON summary with fields: phase, model, kernel_family, p50/p95/p99, median_resilience_time_ms, fraction_keys_evicted, repriming_rate_10s. Checklist: - [x] seqswitch runner implemented with config-driven phase scripts - [x] batched kvcache sampler with snapshot sync - [x] reporter CSV/JSON outputs + unit tests - [x] end-to-end integration in bench harness - [x] docs: README with example configs and interpretation guide Commits (high level): - a1d3f9a: initial seqswitch scaffold and config grammar - b7c4e92: implement burst-switch scheduling and sampling hooks - c2d9f77: add batched kvcache sampling and proto exporter - 5e8a1c0: quantile_resilience reporter and CSV schema - 9f4b2a6: glue tests and harness integration + docs Changes (high level files modified): - bench/seqswitch/src/main.rs (new) - bench/seqswitch/configs/sample_hybrid.yaml (new) - bench/samplers/batched_kvcache.rs (new) - bench/reporters/quantile_resilience.rs (new) - bench/harness/integration.rs (modified) - bench/metrics/README.md (modified) - bench/tests/seqswitch_integration.rs (new) - bench/tests/kvcache_sampler_unit.rs (new) - ci/workflows/benchmark.yml (modified: added job run for seqswitch) - tools/plots/resilience_plotter.py (new) - docs/benchmark-lab/seqswitch.md (new) Review conversation (trimmed timeline): "Maria Kovacs": "Nice focused change. Two concerns: how do we ensure snapshots don't perturb latency? and can we run this on the mini-cluster locally?" "Jonah Patel (author)": "Snapshots are taken only at batch commit boundaries using the runtime's snapshot hook; I've added a flag --sync-snapshot that enforces that. For local mini-cluster, see sample_hybrid.yaml which runs with smaller concurrency and the harness autodeploy target 'mini'." "Ellen Park": "Can the sampler be adapted to test quantized kernels where KV representation differs?" "Jonah Patel": "Yes — sampler reads runtime kernel tags and normalizes keys by (model, quantization_level) so reports are comparable. I added a unit test kvcache_sampler_unit.rs to cover a quantized pseudo-kv layout." "Samir Rao (SRE)": "CI failed on first run: test timeouts in integration harness. Re-run once fixed?" "Jonah Patel": "Fixed a race in harness startup by adding a readiness probe and increasing default timeout; re-ran CI." CI summary: - ci/unit: pass - ci/integration: pass (initial failure on 2024-09-11 due to race; subsequent run on 2024-09-12 passed) - bench-suite: pass - lint: pass How to use (short): - example config: bench/seqswitch/configs/sample_hybrid.yaml - run: ./bin/bench run --runner seqswitch --config sample_hybrid.yaml - outputs: bench/out/<run-id>/quantile_resilience.json and .csv Notes on interpreting results: - The reporter aligns per-batch kvcache snapshots with latency buckets by matching run-phase timestamps; use resilience_plotter.py to plot "repriming_rate" vs p95 to identify unstable kernels. - Typical signal: rising p95 concurrent with a drop in median_resilience_time_ms implies eviction-driven tail amplification. Backwards compatibility: - The changes are additive; existing harnesses that don't opt into seqswitch or the kvcache sampler will not be affected. Performance impact: - seqswitch adds negligible overhead when idle; sampler sampling cost is proportional to sampled-key-count (default 200 keys) and is documented in metrics/README. Tests: - Unit tests for sampler normalization and config parser added. - Integration test runs a 30s mini-run on the mini-cluster verifying CSV output and schema. Merge: Squashed and merged to main on 2024-09-18 (merge method: squash). Follow-ups: - ENG-2310: add cross-run aggregator to group resilience metrics across multiple runs for baseline regression detection. - ENG-2211: run this experiment across the dedicated cluster fleet to generate a baseline report for Q4.
Adds a lightweight sequence-context-switch emulator and a batched KV-cache sampler; new reporter exports quantile-resilience metrics and per-phase cache hit trajectories. Useful for multi-tenant and small-batch latency experiments.

Motivation: We observed intermittent P99 regressions that correlate with input sequence diversity across customers. Existing workload generators focus on sequence length and concurrency but underrepresent token-level entropy and primer-to-response variability that exercise KV-cache pressure and attention kernel branching. This PR introduces a new benchmark runner and reporting pipeline to quantify 'session entropy' effects and provide a stability score that aggregates latency tail, memory jitter, and KV cache miss-rate.

What this PR adds: session-entropy-prober runner (configurable entropy profile, primer strategy, and sticky-token probability); deterministic seed-based sampler; stability-score reporter that emits CSV/JSON and a compact delta report; instrumentation hooks to tag flamepoints and KV-cache spill events; CI smoke harness for quick fidelity checks.

How to run (local): ./bin/bench run session-entropy --config=examples/entropy/profiles/high_variability.yaml --target=localhost:8080 --concurrency=32 --duration=10m --out=artifacts/entropy-high.json

Checklist: [x] runner implementation + unit tests; [x] end-to-end reporter + example profile; [x] deterministic sampling with seed option; [x] lightweight smoke CI that runs under 10m; [x] documentation snippet in README/entropy.md.

Behavioral summary: The runner supports three entropy axes: lexical diversity (vocab sample skew), structural variance (primer/template switching), and temporal stickiness (probability of token repeats within a session). Default 'stability score' is a weighted combination: 0.5*p95_latency_norm + 0.3*mem_jitter_norm + 0.2*kv_miss_rate_norm (lower is better). The reporter also computes cohort deltas between baseline and experiment and emits a small text summary for quick triage.

Why this is different from existing tools: Unlike the seq-mixer and hotpath generators, session-entropy-prober focuses on micro-level token distributions and their interaction with KV cache and attention kernel branching. It reproduces rare tail events that previously only surfaced in production traces, enabling earlier detection in CI and bench lab experiments.
Evan Chen (review): Nice addition — please add a short explanation of the stability score weights and a pointer to how we might tune them per workload. Also prefer using the existing metrics namespace 'bench.kv' instead of 'kv_meta'.
Author reply (Priya): Switched to bench.kv and added explanation in docs/bench/entropy.md. Made weights configurable via reporter config (defaults preserved).
Marina López (review): Found a flake when running smoke on p3.2xlarge - p99 was occasionally high due to driver scheduling; request adding a retry and marking the smoke as 'best-effort' in CI metadata.
Author reply (Priya): Added retry in ci job and a 60s warmup. Also added guidance in README about isolating driver noise for GPU runs.
Daniel Foster (approval): LGTM after fixes. Verified stability_score outputs for baseline/experiment and validated reporter CSVs load into the bench ingestion pipeline.
Add session-entropy benchmark runner and stability-score reporter. Useful for detecting tail regressions caused by token-level input diversity and KV cache pressure. Includes example profiles and CI smoke job.

payload.body:
Motivation: We need a compact, reproducible harness to evaluate prefetch and KV-cache strategies across heterogeneous model mix workloads and to stress token churn patterns that expose kernel pressure and microburst tail behavior. This PR adds the Prefetch Fidelity Matrix (PFM) runner and the Cross-Model Token-Churn Harness (CMTC) plus a reporting pipeline that emits a kernel-pressure matrix and an occupancy heatmap for per-kernel attribution.

What this contains: - A modular runner that composes: (1) session priming and configurable prefix distributions, (2) an adaptive prefetcher shim that can simulate dead/overfetch and partial-key eviction policies, and (3) a token-churn injector that creates correlated short bursts and long-tail churn with per-session variability. - Telemetry exporters that emit per-step kernel occupancy estimates, async-kernel queue lengths, and a kernel-pressure matrix (CSV + JSONL) compatible with our flamegrid visualizer. - A lightweight evaluator harness that runs baseline and candidate prefetch policies, computes p50/p95/p99 delta matrices, and generates a fidelity score that weighs latency, token-cost, and quality regressions (relative perplexity on synthetic masked prompts). - Config-driven YAML workload descriptors for easy reproduction and a small sample corpus used in internal benchmarks.

Why it's different: Existing runners focus on sequence-mix and steady-state bursts. This harness targets cross-model interference and token-turnover stability: e.g., scenarios where short high-entropy prompts repeatedly evict prefetched KV pages and produce tail amplification on specific kernels. The kernel-pressure matrix maps model-layer/kernel combos to observed tail amplification so teams can prioritize kernel optimizations.

Compatibility & safety: - No production serving changes; runner lives entirely in benchmark-lab and uses existing mock serving interfaces. - Default workloads use conservative resource parameters; a separate opt-in config triggers adversarial churn.

Checklist: - [x] Prefetch shim and eviction policies implemented - [x] Token-churn injector with parameterized distributions - [x] Kernel-pressure exporter and occupancy heatmap generator - [x] YAML workload descriptors and quickstart README - [x] Unit tests for sampling and exporter logic - [x] End-to-end smoke runs in CI with synthetic corpus

How to run (summary): ./benchctl run --workload workloads/pfm/cross_model_churn.yaml --out reports/pfm/round-001 --policy prefetch:conservative

Expected outcomes: The first internal run shows a 12% p95 reduction for the conservative prefetch policy vs no-prefetch on mixed-bert-compat models, but a 4% p99 increase for aggressive prefetch in high-churn configs. Results and artifacts are attached to the PR CI job for quick inspection.

Aisha Patel: occupancy_est is a heuristic derived from token footprint and inferred CUDA occupancy; added comments and a unit test to ensure it runs quickly in CI.
Daniel Kim: The YAML descriptors are convenient. Can we add a stress variant that runs fewer sessions but higher churn for quickdog runs?
Aisha Patel: Added workloads/pfm/cross_model_churn_quick.yaml and updated bench-smoke CI to run it.
Priya Rao: I saw the p99 regression in aggressive prefetch config. Can we add an automated check that flags >3% p99 regressions compared to baseline?
Aisha Patel: Added delta thresholds to fidelity_score.py; CI will annotate artifacts when regression exceeds threshold.
Add Prefetch Fidelity Matrix runner and Cross-Model Token-Churn harness. New reporting artifacts: kernel-pressure matrix and occupancy heatmap. Useful for prioritizing kernel-level optimizations and prefetch policy tuning.
This PR is intended for internal benchmark-lab usage only. The next follow-up will add a scheduler-aware variant that exercises node-local contention and GPU oversubscription scenarios.

Summary: Introduce a microtemporal "entropy" synchronizer that detects and coalesces short-lived burst events across worker threads and a complementary spectral sample encoder that compresses sampled telemetry for long-term fidelity analysis. Motivation: our existing burst detectors miss correlated microbursts that span CPU/GPU kernel boundaries; this patch implements cross-stream correlation and a compact export format to retain enough signal for offline spectral analysis without exploding storage.

What changed (design + behavior):
- benchlab/samplers/burst_entropy_sync.cc: new lightweight synchronizer that collects sub-10ms burst markers, aligns them using monotonic timestamps, computes per-kernel entropy metrics and emits aligned events to the reporting queue. Built to be non-blocking and tolerant of clock skew between processes.
- benchlab/encoders/spectral_sample_encoder.py: spectral encoder that converts event streams to a compressed spectral slice (.ssf) format using a small DCT-based projection + run-length packing. Designed for downstream spectral heatmap generation and correlation with KV-cache pressure traces.
- benchlab/tools/benchctl/commands.py: new CLI command `benchctl export-spectral` to generate compressed exports from a run; supports streaming to S3/local and configurable retention window.
- benchlab/reports/compressed_fidelity_format.md: spec for the .ssf export, fields, and suggested decoder algorithms for offline analysis.
- benchlab/tests/test_entropy_sync.py: unit and deterministic fuzz-style tests; added seeding harness to make bursts deterministic in CI.
- benchlab/ci/bench_profile_pipeline.yaml: CI job that runs a short synthetic workload to validate synchronizer + encoder and asserts size and latency regressions.

Performance notes: In a synthetic multi-kernel workload (3 concurrent kernels with artificially injected sub-15ms bursts), the synchronizer identified 98% of correlated bursts vs 63% for the previous thresholded detector. End-to-end export overhead measured at ~1.8% CPU and <2ms p95 added latency in a profiling run (defaults are conservative). Compressed .ssf output reduced raw event payloads by ~8x on our sample runs.

Testing and CI: The bench_profile CI job runs the deterministic workload locally and then validates that produced .ssf files decode and contain expected spectral peaks. One transient flaky assertion occurred on the first run due to a race in the test harness; fixed by adding an explicit flush and retry in tests. All CI checks green on final push.

Review conversation (high level):
- Priya: requested that the synchronizer avoid allocation in the hot path; addressed by switching to a fixed slab allocator and reusing event buffers.
- Diego: asked for stronger determinism in tests; I added seeded timers and a replay harness to guarantee event placement.
- Ava: questioned the compression format and backward compatibility; added a short format spec and provided a compatibility shim for the old JSON-based exports.
The comments thread closed after two follow-up commits that tightened concurrency guards and improved test coverage.

Backward compatibility and migration: The new .ssf export is opt-in; benchctl continues to produce the previous JSON exports. The report spec documents a migration path and a small Python shim (in encoders/) to decode .ssf into legacy JSON for downstream tooling during rollout.

Related tickets: ENG-4821 (multi-kernel microburst detection), ENG-4890 (compressed profile exports for long-term storage).

Release notes: (internal) Add a new microburst alignment sampler and compressed spectral export to benchlab. Opt-in export via `benchctl export-spectral`. Expected to reduce profiling storage by ~8x for burst-heavy workloads and improve correlated-burst detection accuracy.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged after approvals and green CI.
Priya Menon: Nice approach, but hot path allocations will kill p95. Can we reuse buffers?
Samir Patel: Switched to fixed slab allocator and reused buffers in the hot path; updated benchmarks in description.
Diego Alvarez: Tests were flaky locally; can we seed timers so the harness is deterministic?
Samir Patel: Added seeded timer replay and a small deterministic workload for CI to exercise the synchronizer.
Ava Thompson: Need format spec and compatibility with current exporters. Add a shim and docs.
Samir Patel: Added compressed_fidelity_format.md and a decoder function in spectral_sample_encoder.py.
Introduce burst entropy synchronizer and .ssf compressed spectral export. Opt-in via benchctl export-spectral; improves correlated microburst detection and reduces profile storage.

payload.body:
Motivation: Kernel auto-selection v2 adds per-request decision telemetry (selected kernel, candidates, features). Before we increase sampling or add more fields, we need a hard bound on (a) kernel-switch overhead during mixed workloads, and (b) selector evaluation cost (feature extraction + candidate generation + scoring) on the hot path.

This PR adds a targeted microbenchmark suite to benchmark-lab that runs on representative SKUs (A100-80GB, H100-SXM, L40S) and measures: 1) steady-state decode with no switches (baseline), 2) forced alternating kernels every N steps (upper-bound switch cost), and 3) selector evaluation (v1 vs v2) with configurable feature vectors and candidate counts.

What’s included: - New bench: kernel_switch_overhead_bench (forces kernel alternation via a bench-only runtime hook) - New bench: selector_eval_cost_bench (pure CPU bench + optional end-to-end invocation) - Support for running against recorded request-shapes (prefill/decode tokens) to mimic real distributions - Standardized output JSON for perf-canary ingestion: p50/p95/p99 in ns/op and derived overhead ratios - Guardrails: fails the benchmark job if selector eval exceeds the configured budget on any SKU (defaults: p95 < 8us CPU-only, p95 < 25us end-to-end)

Results summary (collected on bench-lab runners; see artifacts): - Selector eval (v2) CPU-only: p95 3.7us (A100), 4.1us (H100), 5.4us (L40S) at 10 candidates; scales ~linear with candidates - End-to-end selector + registry lookup: p95 14–19us depending on SKU + registry size - Forced kernel alternation every step (worst-case): +1.2–2.8% throughput hit on decode-only loops; alternation every 16 steps is within noise on A100/H100, small but measurable on L40S

How this is used: - Provides the perf budget used by ENG-4824 to set telemetry sampling defaults and to justify adding candidate lists behind sampling - Provides a regression gate for future selector logic changes (ENG-4821/ENG-4825) - Serves as a reference for SRE when investigating tail spikes attributed to selector overhead

Notes/limitations: - This does NOT try to model full scheduler interactions or compilation cache misses; it’s intentionally scoped to isolate kernel-switch and selector evaluation overhead. - Kernel alternation uses a bench-only hook (compiled under BENCHMARK_LAB) to avoid exposing unstable knobs in production builds.

Checklist: - [x] Added benchmarks + docs - [x] Added CI job (runs on CPU always; GPU subset nightly + manual) - [x] Added artifact export for perf-canary - [x] Validated on A100 + H100 runners - [x] Linked to Linear tasks (ENG-4824/4825)

Follow-ups: - Add a mixed prefill+decode scenario with a long-context tail bucket (ties into ENG-4825). - Consider exporting an additional metric: selector_candidate_count distribution for correlation in perf-canary dashboards.
Claire Dubois: Can you clarify what exactly you mean by “kernel switch” here? Is this a host-side dispatch cost, a cache invalidation, or something else? We should be careful about conclusions.
Isabella Rossi (author): Good call. In this context it’s the incremental overhead observed when alternating between two already-compiled kernel variants in a tight decode loop, so it captures host dispatch + any device-side state changes that show up as throughput/latency deltas. It explicitly excludes compile/plan creation. I added a note in the README and renamed metrics to “forced alternation overhead” to avoid implying a single mechanism.
Omar El-Sayed: The selector eval numbers are the most important for telemetry. Can we emit both CPU-only and end-to-end (including registry lookup) and set budgets on p95? Also please add a way to scale candidates to 5/10/20/40.
Isabella Rossi (author): Done in 4b9c1c2. We now report selector_eval_cpu_ns and selector_eval_e2e_ns plus overhead ratio vs baseline. Candidates are parameterized; default run includes 5/10/20/40 and exports per-param stats. Budget defaults are p95 < 8us CPU-only and < 25us e2e; configurable via env vars in CI.
Sahana Iyer: CI concern: GPU runners are limited; can we keep presubmit CPU-only and move GPU to nightly + manual dispatch? Also ensure artifacts don’t explode in size.
Isabella Rossi (author): Updated workflow. Presubmit runs CPU-only (fast). GPU job is nightly + workflow_dispatch with SKU matrix. Artifact export is trimmed to percentiles + param metadata only (no raw samples).
Marcus Reed: Can we add a fixture-based request shape mode so we can approximate “real” distributions? It doesn’t need to be perfect; just keep it deterministic and small.

Marcus Reed: Looks good. Approving with one nit: make sure the bench-only hook is clearly compiled out for production builds.
Isabella Rossi (author): Added BENCHMARK_LAB guard + a comment in the hook header and README. Thanks.
Claire Dubois: Approved after the terminology tweak + README clarifications.
Omar El-Sayed: Approved. This gives us the perf budget we needed for ENG-4824.

Motivation: We need a lightweight, reproducible runner that exercises both steady-state and phase-shifted burst patterns while simultaneously measuring cold-start latency across different model variants and runtime kernel configs. This PR introduces a phase-shifted latency sweep runner and a paired cold-start prober that can be composed to produce joint distributions (latency vs cold-start tail) used by the regression detector pipeline.
Design:
- phase_sweep_runner: Python runner that generates a sequence of workload phases with configurable duration, RPS, sequence length distribution and an adjustable phase-offset parameter to produce controlled interleaving across client shards.
- coldstart_prober: small Go probe that issues warmup-less single-shot requests on a configurable model selection (quantized/FP16/FP32) to capture cold-start percentiles under concurrent load.
- reporter bridge: new CSV+JSON reporter that tags samples with phase-id, shard-id, kernel-profile and coldstart-epoch for downstream aggregation.
- CI harness changes: bench job integration and a perf-regression threshold test that runs an abbreviated sweep in CI with synthetic small-models.
How to run: bench/README contains examples; typical run: python bench/runners/phase_sweep_runner.py --profile profiles/low_mem.yaml --phases 6 --phase-duration 30s --phase-offset 7s --out reports/run-<ts>.csv
The coldstart probe is compiled with go build and invoked alongside the runner to annotate early-epoch samples.
Implementation notes:
- Uses existing bench client abstraction for request generation and adds a deterministic pseudo-random seed to make runs reproducible.
- Phase IDs are encoded into the request metadata header X-Bench-Phase so runtime traces can correlate tokens to phase.
- Reporter writes a compact JSON lines stream and a summary CSV compatible with the regression detector.
- Adds a small integration test that validates phase interleaving logic and a smoke perf check for the probe binary.
Commits:
- "initial phase_sweep_runner implementation, core API and simple CLI"
- "add coldstart_prober (go) and CI smoke job"
- "reporter: csv + jsonlines bridge and header tagging"

- "fix: deterministic seeding + durable temp file cleanup"
Files changed (high level):

- bench/probers/coldstart_prober/main.go (new): standalone probe binary
- bench/reporters/csv_json_bridge.go (new): reporter bridge for CSV/JSONL outputs
- bench/configs/profiles/phase_sweep_low_mem.yaml (new): example profile

Reviewers requested small API changes (explicit --seed flag, clearer exit codes for the probe) and asked for a more conservative default for phase-offset to avoid self-synchronization artifacts on noisy CI hosts. I iterated on the runner CLI, added --seed and made the default phase-offset randomized within a small jitter when running in CI mode.

Context: As part of the Quantization Profile Library rollout, we need a repeatable, reviewable set of benchmark outputs that quantify the impact of enabling a published quantization profile vs baseline precision on (a) unit economics (approx cost/token) and (b) latency/throughput across supported GPU SKUs. This PR adds a small publishing pipeline in benchmark-lab that generates normalized CSV summaries per model/profile/GPU and uploads both raw run logs and the rolled-up tables as CI artifacts. The goal is to let Applied ML + Runtime + Platform point to a single source of truth for “expected deltas” used by Console previews, rollout gates, and incident triage.

What’s included: (1) A new runner entrypoint that executes baseline + profile-enabled scenarios back-to-back with consistent warmup and pinned runtime build/commit; (2) CSV summaries under artifacts/quant_profiles/ summarizing p50/p95 end-to-end latency, decode latency, tokens/sec, VRAM peak, and derived cost/token; (3) A stable “schema_version” for the CSV format plus embedded metadata columns (model_id, variant, profile_id, profile_version, gpu_sku, runtime_commit, run_id, timestamp); (4) A README documenting how to reproduce locally and how to interpret cost/token.

Cost/token methodology: We compute cost/token as (gpu_hourly_usd / tokens_per_hour). gpu_hourly_usd comes from a static price table in this repo (documented as “estimates for comparison only”, not customer billing). tokens_per_hour is taken from measured tokens/sec after warmup and excluding initial prefill window. This is meant for relative deltas between baseline and profile-enabled on the same hardware + workload; absolute numbers will vary by fleet utilization and batching.

Workloads: This PR publishes deltas for the standard quant-profile perf suite workloads (short chat, long-context chat, and tool-call shaped prompts) at fixed concurrency points (1, 4, 16) for A100-80GB, H100-80GB, and L40S-48GB. Models currently included are the first beta targets (internal IDs): llama3.1-8b-instruct (x2), llama3.1-70b-instruct (x1), and qwen2.5-32b-instruct (x1) where profiles exist.

Example excerpt (see full CSV artifacts):
- llama3.1-8b-instruct:x2 INT8 profile (A100-80GB, conc=16, long-context): tokens/sec +22.8%, p95 e2e latency -6.1%, derived cost/token -18.6%
- llama3.1-70b-instruct:x1 FP8 mixed profile (H100-80GB, conc=4, short chat): tokens/sec +15.2%, p95 e2e latency -3.4%, derived cost/token -12.9%
- qwen2.5-32b-instruct:x1 INT8 profile (L40S-48GB, conc=16, tool-call): tokens/sec +9.7%, p95 e2e latency +2.1% (tail sensitivity), derived cost/token -7.8% (flagged for follow-up; see notes in README)

Notes / guardrails: This PR does not change any production defaults. Benchmarks are informational and intended to help validate expected savings and catch perf regressions. Profile compatibility is assumed pre-validated; this runner will fail fast if the runtime reports fallback or incompatibility (we export fallback_rate and enforce it == 0 for benchmark runs).

Follow-ups: (a) Add a lightweight “trend” job that compares latest results vs previous main commit and comments on PRs that touch runtime quantization paths; (b) Expand model coverage as new profiles are published; (c) Optionally export a JSON snapshot for Console preview ingestion once the Console team finalizes the ingestion path.

Screenshots/artifacts: CI run for this PR uploads: raw_run_logs.tgz, quant_profile_summary.csv, quant_profile_summary_by_gpu.csv, and per-model CSVs under artifacts/quant_profiles/<model_id>/.

Risk: Low. Changes are isolated to benchmark-lab scripts and CI. No customer-facing behavior change.

Refs: Confluence perf suite doc (quantization-profile-perf-benchmark-suite), runtime metrics naming from redwood/pr-18512, and rollout requirements from prd-quantization-profile-library-opt-in.

Jonas Weber (author): Good call. Currently we drop the first 60s warmup and compute tokens/sec over the remaining steady-state window; decode latency is taken from runtime metric decode_latency_ms aggregated over the same window. I pushed a commit adding runtime_commit + run_id + timestamp columns and documented the steady-state definition in README.
Nadia Rahman (review): For cost/token, please add a disclaimer that the $/hr table is for relative comparisons only. Also can we add schema_version as an explicit column so downstream tooling can detect changes?
Jonas Weber (author): Added both: schema_version column (v1) and a prominent disclaimer in README + schema_v1.md that cost/token is derived from an internal comparison table and not billing.
Arjun Desai (review): Can we export a per-profile summary table that shows delta vs baseline (percent) rather than only absolute numbers? That would make it easier to share with Console/PM without people doing spreadsheet math.
Jonas Weber (author): Added quant_profile_summary_by_gpu.csv which includes baseline vs profile rows plus computed delta columns (pct) for key metrics. Kept the raw absolute tables as well for auditing.
Logan Wright (review): Any concerns about metric naming drift? We’ve had a few runtime renames recently. If the runner can’t find the metric, it should fail loudly rather than publish partial data.
Jonas Weber (author): Implemented validate_metrics_present() and a hard fail if any required metric is missing; also added validate_no_fallback.py to enforce fallback_rate == 0.

Jonas Weber (author): Updated workflow: PR runs a reduced matrix (single model + A100 + conc=4/16); main branch runs full matrix and uploads artifacts. PR artifacts still include CSV schema + sample outputs.

Motivation: We need a deterministic harness that reproduces short-lived queue contention and scheduler jitter seen in production LLM serving clusters. This PR introduces two cooperating pieces: (1) an epochal worklet stitcher that composes short-lived microtasks (worklets) into synthetic request trajectories with explicit epochs (warmup, steady, spike, cooldown) and (2) a queue contention replayer that can inject multi-consumer queue lengths, consumer sleep/jitter profiles, and CPU affinity switches to reproduce head-of-line blocking and tail amplification. Design summary: the worklet stitcher is a lightweight DSL (YAML/JSON) for expressing per-epoch distributions (arrival, size, KV cache hit rates, prefix lengths) and inter-epoch transitions. The contention replayer accepts recorded schedule traces (produced by the collector in this PR) and drives a local multi-threaded runner that models queue lengths and backpressure signaling. Both tools can be used independently or together in end-to-end suites. Implementation: new package bench/worklet_stitcher with a small runtime and generator; bench/contention_replayer that includes an efficient lockless queue emulator and a pluggable CPU-affinity shim on Linux (using sched_setaffinity). Added a trace exporter compatible with existing flamegraph pipeline. Usage: examples/recipes/epochal_small.yaml demonstrates a 10-minute run reproducing a production spike pattern. Invocation: benchctl run --recipe examples/recipes/epochal_small.yaml --replayer traces/spike-2025-11-18.json --out reports/epochal-2026-01-12.json. Backwards compatibility: existing workload runners continue to work; the stitcher adds an opt-in recipe format. Testing: unit tests for the stitcher grammar, integration test that compares steady-state latency histograms with a golden trace (CI runs a short mode). Why unique: this targets micro-scheduler level artifacts (queue contention + affinity churn) instead of just request mixing; helps validate runtime preemption and kernel scheduling heuristics.
Maya Patel: Nice DSL. Question: can the stitcher express correlated KV cache hit patterns across epochs? (e.g., cache warms then drifts).
Ethan Kline: Yes — recipe supports 'cross_epoch_seed' and an optional 'session_affinity' block. Added example in epochal_small.yaml.
Lucas Morin: affinity shim is Linux-only; add a no-op shim for macOS and Windows to avoid build breaks.
Ethan Kline: added platform stubs and conditional build tags; CI short-mode verifies build on macOS runner.
Priya Suresh: Integration test is flaky in CI (timing-related). Can we reduce reliance on wall-clock exactness?
Ethan Kline: switched to quantile-based assertion (p50/p95 ranges) and added retries in CI short-mode; also instrumented test to use a deterministic RNG seed.
Add epochal worklet stitcher and queue contention replayer to benchmark-lab. New recipes and replayer traces enable deterministic reproduction of short-lived queue contention and affinity churn. CI includes a short-mode to run smoke validation.
Introduce epochal workload composer and queue contention replayer for deterministic micro-scheduler stress tests.
1) checkout repo; 2) make build; 3) cp examples/recipes/epochal_small.yaml .; 4) benchctl run --recipe epochal_small.yaml --out /tmp/epochal.json; 5) open reports/epochal-*.json in bench/docs/viewer or run scripts/plot_latency.py
When running long recipes against production-scale traces, use --profile-kernel to capture kernel-level scheduling samples; replayer uses raw sched_setaffinity and requires CAP_SYS_NICE or equivalent in some environments.
Planned follow-ups: integrate with perf-canary to run targeted epoch recipes in canary clusters, add GPU-aware worklets that exercise host->device transfer stalls, and add a cloud-scale distributed replayer variant.
Addressed platform stubs, made integration tests deterministic, added documentation and recipes, and squashed commits per reviewer requests.

Adds a new sequencer (holo-surge) for generating temporally correlated microbursts and a crossframe occupancy exporter for GPU/kernel-level attribution. No user-facing API changes.
Motivation: we observed sustained mid-tail p95 instability when replaying multi-sequence conversational traffic with interleaved priming and varied KV cache hits. Existing synthetic runners produce either Poisson-like bursts or deterministic ramps; they do not emulate the fractal-like, multi-scale surges we see in production that cause cross-frame resource contention and transient kernel occupancy spikes. This PR introduces the 'holo-surge' sequencer (a compact workload generator that composes deterministic priming, stochastic microbursts, and long-period envelope modulation) and a crossframe occupancy exporter that records per-step GPU occupancy signatures and correlates them with logical request frames for downstream reporters.

What this change does: adds a new sequencer (cmd/holo-surge) and a reporting pipeline that serializes occupancy traces in a compact delta format compatible with the benchmark-lab downstream stats pipeline. The exporter uses platform-specific probes (NVIDIA SMI sampling hook or synthetic occupancy estimator when SMI is unavailable) and annotates traces with primer-id, sequence-hash, and KV cache-hit ratio. The sequencer supports deterministic seeds, phase locking across parallel nodes, and variable inter-sequence offsets for interference testing.

Checklist: [x] design doc (ENG-3124) reviewed; [x] unit tests for sequencer RNG and phase-lock logic; [x] integration test that runs holo-surge against mini-cluster and validates exporter schema; [x] perf benchmark comparing p50/p95/p99 and occupancy histograms before/after (summary below); [ ] follow-up: dashboard panels and alerting queries (separate PR).

Testing and validation: ran 5 controlled cohorts on the perf-lab cluster (4x A100 nodes) with identical model and prompt mixes to reproduce production-like priming distribution. All CI checks and integration heartbeat succeeded. Exported traces were consumed by an offline analyzer and matched expected event counts and envelope shapes.

Performance summary (representative): baseline sequencer (seq-ramp) vs holo-surge (same aggregated qps): p50 delta: +3ms, p95 delta: +18ms, p99 delta: +42ms; peak transient GPU occupancy increased by ~12% during synchronized microbursts, with tail correlation to KV cache misses. These numbers are included as CSV artifacts in the PR build.

Usage: examples/holo-surge/README.md demonstrates how to run a single-node holo-surge with deterministic seed, how to enable SMI sampling, and how to post-process the delta-occupancy traces with existing reporters. The sequencer exposes knobs: --envelope-period, --microburst-shape, --phase-lock, --primer-set, --seed, and an output sink compatible with our tracer service.

Related: builds on ideas from ENG-2710 (multi-sequence priming) and pairs with the compact-flame exporter work (PR #50271) for visualization.

Notes: the exporter includes a lightweight fallback estimator when SMI is not available; this avoids hard dependency on privileged runtime, but estimator accuracy is lower (documented in the README). This work intentionally does not change any public HTTP endpoints or the benchmark-lab stable dataset formats; it adds a new export flavor 'occupancy-delta-v1'.
Ethan Park: Nice focused PR — can we decouple SMI dependency from the default exporter? (commented inline on smi_adapter.go)
Marina Lopez: yes, added a runtime probe switch and estimator fallback in commit 2 (reply)
Sasha Gupta: Tests look good; please add a short note in docs about estimator accuracy tradeoffs (requested change)
Marina Lopez: added a section in examples/holo-surge/README.md explaining estimator bounds and a link to the diag CSVs (reply)
Liam O'Connor: Verified p95/p99 artifacts and gave approval — small nit about log verbosity (approved)
CI Bot: all checks passed on rerun, integration completed

Motivation: We need a workload generator that can reproduce complex keyspace skew patterns observed in production: interleaved tenant hotspots, time-varying working sets, and KV-cache sparsity transitions. Existing mix runners sample by sequence length or simple percentile weights but do not provide coordinated stratification across key dimensions (tenant, route, prefix). This PR adds a Stratified Keyspace Mixer (SKM) runner and an accompanying KV-Coverage Reporter that measures effective cache coverage and the resulting token-level cost/latency delta across epochs.

What this change introduces: 1) skm_runner: an epochal traffic generator that accepts a stratification schema (tenant buckets, prefix shards, cold/hot cohorts) and emits request traces compatible with the benchmark-lab runner interface. 2) kv_coverage_reporter: post-run analyzer that computes per-bucket cache hit estimates (prefix+kv-key level), cold-start contribution, and differential p95/p99 delta against a baseline run. 3) sample primer and deterministic seeding so runs are reproducible across CI and local envs. 4) Small harness for staged noise injection (temporal jitter, burst spikes) to exercise batching and scheduling heuristics.

Checklist: - [x] Implement core SKM runner and config parser - [x] Add single-node microbench that validates reproducibility - [x] Integrate reporter into the existing report pipeline - [x] Add docs/quickstart YAML + example workload - [x] Add unit tests for stratification sampler - [x] Run full suite in perf-candidate CI and compare to baseline.

Design notes: - The stratification schema is a compact YAML structure that maps "tenant" -> {weight, shards, hot_ratio} and an optional prefix_transformer to control synthetic key prefixes that influence KV cache locality. - SKM produces sequences annotated with `tenant_id`, `prefix_id`, and `shard_id` so the runtime's KV instrumentation can correlate observed hits. - Epoch boundaries are explicit: each epoch can change the hot_ratio or promote a cold cohort to hot to simulate cache churn. - The reporter uses conservative heuristics to estimate KV hits from observed token outputs and request hashes; it also optionally accepts ground-truth cache logs when available to compute precise coverage.

CI and performance notes: The PR triggered flaky rounds in the GPU integration test due to timing sensitivity in the burst injector; added a small backoff and stabilization sleep. CI summary: initial run had one flaky gpu-smoke failure, rerun passed all perf and unit checks.

Files of interest and how to run: - examples/stratified/README.md documents the YAML schema and quickstart - examples/stratified/tenant_mix.yaml is an opinionated baseline used in our perf deck - bench/runners/skm_runner.py is the runner implementation - bench/reporters/kv_coverage_reporter.py is the post-processor - tests/bench/test_skm_sampler.py covers deterministic seeding.

Why it matters: This runner surface lets us model real multi-tenant effects that drive tail latency and cache inefficiency; it is already useful for validating caching heuristics, scheduling improvements, and quantization tradeoffs across workloads.

Related: Linear ENG-5123 (kv-cache telemetry improvements), ENG-4981 (batcher scheduling experiments).
Tomás Ortega: Nice isolation of the sampler; can you add a short note about memory footprint when running 10k tenants? Asked for a microbenchmark of memory usage.
Asha Raman: Added mem profile snippets to examples/stratified/README.md and a small guard to cap in-memory trace buffers when tenant_count > 5000.
Li Wei: Reporter looks good; one nit about decimal precision in the coverage table (pct -> 2 decimals).
Asha Raman: Fixed precision and added an extra assertion in the reporter test that validates formatting.

payload.body:
Motivation: regressions in allocator behavior and subtle KV-cache inconsistencies were observed during the November perf sweep on multi-tenant clusters. This PR adds a targeted stress runner that intentionally induces fragmentation and compaction patterns on GPUs and a complementary telemetry summarizer that validates KV-cache coherence across warmup, eviction, and re-prime cycles. Summary of changes: 1) new runner binary `gpu_mem_compactor` that (a) allocates variable-length token buffers to produce fragmentation, (b) performs controlled free/alloc cycles with configurable 'cooldown' and 'burst' phases, and (c) emits per-step allocator histograms and CUDA memory metrics; 2) a KV-cache consistency probe that performs round-trip primer->evict->reprime sequences against single- and multi-model serving stacks and records divergence rates, primer hit ratios, and rehydrate latencies; 3) a summarizer pipeline that ingests the runner output and produces a compact CSV/JSON report with per-epoch failure categories (allocation-failures, stale-lookup, rehydrate-timeouts) and heatmap-ready sparklines; 4) test harness integrations and small helpers for local reproducibility. How it works (high-level): the runner spins a configurable number of agent threads that simulate session priming with skewed length distributions, then runs a controlled eviction pattern to force allocator interaction and KV fragmentation. The KV probe injects known token sequences (deterministic primers) and validates equality of returned logits/embeddings after eviction+rehydration. The summarizer performs delta analysis per-epoch and tags results with kernel IDs and approximate GPU memory occupancy. Why this is unique: previous bench runners focused on latency shapes; this one isolates allocator and KV-cache correctness under adversarial memory patterns, making it easier to triage regressions introduced by kernel-level memory layout changes or new allocator heuristics. How to run locally: `bazel run //benchmark-lab/runners:gpu_mem_compactor -- --agents 16 --burst-ms 250 --cooldown-ms 800 --kvcache-check true --out /tmp/gpu-compact-run.json` and then `python3 tools/summarize_kv.py /tmp/gpu-compact-run.json --out /tmp/kv-summary.csv`. Testing and results: ran overnight on a p3.8xlarge equivalent; baseline run shows 0.6% KV divergence and 1.3% allocation backpressure at 95th percentile; after two iteration fixes the divergence drops to 0.02%. Related linear tasks: ENG-1289 (investigate allocator regressions), ENG-1302 (kvcache evictions triage).
Liam O'Connor: Nice separation of concerns. Two suggestions: reduce default agents to 8 for CI and add more logging around cudaMalloc failures.
Aisha Patel (author): Updated CI defaults and added exponential backoff on cudaMalloc failures. Pushed patch to address logging (see commit b4c2a29 and d2f6a00).
Marta Ruiz: The KV-checker should also validate embeddings' L2-norm to detect silent bit flips; can you add a threshold check?
Aisha Patel (author): Added L2-norm delta check with configurable threshold; included in summarizer (commit c7e8f11).
Devon Chen: Approve after CI green and small doc tweak to README about GPU permissions.
Adds a GPU memory compaction stress runner and kvcache consistency summarizer; useful for diagnosing allocator regressions and KV rehydrate correctness under adversarial memory patterns. Includes local run instructions and example summary outputs.

payload.body:
Motivation: We frequently see spiky tail amplification in multi-sequence runs where a small cohort of long sequences drives kernel saturation and masks improvement signals. entropy-baker introduces a compressive sampler that biases synthetic sessions toward informative tail events while still keeping overall sequence distributions realistic. Paired with a per-kernel tail normalizer, this helps make small performance deltas visible in CI and reduces noise in regression detection.

What this PR does: Adds a new workload generator: entropy-baker, which synthesizes session traces by (1) building a histogram of observed sequence prefixes from corpus traces, (2) sampling rarer long-prefix events with importance weights derived from prefix entropy, and (3) emitting interleaved batches that preserve short/long ratio targets. Introduces a reporting pipeline stage: kernel_tail_normalizer, which ingests flame/timeline histograms and applies a robust scaling per kernel to remove cohort-level tail skew before aggregating quantiles.

Key benefits: - Reduces false-positive regressions from tail-saturated kernels in small sample CI runs. - Amplifies signal from long-sequence microbenchmarks so that optimizer changes (e.g., KV cache pruning, attention kernel tweaks) show consistent delta. - Lightweight: sampler runs client-side in the benchmark harness and adds <6% overhead to runner time for typical datasets.

Usage: New harness flag --enable-entropy-baker; config supports target_long_ratio, entropy_weight, and seed. Normalizer is enabled in reporting by default for benchmark-lab CI jobs that set report.normalizer=auto.

Validation: - Microbench: ran on 8-node local cluster, 4 model variants; entropy-baker increases long-seq sample density by 9x while keeping mean tokens-per-request within 5% of baseline. - Regression sensitivity: introduced a controlled 2% slowpath delay in attention kernel; without normalizer the delta was obscured (p95 delta 0.8%), with normalizer the delta surfaces at p95=2.1% and p99=3.4%. - Stability: 30 end-to-end runs show standard deviation of p95 reduced from 1.9% to 1.1% with normalizer. Full numbers in the commit benchmark output.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for sampler weighting and seed determinism. - [x] Integration test in bench-harness that toggles long/short mixes. - [x] Reporting tests validate scaled histogram aggregation. - [x] CI workflow adds a smoke run to benchmark-lab nightly.

Commits summary: - 9c4f5b1: initial entropy-baker sampler implementation and unit tests - 2a7d6be: integrate sampler into bench-harness and add config bindings - f1b8c3e: kernel_tail_normalizer implementation + histogram serializer changes - a4d2b8f: add e2e integration and benchmark payloads - d21f5ea: test fixes, docstrings, and CI workflow updates

Files changed (high-level): - bench/harness/samplers/entropy_baker.py: new sampler module, weighting algorithms, unit tests - bench/harness/config.yaml: new sampler flags and defaults - bench/reports/normalizers/kernel_tail_normalizer.py: new reporting stage + docs - bench/reports/serializers/histogram_v2.proto: serializer extension to carry normalized buckets - ci/workflows/benchmark-nightly.yml: add nightly smoke job using entropy-baker - docs/bench/entropy-baker.md: usage + tuning guidance - tests/bench/test_entropy_baker.py: deterministic tests - tests/reports/test_kernel_tail_normalizer.py: normalization edge cases

Notes on design decisions: - We intentionally keep the sampler separate from the core request generator to allow opt-in through flags without perturbing existing stress runs. - Normalizer uses a robust median-based scale with outlier clipping to avoid over-correcting for genuine regressions. - Serializer was extended to keep a normalization metadata field so downstream dashboards can toggle views with/without normalization.

Limitations and future work: - Current importance weighting uses prefix-frequency entropy; future iterations could incorporate latency-weighted entropy to bias on cost-sensitive events. - Normalizer is tuned for GPU attention kernels; additional kernel categories (quantized matmul paths) may need per-backend params.

Related: BENCH-78 for regression sensitivity improvements, ENG-4012 for CI false-positive reduction.
Adds a new workload generator (entropy-baker) and a reporting stage that normalizes per-kernel tail metrics. No config changes required for existing workloads; opt-in via new harness flag.
Liam O'Connor: Nice approach — the entropy-weighting is intuitive. Two requests: add an explicit seed propagation path so CI reproducibility isn't relying on global RNG and include a sanity-check in the normalizer to avoid scaling tiny-sample kernels.
Esther Park: Thanks Liam — added deterministic seed plumbing and a sample_count threshold in kernel_tail_normalizer to skip normalization for buckets with <64 observations (see f1b8c3e).
Priya Deshmukh: Can you add a short-run CI job that asserts the normalizer reduces variance? Also add telemetry for scaled_vs_raw_sample_ratio so we can monitor effects in prod.
Esther Park: Added nightly smoke job and telemetry counter (ci/workflows/benchmark-nightly.yml, kernel_tail_normalizer emits normalized_ratio metric).
Marco Silva: Code looks good. One nit: histogram serializer change should be backward compatible with existing dashboards. Please confirm the metadata field is optional when reading older payloads.
Esther Park: Confirmed — serializer uses presence check; dashboards default to raw when metadata absent. Added doc note in bench/reports/README.md.
All checks passed on merge: unit, integration, lint, static-analyzer; benchmark-nightly smoke passed once and scheduled for nightly. Performance regressions check (golden) shows no negative impact on short-run medians.
Merged via squash on 2025-11-25 by Priya Deshmukh. Merge message includes summary of usage and CI additions.
