payload.body:
Motivation: teams increasingly optimize for cost-per-token as well as latency; existing benchmark harnesses measure latency and tail quantiles but do not model token-level economics across batching, quantization and cache hit patterns. This PR adds a reproducible benchmark and a lightweight throughput calibrator that quantifies cost vs latency trade-offs for common inference strategies and outputs standardized CSV/JSON summaries suitable for the reporting pipeline.

What this PR introduces: a) bench/cost_econ/runner: a runner that synthesizes request streams with configurable sequence-length distributions, session affinity, and cache-hit models, instrumented to track token counts attributed to model variants, quantization level, and batch size. b) bench/cost_econ/calibrator: a sweep driver that runs multi-dim experiments (batch size, max-seq, quant-level, kv-cache-enabled) and produces normalized cost metrics using a pluggable cost model (supports our hosted rate card and a local nominal model for private deployments). c) reporting/cost_econ/transform: lightweight processors that aggregate runs into cost-latency curves, per-token unit-cost estimates, and a rollup JSON for Redwood Console ingestion. d) example workloads and README: a short tutorial showing how to reproduce a regional sweep and how to feed results into Optimize.

Why it's different: unlike previous throughput-focused runners, the calibrator models token economics: accounting for wasted tokens due to overpadding, impact of prefix caching, and cost delta from quantization. The output is intended to drive two downstream use cases: (1) automated Optimize recommendations (batch/quant profiles) and (2) SKU/capacity planning for Dedicated pools.

Scope of changes: small, self-contained additions under benchmark-lab with no runtime changes to the serving binary. The calibrator reuses the existing workload harness and telemetry collectors to remain compatible with the ingestion pipeline.

How to run locally: ./bench.sh cost-econ --config examples/sweeps/hosted-small.yaml --out-dir /tmp/cost-run; the README contains a one-liner to upload results to the reporting topic.

Metrics and expected stability: example runs in CI (see attached matrices) show stable p50/p95 latencies within 5% of baseline when batch sizes are < 8; cost-per-token delta tables are produced for each sweep and include confidence intervals across 5 repeats.

Notes: this is intended as a baseline generator for Optimize; the cost-model is intentionally simple but pluggable. Future follow-ups will add more sophisticated spot-price modeling and cross-region arbitrage simulations.
Added smoke integration that runs a small hosted sweep in CI (approx 3m) and a dedicated smoke run under a mocked rate card. Tests assert stable latencies and presence of per-token accounting fields; CI matrix added for nightly longer sweeps.
Focus on schema compatibility in reporting/transform.py and on the cost_model interface; the runner is intentionally conservative in concurrency to avoid perturbing latency baselines.
Leo Martinez: Can we expose kv-cache hit-rate as an output dimension so Optimize can learn a policy? -> Author: yes, added an explicit 'kv_hit_rate' field in the run schema (calibrator and runner).
Priya Nair: The cost model should allow a per-region multiplier for cloud egress and reserved capacity. -> Author: added region_multiplier to RateCard and documented how to provide a JSON override.
Samir Kapoor: CI flaked on one run; please add retry and increase repeat count to 5 to get stable CIs. -> Author: increased repeats and added retries in calibrator, re-ran CI matrix.
Add cost-aware benchmarking harness and a calibrator to produce cost vs latency curves; useful for Optimize recommendations and Dedicated capacity planning.
payload.title: Introduce cost-aware token economics bench and throughput calibrator

payload.body:
Motivation: We've seen recurring intermittent p95 regressions across long-running multi-epoch workloads where the signal only appears after many warmup cycles. Root-cause is often a narrow commit window interacting with kernel scheduler behaviour and warmup timing. This PR introduces two complementary tools: (1) an epochal hotpath bisector that runs compact workload epochs across commit ranges to quickly narrow offending commits, and (2) a phase-stress harness that injects controlled scheduling/jitter/prefetch delays into the runtime to reliably amplify the rare p95 event so it becomes reproducible in CI/local benches.

What this change does: Implements a bisector CLI that (a) shards an epochal workload into deterministic micro-epochs, (b) runs them across a git commit range with parallel workers and conservative resource isolation, and (c) aggregates per-epoch phase-bucket histograms to highlight commit-correlated shifts. Adds a phase-stress harness that can shim the runtime with configurable preemption latency, simulated kernel prefetch stalls, and induced KV-cache fragmentation to stress the hotpath under controlled conditions. Also adds a compact serializer (phase-bucket format) and a small reporting pipeline that generates a delta summary highlighting shifted quantiles and hotpath stack tags.

How to run (short): 1) Install bench Docker image: docker build -f Dockerfile.bench -t rwl-bench:phase . 2) Run bisector: bench/bisect --start <commit> --end <commit> --epochs 50 --workers 6 --mode phase-stress --stress-config bench/phase_stress/config.yaml 3) Inspect reports in benchmarks/reporting/<run-id>.phase.json and open docs/benchmarking/hotpath-bisector.md for guidance.

Checklist: - [x] Bisector core CLI, control plane, and parallel runner - [x] Phase-stress harness with 3 stress primitives (preemption, prefetch stall, kv-frag) - [x] Phase-bucket serializer and delta reporter - [x] Unit tests for serializer and small integration test for harness - [x] CI workflow to run a fast smoke bench on PRs - [x] Docs + example primer JSON - [ ] Long-run nightly job wiring (follow-up ENG-1708)

Testing and results: Local reproduction: used a historical regression window and reduced the commit range from ~2k commits to a 6-commit candidate using the bisector in ~45 minutes (6 workers, 50 epochs). Phase-stress amplified the original intermittent p95 from ~850ms to a stable 1.4–1.8s under the stress profile used in the reproduction (config included). CI: fast smoke run in PR pipeline completes within ~12 minutes (benchmarks.yml) and all checks passed after two re-runs on flaky network-injected step.

Limitations and risk: This is experimental and intentionally feature-flagged. The phase-stress primitives are intrusive (they modify scheduling hooks in the bench runtime) and can perturb other telemetry; their use should be limited to debug runs. Bisector increases CI compute usage when run across large commit ranges; the default parallelism is conservative.

Rollout plan: merge gated under label "experimental" and enable for internal SRE+perf teams. Nightly long-run job wiring and a small Linear task to auto-create candidate PRs when a bisect run identifies a single offending commit is tracked under ENG-1708.

payload.body:
Motivation: We need a repro-friendly runner that simulates long-running production inference workloads while exercising kernel selection and memory-pressure edge cases. Current bench runners focus on short bursts or single-phase warmups and miss gradual drift in sequence mixes and KV-cache pressure that lead to late regressions. This PR introduces a longitudinal fidelity runner and an accompanying reporting pipeline to capture phase transitions, kernel selection traces, and GPU memory-safety events.

What this PR adds (high level):
- A new runner: bench/longitudinal_runner.py (config-driven, supports sequence-mix schedules, time-decayed priming, and cohort splitting).
- Adaptive kernel probe: runtime/probes/kernel_probe.cc + probe harness that issues benign synthetic micro-requests that trigger alternate kernel paths without changing model weights. Probe backs off if it detects memory fragmentation or OOM proximity.
- Memory-safety monitor: tools/telemetry/gpu_memory_watcher which annotates traces with allocation failures, fragmentation heuristics, and resident set samples.
- Reporting pipeline: reports/longitudinal_exporter (CSV + compact flame segments) and an HTML quicklook summarizer for offline triage.
- New test fixtures and CI job: ci/workflows/longitudinal-bench.yaml that runs a fast smoke run in CI and stores artifacts.

Design notes:
- Runner is config-first: YAML schedule with phases (steady, drift, spike, decay) and a stochastic token-length generator to emulate nonstationary seq distributions.
- Prober is conservative: probes run on a separate worker thread group, honor runtime SLO settings, and use a kernel-candidate list derived from the model profile. Probes are annotated in traces as 'probe.'
- Memory watcher uses a lightweight sampling policy to avoid perturbing the system; it prefers resident set sampling and CUDA meminfo when available.

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests for schedule parser and token generator
- [x] End-to-end smoke benchmark that produces CSV output
- [x] Kernel probe safety backoff verified in local stress test (no OOMs triggered)
- [x] CI pipeline added and green on main smoke run

Why different from existing runners: This focuses on longitudinal behavior (hours-scale simulated via compressed replay), adaptive kernel probing tied to observed kernel selection drift, and explicit GPU memory-safety annotations to help correlate late failures with kernel choices and sequence-mix drift.

Potential follow-ups:
- Integrate probe results into model-routing policies to enable automatic fallback to conservative kernels when drift is detected.
- Add per-cohort QoS budgeting to measure economic impact of probe traffic.

Diego Ramos: 'Nice shape — I like the conservative probe approach. Can we reduce probe privilege to avoid touching the KV cache directly?'

Aisha (author): 'Probe traffic uses read-only prefix patterns and never injects priming that would mutate KV cache entries; added explicit assertion in probe harness and unit test to ensure no writes.'

Linus Park: 'Memory watcher looks good; can we expose fragmentation metric as a tag on traces so alerting can use it?'

Aisha: 'Added fragmentation tag in the exporter and a minimal histogram metric. See reports/longitudinal_exporter.py changes.'

Maya Bennett (approval): 'Approach validated locally on p3 and p4 hardware. Approving for merge.'
Introduce longitudinal benchmark runner with adaptive kernel probing and GPU memory-safety telemetry. Adds CI smoke coverage and reporting exporter for longitudinal traces.

Adds a new synthetic cohort re-teaming runner plus a subsequence-entropy reporter and an exporter pipeline. Motivation: previous workload runners treated user sessions as independent traces which lost signal about short-lived cohort affinity (sticky sequences that reappear within minutes). This PR implements a lightweight cohorting layer that can remap and coalesce request sequences into synthetic cohorts for more realistic load synthesis, and a downstream reporter that computes subsequence entropy across rolling windows to quantify stickiness. The description below covers design, tests, and usage. Design summary: 1) Reteamer: an offline + streaming runner that ingests sampled trace sessions, groups sequences by structural similarity (token-level n-gram overlap and KV-cache access patterns), and emits synthetic cohorted sequences with tunable churn parameters. The runner supports shuffling, prefix-preservation, and optional token-scrubbing for privacy. 2) Subsequence entropy reporter: sliding-window estimator that computes conditional entropy for variable-length subsequences and attributes entropy deltas to kernel-level execution buckets (via lightweight telemetry markers). This allows us to correlate sequence stickiness with kernel hotspots. 3) Exporter pipeline: compact parquet and newline-delimited JSON exporters with per-cohort statistics and per-kernel attribution lines for downstream visualization. Checklist: - [x] Runner implementation and CLI - [x] Entropy reporter algorithm and tests - [x] End-to-end DAG in benchmark pipelines - [x] Unit tests and integration tests - [x] Basic perf baseline in CI harness Commands and example run: benchlab run cohort-reteamer --input samples/session-sample.parquet --cohort-window 5m --churn 0.2 --output ./out/cohorts.parquet benchlab report subseq-entropy --input ./out/cohorts.parquet --window 60s --k-buckets 8 --output ./out/entropy.ndjson Backwards compatibility: defaults keep previous runner behavior when cohort-window is disabled. Privacy: token-scrubbing is enabled by default to avoid PII leakage. Related work: follows prototypes from ENG-2312 and extends ideas in ENG-2407 about session affinity modeling.
Diego Martinez: Nice work. Two requests: include a short note about privacy guarantees in the README and add one more integration case with high-churn traffic.
Maya Patel: Added privacy paragraph and enabled token-scrubbing by default; added churn test in tests/test_entropy.py (commit b7c2f11).
Omar Singh: I ran the kernel attribution helper on a small cluster; attribution looks plausible but watch the coarse bucket boundaries. Can we expose a finer k-bucket param?
Maya Patel: Exposed k-buckets in the reporter CLI and added a doc note about choosing bucket size; default remains 8. Added unit test for edge-case empty-window.
Liam Walker: CI flaked on python lint; fixes applied. Approving pending final CI run.
CI: All checks green on rerun. Approved and merged by Diego Martinez.
Local synthetic runs (8x A100-ish nodes) show cohorted workload p95 increase of 3.1% vs uncoalesced baseline but end-to-end cost per useful token decreases by 6.8% due to improved batching and KV-cache reuse. Subsequence entropy reporter reveals two low-entropy cohorts responsible for 40% of identical prefix hits; kernel attribution maps those to a single attention kernel with elevated L2 miss ratio in our microbenchmarks.
Add a new cohort re-teaming workload generator and a subsequence-entropy reporter for quantifying sequence stickiness and kernel-attributed hotspots. Useful for improved batching simulations and targeted kernel optimization.

Motivation: We need a reproducible way to surface cross-worker temporal correlations (e.g., multi-node p99 spike alignment, priming side-effects) that are lost when runs are treated as independent epochs. This PR introduces two cooperating pieces: (1) an epoch_synchronizer runner that coordinates epoch boundaries and priming windows across a distributed cohort of workers, and (2) a latency_correlation_graph generator that post-processes traces/latency buckets from synchronized epochs and emits a correlation graph and aligned heatmap artifacts suitable for downstream reporting and regression detection.

What this PR does: adds a new distributed runner (benchmark/runners/epoch_synchronizer.py) with an optional central coordinator mode and a peer-sync mode (gossip-based), implements a small clock-drift-tolerant barrier protocol to guarantee causal ordering of epoch markers, extends the runner harness to record an explicit epoch_id and wall-clock offsets per worker, and adds a post-processing tool (benchmark/reporting/latency_correlation_graph.py) that: ingests time-aligned latency streams, computes pairwise Spearman/Kendall correlations between worker-series, identifies likely causal lead/lag relationships via cross-correlation with significance testing, and emits: an annotated DOT graph (for quick visual inspection), an aligned epoch heatmap (Parquet + PNG), and a compact JSON summary suitable for automated regression pipelines.

Backwards compatibility: epoch_synchronizer is opt-in. Existing runners and reporting pipelines are unchanged unless the coordinator flag is enabled. The post-processor can consume legacy logs if a simple mapping layer is used (a short adapter script is included).

Checklist:
- [x] epoch synchronizer implementation with unit tests and integration harness emulation
- [x] post-processing tool with graph export and heatmap pipeline
- [x] CI workflow updates to run a small multi-node integration on PR builds
- [x] docs: new README and usage examples for running synchronized experiments
- [x] sample dataset and a short notebook for visualization (examples/latency-corr-demo.ipynb)

Performance/validation notes: Local integration runs (3-worker cohort, 1h synthetic workload) showed the synchronizer introduces 2-8ms median overhead to request scheduling (coordinator mode), but removes inter-epoch misalignment that previously caused false-positive correlations in p99 regressions. The correlation generator correctly recovered injected lead-lag patterns in synthetic tests (see bench/reports/controlled_injection_v0/*).

Testing and CI: Added unit tests for the barrier protocol, property tests for the adapter mapping, and an integration job (ci/bench-integration.yml) that spins up a lightweight 3-node emulator in the PR runner. CI initially failed due to flaky timeouts in the emulator; fixed by increasing the default sync window and adding jitter to the peer gossip path. All checks are green on merge.

Docs and examples: Added a short guide under docs/bench/latency_correlation.md describing when to use synchronized runs, interpreting the correlation graph, and guidance on choosing coordinator vs peer-sync modes. The quickstart notebook demonstrates generating the DOT graph and exporting a PNG/Parquet pair for ingestion into the reporting pipeline.

Risks and future work: Current coordinator mode is single-point-of-coordination; future work will add an elected-leader mode with transparent failover. We also plan to add an ML-based anomaly scorer that uses the correlation graph as input to detect emergent cross-worker regressions automatically.

Related: ENG-8241 (evaluation of cross-node regression noise), ENG-8307 (benchmark suite reliability).

Motivation: We observed intermittent p95/p99 regressions on multi-GPU clusters during mixed-sequence workloads that appear correlated with KV cache churn and cross-GPU memory bus contention. This PR introduces a lightweight reproducible sampler and replay harness that synthesizes sparse-KV reuse patterns across simulated tenants, plus an energy/thermal exporter to correlate occupancy and kernel energy with latency spikes. Scope: 1) bench/samplers/multi_gpu_congestion.py: new sampler that coordinates token streams across multiple simulated GPUs, supports per-tenant priming and controlled KV-eviction pulses; 2) bench/replay/sparse_kv_player.py: deterministic replay engine that replays sparse key access patterns with configurable skew and inter-arrival distributions; 3) bench/reporters/energy_exporter.rs: small Rust-based exporter that hooks into our GPU energy counters and emits compact CSV/JSON summaries for downstream visualization; 4) bench/tests/test_congestion_sampler.py: unit + integration tests validating determinism and seed control; 5) docs/bench/multi_gpu_congestion.md: design notes, knobs, and recommended experiment recipes; 6) ci/workflows/benchmark.yml: adds a nightly job invoking the new sampler with a reduced corpus for regression detection. High-level commits: - Seeded sampler core and API (multi_gpu_congestion.py) - Deterministic sparse-KV player and seedable stochastic drivers - Energy exporter, small C-bindings and CSV serializer - Integration test harness and small test corpus - Docs and experiment playbook - CI job and CI matrix tweak to tolerate energy-counters on runners. Commits summary: "seedable sampler and core loop", "sparse kv player + fixtures", "energy exporter and cbindgen stubs", "tests: integration and determinism checks", "docs: bench recipe and knobs", "ci: add nightly benchmark job". Changed areas: bench/samplers/, bench/replay/, bench/reporters/, bench/tests/, docs/bench/, ci/workflows/. Motivation/context: This is a focused benchmark-lab addition to help reproduce and quantify multi-GPU tail events caused by inter-GPU KV eviction pressure and bus saturation. The sampler intentionally generates cross-tenant overlapping priming windows and intermittent cold-primed eviction pulses so we can surface brittle kernel hotpaths and scheduling interactions that do not appear in single-GPU synthetic workloads. The energy exporter is deliberately compact to avoid adding heavy runtime dependencies to the benchmark runner; teams can opt in to additional counters via environment vars. Testing/validation: unit tests assert deterministic outputs given a seed, integration runs produce similar latency distributions across repeated runs (KL divergence < 0.02 under default corpus), and the exporter was validated on a small on-prem cluster (internal lab) against hardware counters. CI notes: The first CI run hit a flaky integration test due to test-machine GPU driver mismatch; we added a driver-check preflight and re-ran — final CI green with nightly job scheduled. Review conversation: "@Arjun: can you add explicit max-memory cap and a graceful fallback if the exporter cannot access hw counters?" Author reply: "Added a soft-fail path and a --skip-energy flag; documented behavior in the README." "@Sana: tests looked non-deterministic on my laptop CI; please ensure seeds propagate to the low-level sampler and to the replay player." Author: "Fixed: seed now threads through the C-binding and the player; added an assert in tests that repeats the run 3x to detect flakiness." "@Diego: minor nit on CSV header naming and prefer jsonl for large runs." Author: "Switched default to jsonl and added a --format flag to exporter." Approvals: Arjun approved after fixes, Sana approved after deterministic test updates, Diego approved cosmetic change. Merge: squash-merged to main. Backwards compatibility: bench APIs are additive and opt-in; no breaking change to existing runners. Release notes: "Added a new multi-GPU congestion sampler and sparse-KV replay harness plus an energy/thermal exporter for correlating kernel energy with latency. Useful for reproducing cross-GPU KV cache churn and bus saturation tail events." Usage notes: docs/bench/multi_gpu_congestion.md contains experiment recipes for reproducing p95/p99 spikes, recommended knobs (seed, skew, inter-arrival, eviction pulse frequency), and guidance for correlating exporter output with per-kernel latency. Related: ENG-4523 (investigation), ENG-4598 (follow-up action: prefetch-policy experiments).

payload.body:
Summary: This PR adds a repeatable baseline generator job in benchmark-lab that computes per-model performance baseline distributions from a controlled prod-like load run. The output artifacts are written in a stable, versioned format that perf-canary can consume for regression evaluation (min samples + percent-change thresholds). Motivation: perf-canary needs a durable baseline per (model, model_version, runtime_build, hardware_sku, region) that reflects real scheduler behavior (queueing/batching) without using customer traffic. Early experiments were using ad-hoc queries on ephemeral metrics, which made it hard to reproduce baselines and triggered baseline drift/cardinality issues during rollout. This job makes baselines an explicit artifact with an audit trail and a consistent schema. Scope / What’s included: (1) New job `baselinegen` that ingests a benchmark-lab load-run result bundle (request-level summary events + runtime counters) and computes: end-to-end latency histograms (p50/p95/p99 + full histogram buckets), runtime-only latency histograms, prefill and decode latency histograms, queueing time histogram, tokens/sec distribution, batch size distribution, and optional KV cache hit-rate summary when present. (2) Baseline artifact format: a single JSON artifact per dimension key, plus an index manifest for discovery. Artifacts are content-addressed and include schema versioning so perf-canary can validate compatibility. (3) Versioning & determinism: the job pins bucket boundaries, uses a seed for any sampling, and stores the exact input run id + git sha + job config in the metadata header. (4) Output location: writes to object storage under `s3://redwood-perf-baselines/perf_canary/v1/` (prod) and `s3://redwood-perf-baselines-staging/perf_canary/v1/` (staging). Includes a thin abstraction so storage backend can be swapped later without touching canary. (5) Guardrails: hard cap on dimensions written per execution (default 200) to prevent accidental wide fanout; rejects any input that contains raw prompts or request payloads (asserts only shape metrics and aggregated counters). (6) Documentation: adds `docs/perf_canary_baselines.md` describing schema, dimension keys, and how to generate/validate a baseline for a new model or hardware SKU. Non-goals: This does not change perf-canary evaluation logic or alert thresholds (handled in perf-canary repo / ADR). This does not add customer-traffic shadowing. Implementation notes: Input contract expects a `loadrun.jsonl.zst` (one line per request summary) and `runtime_metrics.pb.zst` (aggregated runtime counters) produced by existing benchmark-lab load runner. For histograms we use fixed bucket edges aligned with existing observability-pack dashboards to avoid mismatch between baseline and live metrics. The artifact JSON is intentionally flat and explicit (no nested structures beyond a small header), to keep it easy to diff/review and to allow simple validation in the canary service. Example artifact key: `model=llama-3.1-70b-instruct|model_version=2026-01-10|runtime_build=redwood-1.42.0|kernel_set=flashattn-v3|hardware_sku=h100-sxm|region=us-east-1|tier=hosted`. Testing: Unit tests cover histogram generation, percentile extraction, bucket edge stability, manifest writing, and schema validation. Integration test runs baselinegen on a small fixture loadrun bundle and asserts stable output (golden files). Added a dry-run mode that prints the computed dimension keys and sample counts without writing artifacts. Rollout plan: (1) Run job nightly in staging for the initial canary model set (2-3 models) and compare variance vs current ad-hoc baselines. (2) After sign-off from Runtime + Telemetry, enable in prod with a manual trigger path (run-id passed explicitly) before moving to scheduled runs. (3) Wire perf-canary baseline fetch to the manifest index (separate PR already in progress in perf-canary repo). Links: Linear ENG-4874 (baseline store + versioning), ENG-4872 (perf-canary MVP), ENG-4873 (metrics definitions). Notes for reviewers: Please sanity-check the dimension key policy (especially `kernel_set` and `runtime_build`), histogram bucket edges, and the cardinality guardrails. Also confirm the artifact header contains enough info for audit/debug but not enough to leak sensitive data.
Rina Kobayashi: Can we guarantee that the input bundle never contains prompts? I want a hard assertion, not just 'we don't use them'.
Nadia Rahman (author): Yep — added an explicit schema check that rejects any field named prompt/input/text, and the loader only accepts the request-shape fields (prompt_tokens, max_new_tokens, observed_new_tokens) plus timing/counter fields. Added a unit test that fails on prompt-like fields.
Noah Patel: Dimension key question: do we really want `kernel_set` as a baseline dimension? It might explode variants and make baselines sparse.
Nadia Rahman (author): Agree on sparsity risk. Proposed compromise: include kernel_set in the artifact header for attribution, but only include it in the key when `--dimension-policy=debug` is enabled. Default policy keeps it out of the key. Updated config + docs accordingly.
Logan Wright: Bucket edges should match our emitted histogram buckets in metrics; otherwise dashboards/regression evaluator will mismatch. Can you link the source of truth?
Nadia Rahman (author): Bucket edges are now imported from `internal/metrics/buckets.go` (same file used by load runner aggregation). Added a test asserting bucket arrays haven’t drifted (hash).
Allison Grant: Add guardrails for how many dimension combos can be written per job run. We need a safety rail against a bad config writing thousands of artifacts.
Nadia Rahman (author): Added `--max-artifacts` (default 200) with a hard fail if exceeded, plus a dry-run summary to view dimension keys before writing.
Allison Grant: LGTM after the guardrail change.
Noah Patel: Approved. Please ensure the manifest contains sample counts per key; canary should enforce min samples.
Nadia Rahman (author): Added `sample_count` and `window_seconds` to manifest entries; canary can reject low sample baselines.
Logan Wright: Approved.

Motivation: We observed recurring, low-amplitude latency tails in multi-tenant experiments that are poorly explained by request-level telemetry alone; root causes often live in kernel scheduling/driver contention and cross-tenant interference. This PR introduces a lightweight, deterministic multitenant interference prober and a pipeline that enriches benchmark traces with kernel-attribution markers so we can systematically reproduce and attribute tail events. What this change does: implements a bench harness (bench/probers/interference_prober.go + python runner) that spins configurable co-tenants with adjustable CPU/IO pressure profiles; adds a kotlin-compatible exporter (bench/exporters/kernel_attribution_exporter.{py,md}) that annotates traces with coarse kernel events (irq, scheduler_slice, cgroup_migrations) sampled via eBPF shim and aggregates them to token-level latency buckets; supplies a profiling baseline and an example runbook (bench/recipes/multitenant_interference_baseline.yaml) and a small dashboard template for the observability team. Determinism: prober supports seedable RNG for request timings and has an optional fixed-prime warmup sequence to stabilize KV cache states. Outputs: per-run JSON with per-quantile attribution summaries, a compact pprof flame-annotated tarball, and a CSV summary for comparison across runs. Backcompat and safety: the prober runs in a user-space container and only enables eBPF collection when the host allows it; all exporters gracefully fall back to synthetic attribution tags when kernel events are unavailable. How to run: see bench/README.md addition that documents a one-line invocation and an optional --compare flag to diff against a stored baseline. Why unique: unlike our existing workload runners this harness focuses on correlated cross-tenant interference patterns and couples per-token latency histograms with kernel-sourced signals to accelerate triage and regression detection. Notes: this PR intentionally keeps the prober light-weight (no long-running cluster changes) and includes CI smoke tests that run the harness at reduced scale in our Linux runner. Related work: builds on ideas from ENG-1190 (kv-warmup) and ENG-1367 (tail-attribution proto).
Add a synthetic multitenant interference prober and an exporter that correlates latency spikes with kernel-level attribution; useful as a new baseline for variance and regression tests.

Motivation: our multi-sequence interleaved workload traces exposed recurring p95/p99 spikes when concurrent sessions caused fragmented KV cache priming. This PR introduces two complementary components to improve steady-state tail latency and to measure headroom: 1) Adaptive Prefetch Coalescer: a lightweight runtime probe that detects small, temporally clustered key lookups across concurrent requests and issues aggregated prefetches for likely KV entries. Prefetch aggressiveness is controlled by an adaptive heuristic that tracks hit-rate delta and backoff on miss amplification. 2) Headroom Prober: a background sampler that injects low-overhead synthetic sequences under production-like concurrency to estimate remaining CPU/GPU headroom and identify noisy neighbors. Changes: - new runtime module benchmark_lab/prefetch/coalescer.go and coalescer tests - headroom prober harness under benchmark_lab/probers/headroom_prober.py with CLI + config - telemetry wiring: metrics and events exported to observability-pack (prefetch.attempts, prefetch.success_rate, prober.headroom_estimate, prober.latency_impact) - small API change in the session replayer to expose lookahead hints for prefetch (opt-in, off by default) - integration harness changes to include the prober in nightly long-tail runs Backwards compatibility: prefetch is opt-in via config; default behavior unchanged. Testing and results: ran the representative interleaved-seq workload (1000 concurrent sessions, mean seq len=210) in the lab. Compared against baseline nightly harness: p50 unchanged (~24ms), p95 reduced from 168ms to 132ms (-21%), p99 reduced from 312ms to 248ms (-21%). End-to-end throughput impact negligible (<1%). The prober adds ~0.3% extra token throughput load when enabled; metric collection overhead is <0.1%. Checklist: [x] unit tests for coalescer heuristics, [x] integration test with kvcache checkpointing, [x] perf run and report attached, [x] telemetry docs updated, [ ] roll-out gating config (follow-up ticket). Related: references ENG-4123 for KV cache regression, follows patterns from earlier adaptive prefetch experiments. Notes for reviewers: focus on correctness/edge cases in coalescer backoff logic (avoid thrashing) and on the prober sampling cadence (defaults tuned conservatively). Long-term: propose adding a canary flag to enable aggressive prefetch for dedicated capacity clusters. Attachments: perf CSVs and flamegraphs stored in run-2026-02-21 artifacts.

Ethan Li: Thanks Maya — tightened backoff coefficients and added a deterministic miss stress test in coalescer_test.go. See commit 3.

payload.body:
Motivation: During a set of production-mirroring benchmark runs we observed repeated short-lived p95/p99 spikes correlated with tight slot contention and abrupt GPU thermal headroom reductions. These microbursts caused transient QoS violations in the scheduler and produced noisy latency tails in our profiling baselines. This PR introduces two coordinated components to make burst injection more predictable in the bench environment: (1) a slot succession sequencer that coalesces and sequences concurrent slot grants to avoid pathological overlap patterns, and (2) a thermal-aware slew controller that adaptively paces mini-batches when telemetry indicates thermal headroom pressure.

Scope: Changes are confined to the benchmark-lab harness and its synthetic workload runners; no production runtime code is modified. Key pieces: a deterministic sequencer implemented in Go (benchmarks/slot_sequencer), a lightweight thermal predictor in Python that consumes telemetry samples and produces a short-term headroom estimate, and a controller that gates burst submission. We also add telemetry exporters and tagging to make post-run attribution easier.

What this does:
- Implements a slot succession algorithm that enforces a soft inter-slot spacing policy based on observed kernel durations and token/sequence length distribution.
- Adds a thermal headroom estimator that smooths temperature/clock samples and exposes a headroom score (0..1) used by the slew controller.
- Introduces a slew controller that throttles mini-batch submit rates when headroom < threshold, with configurable aggressive/recovery modes.
- Exposes new metrics: bench_slot_latency_ms, bench_slot_overlap_count, bench_thermal_headroom (gauge), bench_slew_throttle_ratio.
- Includes a new deterministic workload playbook (sample_playbooks/slot_succession.yaml) to reproduce the scenario and a docs page with reproduction steps.

Benchmarks & results: Microbench runs against the 2026-01-30 baseline show: median latency unchanged, p95 improved by ~12-18% under high-concurrency bursts, p99 tail reduced by 20-35% in the synthetic token-surge scenario, and GPU thermal oscillation amplitude reduced by ~40%. These runs are attached in the CI bench-regression artifacts.

Testing & QA: Unit tests for sequencer logic and predictor added. Integration harness that runs the playbook for short and long durations (5m/1h) included. I ran the integration suite on an m6 GPU instance matrix. Checklist: 
- [x] Unit tests added and passing locally
- [x] Integration playbook validated on staging cluster
- [x] Bench regression run (baseline comparison) attached to CI
- [x] Docs page draft added under docs/benchmarks
- [x] Performance dashboards updated with new metric mappings

Backward compatibility & safety: Default knobs are conservative: sequencer disabled by default in existing playbooks unless the new playbook is used; slew controller is opt-in via config. No breaking changes to existing harness APIs.

How to run locally: 
1) cd benchmarks/slot_sequencer

Motivation: We observed recurring fatigue in p95/p99 during short-lived microbursts where naive batching either over-aggregates unrelated sequences or leaves hot strands undersampled. This PR adds two complementary pieces: 1) a strand-aware request bundler that groups concurrent requests by inferred request 'strand' (derived from session metadata and request fingerprinting) to keep logical locality and avoid mixing cold/warm hotpaths, and 2) an SLA-sensitive ramp calibrator that automatically shapes synthetic ramp traffic used by benchmarks to honor per-cohort latency SLOs while still exercising tail behavior. Design: The bundler runs as a lightweight pre-batcher stage in the bench runner pipeline. It computes a 64-bit strand key using a two-stage hash (session id + tokenized prompt signature) and maintains short-lived strand windows to enforce affinity for microbatch assembly. Bundles are limited by both token budget and strand diversity thresholds to prevent head-of-line blocking from long sequences. The calibrator observes running telemetry (p50/p95/p99 and queue depth) and adjusts derived ramp slopes and inter-arrival jitter to match target SLOs per cohort. It supports fixed-profile, closed-loop, and hybrid modes (default: hybrid). Implementation summary: - New module benchlab/bundler/strand_bundler.go (Go) and a small shim benchlab/bundler/bundler_test.go covering deterministic hashing and window eviction invariants. - New calibrator benchlab/ramp/calibrator.py (Python) used by the orchestration harness; it exposes a dry-run mode and a live mode that emits adjustment signals over an internal control topic. - Integration glue in benchlab/orchestrator/synth_runner.go that wires bundler output into the existing microburst generator. - Added a lightweight prometheus exporter benchlab/metrics/strand_metrics.prom with strand-level counters and a sampling histogram for bundle sizes. Testing: Unit tests cover hashing corner cases and bundler eviction. End-to-end benchmarking run against a 4-GPU mini-cluster (g4dn-style nodes) with seq-length mixes: 8/32/128. Results: Compared to baseline microburst runner, hybrid bundler+calibrator reduced p99 CPU latency amplification events by ~22% and lowered synthetic-run cost (measured tokens/sec-to-sla ratio) by ~13% on our steady-state profile. Docs and examples: Added README with configuration knobs and a short quickstart script to reproduce local runs. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration test (local mini-cluster) - [x] Perf comparison (results attached below) - [x] Prometheus metrics wired - [x] Added Linear links and runbook notes Migration notes: No infra migration required. Default mode is off; opt-in via orchestrator config. Related: ENG-1289 (microburst stability epic), ENG-1334 (cohort-aware sampling).
Kenta Mori: Nice work. Two quick asks: (1) can we expose the strand window TTL as a config knob (default 200ms) and document expected tradeoffs? (2) the bundler's deterministic hash seems to use the raw prompt; can we normalize whitespace to avoid churn?
Author (Anya Petrov): Reply: Added a config knob strand_window_ttl_ms and normalized prompt before hashing. See benchlab/config/synth_profiles.yaml and bundler_test for coverage.
Riley Thompson: Tests look good. Calibrator logic LGTM but please add a short note in the runbook about failure modes when telemetry is noisy.
Author: Added failure-mode notes in benchlab/README/strand_bundler.md and added an e2e flag --calibrator-noisy-check to gate live adjustments.
Sofia Martinez: Approve after CI green + one minor nit on metric naming (use benchlab_strand_bundle_count_total).
Author: Renamed metric to benchlab_strand_bundle_count_total and updated dashboard; CI rerun queued.
Added a strand-aware bundler to reduce microburst tail amplification and an SLA-sensitive ramp calibrator to generate ramp traffic that respects per-cohort latency SLOs. Opt-in behind config; improves tail stability and synthetic-run cost efficiency.

Motivation: production traffic shows prefix distribution drift compared to training / eval traces leading to poorer KV cache effectiveness and warmup inefficiencies. This PR introduces a simulator and reporting pipeline that (1) emits synthetic requests with contextual prefix drift patterns (topical shifts, truncation/pad noise, prefix-repeat bursts) and (2) aggregates multi-window performance profiles (per-sequence-length buckets, sliding windows at 1s/10s/60s) to reveal how drift affects p50/p95 latency, KV-hit-rate, and kernel alignment metrics. Goals: 1) provide a compact, configurable runner teams can use to reproduce prefix drift failure modes observed in the field; 2) produce compact profile artifacts suitable for long-term storage and automated regression checks; 3) add a small, low-cost reporting pipeline that converts in-memory windows into Parquet exports and uploads to the benchmark artifact storage bucket. High level changes: added a new runner binary `prefix-drift-runner` (Go) with a lightweight simulator that consumes a seed corpus and applies configurable drift transforms (topic-swap, prompt-chopping, leading-fill, prefix-repeat). Added `prefix_profile_aggregator` (Python) that accepts a continuous stream of telemetry (latency, tokens, kv_hit, kernel_id) and emits multi-window stats and kernel-alignment histograms. Added a minimal Parquet export and s3 uploader component and a config-driven CI perf job that runs the runner against a 2-minute synthetic scenario and validates no regressions beyond configured thresholds. Backwards compatibility: runner uses existing benchmark-lab telemetry envelope; aggregator implements a translation shim for older envelope versions so existing dashboards remain functional. Usage: see examples/prefix-drift/README for run commands and sample configs. Why this is different: existing labs focus on burstiness and sequence length mixes; this work focuses on contextual content drift and its specific impact on KV cache warmup, prefetch heuristics, and kernel selection alignment across windows.
Marta: Nice work—this surface (contextual drift) has been a blind spot for us. A couple of things: the aggregator looks like it keeps all windows in memory; can we bound that and spill to disk? Also can you add an example of model variant switching so we can see kernel alignment changes?
Eleni: Good catch—added a max_window_memory_bytes cap and a spill-to-temp-file path with configurable policy. Also added an example scenario in sample.yaml showing a model-variant toggle (fp16->int8) mid-run and the resulting kernel_id change is emitted to the histogram.
Ravi: Perf CI flagged a +0.18% p95 regression on the 2-minute micro-scenario vs baseline. Is that noise? Can we tighten variance?
Eleni: The regression is within expected variance for the chosen seed corpus; I added deterministic seeding for CI runs and a retry policy for the perf job to reduce flakiness. Re-ran CI and p95 delta is now +0.03%—within threshold.
Tomás: Two nit: use context.Context in the collector for shutdown, and prefer structured logs for the uploader so we can correlate attempts.
Eleni: Addressed both—collector accepts ctx and uploader switched to JSON lines; updated tests to exercise graceful shutdown.
Marta: Approving after the memory bounding and CI fixes—this will be useful for SRE and runtime teams.
Tomás: LGTM after last comment; squashed and ready to merge.
Added a new benchmark runner (prefix-drift-runner) and aggregator (prefix_profile_aggregator) to emulate contextual prefix drift and produce multi-window performance profiles. Includes Parquet export and S3 uploader for artifact storage. Useful for reproducing kv-cache warmup regressions and kernel alignment issues.
Run `go build ./cmd/prefix-drift-runner && ./prefix-drift-runner --config configs/prefix-drift/sample.yaml --duration 120s` then start aggregator `python3 aggregator/prefix_profile_aggregator.py --config configs/prefix-drift/sample.yaml` and confirm Parquet file appears in ./out or uploaded to s3 when configured.
CI perf job added at benchmark-lab/.github/workflows/perf-prefix-drift.yml. The job uses deterministic seeds to minimize flakiness. S3 uploader uses benchmark-artifacts bucket and assumes CI role has write access. Ops should verify bucket lifecycle to avoid long-term storage costs.
examples/prefix-drift/README.md contains quickstart, sample.yaml demonstrates model-variant toggle scenario and how to run aggregator locally. See configs/prefix-drift/sample.yaml for all tunable parameters.

Motivation: reproducing cross-tenant interference reliably has been a recurring blocker for debugging tail latency regressions. Randomized noise injection and ad-hoc replay scripts made experiments hard to reproduce across runs and clusters. This PR adds two complementary pieces: (1) a configurable cross-tenant noise injector that can playback a small 'background traffic' trace with deterministic seeding and time-anchoring, and (2) an anchored replay runner that ties foreground request traces to fixed wall-clock anchors so repeated runs are bit-for-bit comparable.

What this PR does (high level):
- Implements a lightweight noise model with pluggable distributions (poisson, bursty, correlated-bursts) and an explicit RNG-seed parameter for reproducibility.
- Adds an "anchor" mechanism: a foreground trace is annotated with anchor timestamps; the runner aligns trace playback to those anchors so warmup/coldstart windows and KV-cache priming are deterministic.
- Introduces a compact exporter (CSV + optional parquet metadata header) that records per-request anchor ids, injected-noise-tags, latency p50/p95/p99, and kernel attribution hints to streamline downstream delta-analysis.
- Adds runtime markers in the runner to expose prefetched primer events to perf collectors (small header in runtime_markers.h and emitted markers in critical path).
- Integrates with existing perf CI: a new perf-suite job wiring leverages the anchored runner for nightly regression baselines.

Why this is different: many previous runners either randomized noise or relied on wall-clock-only replays; combining anchored timestamps + deterministic seeds removes two big sources of nondeterminism (schedule jitter and PRNG variance) and lets us produce reproducible diffable telemetry.

Checklist:
- [x] Core noise model implementation and tests
- [x] Anchored replay runner with anchor alignment algorithm
- [x] Compact exporter and sample schema docs
- [x] Unit and integration tests validating determinism across cluster restarts
- [x] CI perf job wiring (nightly)
- [ ] Long-running soak trials (tracked separately in ENG-1984)

Commits summary:
- 9cf2a1b: add noise_model.py (Poisson / burst / correlated burst generators, deterministic seed)
- 3f847d2: introduce anchored_replay.py (anchor alignment, priming windows, marker emissions)
- 7b1e4c5: compact_exporter + parquet header writer (optional dependency gated behind feature flag)
- de92a6f: add runtime_markers.h and small emitter helper used by anchored_replay
- 51fae10: tests: deterministic replay tests + CI perf-suite wiring

High-level files changed (illustrative):

(2) The markers in runtime_markers.h look fine, but can we make the emission a no-op behind a build flag to avoid perf noise in production?

payload.body:
Context: We need a lightweight, reproducible session-level workload synthesizer that can generate short-lived burst patterns (temporal spikes) and multi-phase sessions to reproduce kernel scheduling and KV cache pressure seen in production p95/p99 tails. Motivation: Existing runners produce steady-state sequences or reproduce long tail distributions but do not emulate multi-phase sessions with rapid intra-session bursts followed by quiet periods. This gap blocks iteration on scheduling heuristics and per-kernel latency drift mitigation experiments.

This PR introduces two components in the benchmark-lab runner suite: 1) Burstwave Session Synthesizer: a configurable workload generator that composes sessions from phases (startup ramp, burstwave, cooldown, intermittent microbursts). It supports parameterized sequence lengths, token emission rate profiles, KV cache warm/cold toggles, and per-session seed control for deterministic replay. 2) Snapshot Reporter: a compact per-run reporter that samples per-kernel latency distributions at snapshot points (pre-burst, peak-burst, post-burst) and emits a small lineage metadata file that ties snapshots to run configuration and random seeds.

Why unique: Instead of only collecting global latency histograms, the reporter captures per-kernel (attention, softmax, GEMM, memcopy) percentiles at three logical snapshots and serializes them for differential analysis across commits. This makes small regressions in a single kernel visible without needing full flamegraphs, enabling faster CI feedback on kernel changes.

High-level changes: - tools/session_synthesizer/burstwave.py: new synthesizer with CLI and YAML profile support. - tools/reporters/snapshot_reporter.py: new reporter that hooks into runner lifecycle and emits compressed snapshots. - benchmark-lab/config/profiles/burstwave-default.yaml: canonical profile used in CI. - tests/integration/test_burstwave_replay.py: deterministic replay + golden snapshot assertions. - benchci/pipelines/burstwave.yaml: ephemeral CI job definition for nightly regression runs. - docs/bench-lab/burstwave-readme.md: usage and tuning guide.

Checklist: - [x] Synthesizer implementation and CLI. - [x] Snapshot serialization and lineage metadata. - [x] Integration tests with deterministic seed replay. - [x] Basic performance sanity checks (no regression in steady-state runner). - [x] Documentation + example profiles.

How to run locally: python tools/session_synthesizer/burstwave.py --profile benchmark-lab/config/profiles/burstwave-default.yaml --out ./runs/test1 --seed 42  --duration 60
Run the reporter as part of the runner: python tools/reporters/snapshot_reporter.py --run-dir ./runs/test1 --emit-json --compress

Testing: Added unit tests for emission schedules and two integration tests: one that validates deterministic snapshots across seed/commit pairs, and one that asserts the reporter writes per-kernel percentiles without signficant overhead (wall time < +5% on a small CI GPU). CI: new benchci job was added and initially flaked due to an environment mismatch (old CUDA image in the benchci runner). I coordinated with infra to pin a lighter image and rerun. All checks passed on re-run.

Impact: Enables fast local reproduction of temporal spike events and simplifies per-kernel regression detection. Expected to reduce time-to-diagnose for scheduling regressions and guide targeted kernel optimizations.

Notes: This is intentionally conservative — the synthesizer provides profiles rather than stochastic generators for initial stability. Follow-up PRs are planned to add an event-driven stochastic mode and integration with the telemetry-backed corpus sampler.

Related: ENG-2241 (profiling baseline), ENG-2299 (scheduling heuristics experiment).

Maya Patel: Good call — factored CLI in 2nd commit (see commit 2).

Maya Patel: Added schema_version and documented compatibility in docs (commit 4).

Maya Patel: Added fast_ci flag and reduced expected wall time in the test; benchci job keeps the full-run as nightly-only.

payload.body:
Motivation: production traffic often contains very short session fragments (single-turn or micro-interactions) that individually don't exercise the model's long-token path or KV cache but collectively create bursts and kernel contention. Existing runners either replay long-session traces or artificially concatenate fragments without preserving timeline semantics. This PR introduces a session-fragment-ensemble-runner that deterministically stitches many short fragments into ensemble requests while preserving original inter-fragment time gaps and token alignment. It also adds a derivative-latency-attribution-reporter that attributes tail (p95/p99/p995) latency to kernel groups, primer pool size, and prefix cache hit characteristics, enabling root-cause signals for long-tail regressions. Design summary: the runner accepts a corpus of short session fragments (jsonl), a timeline map (timestamps per fragment), and a seeding policy to deterministically group fragments into ensembles. It simulates real-world burstiness by replaying ensembles across configurable concurrency lanes and supports two priming strategies: pooled-priming (shared primer buffers) and isolated-priming (per-ensemble primer). The reporter ingests per-request telemetry (latency, kernel tags, kv-hit-rate, primer-size) and emits compact attribution vectors that break down the incremental contribution to tail quantiles by dimension. Implementation notes: added a new runner package (bench/runners/fragment_ensemble), a reporter backend (bench/reporters/deriv_attribution), and lightweight adapters to the existing harness to export deterministic flame snapshots and small tar artifacts for CI. Performance and safety: the runner is implemented in Rust/Go hybrid (Go harness + Rust hotpath for deterministic shuffling) to minimize allocation noise and ensure reproducible runs. We added a deterministic RNG seed derived from Linear ticket + PR number by default so CI comparisons are stable. The reporter uses streaming, constant-memory quantile sketches and offloads heavy aggregation to a worker thread to avoid perturbing latency. Test and verification: included unit tests for deterministic grouping, integration tests that validate end-to-end telemetry pipeline against a golden fixture, and an e2e CI benchmark that runs a small corpus and uploads artifact to build storage. How to run locally: benchctl run fragment-ensemble --corpus testdata/short_fragments.jsonl --timeline testdata/timeline.json --priming pooled --concurrency 16 --seed 43862. Output will appear in bench-out/<run-id>/report.json and flame/* snapshots. Backwards compatibility: runner is additive; existing runners and report formats unchanged. This PR also includes a small compatibility shim in the harness to interpret the new reporter format when present. Related: ENG-2148 (bursty-fragment-fidelity project), SUP-3421 (customer incident that motivated tail attribution).
Adds a session fragment ensemble workload runner and a compact derivative-latency attribution reporter. Intended for advanced tail attribution and small-fragment priming fidelity tests. No breaking API changes.
1) Add fragment_ensemble runner skeleton and CLI wiring (bench/runners/fragment_ensemble) 2) Implement deterministic grouping + Rust shuffler + Go FFI 3) Add deriv_attribution reporter and constant-memory sketches 4) CI workflow to produce artifacts and upload flamegraphs 5) Tests: unit, integration, and e2e golden fixture 6) Docs: runner README and runbook snippets
Evan Liu: Please add a short note on the determinism guarantees of the Rust shuffler; what parts are non-deterministic if we change the Go runtime. Reply (Marina): Added a section in runner README and an integration test that validates identical output across Go 1.20/1.21 in CI.
Sofia Ramirez: The reporter looks great but we should avoid heavy allocations on the request path; can heavy aggregation be fully offloaded? Reply (Marina): Aggregation is offloaded to a single worker thread and reporter.go includes a bounded queue; updated tests to make sure backpressure never exceeds 4x the median latency window.
Jonah Brooks: Could we expose primer pool metrics to the console? Reply (Marina): Exposed primer_pool_size, primer_shared_hit_rate, and primer_eviction_count to the existing telemetry and added them to per-route dashboard templates.
SRE Bot: flakiness detected on initial CI run (p99 drift). Marina: Fixed by making the default seed explicit and reducing timer jitter in test fixture. Re-ran CI and all checks passed.

payload.body:
Motivation: benchmarking long-tail cold starts and per-cohort variability in token-serving hotpaths is difficult with global replayers. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: (1) a Cohorted Warmup Replayer that runs short epochal warmup sessions per user/workload cohort to produce realistic KV-cache warm states, and (2) a Token Hotpath Tracer that records lightweight per-token timing buckets to map hotspots to kernels. Together these enable quantile-stratified export reports that are much better at reproducing p99+p999 tail behaviors in heterogeneous mixes.

What I changed (single-string summary, with checklist):
- Implemented a cohorted warmup engine that groups traces by sequence shape and recent latency signature; epochs are triggered before main replay batches.
- Added a token hotpath tracer that samples token emission timing (microsecond buckets) and annotates traces with kernel hints (when available).
- Built a quantile-stratified exporter that merges cohort epoch stats into reports consumable by existing reporting pipelines.
- Integration tests and a small local end-to-end harness for reproducing p95/p99 regressions.
- Docs: benchlab README update with example experiment config and cohort definitions.

Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] integration harness, [x] local perf microbench, [x] docs updated, [x] Linear items linked.

Commits (high-level):
- 1a2b3c4: feature: initial cohorted warmup engine skeleton and epoch scheduler
- 2b3c4d5: perf: add KV-cache priming path and cohort selection heuristics
- 3c4d5e6: feat: token hotpath tracer and micro-bucket timer util
- 4d5e6f7: export: quantile-stratified report serializer and CSV + JSON exporters
- 5e6f7g8: test: add e2e harness and deterministic replay fixture
- 6f7g8h9: docs: usage examples, configuration guide and analysis notebook

Files changed (high-level):
- benchlab/replayers/cohorted_warmup.py (new) — core engine, cohort selectors, epoch lifecycle
- benchlab/tracers/token_hotpath.py (new) — micro-bucket timing, kernel-hint annotations
- benchlab/exporters/quantile_stratified.py (new) — merges cohort epochs into reports
- benchlab/harnesss/e2e_epochal_runner.py (new) — small runner for reproducible experiments
- benchlab/tests/test_cohorted_warmup.py (new), test_token_hotpath.py (new) — unit tests
- docs/benchlab/cohorted_warmup.md (modified) — usage and config examples
- CI/workflows/bench-e2e.yaml (modified) — adds optional bench-e2e job (runs on schedule)

Design notes and rationale: the replayer runs short warmup epochs sized to median sequence length of the cohort to avoid over-warming high-cost long sequences while still priming KV caches for typical tails. Cohorts are defined by a small set of attributes (sequence length bucket, average tokens/sec observed, and template fingerprint). The token tracer samples 1 in N tokens (configurable) and records emission time deltas in coarse microsecond buckets plus an optional kernel-hint tag when the runtime exposes the kernel selection. This keeps overhead <2% in microbench runs.

Review thread (abridged):
- Diego Morales (reviewer): "Nice approach. Two questions: 1) how stable are cohorts across deployments? 2) Can we avoid storing tracer payloads in-memory for long runs?"
- Maya Patel (author): "1) cohorts default to ephemeral per-run but we persist cohort fingerprints in the report to allow cross-run mapping; we can add a persisted catalog if needed. 2) tracer payloads are streamed to the exporter; we keep a small ring buffer and flush on epoch boundary. See benchlab/replayers/cohorted_warmup.py lines 212-245 for the ring buffer impl."
- Eileen Zhang (reviewer): "CI flakes on the e2e job in the first run. I ran locally and saw an intermittent timing assertion in test_token_hotpath — likely due to timer resolution on macOS. Can you add a small relaxation?"
- Maya Patel: "Added a 10us slack in timer assertions and moved the test to use a deterministic fake-timer in CI-only path. PTAL."
- Ravi Singh (reviewer): "Question on exporter schema: downstream dashboards expect 'cohort_id' and we now emit 'cohort_fingerprint'. Is that mapped?"
- Maya: "Added a compatibility shim in quantile_stratified.py that emits both cohort_id (stable hash) and cohort_fingerprint. Updated docs section."

CI summary and reruns: initial CI run (linux-build/test) failed on bench-e2e (timing assertion). After test fix and rebase, CI passed. Bench-e2e is gated to optional workflow to avoid blocking main merges; nightly scheduled runs collect epochal outputs. Final CI status: pass (all required checks green).

Performance notes from local microbench: in a mixed sequence workload (60/30/10 short/med/long) with cohorted warmup enabled, tail p99 reduced by ~18% and p999 by ~9% compared to baseline global replayer; median unaffected. Token tracer overhead measured ~1.6% in a 10k request microbench with sampling 1:50.

Compatibility and rollout: feature is behind a feature-flag in benchlab config (warmup.cohorted.enabled, tracer.enabled). Default flags are off to ensure reproducibility. We plan to enable the warmup replayer in nightly benchmark runs for two weeks and then promote to CI gated experiments if stable.

Follow-ups (tracked in Linear):
- ENG-2050: persistent cohort catalog and matching service for cross-run cohort identity
- BENCH-117: integrate exporter with reporting pipeline to auto-generate p95/p99/p999 regression alerts for cohorts
- BENCH-118: add server-side optional kernel-hint enrichment from runtime telemetry

Merge outcome: squashed and merged by Maya Patel via squash merge on 2026-02-24. Release note added to benchlab CHANGELOG under unreleased.

Notes for reviewers/maintainers: this PR intentionally keeps runtime hooks optional and lightweight. If we see any regressions in nightly runs, the feature flags make it trivial to roll back. The documentation contains an analysis notebook and an example that reproduces the local microbench numbers.
Adds a cohort-aware warmup replayer that generates epochal warmup sequences per-cohort, plus an optional lightweight token-level hotpath tracer and a quantile-stratified summary exporter. Improves cold-start tail stability for mixed sequence workloads; no breaking changes.

payload.body:
Motivation: Production workloads show that high-priority short bursts can create transient backpressure that amplifies latency for lower-priority models sharing the same serving pool. Existing bench scenarios exercise steady-state mixes but do not quantify cross-priority cascade effects or attribute tail amplification to specific batches/kernels. This PR introduces a simulator and reporter to quantify cross-batch/backpressure effects and provide actionable signals for routing and batching heuristics.

What this PR adds: 1) priority-backpressure scenario runner (benchlab/scenarios/priority_backpressure.go): simulates multiple model queues with configurable priority classes, burst profiles, and backpressure propagation rules (queue headblocking, preemption, soft-eviction). 2) cross-batch attribution reporter (benchlab/reporters/crossbatch_attribution.py): consumes scenario traces and outputs per-batch and per-kernel attribution for p50/p95/p99 deltas attributable to higher-priority interference. 3) occupancy census telemetry (benchlab/metrics/occupancy_census.proto + exporters): collects per-GPU occupancy and per-kernel busy/idle epochs for finer granularity of kernel-level contention. 4) CI bench job updates (scripts/ci/bench-suite.yml): new deterministic seed mode and a perf-smoke stage. 5) docs and runbook (docs/bench/priority-backpressure.md) with instructions, recommended thresholds, and mitigation playbooks.

Design notes: - Simulator models both synchronous batching and continuous batching pipelines; it supports KV cache warm/cold starts and optional priming behavior. - Attribution reporter uses event-aligned difference-in-paths: it constructs cohorts of high-priority bursts and compares tail quantiles of co-located low-priority cohorts after aligning warmup windows; output includes JSON per-run and a compact Prometheus-compatible metrics export. - Config-driven: any bench scenario can be augmented with a priority-tier definition and backpressure policy to test rollout strategies.

Checklist: - [x] New scenario implementation with unit tests and deterministic seed. - [x] Reporter outputs validated against synthetic traces. - [x] CI bench-suite updated to include a fast-smoke run. - [x] Docs and runbook added. - [x] Performance regression guard added (bench-suite will fail PRs with >15% p99 regression unless opt-in).

How to run locally: ./benchlab run --scenario priority-backpressure --config ./benchlab/configs/priority_backpressure.yaml --out ./artifacts/pb_run.json

Expected outputs: - artifacts/pb_run.json (detailed trace + cohort attribution) - prometheus endpoint /metrics exposing bench_priority_backpressure_{p50,p95,p99}_delta and occupancy_census_{kernel}_{epoch} metrics.

Risk and mitigation: The new reporter runs offline and does not change serving code paths. The simulator is isolated to the bench harness but exercises code paths similar to our runtime; we added a safeguard to avoid any live cluster calls.

Related: ENG-7812 (routing policy experiments), ENG-7920 (KV cache warmup heuristics), SUP-1345 (customer incident analysis that motivated this work).
Nate Reeves: Good surface area, +1 on telemetry shape. Can we make the cohort window configurable and add an explanation of the default in the docs?
Sofia Alvarez: Added cohort_window_ms to configs and documented default (300ms) in docs/bench/priority-backpressure.md — uses conservative value to avoid warmup bleed-through.
Priya Menon: The attribution math looks right but we saw a notable variance when the KV cache is cold. Please show how the reporter separates cache-warm vs cache-cold cohorts.
Sofia Alvarez: Reporter now tags cohorts by cache_warm boolean and exports separate quantile deltas; added unit test to validate separation using fixtures/priority_traces.json.
Derek Huang: CI bench-suite failed once on p99 flaky test; after adjusting deterministic seed the run is stable. Please ensure the smoke job uses a very small workload so it stays fast.
Sofia Alvarez: Reduced smoke run length and added explicit seed in CI config. Reran bench-suite; all checks passed.
- Add 'priority-backpressure' benchmark scenario to benchlab for quantifying cross-priority interference and tail amplification.
- New cross-batch attribution reporter that produces per-batch kernel attribution and Prometheus metrics.
- Occupancy census telemetry for kernel-level contention analysis.
- Documentation and runbook with mitigation recommendations (routing rules, preemption, batching adjustments).
This PR aims to make it easier for SREs and runtime engineers to reason about priority-induced tail effects and to test routing/quantization mitigations in the lab before rolling them to Dedicated/Private deployments. Follow-up work: automate cohort-based alerting and integrate with Optimize recommendations.

Motivation: Our existing workload replayers produce high-variance profiling baselines when sequence lengths and batching patterns vary. That noise makes it hard to attribute tail-latency regressions to kernel scheduling vs model changes. This PR adds a deterministic session trajectory slicer plus an offline kernel occupancy estimator that together produce repeatable steady-state runs and a small summarizing artifact used by the perf dashboard.

What this changes: single logical string describing the change—no sub-JSONs. Implements a new replayer module (trajectory_slicer) that slices long session traces into deterministic, time-aligned sub-trajectories, preserving inter-request gaps and token-length distributions. Adds kernel_occupancy tool that consumes runtime telemetry (per-step CPU/GPU utilization, batch sizes, KV cache hits) and outputs a compact occupancy profile used to normalize throughput/latency comparisons across hardware. Adds a reporter that emits a per-cohort summary suitable for downstream p95/p99 stability charts.

payload.body:
Summary: Reduce streaming first-byte latency by aligning per-stream emission windows to kernel batch boundaries, adding a compact KV-prefetch path for stalled streams, and introducing a light-weight handoff to next microbatch when kernels are warm.

Motivation: we observed recurring small delays at stream boundaries where the emitter would flush a tiny payload that did not match the GPU kernel batch size; that triggered kernel invocation overhead and inefficient CUDA launches for micro-batches. For long-lived conversations, cold KV pages and scatter prefetches also introduced tail spikes.

Goals: 1) shape emission timing so emitted tokens more often land inside a kernel-sized bundle; 2) avoid kernel invocation for sub-threshold emissions by deferring via a short, adaptive hold window; 3) provide a compact KV compaction/prefetch path that warms only actively referenced KV shards without full rehydrate; 4) keep changes opt-in via a scheduler flag and a conservative default.

Design:
- Emission window alignment: emitter calculates a per-stream phase based on recent sequence lengths and kernel target_batch_size. Instead of flushing immediately on token availability, emitter waits up to align_window_ms (default 4ms, configurable) to try and batch into an already-scheduled kernel slot. The window is bounded and won't exceed configured latency SLOs.
- Kernel boundary hints: runtime now exposes lightweight kernel_batch_boundary() hints that the scheduler can use to group streams with similar phase into the same kernel invocation.
- Adaptive hold policy: a soft hold with exponential backoff for cold streams; holds are preemptible by latency-critical streams and honor stream deadlines.
- KV compaction prefetch: introduces kv_compact_prefetch mode which maintains a compact working set summary per stream and issues narrow prefetches for only hot KV ranges on handoff; this avoids rehydrating large KV pages for small shifts in attention.
- Microbatch handoff API: small change to the executor internals to support preemptive microbatch handoff when a kernel reports "hot" caches and the queued streams are aligned.

All changes gated behind feature flag: runtime.optim.emit_align_v1 and runtime.kv.compact_prefetch.

Commits (high-level):
- 7 commits: initial design + phase calculator, scheduler hook, kernel hint plumbing, KV compact prefetch implementation, unit tests, perf harness + benchmark results, docs for flags.

Files changed (high-level):
- runtime/emitter/phase_calculator.rs: new logic for per-stream phase and window timers
- runtime/scheduler/batch_planner.rs: uses kernel boundary hints to form kernel groups
- runtime/kernel/metadata.rs: adds boundary hint API
- runtime/kv/compact_prefetch.rs: new compact prefetch implementation and small LRU summaries
- runtime/executor/microbatch_handoff.rs: handoff path and low-overhead signaling
- tests/unit/emit_align_tests.rs
- docs/flags/emit_align.md (docs + quick tuning guide)

Benchmarks:
- Local perf-harness run on p3dn (48GB) using chat-bench scenario (avg prompt length 80 tokens, mean response 32 tokens)
- Results: median TTFB down 18% (from 28ms→23ms), P95 TTFB down 33% (from 94ms→63ms) on mixed workload; small throughput regression (<2%) at very high concurrency due to slightly increased batching wait; KV compaction reduced cold-stream tail spikes by ~45% in targeted long-conversation tests.

Backwards compatibility: no API changes. Feature gated and off by default for safety in production.

Rollout plan:
1) land behind flags, internal canary on dedicated infra
2) enable compact_prefetch on low-traffic regions
3) widen kernel-alignment flag after 2 weeks of monitoring.

Reviewer notes & discussion (excerpted, chronological):
- Marco: "Nice approach. Please document how this interacts with existing prefix caching and the KV evictor."
- Author: "Added section in docs/flags explaining interaction: compact_prefetch only reads summary-based ranges and will not evict; full rehydrate still happens for full-checkpoint restores."
- Priya: "Concern: how do we avoid a pathological case where all streams align and create enormous kernels?"
- Author: "We cap group sizes by kernel_target_size and introduce fair scheduling heuristics; added unit test to simulate alignment storms."
- Noah: "Can we get an opt-in metric for held-milliseconds per stream for SLO monitoring?"
- Author: "Added metric runtime.emit_align.hold_ms and a console dashboard note in the docs."

CI and validation:
- CI flaky on first run: lint failure fixed (trailing whitespace)
- Unit tests: all green locally and in CI after fix
- Perf harness: included microbench scripts under tools/perf/emit_align/
- CI summary: build — pass, unit-tests — pass, bench-smoke — pass, lint — pass (after 1st fix), e2e on small dedicated cluster — pass.

Merge notes:
- After reviewers approved, squashed and merged via "squash-merge" to main.
- Deploy toggles added to internal rollout script.

Related work and references:
- Related PRs on kernel grouping in the past: see ENG-2859 design notes and follow-on ENG-3412 (kernel affinity improvements).
- This PR's linear tickets: ENG-3621 (emit window feature), ENG-3679 (kv compact prefetch).

Caveats and limitations:
- Works best when median response tokens per turn > 6; for extreme sub-token responses benefit is limited.
- Small increased batching wait may slightly increase tail throughput in the highest concurrency regimes; tuned defaults optimize for latency SLOs, not raw throughput.

Checklist:
- [x] design doc attached
- [x] perf benchmarks included
- [x] unit and integration tests
- [x] docs and flags guide
- [x] metrics and dashboard notes
- [x] feature flags for safe rollout

Merge outcome: merged to main on 2025-10-06 via squash-merge.
Align emission windows with kernel batch boundaries to reduce first-byte latency; introduce lightweight KV cache compaction and prefetch hints for long-lived streams; no API changes.

payload.body:
Motivation: We frequently see run-to-run variance from cross-session interference and microburst alignment when replaying production traces. This PR adds a new runner and an associated compact reporting pipeline to (1) reproduce steady-state microbatching behavior across sessions by grouping requests with token-affinity heuristics, and (2) emit a compact delta-serialized telemetry stream suitable for long-term per-kernel occupancy analysis.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Implements a Cross-Session Affinity Microbatch Replay runner that uses a time-windowed "turnstile" packer to form microbatches across session boundaries, an adaptive jitter mechanism to avoid synchronized batching spikes, and a delta-serializer output that compresses repetitive telemetry records between iterations. The runner ships with a lightweight kernel-occupancy mapper that folds GPU-side slot attribution into compact heatmap tiles.

Design highlights and trade-offs:
- Affinity metric: token-sequence fingerprinting (fast, low-cost hash) used to prefer co-location in microbatches; this favors cache reuse but can increase cold-priming for rare prefixes.
- Turnstile window: bounded (configurable 5-50ms) to balance latency realism and batch packing rate.
- Jitter scheduler: small randomized offsets prevent pathological alignment across simultaneous session replays.
- Delta serializer: protobuf-ish compact format (binary) that stores only changed fields per-report to reduce long-run telemetry size; integrated with existing benchmark-lab reporters.
- Backpressure simulation: the runner can inject kernel-level backpressure events to exercise slow-path scheduling and observe occupancy drop/recovery.

Files changed (high level):
- benchmark-lab/runners/affinity_microbatch_run.py: new runner (core logic, config)
- benchmark-lab/packers/turnstile_packer.py: turnstile window and jitter logic
- benchmark-lab/reporters/delta_serializer.go: compact delta serialization for telemetry export (binary)
- benchmark-lab/reporters/occupancy_mapper.py: heatmap tile generator and per-kernel slot attribution
- benchmark-lab/tests/test_affinity_replay.py: unit + integration tests for deterministic replay modes
- benchmark-lab/configs/affinity-defaults.yaml: default knobs for experiments
- docs/benchmarks/affinity-runbook.md: how to run and interpret outputs

Testing and validation performed:
- Unit tests: packer/jitter/serializer correctness vectors added.
- Local integration: replayed a 30k-session production-derived trace in local-mini-cluster and validated no regressions in runner liveness.
- Perf baseline: compared legacy single-session replayer vs new cross-session microbatch on an rtx-8x node with a representative multi-tenant trace: p95 latency decreased 12% under sustained load; mean GPU active time improved by ~8%; telemetry payloads reduced by ~65% storage when using delta-serializer on 1M events.
- Stability: exercised runner for 24h continuous run with periodic backpressure injections — no memory leaks, KV cache hit rate stable.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implement runner and packer
- [x] Add deterministic unit and integration tests
- [x] Add basic docs and runbook
- [x] Add CI bench job that validates smoke metrics
- [x] Wire up delta-serializer to existing reporters
- [x] Performance measurements recorded and attached

How to run (quick): 
1) python -m benchmark_lab.runners.affinity_microbatch_run --trace traces/prod-30k.json --config configs/affinity-defaults.yaml --emit=delta_stream.bin
2) go run benchmark-lab/reporters/delta_serializer.go decode --in delta_stream.bin --out decoded/ --compact-heatmap=decoded/heatmap.tgz
3) Use docs/benchmarks/affinity-runbook.md to interpret heatmap tiles and per-kernel slot traces.

Open items / follow-ups: 
- Integrate delta-serializer as a sink for long-term S3 archival with a CLI tool for index creation (ENG-1350).
- Tune affinity hashing for longer prefix reuse; could be gated behind a config knob for high-variance workloads.

Why this is different: Existing runners primarily replay within single-session or simple interleaving; this PR explicitly targets cross-session microbatching effects and provides a space-efficient telemetry export designed for long-running baseline collection, making it practical to keep high-fidelity per-kernel occupancy history for regression detection.
