feat(packer): implement turnstile window and jitter scheduler
feat(report): add delta-serializer (binary compact) and occupancy mapper
test: add deterministic replay tests and integration smoke bench
docs: runbook and example configs
perf: tune packer thresholds and serialization framing
Evan Chen: Can you make the affinity hashing pluggable? Some traces may benefit from token-weighted fingerprints.
Priya (author): Good call — added a simple hashing interface and a default implementation; added tests to verify swap-in.
Aisha Raman: The jitter parameters look potentially risky for latency-sensitive experiments; can we make it opt-in per config?
Priya: Jitter is configurable (defaults small); docs updated to call out when to disable.
Tomás López: CI bench flaked once on memory pressure; suggested adding a small heap assertion after long runs.
Priya: Added a regression test that asserts resident size growth and re-ran 24h smoke locally.
Approvals: Evan Chen — approved, Aisha Raman — approved after changes, Tomás López — approved.

Introduce cross-session affinity microbatch replay runner and compact delta serializer. Adds a new toolset for reproducing microbatch alignment and generating compressed per-kernel occupancy telemetry for long-term regression tracking. Performance: reduced p95 by ~12% in representative runs and decreased telemetry storage by ~65% on sampled workloads.
Backfill: Run the new runner on the nightly workload-capture job for 7 days to create occupancy baselines before enabling automatic alerts tied to occupancy regressions. See ENG-1284 for rollout plan.

payload.body:
Motivation: we need a low-overhead harness to (1) reproduce cold-start micro-latency artifacts seen in noisy multi-tenant clusters and (2) tie those artifacts to per-kernel execution signatures across GPU families. This PR introduces two components: a lightweight 'ghost-runner' that injects deterministic, intermittent coldstart-like sequences into existing workload traces, and a kernel fingerprint reconciler that captures compact kernel execution signatures for later offline correlation.

What this changes: ghost-runner: a user-space benchmark runner that can replay a subset of sequences from the benchmark corpus with configurable primer sparsity and partial KV priming. It supports: deterministic seedable replay, per-request metadata tagging (ghost=true), an option to inject micro-bursts with configurable inter-burst jitter, and a CLI to export a compact run manifest. Kernel fingerprint reconciler: a small agent that hooks into the profiler probe points and emits kernel-level fingerprints (opcode hash, duration distro summary, occupancy hint) tied to the ghost-runner manifest id. A post-processor reconciles run telemetry and kernel signatures into an epochal report used by the perf dashboards.

Backward compatibility: no changes to runtime product code paths. All instrumentation is gated behind benchmark lab flags and the reconciler runs in a sidecar/prometheus-exporter mode for offline ingestion.

How to run locally: ./bench/ghost_runner/run.sh --manifest examples/manifests/mini-ghost.json --seed 42 --primer-sparsity 0.15 --burst-size 8 --output /tmp/ghost-out.json Then: python tools/reconcile_fingerprints.py --runs /tmp/ghost-out.json --profiles /tmp/prof-*.ndjson --out /tmp/epoch-report.json

Testing and verification: added deterministic unit tests for manifest parsing, a small e2e benchmark that runs on the CI ephemeral GPU job (approx 6 minutes), and offline reconciler smoke checks that validate signature stability across two representative kernels. The CI perf-check step is configured to run on the nightly perf runner for broader time series comparison.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Small e2e bench - [x] CI integration + job config - [x] Dashboard export schema update - [x] Documentation for running and interpreting reports

Rationale and tradeoffs: We intentionally keep the ghost-runner lightweight: it emits metadata and relies on existing tracer/profiler pipelines for heavy telemetry. The reconciler produces compact signatures (not full traces) to avoid storage blowup while still enabling root-cause correlation for tail events.

Lena Horvath: Can we make the primer-sparsity parameter a fraction or absolute count? Prefer fraction for portability across manifests.
Arjun Mehta: Updated manifest schema to accept 'primer_sparsity' as float in [0,1] and added validation tests.
Diego Ramos: I observed nondeterministic seeds on the ephemeral CI; looks like thread scheduling changed ordering. Please add an explicit single-threaded replay mode.
Arjun Mehta: Added --single-threaded flag and updated CI job to run the bench under that mode for the unit e2e.
Priya Kapoor: Reconciler emits a field 'kernel_hint' that overlaps with existing profiler tags; ensure namespaced export to avoid collisions.
Arjun Mehta: Namespaced reconciler fields under 'ghost_reconciler' and updated dashboard mapping.
Initial micro-bench on T4 and A100 showed a 0.8%-2.4% p95 tail shift when ghost sequences are interleaved with steady-state traffic; reconciler signatures matched a kernel variant on older driver stacks. Nightly runs will confirm stability.
Register epoch-report exporter in perf pipeline (done)
Schedule nightly ghost-run in perf lab (ticket ENG-5401)
Add reconciler signatures to kernel-attribution index (follow-up PR)
Key files to inspect: bench/ghost_runner/main.py for replay determinism, bench/reconciler/reconciler_agent.py for fingerprint format, and ci/jobs/ephemeral-gpu-bench.yml for reproducibility in CI. The reconciler intentionally emits compact summaries; if more detail is required we should gate it behind a verbose flag.

payload.body:
Motivation: We’ve been seeing small but persistent drift between benchmark sweeps run from different runner hosts (package resolver differences, CUDA/PyTorch mismatches, minor lib updates). For the public benchmark report we need deterministic reruns (or at minimum: a fully captured environment we can replay) when data validation or Legal asks for substantiation. This PR introduces a Dockerized benchmark runner image with pinned dependencies and a small amount of metadata plumbing so each run manifest records the exact container digest + runtime versions used.

What’s in this PR: Adds a GPU-capable Docker image for benchmark-lab runners based on NVIDIA CUDA runtime, with pinned Python + pip deps, and a reproducible build process (no floating tags). Adds `requirements.lock.txt` (generated from `requirements.in`) and a build arg for CUDA minor version to support our current fleet (12.1/12.2). Adds `bench env` command to dump versions (Python, torch, transformers, CUDA, driver, kernel) and writes them into the run manifest automatically. Adds documentation in README: how to build locally, how to run on a GPU host, and how to run region sweeps via the same container.

Non-goals: This does not change benchmark logic/metrics. It does not attempt bit-for-bit determinism of kernels across driver versions; it’s about making the environment explicit and reproducible enough that reruns are comparable and explainable.

Implementation notes: Uses multi-stage build to keep image size reasonable; wheels are installed from pinned hashes where available. The runner defaults to non-root user and only mounts a working directory (no implicit access to host credentials). Adds a smoke-test GitHub Action that builds the image and runs `bench --help` plus a tiny CPU-only unit test shard to ensure packaging stays healthy.

Checklist: - [x] Image builds in CI and locally - [x] Runner prints captured env info - [x] Run manifest includes container digest + dependency versions - [x] README updated with usage + troubleshooting - [x] Confirmed no secrets/baked-in tokens - [x] Confirmed license headers for base image are referenced in NOTICE

Rollout: Once merged, Infra will update the region sweep runners to use `ghcr.io/redwoodinference/benchmark-lab-runner:<git_sha>` and pin by digest in the scheduler config. We can keep existing bare-metal instructions for now but should prefer Docker for all report-bound runs.
Example: running a sweep via Docker

  docker run --rm --gpus all \
    -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work \
    ghcr.io/redwoodinference/benchmark-lab-runner@sha256:<digest> \
    bench run --config configs/prod_mix_v3.yaml --out artifacts/run.json

Manifest now includes:
  container_image: ghcr.io/redwoodinference/benchmark-lab-runner
  container_digest: sha256:…
  env: { python: 3.11.8, torch: 2.3.1+cu121, transformers: 4.44.2, cuda_runtime: 12.1, driver: 550.54.15, … }
Claire Dubois (review): Can we guarantee the lock file is actually used in the image build (vs pip resolving at build time)? Also please clarify in README that driver versions can still impact p95.

Rina Kobayashi (author): Yep — Docker build now copies `requirements.lock.txt` and installs with `--require-hashes` where hashes are present; otherwise it pins exact versions. Added README note about driver/kernel impact and that we record driver version in the manifest.

Jonas Weber (review): Image size looks high in the build logs (~9.8GB). Can we drop dev tooling (gcc, git) from final stage? Also please add a way to print the container digest from inside the runner.

Rina Kobayashi (author): Switched to multi-stage: build wheels in builder stage, runtime stage only has Python venv + shared libs. Size down to ~4.1GB compressed in GHCR. Added `bench env` output includes `RUNNER_IMAGE_DIGEST` when present (CI injects label + env).

Omar El-Sayed (review): Any risk we bake in AWS creds via build context? Please ensure `.dockerignore` excludes local config and artifacts.

Rina Kobayashi (author): Added `.dockerignore` patterns for `.aws`, `.gcp`, `artifacts/`, `datasets/`, and common dotenv files. Build action runs in clean workspace.

Neha Kapoor (review): For fleet runners, we need a stable tag policy. Can we publish SHA tags and recommend pinning by digest in production configs?

Rina Kobayashi (author): Updated README + added note in description: publish `:<git_sha>` but recommend digest pinning for report runs. Infra can still use floating tags for dev.

Jonas Weber (follow-up): One more: can we ensure the container runs as non-root and doesn’t write outside /work?

Rina Kobayashi (author): Final stage uses `USER bench` with UID/GID set; default workdir is `/work`. Added a quick smoke test to verify uid != 0.

Result: Approved by Claire/Jonas/Omar/Neha. Squash merged.

payload.body:
Motivation: We need a compact, repeatable way to sweep throughput and batch-size configurations while preserving kernel-level signal for short (2–5s) microbench runs. Existing sweep runners produce bulky trace bundles that are slow to upload and hard to diff. This PR introduces a progressive sweepbench runner that performs stepped load ramps and a compact 'heatline' serializer that compresses per-window latency histograms and kernel-sample signatures into a small, diff-friendly artifact.

What this PR adds: 1) bench/sweep/progressive_sweepbench.py — orchestrates stepwise QPS/batch sweeps with adaptive dwell times (auto-extend for noisy tails). 2) bench/reporters/heatline_serializer.py — emits compact TSV/JSONL heatline artifacts (time window, qps, batch_size, p50/p95/p99, microkernel-hash). 3) bench/profiles/kernel_sampler.c — lightweight JNI/extension that samples GPU kernel events for 1–2ms windows and summarizes hot kernels into a stable 64-bit fingerprint. 4) docs/benchmark/sweep_playbook.md — guidance for reproducing runs and interpreting heatlines. 5) CI integration: add a smoke bench job that validates serializer output schema.

Design notes: - Progressive sweeps: rather than fixed-duration steps, the runner watches for quantile convergence and extends the dwell when p99 variance exceeds threshold. This reduces noisy measurements and produces more reliable trendlines. - Heatline format: each line encodes a window with fields [timestamp, qps, batch_size, p50, p95, p99, kernel_fingerprint, sample_count, cpu_rps]. The kernel_fingerprint is a stable hex digest derived from sorted kernel name+duration buckets; it's intentionally low-entropy to keep artifacts small while being useful for correlating hotpaths. - Compactness: the serializer supports gzip and an experimental delta-encoding mode that emits only changed lines relative to a baseline run.

Testing and validation performed: - Unit tests for serializer (schema, delta mode, roundtrip) included. - Local runs on a 4xA100 node comparing standard profiler bundles vs heatline artifacts showed >10x size reduction (avg 2.8MB vs 35MB) with preserved top-3 kernel fingerprints for each window. - Two staged CI runs: initial smoke job failed on first iteration because the kernel sampler needed a higher ulimit; fixed in commit 3.

Safety and rollout: non-breaking. Feature gated behind BENCH_HEATLINE env flag. Default behavior unchanged until flag enabled.

How to use (short): 
$ BENCH_HEATLINE=1 python -m bench.sweep.progressive_sweepbench --model gpt-j-6b --qps-start 5 --qps-end 200 --batch-sizes 1,2,4,8 --out ./runs/sweep01

Next steps / follow-ups: - Add automatic baseline diffing in the benchmark dashboard. - Wire heatline uploader to benchstore with lineage metadata.

Related: ENG-3245 (benchmark stability), ENG-3298 (kernel fingerprinting prototype).
Liam Chen: Can we avoid sampling kernel names on every window? The initial runs showed a small CPU spike.
Ava Patel: We sample at 1–2ms per-window and aggregate; CPU overhead is ~1–2%. I've added README notes and the sampler uses eBPF filter + adaptive duty cycle.
Sofia Ramirez: Need clearer guidance on when to extend dwell. "We should avoid overextending for noisy GPUs."
Ava Patel: Added CLI flags --max-extend-seconds and --variance-threshold and defaults tuned from lab runs.
Noah Green: Approved after the ulimit fix and smaller test matrix in CI.

Motivation: We've observed non-deterministic p95/p99 spikes in a subset of long-running throughput benchmarks that correlate with kernel-level contention and uneven warmup behavior across workers. This PR introduces two complementary components: (1) KernelTide — a contention visualizer that aggregates per-kernel occupancy, stall-reasons and scheduling collisions into time-aligned heatmaps and compact contention-curves; (2) ProbabilisticWarmupCoordinator — a controller that runs randomized preflight primer passes across cohorts to probabilistically cover different KV cache and memory-placement states before measurement windows.

What this PR does (summary): Adds a lightweight sampling probe that annotates kernel events in the benchmark worker (Linux perf + runtime hooks), a postprocessor that synthesizes per-request kernel timelines into a compact parquet-friendly schema, an interactive visualizer (static HTML + JS) for heatmaps and contour plots, and a coordinator that schedules warmup primers with configurable coverage confidence and early-stop heuristics. Integrates with existing bench orchestration and the CI regression pipeline so nightly runs produce kernel-contour artifacts and the stable-run coordinator reduces variance for p95/p99 assertions.

Why this is different: Existing tools produce flamegraphs and token-latency histograms, but none expose the time-correlated kernel-contention signal mapped back to sequence phase and KV-cache state. KernelTide surfaces short-lived contention modes that cause ephemeral long-tail spikes. The ProbabilisticWarmupCoordinator reduces false-positive regressions by ensuring a statistically representative warmup set prior to capture windows.

Compatibility and runbook: Backwards compatible with existing bench manifests. To opt-in add "kerneltide: true" to a workload stanza; warmup coordinator config is optional and defaults to conservative settings. New artifacts are stored under artifacts/kerneltide/{run_id} with a _contours.parquet file and an index.json. README includes visualization usage and troubleshooting steps.

Notes on measurement: We ran the stability suite against a 16-node mini-cluster (mixed A100/V100) with synthetic seq-mix and real prompt traces; KernelTide flagged a scheduler thrash on one node that correlated with a p99 increase of ~18%. After applying the coordinator, p99 variance decreased 34% across 30 runs. Full benchmark logs and the reproduce script are attached in the PR files.

Related: ENG-8342 (noise reduction workstream), ENG-8401 (observability exports), SUP-231 (customer incident that prompted deeper per-kernel analysis).
Add KernelTide visualizer (per-kernel contention curves and heatmaps) and probabilistic warmup coordinator to reduce noisy tail variance in long-running benchmarks. Exposes parquet export for downstream analysis and hooks into baseline regression checks.

Riley: Add schema versioning to parquet output — author: added schema version and compatibility tests (see exporters/parquet/kernel_contours_schema.py).
Maeve: Need clearer runbook for opting-in and disk retention — author: expanded README and set default retention to 7 days behind a feature flag.
Kenji: Approve after two small nits fixed — reviewer approved.

payload.body:
Motivation: Our existing reporters capture latency quantiles and heatmaps but store large traces or coarse aggregates that make long-term trend analysis and root-cause attribution expensive. This PR introduces a sampled epochal latency atlas (compact, per-epoch histograms with context stratification) plus a top-k hotpath detector that extracts the most impactful kernel/token paths contributing to long-tail latency. The design aims to keep storage and ingest cost low while preserving signal required for regression detection and debugging.

Design summary: The atlas reporter samples requests at configurable epoch intervals (epoch == N requests or fixed time windows) and records a small number (configurable M) of per-epoch items: a compact 64-bin quantile histogram keyed by (model_family, sequence_length_bucket, batch_size_bucket), an optional flamepoint signature (top token n-gram fingerprint), and a lightweight kernel-attribution vector (per-kernel busy-time fraction for the sampled request). Samples are serialized to a columnar parquet-like compact proto and uploaded to the telemetry sink. The top-k hotpath detector consumes the atlas stream and runs a sliding-window aggregation that scores (kernel_combination, token_fingerprint) tuples by their incremental contribution to the tail (p95+/p999). Outputs are TopK reports and concise flame-snapshots suitable for on-call triage.

Why sampling: Full-trace capture is too expensive at production scale. We focused on controlled probabilistic sampling with stratification so that rare long-tail patterns are still discoverable while keeping sustained storage under existing telemetry budgets. There are knobs for sample rate, epoch size, and sequence-length stratification.

Testing and validation: Added a new benchmark suite (benchmarks/atlas_fidelity_suite) that replays representative sessions (short chat, long completion, multi-turn) and compares atlas-derived quantiles against ground-truth full-trace quantiles. The suite runs locally in CI as a smoke fidelity check and in the lab as a heavier regression test. Perf impact on the serving host was measured: sampling at 0.5% adds ~0.6ms mean CPU per request and negligible memory pressure.

Rollout plan: Feature gate turned on by default in bench clusters only. After one week of monitoring for ingestion stability and tail-detection false positives, we'll enable generation for nightly historical runs. Operator docs and dashboard tiles are included in this PR.

Notes: The description below includes commits and a short review thread. All code paths have unit tests and a small end-to-end integration test that runs the atlas reporter against a synthetic runner.

- Add sampled epochal latency atlas reporter for compact distribution storage and visualization
- Add top-k hotpath detector to identify kernel+token hotspots contributing to p99/p999
- New example workloads and e2e benchmark to validate sampling fidelity vs storage cost
Evan Brooks: Nice design. Two questions: (1) how do we guarantee sample representativeness across long sessions? (2) please quantify storage overhead for a 30-day retention at 0.5% sampling.
Author (Maya Chen): For long sessions we stratify by sequence_length_bucket and epoch boundaries; long sessions typically span multiple epochs so they get sampled proportionally. Storage estimate: at 0.5% sampling, our synthetic replay projects ~12GB/month for the entire lab fleet (detailed numbers in docs/benchmarks/atlas.md).
Priya Nair: The scoring function in topk_hotpath looks expensive in the worst case. Can we cap cardinality? Consider approximate heavy-hitter sketch first and exact top-k only for candidates.
Author (Maya Chen): Good call. Implemented a two-stage pipeline: lightweight Count-Min sketch for candidate selection, then exact Top-K on the candidate set. Benchmarks in the commits show sketch reduces memory by ~10x with negligible recall loss.
Daniel Ortiz: Tests look good; CI initially failed linting in epochal_atlas.py -> fixed. Also flagged a missing metric export for sample_rate; added atlas_metrics.py to expose sample_rate, sample_count, and drop_count.
Evan Brooks: Approved after sketch change and docs updates.
Initial pipeline: lint failed (flake8: line-length in epochal_atlas.py) -> fixed. Unit tests: pass. Integration atlas smoke job: pass after increasing test timeout to account for synthetic replay. Performance lab run: pass; fidelity suite shows atlas quantiles within 2% of full-trace p95/p99 for benchmark workloads at 0.5% sample rate.
Operators: config knobs are benchmark_lab.atlas.sample_rate, epoch_size, sequence_length_buckets, topk.window_seconds
Storage format: compact parquet-like proto (see protos/atlas.proto) with columnar-friendly fields to support fast ingestion
Future work: integrate atlas-backed alerting for p99 drift and couple with Optimize to suggest sampling adjustments

Context & motivation: We observe noisy p95/p99 tails in mixed-length session replays where short and long sequences interleave. Root cause analysis shows suboptimal token-level scheduling and premature KV cache evictions when boundary alignment is poor. This PR introduces two cooperating components: (1) a Token Flow Orchestrator that proactively groups in-flight requests by soft token window and preferred kernel occupancy, and (2) a Sequence Boundary Reconciler that applies lightweight heuristics to maintain primer continuity and avoid unnecessary KV cache churn.

Design summary: The orchestrator maintains a tiny, per-worker token-slot map and a scheduler that assigns arriving requests into micro-batches constrained by a token-window score (priming affinity, recent kernel selection). The reconciler runs as a short-lived pass before batching to realign primers across requests from the same logical session and to optionally stall short requests for up to a configurable ms threshold to allow better coalescing. Both features are guarded by feature flags and incremental config knobs so rollout is safe.

Commits (high-level):

- Add boundary_reconciler module with primer-aware heuristics and unit tests
- Integrate orchestrator into bench-runner main path behind flag
- Add telemetry hooks: per-window occupancy, coalesce_ratio, primer_hit_rate
- Add e2e microbench scenario and new golden baseline for mixed-length sequences
- Fix race in kv_cache warmup path exposed by staging tests

Changed areas / files (high-level):

Performance validation: Local microbench runs (staging cluster) show a median p95 improvement of 8-12% and p99 improvement of 7-15% for our synthetic mixed-length session workload at 32-concurrency. Memory overhead is small (~2-3% extra RSS) due to the per-worker token-slot map.

Rollout plan: Feature-gated; default off. We will enable in canary by job bench/canary-mixed-merge, monitor metrics token_flow.coalesce_ratio, primer_hit_rate, and bench baseline deltas for 48 hours before gradual ramp.

Backward compatibility: No breaking changes; all API/runner configs are additive and behind flags.

Additional context: This PR is intended to be a pragmatic middle ground between aggressive batching (which severely increases latency for short sessions) and naive per-request scheduling. It should reduce tail variance in multi-modal workloads and serve as a building block for future kernel-aware batch placement work.

payload.body:
Motivation: We frequently see production microbursts with varying amplitude (requests per second per tenant) that expose different kernel hotspots and scheduler contention compared to steady-state or single-amplitude bursts. Existing synthesizers in the benchlab cover sequence mix and temporal bursts but do not explicitly model amplitude variation across short epochs. This PR introduces an amplitude-aware burst fuzz workload generator and a lightweight kernel sampler that captures per-burst kernel execution profiles. The goal is to provide a representative, easy-to-run harness that surfaces scheduling regressions and kernel hotspots that only appear when burst amplitude varies within an epoch.

What this change does: Adds two new components under benchlab/runner: (1) amplitude_burst_fuzzer: a workload runner that generates epochs of bursts where each epoch has randomized amplitude envelopes (triangular, plateau, spike) with configurable intra- and inter-epoch jitter, sequence-length distributions, and optional KV-cache priming. (2) kernel_sampler: a synchronous sampler that inserts short trace probes to collect per-kernel aggregated metrics (time, samples, p95, p99) tied to burst ids and relative amplitude. Also adds burst_level_reporter: post-run pipeline that aggregates token-level latency into burst-aligned quantiles and amplitude histograms and produces a small JSON summary and a flamepoint CSV for interactive flamegraphs.

Checklist implemented: - [x] amplitude_burst_fuzzer CLI and Python API with configurable profiles and JSON config files - [x] kernel_sampler lightweight probe using existing benchlab tracing hooks (no runtime-internal changes) - [x] burst_level_reporter that emits per-epoch p50/p95/p99 + amplitude histogram and kernel flamepoint CSV - [x] unit + integration tests (fast-mode) and a longer local smoke test script - [x] docs/quickstart example and a README describing recommended knobs for reproducing production bursts - [x] CI jobs added to run linter, unit tests, and short bench smoke on PRs

How to run locally: 1) pip install -e benchlab 2) python -m benchlab.runner.amplitude_burst_fuzzer --config examples/amplitude_profiles/spike_plateau.json --out /tmp/run.json --sample-kernel true 3) python -m benchlab.reporters.burst_level_reporter --input /tmp/run.json --out /tmp/summary.json --flame /tmp/flamepoints.csv

Key design notes: - The fuzzer intentionally correlates amplitude envelopes with sequence-length distributions to reproduce real-world patterns where long requests cluster during high-amplitude periods. - kernel_sampler samples at burst boundaries and during peak windows to avoid excessive overhead; sampling rate is configurable. - Reporter keeps output compact (one JSON per run + CSV flamepoints) so it can be archived in S3 and consumed by existing dashboarding scripts.

Observations from internal runs: On our 8-GPU cluster profile, a mixed amplitude profile increased the p99 of token generation by ~18% compared to a static amplitude run with the same total QPS, and kernel_sampler identified a single attention kernel path that accounted for 42% of added tail time during spikes. These findings are recorded in the example run outputs included in this PR.

Related: ENG-2741 (burst analysis), ENG-3110 (kernel hotpath triage).
Aisha Patel: Can you add a guard so sampling is disabled for runs where total qps < 1? Sampling caused flakiness in small CI runs.
Diego Marquez: Good catch — added a guard and a unit test (see fix commit).

Motivation: Long-running sequence workloads show phase-locality (repeated token patterns and KV cache hotpaths) which our current batcher treats uniformly. This PR introduces a small runtime shim (SeqPhase affinity splitter) that tags requests with a lightweight phase fingerprint and routes them to device pools optimized for their phase characteristics, reducing cache churn and avoiding cross-phase interference. In parallel, the PR adds a compact telemetry encoder to reduce trace payload sizes from the bench harness and reporting pipeline, lowering upload bandwidth and storage costs for long experiment runs.

Design summary: The change has three parts in one cohesive patch: 1) a splitter component in the workload runner that computes a 64-bit phase hash based on n-gram token windows and recent sequence boundary markers, plus a scoring heuristic to decide affinity buckets; 2) a device-pool policy extension so the runner can express affinity hints (prefer_same_phase / prefer_diverse) to the scheduler; 3) a compact telemetry encoder that packs event streams with delta-encoded timestamps, token-delta compression, and optional zstd-lite compression for large traces. The encoder is pluggable and defaults to no compression for interactive runs.

What I changed (high-level): Added a new workload runner variant (seqphase-runner) and a reporter pipeline stage (compact-telemetry-encoder). Introduced an internal API surface for phase fingerprints and affinity metadata that is intentionally minimal (two fields on the request envelope) to keep compatibility with existing schedulers. Updated the benchmark harness to exercise heterogeneous device pools (GPU/CPU mix) and added golden test vectors for the phase hash to ensure determinism across languages. Updated docs and examples to show how to opt into affinity routing and telemetry compression.

Checklist: - [x] Runtime shim implemented and unit-tested - [x] Integration tests with multi-pool scheduling - [x] Telemetry encoder unit tests and roundtrip verification - [x] Bench runs on small and medium clusters (results attached) - [x] Docs and examples updated - [x] Security and privacy review for fingerprinting heuristic (no user PII used)

Testing and results: I ran the full benchmark suite on a 4-node GPU test cluster and compared baseline runner vs seqphase-runner across three representative workloads (chatty short-turns, long-coherent completions, mixed-burst). Results (median of 10 runs): - Chatty short-turns: p50 latency unchanged, p95 reduced by 12% (less KV cache eviction) - Long-coherent completions: throughput +6% (more stable KV reuse), p95 tail slightly improved - Mixed-burst: p95 reduced by 18%, sustained throughput +9% Telemetry bandwidth: compact encoder reduced average trace payload size by 4.1x and archive storage by ~3.5x for long runs.

Backward compatibility: The affinity hints are optional and ignored by older schedulers. The phase fingerprint algorithm is deterministic and versioned; the runner emits a version field so older consumers can safely ignore it. The telemetry encoder is a reporter option and will not be used unless enabled in pipeline config.

Related work: This complements earlier kernel batching optimizations (see ENG-3119) and the KV cache priming patches. The fingerprint idea was prototyped in an internal spike (ENG-4388) and reviewed by the serving/runtime team.

Notes for reviewers: Focus on the deterministic properties of the phase fingerprint, the scheduler API surface (small, intentionally conservative), and the telemetry encoding format (compact but auditable). I included bench artifacts and raw traces in the attached CI artifact for reproducibility.

Motivation: benchmarking single-model synthetic workloads misses interactions that appear when live traffic mixes multiple model variants (quantized, fp16, small vs large). This PR adds a lightweight orchestrator to run heterogeneous model mix workloads, a fidelity-based sampler to reduce expensive full-profiling runs, and a cost-attribution reporter that slices latency/cost by model mix and sequence-length quantiles. Motivation: production latency tails are often driven by small transient cohorts and phased transitions; existing synthetic runners in benchmark-lab exercise steady throughput but do not faithfully reproduce cohort-driven tail amplification. This PR introduces a lightweight steady-state latency simulator plus a differential cohort sampler that can inject small cohorts with configurable lifecycle, weight, and state-transition patterns. Design highlights: 1) a steady-state detector that learns sequence length distribution and warmup plateau to avoid cold-start bias; 2) cohort sampler that supports temporal cohorts (start, lifetime, fade) and differential noise/priority profiles; 3) a compact stats pipeline that emits per-cohort p50/p95/p99 p99.9 and a small pre-aggregated bucketed histogram suitable for storage in S3; 4) deterministic seeding mode for reproducible regression runs; 5) compatibility layer so the simulator can run as a normal benchlab workload or as a microprobe from perf-canary. Checklist: [x] simulator implementation, [x] sampler logic, [x] exporter and summary CSV, [x] unit + integration tests, [x] docs and quickstart. How to run: python -m benchlab.simulators.steady_state_sim --config=benchlab/configs/cohort_smoke.yaml --seed=42; CI runs a reduced smoke and a full local sample run was executed on a ci-small-gpu pool. Results summary: using the default cohort profile we observed a reproducible p99.9 delta of +14ms when injecting a 3% high-latency cohort (baseline p99.9 210ms -> 224ms) and the sampler scales to 10k req/s with <3% overhead. This PR is intended to provide a more realistic steady-state baseline for subsequent scheduler and KV-cache mitigations and to enable targeted tail-suppression experiments.

payload.body:
Motivation: In production we observed intermittent tail regressions that correlated with sudden expansion of active keyspace driving K/V cache spill events on GPUs. Existing workload runners focus on steady-state sequence mixes or bursty arrival patterns but do not explicitly exercise the interaction between expanding keyspace, eviction churn, and CPU/GPU memory page behavior. This PR introduces two cooperating test artifacts: 1) a Keyspace Spill Prober (ksp-prober) that drives controlled, configurable keyspace expansion and spill pressure against the serving runtime, and 2) a Fidelity-Aware Replayer that records traces from a target cluster and replays them while injecting spill events to measure metric sensitivity and identify thresholds where quality or latency regress.

Design/Implementation: - ksp-prober: Go binary under benchmark-lab/cmd/ksp-prober. Generates sequences with a parameterized key cardinality curve (linear, exponential, and randomized ramps) and per-sequence eviction hints. The prober supports three modes: dry-run (no model calls, validates traffic shaping), sampling (periodic short requests with real model calls), and saturate (sustained ramp until eviction rate stabilizes). It exposes a small HTTP admin port for health and dynamic parameter adjustments. - fidelity-replayer: Python tool under benchmark-lab/tools/fidelity_replayer.py. Consumes existing trace exports (protobuf or ndjson), attaches synthetic KV keys to tokens via a configurable hash function, and replays the traffic against an instrumented endpoint while toggling explicit cache-seed/evict calls (simulated via SDK hooks). The replayer collects token-level latencies, eviction counts, model output deltas (via deterministic prompt hashing), and anomaly markers. - Telemetry & reporting: Adds a new exporter plugin (benchmark-lab/exporters/kv_spill_reporter) which emits per-epoch CSV/JSON that include: epoch_start, epoch_end, active_keyspace_size, eviction_rate, p50/p95/p99 gen latency, token-invalidation-count, and output-regression-score. The reporter is designed to be consumed by existing bench dashboards.

Test Plan and Baseline Results: - Added unit tests for simulation curves and admin API (Go: 3 new tests). - Integration tests run in CI using a containerized runtime image (lightweight LLM shim) to validate end-to-end replay mechanics. - Local experiments on a staged cluster: exponential ramp to 2x active keyspace produced a median eviction increase from 0.3/s to 4.1/s and p95 latency degradation of ~18% in the saturate mode; in sampling mode the fidelity-replayer detected output delta > 0.02 (cosine similarity drop) when eviction_rate > 2.2/s for the small RAG-like prompt set used.

Commits Summary: - feat(ksp-prober): initial Prober CLI with linear/exp/random ramp models
- feat(fidelity-replayer): trace ingestion + synthetic key attachment + SDK replay hooks
- feat(exporter): kv_spill_reporter with CSV/JSON outputs
- test: unit tests and lightweight integration job

Motivation: Private installations running in multi-region VPCs need deterministic, auditable wiring of audit-log export sinks per jurisdiction and a reconciler that is safe to re-run during installer upgrades and rollbacks. Current behaviour relied on imperative hooks in the installer which caused drift when upgrades failed mid-flight and made it difficult to guarantee retention policies in cross-region setups. This PR introduces a jurisdiction-aware sink orchestration controller and wiring hooks for the private installer + Terraform modules so audit sinks are created and reconciled idempotently.

Summary of changes: 1) Add a small long-running reconciler (go controller) that watches AuditSink CRs and desired sink mapping from the installer; it performs create/update/delete with strong idempotency guarantees and emits detailed audit events (sink-reconciler.* metrics). 2) Extend terraform modules with new outputs and lifecycle-driven hooks so the private-installer can emit a desired-state manifest into the cluster (terraform/modules/audit_sink/*). 3) Helm chart changes: templates now include jurisdiction labels, retention annotations, and optional lifecycle hooks to defer reconciliation until KMS/secret rotation completes. 4) Installer: on the private-installer side we add a declarative sink-write step that applies the desired-state manifest and waits for the reconciler to report success; this replaces the previous ad-hoc shell provisioning. 5) Tests and e2e: add deterministic e2e that simulates mid-upgrade failures and validates rollback idempotency and retention enforcement.

Checklist: - [x] Controller implemented with retries and backoff, idempotent create/update path - [x] Terraform module hooks and docs added - [x] Helm templates updated for jurisdiction and retention annotations - [x] Installer wiring uses desired-state manifest for reconciliation - [x] Unit + e2e tests added and passing - [x] tfsec and helm linting addressed (one warning suppressed with justification)

Deployment notes: - This is backward compatible: the reconciler will adopt existing sinks by matching labels, so rollout can be done with a simple Canary (deploy reconciler -> enable terraform desired-state output -> flip installer to use manifest). - For air-gapped installs the reconciler image is included in the private registry bundle; ensure registry credentials are present prior to enabling the controller. - KMS-backed sinks: reconciler respects annotated kms_key_ref and will wait for secret readiness before finalizing sink wiring.

Rollback behavior: the reconciler is intentionally conservative: on deletion it removes only sink resources it created or owns (ownerReferences + managed-by label). If an installer rollback is triggered mid-upgrade, re-running the installer applies the same desired-state manifest and the reconciler converges back to the prior state without orphaning temporary resources.

Related work and references: Linear tickets ENG-2147 and ENG-2153 track the reconciler and terraform integrations. See internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/board/ENG-2147/jurisdictional-sink-orchestration and runbook: docs/private/audit-sink-orchestrator.md

Why this is different from previous PRs: previous changes focused on retention lifecycles and sink rotation; this change focuses on making sink wiring declarative and upgrade/rollback safe at the installer and terraform boundaries so compliance operators can guarantee retention and export topology after any control-plane operation.

payload.body:
Summary: This PR introduces a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for audit export batches that fail delivery after exhausting retries, and adds an operator-facing replay tool with guardrails. This is a reliability/safety feature for the SIEM-ready audit export beta (Splunk HEC / Datadog Logs / S3) to ensure we never silently drop events while still protecting the platform and customers from accidental replay storms. Context / Motivation: During downstream outages (e.g., sustained 429s from Splunk HEC or 403s from mis-scoped Datadog keys), the exporter currently retries with backoff and then surfaces a per-destination error. Without DLQ persistence we risk either (a) losing batches on process/queue churn or (b) having no safe operational path to replay specific failures once a customer fixes credentials/quotas. ENG-5164 calls for a DLQ + replay tooling with explicit operator controls. Design highlights: (1) DLQ record model: When a batch hits max_delivery_attempts OR we detect a non-retryable adapter error, we persist a DLQ record keyed by (tenant_id, export_config_id, checkpoint_range) and store the batch payload (newline-delimited JSON events) in object storage under a structured prefix. DLQ record includes: dlq_id, created_at, tenant_id, export_config_id, destination_type, reason_code, reason_detail (redacted), first_event_ts, last_event_ts, event_count, byte_size, last_attempt_at, attempt_count, and a payload_ref. (2) At-least-once compatibility: Replays may cause duplicate deliveries. We intentionally do not attempt exactly-once; downstream should dedup using event_id (per ADR on delivery semantics). Replay CLI logs a reminder and requires an explicit --ack-duplicates flag. (3) Operator replay CLI: Adds bin/audit-exporter-replay (Go) to list DLQ items and replay in a controlled fashion. Guardrails include: required --tenant-id and --export-config-id; default is dry-run; interactive confirmation unless --yes is provided; bounded selection via --since/--until and --max-items; token-bucket rate limiting (--max-events-per-minute) to avoid spiking adapters; refuses to replay if export config is disabled OR if exporter feature flag is off for that tenant (unless --override-feature-flag is provided, which is restricted to on-call breakglass role). (4) Safety checks: Replay validates destination configuration hash matches the DLQ record by default (prevents replaying old payloads into a newly re-pointed sink). Can be overridden with --ignore-config-hash-mismatch for incident response, but emits a prominent warning. (5) Redaction: DLQ reason_detail is run through the same redaction helper used by adapter logs to avoid accidentally persisting tokens/keys/PII. Payloads contain audit events only (already subject to audit schema/PII policy); we do not include request/response bodies. (6) Observability: Adds metrics: audit_exporter_dlq_enqueued_total{tenant_id_hash,destination_type,reason_code}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_items{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_events{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_replay_total{result}, and audit_exporter_dlq_replay_latency_seconds. Also adds structured logs for DLQ enqueue and replay runs (with correlation_id). User-visible / Ops workflow: - When an adapter can’t deliver a batch and we exceed retry limits, exporter transitions the batch to DLQ and advances the live pipeline checkpoint to prevent system-wide backpressure. - On-call or Support can instruct customer to fix auth/limits, then run replay for the impacted tenant/config/time window. - Replay is incremental and rate-limited; any failures during replay are re-DLQ’d with a new reason_code (replay_failed_*). Example commands: - List backlog: ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq list --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --until 2025-02-09T06:00:00Z - Dry-run replay (default): ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq replay --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --max-items 10 - Execute replay with explicit acknowledgements: ./bin/audit-exporter-replay dlq replay --tenant-id tnt_123 --export-config-id aex_456 --since 2025-02-09T00:00:00Z --max-items 50 --max-events-per-minute 12000 --ack-duplicates --yes Testing: - Unit tests for DLQ persistence, reason_code mapping, and redaction - Integration tests using adapter stubs: force 429/403/non-retryable to verify DLQ enqueue and payload roundtrip - Manual: replayed a synthetic backlog into Splunk stub with rate limiting and verified dedup by event_id Related: - Linear: ENG-5164 - ADR: delivery semantics and idempotency (at-least-once + event_id) - Support context: SUP-18531 (perceived missing events during throttling) Notes / Follow-ups: - Dashboard panels/alerts for DLQ backlog are tracked separately (we add metrics here, panels in observability-pack). - For beta, replay CLI is intended for on-call / SRE / Support escalation only; we are not exposing self-serve replay in Console.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Can we confirm advancing the live checkpoint after DLQ enqueue won’t violate at-least-once? If we advance, aren’t we skipping events? Diego Santos (author): We’re not skipping generation; we’re persisting the batch payload + checkpoint range and treating replay as the at-least-once path. Without advancing, a stuck tenant can backpressure worker resources and starve other tenants. This matches ADR guidance: preserve payload, allow replay, accept duplicates. Marcus Lin (Security): Please ensure DLQ reason_detail doesn’t store adapter error blobs that may include tokens. Also confirm payload only contains audit events (no request bodies). Diego: Added redaction on reason_detail and a unit test that simulates Splunk error strings containing 'Authorization: Splunk <token>' and verifies it is redacted. Payload is the normalized audit event schema only; no HTTP request/response is serialized. Hanae Suzuki (Secrets/KMS): Where are DLQ payloads encrypted? Diego: Uses existing object storage client with SSE-KMS enabled in beta environments; added config validation to refuse startup if DLQ payload store is configured without encryption in hosted/dedicated. Aisha Bello (SRE): CLI needs stronger guardrails. Can we require --ack-duplicates and make dry-run default? Also add a cap to prevent replaying >N events unless explicitly set. Diego: Updated CLI: dry-run is default; execution requires both --ack-duplicates and --yes; added --max-items default 100 and hard cap 10k unless --breakglass is used. Logan Wright (Telemetry): Metrics label cardinality: do not label by raw tenant_id. Diego: Updated to tenant_id_hash and destination_type/reason_code only. Added note in docs about support workflow for identifying tenant via internal tooling. Approvals: Sean approved after guardrails changes; Marcus approved after redaction changes; Hanae approved after encryption validation; Logan approved after label change.
Exporter now persists terminal delivery failures to a dead-letter queue and provides an operator replay CLI with safety guardrails (beta feature; intended for on-call/support use).
payload.title: Add dead-letter queue + guarded replay CLI for failed export batches

Motivation: Private deployments need finer-grained retention and export controls for tenant audit streams so compliance teams can place tenant data into different archival tiers and lifecycle policies. This PR implements dynamic tenant-level routing for the audit-log-exporter, adds Terraform modules to provision S3 lifecycle policies and cross-account roles, and updates the Helm chart to include pre-upgrade snapshot hooks and a conservative rollback path. Summary of changes: 1) Runtime: introduce a pluggable routing layer that inspects tenant metadata and routes audit events to either existing sinks or to per-tenant S3 buckets; supports regex-based tenant selectors and a default fallback sink. 2) Terraform: new module redwood_audit_bucket with lifecycle_rule and policy templates for infrequent access transition and 365/90/30-day retention presets; creates an IAM role with assume-role trust for the exporter service. 3) Helm: values schema extended with tenantRouting and lifecyclePolicy sections; a pre-upgrade Job is added to snapshot in-flight offsets to a PVC and an annotation that enables rolling back to the previous chart with minimal data loss. 4) Private installer: installer manifest generator gains a new auditBuckets mapping and KMSKeyRef wiring; on-prem package supports filesystem archival sink alongside S3. 5) Migration scripts: provided scripts/terraform-to-helm-migration.sh that converts existing terraform bucket configs into Helm values for clusters that are migrated from Dedicated/Terraform-managed infra to a Helm-managed Private install. 6) Tests & CI: added integration tests that spin up a minio instance and exercise routing, lifecycle transitions, and restore from snapshots. Rollout plan and safety: feature guarded behind a feature flag (AUDIT_ROUTER_V2) and defaulted off for existing private installs. The PR includes a straightforward rollback plan (disable flag, redeploy previous chart, run restore job that replays buffered events from PVC or S3). Also documents KMS key rotation considerations and an automated secrets sync hook for cross-account role credentials. Backwards compatibility: default behavior remains unchanged when tenantRouting is unset. Compliance notes: per-tenant retention is auditable via emitted metrics and structured events; Terraform module emits audit trail tags. See linked Linear tasks for scope and migration coordination.

Context and motivation: On many post-incident reviews we see runbooks that are either stale (steps in wrong order), over-verbose (too many low-value probes), or brittle (expensive probes executed too early). This PR adds a small, production-safe system that proposes ephemeral runbook reorderings and probe prioritization using only short-lived telemetry windows. The goal is not to auto-modify canonical runbooks, but to produce actionable, human-reviewable suggestions and to let responders rehearse suggested flows in a sandbox before applying changes.

What this PR does (single-string description): - Adds a lightweight runbook tuner that ingests the last 30 minutes of relevant telemetry (traces, p95 latencies, error spikes, alerts) and scores each runbook step for: expected time-to-signal, evidence-value (how often the probe returns a decisive signal), and cost (estimated resource impact). - Produces a ranked suggestion list and a compact alternative runbook (ephemeral) that reorders high-value quick probes first, defers noisy/expensive probes to later, and inserts safety-checks for destructive remediations. - Exposes a /v1/sandbox/replay endpoint and a local replay harness (incident-bot/sandbox/replay_harness.py) so on-call can execute the suggested sequence against a mocked telemetry replay (no write effects) and see a summarized delta vs the canonical runbook. - Adds conservative safety gates: suggestions are only generated for runbooks with >= 5 historical incidents and only when telemetry window passes a stability check (no active high-velocity noise). Feature toggles live under incident-bot.feature.ephemeral_tuner and incident-bot.sandbox.enabled.

Checklist (what's in this PR): - [x] core tuner algorithm and scoring (incident-bot/runbook/tuner.py) - [x] sandboxed replay harness and HTTP endpoint (incident-bot/sandbox/replay_harness.py, incident-bot/api/sandbox_handler.py) - [x] UI signals (compact suggestion payload only; UI-side will be in a follow-up PR) - [x] unit + integration tests for scoring and replay simulator - [x] e2e rehearsal test that runs a real incident trace through sandbox (CI flakiness noted, retried once) - [x] config flags and docs (docs/runbook-tuner.md)

Summary of commits: - 8c4a5b2: initial tuner scaffolding and schema - 2f9b12d: implement scoring heuristics and cost model - c3d7f44: sandbox replay harness + deterministic mock telemetry - 7eaf811: add safety-gates and feature flag hooks - 9b0d22e: tests and CI flakiness mitigation - b10a6cc: docs and release notes

Files changed (high level): - incident-bot/runbook/tuner.py (new) - incident-bot/runbook/score_model.py (new) - incident-bot/sandbox/replay_harness.py (new) - incident-bot/api/sandbox_handler.py (new) - incident-bot/config/feature_flags.yaml (updated) - docs/runbook-tuner.md (new) - tests/runbook/test_tuner_scoring.py (new) - tests/sandbox/test_replay_harness.py (new) - examples/sandbox/example_replay_payloads.json (new) - incident-bot/metrics/metrics_registry.py (updated) - incident-bot/ci/rehearsal_e2e.yml (updated) - incident-bot/README.md (update: quickstart for sandbox)

Design notes and safe-guards (important): - Non-destructive: ephemeral suggestions are stored only in-memory and expire after 24 hours; they never auto-apply to canonical runbooks. - Low blast radius: tuning only runs if the number of matching historical incidents >= 5 and the telemetry sample passes a simple signal/noise ratio test (implemented in tuner.is_stable_window). - Explainability: each suggestion item includes attributes {reason, evidence_count, estimated_time_saved_ms, estimated_cost_delta} so responders can quickly decide. - Human-in-the-loop: UI will show a "Run in sandbox" button; the replay harness returns a deterministic summary and an optional timeline to assist live rehearsals. - Auditable: suggestion generation events are logged to the incident-bot audit log with non-sensitive fingerprints for later review.

Testing and CI: Unit and integration tests added. One CI run initially showed a flaky e2e rehearsal test (timing-dependent); we pinned the mock time source and retried. CI: passing (build, lint, unit, integration, rehearsal-e2e). See CI notes below for the transient failure and resolution.

Review conversation (condensed single-string): - Marcus Lee (reviewer): "Nice work — can we make the stability check stricter? I've seen windows that look stable but are actually churned by infra restarts." Aisha: "Agree, bumped the default threshold and exposed it as incident-bot.tuner.stability_threshold (0.7 -> 0.85) and added an integration test that simulates infra restarts." - Evelyn Chen: "How do we prevent suggestions from being noisy for small teams?" Aisha: "Added a min-historical-incidents config (default 5) and a rate limiter (max 1 suggestion per runbook per 24h)." - Rohit Singh: "Make sure audit logs don't contain PII." Aisha: "Logs only include hashed fingerprints and non-identifying counters; added a test to validate no raw identifiers are written." - Marcus Lee (final): "LGTM after the stability threshold change and docs update" (approved).

CI status and notes: - Initial CI: one failing e2e (tests/sandbox/test_replay_harness.py) due to non-deterministic mock clock. - Fix: replace time.time() usage with injected monotonic clock in the harness and add a deterministic mock in tests. - Final CI: all checks passing (build: pass, unit: pass, integration: pass, rehearsal-e2e: pass).

Rollout plan: - Feature is behind two flags; start internal alpha (on-call team) for 2 weeks, gather feedback and adjust scoring weights. - After alpha, enable opt-in for a small set of customers in dedicated deployment via infra toggle. - Full public rollout only after UX follow-up PR (UI for reviewing suggestions) and an additional 2-week soak.

Operational metrics to watch after rollout: - suggestion_accept_rate (how often suggested order was adopted by humans) - average_time_saved_ms (estimate from tuner) - suggestion_false_positive_rate (manual rejects / suggestions) - replay_success_rate (sandbox runs that complete without errors) - incident_response_latency_90 (primary SLO to verify no regression)

Backward compatibility and config: - Defaults preserve current behavior: feature flags off, no change to canonical runbooks or existing endpoints. - All new endpoints are namespaced under /v1/sandbox and require incident-bot.sandbox.enabled=true.

Follow-ups (tracked in Linear): - ENG-2049: UI for viewing & approving suggestions - ENG-2050: Auto-snapshot suggested runbook metadata to incident timeline (opt-in) - ENG-2077: Expand evidence extractors to include logs and runbook outcome classification

Why this is different from previous work: Rather than trying to auto-edit canonical runbooks, this PR focuses on a safe, ephemeral layer that helps responders rehearse and accept improvements with low friction. The replay harness gives a deterministic, no-op rehearsal path that hasn't been in the codebase before and reduces cognitive friction when trying suggestions.

Contact and owner: Aisha Patel (author) — tuned the scoring and drove the sandbox implementation.

Adds an opt-in ephemeral runbook tuner which suggests compact runbook step orders and probe priorities based on recent telemetry; includes a sandboxed replay harness for validating suggestions before rollout. Feature is off by default and gated behind incident-bot.feature.ephemeral_tuner=true.

payload.body:
Summary: This PR adds first-pass Prometheus metrics + basic tracing + structured logging to the audit-log-exporter service. Metrics are aligned to Redwood observability naming/cardinality standards (per Allison/Logan feedback) and provide the signals needed for initial dashboards/alerts (lag, throughput, retries, adapter errors). This work is scoped to exporter-side instrumentation only; the control plane status endpoint will consume these signals via existing health paths and the observability pack dashboards will be done separately. Context: ENG-5168. Motivation: During beta soak we’ve been debugging exporter lag spikes and downstream 429/backpressure mostly via ad-hoc logs. We need stable metrics to (a) quantify export lag vs SLO, (b) separate downstream throttling from internal queueing, (c) support paging policy (page on sustained lag / hard failures, ticket on transient retries), and (d) give Support/CS a consistent way to answer “are we exporting?” Implementation details (metrics): Adds a dedicated Prometheus registry for the service and standardizes metric names under the audit exporter namespace. Key metrics: 1) redwood_audit_exporter_export_lag_seconds (gauge): computed as now() - last_successful_checkpoint_timestamp, exported per destination_type and tenant_tier only (no tenant_id/export_config_id labels). 2) redwood_audit_exporter_events_exported_total (counter): increments per event successfully handed off to an adapter (post-filtering), labels: destination_type, result=success|retryable_error|fatal_error. 3) redwood_audit_exporter_batches_exported_total (counter): increments per batch attempt, labels: destination_type, result=success|retryable_error|fatal_error, http_status_class=2xx|4xx|5xx|none (where applicable). 4) redwood_audit_exporter_batch_send_duration_seconds (histogram): adapter send latency, labels: destination_type, result; buckets tuned to cover typical HEC/Datadog/S3 behavior (including a long tail for throttling scenarios). 5) redwood_audit_exporter_retries_total (counter) and redwood_audit_exporter_retry_backoff_seconds (histogram): records retry loop activity and backoff durations. 6) redwood_audit_exporter_dlq_batches_total (counter) and redwood_audit_exporter_dlq_depth (gauge): DLQ health signals. 7) redwood_audit_exporter_config_sync_success_total / _failure_total (counters) and redwood_audit_exporter_config_sync_age_seconds (gauge): config sync observability. Notes on naming/cardinality: Per observability standards, labels avoid high-cardinality identifiers (tenant UUID, export_config_id, destination host). Those identifiers are emitted in structured logs only. destination_type is one of: splunk_hec|datadog_logs|s3. tenant_tier is derived from config (hosted|dedicated) for now; private is not expected in beta. Implementation details (tracing): Adds OpenTelemetry spans around the exporter batch lifecycle (fetch -> filter -> adapt/send -> checkpoint). Span names follow Redwood conventions: audit_exporter.fetch, audit_exporter.filter, audit_exporter.adapter.send, audit_exporter.checkpoint.write. Attributes include destination_type, batch_size_events, and retry_attempt (bounded). Trace context is propagated through internal goroutines; adapter HTTP clients now attach trace headers where applicable. Tracing is intentionally lightweight (no per-event spans) to avoid overhead and cardinality explosions. Implementation details (structured logs): Switches exporter logs to a consistent JSON structure with stable keys: service=audit-log-exporter, component=exporter|adapter|checkpoint|config_sync, destination_type, export_stream=primary, attempt, batch_id (opaque UUID), and error_kind (classification for retry/backoff policies). tenant_id/workspace_id are included only at INFO for control-plane initiated operations and at DEBUG for hot paths; by default we log export_config_id only when errors occur (to help CS/SRE triage) and we explicitly do not log payload/event bodies. Also adds log redaction safeguards for credential fields (ensures tokens/keys never render via fmt/%+v). Testing: - Unit tests for metric label validation and histogram bucket sanity. - Updated adapter tests to assert that errors are classified consistently (retryable vs fatal) and emit the right counters. - Manual: ran local harness with Splunk/Datadog stubs and confirmed metrics scrape at /metrics, spans in local collector, and logs include trace_id/span_id. Ops/rollout: Metrics are behind the existing service config flag observability.metrics_enabled (default true in staging, false in local unless explicitly enabled). Tracing is gated by OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT presence; if not set, spans are no-op. No changes to request processing semantics. Follow-ups: - Add dashboards/alerts in observability-pack (separate PR). - Revisit export_lag_seconds definition when we add per-destination checkpoint streams (currently one checkpoint per destination config). - Confirm alert thresholds with SRE once we have beta traffic baselines. Changelog/notes: No API changes. No customer-facing behavior change beyond improved operational visibility.
Allison Grant: Please avoid tenant_id/export_config_id labels; we’ve had incidents with cardinality blow-ups. destination_type + tenant_tier is fine. Also: can we align histogram buckets with our defaults (0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 30, 60)?
Caleb Johnson (author): Agreed. Removed tenant_id/export_config_id labels and moved those fields to structured logs. Updated send duration buckets to match standards and added a longer tail bucket (120s) for downstream throttling scenarios.
Logan Wright: Lag metric definition: is it last successful checkpoint time or last attempted? For SLO we care about successful delivery. Also, please make sure gauge is monotonic-increasing during outage (shouldn’t reset due to retries).
Caleb Johnson (author): Lag is based on last successful checkpoint write. It only resets on success. During downstream outage it will increase with wall time; retries do not change it.
Sean Gallagher: For paging we’ll likely alert on sustained lag + sustained failures. Can we add a per-destination “last_success_age_seconds” gauge as well? It’s easier to reason about than lag when clocks drift.
Caleb Johnson (author): Added redwood_audit_exporter_last_success_age_seconds as an alias gauge computed the same way (now - last_success_ts). We can pick whichever reads better in dashboards.
Aisha Bello: Please ensure /metrics endpoint is protected by the same internal auth as /health (or at least not exposed publicly). What’s the exposure in hosted?
Caleb Johnson (author): /metrics is served on the internal admin port only (same listener as /healthz). In k8s, it’s behind cluster network policy; no external ingress. Added a note to docs/ops/metrics.md.
Allison Grant: Structured logs: confirm we never log headers/tokens. I saw a %+v on adapter config in one place.
Caleb Johnson (author): Fixed: removed %+v on destination config; added explicit redaction wrappers and a unit test that fails if known secret keys appear in log output.
Logan Wright: Looks good. Approving once CI is green.
Logan Wright: Approved.
Sean Gallagher: Approved.

Motivation: Several customers surfaced subtle differences between Redwood's chat v1 adapter and OpenAI's /v1/chat.completions around (1) how we treat multiple stop sequences when decisions are ambiguous mid-stream, and (2) edge cases where a streaming functioncall path would emit partial tool output and then close the stream causing callers to see invalid JSON. This change introduces a stop-weighting mechanism (configurable, opt-in for now) that biases candidate stop matches based on token alignment heuristics, and hardens the streaming functioncall handshake so partial tool output is buffered and re-framed into the structured JSON envelope expected by OpenAI clients.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a stop-weighting layer in the chat param translator to reconcile multiple stop specs and prefer the longest/earliest-weighted candidate in parity with OpenAI heuristics.
- Implements a streaming stabilizer that buffers function/toolcall fragments until a complete framed JSON object or safe flush boundary is seen; this prevents truncated JSON being delivered to SDKs.
- Normalizes logprobs emitted during stop events so token probability attribution mirrors OpenAI's reported token slices (adjusts KV-cache flush timing during stop handling).
- Adds structured envelope validation with a recovery path that attempts a best-effort JSON merge for near-complete fragments (experimental, behind the feature flag).
- Exposes a new map of 2 config knobs: chatv1.stop_weight_mode ("off"|"len_bias"|"prob_bias") and streaming.tool_buffer_ms (integer, default 50ms) that customers can set per-route.

Compatibility notes: Default behavior is unchanged (stop_weight_mode=off). When teams opt into len_bias/prob_bias, some legacy prompts that relied on shortest-stop precedence may see different cut points — these are deliberate to match OpenAI parity in our internal evals. The streaming tool buffering is safe and defaulted to 50ms; we did not observe measurable latency regression in our canary tests for common seq lengths.

Testing and verification:
- Unit tests for the stop-weight matcher with 120+ crafted cases covering overlapping stops, multi-byte tokens, and role-prefixed stop sequences.
- Integration tests that spin up the chat v1 adapter + runtime streamer and run scripted toolcall sessions with deliberately fragmented outputs.
- E2E compatibility harness that compares Redwood vs OpenAI responses on 500 prompt/toolcall pairs (pass threshold: 95% parity on stop placement, 99% JSON validity).
- Canary rollout to perf-lab and 3 beta customers for 72h; telemetry shows 0.4% increase in average token latency for small responses and no increase in error-rate.

Rollout plan: Feature gated behind chatv1.experimental.stop_weighting; initial rollout via per-customer config in console with a 2-week canary followed by global opt-in default. If metrics regress >1% error-rate or JSON-MALFORMED anomalies appear, the flag will be auto-reverted.

Related work: ENG-9876 implements a related KV-cache timing fix that reduced misaligned logprobs; PM-3321 requested a customer-facing knob for stop behavior. SUP-412 tracks a customer incident that motivated the streaming JSON hardening.
Diego Morales: Can you add a short explainer in the adapter code about why len_bias reproduces OpenAI behavior?
Asha Patel: Added a detailed code comment and a link to our internal parity doc. Also added unit cases for multi-byte unicode stops.
Ruth Kim: The streaming buffer default looks fine, but please add a metric for buffered_ms to monitor in realtime.
Asha Patel: Added telemetry 'streaming.tool_buffer_ms.p95' and a dashboard tile for the canary.
Evan Zhou: CI flaked on the canary integration once, rerun fixed it — approved after green CI.
payload.title: v1/chat.completions: tolerant stop-weighting + streaming functioncall stabilization

## Summary
This PR enhances `audit-log-exporter` to support compliance/evidence workflows by adding (1) explicit time-windowed exports and (2) optional filters for actor + event types. It also introduces a small report-template layer so the compliance reporting pack can request a known preset ("last_90_days_admin_activity", "rbac_changes", etc.) without re-encoding filter logic in multiple places.

Motivation: enterprise security reviews are consistently asking for "audit logs for a defined period" and "only admin/security-relevant events". We also had a support report (SUP-3917) where customers believed exports were missing event types; part of that was unclear defaults and lack of an explicit event-type filter list in the export request.

## API changes
### New request fields (non-breaking)
- `start_time` (RFC3339, inclusive)
- `end_time` (RFC3339, exclusive)
- `actor_ids` (optional array of strings)
- `actor_types` (optional array: `user|service_account|api_key`)
- `event_types` (optional array of strings; validated against known types)
- `template_id` (optional string; mutually exclusive with providing filters directly unless `allow_override=true`)

Behavior:
- If `start_time`/`end_time` are omitted, behavior remains "export all available within retention" (existing behavior).
- If provided, exporter enforces the window at query time and re-checks in stream/iteration to avoid boundary drift.
- `event_types` is an allowlist filter; unknown types return 400 with a list of valid types.
- `actor_ids` and `actor_types` are ANDed with the time-window and event filter.

### Report templates
Adds `templates/*.yaml` defining a stable set of presets that map to filters + default time windows. Example preset:
- `rbac_changes_last_180d` -> `event_types=[rbac.role.created, rbac.role.updated, rbac.binding.created, rbac.binding.deleted]`, window=180d

Template contract:
- Templates are versioned by exporter release; template IDs are stable.
- Export response includes `applied_filters` so customers/auditors can see exactly what was used.

## Implementation notes
- Query layer updated to accept a `FilterSpec` that compiles to SQL WHERE clauses + parameter binding.
- Streaming export code now emits a header block with: `export_id`, `generated_at`, `window`, `filters`, `template_id` (if any).
- Added a canonical "known event types" registry and tests ensuring registry coverage matches the producer schema we expect.
- Pagination: time-windowed exports use `(timestamp, id)` cursor to avoid duplicates when multiple events share the same timestamp.

## Security/Compliance considerations
- Filters are validated server-side (no raw SQL fragments; strict param binding).
- `actor_ids` is limited to 200 entries to cap query size.
- Maximum export window defaults to 365 days unless `--allow-large-windows` is enabled (intended for internal GRC workflows only).
- Added explicit audit event for `audit_log.export.generated` that records: caller identity, window, filters, and bytes written.

## Testing
- Unit tests: filter compilation, RFC3339 parsing, template resolution, unknown event-type validation.
- Integration tests: seeded audit events across boundary timestamps; verifies inclusive/exclusive semantics.
- Load sanity: ran export for 90d in staging with 1.2M rows; query time stable and memory constant in streaming mode.

## Rollout
- Default behavior unchanged. Consumers can adopt templates incrementally.
- Follow-up: wire `template_id` usage into compliance report pack generator (ENG-18441) once this merges.

## Example request
`POST /v1/exports`
{
  "template_id": "rbac_changes_last_180d",
  "start_time": "2024-08-01T00:00:00Z",
  "end_time": "2025-02-01T00:00:00Z"
}

## Checklist
- [x] Backwards compatible
- [x] Tests added
- [x] Docs updated (README + examples)
- [x] Security review notes captured (filters + limits)
- [x] Added exporter-side audit event for export generation
Marcus Lin: Please confirm window semantics (inclusive/exclusive) are documented and tested, and ensure we’re not vulnerable to massive `actor_ids` payloads. Also: do we need an exporter audit event for generating an export?
Kevin Osei (author): Documented in README + added integration tests for inclusive start/exclusive end. Added max 200 actor IDs and a request size cap. Implemented `audit_log.export.generated` event emitted on successful export start (includes window/filters/template).
Olga Petrov: Template IDs need to be stable and customer-safe. Can we include the applied filters in the export output so auditors don’t have to trust our template mapping?
Kevin Osei (author): Added `applied_filters` header block (JSON) at the start of the exported artifact and also in the API response metadata. Template IDs are now validated against a registry and treated as public identifiers.
Sean Gallagher: Cursor should be deterministic. Using timestamp-only can duplicate/skip on high volume; recommend (timestamp,id) ordering and ensure we have an index. Also add guardrails for >365d windows.
Kevin Osei (author): Updated pagination to order by `(timestamp, id)` and added/verified index in migrations. Added 365d default max window with an explicit server flag for internal workflows.

Motivation: Private deployments require strict per-tenant control of where audit data flows and which events are retained or redacted. Customers asked for (1) the ability to route audit events from different tenants to different sinks (local archive, S3/GS remote archive, SIEM) and (2) a configurable, auditable sensitive-event filter that prevents PII or regulated events from leaving private networks. This PR implements tenant-aware sink routing, a policy-driven sensitive-event filter, upgrade/rollback hooks in the private installer, and accompanying Terraform/Helm changes so operators can opt into the wiring with minimal manual steps. Operators may opt-in to per-tenant routing and to filter rules via values and a managed ConfigMap. Context: Private installs in regulated regions often onboard long-running S3 sinks created before the audit-exporter reconciler existed. We saw multiple incidents where old sinks had no lifecycle/TTL or inconsistent manifesting, causing retention policy gaps and failed replays. This PR introduces an idempotent backfill job that generates 'sink-manifest' objects for existing private S3 buckets, plus a conservative TTL enforcement policy and Helm hooks to wire the job into Private installs. Motivation: ensure compliance (jurisdictional retention and guaranteed export manifests) during upgrades and migrations without forcing immediate manual work for customers. What this PR does: 1) backfill job: a Kubernetes CronJob + a one-shot Job mode that discovers buckets referenced by cluster config and creates SinkManifest CRs with source metadata and inferred retention. The job is fully idempotent and rate-limited to avoid S3 throttling. 2) manifest CRD: lightweight SinkManifest CRD + controller to reconcile manifests into the existing export pipeline (audit log exporter -> tombstone/manifesting stage). 3) TTL enforcement: adds a TTL controller that adds S3 lifecycle hints and emits audit events when retention < minimum for region/compliance tier. This is configurable via helm values and guarded by a feature flag 'backfill.enable'. 4) Helm: chart changes add pre-upgrade and post-upgrade hooks to run the one-shot backfill during upgrades and to roll back in case of failure. 5) Terraform: module updates to add IAM role bindings for the backfill job in Private installer docs; also a migration helper to grant read/list permissions only during backfill window. 6) tests and e2e: unit tests for controller logic, integration test that runs the job against a local-minio fixture, and a smoke test that validates manifests are created and reconciled. Rollout plan: feature-flagged rollout across Private installs; default disabled for air-gapped customers. Backwards compatibility: controller no-ops if SinkManifest CRD already exists and handles duplicate buckets gracefully. Checklist: - [x] CRD and controller - [x] Backfill job (CronJob + one-shot) - [x] Helm hooks and values - [x] Terraform IAM docs + migration helper - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Migration README + runbook for SRE - [x] Feature flag gating - [x] Observability: metrics for backfilled count, failures, S3 errors Migration notes: operators should run the one-shot in read-only mode to preview manifests (helm value backfill.preview=true) then flip to backfill.preview=false to create manifests. For very large tenants we provide a chunked mode (backfill.chunkSize) and backoff settings. Security notes: backfill job uses short-lived credentials and requires explicit consent via terraform migration helper. This description is intentionally long to capture the compliance and operational requirements for Private deployments.
Jordan Alvarez: Can the backfill job be paused via a helm value? Need an emergency kill switch for customers in air-gapped installs.
Maya Chen: yes, added backfill.enabled and backfill.preview flags; job will not start when enabled=false. Also added a KillSwitch annotation handled by the helm hook.
Priya Nair: We should limit concurrent S3 ops to avoid throttling. Add rate limiter and chunking defaults.
Maya Chen: added chunkSize + rateLimit config (defaults conservative). Integration tests cover chunking edge cases.
Samir Patel: suggest logging of manifest diffs for audit tracing and an event when enforcement changes retention below minimum.
Maya Chen: added manifest diff logs and TTL enforcement events; also wired metrics (backfill_jobs_total, manifests_created_total, ttl_violations_total).
Added idempotent backfill tooling to generate SinkManifest CRs for existing S3 buckets in Private installs; Helm hooks to run backfill during upgrades; TTL enforcement controller and Terraform migration helper for IAM; feature-flagged and disabled by default for air-gapped customers.
