payload.body:
Introduce a context-aware interruption 'snooze' flow plus a runbook resumption token so on-call engineers can safely defer noisy alerts while preserving ephemeral troubleshooting context. Motivation: recurring low-value interruptions during live debugging force responders to lose playbook state and trace anchors; we need an opt-in way to reduce noise without losing the captured context used to resume an investigation. This PR implements: 1) snooze manager with context fingerprinting: when an on-call user snoozes an alert via Slack or the web UI, the snooze attaches a lightweight context token that includes playbook id, active probe snapshot id, and optional KV anchors (sanitized). The token is encrypted with the cluster KMS and stored with a TTL. 2) deferred-checker: a background watcher that re-evaluates the underlying metric/alert conditions; if the metric crosses a configurable recovery delta, the snooze is auto-cancelled and escalation continues. 3) runbook resumptions: a safe resume API that accepts the token and rehydrates the ephemeral runbook workspace (playbook steps, last-queried telemetry snapshot, recent commands) into a temporary session for the user who created the snooze or a designated delegate. 4) guardrails: strict scope enforcement (tokens are single-use, bound to user id and repo/namespace), audit events for snooze/create/resume, and automatic expiry fallback to avoid stale claims. 5) UX: Slack quick action updates and a new compact 'Resume runbook' button in the incident web UI; both surface the token ID and expiration. 6) Feature flag and configuration: rollout is gated behind incident-bot.snooze_context.enabled=false by default and exposes recovery thresholds and permitted-scope lists via environment config. Implementation notes: added internal/snooze for core logic, telemetry/snapshotter to capture probe snapshots at snooze time, a minimal resume token codec (AES-GCM + KMS envelope) and server-side checks in the resume endpoint. Security review included KMS usage and audit logging; we restricted KV anchors to a redaction whitelist. Rollout plan: feature-flagged beta for 10% of teams, opt-in via console and Slack workspace deploy, monitor metrics: snooze-accepted rate, resume-success rate, unintended-escalation count. Testing: unit coverage for token lifecycle, e2e Slack flow test, integration test for deferred-checker including simulated metric recovery. Performance: background watcher runs in batches; an opt-in sampling mode prevents explosion of checks for high-cardinality signals. CI: initial flake observed in e2e auth test; re-ran and CI passed. Changelog/notes included. This PR is the foundation for a broader on-call ergonomics effort and is intentionally conservative in what it stores in tokens to avoid leaking sensitive payloads.
Maya Chen: Nice end-to-end. Question: what prevents a delegate from resuming a token after the original owner leaves the org? Should we scope tokens to an expiry + allowed-delegates list?
Author (Priya): We scoped tokens to the creating user's id by default; delegates are allowed only when the creating user explicitly sets a delegate in the UI or when the team has a delegation rule in config. Added unit tests for delegate scoping.
Diego Alvarez: Deferred-checker batch loop looks like it could create a hot-loop under flapping signals. Can we add jitter and exponential backoff per signal?
Author (Priya): Added per-signal exponential backoff plus a global QPS cap and a sampling mode. Updated deferred_checker.go and added integration tests that simulate flapping metrics.
Aisha Gupta: audit entries are great, but ensure PII redaction for KV anchors. Are we using the redaction whitelist?
Author (Priya): Yes, token_codec.go enforces the redaction whitelist and we log sanitized anchors only. Security reviewed and approved.
Add: context-aware snooze flow with runbook resumption token (opt-in behind incident-bot.snooze_context.enabled). Add: deferred-checker to auto-cancel snoozes on metric recovery. Improve: telemetry snapshot capture at snooze time. Fix: race in previous snooze expiry handler. Note: audit logging and KMS envelope used for token security.

Context: As part of the Status page transparency upgrades initiative, we’ve standardized comms templates and added Comms Lead reminders. One gap that came up repeatedly (Support escalations + game days) is that during Sev0/Sev1 incidents we sometimes publish status updates with wording that Support has to immediately clarify, or we publish a component impact that later turns out to be wrong (especially when impact is limited to a subset of customers/regions). This PR introduces an optional approval step in incident-bot before publishing status page updates for Sev0/Sev1, allowing either (a) the on-call Incident Commander or (b) an on-call Support lead to approve the draft. This is intended to improve accuracy without adding overhead to Sev2+ events.

What’s changing:
- Adds a configurable “publish requires approval” gate that activates only for Sev0/Sev1 incidents and only when the action is “publish to Statuspage” (drafting continues to work without approval).
- Approver can be one of:
  - Incident Commander (IC) (default)
  - Support Lead (optional, enabled via config per environment)
- Approval is time-bound: if no approval within N minutes, bot posts a reminder in #incidents and DM’s the Comms Lead + IC. (Does not auto-publish.)
- Adds an explicit “urgent publish” override for IC only (requires a typed confirmation string) for cases where status page time-to-first-update is at risk and Support is unavailable.
- Audit logs: records who approved, when, and the exact message payload + components/regions at publish time (for later accuracy audits).

Key behavior details:
- Sev2+ incidents: no approval gate; behavior unchanged.
- Sev0/Sev1 incidents:
  - /statuspage draft works as today and posts the draft to the incident channel.
  - /statuspage publish triggers approval gate unless config disables it.
  - Approval can happen via Slack button (“Approve publish”) or slash command (/incident approve statuspage).
  - If Support approval is enabled and Support Lead is assigned, Support Lead can approve; otherwise IC approval is sufficient.
- If the incident has no statuspage components selected, publish is blocked with a clearer error pointing to the component fields (ties into the earlier component validation work).

Why optional (and not mandatory): Not all incidents have active Support coverage in the first minutes, and we don’t want to regress TTFU for Sev0/Sev1. The gate can be enabled per workspace/environment. For now we’ll enable in prod for Sev0/Sev1 only, with the IC urgent override available.

Implementation notes:
- Introduces a small “ApprovalGate” interface with a StatuspagePublishGate implementation.
- Slack interactivity: new block actions for approve/deny; deny requires a short reason which is posted back into the incident channel thread.
- Permissions: only users in roles {incident_commander, support_lead} can approve. Role mapping uses the existing incident roles source (no new directory/service).
- Config:
  - statuspage.publish_approval.enabled: true|false
  - statuspage.publish_approval.severities: ["sev0","sev1"]
  - statuspage.publish_approval.approvers: ["ic","support_lead"]
  - statuspage.publish_approval.reminder_minutes: integer

Changed areas/files (high level):
- src/workflows/statuspage/publish.ts: wrap publish action with approval gate
- src/workflows/approvals/gates/statuspage_publish_gate.ts: new gate
- src/slack/blocks/statuspage_publish_approval.ts: Slack UI blocks + actions
- src/slack/handlers/actions.ts: wire approve/deny actions
- src/audit/audit_log.ts: append approval metadata fields
- config/schema.ts + config/defaults.ts: new config entries
- docs/runbooks/statuspage.md: operator guidance for Comms Lead + IC
- tests/workflows/statuspage_publish_approval.test.ts: new coverage for gating + override

Screenshots/UX:
- Added a minimal approval card in the incident channel thread with buttons: Approve publish / Deny (reason required) / IC urgent override.

Rollout plan:
1) Deploy behind config flag off in staging.
2) Enable in staging for Sev0/Sev1 and run through game-day checklist.
3) Enable in prod for Sev0/Sev1 with approvers=[ic,support_lead] and reminder_minutes=5.
4) After 2 weeks, review metrics: time-to-first-update, number of denied publishes, and support escalations about inaccurate status updates.

Risk/mitigations:
- Risk: delays publishing. Mitigation: gate only Sev0/Sev1, reminders at 5m, IC urgent override.
- Risk: role assignment wrong -> no approver. Mitigation: falls back to IC if Support Lead not present; explicit error includes command to assign roles.

Release notes:
- incident-bot: Optional approval step for status page publish actions during Sev0/Sev1 incidents; adds audit logging of approver + timestamps.

Refs:
- Linear: ENG-4860 (approval workflow), ENG-4822 (statuspage integration)
- Jira: INT-10430 (support macros alignment), SUP-28436 (disputed accuracy during US-East degradation)

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests for approval gate + override
- [x] Updated runbook docs
- [x] Verified no behavior change for Sev2+
- [x] Added audit log fields and verified in staging


Rafael Mendes: Can we ensure this doesn’t block the very first Investigating update? We’ve got TTFU targets.
Devon Price (author): Yep—drafting is unchanged and can be posted immediately. The gate only triggers on the publish action to Statuspage. Also added IC urgent override with explicit confirmation to avoid accidental bypass.
Dev Patel: Support Lead approval should be optional; sometimes we don’t have someone available in the first minutes. Also please require a denial reason so we can track patterns.
Devon Price (author): Done. Config now controls approvers=[ic] vs [ic,support_lead]. Deny action prompts for a short reason and logs it to audit + posts it in-thread.
Wei Chen: Copy nit: replace “customer impact” with “impact” (we shouldn’t imply we know it’s customer-wide early). Also remove “we believe” from the approval card header.
Devon Price (author): Updated wording in the approval card + related prompts.
Christine Wong: Can the audit log include the component ids/regions that were published? This will help the weekly accuracy audit job.
Devon Price (author): Added component_ids + regions + incident_id + statuspage_incident_id to the audit payload; tests updated.
Follow-up: enable config flag in prod after next incident-bot deploy window; add a short training note to Comms Lead rotation doc (handled in Confluence/enablement track).

Motivation: customers in regulated regions require per-request consent checks to ensure KMS usage and data residency are aligned with tenant preferences and policy. This PR introduces a small, auditable service (the 'KMS consent oracle') plus an in-path audit sequencer that ensures every request that touches a cross-region or fallback KMS publishes a signed 'consent attestation' and an ordered audit record. Design summary: 1) Consent Oracle: a read-through service consulted by the request-authorizer. It resolves tenant consent profiles, residency constraints, and approved KMS provider lists, returning a canonical consent token. 2) Audit Sequencer: a lightweight sequencer that attaches monotonically increasing audit sequence IDs per-tenant-request-window, emits signed audit envelopes to the audit-log-forwarder, and rejects requests where attestation was not captured. 3) KMS Fallback Policy: a policy engine that allows fallback to approved alternate KMS providers only when explicit consent and policy scope permit it; otherwise the request is denied with clear error codes for clients. Implementation notes: service implemented in go/services/kmsconsent; auth hook added to gateway/authz to consult oracle during preflight; audit sequencer middleware added to runtime/handler and to the private installer flow for on-prem parity. Backwards compatibility: the oracle returns a v1 token; older runtimes will treat missing token as 'unknown' and will be denied by default unless the tenant has an explicit legacy-allow flag. Checklist: - [x] implement oracle service with in-memory cache and Redis backing - [x] add policy rules and unit coverage - [x] add sequencer middleware and integration tests - [x] wire signed audit envelopes into audit-forwarder - [x] add Linear tasks and update runbook - [x] update API docs and console messaging - [x] add migration to populate default consent profiles Testing and validation: local unit tests (go test) and integration tests using the perf-canary harness; added a synthetic scenario that simulates a primary KMS outage to validate fallback behavior and audit sequencing. Load testing: sequencer adds ~0.4ms median overhead in our canary workload at 12k RPS; cache hit paths reduce oracle resolution to sub-ms. Rollout plan: canary in staging behind a feature flag (security.kms_consent=true) for 48h, then staged rollout to 5% of requests on main cluster for 72h, monitor audit delivery (SLO: 99.99% delivery within 60s) and error rate. If errors or missing attestations exceed thresholds, auto-roll back. Ops runbook and Linear tasks are linked to ENG-9742. Why this is different: instead of embedding consent checks into the KMS allocator itself, the oracle centralizes consent resolution and makes attestations first-class auditables so compliance teams can prove per-request consent decisions. Commit summary:
 - initial commit: add oracle service scaffolding and interface (a7d3f9b)
 - add in-memory cache and redis backing, policy parser (b2c4e12)
 - gateway authz hook and tests (c4f1a0d)
 - audit sequencer middleware and sequencer persistence shim (d9b7ef4)
 - integration tests and canary harness config (e3a9b11)
Changed files (high level):
 - go/services/kmsconsent/oracle.go (+312 -14)
 - go/services/kmsconsent/cache.go (+84 -12)
 - runtime/middleware/audit_sequencer.go (+176 -25)
 - gateway/authz/consent_hook.go (+48 -3)
 - audit/forwarder/envelope_builder.go (+92 -8)
 - tests/integration/kms_consent_test.go (+210 -0)
 - docs/security/kms-consent.md (+60 -0)
 - deploy/helm/templates/kmsconsent.yaml (+24 -5)
 - private-installer/ops/consent-migration.sh (+20 -6)
 - perf-canary/config/kms_consent_canary.yaml (+16 -0)
 - scripts/populate_default_consent_profiles.go (+6 -0)
Review conversation (summary): "Diego: Nice separation; can you clarify TTL and cache invalidation strategy?" "Nora: TTL defaults to 5s, Redis pub/sub used to invalidate on profile change; added tests." "Marina: audit envelope should include request-route and model-id; please add fields." "Nora: added route/model to envelope_builder and tests updated." "Samir: need to ensure sequencer persistence doesn't become a hotspot; consider batching signatures." "Nora: added batching option and metrics; sequencer persists only window anchors by default." "Marina: approve after 2 minor nits; Diego: approved; Samir: approved with no further comments." CI notes: initial flaky failing test in integration (timing-related) was fixed by increasing wait timeout for the canary harness; CI green on final run. Merge outcome: merged via squash, commit message consolidates implementation notes and runbook links. Release notes: "Adds tenant-level consent resolution service and audit sequencer to ensure every cross-region or fallback KMS use is accompanied by a signed consent attestation and ordered audit record. Introduces opt-in feature flag and staged rollout plan." Security rationale: improves our ability to produce immutable per-request consent proof for audits, reduces silent fallback risk, centralizes policy interpretation. Rollback plan: disable feature flag and remove gateway hook; sequencer will stop emitting new envelopes but audit-forwarder will continue to accept queued envelopes until drained. Operational metrics to monitor: audit_envelopes_sent, audit_envelope_failures, consent_oracle_latency_ms, sequencer_persist_latency_ms, kms_fallback_rate. Contact: nora@redwood.ai
Diego: can you clarify TTL and cache invalidation?
Nora: TTL defaults to 5s; added redis pub/sub invalidation and tests.
Marina: include request-route and model-id in envelope;
Nora: added fields and tests.
Samir: sequencer persistence could be hotspot; consider batching signatures.
Nora: added batching option and metrics. Approved after nits.
Adds a tenant-level consent oracle and audit sequencer to require signed consent attestations for cross-region or fallback KMS usage; introduces an opt-in feature flag and staged rollout.
Unit tests for oracle and policy parser; integration tests in tests/integration/kms_consent_test.go; perf-canary run validated latency impact; manual canary in staging prior to rollout.
Feature-flagged canary (48h) -> 5% traffic for 72h -> increase to 25% -> global if no issues. Monitoring: audit delivery SLO, error rate, sequencer latency.
Centralizes consent logic to produce auditable tokens and signed envelopes, preventing silent KMS fallbacks and giving compliance teams per-request attestation proof.

Motivation: We need a way for runbook authors and SREs to validate on-call runbooks against realistic past telemetry and exercise commands in a sandboxed environment without impacting production state. This PR adds a 'shadow' on-call runner that replays captured telemetry bundles into a sandboxed execution path and optionally performs dry-run vs reversible actions. The feature enables deterministic playback, automatic safety checks, and a small set of rollback hooks that undo side effects created during replay.

What this change does: adds a new internal service (shadow-runner), a telemetry-playback engine, a sandboxed action-executor with reversible action registry, a CLI for seeding telemetry bundles, and feature-flag gating so teams can opt-in. The design favors safety: destructive actions are run in 'reversible mode' and persisted changes are recorded with rollback tokens. The playback runner can be scheduled or triggered by PRs to run playbooks against a captured bundle.

High-level checklist: [x] design doc linked in Linear ENG-1427. [x] core playback loop implemented and unit-tested. [x] reversible action registry with two built-in rollback handlers (user-message purge undo, synthetic-kv rollback). [x] CLI `rb-playback seed` and `rb-playback run --bundle` added. [x] metrics and tracing added for playback latency, failures, and rollback success. [x] e2e sandbox test harness under test/fixtures that replays a small bundle. [x] feature-flag gating in runtime config and a canary rollout plan.

Backward-compatibility and rollout: The shadow-runner is entirely opt-in; default is disabled. No production request path changes for normal incident-bot consumers. The CLI and seeding tools are additive. We will enable the feature for the oncall-sim org initially (10% canary), monitor metrics (incident.shadow.playback.success_rate, incident.shadow.rollback.rate), then broaden to SRE teams.

Risks and mitigations: potential for accidental state changes if a new action is registered without a rollback handler. Mitigation: PRs that add actions must provide a rollback handler or explicitly mark the action as non-productive for shadow-runner. Tests assert that every registered action either declares reversible or is noop in shadow mode. An additional runtime safety gate will abort playback if an action invokes an I/O-write outside the sandboxing policy.

Related work: ties into ENG-1490 (playbook QA harness) and SUP-1887 (customer-replay-request workflow).
Morgan Lee (2026-02-18): Can we ensure metric names are stable? Suggest prefix incident.shadow.* to avoid collisions. Response: updated metrics and added metrics_registry entry (commit e5b3c4f).
Diego Flores (2026-02-20): Add explicit feature flag gating and a kill-switch for canary. Also request an emergency abort endpoint. Response: added feature_flags.yaml entries and /shadow-runner/abort endpoint with admin auth (commit f6c4d5a).
Nina Kapoor (2026-02-23): Tests look good but one flaky e2e failed on CI due to timeouts. Can we make replay timing deterministic? Response: switched to deterministic wallclock in tests and reduced bundle size; CI rerun passed (commit g7d5e6b).
Morgan Lee (approval, 2026-02-28): Approve after addressing metrics and adding docs.
Team discussion focused on safety-first design. We agreed to require explicit rollback handlers for any action added going forward, gate by feature-flag, and limit initial rollout to a small canary. Documentation and a quick ops runbook were added to reduce accidental misuse.
Merged by Morgan Lee via squash merge. Squashed into single commit 9h3k5b and pushed to main. Canary enabled for org:oncall-sim via feature flag. Rollout note: monitor incident.shadow.playback.success_rate for two days before expanding.
Adds experimental shadow-runner: a sandboxed on-call runner that can replay captured telemetry bundles against runbooks for QA and validation. Includes reversible action registry and CLI tools to seed/run bundles. Disabled by default; opt-in behind feature-flag. See incident-bot/docs/shadow-runner.md for usage and safety guidelines.
1) Run `rb-playback seed --file test/fixtures/sample_bundle.json` 2) `rb-playback run --bundle <id> --mode shadow` 3) Confirm no production side effects and check metrics incident.shadow.playback.* 4) Test abort via POST /shadow-runner/abort with admin token
Enable feature-flag. Seed small test bundle (tools/rb-playback seed --sample) before flipping canary. Observe metrics and if rollback.rate > 0.05 or errors spike, flip feature off immediately and open SUP ticket.

Motivation: On-call responders often need short-lived, read-only probes (log tailing, metric snapshot, safe config queries) that run in an isolated environment and do not change runtime state. The incident-bot currently supports scripted runbooks but lacks an opinionated, safe orchestration layer for ephemeral diagnostics. This PR introduces an Ephemeral Debug Orchestrator and a Safe Probe Runner that: (1) schedules and executes pre-approved diagnostic probes in a sandbox, (2) enforces time/CPU/memory limits and read-only constraints, (3) automatically collects artifacts and attaches them to the incident context, and (4) provides a responder-facing CLI and HTTP endpoints gated by a feature flag. Changes are opt-in and behind INCIDENT_EPHEMERAL_DEBUG with granular RBAC checks.

What this PR contains: - new orchestrator that manages probe lifecycle, lease tokens, and backoff for noisy systems - a safeexec sandbox with syscall restrictions, chroot-like file access limiting, and per-probe resource caps - probe registry with small curated probes (logs-sample, metric-snapshot, config-dump-readonly) - responder CLI helpers (tools/oncall/ephemeral-cli) for requesting a probe and downloading artifacts - observability: probe metrics, traces, and audit events for every probe run - e2e tests that run probes against a local fake target and validate sandbox constraints

Design notes: The orchestrator uses the existing worker queue but adds a short-lived lease manager (15s - 5m) to ensure probes do not hang. Probes are run inside safeexec and are strictly read-only wrappers around existing diagnostic utilities. Results are uploaded to the incident attachment store with tags indicating sensitivity level. The orchestrator defaults to deny for non-admins; requester must have the new permission scope "incident:ephemeral_probe:invoke".

Migration & rollout plan: - Feature gated by INCIDENT_EPHEMERAL_DEBUG=false by default. - Step 1: Deploy with flag disabled and telemetry only (probe_attempts metric) - Step 2: Enable for a small pilot SRE squad and manual canary (1 week) - Step 3: Gradual enable for all on-call rotations with opt-out controls.

Checklist: - [x] Implementation of orchestrator and sandbox - [x] Unit tests for safeexec restrictions - [x] Integration tests for lease/timeouts - [x] Documentation (tools/oncall/ephemeral-cli.md) - [x] Feature flag + RBAC entries - [x] Observability dashboards (minimal)

Security considerations: The sandbox uses seccomp-style filtering and disallows network egress. All probe binaries are run with a dedicated, unprivileged UID. The code path records full audit events and stores artifacts in an access-controlled bucket. We intentionally avoided any writable access to production config or mutation APIs.

Operational notes: The orchestrator emits probe_attempts, probe_success, probe_failure, probe_timeout, and probe_resource_violation metrics. Alerts are suggested in the README for probe_failure rate spikes. The PR also adds a backpressure policy to avoid overwhelming a target service during repeated probe runs.
Marco Ruiz (2024-11-13): Important PR — please call out failure modes and ensure we do not allow probes to hit high-cardinality logs. Also request explicit test demonstrating resource limit enforcement.
Aisha Patel (2024-11-14): Reply: added resource enforcement unit tests and a 'probe_resource_violation' metric. We also added throttling on probe attempts per-incident to limit cardinality.
Linnea Sørensen (2024-11-15): Suggestion: extract seccomp profile to a reusable package and add CI lint for profiles. Also request a short diagram in docs showing artifact flow.
Aisha Patel (2024-11-16): Reply: extracted profile to internal/safeexec/profiles.go and added profile lint step to CI. Documentation updated with artifact flow diagram in tools/oncall/ephemeral-cli.md.
Devon Carter (2024-11-18): nits on log messages and retry backoff parameters. Also noted an e2e flake on CI (timing) — recommended increasing backoff and explicit sleep in the fake target to stabilize test.
Aisha Patel (2024-11-19): Reply: increased backoff, improved logging to include probe_id and lease token, and addressed the e2e flake with a deterministic readiness handshake in the test harness. CI green on final run.

Motivation: On-call responders often need to validate multi-step runbooks before applying changes in production. This PR introduces a lightweight "rehearsal" flow to the incident-bot that executes playbook steps in a dry-run mode against captured synthetic telemetry and read-only control-plane APIs. The goal is to give responders confidence in step ordering, guardrail behaviour, and external integration wiring without performing live mutations.

What this PR adds (high level): 1) playbook-rehearsal CLI: new subcommand 'incident-bot rehearse <playbook-id> --context <snapshot>' that runs steps in dry-run and outputs a step-by-step report with proposed API calls and predicted outcomes; 2) safe dry-run executor: an execution layer that enforces side-effect policies, substitutes mutating calls with simulated responses, and tracks intended state transitions; 3) synthetic traffic harness: a small harness that replays sanitized telemetry events (traces, logs, metrics) from a captured snapshot to validate queries used in runbook conditions; 4) authoring hints: ephemeral checks that lint playbook steps for missing assertions and suggest a sanity-check step where appropriate; 5) telemetry and safety audit: add events that record rehearsal runs to the audit log (no secrets persisted).

Usage notes: The rehearse command accepts either a stored snapshot (snapshot-id) or a live-sanitized capture (--live-snapshot) for short, low-risk rehearsals. Output formats: human, json, and compact-summary. By default the CLI runs with a strict policy that blocks any network calls flagged as "dangerous"; operators can supply an allowlist for approved endpoints via --allowlist (only allowed in admin mode).

Safety and threat model: Rehearsal runs are read-only by default. The executor replaces mutation HTTP calls (POST/PUT/DELETE) with deterministic simulated responses based on simple response templates and historical call traces. Secrets are never sent to the rehearsal harness; we added explicit checks to fail-fast if a playbook references a secret directly. Rehearsals are tracked and visible in the audit timeline so reviewers can see when a playbook was tested and by whom.

Testing and rollout: The feature is behind a feature-flag (rehearsal.cli) gated per-org. Unit and integration tests simulate common runbook patterns (service restart, routing failover, config toggles) against the synthetic harness. We rolled the feature to a small pilot org for two weeks before broad enablement.

Related work: Complements the incident-bot runbook linter and oncall rehearsal ideas in ENG-9071; ties into rollout policies in ENG-9123.
Ethan Chen (2026-02-21): Nice ergonomics for the CLI. Two asks: (1) ensure the simulated responses include realistic rate-limit headers so retry logic is exercised; (2) add a small benchmark for rehearsal runtime on large snapshots.

Marisol Gomez (2026-02-22): Addressed both: added rate-limit header emulation and a microbenchmark test. Also documented expected runtime scaling in rehearsal.md.

Priya Kapoor (2026-02-23): Security note: make explicit that secrets are never included in snapshots — add a canonical sanitizer and an assertion that fails the rehearsal if a secret placeholder is detected.

Marisol Gomez (2026-02-23): Added snapshot sanitizer and explicit assertion; included a CI check to enforce snapshot hygiene.

Jordan Lee (2026-02-24): Left a minor nit on CLI output verbosity flags; approved after Marisol pushed the formatting tweak.

Ethan Chen (2026-02-24): Approved.

Maintainer (automation) (2026-02-25): CI green, merging with squash-merge.
Added a CLI-driven playbook rehearsal and dry-run executor that lets responders validate runbooks against sanitized telemetry snapshots before executing live changes. Feature behind feature-flag 'rehearsal.cli' and audited.
Enablement: org admins must opt in via feature flag and provide allowlist for any approved non-read endpoints. Snapshots must pass the new snapshot-hygiene-check in CI before use in rehearsals.

Motivation: On-call teams see frequent duplicate or conflicting automatic playbook triggers during multi-service incidents. That leads to noisy pagers, duplicated work, and occasional race conditions when multiple runbooks try to act concurrently. This PR introduces an "oncall optimizer" that deterministically sequences competing playbook actions and a lightweight "silent debounce" window to suppress rapid-fire automated escalations.

Design summary: Implement a sequencing layer inside incident-bot that: 1) assigns a deterministic order to candidate playbook runs using a stable hash of (incident_id, service, rule_priority, timestamp_bucket); 2) evaluates simple conflict predicates (resource lock, overlapping mitigation targets) and rewires lower-priority actions to delayed/no-op outcomes; 3) establishes a configurable silent debounce window per-service that suppresses non-critical automatic escalations for a short period after an initial mitigation attempt. The sequencing algorithm is intentionally conservative and synchronous in the controller to minimize surprises.

Key features and behaviors: - Deterministic sequencer: ensures same ordering across restarts within a short time-bucket. - Conflict autocorrector: if two playbooks would modify the same resource (e.g., routing table), the sequencer marks the lower-priority action as deferred and surfaces a single combined action to responders. - Silent debounce: low-confidence automated escalations are suppressed for a configurable window (default 90s) after a mitigation attempt; suppression events are emitted to metrics. - Local dry-run simulator: CLI mode `incident-bot simulate-sequence` validates a set of active rules against a sample incident to preview ordering and suppression decisions. - Telemetry: new metrics incidentbot.playbook.sequenced_count, incidentbot.playbook.suppressed_count, incidentbot.playbook.deferred_actions and tracepoints for sequencing decisions.

Files changed (high-level): - controller/sequencer.py: new sequencer and conflict resolution engine. - controller/simulator.py: local simulation CLI and unit harness. - config/defaults.yaml: added sequencer and debounce configuration knobs. - telemetry/metrics_registry.py: metrics registration and export hooks. - tests/test_sequencer.py: unit tests covering ordering, conflict cases, and debounce behavior. - cli/commands.py: added simulate-sequence command and flags. - docs/operational/playbook-sequencer.md: usage, tuning guide, and migration notes.

Commits (summary): - Add deterministic hashing and sequencing core (Priya K.) - Implement conflict autocorrector and resource lock model (Alex P.) - Add silent debounce implementation and config knobs (Miguel T.) - Add simulate-sequence CLI with sample fixtures (Priya K.) - Wire telemetry and dashboards (Rina S.) - Tests, docs, and release notes (Priya K.)

Testing and CI: - Extensive unit tests added (test coverage + sequencer edge cases). - Integration smoke test run in CI (incident-bot/integration/seq-smoke) flaked once on first run; fixed race by adding short randomized jitter and re-ran. - CI status: all checks passed after second run.

Review conversation (highlights): - Alex Park: "Please ensure sequencing does not increase mean response latency for high-priority actions; recommend a fast-path bypass for priority >= 100." Author reply: "Added bypass for priority >= 100 in the sequencer pipeline; documented behavior and tests added." - Miguel Torres: "Need visibility when two playbooks are merged into one action so responders can audit decisions." Author reply: "Added structured tracepoint 'sequencer.merge' and emitted a human-readable summary to the incident timeline when a merge happens." - Rina Shah: "How do we prevent deadlocks when two sequencers run concurrently in multi-controller setups?" Author reply: "Sequencer uses optimistic locking with a short lease and falls back to delay+retry; added a sim test that reproduces and verifies safety."

Rollout plan: - Feature gated behind incident-bot.sequencer.enabled (default false). - Canary rollout to 10% of customers for 48 hours with increased logging and telemetry. - If telemetry shows suppressed_count/spike in deferred actions but no errors, expand to 50% for 72 hours. - Full rollout only after no regressions in latency SLOs and positive pager noise reduction signal.

Migration notes and compatibility: - Existing playbook YAML files are unchanged; sequencing is opt-in. - Customers that rely on side-effect ordering should test with simulate-sequence. - The sequencer may alter the observed execution order of automatic actions; manual escalations are not affected.

Observability and dashboards: - New Grafana panels for sequenced_count, suppressed_count, and average debounce window per-service. - New alert: incidentbot.sequencer.error_rate > 0.5% for 10m triggers an investigation runbook.

Security and safety: - No privileged credentials introduced. - The conflict autocorrector intentionally avoids destructive merges; if uncertainty > threshold, action is deferred and a human hook is created.

Conclusion: This PR reduces noisy duplicate automations and prevents simple action collisions by providing a deterministic sequence and suppression semantics. It is conservative, opt-in, and accompanied by simulation tooling and telemetry to enable safe rollouts.

Motivation: on-call responders are overwhelmed by alert noise and often run a suite of irrelevant playbooks. This PR implements a lightweight root-cause scoring layer + playbook prioritizer that surfaces the most likely mitigations.

What it does (single-pass summary):
- Adds a signal fusion module that scores candidate root causes from alert metadata, recent SLO burn-rate windows (via slo-toolkit hooks), and recent deploy/rollout activity.
- Introduces a playbook prioritizer that ranks runbooks by expected mitigation probability and time-to-mitigate (TTM).
- Adds a new /incident suggest-playbook command for Slack that returns 1-3 prioritized actions and confidence bands.
- Exposes an opt-in per-service configuration to tune weights and to pin preferred playbooks.
- Includes metrics and tracing for the scoring decisions to aid audits and regression debugging.

Why this is different from previous runbook helpers: the prioritizer is probabilistic and time-aware (uses historic mitigation durations) rather than a static tag-matching engine. It is intentionally lightweight (no heavy ML infra) so it can run in the incident-bot process and be used in private deployments.

Compatibility notes: integrates with existing slo-toolkit event API (v2) and incident-bot's existing alert enrichment pipeline. Backwards compatible: if slo-toolkit data is not present the scorer gracefully degrades to metadata-only heuristics.

Testing and rollout: feature guarded behind a runtime flag; telemetry opt-in enforced per-organization. Can be enabled for a single team for staged rollout.

Files changed: high level list included below.

Problem: on-call responders often need a compact, sanitizable snapshot of service state plus a minimal, actionable playbook skeleton to triage quickly. Current incident-bundles are heavyweight and require manual extraction; runbooks stored in the wiki are long and not tailored to the specific alert fingerprint. This PR implements a lightweight 'Snapshot Curator' and a Playbook Stub Generator that produce compact, prioritized diagnostic bundles and tiny playbook skeletons suitable for chat/Slack handoffs and pager messages. Goals: 1) generate a 1-2 screen snapshot that groups key traces/metrics/log-excerpts with sanitized context and concise signal summary; 2) auto-generate a 5-step playbook stub prioritized by probable root-cause signals; 3) provide a safe "preview" mode and redaction hooks for PII-sensitive customers; 4) offer a CLI and Slack action to produce stubs in-line from alerts. Main changes: - new snapshot curator service: heuristics-based selection (error fingerprinting, high-signal metric deltas, recent deployment tags) - playbook-stub generator: maps snapshot features to prioritized actions + suggested queries - telemetry-sampler: adaptive sampling policy (preserves pre/post-deploy windows) to keep snapshots terse but reproducible - CLI: incident-snapshot create --alert-id/--query + --preview flag - Slack action: /snapshot preview (returns ephemeral message with playbook stub) - redaction layer: pluggable redactors and customer opt-out via config - unit+integration tests, updated docs, and small UX flow in incident-bot UI Why this approach: producing smaller, decision-focused artifacts reduces cognitive load and speeds mean-time-to-resolution. The playbook stubs are intentionally conservative (suggest quick probes and safe mitigations) and include an explicit escalation anchor. Backwards compatibility: existing full incident bundles remain unchanged; curator and generator are opt-in behind a feature flag and RBAC scope. Context: During Dedicated burst beta we observed brief "denial storms" where one tenant would get disproportionately denied burst admissions for ~30–90s after a telemetry delay event. This manifested as burst capacity being available (per fleet dashboards) but the admission controller continuing to deny with reason=POOL_SATURATED / FAIRNESS_THROTTLE for that tenant, while other tenants recovered faster. Root cause: the fairness + pool-availability calculation in the admission controller was using a raw (unsmoothed) free-capacity signal derived from fleet telemetry. When telemetry arrived late/out-of-order, the computed free_capacity could transiently drop to ~0 and stay pinned until the next sample; the token-bucket refill path treated that as hard saturation and stopped refilling, effectively starving tenants that had recently spent tokens. Fix: (1) add EWMA smoothing and monotonic guards for free-capacity + utilization signals, (2) add telemetry staleness detection (age > telemetry_max_age_ms) and switch to a conservative "stale mode" that prevents starvation by allowing minimal refill and limiting denial amplification, while still respecting per-tenant burst caps and global fleet safety caps, and (3) add explicit guard conditions to avoid negative/implausible deltas causing refill=0 for an entire window. This PR is intentionally scoped as a hotfix: no API shape changes, no new config required for existing tenants; defaults are safe and feature-flagged (burst.telemetry_smoothing_enabled) for rollback. Test plan: unit tests for smoothing + stale mode; simulation test that replays out-of-order telemetry and verifies no tenant sees >X consecutive denials solely due to telemetry staleness; staging canary with synthetic telemetry lag injection. Rollout: enable flag for internal dogfood tenants first, then beta allowlist (us-east/H100) after 24h with no SLO regression; keep kill-switch available via config bundle.
Jordan Lee (author): We saw repeated FAIRNESS_THROTTLE denials on Aurora tenant right after a telemetry lag spike in eu-west staging. Traced to free_capacity computed from delayed samples going to 0 and pinning refill. This hotfix adds smoothing + stale-mode to avoid starvation. Please focus review on correctness/guardrails; perf impact is minimal (single EWMA per pool).
Keiko Yamamoto (reviewer): In stale mode, are we risking over-admitting and hurting neighbors? What stops a tenant from getting a "free pass" when telemetry is stale?
Jordan Lee (author): Stale mode still enforces: (a) per-tenant burst_gpu_limit, (b) per-tenant max_burst_ratio, (c) global fleet safety cap (existing circuit breaker path), and (d) a reduced refill rate (min_refill_qps) so we only prevent starvation; we don't increase tenant throughput beyond caps. Also if telemetry is stale for >2 windows we bias towards deny-with-retry rather than admit.
Peter Holtz (reviewer): Can we make the stale detection visible in dashboards? Otherwise oncall won't know why denials are changing.
Jordan Lee (author): Added burst_telemetry_stale_total + burst_telemetry_age_ms histogram and a smoothed gauge. Also added a short internal runbook note with "what to look at". I can add alert annotations in the follow-up PR (trying to keep this one hotfix-sized).
Allison Grant (reviewer): Please confirm label cardinality is bounded for the new metrics. No per-tenant labels on the histogram.
Jordan Lee (author): Confirmed: metrics are per pool (region, hardware_class, pool_id), no tenant_id labels. Tests include a guard to prevent adding tenant_id to stale metrics.
Mina Haddad (reviewer): Routing expects deterministic denial reasons. Any changes to reason codes?
Jordan Lee (author): No new reason codes. In stale mode we still return the same codes but we reduce consecutive denials caused solely by telemetry. Determinism preserved within a decision window given the same inputs; we include telemetry_age_ms only in internal debug logs/context.
Sean Gallagher (reviewer): What’s the rollback plan if this changes admission rates unexpectedly?
Jordan Lee (author): Feature flag burst.telemetry_smoothing_enabled; can be flipped off per region via config bundle. Also safe-guard: if smoothed signal diverges >20% from raw for >N samples, we log + fall back to raw (to avoid hiding real saturation).
Keiko Yamamoto (reviewer): Requested change: please clamp EWMA input to [0, pool_capacity] to avoid outliers; and add a test for negative capacity sample.
Jordan Lee (author): Done. Added clamp + unit test for negative sample and out-of-range sample. Also added comment explaining why we clamp (telemetry jitter + collector bugs).
Peter Holtz (reviewer): Approved after clamp + metrics. Please file a follow-up to add an alert when telemetry stale rate spikes.
Jordan Lee (author): Will do; tracking under ENG-4881 follow-up checklist.
Keiko Yamamoto (reviewer): Approved.
Mina Haddad (reviewer): Approved.
Sean Gallagher (reviewer): Approved; please ensure staged rollout per beta allowlist only.
Jordan Lee (author): Rollout is gated by existing per-tenant allowlist + env flag. Merging now.
Burst admission controller now smooths fleet capacity telemetry and detects stale telemetry to prevent unfair burst denials during transient telemetry lag.
New internal metrics: burst_telemetry_stale_total, burst_free_capacity_smoothed, burst_telemetry_age_ms.

Context and motivation: Oncall handoffs frequently lack the minimal telemetry snapshot responders need to triage quickly (recent errors, recent deploys touched, top-5 traces). This PR introduces two cooperating features: a lightweight local probe-queue sidecar that prefetches a bounded set of telemetry artifacts during an incident, and a Sensible Runbook Composer (SRC) that instantiates short, contextual handoff templates based on severity, affected services, and prefetch results. Goals: reduce first-response time, reduce noisy handoff messages, and provide safe auto-suggested responders. Non-goals: replace full incident capture/export systems or store long-lived PII-laden artifacts.
Adds an ephemeral local probe queue sidecar and a context-aware runbook template composer. Improves handoff quality by prefetching minimal telemetry and supplying responder suggestions. No infra changes required for hosted deployments; Private deployments can opt-in via config.
Not user-facing API change; incident /oncall/handoff returns an additional 'suggested_responders' field when enabled. Backwards compatible: field is omitted unless feature is on. No breaking change.
Feature gated with incident.sidecar.enabled; config default=false for Private installer. Sidecar uses a bounded in-memory store, no disk persistence, and explicit PII redaction on traces/log snippets. Added a config 'max_probe_bytes' with sane defaults.
Operators can enable via helm values (charts/incident-bot/values.yaml) and validate with the provided smoke test (tests/integration/test_handoff_flow.go). Rollout recommendation: canary to 10% of oncall rotation for 48 hours, monitor handoff latency and duplicate-notes alerts.
Added quick-handoffs.md with example handoff payloads and a checklist for enabling in Private deployments. README.md updated with sidecar image and resource recommendations (cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi).

Adds a confined oncall rehearsal playground for replaying recent incidents and running safe experiments against sanitized telemetry. Motivation: teams need a low-friction way to rehearse runbooks and validate mitigations without touching production state or leaking PII. This PR introduces a sandboxed playback engine, a query sanitizer, an opt-in dry-run token for safe action simulators, and a safety harness that enforces rate/cost/side-effect limits. Key behaviors: deterministic replay using time-offsets, injected small-scale fuzzing of metric values to test threshold robustness, RBAC gating so only users with `rehearsal.run` can execute live-like scenarios, and a canary gating step that requires a staged approval for any experiment that includes write-side effects. The description below lists changes, checks, and rollout plan. Checklist: - [x] telemetry ingestion slice and time-offset replay - [x] query sanitizer that strips identifiers and rewrites agg windows - [x] dry-run token and simulated action driver - [x] safety harness with cost/rate caps and write-effect blockers - [x] UI controls in the incident-bot dashboard to create rehearsal snapshots - [x] unit + integration tests for replay determinism - [x] Linear link for tracking: ENG-5123 Deployment plan: feature-flagged for 2 weeks in staging, invite-only beta for SREs, then gradual enablement with audit logs and automatic revert on assertion failures. Known limitations: large trace replays are sampled to avoid runaway costs; external downstream hooks are stubbed in dry-run mode. Related work: builds on prior snapshot exporter PRs and the ephemeral-playbook architecture.

Context: On-call handoffs are noisy and current priority tags are static. Teams repeatedly rebalance duty weights manually after high-traffic windows resulting in inconsistent alert routing and unfair pager distribution. This PR adds an automatic priority calibrator for handoff cards and a compact telemetry sampler that reduces event payloads while preserving incident fidelity. Motivation: reduce on-call cognitive load, stabilize priority ordering during shift boundaries, and cut downstream telemetry costs without losing triage signal. What this PR does (high level): - Introduces a priority-calibration service that computes a calibrated priority score per responder based on recent response latency, current active incidents, past on-call load (rolling 7d), and soft-capacity (user-configurable). - Adds an adaptive telemetry sampler that reduces per-attachment payload by switching to summary-mode for non-incident windows and high-volume teams; it keeps high-fidelity (full traces/logs) when the calibrator flags a responder or team as incident-relevant. - Implements a feature flag ff_autohandoff_v1 and a staged rollout plan (10% -> 50% -> 100%) with canary checks. - Provides migration notes and a single safe default (no change to routing until flag is enabled). Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for calibrator score logic and edge cases - [x] Integration test for sampler flow with synthetic high-volume and quiet windows - [x] Canary rollout gating by metrics (median response latency, dropped attachments) - [x] Docs: runbook and operational playbook entries added - [x] Backwards compatibility: old priority tag preserved as metadata field Implementation notes: - Calibrator runs as a lightweight worker in incident-bot with per-team caching and TTL=30s to limit churn. - Scoring function is tunable via team settings: weights for latency, active_incidents, historical_load. Defaults chosen after offline simulation (see ENG-11234 notes). - Sampler is implemented in Go in telemetry/pipeline with two modes: full and compact. A probabilistic admission ensures a minimum of 0.5% full fidelity per 1k events to support downstream ML and postmortem sampling needs. - The PR contains a migration job (idempotent) that annotates existing handoff records with calibrated_priority=null to allow a gradual backfill. Rollout plan: 1) Deploy to staging, run smoke and load tests (staging metrics targets documented in ENG-11234). 2) Enable ff_autohandoff_v1 for 10% of teams for 24 hours; monitor: response latency p50/p95, sample-droprate, unit test and integration test stability. 3) If stable, increase to 50% and then 100%. Safety gates and rollback: - If dropped_attachments > 0.2% above baseline or responder-misroutes detected, immediately revert flag via console. - Feature toggle supports per-team opt-out. Observability and dashboards added: - New dashboards: "Handoff Priority Distribution", "Telemetry Sampler Loss Rate", "Calibrator Decision Log (sampled)". - Alerts: sampler_drop_rate > 0.3% sustained for 30m; calibrator_score_flip_rate > 2% per hour. Related work and references: - Linear: ENG-11234 (simulation + weight tuning), PM-458 (product acceptance criteria). - Internal doc: /docs/oncall/autohandoff-design.md Testing: - 34 new unit tests (Python), 6 Go integration tests. - A small chaos test that simulates burst alerts and verifies sampler retains at least 1 sample per 2000 events per team. Migration and backwards compatibility: - No forced migrations; existing handoffs keep old_priority tag. - Backfill migration annotates records but can be skipped. - API is additive: clients continue to read priority field; calibrated_priority is optional. Security and data governance: - Sampler preserves hashes for dedup and supports PII redaction rules in compact mode. - No telemetry leaves region boundaries; respects regional KMS settings. Rollback steps (quick): - Flip ff_autohandoff_v1 to off -> worker stops emitting calibrated_priority -> sampler switches to full mode for flagged teams -> run revert backfill if needed. Notes for reviewers: - The calibrator scoring function is intentionally conservative; weight defaults are documented and can be tuned via admin UI. - I included micro-benchmarks for worker overhead under 1000 req/s per instance. Please check the canary gating thresholds and the safety alerts.

Maya Chen: addressed both: added 'missing_data_fallback' to schema and exposed latency_weight via team settings. pushed a new commit.
Sofia Martinez: Integration test is flaky on CI (sampler admission probabilistic). Can we deterministic-seed the test and add a retry?
Maya Chen: updated integration test to use a deterministic RNG seed and added a retry for the admitted-sample assertion. CI rerun requested.
Noah Gupta: Approved after verifying dashboards and alert thresholds in staging. Left a minor nit about log verbosity level.
Ops (automated): Canary gating reference metrics registered: handoff_median_latency, sampler_drop_rate.
Incident-bot: Add autohandoff priority calibrator and adaptive telemetry sampler behind ff_autohandoff_v1. Provides smarter handoff ordering and reduces telemetry costs. Rollout is gated by canary metrics; no behavior change until flag enabled.

Adds two complementary operational tools: a lightweight on-call shift simulator that models responder availability, escalation probability, and alert handoff latency; and an ephemeral brief-bridge service that creates one-time WebRTC brief channels for responders to share audio/text context during high-severity incidents. Motivation: teams frequently ask for a way to estimate how changes to rotation policies (shift length, overlap windows, responder weights) affect mean time to acknowledge/escalate, and they need a low-friction way to share live context without SMS/Slack fatigue. This PR bundles a simulator CLI, a small in-process simulator library for scheduling heuristics, and a minimal brief-bridge shim that integrates with the incident-bot UI and the ephemeral attachments flow. Checklist: - [x] Simulator CLI and library with unit tests - [x] Brief-bridge service and UI path (opt-in behind flag) - [x] End-to-end smoke test for brief channel creation - [x] Documentation and runbook notes for SRE - [x] Feature gated via `ENABLE_BRIEF_BRIDGE` and `SIMULATOR_MODE` env vars Security note: brief-bridge tokens are single-use, short TTL (60s), and do not persist audio to disk by default. See docs/oncall-briefbridge.md and docs/oncall-sim.md for operational controls and recommended RBAC. Limitations: simulator currently models responder availability as a three-state Markov chain (on, muted, away) with configurable transition rates; it does not yet ingest historical paging data (follow-up linear item queued).

Summary:
This PR introduces two complementary features for incident handoffs: a 'telemetry zipper' that consolidates fragmented telemetry pieces into a single, size-aware handoff bundle, and a 'responder-context escort' that creates ephemeral, scope-limited tokens and applies attachment sanitization policies for safe context transfer between responders or external tools.

Motivation:
Oncall handoffs frequently suffer from fragmented traces and partial logs spread across multiple services (small files, incremental snapshots, presigned attachments). That fragmentation makes triage slow and increases leakage risk when attachments travel outside the platform. The zipper reduces noise and request-count overhead; the escort enforces least-privilege context sharing with auditable tokens and an attach-sanitize policy DSL.

What changed (high level):
- telemetry zipper service: server-side component that collects telemetry fragments (logs, traces, metrics snapshots) emitted by incident-bot during an incident, collates them deterministically, and returns a single bundle URL. It performs size-aware chunking and optional compression.
- responder-context escort: new handoff flow that mints short-lived escort tokens, applies a configurable sanitization policy (regex redaction, filetype allowlist, size truncation), and records an immutable handoff audit entry.
- API: added /v1/handoffs/zip and /v1/handoffs/escort endpoints, plus SDK helpers for token exchange and bundle retrieval.
- UI: small console addition to trigger a zipper bundle on handoff and display escort token TTL and sanitization summary.
- Tests and docs: coverage for bundling logic, sanitization rules, and e2e handoff flows; added runbook hints generation for zipper bundles.

Backward compatibility and rollout:
- Both features are opt-in. Existing handoff APIs continue to work; zipper is triggered explicitly via a query param or new handoff button in the UI. Escort token issuance requires a new RBAC capability (handoff.escort). Default RBAC denies issuance until toggled by admins.
- Rollout plan: feature-flag behind 'telemetry_zipper' and 'responder_escort' flags. Canary to internal SRE first, then gradual production enablement.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for bundler ordering, chunking heuristics, and compression fallback.
- Integration tests for token exchange with KMS-backed signer and audit log entries.
- Load tests ensuring zipper request latency stays within 500ms P50 for typical 10-attachment handoffs.

Security considerations:
- Escort tokens are short-lived (default 5 minutes) and scoped to a single handoff id and principal.
- Sanitization policies are executed in a sandboxed worker process; unsafe attachments are blocked and replaced with a fingerprint.
- Audit entries include fingerprint hashes for blocked attachments to support future retrieval requests under compliance workflows.

Revert plan:
- Disabled via feature flag if any regressions are observed. The zipper is stateless (builds bundles from existing fragments) so disabling simply returns to per-fragment handoff with no data loss. Escort can be revoked by disabling RBAC capability and revoking outstanding tokens via audit-record TTL enforcement.
Adds telemetry zipper to consolidate fragmented telemetry and a secure responder context escort that issues ephemeral tokens and sanitizes attachments during handoff.
Priya: please add a migration note about the new RBAC capability and default deny behavior; also expand docs on audit retention.

Motivation: On-call automation needs a way to schedule runbooks to execute outside peak windows, run a non-destructive dry-run before live execution, and ensure safe automatic rollback when automation makes state changes. This PR adds a Deferred Playbook Executor that accepts scheduled windows and optional dry-run payloads, a scheduled dry-run runner that simulates playbook steps without side effects, and pluggable safe-rollback hooks that capture pre-change snapshots and provide an automated revert path. Key design points: (1) All deferred executions are stored as immutable scheduling tasks with idempotency tokens, (2) dry-run mode routes actions to a simulator layer that returns predicted outcomes and a list of mutated resources, (3) rollback hooks register resource snapshotters and revert actions, and (4) RBAC/feature-flag gating prevents accidental live scheduling. This change also adds telemetry (metrics and logs) for scheduled_task.created, scheduled_task.executed, dry_run.result, and rollback.invoked, plus tracing tags for schedule_id and runbook_id. Rollout: feature-flag gated, initial rollout to staging for 2 weeks with synthetic scheduled dry-run tests, then canary to 10% of production namespaces. See linked Linear items for acceptance criteria and SLO checks.
Diego Morales: Nice to see idempotency tokens; request: surface the schedule failure reason in UI events so SRE can triage quickly.
Author (Ava Chen): Added schedule_failure_reason field to the task store and included events emitted with failure metadata.
Priya Kapoor: Please add an explicit max-scheduled-tasks-per-namespace limit and a metric for throttled schedules.
Author (Ava Chen): Added config and metric scheduled_tasks.throttled_count; default limit 200 per namespace and can be overridden by admin settings.
Ethan Park: Danger: rollback snapshot size could be large for some resources — add safeguards and a TTL for snapshots.
Author (Ava Chen): Implemented snapshot TTL and size cap; large snapshots are stored in object storage with a short retention window and an audit log entry.
Unit tests added for scheduler, simulator, and rollback interfaces. Integration test harness simulates K8s resources and verifies dry-run returns no mutations while live run mutates resources and rollback restores state. Added e2e preflight CLI script 'tools/e2e/schedule_dryrun.sh'.
Dry-run mode prevents write operations by routing through an action simulator. RBAC checks are enforced at API layer; only users with 'runbook.schedule' permission can create deferred tasks. Snapshots stored in object storage are encrypted with customer KMS when available. Audit events emitted for schedule creation, execution, dry-run, and rollback.
1) Run DB migration 20250214_add_scheduled_tasks_table.sql; 2) Deploy object-storage credentials secret 'rollback-snapshots'; 3) Enable feature flag 'deferred_playbooks' in staging; 4) Run smoke scheduled dry-run jobs from CLI for two namespaces; 5) Promote flag to canary and monitor metrics for 48 hours.
When enabling the feature flag in production, ensure the scheduled_task store has been migrated and object storage credentials are configured for snapshot storage. Monitor scheduled_task.* metrics and dry_run.result outcomes during canary. If rollback.invoked rises unexpectedly, roll back the feature flag and inspect snapshot retention settings.
Added Deferred Playbook Executor with scheduled dry-runs, safe rollback hooks, telemetry for scheduled tasks, RBAC gating, and CLI examples. Feature-flag gated rollout.

Motivation: on-call teams have asked for a low-friction way to collect anonymized, structured telemetry about common triage patterns (commands run, top signals inspected, mean time-to-first-action) so we can surface repeatable playbook candidates and quiet-window suggestions. This PR adds an opt-in "oncall-habit-harvester" to incident-bot that captures compact provenance + anonymized event histograms and ships them to a customer-configurable sink. Privacy is the priority: no raw logs, deterministic hashing of identifiers, histogram aggregation, and a configurable redaction pipeline.

What this PR does (high-level):
- Adds a new CLI subcommand and background worker: incident-bot harvest start/stop/status. The worker aggregates events into per-shift buckets and emits periodic summaries.
- Implements a lightweight sampling layer that can operate in two modes: event-sampler (probabilistic) and behavior-aggregator (counts and top-k actions). Both modes support a customer-set sampling rate and an explicit allowlist for signal groups.
- Introduces an anonymization/redaction pipeline: stable salted hashes for user IDs, removal of known PII patterns, and token-level entropy checks to drop noisy, sensitive blobs.
- Adds telemetry metrics and traces: harvest.job.count, harvest.events.aggregated, harvest.redactions.skipped, harvest.ship.errors and tracing spans for harvest.lifecycle.
- Adds tests (unit + integration harness) and CLI docs with examples and upgrade notes.

Design decisions and privacy guards:
- Default is OFF. Customers must explicitly enable by setting harvest.enabled = true in incident-bot config or via CLI flag.
- No attachments or raw stack dumps are included in summaries; raw payloads are only used transiently inside the process and never persisted.
- Aggregation windows are coarse (default 4h) to avoid reconstructing individual sessions.
- Salt rotation: we support a rotation window; when rotated, older hashes are dropped from the aggregator to avoid long-lived linkability.

Files changed (high level):
- cmd/incident-bot/harvest.go - new CLI entry and runtime flags
- internal/harvest/worker.go - worker loop and aggregation logic
- internal/harvest/redact.go - redaction & hashing pipeline
- internal/harvest/sampler.go - sampling strategies and configuration
- docs/ops/harvest.md - admin-facing enablement and privacy FAQ
- test/integration/harvest_harness.go - ephemeral harness for end-to-end sampling tests
- pkg/metrics/harvest_metrics.go - new metrics exported to prometheus

Commits (summary):
- feat: add harvest CLI and worker scaffolding
- feat: implement probabilistic sampler and behavior aggregator
- feat: add redaction pipeline with black/allow lists and hashing
- test: integration harness for harvest pipeline and flakiness guards
- docs: admin enablement guide and privacy FAQ
- fix: retry logic for sink failures and graceful shutdown handling

Rollout and backward compatibility:
- no behavioral changes unless enabled. The new CLI is additive.
- Metrics use new names with a harvest.* prefix; dashboards should be added under the observability team guidance.
- If a customer enables the harvest sink but sink is misconfigured, worker will log a single incrementing error and back off; this prevents log storms and accidental data egress.

Testing and CI:
- Local unit tests for redaction rules and sampler determinism.
- Integration harness that starts a local sink and validates the aggregated payloads meet size/PII constraints.
- CI initially showed lint failure (flake: formatting in harvest.go) and a unit test race in the integration harness. Fixes: formatting, and a mutex around the test harness registry. Final CI run: all checks passed.

Operational runbook notes:
- harvest.enabled defaults to false; on enablement, ops should verify harvest.ship.success metric within first hour.
- Alert: harvest.ship.errors > 5 over 10m triggers a temp disable for that instance and an automatic ticket to the ops channel (kept intentionally conservative).

Migration plan:
- Documentation provides a minimal checklist for customers: enable flag, set sink endpoint, choose sampling mode, run in audit mode for 24h to review sanitized summaries.

Related work: ENG-5123 (triage pattern discovery), PM-204 (quiet-hours product spec). This PR implements the backend scaffold required by the PM deck and provides a conservative privacy-first default.

Next steps: add a lightweight UI in the oncall console to visualize per-shift summaries and export candidate playbook snippets (follow-up PR).
Adds an opt-in on-call habit harvester and privacy-first telemetry sampler for incident-burst analysis. Default sampling is off; opt-in required. Includes new CLI, docs, and metrics.
Priya Patel: Nice end-to-end. Two privacy questions: 1) Why remove attachments instead of offering a configurable allowlist? 2) Can we make salt rotation explicit in the config and mention retention in the docs?
Morgan Lee: Good points. We intentionally exclude attachments by default to avoid accidental exfil. I've added an allowed-attachments list behind an "allow_attachments" admin flag and documented the risks. Salt rotation is configurable and documented; defaults to 90 days.
Ravi Singh: Code looks fine. Left a couple of nit comments about error messages in worker.go and a race on the test harness. Also: prefer smaller default aggregation window for dedicated deployments (opt-in override).
Morgan Lee: Addressed nit comments; added aggregation.window override and clarified behavior in comments. Fixed mutex on harness.
Dana Ortiz: CI flake fixed. Integration run passed locally. Approved pending a short changelog entry.
Priya Patel: Approved — privacy FAQ is clear and admin-facing examples look good.

Context and motivation: On-call responders often see runbooks/playbooks that either assume telemetry that doesn't exist for the service, or include remediation steps that are costly or irreversible. This PR introduces a telemetry-aware playbook scoring engine plus a small staged auto-remediation framework to make playbooks safer and easier to evaluate (ENG-4521). The change focuses on three user problems: 1) quickly surface gaps between a playbook's assumptions and the telemetry actually available; 2) estimate the operational cost/risk of executing each step; 3) provide a gated staged-remediation runner that enforces safety checks and provides automated undo suggestions.

What this PR does (summary): - Adds a new playbook-scoring service under incident-bot/services/playbook_scoreer that computes a 0-100 score per playbook based on telemetry coverage, action risk, average execution cost (time/queries/calls), and a confidence metric when telemetry is incomplete. - Introduces a small staged remediation runner (incident-bot/runner/staged_runner) that executes playbook steps in discrete stages with preflight checks, simulated dry-run capability, and automatic undo-step registration when a step is annotated with "undo:" metadata. - Adds a git-hook / GitHub Action (ci/playbook_score_check.yml) which runs the scorer on any modified playbook YAML in PRs and blocks merges below a configurable threshold. - Includes a tiny CLI (bin/ib-playbook-score) for on-call engineers to locally score and simulate playbooks against a target environment (supports --dry-run and --simulate-cost flags). - Adds lightweight schema extensions to playbooks to declare telemetry expectations and cost hints (docs/playbook_schema.md).

Implementation notes: - Scorer uses a three-part signal: telemetry_presence, step_risk_model, and historical_execution_stats. Telemetry presence is computed by matching required metrics/logs/traces declared in the playbook against the telemetry index service (a contributed adapter; not changing the core telemetry index). Step risk leverages a small rule set mapping actions (restart, rollback, db-migrate, toggle-feature) to risk buckets; teams can extend via playbook metadata. Historical stats are optional and used only when present to improve cost estimates. - Staged runner enforces timeouts per stage and records a reversible action list when playbook authors provide undo instructions. The runner exposes a JSON-serializable execution trace that can be attached to incidents for postmortem and cost accounting. - The GitHub Action executes the scorer inside a PyPI-packaged wheel we publish to the repo GH package registry; action fails fast on missing telemetry adapter but can be configured to warn in non-blocking mode.

Commits (high-level): - commit 1: scaffold service + CLI entrypoint and schema docs - commit 2: implement telemetry presence matcher and risk model - commit 3: add staged runner with dry-run mode and trace format - commit 4: add GitHub Action + unit tests - commit 5: fix lint and type issues, add reviewer-requested telemetry adapter fallback

Files changed (high level): - services/playbook_scorer/* (core scoring logic, tests) - runner/staged_runner/* (executor, dry-run, undo registration) - bin/ib-playbook-score (CLI wrapper) - ci/playbook_score_check.yml (GitHub Action) - docs/playbook_schema.md (new schema and examples) - examples/sample_playbooks/* (two annotated example playbooks) - tests/integration/test_scoring_pipeline.py - README updates in incident-bot/README.md

Example usage: ib-playbook-score score examples/sample_playbooks/db_incident.yml --simulate-cost --output report.json; the report includes score breakdown: telemetry_coverage: 62, step_risk_median: 28, estimated_cost_seconds: 420, confidence: low.

Review conversation (condensed): - Arjun Patel (2026-02-11): "Nice direction. Two asks: 1) make the action undo annotation mandatory only for high-risk actions; 2) ensure the GH Action can be opt-out per repo via .github/config.yml". Author reply (Maya Chen 2026-02-12): "Implemented conditional enforcement (configurable threshold) and added repo opt-out config; updated docs and tests." - Lena Rodriguez (2026-02-13): "Can the runner operate in a sandboxed namespace for K8s actions? Concerned about accidental deletes." Author reply (Maya Chen 2026-02-14): "Added --sandbox flag and a K8s dry-run adapter that uses server-side dry run + mock apply to validate undo steps. See runner adapters." - Tomás Silva (2026-02-15): "CI initially failing lint and type checks; after fixes looks good. Please add a small metric for playbook_score_histogram to help product analyze distribution." Author reply (Maya Chen 2026-02-15): "Added playbook_score_histogram metric and dashboard stub in observability-pack/queries.md".

CI and checks: - Initial run: lint failed (flake8-coded style and a mypy issue) - After commit 5: all unit tests pass, integration tests for scorer run in ~40s on CI runner, lint and type checks pass - Final CI status: pass. Action run also validated the examples.

Backward compatibility and safety: This PR does not change runtime APIs used by incident-bot other than adding an optional telemetry adapter interface. Playbook schema extensions are additive and the GitHub Action is opt-out via repo config. Staged runner is opt-in: playbooks must include a new 'runner: staged' annotation to be executed by the staged runner. Undo steps are recommended for high-risk steps; enforcement is configurable.

Migration and rollout plan: - Soft launch: Add GH Action in warn-only mode for three internal infra repos for 2 weeks to gather score distribution. - Opt-in: recommended for teams building automated remediations; provide training doc and two example playbooks. - Block mode: enable enforce mode for critical infra repos once recommended score threshold is stabilized.

Testing performed: Unit tests for scoring heuristics (coverage and edge cases), integration test that runs scorer against synthetic telemetry datasets, manual validation of staged runner against a k8s test cluster (sandbox mode), and smoke tests for CLI.

Known limitations and follow-ups: - Current cost models are heuristic-based; follow-up work tracked in ENG-4590 to plug realtime execution metrics pipeline to refine estimates. - Telemetry adapter coverage must be improved for some legacy services; added a ticket SRE-1084 to onboard missing indices. - Will follow up with analytics dashboard to visualize playbook score trends and to correlate with incident MTTR (SRE-1070).

Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main by Arjun Patel after approvals from all reviewers and final CI green. Changelog entry and release notes pushed to docs/releases/2026-02.md.
Adds an automated playbook scoring engine that surface coverage gaps, estimated execution cost, and proposes gated staged-remediations with safe undo steps. Includes a GitHub Action check and a lightweight CLI to run scores locally.
CLI and GitHub Action added; internal rollout plan included in PR body. See ENG-4521 and SRE-1070 for followups.

Motivation: on-call engineers repeatedly ask for a compact, executable runbook that is generated from incident context (alerts, recent errors, and top traces). This PR adds a lightweight CLI and an incident-bot integration that synthesizes a short runbook (commands, prioritized checks, and escalation steps) and an optional contextual diagnostics payload. Key goals: 1) reduce time-to-first-action for pagers, 2) avoid noise by surfacing only high-confidence runbook steps, 3) keep sensitive traces private by opt-in sampling and obfuscation. What this PR includes: - incident-bot: new /runbook action that can be invoked via Slack or REST to generate a runbook based on the incident object. The generated runbook is markdown with actionable shell snippets and suggested queries. - oncall-cli: a small commandline tool (go) that accepts an incident id or JSON blob and emits a runbook to stdout or a file. Useful for SREs who prefer terminal workflows and for automation in runbooks-as-code. - diagnostics contextualizer: a module that collects top-N spans and error messages, applies configurable redaction rules (email, PII, long stack frames), and summarizes probable root-cause signals. - opt-in privacy flow: traces and logs are only attached when the incident has `attach_diagnostics: true` or when the user requests via Slack button. By default we provide only metadata and pointers to SLOs/dashboards. - tests: unit tests for CLI parsing, diagnostics obfuscation rules, and runbook templates; end-to-end integration test that exercises Slack flow (mocked). - docs: update docs/runbooks.md with examples and a short security note. Backwards compatibility: existing /triage and /runbook-short commands are unchanged; this new flow is additive. Checklist: - [x] CLI implementation and build script - [x] Slack command + REST endpoint - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Documentation updates - [x] Privacy/obfuscation review Notes and limitations: - The generated runbook is intentionally conservative (3 prioritized steps max) to avoid prescriptive automation. - Diagnostics attachments are limited to 10MB; larger payloads fall back to links. - This PR wires in a dependency on the slo-toolkit helper for SLO metadata lookup; that is a lightweight, vendored package.
