Context: As part of the Reliability Program “Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping”, we’re making incident_type a required field at incident creation time, and we want the bot to resolve an owner team consistently (single primary owner) to reduce time-to-engage and improve reporting quality.

This PR updates the Slack modal + slash command flow to require incident_type and incident_subtype (from the v1 allowlist), then performs owner resolution (type/subtype -> primary owner + escalation channel) and posts the result into the incident channel. The goal is: (1) classification is required and auditable, (2) owner is consistently derived from a versioned mapping, and (3) the IC gets an immediate “who owns this” + “where to escalate” suggestion.

User-facing changes:
- /incident create now blocks submission until incident_type is selected.
- incident_subtype is required when the type has subtypes; otherwise the field is hidden.
- After incident is created, bot posts a short summary: incident_type/subtype, resolved owner team, escalation channel, and a reminder that IC can override classification if needed.
- If mapping is missing (e.g., new subtype), we fall back to SRE on-call owner and label classification as “needs-mapping”; bot also files a lightweight internal warning event.

Implementation notes:
- Added TaxonomyAllowlist (static JSON in-repo for now) with strict validation + display labels.
- Added OwnerResolver that consults the mapping (fetched via config service; local fallback for dev/test).
- Added “override owner” admin-only action in the incident channel (logs audit event; does not change the canonical mapping).
- Added structured fields to incident record: incident_type, incident_subtype, owner_team, escalation_channel, owner_resolution_source.

Out of scope:
- Auto-suggest incident_type from symptoms (tracked separately).
- Retrofitting historical incidents (backfill job lives in redwood/observability).

Rollout:
- Behind feature flag: incident_taxonomy_required_fields.
- Enabled for eng-sre workspace first; then global after 1 week if no issues.

Checklist:
- [x] Slack modal validation for required fields
- [x] Owner resolution + fallback behavior
- [x] Audit/event logging for overrides
- [x] Unit tests for allowlist parsing + resolver
- [x] E2E test for create flow
- [x] Docs snippet in /help output

Screenshots/GIF: attached in PR (Slack modal with incident_type dropdown + subtype conditional).
Rafael Mendes (review): We need to be strict about low-cardinality values. Can we guarantee incident_type/subtype only come from an allowlist, and that freeform is impossible via API? Also please ensure the incident record stores the canonical key, not the display label.
Devon Price (author): Yep. Modal options come from taxonomy_allowlist_v1.json; command handler re-validates keys server-side (rejects unknown). Stored fields are canonical keys (e.g., "capacity_fleet_shortage"), display labels are only for Slack UI.
Allison Grant (review): Please add a hard fallback bucket for unknown mappings that doesn’t explode metrics. Suggest: owner_resolution_source="fallback_sre" and incident_type stays as selected, but add needs_mapping=true (internal only). Also confirm we’re not adding subtype as a metric label anywhere in this repo.
Devon Price (author): Implemented needs_mapping as an internal incident attribute; emitted an internal warning event for SRE tooling but no new metrics labels here. Owner resolution source is one of: config, local_fallback, fallback_sre.
Ethan Park (review): For owner mapping, please confirm cache behavior + failure modes. If config service is down we shouldn’t block incident creation. Also, can you align the mapping schema with the control plane versioning approach (ENG-4825)?
Devon Price (author): Resolver never blocks creation. If mapping fetch fails, we fall back to SRE and note owner_resolution_source. Schema matches the draft fields (type/subtype -> owner_team, escalation_channel, runbook_url optional). We’ll swap client to control-plane-backed endpoint once that’s live; tracking in ENG-4825.
Dev Patel (review): From Support/CS POV, escalation channel names should be stable and non-ambiguous (e.g., #eng-fleet-oncall vs #fleet). Can we enforce format + add a note that CS should not use the override action?
Devon Price (author): Added validation that escalation channels must start with # and match a configured allowlist prefix. Override action is restricted to admin role; updated README operator notes to clarify intended use (IC/SRE only).
Dylan Brooks (review): Small UX request: in the incident summary message, include a one-liner: "If classification is unclear, pick best match and add contributing factors in notes". This will reduce folks choosing “unknown” by default.
Devon Price (author): Added the guidance line + link to the decision tree doc (placeholder URL for now; will update when Confluence page is finalized).
Rafael Mendes (approval): LGTM. Thanks for adding server-side validation + non-blocking fallback. Please coordinate rollout window with SRE on-call so we can watch for modal failures (INT-772 history).
Devon Price (author): Ack; will enable flag in eng-sre workspace Monday 10am PT and monitor #eng-sre + internal error dashboard.

Motivation: during on-call war rooms we repeatedly lose time mapping which downstream services will be impacted and what safe mitigations (rate-limit, proxy fallback, read-only-mode) are viable. This PR adds a lightweight oncall dependency mapper service and a 'fallback fabric' suggestion layer that integrates with incident-bot's runbook recommender so responders get ranked, actionable fallback options alongside evidence. Summary: 1) dep-mapper: agent and aggregator that consumes service topology from service-registry and lightweight span-sampling (optional) to build a real-time dependency graph with health annotations; 2) fallback-fabric: rules engine that synthesizes safe mitigation suggestions (proxy failover, degraded routes, client-side throttles) based on dependency blast radius, traffic patterns, and configured safety policies; 3) incident-bot integration: runbook payloads now include a "Fallback candidates" section with confidence scores and automated rollback notes; 4) config and kill-switches: feature flag + per-team opt-out; 5) observability: new metrics, traces, and a small dashboard added. Checklist: - [x] unit tests for dep graph builder - [x] integration tests for rule engine - [x] e2e local simulation harness - [x] docs/ops guidance and playbook examples - [x] rollout plan and feature flag gating Backwards compatibility: default behavior preserved — suggestions are read-only until operator triggers a mitigation. Security & safety: all automated actions are advisory by default; hard mitigations require explicit oncall confirmation and RBAC check. See linked Linear ENG-7886 for design notes and SUP-3472 for an on-call incident that motivated the feature.
Luca Romano: Can we ensure the dep-mapper honors environment-level privacy flags? We should redact sensitive service metadata before storage.
Asha Kapoor: Agreed, added a redaction step in collector.go and tests (see commit e8a2c00).
Priya Das: Requested a unit test for the rule engine that covers chained fallbacks (proxy -> read-only). Also ask for throttling safety limits to be configurable per team.

Jordan Lee: CI flake on the e2e harness, appears to be timeout. Can we make the simulation harness retry on transient network errors?

Motivation: On-call handoffs often arrive with large telemetry attachments and ambiguous next steps. This PR introduces a compact telemetry compressor and a humanized handoff note generator to reduce payload size, remove PII, and provide a cognitive-load estimate and a canary-safe rollback playbook seeded from the collected snapshot. The snapshot collector produces a small 'repro trailer' containing minimal trace slices, top-k logs by error signature, sampled heap/disk metadata and a KV diff bundle. The compressor uses a delta-based rolling window (inspired by rsync-style chunking) plus optional gzip fallback to guarantee size and decompression determinism across platforms. The handoff note generator templates the critical actions, suggested playbook steps, and a short 'operator confidence' metric based on recent similar incidents and successful mitigations. Implementation: adds a new CLI verb incidentctl snapshot gather --compress --seed-playbook and a library package pkg/snapshot with Collector, Compressor and Trailer types. A separate pkg/handoff contains the seeder that turns a trailer into a markdown handoff and an optional canary rollback playbook with explicit verify steps and automated guard rails. Security and privacy: redaction is performed by pkg/sanitize with configurable KMS-backed rules and a strict opt-in flag for payload upload to shared storage. Backwards compatibility: the compressor emits a stable v1 blob header; receivers without decompressor will still get an uncompressed JSON summary. Tests: end-to-end tests simulate 3 incident shapes, compression roundtrip checks, and a small fuzz harness for redaction rules. CI: initial run surfaced a flaky TestHandoffTemplate which was fixed by adding deterministic timestamping in tests. Rationale and impact: expected to reduce average snapshot upload size by 6x for verbose cases, speed up multi-region handoffs, and reduce cognitive overhead for the next responder through structured notes. Commit summary: see commits field. Files changed: see files_changed list. Review: requested tighter PII redaction and explicit opt-in semantics, added audit logs for redaction decisions, added unit tests for compressor edge cases, approved after second iteration. Merge: squash merged to main after CI green and two approvals. Related work: referenced ENG-1423 for handoff UX and SRE-88 for snapshot retention policy. Manual rollout: feature gated behind INCIDENT_SNAPSHOT_V2 and off by default in hosted instance.

Maya Chen: Added a synthetic payload test and optimized chunk window to avoid pathological memory use.

Motivation: On large incidents the incident-bot collects large evidence bundles and the runbook list grows with many low-value, stale playbooks. This inflates on-call load, slows handoffs, and increases S3 storage costs. This PR introduces two cooperating subsystems: 1) an Ephemeral Evidence Curator that captures short-lived diagnostic snapshots ( TTL-limited, compressed, and indexed) and exposes a compact summary to handoffs; 2) a Runbook Pruning Engine that applies safety-first heuristics to hide low-utility runbook variants from default handoffs while keeping them discoverable in advanced views. Both features are opt-in and guarded by a canary flag for incremental rollout.
What this PR does (high level):
- Add internal/collector/curator.go: ephemeral snapshot capture, compression, metadata index, TTL enforcement, and a lightweight tokenized summary used in handoff cards.
- Add internal/runbook/pruner.go: pruning policies (age, signal weight, failure rate, manual votes), a conservative default policy, and safe unprune hooks for diagnostics.
- Wire curator into cmd/incident-bot/main.go to emit ephemeral evidence handles instead of embedding full artifacts in primary handoff messages.
- Add pkg/evidence/storage.go with in-memory + S3 fallback eviction strategy and metrics for ephemeral retention and eviction counts.
- Tests: unit coverage for pruning rules and curator TTL eviction; integration test that verifies handoff payload size reduction.
- Docs: docs/runbook-pruning.md describing policy knobs and operational playbooks for rollback.
Checklist:
- [x] Design review: architecture doc linked in Linear ENG-3241
- [x] Unit tests for core pruning heuristics
- [x] Integration test for end-to-end flow (collector -> curator -> handoff)
- [x] Metrics and tracing hooks added
- [x] Docs and runbook for operators
- [x] Canary gating in feature flags
Commit summary:
- 1a2b3c4: initial curator IPC and TTL store
- 2b3c4d5: runbook pruner core heuristics and policy interface
- 3c4d5e6: wire curator into handoff pipeline, replace raw attachments with ephemeral handles
- 4d5e6f7: add S3 fallback and eviction metrics
- 5e6f7g8: docs and test fixes, canary config
Files touched (high level):
- cmd/incident-bot/main.go - add curator bootstrap and feature flag check
- internal/collector/curator.go - ephemeral capture + summarizer
- internal/runbook/pruner.go - pruning engine and policy registry
- pkg/evidence/storage.go - TTL store + s3 fallback
- test/fixtures/ephemeral_snapshot.json - sample snapshot payloads for tests
- docs/runbook-pruning.md - operator-facing docs and rollback playbook
Small diff snippets (illustrative):
- internal/runbook/pruner.go: added PolicyEvaluator interface and SafeUnprune(handleID string) method
- cmd/incident-bot/main.go: replaced SendHandoff(artifact) -> SendHandoff(artifact.Handle)
Performance and safety notes:
- Handoff payloads are reduced by ~78% in our synthetic canary (median payload 1.9KB -> 420B), cutting transfer latency by ~120ms on handoff-heavy workflows.
- The pruner defaults to a conservative policy: never auto-prune runbooks with >3 recent successful uses or those explicitly pinned by a responder vote. Pruning only hides runbooks from default handoffs; they remain discoverable through the "advanced" menu and via API.
- Ephemeral evidence has a default TTL of 24h, configurable per-tenant; curator emits metrics: evidence.curator.retained, evidence.curator.evicted, runbook.pruner.pruned_count.
- Safe-unprune is implemented: any pruned runbook can be unpruned by on-call via the UI or by a direct API call that also triggers a diagnostic snapshot reattach.
Review thread (abridged):
- Arjun Patel (reviewer): "Nice separation of concerns. Two asks: (1) add integration test for S3 fallback eviction; (2) ensure pruner decisions are logged with deterministic hashes so we can correlate later." 
- Maya Chen (author): "Added new integration test for S3 fallback and deterministic decision log (see commit 4d5e6f7). Also left TODO to expose TTL metrics per-tenant; will follow up in a small patch."
- Liam O'Connor (reviewer): "Can we add a feature flag to make pruning read-only first (i.e. annotate runbooks with pruned=true but not remove them)? That'll make rollback safer for enterprise tenants." 
- Maya Chen: "Good idea — implemented read-only mode behind flag incident.pruner.readOnly (default false for canary). See main.go changes."
- Sofia Martinez (approver): "Verified canary in staging: pruner hid ~12 low-value runbooks and curator reduced handoff noise. Approving after CI green." 
CI and merging:
- CI matrix: unit (go test), lint (golangci-lint), integration (small infra fixture), e2e smoke on staging (canary enabled). Initial lint failed for a few exported comments; fixed in 5e6f7g8. Integration passed on rerun.
- CI summary: unit: pass, lint: pass, integration: pass, e2e-staging: pass
- Merge method: squash and merge. Squash commit message: "ephemeral evidence curator + safe runbook pruner (ENG-3241)"
Operational rollout plan:
- Day 0: merge to main with feature flags off.
- Canary week: enable incident.curator.canary=true for 10% of tenants; monitor evidence.curator.evicted and handoff.size reduction.
- Week 2: enable runbook pruning in read-only mode for 20% of tenants and gather responder feedback.
- Week 4: flip pruning to active mode for trusted tenants; provide operator toggle to disable per-tenant.
Rollback and safety:
- The curator stores full artifacts in S3 until TTL; if immediate rollback needed we can rehydrate attachments from S3 using evidence handles.
- Pruner supports readOnly and a per-tenant opt-out. We added an operator playbook in docs/runbook-pruning.md that describes steps to unprune and reattach runbook artifacts.
Notes and follow-ups:
- Follow-up ticket to add runbook usage telemetry to the telemetry dashboard for easier product feedback (Linear ENG-3305).
- Consider introducing a small ML model to classify runbook usefulness using responder feedback signals (future work).
Merge outcome: Squash merged by Maya Chen on 2026-02-18 after approvals and green CI.
Adds ephemeral evidence collection and a safe runbook pruning step to limit on-call cognitive load; opt-in via config and behind a canary flag.

Motivation: In production we observed two classes of failures when using the OpenAI compatibility layer for function/tool calling: 1) streaming fragmentation could cause transient, inconsistent 'tool_choice' decisions when partial fragments arrived at the runtime, and 2) heterogeneous tool schemas (legacy function defs from older integrations) created noisy mappings that increased false positives for tool selection and made deterministic repros difficult. This PR introduces a compatibility bridge and a deterministic path to stabilize tool selection during streaming and to normalize tool/function schemas for downstream consumers.

What this change does (summary): canonicalizes tool schemas at ingress, introduces a compact tool_choice_v2 envelope with deterministic tie-break semantics, and adds a streaming coalescer that protects the tool selection decision from transient fragment reorder/partial updates. The compatibility bridge performs non-destructive mapping from legacy function signatures to the canonical runtime shape; mappings are recorded as schema provenance metadata that flows with the request for auditability.

Key user-visible behavior: clients using the OpenAI-compatible /v1/ functions/tool-call surface should see no breaking changes. On the server side, tool invocations are more stable during streaming: we avoid flip-flopping tool choices mid-response, and we attach provenance and schema_hash metadata to each resolved invocation. Feature rollout is behind the openai.invoke_compat_v2 feature flag.

Implementation notes: the PR touches three logical areas: api/openai_adapter (compat bridge and normalizer), serving/stream (coalescing and boundary markers), and serving/dispatch (deterministic tool_choice resolver). The resolver uses a deterministic ranking key composed of (rank_score, schema_hash, provenance_age, deterministic_fallback_counter) to ensure always-reproducible selection across replays. The streaming coalescer implements a short (configurable) stabilization window for tool choice decisions that merges adjacent fragments unless a final 'invoke_commit' marker is received. This keeps latency impact minimal while preventing false mid-stream choice flips.

Testing and telemetry: added unit tests for the normalizer, fuzz tests that validate deterministic resolver properties, and integration tests that exercise fragmented-stream scenarios with reorder and partial frames. Benchmarks show the stabilization window introduces ~1.1ms median added latency in the worst-case path and reduces choice flip rate by ~98% on our canary workload. New telemetry events (tool.choice_resolved, tool.schema_mapped, tool.choice_stabilized) are emitted to assist rollout monitoring.

Migration notes: platform teams do not need to change function definitions, but large integrators that previously relied on ad-hoc parameter shapes should validate the canonical mapping. The compatibility bridge logs any lossy mappings to the audit log and surfaces suggested schema fixes in the Console guidance panel.

Related tasks: ENG-4312 (compat bridge), ENG-4400 (stream coalescer), PM-217 (rollout plan), SRE-98 (canary and alerting).

Maya Chen: Added tie-break unit test and updated tool_choice.go to prefer schema_hash before provenance_age; pushed fix.

Sofia Patel: Approved after CI green and two approvals. Noted that SRE should watch tool.choice_stabilized alerts during rollout.
Improves stability of OpenAI-compatible function/tool invocations during streaming. Adds a canonical schema mapping layer and deterministic tool_choice resolution to prevent mid-stream flips. No breaking changes to the public /v1/ function/tool-call API. Operators: enable 'openai.invoke_compat_v2' feature flag and monitor 'tool.choice_stabilized' telemetry. See docs/openai_compat_migration.md for mapping guidance.
Unit tests added for normalizer and resolver (coverage +7%), fuzz test found and fixed a reorder bug, integration tests simulate fragmented streams and validate no mid-stream tool flips. CI flake: one intermittent e2e timeout was rerun and passed.

payload.body:
Motivation: paging fatigue from repetitive low-value alerts continues to erode oncall bandwidth. This change adds an adaptive pager-suppression subsystem to incident-bot that builds and uses per-service noise profiles to decide when to suppress, group, or throttle notifications. Key goals: reduce noisy low-action pages by ~40% in a test cohort, provide clear feedback to oncall (why a page was suppressed), and make suppression policies configurable and auditable.

What this PR does: 
- Adds a lightweight noise profiler that accumulates sketch summaries of alert fingerprints (hash, signature dimensions) and computes short-window noise scores (noise_rate, dedupe_entropy, throttle_suggestion).
- Implements an adaptive suppression policy engine that can: suppress (no page), group (single consolidated page for an incident burst), or debounce (delay page by Xs) based on policy rules and the noise score. Policies are evaluated per-service and fall back to org defaults.
- Adds a user feedback loop: suppressed pages include a one-click feedback link which updates the profiling signals (helpful/not-helpful) and is exposed to SRE dashboards.
- Integrates the profiler with slo-toolkit so teams can import noise budgets and weight suppression aggressiveness by SLO risk.
- Exposes runtime metrics and trace hooks to aid debugging and post-incident analysis.
- CLI flags and runtime config documented for ops teams, with safe opt-out (disable suppression per service).

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc linked in PR (Linear ENG-2914)
- [x] Unit tests for policy engine and profiler aggregation
- [x] e2e smoke test exercising suppression path + feedback loop
- [x] Metrics (Prometheus) and tracing instrumentation added
- [x] Docs: incident-bot README + onboarding note in docs/incidents/

Notes: the algorithm deliberately uses approximate sketches to bound memory and keep profiler replica-safe. This PR is conservative about default aggressiveness and ships with a 30-day telemetry-only mode before auto-suppression is engaged (configurable).

Related links: Linear ENG-2914, RFC: /docs/rfcs/2024/noise-profiling.md, internal dashboard: /dashboards/ops/noise-profile-summary

Release notes: see release_notes field.
Priya Nair: Nice approach. Can you add a brief note on how the sketch parameters were chosen and whether they adapt to cardinality?
Ava Chen: Responded - added comments and a short helper to autoscale sketch buckets based on rolling cardinality; leaving defaults conservative.
Elliot Brooks: Please ensure the feedback link does not leak any PII; verify telemetry scrubber runs before storing signals.
Ava Chen: Confirmed - scrubber added to feedback pipeline and tests updated.
Samir Patel: CI flaked on lint on first run; rerun resolved it. Approving after e2e green.
Maintainer (Roberto Diaz): Merged via squash after approvals.
- Adds adaptive pager suppression using noise profiling.
- Integrates suppression decisions with SLO noise budgets (via slo-toolkit).
- New metrics: incidentbot_noise_rate, incidentbot_suppressed_pages_total, incidentbot_feedback_ratio.
- Safe-default: starts in telemetry-only mode for 30 days unless enabled.

Ops: Use charts/incident-bot/values.yaml to opt into suppression per-service.

payload.body:
Motivation: On-call rotations often require reconstructing a short lived diagnostic session (logs, traces, selected metrics, and the sequence of investigation steps) so that a responder can replay and validate mitigations without having to re-run noisy or expensive data pulls. This PR adds a lightweight "trace-replay" component and a small templating runner for scripted callouts (actions that suggest the next steps to responders). The implementation focuses on: compact, auditable session manifests, safe dry-run execution, and an embeddable UI player for post-incident review.

What this PR does (high level):
- Introduces a session manifest format (JSON) that packages an ordered list of diagnostic artifacts (trace snippets, metric snapshots, logs pointers, and recommended CLI commands).
- Adds a trace-replay service that can reconstruct a timeline view and step through artifacts in the web UI; supports playback speed, step annotations, and jump-to-event.
- Adds callout templates (YAML) and a runner that renders templates with session context and can enqueue human-facing notifications (Slack/Email) or show inline suggestions in the player.
- Adds server-side validation and a safe-execution mode: callout runner supports only whitelisted action types and will never execute destructive commands in non-admin contexts.
- Adds unit + integration tests, and a small docs page with usage and example manifests.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc linked (Linear ENG-1124).
- [x] Session manifest schema stable (v1).
- [x] Safe runner mode & whitelist implemented.
- [x] Tests for replay logic + template rendering.
- [x] UI player with keyboard controls.

Usage notes: To create a replayable session, produce a manifest (examples/docs/trace-replay.md). Upload via the incident-bot API (POST /v1/sessions) or attach to an incident. The player can be opened from the incident timeline and supports exporting the manifest for offline review. Callout templates live under src/templates and can be previewed in the UI.

Security & operational constraints:
- Callout templates are evaluated server-side but only support safe rendering variables and pre-approved delivery channels.
- The runner includes a dry-run flag to prevent accidental side-effects during drills.
- Session manifests do not store raw sensitive logs by default; they point to redacted storage locations. Users must opt into full log capture and provide consent.

Related changes and links: Linear ENG-1124; SRE-73. Design notes: ./docs/design/trace-replay.md. Demo recording: internal link to recording.

Migration: This is backward compatible. Old incidents without manifests are unaffected. The manifest schema includes a version field for future migration.

Rollout plan: feature gated behind `trace_replay.enabled` config flag. Enable in staging, run warm-up traffic, then flip for small oncall group before broader rollout.
Marek Novak (reviewer): Overall looks good. Two concerns: 1) whitelist maintenance model for callout actions; 2) ensure manifest pointers never leak S3 credentials. Can we centralize the whitelist in pkg/config and add an automated alert when new action types are added?
Asha Desai (author): Answered - moved whitelist into pkg/config and added a small CI check that fails when new action types are introduced without a corresponding config entry. Also updated docs to explicitly state we only store pointer metadata (no credentials).
Jordan Li (reviewer): Suggested improving test coverage around race conditions in the timeline stepping (rapid forward/back). Added a small integration test that simulates concurrent step commands. CI showed a timing flake, I tuned the backoff in the player code.

Sofia Martínez (reviewer): UX nit: keyboard shortcut should use 'n'/'p' instead of arrow keys for accessibility. Also requested that callout preview render sanitized markdown. Made both changes and added automated sanitizer in the renderer.

Marek Novak (approver): Approved after changes. Ran a manual end-to-end in staging; player worked and callout dry-run mode prevented side effects.
Adds a replayable diagnostic session manifest and embeddable player in the incident timeline. Introduces safe callout templates with a server-side runner and whitelist enforcement. Feature is gated behind the trace_replay.enabled config flag.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: On-call teams are overwhelmed by low-impact recurring alerts that consume cognitive bandwidth but do not represent material customer impact. This PR implements a probabilistic alert-impact scorer and an adaptive quiet-window mechanism that dynamically suppresses low-likelihood, low-impact repeats while preserving immediate escalation for high-impact signals. Key ideas: compute per-alert posterior impact probability by combining SLI deltas, error-rate magnitude, failing shard cardinality, and inferred customer-facing weight using a lightweight Bayesian prior and feature-normalization; use a short-term adaptive quiet-window that grows with repeated low-impact occurrences and decays faster when upstream error fraction increases; provide explicit safety gates (minimum retention count, per-service opt-out, manual override) and an audit trail so suppressed events are recorded and can be surfaced to oncall during post-incident reviews. What changed: 1) core scorer service: incident-bot/score/prob_impact.py - new scoring pipeline with pluggable feature transforms and a small distilled model for on-device inference; 2) suppression controller: incident-bot/suppression/adaptive_window.go - adaptive state machine that tracks occurrence history and computes suggested suppression durations with exponential backoff and jitter; 3) telemetry hooks: metrics added (incidentbot.prob_impact.score, incidentbot.suppression.duration_suggested, incidentbot.suppression.suppressed_count) and traces for decision paths; 4) config and rollout: incident-bot/config/schema.yaml adds feature flags and per-service thresholds; 5) simulation harness: tools/alert-sim/runner.py to run replay experiments against historical alerts to estimate false-suppress/false-pass tradeoffs; 6) console: small UI cards and dashboard panels wired in observability-pack/dashboards/quiet_window.json to visualize suppression churn and missed-high-impact regressions; 7) docs: a single-page operational guide with examples and escalation flows. Safety and rollout: feature is opt-in per-service, default off. CI includes integration tests that replay a small anonymized alert history to validate suppression decision boundaries and a canary job that runs the scorer in a constrained environment. Checklist: - [x] core scoring algorithm implemented with unit tests - [x] suppression state machine with persistence and TTL handling - [x] telemetry events and dashboards wired - [x] simulation harness and a first-pass replay recorded - [x] documentation and runbook additions - [x] reviewers addressed comments and edge cases - [x] feature gated behind config flag and rollout steps documented Related work: follows discussion in ENG-1245 and complements the noisy-alert attenuator in slo-toolkit; incident where noisy cache-miss alerts flooded a pager on 2025-11-07 motivated the design. Links: Linear ENG-1245, replay artifacts: tools/alert-sim/recordings/2025-11-07.json. Testing notes: unit and integration suites passed locally; CI initially failed a flakey tracing test and was rerun; final CI green. Migration notes: no DB migration required beyond adding an optional suppression table (non-blocking), default retention 7d. Operational play: oncall can toggle suppressions per-service, and a manual "resurface" action sends suppressed events into a briefing queue. Rollout plan included in the PR description below.
Adds a probabilistic impact scoring model and adaptive quiet-window feature to reduce alert noise while preserving high-impact signal. Includes metrics, dashboards and a simulation harness. Backwards compatible and off by default; opt-in via incident-bot config.
Ben Matthews: The Bayesian prior feels sensible but can we surface the feature importance in logs for the first deploy? Requested: add a debug flag to emit feature weights.
Priya Shah: Added debug flag and a sampling mode to only log 0.1% of decisions in prod; updated tests to assert debug output shape.
Lina Ortega: Please ensure suppression durations never exceed SLA-mapped maxima. Requested change: cap duration by service SLA metadata.
Priya Shah: Added cap based on service metadata with a fallback default; documented behavior in schema.yaml and runbook.
Marco Ruiz: Approved after minor nits (typo in runbook and a missing metric label).
Marco Ruiz: Merged — squash merge by Priya Shah at 2026-03-02 17:24:12 UTC.

payload.body:
Adds a pre-merge runbook linter and a non-destructive sidecar sanity prober to reduce on-call friction and prevent dangerous runbook edits. Motivation: multiple post-incident rollbacks were traced to malformed or incomplete runbook steps (missing timeouts, missing rollbacks, plaintext secrets in examples). The linter enforces a small, opinionated policy surface (timeouts, required rollback step, redaction checks, approved command whitelist) and integrates as a fast GitHub Action. The sidecar prober runs as a staging-only job that exercises read-only telemetry queries and zero-impact verification of expected artifacts referenced by the runbook (config maps, dashboards, alert selectors) so we catch mismatches before a runbook is merged.

What changed (summary):
- New CLI tool `rb-lint` (Go) with rules: RULE_TIMEOUT_PRESENT, RULE_ROLLBACK_PRESENT, RULE_REDACT_EXAMPLES, RULE_WHITELISTED_CMDS. CLI returns machine-readable JSON and human-friendly summary.
- GitHub Action `runbook-lint.yml` that runs `rb-lint` on PRs touching `/runbooks/**` and fails the check on policy violations. Action is cached and horizontally parallel for large diffs.
- Sidecar prober service (lightweight Python worker) and Kubernetes Job manifest `runbook-prober-job.yaml` for staging. Prober performs read-only checks: validates referenced resource paths, queries Prometheus metrics to assert metric selectors exist, and validates that dashboard panels referenced by the runbook are resolvable. Prober intentionally does not execute any commands listed in runbooks.
- Unit tests for lint rules and an integration test that spins up a fake Prometheus and mock K8s API server to validate the prober's behavior.
- Docs: CONTRIBUTING.md additions describing how to author runbooks to satisfy lint rules and a new `docs/runbook-lint.md` with examples and remediation guidance.

Why this is safe: the linter is non-destructive; the prober uses read-only creds in staging only and is gated by an opt-in label `prober/staging-ok`. The GitHub Action gate prevents merging runbooks that fail policy checks unless an explicit `bypass/runbook-lint` label is present (requires two approvers).

Rollout plan: enable lint on all PRs in `incident-bot` repo first; enable the prober as an optional staged job for teams that opt-in for two weeks, then enable by default for staging deployments. We will monitor false positives and tighten rules over time.

Related work: ENG-1942 runbook hardening spike, ENG-1987 staging telemetry validation.

Notes on implementation trade-offs: the linter uses an allowlist-first approach for commands to keep the policy small; we purposely delayed adding a full DSL for runbook assertions to iterate on rules. The prober is intentionally conservative (read-only) to minimize blast radius.

Checklist:
- [x] Implement rb-lint rules and CLI
- [x] Add GitHub Action pipeline
- [x] Implement sidecar prober + k8s job manifest
- [x] Unit + integration tests
- [x] Docs and contributor guidance

Additional context for reviewers: pay attention to the redaction heuristics (heuristic-based regex) and give feedback if you see false positives for common multi-line examples. The `rb-lint` output includes file:line markers to make remediation quick.
Ethan Blake: The redaction regex flagged a common CI placeholder - can we whitelist the 'REDACT_ME' pattern?
Priya Patel: Added whitelist for CI placeholder and added unit test (see last commit).
Soraya Khan: Please add an explicit test for a runbook missing a rollback step (edge case: rollback labelled as 'undo' rather than 'rollback').
Priya Patel: Added detection for 'undo' alias and updated rule description. Also expanded docs with remediation examples.
Miguel Alvarez: Integration test failed on first run due to race in fake prometheus startup; recommend retry/backoff in harness.
Priya Patel: Introduced a 15s backoff in test harness and re-ran CI. All green now.
Ethan Blake: Approved pending CI.
Soraya Khan: LGTM.

payload.body:
Context and motivation:
We frequently see flights where responders take ad-hoc actions that drift from the canonical playbook. That drift increases MTTR variance and hides repeatable automation opportunities. This PR introduces an "autograder" that scores on-call actions against the canonical playbook guidance and a playbook-deviation detector that flags incidents where the deviation pattern crosses a threshold. The goal is to make deviations visible, provide seed feedback to runbook authors, and enable safe automation recommendations without changing any on-call workflow by default.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds an action-scoring pipeline in incident-bot that consumes telemetry checkpoints (commands run, timeline events, console outputs, key alerts acknowledged) and computes a normalized 'alignment' score against the recommended playbook steps.
- Adds a playbook-deviation detector that computes per-incident deviation profiles (sequence-level and step-level) and emits signals when deviation rate or semantic divergence exceeds tunable thresholds.
- Stores checkpointed graded snapshots (hashed) for auditing and human-in-the-loop review; no PII is stored — sanitized fields only.
- Exposes a lightweight API and a console view (feature flag) for SRE leads to inspect high-deviation incidents and suggested playbook edits.
- Implements a safe rollout: feature-gated, org opt-in, and initially read-only (no automated remediations).

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Scoring model: rule-backed heuristic with a small trained ranker (ensemble). The heuristics cover timing, step presence, and argument similarity; the ranker helps disambiguate semantically-similar freeform actions. We deliberately avoided a fully opaque ML policy for the first rollout to keep auditability high.
- Telemetry checkpoints: checkpoints are sampled at step boundaries to keep cost manageable; we also provide a high-fidelity sampling mode behind a separate flag for pilot orgs.
- Privacy and safety: explicit sanitizers applied to CLI outputs and snippets; only feature-flagged orgs will have graded snapshots persisted. All persisted artifacts are hashed and linked to incident IDs for audit.

Implementation details (files changed, high level):
- incident-bot/pkg/autograder/*: scoring engine, heuristics, ranker wrapper (GO).
- incident-bot/api/v1/autograder.go: new HTTP endpoints (POST /autograder/score, GET /autograder/incident/{id}).
- incident-bot/web/console/autograder-panel: read-only UI with deviation timeline and example action snippets.
- incident-bot/cmd/checkpoint-agent: small change to include graded metadata in checkpoint envelope.
- infra/k8s/incident-bot-configmap.yaml: feature flag defaults and sampling params.
- test/*_autograder_test.go: unit tests and a small end-to-end fixture that replays synthetic incidents.

Commits (high level):
- feat: initial scoring pipeline and heuristics (3 commits)
- feat: ranker integration and unit tests (2 commits)
- feat: API + console view + feature flag (2 commits)
- chore: sampling knobs, config, and docs (1 commit)
- test: add e2e replay fixture and CI flake fixes (1 commit)

Testing and CI notes:
- CI initially showed a flaky e2e replay test on Linux macOS matrix (repro: timing-dependent assertion). Fixed by switching to event-driven assertions in tests. All checks green on final runs.
- Integration smoke: deployed to staging incident-bot with the autograder flag enabled for the "eng-sre" org only. Observed no detectable increase in CPU at the pod level when sampling rate was 5%.

Metrics and monitoring introduced:
- autograder.alignment_score.p50/p95 (histogram)
- autograder.deviation_incidents.count (counter, per-org)
- autograder.storage.bytes (gauge)
- autograder.latency.p99 (histogram)
- Console: deviation incidents list with links to sanitized checkpoints

Rollout plan and gate control:
1) Canary: stage for 'eng-sre' org with sampling=5% (2 days) — done in staging.
2) Pilot: enable for opt-in beta orgs (feature flag) with sampling up to 20% and UI enabled for SRE leads (1 week).
3) General availability: roll to any org via console opt-in and default sampling 1%.
Feature toggles implemented via configmap and dynamic refresh; we also added an org-level opt-in switch in the console.

Migration and data: none required. Existing incident checkpoints are compatible. Storages are on a new table incident_autograde_snapshots with TTL default 90 days.

Review conversation (high-level):
- Ethan Cole: "This looks promising. Two asks: (1) add an audit trail for any score changes after manual review, (2) ensure we can turn sampling down without redeploy."
- Priya (author): "Added score_change_audit table and implemented dynamic sampling via ConfigMap refresh. See commit feat: add audit trail + dynamic sampling (hash: a12b3c)."
- Marta Ivanova: "Can we redact more CLI arg content by default? I worry about accidental secrets in snapshots."
- Priya: "Expanded the sanitizer list and added a conservative redact-first policy. Sanitation test cases added to test suite."
- Jun Park: "Approach seems fine; please ensure UI is read-only initially and that no automations are wired to the detector yet."
- Priya: "Confirmed — UI is read-only and webhooks for automation exist but remain disabled behind 'auto_recommendations' flag (off by default)."
- Approval flow: Ethan gave LGTM after audit trail added; Marta approved after sanitizer uplifts; Jun gave final approval.

Operational concerns and mitigations:
- Cost: snapshot storage controlled by sampling + TTL; added autograder.storage.bytes gauge and alert at 1GB/week per org.
- False positives: detector emits an initial 'suspect' state; human review is required to mark as 'confirmed deviation' for learning dataset ingestion.
- Abuse: access to graded snapshots gated to org admins and SRE leads only; toggles require owner-level to flip.

Follow-ups and next steps:
- ENG-4199: pipeline to convert confirmed deviations into suggested playbook diffs for authors (separate PR).
- Experiment: run A/B on sentinel suggestions vs no suggestions to measure MTTR improvement.
- Longer-term: investigate replacing the ranker with a small explainable transformer if we can ship more rigorous audits.

Merge outcome:
- Merged via squash on 2026-03-04 after required approvals. Release notes added.

Notes for reviewers and ops: this PR intentionally keeps the first iteration read-only and opt-in. Please coordinate with Security for any org pilot that wants to enable higher sampling rates.
Add on-call action scoring and playbook-deviation detector. Feature gated, opt-in for orgs. Improves incident postmortems and surfaces automation candidates.
payload.title: Oncall autograder and playbook-deviation detector

payload.body:
Title: Add /rollback shortcut command to post rollback UI + runbook links in incident channels

Context
During recent gamedays + the SUP-18421 escalation, the biggest time sink was not executing rollback itself, but getting responders to the right place quickly (Console rollback view + the canonical runbook) while context switching across tabs. This PR adds a tiny “fast path” in incident-bot: a slash command that posts the correct links and a short checklist directly into the incident channel.

What’s included
- New Slack slash command: `/rollback` (alias `/rw-rollback`).
- Posts a message with:
  - Link to Console Rollback UI (Optimization Config history view with the rollback modal entry point).
  - Link to the runbook: “Rollback Optimization Config”.
  - A reminder of the expected decision criteria (p95/p99 regression + 5xx) and the post-rollback verification checklist.
- Optional args:
  - `--env` (default: prod)
  - `--tenant <tenant_slug>`
  - `--model <model_id>`
  - `--region <region>`
  - `--scope <hosted|dedicated|private>` (default: hosted)
  These args don’t mutate anything; they’re used only to build a more specific Console deep link and to display the blast-radius header in the message.
- Safety/guardrails:
  - Only allowed in channels matching `^#incidents(-.*)?$` or `^#oncall(-.*)?$` (configurable via `INCIDENT_BOT_ALLOWED_CHANNELS_REGEX`).
  - If invoked elsewhere, command responds ephemerally with guidance and does not post any internal links.
  - If `--scope private` is provided, we do NOT link to hosted Console rollback UI; we instead post the private operator guide link and the generic runbook section.
  - Requests are logged (structured) with `request_id`, `slack_user_id`, `channel_id`, and parsed args to simplify debugging (no customer payloads).

Why incident-bot vs Console
This is intentionally not part of the rollback product surface area. It’s an operational shortcut for responders to reduce MTTR during active incidents while the Safe Apply + Rollback feature rolls out more broadly (PM-904).

Implementation notes
- Adds a new handler module `commands/rollback.ts` wired into the existing Slack command router.
- Centralizes link construction in `lib/links.ts` to avoid hardcoding Console hostnames across command handlers.
  - Uses `CONSOLE_BASE_URL` and `DOCS_BASE_URL` env vars.
  - Adds `consoleRollbackUrl({ env, tenant, model, region })` helper (returns a deep link with query params when provided).
- Adds a small args parser with strict allowlist flags (reject unknown flags and return help text).
- Includes unit tests for:
  - Channel allow/deny behavior
  - Arg parsing + help
  - Link construction for hosted/dedicated/private scopes

Screenshots (Slack output)
- Example: `/rollback --tenant northbridge --model llama-3.1-70b --region us-east-1`
  Posts:
  - “Rollback links (prod / hosted) — tenant=northbridge model=llama-3.1-70b region=us-east-1”
  - Button: “Open Rollback UI”
  - Button: “Rollback Runbook”
  - Bullet: “After rollback: verify p95 <= baseline + 5xx back to normal; annotate the incident timeline with config_version.”

Testing
- Unit: `pnpm test` (added coverage around new command router path).
- Lint/typecheck: `pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck`.
- Manual:
  - Verified in #incidents-sandbox: message posts correctly and buttons render.
  - Verified in #random: command responds ephemerally and does not post links.

Rollout
- This is behind Slack app permission already granted to incident-bot; no new scopes required.
- Deploy with next incident-bot release (no migration).

Checklist
- [x] Unit tests added for allowlist and arg parsing
- [x] Verified command behavior in non-allowed channels (ephemeral response)
- [x] Links use env-configured base URLs (no hardcoding)
- [x] Reviewed with SRE for incident channel patterns

Commits
1) Add rollback slash command handler + routing
2) Add link helpers + env config
3) Add tests for command allowlist and link output

Changed areas (high level)
- src/commands/rollback.ts
- src/router/commands.ts
- src/lib/links.ts
- src/lib/args.ts
- test/rollback_command.test.ts
- config/env.example

Review conversation
- Sean Gallagher (requested changes): “Can we ensure we don’t leak internal Console URLs into customer shared channels? Some incident channels are bridged.”
  - Aisha Bello: Added channel regex allowlist + explicit deny behavior (ephemeral-only) and made it configurable via env.
- Hannah Rivera: “The copy should remind responders that rollback is a control-plane action and still needs confirmation in Console; avoid implying this command performs rollback.”
  - Aisha Bello: Updated message header + button labels to say ‘Open Rollback UI’ and added ‘This command does not execute rollback’ note.
- Marcus Lin: “Any authz concerns? At minimum, log invocations for auditability.”
  - Aisha Bello: Added structured log event `incident_bot.command.rollback.invoked` with request_id + slack identifiers. No tokens or sensitive params.

CI
- build: pass
- unit-tests: pass
- lint: pass
- typecheck: pass

Merge notes
Squash merged after approvals. No runtime behavior changes outside Slack command surface. Safe to deploy independently of the control-plane rollback feature flag (PM-904), since this only links to UI/docs.
- New Slack slash command `/rollback` (alias: `/rw-rollback`) posts one-click links to Optimization Config rollback UI and rollback runbook in incident channels.
- Adds channel safety checks to prevent posting internal-only URLs outside approved incident/oncall channels.

payload.body:
Motivation: production incidents and internal fuzzing uncovered multiple edge cases in the /v1/chat.completions compatibility layer during streaming: (1) mixed stop tokens and framed JSON tool outputs would cause stream boundary misalignment, (2) role aliasing (user/assistant/function/tool) metadata was being lost during the stream->finalize transition leading to incorrect attribution in logs/metrics, and (3) logprob fallbacks were omitted when structured responses were negotiated in framed-json mode. This PR introduces a lightweight role serializer and a deterministic stop normalization pipeline to achieve parity with OpenAI /v1 semantics while preserving Redwood streaming guarantees. Summary of changes and rationale: 1) role serializer (api/compat/role_serializer.py): canonicalizes incoming message roles and preserves arbitrary role metadata in a compact JSON envelope attached to streaming chunks. This lets the runtime rehydrate message attribution at finalize time without blocking on full payloads. 2) stop normalization pipeline (api/compat/stop_normalizer.py): accepts OpenAI-style stop variants (string, array, regex-like tokens) and produces a prioritized sentinel sequence plus a short-circuit predicate used by the stream coordinator to detect boundaries deterministically. Normalizer also records original stop semantics for telemetry. 3) stream handshake extension (runtime/stream/handshake.cpp / handshake.py): adds a 3-way handshake for framed-json/toolcall streams that negotiates "framed-json-v1" capability and provides an escape-mode marker so tool outputs that embed stop-like tokens do not prematurely terminate the stream. 4) logprob fallback and structured-output adapter (api/compat/response_shaper.py): when clients request framed-json or structured output, the adapter will include best-effort token-level logprob summaries and a low-cost fallback that avoids invoking the heavy scorer when latency SLOs are tight. 5) SDK mappings (sdk/python/redwood/openai_compat.py and sdk/typescript/src/compat.ts): add role hints and an opt-in param "normalize_stops" to mirror parity behavior. 6) tests and harness: comprehensive unit tests and a new integration scenario under tests/integration/compat_streaming_tool_handoff.test that reproduces the incident condition. Implementation notes: - Conservative defaults: role serialization is enabled by default in the compatibility adapter but the opt-out flag (X-Redwood-Compat-Role-Serialize) is available for debugging. - Backwards compatibility: if a non-parity client doesn't set streaming frames, behavior falls back to the previous path. No existing stable API is removed. - Performance: microbenchmarks show ~3% median token latency overhead in worst-case framed-json negotiation; batching improvements in the runtime reclaim ~70% of this cost in steady-state. - Observability: added two new metrics: compat.role_serializer.malformed and compat.stop_normalizer.rewrites to detect malformed inputs and normalization frequency. Rollout plan: staged canary on dedicated clusters for 48 hours with traffic shaping (10%->30%->100%) and a kill-switch feature flag. If compat.role_serializer.malformed > 0.5% in canary traffic, the rollout will automatically roll back. Testing: added unit tests for role alias edge cases, stop normalization coverage for mixed stop arrays + tool content, and an end-to-end scenario that runs the framed-json handshake with toolcall resume. Also ran load tests against Dedicated with 1k concurrent streams to verify KV cache and batching interactions. Migration notes: clients using undocumented stop heuristics that relied on raw token echoes may see semantic difference when normalize_stops=true; recommended to opt-in and validate test prompts. See release_notes.

Motivation: On-call responders frequently spend the first 5-15 minutes gathering context after alert claim (top traces, recent deploys, error logs). This PR introduces a lightweight, time-bounded telemetry snapshot that incident-bot can capture proactively at claim time to reduce cognitive load and improve mean-time-to-resolution.

What this PR does: Adds a transient telemetry capture pipeline that collects a small set of artifacts (top-3 spans by error rate, last 100 log lines for a target service, recent deploy metadata, and metric deltas for key SLOs). Snapshots are stored encrypted for a configurable TTL and are surfaced in the incident thread and the incident-bot UI. Snapshot capture is async and rate-limited to avoid amplifying load during incidents.

Key design points:
- Opt-in by default for hosted (requires admin toggle); enabled-by-default in private installs used in internal QA.
- Snapshot TTL defaults to 1 hour; configurable via incident-bot configmap or admin console.
- Payload is intentionally small (~50-200KB) and sampled to avoid collecting PII.
- Capture runs in a sidecar worker pool with backpressure: at high alert rates, sampling windows widen rather than blocking alert intake.
- All artifacts are labeled with incident metadata and hashed IDs for cross-correlation with observability backends.

Rollout plan:
- Feature gated under feature flag "transientTelemetrySnapshots".
- Canary rollout for 10% internal traffic, monitor CPU/IO, snapshot success ratio, and customer-facing latency.
- Gradual increase while monitoring rate-limiter metrics and storage TTL eviction behavior.

Testing done:
- Unit tests for capture orchestration and TTL logic.
- Integration test harness that simulates bursty alerts and validates that sampling/backpressure prevents overrun.
- End-to-end smoke in staging with real observability stubs.

Usage notes:
- Admins can configure what artifact types to include and adjust TTL.
- Responders see a "Snapshot" card in the incident thread with links to the captured artifacts and quick actions (open trace, tail logs).

Related: ENG-4128 implements the UI surface; SUP-2043 documents support workflow for snapshot data access.
Add opt-in transient telemetry snapshotting to incident-bot: captures a configurable minimal telemetry bundle at responder claim time to accelerate blameless handoffs and root-cause pivots. No default on in hosted customers; admin-configurable in private/dedicated installs.
Aaron Patel: Nice idea. Question: how do we ensure the capture doesn't add load during a P0? Suggest adding an explicit circuit-breaker metric and a fallback path that returns a minimal placeholder when sampling fails.
Maya Chen (author): Added a circuit-breaker metric (snapshot.circuit_tripped_total) and fallback placeholder; updated tests to assert placeholder path when worker pool is saturated.
Sasha Ivanov: Security review: ensure scrubbers run before snapshot persists. Also we should confirm KMS usage in private installs.
Maya Chen (author): Implemented scrubber pipeline and added KMS config validation in store.go; added docs section about allowed artifact types.
Leah Park: Approve after CI green and an e2e smoke verifying TTL eviction.

Context: As part of the Reliability Program "Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping" we’re making incident_type/subtype required in incident-bot. This PR adds lightweight heuristics to auto-suggest a likely incident type based on the initial symptoms so we reduce time-to-classify during live incidents while keeping the human as the source of truth.

What’s in this PR: 1) Suggestion engine: Adds a new suggestion module that generates a (type, subtype, confidence, rationale) suggestion from the incident creation context. Inputs include: incident-bot symptom selections (5xx spike, p95 latency regression, streaming disconnects/resets, capacity/fleet alerts), any attached alert payload (title + common labels), and a small set of structured hints we already capture (tier, region, affected surface: hosted/dedicated/private). The output is always constrained to the v1 taxonomy allowlist; if we cannot match, we return incident_type=Unknown with confidence=low.

2) UX changes (Slack modal + /incident create): When the modal opens, we compute a suggestion and pre-select the incident_type/subtype dropdowns only if the user hasn’t already picked a value. The UI shows a compact hint line: “Suggested: <type>/<subtype> (confidence: <high|medium|low>) — <rationale>”. A new “Use suggested type” toggle is included for cases where preselecting felt too aggressive during review; by default the dropdown is set but the hint is explicit and the user can change it. Any user selection overrides the suggestion immediately and we keep the final selected value as the incident’s incident_type.

3) Auditability: We store suggestion metadata alongside the incident record: suggested_type, suggested_subtype, suggestion_confidence, suggestion_reason_codes, and a boolean suggested_was_overridden (true if final != suggested). This lets SRE report on suggestion accuracy and helps iterate without changing the taxonomy (aligned with the goal of keeping taxonomy stable/low-cardinality).

4) Guardrails: Suggestions are based on an allowlist of patterns and structured symptom flags, not arbitrary freeform strings. Regex usage on alert titles is intentionally limited and reviewed to avoid brittle behavior and accidental cardinality explosions. If multiple heuristics match, we pick the highest-confidence category and include secondary matches in rationale (without auto-setting contributing factors; those remain manual).

Heuristic rules (v1): - 5xx spike: If symptom flag includes “5xx spike” OR alert title/labels match known gateway error alerts, suggest Availability > Elevated 5xx (confidence high). If error hints include “overload”/“queue depth”/“shed”, bias to Availability > Overload/Load shedding (confidence high). - p95 latency regression: If “p95 latency regression” selected and 5xx is not selected, suggest Latency > p95/p99 regression (confidence medium). If alert mentions “runtime scheduler stall” or “kv cache thrash” (known runtime alert names), suggest Latency > Runtime regression (confidence high). - streaming resets/disconnects: If “streaming disconnects/resets” selected OR alert title matches SSE/WebSocket reset monitors, suggest Streaming > Disconnects/resets (confidence high). - capacity/fleet alerts: If symptom flag includes “capacity event” OR alert matches fleet provisioning/insufficient capacity monitors, suggest Capacity > Fleet shortage (confidence high). - Default: Unknown (confidence low) with a short prompt to pick the closest taxonomy category manually.

Testing: - Unit tests for the suggestion engine with representative inputs (symptom-only, alert-only, mixed). - Snapshot tests for Slack modal rendering to ensure the hint line and override behavior stay stable. - Added a small golden test set pulled from recent incident titles (sanitized) to ensure we don’t regress matching behavior.

Rollout: Feature flag `incident_type_suggestions_enabled` (default on for eng-sre + oncall workspaces, off for other internal workspaces until we confirm no UI surprises). A follow-up will enable globally once we have a week of data and review accuracy/overrides.

Notes/Non-goals: This does not auto-route paging or change ownership mapping (handled by control plane + alert routing work). This does not attempt deep multi-cause classification; it’s a first-pass guess to accelerate humans.

References: ENG-4822 (require incident_type + owner), ENG-4821 (taxonomy definitions), ENG-4823 (pager routing), INT-772 (modal field edge case).
Rafael Mendes (review): The overall direction is good. Two asks: (1) please avoid auto-overwriting a value if the IC already picked a type before selecting symptoms; (2) make sure the suggestion is visible even if we don’t preselect (so people understand why it guessed).
Devon Price (author): Updated modal logic so we only preselect when type/subtype are unset, and we always show the hint line. Also added suggested_was_overridden for reporting.
Allison Grant (review): Concern about regexes on alert titles. Can we constrain matching to a small allowlist of known alerts + specific labels? Also ensure we’re not adding any freeform strings to metrics labels downstream.
Devon Price (author): Agree. Moved matching to `allowlist.ts` with explicit patterns for ~18 known monitors and a few label keys. The suggestion engine returns only taxonomy enums + reason codes (no raw alert titles). Added tests for unknown titles returning Unknown/low.
Sofia Ivanova (review): For latency rules: the runtime-specific ones should prefer Runtime regression only when we see known runtime stall/KV thrash monitors. Otherwise keep it generic latency regression. Also, can you include rationale text that doesn’t over-claim root cause?
Devon Price (author): Adjusted latency rule precedence and updated rationale strings to be symptom-based (e.g. “latency regression detected”) rather than causal (e.g. removed “runtime is broken”).
Dev Patel (review): From Support perspective: great. Request: keep confidence + rationale short enough to paste into customer comms, but don’t assume we’ll share it externally. Also, any chance we can make it easy to override when customer reports mismatch (e.g., streaming vs client SDK)?
Devon Price (author): Rationale is now one line and explicitly internal. Override is just changing dropdown; we also show “You changed the suggested type” so ICs know it was overridden.
Rafael Mendes (review): One more: add a feature flag defaulting on only for oncall workspaces to start. Approve after that.
Devon Price (author): Added `incident_type_suggestions_enabled` and set default workspace allowlist in config. Ready for re-review.
Allison Grant (review): Re-reviewed. This is now appropriately constrained. Approved.
Rafael Mendes (review): Approved. Let’s monitor override rate and iterate.
incident-bot now suggests an initial incident_type/subtype based on selected symptoms and attached alerts, with explicit confidence and easy override
suggestion metadata is stored for accuracy/override reporting (no impact to external APIs)

Context and motivation: On high-severity incidents responders often need to run small, targeted probes (health checks, query samples, memory snapshots) across multiple services to validate hypotheses. Existing 'one-shot' diagnostics are ad-hoc and hard to correlate with runbooks. This PR adds a lightweight live probe orchestrator that executes short-lived probes in a safe sandbox, captures annotated snapshots (logs, traces, minimal heap/stack hints where permitted), and packages them into a replayable 'snapshot pack' linked to incident runbooks. The feature also adds a compact UI panel in incident-bot so responders can trigger predefined probe sequences and see suggested guided mitigations based on probe results.

What this PR does (overview): - Implements a probe orchestration engine with safe execution policies, timeouts, and permission gating. - Adds an annotated snapshot pack format (JSONL + attachments manifest) that can be attached to incidents for later replay and postmortem. - Provides a small incident-bot UI panel to run probe sequences, visualize results, and surface remediation suggestions from runbook metadata. - Adds test coverage for orchestration logic and end-to-end smoke tests for probe execution and capture. - Adds docs and a playbook template for teams to define safe probe sets for services.

Design notes and safety: - Probes run in a preconfigured sandbox with network egress restrictions and resource/time caps. - Only on-call roles with the 'probe:execute' permission can run destructive probes; defaults use read-only checks. - Snapshot packs redact secrets and truncate large payloads by policy; a sampling policy controls trace/stack capture to limit PII exposure. - The orchestrator supports dry-run mode which simulates actions without side effects for training/oncall drills.

Checklist: - [x] Orchestrator core implementation - [x] Snapshot pack schema and serializer - [x] UI panel and minimal UX flows - [x] Permission gating and dry-run support - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Docs: docs/oncall/probe-playbook.md - [x] Labeling: incident-bot, sre, telemetry

High-level commits summary: See commit messages below for details. CI: all pipelines passed on squash merge after a flaky unit test was retriggered once.
Luca Moretti (reviewer): Nice approach — can we make the default probe timeout configurable via RBAC scope? I want teams to enforce shorter timeouts in prod.
Maya Chen (author): Good call — added timeout policy bound to team config and a fallback in orchestrator.go (see runner_test.go updates).
Priya Nair (reviewer): Tests look solid. One request: the UI shows raw error traces in the panel — can we redact stack frames that match internal secrets or paths?
Maya Chen (author): Updated UI to apply redactors on display and added unit test for redaction in probes_test.go. The snapshot pack still keeps full stack in encrypted attachment for authorized auditors only.
Oliver Grant (reviewer): Security sign-off pending: need explicit opt-in for heap/stack capture per-team. Also require audit log entries for each probe run.
Maya Chen (author): Added per-team opt-in flag and audit events (orchestrator/audit.go). PTAL.
Luca Moretti (reviewer): Approved after changes.
Merged by squash on main. Commit message consolidated to: feat(incident-bot): live probe orchestrator + annotated snapshot packs

Includes UI panel, pack schema, permission gating, and docs. CI green after retriggering flaky test.

payload.body:
Motivation: In production KV workloads we observed long-tail memory amplification caused by small, heterogeneous slot allocations and conservative eviction scoring. This PR introduces two coordinated components: (1) an occupancy-align allocator that reduces internal fragmentation by biasing allocations into a small set of triangular size bins and (2) the Triangle Evictor — a three-axis eviction heuristic that blends recency, occupancy-impact, and size-gradient to choose victims more robustly under mixed workloads.

Design summary: The allocator groups allocation sizes into triangular buckets (bins whose boundaries follow a geometric progression with controlled overlaps); new allocations prefer the lowest-overhead bin that satisfies alignment constraints. The allocator exposes a lightweight occupancy hint per tenant/shard used by the evictor. The Triangle Evictor computes a composite score = w_recency*recency_score + w_occ*occupancy_impact + w_size*size_gradient. occupancy_impact estimates how much contiguous free space will be recovered if an item is evicted (favoring items that unblock larger coalesced regions). size_gradient penalizes tiny allocations that would worsen fragmentation if kept. The evictor also integrates a spillover gate: when physical memory pressure crosses a soft-threshold, large cold regions are asynchronously compacted and spilled to the configured backing store via a low-priority spill worker.

Compatibility & safety: Runtime feature-flag guarded (kv.triangle_evictor.enabled=false by default). Evictor falls back to previous LRU-ish policy on mismatch, and the allocator supports a compatibility mode that preserves previous bucket boundaries. All code paths respect tenant isolation quotas and the existing accounting metrics.

Checklist:
- [x] allocator implementation and unit tests
- [x] evictor algorithm + integration tests
- [x] async spill worker and backpressure controller
- [x] metrics and trace points for eviction decisions
- [x] perf harness runs and benchmark artifacts attached
- [x] feature flag gating and k8s config knobs for private/dedicated deployments

Notes: This is focused on memory-management/eviction; it intentionally does not change continuous-batching or kernel selection code. Follow-ups will include an optional compaction pass in the continuous-batcher hot path and a tenant-aware prefetch when spilled pages are rehydrated.
Marco Ruiz (review): Can you add a short explanation of the geometric progression constants and why overlaps are necessary? Also please document worst-case CPU overhead when eviction rate spikes.
Aisha Patel (author): Added section to docs and comments in triangle_allocator.rs explaining bin growth factor and overlap rationale; worst-case CPU path is limited by a rate-limited evictor loop and we bound per-iteration candidate checks to 64 entries (documented).
Leah Chen (review): We saw a small regression in a tight 99th p99 latency microbenchmark with tiny-alloc-dominant workload. Can we make occupancy_impact weight configurable by tenant?
Aisha Patel (author): Made occupancy weight tenant-configurable via kv.tenant_defaults.eviction_weights. Benchmarks included in PR updated to show improvement when tuned per-tenant.
Omar Siddiqui (review): Please ensure spill worker obeys disk QoS and doesn't impact critical IO lanes in dedicated deployments.
Aisha Patel (author): Spill worker uses the platform IO QoS token bucket and falls back to a background queue; added integration test that simulates IO contention.
Unit tests cover allocator bin placement, overlap edge cases, and evictor scoring. Integration tests validate tenant quotas and fallbacks. Perf harness: ran against three workloads (small-alloc churn, mixed-sizes, large cold objects) in the internal benchmark lab. CI runs exercised cross-platform builds (x86/arm) and the spill worker tests ran on a simulated backing store. All CI checks passed.
Benchmarks (internal harness, median of 5 runs):
- Small-alloc churn workload: memory amplification reduced from 2.3x -> 1.25x, eviction rate down 48%, p99 latency +2% (config-tuned per-tenant eliminated regression).
- Mixed-size throughput workload: throughput +6-9% and 95th token latency -12%.
- Large-object workload with async spill: peak RSS lowered 28% and spill I/O bandwidth stayed within configured rate limits.
Detailed CSV artifacts uploaded to perf/harness/artifacts/pr-631942/
Introduces Triangle Evictor and Occupancy-Align allocator (opt-in via kv.triangle_evictor.enabled). Reduces memory fragmentation and lowers average eviction churn under mixed-size workloads. Config knobs: kv.allocator.bin_growth, kv.eviction_weights, kv.spill.soft_threshold, kv.spill.rate_limit.

payload.body: Motivation: On-call runbooks and replay tooling are valuable for training and post-incident validation but previous replay utilities at Redwood risked noisy side effects (outbound webhooks, alert fog, metric skew). This PR implements an 'incident sandbox simulator' and a 'safe mock-runner' that lets responders replay recorded incident traces against candidate runbooks and automations in an isolated environment with configurable side-effect policies. High level: adds a sandbox runner service that replays events and telemetries, a mock external connector layer with strict allowlist/denylist and response stubbing, and a traffic-shaping timewarp that lets teams speed up or slow down traces for long-running incidents. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked ENG-2189 summarizing safety model and policies - [x] Sandbox service + CLI to start ephemeral run - [x] Mock connector interface and adapters for PagerDuty, Slack, Metrics, and internal webhook endpoints - [x] Timewarp + deterministic clock for replay - [x] E2E tests and CI job for the sandbox runner - [x] Documentation updates and quickstart example Usage summary: run "inc-sandbox start --trace-id <id> --policy deny-all --timewarp 100x" to launch an ephemeral environment that replays telemetry and executes runbook steps without touching production endpoints. The mock-runner supports three safety modes: deny-all (no external calls), stubbed (pre-seeded responses), and shadow (send but tag and discard results), plus a dry-run output-only mode. Commits: - initial scaffold for sandbox service and CLI (inc-sandbox) - add connector abstraction and PagerDuty/Slack stubs - implement timewarp and deterministic clock - tests: trace fixtures and CI e2e harness - docs: quickstart and safety-model writeup Changed files (high level): incident-bot/cmd/inc-sandbox/main.go incident-bot/internal/sandbox/service.go incident-bot/internal/sandbox/runner.go incident-bot/internal/sandbox/connector_stub.go incident-bot/internal/sandbox/timewarp.go incident-bot/test/fixtures/traces/ longrunning-oom.trace incident-bot/test/e2e/sandbox_e2e_test.go docs/sandbox-quickstart.md docs/sandbox-safety.md Key implementation notes: the sandbox runs as a separate binary to avoid accidental production hooks, uses a plugin-based connector registry so teams can add safe adapters for new integrations, and stores ephemeral state in a namespaced in-memory store with optional persistence to a local temp file for replay debugging. The timewarp multiplies wall-clock intervals and advances a deterministic monotonic clock used throughout the runner to ensure timing-sensitive automations behave reproducibly. Review thread summary: Ethan: "Overall good direction. Two requests: tighten the default denylist and add a warning when stubbed mode is used in CI." Response (Maya): "Agree, tightened denylist and added an explicit CI guard; stubbed mode requires opt-in via sandbox.allow_stubbed_in_ci in CI config." Priya: "Can we add an adapter that simulates rate-limited 429 responses to validate backoff logic?" Response: "Added a test adapter and a trace fixture that injects synthetic 429 bursts; documented how to enable in quickstart." Diego: "Make sure the deterministic clock doesn't leak into production libs." Response: "Sandbox-only clock is namespaced and not exported; added linter check to prevent accidental import into core runtime." CI: The new sandbox_e2e job runs in a hermetic container with network disabled; initial CI run failed due to a flaky timewarp edge case, fixed in follow-up commit that stably passes in current pipeline. Migration and rollout: this is an opt-in developer tool. Configuration defaults to disabled in on-call clusters; quickstart shows how to run locally or in a dedicated ephemeral namespace. Backwards compatibility: no changes to runtime or production connectors. Release notes: Adds an incident sandbox and safe mock-runner for replaying incident traces in an isolated environment. Known limitations: current Slack/PagerDuty stubs do not emulate all edge cases such as enterprise SSO redirects; future work tracked ENG-2245 will add richer stubs and a library of synthetic fault injections. Related: incident postmortem toolkit and on-call training examples. Merge outcome: merged via squash after approvals and a passing CI run. This PR is intended to reduce risk when validating runbook changes and to provide a reproducible playground for on-call exercises.

Motivation: On-call responders frequently spend the first minutes of an incident figuring out what runbook or checklist applies. This PR implements a lightweight, context-aware playbook ranking service plus a synthetic runbook generator that can produce concise, executable checklists for low-confidence matches. The goal is to reduce time-to-first-action by surfacing the top 3 playbooks with per-step confidence and a short, runnable fallback when no high-confidence playbook exists. Key design points: 1) A ranking model that scores playbooks by signal blend (alert fingerprinting, recent cluster-level events, recent triage comments, affected services). 2) A synthetic-runbook generator that emits a minimal checklist using existing templates and a constrained language model with deterministic scaffolding. 3) Opt-in rollout flagged by a config gate and telemetry to validate utility before enabling on-call autopopulation. Backwards compatibility: the default behavior preserves existing runbook selection flows unless the feature flag is enabled. Checklist: - [x] Implement playbook ranker service and API - [x] Add synthetic runbook generator with deterministic template mapping - [x] Hook ranking output into incident slack/cards UI as an opt-in toggle - [x] Add unit and integration tests that run on CI - [x] Add telemetry: selection_rate, acceptance_rate, median_time_to_first_action - [x] Provide documentation and admin toggle in Console Rollout plan: start behind the feature flag for 10% of incidents by volume for 2 weeks, collect metrics and qualitative feedback, then scale to 50% / 100% after sign-off. Safety and audit: generated runbooks include a provenance header and a checksum; generation is logged to the incident audit trail. Related work: Linear ENG-4921 (playbook discovery), ENG-4999 (oncall UX experiment).
Adds an opt-in ranking service that scores candidate playbooks and a synthetic-runbook generator for fallback. Integrates ranked candidates into Slack/card UI and adds telemetry hooks. Includes unit/integration tests and docs. Keeps existing behavior behind a feature flag.
Add an opt-in contextual playbook ranking and synthetic-runbook generator to reduce time-to-first-action for on-call responders. Disabled by default behind a feature flag. Telemetry and admin controls included.
Run unit tests: pytest tests/test_playbook_ranker.py tests/test_synth_generator.py. For integration: run ci/pipeline.yml job 'integration-smoke' or run locally with the provided fixture incidents. Enable the feature flag in staging to exercise the Slack card UI.
Feature is disabled by default. To enable: set incident.playbook_ranking.enabled=true in the admin Console and configure rollout percentage. Monitor metrics: incident.playbook.selection_rate, incident.playbook.acceptance_rate, incident.time_to_first_action.
Adds metrics: incident.playbook.ranked_count, incident.playbook.selection_rate, incident.playbook.acceptance_rate, incident.playbook.generator_confidence_histogram. Adds tracing spans for runbook.ranker.score and runbook.generator.generate.
Generator output includes provenance and checksum; a sanitation pass disallows inline secrets and strips raw keys. Steps matching destructive patterns are marked to require explicit human confirmation.
Opt-in; when enabled users will see ranked playbooks in the incident view and a short generated checklist if no high-confidence playbook is found. Expected positive impact: faster triage and fewer handoffs.
If customers report unexpected runbook content, disable incident.playbook_ranking.generator.enabled and collect the incident ID and generator logs (runbook.generator.trace_id) for debugging.
Liam Chen: Nice work. Two quick asks: add a test for the case where multiple playbooks have identical scores, and make the feature flag expire after 90 days if not promoted.
Maya Patel: Added deterministic tie-breaker in ranker (timestamp + id) and included a flag expiry policy in the admin docs.
Renee Ortiz: Can we ensure the generated runbook never includes destructive commands without a human confirmation step?
Maya Patel: Generator now tags steps with 'requires_confirmation' when a step matches destructive patterns; the UI renders a confirmation prompt. Added unit tests.
Diego Morales: CI flaked on the first integration run; reran and green now. Looks good to me. Approving.
