payload.body:
Context: As part of tiered batching defaults, the fast tier is expected to maintain tight tail latency under mixed workloads and bursty concurrency. Early bench + canary runs showed that continuous batching heuristics that are acceptable for standard/cost-efficient can cause fast-tier p99 regressions when the scheduler accumulates queue depth (especially with mixed prompt lengths and simultaneous streaming + non-streaming traffic). This PR adds fast-tier-specific protections: (1) admission control in overload to keep queue depth bounded, (2) a strict max wait budget (queue time) for prefill admission, and (3) anti-starvation tweaks so long prompts don’t indefinitely block short/older requests when batching is constrained.

What changed: 1) Fast-tier max wait budget: The scheduler now enforces a per-request max_queue_wait_ms when tier=fast. Requests that exceed the wait budget while still queued are dropped early (with a clear reason code) rather than being admitted into an oversized batch that would blow p99. This is implemented at the queue->prefill transition (admission point), using monotonic enqueue timestamps. 2) Fast-tier admission control: When the fast-tier queue is above configured thresholds (queue_depth or estimated_queue_delay), we reject new requests with a retryable overload error (HTTP 429 via gateway mapping; internal status: OVERLOADED_FAST_TIER). This is intentionally stricter than standard tier; goal is predictable degradation rather than slow melting latency. 3) Anti-starvation policy: Fast tier now uses an age-aware selection rule for prefill candidates: prefer older requests within a short window, then apply a short-prompt bias to keep interactive workloads snappy. This reduces cases where the scheduler continuously selects large-prefill requests that maximize throughput but starve small prompts that arrived earlier. The policy is scoped to fast tier only and is gated behind a config flag so we can tune it during canary.

Why this approach: The workload-aware batching project explicitly prioritizes tail latency stability for fast tier. A strict wait budget + overload admission is a common pattern we can explain and monitor. It also provides clean reason codes for debugging (budget exceeded vs rejected at admission) and aligns with the SRE preference: if we can’t meet fast-tier SLO, fail fast with backpressure rather than silently degrading.

Config: Added fast-tier fields under scheduler.tiers.fast: max_queue_wait_ms (default 3ms), admission.max_queue_depth (default 64), admission.max_estimated_queue_delay_ms (default 6ms), starvation.age_bias_window_ms (default 10ms), starvation.short_prompt_tokens_threshold (default 256), and a kill-switch flag scheduler.tiers.fast.enforce_wait_budget. Defaults are set conservatively for the initial rollout; final values will be tuned based on benchmark-lab and perf canary baselines.

Metrics/observability: Added tier-labeled counters and histograms: scheduler_admission_reject_total{tier,reason}, scheduler_wait_budget_exceeded_total{tier}, scheduler_queue_age_ms{tier} (histogram), scheduler_prefill_candidate_age_ms{tier}, and an event in tracing span scheduler.admission with tags tier, admission_decision, and drop_reason. Cardinality controls: reason is a small enum; no route/model labels are added here (those are handled in a separate metrics PR).

Tests: Added unit tests for monotonic queue time accounting and for admission decision boundaries (queue depth/delay). Added a scheduler simulation test covering starvation behavior: mixed request sizes under fixed arrival rates should not allow 90th percentile queue age for small prompts to diverge when fast tier protections are enabled.

Performance notes: On A100-80G, Llama-family 8B chat mix, concurrency ramp 32->256: fast-tier p99 improved ~18–25% in our internal perf harness when bursts occur (at the cost of a small increase in 429s under overload). Under normal load (<= p95 capacity), throughput impact is negligible (<2%). More detail in the benchmark-lab run linked below.

Rollout plan: This PR is meant to land ahead of the tiered defaults feature flag. In canary, we will enable enforce_wait_budget for fast tier on 1% traffic in one region, watch scheduler_wait_budget_exceeded_total and scheduler_admission_reject_total; abort if 429 rate exceeds 0.5% for fast-tier routes at steady state or if p99 does not improve. A follow-up PR will wire these metrics into dashboards/alerts.

Links: Linear: ENG-18424. Related: PR-28445 (workload signals), PR-28431 (tier schema). Customer signal: SUP-48219 (p95 regression during early canary in us-east). Bench run: benchmark-lab job BL-77132 (attached in internal comment).

Checklist: [x] Unit tests added/updated [x] Perf harness run for top model families (A100, H100 spot-check) [x] Metrics + tracing emitted with bounded cardinality [x] Config defaults documented inline and in runtime config docs [x] Feature-flag friendly (kill switch) [ ] Dashboard panels (tracked separately in observability-pack)

Notes for reviewers: The tricky parts are (a) where to enforce wait budget (queue->prefill), and (b) ensuring we never starve streaming decode work by spending too long on prefill selection. Please focus review on scheduler fairness and error mapping semantics.
Sofia Ivanova: The wait budget drop path currently returns a generic overload. Can we distinguish 'budget exceeded' vs 'admission rejected' for telemetry + customer debugging? Omar El-Sayed: Yes—added DropReason::WaitBudgetExceeded and separate counter scheduler_wait_budget_exceeded_total; gateway maps to 429 with a distinct internal code for logs. Noah Patel: Concerned about fairness: short-prompt bias could starve large prompts in fast tier under sustained load. Do we have an escape hatch? Omar: The selector is age-first within a small window; after that it falls back to length-aware batching. Also gated behind scheduler.tiers.fast.starvation.enable_age_bias (default true) so we can disable quickly. Marcus Reed: Please ensure we’re not doing expensive queue scans each tick. Omar: Prefill candidate selection uses a bounded scan (max N=64) and maintains a small heap keyed by enqueue_time for fast tier; worst-case O(N log N) per tick is acceptable at current tick rate. Sean Gallagher: From SRE POV, I’d prefer explicit thresholds and a documented abort condition. Also: what’s the intended 429 rate under overload? Omar: Added defaults + comment block; for canary we’ll abort if >0.5% at steady state for fast-tier routes and if p99 doesn’t improve. Allison Grant: Metrics labels look fine; please avoid adding route/model here to prevent cardinality blowups. Omar: Confirmed—tier + small enum reason only. Sofia: Requested change: enforce monotonic time usage; wall-clock drift would break budget logic. Omar: Updated to use Instant-based enqueue timestamps; added unit tests for drift scenario. Approvals: Sofia Ivanova (approved), Noah Patel (approved), Sean Gallagher (approved), Allison Grant (approved).
payload.title: Fast-tier tail-latency protections: admission control + strict wait budget + anti-starvation

payload.body:
Motivation: During recent regional spikes we observed cascading circuit flips caused by aggressive global fallback heuristics and a lack of short-lived isolation for noisy tenants. This PR introduces two complementary runtime components: 1) a fallback sampler that probabilistically exercises lower-cost fallback paths to maintain observability of fallback quality and avoid cold surprises, and 2) an ephemeral quarantine controller that isolates tenants showing short-lived pathological behavior into a soft-eviction lane for a bounded window. Design summary: - Fallback sampler: routes a controlled fraction of traffic (configurable per-tenant, default 1%) to candidate fallback models/regions to gather quality metrics without impacting live traffic. Sampling policy is weight-decayed and tied to per-tenant SLO delta signals so we increase sampling when drift is suspected. - Ephemeral quarantine controller: detects rapid SLO deterioration patterns (burst error-rate, latency amplification, KV-thrashing) and moves matching traffic into a low-priority quarantine bucket for N seconds (configurable TTL). Quarantine is non-blocking: requests are still served with lower resource priority and the controller stages a gradual readmit with a short warmup. Key goals: reduce global circuit oscillations, limit blast radius of noisy tenants, and get early feedback on fallback model regressions. Checklist: [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-2489) [x] unit + integration tests for sampler toggles and quota accounting [x] runtime metrics + dashboards added [x] safe defaults and feature flags for rollout [x] short-lived hotfix path to disable quarantine if needed Rolling strategy: feature gated behind runtime flag fallback_sampler.enabled and quarantine.enabled. Default rollout: 0.5% global, 1% on suspect tenants; quarantine TTL default 60s with exponential cool-off on repeated isolates. Includes runtime knobs for teams to tune per-customer. Backwards compatibility: no protocol changes; all behavior controlled server-side. Hotfix plan: single-command disable via console toggle and emergency cluster-level env var REDWOOD_QUARANTINE=off. Related work: follows ideas from ENG-2410 (graceful-degradation-experiments) and complements the selective-shedder work. Why different from previous PRs: rather than hard failover or broad load-shedding, this PR emphasizes short, observable isolation plus active sampling to reduce surprise regressions when fallback models are used.
Marco Jensen: Strong idea. Please add a metric for 'quarantine.injected_rate' and group by tenant tier. Also add an alert for repeated quarantines in a 5m window.
Aisha Patel (author): Added quarantine.injected_rate and new alert rule. Grouping by tier is implemented with the 'tier' label on the metric. PTAL.
Sofia Romero: Concern: warmup path may momentarily spike kv cache misses. Suggest adding a short KV-cache prefetch step during readmit. Can we also ensure the sampler respects privacy knobs?
Aisha Patel (author): Implemented prefetch warming for readmit (controller now triggers async kv-prefetch up to configured lookahead keys) and sampler includes opt-out flag per-tenant. Also added a unit test for opt-out behavior.
Evan Li: CI flaked on a stress integration. Re-run requested. After second run green. Approving with one comment to document the opt-out in the tenant onboarding guide.
SRE Bot: auto-comment: deployment-preview created at https://preview-ci.internal/redwood/pr/178205; canary on us-west-2 applied to 2 nodes.
SLO Guard: auto-note: this change modifies sampling rates; ensure product teams are notified before ramping beyond 1%.
Marco Jensen: Approve (after follow-ups).
Introduce a fallback sampling mechanism (default 1%) and an ephemeral tenant quarantine controller to reduce cascading circuit flips. Feature is off by default; enable via runtime feature flags. Improvements: reduced oscillation, better fallback telemetry. Hotfix: single-command disable available.
1) Toggle runtime flags: set fallback_sampler.enabled=false and quarantine.enabled=false via console; 2) If console unavailable, set env REDWOOD_QUARANTINE=off and restart controller pod; 3) Monitor 'quarantine_active_gauge' and 'sampled_requests_total' until zero; 4) If KV-prefetch caused issues, revert commit 5 in the PR and redeploy.

This is a small documentation-only PR to make the new prefix/KV cache telemetry usable by oncall and platform operators without having to hunt through Slack threads or dashboard PRs. It adds an internal README section that (1) defines the cache metrics in plain language (including what counts as hit/miss, partial reuse, and how streaming retries are handled), (2) provides “how to interpret” guidance with common failure modes (capacity/eviction pressure, TTL expiry, policy disabled, hash/version mismatch), (3) documents label/aggregation expectations to avoid cardinality surprises, and (4) links directly to the dashboards + runbook.

Motivation: We’ve had a few iterations on naming + semantics (see the ADR and the recent rename PR) and SRE asked for a single canonical place to point oncall when hit-rate dips or when metrics appear to go missing.

What’s included: - New README section: “Cache Telemetry (prefix + KV): metrics, semantics, and triage” - Quick links to Grafana dashboards (prod + canary) and the incident runbook - Guidance on dashboards: which panels answer which questions (hit-rate vs eviction pressure vs wasted prefill) - Notes on sampling and why some counters/histograms may not match 1:1 with request totals - “Gotchas” section: streaming retries, continuous batching attribution, rollout mismatch between gateway tags and runtime allowlists

Not included: No runtime/instrumentation changes, no dashboard changes, no alert rule changes.

References: - ADR: prefix/KV cache hit-rate definition - Observability standards: cache metrics naming + cardinality policy - Dashboard spec: cache hit-rate dashboards + alerting panels

Testing: Docs only.

Rollout: None (internal docs).
Omar El-Sayed (review): Can we be explicit about whether hit-rate is computed over requests, sequences, or tokens? A bunch of confusion in the earlier thread came from “hit-rate” meaning different denominators.

Nadia Rahman (author): Good call. Updated the README to include (a) request-level hit boolean vs token-level reuse ratio, and (b) which dashboard panels use which denominator. Also added a short note on why token-level is preferred for workload mix changes.

Logan Wright (review): Please add a warning about label cardinality: route_id + model_version is ok, but we should discourage tenant_id and raw prompt hash. Also call out that prompt length is bucketed.

Nadia Rahman (author): Added a “Cardinality / Labels” section with an allowlist summary and examples of safe queries. Explicitly called out that we do not emit raw prompt text and that prompt-length/token-count are histogram buckets.

Allison Grant (review): Dashboard links: can you include both prod and perf-canary, and link the runbook for pipeline drops? Also, suggest a first triage order when hit-rate dips (check ingestion health vs real miss reasons).

Nadia Rahman (author): Done. Added links for prod + canary dashboards and the pipeline incident runbook, plus a 5-step triage checklist: (1) ingestion drop panel, (2) hit-rate trend by region/model, (3) miss reason breakdown, (4) eviction/pressure, (5) wasted prefill.

Noah Patel (review): Minor: align terminology—use “prefix cache” consistently and note how it relates to KV reuse. Also mention streaming retry double-counting was fixed in 18428.

Nadia Rahman (author): Updated terminology and added a short “Recent fixes” note referencing the retry double-counting fix and batched-prefill attribution fix.

Approvals: Omar approved. Logan approved. Allison approved.

Merge: Squash + merge after CI green.

payload.body:
Context: PR #1459 introduced incident taxonomy dashboards and alert rules. During rollout review, Observability flagged that naively labeling high-volume request/edge metrics with incident_type can explode series cardinality (especially when incident-bot classification is missing/late, or when teams attempt to encode subtypes/notes). This follow-up tightens the metric labeling contract and adjusts recording rules to keep the dashboards useful without putting Prometheus/Mimir under stress. What changed: 1) Added an explicit allowlist for incident_type values used in metrics (top-level types only, no freeform). 2) Introduced two stable buckets for missing/invalid classification: incident_type="unknown" (not set) and incident_type="unclassified" (set but not in allowlist / failed validation). 3) Moved incident_type labeling off the highest-cardinality per-route/per-model series and onto lower-cardinality rollups used by the dashboards (recording rules). 4) Added a conservative sampling strategy for the remaining labeled raw series (only for error events and only for a limited set of metrics), with clear comments and defaults. 5) Updated dashboard queries and alert annotations to treat unknown/unclassified explicitly and to keep them visible (we want to drive down unknowns, not hide them). Guidance / policy baked into this repo: - Metrics must only use the top-level incident_type enum (no subtype) and must not include user/customer identifiers. - If classification is missing at emission time, emit incident_type="unknown". If a value is present but not in allowlist, normalize to incident_type="unclassified" and emit a counter for visibility. - Dashboards should break out unknown/unclassified as first-class categories so SRE can track adoption and decision-tree gaps. Rollout notes: This should be safe to deploy independently of incident-bot changes. It assumes the incident_type field exists in log/metric enrichment but tolerates it being absent. After merge, please re-run the cardinality check job in staging and confirm series counts stay within the thresholds in docs/metrics/cardinality.md. Related: ENG-4826 (metric label guardrails), ENG-4828 (dashboard build), and the earlier dashboard PR #1459.
metrics: add incident_type allowlist + normalization (unknown/unclassified)
rules: shift incident taxonomy panels to recording-rule rollups
alerts: annotate unknown/unclassified and adjust grouping keys
docs: document cardinality contract and sampling defaults
ci: add cardinality check budget for incident taxonomy rules
Allison Grant (review): We need a hard contract that incident_type is top-level only. Subtype belongs in incident tooling/events, not metrics. Please add doc language and enforce normalization to unknown/unclassified. Also please confirm dashboards still show unknown explicitly so we can track compliance.
Sergio Costa (author): Added docs/metrics/incident-type-labeling.md with the contract + examples; updated normalization to bucket missing as unknown and invalid as unclassified; updated dashboards to render unknown/unclassified as separate series and added an 'Unknown rate' stat panel.
Aisha Bello (review): Recording rules look good, but the alert grouping key still includes route in one place, which defeats the point. Can we group by tier + incident_type + owner only?
Sergio Costa (author): Good catch. Removed route/model from grouping; kept them in annotations via topk query so the page is still actionable without exploding series.
Rafael Mendes (review): Please add a metric/counter for 'normalized_to_unclassified' so we can chase down emitters. Also add a note on how incident-bot should behave if it can’t determine a type.
Sergio Costa (author): Added redwood_observability_incident_type_normalization_total{reason="unclassified"|"unknown"} and a short guidance section: emit unknown when unset; do not invent new values; add to allowlist via PR if needed.
Mei Lin (review): Can we add a simple before/after estimate for series count impact? Helpful for the program update.
Sergio Costa (author): Added numbers from staging replay in docs/metrics/cardinality.md: incident taxonomy dashboards now rely on 18 rollup series per tier vs ~400+ in the raw per-route view. Included the command to reproduce.
Internal-only: Tightened incident_type metric labeling to prevent cardinality blowups; dashboards/alerts now treat unknown/unclassified explicitly and rely on lower-cardinality rollups.

payload.body:
## Summary
Adds Grafana dashboard panels for Kernel Auto-selection v2 rollout monitoring:
- Selection distribution (chosen kernel + selector version) sliced by model family, GPU SKU, and seq-length bucket
- Latency deltas (v2 vs v1) with p50/p95/p99 overlays and error-rate context
- Cardinality controls (topK, label normalization, and aggressive label dropping) to keep queries safe during canary

This is intended to be the primary dashboard referenced during runtime 1.21 canaries and Dedicated pool enablement.

## Why
During early v2 testing we had enough signal to see shifts in kernel choice, but it was hard to correlate selection changes with tail latency regressions by SKU/seq regime without ad-hoc queries. This PR standardizes the panels + templating variables and bakes in guardrails to avoid exploding series count.

## What’s included
### New panels
1) **Selection share (Top kernels)**
- “Chosen kernel (top 10) by requests”
- “Chosen kernel by seq_bucket (short/medium/long/xlong)”
- “Chosen kernel by GPU SKU (normalized)”
- “Selector version share (v1 vs v2) over time”

2) **Latency impact (v2 - v1)**
- “p95 latency delta (ms) by GPU SKU”
- “p99 latency delta (ms) by model family”
- “Latency delta heatmap by (seq_bucket x gpu_sku)”
- “Error rate + fallback rate overlays”

3) **Safety / guardrails panels**
- “Fallback reason rate (missing kernel / denylisted / unstable / guardrail-disabled)”
- “Telemetry sampling rate (expected vs observed)”

### Variables / templating
Adds dashboard-level variables to avoid per-panel hardcoding:
- region
- env (hosted|dedicated|private)
- pool (for Dedicated)
- model (optional; defaults to all)
- model_family
- gpu_sku (normalized)
- seq_bucket
- selector_version

### Cardinality controls
- Default view is aggregate by (model_family, gpu_sku_norm, seq_bucket, kernel_name, selector_version)
- Drops high-card labels where present (e.g., route, build_sha) via recording rule inputs (see below)
- Panels use topk(10) / topk(15) and show “Other” via Grafana transformations where applicable
- A single normalization mapping for GPU SKU strings (A100 variants, MIG, cloud instance suffixes) is applied through label_replace in one shared query helper, not copy/pasted

## Example queries (PromQL)
> Note: metric names follow current runtime telemetry contract; these panels expect the selector to emit `gpu_sku`, `kernel_name`, `seq_bucket`, `model_family`, and `selector_version` labels.

**1) Selection distribution (top 10 kernels) – last 5m**
```
topk(10,
  sum by (kernel_name) (
    rate(runtime_kernel_selection_chosen_total{
      env="$env",
      region=~"$region",
      selector_version=~"$selector_version",
      model_family=~"$model_family",
      seq_bucket=~"$seq_bucket"
    }[5m])
  )
)
```

**2) Selection share by GPU SKU (normalized)**
```
sum by (gpu_sku_norm, kernel_name) (
  rate(runtime_kernel_selection_chosen_total{
    env="$env",
    region=~"$region",
    model_family=~"$model_family"
  }[5m])
)
```
Where `gpu_sku_norm` is derived via:
```
label_replace(gpu_sku, "gpu_sku_norm", "$1", "gpu_sku", "^(A100|H100|L40S).*" )
```
(Full mapping in lib helper; includes MIG and common cloud naming suffixes.)

**3) p99 latency delta (v2 - v1), by gpu_sku_norm**
```
(
  histogram_quantile(0.99,
    sum by (le, gpu_sku_norm) (
      rate(runtime_request_latency_ms_bucket{selector_version="v2", env="$env", region=~"$region"}[5m])
    )
  )
-
  histogram_quantile(0.99,
    sum by (le, gpu_sku_norm) (
      rate(runtime_request_latency_ms_bucket{selector_version="v1", env="$env", region=~"$region"}[5m])
    )
  )
)
```

**4) Fallback reasons rate**
```
sum by (fallback_reason) (
  rate(runtime_kernel_selection_fallback_total{env="$env", region=~"$region"}[5m])
)
```

## Screenshots
- Attached in PR UI: “Selection share (Top kernels)” and “p99 delta by sku” panels (Hosted us-east-1 canary).

## Rollout / compatibility notes
- No runtime changes here; panels will show partial/empty data until ENG-4824 telemetry lands everywhere.
- If `gpu_sku` label is missing in an environment, dashboard falls back to “unknown” bucket.

## Testing
- jsonnetfmt
- dashboard lint
- rendered dashboards validated in local Grafana

## Related
- Linear: ENG-4824 (telemetry fields + sampling), ENG-4826 (rollout gate)
- Runtime 1.21 canary dashboard link will be added to release checklist once merged.
Aisha Bello (review): The latency delta panels look good, but I’m worried about series blowup when people set model=All + gpu_sku=All. Can we hard-cap kernel_name to topk and hide the long tail? Also suggest defaulting selector_version to (v1|v2) not “.*”.

Allison Grant (author): Added topk(10) on the main kernel distribution panels and set selector_version default to /v1|v2/. Also added a note in dashboard description about narrowing filters for Dedicated pools.

Caleb Johnson (review): +1 on cardinality. Also: can we drop `route` and `build_sha` from the latency histogram panels? Some envs still attach those labels and it will make histogram_quantile painful.

Allison Grant (author): Updated queries to use the recording-rule-backed metric variant when present (the `_agg` suffix) and left a fallback path. Also added an explicit `sum by (le, gpu_sku_norm, model_family, selector_version)` so extra labels don’t leak in.

Omar El-Sayed (review): For debugging tail spikes, we need to see fallback reasons alongside latency deltas. Can you add fallback_reason rate as a right-axis overlay or at least in the same row? Also please ensure we’re not graphing request_id anywhere.

Allison Grant (author): Added “Fallback reason rate” and “Fallback %” panels in the same row as p99 delta. Confirmed we never ingest request_id into metrics (only traces). Dashboard uses only bounded labels.

Paula Mendes (review): Minor: panel descriptions should match the telemetry standard language (‘selector_version’, ‘seq_bucket’). Also please add a short blurb about sampling so folks don’t over-interpret low-traffic cells.

Allison Grant (author): Updated panel text + added sampling panel showing observed rate vs expected; also added a tooltip note on heatmap panels.

Aisha Bello (final): Approved after changes. Please link this dashboard from the runtime 1.21 rollout checklist in the next PR.

Merge: Squash merged by Allison Grant after green CI.
- Added Kernel Selection v2 rollout dashboard panels (selection distribution, latency deltas, fallback/sampling guardrails) with safe defaults and cardinality controls.
payload.title: Add kernel selection v2 dashboard panels (distribution + latency deltas) w/ cardinality controls

payload.body:
Motivation: SRE/on-call and customers need a consistent way to answer “are backups running?” and “why did the last restore drill fail?” across VPC + on-prem Private installs. We already log backup/restore steps in the installer, but logs alone are hard to alert on and don’t support reliable aggregation. This PR adds: (1) structured Prometheus metrics for backup + restore operations (success/failure, duration, bytes, last success timestamps), (2) OpenTelemetry tracing spans with consistent attributes for per-step visibility, and (3) explicit error categorization to drive dashboards/alerts and reduce pager noise. Scope: This instruments the control-plane backup/restore path (installer-driven + control-plane endpoints) and adds common helpers used by both “backup create” and “restore apply”. It does not change backup artifact format or encryption behavior. Metrics (Prometheus): - redwood_private_backup_runs_total{result,storage_backend,component,format_version} (counter) - redwood_private_backup_duration_seconds_bucket{result,storage_backend,component} (histogram) - redwood_private_backup_bytes_total{result,storage_backend,component} (counter) - redwood_private_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds{storage_backend,component,format_version} (gauge) - redwood_private_restore_runs_total{result,source_backend,target_env,format_version} (counter) - redwood_private_restore_duration_seconds_bucket{result,step} (histogram) - redwood_private_restore_validation_failures_total{check_name,error_category} (counter) - redwood_private_backup_restore_errors_total{operation,step,error_category} (counter; emitted on failure paths only) Tracing (OTel): Adds a top-level span per operation: “private.backup.create” and “private.restore.apply”, with child spans for steps: preflight, quiesce, snapshot, encrypt, upload, verify, bootstrap, migrate, validate. Spans include attributes: deployment_id, cluster_id (if known), namespace, storage_backend, artifact_manifest_version, backup_id/restore_id, step, result, error_category. Error categorization: Introduces a shared enum + mapping helper that classifies common failure types in a stable way for alerting/reporting. Categories include: preflight_failed, quiesce_failed, snapshot_failed, encrypt_failed, upload_failed, download_failed, verify_failed, bootstrap_failed, migrate_failed, validation_failed, compatibility_failed, permission_denied, kms_unavailable, timeout, rate_limited, unknown. Mapping is conservative: if we can’t confidently classify, we emit unknown and preserve the raw error message in logs/traces (not as a metric label) to avoid high-cardinality explosions. RBAC / permissions: No new privileges are required for the control plane, but installer pods/jobs must be allowed to emit metrics to the existing collector in Private installs. This PR reuses existing OTEL exporter wiring and the in-cluster Prometheus scrape config. Testing: - Unit tests for error classification mapping and label sanitization - Integration test in staging that runs a forced failure (bad bucket creds) and asserts metrics increments + spans have error_category - Manual validation: ran backup create / restore apply in dev VPC env; verified dashboard panels populate (see follow-up in observability-pack PR). Notes on cardinality: - No metric labels include backup_id, restore_id, customer name, or raw error strings - deployment_id is included only as a tracing attribute (not a metric label) - component label is constrained to a small set (control_plane_db, control_plane_config, k8s_manifests, audit_logs_export) - step label is constrained to known step names and used only on histogram for restore duration per step (bounded) Follow-ups: - Alert rules + dashboards land in observability-pack (PR-94) - SLO definitions tracked in slo-toolkit (PR-67) - Backup status endpoint is in PR-24318 (separate) which will consume these metrics for UI surfacing
Allison Grant (review): Please avoid high-cardinality labels. Specifically: do not include deployment_id as a metric label, and ensure step/component are bounded enums. Also add a short note in-code about why we don’t attach raw error strings to metrics.
Sergio Costa (author): Updated. deployment_id is trace-only now; component + step are constants with a compile-time list; raw error strings remain logs/traces only. Added comments + a label sanitizer that rejects unknown values.
Sean Gallagher (review): Can we add a metric to support paging on “no backups in X hours” without querying counters? A last_success gauge would help. Also, can restore validation failures be separated from “restore failed to run” so we can alert differently?
Sergio Costa (author): Added redwood_private_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds (gauge) emitted only on successful completion. Added restore_validation_failures_total with check_name + error_category to separate validation outcomes from workflow failures.
Ethan Park (review): Error categorization: please ensure compatibility failures (format version mismatch) are separate from generic verify_failed, and that it’s deterministic across versions. Also prefer stable names (snake_case) since SRE will write alert rules against them.
Sergio Costa (author): Added compatibility_failed and mapped version mismatch/manifest parse issues there. Enum names are snake_case and tested for stability.
Marcus Lin (review): Confirm we’re not leaking sensitive info via attributes/labels. Traces may include deployment_id; ensure that’s not customer-identifying beyond our internal UUID. Also avoid putting bucket names or KMS key IDs on spans.
Sergio Costa (author): Confirmed. No bucket names, no KMS key IDs. deployment_id is an internal UUID and only in traces. Added a denylist in attribute builder for common URL/bucket patterns.
Neha Kapoor (approval): Looks good. The last_success gauge + error_category should unblock alerting. Please make sure histogram buckets are reasonable; overly fine buckets can be noisy.
Sergio Costa (author): Buckets set to [1, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 1200, 1800] seconds for operation-level and tighter for step-level. Happy to tune post-merge based on staging data.
Allison Grant (approval): Approved with the label/cardinality changes.
payload.title: Emit metrics + tracing for Private backup/restore operations (with error categorization)

payload.body:
Summary: Adds a Grafana dashboard pack for Redwood Private upgrade health, focused on the new installer-driven upgrade workflow (prechecks -> backup -> control plane rollout -> data plane rollout -> migrations -> postchecks, with rollback entry points). Dashboard set covers (1) precheck failure rates + breakdown by check_id/severity, (2) DB migration durations and timeouts/lock waits, (3) API/control-plane error rates during upgrade windows, and (4) rollback frequency + outcomes. Motivation: SRE and Release Eng asked for a single place to validate upgrade readiness and spot regressions during beta rollouts; today we rely on scattered logs and ad-hoc queries. This PR makes upgrades observable with consistent panels and variables that work in Hosted VPC Private and on-prem (including air-gapped) where only Prometheus + Loki are available. What’s included: - New dashboard: "Private Upgrades / Overview" (upgrade success rate, active upgrades, error budget impact proxy, rollbacks). - New dashboard: "Private Upgrades / Prechecks" (fail rate, top failing checks, blocking vs warning, remediation link rendering). - New dashboard: "Private Upgrades / Migrations" (p50/p95 duration by migration_name, lock wait time, failed migrations, timeouts). - New dashboard: "Private Upgrades / Upgrade Window Errors" (HTTP 5xx/429, gRPC error codes if present, control-plane reachability, installer command failure count). - Optional annotation integration: upgrade window markers derived from audit/installer events when present; otherwise uses a manual label/annotation query. Metrics/log sources: - Prometheus metrics emitted by installer/controller-plane components: redwood_private_upgrade_runs_total, redwood_private_upgrade_precheck_results_total{check_id,severity,result}, redwood_private_upgrade_stage_duration_seconds_bucket{stage}, redwood_db_migration_duration_seconds_bucket{migration}, redwood_db_migration_failures_total{migration,reason}, redwood_private_rollback_runs_total{result}. - Loki log-derived counters for older installs missing a subset of metrics (best-effort fallback queries). Installation notes: Dashboards are templated with common labels (cluster, environment, customer, deployment_mode). On-prem guidance included: set prometheus external_labels for customer + cluster; if unavailable, dashboards still work but variables are limited. Screenshots: attached in PR (Overview + Prechecks + Migrations). Risks/rollout: purely additive dashboards/queries; no alert changes in this PR. Follow-ups: add alerts for migration timeout and elevated rollback frequency once beta thresholds stabilize; wire in audit event fields after redwood/pr-29187 lands everywhere.
Connor O'Brien (review): Can we align naming with the installer upgrade-plan stages? I want SREs to correlate stage names with the plan output. Also, please ensure dashboard variables don’t assume hosted-only labels. Allison Grant (author): Updated stage mapping to match the plan vocabulary (prechecks, backup, control_plane, data_plane, migrations, postchecks). Also switched variable defaults to use cluster/environment labels and made customer optional. Sean Gallagher (review): The precheck fail rate panel looks good, but can we separate blocking vs warning and show top failing checks over the last 24h? Also: please add a "no data" hint for air-gapped installs that don’t have Loki wired. Allison Grant (author): Added a row that splits by severity and a Top 10 failing checks table (by check_id). Added panel description text for Loki fallback and a note in README. Rafael Mendes (review): Migrations dashboard: can we include lock timeout count? We saw lock wait issues in staging and it’s a key signal during upgrades. Also ensure we graph p95 by migration for spotting regressions. Allison Grant (author): Added redwood_db_migration_failures_total{reason="lock_timeout"} and included p50/p95 stat panels by migration. Kira Thompson (review): Please add a short operator note in docs on how to interpret "rollback frequency" and not panic on drills; also mention what counts as a rollback run. Allison Grant (author): Added docs section clarifying rollback run semantics (installer rollback command invocation + result label) and how to filter out drills using the run_reason label when present. Sean Gallagher (final): Approved after the stage naming update and lock-timeout panel. Connor O'Brien (final): Approved; please ensure CHANGELOG entry calls out dashboards only (no functional changes).
payload.title: Add Private upgrade health dashboards (prechecks, migrations, error rates, rollbacks)

payload.body:
Adds a tenant warmup sampler (cost-sentry) that generates lightweight sample traces and a quant-profile bridge that converts sampler-derived metrics into safe quantization presets. Includes telemetry, a small CLI to export/import profiles, and a gradual rollout plan with canary and soft-fallback to full-precision models.
Motivation: tenant onboarding and bursty traffic patterns were producing unpredictable token costs for smaller customers; manual tuning of batch/cache defaults and quant profiles is slow and error-prone. This PR introduces a lightweight sampler (cost-sentry) that collects representative traces at low QPS, scores unit economics, and produces candidate quantization profiles plus batch/cache recommendations via a quant-profile bridge. Summary of changes: 1) new sampler service under runtime/sampler that emits compact workload signatures and token-latency histograms; 2) quant-profile bridge that maps sampler signals to a ranked set of quant presets with safety thresholds (per-tenant); 3) a CLI tool (bin/rw-econ) to export/import candidate profiles and run simulated cost projections; 4) metric + tracing hooks for per-tenant econ-score, sample-coverage, and fallback-triggers; 5) rollout and migration: sampler disabled by default, opt-in via tenant config; staged rollout with 5% canary, 25% limited, then global with automatic rollback on regen-rate or quality regressions. Why this approach: automating warmup and profile generation reduces manual ops, shortens time-to-savings, and provides a safety-first path to quant adoption. Backwards compatibility: sampler output is stored as telemetry only until profile import is approved; runtime respects existing model pins and will only apply quant profiles when tenant config allows it. Testing: unit tests for sampler sketching and bridge heuristics, integration tests for CLI projections, e2e canary in perf-canary harness with synthetic workloads. Rollout plan: canary on dedicated infra for a select tenant cohort, monitor econ-score, output-quality tests (prompt suites), and latency SLOs for 48h before broader rollout. Related work: follows from ENG-1987 (tenant warmup requirements) and ENG-2022 (quant-safety thresholds). Checklist: - [x] sampler service implementation - [x] quant-profile bridge logic - [x] CLI for export/import and local simulation - [x] telemetry and dashboards - [x] unit/integration tests - [x] canary rollout configuration and feature flag
1) Implement cost-sentry sampler core loop and lightweight sketching (runtime/sampler)
2) Quant-profile bridge: heuristics + safety gates + profile serializer (runtime/quant-bridge)
3) CLI: rw-econ export/import and simulate commands (bin/rw-econ)
4) Telemetry: econ_score, sample_coverage, quant_suggested metrics (observability/metrics)
5) Tests and perf-canary harness config (tests/, perf-canary/)
Alejandro Ruiz: Could we avoid adding another process by folding the sampler into the existing prefill agent? Concern: cross-contamination of resource accounting.
Maya Chen (author): I considered folding into prefill but kept it separate to allow different lifecycle and scheduling. Sampler is extremely low CPU (stateless sketches) and runs on a separate thin worker; we'll add resource caps and a scheduler group to avoid interference.
Priya Nair: The safety thresholds look conservative; do we have a mechanism to quantify false positives where quality drops but econ-score still improves?
Maya Chen: Bridge emits a 'projected-quality-delta' and we run existing eval prompt sets as a gating check in the CLI; also feature flag prevents auto-apply unless tenant opted in. We'll add a regression-alert rule in the post-merge follow-up.
Samir Patel: CI showed one flaky test on quant heuristics that passed after rebase; ensure tests are stable before wide rollout.
Maya Chen: Flaky test was due to non-deterministic RNG in a mock; fixed by seeding the mock RNG and added a determinism assertion in the test.
Merged by Alejandro Ruiz using squash-merge on 2026-03-07. Commit message summarizes sampler and bridge and references ENG-1987 ENG-2022. Post-merge: created dashboard 'econ/warmup/candidate-profiles', added a follow-up ticket ENG-2134 to add automated regression alerts and a migration script for tenant owners.

Context: We’re rolling out a formal Dedicated throughput SLO and need a consistent, low-friction dashboard experience for SRE/CS and (later) a curated subset for customers. This PR extends the dedicated mixin dashboards with panels that (a) track throughput floors over time per customer/deployment, (b) show saturation signals that correlate with SLO misses, and (c) provide drilldowns into the exact deployment/model/region slice.

What’s included: 1) “Throughput floor vs actual” panels: tokens/sec (per deployment_id) overlaid with computed floor (tier + shape) and SLO evaluator compliance; includes 5m/30m rollups with clear “below floor” highlighting. 2) “Saturation signals” row: admission-control shed rate, queue depth, in-flight requests, batcher wait time, KV cache hit ratio (when available), and GPU utilization proxy (SM occupancy / active time from node exporter where present). 3) Drilldowns: links from customer-level panels → deployment-level panels, and deployment-level → explore queries + logs/traces (requires `deployment_id` label) with pre-filled time range and filters. 4) Variables & filtering: standardized template variables (`customer_id`, `deployment_id`, `tier`, `region`, `model_family`) and a default view that emphasizes Dedicated pools only. 5) Runbook hooks: adds inline links to the Dedicated throughput SLO escalation runbook and the tier-aware routing/overload protection runbook.

Query semantics: Uses the canonical per-deployment throughput metric emitted by runtime (`redwood_inference_tokens_total` / `rate`), with streaming-aware token accounting (relies on the runtime fix merged separately; this PR avoids older `stream_tokens_total` series). Floor overlay is sourced from the SLO evaluator summary series (`dedicated_throughput_floor_tokens_per_sec`) when available; falls back to a static tier mapping panel note when the evaluator series is missing in a region.

Screenshots: Not attached; dashboards can be rendered locally via `make dashboards` and compared in Grafana using the “mixin-preview” folder output.

Rollout: Safe to merge; panels are behind the existing Dedicated dashboard folder and only appear where the required metrics exist. Follow-up: once the customer-facing Console widget lands, we’ll likely want a simplified “status” view fed by the same evaluator series.
Adds tier-aware Dedicated throughput panels (floor vs actual) with per-customer and per-deployment drilldowns.
Adds saturation signals (admission control shed rate, queue depth, GPU utilization proxies) to speed up triage.
Standardizes variables and link-outs to runbooks and SLO evaluator summaries.
Allison Grant (review): The variable naming is drifting from our conventions. Can we use `customer_id`/`deployment_id` consistently across all Dedicated dashboards, and avoid `acct`? Also please ensure panel titles are actionable (include units + window).
Sergio Costa (author): Updated vars to `customer_id`/`deployment_id` everywhere and removed `acct`. Panel titles now include `tokens/sec (5m rate)` or `tokens/sec (30m avg)` where relevant. Pushed commit a3e7710.
Sean Gallagher (review): For the floor overlay: please make it explicit that the floor is computed from evaluator series and not derived in-dashboard. We don’t want ad-hoc PromQL copies of the SLO logic. Also double-check you’re not using the old streaming counters.
Sergio Costa (author): Agree. The overlay pulls `dedicated_throughput_floor_tokens_per_sec` + `dedicated_throughput_compliance` (when present). No ad-hoc floor math in PromQL; I added a short panel description to that effect. Queries are on `redwood_inference_tokens_total` and not the older streaming series.
Aisha Bello (review): The saturation row is useful, but the GPU utilization proxy will be missing in some private clusters. Can we make it not look “broken” when absent, and add a note on expected availability? Also, can we add a panel for admission-control queue time / shed reason if available?
Sergio Costa (author): Made the GPU proxy panel show a neutral empty-state (no thresholds) and added a note: “present in hosted/dedicated regions with node exporter”. Added shed rate + queue depth; we don’t yet have shed reason labels consistently, so I left that as a follow-up (noted in panel description).
Rafael Mendes (review): Drilldowns: link-out query params look good, but please ensure we’re not leaking customer identifiers into shared URLs outside our Grafana domain. Also, time range should default to last 6h rather than 1h for incident triage.
Sergio Costa (author): Links are relative to Grafana and Explore only; no external destinations. Updated default drilldown to last 6h. Thanks.
Allison Grant (approval): Looks aligned with the Dedicated dashboard standards now. Approved.
Sean Gallagher (approval): Approved. Thanks for keeping floor logic centralized in the evaluator series.
Rafael Mendes (approval): Approved. Merge when green.

payload.body:
Context: Tenant burst models at scale were causing long-tail capacity contention even when overall cluster utilization was within targets. Existing burst token pools did not account for temporal satiation (a tenant over-consuming repeatedly in short epochs) which led to noisy eviction cycles and degraded p99 latency for best-effort workloads. Motivation: provide a controller that (1) detects and dampens repeated burst hunger per-tenant (satiation), (2) exposes a smoother per-tenant utilization mapping for autoscaling decisions, and (3) emits bounded, low-cardinality telemetry that operations can use for SLA reconciliation and chargeback. This PR introduces the 'satiation controller' and an accompanying 'utilization mapper' that together improve fairness and stabilize autoscaler signals. Design summary: - Satiation controller: tracks tenant burst consumption as an exponentially-weighted satiation score (alpha tunable per-tenant profile). When a tenant's score exceeds a profile-dependent threshold, the controller applies a soft drawdown that reduces burst token replenishment rate for that tenant for a decay window. This is different from hard quota enforcement — it smooths behavior while avoiding abrupt rejections. - Per-tenant utilization mapper: a rolling-window mapper that converts raw GPU occupancy and request-side observed throughput into a normalized utilization metric used by the autoscaler. The mapper reports both a short-window (30s) and long-window (10m) percentile-based utilization (p50/p95) to capture both microbursts and sustained load. Mapping uses sample weighting to prefer recent samples but protects against single-request noise by percentile aggregation. - Telemetry & cardinality control: to avoid high-cardinality metrics, the mapper emits per-tenant aggregated tags only for tenants flagged as 'paying' or 'trial-instrumented' and otherwise funnels detailed traces to the event store sampled at 1%. Aggregated metrics include: tenant_id (hashed bucket), satiation_band (OK/WARM/COOLDOWN), short_p95_util, long_p95_util, burst_replenish_rate. Implementation notes: - runtime/controller/satiation_controller.go: new control loop with light-weight in-memory ledger (bounded to 10k tenants via LRU). The ledger persists minimal state to etcd for leader failover. - controlplane/autoscaler/mapper.go: new mapper with percentile reservoir per-tenant using P^2 algorithm to minimize memory. - api/tenant_profiles.proto: added profile fields (satiation_alpha, cooldown_seconds, replenish_rate_base) with backwards-compatible defaults. - telemetry/metrics_transformer: new aggregation stage that hashes tenant_id into 128 buckets and attaches non-identifying tags. - e2e/test_satiation.py + unit tests for P^2 mapper + CI fixtures. Rollout plan: staged rollout via canary: 1) deploy controller in passive mode (no drawdown) for 24h in canary region, compare p99 latencies and autoscaler churn metrics; 2) enable drawdown for 10% of dedicated fleet; 3) expand to 50% after 48h if no regressions; 4) global enable with monitoring playbooks in place. Metrics to watch: cluster-wide p99/generation latency, dedicated-node eviction count, autoscaler scale events/minute, tenant satiation band distribution, and token pool average utilization. Backout plan: controller runs with a feature flag. Reverting the flag restores previous behavior immediately; persistent state expiry is bounded by cooldown_seconds per profile to avoid long-term effects. Testing: unit test coverage for mapper and controller logic, synthetic canary load tests exercising repeated bursts and mixed workloads, telemetry validation asserting that cardinality remains <= 128 buckets in production traffic sample. Related: ENG-1984 (autoscaler signal noise reduction), ENG-2041 (tenant-level fairness experiments).
feat(satiation): add satiation controller loop and ledger persistence
feat(mapper): implement P^2 percentile mapper and short/long window exposers
chore(proto): extend tenant_profiles.proto with satiation fields
perf(telemetry): add hashing-based aggregation and 1% sampling for detail streams
test(e2e): synthetic canary workload and unit tests for mapper/controller
docs: add operational runbook and rollout checklist
Miguel Ortega: Can we make the default cooldown_seconds conservative (>= 300s) to avoid oscillation? Also please add a rollout experiment ID to telemetry for equal comparison.
Aisha Park: Agreed on default; bumped to 600s and added rollout_experiment_id tag. Also added a doc section about expected effects on token pool utilization.
Ravi Kapoor: Mapper looks good; one nit: prefer a decaying sampling weight rather than hard 1% for detailed streams to capture initial-onboarding anomalies. Tests please.
Aisha Park: Implemented decaying sampling: 5% for first 10k requests per tenant, then asymptotes to 1%. Added unit tests and CI fixture.
Dana Li: Verified etcd persistence handles leader failover in local sim; please ensure the ledger LRU limit is observable via metrics.
Aisha Park: Exposed metric runtime.satiation.ledger_size and added alert for >80% of configured capacity.
satiation controller: smoother handling of consecutive tenant bursts, new per-tenant utilization mapper (short and long window percentiles), telemetry aggregation to control metric cardinality, and rollout runbook. Improves p99 stability and reduces autoscaler churn in mixed-burst workloads. Backwards-compatible proto additions.
payload.title: Burst satiation controller and per-tenant utilization mapper

payload.body:
## Summary
Adds the initial Grafana dashboard panels for the production performance canary. The goal is fast triage for per-model regressions (p95 latency and tokens/sec) with enough breakdowns to distinguish kernel/runtime execution regressions from scheduler/queueing and infra issues.

This PR is dashboards-only (no alert rules). Alerts are tracked separately so we can iterate on panel queries/labels before we encode anything into paging logic.

## What’s included
- New dashboard: **Perf Canary / Per-model Performance (Prod)**
  - Topline panels per selected model:
    - End-to-end latency p50/p95/p99 (histogram quantiles)
    - Runtime-only latency p50/p95/p99 (when available)
    - Tokens/sec (overall) + tokens/sec (decode-only) where emitted
  - Breakdown panels:
    - Prefill latency vs decode latency (stacked / side-by-side)
    - Queueing time (scheduler) and queueing fraction of end-to-end
    - Batch size distribution (p50/p95 + histogram heatmap)
    - KV cache hit rate (if the metric is present for the target model/runtime)
  - Correlation / attribution helpers:
    - Runtime build tag and kernel selection tag (as table + annotation)
    - GPU hardware SKU selector and region selector (to isolate fleet changes)
  - Drilldowns:
    - Explore link to raw series (preserves template vars)
    - Trace search link (where trace_id exemplars exist) for recent spikes

## Template variables (kept intentionally small)
- `model` (required)
- `region` (defaults to `us-east`, multi-select enabled)
- `tier` (hosted|dedicated|private, defaults to `hosted`)
- `hardware_sku` (optional; hidden by default to avoid casual cardinality blowups)
- `runtime_build` (optional; used primarily during rollouts)

Note: we do **not** template on `prompt_shape` / `bucket` even though canary emits shape buckets. Those panels are included as a separate collapsed row (opt-in) because we saw the label surface expand quickly during early experiments.

## Metric/query notes
- Uses the canonical perf-canary metric names agreed in ENG-4873:
  - `perf_canary_request_latency_seconds_bucket` (e2e)
  - `perf_canary_runtime_latency_seconds_bucket` (runtime-only)
  - `perf_canary_tokens_per_second` (gauge)
  - `perf_canary_queueing_seconds_bucket` (scheduler)
  - `perf_canary_batch_size` (histogram)
  - `perf_canary_kv_cache_hit_ratio` (gauge)
- Histogram quantiles are computed with `histogram_quantile()` over `rate(<bucket>[5m])`.
- Tokens/sec uses `avg_over_time(...[5m])` with a 1m min step to reduce graph jitter.
- All panels include `model`, `region`, and `tier` in the legend; other dimensions are shown only when explicitly filtered.

## Runbook links
Each top-level row includes a link to the on-call runbook for canary regressions:
- Confluence: `eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert`
- The link is parameterized via dashboard variables (model/region/tier) so the runbook opens with context in the URL.

## Screenshots
- Attached in the PR UI (see: “Per-model overview row”, “Breakdown row”, “Annotations + drilldowns”).

## Rollout plan
- Land in observability-pack, then enable in `prod` Grafana folder via the normal dashboard sync job.
- Runtime/SRE will sanity check the panels during Phase 1 rollout (us-east, 2–3 models).

## Testing
- `make dashboards-lint`
- `make dashboards-render` (jsonnet render)
- Verified in staging Grafana against canary metrics (us-east) for: `llama-3.1-70b-instruct` and `qwen2.5-32b-instruct`.

## Follow-ups
- Add annotation feed for control-plane canary model list changes (so changes in coverage are obvious on the graphs).
- Add a small “alert preview” row (not rules) showing computed deviation vs baseline once baseline store is stable.

Refs: ENG-4877, ENG-4873
Logan Wright: Can we ensure we’re not encouraging people to template on high-cardinality labels (prompt_bucket, seed, request_id)? Also please add a note about `hardware_sku` being hidden by default.
Allison Grant (author): Yep. I hid `hardware_sku` behind an “Advanced” toggle and I’m not exposing prompt bucket as a template var; it’s a collapsed row with fixed queries. Added README note on label guidance + why.
Nadia Rahman: The p95 panels look good. One tweak: can we standardize the histogram window to 5m across the board? I see 1m in a couple queries which will be noisy at low QPS.
Allison Grant (author): Good catch. Updated all histogram quantiles to `rate(bucket[5m])`. Left tokens/sec as `avg_over_time([5m])` for smoothing.
Noah Patel: Please add a panel showing runtime_build + kernel_tag as a table so when a regression hits we don’t have to click around. Also, the runbook link should include model + region at minimum.
Allison Grant (author): Added a small table panel in the header row with `runtime_build`, `kernel_tag`, and `model_version` (when present). Updated runbook and Explore links to carry `var-model` + `var-region` + `var-tier`.
Aisha Bello: Can you align the dashboard naming + folder path with the SRE conventions? Also please add a short “how to use this dashboard” blurb at the top so oncall isn’t guessing what panels matter first.
Allison Grant (author): Renamed to `Perf Canary / Per-model Performance (Prod)` and added a dashboard description block (top). Folder path is now `Prod/Perf Canary` per convention.
Caleb Johnson: For the trace link, is this safe if traces don’t have exemplars? I’d rather have it degrade gracefully than show a broken link.
Allison Grant (author): It’s a soft link (panel link) to the trace search page filtered by model/region/time range; no exemplar dependency. I removed the exemplar-specific wording from the dashboard text.
Logan Wright: Looks good. Approving once CI is green.
CI: dashboards-render failed (jsonnet) due to missing import path in `links.libsonnet`.
Allison Grant (author): Fixed import path; reran CI.
CI: pass.
Logan Wright: Approved.
Noah Patel: Approved.
Aisha Bello: Approved.

Summary: Introduces a SessionFactory abstraction in the Go SDK to harmonize credential lifecycle and to make cross-sdk session semantics parity with the Py/TS SDKs. Adds lightweight stream helpers (StreamReader, PullIterator) to simplify pull-style streaming ergonomics, and exposes telemetry hooks for credential events. Motivation: customer work (SUP-3321) surfaced inconsistent session control between language SDKs which made implementing transparent credential handoffs and prefetching brittle. This PR centralizes session creation, offers an opt-in SessionFactory for advanced consumers, and provides small ergonomic helpers to reduce boilerplate when consuming streaming endpoints. Changes: 1) core/auth: add session_factory.go with SessionFactory interface, RegisterCredentialProvider, and a default DelegatingSessionFactory that composes existing token caches; 2) stream: add stream_reader.go and pull_iterator.go with simple buffering and context-aware cancelation hooks; 3) retry: extract common retry profiles into retry/presets.go and wire the adaptive backoff preset to the SessionFactory; 4) telemetry: add cred_events interface and a small hook in session_factory to emit telemetry tags for lease/refresh/fail events; 5) examples: add examples/session_fanout and examples/stream_reader_usage in the repo root demonstrating multi-connector setups; 6) docs: update SDK CHANGELOG and docs/auth.md to describe SessionFactory usage and migration notes; 7) tests: add unit tests for factory composition, stream cancellation, and a small integration test using the local mock auth server. Commits: c3f5a9b Add SessionFactory interface and default delegating implementation; b2a1d46 StreamReader and PullIterator helpers with buffering; 5d7e0c3 Extract retry presets and wire into factory; 9a4f8b1 Add telemetry hooks and tests; e6c3af2 Docs and examples; 7f2b9d0 Fix lint/test failures after reviewer feedback. Files changed (high level): core/auth/session_factory.go, core/auth/delegating_factory.go, stream/stream_reader.go, stream/pull_iterator.go, retry/presets.go, telemetry/cred_hooks.go, examples/session_fanout/main.go, examples/stream_reader_usage/README.md, docs/auth.md, tests/session_factory_test.go, tests/stream_reader_test.go, go.mod, go.sum. Migration notes: SessionFactory is optional and default behavior remains unchanged for existing consumers; to opt-in to advanced orchestration, instantiate your own SessionFactory and pass it to NewClientWithOptions or set REDWOOD_SESSION_FACTORY env to the factory name. Telemetry hooks are nil by default; SDK will not emit cred events unless a hook is registered. Review conversation snapshot: Reviewer Maya Chen: "Nice consolidation; two asks: add a small e2e verifying the retry preset actually reduces refresh frequency under flakey auth, and can you make the StreamReader buffer configurable?" Author (Liam Ortiz): "Added an integration test using the local mock auth server and exposed BufferSize option on StreamReader, default remains 64KB. Thanks for the pointers." Reviewer Arjun Patel: "Please drop the public NewSessionFactory function and prefer constructor NewDelegatingFactory to avoid export churn." Author: "Switched to NewDelegatingFactory and added a deprecated comment on the removed symbol for the next minor release notes." Reviewer Sofia Martinez: "CI failed lint on first run due to a mixed import grouping and a race in stream tests." Author: "Fixed imports and added a short sleep+retry in flaky test to make it deterministic; flagged a follow-up to rework the test harness (ENG-9201)." CI: First run reported lint fail and one flaky test failure, rerun succeeded. QA & rollout: Manual smoke tested with py/ts example harness to validate session handoff parity. Added a small backwards compatibility test ensuring old behavior unchanged if no factory provided. Performance: microbenchmarks show negligible overhead for default factory (~0.5% latency at 95th p99 of small token refresh scenarios), and stream helper reduces user code complexity based on internal ergonomics review. Risks and mitigations: exposing SessionFactory could encourage custom implementations; guidance in docs recommends composing DelegatingFactory and using provided retry presets. Follow-ups: 1) implement credential warmup hooks in Python/TS SDKs to match Go factory semantics (tracked ENG-9182), 2) add an opt-in telemetry aggregator for cred events in Console pipeline (ENG-9201). Merge: Squash-merged after approvals from all reviewers, CI green. Additional metadata: small version bump in go.mod to v1.5.0-beta.Notes: kept description compact and single-line for PR export compatibility.
Add SessionFactory to Go SDK, expose compact stream helpers, improve telemetry hooks and auth retry presets. Backcompatible for most consumers; small opt-in API surface for advanced session orchestration.
This file models a merged SDK PR that coordinates auth/retry/stream ergonomics across languages and is intentionally focused on Go with follow-ups for Py/TS parity.
payload.title: Unify auth interfaces: add SessionFactory and lightweight stream helpers

Context: As part of the Quickstart Templates launch, we want to ship a recommended alerting baseline that users can enable without getting paged to death. This PR adds an opt-in alert rule group for template apps (RAG/agents) plus example SLOs and burn-rate alerts. The rules are designed around the metrics emitted by the templates + OTel collector configs from PR-156/158, and they intentionally avoid high-cardinality dimensions (no user_id, prompt hash, raw path, or tool args). What’s included: (1) SLO examples: availability + latency SLO recording rules with suggested targets and notes on how to adapt per workload; (2) Alert rules: multi-window burn-rate (fast/slow) alerts for the SLOs, plus a small set of “hard failures” (collector down, exporter errors) and “symptom alerts” (tool failure spikes, streaming disconnect spikes, retrieval empty-result spikes) with conservative defaults; (3) Noise avoidance guidance: documentation on paging vs ticketing alerts, minimum traffic gating, for/hold durations, and recommended grouping to avoid alert storms during deploys/traffic spikes. Rollout: Alerts are opt-in via the template dashboards pack jsonnet entrypoint; we’re not enabling anything by default in the published Grafana Cloud pack. Related: ENG-4184 (observability pack integration), ENG-4186 (smoke tests incl. streaming stability), and the templates’ error taxonomy work (draft).
- Added opt-in alerting rules for quickstart template apps (RAG + agents)
- Added SLO example recording rules and burn-rate alerts
- Added guidance on avoiding noisy/high-cardinality alerting defaults
Allison Grant (review): Please make sure none of the alert expressions include high-cardinality labels. In particular, I see `tool_name` in the tool failure alert. That’s borderline—can we drop it from the alert labels and keep it only in annotations (or not at all) to avoid per-tool alert fanout?

Sergio Costa (author): Good catch. Updated to remove `tool_name` from alert grouping/labels. Keeping a top-N panel in the dashboard for tool_name breakdown; alerts now fire per service/env only. Added a note in README about safe label sets.

Christine Wong (review): Thresholds: the latency burn-rate is currently based on p95>2s for 10m. That’s going to be noisy for small traffic. Can we gate on request volume and use multi-window burn rate instead of a single window? Also, please add explicit severities and a runbook link annotation.

Sergio Costa (author): Updated to multi-window burn rate (5m/1h page + 30m/6h ticket) using the SLO recording rule error budget. Added `min_requests` gating (skip firing if < 50 req in the fast window). Added `severity` labels and `runbook_url` annotations across the group.

Caleb Johnson (review): For the collector/exporter alert, consider differentiating between "collector down" vs "exporter failing". Collector down is usually a scrape issue; exporter failing is often auth/endpoint misconfig. Also please avoid alerting on transient 401s at startup.

Sergio Costa (author): Split into two alerts: `OTelCollectorDown` uses `up{job="otel-collector"}==0` with a 10m `for`. Exporter failing uses a rate of `otelcol_exporter_send_failed_spans` with `for: 15m` and volume gating. Also added a suppression note for first 5 minutes after rollout in the runbook (recommended to use your deploy annotation + Alertmanager inhibition if available).

Logan Wright (review): Can we align naming conventions with the template metrics mapping sheet? Specifically `service.name` vs `app` label usage. Also, the annotation text should mention the template tag filter users can apply in Console/Grafana.

Sergio Costa (author): Normalized to `service.name` and `deployment.environment` and removed legacy `app` references. Added note on filtering to template traffic using `redwood.template_id` (if present) but kept alert rules not depending on it.

Allison Grant (final): LGTM after last push. Thanks for being conservative on defaults.

Christine Wong (final): Approved. Please make sure the docs call out "start as ticketing" for most alerts.

Sergio Costa (author): Done—README now includes a "Paging vs ticketing" section and recommends enabling only SLO page alerts initially.
payload.title: Add recommended alert rules + SLO examples for Quickstart Template apps

payload.body:
Motivation: We observed sustained small microbursts from several tenants that caused headroom churn and elevated P95 latency due to aggressive binary scale-ups. Existing proportional and step scalers overshoot or react too late. This PR introduces a sigmoid-based autoscaling controller that produces a smooth, saturating score for scaling decisions, combined with a per-tenant burst-floor token pool and a graceful shedding path when capacity is exhausted.

What it does: Implements a sigmoid scoring function that maps recent utilization and request slope into a continuous scale signal (0..1). The signal feeds into a capacity allocator that respects a tenant-specific burst_floor_tokens budget and a global gentle_shed_ratio. When capacity is scarce, the controller first attempts to reallocate soft tokens from low-priority tenants, then gracefully shed (queue with prioritized timeouts and optional 503s) according to configured shed_ratio instead of instantaneous hard throttles.

Key knobs added: burst_floor_tokens (per-tenant, default 200 token-equivalent), sigmoid_sensitivity (controls slope), min_scale_score (floor for scale to prevent flapping), cooldown_ms (per-tenant cooldown), gentle_shed_ratio (percent of requests to shed under severe contention). All knobs are exposed via the existing autoscaler CRD and through the Redwood Console config surface.

Telemetry and observability: emits tenant_sigmoid_score, tenant_burst_budget, tenant_burst_floor, shed_decision{yes/no}, graceful_shed_ratio_active, and allocator_rebalanced events. Dashboards updated in docs/observability/autoscaler-metrics.md. Included Prometheus histograms for decision latency and exporter labels for tenant_id and priority class.

Safety and rollout: Feature is gated by a feature-flag (autoscale.v2.sigmoid) and disabled by default. Rollout plan: enable in staging, run a 24h controlled canary on a subset of low-risk tenants, monitor P50/P95 latency and dropped request rate; then expand to bursty tenants with gradual sensitivity increments and final global rollout. Backout path: revert flag, automatic fallback to legacy proportional scaler.

Tests and validation: unit tests for sigmoid math and thresholding, integration tests that simulate mixed-tenancy bursts and verify that total headroom and P95 latency improve vs. baseline. Benchmarks show a 12% reduction in unnecessary scale-ups for synthetic burst patterns used in benchmark-lab.

Related work: follows proposals in ENG-1892 and ties into the tenant-reservation ledger changes in ENG-2034. Addresses customer reports in SUP-473 about repeated transient scale flaps in Dedicated clusters.
Alexei: The sigmoid math looks good but I saw potential contention in metrics_collector when updating per-tenant budgets — can we make those atomic or use a sharded lock?
Maya: Updated metrics_collector to use atomic.Int64 for budget deltas and added a unit test for concurrent updates (ff12aa0).
Priya: Please add a test that simulates a tenant with zero burst_floor_tokens to ensure fallback behavior is correct.
Maya: Added integration scenario 'no-burst-floor' which confirms fallback to global allocator; test added in tests/integration/autoscaler_sigmoid_test.go.
Jordan: Can we include a cost impact estimate for Dedicated customers (expected reduction in unnecessary scale-ups)?
Maya: Added benchmark results and the summary in docs; ~12% reduction in synthetic microburst cases, appendix includes raw numbers and methodology.
Implemented sigmoid_scaler.go (core algorithm ~180 LOC), allocator changes to respect burst_floor_tokens and soft reallocation policy, small CRD addition, and documentation/observability updates. Kept runtime hot paths optimized and added microbenchmarks for score computation.
Introduce sigmoid-based autoscaler with per-tenant burst floors and graceful shedding. Improves stability for microburst workloads and reduces unnecessary scale-ups. Feature gated; disabled by default. See observability guide for new metrics.
Feature-flag gated; staging validation -> 24h canary on low-risk tenants -> expand sensitivity -> global enable. Quick revert by disabling autoscale.v2.sigmoid flag or rolling config to previous autoscaler version.
+5% controller CPU for score computation under worst-case high-tenant churn; net cluster cost reduction observed in benchmarks due to fewer scale events.
This PR focuses on control-plane policy and allocator behavior only. It does not modify model-serving runtime or per-model concurrency limits. Operators should handle knob tuning per-cluster based on traffic profiles.
payload.title: sigmoid-backed-autoscaler-with-tenant-burst-floors-and-graceful-shedding

Context: We’ve seen intermittent elevated 5xx correlated with upstream KMS throttling (SUP-19377) and a near-miss retry amplification event that required a hotfix (pr-18563). While the wrapper now has sane retry/jitter defaults and circuit breaking, we still had a failure mode where a large burst of decrypt/envelope ops (e.g. cache cold start + traffic spike) could saturate KMS and extend the incident blast radius.

This PR introduces an explicit "KMS throttle budget" and integrates KMS calls with the existing request admission/backpressure path so we shed/queue work earlier rather than stampeding KMS.

What’s included (high level): (1) Per-process token-bucket budget for KMS operations: A lightweight budget that is decremented on KMS requests and refilled at a configured rate. When depleted, KMS calls are delayed (bounded) or rejected with a typed error depending on caller policy. This keeps concurrency and request rate within a predictable envelope even if upstream is degraded. (2) Adaptive refill + penalty on throttling: When KMS returns throttling (e.g., AWS ThrottlingException / 429 equivalents), we apply an immediate penalty to the budget refill rate for a short window. This quickly reduces pressure and avoids repeated throttles. (3) Backpressure integration: The KMS client wrapper now plugs into `admission.Controller` so callers can either: (a) block up to `kms.backpressure.max_wait_ms` and then fail fast, or (b) fail immediately (for latency-sensitive paths) with a clear error category (`KmsBudgetExhausted`). (4) Metrics + tracing: Exposes budget state and decisions, and tags spans with the backpressure outcome.

Config knobs (all have safe defaults; prod guardrails still enforced by pr-18502): - `kms.budget.refill_rps` (default: 200 ops/sec) - `kms.budget.burst` (default: 400 ops) - `kms.backpressure.max_wait_ms` (default: 50ms) - `kms.budget.throttle_penalty_window_ms` (default: 30000ms) - `kms.budget.throttle_penalty_factor` (default: 0.5)

Behavioral notes: - This budget is per-process (not global) by design. It limits local amplification and works well with our horizontal scaling/admission control. If we need global limits later, we can layer it via control plane config + per-pool budgets. - We do NOT silently drop decrypts. If we can’t meet the wait bound, we return a typed error and let the caller’s policy decide whether to fail the request, fall back, or rely on cached material (where allowed). - When combined with the circuit breaker, the system now transitions more cleanly: budget starts slowing requests first; if KMS remains degraded, the breaker opens and callers follow degrade-mode policy.

Implementation details: - `kmsbudget.Bucket`: token-bucket with penalty hooks; uses monotonic clock; jittered sleeps to avoid herd effects at refill boundaries. - `kmsclient.Client`: wraps `Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey` calls with `Acquire(ctx)`; all outcomes emit structured logs and metrics. - `admission.Controller`: added a dependency-specific limiter hook (KMS only for now) so we can reuse the backpressure path without leaking KMS specifics into product code.

Metrics added: - `redwood_kms_budget_tokens{env,region,service}` (gauge) - `redwood_kms_budget_acquire_total{outcome="immediate|waited|timeout|rejected"}` (counter) - `redwood_kms_budget_wait_ms` (histogram) - `redwood_kms_throttle_penalty_active` (gauge) - Existing `redwood_kms_errors_total{category=...}` is now incremented for `BudgetExhausted` and `BackpressureTimeout` (maps to the canonical taxonomy).

Example log fields (new/standardized): `kms_op`, `kms_budget_outcome`, `kms_budget_wait_ms`, `kms_budget_tokens_after`, `kms_error_category`, `trace_id`.

Testing: - Unit tests for token bucket correctness and penalty behavior (including time skews). - Integration harness updated to simulate 429/throttling and verify that request rate to the KMS stub decreases within 2s and that tail latency stays bounded (ties into ENG-4825). - Added a regression test ensuring we don’t exceed retry+budget wait combined latency cap.

Rollout plan: - Behind `kms.backpressure.enabled` (default ON in staging, OFF in prod until we flip per environment). - Canary in us-east Dedicated + Hosted data-plane: monitor `redwood_kms_budget_wait_ms p95`, KMS 429 rate, and request 5xx. - Flip prod flag gradually per region; rollback is a single flag change.

Checklist: - [x] SRE reviewed paging/threshold implications (no new pages by default; dashboards use derived panels) - [x] Security reviewed failure semantics (no weakening of envelope decrypt correctness) - [x] Added metrics + trace tags per observability conventions - [x] Added tests for throttle + backpressure scenarios

Follow-ups: - Consider exposing recommended budget defaults in the Private operator guide once we validate prod behavior across 2+ regions. - Evaluate whether control plane should push pool-specific budgets for Dedicated customers with known KMS quotas.

Related: ENG-4821, ENG-4825, ENG-4828; incident context SUP-19377; complements pr-18563 (retry storm hotfix), pr-18449 (circuit breaker), pr-18502 (config guardrails).
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Can we guarantee backpressure wait is bounded even when ctx has long deadline? We should not add unbounded latency. Also please add a metric that clearly distinguishes waited vs rejected outcomes.
Diego Santos (author): Updated `Acquire()` to cap waits at `min(ctx_deadline, max_wait_ms)` and emit `kms_budget_acquire_total{outcome=...}` + wait histogram. Added a test that combined retry+budget wait never exceeds configured latency cap.
Allison Grant (Observability): Metric namespacing: prefer `redwood_kms_budget_*` and avoid mixing into generic admission metrics. Also add `service` tag for multi-service dashboards.
Diego Santos (author): Renamed metrics to `redwood_kms_budget_*` and added `service` tag (consistent with other dependency health panels).
Marcus Lin (Security): Confirm we’re not caching decrypt failures or falling back to stale key material. Also ensure BudgetExhausted maps cleanly into the error taxonomy.
Diego Santos (author): No caching changes in this PR. Budget errors are typed and map to `KmsDependencyOverload` -> `BudgetExhausted` detail in logs/metrics; no fallback to stale material is introduced.
Rafael Mendes (SRE/Game day): Please add a note in the rollout plan about verifying KMS 429 rate decreases and watching p95 budget waits; otherwise +1.
Diego Santos (author): Added explicit canary criteria in the rollout section.
Ethan Park (Platform): Looks good. Small ask: keep the admission hook KMS-only for now to avoid API churn; we can generalize later.
Diego Santos (author): Agreed; hook remains dependency-specific with minimal surface area.
Approvals: Sean Gallagher, Allison Grant, Marcus Lin, Ethan Park
