payload.body:
Context and motivation: Large-scale A/B experiments and canaries at Redwood have limited combinatorial coverage when multiple model axes (model family, quantization, prompt template) are changed simultaneously. That gap exposes us to blindspots where interactions between axes cause regressions that single-dimension canaries miss. This PR implements a "matrixed A/B runner": a coordinator that schedules small, timeboxed micro-experiments that exercise combinations of variants across user slices, plus a fallback saga that can escalate to automated rollback or graceful degradation when composite signals breach configurable safety gates. The runner also includes an opt-in "telemetry synthesis" mode that injects controlled synthetic signals into metric streams for rehearsal runs (smoke, error-injection, latency-pressure) so we can verify alerting and rollback plumbing end-to-end without affecting live user metrics. -- What this changes: 1) rollout/runner: new MatrixedRunner controller that expands a candidate PromotePlan into N micro-experiments using combinatorial sampling heuristics (pairwise by default, configurable to full-factorial for small matrices). 2) workflow/saga: FallbackSaga orchestrates progressive mitigation steps (reduce traffic fraction -> promote degraded model variant -> initiate snapshot-replay -> rollback) with audit events written to rollout-ledger. 3) telemetry: TelemetrySynth module (opt-in) produces labeled synthetic traces/metrics and ties them to experiment IDs so they can be filtered/queried. 4) API: a lightweight PromotePlan v2 CRD (API surface) and CLI flags for dry-run, synth-mode, and timebox. 5) tests: end-to-end smoke harness, unit coverage for combinatorial sampler, and integration test that runs a matrixed micro-experiment in the local devstack. -- Checklist: - [x] MatrixedRunner core implementation - [x] FallbackSaga control flow + audit events - [x] TelemetrySynth with non-production partitioning - [x] PromotePlan v2 API and validation - [x] CLI flags and docs in /docs/rollouts/matrixed-runner.md - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Canary playbook excerpt for SRE runbook -- Linear/Jira ties: ENG-2143 (matrixed rollout work), ENG-2201 (fallback saga+audit), SUP-981 (customer incident that motivated matrixed experiments). -- Risk and mitigations: TelemetrySynth is opt-in and writes synthetic metrics to a dedicated test namespace and tag to avoid polluting global aggregations. The Saga's default policy is conservative: micro-experiments start at 0.1% traffic slices and scale only after passing multiple SLO checks. Rollback is a guarded operation requiring either automated consensus of metric gates OR a manual override from SRE. -- Rollout plan: 1) deploy to staging (this PR includes the k8s Job manifest for a devstack run) 2) run a dry-run matrix with synth-mode enabled 3) enable in limited production namespace behind feature flag and monitor for one week 4) flip on auto-fallback after two successful days. -- Notes: this complements existing cohort-based canaries (does not replace them); the matrixed runner is intended for multi-axis changes where existing single-dimension canaries are insufficient.
Marco Duarte (reviewer): Great direction — I want clarity on how experiments are mapped to user slices. Can we ensure the combinatorial sampler supports per-customer affinity constraints?
Priya Rao (author): Reply: yes — sampler supports an optional affinity policy. I added validation and a test case (tests/affinity/test_affinity_policy.py) to demonstrate the constraint behavior.
Jonas Kline (reviewer): The fallback sequence has multiple side effects (snapshot replay, model swap). We should TTL these operations and ensure idempotency. Please add expiring locks and idempotency keys.
Priya Rao: Added expiring saga locks and idempotency keys persisted in rollout-ledger. Updated docs and unit tests to assert idempotent replays.
Ariella Chen (reviewer): CI flaked on the sampler randomness test — deterministic seed required for CI. Also request small perf benchmark for sampler at 1k variant combinations.
Priya Rao: Fixed test to inject deterministic RNG in CI; added a microbenchmark and a flamegraph output for the 1k case. Benchmarks show <120ms overhead for sampler with default pairwise heuristic.
Marco Duarte: Approving after minor doc edits were addressed.
Jonas Kline: Approving — verified saga idempotency locally.
payload.title: Matrixed A/B Runner with Fallback Saga and Telemetry Synthesis

payload.body:
Motivation: In multi-tenant production workloads we observed sustained KV cache fragmentation and oscillating spill events during load spikes. This behavior amplifies tail-latency for inference requests because active prefixes get evicted during aggressive global reclamation and continuous batching bursts interfere with reclamation quiesce points. The goal of this PR is to reduce fragmentation-driven spillovers and eviction-induced latency spikes by introducing a tenant-aware slab reclamation policy and a paging hysteresis guard that prevents thrash.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Adds a tenant-prioritized slab reclaimer that prefers cold-tenant segments, integrates a hysteresis window around page reclamation (avoid immediate reclaim after short-lived spikes), introduces a spillback failsafe to gracefully throttle new allocations when spill rates exceed a threshold, and wires these behaviors into the runtime scheduler and continuous-batching quiesce points. Also adds metrics and dashboards for visibility and synthetic benchmarks used for validation.

Design highlights: - Tenant scoring: each tenant is scored based on recent access heat (EWMA of lookups and prefix hits), write pressure, and resident fraction. The reclaimer targets slabs with the lowest tenant-weighted residency score. - Hysteresis window: reclamation of newly-created pages is deferred for a configurable hysteresis period (default 10s) to prevent reclaiming pages that were created during a short burst. - Spillback failsafe: if spill events/sec > 5 for > 30s, the allocator enters a soft-fallback that reduces per-tenant allocation pace and routes new requests to a higher-latency but lower-memory model variant (configurable policy). This avoids hard OOM and maintains availability. - Continuous batching interaction: introduced a batching quiesce hook so reclamation only runs between batch drain points; this prevents mid-batch eviction of KV entries needed by the same request. - Kernel hinting: added lightweight metadata to mark compacted slabs so the runtime kernel selector favors fast-path lookup kernels when accessing compacted regions.

Implementation notes: - New package: internal/kv/reclaimer containing TenantReclaimer, HysteresisTracker, and SpillbackController (core algorithms implemented in ~280 lines). - Integrations: runtime/scheduler to register quiesce hooks; serving/runtime allocator to consult SpillbackController before admitting large allocations; observability to emit kv.reclaimer.* metrics and tenant.breakdown.*. - Tests: unit tests for hysteresis logic, tenant scoring, and spillback transitions; integration test with 5-tenent load generator simulating bursty writes.

Benchmark results (staging cluster, G4dn-like hardware): - Baseline (main, before change): median L40 token latency 36ms, p95 210ms, spill events/day: 1,280. - After PR (default config): median 34ms, p95 120ms (43% reduction), spill events/day: 410 (68% reduction), steady-state throughput within 3% of baseline. - Cost: memory headroom increased by ~12% after compaction cycles, reducing emergency spill frequency.

Checklist: - [x] Algorithm implemented and unit-tested - [x] Integration tests and perf harness updated - [x] CI green after flaky test rerun - [x] Metrics & dashboards added - [x] Docs (internal ops runbook) updated

Safety and rollout: default configuration is conservative (hysteresis=10s, spillback threshold conservative) and feature is behind a runtime config flag (kv.tenant_reclaimer.enabled=false by default). Rollout plan: enable on one region with canary capacity, monitor kv.reclaimer.spill_rate and tenant.p95_latency for 48 hours before wide rollout.

Files changed (high-level): internal/kv/reclaimer/reclaimer.go (new), internal/kv/reclaimer/hysteresis.go (new), internal/kv/reclaimer/spillback.go (new), runtime/scheduler/quiesce_hooks.go (mod), serving/allocator/tenant_allocator.go (mod), serving/allocator/allocator_metrics_test.go (new tests), integration/perf/kv_multi_tenant_loadtest.go (new), docs/ops/kv-reclaimer.md (new), dashboards/kv-reclaimer.json (new), go.mod (tweak). Small illustrative change: in quiesce_hooks.go we add: 

  // before: no-op 
  func RunQuiesceHooks() { /* drain batches */ } 
  // after: register tenant reclaimer to run between batch drains 
  func RunQuiesceHooks() { /* drain batches */ tenantReclaimer.RunCycle() }

Review thread summary (single-string conversational transcript): 
Reviewer: Asha Patel - "This looks promising. Can we make the hysteresis tunable per-tenant? Some tenants have short-lived bursts that we shouldn't penalize long-term." 
Author: Jordan Lee - "Agree; made hysteresis per-tenant with a global ceiling in the latest commit (hysteresis is min(global, tenant_bias*10s))." 
Reviewer: Diego Rivera - "Can we ensure the spillback policy doesn't route sensitive tenants to lower-quality models automatically? We need an allowlist." 
Author: Jordan Lee - "Added allowlist support and a second-tier policy flag kv.spillback.allowlist. Default behavior is opt-in; sensitive tenants must be explicitly configured." 
Reviewer: Marta Kline - "Found a flaky test in allocator_metrics_test on macOS runners, it's timing-sensitive." 
Author: Jordan Lee - "Adjusted test timing and added deterministic clock in tests; reran CI." 
Reviewer: Samir Gupta - "Approach LGTM, but please add a note in release notes about possible transient increase in eviction count during the first compaction cycle." 
Author: Jordan Lee - "Added release note and ops runbook guidance." 

CI: initial pipeline had a transient failure in allocator_metrics_test (timing), which was fixed in commit 3; final CI run passed (linux/amd64, linux/arm, integration perf harness).

Merge: squash-merged to main after approvals and perf sign-off.

Related work and follow-ups: - Follow-up: expose per-tenant hysteresis tuning in Console + UI (ENG-2145) - Follow-up: move spillback policy into routing layer for more granular fallbacks (ENG-2201)

Note: description is intentionally detailed to aid reviewers and on-call engineers during rollout.
payload.title: Tenant-aware slab reclaimer with paging hysteresis and spillback failsafe

payload.body:
Context and motivation: production clusters serving bursty chat workloads were repeatedly observing elevated KV cache fragmentation which caused premature paging and aggressive spillovers under tenant contention. This manifested as 95th percentile token generation latency regressions and +20-40% extra disk spill I/O during high-concurrency experiments. Goal: reduce fragmentation-driven spill events, improve memory residency for hot prefixes, and provide a per-tenant backpressure/priority mechanism to avoid noisy-tenant tail behavior.

Summary of changes: Implement an anti-fragmentation defragmentation scheduler that coalesces adjacent free slots proactively during low-load windows and opportunistically during continuous-batching idle gaps. Introduce a tenant-priority allocator that prefers warm-run allocations for pinned tenants and gracefully demotes low-priority tenants during memory pressure. Add a spill throttle module that exposes a token-bucket-like pacing per-tenant and a global spill budget with soft quotas to avoid cascade spill storms. Feature-flagged behind kv.anti_frag_defrag and kv.spill_throttle for staged rollout.

Key behavioral changes and rationale: 1) Defrag scheduler: uses a lightweight hinting API from the allocator to identify fragmentation hotspots (small free islands). Rather than compacting aggressively, the scheduler coalesces neighbors into a small contiguous slab and updates the allocator metadata atomically to minimize stalls. This approach trades a small background CPU cost for reduced page churn and fewer writebacks. 2) Tenant-priority allocator: tenants can be assigned a steady-state priority (derived from billing tier and recent SLA). The allocator attempts in-order placement to maximize prefix locality; on pressure it lowers placement preference for low-priority tenants and exposes a graceful admission signal to the spill throttle. 3) Spill throttle: when global memory pressure exceeds thresholds, the throttle enforces per-tenant pacing and refuses immediate spillbacks that would exceed the global budget. This smooths downstream IO and reduces head-of-line eviction storms.

Perf results (canary): - Controlled canary across 10 clusters: average reduction in spill size per-minute: 28% (median); - 95th token latency improvement: 9-12% across chat workloads with sequence lengths >1024; - Tail variance reduced: observed 2x fewer spill-induced latency spikes in the canary window. Microbenchmarks show the scheduler adds ~0.7-1.5% CPU overhead during peak compaction windows but decreases overall IO wait time.

Testing and rollout: includes new unit tests, deterministic integration tests that simulate tenant contention and fragmentation, and a perf canary harness. The rollout plan is staged: feature flag off by default -> internal canary -> gradual percent rollout -> full on by default after 2 weeks of telemetry.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-9034) - [x] Feature flags added - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Perf canary passes - [x] Observability (metrics + dashboards) - [x] Docs/operational runbook updated

Operational notes and metrics added: kv.defrag.coalesces_total, kv.defrag.coalesce_latency_ms_p50/p95, kv.spill.throttle_tokens_granted, kv.tenant.allocation_priority, kv.eviction.spill_events_by_tenant. Dashboards ship under docs/operational/kv-eviction.md.

Risk and mitigations: defrag activity can cause CPU pressure; limited by windowed scheduling and guarded by a dynamic backoff. Spill throttle could introduce temporary memory oversubscription if misconfigured; default conservative budgets and an auto-fallback that disables throttle at extreme pressure.

Related work and references: builds on earlier work around soft-quarantine and spill smoothing (see ENG-8721) but differs by combining proactive coalescing with tenant-aware allocation and an explicit per-tenant spill budget.

Miguel Cruz: The coalescing is promising but can we expose a per-cluster backoff to avoid noisy neighbors? Please add a control for maximum coalesces/sec.
Asha Patel: Added config kv.defrag.max_coalesces_per_sec with sane defaults and cluster-level override. Updated tests to validate backoff behavior.
Jordan Lee: Can the allocator hint be abused by a malicious tenant to pin memory? Ensure authorization checks and an escape hatch.
Asha Patel: Allocator hint now validated against tenant allocation policy. Added a config path to globally disable priority hinting for private deployments.
Lina Becker: Requesting additional metrics for debugging spill throttle rejections (reason codes).
Asha Patel: Added reason-tagged metrics and a small doc section describing common rejection codes and remediation steps.
Introduce anti-fragmentation defrag scheduler and tenant-aware spill throttle to reduce spill I/O and improve KV cache residency under tenant contention. Feature flagged for staged rollout. See docs/operational/kv-eviction.md for configuration and runbook.

Summary: Adds a progressive, per-tenant fallback hedging layer that cooperates with existing SLO enforcement and circuit state. This change integrates a lightweight liveness probe into regional proxies so hedging decisions can defer to recent probe results when deciding whether to trigger an aggressive fallback for a tenant. Motivation: During recent incidents (see ENG-8372) we observed tenants entering cascade fallbacks when regional KPIs briefly spiked; hedging too eagerly made recovery slower. This PR implements three coordinated behaviors: 1) a tenant-scoped fallback budget that ramps fallback aggressiveness based on short-window SLO burn and long-window sustained pressure; 2) hedged-request coordination that avoids duplicating load on the same region by consulting a fast in-process probe cache; 3) liveness-probe integration so that a region marked as recovering (probe success within 10s) will be given a controlled re-admission window rather than being blackholed immediately. The aim is to reduce false-positive quarantines and speed up recovery while preserving SLO guarantees.
Introduce tenant_fallback_budget store with TTL and epochal decay
Expose /internal/probe-status endpoint on regional proxy and short-lived cache in router
Add hedging coordinator that gates duplicate hedges and consults probe cache
SLO enforcer hook to adjust tenant budgets based on 1m/5m/1h burn windows
Unit and integration tests for hedging logic and probe cache interactions
Docs: operational runbook and Console dashboard feature flags
Liam O'Connor: Can the probe cache be sharded? Concern about thundering herd on warmup. Suggested metrics for probe cache hit/miss.
Maya Chen: Sharded by region+slot in next patch — implemented as lightweight modulo sharding. Added probe_cache_hit probe metric.
Sofia Reyes: Please make the default tenant fallback budget conservative and gated behind console feature flag for 2 weeks.
Maya Chen: Added console gating flag, default off for GA; enabled by canary rollout config in deployment manifests.
Arjun Patel: Integration tests look solid; one minor nit on context timeouts in router hedging path (fixed).
Local unit tests + CI integration harness exercised hedging under synthetic SLO burn patterns. Bench results show a small tail increase for median router latency when hedging is enabled; hedging coordinator avoids duplicate hedges to keep p95 impact <3%. E2E used staging canary with 5% traffic to validate no tenant regressions.
Feature-flagged in Console. Canary rollout: 5% tenants -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over 48h with automatic rollback if regional SLOs degrade beyond configured thresholds. Observability: add dashboard widgets for tenant_budget usage, probe_cache hit-rate, hedging-suppressed-count.
Add tenant-scoped, progressive fallback hedging with probe-based re-admission heuristics. Feature-gated; no behavior change unless enabled. Improves recovery speed and reduces unnecessary tenant quarantines under short transient spikes.

Context: customers operating across multiple jurisdictions need a deterministic way to express data residency constraints and get reproducible enforcement + succinct audit trails. This PR delivers three coordinated pieces: (1) a policy compiler that converts high-level residency rules (service-level claims, geozone allows/denies, operator exceptions) into compact OPA bundles suitable for runtime evaluation and policy diffing; (2) an audit-sampling shim that reduces storage and ingest costs by sampling non-residency-impacting requests while preserving dense traces for cross-region or KMS-bound events; (3) a KMS path sanitizer that normalizes provider-specific KMS resource paths into a canonical internal form so residency checks and audit indexing are reliable regardless of KMS provider syntax. Motivation: previous enforcement relied on distributed ad-hoc checks that led to mismatches between audit logs and RBAC decision outcomes, and caused several edge-case incidents where a KMS ARN variant bypassed residency matching. This implementation centralizes the translation and makes decision artifacts auditable and diffable.

What I changed (summary):
- pkg/policy/compiler: new IR -> OPA translator that accepts residency rule YAML and emits a policy bundle (policy metadata, constraints, fingerprint). The compiler includes a small optimizer to dedupe overlapping allow rules.
- pkg/audit/sampler: introduces a sampling policy engine (configurable sampling rates by route, by geozone, with overrides for KMS-bound ops) and a retention metadata marker for sampled records so the audit-store can apply TTLs.
- pkg/kms/sanitizer: canonicalizes provider variants (AWS ARN, GCP resource-name, Azure keyvault URIs) into a stable key identifier used by policy and audit subsystems.
- cmd/policyctl: CLI additions to lint, compile, and preview residency bundles; added `policyctl diff --live` to compare compiled bundle against runtime decisions for canary/rollouts.
- helm/redwood/templates/rbacv2.yaml: feature-flag gates and RBAC templates to enable the compiler and sampling shim in staged rollout.
- docs/security/residency-compiler.md: specification and examples for writing residency rules, sampling profiles, and KMS canonicalization rules.
- tests/*: unit and e2e tests covering translation correctness, sampler determinism (seeded), and sanitizer idempotence.

Checklist: - [x] Compiler emits OPA bundle and fingerprint metadata - [x] Sampler marks records and exposes retention hint header - [x] Sanitizer covers AWS/GCP/Azure syntaxes and includes unknown-provider fallback - [x] End-to-end test against policy mock service - [x] Telemetry counters (policy.compile.success/fail, audit.sampler.sampled, kms.sanitize.mapped)

Security notes: sampler retains high-fidelity traces when a residency decision is NOT a simple allow (i.e., any deny, cross-region, or uncertain decisions are always fully retained). Sanitizer rejects unknown providers by returning a decision 'unknown_kms_format' which surfaces in the audit stream and increments a security alert metric to prompt operator review.

Rollout plan: feature gated behind `residency_compiler` and `audit_sampler` toggles. Default off for existing clusters. Gradual rollout to staged tenants with canary bundles via `policyctl diff` and a 48h monitoring window. If mismatch rate > 0.5% for canary tenants (measured as diffed decisions vs current runtime), rollback the feature flag and open ENG-rollback Linear task.

Related work: builds on ENG-2145's residency schema and extends the earlier kms-normalizer prototype from SEC-402. See linked Linear tasks for design notes and attack surface review.
Adds a declarative residency policy compiler that emits OPA bundles, an audit-sampling shim for high-volume non-critical calls, and a KMS resource path sanitizer to canonicalize provider bindings. No user-facing API changes; rollout behind feature flag. Backfills audit retention TTL for sampled records.
Diego Alvarez: Can the compiler attach stable fingerprints when rule reordering occurs? I want diffs to be meaningful across minor reorderings.
Asha Kapoor: Yes — the compiler normalizes rule ordering and computes a semantic fingerprint (sha256 of normalized AST). Added tests for reorder invariance.
Maya Li: Audit sampling policy seems risky for high-security tenants. We should ensure opt-out and per-tenant whitelist.
Asha Kapoor: sampling is opt-in per tenant by default; for enterprise tenants the default sampling rate is 0 and there is a per-tenant policy override. Added config and docs.
Evan Brooks: KMS sanitizer mapping should fail closed on unknown formats. Prefer returning explicit decision and incrementing alert counter.
Asha Kapoor: Agreed, implemented unknown_kms_format decision and metric kms.sanitize.unknown (see tests).
Diego Alvarez: CI flake on e2e was due to race in sampler metrics — re-run fixed it. Approving post-fix.
Maya Li: Security review complete, no blockers. Approving.

Motivation: Customers running Redwood Private in air-gapped/on-prem environments require cryptographic proof that the KMS provider used for tenant keys is an approved, on-prem-backed HSM or brokered key service. At the same time, some installers still run RBACv1-style bindings; we need a migration adapter that enforces RBACv2 contracts during upgrade while emitting strong audit evidence that is compact and safe to ship out of the air-gapped site for compliance ingestion.

This PR implements a minimal attestation handshake for air-gapped KMS providers (attestation blob + allowlist verification) and an RBACv2 migration adapter that performs non-destructive policy translation and emits an "audit cohort" record that can be sanitized and batched for export. The goal is to give installers a path to upgrade without requiring live cloud reachability and to provide security teams with verifiable artifacts for policy decisions.

What this changes (high level):
- Adds kms/attestor service used by the private-installer that validates provider-signed attestation blobs and resolves provider metadata against an allowlist bundled with the installer.
- Adds rbac/migration adapter that consumes existing binding manifests (v1) and emits equivalent RBACv2 manifests plus a migration-audit cohort entry per tenant.
- Adds audit/cohort sanitizer that redacts secrets, normalizes timestamps, and replaces machine-friendly operator principals with stable pseudonyms before any export.
- Installer integration: private-installer now has a new --kms-attest-mode flag and a controlled upload workflow that writes cohort files to /var/redwood/cohorts/ for offline transfer.

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests for attestation blob parsing and allowlist checks
- [x] Migration adapter unit tests covering role/permission translation edge cases
- [x] E2E test in private-installer harness that runs entirely offline
- [x] Audit cohort sanitizer tested with fuzzed operator names
- [x] Documentation in docs/private/airgap-kms.md and docs/rbac/migration-guide.md
- [x] Compatibility shim added so upgrades from older installer versions are non-destructive

Security notes:
- Attestation blobs are validated using provider public keys packaged with the installer; we accept only SHA256-signed metadata and reject any unsigned or expired assertions.
- The cohort sanitizer ensures no raw KMS key IDs or plaintext secrets are present in exported artifacts. Sanitizer replaces KMS key ids with stable hash prefixes (first 8 chars) and drops any encryption context entries that contain tenant PII.

Operational notes:
- The default allowlist is conservative; operators can extend it via an allowlist.yaml provided at install time, which is itself signed by a customer operator key and validated by the attestor.
- The cohort upload path is intentionally file-based; we did not add network transfer helpers to keep the initial MVP air-gap friendly.

Backwards compatibility:
- RBACv1 bindings are read-only during migration; the adapter produces new RBACv2 manifests in a separate directory and never mutates the original manifests in-place. The installer will only swap to RBACv2 if an explicit --apply-migration flag is set.

Related work and tickets: ENG-2142 (migration), SEC-78 (attestation requirements), SUP-4312 (customer support case referencing air-gapped KMS verification).

- b2c3d4e: add rbac migration adapter + translation unit tests (rbac/migrate)
- c3d4e5f: installer integration + cohort sanitizer + docs (installer/, audit/)
Each commit kept small to ease cherry-picks into release branches.

Motivation: production incidents showed opaque correlation between client requests and streaming connections and gaps in structured logs from the OpenAI-compat gateway. This PR implements deterministic request_id propagation, W3C traceparent passthrough, structured log enrichment, and per-endpoint metric tags across the API stack including the streaming path and the openai-compat layer. Design summary: 1) Generate a strong request_id at gateway entry when none is provided (X-Redwood-Request-Id / OpenAI-Request-Id fallback). 2) Attach request_id and traceparent to all downstream internal RPCs and to the streaming connection lifecycle (connect, chunk, error, close). 3) Enrich structured logs emitted by the gateway, runtime, and function-caller with request_id, trace_id, span_id, endpoint Tag, model.variant, and routing policy. 4) Add metric label 'endpoint' to per-route counters/histograms, with cardinality bucketing rules described in docs to avoid high-cardinality explosion. 5) Update the OpenAI-compat layer to accept and propagate openai-style request IDs and to map them to internal request_id for trace continuity. Checklist: - [x] Request ID generation and header mapping implemented at gateway - [x] Traceparent passthrough and creation if missing - [x] Streaming lifecycle hooks instrumented with request and trace metadata - [x] Structured log schema extended and validated against logging contract - [x] Metrics labels added and unit tests for cardinality guardrails - [x] Integration tests with OpenAI-compat to verify header passthrough - [x] Docs updated (console + API reference) - [x] E2E verified in staging with simulated multi-chunk streams and function/tool calls Compatibility: existing clients are unaffected; if clients send X-Request-Id or OpenAI-Request-Id we preserve and surface it. For legacy proxies that strip traceparent, we generate and return trace parent details in response headers for operator correlation. Security/Privacy: request_id is opaque UUIDv4; no PII added to logs. Rollout plan: staged rollout by gateway pods behind feature flag for 48h, monitor errors/traces and metric cardinality. Added a feature-flagged Policy Transparency endpoint that serves signed, pseudonymized policy/audit exports for certified auditors and compliance owners. Introduces a KMS pseudonymization adapter and RBAC v2 policy exporter. Backwards-compatible and feature-flag gated.
Motivation: Customers and auditors increasingly ask for exported proofs of access and policy state that do not leak tenant PII or raw key material. Current audit exports are rich but contain operator identifiers and exact key ARNs that some customers cannot share with external auditors. This PR introduces a feature-flagged Policy Transparency endpoint (GET /internal/compliance/policy-transparency) which returns a signed bundle containing: a diff of RBAC v2 policies (human- and machine-readable), KMS usage summaries with pseudonymized key identifiers (via the new KMS Pseudonymization Adapter), and an attestable audit log slice (time-windowed) where sensitive fields are redacted or replaced with stable pseudonyms. Design highlights: - KMS Pseudonymization Adapter: a pluggable layer in the key-usage exporter that replaces exact key ids with deterministic pseudonyms per-tenant + per-audit-session salt. Pseudonyms are stable within an audit run but irreversible without the session salt, which is exposed only to the auditor via a short-lived, auditable grant. - RBAC v2 exporter: walks the policy store, computes normalized diffs between the requested window and the prior snapshot, and includes policy fingerprints and human-readable rationale fields. - Signed bundles: bundles are signed with the compliance service key (stored in KMS) and include a hash manifest so downstream verification is trivial. - Feature gating: exposed under feature gate policy_transparency_v1 and an RBAC guard requiring org:compliance-reader role. - Privacy controls: default export redacts operator emails and replaces them with stable pseudonyms; optional pseudonym reveal is gated by an explicit auditor grant backed by SUP-8841 workflow. Checklist: - [x] Adapter for pseudonymization added and unit-tested - [x] RBAC v2 exporter implemented with diff & fingerprinting - [x] Signed bundle format defined and documented (docs/internal/compliance) - [x] Feature flag + rollout plan (5% beta, org opt-in) - [x] E2E test exercising signer and verification flow - [x] Security review and threat model updated Context and scope: This PR does not change actual KMS key usage, key policy enforcement, or tenant key scoping. It only transforms what is present in exported artifacts and adds an access-controlled endpoint for compliance. The session-salt reveal mechanism is implemented in a companion PR for the auditor-access service (SUP-8841) and is intentionally separate to keep the data-plane export immutable and verifiable. Commits summary: - Add KMS pseudonymization adapter and deterministic pseudonym generator - Implement RBAC v2 policy walker and diff engine - Add bundle signer + verification helpers - Hook endpoint into compliance service with RBAC guard and feature gate - Add e2e tests and integration test harness updates - Documentation: internal spec and migration notes Changed files (high level): - services/compliance/api.go (new endpoint + handler) - services/compliance/exporter/pseudonym_adapter.go (new) - services/compliance/exporter/pseudonym_test.go (unit tests) - services/compliance/exporter/pseudonym_impl.go (deterministic salt logic) - core/rbac/exporter/exporter.go (policy walker + diff engine) - core/rbac/exporter/serializer.go (fingerprint + human readable output) - infra/iam/roles.yaml (new org:compliance-reader role) - docs/internal/compliance/policy-transparency.md (spec) - tests/e2e/compliance_transparency_test.go - build/ci/compliance_exporter_pipeline.yml - pkg/crypto/signature.go (bundle signer helpers) - scripts/rollout/feature_flag_policy_transparency.sh Review conversation (selected): - Marcus Li (reviewer): "This looks comprehensive. Two concerns: 1) the deterministic pseudonym generator — how do we handle key rotation on the backend KMS? Could the pseudonym map break when a key is replaced? 2) performance when exporting a large window (multi-day)." - Author (Anya): "Answers: 1) pseudonymization operates on key fingerprint (SHA256 over key public metadata + key-id). When a key is rotated, the fingerprint changes and the pseudonym will change — which is intended (the export will show a different pseudonym, and the diff engine will surface that as key-rotation). For stable cross-window mapping we also include an optional 'alias hint' field that points to tenant-provided aliases if available. 2) Export path is stream-processed; we implemented a streaming serializer and the exporter supports chunked signatures to avoid OOMs. Benchmarks in tests show 2x memory reduction vs naive buffering." - Sofia Morales (reviewer): "Please add a note to the threat model about an attacker who obtains a session salt. What mitigations exist?" - Author (Anya): "Added threat model section and an auditor-secret TTL + KYC gating note. Session salts are short lived, logged to the auditor grant ledger, and we rotate the grant after use (see docs)." - Devon Harris (approver): "Approve after nits: make the feature-flag default off and add a metrics counter for exports per org." - Anya: "Addressed: feature flag defaults to off, plus export_counter{org} metric added and linked to Console dashboard." CI summary: - unit tests: pass - integration tests: pass (compliance exporter harness) - lint: pass with minor golint warnings fixed in subsequent commit - security scan: pass with low-severity findings (noted in PR) Merge outcome: merged via squash on 2026-03-01 by repository maintainers. Post-merge actions: - Rollout plan in docs/ops/rollouts.md (staged 5% -> 50% -> org opt-in) - Follow-up PRs: auditor-access grant flow (SUP-8841) and console UI for granting reveal (ENG-9278) Monitoring and observability: - export_counter{org} metric added - bundle_sign_latency histogram - compliance_export_errors counter - dashboard and alert runbook added under observability/compliance Export privacy guarantees (short): - Raw KMS key IDs are never present in exported bundles unless an auditor grant reveals them. - Pseudonyms are deterministic per-session and tenant and are irreversible without the session salt. - Signed bundles allow auditors to verify the integrity of exports without relying on live access. Operational notes: - Because the bundles are signed with the compliance service KMS key, rotation of that key will result in new signatures; we include signer-key-id in the manifest so auditors can verify previous bundle signatures against archived signer keys. - Feature gate controlled: disable quickly via feature flag if unexpected privacy concerns appear. Documentation: docs/internal/compliance/policy-transparency.md contains API schema, bundle format, threat model, rollout steps, and verification example. Migration: No customer migration required; org admins must opt in to enable exports. Known limitations: - Pseudonym reveal workflow is out-of-band (separate PR) - Very large exports can still be slow; we recommend limiting window to 7 days for initial rollout.

Anya: 'pseudonymization is based on key fingerprint; rotation changes fingerprint and will show as rotation; alias hints exist for stability'

Adds Early-Exit Load Shepherd and Transparent Slowpath Attenuator to improve SLO adherence during transient bursts; telemetry and rollout toggles included.
Motivation: in recent incidents we observed slowpath requests (long KV/drain + heavy decoding) saturating GPU queues under short bursts and causing tail-latency SLO violations. This change introduces an "early-exit load shepherd" that probabilistically prefers fastpath execution when capacity is tight and a "transparent slowpath attenuator" that gently reduces admission to slowpath workers rather than hard-shedding. The goal is graceful degradation: preserve p50/p90 latency for high-priority traffic while allowing lower-priority slowpath work to be delayed/backed off with observable bounds.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a lightweight early-exit decision in the scheduler: if estimated remaining KV pressure + queue depth exceeds adaptive thresholds, low-priority requests are signaled for early-exit and returned with a short-circuit response (with structured telemetry to drive retries).
- Implements a slowpath attenuator that applies probabilistic admission based on recent slowpath dwell time and regional SLO credit. Attenuator decays probability back to 0 over a configurable window to avoid long tail suppression.
- Adds per-tenant & per-region metrics (early_exit.rate, slowpath.attenuation_ratio, early_exit.latency_impact) and dashboard panels to the SLO console.
- Introduces feature flags and rollout toggles (canary_fraction, region_whitelist, soft_mode) to enable gradual adoption and quick rollback.
- Fixes a KV drain race discovered during testing where early-exit could leave partial KV state; added a small sync guard and unit tests.

Checklist: 
- [x] Scheduler decision logic and unit tests
- [x] Slowpath admission policy + property tests
- [x] Knobs & feature flags with defaults tuned off for existing clusters
- [x] Telemetry + dashboard YAML + alert baseline adjustments
- [x] Load test scenario and CI gating
- [x] Rollout runbook included in docs/degradation.md

Related: Linear ENG-3492 (early-exit prototype), ENG-3580 (slowpath admission tuning), incident SUP-987 (regional KV saturation).

Evelyn Park (author): 'Added a note in the dashboard YAML with expected baseline ranges; also added a TTL-based sample to reduce noise.'

Luca Moreno: 'Concern: probabilistic admission could bias multi-tenant fairness. Can we add tenant_weighted backoff?'

Evelyn Park: 'We intentionally kept tenant weighting orthogonal in this first pass to simplify the canary. Added a follow-up Linear card (ENG-3641) to evaluate tenant_weighted rollout. I also added a guard that refuses to attenuate primary-tier requests.'

Grace Chen: 'Unit tests look good. Load testing flaked once — re-ran and green. Approving pending one doc tweak.'

Grace Chen (after doc tweak): 'Approved.'
Checks run: unit-tests (passed), integration-slo-tests (flaky -> rerun passed), lint (passed), load-profile/short-burst (initial run showed p99 degradation; adjusted attenuator defaults and re-ran -> pass), grafana-render (passed). Investigation: the first load test exposed a KV drain race which the PR fixes; rerun included the fix and passed. CI pipeline ID: build/829104. Detailed check logs are attached to the PR (link omitted for dataset).
Merged by squash on 2026-02-14 after approvals from reviewers. Merge method: squash and merge. Release note added to changelog. Rollout plan: start canary at 1% in us-west, expand to 5% after 24h if no SLO regressions, add eu-central mirrored canary the following day, full enable only after telemetry shows attenuation_ratio < 0.15 and no >5% regression in p99 for primary tier. If customers report increased immediate 429-like early-exit short-circuits, set runtime.early_exit.soft_mode=true to return a 202 (delayed) instead of hard short-circuit so clients can hedge. Background: Production workloads with mixed sequence lengths were showing elevated transient GPU memory usage due to long-lived scratch allocations and conservative KV retention. Motivation: Reduce peak working set without regressing latency SLOs by compacting scratch buffers along a chronological lifetime axis and introducing an ephemeral KV binning layer to enable low-overhead short-term eviction. Design summary: 1) Chronological scratch compaction: a micro-slab allocator subdivides large scratch arenas into thin chronological slabs keyed to request arrival time windows. Slabs are compacted (coalesced and zeroed) once all active kernels referencing that slab have completed; we prioritized an optimistic fast-path for single-kernel consumers and a fallback slow-path that defers compaction for multi-kernel overlap. 2) Ephemeral KV binning: add a short-lived in-GPU bin layer for KV cache entries produced by streaming/continuous-batching traffic. Bins are sized by recent token reuse statistics and are evicted in short time windows (seconds) before falling back to the regular LRU eviction policy. 3) Kernel handshake and scheduler hints: small ABI extension lets kernels declare scratch slab affinity and earliest-safe-evict timestamps to avoid races during aggressive compaction. 4) Safety/fallbacks: compaction is gated behind runtime flags and a conservative heuristics mode that disables binning for pinned sessions (dedicated capacity). Checklist: - [x] implementation of micro-slab allocator and slab lifecycle manager - [x] ephemeral KV binning + telemetry - [x] scheduler handshake + kernel ABI extension - [x] unit & integration tests - [x] microbench/perf runs and SLO verification - [x] rollout plan with runtime flag & canary gating Testing & results: Unit tests added for allocator invariants and KV bin rotation. Integration tests simulate mixed-length streaming workloads and show median peak GPU working set reduced by ~18% on T4/GPU mix and up to 27% on p4d tests with heavy continuous-batching. P99 latency change: +1.3% (within allowable SLO); throughput unchanged. Safety: feature off by default for hosted API; enabled behind canary boolean for Dedicated. Rollout: staged canary (10% nodes) for 48h then ramp to 100% if no regressions. Related: touches runtime/scheduler, runtime/scratch_allocator, runtime/kv_cache, and a small API bump for kernel metadata. Notes: This PR is focused on runtime memory and low-risk integration—there are follow-ups planned to expose additional telemetry and per-customer tuning knobs in Redwood Console.
Diego Alvarez: Impl looks solid; main concern is race between kernel evict hint and compaction. Can we add an assert in debug builds?

Problem: SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go) diverged in retry defaults and streaming ergonomics after several incremental fixes. This caused mismatched failure modes in production: some clients aggressively retried transient 5xxs and caused thundering retries; others exposed low-level streaming primitives that made simple restart/reauth flows awkward. Goal: unify retry heuristics (backoff shape, max attempts, idempotency heuristics) and introduce a compact, cross-language lightweight StreamAdapter facade that simplifies resumable stream consumer code and standardizes token-refresh hooks. This PR implements the following across SDKs and docs: - A shared retry profile DSL (exposed as config objects in each SDK) with default presets: conservative, standard, aggressive - Uniform default: "standard" with jittered exponential backoff (base=100ms, factor=2, cap=10s, max_attempts=4), plus opt-in aggressive preset for batch workloads - Idempotency-based retry gating: automatically reduces retries for non-idempotent operations unless caller explicitly marks them safe - StreamAdapter: a tiny facade that wraps underlying WS/HTTP chunked streams to provide resume, heartbeat, and credential-refresh hooks with a minimal callback surface - Session priming helper to pre-warm credential leases for long-lived streams - Cross-SDK tests and integration harness updates (local smoke + downstream example app) - Version bumps: python sdk -> 1.7.0, typescript sdk -> 2.4.0, go sdk -> v0.13.0 Rationale: having consistent retry behavior reduces production surprises and makes server-side load profiles predictable. A compact, well-specified stream adapter lowers the cognitive load on app authors integrating streaming LLM responses while enabling consistent token refresh semantics for private/dedicated deployments. Checklist: - [x] Implement retry DSL in each SDK - [x] Implement StreamAdapter facade in each SDK - [x] Add unit and integration tests (cross-sdk harness) - [x] Update changelogs and version numbers - [x] Update docs and quickstart examples - [x] Run perf smoke tests and adjust defaults as needed Related: Linear ENG-2043 ENG-2198; internal incident notes INT-582 (stream reconnect storm). See design doc: https://linear.redwood.ai/notes/ENG-2043-unified-retry-and-stream-adapter for full rationale and migration notes.

Priya Nair: tests look good, but TS adapter needs clearer typings for the credential refresh callback; suggested signature change and added an example in the README.
Maya Thompson: updated TS types and added example snippet; also added an integration smoke test that simulates token rotation.

Context & motivation: Customers integrating with OpenAI /v1/chat.completions expect predictable parity for a) parameter semantics (temperature/top_p/n), b) role and stop handling, c) function/tool calling determinism, d) streaming stability and e) structured output formats. This PR implements a lightweight 'param orchestrator' plus stream resilience and a compact framed-json envelope to reduce client parsing ambiguity. Design highlights: - Param orchestrator: canonicalizes v1 params into our internal runtime hints (temperature->sampling_bias, top_p->nucleus_hint, n->parallel_copies), enforces safe ranges, and emits warnings for ambiguous combinations. - Stop handling: supports both legacy stop arrays and a new weighted-stop list (token + weight). The orchestrator deduplicates equivalent stop sequences, orders stable by token hash, and implements a stop-short-circuit that avoids duplicate fragments in streaming mode. - Streaming stability: introduces a fragment sentinel boundary (\u241E) paired with a heartbeat ping when fragmentization is long-lived; backpressure heuristics reduce jitter seen in high-concurrency workloads. - Function/tool calling deterministic preflight: a lightweight intent-scoring preflight runs in the coordinator so model responses that indicate tool invocation are matched to the highest-confidence registered tool deterministically to avoid flakiness in canary and multiprocess setups. - Structured output: adds an opt-in 'framed_json' response_mode that wraps model output in a small envelope {"frame_v":1, "payload_type":"assistant_response|tool_call|eval", "body":...}. This reduces ambiguity when streaming toolcall metadata and logprob arrays. - Logprobs normalization: canonicalize top_logprobs to a list-of-maps structure, normalize -Inf/NaN to null, and include a token_index map so downstream clients have stable indexing. Checklist: - [x] Param translation and validation + unit tests - [x] Weighted-stop parsing and dedupe algorithm - [x] Stream sentinel & heartbeat implementation + integration test - [x] Deterministic tool preflight and coordinator changes - [x] Framed JSON envelope + docs example - [x] End-to-end compatibility tests against OpenAI fixtures - [x] SDK guidance updates (python/ts) Rollout plan: staged on internal canary -> dedicated infra -> hosted fleet. Feature gated: framed_json is opt-in via response_mode; orchestrator applied for requests that declare api_version: "v1" to minimize risk. Related: ENG-2147, PM-489, SUP-1123. Links: linear/ENG-2147, api-design-doc (private), docs PR will follow.
Adds a compatibility layer that maps /v1/chat.completions params to Redwood's runtime, stabilizes streaming boundaries, introduces a deterministic preflight for function/tool selection, normalizes logprobs payloads, and emits a compact framed JSON envelope for structured outputs. Backwards-compatible for existing clients; opt-in behavior for framed JSON via response_mode parameter.
Opt-in framed_json via response_mode. Orchestrator applied when api_version=v1. No breaking changes for existing clients. SDKs updated with examples. Monitoring: compat_preflight_count, stream_fragmentation_rate (should drop), weighted_stop_dedup_rate.
Run tests in tests/integration/test_v1_compat_fixtures.py against the OpenAI fixture dataset. For canary: enable framed_json for 5% of traffic and monitor error rate and parsing failures in the SDKs. Validate that top_logprobs map indexing matches token offsets when framing is enabled.

Motivation: customers with strict regulatory envelopes asked for stronger guarantees that KMS usage and RBAC decisions respect declared service boundaries (e.g. datasets, operator roles, and tenant pinning) while keeping the policy model declarative and auditable. This PR implements a service-boundary enforcer that validates request-scoped claims against a declarative KMS-binding policy and routes audit events through a shard-aware audit sink. The change is split into three logical pieces: 1) policy/decl-mapper: a compact DSL and evaluation engine to map service/tenant attributes to allowed KMS provider bindings (supports multiple providers, per-tenant allowlists, and temporary operator overrides), 2) runtime/enforcer: a lightweight middleware that performs enforcement at the request edge, emits canonical audit markers, and short-circuits unsafe KMS calls with a clear error and remediation hints, and 3) observability/audit-router: a configurable router that shards audit events by jurisdiction and retention class to separate sinks (S3/BigQuery/GCS) and attaches signed provenance headers. Checklist: - [x] DSL spec and examples - [x] Decl-mapper implementation + unit tests - [x] Enforcer middleware and integration tests - [x] Audit router with sink adapters and provenance headers - [x] Helm chart changes for private installers - [x] Documentation and upgrade notes Backwards compatibility: The DSL defaults are permissive for existing deployments; operators must opt-in to stricter enforcement in the Console or via the new ConfigMap. Rollout plan: staged enablement by tenant cohort using a rollout flag and safe-fallback to previous KMS behavior when policy evaluation fails (fail-open for non-enforced tenants; fail-closed optional per organization). Related work: ENG-3456 (service-boundary policy), SEC-112 (audit provenance), PM-789 (compliance rollouts).
Adds a declarative service-boundary policy DSL and runtime enforcer that can be opted into per-tenant; introduces audit-sink sharding for region-aware retention. No immediate breaking changes; operators must enable enforcement explicitly. See docs/security/service-boundary.md for migration steps.
Initial reviewers requested stricter error codes and clearer remediation text when a request is blocked. Diego asked for a performance microbenchmark; we added a small load test showing ~1% p99 overhead in the edge path. Priya requested an extra integration test covering operator-scope override TTLs, which was added. A transient flaky test in CI caused one rerun; after the rerun all checks passed. Final sign-off granted by Samir (security lead).
Operators should review the example policy files in policy/decl-mapper/README.md and enable enforcement via the Console feature flag or the helm value 'security.serviceBoundary.enforce=true'. When enabling for the first time, run the migration script tests/integration/kms_binding_residency_test.go against a staging cluster to confirm KMS provider mappings. Audit router requires credentials for configured sinks and an HSM/KMS key for signing provenance headers; fallback to unsigned mode is available but not recommended.

Context: Our existing lint pipeline is heavy (Docker-based linters and full repo checks on every PR) which slows feedback and increases CI cost. Release hooks were tightly coupled to the monolithic workflow, making staged releases fragile when we split artifacts. This PR introduces three coordinated changes: 1) a lightweight lint harness (fastpath) that runs staged checks locally and in CI for touched files only; 2) a dep-rotation tool that automates safe, staged upgrades/removals of transitive dependencies; 3) a refactor of release hooks into a two-stage flow (prepare + smoke) to improve reliability and enable canary releases.

What changed (high level): implemented a new fast lint harness written in TypeScript that caches parsed ASTs and computes minimal lint sets for PR diffs; replaced a number of heavyweight Docker lint invocations in CI with node-run fastpaths and fallbacks to the legacy image for full scans on demand; added tools/dep-rotation (small Go binary + orchestration script) that iterates through candidate transitive deps, generates rotation PRs with lightweight test matrices, and annotates each candidate with rollout status; refactored workflows/.github/workflows/release.yml into prepare-release.yml and release-smoke.yml and added a new staged-release label that gates automated canaries; added a simple preflight compatibility check that runs a pinned set of integration samplers against the candidate build before promoting artifacts.

Motivation: reduce PR feedback time by ~3x for typical code changes, reduce CI spend on lints for high-volume PRs, and make dependency churn safer by automating gradual rollouts and rollbacks. Separating release steps reduces failed release rollouts and makes the failure modes more observable and recoverable.

Checklist:
- [x] Add fastpath lint harness and integrate into PR pipeline
- [x] Add fallback path to legacy docker linter for full scans
- [x] Implement dep-rotation tool with PR templating and light test matrix
- [x] Split release workflow into prepare + smoke and wire staged-release label
- [x] Update CONTRIBUTING.md with new fastpath instructions and howto for dep-rotation
- [x] Add smoke job to console dashboards for release-failure alerts

How to exercise locally:
- Run the fast lint harness: ./scripts/lint-fast --staged
- Create a trial rotation: ./tools/dep-rotation/rotate --dry-run --candidate lodash@4.18.0
- Trigger staged release locally with: gh workflow run prepare-release.yml --ref feature/branch

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: fastpath lint may miss some cross-file lint rules. Mitigation: CI still runs full scan on main branch and the fallback job runs full lints on PRs touching build/infra.
- Risk: dep-rotation may generate many noisy PRs. Mitigation: tool defaults to dry-run and has an auto-throttle; rotation PRs are created under tools/automation and labelled rotateme.

Related work: builds on ENG-3742 (perf-oriented CI slicing) and ENG-3890 (release resiliency). Also complements recent cache work in pr-71220 and pr-833000.
Aidan Cole: Nice, big win for feedback velocity. A couple of questions on the fallback invocation and caching semantics — see inline.
Maya Patel: replied with rationale for cache TTL and fallback ordering; updated scripts to make TTL configurable via CI input.

Context: as we roll out the hardware tuning profiles pack + override precedence (fleet default -> per-deployment -> per-route -> env/flags), Support and SRE need a fast way to answer “what config is this runtime *actually* using right now?” without grepping logs or reverse-engineering values.yaml + env vars. This PR adds a small CLI/tooling command that prints the effective runtime config after profile selection and all overrides are applied, including the source/precedence for each key, and with safe redaction of secrets. What’s included: (1) New CLI subcommand: `redwood-runtime config dump` (alias: `redwood-runtime dump-config`) (2) Supports YAML and JSON output: `--format=yaml|json` (default: yaml) (3) Includes optional provenance: `--explain` adds a per-key “source” (profile_pack / runtime_default / config_file / env / flag / route_override) and the profile id/version chosen (4) Redaction by default: any key matching `*token*`, `*secret*`, `*password*`, `*api_key*` is replaced with `"<redacted>"`; `--no-redact` requires `--i-understand-this-prints-secrets` (5) Stability for runbooks: output is sorted deterministically and emits a single header line with runtime version, profile pack version, detected hardware, and override summary (counts by source). Example usage: `redwood-runtime config dump --explain --format=yaml` prints the config used by the running process (or from a config file via `--config /path/runtime.yaml`). Operator workflow: oncall can `kubectl exec` into a pod, run the command, and paste into incident threads; Support can ask Private customers to run the command and attach output (safe by default). Non-goals: not a full “doctor” tool; does not attempt to validate fleet health; does not persist output anywhere. Notes: This builds on the precedence rules implemented in PR-21991 and adds a single shared `EffectiveConfig` snapshot that is already used by startup logs. This PR reuses that logic rather than duplicating config resolution. Follow-ups: we may want to wire the same output into the debug endpoint added in PR-22027 so that we can fetch it remotely when permitted by policy.

Implementation details: CLI is implemented in `cmd/redwood-runtime/config_dump.go` and uses the existing config loader to compute `EffectiveConfig`. Provenance is carried by `ResolvedValue{value, source, source_detail}`; `source_detail` includes e.g. env var name or config file path. YAML output uses our existing internal serializer (no anchors) for readability in tickets. The command exits non-zero if config parsing fails; with `--strict`, it also exits non-zero if hardware detection is ambiguous (mirrors loader behavior).

Testing: unit tests cover redaction patterns, deterministic ordering, provenance output, and a golden-file test for YAML output. Added an integration test that runs the CLI in a minimal container entrypoint to ensure it can execute without GPU present (important for CI + support tooling containers).

Docs/Runbooks: added short snippet to the internal runbook template referenced by SRE (not public docs).

Motivation: perf-canary is showing end-to-end latency regressions that are hard to attribute (kernel/runtime execution vs scheduler pressure). This PR exports scheduler queueing-time metrics and batch-size distribution at the runtime layer so we can: (1) split latency into queueing vs execution for canary attribution, (2) detect regressions caused by batching heuristics / admission control changes, (3) avoid relying on sampling-heavy trace-only approaches. What’s included: - New histogram metric for scheduler queueing time (enqueue -> execution start). - New histogram metric for batch size at execution start (effective batch after coalescing). - Structured dimension set aligned with telemetry cardinality constraints (no per-request identifiers). - Wiring to existing runtime metrics registry + export path. - Unit tests for metric emission + bounds (no negative durations, no zero/negative batch sizes). Metric definitions (names / units): - redwood_runtime_scheduler_queueing_time_ms (histogram, ms) - redwood_runtime_scheduler_batch_size (histogram, count) - redwood_runtime_scheduler_queueing_time_ms_count / _sum / _bucket (exported by histogram backend) Dimensions (labels): model (canonical name), model_version (registry version id), region, tier (hosted|dedicated|private), pool (logical serving pool), hardware_sku, runtime_build_id, scheduler_policy (coarse enum). Notes: - scheduler_policy is intentionally coarse ("classic" | "continuous" | "unknown") to avoid config-cardinality blowups. - We do NOT emit request_id, tenant_id, prompt_length, or any user identifiers. - Metrics are emitted at the point a request leaves the scheduler queue and is assigned to a GPU execution slot; for batched execution, queueing time is tracked per request, and batch_size is tracked per batch. - Backfill: none; this is new time series. Canary and dashboards can start querying once the runtime rolls out. Rollout plan: ship behind runtime flag RuntimeMetrics.SchedulerQueueing (default ON in staging, ON in prod after canary validates). If metrics volume is higher than expected, we can disable via the flag without runtime restart (dynamic config refresh). Validation: verified under synthetic load in staging (benchmark-lab runner) that queueing time rises with induced scheduler saturation and returns to baseline when load is removed; batch-size histogram shifts as expected when toggling continuous batching depth. Related: ENG-4875 adds scheduler-level instrumentation; perf-canary dashboards/alerts will follow in observability-pack. Screenshots: none (metrics-only).

Omar El-Sayed (author): Yep, this is enqueue->execution start (after batch formation + slot assignment). I clarified in docs/ops/metrics/runtime-metrics-catalog.md and added a code comment in dispatcher.go near the dequeue path.

Omar El-Sayed (author): Done. Updated buckets to match runtime latency standard buckets and added a unit test that asserts bucket boundaries.

Sofia Ivanova (approval): Looks good with clarified semantics + bucket alignment. Approving.

Introduce a contractual throughput admission controller and a burst attenuator to provide per-tenant guaranteed throughput while smoothing microbursts. Motivation: customers using Dedicated capacity require clear guarantees against noisy neighbors and predictable tail latencies during bursty traffic. This PR implements an admission layer that negotiates a tenant's committed throughput from their reservation metadata and enforces it via a tokenized admission queue plus a short-term burst attenuator that decays credits based on recent consumption. The change touches scheduler admission logic, the tenant reservation API, autoscaler signals, and telemetry. Key behaviors: 1) When a request arrives the admission controller checks committed_throughput and current_reserved_headroom; if within committed rate it admits immediately; if the tenant has burst credits the attenuator allows the request but debits burst_credits; if neither condition is met the request is queued behind guaranteed work and may be backpressured or overflowed to a secondary tier depending on policy. 2) Burst credits accumulate when a tenant consumes below committed throughput and decay with an exponential half-life when idle; a safety cap prevents unbounded credit accumulation. 3) The autoscaler receives a new metric (committed_utilization_ratio) that excludes transient burst-driven spikes so scaling decisions stay aligned to contractual load. 4) Rollout is opt-in per-tenant through a ReservationPolicy flag so we can pilot with a handful of customers before global rollout. This single commit description covers design, implementation, tests, docs, and migration notes. Checklist: [x] Design doc linked [x] Unit and integration tests [x] Telemetry and dashboards updated [x] Backwards-compatible API changes [x] Migration guide included. Related work: ENG-2148 (reservation contract schema), ENG-2201 (autoscaler signal filtering), SUP-587 (customer incident that motivated smoother admission).

payload.body:
Motivation: We observed recurring warmup regressions in mixed-workload tenants where continuous batching interleaves short and long sequences. Captures taken across interleaved KV cache offsets produced graphs that were fragile to small kernel-selection differences; replays would either miss hot paths or trigger repeated fallback recompilations, causing 30–70% p50 latency degradation during warmup windows. This PR introduces a split-capture (tiling) strategy combined with a kernel-hash compatibility fallback to minimize thrashing and dramatically shorten warmup.

Design summary: single-string design doc below.

- Split-capture tiling: instead of capturing one large graph covering a wide sequence-length distribution, the capture manager partitions incoming requests into "tiles" by sequence-length and KV-offset proximity and performs targeted captures per tile. Tiles are small, deterministic buckets (configurable: default 16 tokens width) so captured kernels are stable and more likely to match replayed kernels.
- Kernel-hash compatibility fallback: when replay encounters a kernel mismatch, we compute a lightweight kernel-hash fingerprint for the active kernels in the current graph and consult a compatibility policy that either accepts the mismatch (if hash distance under threshold), triggers a fast-local patch (stitching minor kernel variants), or falls back to recompiled capture. This reduces full fallbacks when only minor codegen differences exist.
- KV-alignment metadata: captures now embed KV-offset markers into the graph metadata so replay aligns the cached KV entries deterministically. This avoids misaligned KV-cache offsets that were a major source of mismatch for interleaved workloads.

- Deterministic incremental warmup: when a new tile is first observed, we perform a short deterministic warmup (default 4 priming requests) with guaranteed kernel-selection seeding to avoid long probabilistic priming.

payload.body:
Introduces the zipper batcher: a seqlen-aware batching heuristic that reduces padding overhead and improves KV cache locality. Default rollout gated by a runtime flag; measurable cost and tail-latency improvements on benchmark workloads.
Summary: Add a new 'zipper' batching algorithm that forms cohorts by interleaving short and long sequences (zippering) while biasing selection toward requests with warm KV cache entries (LRU score) and stable kernel-cost profiles. Motivation: Traditional bucketing or pure seqlen-first packing either wastes tokens (padding) or causes frequent kernel-path switching and KV cache churn. The zipper approach aims to reduce padding overhead without scattering requests that would evict hot KV cache lines, and to smooth kernel selection transitions so the runtime can reuse optimized kernels longer. Design: 1) Each incoming request is annotated with sequence_length, lru_score (derived from per-request cache footprint and last-access timestamp), and an estimated kernel_cost vector (small fingerprint mapping to an internal kernel profile). 2) The batcher maintains short and long shelves; instead of flushing full buckets, it pulls from both shelves in zipper order: short,long,short,long,... up to target batch_size or pad-overhead budget. 3) When choosing the next candidate, zipper_batcher scores candidates by combined metric: score = alpha*pad_savings_estimate + beta*lru_preservation + gamma*kernel_cost_alignment. Parameters alpha/beta/gamma are tunable via config; defaults chosen to prioritize pad savings but penalize negative LRU impact. 4) If a potential zipper cohort would change the dominant kernel path for the batch beyond a threshold, the cohorter will bias toward same-kernel candidates or split into two sub-batches to avoid kernel thrash. 5) Integrated backpressure: if latency SLOs start degrading, zipper reduces cohorting aggressiveness and favors immediate flush. Implementation details: - New module src/runtime/batcher/zipper_batcher.rs implementing the heuristic, exposing a runtimeflag enable_zipper and config knobs (alpha,beta,gamma,pad_budget_pct,max_kernel_switch_per_batch). - Added cost-model hook in src/runtime/scheduler/cost_model.rs to return a compact kernel profile id for active models. - KV-awareness surfaced via an LRU-proxy in serving/kv_cache/eviction_policy.rs that produces a per-request lru_score without changing eviction semantics (read-only view). - Small changes in runtime/batcher/mod.rs to register zipper option and wiring into continuous batching loop. - Tests and benchmarks added: tests/perf/zipper_benchmark.py and tests/unit/test_zipper_cohorting.rs. Performance: Benchmarked on A100 and H100 medium/long tail workloads. Representative results vs current default cohorter using 8-shard 40b model: average token cost -11.8%, throughput +17.6% under mixed seqlen traffic, median latency ~unchanged, 95th tail latency -5.1%. When combined with KV-friendly routing these gains improved to token cost -14.2% and tail -8.0%. We also saw a ~10% reduction in kernel-switch events, leading to more stable GPU utilization. Commits: - feat(batcher): zipper batcher core algorithm and config - perf(scheduler): kernel profile id and cost smoothing hook - infra(kv): add lru_score proxy view (read-only) - test(perf): zipper benchmark harness - docs: operator guide and rollout notes Changed files (high level): src/runtime/batcher/zipper_batcher.rs, src/runtime/batcher/mod.rs, src/runtime/scheduler/cost_model.rs, src/serving/kv_cache/eviction_policy.rs, tests/perf/zipper_benchmark.py, docs/operators/zipper-batcher.md Testing and CI: Initial CI run failed integration perf (bench harness timeout) on first push due to lock ordering in LRU proxy. Fixed by introducing a read-lock pattern and adding a stress test. Final CI: unit tests pass, perf harness runs in CI microbench, e2e bench on internal infra completed manually. Rollout plan: Feature gated across runtime via enable_zipper flag. Start with 5% of hosted traffic for 24h, monitor pad_overhead, kernel_switch_events, kv_miss_rate. If metrics stable, ramp to 50% then full. Observability: added metrics zipper_cohort_size, zipper_pad_savings_pct, zipper_kernel_switch_count, zipper_lru_impact_score, and a tracing tag for cohort_id to link traces. Backwards compatibility and safety: zipper is off by default; no changes to on-disk artifacts; LRU proxy is read-only so no cache semantics change. Migration: none required. Review conversation: - Evan Rogers: "Nice idea. Please add a hard safety cap to avoid pathological cohorts that exceed pad budget under bursty short-sequence arrival." Author reply: "Added pad_budget_pct config and enforced at selection time; default 12%" - Priya Singh: "Concerned about kernel switching heuristics; will this hurt tail latency for long conversation workloads?" Author reply: "We added a kernel_switch_threshold and sub-batching path; if threshold exceeded we prefer split batches which preserves tail SLAs." - Luca Moretti: "Please add more unit tests around concurrency with the LRU proxy." Author reply: "Added stress unit test that surfaced lock ordering bug, addressed and documented." Approvals and merge: After two follow-up fixes and CI green, PR approved by Priya Singh and Luca Moretti. Merge method: squash and merge. Related work: complements ENG-4021 (batching cost model refactor) and ENG-4087 (kv-cache telemetry). Notes: This PR purposefully trades a bit more scheduler complexity for measurable token savings and more stable kernel utilization. Operator docs added with guidance and sample config. Known limitations: very high variance seqlen workloads with adversarial arrival patterns still benefit from explicit seqlen bucketing; zipper should be used as a middle-ground heuristic. Future work: adaptive alpha/beta tuning from live metrics and auto-rollout suggestions in optimize service.
payload.title: LRU-aware zipper batcher for seqlen cohorting and kernel-cost smoothing

payload.body:
Context: long-context workloads and mixed-size batches reveal inefficiencies in block-local attention kernels: boundary handoff between tiles forces repeated loads and prevents KV cache warm paths from being effective. Motivation: reduce cross-block memory traffic and enable early KV warmup while preserving numerical parity and compatibility with existing rotor/rope encodings. This PR implements a hybrid execution strategy called Cross-Block FlashMerge that splits attention computation into two cooperating phases: local-block compute (fast, Flash-optimized) and a lightweight handoff phase that merges partial results across neighboring blocks. The design also adds a prefetch-compression step for rotary/rope embeddings to reduce memory bandwidth when streaming long sequences, and a proactive KV warmup path that populates small warm KVs for expected next tokens using a cheap predictive sampler. Key features: 1) FlashMerge kernel: new CUDA kernel that fuses q,k,v GEMM + scaled-dot + softmax + out projection for intra-block work while exposing a compact handoff envelope for inter-block reduction; 2) Cross-block handoff: small fixed-size metadata buffers exchanged between adjacent tiles to avoid reloading full KV slabs; 3) Prefetch compression: lightweight delta-encoded rotary/rope transform that reduces per-token bandwidth for long sequences by ~2x with negligible compute overhead; 4) KV warmup: scheduler hook that issues background warmup requests for recently seen conversation prefixes; warm KVs are retained in the LRU hotset until eviction pressure; 5) Scheduler integration: continuous-batcher updated to honor handoff-aware batching windows and to start warmup for small-latency targets. Performance summary: microbenchmarks on p4d.24xlarge, fp16, sequence length 8k: end-to-end throughput +27% vs baseline flash-attn, median latency (p50) down 18% at batch size 1 for 2k contexts, peak GPU memory reduced by ~6% on hot-paths. Accuracy: numerical differences are within 1e-5 of the previous Flash kernel for fp16 accumulation; no quantization regressions observed in our eval harness. Safety and compatibility: feature is gated behind runtime flag --attn-crossblock-flashmerge and kernel selection policy prefers proven flash variant for small sequence lengths. Rolling deploy plan: canary on Dedicated first (10% traffic), collect trace-level latency and rand-eval quality metrics for 48h, then phased rollout. Tests and validation: unit tests for kernel math, deterministic small-sequence validation, integration bench harnesses added, end-to-end regen tests for chat service. Notes: runtime knobs exposed: attn.crossblock_enabled (bool), attn.prefetch_compression (enum: none|delta), attn.kv_warmup_window (int). How to review: focus on kernel correctness (tests in tests/kernel/), scheduler interactions (scheduler/continuous_batcher.cpp), and perf regression risks in mixed small/large workloads. Related: ENG-1284 (attention scheduling), ENG-1299 (kv cache hotset).
Introduces Cross-Block FlashMerge attention kernel with prefetch compression and KV warmup. Improves p50 latency and throughput for long-context workloads. No public API changes. Opt-in behind runtime flag --attn-crossblock-flashmerge.
Ben Hollis: Can you explain why we need the handoff buffer format rather than simply concatenating partial reductions? Please add a short comment in flashmerge_kernel.h, and include a size/alignment note.
Aisha Kapoor: Added comment and alignment table in flashmerge_kernel.h; handoff buffer keeps 64B metadata per tile to avoid atomic ops across SMs.
Priya Natarajan: Scheduler changes look invasive for the continuous-batcher. Did you measure impact on small-sequence throughput (<=128 tokens)?
Aisha Kapoor: Yes, we ran mixed-traffic microbenchmarks; small-sequence p95 latency saw <2% regression in worst-case. Added opt-out path for small sequences and a unit test in tests/bench/ to validate. Updated PR with results and graphs.
Luca Moretti: Prefetch compression seems heuristic. How robust is it to variable rotary scales? Any precision loss?
Aisha Kapoor: Prefetch compression is delta-encoding of rotary phases and uses a fallback to full representation if variance exceeds threshold. We added unit tests to exercise extreme scales; numerical diff <1e-5 in fp16 accumulative tests.
CI Bot: gpu-integration (flaky) failed on first run (OOM in long-seq smoke).
Aisha Kapoor: Reduced temporary buffer footprint, added guard to avoid launching flashmerge for sequences below min_tile_size. Reran CI; passed.
