Introduces an affinity-driven slab rebalancer with a write-through reservation window and soft handoff to improve locality and reduce allocation latency. Lowers 99th percentile token latency under mixed workloads; no API changes.
Summary: Adds an affinity-driven slab rebalancer and a small write-through reservation window to the paged KV block allocator. Motivation: mixed inference workloads with varying sequence-length distributions revealed pathological allocation churn and cross-stream cache pollution. This resulted in elevated 95/99p token latency and extra CUDA kernel contention during heavy batching. Goals: 1) Reduce allocation stalls under bursty concurrency, 2) Improve per-stream locality for KV cache reuse, 3) Avoid global pauses during slab compaction.
Design: affinity score combines recent-access locality, owner stream id fingerprint, and slab coldness. Scoring is lightweight (single 64-bit counter updates) to avoid extra atomics on the hot path.
Reservation window: short-lived write-through reservations (default 20ms) let in-flight streams hold a micro-reservation for contiguous KV blocks. This increases reuse for follow-up tokens without long-term fragmentation.
Soft handoff: when rebalancer moves blocks between slabs, it marks ranges read-only and lets existing owners finish using them before finalizing the migration, avoiding global stop-the-world compactions.
Scheduler integration: worker pool now exposes a fast path to prefetch allocator hints into local per-worker alloc caches to reduce contention at high concurrency.
Safety: added invariants and sanitizers that run in debug builds to catch double-free or stale-KV access during handoffs.
Performance: benchmark results (mixed short+long sequences, 128 concurrent streams) show 12% lower 95p token latency and 18% fewer allocation stalls on p4d. Memory overhead increase is <1.8% due to short reservations and per-worker caches.
Testing: microbench harness covers reuse ratio, reservation expiration, and soft handoff correctness. Added integration test that replays a real customer trace to validate end-to-end behavior.
Risk: under extremely skewed workloads reservation windows could temporarily hold hot blocks; mitigated by per-slab cap and decay policy. Monitoring added to alert if reservation hold ratio exceeds 15% for longer than 5 minutes.
Rollback: feature flag and safe path to disable rebalancer without restart; disabling drains reservations and restores previous allocator policy immediately.
Related: ties into ENG-6732 (allocator stability) and ENG-6870 (kv-cache telemetry).
Daniel Cho: Please add a short note in docs about the reservation window tunables and the default values. Also, add a comment explaining why we prefer soft handoff over immediate forced migration.
Ava Martinez: Added docs and inline comments. The reservation defaults were picked after running the benchmark harness across p4d and g5 clusters (see bench results in the PR).
Priya Rao: Perf numbers look good but please add a guard to avoid reservation growth under pathological churn. Suggest a decay timer and a per-slab cap.
Ava Martinez: Implemented per-slab cap and decay timer; added unit tests to validate scavenging behavior.
Liam O'Connor: Verified allocator invariants and memory accounting. Approving pending CI green.
CI: Flaky GPU smoke test failed once; rerun successful.
payload.title: affinity-driven-slab-rebalancer-and-write-through-reservation-for-paged-kv

payload.body:
Motivation: TP workloads continue to be dominated by periods where collectives stall local kernel work or where KV-cache misses force synchronous prefetches that block dispatch. On modern multi-GPU hosts these stalls amplify tail latency and hurt sustained throughput for small-to-medium microbatches used by Redwood hosted customers.

This PR implements a 'commcompute conductor' that coordinates three complementary optimizations for tensor-parallel runtimes: (1) hierarchical collective scheduling and NCCL stream affinity to permit asynchronous overlap with compute across heterogeneous link rates; (2) an adaptive KV-cache prefetcher that issues speculative prefetches based on per-request prefix hit probability and observed token arrival patterns; (3) kernel-swap hinting and lightweight state migration so we can opportunistically launch lower-latency kernels while a large allreduce is in-flight.

Summary of changes (high-level):
- New runtime component: src/runtime/tp/commcompute_conductor.cc/h (C++): orchestrates per-layer schedules, establishes per-peer affinity groups and issues NCCL group launches with calibrated concurrency windows. Contains a compact state machine and exposes hooks for the prefetcher and kernel-swap controller.
- NCCL tuning: src/runtime/nccl/pacing_policy.cc and config: adds per-link bandwidth smoothing and backoff heuristics to avoid oversubscription on mixed NVLink/PCIe topologies.
- KV-cache prefetcher: src/runtime/cache/kv_prefetcher.*: lightweight sampling-based predictor using exponential decay on prefix-hit counts; issues async prefetch RPCs to local caching layer and records soft-failure histograms to tune aggressiveness at runtime.
- Kernel swap: src/runtime/launcher/kernel_swap.*: annotate kernels with 'swap_hint' metadata, enable faster microkernel fallback paths when large collectives are active; migrate minimal KV pointer state so swapped kernels can resume without full recompile.
- Batching interaction: adjustments to scheduler to keep continuous batching work-stealing compatible with prefetcher decisions.
- Tests and perf harness: tests/tp/test_commcompute_conductor.py, bench/tp/bench_collectives.py and additions to perf-canary workflows.

Design notes and rationales: 
- Hierarchical scheduling groups GPUs into 'affinity shards' per-layer rather than forcing global synchronous collectives. This reduces head-of-line blocking for layers with small activations while preserving correctness for large-layer collectives. We calibrated window sizes with microbenchmarks on p4/p5 nodes.
- The prefetcher is intentionally conservative: it requires a prefix probability threshold before issuing Cross-node KV fetches; thresholds decay based on measured miss penalties to avoid flooding the network for bursty workloads.
- Kernel-swap provides low-cost fallbacks: we don't replace kernels wholesale, we annotate choices and perform fast pointer/mmap swaps; that keeps most of the runtime stable and minimizes JIT churn.

Commits in this PR (summary):
- commit 1: initial commcompute conductor state-machine and public hooks (author: Ethan Park)
- commit 2: KV prefetcher and metrics (histograms, per-peer counters, config knobs)
- commit 3: kernel swap paths and scheduler integration; tests + perf bench harness; docs update about rollout

Files changed (representative list):
- src/runtime/tp/commcompute_conductor.cc
- src/runtime/tp/commcompute_conductor.h
- src/runtime/nccl/pacing_policy.cc
- src/runtime/cache/kv_prefetcher.cc
- src/runtime/launcher/kernel_swap.cc
- src/runtime/scheduler/continuous_batching_integration.cc
- tests/tp/test_commcompute_conductor.py
- bench/tp/bench_collectives.py
- docs/notes/commcompute-conductor.md

Small illustrative diff (kernel annotation):
- @kernel(name="matmul_f16")
+ @kernel(name="matmul_f16", swap_hint="low_latency_fallback")

Benchmarks and results:
- Microbench on 8xA100-pod (tensor-parallel 4): end-to-end latency for 8-token generation workloads improved by 18% p50 and 24% p95 for typical prompt length (128 tokens) under continuous batching load.
- Allreduce overlap: measured 35% reduction in idle GPU cycles during large collective windows due to schedule interleaving.
- KV prefetch hit rate increased from 72% -> 88% for steady-state conversational traces in the internal perf corpus when prefetching enabled with threshold=0.6.

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests added for conductor state transitions and prefetcher decay logic.
- Integration bench runs added to perf-canary pipeline to capture throughput/latency regressions.
- Initial CI flakiness: one GPU integration test failed on first run (OOM in python integration harness). Fixed by reducing temporary buffer sizes in kernel_swap and reran. Final CI status: all checks green.

Review conversation (high level, selected):
- Laura Mitchell (review): "Great high-level design. Please add explicit invariants for when prefetches are canceled (e.g. on model switch or prompt truncation). Also we should expose a runtime metric for speculative prefetch bandwidth."
  - Reply (Ethan): "Added prefetch cancellation hook and new metric prefetch_bytes_speculative. See kv_prefetcher.cc lines ~210-245."
- Ravi Kapoor (review): "Concern: kernel swap state migration could interact poorly with persistent caching; can we fail-safe to original kernel when migration fails?"
  - Reply (Ethan): "Yes — swap is guarded by atomic 'swap_ready' and we added fallback path to rebind original kernel; documented in comments and tests. Added unit to force swap failure to validate fallback."
- Anya Petrova (approval): "Bench look solid; happy to merge after CI is green and release notes."

Rollout plan:
- Canary: deploy conductor behind runtime flag on perf-canary and 5% of hosted traffic for 48 hours. Monitor p50/p95 latencies, prefetch bytes, speculative miss rate, and GPU idle cycles.
- Gradual ramp: if canary metrics are stable (<2% reg on p50, improvement on tail), increase to 50% over 24h then full.
- Fallback: runtime flag disables all three components atomically if regression seen.

Backwards compatibility and safety:
- No public API changes. Default prefetching is off for older models; conductor is controlled via runtime config flags. Kernel swap is opt-in via model-provided annotations.

Related work: links to ENG tickets and earlier PRs for NCCL pacing and KV-cache improvements (ENG-1345, ENG-1199). This PR integrates previously separate heuristics into a single conductor to reduce cross-component oscillation.

Notes for reviewers:
- Focus review on: conductor state transitions (commcompute_conductor.h), prefetch threshold tuning code, and kernel swap fallback tests.
- Perf numbers included above were collected with the bench harness at bench/tp/bench_collectives.py; dataset used is internal-perf/conv-v2.

Merge outcome: PR was squashed and merged to main after CI passed and perf-canary smoke showed expected improvements.

Changelog (user-facing):
- Improved multi-GPU tensor-parallel latency and throughput for many small-to-medium generation workloads via smarter overlap of collectives and compute, improved KV-cache prefetching, and low-cost kernel fallbacks.

If you want a walkthrough I can run a short demo showing conductor metrics in the console and the perf-canary dashboard.
Improve multi-GPU tensor-parallel runtime: hierarchical comm/compute conductor that overlaps NCCL collectives with kernel execution; adaptive KV-cache prefetching; kernel swap hinting to reduce stall time. Rollout: canary then full. No API changes.
payload.title: commcompute-conductor-hierarchical-prefetch-kernel-swap

payload.body:
Motivation: large tenants exhibit multi-modal request patterns that make single-strategy batching suboptimal. This PR introduces a sampled-batch consensus allocator that forms lightweight consensus decisions across concurrent samplers and attaches a tenant-aware quant stitcher that composes conservative quantization profiles at rollout time. The goal is to reduce per-token cost without regressing p95 latency or quality for high-variance workloads.

What this change contains: implementation of a sampled consensus layer in the runtime batcher so multiple samplers can propose batch groupings and a consensus step selects the batch plan with best predicted unit-econ score; a new quant stitcher service that merges safe quantization presets (CPU/GPU/INT8/FP16) based on historical eval signals and per-tenant safety thresholds; telemetry hooks (unit_econ.* and batch.consensus.* metrics) and a small CLI to generate dry-run profiles for tenant owners.

Design notes: consensus uses a probabilistic sampling window (configurable, default 150ms) across N samplers to estimate expected token/latency tradeoffs. Scoring function is pluggable and evaluates expected cost delta against a latency SLO penalty. Quant stitcher merges candidate quant profiles by ranking them on a loss-tolerant score computed from recent eval sets and sentinel prompts; the stitcher emits a safe combined profile and a degradation estimate. Rollout uses canary rules in the console (canary weight + rollback thresholds) tied to the new telemetry alarms.

Backward compatibility: runtime defaults unchanged. New behaviors gated by two flags: runtime.batcher.consensus.enabled (off by default) and quant.stitcher.automerge (off by default). This lets operators evaluate via dry-run.

Testing: unit tests for the consensus allocator, synthetic workloads in perf-canary, integration tests for stitcher + eval harness, and a smoke test that runs a tenant-level dry-run and verifies no p95 regression under 99% simulated traffic.

Migration and rollout: docs/blueprints/sample-consensus.md contains a step-by-step tenant migration guide. Recommend enabling consensus in staging with automerge=false for 2 weeks before gradual canary.

Related: ENG-1952 (tenant economizer RFC), ENG-1960 (quant safety signals), SUP-421 incident followup where bursty tenants saw cost spikes.

Checklist: - [x] Runtime consensus allocator implementation - [x] Quant stitcher service and API - [x] Telemetry and alert rules - [x] CLI dry-run + docs - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf canary run and baseline attached to the PR

Notes: This PR is intentionally conservative in default behavior to avoid surprise regressions. The quant stitcher emits both a recommended profile and a conservative fallback; the platform will only activate the recommended profile when tenant owners opt in or when policy allows automated rollouts with safe thresholds.
Jonah Becker: Overall clean. Two asks: add a short runbook for operators when consensus causes mix of tiny and huge batches, and ensure the scoring function exposes a stable seed for tests.
Mira Patel: Added runbook section and injected deterministic seed in tests (consensus_test.go lines 84-96).
Priya Shah: Can you clarify the safety delta threshold used by the stitcher? How do we make it tenant-configurable?
Mira Patel: stitcher exposes quant.stitcher.safe_delta_pct and tenant override via tenant.policies.quant.safe_delta_pct. Added docs and example override in configs.
Luca Romano: CI flaked on integration test (timeout on perf-canary). Re-ran CI and added tighter timeouts in the harness. Also suggested moving metrics to unit_econ.v2 namespace for future-proofing.
Mira Patel: Addressed timeouts and moved primary metrics to unit_econ.v2 while keeping backwards-compatible aliases.

Context: Several enterprise customers in EMEA and APAC require explicit enforcement that tenant data and cryptographic operations remain bound to declared legal jurisdictions. This PR introduces a lightweight jurisdictional assertion signal that is carried alongside requests and evaluated by a new conditional KMS guard. Motivation: allow policy-driven decisions for key selection (per-tenant regional CMKs, multi-provider fallbacks) while preserving existing RBACv2 workflows and audit trail integrity. Changes: 1) Add X-Jurisdiction and internal X-Redwood-Jurisdiction assertion headers and plumbing in gateway middleware; these are validated by the new pkg/rbac/assertions subsystem which canonicalizes asserted jurisdiction claims against tenant profiles. 2) Implement pkg/kms/guard.go: a conditional guard that maps jurisdiction assertions + tenant policy -> allowed KMS providers and key aliases. The guard supports explicit deny lists, soft-fallback to a global-cmk if tenant policy allows emergency fallback, and an operator-ttl delegation path. 3) RBACv2 policy update: extend role assertions to include jurisdiction claim predicates and timebound delegations (operator TTL) that can be granted only by 'residency-admin' roles. 4) Audit: audit service now tags events with audit.jurisdiction.{tenant,claim,decision} and includes sealed metadata for non-repudiation when keys are used for encryption/decryption. 5) Feature gating & rollout: feature flag 'jurisdiction-guard' default off; rollout plan in docs/migration with a staged canary across regions. Tests & docs: unit + integration tests added, and documentation + migration notes included. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for assertion parsing and policy evaluator - [x] Integration tests for KMS selection and fallback behavior - [x] Docs and migration guide - [x] Security scan and static analysis - [x] Feature flag gate and Helm values entry Deployment notes: When enabling in Dedicated or Private installs, operators must supply per-tenant jurisdiction profiles (examples in examples/tenant/jurisdiction.yaml) and optionally configure KMS provider mapping in helm values. Backwards compatibility: default behavior remains unchanged when feature flag is off; when enabled, requests without asserted jurisdiction use tenant default if present or proceed with existing KMS selection logic. Rollback: the flag can be disabled cluster-wide to restore prior behavior. Related work: ties to ENG-1987 (tenant residency index) and SEC-302 (audit sealing for region-bound cryptography).
2024-11-16 - Luis Ortega: Requested clarification on operator TTL semantics and whether delegation tokens are revocable. Action: added TTL revocation hook and tests; updated docs to call out revocation window.
2024-11-17 - Priya Raman: Suggested tightening the default fallback policy to require explicit tenant opt-in for global CMK fallback. Action: made fallback opt-in via tenant policy, kept emergency override for SRE with audit stamp.
2024-11-18 - Ethan Park: Noted potential performance impact from additional assertion validation on hot path. Action: added in-memory LRU cache for tenant jurisdiction profiles and metrics for cache hit/miss; benchmark numbers added to docs.
2024-11-19 - Nora Chen (author): Addressed feedback, ran full CI, pushed final squash commit and requested merge.
Adds a gated feature 'jurisdiction-guard' that enables per-tenant jurisdiction assertions and a conditional KMS guard. When enabled administrators can require region-bound key usage, configure provider mappings, and obtain richer audit signals. Backwards compatible while gated. See docs/security/jurisdiction-guard.md for configuration and migration steps.
Helm: set jurisdictionGuard.enabled=true to enable. Provide tenant profiles at config map path /etc/redwood/tenants/jurisdiction.yaml or via API. Ensure KMS provider mappings are supplied under values.kms.jurisdictionMap. Monitor metric kms.guard.decision and audit.jurisdiction.* events after enabling.
Low/Medium: introduces policy evaluation on request path (mitigated by caching) and cross-service header propagation. Controlled by feature flag and rollout instructions. Security review completed and SCA passed.

Context and motivation: We observed nondeterministic tool selection and silent failures when downstream tool processes returned transient backpressure (rate-limit / overload) during streaming tool/function invocations. This manifested as partial tool messages, missing tool_choice resolutions, and inconsistent retry behaviors across SDKs. This PR introduces two coordinated changes: 1) a deterministic error schema for tool_choice resolution so callers can programmatically react to selection failures, and 2) an explicit envelope-level backpressure indicator that can be emitted during streaming to signal temporary unavailability of a tool and a suggested retry window.

What this changes (high level):
- Add `tool_choice_error` object to OpenAI-compat invoke responses and stream fragments. The object is deterministic (fields: code, reason, suggested_retry_ms) and is emitted when the platform cannot finalize a tool assignment due to capacity or schema mismatch.
- Add envelope-level field `backpressure_hint_ms` to streaming fragments (optional integer). When present clients should postpone immediate retries of the same tool for the specified window.
- Make streaming fragments emit explicit boundary frames around tool messages to avoid partial payload confusion in the client. Boundary frames are idempotent markers and do not change payload semantics.
- Update compatibility adapter to map internal executor backpressure/error states into the new OpenAI-compatible fields.
- SDK and docs updates: python and typescript SDKs updated to surface the new fields with improved parsing helpers and examples.

Commits (summary):
- 1f4c2b2: core(adapter): map executor backpressure to openai envelope fields
- 8a7d9f1: runtime: emit boundary frames around tool streaming fragments
- b3d9a0c: api: add deterministic tool_choice_error schema and marshallers
- d2e5f8b: sdk/python: add parser helpers and unit tests
- e9a7c11: sdk/ts: update streaming client example and docs
- 4c0b2a7: test: integration test for transient backpressure and retry behavior

Files changed (representative paths):
- internal/openai_adapter/adapter.go (mapping logic + marshalling)
- runtime/streaming/envelope.go (boundary frames + backpressure hints)
- api/contracts/openai_tool_errors.proto (new schema + docs)
- sdk/python/redwood/streaming.py (parsers + tests)
- sdk/ts/streaming-client.ts (example and helper typings)
- docs/openai_compat/tool_calling.md (compat guide + migration notes)

Review conversation (high level):
- Liam: requested a deterministic error code set and suggested using single byte markers for boundaries to keep bandwidth low. Also asked for metrics (counter for backpressure events).
- Anika: added error codes (TOOL_UNAVAILABLE, TOOL_SCHEMA_MISMATCH, TOOL_TIMEOUT) and added a low-entropy one-byte boundary marker; pushed an extra commit adding metrics.backpressure_events counter.
- Jin: flagged potential client breakage if SDKs assume no extra fields. Requested SDK tests and migration notes. Anika added SDK parsing helpers, unit tests, and the docs migration note.
- Marta: ran perf canary and requested microbenchmark numbers. Anika added a microbenchmark and updated the PR with results (median overhead < 1.2% on steady-state streaming workloads).
- Final: reviewers approved after fixes; CI green.
Introduces a deterministic tool_choice error schema and streaming envelope backpressure indicator; clients should tolerate new optional fields. Non-breaking for existing OpenAI-compat consumers.
Follow-ups: expand error taxonomy (ENG-1601), observability histogram (ENG-1678); coordinate with Dedicated team for capacity signaling in private deployments.

payload.body:
Context: As part of the Reliability Program (incident taxonomy + ownership mapping), we need a single source of truth for incident owner resolution that is (1) versioned and reviewable, (2) validated to avoid typos / ambiguous matches, (3) auditable (who changed what + when), and (4) safe to roll forward/back without paging the wrong teams mid-incident. This PR introduces a control-plane managed config for mapping incident_type + subtype -> owning team metadata, plus guardrails and rollout tooling.

What this PR does: Adds a new control-plane config kind `incident_owner_mapping.v1` stored and served by the config service. The config maps {incident_type, incident_subtype} to: primary_owner_team, secondary_owner_team (optional), consulted_teams (optional), escalation_channel, and runbook_links (optional). Adds server-side validation (schema + allowlists + uniqueness + cardinality checks), audit logging on every publish, and a staged rollout mechanism with canary + automatic rollback on validation/serve errors.

Key behaviors / safeguards: 1) Uniqueness + precedence rules: exact match on (type, subtype) wins; type-only match (subtype="*") is allowed as a fallback; multiple matches are rejected at publish time. 2) Unknown handling: if a lookup misses, the API returns owner="UNRESOLVED" with a reason and a suggested next action ("pick owner manually") to avoid silently assigning the wrong team. 3) Validation: type/subtype must be in the taxonomy allowlist (pulled from `incident_taxonomy.v1` config); team ids must be in the org/team registry; escalation_channel must be a known Slack channel format; runbook_links must be https and match an allowlist of domains (Confluence + docs). 4) Rollout: publish supports `--stage=canary` (serves to 5% of lookups, based on stable hash of incident_id) then promote; rollback supports `--to-version=<n>` with a one-command revert.

API surface: Adds `GET /control-plane/v1/incident-owner/resolve?type=...&subtype=...` used by incident-bot and internal tooling. Response includes resolved owner metadata plus the mapping version and the matched rule key for auditing/debug.

Audit logging: Every publish/rollback writes an immutable audit record with: actor, request id, diff summary (added/removed/modified rules count), config version, and a sha256 of the full payload. Audit records are queryable in the existing control-plane audit UI and emitted to the central audit log stream.

Testing: Unit tests for schema validation, match semantics, and unknown resolution; integration tests in `control-plane-api` verifying versioned reads + staged rollout; property-based test generating random mappings to ensure no ambiguous precedence slips through.

Migration/ops notes: This PR ships the config kind + resolver API but does not yet flip incident-bot to use it by default (that is in PR(s) tied to ENG-4822). Initial seed mapping lives in `config/seed/incident_owner_mapping.v1.json` and will be managed by SRE going forward. If this config is unavailable, callers should continue to fall back to existing static lookup tables until rollout is complete.

Follow-ups: (a) Add per-type runbook suggestion wiring in incident-bot output (tracked separately), (b) enforce required incident_type/owner on close once owner mapping is stable for 2 weeks, (c) add dashboard panel for unresolved owner lookups.

Refs: ENG-4825, ENG-4822. Related PRs: pr-28411 (add incident_type tag to alert payloads), pr-28503 (expose incident_type in ops console api).
Allison Grant (Observability): "Can you confirm we won't create a high-cardinality label explosion by letting subtype be arbitrary?" Ethan Park (author): "Subtype is validated against `incident_taxonomy.v1` allowlist; we reject unknown/novel subtypes at publish time. Also, the resolver returns the matched rule key but we don't emit it as a metric label. Metrics will only use the bounded incident_type/subtype enums." Allison: "Please add a test that fails publish if subtype isn't in taxonomy." -> Added in 7c2a9b1.

Rafael Mendes (SRE): "We need to know who changed owner mapping during an incident. Audit record should include before/after summary and version." Ethan: "Added audit emit with actor + diff counts + sha256, and we log matched_rule in resolve responses so we can correlate." Rafael: "Make sure rollback is one command." -> Added `config rollback --kind incident_owner_mapping.v1 --to-version N` and documented.

Mina Haddad (Routing): "What happens when routing/fleet dispute subtypes get updated and the config hasn't rolled out?" Ethan: "Resolver returns mapping_version and is served from config service; rollout supports canary -> promote. Callers can pin minimum version if needed. During rollout window, incident-bot will remain on static mapping." Mina: "OK, but add a default type-only fallback for Routing.*" -> Seed mapping updated to include subtype="*" for a few top-level types.

Dylan Brooks (Tooling): "Do we have a safe failure mode? If the config service is down, incident-bot can't resolve." Ethan: "Resolver endpoint returns 503 but callers are expected to fall back to their static mapping until we flip the default. Added explicit note in docs." Dylan: "Please add a header indicating failure reason." -> Added `x-owner-resolution-status: UNAVAILABLE|OK|MISS`.

Aisha Bello (Dashboards/SLO): "Can we export an unresolved counter so we can monitor adoption?" Ethan: "Added `control_plane.incident_owner_resolution.miss_count` + `unavailable_count` with no extra labels beyond {env, region}." Aisha: "Ship it."
Internal: Control plane now supports `incident_owner_mapping.v1` config with validation + audit logging and a resolver endpoint used for incident owner resolution. Includes staged rollout and rollback tooling.
payload.title: Add incident owner mapping config to control plane (versioned + validated + audited)

Context and motivation: Our multi-SDK surface has accumulated several ad-hoc credential helpers and divergent retry/backoff defaults. Production teams reported higher p99 latencies during token refresh storms and confusing ergonomics when wiring streaming consumers. This PR introduces a compact, opt-in credential facade (CredFacade) and a latency-aware backoff profile that unify behavior across Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs, plus a small typed streaming context object to carry request-level auth metadata.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Adds CredFacade core + lightweight adapters for existing TokenProvider interfaces, introduces BackoffProfile.v2 (latency-aware jitter and per-operation bias), extends streaming client APIs with TypedStreamContext for cross-language parity, and bumps SDK versions: python 4.1.0, typescript 2.7.0, go 1.6.0. Changes are intentionally opt-in: old constructors still work and deprecated helpers log a single WARN.

Python SDK changes: new redwood.auth.facade.CredFacade that wraps existing refreshers; redwood.backoff.LatencyAwareProfile with three presets (interactive, balanced, throughput); StreamContext dataclass carries request_id/tags/auth_hint and is passed into stream iterators; added integration tests that simulate token-service latency and ensure backoff throttling does not starve generation loops.

TypeScript SDK changes: exported CredFacade from @redwood/sdk auth package; BackoffProfile options added to client constructors; StreamContext typed interface and updated AsyncIterable consumer helpers to accept context param. Added migration notes in README and examples/streaming/typed_context.ts.

Go SDK changes: compact facade implemented as credfacade package with two small adapters for existing TokenProvider implementations; backoff package receives LatencyAware option; StreamContext struct added to streamproto package and plumbing added in stream client builder.

Migration and compatibility: All changes are backward-compatible by default. Teams can opt into the new facade by passing CredFacade into client constructors or call Client.with_backoff_profile('balanced') to enable latency-awareness. Deprecation warnings added where older helpers remain. No runtime breaking changes expected.

Testing and rollout: Multi-SDK unit + integration test matrix added (local mock token service + real-model smoke tests on perf canary infra). A gradual rollout was performed: first enable on internal staging tenants for 48h, then 1 week on canary customers before general availability.

Notes on performance: Benchmarks indicate median token latency unchanged; p99 token refresh failures reduced by ~62% under bursty refresh load due to added jitter and bias in the backoff profile. Streaming memory overhead is negligible (StreamContext is small <256 bytes).

Acceptance criteria: reviewers confirmed API ergonomics, all CI green after one retry for flaky e2e, documentation updated, and version bumps added to SDK release manifests.
Lena Torres: Nice consolidation. Two requests: add a small example showing how to wrap legacy TokenProvider with CredFacade, and please confirm that the facade doesn't change concurrent refresh semantics.
Maya Patel (author): Added example in examples/streaming/typed_context.ts and added an adapter in redwood-sdk-python/redwood/auth/adapter.py. Concurrent refresh keeps same mutex semantics; added unit that asserts single refresh under contention.
Omar Haddad: Backoff presets look sensible. Suggest making 'interactive' slightly more aggressive for sub-300ms latencies. Also flag: CI e2e failed once on canary due to test flakiness — rerun required.
Maya Patel: Tuned interactive preset alpha and reran e2e; CI now green after one retry. Added note in the docs about tuning for low-latency regions.
Priya Nair: API ergonomics LGTM. Minor nit: prefer StreamContext to carry an optional 'hint' rather than raw token to avoid accidental leakage.
SDKs: Added a compact CredFacade to standardize credential refresh behavior; introduced LatencyAware backoff profiles (interactive/balanced/throughput) to reduce p99 token refresh stalls; added typed StreamContext to standardize streaming metadata across languages. Backwards-compatible and opt-in. Bumped SDK versions: python 4.1.0, typescript 2.7.0, go 1.6.0.
Enhancement: compact credential facade + latency-aware backoff + typed stream context (py:4.1.0, ts:2.7.0, go:1.6.0)
payload.title: Introduce concise credential facade with latency-aware backoff and typed streaming context across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs

Context and motivation: Production teams need faster root-cause for cost spikes that happen inside long-running chat sessions and better visual tools to reconcile traces with cost signals. Existing token-level and span telemetry gives good signal but is hard to correlate at the session/fragments level for ops and product teams. This PR introduces two complementary features: 1) session-sliced cost attribution — a backend aggregation and set of derived metrics that break down per-session cost and latency into contiguous 'slices' (prompt fragments, model-variant boundaries, KV-cache resets) so you can answer questions like 'which fragment of this session consumed 60% of the cost' quickly; 2) span-join visualizer — a console widget that joins contiguous spans and log events into a compact timeline view with cost/latency overlays and clickable links back to traces and the new session slices. Summary of changes: - New aggregator service: observability/session_slicer service (Go) that consumes traces + token cost events and emits slice-level rollups (rw_session_slice_* metrics) and a lightweight JSON join artifact stored in S3 for UI retrieval. - Tracing pipeline change: tracing/span_joiner processor (Python) that synthesizes contiguous span groups and enriches them with the slice id from the session_slicer. - Console: dashboards/session-cost-explorer and console widget span-join-visualizer (React/TS) with timeline, per-slice cost bars, and a filter for model-variant and cache-hit state. - Alerts: a new adaptive alert rule (observability/alerts/session_slice_burn_rate.prom) that compares slice burn-rate to a session baseline and suppresses noisy transient spikes by requiring multi-slice persistence. - SDK & ingestion: small opt-in telemetry flag in runtime to emit per-slice annotations for high-cardinality sessions to reduce downstream join load. - Tests: unit and integration tests for the pipeline, e2e storybook for the UI widget, and a load test harness demonstrating slice throughput at 10k sessions/minute. Migration and rollout: The session_slicer initially runs on a dedicated observability queue (no replacement of existing token rollups). We will run the slicer in shadow mode for 2 weeks and run a limited console beta. Rollout steps: 1) Deploy backend in shadow mode -> 2) Enable UI for beta orgs (feature flag) -> 3) Flip ingestion opt-in for consenting customers -> 4) Promote to default. Why this is different: instead of trying to attribute cost purely to tokens or spans, slices represent contiguous logical units inside a session (prompt, tool-call, external context), which is more actionable for product owners. The span-join visualizer is designed to be low-cardinality and link back to full traces when operators need detail. Testing notes: - Local unit tests and integration tests in ./tracing/span_joiner/tests pass. - Load test harness (observability/loadtests/session_slicer/) simulates 10k sessions/min and shows CPU/latency within expected SLOs (cluster sizing notes in runbook). - CI initially failed lint due to TS type and a flake8 rule; both were fixed in subsequent commits. Observability & cost: new metrics introduced: rw_session_slice_count, rw_session_slice_token_cost_total, rw_session_slice_latency_ms_p50/p95, rw_span_join_count. These metrics are emitted with low-cardinality tags (slice_type, model_family, region) and a session_bucket id that reuses existing sampling keys to avoid explosion. Rollback plan: disable feature flag and stop emitting slice artifacts; slice rollups are additive and do not replace existing billing signals. Related: ENG-1284 (slo-driven alert tuning), PM-482 (console explorer for billing teams). Checklist: - [x] Backend aggregator implemented - [x] Tracing joiner implemented - [x] Console widget + dashboard - [x] Tests and load harness - [x] Runbook and rollout flag - [x] Docs (observability/docs/session-slices.md)
Samir Patel: This looks great overall. Two questions: how are we preventing cardinality explosion for multi-tenant customers that have long-lived sessions? Can you add documentation on how session_bucket works?
Priya Menon (author): We already reuse the existing sampling key (session_bucket) and explicitly drop per-token annotations unless the session is opted-in. Added docs at observability/docs/session-slices.md describing the bucketing and sampling policy.
Claire Huang: The alert suppression rule seems complex. Can we simplify the logic so on-call can reason about it quickly? Maybe prefer a refractory window rather than a multi-slice persistence counter?
Priya Menon: Happy to iterate. We started with refractory windows but observed oscillation in canary tests. The multi-slice persistence gate reduces noise from short-lived tool calls. Added comments and a README explaining tradeoffs.
Daniel Reilly: UI looks solid. A couple of accessibility items and keyboard nav for the timeline would be nice. Also consider linking directly to the trace span id when available.
Priya Menon: Addressed keyboard nav (tab focus) and added deep-links to trace/span ids where present.
Add session-sliced cost attribution and span-join visualizer: new low-cardinality metrics and console widget for per-session cost/latency breakdowns. Beta rollout behind feature flag. See observability/docs/session-slices.md for details.
payload.title: introduce-session-sliced-cost-attribution-and-span-join-visualizer

Adds Dedicated drain progress metrics (percent/ETA/states) and emits annotations for dashboards during drain workflows. No customer-facing API changes.
Context: As part of the regional failover automation upgrade, we added a Dedicated pool drain workflow (PR #19822) but on-call has had limited visibility into whether a drain is making forward progress vs stuck (and how close we are to a safe cutover). This PR adds drain progress metrics emitted by the drain coordinator and wires those metrics into the existing failover signal dashboards so the game day runbook can validate drain progress in real time. What’s included: 1) New metrics for Dedicated drain lifecycle and progress, emitted from the dedicated-drain coordinator and keyed by pool_id (bounded) + region + customer_tier. 2) A periodic progress sampler that computes remaining nodes/replicas, in-flight request counts, and an ETA based on recent completion rate; sampler is explicitly best-effort and will not block drain execution. 3) An annotation event emitted when a drain starts/stops/aborts (to reduce manual timeline stitching). 4) Dashboard hooks: update the failover dashboards spec wiring (Grafana json in observability-pack is handled in PR #907; this PR provides the metric contract and internal dashboard wiring behind the same feature flag). Metric definitions: - dedicated_drain_state{region,pool_id,tier,state}: gauge (0/1) for states: requested|running|paused|completed|aborted|failed. - dedicated_drain_progress_percent{region,pool_id,tier}: gauge 0..100 (reported as float; rounded in dashboard). - dedicated_drain_remaining_nodes{region,pool_id,tier}: gauge. - dedicated_drain_inflight_requests{region,pool_id,tier}: gauge from gateway/routing counters (best-effort snapshot). - dedicated_drain_eta_seconds{region,pool_id,tier}: gauge; -1 when unknown (e.g., insufficient samples). - dedicated_drain_transition_total{region,tier,reason}: counter (pool_id intentionally excluded to keep cardinality bounded; pool_id is available via logs/audit events). Cardinality + safety: pool_id is bounded by Dedicated pools and is already an existing bounded identifier in internal metrics; we enforce a max distinct pool_id per region in the emitter (drops + logs once exceeded). We intentionally do not label by tenant_id/customer_id. For event-style visibility and audits, the drain workflow already emits audit events; this PR adds a short annotation emitter that references the audit event id. Testing: unit tests cover ETA calculation behavior (including noisy/stalled progress) and state transitions; integration test uses the staging drain simulator to ensure gauges get updated and cleared on completion/abort. Rollout: guarded by feature flag dedicated_drain_progress_metrics (default off). We’ll enable in staging during rehearsal; production enablement will be scoped to game day allowlist tenants/pools per ENG-2420 and the runbook checklist. Follow-ups: - Add an alert on “drain running with no progress > N minutes” once we have staging data (tracked in ENG-2426). - Add better correlation to incident timeline tooling (planned in PR #19844).
Allison Grant: Please confirm we’re not adding tenant/customer labels here; pool_id seems OK but I’m worried about high-cardinality if we include per-replica identifiers. Also: can eta_seconds be -1 vs NaN so alerts can treat it explicitly?
Sergio Costa (author): Confirmed: no tenant/customer id, no replica ids. Labels are region,pool_id,tier (+ state for the state gauge). eta_seconds returns -1 when unknown; dashboards will map -1 to “unknown”. Added a unit test to cover this path.
Vanessa Ortiz: How do we prevent this from becoming a hot loop when drain is running for large pools? Also ensure we don’t make drain completion dependent on metric emission.
Sergio Costa (author): Sampler runs every 15s with jitter; uses cached coordinator state and a single aggregated read for inflight. Errors are swallowed and logged; drain state machine does not await metric emission. Added a benchmark and a note in code comments.
Miles Thornton: For the transition counter, can we standardize reason values with the rollback ADR language (abort, rollback, capacity_gate, operator_cancel) so dashboards are consistent with failover controller metrics?
Sergio Costa (author): Good call—updated reason enum to align with controller audit reasons + documented allowed values; also added a mapping for legacy abort codes to keep compatibility with existing logs.
Rafael Mendes: Please add a quick query example in the PR description or code comment for on-call: how to tell “stuck drain” vs “paused drain” and where to look.
Sergio Costa (author): Added query examples in a comment near metric definitions and updated the internal runbook reference section with two PromQL snippets.
Enable flag in staging for rehearsal: dedicated_drain_progress_metrics=true (SRE allowlist only).
Coordinate dashboard panel additions in observability-pack PR #907; metric contract is now stable.
Track alerting thresholds after first production game day (ENG-2426).
payload.title: Dedicated drain: add progress metrics + dashboard hooks

Background and motivation: We need richer telemetry for RBACv2 policy decisions so security teams can correlate decision signals with CMK (customer-managed key) usage and data-residency enforcement while preserving an immutable audit trail. This change adds a lightweight policy-telemetry adapter that emits per-decision metadata to the audit sealer and wires a CMK handoff flow that records proof-of-handoff for cross-region key delegations. Goals: (1) capture policy input vectors and scoring metadata for RBACv2 decisions, (2) stamp audit envelopes with CMK provenance when a delegated key is used or handed off, (3) keep latency impact sub-5ms on hot paths and run in shadow mode by default for the initial rollout. What this PR does (high level): - New adapter service: src/server/policy_telemetry/adapter.go and internal protobufs for a compact per-decision telemetry payload. The adapter lives behind the policy engine and exports a non-blocking gRPC/HTTP endpoint that the audit sealer can consume. - Audit sealer integration: pkg/audit/sealer/service.go updated to accept TelemetryEnvelope objects and include a CMK-proof section when the CMK handoff occurs. - CMK handoff protocol: small state machine added to pkg/crypto/cmk_handoff.go to produce a signed CMK-handshake ticket that is stored alongside the audit envelope (sealed by our root-key and including the original request's residency hint). - DB migration: migrations/20260210_add_policy_telemetry_table.sql introduces telemetry_store for long-term sampling and bloom-index keys for fast lookup. - RBAC rules: rules/policy_templates/added_labels.yaml adds optional scoring labels that the policy engine can populate; this is backward compatible and ignored when the adapter is disabled. - Ops and deployment: deploy/privileged-role.yaml grants the sealer the minimum KMS wrap/unwrap permission; deploy/helm/values.yaml includes a feature flag policyTelemetry.enabled defaulting to false. - Tests and CI: tests/integration/test_policy_telemetry.py and tests/e2e/test_cmk_handoff_flow.sh simulate cross-region handoffs in the integration environment. Rollout plan: default is shadow mode (telemetry recorded but not used in auth decisions). After 2 weeks of sampling and a brief regression window with quality gates, we'll flip the runtime flag and enable per-route enforcement for a small set of internal operator teams. Backwards compatibility: adapter is optional; when disabled the sealer continues to write audit envelopes without telemetry sections. Security review notes: CMK handshake ticket is signed with our internal attestation key and includes a nonce + residency claim; no plaintext key material is written to telemetry_store. Migration path: a write-only collector is safe for first deploy. See docs/security/policy-telemetry.md for operational runbook and sampling guidance.
Avi Patel (2026-02-16): Can the adapter operate in-process to avoid RPC overhead? Concern: extra hop on hot policy path.
Marisol Chen (2026-02-16): We measured the in-process approach in a prototype; separating via non-blocking gRPC gives better isolation and allows independent scaling. We added micro-batching to keep p99 impact <5ms.
Gabrielle Ortiz (2026-02-17): Please ensure the CMK handshake ticket contains no key material and is forward portable for third-party auditors. Add field-level docs to telemetry.proto.
Marisol Chen (2026-02-17): Updated telemetry.proto with explicit provenance fields and a non-exportable key-id reference. Confirmed no plaintext keys are stored.
Liam O'Connor (2026-02-18): Tests pass but noticed the sealer might retry KMS unwrap synchronously. We should offload retry/backoff to the async worker to avoid blocking envelope writes.
Marisol Chen (2026-02-18): Moved KMS retry into the worker queue and added circuit-breaker metrics; added integration test for transient KMS failures.
Avi Patel (2026-02-19): Approved after minor nits; please add release-note summarizing operations impact.
Gabrielle Ortiz (2026-02-20): Security review complete; LGTM.
Add optional policy-telemetry adapter and CMK handoff audit sealing. Defaulted to shadow mode; no behavior change for existing tenants until policyTelemetry.enabled=true. Operators must provision new minimal KMS wrap/unwrap role before enabling. Includes DB migration to add telemetry_store (write-only by default).
Improves forensic capability for RBACv2 decisions and provides auditable CMK handoff proofs. No secret materials are written to telemetry storage. Access to telemetry_store requires audit-logged roles; deploys gated by security review.
payload.title: Introduce policy-telemetry adapter and CMK handoff audit sealing

Motivation: we observed sporadic cudagraph replay regressions when request batch shapes are highly fragmented (short prefix tokens followed by long continuations) and when op-level kernel selection switches between fast-path and fallback implementations. This PR introduces a hybrid capture strategy that records a compact shape-invariant fingerprint, uses a lighter-weight runtime validator at replay time, and integrates a dynamic kernel selector to prefer capture-stable kernels during warmup. The change reduces replay failure rates and avoids conservative shape guards that previously prevented reuse. Approach summary: 1) Add a CaptureFingerprint produced during initial capture that summarizes sequence-length histogram, KV cache usage flags, and quantization mode so that replay can quickly decide compatibility without exact-shape guards. 2) Implement a HybridFallbackManager that tries the captured graph, runs a micro-warmup (<=8 tokens) using the new validator, and falls back to per-step execution only on mismatch. 3) Extend KernelSelector to expose a "capture-stability" metric; the scheduler prefers kernels marked stable when running in cudagraph-enabled routes or during canary warmups. 4) Add telemetry (cudagraph.replay.{attempts,successes,validated_fallbacks}, kernel.selector.choice) and a feature flag runtime.cudagraph.hybrid_fallback to allow staged rollout. Performance/regression results: canary run across 20 instances with synthetic shard workloads shows 6-12% throughput improvement for long-seq workloads versus current main while reducing replay failure rate from ~7% to 0.3% on fragmented traffic. Median latency p50/p95 unchanged within noise; p99 improved slightly for batched workloads due to fewer fallback hot paths. Compatibility notes: this does not change model formats. The hybrid fingerprint is backward-compatible; nodes without the new runtime will ignore the fingerprint. We ship the feature behind the runtime flag and add a 2-week progressive rollout. Migration checklist: - Enable runtime.cudagraph.hybrid_fallback on staging; - Run perf benchmark-lab suite (bench/cudagraph) under both contiguous and fragmented batch profiles; - Monitor new metrics in console and SLO alerts. Related: ENG-1423 kernel-selection tuning, ENG-1458 canary rollout plan. Testing: unit tests for fingerprint equality and validator, integration perf tests, and end-to-end canary with real traffic. See docs/ops/cudagraphs.md for operator rollout steps and a short note in CHANGELOG about the flag.
Marco Liu: The fingerprint looks promising but we should ensure it does not add CPU overhead on hot paths. Can the serializer be caching-friendly?
Asha Patel: The serializer uses a fixed-size bitmap and a preallocated buffer; microbenchmarks show <0.5% CPU overhead on capture path in our perf lab.
Priya Rao: We need clearer guidance in docs about when to disable hybrid_fallback for low-memory devices.
Asha Patel: Added section in docs/ops/cudagraphs.md about memory tradeoffs and a knob runtime.cudagraph.max_warmup_tokens (default 8).
Daniel Kim: Can we add a quick telemetry-based alert to detect increased validated_fallbacks?
Asha Patel: Added cudagraph.replay.validated_fallbacks to console dashboard and a leak-style alert rule in ci/canary/manifest.yaml.
Feature: hybrid cudagraph fallback and dynamic kernel selection to improve replay robustness on fragmented batch shapes. Improvements: lower replay failure rate, modest throughput gains for long sequences. Ops: new runtime flag runtime.cudagraph.hybrid_fallback (default off), new metric cudagraph.replay.validated_fallbacks, rollout steps in docs/ops/cudagraphs.md.
payload.title: hybrid-cudagraph-fallback-and-dynamic-kernel-selection-for-fragmented-batches

Summary: Adds an Invocation Health Index (IHI) that synthesizes latency, error-rate, token-cost drift, and KV-cache miss impact into a single 0-100 health score for routes and tenants; introduces an Alert Escalator which raises alert severity based on short-term IHI trend and a configurable business-impact model; ships a lightweight streaming-sample adapter that collects the first N tokens and key trace anchors for low-bandwidth trace capture; and adds dashboards and runbook snippets for on-call response. Motivation: existing observability artifacts capture many orthogonal signals (latency histograms, token cost histograms, span traces, kv-cache miss counters) but there is no compact operational signal teams can use to triage and automate alert routing/escalation. IHI provides a deterministic composite signal that is cheap to compute at ingestion and indexes into the escalation policies. What this PR does: - Compute IHI at ingestion using weighted, z-normalized submetrics (latency p95/p99 drift, error rate, token-cost delta from baseline, kv-cache miss rate) - Persist IHI as a metric label per-invocation and emit rollups (per-tenancy, per-route, per-model) - Introduce Escalator service that subscribes to IHI rollups and applies escalation policy (severity, paging, auto-ack suppression windows, SLA-aware dedup) - Add streaming-sample adapter in tracer pipeline that stores trimmed token payload (first N tokens) + span anchors to S3/short-term store for manual inspection; adapter is opt-in per-tenant and obeys PII redaction rules - Dashboards: Invocation Health Overview, IHI trend explorer, Escalation queue, Token sampling spot-check panel - Alert tuning: new alert rules that reference IHI sustained drops and modeled business-impact to adjust PagerDuty routing - Tests: unit tests for aggregator, integration test with local tracer adapter, load bench showing <0.6% ingestion overhead at 10k inv/s Checklist: - [x] Implementation: IHI ingester, escalator service, streaming-sample adapter - [x] Metrics emitted + tags added to rollups - [x] Dashboards and playbook snippets - [x] Tests and bench fixtures - [x] Docs: observability runbook updated and tenant opt-in docs added Rollout plan: 1) Deploy IHI ingester behind feature flag and emit metric to internal debug namespace 2) Enable per-route rollups for a small cohort of tenants (10 internal + 3 customers) 3) Turn on Escalator in alert-only mode (no paging) for 48h, tune thresholds 4) Enable paging for critical customers after sign-off Migration notes: No breaking API changes. Metric names and labels are additive. Tenants must opt-in for streaming-sample adapter; default is off. Privacy: token payload sampling enforces redaction pipeline and retention TTL. Impact: small ingestion CPU increase (~0.4 cores per 1000 inv/s) and additional short-term storage for samples. Links: runbook: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/OBS-2042-invocation-health-runbook, design doc: https://docs.redwood.ai/design/obs-invocation-health
Asha Patel (reviewer): Nice work, the IHI concept should help oncall signal clarity. Left two questions about normalization weights and the token-cost baseline window.
Evan Brooks (author): Answered — default weights are 0.4 latency / 0.3 error / 0.2 token-cost / 0.1 kv-miss. Baseline uses a rolling 7-day median by route; config is surfaced in config/feature_flags.yaml.
Miguel Torres (reviewer): Please add an integration test that demonstrates IHI stability during transient spikes (e.g., short 5-minute p99 spikes).
Evan Brooks (author): Added ihi_spike_sim in tests/ingestion; updated bench to produce synthetic jitter and validated stability.
Grace Lin (reviewer): Streaming-sample adapter must not persist full token text for PII-sensitive tenants. Add opt-out and redaction enforcement.
Evan Brooks (author): Adapter honors tenant opt-in and enforces redaction via rules in scripts/redaction/redaction_rules.yaml. Added tests and docs.
Add Invocation Health Index (IHI): single-score health metric for routes/tenants
Introduce Alert Escalator: SLA-aware alert escalation and automated severity adjustments
Add streaming-sample adapter: opt-in low-bandwidth token sampling with PII redaction
New dashboards: Invocation Health Overview + Escalation queue
payload.title: Introduce Invocation Health Index + alert escalator and lightweight streaming sample adapter

Context: customers running Dedicated fleets reported transient SLA pressure during short spike patterns that are not well-served by the existing autoscaler which focuses on steady-state util signals. This PR introduces the Capacity Horizon Advisor (CHA), a lightweight controller that computes short-term capacity reservations per-tenant based on recent arrival curves and burst risk scores, and a Granular Burst Quota Mapper (GBQM) that exposes per-tenant, timeboxed burst allowances to the serving path. Motivation: reduce tail latency and failed requests during intermittent surges while avoiding long-lived overprovisioning. High level change: 1) CHA service (controller) ingests sampled request timestamps and the utilization sampler to estimate a 1m/5m/15s horizon demand curve, applies an exponential-decay uncertainty model, and outputs a suggested reservation token quota per tenant for the next 60s interval. 2) GBQM maps CHA suggestions to an internal burst-token account per-tenant with soft and hard limits and a decay/return policy; it integrates with the existing token-bucket admission path and emits headroom_curve telemetry. 3) Autoscaler adaptions: the main autoscaler now accepts CHA hints as advisory reservations (configurable via feature flag) and treats them as short-lived soft commitments for prioritization in the warmpool and prewarm steps. 4) Telemetry: new metrics (cha_suggested_tokens, gbqm_active_quota, headroom_curve_p50/p90, cha_confidence) and a small exporter that writes headroom curves to the observability service for slice-by-tenant analysis. 5) Controls: operator knobs added to the dedicated config for horizon window, risk_sensitivity, and decay_rate; sane defaults applied. Design notes: CHA is intentionally advisory—no forced capacity changes without explicit operator opt-in; suggestions are timeboxed and auto-expire to avoid stale reservations. The uncertainty model penalizes suggestions that require >20% short-term cluster commitment and gradually downgrades suggestions when system-wide spare capacity is low. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag "cha.enabled" default false; canary rollout to a single warmpool in us-west-2 serving low-volume tenants; monitor headroom_curve and p99 latency for 72h; expand to additional pools on green signals. Migration: no customer migrations needed; default behavior unchanged until flag enabled by SRE. Backwards compatibility: GBQM integrates with token-bucket admission via an additive allowance path and falls back to preexisting admission logic when disabled. Testing: unit tests for the uncertainty model and mapper rules, integration test harness simulating spike patterns, and a perf canary run in benchmark-lab showing a 35-60% reduction in spike-induced dropped requests for a synthetic 10x short burst workload with <3% steady-state cost increase. Security: no new exfiltration paths; suggestions are internal-only and logged at debug level. Observability and alerting: new dashboard panels and alerts added for anomalous suggestion rates and suggestions rejected due to cluster constraints. Safety: CHA suggestions are capped by per-tenant max_quota and global soft_budget to avoid capacity starvation. Implementation files: controller implementation in controllers/cha/ (Go), GBQM admission in serving/admission/burst_mapper.go, autoscaler hook in autoscaler/hints_consumer.go, metrics/exporter in telemetry/cha_exporter.go, Helm values patch for dedicated, and documentation. Performance: bench runs on a 200-node dedicated test cluster indicate steady-state 0.5–2% CPU overhead and memory footprint +12MB per CHA replica; latency improvement primarily visible at p95-p999 during bursts. CI: runs unit/integration/lint and a short canary scenario; all checks passed after a flaky test fix. See commits and changed files below for exact diffs.
Daniel Park: Can we tighten the default decay_rate for experimental rollout? I saw a couple of cases in the integration where suggestions lingered longer than expected.
Aisha Kaur: Replied: tightened default to 0.6 from 0.8 and added explicit expiry enforcement for suggestions >60s. Also added an integration assertion to validate expiry behavior.
Erin Zhao: Please add more conservative gating for low-capacity clusters - do not let CHA suggestions push cluster commit > 15% by default.
Aisha Kaur: Replied: added global soft_budget cap (15% default) and a cluster-level override for operator use. Documented in helm values and runbook.
Leo Martínez: lgtm with one nits: move exporter registration to telemetry/init.go and avoid noisy debug logs by sampling at 1% for high-volume tenants.
Aisha Kaur: Replied: moved registration and added sampling; adjusted logging levels and added a feature flag to increase sampling for debugging.
CI Bot: Integration flake detected in benchmark-lab spike harness; rerun fixed failure after seeding randomness.
Introduces Capacity Horizon Advisor (opt-in) and Granular Burst Quota Mapper to reduce burst-induced dropped requests; new metrics: cha_suggested_tokens, gbqm_active_quota, headroom_curve_p50/p90; operator knobs added to helm values for controlled rollout. Default behavior unchanged until enabled.
payload.title: Capacity Horizon Advisor and Granular Burst Quota Mapper

payload.body:
Context: We continue to see autoscaler thrash in medium-load bursts where short-lived demand spikes cause the fleet to scale up then immediately scale down, destabilizing warm pools and increasing cost. Small tenants with occasional microbursts are starved by aggressive proportional allocators and end up timing out while larger steady tenants consume most freshly provisioned slots. Motivation: Reduce churn from transient headroom changes, provide a bounded short-term priority channel for microbursts, and surface observability for fence violations and ephemeral allocations. This PR introduces two cooperating mechanisms: 1) A soft capacity fence that prevents immediate reclamation of recently provisioned capacity for a configurable grace window and a decay curve rather than an instantaneous release. The fence is applied per-fleet and per-tenant reservation waterfall; it is soft because it permits reclamation for higher-severity events (e.g., critical safety drains) but biases the autoscaler to prefer gentle ramp-down. 2) An ephemeral priority allocator: a transient, time-bounded pool of priority credits that can be loaned to tenants when they emit validated microburst requests. Credits are repaid via a short throttling phase or via scheduled background demotion; the allocator enforces strict fairness windows to prevent long-term priority accumulation. Design notes: - The soft fence is implemented as a headroom token ledger with timestamps and a decaying headroom score (RFC-style parameters: fence_window_seconds, decay_half_life_seconds, reclaim_threshold_percent). - Ephemeral allocator is a scoped priority pool (config: pool_size_slots, max_credit_duration_seconds, per_tenant_credit_cap) and integrates with the request admission path so that ephemeral allocations are only granted when latency SLO for the router is preserved. - Both features are behind an operator-controllable feature flag (feature.gate.soft_capacity_fence / feature.gate.ephemeral_allocator) and default to off for existing Dedicated fleets. - Telemetry adds metrics: redwood_fence_allocated_seconds, redwood_fence_reclaims_total, redwood_ephemeral_credit_grants_total, redwood_ephemeral_credit_rejections_total, redwood_ephemeral_grant_latency_ms. Also added tracing spans for fence-eval and ephemeral-grant with contextual tags (tenant_id, fleet_id, reason). Migration & rollout: - Default to gated rollout for 72 hours in staging fleets, then gradual rollout across small fleets (<= 50 GPUs) with canary monitoring. - If fence_violation_rate > 1% or ephemeral_grant_rejection_rate > 10% in canaries, the feature gate will be rolled back automatically by the ops runbook. Testing: - Unit tests for ledger decay math, allocator fairness window, and gating logic. - Integration harness: synthetic microburst scenarios showed 48% reduction in scale-up events vs master and 22% lower cold-start tail latency for microburst tenants. - Load test: 6-hour rerun on perf-canary cluster with mixed tenant profiles (50% steady, 50% bursty) preserved 99th-percentile generation latency within SLO and reduced total scale events by 34%. Backwards compatibility: - Existing reservation semantics are preserved when the feature flags are off. - Rollback is safe because reclamation remains policy-governed; no immediate resource leaks. Configuration: - New API surface in fleet config: soft_capacity_fence: {enabled, fence_window_seconds, decay_half_life_seconds, reclaim_threshold_percent} and ephemeral_priority: {enabled, pool_size_slots, max_credit_duration_seconds, per_tenant_credit_cap}. Observability: - Console dashboard tile added for fence state per-fleet and ephemeral pool utilization. - Alerts: fence_violation_rate (warning) and ephemeral_pool_exhaustion (critical). Security/permissions: - Only operators with fleet-admin role can toggle the feature gates. Related work: ENG-1482 (autoscaler stability spike investigation), ENG-1709 (microburst fairness doc).
Adds a configurable soft capacity fence to reduce scale-up/scale-down oscillation and a short-lived ephemeral priority allocator to fairly distribute microburst credits across tenants. Includes telemetry and feature flag gating.
Jonah Pierce: High-level LGTM. Two requests: (1) can we make the default decay_half_life conservative so small canaries are safe? (2) Add a metric to count per-tenant grant latency buckets
Aisha Khan: Answered — default decay_half_life_seconds is 600s in config; increased canary to 1200s for initial rollout. Added per-tenant grant latency histogram in telemetry commit.
Lin Wei: Thread-safety nit in headroom_ledger.go: prefer atomic.RWMutex vs atomic counters for map ops. Also question about reclaim priority vs safety drains.
Aisha Khan: Addressed with a map-level RWMutex and microbenched; added early-return path to allow immediate reclaim on operator/drain events.
Caroline Voss: Tests look good; please add an e2e assertion that ephemeral grants do not exceed per_tenant_credit_cap under high contention
Aisha Khan: Added e2e assertion and extended perf-run to 6 hours. Reran CI and green.
Merged into main after addressing concurrency nit and adding e2e cap assertion. CI passed on final run (all checks green). Rollout gated; ops instructed to follow canary runbook. Observed 34% fewer scale events in perf canary with preserved latency SLOs.
payload.title: Introduce soft capacity fence and ephemeral priority allocator to reduce autoscaler thrash and improve microburst fairness

Context: Dedicated fleets need finer-grained admission controls to preserve tenant throughput guarantees during transient spikes without wasting reserved capacity. Motivation: existing backpressure and burst-token systems react after congestion has already impacted latency/SLOs; we want a conservative, forward-looking gate that prevents risky admissions when headroom is predicted to be insufficient. What this PR implements: a lightweight "threshold oracle" that synthesizes short-term utilization forecasts (EWMA + percentile sampler) and a risk sigma coefficient to produce a per-tenant safe-admission threshold, plus a deferred-throttle gate that pauses burst admissions for a configurable window when predicted risk crosses the configured threshold. The implementation is conservative by default and opt-in per fleet/tenant (config flag is off for existing fleets). Key behaviors: 1) Oracle computes a 30s and 5m smoothed utilization window, combines them with a tunable sigma multiplier and a percentile-of-samples safety margin to produce a numeric "admission headroom" score. 2) Deferred-throttle gate integrates with the existing admission pipeline (AdmissionController -> BurstTokenPool) and can defer acceptance of burst tokens for a tenant for a configurable cooldown when the oracle signals elevated risk. 3) Telemetry: emits new metrics (tenant_admission_headroom, tenant_risk_sigma, deferred_throttle_events) with tags for tenant_id, fleet_id, and policy_version. 4) Rollout: feature gated, default disabled; can be enabled per-fleet in dedicated config; operator can choose conservative defaults used in initial rollout. Design notes: - Oracle is intentionally local and stateless (uses sliding-window counters and percentile sampler) to avoid cross-fleet coupling and to make rollout lower-risk. - The gate uses exponential backoff for repeated deferrals to avoid oscillation and includes an override annotation for emergencies. - We preserve existing burst-token accounting (no change to token economics) but reduce accidental admissions when predicted headroom is insufficient. Migration: no required DB migrations. Config knobs added for fleet config proto (threshold_oracle.enabled, threshold_oracle.sigma, threshold_oracle.window_seconds, deferred_throttle.cooldown_seconds). Testing: unit tests for oracle math and gate, e2e in perf-canary harness with synthetic tenant spike. See related Linear items ENG-3241, ENG-3308.
Jordan Rivera: Nice isolation between oracle and gate. Question: why percentile sampler instead of full histogram? Response: sampler reduces memory pressure for large tenant counts and gives sufficient tail signal for admission decisions.
Sana Malik: Can we expose a diagnostic export for the oracle's internal state? Reply: added a debug endpoint behind admin auth that returns last N samples and EWMA state (see telemetry/metrics.yaml change).
Omar Ibrahim: Concerned about oscillation with backoff windows. Reply: the gate now uses exponential backoff with jitter and a min-cooldown floor; added tests simulating repeated spikes.
unit: oracle math edge cases and sampler correctness (pkg/autoscaler/oracle_test.go)
integration: admission path with oracle enabled against local BurstTokenPool simulator
perf-canary: synthetic tenant spike scenario run in staging (cmd/perf-canary/scenarios/threshold-oracle.yaml) showing 42% fewer SLO breaches under default conservative config
step 0: keep feature disabled in global defaults
step 1: enable for non-critical fleets in staging for 7 days; monitor tenant_admission_headroom and deferred_throttle_events
step 2: enable for a small set of production fleets (opt-in) with sigma=2.5 conservative setting
step 3: evaluate telemetry for 2 weeks; consider lowering sigma or adjusting windows per workload
Added Threshold Oracle and Deferred Throttle Gate for dedicated fleets (opt-in).
New telemetry: tenant_admission_headroom, tenant_risk_sigma, deferred_throttle_events.
No changes to burst-token accounting; default behavior unchanged until enabled per-fleet.
payload.title: introduce-threshold-oracle-and-deferred-throttle-gates-for-dedicated-fleets

Context: Several customers and downstream SDK teams reported jitter and unnecessary reauth churn when a single application multiplexes multiple logical streams over long-lived connections. Motivation: introduce a lightweight orchestrated credential profile model plus a small pullstream adapter that lets SDKs pin a credential profile per logical stream while sharing transport-level heartbeats, reducing reauth noise and improving burst behaviour. This PR implements a cross-language surface and coordinated runtime invariants and ships companion version bumps for the three SDKs. Scope: 1) credential profiles v2 (shape-stable, smaller footprint) implemented in Python/TS/Go SDKs, 2) a PullstreamMultiplexer shim that exposes a typed StreamHandle->Profile mapping for callers and handles on-the-wire multiplexing, 3) a small backoff harmonizer that aligns retry jitter windows across SDKs to avoid thundering reauth storms, and 4) docs + migration guide and unit/integration tests. Design highlights: credential profiles are declarative presets (idle_ttl, reauth_threshold, prewarm hooks) that can be composed; the PullstreamMultiplexer stitches an id-assigned logical stream into a single transport connection while maintaining per-stream credential leases and allows graceful checkpointed resume. Rollout plan: feature-flagged at runtime, staged rollout behind canary config for dedicated customers, with telemetry gates for reauth-rate and connection churn. Backwards compatibility: default profile maps to existing behavior so this is non-breaking for consumers unless they opt-in. Testing: added cross-sdk unit tests, e2e with local multiplexed harness, and a small chaos scenario that simulates credential expiry and prewarm flows. Related: builds on prior session-lease work (ENG-8710) and the credential prefetch RFC (ENG-9302).
Aisha Patel (2026-01-13): Nice isolation of profile serialization, can we tighten the JSON schema to reject unknown top-level keys? Suggest adding a validation layer so future changes are explicit.
Diego Morales (2026-01-13): Good call, added a schema validator in profile_v2.py and schema docs in docs/sdk/cred-profiles.md in the next commit.
Ryan Chen (2026-01-14): Multiplexer looks clean. Question: under high load, does the id->lease map become a contention point? Could we shard the reconciler per CPU core in the Go implementation?
Diego Morales (2026-01-14): Added a note and a simple sharded reconciler in multiplexer.go behind a build flag; left single-shard default for safety. We can enable after perf tests.
Lena Fischer (2026-01-16): Tests look good. Minor nit: add a short example snippet in the TS README showing typical usage with async iterators.
Diego Morales (2026-01-16): Added the TS snippet and an example to the docs + bumped the TS test harness timeout to reduce flakiness.
Introduce credential profiles v2 and PullstreamMultiplexer shim. Adds non-breaking opt-in API for per-logical-stream credential presets, reduces reauth churn for multiplexed workloads, and harmonizes retry jitter across SDKs. SDK versions bumped: python -> 1.12.0, typescript -> 2.34.0, go -> v1.9.0. See docs/sdk/multiplexing-migration.md for migration steps.
payload.title: Orchestrated credential profiles and multiplexing pullstream shim

Summary: Add a policy-assertion mapper that converts incoming operator/service JWT claims into RBAC v2 directives, enforce KMS region pinning during the KMS handshake, and introduce a lightweight audit watermarking header for cross-region key-usage detection. Motivation: Recent compliance reviews and an internal incident (SUP-1193) showed ambiguous operator claims leading to accidental cross-region KMS calls and noisy audit streams that made investigating residency violations slow. This change tightens the policy -> RBAC mapping, rejects KMS requests incompatible with tenant region policies earlier, and tags audit events with a stable watermark for easier deduplication and correlation.

What this PR does (high level):
- policy/mapper: new PolicyAssertionMapper component that validates and normalizes JWT claims (operator.scope, tenant.region, service.zone) and emits RBAC v2 grant objects consumed by request-authorizer.
- kms/validator: KMS region pin checks during handshake and an opt-in strict-mode that returns a 412 (Precondition Failed) when a key operation is out-of-region for a tenant pinned by policy. Backwards-compatible default remains permissive with audit-only mode.
- audit/watermark: add X-Audit-Watermark (sha256 over request meta + timestamp bucket) to trace and dedupe cross-service audit lines, with config toggle and retention hints for downstream sink.
- rbac: small adjustments to rbac-v2 policy loader to accept mapped grant objects and to prefer explicit regional deny rules over generic allow rules.
- docs: security runbook and migration guide for operator teams to verify claims and enable strict KMS pinning.

Implementation notes:
- PolicyAssertionMapper lives under services/policy and is designed as a sidecar-friendly library so Dedicated/Private deployments can opt into translation without changing the control plane. It performs conservative normalization only (no claim augmentation).
- KMS region checks happen pre-encryption/decrypt attempt to fail fast and avoid potential cross-region telemetry leaks. There is a feature-flag (KMS_REGION_STRICT) that can be flipped per-tenant.
- Watermarking uses an HMAC-free SHA256 over canonicalized values (tenant_id, request_path, short-timestamp-bucket) so sinks can correlate without storing sensitive payloads. We intentionally avoid embedding key material in the watermark.

Checklist: [x] Unit tests for mapper normalization and rbac grant generation [x] Integration tests for KMS pre-checks in permissive and strict modes [x] End-to-end audit flow validation with watermark enabled [x] Documentation and migration guide [x] Feature flags and telemetry counters added

Testing and CI: Ran unit tests (services/policy/*), integration suite cover KMS region pinning scenarios, and an end-to-end smoke test that verifies watermark appears in all configured audit sinks. One flaky test in canary CI (integration/network) was retried and passed on rerun. Security scan (SNYK/Trivy) showed no new high/critical findings.

Rollout plan:
- Canary in us-west-2 with watermark and mapper enabled in audit-only mode for 48 hours.
- Enable KMS_REGION_STRICT for a small tenant cohort with customer opt-in and monitor errors for 7 days.
- Gradually expand strict mode after operator signoff; policy migration tooling included in docs to help tenants update claims.

Rollback: revert feature-flag or toggle mapper to audit-only mode. A small compatibility shim ensures older RBAC v1 checks will continue to operate until migration completes.

Related: ENG-4821 (policy mapping RFC), SEC-92 (compliance gap triage), SUP-1193 (incident follow-up).
Arjun Patel: Can we avoid blocking all requests in strict mode for now? Suggest returning 412 with a clear remediation message. (resolved)
Leah Chen: Mapper ok overall but add a defensive check for missing tenant.region claim; mapped grants should default to 'region: unknown' rather than fail hard. (addressed)
Omar Haddad: audit watermark looks good — please ensure sinks respect the retention hint header. (added note in watermark.go)
Arjun Patel: CI showed a flaky integration test; saw a retry and green, please add a non-flaky variant if possible. (follow-up ticket created: ENG-4907)
Maya Ortiz: Thanks all — addressed comments and added migration docs.
Add PolicyAssertionMapper to convert operator claims into RBAC v2 grants; KMS region pre-checks with per-tenant strict mode; audit watermarking header to correlate and dedupe cross-region audit events. Non-breaking by default; opt-in strict mode requires tenant claim migration.
payload.title: Policy assertion mapper, KMS region hardening, and audit watermarking
