Context: We currently emit token-level traces and basic invocation spans but lack a way to see invocation topology (call/child relationships across microservices and runtime stages) coupled with a lightweight cost mosaic that surfaces expensive invocation segments. This makes SLO triage and cost debugging for multi-stage requests slow (ENG-3210).

Motivation: Provide engineers and SREs an end-to-end investigatory surface that links: 1) per-invocation topology (entry -> kernel queue -> runtime -> kv-cache -> fallback), 2) sampled token phase timing, and 3) a compact cost 'mosaic' view that highlights which stage(s) contributed most to token/unit cost. This PR introduces a topology tracing library, a mosaic writer that aggregates cost slices for dashboards, and a companion dashboard JSON and docs.

What changed (high level): Adds a topology tracer that synthesizes parent/child relationships from existing span IDs and lightweight edge heuristics; introduces a token-phase snapshot event that attaches phase timings to invocation spans; adds a cost-mosaic writer that reduces per-invocation token cost into 5 buckets and emits rollup documents for dashboards; includes a Grafana dashboard JSON for the mosaic and a docs page with rollout and troubleshooting steps.

Design notes: - Topology tracer attaches a deterministic topology_key to each span derived from (service, stage, kernel_hint). It does not change the public trace IDs. - Snapshot events are sampled 1% by default with a configurable per-tenant multiplier (config key: observability.snapshot_rate). - Cost mosaic aggregates per-invocation tokens into buckets: compute, kv-cache, kernel-queue, network, misc. Buckets are derived from existing token attribution tags; where missing, we fall back to phase-duration heuristics. - Writer is implemented as an async, bounded worker to avoid applying backpressure to critical request paths. Backpressure is mitigated by a small token buffer and drop-policy metrics exposed as observability:observability.mosaic_drop_count.

Checklist: 
- [x] Topology tracer library (src/observability/topology_tracer.go)
- [x] Token-phase snapshot event (pkg/telemetry/snapshot.go)
- [x] Cost mosaic writer (services/mosaic/writer.go)
- [x] Grafana dashboard JSON (dashboards/cost-mosaic.json)
- [x] Docs and runbook (docs/observability/cost-mosaic.md)
- [x] Unit + integration tests (perf/bench/invocation_sampler_test.go, pkg/telemetry/snapshot_test.go)
- [x] Load-tested write path (benchmarks/mosaic_write_bench.md)

Backwards compatibility and rollout: Default sampling is low (1%) and feature gated via config and feature flags. No trace ID or span schema breaking changes. The writer will start in 'dry-run' mode in the rollout plan for 24h to validate telemetry volumes; after that we enable persisted rollups. See docs/observability/cost-mosaic.md for the toggle and runbook.

Benchmarks: On a 32-GPU staging cluster with representative workload: - Mosaic writer avg CPU overhead per 1k invocations: +0.07 CPU-seconds - Median added p99 latency on hotpath (measured at service ingress): +1.4ms (within SLO) - Observed mosaic payloads: ~34KB per 1k sampled invocations (rollup compressed to ~10KB before storage) - With default sampling (1%), storage estimate: ~2.5GB/day for a mid-tier customer (guidance in docs).

Commit summary: 
- 8b3f2c2: add topology tracer and unit tests
- d1a9e77: implement token-phase snapshot events, add serialization layer
- 5f4b0a1: cost mosaic writer and async worker, add drop metrics
- 3a7c11f: add Grafana dashboard and dashboard generator tooling
- 9d2e4b3: docs and runbook; add feature flag and config knobs

Files changed (representative): 
- src/observability/topology_tracer.go
- pkg/telemetry/snapshot.go
- services/mosaic/writer.go
- services/mosaic/worker_pool.go
- dashboards/cost-mosaic.json
- docs/observability/cost-mosaic.md
- pkg/telemetry/serializer.go
- perf/bench/invocation_sampler_test.go
- tests/integration/mosaic_integration_test.go

Testing and CI: Unit tests and integration tests run in CI. Initial CI run had a flaky test (perf/bench/invocation_sampler_test.go) due to timing, fixed by replacing wall-clock dependency with a fake clock. All checks passed on the final run (lint, unit, integration, e2e smoke).

Migration: No DB schema changes. Rollup storage uses an existing compressed blob table (mosaic_rollups) with a new jsonschema version header for graceful migration. We increment schema_version in the writer to 3.

Rollout plan: 
1) Merge to main with feature flag off.
2) Enable dry-run (emits rollup to internal sink only) for 24 hours, monitor observability.mosaic_drop_count and writer queue depth.
3) Turn on persisted rollups for 5% traffic for 48 hours.
4) Ramp sampling/config to 1% tenant default.
5) Open dashboard to SREs and run RCA playbook for 7 days.

Related: ENG-3210 (cost-mosaic), ENG-3301 (topology tracing).
Asha Patel (2025-11-22): Nice end-to-end. A couple asks: please add a metric for writer queue latency distribution and expose the default snapshot rate as a gauge. Also prefer a smaller default buffer for the worker pool (you had 10k queued tokens).
Jamal Ortiz (2025-11-23): Addressed — added writer.queue_latency_histogram and observability.snapshot_rate_gauge. Reduced default buffer to 2k and made it an env-configurable value. Added notes in docs explaining tradeoffs.
Luca Moretti (2025-11-25): Can you justify the phase-bucket heuristics when attribution tags are missing? I worry about noisy attribution leading to misleading mosaics.
Jamal Ortiz (2025-11-25): Added fallback confidence score with the rollup. Mosaic now includes a confidence float per bucket and the dashboard highlights low-confidence rollups. Also added a sampling knob to force higher confidence on a small proportion of invocations to validate heuristics.
Renee Kim (2025-11-28): Tests look good. Please add a short snippet in docs showing how to query mosaics for a given tenant and timeframe. Also, can we add an alert to watch mosaic_drop_count?
Jamal Ortiz (2025-11-28): Added query examples to docs and a recommended alert rule (SLO: if mosaic_drop_count > 100/min then pager). Updated dashboard description with link to runbook.
Add invocation topology tracing and a cost mosaic rollup writer. Default sampling off; feature gated. Provides a Grafana dashboard and runbook to accelerate SLO triage and token-cost debugging.

Context and motivation: production retention and key-scoping gaps were identified during a compliance review (ENG-4982). Existing audit logs could be retained beyond policy TTLs due to missing enforcement and operator RBAC guards; similarly, a subset of customer CMKs lacked standardized residency tags which complicates region-aware KMS routing. This PR introduces three coordinated pieces: 1) retention-enforcer service and RBAC v2 bindings to manage tombstone jobs, 2) an idempotent KMS tagging migration with verification and rollback, and 3) an audit-sink fanout so compliance consumers (long-term archive, e-discovery, and analytics) receive consistent copies while tombstone runs proceed.

Changes (high-level commits): - Add retention-enforcer microservice + API surface (tombstone scheduler, dry-run mode, metrics) - RBAC policy templates (rbacv2) and a new role: AuditTombstoneOperator scoped to org/tenant boundaries - Migration: kms-tag-migration script (aws/gcp wrappers) with verification hooks and a dry-run flag - Audit sink: fanout adapter to forward canonical audit records to the compliance-collector and s3-archive - Unit + integration tests for policy evaluation and migration safe-paths - Console docs and runbook: how to run migration, roll back, and incident playbook

Files changed (selected): - services/retention-enforcer/main.go (new) - services/retention-enforcer/scheduler.go (new) - infra/rbac/v2/audit_tombstone_role.yaml (new) - tools/migrations/kms_tagging/migrate_tags.py (new) - tools/migrations/kms_tagging/verify.py (new) - observability/metrics/retention_enforcer.prom (new) - api/openapi/retention-enforcer.yaml (new) - docs/rbac/retention-runbook.md (updated) - docs/ops/kms-tagging.md (new) - services/audit-proxy/fanout_adapter.go (updated)

Review conversation: Marcus Lee: "Can the tombstone job be constrained by both tenant and region? We must ensure no cross-region deletion logic." Author: "Yes — the scheduler enforces scope the same way operator role assertions do; tombstone jobs are always evaluated with the request's residency claim and the KMS tag verifier will block deletion for keys missing the matching region tag. Added unit tests to cover multi-tenant scenarios." Priya Patel: "Migration script looks good but we need a way to verify the tags before enabling automatic routing." Author: "Added verify.py and a two-phase migration in the runbook: dry-run -> tag application -> post-verify -> enable routing. The migration supports explicit allowlists for initial rollout." Diego Ramos: "CI flake on integration: kms emulator timeout." Author: "Increased emulator timeouts and added retry on transient errors; re-ran CI." Approvals: Marcus approved after minor comments; Priya approved after runbook additions; Diego approved after CI green.

CI and checks: - unit-tests: pass - integration-tests (kms-emulator): initially fail due to timeout, retried, pass - linters: pass - policy-compat-checker: pass - security-scan (deps): warn on one dev dependency (not in production path)

Migration and rollout notes: - Default behavior: migration runs manually via tools/migrations/kms_tagging with --dry-run. - Opt-in: tenant admins can opt-in to automatic tag application per-tenant via the console flag. - Flag gating: the retention-enforcer is deployed disabled by default; enable per-region after migration verification. - Rollback: migration includes a rollback script that unsets tags applied by the run. - Observability: retention-enforcer exposes per-tenant metrics (tombstone_count, dry_run_warning_count, failed_verifications) and audit entries for every deletion.

Security considerations: - New RBAC role (AuditTombstoneOperator) is scoped and requires: operator:region, operator:tenant claims. - KMS tag migration adds no new key material; tags are metadata only. Scripts follow least privilege: separate IAM role for tag writes with allowlist. - Audit-sink fanout preserves canonical audit envelopes and signs forwarded copies to prevent tampering.

Testing performed: end-to-end staging run with synthetic tenants (3 tenants across 2 regions), ran full migration in dry-run and verified no tombstones were scheduled until tags were verified. Load test of tombstone scheduler at 10k records/minute sustained under SLOs.

Merge outcome: squash and merge on 2024-11-20. Notes: tagged as release-note:infra and rolled out to staging immediately; production rollout planned after compliance signoff and an operator training session.
Introduce a retention enforcement service and RBAC bindings to allow automated tombstone of audit records; add a migration to tag existing customer CMKs with region/residency metadata and a safe rollback path; add an audit-sink fanout to the compliance collector. No public API changes; internal infra and policy updates only.

payload.body:
Motivation: intermittent regional reconnections were causing abrupt connection churn and KV-cache loss during rapid failback windows. This increased tail latency and produced SLO violations for a subset of customers during rolling network flaps. This hotpatch introduces a 'traffic bleedoff' path and an inflight-preserve escape hatch that prioritizes completing active KV-backed sessions while gently shedding new requests. The change is intentionally conservative: it nudges circuit thresholds and sashays new-connection admission rather than hard-killing. Key goals: 1) maintain customer-visible session continuity for in-flight requests, 2) reduce SLO noise during short-lived regional instability, 3) provide immediate telemetry to validate efficacy.
Hotpatch: introduce a traffic bleedoff coordinator and inflight-preserve escape hatch to reduce SLO violations during short regional reconverges. Defaults are conservative; opt-in canary via runtime flag. Adds metrics: runtime.bleedoff.engaged, runtime.bleedoff.duration_ms, runtime.inflight.pinned_count.
Design summary: The bleedoff coordinator is a thin admission controller inserted at the regional egress gateway. When a region reconverge signal or elevated egress latency is detected, the coordinator enters a bleedoff window: new low-priority requests are placed into a short admission delay (randomized 100-400ms) and then rejected if capacity remains constrained. High-priority/inflight sessions are marked with an ephemeral preserve token; the KV-preserve patch pins the session's small working set and avoids evicting its KV cache for up to 60s or until completion. Circuit reopen backoff was softened: reopen attempts now use an exponential jittered cooldown with a higher base to avoid rapid flip-flopping. Canary rollout: flag runtime.canary.bleedoff enabled for 10% of hosts for 48h, with automated rollback if error budget burn >2*slo_baseline in that window.
Unit tests simulate coordinator transitions and validate that pinned inflight sessions are not evicted during reconverge. Integration staging run against a replayed incident trace shows 72% reduction in KV cache miss storms and a 30% reduction in 95th percentile tail latency during brief region flaps. CI initially had a flaky test (coordinator_test.go:TestStagger) failing under race timing; fixed by switching to deterministic clock injection and re-ran pipelines. Load canary in staging for 24h before merging to main.
Flag-based quick rollback: flip runtime.canary.bleedoff=false for canary hosts; global rollback by disabling bleedoff coordinator at runtime via feature gate. If unexpected persistent errors occur, revert patch and restore previous circuit thresholds. Post-merge monitoring dashboard created and an on-call playbook added to docs/ops/bleedoff-runbook.md.
Expected benign: slight increase in short-term rejection rates for low-priority traffic during bleedoff windows; improved completion rate for inflight sessions. Operators will see new metrics; SRE will evaluate burn rate over the next 72h and may adjust preserve TTL and admission delay windows.
1) Promote console alerts for runtime.bleedoff.engaged to paging at a 10m sustained threshold. 2) Monitor canary host telemetry and collect sample traces where bleedoff engaged. 3) Run a follow-up perf PR to make the pinning lighter-weight if memory pressure observed.
Diego Alvarez: Can we avoid pinning large KV objects for more than 30s? Suggest cap + LRU fallback. (addressed)
Marina Chen: Please add a short-circuit in the coordinator to prevent double-shed on cascaded region failures. (added guard)
Anika Patel: Metrics look good; add a histogram for bleedoff duration to help tuning. (added metric)
Rebecca (SRE): Observability: include an alert that fires when bleedoff engages >3 times in 10m. (docs updated)
This PR is intentionally conservative and contains feature flags for immediate rollback. The implementation avoids broad behavioral changes to eviction policies; instead it biases admission and short-term cache pinning to preserve user-visible sessions. SRE verified the runbook and approved the pager thresholds.
Related to incident SUP-3122 (2026-02-18): regional egress flapping caused repeated KV cache thrash and elevated tail latency. This PR mitigates recurrence for short windows but is not a replacement for long-term egress stability fixes.
payload.title: Traffic bleedoff and inflight-preserve emergency SLO guard (hotpatch)

payload.body:
Context: Customers running Dedicated fleets occasionally see transient throughput shortfalls when cross-tenant preemption, node reboots, or maintenance windows cause short-lived capacity loss. Existing autoscalers smooth utilization but do not account for small intermittent losses which cause conservative headroom shrinkage and result in repeated over-provisioning.

Motivation: Introduce explicit bookkeeping for short-lived capacity loss and a bounded 'amnesty' mechanism that lets tenants recover unused commit credits over a short window instead of being penalized by long-term reservation recalculation. This reduces oscillation in reserved capacity, improves throughput guarantees for tenants with bursty patterns, and lowers steady-state reserved capacity.

What this PR does: Adds two coordinated components: 1) capacity-book, a lightweight ledger that records short-lived capacity deltas (node drains, preempt events, maintenance) and attributes lost capacity to clusters/pools; and 2) amnesty-controller, a bounded forgiveness policy that reconciles per-tenant commit valuations when the capacity-book indicates loss was transient and within configured thresholds. The controller can proactively issue ephemeral credits or relax reservation enforcement to avoid hard reservation churn. The change is fully feature-flagged behind "capacity_book_amnesty_v1".

Design notes: - Capacity-book is implemented as an append-only time-windowed ledger (TTL 10m by default) that exposes summarized loss histograms to autoscaler components. It intentionally avoids strong consistency — eventual aggregation is sufficient for amortized decisions. - Amnesty-controller consumes the loss histogram and a tenant's recent commit history; it applies a decayed forgiveness function (alpha=0.6 default) to convert lost tokens into temporary credits capped by a per-tenant budget. - The system maintains invariants: amended capacity never violates cluster hard-limits; amnesty credits are ephemeral and expire within 5 minutes; chargeback metrics are emitted for audit.

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for ledger rollup, decay math, and safety caps. - Integration tests simulate node preemptions + tenant traffic to validate no SLA regressions. - Load test against perf-canary harness with 500 tenants to measure steady-state reserved reduction and burst success rate. Results: average reserved capacity reduced by ~6.8% across runs; 95th percentile tail recoveries improved by ~22ms for burst admissions.

Rollout plan: - Feature flag default off. - Step 1: Enable in canary clusters during a 2-week observation window (ops + QE). - Step 2: Enable for low-risk customer pools with telemetry gates. - Step 3: Gradual ramp to remaining Dedicated clusters with a global kill-switch.

Telemetry and dashboards: New metrics emitted: "capacity_book.loss_events", "capacity_book.loss_histogram", "amnesty_controller.issued_credits", "amnesty_controller.expired_credits", and audit logs for reconciliation decisions. Added Grafana panels under Dedicated -> Capacity Book and a set of SLO checks to detect accidental over-admission.

Backward compatibility: All API surfaces are internal; no public API changes. Configuration knobs added to Dedicated config (defaults preserved).

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests added/updated - [x] Integration tests added - [x] Perf canary run completed - [x] Docs stubbed in /docs/dedicated/capacity-book.md - [x] Release notes drafted

References: Linear ENG-1782, ENG-1799; related older work: ENG-903210 (hedged-autoscaler) and pr-421314 (latency-indexed-provisioner) for telemetry patterns.

Notes: This approach is intentionally conservative — amnesty only reduces churn for short transient blips. Long outages still trigger normal reservation reconciliation and customer notifications.
Marco Santoro: Can we add a safety valve so amnesty cannot issue credits during maintenance windows?
Ellen Park: Added maintenance window check and unit test in controller_test.go
Priya Sharma: Please quantify the worst-case risk of over-admission in the PR description - how many ephemeral credits could be active cluster-wide?
Ellen Park: Added a paragraph to the description and a config knob (amnesty_cluster_cap) defaulting to 0.5% of cluster capacity
Jae Kim: lgtm modulo CI flake seen on integration tests (timeout on perf-run).
Ellen Park: increased test timeouts and re-ran canary; CI OK now.
payload.title: Capacity bookkeeping and burst-amnesty orchestrator (capacity-book + amnesty-controller)

Motivation: frequent fine-grained scale events on Dedicated clusters cause allocation churn and transient latency spikes for steady sustained workloads. This PR introduces two coordinated changes: (1) a deferred scale granularity layer (Scale Decoupler) that groups candidate scale actions into a configurable time bucket and emits a single reconciled action to the provisioner, and (2) a low-overhead utilization census service that samples per-pool signals with adaptive sampling to provide a robust decayed-utilization picture for the autoscaler. Both changes aim to reduce flapping, improve tail latency during scale transitions, and preserve burst capacity guarantees.

What changed (high level):
- New Scale Decoupler component in controller plane that buffers per-tenant and per-pool scale intents for a configurable window (default 30s) and merges them using policy heuristics (favor sustained growth, respect emergency fast-paths).
- Utilization Census daemon that replaces expensive full-pool scans with lightweight randomized probes + exponential decay windows; exports cohorted histograms and percentile summaries to the metrics pipeline.
- Autoscaler updated to query Census summaries and to respect decoupler-recommended consolidated actions; introduces hysteresis knobs and a min-delta threshold to avoid sub-token scale churn.
- Telemetry: added ring buffer counters, 'census.sample_rate' and 'decoupler.emitted_actions' metrics, and tracing spans for the merge decision path.
- New unit and e2e tests for decoupler merge semantics and census sampling accuracy; stress test added to perf-canary harness.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked in description (Linear ENG-2247)
- [x] Unit tests for merge policy and utility functions
- [x] Integration tests for end-to-end scaling on a small dedicated cluster
- [x] Metrics and traces wired to observability console
- [x] Backwards-compatible (decoupler is opt-in, census can fall back to full-scan)

Impact: rolling this out cluster-by-cluster should reduce the number of scale actions per hour for steady workloads by ~60% in our internal perf runs, reduce allocation churn and lower 99th percentile latency during scaling by ~8-15%. The change preserves existing SLA fast-paths (emergency preemption when backlog exceeds threshold).
Mateo Ruiz: Nice isolation between decoupler and provisioner. Request: expose a metric for 'merged_action_size' to monitor consolidation ratios.
Asha Menon (author): Added 'decoupler.merged_action_size' histogram in the latest commit and documented threshold implications.
Lena Cho: Census looks promising, but sampling rate defaults may be aggressive for very small pools. Please add a config knob and a fallback to full-scan for pools < 5 nodes.
Asha Menon: Added 'census.min_pool_size' config and a small-pool fallback path, plus unit tests that cover the behavior.
Dmitri Petrov: Found a race in merge decision under concurrent intent updates (flaky in integration). Suggest using a compare-and-swap guard or serializing per-pool intent commits.
Asha Menon: Reworked intent buffering to use per-pool mutexes and added deterministic test harness; integration flakiness resolved.
Mateo Ruiz: CI green, approving for canary. Please add a rollout plan in the ops doc before GA.
Lena Cho: Approved after small nits fixed in docs.
Introduce Scale Decoupler (opt-in): groups scale intents to reduce churn and allocation noise.
Introduce Utilization Census: low-overhead adaptive sampling for per-pool utilization reporting.
Autoscaler now consults census summaries and respects decoupler-consolidated actions; conservative defaults ensure backwards compatibility.
New metrics: decoupler.emitted_actions, decoupler.merged_action_size, census.sample_rate.

Motivation: Dedicated fleets saw periodic noisy preemptions during short-lived demand spikes which caused tail latency regressions for pinned workloads. This PR implements a tiered commit window and a graceful preempt reserve controller that reduces premature preemption while preserving capacity elasticity. Summary: add a new controller (pkg/fleet/preempt_reserve_controller.go) that maintains per-tenant tiered commit windows and a soft reserve ledger. The default policy creates three tiers (burst, sustained, committed) with decaying reserve weights. Additions to the autoscaler allow the scale decision to consult the reserve ledger and favor graceful shrinkage over immediate slot reclamation. Telemetry: new metrics exported under telemetry/fleet_reserve.md including histograms for reserve_utilization_seconds, gauge for tiered_reserve_bytes, and a counter for graceful_preempt_events. Config and ops: charts/dedicated/values.yaml exposes reserve window knobs and rollout safety flags. Tests: unit tests for the ledger and decision policy plus an e2e test (tests/e2e/preempt_reserve_test.go) that validates no-regressive tail latency under synthetic microbursts. Commits: a) feat(reserve): add preempt reserve controller and ledger b) feat(autoscaler): consult reserve ledger in scale-down decision c) perf: reduce lock contention in ledger updates d) docs: operations guide and config knobs e) test: add unit and e2e tests f) ci: flake fixes and test orchestration tweaks. Files changed (high level): pkg/fleet/preempt_reserve_controller.go, pkg/autoscaler/decision.go, pkg/allocator/slotmanager.go, charts/dedicated/values.yaml, telemetry/fleet_reserve.md, docs/ops/preemption.md, tests/unit/ledger_test.go, tests/e2e/preempt_reserve_test.go, scripts/ci/orchestrate_tests.sh, examples/dedicated/commit-policy.yaml, Makefile. Review thread: initial review by Samir requested lowering the default conservative reserve from 25% to 12% and adding a short-circuit for tenants with hard SLAs; implemented in second commit. Anya asked for clearer invariants around ledgers during partial failures; added stronger invariants and an extra integration test that simulates controller restarts. Miguel flagged a potential CPU hotspot in the ledger update path; resolved by moving to per-shard update queues and adding benchmarks. CI notes: first CI run failed due to a flaky e2e harness timeout; timeout increased and harness resilience improved, subsequent runs passed. Performance results: internal canary showed 18% reduction in scale-down-induced tail latencies for affected tenants and a 5% reduction in unnecessary preempt events during 30s microbursts. Backwards compatibility: default behavior preserves current autoscaler semantics unless the reserve controller is enabled via charts values. Rollout plan: staged rollout with canary on 10% of fleets then 50% then full, with automatic rollback on increased tail latency. Merge: squashed and merged after approvals and green CI. Related work: follows up on ENG-1284 (surge smoothing prototype) and complements pr-309452 probing provision controller. Notes for operators: tune tier windows and reserve weights based on workload burstiness; use provided dashboards to inspect reserve_utilization_seconds histogram when debugging preempt patterns.
Introduces a tiered commit/reserve controller to reduce noisy preemptions and improve sustained throughput across Dedicated fleets. Backwards-compatible defaults; ops can tune reserve windows per-tier.

payload.body:
Motivation: We need a compact, safer defaults engine that recommends batching, cache and quantization presets per workload profile to reduce per-token unit cost without manual tuning. This PR introduces 'Cost Sculptor' (internal name) - a prescriptor service and small console UX that suggests conservative defaults and optionally auto-applies them behind a feature flag. Context: large customers frequently under-tune batching/cache/quant settings and see high unit costs. Existing autotuners are aggressive and require long profile runs. Cost Sculptor provides quick, explainable presets computed from short sampling windows and historical telemetry.

What this PR does (summary): Adds a prescriptor microservice (pkg/econ/prescriptor) that consumes workload profiles and returns batching/cache/quant presets; exposes a REST endpoint and a CLI shim; wire the console to surface suggestions; adds an opt-in auto-apply rollout; records telemetry for applied suggestions and a light-weight A/B metric for unit cost delta.

Design notes: - Prescriptions are generated by a rule+heuristic engine (no ML model in this PR) with tunable thresholds to avoid regressions. - Safe fallbacks: suggestions include safety caps (max batch size, quant aggression limits) and a rollback window. - Telemetry: adds metric tags (suggestion_id, policy_version, candidate_profile) so we can measure impact and do experiments. - Feature flag: cost_sculptor.suggest_enabled and cost_sculptor.auto_apply for controlled rollout.

Checklist:
- [x] Core prescriptor engine and REST API
- [x] Console panel with suggestion preview + apply button
- [x] CLI shim for ops teams: redwoodctl econ suggest --sample <job>
- [x] Integration tests including simulated workloads
- [x] Telemetry and event schema registration
- [x] Docs: docs/operator/cost-sculptor.md and quickstart
- [x] Feature-flag gating and rollout plan

How to test locally: 1) run `make dev-prescriptor` which brings up prescriptor on :8089; 2) run sample generator scripts/scripts/sample-workload.sh to produce a short profile; 3) curl POST /v1/prescribe with the profile or use `redwoodctl econ suggest`; 4) in console -> Advanced -> Cost Suggestions you can preview and apply. See tests/e2e/cost-prescriptor.spec.ts for end-to-end smoke tests.

Bench summary: On a 7-day sampled trace from a mid-market customer (mixed short/medium sequences): - Median token-cost reduction: ~18% (range 11-26%) - P95 tail latency increased < 2% in worst case when auto-apply used conservative presets - Quantization suggestions applied q4->q4f gave ~9% decrease in GPU memory and enabled 1.15x request throughput for small-medium sequences. Bench scripts are in scripts/eval-profiles.sh and results logged under tools/benchmarks/cost-sculptor/.

Rollout plan: Start behind suggest_enabled for all customers (UI visible) but auto_apply only for internal tenants. Stage: internal -> beta customers (by invite) -> gradual ramp controlled by metric unit_cost_delta and latency_95. We will monitor the rollback window flag and have a kill-switch in console.

Related: ENG-1982 (prescriptor MVP), ENG-2043 (telemetry schema for econ suggestions). See docs link: https://internal.redwood/docs/operator/cost-sculptor

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps the prescriptor deterministic and conservative; a follow-up (ENG-2067) will add a learned ranking model and simulated A/B evaluation harness.

Motivation: During a regional surge incident we observed oscillating circuit transitions causing tenant-visible latency spikes and partial degradations. This PR introduces the 'degradation ward' - a lightweight transparent fallback governor that provides a conservative SLO relay and ephemeral fallback sentinel to avoid aggressive circuit flips and reduce cross-region failovers. Changes: 1) SLORelay operator that computes a smoothed SLO deficit metric per-tenant with exponential decay and time-weighted buckets, 2) DegradationGate middleware that applies a graded allow/deny decision with probationary windows, 3) EphemeralFallbackPlanner that reserves a tiny warm standby route and coordinates transparent KV-preserve handoff, 4) Telemetry hooks and new metrics: ward.slo_deficit, ward.probation_events, ward.fallback_reservations, and associated alert thresholds. Why this approach: targets failure modes observed in incident INC-2026-02-09 where fast reopen+failover churn amplified load; aim to prefer soft degrade and tenant probation over hard regional failover. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is opt-in via config flag 'ward.enabled' set to false in cluster config; when disabled runtime is unchanged. Testing: unit tests for SLO relay smoothing and DegradationGate decision matrix, integration test that simulates KV drain and verifies transparent fallback reservation, load test that demonstrates 12% reduction in cross-region failovers at 90th percentile latency under synthetic spike. Commits: - Add SLORelay and smoothing logic (samantha/ward/slo_relay) - Implement DegradationGate middleware with probation windows (samantha/ward/gate) - Add EphemeralFallbackPlanner and reservation protocol (samantha/ward/planner) - Telemetry and dashboards (samantha/ward/telemetry) - Tests and docs (samantha/ward/tests_docs) Files changed: runtime/ward/slo_relay.go, runtime/ward/gate.go, runtime/ward/planner.go, runtime/ward/telemetry.md, runtime/ward/README.md, infra/config/ward_defaults.yaml, telemetry/dashboards/ward_overview.json Reviewers and conversation: Rajiv requested clarifications on SLO smoothing constants and suggested replacing a hard 30s window with exponential decay, author updated smoothing code and added tests; Elena flagged potential lock contention in planner reservation; author introduced sharded reservation map and a benchmark showing negligible contention; Kai approved after CI green and asked to add an emergency disable flag which was added to config. CI: go build/test passed, linters passed, e2e flake on integration reran and passed. Files changed count: 7. Size: +312/-58. Release notes: 'Introduce Degradation Ward: opt-in SLO-relay and transparent fallback planner to reduce failover churn and improve stable degraded operation. Default disabled.' Merge: merged on 2026-02-20 via squash. Followups: rollout plan in Linear ENG-4981 for staged canary, post-deploy smoke tests, and incident retro action items. Related: SUP-3321 and INC-2026-02-09.
Rajiv: Can you make the smoothing window configurable instead of a fixed 30s? Consider exp decay to reduce sensitivity to spikes.

Elena: Planner reservation looked like a global lock under contention in the benchmark; please shard the reservation map.

Motivation: multiple SDK teams requested a small, predictable surface for credential handoff and a compact pullstream-friendly streaming facade that is consistent across Python, TypeScript, and Go. This PR introduces a lightweight "credential fabric" (orchestrated credential wrappers + fallback registry) and a compact PullStreamAdapter across SDKs to improve ergonomics for streaming consumers, smooth credential rotation, and reduce duplication in app code. Work covers three SDK packages and a central internal crate used for shared protocol types. Summary of changes: 1) Credential fabric: introduces CredentialRegistry (language-specific API names: CredentialRegistry / CredFabric) and a CredentialChain composable that accepts multiple providers (static tokens, delegated channels, rotating leases). It exposes a small lifecycle: acquire(), refresh_hint(), and release() to make lease semantics explicit for streaming sessions. 2) PullStreamAdapter: a minimal streaming facade that normalizes chunk buffering, backpressure hints and reauth callbacks; it intentionally avoids heavyweight session objects so callers can easily await chunks in tight loops. 3) Retry presets: adds an "sdk:streaming-compact" retry profile that defaults to lower backoff jitter for short-lived streams and a conservative retry window for credential-refresh scenarios. 4) Cross-sdk parity: brings the same API names and idioms to Python, TypeScript and Go with shims to preserve backwards compatibility. 5) Version bumps: py-sdk -> 0.11.0, ts-sdk -> 2.4.1, go-sdk -> v1.8.0. Migration notes / compatibility: - Python: introduces redwood.session.CredentialRegistry and redwood.stream.PullStreamAdapter. Existing SessionManager remains; a compatibility shim SessionManager.migrate_to_registry() is provided to ease rollouts. - TypeScript: adds CredFabric and pullstream.light() convenience factory. Old streaming constructors still supported but marked deprecated with console warnings. - Go: renames SessionHandle->SessionHandleV2 in public surface and provides SessionHandle (thin wrapper) for compatibility during the deprecation window. Tests and runtime: comprehensive unit tests added across SDKs including new integration tests that simulate token rotation during active streaming and ensure no dropped chunks or double-invocation of auth hooks. Performance: minor overhead for the registry path on cold start (~0.8ms median) but steady-state throughput unchanged. Rollout plan: library level releases were coordinated; feature gate in the hosted API will toggle registry-backed delegation for enterprise customers first, then default for all in 2 weeks. Commits and rationale: - feat(cred): introduce credential fabric and registry with composable chain - feat(stream): add compact PullStreamAdapter and stream retry preset - refactor(py/ts/go): centralize token exchange infra into shared-types crate - test: add rotation/integration tests and CI matrix - docs: add migration guide and quickstart examples Known limitations and followups: - The Go wrapper increases binary size slightly due to shim layers; follow-up PR will peel shared helper to a submodule. - There are a couple of non-blocking lint warnings in ts examples that were deferred to a docs cleanup PR. Full description ends here.
Marcus Nguyen: Nice consolidation — can we make refresh_hint non-blocking in Python? It's currently a sync call and may be invoked from async stream handlers.
Aisha Patel: Good catch, updated to return an awaitable in Python and added a small adapter to keep the sync path for legacy users. See commit b2d4e11.
Sofia Alvarez: TS API looks ergonomic. Minor nit: prefer 'credentials' over 'credfab' in the factory function name for clarity.
Aisha Patel: Renamed factory to 'CredFabric' but preserved credfab() as deprecated alias with a console.warn.
Ethan Brooks: CI flakes in go test on macos-latest, seems related to race in TestStreamRotation — added a short mutex in the test harness, re-ran pipeline.
CI Bot: All checks passed on rerun (linux/go/ts/py matrices).

Merged to main via squash. Release artifacts published to internal registry and packages pushed to PyPI/NPM/Go proxy. Feature gate will enable for enterprise customers and then roll out globally.

Docs cleanup PR scheduled (ENG-8632)

payload.body:
Problem: With RBAC v2 deny-by-default landing across Gateway + Control Plane, Support and Console UX need consistent, structured signals to answer “why was I denied?” without leaking policy internals or creating side-channel disclosure. Today we return a generic 403 from several stacks and each service/gateway path formats errors differently, making troubleshooting slow (and leading to tickets like SUP-48305/INT-19022). This PR introduces a shared set of denial reason codes and a gated, optional debug header mechanism for admin troubleshooting. Summary of changes: (1) Add canonical AuthzDenialReasonCode enum (and mapping helpers) in the shared authz package. (2) Standardize PermissionDenied error payload shape across gateway + control-plane HTTP handlers (no policy details; includes stable reason code + request id). (3) Add opt-in debug response headers behind BOTH a feature flag and an admin-only permission check, so authorized admins can see a high-level explanation in-flight without needing server logs. (4) Add metrics and logs to quantify deny reasons (for rollout dashboards) while keeping user-visible errors minimal. API/behavior details: - Default behavior (no debug): 403 with error code PERMISSION_DENIED and a structured denial_reason_code field (string) plus request_id; message remains generic ("permission denied"). - Debug behavior (admin-only): if request includes header X-Redwood-Debug-Authz: 1 AND caller has permission rbac.debug_authz AND rbac_debug_headers_enabled flag is on, then response includes headers: X-Redwood-Authz-Decision: deny|allow, X-Redwood-Authz-Reason: <reason_code>, X-Redwood-Authz-Required-Permission: <permission>, X-Redwood-Authz-Scope: <scope_type>:<scope_id>. We intentionally do not include the evaluated role names, bindings, group ids, or full policy graph. - For non-admins or when flag disabled: the request proceeds normally but debug headers are not included; we do not return a different error to avoid oracle behavior (we only log internally that a debug header was requested but suppressed). Denial reason codes included (initial set): - MISSING_PERMISSION (subject lacks required permission for action) - SCOPE_MISMATCH (permission exists but not for requested scope) - SUBJECT_UNRESOLVED (no subject / token mapping failed) - POLICY_VERSION_UNAVAILABLE (policy fetch failed / stale) - EVALUATION_TIMEOUT (authz evaluation exceeded budget) - BREAK_GLASS_REQUIRED (endpoint requires break-glass elevation) - ENDPOINT_UNANNOTATED (sensitive endpoint missing permission annotation; treated as deny in v2 mode) - FEATURE_FLAG_DISABLED (v2 enforcement / endpoint guard disabled; used internally for debug + metrics) Notes on info disclosure: Debug headers are only emitted for callers who already have rbac.debug_authz. This is designed for Org Admin/Security Admin flows in Console and for Support during guided troubleshooting with customer administrators. We also redact in Hosted multi-tenant environments by default (flag off), but enable in dedicated/private dogfood and pilot envs. Test coverage: unit tests for reason code mapping and redaction, gateway integration tests for header gating and consistent payload shape, and a control-plane handler test to validate ENDPOINT_UNANNOTATED denies when v2 enforcement is enabled. Follow-ups: Console “Why denied?” UX will consume denial_reason_code + request_id immediately; debug header view will be exposed only in admin troubleshooting pane (separate PR in console repo).
Marcus Lin (Security Eng): “I like the direction, but I’m worried about leaking required permissions/scope IDs to non-admins. Can we guarantee headers never show up unless the caller is explicitly privileged? Also please confirm we aren’t creating an oracle where requesting debug changes the response.” Kaitlyn Nguyen (author): “Yep. Debug headers require: (1) request header present, (2) rbac_debug_headers_enabled flag enabled, (3) allow decision by authz check for permission rbac.debug_authz. If any condition fails, we do not alter the response body/status; we only omit debug headers. Added test cases for ‘requested but suppressed’ paths.” Amara Diallo (Gateway): “Can we ensure header emission happens after authz evaluation and is consistent for streaming routes? Also standardize casing and prefix. Suggest we use X-Redwood-Authz-* only.” Kaitlyn: “Updated to only emit X-Redwood-Authz-* headers and moved header population into a shared helper called after evaluation. Streaming route path uses the same middleware; added regression coverage.” Chloe Martin (Console backend): “Console needs a stable denial_reason_code in the JSON body, not only headers. Please confirm that it’s always present on 403 in v2 mode and that codes are stable.” Kaitlyn: “Added denial_reason_code to the error body for PermissionDenied in both gateway and control-plane. Codes are treated as stable API surface (documented in internal doc; customer-facing doc later).” Felix Schneider (Console): “For ‘why denied?’ we also need request_id. Is that present for both gateway and service errors?” Kaitlyn: “Yes; both paths include request_id and we align with our existing request id propagation header. Added tests to ensure request_id is present.” Jordan Lee (Policy engine): “Reason code mapping: EVALUATION_TIMEOUT vs POLICY_VERSION_UNAVAILABLE. Make sure timeouts are not conflated with cache misses.” Kaitlyn: “Separated evaluation budget timeouts from policy fetch failures; the evaluator returns distinct error types now and mapping reflects that. Added unit tests for each mapping.” Requested changes were addressed (naming/prefix, oracle behavior, mapping correctness), then approvals were given.
RBAC v2 permission denied responses now include a stable denial_reason_code and request_id for troubleshooting.
Admin-only, feature-flagged debug headers can be enabled for guided “why denied?” investigations without exposing policy internals.
payload.title: RBAC v2: structured denial reason codes + optional authz debug header

Motivation: We observed several canary failures where transient infra flakiness or external API hiccups caused noisy metric signals and unnecessary rollbacks. This PR implements an automated 'replay-and-heal' step for blue/green promotions: when a canary batch trips metric failure thresholds, the platform will optionally (configurable per-rollout) pause, capture the failing canary traffic snapshot, and replay it deterministically against the previous stable variant and against an isolated replay harness to identify whether the failure is reproducible or transient. If the replay shows non-deterministic failures (i.e. stable variant succeeds or errors don't reproduce), the rollout resumes with an automated "heal" path that can: 1) clear transient cache/connection buckets, 2) retry canary at reduced weight, or 3) perform a targeted rollback with snapshot auditing. Key features: - Session-aware canaries: traffic sampling preserves session-affinity groups to avoid mixing stateful sessions across variants. - Deterministic replay harness: recorded requests, headers, and session keys are replayed in the same order with preserved timing window metadata to improve reproducibility. - Replay comparison policy: configurable similarity metrics (latency delta, error-class match, token-level divergence for LLM outputs) with pluggable thresholds. - Audit trail: all replays, snapshots and decisions are written to the rollout ledger and exposed in Console for post-mortem. - Minimal infra impact: replay jobs run on isolated pod pool with capped concurrency and token-cost budget. - Backwards compatibility: rollout manifests gain an optional 'replay_heal' block; existing rollouts default to off.

What this PR changes (summary): 1) rollout/engine: add ReplayHealExecutor with state machine states {RUN_CANARY, PAUSE_CAPTURE, RUN_REPLAY, ANALYZE, HEAL_OR_ROLLBACK, PROMOTE}. 2) rollout/api: extend rollout schema with 'replay_heal' stanza and new validation. 3) runtime: session-affinity sampler and deterministic request recorder. 4) console: new UI timeline entry and buttons for manual replay/force-heal. 5) tests: end-to-end canary replay flow tests and unit tests for comparison heuristics.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (Linear ENG-3412). - [x] Unit tests added for executor transitions and comparison logic. - [x] E2E smoke harness added (flaky on first run, rerun fixed). - [x] Console timeline elements implemented and behind feature flag. - [x] Documentation stub in docs/rollouts/replay-heal.md.

Commit summary is below; files changed and review thread follow.
Adds an automated replay-and-heal executor for blue/green rollouts. New safety gates: session-aware canary sampling, deterministic replay harness, and audit-backed rollback. Backwards compatible with existing rollout policies.
Evan Cho (Reviewer): Nice clear state machine. Two asks: (1) ensure we cap token budget per replay job and surface that in the manifest; (2) move deterministic recorder to runtime/recorder package to make it reusable by other features.
Priya Menon (Author): Addressed both in subsequent commits: added 'replay_budget_tokens' to manifest proto with validation and moved recorder implementation to runtime/recorder. Updated docs to call out limits.
Lena García (Reviewer): Tests look good. The e2e was flaky on first CI run — can you add retry logic to the harness and an assertion about audit entries being created?
Priya Menon (Author): Added retry for the harness and asserts for ledger entries in tests; pushed new commit. CI reran and passed.
Marcus Holt (Reviewer): Concern about auto-heal producing inconsistent user-visible outputs for LLM responses. Suggest we expose an opt-in policy per rollout for 'strict_output_match' which forces rollback on divergence. If not opted-in, heal path may proceed conservatively.
Priya Menon (Author): Added 'strict_output_match' boolean to replay_heal policy; default false to preserve existing behavior. Updated comparison thresholds and docs.
Lena García (Approver): Approving after tests green and policy flag added. (LGTM)
Evan Cho (Approver): Approved — code quality and docs reviewed. (Approved)

Context and motivation: production customers reported intermittent long-tail stream stalls when upstream routing briefly failed or when idle connections were reclaimed by intermediate NAT timeouts. Different SDKs had slightly divergent approaches: TS refreshed tokens on different timers, Go relied on TCP keepalive defaults, and Python had a separate health ping implementation. This PR harmonizes a cross-sdk connector heartbeat and a small ergonomic typed stream surface, and standardizes an adaptive, jittered backoff profile for streaming reconnects.

Goals (high level):
- Provide an opt-in connector heartbeat on long-lived stream connections to improve server-side detection and faster failover when routing changes occur.
- Standardize a jittered exponential backoff profile shared by all SDKs to reduce thundering herd reconnections and improve SLOs.
- Offer a simpler typed stream consumer surface that centralizes cancel/resume semantics across Python/TS/Go.
- Bump SDK versions and update CHANGELOGs.

What changed (summary of commits):
- Add connector/heartbeat logic to runtime client library (lib/connector/heartbeat.*).
- Implement jittered backoff profiles and configs (sdk/common/backoff_profiles.go / py / ts).
- Introduce StreamHandle / TypedStreamConsumer abstractions for each SDK to unify cancel, pause, resume, and health checks.
- Add opt-in feature flagging and env var knobs (REDWOOD_SDK_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS, REDWOOD_SDK_HEARTBEAT_TTL_MS).
- Docs: update quickstarts and examples across redwood-quickstarts and SDK docs with code samples.
- Tests: E2E streaming tests updated to cover heartbeat behavior and reconnection profiles.

Files touched (high level):
- sdk/common/backoff_profiles.go (new)
- sdk/ts/src/stream/typed_consumer.ts (new)
- sdk/py/redwood/stream/typed_consumer.py (new)
- runtime/connector/heartbeat.go (new)

- CHANGELOGs and package.json / setup.py bumps

Checklist:

- [x] E2E tests covering reconnect and idle reclaim scenarios

Review conversation (high level extract):
- Diego: "Can we make the heartbeat opt-in by default and expose both interval and ttl? Also request tests for NAT timeout scenario."
  - Aisha: "Yes — default is off. Added env var knobs and new e2e that simulates NAT timeout via idle timeouts in the harness."
- Lina: "TS linter flagged some types; please ensure API surface matches the other SDKs (cancel/resume naming)."
  - Aisha: "Adjusted names to TypedStreamConsumer.{cancel,resume,healthCheck} and added deprecation notes for old methods in the TS adapter."

Motivation: several incidents over the past quarter showed that binary drop/allow load-shedding causes unacceptable SLO regressions for high-priority customers and noisy neighbor effects for bursty inference workloads. This PR introduces a soft-degradation execution path that preserves latency SLOs for SLO-tagged traffic while allowing best-effort degradation for low-priority work. The approach combines per-route priority queues, headroom tokens, and a lightweight fallback executor that runs model-lite variants or cached responses when the main runtime is congested.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a per-request priority label that can be set via x-redwood-priority header or inferred from token quotas.
- Implements a priority queue scheduler in the serving proxy: high/normal/low queues with configurable time-to-serve thresholds.
- Introduces "headroom tokens" per GPU worker group to reserve capacity for SLO-critical requests; headroom is replenished on request completion and decays under sustained load.
- Adds a fallback execution policy: when a request exceeds its time-to-serve threshold, the scheduler routes it to a fallback executor which can: a) serve from prefix KV cache, b) call a quantized model shard with a reduced max_tokens, or c) return a guarded canned response indicating transient degraded fidelity.
- Provides operator toggles and rate limits: per-tenant priority caps, global fallback ratio, and emergency circuit-breaker to cut fallbacks entirely.
- Adds metrics and tracing spans for priority queue depth, headroom utilization, fallback invocations, and per-tenant degradation rates.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc linked (ENG-4873)
- [x] Unit tests for scheduler and fallback routing
- [x] Integration tests in perf-canary using synthetic overload patterns
- [x] Feature flag gating + rollout configuration in Console
- [x] RBAC update to allow ops to change priority caps

Risk and mitigation: The main risk is introducing scheduling jitter under mixed workloads. Mitigations included tight end-to-end latency SLO tests, conservative default configs, and a toggle to revert to legacy load-shedding instantly via emergency circuit-breaker.

Rollout plan: Gradual rollout behind feature flag: start with internal customers (10% of traffic), monitor headroom/utilization and fallback rate. If stable, increase to 50% then global. Automated SLO regression alerts will rollback the flag.

Related: SUP-1122 (support ticket reporting noisy neighbor latency spikes), ENG-4898 (observability dashboard for degradation metrics).
Arjun Patel: Nice clear design. Two nits: 1) prefer exponential decay for headroom tokens rather than linear to avoid oscillation; 2) add tenant-scoped unit tests.

Maya Chen: addressed both; switched to exponential decay and added tenant-scoped tests in f2a88be.
Sofia Martinez: Can we avoid exposing x-redwood-priority as an arbitrary header from public clients? Suggest map header values to vetted priorities in gateway.

Maya Chen: updated gateway mapping and added validation; only values (high, normal, low) accepted. SDK helper added to set safely.
Liam O'Connor: How will this interact with existing circuit breakers? If fallback starts returning canned responses, operator shouldn't see errors bubble up as 5xx.

Maya Chen: fallback responses are 200 with a response-metadata header x-redwood-degraded:true and a trace tag. Circuit-breaker thresholds unchanged; we added a new metric fallback_rate for alerting.
CI Bot: lint check failed on first run (gofmt).

Maya Chen: fixed formatting and force-pushed; CI passed on second run.
Squash and merge. Commit message summarizes feature, risk mitigations, and rollout plan. Feature gated behind runtime.feature.soft_degradation. Ops runbook added to docs/operations/soft-degradation.md.
Added soft-degradation priority queues and fallback executor to improve SLO preservation under congestion. Configurable headroom tokens and per-tenant priority caps. Backwards-compatible and feature-flag gated.
1) Default config is conservative; monitor metrics/redwood.degradation.fallback_rate and metrics/redwood.headroom.utilization. 2) To disable, flip runtime.feature.soft_degradation=false or set fallback_ratio=0. 3) Emergency circuit-breaker toggle available in Console -> Runtime -> Fallbacks.

Motivation: We observe that some tenants experience sudden cost spikes when defaults for batching and quant profiles are too aggressive for their traffic shape. This PR introduces a lightweight 'budget-nudge' controller that applies soft, tenant-scoped adjustments to batching/caching defaults and a complementary 'quantization safety limiter' that prevents risky profile rollouts when unit-econ signals degrade. The goal is automated, reversible nudges (not hard overrides) with observability and an easy opt-out path.

What this PR does (summary): 1) Adds budget_nudge_controller service that monitors per-tenant unit-econ signals (cost per token, recent latency percentiles, warm-start hit rates) and computes conservative adjustments to: - target_batch_size - prefix_cache_ttl - microbatch_warmup_steps 2) Introduces quant_safety_limiter which blocks automated quantized-profile rollouts when the simulated delta in unit-econ or the loss-estimate exceeds configured thresholds; exposes a dry-run mode that outputs estimated token-cost delta and estimated p95 latency impact. 3) Provides a defaults-suggestion CLI (rwictl econ suggest) that emits a JSON patch of suggested defaults per tenant for review. 4) Ships telemetry hooks and alerts: new metrics, dashboards, and a Lightstep tracing span naming convention for nudge decisions. 5) Includes integration tests (simulated traffic replay) and a follow-up migration job to persist soft-nudges to the tenant defaults table.

Design notes and safety: - Nudges are conservative by default: we only shift parameters slowly (max +10% batch size per 24h, TTL adjustments capped) and always attach a confidence score. - Nudges can be auto-rolled back if cost increases > configured window or if latency regressions cross threshold. - Quant safety limiter runs a fast simulation path (sampled tokens + cached KV warmstart model) and refuses rollout if regression risk > 2% or if loss-estimate increases beyond guard rails. - All decisions are logged and surfaced in Console under the "Budget Nudges" section.

Checklist: - [x] Budget_nudge_controller implementation (Go) - [x] Quant_safety_limiter implementation (Python worker) - [x] rwictl econ suggest CLI and dry-run output - [x] Telemetry: metrics, traces, dashboard seed JSON - [x] Integration tests with synthetic traffic harness - [x] Docs: console UX and opt-out guide - [x] Add feature flag (feature.budget_nudge) with default off for new tenants

Related: ENG-3045 (tenant cost stability), ENG-3187 (unit-econ telemetry), SUP-1123 (customer incident that motivated soft rollbacks). See design doc: internal.redwood/notes/budget-nudge-controller (link internal only).

Commits (summary): - initial budget-nudge controller scaffold, metrics and config schema - add heuristic engine and rate limiter for parameter deltas - implement quant-safety worker + simulator endpoint - rwictl econ suggest CLI + JSON patch writer - add integration tests and fixtures - docs and dashboard seeds - minor test fixes and CI flakiness fixes

Files changed (high-level): - src/econ/budget_nudge_controller/controller.go (core controller loop, decision engine) - src/econ/budget_nudge_controller/heuristics.go (heuristic rules for batch/cache nudges) - src/econ/quant_safety/worker.py (simulation and gating logic) - src/cli/rwictl/econ/suggest.go (CLI dry-run and patch exporter) - infra/telemetry/dashboards/budget_nudge_dashboard.json - tests/integration/econ/replay_nudge_test.py - migrations/2026_02_15_persist_nudges.sql - docs/console/budget_nudges.md - docs/operational/quant_safety.md - helm/values.yaml (feature flag defaults)

Small illustrative diff (controller loop sketch): "for tenant in enabledTenants { metrics := fetchUnitEcon(tenant); suggestion := heuristics.Suggest(metrics); if suggestion.Confidence > cfg.MinConfidence && withinRateLimit(tenant) { persistSoftNudge(tenant, suggestion); emitTrace(span, suggestion) } }"

Operational notes: - Feature gated under feature.budget_nudge; rollout plan: start with 10 pilot tenants, observe 48h windows, then progressive ramp to 30% of tenants. - Alerts created: BudgetNudge::RollbackNeeded, QuantSafety::BlockingRollout (SLO: <5 noisy alerts per week during ramp). - Migration persists soft nudges as JSON blob in tenant_defaults.nudges (reversible).

Testing: - Unit tests for heuristic thresholds and rollback logic included. - Integration replay harness simulates ten tenant shapes (burst, long-tail, interactive) and validates no >5% cost increase regressions under nudges. - Quant safety simulations include golden baseline and random seed to detect flakiness.

Backward compatibility and opt-out: Nudges are stored as separate metadata and do not replace explicit tenant overrides. Admins can disable auto-nudges per tenant from Console or via API.

payload.body:
Context: Dedicated fleets currently allocate capacity using coarse reservation windows (minutes-to-hours). For bursty tenants this leads to either over-provisioning or repeated emergency fallback to cheaper model variants. Motivation: Introduce a lightweight per-tenant micro-reservation primitive ("commitlet") plus a cross-pool negotiation agent that dynamically brokers transient throughput across sibling pools when headroom is available. Goals: 1) Improve tail throughput for short-lived bursts without enlarging long-term reservations. 2) Provide a predictable, auditable accounting unit for transient allocations. 3) Keep latency impact negligible and keep scheduler complexity bounded.

What this PR does: Adds a Commitlet Oracle service that issues timeboxed micro-commitments (commitlets) backed by an elastic safety credit. Commitlets are small (tokenized) allocations that attach to incoming requests and are consumable for a short window (30s–5min). A new Throttle Negotiator module coordinates soft transfers between pools: when one pool has spare tokens it publishes a transferable budget; neighboring pools can claim up to a configured fraction subject to SLO guardrails. The Negotiator prefers local warmlets and prefers cross-pool transfers only when local latency headroom is observed.

Implementation notes: - New service pkg/autoscale/commitlet_oracle.go with a minimal in-memory ledger + persistent tombstone store for idempotency. - Negotiator implemented under pkg/orchestrator/throttle_negotiator.go exposing a gRPC API used by pool controllers. - Control plane: small additions to control-plane API (v2) for commitlet issuance and redemption; backward compatibility preserved: pools without the feature will ignore the new fields. - Metrics & telemetry: commitlet_issue_count, commitlet_redeem_latency_ms, crosspool_transfer_attempts, negotiated_transfer_success_rate. - Config: feature gated behind operator flag --enable-commitlets and per-tenant quota caps.

Migration and rollout: Workload-safe by default: commitlets disabled on old clusters. Rolling upgrade plan in docs: install operator flag, enable commitlets in a single staging pool, run smoke + synthetic burst profile, gradually enable on production pools with progressive quota. A migration job will backfill any missing tombstones in the oracle store but is conservative (no retroactive accounting changes).

Testing and validation: Unit tests for ledger and negotiator state machine. Integration harness uses benchlab synthetic bursts (see tests/integration/commitlet_oracle_test.go) to validate that 95th/99th percentile throughput improves for burst traces while p99 latency impact is <5ms for the runway cases. A canary run on a subset of Dedicated fleet (us-west-2) showed a median cost delta of +0.8% with 18% fewer fallback events for targeted tenants.

Backward compat: No breaking API changes. Config default is off. Operators must opt in and set per-tenant caps to avoid unbounded spend.

Related: ENG-3419 (commitlet design), PM-504 (product requirements), incident SUP-1120 (context for emergency fallbacks).
6 commits: initial oracle and negotiator prototypes; add control-plane API v2 extensions; ledger persistence and tombstone backfill; metrics and dashboards; integration test harness; docs and operator flag. Each commit is focused and namespaced to relevant packages.
Jonah Kim (2025-08-14): Nice design. Two requests: add a fast-path for local warmlet claiming and clarify tombstone retention policy.
Maya Patel (2025-08-15): Added fast-path in throttle_negotiator.go and documented tombstone retention (14 days, configurable).
Lina Gómez (2025-08-20): Request change - need additional unit test for double-issue prevention when oracle restarts mid-window.
Maya Patel (2025-08-22): Added ledger restart test and a small refactor to make state writes idempotent. Updated tests/integration accordingly.
Arjun Desai (2025-08-28): Verified metrics and load characteristics in local canary; left a minor nits comment on variable naming (fixed).
Lina Gómez (2025-09-01): Approved after tests and docs updates.
Introduces Commitlet Oracle and Throttle Negotiator (opt-in). - New micro-reservation primitive (commitlet) for short-lived burst throughput. - Cross-pool soft transfers mediated by Throttle Negotiator. - Metrics: commitlet_issue_count, commitlet_redeem_latency_ms, crosspool_transfer_attempts. Operator action: enable with --enable-commitlets and set per-tenant caps.
Risk: misconfigured caps could allow transient spend increases or affect fairness. Mitigations: feature is off by default, per-tenant caps and global safety credit, audit logs captured for every transfer, canary rollout guidance provided in docs.
Unit + integration + benchlab. Integration showed improved burst throughput with limited cost impact in canary. Ran synthetic burst profiles from benchlab (config bspec/short_burst.yaml). No regression observed on existing autoscaler unit tests.
Microbenchmark: commitlet issuance adds ~0.6ms median to request control-plane path; negotiated transfers are asynchronous and do not affect request latency directly. End-to-end p99 latency impact observed <5ms in canary for typical request sizes.
If operators see a large number of 'transfer_rejected_quota' events, verify tenant cap configuration and global safety credit level. Tombstone backfill job may show transient I/O pressure; backfill runs at low priority. To emergency-disable: set --enable-commitlets=false and drain commitlet queues via the operator endpoint.
