Adds language-specific ergonomics for typed retry annotations: decorators in TS, context-managers in Python, functional options in Go. Backwards compatible; opt-in via new SDK config flag. Includes synced heartbeat helper for long-lived streaming sessions.
Motivation: customers have repeatedly asked for clearer, type-level retry intent that can be enforced by SDKs and surfaced in telemetry. This PR introduces a small, language-native surface that lets callers declare retry semantics close to callsites and gives runtime helpers (heartbeat + soft-fail policy) for long-lived streaming sessions to avoid transient auth flaps.

Summary of changes (single continuous description):
- Introduce a portable "RetryAnnotation" model and language-specific bindings: TypeScript uses a @retry({policy}) decorator for generated client methods; Python exposes RetryAnnotation as a typed dataclass and a contextmanager helper; Go exposes a functional option RetryAnnotation(...) and a typed RetryPolicy enum.
- Heartbeat wrapper: a lightweight session.Heartbeat helper that pins a background heartbeat + jittered backoff to keep token leases alive for streaming connections. Designed to be safe with existing heartbeat/keepalive primitives.
- Telemetry hooks: the SDKs will emit retry.annotation and retry.decision tags so backends can correlate policies to observed retries.
- Migration notes: default behavior unchanged; new API is opt-in behind `enableTypedRetryAnnotations` feature flag in SDK config; small samples added to each SDK's docs and examples.
- Tests: unit tests for annotation parsing and examples, integration tests exercising heartbeat with a mock auth proxy (flaky on windows, retried in CI).

Implementation detail summary: commits touch language-specific client generators (ts-client-gen, py-client-gen, go-client-gen), a small shared proto/json schema for the annotation payload, and adapters in each SDK runtime that translate the annotation into per-transport retry hooks.

Checklist: [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-5941) [x] automated unit tests [x] integration smoke tests [x] docs examples updated [x] telemetry events instrumented [x] feature-flag gate added

Notes:
- Kept primitives minimal; the goal is ergonomic opt-in that doesn't expand surface area drastically.
- This PR intentionally does not replace existing retry presets or the retry DSL; it layers a thin, typed hint on top.
- Performance impact: microbenchmarks show <0.5% added latency on cold-paths and negligible memory impact.
- Follow-ups: telemetry dashboards (ENG-6012) and an example migration guide for large codebases.
Alex Kim: Overall nice shape. Two asks: 1) can we make decorator metadata non-enumerable in TS so it doesn't leak into console logs? 2) add an example where annotation is overridden by per-route server-side hints.
Priya Desai (author): Good catches. Made decorator metadata non-enumerable and added override example in examples/typed_retry/README.md. Pushed an extra commit to address both.
Miguel Alvarez: The Python contextmanager API looks good but please add a short example showing use with nested backoff contexts.
Priya Desai (author): Added nested backoff example and a note in docs about precedence.
Sofia Ivanova: Flaky e2e on Windows — I saw the rerun pass. Please add an env guard around the flaky test and a TODO referencing infra ticket.
Priya Desai (author): Wrapped the flaky case with a platform skip and filed SUP-2101 to track reworking the mock auth proxy on Windows.
CI Bot: e2e failed on first run due to timing; rerun passed; final CI green.

Context: Large tenants with volatile traffic were incurring unnecessary token costs due to conservative prefill settings and broad quantization rollouts. This change introduces a Frugal Prefill Orchestrator (FPO) that combines short-horizon workload forecasts, tenant-level warmup lanes, and quantization guidance to reduce unit econ while preserving tail latency SLOs. Motivation: give operators a single place to reason about prefill budgets and quantized-serving rollouts, and provide a dry-run simulator so customers and SREs can validate cost/latency tradeoffs before enabling defaults. What this PR does: - Add a Prefill Orchestrator that computes per-tenant prefill budgets from recent traffic shapes and heatmap-derived cold-start probabilities. - Add a Quant Guidance API that recommends quant profiles (fp16/8bit/ptq) per model + tenant segment and can emit rollback signals when quality drift is detected. - Wire telemetry enrichment so the Console can show estimated per-tenant token savings and projected latency regressions when a quant profile or prefill policy is applied. - Add rwctl subcommand (rwctl prefill dry-run) to simulate a tenant rollout with synthetic request traces. - Add safety gates: conservative initial budget, canary rollout by tenant cohort, automatic fallback to full-precision if hallucination metrics or eval regressions cross thresholds. - Add unit and integration tests and a small load test harness used by CI. Checklist: [x] core orchestrator implementation; [x] telemetry + console enrichment; [x] rwctl CLI dry-run; [x] unit/integration tests; [x] docs draft. Related: Linear ENG-3245, ENG-3301. Risk: medium — changes affect routing and quant selection logic. Revert plan: the orchestrator can be disabled via a feature flag and a server-side kill switch that restores previous prefill defaults and quant profiles.
init: add prefill orchestrator core and interfaces
telemetry: enrich batch/prefill metrics and tags (tenant_id, forecast_bucket)
cli: introduce rwctl prefill dry-run and report generator
quant: add guidance heuristics and safe-fallback hooks
tests: add integration tests and CI load harness
Diego Ruiz (review): Please add a fallback path when prefill budget computation fails; observed a nil-pointer in staging if tenant metadata is missing.
Asha Menon (author): Added conservative fallback budget and hid nils behind an accessor; added unit test (TestBudgetFallback).
Priya Patel (review): Telemetry tags look good but we should avoid high-cardinality tag explosion for small tenants.
Asha Menon (author): Collapsed tenant dimension into tenant_cohort for low-volume tenants; added sampling to high-cardinality traces.
Marcus Li (review + approval): Verified dry-run outputs and simulated canary rollout; performance numbers look reasonable. Approving.
Introduce Frugal Prefill Orchestrator: per-tenant prefill budgets, quantization guidance, rwctl dry-run simulator, telemetry console enrichment; safe canary rollout and automatic fallbacks.
1) Merge feature behind FF; 2) Enable for internal tenants only and run rwctl dry-run for 24h; 3) Canary cohort (5% tenants) for 48h with automated rollback thresholds; 4) Gradually expand to 25/50/100% if metrics stable; 5) Monitor Console "prefill-savings" panel and regression alerts.
Feature flag: prefill.orchestrator.enabled. CLI: rwctl prefill dry-run --tenant=<id> --simulate-traffic=<profile>. If rollback triggers, set prefill.orchestrator.enabled=false and reapply previous policy via admin console.
Synthetic tenant sim: projected token reduction 22%-36% depending on cold-start rate; median tail latency increase <3ms for 8-bit profiles in canary runs.
Customers: introduces safe cost-optimization defaults that we will offer as a managed opt-in; initial availability limited to Dedicated and Hosted tiers with SLO guardrails.

Context: Customers deploying Private and Dedicated silhouettes asked for stronger guarantees around delegated KMS usage and auditable snapshots for regulatory review. This change introduces a KMS delegation verifier (server-side policy enforcer + offline verifier) that prevents transient operator credentials from being used to access keys outside an allowed tenancy/region envelope, and an immutable audit snapshotting pipeline that creates tamper-evident, redacted audit exports for compliance teams.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a runtime middleware that validates KMS request contexts against RBAC v2 delegation assertions and the tenant's declared region pin. Requests that fail verification are rejected with a 403 and a structured denial which includes the policy failure reason code.
- Introduces an offline verifier binary (cmd/kms-delegation-verifier) that can replay request traces and validate that historical delegations complied with policy; useful for audits and post-incident validation.
- Adds an immutable audit snapshotter service that batches and writes signed, chunked snapshots to an object store. Snapshots include a redaction layer (configurable by data classification) and a signature envelope (ed25519) plus a SHA256 ledger file for integrity checks. Customers can configure the destination S3/GCS bucket or opt into Redwood-managed archival.
- Adds RBAC v2 policy templates and a small policy compiler that synthesizes operator-scoped assertions into runtime checks; includes policy for cross-region delegation deny-by-default.
- Adds Linear/Jira links in alerts and a migration guide for customers using older delegation semantics.

Why this approach:
- Runtime protection prevents new delegations from being abused in real-time.
- Offline verifier supports compliance review and forensic replay without touching production servers.
- Snapshotter design intentionally keeps a signed ledger and redact rules outside of customer keys to allow regulatory review while preserving PII minimization.

Rollout plan: staged feature-flag rollout:
1) Dry-run: runtime middleware runs in audit mode only for 48 hours (collects denials but does not enforce).
2) Canary (10%): enforce denies for non-critical tenants.
3) Full: enforce denies for all tenants after 7 days with monitoring and rollback playbook.

Migration notes and config flags:
- New flags: --kms-delegation-enforce=(off|audit|enforce), --audit-snapshot-target=(redwood|customer-bucket), --snapshot-retention-days.
- Policy templates added under deploy/policies/rbacv2/kms_delegation_templates.yaml.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests added for verifier logic and redaction rules.
- Integration tests added that exercise cross-region KMS attempts (mocked KMS providers).
- End-to-end snapshot integrity test verifies signature + ledger chain.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: false positives for complex delegations (mitigated by dry-run and policy compiler warnings).
- Risk: snapshot storage costs (mitigated via retention flags and customer-managed buckets).

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc (Linear ENG-1942) linked and reviewed
- [x] Unit/integration tests added
- [x] Policy templates included
- [x] Monitoring dashboards draft (observability)
- [x] Rollback playbook authored

Related: SUP-887 (support case where a delegated operator key was used from an unexpected region).
Evan Morales (2026-01-31): Please split the middleware validation path so high-latency verification (policy compiler lookups) does not block fast-path KVS ops. Also add metrics for validation latency.
Priya Natarajan (2026-01-31): Split into fast-path (cached assertion lookup) + background policy refresh implemented; added metrics `verifier.latency_ms` and cache hit ratio.
Jonah Li (2026-02-01): The offline verifier binary is great. Can we add an option to produce a CSV report of failures for legal teams?
Priya Natarajan (2026-02-01): Added --export-csv flag and documentation in the migration guide.
Marisol Ruiz (2026-02-02): LGTM after CI re-run. One minor nit about error codes; suggest adding a mapping table to docs.
Marisol Ruiz (2026-02-02): Approved
Security: Add KMS delegation verifier to enforce tenant/region-bound key usage; Compliance: Immutable audit snapshotting with redaction and signed ledger; Ops: New flags for dry-run and snapshot retention.
Default rollout is audit-mode. Operators must ensure the snapshot bucket has write permissions and key rotation for signing keys is coordinated with Security. See docs/ops/kms-delegation-migration.md for playbook.

Summary: This PR adds the initial implementation of the Region Health Service (RHS): a small control-plane service that aggregates multiple signal streams into a single cached health view per region, per product surface (Hosted API vs Dedicated), and per routing "route class" (chat/generate/embeddings). This is a foundational building block for the Regional Failover Automation Upgrade; routing and the failover controller will consume RHS rather than each team independently interpreting raw metrics. Scope in this PR is intentionally limited to: (1) ingest + aggregate a minimal set of signals, (2) expose a stable internal API, (3) ship tests and canned fixtures, and (4) add integration stubs for routing/policy evaluation behind a feature flag. Motivation / context: Today our failover decisioning pulls from several places (burn alerts, reachability probes, ad-hoc dashboards) and the interpretation differs across Hosted vs Dedicated paths. During staging rehearsals we’ve also seen missing/late signals cause inconsistent decisions or controller crashes. RHS provides a single, defensive, typed interface with explicit freshness requirements and a "degraded vs unknown" distinction. This PR is a prerequisite for deterministic trigger hierarchy evaluation (ADR-042) and for building safe automation + rollback guardrails (ADR-043). Design highlights: Aggregation model: RHS evaluates region health as a set of per-signal observations + a computed status. Status is one of {HEALTHY, DEGRADED, UNHEALTHY, UNKNOWN}. UNKNOWN is reserved for cases where we cannot produce a trustworthy view (e.g., missing reachability feed + stale metrics), and is intended to be treated as "do not auto-failover" by the controller unless corroborated elsewhere. Signals included in this first cut: (a) reachability probe status from perf-canary (cross-region HTTP + TCP probe), (b) service-level 5xx burn (1m/5m rolling) from the SLO metrics pipeline, (c) tail latency burn (p95/p99 vs SLO target) from the same pipeline, (d) capacity headroom placeholder (stubbed interface; returns UNKNOWN until ENG-2414 lands), (e) control-plane dependency check (basic: routing config store + policy engine RPC health). Freshness + caching: RHS caches computed health views for 5s with jitter (±20%) to avoid stampedes during partial outages. Each signal includes last_updated_at and a max_age budget; if any required signal exceeds its max_age the final status becomes UNKNOWN (unless an authoritative reachability failure is present). API (internal): GET /internal/v1/region-health?surface=hosted|dedicated&region=us-east&route_class=chat returns the computed health, per-signal observations, and a "reason_summary" string intended for audit logs. GET /internal/v1/region-health/summary?surface=hosted returns all regions for that surface in one response to support controller loops. Note: This is internal-only (mTLS + service auth); no external customer endpoints. Observability: Exposes rhs_cache_hit_total, rhs_compute_latency_ms, rhs_signal_staleness_seconds{signal=...}, rhs_region_status{surface,region,route_class,status}. Logging is structured with request_id and evaluation_id so routing/controller can reference exact computations in their own audit events later. Integration stubs: Adds a RegionHealthClient in routing/policy-engine with a disabled-by-default path (feature flag: routing.region_health.enabled=false). When enabled, routing fetches RHS summary on a background ticker and stores it in memory for policy evaluation predicates (currently predicate returns "unknown" unless explicitly enabled; no routing decisions change in production as part of this PR). Tests: Unit tests: coverage for status computation, freshness handling, and precedence rules (reachability failure overrides stale error metrics; stale required signals yield UNKNOWN). Integration tests: spins up RHS with fake signal providers (fixtures) and asserts the API output schema + caching behavior. Contract-ish test: small routing-side test that ensures the client handles partial/missing fields and timeouts without crashing (returns UNKNOWN). Security / safety: RHS has explicit timeouts for each upstream signal provider and fails closed to UNKNOWN instead of inferring HEALTHY from missing data. Rate limiting: internal per-caller QPS limit (configurable) to prevent controller/routing thundering herd. AuthZ: restricted to allowlisted service identities (routing, failover-controller, incident-bot in later PR). Rollout plan: Land RHS as a standalone service in staging first; routing integration is present but disabled. Follow-ups: (1) ENG-2414 integrate real capacity headroom signal provider; (2) ENG-2417 wire reachability probes as first-class ingestion rather than polling; (3) PR to add cache TTL tuning based on observed load (likely 2s-10s); (4) formalize schema versioning once controller consumes it; (5) add dashboard panels for rhs_region_status and staleness. Commits (squash summary): 1) region-health-service: skeleton service + config wiring; 2) rhs: signal provider interfaces + aggregation engine; 3) rhs: internal HTTP API handlers + auth; 4) routing: add RegionHealthClient (flagged) + predicate stub; 5) tests: fixtures + integration harness; 6) obs: metrics + structured logs; 7) docs: internal README + runbook stub. Changed areas (high-level): services/region-health-service/* (new) for service code and deployment manifests; pkg/regionhealth/* for shared types; routing/policy-engine/* for client + predicate stub (flagged); deploy/helm/* adds chart and default values for staging; tests/integration/region-health-service/* adds fixture-based tests. Reviewer discussion (highlights): Ravi Menon: asked for a hard stance on UNKNOWN semantics and how routing should treat it. Resolution: added explicit docstring and a unit test that UNKNOWN does not imply healthy; routing predicate now requires explicit enablement + non-UNKNOWN to be used. Allison Grant: flagged metric label cardinality risk if we include tenant identifiers. Resolution: no tenant dimensions added; surface/region/route_class only, plus a note in README for future additions. Victor Alvarez: requested clarity on reachability probe sources and how to distinguish provider DNS issues vs regional impairment. Resolution: added probe_source and probe_type fields internally (not labels) and improved reason_summary string to include "reachability:tcp_fail" vs "reachability:http_5xx". Jordan Lee: asked for deterministic ordering of reasons to support audit logs. Resolution: reason_summary now uses a stable ordering and includes the evaluation_id. CI: build/test/lint all green after rerunning integration tests once (flaky due to clock mocking; fixed by using monotonic test clock). Checks: //ci/redwood:unit-tests PASS, //ci/redwood:integration-tests PASS, //ci/redwood:lint PASS, //ci/redwood:container-build PASS. Merge: Squash merged into main after approvals from routing + observability + network.
Internal-only: introduces Region Health Service used by failover controller/routing (behind flags). No customer-visible API changes.

Context: Ops and SREs are spending a lot of time triaging transient token/latency spikes that are noisy (short-lived) and not indicative of systemic regressions. This PR introduces a lightweight per-invocation 'Invocation Stability Index' (ISI) and a downstream 'Noise Attenuation Adapter' for alert routing to reduce noisy alerts while preserving SLO-sensitive signals. Motivation: provide a single derived signal that captures dispersion in token latency, retry/early-termination rate, and KV-cache miss jitter so that alerting rules can differentiate stable regressions from ephemeral noise. Design summary: - Runtime: compute ISI (0-100) per invocation as a normalized aggregation of: latency variance across token phases, token-count jitter vs baseline, retry/early-termination events, and kv-cache-miss ratio. Implementation emits a span tag stability.score and a prometheus histogram redwood_invocation_stability_bucket with labels {route, model, tenant, region}. Cardinality controls: we explicitly avoid per-invocation IDs on metrics and only tag traces with invocation_id for post-hoc joins. - Alerting adapter: a middleware in alertd that consults short-term ISI rollups and applies dynamic suppression rules: if stability.avg_1m < 30 and spike duration < 2m, suppress non-critical alerts and route to 'quiet' channel for 10m; critical SLO alerts still bypass the adapter. The adapter records decisions in telemetry (noise_attenuator.decision{action=suppress|allow}). - Dashboards/UI: added Stability Cohorts panel (percent of invocations by ISI bucket), Stability Heatmap (route x time), and Noise Attenuation Actions table (recent suppressions, reason, affected routes). A compact StabilityBadge component shows in the Console invocation view. - Rollout: gated behind feature-flag rtev.stability_index. Canary plan: 1% (staging) -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 7 days with SLO guardrails. - Performance: measured overhead in synthetic load tests: ~0.4ms median added p95 latency for runtime tagging and ~2% CPU for collectors under 50k invocations/s; metric cardinality kept low. - Tests: unit tests for scoring logic, property tests for normalization boundary cases, integration e2e that replays synthetic noisy spikes and validates suppression behavior; added load test scenario. - Docs: operational runbook explaining how to tune ISI thresholds and how to disable suppression per-tenant. Checklist: [x] Implementation of ISI in runtime and tracer enrichment | [x] Prometheus metrics and rollups | [x] Noise Attenuation Adapter and policy YAML | [x] Console panels and StabilityBadge | [x] Unit / integration / load tests | [x] Docs and runbook | [x] Feature flag and canary rollout plan Commit summary: (see commits field). Changed files (high-level): runtime/metrics (stability index), tracing (span enrichment), observability pipeline (adapter), dashboards and console components, docs, featureflag config. See changed_files list for specifics. Why unique: focuses on signal composition (stability index) + policy adapter to suppress alert noise rather than only adding more telemetry.
Lucas Chen: Nice approach. Please ensure metric cardinality is bounded — drop invocation_id and avoid high-cardinality labels.
Maya Patel (author): Reworked metrics to only include {route,model,tenant,region}; retained invocation_id only on spans for trace joins.
Priya Natarajan: Can we reduce the suppression window to 2m max? Also suggest exponential backoff for repeated suppressions on the same route.

Introduces an Invocation Stability Index (ISI) and a Noise Attenuation Adapter to reduce alert noise from transient token/latency spikes. Highlights: new stability metrics and dashboard, an alerting adapter that applies dynamic suppressions, and an operational runbook for tuning. Rollout behind feature flag rtev.stability_index.

If suppression is causing missed regressions, set policy 'allow_all' and file ENG-1921 for follow-up. Policy files live in observability/adapter and are tenant-overridable.

1) Rollout canary per plan; 2) Schedule 24h alert reduction review with SRE; 3) Add per-tenant opt-out flag and document in onboarding; 4) Sweep dashboards for customers on Dedicated/Private to ensure visibility.
This PR couples a derived score with an active adapter that mutates alert routing decisions; unlike previous work that only added telemetry, this change actively reduces noise by making suppression decisions based on a composite signal.

Introduce opaque session propagation token to preserve session affinity across stream reconnects; add non-intrusive StreamTap adapter for telemetry and debugging without changing backpressure semantics; SDK surface parity and minor version bumps.
Context: Customers reported resumed streaming sessions lost context on reconnect and telemetry hooks were invasive for production use. This PR introduces an opaque session token propagation mechanism across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs and a StreamTap adapter that lets observability and local debugging tools inspect stream events without altering timing or backpressure. Motivation: Provide a small, low-risk surface that solves two operational problems: 1) make reconnect/resume deterministic for applications using session affinity and 2) enable safe passive telemetry for streaming workloads. Summary of changes: Added opaque session header (X-Redwood-Session) and a lightweight session encoder/decoder; implemented session-preserve logic in the streaming reconnect shim; added StreamTap adapter (pluggable middleware) that exposes a read-only stream of events for observers; harmonized retry presets so resume attempts are marked idempotent to avoid double-exec semantics; bump SDK versions: python->1.9.0, typescript->2.4.3, go->v1.6.1; included unit and e2e streaming tests and an integration test that simulates reconnect sequences and in-flight KV cache reuse. Checklist: - add session header and helpers across SDKs; - add StreamTap adapter and examples; - ensure backpressure invariants hold under adapter; - update SDK docs and changelogs; - add e2e harness and flaky test allowances. Commits: ["c1a7f2a: introduce opaque session header and encoder/decoder","d4b8e9f: stream reconnect shim: preserve session token and KV cache hinting","f6c12b3: typescript SDK: streamTap adapter + examples","a8e4d01: python SDK: add tap adapter + tests","b2f7c8d: go SDK: stream tap & session propagation implementation","e9a0d5e: integration tests and e2e harness for reconnect flows","ff12aa0: update changelogs and bump version numbers"]. Changed areas: ["sdk/python/redwood/streaming.py","sdk/typescript/src/stream/streamTap.ts","sdk/go/stream/adapter/tap.go","sdk/common/session/session.go","docs/sdk/streaming.md","tests/e2e/stream_reconnect_sim.py","examples/stream-tap/README.md","changelogs/python.md","changelogs/typescript.md","changelogs/go.md","ci/e2e-stream-harness.yml"]. Patch snippets (illustrative): ["// streamTap: observe events without modifying data or timing; read-only interface","const tap = new StreamTap(observer => { observer.on('chunk', c => log(c)); });","// server-side: accept X-Redwood-Session header and route to affinity pool","sessionToken := req.Header.Get(\"X-Redwood-Session\") // opaque string"]. Review thread summary: "Initial review requested smaller surface for Go impl. Diego called out potential race on session cache invalidation and asked for a stronger test that simulates concurrent reconnects; addressed by adding a mutex around cache promotion and a dedicated concurrent_reconnect test; Samir requested ergonomics tweaks for TypeScript (StreamTap factory signature) which were applied; Lena verified python tests and asked for doc examples demonstrating telemetry use-cases; author responded with examples and a short video capture for reviewers. One CI flake on integration tests caused a rerun; fixed a timing race in the e2e harness and re-ran. Merge: squash merge after final signoff. Merge method: squash. Motivation/risks: The changes are additive and guarded behind a feature flag in the SDKs (enabled by default for 1.9.0/2.4.3/v1.6.1). Risk surface: small risk for customers that proxy headers are stripped by intermediate infra; added robust fallback to a generated ephemeral session. Rollout plan: gradually enable GA by flipping the feature flag for Hosted API customers in the next 2 weeks; monitor metrics (session-resume-rate, duplicate-event-rate, latency p95) via new dashboards. Post-merge tasks: create a compatibility note for on-prem/private installers (redwood-private-installer), land a small patch to server routing to accept the opaque token in legacy gateways, coordinate marketing changelog entry, and file a follow-up to add optional HMAC signing (ENG-21110). Related items: ENG-20934 (session affinity work), PM-4101 (obs requirements), SUP-782 (customer incident).

Summary: Introduce a lightweight 'mini-bisect' canary mode and traffic snapshotting to speed up diagnosis and automate rollback for warmstart regressions. Motivation: We observed slow, manual bisect workflows when a canary exhibits intermittent regressions related to cache warmstart/kv-cache priming. This PR implements a controller pattern that runs short-window bisect-style probes, records traffic snapshots (input distribution, sequence-length buckets, metadata tags), and evaluates a compact set of metric comparisons to decide an automatic rollback. Design: 1) controller: new MiniBisectController that coordinates N short probe waves (default 3), each wave splits a small, orthogonal slice of traffic to the candidate model. 2) traffic snapshots: proto-compact JSON blobs capturing token-length histograms, request metadata tags, and sampled request hashes; snapshots are stored in the rollout namespace and retained for 48h. 3) warmstart oracle: compares per-wave latency p95, kv-cache hit-rate estimate, and loss-proxy signal (existing quality metrics) against baseline with configurable thresholds and a decay-weighted scoring; if oracle score crosses rollback threshold, controller triggers an immediate revert to previous model and emits forensic snapshot bundle to the audit log. 4) Autoscaling safety: the controller coordinates with scheduler to throttle probe concurrency to avoid autoscaler thrash. 5) Opt-in config: rollout policy field 'mini_bisect: {enabled:true, waves:3, snapshot_ttl:48h}' and feature-flag rollout.mini_bisect.enable. Backwards compatibility: defaults disabled; no surface change to SDKs. Testing: unit tests for snapshot serialization + controller simulator harness; e2e in perf-canary lab using synthetic traffic. Rollout plan: behind feature flag, staged on staging, then limited production on internal customers for 2 weeks. See linked Linear tasks ENG-4812 ENG-4890 for follow-ups.
Adds a mini-bisect canary controller that snapshots traffic distributions and supports automatic rollback if warmstart regressions are detected. Opt-in via rollout policy flag. No changes to public API surface unless feature flag enabled.
~410 additions across controller, snapshot, and tests; key changes add snapshot storage and scoring logic. Small change to scheduler to honor per-rollout probe budget.
Aisha: Nice approach — can we keep snapshots size-bounded? Please add a deterministic truncation policy.
Author reply: Added snapshot TTL and size cap (1MB) with streaming compression; updated serializer.
Daniel: How do we avoid cascading rollbacks if baseline is noisy? Suggest decay-weighted scoring and min-probe floor.
Author reply: Implemented decay-weight, min_probes floor = 2 and conservative default thresholds; documented rationale.
María: Add explicit audit fields for forensics (request_sample_ids + snapshot_version). Also ensure RBAC prevents snapshot export.
Author reply: Added export_safe flag and RBAC check in audit_writer; tests added.
CI bot: unit tests failed on first run (race in scheduler throttle). Author pushed fix and re-ran CI.
Daniel: approved after CI green and one nit fixed on log verbosity.

Context: During a recent multi-region incident we observed bursty latency tails that caused aggressive load-shedding to kick in too early for small cohorts. This PR introduces a lightweight "latency cushion" admission policy plus a regional fallback orchestrator that coordinates staged drains and accelerated KV-preserve handoffs across candidate regions. Goal: reduce unnecessary tenant evictions and avoid cascading regional failovers while preserving SLOs under transient latency tail events. This change is targeted at the serving runtime and the control plane routing logic; it is backward-compatible and feature-flagged.
Latency cushion: per-tenant adaptive cushion computed from observed p95/p99 baseline and recent tail excursions. Admission policy categorizes incoming requests as immediate/admit-with-cushion/evict. 'Admit-with-cushion' allows a short additional wait window (configurable, default 150ms) where we accept the request but mark it as cushion-tracked; the request participates in KV-preserve fastpath and receives priority in KV cache reuse. Cushion windows are bounded and decay per-tenant to avoid long-lived exemptions. Regional fallback orchestrator: a control-plane coordinator that, when triggered by sustained regional KV pressure or probe failures, sequences candidate failover steps: mark-sticky-quiet -> staged drain -> prefetch target slot -> expedited KV-snapshot -> atomic switch. Orchestrator integrates with existing rollout and canary logic; it includes a probe protocol with exponential backoff and jitter. Feature flags: Safe rollout behind flags: runtime.latency_cushion.enabled and routing.fallback_orchestrator.v1.
Unit tests: 42 new cases covering cushion state machine, decay, and eviction edge cases. Integration: added a synthetic burst scenario to perf-canary harness simulating p99 spikes across 50 tenants to validate no regression in median latency and SLO preservation. Load tests: 1h soak in benchmark-lab showed 6-8% reduction in tenant evictions during transient tails with <1% change in p50/p90. Telemetry: new metrics registered: runtime.latency_cushion.admits, runtime.latency_cushion.evictions_saved, orchestrator.step_durations, orchestrator.probe_failures. Added tags for tenant_id and region to facilitate incident triage.
Rollback plan: feature flags allow immediate disable. Emergency revert commit included (revert feature flag initialization and orchestrator registration). Runbook: SRE runbook updated with steps to globally disable runtime.latency_cushion.enabled and routing.fallback_orchestrator.v1 via controlplane toggle + restart-less config push. If observing increased p99 or KV pressure, revert orchestrator and disable cushion.
Arun Gupta: asked for clearer bounds on cushion decay and vector attack surface (malicious clients sustaining cushion). Response (Lena): added per-tenant credit tank with max tokens and observable depletion metric; updated tests. Morgan Lee: requested telemetry to separate 'saved eviction' events from 'soft-admit' timeouts — implemented in commit 3. Tara Singh (SRE): requested an emergency disable path and explicit knob in the health dashboard; added flag + dashboard patch. Final: approvals from Arun and Tara after a CI rerun. Morgan gave LGTM for telemetry clarity.
CI pipeline: lint -> unit tests -> integration (perf-canary emulator) -> e2e smoke. First run: unit failure (race in cushion state machine) detected; fixed by atomic state update and retry backoff. Second run: all checks green. Perf-canary reported expected eviction reduction; nightly stability run scheduled.
Merged via squash on 2026-03-05 by Lena Chen after approvals. Merge notes: enabled feature flags default to off; rollout schedule: staged enable for non-production regions for 48h, then progressive enable in canary tenants, and finally global opt-in. Added release note entry for ops and SDK teams.
- Introduced 'latency cushion' admission policy to reduce premature tenant evictions during transient tail spikes (feature-flagged).
- Added Regional Fallback Orchestrator to coordinate staged drains with KV-preserve handoff (feature-flagged).
- New telemetry: runtime.latency_cushion.admits, runtime.latency_cushion.evictions_saved, orchestrator.step_durations.
- Rollout is gated via runtime.latency_cushion.enabled and routing.fallback_orchestrator.v1 flags. Ops: follow updated runbook if enabling.
Coordinate with Dedicated on a canary window because the orchestrator changes routing semantics during staged drains. Notify customer-facing incident team and update support playbooks with new flag names.

Context: As part of the Regional Failover Automation Upgrade (ENG-2411), we need a safe, deterministic way to drain Dedicated GPU pools during regional impairment and controlled failovers. Today, draining is a manual sequence across fleet tooling + routing toggles, which is slow and error-prone during an incident. This PR adds an internal endpoint and workflow to request/observe a drain, with explicit safety gates and auditability.

What’s in this PR: 1) New internal control-plane endpoint: POST /internal/dedicated/pools/{pool_id}/drain (and GET /internal/dedicated/pools/{pool_id}/drain/{drain_id}) that initiates a drain request and returns a drain_id for tracking. Requests are idempotent via Idempotency-Key and constrained by RBAC (internal operator + automation controller only). 2) Drain workflow/state machine: QUEUED -> VALIDATING -> DRAINING -> WAITING_FOR_ZERO -> COMPLETE (or FAILED/CANCELED). The controller will: (a) validate pool eligibility (tier, region, model family constraints), (b) coordinate with routing to stop new allocations to the pool, (c) gradually reduce schedulable capacity (rate-limited, configurable), (d) wait for active sessions/in-flight requests to fall below thresholds, and (e) mark drain complete only after a stable window. 3) Safety gates: max concurrent drains per region, max drain rate, minimum regional headroom requirement (signals from fleet capacity service), and explicit “do not drain” for pools with pinned single-region residency. For production, execution is behind the feature flag dedicated.drain_endpoint.enabled and also supports dry-run mode via ?mode=dry_run to compute the plan + validations without mutating state. 4) Observability: new metrics dedicated_drain_requests_total, dedicated_drain_state (gauge by state), dedicated_drain_progress (0-1), dedicated_pool_active_sessions, and structured audit events emitted on request/transition/complete/fail (used by incident-bot summaries and game day timelines).

Why this approach: Drain is treated as a first-class operation with an auditable state machine, rather than a pile of one-off scripts. The endpoint is intentionally internal-only and designed for integration with the failover controller; on-call can also invoke it during manual mitigation with clear rollback/cancel behavior.

Rollout plan: 1) Staging: enable flag globally; run soak tests + simulated drains during rehearsals. 2) Production: enable for a small allowlist of test tenants/pools used in controlled failovers; require approval hooks at the controller layer (separate PR). 3) Expand to more Dedicated tiers after game day success criteria are met.

Risks + mitigations: Main risk is draining too aggressively and causing customer-visible errors. Mitigations: validation gates require headroom, rate limits on capacity reduction, and routing coordination to stop new placements first. The workflow can be canceled (POST .../cancel) which halts further drain steps and restores target schedulable capacity to the last known good value.

Testing: Unit tests cover state transitions, idempotency, and validation logic; integration tests run against a fake fleet backend; e2e staging test demonstrates drain completes with active sessions decreasing to zero. Added docs in code comments for on-call usage; runbook updates tracked in ENG-2423.

Follow-ups (not in this PR): wiring this into automated regional failover workflows (controller calls drain endpoint), dashboards panel additions, and tightening residency policy validation based on enterprise contracts (tracked separately).
- Internal-only API to request a Dedicated pool drain (idempotent, audited)
- New drain state machine with safety gates + progress metrics
- Runbook hooks and structured audit events for on-call visibility

Motivation: Small but frequent multi-stream prefill workloads show long tail latency when prefill KV commit/flush serializes decode start for a subset of shards. This PR introduces a lightweight 'decoder bridge' microkernel and an adaptive token synchronizer that allow decode work to start opportunistically while guaranteeing KV coherence; additionally we reorder background KV flush/writeback to prioritize in-flight slices to reduce stall probability. Design summary: 1) decoder_bridge microkernel exposes a narrow ABI that accepts partial prefill completion tokens and a safe continuation point for decode kernels so that decode can start for slices whose KV is ready while the rest of the prefill continues in background; 2) token_synchronizer tracks per-request slice readiness and uses an adaptive threshold (configurable percentile + min-slices) to decide early decode handoff; 3) kv_flush_reorderer introduces a prioritized writeback queue that promotes writes for slices with active decode handoffs and demotes cold writebacks; 4) integration with the scheduler: small change to Scheduler::sliceApply to publish readiness events to the synchronizer; 5) safety: full correctness ensured by a KV pin + read-after-write validation step in the bridge kernel before final decode commit. Checklist: implementation and unit tests implemented; perf harness and synthetic multi-stream tests added; runtime flags for toggling feature and tuning thresholds; documentation update and migration notes added. Testing: local microbenchmarks across 4 GPU shapes, cluster perf runs on staging with mixed small/large request mixes; canary rollout planned. Benchmarks: on mixed-small workload (mean 6 tokens prefill, 120 concurrent streams) P95 latency reduced ~12% and 99th reduced ~18% compared to baseline; end-to-end token cost unchanged within noise. Backward compatibility: feature gated and off by default; non-breaking by default. Rollback plan: revert feature flag or disable via console; migration safe because no on-disk state changes. Related work: ENG-1442 (prefill scheduling work), PRs: pr-82763, pr-89901 for context. Merge method: squash. Notes: avoided major changes to KV store internals; kept kernel ABI minimal to ease backporting to release branches.
Ethan Cole (2026-02-13): Can we simplify the public API on decoder_bridge.h to reduce maintenance surface? Suggest combining two callbacks into a single enum-driven callback.
Nina Patel (2026-02-14): replied: refactored to single callback and kept the old API internal for backward compat; added unit tests covering both paths.
Ravi Singh (2026-02-16): Observed perf regression on large-batch-only workloads in first run; noted configuration should be gated by config thresholds. Nina: adjusted adaptive threshold logic and added a guard to bypass synchronizer for >N tokens per slice.
Marta Li (2026-02-18): Approved after second perf run; flagged a small doc nit which was fixed.
CI Bot (2026-02-17): perf-bench flaky on first try; rerun passed and posted artifacts.
MergeBot (2026-02-19): merge/squash complete, merge commit sha: e7b9a1c3d4f2
Introduce decoder bridge and adaptive token synchronizer to reduce prefill tail latency. Feature gated and off by default. Gains: up to 12% P95 latency reduction on small multi-stream workloads. Tuning knobs: prefill_token_sync_percentile, prefill_token_sync_min_slices.
payload.title: Decoder bridge: adaptive token synchronizer and KV flush reorder to reduce prefill tail latency

Motivation: Add a consent-driven KMS provisioning path that ties tenant-level consent events to ephemeral CMK leases and RBAC v2 temporal grants. This addresses compliance requests to ensure cryptographic keys used for customer workloads are provisioned only after an auditable consent event and that operator/service privileges to those keys are timebounded and revocable.

What this PR does: Implements a small service (kms-provisioner) that receives signed consent assertions, performs lightweight policy checks, mints ephemeral CMK grants via the KMS adapter, records a provenance envelope to the audit log, and issues RBAC v2 temporal grants to operator principals scoped to the key for the lease duration. The design favors clear auditability, conservative defaults (deny until consent), and operator observability.

Key behaviors and guarantees: - Consent assertions must be signed by an allowed consent issuer (tenant or delegated controller) and include a nonce and expiry. - Ephemeral CMK leases default to 1 hour and are configurable per-tenant policy. - RBAC temporal grants are encoded as role bindings with start/expiry timestamps and an auditable decision id. - All provisioning actions write an immutable audit envelope to the audit-writer with provenance headers and a hash of the consent assertion for dedupe. - Automatic revocation: if lease expires or consent is revoked, the provisioner triggers a revoke flow that removes RBAC temporal grants and requests KMS to revoke access.

Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.consent_kms_provisioner (default off). Gradual rollout to internal tenants for 2 weeks, then to early enterprise customers with a migration runbook. We included a dry-run mode that simulates KMS calls and writes audit envelopes marked as simulated.

Testing and validation: unit tests for policy engine, integ tests with local KMS emulator, e2e exercise in benchmark-lab with a tenant fixture. CI includes static analysis, contract tests for the RBAC policy writer, and an audit-log ingestion smoke test.

Related work: Linear ENG-1734 (consent + key lifecycle), ENG-1810 (rbac temporal grants), and acks to previous residency/kms PRs for audit envelope formats.

Checklist: - [x] Service scaffolding and configs - [x] Policy engine + validation - [x] KMS adapter integration with lease+revoke - [x] RBAC v2 temporal grant writer - [x] Audit envelope producer - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Migration/runbook draft (docs/consent_kms_migration.md)

Notes: This change introduces no global default CMK creation; provisioning is tenant-triggered. The provisioner runs as a low-privilege operator and obtains a short-lived operator lease (separate from the tenant CMK lease) when performing KMS operations to reduce long-lived credentials exposure.
Reviewers requested additional hardening around replay protection, observability for consent failures, and robust revoke semantics. The author implemented nonce-store, added metrics + alerts, and improved revoke retry/compensation logic. Staging smoke validated the happy path and simulated revocations.
Arjun Patel: Please clarify threat model for consent issuer compromise — can an attacker replay signed assertions? Consider enforcing one-time nonces and binding to request origin. (requested changes)
Maya Chen: Added nonce-store with TTL and included request origin binding in assertion validation. Also signaled dedupe by hashing assertion into audit envelope. Reply to Arjun. (resolved)
Sofia Martinez: Audit envelopes look good; add a metric for failed consent validations so SRE can alert on unusual rates. (requested changes)
Maya Chen: Added metrics + dashboard and alert for high failed-consent-rate. Updated observability/dashboards and alerts. (resolved)
Liam O'Connor: RBAC temporal grant revocation path needs to handle partial failures when KMS revoke succeeds but RBAC write fails; added retry/compensating logic and clearer logs. (approved)
Sofia Martinez: Approving after a quick smoke run in staging. (approved)
security-team@redwood reviewed key handling and confirmed there are no long-lived operator secrets introduced; recommended KMS adapter run with an operator lease and for the provisioner to be deployed in a reserved namespace with a restricted RBAC role. Recommendations implemented.
Provisioner designed for async KMS ops; synchronous path only used during initial lease issuance. Benchmarked in benchmark-lab: median issuance latency 180ms (emulator), expected 300-500ms in managed KMS. Bulk provisioning uses batch consent mode (future work).
docs/consent_kms_migration.md includes operator runbook: enable feature flag, run dry-run to surface policy mismatches, migrate tenants via admin console, and monitor failed-consent-rate. A rollback path disables feature flag and revokes any ephemeral grants that were issued during rollout.
Add consent-driven KMS provisioning and RBAC v2 temporal grants. Feature-flagged: feature.consent_kms_provisioner (default off). See docs/consent_kms_migration.md for migration steps.
Deploy in its own namespace with network policy restricting egress to KMS endpoints and audit-writer. Ensure KMS adapter credentials are bound to short operator leases. Monitor metrics: consent_requests, consent_failures, lease_issued, lease_revoked, rbac_grant_errors.

Motivation: During the 2025-10-30 regional incident we observed large cohorts of connections performing KV-sync + prefix rehydrate at near-identical times when new nodes came online or during controlled rollouts. The synchronized work created short egress spikes that tripped tenant SLO enforcement and caused downstream circuit hysteresis. This PR introduces two orthogonal mitigations: (1) a connection sync holdoff that staggers KV/rehydration work based on an epochal jitter + server-load probe, and (2) a surge-insulation policy that places a short smoothing buffer on tenant egress accounting so the SLO enforcer prefers transient slowdowns and probing over immediate hard shedding. This is implemented as a conservative default that can be tuned per-deployment.

What changed (summary):
- runtime: add connection_sync_holdoff (epochal jitter + load-aware delay) to the serving runtime connection manager; this delays synchronous KV rehydrates and batches them into micro-waves to avoid spike amplification.
- slo: new surge_insulator policy that applies an exponential smoothing window to tenant egress rate before it contributes to short-window SLO violation counters; configurable via defaults and per-tenant overrides.
- fix: address race in circuit state transitions when manual unpark and automatic reopen occur concurrently; introduce a lightweight state mutex and ordering invariant.
- telemetry: new metrics (conn_sync.delay_ms, surge_insulator.smoothed_egress, surge_insulator.drop_reason) and a new debug view for correlated connection sync spikes.
- ops: helm values and defaults.toml knobs to opt-in/out and tune windows for Dedicated/Private installs.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc reviewed with SRE and Runtime (ENG-2872)
- [x] Unit tests for connection_holdoff jitter and ordering
- [x] Integration test exercising warmup-inserted micro-waves
- [x] Canary deployment in us-west-2 for 24h
- [x] Telemetry dashboards and alerts added

Commits:
- "add: connection_sync_holdoff gate + epochal jitter (runtime)"
- "feat: surge_insulator smoothing policy and config plumbing (slo subsystem)"
- "fix: circuit state raceguard and tests"
- "docs: add operational knobs and example helm values"

Changed files (high level):
- src/runtime/connection_manager.rs (new holdoff logic, unit tests)
- src/slo/surge_insulator.go (policy implementation + config hooks)
- services/slo/enforcer.rs (integration with smoothed metrics)
- telemetry/telemetry_schema.yaml (new metrics)
- deploy/helm/values.yaml (tunable knobs + docs)
- config/defaults.toml (insulation defaults for hosted/dedicated)
- tests/ci/connection_sync_test.py (new integration test harness)

Testing and CI:
- Local unit-tests: all green
- Integration: connection_sync_test added and run in CI, initially flaky under race conditions; fixed by adding a deterministic wait in harness and re-running.
- CI checks: lint, unit, integration, e2e-canary. First run: integration flake (timeout); rerun passed. Final CI: all checks green.

Review notes / conversation (highlights):
- Marco Liu (reviewer): "Nice approach separating smoothing from enforcement. Please add a high-cardinality knob off switch for hot paths and ensure the egress smoothing metric tags tenant and route." — addressed in surge_insulator.go and telemetry_schema.yaml in commit 2.
- Sofia Patel: "Can you quantify added latency for connection warmups under holdoff? We should ensure 95p isn't increased materially." — author reply: "Added micro-benchmarks in connection_manager.rs; median increase is ~4ms for first token rehydrate, 95p < 15ms under our simulated warmup. Bench numbers included in PR description and surfaced to telemetry as conn_sync.delay_ms." — Sofia approved after bench numbers were attached.
- Dinesh Ramesh: "Concern: SLO enforcer might hide persistent noisiness if window is too wide. Suggest a decay-based fallback into hard-shed for sustained violations." — author: "Surge_insulator is exponential-smoothing with configurable half-life; added a fallback threshold that short-circuits to the enforcer if smoothed_rate > sustained_threshold for duration X. Context and motivation: production workloads showed long-tail memory amplification from small long-lived KV entries combined with transient hot entries. Existing single-slab allocators cause fragmentation and cascading spill events under bursty workloads. This PR introduces a generational slab allocator plus an adaptive preemptive evictor that cooperates with the scheduler and compaction feedback loop to reduce tail latency and decrease spill-to-disk rates.

What this PR does (high level): adds a 2-generation slab allocator (young/hot + old/stable), a lightweight predictive preemptive evictor that uses short-term access heat and sequence-length-aware heuristics to preemptively compact and spill low-utility objects, and an idle-time compactor that coalesces small free segments when the node is below CPU load threshold. Integrates eviction signals with the request scheduler so that large batching decisions can trigger opportunistic compaction outside of SLO windows.

Design details: generational slab keeps small fixed-size regions for young objects that are expected to be reaccessed; objects surviving an age threshold are promoted to the old slab where larger contiguous segments are favored to reduce fragmentation. The preemptive evictor maintains a lightweight priority queue keyed by exponentially-weighted recency/frequency and predicted remaining lifetime (based on access pattern and model-agnostic heuristics). When memory pressure approaches a high watermark the evictor will compact within the old slab first and then select preemptive candidates from young->old cross-boundary candidates to avoid leaving behind fragmented pockets. Compaction-feedback loop: compaction run statistics (reclaimed bytes per work unit, CPU cost, spill reduction) are fed to an adaptive cost model that tunes compaction aggressiveness and the promotion age threshold at runtime.

Compatibility and migration: allocator exposes a backward-compatible config knob (kv.generational.enabled) defaulting to off for rolling release; when enabled, a cooperative draining protocol migrates in-memory objects in small batches to avoid pause spikes. Private customers can toggle the preemptive policy independently (kv.evictor.mode = passive|adaptive|preemptive).

Benchmarks (summary): microbench with mixed read/write 80/20, 128B median item, bursty tail: peak resident set reduced by ~22%, observed spill-to-disk events reduced 3.7x, 95p latency improved by ~18% on p3.2xlarge profiled nodes. Production canary on a small Dedicated cluster reduced emergency spill incidents from 5/week to 1/week over a 48h window. See bench/kv_memory_bench.toml and attached plots in the internal artifact link.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for slab promotion/demotion and compaction boundaries - [x] Integration test for cooperative draining during rolling upgrade - [x] Bench harness and regression tests - [x] Feature flag and runtime tuning knobs - [x] Documentation: design doc and ops runbook

Notes: this PR focuses on allocator/evictor logic; it intentionally leaves deeper ML-based lifetime predictors for follow-ups (ENG-2034). The compactor runs are gated by a CPU threshold to avoid contention with kernel-bound batching during high-throughput windows.

Related: ENG-1892 (kv memory fragmentation), ENG-2034 (predictive TTL follow-up), infra/ops ticket for Dedicated canary scheduling.
Evan Cho: Can you clarify how promotions avoid copy amplification under large-value workloads? Suggest measuring copy bytes in bench.
Maya Singh: Response: promotions are size-class aware; values > 16KB are kept out of young slab by default and use a direct allocation path. Added copy-bytes metric to bench and a note in docs.
Lena Hoffman: Request change: prefer configurable promotion age via runtime flag, and ensure compaction is throttled below N% CPU. Also add e2e canary steps.
Maya Singh: Response: added kv.promote_age_ms and compactor.cpu_threshold_pct config, updated ops runbook and canary checklist.
Marcus Li: Approve after CI passes and minor nits fixed (log level + comment).
- Add generational slab allocator for KV cache to reduce fragmentation and tail spill events.
- Add adaptive preemptive evictor that uses short-term heat to preemptively compact and spill low-utility items.
- Idle-time compactor with runtime tuning to coalesce free segments.
Operators: enable via kv.generational.enabled; tune kv.promote_age_ms and kv.compactor.cpu_threshold_pct for your workload.
Rolling deploy: enable feature flag in staging and run the cooperative draining job (ops/kv/drain.sh) during low-traffic windows. Monitor kv.reclaimed_bytes, kv.spill_events, and system cpu utilization. Canary instructions in docs/kv-generational-design.md.

Motivation: We observed two incidents where short-lived regional spikes triggered wholesale tenant evictions because SLO enforcement consumed tenant credit abruptly and synchronous KV replication races caused stale penalty state to persist across nodes. This PR introduces a transient SLO reserve orchestrator (per-tenant decaying credit pool with soft-shed rules) plus a small hotfix to the regional KV replication path that prevents raceback of penalty counters. Summary: 1) Add a transient_slo_reserve service that maintains a short-duration credit buffer per tenant, decays credits over a configurable half-life, and can be consulted by the SLO enforcer to allow short bursts without triggering eviction. 2) Implement a soft-shed policy that temporarily lowers batching windows and switches to cached responses for non-critical endpoints when reserve is exhausted instead of evicting. 3) Introduce an idempotent apply and fencing token in the region_kv_replicator to avoid a race where a delayed replicate could reapply an old penalty delta (the hotfix). 4) Add feature flag (ff.slo_reserve_v1) and rollout plan (canary regions -> global). If stable, enable globally over 48h with automatic rollback key if eviction_rate rises >10% over baseline Observability and alerts added: - slo.reserve_miss_rate (per-tenant, per-region) - slo.shed_rate - replicator.fence_rejects - Alert: reserve_miss_rate > 5% sustained 15m in canary -> auto-disable feature flag Release notes: "Adds a transient SLO reserve that prevents transient spikes from causing tenant evictions and introduces a hotfix preventing regional replication races that could reapply historical penalty deltas. Feature is behind ff.slo_reserve_v1; canary rollout is scheduled. Operators: see docs/operational/slo_reserve.md for rollback steps." Deployment notes: - The change is backward compatible and gated by a feature flag; no DB migration required. - The replication fencing requires a small persisted token (string) per-region; the first rollout will write the initial token automatically. - Recommended canary: low-traffic regions with active SLO monitoring. Post-merge actions: - Monitor telemetry for 72h and be prepared to toggle ff.slo_reserve_v1 - Follow-up ticket: ENG-1354 to add a persistence-backed reserve snapshot for long restarts Edge cases and risk mitigation: - Risk: mis-sized decay halves may let bursts leak through; mitigated by conservative defaults and operator-facing config - Risk: soft-shed could affect downstream SLAs; mitigated by endpoint allowlist and gradual rollout - Risk: race conditions in replication; mitigated by fence token persisted and integration tests added Additional notes: This PR is intentionally kept to a minimal hotfix on the replicator to minimize scope; the larger persistence-backed reserve (ENG-1354) will be follow-up. Summary: Adds a 'promote latch' primitive to the rollout runtime that enforces telemetry-driven checkpoints during canary/promote phases and wires an automated graceful backout playbook. Motivation: We've seen several incidents where a quick promote followed by a manual rollback caused session disruption and inconsistent user experience. This change makes promotion decision points explicit, observable, and abortable by the system when health signals deteriorate.

What this PR changes: Implements a latch state machine that can be attached to promotion plans. The latch evaluates a configurable set of telemetry checks (latency P95, error rate, semantic-regression signal from eval hooks, user-facing anomaly detector) at defined holdpoints. If thresholds are exceeded the latch triggers one of three actions: pause, slow-reduce-traffic, or backout. Backout is a graceful revert that preserves active session affinity and replays a small percentage of traffic to snapshot-mode for forensic capture.

Design details: - New API surface: rollout.spec.latches[] with 'checks', 'holdpoint_ms', 'action_on_violation' and 'grace_window_ms'. - Latch executor runs as part of promote coordinator (coord/promote_latch.go). It subscribes to the telemetry bus and evaluates windowed signals with exponential smoothing to avoid flapping. - Added a compact policy DSL for composite checks (e.g. "p95(latency, 60s) > 250ms and semantic_regression > 0.02"). - Backout path triggers a snapshot-and-drain flow: mark new model variant as draining, continue serving existing sessions for up-to 60s (configurable), persist recent requests to replay buffer for debugging, and reduce traffic fractions per-step to avoid sudden capacity shock. - Session affinity: when backout occurs we keep sticky sessions routed to the previous variant for their session TTL. That required plumbing session-cookie metadata through the swap plane.

Files touched (high level): - coord/promote_latch.go (new) - coord/latch_policy.go (new) - telemetry/telemetry_bus.go (mod) - controlplane/api/v1/rollout.proto (mod) - controlplane/server/rollout_handlers.go (mod) - runtime/drain_replay.go (new) - acceptance/e2e/promote_latch_test.go (new) - docs/rollouts/promote-latch.md (new)

Commits (summary): - Add promote latch state machine and executor - Add telemetry composite-check parser and evaluator - Wire latch into promote coordinator and API - Implement graceful backout drain + replay buffer - Unit + integration tests for latch + backout scenarios - Docs and rollout playbook

Testing done: - Unit tests for policy parser and executor: coverage for composite boolean expressions and time windows. - Integration e2e harness: simulate canary with injected latency/error, assert latch pauses promotion at configured holdpoints and triggers backout when condition persists. - Load test: 5k RPS synthetic traffic with model swap; verified no p95 regression during drain window. - Manual smoke: verified session stickiness preserved during backout in both hosted and dedicated modes.

Rollout plan: This is gated behind a feature flag rollout.promote_latch_enabled. Default remains off. Staged rollout plan: 1) Enable for internal org (1%) for 24h with verbose logging and wired smoke checks. 2) Increase to 10% after 48h if no backouts and health signals stable. 3) Expose to public customers as opt-in in Redwood Console.

Operational runbook (short): - Triggered when latch performs backout: check telemetry dashboard (new 'PromoteLatch' pane) for signals and recent decision trace. - If false positive: use 'resume' action to let coordinator re-evaluate after a manual holdpoint override. - For persisted replay buffer: run replay tool (scripts/replay_tool) against a staging cluster for reproduction. - For prolonged failures: revert feature flag and open incident with 'rollout-latch' tag.

Safety considerations: - To avoid noisy backouts, we use smoothed windows and require violation persistence > grace_window before backout. - Backout is conservative: we prefer pause or step-down traffic before full revert. - All decision traces are recorded and can be audited.

Related items: Linked Linear tasks ENG-1427 (promote latch design) and ENG-1433 (telemetry integration). This PR references prior incidents documented in INT-2041.

Why this is different from previous rollouts: Instead of ad-hoc holdpoints, this makes checkpoints first-class, pluggable, and machine-enforceable. The goal is to reduce manual intervention and make rollouts reproducible and auditable while reducing user-visible disruption during rollbacks.

Summary: Introduces a saga-based rollout orchestrator that checkpoints rollout state to a persistent snapshot store so canary and A/B rollouts can be paused, resumed, and replayed deterministically. Motivation: customers requested resumable canaries after several incidents where long-running experiments were interrupted by infra maintenance. This PR provides a first-class primitive (rollout saga + snapshot store) to avoid manual replays and brittle ad-hoc recovery scripts. Design highlights: 1) Saga orchestrator manages step sequence (canary phase, ramp, smoke checks, promote) and writes compact snapshots of progress and cohort assignments to the snapshot store after each state transition. 2) Snapshot store is pluggable: default implementation uses our existing durable-metadata service (with TTL + versioning) and an optional S3-backed archival plugin for long retention. 3) Resumable canaries: when a rollout is resumed, the orchestrator rehydrates state, replays pending validation windows, and continues traffic phasing with identical cohort mapping to preserve session affinity. 4) Safety: checkpoints include deterministic pseudo-random seeds for sampling, metric anchors, and active safety gates; resumptions re-run smoke checks before increasing traffic. 5) Rollback tokens: each snapshot includes a reversible rollback token that enables fast snapshot-based rollback to any previous checkpoint. 6) Observable timeline: console UI gains a new timeline view that shows snapshots, resume points, and reasons for pause/auto-hold. Checklist: - [x] Saga state machine and persistent snapshot API - [x] Default durable-metadata adapter + S3 archiver plugin - [x] Resume/replay logic with deterministic cohort mapping - [x] Rollback token generation and replay-based rollback path - [x] E2E tests covering simulated infra interruption and resume - [x] Console timeline UI and docs runbook - [x] Load test showing snapshot write latency impact (<5ms p50) Migration notes: Existing rollouts will continue to use the legacy in-memory state unless migrated. An opt-in flag rollout.spec.resumable=true will enable persisting snapshots for new rollouts (we will provide a migration job in a follow-up PR to convert active runways). Related: ENG-2345 (resumable canaries), ENG-2380 (snapshot retention policy). Links: design doc https://linear.app/redwood/notes/ENG-2345/resumable-canaries-design; runbook draft at docs/runbooks/resumable-canaries.md. Testing: unit + integration tests included; e2e harness simulates coordinator failover; performance microbenchmarks for snapshot writes. Backwards compatibility: headless rollouts with resumable=false unaffected. Rollout failure modes and mitigations are documented in runbook. Merge plan: squash merge; gradual console feature flag after rollout controller rollout.

Motivation: tenant warmstart and prefill heuristics currently produce suboptimal cache utilization for low-cardinality workloads which inflates per-token cost. This PR adds a lightweight runtime 'prefill sentinel' that compacts low-value KV entries and a companion CLI to synthesize tenant prefill profiles and surface conservative quantization suggestions. The goal is to reduce tail token spend and improve contiguous cache hit rates without changing public API behavior. Implementation summary: added a sentinel compactizer algorithm in the runtime prefill path to detect stale/low-reuse KV prefixes, a tenant-level sampler and scoring function to derive compacting thresholds, a compact-while-warmup mode for Dedicated instances, metrics/tracing hooks for hit-rate impact, and a small CLI tool (prefillctl) that generates recommended batch/cache/quant presets from historical traces. This single-string description contains the full PR context, design tradeoffs, testing notes, and rollout plan: design decisions (heuristic thresholding, safety fallthroughs, per-tenant opt-out), testing (unit tests for compactizer, integration smoke in benchmark-lab with 100k synthetic requests, manual QA on staging Dedicated), rollback plan (feature flag disable and config revert), rollout (canary on 3 tenants -> 15% -> 50% -> global), and backward-compatibility assurances.

Background: During a regional capacity spike we observed a pattern where long-running slowpaths caused connection pileups and aggressive tenant eviction, leading to cascading SLO drops for mid-tier customers. This PR implements a compact "contingency fuse" in the serving runtime and a progressive evacuation safeguard at the routing layer to reduce oscillation and allow graceful degradation under transient overload.
Motivation: Existing circuit breakers flipped aggressively when downstream kv pressure rose; that behavior is correct for severe faults but caused unnecessary tenant reinstates and noisy metrics during short-lived surges. The contingency fuse is a lightweight short-window gate that combines health signals (local latency quantiles + kv pressure) to temporarily divert traffic to standby routes before full eviction. The progressive evacuation safeguard introduces a staged drain with time-decayed backoff so tenants are not immediately evicted for brief infra perturbations.
Key changes: 1) runtime/evacuator/contingency_fuse.go — new fuse with configurable thresholds and exponential cooloff. 2) routing/fallback_policy.go — staged evacuation orchestration and fallback scorer adjustments. 3) controller/telemetry/evac_metrics.go — new metrics and tags for contingency decisions. 4) deploy/hotfix-release.yaml — rollout config with 5% canary and 10m observation window. 5) tests/integration/evacuation_sim_test.go — deterministic scenarios that simulate kv pressure spikes, short surges, and regional failover.
Design notes:
- Fuse window is intentionally short (250ms sampling) to catch fast surges without impacting steady-state.
- Fuse decision is a composite: p90 latency > X AND kv_queue_ratio > Y; both thresholds are configurable per-region and per-tier.
- Progressive evacuation uses three phases: warn (no eviction, ramp weights), partial-evac (soft-evict lowest priority), full-evac (hard-evict). Each phase has decaying TTLs to allow automatic healing.
- Telemetry includes decision_reason tag to help correlate fuse hits with SLO deltas.
Testing and validation: Unit tests cover decision logic and backoff; integration harness runs a 2-hour simulated surge that previously repro'd the incident and shows reduced eviction events by ~72% while SLO hit rate improved 48% in the mid-tier cohort.
CI: initial run showed a flaky integration test (timeout), fixed by tightening wait conditions; full CI green on rerun.
Rollout plan: Canary 5% across two low-risk regions for 30 minutes, observe contingency_fuse.hit_rate, tenant_evictions, and p95 latency regressions. If metrics stable, ramp to 50% over 2 hours, then full rollout.
Rollback: feature flags gate fuse and progressive evacuation separately; revert the feature flag to disable behaviors without code rollback.
Related: linear ENG-2148 captures the incident timeline; SUP-9123 includes customer reports.
Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests added
- [x] Integration simulation added
- [x] Telemetry and dashboards updated
- [x] Rollout plan + feature flagging
- [x] Postmortem link prepared (internal)
Migration/compatibility: Default thresholds are conservative; no customer-visible config changes required.
Hotfix notes: Backported a minimal patch to the 2026-02-15 maintenance branch to stop immediate re-evictions in the middle of the previous incident.

Motivation: During a recent outage window we observed repeated rapid reopen cycles for tenant circuits in some regions. The root cause was a combination of transient infra flakiness and an aggressive per-tenant penalty decay which allowed a tenant to re-enter normal routing too quickly, only to trigger another short-lived failure and cause oscillation. This PR introduces a 'Sticky Penalty Tracker' that records recent circuit transition history and applies a progressively longer soft-stall (slo-relaxation window) for tenants that show repeated failures within a short time window. The feature is intentionally non-blocking: it surfaces a soft-stall that influences routing and request admission but keeps logs, metrics, and an override path for emergency rollback.

What this changes (summary): - New in-memory StickyPenaltyTracker component used by the routing and SLO enforcer to compute an additional soft-stall multiplier for tenants with repeated circuit flips. - Cross-region coordinator shim (best-effort pubsub via region heartbeat channel) so adjacent regions can avoid immediate failover loops by learning about sticky penalties without requiring strong consistency. - Backward-compatible API flags: feature gate redwood.runtime.sticky_penalty.enabled (off by default for canary), and redwood.sre.stall_override for emergency bypass. - Telemetry: new histograms and tags (sticky_penalty.age_buckets, sticky_penalty.count) plus event logs for penalty application. - Tests: unit tests for penalty decay math, integration tests simulating flip cycles, and a small perf bench to validate negligible added p99 latency.

Design details: - Penalty calculation is time-decayed exponential: penalty = base * (1 + alpha)^{n_recent} clipped to max_penalty; n_recent counts flips in sliding window. Decay half-life is configurable per-tenant. - StickyTracker persists minimal state in the existing tenant metadata store (one small protobuf record per tenant) with tombstoning to avoid metadata churn; on Private installs this is optional and defaults to in-memory only. - Cross-region exposure is publish-only: regions emit short-lived announcements (tenant id + penalty snapshot) to the heartbeat channel; recipients treat these as advisory. This prevents aggressive cross-region failover when one region is oscillating.

Rollout plan: - Feature gated and disabled by default. - Step 1: Enable in internal canary (hosted internal cluster) for 48h, observe penalty histograms and failure-rate correlation. - Step 2: Enable for 10% of production tenants (weighted by traffic) and monitor p95/p99 latency, SLO violations, and failover events. - Step 3: Gradual ramp to 100% with staged decay tuning. The PR includes a runbook section for emergency disable (flip redwood.runtime.sticky_penalty.enabled=false) and a fast override via redwood.sre.stall_override.

Testing & validation: - Unit tests cover decay math, edge cases for max clipping, and garbage collection of old entries. - Integration test harness simulates repeated short failures and shows reduced oscillation and fewer cross-region failovers. - Small perf microbenchmark shows ~0.05ms median overhead on the routing hot path and no measurable p99 change under 1000 concurrent requests in CI.

Acceptance criteria: - No increase in p99 latency in production canary over 24h. - Reduction in repeated failover count by >=40% for affected tenants in the test scenario. - CI green and security review completed.

Notes and related work: This complements earlier SLO relaxation features by adding temporal stickiness to avoid rapid reopen cycles. See linear items ENG-2481 and follow-up notes in SUP-7790. For Private installations that enable persistent tenant metadata, there is a migration note: new tiny protobuf record id=sticky_penalty_v1.

References: internal runbook link: https://linear.app/reports/ENG-2481/notes, design doc: docs/runtime/sticky-penalty-tracker.md.

Diego Ramos: Minor nit on metric tag cardinality; prefer bucketing tenant_role instead of tenant_id where possible. (addressed)
Linh Tran: Question about persistence -- can private installs cause metadata explosion? You added tombstoning, please highlight GC policy in runbook. (added)
Maya Patel: Approve after you add canary rollout notes and the emergency toggles to the runbook. (approved)
Asha Menon: replied: added runbook section, GC policy, and metric buckets per reviewer feedback.

Adds a reconciliation report and warehouse view that compares the Unit Economics pipeline aggregates (blended $/1M output tokens and underlying $ + tokens) against billing totals for the same time window. This is intended as a Finance sign-off tool and a recurring data quality guardrail for exec reporting (QTD/MTD). The report is internal-only and intentionally conservative about what it claims to reconcile: we reconcile compute-related cost attribution and token-metered usage to billing line items that are attributable to inference usage; we explicitly exclude taxes, one-time fees, manual adjustments, and contract-specific true-ups that are not represented in metering. Implementation overview: (1) introduces a canonical reconciliation window definition (UTC by default, with a documented option to run in Finance reporting TZ), (2) materializes daily and monthly reconciliation tables keyed by customer_tier + region + model_family (optional drilldown) and a top-level rollup, (3) implements tolerance-based pass/fail gates with reason codes (e.g., missing metering hours, rate-card version mismatch, billing lag), and (4) wires a lightweight CLI + scheduled job to publish a daily snapshot and a CSV export for FP&A. Guardrails: we hard-fail the report if metering completeness is below threshold (see econ_pipeline_completeness_pct), if the billing extract is missing the last N hours for the requested window, or if the GPU rate card version differs from the one pinned for the window; we soft-warn for low-volume segments where rounding dominates. Known limitations (documented in the report header and README): refunds/credits are applied at invoice time and may land outside the usage window; dedicated/private contracts often bill at committed capacity rather than metered tokens (we still provide a reconciliation section, but it is labeled "not expected to match" unless contract flags indicate usage-based billing); resellers can aggregate billing across multiple internal org_ids; and streaming output token parity issues can bias the token side if a regression occurs (this report surfaces the discrepancy but does not correct it). Testing: added unit tests for billing line-item classification, window alignment, tolerance math, and reason-code prioritization; added an end-to-end test with a fixture billing export and a fixture metering aggregate for a known-good day. Rollout: behind internal feature flag UNIT_ECON_RECONCILIATION_REPORT; Finance (Laura/Rishi) requested this as a go/no-go artifact for v1; once merged we will run in shadow mode for 1 week and tune tolerances before gating the exec KPI pack.
warehouse: add econ_reconciliation_daily + econ_reconciliation_monthly tables
billing: classify billable inference line items and normalize invoice timestamps
reconcile: compute deltas, pct deltas, and reason codes with tolerance policy
cli: add `rw econ reconcile` export (csv + json) and scheduled snapshot job
tests: add fixtures + reconciliation math tests; docs: add limitations + runbook link
