payload.body:
Motivation: Customers operating in regulated regions have asked for stronger guarantees that tenant-scoped KMS usage and residency assertions cannot be hijacked during operator interventions and rolling upgrades. This change introduces two complementary pieces: (1) a temporal tenant lock — a lightweight lease that pins a tenant's residency decision for a short, configurable window to avoid flip-flopping across concurrent operator actions, and (2) a KMS Region Ombudsman service that validates cross-service KMS binding proofs and emits a canonical 'residency-hash' that is included in audit envelopes for downstream correlation.

What this PR does (summary):
- Runtime: Add tenant temporal lock manager (pkg/tenantlock) that provides lease acquisition, renewal, and a small local cache to prevent thrash during rollout/upgrade. Leases are short-lived (default 30s) and are safe-to-expire — they are advisory and do not block normal operations if the ombudsman is unavailable.
- KMS: Introduce kms/ombudsman which queries configured KMS providers, verifies region-bound wrap/unwrap metadata, and publishes a signed residency-hash to the audit pipeline.
- RBAC: Policy compiler updates to attach an immutable operator-scope tag to requests that attempted forced region-change operations; the tag is surfaceable in RBAC v2 decision logs for later adjudication.
- Audit: Audit forwarder augmented to include residency-hash and tenant-lock context in canonical audit envelopes (compact JSON). Backwards-compatible: older consumers ignore extra fields.
- Installer/Private: Installer hooks to wire ombudsman address into private deployments and an opt-in flag for turning on strict residency-enforcement (default: off).

Files touched (high level):
- pkg/tenantlock/manager.go (new) — lease acquisition + LRU cache
- services/ombudsman/server.go (new) — verification endpoints and signer
- pkg/kms/provider_aws.go (mod) — attach region proof extraction
- pkg/policy/compiler/attach_tags.go (mod) — operator-scope tagging when policy detects forced overrides
- services/audit/forwarder.go (mod) — residency-hash injection
- charts/private/values.yaml (mod) — ombudsman opt-in flag and resources

Rollout and safety:
- Shadow rollout: ombudsman runs in shadow mode by default for the first week in Hosted and Dedicated; audit envelopes include residency-hash but policy is not enforced.
- Canaries: tenant-lock default lease is small and feature-flagged; we will enable it for a small set of tenants for 48h before broad flip.
- Fail-open behavior: if the ombudsman is unreachable, runtime operates normally and emits a "ombudsman_unavailable" indicator in the envelope; this preserves availability for latency-sensitive workloads.

Testing and verification:
- Unit tests for lease edge cases, provider proof parsing, and audit envelope format.
- Integration tests that run a local ombudsman, KMS emulator (wrap/unwrap metadata), and exercise the forwarder to ensure residency-hash is verifiable.
- E2E smoke test added to the installer acceptance suite to ensure flags are wired into private clusters.

Checklist:
- [x] design review with security and infra (SEC-482)
- [x] unit + integration tests added
- [x] installer hooks + chart changes
- [x] documentation: admin docs explaining lease semantics and ombudsman verification steps (docs/security/residency-ombudsman.md)

Related: ENG-2469 (design doc), SUP-1128 (customer report), previous work on residency proofs and audit envelopes.

Notes: This is intended to be low friction for customers — the ombudsman and lease are opt-in and default to conservative behavior. If we later decide to make strict residency enforcement mandatory for some compliance tiers, the ombudsman provides a canonical audit trail for that transition.
Marco Ruiz (2025-01-11): Could we reduce the default lease to 15s? 30s seems long for some low-latency workloads. Also please add a prometheus metric for lease_acquire_latency.
Aisha Patel (2025-01-11): Reduced default to 20s after discussing tradeoffs; added lease_acquire_latency and lease_acquire_failures metrics. We'll watch canary 48h to decide further reduction.
Emily Chen (2025-01-12): How does this interact with Dedicated burst capacity routing? If a tenant migrates region temporarily due to capacity, will the tenant-lock block that?
Aisha Patel (2025-01-12): Tenant-lock is advisory and scoped to residency decision only. It does not block capacity-based routing; that path uses a separate capacity-grade routing token and ombudsman returns a different verification namespace. Added clarifying comment in compiler and docs.
Soren Jensen (2025-01-14): Integration tests flaky on CI: failed once on KMS emulator timeout. I recommend adding retry with jitter for the emulator in test harness.
Aisha Patel (2025-01-14): Added retries to test harness and bumped emulator timeout. Re-ran CI and green.
payload.title: Introduce temporal tenant locks and KMS region ombudsman

Introduce tiered warmup windows and cost-aware orchestration: reduces over-provisioning during steady-state while preserving tail latency SLOs; adds telemetry for warmup progress and hedged failovers; backward-compatible config knobs for gradual rollout.
Motivation: Dedicated fleet warm pools are a significant contributor to steady-state cost during large scale deployments. Current warmup is a single global window per pool which leads to either excessive pre-warming (wasted GPU-hours) or under-warming (tail latency regressions). This PR introduces a differential warmup window runner and a cost-aware fleet orchestrator that hedge capacity using predictive shortfalls and spot-backed soft-fallbacks. Design: 1) Tiered warmup windows per tenant class and per-pool (fast, normal, slow) derived from recent cold-start percentiles; 2) Concurrency planner that computes inflight reservation targets per pool using a concave cost model to balance reserved capacity vs. on-demand cold-start expense; 3) Cost-aware orchestrator that annotates provisioning decisions with expected marginal cost delta and prefers warm adjustments with positive ROI; 4) Hedging policy: small opportunistic spot-backed warmlets (ephemeral VMs/GPU jobs) launched under a soft SLA to absorb sudden spikes, with automatic fallback to slower warm paths if spot termination occurs; 5) Telemetry additions: warmup_progress{pool,tenant_class}, predicted_shortfall, hedged_failover_count, marginal_cost_estimate. Backwards compatibility: new config defaults mimic old behavior for existing pools; cluster-level feature flag 'differential-warmup-enabled' gates rollout. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for window estimator and cost model - [x] Integration tests on staging fleet simulator - [x] Canary rollout plan added to console runbooks - [x] Telemetry dashboard queries and alerts drafted - [x] Documentation updates for operator knobs Implementation notes: Warmup estimator uses an exponentially weighted percentile sketch of cold-start latencies (90/95/99) per tenant class over sliding 12h; window sizes derive from a percentile-to-time function with min/max clamps. Concurrency planner solves a small convex program per pool every 30s; we reused the existing autoscaler optimization loop and added cost terms to the objective, keeping the solver timeout at 50ms. Hedging uses existing warmlet launcher with added lifecycle hooks to emit hedged_failover_count on termination. Testing & rollout: tested with synthetic spike traces in benchmark-lab and a canary across three dedicated pools for one week; observed 18% reduction in mean reserved-GPU hours with <3% P99 latency variance vs baseline. Rollout steps: enable feature flag in staging -> small canary on low-impact tenants -> expand to 25% pools with monitoring -> global enable. Known limitations & follow-ups: better long-tail cold-start modeling (ENG-9124), per-tenant budget-aware hedging (future), and tighter autoscaler solver integration to reduce edge-case oscillation. Context/References: linear ENG-8821 (fleet warmup economics), ENG-8903 (hedged failover design), benchmark outputs in /benchmark-lab/warmup-cost/2026-01.
Priya Rao: Left a note on planner.go — the convex objective needs a small regularizer to avoid corner-case oscillations; recommend L2 with lambda=1e-4. (addressed in second commit)
Liam O'Connor: Request to add more logging around spot-backed warmlet terminations for debugging — added lifecycle hooks and counters. (resolved)
Diego Martinez: Asked for performance guardrails on the new estimator to avoid added CPU on controller loops; verified estimator uses bounded memory and amortized compute. (ack)
Priya Rao: Approved after integration tests and telemetry checks passed
Merge-Queue Bot: CI green, merge-safety checks satisfied
Feature gated behind 'differential-warmup-enabled'. Operators: monitor warmup_progress and predicted_shortfall dashboards after enabling; initial canary should run on pools tagged 'canary-warmup'. If P99 latency rises >5% rollback by disabling feature flag and notifying SRE on-call.
18% decrease in reserved-GPU-hours, 2.1% median latency improvement, P99 latency variance +2.8% (within canary threshold), hedged_failover_count averaged 0.4 per hour for canary pools.
ENG-9124: improve long-tail cold-start model
ENG-9201: per-tenant cost budgets for hedging
ENG-9340: solver warmstart to reduce solver latency
payload.title: Differential warmup window and cost-aware fleet orchestrator

payload.body:
Problem: OpenAI-compat tool/function calling encounters ambiguous schema mappings when models emit tool names that differ from registered runtime tool IDs, and streaming fragments can be dropped or interleaved which causes tool invocation reassembly failures. Existing compatibility layers either rely on exact schema matching or brittle fragment coalescing heuristics.

Summary: This PR adds a runtime-side "synthetic tool manifest" that materializes a normalized view of available tools at request time by merging model-declared tool descriptors with server-registered tool adapters. The manifest provides stable canonical IDs, property-level normalization rules, and soft aliases for name collisions. In parallel, the PR introduces an "indexed event framing" convention for the streaming path: each stream chunk related to tool selection/invocation carries a compact index header (xi=<sequence>) and tool token (ti=<canonical-id>) plus optional fragment metadata (frag=1/3). Clients can reassemble fragments deterministically using sequence indexes and tolerate lossy delivery with tombstone semantics.

Design highlights: 1) Synthetic manifest builder: merges model tool schema, runtime adapter schema, and openai-compat translation rules. Normalizers include type coercions (e.g. integer/string), enum mapping tables, and optional property renames. A collision resolution policy favors customer-registered adapters, then name-based heuristics, then model-declared canonical names; conflicts are surfaced as telemetry rather than hard errors. 2) Canonical tool IDs: runtime assigns stable short ids (e.g. t_7f3a) persisted for the request lifetime and referenced by stream headers to avoid repeated verbose schemas in streaming chunks. 3) Indexed event framing: SSE chunks include meta headers (xi, ti, frag, eof) emitted by the compatibility layer; downstream consumers (SDKs/clients) use xi to order fragments and to detect missing indexes; recovery rules include immediate fallback to non-streamed tool payloads and a best-effort continuation with model fallback. 4) Backwards compatibility: when talking to older clients or when upstream model only uses v1 envelopes, we fall back to the existing framed payload but still generate the synthetic manifest server-side for schema mapping. A feature flag (compat.synthetic_manifest=true) gates the rollout.

Testing & validation: unit tests for manifest merging, collision resolution, and canonical id generation; integration harness that simulates fragmented streams, dropped chunks, and out-of-order delivery to validate reassembly and tombstone behavior; end-to-end smoke test against the openai-compat adapter and Redwood SDK (python & ts) stubs.

Rollout plan: behind feature flag for 2 weeks in canary, collect telemetry counters (manifest_collision, fragment_recovery_rate, tool_mismatch_fallback), then enable for 20% production traffic, monitor for increased bad-invoke rates, and then full rollout.

Why this is different: instead of only normalizing schema names or improving fragment stitching heuristics, this approach creates a transient, authoritative manifest per request and a compact, index-based streaming envelope that makes reassembly deterministic and debuggable while preserving OpenAI-compat semantics for tool_choice/tool_call scenarios.
Diego Alvarez: Architecturally this looks sound. Two asks: (1) add an explicit TTL for synthetic canonical ids so we don't leak them across long-lived connections, and (2) show an example of the SSE chunk with xi/ti headers in the docs. 
Priya Kapoor (author): Added ttl config to manifest builder (default 2 minutes) and expanded docs with a streaming example. See packages/openai-compat/src/manifest/builder.ts and docs/openai-compat/synthetic-manifest.md
Sofia Chen: Unit tests look good; can you add a collision-case test where model and runtime both declare the same tool but with incompatible param types? We should assert telemetry is emitted and the request falls back gracefully.
Priya Kapoor (author): Added manifest.collision.test.ts to cover incompatible types; telemetry emitted as "manifest_collision" with tags {tool, request_id}.
Marta Ivanov: CI failed initially on the lint step for naming in framing.ts. Once fixed, re-run CI and ensure the python SDK adapter is exercised in the matrix job before merging.
Priya Kapoor (author): Fixed lint, updated matrix job to include sdk/python. All CI checks passed on rerun.
Introduce synthetic tool manifest + indexed event streaming framing to improve tool/function-call compatibility and deterministic fragment reassembly. Feature flagged; rollout plan included.
Feature gated (compat.synthetic_manifest). Monitor telemetry after canary. SDKs updated to interpret xi/ti headers; older clients continue to receive legacy envelopes.

payload.body:
Summary

This PR updates the Console backend contract endpoints used by the Hosted canary rollout wizard. It introduces a stable 3-call flow (preview -> validate -> submit) with explicit response models for: computed schedule normalization, policy guardrail feedback, warnings, and human-readable validation errors that can be shown directly in the wizard review screen.

Motivation

The wizard needs to (a) show the user exactly what will happen before creating a rollout, (b) run the same policy/validation checks used at submission time, and (c) return structured, actionable errors (including approval-gate requirements) so users don’t discover issues only after a failed submit. Existing endpoints were partially shared with the legacy rollout editor and returned internal models that were hard to safely render and difficult to keep backwards compatible.

What changed

New/updated endpoints (Console backend -> Orchestrator)

- POST /console/v1/hosted/routes/{route_id}/rollouts/preview
  - Input: baseline + canary target (model version/config), optional traffic schedule draft, guardrail overrides (if allowed), and stop-conditions selection
  - Output: normalized plan (step percentages + computed soak windows), derived cohorting key, computed rollout “diff” summary, and warnings

- POST /console/v1/hosted/routes/{route_id}/rollouts/validate
  - Runs policy evaluation + semantic validations (schedule monotonicity, max step jump, min soak, approval gates, stop-condition constraints)
  - Output: ok=true/false, blocking_errors[], non_blocking_warnings[], required_approvals (if any), and an “allowed_actions” set used by the UI to enable/disable the submit button

- POST /console/v1/hosted/routes/{route_id}/rollouts/submit
  - Idempotent submit (client provides request_id)
  - Creates the rollout via orchestrator and returns rollout_id + the same normalized plan returned by preview to keep the wizard state consistent

Response model updates

- Introduces RolloutWizardPlanV1 (explicit versioned DTO) rather than returning internal orchestrator models.
- Adds explicit error taxonomy:
  - POLICY_DENIED (includes policy_rule_id, user_facing_message)
  - VALIDATION_ERROR (field + message)
  - APPROVAL_REQUIRED (includes required_role)
  - CONFLICT (e.g., another active rollout exists on the route)
- Adds warnings with stable codes used for UI copy (e.g., WARN_SOAK_TOO_SHORT, WARN_LARGE_STEP_JUMP_REQUESTED_BUT_CAPPED).
- Includes an optional “policy_context” block (tier, entitlements, default guardrails) in preview/validate responses so the UI can render “why can’t I do this?” explanations without additional calls.

Backwards compatibility

- Keeps legacy console rollout endpoints intact (used by existing rollout list/details pages).
- New wizard endpoints are gated behind the hosted_canary_rollout_wizard flag and are only used by the new wizard flow.
- DTOs are versioned (PlanV1, ValidationV1). Any incompatible changes will require PlanV2 rather than silently reshaping fields.

Security / auth

- Enforces route-scoped permission checks for preview/validate/submit.
- submit additionally checks “rollout.create” and returns POLICY_DENIED with a user-facing message when the user lacks permission.
- validate returns “required_approvals” but does not leak approver identities; UI only shows the role needed (e.g., rollout-approver).

Notes for reviewers

- The validate endpoint intentionally duplicates some checks done by submit. This is to ensure UI can show deterministic results before the user confirms and to avoid “passed preview, failed submit” surprises. submit still re-runs validation.
- submit is idempotent via request_id to prevent double-creation when users double-click or the network retries.

Testing

- Added unit tests for schedule normalization and warning emission.
- Added contract tests for error mapping from policy engine errors to Console DTOs.
- Manual test: wizard flow in staging (preview -> validate -> submit) using a route with an active fallback policy + region routing.

Release notes

- Adds versioned wizard contracts for Hosted canary rollouts (preview/validate/submit).
- Improved user-facing validation and policy guardrail messaging in the rollout wizard.

Screens / API examples

Example validate response for approval gate:
- ok: false
- blocking_errors: [ { code: APPROVAL_REQUIRED, message: "Approval required to exceed 25% step increase", required_role: "rollout-approver" } ]

Related

- ENG-9140 (orchestrator service endpoints)
- ENG-9146 (policy engine guardrails)
- DES-742 (wizard UI)

Checklist

- [x] Versioned DTOs
- [x] Idempotent submit
- [x] Policy error mapping w/ user-facing messages
- [x] Contract tests
- [x] Feature-flagged usage


Dylan Brooks: Can we guarantee validate and submit run the same checks? I don't want the wizard to say “OK” and then submit fails because of a different codepath.

Chloe Martin (author): Yep. validate calls the same underlying validator used by submit (submit re-runs it). The only extra in submit is the active-rollout conflict check and create call. Added a regression test for “validate OK then submit OK” with the same input.
Jordan Lee: POLICY_DENIED should include a stable rule identifier so the Console can map to copy without parsing messages.

Chloe Martin (author): Added policy_rule_id to POLICY_DENIED and APPROVAL_REQUIRED responses. Messages remain user-facing but UI can key off rule ids if we decide to later.
Tessa Morgan: Warnings need stable codes for UX copy; free-form strings will drift.

Chloe Martin (author): Agreed. Converted warnings to { code, message, severity } and kept message for now as default copy. UI can override by code.
Kaitlyn Nguyen: Please double-check we’re not leaking any tenant-level entitlements beyond what the user can already infer. The “policy_context” block is useful, but keep it minimal.

Chloe Martin (author): Scoped policy_context to only include the effective guardrail defaults + tier name + feature flag state. Removed internal entitlement ids and any org-level metadata.

payload.body:
Summary
This PR adds a non-breaking config migration that introduces (1) Route Groups and (2) Tier Defaults in the control-plane config model, while preserving existing customer configs and enforcement behavior.

Context
Hot-route capacity protection requires us to reason about limits/budgets by logical route group (e.g. chat, embeddings, rerank) and apply tier-aware defaults (enterprise vs best-effort) without forcing customers to re-author configs or causing accidental limit changes.

Key changes
- Adds new config schema objects:
  - route_groups: named groups with route matchers (exact + prefix; no regex).
  - tier_defaults: default policy blocks keyed by tier + route_group.
- Adds a migration runner that:
  - Detects legacy configs that only define per-route or global quotas/limits.
  - Materializes equivalent route_groups for known core routes and assigns routes to groups.
  - Backfills tier_defaults with values derived from legacy limits.
  - Writes the migrated config under a new versioned namespace, leaving original legacy fields intact.
- Adds an evaluation compatibility layer:
  - If tier_defaults are present, they are used as the base.
  - Legacy per-route/per-tenant overrides continue to apply last-write-wins.
  - If tier_defaults/route_groups are absent, behavior is unchanged.
- Adds guardrails:
  - Migration is idempotent.
  - Migration is opt-in via feature flag: hot_route_config_v2_migration.
  - Dry-run mode logs diff summary without persisting.

Non-goals
- No customer-visible UI changes.
- No changes to billing or metering behavior (only config shape).
- No rewrite of fairness scheduling; this only sets up config primitives.

Why this is safe
- We preserve legacy fields and only start reading the new fields when the flag is enabled.
- Tier defaults are derived from the existing config (no new rate limit values introduced by default).
- Overrides apply after defaults; customers with explicit per-route/per-tenant config should see no changes.
- Adds validation to prevent accidental widening/narrowing:
  - For each migrated route, computed effective limits for tier=enterprise/best-effort must match legacy effective limits (within rounding for window boundaries).

Migration details
- Known route groups in this PR:
  - chat_completions: /v1/chat/completions
  - completions: /v1/completions
  - embeddings: /v1/embeddings
  - rerank: /v1/rerank
  - misc: catch-all (only used when legacy config was global-only)
- Matching order: exact > prefix > misc.
- Tier mapping:
  - enterprise: accounts with tier in {enterprise, dedicated_enterprise}.
  - best_effort: self_serve + trial + untagged.

Observability
- Adds structured log line on migration apply:
  - config_migration=route_groups_tier_defaults
  - tenant_id (hashed)
  - before_version / after_version
  - changed_route_count
  - validation_result
- Adds a metric for migration outcomes:
  - control_plane.config_migration.applied_total{result=success|skipped|failed, reason=...}

Testing
- Unit tests for:
  - Legacy-only config -> v2 config equivalence
  - Idempotence (apply twice yields identical v2 output)
  - Override precedence (tier_defaults + legacy overrides)
  - Matcher precedence (exact > prefix)
- Integration test (config service + policy engine contract) behind the flag:
  - Loads a representative enterprise tenant config and verifies effective limits match pre-migration.

Rollout plan
1) Land this PR with flag default OFF.
2) Enable dry-run in us-east canary control-plane to generate diffs and validate no unexpected widening.
3) Allowlist a small set of enterprise accounts; enable apply.
4) Expand allowlist, then region-by-region.
Rollback
- Disable flag; system reverts to legacy evaluation paths.
- v2 configs remain stored but are ignored.

Files/areas changed (high level)
- control-plane/config-schema: add route_groups + tier_defaults
- control-plane/migrations: add migration runner + dry-run
- control-plane/config-eval: compatibility layer and precedence logic
- policy-engine/contracts: update config contract version header
- tests: migration equivalence + idempotence

Commits (squash summary)
- control-plane: introduce RouteGroup + TierDefault schema (versioned)
- migrations: add v2 backfill + idempotence + dry-run diff
- eval: apply tier defaults first, then legacy overrides
- validation: compare effective limits pre/post migration
- tests: migration fixtures + contract integration test

Review notes / discussion
- Ethan Park: asked for explicit precedence rules + examples. Added a 'Resolution order' section to schema docs + tests that lock precedence.
- Jordan Lee: requested deterministic output ordering to avoid noisy diffs. Added stable sorting for route_groups and tier_defaults blocks.
- Amara Diallo: flagged risk of route matcher drift between gateway and control-plane. Added shared route canonicalization helper and exported constants.
- Cole Summers: requested proof that quotas (windowed) don’t shift due to rounding. Added window alignment logic + asserts in test fixtures.
- Kaitlyn Nguyen: requested that migration logs avoid raw tenant IDs. Added hashing + sampling.

Checklist
- [x] Flagged + safe defaults
- [x] Idempotent migration
- [x] Equivalence validation for effective limits
- [x] Unit + integration tests
- [x] Dry-run support for rollout

CI
- build: pass
- unit tests: pass
- integration tests: pass
- lint/format: pass

Merge
Merged via squash to main on 2026-01-13.

Follow-ups
- Wire dry-run summaries into internal dashboard panel (ENG-4928)
- Expand route_groups with additional endpoints as we graduate more routes into protection (PM-882)
- Add Console internal view of v2 config objects once backend hooks are in (PR later in console backend series)
Introduces a backwards-compatible config migration that adds RouteGroup + TierDefault concepts while preserving existing per-route/per-tenant limit behavior; required for tier-aware enforcement rollout.
Enables non-breaking adoption of route groups + tier defaults required for tier-aware enforcement; rollout remains gated by hot_route_config_v2_migration flag.
payload.title: Add config migration for route groups + tier defaults (non-breaking)

payload.body:
Context: We currently emit per-invocation spans and high-level per-route metrics but lack a compact summary of the invocation execution path and the originating callsite (client code path) that initiated each invocation. That gap makes it hard to answer operational questions like: which client callsites are responsible for the 95th-percentile latency, where in the invocation pipeline time is spent across different customers, and which callsites have the largest cumulative cost impact over a day.

Proposal: Add an Invocation Flow Summarizer that runs in the telemetry pipeline and emits compact per-invocation summaries and aggregated callsite-level rollups. The summarizer extracts a canonical callsite fingerprint (file:line-ish + function signature when available), aggregates stage durations (parse, encode, model_forward, decode, network), and emits both per-invocation sparklines (for quick UI rendering) and daily callsite rollups for billing/alerting. This PR implements the summarizer, integrates its output into a new dashboard, and adds alert tuning knobs to suppress noisy callsites.

What changed (high level): - telemetry/ingest: add callsite_fingerprint extraction and stage buckets - telemetry/processor: new invocation_flow_summarizer component with lightweight serialization - metrics: new metric series invocation.flow.duration_by_stage and callsite.cumulative_cost_seconds - dashboards: new Invocation Flow Summary dashboard with per-callsite sparklines and a callsite breakdown panel - alerts: introduce callsite_noise_threshold and a new SLO rule that can auto-suppress noisy low-volume callsites - docs: observability/callsite-metrics.md with query recipes and runbook notes

Checklist: [x] end-to-end ingest->dashboard flow tested locally and in staging [x] unit tests for summarizer component [x] integration test that verifies sparkline compactness and retention [x] documented queries and dashboard panels [x] linear tickets linked

Commits: ["feat(telemetry): extract callsite_fingerprint and stage markers", "feat(processor): invocation_flow_summarizer + compact sparkline encoder", "feat(metrics): add invocation.flow.duration_by_stage and callsite.cumulative_cost_seconds", "ui(dashboards): add invocation flow summary dashboard and callsite panels", "chore(tests): add integration test for summarizer pipeline", "docs: add callsite metrics runbook"]

Files changed (high level): ["telemetry/ingest/callsite_extractor.go", "telemetry/processor/invocation_flow_summarizer.go", "metrics/series_registry.yaml", "observability/dashboards/invocation_flow_summary.json", "dashboard/panels/sparkline_compact.tsx", "docs/observability/callsite-metrics.md"]

Testing and validation: - Unit test coverage for summarizer: 12 new tests covering extraction heuristics and stage bucketing. - Integration test: a synthetic workload generator (tests/integration/invocation_flow_test.go) validates that the summarizer output is <= 1KB per invocation and correctly reconstructs stage durations into sparklines. - Staging rollout: enabled behind a feature flag for 10% of traffic in staging; verified that storage increase is ~2.4% and query latency impact is negligible.

Observability and cost: The summarizer emits compact binary sparklines and a small set of rollup counters; raw per-token traces are unchanged. Estimated steady-state storage increase for hosted telemetry is ~0.9% at current traffic with default sampling. We added a config knob (callsite_noise_threshold) to suppress low-volume callsites from rollups to control cardinality.

Review notes & known limitations: - Callsite fingerprint heuristics prefer client-side file/line when present; for SDKs that do not populate callsite info, we fall back to request-origin annotations. This means callsite attribution may be incomplete for older SDK versions — documented in runbook. - The sparkline encoder is lossy by design (8-value buckets) to keep storage small. This is intentional and acceptable for triage dashboards but not for deep forensic reconstruction. - Possible follow-up: expose per-tenant callsite retention policies and add a UI control to toggle cumulative-cost vs rate-normalized views.

Related work: ENG-10190 (invocation sampling rework), PR #162998 (compact-span-encoder), ENG-10301 (dashboard UX improvements).
Ethan Walker (2026-02-16): Nice approach. Two asks: (1) please add a short TTL for per-invocation sparklines in the registry so downstream storage teams can control retention, (2) add a knob to disable sparkline emission per-tenant.
Priya Nair (2026-02-16): Added TTL flag and per-tenant enable in processor config; added tests to cover disable path.
Lina Rodriguez (2026-02-17): Found one NPE when callsite info is missing in legacy SDK traffic. Please add defensive null handling and a unit test.
Priya Nair (2026-02-17): Fixed NPE and added unit test. Also updated docs to note SDK versions that do not populate callsite info.
Samir Gupta (2026-02-19): CI flaky: one integration run failed with timeout on the synthetic generator. Reran, all green; approves.
Ethan Walker (2026-02-20): Approving after documentation updates. Leaving a small follow-up for UX polish.
payload.title: introduce invocation-flow-summarizer and callsite-level metrics

payload.body:
Motivation: Customers observed hard reservation churn when short spikes used up committed slots, causing aggressive decommits and long tail latency. This PR introduces the Commitment Softening Adapter and Burst Tempering Operator to reduce churn and provide predictable sustained throughput guarantees while preserving headroom for transient bursts. Design summary: 1) Commitment Softening Adapter (controller) applies a dynamically-smoothed effective_commitment value per tenant. It blends the tenant's raw reservation with a time-weighted EWMA and a configurable softness window so short spikes do not immediately drive the committed allocation. 2) Burst Tempering Operator is a runtime admission-layer policy that enforces a short-term burst budget token bucket for each tenant backed by a decaying escrow. When a tenant exhausts its burst escrow the operator signals a gentle throttle path and coordinates with the autoscaler to request transient warm capacity instead of immediate hard decommit. 3) Telemetry hooks: we emit new metrics tenant_effective_commitment, burst_escrow_level, burst_tempering_actions, and commit_softening_delta. These are annotated with percentile labels and exported to the existing tenant-utilization-sink. Backwards compatibility: default softness window is disabled (0s) for tenants without opt-in; cluster-wide default set in feature flag softening.enabled=false. Configuration: operator settings exposed via CRD fields and Redwood Console feature flags: softness_window_ms, softness_alpha, burst_escrow_capacity_tokens, escrow_decay_ms, burst_tempering_threshold_pct, emergency_fallback_policy. Implementation notes: admission path changes are minimal and gated behind feature flags. We add a lightweight cache in the autoscaler for effective_commitment to avoid N round-trips, TTL aligned with softness_window. The adapter runs as a separate controller to keep responsibility boundaries clear and allow per-tenant opt-in rollout. Tests and validation: unit tests for EWMA blending and escrow decay, e2e synthetic-driver scenario that simulates 100 tenants with mixed bursty/sustained patterns, and a perf canary on a subset of Dedicated fleet using 3k QPS synthetic traffic. The canary showed 18% reduction in decommits and 12% tail latency improvement at p99 for tenants that opt in. Rollout plan: feature-flagged rollout, start with internal customers and 5 pilot tenants, then staged ramp to 25% of production tenants, monitor commit_softening_delta and burst_tempering_actions, watch for increased cold-starts and warm-pool pressure, and set rollback threshold if sustained decommits > baseline + 5% for 30m. Related work: builds on warm-pool heuristics from ENG-2187 and leverages util reporting contracts introduced in ENG-3310. Linear: ENG-5492, ENG-5511. Jira: SUP-2229 (customer incident that motivated this). Breaking change: no. Security: no new surface area beyond standard CRD RBAC. Notes: this description compresses design, configuration, testing, rollout, telemetry, and related tickets into one narrative.
Marco Chen: Please clarify how the softness window interacts with autoscaler TTLs. If we have a long softness window will the autoscaler underprovision?
Priya Kaur: The adapter exposes the effective_commitment via the autoscaler cache TTL which we set to min(softness_window, 30s) by default. Autoscaler reacts to effective_commitment rather than raw reservation so it will not overreact to short spikes.
Aisha Gupta: I worry about warm-pool pressure and billing spikes when we request transient warm capacity instead of decommit. Can we cap transient requests?
Priya Kaur: Added burst_escrow_capacity_tokens and a cluster cap parameter. The operator will not request more warm capacity than escrow_cap*2 within a rolling minute. Also console exposes transient-request-cap.
Daniel Ortiz: Tests look good; can we add a stress test that flips softening.enabled=true/false under load to ensure stability?
Priya Kaur: Added flip-state stress harness in integration tests and validated no panics; included in canary run notes.
Author: this PR intentionally keeps default softening disabled to avoid surprising tenants; pilot rollout is recommended.
Perf note: canary data attached to PR pipeline artifacts (see integration-tests link) shows reduced decommits and improved tail latency for opt-in tenants.
Ops note: monitor telem metrics tenant_effective_commitment and burst_escrow_level during ramp, plus dedicated warm-pool utilization dashboard updated.
Introduce Commitment Softening Adapter (opt-in) and Burst Tempering Operator to reduce reservation churn and improve p99 latency for bursty tenants. Default disabled. Configurable via CRD and Console feature flags.

payload.body:
Motivation: Clients of the OpenAI compatibility shim and our native API have been handling rate-limit responses inconsistently due to differing header shapes and an unbounded Retry-After policy coming from the gateway. This causes two classes of customer-facing issues: (1) clients requeue aggressively on short windows and get immediate subsequent 429s, or conversely back off for excessively long windows; (2) tool/function call semantics that trigger side effects have no well-defined client-facing idempotency guidance, which makes it hard for callers to safely retry streaming or tool-invocation failures.

This PR does three things in a single change set to improve API robustness and cross-compatibility: 1) Clamp and canonize Retry-After semantics across the gateway and OpenAI shim, 2) Standardize response header names and structured error codes for rate/limit conflicts, and 3) Add a documented idempotency contract for tool/function calls exposed via function-calling tooling to make retries safe and observable.

What changed (high level):
- Introduced a configurable Retry-After clamping policy in gateway/rate_limiter.go. By default Retry-After values returned to clients are clamped to [1s, 120s] unless tenant overrides are configured. The gateway still observes internal longer windows for internal routing, but the outward-facing header is normalized to prevent pathological client backoffs.
- Canonicalized rate headers in adapter/openai_headers.go: we now set both X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After, plus an optional X-RateLimit-Reset (unix epoch seconds) for callers that prefer deterministic resets. Header names are intentionally additive to preserve OpenAI-compat where present.
- Introduced structured error codes (api_error.code) on HTTP JSON error responses and an OpenAI-mapping table so that clients get consistent strings like "rate_limit.exceeded", "rate_limit.in_flight", "tool.execution_conflict", and "request.timeout". The response shape maintains the OpenAI-compatible fields but adds a top-level "code" key for programmatic checks.
- Tool/function calling: added an explicit idempotency contract for tool invocations (api/tool_invoker.go). Callers may opt-in to a per-invocation Idempotency-Key header. When present, the invoker guarantees at-least-once semantics but deduplicates executions for the lifetime of the stored key (default 5 minutes). If the tool is side-effectful and cannot be deduplicated, the invoker returns 409 with code "tool.execution_conflict" and details explaining the partial state and a suggested retry window.
- Streaming stability: improved backpressure handling in the OpenAI shim streaming adapter (adapter/streaming_backpressure.go) so that Retry-After is not emitted mid-stream; instead we surface well-formed terminal error events with structured codes. This reduces ambiguous client behaviour on half-closed streams.
- Tests and docs: added e2e tests for corner cases and updated docs in docs/openai_compat.md and docs/tool_idempotency.md.

Checklist (approx):
- [x] Gateway clamping implementation and feature flag
- [x] OpenAI header canonicalization and compatibility layer
- [x] Structured error codes + mapping table
- [x] Tool invoker idempotency flow + 409 semantics
- [x] Streaming adapter adjustments to avoid mid-stream Retry-After emissions
- [x] Unit and integration tests
- [x] Docs (OpenAI shim + tooling idempotency)

Backwards compatibility and migration notes:
- Existing clients will continue to receive OpenAI-compatible fields. We avoid removing headers; instead we add canonical ones. The only visible change is the clamped Retry-After maximum and the presence of a programmatic "code" field in error responses. To minimize surprise we gate the clamping behind a runtime toggle that is enabled for new tenants and rolled out to existing tenants over 2 weeks.

Operational notes:
- Default clamping upper bound is configurable via env REDWOOD_RATE_RETRY_MAX_SECONDS (default 120). Tenants with strict regulatory requirements can opt out via tenant config.
- Tool idempotency store uses our existing short-lived cache (KV store) with a 5 minute TTL default; this is tunable per-tenant for high-volume tool callers.

Why this approach?
- Clamping aligns client semantics and avoids extreme backoffs.
- Structured codes give deterministic programmatic behaviour for SDKs and customers migrating from other APIs.
- Explicit idempotency contract makes tool retries safe without forcing consumers to build custom locking.

Related work: Linear ENG-5123 (rate semantics audit), PM-241 (compatibility migration), prior PRs that touched Retry-After and idempotency surfaced behaviour.

Testing and rollout:
- Unit and integration tests added under tests/ (simulate short/long Retry-After, tool retry races, streaming mid-error).
- Feature-flagged rollout to a small subset of tenants, followed by metrics observation (rate.limit.adjustment, tool.idempotency.hits, streaming.errors).

If anything needs to be split out before merge (size concerns), I can extract the header canonicalization into a follow-up, but reviewers requested keeping the end-to-end semantics visible in this single PR for quicker verification in the staging environment.
Miguel Torres (2025-07-21): Strongly 👍 on clamping. One operational question: can we emit both Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Reset? Author: yes, both are emitted; Retry-After is clamped and Reset is authoritative epoch time.
Laura Chen (2025-07-22): Tool idempotency looks good, but we need an explicit note in docs that 409 semantics may include partial execution metadata. Author: added docs/tool_idempotency.md with suggested client behavior and example responses.
Samir Bhandari (2025-07-24): CI flake on e2e intermittent; re-ran and green. Also requested a small change to log metric when dedupe hits occur. Author: added metric tool.idempotency.hits in pkg/metrics.
Miguel Torres (2025-07-28): Approved after minor nits addressed.
- Normalize rate-limit headers and clamp Retry-After to an adjustable default max (120s).
- Add X-RateLimit-Reset (epoch) and stable error code field for programmatic checks.
- Define idempotency-key semantics for tool/function calls; returns 409 with code 'tool.execution_conflict' for non-dedupable conflicts.
- Streaming adapter no longer emits Retry-After mid-stream; terminal structured errors are emitted instead.
Rollout is feature-flagged. Watch metrics: rate.limit.adjustment, tool.idempotency.hits, streaming.errors. Default Retry-After max is 120s; change via REDWOOD_RATE_RETRY_MAX_SECONDS env or tenant opt-out.
SDKs should prefer checking top-level 'code' on errors for programmatic handling; SDKs may map 'rate_limit.exceeded' to backoff strategies and treat 'tool.execution_conflict' as non-idempotent conflict with suggested retry delay extracted from error details.

Context: customers asked for clearer schema validation behavior when using response_format and for better UX when streaming partially-invalid structured outputs. This PR introduces a negotiated strictness mode with developer hints, a human-friendly error mapping layer, and safer streaming semantics to preserve tool/function-calling integration. Motivation: previously streaming clients would receive raw JSON errors or abrupt disconnects when schema validation failed mid-stream and tool-calls could be interleaved in invalid states. Goals: 1) let callers express a preference (response_format.schema_version + response_format.strict_hint) without breaking compatibility, 2) emit deterministic machine-level error frames and friendlier human-facing diagnostics, 3) ensure tool/function calls remain fenced and either committed or cleanly aborted on schema failure, 4) keep OpenAI-compat adapter behavior backward compatible for v1/chat and completions. What changed (high level): added a response_format.hint header and an enum for strict_hint (prefer_coercion|strict|soft), implemented a negotiation step in the compatibility layer that chooses coercion/retry/fallback strategies, introduced a "schema-error-frame" streaming chunk type with an attached "human_message" string for client UX, and added fences around tool_call lifecycle so partial outputs don't trigger tool execution. API surface: new optional fields in request payload: response_format.schema_version (string), response_format.strict_hint (string), response_format.hint_metadata (string). The OpenAI-compatibility adapter maps these into internal negotiation decisions while preserving existing v1 endpoints when these fields are absent. Streaming semantics: when a schema violation is detected mid-stream the runtime emits a schema-error-frame then either attempts one soft coercion pass (when prefer_coercion is set) or terminates the stream with a final_error_frame. For strict mode the stream halts immediately and the model output is captured as a diagnostic artifact available via the execution id. Tool/function calling: tool calls are now gated behind a committed-output marker; the runtime will not forward a tool_call to the tool process until a checkpoint confirms the preceding structured tokens conform to the schema or until strict_hint allows speculative tool execution. This prevents side effects from partially-invalid outputs. Error mapping: introduced a compact error taxonomy (schema_mismatch, coercion_failure, stream_truncation, tool_call_fenced, adapter_incompatible) and each error includes a short human_message and actionable_hint. Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged when response_format fields are omitted. Testing: unit tests for negotiation logic, integration tests for streaming error frames and tool fences, e2e with OpenAI-compat endpoints. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind ff/structured-negotiation for 2 weeks, default to opt-in via header. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked - [x] unit tests - [x] integration tests - [x] docs updated - [x] feature flag added - [ ] perf soak in staging

Maya Thompson (reply): Added ff/structured-negotiation to allow opt-in legacy behavior. Migration notes updated in docs/api/response_format.md.

payload.body:
Add circuit breaker + fallback behavior around KMS calls to prevent cascading latency/5xx during KMS degradation. Operators will see explicit KMS_CIRCUIT_OPEN errors and new metrics for breaker state/transitions.
Context: During recent KMS throttling/timeouts (see SUP-19377), application-side retries amplified load and created a request storm against KMS, worsening tail latency and elevating 5xx. We’ve already standardized timeouts/retries in the KMS wrapper (PR #18421); this change adds circuit breaking + a documented degrade/fallback policy so we fail fast and shed load instead of stampeding KMS.

What this PR does:
- Adds a per-key (key ARN) circuit breaker in the shared KMS client wrapper with CLOSED/OPEN/HALF_OPEN states.
- Introduces a fallback mode policy for decrypt/envelope operations:
  - If circuit is OPEN: do not call KMS; attempt to serve from in-memory DEK cache if present (bounded TTL, non-persistent); otherwise fail fast with a mapped KMSUnavailable error (no retries).
  - Encrypt/new key generation paths: fail fast when OPEN (no cache fallback), returning a distinct error class to avoid queuing / retry loops.
- Caps concurrency to KMS with a small in-flight semaphore (prevents spikes during HALF_OPEN).
- Emits metrics + logs needed for on-call triage:
  - redwood.kms.circuit_breaker.state (gauge)
  - redwood.kms.circuit_breaker.open_total / half_open_total (counters)
  - redwood.kms.circuit_breaker.blocked_total (counter)
  - Structured log fields: kms.key_arn, kms.op, kms.error_category, kms.circuit_state, kms.circuit_open_reason
- Adds unit tests with fake clock to validate: state transitions, half-open probe behavior, and that OPEN short-circuits before any retry logic.
- Documents the operational behavior in-code (module docs + inline comment block) with explicit non-goals: we are not changing cryptographic primitives, not persisting plaintext key material, and not altering key rotation semantics.

SRE-requested changes included here:
- HALF_OPEN uses jittered probe scheduling to avoid synchronized thundering herd after an incident clears.
- OPEN duration is bounded; we re-check via controlled probes rather than staying OPEN indefinitely.
- Separate breaker keys for decrypt vs metadata calls (avoid a metadata blip taking down decrypt).
- Explicit error mapping for OPEN-short-circuit -> KMS_CIRCUIT_OPEN (distinct from timeout), and we do not apply caller retry policy to this class.

Config (defaults are safe for prod):
- kms.circuit_breaker.enabled=true
- kms.circuit_breaker.failure_threshold=8 (rolling window)
- kms.circuit_breaker.window=30s
- kms.circuit_breaker.open_cooldown=45s (+/- 20% jitter)
- kms.circuit_breaker.half_open_max_in_flight=2
- kms.circuit_breaker.cache_fallback_ttl=5m (decrypt only; bounded, memory-only)

Rollout notes:
- This is behind a feature flag kms.circuit_breaker.enabled (on by default in staging; gradual enable in prod per-region).
- Please coordinate with ENG-4828 (dashboard/alerts) before broad prod enablement.

Test plan:
- Unit tests for breaker transitions and short-circuit behavior.
- Staging: simulate KMS 429/timeout using the fault injection harness; verify: request rate to KMS drops sharply once OPEN, p95 latency stabilizes, and error responses are consistent and actionable.

Follow-ups (not in this PR):
- Update runbook playbook examples to include KMS_CIRCUIT_OPEN and recommended mitigations (ENG-4821 docs workstream).
- Extend integration tests to assert breaker behavior under sustained throttling (ENG-4825).

Screenshots / evidence:
- Added a short “expected graphs” note to help validate in staging: look for breaker_open_total increments and a drop in kms.request_total during simulated failures.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): The high-level approach looks right, but we need to guarantee that when the circuit is OPEN we do not accidentally enter the retry loop. Can you ensure OPEN short-circuits before retry middleware and emits a distinct error class so clients don’t retry?
Rafael Mendes (author): Yep. I moved the breaker check to the top of the wrapper call path (before retry/backoff). Added error KMS_CIRCUIT_OPEN and the retry classifier now treats it as non-retryable. Added tests to assert 0 KMS calls while OPEN.
Allison Grant: Metrics need to be consistent with our naming/tags. Please add key_arn as a tag but also cap cardinality. We’ve been burned by raw ARNs exploding series count.
Rafael Mendes (author): Good catch. I’m tagging by key_alias when present (normalized) and falling back to a hashed key_id label (first 12 chars) rather than full ARN. Full ARN is only in logs/traces.
Marcus Lin: Please confirm the cache fallback is memory-only and bounded TTL. We should not persist plaintext DEKs or extend lifetime beyond what’s already acceptable.
Rafael Mendes (author): Confirmed. This uses the existing in-memory DEK cache, TTL default 5m, and is only used for decrypt when circuit is OPEN. No persistent storage; no change to crypto primitives.
Ethan Park: For control-plane metadata calls (DescribeKey / GetKeyPolicy etc.), can we isolate the breaker so those failures don’t take down decrypt? We’ve seen IAM/permission issues on metadata while decrypt is fine.
Rafael Mendes (author): Implemented separate breaker keys per op class: decrypt/encrypt vs metadata. Also added separate metrics by op_class to help diagnose.
Nadia Rahman: CI integration-smoke failed once with flake in the fault injector. Please rerun and link the staging run output.
Rafael Mendes (author): Reran; green now. Linked the staging harness run in the check output; also reduced probe frequency in the test to avoid timing sensitivity.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): One more change request: half-open probes should be jittered; otherwise after a regional KMS blip every instance will probe at once when cooldown ends.
Rafael Mendes (author): Added +/-20% jitter to open_cooldown and randomized initial probe delay per process. Added a test that validates probe schedule uses jittered duration bounds.
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Approved with the jitter + non-retryable error mapping. This should materially reduce blast radius during throttling events.
Allison Grant: Approved after the tag cardinality fix.
payload.title: Implement KMS circuit breaker + fallback mode to prevent retry storms during KMS incidents

Introduces an adaptive throttle calibration controller that smooths SLO violations by adjusting tenant-level throttle setpoints with a PID-inspired feedback loop. Improves stability during short regional surges and reduces oscillation between shed and reopen states. Backward compatible; default disabled behind feature flag slo_throttle_cal_v1.
Context and motivation: We continue to see short, noisy spikes in tail latency that cause reactive load-shedding to oscillate (shed → reopen → shed). That behaviour produces high churn for long-running KV-cached sessions and causes tenant-visible error bursts. This PR introduces a controller that observes smoothed SLO deltas and proactively nudges tenant throttle setpoints using a calibrated feedback rule (proportional + integral term) to reduce oscillation and preferentially favor short recovery windows over aggressive immediate shedding.

Goals: reduce oscillatory shedding across regional surges, shorten recovery jitter, keep per-tenant throughput close to target SLO without causing large error spikes, and provide safe rollout controls (feature flag + canary policy).

What this changes: single continuous change set that touches the regional shed executor, the tenant throttler, and the telemetry pipeline: 1) new controller module (slo_throttle_calibrator) implementing a lightweight feedback loop with configurable windowing and rate caps; 2) tenancy API extension for a soft-setpoint (soft_throttle_hint) that the controller can update without overriding operator-set hard limits; 3) metric exports (slo_delta_smoothed, throttle_hint_applied, hint_conflict_count) and traces for decision points; 4) conservative default tuning and a runtime feature flag slo_throttle_cal_v1.

Design notes: the controller operates on a 10s aggregation window by default, computes an exponentially-weighted-smoothed SLO delta, applies a proportional + integral correction (bounded by per-tenant rate of change), and writes a hint to the tenancy config server. The actual enforcement still runs through the existing throttler which treats hints as advisory unless an account-level opt-in flag is set. This minimizes risk while still enabling meaningful smoothing.

Rollout and safety: feature gated behind slo_throttle_cal_v1. Plan: enable in internal canary (5% traffic) for 24h, inspect metrics and traces (tail-latency, hint_conflict_count, shed/reopen frequency); advance to 25% if stable, then 100% across non-enterprise accounts. Enterprise/Dedicated customers default to off unless they opt-in via console toggle. We added an emergency kill-switch that reverts hint application in <1s.

Testing and validation: unit tests for controller math and boundary conditions; integration harness that replays historical surge workloads (simulated tenant skews) to verify reduced shed oscillations; chaos test exercise where a region loses 20% capacity for 3 minutes — we observe 32% fewer reopen events and 18% lower 95th latency volatility in the canary. CI exercises lint, unit, and end-to-end replay job.

Observability: new dashboards (SLO -> Throttle Calibration) and alert: slo_calib_conflict_rate > 0.5% for 15m. Telemetry includes an event stream of hint writes to support postmortems.

Backward compatibility & migration: controller writes only to soft_throttle_hint. Existing operator-set hard_limits remain authoritative. If hint_conflict_count grows, controller backs off and emits a diagnostic trace.

Related work: builds on ENG-2876 (tenant throttler refactor) and ENG-3011 (telemetry v2).

Checklist: 
- [x] Controller implementation + unit tests
- [x] Throttler integration (advisory hint handling)
- [x] Telemetry exports and dashboard skeleton
- [x] Canary rollout plan and feature flag
- [x] Docs (internal runbook)

Potential risks: over-aggressive integral accumulation during long sustained under-provisioning (mitigated by anti-windup and bounded integral), unintended interference with operator-initiated maintenance (mitigated by hard limit precedence), and metric skew due to cross-tenant aggregation (we added per-tenant bucketing).

Next steps after merge: schedule a 24h canary, monitor the new metrics, and collect two incident-free days before wider rollout. If we see hint_conflict_count spikes, revert via feature flag immediately.
Miguel Rivera: Please add a brief note about anti-windup strategy and why integral is bounded to X in the controller config. Also add unit tests for integral boundary conditions.
Claire Zhang: Added anti-windup with per-tenant cap and tests for saturation cases. See commit 'fix: handle tenant hard_limit precedence and exponential-backoff on conflict'.
Asha Patel: Can we ensure the telemetry export uses per-tenant sampling to avoid cardinality explosion? If so, include sampling knobs in the config.
Claire Zhang: Telemetry now uses per-tenant bucketing and a 0.1% default sampling for detailed event stream. Documented in telemetry/metrics/exports.go.
Tom Becker: Approving pending canary plan and ensuring emergency kill-switch is wired to ops console. Left a minor nit around naming in the proto; not blocking.

Motivation: provide a small, opinionated orchestrator that wires tenant-level savings templates (batching, cache ttl heuristics, quant profiles) into runtime defaults and exposes a dry-run savings estimator. This PR adds a 'Savings Playbook' concept to the econ service to make tenant defaults declarative and traceable. Scope: 1) orchestrator service and CLI to apply per-tenant templates; 2) a lightweight cache-thermostat controller that adjusts prefix caching TTLs based on recent hit-rate/latency; 3) a small set of curated quantization profiles tied to tenant SLAs; 4) a dry-run estimator that simulates cost delta for a template without changing production routing. Checklist: - [x] add SavingsPlaybook API and storage model - [x] implement cache-thermostat with safe ramping - [x] provide three starter tenant templates (startup, scale, enterprise) - [x] wire telemetry (savings_estimate, applied_templates, cache_ttl_adjustments) - [x] add CLI dry-run mode and unit tests - [x] docs and examples in docs/savings-playbook.md How to review: focus on the orchestrator safety gates (rollback window, manual approval for >20% estimated change) and cache-thermostat ramp algorithm. Related: ENG-2041 implements templated defaults workstream; SUP-8721 surfaced a customer request to automate tenant defaults. Motivation: Intermittent corruption was observed when multiple eventstream fragments arrived with overlapping logical epochs, causing partial JSON payloads to be incorrectly attributed to adjacent tool/function-call events. This manifested as truncated toolcall objects and misordered assistant tokens in downstream consumers. This PR introduces an epoch alignment pass in the SSE reassembler, a soft handoff window for function-call sentinels, and heuristics to preserve JSON object boundaries across chunk boundaries. The changes reduce the chance of partial JSON merges and avoid emitting duplicate delimiters when fragments overlap. Summary of changes: 1) Add an epoch-indexed buffer that tags incoming fragments with an epoch token derived from the stream header and sequence offset. 2) Introduce a soft handoff window that delays function/tool-call emission for up to 8ms when an overlapping fragment could contain remaining sentinel bytes. This is a conservative, configurable default to balance latency and correctness. 3) Implement a JSON boundary guard that favors completing a top-level JSON object when the fragment tail suggests a continuation, rather than slicing and emitting an incomplete token. 4) Update the SSE parser unit tests and add an integration scenario that replays interleaved fragments with simulated reorder and partial loss. 5) Add telemetry spans and metrics (sse.epoch_gap_recovered, sse.handoff_delays_ms.histogram, sse.partial_json_rescue) to aid future debugging and rollouts. Backwards compatibility: Default handoff window is small and can be disabled via feature flag sse.handoff.window_ms. No public API changes. Risk: Slight increase in median streaming latency in pathological overlap cases due to the handoff window; metrics are included to monitor impact. Related work: builds on prior fragment-reassembly work in ENG-1987 and complements the partial-json-rescue experiments in ENG-2345. The PR includes a canary rollout plan and escalation steps for reverting the handoff flag if latency regressions exceed thresholds.
Arjun Patel: The epoch tagging looks good but we should ensure we never grow the buffer unbounded. Please add compaction invariants to the reassembler and a max_bytes config.
Maya Thompson: Added compaction and a soft limit of 4MB with heap-clearing behavior in the next commit. Also added a failing unit test that reproduced prior OOM in CI.
Sofia Morales: The handoff window looks conservative. Can we make it adaptive based on observed fragment gaps reported by the telemetry?
Maya Thompson: Added a follow-up TODO and config hook; plan to iterate in a follow-up PR after rollout metrics are gathered.
Ben Cho: Tests look thorough. Please add a short note in the changelog about the feature-flag and how to disable it for dedicated/private installs.
Maya Thompson: Changelog entry added to docs/rfc/sse-epoch-handoff.md and included in the release_notes field.
Improve SSE stream resilience by aligning overlapping fragments to logical epochs and introducing a configurable soft handoff window to prevent partial JSON and tool-call truncation. Enable via feature flag sse.handoff.window_ms. Metrics and tracing added to monitor behavior.

Summary: This PR emits structured, machine-readable audit events for rollout auto-decisions (AUTO_PAUSE, AUTO_ROLLBACK, AUTO_SUPPRESS) onto the existing audit event stream. These events are consumed by Console backend, incident-bot, and downstream retention/export tooling.

Motivation: As we wire SLO breach evaluation into the rollout controller, we need a durable and queryable record of what happened (decision, inputs, and who/what initiated it). This enables (1) Console “why did we rollback?” views, (2) incident notifications with correlation IDs, and (3) compliance/auditability expectations for Dedicated/Private customers.

What’s included: - New event type: rollout.auto_action (versioned schema v1) - Correlation IDs: propagate rollout_correlation_id across evaluator -> controller -> executor; include decision_correlation_id per decision emission - Monitor linkage: include monitor_provider + monitor_ids and monitor_definition_url (when available) for the evaluated SLOs - Policy linkage: include policy_id + policy_version (hash) used for the decision - Decision details: action (pause|rollback|suppress), scope (route/model_version/region/customer_tier), and suppression reason (admin override, incident window, telemetry stale, min sample not met) - Privacy/safety: no prompt text, no customer payloads; IDs only. Metrics are referenced via snapshot_ref (pointer) rather than embedding raw time series.

Notes: - Schema is designed to align with ADR-0128 requirements (required fields + retention constraints). - This PR does not change controller behavior; it only emits events when other components call AuditEmitter.emitAutoAction(...). (Behavioral changes live in the controller hook PR.)

Testing: - Unit tests for schema serialization + required fields - Integration test with local event-bus harness validating routing key + consumer compatibility

Rollout: Feature-flagged behind audit.emit_rollout_auto_actions (default off). Enabled in staging in follow-up once Console API consumer is deployed.

Follow-ups: - Wire Console timeline UI to decision_correlation_id filtering (ENG-4833) - Add alert routing to include decision_correlation_id in Slack notification (ENG-4872)
Allison Grant (review): Can we avoid embedding any metric values directly to keep event size + privacy under control? Suggest making snapshot_ref required and explicitly documenting that it points to Grafana/explorer with RBAC.

Felix Schneider (author): Agreed. Updated schema: snapshot_ref is now required for breach-driven decisions, and we only include high-level booleans for evaluation gating (min_sample_met, telemetry_stale) rather than numeric p99 values. Added docs + tests.

Kevin Osei (review): For INT-8832/RBAC: ensure suppression events do not leak admin identity beyond actor_id (internal) and that actor_type is constrained. Also confirm we’re not including customer identifiers beyond customer_tier.

Felix Schneider (author): Implemented actor_type enum (SYSTEM|ADMIN|SERVICE) and actor_id is the internal principal id. No customer_id/org_id in payload; scope includes customer_tier only. Added a lint check to reject forbidden labels.

Jada Williams (review): Partition key should be rollout_id (not route) to preserve ordering for a given rollout. Also can we include the step_id to correlate to state machine transitions?

Felix Schneider (author): Updated publisher to use rollout_id as partition key. Added step_id and step_name fields; step_id is stable across retries. Also added idempotency guard: emit once per decision_correlation_id.

Logan Wright (review): Please document expected QPS and event volume. Event stream team wants to confirm topic retention and size constraints.

Felix Schneider (author): Added doc section with volume estimate: <= 1 event per decision per rollout step (typical 0-3), plus suppress/override events. Included payload size budget (<2KB) and confirmed current audit topic retention (30d) is sufficient for MVP.

Allison Grant (approval): Looks good with snapshot_ref requirement and ordering fix.

Kevin Osei (approval): Approved; privacy constraints satisfied.

Jada Williams (approval): Approved; thanks for step_id and partitioning change.

Motivation: Production observability is overwhelmed by full-span captures for low-value invocations which inflate storage and increase query latency. This PR introduces two cooperating subsystems: (1) an adaptive span prioritizer that scores and marks spans for deep collection based on cost, error-signals, and session importance; (2) a low-priority 'cost-shadow' mirroring sink that asynchronously mirrors token-level cost and phase metrics to a cold store for long-tail analysis without touching the hot metrics pipeline. Goals: reduce full-trace ingestion volume by targeting high-signal invocations, preserve ability to analyze rare expensive cases via mirrored shadow data, avoid any change to customer-facing metrics semantics. What changed: added prioritizer service with policy rules, sampling heuristics and pluggable scoring; introduced a new telemetry sink that mirrors a compact cost-only envelope to S3/Cold ES; added routing and safe-fallback so if the prioritizer is down we default to legacy sampling; added end-to-end integration tests and dashboard updates. Checklist: [x] prioritizer core logic implemented; [x] cost-shadow sink + backpressure handling; [x] feature flag gate (observability.prioritizer.enabled=false by default); [x] docs and runbook; [x] infra helm values for toggling mirror retention; [x] e2e tests and load test validation. Rollout plan: feature gated rollout to internal canary tenants for 2 weeks, monitor SLOs and ingestion-queue lag, then enable for low-volume customers and increase. Linear: ENG-9231 implements prioritizer rules; ENG-13104 wires mirror sink and storage lifecycle. Related work: builds on prior token-cost-attribution infra (see ENG-7425) and complements the prefetched-kv warmup traces work. Risks and mitigations: risk of losing rare-context detail if prioritizer mis-scores; mitigation includes conservative defaults, a short-term default TTL on mirrors and a manual override to force-capture by trace ID. Backwards compatibility: hot metrics stream and existing dashboards unchanged unless mirror flag enabled. Performance: local microbench and canary load tests show ~35% reduction in full-span ingest and <3% CPU overhead on proxy path while mirroring adds negligible tail-latency due to async buffering. Merge notes: squash-merged after addressing final review comments and flaky test re-run.
Liam: asked for clearer failure-mode semantics and a short-circuit when the mirror sink falls behind; Noah: requested additional unit tests for policy edge-cases and tighter typing on sink envelopes; Marisol: asked to add a runbook section for an operator to force-capture a trace ID and to confirm retention requirements for mirrors. Author replies: clarified backpressure behavior and added an emergency capture API; added requested tests and typed encoder; documented retention defaults. CI: initial lint found style nits, one flaky integration test 'test_cost_shadow_integration' failed on first run due to race on bucket teardown — retried and passed. Approvals: reviewers approved after fixes. Merge: squash merge into main with feature flag off by default.
payload.title: Add adaptive span prioritizer and cost-shadow mirroring

Context: Sales Engineering needs a repeatable way to stand up a production-like “demo tenant” (org + projects + routes + model pins) and reset it between demos without manual Console clicking. This PR adds an internal CLI command to bootstrap the demo tenant in an idempotent way and with explicit safety rails to prevent accidental execution against non-demo environments.

What’s included:
- New CLI command: `rw demo bootstrap` (internal-only) that creates/updates:
  - Demo org `redwood-demo`
  - Projects: `core-api`, `prod-econ`, `reliability`, `observability`
  - Routes for each project with pinned model versions (via route config), and baseline policy stubs for fallback (full policy enforced in ENG-4840)
  - Seeded API keys (scoped) for SE usage (key scoping tightened further in ENG-4855)
- Idempotent creation semantics: re-running the command is safe; resources are looked up by stable external IDs + naming convention, then patched to match the desired spec.
- Environment guards:
  - Requires `--env demo` OR `REDWOOD_DEMO_TENANT=1`.
  - Refuses to run if control-plane reports a non-demo org already exists with the same slug, or if billing account is not `billing-sandbox`.
  - Requires explicit `--confirm` for destructive updates (route overwrite, key rotation).
- Dry-run mode: `--dry-run` prints intended actions and exits non-zero if drift is detected (useful for pre-demo checks).
- Structured output: `--format json` emits a machine-readable summary used by the runbook/healthcheck followups.

Why this approach:
- Deterministic bootstrap makes demos resilient to Console/UI changes and avoids “dashboard emptiness” from missing routes/projects.
- Idempotency + drift reporting supports quick resets between demos and parallel demo namespaces (later work in ENG-4894).
- Guardrails reduce the blast radius risk (learned from prior internal RBAC/environment confusion in INT-993).

Testing:
- Unit tests for spec->API calls mapping, idempotent behavior, and env guard refusal logic.
- Manual: ran against `demo-control-plane` and re-ran bootstrap 5x to validate no duplicate org/projects/routes; verified output summary consumed by SE runbook.

Rollout notes:
- Behind internal feature flag `internal_tools.demo_bootstrap_cli`.
- Documentation stub added to internal docs (full runbook lives in Confluence; Elliot will link once published).

Follow-ups:
- ENG-4833: synthetic traffic generator to populate Console dashboards.
- ENG-4840: formalize model pinning + safe fallback policy and alerting on catalog drift.
- ENG-4855: key rotation + least privilege tightening.

Add presubmit cost estimator to reduce CI spend and a reproducible dependency-snapshot stage; split lint into fast/type/style lanes and update CI docs.
Context: Our CI costs and noisy presubmit matrix have grown as we added more integration shards and cross-language test profiles. This PR introduces a lightweight presubmit cost estimator and a reproducible dependency-snapshot stage to reduce unnecessary full-matrix runs and make premerge runs easier to reason about.

What this change does: Adds a new presubmit analyzer that performs a fast file-change impact analysis, maps changed paths to a recommended test profile and an estimated CI compute cost (seconds/minutes and USD-equivalent) based on runner profiles. The estimator runs as an early job and writes decision labels that downstream composite workflows use to select a narrow test subset (fast lint/type checks by default, full integration matrix only when high-impact files are touched). Also: introduces a dependency-snapshot stage that records package manager lock/metadata (go.mod + sum, poetry.lock, package-lock.json) into an artifact and a short reproducibility check to ensure lockfile parsing succeeds across CI images.

Secondary changes: Split lint pipeline into three targeted lanes (fast-style, typecheck, and slow-regex-safety) so the estimator can opt into only the lanes that matter. Bumped a few CI helper deps (ci-tools v2.8.0, premerge-sdk v1.5.1) and canonicalized the runner profiles used for cost estimation. Updated docs/ci/presubmit.md with guidance and rollout flags.

Why: We observed a median presubmit runner time of 9m per PR for the typical change; internal A/B on ~700 PRs showed this estimator plus selective lanes reduced aggregate CI minutes by ~12% without increasing post-merge failures. The dependency snapshot reduces flakiness caused by transient registry differences during gated builds.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for the estimator logic (path-to-profile mapping and cost model) + integration test that exercises the label gating (simulated PR event). Ran a two-week canary on the infra and platform repos with feature-flagged enabled; metrics collected in the console show a 10-15% drop in minutes billed and no observed increase in merged-breakages.

Rollout plan: Feature-flag default off. Initial rollout to infra and sdk teams for 48h canary, then +engineering team. After telemetry review enable by default and remove flag in 6 weeks if stable. A one-button revert lives in the console to disable estimator gating across repos.

Notes and followups: We will follow up with an RFC to make the estimator configurable per-repo (thresholds and cost model). We also plan to add an optional heuristics ML model in a future PR to improve precision for borderline changes. Links: Linear ENG-2123 for estimator algorithm, ENG-2199 for dependency snapshot work.
Arjun Patel: Nicely scoped; can we make the cost model config per-repo? (requested change)
Maya Chen: yes, added runners.yaml and made config overrideable via repo settings; updated docs (reply)

Summary: This PR introduces a small, cross-platform Go utility (tools/mergestate-prober) that evaluates merge readiness by inspecting recent CI flakiness, re-run counts, and commit graph churn; it also replaces the brittle shell-based release script with a slim, declarative release adapter (cmd/releasectl + releases/*.yaml). Motivation: We've observed multiple late-stage regressions and noisy merges where intermittent CI flakiness or concurrent rollups caused post-merge rollbacks. The goal is not to gate merges aggressively, but to give maintainers a deterministic signal (and optional auto-quarantine) when a PR lands during high churn or when CI instability is present. What changed: 1) New tool: tools/mergestate-prober - Go binary that aggregates: recent check-run reruns, failure rates for top 5 flaky tests, and a small heuristic for merge collisions (multiple dependent PRs touching the same packages). 2) Presubmit split: ci/presubmit/lint-quick.yml (fast rules: formatting, TS typecheck subset, go vet) and ci/presubmit/lint-full.yml (full linters + slower codegen checks). Jobs are orchestrated so quick checks unblock author feedback quickly while full checks run in a separate lane. 3) Release refactor: remove scripts/release.sh and add cmd/releasectl which reads declarative release manifests in /releases and performs staged artifacts, signing, and publishing steps. The adapter has pluggable backends for hosted vs private deployments. 4) Repo hygiene: remove deprecated .ci/cache-tarballs/ and update pnpm-lock.yaml and go.mod to current minimal supported toolchains. 5) CI actions: bump actions/checkout to v4, switch some runners to ubuntu-24.04 images, and add lightweight caching policy to speed quick-lint. Testing and verification: - Unit tests for mergestate-prober (mocked GH API) - Integration smoke run of releasectl against a dry-run registry - Presubmit CI run (quick + full) passed after two minor fixes. Rollout plan: merge to main behind a short feature-flag (MERGESTATE_PROBER=enabled by default for maintainers). We will monitor the new metric (merge_prober/alert_rate) in the Console for two weeks and opt-in the auto-quarantine behavior only if the signal proves accurate. Related: ENG-1427 (CI stability), ENG-1843 (release reliability).
