payload.body:
## Context
We’ve been seeing inflated counts at the top of the activation funnel (signup stage) since the lifecycle growth sprint instrumentation landed. This has been most visible in regions with higher auth callback latency and for users who refresh the console during the post-signup redirect.

Root cause: `signup_completed` was emitted from *two* places:
1) Auth callback handler (server) when we exchange the OAuth/session token
2) Console bootstrap (client) when `currentUser.isNew == true`

In the happy path these happen once each (still bad), but in the presence of retries/refresh, the client-side emission could occur multiple times, leading to 2–4 events per new user. This skewed the funnel conversion rate, especially when computing “% of signups completing first request within 7 days” with naive event counting.

## What changed
- Make the server-side emission the single source of truth for `signup_completed`.
- Remove client-side fallback emission and replace it with a debug-only log (behind an internal flag) to preserve troubleshooting signal without polluting analytics.
- Add idempotency guard on the server event publisher:
  - Dedupes `signup_completed` per `user_id` for a short window (30 minutes) using an event-key in Redis.
  - Also dedupes `activation_signup` alias to avoid re-introducing duplicates via legacy event name.
- Add a regression test for the callback handler to ensure repeated callbacks do not emit additional signup events.

## Why this is safe
- The event is informational/analytics-only (no product logic is gated on it).
- Server is already the canonical place where we know the signup is complete.
- Dedup window is short and keyed by user, so it won’t suppress legitimate re-signups (new user id) or later lifecycle events.

## Validation
### Before
- Sample (2026-01-27 UTC): ~1.82 `signup_completed` events per distinct `user_id` (p50=2, p95=3)
- Funnel dashboard showed occasional >100% “signup → api_key_created” conversion for small cohorts (clear sign of duplication)

### After (staging + prod canary)
- Staging load test (forced refresh + retry): 1.00 `signup_completed` events per distinct `user_id`
- Prod canary (5% of traffic for 3 hours): 1.01 events per distinct `user_id` (small remainder due to legacy clients still in flight)
- Funnel conversion rates returned to expected ranges and the signup stage volume dropped ~35% relative to distinct users (consistent with prior duplication rate)

## Rollout
- Ship as hotfix to `main`
- No migrations
- Dashboard owners: Sergio Costa / Allison Grant are aware; update their sanity-check query to use distinct users as a guardrail until the canary completes.

## Checklist
- [x] Confirmed no downstream systems require client-side emission
- [x] Added tests
- [x] Verified event schema unchanged (only emission sites)
- [x] Coordinated with Growth (Ben Carter) on expected dashboard deltas

Refs:
- INT-3310 (activation funnel discrepancy)
- Lifecycle growth sprint instrumentation (ENG-10492)
- Activation funnel dashboard work (ENG-10533)
Logan Wright (review): Can we confirm we’re not suppressing legitimate replays if a user opens two tabs during signup? Also, why 30 minutes for the dedupe window?
Nadia Rahman (author): Yes—two tabs will hit the same user_id and we *do* want one logical signup event. 30m is meant to cover retries/refreshes around auth callback + console bootstrap; we can tune shorter if you prefer. Also keyed by (event_name,user_id) only, so it won’t affect other funnel events.
Dylan Brooks (review): Removing the client emission makes sense. Any chance older console builds still rely on the client event for experiment cohort assignment?
Nadia Rahman (author): Cohort assignment is via feature flag service on signup timestamp + user id; not tied to this event. Confirmed with Ethan/Benji on ENG-10501 thread; this event is analytics-only.
Paula Mendes (review): Please add a note in the PR about the legacy alias event name (`activation_signup`) so we don’t get bitten again in SQL.
Nadia Rahman (author): Added to “What changed” + validation section; also dedupes both names. Good call.
Logan Wright (review): Test looks good. One suggestion: make the redis key include environment to avoid any weirdness in shared infra.
Nadia Rahman (author): Updated key prefix to include env namespace (already present in redis client config, but now explicit in the key builder).
CI (bot): ✅ build / unit-tests (pass) | ✅ lint (pass) | ✅ console-e2e-smoke (pass)
Dylan Brooks (review): Approved. Let’s monitor funnel dashboard after merge; we should expect a visible drop in signup counts.
Logan Wright (review): Approved.
Paula Mendes (review): Approved after key prefix change.

payload.body:
## Context
As part of the Lifecycle Growth Experiments sprint, we’re increasing volume of onboarding/lifecycle emails. Support has seen an uptick in "didn’t receive onboarding email" and "please stop emailing me" tickets (SUP-24871). We also need a clear, self-serve way for developers to manage email preferences that’s consistent across email + console, and meets CAN-SPAM/GDPR expectations.

This PR adds an Email Preferences page in the Redwood Console and wires lifecycle sends to respect those preferences. It also implements a one-click unsubscribe link suitable for inclusion in the onboarding drip v2 templates.

## What’s included
1) Console UI
- New Settings page: Settings → Notifications → Email preferences
- Users can:
  - Unsubscribe from onboarding/lifecycle emails (transactional-ish but not strictly required for account access)
  - Opt out of marketing announcements
  - View a brief explanation of what each category means
- State persists per user and is reflected immediately in subsequent sends.

2) Backend/API
- Adds `GET /console/api/email-preferences` and `PUT /console/api/email-preferences`
- Adds `GET /unsubscribe` one-click handler used by email templates. The handler accepts a signed token (HMAC) containing user_id + category + issued_at.
- Updates lifecycle send pipeline to enforce suppression:
  - If `lifecycle_onboarding=false`, suppress the onboarding drip
  - If `marketing_announcements=false`, suppress non-onboarding marketing campaigns
  - Transactional/security emails remain unaffected (explicitly not controlled by this page)

3) Telemetry + audit
- Adds events:
  - `email_preferences_viewed`
  - `email_preferences_updated` (includes category + new value)
  - `email_unsubscribe_link_clicked` (category)
- Emits an audit log entry on preference changes for compliance review.

## Why console + one-click unsubscribe?
- Console: gives users a stable place to manage preferences even if the email client blocks images/links.
- One-click: reduces friction and complaint rates; satisfies practical CAN-SPAM expectations; aligns with internal compliance guidance.

## UX notes
- Copy uses approved messaging guidelines: direct language, no dark patterns, clear distinction between onboarding vs marketing.
- We intentionally avoid pre-checked boxes and avoid bundling unrelated preferences.
- Success state is explicit (toast + updated toggle).

## Security & privacy
- Unsubscribe tokens:
  - Signed, not encrypted (payload has no email address; only user_id + category + timestamp)
  - TTL: 30 days
  - Single-use is not enforced (acceptable per legal review); token is category-scoped
- Rate limiting: per-IP on `/unsubscribe` to avoid abuse; returns 200 even if token is invalid/expired (does not reveal user existence).
- Data retention: preference row stored as part of user profile; audit events follow existing retention policy.

## Feature flag / rollout
- UI is guarded behind `lifecycle_growth_email_preferences_console` (on for dogfood + growth cohorts first).
- Send pipeline enforcement is NOT behind a flag (preferences should always be respected when present). Default behavior for users without a preference row is unchanged.

## Testing
- Unit: token signing/verification, category scoping, TTL behavior
- Integration: lifecycle send suppression for onboarding + marketing categories
- E2E (Playwright): navigation to settings page, toggle behavior, persistence

## Screens
- Settings → Notifications → Email preferences (desktop + mobile)
- Unsubscribe landing state (success + optional link to Console preferences)

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- Add “Email preferences” link to the user menu (not just Settings) (tracked in ENG-10518 comments)
- Extend to team-level preferences (org admin) for enterprise accounts (out of scope for sprint)

## Checklist
- [x] Legal/compliance review requested (Michael/Olga)
- [x] Docs/templates PR will include updated footer links (tracked separately)
- [x] Event taxonomy approved by Nadia (see comment thread)
- [x] Dashboard panels will be added in observability pack PR (separate)

References: ENG-10518, PM-659, PM-651, SUP-24871
- Adds an Email preferences surface in Console Settings (opt out of onboarding/lifecycle emails and manage marketing communications)
- Implements one-click unsubscribe endpoint used by lifecycle email templates
- Ensures lifecycle send pipeline honors preferences and logs audit events
Dylan Brooks (requested changes): "Can we ensure the unsubscribe handler doesn’t leak whether a user exists? Also please add rate limiting on the route." Ethan Park (author): Updated handler to always return 200 with a generic success body; added per-IP rate limit middleware + tests.

Marissa Cole (comment): "Copy looks good, but can we clarify that transactional/security emails are not affected? Also move the section above the toggles." Ethan: Adjusted copy + layout; added explicit note and linked to internal help doc.

Tyler Benson (comment): "We need the lifecycle pipeline to emit an event when suppression occurs so we can monitor impact on activation vs deliverability. Can we add `email_send_suppressed`?" Ethan: Added `email_send_suppressed` with reason=`user_preference` and category.

Michael Grant (legal): "Token payload should not include email address; TTL should be reasonable; avoid pre-checked opt-outs." Ethan: Confirmed payload is user_id only; TTL set to 30 days; UI uses explicit toggles defaulting to current state.

Olga Petrov (GDPR): "Add a link to privacy policy and note how to contact support for data requests." Ethan: Added footer link and a short note on data requests.

Logan Wright (analytics): "Event names/properties should match the lifecycle taxonomy doc; ensure dedupe if user toggles quickly." Ethan: Updated to match taxonomy (`email_preferences_updated`), and server-side dedupe on identical updates within 2s.

Approvals: Dylan Brooks ✅, Marissa Cole ✅, Michael Grant ✅, Olga Petrov ✅

Motivation: reduce noisy rollouts during scheduled release windows while improving visibility into risky transitive dependency updates. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: 1) a small, opt-in 'merge-sigil' quiet gate that defers non-urgent merges to configured quiet windows and exposes a lightweight scheduler for release engineers; and 2) a 'dep-curator' CLI that performs fast transitive-dep heuristics, produces a human-readable risk summary, and emits metadata used by the merge gate. Additionally, lint/test pipelines are split into 'quick' and 'strict' profiles so routine changes get fast feedback while release-critical branches still run the full verification.
Diego: Requested unit tests for the dep-curator rule loader and a clearer sample rule. Marked as changes requested.
Ava: Added rule loader tests and expanded default ruleset (see commit b0e7c9a). Included docs showing expected rule schema.
Ethan: Flagged a potential scheduler N+1 when many repos opt in; suggested debouncing and a max-backoff. Left a suggestion inline in action.yml.
Ava: Implemented debounce and backoff defaults; added configuration to action.yml and updated docs.
Maya: Ran full release workflow in staging, reported minor flake in strict lint job which required a cache-bump; approved after re-run.
CI: One flaky lint job failed on first run; re-run succeeded. Final CI status is green.
Adds an opt-in 'merge-sigil' quiet gate for scheduled release windows, a lightweight dep-curator that emits dependency risk summaries, and splits lint into quick/strict profiles to speed feedback. Operators: enable merge-sigil via .github/merge-sigil.yml and configure quiet windows. Dep-curator provides a --summary flag for CI integration and a --rules file to tune heuristics.

Context
We’re landing new prefix/KV cache telemetry (hit/miss, eviction/pressure, wasted prefill) across a series of PRs. SRE/Telemetry requested explicit runtime-side flags so we can (a) gate rollout per env and (b) dial sampling/rate limiting without code changes.

This PR introduces a single, typed config surface for cache telemetry and updates the internal runtime config docs with recommended defaults + rollout notes.

What’s in this PR
- New runtime config block: cache_telemetry
  - cache_telemetry.enabled (bool): global kill switch for all new cache telemetry emissions
  - cache_telemetry.metrics_enabled (bool): metrics-only gate (allows traces off/on separately)
  - cache_telemetry.traces_enabled (bool): enables span annotations for cache events (kept off by default in prod)
  - cache_telemetry.sample_rate (float 0.0–1.0): sampling for high-volume counters/histograms where we’ve approved sampling (implementation uses probabilistic sampling at request start)
  - cache_telemetry.event_rate_limit_per_sec (int): per-process token bucket for cache event annotations (primarily traces) to avoid bursty cost
  - cache_telemetry.emit_miss_reason_breakdown (bool): gate for miss reason label emission (kept on in staging/canary; prod default on with allowlist enforcement handled elsewhere)
- Wiring
  - All new cache metrics introduced in pr-18421/pr-18422/pr-18423/pr-18424 are now guarded by CacheTelemetryConfig checks.
  - Tracing annotations (added in a later PR) are prepared to use traces_enabled + event_rate_limit_per_sec.
  - Config is read once at runtime init; no hot reload in this PR (intentional to avoid partial-tag mismatches).
- Defaults
  - staging: enabled=true, metrics_enabled=true, traces_enabled=true, sample_rate=1.0, event_rate_limit_per_sec=500
  - canary: enabled=true, metrics_enabled=true, traces_enabled=false, sample_rate=0.25, event_rate_limit_per_sec=200
  - prod: enabled=true, metrics_enabled=true, traces_enabled=false, sample_rate=0.05, event_rate_limit_per_sec=100
  - NOTE: these defaults are conservative for prod; we can raise sample_rate once we confirm series cost with the ingestion-side cardinality guards.
- Docs
  - Adds a short “How to roll out cache telemetry safely” section that aligns with SRE canary gates: enable in staging -> enable in perf-canary at 25% sample -> prod at 5% sample -> tune.
  - Documents which signals are sampled vs unsampled (eviction pressure gauges remain unsampled).

Why this approach
- One top-level kill switch is necessary for incident response (telemetry cost spikes, unexpected overhead).
- Separating metrics_enabled vs traces_enabled matches how we control cost/cardinality: metrics are heavily constrained; traces can still get expensive quickly if enabled broadly.
- Keeping config read-only at startup avoids “mixed config” within a process that could produce confusing partial-series.

Testing
- Unit tests validate config parsing/validation (sample_rate bounds, negative rate limits, default application).
- Local load test sanity: toggling enabled=false removes all new cache series.
- Perf smoke runs included for instrumentation off/on at 5% sample (see CI).

Rollout
- Intended to ship before enabling cache telemetry in prod. Oncall can flip enabled=false via runtime config push if we see unexpected cost/overhead.

Links
- Linear: ENG-4821 (definitions/tags), ENG-4822 (runtime instrumentation)
- Related PRs: pr-18425 (sampling + rate limits), pr-18431 (naming reconciliation)

Open questions (not blocking)
- Do we want hot reload for sample_rate only? SRE asked for it, but it’s easy to introduce partial-series; proposing we revisit once ingestion drop detection is in place.

Reviewer notes / conversation summary
- Omar El-Sayed: requested that “enabled=false” must be a hard guarantee (no side-channel emissions). Author: updated guards to short-circuit before any miss-reason computation and added a regression test asserting zero increments.
- Nadia Rahman: asked to clarify which metrics are sampled and to avoid naming drift vs observability standards. Author: updated docs and aligned the config key names to match other telemetry blocks.
- Caleb Johnson: flagged risk of operators raising sample_rate without considering cardinality budgets. Author: added comments in defaults YAML + a doc callout that sample_rate > 0.25 requires ingestion guard verification.
- Marcus Reed: requested perf evidence that the flag checks don’t regress hot path. Author: ensured checks are branch-predictable and cached; posted perf smoke numbers in CI comment.
- Allison Grant: asked for explicit runbook snippet (“what knob to turn when dashboards go flat vs when cost spikes”). Author: added a small section to ops/runbooks/cache-telemetry-rollout.md.

Merge
Squash merged to main after CI green and approvals from Runtime + Telemetry + SRE.
- Adds runtime config flags to enable/disable cache telemetry and tune sampling/rate-limits per environment
- Documents recommended defaults for staging/canary/prod and how to roll out safely

Context: We’ve been hardening TP watchdog + abort/drain semantics (ADR-0127, ENG-4826) and adding stall detectors/metrics (ENG-4823). We didn’t have regression coverage that proves: (1) a rank/collective “silent stall” actually triggers the watchdog within the configured threshold, (2) the abort path returns the expected structured error, and (3) the replica drain/overload hooks fire so we don’t wedge GPUs indefinitely.

This PR adds a small fault-injection surface and an integration test suite that runs a multi-rank TP replica in-process (test harness spawns N ranks) and intentionally introduces controlled stalls. The goal is deterministic coverage without relying on real NCCL deadlocks.

What’s included:
- Fault injection knobs (test-only) to simulate the major stall classes we see in the wild:
  - "collective_never_completes": rank 0 blocks before a collective and never reaches the call site (simulates ordering mismatch/starvation without hanging the driver).
  - "collective_slow_path": inject an artificial delay before/after ncclGroupEnd to validate watchdog thresholds and false-positive behavior.
  - "scheduler_starvation": pause the TP collective scheduling lane while prefill work continues (validates fairness/guardrail integration).
  - "client_cancel_mid_decode": triggers cancel path during streaming decode to ensure watchdog/abort doesn’t leak in-flight state.
- New tests asserting the end-to-end semantics:
  - Watchdog fires and returns a stable error code (RuntimeError::kTpStallWatchdog) within bounds.
  - Abort propagates as a request-scoped failure and does not block unrelated replicas.
  - Replica drain is emitted once (deduped) and surfaces in logs/metrics.
  - Stall reason tagging is present in structured logs (compute vs comms vs scheduler) and increments the appropriate counters.
- CI reliability notes + gating behavior:
  - The suite is GPU-required and runs only on CI pools with multi-GPU nodes.
  - The “never completes” test uses a cooperative stall (condition variable + timeout) rather than blocking CUDA/NCCL, so the test process can still exit cleanly.
  - Default runtime watchdog thresholds are overridden in tests to keep runtime < 60s total.

Why this is safe:
- Fault injection is guarded behind a build flag and a runtime check: enabled only for tests (RW_ENABLE_FAULT_INJECTION=1) and only in non-release builds.
- No behavior changes in production builds.

How to run locally:
- bazel test //runtime/tp/tests:tp_watchdog_fault_injection_test --config=cuda
- RW_ENABLE_FAULT_INJECTION=1 RW_TP_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT_MS=8000 bazel test //runtime/tp/tests:tp_watchdog_fault_injection_test

Follow-ups:
- Once perf-canary has the TP stress scenarios live (ENG-4828), we should add a “simulated stall canary” run in benchmark-lab to validate alert routing end-to-end (SRE).

Checklist:
- [x] Deterministic repro of watchdog firing
- [x] Verifies structured error propagation to API boundary (via internal request wrapper)
- [x] Ensures replica drain hook called exactly once
- [x] CI configured to avoid flakiness / hangs
- [x] Docs/comments added near injection points explaining constraints

Refs: ENG-4826 (watchdog + drain), ENG-4823 (stall metrics/reasons), INT-2219 (extra debug logging window during canary).
runtime/tp: add test-only fault injection hooks for TP collective lane
runtime/tp/tests: add watchdog fault-injection integration tests
runtime/observability: expose stall reason tag in test harness assertions
ci: add multi-gpu test target to gpu-integration shard with timeouts
docs: add notes on running TP fault-injection suite locally
Noah Patel: Can we guarantee the “never completes” case doesn’t wedge NCCL/CUDA and leave the CI worker unusable? We’ve been burned by tests that intentionally hang.
Sahana Iyer (author): Yes — the “never completes” injection blocks before any CUDA/NCCL call and uses a cooperative gate released by the harness on teardown. There’s also a hard test timeout and a watchdog override to keep it bounded.
Rafael Mendes: Please add an assertion that the drain event is deduped. During the Feb incident we saw repeated drains spamming alerts.
Sahana Iyer (author): Added an explicit expectation on drain counter == 1 for the request and a log match asserting single drain emission; also updated the test harness to clear metrics between cases.
Julian Moore: For scheduler_starvation, can we ensure it’s actually testing the same lane that the runtime uses for collectives (not a no-op)?
Sahana Iyer (author): Updated injection point to pause the TP collective scheduling lane (CollectiveLane::Run) and asserted queue depth increases while prefill continues; the watchdog then triggers with stall_reason=scheduler.
Omar El-Sayed: The tests currently hardcode label values. Prefer using the stall reason enum names to avoid churn if we rename label strings.
Sahana Iyer (author): Done — assertions now compare against StallReason::ToString() output and only spot-check a couple of stable substrings for logs.
Kira Volkov: CI: we should keep this in the GPU integration shard but add a retry-once wrapper. GPU nodes sometimes hiccup and we don’t want to block merges on infra flake.
Sahana Iyer (author): Added one rerun-on-infra-failure to the gpu-integration job only (not for assertion failures). Also tightened timeouts to fail fast if a node is unhealthy.
enum class TpFault { kNone, kCollectiveNeverCompletes, kCollectiveSlowPath, kSchedulerStarvation, kCancelMidDecode };
RW_FAULT_INJECT("tp", "collective_never_completes") { gate_.Wait(); } // cooperative stall; test harness releases on teardown
EXPECT_THAT(err.code(), Eq(RuntimeError::kTpStallWatchdog)); EXPECT_THAT(err.details(), HasSubstr("stall_reason=comms"));
EXPECT_THAT(metrics.Get("runtime_tp_replica_drain_total", {"reason","watchdog"}), Eq(1));
Internal: Adds TP watchdog fault-injection integration tests (no production behavior change).

payload.body:
Context: As part of the hardware tuning profiles pack, we want predictable and measurable H100 behavior across a wide mix of prompt/response lengths. Our current kernel selection logic is too coarse (mostly based on “model family + attention impl availability”), which leaves meaningful perf on the table for short-prefill / mid-context / long-context buckets, and occasionally picks kernels that are stable but suboptimal for certain seq-len distributions.

What this PR does: Updates the H100 kernel auto-selection heuristics to bucket by effective prefill seq length and decode context length, and to select kernels accordingly. The intent is not to introduce new kernels; it’s to improve routing among existing implementations and to make the choice more robust under mixed workloads (including streaming).

Heuristic changes (H100 only): 1) Add seq-len buckets for prefill: S (<=512), M (513–2048), L (2049–8192), XL (>8192). 2) Add a separate decode-context bucket (ctx <=4096 vs >4096) to avoid the “one-size-fits-all” pick under long-running chats. 3) Prefer FA2 persistent kernels for S/M buckets when head_dim and layout are compatible; prefer FA2 split-k for L when batch is high; prefer paged-attn path for XL or when KV is paged due to cache budgeting. 4) Add explicit guardrails to avoid selecting the “aggressive” kernels when streaming + small batch + tight p95 SLO (these cases showed instability in earlier runs). 5) When detection is ambiguous (MIG partitions, vendor SKU string variants), fall back to the prior stable choice and emit a selection_reason metric tag.

Performance summary (microbench + perf-canary): Microbench (runtime/bench/h100_kernel_sweep) indicates net gains in tokens/sec primarily in S/M buckets, with neutral-to-slight improvements in L and no regressions in XL (where we usually end up in paged-attn anyway). Perf-canary job: https://perf-canary.redwood-inference.net/jobs/rc-145982 (H100 SXM, us-east) and https://perf-canary.redwood-inference.net/jobs/rc-146104 (H100 PCIe, us-west). Aggregate deltas vs main (median across matrix): S (<=512): +6–9% decode tok/s, p95 latency -2–4% at concurrency 16; M (513–2048): +4–7% decode tok/s, p95 latency ~flat; L (2049–8192): +0–3% tok/s, p95 latency +0–1% (within gate); XL (>8192): ~flat (within noise).

Correctness/stability: No changes to numerics expected; we’re only changing kernel selection. Added tests to ensure bucket boundaries behave as expected and to keep the fallback path intact. Also added log/metrics breadcrumbs so oncall can see (a) selected kernel impl, (b) seq bucket, (c) why we avoided a faster kernel.

Rollout plan: This is intended to be consumed by the H100 tuned profile, but it is safe as a standalone change. We will stage behind the existing runtime knob `runtime.kernel_autoselect.h100_seq_bucket_enable` defaulting ON for H100 in hosted canary pools only, and keep the ability to override OFF per pool if we see tail latency regressions.

Links: Linear ENG-4824, ENG-4821. Related PRs: PR #22003 (H100 scheduler presets), PR #21991 (profile selection logic). Microbench notes: internal bench artifact “h100-kernel-sweep-2025-12-09” (Benchmark Lab run ID bl-77219).
runtime/kernels: add H100 seq-len bucket helper and enums
runtime/kernels: update autoselect to choose FA2 persistent vs split-k by bucket
runtime/kernels: add guardrails for streaming + low batch and long ctx
runtime/metrics: emit selection_reason + seq_bucket tags
runtime/tests: add bucket boundary tests and fallback coverage
bench: extend h100 kernel sweep script to print chosen kernel and bucket
Grace Kim: Can you clarify why the cutoff for S/M is 512/2048? We’ve seen some models behave differently around 1k.
Yuki Sato: Cutoffs are based on the sweep where FA2 persistent wins pretty consistently <=512. Between 513–2048 the win is still there but smaller; beyond 2k split-k tends to catch up at higher conc. I added a note in code and the bench script prints the crossover points for head_dim=128/64 so we can revisit.
Sofia Ivanova: Any risk that the new selection changes tail latency under streaming? Scheduler already has fairness toggles, but I’d like to avoid compounding.
Yuki Sato: Added an explicit guardrail: if streaming && batch<4 && target_p95_ms is set (SLO mode), we keep the previous “stable” kernel. Also emitting selection_reason so we can correlate in dashboards.
Rina Kobayashi: Please link the perf-canary job IDs and include the exact workload rows where you saw the largest gains.
Yuki Sato: Added links in PR description + attached the two summary artifacts. Biggest gains are in rows: chat_short_prefill_high_conc and summarize_1k_to_2k_prefill (both non-streaming).
Hiro Tanaka: Bucket XL (>8192) defaulting to paged-attn makes sense, but can you ensure we don’t pick it for 8193 when KV paging isn’t enabled? That could be a perf cliff.
Yuki Sato: Good catch. Updated to require kv_cache_mode==PAGED for the paged-attn preference; otherwise we use FA2 split-k for XL as long as memory headroom is sufficient, and we log if we override due to kv budget.
Kira Volkov: Metrics naming: please prefix with runtime_kernel_ and make bucket labels consistent with the dashboard panels.
Yuki Sato: Done. Renamed `kernel_autoselect_bucket` -> `runtime_kernel_autoselect_seq_bucket` and aligned labels to {S,M,L,XL}.
Aisha Bello: Perf gates look OK. Please add a note on expected variance; otherwise we’ll get noisy alerts when the buckets shift the mix.
Yuki Sato: Added a short note to the perf-canary README and linked it in the description. Also tagged the metric so we can segment by selected kernel.
H100 only: improved kernel auto-selection by sequence-length buckets; adds selection metrics and guardrails to avoid streaming tail-latency regressions.

payload.body:
Stabilize SSE streaming by introducing a packetizer/window coordinator and deterministic call serializer to prevent partial-JSON emissions and function-call reordering on reconnect/replay.
Background: customers saw rare but high-impact cases where SSE fragment coalescing and transport-level reordering produced truncated JSON frames or out-of-order tool/function call events during reconnects and HTTP/2 headroom shifts. This PR introduces a buffered packetizer + window coordinator inside the streaming stack plus a deterministic call serializer (call-seq) and idempotency token handshake so clients and the OpenAI-compat layer can reliably resume and preserve fncall ordering. Motivation: reduce broken/partial JSON emissions, minimize application-level compensating logic, and make reconnect/replay deterministic. Implementation summary: 1) packetizer: aggregates incoming runtime tokens into bounded windows (configurable via env/route param) and emits well-formed SSE events only at window boundaries or when explicit epoch markers appear; 2) window coordinator: assigns a monotonically increasing window_id + window_checksum and exposes an optional checkpoint token (sse-checkpoint) that clients may ACK — used only for resume heuristics; 3) deterministic call serializer: when an event contains a tool/function call, serializer attaches call_meta: {call_seq, call_idempotency_token}. Calls are emitted in strict call_seq order and the OpenAI-compat adapter preserves call_seq across model fallbacks; 4) reconnect/resume behavior: on reconnect with a checkpoint, server attempts a fast-resume by replaying buffered windows from the last ACKed checkpoint. If checkpoint mismatch, server falls back to re-stream-from-start + explicit resync hint. 5) compatibility shim: openai-compat now maps call_meta to OpenAI-style function_call sentinel plus an embedded __call_seq to avoid breaking older clients. Tests & metrics: added deterministic replay unit tests, end-to-end integration that fuzzes HTTP/2 coalescing, and a perf microbenchmark to ensure added buffering does not regress 99th percentile latency in common short-response workloads. Rollout: feature guarded by route flag streaming.packetizer.enabled (default off). Progressive rollout: beta to select tenants for 48 hours, then broader ramp if no regressions. Backwards compatibility: default behavior unchanged when feature is disabled. See changed files for implementation details.
Maya Chen (review): Can we make the default packet window conservative for now (e.g., 16KB or 50ms) to avoid latency regressions on short responses? Also please add metrics for dropped partial-json events.
Priya Desai (author): Updated default to 16KB / 50ms and added metrics sse.packetizer.window_bytes and sse.packetizer.window_duration_ms. Added test that asserts no regressions for sub-1KB responses.
Ethan Li (review): Lgtm overall. A few nits: rename call_seq to __call_seq for the OpenAI shim only; ensure we don't leak internal window_id into public headers. Also please add a safety timeout to avoid indefinitely buffering a stalled connection.
Priya Desai (author): Addressed all nits: OpenAI shim uses __call_seq; window_id now only appears in internal logs and checkpoint tokens (opaque). Added 2s safety flush timeout configurable by route.
Rohan Kapoor (approval): Verified deterministic replay tests locally and ran the http2 fuzz harness. Approving pending CI green.
Feature gated; must enable streaming.packetizer.enabled per-route before traffic. Observability: new metrics and logs added; dashboards updated under Redwood Console > Streaming > Packetizer.
1) set route flag "streaming.packetizer.enabled=true"
2) monitor sse.packetizer.window_bytes and sse.packetizer.buffered_windows metric
3) if partial JSON regressions occur, set streaming.packetizer.enabled=false and file ENG ticket.
Added follow-up ENG-5239 to audit client SDK behavior and roll-forward a user-facing migration note in the SDK changelogs. Scheduled canary rollout for Nov 10 2025.
payload.title: Buffered SSE window coordinator and deterministic call serializer

Motivation: In the last week we observed a recurring production pattern where regions with transient KV-store staleness would cause circuit-breaking state to stick for tenant shards. That in turn amplified load on neighboring regions during rejoin windows and produced a class of tail-latency spikes and SLO breaches. This PR introduces a conservative 'soft-deny fuse' at the regional ingress and a lightweight KV-drift reconciler to avoid persistent sticky circuits. The goal is graceful degradation: quickly shed a small fraction of load during suspected KV inconsistency while ensuring tenants can reestablish healthy state without a hard network-level deny. Changes include: - soft-deny fuse middleware that returns a deterministic 429-like JSON payload with retry-after hints when the regional fuse trips; the fuse is metric-driven (error-rate + kv-lag signal) and uses an exponential cooldown plus token-bucket fraction to limit collateral impact - KV-drift protector that watches per-tenant KV sync lag and performs a jittered resync probe when drift is suspected; the probe attempts a read-then-compare before pushing a corrective update to avoid write storms - short TTLs added to sticky-circuit annotations and a background reconciler that clears orphaned circuit state after a conservative timeout - feature-flag + rollout strategy: feature flag enabled by default in hotfix, gate available for canary populations via rollout config - telemetry: added metrics for fuse trips, kv-resyncs, reconciler clears, and a new alert rule that triggers at 3x baseline fuse-trip rate for 5m - tests: unit tests for fuse logic, simulated integration harness that reproduces KV-lag patterns, and a small e2e canary job run in staging Checklist: - [x] unit tests - [x] integration replay harness - [x] e2e canary in staging - [x] added dashboards and alerts - [x] rollout plan included Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main and build hotfix artifact 2) Canary to 2% of traffic in us-west via rollout flag for 30 minutes 3) Monitor fuse trips / kv-resyncs and latency SLOs for 60 minutes 4) Gradually increase canary to 25% then 100% if stable Rollback: Flip feature flag off; the fuse and reconciler are designed to be side-effect-free when disabled. In case of unexpected behavior, revert the hotfix and deploy the previous artifact Notes on risk: The reconciler performs corrective writes only after a read-compare step and respects per-tenant write rate caps to avoid cascading writes. The soft-deny payload includes client-friendly guidance and retry-after to encourage backoff from SDKs. Related items: Linear: ENG-3421 (investigate sticky circuit incidents), ENG-3499 (regional kv-lag telemetry).
Diego Morales: Left a couple small suggestions in soft_deny_fuse.go about metric labels and cardinality; please ensure fuse reason is tagged.
Lena Park: Reply: addressed metric label comments and added unit test for reason tag (see commit c4e1f56).
Priya Raman: Question on reconciler safety - can it write over a forward-moving state?
Lena Park: Reply: reconciler does read-compare and abides by tenant write caps; added doc note and per-tenant rate limiter; see reconciler.go comments.
Samir Gupta: Approved after canary metrics looked stable at 2% traffic.
Hotfix: add regional soft-deny fuse and KV-drift protector to reduce sticky-circuit incidents and improve SLO stability under transient KV inconsistency. Includes telemetry and canary rollout.

Context: As part of the KMS hardening initiative (ENG-4821/ENG-4825) we need repeatable, non-flaky coverage for the most common real-world failure modes we’ve seen (timeouts and throttling) and guardrails to prevent retry amplification. This PR introduces an integration-test harness that can deterministically inject KMS failures and validate that our KMS wrapper obeys configured budgets (max retries + max wall-clock) and that upstream services surface the correct error category without masking (e.g., Throttling vs Timeout vs AccessDenied). What’s included: (1) A small “kms-fault-injector” sidecar used only in integration tests (runs in docker-compose and the CI integration job). It proxies KMS requests and can inject (a) fixed latency, (b) probabilistic timeouts (connection stall), and (c) throttling responses (AWS-style ThrottlingException / HTTP 429 equivalent) based on per-test configuration. (2) New integration tests for envelope decrypt paths in the control-plane and data-plane adapters that cover: timeout -> retry with jitter -> fail fast within latency cap; throttling -> bounded retries -> correct error taxonomy; and “mixed” failure where first N requests throttle then succeed, asserting the wrapper eventually succeeds without exceeding retry budget. (3) Assertions for total wall-clock budget and retry counts using emitted metrics/spans from the wrapper: kms.client.attempts (counter), kms.client.latency_ms (histogram), kms.client.errors{category=...} (counter). These assertions are done by reading the local in-memory test metrics exporter (not scraping Prometheus) to keep tests hermetic. (4) A CI job wiring (integration-kms-failure-modes) that runs these tests in parallel with other integration suites, gated on main and release/*, and skips on fork PRs (requires docker service). How to run locally: `make itest-kms-failure-modes` (requires docker). Notes/constraints: This is AWS-mode only for now; the harness is intentionally provider-agnostic at the proxy layer, but the error-shape fixtures currently match AWS responses. We’ll extend with GCP/Azure once those wrappers land behind the same error taxonomy (ENG-4822). We intentionally avoid testing circuit-breaker behavior here; that is covered in ENG-4824/PR-18449. Risk: Low product risk (test-only code paths), moderate flake risk; mitigations include deterministic seeds, fixed injection windows, and conservative latency thresholds. Evidence: This PR adds regression coverage for SUP-19377 patterns (intermittent 5xx correlated with KMS throttling) and enforces the retry cap/latency cap behavior agreed in ADR-007.
Rafael Mendes (SRE): Can we ensure the timeout scenario doesn’t hang the job if docker networking flakes? Please add a hard upper bound per test and fail with actionable logs.
Sahana Iyer (author): Added per-test `context.WithTimeout` (20s) and a harness-level watchdog (2m) that dumps the injector config + last 200 proxy events on failure.
Hanae Suzuki (Security): For throttling, please validate we’re mapping to the canonical category name agreed in ENG-4822 (Throttling, not RateLimited). Also confirm we don’t leak provider-specific error text into customer-visible messages in the test assertions.
Sahana Iyer (author): Updated assertions to check `category=Throttling` and only verify internal log fields; no customer-facing strings are asserted.
Allison Grant (Obs): Metric namespacing should match our standard (`redwood.kms.*`). The harness helper currently searches for `kms.client.*` directly; please update to the final names so tests protect us from future renames.
Sahana Iyer (author): Updated to `redwood.kms.client.*` and added a small compatibility shim so the suite fails loudly if names drift.
Diego Santos (Platform): The wall-clock caps seem tight (1.5s) for CI. Suggest bump to 2.5s and assert on retry count + max backoff instead, to avoid flakes.
Sahana Iyer (author): Bumped caps to 2.5s in CI, kept tighter defaults for local runs, and added explicit assertions on attempt count + backoff ceiling. Re-ran suite 20x on CI runner image; no flakes observed.
Tomáš Novák (On-call/runbooks): Can we print the error taxonomy mapping when a test fails? That would help triage quickly.
Sahana Iyer (author): Added failure output showing observed error categories, retry counts, and last span status for the KMS call.

test(kms): add throttling + timeout scenarios for envelope decrypt integration suite
test(metrics): add in-memory exporter helpers for asserting attempt counts and error categories
ci: add integration-kms-failure-modes job + docs for running locally
chore: tighten timeouts and stabilize tests with deterministic seed + retryable container startup
Adds CI/staging integration tests that simulate KMS timeout + throttling and assert retry budgets/latency caps/failure propagation for envelope decrypt paths.

payload.body:
Motivation: customers with strict data residency requirements were observing KMS usage that did not always preserve the tenant-declared jurisdiction header across retries and service boundaries. This PR introduces a lightweight KMS adapter service plus RBAC decision hooks and audit preservation middleware to ensure: 1) KMS requests are pinned to an allowed geozone based on operator and tenant claims, 2) audit metadata (region, operator-assertion, provenance) is carried end-to-end and de-duplicated at ingest, and 3) runtime fallbacks are explicit and observable when region enforcement is relaxed for operational reasons.

What this changes: single continuous change set that touches the adapter service, runtime auth hooks, audit writer, helm chart and tests. Key behaviors: - A new internal service services/kms-adapter that validates KMS target region against RBAC v2 decision; it returns an explicit consent token for callers. - RBAC hook (internal/auth/rbacv2/kms_binding.go) consults the policy engine and annotates the request context with a region-assertion claim. - Audit middleware (pkg/audit/preservation.go) attaches an immutable audit-stamp and preserves jurisdiction-relation headers across async handoffs. - deploy/helm/kms-adapter-chart.yaml adds a low-privilege deployment with resource limits and an opt-in toggle in values.yaml.

Rollout and compatibility: adapter is opt-in via feature flag (redwood.feature.jurisdiction_kms_adapter). Existing code paths continue to call the previous KMS client until a config flip is applied. We included a staged rollout plan in docs/compliance/jurisdiction-kms.md and feature gating on Dedicated/Private deployments only for the first quarter.

Security considerations: RBAC checks are mandatory for adapter-backed requests; a fallback mode allows explicit operator consent (audit-only) and is logged at WARN level. The adapter performs strict signature checks on incoming operator assertions and rejects mismatched territory codes. All KMS credentials remain encrypted in our KMS; the adapter authenticates to KMS using a service principal with a scoped CMK.

Testing: unit tests for RBAC decision mapping; integration tests that simulate multi-region operator-tenant combinations; e2e test which asserts audit header presence in the ingestion pipeline. CI initially had a flaky e2e that failed due to timing in KV cache warmup — that was fixed by increasing retry window and adding a health probe.

Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (ENG-3421) - [x] unit tests - [x] integration tests - [x] helm chart and values - [x] docs added under docs/compliance - [x] rollout plan and feature flag - [x] security review by SRE and Product Security

Notes: This PR is intentionally coarse-grained to keep the adapter and RBAC integration in a single merge to simplify rollout testing. Follow-ups planned: - split adapter to its own repo for large customers - telemetry upgrade to add per-tenant KMS usage cost attribution (ENG-3502)
Adds a jurisdiction-aware KMS adapter and RBAC v2 hooks to enforce region pinning and improve audit header preservation. No breaking public API changes; install notes in docs/compliance/jurisdiction-kms.md.
Aisha Rivera: high level - this looks reasonable. Please add a note describing the intended behavior when RBAC is unavailable (circuit-breaker semantics).
Jonah Patel: replied - added circuit-breaker semantics and config knobs (adapter.timeout_ms, adapter.circuit_threshold) in deploy/helm/values.yaml; documented behavior in docs/compliance/jurisdiction-kms.md.
Markus Li: nit - prefer a shorter default retry window in the e2e to avoid long CI runs; otherwise +1 after tests pass.
Jonah Patel: replied - shortened default retry and added a CI-only override; pushed a fix in a3f7b2c.
Eleanor Chen: security review - confirm that audit stamps are immutable and signed; also request a short design note about how operator consent is recorded.
Jonah Patel: replied - audit stamps use HMAC with rotating key and are stored in the audit envelope; added design note in docs/compliance/jurisdiction-kms.md and implementation in pkg/audit/preservation.go.
Aisha Rivera: approved - LGTM after the minors.

payload.body:
Adds low-overhead runtime metrics (scheduler lag + queue depth) to support overload protection triggers and SRE dashboards. No API changes.
Context: Hot-route capacity protection needs a small set of runtime-originated pressure signals that are (a) cheap to compute in the data plane, (b) stable under high load, and (c) low-cardinality enough to be safely shipped at high frequency. This PR adds two primary signals to the runtime metrics pipeline: scheduler lag (time between eligible-to-run and actually scheduled) and queue depth (pending work items) with limited dimensionality.

What’s in this PR: 1) Scheduler lag histogram (ms) emitted at the scheduling boundary per engine instance. Lag is computed as (now - enqueue_ts) at the moment the request enters a runnable slot. 2) Queue depth gauge emitted from the admission queue, representing pending requests waiting for runtime scheduling. 3) Optional route_group attribution: runtime does NOT attach raw route/path; it accepts a pre-aggregated route_group identifier from the router (small fixed set) and will emit per-route_group metrics only when explicitly enabled for protected routes. 4) Sampling + emission controls to keep overhead bounded: fixed-rate emission for gauges (default 1s), capped label sets, and a safety circuit that disables route_group attribution if distinct values exceed a threshold.

Why: These metrics are used by the routing/admission control layer (ENG-4924) to gate best-effort traffic earlier, and by SRE dashboards/alerts (ENG-4926) to understand when load shedding / admission control is expected vs when tail latency is caused by other runtime regressions.

Key design points: - Low overhead: all hot-path math is integer/monotonic clock only; no string formatting in the scheduling loop. - Low cardinality: label set is strictly bounded (region, pool, model_family, route_group when enabled). No tenant/customer labels. - Deterministic meaning: scheduler_lag_ms measures time waiting specifically for runtime scheduling capacity, not network queueing or router queueing.

Metrics (names + labels): - redwood.runtime.scheduler_lag_ms (histogram) labels: region, gpu_pool, model_family, route_group(optional) - redwood.runtime.queue_depth (gauge) labels: region, gpu_pool, model_family, route_group(optional) - redwood.runtime.overload_signal_enabled (gauge) labels: region, gpu_pool (1/0)

Operational notes: - Default: route_group attribution disabled. Router team will enable only for the protected route groups via config in a follow-up PR, after validating cardinality in staging. - If route_group attribution is enabled and the runtime observes >32 distinct route_group values in a 5m window, it will automatically drop route_group labeling and emit a structured warning log once per window.

Testing: - Unit tests validate lag calculation and monotonic clock usage. - A micro-benchmark validates <0.3% CPU overhead at 10k req/s synthetic scheduler throughput with gauges at 1s and histogram sampling at 1/10. - Integration smoke in staging: dashboards show stable cardinality and no increased scrape payloads.

Rollout: - Behind flag RUNTIME_OVERLOAD_SIGNALS. - Staging enabled by default for 48h; prod canary in us-east on one pool after SRE sign-off.

Follow-ups: - Add burn-rate alert wiring in slo-toolkit once dashboards confirm stable behavior. - Align routing thresholds once we have a week of baseline distribution under normal traffic.

References: Linear ENG-4925, ENG-4924. Related: postmortem 2025-11-03 (fleetwide latency cascade).
Sofia Ivanova (requested changes): We should be explicit about what scheduler_lag includes/excludes. Right now it looks like it could be conflated with router queueing. Also: make sure enqueue_ts uses monotonic clock; wall time will break during NTP adjustments.

Julian Moore (author): Updated docs in the metric comments + PR description: lag is measured strictly between runtime queue enqueue and scheduler pick-up. Swapped to monotonic clock source and added unit test that fails if wall-clock is used.

Logan Wright: Please keep label dimensions minimal. We can’t afford tenant_id or raw route path. Is route_group guaranteed small and bounded?

Julian Moore: route_group is optional and disabled by default. Added a runtime-side cardinality guard: if >32 distinct route_groups per (region,pool) in 5m, we drop route_group labeling and emit a warning. Also added a gauge overload_signal_enabled for visibility.

Rafael Mendes: For triggers we care about sustained queue depth (e.g., >N for >T). Are gauges emitted frequently enough and stable?

Julian Moore: Default 1s cadence; should be sufficient for admission control loops that run at ~1-5s. Added note in rollout plan and verified scrape payload is stable in staging.

Allison Grant: Please align metric names with observability standards (namespace + units). scheduler_lag_ms is good; queue_depth should be unitless. Also add a short section on cardinality risk.

Julian Moore: Renamed to redwood.runtime.* and added explicit units + the cardinality guardrail section.

Nadia Rahman (approval): Looks good. Thanks for keeping this low-cardinality and adding the safety cutout. Approved.

Sofia Ivanova (approval): Approved after monotonic time change + extra tests.
payload.title: runtime: export scheduler lag + queue depth metrics for overload protection

payload.body:
Motivation: after rolling out CUDA graph capture/replay we observed intermittent regressions in latency and correctness on mixed-shape workloads. Root causes included unstable capture sequences when KV-cache priming and continuous batching interact, and aggressive kernel specialization during early captures that later mismatches runtime conditions. This PR introduces an adaptive warmup strategy plus a lightweight dynamic shape-guard mechanism and a conservative kernel-selection fallback to eliminate those regressions while preserving the latency wins from replay.

What changed (high level):
- Introduces an adaptive warmup controller that tracks capture success/failure rates per-device and per-model-variant. The controller increases warmup iterations for captures showing instability and temporarily disables aggressive kernel specialization until captures stabilize.
- Adds a dynamic shape-guard implementation: at replay start a tiny runtime check validates captured tensor shapes against the incoming request and routes to the non-graph execution path when mismatches are detected. Guards are inserted automatically and retired after a configurable stability window.
- Implements a conservative-kernel fallback: first N replays prefer fallback kernels that are correct across small shape variations (slightly lower peak throughput but far more robust), then switch to optimized kernels after stability is observed.
- KV-cache reconciliation adjustments: delay capture start until prefix KV cache is fully materialized for requests marked as "hot-prefix"; this avoids partially-filled KV states causing different capture traces.
- New telemetry probes and metrics for graph capture status: capture_attempts, capture_failures, guard_trips, kernel_fallback_count, warmup_iterations. These feed the console and new alerting rules.
- Unit + integration tests covering shape-guard paths, KV-cache delay path, and an e2e synthetic mixed-shape workload. Benchmarks added to perf suite.

Compatibility and safety: The shape-guard path is opt-out per-deployment and defaulted on for hosted/Dedicated. The fallback is conservative and only used during warmup; no persistent change to kernel selection unless stability thresholds are met. We also provide a runtime toggle and a per-model annotation to force strict graph-only behavior for advanced users.

Results: On our mixed-shape synthetic workload (sequence length variance 8-1024, batch size 1-8) this PR removes previously observed 5-15% latency regressions and eliminates rare incorrect outputs triggered by mismatched KV caches. End-to-end P95 latency improved by ~3% relative to the baseline graph-replay with previous heuristics, and the number of incident-causing regressions in staging dropped to zero across a multi-day soak.

Related work and tickets: Linear: ENG-3421 (graph warmup instability), ENG-3488 (kv-cache capture timing). A followup will expose warmup tuning in the Console UX (ENG-3580).

Notes for reviewers: focus on the correctness of guard insertion/removal and the potential perf impact of conservative kernels; the fallback path is intentionally simple and only active during warmup to minimize long-term overhead.

Small code snippet (illustrative):
if (!captured_shapes.match(incoming_shapes)) {
  // fast path: route to non-graph executor and record guard_trips metric
  executor = non_graph_executor;
} else {
  executor = graph_replay_executor;
}

This description is a single continuous string; see commits and changed files below for details.
Liam Chen (2026-02-16): Can you clarify how shape_guard impacts tail latency? I want numbers for worst-case guard trips.
Maya Rodriguez (2026-02-16): Added P99/P95 numbers to the description and perf bench; worst-case guard trip adds ~0.8ms in our staging runs.
Priya Patel (2026-02-17): Suggest moving the KV-cache delay threshold to a per-model tunable. Otherwise LGTM.
Maya Rodriguez (2026-02-17): Done — added a per-model config and runtime toggle, documented in tools/console/graph_warmup_toggles.md
Ethan Moore (2026-02-18): I saw flaky failure on cuda-integration on a different CUDA minor; added a guard around kernel selection for older drivers.
Maya Rodriguez (2026-02-18): Addressed — now we probe driver capabilities before enabling specialized kernels.
payload.title: Adaptive CUDA-graph warmup with dynamic shape guards and conservative kernel fallback

Background: In recent region surge incidents we observed frequent circuit flips and aggressive tenant eviction spikes when health probes and SLO scoring converge during bursty ingress. That behaviour amplified recovery time because short-lived noisy failures triggered hard quarantines and large SLO penalty accruals. This PR introduces an interruptible quarantine window and an SLO compaction bridge aimed at reducing oscillation while preserving fair shedding for overloaded tenants.

What this changes (single continuous description): Adds an interruptible quarantine controller that marks a node/tenant as 'soft-quarantined' for a configurable window (default 30s) during which eviction is interruptible by sustained healthy probes and KV-drain progress; introduces an SLO compaction step which caps incremental SLO penalty accrual per-tenant to a smoothing function over a sliding window (configurable, default 5m) to avoid runaway penalty spikes; adds a bridge in the load-shed decision path that blends hard eviction signals with the new soft-quarantine state to prefer gradual eviction and KV-prefetch-affine throttling instead of immediate hard disconnection.

Key motivations: reduce cross-region failover churn, prevent collateral tenant evictions from transient probe noise, provide an operational knob to trade short-term SLO strictness for stability during known region-level capacity events.

Implementation summary: changes in services/slo-manager: new interruptible_quarantine.go controller and compaction policy implementation; runtime/shedder: decision path updated to consult QuarantineBridge and to allow staged eviction with TTL-backoff; sequencer: small backpressure hook to surface kv-drain progress for interrupt logic; config: feature flag slo_compaction.enable and parameters under runtime.features.slo_compaction; tests: unit tests for compaction math and e2e stability test that simulates probe flapping.

Behavioral notes and knobs: the feature is off by default. When enabled it introduces three knobs: quarantine_window_seconds (default 30), slo_compaction_window_seconds (default 300), and max_penalty_delta_pct_per_window (default 20%). Operators can tune via the runtime config map or via the Console feature toggle.

Rollout plan: 1) Canary in eu-west-1 for low-traffic tenant cohort (2% traffic) for 2h, 2) expand to regional pool for 24h while monitoring slo_burn, circuit_state_flip_rate, and tenant_eviction_rate, 3) full rollout if metrics are stable (<10% change to user-visible latency and <5% change to permanent_eviction_rate). Rollback is a single flag flip.

Testing & verification: added unit coverage to slo-manager (compaction math), added integration harness scenario that replicates probe noise; ran a 2-hour canary window during which circuit flips dropped by 42% and permanent evictions dropped by 31% in simulated bursts (see commits for logs).

Related: references SUP-2041 root-cause and ENG-1284 followup investigation.

Checklist: - [x] Implementation compiled and unit-tested - [x] Integration test added to perf-canary harness - [x] Feature-flag gating and Console toggle wired - [x] Rollout/monitoring doc added - [x] Post-merge incident watch scheduled
Marco Li: Can we keep the default compaction window at 5m? If customers have very bursty traffic it could hide real regressions. Suggest adding a circuit flip counter override for critical tenants.
Aisha Kapoor: Agree on the concern. Kept default 5m but added max_penalty_delta_pct_per_window and an override for tenants labeled 'critical' to bypass compaction. Added note in runbook.
Elena Martinez: CI failed on integration first run due to a mock time dependency — please avoid global time.Now() in tests.
Aisha Kapoor: Addressed — switched to injected clock in tests and runtime. Pushed fix in commit 4.
Jonah Price: Approved after the clock fix and adding a short e2e canary in eu-west-1. Leaving a follow-up to add dashboard panel for 'quarantine_interrupt_rate'.
Merged by Elena Martinez on 2025-03-15 via squash merge. Merge commit message: 'hotfix(slo): interruptible quarantine + compaction bridge — reduce eviction churn on regional surges'. Backout plan documented in docs/runbooks/slo-compaction.md.
Introduce interruptible quarantine and SLO compaction bridge to reduce eviction and circuit-flip churn during short-lived region surges. Feature gated and off by default. Operators can enable via runtime.features.slo_compaction and tune quarantine_window_seconds, slo_compaction_window_seconds, and max_penalty_delta_pct_per_window.

payload.body:
Summary: Introduces a segmented activation materialization strategy ("segmented activation stitching") combined with opportunistic scratch buffer deflation and a memory-aware microbatch scheduler to lower peak GPU workspace for long-sequence generation workloads. Motivation: large sequence generation and dense KV-cache workloads expose temporary allocation spikes from full-layer re-materialization and transient scratch buffers. Rather than a full-layer checkpoint/restore, this PR divides activations into smaller immutable segments that are stored in a compact delta representation and stitched on demand, enabling finer-grained eviction and smaller transient buffers. Key changes: (1) segmented activation store and stitcher for re-materialization paths; (2) a deflation routine for scratch buffers that compacts and coalesces empty slots during idle windows; (3) microbatch scheduler changes that tag batches with a memory-envelope and stagger allocations to avoid concurrent peak alignment; (4) lightweight KV-window hints that bias eviction for seldom-accessed KV windows during high pressure; (5) telemetry and smoke tests for end-to-end regression on 2x and 8x GPU configs. Compatibility: keeps the public serving API unchanged and includes a runtime flag to opt into the segmented stitcher for canary rollout. Performance summary: on internal GPT-style 8k benchmarks we observe a median 28% reduction in observed peak GPU memory and a 38% reduction in transient workspace allocations for steady-state continuous-batching workloads, with a P95 latency increase of ~2ms for worst-case re-materialization paths. Risk and mitigation: materialization-on-demand can add a small CPU/GPU recompose cost; mitigations include a per-request cold-window prefetch policy and a conservative default canary rollout. Related work: complements recent allocator tuning changes (ENG-61642, ENG-70188) and is orthogonal to quantized kernel work. Testing: unit tests for segment serialization, integration stress tests on multi-concurrency workloads, and a replay harness that validated no correctness regressions across sampled prompts. The description below lists commits, changed areas, review conversation, CI history, and the merge outcome.
a1f4d3c: introduce segmented activation store and stitcher (initial design, serialization format)
b2e7f91: implement scratch buffer deflation and opportunistic coalescer; add microbatch memory-envelope tags
c9d2b5e: add KV-window hinting, telemetry metrics, tests and canary flag; address review comments

Summary: Wires the new FP8 attention kernel path into the serving runtime behind a feature flag, adds kernel-registry entries for supported GPU SKUs, and includes basic correctness tests to ensure safe rollout in the FP8/INT8 benchmarking sprint.

Motivation: As part of the FP8/INT8 kernel benchmarking sprint (ENG-7423), we want to evaluate quantization-friendly attention kernels under realistic prefill/decode mixes without risking global regressions. This PR introduces an opt-in dispatch path with explicit guardrails and a clean fallback to the baseline attention implementation when unsupported.

What’s included: (1) Feature flag: adds `runtime.kernels.fp8_attention.enabled` (default: false) and a per-model override hook used by perf-canary cohorts; (2) Kernel registry/dispatch: registers the FP8 attention kernel variant for H100 (SM90) with shape constraints and runtime checks, and routes eligible attention ops to FP8 when the flag is enabled; (3) Guardrails + fallback: validates alignment constraints (head_dim, qkv strides), mask support, and min/max sequence-length regimes; falls back to baseline attention if any constraints are not met, or if CUDA / driver capabilities are insufficient; (4) Correctness tests: adds a small set of deterministic unit/integration tests comparing FP8 attention outputs to the baseline within tolerance across a few representative shapes (single-batch and small-batch, masked and unmasked). These tests are not performance tests; they are intended only to catch blatant numerical/correctness failures.

Out of scope: no heuristic auto-selection logic (will land in a separate PR tied to ADR-019); no scheduler changes; no canary gating logic. This PR is solely the wiring so we can start measuring.

Implementation notes: - This uses a runtime-level kernel-mode selector with explicit tagging for observability; when enabled, metrics include `kernel_mode=fp8_attn` at the op-level to aid perf triage. - Support is restricted to H100 initially. A100 is intentionally excluded in this PR due to incomplete coverage and higher regression risk; enabling on A100 requires additional kernel variants and validation.

Testing: - `runtime-kernels-unit` (CPU) - `runtime-gpu-smoke` (H100) - Added `fp8_attention_correctness_test` suite gated to run only on H100 CI runners - Manual: ran microbench sanity for 3 shapes (see internal note in ENG-7423)

Rollout plan: Default disabled. Perf team can enable via flag for benchmark harness runs and later canary cohorts (handled elsewhere).
Hiro Tanaka (review): Can we make the fallback behavior explicit in logs/metrics? I want to avoid silent partial enablement during benchmarks. Also, please document the exact shape constraints (head_dim/alignment) in the PR description and in code comments near eligibility checks.

Grace Kim (author): Added a `fp8_attention_fallback_reason` counter (tagged) and a debug log behind `RUNTIME_DEBUG_KERNEL_DISPATCH`. Also expanded comments in `is_fp8_attention_eligible()` and updated the PR description with constraints.

Yuki Sato (review): The flag name should match the convention used in other kernel toggles. Suggest `runtime.kernels.fp8_attention.enabled` (boolean) plus a future-proof enum for modes if needed. Also: ensure we don’t accidentally enable this for models that don’t use the supported attention layout.

Grace Kim (author): Renamed to `runtime.kernels.fp8_attention.enabled` and enforced model-layout checks (requires packed QKV layout + supported mask type). Added a unit test that exercises a non-eligible layout and asserts baseline path is taken.

Rina Kobayashi (review): Correctness tests: please fix random seed determinism and add a tolerance note. We should also include at least one test with causal masking because we’ve historically had mask edge cases.

Grace Kim (author): Seed is now fixed; test vectors are generated deterministically. Added causal mask test + clarified tolerances (`atol=3e-2`, `rtol=3e-2`) and why (FP8 accumulation).

Noah Patel (review): Metrics tagging: make sure the kernel_mode tag doesn’t explode cardinality. Please keep it as a small fixed set of values.

Grace Kim (author): Tag values are now limited to `baseline` | `fp8_attn` and only emitted for attention op spans; no per-shape tags. Also updated metrics doc comment.

Final: All reviewers approved after the second round. No requested changes outstanding.
payload.title: runtime: integrate FP8 attention kernel behind feature flag

Context: During a regional egress surge we observed repeated failover churn where parallel fallback paths triggered contention and caused SLO regressions for steady tenants. This hotpatch introduces an ordered fallback rail to serialize fallback decisions at per-tenant granularity and a probing safeguard that gates regional failover triggers while KV-sync and ephemeral drains are in-flight. Motivation: reduce oscillation and prevent unnecessary regional evacuation during short-lived pressure spikes, improving SLO stability and reducing cold-cache retries. Changes and rationale: 1) ordered fallback rail: a lightweight in-memory per-tenant rail that enqueues fallback transitions and enforces a max-concurrent-fallback of 1 per tenant, with a time-window hysteresis to avoid rapid reopens; 2) probe gating: region health probes now require two sustained probe failures (configurable) and will be suppressed while KV pressure metrics (kv_cache_pressure, inflight_prefetch) exceed thresholds; 3) pretrim pass for queued requests: best-effort trimming of low-priority queued requests to keep admission queues bounded during failover; 4) telemetry: emit fallback_rail.event and probe_gate.reason with tags for tenant, region, and prior_state to aid post-incident analysis; 5) runbook/docs: emergency rollback steps and a checklist for operators added. Checklist: - [x] implement ordered rail with hysteresis - [x] add probe gating condition and metrics hooks - [x] unit + integration tests for rail semantics - [x] e2e scenario reproducer and mitigation test - [x] add runbook fragment and rollout notes Commits summary: feat(fallback): add ordered fallback rail and per-tenant queueing; fix(probe): gate region probe during kv pressure; perf(queue): pretrim low-priority requests; telemetry: baseline fallback_rail and probe_gate events; docs: runbook and rollout. Files changed high-level: runtime/fallback/ordered_rail.go (core logic and tests), runtime/metrics/pressure.go (pressure thresholds), probes/region_probe.go (gating logic), telemetry/events.go (new event types), helm/templates/evacuation-config.yaml (runtime toggles), docs/runbooks/regional-fallback.md (operator steps), test/e2e/fallback_rail_surge_test.go (scenario). Review conversation (high level): "Luca Moretti: Could the ordered rail become a hotspot for high-throughput tenants?" Author reply: "Marisa: We bound rail cost—rail state is sharded by tenant hash and only holds a tiny token + timestamp; benchmarking shows <1% p95 CPU on synthetic 100k tps tenant." "Ayesha Rahman: Probe gating thresholds look conservative; can we expose them as feature flags?" Author: "Added helm toggles and runtime feature flags; defaults mimic previous behavior until rollout." "Benji Ortiz: Add a safety valve to bypass rail during manual evacuations." Author: "Added admin override endpoint and documented the rollback steps in the runbook." CI details: Build: pass; Unit tests: pass; Integration: pass; E2E: failed once due to unrelated flaky network simulator, rerun passed; Lint: pass with one style warning fixed in follow-up commit. Metrics and canary plan: Roll out to 10% of capacity in region-us-east-1 for 1 hour, monitor p50/p95 latency, fallback.count, slo.error_budget_spent, kv_cache_pressure. If fallback.count does not drop and error budget continues to burn, rollback immediately. Merge: squashed and merged by Ayesha Rahman (squash), merge commit 0a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d. Backport/hotfix: cherry-picked to release/2026-02-13 as part of the emergency patch. Notes for operators: To disable the ordered-rail set helm value fallback.orderedRail.enabled=false and restart control-plane pods; to force a region failover during maintenance use admin override endpoint /admin/fallback/force with tenant-scoped flag. Related: ENG-6543 tracks a follow-up to evaluate per-tenant sharding with cross-region stickiness and SRE-112 is the postmortem action item to tune probe thresholds.
Hotpatch: introduce ordered fallback rail to reduce cross-tenant thrash during regional egress spikes; add probe gating to avoid false positive failovers. Backported to main as emergency fix.
Luca Moretti: Could the ordered rail become a hotspot for high-throughput tenants? Please include microbenchmarks.
Marisa Chen: Added microbenchmarks in ordered_rail_test.go and a short perf table in the PR description. Sharding and memory caps added.
Ayesha Rahman: Prefer feature-flagging for probe thresholds so we can tune without redeploys.
Marisa Chen: Exposed helm/runtime flags and added instructions to docs/runbooks/regional-fallback.md.
Benji Ortiz: Need an escape hatch for manual evacuations to bypass rail enforcement.
Marisa Chen: Implemented /admin/fallback/force and documented usage; requires admin token.

Motivation: teams need a low-friction, auditable way to validate unit economics before rolling quantization or batching defaults into production. This PR adds a lightweight CLI tool (unit-econ-audit) that simulates request mixes, applies conservative quantization profiles, and produces an audit report with token-level cost projections and tail-latency risk bands. Summary: add CLI wrapper, new conservative quant profile YAMLs, a small simulation engine that reuses existing sampling primitives, integration tests, and docs. The CLI is intentionally conservative by default (won't recommend aggressive int8 fallbacks) and outputs a set of recommended safe profiles plus warnings for tail latency or accuracy risk. Checklist: - [x] Implement CLI entrypoint and flags for workload slice, sample size, and risk tolerance. - [x] Add conservative quant profile catalog and profile validator. - [x] Reuse workload sampler framework and extend sample tiler for bursty arrival patterns. - [x] Add unit + integration tests and fixtures. - [x] Add docs and a usage example (dev docs and example repo snippet). - [x] Add Linear ticket references and changelog entry. Commits summary: 1) feat(auditor): initial simulator and CLI scaffolding, 2) feat(profiles): add conservative quant catalog and validator, 3) perf(sampling): extend sample tiler to model microbursts and tail latency, 4) test: add integration scenario for tenant-like traffic, 5) docs: usage guide and example walkthrough. Changed areas (high-level): - rwb/tools/unit_econ_audit.py: new CLI and orchestration glue. - rwb/sampling/tiler.py: extend tiler with bursty pattern generator and deterministic seeding. - rwb/quant/profiles/conservative/*.yml: three new conservative profiles for GPU/CPU/edge tiers. - rwb/quant/validator.py: profile schema validator and safety checks. - rwb/tests/integration/test_unit_econ_audit.py: adds end-to-end scenario. - docs/dev/unit-econ-audit.md: walkthrough and examples. - examples/cost-audit/sample-config.json: sample config for customers. Review notes and conversation: - Evan: "Nice end-to-end story; can we expose an option to export recommendations as a JSON policy for the defaults compiler?" Reply (Amina): "Yes, added --export-policy flag to CLI and documented mapping to defaults compiler schema." - Priya: "How are we measuring accuracy regressions for quant profiles?" Reply: "CLI runs a small eval set when --eval-path is provided and reports relative delta; we also emit warnings when delta crosses the risk tolerance threshold." - Marcel: "Integration CI flaked on the tiler seed; make seeding deterministic for test mode." Reply: "Fixed: added --seed and deterministic mode used by tests." CI and stability: initial CI run failed one integration test because of non-deterministic tiler seeding; test retried with deterministic seed and all checks passed. Lint, unit tests and integration scenario run in under 12 minutes on CI. Security review: no secrets, CLI only reads local files; profile validator prevents malformed YAML from being applied. Performance: lightweight simulator targets <1s/sample for default sample sizes; larger sims are limited by --sample-size. Backwards compatibility: conservative profiles and CLI are additive; no behavior change to runtime defaults until exported policies are applied. Merge outcome: merged via squash with commit message summarizing feature and linking ENG-5123. Release notes: "Add unit-econ-audit CLI: simulate workload mixes with conservative quant profiles and export safe policy recommendations for defaults compiler. Useful for pre-flight cost/regression checks." Notes for backport: none. Manual steps: update docs site navigation to include the new dev guide (will be done in docs release PR).
Evan Chen: 'Nice end-to-end story; can we export JSON policy for defaults compiler?'
Amina Patel: 'Added --export-policy flag and mapping in docs.'
Priya Kumar: 'How do we track accuracy regressions with these conservative profiles?'
Amina Patel: 'Optional --eval-path runs a curated eval and reports delta; we warn when above tolerance.'
Marcel Diaz: 'CI flaked due to tiler non-determinism.'
Amina Patel: 'Added deterministic seeding in test mode and --seed flag for reproducibility.'
