Context and motivation: The KV cache has been the primary driver of tail latency spikes and memory churn on multi-tenant serving nodes. Previous approaches (compaction, slab segregation, proactive spill) helped but left two recurring issues: 1) fragmentation across sparse collector regions that prevents reclaiming idles without evicting hot keys, and 2) uncontrolled spill-over that floods the disk path and backpressure cascades into request queues. This PR introduces two coordinated subsystems: (A) sparse-region reclaimer (SRR) which does fine-grained region-level free-list reclamation and compaction hints, and (B) spill backpressure controller (SBC) that applies adaptive admission control to spill workers and integrates with scheduler kernel-selection to avoid contention with hot inference kernels.

Design summary: (A) SRR splits large KV arenas into sparse regions and maintains a per-region occupancy estimate and fragmentation score; regions with low utilization are reclaimed asynchronously with a conservative eviction budget to avoid removing recently-accessed items. Reclamation prefers cold regions determined by an exponential decay of access counters plus a hotness hysteresis window to reduce oscillation. (B) SBC monitors current disk spill queue length, average spill latency, and tail CPU load. When any signal crosses configured thresholds, SBC throttles new spill tasks by moving them into a timed backoff queue and signals the scheduler to deprioritize maintenance threads in favor of inference kernels. SBC exposes a soft-reservation API so the serving runtime can opt-in to reserve a small protected KV pool for critical routes.

What changed (high level): - Implemented sparse region metadata and reclamation loop in redwood/serving/kv/region_reclaimer.{cc,h} - Added fragmentation scoring and eviction budget controller in redwood/serving/kv/evictor.cc - Introduced spill backpressure controller in redwood/serving/kv/spill_controller.{cc,h} and integrated with the existing spill worker. - Scheduler integration layer: scheduler/hints.cc to accept maintenance hints (deprioritize, throttled) and kernel selection glue that prefers lower-latency kernels when SBC signals high IO contention. - New telemetry: metrics for region_fragmentation_score, srr_reclaims, spill_backpressure_level, spill_throttle_events. - Unit and integration tests under redwood/serving/kv/tests/*, bench harness in benchmark-lab/kv-spillback to reproduce backpressure scenarios.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked and reviewed (ENG-3986)
- [x] Unit tests for SRR and SBC
- [x] Integration tests for end-to-end spill scenarios
- [x] Benchmarks showing improved tail latency under mixed workloads
- [x] Rollout plan with gradual canary and feature flag

Commits summary: - Add sparse-region reclaimer core loop and metadata (A. Martinez) - Add fragmentation scoring and eviction budget (A. Martinez) - Implement spill backpressure control & scheduler hooks (R. Patel) - Add soft-reservation API and route-level opt-in (J. Li) - Add tests and benchmarks (M. Chen) - Docs and telemetry (A. Martinez)

Changed areas (representative files): - redwood/serving/kv/region_reclaimer.cc - redwood/serving/kv/region_reclaimer.h - redwood/serving/kv/evictor.cc - redwood/serving/kv/spill_controller.cc - redwood/serving/scheduler/hints.cc - redwood/serving/kv/tests/test_reclaimer.cc - benchmark-lab/kv-spillback/README.md

Example snippet (region reclaim hint):
  // pseudo: mark region for compact if fragmentation_score > threshold && age > min_age
  if (score > cfg.reclaim_fragmentation_threshold && now - region.last_touch > cfg.min_cold_age) {
    reclaim_queue.push(region.id);
  }

Benchmarks: Synthetic mixed workload with 40% large seq generation + 60% short-chat showed: - 95th token latency reduced by ~18% on nodes under memory pressure - Disk spill queue length 6x lower during peaks after SBC engages - No measurable regression (<1%) in median latency for cold-only workloads

Testing and verification: Added deterministic unit tests for region metadata transitions, property-based tests for eviction budget not exceeding configured bounds, and integration test that simulates sustained spill throughput while verifying SBC transitions through green->yellow->red states. Canary rollout: feature flag redwood.kv.srr enabled off by default; enable for 5% of serving nodes for 48 hours with increased telemetry before wider rollouts.

Risk and mitigations: - Risk: Overly aggressive reclamation could evict keys that are about to be used. Mitigation: conservative default thresholds, hotness hysteresis, and a canary rollout. - Risk: SBC could starve maintenance leading to long-term fragmentation. Mitigation: SBC uses a weighted-leaky-bucket that always allows a minimum background maintenance budget.

Related work / follow-ups: - Followup planned to add cross-node cooperative eviction hints for Dedicated clusters (ENG-4210). - Next iteration will add async kernel-safe compaction to enable reclaim without stop-the-world pauses.

Rollout and merge notes: Feature gated. CI green after two reruns (flake in perf test). Merged via squash.
Jordan Li: Please add a small stress harness that exercises threshold transitions — can we reproduce the yellow->red oscillation?
Ava Martinez: Added harness under benchmark-lab/kv-spillback and an integration test that asserts monotonic backpressure state transitions.
Ravi Patel: We should make the soft-reservation configurable per-tenant. Also ensure scheduler hints have a bounded cost to avoid scheduling thrash.
Ava Martinez: Soft-reservation can be toggled per-route via the API; scheduler hint rate limiting added (max 10 hints/s).
Maya Chen: Verified tests locally and ran the bench profile; observed 15-20% 95th improvement on our CI-sized instance. Approving once CI stabilizes.
Add sparse-region reclamation and adaptive spill backpressure to reduce KV cache-induced tail latency and disk spill storms; feature is behind a feature flag and can be gradually enabled per-cluster.

Context: Recent incidents under regional slowpath spikes (SUP-9123) showed large bursts of open backend connections and a cascade of slowpath requests that pushed SLOs past the alert threshold. The canary deployed the initial admission gate but revealed oscillation (rapid open/close) when burst traffic subsided. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: (1) a Connection Thermostat layer that caps and smooths new outgoing connection ramp-ups per-region per-pool, with a PID-inspired dampener to avoid rapid reopen cycles; (2) a Slowpath Trickle-Shedder that converts abrupt slowpath admission into a tokenized trickle stream when queue depth and avg latency cross configured SLO markers. Both changes are guarded behind runtime flags and include an emergency rollback switch. Checklist: - implement thermostat algorithm and bounded queueing - implement trickle-shedder token allocator and backpressure hooks - add metrics (thermostat_setpoint, trickle_tokens_granted, slowpath_sat_rate) and traces for handoff paths - unit tests for edge windows, scheduler fairness, and stepdown - integration canary: 10% traffic region for 2h, telemetry gating - add documentation of config knobs and safety rollback Notes on design: Thermostat keeps a soft target for concurrently opening backend connections and slowly adjusts the target based on short-term latency and connection success rate. A short cooldown prevents immediate reopen after a hard clamp. Trickle-shedder uses a leaky-token approach: when slowpath load exceeds threshold, new slowpath admissions are scheduled into a paced stream (configurable burst+rate) instead of immediate admission; this flattens downstream KV and GPU load while preserving prioritized throughput for high-SLO tenants. Testing & rollout: Ran synthetic spike tests against perf-lab and a 6-hour canary in us-west-2 with traffic mirroring. Initial CI run hit a flaky test (scheduler/alloc_test.go) which was fixed by guarding timeouts; final CI passed. Rollout plan: enable runtime flag in main->canary 10% region->observe 24h->ramp to 100% with 1h pauses and alert thresholds. Revert plan: runtime flag off + immediate connection drain (fast-drain=false) and regional rollback script in runbooks. Related: ENG-1982 (SLO enforcement work), SRE-54 (incident follow-up).
Ethan Martinez: Good idea to smooth connection ramps. Two asks: expose the thermostat setpoint as a tag and add an emergency disable in flags. Also, can you explain the choice of PID constants and where we surface them in the UI?
Nadia Thompson: Added flags.runtime.thermostat.disable and metric thermostat_setpoint with region tag. PID defaults are conservative; moved constants to flags and documented rationale in runbook. Will surface short form in console in a follow-up (ENG-2149).
Priya Kapoor: Concern about tenant fairness when trickle is enabled — will this starve small high-priority tenants?
Nadia Thompson: Trickler honors tenant priority weights; added unit tests for priority-preserving allocation and a fairness meter metric trickle_priority_violation (should be zero).
Liam O'Connor: CI flake on alloc_test.go — repro shows time.Sleep races. Please replace with clock mock/WaitGroup.
Nadia Thompson: Replaced test sleeps with injectible clock; pushed fix (commit b7c8d9e). CI retriggered and passed. Approved by SREs after canary telemetry review.
Add Connection Thermostat to smooth outgoing connection ramp-ups and reduce reopen oscillation.
Introduce Slowpath Trickle-Shedder to pace slowpath admissions during overloads; reduces downstream latency spikes.
Telemetry: new metrics thermostat_setpoint, trickle_tokens_granted, trickle_priority_violation added.
Hotfix: fixes flaky alloc_test and adds canary rollback script.

Introduce a polyphase surge controller to smooth tenant bursts and new utilization telemetry rollups for more accurate per-tenant headroom accounting; no API contract changes.
Summary: Adds a 'polyphase' surge controller that staggers temporary burst allowances across short, medium, and long time windows to avoid synchronized warm-pool pressure during cross-tenant spikes. Also introduces a lightweight tenant utilization rollup pipeline (percentile + EWMA sketches) consumed by the autoscaler and the Console. Motivation: recent incidents showed many tenants taking simultaneous short bursts which forced large warm-pool spin-ups and produced noisy utilization signals. The polyphase approach spreads transient credits and produces smoother admission decisions while preserving short burst responsiveness. Key changes: 1) controller/core/polyphase_controller.go: new algorithm and decision interface; 2) controller/api/telemetry_ingest.go: new rollup ingestion path and schema; 3) telemetry/rollups/percentile_sketch.go: compact sketch implementation tuned for low-cardinality tenant series; 4) autoscaler/integrations.go: uses rollup ETS metrics to adjust warm-pool sizing; 5) console/frontend/tenant-utilization.tsx: new per-tenant 50/90/99 histograms and a 'burst posture' indicator; 6) e2e/bench/scale_surge_test.go: regression test and load harness. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-1324) - [x] Unit tests for sketch and controller - [x] Integration test with warm-pool emulator - [x] Console visualization wired to telemetry - [x] Backwards-compatible telemetry schema (ingest uses feature-flag) Behavior notes: - Polyphase credit windows: 1s (immediate), 30s (short), 5m (sustained). Credits are proportional to tenant commitments with soft upper bounds; controller may defer granting long-window credits if warm pool headroom is low. - Rollups publish: p50, p90, p99, ewma rate, and a burstiness score (0-1). - Default behavior behind feature-flag rollout for 2 weeks then enabled cluster-wide. Commits: ["feat: add polyphase controller core and interfaces", "perf: compact percentile sketch with streaming merge", "chore: telemetry schema version bump and feature flag", "feat: console burst posture UI and API wiring"]. Files changed (high level): ["controller/core/polyphase_controller.go", "controller/core/polyphase_controller_test.go", "telemetry/rollups/percentile_sketch.go", "telemetry/rollups/percentile_sketch_test.go", "telemetry/ingest/ingest_pipeline.go", "autoscaler/integrations.go", "console/frontend/tenant-utilization.tsx", "console/api/handlers/telemetry.go", "e2e/bench/scale_surge_test.go", "deploy/k8s/configmap-rollup.yaml", "scripts/bench/run_surge_harness.sh", "docs/ops/polyphase-deploy.md"]. Runtime impact: microbenchmarking shows 6-8% CPU overhead on the telemetry pipeline at peak ingest but reduces warm-pool spin-ups by ~22% in simulated multi-tenant surge tests. Reviewed perf tradeoffs and added sampling thresholds to avoid unbounded cost. Backwards compatibility: ingest preserves v1 schema; rollup feature requires opt-in flag. Rollout plan: staged rollout to canary clusters (2 days) -> regional pools (5 days) -> global (toggle off if regression).
Sophie: Can we get a deterministic unit test that simulates three tenants bursting at offset phases? Marcus: Added polyphase_controller_test.go with a deterministic clock and a table of staggered spikes. Omar: I'm worried about memory amplification from sketches at high cardinality. Marcus: Sketch defaults to per-tenant sampling; added a global sampler and a hard cap. Priya: Console UX looks good; request minor copy change for 'burst posture' tooltip. Marcus: Updated copy and added docs/ops polyphase-deploy.md with rollout and rollback steps. QA: Ran e2e harness in staging, observed 22% fewer warm pool spins in simulated traffic, no regression on latency p95. Approvals: Sophie approved, Omar approved after cap change, Priya approved after copy tweak.

Motivation: Long-running production incidents showed noisy logs and high-cost tail invocations where token cost spikes correlate with unbounded logging. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: (1) a TokenBudgetEstimator that predicts per-invocation token budget (expected tokens + safety margin) using light-weight features (model, route, historical prompt shape) and (2) an adaptive log-gating middleware that uses the estimator at request time to decide logging fidelity and span enrichment. The goals are: reduce observability noise for low-value heavy invocations, preserve high-fidelity traces for risky/expensive invocations, and expose token-budget-derived metrics for dashboards and alerting.

What this changes (summary): adds a new estimator implementation (observability/metrics/token_budget_estimator.py) with a pluggable config, adds a tracing/log-gate integration (observability/tracing/log_gate.py) that tags spans with budget_decision and gated_fields, a compact dashboard (console/dashboards/token_budget_overview.json) showing predicted budget vs actual token spend, and new alert rules (alerting/policies/budget_alerts.yaml) to surface cases where actual > predicted * 1.5 for high-SLA tenants. There are docs explaining configuration knobs and rollout plan (docs/observability/token-budget.md). Tests included cover estimator calibration and gating heuristics.

Implementation notes and constraints: the estimator is intentionally conservative and runs synchronously in the request pre-hook with a bounded CPU budget; model pedigrees (model family + tokenization scheme) are considered to keep predictions stable across quantized variants. The gating middleware currently supports two levels: minimal (error + span id) and full (token deltas + KV samples). Gating decisions are emitted as a metric token_budget.gate_rate{decision=minimal|full} for monitoring and can be toggled per-tenant via helm values (deploy/helm/values-observability.yaml).

Rollout plan: behind feature flag (ff_observe_token_budget) and default-off for enterprise tenants. Staged rollout: 1) internal Canary (1% traffic) for 48h with token_budget.gate_rate SLO checks, 2) expand to all internal tenants (7 days), 3) optional customer opt-in. Alerts: added budget overrun alert (SEV3) and gate-rate drift alert (SEV4) with automated quiet-windowing for known maintenance windows.

Risks and mitigations: wrong budget calibration could over-suppress valuable logs; mitigated by conservative multiplier and retaining full logs when spans show error states or when cost > 3x predicted. We also emit a debug telemetry stream (sampled) of gated events for offline QA. Performance: estimator adds ~150us median latency on our canary (measured in local perf bench). Load tests included in this PR run showed <1% p50 latency increase at 99th percentile load for the canary configuration.

Motivation: Under high client backpressure and aggressive batching we observed a class of desynchronization issues where partial JSON payloads lost delimiter context or retransmitted fragments interleaved function-call sentinels, causing OpenAI-compatible SDKs to fail to reconstruct structured output or to apply function calls out of order. Summary: Introduces a lightweight resynchronization protocol and parser hardening without changing the public API: 1) add a small fragment header with a 8-bit rolling window checksum and frag_seq per request so receivers can detect gaps quickly and trigger resync; 2) emit an opt-in resync_marker SSE event from the server when sequence gaps or overlap are detected to allow clients to fast-resynchronize state; 3) parser: delimiter-aware coalescing with a bounded lookback and a quoted-boundary heuristic to avoid treating delimiter bytes inside JSON strings or escapes as stream boundaries; 4) retransmit/replay path: stash in-flight sentinel tokens (function-call sentinels, tool markers) and enforce stable replay ordering on retransmit to avoid interleaving; 5) OpenAI-compat adapter: expose an opt-in "resync" mode so SDKs can opt into marker-aware reconstruction during staged rollout. Tests: deterministic backpressure simulator, randomized fuzz harness against the SSE parser (500k runs), targeted integration tests ensuring function-call ordering across retransmits, and a small perf bench to quantify cost. Rollout: staged canary at 5% then 25% with monitoring for resync_marker emission rate and tail latency; rollback criteria documented. Related work: builds on ENG-2419 and addresses customer incident SUP-9876. No breaking API changes and SDKs can opt-in. Detailed commit history, changed areas, reviewer discussion, and CI results follow.
Julian Meyers: Overall approach looks good — can you quantify the perf cost of the header/checksum in the common case? Please add a microbenchmark and document the cost in docs/sse.md.
Aisha Khatri: Added microbenchmark in sse/bench_checksum.go and included results in docs; median token latency regression under synthetic backpressure was 0.4% at canary settings.
Chen Li: The quoted-boundary heuristic looks fragile on nested escapes. Please add a unit test that fuzzes nested string escapes and confirm no false boundaries.
Aisha Khatri: Added nested-escape fuzz test and extended fuzz corpus; CI fuzz pass included in results.
Sofia Morales: Needed a TTL on stashed sentinel tokens to avoid unbounded memory during extreme retransmit storms. Please add a soft TTL and metrics for dropped stashed tokens.
Aisha Khatri: Implemented 30s soft TTL and exported metrics sse.stash.dropped_ttl and sse.resync_marker.count; added test and docs.
Julian Meyers: Approving pending documentation updates and CI green. Thanks for the thorough tests.
Fixes rare stream desyncs caused by backpressure-induced fragmentation: improves SSE parser resynchronization, adds a fast-path for delimiter-prefixed fragments, stashes and reorders sentinel tokens during retransmit to preserve function-call ordering. No API changes.

Context: We need a safer, low-noise promotion path for multi-arm A/B experiments that mixes shadow verification and canary traffic with adaptive fidelity controls. Existing staged rollouts are brittle when metric signal is noisy across cohorts and when traffic heterogeneity creates false positives that trigger rollbacks. This PR implements a 'gradient fallback funnel': a compact orchestrator stage that gradually introduces live traffic to candidates with a fidelity hedging policy that autoscatters decisions across shadow-check passes and low-fraction canaries before committing. Motivation: reduce unnecessary rollbacks, improve signal-to-noise when A/B arms show small effect sizes, and provide a clear behavioral contract for automatic fallback when telemetry is inconclusive. Changes: 1) rollout/orchestrator/funnel.go: new GradientFunnel controller implementing staged phases - shadow-validate -> low-fraction-safety -> ramp -> commit/rollback. 2) rollout/policies/fidelity_hedge.py: fidelity hedging policy (configurable alpha/beta, shadow passes, entropy threshold). 3) routing/bridge.go: light-weight shadow bridge to mirror traffic with sampling and deterministic session-affinity. 4) telemetry/partitioned_metrics.md: docs for new partitioned SLOs and recommended thresholds. 5) docs/rollout-playbooks.md: new runbook for handling ambiguous signals and operator overrides. 6) e2e/experiment_integration_test.py: new integration test that simulates noisy cohorts and validates fallback behavior. 7) api/rollouts.proto: API extension to expose fidelity parameters and runbook links. Design highlights: - Gradient phases are tunable by duration and fraction; defaults are conservative (2 shadow passes, 0.5% initial ramp). - Fidelity hedging uses a small held-out comparison window and an entropy-based abort when cohorts diverge with high variance. - Automatic fallback paths: fast rollback (immediate revert on catastrophic SLO breach), graceful fallback (move candidate back to shadow only for N minutes), and locked-operator state. - Observability: added debug spans, phased metrics (shadow_passes, hedge_aborts, ramp_progress) and a new dashboard template. Migration: rollout controller is backward-compatible; existing A/B configs can opt into gradient funnel by setting strategy: "gradient_fallback". Linear/Jira: relates to ENG-4820 (rollout safety) and SUP-2110 (customer incident prompting better hedging). Checklist: - [x] Implementation of controller and policy - [x] Unit tests for hedging logic - [x] Integration test with synthetic noise - [x] Docs and runbook - [x] Backwards compatibility and proto bump - [x] Canary in staging for 24h before merge Tests and CI: initial CI run showed a flaky integration test (timeout) which was addressed by increasing test timeouts and adding a deterministic RNG seed. All checks green on the final run. Rollout plan: merge to main, canary in staging for 24 hours targeting internal traffic, enable for one internal product team as opt-in for 2 weeks, then expose to platform config page. Rollback behavior: merged as a safe strategy with clear audit trails and operator overrides. Related: builds on ideas from ENG-3891 (shadow verification) but is intentionally narrower and focused on multi-arm AB patterns.

Author (Eleni): Added example formula and staging thresholds; defaults are conservative and can be overridden. See telemetry/partitioned_metrics.md lines 32-46.
Ravi Kapoor: Performance question — will shadow bridge increase CPU overhead on the frontends? Suggest making sampling pluggable and defaulting to server-side offload.
Author (Eleni): Shadow bridge does sampling at the edge proxy level; updated routing/bridge.go comment and added config to allow offload to a sidecar. Also added benchmark notes to docs/rollout-playbooks.md.

Maya Chen: Approve after minor doc tweaks.
Ravi Kapoor: Looks good to me; eager to see staging results.
Benji Alvarez: Approved.
Introduce 'gradient_fallback' rollout strategy: conservative shadow-first validation, fidelity hedging for noisy cohorts, and phased ramp with automated fallback paths. Includes docs, runbook, and dashboard template.

Adds a tenant-aware cost sampler (cost-radar) and a conservative quantization fallback operator (quant-attenuator). New defaults are non-invasive and gated behind feature flags. Improves unit economics visibility and reduces token-cost spikes from cold/micro-burst traffic.
Context and motivation: production traffic exhibits transient micro-bursts and tenant coldstart patterns that inflate per-token cost when aggressive quant profiles are applied globally. This PR introduces two cooperating components: (1) cost-radar sampler: a lightweight, tenant-scoped sampler that continuously profiles batch shapes, coldstart frequency, and KV-cache hit patterns; (2) quant-attenuator: a runtime policy agent that applies a conservative quantization fallback for affected tenants during detected cost-surge windows.

Design summary: cost-radar runs as a low-overhead sidecar inside the serving mesh and emits aggregated sketches to the econ inspector. It ships tenant summaries on a 1m cadence (configurable) and triggers a policy decision when the sampled unit-econ delta exceeds a threshold. The quant-attenuator translates policy decisions into guarded runtime actions: temporarily switch to a compatible, higher-precision profile (e.g., q4 -> q8 fallback) for the tenant's warmup lane, optionally increase batch sizing and invoke a short-lived KV-cache prefill. Both components are opt-in by default and controlled by tenant flags and the admin console.

Checklist: - [x] cost-radar sampling prototype implemented (Go) - [x] quant-attenuator policy and runtime hooks (Rust) - [x] telemetry and Grafana dashboard (docs) - [x] unit + integration tests covering policy arbitration - [x] feature-flag gates and rollout plan - [x] CLI dry-run mode for policy simulation

How to test locally: 1) enable feature flag: `redwoodctl flags set tenant:<TENANT> cost_radar=true` 2) run `./dev/local-sampler --tenant <TENANT> --trace` to stream snapshots 3) simulate micro-burst with `tools/simulate_traffic --bursts 50 --shape short` 4) run `redwoodctl econ simulate --dry-run` to validate the quant-attenuator decision without applying changes.

Migration notes: defaults are conservative and opt-in. No automatic tenant-wide quant changes occur until the attenuator policy is enabled for a tenant. Existing autoscale and rollout logic is compatible; tie-breakers when both autoscale and attenuator want to change batch sizing prefer autoscale unless a `force-fallback` flag is set.

Related work: references ENG-9981 (cost signal pipeline), ENG-10012 (tenant warmup strategy), and SUP-2143 (support ticket motivating conservative fallbacks).
Diego Ramos (2026-02-16): Nice design. Please add a metric for 'attenuator.decisions' with tenant label so SRE can slice it. Also request adding a unit test for a churny tenant.
Aisha Kaur (2026-02-16): Added metric and a churny-tenant unit test. PTAL.
Markus Feldman (2026-02-18): Question: how does this interact with Dedicated capacity policies? If a tenant is on Dedicated, we should avoid switching quant profiles without ops approval.
Aisha Kaur (2026-02-18): Good catch — added a dedicated_tenant guard in policy.rs; attenuator becomes no-op unless 'allow_dedicated_fallback' is set in tenant settings. Documented in migration notes.
Hannah Lee (2026-02-20): CI flake observed on the sim test; re-ran and green. Approving after minor naming change to metric label.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Customers struggle to pick safe yet cost‑effective defaults for batching and caching across tenants with diverse request shapes. Large config surfaces (stride, max_batch_delay_ms, KV prefill hints, and quant profile selection) mean teams either overprovision latency targets or accept expensive per‑token costs. This PR introduces 'cost-beacon', a lightweight tenant profiler and adaptive default generator that observes a short bootstrap window for a tenant and suggests conservative batch-stride defaults, cache prefill hints, and a per-tenant quant profile candidate.

What this change does (high level): Implements a runtime component (cost-beacon) plus a small CLI/agent (costctl) to run a 1–5 minute sampling pass per tenant (or for a subset of requests) to: 1) estimate effective sequence-length distribution and concurrency footprint, 2) compute an adaptive batch stride (micro-batching stride) that balances latency SLO vs unit-cost for that tenant, 3) suggest KV/prefix cache prefill thresholds and TTL hints to reduce repeated prefix work, and 4) run a lightweight quant profile probe (quant-thermostat probe) that scores candidate quantization points on a tiny eval set to recommend a conservative quant profile for production rollout.

Implementation notes: The profiler runs as an opt-in sidecar in Dedicated/Private deployments and as an account-level sampler in Hosted. The runtime side includes: runtime/batcher/stride_scheduler.go (new scheduler that accepts adaptive stride overrides), runtime/cache/prefill_hint.go (hint propagation / telemetry tagging), components/cost-beacon/collector.go (sampling, sketching histograms, and tenant model), components/cost-beacon/strategy.go (heuristics that map signals to defaults), cli/costctl/probe.go (CLI for dry-run and dry-simulate), and docs/quickstarts/cost-beacon.md. Config surfaced to Console: suggested defaults and a confidence score. We intentionally keep the initial heuristics conservative (favoring latency for interactive tenants) and provide an automatic rollback window controlled by rollout policies.

Checklist: - [x] Sampling pipeline and TTL-limited sketches implemented - [x] Stride calculator + scheduler integration - [x] KV prefill hinting into runtime traces - [x] Small quant probe harness with per-tenant candidate scoring - [x] CLI (costctl) dry-run and apply flow - [x] Unit and integration tests + perf microbenchmarks - [x] Docs + console annotations - [x] Canary rollout plan + feature flag gating

Testing and validation: Unit tests for stride math, cache hint propagation, and quant probe scoring included. Integration test spins up a 2-GPU local harness and verifies that stride override yields expected latency/cost tradeoffs for three synthetic workloads (short-chat, long-composition, high-concurrency inference). Perf bench was run using benchmark-lab with tenant workloads; measured median token-cost reduction of 8–14% for chat-like tenants with unchanged 95th-percentile latency under the conservative profile. CI initially failed lint (gofmt) and a flakey bench test (BenchStrideScheduler) — both addressed in follow-ups and re-ran CI passing.

Rollout plan: 1) Feature gated behind acct-level flag and a Console toggle. 2) Internal canary: 5 tenants on Dedicated for 48h with telemetry dashboards (latency SLOs, unit-cost, cache hit-rate). 3) Gradual expansion to Hosted with default 'suggest' mode (no automatic apply) before enabling auto-apply for tenants that opt in.

Risk and mitigations: - Incorrect quant recommendation: probe uses a conservative penalty for any loss of output coherence; recommendations are advisory until explicitly accepted. - Over-aggressive batching: scheduler enforces latency SLO ceilings and automatically reduces stride on observing SLO erosion. - Telemetry cost: sampling window is limited and sketching uses low-memory summaries.

Related work: This complements prior autotune efforts (prefill/autotune) by focusing on a short-lived, tenant-specific bootstrap that produces high-confidence conservative defaults rather than complex long-running autotuners. Linear refs: ENG-3482 (profiler), PM-112 (productization).

How to validate locally: run `make dev-costbeacon` to start the sidecar sampler against local redwood runtime; `costctl probe --tenant-id=demo --dry-run` will print suggested stride/cache/quant with confidence and simulated cost delta.

Notes: This PR purposefully keeps the decision mapping white-box and human-readable so SEs can audit suggested defaults for enterprise customers. Future follow-ups will add model-based suggestion and multi-tenant cross-signal aggregation.

Maya Chen: Added safety clamp in stride_scheduler.go and unit tests (clamp value landed behind config flag).
Sophie Alvarez: The quant probe harness looks promising but add a test that verifies recommendation is advisory until user-apply path is used.
Maya Chen: Added CLI flow to require explicit 'costctl apply --confirm' for Hosted, and feature-flaged auto-apply only for Dedicated in the canary. Tests updated.
Liam O'Neill: Approving pending CI green. Observability: add a Grafana dashboard link in docs.
Maya Chen: Added dashboard link and a short dasboard JSON export to docs/quickstarts. CI re-ran and passed.
Introduce cost-beacon (tenant profiler) and adaptive batch-stride defaults plus a conservative quant probe. Adds costctl CLI with dry-run and apply. Feature gated; default mode = suggest. Reduces token unit-cost for chatlike tenants in early tests by 8–14% while preserving latency SLOs.
Adds a conservative tenant profiling component that recommends batch and cache defaults plus quant candidates; CLI and docs included, canary-ready.

Motivation: During recent regional surges we observed tenant-level SLO violations triggering aggressive global circuit flips and mass eviction of low-priority requests. That behavior caused unnecessary cold-path rebuilds and DLL cache churn for tenants that were transiently hot in a small window. This PR implements a tenant-aware SLO windowing mechanism plus an ephemeral local fallback circuit that lets tenants degrade softly for short windows without affecting global circuit state.

What this change does (single-string summary): Adds a sliding tenant SLO window allocator (configurable window length and weight decay), a short-lived "ephemeral" local fallback circuit that can be raised/lowered per tenant-region for a configured grace period, and a prioritized token drain that preserves high-importance tokens (system, admin, and paid-priority) while shedding best-effort traffic. Also wires metrics, tracing, rollout flags, and an emergency hotfix toggle.

Key benefits and rationale: 1) Limits blast radius of transient spikes by keeping global circuits stable; 2) Enables soft degradation for tenants experiencing micro-surges without impacting sibling tenants; 3) Reduces cold-cache rewarm costs by avoiding full-eviction; 4) Gives product teams control via tenant-level knobs and short automatic decay.

Design notes: - Tenant SLO windows are tracked per (tenant, region, model_variant) and aggregate into a single moving-average score used by the SLO enforcer. The allocator uses a decayed sum with configurable half-life to avoid overreacting to single anomalies. - Ephemeral fallback circuit is a separate state machine with a short TTL (default 45s) and exponential backoff; it only controls soft-shed actions (priority-based token dropping and low-quality model variant routing). It does not flip global region circuit state. - Token prioritization: tokens are annotated at ingress; drain respects token classes (system>paid>free). Low-class tokens are dropped probabilistically with a ramp based on measured token pressure. - Rollout strategy: feature gated behind runtime flag slo.tenant_windowing; default off for 24-hour canary on selected tenants, then staged ramp.

Checklist: - [x] Implement window allocator and state persistence (- compact protobuf snapshot) - [x] Implement ephemeral circuit state machine and TTL-based decay - [x] Implement token prioritization and draining hooks in the request router - [x] Add metrics and tracing spans (tenant.window_score, tenant.ephemeral_state, token.drop_rate) - [x] Add configuration knobs and runtime feature gate - [x] Unit tests for allocator and circuit transitions - [x] Integration test with synthetic surge harness - [x] Docs and runbook updates - [x] Canary rollout and monitoring dashboard prepared

Backward compatibility and safety: Behavior is opt-in. Default runtime flag is off; when on we exercise only soft-shed paths. No breaking API changes. Config values have sensible conservative defaults to minimize false positives.

Performance: Local microbenchmarks show the allocator adds ~0.3% CPU and <1ms p90 request decision latency on our canary nodes. In synthetic surge tests we reduced global circuit flips by 78% and cache rewarm-related 95th latency by 22%.

Files changed (high level): see files_changed list for full paths. Key files include the SLO allocator core, ephemeral circuit manager, router draining hook, protobuf snapshots, runtime flags, tests, and docs.

Rollout plan and monitoring: - Stage 0: Internal canary (4 nodes) on dev cluster with slo.tenant_windowing=true for test tenants for 24h. - Stage 1: 10% tenant population in us-west for 48h with tight dashboards. - Stage 2: 50% ramp with automated abort if token drop_rate > 2.5% or tenant.window_score false-positive spikes > 3x baseline. Emergency toggle slo.disable_ephemeral=true to disable immediately.

Related work: complements ENG-4210 (regional soft-failover), refactors parts of ENG-4122 (per-tenant quotas). Supports SUP-1182 incident mitigation playbook.

Notes for reviewers: Focus on correctness of circuit transitions, serialization of allocator state across restarts, and ensuring drain preserves high-priority token semantics. The hotfix toggle path is intentionally minimal and covered by e2e.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged after two approving reviews and a green CI run.

Julian Park: Can we ensure allocator snapshots are written atomically to avoid partial restores? (see comment inline about temporary file rename) - Asha: Yes, using atomic tempfile+rename, added tests.
Leah Moreno: The token drain probabilities need a guard to avoid starving paid tokens under extreme noise. Suggest adding min_preserve for paid tokens. - Asha: Added min_preserve=0.98 for paid and system tokens; config default in flags.toml.
Samir Iqbal: CI flake on first run due to test harness timeout; reran and passed. Also suggested clearer dashboard alerts—updated.
Ops (post-merge): Confirmed canary tenants behaved as expected over 36h with no global flips.
Introduces opt-in tenant SLO windowing and ephemeral local fallbacks to enable soft degradation during short tenant surges. Feature is behind runtime flag slo.tenant_windowing and includes a hotfix toggle slo.disable_ephemeral. Reduces global circuit flips and cache rewarm costs. See docs/ops/tenant_slo_windowing.md for runbook and config.

Motivation: Our presubmit matrix has grown organic profiles encoded in bash + make targets. That makes on-call triage and staged fastpaths brittle and hard to reason about. This PR introduces a typed presubmit profile abstraction implemented as a small TypeScript action and a compact release dry-run prober that exercises release hooks without performing real deploys. Goals: 1) standardize presubmit profiles (fast, full, infra-smoke) as typed JSON schema so CI can select lightweight lanes deterministically, 2) replace ad-hoc shell scripts with a single typed action to reduce flakiness and enable incremental test-slicing, 3) add a non-invasive release dry-run prober to validate release choreographies and ensure that release automation hooks (signing, artifact promotion, rollback policies) are runnable in CI without impacting production. Design summary: - presubmit profiles: schema v1 under .github/presubmit/profiles.schema.ts and profiles/ directory with canonical profiles. Profiles are validated at PR time by the new action .github/actions/typed-presubmit. - typed action: small node-based action (TS compiled) that resolves changed paths, maps to profile buckets, and emits annotations consistent with our existing presubmit telemetry. The action supports a --dry-run mode used by local devcontainers. - release dry-run prober: lightweight Go binary under ci/probers/release_dryrun that simulates release hooks (artifact signing stub, permission checks, rollout-fallback path) against a mocked control-plane. The prober runs as part of a staged release-check job and produces structured JSON reports which are then stored as artifacts for later inspection. Implementation notes: - Migration path: legacy make targets still work; a temporary compatibility shim maps old target names to profiles for two weeks before deprecation. - Rollout: gated behind a feature flag in CI config (ci/flags.yaml) and will be flipped after two successful nightly runs. - Performance: end-to-end presubmit latency for incremental changes reduced on average by 22% in internal experiments by skipping heavyweight E2E in fast profile. - Safety: the release dry-run uses mocked signing and does not touch production credentials; integration tests verify no network calls to production endpoints. Why not a monolithic refactor: typed action is intentionally tiny (approx 280 LOC) to make future audits easier. Follow-ups: create a presubmit-dashboard card (ENG-10235) to visualize profile distributions. Backcompat: none for external consumers. This long description contains context, motivation, implementation details, rollout plan, and follow-up work in one continuous string per repo conventions.

Context: We observed persistent streaming first-byte tail latency for medium-length responses (tokens 8..128) caused by misaligned emitter ticks, inefficient microbatching at low emission density, and cold KV lookups triggered just-in-time. This PR introduces a coordinated emitter layer (the "harmonic emit coordinator") that aligns emission ticks to kernel execution windows, applies graded per-stream backpressure using harmonic credit shaping, and plugs in an anticipatory KV prefetcher that uses short-horizon sequence hints to warm the KV cache before kernel execution. The combined change targets stable TTFB improvements without sacrificing peak throughput. What changed (high-level): - New coordination layer: runtime/emitter/harmonic_coordinator.rs implements a lightweight tick harmonizer that observes kernel run windows and schedules flushes on harmonic boundaries to reduce interleaved kernel churn. - Graded backpressure: emitter now applies a per-stream harmonic credit curve (fast-path for hot streams, gentle damping for cold streams) to avoid sudden flushes that cause kernel scatter. - KV synergy: runtime/kv/prefetcher.rs introduces a predictive prefetch hook; when a stream's emission density and token context match a learned warmup pattern, we probe the KV cache early and bias kernel placement to nodes with warmer caches. - Continuous microcoalescer: runtime/batcher/continuous.rs coalesces sub-token microbatches within a short adaptive window when pending emissions are sparse; avoids draining immediate credits to preserve kernel affinity. - Kernel policy: runtime/scheduler/kernel_policy.rs updated to consider emission_density and kv_warmth_score when selecting execution kernels and packing microbatches. - Tests and docs: added integration tests and a performance explainer in docs/perf/emit-coordinator.md. Rollout plan: Canary at 5% traffic in the US region, metric gates on median TTFB, p95/p99, and overall token/s GPU efficiency; automatic rollback if p99 regresses > 8% during canary. Observed outcomes in internal benchmarks: - Median TTFB reduction: 12% - p95 reduction: 22% - p99 reduction: 35% on medium-length responses under mixed workload in our perf lab - End-to-end throughput unchanged within noise (+/-2%) on dense generation workloads; slight throughput dip (~2%) in extreme microburst scenarios but with much lower tail latency tradeoff. Backwards compatibility: behavior is feature-flagged as "harmonic_emit" and off by default for Dedicated/Private until customer opt-in. Compatibility with model variants: kernel selection fallbacks remain in place; if KV hints are unavailable, coordinator degenerates to conservative flush cadence. Related: builds on ideas from earlier credit/granularity PRs but rethinks scheduling from a coordinator-first perspective. This description includes the motivation, design, and rollout plan in one continuous narrative.
Priya: Why harmonic boundaries? Can you include a microbenchmark showing kernel affinity improvements versus a simple fixed-interval flush?
Evan: Added bench in examples/benchmarks and included kernel-affinity metric (emit_alignment_ms) in the perf dashboard queries.
Luca: The KV prefetch probe looks like it could add latency for cold paths. Can we gate it with a low false-positive budget?
Evan: Prefetch is gated by a warmth_score threshold and a sampled rate; added explanatory comments and a metric to track prefetch hit/miss ratio.
Janelle: Integration test flaked on macOS runner (timing-based). Suggest switching to wall-clock tolerant assertions.
Evan: Updated tests to be tolerant and added CI retry annotation for flaky_networked_test.
Priya: Approve after the test flake patch and a short note in docs about the canary rollback conditions.
Luca: Approved. Recorded performance numbers look solid for canary rollout.
Introduce harmonic emit coordinator to align emitter ticks with kernel windows, graded per-stream backpressure, anticipatory KV prefetch hooks, and an adaptive microcoalescer — reduces streaming TTFB and p99 for medium-length responses with minimal throughput impact. Feature flag: harmonic_emit. Canary rollout with automatic rollback on p99 regression.
Canary telemetry: emit_alignment_ms, kv_warmth_score, prefetch_hit_ratio, microcoalesce_rate
Known limitation: small throughput regression under pathological microburst workloads; tracked in ENG-1320
Next steps: extend KV hinting to cross-request patterns and evaluate kernel packing heuristics for very long-context models

Background: Our presubmit pipeline has grown heavy as we accumulate transient devdeps and broad lint/test coverage. This PR introduces a small, low-risk refactor that: (1) partitions CI-facing dependencies into stable and ephemeral buckets to reduce install churn, and (2) adds a lightweight presubmit prober that runs a curated set of end-to-end smoke checks (including a few representative LLM prompts against the OpenAPI-compatible inference API) to detect regressions in streaming/structured-output behavior before full integration tests run. Motivation: reduce CI setup time, limit noisy dependency churn, and catch API contract regressions earlier with a cheap smoke stage. What this changes: - CI dep bucketing: a new ci/deps/manifest.yaml describes two groups: stable (pinned semver, cached) and ephemeral (fast-refresh, optional). The presubmit image build uses the manifest to only install ephemeral deps when changed. - Presubmit prober: a thin Go binary (ci/presubmit/prober/main.go) that loads a small prompt set (ci/presubmit/prompts/*.jsonl) and runs lightweight checks (tokenization sanity, streaming frames received, basic structured JSON validation). It returns non-zero only for clear contract breaks. - Staged presubmit lanes: workflow now has quick-lint -> prober -> full-integration gates. The prober gate is short (<= 30s on average) and can be toggled via labels. Migration and rollout: default opt-in for repos under redwood/; rollout plan included in the checklist below. Rollback: revert workflow YAML or label toggle to disable prober immediately. Risks: false positives for model output are mitigated by using deterministic synthetic prompts and schema checks only. Implementation notes: - Added caching key changes to workflows to include bucket manifest checksum so caches are invalidated only when stable bucket changes. - Adjusted lint runner to skip heavy linters in the quick-lint lane and surface them in the slower lanes. - CI images updated to include a minimal runtime for the prober (Go1.21, small curl shim). Checklist: - [x] Add ci/deps/manifest.yaml and install harness - [x] Implement presubmit prober and sample prompt set - [x] Wire prober into .github/workflows/presubmit.yml as a staged check - [x] Add doc snippet to docs/contrib/ci.md describing bucketing TTLs - [x] Run in canary mode on redwood/* and redwood-sdk-* for 72h before org-wide rollout Related work: Linear ENG-4022, ENG-4098. This description contains the end-to-end context, migration notes, and rollback plan.
Canary run: 72h across redwood/redwood, redwood-sdk-python, redwood-sdk-typescript. Observed median presubmit setup time reduced 28% (from 86s to 62s) on canary projects. Cache hit rate for stable bucket ~94% across canary. Prober false-positive rate: 0/48 synthetic checks; one flaky network failure on test runner was mitigated by retry logic. Metrics tracked in Console: ci.presubmit.setup_ms, ci.prober.duration_ms, ci.cache.hit_ratio.
1) Merge to main behind 'canary' label. 2) Monitor canary for 72h. 3) Expand label targeting to more repos. 4) After 1 week, flip default to enabled org-wide and deprecate old heavy quick-presubmit job. See docs/contrib/ci.md for TTL knobs.
Ops: when deploying org-wide, watch cache-hit ratio and presubmit queue depth. If presubmit_prober begins to fail due to infra slowness, disable by adding label 'prober-disable' to the workflow_dispatch or revert .github/workflows/presubmit.yml. The manifest checksum (ci/deps/manifest.yaml) is used in cache keys; rotating stable bucket should be done with a follow-up PR that notes cache invalidation.
Introduce dependency bucketing for CI and a lightweight presubmit prober that runs schema/smoke checks on a small representative prompt set. This reduces presubmit latency and catches contract regressions early. Backwards compatible: prober is opt-in via labels during canary, and bucketing is transparent to dev workflows.
Claire Huang (requested changes): The prober is great, but can we reduce default concurrency to 2 to avoid thundering on the canary infra? Also request that the prompt set be clearly labeled synthetic vs production so we don't accidentally leak customer prompts. - Aisha: updated main.go to limit concurrency via --workers flag and added metadata fields to prompts. Pushed commit a6e4d21.
Miguel Santos: Suggest adding an explicit cache key tie to ci/deps/manifest.yaml checksum to avoid invalidating cache on unrelated changes. - Aisha: implemented cache_key_util and adjusted workflow, see f14b0d2.
Ben Walker (approval): Verified canary run results and infra metrics. Approve after CI green and a short observation window.

Motivation: Production customers increasingly ask not just for current token/latency cost telemetry but for short-term forecasts that help platform and customer teams answer: how long will a given token budget or latency SLO hold at current load and growth trends? This PR adds a lightweight prognostics pipeline and an interactive dashboard that surfaces per-tenant and per-route 'token runway' estimates and probabilistic SLO breach forecasts.

Scope and changes: single continuous set of changes across instrumentation, ingestion, forecasting, dashboard, and alert tuning: 1) metric instrumentation: new rolling-window metrics (runway_tokens_remaining, runway_rate_trend, latency_slo_tail_prob) exported from the gateway and runtime with tenant+route labels; OTEL spans enriched with forecast_anchor tags so traces can be correlated with forecasts. 2) forecasting worker: a small streaming estimator (exponential smoothing + short-window AR) that computes 5/15/60-minute horizon percentiles for token consumption and latency tail probability per tenant/route; published as Prometheus-style metrics and a compact protobuf payload to the observability ingestion topic. 3) dashboard: Grafana panels (JSON) that show runway horizon, forecast bands, probability heatmap of SLO breach, and an interactive selector for tenants/route groups. 4) alert tuning: new alert rules that switch to probabilistic mode—alert fires only when 95th percentile breach probability exceeds threshold for two consecutive windows; provides auto-suppression for noisy short bursts. 5) runbook + rollout: runbook for on-call and migration steps, and a controlled rollout via feature-flag gated by tenant tier.

Implementation notes: forecasting worker is implemented as services/observability/runway/estimator with a bounded in-memory state keyed by tenant_id+route_hash and a fallback path that uses simple linear extrapolation if windows are sparse. Forecast payloads are intentionally compact (utf8 proto) and published to the existing observability topic (obs.forecasts.v1). We reuse existing ingestion parsers and added a scheduled consumer to hydrate timeseries for Grafana streaming panels. To keep runtime overhead low, token-level counters are emitted at 15s intervals and aggregated to 1m for forecasting.

Backward compatibility & data retention: metrics have additive names (runway_*) and do not change existing metrics. Forecast payloads are optional: dashboards fall back to raw time series if forecasts are missing. We included an integration test mode that runs the estimator against historical traces for accuracy regression checks.

Rollout plan: 1) deploy forecasting worker to staging with feature flag off for all tenants; 2) enable for internal tenants and validate dashboard and runbook playbook for 48h; 3) enable on a small set of tier-2 customers for 72h while monitoring false positive rate; 4) gradual ramp to all customers over two weeks with opt-out.

Risk and mitigation: false positives from over-sensitive thresholds are mitigated by requiring two consecutive windows and a minimum traffic floor before alerts are eligible. Forecasting worker is stateless enough to be restarted without data loss. We added metrics for estimator health: forecast_lag_seconds, model_fail_rate, and fallback_rate.

Testing performed: unit tests for estimator logic (exponential smoothing math, input sanitization), e2e test that replays a recorded week of traffic to validate runway estimates vs ground truth, integration tests for dashboard ingestion and alert rule evaluation, and CI checks for linter and proto compatibility.

Related work: builds on ENG-1683 (per-tenant token budget counters) and ENG-2011 (dashboard streaming panels). Linear/PM refs: ENG-2145, PM-1987.

Checklist: - [x] instrument metrics and spans - [x] implement streaming estimator - [x] dashboard panels added - [x] alert rules and runbook - [x] unit + integration tests - [x] staged rollout plan documented

Notes: this PR is observability-only, no changes to public API or hosted inference runtime behavior beyond low-overhead metrics emission.
Arjun Patel: Nice end-to-end. Two questions: 1) how stable are the forecasts under diurnal traffic? 2) can we avoid adding more high-cardinality metrics?
Maya Chen: Reply: Forecast uses short-window seasonality-aware smoothing plus a traffic-floor check; we only emit runway_* metrics for tenants with traffic over the floor and aggregate route->route_group in high-cardinality cases.
Leila García: Suggestion: include a 'confidence' sparklines panel next to the runway so oncall can eyeball model certainty quickly.
Maya Chen: Added confidence band panel in runway-dashboard.json and implemented model_confidence metric exposed by the estimator.
Samir O'Neill: CI flaked on proto-compat; re-run fixed it. Approving with a follow-up to add an adaptive smoothing hyperparameter for specific tenants.
Leila García: Approved after verifying the runbook steps in staging.
Arjun Patel: Merging — please follow the rollout plan strictly and ping SRE during tenant ramp.
Maya Chen: Will do; feature flag gating and rollback plan included in runbook.
Add token runway prognostics and probabilistic SLO forecasting: new runway_* metrics, forecasting worker, Grafana dashboard, probabilistic alert rules, and runbook. Provides short-horizon (5/15/60m) forecasts and SLO breach probabilities to reduce noisy alerts and enable proactive capacity planning.

payload.body:
Motivation: Many tenants experience transient unit-econ regressions during sudden traffic spikes where microbatching and cache policies drive up per-token cost without corresponding latency improvements. This PR introduces two cooperating runtime components plus defaults and tooling to automate safe, reversible cost controls: 1) Cost Pause Batcher: a lightweight batcher wrapper that pauses non-critical micro-batches when per-tenant unit-econ metrics (cost-per-request, token-utilization) exceed configured thresholds; it preserves latency SLOs by only pausing batching for request classes marked as 'thrifty' and keeps a small hot-path queue for latency-sensitive traffic. 2) Quant Throttle Controller: a runtime controller that incrementally increases quant aggressiveness (int8 -> int4 simulated pathways / lower-precision kernels where available) when a tenant's cost trajectory breaches thresholds and latency headroom exists. The controller uses a conservative ramp with immediate rollback on quality regressions tied to eval hooks. Changes include: - new runtime modules: runtime/batcher/cost_pause.go, runtime/quant/throttle_controller.go - config: defaults for batching/cache/quant in runtime/config/cost_defaults.go and helm values.yaml - metrics and alerts: unit_econ dashboard widget and alerting rules (console/widgets/unit_econ_dashboard.yaml, monitoring/alerts/unit_econ.rules) - CLI and examples: sdk/python/examples/cost_pauser_example.py, tools/cost-simulate --dryrun - docs: docs/ops/cost-automation.md and an ops playbook for incident response Design highlights: - Decision boundary: thresholds are tenant-configurable with a safe default derived from historical median unit-econ + 2 sigma. - Graceful pause: pausing only applies to non-critical batchable routes; the batcher drains existing in-flight batches and keeps capacity for immediate small batches. - Quant ramping: controller applies staged quant profiles; each stage includes synthetic eval (short run against golden prompts) before promotion. - Observability: new tracing spans for pause/ramp events and token-level cost attribution recorded per tenant. Backwards compatibility: defaults are opt-in via tenant flag; runtime behavior without the flag is unchanged. Testing: unit tests for controller logic, integration tests under perf-canary with synthetic traffic and golden prompt evals were added. CI: full linters, unit and integration tests passed after one iteration to fix race conditions found in initial run. Rollout plan: - Canary (1% tenants) for 48h with aggressive telemetry - Gradual ramp to 25% over 7 days if no regressions - Full rollout gated by cost-savings signal and no increase in quality-regression alerts Notes: this PR is conservative by design (safe defaults, immediate rollback, manual override) and intended as an enabler for automated cost mitigations rather than aggressive cost-savings defaults.
Arjun Sinha (2026-02-14): Nice separation of concerns. Can we ensure the batcher pause decision is deterministic under concurrent evaluation? I saw a race in CI on the first run.
Maya Patel (2026-02-14): Addressed: added a small lock around the pause window and an atomic state machine. CI reran and the race is fixed.
Liam Chen (2026-02-16): The quant ramp stage names need to be stable across restarts for telemetry correlation. Suggest including explicit GUID in config for each stage.
Maya Patel (2026-02-16): Accepted; added stable stage IDs and persisted last-applied-stage in tenant metadata so we can correlate events.
Zoe Martinez (2026-02-18): What are the SLO/latency guarantees when batching is paused? Need a short playbook for oncall to force-disable per-tenant behavior.
Maya Patel (2026-02-18): Added ops playbook (docs/ops/cost-automation.md) and a CLI flag to force-disable per-tenant. Updated release notes to call this out.
Liam Chen (2026-02-19): Integration test results look good. One minor nit: add a synthetic eval timeout to avoid blocking controller loop on flaky eval infra.
Maya Patel (2026-02-19): Added 3s synthetic-eval timeout and fallback scoring. Reran integration tests; all green.
- Introduces 'Cost Pause Batcher' to automatically pause non-critical micro-batches when tenant unit-econ thresholds are exceeded.
- Adds 'Quant Throttle Controller' for staged, reversible quantization ramps with rollback on quality regressions.
- New defaults for batching, cache and quant profiles (opt-in per tenant).
- Unit-econ dashboard widget and alert rules.
- CLI tool: tools/cost-simulate supports dry-run scenarios for tenant policy evaluation.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Customers and internal tenant simulations often need to understand how different prefill strategies, cache sizes and quantization tiers interact before rolling changes into Dedicated/Private clusters. Existing prefills were tested with simple traffic replays; we lack a compact, deterministic runner that can synthesize tenant-level cold/cold-to-warm transitions and export compatible quant profiles for downstream deployment. This PR adds a lightweight 'ghost' scenario simulator that (1) runs sampled prefill scenarios deterministically, (2) produces compact telemetry artifacts (batch shape histograms, cache hit traces, kv-cache footprints), and (3) emits an opinionated quant profile export that can be consumed by the optimizer pipeline.
Design summary: - New package pkg/prefill/ghost: deterministic runner with scenario definitions. Scenarios are small YAML files (samples included) that define tenant traffic mix, sequence length distributions, and warm/cold windows. - CLI integration via redwoodctl prefill run-ghost: lets operators run local quick simulations and output a tarball with telemetry.json and quant_profile.yaml. - Quant exporter in pkg/quant/exporter: takes steady-state token statistics from the simulator and produces an annotated quant_profile.yaml with recommended quant tiers and fallback thresholds for per-layer quantization. - Telemetry adapter: telemetry/metrics/prefill.go emits a compact telemetry envelope compatible with our ingestion pipeline (prefill.* metrics and prefillsim.batch_shapes histogram).
Files changed (high-level): - cmd/redwoodctl/prefill.go: add run-ghost command wiring and flags (-scenario, -seed, -output). - pkg/prefill/ghost/ghost_sim.go: core simulator, deterministic RNG, scenario interpreter, warmup/warmdown logic. - pkg/prefill/ghost/scenarios/sample_profiles.yaml: sample scenarios for quickstarts. - pkg/quant/exporter/export.go: quant profile generation and heuristics. - telemetry/metrics/prefill.go: metric export helpers and envelope serialization. - docs/prefill/ghost-runner.md: user-facing guide and examples. - test/e2e/prefill_ghost_test.go: e2e smoke tests and deterministic checks. - ci/pipelines/ghost-sim.yml: lightweight CI job for simulator lint/test. - internal/config/samples/prefill_profiles.yaml: seed scenario samples used by integration tests. - Makefile, go.mod updates for new packages.
Checklist: - [x] Simulator core implementation and deterministic tests - [x] CLI wiring and quickstart scenario - [x] Quant exporter and header annotations - [x] Telemetry envelope and ingestion smoke test - [x] Unit + e2e tests - [x] Documentation and quickstart examples
Backwards compatibility: The simulator and exporter are additive. Quant export format uses a new top-level key 'redwood_quant_profile_v1' to avoid confusion with older downstream parsers.
Migration notes: When using exported quant_profile.yaml in a live rollout, follow the normal canary flow (create a compact quant variant, run traffic shadow for 24h, then canary).
Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - The simulator intentionally does not attempt to emulate GPU kernel-level scheduling; it produces higher-level signals (batch sizes, cache hits, kv footprint) and a conservative quant suggestion. The goal is early-stage signal for tenant owners, not final production calibration. - Quant heuristics are conservative: prefer higher precision when observed per-layer token variance is high. - The CLI includes a --dry-run mode that prints top-5 quant suggestions without producing artifacts.
Security and privacy: Scenario YAMLs must not include PII; sample scenarios are synthetic. Telemetry envelope redacts any tenant identifiers by design and tags runs with a local-run marker.
CI and validation: The initial CI run failed due to a race in the deterministic RNG seeding; fixed by replacing global rand with a seeded xorshift64+ in ghost_sim.go. Final CI status: all unit tests and e2e smoke passed on linux/amd64.
Release notes: "Add a tool (redwoodctl prefill run-ghost) to simulate tenant prefill scenarios and export a conservative quant profile to aid rollout planning and cost optimization."
Related work: follow-ups include hooking this output into the autotune pipeline (ENG-7605) and adding a UI surface in the Console for one-click simulation (PM-412).
Noah Patel: Nice approach. Two requests: (1) can we make the scenario schema stricter (explicit max/min fields for seq length)? (2) please add a short note in docs about how this differs from existing replay-based prefill.
Asha Verma: Responded - added stricter schema and validation in scenario_parser.go; doc updated with comparison section and example outputs.
Priya Singh: Found a potential N+1 when serializing envelope in telemetry; prefer streaming encoder. Also request small unit test to assert redaction of tenant IDs.
Asha Verma: Switched to json.Encoder streaming API and added test redaction_test.go. CI flake was due to RNG; replaced with xorshift64+.
Marco Rossi: Approving - flagged a follow-up for Console integration (PM-412) and a telemetry retention question; OK to merge after CI green.
GitHub Actions: CI run #42 - initial unit failing tests (race) -> fixed in commit 6; final run passed all checks.
Added 'redwoodctl prefill run-ghost' simulator and quant exporter to help teams preview cost/quality tradeoffs before rollout. Produces a telemetry bundle and a conservative quant_profile.yaml for downstream autotune or manual canaries.
This change is additive; the simulator writes only to the provided output path. If customers run the tool in dedicated/private clusters, ensure their telemetry ingestion policy allows prefill.* metrics. The exporter uses conservative defaults; any sudden production regressions should be investigated by disabling new quant tiers in rollout and reverting to pinned model variants.
payload.title: Introduce Prefill 'ghost' scenario simulator and quant profile exporter

Motivation: teams continually ask for recommended defaults that balance cost and latency across heterogeneous workloads. Current manual presets are hard to maintain and often conservative or overfit to specific tenants. This PR introduces HintEngine: a small policy/scoring layer that synthesizes unit-econ signals, sample latency distributions, and KV-cache hit heuristics to emit per-tenant 'cost hints' (suggested batch size, cache TTLs, and quant profile families). The PR also adds a compact, audit-friendly 'quant template' catalog (three conservative/balanced/aggressive templates) plus a dry-run simulator that shows estimated unit-econ impact before apply. What changed: 1) runtime/hintengine: new hint engine service (lightweight scoring, deterministic priority tie-breakers, eviction-safe cache of tenant signatures). 2) policy/catalogs: compact_quant_templates.yaml with three vetted profiles and compatibility matrix for common model families. 3) api/cli: `redwoodctl cost-hint apply --dry-run` that outputs estimated token savings and projected p95 latency delta. 4) telemetry: new metrics (hint_score, hint_rationale, simulated_unit_econ) and a small dashboard manifest. 5) e2e tests & integration harness: workload simulator that verifies suggestions do not push p99 > 2x baseline for the conservative template. Design notes: HintEngine is deliberately conservative by default: it prefers cache-first suggestions, enforces model-compatibility checks for quant templates, and annotates each suggestion with a confidence bucket (low/medium/high) plus an estimated cost delta. The compact quant catalog uses quant-aware fallbacks: when a template is incompatible we suggest the nearest compatible profile and add a fallback flag so runtime can gracefully degrade. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for scoring functions - [x] Integration tests with warm/cold KV-cache scenarios - [x] Telemetry gated behind feature flag - [x] CLI dry-run implemented - [x] Docs stub for operations (cost-hints.md) Rollout plan: enable HintEngine in canary for 10 tenants for 48h, collect simulated_unit_econ and actual token consumption, then increase gradually. Linked items: ENG-1452 (HintEngine MVP), ENG-1453 (quant templates catalog). Backwards compatibility: config files are additive; no breaking API changes.
Miguel Soto: Please add a safety gate if telemetry is unavailable (we shouldn't apply hints blind). Author: Added telemetry gating; dry-run will refuse to apply if simulated_unit_econ is missing and --force not set. Evelyn Cho: Can we ensure quant templates are validated against model shims to avoid runtime OOMs? Author: Added a runtime compatibility check and explicit fallback behavior; unit tests added for T5/GPT-family shims. Liam O'Connor: CI was flaky on the simulator run; re-run fixed it but please refactor to reduce nondeterminism. Author: Stabilized simulator seeding and added retries; CI green on rerun. Final: Approved by all reviewers, minor docs nit fixed in follow-up commit.

Motivation: Our monorepo CI has accumulated duplicated lint/test steps and a growing GitHub Actions matrix that increases queue times and flakey windows. This PR introduces a composite action that consolidates linting, unit tests, and type checks into a single reusable step, prunes unnecessary matrix axes for non-runtime packages, and updates a small set of GitHub Action dependency pins to the latest stable versions. Goals: 1) reduce workflow code duplication (move repeated steps into .github/actions/composite/lint-test), 2) shorten average runner time for non-Critical CI by ~20-30%, 3) make future CI changes atomic via the composite action, and 4) unblock release automation refactors by providing a single action consumers can adopt.

Summary of changes: - Added a new composite action at .github/actions/composite/lint-test/action.yml. The action runs ESLint, mypy, pytest (selected packages), and a light-weight JS build verification. It exposes inputs for 'scope' and 'fast-fail' and returns annotations for failures so GH UI surfacing is preserved. - Replaced duplicated job steps in workflows: .github/workflows/ci.yml, .github/workflows/ci-python.yml, and .github/workflows/verify-release.yml to call the composite action. - Pruned the test matrix for several infra packages: removed node-version from the matrix for packages that are node-agnostic and collapsed redundant environment combinations. - Bumped actions/checkout v2 -> v4, actions/setup-node v2 -> v4 (minor config changes handled), and actions/cache pin for improved cache key stability. - Small repo hygiene: removed a legacy script runner wrapper scripts/ci/run-tests.sh in favor of the action input. - Updated README CI section with adoption notes and a migration checklist.

Commits (high-level): - 0a3c9f4 chore(ci): add composite lint-test action - 7b2d6a1 chore(ci): wire composite action into main CI workflow - 9f44a12 chore(ci): prune matrix for infra packages to reduce runs - a1d7b8e deps: bump actions/checkout/setup-node/actions-cache pins - d4e2f05 docs: update CI docs and migration notes - 3c0e9b2 refactor: remove legacy ci wrapper script

Changed files (high-level list): - .github/actions/composite/lint-test/action.yml - .github/actions/composite/lint-test/Dockerfile (lightweight node/python image) - .github/workflows/ci.yml - .github/workflows/ci-python.yml - .github/workflows/verify-release.yml - scripts/ci/run-tests.sh (deleted) - docs/ci.md - package.json (devDeps alignment for lint/test) - .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ci-bug.md (updated guidance)

Testing: Local smoke runs via act and multiple sample workflow runs on a dedicated test branch. Measured wall-time on an average CI matrix entry before/after: main repo lint+tests job reduced from ~12m to ~8.5m (28% improvement) for infra packages where matrix was pruned. Verified sarif annotations still appear in PR checks for ESLint and mypy. Ran release verification workflow against a staging tag: composite action worked as a drop-in replacement and respected the 'fast-fail' input to stop early on critical failures.

CI timeline / flakes: Initial workflow run on 2026-02-18 failed due to actions/checkout v4 needing permission change for token access (caught by Samir). Follow-up commit adjusted permissions and re-ran; subsequent runs passed. Minor transient network flake observed in actions/cache on 2026-02-20, reran successfully.

Review conversation (condensed): - Ethan: "Nice consolidation — can we keep the npm cache separation for yarn v3?" Author: "Yes, added an optional cache-key input and kept separate paths when scope includes node-packages." - Marta: "Please add a short migration note for any external consumers of the old script." Author: "Added docs and a small migration checklist in docs/ci.md." - Samir: Requested that the matrix pruning be opt-in per-package. Author: "Made pruning opt-in by adding ci-matrix: minimal flag in package metadata; default unchanged for runtime packages." Approvals: Ethan and Marta approved after requested changes were addressed. Samir approved after the pruning opt-in was implemented.

Merge: Squash and merge on 2026-02-24. Post-merge actions: opened a short follow-up ticket (ENG-3191) to roll the composite action into the dedicated CI for Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private (these targets need different caching semantics). Also added a small follow-up PR planned to add telemetry for composite action runtime.

Release notes: "chore(ci): add reusable composite lint/test action and reduce redundant matrix runs; bumps actions pins. Improves CI runtime and reduces duplication. No functional changes to runtime code."

Notes for adopters: - To adopt the composite action, replace repetitive steps with: uses: ./github/actions/composite/lint-test with inputs.scope and inputs.fast-fail as needed. - If you rely on legacy scripts, check scripts/ci/run-tests.sh for behavior and follow migration checklist in docs/ci.md. - If you are in a runtime package, set ci-matrix: minimal=false in package metadata to retain prior matrix coverage.

Priya Nair: Added optional cache-key input and preserved separate paths when scope includes node-packages.
