Context: Several incidents in Q4 revealed race conditions in the audit-forwarder when operator-scoped retries + multi-region KMS failover triggered duplicate audit envelopes. This PR introduces three coordinated pieces: (1) an operator-scoped audit lock that serializes audit envelope creation for operator sessions, (2) a KMS tiering policy that allows an operator to specify preferred KMS backend tiers (hot/warm/cold) and provides deterministic fallback ordering, and (3) an RBACv2 safelist enforcement for operator roles that prevents elevated operator templates from being applied to tenants with residency constraints. Motivation: reduce duplicated audit entries, make KMS failover deterministic and observable, and close a gap where operator role templates could inadvertently elevate tenant access during emergency workflows.
Added operator-scoped audit lock to prevent duplicate audit forwards; introduced KMS tiering config and RBACv2 safelist enforcement for operator roles. Backwards compatible behind feature flags.
Ethan Cole: The redis lock fallback looks fine but we need to ensure we don't block critical path requests for more than 150ms — can we add a non-blocking fast-fail option?
Maya Chen: Added fast-fail option behind 'operator_audit_lock_nonblocking' flag. See pkg/config changes. Also added metrics for lock_wait_ms.
Priya Nair: RBAC safelist check should emit an audit event when it rejects an operator-template apply so we can track attempted escalations.
Maya Chen: Implemented an 'operator_safelist_reject' audit event and updated the audit schema with minimal fields (operator_id, tenant_id, reason).
Jordan Park: Integration tests flaky on CI (kms proxy timing). Please add retries and bump timeouts; also add a deterministic seed to e2e harness.
Maya Chen: Increased e2e timeouts and added deterministic seed. CI runs green locally and in AWS test fleet.
payload.title: Introduce operator-scoped audit locking, KMS tiering, and RBACv2 safelist enforcement

payload.body:
Context and motivation:
This PR implements a new admission layer for the continuous-batcher we call the 'elastic lane throttler'. The goal is to reduce starvation of small/latency-sensitive lanes while retaining batching efficiency for throughput-heavy lanes. The previous continuous-batcher showed occasional head-of-line and lane-starvation spikes when a small number of long-sequence requests monopolized slots; debugging traces pointed at aggressive slot grabs + KV-prefetch noise.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds lane-based admission tokens: each incoming request is assigned to a lane (latency, balanced, throughput) by heuristics in scheduler based on sequence length, model hint, and request metadata. Lanes have token buckets with adjustable refill rates to shape steady-state admission.
- Introduces "patience credits": every request accrues a tiny aging credit while queued; the scheduler uses the decaying-credit to break starvation by temporarily elevating aged requests across lanes. Credits decay exponentially after dispatch to avoid long-term priority inversion.
- KV cache warmup hint propagation: requests that touch warm KV keys now annotate the admission token so they can be coalesced or admitted preferentially when cache locality can reduce per-token cost.
- Soft-timeout + jittered backoff: instead of a single hard queue timeout that would force-drop or preempt, the scheduler now installs a soft-timeout that triggers a gentle admission boost for aged requests and a jittered backoff to avoid synchronized mass-promotions.
- Kernel-aware slot sizing: scheduler consults kernel selector with a small scoring API (seq_len_estimate + quantized_cost_hint) to pick more appropriate slot sizes when mixing short and long sequences in a batch. This reduces wasted kernel occupancy and tail latency for short lanes.

Files changed (summary):
- runtime/batcher/elastic_lane_throttler.go: new admission layer with lane definitions, token buckets, patience credits and soft-timeout logic.
- runtime/scheduler/score_advisor.go: small API to expose seq-length/cost hints from kernel selector to scheduler.
- runtime/kv/cache_manager.go: add warmup-hint annotation on requests and a helper to surface KV locality to scheduler.
- runtime/kernel_selector/score.rs: add a compact estimator used by the scheduler for slot-sizing.
- pkg/metrics/queue_metrics.go: new metrics for lane_fill, patience_credits, soft_timeouts_triggered, kv_locality_hits.
- runtime/batcher/elastic_lane_throttler_test.go: unit and integration tests covering fairness, starvation scenarios and warmup-hint flows.

Commits (high-level):
- a1f9d8c: initial implementation of elastic lane throttler + basic token buckets
- b2c3e4a: add patience credit model and soft-timeout/jitter behavior
- c8d7e12: wire KV warmup hints into scheduler path, metric plumbing
- d3f5b8f: kernel score advisor and slot-sizing tweaks
- e7a12b4: tests, benchmarks, and docs updates

Testing and results:
- Unit tests: deterministic tests for token refill and patience credit accrual (fast).
- Integration: a replay harness with mixed short/long traffic (90th/99th latency targets) shows 20-35% reduction in short-request tail latency under heavy long-request pressure, with <3% throughput regression on large sequences. KV locality-aware paths reduced per-token compute by ~6% for workloads with >30% warm-key reuse.
- Canary: gradual rollout on a single machine pool for 48h with active tracing and SLA gates. No regressions observed; a few edge-case races found and fixed (see review thread).

Rollout plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag (default off).
2) Enable on canary pool (single region) for 48h.
3) Gradually increase to 10% of pools, monitor lane_fill, patience_credits, soft_timeouts_triggered, latency SLOs.
4) Full rollout if no regressions and after ops sign-off.

Backward compatibility and configuration:
- Feature gated (config flag continuous.batch.elastic_lane_throttler).
- All parameters (bucket refill rates, patience decay, soft-timeout values) exposed via runtime config and per-customer overrides for Dedicated/Private.

Notes on safety and risk:
- The algorithm is conservative: token buckets default to generous refill for latency lane and small refill for throughput lane to avoid harming short requests.
- Soft-timeout uses jittered promotions and is intended to avoid synchronized wake-ups; still possible to see transient metric spikes — dashboard alerts added.

Related Linear tickets: ENG-4129 (Continuous batch fairness), ENG-4151 (KV hint propagation).

Test plan: unit/integration/e2e described above, new benchmarks added to benchmark-lab.

Samir Rao: Can the patience credits cause long-running requests to starve again if we mis-tune decay? Recommend a circuit-breaker cap on promotions (author: added cap and test).
Ellen Park: Found a race in token bucket refill during pool shutdown (author: added mutex + unit test; CI rerun passed).
Diego Morales: Kernel score advisor looks good; suggest logging when slot-sizing changes batch composition to aid debugs (author: added sparse log at debug level).
Ops (Helen Tsai): Add dashboard panels for patience credits and soft-timeouts; set alert if soft_timeouts_triggered > 100/min on a pool (author: added panels and alert rules).
Introduce elastic lane throttler: lane-based admission + patience credits, KV locality hints, kernel-aware slot-sizing and soft-timeouts to reduce starvation and short-request tail latency. Feature gated; disabled by default.
payload.title: Introduce elastic lane throttler and fairness smoothing for continuous-batcher

Context: compliance teams requested better observability and deterministic decisioning for RBAC v2 evaluations when KMS-bound resources are used. The current policy decision path does extra lookups to resolve KMS provenance which increases tail latency and makes post-hoc audit correlation expensive. This PR adds two small, tightly-scoped components: (1) a policy-index service that maintains compact fingerprints and quick-match indices for RBAC v2 policy templates and (2) a KMS provenance adapter that attaches canonical KMS usage metadata to the audit envelope and exposes a provenance lookup API used by the policy index. Motivation: reduce per-decision latency, make audit logs richer and machine-friendly, and enable safe incremental rollout of residency-sensitive KMS checks. Changes: - New service: internal/policyindex: stores policy fingerprints, matching rules, and a lightweight cache with TTLs; exposes /v1/match and /v1/refresh endpoints. - KMS adapter: internal/kms/provenance: extracts KMS key origin, provider, region-assertion and returns a provenance token included in Authorization-Audit headers. - Audit envelope enrichment: audit/encoder now includes kms_provenance.token and provenance_fingerprint fields; audit forwarder accepts provenance tokens and stores them in the canonical audit index. - Policy decision path: authz/engine calls policy-index/match first; if no match falls back to full policy evaluation. Feature flag: rollout.policy_index=true gates behavior. Backwards compatibility: when the feature flag is disabled, system behavior is unchanged. When enabled, the fallback path guarantees identical decisions. Testing and validation: unit + integration tests added (authz engine, policy-index, audit pipeline). Load test harness shows p95 decision latency reduced by ~0.8ms on our benchmark workload with 10% policy cache hit rate; no regressions on throughput. Security review: key materials are never persisted in the index; provenance tokens are short-lived and signed with the platform KMS. Migration and rollout notes: - Step 0: deploy policy-index in shadow mode (feature flag off) for 24h and collect match metrics. - Step 1: enable rollout.policy_index=shadow to populate index and verify audit correlations. - Step 2: toggle rollout.policy_index=true for 10% of traffic and monitor decision parity alerts. - Step 3: increase rollout to 100% after 72h with no parity errors. Monitoring: new dashboards added: AuthZ / decision parity, PolicyIndex hit-rate, KMS provenance errors. Alerts: parity-drop >0.1% for 30m escalates to SEC-ONCALL. Checklist: - [x] Security review completed (SEC-77) - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests with audit forwarder - [x] Load benchmark run - [x] Documentation: README for policy-index and ops runbook - [x] Feature flag gating added Notes: This PR touches only internal APIs and the audit envelope schema; migration is non-breaking because fields are additive and the policy-index is optional. Follow-up work: garbage-collection of old provenance tokens (ENG-4202), extend index to support conditional attributes (ENG-4210).
Ethan Rivera: can the policy-index fingerprint collide with templated policies? please include the algorithm rationale. -> reply (Maya Chen): fingerprint uses a canonicalized AST + HMAC with per-deployment salt to avoid accidental collision; doc string added to proto and tests cover near-collisions.
Samira Patel: audit schema change looks additive, but ensure downstream sinks ignore unknown fields. Suggest adding a schema version header. -> reply (Maya Chen): added Audit-Schema-Version header and compatibility tests to forwarder; forwarder now logs and drops unknown fields safely.
Luca Moretti: load test numbers look promising; what about worst-case where provenance service is down? -> reply (Maya Chen): policy-index match has a strict 50ms local timeout and falls back to full policy evaluation; added circuit-breaker metrics and a unit test that simulates gateway failures.
Ethan Rivera: security team should confirm token lifetime is safe. -> reply (Samira Patel): SEC reviewed and approved token lifetime 5m (SEC-77).
payload.title: Introduce policy index and KMS provenance adapter

Context: Production rollouts have an increasing need to validate model behavior on shadow traffic with deterministic checks before promoting to live traffic. This PR introduces a light-weight shadow validation adapter that runs a configurable suite of checks (SLO/metric thresholds, semantic drift signals, and deterministic prompt-set regression checks) and hooks into the rollout controller to trigger automatic rollback or quarantine when safety gates fail. Motivation: Reduce manual toil for transient regressions and make rollback decisions auditable and consistent across hosted/dedicated/private deployments. Change summary: 1) Add server-side adapter that subscribes to mirrored requests, computes validation signals, and emits decision tokens. 2) Extend the rollout controller with a new 'validation-policy' stage that consumes the adapter decisions and supports timeboxed tolerances, failure budgets, and quarantine windows. 3) Add integration tests, observability metrics, and a docs runbook for incident responders. Checklist: - [x] Implementation of adapter and controller hooks - [x] Unit tests for adapter logic - [x] Integration tests within the canary harness - [x] Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboard snippets - [x] Runbook and rollback playbook - [x] Security review for request mirroring path Design notes: The adapter processes mirrored requests asynchronously and maintains per-cohort sliding windows for metric aggregation. It supports pluggable validators: threshold, delta-from-baseline, and token-level regression checks. Decisions are signed with the rollout controller's service identity and persisted to the rollout journal so historical rollbacks are reconstructible. Performance consideration: adapter is implemented with a bounded worker pool and priority queue to avoid head-of-line blocking on serving nodes; default flavor samples 1:10 of mirrored traffic for heavy routes to keep cost predictable. Rollout behavior: When the validation-policy fails hard thresholds, the controller will immediately flip canary traffic to fallback and optionally quarantine the model variant; soft failures accumulate into a failure budget which can trigger automated mitigations (e.g. reduce traffic, extend canary). Testing & CI: added integration test harness that runs synthetic shadow traffic, asserts metrics emission and controller decision flow, and runs against a small colocated runtime using qkv-mock model. Observability: metrics prefixed rollout_validation_* (count, error_rate, drift_score), traces instrumented for per-request validation path, and an example Grafana panel in docs. Security & privacy: mirrored payloads are redacted according to existing redaction pipeline before being processed; KMS keys used to sign decisions. Migration: feature-gated by default; rollout-controller config flag 'enableShadowValidation' must be set. Rollout plan: staged rollout to internal tenants for 2 weeks behind a feature flag, then enable for low-traffic customers, progressively widen cohort. Backout: feature flag off or controller rollback. Related: linear ENG-1824 (validation service), ENG-1899 (canary-controller extension), SUP-3328 (customer incident that motivated auto rollback).
Added a shadow-traffic validation adapter and automated rollback orchestration that enables safe canary validations against golden prompt sets and a configurable abort policy.
Miguel: Please add a safety net to prevent the adapter from holding onto large request payloads; are we enforcing the redaction step? 
Author (Aisha): Adapter now rejects non-redacted payloads and logs an alert; added size cap and eviction policy.
Riley: The failure budget math needs a doc section and a clear default; what are the defaults?
Author: Added default failure budget (5 failures per 10k requests) and a math appendix to docs.
Priya: Can we make the sampling configurable per-route to control cost?
Author: Added per-route sampling in rollout manifest and updated integration tests.
Miguel: unit tests look good, integration was flaky on first run. CI team reran e2e and got green; approving for merge.
Feature gated behind 'enableShadowValidation'. Opt-in for early customers; recommended to enable only with monitoring dashboards and alert thresholds configured.
Risk: noisy false positives causing unnecessary rollbacks. Mitigation: conservative defaults, failure budget, quarantine window, audit logs, and a manual override in the console.
Unit tests covering validators; integration tests simulate mirrored traffic with golden prompt sets and assert metric thresholds; staging rollout to internal tenants for 2 weeks with canary at 5% then 20% before wide rollout.
payload.title: Add shadow-traffic validation adapter with automated rollback orchestration

This PR introduces a tolerant retry adapter and an async pullstream compatibility shim across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs to reduce friction around transient auth failures and to provide a stable, ergonomic async iterator for streaming responses across languages. Motivation: customer-facing incidents showed frequent transient token handshake failures and inconsistent stream ergonomics between SDKs which made cross-team integration tests brittle. This change: 1) Adds a lightweight "tolerant" retry adapter that treats short-lived 401/429 windows as retryable with a configurable credit window and jittered backoff presets. 2) Implements a small polyglot async pullstream shim that standardizes the semantics of pull-based streaming (peek/prefetch/pause/resume) and exposes a minimal, typed surface in each SDK. 3) Harmonizes default retry/backoff profiles used by the hosted client to avoid cross-language divergence. 4) Adds interop tests and examples demonstrating token swap + stream resume scenarios. The description below documents design decisions and checklist.
feat(retry): tolerant adapter with credit window; feat(stream): async pullstream shim (py/ts/go); refactor(sdk): unify backoff presets; test: add crosslang interop tests and fixtures; ci: add pipeline matrix for cross-sdk smoke; docs: API examples and migration notes
- Introduce tolerant retry adapter (configurable credit window + jittered backoff) across SDKs
- Add async pullstream polyglot shim to standardize streaming ergonomics (peek/prefetch/pause/resume)
- Bump SDK packages: python -> 1.12.0, typescript -> 2.4.1, go -> v1.5.3
- Add cross-language integration tests and examples for token-swap + stream-resume
Clients relying on immediate 401 propagation: if you previously relied on instant auth failure surfacing, set tolerant_adapter.enabled=false or reduce credit_window_ms to 0. Default behavior preserves UX for most apps but smooths transient blips. See docs/sdk-migration/tolerant-retry.md for examples.
Key things to validate: 1) Backoff presets in internal/compat/retry_presets.go match the values in sdks/python and sdks/typescript. 2) No new goroutine leak in pullstream prefetch worker on cancel. 3) Python async iterator exposes 'peek' and 'resume' semantics consistent with TS/Go.
1) Run cross-sdk matrix in ci/pipelines/cross-sdk-matrix.yml. 2) Exercise examples/multi-sdk/stream-resume/ to verify resume after token-swap. 3) Run long-running soak (10m) with simulated token rotation to ensure tolerant adapter does not mask real auth expiry unless configured.
Liam O'Neill: Nice consolidation. Please clarify why tolerant adapter defaults to a 5s credit window instead of per-request tokens. Also add a short note about when this is unsafe (long-lived auth rotations).
Author(Maya Chen): Added explanation in docs and added 'unsafe_for_long_rotations' flag to the adapter. Kept default conservative (5s) after benching -- prevents extra retries for slow clients.
Priya Kapoor: Found a race in Go pullstream when cancel is called during prefetch; suggested chan close pattern and an additional unit test.
Author: Fixed race by switching to a context-aware prefetch worker and added the unit test the reviewer requested. PTAL.
Jonas Berg: CI flake in TypeScript tests (timing-sensitive). Recommend using fake timers in the spec to avoid flaky waits.
Author: Updated TS tests to use lolex fake timers; re-ran CI, all green.
This PR intentionally keeps the adapter implementation minimal (no persistent token cache or credential orchestration) — integration with the credential mediator will be done in a follow-up to keep review scope manageable.
payload.title: Add tolerant retry adapter + async pullstream polyglot shim to align SDK ergonomics

Context and motivation:
Large KV cache fetches are a frequent source of head-of-line blocking and IO bursts during eviction-driven reclaim. On multi-tenant inference workloads this shows up as sporadic p99 latency spikes and reduced sustained throughput when reclaim background work coincides with hot request batches.

Goal:
- Reduce H-o-L blocking caused by large contiguous KV fetches by breaking them into smaller prefetch chunks that interleave with the request execution path.
- Smooth background reclaim/eviction IO by adding an eviction-throttle that rate-limits eviction work based on current SLO pressure and a small token-bucket tied to per-GPU IO budget.
- Surface scheduler/batcher hints so the serving runtime can avoid issuing fetch+evict storms while maintaining high throughput for short requests.

What this PR changes (high level):
- pkg/kv/cache/prefetcher.go: new chunked prefetcher that fetches blocks in configurable chunk sizes and yields to the scheduler between chunks. Prefetcher uses an adaptive chunk-size heuristic (defaults tuned via canary) that grows/shrinks based on observed fetch latency and KV hit ratio.
- pkg/kv/allocator/eviction_throttle.go: eviction-throttle controller implementing a small token-bucket and backoff policy. Throttle is SLO-aware: it samples request latency percentiles published by the serving runtime and reduces eviction drain rate when tail latency increases.
- pkg/serving/scheduler/batcher.go: adds prefetch-yield hooks to allow continuous-batching to interleave I/O with token processing, reducing stall windows for other batches. Also plumbs a batch-priority hint that lowers eviction allowed rate while high-priority user batches are in-flight.
- cmd/redwood/flags.go + config/defaults.go: new feature flags and default parameters for canary: chunk_size_pages, max_chunks_per_request, eviction_tokens_per_second, slo_latency_threshold_ms. Defaults off for global rollout; enabled for canary nodepool.
- tests/unit/prefetcher_test.go and tests/integration/prefetch_eviction_test.go: coverage for chunked fetch ordering, interleaving correctness, and throttle behavior under synthetic SLO violation.
- bench/kv_prefetch_bench.yaml: bench config used for local and CI regression tests.

Design notes and rationale:
- Chunking vs. full fetch: empirical runs in benchmark lab showed that breaking 256-page fetches into 8x32-page chunks reduced median stall time by ~38% and p99 by ~22% under mixed workloads because it gives the runtime scheduler opportunities to schedule other small batches.
- Eviction-throttle instead of disable reclaim: simply pausing reclaim leads to memory pressure spikes. Throttle lets reclaim continue at a controlled rate so long-running background compaction does not synchronize across GPUs and cause IO bursts.
- SLO feedback loop: throttle uses a conservative low-pass filter on p95/p99 signals to avoid oscillation. We also emit internal metrics (prefetch.chunk_count, evict.throttle_tokens, evict.drain_rate) for alerting and tuning.

Benchmarks (canary nodepool, synthetic mixed workload):
- p50 latency: -6% (improvement)
- p95 latency: -14%
- p99 latency: -22%
- sustained throughput: +7%
- Background IO variance (stddev): -45%
Notes: numbers aggregated from 6 runs, canary enabled with defaults. Full benchmark scripts are in bench/ and were run with bench infra id bench-20241107-12.

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests added for prefetcher and throttle. Integration test simulates SLO violation and asserts eviction drain rate reduces and that in-flight batches are not stalled.
- CI initially failed flakily on integration test (race in allocator stats). I added a small synchronization in allocator stats update and reran CI; all green.

Review conversation (high level):
- Aaron Liu: "Can we show the cost regression for cold-starts? Chunking could add small extra latency if the first chunk misses and subsequent chunks are needed."
  - Priya: "Added a benchmark for cold fetch penalty and tuned initial chunk size. Cold-start p50 increased by <2ms for very large multi-page misses; we consider this acceptable vs tail improvements. Documented in bench/README and release notes."
- Camille Dubois: "Please add metrics and a flag to disable chunking per node. Also add a rollout plan for Dedicated customers."
  - Priya: "Added metrics and cmd flags. Default remains off for global; enabled on canary nodepool. Dedicated will get opt-in via runtime config."
- Jorge Ramirez: "CI showed a data-race in allocator stats on the first run; please fix and re-run."
  - Priya: "Fixed by moving stats write to a single updater goroutine and added unit test to surface regression. CI green afterwards."

Operational notes and rollout:
- Feature gated: default off at global scale. Canary nodepool in us-west-2 enabled for 2 weeks under monitoring.
- New metrics: prefretch.chunk_size, prefetch.chunks_per_req, evict.throttle_tokens, evict.drain_rate, kv.prefetch_yields. Dashboards updated in observability-pack (PR referenced in Linear ENG-6324).
- Alerting: added a burn-rate style alert if evict.drain_rate drops while p99 latency climbs > 15% for >5m.

Motivation: Users reported rare but reproducible downstream failures when the OpenAI-compat SSE proxy emitted fragments that split inside critical token boundaries (eg. 'data: {' split across TCP frames) or where function-call sentinel events interleaved with regular events and were delivered out-of-order under high concurrency. These manifested as partial JSON parse errors, duplicated event delivery, or function-call arguments arriving before their leading sentinel. Root cause: the streaming parser allowed a tight race between chunk coalescing and event-window flush: a trailing partial 'data:' line could be considered complete by the socket layer, triggering a flush that the reassembly state machine interpreted as a terminal event even though the JSON body was incomplete. Approach: 1) Introduce a short, bounded reassembly window that holds non-terminal data fragments and performs a lightweight lookahead to determine whether a trailing fragment could be the prefix of a JSON object or an 'event:' header. 2) Add a brace-balance sentinel heuristic for JSON payloads: the parser keeps track of net braces and only emits a completed JSON event when braces are balanced and a following SST delimiter (blank line) or stream terminator is observed. 3) Implement ordered-event flush: each logical SSE event is assigned a monotonic stream-seq (local to the connection) at parse-time; the emitter guarantees in-order delivery semantics for events and function-call sentinels even when chunks are received out of order by the lower-level socket reassembly (this is enforced with a tiny per-connection queue that expires items after a configurable soft timeout to avoid head-of-line blocking). 4) Backcompat: default soft timeout is conservative (10ms) and can be tuned via redwood.openai_compat.sse.reassembly_window_ms. The parser preserves existing event prefixes and only changes when a potential split is detected, minimizing churn. Changeset summary: small state-machine changes in the SSE parser, a new reassembly queue and tests, and a minor shim in the OpenAI-compat adapter to propagate the config. Testing: added unit tests to cover partial 'data:' prefixes, fuzz-run reproductions with randomized chunk boundaries, integration test that simulates interleaved function_call + message events under a concurrency profile used in customer incident reproduction. Benchmarks indicate <1% median latency increase for streaming clients under normal load and significantly reduced incidence of parse errors under adversarial chunking. Rollout: feature-flagged behind openai_compat.sse.stable_reassembly (default on in main after this PR); we will monitor metrics (sse.parse_errors, sse.reassembly_time_ms, openai_compat.event_reorder_count) on the canary cluster for 72 hours before full cutover. Checklist: - [x] Repro-case unit and integration tests - [x] Fuzz harness added and CI integration - [x] Reviewer feedback addressed - [x] Bench numbers and dashboards updated - [x] Feature flag and runtime knobs added - [x] Release note prepared
Fix: Resolve sporadic SSE reassembly races that produced partial/invalid JSON when chunk boundaries split tokens or `event:` lines; ensure deterministic ordering for interleaved function-call and normal events. Backwards-compatible parsing changes; no API break.
Ava Chen: Can we avoid introducing head-of-line blocking with the reassembly queue? Suggest adding an expiry + immediate fallback path that emits an unbalanced JSON with a parse-error metric rather than stalling indefinitely.
Marta Velasquez: Addressed in commit 3: expiry implemented (default 10ms) and fallback emits parse-error metric sse.partial_emit with payload for post-mortem. Added comment to make behavior explicit.
Luis Martinez: The brace-count heuristic might fail for strings containing braces. Add string-aware counting or rely on a small JSON tokenizer.
Marta Velasquez: Switched to a lightweight tokenizer that tracks string state and escapes; now only counts braces outside strings. Tests added for edge cases like '\"{"' sequences.
Evan O'Neill: CI flaked on the new fuzz job; please make the harness deterministic in CI (seed) and limit runtime.
Marta Velasquez: CI change added: fuzz job now runs with a fixed seed in CI and is randomized nightly without a seed. Also added a 30s cap for CI runs.
payload.title: Minimize SSE split-boundary races and ordered event flush

Summary: This PR introduces a new lightweight 'policy-decision-audit-bridge' service inside the policy stack and a KMS-backed assertion middleware that signs decision digests before they are emitted to the audit pipeline. Motivation: customers and compliance teams have requested cryptographic proof that RBAC decisions were evaluated within the configured jurisdiction and that audit events are tamper-evident during transit. This change provides two capabilities: (1) attach an auditable, content-addressed assertion to every policy decision using a customer/region-aware KMS envelope, and (2) migrate existing audit events into the new bridge so downstream consumers receive a signed assertion + canonicalized event. Key goals: - Ensure assertions are region-anchored (respecting tenant/namespace region pinning) by consulting region hints from the request context. - Keep overhead minimal: signing occurs asynchronously with bounded retries and a local signing cache to avoid blocking critical request paths. - Provide observability and fallbacks: when KMS is unavailable, the bridge emits a signed-placeholder and marks events with 'kms_status: fenced' to be reconciled later. Design: - policy-decision-audit-bridge: a new component receiving canonical policy decisions over an internal pub/sub (existing decisions topic). It canonicalizes the decision payload (deterministic ordering of keys), computes a digest (SHA-256), optionally encrypts the digest with the tenant-scoped CMK, requests a KMS signature/attestation, and forwards combined payload to audit-writer. - kms-assertion-middleware: plumbs into the policy evaluation path and emits a small signed assertion (digest + kms_metadata) for synchronous callers that need proof. Middleware consults namespace-level key-binding policy; if the tenant has 'kms_disabled' flag, it emits 'assertion: unsigned:policy' and a metric. - Signing cache & batching: local LRU cache for recent digests, and batch-sign worker to reduce KMS calls for spikes. - Fallback behavior: on transient KMS failures (<30s), the bridge retries with exponential backoff; for persistent failure, it marks event with 'kms_status: failed' and triggers alert with runbook. Compatibility & rollout: - Backwards compatible: audit-writer can accept both old and new envelope shapes; a compatibility shim added to audit-consumers will read signed_assertion when present. - Rollout plan: feature-flagged (policy.audit.bridge.enabled) rolled out to 5% -> 50% -> 100% tenants. Bridge produces signed assertions in shadow for 2 weeks before enabling enforcement mode. Security considerations: - Tenant-scoped key usage: we enforce that KMS keys are tenant-scoped and validate key location against namespace region. - No plaintext keys stored: only key identifiers and key-policy hashes cached. - Observability: counters for signed/unsigned/placeholder events, KMS latency histograms, and an audit-signing histogram exported to console dashboards. Checklist: - [x] Implement bridge service and middleware - [x] Add unit and integration tests for canonicalization and signing flow - [x] Add metrics and dashboard panels - [x] Feature flag and staged rollout config - [x] Add runbook entry for KMS failure mode - [x] Add Linear ticket references and doc link Documentation: Added docs/ops/policy-decision-audit-bridge.md describing configuration, runbook, and migration notes. Related work: builds on earlier 'region-assertor' work (ENG-6112) and ties into SUP-4127 for customer support triage. Testing: Verified with local KMS emulator and staging tenant with multi-region pin; end-to-end test exercised audit-consumers to validate signature envelope. Impact: Minor additional latency for synchronous middleware path measured at +3ms p50 when cached, +18ms p99 without cache. Cost: Expected KMS request volume reduced by caching and batching; projected increase ~0.6% on average for signing cost for typical workloads.
Adds Policy Decision Audit Bridge and a KMS-backed assertion middleware. No customer-facing API changes. Enables richer, tamper-evident audit records for cross-region RBAC decisions.
Marco Silva: Please add unit tests for the deterministic canonicalization when map keys include numeric strings. I saw a potential non-determinism in ordering in canonicalizer.go:SerializeMap().
Priya Rao: @Marco added three unit tests that cover numeric key ordering and an explicit sort. SerializeMap now uses stable sort with type-aware comparator.
Elena Dimitrov: We need to ensure the KMS client respects role-bound credentials for operator accounts. Can you scope the signer to use tenant-service-account roles?
Priya Rao: Added KMS role binding lookup and enforced scope; updated docs and added a test to validate role mismatch returns a 403 and placeholder assertion.
Riley Park: Approving after address comments. Small nit: rename 'kms_status' enum to 'kms_assertion_state' to be explicit.
Priya Rao: Renamed field across bridge, middleware, and docs. Adjusted alerts and dashboards accordingly.
Focused reviews on canonicalization determinism and KMS scoping.
Decided on feature-flagged rollout with shadow signing phase for 2 weeks.
Added runbook and dashboard before enabling enforcement mode.
All reviewers approved; CI green before merge.

Motivation: We observed sustained KV cache fragmentation under mixed chat+embed workloads which causes frequent small-page spillovers and I/O amplification during tail-loads. This PR introduces a new fragmentation gradient metric and an adjacent proactive layered reservation controller to reduce fragmentation-induced paging. Summary of changes: 1) Introduce 'fragmentation gradient' telemetry that measures per-shard contiguous free-run distribution and short-term slope to predict imminent fragmentation events. 2) Add a proactive reserve controller that maintains a small pool of contiguous reservation slices in a layered fashion (hot, warm, cold) and replenishes them during low-utilization windows. The controller integrates with eviction and the scheduler so reservations are pre-emptively allocated on nodes that will receive bursty workloads. 3) Modify the KV allocator to prefer adjacent-slot allocation when gradient predicts increasing fragmentation; fall back to best-fit otherwise. 4) Hook controller signals into the continuous-batching scheduler to avoid batching across boundaries that would force extra KV copying. 5) New metrics/endpoints and retrofit to the Console: fragmentation_gradient, reserve_pool_utilization, reserve_replenish_events. Why this matters: experiments on canary clusters show a 18% reduction in spill I/O bytes and a 12% improvement in p95 latency for tokenize-heavy chat traces (90th-99th percentile heavy tails). Implementation notes and compatibility: changes are opt-in via config flags (kv.fragmentation_gradient.enabled, kv.reserve_controller.mode=proactive|passive) and default to off for Dedicated until we validate at scale. No API changes to external users. Rollout plan: enable in benchmark-lab and perf-canary for 2 weeks, monitor fragmentation_gradient and spillback metrics, then staggered enablement on Dedicated min groups. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (ENG-3145) - [x] unit tests for allocator heuristics - [x] integration tests with continuous batching toggled - [x] bench runs and flame graphs attached - [x] Console metrics wired - [x] feature-flag gating - [x] docs/notes in runbooks (for SRE) See also related work: this PR complements the KV-prefetch work (ENG-2971) and interacts with spillback-rate limiting (ENG-3210).

Motivation: We need a promotion path that respects cohort ownership and avoids aggressive cutovers that cause user-facing regressions. This PR implements a 'deferential promote bridge' that (1) acquires a short-lived cohort lease before increasing traffic to a model variant, (2) runs parallel shadow validation for the cohort during a soft ramp, and (3) triggers automated rollback or hold when cohort-level SLO regressions or counterfactual regressions are detected. High level: orchestration controller + bridge runtime hooks + runbook wiring to Console. Design goals: preserve session affinity, reduce blast radius per cohort, enable fast automatic backout for transient regressions, and provide clear telemetry for post-mortem. Changes in this PR: new controller (promotebridge) that coordinates lease acquisition, shadow sample routing, and delta-safety checks; lightweight cohort-lease CRD with TTL; runtime hook to attach a short-lived shadow siphon to cohort requests; metrics and alerts emitted under rollout.promote_bridge.*. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-1982) - [x] Cohort lease CRD and controller - [x] Runtime hook and gateway routing change - [x] Telemetry metrics and dashboards - [x] Integration tests for lease lifecycle and rollback triggers - [x] Runbook and Console wiring - [x] Canary rollout tested in staging How it differs from existing promote controllers: instead of global fraction-based ramps this uses cohort-leases and an orchestrated soft ramp inside the cohort boundary. The bridge is 'deferential' because it yields to any active session-affinity constraints and avoids preempting other cohort leases. Rollback policy: immediate rollback if any of the following are observed within the grace window: cohort latency P95 increases > 30ms AND error rate delta > 0.5%; or offline regression detection on model outputs (semantic drift score threshold). On soft anomalies the controller will hold and widen shadow sampling for 10 minutes and re-evaluate. Migration/rollout plan: merge to main, deploy promotebridge controller to staging for 48h with two controlled cohorts (marketing-early, search-beta), then scheduled canary to 3 additional cohorts. Post-merge tasks: dashboard link, update operator docs, and announce on #deploys. Related linear items: ENG-1982 tracks follow-ups for tenant-configurable TTLs and telemetry cardinality. Rollout timeline: target GA in 3 weeks after staged validation.
Asha Rao: Overall LGTM; please add a short explanation of the lease TTL rationale and why 60s was chosen (concern: churn on high QPS cohorts).
Sofia Martinez: Responded - TTL set to 60s to bound lease hold time and allow rapid backfills; added follow-up ENG task to make TTL per-tenant configurable.
Eliot Chen: Found a race in controller state transitions when leases expire mid-ramp; requested deterministic retries and idempotency.
Sofia Martinez: Fixed - added idempotent transition logic and retry backoff; added unit tests for expired-lease path.
Marcel Nguyen: Asked about observability costs of widened shadow sampling; requested adjustable sampling cap.
Sofia Martinez: Added sampling cap config and surfaced default in the Console; documented cost implications in runbook.
Asha Rao: CI flaky test (integration/promote_bridge) failed initially; reran and passed after fix. Approved and merged via squash.
Introduces Promote Bridge: cohort-lease based promotion controller, shadow siphon for cohort-scoped validation, and automated rollback rules. Admins can configure lease TTL and shadow sampling caps via Console. Intended to reduce blast radius for canaries and speed safe rollbacks.
Default rollout disabled; operator flag 'enablePromoteBridge' must be set to true. Staged rollout plan restricted to opt-in cohorts. Alerts created for rollout.promote_bridge.rollback and rollout.promote_bridge.holdpoint. Added automatic mitigation to drain new cohort traffic and restore previous model snapshot on critical rollback.

Motivation: Our monolithic lint executor has grown slow and brittle as we added language-specific rules and formatters. This PR splits the lint runner into language-aware shards (js/ts, python, go, docs) so presubmit latency improves on common change types and tooling installs are scoped.

What this does (single-line description + checklist):
- Introduces a small lint-shard runner binary (go) that fans out to language workers based on changed paths and manifest hints.
- Adds a release-quarantine gate in release automation: PRs that touch release/*, changelog, or package manifests must pass a release metadata validation job before merge.
- Moves heavy toolchain bootstrap steps into optional per-shard init steps so the default fastpath avoids installing rust/cargo/golang for JS-only changes.
- Updates CI templates and local dev shim to retain backward compatibility for local docker-based runs.

Checklist: 
- [x] Split runner and add per-language job manifests
- [x] Add release-quarantine check and validator script
- [x] Update GH Action templates and workflow matrix to use shard hints
- [x] Add docs for contributors (CONTRIBUTING.md additions)
- [x] Smoke-tested on staging branch

Related context: ENG-1182 tracks presubmit latency for js-only PRs; ENG-1199 is the release automation hardening work triggered by a missed release-note incident (SUP-3421). This change is intentionally conservative: default behavior is unchanged unless shard hints or path globs indicate a language-specific fastpath.

Notes on backwards compatibility and migration: The old monolithic lint action remains available under workflows/legacy-lint.yml for two weeks and is removed in a follow-up cleanup. The new shard runner will log telemetry (metric: ci.lint.shard_hit) to help tune default shard mappings.

Runtime/operational notes: The shard runner is small (stateless) and can be packaged into the existing actions/runner image. The release-quarantine hook runs as a required check on release branches; it validates presence of release metadata and verifies release note format. Failure causes an explicit blocking status and a short human-readable remediation hint.
1) introduce lint-shard runner and per-language manifests
2) wire GH Actions workflows to use shard hints and path filters
3) add release-quarantine validator and action wrapper
4) update CONTRIBUTING.md and workflow docs
5) add telemetry hooks and fallback to legacy runner

(5 commits, authored by Priya Natarajan)

Motivation: Customers with strict output-quality contracts were seeing silent regressions when aggressive quant profiles and batch heuristics were applied. This PR implements a safety-normalized quant profile generator plus an adaptive batch defaults controller that biases for cost while keeping a lightweight continuous QA probe to guard against quality regressions.

What this changes: generates candidate quantization profiles normalized by a safety floor (measured on a small labeled prompt set) and ships an adaptive suggestion pipeline that adjusts batch_size and cache hints per model+workload fingerprint. The system produces human-readable scoring, expected cost delta, and rollback triggers tied to quality thresholds.

Checklist:
- [x] quant profile generator (Python) with CI unit tests
- [x] runtime hooks for applying profile metadata at model load (Go)
- [x] adaptive batch defaults controller with workload fingerprinting (Rust service)
- [x] lightweight evaluation probe that runs continuous micro-evals against canary traffic
- [x] docs and console suggestions plumbing
- [x] safety rollback path + monitoring alerts

Related: Linear ENG-4321 (quant safety baseline), ENG-4390 (adaptive batching pilot). Also references design notes: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4321/quant-safety-baseline and a small internal spec: docs/design/safety-normalized-quant.md.

Summary of work:
- Adds a profile tuning pipeline (optimize/quant_profile_tuner.py) which scores candidate quant matrices by: (1) expected compute delta, (2) loss in rerank/LL metrics on eval set, (3) a safety-normalized penalty if metric loss exceeds a small epsilon. This produces profiles annotated with "safety_score" and "expected_cost_savings".
- Adds runtime flagging to model metadata and a deterministic application path in serving/runtime/loader.go so Dedicated and Private deployments can pin or accept suggested profiles.
- Introduces an adaptive batch defaults service (scheduler/batch_advisor.rs) that watches windowed latency/coldstart stats and suggests per-route batch_size/cache_ttl defaults to console via the suggestions API.
- Adds a canary micro-eval harness (evals/micro_probe.py) that runs a 20-sample prompt set against suggested profile+batch combo and emits a quality delta. The controller uses the probe to automatically reject suggestions that exceed the safety threshold.

Commit summary: see commit_summaries field.

Files changed (high level): serving/runtime/loader.go, serving/runtime/batcher.go, optimize/quant_profile_tuner.py, scheduler/batch_advisor.rs, evals/micro_probe.py, console/api/suggestions.rs, docs/design/safety-normalized-quant.md, tests/quant_tuner_test.py, tests/micro_probe_integration.sh

CI and checks: pipeline runs include unit, integration, and smoke benchmarks. One intermittent performance flaky in the scheduler integration (rust test) was fixed by reducing a synthetic timeout. All checks passed on final run.

Merge rationale: combines safety-first quant recommendations (preventing silent quality regressions) with an automated, observable batching suggestion pipeline that reduces unit cost for the common case while providing safe rollback. This is intended as an opt-in suggestions feature for Hosted and an opt-in default for Dedicated trials.
Reviewer: Evan Cheng: Can you clarify how the safety-normalized penalty is computed? Also request stronger integration test coverage for large-sequence scenarios.
Author (Maya): @Evan the penalty is a multiplicative term that scales linearly when metric loss > epsilon; details in docs/design/safety-normalized-quant.md (section 3). I added a new integration that runs a sampled long-seq profile to tests/micro_probe_integration.sh.
Reviewer: Priya Nair: The console suggestions look noisy for very low-volume routes, can the advisor suppress suggestions below a min-op threshold?
Author: added a min_request_threshold config and a suppress_until window for routes with < 100 requests in 24h.
Reviewer: Carlos Ruiz: Did you consider tying the probe to the existing evals infra so we reuse golden prompt sets?
Author: yes — the probe uses a compact golden set indexed under evals/golden/mini_probe_v1.txt and is configurable; I included a migration note for later consolidation.
Reviewer: QA (Lena): Where are the rollback alerts wired?
Author: alert rules live in observability/alerts/quant-safety.rules and console will show rejected suggestions with reasons (safety_score/exceeded_delta).
Approvals:
- Evan Cheng: APPROVED after comments addressed
- Priya Nair: APPROVED
- Carlos Ruiz: APPROVED
QA signoff: Lena: PASS

Motivation: customers observed short-lived regional instability where controllers would rapidly flip local circuits during transient KV pressure spikes; these flips caused cascading failovers and SLO violations. This PR introduces a conservative holdoff and dampening path for regional circuit transitions, adds a short-lived soft-evict sampling window to reduce aggressive tenant eviction, and tightens telemetry to detect oscillation patterns earlier. Key goals: 1) avoid rapid circuits flips during transient pressure, 2) reduce tenant blowout from overly aggressive load-shedding, 3) produce richer signals for runbooks and automated rollback. Changes: - new configuration knobs: regional_circuit_holdoff_ms (default 5000), circuit_reopen_backoff_jitter_pct (default 0.15), soft_shed_sample_window_s (default 10) - add a lightweight in-memory oscillation detector that counts circuit state changes per-region and raises a noisy-but-actionable metric when thresholds are crossed - integrate detection with the admission controller so an oscillation flag pauses new evictions for a short window and switches to slower, proportional shedding - tweak the fallback routing policy to prefer standby nodes in the same geo when local circuits are in dampened mode Rollout plan and canary: 1) ship to dedicated canary cluster in us-west-2 with conservative defaults and 15-minute telemetry retention for the new metrics 2) open a 48-hour canary and monitor SLO error budget burn, circuit-flip-rate, tenant-evict-rate and tail-latency P99 3) if metric regressions appear, automatic rollback path is enabled via feature flag and an emergency quick-revert playbook in docs/runbooks/regional-failover.md Checklist: - [x] config knobs added and validated against config-schema - [x] unit tests for holdoff/backoff logic - [x] integration sim covering oscillation scenario - [x] telemetry emitted for flip-count and soft-shed-sampler - [x] runbook updated - [x] perf run for latency overhead (<1% median CPU in runtime path) Notes: conservative defaults chosen to avoid user-visible changes; operators can tune by region. Motivation: Dedicated fleets occasionally overcommit short-lived batch reservations in the presence of high churn and cross-zone routing. This causes noisy eviction storms during drain and suboptimal locality placement which increases p99 latency for latency-sensitive tenants. This PR introduces two coordinated features: 1) reservation shadowing for short-lived batch allocations so that transient reservations do not immediately claim global reservation quotas and 2) a locality-aware drain policy that prefers draining non-local slots first and emits additional telemetry for per-pool locality pressure. Approach: reservations.go adds a lightweight shadow buffer that holds ephemeral batch reservations for a configurable shadow window (default 30s). Shadow entries contribute to soft capacity checks but are eligible for immediate reclamation during tight capacity events. locality_drain.go implements a drain scorer that weights slots by locality affinity, recent KV cache hits, and tenant SLA class to prefer evicting non-local and opportunistic work. Both features are opt-in via DedicatedFleetConfig flags and have rollout feature gates. Telemetry: new metrics (dedicated.reservation.shadowed_count, dedicated.drain.locality_skew, dedicated.drain.eviction_reason) and a histogram for shadow eviction latency. Design tradeoffs: Shadowing reduces false positive quota exhaustion at the cost of slightly more complex accounting and a small window where global utilization appears lower; locality drain reduces cross-zone KV warmup but may delay full cluster defragmentation in extreme imbalance cases. Rollout plan: feature gated, default off for 2 weeks in prod; enable for experimental fleet pools with gradual ramp and live dashboards. Tests: unit tests for reservation lifecycle, integration test simulating churn-driven eviction, and an end-to-end perf benchmark showing 12% reduction in tenant p99 under synthetic churn. Backwards compatibility: no API changes; behavior is controlled by config flags. Related work: follows up on ENG-4219 and integrates with the warm-pool heuristics from ENG-4330. Notes: left a TODO to surface shadow window tuning in the Console once telemetry has 24h retention.

Context and motivation:
This change introduces a prefill safeguard layer and a compact quantization fallback ("quant-fx") that together reduce unexpected cost overruns caused by aggressive prefill + quant combos in tail workloads. Several customers hit scenario where aggressive 4-bit presets + prefill heuristics produced regressions in unit economics for low-throughput tenants. The goal is to add a safety net that: (1) estimates per-request cost delta for a prefill decision, (2) applies a conservative fallback quant profile when predicted unit econ crosses a tenant-configurable threshold, and (3) exposes a small operator CLI to inspect and simulate decisions for troubleshooting.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds an online Prefill Safeguard Cost Calculator that computes expected token-cost delta and an associated risk score derived from recent token distribution and KV cache hit ratios.
- Implements Quant-FX: a thin runtime hook that can switch between quant profiles (8-bit->4-bit or 4-bit->8-bit) for a single request when the safeguard deems the expected cost/regression unacceptable. This is implemented as a lightweight runtime hint (no cold-restart).
- Adds a CLI (prefillctl) for operators to run dry-run simulations against a tenant's recent traffic, and a --what-if flag to show estimated cost delta for different quant profiles.
- Adds telemetry metrics: econ.prefill.estimated_delta_usd, econ.prefill.risk_score, econ.quantfx.fallback_count, and prefillctl CLI events.
- Provides unit tests and integration smoke tests; docs for ops and a short quickstart.

Checklist:
- [x] Safeguard algorithm implementation and hooks in serving runtime
- [x] Quant-FX runtime fallback implementation (patch-level, non-disruptive)
- [x] Operator CLI and dry-run mode
- [x] Telemetry metrics and dashboard skeleton (Grafana JSON in docs)
- [x] Unit & integration tests
- [x] Documentation for on-call and SRE runbook

High level changes (files):
- src/econ/safeguard_calculator.py: main algorithm + tenant config lookup
- src/runtime/quant_fx.py: runtime hint handler, lightweight switch logic + fallbacks
- cli/prefillctl.py: operator CLI to simulate and inspect decisions, supports --tenant, --lookback and --what-if args
- telemetry/metrics.yaml: metric definitions and dashboard skeleton used by Console
- docs/ops/prefill-safeguards.md: ops runbook and rollout notes
- tests/unit/test_safeguard.py: unit coverage for edge cases (zero-prefill, extreme-long tails)
- tests/integration/test_quantfx_smoke.py: integration smoke test against local runtime simulator

Commits (summary):
- 0c1e5a2: introduce safeguard calculator core and tenant thresholds + config parsing
- 1a9b4d7: wire Quant-FX runtime hook and add lightweight runtime switch APIs
- 2f7b8c0: add CLI prefillctl with dry-run and what-if simulation paths
- 3b4c6d1: add telemetry metrics + Grafana skeleton + docs draft
- 4d8f9e2: unit/integration tests, fix flake found in CI

Testing and verification:
- Local unit test suite passes (tests/unit/*) with coverage for risk bucketing and fallback decisions.
- Integration smoke used runtime simulator to verify quant-fx fallback does not require model reload and has sub-1ms decision overhead in hot path (measured in dev environment).
- Ran prefillctl --what-if against a sampled tenant trace (1k requests) and validated cost delta estimates matched simulated accounting within 3%.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge to main as feature-flagged off by default.
2) Enable for internal staging tenants and run prefillctl campaigns for 48h.
3) If results are within thresholds, enable for a subset of low-throughput tenants with opt-in.
4) Iterate on thresholds and expose per-tenant override in Console.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: quant-fx runtime switching could introduce regressions in output quality for edge cases. Mitigation: fallback is gated by risk_score and tenant opt-in; we log samples for quality evals and throttle fallbacks to <1% of traffic for first week.
- Risk: inaccurate cost estimator may oscillate. Mitigation: estimator contains smoothing over 1-hr windows and conservative bias; operator CLI allows dry-run verification before enabling.

Notes for reviewers:
- Focus review on: correctness of cost delta math in safeguard_calculator.py, lightweightness of runtime hook in quant_fx.py, and that prefillctl does not leak sensitive traces (we only surface derived metrics unless --export-samples is explicitly provided).

Related work:
- Builds on ideas from ENG-2981 (prefill economics explorer) and uses sampling plumbing added in ENG-3050.

Improves continuous-batcher fairness by introducing a probabilistic queue sampler and per-key TTL on KV cache pins to prevent starvation of low-weight requesters; reduces tail latency spikes and reduces long-lived cache pin buildup.
Context: In high-concurrency, mixed-weight workloads we observed long-lived KV pin clusters and unlucky queue ordering causing starvation of occasional low-weight traffic and microbursts that bypass batching fairness; this produced 95th/99th tail regressions on multi-tenant hosts. Motivation: Rather than hard-demoting flows or introducing heavyweight admission controls, this change adds a lightweight probabilistic sampler to the continuous-batcher queue plus a configurable TTL for KV cache pins so stale pins are evicted proactively. Summary of changes: 1) Add queue_sampler component that periodically samples queued requests and nudges under-served requesters toward priority slots using a randomized jittered backoff to avoid synchronized probes. 2) Wire sampler into scheduler decision path with a low-overhead path that only touches head-of-queue metadata to keep hot paths fast. 3) Introduce per-key pin_ttl and a soft-eviction policy in runtime/kv/cache_manager to age KV pins that have not been accessed by multiple windows, plus a pin_renew hook when requests observe repeated hits. 4) Add metrics and tracing: sampler.probes, sampler.nudges, kv.pin_ttl_evictions, kv.pin_renewals, and a sampler_latency histogram. 5) Provide a set of tunable knobs exposed through the console and runtime flags: sampler_min_interval_ms, sampler_probe_rate, pin_ttl_ms, pin_renew_threshold, sampler_jitter_pct. Implementation notes: The sampler uses an exponential backoff schedule per-cohort to limit probe volume under overload and a tiny bloom-style recent-sample filter to avoid reprobing the same queue item within a short interval. Pin TTL is intentionally conservative (default 5m) and only triggers soft-eviction that yields pins back to the allocator while allowing a fast re-pin on demand. Testing: Unit tests for sampler scheduling, filter correctness, and pin soft-eviction were added. Integration tests simulate mixed-weight flows and validate no regressions in aggregate throughput. Load experiments on staging used a synthetic 50/50 mix of heavy/ephemeral callers and a replay of production interleaving. Observed results: median latency unchanged, 95th down ~8-12% on heavy hosts, 99th down ~15-22% on hosts previously experiencing starvation, overall KV pin count per-host reduced by ~30% after warmup. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag and staged to Canary pool, then to 25% of capacity for 48h with observability dashboards and automated rollback triggers on error_rate or latency_breach. Related: builds on patterns from ENG-8421 and complements the batch-slot rebalancer. Checklist: [x] unit tests [x] integration tests [x] perf benchmarked in staging [x] metrics/dashboards added [x] feature-flagged [x] docs notes added. Motivation, design doc, and tuning guidance linked in Linear ENG-8421.

Ava: Addressed. moved sampler bitmap to a preallocated slice and added a canary script under tools/canary/sampler_smoke.sh.
Sofia: Tests look good; add a note about pin_renew race with concurrent re-pins.
Ava: Added lock-free fastpath for pin_renew to minimize contention and documented it.
Noah: Approved after verifying metrics in staging run.
Follow-up work: 1) expose sampler cohort thresholds in console (ENG-8670), 2) consider adaptive pin_ttl based on host memory pressure, 3) evaluate interaction with ranker-driven coalescing.

Motivation: Multiple SDKs had divergent retry semantics and fragmented telemetry hooks which made cross-language integrations and debugging harder for customers running mixed deployments. This PR consolidates a compact connector surface, introduces a small declarative retry DSL for common retry strategies, and enriches streaming telemetry (span tags + token-level counters) across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs.

What changed (high level):
- Introduced a compact connector abstraction that normalizes credential lookup and heartbeat hints; implementations in py/ts/go delegate to language idiomatic factories.
- Added a declarative retry DSL (RetryPreset) supporting: no-retry, idempotent-only, hedged-read, and latency-aware backoff. Presets are documented and serializable in SDK telemetry.
- Streaming adapters: added a lightweight stream-metadata envelope with per-chunk metrics (latency, chunk-size, credentials-state) and optional span annotations.
- Telemetry: emit connector_id, retry_preset, and session_warmup flags as consistent tags across SDK spans/traces.
- Version bumps: python -> 1.20.0, typescript -> 1.37.0, go -> 1.9.0.
- Docs: added cross-SDK migration guide and examples for combining RetryPreset with stream handlers and connector factories.

Context and motivation: We observed recurring tenant cost spikes caused by suboptimal batching shapes combined with overly conservative quant profiles. This PR introduces the Budgeted Slimmer engine which proactively trims batch shapes for tenants hitting budget thresholds and a Quant Tactician service that suggests tiered quantization profiles with safe rollback heuristics. The goal is to reduce per-token cost variability while preserving 99p latency SLOs. Summary of changes: 1) runtime/budgeted_slimmer: new adaptive batch-shape pruner with a safe backoff policy, 2) optimize/quant_tactician: recommendation engine that scores tenant workloads and proposes quant profiles per model family, 3) cli/econ_sim: a simulator to run deterministic dry-runs against historical traces and produce unit-econ delta reports, 4) telemetry: new econ.tactician and econ.slimmer metrics and dashboards, 5) tests: tenant-level integration tests and a smoke test in perf-canary. Rollout plan: gated feature flag redwood.econ.budgeted_slimmer default off, staged activation for 5 internal tenants then opt-in for customers; quant tactician suggestions are proposal-only until accepted by tenant policy. Checklist: - add feature flag and default off, - include unit tests and integration smoke tests, - add telemetry and dashboards, - implementation includes safe rollback and explicit audit logs. How to test locally: use cli/econ_sim with --trace sample_traces/tenant_small.json then inspect outputs in outputs/delta_report.json. Monitoring and safety: recommendations are recorded to audit log and include confidence score; the runtime will not apply aggressive trimming below configured latency floor and will immediately revert on latency regression detected by the canary alert rule. Docs: brief usage guide added to docs/ops/econ-automation.md. Related: builds on prior cost tooling work in ENG-3245 and addresses SUP-5021 incident mitigations.
Add Budgeted Slimmer runtime module, tenant quant tactician and CLI simulator for unit-econ dry run; no breaking API changes

Context: customers and SRE teams asked for safer RBAC policy rollouts and lower-noise audit telemetry in large orgs. This PR adds a server-side RBAC policy linter, a Console dry-run toggle so operators can preview the effect of policy changes without committing enforcement, and an audit-sampling enforcer that reduces event volume while preserving key forensic signals. Motivation: reduce rollback incidents during RBAC changes, cut audit ingestion costs for high-volume tenants, and give platform engineers a clear safety net when evolving policy templates. What this PR does: 1) policy/linter: new rule engine (yaml-based rules) that validates for common misconfigurations (wildcard service principals, overly broad role bindings, missing residency constraints) and surfaces human-friendly messages; 2) api: /rbac/lint endpoint and server-side pre-merge check that runs as a GitHub App webhook and as a CI guard; 3) console: dry-run UI component and an admin toggle that wires to a new server flag so teams can preview effective decisions per-request without mutating enforcement state; 4) audit/sampler: lightweight pipeline stage that applies tenant-configurable sampling profiles (preserve-error/deny traces, sample allow events down to target rate, keep burst windows); 5) KMS tag checks: the linter now includes optional policy checks that verify KMS key tags and region attributes on bindings to catch residency-policy regressions; 6) docs and runbooks: new docs/rbac-lint.md and an incident runbook describing steps to convert a dry-run to enforcement and how to interpret sampler metrics. Testing and rollout: unit + integration tests added for the rule engine, nightly e2e against an internal staging cluster, and a gradual rollout gated by a feature flag with a canary cohort (10% tenant traffic) for two weeks before global enablement. Backwards compatibility: dry-run is read-only by default and does not change enforcement until flipped by admins; sampling defaults to pass-through for existing tenants unless a profile is specified. Motivation: Dedicated fleets need a way to allow short-term bursts without violating long-term throughput guarantees. Current burst token pools are too binary (grant/reject) and produce utilization spikes that complicate autoscaler decisions. This change introduces a probabilistic burst contract (PBC) that smooths admission, plus a smoothed utilization reporter that feeds the autoscaler and telemetry with stable percentile-based signals.

What this PR does (single-line sections kept contiguous): Implements a leaky-bucket style contract where 'burst credit' is accrued and decayed with a tunable half-life; admissions are probabilistic when credit is depleted (admission probability = min(1, credit_ratio * scale + base_prob)) to allow graceful degradation under contention. Adds a new reporter that samples per-tenant request latencies and compute-utilization and publishes both raw percentiles (p50/p90/p99) and an EWMA-smoothed utilization metric used by the fleet autoscaler to avoid oscillation. Exposes config knobs in Dedicated API: burst_size, decay_half_life_seconds, base_admit_prob, admit_scale, reporter_window_seconds, reporter_sample_rate. Adds feature flag `pbc_enabled` for gradual rollout.

Design notes: The PBC keeps a token balance per-tenant; tokens refill at a steady rate proportional to the tenant's committed throughput and decay exponentially (configurable half-life) to prevent long-term hoarding. When tokens are insufficient we no longer block deterministically; instead we compute an admission probability that preserves long-term expected throughput while enabling intermittent bursts. The probabilistic approach reduces synchronized reject storms and smooths queueing. The reporter uses reservoir sampling for percentiles and an exponentially-weighted moving average for utilization (alpha derived from window_seconds).

Backward compatibility and safety: Behavior is opt-in via feature flag and per-tenant config. The deterministic admission path remains available (`pbc_enabled=false`) and default values align with current burst semantics (burst_size=2x alloc, base_admit_prob=0.0 yields approximate current behavior). All new metrics are additive and do not change existing metric names.

Telemetry and dashboards: New metrics added: `dedicated.burst.admitted_ratio`, `dedicated.burst.token_balance_ewma`, `dedicated.util.p50_ms`, `dedicated.util.p95_ms`, `dedicated.util.p99_ms`, `dedicated.util.smooth_ewma`. Dashboard JSON and Grafana snapshots included.

Testing and rollout: Unit tests for admission math and decay; integration test harness simulating 1000 tenants with mixed load; canary rollout plan: enable PBC for 1% of tenants for 24h, monitor admitted_ratio and tail latencies, ramp to 25% then 100% if no regressions.

Checklist:
- [x] Core algorithm implementation and unit tests
- [x] Integration tests against autoscaler simulation
- [x] Telemetry metrics and dashboard assets
- [x] API surface and config validation
- [x] Docs and feature-flag gating

References: Linear ENG-2201 (autoscale stability), ENG-2310 (dedicated burst design). Related incident SUP-412 inspired the probabilistic approach to avoid large reject waves.

Notes for reviewers: Focus review on parameter defaults and the interaction between reporter smoothing and the autoscaler's hysteresis. Performance-sensitive code is in `pkg/fleet/pbc` and `pkg/fleet/reporter` — those files contain hot paths where allocation/GC was carefully minimized.

Introduce a token-stage attribution atlas and compact trace digests that auto-prioritize retention by an entropy-weighted signal to reduce storage while preserving investigatability and alert fidelity.
Motivation: Long-tail incidents and cost/latency investigations often require understanding not just per-invocation aggregates but the per-token stage progression (tokenization, encoding, KV-access, self-attention, decode) across the invocation timeline. Full traces are large and expensive to retain; our current sampling misses many subtle degradations that start as stage-level skew. This PR introduces two coordinated features: (1) a Token Stage Atlas metric and dashboard that synthesizes per-stage timing histograms and stage transition counts per route/model, and (2) a compact Trace Digest format (trace-digest) with an auto-prioritization policy that keeps a small, information-rich subset of spans for long-tail investigation.

What this PR does (high level): Adds a Token Stage Atlas generator that rolls per-invocation phase timings into compact stage histograms and a per-route stage SLI time series. Implements a trace-digest encoder that produces a highly-compressed representation (span-level summaries + token-phase deltas + small KV-hit bitmaps) and a retention prioritizer that scores digests using an entropy-weighted heuristic (combines token-phase variance, error/exception signal, and anomaly score from the local anomaly service). Provides a new dashboard with drilldowns, a synthetic replay hook for reproducing digest-edge cases, and a migration shim so existing downstream consumers can opt into the digest stream via feature flag.

Design notes and constraints: - Trace-digest is intentionally lossy: full spans are not reconstructed; digests are meant for triage and RCA. - Prioritizer runs as a best-effort async op in the telemetry pipeline and is tunable by tenant. Scores are (0.0-1.0) and stored alongside the digest metadata so queries can filter by score. - Atlas histograms are downsampled into exponential buckets to control cardinality while preserving fat-tail detail. - This PR includes a dry-run mode which emits digests and prioritization scores to a side-index (no change in retention) for 7 days to allow ops validation.

Ops runbook highlights (single string): To enable for a tenant: set feature flag observability.token_stage_atlas=true and observability.digest_prioritizer=enabled|dry-run in the tenant console or via the CLI. Dry-run will produce digests and scores but not change retention. Rollout plan: start in dry-run for 48-72h, verify digest entropy distribution on the new dashboard, then enable for 10% of traffic and monitor SLOs and storage delta. If alerts spike, revert to dry-run immediately.

Motivation: Dedicated fleets occasionally suffer from longtail microbursts that are small in amplitude but long in duration and evade the existing burst token window, causing tail latency violations for premium tenants. This PR introduces two complementary mechanisms: (1) an adaptive reserve window that dynamically extends committed capacity reservation at cohort granularity based on sustained shortfall signals, and (2) a longtail burst protector that gates transient spillover by applying a token drain budget informed by utilization heartbeat telemetry. Summary: Implement an adaptive rolling window allocator that smooths reservation decays using an exponential decay tuned to each tenant's recent miss-rate; add a longtail protector as a soft admission layer that temporarily reduces opportunistic allocation for pools that show sustained >p90 latency slippage. Design notes: The reserve window is parameterized by target_percentile, decay_half_life, and cohort_weight and integrates with the existing reservation ledger via a new ReserveWindowController. The longtail protector runs as a lightweight admission controller that consumes from a reservoirized budget attached to each pool; the budget refills based on a sampled utilization heartbeat and a probabilistic backoff when sustained tail events are detected. Both features are opt-in via Dedicated config and are backward compatible when disabled. Files changed: pkg/autoscaler/reserve_window.go implements the rolling window logic and exposes a small control API; pkg/autoscaler/longtail_protector.go contains the admission and budget logic; observability/metrics/reserve_telemetry.prom and observability/metrics/longtail_metrics.prom add new metrics (reserve_window_size, reserve_adjustments_total, longtail_budget_level, longtail_shed_events_total); deploy/helm/values-dedicated.yaml adds feature gates and defaults; docs/ops/reserve-window.md explains knobs and runbooks; tests/autoscaler/test_longtail_protector.go and tests/autoscaler/test_reserve_window.go include unit and integration scenarios. Backwards compatibility and safety: Default settings are conservative (feature gate off). When enabled, the controller performs gradual adjustments only after crossing configurable confidence thresholds to avoid oscillation. There is a built-in hard ceiling so no new capacity will be created beyond configured pool limits. Rollout plan: Canary 5% of dedicated fleets for 48 hours with telemetry dashboards and a synthetic steady-and-longtail workload; expand to 25% after stability and finally to 100% in staged increments. Monitoring and alerts: New SLI dashboards and alerts added for percentage of longtail_shed_events, reserve_adjustment_rate, and per-cohort p95 latency drift. Performance: Microbenchmarks show median scheduling latency unchanged; p99 tail latency for simulated sustained microbursts improved by 18-27% in our emulated dedicated clusters. Related work: builds on ENG-4320 (reserve ledger refactor) and ENG-4876 (heartbeat sampler).
Miguel Torres: The decay_half_life default seems optimistic for smaller tenants; can we add a per-tenant floor?
Aisha Kapoor: Added tenant_floor parameter and unit tests to exercise it (see commit 3).
Lena Müller: Can the longtail protector starve opportunistic workloads during recovery? Add a safety decay so budget drains exponentially slower when p95 improves.
Aisha Kapoor: Implemented safety decay and added a flaky-guarded integration test demonstrating recovery behaviour.

Aisha Kapoor: Confirmed through local runs that CPU increase is within expected bounds; added tuning to sample rate and lowered telemetry cost. Re-ran benchmarks; numbers attached.
Lena Müller: Approved pending a short canary and ops sign-off.
Ops Bot: Canary config created for 5% of dedicated fleets for 48h (canary-id: canary-207210).

Context: Several teams reported cognitive overhead when wiring credential refresh hints into streaming consumers and inconsistent retry presets across SDKs. This PR harmonizes a lightweight 'CredentialHint' surface across Python/TypeScript/Go, standardizes retry preset names and defaults, and eliminates an awkward streaming iterator pattern that caused frequent user codeworkaround. Motivation: reduce integration friction for customers moving between SDKs and improve production defaults for auth/retries. Changes in this PR: 1) Introduce CredentialHint (optional, minimal): transports can accept an opaque hint (e.g. {lease_window: "short"} or a token expiry timestamp) that SDKs forward to the runtime and credential mediators to prioritize refresh windows. Hints are optional and backward compatible. 2) Retry presets: rename and map presets (fast|balanced|stable) across all SDKs; unify default backoff floors and jitter bounds, and document recommended presets for streaming vs request/response. 3) Stream ergonomics: replace the previous callback-heavy streaming adapter in TS/Go with a thin async iterator/pullstream facade that mirrors the Python async iterator ergonomics; add a small 'with_stream' helper in Python for context-managed resource cleanup. 4) Telemetry hooks: attach a small 'retry_preset' tag to SDK-side telemetry to enable cross-SDK aggregation. 5) Version bumps: python -> 0.14.2, typescript -> 1.6.0, go -> v1.8.3 (patch bumps only).
