Context: The paged KV cache eviction/reuse behavior has been a persistent source of tail latency and wasted GPU cycles during mixed-model workloads. Simple LRU/clock approximations cause thrashing when small hot prefixes collide with larger less-frequent blocks, and the allocator lacks a way to bias retention toward blocks that deliver higher downstream kernel-cost reductions.

This PR introduces an adaptive block retention policy (Weighted Frecency) for the BlockManager used by the paged KV cache. The policy computes a compact frecency score per resident block that blends three signals: access frequency (count), recency (exponential decay window), and a model-specific hotness weight derived from recent inference samples. The score is further adjusted by a small cost factor representing estimated kernel miss penalty (measured in ms) so the allocator prefers to keep blocks that are cheap to keep but expensive to recompute.

Key changes and goals: 1) Add WeightedFrecencyScore and decay window infrastructure (configurable via allocator.config.block_retention). 2) Replace the eviction ranking comparator with a score-first comparator while keeping a soft LRU fallback to avoid pathological cases. 3) Introduce a short soft-pin window for blocks that were prefetched or used by the current continuous-batching pipeline to prevent immediate eviction during bursty access. 4) Add a background micro-coalescer to merge adjacent free segments to reduce fragmentation in the block arena and improve allocator decision granularity. 5) Expose a feature flag (runtime.feature_flags.block_retention_v2) and safe rollback path to the legacy allocator.

Performance: Microbenchmarks on the perf-lab (n1-standard GPU-backed nodes) show: - 6-9% sustained throughput improvement on mixed-chat workloads with heavy model multiplexing. - 12-22% reduction in p99 generation latency for a realistic e2e test harness that simulates small hot prefixes and occasional large context fetches. - Allocator churn (evictions/sec) reduced by ~35% on the same workloads. The improvements are most substantial when model hotness is skewed; synthetic uniform access patterns see neutral behavior.

Safety and rollout: Policy is gateable via the feature flag and has conservative defaults (longer decay half-life, low cost-weight) to avoid regression risk. The PR includes a canary plan: enable for 5% of traffic in Dedicated canaries for one week with latency and eviction metrics monitored. We also maintain per-model retention overrides in config for customers who need deterministic behavior.

Tests and validation: - Unit tests for score decay math, ties, and boundary conditions. - Integration tests that validate soft-pin semantics under continuous-batching. - Perf harness additions and an automated comparative benchmark. - Stress test that runs with the legacy allocator fallback enabled and verifies no data corruption.

Docs: Added allocator design notes and a short troubleshooting section describing how to tune decay/weight parameters and interpret the new metrics exposed in Console (block_retention.score_distribution, block_retention.eviction_rate).

Checklist: - [x] Feature implemented behind flag - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Perf benchmarks included - [x] Canary/rollout plan - [x] Docs updated

Motivation and follow-ups: This is a low-risk, high-payoff change to reduce eviction oscillations and bias caching toward blocks that materially reduce kernel work. Follow-ups include autoprobing of kernel miss penalty, adding a tiny ML model to predict block hotness, and exploring tighter integration with the scheduler for co-located eviction decisions.

Motivation: regional failovers combined with aggressive reopen behavior were causing tenant-level oscillation and repeated cold KV-cache misses leading to SLO flaps. This PR implements a low-risk hotfix that (1) primes tenant KV prefixes during region handoff windows, (2) staggers circuit-thaw operations across nodes to avoid synchronized reopen spikes, and (3) adds a feature flag and telemetry gates for progressive rollout. Technical summary: added a PrimingManager in the SLO enforcer runtime that schedules lightweight KV prefetch jobs for tenants that are in the failover window; modified the circuit thaw scheduler to use randomized stagger + per-tenant backoff so nodes do not simultaneously move circuits from CLOSED->HALF_OPEN; introduced a feature flag runtime.config.slo.tenant_priming (default: off) and a conservative default thaw_delay_seconds=9 with canary override. Risk mitigation and rollback: the changes are behind a feature flag and guarded by quota controls (concurrent_primers_limit). If telemetry shows increased error rates, the flag can be turned off instantly and thaw_delay can be set to a very large value to keep circuits closed. Canary and results: rolled out to us-east-1 Canary cohort (5% traffic) for 36 hours; observed 42% reduction in cold-KV miss latency spikes and no increase in 5xx rates; one transient flake in e2e-regional-failover tests prompted a delay tuning from 6s->9s. Testing: unit tests for PrimingManager and scheduler jitter, integration test that simulates regional handoff and verifies priming jobs run and succeed, canary harness tests for telemetry emission. Followups: expand priming to include prefix frequency heuristics (ENG-4287), expose tenant-level priming metrics in Console, and evaluate datacenter-local priming when Private deployments are used.
Marcus Nguyen (reviewer): Comment: ensure concurrent primer tasks are capped per-region to avoid adding load during recovery. Suggest adding a region-level semaphore.
Aisha Koenig (author): Reply: implemented concurrent_primers_limit and region semaphore; default set to 12 and configurable via runtime config.
Priya Shah (reviewer): Comment: please add unit tests for jitter behavior and a canary dashboard to track priming latency improvements.
Aisha Koenig (author): Reply: added deterministic jitter tests and wired priming_latency_50/95/99 into canary metrics; dashboard link in PR description.
Derek O'Connor (approver): Approval: verified canary graphs and test results; OK to merge behind flag.
Hotfix: reduces post-failover oscillation by priming tenant KV prefixes and staggering circuit thaw operations. Rollout is gated by feature flag runtime.config.slo.tenant_priming; default OFF. Backwards-compatible and reversible.
If increased 5xx or CPU usage is observed after enabling the flag, toggle runtime.config.slo.tenant_priming to false and increase runtime.config.slo.thaw_delay_seconds to a large value; check priming_retry and primer_failure metrics to investigate underprovisioning.

Motivation: long-tail invocation cost/latency signals are noisy and siloed between token-level billing metrics and kernel/runtime latency slices. This PR adds a lightweight wireflow tracer that stitches token cohorts (by prompt shape and prefix warmup state) to kernel-level latency slices and produces an attribution trellis consumable by dashboards and alerting. Goals: 1) surface which token cohorts are driving cost spikes at the kernel/batching level, 2) enable low-noise alerts that combine cohort-level delta and kernel contention signals, 3) provide a tenant-aware trellis dashboard for SREs/Platform to triage cost regressions without deep trace joins. Changes are split across runtime instrumentation, a small aggregation sidecar, metric rollups, and a Grafana dashboard. Notable design points: the wireflow tracer emits a concise span (wireflow.token_slice) with attributes {cohort_id, kernel_hint, kv_warm, batch_size_hint, tenant_id, token_cost_est}. Cohort assignment is probabilistic and low-overhead (1% default) and is configurable by deployment. The aggregation sidecar consumes these spans, produces cohort histograms, and emits compact rollups: wireflow.cohort.cost_p50/95, wireflow.cohort.kernel_latency_p50/95, and wireflow.cohort.contention_index. The dashboard uses a trellis layout: rows = tenant, columns = cohort; panels include compact heatmap of per-token-cost delta, stacked kernel-latency waterfall, and a ranked callsite attribution list. Alerting: new rule wireflow_high_delta combines cohort.cost_p95 delta > 3x baseline AND cohort.contention_index > 0.2; it suppresses noisy one-off invocations by requiring sustained delta over a 30m window. Rollout: feature-gated, disabled by default on hosted; enabled for Dedicated trial clusters and Private via installer flag. Backfill: a backfill script is provided to derive cohort baselines from 7 days of sampled spans. See release_notes for operator-facing notes.

Motivation: Cold-starts and tenant-tail workloads are a dominant contributor to per-token cost and latency variance in production. Existing warmup logic is coarse-grained (global prefill budgets per GPU pool) and interacts poorly with mixed quantization lanes (8/4-bit variants), leading to either wasted cold-prefill or unexpected quality regressions when aggressive quant profiles are selected. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: (1) a Granular Warmup Allocator that assigns probabilistic warmup budgets per-tenant and per-shape window based on recent traffic and signalized unit-econ thresholds; (2) a Quant-Compatibility Fallback Layer (quant-compat) that detects when a chosen quant profile may produce outlier loss on sampled eval prompts and routes the request to a compatible fallback model/quant lane automatically.
Summary of changes:
- allocator: new service and runtime hook (warmup-allocator) that maintains lightweight sliding-window counters, probabilistic budget tokens, and an admission policy that prefers small, high-value prefill allocations; supports tenant overrides and a dry-run telemetry mode
- quant-compat: compatibility matrix + lightweight evaluator that runs a fast-loss heuristic on a small prompt set and consults policy rules to choose fallback variants; integrates with serving router to enforce graceful fallback and emits structured telemetry when fallbacks occur
- telemetry: new econ-prefill and quant-compat events, dashboards, and alerts (updated docs link below)
- config: new tenant-level fields for warmup_budget_mode, sample_rate, and quant_compat_policy
- CLI: warmup-sim tool to simulate budgets and visualize unit-econ impact
Motivation continued: the goal is to reduce wasted GPU tokens spent on prefill while bounding tail latency and preventing silent quality regressions from aggressive quantization.
Design notes:
- Probabilistic token issuance uses a reservoir with deterministic seeding per-tenant to enable reproducible sampling in A/B tests
- Shape windows are keyed by (model_family, sequence_bucket) to keep state small
- Quant-compat uses a two-stage check: quick divergence heuristic (latency < 2ms) + optional micro-eval (bounded to 5ms) before deciding fallback
- All decisions are logged and can be toggled to dry-run to collect telemetry before enforcement
Checklist:
- [x] Implementation of warmup allocator server and runtime hook
- [x] Quant-compat compatibility matrix and decision flow
- [x] Integration tests for allocator admission across tenant cohorts
- [x] Unit tests for quant-compat heuristics and fallback routing
- [x] Telemetry events and Grafana dashboard templates
- [x] Backwards-compatible config parsing and tenant override validation
- [x] Upgrade plan for existing clusters (migration steps in upgrade_notes.md)
Testing and results: In staging with three representative tenants (chatbot, search, assistant) we ran a 48h dry-run. Results vs baseline:
- Prefill token spend: -22% on average (peak -35% for search tenant)
- Tail 99.9 latency: improved 8-12ms for mixed-quant lanes
- Observed quality regressions from quant fallbacks: 0 (when fallback policy enabled)
- CI: all unit/integration tests green. See simulation artifacts in s3://redwood-econ/sim/582431/
Deployment and rollout:
- Start in dry-run on dedicated pools for 1 week to validate telemetry
- Enable enforced mode with conservative budgets and quant_compat_policy: "safe" rollout for next 2 weeks
- Expose tenant-level opt-outs for customers with strict prefill SLAs

Motivation: production customers running latency-sensitive endpoints (chat and short-completion inference) observed intermittent tail-latency spikes during cluster-level bursts. Existing capacity allocators react to utilization signals that correlate poorly with the 95th/99th token latencies we target. This PR introduces a latency-budgeted reservoir scheduler that reserves a small, elastic pool for latency-critical tenants and a lightweight utilization probe that samples per-pool latency percentiles and effective concurrency. The goal is to reduce tail latency regressions during transient load while preserving overall throughput and cost-efficiency.

Design summary: add a ReservoirController that maintains a dynamically-sized "latency reservoir" per-pool. The controller computes a reservoir target from a latency budget (ms per request percentile) and recent qps/kv-cache hit patterns. The controller prefers soft reservations (slot tokens that can be borrowed by opportunistic workloads) and decays reservations when headroom is available. A UtilizationProbe component periodically samples per-pool latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), queue lengths, and GPU-utilization-derived throughput estimates and publishes compact telemetry for autoscaler and alerting consumption.

Key behaviors implemented: 1) Admission path modification — latency-reserved tokens are considered first for critical routes, falling back to the main admission when exhausted. 2) Soft-borrow semantics — opportunistic queues may borrow reservoir tokens; borrowings are tracked and prioritized for fast reclamation when latency budgets are under pressure. 3) Reservoir decay — exponential decay with a configurable half-life to release capacity gracefully after spikes. 4) Sampling strategy — util probe uses reservoir-weighted histogram windows to estimate p95/p99 with minimal overhead. 5) Metrics — new time-series: reservoir_target_slots, reservoir_in_use, reservoir_borrows, probe_latency_p95, probe_latency_p99, probe_effective_concurrency and related tags (pool_id, tenant, route).

Configuration and operator controls: new CRD fields under FleetAutoscalerSpec: latencyBudgetMs (string, e.g. "p95:120,p99:240"), reservoirMaxSlots, reservoirHalfLifeSeconds, probeSamplingIntervalSeconds, and borrowPriority. Defaults chosen to be conservative and off by default; rollout plan below flips feature gate in staging clusters first.

Rollout and safety: implemented feature flag "LatencyReservoirV1" gated at runtime. Default disabled. Canary rollout plan: enable for a single low-risk tenant in staging -> 3 canary pools in prod with guardrails (max reservoir <= 5% capacity) -> ramp to additional pools once p95/p99 regressions are <5% and cost delta <2%. Automatic fallback to non-reservoir admission on controller failure.

Testing and telemetry: unit tests for reservoir math, borrow/reclaim logic, and probe histogram aggregation. Integration tests included: admission path acceptance tests, simulated spike e2e that asserts p95 improvement, and a small loadtest script used in bench lab to validate resource overhead. CI smoke and integration pipelines added.

Why different from prior work: unlike prior soft-burst token and warm-pool features, this controller computes reservation targets directly from latency percentiles and request characteristics, not purely utilization. The probe provides a low-latency feedback signal for P95/P99 that is cheaper than end-to-end synthetic probes and integrates with autoscaler decisions.

payload.body:
Adds a stable RBACv2 policy packager CLI for compiling role templates with residency labels; introduces per-request CMK attribution headers for clearer KMS billing and audit; deploys an audit-ingest deduper to reduce duplicate audit noise in high-throughput environments. Backwards compatible; opt-in via feature flag.
Summary: This PR introduces three coordinated pieces to improve compliance operations and reduce audit noise: (1) rbac-packager: a CLI and library that composes RBACv2 policy templates with tenant/geo labels and outputs a validated bundle for staging and canary rollouts; (2) cmk-attributor: middleware that attaches deterministic CMK attribution metadata to KMS usage events so audit records can tie CMK use to tenant-level contracts; and (3) audit-deduper: an ingest pipeline stage that coalesces identical audit events within a short time window to avoid alert and storage storms from retries and high-frequency service calls.
Motivation: customers operating across multiple jurisdictions requested clearer policy bundles for compliance reviews, more precise KMS usage attribution for billing and key-residency proofs, and lower audit noise to make incident signals actionable.
How it works:
- rbac-packager: takes role templates (templates/roles/*.yaml), tenant claims, and a residency map, validates constraints (no cross-zone elevated grants), and emits a signed bundle (rbac-bundles/<tenant>-v<N>.json) plus a compact manifest used by the policy deployer. Packaging performs static checks (mutually exclusive grants, temporal bounds) and produces an explainability map for auditors.
- cmk-attributor: small middleware inserted in the kms-proxy path (service/kms/proxy/attributor.go) that: 1) resolves the effective CMK used (explicit or derived), 2) attaches an attribution header X-Redwood-CMK-Attribution: tenant=<id>;bundle=<bundle-id>;hash=<short-hash>, and 3) emits a trace/span with cmk.attribution=true. The header is HMAC-signed with the service key so downstream audit processors can validate provenance.
- audit-deduper: a streaming operator in audit-ingest that groups events by (principal, action, resource, cmk-attribution, event-type) and coalesces events when they are bitwise-equal in payload within a 4s sliding window (configurable). Coalesced entries include a count and a first/last timestamp to preserve fidelity while reducing downstream fanout.
Implementation notes and tradeoffs:
- Default dedupe window is conservative (4s) to avoid collapsing unrelated events; operators can tune it per pipeline.
- CMK attribution header intentionally uses a short hash (first 8 bytes of SHA256) to avoid exposing full key IDs in logs while preserving uniqueness for auditing.
- Packager outputs are signed with the org signing key to ensure deployer integrity; signing key rotation is supported via signer plugin.

Motivation: We need stronger non-repudiable audit evidence for operator-driven RBAC delegations (temporary grants, operator-on-behalf flows) and a way to control audit retention per tenant without exposing KMS keys to the control plane. This PR implements a KMS-signed audit envelope for delegated RBAC events and introduces per-tenant KMS retention profile metadata that drives downstream retention policies in the audit indexer.

What this changes: Adds a new audit envelope signer that wraps delegation events with a compact signed envelope (signed by tenant-scoped KMS / tenant key proxy), a retention_profile field propagated on tenant metadata and embedded into signed audit envelopes, and a new retention-profile-to-mlog TTL mapping used by the audit-indexer. The RBAC delegator now emits both the canonical audit event and the signed envelope for high-confidence verification by downstream compliance tooling.

Design notes: - The envelope format is intentionally compact (protobuf v3) and includes: event_id, delegation_request, actor_claims, service_context, retention_profile, signature_meta. The signature is created by the tenant KMS proxy (no plaintext key material in control plane). - Per-tenant retention_profile is a symbolic string (e.g. "standard", "sovereign-90d", "short-30d") which is validated against an allowlist during tenant onboarding and surfaced to the control plane as immutable tenant metadata. - The signer is a small, well-isolated component under services/audit/envelope to reduce blast radius; signing requests are rate-limited and retried with backoff. - Audit-indexer consumes signed envelopes and uses retention_profile to derive storage TTL; mismatches between an unsigned canonical event and a signed envelope are flagged as high-severity anomalies.

Rollout plan: 1) Feature gated by an ops flag (audit.envelope.enabled=false by default). 2) Deploy signer in read-only mode (emit envelopes locally to staging index) and verify consumer compatibility. 3) Enable signing for a small set of test tenants (ENG-8432) and exercise end-to-end verification. 4) Gradually flip the flag to enable for all tenants, enforcing allowlisted retention_profiles.

Backward compatibility: The canonical audit event shape is unchanged; consumers that do not understand signed envelopes will continue to ingest the unsigned event. Envelopes are published to a parallel topic (audit.envelopes.v1) so consumers can opt in.

Security considerations: - Tenant KMS usage is proxied via a tenant-escrow component that only exposes a Sign API. - Retry/backoff and rate limits prevent accidental KMS storms; the signer will fall back to emitting unsigned events with an audit annotation if signing fails for >5 minutes. - Retention profiles are validated by policy and cannot be escalated by operators without a signed change request (Linear ENG-8432).

Testing: Unit tests for envelope serialization/signature verification, integration tests that exercise the KMS proxy (mock), and an e2e test that verifies retention_profile propagation through onboarding -> delegator -> indexer. A flaky e2e test was observed in CI related to an unrelated indexer timing assumption and was retried (see CI details).

Migration and data: A migration adds tenant.retention_profile to the tenants table (nullable, default "standard"). Existing tenants will be backfilled to "standard" with a background job after rollout. Audit-indexer will interpret missing profiles as "standard".

Checklist: - [x] Schema and migration for tenant retention profile - [x] Envelope protobuf and signer implementation - [x] KMS proxy Sign API integration (mocked in unit tests) - [x] Audit-indexer TTL map and anomaly detector - [x] Docs: security/delegated_rbac_kms.md - [x] End-to-end tests and load sanity check

Related: ENG-8432 (linear), SUP-1123 (support note for test tenant), SEC-214 (threat modelling work).
Diego Alvarez: Strong design. Two requests: 1) Add a mechanism to surface signing latency to the tracing spans; 2) ensure signer errors are recorded as a non-fatal metric so SRE can alert without dropping events.
Asha Menon: Added tracing instrumentation to signer (commit f6d7e2a) and added metrics.signer.failures & metrics.signer.latency. Updated docs to include operational runbook.
Priya Raman: Please validate the protobuf backward compatibility guarantees and add explicit versioning in proto namespace. Also request a short security review on the KMS proxy auth flow.
Asha Menon: Proto is namespaced audit.envelope.v1; added explicit version field in envelope.proto and recorded SEC review ticket SEC-214 in the PR. Updated tests to assert version roundtrip.
Evan Cho: Small nit—retention_profile allowlist should be configurable via infra config; otherwise LGTM.
Asha Menon: Moved allowlist into infra/config/defaults.yaml and added validation at tenant-onboard time.
Added KMS-signed audit envelopes for delegated RBAC events and per-tenant retention_profile metadata. Feature is gated and rolled out gradually; existing audit consumers continue to work with unsigned canonical events.
Monitoring: metrics.signer.latency, metrics.signer.failures, audit.envelope.mismatch.count. Trace span: audit.envelope.sign. Fallback behaviour: after 5 minutes of consecutive signing failures signer switches to annotated unsigned events and emits ops alert.

payload.body:
Motivation: Recent incidents showed oscillation when regional circuits reopened under short-lived load spikes. The tenant limiter combined with aggressive reconnects caused brief throughput collapse in neighboring regions. This PR introduces an ephemeral fallback arbiter that probes candidate fallbacks with paced connection timeouts (connection pacing) and a temporal SLO bridge that grants short-term acceptance credits which decay deterministically. The arbiter reduces noisy reopen attempts and prevents rapid circuit flip-flops while allowing fast failover when capacity is truly available.

Design summary: single continuous description below. The arbiter sits between the routing decision and the fallback commit. Instead of immediately switching traffic to a fallback region/variant, the arbiter issues controlled probe connections with an exponential pacing timelock per candidate (initial delay + jitter + backoff). Probes use a soft connection timeout tuned to avoid long-hanging sockets. Successful probes consume a small temporal credit from a per-tenant SLO bridge; credits are earned on sustained success and decay with a configurable half-life. If enough credits accumulate within a short window, the arbiter performs a controlled failover. If credits decay or probes fail, the arbiter throttles subsequent attempts and escalates to a more conservative fallback (lower capacity variants) or returns an overloaded response to the caller (guided SLO degradation).

Implementation notes: 
- New package: internal/arbiter with two main components: probe_scheduler and slo_bridge (credit ledger).
- Probe scheduler implements connection pacing and timelock, uses region health metrics and short-lived TCP connect+TLS handshake probes to validate candidate nodes.
- SLO bridge implements per-tenant ephemeral credits, deterministic decay (half-life seconds), and a safety cap to avoid amplification.
- Integration with routing: router/decision now calls arbiter.ProbeAndDecide(ctx, candidate_list, tenant_id, policies). Backwards compatible: if arbiter disabled via flags, behavior is unchanged.
- Rollback fix: previous tenant limiter change (feature/tenant-limiter-warmup) introduced a fast-path that allowed bursts which can interact badly with immediate fallback. This PR reverts that fast-path for mainline and introduces a gated warmup only for Dedicated pools behind feature gate.

Checklist: 
- [x] unit tests for slo_bridge (decay semantics, cap enforcement)
- [x] unit tests for probe_scheduler (pacing backoff, timeout)
- [x] integration test that simulates regional reopen flapping
- [x] CI passing on linux/amd64 and linux/arm64
- [x] canary rollout plan added to docs/ops/fallback-arbiter.md
- [x] observability: added metrics (arbiter.probes_total, arbiter.credits, arbiter.failover_attempts) and traces for probe lifecycle

Testing and rollout: 
- Local integration with the benchmark-lab harness reproduced a previous incident sequence and verified that the arbiter prevented cascade failures.
- Canary rollout: 2% traffic in us-west initially for 24h, then 10% for 6h, then 100%. Health checks and SLO regressions monitored; automatic rollback on latency >10% or error-rate >0.5% relative to baseline.

Risks and mitigations: 
- Risk: probe load could add overhead. Mitigation: probes are short-lived, capped per region, and scheduled with backoff; metrics included to watch probe cost.
- Risk: incorrect decay parameters could delay legitimate failovers. Mitigation: conservative defaults and feature flags to tune half-life and credit thresholds at runtime.

Related work: ties to ENG-2182 (failover stability initiative) and SRE-501 incident postmortem.

Notes: description intentionally continuous. See changed_files for high-level diffs and commits for stepwise history.
Introduces an ephemeral fallback arbiter that paces connection timeouts and a temporal SLO credit bridge to reduce circuit flapping. Includes rollback safety for tenant limiter behavior. Safe rollout via canary, no user-facing breaking changes.
Evan Brooks: Nice design. Two questions: 1) how do we bound probe concurrency across many tenants? 2) please add an integration simulation for a 3-region reopen scenario.
Maya Singh (author): Answered: probe concurrency is bounded by per-region shared semaphore and per-tenant token; added tests for 3-region scenario in integration test. See commit b2a77e9 and tests/integration/fallback_arbiter_flap_test.go
Lena Morrison: Can we add a metric for average probe latency and a debug flag to force immediate success for chaos testing?
Maya Singh (author): Added arbiter.probe_latency_ms histogram and a testing override flag (arbiter.test.force_probe_success) guarded to local/dev only. See commit e7d1a99
Samir Patel: The tenant limiter revert needs a short note in the changelog to make SRE aware of the behavior change during rollout. Also request to add a telemetry alert for probe-error-rate > 2% sustained over 5m.
Maya Singh (author): Added changelog entry and alert in deploy/monitoring/alerts.yaml; pushed in e7d1a99. Also included runbook steps to reduce probe concurrency if cost observed.

payload.body:
Summary: Adds a tenant-level latency-bucketed reservation system and a configurable surge threshold gate to Dedicated fleet admission and the autoscaler pipeline. The change introduces a small, opt-in admission controller that tracks recent latency percentiles per-tenant, maps requests into latency buckets (p0, p50, p90, p99), and enforces soft reservations per-bucket. When a tenant exceeds its budgeted bucket, requests are conditionally routed to a surge queue with rate-limited admission; if the surge queue fills, requests are gracefully degraded or routed to an overflow model variant based on policy.

Motivation: We observed repeated incidents where single-tenant tail latency spikes (p99) triggered autoscaler upsizing and burst credits consumption while average-throughput remained low. This caused suboptimal capacity churn and degraded multi-tenant fairness. The latency-bucket model lets us reason about and reserve headroom for critical latency tiers while still allowing controlled bursts above the reservation. It reduces reactive autoscaler upsizing from tail noise and gives the operator explicit surge controls.

Design highlights: - Latency buckets: p0 (best-effort), p50, p90, p99. Tenants declare a target distribution and an overall reservation budget. The admission controller maintains an exponential-weighted moving percentile estimator per bucket. - Reservation accounting: soft credits allocated per-bucket; credits decay with time and refill at tenant-specific rates. Credits are consumed on admitted requests; burst consumption is charged against a surge allowance. - Surge threshold gate: a configurable threshold (utilization or absolute concurrent requests) triggers surge gating. When gate open -> allow spike up to ephemeral surge allowance; when closed -> divert to overflow or enforce throttling. - Autoscaler integration: autoscaler now consumes aggregated bucketed-utilization signals rather than only raw QPS/CPU. It uses a hysteresis policy tuned to ignore isolated p99 spikes when they do not align with sustained bucket utilization. - Telemetry: new metrics per-tenant: tenant.latency_bucket.{p0,p50,p90,p99}.utilization, tenant.reservation.credits, tenant.surge.fill_ratio, tenant.surge.admissions, fleet.bucketed_utilization_percentiles. Added tracing spans for admission decisions and charge attribution. - Config surface: YAML knobs for Dedicated: per-tenant reservation profile, surge allowance, refill rates, p99 hysteresis window, overflow model mapping. Exposed via Console and CLI for operators.

Commit summary: - feat(admission): add latency bucket estimator and per-tenant ledger (7 commits) - feat(autoscaler): consume bucketed signals and implement hysteresis decider - feat(telemetry): emit new tenant-level metrics and dashboard queries - test: unit tests for estimator, integration test harness updates for multi-tenant microburst scenarios - docs: operator guide and console UI knobs explained

Files changed (high level): - services/admission/controller.go (new admission flow + attach points) - packages/reservations/ledger.go (credit accounting, refill logic) - autoscaler/decider/bucketed_decider.go (hysteresis + decision logic) - observability/metrics/tenant_buckets.prom (metric definitions and labels) - ci/integration/microburst_harness_test.go (new integration scenarios) - docs/operations/dedicated_reservations.md (operator guide) - web/console/src/pages/dedicated/tenantProfiles.tsx (console controls)

Small illustrative diff snippets (high-level): - reservations/ledger.go: added DebitBucket(tenantID, bucket, weight) and RefillLoop() with time.Ticker-backed refill. - autoscaler: replaced rawQPS signal with bucketedUtilSignal.Aggregate(window) and applied sigmoid-backed hysteresis.

Tests and CI: Unit tests added for percentile estimator and ledger edge-cases (credit exhaustion, refill race). Integration harness runs a 20k request synthetic microburst across 50 tenants and asserts fleet-level p99 tail is within targets while ensuring no tenant consumes >3x allotted surge allowance. CI showed a transient flake in integration which was fixed by increasing test harness timeouts; all checks green on final run.

Review conversation: - Ethan Morales (reviewer): "Overall clean design. A couple of questions: 1) how is the refill rate tuned for tenants with steady vs spiky workloads? 2) can operators observe charge attribution per route?"
- Priya (author): "Refill rates default to a conservative per-minute token refill based on historical average QPS; we expose per-tenant override in the YAML profile. Charge attribution is emitted via tenant.surge.admissions with route label — added to telemetry and dashboard in this PR."
- Lina Chen (reviewer): "Need stronger safety when ledger storage falls behind (e.g., control plane partition). Propose fail-open for a rolling window and escalate to ops alert; otherwise risk widespread throttling."
- Priya: "Added a fail-open window (configurable 30s default) and an ops alert metric tenant.reservation.stale_detected. Documented behavior in ops guide."
- Marcus Rivera (approver): "Approved after tests and ops docs. Verified dashboard queries and that autoscaler does not react to isolated p99 blips in staging."

CI summary: - unit: pass - integration: pass (rerun once) - lint: pass - e2e-console: pass

Deployment notes: Rollout is gated behind a feature flag per-dedicated-cluster. Default configuration is non-invasive (all tenants soft-unlimited) and operators can opt in per-tenant. We plan a gradual rollout: enable for a pilot set of 5 tenants, validate metrics for 48h, then expand. Console UI controls are behind same flag.

Rollout validation checklist (in PR description for operator runbook): - enable feature on pilot cluster - create two tenant profiles (steady and spiky) and set reservations - run microburst harness to validate p99 isolation - monitor tenant.surge.fill_ratio and tenant.reservation.credits - if unexpected throttling: increase burst allowance or fail feature off

Related work and follow-ups: - ENG-7340: integrate with Commitment Safety Reservoir to provide cross-tenant hedging for long surges - ENG-7259: UI for visualizing per-route charge attribution - follow-up: tune autoscaler hysteresis constants with 2 weeks of pilot data

Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main. Release notes added to changelog.

Why this is different from earlier PRs: Earlier work focused on utilization and burst token pools; this PR introduces latency-aware reservations so we can separate throughput-driven capacity decisions from tail-latency driven transient spikes. It complements existing burst banking approaches by adding a latency signal and explicit surge gating policy.

Contact: Priya Natarajan (author) for implementation details; Lina Chen for ops validation and dashboard queries.
Introduce per-tenant latency-bucket reservations, surge threshold gating, and new utilization/latency telemetry. Improves isolation under microbursts and reduces tail-latency driven over-provisioning.

Context: production traces showed recurring short-duration high-concurrency spikes ('glitches') that push the serving stack into suboptimal batching and cache-miss behavior, increasing unit cost for low-traffic routes while degrading p95 latency for tail requests. Motivation: existing econ defaults are great for steady-state workloads but oscillate badly on bursty tails; operators end up widening SLAs or creating ad-hoc route overrides. This PR introduces a two-pronged, conservative change set to reduce unit-cost oscillation and make defaults safer for bursty, low-volume routes: 1) A lightweight 'workload deglitcher' signature detector integrated in the request router that detects short spikes (configurable 1-5 minute windows) and applies a transient smoothing policy: prefer smaller micro-batches, enable conservative KV prefix caching prioritization, and temporarily pin to a lower-quantization fallback when latency SLOs are relaxed. 2) A 'tail-response smoothing' module in the runtime scheduler that stretches the effective batching window only for detected glitch windows to trade a few ms of median latency for dramatically lower per-token cost at the tail. 3) A small companion CLI tool (redwood-cost-tuner) and library under tools/econ-sim that lets SREs/Platform engineers run fast Monte Carlo simulations of route-level unit economics across combinations of batch_size, kv_cache_policy, and quant_profiles; the tool includes presets and an automated 'safe-default' suggester that writes YAML snippets for per-route defaults. Changes: added workload_deglitcher.py (router integration), tail_smoother.py (scheduler hook), a new conservative quant profile (qsafe-i16) with runtime gating, the cost-tuner CLI (tools/econ-sim/cli.py) and a lightweight simulation engine (tools/econ-sim/sim.py), and docs + smoke tests. Backwards compatibility: all behavior is opt-in by default; the global config flag runtime.enable_deglitcher is false unless set by ops or via the safe-default suggester. Rollout plan: feature gate off, deploy to staging; run cost-tuner against staging traffic and generate suggested per-route configs; flip feature gate to enabled only for routes in a canary list for 72 hours and monitor p50/p95/units-per-req. Observability: new tracing spans (router.deglitch.detect, scheduler.tail_smooth.apply) and metrics (deglitch.window_count, tail_smooth_applied, econ_sim_recommendations) included. Risks & mitigations: initial perf run indicated qsafe-i16 caused a 2% token throughput regression on LLM-7B float paths; we narrowed the runtime gate for qsafe-i16 to routes with sequence_length < 1024 and added a GC-friendly quant fallback. Tests: unit tests for detection heuristics and simulation engine; integration smoke for router->scheduler wiring. Deployment notes: config schema bump (runtime.enable_deglitcher boolean, econ_suggester.bucket_ms int). Related: ENG-1423 (workload stability), ENG-1487 (unit econ tooling).
Diego Ramirez: Overall this looks promising. Two concerns: make the detection window configurable per-route and ensure metric cardinality doesn't explode when used org-wide.
Sofia Liang: Addressed both — detection window is now per-route with global fallback and deglitcher emits aggregated metrics by route-prefix only (dropped fine-grain user ids). Added docs section on cardinality.
Maya Patel: The qsafe-i16 profile causes a 2% throughput regression on some kernels in perf runs. Can we gate it by seq_len and add a fast fallback?
Sofia Liang: Yes — updated runtime gating so qsafe-i16 is only selected for seq_len < 1024 and added a hysteresis-based quick-fallback when observed throughput drops >3%.
Alexei Volkov: Add a canary rollout playbook and a pre-merge smoke job that runs econ-sim against recorded traces. Also please add a small e2e test verifying the suggester emits valid YAML.
Sofia Liang: Added playbook and the e2e test. CI now runs econ-sim against a tiny trace blob (deterministic seed).
New opt-in workload deglitcher and tail-response smoothing to reduce unit-cost oscillation for bursty routes. Includes redwood-cost-tuner CLI to simulate unit economics and generate safe-default route configs. Qsafe-i16 quant profile added (gated).

payload.body:
Summary: Introduces a first-class compatibility policy for Redwood Private upgrades (VPC + on-prem) to deterministically block unsupported upgrade paths and warn on risky jumps. This is the policy layer consumed by the installer upgrade-plan generator and (in follow-ups) the control-plane / Console to provide consistent messaging. Motivation: We’ve had multiple upgrade-related incidents/near-misses driven by customers attempting multi-version jumps (or mixing control-plane/data-plane versions) without clear guardrails. This PR makes the supported upgrade surface area explicit and testable. Scope: - Adds a version compatibility matrix (source-of-truth) under `private/compat/compat-matrix.yaml` with explicit allowed transitions and constraints. - Adds a policy evaluator library (`private/compat`) that takes `current`, `target`, deployment mode (vpc|onprem), and optional Kubernetes/storage signals, then returns: `ALLOW`, `WARN`, or `BLOCK` with machine-readable reason codes and operator-facing messages. - Adds a CLI helper used by `redwood-private-installer` to render a stable summary (this is used by plan generation; the installer wiring lives in its repo). - Adds unit + golden tests for common paths and known failure cases (including SUP-18421 pattern: DB migration expectations when skipping intermediate minors). Compatibility semantics (v1): - Default supported path is N-1 -> N for Private platform versions (minor-to-minor or patch-to-patch), ALLOW. - N-2 -> N is WARN (supported for selected versions only; requires explicit operator acknowledgement in the installer). - Any cross-major jump is BLOCK unless explicitly whitelisted in the matrix. - Patch downgrades are BLOCK (rollback is handled by the upgrade state machine + artifacts; not by "downgrade to arbitrary patch"). - Control-plane and data-plane version skew: ALLOW within a bounded window defined in the matrix (currently: CP can be at N while DP at N-1 during staged rollouts; DP at N while CP at N-1 is BLOCK). - On-prem/air-gapped constraints: evaluator can return WARN when target version requires artifacts not present in the bundle manifest (reason code emitted; bundle verification lives elsewhere). Files/areas changed (high level): - `private/compat/compat-matrix.yaml`: initial matrix entries for 2025.04 -> 2025.05 and 2025.05 -> 2025.06; includes CP/DP skew bounds and notes. - `private/compat/evaluator.go`: semver-ish parser for Redwood Private version scheme + policy evaluation function. - `private/compat/reasons.go`: stable reason codes for auditability and support playbooks (e.g., `UNSUPPORTED_MAJOR_JUMP`, `DP_AHEAD_OF_CP`, `SKIP_TOO_MANY_MINORS`). - `private/compat/render.go`: canonical formatting for CLI/installer output (kept stable for docs and screenshots). - `private/compat/testdata/*`: golden test fixtures. - `docs/internal/private/compatibility.md`: internal notes for release engineering on updating the matrix per release train. Operator UX (as emitted by evaluator): - BLOCK example: "Upgrade blocked: current=2025.04.3 target=2025.06.0. Reason: unsupported upgrade jump (skips 2025.05). Remediation: upgrade to 2025.05.x first, verify health checks, then proceed to 2025.06.0." - WARN example: "Upgrade warning: N-2 -> N path allowed for this target but requires acknowledgement. Risks: longer DB migration time; ensure 2x storage headroom and maintenance window >= 60m." Checklist: - [x] Matrix is human-editable and code-reviewed - [x] Reason codes are stable and documented - [x] Unit tests cover allow/warn/block for common transitions - [x] Golden tests ensure CLI rendering stability - [x] Added "matrix freshness" CI check: fail if current release train target is missing from matrix (see notes in docs) Follow-ups (not in this PR): - Wire evaluator into installer prechecks + plan generation output (tracked in ENG-4821 / installer PR). - Emit evaluator outcomes to audit logs (planned in PR-29187). - Extend matrix with Kubernetes version constraints + storage backend notes once CI matrix is finalized (ENG-4877).
Private upgrades now evaluate a compatibility policy before proceeding: unsupported version jumps are blocked; risky but supported paths emit warnings with remediation guidance.
Ethan Park (review): Can we clarify where this policy is enforced today vs future? I’m concerned we’ll have matrix + library but no hard gate. Also: DP-ahead-of-CP rule should be BLOCK even if matrix would otherwise allow (safety). Quentin Harris (author): Added explicit notes in description + docs: enforcement in installer plan generation first; control-plane gating later. Also updated evaluator ordering so CP/DP skew checks run before matrix transition allowlist. Connor O'Brien (review): Matrix update workflow: who owns it and how do we prevent drift across release trains? Suggest a CI check that ensures the current release train has entries. Quentin Harris (author): Added `private-compat-matrix-check` workflow that validates matrix contains target versions listed in `release/PRIVATE_RELEASE_TRAIN` (simple text file). Also added docs section "Ownership" with Release Eng + Quentin as DRI and required reviewers. Sean Gallagher (review): WARN messaging should include concrete remediation requirements (maintenance window, storage headroom). We need consistent text so Support can copy/paste. Quentin Harris (author): Added renderer templates to keep messages consistent; included storage headroom + window suggestions in WARN output for skip paths. Naomi Feldman (security review): Ensure no sensitive environment details are included in rendered messages by default; reason codes are fine, but avoid leaking cluster names/URLs. Quentin Harris (author): Confirmed renderer only prints versions + reason codes; removed optional debug print of cluster identifier (was in an early commit). Rafael Mendes (SRE): For BLOCK: include explicit "do not proceed" language + link to runbook section, otherwise operators try to brute-force. Quentin Harris (author): Updated BLOCK template to include "Upgrade cannot proceed" and internal doc link placeholder used by installer docs. Approvals: Ethan Park approved after changes; Connor O'Brien approved; Sean Gallagher approved; Naomi Feldman approved with note to ensure audit log fields are handled in follow-up; Rafael Mendes approved. Merge: Squashed and merged to main.

Motivation: production incident INC-2026-02-14 showed repeated circuit flips in regional slowpaths as capacity returned after an outage. Rapid reopen/close oscillation caused request churn and SLO violations for a subset of tenants. Root cause: when nodes rejoin, transient latency spikes and KV-cache warmups briefly increase error/latency signals that the circuit controller treats as persistent failures. This PR introduces two coordinated mitigations: 1) a configurable reopen debounce (default 5s) that prevents immediate reopen attempts when a circuit has just tripped, allowing validation of sustained healthy signals; 2) a regional rejoin policy that places newly-joined nodes into a short 'quiesce' window where they are eligible for gradual traffic reintroduction with exponential backoff and jitter. Changes are behind a feature-flagged rollout and include additional telemetry spans and metrics to surface reopen attempts, debounce firings, and rejoin progression. This PR is a hotfix: it targets main and is intended for quick rollout with an immediate canary followed by staged increase. The description below summarizes commits, changed areas, tests, CI behavior, review comments, and merge details.
Ethan Zhao (2026-02-16): Nice concise patch. Two quick asks: 1) add an integration test that simulates node flapping +KV warmup so we can assert no reopen churn; 2) expose metric labels for tenant_id and region on reopen_attempts_total.
Ava Martinez (2026-02-16): Added integration test and extended metric labels to include tenant and region. Integration test lives in integration-tests/regional_rejoin_test.go. Commented on the latency impact — debounce default 5s chosen after load testing.
Priya Nair (2026-02-17): Can you double-check the default flag is off for non-hosted Dedicated customers? We should avoid surprises for reserved capacity workloads. Also request a small note in rollout docs about rollback steps.
Ava Martinez (2026-02-17): Default feature flag is off for Dedicated and Private install manifests; updated docs/rollout-notes/reopen-debounce.md with explicit rollback steps (rollback: revert feature flag and drain any nodes in rejoin stage).
Luca Romano (2026-02-17): Approve after CI green and a successful canary on us-east-1. Please ensure tracing spans are low overhead.
Ava Martinez (2026-02-18): Confirmed canary run on us-east-1 (see CI checks) and trace overhead measured <1% p50 increase. Marking as ready to merge.
Hotfix: Adds reopen-debounce to circuit controller and a regional rejoin policy to prevent reopen/close oscillation during capacity recovery. Default feature-flag off for Dedicated/Private. Improves SLO stability during rapid node rejoin events; exposes new metrics for observability: reopen_attempts_total, reopen_debounce_fired_total, rejoin_stage_gauge. Rollout: canary in one region then staged ramp.
payload.title: Prevent rapid circuit flips during capacity spikes: reopen-debounce and regional rejoin policy (hotfix)

payload.body:
Context / Motivation: Tensor-parallel inference workloads spend a non-trivial fraction of wall time in many small collectives (alltoall/allreduce) and short-lived kernel launches when sequence lengths and micro-batch packing vary. This PR adds an opportunistic collective coalescer that merges closely-timed small collectives into a consolidated launch when safe, plus a lightweight kernel resynthesis component that generates tuned microkernels for the hot small-sequence paths at runtime. The goal is to reduce NCCL/kernel launch overhead and improve overlap between comm and compute, without changing existing APIs or requiring offline compile steps.

What this PR changes (single-string summary): Implement runtime/collectives/coalescer that buffers and coalesces eligible collectives within a configurable window; add runtime/compiler/kernel_resynth which JITs small fused kernels specialized for common (seq_len, hidden) tuples; adjust scheduler to prefer compute-forward stream ordering and to annotate coalesced collectives for KV-cache-friendly ordering; add perf harness, unit/integration tests, and docs.

Key design points: - Opportunistic coalescing window is adaptive: starts at 100us and grows/shrinks based on observed inter-collective gaps and overall SLO headroom. - Safety: coalescer observes token-level dependency metadata; it will not merge collectives across operations that would change correctness (e.g., KV cache writes or model-ordered reductions). - Kernel resynthesis is bounded: compiled kernels are small, cached per-(device,seq_len,hidden) triplet, and evicted by LRU to avoid memory bloat. The resynth path falls back to precompiled kernels on memory pressure or when JIT fails. - Scheduler changes include a heuristic to launch compute-heavy projection kernels on the compute stream immediately and delay non-critical launches until NCCL progress is in flight, improving overlap.

Performance: Microbenchmark numbers (internal perf-lab, TP-8, A100s, sequence distribution from real prod traces): - End-to-end throughput up to +26% for chat-like workloads with many short sequences (median +18%). - P95 latency reduction on small prompts: ~12–18% depending on batching. - NCCL launch/latency tail reduced by ~30% as measured by collectives/s and avg latency per collective. - KV-cache hit path unchanged; some small improvement (~4%) due to reordered coalesced launches avoiding redundant KV buffer syncs.

Commits (high-level): - Implement coalescer: runtime/collectives/coalescer.cpp/.h, +tests/perf/bench_collective_coalescer.py - Add kernel resynth module: runtime/compiler/kernel_resynth.cpp/.h, +runtime/compiler/Makefile tweaks - Scheduler integration: serving/scheduler/stream_optimizer.cpp - Tests: tests/unit/collective_coalescer_test.cc, tests/integration/tp_end2end_coalesce.sh - Docs: docs/perf/collective_coalescer.md - CI: ci/perf-lab.yml additions + a small windows to disable resynth in GPU-less CI

Files changed (high-level): - runtime/collectives/coalescer.cpp/h - runtime/compiler/kernel_resynth.cpp/h - serving/scheduler/stream_optimizer.cpp - tests/unit/collective_coalescer_test.cc - tests/perf/bench_collective_coalescer.py - docs/perf/collective_coalescer.md - ci/perf-lab.yml

Compatibility and safety notes: - No API/ABI changes. - Coalescer disabled by default in release builds; opt-in via REDWOOD_COALESCE=1 or per-deployment config in console. - Kernel resynthesis requires a writable tempfs on device; when unavailable the path is a no-op and the runtime uses fallback kernels. - Added extensive unit tests to exercise correctness across heterogenous GPU topologies; we also ran a canary suite on Dedicated clusters (TP-2/TP-8) before merge.

Review conversation (abridged): 
- Ethan Zhao (reviewer): "Nice direction. Two correctness asks: 1) ensure we never reorder collectives that cross KV cache write boundaries; 2) add a deterministic seed for the coalescer's adaptive backoff so tests are stable."
- Sofia (author): "Addressed both: coalescer tags ops with KV write flags and we added COALESCE_TEST_SEED env var for deterministic behavior in tests. Updated tests accordingly."
- Priya Nair (reviewer): "Kernel resynth looks promising but we should bound JIT memory. Please add eviction metrics and a hard cap. Also add a guard that disables resynth on preemptible instances."
- Sofia: "Added eviction metrics (collective_resynth_evictions) and RESYNTH_MAX_CACHE_MB config. Also added a cheap instance-type check to disable on preemptible/spot instances in the resynth manager."
- Lucas Reinhardt (reviewer): "CI failed on first run due to flaky timing in bench harness. Reran perf CI and added a 2s stabilization sleep in bench harness to reduce flakiness. LGTM after CI pass."

CI summary: - Static checks: passed - Unit tests: passed (collective_coalescer_test, kernel_resynth unit) - Integration: perf-lab required two reruns; first run showed a transient timing flake in bench_collective_coalescer; second run green. - Merge gating: all checks green at merge time.

Post-merge notes and follow-ups: - Created follow-up ENG tasks to: 1) expose per-tenant coalescer tuning in Console (ENG-4902), 2) explore combining coalescer with adaptive batching heuristics (ENG-4916), 3) add TPU-simulated sanity checks (ENG-4920). - Performance dashboards added to Console: new metric group "collective_coalescer" (collectives_coalesced, avg_coalesce_window_us, resynth_invocations).

Why this is different from previous work: earlier PRs focused on static NCCL tuning, stream prioritization, or KV prefetch heuristics. This change introduces an adaptive, correctness-aware consolidation layer plus an on-host microkernel JIT that together attack the high-overhead case of many small collectives + short kernels. The approach is intentionally opportunistic (runtime opt-in) to reduce blast radius and provide a safe migration path.

Notes for on-call / SRE: - The coalescer can be disabled via REDWOOD_COALESCE=0. - Watch metrics: collective_coalescer.coalesced_rate, resynth_errors, resynth_evictions. - In the unlikely case of deadlock symptoms, set REDWOOD_COALESCE=0 and restart serving workers; safe fallback to precompiled kernels is automatic.

Merge: Squash and merge after final approvals.

End of PR description.
Introduce opportunistic collective coalescer and a small-kernel resynthesis path that reduces per-collective overheads on TP workloads; measurable throughput and latency improvements for multi-GPU inference.

Motivation: customers relying on the /v1/chat.completions semantics reported two classes of regressions after stricter param normalization: (1) streaming sessions that assumed legacy stop/role behaviors would produce truncated frames or fail to surface function toolcall handoffs, and (2) integrations that relied on legacy parameter names (e.g. stop_words, role_hint) started silently dropping fields. This PR introduces a non-breaking 'gentle deprecation' layer in the OpenAI compatibility middleware to map legacy parameters and role aliases to the canonical internal representation, plus a small runtime change to ensure the streaming coordinator emits a structured fallback envelope when a tool/function call boundary is detected but the client cannot accept the preferred framed JSON toolcall. What changed (high level): - compatibility/param_shim: add backwards-compatible mappings for legacy params (stop_words -> stop, role_hint -> role), with telemetry and warning header injected in responses so downstream integrators can detect usage. The mapping is opt-out via a compat header. - runtime/stream/coordinator: when stream handoff to a tool is required but the active client capability negotiation indicates 'framed-json' is unsupported, coordinator now emits a stable 'structured-fallback' envelope that contains: last_delta_tokens, truncated_stop_reason, and a serialized toolcall summary. This preserves functioncall semantics for older clients and reduces silent message loss. - api/openai_v1/normalizer: normalize stop arrays vs string stops, surface logprob field consistently under choices[*].logprobs.normalized for both streaming and non-streaming paths. - sdk/python/openai_compat.py and sdk/ts/client_adapter.ts: add explicit opt-in flag openai_compat_warns to surface deprecation warnings to application logs (default true in SDKs). - docs: migration guide describing the new header, how to opt-out, and examples for both framed and fallback envelopes. Commits (summary): - 7b2f4c1 add param shim + telemetry header - 2d9e7a8 streaming coordinator: structured fallback envelope - a8c3b21 normalize logprobs path across streaming/non-streaming - 145f9ab sdk: expose openai_compat_warns toggle and tests - c3179ef docs: migration guide + example curl sequences Changed files (representative): ["compat/param_shim.go", "runtime/stream/coordinator.go", "api/openai_v1/normalizer.go", "sdk/python/openai_compat.py", "sdk/typescript/client_adapter.ts", "docs/openai-v1-migration.md", "tests/integration/openai_compat_streaming.test.js", "tests/unit/param_shim_test.go", "ci/flow.yml"] Testing and CI: initial CI run failed on an edge unit test around role alias mapping (tests/unit/param_shim_test.go) due to an overlooked empty-role case; fixed in commit a8c3b21 and CI was manually retriggered. Integration tests for streaming + toolcall were added and exercised against a local framed-json-capable client and a legacy client that only accepts line-delimited JSON. Performance: added a microbenchmark for stream coordinator path to ensure fallback envelope does not add >1ms median latency per handoff at 99th percentile under our standard load; results showed ~0.6ms delta and are checked into perf/benchmarks/stream_fallback.md Rollout and risk: - This change is additive and guarded by the compat header toggles; no change in default model semantics for canonical API consumers. - We intentionally emit a deprecation warning header and SDK-level logs to encourage migration; the default shim remains enabled for six months before we will consider flipping to a stricter mode (ENG-1422). - Backwards-incompatible risk is low but possible for clients that parse streaming frames by byte offsets; we include docs and a migration snippet to detect the header and switch to framed-json when available. Review thread (high-level): - Aisha: flagged concern about header key naming and potential header bloat; suggested standardizing under x-redwood-compat and adding a short TTL to warnings. Author response: implemented x-redwood-compat-deprecation in 2d9e7a8 and added TTL logic. - Marco: requested clearer schema for structured-fallback envelope and example for Python SDK; added envelope schema to docs and sample snippet in sdk/python/openai_compat.py. - Dmitri: asked for perf numbers and a reproducible benchmark; author added microbenchmark and perf notes. Merge notes: approved by reviewers on 2025-11-21, CI green on re-run, merged via squash on 2025-11-22. Related work: follow-up ticket ENG-1499 to track removal plan and ENG-1500 to add server-side telemetry that surfaces top legacy params by customer.
Reviewer comments requested header standardization, clearer envelope schema, and perf measurements. Author implemented changes and added microbenchmarks; reviewers approved after updates.
Added a backwards-compatible parameter shim for OpenAI /v1/chat.completions, streaming coordinator now emits a structured fallback envelope for legacy clients during tool/function handoffs, SDKs expose an opt-in deprecation warning toggle; documented migration steps.

Motivation: Customers frequently ask for automated defaults that pick batching/caching and quantization presets per tenant while respecting spend ceilings and latency SLOs. This PR adds a price-ladder autotuner: a runtime component + CLI tooling that synthesizes a small set of tiered defaults (bronze/silver/gold) per tenant. Each tier encodes a pipeline of preferences (batch target, prefix cache policy, quant profile preference, and fallback order). The autotuner derives tiers by replaying a brief synthetic workload (sampled request shapes), scoring candidate presets by unit-econ (tokens/cost) and 95th-percentile latency. Design summary: 1) price_ladder service (go): orchestration for running quick simulations, emitting candidate tier manifests; 2) price-ladder CLI (ts): dry-run, apply, export as presets-as-code; 3) config schema updates: TenantDefaults API gains price_ladder field and tier manifests; 4) runtime hooks: small decision point in route selection to prefer tier-specific presets and fall back gracefully; 5) telemetry: new telemetry keys price_ladder.run_id and pricing_metrics.{tier}. Outcome: default generator produces conservative tiers that improve unit-econ by ~18% on our benchmark trace while keeping p95 latency within SLO (<= 120ms) for silver/gold tiers. Rollout: feature gated behind feature_flag.price_ladder and initially enabled for internal tenants. See checklist below.
Ethan Marlow: Nice end-to-end. Please add a comment about safety margin used during simulation (we don't want aggressive quant that breaks hallucination rate).
Priya Natarajan: Added safety_margin parameter documented in synth_replay.go and exposed via CLI flag --safety-margin (default 0.12). Also added a unit test asserting chosen quant profiles are not lower than tenant_min_quant when set.
Diego Alvarez: Can we avoid running heavy synthetic replays in the hot path? Make sure the service uses permissive CPU/GPU quotas and a single-shot worker per tenant.
Priya Natarajan: Generator is async and scoped to a short-lived worker. The route hook uses only the previously computed manifest; if no manifest exists we fall back to system defaults. Clarified in main.go comments.
Zara Kim: Add e2e assertion for p95 latency with the price ladder applied. Also check telemetry contains run_id for every apply.
Priya Natarajan: Added integration test that validates p95 <= 120ms for silver/gold under our benchmark trace and verifies telemetry.record contains price_ladder.run_id.
Merged by squash on 2026-02-20 by Zara Kim. Commit message consolidated to: 'price-ladder: autotune tenant-tiered batching/caching/quant presets; add CLI and telemetry'. Backwards compatible: TenantDefaults schema adds optional price_ladder field. Migration writes empty manifests for existing tenants. Feature gated behind feature_flag.price_ladder.
Add price-ladder autotuner: generate tenant tier manifests that recommend batching, cache, and quant presets to optimize unit economics while respecting latency SLOs. Feature off by default; enable via feature_flag.price_ladder. CLI: price-ladder dry-run/apply/export. See docs/platform/price-ladder.md for details.
1) Deploy service to staging; 2) Run price-ladder dry-run against sampled internal tenant traces; 3) Review candidate manifests via console; 4) Enable feature_flag for internal tenants; 5) Monitor pricing_metrics and latency p95 for 48h; 6) Gradually expose to opt-in customers; 7) After stabilization, enable rollout automation
Integration tests include synthetic replay harness, p95 assertions, and telemetry verification. Bench numbers: on benchmark-trace-v3, silver tier reduced token-cost by 18% with p95 latency +8ms (within target). Added regression test to prevent quant profile regressions when tenant_min_quant is present.
New metrics: price_ladder.replay_duration_ms, price_ladder.candidate_score, pricing_metrics.{tier}.unit_cost_estimate, pricing_metrics.{tier}.p95_latency_ms. Added tracing span 'price-ladder.generate' and run_id propagated as baggage. Metric dashboards added under Console -> Cost Optimization -> Price Ladder.
Autotuner runs only on sampled traffic and does not persist raw request payloads. All generated manifests are stored encrypted at rest. Access to apply manifests gated by RBAC (role: infra:price_ladder_apply).
This PR focuses on safe defaults and auditability. Follow-ups: 1) automate tenant opt-in heuristics; 2) expose recommended presets via SDK; 3) support cross-tenant compare mode for marketplace customers.
payload.title: Introduce inference price-ladder autotuner (tenant-tiered batching & quant presets)

Purpose: improve parity with OpenAI /v1/chat.completions while reducing stream instability and making tool/function calling resumable and machine-parseable. This PR adds a parameter gateway that unifies deprecated aliases and enforces sane defaults, implements a stream-resilience controller that sends heartbeat frames and enforces inflight token caps, and defines a lightweight TOOL_SESSION handshake and resumable partial-result protocol. Additionally, json_mode negotiation with a schema_hint header lets clients opt into structured outputs without surprising human-facing callers. The gateway maps legacy params (e.g., top_p vs nucleus) deterministically, coalesces stop strings and arrays, and preserves semantics when n>1 by explicit deterministic seeding. Streaming safeguards include heartbeat intervals, client ACK timeouts, and an adaptive inflight limiter that reduces token send rate if ACK latency rises. Tool session behavior: clients receive a TOOL_SESSION frame with session_id, expected_content_type, and resume_token; tool outputs are emitted as PARTIAL_RESULT frames and closed with TOOL_RESULT frames containing status and canonicalized output. JSON negotiation: json_mode values are off|loose|strict; strict enforces shaped output via a server-side shaper and rejects non-JSON tokens after a grace threshold. Rollout plan: feature gated, will rollout to canary and 10% of hosted traffic for 7 days before expanding. Backcompat: default paths maintain legacy framing; openai_compat flag enables the strict mapping and tool/session frames.
Aisha Rahman (reviewer): How will strict json_mode affect existing customers who rely on free-form text?
Jonah Park (author): strict is opt-in and gated by json_mode header or tenant flag. For canary we also provide a per-tenant toggle and a graceful fallback that emits a LAST_TRACE token and switches to loose mode if shaping fails repeatedly.
Sergei Petrov (reviewer): The inflight limiter could interact poorly with our autoscaler; did you run synthetic burst tests?
Jonah Park (author): yes, we ran burst tests against the Dedicated canary pool and observed <5% additional tail latency. The limiter exposes tuning knobs and emits metrics stream.inflight_limit_ratio and stream.ack_latency for operator tuning.
Nora Alvarez (reviewer): Tool session resume semantics look solid. Request: include resume_token rotation and TTL to avoid stale resumes.
Jonah Park (author): added resume_token_ttl (default 15m) and rotation on TOOL_RESULT success; documented the TTL and added tests to ensure stale tokens are rejected.
Aisha Rahman (reviewer): CI had one flaky e2e run; re-ran and green. Approving pending release note.
Added v1 chat compatibility layer: parameter gateway for legacy aliasing, streaming resilience with heartbeat and inflight limiting, TOOL_SESSION handshake and resumable partial tool outputs, and json_mode negotiation for structured responses. Feature is opt-in and rolled out gradually.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: In production we continue to see head-of-line blocking when a small number of KV-cold, heavy requests occupy batcher slots during continuous batching windows. This increases tail latency for small/short requests and drives up token cost due to repeated KV misses. This PR implements a windowed admission layer that is prefetch-aware and a client-weighted fairness shaper to reduce starvation and improve SLO adherence.

What this change does (high level): Adds a new 'PrefetchWindowedScheduler' that slices continuous-batcher admission into short windows (configurable, default 12ms) and tracks per-window expected kernel cost and KV-warmth hints. The scheduler: (1) prefers admitting requests that have KV-warmup hints or low expected kernel cost to reduce head-of-line blocking; (2) enforces a client token-bucket so noisy neighbors cannot consume all window slots; (3) emits soft-preemption signals for requests that exceed a configurable 'kindly-yield' timer so the batcher can reshuffle without hard-killing; (4) propagates KV-warmup hint metadata into the KV layer so prefetchers can warm embeddings/kv entries ahead of scheduling.

Implementation notes: - runtime/scheduler/prefetch_windowed_scheduler.go: new scheduler implementation with admission windows, per-client token buckets, and yield timers. - runtime/kv/cache_warmup_hint.cc + .h: C++ side hook to accept warmup hints and touch hot-keys without blocking main path. - runtime/bench/bench_prefetch_scheduler.py: added microbench harness to measure windowed admission effects. - runtime/metrics/scheduler_metrics.go: new metrics (window_slots_offered, warmup_hit_rate, kindly_yield_count). - configs/flags.yaml: feature flag prefetched_window_scheduler (off by default) and tuning knobs.

Design trade-offs: We intentionally keep windows short to avoid added admission latency; longer windows improve batching efficiency but increase H/o-L blocking risk. The client token bucket is leaky and decays reservation slowly to avoid lock-in. Soft preemption is cooperative: kernels need to support quick checkpoint/yield for long lived requests — fallback is still safe because we don't preempt work mid-kernel.

Benchmarks (perf-lab; representative load with mixed short/long requests): - Baseline (continuous-batcher vX): 95th latency = 380ms, 99th = 630ms, KV miss rate = 18% - With feature on (default knobs): 95th latency = 335ms (-12%), 99th = 565ms (-10%), KV miss rate = 12% (-33%), sustained throughput +7% before SLO degradation. Token cost per 1M tokens down ~6%. Microbench harness attached for reproducibility.

Testing: - Unit tests for windowing and token-bucket logic. - Integration tests exercising KV warmup hook (simulated cold-hit and warm-hit) in bench cluster. - Load tests across perf-canary with feature flag ramp: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%. All stages passed; two reruns needed for a flaky bench job that was unrelated (disk image pull timeout).

Rollout plan: Gate behind feature flag (off by default). Start 10% on perf-canary, observe warmup_hit_rate and kindly_yield_count, then follow canary ramp. If any regression >5% on 99th latency, auto rollback.

Checklist: - [x] Scheduler implementation - [x] KV warmup hook - [x] Metrics + dashboards - [x] Bench harness + reproducible numbers - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Documentation: runtime/ops/README.md updated with knobs and troubleshooting notes.

Related work: builds on previous fairshare/cohort batching efforts but focuses on prefetch coordination with KV cache and cooperative yield rather than hard preemption. Linear refs: ENG-2345 (kernel affinity hints), ENG-2411 (kv warmup roadmap).

Notes for reviewers: Focus review on the admission loop and token decay math; the yield-handling path must not drop kernel state. Prefetch hooks are opt-in and non-blocking by design. 
Introduce a prefetch-aware windowed admission policy and client-weighted fairness shaping on the continuous batcher. Default gated behind feature flag 'prefetch_windowed_scheduler'. Improvements: lower P95/P99 tail, fewer KV cold-misses, smoother throughput under skewed clients.
Ethan Rios: Nice direction. Two requests: (1) add a small linearizability test for token decay when multiple clients burst; (2) clarify how kindly-yield interacts with time-sliced kernels.
Maya Patel (author): Added unit test for token decay and extended doc comments on yield interaction; kindly-yield triggers a cooperative checkpoint request, not a hard interrupt — clarified in comments.
Claire Nguyen: Benchmark numbers look promising. Can we add an experiment where prefetch hints are noisy (false positives) to show robustness?
Maya Patel (author): Added bench scenario 'warmup_false_positive' and verified regression is <1% on throughput; added to bench scripts.
Omar Haddad: LGTM after one nit: use exponential backoff for token bucket refill when a client is repeatedly throttled to avoid oscillation.

Motivation: Customers running Dedicated fleets observed sudden SLA regressions under sustained burst patterns where per-tenant credit pools were exhausted and the cluster dropped from optimal throughput to hard-throttle mode. This PR introduces a scalable credit-capping controller and a gradual-degradation reconciler that: 1) enforces per-tenant soft caps and dynamic overflow gates, 2) applies a time-decayed degradation path (graceful throttling) instead of abrupt eviction, and 3) emits high-resolution tenant utilization quantiles for downstream billing and SLO reports. Changes include a controller that reconciles tenant credit state in bounded batches, a token gate that performs probabilistic admission when credits are low, and an exporter that produces p50/p90/p99 histograms per tenant window. Rollback: flip feature flag off; reconciler runs idempotently and previous ledger state is preserved. Related: complements ENG-1398 (headroom hedging) and fixes SUP-4421 customer incident summary. No API changes to public Redwood API surface. This description is single-line for PR export consistency.

Add stratified sampling probe scheduler with entropy-normalized cohorting; introduce deferred fallback orchestrator to reduce noisy rollbacks; config knobs for sampling budgets and stability escrow.
Context: we see frequent spurious rollbacks during gradual rollouts when small cohorts produce high-variance latency signals. This PR introduces a two-part solution: a stratified sampling guardrail that ensures probes sample across traffic modalities and an orchestrator that defers fallback decisions until an aggregated stability escrow is satisfied. Motivation: reduce noisy rollbacks and improve signal-to-noise for regression detection without adding significant probe traffic. Design summary: 1) Stratified sampler: samples requests into cohorts by three axes (route, tokenized length bucket, and tenant weight class). Sampling budget is enforced per-cohort and normalized by an entropy metric so low-variance cohorts get proportionally fewer probes. Rough pseudocode: func selectCohort(req) -> cohortID { /* routeHash % N, lengthBucket(req.length), tenantBucket(req.tenantWeight) */ } func shouldProbe(cohort) -> bool { /* uses budgetRemaining[cohort] and entropyNormalizer */ } 2) Deferred fallback orchestrator: when a canary metric crosses a threshold, instead of immediate rollback, we allocate a stability escrow (a short time window and probe budget) to confirm regression across cohorts and time slices. The orchestrator maintains decay-weighted evidence and only triggers fallback when evidence > configured quorum. This reduces churn from transient spikes. Key knobs: - per_cohort_budget (int) - entropy_normalizer_alpha (float) - escrow_window_seconds (int) - fallback_quorum_fraction (float) Backwards compatibility: default configs keep current sampling behavior; feature gated under canary.feature.stratified_sampling=true Migration: operator migration is a config toggle (no rolling restart required). Checklist: - [x] Core sampler implementation and unit tests - [x] Orchestrator finite-state machine + integration tests - [x] Perf microbenchmarks (latency of sampler decision < 50us) - [x] Observability: metrics, histograms, and events emitted - [x] Helm values and example configs - [x] Docs with rollout guidance Testing: unit and integration tests included under perf-canary/tests. Local load tests were run with scripts/loadtests/stratified_probe_runner.py against a staging canary. Perf results: average added CPU per probe: +0.9%, median decision latency: 18us (p95 42us). On a controlled noisy workload, the deferred fallback prevented 3/4 spurious rollbacks compared to baseline over a 4h window. Commits (summary): - feat(sampler): implement stratified cohort selector and budget accounting - feat(orchestrator): add deferred fallback FSM and escrow accounting - test: add unit and e2e tests for sampling and orchestrator - perf: microbench harness and measurement scripts - docs: operational guide and example configs - ci: add canary perf pipeline job Review notes: this is intentionally conservative with defaults to avoid changing behavior for existing installs. The stratified sampler exposes a simple metrics surface: canary_probe_count_total{cohort="..."}, canary_entropy_score, canary_escrow_state{state="pending|active|committed|aborted"}. Observability: added Prometheus metrics (observability/metrics/canary_metrics.prom) and a dashboard template in docs. Rollout plan: feature-flag on in staging for 48h, evaluate canary success rate and rollback count, then enable in limited production tenant slice (5%) for 72h with close monitoring, then scale up. Admin override: immediate forced-fallback endpoint available for on-call. Runtime considerations: sampler is written to be lock-free for fast path; budget accounting uses sharded counters to minimize contention. Known limitations: - sampling across many tiny tenants can dilute budgets; recommended to group low-volume tenants into 'micro' bucket - current entropy normalizer uses exponential smoothing; long-tail pattern shifts may need recalibration Future work: adaptive per-cohort thresholds based on historical variance, integration with traffic-curation probe scheduler for load shaping.
Maya: Nice approach, can you clarify how escrow decays across windows?
Omar: Escrow uses exponential decay keyed by canary id; details in deferred_fallback.go comments.
Ethan: Unit tests look comprehensive but add a failing-case test for partial cohort loss.
Omar: Added test and pushed fix for edge-case where cohort budget underflowed.
Zara: Approved after CI pass and perf numbers.
Ops: noted a helm value request for default escrow window increase to 120s for high-latency regions (applied).
