Context: Teams reported friction wiring multiple credential sources (env, KMS-backed secrets, delegated tokens) into SDK session lifecycles and inconsistent streaming ergonomics across Python/TypeScript/Go. Motivation: simplify credential composition, make SDKs share a single small surface for pull/generator-style streams, and avoid divergent ad-hoc shims that increase cognitive load. Changes: add a lightweight CredentialComposer interface that composes ordered credential providers with precedence rules, cache hints, and proactive prime hooks; introduce a SlimStreamFacade that normalizes pull-generator and async-iterator ergonomics across languages (Session.prime API to warm credentials and optional resume tokens); implement language-specific adapters in python/ts/go under sdk/{python,typescript,go}/session to preserve idiomatic usage while achieving parity; add deprecation shims that map legacy Session.prefetch calls to Session.prime with logging for two release cycles; wire credential telemetry hooks and new retry presets that bias early-auth retries differently from request-level retries to avoid double-retries during auth window failures; update samples and E2E tests and bump SDK versions (py v1.34.0, ts v1.28.0, go v1.8.3). Backwards compatibility: behavioral-preserving for most users; a non-breaking rename is offered via deprecation shims; internal telemetry field names changed (telemetry.auth.strategy) and documented. Testing: unit tests added in all three SDKs, integration tests against a local auth-proxy, cross-language smoke harness, and perf runs showing median stream connect latency unchanged and 12% reduction in duplicate auth attempts under high concurrency. Rollout: merged behind feature flag and will be ramped for paid tenants first.
Simon Huang: Love the Composer abstraction; please ensure provider ordering is stable across runs and add deterministic fallback tests.
Author (Asha Patel): added deterministic ordering tests and a tie-breaker based on provider registration order.
Leah Ortiz: TS ergonomic surface looks good but prefer rename of 'prime' param 'resumeToken' -> 'checkpoint' for clarity.
Author (Asha Patel): updated TS adapter and docs to use 'checkpoint' and left compatibility alias 'resumeToken' for one release.
Tomás Rivera: Go adapter needs clearer ownership rules for goroutine lifetimes in the SlimStreamFacade; potential leak found.
Author (Asha Patel): revised Go adapter to use context cancellation and added a goroutine leak detector test.
Introduce CredentialComposer to compose multiple credential sources with precedence and prime hooks.
Add SlimStreamFacade to harmonize pull/generator stream ergonomics across Python/TypeScript/Go.
Session.prefetch deprecated in favor of Session.prime; prefetch is auto-mapped for two release cycles with a warning.

Motivation: Production rollouts at Redwood increasingly need deterministic rollback behavior plus a low-latency fast-fail safety gate that operates across heterogeneous cohorts. This PR implements an atomic swap rollout primitive driven by a traffic-quorum policy and pairs it with a compact reproducible playback (repro-playback) artifact to warm caches and recreate in-flight behavior at rollback time. Design summary: 1) Traffic-quorum router: a policy layer that requires a configurable quorum of cohort acceptance signals before the swap is committed cluster-wide. Cohort signals are aggregated from per-route SLO checks (latency, p50/p95, error-rate, and a lightweight quality delta if available). 2) Swap transaction: swaps are executed as a two-phase transaction: prepare (shadow swap + quorum voting), then commit (atomic swap). If quorum is not met within the window, the prepare is aborted and traffic remains on the incumbent model. 3) Repro-playback artifact: during the prepare phase we capture a bounded deterministic sample (request fingerprints, prefix KV snapshots, and tokenization deltas) into a compressed playback bundle stored in the replay-store. On abort or post-commit rollback, the playback is run against the previous model/component in an isolated sandbox to validate behavior and to warm KV caches deterministically. 4) Metrics gating and backoff: the quorum evaluator supports weighted voting by cohort size and a backoff policy that escalates to traffic-splitting if partial acceptance is observed. 5) Operator UX and safety: exposes a single CLI for initiating atomic swaps with flags for quorum size, sample window, and repro-playback retention. Also adds detailed events to the rollout journal for audit and postmortem. What changed (files): controller/atomic_swap.go orchestration/quorum_router.go orchestration/quorum_evaluator_test.go replay/replay_store.go replay/replay_serializer.go cli/swapctl.go telemetry/rollout_journal.proto docs/runbooks/atomic-swap.md examples/atomic-swap-example.yaml CI/workflows/atomic-swap.yml High level commits: - feat(atomic-swap): add two-phase swap controller and quorum router - perf(replay): compact binary serializer for playback bundles - test(quorum): add end-to-end acceptance tests with synthetic cohorts - docs: runbook and example usage - ci: workflow and end-to-end smoke job Review summary: Initial review requested on 2026-02-17. Liam: requested stronger invariants on the prepare abort path and clearer eventing for audit logs (addressed: added explicit prepare-abort event and idempotent cleanup). Maya: flagged potential N+1 metric queries in the quorum evaluator (addressed: added aggregate metric snapshotting and cache). Chen: asked for staged rollout path if quorum partially passes; implemented weighted-split fallback with operator opt-in. CI: The first CI run showed a flaky integration test in orchestration/quorum_evaluator_test.go due to time-dependent sampling; fixed by introducing deterministic clock in tests. Final CI: all checks green. Testing and canary plan: - unit/integration coverage added for quorum lifetime, abort/commit paths, and repro-playback execution. - End-to-end smoke on staging with two synthetic cohorts (region-us / region-eu) and production-like load. - Canary: initial usage gated to 5% traffic with manual approval for 25% then 100% after 24h and automatic rollback on failed quorum windows. Migration notes and compatibility: - No data-format changes to persisted models. Replay bundle storage is compatible with existing replay-store but uses a new serializer version; migration path included to rehydrate older bundles. - Operators should review default quorum (set to 0.6 weighted) and sampling window (default 120s) in the rollout config. Rollback semantics: - Abort during prepare leaves incumbent untouched and deletes ephemeral bundles older than retention threshold. - Post-commit rollback triggers repro-playback to warm former model and validate behavior before switching live traffic back. Audit trail: All prepare/commit/abort/rollback events are written to telemetry/rollout_journal.proto and surfaced in Console under the rollout activity tab. Security and perf considerations: - Bundles are encrypted at rest using cluster KMS keys and access-controlled. - Repro-playback runs are throttled to avoid spike load; KV cache warmup uses controlled prefix-inserts. Runbook and docs: added docs/runbooks/atomic-swap.md with step-by-step operator guidance, escalation playbook, and CLI examples. Linear/JIRA references: ENG-9123 covers the core runtime changes; PM-204 tracks the UX and rollout defaults. Checklist: [ ] Add canary to staging and validate metrics [x] Add deterministic-clock to tests [x] Add event journaling for audit [x] Add CLI and example [x] Secure bundle storage [x] CI passing Merge outcome and rationale: Given green tests, addressed reviewer changes, and an explicit staging canary plan, this PR was merged via squash-merge to main on 2026-02-24. The feature enables safer, auditable atomic swaps with deterministic rollback behavior and reproducible cache warmup which reduces rollback flakiness in production.
Liam: Please add an explicit prepare-abort event so auditors can see partial attempts.  Asha: Added prepare-abort and idempotent cleanup.
Maya: Quorum evaluator may hit N+1 when fetching cohort metrics.  Asha: Introduced aggregated metric snapshot and cache (see orchestration/quorum_router.go).
Chen: What happens if we only partially meet quorum? Suggest fallback to traffic-splitting.  Asha: Implemented weighted-split fallback and operator opt-in flag.
Initial CI: flakey integration (time-dependent sampling) -> fix: deterministic clock -> rerun -> all checks passed. Coverage: +6% in quorum code paths. E2E smoke job passed on staging.
merged via squash-merge on 2026-02-24 by Maya Singh. Commit summary preserved in PR description. Tags applied: release/next, rollout/atomic-swap.

Context: Dedicated fleets sometimes oscillate when reservation adjustments are applied mid-window and when sampled utilization signals disagree across pools. Customers see transient SLA blips during aggressive commit rebalancing (notably under variable traffic patterns from bursty tenants). This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: 1) a commit-window aligner that delays and groups reservation adjustments to commit boundaries to reduce churn and enable amortized scale decisions; 2) a thresholded utilization-signature exporter that emits compact, percentile-aware utilization sketches (HDR-based) per-pool and per-tenant window, enabling the autoscaler and the headroom controller to make decisions from smoothed, robust signals. Goals: reduce reservation churn, lower scale-up/scale-down reversals, and improve telemetry fidelity for long-tail utilization so that autoscalers can tune headroom with fewer false positives. Changes: - New controller commit_window_aligner (pkg/autoscaler/aligner) which buffers reservation deltas and applies them at commit window boundaries with configurable alignment tolerances and safety backoff. - util_signature proto and exporter (pkg/telemetry/util_signature) that samples per-slot utilization and exports HDR sketch summaries + checksum-based signatures to the telemetry pipeline. - Autoscaler integration: autoscaler now consumes util_signature summaries to compute trimmed percentiles (p50/p90/p99) and uses commit-window-aligned deltas when making scale decisions. - Backwards-compatible flags: feature gating via runtime flags to enable progressive rollout per-cluster. - Tests: unit tests for alignment logic, integration test harness simulating bursty tenants (test/e2e/commit_alignment_test), and a perf microbench for exporter overhead. Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-2481) - [x] Proto + exporter implemented - [x] Aligner controller implemented with safety backoffs - [x] Unit + integration tests added - [x] Benchmarks captured and added to CI (flaky benchmark isolated) - [x] Feature-flag gated rollout and config defaults noted Migration notes: default behavior preserves current autoscaler semantics when feature flag is off. Enabling the aligner on existing fleets will cause reservoir adjustments to be applied at the next commit window; customers with tight SLA margins should schedule rollout during maintenance windows. Related: design doc link: https://linear.app/redwood/ENG-2481/commit-window-aligner-design; internal convo: #infra-autoscale.
1) add util_signature proto + exporter (A. Martinez)
2) commit window aligner implementation and controller scaffolding (A. Martinez)
3) autoscaler consumer: integrate util_signature p99/p90 selection, apply aligned deltas (L. Romano)
4) e2e harness and tests for burst smoothing (P. Nair)
5) docs + rollout flags + defaults (A. Martinez)

payload.body:
Motivation: Dedicated fleet onboarding spikes and oscillatory provisioning have caused transient overshoot of node starts and increased preemption-induced throughput loss for multi-tenant pools. This PR adds two coordinated pieces: (1) a provisioning-rate-limiter in the control plane that smooths out node launch requests per-pool based on a velocity-aware token window, warm-pool occupancy, and recent failure signals; (2) a utilization-loss-reconciler that attributes lost effective throughput to provisioning/preemption events and reports a corrected per-tenant utilization metric used by the autoscaler and billing-reporter.

Summary of changes: added a new provisioner/ratelimit package that exposes a RateLimiter interface and an implementation ProvisionWindowLimiter which enforces a dynamic per-pool QPS of provisioning actions. The limiter uses EWMA of recent launches and a warm-pool factor to let bursts when warm capacity exists while preventing repeated start storms. The reconcilers/telemetry changes include a UtilLossReconciler service that listens to allocation events, preemption notices and reservation reconciliations to compute 'lost tokens' (tokens that would have been served absent preemptions or fractional deallocations). These are exposed as metrics (reconciler.lost_tokens_total, reconciler.reconciled_utilization_ratio) and a compact per-tenant CSV export for offline billing audits.

Implementation notes: - Rate limiter operates at the ProvisionCoordinator RPC boundary so decisions are deterministic and easy to audit. It supports a per-pool override map and a conservative default derived from fleet size and recent per-pool headroom. - The limiter has a bypass flag for emergency operator commands and for on-demand manual scaling via the console. - UtilLossReconciler relies on an event-sourced view (allocation events, preemption logs, and reservation adjustments) and performs a nightly reconciliation job to surface mismatches; a fast-path real-time sampler provides immediate feedback for autoscaler heuristics. - New config knobs: max_provision_rate_per_pool, provision_rate_ewma_alpha, warm_pool_burst_multiplier, reconciler_sampling_window_seconds, reconciler_min_event_threshold. Defaults are conservative (no behavior change for existing pools) and documented in config/README.

Testing & rollout: unit tests for limiter token mechanics and reconciler attribution were added. Integration test harness simulates 3 pool topologies (steady, ramp, flapping) and assertions verify limiter prevents >30% overshoot during synthetic ramp and that reconciler reports >=95% of known lost tokens in integration traces. Staged rollout: feature gate off by default; gradual enable across Canary->Staging->Prod with per-pool opt-in. Rollback plan: disable feature gate or set per-pool max_provision_rate_per_pool to very high value to restore previous behavior.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked: /docs/design/provisioning-rate-limiter.md - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Metrics + dashboards (Grafana dashboard template added) - [x] Release notes entry added

Related: builds on prior autoscaler headroom work (ENG-3881) and complements the warm-pool prewarming improvements in ENG-3977. Not a breaking change: defaults preserve current behavior.

Marcus Nguyen: Can the limiter cause headroom starvation for pools with aggressive fractional reservations? Please include a safety check to avoid blocking guaranteed reservations.
Priya Shah: Good point — added a reservation bypass: guaranteed reservations and SLO-backed commit windows are exempt. See provisioner/coordination/coordinator.go:ReserveAndLaunch now checks bypass list.
Evelyn Ortega: Telemetry looks good; ensure reconciler only samples sensitive tenant IDs with redaction. We need PII hygiene.
Priya Shah: Reconciler exporter now redacts tenant identifiers in the CSV and emits a tenant hash for correlation. Updated exporter.go and added unit tests.
Samir Kulkarni: Integration tests pass locally but flake reproduced once in CI; investigator note attached.
Priya Shah: CI flake was due to time skew in test harness, tightened clock mocks and retried. All CI runs green after fix.
payload.title: Introduce provisioning-rate-limiter and utilization-loss-reconciler for dedicated fleets

Adds operator-scoped circuit breaker to prevent unintended cross-region KMS usage, a residency prober for service claims, RBAC v2 policy mapper adjustments, and offline audit collector hardening. Controls are behind feature flags and rollout is canaryed by tenant.
Motivation: Several internal incidents revealed that operator-scoped service claims could accidentally exercise KMS keys in non-resident regions when fallback heuristics engaged. This PR adds a defensive circuit breaker at the service-claim layer that blocks KMS operations when residency constraints fail a liveness/prober check, plus a self-contained residency prober that continuously verifies service-to-region affinity. The change also tightens RBAC v2 mapping so operator-scoped grants are rejected if the claim does not match residency assertions, and hardens the offline audit collector to include provenance tags and scrubbed context for any breaker-triggered events. Implementation overview: 1) New package services/kms/circuit_breaker.go implements a token bucket backed circuit breaker with exponential backoff and a short-term denylist keyed by (service, tenant, attempted_kms_region). The breaker exposes metrics: kms.breaker.allowed, kms.breaker.denied, kms.breaker.backoff_seconds. 2) services/kms/residency_prober.go implements a residency prober that runs a lightweight key-assertion handshake against configured KMS endpoints and caches results with TTL and jitter. Prober results are surfaced to the breaker via a compact status struct. 3) RBAC v2 policy mapping adjusted in rbac/policy/mapper.go to evaluate residency claims (attribute: residency.region) during decision time; missing residency attributes cause a soft-deny path which the breaker can escalate to a hard block when the feature flag is enabled. 4) audit/offline_collector.go extended to include event provenance (prober_result, breaker_reason) and to redact tenant PII for any breaker-related audit forwards. 5) Helm values and operator docs updated to include feature flags rbac.v2.residency_enforce and kms.breaker.enabled and rollout knobs per-tenant. 6) New unit and integration tests covering prober race conditions, breaker backoff behavior, and RBAC attribute evaluation. Migration: tenants with custom KMS mappings must add residency.region claim to service bindings or opt-out by annotation until migration is complete.
Evan Li: Asked for explanation of breaker keying semantics and suggested using tenant-scoped denial histogram; author clarified key is (service, tenant, attempted_region) and added tenant histogram metric; Evan approved after metric added.
Marcus Kim: Noted potential jitter edge-case when prober TTLs align across hosts causing thundering rechecks; requested exponential backoff and randomized jitter; author implemented backoff and updated tests; Marcus requested an additional integration scenario covering network stalls; author added a flakey-tolerant test and Marcus approved.
Sofia Delgado: Security review requested proof that audit redaction removes tenant PII and that provenance tags do not leak keys; author added redaction unit tests and described provenance as summary enums only; Sofia approved with minor doc wording request which was addressed.
QA (Lina Park): Reported intermittent failure in integration test when CI uses mocked KMS with strict timing; added a 50ms tolerance to prober timing in CI and reran; CI passed.
Author (Asha Patel): Responded to all comments and pushed follow-up commits addressing backoff/jitter and audit redaction; requested squash-merge.
Risk: false-positive breaker activations causing client errors. Mitigation: staged rollout with log_only mode and alerting, 48h canary window, quick revert flag kms.breaker.enabled=false.
Risk: increased latency from prober calls. Mitigation: prober uses cached status with TTL and jitter, local cache on each host, and prober calls are async where possible.
Risk: RBAC policy eval path change could affect non-residency tenants. Mitigation: default policy path still allows access unless residency_enforce is turned on; documented opt-out annotation for legacy tenants.
Metrics: kms.breaker.denied, kms.breaker.allowed, kms.breaker.backoff_seconds, rbac.residency_checks.total, audit.breaker_events.count
Dashboards: Security / KMS Residency -> added panel for breaker spikes
Runbook: docs/runbooks/kms-residency-rollout.md contains rollback steps, metrics to watch, and how to disable per-tenant via annotation
payload.title: Introduce service-claim circuit breaker and KMS residency prober

Motivation: Some model regressions (e.g., delayed coherence drift, rare token hallucinations, multi-turn state corruption) manifest only after a short window of downstream interactions. Immediate canary signals can miss these delayed failure modes and either produce false negatives or force overly conservative rollouts. This PR introduces a Deferred Shadow Buffer + Replay Rollout Controller that captures a configurable sample of shadow requests, buffers their inputs and immediate responses for a short evaluation window, and then replays them asynchronously against candidate model variants to compute delayed-signal metrics and a deterministic rollback score. Main goals: (1) give operators a lightweight way to detect delayed degradations before completing a traffic promotion, (2) enable A/B evaluations where metric windows differ (e.g., immediate latency vs. 5-minute coherence checks), and (3) provide an operator-friendly simulator to estimate rollback probability over historical traffic. Changes in this PR: implemented a rollout controller that manages a per-cohort shadow buffer with TTL and replay policies; added a replay-based metric sink that computes windowed deltas (supporting mean/percentile and custom loss functions); integrated a rollback score calculator with configurable thresholds and weightings; added a deterministic simulator that can run a replay pass against stored traffic (used in CI and by SRE to estimate risk); surface new rollout knobs in the API (api/v1/rollout_types.go) and console docs. Backwards compatibility: the controller defaults to a disabled shadow buffer; enabling requires opt-in in the rollout spec. Checkout checklist: - implement controller + buffer (controllers/deferred_shadow_controller.go) - add simulator (pkg/simulator/replay_sim.go) - expose API fields and validation (api/v1/rollout_types.go) - add e2e test harness and CI job (test/e2e/deferred_shadow_replay_test.go) - docs and console notes (docs/rollouts/deferred-shadow.md). Testing summary: unit tests for buffer correctness and TTL, integration test that drives replay and asserts expected rollback_score computation, e2e experiment against a synthetic historical corpus to check simulator stability. Risks and mitigations: buffer growth under heavy traffic mitigated by stochastic sampling and dynamic rate cap; possible metric misalignment mitigated by conservative default thresholds and an evaluation-only "simulation" mode that runs fast but does not block promotions. Usage notes: the rollout spec accepts shadow.buffer_size, shadow.sample_rate, shadow.replay_delay, and rollback.score_threshold; recommended default values included in docs. Related work: builds on prior staged-rollout and shadowing infra but focuses on delayed-signal detection and deterministic replay to support safe promotions. The description below contains a short example of a rollout snippet: {"rollout_strategy": "deferred-shadow", "shadow": {"sample_rate": 0.05, "buffer_ttl_seconds": 300, "replay_delay_seconds": 120}, "rollback": {"score_threshold": 0.8}}. Please see the changed files for implementation details and the simulator for how to run historical risk estimates.
Marco Diaz (reviewer): Can we avoid storing full request payloads in the buffer? Suggest storing a normalized fingerprint and replay seed to reduce memory. Which sensitive fields are redacted?
Aisha Khanna (author): We store a sanitized request plus a small provenance envelope. Sensitive fields are redacted via existing request-sanitizer pipeline; I added a unit to validate redaction and updated the docs to call out redaction rules.
Lina Zhao (reviewer): The rollback_score uses a weighted sum of metric deltas. Would be good to add a configurable smoothing window and expose weights via the rollout spec for experiments.
Aisha Khanna (author): Added smoothing_window_ms and exposed metric_weights in the spec. Default weights keep latency lower-priority to avoid false positives on noisy networks.
Evan Park (reviewer): e2e flakes observed on nightly due to simulator relying on local timezone and time.Now() in tests. Please inject clock interface for determinism.
Aisha Khanna (author): Rewrote simulator to use injected clock; e2e now deterministically seeds replay runs in CI.
Marco Diaz (approver): LGTM after minor nits; please follow up with a separate PR to add observability metrics for buffer size and replay latency.
Lina Zhao (approver): Approved - the simulation harness is useful for SRE risk analysis.
Operator-facing: add 'deferred-shadow' rollout strategy with buffered shadowing and replay-based rollback scoring; defaults off; see docs/rollouts/deferred-shadow.md for sample spec and recommended defaults.
Added Deferred Shadow Buffer + Replay controller and simulator; API fields in api/v1/rollout_types.go; e2e tests and docs.

Motivation: Different SDKs had subtly divergent streaming semantics and retry behaviors which caused hard-to-debug client edge-cases (double-cancel, lost error events, and inconsistent backoff telemetry). This PR introduces small, opt-in typed guards and a tiny cross-SDK backoff shim to align runtime behavior and improve ergonomics when consumers migrate between Python/TS/Go.

Summary of changes: 1) Add typed stream-safety guards: a lightweight consumer-side guard that enforces single-terminal event semantics (only one of close/error) and surfaces a consistent error envelope across languages. Implementations: TypeScript guard + tests (sdk/typescript), Go guard + tests (sdk/go), Python wrapper with typing annotations and context-manager helper (sdk/python). 2) Cross-SDK backoff shim: a small, language-agnostic policy spec serialized as JSON in the SDK root; SDKs adopt the shim to produce identical retry timing and telemetry tags for the most common transient errors (auth refresh, 429, connection reset). 3) Ergonomic minor API change: introduce Stream.cancel(reason: str|None) / Stream.close() parity doc and deprecation shim (old cancel() still available for one release). 4) Coordinated version bumps and changelog updates: python 2.4.1 -> 2.5.0, typescript 3.1.0 -> 3.2.0, go v0.9.7 -> v0.10.0.

Checklist: - [x] Implement TS guard and unit tests - [x] Implement Go guard and unit tests - [x] Implement Python wrapper, typing and integration tests - [x] Add shared backoff JSON and normalization code in each SDK - [x] Update SDK changelogs and release manifest - [x] Run cross-language integration matrix in CI - [x] Docs: streaming best-practices and migration note

Testing and rollout: Local integration matrix exercised against the hosted QA runtime (stream smoke, auth refresh fault-injection, and 429 storms). CI initially flagged a flaky Go race in the stream test; reproduced locally and fixed by a short mutex around the internal state transition. After fix the full matrix passed. Rollout plan: merge to main and publish SDKs in a coordinated window; leave deprecation shim for one release and call out migration in the changelog and docs site.

Notes: The changes are intentionally small and additive. Consumers that rely on the old multi-terminal behavior should not break immediately due to the guard being opt-in via an instantiation flag (enable_stream_safety=true) for the first release; we plan to enable it by default in next minor once telemetry shows insignificant breakage.
Miguel Ramos: Please add one sentence in the docs about the opt-in flag and the telemetry tag we will use so SRE can filter consumers.
Author (Asha): Added docs and telemetry tag description (redwood.telemetry.stream_guard=enabled).
Lina Cho: The Go test 'TestStreamStateTransition' flaked in CI. Can you add a deterministic wait or remove timing assumptions?
Author: Reproduced locally, added a short mutex around state transitions and removed timing-based assertions; pushed fix in 4d2e8c7.
Ethan Ford: Can the backoff JSON schema become part of our public SDK spec? Suggest we document it under docs/api/backoff-policy.md.
Author: Agree, added a short section and linked it in the CHANGELOG.
Miguel Ramos: approved with a minor nit about changelog wording.
Merge: Approved and squashed after CI green.
Checks: build (ts/go/py) - passed, unit tests (ts/go/py) - passed after fix, integration matrix - passed, lint - passed, typecheck - passed. Timeline: initial CI run reported a flake in go unit tests (race detector) at 2026-02-22 02:41 UTC; fixed and rerun, final green at 2026-02-26 10:03 UTC.
Special note: cross-language integration suite exercises auth refresh fault injection; observed expected retry telemetry tags once shim adopted.
Add opt-in stream safety guards to TS/Go/Python SDKs; introduce standardized cross-SDK backoff policy; minor ergonomic parity for Stream.cancel/close; coordinated SDK version bumps (python 2.5.0, typescript 3.2.0, go v0.10.0). Migration: enable_stream_safety is opt-in for 2.5/3.2/0.10; enable by default in the next minor release after monitoring. See docs/sdk/streaming-migration.md for migration steps and examples.
Backport readiness: change is additive and small; mark as backport-ready for any stable release branches if needed. Telemetry: tag redwood.telemetry.stream_guard=enabled for consumers that opt in.

Adds batch-affinity optimizer to improve request packing for tenant/route locality and introduces a new quantization profile 'quant-sentinel' that allows graceful degradation across capacity tiers. Includes telemetry hooks and a unit-econ dry-run CLI to simulate cost/latency tradeoffs.
Motivation: We have recurring tenant noise and suboptimal packing when multiple small requests with similar token shapes hit the same serving pool. Current batching is agnostic to tenant affinity which causes more KV cache misses and inefficient GPU utilization. Additionally, aggressive quantization rollouts have caused occasional quality regressions for tail workloads. This PR introduces two coordinated features: (1) a batch-affinity optimizer that prefers packing requests with high locality (tenant, route, prompt-shape signatures) while respecting latency SLOs and (2) a conservative 'quant-sentinel' quantization profile that progressively reduces precision by lane and includes a rollback sentinel that forces fallback to a safe quantized variant on quality regressions. Design/changes summary: - Routing/packing: new affinity scoring module (affinity_score) that computes a lightweight locality score using tenant_id, model_version, prefix hash, and token-length bucket. The packer will bias towards high-affinity groups while still respecting pack size and latency headroom. - Prefill/cache: added an affinity-aware prefill hint that enables soft KV cache pinning for high-affinity lanes (TTL-based, configurable per-tenant). - Quantization: added a new profile 'quant-sentinel' that annotates model variants with a sentinel threshold and a staged degradation path: fp16 -> int8-symmetric -> int8-symmetric+kv-compress. Each stage has quality gates and automatic fallback to a verified baseline when regressions are detected. - Telemetry/metrics: new metrics (batch_affinity_ratio, affinity_pack_efficiency, quant_sentinel_fallbacks) and tracing tags (affinity_group_id, quant_stage) for post-deploy analysis. - CLI/tooling: unit-econ dry-run flag to 'redwood-econ' CLI to simulate per-tenant cost delta with current traffic shape and proposed affinities/quant profiles. Rollout plan: 1) Canary deploy optimizer into one region with 5% traffic for non-enterprise tenants for 48 hours. 2) Collect metrics and run quality probes (eval set + live A/B) using the quant sentinel gate. 3) Ramp to 50% with telemetry gates, then to 100% if no regressions. Checklist: - [x] affinity scoring unit tests - [x] packer integration tests with latency SLOs - [x] quant-sentinel unit tests and sentinel regression hooks - [x] telemetry dashboards (draft) - [x] CLI dry-run implemented - [x] e2e smoke test in benchmark-lab Observability notes: initial smoke benchmarks show a 9-12% token/sec utilization increase for mixed small-request workloads and a 7-9% median latency decrease for 0-128 token requests under load. Quality gate simulated on our eval set shows <0.5% delta for the first quant stage, and 1.5-2.1% for stage 2 for large-context prompts (above 1024 tokens) — hence the sentinel fallback behavior. Motivation references: ENG-1892 (tenant packing problems), ENG-2041 (quant rollout safe paths), SUP-4123 (customer incident showing regression during quant rollout).
Diego Marquez: Nice end-to-end. Two questions: 1) affinity_score weight defaults — do we expose them per-tenant or keep globally tuned? 2) any extra memory / KV pin risk under heavy churn?
Ava Chen: Reply: default weights are global tuned but exposed via tenant override flags; KV pin uses TTL and eviction heuristics to prevent unbounded memory growth (added tests).
Priya Nair: Please add canary gating based on affinity_pack_efficiency and quant_sentinel_fallbacks; ensure rollback hook can be invoked from console.
Ava Chen: Reply: added telemetry gates and console runbook; rollback is a one-click toggle that flips traffic to baseline variant (documented in docs/deployment/quant-sentinel.md).
Samir Patel: Lgtm after minor nits — prefer explicit timeouts in packer loop and a small comment about potential fairness regressions for small tenants. Added a requested change on packer.go
Ava Chen: Addressed nits, added timeout and fairness limiter; ran bench again and attached numbers.
payload.title: Introduce batch-affinity optimizer and 'quant-sentinel' graceful quantization profile

Context: Multiple teams asked for a small, embeddable bridge to unify session/token lifecycle across SDKs while making retries and streaming ergonomics consistent. This PR introduces a compact session-bridge interface implemented in Python/TS/Go, ergonomic per-language retry wrappers, and an opt-in compat mode for older SDK consumers. Motivation: reduce duplication of token-refresh logic across service clients, make stream resumptions default-ergonomic, and provide a clear upgrade path with minimal breaking surface.

What this changes: - New core interface 'SessionBridge' (language idiomatic wrappers) that centralizes lease/renew/hand-off semantics. - Per-language retry profiles: 'default', 'interactive', 'high-throughput' with consistent backoff math and jitter shapes. - Stream ergonomics: a small cursor API for resuming chunked streams and an automatic token-warmup hook for first request in a session. - Opt-in compatibility mode: SDKs honor legacy token callback signatures when 'compatMode=true'. - Tests + CI: cross-sdk interop tests and matrix updated to run a lightweight interop job.

Checklist: - [x] design doc, ENG-2141 - [x] types and user docs - [x] integration tests - [x] version bumps for all three SDKs - [x] telemetry for token refresh events (new event type)

Review summary (summary of the review thread): Liam: asked for clearer failure semantics on session handoff; asked to guarantee idempotent handoff. Action: added handoff_id and idempotency checks in bridge implementation. Priya: requested smaller public surface for Python session manager and suggested default retry names; actioned and reduced exported symbols. Mateo: noted a flaky test on CI (ts stream resume) — root cause was a timing race in test harness; I switched to deterministic mock time and re-ran CI.

CI: initial run had one flaky TS test fail; re-run completed successfully across all matrix entries (linux/py, linux/ts, linux/go, macos/py). Coverage: +0.4% on cross-sdk tests.

Migration notes: bump SDKs to the versions in release notes. Existing consumers who relied on the older token callback should enable compatMode=true and migrate to the new async-friendly token provider by the next minor. Docs: added migration guide and example helpers in examples/streaming.

Risks & mitigations: The change surfaces auth lifecycle in more places — to mitigate we kept compatMode and added a feature-flagged rollout in the console for dedicated/private customers. No breaking changes expected by default.

Merge: Squash-merged after approvals from Liam and Priya and green CI.
Adds a lightweight session bridge and per-language ergonomic retry wrappers for streaming and non-streaming flows; bumps SDK versions: python v2.10.1, typescript v1.9.4, go v1.5.0. Opt-in compatibility mode for older consumers.
Follow-up: instrument end-to-end latency for first token warmup (ENG-2178)
Follow-up: backfill SDK release pages with migration snippets

payload.body:
Motivation: Build a lightweight saga-style rollback orchestration layer for canary commits that coordinates cross-service compensation actions, provides an auditable playback for incident repro, and exposes staged decision points for human escalation. Many existing controllers handle traffic phasing and metric gates; this PR focuses on the commit/compensate lifecycle and forensic replay so on-call can reproduce and unwind complex promotes across model variants and downstream transforms.

What this PR adds: a) a SagaExecutor component that records atomic commit steps (traffic transition, KV migration, cache invalidation, feature-flag flips) and associated compensation actions; b) decision checkpoints wired to telemetry gates (latency/error/qa-regressions) that can auto-run compensations or escalate to a human reviewer; c) a synthetic-smoke runner that executes a configurable suite of synthetic requests against the canary variant and stores trace-correlated snapshots; d) an audit-playback tool that replays recorded traffic slices deterministically in a sandboxed dry-run to reproduce observed regressions; e) a compact JSON-based saga journal (append-only) with signatures for forensic integrity and optional encryption hooks for Private deployments.

Design notes: the saga journal is append-only and arranged as discrete steps with idempotency keys to allow safe retries. The SagaExecutor exposes a finite-state machine: PREPARE -> EXECUTE_STEP -> CHECKPOINT -> ON_FAILURE -> COMPENSATE -> COMPLETE. Checkpoints evaluate telemetry rules (configured with SLO thresholds and rate-aware heuristics). If a checkpoint is tripped, the executor will first attempt automated compensation and then open a human review ticket when configured thresholds are exceeded. The audit-playback replays in a constrained environment: synthetic smoke first, then traffic-replay with session affinity preserved if available.

Rollout safety: to avoid split-brain between autoscaling and staged promote we added a lease token per saga commit; only the token-holder may mark a saga as COMPLETE. Leases are short-lived and renewed automatically; orphaned leases trigger a conservative auto-compensate path.

Backward compatibility: defaults keep existing rollout controllers intact. The SagaExecutor is opt-in per rollout via a single flag in the rollout spec: "saga: enabled", and an optional "audit_playback: enabled" flag for environments that allow replay.

Checklist: - [x] Saga journal schema and migrations - [x] SagaExecutor FSM and API surface - [x] Telemetry gate integration and SLO mapping - [x] Synthetic-smoke runner and CI harness - [x] Audit-playback CLI and sandbox mode - [x] Tests: unit + integration + a replay smoke test in staging - [x] Docs: rollout cookbook and runbook snippets

Impact: Intended to improve on-call confidence for staged promotions by enabling deterministic repro and safe cross-service unwind. It provides a clear audit trail for compliance and a programmable way to encode compensations for complicated model swaps.

Motivation: several production deployments surfaced intermittent auth probe failures that caused streaming consumers to retry aggressively and lose backpressure semantics. This PR introduces a pluggable credential fallback chain, harmonizes a typed stream contract across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs, and wires lightweight retry presets that prefer fast local fallbacks before hitting network refresh endpoints. The goals are: 1) make credential lookup resilient (local cache -> delegated proxy -> remote refresh) with a clear TTL/priority model; 2) propagate backpressure hints and a minimal typed envelope so SDKs can interoperate without behavioral surprises; 3) introduce small, opt-in retry presets tuned for streaming consumers to reduce noisy retries in client apps. Changes are split across SDK surfaces and the mono-repo coordination layer. See linked Linear items for rollout plan and metrics to watch. Checklist: [x] design doc linked in Linear ENG-2191; [x] unit tests for credential fallback and stream contract in each SDK; [x] integration test matrix against the proxy dev environment; [x] telemetry hooks for credential-fallback-count and stream-backpressure-events; [x] doc snippets for migration and example usage; [ ] follow-up: opt-in feature flag for legacy behavior for 1 release cycle. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is compatible but exposes a new opt-in policy field on client constructors. Rollout plan: merge to main, staged canary on Dedicated infra, 48h metrics review, then wide rollout.

Context and motivation: Customers running cost-sensitive tenant workloads repeatedly ask for prescriptive, per-tenant defaults that balance latency SLOs and unit economics without deep runtime tuning. ENG-2314 requested an experimental set of presets for low-traffic tenants; ENG-2407 asked for clearer operator guidance on quantization tradeoffs. This PR introduces the "WalletWise" batch sculptor (a set of tenant-aware batch/cache/quant presets), runtime rollout hooks to enable safe gradual opt-in, and a developer-facing guidance doc that codifies heuristics used by the presets.

What this changes (single-string checklist and detail): 
- Add: walletwise presets under configs/presets/walletwise/* (profiles for tiny, small, medium tenants).
- Add: runtime hook (pkg/runtime/prefill/walletwise.go) that selects a conservative preset when tenant capacity or cost tier is flagged.
- Add: quant guidance doc and interactive checklist (docs/operator/walletwise-quant-guide.md).
- Update: default batcher config merge logic to prefer tenant-specific profiles if present (pkg/config/merge.go).
- Add: telemetry tags for WalletWise decisions (telemetry/metrics.yaml) and sample dashboards (observability/dashboards/walletwise.jsonnet).
- Tests: unit tests for merge behavior and preference fallbacks; a small e2e smoke that runs in the perf-canary suite.

Commits (high-level): 
1) aisha/add-walletwise-presets - add YAML presets for three tenant classes + unit tests for YAML validation.
2) aisha/walletwise-runtime-hook - implement selection hook with feature-flag gated rollout and basic caching integration.
3) aisha/quant-guide - operator doc + examples + small script to validate quant profiles against known-good model artifacts.

Changed areas (high level, illustrative): 
- configs/presets/walletwise/
  - tiny.yaml (prefill: enabled, batch_size_target: 1-4, kv_cache_policy: conservative, quant_profile: q4_8_safe)
  - small.yaml (prefill: enabled, batch_size_target: 4-16, kv_cache_policy: balanced, quant_profile: q4_0_mixed)
  - medium.yaml (prefill: enabled, batch_size_target: 16-64, kv_cache_policy: aggressive, quant_profile: q3_4_perf)
- pkg/runtime/prefill/walletwise.go 
  - adds SelectWalletwiseProfile(tenantMeta, workloadSig) and unit tests 
  - safe fallback to global defaults when instrumented signals are missing
- pkg/config/merge.go 
  - updates merge logic to consult tenant presets before applying global heuristics
- docs/operator/walletwise-quant-guide.md 
  - step-by-step: sample evaluation harness commands, token/latency tradeoff table, guidance for fallback quant profiles 
- observability/dashboards/walletwise.jsonnet 
  - new dashboard showing per-tenant unit cost delta and prefill hit-rate

Review conversation (abridged and inline): 
- Marco Ruiz (request changes): "Nice approach. Two concerns: ensure the runtime hook does not introduce contention on the prefill path, and add a canary-only env var so we can test without hitting production tenants."
- Aisha (author): "Thanks Marco — hook uses non-blocking read path and writes decisions to a per-tenant cache with TTL. Added WALLETWISE_CANARY_ONLY flag (defaults to true in rollout). See pkg/runtime/prefill/walletwise.go: lines 38-76 for the gating logic."

CI and validation:

Rollout plan and safety: 
- Feature flag WALLETWISE_CANARY_ONLY true by default. Ops can flip to tenant opt-in via tenant metadata, then to global opt-in after monitoring.
- Telemetry emits walletwise.decision.{tiny,small,medium} and walletwise.fallback.* to detect misclassification.
- Added SLO guard: if prefill hit-rate < 30% and 95th p99 latency regresses > 10% for two consecutive 1h windows, an automated rollback signal will be emitted to alerting.

Docs and operator guidance summary: 
- docs/operator/walletwise-quant-guide.md: contains a short script to run the quant-sanity-check on a model artifact, recommended thresholds (quality drop <= 2% on the standard eval set), and a small table mapping quant_profile -> expected token throughput improvements.

Motivation: Customers need deterministic errors from structured-output endpoints that are actionable for client SDKs and observability stacks while preserving streaming latency and tool/function-calling semantics. This PR introduces a telemetry-friendly error contract for response_format=json_schema used with streaming and tool calls, plus a lightweight streaming checkpoint used to fence tool invocations for safe resumption. Summary: 1) Introduce a thin header X-Redwood-Contract-Error that surfaces a short machine code (e.g., SCHEMA_MISMATCH, STREAM_TRUNCATED, TOOL_FENCE_VIOLATION) and a stable telemetry tag. 2) Add an in-stream checkpoint token ("checkpoint_id") emitted before tool/function calls and at schema validation boundaries so clients can resume from the last acknowledged checkpoint on retry. 3) Extend OpenAI-compat mapping so legacy clients receive compatible error types but SDKs can opt-in to structured error payloads via Accept: application/vnd.redwood+json. 4) Implement a runtime validator that performs streaming-aware schema checks: lightweight progressive validation with final strict pass before commit. Design details: - Checkpointing: the runtime emits a minimal JSON fragment "{\"_checkpoint\": \"<uuid>\"}" as a discrete event on the stream prior to any tool call or schema-critical token boundary. Checkpoints are advisory by default; in strict mode they become fencing points (the runtime records tool-call side effects only after the strict checkpoint is acknowledged by the client via a follow-up acknowledgment API or by an idempotent toolcall token). - Error contract: errors include three fields in the header and, when Accept indicates Redwood structured error support, the final error event includes a machine_code, human_message, client_hint (e.g., "retry_with_backoff"/"adjust_schema"), and telemetry_tags. When mapping to OpenAI-compat errors the runtime preserves the human_message and maps machine_code to a short code placed in error.type for easy ingestion by third-party clients. - Streaming validation: to avoid latency regressions we run a progressive validator that checks incremental token sequences for major structural violations (unclosed arrays/objects, type mismatches that are deterministically provable) and defers non-deterministic checks until finalization. On finalization we perform full jsonschema validation; if strict mode is enabled we emit SCHEMA_STRICT_VIOLATION and close the stream with a clear checkpoint id for restart. - Tool/function-calling safety: toolcalls now include a toolcall_token and a pre-call checkpoint emitted in-stream. If a tool reports a side-effect failure, the runtime includes TOOL_FENCE_VIOLATION with the checkpoint id so downstream systems can reconcile or retry idempotently. Backward compatibility: older clients get minimal header-only errors (no structured JSON) and will see canonical OpenAI-style error.text. New SDKs (python/ts/go) will decode structured errors and surface client_hint and telemetry_tags in exceptions/LogRecords. Migration: - Console and Optimize teams will receive a small telemetry column for contract error codes. - SDK teams get a small API addition: Response.contract_error (nullable) and Stream.on_checkpoint(callback). Testing: unit tests for progressive validator, e2e integration tests with the tool-runner (simulated idempotent and non-idempotent tool outcomes), load tests to verify <2% p50 latency impact under typical streaming workloads. Checklist: - [x] Runtime: emit checkpoint tokens and structured header - [x] Runtime: progressive validator + final strict pass - [x] API: Accept header negotiation and OpenAI-mapping layer - [x] SDK: python/ts basic decoding and streaming callbacks - [x] Docs: Console and API docs describing new headers and migration - [x] Telemetry: contract error tags in trace/span attributes - [x] Load tests run on perf-canary Observability notes: added contract_error and checkpoint_id as stable span attributes (redwood.contract_error, redwood.checkpoint_id) and a dashboard tile that breaks down top 10 contract_error codes. Security: no secrets exposed; checkpoint tokens are UUIDv4 and do not encode PII. Related: ENG-2145 for validator work, PM-87 for product acceptance criteria, SUP-4123 for a troubleshooting playbook. Rollout plan: - Stage 1 (canary): enable structured headers and checkpoints in canary region with feature flag rschema.streaming.telemetry=false (header-only) - Stage 2: enable progressive validation and sdk opt-in for structured errors - Stage 3: strict-mode gating for paid tiers only and documentation updates - Rollback: feature flags to disable checkpoint emission and revert to legacy OpenAI-compatible behavior.
Ethan Cole: Nice end-to-end. Two requests: 1) add a clear TL;DR for SDK consumers in the top of docs so they can opt in quickly, 2) ensure checkpoint UUIDs are rotated per request so they cannot be guessed across sessions.
Priya Nair (author): Added TL;DR to docs and ensured checkpoint UUID is per-request (see emitter.go change).
Marco Liu: Can we include a small backoff recommendation in the client_hint? Many infra teams want deterministic retry windows for billing reconciliation.
Priya Nair: Added client_hint examples (retry_with_backoff: 2s, exponential up to 30s) and added in docs.
Added streaming checkpoints and structured contract error telemetry for response_format=json_schema. New header X-Redwood-Contract-Error with machine codes and opt-in structured error payloads. SDKs updated to surface checkpoints and structured errors. Backward compatible with OpenAI-compat clients.
Canary observations: small uptick in error telemetry during first day as customers opt-in; no increased tail latency observed in perf-canary runs.
Follow-ups: 1) automated client-acknowledgment API for strict checkpoints (ENG-2210), 2) richer tooling for automated schema-guided prompt repair in Optimize (PM-121).

Motivation: During recent regional evacuations we observed sudden, near-immediate global load-shedding spikes as nodes reclaimed capacity and regional routing switched. This caused expensive error budgets and flapping circuit states for mid-priority tenants. This PR introduces an 'evacuation grace reserve' which conservatively holds a small capacity reserve and a token-based grace budget per-region so that staged failovers preserve the highest-priority inflight work and avoid simultaneous full-shed waves. --- Design summary: Add a lightweight controller (EvacGraceReserve) that tracks regional evacuation signals and maintains a per-region reserve token pool derived from the region's current SLO headroom. When an evacuation/failover is signaled, the controller allocates tokens to steward a gradual admission taper: requests can draw a reserve token to bypass coarse load-shed gates for a bounded window. Tokens expire and are replenished on a conservative cadence. The runtime shedder integrates a non-blocking reserve consumer that prefers KV-preserving work and short-lived requests. The mechanism is opt-in via the runtime config and feature-flagged behind runtime.evacuations.grace_reserve.enabled. --- Config knobs: runtime.evacuations.grace_reserve.enabled (bool), runtime.evacuations.grace_reserve.initial_percent (string decimal, default "0.03"), runtime.evacuations.grace_reserve.max_burst_tokens (int as string), runtime.evacuations.grace_reserve.token_ttl_secs (int as string), rollout.evacuations.grace_reserve.stable_window_secs (int as string). --- Behavioral guarantees: 1) Does not increase total committed capacity: reserve is a conservative fraction of ephemeral headroom only; 2) Tokens are strictly bounded by a region-local cap; 3) Token consumption is best-effort and honored only when the global shedder would otherwise evict; 4) Failure modes: if the controller panics or is OOMed, system falls back to current shedding semantics (no tokens). --- Testing and validation: Added unit tests for token accounting, integration test that simulates a two-region failover and asserts smoother tail-latency and fewer circuit flips, and a staging canary that ran for 48 hours under synthetic traffic patterns. Telemetry: added metrics evac_reserve.tokens_allocated, evac_reserve.tokens_consumed, evac_reserve.replenish_rate and histograms for reserve-bypass latency. --- Rollout plan: 1) feature-flag disabled by default; 2) enable in staging and run 72h soak; 3) enable for 10% of region traffic with canary header; 4) expand to 50% and monitor SLOs and circuit-flip rate for 24h; 5) global on if metrics look stable. Rollback: flip feature flag off; controller will gracefully expire tokens and revert to baseline. --- Why unique: Prior work focused on reactive shedding thresholds and cooldowns. This PR adds a proactive, bounded headroom reservation tuned for evacuation windows to reduce simultaneous global shedding and improve graceful degradation behavior.
Samir Patel: Could we avoid holding the token pool in memory per region? Consider using the existing slot-reservation service to persist token state across controller restarts. Response: We deliberately kept it ephemeral to minimize cross-region write amplification; added resilience path to reconstruct from headroom metrics on restart (see controller.go#rebuildFromMetrics).
Eve Torres: Add a guard so that tenant-priority metadata is respected when bypassing shedding (we can't let low-priority tenants jump the queue). Response: Added priority check in reserve_consumer.go; only tenants above configured threshold may consume tokens and we emit evac_reserve.token_denied metric.
Liam O'Connor: CI flake observed in TestIntegration_EvacReserve under heavy CPU; add backoff and rerun. Response: Increased test timeouts and added deterministic scheduling to reduce flakiness; CI rerun passed.
Introduce Evacuation Grace Reserve: opt-in feature that preserves bounded capacity during regional evacuations to reduce simultaneous shedding and circuit flapping. Configurable via runtime.evacuations.grace_reserve.*.
payload.title: Introduce evacuation grace reserve to smooth regional failovers and SLO enforcement

Motivation: Improve observability across the API surface for streaming, function/tool calls, and the OpenAI-compat shim by introducing a request-scoped telemetry header that carries tracing context and function-call baggage, emitting structured JSON access logs with fine-grained fields (route, model_family, mode, tokens_sent, tokens_received, tool_call_id, partial_stream_checkpoint), and tagging per-endpoint metrics with programmatic labels. This PR introduces: (1) middleware that injects and forwards an x-rw-telemetry header (traceparent+baggage) and preserves request IDs across proxy hops, (2) a lightweight func-call span bag that attaches tool call metadata to spans and is included in structured logs when tool/function calling occurs, (3) a JSON access log formatter that emits stable schema fields for downstream log pipelines, (4) metric label enrichment at the routing layer so per-endpoint counters and latency histograms include route_name, model_family, and request_mode (chat/completion/embedding), and (5) OpenAI-compat shim updates so clients using the shim automatically get propagated trace headers and per-chunk streaming checkpoint events logged. Backwards compatibility: the new middleware is opt-in via config flag `observability.request_scoped_telemetry=true` for Dedicated/Private until rollout completes; shown fallback behavior ensures older clients see no change. Motivation: Several customer incidents showed user sessions getting inconsistent results during shadow -> canary transitions when per-session stickiness and long-lived KV cache entries existed. This PR introduces a session handoff protocol with an explicit deadline and replay-safe drain to ensure session-consistency during shadow-to-canary transitions, plus observable probes and operator controls. Summary of changes: - Add SessionHandoffCoordinator service that tracks per-session phase (shadow, pending-handoff, active-canary) and enforces a configurable deadline for handoff. - Implement graceful deadline semantics: when the deadline expires, active user requests are allowed to complete on the origin model; subsequent requests are routed to the canary, and any in-flight KV cache entries are checkpointed for safe replay. - Introduce per-session tokens for stickiness that are transparently reissued during the handoff window to avoid split-brain routing on retries. - Add replay-safe drain helpers for runtimes that manage KV caches and streaming sessions (hooks for cuda/kv cache flush). - Console: new handoff dashboard with per-rollout countdown, stalled-session list, and operator-triggered immediate-cutover button. - E2E: extended the rollout integration harness to simulate long-lived sessions and network flaps. - Tests: unit tests for coordinator state machine, integration tests for token reissuance and deadline behavior, and load-scenario validation in perf canary harness. Backwards compatibility: defaults keep current behavior (no session handoff) unless a rollout specifies "handoff_deadline_ms" or uses the new "session_handoff" flag. Checklist: - [x] Design review (ENG-1724) - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Console UX mockups - [x] Perf validation in canary lab Known limitations: - On extremely high churn of short sessions, additional token issuance load was observed in perf tests; we added rate-limiting but further optimization may be follow-up (ENG-1789). - On on-prem installs with very old runtimes, the replay hooks are no-op; installer will surface a warning. Related work: builds on the traffic-anchoring and shadow drain utilities (see ENG-1629 and PRs that added per-cohort anchoring).
Arjun Patel (2026-02-19): Can we avoid a synchronous KV checkpoint on the critical path? Suggest yielding and using a best-effort background flush with a strong idempotency token.
Maya Thompson (2026-02-19): Implemented background checkpointing and added idempotency tokens; updated tests to cover double-flush scenarios.
Elena García (2026-02-20): Need clearer operator guidance for when to press immediate-cutover. Add guardrails to prevent accidental mass-cutovers.
Maya Thompson (2026-02-21): Added modal confirmation, per-rollout RBAC check, and operator audit log entry.
Add optional session handoff protocol for rollout transitions: configurable deadline, replay-safe drain hooks, console handoff dashboard, and operator controls. Off by default; enable via session_handoff in rollout spec.

Motivation: Operators need a compact, explainable way to pick batching/caching defaults and quantization profiles tuned to their workload mix without manual trial-and-error. This PR introduces a Decision Graph Cost Advisor that ingests workload traces and generates opinionated default templates (batching, prefix caching, and quant profiles) plus a lightweight CLI previewer that computes estimated unit economics for a candidate template. Changes are intentionally conservative: defaults are suggested but not auto-applied; rollout helpers are included for canarying. Summary of changes: new econ decision graph engine, CLI "rwctl cost preview", templates for batch/cache/quant, telemetry hooks for economic impact simulation, unit tests and perf smoke harness. Why this differs from prior autosuggesters: instead of a monolithic heuristic, the decision graph composes independent decision nodes (latency SLO, token distribution, cold-start ratio, model quantizability) and performs forward simulation with cost and SLA scoring to produce ranked templates and an explainable reason string. Checklist: - [x] engine implementation and tests - [x] CLI previewer + YAML template format - [x] integration with telemetry replay harness - [x] docs and rollout guide - [x] perf smoke on unit-econ simulator - [x] manual review and approvals How to validate locally: 1) run `make econ-smoke` to spin lightweight simulator with sample trace in examples/cost-presets/ 2) `./bin/rwctl cost preview --template examples/cost-presets/sample-config.yaml --trace examples/traces/chat_small.json` prints estimated tokens/cost/latency percentiles and recommended changes 3) run unit tests `go test ./pkg/econ -run TestDecisionGraph` Notes on rollout: configuration is gated behind a feature flag "econ.decision_graph.enabled" and the default templates are placed under config/econ/templates/*.yaml; operators must opt-in to apply them to runtime. The PR also documents a canary sequence: sample workload -> template apply to 5% route -> monitor econ.delta metric -> promote at 95th percentile pass threshold. Risks and mitigations: risk of over-aggressive batching harming tail latency. Mitigation: every template includes a conservative latency cap and a server-side per-route emergency throttle that will revert to previous policy when observed p99 > configured cap. Related work: builds on telemetry replay infra added in ENG-3311 and quant profile scaffolding from ENG-4120.
Miguel Torres: Could we add a simple end-to-end regression that runs a 1k request trace to ensure no regression in p99?

Motivation: production SREs see alert noise from occasional short-lived latency spikes that originate in different stages of the inference pipeline (gateway queuing, runtime batching, kernel stalls). Existing per-route percentiles conflate stage-level behavior and cause noisy paging. This PR introduces a compact cross-stage 'latency fingerprinter' that emits a small per-invocation signature describing relative stage contributions and a 'quiet-window alert attenuator' that reduces alert weight during controlled low-volume windows. Design summary: 1) Fingerprinter: lightweight sampler attached to the invocation lifecycle that records per-stage token-timing buckets (gateway, auth, routing, runtime-prep, runtime-exec, postprocess) and encodes them into a fixed-length base64 signature and numeric vector for rollups. The implementation uses reservoir sampling to cap overhead and amortized histogram buckets for compactness. 2) Quiet-window attenuator: a policy layer in the alerting pipeline that detects scheduled or observed low-volume periods (customer deployments, maintenance windows, regional off-hours) and temporarily increases alert thresholds and groups alerts by fingerprint similarity to avoid duplicate paging. 3) Backwards compatibility: emits new metrics and trace attributes but preserves existing spans and alerts until rollout is gated. Checklist: - [x] implement fingerprinter and proto for telemetry - [x] expose new metrics via prometheus/metrics-exporter - [x] add trace enrichment hooks and OTEL attribute mapping - [x] implement quiet-window attenuation policy with feature flag - [x] end-to-end tests + staging canary - [x] docs + runbook updates Impact and rollout: default-off feature flag, feature gated by env var and Linear tickets. We plan a 2-week canary on a subset of customer traffic (10% of production) followed by gradual ramp. The change reduces alert churn for low-volume windows and provides a new dimension for SRE to group similar invocations during triage. Observability UX: console change adds a compact fingerprint column to invocation tables and a new 'fingerprint rollup' dashboard with heatmap and top contributing stages. No customer-facing API changes.
Ravi: Can we bound the extra memory/cpu per worker? Reply (Maya): reservoir sampler caps to 256 samples per-second and we track only 6 stage buckets; measured <1% mem and CPU on p3-medium in staging. Sofia: How does grouping interact with existing alert dedup? Reply: Attenuator augments dedup by adding a fingerprint similarity key (Hamming distance on bitvector) and only suppresses if similarity > 0.85 and volume is low. Liam: Add a feature-flag and rollout doc. Reply: done, added env var REDWOOD_OBS_FINGERPRINT and rollout steps in docs/observability/fingerprint.md. CI: initial run had one flaky integration failing on trace-sampler; rerun passed and full e2e suite green.
Adds a compact per-invocation cross-stage latency fingerprint and a quiet-window alert attenuator that groups similar invocations to reduce alert noise during low-volume windows. Feature is gated by feature flag and rolled out via canary.
unit tests for fingerprinter buckets and reservoir sampler; integration tests for metrics export + OTEL enrichment; e2e canary run against staging with 48h of synthetic and real traffic; smoke tests on console UI column rendering; alerting policy simulation to verify attenuation behaviour
Default off. Step 1: enable in staging (48h), run canary job (10% traffic) for 7 days while monitoring token-cost and latency SLOs. Step 2: enable on 25% of traffic and review alert churn metrics for 3 days. Step 3: full rollout if no regressions. Feature toggle via REDWOOD_OBS_FINGERPRINT; immediate rollback flips flag off.
Measured overhead: +0.6% CPU and <0.8% memory on p3-medium for typical traffic pattern. Metric ingestion increases cardinality slightly; export uses aggregation windows to limit high-cardinality churn.

Add Signal Preservation Matrix (SPM) to preserve minimal invocation context across async stages; New latency-attribution grok for mapping span phases to token phases; Dashboard panels and an alert-sensitivity tuner to reduce noisy SLO alerts; Migration script for telemetry index; Backwards-compatible telemetry enrichment
Context: long-running and async inference pipelines were losing small-but-critical invocation context across stage boundaries (streaming proxies, sidecars, queued workers). This caused noisy alerts, broken token-level latency attribution, and poor rollback signals during incidents. This PR introduces the Signal Preservation Matrix (SPM): a compact, TTL-bound context envelope propagated with spans/metrics/logs; and a latency-attribution grok that maps low-level span phases to token-phase buckets so we can attribute cost/latency consistently across stages. Changes include telemetry enrichment in the serving runtime, an ingestion-time marker that tags preserved signals, a small schema migration for the telemetry index to support SPM keys, three dashboard panels for SPM preservation rate / cross-stage latency-bridge / token-phase waterfall, and an interactive alert-sensitivity tuner that recommends per-route alert thresholds and noise-reduction knobs. Commits: 1) add SPM envelope and propagation hooks to runtime (propagate via headers, span tags, and metadata blobs); 2) ingest-time SPM hydratator and index migration; 3) latency-attribution grok and mapper service with unit tests; 4) dashboard json + widgets and example saved queries; 5) alert-sensitivity tuner backend + UI; 6) docs, migrations, and explainable telemetry-runbook. Impact: staging runs show a 42% reduction in duplicate/noise alerts on busy routes, end-to-end token-phase attribution accuracy improved on sampled traces (measured F1 increase from 0.74 to 0.88), and the additional ingestion CPU cost measured <1.5% at p95 under our staging traffic profile. Backwards compatibility: SPM is opt-in per-route (default off for existing customers) and falls back to current behavior if missing. Testing & CI: added unit tests for propagation and mapper logic, integration tests for enriched traces across a 3-stage async pipeline, and dashboard smoke tests. The first CI run had a lint failure (missing import in the dashboard generator) which was fixed in the second commit; e2e tests passed on the final run. Migration: add migrations/20260220_spm_migration.sql; the migration adds a small index column and a one-time backfill; migration guide included in docs/observability/spm.md. Runbook: brief incident playbook added with steps to toggle SPM per-route, run alert-sensitivity calibration, and roll back the index migration if necessary. Merge: Approved by Diego and Priya after one round of changes; squashed and merged to main. Notes: keep sampling of preserved signals low by default to limit cardinality; the alert-sensitivity tuner will suggest conservative defaults and can be gradually widened by SRE during rollout.

Motivation: We observe intermittent cost/latency spikes driven by invocation payloads that exhibit highly sparse token usage patterns (e.g., long prompts with many inert tokens or templates). Current token-level cost metrics miss structural sparsity signals that correlate with kernel occupancy and prefetch inefficiencies. This PR introduces a lightweight token_sparsity_index telemetry metric, an invocation-level token_alignment_score for trace correlation, a dashboard that surfaces cross-stage alignment heatmaps, and an alert multiplier that increases alert sensitivity for cohorts with high sparsity entropy. Scope: instrumentation changes in the runtime telemetry pipeline, exporter mappings, a new dashboard JSON, updated alerting rules, unit and integration tests, and a short runbook describing troubleshooting steps and an automated synthetic replay to validate alert behavior. Checklist: 1) Add token_sparsity_index and token_alignment_score to telemetry schema and exporter mapping. 2) Compute per-invocation sparse-token histogram and export as sparse_bucket label. 3) Add dashboard panels: sparsity distribution, crossstage alignment heatmap, kernel-occupancy correlation scatter, and cohorted alert history. 4) Add alert rule with adaptive multiplier based on cohort sparsity entropy and safety cap to avoid alert storms. 5) Feature flag telemetry.feature.token_sparsity to gate rollout. 6) Add unit tests for metric computation and CI replay test. 7) Add runbook and example query snippets to docs. Commits summary: - Add metric computation and unit tests (aisha/telemetry/sparsity) - Wire exporter label mappings and feature flag (aisha/telemetry/exporter) - Dashboard and alerting rules (aisha/observability/dashboards) - Runbook and synthetic replay harness (aisha/observability/runbooks) Changed areas: telemetry/schema.go (new metrics, label enums), telemetry/sparsity_calculator.go (core computation), exporters/prometheus_mapper.go (label mapping), observability/dashboards/token_sparsity.json (new dashboard), alerts/token_sparsity.rules.yml (new alert), docs/observability/token-sparsity.md (runbook), tests/telemetry/sparsity_test.go, integration/synthetic_replay/sparsity_replay.go. Review conversation highlights: Marco Velasquez: "Nice signal, but compute cost on hot path? Please ensure sparsity index is O(n) and bounded memory." Author: "Implemented streaming histogram with bounded buckets, added tests to assert memory usage remains constant for long sequences." Emily Zhang: "Alert multiplier looks promising but could amplify noise for low-volume tenants." Author: "Added entropy-based floor and a per-tenant minimum sample window; also feature-flagged rollout so we can A/B for selected tenants." Jonas Müller: "Please add a dashboard panel that ties kernel occupancy percentiles to sparsity buckets." Author: "Added kernel-occupancy correlation scatter and a percentile rollup panel." CI summary: initial run failed due to a flaky integration test in synthetic replay (timeout). Fixed by increasing replay timeout and adding retry logic. Subsequent CI run passed all unit, lint, and integration checks. Deployed behind feature flag and rolled out to 10% of traffic for internal tenants for two days; collected telemetry and validated alert sensitivity without increased false positives. Merge outcome: merged via squash into main after approvals from Marco and Emily. Release notes: "Add token sparsity telemetry and token alignment dashboard. New alert rule to surface sparsity-driven cost/latency regressions. Rollout behind feature flag. See docs/observability/token-sparsity.md for runbook and mitigation steps." Runbook excerpt: "When an alert fires, open the token_sparsity dashboard, filter for the tenant and time window, inspect cross-stage alignment heatmap for mismatched prefixes, run the synthetic replay harness to reproduce, and if confirmed reduce model sequence length or enable prefix warmup cache for the affected route." Testing and validation: unit tests assert correctness over synthetic token shapes including all-uniform, interleaved sparse patterns, and pathological long-template cases. Integration replay generated 5k synthetic invocations across 3 sparsity cohorts and validated that alert multiplier increased sensitivity by 2x for high-entropy cohorts while keeping baseline false positive rate <1%. Backwards compatibility: telemetry schema additions are additive and exported label names are prefixed with sparse_ to avoid collisions. Rollout plan: enable feature flag for internal tenants -> monitor false positive rate and CPU overhead -> gradually expand to 50% -> full rollout after 2 weeks if metrics stable. Notes: I intentionally kept the runtime changes minimal and added comprehensive tests and a defensive feature flag. This PR is observability-first: it provides signal, tooling, and actionable runbook to debug sparsity-related cost anomalies.

Context and goal:
We observed repeated CI flakiness and long cold-start times caused by the ad-hoc collection of shell bootstraps for language toolchains (node/rust/go/python) and a heavy, monolithic lint runner that executes all rules for every PR. This PR introduces a two-part change: (1) a small, hermetic Go-based toolchain anchoring shim that canonicalizes bootstrapping steps and reduces runtime variability; (2) a lightweight lint 'minifier' runner used in fast-feedback lanes that runs a safe subset of rules and defers expensive or batch-only checks to nightly or staged lanes.

What changed (summary):
- Add tools/toolchain/anchor (Go) and migrate existing bootstrap snippets to canonical manifests. The shim consults a simple manifest (toolchain.yaml) and exposes a uniform local cache + lease mechanism for CI runners.
- Introduce tools/lint/minifier which implements a fast rule selector: rule tags, path-aware selectors, and a deterministic dry-run mode for presubmit.
- Add a lockfile anchoring step: ci/lock-anchors/anchor-check runs on PRs that change package manifests to ensure lockfile drift is deliberate. Anchoring tries to avoid full installs by validating lockfile checksums against curated anchors for transitive sets.
- Split CI workflow: .github/workflows/presubmit-fast.yml (uses minifier & anchor-check) and .github/workflows/presubmit-full.yml (daily/merge-only heavy runner).
- Migrate a set of existing bootstraps (ci/scripts/bootstrap-*.sh) to the new Go shim and remove duplicated logic.

Why this approach:
- Reduce presubmit latency by ~35-50% for common PRs via targeted linting and cache-friendly bootstraps.
- Reduce CI flakiness from environment drift by centralizing the bootstrap logic and blessable anchors.
- Make it easier to reason about which rules run in fast lanes and which run later (fewer noisy failures).

Checklist:
- [x] Add Go shim and minimal unit tests for manifest parsing
- [x] Implement minifier with path-aware rule selection and unit tests
- [x] Wire fast presubmit to minifier and anchor-check
- [x] Migrate 7 bootstrap scripts to toolchain anchor manifests
- [x] Update docs/ci/toolchain.md and docs/ci/lint-minifier.md
- [x] Run bench-scripts/presubmit-latency to validate improvement

Migration notes and rollback plan:
- New workflows default to opt-in on a subset of repos. Rollback involves re-enabling legacy bootstrap scripts (kept in tools/legacy-bootstraps) and reverting the workflow YAML. Anchor manifests are additive and safe to remove if rollback is required.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Anchor-check false positives when lockfile changes are legitimate (e.g., pinned transitive updates). Mitigation: anchor-check emits a clear remediation hint and a bypass label flow for trusted maintainers; it will not block merges by default until opt-in is complete.
- Risk: Minifier misses an important lint rule required for correctness. Mitigation: maintain a small required-rule tagset that always runs in fast lane; other rules are promoted via a staged rollout and telemetry.

Notes for reviewers:
- Focus on toolchain/anchor correctness and the deterministic nature of the lease cache. The Go shim is intentionally small; avoid bikeshedding the lease implementation unless correctness gaps are evident.
