Context: We observed fast fractional decommits (capacity reclamation/spot churn) causing synchronized quota chops that produced transient throughput and latency SLO regressions for mid-tier tenants. This PR implements a tenant-aligned commit rescheduler plus a proactive erosion guard to make decommits gradual, reduce KV-cache thrash, and preserve downstream SLAs. Motivation: avoid immediate, simultaneous capacity reductions across pools and instead apply tenant-scoped, observable, reversible changes. High-level changes: 1) Commit Rescheduler (controller): batches commit/delta events per tenant and applies them in an idempotent transactional window; enforces per-tenant commit pace and adds randomized jitter to avoid cross-tenant sync. 2) Transactional Apply Path: lightweight two-phase apply for reservation changes (prepare -> validate -> commit) with rollback hooks on transient failures (e.g., warm pool shortfall). 3) Proactive Erosion Guard: converts immediate fractional decommits into a decayed ramp-down using exponential decay plus a minimum hold window to prevent abrupt SLA impact. 4) Telemetry & Auditing: new metrics and audit events (tenant_commit_applied, tenant_commit_deferred, erosion_guard_triggered) and an SLI probe for per-tenant decommit latency. 5) Tests & scenarios: integration test simulates spot preemptions across two zones and asserts <=2% 95th percentile latency regression for protected tenants. Checklist: [x] design doc ENG-3245 linked; [x] controller + reconciliation implemented; [x] transactional apply + rollback; [x] erosion guard algorithm + knobs; [x] telemetry + dashboards; [x] unit + integration tests; [x] docs and helm samples. Commits summary: feat(rescheduler): tenant commit rescheduler and reconciliation window; feat(apply): transactional reservation apply API and rollback helpers; feat(erosion): proactive erosion guard with decay policy; feat(metrics): tenant_commit_* metrics and audit events; test(e2e): simulated-spot-decommit scenario; infra: helm values and console flags for rescheduler. Config knobs (defaults): rescheduler.window_ms=2000; rescheduler.max_batch_per_window=5; rescheduler.jitter_ms=150; erosion.decay_half_life_s=120; erosion.min_hold_s=30. Files touched (high-level): services/autoscaler/controller/rescheduler.go (new); services/autoscaler/apply/transactional_apply.go (new); services/autoscaler/erosion/guard.go (new); pkg/telemetry/metrics.go (metrics additions); web/console/src/features/dedicated/commit-controls.tsx (UI toggles); helm/redwood/values.dedicated.yaml (config knobs); test/e2e/spot_decommit_sim_test.go (integration); test/unit/rescheduler_test.go (unit coverage). Small loop excerpt: for each tenant in pendingQueue { batch := drainBatch(tenant, cfg.maxBatch); if shouldApply(batch) { applyTx(ctx, batch); } else { deferWithJitter(tenant, cfg.jitterMs); } } Metrics added: tenant_commit_attempt_total (counter), tenant_commit_applied_total (counter), tenant_commit_deferred_total (counter), erosion_guard_events_total (counter), tenant_decommit_latency_ms (histogram). Backwards compatibility: transactional apply is opt-in via feature flag "enableTransactionalApply" and defaulted on for Dedicated clusters after a soft rollout. Review conversation (abridged): Evan Brooks: "Add audit log entry for every deferred commit and per-tenant deferred counters"; Maya Patel: "Added tenant_commit_deferred_total and audit event; surfaced deferred_window_count metric"; Samira Liu: "Concerned about rescheduler queue memory during bursts"; Maya Patel: "Per-tenant queue length limited to 100 with eviction and tombstone audit events; tests added"; Carlos Ortega: "CI flake on e2e timing, suggest looser timing assertion"; Maya Patel: "Adjusted e2e tolerance to +/-200ms and reran CI". CI summary: Build: passed; Unit tests: passed (coverage +0.6%); Integration/e2e: initially flaky then passed on rerun; Lint: passed; Helm/chart check: passed. Merge outcome: Merged via squash on 2025-02-18 by Samira Liu. Rollout plan: canary to 10% Dedicated clusters for 48h (feature flag off by default, enable via console toggle in canary); monitor tenant_commit_deferred_total and tenant_decommit_latency_ms; rollback if >3% increase in protected-tenant 95th latency; ramp to 100% over 7 days if stable. Notes: This moves immediate synchronous quota cuts to an intention-first, tenant-scoped commit cadence that is observable and reversible, reducing synchronized KV cache invalidation and spikey traffic patterns at the cost of small eventuality. Related work: ENG-3245 design doc, PR 31102 (utilization metrics), PR 33457 (autoscaler signal smoothing). Backports: will prepare a backport to release/2025.02 if QA agrees.
Introduce commit rescheduler and proactive erosion guard to smooth decommits and reduce tenant-facing SLO violations during capacity churn.

Motivation: Customers running production LLM inference need a way to run targeted, debuggable canaries that: 1) allow engineers to sample and inspect shadow traffic without affecting production telemetry; 2) keep an auditable trail for regulatory/compliance review; and 3) trigger deterministic, explainable rollbacks when defined safety gates breach. This PR introduces a declarative 'LiveDebug Canary' feature that wires into the existing rollout runtime and operator with minimal disruption.

What this PR does (single-string sectioned description): Adds a declarative rollout spec (api/v1/rollout_livedebug.yaml) that supports: debug_sample_rate, debug_storage (audit KMS-backed S3), differential-metrics (compare shadow->live output for drift), and rollback_rules (thresholds and chained actions). Implements a shadow-decoupling layer in the router so debug-shadow requests are routed to an isolated consumer pipeline that: a) persists full inputs/outputs + metadata to secure audit storage; b) exposes a debug-stream endpoint for engineers (RBAC guarded) to inspect sampled traces without polluting production logs; c) optionally sends sanitized traces to the telemetry cluster for aggregated metrics. Adds a safety-policy engine that evaluates multiple signal inputs (latency, token-error-rate, semantic-drift-score) against configured gates and can execute the declarative rollback-playbook (graceful drain, traffic-rewind, model-swap, and incident annotation).

Checklist: [x] API schema and CRD for rollout_livedebug [x] Router and shadow-decoupling implementation [x] Auditable storage pipeline + KMS integration (opt-in) [x] Safety policy evaluator with unit tests [x] End-to-end integration tests that simulate regressions and auto-rollback [x] Console docs + runbook page + example Linear ticket template [x] Perf smoke to verify baseline tail latency impact < 1%

High-level implementation notes: - New CRD: rollout_livedebug.v1 (api/v1/rollout_livedebug.yaml) mirrors staged-rollout fields but with debug-specific knobs. - Router change: added a small policy gate (router/decoupled_shadow.go) that marks sampled debug requests and forwards them to the debug pipeline; normal shadow mirroring remains unchanged unless decoupling enabled. - Safety engine: policy/evaluator.go takes time-windowed signals (PromCounter, latency histogram, embedding drift) and produces a deterministic decision with a signed audit event for every rollback decision. - Auditable playbook: playbooks/rollback_playbook.go encodes the chain of actions; each step emits an immutable audit entry and link to the incident ticket. - Console and docs: docs/rollouts/livedebug.md and console UI wiring for 'Inspect debug stream' (RBAC: rollout.debug.view).

Why unique: Existing shadow/canary flows at Redwood mirror requests into production paths. LiveDebug intentionally separates sampled debug traffic into a locked-down path with stronger auditing and explicit rollback bindings — enabling safe live debugging for regulated customers and SRE teams.

Risks and mitigation: - Performance: router adds ~0.5ms median overhead when decoupling enabled; fallback path keeps previous behavior. Mitigated by opt-in and sampling default 0.1%. - Storage cost: audited traces can be large; rollup policy compresses traces older than 7 days and supports redaction. - Security: audit storage encrypted with customer-provided KMS when requested and access controlled via console RBAC.

Testing notes: e2e harness simulates a semantic regression by applying synthetic perturbations to responses; the safety engine triggers rollback when semantic-drift-score > 0.22 and latency p95 increases > 25%. Integration test artifacts are added under test/e2e/livedebug.

Related work: builds on the staged-rollout primitives (ENG-1452) and the telemetry drift detectors that landed in ENG-2099. For customers with on-prem Private deployments, this feature is gated behind an operator flag and validated in redwood-private-installer smoke runs.

How to review: focus on the policy/evaluator deterministic behavior, router decoupling correctness, and the audit trail immutability. The UI wiring is small and can be reviewed in a separate UX PR if needed.

Links: Design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1452/design-livedebug-canary; Runbook draft: docs/runbooks/livedebug-rollbacks.md
Ethan Moore: Please confirm evaluator is deterministic across restarts and that the signed decision contains the full input signature (approved after small change)
Priya Shah: Added signed decision payload and persisted decision snapshot to audit store; updated tests to assert reproducibility
Lina Kovacs: Small nits on docs and API naming; requested a follow-up to split UI PR - addressed in docs commit
Marta Ruiz: Verified KMS integration and that the operator flag gating works in private smoke; approved

payload.title: Declarative LiveDebug Canary with Auditable Rollback Playbook and Shadow Decoupling

Motivation: Our repository accumulated a number of near-duplicate CI workflows (lint/test/build/release) that drifted independently. This increases maintenance cost, slows adding new checks, and causes subtle differences between repos and components. This PR centralizes common CI job definitions into a small set of reusable workflow templates under .github/workflow-templates/, migrates existing workflows to call those templates, and provides a one-shot migration script and docs to finish the transition. Key changes: 1) New reusable templates: build.yaml, lint.yaml, test.yaml, release.yaml. Templates capture standardized caching, matrix axes, and logging/annotations (annotations support for test failures). 2) Migration: added scripts/ci/migrate_workflows.sh that rewrites existing .github/workflows/* to reference templates and annotates deprecated files with a deprecation header. Script is idempotent and prints a migration report. 3) Dependency hygiene: bumped several widely-used GH actions and pinned to stable minor versions (actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-node@v4, actions/cache@v4). 4) Repo hygiene: remove duplicated job definitions from 9 workflows and keep a thin shim for any special-case jobs. 5) Observability: added lightweight CI metrics emission helper (scripts/ci/emit_ci_metrics.py) called by templates to record duration and cache hit/miss tags (opt-in). 6) Docs: docs/ci/README.md describes how templates work, how to call them from component-level workflows, and a migration checklist for maintainers. Migration notes & compatibility: - The templates are intentionally conservative: default matrix sizes and concurrency limits mirror current behavior to avoid instant resource spikes. - Workflows that rely on specialized ephemeral runners or privileged steps (e.g., on-prem installer tests) are left as shims, with comments on how to extend templates. - Breaking changes: none by default; component workflows keep the same triggers after migration. For teams that had bespoke caching steps, the migration script leaves a marked TODO block so maintainers can reconcile. Testing & rollout: - Ran migration across core packages (redwood/, redwood-sdk-python/, redwood-examples/) in a dry-run; validated lint and unit job exit codes and timing. - Ran full CI with templates on redwood core; observed a 7% average improvement in queue/wait time due to fewer duplicated job preparation steps. - Added a short-lived deprecation job that runs for two weeks after merge and prints a pointer to the migration guide. Backwards compatibility guard: templates include a feature-flag input (enable_experimental_caching) to gate experimental cache policy changes. Follow-ups: - Schedule a short RFC/office-hours for integrators to discuss template knobs (ENG-1302). - Add an automated bot to propose migration PRs across auxiliary repos (follow-up ticket ENG-1310). Motivation: SDKs have continued to drift in how they choose and refresh credentials and in how pull-style streaming APIs are consumed by application code. This PR introduces a compact, language-agnostic token router plus a tiny pullstream shim to bring ergonomics and parity across Python/TypeScript/Go without forcing large surface API changes. What this does: (1) adds a lightweight TokenRouter abstraction that centralizes credential selection logic, precedence rules, and a small lease/refresh hint API so SDKs can implement identical fallback behavior and telemetry hooks; (2) introduces PullstreamShim helpers for each SDK to normalize async/pull streaming semantics and provide a simple resume/cancel contract for callers; (3) updates the SDKs to use the router/shim in the default client path with a feature flag to preserve backwards compatibility during rollout; (4) includes tests, end-to-end smoke harness updates, and example snippets for each language; (5) bumps package versions: python->0.18.0, typescript->1.12.0, go->1.8.3. Backwards compatibility: router is additive and initially off behind feature flag "sdk.token_router_v1"; existing credential env vars and explicit credential objects continue to work. Migration notes: clients can opt-in by setting feature flag or by passing TokenRouter to Client() constructors; applications using bespoke streaming helpers will see minimal API differences and are provided an adapter in sdk/examples/compat. Tests & CI: added unit tests for router precedence and simulated lease expiry, integration test that spins up a token mock and validates cross-language resume behavior. Telemetry: emits lightweight metric labels (sdk.token_selection, sdk.stream_resume_reason) and logs on refresh failures. Release notes: see release_notes field. Linked work: ENG-1987 standardize client-side credential precedence; ENG-2034 streaming ergonomics parity. Checklist: ensure feature flag rollout coordinated with server-side token-lease endpoints, confirm package registry artifacts for three SDKs, announce migration in SDK changelogs and upgrade guide.
Luis Ortega: Nice consolidation. Two asks: a) can we avoid exposing lease internals in public headers and b) add a short changelog snippet explaining fallback semantics?
Maya Chen: Responded that lease hint is intentionally minimal (expiry + approx ttl) and we've kept it out of public surface except in TokenRouterHint struct which is marked experimental; added changelog blurb in docs/ and extra unit test for precedence.
Priya Kapoor: CI flakiness on Go integration initially; test harness missed context cancellation path. Please add context timeouts to the integration harness.
Maya Chen: Added context timeouts and re-ran CI. Go integration stabilized on the second run.
Samir Patel: Approved after verifying telemetry labels and that feature flag gating is correct for existing clients. Left one minor nit inline about a log message level.
Add TokenRouter abstraction and PullstreamShim to unify credential selection and pull-style streaming across SDKs. Feature-gated rollout; non-breaking by default. Bumped versions: python 0.18.0, typescript 1.12.0, go 1.8.3. Telemetry: sdk.token_selection and sdk.stream_resume_reason labels added. See docs/sdk/token-router-and-pullstream.md for migration details.

Context: Customers reported intermittent malformed JSON being emitted from the SSE endpoint when streams are under bursty load and when tool/function call handoffs occur. Root causes identified: (1) jitter in chunk boundary alignment that produced half-escaped UTF-8 sequences across SSE events, (2) race between the streaming flusher and the fncall sentinel insertion which could reorder sentinel tokens relative to trailing delimiters, and (3) OpenAI-compat adapter rebuffering that coalesced unrelated events into a single SSE data frame. Motivation: fix hard-to-reproduce partial-JSON cases without regressing latency or throughput. Summary of changes: 1) Introduce a lightweight chunk anchoring metadata byte (anchor flag) in the stream encoder so that receivers can detect when a chunk boundary is semantically safe to reemit a delimiter; this avoids the heuristics that previously caused delimiter duplication or loss. 2) Add a JSON seam repair step in the SSE reassembler that detects incomplete UTF-8/JSON spans at the chunk edge and emits a deterministic continuation marker ("__REDWOOD_JSON_SEAM__") only when necessary; the OpenAI compatibility layer rewrites these markers to a safe no-op event for downstream SDKs. 3) Tighten the fncall handshake: we now reserve a one-byte fence and apply ordered publish semantics so function-call sentinel insertion wins the race against the flusher without introducing extra buffering. 4) Reduce coalescing in the OpenAI adapter: switch from block-coalesce to affinity-based coalesce so events from different logical streams are not merged in the same SSE data block. 5) Add comprehensive unit + fuzz tests that simulate chunk splits at UTF-8 and JSON token boundaries and end-to-end integration tests using the openai-compat shim. Migration & compatibility: default behavior is backward-compatible; the chunk anchoring flag is opt-in for private deployments via config sse.chunk_anchor=true and is enabled for Hosted rollout after a staged canary. OpenAI-compat consumers see no breaking behavior: the repair marker is transformed to an internal no-op event. Checklist: - [x] Implement chunk anchor encoding/decoding - [x] Implement JSON seam repair and seam-to-noop mapping in openai-compat - [x] Tighten fncall handshake and add ordered publish path - [x] Swap coalescing strategy in openai adapter - [x] Add unit/fuzz/integration tests - [x] Update streaming docs and SDK guidance - [x] Run canary and smoke test on dedicated cluster Tests & validation: unit tests cover 92% of the new streaming module, fuzz tests run 50k iterations covering splits on multi-byte UTF-8 and nested JSON tokens, integration test uses local harness to validate toolcall ordering under 1000 concurrent streams. Linked issues: SUP-1142 (customer incident), ENG-8423 (streaming robustness epic).
Liam Chen: Can you explain why we need a marker instead of attempting to reassemble at the consumer? Author: The marker is a cheap sentinel that avoids repeated expensive reassembly attempts under backpressure and is only emitted when a true seam is detected.
Marceline Duarte: The fence byte sounds risky for portability across proxies. Author: We keep it as an internal in-band flag, encoded as a low-entropy prefix in the chunk header; adapters that can't parse it will ignore and fall back to heuristics (backwards-compatible).
Priya Nair: Please add an observability metric for seam events. Author: Added metric streaming.seam_repaired_count and dashboard tile in streaming ops bar. Reviewers: LGTM after tests pass.
Fixes a rare class of malformed partial-JSON responses emitted by the SSE streaming endpoint under bursty load and function-call handoffs. Adds chunk anchoring to improve delimiter stability and a deterministic seam repair path. Backwards-compatible; opt-in via sse.chunk_anchor config for private deployments. Recommended for all Hosted users once canary completes.
Rollout plan: enable in a 5% hosted canary for 48 hours, monitor streaming.seam_repaired_count and error.rate, then 25% for 24h, then full rollout. For Dedicated/Private, enable via config or coordinate upgrade with infra team. Observability: new metrics and a Grafana dashboard tile were added (streaming.seam_repaired_count, streaming.chunk_anchor_accepted).

payload.body:
Motivation: Short interactive requests (few-keystroke completions) suffer from prefill-decode handoff overhead when the prefill window is small and decode is idle. The runtime spends GPU cycles priming KV cache and scheduling tiny kernel launches that often block decode progress and increase tail latency under load. This PR implements a runtime coordinator that adaptively 'skips' trivial prefill windows and tightens the interstage handshake to let decode proceed opportunistically when prefills would provide marginal benefit.

What this PR does (single-line summary): Adds an adaptive Prefill Gap Skipper, a stage Coordinator for handshake reductions, scheduler hints for kernel selection, and a KV-warmup policy to avoid redundant priming on micro-prefills.

Key components and files touched: src/serve/pipeline/handshake.rs - new StageCoordinator and handshake state machine; runtime/scheduler/prefill_gap_skipper.cpp - skipper logic and backoff estimator; runtime/kernel/kernel_hints.h - new hint flags used by kernel selector; runtime/kv/kv_warmup_policy.cc - conservative warmup sampler and TTL; tests/bench/prefill_handshake_bench.py - microbench harness with synthetic short/query traces; docs/optimizations/prefill-gap-skipper.md - design doc and tuning knobs.

Commits (high level):
- Add Prefill Gap Skipper and basic estimator (S. Patel)
- Wire StageCoordinator into pipeline handshake and expose handshake_time budget (D. Kim)
- Add kernel hints and scheduler integration (M. Silva)
- KV warmup sampler and microbench harness (S. Patel)
- Unit tests and perf baselines, bench fixes (O. Haddad)

Implementation notes: The Prefill Gap Skipper observes the recent sequence-length histogram and the observed decode-ready latency; it computes an expected utility for a prefill window using a simple cost model: expected token savings vs prefill latency and kernel startup overhead. When expected utility < threshold the skipper defers prefill and increments a short-gap counter which is used by the StageCoordinator to relax handshake barriers for the next decode stage. The StageCoordinator reduces the handshake's strictness (allowing decode to pull KV entries directly or proceed with partial KV warming) when the pipeline is dominated by low-utility prefills.

KV warmup policy: Instead of aggressive priming on every prefill, we now sample a subset of recent keys based on sequence overlap heuristics and maintain a lightweight TTL on cache entries to avoid repeated synchronous loads. This reduces device memory churn and copy overhead on prefill bursts. The policy is conservative by default with a config flag to be more aggressive for specialized workloads.

Scheduler and kernel hints: Prefill Gap Skipper emits a kernel_hint (SKIP_SMALL_PREFILL) when skipping. The scheduler respects this hint to avoid spinning up small decode-optimized kernels that would otherwise be chosen for tiny prefill windows. We also added a 'fast-path' microkernel for decode that can run with partial KV availability, enabling earlier token emission while background warmup continues.

Benchmarks: Microbench harness was run on a 4xA100 cluster (simulated multi-tenant load). Representative results (median of 10 runs, synthetic short-query trace - mean tokens/request ~ 12):
- Baseline (main): p50=18ms, p95=62ms, tail(99)=210ms
- This PR: p50=16.5ms (-8%), p95=54ms (-13%), tail(99)=168ms (-20%)
Under high concurrency (500 concurrent streams) the number of small kernel launches reduced by ~42% and total GPU cycles used for prefill dropped ~28%.

Safety and compatibility: All new features are gated behind runtime flags and config knobs: ENABLE_PREFILL_GAP_SKIPPER (default: true in this PR for validation), PREFILL_UTILITY_THRESHOLD (float), KV_WARMUP_SAMPLING_RATE. We made sure the default behavior preserves semantic correctness: decode correctness is unchanged — we only opportunistically delay prefill when utility is low and allow decode to proceed with partial KV in the microkernel path.

Tests: Added unit tests for handshake transitions and skipper estimator edge cases, and integration bench tests that assert no correctness regression on greedy/beam decoding. The bench harness includes regression detection (assert p95 does not increase >5% vs baseline) and was used locally; CI runs the integration bench in a small emulation mode.

Review timeline and conversation summary:
- Daniel Kim (reviewer): "Nice design — can you clarify how the utility threshold is auto-tuned? Concern about oscillation when load varies rapidly."
- Sofia (author): "Threshold is currently static; added a note to follow-up to add an EWMA-based auto-tuner. For stability we clamp step changes; also StageCoordinator tracks short-gap counters to avoid flip-flopping."
- Marta Silva: "Kernel hinting looks good. Please make sure default kernel selection still wins for long-prefill workloads."
- Sofia: "Added unit test to ensure long prefills still pick the heavy prefill kernels; preserved existing kernel selector priority when hint absent."
- Omar Haddad: "KV warmup TTL tuning needs docs; observed a case where overly-aggressive TTL eviction increased loads."
- Sofia: "Added doc and conservative defaults; also included a flag to disable TTL for customers who want max cache retention."

CI and rollout: CI passed all unit and integration checks; a single flaky bench run was observed in one job (bench run timeout) and was re-run successfully. Merge method: squash merge. Post-merge, we deployed the feature to canary fleet with a 10% traffic ramp and monitored latency, cache hit-rate, and kernel launch counts for 48h. Canary telemetry matched local benchmarks and showed stable behavior.

Follow-ups (future work):
- Add an EWMA auto-tuner for PREFILL_UTILITY_THRESHOLD (ENG-1989)
- Evaluate adaptive sampling for KV warmup under multi-tenant variance
- Surface a console metric for skipped-prefill-rate and handshake-relax events for easier observability

Related work: contrasts with staged-prefill approaches that aggressively overlap prefill+decode; instead this change focuses on avoiding low-utility prefill work and enabling decode progress when it's the better path. See design doc at docs/optimizations/prefill-gap-skipper.md and Linear ticket ENG-1743 for planning notes.

Merge notes: Squashed commits. No database or public API changes. Feature is opt-in via flags and can be disabled remotely if any customer regression is observed.

Files changed (high level):
- src/serve/pipeline/handshake.rs (+248 -34)
- runtime/scheduler/prefill_gap_skipper.cpp (+312 -12)
- runtime/kv/kv_warmup_policy.cc (+142 -26)
- runtime/kernel/kernel_hints.h (+18 -0)
- tests/bench/prefill_handshake_bench.py (+96 -0)
- docs/optimizations/prefill-gap-skipper.md (+82 -0)
- tests/unit/handshake_tests.rs (+44 -122)

If merged, deploy plan: graduate from canary (10% -> 40% -> 100%) over 6 hours per step with rollback on p95 regress >5% or cache hit-rate drop >7% for critical workloads.

Signed-off-by: Sofia Patel

Introduce an adaptive prefill skipper that reduces needless short-window prefill work and a tightened interstage handshake that reduces backpressure between prefill and decode. Expected latency improvement for short queries: 8-15% p95; tail improvement under high-concurrency: ~20%.
payload.title: Adaptive Prefill Gap Skipper and Interstage Handshake Optimizer

payload.body:
Context: During staging rehearsal for regional failover automation, the failover controller crashed with a nil pointer dereference when one of the signal streams (capacity/headroom) was absent for a subset of regions/routes. This can happen during partial outages of the signal publisher, misconfigured routing configs in staging, or when a region is newly added and the signal pipeline hasn’t started publishing yet. The controller should degrade safely (no action + clear evidence) rather than crash-loop.

What changed: 1) Make signal reads total: convert all signal fetch paths in the controller to return an explicit tri-state (present/absent/stale) instead of a nil map/struct. Missing signals no longer cause an NPE. 2) Deterministic behavior on missing inputs: if a signal required for corroboration (per ADR-042) is missing, the controller marks the evaluation as `insufficient_evidence` and produces a no-op plan; we do not flip policies based on partial evidence. If the missing signal is non-authoritative for the decision path, we proceed but record `missing_signal_sources` on the evaluation log/audit event. 3) Observability: add `failover_controller_missing_signal_total{signal=<name>,region=<region>}` counter and emit a structured log + audit event annotation when a required stream is missing for >2 evaluation intervals. 4) Safety: add a short circuit to avoid writing partial plans when evaluation errors occur; controller returns a stable empty plan and increments `failover_controller_eval_errors_total`.

Tests: Adds a regression test that reproduces the panic (signal store returns absent for a configured signal). Adds table-driven tests for the new evaluation contract (required vs optional signals) and verifies the controller produces a no-op plan and emits the missing-signal metric/log.

Impact/Risk: Low functional risk (hotfix + behavior only affects missing-signal cases). This reduces the chance of controller crash-loop during impairment, and avoids acting on incomplete evidence.

Rollout: Merge to main and deploy to staging immediately. After 30 minutes of stable evaluations (no panic, expected metric increments only), promote to production via standard controller rollout (helm chart values unchanged; behavior is code-only). On-call notes included below.
Miles Thornton (review): Can we confirm we never flip when a required corroboration signal is missing? I want this to be strictly safer than before.
Benji Okafor (author): Yes. `required=true` signals now gate the evaluation: we return `insufficient_evidence` and emit a no-op plan. Added test `TestEvaluator_MissingRequiredSignal_NoOpPlan`.
Jordan Lee (review): Please ensure this doesn't introduce hidden oscillation if signals flap between absent/present. Do we have any dampening on the 'missing required signal' state itself?
Benji Okafor (author): We don't change routing when absent; the controller keeps existing policy state. For noise, we only alert/annotate after >2 consecutive intervals missing (see `missingSignalHoldDown=2`).
Allison Grant (review): Metric label cardinality: please avoid route/model labels. Region + signal is fine. Also add log field listing which sources were missing.
Benji Okafor (author): Updated metric to only include {signal, region}. Added `missing_signal_sources` array in structured logs (no route/model).
Rafael Mendes (review): Add a note in rollout steps for on-call: what to look for in dashboards and how to verify no panic-loop.
Benji Okafor (author): Added rollout notes + suggested queries to the PR description and troubleshooting doc.
Staging: Deploy immediately after merge. Verify `failover-controller` pod restarts == 0 and `failover_controller_eval_errors_total` remains flat. If testing missing-signal behavior, expect `failover_controller_missing_signal_total{signal="capacity_headroom"}` to increment for the affected region(s), and controller should keep emitting no-op plans (no policy writes). Production: Standard rolling deploy. No feature flags required. If `missing_signal_total` spikes in prod, treat as signal pipeline issue (not routing); do not attempt manual failover based on incomplete evidence—follow runbook troubleshooting section 'Missing signal streams'.
Reliability: Failover controller no longer crash-loops when a signal stream is missing; missing required corroboration signals result in safe no-op decisions with improved metrics/logging for triage.
payload.title: Hotfix: prevent failover controller NPE when a signal stream is missing

Adds OpenAI compatibility shim for deterministic tool selection during streaming and a structured-output normalizer; non-breaking, opt-in via config flag openai.compat.tool_hinting
Summary: This PR adds a lightweight 'tool hint' encoder to the OpenAI compatibility adapter and a 'fragment guard' layer that prevents mid-stream tool_choice flips when the model emits fragmented function/tool call messages; Motivation: We observed nondeterministic tool selection when large responses were streamed in fragments; downstream invocation systems would receive partial evidence and flip the chosen tool mid-stream causing duplicate tool invocations or aborted handoffs; Goal is to stabilize tool_choice semantics without changing the OpenAI-compatible API surface; Changes: 1) tool hint encoder: encodes deterministic, order-preserving per-tool hints into the stream as opaque, short provenance tokens (header: x-rw-tool-hint) that the invoke layer uses to lock the selected tool for the lifetime of a response; 2) fragment guard: coalesces contiguous tool-invoke fragments and defers decision until fragment boundary or signature-confidence threshold; 3) schema normalizer: aligns tool parameter schemas from external registries to the OpenAI function schema (type coercions, required->optional mapping, canonical name aliases); 4) tie-break policy: deterministic score+id tiebreak to avoid nondeterminism when scores are near-equal; 5) telemetry: new metrics rw.compat.tool_choice.locked_count and rw.compat.fragment_coalesce_rate; 6) opt-in config: openai.compat.tool_hinting (default false for now) and rollout plan; 7) docs and SDK: TS + Python compat tests and example; 8) e2e test harness that simulates fragmented streams and validates at-most-once tool handoff; Backwards compatibility: no API schema changes; behavior is gated by config and flag rollout for Dedicated/Private; Risk: subtle differences when models already rely on token-level heuristics; mitigation: gradual rollout and A/B canary; Why unique: instead of changing model scoring we add a streaming-level coordination primitive that is transparent to most callers; Technical notes: the tool hint tokens are HMAC'd short strings carrying (tool_id, seq, partial_hash) and are stripped before user-facing output; they are applied only in internal streaming frames; The fragment guard uses a small state machine per-stream to coalesce fragments up to 512 tokens or until an explicit end_of_function marker is observed; This avoids re-parsing partial JSON fragments mid-stream; See commit list and file changes below for implementation detail and tests.
Ivan Petrov: 'Conceptually this looks good; worried about HMAC key rotation and leak risk. Please document KMS integration and ensure hints are not logged.' || Aditi Shah (author): 'Ack. Added KMS/HSM note to docs and redacted logging for hint tokens; hints are stored only in memory and never emitted to logs. See docs/compat/rollout-plan.md.' || Lena Gomez: 'Can we avoid the extra header and instead piggyback on existing invoke metadata? Headers are easier to miss in the proxy.' || Aditi Shah: 'We considered piggybacking; header chosen for minimal change to existing wire protocols and to keep hint opaque to model clients. Added comment in router to allow future switch to metadata field.' || Samir Kaur: 'Tests are comprehensive but there is a flaky case when coalescing large fragments; we should add a 2s fail-safe timer to avoid head-of-line blocking.' || Aditi Shah: 'Added timeout to fragment_guard and a unit test for timer expiry; reran flaky suite.' || Ivan Petrov: 'Approving pending docs and CI green.' || CI bot: 'All checks passed after rerun.'
Rollout: enable openai.compat.tool_hinting=true in Canaries (5% traffic) for 48h, monitor rw.compat.fragment_coalesce_rate and tool_choice.deviation. If any increase in tool mis-invocations, revert via feature flag. Support: linked SUP-4128 for customer repro that motivated this change.
unit tests added for fragment coalescing and tie-break policy
e2e harness validates at-most-once handoff under fragmentation
docs updated with config and KMS guidance
canary + rollback steps defined
payload.title: Introduce OpenAI-compat tool hint encoder and fragment guard to stabilize tool selection across streams

payload.body:
Motivation: Our continuous perf canary pipeline is sensitive to short, high-magnitude bursts and noisy client-side variance which produce false-positive regressions and unnecessary rollbacks. This PR introduces a windowed signal denoiser and a tiered adaptive failover policy to reduce noise-induced alerts while preserving sensitivity to sustained regressions.

What this PR does: Implements a Tukey-weighted sliding-window denoiser with robust median/IQR trimming, integrates a cross-cohort smoothing layer for low-traffic tenants, and adds a staged failover controller that performs: 1) soft-fallback to a cheaper model variant or cached responses, 2) traffic corking at cohort-level, and 3) last-resort rollback. The controller includes a 'staged-escape' detector that disables denoising if smoothed signals decorrelate from raw signal for N windows (prevents hiding true regressions).

Why this approach: Tukey tapering reduces influence of isolated outliers compared to simple EWMA; the robust central tendency preserves step changes while reducing spike sensitivity. Cross-cohort smoothing borrows statistical strength from similar traffic slices to avoid noisy signals for small tenants. Tiered failover provides graceful degradation and gives operators time to investigate before a hard rollback.

Testing performed: Unit tests for denoiser edge cases, integration tests plugging the denoiser into the canary evaluator, and e2e perf scenarios using the synthetic traffic harness (single-spike, burst trains, traffic ramp, and gradual model drift). Benchmarks run across three hardware profiles. Telemetry validated in staging and dashboards added for signal inspection.

Rollout plan: Feature-flag gated (canary_denoiser.enabled=false by default). Staged rollout: 1) enable for internal test tenants (1h), 2) enable for 5% of canaries (24h), 3) enable progressively to 50%+ after monitoring. If anomalies occur, toggle feature-flag off to revert instantly.

Checklist:
- [x] Algorithm implementation (denoiser) and unit tests
- [x] Integration into canary pipeline and evaluator
- [x] Telemetry and dashboards
- [x] Runbook and rollback steps
- [x] Performance microbench and e2e verification

Notes: This PR touches only evaluation logic and controller paths; there are no public API changes. See linked Linear tasks for background (ENG-5421 describes noise patterns; ENG-5503 requested staged failover).
Liam Chen: Can you explain why we prefer Tukey-style weights vs exponential smoothing for short bursts?
Response: The Tukey taper reduces sensitivity to single outliers and preserves step changes; we include an adaptive lambda that shifts toward exponential smoothing when sustained drift is observed.
Rosa Vega: Telemetry cardinality looks high; consider aggregating percentiles at cluster-level.
Response: Aggregation added and new metric canary_signal_bucket now emitted at 5m granularity to avoid cardinality explosion. See internal/telemetry/canary_metrics.go for implementation.
Anand Iyer: We need safety gates for release; what happens if denoiser hides signal prior to rollback?
Response: Added 'staged-escape' detection that disables denoiser if decorrelation between raw and smoothed >= threshold for 3 windows; controller will evaluate raw signal and escalate directly to rollback if necessary.
- Add windowed denoiser to canary pipeline to stabilize latency signals under bursty traffic
- Introduce adaptive failover policy with staged soft-fallback before full rollback
- New telemetry: denoiser_signal_strength, denoiser_disabled_reason, failover_state
- Runbook: docs/runbooks/perf-canary-denoiser.md
This change affects canary evaluation logic only; default feature flag is off for 1 week of gradual rollout. If regressions appear, flip canary_denoiser.enabled=false and the pipeline will revert to previous signal path. Emergency rollback tested in staging with toggle and verified in 30s.
E2E: synthetic traffic scenarios including single-spike bursts, multi-burst patterns, and gradual drift. Results: false-positive rate reduced from 6.3% to 0.9% on test corpus; detection latency unchanged. Benchmarks: CPU overhead approx +2% per controller replica; memory +30MB. Load tests run at 2x production load for 24h.
Merged via squash with release note: "Add windowed signal denoiser and adaptive failover policy to reduce false-positive canary regressions under bursty traffic. Backfill: ENG-5421."

Motivation: intermittent regressions during canaries were often due to aggressive traffic ramps and cold-path performance variance in small cohorts. This PR introduces a Cohort Stabilizer controller and a 'slow-start' ramp policy for staged rollouts, plus explicit rollback clauses and an automated playbook hook. The change bundle includes: 1) a new controller that enforces a minimum warmup window per cohort and monitors rolling-window latency/quality signals; 2) a slow-start ramp schedule that increments traffic only after passing per-cohort SLO checks; 3) conservative backpressure: when the controller sees latency or error spikes for a cohort it reduces ramp velocity and pauses promotion; 4) rollback clauses that capture snapshot reasons, create an auditable rollback ticket, and optionally trigger immediate swap to the previous stable model variant; 5) telemetry probes and a lightweight audit trail for replay; 6) an operator-facing CLI command and console UI hints to visualize cohort state and manually trigger/override holds. This description contains the checklist and links: - Checklist: [x] controller implementation, [x] unit + integration tests, [x] e2e replay test harness, [x] console hints, [x] documentation pages updated, [x] rollback playbook drafted. - Related Linear tasks: ENG-1892, ENG-1901. - Design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/doc/COHORT-STABILIZER-DESIGN. Notes: the controller aims for conservative behavior by default (slow-start fraction=0.02 initial, step=+2% every condition pass) and exposes tunables for enterprise Dedicated/Private deployments. The rollback clauses are policy-as-data so tenants can opt for automated reversion or manual incident-driven revert. Rolling is safe across region/replica topologies and respects session affinity by default.
Luca Moretti: Can we make the initial slow-start fraction configurable via tenant YAML? Prefer default conservative but allow enterprise tuning.
Maya Singh: Yes, exposed as cohort_policy.slow_start.initial_fraction and documented in rollout-playbooks.md.
Priya Raman: Suggest adding a TTL to rollback tickets to avoid stale auto-reverts.
Maya Singh: Added TTL handling and tests that simulate ticket expiry before auto-revert triggers.
Samir Patel: Integration looks good; one nit about log verbosity in high-traffic canaries.
Maya Singh: Reduced stabilizer logger to debug for per-request traces; kept info for holds and rollbacks.
Introduce Cohort Stabilizer controller to slow-start canaries and reduce false-positive regressions.
New policy fields: slow_start.initial_fraction, slow_start.step_percent, stabilizer.backpressure_thresholds.
Automatic rollback clauses with auditable tickets and optional auto-revert behavior.
Console: cohort timeline visualization and 'cohort inspect' CLI.
If hosts report unexpected holds: check controller metrics (stabilizer.holds_total, stabilizer.backpressure_events) and the e2e replay queue. Use 'redwoodctl cohort inspect <cohort>' to view state and trigger manual override. Rollback tickets are created under the 'rollout-auto' queue with tag 'stabilizer'.

Context: During the NA pilot we’re seeing a non-trivial number of “vanity” intent triggers and a couple of true false positives (notably Quartz Commerce) resulting in unwanted outreach (see SUP-3392). This PR adds a set of guardrails to reduce noise while keeping recall for genuinely sales-worthy signals. Summary of changes: (1) Suppression windows: prevent re-routing the same signal type for the same account within a configurable cooldown (default 14d for intent, 7d for reliability/usage) unless severity increases. We store last_routed_at by (workspace_id, signal_type) and compare against current signal_score + severity. (2) Internal/test org filtering: blocklist/allowlist logic for Redwood-owned workspaces and known test tenants; also filters “example.com” style seeded domains and sandbox workspaces tagged by billing. This is applied before scoring so we avoid polluting analytics tables and HubSpot with internal activities. (3) Minimum-volume gates: require minimum sustained volume for threshold signals (tokens/spend/429s) to reduce one-off spikes; add a separate gate for “docs intent only” that requires either (a) 2+ distinct sessions across 48h or (b) docs intent + at least one supporting product event (workspace invite spike, API key rotation, or repeated rate-limit). (4) Confidence floor: enforce a minimum confidence threshold for routing (default 0.65) with per-signal overrides, and write suppressed candidates to a side table for tuning. (5) Auditability: whenever we suppress we emit a structured log and a metric with reason codes (cooldown, internal_org, min_volume, confidence_floor). Tradeoff notes: This will reduce total routed tasks (expected 25–40% drop based on pilot cohort replay), but should materially reduce spam/false positives. We explicitly bias toward fewer tasks while we tune thresholds; suppressed events remain queryable for later adjustment. Testing: Added unit tests for suppression keying + cooldown behavior, internal org matching, and min-volume gating; added a replay test against a sanitized subset of the pilot cohort to validate volume impact. Follow-ups: (a) Add UI surfacing of “suppressed signals” for triage (see DES-412), (b) Re-evaluate doc intent heuristics once we have docs instrumentation improvements from Elliot (docs session identifiers), and (c) Consider account-level suppression when Marketing nurture is active (separate workstream with Tyler/Camila).
Key changes: services/plg_signal_router/suppression/guardrails.ts (new guardrail evaluation pipeline and reason codes); services/plg_signal_router/config/signal_guardrails.yaml (defaults for cooldown, min-volume gates, confidence floor); analytics/jobs/daily_signal_aggregator/min_volume.sql (add sustained-volume windows + distinct-day checks); services/plg_signal_router/internal_org/filter.ts (new internal org matching + explicit deny/allow lists); services/plg_signal_router/hubspot/route.ts (skip routing on suppressed results; still write suppressed to analytics); services/plg_signal_router/metrics.ts (new counters: suppressed_total{reason}, routed_total{signal_type}, candidate_total); tests/plg_signal_router/guardrails.test.ts (unit tests for cooldown/severity escalation, min-volume gates, internal matching); tools/replay/pilot_cohort_replay.ts (sanitized replay runner used for before/after counts). Illustrative snippet (guardrail evaluation): if (isInternalOrg(account) && !isExplicitlyAllowed(account)) return suppress('internal_org'); if (!passesMinVolume(signal)) return suppress('min_volume'); if (!passesCooldown(lastRoutedAt, signal)) return suppress('cooldown'); if (signal.confidence < confidenceFloor(signal.type)) return suppress('confidence_floor'); return allow();
Logan Wright (requested changes): Cooldown keying looks right, but can we ensure severity escalation bypasses cooldown only when we have a material delta? Right now it’s >0.01 score, which is too sensitive and will re-spam on minor fluctuations. Also please make sure suppressed candidates are still written with enough context (signal_type, score, reason, window_start/end) so we can tune. Mei Lin (reply): Good call. Updated severity bypass to require either (a) score delta >= 0.15 or (b) severity enum increases (e.g., MED->HIGH). Also added window_start/window_end and score/confidence into suppressed_candidates table + logs. Priya Natarajan: For internal org filtering, I like the deny-by-default for Redwood domains, but please confirm we’re not accidentally suppressing legitimate customers with shared email domains (contractor scenarios). Can we rely primarily on workspace flags rather than email domain? Mei Lin: Agreed; updated to prioritize workspace.billing_account_type==INTERNAL or workspace.tags includes 'redwood-internal'. Domain-based suppression is now a fallback heuristic only when billing metadata is missing, and it requires both domain match AND org_created_by seed script flag. Isabelle Laurent: From an ops standpoint, can we tune cooldowns per region/tier without code changes? (Pilot EMEA wants longer cooldown on intent-only docs views.) Mei Lin: Yes—cooldowns are now config-driven in YAML and read at runtime. Added keys for intent_docs_only_cooldown_days and per-tier overrides (self_serve vs enterprise_trial). David Kim: HubSpot side effects: please ensure we aren’t creating tasks and then immediately suppressing in retries (idempotency). We’ve had issues where the candidate is evaluated twice in the same run. Mei Lin: Added an idempotency guard: suppression decision happens before HubSpot calls; also ensured we persist last_routed_at only after successful HubSpot task creation. Added a test for double-evaluation. Dr. Aisha Rahman: Privacy review: internal org filtering is fine, but ensure the suppressed_candidates table doesn’t include raw URLs or page titles from docs views—keep it to enums/counts. Mei Lin: Updated schema: docs intent stored as doc_category enum + count + distinct_sessions, no raw URLs/titles. Approvals: Logan approved after severity change; Priya approved after internal filter adjustment; Isabelle + David approved with config/idempotency; Aisha approved with docs intent sanitization.
Internal: Reduce PLG signal noise by adding cooldown suppression, internal org filtering, and min-volume gating; emit suppression reason metrics for tuning; mitigates false-positive outreach risk noted in SUP-3392.

Motivation: reduce tail latency and unit cost for short-to-mid sequence inference workloads while keeping KV memory footprint under budget. This PR introduces a channelized attention microkernel that stripes Q/K/V across SIMD lanes/warps to improve L2 and shared-memory utilization for small batch, low-sequence scenarios, and a complementary KV soft-evict scheduler that probabilistically compacts and evicts cold KV entries to lower resident memory pressure during sustained continuous-batching.

Summary of changes: single continuous description string (no sections elsewhere) covering the kernel, scheduler, and rollout plan. The channelized microkernel reorganizes the inner-loop compute so that each warp processes interleaved channels of Q/K/V (instead of full-head blocks). This increases arithmetic intensity for narrow sequences and reduces bank conflicts seen on small sequence lengths. We add a small in-kernel rotary delta compaction step that applies a lightweight rematerialization-friendly encoding for rotary/rope components in the KV store (compact_rotary_storage) to reduce per-token KV bytes when rotary embeddings dominate. The soft-evict scheduler implements an occupancy- and recency-aware probabilistic eviction policy (soft_evict) with a tunable pressure parameter; it signals warmup/backpressure to the continuous-batcher to slow batching when memory thresholds approach configurable SLOs.

Why this is different: Unlike previous head/block tiling approaches, channelized striping is optimized for the common PLG short-seq patterns (seq_len <= 128, bursty arrivals) and purposely trades a small compute reordering latency for improved cache reuse and fewer warp replays under contention. The KV soft-evict is a non-blocking heuristic intended for Dedicated & Private deployments where memory isolation and predictable degradation are important; it intentionally avoids synchronous spilling to host storage and instead degrades gracefully while emitting observable metrics for automatic rerouting.

Checklist:
- [x] Microkernel: channelized striping compute + rotary delta compaction implemented in runtime/attn/channelized_kernel.cu
- [x] KV: compact rotary-backed storage and accessors in runtime/kv/compact_rotary_storage.cc/h
- [x] Scheduler: soft-evict implementation and config knobs in runtime/scheduler/soft_evict_scheduler.cpp
- [x] Continuous-batcher: backpressure hook and smoothing added to runtime/batching/continuous_batcher.cpp
- [x] Benchmarks and unit tests added (tests/bench/attn_channelized_bench.py, tests/unit/kv_compact_test.cc)
- [x] Docs + rollout notes (docs/perf/attn_channelized.md)

Performance results (canary/LAB):
- Mixed short-seq synthetic workload (batch=1..8, seq=32..128): 8-12% p99 latency reduction vs. current main microkernel, 14-22% throughput improvement for mixed request distributions.
- End-to-end token cost reduced by ~7% in continuous-batcher steady-state when soft-evict reduces KV resident size by 18% on average for rotary-heavy models.

Backward compatibility & safety: Defaults are off for Hosted customers. Dedicated/Private deployments get the scheduler behind a runtime flag (runtime.config.attn_channelized.enabled = true) and can tune soft-evict thresholds. No API surface changes. There are additional metrics exposed (attn.channelized.enabled, kv.soft_evict_pressure, kv.rotary_compaction_ratio) and a canary rollout plan described in docs/perf/attn_channelized.md.

Rollout plan: Canary across 5 dedicated clusters with runtime flag enabled, monitor p99 latency, kv.resident_bytes, continuous_batcher.rate. If regressions >5% in token quality or >10% in p99 latency appear, automatic rollback.

Marcus Li (reviewer): Strong idea. Please annotate the kernel with expected lane occupancy and add a micro-benchmark that isolates L2 reuse. Also add a short paragraph describing numerical stability for rotary delta compaction.
Author (Rina): Added micro-bench and inline occupancy comments. Rotary compaction is reversible and uses int8 delta with bias accumulation to preserve fp16 fp32 accumulation paths; details in comments and tests.
Sofia Nguyen (reviewer): Concern: soft-evict may interact poorly with KMS-backed memory reporting in Private. Can we add a guard that disables evict when host-spill is configured?
Author (Rina): Added guard (runtime.config.kv_disable_soft_evict_when_spill=true by default false) and test coverage for the behavior. Also emitted a metric kv.soft_evict_disabled_reason for audit.
Diego Ramos (reviewer): CI flakes on cuda-smoke; requested smaller shared-memory footprint in the kernel.

Context: Follow-on to the multi-SDK credential and streaming work — this PR standardizes a credential priming + retry diagnostic matrix across Python/TS/Go SDKs, improves ergonomics for PullStream consumers, and surfaces a deprecation path for the legacy PullStream resume API. Motivation: teams have reported inconsistent retry behavior when a token swap occurs during active streaming; additionally, our telemetry for retry predicates made it hard to correlate client-side retry decisions with server-side throttles. This change groups three coordinated efforts: 1) introduce an explicit "credential priming" handshake that SDKs can opt into to warm token caches prior to heavy streaming workloads, 2) add a compact, human-readable retry diagnostics payload that is emitted to SDK telemetry hooks (and to the Console events), and 3) provide a compatibility shim plus deprecation warnings for the old PullStream resume()/cursor style in favor of the newer resumable checkpoint API. Summary of changes (high level): - Python SDK: add CredentialPrimer class, expose enable_credential_priming flag on Client, add retry_diagnostics callback hook in async streaming client, bump package to 1.12.0-rc1. - TypeScript SDK: add credentialPriming middleware, small ergonomic changes to AsyncIterable stream consumer (stop() -> closeGracefully()), emit diagnostics to telemetry collector, bump to 2.8.0-rc3. - Go SDK: expose Primer interface and default implementation, add Diagnostics struct to stream events, update PullStream helper to log deprecation on first use, bump to v0.18.1-rc2. - Core: add compact retry diagnostics proto and Console wiring so events show up under "client-retries" timeline. Compatibility notes: - All SDKs include a runtime opt-in for priming; default remains off. - The legacy PullStream resume() remains available but now logs a deprecation advisory on first invocation; a migration guide is included in docs/ and linked in release_notes. Checklist: - [x] Credential priming implementations for py/ts/go - [x] Retry diagnostics emission to telemetry hooks - [x] Deprecation warning and migration doc - [x] Unit + integration tests for priming and diagnostics - [x] Console event plumbing for client-retries - [x] Docs and changelog updates Commits (summary): - 6f1d3b4 Add CredentialPrimer and tests (python) - 9b2a7e1 Add credentialPriming middleware and telemetry hook (typescript) - a1c4d2e Expose Primer interface and diagnostics (go) - 2c3f4b0 Add compact retry diagnostics proto + console hook - d5e6f77 Docs: migration guide and examples - 3a4b5c6 Fix flaky integration test: streaming-retry-timeouts Tests/CI: First CI run failed on python/integration/stream_warmup due to a timing assumption (test asserted metrics event ordering). Adjusted test to wait for priming ack and re-ran; subsequent run passed. E2E permutations: ran a matrix across py/ts/go client versions + server throttling mode (leaky-bucket/fast-fail) to validate that diagnostic payloads are emitted and that priming short-circuits the first-token-exchange latency spike. Files changed (high level): - sdk/python/redwood_client/credential_primer.py - sdk/python/tests/test_credential_primer.py - sdk/python/redwood_client/__init__.py (version bump) - sdk/typescript/middleware/credentialPriming.ts - sdk/typescript/streams/async_consumer.ts - sdk/typescript/telemetry/retryDiagnostics.ts - sdk/typescript/package.json (version rc) - sdk/go/primer/primer.go - sdk/go/stream/diagnostics.go - proto/telemetry/retry_diagnostics.proto - docs/migration/pullstream-resume-to-checkpoint.md - console/events/client_retries_handler.go - tools/ci/e2e/matrix-config.yml Review conversation (high level): - Jonah Kim (reviewer): Requested clearer guarantees around priming: what happens if priming fails? Author reply: Priming is best-effort; SDKs expose a priming_timeout and on failure we fall back to the normal token fetch path while emitting a diagnostic with "priming_failure". Updated README and added test that simulates priming failure. - Lucia Moreno: Asked to avoid noisy deprecation logs in high-throughput apps. Author reply: switched to a once-per-process deprecation counter and added an environment variable REDWOOD_SDK_SUPPRESS_DEPRECATION to silence. - Evan Zhang: Asked for a smaller default diagnostic payload to avoid telemetry cost. Author reply: made payload compact (enum codes + short reason strings) and added opt-out at init. Merge details: - Merge method: squash and merge - PR merged by: Jonah Kim - Merge commit summary: "Unify credential priming and retry diagnostics across SDKs; surface PullStream resume deprecation; bump SDK release-rcs." Release notes (user-facing): - SDK: opt-in credential priming to reduce first-request latency for streaming workloads (opt-in via enable_credential_priming / credentialPriming middleware / Primer option). - SDK: new retry diagnostics emitted to telemetry hooks and Console (human-readable timeline events). - Breaking changes: none by default; legacy PullStream resume is deprecated but still available. Migration guide: docs/migration/pullstream-resume-to-checkpoint.md
Jonah Kim: Please clarify priming failure semantics and add a test that simulates token service latency.
Asha Patel: Added priming_timeout, documented fallback behavior, added integration test that injects latency to token service.
Lucia Moreno: Deprecation spam risk for PullStream.resume observed in perf tests; consider rate-limited warning.
Asha Patel: Implemented once-per-process deprecation counter and env var to mute warnings.
Evan Zhang: Diagnostics size concerns — can we make the default payload tiny?
Asha Patel: Switched to enum codes + short reason strings and added opt-out flag at client init.
Initial CI: 1 failing python integration test (timing). Reran after test fix; final CI status: all checks passed (unit, linters, integration matrix, e2e).
- Opt-in credential priming for streaming (improves first-request latency)
- Compact retry diagnostics emitted to SDK telemetry and Console
- Legacy PullStream.resume deprecation path and migration guide

Motivation: multiple incidents during near-midnight rollouts and repeated fallout from transitive dependency upgrades motivated a small, focused refactor: introduce a windowed release orchestrator that gates merges to safe roll windows and a dependency-compatibility adapter that runs lightweight ABI/behavior checks before auto-bumping deps. This PR bundles the orchestration glue, a slim preflight runner, and a dep-compat shim intended to be cheap to run in presubmit.
Summary of changes:
1) ci/release-orchestrator: new Go binary (cmd/release-orchestrator) that coordinates merge windows, quiet periods, and graceful drain signals to downstream pipelines.
2) ci/presubmit-hooks: add hook shim to call the dep-compat adapter and short smoke pipeline; hooks are configured as opt-in per-repo via .github/presubmit-config.yaml.
3) tooling/dep-compat: Python adapter that, for a candidate bump, installs the package into an ephemeral venv, runs a curated short test matrix (sanity import, API surface smoke, small model-run smoke where applicable), and emits a compact compatibility report artifact.
4) buildkite/pipeline-stages: reorganize release stages into window-aware lanes and add backoff policy on transient infra failures.
5) docs/ci/release-windows.md and docs/ci/dep-compatibility.md describing behaviors and opt-in migration steps.
Commits (high-level):
- init: release-orchestrator main loop and config parsing
- add: presubmit hook wiring and config schema
- add: dep-compat adapter v0 with import+api smoke checks
- refactor: pipeline stage definitions and backoff policy
- fix: avoid deadlock on drain sequence (race condition fix)
- test: unit/integration harness for the adapter
- docs: usage & migration notes
Changed areas (high-level file list):
- cmd/release-orchestrator/main.go
- ci/hooks/presubmit_runner.go
- tooling/dep_compat/checker.py
- .github/presubmit-config.yaml (new, small opt-in map)
- buildkite/release-pipelines.yml
- docs/ci/release-windows.md
- docs/ci/dep-compatibility.md
- scripts/ci/fixtures/dep-compat-sample
- Makefile entries and CI job templates
Notes on approach and tradeoffs: The orchestrator enforces wall-clock windows defined in org-level config and per-repo overrides. It is intentionally conservative: default rollout windows are UTC 14:00-21:00 but can be narrowed by security or compliance labels. The dep-compat adapter is intentionally lightweight: it is not a full test runner, but a fast preflight that detects common breaking changes surfaced by import/name errors, changed call signatures (via a thin reflection/checklist), and model-based smoke runs when present. We accept occasional false-positives and tuned to allow quick follow-ups; false negatives are minimized by keeping the test matrix aligned with critical integration points.
Checklist:
- [x] design doc linked in ENG-7843
- [x] unit tests for Go orchestrator loop
- [x] adapter smoke harness and sample fixtures
- [x] pipeline YAML updated and tested in a ephemeral buildkite org
- [x] docs and migration notes
- [x] opt-in gating so repos can adopt incrementally
Review conversation (condensed into single string): Ethan Patel: "Can orchestrator handle multi-tenant pipelines where multiple repos try to claim the same window?" Author (Maya): "Yes, orchestrator uses a lightweight lease in Dynamo (ci-lease table) and will serialize ownership; added retries and jitter to reduce contention." Rosa Kim: "Dep-compat adapter looks good but I'm worried about test flakiness for model smoke runs." Author: "Adapter will skip model smoke by default unless repo opt-in flag present; model smoke uses cached small models and a 10s timeout — documented in dep-compatibility.md." Liam O'Connor: "Need telemetry hooks for rollout failures and backoff counts." Author: "Added metrics (release_window_claim, backoff_attempts, compat_check_result) emitted to statsd; dashboards are in observability-pack PR follow-up."
Requested changes and responses:
- request: make presubmit-config opt-in per default -> addressed by defaulting to false and adding migration guide.
- request: enforce max runtime for adapter jobs -> added 120s hard cap and graceful cancellation path.
- request: better error messages for compatibility reports -> added compact JSON report with human-friendly summary lines.
CI summary: initial runs showed a failing unit test (race in drain handling) and a lint warning in checker.py. Both fixed in follow-up commits; final CI status green: unit tests 120/120, integration smoke 12/12, linters pass, pipeline deployment dry-run passed.
Release notes: "Introduce windowed release orchestrator to schedule merges into defined rollout windows and add a lightweight dependency compatibility adapter for preflight checks on automatic upgrades. Opt-in per repo via .github/presubmit-config.yaml. See docs/ci/release-windows.md and docs/ci/dep-compatibility.md for migration steps."
Rollout plan: staged rollout across infra repos first (ark, infra-config), then core runtime (redwood) opt-in, followed by SDKs.
Breaking change: "false" (not a breaking API change).
Files changed count and delta provided above.
Follow-ups: add an automated dashboard import for the new metrics, a cross-repo adoption tracker script, and extend dep-compat checks to run on scheduled nightly bump candidates to reduce burstiness.
Merged via squash on 2025-11-08 after approvals from Ethan, Rosa, and Liam.

Summary: Adds a compact per-invocation lineage identifier, a deployable event-sidecar that performs reservoir sampling of structured invocation events, and a phase-aware token chargeback dashboard (UI + queries + alert tuning). Motivation: customers asked for faster root-cause access when token cost spikes and for cheaper, correlated logs that don't increase cardinality in primary traces. The lineage ID lets teams surface a single stable key in traces, logs, and billing lookups; the sidecar samples rich structured events (prompt/phase markers, quantization flag, kernel hints) and forwards them to the telemetry bus; the dashboard ties token counts to invocation phases so teams can reason about chargebacks per-phase. Design highlights: - Lineage ID: deterministic 64-bit stable ID derived from request id + model-version + route fingerprint (collision resistant, reversible for debug only via internal index). Stored in span attribute "inv.lineage" and emitted in HTTP header X-Inv-Lineage for private deployments. - Event sidecar: Go service (pkg/sidecar/event_sampler.go) runs as a per-node sidecar, attaches to the local ingestion socket, performs time-windowed reservoir sampling, emits compact JSON events to the telemetry bus (Kafka/KSQ) and writes a minimal sidecar metric (sidecar.sample.rate, sidecar.drop.rate). Sampling policy is multi-tier: always-sample on errors, adaptive reservoir for heavy tenants, and static 1-per-100 for low priority routes. - Phase-aware token chargeback: new dashboard observability/dashboards/token_phase_chargeback.json that aggregates tokens by labeled phases (init/prefix/gen/postprocess), attributes GPU/CPU split where available, and computes per-tenant per-route chargeback tables for accounting. Alerts: a new alert (TokenPhaseChargebackSpike) triggers when a route shows >20% increase in tokens for 'postprocess' over a rolling 30m baseline with adaptive hysteresis to reduce churn. Checklist: - [x] Add lineage generator and attach to serving runtime (src/serving/lineage_id.py) - [x] Emit header in private/VPC variants - [x] Implement event sidecar (pkg/sidecar/event_sampler.go) with unit tests - [x] Add sampling metrics and dashboards - [x] Create chargeback dashboard and alert rule - [x] Add runbook and playbook links (docs/runbooks/token_chargeback_playbook.md) - [x] Add integration tests and perf microbenchmarks Commits (summary): - a1f3b2c: feature(lineage): deterministic per-invocation lineage id + header emission + unit tests - b7c4d99: feat(sidecar): add reservoir sampler, config knobs, and telemetry sinks; add sidecar e2e harness - c3d9f11: obs(dashboard): token phase chargeback dashboard + alert rule + runbook link - d5e0a20: test: integration tests for sampled events and lineage correlation - f0b6c6a: perf: microbenchmark for lineage overhead and sidecar CPU utilization Changed files (high level): - src/serving/lineage_id.py (new) - internal/trace/attributes.go (add inv.lineage propagation) - pkg/sidecar/event_sampler.go (new) - pkg/sidecar/config.yaml (new) - observability/dashboards/token_phase_chargeback.json (new) - monitoring/alerts/token_phase_rules.yaml (updated) - docs/runbooks/token_chargeback_playbook.md (new) - tests/integration/test_sidecar_sampling.py (new) - tests/perf/test_lineage_overhead.bench (new) - pkg/telemetry/forwarder_kafka.go (small hookup) - go.mod / python requirements (minor bumps) Testing & perf: - Unit tests: all pass locally and in CI. - Integration: sidecar e2e ran in staging; validated that ~1% sampling yields <0.4% CPU overhead on a busy node. - Perf: microbenchmark shows lineage_id generation adds ~55ns on hot path; negligible impact on 99th latency in our bench. - Security: header emission gated behind deployment config and KMS access; no PII stored in sampled events. Review conversation (condensed timeline): - Riley Chen (reviewer): "Nice design. Please add a metric for sidecar queue length and make sampling policy pluggable per-tenant." - Asha (author): "Added sidecar.queue.length and tenant_policy config; updated tests." - Jonah Li: "I saw the dashboard queries show an unexpected bump in 'init' tokens — is this real or a query bug?" - Asha: "That was due to double-counting in a prior staging export; fixed the rollup key in observability pipeline and re-verified." - Nadia Kumar (approver): "Left two minor nits on config docs and runbook escalation thresholds; otherwise LGTM." - Asha: "Addressed both nits, adjusted threshold to match SRE guidance, added runbook link to alert annotations." CI summary: - lint: pass - unit: pass - integration: pass (staging run flake → rerun → pass) - e2e: pass - perf-bench: pass - security-scan: pass Merge notes: Merged via squash by Nadia Kumar after approvals. Squash commit message: "inv-lineage + event-sidecar + token-phase-chargeback: add lineage IDs, sampled event sidecar, UI and alerts" Rollout plan & follow-ups: - Feature gated; default sampling set low for all tenants. - Recommend enabling lineage header in Private customers with opt-in; add telemetry->billing join job in next sprint to populate chargeback tables. - Follow-up tasks created: ENG-1102 (billing-join job), ENG-1103 (enable tenant-level sampling UI), ENG-1104 (add long-term retention pipeline for sidecar events). Links: - Linear board: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1045 - Runbook: docs/runbooks/token_chargeback_playbook.md - Staging dashboard (internal): /dashboards/token_phase_chargeback (internal URL) Notes: This PR focuses on low-overhead observability improvements for token-cost and latency debugging without increasing trace cardinality; design favors sampled structured events and a stable lineage key to quickly correlate traces, logs, and billing.
Adds per-invocation lineage IDs for trace correlation, a lightweight sampled-event sidecar for low-overhead structured logging, and a new token-phase chargeback dashboard with alert hooks and runbook links.

Context and motivation: We observed recurring SLA blips when tenants with spiky traffic consumed short-lived bursts that later forced aggressive eviction of warm capacity. Existing autoscaler policies allocate headroom primarily from point-in-time utilization and conservative percentiles; they do not explicitly budget for variance in bursty tenants. This PR introduces a variance-budgeted autoscaler policy and a deferred-burst commitment mechanism to reduce unnecessary warm pool churn and preserve throughput guarantees.

What this change does (single-string body): Implements a variance-budgeted allocator that maintains a per-tenant 'variance budget' derived from historical traffic variance and a configurable confidence window. The budget is consumed when a tenant requests burst capacity; instead of committing immediately, the controller places the request into a short deferred-commit queue where capacity checks and global headroom sampling continue for up to a configured grace period (default 6s). If capacity remains available at commit time the burst is finalized; if not, the request is either partially granted (scaled-down commit) or rejected with a clear telemetry event.

Key motivations: 1) Smooth transient overprovisioning spikes that arise from simultaneous microbursts, 2) Preserve guaranteed throughput for steady tenants by avoiding preemptive eviction of long-running reservations, 3) Improve utilization signals by accounting for variance rather than relying solely on fixed percentiles.

Behavioral changes and config knobs: A new policy type 'variance_budget' can be selected per-tenant; parameters added: budget_window_seconds, bootstrap_percentile, commit_grace_seconds, max_partial_commit_ratio. Backwards compatibility: default remains existing percentile-based policy. The deferred commit flow is guarded behind a feature flag (autoscaler.deferred_burst.enabled) to allow staged rollout.

Observability and telemetry: adds metrics: redwood_autoscaler_variance_budget_available, redwood_autoscaler_deferred_queue_length, redwood_autoscaler_deferred_commits_finalized_total, redwood_autoscaler_partial_commits_total, and an event tag 'deferred_burst_rejection_reason'. Dashboards and alert rules added under observability/metrics to highlight growing deferred queue length and sustained budget depletion.

Testing and validation: unit tests for variance_budget math and partial commit scaling added; integration test simulates 200 tenants with randomized microbursts and verifies 95th pct latency and eviction counts do not regress compared to baseline. Local perf runs show ~3% improvement in steady-state utilization for mixed workloads and a 30% reduction in warm-pool churn during synthetic burst storms.

Rollout plan: Enable feature flag in canary clusters for 48 hours with extended telemetry; promote to staging with default budget_window_seconds=300 and commit_grace_seconds=6; observe deferred queue and partial commit metrics for regressions before enabling in production.

Implementation notes and non-obvious details: - Variance budget is maintained as an EWMA of per-tenant short-window variance with a decay that prioritizes recent bursts. - Deferred commit queue is in-memory on the controller and durable across leader elections via small in-cluster lease tokens; commit pre-checks use a sampled lookahead on capacity to avoid over-committing. - To avoid priority inversion we add a soft-fairness gate that prevents long-lived low-priority commit retries from starving new short bursts.

Files changed summary: moved core algorithm into pkg/autoscaler/variance_budget.go; deferred commit state machine in deferred_commit.go; small wiring and config in policy_config.go; controller bootstrap hooks in cmd/controller/main.go; metrics YAML and dashboard scaffolding under observability; integration test and example tenant profile.

Related tickets: ENG-1287 (variance-budget proto and policy), ENG-1310 (deferred commit design spike).

Risks and mitigations: Risk of mis-tuned budgets causing undercommit -> configured conservative bootstrap_percentile and a gradual ramp. Feature flag allows rollback. CI coverage added for the race we observed in drain cancellation.
