Context: multiple customers and internal teams asked for a small, well-tested primitive to let SDK users supply multiple credential sources (short-lived tokens from vaults, rotating delegated creds, and long-lived API keys) without wiring custom orchestration in app code. Separately, TS/Python/Go SDK consumers requested a simpler async composition primitive for chunked streaming responses (concatenate+throttle semantics) that preserves backpressure and parity across languages. This PR implements a lightweight "mux credential proxy" plus an ergonomic asyncZipStream helper in all three SDKs, reconciles retry window defaults across languages, and bumps SDK minors so applications can opt into the new primitives.

Changes in this PR (single-string description): - Add mux credential proxy: a small in-SDK coordinator that accepts an ordered list of CredentialProviders and exposes a single provider surface with deterministic rotation and lease metadata. It supports optional warmup hooks and pluggable clock (test-friendly). - Add asyncZipStream helper: accepts multiple chunked-async iterables (or Node streams) and yields zipped/interleaved chunks with configurable windowing and per-source backpressure policy. Replaces previous ad-hoc helper in examples and standardizes grammar across SDKs. - Normalize retry config: default connect/idle retire windows aligned to 2s connect / 60s idle across SDKs, introduce RetryProfile v2 that is opt-in. Documented migration notes. - Minor public API tidy: small ergonomics changes to StreamHandle.close() -> .stop(), clearer error subclassing for AuthError vs RetryExhausted, and documented stable deprecation of old helpers in favor of asyncZipStream. - Bump versions: ts 1.9.0 -> 1.10.0, python 0.18.4 -> 0.19.0, go v0.16.7 -> v0.17.0 (all semver-minor). Motivation: improve cross-language parity and reduce customer glue code for credential rotation and stream merging. Backwards compatibility: default runtime behavior preserved; rotation semantics only change when consumers pass multiple providers or opt into RetryProfile v2; the StreamHandle API rename includes a compatibility shim for one release.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc & compatibility review (ENG-2147) - [x] Tests added: unit + integration + interop smoke tests across local CI matrix - [x] Benchmarks: microbench for stream interleave latency and credential swap overhead - [x] Docs updated: SDK changelogs + migration snippet - [x] Version bumps and changelogs prepared - [x] Confirmed no behavioral change for single-provider consumers

Testing notes: Ran matrix in CI (linux/py38/py310, node14/node18, go1.21) + simulated vault lease rotation tests in python/ts. Benchmarks show mux proxy adds ~0.6ms median per-token for token-swap scenarios and asyncZipStream reduces end-to-end throughput variance in multi-source streams by ~18% at small window sizes. Migration: users should replace old example helper with asyncZipStream or keep the old helper for one cycle (compat shim present). If you supply multiple providers, consult README: merging semantics are FIFO by provider order.
Diego Morales: +1 overall, left two nit comments about naming (stop vs close) and a comment about exposing lease metadata as part of Token object.
Lily Chen: requested clearer retry docs and an explicit migration section for users who depended on old shuffle semantics. Also asked for a perf test to measure rotation under load.
Samir Gupta: found a concurrency race in the Go mux when a provider returned error during swap; asked for a retry-with-backoff inside the rotation path. Patch pushed to address and tests added.
Asha Patel (author): replied to all comments, added compatibility shim for StreamHandle.close -> .stop(), clarified lease metadata surface, and added the requested perf test to the CI matrix.
Introduce mux credential proxy (allows multiple credential providers with deterministic rotation and lease metadata); asyncZipStream helper for ergonomic multi-source chunked streaming; normalized retry defaults and opt-in RetryProfile v2; minor SDK bumps (ts 1.10.0, python 0.19.0, go v0.17.0). See docs/sdk-migration/mux-proxy-and-zipstream.md for migration guidance.

payload.body:
Motivation: During a recent regional surge incident we observed repeated oscillation between regional eviction and full failover for mid-tier tenants. Root cause analysis showed aggressive immediate-eviction heuristics + global failover triggers interacting with best-effort KV-syncs and warm-up penalties. This PR introduces a lightweight fallback reservoir and a graceful containment controller that (1) absorbs short transient surges without triggering cross-region failovers, (2) staggers tenant eviction windows to reduce thundering rejoin, and (3) exposes a tunable containment tier that can be exercised by SLO enforcement policies.

What this changes: Implement a fallback reservoir (in-memory scoring + soft-lease) that temporarily holds eviction candidates for a configurable duration instead of evicting immediately. Add a containment controller that applies a progressive penalty schedule: initial soft-shed -> partial token cap -> full eviction only after reservoir expiry and penalty escalation. Introduce telemetry hooks and tracing spans for the reservoir lifecycle to aid incident analysis. Provide default conservative config that can be tightened by SRE on high-pressure events.

Design notes: The reservoir is per-region and tenant-aware; entries are lightweight structs (tenant_id, score, inserted_at, expiry_hint). Scoring uses a normalized SLO breach probability combined with recent CPU/RAM/queue-depth metrics. The containment controller runs as part of the regional load-shed orchestrator and defers actual node eviction calls for items in the reservoir until the penalty schedule advances. The controller also integrates with the existing circuit-breaker state machine; this PR adds a new reservoir state that circuit-breaker transitions can consult when deciding failover.

Backward compatibility: Runtime defaults to disabled if a feature-flag is not set. When enabled, the system falls back to the old eviction path if reservoir state cannot be loaded (safe fallback). No API changes to public endpoints.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for scoring, TTL eviction, and penalty escalation. Integration test simulating a burst workload to assert that immediate cross-region failover is avoided and that reservoir drains correctly under sustained pressure. Load tests against the canary fleet showed a 32% reduction in cross-region failover events for the simulated tenant mix and no measurable increase in tail-latency for surviving requests.

Deployment notes: Feature-flag gated rollout: start disabled, enable in a canary region for 24h, then roll global. Operators can tune reservoir_size, soft_shed_threshold, and initial_hold_ms via the console or configmap. Observability: new metrics (reservoir_size, reservoir_hits, reservoir_evictions, containment_penalty_level) and traces (reservoir.insert/reservoir.drain/containment.apply).

Related: ENG-2319 tracks the follow-ups to add automated canary tuning; SRE-502 covers runbook updates and alert threshold adjustments.

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests added
- [x] Integration tests for surge scenario
- [x] Metrics emitted with sensible names
- [x] Feature-flag and default disabled
- [x] Runbook draft attached to SRE-502

Notes: This is a pragmatic mitigation for repeated oscillation; follow-up PRs will refine scoring and introduce a bounded persistent reservoir for multi-process durability.
Owen Brooks: Can we bound memory usage of the reservoir under pathological tenant counts? Suggest adding a max_entries config and LRU eviction as a safety net.
Author (Elena Ramos): Added max_entries with LRU fallback in the latest commit; reservoir.go now enforces a hard cap and tracks eviction reasons.
Priya Patel: The scoring function mixes QPS and CPU signals; please confirm the scales are normalized and add a short comment with rationale so future maintainers understand weights.
Author (Elena Ramos): Expanded scoring comment and added unit tests that assert proper normalization across nominal ranges.
Marcus Li: CI flake on integration test initially; re-ran and tests passed. Approving pending minor logging cleanup.
Marcus Li: Approve (after logging tidy).
Owen Brooks: Approve.
Introduce a feature-flagged per-region fallback reservoir and containment controller to reduce unnecessary cross-region evictions during transient surges. Defaults disabled; operators can enable and tune via config. Metrics/traces added for observability.
Enable via feature flag 'containment_reservoir' in canary region; monitor reservoir_evictions and containment_penalty_level. If you see reservoir saturation, increase max_entries or lower soft_shed_threshold. See docs/runbooks/containment-reservoir.md for emergency rollback steps.

Context: our current GitHub Actions matrix runs large monolithic jobs which cause long queuing times, brittle cache keys, and repeated work across similar tasks. Motivation: reduce CI minutes, make failure modes easier to triage, enable incremental execution, and provide deterministic toolchains for reproducible builds. This PR introduces a lightweight task-graph runner for our CI pipelines, decomposes the large matrix into smaller named tasks (checkout -> bootstrap -> lint -> unit-test -> integration-smoke -> build-artifacts -> publish), and adds per-job dependency isolation + lock verification to prevent dependency drift. To improve reproducibility we pin the LLVM/rust/node toolchain snippets used in native builds and add a per-PR toolchain override for emergency rollbacks. The description below summarizes the surface changes, migration notes, and testing performed. Features: 1) CI task graph YAML templates: new .github/ci/task-graph.yml and reusable job templates under .github/ci/templates/*.yml so individual repos can opt-in to the graph. 2) Task runner shim: a small Go binary tools/ci/graph-runner that interprets the graph and enforces parallelism/ordering and exit semantics (used only in Actions runner). 3) Per-job virtualenvs and node_modules caches keyed by repository+lockfile-hash to reduce cross-PR cache contamination. 4) Dependency lock verification step: CI now fails fast if installed deps diverge from lockfile; an opt-out for legacy branches exists. 5) Toolchain pin manifests: .ci/toolchains.yaml with pinned versions and a small bootstrap script .ci/setup-toolchain that fetches exact versions for llvm/clang/rustup/node. 6) Release artifact naming standardized to redwood-<repo>-<commit>-<platform>.zip to make downstream publishing idempotent. Migration: the change is opt-in — older repos will continue to use the matrix until maintainers flip the workflow reference. Rollout plan: opt-in for core redwood packages this week, monitor CI minutes and flaky tests, then expand to SDK repos. Testing: validated against redwood/core, redwood-sdk-python, and redwood-helm-charts in a dogfood run. Observed ~34% reduction in total runner minutes for the core repo and fewer cache misses. See commits and files changed for details.
Marco Bell: Nice decomposition — two asks: (1) can we tighten the default per-task timeout to 20m for lint/unit to avoid runaway jobs? (2) please document how cache key rotation works for infra ops.
Anika Shah (author): lowered lint/unit default timeout to 20m, added TTL config for caches in .github/ci/task-graph.yml and documented cache rotation in docs/ci/migration-to-task-graph.md
Sofia Nguyen: graph-runner looks good but please add a health endpoint or verbose logs when a step is stuck to aid debugging in Actions logs.
Anika Shah: added verbose --debug flag and a simple /metrics/prometheus endpoint behind a local-only listener for e2e debugging; documented invocation in README of tools/ci
Evan Park: CI flakiness triage -- we should surface flaky test metadata into PR checks so maintainers can see historical flakiness per test. Recommend a follow-up (ENG-3499).
Anika Shah: ACK; added ENG-3499 to linked_linear for flaky-test telemetry follow-up
Opt-in CI task-graph + per-job dep isolation; pinned toolchains (LLVM/Rust/Node) for reproducible builds; lockfile verification added; standardized release artifact naming. No runtime behavior changes to production services.
Operators: toolchain pins live in .ci/toolchains.yaml; to temporarily override a pinned toolchain for emergency builds set CI_TOOLCHAIN_OVERRIDE env on the runner. Cache keys are now keyed by <repo>-<lock-hash>-<package-manager>-<platform>. If you need to evict caches manually use the 'ci:evict-cache' Makefile target which calls the cache API with prefix matching.
If the graph introduces regressions, revert by changing workflow refs back to the legacy matrix (branch: main) and re-enable the previous matrix workflow copy located at .github/workflows/ci-legacy.yml. A temporary feature flag CI_FORCE_LEGACY=true is supported to force the legacy path per-run.
Dogfood runs against core packages + SDKs across linux/ubuntu-latest and macos-latest. Measured a 34% reduction in total runner minutes for core package; cache hit rate improved from ~52% to ~78%. No regressions in smoke integration runs. Observability: added basic traces for task durations to be ingested into existing tracing pipeline.
1) Enable task-graph workflow for redwood/sdk repos over next 48 hours. 2) Run dependency lock enforcement on the weekly maintenance cron to surface legacy drift. 3) Follow-up ENG-3499 for flaky-test telemetry.
This PR is intentionally conservative: the graph-runner is used only as an orchestration shim inside Actions and does not replace our internal runners. We kept an opt-out path to minimize disruption to release automation while enabling fast iteration on cache and parallelism strategies.
payload.title: Modernize CI: introduce task graph, per-job dep isolation, and toolchain pinning

Context and motivation: customer platforms observed intermittent stalls during high-concurrency function-invocation (fncall) streams when small payloads interleave with larger routing requests. The gateway's previous pacing assumed uniform per-request cost and used a fixed write/window/flush schedule that caused head-of-line blocking for low-token fncalls and occasionally dropped tool-call boundaries when proxied to the OpenAI compat shim. This PR introduces a rate-aware routing policy plus a connection-level stream resilience layer to prioritize small fncall payloads while protecting overall route capacity. The change is conservative and feature-flagged behind gateway.config.enable_rate_aware_routing and gateway.config.fncall_stream_backoff_ms. Key pieces delivered: 1) Rate-aware routing policy: routes maintain a short-term cost estimate (tokens-per-second equivalent) and the router weights inflight request scheduling to avoid starving low-cost fncalls. 2) Write window smoothing: the proxy writer uses an adaptive smoothing window that shortens for connections with frequent small fragments and lengthens for long-running generation streams; this reduces latency for function-invocation toolcalls without increasing load on backend shards. 3) Early-boundary signaling: introduce an optional fncall boundary header (X-Redwood-Fncall-End) that the compat shim and model adapters can use to finalize KV-cache flushes and avoid accidental continuation of structured-tool-output into subsequent payloads. 4) Backoff and retry heuristics: connection-level exponential backoff for stream handshake failures with jitter, plus a fast-fallback route to a compatibility shim for models that do not support streaming fncall tool boundaries. 5) Telemetry and dashboards: new metrics added (gateway.route_rate_score, connection.small_payload_ratio, fncall.boundary_missed) and Grafana panel templates for canary monitoring. 6) Canary plan and rollout: behind flags, enabled for 10% of traffic by routing weight, with automatic rollback on spike of fncall.boundary_missed or >5% increase in p50 latency for fncall routes. Checklist: - [x] Design doc: internal doc at linear/ENG-4921 (linked). - [x] Unit tests for router scoring and writer smoothing. - [x] Integration e2e: simulated bursty fncall load against compat shim. - [x] Perf bench: latency and tail comparisons vs baseline. - [x] Telemetry dashboard patches. - [x] Feature-flagged and canary rollout plan. Links: linear/ENG-4921 design notes and perf results: https://linear.app/redwood/ENG-4921/design, internal bug SUP-305 incident notes. Backwards compatibility: default disabled; when enabled, behavior prefers small fncall payloads but preserves route quotas and global capacity accounting. Why this is different from previous gateway PRs: instead of only clamping or changing buffer TTLs, this PR adjusts routing decision weights and adds boundary signaling to reduce cross-request contamination and give deterministic treatment for fncall streams. Testing notes: e2e validated with a mix of 500 concurrent short fncalls (avg 12 tokens) and 120 concurrent long generation requests (avg 1600 tokens) for 10 minutes; observed 35% reduction in fncall p95 and no throughput regression on backend shards. Rollout: merged after canary at 10% for 48h with no regressions, then progressively rolled to 50% and full enabling under monitoring.
Gateway: introduce rate-aware routing policy and connection-level stream backoff; improves function-invocation handshake stability and reduces streaming stalls under bursty workloads.
Jonah Park: The router scoring looks reasonable, but can we expose the short-term window size via config and make it per-route? Request to add route-level override in defaults.yaml.
Aisha Menon: Added route-level override and documented defaults; kept system-wide fallback to avoid config explosion. See commit d2e7a18.
Priya Kapoor: The X-Redwood-Fncall-End header is a nice addition. Need a security note in compat shim to strip/validate header to avoid header-injection attacks.
Aisha Menon: Validated and canonicalized header values in compat shim; added unit tests for malformed header handling (commit b3c8f42).
Marco Giannini: CI e2e failed the first run with intermittent timeouts in the writer smoothing test. Please investigate flakiness and add a retry helper for the test harness.
Aisha Menon: Reproduced flaky timing locally, added deterministic clock injection in tests and a retry wrapper for the e2e harness. Re-ran CI; all green.
Priya Kapoor: Approved after test flakiness addressed and telemetry added. Please add a brief note in release notes about the feature flag default-off behavior.
Aisha Menon: Release notes entry added and verified with docs owner.

Context: Long-tail SLO noise and prefetched-token accounting have been recurring pain points for customer-facing observability. Root cause: (1) existing samplers capture only past spans and biased warm traces, making it hard to surface which future-prefetch decisions (eg. cache pre-warm or assistant tool calls) actually drove cost spikes, and (2) token cost attribution treats all generated tokens as a monolith and loses origin semantics (system vs user vs prefetch vs tool).

Proposal: Introduce the Invocation Horizon Sampler (IHS) + Token Cost Origins mapper. IHS gathers an invocation-centric micro-window spanning pre-invoke signals, request lifetime, and a short "horizon" of downstream prefetch/tool invocations (up to 2s after invocation start) and emits a single sampled digest. The Token Cost Origins mapper annotates per-token cost/latency with an origin tag and phase (prompt, generation, tool, postprocess) so dashboards and alerts can attribute SLO noise to the correct causal surface.

What this PR changes: single-continuous description of changes and rationale. 1) Telemetry: add horizon-sampled invocation digest event, new schema fields: horizon_id, origin_tags, phase_breakdown, cost_signature. 2) Sampler: implement IHS in observability-sidecar with an adaptive sampling budget that prefers low-cardinality route+model pairs and keeps reservoir per-tenant. 3) Token attribution: enrich token emission pipeline to attach origin metadata pulled from the request graph (caller, tool, prefetch module). 4) Dashboard: add "Origin Cost Explorer" dashboard and an "Horizon Spike Investigator" panel that correlates horizon samples with kernel/backpressure metrics. 5) Alerts/playbook: add tuned alert rules that can suppress noise when origin is prefetch and route low-traffic. 6) Docs: add an observability-runbook section describing how to interpret origin tags and an example incident triage flow.

Motivation and tradeoffs: This approach increases event cardinality modestly but improves signal-to-noise for SLO debugging and cost RCA. The horizon window is conservative (2s default) to avoid unbounded correlation. We intentionally keep origin tags coarse (system/user/tool/prefetch/unknown) to prevent cardinality explosion.

Backward compatibility: New fields are additive; older consumers ignore horizon_id and origin_tags. Default sampling rate is off for free-tier tenants and enabled in staged rollout for prod tenants.

Rollout plan: staged in three waves: canary (internal + dev tenants), limited prod (5% traffic routed), wide (config to all). Monitoring: added dashboards and a synthetic probe (observability/ci job) to validate horizon sample capture.

Checklist:
- [x] Implementation: sampler + token mapper + ingest schema
- [x] Unit/integration tests for horizon sampler and mapper
- [x] End-to-end synthetic replay test to ensure deterministic attribution
- [x] Docs + runbook update
- [x] Dashboard panels and alert rules added

Notes: Related to ENG-4521 (reduce SLO noise) and OBS-110 (prefetch accounting). This PR purposely avoids adding high-cardinality free-text origin labels; we can expand origin taxonomy in a follow-up after measuring cardinality.
Arjun Patel (reviewer): Can we validate that adding origin_tags won't push high-cardinality metrics downstream? Requested a cardinality cap and fallback to 'unknown' when cardinality threshold is exceeded.
Leah Martinez (author): Added reservoir per-tenant + cardinality cap (configurable via OBS_CARDINALITY_CAP). Fallback behavior documented in runbook. See commit b2e8f12.
Maya Chen (reviewer): Alert suppression LGTM but please include a manual override to disable suppression during incident drills.
Leah Martinez (author): Added 'suppress_prefetch_noise' toggle and documented drill overrides in alerts YAML. See commit d44a6ee.
Tomás Rivera (reviewer): Add a test that simulates tool-driven token storm to ensure cost attribution resolves to 'tool' origin.
Leah Martinez (author): Added replaybench fixture and deterministic test. See tests/observability/test_horizon_sampler.py.
Unit tests cover sampler reservoir, cardinality cap, and token-origin mapping. Integration replaybench runs a synthetic workload that exercises prefetch and tool calls; asserts tokens are labeled correctly and cost tallies by origin match ground truth. E2E will run in canary with synthetic probe that emits known prefetch sequences to validate end-to-end capture.
Introduce Invocation Horizon Sampler and Token Cost Origins: improves observability for prefetch/tool noise and enables origin-aware cost attribution. Add new dashboard 'Origin Cost Explorer' and 'Horizon Spike Investigator'. Alerts include origin-aware suppression toggles.
Ops: enable OBS_HORIZON_SAMPLER=false to roll back runtime capture immediately. To disable origin-aware suppression set alerts.suppress_prefetch_noise=false in alerts config. Watch dashboard 'Horizon Spike Investigator' and synthetic probe for regressions.

Context and motivation: Our presubmit lanes have been a major source of noisy CI and developer friction — long lint runs, transient toolchain drift, and repeated full-test shards for small changes. This PR introduces two complementary features: (1) presubmit-lite mode, an opt-in path that runs a warm-cache light lint + targeted test shard selection for small/iterative commits, and (2) a toolchain snapshotter that records the devcontainer/tool versions used when a developer runs a local presubmit, then reuses that snapshot to stabilize fastpath CI runs. The goal is to reduce average presubmit feedback time and lower unnecessary CI resource consumption without changing the strong-of-main presubmit guarantees.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a presubmit-lite orchestration mode behind a feature flag and repo config: .github/presubmit-lite.yml. Teams can enable for folders with fast feedback constraints.
- Implements a lightweight lint cache warmer that pre-populates the node/rust/python linters' caches on ephemeral runners to avoid cold-start penalties.
- Adds an adaptive test-shard router: small changes (determined by path-aware heuristics and a delta token budget) are routed to targeted shards; larger changes fall back to full integration presubmit.
- Introduces toolchain snapshotter: command-line shim (tools/snapshotter) that captures and uploads a compact snapshot (tool versions, package-lock hash, devcontainer digest) as a repo artifact and a presubmit label. CI reuses snapshots to create hermetic fastpath runner images.
- Adds telemetry hooks (metrics + a compact presubmit audit log) so we can measure latency, hit-rate, and cache-warm success.

Why this is safe: The main presubmit path is unchanged; presubmit-lite is opt-in and gated by a repository config value with an allowlist. All fastpath runs include a final lightweight merge-base consistency check and a forced full presubmit for PRs touching critical paths (runtime/, infra/, release/). The snapshotter only affects the runner image used for fastpath; it does not alter build artifacts or production runtime images.

Commits (summary):
- feat(ci): presubmit-lite orchestrator and config parsing
- feat(ci): implement cache-warming helper for eslint/ruff/cargo
- feat(ci): adaptive test shard router with path heuristics
- feat(ci): tools/snapshotter CLI and upload hook
- perf(ci): use snapshot digest to seed ephemeral runner images
- test(ci): add end-to-end integration harness + unit tests for heuristics
- docs: presubmit-lite README and ops playbook

Files changed (high level):
- .github/presubmit-lite.yml - new opt-in config
- .github/workflows/presubmit-lite.yml - presubmit-lite workflow that reuses existing actions with warmers
- tools/snapshotter/* - CLI shim (Go) that captures toolchain state and uploads artifact
- infra/runner-seed/seed-image-helpers.sh - small helper to apply snapshot to runner bootstrap
- ci/warmers/{lint_warmer.rs,lint_warmer.py} - language-specific cache warmers
- ci/shard-router/*.ts - router logic and heuristic tests
- docs/ops/presubmit-lite.md - rollout and troubleshooting

Testing and CI:
- Local unit tests added for router heuristics and snapshot parsing.
- Integration test in a lightweight matrix (node/python/rust) that validates end-to-end: snapshot capture -> seeded runner -> warm-cache -> targeted shard selection.
- CI initially flaked on the Rust warmer due to a path race in cache initialization (see reviews). Fixed by adding a temp directory lock and retry logic.
- Final CI status: all checks passed (lint, unit, integration, e2e matrix). Full details available in the checks summary.

Review conversation (high level):
- Ethan Morales (review): "Nice reduction in complexity compared to earlier proposal. Two asks: tighten the allowlist semantics and add an opt-out label for the PR UI so reviewers can force a full presubmit. Also can we make the snapshot upload size limit explicit?"
- Priya (author reply): "Addressed: added allowlist semantics to .github/presubmit-lite.yml and implemented a PR label override (ci/force-full-presubmit). Snapshotter now enforces a 512KB compressed payload limit and will fall back to a toolchain digest-only mode if exceeded."
- Lena Park (review): "Concern: adaptive router heuristic might under-approx small-but-impactful changes (e.g., proto changes). Suggest explicit file pattern blockers."
- Priya: "Added blocker patterns for runtime/, models/, schema/ and a final merge-base check. Documentation updated with examples."
- Omar Haddad (review): "Telemetry looks good but add a simple dashboard query for median presubmit latency and cache-warm hit rate."
- Priya: "Added metrics and a Grafana panel link in ops docs; will follow up with dashboards in infra repo."
- Approvals: Ethan/Merged after a squash-and-merge once CI green.

Migration and rollout plan (ops notes):
- Feature is opt-in. Teams enable by adding .github/presubmit-lite.yml to their repo root and toggling the allowlist.
- Pilot with SDKs (redwood-sdk-python and redwood-sdk-typescript) for two weeks. Measure: 40% reduction in median presubmit latency and 25% fewer full-run CI hours.
- After pilot, default enable for non-runtime repos with a coordinated announcement and training doc.

Known limitations and follow-ups (todo):
- Snapshotter currently records package-lock yarn.lock and cargo.lock hashes; we plan to extend to Dockerfile hashes for container toolchains.
- Heuristics will be refined after we have more telemetry — follow-up ENG tasks created (ENG-2160).
- We observed occasional checksum mismatches for devcontainer digests on older runner images; infra ticket created (ENG-2161).

Merge details:
- Merge method: squash and merge
- Squash title: "presubmit: add presubmit-lite orchestrator + toolchain snapshotter"
- Merged by: Ethan Morales on 2026-02-20

If you want to test locally:
- ./tools/snapshotter capture --out ./snapshot.json
- ./tools/snapshotter upload --file ./snapshot.json --repo redwood --pr 1234
- Run the lightweight workflow using the presubmit-lite label or by committing .github/presubmit-lite.yml with your allowlist entry.

Contact: Priya Choudhary (author) for rollout questions and infra follow-ups.
Adds an opt-in presubmit-lite mode that warms lint/test caches and a toolchain snapshotter that pins devcontainer/tool versions to reduce presubmit variance and speed feedback.

payload.body:
Motivation: Reduce presubmit latency and improve dependency hygiene by introducing a lightweight presubmit plugin that runs a fast dependency-audit pass and orchestrates staged lint/test lanes. This PR introduces an orchestrator service and a GitHub Actions plugin wrapper that performs targeted checks based on changed paths, runs a fast dependency snapshot + vulnerability audit, and fences slow checks into staged lanes.

Summary of changes: - new presubmit plugin (go) that inspects changed files and emits a compact manifest for the runner - dependency-audit harness that generates a lockfile snapshot and runs safety checks against a curated advisory feed - action composite wrapper and action.yml to wire the plugin into existing workflows - small upgrades to makefile and ci tooling to expose path-matching predicates - migration of the monolithic lint job into three staged lanes (fast, medium, slow) with a coordinator step - integration tests for the plugin and sample workflow templates under .github/quickpaths

Checklist: - [x] implement plugin core and CLI - [x] composite Action wrapper + action.yml - [x] unit tests for path-matching and audit logic - [x] integration workflows in repo: ci/integ-presubmit.yml - [x] docs: docs/ci/presubmit-plugin.md - [x] staged rollout via feature flag

Rollout plan: Feature-flag off by default. Motivation: teams building long-lived streaming flows need consistent session semantics, predictable credential handoff, and compact retry profiles across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. This PR consolidates previous ad-hoc session shims into a small cross-language SessionMiddleware plus a compact RetryPolicy abstraction that encodes per-stream backoff hints and warmup directives. The goal is pragmatic parity: single conceptual model for session lifecycle + minimal ergonomic primitives for users to adopt without rewriting existing streaming code.

Summary of changes: added a new SessionMiddleware interface and reference implementations in python/ts/go; introduced RetryPolicy compact profile and three defaults (fast, balanced, patient); replaced legacy StreamCursor+Resumer plumbing with a simplified PullStreamCursor that exposes a single async iterator/chan-friendly API per language; added a compact credential-swap adapter that performs background token refresh and exposes a lightweight event hook for telemetry; bumped SDK package versions (py 2.4.0, ts 1.7.0, go 1.5.3); updated docs and migration guide.

Notable files and diffs (high level): see files_changed for concrete list. Changes are intentionally small per-language: python focuses on async iterator ergonomics, typescript adds an ergonomic pullstream facade and a Promise-based warmup API, go focuses on channel-friendly PullStreamCursor and low-allocation retry loop. No changes to server APIs or wire protocol.

Compatibility & migration notes: default behavior is backward compatible. New functionality is behind opt-in flags: SessionMiddleware is not injected by default; SDKs provide a one-line opt-in helper (e.g. RedwoodSession.enable_default_middleware()). Applications that previously depended on internal cursor rehydration should follow the migration guide included in docs/migration/session-unifier.md.

Testing and validation: unit tests and integration matrix added for each SDK; added cross-language integration test that exercises a long-lived streaming scenario, credential rotation, and failover to fallback model. Performance bench: small improvement in median tail-latency under high concurrent stream counts due to reduced allocation churn and simplified cursor state.

Rollout plan: merged to main behind feature-flag in platform; gradual rollout to hosted and dedicated customers using canary groups. Follow-ups: telemetry enrichment for per-stream retry buckets (ENG-2104), a docs RFC to align examples across languages (ENG-2112), and a future opt-in server hook to surface session state for observability (ENG-2176).
Introduce cross-language SessionMiddleware + compact RetryPolicy; bump python/sdk -> v2.4.0, typescript/sdk -> v1.7.0, go/sdk -> v1.5.3; ergonomics improvements for streaming iterators and credential warm-up. No breaking API changes for public surface; opt-in config flags for advanced behaviors.

Adds elastic reserve windows and stochastic timeout jitter to the continuous batching scheduler. Improves p95 latency and reduces starvation for KV-heavy workloads. Config knobs added under scheduler.defaults. Rollout controlled by continuous-batcher.v2 feature flag.
Motivation: Continuous-batcher has been the primary low-latency path for short-sequence requests, but we still observe tail spikes and intermittent starvation under mixed KV and compute-heavy workloads. This PR introduces two complementary scheduler features: (1) elastic reserve windows - a per-queue dynamic reservation that adapts to short-lived queue pressure to protect latency-sensitive flows without statically reserving capacity; and (2) stochastic timeout jitter - small randomized timeout offsets applied to order-sensitive probes to reduce synchronized timeout storms and thundering herd effects. Both changes are designed to be low-risk and behind a feature flag (continuous-batcher.v2) for staged rollout.

Design summary: elastic reserve windows maintain a small movable budget (in slot units) that adjusts on an EWMA of queue horizon and recent service time. When a queue's horizon grows above a threshold the window expands to ensure a minimum number of immediate dequeues for latency-critical requests; when pressure subsides the window decays so global throughput is not harmed. Stochastic timeout jitter injects bounded, deterministic randomness into inter-probe timers and soft-timeout promotions so that multiple probes don't escalate simultaneously. To avoid negative interaction with autoscaling and admission heuristics we clamp jitter to a small fraction of the timeout (default 5-8%) and expose the profile via configuration.

KV-awareness: To prevent KV-heavy tenants from monopolizing reserve windows we added a lightweight tenant scoring heuristic that downweights requests with heavy KV pin usage and upweights low-KV short requests. The score is computed from recent KV hit/miss ratios and sequence-length histograms (EWMA). This heuristic participates in elastic reserve admission but does not change global priority ordering; it only biases eligibility for reserve slots.

Kernel hints: The scheduler now emits an optional kernel-hint flag with each dequeued batch indicating expected average sequence length and whether KV-cache lookups are likely. The backend inference runtime uses this flag to prefer short-sequence kernels or prefetch KV lanes. This is explicitly advisory and has no semantic effect if the runtime ignores the hint.

Testing and benchmarks: Microbenchmarks on a mixed workload (60% short chat, 30% KV-lookup rerank, 10% long completion) show a median p95 latency improvement of ~15% for short requests and a global throughput increase of ~4% when the feature flag is enabled with default knobs. KV hit rate improved +8% in tests where the prefetcher used kernel hints. Regression tests cover reserve window growth/decay, jitter bounds, and fairness properties; stress tests run for 6 hours to detect slow drift. A flaky test in CI (continuous_batcher_timing_test) failed once during the first run due to an unrelated timing race; it was retried and passed on the second run. All other suites passed.

Rollout plan: Feature gated via continuous-batcher.v2. Step 1: internal canary on a small dedicated pool (1 week). Step 2: staged tenant opt-in for Dedicated customers with traffic probes (2 weeks). Step 3: gradual ramp to default-on for hosted where SLOs are met (3 weeks). Immediate rollback by toggling continuous-batcher.v2 off; the code path intentionally preserves previous behavior when the flag is false. We will monitor p95/p99, tail drop counts, and KV hit metrics during rollout.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-2013) - [x] Unit + integration tests added - [x] Microbenchmarks with baseline and deltas - [x] Feature flag and config knobs - [x] Docs updated (scheduler knobs) - [x] Rollout playbook added

Risks and mitigations: Elastic reserve windows could reduce global batching efficiency if misconfigured; we mitigate by conservative defaults (small window size, slow growth EWMA) and an automatic decay policy. Jitter could mask real systemic timeouts if set too large; we clamp and log any repeated promotions for visibility. KV scoring is intentionally lightweight to avoid per-request overhead; we sample-heavy paths for scoring updates.
Liam Chen: Can you clarify the growth rate constants used by the EWMA for the reserve window? Small changes there can flip behavior under bursty traffic.
Author (Maya Ortiz): Added comments next to the constants and exposed them as config knobs. We tuned them from 0.15 to 0.05 alpha after observing overshoot during local replay.
Sofia Patel: The kernel-hint field is a useful signal but we should avoid coupling the runtime. Please make it optional in the protobuf and document the advisory semantics.
Author (Maya Ortiz): Made kernel-hint optional and added documentation; also added a no-op path in the runtime so older binaries ignore it safely.
Arun Iyer: LGTM pending one test flake fix in continuous_batcher_timing_test (race on simulated clock).
Author (Maya Ortiz): Fixed race by pinning simulated clock to a monotonic source in the test harness; pushed fix.
Liam Chen: Approved and merged. Noted a small follow-up to evaluate different jitter distributions (gaussian vs uniform) in ENG-2067.
SRE (automated): CI rerun due to flaky timing test. All checks green on second run.

Context: Our presubmit lanes have accumulated a large universe of dependency bumps and full-lane lint runs which lengthen feedback and increase flakiness. Recent incidents during a Dedicated rollout highlighted a transitive dependency mismatch that slips past staged checks because dependency rotation runs are coarse-grained and run infrequently. This PR introduces a targeted dependency rotation mechanism and a stage-aware presubmit orchestration layer that reduces CI noise, speeds feedback for common edits, and ensures dependency updates exercise the same staged lanes used for release candidates.

Summary of changes: 1) Add a small service/runner component (presubmit-orch) that computes a minimal set of lanes to run based on changed paths plus a targeted dependency-rotation plan when package-locks or go.sum change. 2) Implement a dependency-rotation scheduler that runs lightweight upgrade probes (no rebuild) and escalates to full integration lanes only when heuristics indicate high-risk (major semver bump, native deps touched). 3) Split lint/test matrix into: quick (fast local checks + staged path sniffing), staged (per-target integration), and rotation (dependency-only probes). 4) Add new YAML templates and a thin action wrapper so repos can opt-in per-folder. 5) Update docs and GraphQL endpoint used by the PR dashboard for visibility.

Motivation: We want fast turnarounds for typical code changes (sub-10m feedback) while still increasing cadence and coverage of dependency rotation without taxing our full integration infrastructure. This preserves quality for release paths by ensuring dependency updates hit the same staged lanes used for release smoke tests.

What changed (high-level): - presubmit/orchestrator/runner: new orchestrator that inspects changed files and kicks off the minimal lane set. - .github/workflows/presubmit-staged.yml: new template that uses the orchestrator decision. - actions/dep-rotation: action to run targeted dependency probes with heuristics and cacheable probes. - buildkite/ci-templates: updated to allow staged lanes to be triggered by the orchestrator for dedicated runs. - docs/dev/ci-presubmit.md: documentation and opt-in guide.

Testing and rollout: Unit tests for the orchestrator heuristics and integration tests running in the benchmark-lab were added. Ran canary on redwood-examples and redwood-sdk-python for two weeks: median presubmit time for code-only edits dropped from ~18m to ~6m; dependency-rotation increased number of shallow probes by 3x but full integration lane runs remained stable. CI on this branch: initial run had two flaky integration failures; both were traced to timing in a test harness and fixed in follow-up commits. All checks passing at merge.

Migration and opt-in: Default behavior is no-op until repo-level opt-in via .github/presubmit-config.yml. We added an opt-in guide and a migration checklist; platform teams can enable orchestrator per folder, and there is a rollback flag to stop orchestrator-triggered lanes if issues arise.

Risks and mitigations: Risk of missing a necessary integration-run for rare transitive changes mitigated by: 1) rotation heuristics conservative for native or major bumps, 2) nightly full-rotation job retained, and 3) dashboard alerting for any dependency probe failures that would escalate.

Related work: ENG-7249 introduced the initial lane-slicing heuristics; ENG-7310 defines rotation semantics and alerting. SUP-1032 tracked the production dependency incident that motivated this change.

Release notes: introduces targeted dependency rotation and stage-aware presubmit orchestration to speed presubmit feedback and centralize dependency probe logic.

Checklist:

- [x] Integration tests for rotation probes
- [x] Canary run on two repositories (redwood-examples, redwood-sdk-python)
- [x] Documentation and opt-in guide
- [x] Rollout plan with rollback flag

Merge notes: Squash merge. Post-merge: deployed orchestrator to the presubmit runner pool and published docs to the internal docs site.

Author (Aisha Patel): Done; heuristics now escalate to full lanes for semver-major changes and when native modules are present.
Lena Hoffmann: The new action runner looks heavier than expected; can we make the probe more cache-friendly?
Author (Aisha Patel): Adjusted probe to reuse lockfile diffs and added a local-state cache to reduce repeated resolution work; benchmark shows 40% CPU savings on probes.
Devon Kim: Tests look good; please add a dashboard alert for failed rotation probes so SRE can triage quickly.
Author (Aisha Patel): Added presubmit.rotation_probe_failed alert and documentation to the SRE playbook section.

Motivation: customers expect /v1/chat.completions parity for legacy OpenAI clients while we preserve Redwood runtime performance and structured tool outputs. This PR introduces a shallow parameter gateway that canonicalizes incoming v1/chat params, enforces a single source of truth for stop/logprob behavior, and hardens the streaming handshake for tool/function calls so that fragmented Deltas are reassembled deterministically.

What changed (summary): consolidated param translation and validation into api/compat/v1_chat_gateway.go; introduced a small translator in api/compat/param_translator.py to centralize role/stop/logprob rules; consolidated streaming boundary handling into runtime/stream/stream_coordinator.rs and added explicit fragment sequence numbers and heartbeat reconciliation; improved KV cache lifetime hints in runtime/kv_cache/cache_manager.cpp to avoid token duplication on retries; added compatibility shims in sdk/python/openai_compat.py to keep existing client semantics.

Behavioral impacts: stop semantics now prefer explicit stop arrays, with fallback to heuristics that match OpenAI historical behavior; logprob reporting is now consistent between streaming and final payloads (we emit a combined logprobs.summary when streaming was used); function/tool call handshake uses a 3-way fragment acknowledgment to avoid mid-stream truncation of tool responses.

Testing and validation: unit tests added in tests/unit for param translation rules; integration tests in tests/integration/test_chat_parity.py cover streaming recovery, stop normalization, and toolcall reassembly across network interruptions. Background: Dedicated fleets serve a mix of steady tenants and bursty tenants. Short, intense bursts are valuable for customer experience but can trigger aggressive preemption/eviction that harms long‑running tenants and causes oscillation. This PR introduces two cooperating pieces: a time‑weighted burst credit allocator (TWBCA) that smooths burst consumption over a configurable half‑life, and a respectful eviction controller (REC) that uses the TWBCA signal plus utilization patterns to prefer reclamation from sustained, low‑priority consumers while avoiding immediate eviction for transient overshoot.

What this changes: added a new crediting model: each tenant now accrues a time‑weighted burst balance that decays with a configurable half_life_ms. When a tenant consumes burst tokens, the draw reduces the balance and increases a short lived "burst_pressure" metric. The autoscaler and preemption path consult both current instantaneous utilization and the TW balance to decide whether to trigger preemption. REC computes an eviction_score that mixes (1) normalized sustained utilization, (2) TW balance (higher balance => lower eviction preference), and (3) preemption_cooldown windows to avoid thrash.

Key goals: reduce eviction churn during short bursts, preserve throughput guarantees for committed tenants, and provide predictable telemetry for capacity planning.

Implementation details: - controller/twbca: new loop that samples per-tenant token consumption and updates a compact EWMA state (64b per tenant) stored alongside reservation metadata. Uses integer math in hot path and converts to double only for export. - controller/rec: integrates with existing leasebook and scorecard pipelines. Supports pluggable scoring weights and configurable preemption_window_ms. - config schema changes: added dedicated.twbca.enabled, dedicated.twbca.half_life_ms, dedicated.rec.preemption_window_ms, dedicated.rec.eviction_weight_factors (sustained, burst_balance, cooldown). Defaults are conservative (TWBCA off by default; REC can be enabled cluster‑wide or per‑pool). - telemetry: new metrics exported via prometheus: redwood_dedicated_twb_balance{tenant}, redwood_rec_eviction_score{tenant,pool}, redwood_rec_preemption_cooldown_active{tenant}. Also added histogram redwood_rec_evict_latency_ms. - tests: unit tests for EWMA math, integration tests with synthetic load to validate eviction prioritization, and an end‑to‑end canary harness that runs in perf‑canary repo.

Rollout plan: start with TWBCA disabled by default. Enable REC in a canary dedicated pool for 2 weeks with verbose metrics. If stable, flip TWBCA on with half_life_ms=300000 (5m) for canary, then progressively increase to 15m for tenants with bursty workloads. Document knobs and recommended values in the Dedicated capacity ops runbook.

Checklist:
- [x] EWMA algorithm and math vetted in design doc (ENG-1298)
- [x] Unit and integration tests added
- [x] Metrics and dashboards (DevOps) wired up
- [x] Backwards compatible config with safe defaults
- [x] Release notes drafted

Risks and mitigation: If half_life too short we fall back to prior behavior; if too long we could underreact to actual overcommit and starve low‑priority tenants. Mitigations: conservative defaults, gradual rollout, automatic kill‑switch that reverts to legacy eviction when global eviction_rate > configured threshold.

Related: references the preemption_window work (ENG-2021) for the cooldown gating. Also ties into the per‑tenant telemetry collector work in metrics team to allow capacity planners to set reservation buffers.

Notes on code hygiene: added a feature flag gate and feature toggle in the runtime feature registry. All new exported config keys are documented in the schema and validated in the bootstrap path.

Sofia: Concern about default off — how will we surface the improvement? Author: added canary dashboard and perf‑canary job to measure eviction churn and tail latency.
Diego: Question on integer math edge cases. Author: added tests for overflow and rounding; moved conversion points out of hot path.
Arun: +1 after addressing race in leasebook read path. Sofia: approved. Diego: approved with minor nits fixed.

Motivation: multiple customers hit friction when upgrading SDKs because streaming consumer ergonomics and credential retry configuration were not aligned across languages. This PR converges three workstreams: (1) introduce a small 'ConsumableStream' consumer surface that normalizes async generator/pull-stream usage patterns, (2) simplify credential bootstrapping by adding a transparent preflight + lightweight backoff preset that is shared across SDKs, and (3) bump SDK minor versions with migration guidance.

What changed (high-level): added a small shim that exposes a single-worker-friendly streaming consumer API with deterministic teardown semantics; centralized credential preflight that attempts fast path token refresh on connection errors and falls back to a conservative backoff (100ms -> 1s -> 2s) before surfacing permanent failure; unified retry config keys (retry_profile -> retryPreset) and documented deprecation. The change is intentionally additive: old call shapes continue to work but will emit a deprecation warning when non-idiomatic patterns are used.

Repos touched: sdk/python, sdk/typescript, sdk/go, docs, examples, CI.

Key design notes: the ConsumableStream surface is minimal: "for await (chunk of stream)" / async for generator in Python / channel consumer in Go all map to a small helper that guarantees: (a) implicit cancellation on handler exception, (b) idempotent close semantics, and (c) consistent telemetry tags (sdk.language, sdk.stream.consumed). Credential flow: added preflight-check in transport layer that runs once per connection and uses credential adapters to try a non-blocking refresh. If refresh fails transiently we retry per the shared preset. This reduces noisy 401s during cold-starts.

Migration & compatibility: existing streaming APIs are compatible but to get the ergonomic surface users should switch to the new helper (examples updated). The retry_profile -> retryPreset rename is backward compatible for one minor: both keys are accepted for now; logs will report which key is used. This PR bumps the Python SDK to 0.19.0, TS SDK to 1.28.0, and Go SDK to v1.9.0.

- [x] TypeScript: add generator->ConsumableStream adapter, TS types + tests

- [x] Update release notes and migration guide

Motivation: reduce KV cache churn and tail latency for mixed workloads by introducing a segmented block pool that separates hot/cold pages and applies kernel-aware allocation hints. This PR implements a soft-pinning layer plus a dynamic eviction policy that accounts for model kernel usage patterns and sequence-length locality. Design highlights: 1) segmented_pool component maintains two logical segments (hot/cold) and migrates blocks based on access frequency and active kernel hints; 2) eviction policy is LRU-ST (LRU with sequence-time decay) so short-lived prefixes don't evict long-running contexts; 3) kernel-aware allocation: callers can attach an allocation hint (e.g. attention-optimized, kv-dense) that biases allocator to choose blocks that match the downstream execution path (reduces rematerialization and kernel fallback); 4) soft-pinning: soft pins mark blocks as preferred for a short window and are honored unless memory pressure forces forced eviction; soft pins are used for canary in-flight requests to avoid thrashing; 5) quotas: per-model soft quotas and burst-reserve to avoid noisy-neighbor regressions. Rollout approach: staged rollout behind a feature flag default-off, smoke tests in Dedicated, canary in Hosted for <100 accounts first, metric gates for increased traffic. Backwards compatibility: falls back to existing paged allocator when flag disabled. Testing and benchmarks: microbench harness added plus cluster-level perf job. Observed improvements: p50 latency for multi-turn chat workload down 9-14% and sustained throughput up 6-9% for batching window=20. CPU overhead small (~1-2% on scheduler path) while reducing GPU stalls from poor KV reuse. See files changed for details and benchmarks.
This targets recurring incidents where mixed small/long sequences caused prefix eviction of long-running KV contexts leading to expensive recompute on GPU kernels. Prior approaches (single paged allocator, softpin v1) reduced some churn but still allowed corner-case oscillation; segmented approach with kernel hints aligns allocator decisions with downstream kernel execution patterns and preserves long-lived contexts.
Introduce segmented block pool with hot/cold migration and kernel-aware allocation hints; add LRU-ST eviction to stabilize multi-turn workloads; add soft-pinning to reduce KV thrash; exposes config knobs: segment_size, soft_pin_ttl_ms, kernel_hint_weight; rollout behind feature flag; expected p50 improvement ~10% for multi-turn chat workloads
bench(cluster/multi-turn-chat): p50 latency -9..-14%, throughput +6..+9% at batching=20; GPU stall rate -18% in sampled traces; scheduler CPU +1.5% median overhead
Feature gated: toggle serve.runtime.segmented_pool.enable in allocator.yaml. Monitor metrics: kv.segment_migrations/sec, kv.forced_evictions, kv.soft_pins_active, scheduler.kernel_hint_miss_rate. Canary rollout recommended; rollback by disabling flag if forced_evictions spike.
Unit tests + microbench; Dedicated smoke; Hosted canary: 100 accounts -> 1k -> open. Add perf jobs to monitor 24h sliding windows during canary. Post-merge: schedule follow-up to evaluate long-tail p99 effects and tune decay constants.
Diego: Nice separation. Concern: migration path under heavy churn—what prevents oscillation between hot/cold? Author: added hysteresis and sequence-time decay to avoid oscillation; tuned defaults. Aisha: please add metric for 'forced_eviction_due_to_pressure' and expose soft_pin TTL via config. Author: added metric and config entry. Oliver: requested a simpler fallback for older private deployments with patched runtime; author: added a compatibility shim and unit tests. CI had a flaky scheduling test that was retried once; rerun green. Final approvers: Diego approved, Aisha approved after metrics added, Oliver approved after shim. Merge performed via squash.
No user-visible API changes. Internal config available. Added a short design doc under docs/perf/block-pool.md.

Motivation: Users have requested more graceful handling when a model's streaming output cannot be fully validated against a declared JSON schema (response_contract). Strict mode today either accepts or rejects a streaming response at the end, which is brittle for long-running streams and tool-calling flows. This PR introduces a soft-strict negotiation mode that: 1) tries to validate incrementally during streaming using lightweight checkpoints, 2) falls back to a best-effort coercion/diagnostic path when schema cannot be satisfied, and 3) emits clear deprecation and migration guidance for the legacy response_format field.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a negotiation backoff policy for response_contract validation that attempts incremental validation while the stream is live and uses backoff thresholds to switch to a best-effort mode instead of hard reject.
- Implements streaming checkpoints: the runtime emits small, signed checkpoint markers at configurable intervals so validators can resume validation when partial fragments arrive out of order. Checkpoints are lightweight and storage-backed with TTL.
- Introduces a "soft-strict" flag on the API surface and SDKs (sdk/python/redwood/schema_options.py) that opts the call into diagnostic-rich validation: validation errors are surfaced as structured diagnostics rather than immediate stream termination.
- Enhances OpenAI compatibility mapper to translate legacy response_format values into response_contract hints so older clients continue to behave predictably (api/openai_compat/response_mapper.go).
- Adds deprecation warnings for response_format in server responses and the CLI; docs updated with migration steps (docs/response_contracts.md).
- Wire up telemetry with reduced cardinality: validation outcome (ok/soft-fallback/hard-reject), time-to-first-valid-chunk, and checkpoint-count. Telemetry rules are in observability/telemetry_rules.yaml (opt-in by default).
- Comprehensive unit and integration tests for streaming validation, checkpoint resumption, and compat mapping.

Design notes:
- Soft-strict semantics: by default the runtime still enforces strict schema validation for non-streaming calls. For streaming calls the soft-strict signal allows the runtime to maintain low-latency response and provide diagnostics via a header + final payload field. This preserves signal for downstream tool callers while avoiding hard failures during transient model tokenization/formatting issues.
- Checkpointing: checkpoints are intentionally minimal (seq_id, kv-hash, byte-offset, signature) to allow fast resume and verification without storing full partial responses. Checkpoints are TTL'd (configurable) and not retained in long-term logs.
- Backoff policy: exponential backoff with jitter; after N failed attempts we emit a soft-fallback state and continue streaming. The thresholds are tunable by customer and default to conservative values validated in perf canary.

Rollout and flags:
- Feature gate: runtime config flag "enable_soft_strict_schema" (disabled by default for enterprise Private installs). Hosted will enable opt-in for beta customers.
- SDKs: Python SDK exposes allow_soft_strict=True on the generation call; TS/Go SDKs will follow in a follow-up patch (tracked in ENG-1587).
- Observability: telemetry is opt-in; verbose diagnostics are gated to avoid PII exposure.

Migration guide (short):
- If you use response_format today, update to response_contract by following docs/response_contracts.md. The server will include migration headers for two release cycles. Quick path: set response_contract to a minimal schema (top-level object with optional fields) and enable allow_soft_strict during testing to observe diagnostics.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implementation in runtime + compat mapping
- [x] SDK flag in Python
- [x] Unit/integration tests
- [x] Docs + migration guidance
- [x] Telemetry rule (opt-in)

CI and perf notes: The integration canary run exercised endpoint-level latency and found <2% p50 increase for typical short chat requests; large-token streaming flows saw ~7% overhead when checkpoints are enabled (configurable). Canaries and perf-lab reports are attached to the Linear ticket.

Merge notes: Squashed into a single commit for readability and small revert path. See merge commit for the final canonical patch.

Related: ENG-1492 (streaming schema strategy), ENG-1587 (SDK flags), SUP-4421 (customer incident that motivated soft-fallback behavior).
Aisha Patel: Nice incremental approach. Two asks: reduce telemetry cardinality for model_name+schema_id combos and add an explicit opt-out for private installs. Please add unit tests for the checkpoint TTL edge case.
Ethan Romero (author): Addressed in commit 5: lowered telemetry granularity to outcome only + added opt-in flag for enterprise private. Added test for TTL expiry and documented caveat.
Liam O'Connor: Question on security: are checkpoints signed to prevent injection? Also please ensure checkpoint metadata doesn't leak user payload.

Author reply: Checkpoints include an HMAC signature and only store offsets/hashes, not raw tokens. Added unit test to verify no payload in checkpoint storage and updated docs to mention signing (docs/response_contracts.md).
Marisol Vega: Observability looks good; can we gate verbose diagnostics behind a role-based permission?

Author reply: Added check in the console and SDK to require permission 'schema.diagnostics:read' for verbose payloads.
Introduce soft-strict response_contract negotiation with streaming checkpoints and backward compatibility mapping for response_format. Adds opt-in telemetry and SDK flags to observe validation diagnostics. See docs/response_contracts.md for migration guidance.
Enable allow_soft_strict in SDKs to observe diagnostics before migrating. Replace response_format with response_contract gradually; legacy response_format will be supported with compat mapping for two release cycles. Follow docs/response_contracts.md for examples.
This PR focuses on production safety for structured output and tool-calling workflows. It is intentionally conservative: feature is opt-in and gated to avoid surprising behavior in strict production workloads. We plan follow-ups to add TS/Go SDK flags and a console toggle for beta customers.
payload.title: soft-strict-schema-negotiation-with-streaming-checkpoints-and-deprecation-messaging

Summary: This PR tightens the deploy gate introduced in pr-28510 (warn-only) by enforcing a release freeze when a tier’s error budget is exhausted. When the gate is in a BLOCK state, non-emergency deploys fail fast in CI and surface a clear remediation message (link to tier dashboard + runbook). Emergency deploys remain possible, but require an explicit override token and incident metadata, and are posted to #eng-sre for auditability. Motivation: We’ve had recurring cases where we continued shipping feature rollouts during active budget exhaustion, prolonging recovery and making ownership ambiguous. This change aligns enforcement with the approved error budget policy (multi-window burn alerts + consequences) and creates a consistent “stop the line” behavior per tier. Policy behavior: (1) Gate evaluates the 30d rolling error budget state for the target tier(s) impacted by the deploy (hosted_shared, dedicated_reserved). (2) If budget_remaining_percent <= 0.0 OR budget_state == EXHAUSTED, gate blocks by default. (3) Exceptions: emergency mitigation/rollback deployments only, with required override fields. (4) Overrides are logged (CI artifact + audit log event) and announced in Slack with a standard template. Emergency override procedure: To perform an emergency deploy when the tier budget is exhausted, set REDWOOD_DEPLOY_OVERRIDE=emergency and provide (a) INCIDENT_ID (PagerDuty/Slack/incidents thread permalink) and (b) REASON (1–2 sentences). The gate validates required fields, attaches them to the deploy metadata, and emits an audit event. If these fields are missing, the deploy is blocked. Implementation details: The gate uses the existing budget computation service endpoint (slo-budget-api) to fetch a tier-scoped status snapshot (window=30d, refresh_tolerance=10m). The gate is intentionally conservative: if the budget service is unreachable or returns stale data beyond tolerance, we fail closed for non-emergency deploys (and fail open only for rollbacks tagged as emergency). We also added unit tests around state transitions and a small integration test for the CI action wrapper. Operator UX: CI output includes (a) detected tier(s), (b) budget state, (c) link to the tiered SLO dashboard, (d) runbook link, and (e) instructions for emergency overrides. Rollout: This is enabled for Hosted and Dedicated pipelines in “enforced” mode. Sandbox/staging remains warn-only to reduce friction. Related: ENG-4941, error budget policy doc, and incident-bot burn summaries. Notes: We intentionally did not add per-model or per-customer gating here to avoid cardinality/ownership confusion; this gate is tier-scoped by design.
CI/CD: Non-emergency deploys are blocked when a tier’s 30d error budget is exhausted; emergency override requires incident context and is fully audited.
Aisha Bello (review): Can we confirm the definition of “exhausted” is strictly budget_remaining <= 0 on the canonical 30d window? We should avoid accidental blocks on short-term burn spikes (burn-rate alerts already cover that).
Connor O'Brien (author): Yes — this only blocks on the 30d budget snapshot reporting EXHAUSTED or remaining<=0. Burn alerts are separate and still page; we’re not blocking on burn-rate here to avoid flapping. Added an explicit comment + test case.
Jordan Lee (review): Fail-closed on budget API outage is good, but we need an emergency path that works even if the budget API is down (e.g., rollback during outage).
Connor O'Brien (author): Added “emergency + rollback” special-case: if override=emergency AND change_type=rollback, we allow deploy even when the budget API is unreachable, and we annotate the audit event with budget_state=UNKNOWN + reason.
Mina Haddad (review): How do we pick the tier(s) for a deploy? Routing changes can impact both hosted and dedicated depending on policy bundles.
Connor O'Brien (author): The gate reads impacted_tiers from the deploy manifest (generated during pipeline) and defaults to “hosted_shared” for gateway/routing bundles unless the manifest explicitly constrains scope. I added a note in docs and a safeguard: if impacted_tiers is empty, we block and ask for explicit scope (prevents accidental broad deploys).
Sahana Iyer (review): Please ensure overrides are not just Slack-only; we need durable audit logs for compliance and post-incident review.
Connor O'Brien (author): Done — override emits AUDIT_EVENT_DEPLOY_OVERRIDE with incident_id/reason/actor/pipeline + linked commit SHA. Slack is just a notification surface.
Rafael Mendes (review): Requesting a clearer runbook link and a standard message in CI so on-call isn’t debugging “why did my deploy fail?”.
Connor O'Brien (author): Updated CI output to include the error-budget breach mitigation runbook and the tiered SLO dashboard deep link. Added examples to docs/internal/deployments/error-budget-gate.md.
Aisha Bello (approval): Approved. This matches the enforcement phase expectations. Please coordinate enablement messaging in #eng-sre and with Release.
Rafael Mendes (approval): Approved.

Context: Customers operating under regional data residency requirements have asked for a safer, auditable enforcement point that prevents requests from being routed to out-of-region KMS or inference pools when a tenant or route is geo-locked. This PR introduces a lightweight enforcement layer (geo-lock enforcer) that evaluates a location claim on incoming requests, validates against a tenant-bound RBACv2 delegated-role mapping, and annotates audit events with KMS provenance. Motivation: Existing residency hooks were dispersed across routing and KMS allocators which made audits hard to reason about and increased the blast radius for misconfiguration. This change centralizes validation and provenance annotations so policy owners and auditors can trace why a request was allowed or rejected. Changes included: - pkg/policy/geo_enforcer.go: new enforcement module that validates request claims (region, geozone, tenant-assertion) against configured residency policies and RBAC role delegations. - pkg/rbac/delegation_mapper.go: RBACv2 helper that maps incoming operator/service claims to effective delegated roles with expiry and scope checks. - pkg/kms/provenance_adapter.go: wraps KMS allocator calls to emit signed provenance headers (kms-origin-prove) for successful key selections. - api/middleware/auth_geo.go: request middleware that wires enforcement into the API ingress path and short-circuits requests that fail geo-lock checks before model selection. - docs/compliance/geo-locking.md: new guide for compliance and SRE runbooks explaining expected audit fields and how to configure tenant-scoped policies. - helm/redwood/templates/config-enforcer.yaml: helm values and default config for the enforcer and delegation mapper. - tests/integration/geo_lock_e2e_test.go and tests/unit/*: tests covering positive/negative cases, expiry of delegated roles, and audit enrichment formats. Rollout plan: 1) Feature flagged behind runtime.enforcers.geo_lock (default off). 2) Canary on infra stage with subset of tenants pinned to geozone eu-west-1. 3) Monitor audit log volume and audit.provenance.kms-origin metrics for two weeks. 4) Gradual enable in production with weekly checks from compliance. Backwards compatibility: No breaking API behavior when flag is off. When on, requests missing a tenant claim will be rejected by default (documented in runbook). Tests: Added E2E test that simulates operators with delegated-role tokens to ensure enforcement allows valid delegated operations while rejecting cross-region key requests. Security review: Token expiry and delegation TTLs are enforced; mapping logic rejects wildcard delegation unless explicitly allowed per-tenant in Helm values. Performance: Enforcer caches delegation mappings for 5 minutes with invalidation on policy refresh; observed median p50 +0.6ms in a small bench. CI: full unit + integration suite passed; lint warnings fixed. Checklist: - [x] Implementation with unit tests - [x] Integration E2E - [x] Docs and runbook - [x] Feature flag and helm values - [x] Security review notes and threat model summary - [x] Telemetry (audit.kms_provenance, enforcer.decisions) Related work: referenced ENG-2547 for the centralized residency model and SEC-89 for KMS provenance requirements. Links: linear/ENG-2547, security/SEC-89. Merge: squash and merge to main after reviewers approved.
Marco Ruiz (reviewer) - please add a clear migration note for tenants that rely on global delegations. Also confirm cache invalidation semantics.
Priya Malhotra (author) - added migration notes to docs and reduced cache TTL to 5m; added policy refresh hook tests.
Ava Patel (reviewer) - can we surface an admin metric for 'delegation_mapped' vs 'delegation_missing' to help support triage?
Priya Malhotra (author) - added telemetry counters enforcer.delegation.mapped and enforcer.delegation.missing and updated observability docs.
Jonah Kim (approver) - security review complete, TTL checks and no-wildcard default are acceptable. Approving.
CI bot - all checks passed (unit, lint, integration).
Adds a feature-flagged geo-lock enforcement module that validates tenant region claims against RBACv2 delegated roles and annotates audit logs with KMS provenance. Off by default; enable via helm value runtime.enforcers.geo_lock. See docs/compliance/geo-locking.md for configuration and runbook.
payload.title: Introduce geo-lock enforcement and RBACv2 delegated-role mapper with KMS provenance adapter

Motivation: We have accumulated multiple ad-hoc session/reauth behaviors in the three SDKs that cause surprising reconnection patterns and duplicate heartbeats for long-lived streams. This PR introduces a harmonized session protocol v2 (wire-compatible fallback to v1) plus a small, ergonomic StreamFactory that produces cancelable async iterators/async generators across Python/TS/Go. Goals: 1) provide a single session lease/heartbeat contract that SDKs can rely on; 2) centralize adaptive reauth window logic and expose conservative defaults; 3) give application teams a simple cancelable iterator abstraction (with drain-on-cancel and optional graceful-finish) to reduce onboarding friction; 4) bump SDK versions with compat shims and add crosslang examples. Summary of changes (high level): - Add session-protocol v2 definitions and negotiation handshake in the client transport layer. v2 adds a lease_id and optional lease_ttl_jitter that servers can use for preferred refresh windows. Clients fall back to v1 when server does not support v2. - Introduce adaptive-reauth window: clients compute reauth_at = lease_expiry - min(max(lease_ttl * 0.15, 5s), 60s) and can apply a tunable jitter. This reduces simultaneous refresh storms. - New StreamFactory API in each SDK: Python: StreamFactory.cancelable_async_iter(stream_handle, on_cancel="drain" | "finish"); TypeScript: createCancelableAsyncIterator(stream, {onCancel}); Go: CancelableIterator wrapper with Context-cancellation integration. - Implement per-SDK compatibility shim that allows existing consumer patterns to keep working; new ergonomic patterns are opt-in. - Tighten telemetry: emit session.lease_acquired, session.lease_refreshed, session.lease_failed with attachable tags (sdk, version, region) and add counters for reauth_attempts and reauth_backoff_ms. - Tests: unit tests for handshake negotiation, simulated lease jitter, and cancel-on-cancel semantics; integration test fixture that runs a mock server that advertises v2. - Docs: cross-sdk example added to redwood-examples and API docs updated with migration notes. - Version bumps: py 1.8.0 -> 1.9.0, ts 1.27.0 -> 1.28.0, go 1.7.3 -> 1.8.0. Checklist: 
- [x] Cross-SDK API design review (ENG-2203)
- [x] Backwards compatibility shim in each SDK
- [x] Unit + integration tests
- [x] Telemetry added and validated in staging
- [x] Docs and examples updated
- [x] Release notes drafted Notes on compatibility and migration: The default behavior is backwards compatible; servers not advertising v2 continue to work. Teams that relied on manual heartbeat/resend loops should migrate to the StreamFactory cancel handlers to avoid duplicate drains. There is no expected breaking behavior, but SDK consumers that relied on implicit duplicated reauth calls in race windows may see fewer redundant refreshes (which is a correctness/perf win).
Diego Alvarez: Can we reduce the default reauth window to 10% instead of 15%? Concern is early churn for very short leases.
Lena Park: I tried 10% initially; 15% gives more headroom for noisy networks and aligns with our current implicit behavior. Added jitter min/max guard to avoid extreme cases.
Maya Chen: The Python cancelable iterator API looks ergonomic but can we document how drain vs finish interacts with in-flight errors?
Lena Park: Added a paragraph in the docs and updated unit tests to assert that onCancel='finish' will drain pending chunks and then close the iterator with the last error preserved.
Omar Rahman: Telemetry tags look good; can we emit a boolean session.v2_supported tag once per process?
Diego Alvarez: LGTMed after small nits (renamed a test helper).
Maya Chen: Approved.
Outcome: Addressed all review comments; Diego requested one last CI run after test flakiness fix and then merged with squash merge.
Added session-protocol v2 with lease-based reauth windows and a new cross-SDK StreamFactory providing cancelable iterators. Telemetry: session.lease_* metrics. SDK bumps: python 1.9.0, typescript 1.28.0, go 1.8.0. Backwards compatible; opt-in ergonomics for cancel behavior. See docs/sdk/session-protocol-v2.md for migration guidance.
QA ran a three-node integration harness with randomized lease_ttl (20-300s) for 6 hours; no unexpected double-refresh events observed, and iterator cancel semantics matched spec in 96/96 test scenarios. One flaky test fixed (handshake timing).
No runtime or infra changes required. For maintenance releases (if backporting to 1.8.x), apply session_shim only and skip StreamFactory for SDKs where major version policy forbids API additions.
- Publish SDK packages (py wheels, npm, go module)
- Notify integrations slack channel with migration notes and example link
- Promote telemetry dashboard for session.* metrics to staging -> prod
- Monitor reauth_attempts for first 72h after release
