Motivation: Over the last quarter we observed increased CI flakiness concentrated in a small number of GitHub Actions shards (slow runners, env misconfiguration, or transient network spikes). Separately, our dependency update cadence has become noisy: Renovate/Open-source bots create many PRs for low-risk transitive bumps that don't require human attention. This PR introduces two production-safe automation pieces and a small refactor to the existing lint/test orchestration to reduce noise and improve CI stability.

What this PR does (single-string description):
- CI shard health-checker (tools/ci/shard_health.py + .github/workflows/ci-health-check.yml): periodic job (every 3h) that aggregates shard runtimes from workflow run artifacts and checks for long-tail failure/retry patterns. It annotates failing workflows, opens an internal issue when a shard crosses predefined thresholds (median runtime > X, failure rate > Y), and can mark a shard as quarantined to avoid scheduling future matrix jobs there for 24h. The health-checker emits metrics (Prometheus pushgateway via internal endpoint) and writes a compact status.json artifact so downstream orchestration can prefer healthier shards.
- Dependency-janitor (scripts/dep_janitor.py + .github/workflows/dep-janitor.yml): weekly scheduled workflow that scans package manifests (go.mod, package.json, pyproject.toml) for low-risk transitive updates (patch releases, semver-safe). For candidates, the janitor creates a single rollup PR per package-ecosystem containing grouped changelogs, test matrix outcomes from a dry-run job, and a suggested merge window label (e.g., "maintenance/low-risk"). The job uses a guarded approach: only PRs that pass our lightweight smoke tests and have no incompatible transitive changes are opened. Overrides are available via repo config (ci/dep-janitor-config.yaml).
- Lint/test orchestration refactor: extracted a small launcher (scripts/ci/runner_launcher.sh) which normalizes environment variables, sets up tool cache, and reuses a single lint job across subpackages to reduce matrix duplication. This reduces redundant setup time and reduced average CI minutes for lint runs by ~18% in our internal benchmark.

Design notes and safety:
- The shard health-checker runs in audit-only mode by default for the first week after rollout (we do not quarantine shards or open issues automatically). It emits detailed logs to the workflow run and an artifact with historical bucketed runtimes. After one week, the job will be flipped to active (a release flag flip in infra-config).
- The dependency-janitor explicitly filters out direct dependency major bumps and any packages in the "do-not-janitor" list. PRs created include an automated label and a required reviewer from the owning team. By default it targets the "dev" branch, not main, so merges are gated behind normal review policies.
- All new scripts are written with idempotency and small memory footprint; Python code pins only runtime deps and vendors a small helper library to avoid transient network fetches during the workflow.

Testing and rollout plan:
- Local unit tests added for shard scoring algorithm (tests/test_shard_health.py) and dep-janitor candidate selection (tests/test_dep_janitor.py).
- Staged rollout: first enable workflows in the redwood/infra and redwood/helm repos for 48h in audit-only mode; then opt-in the rest of core repo.
- Observability: dashboards added (dashboards/ci-shard-health.json) with run-rate, median/95th runtime per shard, quarantined shards, and janitor-created PR delta. Alerts created for sustained median > 2x baseline.

Checklist (what I did):
- [x] Implement shard health-checker script and workflow
- [x] Implement dependency-janitor script and scheduled workflow
- [x] Refactor lint/test runner launcher and simplify matrix configs
- [x] Add unit tests and smoke workflow for new jobs
- [x] Add dashboard and alert rules for visibility
- [x] Update CONTRIBUTING.md and internal runbook for janitor behavior

What I did NOT change: release automation pipelines, deploy hooks, or any customer-facing release steps. The changes are scoped to CI, repo maintenance automation, and observability.

Related work: ENG-1428 (CI stability initiative), ENG-2103 (repo hygiene roadmap), SUP-88 (support ticket that surfaced dependency noise).

Notes for reviewers: focus review on the shard scoring heuristics (shard_health.py) and the safety gates in dep_janitor.py. The lint/test refactor is intentionally small (move + small wrapper) to minimize merge conflict surface.

Add CI shard health checker that detects long-tail flaky shards and rebalances jobs; introduce dependency-janitor scheduled workflow that creates safe update PRs for low-risk transitive deps; refactor lint/test orchestration to share lightweight launcher and reduce matrix duplication.
Jonah Kim (requested changes): Can we reduce permissions scope for the janitor bot? Suggested: use checkout-with-token and fine-grained token with repo:status and pull_request scope only.
Aisha Patel (response): Updated janitor to use fine-grained token; added fallback branch protection check to avoid accidental direct merges.
Mariela Costa (approved): Verified shard scoring tests and smoke run on infra repo; logging is sufficient for audit-mode.
Evan Brooks (comment): Consider adding a small canary that targets low-risk packages for the first 2 weeks. (Followed-up by janitor config change)
Aisha Patel (reply): Added canary flag and updated ci/dep-janitor-config.yaml to default to canary=true for first 2 runs.
payload.title: Introduce CI shard health-checker + dependency-janitor cron; refactor lint/test orchestration

Context: Customers increasingly require per-endpoint data residency guarantees and stronger audit proofing when KMS operations cross regions. This change introduces three coordinated pieces: 1) a per-route residency enforcement layer that validates route-level residency policies before request routing; 2) a KMS-consent middleware that surfaces explicit consent/consumption traces when a request would cause cross-region key usage; 3) an immutable audit checkpoint mechanism that signs and seals critical audit events with a cluster CMK and writes checkpoint references to the audit store. Motivation: close gaps where a request on a global route could inadvertently use a regionally-scoped CMK or be routed through an incompatible region without tenant consent. This improves compliance posture for geo-sensitive customers and enables certified audit trails for SOC/ISO work. Changes included (high level): - New config: service.routes[].residency_policy {allowed_regions, deny_cross_region, require_kms_consent} - Residency enforcement middleware in gateway/router that rejects or annotates requests based on route policy - KMS-consent middleware that injects consent tokens, records the consent event in the audit trail, and rejects requests when consent is required but absent - Audit checkpoint service: signs a compact checkpoint blob with cluster CMK, stores signed reference in audit-store, and emits a sealed_event marker to the audit stream - RBAC v2 adapter: small converter that maps existing service-account role bindings to the new attribute-driven checks used by the residency enforcer - Tests & infra: e2e tests, unit coverage for middleware, integration test with kms-emulator, and a performance microbenchmark to quantify latency impact on cold-paths Rollout and feature-flagging: This is gated behind feature.residency_enforcer_v1 (default off). The rollout plan in the PR description includes: canary 5% of requests to region-us-east-1, collect KPI: reject-rate, latency p95, audit store write latency, and KMS-op deltas. If metrics are stable, ramp to 100% in two-week windows. Checklist: - [x] API + config schema - [x] Residency enforcement middleware implemented - [x] KMS-consent middleware and consent token flow - [x] Immutable audit checkpoint signer and persistence - [x] RBAC v2 binding adapter (compat-mode) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] E2E with kms-emulator - [x] Documentation: config, rollout, troubleshooting - [x] Security review by SEC team

Commit summary: - feat(residency): add route policy schema and enforcement hooks - feat(kms-consent): implement consent token flow and audit emission - feat(audit): checkpoint signer that uses cluster CMK and exposes checkpoint API - chore(rbac): add compat adapter from legacy bindings to v2 attribute checks - test: add e2e and perf microbenchmarks - docs: add residenty.md and migration guide

Changed areas (high-level): - gateway/router/middleware/residency_enforcer.go - gateway/middleware/kms_consent.go - services/audit/checkpoint_signer.go - config/schemas/route_residency.yaml - rbac/adapter/legacy_to_v2_converter.go - tests/e2e/residency_canary_test.go - docs/security/residency.md - infra/ci/kms_emulator.yml - examples/route-policy-samples.yaml - helm/values.residency.example.yaml - internal/observability/metrics_residency.go - perf/bench/residency_coldpath_bench.go

Review conversation (excerpt): "Jordan Kim (reviewer): Why do we need a separate consent token instead of reusing existing audit headers?" Author reply: "Aisha Kapoor: We considered reusing x-audit-token but needed a tamper-resistant consent artifact that can be validated independently by downstream KMS proxies; consent tokens are short-lived and signed by the gateway to prevent replay. We still emit audit headers for correlation." "Lena Müller: Can this accidentally increase p95 for small requests?" Author reply: "Aisha Kapoor: We added a fast-path that skips signing when policy is allow-local and no cross-region operation is detected; the perf microbenchmark shows a median increase of 1.2ms on cold-paths and <0.2ms on warm-paths. We'll monitor during canary." "Ravi Patel: Is the checkpoint signer single-writer? What happens if signer fails?" Author reply: "Aisha Kapoor: The signer uses a leader-election-backed single-writer in hosted; fallback writes an unsigned provisional checkpoint with a retry loop and emits a diagnostic alert. Signed checkpoints are required for final audit ingestion; provisional ones are marked until re-signed." "SEC team (comment): Please ensure the CMK rotation plan and key access list are documented." Author reply: "Added KEY_ROTATION.md and scoped the signer to cluster CMK with ACLs; SEC approved on 2024-11-08." 

CI summary: - unit/tests: pass - integration/kms-emulator: pass - lint: pass - build: pass - e2e/residency_canary_test: pass - perf/bench: completed (bench run artifacts attached) Flaky checks: none.

Migration notes: - Existing route config without residency_policy is treated as allow-global (preserves current behavior). - We provide rbac/adapter/legacy_to_v2_converter to auto-generate suggested attribute bindings; maintainers should review generated bindings before enabling strict enforcement. - If you enable require_kms_consent on a route, clients must present consent tokens or requests will be rejected (400/consent_required). Troubleshooting: - diag/residency-rejects exposes reasons and matching policy; - audit/checkpoints expose last_signed_checkpoint_id and status; - gateway logs include consent token validation outcome.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged after approvals from Jordan, Lena, and Ravi and SEC signoff. CI green. Feature flag created and documented. Post-merge tasks: schedule rollout with SRE, add dashboard panels for reject-rate and checkpoint write latency, and add an entry to the next compliance audit checklist.
Added per-route data residency enforcement and KMS-consent middleware; introduced immutable audit checkpointing and RBAC v2 binding adapter. Backwards-compatible config flags; rollout via feature flag 'residency_enforcer_v1'.
feat(residency): route residency policy schema and enforcement hooks
feat(kms-consent): consent token generation & validation, consent audit events
feat(audit): checkpoint signer that signs with cluster CMK and writes sealed checkpoint refs
chore(rbac): compatibility adapter from legacy bindings to RBAC v2 attribute checks
test: e2e residency canary + kms-emulator integration
Jordan Kim: Why a new consent token instead of reusing existing audit headers?
Aisha Kapoor: Consent tokens are short-lived, signed, and validateable by downstream KMS proxies; audit headers are still emitted for correlation.
Lena Müller: Concerned about p95 regressions.
Aisha Kapoor: Fast-path avoids signing for local-only policies; perf microbench shows small median impact.
Ravi Patel: What are failure modes for the checkpoint signer?
Aisha Kapoor: Leader-election single-writer; falls back to provisional unsigned checkpoint with retry and diagnostic alert.
SEC: Document CMK rotation and ACL for signer.
Aisha Kapoor: KEY_ROTATION.md added; SEC approved on 2024-11-08.

payload.body:
Motivation: Production incidents and customer feedback showed gaps in observability across the public API surface: missing/unstable request ids for streaming responses, inconsistent trace propagation through the OpenAI compatibility layer, and insufficient per-endpoint metric tags for cost/latency attribution. This PR adds a unified request ID and trace propagation model, structured JSON logging augmentation, and per-endpoint metrics tags so latency/cost dashboards and alerting can attribute behavior correctly.

What this change does (summary): - Assigns a stable request_id at the API ingress for every request (hosted/dedicated/private). The request_id is included as: X-Request-Id response header, a top-level field in structured JSON logs (request_id), and injected into streaming chunk envelopes so that partial responses can be correlated to a single request. - Propagates tracing headers (traceparent and b3 where present) to internal services and exporters; integrates with our OpenTelemetry pipeline. We canonicalize trace ids to trace_id in structured logs. - Enhances the OpenAI compatibility layer: preserve incoming OpenAI-style request ids (if present) and map them onto internal request_id while returning OpenAI-compatible response ids; ensure the x-request-id header is forwarded and mirrored to openai response 'id'. - Adds per-endpoint and per-model metric tags (route, operation, model.family) emitted to metrics backend so dashboards can slice latency and token cost by API route (completion/chat/embeddings), model family, and plan tier. - Structured log fields: request_id, trace_id, route, http_method, user_id (when present), model, tokens_in, tokens_out, response_status, tool_call_id (for function/tool calls). - Streaming stability changes: ensure server assigns request_id before handshake completes with client; streaming chunks now include metadata envelopes with request_id and sequence numbers. This reduces misattribution for aborted/partial streams. - Function/tool calling observability: each tool call receives a tool_call_id and is correlated to the parent request trace; logs include tool_call_id/tool_name and duration. - Tests and CI: unit tests for header mapping, integration tests for streaming chunk envelopes, and a smoke test to validate metrics tags are emitted.

Design notes: - We intentionally keep the internal canonical ID as rr_request_id but expose it as X-Request-Id for HTTP compatibility and map it to OpenAI 'id' when using the compatibility endpoint. This avoids breaking customers who rely on existing OpenAI response id semantics while giving internal services a consistent key. - Trace propagation supports both W3C traceparent and B3. When both are present we prefer W3C and log both in debug mode. Traces are exported via our existing Otel collector config; no schema changes to the tracing backend. - Metrics tag cardinality is constrained: model.family is used rather than full model version in high-cardinality metrics. Route is normalized (chat.completions -> chat, completions -> completion, embeddings -> embedding). - Streaming envelope format: each chunk begins with a lightweight JSON prefix: {"request_id":"...","seq":42,"trace_id":"..."} followed by payload. The prefix is base64-safe and parsed by our SDKs; fallback behavior: legacy clients ignoring the prefix still receive the payload uninterrupted (we validated parsing safety).

Files changed (high level): - api/gateway/handler.go: assign request_id early, header mapping, trace extraction. - api/gateway/streaming.go: chunk envelope implementation and handshake update. - compat/openai/translator.go: map x-request-id <-> openai id and ensure streaming envelope compatibility. - runtime/observability/logging.go: structured logger helpers and keys. - runtime/observability/metrics.go: metric tag extraction and emission code, tag normalization helpers. - runtime/tooling/tool-calls.go: tool_call_id generation and correlation instrumentation. - integration_tests/test_observability_streaming.py: end-to-end streaming + header assertions. - unit_tests/test_openai_compat_header_mapping.go: mapping edge cases. - docs/api/observability.md: new docs section explaining headers, logs, and metric tags.

Commits (summary): - 0a3d8f2: initial gateway instrumentation and request id generation - 3b9f1c7: implement streaming chunk envelopes and SDK-friendly prefix - b1e4c6a: add OpenAI compatibility header mapping and translator tests - 6f7d2a1: structured logger helpers and trace canonicalization - f2c11b9: metrics tags emission and normalization + unit tests - 9d2b4e0: tool calling instrumentation and tool_call_id propagation - a7e8f33: docs and changelog entry; added rollout plan

Testing and CI notes: - Initial CI run had an intermittent failure in streaming integration (integration_tests/test_observability_streaming.py) due to race on request_id injection; fixed by ensuring request_id is assigned before stream handshake completes and adding a short synchronization point in the test harness. - All unit tests + integration tests passing after fixes; end-to-end smoke run on staging validated traces appear in OTEL backend with correct trace_id and request_id tags, and metrics dashboard received route/model tags. CI status: pass.

Review conversation (high level): - Miguel Alvarez: "Can we avoid increasing tag cardinality for metrics? We should prefer model.family not full model names." Author reply: "Agree — changed emission to use model.family for high volume metrics; full model appears only in debug traces." - Priya Nair: "Will OpenAI compat clients see any header changes?" Author reply: "No breaking change. We mirror internal rr_request_id to openai 'id' and return X-Request-Id as before. We document a new X-Redwood-Request-Id alias for debug." - Evan Brooks: "Streaming envelope looks good. Make sure SDKs handle prefix safely." Author reply: "Added parsing helpers in SDK interface and verified TS+Python SDK unit tests in their repos in follow-up PRs." - QA (Marcos): "Observed a case where aborted streams left dangling metrics. Can you increment a 'stream.aborted' metric?" Author reply: "Added stream.aborted counter emitted when connection closed before final chunk; included in metrics change set."

Backward compatibility and rollout: - Backwards compatible by default. Legacy clients that ignore the chunk envelope still receive payload; envelopes are designed to be safely ignored if not parsed. - Rollout plan: feature gated behind a runtime flag. Step 1: deploy to staging and run smoke tests (done). Step 2: deploy to canary subset of Hosted API (5% traffic) for 24 hours and monitor error/latency/trace correspondence dashboards. Step 3: full rollout with a 1h pause and rollback criteria defined in docs. We used canary run results to validate no increase in tail latency.

Operational impact and alerts: - New dashboards added: API Request ID heatmap, Route x Model latency with request_id tagging, Streaming chunk success rate. - Alerts: increase in stream.aborted > 0.5% over baseline, mismatch count where request_id missing in logs > 0.1% of requests, and drop in trace sampling/ingestion.

Follow-ups and TODOs: - SDK PRs to consume streaming prefix and surface request_id in client logs (TS+Python open follow-up PRs). - Instrument cost attribution pipeline to use model.family metric tags for billing experiments. - Add optional opt-out header X-Redwood-No-Request-Id for customers with specific privacy constraints (follow-up RFC).

Summary: This PR improves end-to-end observability of Redwood's API surface by unifying request IDs, ensuring trace propagation throughout the stack, adding structured logs and per-endpoint metric tags, and keeping compatibility with OpenAI-style clients. The change was reviewed, tested, and merged (squash merge) to main on 2026-02-23.
Added request id + trace propagation across API surface, structured logs with request/trace fields, per-endpoint metrics tags, and OpenAI-compatibility header mapping. No user-visible breaking changes; opt-in header behavior documented.
Miguel Alvarez: Can we avoid increasing tag cardinality for metrics? We should prefer model.family not full model names.
Priya Nair: Will OpenAI compat clients see any header changes?
Evan Brooks: Streaming envelope looks good. Make sure SDKs handle prefix safely.
Marcos (QA): Observed a case where aborted streams left dangling metrics. Can you increment a 'stream.aborted' metric?
Merged after CI fixes. Staging canary saw no regression in p99 latency. SDK follow-ups scheduled in respective repos. Documentation updated under docs/api/observability.md.

payload.body:
Motivation: Customers in regulated industries asked for stronger, auditable RBAC primitives after the recent compliance review (linked ENG-8423). This PR delivers three coordinated changes: 1) RBAC v2 policy tightening and a migration tool that preserves existing role bindings while enforcing least privilege; 2) audit-forwarding hooks and structured audit entries to support SIEM ingestion; 3) KMS envelope encryption support for customer-managed keys and region pinning controls so workloads can be constrained to approved regions.

Summary of changes (single-line list): migration script, rbac policy schema bump, audit formatter + forwarder, kms envelope adapter, routing middleware region-pin flag, tests and docs.

Checklist (worked through in commits): 
- [x] RBAC v2 schema bump and validator (schema_v2.json + validation code)
- [x] Migration tool: rbac/migrate_v1_to_v2.go with dry-run and apply modes
- [x] Audit: emit structured audit events for role/grant/revoke actions and request routing; add forwarder plugin that posts to configured HTTP endpoint (with backoff/retry)
- [x] KMS: kms/envelope_adapter.go implementing envelope encrypt/decrypt using AWS KMS and generic KMS interface for GCP/Azure future plumb
- [x] Region pinning: route layer checks cluster/region tags and rejects/rewrites requests per tenant policy; admin console toggle + API flag
- [x] Integration tests: rbac e2e (happy/failure paths), audit forwarder unit tests, kms adapter unit test with KMS mock, region pin policy functional tests
- [x] Docs: security/rbac_v2.md, ops/kms_integration.md, compliance/region_pinning.md

Commits (high level):
- a1b2c3: rbac: add v2 schema and validator (includes policy examples and commentary)
- d4e5f6: tooling: rbac migration CLI and dry-run support
- 7a8b9c: audit: structured event format and forwarder plugin (http/backoff)
- 0f1e2d: kms: envelope adapter skeleton + tests + docs
- 3c4b5a: routing: region pin enforcement and admin-api flag
- 6d7e8f: tests/docs: add e2e tests and example configuration for SOC customers

Files changed (high-level):
- rbac/schema_v2.json
- cmd/rbac-migrate/main.go
- internal/rbac/validator.go
- internal/audit/formatter.go
- internal/audit/forwarder/http_forwarder.go
- internal/kms/envelope_adapter.go
- internal/router/region_pin.go
- docs/security/rbac_v2.md
- docs/ops/kms_integration.md
- docs/compliance/region_pinning.md
- test/integration/rbac_e2e_test.go
- test/unit/kms_adapter_test.go

Notable implementation details: 
- RBAC v2 introduces role constraints and condition expressions (small DSL). Validator rejects grants that would expand privileges beyond existing bindings in dry-run migration mode; migration logs explicit transform steps to help audits.
- Audit entries are JSON objects with fields: timestamp, actor_id, tenant_id, action, target_type, target_id, before, after, request_id, region_hint. Forwarder supports HMAC-signed payloads if customer provides a secret.
- KMS envelope implementation follows the envelope pattern: generate data key locally, encrypt payload with AES-GCM, and encrypt data key with customer KMS key. Adapter supports AWS KMS GenerateDataKey and Encrypt/Decrypt; generic interface allows other providers. Key use is optional per-tenant; when enabled, encrypted blobs are stored in object storage with metadata describing the wrapping key ARN and region.
- Region pinning is enforced at the routing middleware: requests carry tenant metadata (tenant.region_policy). If tenant policy specifies allowed regions, requests routed to incompatible region are rejected with 403 and a structured audit event. Admins can override with an emergency bypass flag (requires separate audit log entry).

Backward compatibility and migration notes:
- Default behavior remains unchanged until migration tool is run. We intentionally ship validator + migration in a single PR so SRE and security can coordinate rollout. Customers on Dedicated/Private will need to run the migration binary against their control plane database.
- KMS envelope is opt-in. Existing server-side encryption remains available.

CI and testing: CI initially failed due to linting around the DSL parser; fixed in second commit. All unit and integration tests pass in CI (see checks below). The audit-forwarder added a flaky test around HTTP retries that required increasing the backoff window; that fix is included.

Operational runbook (short):
1) Run rbac-migrate --dry-run and review generated transform log.
2) When ready, run rbac-migrate --apply during maintenance window.
3) If using KMS envelope, configure tenant KMS ARN and verify KMS IAM access from control plane.
4) To enforce region pinning, set tenant.region_policy in admin console and monitor audit events.

Reasonable follow-ups (future PRs): automated policy suggestions from usage telemetry, GCP KMS adapter, and per-tenant SIEM batching sink.

Michael: Strong work on the schema; please expand on condition DSL docs and add an example for temporal constraints.
Author (Aisha): Added temporal constraint examples in docs and a short parser example.
Lena: Audit forwarder should redact PII from before/after snapshots by default.
Author: Implemented redaction hook and added a configuration option to disable redaction for customers who manage retention.
Omar: KMS adapter looks good; add more mocks for failure modes and validate retry behavior.
Author: Expanded KMS adapter tests to include network errors and KMS Throttling simulation.
Security review (Michael): Approved after tests; noted we need an ops checklist for private deployments.
Qa: Ran e2e, flagged region-pin 403 behaviour change; added acceptance test.
Merge: Squash and merge after approvals and green CI. CI required a re-run once; final run passed.
Merged after approvals from security and infra, CI green. Migration tool included; ops runbook added. No rollback needed. Monitoring alerts created for audit forwarder error rate and KMS errors.

payload.body:
Motivation: Prefill (context encoding) and decode have traditionally been serialized at the pipeline level which leaves GPUs underutilized for long-context prompts or when using KV cache. This PR decomposes the pipeline into explicit stages so we can: 1) split prefill into fixed-size chunks (chunked prefill) to produce KV segments early, 2) speculatively start decode on available tokens while later prefill chunks are computed, and 3) overlap prefill and decode stages via an explicit stage scheduler. Design summary: implement a PrefillChunker that emits KV checkpoints, add a SpeculativeDecode orchestrator that monitors token-level readiness, and replace monolithic PipelineRunner with a StagedPipeline that can run prefill/decode tasks on different streams. Changes include lightweight kernel hooks to accept partial KV inputs, scheduler heuristics to prefer low-latency decoding on tail tokens, and KV cache eviction guards to avoid double-use races. Results: see perf_results_summary. Checklist: [x] design doc link: https://redwood.internal/docs/prefill-decode-stage-design [x] unit tests added for chunker and stage transitions [x] integration test for KV consistency [x] perf harness runs included [ ] finalize docs. Related: ENG-4021, ENG-4130. Merge notes: squash-merged after perf run confirmed 12-28% P50 improvements on long-context generative workloads, and no regression on short-context fast-paths.
Improves end-to-end latency for long-context prefill workloads by enabling chunked prefill, speculative decoding to overlap compute, and scheduler adjustments to maximize GPU utilization. No API changes.
Long-context (16k tokens) generation P50 latency: baseline 1420ms -> 1248ms (12% improvement)
Tail-latency (first decode token readiness): baseline 84ms -> 62ms (26% improvement)
Throughput (batched continuous) on 4xA100: +18% tokens/sec for mixed short/long workload
Memory: peak GPU memory up by 3% due to chunk buffers; KV consistency tests show no extra leaks
Marco Ruiz: The new kernel hook looks good but we need to ensure memory alignment for partial KV writes; please add assertions and a fallback path.
Lina Park: Added alignment checks and a fallback memcpy path to the kernel; updated unit tests to cover misaligned edge cases.
Asha Patel: Scheduler heuristics look promising. How do we prevent speculative decode from consuming tokens that later get invalidated due to out-of-order prefill?
Lina Park: We add a lightweight token versioning stamp and validation before decode commits to output; described in comments and tested in integration test.
Devon Li: CI perf job flagged a small regression on 8k sequence when chunk_size was 64; recommend exposing chunk_size and auto-tuning heuristic.
Lina Park: Exposed chunk_size to config and added an auto-tuner which samples 3 sizes at startup. Added notes to release notes.
This PR touches both runtime and kernel layers; coordinate with release engineering for backported patches to release/1.8 if needed.
Follow-up work: tighter kernel fusion for multi-chunk decode path and better memory reclamation for ephemeral chunk buffers.
payload.title: Decompose prefill/decode pipeline to enable chunked & speculative prefill with stage overlap

payload.body:
Motivation: shipping model or runtime changes without continuous guardrails has resulted in two production regressions in the last quarter. This PR introduces a continuous performance-canary pipeline that runs steady-state microbenchmarks and short ramp tests against staged model/runtime variants, computes a composite canary score (latency p50/p95/p99 + throughput stability + error rate), and wires automated rollout-guard actions into the Redwood Console. The goal is to detect sustained regressions early (nightly/scheduled + on-PR short runs) and block automated rollouts until regressions are triaged.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a new perf-canary service and pipeline: scripts and a GH Actions job (.github/workflows/perf-canary.yml) to execute microbenchmarks against a canary environment and baseline.
- Implements a canary scoring library (scripts/perf_canary/score.py) that computes composite scores using weighted percentiles and a simple Bayesian uplift check to avoid noisy false positives.
- Integrates the canary runner with Redwood Console: canary results are sent to the new /api/internal/canary endpoint; console shows pass/fail and time-series.
- Rollout guard controller (controllers/rollout_guard.go): subscribes to canary results, enforces per-deployment threshold policies, and can (1) pause a rollout, (2) rollback to previous model snapshot, and (3) open a Linear ticket automatically when configured.
- Alerting hooks: Prometheus metrics (metrics/perf_canary.prom), Grafana dashboard panels (observability/dashboards/canary.jsonnet), and Slack notifications for degradations.
- E2E smoke + integration tests for the runner and controller (integration/perf_canary_test.go).
- Docs and runbook: docs/perf-canary.md + runbooks/incident-perf-canary.md.

Checklist: [x] perf runner + scoring library added, [x] CI job + scheduling, [x] console endpoint + UI hook, [x] rollout controller + policy config, [x] metrics + dashboards, [x] tests, [x] docs.

Notes on design and tradeoffs:
- We intentionally run a mix of short PR-level runs (3min, synthetic traffic) and longer scheduled steady-state runs (30–60min) to catch both regressions in startup/steady-state and throughput tail behavior.
- Composite canary score is conservative by default; teams can opt-in to stricter policies at deployment time via deployment.yaml -> rolloutGuard section.
- We added a small amount of latency to the console API path to avoid blocking the control plane on canary analysis; results are posted asynchronously and control decisions are made by the rollout controller which reads canonical results from Prometheus + the internal canary store.

Migration / rollout plan: enable default nightly canary job for most services in staging first; expose policy toggles in the UI; after two weeks of low-noise results, flip on canary enforcement for select services.

Related: Linear ENG-873 (perf canary spec), ENG-912 (rollout guard API), ENG-995 (console canary UI).
Marcus: 'Big picture LGTM — two things: the Bayesian check needs stronger comments, and please add a flake-tolerant mode for nightly runs.'
Ava: 'Added docstring comments and new --tolerance flag; updated docs to explain nightly vs PR runs.'
Priya: 'Can we ensure the controller only performs rollbacks if the error rate is increasing, not just latency? I saw a spike in p99 once without error NACKs.'
Ava: 'Controller policy now uses a combined signal: error_rate delta + latency delta; policy is pluggable and default requires both signals.'
Liam: 'Integration tests are failing on the second run in CI with a timing issue.'
Ava: 'Fixed test flakiness by stabilizing mocked clock and added retry for the Prometheus scrape in tests.'
Marcus (approval): 'Approved after test fix and docs update.'

Context and motivation: Customers using structured output and the OpenAI-compat layer continue to hit edge cases when models stream tokens that transiently violate the declared JSON schema (for example: truncated objects mid-stream or tokens that later get corrected). This PR implements a new response_format value json_schema_v2 that performs lightweight, streaming-aware partial validation during token emission, surfaces structured schema_violation events to clients, and provides a strict_mode toggle that upgrades behavior to immediate request rejection on strong violations.

What this change does (single-string summary): Adds a streaming-safe JSON Schema v2 validator to the runtime, maps OpenAI-compat response_format json_schema_v2 to the new validator, updates SDKs to surface structured error events, and introduces a fallback path where strict_mode=false will gracefully fall back to best-effort streaming with a final post-stream validation result.

Detailed behavior: - response_format=json_schema_v2 (default strict_mode=false): runtime performs incremental token-level validation and emits progress events of type 'schema_hint' and final 'schema_result'. If final validation fails, the response contains an explicit structured error block and a new error code SVC-1003. The streaming connection itself remains open unless strict_mode=true. - response_format=json_schema_v2 & strict_mode=true: runtime attempts incremental validation and will abort the stream and return an immediate structured error when a non-recoverable violation is detected (e.g. unmatched braces in a way that cannot be reconciled by later tokens, or missing required top-level keys when end-of-stream is reached). - Backwards compatibility: response_format=json_schema (legacy) behavior unchanged. Clients that do not opt into json_schema_v2 continue to get current behavior.

OpenAI-compat specifics: The compatibility shim accepts the parameter response_format=json_schema_v2 (same semantics), and maps incoming strict=true to strict_mode=true in Redwood API. We explicitly document that OpenAI-style field names 'response_format' and 'strict' are translated. This allows smooth migration for customers currently using the OpenAI-compat endpoint.

Runtime changes (high-level): - Added runtime/validation/jsonschema_v2.py: incremental validator with token buffer heuristics and a light-weight recovery model to avoid false positives mid-stream. - Serving runtime hooks: emit structured stream control events (schema_hint, schema_violation, schema_result). - Fallback policy: when strict_mode=false, the runtime will continue streaming but annotate the response with final schema_result metadata and include a structured error if validation fails.

SDK and API surface updates: - Python and TypeScript SDKs: new response event types and helpers to subscribe to schema_hint/result events. - openai_compat layer: accepts response_format=json_schema_v2 and strict=true/false mapping. - Console/docs: new page documenting migration path and examples.

Testing and rollout: - Added unit tests and e2e streaming tests that simulate incremental partial outputs and model fluctuations (tests/e2e/test_stream_schema.py). - Canary rollout plan: feature flagged; start at 5% of hosted traffic for 48 hours, monitor schema_violation metric and client error rates, then 50% for 24 hours, then 100% if metrics are green.

Migration notes for customers: Clients that want strict enforcement should pass strict_mode=true (or strict=true on OpenAI-compat). If you rely on legacy lenient behavior, do nothing. SDKs will include helpers to parse the structured error block and to receive schema_hint events to progressively build the validated payload.

Checklist: - [x] Runtime validator implementation - [x] OpenAI-compat mapping - [x] SDK surface updates (Python + TS) - [x] Docs and examples - [x] Unit and e2e tests - [x] Feature flag and rollout configuration

Related work: ENG-2476 (validation infra), PM-632 (product requirements for strict structured output).

CI and merge notes: initial CI run failed on a flaky test in tests/infra/test_rate_limiter; reran and all checks passed. This PR is merged by squash to keep history focused.
Ethan Liu (2026-02-11): Can you clarify the recovery heuristics used by the incremental validator? I want to ensure we're not too permissive mid-stream.
Asha Patel (2026-02-11): The validator uses a two-token lookahead heuristic and a small stack-based bracket matcher; comments added to runtime/validation/jsonschema_v2.py explaining thresholds.
Marina Ortega (2026-02-12): Please add an e2e that simulates a model that emits a corrected value after an earlier violation (to ensure we don't false-positive).
Asha Patel (2026-02-12): Added tests/e2e/test_stream_schema.py that covers the corrected-value case and edge-case truncated-object behavior.
Diego Ramos (2026-02-13): CI failed on a flaky rate limiter test -- looks unrelated. Rerun CI.
Asha Patel (2026-02-13): Reran CI and pushed a small test timeout bump to stabilize infra tests. CI green on rerun.
Ethan Liu (2026-02-15): Approving after verifying the metrics dashboard and canary config. Leaving a note to monitor SVC-1003 counts on rollout.
Marina Ortega (2026-02-15): Approved. Documentation and examples look good.

payload.body:
Problem:
SSE streaming to OpenAI-compatible clients occasionally emitted event tokens that split valid JSON objects across chunk boundaries. When combined with request-side backpressure and the runtime's eager flush behavior, this led to: partially emitted JSON frames, duplicated delimiters, and misordered tool/function-call sentinel events.

Goals:
1) Avoid emitting syntactically invalid or truncated JSON payloads to downstream consumers unless a hard timeout occurs.
2) Preserve emitter ordering guarantees for application-level sentinels (function-call/tool events) relative to the final assembled JSON object.
3) Keep latency impact minimal for common-case small events and maintain graceful degradation under degraded network/worker conditions.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a lightweight "cork" layer to the SSE stream coordinator that buffers incomplete logical frames until a) a JSON boundary is seen, b) a max cork-timeout elapses, or c) the cork is explicitly flushed by priority events.
- Implements an atomic-span recovery algorithm: frames buffered across cork boundaries are reassembled using a small boundary-check heuristic and an optional 16-bit rolling checksum to detect silent corruption from mid-chunk truncation.
- Introduces a call-order watermark: function-call/tool-call sentinel tokens are sequenced and only emitted after their associated JSON payload is fully reassembled (or after cork-timeout), avoiding toolcall-before-body races.
- Adds conservative safeguards to avoid unbounded memory growth for pathological clients (max-span-bytes + span-count quotas, eviction metrics).
- Adds end-to-end unit and integration tests targeting partial JSON injection, deliberate delimiter duplication, and interleaved heartbeat scenarios.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Corking is optimistic: for single-chunk small events (~<1KB) we pass them through immediately. Corking engages only when a chunk does not contain a complete top-level JSON boundary or when parsing heuristics indicate a likely mid-object split. This keeps latency low for 95th percentile events.
- The checksum is intentionally small and fast (rolling 16-bit) to catch most accidental corruption without heavy CPU cost. It is not a substitute for transport-level guarantees; checksum failures fall back to best-effort emit with a diagnostic header.
- Timeouts are tuned conservatively (default 80ms) and are configurable per-route. We expose this as an opt-in compatibility knob for customers who require strict OpenAI-compat behavior vs minimal-latency behavior.

Checklist:
- [x] Implement cork coordinator and reassembler logic in runtime core.
- [x] Add call-order watermarking and ordering guarantees for tool/function sentinel events.
- [x] Add quota checks and eviction metrics.
- [x] Unit tests for fragment reassembly and checksum mismatch paths.
- [x] Integration tests exercising backpressure + heartbeat interleaving.
- [x] Add short doc note in streaming compatibility changelog.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(sse): introduce cork coordinator and buffer API (Avery Chen)
- feat(sse): implement atomic span reassembler and rolling checksum (Avery Chen)
- fix(api): sequence toolcall sentinel emission behind call-order watermark (Avery Chen)
- perf(sse): avoid allocation churn in common-pass-through path (Ethan Wallace)
- test(sse): add regression tests for partial-json and duplicate-delimiter scenarios (Marisol Vega)
- docs: add streaming-changelog entry and compatibility flag docs (Avery Chen)

Files changed (high level):
- runtime/sse/stream_coordinator.rs  (new cork coordinator + core flow changes)
- runtime/sse/cork.rs  (buffering primitives, timeout handling)
- runtime/sse/reassembler.rs  (atomic span reassembly, checksum)
- openai_compat/sse_reassembler.go  (compat shim to ensure same behavior for OpenAI layer)
- api/streaming/handler.py  (expose per-route cork config and metrics)
- tests/sse/test_partial_json_reassembly.py  (integration)
- tests/sse/test_toolcall_ordering.py  (unit + integration)
- docs/streaming_compatibility.md  (note + config)
- metrics/streaming.prom  (added new cork_* metrics)

Small illustrative snippet (reassembler heuristic):
"""
// rough pseudo: only shown in PR for reviewer context
if !hasTopLevelBoundary(chunk) {
  corkBuffer.append(chunk)
  if (corkBuffer.size > maxSpanBytes) evictOldestSpan()
  scheduleFlushAfter(timeout)
} else {
  emit(reassemble(corkBuffer + chunk))
}
"""

Review conversation (high level):
- Priya Kumar: "Latency impact looks acceptable in flame graphs, but pls add a stress test where 1000 concurrent tiny streams flip on cork to ensure we don't hit GC pressure."
- Avery Chen: "Added stress test and micro-optimizations to pass-through path; results included in CI run 42."
- Ethan Wallace: "Minor nit: move default timeout into runtime config struct and document it. Also renamed a counter for clarity."
- Avery Chen: "Addressed both; updated docs/ and ran benchmarks."
- Marisol Vega: "Tests uncovered an edge when heartbeat and toolcall arrive the exact same tick; added deterministic ordering in code path."
- Priya Kumar: "Approving after CI green and stress test numbers look stable."

CI summary:
- unit: pass
- integration(sse): pass (includes new partial-json scenarios)
- lint: pass
- bench: flake on first run (memory benchmark timeout), rerun succeeded
- security-scan: pass

Motivation: Teams running A/B tests and canary promotions need deterministic cohort anchoring plus an automated fast-fallback when latency, error-rate, or quality regressions are detected. This PR introduces a controller and API surface that: 1) pins user/query cohorts to a stable treatment (anchor) during long-running A/B experiments, 2) provides promotion hooks to move anchored cohorts from shadow->canary->primary on a schedule or metric gate, and 3) implements a fast-fallback path that immediately drains traffic from a failing variant and re-anchors affected cohorts to the last known-good variant.

Changes include: controller implementation (orchestration/scheduler), a new lightweight cohort store (kv-backed, optional in Dedicated/Private), API surface for experiments (create/update/pause/promote), telemetry and probe instrumentation (per-cohort latency/error/quality counters), and end-to-end integration tests and docs. The description below summarizes the components and rationale.

Design highlights: - Cohort anchoring: a deterministic hashing and sticky assignment ensures the same caller/session lands in the same treatment for the experiment duration. Anchors are stored with TTL and versioned keys so rollbacks can replay previous assignments. - Promotion hooks: experiments can declare promotion policies (time-based, metric threshold, linear ramp). Promotions go through a two-phase commit: dry-run observation then switch, with a snapshot of cohort mapping. - Fast-fallback: when a policy gate trips (latency > SLO, error spike, or model-quality delta beyond threshold), the controller triggers immediate drain of failing variant and reassigns cohorts to the last healthy variant; a short-lived quarantine lane accepts replayed requests for diagnostics. - Safety and audit: all assignment changes and fallback events are journaled; operators can view the journal and roll forward/back via the console or API.

Backward compatibility: experiments default to the older routing behavior if no experiment config is present. The cohort store is optional — when disabled the controller falls back to probabilistic assignment but still enforces promotion/fallback flows.

Testing and rollout: unit and integration tests added under integrations/ab_anchor. Performance microbenchmarks show assignment latency <200us p95 and fallback completion time under 2s in a local Dedicated environment.

Why this is different from prior rollout work: prior PRs focused on traffic-splitting and staged canaries; this adds persistent cohort assignment and a fast, auditable emergency fallback designed for long-lived A/B experiments where reassigning users mid-experiment is unacceptable.

Related: Linear ENG-2345 (AB experiment lifecycle), ENG-2419 (fast-fallback SLO integration).
Leo Zhang: Can you clarify how the store behaves in the case of network partitions? We should avoid double-assignments — suggested adding optimistic locking and a conflict counter (see commit 'Fix: handle concurrent promotions').
Priya (author): Added optimistic locking and a conflict counter; on partition the controller marks affected cohorts as 'quarantined' and routes traffic through the replay lane until resolved.
Marta Kowalski: Are promotion dry-runs exposed in the console? We need a way for product to eyeball sample traffic before a full promotion.
Priya: Yes — dry-run is now surfaced under the 'Preview' tab in the console and via the API - see api/v1/experiment.proto changes and the new anchor_playbook.md.
Ben Carter: CI integration tests occasionally failed on macOS runners due to timeout; increased test timeout in CI and added retry for flaky network op. CI now green.
Leo Zhang: Please add a short migration note for Dedicated/Private customers about enabling the cohort store and recommended KV backends.
Priya: Added docs/rollouts/ab_anchor.md and helm values for toggling the feature. Also added a console blurb under operator playbook.
New orchestrator for long-running A/B experiments: persistent cohort anchoring, promotion hooks (dry-run, schedule, metric gates), fast-fallback with quarantine/replay, and optional cohort KV store. Includes API additions and console playbook.

Motivation: tenants on Dedicated occasionally approach committed latency SLOs during short spikes. Current strict admission controls either throttle aggressively (hurting tail latency) or immediately fall back to hosted variants (increasing cost and losing isolation). This PR introduces a "soft SLA contingency router" that probabilistically diverts a tunable fraction of incoming requests to reserve lanes or to hosted fallback based on short-term predictive headroom and tenant contract thresholds, combined with a nightly "usage reconciliation" pipeline that compares billed reservation credits to observed GPU utilization to surface over/under allocation and generate recommended reservation adjustments.

This is a production-focused change: behavior is off by default and gated behind a feature flag (ops.contingency.enabled). Main goals are: 1) preserve critical tenant latency SLOs gracefully during microbursts, 2) avoid wholesale fallback unless necessary, 3) provide visibility and automated recommendations to correct reservation drift.

What I changed (high level):
- runtime/controller/contingency_router.go: new router component implementing soft diversion policy, short term headroom estimator, and per-tenant contingency token accounting.
- pkg/sim/sla_simulator.go: lightweight deterministic simulator used by unit tests and can be run locally to validate routing behavior under synthetic burst patterns.
- ops/reports/usage_recon.py: nightly reconciliation job that aggregates per-GPU utilization samples, cross-references reservation ledgers, and emits recommended reservation deltas to Linear.
- docs/ops/contingency_routing.md: operator runbook (feature flag, metrics, rollback).
- test/unit/contingency_router_test.go: deterministic tests for token accounting, diversion probability bounds, and concurrent update safety.
- charts/redwood/values.yaml: small values to expose feature flag to Helm for Private installs.

Checklist: [x] design doc linked (ENG-1412) [x] unit tests added [x] e2e smoke script (manual) [x] feature flag gated [x] docs & runbook updated [ ] migration script (not required; migration is zero-downtime)

Notes on behavior and safety: The router maintains a sliding-window headroom estimate per fleet (default 30s window) and computes a diversion ratio r(t) = clamp(0,1, alpha * (1 - remaining_commit_fraction)). Remaining_commit_fraction uses an exponentially decayed observed utilization vs reservation baseline. When r(t)>0 the router probabilistically routes requests: some to dedicated reserve lanes (if tokens available), some to hosted fallback (if configured), otherwise to a best-effort queue. Contingency tokens are sourced from a soft reserve ledger that decays when used and replenishes at a configurable rate to avoid persistent stealing from other tenants.

Monitoring and alerts: New metrics are emitted: contingency.router.diversion_ratio, contingency.router.tokens_consumed, usage_recon.recommendation_delta_count, usage_recon.unmatched_samples. Dashboards and alerts are documented in docs/ops/contingency_routing.md.

Migration & rollout plan: feature flag off by default. Canary rollout to two small fleets for 48h, validate contingency.router.tokens_consumed < 5% of committed capacity and nightly usage_recon false-positive rate < 2%. If metrics spike, operator can toggle ops.contingency.enabled=false and abort.

Related: ENG-1419 covers reconciliation alerting thresholds. SUP-827 flagged discrepancy cases that motivated the reconciliation job.

Aisha Kumar (reviewer): Nice direction. Two immediate concerns: 1) race on token ledger increments when many goroutines try to claim; please add CAS/compare-and-swap or a per-shard mutex. 2) metrics are great but we need an SLA-preserving alert if diversion_ratio>0.3 for >5m.
Maya Chen (author): Added per-shard mutex in commit b4c5d6e and exposed contingency.router.diversion_ratio alert with 5m burn-in. Also tightened diversion cap to 0.4 from 0.6 per product request.
Daniel Park (reviewer): Unit tests look good. Could we add one integration smoke that runs simulator + reconciliation job? Concerned about nightly job cost scanning all samples.
Maya Chen: Reworked reconciliation to sample at 1m granularity and sample 10% of GPUs by default. Added integration smoke script under scripts/smoke/contingency_smoke.sh (not included in this PR) and documented cost tradeoffs.
Luca Romano (approver): Verified metrics on canary fleet. Small nits: document helm flag location and add release note. Approving pending doc tweak.
Maya Chen: Addressed doc tweak and added release notes. Ready to merge.
Add a feature-flagged soft SLA contingency router that probabilistically diverts requests to reserve lanes or hosted fallback during microbursts; add nightly usage reconciliation job that recommends reservation adjustments based on observed GPU utilization. Operator docs and metrics included.

Motivation: fragmentation in the paged KV block pool increases allocation stalls during bursty steady-state workloads, especially when short-lived prefixes intermingle with long-lived cache entries. This PR introduces a TTL-aware eviction policy combined with a low-interference background compaction pass that reduces high-frequency churn while preserving pin guarantees for hot tails. The goal is to reduce tail latency from allocator stalls without regressing throughput or increasing write amplification.

What this change does (single continuous description): Adds an adaptive TTL estimator that clusters entries by observed access lifetime and assigns eviction priority buckets. New eviction buckets are promoted/demoted based on online decay counters to avoid thrashing at bucket boundaries. A background "stable compaction" worker walks weakly-referenced pages (configurable concurrency) and coalesces partially-filled blocks into contiguous spans to reduce internal fragmentation; compaction is prioritized for buckets with high fragmentation scores. Pinning behavior is updated: soft-pins now carry a sticky-decay counter so recently unpinned but frequently re-referenced spans are protected for a short grace window to avoid repeated reallocation. Integration with continuous batching: the allocator exposes a fast-path that allows the batcher to reserve N inline pages for immediate allocation to avoid synchronous stalls during hot-burst scheduling.

Testing and metrics: Microbenchmarks show allocator stall incidence reduced by 3.2x on our single-GPU latency-sensitive workload (batch size=1, seq=512). End-to-end infer p95 within a mixed workload improved by ~14% and p99 improved by ~9% at equivalent throughput. Background compaction added ~0.4% CPU on the host under default settings; compaction concurrency is tunable. System tests: new unit/bench suites for bucket promotion, compaction correctness, and a stress harness reproducing fragmentation patterns.

Compatibility and safety: Backwards-compatible config toggles behind a feature flag kv.experimental.adaptive_ttl. Default behavior is opt-in for dedicated/private customers via config rollout; can be enabled in-hosted after a staged canary. No breaking API changes.

Checklist: - [x] Add TTL estimator and promotion logic - [x] Implement stable compaction worker - [x] Update soft-pin sticky-decay semantics - [x] Add allocator reservation fast-path for batcher - [x] Unit tests and benches - [x] Docs (architecture note and config guide) - [x] Perf graphs attached to PR

Related: ENG-4274 (allocator tail latency project), ENG-4321 (KV fragmentation runbook).
Diego Ramirez (reviewer): Please add a short-circuit on compaction if fragmentation score < 0.12 to avoid wasted CPU cycles. Also suggest a unit test that simulates repeated allocate/free of large spans to validate no regression in allocation latency.
Maya Chen (author): Added threshold short-circuit and new stress test (kv_fragmentation_stress.rs). Bench shows CPU overhead negligible when threshold is met. Responded with updated commit f6b22a9.
Priya Nair (reviewer): Can you add a safety toggle so operators can disable compaction without redeploying? Concern about noisy neighbor effects in multi-tenant Dedicated clusters.
Maya Chen (author): Added kv.experimental.compaction_enabled toggle in configs/defaults/kv.toml and documented operator guidance in docs/architecture/kv-eviction.md.
Evan O'Connor (reviewer): Please ensure metrics emitted for compaction work units, moved bytes, and sticky-pin hits/misses so SLO owners can observe impact.
Maya Chen (author): Emitted metrics: kv_compaction_runs, kv_compaction_bytes_moved, kv_sticky_pin_hits, kv_sticky_pin_misses. Hooked into console dashboards via perf-monitoring team (screenshot attached in PR).

Context: Large tenants with bursty tail traffic waste tokens and GPU cycles during cold KV-cache windows. Goal: introduce a tenant-scoped prefilling heuristic and a quantization-tier manager that automatically picks safe, cost-effective quant profiles per workload bucket while preserving latency SLOs. Context and motivation: We need a unified conductor that lets product teams express cohort-anchored traffic phasing policies (canary, A/B, and shadowing) with automated failsafe behavior tied to deterministic rollback reasons so operators can reason about regressions. Current rollout primitives are fragmented across the orchestration layer and the legacy traffic proxy; recovery semantics are ad-hoc and hard to audit. This PR introduces a first-class Traffic Conductor that centralizes policy evaluation, variant sculpting (fractional shaping per cohort), and deterministic failsafe triggers (latency/accuracy/telemetry anchors) so model swaps and experiments run with predictable rollback behavior.

What this PR does (high level): Implements a policy-driven conductor that: 1) assigns cohorts to variant lanes and sculpts traffic fractions using a decay-aware allocator so small cohorts do not overshoot; 2) preserves session affinity during phased drains to avoid user-facing churn; 3) supports decayed shadowing (shadow traffic that ramps down automatically as signatures stabilize) to reduce cost during long-running experiments; 4) surfaces deterministic rollback reason codes (e.g., SLO_LATENCY, REGRESSION_ACCURACY, TELEMETRY_DROP) and stores them in the rollout journal for audit and replay; 5) adds a "rehearsal" playback mode that replays sampled production traffic against candidate variants prior to increasing live traffic; 6) implements telemetry gates that tie to existing metrics pipelines (via MetricsProxy hook) and allow multi-metric gating with configurable windows.

payload.body:
Introduce delta-driven pin throttling and a tiered reuse pool for paged KV; reduces tail latency and lowers memory churn under mixed workloads.
Motivation: Our paged KV block manager saw high tail latency and frequent pin-induced stalls when conversational workloads produce short bursts of focused hot prefixes. Existing heuristics pinned aggressively on first-detect hotness and coalesced eagerly, which increased contention and caused kernel scheduling jitter. This change introduces a delta-driven pin heuristic plus a lightweight tiered reuse allocator to smooth pin activity and defer expensive coalesces into the background.
- Delta-driven pin throttle: compute a per-span "delta" metric = recent_access_rate - historic_access_rate; only escalate pin priority when delta crosses a configurable hysteresis threshold. This prevents immediate hard pins for transient bursts and reduces pin churn.
- Tiered reuse allocator: hot/warm/cold lanes for freed blocks. Blocks evicted into warm can be rehydrated quickly without full reallocation; cold lane is low-priority and compacted in background. The allocator uses a compact epoch-based reclamation to avoid locking hot paths.
- Deferred coalesce worker: coalesce and merge adjacent free spans in a low-priority background worker; opportunistic coalesces happen inline only when contention is low.
- Pin throttling backpressure: when overall pin rate exceeds budget we throttle new high-priority pins and apply an exponential backoff per-request to avoid head-of-line stalls.
- Scheduler hints: the runtime's request router receives a lightweight hint about expected hot-span locality (hot/warm/cold) so continuous-batcher can favor batches that avoid heavily pinned spans and the kernel selector can choose low-latency kernels when locality is high.
- Tests and perf harness: added unit tests for delta metric, integration tests for epoch reclamation, new stress profile in perf-canary that simulates rapid conversational prefix changes, and updated observability to expose delta, pin_budget, and tier occupancy metrics.
Perf canary (mixed chat, 32-client, variable prefix churn): p50 throughput +9%, p95 latency -12%, p99 latency -18% on average across 3 runs. Memory churn (alloc/free cycles) reduced ~22% due to warm-lane reuse. On a synthetic write-heavy workload the change had neutral throughput but lowered tail latency by ~5%.
- Unit tests for delta calculation and hysteresis edge cases.
- Integration test exercising warm rehydration path under contention.
- TSAN run to catch race in deferred coalesce (fixed).
- Perf-canary profile added and executed three times in staging.
- Manual validation: exercise streaming scenarios to confirm scheduler hints reduce kernel jitter.
Risks: throttling could delay legitimate long-running pins causing extra load; mitigation: conservative defaults, runtime toggle, and metrics to observe throttle ratio. Deferred coalesce introduced a small window of fragmentation; mitigation: bounded epoch ages and opportunistic inline coalesces when low contention is detected.
Aaron Chen: Nice approach. Can you quantify the extra memory footprint for warm-lane staging? Also ensure the default hysteresis isn't too aggressive for low-QPS customers.
Sofia Patel (author): Warm-lane adds a small per-span tag and a freelist pointer; measured at ~0.8% memory overhead in our canary. Hysteresis default tuned from perf runs; added config and notes in RFC.
Priya Natarajan: How does this interact with dedicated capacity autoscaler? If pins are throttled, will we cascade to scaling decisions?
Sofia Patel: We emit pin_budget and pin_throttle_ratio metrics. Autoscaler policy in Dedicated can factor pin_throttle_ratio as a signal; added a short note in docs about suggested autoscaler thresholds.
Jordan Lee: Suggest adding a debug dump for tier occupancy and top-delta spans to help SRE during incidents.
Sofia Patel: Added a /debug/kv/tier-occupancy endpoint and top-delta spans to the existing debug dump (secured behind RBAC).
Aaron Chen: One nit: rename "cold" lane to "archival" to avoid confusion with 'cold start' semantics.
Sofia Patel: Renamed in allocator and docs (archival lane).

payload.body:
Background: Multiple customer bug reports and internal integration tests showed inconsistent behaviors in the OpenAI compatibility layer and streaming endpoints when rate limits, idempotency conflicts, or internal errors occur. Symptoms included: (1) missing or ambiguous Retry-After semantics across hosted vs dedicated; (2) idempotency keys that sometimes returned a 500 on duplicate requests instead of a deterministic 200/409; (3) streaming clients receiving partial SSE/HTTP chunks with no canonical error envelope; (4) OpenAI-compat mappings returning different error shapes from the main API which caused SDKs to mis-handle retries. Motivation: unify error surface and retry semantics so clients (and our SDKs) can implement robust backoff/retry, and so streaming consumers get a machine-readable error payload at the end of a stream. Changes in this PR: - Standardize HTTP rate-limit headers and Retry-After behavior: always return Retry-After in seconds when throttled and include X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset (unix epoch seconds). For sub-second guidance, include X-Retry-After-Ms only for internal fast-paths (e.g., burst throttles). The OpenAI compat layer maps internal throttles to 429 + {"type":"rate_limit","code":"rate_limit_exceeded"}. - Idempotency key lifecycle: persist Idempotency-Key for successful and in-progress requests for a configurable TTL (default 24h). On duplicate non-mutating calls we now return the original response (200), on duplicate conflicting side-effect attempts we return 409 with code "idempotency_conflict" and an explanatory message. Internal transient errors during idempotency write will trigger a 503 with code "idempotency_unavailable" to avoid unsafe retries. - Streaming stability & error envelope: streaming responses (SSE and chunked JSON) will terminate with a final structured error chunk/trailer when an error occurs mid-stream. The final chunk uses a canonical shape: {"error":{"type":"<type>","code":"<code>","message":"<message>","request_id":"<id>"}} so SDKs can detect and act on the error deterministically. OpenAI-compat GET /v1/chat/streams mapping will include this final JSON chunk and then close the connection. - OpenAI compatibility layer mappings: introduced a single map in openai_compat/error_map.go that translates internal codes (e.g., QUOTA_EXCEEDED, THROTTLE, KV_WRITE_FAIL) into OpenAI-like codes and types so downstream SDKs see consistent errors. - Client-facing docs & tests: updated API reference and added end-to-end tests for rate limit headers, idempotency key replays, and streaming error trailers. - Observability: added new metrics (errors.openai_compat_mapped_total, idempotency.key_hits_total) and traces for idempotency lookups to ease debugging. Related: ENG-2013 implements the idempotency storage change; SUP-432 reported the original customer issue. Checklist: - [x] Rate-limit header canonicalization implemented and tested - [x] Idempotency persistence with TTL and conflict semantics - [x] Streaming final-error envelope implemented for SSE and chunked JSON - [x] OpenAI compat error map and test cases - [x] Docs and SDK compatibility notes updated - [x] End-to-end tests added (CI passing) Notes/Tradeoffs: - We keep Retry-After in seconds as the canonical header to match broad client expectations; X-Retry-After-Ms is best-effort and only available on some throttles. - Persisting idempotency keys increases storage/coordination cost; we use a sharded TTL map and a background compaction job to bound cost. - This PR intentionally avoids changing public error codes used by large enterprise customers; instead we map internal codes to the stable OpenAI-like set. Migration: SDKs should start reading the canonical error envelope on streams and respect the Retry-After header (seconds). For idempotency, clients should pass Idempotency-Key for safe retries and handle 409/idempotency_conflict by surfacing the conflict to the caller.
Rosa: Can you confirm that Retry-After is always in seconds? Maya: Yes; we kept seconds as canonical; X-Retry-After-Ms is optional and only present for burst throttles. Ethan: LGTM pending minor nits in tests. Devon: Please add a tracing span around idempotency lookup. Maya: Added span and metric. CI initially failed on e2e streaming test due to race; fixed by adding a short stabilization wait and asserting final trailer. Approvals: Ethan approved 2026-02-24, Rosa approved 2026-02-25.
payload.title: consistent error schema, retry-after semantics, and idempotency handling for streaming / openai-compat

payload.body:
Context: During a regional transient last week we observed correlated tenant reopen storms when region health probes flapped; simultaneous reinstate attempts caused KV cache churn and surge-evictions that amplified SLO breaches. Motivation: introduce a short, tenant-scoped "quiesce window" on region failover that serializes reinstate attempts with jittered backoff and a staggered-reinstate coordinator. This reduces bursty rejoin traffic and gives the serving runtime time to warm KV caches and stabilize before accepting full traffic. What this PR does: 1) Add a tenant_quiesce_window (default 30s) to the failover coordinator that marks tenants as "quiesced" on an outbound region handoff. 2) Implement a staggered reinstate scheduler that assigns reinstate slots using tenant weight and historical request rate. 3) Add a soft circuit coalescer that prevents immediate circuit resets for tenants that rejoin within the quiesce window. 4) Expose two new metrics (quiesce.window_applied, reinstate.slot_latency) and a debug-only trace path. 5) Hotfixes in the runtime to avoid duplicate KV drain on simultaneous reinstate. Rollout plan: feature gate off by default -> rollout to canary region -> metric validation -> global enable. Related work: ENG-1298 (regional failover stabilization), SUP-4983 (customer incident #42). Context: Customers operating under strict data residency and key-governance requirements need stronger guarantees that requests which used tenant CMKs originated from acceptable regions and operator contexts. Additionally, a number of enterprise integrations require RBAC grants that are valid only for tight temporal windows (e.g., emergency operator escalation). This PR introduces a compact server-side flow that attests KMS origin on each request, evaluates temporal RBAC grants, and surfaces an audit-sampling override for high-sensitivity flows.

What this change does: implements a light-weight KMS provenance attestor (pkg/kms/provenance_attestor.go) that validates key metadata and produces a signed provenance header. Adds a temporal RBAC evaluator (svc/authz/temporal_rbac.go) that consumes Linear/JWT claims plus a timebound grant store. Hooks are added to the request pipeline (http/middleware/provenance_middleware.go) to enforce provenance checks for routes labeled with the new annotation `security.kms.provenance: required`. Audit pipeline changes include an audit-sampling override flag (audit/override_probe.go) that forces 100% capture for provenance-failures or temporary-operator sessions.

Design notes: provenance attestation is intentionally non-blocking for routes without the annotation to preserve backward compatibility. For annotated routes, provenance failures return 403 with a structured failure code and include a sanitized audit header to allow downstream forensics. Temporal grants follow an additive policy: an ephemeral grant record is stored in the grant-store with start/end timestamps and a signed grant token is issued; the evaluator validates token integrity + time window. Key origin checks compare KMS key metadata (region, provider, role) against tenant policy and use a small TTL'd cache for performance.

Migration and rollout: feature-gated behind `feature.kms_provenance` and rolled out via console flags. Default rollout: stage -> canary (10%) -> broad. We provide a compatibility shim that emits provenance headers even when checks are disabled to help downstream systems opt-in. Operators must run a one-time migrate script that backfills grant metadata for existing temporary grants (scripts/migrate_backfill_grants.go).

Checklist:
- [x] provenance attestor core implementation
- [x] temporal RBAC evaluator + grant store API
- [x] middleware integration for annotated routes
- [x] unit + integration tests (authz + kms simulator)
- [x] docs: config guide + runbook (docs/security/kms_provenance.md)
- [x] migration script and console flag wiring

Security considerations: signed provenance tokens are HMAC'd with platform KMS-managed secrets, rotated via existing key rotation pipeline. Audit-sampling override can be toggled by SRE and is logged as a privileged action. No tenant secrets are exposed in logs; all provenance headers redact sensitive attributes by default.

Related: ENG-4820 (temporal grants), SEC-117 (audit capture for residency failures).
- Security: add per-request KMS provenance attestation and validation
- Access control: introduce timebound (temporal) RBAC grants and evaluation hooks
- Observability: audit-sampling override and structured provenance headers

Marcus Li: Approve after CI passes and migration script has idempotency checks.
Priya Natarajan: Migration script now checks existing grant tokens and skips duplicates; added unit tests.

Context: Teams report inconsistent retry behavior across SDKs and awkward ergonomics when consuming streaming responses (different iterator/callback patterns per language). This PR unifies the developer experience by introducing: 1) a config-driven retry profile abstraction (gentlebackoff/adaptive/strict) that is serializable and can be passed to SDK constructors; 2) a consistent iterable/pull-stream surface for streaming responses in Python, TypeScript, and Go; 3) lightweight adapter layers for existing callbacks to maintain backwards compatibility; 4) a credential lease hook to smooth token rotation during long-lived streams.

Motivation: reduce cognitive load for cross-platform teams, enable server-side recommendations (Optimize) to suggest retry profiles, and fix edge cases where reauth during stream reconnects caused duplicate events or lost messages.

Design summary: - Retry profiles are plain objects with named profiles (gentlebackoff, balanced, aggressive) and pluggable backoff strategies. SDKs expose a `RetryProfile` config and a `retry_profile` field in client constructors. - Streaming surface: introduce `iter_stream()` in Python (async iterator + sync iterator fallback), `streamIterable()` in TypeScript (AsyncIterable + friendly for for-await), and `StreamIterator` in Go that supports Pause/Resume and Idempotent Resume tokens. - Auth lease hook: credential providers can optionally implement `lease()` returning a short-lived token window; the runtime will prefetch and swap tokens gracefully while preserving a per-stream handshake. - Backwards compatibility: existing `.stream()` methods are shims that call into the new iterables; we provide migration docs and a small compatibility adapter shipped in each SDK package.

Implementation notes: changes touch SDK surface layers only, with minimal runtime changes in the core redwood server to honor the named retry profiles for hosted routes.

Tests: added cross-sdk integration tests that exercise reconnect during token rotation, retry profile effect on transient 5xxs, and stream resume semantics.

Checklist: - [x] TypeScript impl and tests - [x] Python impl and tests - [x] Go impl and tests - [x] Auth lease hook integrated - [x] Migration docs and examples - [x] CI green - [x] Release notes Draft

Commits summary: short, focused commits each per language and docs.

Files changed (high level): - redwood-sdk-typescript/src/stream/iterable.ts (new unified iterable implementation) - redwood-sdk-python/redwood/stream/iterable.py (new async/sync iterator) - redwood-sdk-go/stream/iterator.go (pause/resume tokens) - shared-specs/retry-profiles.yaml (canonical profiles) - docs/sdk/migration/retry-profiles.md - examples/streaming/typed-iterables/* - tests/integration/stream-resume-reauth.test.ts - tests/integration/stream-resume-reauth_test.py - tests/integration/stream_resume_reauth_test.go

Review notes and discussion: - Ethan: requested clearer guarantees for ordering during token swap — added a short section in the body and tests that validate ordering is preserved for per-request monotonic sequence ids. - Sofia: asked to ensure the new retry config can be passed via environment/JSON for Redwood Optimize to suggest overrides — implemented parsing of env var REDWOOD_RETRY_PROFILE and added docs. - Diego: requested smaller surface area for Go ergonomics — we trimmed the iterator API to fewer exported methods and provided a small helper to expose Pause/Resume semantics. CI: initially flaked on e2e streaming; re-run fixed intermittent infra flakiness and all checks passed.

Merge plan: squash-merge into main after approvals; post-merge we will publish SDK minor releases: python 1.12.0, typescript 2.4.0, go v1.9.0 and update CDN docs.

Rollout: behind feature flag on the hosted API to opt-in retry-profile forwarding; SDKs default to "balanced" to keep behavior steady.

Migration guidance: short adapter example in migration doc showing how to convert old stream callback usage to the new async iterator (TS) or sync iterator (Python).

Fix: redundant heartbeat guard to reduce cascading failovers; Hotfix: fast-recovery fuse to avoid oscillatory reopens during transient probe flaps.
Summary: Adds a conservative redundant heartbeat verifier and a fast-recovery fuse to prevent rapid reopen oscillations seen in multi-region ingress spikes. Motivation: Recent incidents (SUP-7123) exposed a pattern where transient probe flaps and concurrent health reconciles triggered repeated region failovers, causing tenant SLO churn. The redundant verifier consults a secondary control-plane probe and recent KV-sync quorum before declaring a region healthy; the fast-recovery fuse enforces an exponential cool-off with jitter for reopen attempts. The feature is behind a feature flag 'redundant_heartbeat_guard' and default fuse parameters are configurable per-region. Changes: runtime/heartbeat_guard: redundant verifier and unit tests; runtime/fuse: fuse state machine with backoff and jitter; telemetry: circuit_transition_reason and fuse_state metrics; infra: pager thresholds and runbook links; ops: hotfix rollout templates and staging canary script; tests: integration e2e simulating probe flaps. Canary rollout plan included. No DB schema changes. Observability: dashboards for fuse_state, verification_latency, reopened_count and short-term alert reopened_count > 5 in 15m.
Squash-merged to main. Hotfix pipeline deployed to canary regions (10%) for 24h then expanded to 100% per rollout plan. Observed 40% reduction in reopen events during staging canary. Owners: Jonah (monitor reopen_count 72h), Infra (probe cost impact after 7d).
