Motivation: We observed transient regional latency spikes and downstream SLO oscillations during rapid regional rejoin events when large numbers of tenant connections returned after an isolate window. This PR introduces a tenanted 'pacekeeper' token-based gating layer plus a soft-rejoin probe that staggers KV warmups and prevents a sharp surge hitting the fast-path. Design summary: The pacekeeper maintains per-tenant windows that limit concurrent fast-path sessions and releases tokens at a measured rate derived from recent successful token consumption and observed P95 latency. The soft rejoin probe runs as part of connection restoration: rather than immediately reattaching a tenant to the regular serving module, the probe exercises a lightweight probe RPC which warms KV cache prefixes and verifies end-to-end tail latency under a capped load before full rejoin. Key features: 1) Token bucket per tenant with exponential decay of peak allowance; 2) Probe RPC with success/fail counters and backoff that feeds into the tenant token rate; 3) Metrics and traces for token availability, token denial rate, probe pass rate, and observed incremental KV hit ratio; 4) Configurable emergency-bypass policy for enterprise customers (safety valve in case of false positives). Backwards compatibility: Pacekeeper operates as a local middleware layer in the serving runtime and is off by default for legacy tenants. We provide a rollout flag that starts in canary for the 'tenanted' rollout group. Tests and validation: Unit tests for token lifecycle, decay scheduler, and probe state machine. Integration test harness simulates 10k tenants rejoining in a 30s window and asserts that fast-path QPS spikes are reduced by at least 70% while average P95 increases less than 10ms. Load tests executed in benchmark-lab region with a shadowing run for 1 hour. Observability: Added 4 new traces and 6 metrics: pacekeeper.tokens.available, pacekeeper.tokens.denied, rejoin_probe.pass_rate, rejoin_probe.latency_p95, tenant_kv_prefix_warm_ratio, tenant_rejoin_delay_dist. Rollout and rollback plan: Deploy behind feature flag on canary (5% of traffic) for 2 hours, monitor metrics and alert on a >5% increase in request error rate or >20% increase in P99 latency for the canary cohort. If triggered, toggle emergency-bypass which immediately drains pacekeeper and allows immediate rejoin. Commits summary: - Add pacekeeper middleware and token store with decay scheduler - Implement soft rejoin probe RPC and state machine - Wire metrics/traces and small console dashboard config - Add unit and integration tests + benchmark harness scenario - Add canary rollout flag and emergency-bypass gate Files changed (high level): src/runtime/pacekeeper.rs (token lifecycle & scheduler), src/runtime/rejoin_probe.rs (probe state machine & RPC client), src/runtime/mod.rs (middleware wiring), charts/console/pacing_dashboard.yaml (dashboard tiles), integration-tests/rejoin_storm_scenario.py (load harness), docs/operational/pacekeeper.md (how to interpret metrics and rollback), infra/featureflags.yaml (canary config), tests/unit/test_pacekeeper.rs (unit tests), tests/integration/test_rejoin_probe.py (integration assertions). Review conversation summary: - Ethan Brooks: "Can we add a per-tenant opt-out flag for compliance customers?" Author: "Added emergency-bypass and an allowlist config; also documented behavior in docs/operational/pacekeeper.md." - Lina Gomez: "Concerned about the token decay math under heavy churn; can we add a stress test?" Author: "Added a 10k-tenant churn scenario to benchmark-lab and uploaded results to the Linear ticket ENG-4621." - Markus Huber: "Looks good, one nit on metric naming and a minor race in token refill." Author: "Fixed metric prefix and added an atomic refill routine; pushed a follow-up commit." CI and checks: - unit-tests: pass - integration-tests (short): pass - lint: pass - benchmark-lab-shadow: pass - e2e: pass Merge notes: Squash merge after final CI green. Release notes: "Introduce tenanted pacekeeper to smooth regional rejoin traffic spikes; enables configurable emergency-bypass and observability for troubleshooting. Improves resilience during large-scale regional restores." Additional context: This PR was implemented as a response to an incident on 2026-02-11 where a region rejoin produced a transient 3x tail-latency spike affecting hosted customers. The approach emphasizes graceful ramping and observability over hard denials; it is intended to be a conservative production improvement and is guarded behind feature flagging for controlled rollout.

Maya Patel: Added emergency-bypass and allowlist; documented in docs/operational/pacekeeper.md

payload.body:
Motivation: We see recurring hard-decommits and noisy SLA violations during cluster-wide reclaim windows. Operators requested a low-risk way to evaluate soft-reservation strategies and emergency capacity behaviors without altering live allocation logic. This PR introduces two related pieces: (1) a 'reservoir stockpiler' subsystem that allows the autoscaler to opportunistically accumulate short-lived capacity credits (stockpiles) for tenants when clusters are underutilized, and (2) a 'deferred SLA experiment' mode that runs a probabilistic simulator inside the control plane to evaluate headroom decay and eviction impacts before applying new autoscaling policies in production.

Summary of changes: single continuous description of code/docs/telemetry and operational tooling added: 1) Core controller: stockpiler manager for dedicated fleets that tracks per-tenant stockpile balance, stockpile decay curve, and redemption rules. 2) Simulator: a background component that replays sampled traffic traces against a configurable policy to estimate SLO violations, mean latency impact, and stockpile exhaustion percentiles. 3) Telemetry: new metrics (reservoir_level_bytes, reservoir_credits, reservoir_decay_rate, reservoir_redeem_success, simulator_predicted_95_latency_delta) and Grafana dashboards. 4) CLI/console controls: experiment toggle, visualization, and an API to export simulated scenarios for on-call review. 5) Safety: a non-invasive opt-in mode that never alters live scheduling decisions; subsequent PR will wire the conservative redemption policy into the live allocator after signoff.

Checklist:
- [x] Reservoir data model and APIs (Create/Consume/Decay)
- [x] Probabilistic replay simulator with scenario seeds and sample replay rate control
- [x] Telemetry + dashboards for stockpile health and simulator outputs
- [x] Unit and integration tests for stockpiler lifecycle
- [x] End-to-end e2e job that runs simulator against canned traces
- [x] Documentation: operator guide and short runbook for experiment adoption

Why this is different: existing autoscaler features control allocation and burst credits at request-time. The stockpiler is an opportunistic pre-allocation mechanism that acts like a short-lived escrow reserve: it captures transient spare capacity and presents it as redeemable credits during future surges. The simulator lets us probe long-tail failure modes (multi-tenant exhaustion, correlated evictions) under realistic workload replays, giving operators quantitative tradeoffs before changing live policies.

Commits summary:
- a1b3d8e: introduce stockpiler store and proto definitions (core types, retention)
- b7f4c2d: stockpiler manager implementation with decay scheduler and redemption hooks
- c3e9f0a: simulator: trace replayer and policy driver (with deterministic seeding)
- d22a7b9: add Prometheus metrics and dashboard JSONs; wire into console UI
- e9b517f: integration tests + e2e runner and sample traces
- f0a4c1b: docs: operator guide and runbook

Changed files (high level):
- src/autoscaler/stockpiler/{manager.go,store.go,types.proto,decay.go} - main logic
- src/autoscaler/simulator/{replayer.go,policy_driver.go,scenarios/} - simulator and sample traces
- src/controlplane/api/{reservoir_api.go,handlers_test.go} - experiment toggle endpoints
- observability/dashboards/reservoir-health.json - new dashboards

This change addresses a class of streaming failures where partial JSON tokens emitted across SSE chunks could be mis-parsed when delimiter bytes (newlines / `data:` markers) were interleaved with token bytes. Root cause: the old parser treated SSE delimiters and JSON byte sequences as independent, which allowed reassembly to drop or reorder delimiter context when incoming TCP/HTTP chunk boundaries split tokens atypically (common with proxies and multiplexed HTTP/2 connections). The fix implements a small lookahead buffer and an explicit synthetic-frame sentinel that is emitted by the stream adapter whenever we detect an incomplete JSON token at a chunk boundary. The parser FSM was updated to (1) prefer consuming delimiter markers only when they are not currently in the middle of a buffered JSON token, (2) treat the synthetic sentinel as an unconditional commit point for any buffered token, and (3) map OpenAI-style terminal sequences (e.g. "data: [DONE]") into the same terminal event flow used internally so tool/function-calling boundaries remain consistent. Also added a set of targeted fuzz tests and an e2e fixture that runs the OpenAI-compat adapter behind a proxy that induces random chunk splits. Backwards-compatible: the streaming wire protocol has not changed; the synthetic sentinel is internal-only. This PR includes docs clarifying streaming error codes and guidance for SDK authors on validating token boundaries. Rollout plan: feature-flagged for 48 hours in canary, then promoted to main if no regressions are observed. See validation_steps for test commands and expected outputs.
Liam Chen: The FSM change makes sense, but can we avoid an extra allocation on the hot path? Suggest reusing a pooled buffer for lookahead.
Nina Roberts: Please add a regression test that reproduces the proxy-chunking symptom we saw in the incident log. Also add a short note to the streaming docs about the error code that indicates a malformed partial token.
Carlos Méndez: Were there any latency regressions in the bench? Even small allocations can amplify at 1k+tps; please include before/after p95 numbers.
Asha Patel: Reworked lookahead to use sync.Pool-backed buffer; added unit that simulates 1k tps with pooled buffers; p95 is unchanged within noise.
Asha Patel: Added a deterministic proxy fixture in pkg/testing and a reproduction test that mirrors the incident. Document updated with streaming error guidance.
Asha Patel: Bench results included in the PR comment thread: p50 unchanged, p95 +1.8ms on microbenchmark (within acceptable SLO); e2e p95 unchanged.
Fix: Streaming API now correctly handles interleaved delimiters and partial JSON tokens split across chunk boundaries. Impact: reduces rare malformed-output and tool-calling failures when proxies or HTTP/2 cause atypical chunking. Migration: none required for API consumers; SDKs updated to include validation helpers.
Run fuzz suite: go test ./pkg/testing -run TestSSEFuzz -fuzz=Fragmentation
Simulate proxy chunking: ./scripts/proxy-chunk-sim --split-pattern=random --target http://localhost:8080/stream and ensure that JSON objects reassemble without loss
SDK smoke: python -m examples.streaming.validate_token_boundaries --endpoint http://localhost:8080/stream (expect: 0 malformed-token errors)

Summary: Introduces the Frugality Horizon autotuner: a tenant-aware automation pipeline that suggests and safely rolls out batching, prefix/KV cache defaults, and per-tenant quantization profile candidates based on sampled telemetry and synthetic workload simulation. Motivation: customers running diverse workloads need predictable unit economics; current defaults are conservative or too generic. This autotuner couples sampled p95/p99 latency, batch hit-rate, token-cost estimates, and model quality regression heuristics to produce prioritized, safe suggestions that can be dry-run via CLI or applied with staged rollouts. What changed: 1) pkg/econ/autotune: core tuning engine, simulation harness, safety gates (latency delta threshold, quality regression window, rollback hooks). 2) cmd/econctl: new CLI for previewing suggestions, running dry-runs, exporting presets-as-yaml, and applying tenant-level rollouts. 3) telemetry/bridge: mapping layer that synthesizes cost-per-token, batch-hit-rate, prefix-cache-hit metrics into the autotuner input format. 4) charts/helm: new helm values for enabling the autotuner and adjusting rollout concurrency. 5) docs/ops: operational runbook, rollback steps, evaluation checklist. 6) tests: unit and end-to-end synthetic-workload tests and a new perf-smoke that runs in CI. Design notes: - Autotuner runs as a controller that processes daily telemetry windows and generates ranked suggestions. - Suggestions include: batching presets (max_batch/target_latency), cache presets (prefix_ttl, kv_cache_allowlist), and quant profiles (int8/llm8/q4_0 variants with estimated PSNR-like quality delta). - Each suggestion carries an estimated delta in unit-cost and a risk score derived from traffic similarity and prior rollouts. - Safety model: suggestions are only applied automatically if they pass low-risk heuristics; otherwise they land in a reviewer queue in the Console and can be applied via econctl with canary/percentage rollouts and automatic rollback triggers. - Dry-run mode: econctl --dry-run produces a synthetic replay of sampled requests against the candidate profile using the simulator and emits a differential report. Checklist: - [x] Core engine implementation - [x] Telemetry mapping and sampling - [x] Simulation harness with synthetic workloads - [x] CLI and docs - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] CI job for perf-smoke Backwards compatibility: the autotuner only produces suggestions; it does not change tenant settings without explicit apply or approved auto-apply policy. The defaults remain unchanged unless opted-in or rolled-out through the Console/CLI. Migration/operational notes: see docs/ops/frugality-horizon-runbook.md for enabling flags, required telemetry retention (30d), and recommended dry-run cadence.

Motivation and summary: We observed that token-level telemetry and token-cost attribution have grown in cardinality as product teams create diverse prompt templates. High-cardinality leads to noisy alerts and expensive ingestion/storage. This PR introduces a cross-tenant token cohort sampler (reservoir-based, LRU decays) that groups similar prompt shapes and token-phase signatures into cohorts for sampling and rollup. A companion component — the contextual alert prioritizer — reorders/reduces alert noise by scoring candidate alerts using cohort-level impact, recent cost delta, and a route-criticality multiplier.

Design highlights: 1) Sampler algorithm: lightweight fingerprinting of prompt-shape + model+seq-dist -> cohort key. Each cohort maintains a capped reservoir of invocation anchors (N=256 default) with LRU-decay on low-traffic cohorts. Reservoir entries carry prefetched KV-cache footprints and a compact phase histogram to enable per-phase latency breakdowns without needing full traces for every request. 2) Prioritizer: Alert candidates are enriched with cohort signal (cost delta, anomaly z-score) and request metadata (tenant SLA tier, route importance). The prioritizer applies a tunable policy to suppress low-impact alerts and to escalate high-impact cohort regressions. 3) Rollup: cohorts emit summarized metrics (token_cost_p50/p95 by phase, cohort_query_count, cohort_kv_miss_rate) with a compact tag set to avoid cardinality explosion. 4) Console: new dashboard 'Token Cohort Overview' summarizes cohort heatmaps, long-tail cohort traces, and prioritized-alert feed.

Files changed (high level): See files_changed_high_level. Key code lives in telemetry/sampler and telemetry/alerts. The console dashboard JSON wires new panels; docs include rollout and migration guidance.

Testing and perf: Unit tests added for sampler edge cases, integration tests validate the prioritizer against replayed production traces (subset sanitized). Microbench: sampler adds ~0.6ms median to request path in optimized build, worst-case +2.4ms for first-seen cohort (prefetch paths mitigate subsequent requests). Memory: capped reservoir keeps per-cohort memory bounded; global cohort table size is configurable and monitored.

Rollout plan: 1) Feature-flagged behind cohort_sampler_v1; opt-in per-tenant. 2) Enable for small number of low-risk tenants for 48h with traffic replay; monitor cohort coverage and missed tail alerts. 3) Gradual ramp to 25% of tenants over two weeks with automatic rollback on error-rate or metric-regression alarms. 4) Default enablement for all non-enterprise tenants after four weeks unless explicitly disabled.

Backward compatibility and migration: Prioritizer is additive: if disabled, existing alert rules remain unchanged. Cohort rollups produce new metric names with stable mapping; existing dashboards unaffected. Migration doc includes a mapping for token-level metric names and recommended alert adjustments.

Checklist: - [x] Core sampler + reservoir store implemented - [x] Prioritizer policy engine and unit tests - [x] Console dashboard and basic visualizations - [x] Integration tests with replay harness - [x] Docs + rollout plan - [x] Feature flag + metrics to monitor enablement

Related work: ENG-4873 (token-cost-scaling) and ENG-4920 (alert-fatigue). This complements earlier token-rollup efforts by moving sampling earlier (in-proxy) and bridging cohorts across tenants to preserve shared signal for rare long-tail templates.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main. Post-merge actions: deploy sampler behind feature flag in staging, schedule a 48h smoke window and fill in observability-runbook entries for the new cohort coverage metrics.

Rollout guarded by feature flag 'cohort_sampler_v1'.
Watch cohort_table_size, cohort_eviction_rate, cohort_kv_miss_rate, token_cohort_p95_phase_latency. If cohort_eviction_rate spikes > 10% sustained, reduce global_cohort_max or increase reservoir cap for impacted tenants. The prioritizer emits metrics 'alert_priority_score' and 'alert_suppressed' to validate suppression behavior.

Motivation: Production workloads show highly variable per-request sequence length and cold-KV cache hit patterns; teams repeatedly tune batch and cache thresholds by hand. This PR introduces a small, opinionated CLI that runs a fast local probe against a workload sample and suggests cost-conscious defaults for continuous batching, prefix/KV cache activation thresholds, and conservative quantization profile hints. The goal is to reduce unit token cost while respecting 99th-percentile latency SLOs and avoiding quality regressions.

What this PR adds: a new CLI command (redwood optimize frugal-tune) that: 1) accepts a workload trace (JSONL of request metadata) or pulls a sampled profile from the console API, 2) runs a lightweight simulator that models batching latency curves, cache hit probability by prefix length, and quantized model throughput deltas, and 3) emits a recommended defaults bundle (batch_size_hint, batch_timeout_ms, cache_min_prefix_tokens, preferred_quant_profile) plus an annotated report with economic tradeoffs (estimated cost per 1M tokens, expected p99 latency impact). The CLI is intentionally conservative: recommendations include a safety margin and explicit rollback instructions.

Technical approach & constraints: The simulator uses the runtime's empirical latency models (extracted from existing perf profiles) combined with a compact queuing model to estimate tail latency at different batching shapes. Cache heuristics are derived from sampled prefix reuse distributions. Quantization guidance is based on precomputed quality-versus-throughput curves for supported model families; the CLI will only recommend a lower-precision profile when estimated token-quality loss is within a user-provided tolerance flag. The tool is offline-only and does not modify live configs; output is a JSON bundle compatible with the platform defaults API.

Changeset summary: adds a new small Go binary under tools/opt-cli/, a simulator package under internal/econsim/, a README and quickstart in docs/opt/, unit tests covering simulation edge cases, and an integration test that validates full CLI flow against a synthetic trace. Also adds small telemetry events (opt_tune.run, opt_tune.apply) gated behind an opt-in flag.

- [x] unit and integration tests
- [x] CLI help and README
- [x] conservative defaults and rollback instructions
- [x] safety telemetry (opt-in)

Usage example: redwood optimize frugal-tune --trace sample.jsonl --max-quality-drop 0.01 --out recommended-defaults.json

Risks and mitigation: Incorrect modeling could suggest aggressive defaults that violate latency SLOs. Mitigations: 1) CLI includes p99 latency estimates and flags when suggestion risk is high; 2) recommendations include explicit canary rollout steps; 3) recommendations default to no-op when sample size is too small.

Follow-ups: Add an optional dry-run mode that can replay a small subset of live traffic against suggested defaults in sandboxed Dedicated capacity (future work, ENG-4207).

Context and motivation:
We see frequent noisy alerting and large trace payloads driven by a small number of high-entropy token sequences (e.g., user-provided code blobs, encoded binary in prompts, or adversarial long random strings). These requests have low signal for SLOs and produce a disproportionate volume of high-fidelity logs and traces, increasing cost and alert churn.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a new metric 'token_path_entropy' emitted per invocation that estimates the Shannon entropy of the token sequence path (rolling window over final N tokens).
- Adds runtime gating to reduce full-trace/log capture for invocations where token_path_entropy > entropy_threshold (configurable per-tenant). This is a sampling/gating control that preserves metadata and light metrics while skipping heavy payload attachment.
- Introduces an alert circuit-breaker rule: when the system detects a sustained increase in high-entropy invocations that drive alert noise without correlated SLO regressions, the circuit-breaker automatically scales alert thresholds and quiets low-signal alert groups for a cooldown window.
- Adds a dedicated Grafana dashboard (Observability / Token Entropy) with panels for entropy distribution, high-entropy invocation rate, correlation to token-cost and latency, and circuit-breaker state timeline.
- Tuning and defaults: entropy_threshold default tuned conservatively to avoid suppressing valid signals; circuit-breaker default uses a 30m warmup and 6h decay.

Checklist:
- [x] Metric instrumentation (ingest + event model)
- [x] Runtime gating flag + tenant config surface
- [x] Dashboard and panels
- [x] Alert rule and circuit-breaker implementation with feature flag
- [x] Unit tests for metric calculation and gating logic
- [x] Integration smoke tests for alert behavior in staging
- [x] Docs: config guide and runbook (docs/observability/entropy-runbook.md)

Commit summary:
- feat(obs): compute token_path_entropy per invocation (lib/telemetry/token_entropy.go)
- feat(obs): emit entropy histogram and percentile rollups to metrics router (telemetry/publishers/metrics_router.go)
- feat(runtime): add gating hook to trace collector and tenant-level config (runtime/tracing/gating.go)
- feat(dash): add Grafana dashboard JSON and README (dashboards/token-entropy.json, dashboards/README.md)
- feat(alerts): implement circuit-breaker orchestration and rules (alerts/circuit_breaker.go)
- test(obs): unit and integration tests for entropy and gating (telemetry/token_entropy_test.go, e2e/entropy-smoke.sh)

Diff highlights (high level):
- lib/telemetry/token_entropy.go: new module with two public functions: EstimateEntropy(sequence[]) and EntropyScoreRollup(invocation). Algorithm: normalized soft-bucketed Shannon estimate (fast, streaming-friendly).
- runtime/tracing/gating.go: new gating path checked at span finalization; adds tenant config lookup and a short-circuit to avoid attaching full log blobs.
- alerts/circuit_breaker.go: state machine with counters and cooldown windows; metrics exported for circuit state changes.
- dashboards/token-entropy.json: dashboard with 6 panels; includes an explainer in panel descriptions and links to runbook.
- docs/observability/entropy-runbook.md: operational guide for oncall: how to diagnose, manually override, tuning knobs.

Testing and validation (summary):
- Unit tests: token_entropy_test covers edge cases (short sequences, identical tokens, unicode payloads).
- Integration: staging run with synthetic high-entropy payload generator; verified that gated traces reduced storage by ~68% and reduced alert volume for a noisy alert group by 84% without any SLO signal change.
- Load: local micro-benchmarks show entropy estimate adds ~0.2ms per invocation on p95 across 8k sequence lengths when implemented with soft-buckets.

Review notes and risk assessment:
- Risk: misconfigured entropy_threshold could suppress legitimate signals. Mitigations: conservative default, config per-tenant, and a manual override in Console. The runbook explains emergency steps to re-enable full fidelity.
- Observability: added explicit metrics for high_entropy_invocations_total and circuit_breaker_state to allow rapid validation after rollout.

payload.body:
Context
We hit an edge case during load tests (see #eng-runtime thread 1770417729) where long-context requests could starve indefinitely when the short queue remains continuously non-empty (e.g., 95/5 mix, short requests arriving at a rate that keeps short queue depth > 0).

Root cause
Our current aging/boost logic only applies when we consider a long request for dispatch. But in sustained short traffic, the dispatch loop effectively never reaches the long queue because the short queue always produces at least one eligible batch each iteration and the per-iteration class share enforcement is soft. In practice this becomes: "short wins every time" and long requests accrue wait time but never trigger a hard preemption.

Fix
- Change aging from a purely additive score to a thresholded "must-serve" promotion: if oldest long request wait_time_ms >= long_starvation_max_wait_ms, we treat LONG as temporarily high priority for at least one dispatch quantum.
- Make the promotion sticky for a bounded number of iterations (long_starvation_burst_iters) so we complete prefill and ensure decode makes progress, but cap it to avoid flipping the system into long-dominant behavior.
- Keep existing token budget guardrails intact: even in promoted mode we still respect per-iteration token budgets, but we allow LONG to consume the class share for that iteration.

Why this is safe
- The promotion only triggers after a long request has exceeded a configured wait threshold; default value tuned for canary to be conservative (2500ms).
- We cap the promoted burst to prevent "long takeover" under pathological long-only scenarios.
- The change is behind the existing mixed scheduler feature flag; no effect when the policy is disabled.

Config knobs
- scheduler.long_starvation_max_wait_ms (new, default: 2500)
- scheduler.long_starvation_burst_iters (new, default: 2)
- scheduler.long_aging_half_life_ms (existing, now used only for tie-breaking rather than progress guarantees)

Tests
- Adds a regression test that replays the starvation scenario: sustained short arrivals + one long request. Asserts:
  1) long request observes bounded time-in-queue (<= threshold + epsilon)
  2) long request receives at least one dispatch within N iterations
  3) short p95 does not blow up (test uses a small simulated scheduler + deterministic clocks rather than GPU runtime)

Bench notes
I ran the synthetic 80/20 and 95/5 mixes in the local simulation harness. This fixes the starvation case; the 80/20 baseline numbers are unchanged within noise. We should still validate on perf-canary once merged into the release branch.

Implementation details
- The dispatch loop now checks oldest_long_wait_ms each iteration (O(1) using tracked head timestamps).
- Promotion sets a local force_class=LONG for the next dispatch selection; it does not reorder queues.
- Metrics: increments scheduler_starvation_promotions_total{class="long"} and records scheduler_oldest_wait_ms{class="long"} to help verify in canary.

Changed areas
- runtime/scheduler/two_queue_dispatch.cc: promotion + sticky burst implementation
- runtime/scheduler/aging.cc: adjust aging semantics (tie-breaker only)
- runtime/scheduler/config.h: add new knobs + validation
- runtime/metrics/scheduler_metrics.cc: add starvation promotion counter
- runtime/tests/scheduler/mixed_workload_starvation_test.cc: new regression test
- docs/internal/runtime/scheduler_policy.md: update with starvation guarantee behavior

Checklist
- [x] Unit/regression tests added
- [x] Metrics added/updated
- [x] Config validation + safe bounds
- [x] Verified feature-flag behavior
- [x] Release branch cherry-pick ready

Review discussion highlights
Lena Fischer: "We need a hard progress guarantee; purely increasing score won’t help if we never look at LONG." -> Implemented thresholded must-serve promotion + sticky burst.
Sofia Ivanova: "Make sure this doesn’t create oscillation with token budgets; keep it bounded." -> Added long_starvation_burst_iters and kept token budget enforcement.
Sean Gallagher: "Add a metric we can alert on during canary." -> Added scheduler_starvation_promotions_total and oldest wait gauge.
Omar El-Sayed: "Ensure prefill/decode separation isn’t regressed." -> Promotion only affects class selection; prefill/decode hooks unchanged.

CI
- build-and-unit-tests: PASS
- runtime-scheduler-tests: PASS
- lint/clang-format: PASS

Merge
Merged via squash into release/runtime-1.18. Follow-up: once perf-canary picks up the new release artifact, we should confirm starvation_promotion counter remains near-zero in normal mixes and only spikes in the synthetic 95/5 scenario.
Fixes a starvation edge case in the mixed-workload two-queue scheduler where long requests could make no progress under sustained short traffic; adds regression coverage.

payload.body:
Motivation: Production shadow traffic often creates transient load spikes during promotion rehearsals and phased seeding. Those spikes can cause autoscalers to misinterpret demand and overprovision, increasing cost and masking regression signals. This PR implements an "epochal shadow reservoir": a lightweight in-memory reservoir sampler and traffic reverberation buffer that smooths shadow bursts, preserves fidelity for replayable smoke, and exposes autoscale-aware heuristics so the inference autoscaler treats shadow rehearsal load as a first-class signal with damped impact.

Design summary: The feature attaches to the shadow ingress path and groups shadow traffic into short-lived epochs (configurable, default 10s). Each epoch keeps a capped reservoir per-model-cohort and emits a controlled, rate-limited replay stream to backend replicas for rehearsal and telemetry. Replays are tagged as rehearsal=true and carry an epoch_id to support deterministic sampling and subsequent bisect/replay. An autoscale adapter publishes a damped load metric (shadow_effective_rps) that is weighted by a tunable damp factor and a decay window. The design aims to: 1) prevent autoscaler overreaction to instantaneous shadow spikes, 2) ensure stable, reproducible rehearsal streams for evaluation, and 3) provide telemetry hooks for signal-level diagnostics and causal attribution.

What changed (high level): added epochal reservoir and replay pipeline; introduced autoscale adapter metric and config knobs; plumbing for rehearsal tagging and epoch provenance; unit and integration tests simulating spike profiles; docs and migration notes; small SDK shim to expose epoch_id in audit logs.

Commits summary: 1) add epochal reservoir core and interfaces; 2) implement epoch grouping and reservoir sampling strategy; 3) replay dispatcher with rate limiter and backoff; 4) autoscale adapter and metric exporter; 5) tests (unit + integration spike harness); 6) docs and config defaults; 7) address reviewer feedback and flake fixes.

Files changed (summary): see changed_files.

Rollout plan: land behind runtime flag `FEATURE_EPOCHAL_SHADOW` default off. Stage rollout in three steps: dev staging (flag on, no autoscale adapter), canary (small percentage of shadow traffic to reservoir, adapter in read-only mode), and progressive promote (enable replay and adapter for monitored clusters). Follow-playbook: monitor shadow_effective_rps, rehearsal success ratio, and autoscale decisions for 48h. Canary guardrails are included in the config and console charting.

Risks & mitigations: incorrect damp factor may hide real load; mitigation: conservative default (0.25) and canary-only initial enablement. Reservoir memory leak risk: bounded caps and epoch eviction implemented; validated via integration memory profiles.

Related work and tickets: ENG-54321 (cohort replay infra), PM-234 (canary observability), INT-88 (incident follow-up for autoscale overprovisioning).

Priya Nambiar (2026-02-15): Addressed: added helm value `epochalShadow.dampFactor`, surfaced epoch_id in SDK shim and audit events, added integration test simulating combined streams. PTAL.
Marina Lopez (2026-02-16): Request small change: make reservoir caps per-cohort configurable via runtime config and not compile-time constant. Also noted a potential N+1 metric export — tracked and fixed in the fixup commit.

Introduce epochal shadow reservoir to smooth shadow traffic spikes, provide damped shadow_effective_rps metric for autoscaler, and add replayable epoch provenance. Feature disabled by default; enable via FEATURE_EPOCHAL_SHADOW or Helm value epochalShadow.enabled.

Motivation: Clients implementing OpenAI-compatible semantics (rate limits, retry-after, idempotency) observed inconsistent retry behavior across hosted and dedicated backends. This caused duplicated tool/function calls and variable backoff behavior for streaming clients when mid-stream transient errors occurred. This PR standardizes retry semantics exposed by the Redwood API and the OpenAI compatibility shim, and strengthens structured error frames for streaming so that clients can make deterministic retry and deduplication decisions.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Adds a small, explicit 'retry contract' surface to errors and streaming frames, introduces a Retry-After-Priority header to disambiguate clock vs quota windows, formalizes Idempotency-TTL semantics returned to clients, and updates the OpenAI shim to map legacy headers into the new structured fields. Also includes integration tests, docs, and SDK compatibility notes.

Key changes (high-level):
- Response error shape now includes: code (string), message (string), retryable (boolean), retry_after_seconds (integer, null if not applicable), quota_bucket (string, for cardinality-based rate windows). These are surfaced for HTTP 429/503/504 and streaming error frames.
- New header 'Retry-After-Priority' with values 'clock' | 'quota' | 'server' to indicate the semantics of Retry-After when present. This allows clients to choose backoff strategies (e.g., clock-based sleep vs jittered retry).
- Idempotency TTL: server adds 'Idempotency-TTL' (seconds) in both success and error responses when an Idempotency-Key was provided, clarifying how long the server will hold deduplication state.
- Streaming frames: error frames are now JSON objects with fields {"error": {<structured error>}, "terminal": true|false}. Non-terminal streaming errors include retryable flag so the client can decide to continue or abort. Terminal=true indicates the stream should be considered closed by the server.
- OpenAI shim mappings: old headers (X-RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After) are translated into retry_after_seconds + Retry-After-Priority and quota_bucket; existing OpenAI-compatible flakey clients will still receive the normal OpenAI headers for backward compatibility but are encouraged to read the structured body.
- Backcompat shim: an optional compatibility mode (env REDWOOD_COMPAT_OLD_RETRIES=yes) writes legacy headers only; disabled by default in new deployments.

Commits (summary):
- Add structured error fields and tests (author: pkothari)
- Implement Retry-After-Priority header and mapping layer
- Streaming: implement structured error frames and update frame serializer
- OpenAI shim: map legacy headers into structured error payloads and add compatibility toggle
- Docs: API contract section, SDK guidance, migration notes
- Integration tests and CI fixes

Files changed (representative, small snippets included where useful):
- redwood/openai/shim/response_mapper.go: add toStructuredError(err) -> returns code/message/retryable/retry_after_seconds/quota_bucket and header mapping (snippet: 'resp.Headers.Set("Retry-After-Priority", priority)')
- redwood/runtime/stream/stream_serializer.go: replace plain-error-frame with structured JSON frames (snippet: 'frame.Data = json.Marshal(struct{Error interface{} `json:\"error\"`; Terminal bool `json:\"terminal\"`}{...})')
- redwood/api/http/headers.go: introduce constants for Retry-After-Priority and Idempotency-TTL
- redwood/tests/integration/retry_contract_test.go: new table-driven tests covering clock vs quota windows and idempotency TTL checks
- docs/api/retry-contract.md: adds examples, client pseudo-code for streaming and non-streaming flows
- redwood/observability/metrics.go: add metric rwd.retry_priority_emitted{priority} to monitor server-side decisions

Notes on compatibility and rollout:
- Backward compatible by default: we keep existing OpenAI headers but prefer structured body fields. SDKs will be updated in follow-up PRs to prefer structured fields first and fall back to headers.
- Feature flagging: the new header and structured frames are gated behind an opt-in config so that we can enable progressively across regions. The PR includes a migration playbook in docs/migrations/retry_contract.md.

Testing:
- Unit tests for mapping logic and serializer (run: make test ./...; all pass)
- Integration tests simulate quota windows and clock-based rate resets; we add a mock clock to deterministically exercise Retry-After-Priority decisions.
- Manual staging run: streaming clients (Node + Python) exercised 1k short lived streams with induced 429/503s. No duplicated tool calls observed when idempotency keys were used.

Operational considerations:
- Metric added to help detect misconfigurations when servers emit 'quota' but clients assume 'clock'.
- Logs include a short reason string when Retry-After-Priority is chosen (e.g. 'quota-window', 'global-quota', 'node-overloaded').
- Rolling enablement recommended: start with non-critical regions and enable compat mode for legacy integrations.

Related: ENG-2104 (retry contract design), ENG-2201 (stream framing for errors).
Alejandro Ruiz (reviewer): Please add a short justification for choosing header + body shape vs only body. Clients often rely on headers for proxies—make sure the shim preserves both.
Priya Kothari (author): Added backcompat behavior to keep legacy headers by default; documented rationale in docs/migrations/retry_contract.md.
Meera Patel (reviewer): Integration tests look good. Is there a plan to limit the cardinality of quota_bucket? We should avoid unbounded cardinality causing metrics cardinality explosions.
Priya Kothari (author): quota_bucket is intentionally coarse (e.g., 'user:global', 'org:region') — clarified in code comments and added a unit test that asserts max 32 distinct buckets in a test run.
Liam O'Connor (reviewer): Streaming changes are significant; can we provide an opt-out for existing streaming SDKs in case of unexpected deserialization errors?
Priya Kothari (author): Added feature flag REDWOOD_COMPAT_OLD_RETRIES for streaming to emit old plain-string frames; off by default. Also added SDK guidance to catch structured frames defensively.
Alejandro Ruiz (reviewer): CI integration flake noted; reran tests after fix. Approving now.
Meera Patel (reviewer): Approve after adding one more comment on docs wording.
- Standardized structured error responses with retry metadata for HTTP and streaming.
- New Retry-After-Priority header to disambiguate retry semantics.
- Idempotency-TTL header added to clarify deduplication window.
- Streaming frames now include structured error objects with terminal flags.
- Backcompat mode available via REDWOOD_COMPAT_OLD_RETRIES.
See docs/api/retry-contract.md for migration steps.

Introduce a set of coordinated changes to improve RBAC v2 maintenance, audit privacy, and KMS residency verification: (1) policy TTLs for RBACv2 role bindings and templates so expiring privileges require re-approval or rotation, (2) a soft-deny gate that routes requests from expired/ambiguous policy states into an enriched audit queue rather than hard-denying production traffic, (3) an audit-entropy mitigator that reduces high-cardinality trace identifiers in audit logs to limit cross-region linkability while preserving integrity hashes for forensic needs, and (4) a lightweight KMS introspection HTTP endpoint used by control-plane components to verify key region affinity during policy evaluation. This PR includes server-side implementations, a migration to add TTL metadata to existing policy objects, unit and integration tests, docs for operators and compliance teams, a console flag to surface expiring policies, and a rollout plan to enable soft-deny by default behind a feature flag. Motivation: customers need short-lived/rotating operator grants for compliance reviews and we need a low-risk migration path that avoids accidental denials during rollout while improving audit privacy for multi-region tenants.

Motivation: Certain customers require privacy-preserving rollouts where requests from users who have not consented to behavioral experimentation must never be routed to canary variants. This PR introduces a consent-aware canary path, explicit feature-gates for experiment eligibility, and an automated revert playbook that triggers on either privacy policy violations or SLO/regression signals. Design: add a ConsentRouter component that evaluates signed consent tokens and user-level flags; extend RolloutPolicy to include consent_gate (opt-in/opt-out/strict) and per-cohort mapping; implement a RevertOrchestrator that listens to telemetry gates (latency/error/quality and privacy_audit signals) and performs snapshot revert, traffic-quarantine, and safe-drain sequences; surface new toggles in Console for admins to preview impacted cohorts. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is off and existing rollouts continue to work; if consent_gate omitted, rollout falls back to legacy routing. Tests and validation: unit tests for router and orchestration logic, integration e2e scenarios simulating mixed-consent cohorts, and a staged canary smoke run in perf-canary lab. Rollout plan: land behind a feature flag, enable in staging with synthetic traffic, then enable for a single low-risk customer cohort, monitor key metrics for 48 hours, then widen. Checklist: [x] router implementation [x] controller integration [x] metrics and audit events [x] runbook + console UI [x] e2e smoke tests [x] Linear ticket tags. Notes: this PR intentionally keeps consent evaluation synchronous at the routing layer to avoid accidental shadowing; future work will explore async pre-filtering cache for latency optimization.

Motivation: Teams repeatedly ask for a lightweight way to reason about tenant-level unit economics (a simple, reproducible sandbox) before applying batch/cache/quantization defaults at scale. This PR adds a developer-facing CLI called "econ-smelter" that runs a Monte Carlo micro-simulator using a tenant's sampled traffic profile and produces deterministic heuristic presets (batch shapes, prefix cache hints, and candidate quant profiles) plus a provenance report that ties heuristics back to simulated cost/latency tradeoffs.

What this changes: single continuous change set that introduces: 1) cmd/econ-smelter CLI (Go) with subcommands `simulate`, `export-presets`, and `explain`; 2) a compact simulator implemented in Python (internal/econ/simulator.py) that can be embedded or run remotely for heavier sim runs; 3) heuristics generator (internal/econ/heuristics.go) that converts simulation results into tenant-safe presets with confidence bands; 4) telemetry adapter (internal/telemetry/econ_exporter.go) to emit structured events to Console for visual diffs; 5) a small presets-as-code YAML schema and examples under examples/econ-smelter/; 6) e2e smoke tests and unit tests.

Key behaviors and guarantees: - The CLI accepts either a recorded sample (ndjson of request shapes) or a synthetic distribution and runs N Monte Carlo trials to compute expected per-token cost, P95 latency, and fallback risk. - Heuristics generator produces up to three candidate presets (conservative, balanced, aggressive) and annotates them with expected unit cost delta and rollback safety score. - Exports include a normalized telemetry manifest so Console can visualize the simulated delta when importing a preset. - Default output is idempotent YAML that can be applied with existing defaults-as-code tooling.

How to review: focus on correctness of simulation maths (internal/econ/simulator.py), the mapping heuristics (internal/econ/heuristics.go), and the telemetry schema (internal/telemetry/econ_schema.md embedded). The PR includes an annotated example run in examples/econ-smelter/run-annotation.md.

Testing notes: included unit tests cover the mapping from simulation percentiles to preset thresholds and CLI integration tests exercise a small synthetic tenant trace. Local smoke run performed with `make econ-smelter-sample` reproduces the sample in examples and prints three preset candidates.

Performance: small-sample simulations (5k synthetic requests, 100 trials) complete in ~6s locally and in CI the Python sim is capped with a 30s timeout. Heuristic generation is O(n) in the number of candidate shapes and negligible.

Backward compatibility: presets produced use the current presets schema and will be validated against the existing presets-as-code validator. No runtime configuration has changed; this is an additive tooling feature.

Security: no secrets or keys are introduced. Telemetry events are scrubbed of request payloads; only shape/size/latency/cost statistics are emitted.

Release notes: new command-line tool `econ-smelter` (developer preview) for tenant-level microeconomic simulation and heuristics export.

Related: ENG-2148 (tenant prefilling simulation prototype), ENG-2199 (presets-as-code import path), and an internal doc link to the Console visualization PR (referenced in the review comments).
Marco Li: Great direction. One question: the simulator assumes independent inter-arrival times per request — can we model burst correlations?
Elena Park: We kept the first pass simple to get an iterative flow. I added a `--burst-model` flag that accepts a small HMM descriptor; docs note the limitation. Will iterate if we see requests that need it.
Dina Rao: The rollback safety score is helpful; please add a short justification for the thresholds used (why 15% delta maps to 'balanced').
Elena Park: Added justification and links to ENG-2148 design notes in examples/run-annotation.md; thresholds come from historical tenant rollouts and conservative bounds used by the rollout service.
Owen Fitzgerald: CI flaked once on the Python sim timeout; can you ensure the sim has deterministic RNG seed for tests?
Elena Park: Test changes: sim_test uses fixed seed and CI config increased test timeout to 45s for Linux runners. Reran CI and all checks passed.

Introduces a session-sticky A/B scheduling lane with retrospective mitigation hooks; adds telemetry for session-level divergence; exposes rollback playbook via API; non-breaking default behavior; opt-in via rollout config.
Motivation: Certain A/B experiments require session affinity (stickiness) across phased rollouts to avoid erratic UX when users bounce between model variants during an experiment. Operators also requested a way to surface and auto-apply retrospective mitigations when cohort-level regressions are detected after a roll-forward window. This PR implements a session-sticky A/B scheduler that pairs: (1) a lightweight session affinity token managed by the gateway, (2) a scheduler that respects session continuity when assigning variants, and (3) a retrospective-mitigation subsystem that computes cohort deltas over a lookback window and applies fast mitigations (traffic shrink, snapshot revert, or sample quarantine) via the rollout controller. Changes: 1) scheduler core: new SessionAffinityManager and AbSessionAllocator with pluggable hashing and TTL; 2) rollout engine: integration hooks for retrospective mitigation policies and a compact policy DSL; 3) telemetry: per-session trace ids, cohort-delta metrics, and an explainability tag emitted on mitigations; 4) API: /rollouts/{id}/mitigation-status and an admin endpoint to replay a retrospective decision; 5) docs/tests: unit, integration, and an end-to-end smoke harness with synthetic sessions. Safety model: default rollout configs remain unchanged unless session_affinity is enabled. Retrospective mitigations are opt-in and require an explicit mitigation_budget in the rollout spec. The subsystem is designed to only enact non-disruptive actions (traffic shrink by fraction, sample quarantine) unless the operator escalates to a full snapshot revert. Implementation notes: decided on deterministic allocation using siphash128 to avoid cross-language variance; affinity token is signed and has a 24h TTL by default; the allocator keeps a tiny cache to avoid recomputing for heavy tails. Testing: added unit tests for allocator boundary cases, integration tests exercising mitigations against the canary simulator, and a stress job that validates memory/latency under heavy session loads. Rollout plan: staged rollout to internal customers for 2 weeks behind a feature flag, then gated beta with SLO checks (latency and quality delta thresholds) before global enablement. Backout plan: if any critical regression is seen, the mitigation subsystem can (a) instantly shrink variant traffic to 0% (fast path), (b) quarantine sessions for sampling and replay, or (c) initiate snapshot revert via the model registry integration. Related: linear ENG-1298 tracks product acceptance criteria; SUP-3421 is the support case that motivated retrospective mitigations. Checklist: - [x] core allocator implemented - [x] mitigation DSL and engine - [x] API and console hooks - [x] telemetry and alert rules - [x] tests and e2e harness - [x] docs and runbook Notes: this PR intentionally keeps the sticky logic out of the canonical decision graph to minimize risk to other rollout modes. Future work: add probabilistic decay for long sessions and automatic mitigation suggestions based on historical signal patterns.
Arjun Patel: Left small nits on allocator locking; please ensure the cache uses a jittered eviction to avoid stampeding.
Maya Chen: Addressed locking and added a microbenchmark for lookup latency.
Diego Rivera: Telemetry looks good; please add a high-cardinality-safety note to the metrics doc.
Sofia Novak: Confirmed API shape; requested a minimal JSON schema change for mitigation events.
Maya Chen: Updated API schema and added contract tests against the admin client.
Arjun Patel: Approving pending one more integration run.
CI: Integration tests passed on second run; initial flake was a timing-related mock.
Squash merged to main after approvals and green CI. Post-merge actions: feature flag set to off by default; internal canary rollout scheduled for 2026-03-02; runbook linked in docs.

Summary: Introduces an attention sparsity mapper that detects per-head and per-layer sparsity patterns at runtime and routes attention kernels to sparsity-optimized codepaths; adds a KV bucket rebalancer that keeps KV-shard occupancy balanced across GPU lanes and proactively migrates small cold-buckets into contiguous slabs to avoid fragmentation. Motivation: MQA/GQA model modes (mixed head widths and grouped attention) produce pathological per-head allocation and microburst patterns that increase p99 latency and cause uneven kernel selection leading to suboptimal GPU utilization. This PR implements two complimentary mechanisms to address these issues: (1) a lightweight runtime mapper that tags requests with a sparsity profile (head-density histogram + token alignment fingerprint) and biases kernel selection towards sparse-friendly kernels when beneficial; (2) a background KV bucket rebalance worker that runs during idle cycles and reclaims fragmented KV slots, coalesces tiny buckets, and pre-warms likely-cold buckets for models with high short-burst variance. Key changes: new runtime/attn/sparsity_mapper.{cpp,h} and runtime/kv/kv_rebalancer.{cpp,h}; scheduler hooks to honor sparsity hints during kernel dispatch; a new continuous-batching window guard that prevents microbursts from breaking batch packing for short-lived interactive sessions; feature flag gating (feature_flags.yaml) and operator-config knobs for rebalance aggressiveness and CPU/GPU resource limits. Benchmarks: end-to-end canary on Dedicated (8xA100 equivalent): Llama-MQA 13B, 8k context: p50 -6.1% latency, p95 -9.4%, p99 -18% (tail wins); throughput +7.8% for steady streams; Qwen-34B GQA mode: p99 -15% under bursty traffic with 16-token microbursts; reduced kernel fallback rate by 62% on average across 50k test traces. Backwards compatibility and safety: default behavior is off; rollout via feature flag; KV rebalance is read-only until operator enables migration mode. Rollout plan: step 1 canary in Hosted in eu-west-1 with small percentage of traffic (1%), monitor p50/p95/p99, kernel fallback rate, KV fragmentation metric; step 2 expand to Dedicated pools with opt-in; step 3 enable background migration for Private with operator approval. Testing: unit tests for mapper heuristics and rebalance FSM, synthetic replay tests with recorded production traces, end-to-end perf jobs run in nightly cluster, additional integration tests to ensure no data corruption during movable KV operations. Related work: builds on prior KV compactor work and head-tiling heuristics but focuses on runtime detection and live rebalancing rather than offline packing. Rollback: disable flags and revert head_branch; extensive observability added to trace kernel choice, sparsity fingerprint, and rebalance actions. Migration notes: for Private deployments operators should disable migration until maintenance window is scheduled. See linked Linear ENG-3491 for perf goals and ENG-3627 for rollout checklist.
Ethan Zhao: Nice focused split. Two high level asks: (1) can the sparsity fingerprint be computed in the fast path without extra allocations? (2) add a safety net to avoid rebalance thrashing if the model has extreme churn.
Priya Nambiar: Responded: fingerprint uses stack-allocated fixed buffer and is computed during tokenization hook; rebalance uses exponential backoff and a throttle window per model shard to avoid thrash.
Lars Håkansson: Please add an integration test that runs with synthetic microbursts and validates no data loss during migration.
Priya Nambiar: Added tests/kv/kv_rebalance_fsm_test.py with a migration dry-run mode; confirmed no corruption on CI and on nightly cluster.
Miguel Ortega: Observability looks good, but add a histogram for 'rebalance_moved_bytes' and a boolean gauge 'rebalance_in_progress' for alerting.
Priya Nambiar: Added metrics and dashboard snippet to observability/metrics.
Ethan Zhao: Approve after small docs tweak.
Lars Håkansson: Approved.
Introduce attention sparsity mapper and KV bucket rebalancer. Opt-in feature flags default to disabled; expected p99 reductions on MQA/GQA models and improved kernel selection for sparse heads. Operators: review rebalance config before enabling migration in Private deployments.
Default off. Flags: runtime.attn.sparsity_mapper.enabled, runtime.kv.rebalancer.mode={dry,rebalance,migrate}, runtime.kv.rebalancer.cpu_limit, runtime.kv.rebalancer.gpu_warmup_budget. Migration must be scheduled in maintenance window for air-gapped installs.

Context: We continue to converge the Redwood API surface with OpenAI /v1/chat.completions expectations while preserving the runtime semantics and safety guarantees of the platform. Customers expect consistent handling of 'stop' semantics, role aliases, and token-level diagnostics (logprobs) across streaming and non-streaming paths. Motivation: Prior implementations duplicated stop heuristics across the streaming coordinator and the batched inference path, which led to subtle differences for edge cases (multi-token stops, weighted stop lists) and made tool/function-calling integration brittle during stream handoffs. This PR centralizes stop ranking and logprob post-processing into a small coordinator layer that sits between the compatibility layer and the runtime, and adds an explicit role-resolution pass to keep role aliasing deterministic.

What this PR does: 1) Introduces a lightweight ChatParamCoordinator that normalizes incoming /v1/chat parameters (stop arrays, stop-weights, role aliases, temperature/nucleus fallbacks) into a single canonical representation used by both streaming and batch paths. 2) Adds a StopRanking module that computes a prioritized stop prediction list using model token boundaries and span-level scoring; it produces a stable stop decision object consumed by the stream-framer and the final message serializer. 3) Extracts logprob abstraction helpers so tooling (SDKs and observability) can request per-token top-k scores without duplicating formatting logic. 4) Adds role resolution mapping (role_alias -> canonical_role) and ensures the mapping is recorded in the response metadata returned both in streaming deltas and the final framed JSON envelope. 5) Small SDK bindings and example demonstrating a predictable fncall handoff when a tool returns a stop-inducing token sequence.

Behavioral guarantees and compatibility: - Backwards compatible default behavior: if a request uses legacy fields, coordinator will map them to the canonical form. - Streaming parity: streamed deltas include a sentinel when a StopRanking decision is reached; clients using framed json will receive identical final message shapes as non-streaming completions. - Logprobs: the abstraction returns scores in OpenAI-compatible arrays (token, logprob, top_logprobs) but the internal representation remains optimized for vectorized retrieval. - Safety: StopRanking enforces a minimum safety filter pass (configured via runtime flag) so that stop tokens flagged by the safety subsystem are treated with priority.

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for coordinator normalization and stop-ranking heuristics (tests/unit/chat/coordinator_test.rs). - Integration tests exercising streaming/non-streaming parity across role aliasing and multi-stop lists (tests/integration/chatv1_stop_compat.test). - Added e2e scenario in examples/compatibility/chat_tooling_example.py demonstrating function-call -> tool -> resume flow when tool output contains stop tokens. - Benchmarked tail-latency impact: coordinator adds ~0.3ms median and <1.5ms p95 on a 512-token window in our canary environment; included micro-optimizations to keep path hot.

Rollout plan: feature gated behind `chatv1_param_coordinator` flag; gradual canary rollout to 10% of hosted traffic for 48h, then 50% for 24h, then full. If regressions observed, flag can be toggled to restore previous per-path heuristics.

Checklist: - [x] Coordinator implementation and unit tests - [x] Stream-framer integration and delta sentinel - [x] SDK example updated - [x] Observability added (trace/span for stop decisions) - [x] Performance microbench and notes included

Notes: This is intentionally non-breaking; however, customers that relied on previous stop tie-breaking may observe deterministic but different choices in certain multi-stop/overlapping token cases. We will surface this in release notes and the console rollout modal.
Mateo Ruiz (Reviewer): Can we avoid copying token arrays twice in the framer? Suggest passing a token view and annotating boundaries instead of cloning. Requested change noted.
Aisha Patel (Author): Switched to token views and annotated in-place; updated framer to hold a small lifetime-bound reference in coordinator path.
Lin Qiao (Reviewer): Add a short note in docs explaining deterministic tie-breaking for overlapping stops so users can anticipate behavior. Approved after docs update.
Jamal Thompson (SRE): Verified canary logs for stop-decision spans and trace spans look sane; minor suggestion to reduce p95 noise in metrics aggregation; resolved.
Mateo Ruiz (Reviewer): LGTM — approving.
Add ChatParamCoordinator to normalize /v1/chat parameters and produce stable stop decisions across streaming and batch paths. Role alias resolution and OpenAI-compatible logprob formatting are now unified. Backwards-compatible by default; customers may see different deterministic tie-breaking in overlapping 'stop' cases.
payload.title: v1/chat: coordinator for stop-ranking, role resolution, and logprob abstraction

## Summary
This PR reconciles naming between "prefix cache" vs "KV cache" metrics in the serving runtime and standardizes metric + label names to match:
- Observability standards: `cache-metrics-naming-and-cardinality-policy`
- ADR: `adr-prefix-kv-cache-hit-rate-definition`

Net effect: dashboards/alerts can rely on one stable namespace and avoid ambiguous (and occasionally inverted) terminology that crept in across earlier instrumentation PRs.

## Motivation / context
During ENG-4821 review + early dashboard wireframes, we found:
- Some metrics used `prefix_cache_*` for what was actually KV reuse (post-prefill), while others used `kv_cache_*` for prefix reuse during prefill.
- Counters were inconsistently suffixed (`_count` vs `_total`) and gauges used mixed units.
- Label keys drifted (`model` vs `model_id`, `route` vs `route_id`, `deployment` vs `deployment_mode`).

This made it hard to build consistent panels and also complicated ingestion-side allowlists and drop rules.

## What changed
### 1) Metric namespaces and canonical names
We now use two explicit top-level families:
- `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.*` for prefix/prompt reuse during prefill
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.*` for KV reuse effectiveness during decode (and related capacity/pressure signals)

Canonical examples:
- `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.reused_tokens_total`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.requests_with_reuse_total`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.hit_tokens_total`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.miss_tokens_total`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.miss_tokens_total{miss_reason=...}`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.evictions_total{eviction_reason=...}`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.memory_pressure_ratio` (gauge in [0,1])
- `redwood.runtime.cache.wasted_prefill_tokens_total` (cross-cutting; kept outside prefix/kv to match earlier dashboard spec)

### 2) Label key normalization
Aligned to standards doc and gateway join keys:
- `deployment_mode`: hosted | dedicated | private
- `region`: e.g. us-east-1
- `model_id`, `model_version`
- `route_id`
- `prompt_length_bucket`: small fixed set (e.g. 0_256, 257_1024, 1025_4096, 4097_plus)

No behavioral changes to allowlists here; this PR just ensures runtime emits the canonical keys that ingestion expects.

### 3) Deprecation / compatibility plan
Legacy metric names remain emitted as *deprecated aliases* for a limited time:
- Runtime will emit both canonical + legacy names for **2 release trains** (or 30 days in hosted, whichever is longer), guarded by `cache_telemetry.emit_legacy_names=true` (default: true in prod for now).
- New names are always emitted when cache telemetry is enabled.
- Legacy names are annotated in docs as deprecated; dashboards should migrate ASAP.

Deprecation mapping (non-exhaustive, see `docs/internal/telemetry/cache_metrics_migration.md` for full list):
- `redwood.cache.kv.hit_rate` -> `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.hit_tokens_total` + `...miss_tokens_total` (hit-rate computed in queries)
- `redwood.cache.prefix.hit_count` -> `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.requests_with_reuse_total`
- `redwood.cache.prefix.reuse_depth` -> `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.reused_tokens_total` (depth now represented via histogram in separate PR; this PR aligns the family name)

Rationale: standards prefer emitting the raw totals/histograms and computing derived ratios in dashboards/queries to avoid confusion around partial-hit semantics.

## Files / areas touched (high level)
- `runtime/telemetry/cache_metrics.*`: renamed instruments + label keys
- `runtime/telemetry/metrics_registry.*`: added alias helper for temporary legacy emission
- `runtime/config/cache_telemetry_flags.*`: `emit_legacy_names` flag + docs
- `docs/internal/telemetry/cache_metrics_migration.md`: mapping table + timeline
- `tests/integration/cache_metrics_*`: updated assertions to check canonical names; retained one test that asserts legacy aliases still show up when enabled

## Testing
- Unit tests updated for canonical metric keys
- Integration test: `CacheMetricsEmitBothNamesWhenLegacyEnabled` verifies both are present
- Validated locally with `telemetry_smoke` target (ensures ingestion schema accepts new label keys)

CI:
- build-runtime: pass
- runtime-unit: pass
- runtime-integration: pass
- lint: pass

## Notes for dashboard/alert owners
- Please update queries to new names. Legacy names will remain for a short window but should not be relied on.
- This PR intentionally does *not* change sampling; see PR-18425 for sampling/rate-limits.

## Review discussion highlights
- Omar El-Sayed: requested we avoid the term "hit_rate" for raw metrics and compute ratios in dashboards to align with ADR partial-hit semantics. Updated accordingly; removed `*_hit_rate` gauges.
- Allison Grant: asked for an explicit migration doc + timeline. Added `cache_metrics_migration.md` and release note.
- Caleb Johnson: confirmed label key normalization is compatible with ingestion allowlists; requested we do not introduce per-tenant labels here. No tenant labels added.

## Checklist
- [x] Names aligned to standards + ADR
- [x] Legacy aliases gated and time-bounded
- [x] Docs include mapping + timeline
- [x] Tests updated

## Commits (squashed)
1) telemetry: rename cache metric instruments + normalize labels
2) telemetry: add legacy alias emission helper + config flag
3) docs: add cache metrics migration mapping + deprecation timeline
4) tests: update integration assertions for canonical names

Merged via squash.

Related:
- Linear: ENG-4821 (finalize metric definitions/tags)
- Downstream dashboards: observability-pack PR-612 (panels) will be updated to canonical names after this lands
- Telemetry: cache metrics renamed to match observability standards and ADR definitions; legacy metric names remain temporarily as deprecated aliases (see runbook/docs for mapping).

Adds a low-volume presubmit cost sampler and a toolchain stabilizer that reduces CI variance (no user-facing API changes). Backfill: recommended for teams experiencing noisy CI due to toolchain churn.
Context: CI noise from transitive dep updates and toolchain version flips has led to intermittent presubmit failures and unpredictable cost spikes in hosted runs. Motivation: reduce noise, gather sample-based cost telemetry, and stabilize the dev toolchain so presubmit failures are actionable rather than transient. What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight presubmit-cost-sampler pipeline (ci/presubmit/sampler.yaml) that runs on ~0.5% of PRs and records job-level time/cpu/mem/infra-cost estimates to the internal CI-telemetry store. 2) Introduces a toolchain-stabilizer service (infra/toolchain-stabilizer/) that: - pins a curated minimal set of tool versions for presubmit lanes, - warms language/OS-specific caches on ephemeral runners, - injects a cache-warm header into existing install steps. 3) Adds an opt-in "quiet-merge-window" gating policy (scripts/merge-window/README.md) that batches non-urgent merges during off-peak windows to reduce peak CI contention. 4) Adds a small metrics exporter (tools/ci-metrics/exporter.go) and a docs page (docs/ci/cost-sampler.md) describing cost metrics and how teams interpret them. Backwards compatibility: all changes are opt-in via two repo-level feature flags (repo settings): ci.cost_sampler and ci.toolchain_stabilizer. Default rollout: ci.cost_sampler=false, ci.toolchain_stabilizer=false. Rollout plan: stage 1 (internal): enable both flags for redwood/* small teams (1 week) and validate stability. Stage 2 (canary): enable ci.toolchain_stabilizer=true for 10% of active repos and ci.cost_sampler=true at 0.5% PR sample rate (2 weeks). Stage 3 (gradual): increase sampler to 2% and stabilizer to 50% if metrics are green. Testing done: - Unit tests for exporter and stabilizer boot sequence - End-to-end smoke against ephemeral runners (ci/presubmit/smoke) - Canary presubmit runs recorded in telemetry (see CI checks) Checklist: - [x] Feature flags implemented - [x] Minimal docs added - [x] Telemetry schema versioned (v1) - [x] Quick rollback path (feature flag off) Known limitations: sampler estimates are model-based and may over/under-estimate infra cost by ~10% initially; we will calibrate over next 2 weeks. Related: ENG-1456 (presubmit-costing), ENG-1489 (toolchain hygiene).
Elliot Reed: Can we make the sampler sample rate configurable per-repo? Suggest adding a repo-level override (addressed in feature_flags.go).
Priya Natarajan: Reply: added repo override and documented in docs/ci/cost-sampler.md; default remains throttled via org policy.
Samir Patel: Request change: cache-warming needs idempotency guard to avoid re-warm storms. Actioned: cache-warmer.sh now contains a lockfile+ttl.
Ava Chen: Approved after verifying telemetry schema and test coverage. Left a small nit about log verbosity (fixed).
Merged via squash (commit a1b2c3d). Feature flags toggled for internal canary: ci.toolchain_stabilizer=true (10% repos), ci.cost_sampler=true (0.5% PR sample). Release notes attached to changelog. Backout: toggle flags off to rollback.
payload.title: Introduce presubmit cost sampler and toolchain stabilizer

Motivation: Canary evaluators are sensitive to short-lived traffic bursts that inflate tail latency and throughput variance, causing noisy false-positive rollbacks and developer friction. This PR implements a probe-rate controller (Temporal Sigmoid Throttler) that dynamically attenuates probe injection when burstiness and SLO gradient indicate transient noise, plus a Graceful Cutover policy that defers final traffic shifts until a stability window passes.

What this changes: Adds a probe rate controller that uses a short-term burst index, SLO gradient, and a configurable sigmoid shaping function to reduce probe intensity during high-variance windows; introduces a Graceful Cutover state machine in the rollout controller so final cutovers only occur after an adaptive stability score is met; expands metrics, traces, dashboards, and test harnesses.

Checklist: [x] Temporal Sigmoid algorithm implemented and unit-tested. [x] Integration tests exercising burst scenarios added. [x] Dashboards and alert rules updated. [x] Feature gated behind canary.temporal_sigmoid feature flag. [x] Rollout plan with progressive enablement prepared.

Why sigmoid shaping: A sigmoid curve provides a smooth attenuation factor between 0 and 1 as burst index increases, avoiding hard thresholds that cause oscillation. The shaping parameters are tunable per-customer workload profile.

Testing and results: Local load tests and perf lab synthetic traces (mixed steady+bursts) show false-positive canary triggers drop from ~14% to ~2% across 1-minute microburst scenarios, while detection latency for sustained regressions increases by <2s on average. E2E stability run on the perf-canary harness (100k synthetic requests over 60m with three injected regressions) passed without spurious rollbacks.

Rollout plan: Deploy to canary evaluator staging, enable feature flag at 10% of experiments for 48h, promote to 50% after automated regression-free window, and enable by default after one week with metric review. Built-in fallback: if stability score decays or new anomaly detectors fire, controller immediately reduces probe weight to zero and falls back to legacy probing.

Operational notes: New metrics emitted: canary.probe.attenuation, canary.stability_score, canary.burst_index, canary.cutover_state. Traces include probe.weight and cutover.decision_reason. Suggested SLO dashboards and alert thresholds included in docs.

Related: Linked Linear tickets ENG-10482 (canary instability), ENG-10490 (rollout guard improvements). Support ticket SUP-4482 documents a customer incident that motivated the approach.

Risks and mitigations: The main risk is over-attenuation delaying detection of real regressions during sustained low-signal periods; mitigated by conservative default sigmoid slope and a safety gate that forces evaluation when SLO degradation crosses a hard threshold.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the burst index calculation (prober_controller.py) and the stability score aggregation (slo/policies/graceful_cutover.policy). The feature flag and config schema live in infra/helm/canary-controller.yaml.
Introduce Temporal Sigmoid Throttler and Graceful Cutover to reduce false-positive canary regressions during traffic bursts. Smoother probe shaping and delayed final cutover lowers noisy rollbacks while preserving sensitivity to real regressions.
Diego Morales: Nice work. Two questions: how is burst_index calculated on multi-region traffic, and can we surface the attenuation factor in trace spans?
Lena Zhang: Burst index is a weighted percentile-based estimator that merges per-region indexes using recent qps weights; I added probe.weight to spans in the latest commit (d4c9a7f).
Aisha Patel: Integration tests look good, but add a test for sustained moderate load to ensure we don't delay detection longer than acceptable SLO window.
Lena Zhang: Added sustained-load scenario and updated the default sigmoid slope to be slightly steeper to reduce detection lag (commit f3e2b7c).
Marcus O'Neill: Approved. Please make sure runbooks and dashboard links are in the release notes.
CI: integration-e2e failed on first run due to a flake in the harness; rerun fixed it (see ci checks).
Release Manager: merged via squash after approvals and green CI.
payload.title: Add temporal-sigmoid-throttler and graceful cutover for bursty canary probes
