Motivation: Clients and platform routing need a clearer, machine-readable separation between per-request idempotency and longer-lived conversation/session idempotency, and operators need a deterministic retry guidance window rather than a single Retry-After hint. This PR introduces two compatible surface changes to the OpenAI bridge and streaming runtime: 1) a new Idempotency-Scope request header (Idempotency-Scope: request|session|conversation) that disambiguates how idempotency keys are interpreted and persisted by the adapter and routing layer, and 2) a Retry-After-Range response header (Retry-After-Range: <min-seconds>,<max-seconds>) which gives callers a recommended retry window to support smarter backoff strategies and smoother autoscaling. In addition, this PR standardizes the structured error envelope returned by the OpenAI-compat shim to include {"code","message","retryable","retry_after_hint_seconds","idempotency_hint"} where applicable and adds a single-line streaming error frame format for tool/function-call streams (frame_type:error payload:<json-string>). Design summary: - Idempotency-Scope is advisory but authoritative for the OpenAI shim: when Idempotency-Scope=request the idempotency-key is treated as a single atomic request key; when session or conversation the adapter will attempt to correlate incoming keys across the session identifier (customer-provided) and preserve a scoped result lease for the configured lease TTL. The default behavior remains request-scoped for existing clients if the header is absent. - Retry-After-Range is emitted by rate-limiters and the serving runtime when we can estimate a best-case and worst-case window (e.g., 30,120). Consumers may choose any retry policy within that range; our SDKs will include an opt-in helper to adhere to the window semantics. For legacy single-value Retry-After we continue to set the header for compatibility. - Streaming errors: tool/function-call streams now emit a dedicated error frame as a single-line event to avoid protocol framing ambiguity. The frame contains the standardized envelope and, when a retry is applicable, includes retry_after_hint_seconds and idempotency_hint (e.g. "retry_after_hint_seconds":45, "idempotency_hint":"session:abcd1234" ). - OpenAI mapping: 429/503 map to code="rate_limit", 409 map to code="conflict" with retryable=false unless accompanied by a Retry-After-Range; validation errors map to code="invalid_request". Implementation notes: - OpenAI adapter: header parsing and mapping implemented under openai/adapter/headers.go, with unit tests and a small compatibility shim so missing headers fall back to prior logic. - Runtime: rate limiter updates in runtime/ratelimit/heuristic.go to compute a conservative min/max window and surface it via HTTP and internal gRPC for Dedicated/Private. - Streaming: new frame serializer in stream/frame.go and new parser in stream/parse_test.go to validate single-line JSON error frames. - SDKs: brief helpers added in redwood-sdk-python/ and redwood-sdk-typescript/ to surface Idempotency-Scope and parse Retry-After-Range; helpers are opt-in and behind a feature flag. Compatibility and rollout: - No breaking change: existing clients that do not send Idempotency-Scope continue to behave as before (request-scoped). Retry-After-Range is additive; we still emit Retry-After for single-value clients. - Feature gated: the adapter toggles for private/dedicated customers are behind feature flags; hosted rollout will start as opt-in for beta customers for two weeks then auto-toggle based on SDK opt-ins. Testing and verification: - Unit tests covering header parsing and mapping (openai adapter unit tests). - Integration tests with simulated throttling to assert Retry-After-Range values are well-formed and that SDK helpers respect the window. - Streaming e2e harness updated to assert single-line error frames are emitted and to validate idempotency_hint propagation during tool-call retries. Docs and migration guidance: - Added a concise spec doc to docs/openai-compat/idempotency-retry.md that describes header semantics, sample flows, and recommended SDK usage. - Migration notes advise clients to start adding Idempotency-Scope when they want session-level deduplication and to rely on Retry-After-Range for smarter backoff rather than tight fixed retries. Rollout checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] SDK helpers behind flag - [x] Docs update - [x] Beta rollout to 5 hosted customers - [x] Monitor telemetry for increased duplicate suppressions Risk and alternatives considered: We considered an opaque lease token approach (analogous to previous "lease" work) but chose an explicit Idempotency-Scope header to make behavior observable and debuggable across the OpenAI mapping layer and user agents. The Retry-After-Range intentionally provides a bounded window to allow servers to communicate uncertainty rather than forcing a single fixed backoff value. Summary of impact: improves client/platform behavior under rate pressure, reduces accidental duplicate tool invocations for session-level workflows, and yields better automated retry policies across SDKs and integrators.
Adds Idempotency-Scope and Retry-After-Range headers for clearer retry semantics; normalizes OpenAI-compatible error envelope; introduces a single-line streaming error frame with structured fields; opt-in header-driven behavior, no forced breaking changes.
Ava Patel: This addresses the ambiguity we saw in the payments team's incident where session-level replays caused duplicate charges. The header naming looks good but please add explicit TTL docs for session scope.
Lina Chen (author reply): Added TTL guidance in docs and clarified that TTL is policy-driven per deployment in the adapter README.
Diego Morales: Can we guarantee Retry-After-Range won't leak internal timing? Suggest rounding to seconds and capping max to a configured threshold. Also add a metrics tag for whether range was provided vs single Retry-After.
Lina Chen (author reply): We round to seconds and cap by runtime config; added metric runtime.rate_retry_range.present in metric exports. PTAL.
Marcus Nguyen: Approve after small nits on test coverage and ensuring SDK flag defaults to false. Tests look thorough.
Lina Chen: Addressed tests and defaulted flags to false; added integration scenario with simulated 429 bursts.
QA (automated): Verified stream error frames are one-line JSON events and SDK helper parses Retry-After-Range correctly.
payload.title: Introduce Idempotency-Scope header and Retry-After-Range for OpenAI compat and tool-stream stability

Context: Dedicated staged rollouts (reserved pools) support promote/abort and automated gate evaluation. During beta we hit cases where (a) telemetry lag/missing metrics made gates "UNKNOWN" and blocked promotion, (b) a canary partition induced transient 429s and operators needed an immediate hold while investigating, and (c) SRE needed an explicit, auditable escape hatch for incident mitigation. This PR adds two admin-only emergency controls: (1) force-promote to advance a rollout stage while explicitly bypassing gate evaluation and (2) hold/resume to freeze a running rollout (no automatic gate polling changes and no stage transitions) until resumed or aborted.

What’s in this PR: - API: Adds POST /v1/dedicated/pools/{pool_id}/rollouts/{rollout_id}:force_promote and POST ...:hold (plus ...:resume) endpoints, reusing idempotency keys + optimistic concurrency from promote/abort. - RBAC: Requires new permission scope dedicated_rollouts.override (admin-only; not exposed to customer-admin). Requests must include override_reason and an optional ticket_ref (SUP/INC/INT) for traceability. - State machine: Introduces HELD as a first-class rollout state; HELD blocks promote/force_promote unless resume is called (abort allowed from HELD). Force-promote is allowed only from RUNNING and only if a next stage exists; it advances stage pointer and updates rollout state consistently with normal promotion logic. - Gate evaluation: Force-promote bypasses policy-engine gate evaluation and marks the stage transition with gate_result=OVERRIDDEN. - Audit logging: Emits explicit audit events for DEDICATED_POOL_ROLLOUT_HELD, DEDICATED_POOL_ROLLOUT_RESUMED, and DEDICATED_POOL_ROLLOUT_FORCE_PROMOTED. Payload includes actor, actor_type, pool_id, rollout_id, from_stage_id, to_stage_id, override_reason, ticket_ref, and request_id/idempotency_key. - API warnings: Adds warnings[] in action responses when an override is used (force-promote) or when a rollout is currently HELD (promote returns 409 with a warning explaining required resume). - Guardrails: Rejects force-promote when gates are currently PASS (to prevent casual bypassing), unless force=true is explicitly set (double-confirmation for admin tooling). Also rejects hold/resume without reason to improve post-incident review quality.

Operational notes: - These endpoints are behind the existing feature flag dedicated_staged_rollouts_v1, but RBAC is still enforced when enabled. - Audit events are emitted from the control plane (same path as promote/abort) to ensure export + retention behavior matches existing rollout actions.

Tests: - Added unit tests for state transitions (RUNNING->HELD->RUNNING), override validation, and RBAC enforcement. - Added integration coverage in the staged-rollouts test harness for: hold during gate evaluation, resume, and force-promote with missing metrics.

Follow-ups: - Console UI will surface HELD state + warnings (separate PR). - Audit log export pipeline needs to be updated to include the new event types (tracked in INT-1951).

Checklist: - [x] RBAC reviewed (Kaitlyn) - [x] Audit schema reviewed (SRE/Compliance) - [x] Added docs strings for admin tooling (errors + warnings) - [x] Added tests for idempotency + concurrency edge cases
Jordan Lee (review): Can we be explicit about semantics when telemetry is missing? I want force-promote to be the only bypass; promote should remain fail-closed on UNKNOWN. Also, please ensure HELD prevents background promotion by any automation.

Benji Okafor (author): Agreed. Promote remains unchanged (fail-closed on UNKNOWN unless policy explicitly allows). HELD now blocks both promote and force-promote with 409 unless resumed; abort remains allowed. Gate polling continues but does not trigger any stage transitions.
Kaitlyn Nguyen (security): dedicated_rollouts.override must not be granted to customer-admin. Where is this permission assigned? Also, require a reason string (min length) and log it.

Benji Okafor (author): Permission is only in the internal admin role bundle (rbac/policies/internal_admin.json). Added validation: override_reason required, trimmed, min 10 chars; stored in audit payload and action response. No changes to customer role bundles.
Rafael Mendes (SRE): Please add an audit field for ticket_ref and make it easy to grep from SIEM exports. Also, can we include from/to stage ids and rollout revision for concurrency debugging?

Benji Okafor (author): Added ticket_ref optional string; included from_stage_id/to_stage_id and rollout_etag in the audit payload. Also added request_id and idempotency_key for correlation.
Ethan Park (platform): Force-promote should be hard to click. Double-confirmation looks good. But why block force-promote when gates are PASS?

Benji Okafor (author): Guardrail based on observed operator behavior in beta: it’s easy to bypass gates “just to move forward.” If gates PASS, normal promote is available and safer. If someone insists, they can set force=true which records an additional override flag in the audit event.
Chloe Martin (console backend): The warnings[] field—can you confirm it won’t break existing clients? Our console backend expects action responses to deserialize strictly.

Benji Okafor (author): We only add a new optional field (warnings) and do not change existing fields. Updated protobuf + JSON tags so unknown fields are ignored in older clients. Added a console contract test in our internal SDK harness to ensure decode succeeds.
Admin-only emergency controls for Dedicated staged rollouts: hold/resume and force-promote (with required reason + audit logging).
Action responses now include warnings[] for override/held guidance (non-breaking additive field).
payload.title: Dedicated staged rollouts: add force-promote + hold/resume with admin guardrails

Motivation: We observed recurring fragmentation spikes and short-lived allocation storms from tenant burst traffic which cause reactive spillover to local NVMe and cascading eviction storms. Those spill/eviction bursts increase p99 latency for inference requests and create noisy neighbor effects on shared Dedicated pools. This PR introduces a combined allocator + eviction control strategy to smooth slab-level free space, pace eviction throughput, and provide soft per-tenant reservation windows to reduce spillovers.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Implements a slab 'smoothener' that migrates small free runs between slabs to reduce fragmentation, introduces an eviction-rate shaper that caps eviction throughput and ramps it based on measured IO/backpressure, and adds tenant-aware short-term reservation windows so active tenants get a stable allocation when under transient bursts. Also includes telemetry, unit and perf tests, and a staged rollout plan.

Design notes: - Slab smoothener: background task that periodically samples slab free-run histograms and executes low-cost free-run coalesces (move/merge) for slabs whose fragmentation score exceeds a threshold. Moves are sized to fit into existing allocation slack and avoid large temporary memory spikes. The task supports a configurable 'aggressiveness' parameter and an idle-only mode to avoid interference with hot allocation paths. - Evictor rate shaper: instead of instantly trying to evict to satisfy a memory shortfall, the shaper enforces an eviction budget (evictions/sec and io_bytes/sec) and uses a PID-inspired controller to ramp up/down eviction throughput based on measured spill queue depth and disk latency. This prevents eviction-induced I/O storms and gives the smoothener time to reclaim space. - Tenant reservation windows: ephemeral soft reservations per-tenant that allocate a small buffer of tokens proportional to recent allocation rate. The reservation is reclaimable but lowers the chance of an otherwise healthy tenant being victim to an eviction wave. Reservation behaviour is tunable by tenant tier. - Continuous batching interplay: added a coordination hook so the batch scheduler can signal expected short-term allocation needs; the smoothener defers aggressive moves if a large batch is in flight to avoid extra copying.

Operational controls and knobs: configuration variables added to src/kv/config.rs (smoothener.enabled, smoothener.aggressiveness, evictor.rate_limit, evictor.io_budget_bytes_per_sec, tenant.reservation_window_ms, reservation.tier_multipliers). Default values are conservative for canary rollout.

Benchmarks: synthetic tenant burst test (100 tenants, 20% heavy bursts) measured on perf-lab: - fragmentation_score (median) down 35% - spill-to-disk events down 18% - steady-state memory overhead +1.8% (due to reservation slack) - p99 latency for 512-token generation decreased by 7% under burst conditions

Rollout plan: 1) Canary on 'redwood-dedicated-canary' (5% capacity) with smoothener.idle_only=true and evictor.rate_limit conservative; 2) Monitor metrics: kv.fragmentation_score, kv.eviction_rate, kv.spill_count, tenant.alloc_stalls; 3) Increase aggressiveness after 72h stable canary; 4) Gradual 25/50/100% ramp with automated rollback on spike in spill_count or p99.

Notes on safety: All background moves are no-copy where possible (relink free-run descriptors) or bounded-copy with atomic handover to avoid corrupting the KV index. Evictor shaper maintains a small emergency bypass for OOM-critical paths.

Michael Lang: Can we quantify the CPU cost of the smoothener at default aggressiveness? Priya Kapoor: Measured ~2-3% CPU at canary fleet on perf-lab under normal load; it's configurable and default is idle_only which reduces CPU. Diego Chen: The move code touches allocation paths — how do you ensure we don't introduce races with concurrent allocations? Priya Kapoor: Smoothener acquires per-slab lightweight epoch pin and uses compare-and-swap handover for descriptors; added unit tests that stress concurrent alloc/free. Sana Patel: We saw a flaky test in evictor unit tests on first CI run (race on io_budget reset) — please add guard and retry. Priya Kapoor: Fixed in commit 4, added deterministic sleep in the test to reproduce; re-ran CI. Michael Lang: LGTM after Diego's nit on error logging; Diego Chen: Approved with comment to include a structured log field 'kv.smoothener.move_reason'. Merge was blocked until the flaky test was stabilized and perf run passed. Final PR author reply: thanks — addressed comments, tightened timeouts, and added additional perf assertions.
CI summary: build: pass, unit-tests: pass (with flaky test fixed), integration-tests: pass, linters: pass, perf/bench: pass (bench run: compare-against-main shows 7% p99 reduction under burst scenario). One rerun required for evictor_test.rs (race) which passed after fix. All checks green before merge.
Merged via squash (squash-merge) into main by Michael Lang on 2026-02-18. Merge commit message: 'kv: slab smoothener + evictor rate shaper + tenant reservation (ENG-3245, ENG-4120)'.
Improves KV memory fragmentation and reduces eviction/spill bursts: adds slab smoothener (background defragmentation), eviction-rate shaper (backpressure-aware eviction pacing), and tenant soft reservation windows. Metrics: kv.fragmentation_score, kv.eviction_rate, kv.spill_count. Configurable knobs under KvConfig.

Impact: Should reduce p99 latency during tenant bursts and lower disk spill events. Conservative defaults enabled for canary rollout.
If rollout causes increase in kv.spill_count or sustained eviction_rate above configured io_budget, disable smoothener.aggressiveness or evictor.rate_limit via remote flags and rollback; emergency bypass exists to free memory but will increase spill events. Monitor disk latency and tenant.alloc_stalls.
payload.title: KV slab smoothener and evictor rate shaper with tenant reservation windows

Motivation: multi-stage rollouts (canary/A-B/shadow) must make incremental progress in a way that survives controller restarts, supports manual intervention at well-defined epochs, and provides deterministic rollback to the last known-good commit. This PR introduces an "epoched fanout" controller that divides a rollout into discrete epochs (batches) and records an append-only snapshot after each epoch commit. Each epoch snapshot contains routing deltas, traffic weights by cohort, and aggregated metrics checkpoints. Key features: 1) stepwise commit: the controller applies changes in small epochs and only advances the commit pointer after a successful safety gate evaluation; 2) resumeable progress: epoch snapshots are durable in the snapshot store so a controller restart can resume from the last committed epoch without reapplying or double-counting traffic; 3) deterministic rollback: when a safety gate trips, the controller computes a rollback plan that replays the last stable epoch snapshot and issues a coordinated fan-in to the previous routing state; 4) multi-mode support: works for canary, weighted A/B splits, and shadow mirroring (shadow epochs are recorded but traffic is never shifted); 5) dry-run and simulation: an integrated simulator validates epoch boundaries and race scenarios during CI; 6) observability: new rollout_epoch, epoch_commit_latency_ms, fanout_progress_percent, snapshot_age_seconds metrics and structured traces that show epoch state transitions. This description includes high-level design rationale, implementation notes and the test checklist. Implementation notes: - New epoch snapshot store (rollout/epoch_snapshot_store.py) backed by the existing configstore with append semantics. Snapshots are small (~2-6KB) and regularly GC'd by snapshot TTL. - Controller changes (rollout/controller.py): epoch state machine, commit/abort/rollback transitions, deterministic hashing for cohort assignment, and safety gate hooks. - Routing layer adapter (routing/traffic_fanout.go): stepwise apply/rollback helpers and compatibility shims for legacy routing plugins. - Tests (tests/unit/test_epoched_rollout.py, tests/integration/epoched_rollout_sim.py) cover loopback, restart-resume, rollback under metric flapping and shadow-only epochs. - Docs and runbook (docs/runbooks/epoched-fanout.md) with operator playbook for manual recovery and rollback commands. Checklist: - [x] Design doc review (ENG-1892) - [x] Unit tests for epoch transitions - [x] Integration simulation for restart/resume - [x] Metrics and tracing added - [x] Runbook and example rollout YAML - [x] Backwards compatibility verification with legacy routing adapter Known limitations: - The snapshot GC TTL is conservative and may need tuning for very long-running experiments; - Very large numbers of cohorts (>>1000) will still be limited by routing plugin performance (future work: shard-aware fanout). Related work: this complements previous staged-rollout efforts (see ENG-1421) but focuses on restart-resilience and deterministic rollback semantics.
Diego Alvarez (2026-02-18): Can we add an explicit idempotency token for epoch commits? If the controller crashes after issuing routing changes but before snapshot write we risk partial application.
Priya Shah (2026-02-18): Added idempotency token (commit_id) to the snapshot record and controller now validates commit_id on resume. See epoch_snapshot_store.py lines ~120-155.
Rina Patel (2026-02-19): I hit a lint failure in routing/traffic_fanout.go during local run. The gofmt diff is noisy; please run 'make fmt' before merging.
Priya Shah (2026-02-19): Fixed formatting and tightened the fanout API; pushed commit c5a1e9b -> d9f7a11 to address lint and an edge-case in rollback order.
Marta Chen (2026-02-21): Tests look good. Please include an inline comment explaining the deterministic hashing seed choice (we use rollout.id + epoch).
Priya Shah (2026-02-22): Added comment and a helper deterministic_hash() in controller.py; updated docs with rationale. Diego + Marta approved.
CI (2026-02-20): initial CI run failed: unit tests (flake) and lint errors. Subsequent run (2026-02-22) green.
Added an epoched rollout controller that enables restart-resilient, stepwise canary/A-B/shadow deployments with deterministic rollback. Operators should consult docs/runbooks/epoched-fanout.md for migration steps and best practices.
On upgrade: controllers will automatically begin writing epoch snapshots under the existing configstore namespace. To minimize snapshot retention during the first 24h, set rollout.snapshot_ttl to 72h in charts/values-rollout.yaml. If you need to abort mid-epoch, use 'redwoodctl rollout abort --epoch <n>' which replays the last committed epoch snapshot and issues the fan-in plan.
Backward compatible with legacy routing adapters. Adds small persistent metadata per rollout (snapshot records ~2-6KB). Improves reliability for long-running staged rollouts and reduces human intervention in rollback scenarios.
payload.title: Epoched fanout controller with stepwise commit and resumeable rollback

Problem: Continuous-batcher workloads with mixed KV-cache and compute-heavy requests still show periodic starvation of latency-sensitive requests under sustained load in multi-tenant nodes. Previous fairness knobs reduced mean tail but regressed throughput for bursty KV-heavy traffic. Motivation: we need a scheduler layer that (1) preserves strict latency SLOs for latency-tiered requests, (2) prevents indefinite starvation of low-priority KV pin requests, and (3) minimizes end-to-end throughput loss. This PR introduces the Tiered Latency Queue Adapter (TLQA) and a complementary Pin Balancer module that cooperatively manage admission and slot allocation in the continuous-batcher runtime. TLQA creates soft priority tiers (fast, normal, background) with time-budgeted fast lanes. Fast-lane requests get preferential early admission but can be demoted after a configurable accrue-time threshold to avoid permanent starvation of background work. The Pin Balancer monitors KV-pin hot-spots and performs bounded pin-relocation and soft-eviction with hysteresis to allow prefetch/kv-cache warmup while avoiding long-lived pins monopolizing slots. Key behavior: - Fast-tier admission uses a short-lived reservation window (default 2ms) per epoch; if fast-tier requests fail to complete in that window the reservation decays exponentially to free capacity. - Demotion: requests older than demote_ms (default 40ms) in fast/normal tiers are moved to background to ensure forward progress. - Pin Balancer keeps per-key low-water marks and issues bounded unpin commands when local slot occupancy exceeds pin_occupancy_threshold (default 0.7). Unpin is cooperative: the runtime asks the KV cache manager for best-effort unpin; if the manager cannot unpin within unpin_grace_ms the slot is force-rotated and the request allowed to continue on a fallback model variant. Implementation highlights: - Scheduler: new adapter layer (tlqa_adapter.cc/h) that sits between the admission controller and the batcher. It tracks per-tier counters, reservation tokens, and decays tokens using a lightweight exponential-backoff timer wheel. - Pin Balancer: pin_balancer.{cc,h} with an async RPC to the kv-cache manager; leverages existing metrics and tracing hooks (metrics: tlqa.reservations.*, pinbalancer.unpin.*) - Kernel selection hints: the adapter surfaces hints for short sequence fast-path kernels (small_seq_kernel) when a fast-tier reservation is used; this reduces kernel invocation overhead for short responses. - Telemetry: new per-route histograms (tlqa.latency_by_tier) and alerts when pin eviction rate > 5%/minute. Tests and validation: - Microbench: synthetic mix (30% fast, 50% normal, 20% KV-pinned) across 8-node canary; result: 99th p50/p95 improvements for fast tier: p95 down 18% and p99 down 12% compared to master under same load; overall throughput loss < 2.5%. - Stress: long-run soak (72h) on perf-canary with KV hotkeys: no request starvation observed; tail spikes reduced. - Integration: added unit tests for adapter token decay, demotion and pin balancer unpin backoff; end-to-end e2e test harness added to perf-canary suite. Rollout plan: staged canary across regions (us-west-2, eu-west-1) with TLQA disabled by default on main; enable per-customer via runtime flag and smoke test on dedicated nodes. Config knobs exposed: tlqa.enabled, tlqa.fast_reservation_ms, tlqa.demote_ms, pinbalancer.enabled, pinbalancer.unpin_grace_ms, pinbalancer.occupancy_threshold. Related work: builds on prior queue fairness work (ENG-1980) and KV warmup heuristics. See Linear ENG-1982 for acceptance criteria and performance targets. Checklist: - [x] Design doc + microbench results attached - [x] Unit & integration tests - [x] Metrics and dashboards updated - [x] Rollout plan added - [x] Feature-flag gated
Lina Chen: Can you justify the default demote_ms=40ms? In our traces fast requests often complete <10ms; 40ms seems conservative. Please add rationale and a sensitivity sweep.

payload.body:
Motivation: Session affinity during canary rollouts causes noisy user experiences when in-flight sessions are cut over to a new model mid-conversation. This PR implements a session-anchored canary primitive that issues short-lived traffic lease tokens to keep ongoing sessions pinned to the original model until a safe handoff point, and adds a deterministic "rewind" rollback mechanism that can replay pinned sessions against a previous model for stateful reconciliation.

What this PR introduces: 1) Traffic Lease Tokens: new lightweight token that the gateway attaches to session-level requests. Tokens are acquired by the node that handles the first request in a session and are enforced by the routing layer for the token's TTL. 2) Handshake + Handoff API: a control-plane API for creating handoff windows so a session can finish a bounded number of turns before being moved. 3) Checkpointed Session Snapshots: at handoff points we persist a compact session checkpoint (KV of conversation pointers and short-term model KV-cache metadata) to the rollout store. 4) Rewind Rollback: when an automated rollback is triggered, the system can replay the checkpointed session against the target model (previous version) and emit reconciliation events and metrics. 5) Safety locks and draining semantics: explicit safety lock prevents model swap until all critical leases are released or max-handshake-timeouts elapse. 6) Observability and playbooks: new metrics, dashboards, and a runbook for operators.

Implementation notes: - Control plane: rollout service gains endpoints /lease/acquire, /lease/release, /handoff/start, /rewind/replay. These are backward-compatible (old gateways ignore lease headers). - Data model: added rollout.leases table (lease_id, session_id, owner_node, ttl, created_at) and session_checkpoints (checkpoint_id, session_id, snapshot_blob, created_at). TTLs are configurable per-deployment. - Routing: router now respects X-Session-Lease header; if absent behavior is identical to current fallback routing. - Performance: lease check is cached in-memory per-router to avoid DB roundtrips on every token check; we added a small consistent-hash lookup path for lease ownership. - Tests: unit tests for lease lifecycle, integration tests for handoff/during-canary, e2e playback test that verifies fidelity of rewind replay.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc (links/ENG-7412) - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] e2e replay test - [x] Observability dashboards - [x] Docs + runbook - [x] Backwards compatibility validation

Risk & Mitigations: The primary risk is lease ownership divergence under transient partitions. Mitigations: (a) conservative TTL defaults (30s), (b) fail-open routing when local lease cache cannot be validated and request is tagged non-critical, (c) automatic lease reconciliation job.

How to test locally: - run ./dev/rollout up - run ./dev/gateway with --enable-session-lease - run tests/integration/test_handoff.py

Related work: This PR complements the existing shadow/replica frameworks (see ENG-6021) and ties into the rollout contracts added in ENG-6993.

Summary: Adds session-anchored canary behavior to reduce user-visible flakiness during model swaps and provides a deterministic rollback "rewind" to reconcile long-running sessions on rollback.

Priya Patel (author): Added deterministic seed and switched the replay to use fixed time.advance in tests. Also added a small jitter window to make timing more realistic while remaining deterministic.
Leo Alvarez: Approve with minor nit on documentation wording for 'lease TTL' defaults. Can we expose env var for QA?
Priya Patel: Exposed ROLLOUT_LEASE_DEFAULT_TTL and documented in session-lease.md. Addressed other nits in follow-up commit.
Samira Khan: Left an inline comment about metrics cardinality; suggest sampling for snapshot_blob size above 2KB.
Priya Patel: Implemented sampling and added a redaction step to the checkpoint serializer to cap stored conversational context length.
Session-anchored canaries: introduce short-lived traffic lease tokens to pin in-flight sessions during model rollouts. Added rewind rollback to deterministically replay session checkpoints against previous model versions. New DB tables rollout.leases and session_checkpoints. Backwards compatible routing when tokens absent. Operators: see docs/rollouts/session-lease.md for runbook and Grafana dashboard.

payload.body:
Motivation: Customers want predictable unit economics without manually tuning batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles for every tenant and workload. This PR introduces the "cost-control-flow" subsystem: a small, opinionated policy engine that synthesizes tenant-level defaults for batching, prefix cache, and quantization fallbacks with safe fallthroughs and a simulation mode.

High level changes:
- Add a lightweight policy engine (pkg/policy/cost_control.go, pkg/policy/engine_test.go) that evaluates tenant policies written as ordered rules. Rules are intentionally limited (match by route, traffic class, and latency bucket) to keep evaluation O(#rules) and auditable.
- Expose tenant config keys under: tenant.config.cost_control.{enabled,policy_id,cache_ttl_secs,batch_target_ms,quant_fallback_priority}. These are stored as JSON blobs in the existing tenant store (no schema migration required).
- Implement server-side defaults synthesizer (cmd/rcost/synthesizer.go) that produces conservative defaults per tenant using recent traffic histograms (20k samples) and a cost budget target. Defaults are designed to never increase tail latency by >3% compared to a baseline.
- CLI: rcost simulate --tenant T123 --policy p-default --workload-file samples/web-chat.json produces a short report (expected unit cost delta, estimated p95 change) so SREs/product teams can iterate offline.
- Runtime integration: the serving runtime now reads an evaluated policy response in routing-time metadata and applies three no-op-safe knobs: target batching window (ms), cache TTL hint (secs), and quantization preference order. The runtime will not apply the policy if doing so would violate a hard SLA (configured per route).
- Observability: added metrics (policy_eval.duration_ms, policy_eval.hit_count, cost_control.applied_count) and two logs for audit (policy_eval.request_id -> rule_id, synthesized_defaults.snapshot_id).
- Safety & rollback: feature gated behind tenant flag and deploy flag. If any CI smoke test fails, rollout is blocked. There is an automatic revert to conservative defaults if policy evaluation error rate > 0.5% over 5m.

Design notes and rationale:
- Keep policy language intentionally small so we can ship quickly and retain strong performance characteristics. This is not a general-purpose policy DSL, it's a cost-control flow aimed at safe defaults and tenant isolation.
- Use post-hoc synthesis (rcost synth) rather than direct learning in the control plane to avoid feedback loops that could destabilize latency.

Behavioral guarantees:
- No policy will be applied if (1) it increases route p95 by >5ms absolute, or (2) the tenant has an SLA tag requiring strict latency.
- Quantization fallbacks are only advisory; runtime refuses to switch to a quant profile that hasn't been validated in the model registry for the target hardware.

Checklist:
- [x] Policy engine implementation + unit tests
- [x] Synthesizer CLI + sample workload and simulation test harness
- [x] Runtime hook integration and guardrail checks
- [x] Observability metrics + sample Grafana dashboard JSON (docs/grafana/cost-control-dashboard.json)
- [x] Docs: docs/operations/cost-control-flow.md with onboarding steps and example policy templates
- [x] E2E smoke: synthetic web-chat workload validated on dev cluster (latency regression within targets)

Migration/rollout plan:
1) Deploy code behind feature flag to canary region; enable only for internal tenants.
2) Run rcost simulate across top-5 tenant workloads to generate candidate policies.
3) Enable per-tenant opt-in with a 2-week monitoring window; if any significant regressions detected revert per-tenant flags.
4) Expand to self-serve tenants after two weeks of stable metrics.

Related work: ENG-2382 (policy engine prototype), ENG-2419 (tenant telemetry sampler).

Notes for reviewers: The synthesizer contains a small heuristic budget allocator; I'm particularly interested in feedback on the cost-to-latency model (pkg/rcost/model_estimator.go). I kept the model intentionally conservative (bias toward not increasing latency).

Evan Park: Can you explain why we opted for ordered rules vs. a priority hash? Looks good but I'd like clarity on complexity guarantees.
Priya Nambiar: Ordered rules keep semantics simple and auditable; evaluation is O(n) and n is expected to be <50 per tenant. Added comment in engine.go to justify choice.
Marisol Ortega: The cost-to-latency estimator seems optimistic for long-tail workloads. Can we bias it more conservatively?
Priya Nambiar: Updated estimator to add a 2% latency safety margin and added an integration test with a heavy-tail synthetic trace. See model_estimator.go change.
Jonah Liu: CI flaked on the gRPC auth test in the canary run. Rerunning...
Priya Nambiar: Flake was unrelated; rebase fixed the transient failure. CI is green now.

Introduce 'Slate' — a tenant-aware balancing layer that coordinates dynamic micro-batching, cold-start prefetch budgets, and staged quantization fallbacks. Adds safety gates to avoid quality regressions and a gradual rollout plan.
Motivation: Many tenants exhibit mixed traffic patterns (bursty tails + steady micro-traffic). Existing defaults either favor latency (small batches) or cost (aggressive quant/large batches), forcing manual tuning. Slate provides an automated balanceer that reasons about tenant SLOs, observed latency quantiles, and token-level unit economics to pick run-time batch sizes, lightweight prefetch budgets, and quantization stepping with automatic rollback on quality regressions.

Design overview: Slate runs as a per-tenant policy agent in the serving control plane. It consumes short-term telemetry (p90/p99 latency, sample size, token mix), tenant SLOs, and cost-per-token estimates. Decision outputs are: target continuous-batch window, max-prefetch-tokens budget, and an ordered quant-fallback list (fp16 -> q4 -> q8-int8-style). To reduce blast radius we added two safety primitives: historical quality watermarking (compares decoded sampled prompts to baseline embeddings) and a rollback circuit that triggers on sudden loss in semantic-similarity or an increase in response divergence metrics.

What this PR includes: single continuous string. Implementation contains: 1) slate agent orchestration + gRPC control contract; 2) batcher adapter to accept dynamic window from Slate; 3) quant-profile manager and on-host soft-switcher; 4) small telemetry hooks for unit-econ counters and quality-watermark sampling; 5) a lightweight CLI to preview suggested slate plans for a tenant.

Checklist: - [x] agent + control contract implementation - [x] batcher adapter + unit tests - [x] quant soft-switch and safety rollback - [x] e2e smoke against synthetic tenant traffic - [x] observability: graphs + alerts - [x] rollout plan and feature flag gating

Testing and results: Local sim harness shows average token cost reduction of 18% for mixed workloads with median latency increase <5ms and p99 impact within SLO for 92% of tenants. Canary on staging ran across 60 tenants for 48h; two tenants saw semantic drift triggered and were auto-rolled back (expected behavior).

Rollout plan: Feature-flagged; opt-in for dedicated customers initially, followed by a 10% gradual ramp on hosted with telemetry review gates and manual hold for high-compliance tenants.

Notes: This is intentionally conservative on quant steps and relies on our existing KV cache to keep latency stable. Follow-up work: cross-tenant coordination for shared GPU pools (ENG-4289), and an analytic to estimate marginal token price per tenant for finer-grained cost decisions.
Ethan Clarke: overall direction looks good; worried about quota interactions when prefilling on multi-tenant nodes — please add a per-node prefetch cap.
Sofia Martinez: added per-node cap and unit test; updated documentation section on quota interactions.
Priya Nair: can we be more explicit about the quality watermark sampling frequency? We should avoid extra token egress when sampling.
Sofia Martinez: changed sampling to asynchronous and batched watermark snapshots (configurable, default 1 per 1000 responses). Added note in runbook.
Lars Johansen: LGTM after nits; please squash the telemetry refactor into the primary commit to reduce noise.
Ethan Clarke: Approved following squash and the added per-node cap.
Merge Bot: merged by Sofia Martinez using squash and merge.

This PR improves drilldown query latency for the internal Unit Economics dashboard by tightening warehouse table layout (partitioning/clustering), removing a few high-cost joins and DISTINCTs in the hot path, and switching the most commonly-hit rollups to pre-aggregated/materialized views. The primary goal is to keep p95 query time for time-series + top-N breakdowns under ~2s for typical Finance/Product filter combinations (7d/30d, group_by=model|region|tier) while keeping hourly freshness and correctness intact. Context: during dogfood we saw a few breakdowns regress to 10–25s when grouping by model+region with additional filters (quantization_profile, streaming) due to full scans on hourly fact tables and an inefficient join to the rate card + region mapping tables. This is follow-on work to the initial aggregation job (PR #19342) and API endpoints (PR #19374). Key changes: (1) Re-partition hourly fact + rollup tables by usage_date (derived from usage_hour) and cluster by (canonical_region, customer_tier, model_id) to align with our most common predicates; (2) Introduce a slim dimension table with integer surrogate keys for model_id/region/tier to reduce row width in the largest fact table and avoid repeated string normalization; (3) Replace COUNT(DISTINCT request_id) and per-row JSON extraction in the dashboard views with precomputed columns emitted by the aggregation job; (4) Add/replace two materialized views: unit_econ_rollup_daily_mv (default for 7d/30d) and unit_econ_breakdown_topn_mv (serves top-N tables without scanning the full hourly set); (5) Rewrite the dashboard views to join rate card + allocation factors after aggregation (per hour/day bucket) rather than per request, and to avoid joining region normalization at query time (use canonical_region already stored). Expected impact (measured on staging warehouse with a 14-day slice): time_series(group_by=model, 30d) p95 12.8s -> 1.9s; topN_regions(7d, model=all) p95 8.4s -> 1.3s; drilldown model+region+tier (30d) p95 21.5s -> 2.6s. Notes: No changes to metric definitions; cost attribution math is unchanged. This PR includes a safe migration path: new tables/MVs are built side-by-side, views are swapped, and we keep the prior views for one release behind a feature flag for quick rollback. Backfill/refresh: materialized views refresh hourly; daily MV uses incremental refresh with a 3-day lookback to accommodate late-arriving telemetry.
Staging validation: (1) Ran 30d dashboard query suite (timeseries + breakdowns) against old vs new views; compared blended_cost_per_1m_output_tokens, total_cost_usd, output_tokens across group_bys for exact match within float tolerance (<= 1e-6 on $/1M, exact match on token counts). (2) Verified MV refresh behavior (hourly) and incremental daily MV lookback logic with simulated late-arriving hours. (3) Load test: 50 concurrent dashboard queries for 10 minutes; ensured warehouse credits stayed within expected envelope and p95 latencies met targets. (4) Verified API responses unchanged (schema and ordering), aside from faster response times.
Logan Wright (review): Can we confirm clustering choice? model_id is high-ish cardinality; worried about clustering degradation. Also, why both daily MV and topN MV vs a single MV? Mei Lin (author): Agreed on cardinality risk; in staging the clustering benefits still dominate for our access patterns because model_id is heavily filtered/grouped. I also capped clustering keys to 3 and moved quantization_profile out of clustering (kept as a projected column only). Re: two MVs: daily MV serves time series with date predicates; topN MV is keyed to common group_bys and pre-sorts/limits, avoiding scanning all groups for every request. Nadia Rahman (review): The rewrite moves rate card join after aggregation—any risk of shifting allocation when rate_card changes intra-day? Mei Lin: Rate card is versioned by effective_date; we join on usage_date/usage_hour bucket. This is equivalent to prior logic (previously rate card was looked up per request but with the same effective timestamp). Added a regression test covering a rate card boundary day. Chloe Martin (review): Please ensure view swap is gated so Console can roll back quickly if we see discrepancies. Also, what’s the API cache TTL assumption here? Mei Lin: Added feature flag ECON_WAREHOUSE_VIEWS_V2 to choose between old/new views at the query layer (default on in staging, off in prod until rollout). API cache TTL unchanged; this PR just reduces warehouse time so the cache can be shorter if we want later. Allison Grant (review): Any SRE concerns: MV refresh failures, monitoring? Mei Lin: Added two new freshness checks to the existing unit-econ pipeline monitor: MV last_refresh_age_minutes and MV rowcount sanity vs hourly fact. Both wired into the existing alert route. Logan Wright: Request change—document the new “dim_keys” table and rationale; also add an EXPLAIN for the slowest prior query so we have a baseline. Mei Lin: Done in docs/unit-economics/warehouse-performance.md; included before/after plans and the exact query templates used. Approvals: Logan Wright approved after docs update; Chloe Martin approved with the feature-flag gating; Nadia Rahman approved after boundary test; Allison Grant approved after monitoring notes added.
Internal-only: unit economics dashboard drilldowns should load significantly faster (esp. 30d + model/region breakdowns). No metric definition changes.

Motivation: Long-running tenants and variable sequence workloads expose pathological KV cache fragmentation and recurring micro-spill events that increase tail latency and IO spikes during eviction. This PR introduces a hybrid map compactifier plus an attenuation layer for spill-over that cooperates with continuous-batching to smooth reclaim pressure and preserve P99 latency.

What this changes (single-line list): 
- Adds a HybridMapCompactifier that performs low-cost in-place compaction for small segments and async remap compaction for large sparse ranges.
- Introduces a SpillAttenuationController: token-bucket backpressure on spill operations with hysteresis and per-tenant fairness weights.
- Evictor policy: age+density scoring and a secondary soft-throttle to prefer coalescing evictions into larger contiguous ranges to reduce write amplification.
- Scheduler hint: a kernel_prefer_local flag exposes low-latency kernel selection for compaction work to reduce kernel-launch jitter on multi-GPU hosts.
- Continuous batching integration: compaction and spill tasks are batched with inference prefix batching windows to avoid competing for GPU kernel time during high QPS.
- Tests & benchmarks: microbenchmarks for fragmentation scenarios and an e2e bench that simulates tenant churn.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implementation and unit tests for compactifier and controller
- [x] Integration with evictor scoring and scheduler hints
- [x] Benchmark harness and regression guardrail (quality + perf)
- [x] Documentation (runtime/kv_allocator/README updated)
- [x] Add Linear references and attach workload traces used for tuning

Performance summary (compared to main, workload: mixed-seq churn RPS 5k): 
- Median memory residency reduced by ~7% due to in-place compaction and coalesced evictions.
- P99 tail latency for inference generation while background compaction is active improved from 132ms to 92ms (=~30% reduction).
- Spill IO peaks reduced by ~55% because SpillAttenuationController batches and rate-limits spill windows.
- CPU overhead for allocator background threads + compaction is ~3% of host CPU on our bench machines.

Why this is different: Existing strategies either run aggressive global compaction (high cost) or rely solely on eviction heuristics. The hybrid compactifier keeps hot small objects contiguous cheaply while async remapping handles large sparse regions; combined with attenuation it minimizes IO storms during reclaim.

Commits summary: 
- a1f3b9c add HybridMapCompactifier implementation and unit tests
- b4d22a1 introduce SpillAttenuationController and rate-limiter primitives
- c2e7f10 integrate compactifier with evictor scoring and add scheduler hint knobs
- e7a4d5b batch compaction/spill tasks into continuous-batching pipeline and add bench harness
- f9b02d3 docs: runtime/kv_allocator/README and design note

Changed areas (high-level): 
- runtime/kv_allocator/compactifier.cc
- runtime/kv_allocator/compactifier.h
- runtime/kv_allocator/spill_controller.cc
- runtime/kv_allocator/evictor_policy.cc
- runtime/scheduler/kernel_hints.cc
- runtime/continuous_batching/integration.cc
- benchmarks/kv/fragments_bench.cc
- tests/kv/compactifier_test.cc
- docs/runtime/kv_allocator/README.md

Notes on deployments and safety: 
- Feature gated behind runtime flag kv.enable_hybrid_compactifier=false by default for canary rollout.
- SpillAttenuationController exposes two tunables (burst_tokens, refill_ms) with safe defaults used in Dedicated clusters.
- No breaking API changes; config additions are additive.

Related work / tickets: Linear ENG-1981 (fragmentation regression), ENG-2027 (spillback rate-limiter), ENG-2064 (batching integration), SUP-87 referenced for a customer incident that motivated the attenuation design.
Ravi Kumar: Can you clarify the heuristics for large-region async remap? I'm worried about increased mutex contention during remap. -- Requested changes
Evelyn Chen: Reply: Large-region remap uses a non-blocking two-phase swap and grabs per-segment locks; I added code comments and a microbenchmark (remap_lock_contention_bench) showing sub-ms median lock hold under our workload. PTAL.
Sofia Martinez: I ran the e2e bench on a multi-tenant Dedicated cluster and saw spill peaks reduced; can we add a guardrail to prevent refill_ms being set too low in user configs? -- Comment
Evelyn Chen: Added config validation and min_refill_ms=50ms. Also added docs entry in README.
Jonah Blake: Approved after minor nits fixed (doc wording + one flaky test removed from stable suite).
CI: Build passed; tests: 128/129 (one flaky test retried and passed on rerun). Check run id: ci/runner/89412

Motivation: Customers using long-lived streaming connections reported uneven retry behaviour and poor backpressure signals when consumers exercised slow sinks or transient auth refreshes. This PR delivers a coordinated change across the three official SDKs to (1) add a small, opinionated set of retry template presets (fast/fallback/hedged) usable out of the box, (2) expose a lightweight 'streamBackpressureHint' on streaming request shapes so servers and proxies can make informed batching/drop decisions, (3) ensure iterator/stream handles support a cancel-safe Close/Finish semantics so KV caches and background heartbeats shut down deterministically, and (4) align credential telemetry tags emitted by SDKs for easier cross-service tracing. Scope: cross-repo edits live in the monorepo under redwood-sdk-python/, redwood-sdk-typescript/, and redwood-sdk-go/; also includes docs and migration guide. Testing: added unit tests for retry-presets and backpressure hint propagation in each SDK, added an integration streaming smoke test that exercises slow consumer scenarios, and updated changelogs. Checklist: [x] add retry template DSL and presets in each SDK; [x] surface streamBackpressureHint in request builders; [x] implement Close/Finish idempotent semantics on stream iterators; [x] harmonize telemetry tags for credential operations; [x] tests and changelogs updated; [x] bump SDK package versions and release notes. Migration notes: users upgrading should switch to the new RetryTemplate presets or map their current RetryPolicy to one of the presets; the new streamBackpressureHint is optional and defaults to "none" for backward compatibility. Backwards-incompatible changes: none expected; if teams rely on implicit Close semantics they should opt into explicit Close/Finish to avoid relying on finalizers.
Python SDK 1.12.0, TypeScript SDK 1.28.0, Go SDK v1.9.0: introduce curated retry-template presets, expose streaming backpressure hints, add cancel-safe iterator close semantics, unify credential telemetry tags; minor bugfixes and docs; see migration notes.
Jonah Ellis: The retry presets look reasonable but please add a short doc blurb explaining the tradeoffs between 'fallback' and 'hedged' in the README; also please add a template for custom policy mapping.
Nina Park (author): addressed in docs and added mapping example; moved the hedged preset to use a slightly higher initial delay to avoid immediate duplicate traffic.
Priya Kapoor: In TS, the streamBackpressureHint felt tightly coupled to internal transport envelope; can you make it a lightweight shape-only field so other transports can ignore it?
Nina Park (author): changed TS surface to be transport-agnostic and added tests demonstrating how to noop the hint in a custom transport.
Marco Li: Go integration test failed with race on first run; looks like the iterator Close needed an extra edge-case for double-close. Please add idempotency guard.
Marco Li (author): added atomic guard and new test; re-ran CI and flakiness resolved.

Motivation: Customers operating across regions need resilient KMS usage with strict residency guarantees. When preferred regional CMKs are unavailable (maintenance, degraded provider regions, or temporary operator throttles) we must enforce a deterministic, auditable fallback that preserves residency constraints where possible and surfaces policy decisions to operators. Additionally, RBAC v2 paths occasionally allow short-lived elevation churn (race during operator delegation) which can be abused; introduce an elevation limiter to bound concurrent temporary grants and emit telemetry when thresholds are exceeded.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a KMS Residency Fallback Planner: a deterministic policy engine that selects a fallback CMK based on residency intent, last-known-affinity, tiered consent (tenant-level consent, org allowlist), and operator-scoped leases. Planner exposes a narrow API used by the kms-allocator and kms-proxy. 2) Adds RBAC Elevation Limiter: middleware that tracks temporary elevation tokens (operator leases) per-operator and per-tenant window, imposes soft and hard caps, and integrates with the policy decision cache so rollbacks are immediate. 3) Emits structured audit events for planner decisions and limiter actions: decision_id, reason, candidate_keys, operator_lease_id, and policy_fingerprint. 4) Add a dry-run mode and opt-in shadowing to allow operators to test new fallback rules without affecting traffic. 5) Updates Helm chart and installer flags to expose planner tuning knobs and limiter thresholds.

Backwards compatibility and migration: default behavior preserves current allocation strategy; planner is behind a feature flag (kms.residency.planner.enabled=false) by default. Audit events are additive (new event types); no change to existing audit schema fields. RBAC limiter defaults to permissive thresholds matching historical maxima to avoid operational disruption.

Testing and validation: unit tests for planner selection rules, property-based tests for deterministic ordering, integration tests simulating region failover, e2e with private-installer in a two-zone cluster, and load tests to validate limiter scale and memory usage. CI includes a new slow integration job gated to nightly runs.

Checklist:
- [x] Feature flagged planner and limiter
- [x] Unit + integration tests
- [x] Helm and private-installer flags
- [x] Audit event docs and examples
- [x] Shadow/dry-run mode for staged rollout
- [x] Linear ticket linked (ENG-4821), support ticket noted (SUP-679)

Risks and mitigations: planner introduces a small deterministic delay (policy evaluation) at allocation time; mitigated by caching decisions for 60s and pre-warming common tenancy keys. Limiter may surface false positives in bursty operator workflows; added a burst window and rate smoothing.

Rollout plan: merge to main behind feature flag, enable shadowing for 2 weeks, flip planner on for 10% of traffic with automatic rollback on audit-anchored anomaly detection, then gradual ramp to 100%.

Notes: This PR intentionally separates decision logic (planner) from enforcement (kms-proxy) to ease future policy audits and allow replay of decisions for provenance. See docs/security/kms-residency.md for full operator guide.
planner: add residency fallback planner with deterministic scoring and caching
rbac: add elevation limiter middleware and in-memory counters with prometheus metrics
audit: emit structured decision events and map to existing audit pipeline
helm: expose kms.residency.* and rbac.limiter.* tunables
installer: add flag to private-installer for planner shadow mode
tests: add unit, property-based, and integration tests for failover scenarios

Maya Chen (author): Added a 60s decision cache and pre-warm hook; attached canary numbers to the CI run showing p99 increase < 3ms under baseline.

Summary: This PR implements a background SLO reconciler that computes desired circuit states off the request path and introduces a non-blocking grace period for circuit reopen decisions to reduce flip-flopping under transient load.
Motivation: During the last two incidents we observed frequent circuit reopen/close oscillation when short-lived bursts pushed regional latency over SLO thresholds. That led to poor tail latency for many tenants and noisy telemetry. The reconciler moves expensive SLO evaluation and candidate state transitions out of the hot path; the grace period applies a short, non-blocking delay window to allow in-flight metrics to settle before applying an immediate reopen.
Design highlights:
1) services/controller/slo_reconciler.go implements a periodic reconciler loop that aggregates per-tenant SLO windows, computes a smoothed violation score (leaky-bucket smoothing), and emits candidate state transitions into the circuit manager queue. The reconciler reads the same metric stream as the runtime but uses independent sampling windows to avoid contention.
2) services/circuit/circuit_manager.go now supports 'deferred_apply' for reopen transitions — the controller enqueues a candidate reopen with a timestamp; the circuit manager will apply reopen only if the candidate remains valid but will never block request handling to wait for reconcile evaluation.
3) Feature gating: new config flag slo.reconciler.enabled in pkg/config/features.yaml (off by default). Operator can enable in staging for canary.
4) Telemetry: added metrics slo_reconciler.evaluations_total, slo_reconciler.transition_candidates, circuit.grace_reopens and tags for region/tenant to internal/telemetry/metrics_registry.go.
Implementation notes:
- Careful to avoid extra heap allocations in reconciliation loop; used a reused buffer for tenant window aggregation.
- Reconciler uses a read-copy-update pattern for config to avoid global locking.
- Circuit manager change uses atomic state transitions for reopen/close and an append-only candidate queue with bounded size to prevent backpressure.
Commits:
- "reconciler: add background SLO reconciler loop and aggregation"
- "circuit: non-blocking reopen grace period and candidate queue"
- "telemetry: register reconciler and grace metrics"
- "tests: add integration test for reconcile-driven transitions"
- "docs: ops guide for enabling and monitoring the reconciler"
- "ci: flaky test stability harness for reconciler"
Files changed (high-level): services/controller/slo_reconciler.go: new reconciler implementation with benchmark scaffolding services/circuit/circuit_manager.go: logic for deferred_apply + atomic state machine pkg/config/features.yaml: new feature flag internal/telemetry/metrics_registry.go: metric registration tests/integration/slo_reconciler_staging_test.go: end-to-end scenario: transient spike -> candidate reopen queued -> grace period prevents immediate flipflop -> reconciler confirms transition docs/ops/slo-reconciler.md: operator instructions + rollout plan Makefile: test target for reconciler integration.
Testing and CI:
- Local unit tests added and passing.
- Integration test simulates transient surge (100ms window) and asserts no more than one reopen/close within 30s for a single tenant.
- CI initially showed a flaky timing test (tests/integration/slo_reconciler_staging_test.go) failing on CI worker with high noise; I adjusted timeouts and added a stability harness (retry-based assertion) and re-ran. Final CI: all green (unit + integration + lint).
Performance/observability notes:
- In staging canary (0.5% traffic) we ran a controlled spike test: reconciler reduced reactive reopen rate by ~78% vs baseline and reduced client-visible 95th latency by ~12ms during the spike.
- Memory and CPU overhead: reconciler loop added ~6% CPU on controller pod during evaluation windows and <30MB RSS increase on the controller; we included autoscaler tweaks in rollout.
Rollout plan:
1) Merge gated behind feature flag.
2) Enable in staging for one week with canary traffic and watch slo_reconciler.transition_candidates and circuit.grace_reopens metrics.
3) If results match expectations, enable in regional canaries (2 regions) and monitor for 48-72 hours.
4) Gradual global ramp with early abort if reopen counts or error rates rise unexpectedly.

Approvals: "Liam Chen: approved" "Sofia Martinez: approved with minor comments" "Noah Rivera: approved" Merge details: merged by Liam Chen via squash merge; commit message summarized reconciler and grace period. Adds a lightweight presubmit guard that skips expensive integration and runtime tests for trivial churn (docs, lockfile bumps, README tweaks) and introduces a dependency metadata index used by CI to make safer dependency-update decisions. No runtime behavior changes. Expected CI median wall-clock improvement for small PRs: ~40%.
Motivation: our presubmit lanes run expensive integrational checks for many PRs that only touch docs, vendor metadata, or lockfile updates. This inflates queue times and developer feedback latency. This PR introduces a compact presubmit guard that computes a small change signature and consults a dependency metadata index to decide if the full integration lane is required. The index encodes package->impact heuristics (runtime vs dev-only, critical paths, known flake-prone updates).

What this PR does: 1) tools/ci/presubmit_guard.py: new guard that inspects changed paths, git diff hunks, and a cached dependency metadata index to return a preflight verdict (skip, run-quick, run-full). 2) tools/ci/dep_indexer.py: builds dependency metadata from lockfiles, module manifests, and a small heuristics config (maintainable YAML). 3) .github/workflows/presubmit.yml: wiring to run the guard as the first step; if verdict==skip it posts a status and short-circuits heavy jobs. 4) scripts/ci_checkpoint_wrap.sh and pkg/infra/checkpoint/*: lightweight checkpoint wrappers used by CI to mark progress and mitigate orphaned runner timeouts. 5) tests/presubmit/*: unit and integration tests exercising guard logic and indexer behavior. 6) docs/ci/README.md: operational notes and how to update the dependency metadata.

Checklist: - [x] Add guard and indexer code with unit tests - [x] Integrate guard into presubmit workflow - [x] Add docs and update on-call playbook - [x] Run canary on staging CI and measure wall-clock improvements - [x] Add telemetry counters for skip/run decisions

Safety and rollout: default behaviour is conservative: the index starts with conservative heuristics and any unknowns result in run-full. We deployed this behind a feature flag for 72h on staging, observed ~37-43% median improvement for small PRs (<50 LOC, docs-only), and no missed regressions in the canary set (100 PRs sampled). We also implemented an automatic fallback: if the guard binary exits non-zero or the index is unavailable, workflow falls back to run-full to avoid silent skips.

Operational notes: updating the dependency metadata is a manual step (tools/ci/dep_indexer.py --update) that will later be automated from nightly lockfile scans. The docs directory includes a CONTRIBUTING section describing signals to mark a package as dev-only or low-impact.

Related: ENG-452 introduces the initial heuristics schema; SUP-210 was an incident where an infra-only bump triggered a long presubmit and contributed to release delay.

CI summary: first run had one flaky test in tests/presubmit/test_guard.py that was fixed in a follow-up commit (deterministic tempdir timing). Final CI: all checks passed.

Merge: squash merge to main.

Priya Desai: Please add a safety net so that an unavailable index does not cause skips — suggested returning 'run-full' on error. (resolved)
Marco Ruiz: Can we add per-repo opt-outs? Not in this PR, but added docs/ci/UPDATE_DEP_INDEX.md describing how to mark patterns. (answered)
Evan Turner: Minor nit: prefer explicit exit codes for the guard (0=skip,1=run-quick,2=run-full,3=error). Updated and tests added. (resolved)

Priya Desai: Approving after seeing telemetry counters and fallback logic. (approved)

Motivation: We continue to see client libraries re-implementing similar streaming lifecycle and retry behavior (token refresh during long-lived streams, cancellation propagation, and duplicate backoff strategies). This PR introduces a lightweight, SDK-friendly CancelableStream abstraction and moves retry decision & backoff logic into a shared retry-shim (redwood/sdk-shared/retry) so Python/TS/Go SDKs can converge on identical semantics without duplicating fragile state machines.

What this PR changes (single-string summary): Adds CancelableStream helpers and context-aware wrappers for streaming endpoints; centralizes retry/backoff/token-refresh decisions in a shared shim used by all three SDKs; small ergonomics helpers (WithContext, StreamCloseNotify); updates examples and tests; bumps client versions.

Checklist: - [x] Design proposal landed in ENG-1423 - [x] Core retry-shim implemented and unit-tested - [x] Python/TS/Go bindings added to call into shim - [x] End-to-end streaming smoke tests updated - [x] Docs snippets refreshed - [x] Version bumps for each SDK

Commits (high level): - feat(retry-shim): introduce shared retry decision module and deterministic backoff profiles - feat(streams): add CancelableStream interface and WithContext helpers in sdk-shared - feat(go-sdk): wire CancelableStream adapter, expose Stream.CloseNotify and Stream.Cancel - feat(py-sdk): add StreamingClient.with_cancelable() helper and token refresh hook during retries - feat(ts-sdk): expose makeCancelableStream and typed iterator wrapper - test: add cross-sdk streaming integration harness (flaky-test guard) - docs: update streaming.md and quickstarts

Files changed (high level): - redwood/sdk-shared/retry/* (new): core retry logic, backoff profiles, token-refresh orchestration hooks - redwood/sdk-shared/stream/* (new): CancelableStream interface, context bindings, utilities - redwood/sdk-go/streaming.go: adapter and exported helpers - redwood/sdk-python/streaming.py: convenience wrappers and small refactor to client handshake - redwood/sdk-typescript/streams.ts: typed iterable wrapper and cancellation token doc examples - docs/quickstarts/streaming.md: replace example with WithContext-using pattern - tests/e2e/streaming_harness: add cross-sdk test case simulating token rotation and mid-stream cancellation

Notes on ergonomics and compatibility: The CancelableStream API is opt-in: existing streaming calls continue to return the older iterator/async-iterator shape. New convenience constructors (e.g. client.stream().as_cancelable(ctx)) provide an ergonomic migration path. The retry-shim exposes a minimal interface (shouldRetry(error, attemptMetadata) -> {decision, backoffMs, refreshToken}) so SDK tongues can keep language-idiomatic wrappers.

Review conversation (abridged, single string): Ethan Cole (reviewer): "Great consolidation. Two asks: make backoff profiles pluggable and add metrics hooks when retry-shim triggers token refresh." Priya (author): "Pluggable profiles added behind RetryConfig; metrics hooks exposed via RetryHooks interface; added tests." Marta Puig (reviewer): "Please ensure TS iterator typings remain compatible for downstream consumers; watch for runtime-heavy allocations in Go." Priya: "TS tests updated to preserve Iterator<T> shape; Go implementation uses a single goroutine with channel-based streaming to avoid allocations on each token and includes microbench." Liu Zhang (final approver): "Tests and CI green; behavior verified by streaming canary locally. Approving for merge."

CI and stability: Initial CI run failed on a flaky e2e that simulates mid-stream token rotations (timeout). I reworked the harness to use deterministic fake-time and retried. Final CI: all checks pass (unit, linters, cross-sdk integration). Post-merge canary run against perf lane showed no regression in median latency for typical 1-2s streams; tail latency improvement in high retry scenarios due to centralized token refresh queuing.

Merge: Squash merge after approvals. Merge commit records authorship and links to ENG-1423/ENG-1668.

Migration guidance for SDK consumers (short): 1) No immediate action required. 2) To opt into cancellable streams, call the new helper on the client: e.g. py: client.stream(...).as_cancelable(context) or ts: makeCancelableStream(client.stream(...), abortSignal). 3) If you implement custom retry policies, switch to RetryConfig to maintain compatibility.

Follow-ups planned: - ENG-1668: metrics instrumentation for retry events and token-refresh counts - Small perf pass to reduce allocation overhead in the Go adapter - Docs: add migration guide and a short video showing cancelation + graceful shutdown

Related: ENG-1423, ENG-1668, and a related internal incident INT-3021 (token-rotation causing duplicate in-flight refreshes).
Introduce cancelable stream primitives across SDKs; centralize retry decision logic into shared retry-shim; bump SDK versions (Python 2.6.0, TypeScript 1.9.0, Go v0.8.0). Backwards compatible: opt-in helpers; no forced client changes.

Motivation: We observe intermittent cold-path latency spikes and unexpectedly high token cost on first-invocation paths for multi-chunk requests. Root cause analysis (ENG-4521) showed that prefetch jobs often don't fully warm kernel/jit/kv caches for sharded serving, and current dashboards lack a compact signal to quantify effectiveness. This PR introduces a derived metric "prefetch_warmup_efficiency" (ratio of useful warmup hits to prefetch attempts) and an autotune pipeline to recommend warmup batch sizes and backoff windows.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Adds the metric at the telemetry collector, surfaces warmup tags on spans, exposes a warmup-efficiency dashboard and an autotune job that suggests config changes, and adds an alert that suppresses noisy flaps with hysteresis. Changes are behind a feature flag (observability.prefetch_warmup) and include unit + integration tests and a small Console UI panel.

Checklist:
- [x] implement prefetch_warmup_efficiency gauge and aggregation windows (1m/5m/1h)
- [x] attach warmup_reason and warmup_outcome tags to invocation spans for correlation
- [x] dashboard JSON with heatmap, efficiency sparkline, and recommended tuning panel
- [x] alerting rule: prefetch_warmup_degradation (30m sustained < 0.6 triggers) with auto-suppress for known deployment windows
- [x] autotune job that runs nightly on sampled traffic and posts recommended batch_size/warmup_lookahead to a suggestions index
- [x] unit tests + synthetic replaybench integration test
- [x] feature-flag rollout + docs blurb in changelog

Backward compatibility and rollout: All telemetry additions are additive. The feature is gated; no change to serving defaults. The dashboard and autotune job are opt-in via console toggle. Alert thresholds are conservative and have a 2-hour quiet-window to avoid noisy pages during releases.

Operational notes: The autotune job outputs recommendations with confidence bins; recommendations include an estimated cost delta and expected tail latency impact. We intentionally cap suggested batch_size to prevent regressions on small-tenant traffic. The alerter includes an annotation with the last successful autotune run ID to aid triage.

Testing and verification: Unit tests validate metric computation for synthetic traces. Integration test replays a warmup-heavy synthetic workload and asserts the efficiency metric rises above 0.85 after warmup. CI initially showed a flaky integration test related to timing; I adjusted the replaybench timings and reran CI (see commits).

Related work: builds on the kernel warmup observability hooks from ENG-5012 and reuses the span-tagging primitives introduced in pr-110999 (span warmup tags). Links: Linear: ENG-4521, ENG-5012; Support ticket: SUP-1189.

When enabling in prod, monitor the suggested batch_size drift and the autotune confidence bins for first 48 hours. The alert includes an annotation for the last autotune run ID. If you see >5% tail latency regressions after applying a recommendation, roll back and file ENG-5012 follow-up.

Motivation: Customers and SREs have asked for a compact, chronologically ordered view of per-invocation work stages (ingest, routing, batching, KV lookup, kernel exec, postprocess, network egress) to speed up incident triage and to attribute cost and latency to precise pipeline segments. At the same time, the observability pipeline has been suffering from high-cardinality log payloads when we attach full request contexts; this PR introduces a log-sample compactifier that keeps representative context while reducing cardinality and payload size.

What this change does (single-line summary): add a lightweight invocation timeline model, emit timeline spans at ingest and runtime boundaries, surface a timeline visualization in the telemetry UI, and add a configurable log-sample compactifier that reduces attached context while preserving keys used for debugging.

Details and rationale: The runtime already emits fine-grained spans, but they are dispersed and heavy when joined with raw request contexts. The timeline aggregates existing span events into a deterministic ordered list of named segments with duration and token counts. The compactifier performs three steps on attached request context before storage: 1) key whitelist/blacklist, 2) sketch-based value summarization for large text blobs (min-hash fingerprint + 64-byte prefix), and 3) reservoir sampling of nested arrays with deterministic seeding to make sampled context reproducible for a given invocation id. This reduces typical attached context size by ~4x in our internal traces while retaining the tokens/keys teams find useful during debugging.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc: ENG-4127 (linked) - [x] Unit tests for timeline aggregation - [x] Integration tests for compactifier sampling and size reduction - [x] Dashboard panels added (telemetry/timelines) - [x] Backwards-compatible: feature gated by runtime flag and server-side toggle - [x] Migration note included for downstream consumers

Behavioral notes: Timeline segments are emitted as a single synthetic span with attribute timeline.v1 containing an ordered list; this keeps trace cardinality low and allows rollup without new trace types. The compactifier runs on ingestion only and is reversible for stored snapshots using the invocation id + sample seed if full context retrieval is enabled via audit storage (opt-in enterprise feature).

Commit summary: - introduce telemetry/timeline aggregator and timeline proto - emit timeline span at runtime flush and after KV-cache hits - add compactifier module and unit tests - add dashboard JSON for timelines and sample size distribution - add feature flag and config knobs for sampling rate and whitelist - update docs/observability/telemetry.md

Files changed (high level): src/runtime/telemetry/timeline_aggregator.go, src/runtime/telemetry/compactifier.go, pkg/telemetry/proto/timeline.proto, web/console/pages/telemetry/timeline-panel.json, infra/helm/values.telemetry.yaml, tests/telemetry/timeline_integration_test.go, docs/observability/telemetry.md

Review & discussion (summary): See review_comments for inline threads. Key threads: memory overhead for compactifier (addressed by bounded buffers and shared pool), determinism of sampling (seed uses invocation id + shard salt), and UI layout for timeline (added compact view for narrow screens).

CI and merge: CI passed after one flaky test rerun. Merged via squash-merge to main. Release-note: Adds invocation timeline visualization and a configurable log-sample compactifier to reduce observability payload sizes without losing actionable context.

Migration: No forced migration; downstream consumers of telemetry spans will see timeline.v1 attribute when the runtime flag is enabled. Docs updated with example timeline JSON and recommended alert adjustments for segment-level latency.

Risks & mitigations: The main risk is under-sampling important context keys — mitigation: whitelist defaults include request_id, user_id, prompt_hash, and top-3 function call signatures; teams can opt to add keys via config. Performance risk mitigated via benchmarks and pooled buffers (see perf numbers in design doc).

Sana Kapoor: Implemented a shared buffer pool and added a circuit-breaker to drop non-whitelisted keys if memory pressure exceeds threshold (see compactifier.go).
Marisol Aguirre: How do we ensure sampling determinism across restarts?
Sana Kapoor: Sampling seed uses invocation_id + telemetry_shard_salt persisted in config; documented in design doc.

Infra: Please add helm values for enabling the feature per environment.

QA: Integration test covers end-to-end timeline and compactifier size assertion.
