payload.body:
Summary: Implements a runtime-level orchestrator that combines per-tenant SLO weights, recent token/connection usage heuristics, and circuit breaker state to decide eviction pressure and fair connection allocation. Motivation: Recent incidents showed that aggressive single-tenant bursts could destabilize local KV caches and connection pools, causing cascading slowpaths in regional failovers. Rather than coarse tenant de-prioritization we need a finer-grained policy that: 1) honors explicit SLO weightings (e.g., premium vs free), 2) smooths transient spikes using an exponential decay window, and 3) coordinates with circuit-breaker health so we avoid pushing degraded tenants into immediate hard eviction. What this PR does: - New orchestration module: runtime/evictor/slo_orchestrator.go that computes a tenant priority score combining SLO weight, recent tokens/sec, connection-hold time, and current circuit state. - Connection fairness: runtime/conn_pool/fair_allocator.go adds soft quotas and a reclaim path that respects per-tenant score. - Eviction soft-exit: runtime/evictor/decay_controller.go implements a configurable decay window and prevents immediate re-open flips by recording ephemeral penalty snapshots. - Telemetry: observability/metrics/evictor.metrics.yaml and docs/telemetry/README.md describing the new counters and dashboards. - Config: ops/configs/evictor_profiles.yaml contains profiles and sane defaults; ops/airbyte/rollout-plan.md has the staged rollout. Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-2149) - [x] Unit+integration tests for fairness allocator - [x] CI green on canary cluster run - [x] Dashboard and alert updates included - [x] Rollout plan with abort criteria included Commits summary: - Initial implementation of slo_orchestrator with scoring function and tests - Add fair_allocator and integrate with conn pool lifecycle - Implement decay_controller and penalty snapshot storage - Telemetry and dashboard wiring - Rollout plan and config profiles - Hotfix: prevent rapid penalty re-apply on reconnect race (follow-up commit) Files changed (high level): - runtime/evictor/slo_orchestrator.go - runtime/conn_pool/fair_allocator.go - runtime/evictor/decay_controller.go - observability/metrics/evictor.metrics.yaml - ops/configs/evictor_profiles.yaml - docs/telemetry/README.md - ops/airbyte/rollout-plan.md Testing notes: unit tests included for scoring boundaries and allocator fairness; integration test simulates multi-tenant burst to validate no single tenant drives more than 65% of connection slots when below a threshold score. Load test on canary (region us-east-1) shows 18% reduction in cascade slowpaths and elimination of repeated circuit flips during replayed incidents. Review conversation snapshot: Arjun: "Score function looks reasonable; can we make weight->score mapping pluggable so we can A/B different curves?" Author(Maya): "Added configurable weight_to_score_curve in evictor_profiles.yaml and default to a capped logarithmic mapping; documented in rollout plan." Leah: "Need stronger unit test around reconnect race, I observed a micro-flip in local repro." Author: "Added hotfix commit to debounce penalty re-apply with per-conn epoch token; added integration test that previously failed." Diego: "Telemetry names LGTM; add a short-lived alert to detect unexpected evictor rejections." Author: "Added evictor.rejection_rate alert in observability file and included abort criteria in rollout-plan.md." CI summary: GitHub actions: unit (pass), integration (pass on canary run), lint (pass after fix), e2e (flaky test xfail annotated). Merge notes: merged to main via squash merge after +2 approvals and canary run. Post-merge actions: - Kick off staged rollout (ops/airbyte/rollout-plan.md) to 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 48h windows - Monitor evictor.rejection_rate and slo-weighted-fairness breach metrics for first 72h - Prepare rollback branch feature/evictor-rollback if we observe >0.5% customer error-rise within 30m of each ramp. Related: ENG-2170 (follow-up: expose per-tenant debug dump for on-call), ENG-2149 (design). Notes: No public API or migration required. This PR is intended to be non-breaking and reversible; configs default to conservative profiles to avoid surprises.
Adds a configurable SLO-weighted eviction policy and connection fairness layer to reduce tenant-induced oscillation under surge. No customer-facing API changes. Rollout as a staged canary with telemetry gated rollback.

payload.body:
Motivation: In long-sequence and chat workloads we observed stalls caused by the existing two-stage dequant -> kernel dispatch pattern. Large KV-cache lookups frequently forced backend transfers that serialized with kernel uploads, increasing p95 latency on INT8/FP8 mixed paths. This PR introduces an "interleaved dequant + prefetch" optimization and a small scheduler handoff that reduces end-to-end stalls and improves KV cache locality.

Design summary: single-pass inspector (runtime/scheduler/interleave_inspector) walks per-request KV usage hints and issues prefetch requests concurrently while the per-layer dequant step is scheduled. The kernel_router was augmented to accept a "prefetch affinity" hint so that when the dequant completes the kernel can be enqueued to the same GPU/stream to avoid device-to-device shuffles. We also added a light-weight soft-fence that allows the continuous-batcher to overlap next-token inputs with backend prefetch operations for re-used KV slices.

Key changes: modified kernel_router.cc to accept affinity tokens and a small RMQ to track in-flight prefetches; added interleave_prefetch_pass.cc which coordinates dequant + kv prefetch ordering and emits runtime hints; updated kv_cache.cc to expose an async peek API used by the inspector; tuned continuous_batcher to allow speculative enqueues when prefetch affinity is present. Minor API additions are internal-only and protected by a runtime feature flag: redwood.runtime.experimental.interleave_dequant_prefetch.

Benchmarks: microbench (bert-large, seq_len=2048) on n1-standard + A100 profile shows throughput +18% and p95 latency -12% for INT8-smoothquant path vs main. End-to-end chat scenario (gpt-3 style, multi-turn 4k tokens accumulated) shows 22% token/sec improvement and 9% lower tail latency when canaryed on dedicated pools. Memory overhead is negligible (<1% resident increase) due to reusing prefetch buffers and avoiding duplicate copies.

Compatibility and safety: the change is opt-in by runtime flag and guarded by kernel compatibility checks (INT8/FP8 smoothquant variants only). If affinity hints cannot be honored (heterogeneous pool or capacity constraints) the scheduler falls back to pre-existing routing. We added health counters and rollout metrics to Console: interleave.prefetch.hits, interleave.prefetch.fallbacks, interleave.kernel.handoff_latency.

Testing: unit tests for new inspector logic and async kv peek were added; integration perf harness added bench_attn_interleave.py for CI perf regression. Stress tests run in perf-lab with mixed precision loads.

Deployment plan: staged rollout: feature flag enabled on canary pool -> observe metrics for 72h -> gradual ramp to 25% -> 100% if no regressions. Rollback is a single flag flip.

Related: addresses ENG-2419 (reduce dequant-induced stalls) and partially complements ENG-2567 (kv-query locality improvements).
Liam Chen: Nice approach. Two questions: (1) how does the inspector scale with large request fanout? (2) can we avoid the extra allocation in async kv peek?
Maya Patel: For (1) inspector is O(#kv_slices) and we cap hints to a configurable window (default 8 slices). For (2) we reused pinned scratch buffers from the allocator pool; allocation path is hot but pooled so amortized cost is low. Added note in code and a new perf test showing negligible allocation overhead.
Rosa Alvarez: Need stronger guards for mixed-precision fallbacks — please add a metrics signal when the scheduler falls back to old path.
Maya Patel: Added interleave.prefetch.fallbacks and increment points in kernel_router and inspector. Also added an e2e test that forces fallback and asserts metrics are emitted.
Devon McCarthy: CI flagged a race in prefetch completion; see my comment on interleave_inspector.cc:line78. Please add ordering fence.
Maya Patel: Added soft-fence using the runtime stream semaphore; updated tests to cover the race. CI green on rerun.

payload.body:
Adds a session-aware ensemble promotion controller and hybrid A/B rollback playbook. Improves safe promotes for stateful session traffic with explainable rollback replay. No API surface changes for customers.
Motivation: Large multi-variant experiments and shadow-to-canary promotions expose a gap when session affinity and small cohorts interact with ensemble routing. This change introduces a 'sessioned ensemble promoter' runtime controller that coordinates rolling promotes for ensemble model groups (heterogeneous variants) while preserving session coherence and providing an automated hybrid A/B rollback playbook when drift or latency regressions are detected. High-level goals: 1) maintain session affinity across promotes so user sessions see consistent model variants during a transition, 2) enable multi-arm A/B promotes where traffic fractions shift smoothly based on telemetry, 3) provide an automated rollback path that can perform sampled replay (dry-run) plus deterministic revert when thresholds hit, 4) be non-invasive to existing API surface and compatible with Dedicated/Private deployments. Design summary: The promoter composes three subcomponents: a session ledger that holds session->variant leases, a fractional orchestrator that applies staged traffic deltas with backpressure and decay windows, and a rollback playbook engine that runs a decision DAG (smoke checks, latency SLO gates, quality regression detectors) to trigger sampled replay or immediate revert. The promoter uses a short-lived in-memory lease (default 5m) with optional persistent snapshotting for long-lived sessions behind stateful routes. It integrates with the console telemetry hooks for per-variant SLOs and with the Optimize recommendations engine to pick safe step sizes. Checklist: - [x] API: add internal controller endpoints for orchestration and diagnostics. No public/customer API changes. - [x] Runtime: implement session ledger and fractional orchestrator. - [x] Safety: add rollback playbook engine and decision traces. - [x] Tests: unit tests for lease logic, integration test for staged traffic shift, e2e smoke with simulated regression. - [x] Docs: operator guide and runbook in repo/docs/rollouts. Implementation notes: Commits are split by logical area: session-lease core, orchestrator state machine, rollback playbook DSL and engine, telemetry adapters, tests and docs. The session ledger uses sharded lease buckets keyed by hashed session id to limit coordination hot spots. The fractional orchestrator monitors both request latencies and token-level cost deltas to apply conservative phasing when cost SLOs trend upward. Rollback playbook: default policy is a two-step action: 1) sample-replay mode where 5% of promoted traffic is routed to the previous stable variant for replay and differential comparison for 10 minutes; 2) if delta on chosen metrics exceeds configured thresholds, trigger immediate revert and create an audit snapshot. Backwards compatibility and rollout: the controller starts in dry-run for 48h in a staging cluster with synthetic traffic and can be toggled per-namespace. The operator guide includes manual holdpoints and an emergency 'cut glass' revert route. Testing summary: Added unit coverage to session lease edge cases, an integration harness simulating session churn and heterogenous variant pools, and a simulator that fuzzes latency/regression signals to validate playbook thresholds. CI: initial lint run flagged formatting on DSL parser; fixed in commit 3. Security review: minimal surface; session ids remain hashed; no sensitive state stored unencrypted. Deployment: feature is behind an operator flag (rollouts.session_ensemble_enable) and defaults to off for Dedicated/private installs. Related work: builds on ENG-1425 (cohort-aware promotes) and ENG-1482 (telemetry-led gates). Linear links and SUP ticket noted for support test matrix. Migration and operator impact: small schema bump to internal controller snapshots (v2) with automatic in-place migration script included. Rollback and audit: every promote and revert emits an audit record suitable for retention in customer audit logs for Private deployments. Merge details: squashed and merged to main after approvals and CI green.
Calvin Huang: Nice design. Question: how do we avoid hot-sharding on large numbers of short sessions? Suggest adding randomized lease jitter and bucket affinity.
Aisha Patel: Reply: added lease jitter and increased shard count; also added a fallback to sticky short leases for high-churn routes. See session_ledger.go changes in commit c1a6d8f.
Priya Natarajan: Please add an integration test that simulates a regression in both latency and quality signals simultaneously to ensure playbook prioritizes latency SLOs.
Aisha Patel: Added ensemble_fuzzer simulator and an integration test that injects correlated latency+quality drift.

Motivation: Prefetch/prefix prefill is a major contributor to wasted token compute for spiky workloads; naive prefetching inflates unit cost when load has poor locality. At the same time, aggressive static quant profiles risk quality regressions for tail requests. This PR implements two coordinated automations: (1) an adaptive prefetch throttle that learns per-model/per-route prefill hit-rate and dynamically reduces prefill aggressiveness for low-locality workloads, and (2) a quantization ramp controller that gradually applies lower-precision profiles during sustained low-sensitivity windows and backs off when eval metrics degrade. Design summary: the prefetch throttle collects a lightweight rolling window of prefix-hit ratios and request inter-arrival statistics, computes an expected prefill ROI score, and adjusts prefill budget (requests per second allowed to prefetch) using a PID-lite controller. The quant ramper registers with the Optimize subsystem and uses production eval hooks to compute a short-term quality delta (bleu/rouge-based or embedding cos-sim proxies) before committing to a lower quant profile; it supports staged ramps (full -> q8 -> q4) with configurable hold periods and rollback triggers. Config/ops: new org-level config keys: econ.prefetch.throttle.enabled (bool, default=false for safety), econ.prefetch.throttle.window_s (int), econ.prefetch.throttle.target_roi (float), econ.quant.ramp.enabled (bool, default=false), econ.quant.ramp.stages (ordered list), econ.quant.ramp.min_hold_s (int). Rollout plan: start off by enabling both features as "opt-in shadow" in Dedicated and Hosted canaries, collect telemetry for 48h, then enable soft-enforcement in a small percentage (5%) of traffic for 7 days, finally flip default off->on for selected perf-sensitive models after product signoff. Tests & telemetry: end-to-end integration tests simulate low- and high-locality traffic to assert throttle converges and prefill budgets fall back to baseline; quant ramp simulated on eval harness with synthetic regressions to verify rollback. Telemetry: added prefill.hits, prefill.misses, prefill.budget_used, quant.ramp.stage, quant.ramp.rollback_count, econ.unit_cost_delta. Benchmarks: internal staging run across three representative workloads shows median unit cost improvement 12% on spiky workloads with <1% quality delta (measured by embedding-sim proxy). Implementation notes: new controllers implemented in serving/runtime/prefill and optimize/ramp; lightweight in-memory stores with optional persistence to kv for operator visibility; new CLI flags and API surface for manual override. Documentation: README updates in docs/econ and examples in redwood-quickstarts showing config snippets and how to revert. Related work: complements ongoing batch/caching heuristics (see ENG-1987) and reuses the cost-scorer from pr-331210. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (linked in linear ENG-2245) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Telemetry + dashboards - [x] API + CLI controls - [x] Docs + quickstart example - [x] Canary deployment notes
Darren Lopez (reviewer): Overall strong design. Two asks: 1) make sure throttle controller has a safe minimum budget to avoid cold-start regressions; 2) add explicit audit logs when quant ramp changes a profile.
Maya Chen (author reply): Added 'min_budget' default to config and emit quant.ramp.audit events; tests updated.
Priya Nair (reviewer): Can we gate the quant ramp on a per-customer opt-in? Some enterprise customers require manual approval.
Maya Chen (author reply): Added per-org override keys and CLI explicit enable flag so ent customers remain opt-in by default.
Samir Gupta (approver): CI green, smoke in canary looks good. Approved.
CI Bot: build/presubmit passed after second run (flake on first).
Introduced adaptive prefetch throttle and quantization ramp controller. Opt-in via econ.prefetch.* and econ.quant.ramp.* flags. Provides measured unit-cost reductions for spiky workloads with automated safeguards and rollbacks.
Default is disabled. To enable in a controlled rollout: 1) set econ.prefetch.throttle.enabled=true in the org config for the canary org, 2) enable econ.quant.ramp.enabled=true in Optimize for the test models, 3) monitor dashboard 'prefill-quant' for regressions. Emergency rollback: set both flags to false or use CLI econ disable-ramp/disable-prefetch. Alerts tuned to fire on quant.ramp.rollback_count > 3 in 5m.

payload.body:
## Context
As part of the provision-to-ready automation rollout, we are standardizing golden image channels (candidate -> stable) and pinning pool image versions. During the us-east/A100 staged rollout we had a quarantine spike and had to quickly determine who/what changed image configuration on the affected pool(s). Today those changes are visible via config history in a few places, but they are not captured as first-class audit events.

This PR emits explicit audit events whenever a pool’s image channel or pinned image version changes (including promotions and rollbacks). These events are designed to be consumable by SecOps/compliance tooling and also useful during incident response/postmortems.

## What’s included
- New audit event type: `fleet.pool.image_config_changed`
- Events emitted on:
  - `image_channel` change (e.g., `candidate` -> `stable`)
  - pinned `image_version` change (e.g., `gpuimg-2025.10.21-1` -> `gpuimg-2025.10.23-2`)
  - explicit “clear pin” operations (pin removed)
- Captured fields:
  - `pool_id`, `region`, `pool_type` (dedicated/shared)
  - `before` + `after` (channel + version)
  - `actor` (service account or user), `actor_type`
  - `reason` (freeform, required for manual changes)
  - `request_id`, `source` (api/automation), and `git_sha` of the control-plane deploy
- Emission is centralized in the pool update pathway (so we don’t miss changes from future callers)
- Guardrails:
  - No per-node identifiers in event payload
  - Size capped + reason truncated (server-side)
  - Event emission is “best effort” but failures are surfaced in metrics and logs

## Why this way
- Compliance needs an immutable record of configuration changes and the identity that performed them.
- Incident response needs to quickly answer: what changed, when, by whom, and what was the intended reason.
- We intentionally avoid logging the entire pool spec to prevent accidental leakage and keep events stable.

## Testing
- Unit tests for:
  - channel-only changes
  - version-only changes
  - channel+version changes
  - no-op updates (no event)
  - actor attribution for service-to-service calls
- Integration test with the audit sink in `dev` using a fake request id.

## Rollout / operational notes
- Event volume expected to be low (pool config changes are infrequent).
- If the audit sink is degraded, pool updates continue; we increment `audit_emit_failures_total{event_type=...}` and log at WARN with request id.
- Follow-up: wire these events into the readiness UI “change history” panel (out of scope for this PR).

Refs: ENG-4826 (image channels), ENG-4822 (readiness state machine control-plane work).
Ethan Park (review): Nice. One request: can we ensure we emit exactly once per update request (even if both channel+version change) so downstream doesn’t have to de-dupe? Also please confirm the event is emitted after the DB transaction commits.
Benji Okafor (author): Updated to emit a single `image_config_changed` event containing both before/after values. Emission now happens post-commit (hooked into the update service return path) and includes the DB commit timestamp used as `event_time`.
Marcus Lin (security review): Please do not include raw request body or arbitrary annotations in the audit payload. Also, require a reason for human-initiated changes; automation can use a fixed reason string. Add size caps to prevent abuse.
Benji Okafor (author): Ack. Payload is now strictly `{pool_id, region, pool_type, before, after, actor, actor_type, reason, request_id, source, git_sha}`. Added `reason` validation: required if `actor_type=user`. Added truncation to 256 chars + rejects control characters.
Vanessa Ortiz (review): This will help a lot. Can we include `image_channel` values normalized (candidate/stable) and add a note about rollbacks? Also add a metric so we can alert if the sink is failing silently during a rollout window.
Benji Okafor (author): Normalization added (enum -> canonical string). Docs call out rollback flows (stable -> candidate + version pin change). Added `audit_emit_failures_total` + `audit_emit_latency_ms` and dashboard hook is tracked separately.
Hanae Suzuki (review): Can we ensure actor attribution works for service-to-service calls from the provisioning orchestrator? I’ve seen `unknown` in a few places.
Benji Okafor (author): Fixed: we now propagate `actor` via request context and default to the mTLS principal when present. Tests cover both user JWT and service principal cases.
Ethan Park (approval): LGTM. Thanks for keeping the emission post-commit and for the no-op guard.
Marcus Lin (approval): LGTM with the caps + reason requirement.
Vanessa Ortiz (approval): Approved. Please ping #eng-infra once merged so we can reference this in the rollout checklist.

payload.body:
Motivation: Tenants with long-standing reserved capacity (committed/contractual reservations) were experiencing abrupt loss of soft-burst credit when admins changed reservation sizes or during autoscaler-driven decommit flows. This caused sudden tail-latency spikes and unhappy downstream SLAs. The goal of this PR is to introduce a backwards-compatible, opt-in "Grandfathered Credit Allocator" that preserves a decaying bucket of credit for legacy reservations and a 'soft revocation' protocol that gracefully drains these credits before hard revocation.

Design summary: The allocator maintains a per-tenant grandfathered_balance which is seeded from the reservation delta when a reservation is reduced or rebalanced. The balance decays on a configurable half-life window (default: 14d) and is eligible for consumption only when primary reservation tokens are exhausted. A soft_revocation handshake (controller -> fleet agent) allows the controller to request a staged revoke; the agent attempts to shed load within a configured grace_period (default: 10m) while emitting progress telemetry. If the tenant cannot shed by the end of grace_period, the controller performs a final hard revocation.

Key properties: (1) Smooth capacity transitions: avoids cliff-like revocations that cause transient QoS failures, (2) Observability: emits new metrics for credit levels, decay_rate, and active_revocations, (3) Autoscaler integration: the allocator signals 'effective_commitment' to autoscaler so scale decisions respect remaining grandfathered credit, (4) Safety: soft revocation is conservative by default and requires explicit opt-in via tenant config or a cluster-wide feature flag.

What this PR includes: implementation of the Grandfathered Credit Allocator, the soft revocation protocol handshake, autoscaler hooks to read effective_commitment, telemetry/metrics registration, unit + integration tests, ops docs and a small migration script to backfill existing reservation deltas for tenants that opt into the new policy.

Commits (high-level): - Add design doc for grandfathering and protocol (docs/ops/grandfathering.md) - Implement allocator core and REST/GRPC endpoints (services/fleet/allocator.go) - Integrate soft revocation handshake in reconciler (controller/autoscaler.go) - Metrics: register grandfathered_credit_* gauges and revocation_histogram (observability/metrics_registry.go) - Add unit and integration tests for decay and graceful revoke (services/fleet/allocator_test.go) - Add Helm config toggles and default parameters (charts/redwood-helm/templates/configmap.yaml)

Files changed (high level): services/fleet/allocator.go (core logic), services/fleet/allocator_test.go (tests and synthetic load harness), controller/autoscaler.go (autoscaler reads effective_commitment), observability/metrics_registry.go (new metrics and tags), docs/ops/grandfathering.md (design + ops runbook), charts/redwood-helm/templates/configmap.yaml (feature flag and tunables), scripts/migrations/backfill_grandfathered.py (migration helper).

Testing and results: - Unit tests cover decay math and edgecases for zero-length windows and negative deltas. - Integration tests simulate reservation shrink events and assert that soft revocation reduces burst-sourced requests over the configured grace_period. - Local load tests (10k QPS synthetic tenants) show reduced 99p latency spikes during reservation changes: median 99p drop from 420ms -> 140ms under a staged revoke with grandfathering enabled.

Rollout plan: 1) Merge behind a feature flag (disabled by default), 2) Canary enable for internal test tenants, 3) Ramp to customers that opt-in via tenant config within 2 weeks, 4) Monitor metrics for unexpected revocations and adjust decay window. Ops doc includes rollback steps and a script to remove grandfathered balances if needed.

Backward compatibility and safety: Feature is opt-in; default behavior unchanged. There is a config knob to set decay window and grace periods cluster-wide. All new metrics have sane cardinality (per-tenant tag only when balance > 0).

Related work and tickets: ENG-5618 (design), ENG-5640 (autoscaler hook), SUP-9082 (customer impact case motivating soft revocation).
Ethan Caldwell: Please avoid exposing per-request locking on the allocator; the test harness showed a contention point at high QPS. Consider sharding by tenant hash and use lock-free atomic updates where possible.
Maya Patel: Addressed in f2b3c4d — switched to a sharded ring buffer + atomic updates and added contention test. PTAL.

Maya Patel: Added histogram and gauge soft_revocation_progress in observability registry; added to the canary dashboard screenshots in the ops doc.

Maya Patel: Fixed tests to inject deterministic clock source; reran CI.

Config knobs exposed via Helm: grandfathering.enabled, grandfathering.decay_half_life, grandfathering.grace_period. Opt-in only; no default behavioral change.

payload.body:
Adds a thresholded descriptor-based eviction policy plus an optional background slotted defragger to reduce memory fragmentation and paging in the KV cache. Defaults are conservative (feature gated) and rollout plan described in PR body.
Summary: Implements a low-latency eviction policy that uses per-descriptor write/read watermarks to preferentially evict whole logical descriptors (buckets of entries) when memory pressure crosses configurable thresholds, combined with a low-priority background slotted defragger that coalesces small free regions into page-sized spans to reduce spillover and paging churn. Motivation: recent load patterns show long-tailed fragment distributions where small stale fragments prevent allocation of contiguous pages, causing frequent spillovers under bursty workloads. This leads to higher latency and cost as the runtime spills working sets to disk or GPU host memory. Goals: 1) reduce reactive spill frequency by reclaiming contiguous regions proactively, 2) keep eviction decisions aligned to descriptor locality so hot descriptors avoid thrash, 3) be safe for multi-tenant workloads and compatible with Dedicated/Private deployments. Design highlights: - Thresholded Descriptor Evictor: tracks per-descriptor metrics (last_access_ms, resident_bytes, fetch_count) in a lightweight ring and computes a dynamic eviction priority that combines an LRU-ish recency factor with a size-awareness term. When global free memory falls below watermark_low, the evictor enters a sampling mode and marks candidate descriptors; when below watermark_critical it drains marked descriptors until free memory meets target. - Slotted Defragger: background worker that scans free region lists and maintains a small fixed set of "slots" (bucketed by size class). It attempts atomic coalesces of adjacent free extents inside a tenant's arena to form page-aligned spans. Coalescing is performed opportunistically and yields to latency-sensitive threads; it can be throttled by a per-tenant CPU budget and backpressure signals from scheduler. - Paging/backpressure interplay: introduces a backpressure token emitted when spill queues exceed configurable depth; when backpressure is active the evictor temporarily raises the low watermark threshold and increases aggressive coalesce budget to avoid repeated spills. - Safety and correctness: uses existing arena locks and adds a defrag reservation handshake to avoid races with concurrent writes and KV promotions. There is a fast-path where single-entry evictions still proceed without defrag reservations to preserve tail latency. Checklist: - [x] Implement eviction policy and descriptor metadata store - [x] Add slotted defragger worker and size-slot bookkeeping - [x] Integrate backpressure signals into evictor heuristics - [x] Unit tests for descriptor selection, slot coalescing, and reservation handshake - [x] Integration tests simulating bursty tail loads and multi-tenant fairness - [x] Perf tests: microbench against synthetic fragmentation workloads - [x] Feature gate + runtime config knobs and docs - [x] Rollout plan (canary + staged ramp) Testing notes: microbench shows 28-36% reduction in spill operations on synthetic workloads with 60-80% fragmentation and similar token throughput. P99 latency under burst load improved ~12–18ms for small reads due to reduced IO on spill path. Compatibility: default off for Hosted customers until validation; enabled behind a runtime flag for Dedicated and Private during initial rollout. Rollout: canary in staging for 48 hours, small percentage canary on Dedicated cluster for 1 week, broader ramp subject to metrics. Related: ENG-1428 (fragmentation incident follow-up), ENG-1499 (kv arena diagnostics), SUP-4021 (customer report of frequent spills). Implementation notes: - Memory accounting uses existing resident_bytes fields and adds descriptor-level counters persisted to in-memory metadata only (no on-disk format changes). - Defragger uses a best-effort transactional coalesce: if a coalesce fails due to racing allocation, the worker drops the attempt and requeues the smaller slot. - Evictor sampling uses an epoch tick to keep cost O(1) per allocation. - Feature gate: redwood.cfg.runtime.kv.descriptor_eviction.enabled = false by default. Observability: new metrics added: kv.evictions.descriptor_count, kv.defrag.coalesce_attempts, kv.defrag.coalesce_success, kv.backpressure.active_seconds, kv.evictions.by_watermark. Also added two new tracing spans: KV:DescriptorEvict and KV:SlotCoalesce. Security/permissions: no new surface area; defragger runs under existing tenant arena permissions. Rollback: feature can be disabled via runtime flag and reverted with a fast rollout script included in this PR.
Miguel Santos: Can you walk through why descriptor-level eviction is better than entry-level LRU for our long-tail fragment case? Author: Descriptor grouping reduces allocator fragmentation pressure by freeing contiguous sets of entries that share physical locality; this trades coarser eviction granularity for fewer spill events.
Rina Cho: Defragger and eviction both touch arena metadata; any risk of deadlock? Author: We use a strict ordering convention (evictor -> reservation -> allocator) and the defragger uses try-lock with backoff, so deadlocks are prevented. Added unit tests that intentionally create contention paths.
Evan Murray: How did you tune the watermark thresholds? Author: Initial defaults derived from historical telemetry (75th/95th memory percentiles). Exposed knobs for percentiles and absolute bytes in runtime flags; recommend canary tuning per workload.
payload.title: Thresholded Descriptor Evictor and Slotted Defragger for KV Cache

payload.body:
Motivation: Several customers and internal SDKs are still emitting the legacy tool-call envelope (v1) while the new schema (v2) for streaming/tool-calls has been rolled out. This mismatch leads to two classes of instability: (1) streaming parser errors during tool/function call handoffs, and (2) partial structured-output fragments that leak into downstream tool orchestration. This PR adds an interim coercion layer in the API gateway/runtime that detects client-declared schema preferences, validates incoming streaming frames, and rewrites v1 tool envelopes into the v2 canonical shape at the stream boundary. The coercion is conservative and reversible: we inject a small per-request flag into request metadata (schema_coercion_applied) and emit telemetry when we rewrite frames. The middleware supports three modes: passthrough (no rewrite), permissive-coerce (rewrite v1->v2 and allow both response modes), and strict (reject unexpected envelopes). Default rollout: permissive-coerce behind the feature flag feature/schema-coercion-v1 with opt-out via the X-Redwood-Prefer-Schema header. Implementation details: - Negotiation: the middleware checks X-Redwood-Prefer-Schema and Accept-Schema headers, then consults the request's declared content-type. If client requests v2 explicitly, we do not coerce. - Streaming rewriter: a small streaming-state machine that transforms v1 tool-call open events into v2 tool_call.start frames, lifts argument envelopes into v2-typed 'args' fields, and ensures chunked structured outputs are framed as complete JSON tokens before forwarding to the model runtime. The rewriter supports partial-kv caching to avoid reserializing large arguments. - Tool-call fallback: for tool invocations where the model returns tool call frames in v1, we translate them to v2 for internal routing; when routing to legacy tool runners that only accept v1 we convert back at the tool adapter boundary. - Telemetry & tracing: new counters schema_negotiation.rewrites, schema_negotiation.rejections and per-route timing metrics added to the console. We emit a deprecation warning header (X-Redwood-Schema-Deprecation) when we detect v1 clients to drive SDK updates. Tests & rollout: unit and integration tests cover streaming reassembly, partial argument buffering, and back-to-back tool-calls. Canary deployment in us-west-2 for 24 hours, followed by region-by-region ramp controlled by the feature flag. Monitoring dashboards added and alerts created for rewrite error rate > 0.1% or client-perceived latency regression > 20ms. Backwards compatibility: users can opt into strict mode via feature flag to force schema errors. The middleware is temporary and will be removed after the v1 sunset window (communication via deprecation header + Linear/Jira). See below for changed files, commit summaries, and review notes.
Adds a runtime-coercion middleware that safely rewrites streaming tool-call envelopes from legacy v1 schema to v2 shaped envelopes, gated behind a feature flag. No user-visible breaking changes expected; opt-out via X-Redwood-Prefer-Schema header.
Liam O'Connor: This direction looks good, but the streaming state machine needs clearer invariants around partial JSON chunks — can you add assertions to ensure we don't emit malformed tokens?
Maya Patel (author): Added buffer invariants and unit tests that assert that partial frames never reach the router. Also added a safety timeout for in-flight partial arguments to avoid forever-waiting streams.
Rina Gupta: Please clarify how this interacts with KV cache eviction and token accounting — if we rewrite frames, do we double-count tokens?
Maya Patel: We only rewrite envelope metadata; token accounting occurs post-rewrite against the normalized payloads. Added metric schema_negotiation.token_delta to track any accounting delta and a test that ensures delta==0 for rewrite paths.
Sophie Keller: Suggest adding a tight canary (5% requests) in addition to region canary so we can verify SDK ecosystems before global rollout.
Maya Patel: Updated rollout plan to include 5% canary via the feature flag and added console chart for canary-specific rewrite rates.
payload.title: Introduce interim schema coercion layer for tool-streaming backward compatibility

payload.body:
Context: Experimental rollouts (canaries, A/B tests, shadow lanes) currently rely on static alerting and manual judgment to abort or roll back. That delays remediation and increases blast radius when subtle regressions (quality drift, distribution shift, latency tail) are only visible in aggregate telemetry.

Motivation: Provide a lightweight, explainable advisor that continuously scores running experiments using multi-signal telemetry windows and recommends safe aborts or automatic quarantines. The advisor is conservative by default (suggest-only) and integrates with the rollout controller to optionally trigger automated actions for high-confidence failures.

What this PR delivers: A new rollback advisor component that: 1) ingests existing rollout telemetry (latency, p75/p95/p99, error rates, inference-quality deltas from eval hooks, and custom experiment metrics), 2) computes a composite risk score with signal-aware weights and a tunable decay window, 3) emits recommendations (suggest_abort, warn, ok) with rationale traces and contributing signals, and 4) exposes a lightweight HTTP webhook API for the rollout controller to poll or subscribe.

Design highlights: - Conservative default policy: suggestions are non-authoritative. Auto-abort requires an explicit rollout annotation. - Explainability: Each recommendation includes the top-3 contributing signals and a short human-readable rationale so SREs and PMs can triage. - Debiasing: The scorer applies cohort-balancing heuristics to avoid false positives when traffic slices are small or skewed. - Safeguards: A quorum-based suppression prevents noisy signals from flipping status during transient blips. - Backfill simulator: an offline replay harness (tests/integration) verifies decision stability over historical traffic.

Developer checklist (in-PR): [x] unit tests for scorer logic; [x] end-to-end integration test with a synthetic canary; [x] docs and example config; [x] presubmit CI; [ ] perf microbench (scheduled).

Usage example (rollout annotation snippet):

  rollout:
    name: my-model-exp
    annotations:
      rollback.advisor/redwood-enabled: "true"
      rollback.advisor/auto-abort: "off"  # options: off|manual-approve|auto-on-critical
      rollback.advisor/threshold: "0.72"

(Annotations control whether the rollout controller will apply suggestions automatically.)

Commit summary: - 7a1d2b3: initial rollback advisor module, public interfaces, and HTTP webhook - 9b4c6d0: telemetry scorer implementation (multi-signal, decay windows) - 0f3e8a1: controller integration: poller and lightweight decision cache - d2c4b77: tests: integration harness with synthetic canary replay - f8a9b21: docs and example rollout annotation; tuning notes; CI fixes

Files changed (high level): - controllers/rollback_advisor.go: new controller that coordinates poll/push and decision caching - telemetry/scorer/scorer.go: multi-signal scoring logic and debiasing heuristics - telemetry/metrics_schema.yaml: schema additions for experiment metrics and quality deltas - docs/rollouts/telemetry-rollback-advisor.md: design + tuning guide + FAQ - examples/experiments/ab-safe-quickstart.yaml: example rollout annotation and sample metrics - tests/integration/rollback_advisor_test.go: replay harness and stable-decision assertions - ci/presubmit-checks.yaml: added integration job entry

Small illustrative snippet (scorer config, for reference):

  scorer:
    window: 120s
    signals:
      - name: p95_latency
        weight: 0.35
      - name: error_rate
        weight: 0.4
      - name: quality_delta
        weight: 0.25
    cohort_balance_threshold: 30
    suppression_quorum: 0.6

Testing notes: - Integration harness replays several historical canaries and asserts that the advisor produces the same recommendation for >= 95% of time windows. - We added guardrail tests that simulate small-cohort skew to validate debiasing heuristics. - One flaky test was stabilized by increasing the metric aggregation window; documented in the commit.

Review conversation (summary): - Ethan Patel: "Concerned about false positives when live traffic is highly skewed. Please add a tuning guide and default cohort_balance_threshold." -> Addressed: added docs and changed default to 30. - Sara Nguyen: "How will this interact with existing alerting? Could we get duplicate noise?" -> Reply: advisor emits a separate recommendation stream; we added a mapping example in docs to dedupe with PagerDuty rules and a short-lived label to indicate advisory vs authoritative. - Diego Morales: "Suggest adding an opt-in path for auto-abort tied to customer SLA tiers." -> Added rollout annotation auto-abort modes and documented fallback behavior. - Sara Nguyen (approval): "Reviewed security around webhook auth and decision payloads; looks good. Approving."

CI summary: - unit-tests: pass - integration-tests: initially failed (race in replay harness), rerun -> pass - linters: pass - e2e-smoke: pass - perf-bench: queued (no blocker) Overall ci_status: pass

Operational considerations: - Default behavior is non-disruptive. Customers must opt-in to automated actions. - Telemetry ingestion depends on the existing metrics pipeline; we added conservative retention and a small memory cap for in-memory windows. - We should run this behind a feature flag for the first month to collect operational telemetry (false-positive rate, decision latency).

Merge: Squash merged on 2026-02-22 via GitHub UI by Maya Chen. Release note included below.

Rationale for uniqueness: This PR focuses on explainable, telemetry-led advisory behavior (suggest-only by default) and a small, auditable webhook integration, rather than an all-or-nothing auto-abort system. It aims to reduce human reaction time to degradations while keeping rollouts safe by default.
Ethan Patel: Concerned about false positives with skewed traffic; request for cohort balancing (addressed)
Sara Nguyen: How will this interact with existing alerts? Added dedupe mapping and label guidance
Diego Morales: Request opt-in auto-abort routes for SLA tiers; added annotations and docs
Sara Nguyen: Security review of webhook and payloads looks good - approved
Add a telemetry-driven rollback advisor that suggests safe aborts for experimental rollouts. The advisor is suggest-only by default; auto-abort is gated via rollout annotations. Includes docs, example configs, and an offline replay harness.

Operational impact: opt-in; monitor advisor false-positive rate before enabling auto-abort for production rollouts.
payload.title: Telemetry-driven Rollback Advisor for Experimental Rollouts

Motivation: Production streaming workloads occasionally need to resume long-lived streams after transient disconnects without replaying the entire conversation. This PR implements a lightweight resumable/checkpoint hinting protocol (session-checkpoint v0.1) and exposes ergonomic helpers in all three SDKs so product teams can opt-in with minimal code changes. Summary of changes: 1) Protocol: introduce an optional 'X-Session-Checkpoint' header and resumable token semantics returned on streaming completion (response metadata). Server will emit stable checkpoint tokens that encode minimal KV cursor + prefix hash; clients can pass checkpoint token on a new stream to resume from that point where supported. 2) SDK surface: Python: add AsyncResumeableStream and helper resume_from_checkpoint(checkpoint: str) on StreamingClient; TypeScript: augment createStream({ resumeToken?: string }) and add generator helper stream.resumeWith(token); Go: introduce ReaderWithCheckpoint and streaming.ResumeFrom(token string) convenience wrapper. 3) Retries/backoff: align retry windows when resuming so clients don't double-retry content; introduce 'jitter_scale' in retry presets and expose opt-in PWM (progress-weighted multiplier) so resumption retries favor shorter windows for resumption flows. 4) Ergonomics/parity: ensure all three SDKs provide an idiomatic way to accept a checkpoint token and return one on normal completion or explicit checkpoint() call. 5) Docs & examples: cross-SDK quickstarts and a migration guide. Commits (high level): - Add protocol docs + OpenAPI extension for X-Session-Checkpoint header - Implement server side checkpoint generator and validation (small shim) - Add Python AsyncResumeableStream + unit tests - Add TS generator helpers + typed resumeToken types + e2e test - Add Go ReaderWithCheckpoint and examples + integration test - Add retry presets and jitter_scale implementation for client-side resume flow - Update changelogs and quickstart examples - Add CI job to run tri-sdk resume e2e matrix Changed files (high level): server/api/streaming_spec.yaml, server/handlers/checkpoint.go, sdk/python/redwood/streaming.py, sdk/python/tests/test_resume.py, sdk/typescript/src/stream.ts, sdk/typescript/tests/resume.spec.ts, sdk/go/stream_resume.go, docs/guides/resumable_streams.md, examples/multi-sdk/resume_quickstart.md, changelogs/py-0.19.0.md, changelogs/ts-1.30.0.md, changelogs/go-1.9.0.md. Testing notes: added targeted unit tests in each SDK and a small end-to-end CI matrix that spins a local handler-sim (lightweight checkpoint mock) and validates resume semantics under network jitter. CI initially failed on a flaky TS e2e due to an intermittent timing assumption; fixed by switching to a polling-based resume readiness probe and re-ran. Backwards compatibility: The transport change is opt-in — servers only emit X-Session-Checkpoint when checkpointing enabled; old clients ignore unknown headers. Clients that want resume must explicitly opt-in via the new helper surfaces. Rollout: feature-flagged on server side; SDK helpers are behind minor versions and documented. Migration: minimal — example included for each SDK. Usage examples (short): Python: stream = client.stream(...); cp = stream.checkpoint(); resumed = client.resume_from_checkpoint(cp) TypeScript: const stream = client.createStream(); const cp = await stream.checkpoint(); await client.createStream({resumeToken: cp}) Go: r := sdk.NewResumeReader(...); token := r.Checkpoint(); resumed, _ := sdk.ResumeFrom(token) Security notes: checkpoint tokens are opaque signed blobs (HMAC) - servers validate; no user data returned in token. Release bumps: python 0.19.0, typescript 1.30.0, go 1.9.0. Links: Linear ENG-2109 for protocol design; SUP-1123 incident that motivated resumption.
Marco Li: Nice, this addresses the SUP-1123 replay storm risk. Two requests: ensure we document expected size/entropy of tokens and add a defensive server-side TTL for tokens.
Aisha Patel (author): Added token TTL enforcement on server (checkpoint.go) and a short section in docs about size/entropy. Tokens are HMAC-signed 48 bytes base64 by default.
Dana Roberts: TS helper API looks good; one nit: prefer resumeToken over token in parameter names for discoverability. Also, can we expose a 'resumeable' boolean on the stream object for feature gating in client code?
Aisha Patel (author): Renamed parameter to resumeToken and added stream.resumeable boolean on TS/py/go stream objects. Update tests accordingly.
Evan Kim: Tests look solid. Suggest adding a test for retry/jitter behavior when resume is used in hot paths — otherwise approving.
Aisha Patel (author): Added resume-specific retry test with jitter_scale=0.6 to the e2e matrix as requested.
Dana Roberts (approval): Approved-by Dana Roberts
Marco Li (approval): Approved-by Marco Li
Introduce optional resumable streaming via session checkpoints. SDKs: Python 0.19.0, TypeScript 1.30.0, Go 1.9.0 provide ergonomic helpers to create, checkpoint, and resume streams. Opt-in feature; see docs/guides/resumable_streams.md for migration steps and security considerations.
payload.title: introduce resumable checkpoint streaming protocol and ergonomic SDK helpers across py/ts/go

Context: As part of the Runtime LTS initiative, we need a low-risk, repeatable way to apply small, curated fixes from mainline onto an LTS release branch (e.g. runtime-1.18-lts) while keeping diffs minimal and auditability high. Today, backports are a mostly-manual process (cherry-pick locally, resolve conflicts, open PR, remember labels/notes), which has already caused missed steps in branch-cut dry runs and slowed down response for Sev1/Sec fixes. This PR introduces a helper script to automate: (1) selecting commits/PRs to backport, (2) cherry-picking onto an LTS branch, (3) detecting conflicts early, and (4) opening a backport PR with an LTS-specific template and required metadata. What’s included: - New script tools/release/lts_backport.py (Python) that wraps git + gh (GitHub CLI) to create an LTS backport PR. - Conflict detection: script attempts a clean cherry-pick in a throwaway worktree; if conflicts occur, it aborts and prints the conflicting files/hunks and the exact commands to reproduce locally. It also supports an optional --allow-conflicts mode for cases where we still want a WIP PR for visibility, but defaults to fail-fast. - PR creation with template: opens a PR against a configurable LTS base branch, with a standardized title, body sections (Risk, Test Plan, Perf Gate, Rollback Notes, Compatibility), and checkboxes aligned with LTS change management. - Labels + reviewers: applies labels (lts/backport, runtime, security when requested) and requests review from a default reviewer set configurable in .github/lts-backport.yml; also supports overrides via flags. - Provenance metadata: includes original PR number, original merge commit SHA, and cherry-pick commit SHAs in the PR body, plus a machine-readable footer so the release notes generator can later associate backport PRs with the upstream PR. - Safety rails: refuses to run with a dirty working tree; refuses to backport merge commits by default (can be overridden with --allow-merge-commit); validates that the target LTS branch exists on origin; ensures the created branch name is unique and deterministic. Usage examples: - Backport by upstream PR: python tools/release/lts_backport.py --lts-branch runtime-1.18-lts --pr 23341 - Backport by commit SHA: python tools/release/lts_backport.py --lts-branch runtime-1.18-lts --sha 7a1c9f0d - Security hotfix (adds security label + tighter template language): python tools/release/lts_backport.py --lts-branch runtime-1.18-lts --pr 23425 --security Notes on naming and semantics: - Backport branches are created as backport/runtime-1.18-lts/<upstream_ref>-<shortsha> (ex: backport/runtime-1.18-lts/pr-23341-7a1c9f0d). - PR title defaults to: [LTS runtime-1.18-lts] Backport <upstream_ref>: <upstream title> - PR body includes a ‘Backport Metadata’ footer used by tooling; please do not edit that section manually. Non-goals: This script does not decide backport eligibility; it’s an execution tool only. The rubric/approvals remain in the LTS policy docs and enforced in review + CI gates. It also does not attempt to auto-resolve conflicts. Follow-ups: - ENG-4824 will wire this into release-manager checklists and CI workflows. - ENG-4826 will ingest the backport metadata footer when generating LTS release notes. - We should consider adding a ‘dry-run’ mode that skips branch push/PR creation once we finalize the template language with Product/Support.
Connor O’Brien (Release Eng): The direction is right. Two asks before merge: (1) default reviewers should include at least one Runtime lead + Release Eng lead, and (2) the PR body should include a dedicated section for perf validation (even if it’s ‘N/A’), since perf regressions are a hard blocker for enterprise. Devon Price (author): Updated .github/lts-backport.yml defaults to include Connor + Samir; added a ‘Perf gate’ section to the template with required link or explicit ‘not run’ justification. Sahana Iyer (CI/Build): Please don’t rely on a globally-installed gh; our release containers have it but some dev laptops don’t. Can we emit a clearer error + install instructions? Also can we avoid requiring write access if someone just wants conflict detection? Devon Price: Added preflight checks: if gh is missing, we print a single-line install hint and exit non-zero. Added --local-only mode that runs the worktree cherry-pick + conflict detection without pushing or opening a PR. Samir Qureshi (Runtime): The ‘refuse merge commits’ default is good. Can we also block ‘cherry-pick a PR merge commit’ by default (those often pull in extra unrelated commits)? Devon Price: Script now resolves PR -> merge commit -> first parent by default; you can override with --use-merge-commit. Also prints the upstream commit list in the PR body so reviewers can sanity check scope. Kira Volkov (tooling): Minor: branch name can exceed Git ref limits if upstream title is used. Looks like you’re only using pr-number/sha; good. Please add unit test for branch naming collisions. Devon Price: Added test case for deterministic suffix and collision retry (adds -2, -3...). Connor O’Brien: Looks good; approved. CI note: first run failed due to missing mypy stubs in the test image; rerun after pinning types-requests in dev requirements passed.
Internal tooling: add lts_backport helper script to standardize cherry-picks and backport PR creation for runtime LTS branches.
payload.title: Release Eng: add cherry-pick helper for LTS backports (conflict detection + PR templates)

Motivation: production workloads observed sustained spill-to-disk cascades under multi-tenant pressure where coarse-grained residency accounting caused over-aggressive eviction of hot fragments and erratic IO bursts. This PR implements three complementary mechanisms to reduce fragmentation, stabilize spill behavior, and give operators deterministic controls: 1) a compact in-memory shadow map that tracks sub-page fragment occupancy and recent access weights (approx 64B entries, low overhead) to enable fragmentation-aware victim selection; 2) tenant pinning primitives that allow the scheduler/allocator to mark a small working set as non-evictable for a configured window (used by Dedicated customers to protect latency-critical tenants); 3) a spillback rate limiter that gates asynchronous spill tasks based on adaptive IO telemetry and global in-flight spill budget to prevent burst saturation and cascading memory pressure. Design summary: shadow map is a separate contiguous region co-located with the KV slab metadata; entries are bloom-augmented to bound memory and maintain per-fragment age/weight counters for fast scoring. Eviction integrates shadow map scores with existing recency counters and tenant priority to produce a composite eviction score. Tenant pinning is exposed via runtime flag and API: tenant_pinning.window_ms and tenant_pinning.max_keys, and is enforced by treating pinned keys as immovable until either the window expires or an explicit unpin call. The spillback rate limiter uses a token-bucket shaped by two signals: measured disk latency tail and total async spill queue depth; when the bucket is exhausted new spill tasks are delayed or coalesced into prioritized writes. Implementation notes: - runtime/kv/shadow_map.{rs,mod} implements the compact table, concurrent-safe bumping, and eviction scoring helpers. - runtime/kv/evictor.rs updated to consult shadow_map.score_for(fragment_id) and tenant_pinning.is_pinned(key) during selection. - spillback controller sits in runtime/kv/spillback_controller.rs and exports metrics exposed to Console: kv.spill.rate_limiter.allowed_tokens, kv.spill.backpressure_events. - compaction worker now supports tenant-aware micro-compaction windows to reduce in-place copying latency. Testing and benchmarks: microbench harness shows p95 latency for small-chat workload reduced by 12% (tail improvements by 18%) under mixed-tenant load; sustained background IO dropped 37% in synthetic hotspot test; fragmentation score (internal metric) improved 23% after an hour of churn; throughput (+write QPS) improved ~9% when using tenant pinning for a 1% protected working set. CI: unit + integration + benchmark CI were run; a flaky race in the initial spillback controller was fixed (race around async cancellation). Rollout and feature flags: guarded behind feature flag kv.shadow_map.enabled and kv.spillback.rate_limiter. Default off for existing Dedicated clusters; opt-in via feature-flags yaml or runtime config. Rollout plan: 1) enable in staging with monitoring dashboards added (kv.spill.* metrics); 2) enable for small subset of Dedicated tenants for 24h; 3) gradual ramp with 2x monitoring cadence for first 72h. Observability: new dashboards and alerts added for sustained backpressure events and spike in kv.evictor.score_mismatch. Migration and upgrade: on upgrade the shadow map region is initialized lazily; no data format migration required. Risk and mitigations: tenant pinning can reduce overall memory elasticity — documented and default conservative limits applied; spillback limiter might delay background cleanup leading to short-term higher memory usage — mitigated by compaction windows and operator quotas. Related work: builds on insights from ENG-1623 (fragment-aware reclaim) and ENG-1870 (spill smoothing).
Ethan Cole: Can you quantify the memory overhead of the shadow map at 1M fragments? Requesting numbers to justify defaults.
Marina Liu: Shadow map uses ~64MB per 1M fragment entries with the default bloom sizing; added numbers to docs and unit tests to validate memory claim.
Priya Natarajan: Need a safety valve for tenant pinning in low-memory scenarios (global forced-unpin).
Marina Liu: Added a global forced_unpin_threshold and a graceful eviction path that logs an audit event; documented behavior.
Liam O'Connor: Observed a CI flake on Windows runner; looks like filesystem latency assumptions in benchmark harness.
Marina Liu: Reworked benchmark to use synthetic latency injection and exempt Windows-specific path; reran benchmarks.
Ethan Cole: Approve after addressing race fixes and adding an integration test for spillback backpressure under heavy IO.
Priya Natarajan: Approved - verified dashboards and alert thresholds in staging dashboard draft.
Introduce a fragmentation-aware shadow map, tenant pinning primitives, and a spillback rate limiter to stabilize KV cache behaviour under multi-tenant load. Default: feature disabled; opt-in via kv.shadow_map.enabled and kv.spillback.rate_limiter. Recommended for Dedicated deployments with observed churn/IO pressure.
Feature requires console dashboards: kv.spill.rate_limiter.allowed_tokens, kv.spill.backpressure_events, kv.evictor.composite_score. Conservative defaults are applied; monitor memory headroom and backpressure events when enabling. To force-disable at runtime set kv.spillback.rate_limiter.enabled=false and trigger a graceful drain.
Added global forced_unpin_threshold and an emergency unpin API. Compaction workers run at lower priority when backpressure is high. All features guarded by runtime flags and can be rolled back without offline data migration.
payload.title: introduce-kv-shadow-map-tenant-pinning-and-spillback-rate-limiter

Summary: Enforces RBAC for Usage Insights cost views and export flows, adds a workspace-level setting to hide cost data, and emits audit log events for export generation/download and share-link access. This is a prerequisite for enabling the Usage Insights beta for enterprise workspaces with stricter governance.

Context / motivation: Usage Insights introduces cost/usage breakdowns by route+model and a CSV export path. Security review flagged two gaps: (1) existing "usage" permissions were sufficient to view token counts but not appropriate for cost visibility, and (2) export/download actions were not consistently audited. We also need a workspace admin control to disable cost visibility in restricted workspaces while still allowing non-cost usage metrics.

What changed:
- RBAC: Introduced a dedicated permission gate for cost visibility and export actions.
  - New permission: cost.read (for cost columns/fields, totals, currency display).
  - New permission: cost.export (for creating export jobs, retrieving signed URLs).
  - Existing usage.read continues to allow non-cost usage metrics where applicable.
- Workspace setting: Added workspace_settings.hide_cost (default false).
  - If hide_cost=true, server returns cost fields as null/omitted and the UI should render "Cost hidden by workspace admin" messaging (UI wiring is in a separate PR).
  - hide_cost does not block non-cost usage views (tokens, request counts), but does block exports that include cost columns.
- Endpoint enforcement:
  - usage-insights query endpoints now require usage.read.
  - Any response including monetary cost requires cost.read AND hide_cost=false.
  - Export endpoints require cost.export AND hide_cost=false.
- Audit logging:
  - Added audit events:
    - usage_insights.export_job_created
    - usage_insights.export_downloaded
    - usage_insights.share_link_viewed (when report links are accessed)
  - Audit payload includes actor_id, workspace_id, project_id (when present), time_range, filters (route/model), export_format, row_count (when available), and client_ip/user_agent.
  - Added fields requested in INT-9140 (download URL redaction + export_job_id correlation).
- Error handling / semantics:
  - 403 for missing permissions (with explicit "required_permission" in error metadata).
  - 412 when workspace setting hide_cost=true and caller requests cost data/export.
  - Ensures consistent behavior across REST and internal RPC adapters.

Security review notes (Marcus/Kevin):
- We intentionally do NOT log raw query strings or prompt content in audit payloads.
- Filter values are constrained to normalized route templates and model identifiers (already normalized/bucketed upstream).
- Signed download URLs are never stored in audit logs; we log export_job_id and a short-lived download token hash.
- Retention: audit events follow existing audit log retention policy; export artifacts follow export retention policy (handled in export service).

Testing:
- Unit tests for RBAC evaluator (permission matrix across roles: Workspace Admin, Billing Admin, Developer, Viewer).
- Integration tests for /usage-insights/* endpoints verifying 403/412 behaviors and field redaction.
- Added golden tests for audit event payload shape (ensures INT-9140 fields stay present).

Rollout notes:
- This is gated behind the existing feature flag for Usage Insights beta; enforcement is server-side and safe to enable before UI changes.
- Follow-up: Console UI will hide cost columns and disable Export CTA based on new "cost_visibility" capability field (tracked in ENG-3820 subtask).

Screenshots: N/A (backend-only).

Risk / mitigations:
- Risk: Some customers rely on existing "usage" roles to see cost in older billing views. Mitigation: cost.read is only applied to Usage Insights endpoints; existing billing pages are unchanged.
- Risk: Export clients may see new 412 errors when hide_cost is enabled. Mitigation: error message includes actionable guidance (admin setting + required permission).
authz: add cost.read and cost.export permissions + role bindings
usage-insights: enforce RBAC and workspace hide_cost gate in query handlers
exports: block job creation when hide_cost is enabled; add required_permission errors
audit: emit export_job_created/export_downloaded/share_link_viewed events with INT-9140 fields
tests: permission matrix + endpoint integration coverage
Marcus Lin: Can we ensure audit logs don’t include raw route strings that might contain IDs? I only want normalized templates in logs.
Kaitlyn Nguyen (author): Yep. Audit payload uses the normalized route_template from the request filter (same canonicalization used for aggregation). Added a guard to reject untemplated paths at the API layer.
Kevin Osei: INT-9140 asked for correlating download events without logging the signed URL. Can we include export_job_id + a stable download token hash?
Kaitlyn Nguyen (author): Added export_job_id everywhere and a sha256(download_token) field. Signed URL is never logged. Updated golden tests to prevent regression.
Ethan Park: Why 412 vs 403 when hide_cost is enabled?
Kaitlyn Nguyen (author): 403 is for missing permissions; 412 is for a workspace precondition (admin policy). This helps support triage and makes it clearer that granting a role alone won’t fix it.
Chloe Martin: Please ensure cost fields are consistently omitted/null so clients don’t misinterpret zeros.
Kaitlyn Nguyen (author): Implemented explicit nulls and removed defaulting to 0. Added integration tests verifying no cost totals returned when gated.
Dylan Brooks: Any impact on existing billing endpoints?
Kaitlyn Nguyen (author): No. Enforcement is only applied to the new Usage Insights endpoints and export routes.
Marcus Lin: Approved after the audit payload update + test coverage.
Ethan Park: Approved.
payload.title: RBAC gating for cost views + CSV export; add audit log events

Context and motivation: Customers reported two recurring issues during canary rollouts: (1) when a canary triggered a rollback, long-lived sessions lost affinity and experienced elevated error rates during the failback window; (2) shadow traffic replay tools could not deterministically reproduce the failing path because session-dependent inputs were lost at promotion time. This PR implements an automated recovery flow that (a) preserves per-session routing affinity across rollbacks, and (b) records/replays 'shadow anchors' — compact session keys and prefix traces — so post-mortem and automated regression checks can replay the exact request context.

Summary of changes: Implement a RolloutRecovery controller that tracks a sticky_session_map for affected cohorts, extends the shadow-capture pipeline to emit lightweight anchors, and adds a replay-based rollback verifier that uses anchors to validate that the rollback candidate matches production failure signals. Changes are backward compatible: when sticky sessions are not enabled for a route, the controller is a no-op.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-4512)
- [x] Unit + integration tests for controller logic
- [x] E2E smoke test in perf-canary lab
- [x] Telemetry: added metrics for anchor hit/miss and session-preserve success
- [x] Rolling upgrade strategy for controller state (no single-point blocking restart)

Commits (high level):
- feat(recovery): add RolloutRecovery controller and APIs (authoritative state machine + reconciliation loop)
- feat(shadow): emit shadow_anchor tokens with session prefixes in capture pipeline
- feat(router): extend router to consult sticky_session_map on promote/rollback paths
- test: add unit tests for anchor serializer and replay verifier
- infra: add small migration to persist sticky_session_map in cluster-backed shard

Files changed (high level):
- services/rollout/controller/recovery_controller.go (core reconciliation logic; 280 LOC)
- services/router/session_affinity.go (session mapping helpers; 60 LOC)
- services/shadow/capture_pipeline.go (anchor emission; 48 LOC)
- pkg/telemetry/metrics.go (new counters: anchor_emitted, anchor_hit, session_preserve_success)
- deployments/migrations/20241010_sticky_session_map.sql (small migration)
- test/rollout/recovery_test.go (integration scenarios)
- docs/rollouts/sticky-session.md (how to enable + safety notes)

Design notes and safety guards (in-line in code):
- Sticky session map is scoped by cohort ID and has TTL eviction; entries are not a persistent user-facing privacy artifact (anchors are hashed with per-tenant salt).
- Anchors are minimized payloads (session prefix + stable-hash of request context) to avoid PII and reduce bandwidth for replay.
- Replay verifier runs on dedicated canary nodes with CPU-limited replay workers to avoid noisy-neighbor effects.
- Rollback only proceeds automatically if replay verifier confirms >95% alignment with observed failure signals OR operator-approved fast rollback is enabled.

Review conversation (summary):
- Diego Alvarez: asked for clarity on consistency model for sticky_session_map during control-plane failover. Author response: added migration to shard map and added reconciliation idempotency checks; noted that ephemeral inconsistencies are tolerated by using TTL and client-side retry.
- Priya Patel: requested privacy audit for anchor payloads. Author response: anchors are salted+hashed per-tenant; added test vectors and a small note in docs/rollouts/sticky-session.md.
- Jonas Müller: flagged potential perf regression for high-QPS routes. Author response: added adaptive sampling in capture pipeline (default 1% for high QPS) and documented policy in README. Jonas approved after perf numbers from perf-canary lab showed median p99 diff < 2ms.

CI and checks:
- unit-tests: passed (202s)
- integration-tests (rollout suite): passed (8m)
- lint: passed
- security-scan (Snyk): passed (no new high severity findings)
- perf-canary (internal): baseline run passed; measured anchor emit path with 1% sampling, CPU increase <1%.

Manual validation performed:
- Deployed feature branch to perf-canary environment with a synthetic cohort that simulates long-lived sessions and deliberate regressions.
- Triggered a canary that fails on a session-scoped bug; validated that (1) sessions remained pinned to fallback model, (2) anchors were recorded and used by the replay verifier, (3) automated rollback proceeded after replay alignment threshold was satisfied.

Backward compatibility and upgrade path:
- Controller can be deployed incrementally: when older routers that do not understand anchors receive traffic, anchors are ignored and no behavior change occurs. Migration writes a shard entry that is optional; controllers reconcile if present.

Operational runbook excerpt (docs/rollouts/sticky-session.md):
- When a canary fails but rollback verifier reports low alignment (<40%), open an incident and consider operator replay with extended anchor window.
- TTL for sticky_session_map defaults to 24h and can be tuned per-route.
- Anchor sampling rate defaults to 1% for routes with >10k RPS, 5% otherwise.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main on 2024-10-17 by Maya Chen after two approvals. CI green on final run. Post-merge actions: rolling deployment to canary fleet staged over 2 hours, perf monitoring dashboard added to Redwood Console under 'Rollouts / Sticky Session Recovery'.

Notes / follow-ups:
- Future: expose replay-based alignment score via API so customers can query rollback confidence per-deployment.
- Future: investigate integrating anchor replay into eval-harness for deterministic regression tests.

Diego Alvarez: please document consistency guarantees during control-plane failover and add idempotency to reconciliation. (addressed)
Priya Patel: ensure anchors don't leak PII; add salt+hash and tests. (addressed)
Jonas Müller: measure perf impact on high-QPS routes and add adaptive sampling. (addressed, perf numbers attached)
QA Lead (automated): integration scenario passed in perf-canary lab.
payload.title: Automated Rollout Recovery with Sticky-Session Preservation and Shadow Replay Anchors

payload.body:
Fixes partial-JSON emit/resume behavior in SSE streams by adding idempotent span anchors, offset correction headers for resumed connections, and a lightweight checksum header. Improves tool/function-call handoffs and structured-output recovery for mid-stream truncation. Backwards compatible with openai-compat mode.
Context: We saw several customer-facing incidents where resumed or retried SSE connections could emit duplicate or truncated structured-output events (function calls / JSON objects) due to out-of-band chunk reassembly and stale KV cache offsets. This PR introduces an idempotent span anchor and an offset-correction header to make resume/reconnect behavior deterministic. Design highlights: 1) Span anchors: every emitted logical span (a contiguous series of SSE events that together form a structured JSON or a function-call handoff) is tagged with an opaque span-id and an incremental span-seq for ordering. Anchors are emitted at the head and tail of spans as sentinel events (comment-prefixed SSE lines) so receivers can detect incomplete spans and avoid double-apply on resume. 2) Offset-correction header: when a client reconnects with a resume token we now include a small offset-correction header (checksum-lite + last-ack-offset) to reconcile the server's buffered byte window and the client's last seen offset. This prevents replaying bytes that would split UTF-8 or JSON tokens. 3) Lazy KV checkpoint: for requests that use large KV caches across resumable streams we introduce a lazily materialized checkpoint marker that ties a KV cache fingerprint to the span-id to ensure resumed requests reattach to the correct cache state (avoids stale cache lookups triggering function-call mismatches). 4) Compatibility: the new sentinel events and headers are added in a way that is backward compatible with openai-compat; old clients will ignore the extra comment-prefixed events and headers but still get stable structured output. Changes made: - Streaming emitter: implements span-id/span-seq, sentinel emission, and tail-anchor flush semantics. - Resume handshake: new resume-response header fields (X-RW-Resume-Offset, X-RW-Resume-Checksum) and server-side reconciliation logic. - Parser: resilient reassembly logic that uses span anchors to detect mid-span truncation and reconstruct or abort deterministic spans. - Function-call handoff: deterministic guard to ensure tool calls are only emitted once per span-id, with a retry-safe ACK path. - Tests: new unit tests (parser, emitter), integration test that replays partial frames and verifies idempotency, and a fuzz integration to exercise UTF-8 split boundaries. Summary of why this is different from previous fragment fixes: instead of heuristically trying to guess JSON boundaries at read-time, this approach makes the stream itself self-describing (anchors + offsets) so both client and server can deterministically agree on resume semantics. This reduces edge-case flakiness (duplicate function calls, truncated JSON) without requiring aggressive buffering or reserialization.
Alex Givens (review): Nice incremental design. Two asks: (1) add a short-living metric for span-anchor mismatches so we can alert on regressions, (2) make the resume checksum algorithm pluggable for future stronger checks.
Priya Nair (author reply): Added span_anchor.mismatch metric and extracted checksum impl behind a trait with default crc32c-lite implementation. See emitter.rs and resume_handler.rs changes.
Rafael Ortega (review): Parser looks good but we should avoid allocating a full reassembly buffer for very long spans. Suggest streaming-validate on the fly and only materialize when necessary.
