Introduce a background lattice defragmenter that reduces KV cache fragmentation and a preemptive spill partitioner that splits spill work into tenant-aware windows. Improves memory efficiency under mixed workloads and reduces p99 latency under memory pressure. Feature gated (kv.lattice_defrag.enabled) and rolled out gradually with automatic fallback.
Motivation: long-running tenants and variable-size KV entries caused severe external fragmentation in the slab-backed KV cache. Under burst workloads this led to aggressive spill storms and CPU/IO jitter as the existing evictor bounced between small free fragments. This PR implements two complementary subsystems: 1) a lattice defragmenter that opportunistically compacts adjacent live slots into contiguous lattice buckets to recover large free extents without full-page rewrite, and 2) a preemptive spill partitioner that slices spill work into prioritized, tenant-aligned windows to avoid single-worker spill storms. Design notes: the lattice defragmenter runs as a low-priority background worker integrated with the scheduler so it only performs work during batching idle windows (continuous-batching aware). It operates on a lightweight bitmap index (lattice map) per shard to identify coalescable runs and emits in-place move operations that update KV handles and the runtime's kernel hints for coalesced memcpy paths. The preemptive spill partitioner builds a heatmap of candidate slots using occupancy and sequence-age heuristics, partitions the work by tenant and allocation hotness, then schedules spill sub-tasks with a soft deadline so the runtime can preempt long spills to honor latency SLOs. Compatibility: no change to on-disk formats. The runtime exposes two flags: kv.lattice_defrag.enabled (default off) and kv.spill_partition.window_ms (default 200ms). Rollout plan: feature gated -> enable for 10% of dedicated capacity -> monitor mem pressure and p99 lat -> progressive increase with automated rollback on error budget breaches. Testing: unit tests for lattice map correctness, stress scenario integration tests that simulate mixed-size allocations, and new benchmarks measuring p50/p95/p99 generation latency and memory footprint under synthetic hot-tenant workloads. Migration: none required, old evictor is fallback path. See linked linear ENG-8212 for benchmark tasks and ENG-8340 for rollout schedule.
1) add lattice map struct and basic compaction worker (nkapoor/lattice-map)
2) implement preemptive spill partitioner + scheduler hooks (nkapoor/spill-partitioner)
3) wire feature flags, config, and unit tests (nkapoor/feature-gate)
4) add integration stress test and perf harness (nkapoor/perf-harness)
5) docs and changelog entry (nkapoor/docs)
src/kv/lattice_defrag.cc (new): core algorithm with bitmap scanner and in-place move ops; src/kv/lattice_defrag.h (new): public API and config types; src/kv/spill_partitioner.cc (new): partitioner and scheduler integration; src/kv/spill_partitioner.h (new); src/scheduler/idle_worker_pool.cc (update): hooks to run low-priority compaction during continuous batching idle windows; tests/kv/lattice_map_test.cc (new); tests/integration/kv_spill_partition_stress.py (new); docs/ops/kv-defrag.md (update): rollout and configuration examples. Small changes in src/kv/evictor.cc to add fallback and telemetry counters.
Asha: 'High level looks good; main concern is safety of in-place moves during concurrent reads — please document memory ordering guarantees and add assertions.'
Author (Nina): 'Added a memory ordering section in lattice_defrag.h and ensured moves go through a two-phase publish with an RCU-style grace window; added assertions and unit tests.'
Liam: 'Benchmarks are promising but we need to ensure CI includes the perf harness for regression monitoring.'
Author: 'Perf harness added to CI as optional job; results are uploaded to internal perf dashboard (link in ENG-8212).'
Marta: 'What are the failure modes? If compaction slips or moves fail, will we leak handles?'
Author: 'On move failure the code aborts the compaction for that run and reverts partial updates; we also emit a sticky metric kv.lattice.move_failures and fallback to slow rewrite path; documented in ops doc.'
Asha (approval): 'Nit: rename internal timer to compaction_idle_budget_ms; otherwise approved.'
Merge: 'squash and merge' by Liam after CI green.
Linux: build+unit-tests (pass), integrations (pass), perf-harness (optional) - results: p99 down ~3.4% on internal benchmark; MacOS: build (pass); Lint: go/clang-format (pass); Fuzzer: kv-fuzzer (pass); E2E: kv-spill-stress (pass). Flaky tests: kv/slot_relocator_test intermittently flaky on older kernels; added retry in CI pipeline.
Microbench: synthetic hot-tenant workload (varied entry sizes 128B-256KB): memory utilization down 9-14% at 95th percentile, p99 inference generation latency reduced by 3.4% under memory pressure, batch throughput stable (+0.6%). Integration stress (24h): spill storms reduced from 3/day to 0/day on our cluster. Observability: added kv.lattice.coalesce_ops, kv.spill.partition.window_ms and kv.lattice.move_failures counters.
Operational knobs: kv.lattice_defrag.enabled=false by default; safe default limits to 1 compaction worker per shard. Admins should monitor kv.lattice.move_failures and evictor.fallback_count after enabling. This PR is intentionally conservative — further tuning (adaptive windowing and kernel memcpy hints) will follow in a follow-up PR (ENG-8907).

Summary: This PR introduces a lightweight fragment-rotation buffer and a delimiter gating policy in the SSE streamer to address a recurring class of production incidents where partial JSON blobs could be emitted to clients during reassembly windows. The bug manifested as truncated or interleaved JSON objects when: (1) upstream partial fragments arrived out-of-order or late, and (2) the streamer emitted a delimiter or tool-call sentinel immediately on flush.

Motivation: We saw two customer incidents where integrations using OpenAI-compatible clients failed to parse streaming responses during brief backpressure events (see SUP-4321). Prior fixes reduced most races but did not cover scenarios where a late fragment would rotate into an active slot after a delimiter was already emitted.

Approach:
- Introduce a circular fragment-rotation buffer (small, per-connection) that holds up to N in-flight fragments and rotates slots when late fragments arrive; rotation preserves original event ordering rather than clobbering the current tail.
- Add a delimiter gating policy: delimiters and tool/fn-call sentinels are deferred until the rotation buffer can be drained to a token boundary. This prevents emitting a boundary in the middle of a JSON token.
- Implement a lightweight seq-check on fragment headers: fragments now carry a 16-bit rotation epoch and a 32-bit offset; the streamer uses these to decide whether a fragment can be stitched or MUST be held for rotation.
- Rework parser state machine to expose a "boundary-safe" check used by gating. The change is non-invasive and falls back to the previous behavior when rotation buffering is disabled (config flag) for easier rollout.

Commits (high-level):
- Add rotation buffer data structures and unit tests (mchen/sse-rotbuf)
- Implement delimiter gating and boundary-safe API (mchen/sse-gate)
- Add OpenAI compatibility e2e harness with fuzz scenarios (mchen/e2e-compat-fuzz)
- Add metrics and tracing (sse.rotation.held, sse.delimiter.deferred, sse.rotate.evicted) (mchen/observability)
- Tests/fixes and CI adjustments after reviewer feedback (mchen/fixups)

Files changed (high level):
- sse/streamer/rotbuf.rs: new rotation buffer and invariants
- sse/streamer/gating.rs: gating policy and boundary-safe checks
- sse/streamer/parser.rs: state machine refactor to expose safe checks
- sse/protocol/fragments.proto: extended fragment header (epoch/offset)
- sse/tests/fuzz/compat_fuzz.go: new e2e fuzz harness using OpenAI client simulator
- sse/tests/unit/parser_tests.rs: additional token-boundary tests
- observability/metrics.yaml: new counters and dashboards
- docs/api/streaming.md: added compatibility notes and rollout toggle
- CHANGELOG.md: release note snippet

Tests and validation:
- Unit coverage added for rotation buffer edge cases (late arrival, eviction, wraparound) and boundary-safe checks.
- Fuzz e2e harness simulates partial deliveries, delayed fragments, interleaved tool-call sentinel injection, and real-world load patterns observed in incidents.
- Local compatibility run against openai-stream-sim shows previously failing cases now parse cleanly.

CI: All checks pass after two iterative fixes to the parser refactor. Notable CI jobs:
- unit: pass
- integration-streaming: pass (30/30 simulated scenarios)
- fuzz-e2e: pass (seeded reproducer cases validated)
- lint/format: pass

Performance: Microbenchmarks show ~0.9% median additional CPU per active stream under pathological rotation load (highly fragmented synthetic workload). Under typical production traffic the overhead is negligible because rotation buffering is rarely used. Observability/tracing added to measure rotation event rates so we can rollback if necessary.

Rollout plan:
- Feature gated behind runtime flag sse.enable_rotation_buffer (default off).
- Canary rollout to 10% of streaming traffic for 48 hours with alerting on sse.rotate.evicted > threshold and sse.delimiter.deferred spikes.
- Full rollout once canary is stable.

Review conversation (abridged):
- Diego Alvarez (review): "Nice design; my main concern is eviction semantics during high fragmentation. Can we ensure eviction never discards the last tool-call sentinel?"
- Maya: "Added an eviction invariant in rotbuf.rs and unit tests to protect sentinel boundaries; see commit mchen/sse-rotbuf."
- Priya Nair (review): "Parser refactor is much cleaner now. Please add a metric for deferred delimiters so we can alert."
- Maya: "Added sse.delimiter.deferred and a dashboard tile. Also added an integration test asserting deferred delimiters are bounded under normal load."
- Elena Petrova (approval): "Approach looks good, tests are exhaustive; approvable once CI green and canary knobs are exposed in config."
- Final thread: minor formatting nits addressed; Diego approved after review.

Merge outcome: merged to main via squash merge on 2026-03-03 by Maya Chen.

Notes on compatibility:
- This change is backward compatible at the wire protocol level; fragment header extension is optional (old agents are treated as epoch 0).
- OpenAI-compat shim updated to tolerate deferred delimiter timing and still synthesize proper function-call handoffs.

Known limitations and follow-ups:
- Current rotation buffer size default is small (4 slots); follow-up task ENG-10234 to experiment with adaptive sizing.
- We still see a corner case when multiple late fragments collide and exceed the buffer; a small number of these will log an eviction metric and fall back to the old behavior (emit delimiter). Those events are expected to be exceedingly rare and will be tracked via the new metrics.

Related work: superset of fixes from ENG-9876 and references to prior SSE fixes (see changelog).
Fixes an SSE edge case that could emit incomplete JSON objects when stream fragments overlap; improves tool/function-call ordering and compatibility with OpenAI-style clients; adds new unit and e2e streaming tests; no API changes.
Merged via squash; migration-safe; rollout behind flag; follow-ups tracked in ENG-10234 and ENG-11000.
payload.title: SSE: introduce fragment-rotation buffer and delimiter gating to prevent partial-JSON bleed-through

payload.body:
Motivation: In highly elastic dedicated fleets we occasionally observe optimistic reservations that look good from passive metrics but collapse under microbursts. This PR introduces a light-weight active probing layer (ProbeProvisionController) that issues short-lived capacity probes and blends their results into a sliding reservation window. The probe stream provides higher-fidelity headroom estimates and allows graceful throttling when observed usable capacity diverges from statistical reservations.

What this changes (high level): Adds a ProbeProvisionController in the dedicated control plane that runs tenant-scoped micro-probes, a BurstInspector telemetry component that reports probe-derived signals, and a small simulation harness used to validate fairness across tenants and burst patterns. The blended reservation is a time-decayed average that mixes soft reservations, recent probe headroom samples, and a safety floor based on node-level allocatable.

Key features: 1) Probe-based headroom metric (probe_success_rate, probe_headroom_ms, probe_tail_latency_p90) emitted per-tenant and per-fleet. 2) Sliding reservation blender with configurable decay window and probe weight (config: reservation.decay_window_seconds, reservation.probe_weight). 3) BurstInspector endpoint for metrics ingestion and a Prometheus exporter that exposes blended_reservation_ratio and probe-derived stability score. 4) Simulator that runs multi-tenant scenarios to validate fairness and quantifies additional cost vs. SLA uplift. 5) Safe fallback: if probes fail or latency increases beyond threshold, controller falls back to conservative reservation and fast-fail throttling to prevent oversubscription.

Backward compatibility & rollout: ProbeProvisionController is feature gated (controller.features.probes = false by default). Helm chart value added under redwood-dedicated.values.yaml to opt-in. Migration path: opt-in in Canary fleet, monitor BurstInspector probe_success_rate and blended_reservation_ratio; default behavior unchanged for non-opted fleets.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for blender math and probe sampling; integration tests that run simulator scenarios (steady, spike, noisy node). Performance tests show median additional CPU < 3% on control plane and < 0.4% p99 scheduling latency change on serving path in our cluster-size 50 simulation. Added e2e smoke that verifies fallback when probes time out.

Risks and operational notes: Active probing increases control-plane traffic; probes are tiny (single RPCs with short TTL) and rate-limited per-tenant. We recommend progressive rollout by enabling probes for low-risk tenants first. Alerting: added alerts for probe_success_rate < 90% and blended_reservation_ratio drift > 15% for > 5m.

Related work: complements the existing headroom scheduler and reservation decayers (see ENG-15230). This PR also implements better observability hooks which are useful for upcoming proportional backfill work.

Documentation: Added design doc and operator runbook describing tuning knobs, required dashboards, and recommended rollout checklist.

Linked Linear: ENG-17482 (probe provisioning), ENG-17610 (burst telemetry). Jira ticket SUP-455 contains customer reproduction used to drive the probe approach.
Daniel Park (2026-02-18): Nice approach. Two asks: 1) ensure probe rate limits are enforced per-tenant (not just global) and 2) please add a small benchmark showing controller CPU impact under 1000 tenants.
Maya Alvarez (2026-02-19): Added per-tenant token bucket & synthetic benchmark in simulator (see commit g7b9c1d). Updated runbook with suggested tenant rollout order.
Priya Singh (2026-02-22): Safety concern: the initial probe_weight default (0.5) looks optimistic. Recommend 0.2 until we get more field data. Also please expose a feature flag for fast-fail throttling threshold.
Maya Alvarez (2026-02-23): Lowered default probe_weight to 0.2 and added controller.features.probes.fast_fail_threshold (docs updated).
Liam O'Connor (2026-02-24): Tests look good. One nit: use context deadlines in simulator RPCs for deterministic failures.
Maya Alvarez (2026-02-25): Switched simulator RPCs to use deadlines; added an integration test that asserts fallback path when probes exceed deadline.
Feature: Probe-based reservation blending (opt-in). Operators can enable controller.features.probes to smooth reservations using active probes. New telemetry: probe_success_rate, probe_headroom_ms, blended_reservation_ratio. Added operator runbook and Helm opt-in values. Safe fallback ensures no regression when probes are unreliable.
Enable probes only in canary clusters. Watch Alert: probe_success_rate < 90% and blended_reservation_ratio drift > 15%. Default probe_weight=0.2; increase only after 48h of stable telemetry. Control-plane CPU impact observed ~3% in tests; ensure control-plane autoscaling buffer before enabling at fleet scale.

Motivation: Multiple SDKs (TS/Python/Go) had divergent approaches to streaming token refresh and retry presets which led to subtly different developer ergonomics and intermittent reconnect bugs in long-running multi-connection workloads. This change introduces a lightweight 'credential fanout' abstraction that allows a single lease/refresh pipeline to fan out credentials to multiple stream connections, plus typed stream lifecycle hooks so SDK consumers can run warmup/cleanup logic deterministically. Scope: 1) core credential/fanout implementation (shared, low-dep runtime) 2) TypeScript SDK surface changes (typed hooks, new RetryProfiles enum, default backoff presets) and minor ergonomic helpers 3) Python/Go companion shims in the monorepo that wire the new contract into existing session managers (non-breaking) 4) test harness updates, docs, and changelog bumps. Key goals: 1) reduce duplicate refresh requests under high fan-out, 2) provide deterministic hook points for warmup/backpressure in streaming consumers, 3) unify retry/backoff presets across SDKS, 4) bump TS SDK to 1.7.0 with clear migration notes. Checklist: - [x] implement credential fanout and fanout-safe refresh semantics - [x] add typed stream hooks (onOpen, onWarmup, onClose) for TS SDK - [x] expose RetryProfiles enum and default presets - [x] add shim adapters for Python and Go SDKs (no behavior change by default) - [x] update e2e streaming treadmill tests and flaky test stabilization - [x] update changelogs and release notes - [x] manual smoke tests with Canary app (stream fanout=12) Changes: commits below and high level file list show exact edits. Testing: Unit tests cover fanout edgecases (concurrent refresh, lease expiry, single-refresh-per-window). Integration tests on CI include streaming treadmill at fanout sizes 1/4/12 and an emulated token expiry. One flaky test (stream-resume-interop) failed on first CI run, was stabilized by a 150ms delay in the test harness to avoid race with test-only hook; CI was re-run and all checks passed. Migration notes: TS SDK consumers who relied on internal session internals should switch to the exported typed hooks; default behavior is unchanged and migration helper is provided in the deprecation guide. Rollout: merged to main and will be included in the 1.7.0 SDK release cut later this week. See release_notes field below for user-facing notes.
Marco Ruiz: Please ensure we don't forget metrics on the fanout path (fanout.size, fanout.refresh_count). Add counters and labels so we can alert if refresh amplification appears.
Nina Patel (author): Added fanout metrics and unit tests for counters in a follow-up commit (see a8f3b1c -> metric additions).
Leah Tan: The typed hooks look good; can we make onWarmup async and document expected latency impact?
Nina Patel (author): onWarmup is async in the exported typings; added note in docs about typical latency expectations and suggested usage patterns.
Danielle O'Connor: CI treadmill flaky test fix makes sense but add a TODO to remove the artificial delay once the event ordering is hardened.
Nina Patel (author): Added TODO in delay_fix.ts and filed ENG-4822 to track hardening work.
QA (internal): Verified TS SDK example against Canary app and saw 4x reduction in refresh calls at fanout=12 compared to the previous baseline.
TS SDK 1.7.0: Introduces credential-fanout abstraction to reduce refresh amplification under high fanout streaming workloads; new typed stream hooks (onOpen/onWarmup/onClose) for deterministic warmup and cleanup; unified RetryProfiles enum with sensible defaults that align with other SDKs; Python/Go shims included for compatibility. Migration: default behavior is unchanged. If you used internal session objects, follow the migration guide at docs/sdk/migration/typed-hooks.md to adopt exported hooks.

Context: As part of the Reliability Program (Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping), we’re adding enforcement around remediation expectations. This PR implements remediation SLA timers and breach alerting (Slack + paging) keyed by incident severity and customer tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private). It ships with conservative defaults, is fully config-driven, and includes safeguards to avoid noisy paging. What’s in this PR: 1) SLA policy evaluation + due time computation: New module computes SLA due timestamps for (a) time-to-mitigate (TTM) and (b) time-to-fix (TTF) based on incident {severity, tier}. We derive start_time from the incident declared timestamp (incident-bot created_at / incident record start_at) and persist computed due_at values into the incident record. Timers are recomputed if severity or tier changes. 2) Breach notifications: Adds two notification thresholds: (a) “approaching breach” at 80% of remaining time (Slack only) and (b) “breach” at 100% (Slack + paging depending on policy). Paging is enabled only for Sev0/Sev1 for Dedicated/Private by default; Hosted Sev0 pages, Hosted Sev1/Sev2 are Slack-only by default. 3) Config defaults + overrides: Adds a versioned YAML config `configs/reliability/remediation_sla.yaml` with defaults for each tier and severity. Also supports per-incident overrides for: pause_reason (force majeure), customer_caused (does not stop timer, but annotates notifications), and suppression window (temporary; requires reason + actor). 4) Telemetry: Emits metrics for compliance reporting and alert tuning: `incident_sla_due_seconds{tier,severity,phase}` and `incident_sla_breach_total{tier,severity,phase,breach_type}` plus structured logs including incident_id, due_at, and whether paging was suppressed. Metrics label cardinality is bounded (tier/severity/phase enums only). 5) Runbook wiring: Adds runbook link in Slack breach message, and includes explicit “how to pause/override” guidance with audit trail requirements. Behavior details: - Timer start: when incident transitions into ACTIVE (declared), not when the first alert fired. - Timer stop: TTM stops when incident is marked MITIGATED; TTF stops when incident is marked RESOLVED. - Severity/tier changes: Recompute due_at from the original start_time for that phase; we also emit an audit log entry noting the policy change. - Pauses: Only supported for force majeure (e.g., cloud provider region outage) and requires `pause_reason` + `approved_by` on the incident record. Paused incidents still send a daily Slack reminder in #eng-sre to ensure they’re not forgotten. - Dual tracking: If Security Ops flags an incident as security-classified, this SLA evaluator continues to run for reliability severity/tier but adds `security_flag=true` to logs and includes a handoff note in notifications. Slack message format (breach): `:rotating_light: Remediation SLA BREACH (TTM) - Sev1 Dedicated` + incident link + owner + due_at + time_over + action buttons (ack, page owner, pause with reason). Pager payload includes incident_id, tier, severity, phase (TTM/TTF), and owner team. Why this approach: - Config-driven to align with evolving customer commitments without code changes. - Low-cardinality telemetry for dashboards and long-term reporting. - Conservative paging defaults to avoid alert fatigue while still making breaches visible and measurable. Follow-ups (out of scope here): - Hooking taxonomy incident_type into SLA policy (phase 2); today it’s keyed only by tier/severity. - Console surfacing for CS/ops (tracked separately). - Backfill for historical incidents (ENG-4827). Testing: - Unit tests for policy evaluator (matrix coverage). - Integration tests for Slack notification payloads and PagerDuty routing suppression logic. - “Time travel” tests using fake clock to validate approaching-breach and breach scheduling. Risk/rollout: - Feature flags: `remediation_sla.enabled` and `remediation_sla.paging_enabled`. - Default rollout plan: enable Slack-only for all tiers for 1 week; enable paging for Dedicated/Private Sev0/Sev1 after tuning. - Includes a kill switch to disable all SLA notifications if noise is higher than expected.
Rafael Mendes: We need to be explicit about the start/stop semantics (ACTIVE->MITIGATED/RESOLVED) and make sure severity changes don’t reset the clock in a way that hides breaches. Also add guidance for when to use pause vs suppression.
Dylan Brooks (author): Updated description + added audit log entry on any recompute; clock is anchored to phase start_time. Added `pause_reason` requirements and a daily reminder for paused incidents.
Allison Grant: Metrics look fine; please confirm labels are bounded enums only (no incident_type, no owner labels). Also please add a single counter for breaches rather than emitting a per-incident gauge that could churn.
Dylan Brooks (author): Confirmed: labels are tier/severity/phase/breach_type only. Switched breach reporting to `incident_sla_breach_total` counter and kept due time as a value emitted on incident state change (not continuously).
Aisha Bello: Can we emit “approaching breach” as a distinct event for dashboards? Also, do we have a knob to disable paging entirely while we tune?
Dylan Brooks (author): Added `incident_sla_warning_total{...}` counter for 80% warnings and feature flag `remediation_sla.paging_enabled` default false. Slack-only remains enabled behind `remediation_sla.enabled`.
Lauren Bishop: Dedicated expectations: paging for Sev1 Dedicated is OK, but we need a carve-out for large cloud-provider incidents (force majeure). Make sure the pause path is auditable and doesn’t silently stop all notifications.
Dylan Brooks (author): Implemented pause with required `pause_reason` + `approved_by` and continued daily Slack reminder in #eng-sre while paused; breach paging is suppressed while paused but the incident record retains due_at and pause metadata.
Ethan Park: Any schema changes to incident records must include migration notes. Also, ensure pause/suppression changes are recorded in the control plane audit log.
Dylan Brooks (author): Added migration for new fields (due_at_ttm, due_at_ttf, pause_reason, pause_approved_by, suppression_until) and added audit log events `incident.sla_policy_recomputed` and `incident.sla_pause_updated`.
Nikhil Sharma: Hosted tier shouldn’t page for Sev1 by default; Slack is fine. Please double-check defaults match that and link the runbook for overrides.
Dylan Brooks (author): Defaults updated: Hosted pages only on Sev0. Added runbook link and quick steps for override/pause in Slack message.
Rafael Mendes: Approving contingent on rollout plan being documented in the PR and feature flags defaulting to safe values.
Dylan Brooks (author): Rollout plan added; paging flag defaults false. Thanks.
Rafael Mendes: Approved.
Allison Grant: Approved.
Aisha Bello: Approved.
Internal: remediation SLA timers + breach notifications are now available behind `remediation_sla.enabled` / `remediation_sla.paging_enabled`. Default config is Slack-only; paging disabled by default.

Context
We’re introducing Hosted data residency enforcement (region pinning) across routing + gateway. The gateway must return a deterministic, consistent error when a request is blocked by residency policy (instead of falling back, timing out, or returning generic 500s in some streaming paths).

This PR implements the public error contract for residency violations:
- Returns HTTP 409 (Conflict) when residency policy blocks a request
- Standardized JSON error payload with stable `error.code`, `error.type`, and `help_url`
- Works consistently for both streaming and non-streaming endpoints
- Propagates `request_id` and `residency.decision_id` for support/debug (without exposing full policy content)
- Maps internal policy-engine outcomes to a small set of public-facing reason codes

Motivation / user impact
- Customers with EU-only pinning should get a clear, actionable error when their request would route outside allowed regions (or when they call the wrong regional base URL)
- SDKs can reliably detect this as a residency issue and surface guidance (instead of treating as retryable 5xx)
- Support gets deterministic identifiers to locate decision logs and troubleshoot quickly

Behavior
- Non-streaming: respond with 409 immediately
- Streaming: if policy block is known before starting the stream, the gateway responds with a normal 409 JSON error (no stream initiated). If a block is discovered after headers would have been sent (should be rare; mostly during phased rollout), we terminate the stream with a final SSE error event using the same error schema and include `request_id`.

Public error schema (example)
{
  "error": {
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "code": "data_residency_policy_violation",
    "message": "Request blocked by data residency policy: allowed regions are [eu-central-1]. Update your project’s residency settings or use an API base URL in an allowed region.",
    "param": null,
    "help_url": "https://docs.redwoodinference.com/errors#data_residency_policy_violation"
  },
  "request_id": "req_01H...",
  "residency": {
    "decision_id": "rdc_01H...",
    "selected_region": null,
    "allowed_regions": "eu-central-1",
    "reason": "target_region_not_allowed"
  }
}

Notes:
- `allowed_regions` is returned as a comma-separated string to keep the payload stable across languages/SDKs and to avoid accidental JSON shape drift.
- We do NOT return `policy_id` in the public response. We do return a `decision_id` which can be looked up in internal logs.
- `help_url` points to docs anchors; docs PR will add that section (tracked separately).

Implementation details
- Adds a dedicated `ResidencyViolationError` type in the gateway domain layer with a strict mapping from internal policy evaluator outcomes.
- Centralizes error serialization in `gateway/errors/public_errors.ts` to guarantee the same shape for REST + streaming adapters.
- Adds regression tests for:
  - /v1/chat/completions (json)
  - /v1/completions (json)
  - /v1/embeddings (json)
  - streaming chat SSE path (ensures no generic 500)
- Adds structured logging fields:
  - `residency.blocked=true`
  - `residency.reason`
  - `residency.decision_id`
  - `http.status=409`

Rollout
- Guarded by feature flag `residency_enforcement_error_contract_v1` (default ON in staging, OFF in prod until routing enforcement is enabled per-region).
- When flag is OFF, behavior is unchanged.

Refs
- Linear: ENG-4833, PM-1490

Background and motivation: Operators want a single, explainable surface to see where time and cost are being spent in a single invocation. Existing per-route latency panels and token-cost histograms are helpful but do not make it easy to attribute time/cost across the request lifecycle (parse -> model compute -> decode/stream). This PR introduces a phase-aware response waterfall visualization, new span phase tags, and an adaptive anomaly damping layer for alerts so that SREs get fewer noisy triggers from harmless phase skews.

What this changes: 1) New telemetry: emits span.level_phase tags (parse, queue, model, decode, stream) and numeric phase_dur_ms for all model-serving spans. Implemented lightweight phase tagging in trace_utils and serving runtime (small fast-path instrumentation to avoid added allocations). 2) Dashboard: adds observability/dashboards/response_waterfall.json (Grafana dashboard schema) with stacked-phase waterfall panels, per-tenant phase breakdown, and a selectable percentile/quantile selector. 3) Token-level correlation: enriches token-cost rollups with phase attribution to show cost-per-token by phase and by model variant. 4) Alerts: adds adaptive anomaly damping algorithm in alerts/anomaly_damping.go which decays alert sensitivity for routes where phase shifts are correlated with known model rollouts or CPU-backed rescheduling. 5) Migration: SQL migration script scripts/migrate-phase-tags.sql to backfill phase_breakdown tables for the last 30 days. 6) Tests and docs: adds e2e test to tests/e2e/response_waterfall_test.py, small unit tests for the damping policy, and runbook/docs/runbooks/phase-waterfall.md with troubleshooting steps and recommended thresholds.

Checklist: - [x] Instrumentation: minimal overhead tagging (microbench shows <1% p99 impact) - [x] Dashboard panels wired to query indices and annotated with rollout metadata - [x] Alert rules unit-tested and dogfooded on staging - [x] Migration script validated on snapshot dataset - [x] Runbook written and linked from the dashboard

How it was implemented (high-level commits): - Added phase tagging into trace emission path with a compact enum to keep tag cardinality low. - Aggregations: updated token-cost-indexer to accumulate phase_dur_ms and phase_cost_estimate. - Dashboard: built interactive waterfall with per-invocation hover showing top 3 contributing phases and approximate token cost. - Alerts: damping runs as an inline preprocessor that adjusts threshold percentile based on historical phase variance and rollout annotations.

Testing and verification: 1) Unit: added mocked span generator tests for phase tagging and aggregator. 2) Integration: response_waterfall_test replays synthetic invocations (varying queue/model/decode ratios) and asserts dashboard queries return coherent stacked sums and that alert dampening suppresses noise for predictable model rollouts. 3) Staging rollout: enabled on staging for two weeks behind a feature flag, compared alert counts to previous baseline (30% reduction in non-actionable alerts for routes with recent rollouts).

Migration and rollout plan: - Step 1: deploy instrumentation + dashboard to staging behind feature flag (0-2 days) - Step 2: run migration script on staging snapshot and validate panels (2-3 days) - Step 3: enable damping in alerts for staging traffic, monitor for under-suppression (3-7 days) - Step 4: incremental rollout to canary tenants (week 2) - Step 5: full rollout and remove feature flag (week 3)

Rollback plan: revert head branch via squash revert; disable damping preprocessor by flipping alert flag; remove dashboard from shared space if visual regressions surface.

Known limitations: backfill uses approximate mapping for older spans that do not have explicit phase markers (heuristic attribution), which can undercount parse vs queue in rare cases. We intentionally keep phase tags low-cardinality to avoid metric explosion.

Related: references ENG-3421 for alerting work and SUP-8891 (support ticket) showing noisy alerts during a recent model rollout.

Notes: performance microbench shows a 0.4% median latency increase and <1% p99; sampling rate for detailed token-phase accumulation is set to 1% by default and can be ramped per-tenant via Console.
Add a phase-aware response waterfall dashboard (per-invocation phase breakdown) and an adaptive anomaly damping layer to reduce noisy alerts during rollouts. Includes instrumentation, backfill migration, and runbook.
1) Enable feature flag console/feature_flags/phase_waterfall.yaml for your staging tenant. 2) Run scripts/migrate-phase-tags.sql against a staging snapshot (see migration notes in docs). 3) Run tests: pytest tests/unit && pytest tests/e2e/response_waterfall_test.py. 4) Verify the Grafana dashboard under Observability -> Response Waterfall shows stacked phases and hover costs. 5) Observe alert counts for 48h to validate damping behavior.
This PR was dogfooded on staging; observed ~30% reduction in non-actionable alerts for rollout-affected routes with no missed actionable alerts in the monitored window. Contact Priya for SLO tuning guidance.

Motivation: Our monolithic lint runner has been a large contributor to CI minutes and noisy signal when rule ownership or rule-surface changes. This PR refactors the lint orchestration layer to separate rule evaluation from runner execution and attaches 'provenance' metadata to rules so we can target fixes, notifications, and owners more accurately. It also introduces a sparse-test scheduler that avoids running full integration/test suites on lint-only or rule-doc changes and coalesces consecutive lint-only pushes into a single CI run when feasible.

Summary of changes:
- Introduce RULE_PROVENANCE manifest (ci/lint-orchestrator/provenance.yaml) that records rule id, owner, last-changed commit, and risk score
- Replace legacy lint entrypoint with a lightweight orchestrator (ci/lint-orchestrator/main.go) that computes minimal job graph and delegates execution to existing runners
- Add sparse-test-scheduler that performs fast impact analysis and schedules only the required test shards for low-risk changes
- Add coalescer to .github/actions/commit-coalescer to merge frequent lint-only pushes into a single queued run (opt-in by label)
- Bump dev deps: eslint-plugin-typescript 5.8.0 -> 6.0.1, @redwood/lint-shim 1.3.2 -> 1.4.0 (minor; includes provenance extractor)
- Docs: new guidance and troubleshooting for rule ownership and how to update provenance
- Tests: unit tests for orchestrator, scheduler, and provenance extractor

Checklists:
- [x] design doc linked (ENG-3245)
- [x] unit tests added for orchestrator and scheduler
- [x] integration smoke run against staging allocator
- [x] shared config migrations scripted (ci/lint-orchestrator/migrate-provenance.sh)

Performance/impact:
- Measured against a 30-day sample of PRs: median lint-only CI minutes reduced by ~48% and median end-to-end feedback time improved from ~9m to ~5m for lint-only changes
- Sparse-scheduler avoided full-test runs for ~37% of non-functional-change PRs in the sample

Rollout plan:
- Feature gated (env REDWOOD_LINT_ORCH=false by default)
- Opt-in via label "ci:orchestrate-lint" for first week and compare telemetry
- After verification, flip default and migrate provenance using scripted job. Migration details and rollback instructions are in ci/lint-orchestrator/README.md

Motivation: We observed a class of production incidents where unusually large user payloads (multipart uploads or long system prompts with embedded toolcall scaffolding) caused amplification in the gateway streaming path: proxy buffers would coalesce many small frames, then the downstream model path would stall on KV-cache handshakes for function/tool calls, resulting in head-of-line stalls and user-facing stalls during streaming. This PR applies two orthogonal mitigations at the gateway surface: 1) a transient route-level size quarantine that detects and isolates anomalously large requests for separate handling (batch-fallback or immediate reject when configured), and 2) an adaptive chunk-ack window for the streaming proxy that prevents the proxy from holding too many unacked chunks during tool/function handshakes, reducing amplification and stray retries. The goal is to improve streaming stability without changing client-facing APIs; OpenAI-compat behavior is preserved with a small compatibility tweak to chunk framing to avoid double-close race in function-call handoffs. Summary of changes and rationale: - Add a route_quarantine state machine that tracks per-route size spikes and applies a short TTL quarantine (configurable) that routes offending traffic to a batch-fallback path or returns a 413-like hint depending on policy. This reduces the number of pathologically large requests entering low-latency streaming pools. - Implement adaptive ack window in the streaming proxy: the window size reduces automatically when a toolcall handshake is detected (based on stream metadata flags and content heuristics), and grows back after a successful handshake. This prevents buffer amplification during the multi-step toolcall exchange. - Small OpenAI-compat change: tweak chunk_framer to emit a stable terminator frame for function-call streams to avoid ambiguous end-of-streams observed in interop tests. - Observability: add metrics (route_quarantine.count, streaming.ack_window.size, streaming.toolcall.handshakes) and an alert hint to SLO playbook. - Tests: unit coverage for quarantine TTL logic, integration test for simulated toolcall handshake under heavy chunking, and e2e compatibility test against the openai-compat shim. Checklist: - [x] Design review with runtime and gateway (ENG-4122) - [x] Benchmarked basic workloads locally (reduced tail stalls by ~45% in synthetic replay) - [x] Added unit and integration tests - [x] Updated observability and runbooks - [x] Docs entry for gateway tuning (docs/changes/streaming-tuning.md) Commits (high-level): - 9a1c2d: add route_quarantine state machine and config knobs - 3f7b44: implement adaptive ack window and proxy integration - 11b3e7: compat: stable chunk terminator for function-call streams - 5d9f2a: tests + metrics + docs Notes on backward compatibility: The route quarantine is opt-in by default and can be enabled per-route. The adaptive ack window is conservative and defaults to the current window size; only active reductions occur when a handshake pattern is recognized. The OpenAI-compat framer change is additive and preserves previous chunk contents; it only alters the closing sentinel to make toolcall handoffs deterministic. Changed areas (high level): gateway/router/route_quarantine.go, gateway/proxy/stream_buffer.go, gateway/proxy/ack_window.go, compat/openai/chunk_framer.go, api/tests/stream_toolcall_integration.rs, docs/changes/streaming-tuning.md, pkg/config/defaults.yaml, pkg/observability/alerts.yaml Review conversation (selected): - Connor Liu (review): "Question: what stops a client from intentionally triggering the quarantine to force batch-fallback?" - Aisha: "We enforce a short cooldown and circuit flag per-client; policy supports client whitelisting. Also quarantine TTL is low (default 30s) and we emit a debug header that clients can examine. See gateway/router/route_quarantine.go:QuarantinePolicy." - Elena Martinez (request changes): "Please add a histogram for ack_window size; counters alone won't show distribution." - Aisha: "Added histogram metric streaming.ack_window.size_buckets in observability patch; also added a note in runbook about interpreting it." - Rajesh Kumar (approval): "Verified integration test under the allocator stress harness; LGTM once CI green." CI summary: - unit-tests: passed - integration-streaming: initially failed (timing-sensitive flake), rerun -> passed - lint: passed - e2e-openai-compat: passed Merge: squashed and merged to main (squash), merge commit: squashed 4 commits into one. Rollout notes: Gate is controlled by config flag gateway.features.route_quarantine.enabled (default false). Ops can enable in a canary region first; metric route_quarantine.count and streaming.ack_window.size_buckets should be monitored for unexpected spikes. Linked issues: ENG-4122 (design), PM-198 (customer impact follow-up), SUP-3221 (customer repro attached).
Connor Liu: Question: what stops a client from intentionally triggering the quarantine?
Aisha Patel: We enforce a short cooldown and per-client circuit flag; debug header emits reason.
Elena Martinez: Please add a histogram for ack_window size.
Aisha Patel: Added streaming.ack_window.size_buckets and runbook note.
Rajesh Kumar: Verified under allocator stress harness; LGTM.
Ops (post-merge): Can we get a dashboard tile for quarantine != 0 in canary regions?
Introduce an opt-in route-level quarantine to isolate very large requests and an adaptive streaming proxy ack window to reduce buffer amplification during tool/function-call handshakes. Opt-in by default; improves streaming stability and reduces tail stalls. See ENG-4122 for design notes and docs/changes/streaming-tuning.md for ops guidance.

Motivation: recurring tenant oscillation and noisy redistribution of burst credits across dedicated pools have caused repeated transient SLA violations during back-to-back surges. This PR introduces a per-pool throughput budgeting abstraction plus a hysteresis controller that smooths admission decisions and prevents rapid open/close oscillations when headroom fluctuates.

Design summary: the controller maintains a moving-window budget for each pool (committed_throughput, soft_budget, expected_burn_rate) and exposes two key behaviors: (1) budget demultiplexing: incoming burst reservations are split into stable vs ephemeral tranches so long-lived reservations draw from a soft_budget while ephemeral spikes are served from a burst cache; (2) hysteresis gating: scale/admit decisions require a budget delta to exceed threshold for a configurable hold period before flipping state. Both behaviors are parameterized per-pool and per-tenant overrideable.

Config knobs added: per_pool.throughput_budget.initial_qps (int), per_pool.throughput_budget.window_seconds (int), per_pool.hysteresis.open_threshold_pct (float), per_pool.hysteresis.close_threshold_pct (float), per_pool.hysteresis.hold_seconds (int), admission.split_ratio (stable:burst). Defaults chosen to be conservative to avoid regressions.

Telemetry and alerts: new metrics exported under redwood_dedicated_pool_*: budget_available, budget_burn_rate, budget_forecast_p50_ms, hysteresis_state (0/1), recent_split_ratio. New alert: DedicatedPoolBudgetDepletion (fires when budget_available/pool < 5% for > 2m). Dashboards: dedicated -> Pools -> Throughput budgets (new panel).

Backward compatibility & rollout: controller is opt-in per Fleet by flipping dedicated.features.per_pool_budget to true. Default remains disabled for existing fleets. Rolling deploy strategy: start with internal canary fleet (5 clusters) -> gradual flag rollout across production pools -> enable automated telemetry-driven ramp.

Testing: unit tests for budget accounting, e2e integration test simulating sustained and bursty load shapes, and a small cluster-level soak run. Benchmarks show 1–3% CPU increase on controller nodes and no measurable increase in p99 latency for admission path.

Notes: Linear ENG-2189 covers follow-ups for multi-cluster budget reconciliation, and SUP-712 documents customer incident that motivated the change.
Diego Ramirez (reviewer): Looks solid overall. Two requests: (1) add a small randomized jitter to hold_seconds to avoid thundering-holds across pools; (2) clarify the accounting semantics when a tenant has both stable and ephemeral slices. See inline comment on hysteresis_controller.go:72.
Lena Fischer (author): Added jitter parameter per_pool.hysteresis.jitter_ms (default 250ms) and clarified comments + unit tests covering the tenant slice accounting. Responded to Diego's inline note and pushed commit 2/3.
Aisha Khan (reviewer): Verified metrics naming and alert thresholds. Requested a minor change to dashboard panel text to call out expected units for budget_forecast_p50_ms.
Omar Patel (approver): Approved after CI green and a successful canary with internal fleet. Left a suggestion to document the migration path for existing alerting rules.
CI flake: one transient e2e failure in the canary job on first run; rerun passed.
Added opt-in per-pool throughput budgets to smooth dedicated fleet admission and reduce SLA oscillation.
Hysteresis controller prevents rapid open/close admission cycles; configurable hold and thresholds.
New telemetry: redwood_dedicated_pool_budget_available, budget_burn_rate, budget_forecast_p50_ms, hysteresis_state.
Opt-in through dedicated.features.per_pool_budget; default disabled.

Context: Streaming tool/function calls and strict JSON schema validation cause many client-side retries when near-well-formed JSON is truncated or has small syntax issues in-flight. This PR introduces a best-effort streaming snapshot repair path and an opt-in permissive schema negotiation mode to reduce application-level retries while preserving strong diagnostics and OpenAI compatibility. Motivation: reduce retry storms and improve streaming stability for structured-output contracts without surprising production behavior. Key ideas: 1) capture short-lived stream snapshots (tail window of bytes/tokens) at schema-check checkpoints and attempt localized repairs (close brackets, remove trailing commas, balanced quotes) before declaring a hard validation failure; 2) when repair is non-destructive and yields a schema-valid object, emit a structured telemetry event and attach a small diagnostics header (x-redwood-schema-repair) to the final response explaining the repair applied; 3) for tool/function-call boundaries, anchor snapshots using the existing toolcall token markers so repairs do not cross toolcall fences; 4) provide a new response_format.mode value permissive_repair that clients can set to opt into this behavior; 5) maintain backward-compatible OpenAI shim behavior by mapping permissive_repair to openai_compat.mode=permissive-with-repair and including the same repair diagnostics in the legacy streaming envelope as platform metadata. Checklist: - [x] design: stream snapshot window and repair heuristics (balanced-parens, trailing-comma strip, quote-fix) - [x] runtime implementation: snapshot capture, in-flight repair pipeline, chained validators - [x] openai-compat shim: negotiate permissive_repair -> permissive-with-repair mapping - [x] toolcall anchoring: token markers and fence tests - [x] telemetry: repair.reason, repair.applied, repair.score, repair.latency - [x] safety: only apply repair when edit distance heuristic < threshold and when no tool boundaries are crossed - [x] tests: unit/integ/e2e sim with flaky generators - [x] docs: API surface and migration notes - [x] perf: benchmark microbench showing <=2.7% median CPU overhead in P50 P95 cases Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged (strict mode). permissive_repair is opt-in and guarded by a per-customer rollout flag for Dedicated/Private customers. If repair cannot produce a valid payload, runtime falls back to the existing soft-fail path (error metadata + stream truncate) and does not attempt destructive edits. Risk and mitigation: - false-positive repairs are possible; mitigated by conservative edit-distance threshold, whitelisting of fixes (no reordering, only closure/trim/escape), and telemetry-based revert if repair rate exceeds preset SLO. - small CPU overhead: measured and acceptable; added rollouts to ramp to broader fleets. Tests and results: harnessed synthetic truncation workloads and real-client traces; found client retry reduction of 38% (median) in test corpus. Migration notes: add response_format.mode=permissive_repair to client options or set openai_compat.mode=permissive-with-repair for legacy clients. See release notes below for detailed client guidance. Related: ENG-9142 (schema stability), PM-3321 (product impact analysis).
Diego Ramos: Nice approach. Two concerns: (1) how do we guarantee we don't repair across toolcall fences? Please show invariants and tests; (2) please add a knob to completely disable repair for Private installs.
Maya Patel (author): We anchor snapshots to explicit fence tokens emitted by the parser; added unit tests under tests/integ and added a feature flag (runtime.featureFlags.RepairSnapshots) exposed via config for Private. See added tests 'fence_anchor_no_repair_cross' and 'private_flag_respects_disable'.
Aria Chen: Can you add a short e2e with the OpenAI-compat shim to validate legacy streaming envelopes still decode metadata?
Maya Patel: Added e2e in tests/integ/openai_compat_repair_e2e.test and verified legacy envelope includes 'x-redwood-schema-repair' in the final metadata chunk.
New opt-in response_format.mode=permissive_repair that attempts conservative in-stream JSON fixes for near-well-formed structured outputs, reducing client retries for truncated/partial streams. OpenAI-compat clients can enable openai_compat.mode=permissive-with-repair. Repair is opt-in and behind a rollout flag; default strict behavior unchanged. See docs/migration/permissive_repair.md for guidance and examples.
If you have transient stream truncation errors with structured outputs or tool calls, consider setting response_format.mode=permissive_repair; monitor 'schema_repair.applied' telemetry and use the x-redwood-schema-repair header to surface diagnostics. For Dedicated/Private customers, administrators can toggle the runtime.featureFlags.RepairSnapshots flag.
Unit tests cover repair heuristics and fence anchoring. Integration tests validate end-to-end OpenAI-compat decoding and toolcall safety. E2E on staging with sampled production traces shows a 38% median reduction in client retries for schema errors. Performance overhead measured at <=2.7% median CPU increase under representative serving load.

Motivation: intermittent regressions observed in production where CUDA graph replay would re-capture too often (different shape guards or stale KV cache state), increasing tail latency and causing noisy SLO violations. This PR implements a small compatibility layer that canonicalizes compatible shapes and a KV-cache safe replay path to reduce unnecessary re-captures. Changes: 1) Add cudagraph_compat.h/cpp: heuristics to determine when two shapes are safe to reuse the same capture (prefix compatibility, token axis padding rules, and kv-cache pointer-stability checks). 2) Update cudagraph_manager.py to maintain a compatibility map keyed by a lightweight shape-signature instead of exact tensors; replays check compat map first. 3) Make scheduler.cpp prefer warmup probes for under-utilized kernels and surface a new metric (cudagraph_reuse_ratio) to console. 4) KV cache patch: kv_cache.cc now stamps ephemeral generation IDs into cache metadata so a replay will detect incompatible KV states and fall back without triggering a full capture for nearby shapes. 5) Tests and docs: added focused unit + integration tests and a short doc page with recommended warmup probes and runtime knobs. Rollout plan: staged on Dedicated pools for one week with observability hooks (cudagraph_reuse_ratio, capture_rate, fallback_count). Linear tickets: ENG-6123 (primary), ENG-6198 (follow-up to remove legacy exact-match path). Checklist:
- [x] Core compatibility algorithm implemented and unit-tested
- [x] Integration tests covering replay fallback and KV cache mismatch
- [x] Metrics emitted and dashboard note added
- [x] Bench script to reproduce capture churn
Notes: this is intentionally conservative — we prefer false negatives (not reusing when safe) over false positives that could cause incorrect outputs. We also retained the exact-match capture path behind a feature flag for a quick rollback.
Added unit tests for shape_signature equivalence classes, integration test that simulates alternating shapes and verifies reuse ratio > 80% under bench workload, and a KV cache mismatch test that asserts safe fallback without capture when generation-id mismatch occurs.
Feature flag: runtime.cudagraph.exact_match_fallback=true/false (default: false). If you see unexpected output regressions after enabling, flip flag off to revert to exact-match captures. Monitor cudagraph_reuse_ratio and fallback_count. If fallback_count spikes > 5% of captures, enable additional warmup probes or increase capture-bucket granularity.
Diego: Can you explain the rationale for the prefix-compat rule? Aisha: Prefix-compat covers the common decode pattern where inputs vary only in trailing padding or short lookahead; it avoids creating a distinct graph per minor sequence-length delta. Lina: The KV-cache generation-id stamp seems safe but we should ensure it doesn't persist across serialization. Aisha: generation-id is ephemeral and excluded from persisted snapshots by the cache serializer; added a unit test to assert this. Vikram: CI GPU integration flaked on the first run (OOM in bench_script) — re-ran with larger instance and pushed a small guard to limit max-warmup-batch in bench. Diego: Approved after tests and minor doc tweak. Merge performed with squash-merge.
Reduced CUDA graph re-captures by introducing a dynamic shape compatibility layer and KV-cache-safe replay path; emits new metric cudagraph_reuse_ratio; conservative default behavior with a feature flag for exact-match fallback.

Problem: When a TP replica is wedged (collective stall / scheduler starvation / heartbeat gap), we currently keep routing new work to it until upstream timeouts/backpressure eventually trigger. This amplifies p99, increases queue depth, and can cascade into autoscaling thrash. This PR wires the TP stall signal into overload protection so that once a replica is suspected-stalled it is immediately marked DEGRADING and stops accepting new requests; callers either get a fast, structured overload response or (when possible) are redirected to healthy replicas. Approach: 1) Introduce a "replica degraded" state driven by TP stall detector signals (from ENG-4823) with hysteresis to avoid flapping. 2) Teach the local admission controller + router to consult degraded state and load-shed before enqueue. 3) Surface a structured error code for clients and for internal retry logic, and export metrics so SRE can alert on load-shed events and correlate to heartbeat gaps. Behavior: - If tp_stall_detector trips for a replica (stall_reason != none) OR heartbeat gap exceeds threshold, set replica_state=DEGRADED for min 30s, then transition to RECOVERING once heartbeat resumes for a stable window. - While DEGRADED, admission controller rejects new requests with error_code=RUNTIME_TP_REPLICA_DEGRADED (HTTP 503 for hosted gateway, internal status for Dedicated). - Router: if other replicas for the same model+profile are healthy, redirect (internal reroute) before rejecting; otherwise fail fast to avoid unbounded queueing. - Existing in-flight requests are not force-cancelled by this change (watchdog/abort in ENG-4826 handles that path); this change only prevents pile-on. Metrics/logging: - runtime_tp_replica_degraded (gauge, labels: model, tp_degree, reason) - runtime_tp_load_shed_requests_total (counter, labels: reason, route, model) - Structured log at state transitions with replica_id, rank, reason, heartbeat_age_ms. Risk/mitigation: Primary risk is false positives causing unnecessary shedding. Mitigations: (a) hysteresis + minimum degraded window, (b) feature flag runtime.tp_load_shed_on_stall (default off in prod; enabled in canary), (c) metrics to quantify shed rate vs real stalls. Testing: Unit tests for state machine/hysteresis; integration test with simulated stall signal verifies that new requests are rejected/redirected while old requests continue (until watchdog in separate PR).
Sofia Ivanova (review): Can we ensure we don’t shed due to a single transient heartbeat miss? We’ve seen short gaps during prefill spikes. Also, what’s the ordering between scheduler backpressure vs this new degraded gate?
Julian Moore (author): Yep. The degraded transition requires either (a) stall_reason emitted (non-none) OR (b) heartbeat_age_ms > tp_stall_heartbeat_gap_ms (default 5000ms). Then we hold DEGRADED for 30s minimum and require 10s of stable heartbeat to exit. Admission controller checks DEGRADED before queueing; existing scheduler backpressure still applies after that for healthy replicas.
Rafael Mendes (SRE): +1 on fast fail. Two asks: 1) please add a counter for shed-by-reason so we can alert on sudden spikes, 2) make sure the error is actionable for on-call (points to runbook/next step).

Also updated error message to include "Replica degraded due to TP stall; see runbook: runtime-tp-hang-mitigation" (internal link).

There is no double-enqueue; request_id is assigned once and only enqueued on the chosen replica. For streaming: behavior is unchanged; if the initial selection is DEGRADED, we fail fast before opening stream; if it becomes DEGRADED mid-stream, this PR does nothing (watchdog/abort handles). Added a test that asserts only one enqueue occurs per request under concurrent state updates.
Aisha Bello (review): Metric naming: please align with the TP heartbeat thread (runtime_tp_* prefix). Also add tp_degree label (we page by degree/hardware).
Julian Moore (author): Renamed metrics to runtime_tp_* and added labels: model, tp_degree, route, reason. Updated docs/internal/runtime/overload-protection.md accordingly.
Sofia Ivanova (review): One more request: make the minimum degraded window configurable. Some customers may want more aggressive recovery during canary.
Julian Moore (author): Added runtime.tp_degraded_min_duration_ms and runtime.tp_degraded_recover_stable_ms under the same flag gate; defaults set conservatively. Flag remains off by default in prod.
Rafael Mendes (approval): Looks good. Please ensure rollout uses canary + Dedicated-first as per ENG-4829; otherwise OK to merge.
Julian Moore (author): Ack. Plan is to enable flag only in perf-canary + one Dedicated canary cluster; Connor coordinating under ENG-4829.
- Runtime: when TP stall signal trips for a replica (heartbeat gap / stall reason), new requests will be load-shed (fast reject) or rerouted to healthy replicas when the feature flag runtime.tp_load_shed_on_stall is enabled. Adds metrics runtime_tp_load_shed_requests_total and runtime_tp_replica_degraded for alerting/correlation.

Motivation: Provide an intentionally minimal, privacy-conscious RAG reference that runs in the browser using an embeddings-first strategy. Many RAG quickstarts rely on server-side vector stores or heavy tool scaffolding; this PR demonstrates a different tradeoff: do light retrieval and filtering client-side (IndexedDB) and keep inference calls to Redwood minimal and deterministic.

What this PR adds: a new example playbook and a tiny TS agent shim that shows how to (1) build an embeddings-first retrieval pipeline in-browser, (2) implement deterministic tool-calling hooks for structured actions (evidence highlighting, link-out), and (3) wire Redwood API calls with streaming while preserving user privacy for local context. Includes a runnable demo (static HTML + wasm-friendly bundling) and docs pages in the handbook with UX and security guidance.

Highlights / design notes: - Embeddings-first: compute or fetch embeddings and store them in IndexedDB; retrieval does cosine search with approximate top-k then re-ranks by simple heuristic to keep latency under 50ms for small corpora. - Deterministic tool-calling: agent shim exposes a small schema and deterministic validation so the server-side decoder can be used in streaming mode without speculative side effects. - Offline/limited connectivity: demo demonstrates graceful degradation when API calls fail (cached answers, fallback to conservative summaries). - Security: guidance for public sites, advice to avoid embedding PII in local stores, and a pattern for ephemeral key rotation when using hosted Redwood.

Files changed include a new example directory (redwood-examples/browser-rag-embeddings-playbook/) and two handbook pages under redwood-docs. The demo is designed to be copy-paste runnable and includes a minimal build step (esbuild) and an optional wasm cosine-distance helper for larger corpora.

Checklist: - [x] Example code and README - [x] Demo HTML + minimal build scripts - [x] Handbook/guide + diagrams - [x] TS SDK sample wiring (browser-safe) - [x] Security section and suggested CSP/KMS patterns - [x] Unit tests for indexing + retrieval shim - [x] CI runs green (one flaky CI lint re-run required)

Related: ENG-3421 (embeddings-first experimentation), PM-118 (docs milestone). Not a breaking change.

How to run the demo locally: 1) cd redwood-examples/browser-rag-embeddings-playbook/demo 2) npm install && npm run build 3) serve -s dist 4) open http://localhost:5000 and follow onboarding to index a small corpus or pull sample embeddings.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the handbook language (clarity for product-facing engineers), the privacy guidance, and the deterministic tool schema shape (agent.ts). The shim and example are intentionally small — we want them to be safe to link-to from the docs site and usable as a starting point for partners building client-side augmentation flows.

Motivation: many tenants run conservative batch/cache/quant defaults which leave cost on the table or cause poor tail latency during bursty traffic. This PR introduces the 'cost-hopper' batcher: a lightweight policy layer that probes multiple batching shapes at runtime, hops between them to maintain latency SLOs, and surfaces per-tenant quantization tier guidance. The feature bundles three pieces: (1) cost-hopper scheduler: a tenant-scoped batching policy that dynamically selects batch shapes based on short-term latency and unit-econ signals; (2) quant-tier advisor: an offline/online guidance engine that recommends safe quantization tiers per model/tenant and produces a confidence score usable by rollout policies; (3) defaults exporter: a CLI and API to export suggested batching+cache+quant defaults as YAML for tenant onboarding. What changed: modified serving runtime scheduler to accept batching policy hooks; added a new 'cost_hopper' policy implementation with probe and decay windows; added quant-tier advisor service and an export CLI command under tools/quantcli; wired policy controls into the Console rollout UI (flags to force a policy or set sampling rate). Safety: default behavior is opt-in and sampling-only for first 24h, the policy refuses to pick quant tiers that the advisor marks 'low-confidence' unless explicitly allowed. Includes unit and integration tests and a canary rollout plan. Checklist: - implemented runtime policy, - added quant advisor and scoring, - CLI exporter and docs, - unit tests and integration tests, - perf bench and tenant-canary plan, - migration to settings API for tenant defaults. Testing summary: local unit tests and linters; synthetic perf bench against small Llama-like model; tenant canary run on staging for 48h; manual QA in Console. Related: ENG-4821 (cost-hopper design), PM-721 (defaults UX).
Rohan: Can you clarify how the probe window size is chosen? It looked aggressive in the first perf run.
Author(Ava): Probe window is tenant-adaptive; default 200ms but we scale up if variance is high. Added comments and a config knob.

Author: expanded docs to include false-positive handling and rollback guidance.

Introduce 'cost-hopper' dynamic batching policy and quant-tier guidance. Opt-in sampling rollout only. Provides per-tenant suggested batching/caching/quant defaults exportable via tools/quantcli. Improves steady-throughput efficiency and can reduce unit cost by ~10% for compatible workloads. See docs/ops/cost_hopper_best_practices.md for rollout steps.
Default is opt-in sampling; to enable for a tenant set tenant.settings.batch_policy = 'cost_hopper' and sampling_rate <= 0.05. Migrations include adding settings key; rollback removes policy entry and reverts to tenant default batcher.

Motivation: continuous-batcher tail latency incidents in multi-tenant workloads indicated intermittent starvation of low-throughput routes when high-concurrency KV-heavy requests arrived in bursts. This PR introduces a windowed adaptive backlog arbitration layer that observes short-term queue horizons and dynamically relaxes slot reservation decay per tenant/model to prevent starvation while preserving global throughput and batching efficiency. Design: 1) backlog window sampler: track per-route backlog distribution over a sliding 250ms window (configurable) and compute a backlog score that combines queue length, mean wait, and recent preemption events; 2) adaptive arbitration policy: translate backlog score into a temporary soft-reservation multiplier with exponential decay tuned to workload shape to avoid long-lived priority inversion; 3) humane soft-timeout: replace hard preempt timeouts with jittered, gradually escalating soft timeouts to give KV-heavy requests a chance to finish in degraded kernel paths; 4) KV-cache hinting: add a small hinting hook so the scheduler can mark certain requests for proactive KV prefetch based on backlog trend; 5) observability: new metrics (backlog_score, soft_reservation_factor, humane_timeout_ms) and a console dashboard tile to visualize arbitration activity. Backwards compatibility: all knobs are feature-gated under runtime.flags.windowed_arbitration, default-on in canary clusters only until validated. Benchmarks: microbenchmarks on an 8xA100 cluster with realistic mixed workloads (chat embeddings + backend reranking) show 95th token latency reduced by ~18% on samples that previously suffered starvation, median unchanged, end-to-end throughput stable (+1%). Cost per token for the workload showed a 2% improvement due to fewer hedged re-requests. Implementation notes: conservative defaults chosen to avoid excessive batching churn; ability to pin per-tenant policies via config file; unit and bench coverage added. Rollout: staged canary -> region rollout with telemetry checks and automated rollback on spike of hedging or token spillover. See release_notes and docs for tuning guidance.
Diego: Can you justify the 250ms window choice? It may be too short for some reranking workloads. Author: perf sweep showed 200-500ms works; 250ms is conservative and configurable via runtime.flags.windowed_arbitration.window_ms.
Lena: Concern about interaction with kv-prefetch causing extra memory pressure. Author: hinting is advisory only and gated; prefetch budget uses same cache admission heuristics to avoid noise.
Marcus: Tests look good but add a flaky guard for bench harness on CI. Author: added retry logic and a bounding cfg so CI bench runs are stable.
Introduce windowed adaptive backlog arbitration for continuous-batcher. Improves tail latency under bursty KV-heavy workloads and reduces unnecessary hedging. New flags: runtime.flags.windowed_arbitration.*, observability metrics added.
payload.title: Windowed adaptive backlog arbitration to reduce continuous-batcher starvation

Context: As we expand shadow traffic dogfood + Dedicated beta, we need a minimal but actionable alert set that (a) catches true quality regressions early and (b) catches pipeline issues (ingestion/scoring lag) that would make the deltas unreliable. This PR adds Alertmanager rules + routing for shadow quality regression detection and scoring pipeline health, with runbook links and sane default thresholds. Scope: (1) New recording rules for shadow quality deltas and confidence gating; (2) Alert rules for quality regression (p0/p1), missing data, and scoring lag/backlog; (3) Alertmanager routing to the Shadow Traffic beta oncall rotation with dedup keys that avoid cardinality blowups; (4) Runbook links and dashboard annotations used in notifications. Key design points: - Regression alerts are gated on minimum sample size + confidence (avoid noisy paging). We only page when both (i) sample count >= threshold and (ii) the 95% CI excludes 0 (or baseline) for the delta; otherwise we open a ticket for investigation. - All alert labels are limited to tenant_tier / deployment_mode / route_group / metric_name / experiment_id (hashed). We explicitly do NOT include customer_id, prompt_id, model_id, or full route paths. - Fail-open principle: these alerts are for visibility only; they do not change routing/rollouts automatically. Follow-up work (separate PR): wire these alerts into Console “Quality deltas” callouts and auto-link the active shadow experiment and rollout timeline entry. Testing: validated rules in staging with replayed shadow events (dogfood tenant) and confirmed page/ticket routing + dedup behavior; verified no high-cardinality label leaks in Alertmanager. Related: ENG-5409, ENG-5415; incident follow-up SUP-28477 (missing deltas were scoring lag). Runbooks: Confluence: Eng Platform Runbooks → Shadow Traffic rollout & rollback (section “Alerts & triage”), and SRE playbook stub added under /runbooks/shadow-traffic-alerts.md.
Adds paging + ticketed alerts for shadow quality regressions and scoring pipeline lag
Routes beta customer regressions to Shadow Traffic oncall (SRE) with product/ML watchers
Links alerts to runbook steps + dashboards for quick triage

Motivation: following a recent incident where simultaneous circuit resets in multiple AZs caused an amplified eviction cascade and a regional failover storm, this change introduces a staggered circuit-reset protocol and 'eviction softening' window to smooth fallback transitions. Goals: 1) avoid synchronized circuit resets across instances and regions; 2) temporarily relax eviction aggressiveness during initial recovery to prevent downstream capacity thrashing; 3) provide observability hooks and bypass flags for on-call. High-level approach: add randomized, tunable delay windows to circuit reset logic (default jitter 10-45s per node) and implement a short-lived eviction softening mode that reduces priority eviction rates and increases token-budget thresholds for in-flight requests for 30s after a region signals recovery. Safety: default parameters are conservative; feature controlled by launch flag runtime.feature.staggeredCircuitReset and can be disabled per-region via config. Rollout plan: canary deploy to eu-west-1 (10% of nodes) for 2 hours, monitor SLO/burst evictions, then increment to 50% and full rollout. Includes hotfix path to force immediate reset for critical infra. Backwards compatibility: no API change; only affects runtime behavior. Checklist: [x] unit tests for jitter logic [x] integration test for softening window [x] observability events added [x] runbook updated [x] canary plan defined. Related work: ENG-5582, ENG-5690, incident INT-2026-02-12. Description of changes and notes on behavior are in PR comments and runbook.

Context: Our presubmit pipeline runs a monolithic linter and a broad dependency upgrade scanner which has been adding latency to author feedback loops and producing noisy dependency PRs. This change splits the presubmit linting into three fast-tiered lanes (fastpath, standard, heavy) and introduces a lightweight dependency safelisting component that quarantines known-flaky devdeps and promotes low-risk dependency bumps to a fast approval path. Motivation: reduce median presubmit latency for code changes (target < 60s for shallow edits), lower noise from dependency churn, and make it easier to roll out targeted linter updates without impacting the whole repo. What this PR does: - Adds a presubmit manifest that maps changed paths to lint tiers (fastpath covers docs, small TS/py edits; standard runs common linters; heavy runs expensive static analyzers and typecheck on larger touch areas). - Introduces a minimal Go-based presubmit agent (ci/cmd/presubmit-router) that reads the manifest, sets workflow inputs, and tags PRs with the chosen tier. - Adds tools/dep-safelister to maintain an allowlist of devdeps that may be auto-approved for minor versions and a quarantine list for flaky packages. - Refactors .github/workflows/presubmit.yml into three composite jobs and a router step that routes to the appropriate lane. - Documentation: docs/presubmit.md describes the tiering rules, signals for escalation, and how to add packages to the safelist. Rollout plan: staged rollout on the repo: 1) deploy presubmit-router in dry-run mode for two weeks, 2) enable fastpath routing for docs and small edits, 3) opt-in standard/heavy lanes for teams, 4) start auto-approving low-risk dep bumps after monitoring. Checklist (author): [x] manifests and tests for tier mapping, [x] unit tests for dep-safelister, [x] end-to-end smoke run in ephemeral branch, [x] docs updated. Checklist (ops): [x] add router to allowed workflows in org policies, [x] prepare rollback (revert to single presubmit workflow). Commits (high-level): see commits field for messages. Changed areas (high level): .github/workflows/presubmit.yml, ci/presubmit/router.go (new), tools/dep-safelister/{main.go,policy.yaml}, scripts/bootstrap-presubmit.sh (reworked), docs/presubmit.md, tests/presubmit/tier-mapping.test.yaml. Testing performed: - Local unit tests for router and safelister (go test). - Full presubmit simulation on a fork with 120 synthetic PRs covering docs, small code, and large refactors. - Canary: enabled fastpath for the docs team for 48 hours, observed median queue time drop from 110s to 47s. Risks and mitigations: - Misclassification could under-run heavy linters: router defaults to next-higher tier when path heuristics are ambiguous. - Auto-approve of dep bumps could surface supply-chain risk: safelist only targets devdeps and minor semver bumps; release notes require manual review for prod deps. Related: ENG-4582 presubmit performance sprint; ENG-4620 dep hygiene initiative. Merge: squash merge after reviewer approvals.
Alexei Morozov: Can we make the router heuristics deterministic by adding a path-weight table? Response: added a tier priority table and unit tests (see tests/presubmit/tier-mapping.test.yaml).
Jordan Kim: Dep safelist seems powerful — how do we revoke an entry? Response: policy.yaml includes a revocation window and safelist entries require 2 approvers from infra. Added documentation in docs/presubmit.md.
Samira Patel: CI flakes in heavy lane might still block merges. Suggest adding an auto-fallback to rerun heavy jobs as separate nightlies. Response: agreed; added fallback to nightly heavy-linting job and a note in the rollout plan.
Introduce tiered presubmit linting (fastpath/standard/heavy) to reduce author wait time and add a dev dependency safelister to reduce noisy dep PRs. No user-facing changes. Ops: follow rollout steps in docs/presubmit.md.
