Summary: Implements a SlotLifecycleManager and a smoothed-pin eviction policy to reduce churn in the paged KV block manager. The change introduces a per-CPU recyclable slot pool, an EWMA-based 'smoothed' pin score for pins that briefly spike, and low-latency background compaction windows to avoid interfering with hot-path token generation. Motivation: Recent canaries and perf lab runs showed that short-lived hot prefixes and bursty access patterns cause repeated pin/unpin churn, increasing CPU time in the allocator and causing tail latency spikes. This PR reduces the frequency of hard evictions and makes pin decisions more stable under bursty workloads.

Design & key changes: - New component: src/kv/slot_lifecycle.rs (SlotLifecycleManager). Responsible for tracking slot states (hot, warm, cold) and scheduling reclaim/compaction work off the critical path. - Smoothed-pin policy: we use a lightweight EWMA on access timestamps to compute a pin_score per slot. Short bursts raise the score but decay quickly; the eviction decision uses a delta threshold to avoid immediate unpin on transient drops. - Per-CPU recyclable slot pools: reduce global contention by returning freed slots to a per-cpu ring buffer; global pooling only used when per-cpu pools are low. - Deferred compaction windows: compaction and slab merge tasks are scheduled by the lifecycle manager and throttled by realtime load signals (continuous batching backlog and CPU utilization). - Config knobs: kv.slot_lifecycle.enabled, kv.smoothed_pin.alpha, kv.percpu_pool_size, kv.compaction.load_threshold. Defaults chosen to be conservative and disabled in private installer until canary completes.

Commits (high-level): - a1b3d7c: Add SlotLifecycleManager scaffolding, metrics and basic lifecycle state machine - 5f2e9a1: Implement smoothed-pin EWMA, per-cpu recycler and fastpath for hot slots - c9d1f4b: Add benches, unit tests, docs, feature flags and rollout knobs

Files changed (high-level): - src/kv/slot_lifecycle.rs (new) - src/kv/allocator.rs (policy hooks and interfaces) - src/kv/slot_table.rs (pin/unpin instrumentation) - runtime/batching/scheduler.rs (load signal hook) - benches/kv_reuse_bench.rs (bench harness) - tests/slot_lifecycle_test.rs (unit + integration) - docs/perf/kv_strategy.md - config/defaults.toml

Benchmarks & results (perf lab): All numbers are median over 10 runs on a Dedicated 4xA100 canary with production-like trace. Workload: mixed read-heavy prefix cache with bursts.
- Throughput (tokens/sec): +18% on steady-state multi-client load. - P99 generation latency: -12% on KV-hit-heavy profiles. - Eviction CPU cycles: -34% measured in allocator flame graphs. - Scheduling contention (lock hold time in allocator): -27%. - Memory fragmentation (internal metric): -8% reduction after longer runs.

Testing & validation: - Unit tests for lifecycle transitions and EWMA math. - Integration tests for per-cpu recycler under concurrency (stress). - Perf bench added and run in benchmark-lab with CI artifacts attached. - Canary rollout plan: enable feature flag for 5% of Dedicated capacity, monitor allocator CPU, p99 tail, and KV hit ratio for 48 hours, then expand.

Rollout & rollback plan: Feature gated. Default OFF for Private installer until we complete enterprise canary (expected 2 weeks). Rollback toggles via kv.slot_lifecycle.enabled=false which immediately returns behavior to previous allocator fastpath. In-flight requests are not affected; background tasks will drain.

Observability & metrics added: - kv.slot_lifecycle.evictions - kv.slot_lifecycle.reclaimed_slots_per_sec - kv.slot_lifecycle.pin_score_ewma_p50/p95 - allocator.percpu_pool_hits

Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-2345) - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Benchmarks in perf lab - [x] Config knobs and PRD/rollout plan - [x] Docs updated

Review conversation (selected): - Noah Kim: "Can you explain why EWMA and not a tiny TTL? What's the expected sensitivity tradeoff?" - Aditi: "EWMA gives us fine-grained sensitivity control and smooth decay without allocating per-slot timers. The alpha is configurable; a TTL would need busy timers or coarse time buckets which had higher overhead in benchmarks." - Ethan Brooks: "Per-cpu pool sounds good, but what about long-tail starving and stealing?" - Aditi: "Pools can be stolen by the global pool when low; stealing is implemented with an O(1) batch move to amortize cost. Tests exercise steal under heavy allocations." - Priya Nair: "Please add a knob to disable background compaction in private installer — I see you did that in defaults, thanks." - Priya (approval): "LGTM after small comment about metric tagging."

CI: All checks passed (unit, integration, lint, benchmark job). One flaky test in earlier run (tests/slot_lifecycle_test::concurrency_stress) failed once and was rerun and passed; added additional backoff in test harness to reduce flakiness.

Merge & follow-ups: Squash-merged to main on 2025-11-20. Follow-up tickets created: ENG-2501 (observability dashboard), ENG-2502 (canary automation for slot_lifecycle), and a small perf tweak ENG-2503 to expose per-cpu pool stats to the console.

Motivation: Tighten the separation between tenant residency metadata and operator-level privileges while preserving necessary operational workflows. This PR implements a 'geo-blindness protector' layer that prevents operator principals from observing tenant geographic residency unless explicitly authorized, and introduces a KMS claim mapper to propagate and enforce residency claims at encryption/decryption time.

Summary of changes: Adds an RBAC v2 policy plugin that evaluates operator tokens against tenant residency claims and denies access when the operator is not allowed to view or act on region-pinned tenants; introduces pkg/kms/claim_mapper which attaches and validates a residency claim to KMS envelope metadata; enriches audit logging with residency_tag and residency_evidence fields so compliance teams can trace decisions; provides a migration tool to backfill residency_tag for historical audit rows based on key usage heuristics; updates the policy compiler with residency-aware predicates and a new operator_scope template; includes unit and integration tests and example policies.

Checklist: 
- [x] RBAC v2 policy module + unit tests
- [x] KMS claim mapper + integration tests (simulated KMS in CI)
- [x] Audit enrichment + backfill migration script
- [x] Policy compiler templates and docs snippets
- [x] E2E regression tests for operator workflows
- [x] Performance baseline (no >2% p95 latency regression on token validation)

Commits summary: 
- a1b2c3d add rbav2 residency predicate and operator_scope template
- b2c3d4e implement kms claim mapper and envelope metadata encoding
- c3d4e5f add audit enrichment and backfill migration script
- d4e5f6a add unit + integration tests and test fixtures

Notes on scope and risk: The residency claim is an opaque assertion (string tag + evidence hash) carried in the KMS envelope metadata. The claim_mapper enforces that decryption requires a residency-scope permit when the envelope has a residency_tag and the requesting principal lacks a residency grant. Motivation: We need a low-friction, deterministic way to prepare and promote model rollout state across environments (hosted, dedicated, private) without long-lived in-memory locks or heavy orchestration dependencies. This PR introduces a lightweight snapshot sequencing mechanism that captures the minimal rollout state needed to drive deterministic cutover and to safely rewind when SLO gates fail. Design summary: 1) compact snapshot format (protobuf-compact) that records cohort allocations, prefix cache hints, KV cache anchors, and cutover tokens; 2) idempotent preflight checks that can be executed against a dry-run replay harness to validate latency/cost smoke signals before promoting traffic; 3) deterministic cutover algorithm that promotes cohorts in a reproducible order (session-anchored) to maintain session affinity guarantees and make post-mortem replay simpler; 4) rollback anchors: snapshots include back-reference anchors so a promotion can be reverted by applying an earlier snapshot without requiring live consensus; 5) operator reconciliation: the rollout-controller CRD accepts snapshot payloads and drives the promotion state machine without mutating live routing paths until cutover completes. What changed: - Serving runtime: new sequencer plugin (serving/rollout/sequencer.go) and snapshot serializer for compact state. - Operator: rollout-controller can accept snapshot CRDs and run preflight/dry-run (operator/controllers/rollout_controller.go). - Console: new snapshot editor and diff view for dry-run results (console/ui/rollouts/snapshot-editor.tsx). - Charts: operator CRD and RBAC updates for snapshot handling (charts/redwood-operator/templates/rollout-crd.yaml). - Tests: integration dry-run and replay harness (tests/integration/snapshot_replay_test.go). Rollout plan and safety: this PR ships behind a feature flag rollout.snapshot_sequencer. Default behavior is unchanged. The sequencer supports dry-run-only runs (no traffic change) and can be toggled to perform a live deterministic cutover once smoke signals pass. Preflight checks are idempotent and safe to run repeatedly. Checklist: - [x] unit tests for serializer and sequencer state transitions - [x] operator e2e dry-run and live promotion tests - [x] console snapshot editor wired to preview API - [x] docs and runbook for disaster recovery and manual revert - [x] CI pipeline updated to include snapshot-e2e stage Security and performance notes: snapshots are encrypted at rest and in-flight (KMS). Compact format reduces operator memory pressure; sequencer runs are bounded and yield to normal request processing. Backwards compatibility: operator tolerates old rollout CRDs; if snapshot payloads are present but feature flag is disabled, they are stored but not executed. Migration: no data migration required. Related work and context: builds on ENG-4521 (stable-session-affinity) and ENG-4680 (rollback-anchors). This is intended to reduce toil during canary/A-B promotions and to make replayable rollouts first-class. Notes for reviewers: look at sequencer preflight idempotency and the operator reconciliation loop where snapshot state is converted into a promote plan. The description above contains the runbook for toggling the feature flag and emergency revert steps.
Marco Liu: Can we guarantee the sequencer run won't starve request threads under heavy load? Suggest yielding every 200ms and adding metrics for run_duration.
Aisha Patel: Added yielding logic + metrics (run_duration_ms, bytes_serialized). Also moved expensive validation off the hotpath into a background verifier.
Kenji Yamamoto: Operator reconciliation looks good but please add an exponential backoff on failed dry-run attempts to avoid tight retry loops.
Aisha Patel: Backoff added and tests updated to assert backoff behavior.
Sofia Becker: Verified the console diff UI and ran the e2e dry-run; approving pending changelog entry.
Sofia Becker: Approved.
Introduce a feature-flagged snapshot rollout sequencer: compact rollout snapshots, deterministic cutover, idempotent preflight dry-run, and console snapshot preview. Disabled by default; enable via rollout.snapshot_sequencer. See docs/runbooks/snapshot-rollouts.md for operator runbook and emergency revert steps.
Feature flagged; recommend limited rollout to internal customers first and monitoring of sequencer.run_duration_ms, rollout.preflight_failures, and snapshot.serialize_bytes.

Motivation: Presubmit latency and noisy dependency churn have been two recurring developer pain points. This PR refactors the presubmit artifact pruner to be stage-aware, introduces a lightweight presubmit runner that does fast lint+type checks for most PRs, and adds a Dependency Steward component (opt-in) that surfaces suspected dev-dep rot and creates curated rotation PRs. Summary of changes: - Stage-aware artifact pruner: pruner now prunes only artifacts for long-running lanes and preserves fastpath caches for tagged fast-lane PRs. This reduces redundant cache eviction and warms fastpath caches more reliably. - Lightweight presubmit runner: a small Go runner that executes a minimal lint/type subset using cached toolchains. New fastpath lane runs in ~30s on average for changed JS/TS/Go packages. - Dependency Steward: watches package lockfiles, runs a lightweight compatibility probe (matrix of latest patch/minor versions) and opens an automated PR template with suggested updates and risk tags. This component is opt-in via a repo label (deps/auto). - CI wiring and release hooks: composer for presubmit lanes adjusted to avoid running full integration matrix on docs-only or trivial changes; release smoke now runs only after merge in release lanes. - Observability: added presubmit-duration and dep-steward-created metrics, and a small dashboard link. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for pruner and runner - [x] E2E smoke in the fastpath lane - [x] Integration test for DepSteward probe harness - [x] Docs updated (devtools/presubmit.md) - [x] Linear tickets linked Implementation notes: commits are structured to separate the pruner refactor from the new runner and the dep steward. The runner is intentionally minimal; any heavy checks are still gated into the existing heavy-lane workflows. Security: DepSteward does not have write-by-default; it opens PRs and requires repo-level approval. The agent uses the existing bot user and KMS keys. Migration plan: rollout is staged: (1) enable fastpath lane for a small set of repos, (2) monitor presubmit-duration and CI failure modes for two weeks, (3) enable DepSteward on opt-in repos and monitor for false positives. Related: ENG-2142 (presubmit performance), ENG-3384 (dep rotation pilot). Links: internal doc https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-2142/presubmit-fastpath-runner and design spec in docs/devtools/dep-steward.md.

Summary: This PR harmonizes three related ergonomic surfaces across the Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs: prefetch/retry profiles used by credential prewarming, the async streaming iterator surface (pull/push parity), and a tiny compatibility shim to smooth credential rotation during streaming bursts.

Motivation: teams building low-latency, high-throughput inference pipelines reported brittle reauth during short-lived spikes (SUP-788) and inconsistent examples across SDKs. This change reduces N+1 credential lookups, tightens retry windows for streaming heartbeats, and exposes a small opt-in shim that keeps long-lived stream cursors resilient during token swap.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-4206) - [x] Py/TS/Go API prototypes implemented - [x] Unit tests for retry windows and prefetch logic - [x] Cross-SDK examples updated - [x] Perf microbenchmark run against perf-canary and passed latency regressions thresholds

What this changes (high level): - Introduces a declarative prefetch profile table that maps workload shapes (short-chat, long-form, embeddings-batch) to pre-warm behaviors (initial token prefetch, credential lease duration, heartbeat cadence). Implemented in each SDK with the same JSON schema. - Normalizes the async streaming consumer to prefer a pull-iterator idiom but exposes a push-friendly adapter in TS and Go for existing callers. Python now exposes an AsyncStream.peek() helper to inspect the next envelope without consuming, matching TS's peekable generator and Go's StreamCursor.Peek. - Adds a compatibility shim (CredentialLeaseMapper) that accepts multiple credential sources and performs a best-effort lease handoff during reauth. The shim is opt-in (enabled via client config prefetch_profiles.enable_lease_mapper). - Tightens default retry/backoff for streaming heartbeats: shorter initial retry (100ms -> 40ms) with capped exponential and jitter tuned to reduce thundering herds observed in oncall traces. - SDK versions bumped: python -> 1.14.0, typescript -> 2.8.0, go -> v1.9.5.

Commits (summary): - "add prefetch profile schema and loader in sdk-core" - "python: implement prefetch profiles, add AsyncStream.peek and tests" - "typescript: introduce PrefetchConfig, add peekable generator adapter, bump to 2.8.0" - "go: add StreamCursor.Peek and CredentialLeaseMapper, bump v1.9.5" - "contrib: update examples/prefetch and docs crosslinks"

Files touched (high level examples): - sdk-core/prefetch/schema.json - python/redwood_sdk/prefetch.py - python/tests/test_prefetch_profiles.py - python/redwood_sdk/streaming/async_stream.py (adds peek, leaner retry settings) - typescript/src/prefetch/config.ts - typescript/src/stream/peekable_generator.ts - typescript/test/streaming/prefetch.test.ts - go/sdk/prefetch/prefetch.go - go/sdk/stream/cursor.go - go/sdk/stream/lease_mapper.go - docs/sdk/prefetch.md - examples/multi-sdk/prefetch-demo/* (ts/py/go short examples)

Design notes and rationale: - Keep the schema stable and language-agnostic: a small JSON table with three canonical workload shapes. This allows ops teams to export/import profile configs between environments. - Opt-in shim: the CredentialLeaseMapper intentionally does not change default auth behavior; customers enabling it get smoother lease handoffs at the cost of an additional prefetch call. - Retry tuning: we conservatively shortened the initial retry to reduce end-to-end cold-start p99s for small batches. Benchmarks showed ~12% p99 improvement on short-chat trace shape.

Review conversation (selected snippets): - Marco Ruiz (review): "Please call out the failure modes when the lease mapper can't find a fresh token; will we end up double-issuing refreshes?" - Aisha (author): "Mapper uses a single-flight guard per client, so refreshes dedupe; added test to assert single-refresh under concurrent triggers." - Linnea Berg: "Is the new peek() API safe for buffered streams? Could consumers accidentally starve prefetch?" - Aisha: "peek() is read-only and bounds-checks against the prefetch buffer; docblock shows recommended patterns. Also added a linter rule note for stream implementations." - Daniel Cho (review): "TS/Go adapters are slightly different in ergonomics; can we add a small migration note?" - Aisha: "Added migration section in docs and examples with 3 patterns: (1) minimal opt-in (enable_lease_mapper), (2) explicit migration (replace push-consumers with pull+peek), (3) compatibility path (use adapter)."

CI and validation: - Initial run: CI failed on Go unit test (race in lease_mapper) and Python lint rule (line-length in docs). - Fixes: added singleflight mutex and trimmed long lines. - Final CI: all checks passed: unit, integration (sample harness against perf-canary), linters, typechecks. Merge: merged via squash commit into main on 2026-02-26.

Post-merge actions: - Publish SDK releases: py 1.14.0 (wheel + sdist), ts 2.8.0 (npm tag beta then latest), go v1.9.5 (module tag) - Update quickstarts in docs site and add a migration snippet under "Streaming and Auth" - Communicate to SRE and Solutions: brief on heartbeat tuning and lease mapper opt-in - Watch perf-canary and telemetry for first 48h for any regressions

Migration notes (concise): - If you rely on push-based streams in TS/Go, use the provided adapter (peekable_generator / StreamCursor.Adapter). - To enable lease handoffs set client config prefetch_profiles.enable_lease_mapper=true and monitor credential refresh metrics. - No change required for basic token-based auth; shim is opt-in.

Follow-ups (tracked): - ENG-4299: expose telemetry hooks for lease handoff events - ENG-4312: experiment with adaptive prefetch profiles based on observed sequence lengths - ENG-4400: add opt-out telemetry to measure mapper adoption
Coordinated SDK changes: introduce prefetch profiles, stabilize stream async-iterator ergonomics, add lightweight compatibility shim for credential rotation. Version bumps: Python v1.14.0, TS v2.8.0, Go v1.9.5. No API-breaking changes expected; migration notes included.
Marco Ruiz: Please call out the failure modes when the lease mapper can't find a fresh token; will we end up double-issuing refreshes?
Aisha Kaplan: Mapper uses a single-flight guard per client, so refreshes dedupe; added test to assert single-refresh under concurrent triggers.
Linnea Berg: Is the new peek() API safe for buffered streams? Could consumers accidentally starve prefetch?
Aisha Kaplan: peek() is read-only and bounds-checks against the prefetch buffer; docblock shows recommended patterns. Also added a linter rule note for stream implementations.
Daniel Cho: TS/Go adapters are slightly different in ergonomics; can we add a small migration note?
Aisha Kaplan: Added migration section in docs and examples with 3 patterns: minimal opt-in, explicit migration, compatibility path.
CI Bot: go test failed (race) on first run; subsequent CI passed after mutex singleflight fix.
QA: Integration tests exercised short-chat and embeddings shapes; observed expected p99 improvement for short-chat.

Motivation: Production canaries today make decisions largely on isolated metrics (latency, error rate). For model rollouts we frequently observe subtle signal cross-talk where small upstream quality shifts (e.g. subtle bias or context-sensitive hallucinations) are not surfaced by any single metric until the rollout is large. This PR implements a \"signal-fused holdpoint\" canary that aggregates orthogonal signals (latency p99, completion error counts, toxicity regression, hallucination proxy score, user satisfaction proxy) into a single holdpoint decision function and wires an automated replay playbook to validate suspected regressions. Design: 1) New canary controller mode: holdpoint-fusion. The controller computes a weighted fusion score from configurable signal streams. When the fusion score crosses a soft threshold, the canary pauses and triggers the replay playbook. 2) Debiasing probe: we add a stratified sampling probe that runs targeted prompts (demographic/edge-cases) against canary and baseline and computes an effect-size for bias regressions. 3) Replay playbook: sampled production requests (shadow) are snapshot and replayed against the candidate model with randomized context variations and adversarial perturbations. Results are summarized into a compact regression report with example pairs to surface human-reviewable diffs. 4) Integration with rollback hooks: on hard-threshold breach the controller can trigger either instant rollback or staged drain with annotated telemetry. 5) New telemetry: fusion_score, bias_effect_size, replay_regression_count, replay_artifacts_s3_key. 6) CLI / API flags: --enable-holdpoint-fusion, --fusion-thresholds, --replay-depth. Checklist: - [x] Controller fusion algorithm with pluggable signal adapters - [x] Stratified debiasing probe and dataset shards - [x] Replay orchestration and safe storage of artifacts - [x] E2E smoke tests in perf-canary lab - [x] Console dashboard panels and alert rules - [x] Docs update (rollouts playbook) Commits summary: - init: add holdpoint fusion controller scaffolding - adds: debiasing probe service and sample datasets - implements: replay orchestrator and artifact uploader - tests: smoke + integration harness updates - docs: rollout-playbook.md and console dashboard config Changed areas (high level): - controllers/canary/holdpoint_fusion_controller.py (new) - probes/debiasing_probe/ (new service and dataset shards) - replay/orchestrator.py (new) - telemetry/metrics_registry.yaml (adds fusion_score and replay metrics) - console/dashboards/holdpoint_playbook.json (dashboard panels) - tests/integration/test_holdpoint_fusion.py - examples/rollouts/playbook_sample.md Review conversation: \"Ava Martinez: Nice end-to-end. A few questions on the replay artifact retention (cost) — can we TTL by default?\" \"Author Rohit Shah: TTL config added, default 7 days; retention is configurable via replay.ttl_days in config.\" \"Ellen Park: Fusion weights need sane defaults; can we expose them as per-customer overrides?\" \"Author Rohit Shah: Yes, weights are per-deployment and can be adjusted via the rollout policy. Added docs section.\" \"Diego Alvarez: Concern about performance impact of the debiasing probe during peak. Suggest sampling cadence and async evaluation.\" \"Author Rohit Shah: Probe runs on a low-priority background pool and honors burst budgets. Updated controller to enforce budget checks.\" CI summary: \"lint: pass\", \"unit-tests: pass (coverage delta < 0.2%)\", \"integration-tests (perf-canary): pass\", \"e2e-smoke: pass (replay harness)\" Merge notes: \"Merged by squashed commit after approvals from Ava and Ellen. Backwards compatible changes only; feature gated behind flags. Release rollout plan: enable in staging for 48 hours with conservative fusion thresholds, then ramp to canary cohorts.\"
Adds a coordinated canary mode that fuses multiple signal streams to create holdpoints, including bias debiasing checks and a replay-based verification playbook. Backwards compatible; adds new metrics and CLI flags for release gating.

Rohit Shah: Weights are configurable via rollout policy.
Diego Alvarez: Ensure probe sampling is low-priority; watch peak impact.

Add a delta-based safeguard switch and drift heuristics to trigger controlled rollbacks during canary/A-B/shadow rollouts.
Context: We observed several partial degradations during staged model rollouts where small but sustained metric deltas among specific cohorts (latency, loss, token-error-rate) progressively violated SLAs before manual intervention could fully mitigate impact. This PR adds a 'delta safeguard' — a feature flag + lightweight evaluation layer that watches cohort deltas and enforces a stop-and-rollback when configured thresholds are breached.

Motivation: Existing rollout controllers support percentage-based gates and multi-metric gates, but they lack a concise mechanism to reason about directional delta (current vs baseline) for cohort slices and automatically perform a safe rollback without operator intervention. The delta safeguard is intended to be low-latency, explainable, and reversible.

What this PR changes: - Introduces pkg/safeguards/delta_switch.go: engine that computes per-cohort deltas against pinned baseline snapshots and exposes a compact decision API to the rollout controller. - Adds lightweight cohort snapshot persistence (sqlite-backed in test/dev, KVS integration hook for production) and a periodic reconciliation loop. - Extends services/rollout/controller.go to call the delta safeguard as an additional gate during canary, A/B, and shadow phases. - Adds a soft-stop path: on first breach, rollout pauses, emits a detailed event and trace span, and runs a secondary validation window (configurable grace period) before executing rollback. - Implements an emergency fast-rollback path when deltas exceed a hard-limit threshold. - Adds end-to-end tests in tests/integration/drift_rollback_test.go that simulate gradual drift and sudden regressions. - Adds runbook docs at docs/runbooks/drift-rollback.md and small Console UI affordance to display delta reasons at the rollout details page.

Design notes and constraints: - Delta computation is intentionally simple (percentage and absolute delta with smoothing) to avoid flakiness; we purposefully avoid complex ML detectors in this first iteration. - The safeguard exposes per-metric advisory scores (0..1) and a combined decision: continue/pause/rollback. Teams can opt-in per-environment via feature flag and tune thresholds per-cohort. - Persistence: production runtime uses the platform KVS; this PR includes an adapter interface so operators can provide etcd/consul/redis-backed stores.

Checklist: - [x] Core delta engine + API - [x] Controller integration (pause + rollback hooks) - [x] E2E tests for soft-stop and hard rollback - [x] Runbook and Console visibility - [x] Feature flag gating and defaults set to off for all tenants - [x] CI green (unit + integration)

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for delta math and smoothing rules. - Integration test simulates a canary where cohort A gradually drifts beyond soft_threshold: controller pauses, waits 60s grace, then marks canary unhealthy and rolls back. - Load smoke run to validate that the delta layer adds <1% CPU cost on the controller under 1000 rps. - Manual validation run on staging with feature flag enabled for a single tenant.

Rollout plan: 1) Merge behind feature flag off by default. 2) Canary enable for platform-internal tenants for 48h. 3) Enable for customer staging environments for 72h with monitoring dashboards. 4) Open opt-in for customer teams via Console toggle. 5) Evaluate metrics and enable by default if no regressions in 2 weeks.

Related work: This complements ENG-2199 (cohort similarity routing) by giving a reactive safety layer and ties to SUP-881 for the customer-reported drift incident in Jan. Docs: docs/runbooks/drift-rollback.md.

Notes for reviewers: Focus review on decision boundaries in delta_switch.go and the reconciliation window semantics in controller.go; both are intentionally conservative. Also please check the adapter interface for persistence for any obvious race conditions.

Introduces a configurable delta-safeguard toggle and heuristics to auto-rollback model rollouts when cohort-level drift or metric delta thresholds are exceeded. No customer-facing breaking changes.
Lina Chen: Can we document the smoothing window defaults and their rationale? I had a concern about sensitivity at short windows.
Author (Maya): Added inline comments and bumped default smoothing to 30s; left config exposed for teams.
Diego Morales: Suggest using existing metrics tags (cohort_key) so dashboards automatically show the delta traces.
Author (Maya): Now emits cohort_key tag on all spans and metrics; updated tests to assert tag presence.
Priya Singh: Approving after CI green. Please squash commits and ensure runbook contains rollback run steps.
CI Bot: All checks passed (unit, integration, lint). e2e flaky test retried once and passed.

Motivation: reduce user-visible failures when clients disconnect during long-running streaming or function-invoke flows and avoid double-execution of tool calls while preserving backwards compatibility. This PR implements a lease-based session ownership model (session leases are short-lived ephemeral tokens that the client can present to resume an in-flight session), a server soft-abort signal that preserves KV cache and allows a short reconnect window, and a small streaming envelope version bump (v2) that separates structured-output frames from toolcall frames to make resume safe for function calls. Key changes: add X-RW-Session-Lease header and server-side lease manager with configurable TTL and jitter; introduce resume token format "lease:<id>:<last_ack_seq>:<sig>" and validation rules; implement soft-abort event code "rw:soft_abort" and a grace window during which server retains the session state; add tool-call fingerprinting to detect and suppress duplicate tool invocations on resume; extend streaming envelope with explicit frame types (emit, tool_call, tool_result, metadata) while translating v1 streams via an adapter for compatibility; expose metrics for lease failures, resume_success_rate, soft_abort_rate, and lease_refresh_latency; add unit/integration tests and e2e scenarios that simulate flaky networks and replayed resumes. Compatibility and rollout: v1 clients continue to work unchanged via the adapter that translates v2 envelope frames back to the v1 wire format; feature gated behind "session-lease-v2" (console flag + API header opt-in) so we can stage traffic 0%->20%->100% following Canary windows and perf guardrails. Security: resume tokens are HMAC-signed (KMS-backed signing key) and time-limited to avoid session hijack. Testing and verification: carried out deterministic replay tests for function call idempotency, 100x flaky reconnect capture tests, and benchmarks showing ~3% throughput improvement from lighter KV retention logic. Rollout plan: 1) enable gate in internal envs; 2) 20% user traffic for 48h with tight tracing; 3) 100% after validating resume success and low soft_abort rate. Checklist: [x] design doc linked; [x] proto and schema changes; [x] tests added; [x] docs and changelog; [x] feature-flag wiring; [x] metrics and alerts configured. Follow-ups: metrics SLO adjustments, add SDK helpers for automatic lease refresh, tighten default TTL based on real traffic patterns.
Introduce lease-based streaming session protocol (v2) with soft-abort semantics, resume tokens with last-ack sequencing, and adapter compatibility for v1 clients; opt-in via feature flag for staged rollout.
5 commits: 1) session lease manager and TTL logic; 2) streaming envelope v2 frames + v1 adapter translator; 3) tool-call fingerprinting and idempotency guard; 4) tests and flaky-network e2e harness; 5) docs, feature-flag wiring, and metrics/alerts.
Ethan Wallace: Nice design. Two concerns: 1) lease TTL default value (30s) may be too aggressive for high-latency mobile; recommend exposing scalar in API config. 2) Please add a unit test where resume token signature fails to ensure we close session gracefully.
Maya Chen: Addressed both. TTL is now configurable via per-customer profile and the handler returns a well-defined 410:rw_lease_expired for expired tokens. Added signature-negative test in streaming_handler_test.go.

Motivation: SDK consumers repeatedly asked for smaller, deterministic integration points for auth warmup and easier streaming consumption patterns. Current SDKs have similar behaviors implemented ad-hoc per-language; this PR unifies the core primitives and surfaces ergonomic facades in each SDK so teams can opt-in to credential priming and a fluent pullstream API without large surface changes.

Summary: This change introduces a compact credential priming policy in the shared SDK surface and language-specific ergonomic wrappers: a small Python priming facade that starts background token warmup, a TypeScript fluent pullstream consumer that turns the async iterator into a chainable DSL, and a Go adapter that provides a low-alloc pullstream handle plus an opt-in priming hook. The PR also adds cross-sdk deterministic retry matrices documentation and a short migration guide.

What I changed (high level):
- Extracted priming logic into sdks/shared/credentials/priming_policy.go and exposed a minimal API used by each SDK.
- Python: sdks/python/redwood/session/priming.py — session.priming.start(prime_before=30s) and a background worker with bounded concurrency.
- TypeScript: sdks/typescript/src/pullstream/fluent.ts — fluent .map/.filter/.batch chainable helpers and a small adapter to convert existing async iterables.
- Go: sdks/go/pullstream/adapter.go — pullstream.Handle and an OptInPriming(ctx) helper to reduce allocations in high-throughput servers.
- Tests: integration and unit tests added for priming behavior and pullstream ergonomics.
- Docs: migration guide and examples for each SDK.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc reviewed with SDK leads (ENG-4952)
- [x] Shared priming policy implemented and covered by unit tests
- [x] Language wrappers implemented and smoke-tested against staging backends
- [x] Changelogs and migration notes added
- [x] CI pipeline green after rerun

Compatibility notes: The priming API is opt-in; no breaking changes to existing public SDK surface are made by default. The new fluent pullstream is additive — consumers can migrate gradually. The shared deterministic retry matrix is documentation-only for now; follow-up PRs will wire it into client-side presets.

Benchmark & safety: Microbenchmarks show <3% latency increase at cold start for priming enabled workloads but >15% tail reduction for sustained streaming scenarios where token refresh races previously occurred. Priming defaults are conservative (disabled) and limited to the session object to avoid unexpected network traffic.

Testing/CI: All language pipelines run; intermittent flaky test in TypeScript pullstream suite was addressed by adding a short jitter in test harness. The CI run associated with this PR passed on the second attempt (flaky e2e rerun).

Review summary: See review conversation below for requested changes and responses.

Merge: squashed and merged into main on 2026-02-26. Release notes appended to SDK CHANGELOGs.

Notes for maintainers: follow-up tasks include wiring deterministic retry presets into SDK constructors (ENG-4988) and adding telemetry for priming hits/misses to the Console observability surface.
Arjun Patel: Please clarify thread-safety of the Python priming worker and ensure it cannot spawn unbounded greenlets in ASGI environments. (requested changes)
Maya Chen: Addressed — worker now uses an explicit concurrency semaphore and ties lifecycle to session.close(). Added tests for asyncio/gunicorn interop.

Added fluent pullstream convenience API in TypeScript and adapters in Python/Go
Integration tests and migration docs added
Small CI changes to stabilize flaky pullstream tests
Adds an opt-in credential priming policy (shared) and language-specific ergonomic facades: Python background priming, TypeScript fluent pullstream API, and a light Go pullstream adapter. No breaking changes by default. See SDK CHANGELOGs for per-language migration steps.

payload.body:
Motivation: multiple SDKs exposed slightly different semantics for credential windows, heartbeat behavior, and iterator ergonomics which caused intermittent token churn and surprising consumer ergonomics when failing over or reauthenticating. This PR introduces a coordinated model across Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs that normalizes credential 'grace periods' (a small buffer before expiry used to trigger preemptive reauth), surfaces a small synthetic heartbeat when the transport cannot emit keepalives, and replaces several low-level iterator primitives with a single consumer-friendly async/pull-iterator abstraction per language. Summary of changes (single continuous description): - Introduce CredentialLease/CredentialWindow: a small, configurable TTL buffer used by the client runtime to decide when to refresh or swap credentials. Default normalized window is 30s across SDKs with opt-out via explicit config. - Add synthetic heartbeat shim in transports: when a connection is idle for more than 10s and the upstream cannot emit keepalives, the SDKs will send a lightweight ping to keep session affinity and reduce accidental session eviction observed on some cloud LB configs. Heartbeat is disabled for on-prem/private deployments by default via a transport flag. - Replace legacy pull/stream iterator variants with a single PullStream/AsyncPullIterator API in TS/Py and PullIterator in Go. The new surface: - Python: AsyncPullStream (async iterator with .close() and .drain() hooks). - TypeScript: AsyncPullIterator (AsyncIterable + explicit .dispose() method). - Go: PullIterator with context-aware Next(ctx) semantics and Close(ctx). The goal: consistent ergonomics for consuming streaming responses and clear shutdown/reauth flow. - Credential fallback: introduce a small delegated-credential-fanout pattern that allows multiple credential providers (env, disk cache, delegated refresh) to race/chain with deterministic fallback order. This reduces hot path latency for common env-based tokens while supporting delegated refresh in background. - Backoff and retry presets: align default retry profile names across SDKs (default -> balanced-retries) and add an explicit short-retry preset used for streaming reconnects. - Telemetry: emit credential.window and stream.heartbeat.enabled tags to runtime traces and metrics so operators can correlate token churn to SDK behavior. - Version bumps: ts-sdk -> 1.10.0, py-sdk -> 0.46.0, go-sdk -> v1.5.3 (changelog entries included). Compatibility/migration notes: - Existing code using low-level iterator types will continue to work but will receive deprecation warnings; migration guide included in docs/ with examples for each language. - The credential window default (30s) is conservative; customers that previously relied on immediate refresh-on-expiry may observe earlier refreshes but no functional regressions. Rollout plan: staged rollout on hosted API for 2 weeks behind feature flag, then account-level opt-in, then default on in 12 weeks. Tests & validation: unit + integration matrix added for all three languages; e2e smoke against a mocked LB that simulates session eviction. See CI checks below for coverage details.
Evan Liu: Nice consolidation. Can we make the heartbeat interval configurable per-client instead of per-transport? Some internal users want per-route tuning.
Asha Patel: Thanks — added client-level override in the latest patch; transport flag remains the ultimate kill-switch for private installs.
María Gómez: TS API looks good; naming nit: AsyncPullIterator.dispose() vs .close() — prefer .dispose() to avoid confusion with stream.close().
Asha Patel: Acknowledged. TS kept .dispose(); Py provides .close() for idiomaticness and both map to the same underlying signal.
Ravi Sundaram: How do we prevent credential race storms during mass refresh? Could add randomized jitter to refresh start times.
Asha Patel: Added jitter to preemptive refresh and a short-term leader election when multiple providers are in fallback mode.
Claire Huang: Add test simulating LB churn and verify no reconnection storms.
Asha Patel: Added test matrix test/integration/streaming/session-eviction-mock.test demonstrating behavior and telemetry tags.
Normalize credential refresh window to 30s across SDKs (configurable)
Add synthetic heartbeat shim to reduce session evictions behind some load balancers (disabled in private by default)
Introduce unified PullStream/AsyncPullIterator/PullIterator consumer surface for streaming responses
Add credential fallback fanout with deterministic fallback order and jittered refresh
Align retry presets and add short-retry for streaming reconnects
SDK version bumps: typescript 1.10.0, python 0.46.0, go v1.5.3

payload.body: Motivation: reduce p50/p95 latency variability for short sequences while improving throughput for mixed-length workloads. We observed tail spikes when the continuous-batcher and the KV cache warmed up simultaneously for traffic with high small-request ratio. This PR introduces a staggered windowed attention scheduler that coordinates small 'subtile' kernel invocations with explicit KV warm-lanes, plus a lightweight subtile fusion pass that reduces kernel-launch overhead on short contexts. Summary of changes: 1) scheduler: add runtime/scheduler/staggered_scheduler.cpp (staggered policy that separates warm-lane traffic from cold misses, assigns micro-tiles to dedicated executors, and prioritizes short-seq hotpaths) 2) kernels: add runtime/attn/subtile_kernel.cu and runtime/attn/subtile_fuse_pass.cc (subtile is a small-window Flash-inspired kernel optimized for seq_len <= 64; fusion pass folds rotary/unapply steps to remove an extra transpose) 3) kv: add runtime/kv/warm_lane.cpp and warm_lane.h (a tiny lane allocator that prefetches KV pages for hot prefixes and exposes a warm token to the scheduler) 4) orchestration: hooks in runtime/orchestrator/continuous_batcher.cpp to surface warm-lane hints and schedule micro-batches without flushing the KV cache 5) tests/bench/windowed_prefetch_bench.py and tests/unit/test_warm_lane.py 6) docs/perf/attn-windowed-warmlanes.md. Key design details: - Staggered policy keeps a short-latency lane and a warm-lane pool; the short lane uses the subtile kernel and avoids preemption by large-batch coalescing. - Warm-lanes maintain a small LRU of KV page IDs and drive async prefetches; scheduler uses a 3-level priority score (latency-sensitivity, cache-affinity, batchable). - Subtile kernel implements a fused rotary application + QK partial reduction, avoiding an intermediate transpose for small windows; uses warp-level accumulators and avoids shared-memory for >32 heads to minimize bank conflicts. - Continuous batching changes: the batcher now exposes 'microbatch affinity' to indicate compatibility with subtile execution, enabling continuous flushless batching for sequences composed predominantly of short tokens. Performance: - Internal bench (g4dn-like node) on mixed chat workload (60% seq<=32, 30% seq 64-128, 10% >256): p50 latency improved 9.4%, p95 improved 12.1%, overall throughput improved 18% at 95% utilization. - Cold-start KV tail (first request after model swap) reduced from median 120ms extra to 72ms extra for hot prefixes (40% reduction). - Microbench of subtile kernel vs generic kernel for seq=32 shows 2.3x reduction in kernel launch overhead and 1.6x token/sec improvement. Backwards compatibility: fallback to existing flash/attn path when subtile guard conditions fail (seq>64 or incompatible head counts). Flags: runtime.feature.subtile=true (off by default for safety) and runtime.feature.kv_warmlane=true. Rollout plan: staged on Dedicated canary pools then Hosted: start with 10% traffic, monitor p50/p95 and KV hit ratio; if regressions occur auto-disable features. Commits: ["Add staggered scheduler and policy (staggered_scheduler.cpp)", "Implement subtile attention kernel (subtile_kernel.cu)", "Subtile fusion pass and build flags (subtile_fuse_pass.cc)", "KV warm-lane allocator and async prefetch (warm_lane.cpp)", "Batcher hooks and affinity propagation (continuous_batcher.cpp)", "Bench and unit tests", "Docs and perf notes"]
payload.title: Staggered windowed attention scheduler with KV warm-lanes and subtile fusion

Motivation: We want structured outputs (response_format/jsonschema) to be practical in the wild: models occasionally emit slightly mismatched types or nested nulls which today either cause full stream rejection (strict_mode=true) or silent acceptance (strict_mode=false). This PR adds adaptive coercion hints and runtime-level strictness controls to reduce operational failures while preserving strong validation options for teams that need them. Design summary: 1) Introduce a new per-request 'strictness' enum that replaces/deprecates the boolean strict_mode. Values: 'reject' (current strict behavior), 'warn' (validate but allow soft coercions during streaming and emit structured errors), 'relaxed' (coerce common mismatches). 2) Add 'schema_coercion_hint' metadata to the response_format payload schema which is a lightweight descriptor (max 1KB) that the serving runtime uses to prefer specific coercion strategies without altering schema semantics. Examples: number-as-string coercion, empty-string->null, boolean-like strings. 3) Streaming behavior: coercion is applied incrementally when safe; ambiguous coercions are emitted as structured 'coercion_warning' events in the stream and final validation will either pass with warnings or fail with an 'schema_violation' error depending on strictness. 4) Error mapping: we standardized new error codes under openai-compat layer (Schema.CoercionWarning, Schema.Violation, Schema.StreamTruncated) and mapped them to human-readable messages; the API surface still returns the OpenAI-compatible status codes but includes 'redwood_error' for more detail. 5) Backwards compatibility: the boolean 'strict_mode' is still accepted for this release and mapped to strictness (strict_mode=true -> 'reject', false->'relaxed') with a deprecation warning in logs and docs. 6) Telemetry: added counters and latency buckets to ensure coercion hot-paths are observable and to detect regressions in per-token latency. Implementation notes: - Core coercion engine implemented in src/core/response/coercion with a compact rule table and fast-path for common cases to avoid adding extra allocations in the hot loop. - Streaming validator hooks placed in streaming_validator.go; they emit structured stream events which the OpenAI compatibility layer forwards as chunked meta events. - SDKs: convenience helpers added to Python and TypeScript SDKs to set 'strictness' and to parse 'coercion_warning' events when streaming. - Docs: upgrade guide for teams converting from strict_mode boolean to strictness enum, and sample recipes for tool/function-calling owners to choose policies per route. Tests & CI: initial run triggered a flaky integration test in response_format_integration.sh due to a timeout in perf-canary; I fixed the test by reducing a synthetic latency injection and restructured the test harness to decouple coercion verification from end-to-end bandwidth variables. Final CI status: all checks passed (unit, integration, lint, mypy, ts-check, e2e-canary). Review summary: - Evan requested clearer telemetry tags (added 'coercion.rule' and 'coercion.outcome'). - Marina asked for more explicit decoupling between function-calling payloads and coercion rules; added a guard that disables coercion for tool-call payloads unless route opts-in. - Derek raised perf concerns; added microbenchmarks and optimized the fast-path allocation to remove measurable regressions in the 95th percentile. - Small followups scheduled: ENG-4990 to add a visual indicator in Redwood Console for per-route coercion failure rate and PM task to evaluate default strictness per template. Migration & rollout: feature gated under 'response.adaptive_coercion' with rollout plan: 1) enable in staging for 48h, 2) enable in canary shard with 1% traffic for 7 days, 3) global opt-in for hosted teams via API flag, 4) allow Dedicated/Private customers to set default via their config. Observability & alerting: added a P99 latency alert for coercion path in observability/telemetry-metrics.yaml and a regression alert if coercion-related errors increase >5% over baseline. Related work: ties to ENG-4921 (streaming stability) and SUP-1173 (support escalations where strict_mode caused production outages). Docs and examples updated to include migration steps and sample prompts. Merge notes: squashed and merged after approvals; release notes added.
Introduces adaptive schema coercion hints and a deprecation path for strict_mode boolean; runtime supports per-request strictness levels (warn/relaxed/reject) and streaming-safe soft-coercion with mapped error codes.
Evan Li: Please add coercion rule telemetry tags so we can filter by rule type in logs. Can you also add unit test coverage for numeric-string coercion edgecases?
Priya Patel (author): Added 'coercion.rule' and 'coercion.outcome' tags; pushed tests for numeric-string and empty-string->null cases.
Marina Raskin: Ensure function-calling payloads are not coerced by default; tool outputs may be JSON-lit and authors expect strict typing.
Priya Patel (author): Added route opt-in guard and documented the change. Default remains conservative for function/tool calls.
Derek Zhou: Microbenchmark showed a small regression at 95th pct — can we avoid extra allocations?
Priya Patel (author): Optimized fast-path, replaced one allocation with stack buffer; reran bench and P95 matches baseline.

payload.body:
Motivation: Customers operating under regional data residency constraints require cryptographically enforceable, observable controls that prevent use of tenant keys outside allowed regions while preserving a predictable rollout path. This PR introduces a residency lifecycle guard and a lightweight KMS proxy to enforce tenant-region pinning at request time, plus audit metadata enrichment so downstream auditors can verify decisions. The goal is a low-risk, staged deployment path that 1) enforces denial-by-default for disallowed KMS operations, 2) emits continuity evidence to audit logs, and 3) provides a configurable tenant fallback policy (fail/route-to-allowed-region/queue-for-review).

What this PR changes (high level): Adds a residency-guard service that evaluates tenant residency attributes and RBAC v2 policies to make per-request allow/deny/reroute decisions; implements kmsp-proxy-lite (a small proxy sitting in front of the KMS client used by the service runtime) that blocks or rewrites KMS calls when keys are out-of-region; introduces an audit-enricher middleware that attaches residency_evidence headers and a signed decision token to every request forwarded to audit ingestion; extends RBAC v2 templates with a new attribute: tenant.residency.region_pin and a policy snippet in rbac/templates/residency.yaml; provides Helm values and an operator flag to enable the guard in Dedicated and Private installs; and ships tests and docs.

Key design notes: residency-guard is intentionally separated from existing authz flow to avoid coupling; it subscribes to tenant catalog changes and caches pin rules with TTL and versioned checkpoints for fast path checks. kmsp-proxy-lite is single-threaded by design and deliberately minimal: it validates key metadata and origin region, short-circuits unauthorized calls with HTTP 403-style errors to the runtime, and emits a structured audit event on each enforcement action. The audit-enricher attaches a base64-encoded decision envelope signed with the platform audit key (rotatable via KMS). Decision envelopes contain: tenant_id, key_id, requested_operation, resolved_region, rule_version and enforcement_timestamp.

Behavior and rollout plan: feature gated behind operator flag and a feature-flag for Hosted customers. Default rollout uses "monitoring-only" mode where decisions are logged but not enforced; after 2 weeks of telemetry validation the guard flips to "enforce" for a subset of tenants (canary group), then broadens to all tenants. Fallback policy options: fail-request, route-to-allowed-region (if cross-region replication configured), or queue-for-manual-review.

Compatibility: No breaking behavior when disabled. If enabled without corresponding RBAC templates the guard defaults to monitoring-only. KMS providers are supported via a pluggable adapter; we ship adapters for AWS and GCP used in our environments.

Testing: unit tests for the policy matcher and envelope signer; integration tests that run kmsp-proxy-lite against a local KMS emulator; e2e tests in the perf-canary lab that validate latency impact under 99th-percentile load. CI noted a flaky e2e on first run (timing in emulator); test was rerun and passed.

Observability: added residency.guard.* Prometheus metrics (decisions_total, blocked_calls_total, envelope_sign_failures_total), an Alert rule to fire when blocked_calls spike for canary tenants, and new tracing spans (residency.guard.evaluate, kms.proxy.enforce). Audit entries include the signed decision envelope for downstream auditors.

Security review: security team reviewed threat model for envelope signing and key management. The envelope signer uses a short-lived signing key protected by KMS with strict access controls. No plaintext tenant secrets are logged.

Release notes: "Add residency lifecycle guard and lightweight KMS proxy to enforce tenant region pinning. Initial rollout is monitoring-only; operator flag required to enable enforcement. See docs/security/residency-lifecycle.md for configuration and migration steps."

Related work: complements ENG-8110 (residency operator UI) and SEC-1041 (residency audit schema).

Checklist: [x] design doc linked, [x] unit/integration tests, [x] docs updated, [x] security review signed, [x] telemetry and alerts added, [x] rollout plan included.
Asha Patel: Please add a unit test that covers TTL cache expiry to avoid stale decisions in long-lived processes.
Marisol Vega: Added unit test and a cache invalidation hook; pushed update (see commit a8b3c55).
Liam O'Connor: We should avoid blocking the main request path on a signing call — what if signing KMS is slow? Consider async envelope signing with best-effort attach.
Marisol Vega: Switched to sync-for-monitoring-only and best-effort async path for enforce mode; documented tradeoffs in design notes.
Nikhil Rao (security): Confirmed key usage policy and rotation strategy; advised to include an incident runbook for envelope verification failures.
This implementation prioritizes minimal performance impact in the fast path. The kmsp-proxy-lite adds ~1.8ms median overhead in internal perf runs; measured increase at p99 is <6ms in canary environment. Operators should monitor residency.guard.latency and blocked_calls_total when enabling enforcement.
Add residency lifecycle guard and lightweight KMS proxy for enforcing tenant region pinning. Operator flag required to enable enforcement. Feature initially ships in monitoring-only mode; see docs for migration steps.
1) Enable feature flag in staging and set mode=monitoring. 2) Run for at least 2 weeks and validate signed decision envelopes in audit logs. 3) Enable canary enforcement for a small tenant cohort. 4) Monitor alerts and metrics; escalate via SEC-1041 process if anomalies seen.
components: security: add residency guard and kms-proxy-lite (monitoring-only by default); add rbac residency templates; add audit envelope signing
Adds structured decision envelopes to audit stream; increases audit event cardinality but improves forensic fidelity. Backfilled envelopes are not provided automatically.
See docs/security/residency-lifecycle.md and ENG-8110 for UI integration plans.

payload.body:
Context: We observed intermittent starvation and long tail latency in continuous-batcher under mixed workloads (short stateless requests interleaved with KV-heavy long-context requests). Root causes: aggressive slot acquisition semantics that allowed long KV-warmup requests to hold batch slots while short requests accumulated, and absence of a staleness-aware aging signal for queued items. This PR introduces a cooperative lease-backoff mechanism plus a staleness-aware queue tuner and lightweight kernel hints to reduce tail latency and prevent starvation without sacrificing throughput.

Design summary: 1) Cooperative lease backoff: requests acquire a soft lease for a batch slot. Long-running requests that exhibit prolonged KV-warmup or kernel contention will yield their soft lease after an adaptive backoff period (exponential with capped jitter). Yielding returns the request to the queue as a higher-priority "warmup-assisted" token so the runtime can try a different compatible slot or schedule smaller micro-batches to keep throughput high.
2) Staleness-aware queue tuner: we compute a per-request staleness score that increases over time but gets a boost if the request is KV-cold (no KV cache hits) or was preempted. The queue's admission policy uses a combined score (age + staleness + fairness credit) to select the next candidate for batching, thus preventing indefinite starvation of older or cache-miss requests.
3) Kernel-hint metadata: admission path propagates a lightweight hint derived from request shape (sequence length, past token delta) so the kernel selector can prefer smaller kernels for mixed-size batches, reducing kernel mis-schedules that cause head-of-line blocking.
4) Timeouts & safety: per-request soft-timeout with jittered probe windows to avoid synchronized yield storms. Feature flagging and a kill-switch are provided: redwood.scheduler.cooperative_backoff and redwood.scheduler.staleness_tuner.

Implementation notes: changes touch scheduler admission logic, batcher coordinator, KV cache metrics plumbing, and the kernel hinting interface. New modules: scheduler/lease_backoff.go (adaptive backoff logic), scheduler/staleness_tuner.go (scoring and fairness credits), admission/kernel_hints.go (hint propagation), plus unit/integration tests and e2e perf harness updates. Backwards compatibility: default flags are off; when enabled the system maintains existing semantics for requests without hints.

Benchmarks: micro-benchmarks run on a 4-GPU dedicated node with mixed synthetic workload (40% short stateless 64-token requests, 60% KV-heavy 2k-token requests with high cache miss ratio). Key results vs main (feature off): - 95th percentile p99 latency for short requests down by ~8% (from 230ms to 211ms). - Tail latency (p99.9) for mixed workload down by ~15%. - Aggregate throughput sustained ~+6% under the same budget due to fewer wasted warmup slots. - KV-cache warmup rate improved: cold-to-warm transition latency reduced by ~12%. These results include canary A/B runs; see attached bench summaries.

Testing & validation: extensive unit tests for backoff math and scoring, integration in the continuous-batcher harness, and an extended perf canary (3-day run) against representative production traces. Safety checks added to prevent thrashing: minimum lease hold time, capped backoff multiply, and back-pressure if the admission queue grows beyond a configured threshold.

Rollout plan: feature-gate behind redwood.scheduler.cooperative_backoff and redwood.scheduler.staleness_tuner. Rollout steps: enable at 1% traffic -> monitor fairness/latency/cold-miss regressions -> 10% -> 50% -> full. Metrics to watch: batch slot utilization, per-request wait-time distribution, KV-cache hit rate, canary error budget, and kernel mis-schedule counts. Emergency rollback is a single flag flip.

Notes and follow-ups: - There is scope for tying the staleness score to long-running model-level signals (e.g., KV eviction pressure) as a future follow-up (ENG-1896). - Suggested follow-up PR: move kernel-hint scoring into the compilation stage so the kernel selector learns profile-based preferences across deployments.

Checklist: implementation, unit tests, integration tests, bench harness updates, docs snippet for flags, canary plan, and metrics dashboards added.
Priya Nair: Nice design. Two asks: (1) can we make the backoff multiplier configurable per-class; (2) please add assertion that yielded requests don't lose trace/span linkage.
Alyssa Chen: Addressed both; added per-class multiplier and span-preserve shim in admission. Updated tests.
Jared Thompson: Observability looks good but please add a histogram for "yield_count" per-request so we can detect thrashing; also add an alert to canary dashboard if yield_rate > 0.5%.
Alyssa Chen: Added yield_count histogram and dashboard tile. Canary playbook updated.
Introduces cooperative lease backoff and a staleness-aware queue tuner for the continuous-batcher to reduce tail latency and prevent starvation in mixed KV workloads. Feature gated; off by default.
payload.title: Cooperative lease backoff and staleness-aware queue tuner for continuous-batcher

Motivation: streaming tool/function-calling paths were fragile under client reconnects and cross-origin environments. Scoped bearer tokens used to authorize tool calls are short-lived and bound to a connection; browsers that reconnect (SSE/WebSocket fallbacks) or intermediary proxies could inadvertently drop or replay Authorization headers leading to tool-call failures or accidental privilege elevation. This PR introduces a session-anchored auth "frame" concept plus a conservative, origin-verified preflight behavior to improve streaming stability and preserve OpenAI-compatible surface expectations.

What this change does: added a lightweight, signed session auth frame carried in a single header (X-Redwood-Auth-Frame). The frame contains minimal claims (session_id, scope, expiry, key_id) and is signed with the project's rotating signing key (JWS compact). Servers validate frames against the project's public keys and ensure the session_id matches the connection lifecycle. For older clients we continue to accept Authorization: Bearer tokens on /v1/* endpoints; however the server will preferentially validate X-Redwood-Auth-Frame for streaming endpoints to avoid header loss on intermediate reconnects.

CORS & preflight: added stricter handling for browser preflight when streaming endpoints are used. The server now returns Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Redwood-Auth-Frame and Access-Control-Allow-Origin is verified against the project's configured allowed_origins metadata. Preflight failures return 403 with structured JSON explaining the mismatch to help debugging.

Compatibility: to ease rollout this PR implements a compatibility shim: clients can send X-RW-Signed-Nonce (short single-use signed nonce) or the new auth frame. The shim is opt-in by header order: frame -> signed-nonce -> Authorization header. SDKs (TS/Python) are updated in companion commits to attach the auth frame automatically when a session manager is available.

Security model: frames are short-lived (default 2m) and bound to session_id. The server rejects frames that do not match the live session binding (on the connection handshake) to mitigate token replay across connections. Keys are rotated via the existing project key API; servers cache public keys with TTL and fall back to live lookup on verification failures.

Testing & rollout: added unit tests for parsing/verification, integration tests with SSE reconnect, and an e2e scenario exercising tool/function call acceptance after browser reconnect. Rollout plan: 5% canary (10 nodes) -> 25% -> 100% over 72 hours; monitor errors/api_auth.failure_rate and streaming.tool_call_drop_rate. Old header deprecation: Authorization-based inference will be deprecated for streaming after 30 days; the non-streaming REST surface continues to accept Authorization for 90 days.

Checklist: 
- [x] Add auth frame parsing and verification in runtime
- [x] Implement origin verification in preflight handler
- [x] Add compatibility shim for signed-nonce
- [x] Update TS/Python SDKs to attach frame when available

Priya: can we make frame expiry configurable per-project? responding: added ProjectConfig.SessionFrameTTL with default 2m (see verifier.go)
Diego: ensure key rotation fallback doesn't cause latencies on hot paths. reply: verifier caches keys for 5m and does background refresh; fallback only on verification failure and logged (metrics: auth.key_lookup_fallback)
Tom: e2e was flaky locally, add retry for SSE reconnect in test harness. reply: adjusted harness and re-ran CI

See docs/auth/session-frames.md for migration steps.

Metrics to watch post-merge: streaming.tool_call_drop_rate, api_auth.failure_rate, auth.key_lookup_fallback_count.
