Motivation: on mixed-cluster deployments we observed long tail latency and suboptimal throughput for tensor-parallel allreduce when nodes have heterogeneous NVLink/intra-node bandwidths or asymmetric cross-node links. Smaller microbatches and low-latency applications (streaming chat) disproportionately hit these tails.

This PR introduces a bandwidth-aware fanout planner and a KV-shard coalescing pass that together reduce cross-node stalls and improve overlap between communication and compute. It also adds a narrow-copy optimized kernel for strided small-chunk merges and a runtime hook that maps comm streams to physical links based on a link-rate profile discovered at startup.

What changed (high level):
- Fanout planner: builds a minimal spanning fanout for allreduce that avoids slow links and increases per-hop concurrency when it detects bandwidth heterogeneity. The planner prefers intra-node NVLink-RDMA pairs, then high-rate cross-node links, and uses low-rate links only as fallback.
- KV-shard coalescer: groups adjacent KV cache shards into aligned coalesced writes to reduce the number of small allgathers. This reduces per-step launch overhead and amortizes DMA for common prefix cache hits.
- Stride-optimized memcpy kernel: a small, vectorized kernel for <4KB strided copies used by the coalescer; reduces memcpy time by up to 3x in microbenchmarks.
- Stream mapper: startup probe collects link bandwidths (via existing topo_probe) and creates stream->link mappings to route collective streams away from congested links.
- Scheduler tweak: a light-weight scheduling hint that encourages launching compute kernels on the stream that finished the local reduce, improving KV reuse and overlap.

Benchmarks: (multi-node, 8xA100-80GB, TP-4)
- Throughput: +18% median for 512-token workloads with batch size 8; +11% median for batch size 2.
- P99 latency: reduced by 24% for streaming microbatch workloads (<=2 microbatches).
- Small allgather count: reduced by 38% for a realistic prefix-caching trace.
- Overhead: startup probe adds ~45ms to init time on first run; negligible once cached.

Compatibility and safety:
- The fanout planner is opt-in via config flag "runtime.bandwidth_fanout.enabled" (default: true for Dedicated and Private, false for Hosted until canary completes).
- Fallbacks: if topology probe fails or detects homogeneous links, planner falls back to existing balanced tree.
- Unit and integration tests added; new runtime flag is gated behind a feature flag at rollout.

Checklist: 
- [x] Perf microbenchmarks
- [x] Unit tests for planner and coalescer
- [x] E2E smoke on CI
- [x] Docs: added runtime flags and rollout notes
- [x] Bench dashboard entry (Linear ENG-4281)

Related: ENG-4219 (heterogeneous link investigation), ENG-4281 (bench dashboard and canary plan).

Notes: this is intentionally conservative in memory use for the coalescer (max 1.5x temporary buffer). We plan a follow-up to expose a memory/perf knob and to extend the stream mapper to NVSwitch-aware topologies.
Diego Alvarez: Nice work — planner looks solid. Two concerns: (1) how do we ensure the planner doesn't create hotspots on high-bandwidth links? (2) can the coalescer accidentally increase mem usage in pathological KV layouts?
Maya Chen (author): For (1) planner bounds per-link concurrent fanout degree and we prefer fanout breadth over depth when bandwidth headroom is available — added comments and a unit test that simulates a single high-capacity link. For (2) coalescer enforces a 1.5x temporary buffer cap; I added a regression test that mirrors EXTREME_KV layout and it passes. See tests/unit/test_kv_coalescer.cc
Priya Natarajan: CI showed a flaky on the e2e smoke (timeout). I reran and it's green. Please add a brief note in the canary doc about rollback steps if p99 increases in the first 24h.
Lucas Meyer: approved
(bench numbers look believable; we should run on a heterogeneous NVSwitch+NVLink cluster before broad rollout).
Improves TP allreduce performance on clusters with heterogeneous link bandwidth by introducing a bandwidth-aware fanout planner and KV-shard coalescing. Adds a small stride-optimized memcpy kernel and stream mapping to reduce comm/computation stalls. Opt-in flag and canary plan included.
payload.title: Heterogeneous-bandwidth-aware allreduce fanout with KV-shard coalescing and comm/compute overlap

Motivation: reduce first-run friction for engineers learning to build RAG-driven agents by shipping a compact 'Lightbook' stepper tutorial plus a small CLI that extracts runnable API snippets from docs. Motivation: We need a low-risk way to evolve request/response schema behavior for the API surface (streaming, tool-calls, and structured output) while preserving compatibility for existing clients. This PR implements a server-side schema gating mechanism driven by an opt-in Beta header, plus a streaming backfill path that gently converts legacy streaming chunks into the new structured event stream format for clients that opt-in. The change is intended as a backward-compatible rollout: default behavior is unchanged unless the client includes the X-Redwood-Beta-Schema header. The implementation includes a short rollback path and metrics to measure conversion fidelity. Highlights: 1) new header handling middleware (X-Redwood-Beta-Schema: v2-preview) and a graceful gate that routes requests to compatibility adapters; 2) streaming backfill controller that translates legacy "delta/text" chunks into structured stream events and reorders tool/function-calling tokens where safe; 3) adapter layer for OpenAI-compat SDKs to rewrite responses client-side when header present; 4) small changes to evaluator harness and integration tests to validate structured output regressions; 5) docs and changelog entries describing the beta opt-in and recommended migration path. Rollout plan: feature flag on, limited Canary region, monitor conversion_success_rate and client_error_rate for two weeks, then expand to all regions before flipping default. Links: Linear ENG-4123, PM-98. Related: previous schema and fallback work (context: schema negotiation efforts), and streaming stability bugs addressed in PERF tickets. CI: initial lint/test failure on streaming order test; fixed by commit 3. Merge: squash merge after approvals and green CI.
Lena Zhou: Please add a comment on the adapter that explains reordering guarantees; worried about edge cases when tool-call tokens split across chunks.
Author (Asha): Added detailed inline comment and an additional unit test that simulates split tokens across chunk boundaries.
Connor Blake: Approve with suggestion to expose conversion_success_rate in the console. Added a follow-up Linear ticket for dashboards.
Ravi Menon: Verified perf budget — <10% p99 increase on small sequences in Canary; OK to proceed.
Sophie Turner: Doc nit: update migration recipe to include recommended retry semantics for clients that mix legacy and beta headers.
Opt-in beta: clients can include X-Redwood-Beta-Schema: v2-preview to receive structured output and the new streaming event envelope. Legacy clients unaffected. Streaming backfill adapter reduces migration friction by converting legacy chunk format into the v2 event stream on the server when the header is present. Monitor conversion_success_rate and client_error_rate. See docs/migration/beta-schema.md for migration steps.
Integration tests added for structured event ordering and tool-call token boundaries. Manual QA in Canary region validated by SRE. Watch metrics: conversion_success_rate >= 99% and post-conversion latency p95 within 10% of baseline.
payload.title: Introduce schema gating with Beta-Schema header and streaming backfill

payload.body:
Background and motivation: In live workloads we observe frequent stalls when the pipeline ties input warmup (prefill) and decode stages at the slice granularity. Large-batch and high-concurrency traces show that a slow decode on one worker can back pressure prefill across other slices leading to elevated p95/p99 tail latency. This PR introduces an asynchronous slice coordinator that decouples input warmup from decode execution so prefill can make forward progress (KV priming + prefix materialization) without waiting for the decode stage to accept the same slice.

Design summary: the async slice coordinator is a small scheduling layer between the prefill producer and decode consumers. Key ideas: (1) slices produced by prefill are transferred into an in-memory non-blocking transfer queue along with lightweight metadata (sequence id, prefix hash, kv-ready flag) so they can be consumed independently; (2) decoders subscribe to available slices and request per-slice admission tokens from the coordinator using a windowed backpressure allocator to preserve latency SLOs; (3) KV cache now exposes a soft-commit operation that marks a slice's KV entries as warm without forcing a full synchronous flush—this enables fast lookup by decode kernels while avoiding immediate global book-keeping; and (4) minimal kernel surface changes: a non-blocking slice descriptor and a tiny handshake API for kernel readiness checks.

Why this is different: instead of speculative duplication of prefill work or heavy-weight handoffs, this approach focuses on slice-level asynchrony and lightweight metadata exchange to keep memory overhead low and reduce decode-induced stalls across unrelated slices. It is complementary to speculative prefill and microbatch coalescing, but targets workloads where inter-slice decode variance is the dominant source of tail latency.

Implementation notes: C++ runtime changes live under src/runtime/scheduler/: async_slice_coordinator.{cpp,h} implements the transfer queue and token allocator; kernel streaming changes are limited to kernel_stream.cpp for the readiness API; src/runtime/kv/cache_sync.cpp adds soft_commit and lookup hints. Unit tests and microbenchmarks were added under tests/benchmark/latency/async_slice_bench.py and tests/unit/scheduler/test_async_slice_coordinator.py. The implementation uses lock-free single-producer single-consumer queues where possible and falls back to wait-free ring buffers for multi-consumer paths.

Testing and verification: local unit tests and CI passed (see checks). Perf harness showed consistent improvements: mixed prefill/decode synthetic traces (seq-len distribution skewed to long decodes) yield 12% throughput improvement under steady load and 18% reduction in p95 end-to-end latency in our internal benchmark cluster. Memory overhead measured at +6% resident set for large model configs (4k token warmup windows) and was within the safety budget.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc linked in ENG-1893
- [x] Unit tests added
- [x] Perf benchmarks added and recorded
- [x] Metrics emitted for coordinator queue depth and per-slice wait time
- [x] No user-facing API changes

Rollback plan: feature is behind a runtime flag (runtime.async_slice_coordinator=false). If we observe regressions in the canary lane we can disable flag and revert commit cluster-wide.

Notes for reviewers: focus on memory reclamation on the ring buffer, metric naming for per-slice timers, and correctness of KV soft_commit semantics under race.
Initial coordinator scaffolding and non-blocking queue implementation
Implement token allocator and admission protocol for slices
Add KV soft_commit API and integrate with slice producer
Kernel readiness API and small kernel_stream changes
Unit tests and perf harness + docs
Rohan Patel: Can you quantify peak memory usage for 4k warmup windows and explain reclamation semantics? Some of our canary traces had larger resident growth previously.
Maya Chen: Measured +6% resident set on our benchmark cluster; coordinator uses an epoch-based reclamation for slice descriptors and we added a config knob to cap queued slices per-model to prevent unbounded growth.
Rohan Patel: Please add a unit test that simulates delayed decoder so we can guard against pathological enqueueing.
Maya Chen: Added delayed decoder test (tests/unit/scheduler/test_async_slice_coordinator.py::test_delayed_consumer) which asserts queue cap behavior and correct soft_commit ordering.
Lena Ortiz: Metric names look fine but prefer suffix '.ms' for per_slice_wait histogram. Also suggest emitting a synthetic 'slice_migration' counter for debugging cross-worker handoffs.
Maya Chen: Renamed per_slice_wait to per_slice_wait_ms and added slice_migration counter. Updated docs/architecture.
Evan Brooks: Verified that kernel readiness API keeps kernel changes minimal and didn't regress streaming decode throughput in my local runs. Approving.
CI bot: buildkite/ci passed, unit tests passed, perf checks improved for target traces.
runtime: add async slice coordinator to decouple input warmup from decode, reducing tail latency for workloads with high decode variance. Controlled by runtime.async_slice_coordinator flag; no public API changes.
Mixed prefill/decode synthetic: +12% throughput, -18% p95 latency; p99 unchanged in steady-state. Memory overhead: +6% RSS for large warmup windows (config cap available). Benchmarks run on internal perf cluster (8xA100), harness scripts added under tests/benchmark.
This change is intended to be a low-risk performance improvement for production workloads. We left the default off on release branches until the canary lane completes a 2-week soak.
payload.title: Decouple input warmup and decode with async slice coordinator

Motivation: Customers building strict structured-output pipelines need predictable behavior when models stream partial tokens, when clients ask for OpenAI-compatible error codes, and when function-calling instruments interact with response_format negotiation. This PR implements bidirectional schema negotiation (client-specified response_format + runtime-augmented hints), a compact error-code mapping layer for OpenAI-compat consumers, and stream-recovery signals so callers can decide whether to retry or fallback.

What this changes at a high level: 1) ResponseFormatNegotiator: a small runtime component that takes the user-supplied response_format (json_schema, text, openai_compat) and the model capability profile and selects a streaming/strictness strategy. 2) StrictMode Opt-in Flag: new request parameter response_format.strict (opt-in) that enables hard schema validation on complete and streaming mode; violations are surfaced as structured errors rather than free-text warnings. 3) Stream Recovery Header: during streaming, when an invalid JSON chunk or schema violation is detected, the runtime emits a small control event (EVENT: schema_error) with a canonical error code and a short token cursor so clients can choose to rewind/skip or fallback to a non-strict route. 4) OpenAI-compat error mapping: new compact mapper that translates internal schema error classes to OpenAI-compatible error categories (e.g., invalid_request_error -> invalid_response_format, resource_exhausted -> model_capacity) and preserves guidance text. 5) Function-calling interplay: the negotiator now marks function call envelopes as tolerant by default unless response_format.strict=true. This avoids hard failures in common function-calling workflows while allowing strict validation for verification flows.

Changes included (summary): commits: add negotiator, add strict flag parsing in API surface, stream event plumbing, error mapper and tests, docs update, TS SDK typing for response_format, Python SDK acceptance tests, small perf tweak to streaming parser to keep latency within SLO.

Compatibility notes: - Default behavior unchanged for existing clients (strict=false by default). - OpenAI-compat explicit mode maps legacy error shapes; behavior only activates if client requests openai_compat or sets compatibility headers. - Private/Dedicated customers can pin default strictness via account config (follow-up PR in dedicated config).

Testing and rollout: unit + integration coverage added for negotiation permutations (json_schema streaming/non-streaming, text, openai_compat). End-to-end canary on perf-canary for 24h with rollback flag. Feature gated behind runtime flag `negotiator_v2` and released via canary->gradual->global rollout.

Follow-ups: - Dedicated: expose account-level default strictness and an importable policy bundle. - Observability: surfaced metric redwood.response_format.violation.count and histogram of recovery latency. - SDK ergonomics: add high-level helper to auto-handle schema_error events.

Related Linear/Jira: ENG-2024, ENG-2121, SUP-891.
Liam Chen (review): overall design LGTM, but please split the big negotiator class into protocol and strategy so it's easier to test in isolation
Maya (reply): split into negotiator/protocol - pushed in c8e71b2 and added unit tests for strategy permutations
Ruth Gomez (request changes): need clearer guidance in docs about how stream control events should be consumed by SDKs
Maya (reply): added SDK helper examples and docs section 'Handling schema_error events'
Evan Brooks (approve): verified canary runs, no CPU/latency regression observed on p95
Adds a negotiated response_format layer with an opt-in strict mode for JSON-schema validation during streaming; introduces schema_error streaming control events and OpenAI-compatible error mapping. Default behavior unchanged. Feature is behind a runtime flag and rolled out via canary.
payload.title: schema negotiation: bidirectional response_format + OpenAI-compat error mapping

Motivation: In the last week we observed an oscillation pattern where regional circuit short-circuits were reopening rapidly during transient telemetry spikes, triggering wholesale tenant evictions and noisy rollbacks. This produced two customer-impact incidents (SUP-9842) where SLOs spiked briefly and then recovered, but the recovery path caused repeated evictions and slowed overall stabilization. Goal: introduce a conservative 'snooze' window for recently-closed short-circuits on a per-fleet basis and add a fleet-leveller that smooths eviction scores across nodes to avoid synchronized evictions. This change seeks to reduce circuit flip frequency, reduce mass-eviction events, and ensure SLO enforcement logic does not cascade under transient noise.
1) 5f3a2b6 - hotfix: introduce short_circuit_snooze_ms config and default 30000ms
2) 7b2d1c9 - safety: add fleet_leveller eviction smoothing weight (0.25 default)
3) 2d9e8a1 - tests: unit tests for snooze window and levelling math
4) 9a1b0ff - telemetry: emit short_circuit_snooze.event and leveller.trace tags
5) ab3c4d5 - docs: describe behavior and operator knobs in runtime-config reference
Luca Rossi: Can we avoid a global default that masks real outages? Suggest exposing env override and adding a per-deployment hard-disable flag. (Addressed in second commit)
Author (Maya Chen): Added runtime flag short_circuit_snooze_disable and documented tradeoffs; kept default conservative (30s) to prevent flapping.
Priya Patel: The leveller weight math looks right but please add a canary gating phase to the Dedicated rollout; small fleets may need a lower weight. (Added gating in config and rollout notes)
Diego Morales: CI flake in integration test on first run (timing). Re-ran and added test stabilization sleep in test harness to avoid nondeterministic timing.
Hotfix: reduce rapid short-circuit reopen/eviction oscillation by adding per-fleet short-circuit snooze (default 30s) and an eviction leveller that smooths eviction scores across nodes. Operators can tune short_circuit_snooze_ms and fleet_leveller_weight. Backfill telemetry tag short_circuit_snooze.event for incident correlation.
If rolling back, disable short_circuit_snooze via runtime flag and set fleet_leveller_weight=0 before full rollback to avoid asymmetric eviction behavior. Watch metrics: circuit.flip_rate, eviction.batch_size, slo.p90_latency. Immediate mitigation for customers: increase tenant priority for critical customers (operator guide section added).
payload.title: short-circuit-snooze-and-fleet-leveller-hotfix

payload.body:
Motivation: streaming tool/function-call payloads frequently break when tokenizer subtokens split anchors used by constrained decoders (CFG/regex). This PR implements a token-span aligner + a lightweight runtime proxy that translates regex constraints to anchored CFG fallbacks when token boundaries are ambiguous, and stabilizes function-call framing in the streaming path. Key goals: 1) prevent truncated or malformed toolcall JSON in stream fragments, 2) maintain OpenAI-compat framing for function calls, 3) reduce false-positive constraint violations caused by subtoken splits.

Summary of changes: implemented a tokenizer-aware span alignment component that maps constraint token indices to byte offsets across BPE/subtoken boundaries; added a regex-to-cfg fallback proxy that synthesizes conservative CFG anchors when regex constraints would otherwise be unsafe to apply during streaming; updated stream framing to buffer partial tokens at chunk edges and to attach deterministic re-emit markers for resumed segments; added unit + integration tests that run against the openai-compat layer and a small internal regression harness.

Design notes: the span aligner hooks into the tokenizer abstraction (tokenizer/aligner.go) and exposes a best-effort mapping with confidence scores; the fallback proxy lives under constraints/proxy and is pluggable (env-controlled) so Dedicated/Private customers can opt-in to the old strict-regex behavior. A new configuration flag (constraints.streaming_mode = "safe-fallback") controls the behavior: SAFE => prefer CFG fallback on low-confidence spans, STRICT => apply regex only if full-token match.

Checklist: - [x] tokenizer span mapping implementation and comments - [x] regex->CFG fallback translator with conservative anchor generation - [x] streaming buffer/edge re-emit markers - [x] OpenAI-compat function-call framing fixes and tests - [x] e2e regression test reproducing earlier SUP-1287 incident - [x] changelog entry and migration notes - [x] performance microbenchmarks (no >3% median latency impact in our bench)

Testing: local unit test suite covers 98% of new code; integration tests run in CI with both small (gpt-lite) and medium (gpt-medium) models; added a new regression file under eval-harness/regressions/toolcall-span-split.json that reproduces the previously flaky case. CI run: build -> unit -> integration -> fuzz (only for constraint proxy). The CI pipeline initially flagged a flaky fuzz worker (seed 2143) which was addressed by tightening the anchor heuristic and re-run; final CI status is PASS.

Risk and rollout: default behavior remains backward-compatible (regex mode unchanged) for existing customers. The new safe-fallback mode is enabled by default for hosted streaming routes that have toolcall=true to mitigate customer impact; Dedicated instances can toggle via their config. We also added an opt-out header (X-Redwood-Constraint-Mode: strict) to maintain compatibility for customers who rely on strict regex behavior.

Related: ENG-3421 (structured-output regressions), SUP-1287 (customer incident), ENG-3499 (streaming reframe RFC).

Notes for reviewers: focus on tokenizer/aligner correctness and the heuristics in proxy/fallback.go; look for edgecases around multibyte UTF-8 boundaries and recursive CFG anchor generation. The fallback synthesizer intentionally errs on the side of permissiveness to avoid false positives that drop tokens.
Ethan Park: Nice isolation between tokenizer and constraints. One concern: aligner confidence thresholds are currently hard-coded; can we make them configurable and document the expected trade-offs?
Priya Nair: Responded: added constraints.streaming_confidence_threshold and documented defaults in docs/constraints.md. Kept conservative defaults used in CI benchmarks.
Luca Moretti: Found a UTF-8 boundary case in chunker.go where a 3-byte char split across chunks could be misclassified as partial token - see inline. Suggest adding a regression to cover emoji sequences.
Priya Nair: Responded: fixed boundary detection and added test case for emoji-surrogate patterns in openai_toolcall_test.go.
Zoe Chen: Ran perf microbenchmarks; median latency impact is +1.8% in our standard throughput test, within acceptable bounds. Approving pending small nits on comments.
Zoe Chen: Approved changes.
Merged via squash on 2024-06-10 after approvals from reviewers. No post-merge hotfixes required. Release notes added to CHANGELOG.md under 'Structured output / streaming'.
Adds tokenizer-aware token-span alignment and a regex->CFG safe-fallback proxy to stabilize streaming function-call framing and constrained decoding across subtoken boundaries. Default behavior remains compatible; new safe-fallback mode reduces malformed toolcall regressions in streaming. See docs/constraints.md for migration and tuning guidance.
payload.title: token-span-aligner-and-regex-fallback-proxy-for-toolcall-streaming

Context:
We have growing CI wall time from running monolithic integration matrices for small changes. This PR introduces a lightweight presubmit prober (codename: Siesta) and a dependency visibility index to reduce premerge feedback time. The prober is intentionally minimal: static-source heuristics, quick-path test selectors, and a small Go probe binary that emits a deterministic 'presubmit fingerprint' for changed paths.

Motivation:
- Reduce developer wait times on common doc/SDK/infra tweaks by avoiding full integration runs unless needed.
- Provide a reproducible preflight check that can be run locally and in CI to gate expensive shards.
- Make dependency visibility explicit so presubmit selection is conservatively correct for transitive changes.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds a new lightweight Go binary cmd/presubmit-prober (approx 120 LOC) that scans a change list and computes a presubmit fingerprint and a list of impacted test tags.
- Adds a dependency-visibility index stored as a small YAML under infra/dep-index.yaml (generated by scripts/dep-indexer). Index is used by the prober to expand impact beyond direct file diffs.
- Introduces a new CI job in .github/workflows/preflight-siesta.yml that runs the prober and conditionally triggers downstream CI lanes via workflow_dispatch with annotated tags.
- Refactors the existing presubmit orchestration script (scripts/presubmit-orchestrator.sh) to call the prober and short-circuit heavy shards when not needed.
- Adds unit tests for the prober and a small e2e harness that validates tag selection against a few representative diffs in tests/fixtures.

Design notes:
- The prober output is deterministic and signed by CI using a job metadata checksum to avoid accidental cache poisoning.
- Dependency index is intentionally conservative (over-approximate) and is regenerated via CI schedule weekly and during major dependency upgrades. The generator lives at scripts/dep-indexer/ and is separate from runtime prober to keep presubmit fast.
- Rollout is gated: new CI workflow runs in parallel but does not yet prevent merges. We will flip the enforcement guard in a follow-up after 1 week of telemetry.

Testing and results:
- Local unit tests added; e2e harness simulates 6 change sets (docs-only, sdk-typo, runtime-scheduler, kvcache tweak, quantization profile change, infra/helm tweak).
- On the repo's mid-sized change set sample, presubmit wall time reduced ~38% for non-runtime changes when prober short-circuits heavy shards.

Migration / rollout checklist:
- [x] Add prober and dep-index generator (this PR).
- [x] Run weekly index generation scheduled job (CI schedule added).
- [x] Monitor presubmit hit/miss rates and errors for 7 days.
- [x] Flip enforcement to block merges if prober indicates a heavy change (follow-up PR).

Notes for reviewers:
- Focus review on presubmit-prober deterministic logic and dep-index schema. The generator is conservative by design; correctness favors over-inclusion.
- I intentionally kept the Go binary minimal and dependency-free (std lib only) to avoid CI image bloat.

Commits (high-level):
- feat(presubmit): add cmd/presubmit-prober (initial implementation and tests)
- feat(ci): add preflight-siesta workflow and integrate with presubmit-orchestrator
- feat(infra): add scripts/dep-indexer and infra/dep-index.yaml (seed index)
- refactor(presubmit): update presubmit-orchestrator to call prober
- test: add fixtures and e2e harness for prober behavior

Changed areas (high level):
- cmd/presubmit-prober/* (new)
- scripts/dep-indexer/* (new)
- infra/dep-index.yaml (new, ~2.1KB seed)
- .github/workflows/preflight-siesta.yml (new CI workflow)
- scripts/presubmit-orchestrator.sh (modified)
- tests/fixtures/presubmit/* (new)
- internal/ci/README.md (documentation for prober usage)
Ethan Cole: Nice approach, helps common-case fast paths. A couple questions on dep-index format - can we make it a bit more compact?
Author (Maya): Index intentionally verbose to aid manual inspection; generator has a compact mode (scripts/dep-indexer --compact) but I want human-readable default for first rollout.
Priya Natarajan: Prober binary should not add a compiled artifact to Docker image. Can we run it from source in CI?
Author (Maya): Yes - CI builds the prober on the runner; no baked image change. I added CI step to build-and-run the prober as part of the preflight job.
Luca Moretti: Tests look good. Please add telemetry counters for 'short_circuit' and 'forced_full_run' so we can observe the hit rate.
Author (Maya): Added two counters and emit them as GitHub job summary annotations; we'll wire them into telemetry in follow-up (ENG-2180).
Ethan Cole: LGTM after telemetry and small doc tweak. Approving.
- Introduces 'Siesta' presubmit prober: a lightweight preflight step that short-circuits heavy CI shards for non-impactful changes.
- Adds a dependency visibility index to improve conservative test selection for presubmits.
- Adds new CI workflow 'preflight-siesta' and refactors presubmit orchestrator to integrate the prober.
- No behavioral changes to production code; rollout is non-enforcing initially.
payload.title: add-siesta-presubmit-prober-and-dependency-visibility-index

Context: We have observed tail-latency spikes and cache pollution during canary drains for models that diverge behaviorally from the primary model. Existing time-windowed drains and traffic-splitting strategies either hold back traffic for too long or abruptly shift traffic causing downstream SLO regressions. This PR introduces a declarative, cohort-aware similarity routing layer that gracefully drains canaries by steering requests based on request-to-model similarity fingerprints.

Summary: Adds a CohortSimilarityRouter to the rollout controller which computes a lightweight fingerprint per request and routes cohorts to model variants according to an operator-specified similarity threshold. The rollout spec (api/schemas/rollout_v2.yaml) includes cohortRules and similarityThresholds that let teams express: targeted A/B splits by cohort, speculative routing for ambiguous requests (dual-call + winner-take-all), and a staged drain that reduces traffic to the canary only for high-similarity cohorts first. The runtime component uses an LRU-backed similarity cache and a compact locality-sensitive hashing index for O(1) approximate similarity checks, minimizing per-request overhead.

Checklist: 
- [x] design doc and prototype spike validated with load tests (see docs/rollouts/cohort_similarity_routing.md)
- [x] rollout API extension and backwards-compatible parsing
- [x] runtime similarity index with micro-benchmarks
- [x] integration tests for drain scenarios and A/B cohorts
- [x] observability: rollout metrics and tracing for similarity decisions
- [x] feature-flag gated rollout (off by default)

Key behaviors and safety: The router is opt-in per rollout and can be enabled only for rosters that opt into cohort routing. Drain progresses in three deterministic stages: (1) similarity-first reduction where only high-similarity cohorts are shifted to canary, (2) progressive blending where threshold relaxes, and (3) full swap. At any stage, if SLO gates in the Console are breached (latency or quality regressions), an automated rollback playback is triggered that replays a bounded sample of requests against the previous model for root-cause collection and then performs an immediate traffic revert. The playback is stored in the rollout journal for auditing.

Performance: Microbenchmarks on c6g-like instances show median per-request overhead of ~0.8ms for the similarity check when the index is warm; end-to-end 95th latency impact across a mixed workload was <2% for 99th token latency. Load test details and artifact links included in the design doc.

Testing and QA: New unit tests cover the similarity index edge cases and hash collisions. Integration e2e uses ci/workflows/rollout_e2e.yml to validate a staged drain under synthetic cohorts; tests simulate SLO regression to verify automated rollback sequence. Manual verification steps are documented under docs/rollouts/cohort_similarity_routing.md.

Files changed at a glance: 
- services/rollout/controller.py: adds CohortSimilarityRouter, new lifecycle states (SIMILARITY_DRAINING, BLEND), and handlers for automated rollback playback.
- services/rollout/similarity_index.py: LSH-based index plus LRU cache and async warming logic.
- services/rollout/drain_policy.py: declarative drain planner implementing the three-stage drain.
- api/schemas/rollout_v2.yaml: rollout spec extension with examples in examples/rollouts/cohort_similarity_example.yaml.
- docs/rollouts/cohort_similarity_routing.md: design rationale, ops runbook, and rollback playbook.

Review thread (high-level): 
- Liam O'Connor (reviewer): "Strong design; two requests: add an integration test that simulates cache cold starts, and ensure the similarity decision is logged at debug level only behind a flag." 
- Maya Chen (author): "Addressed: added test for cold start in test_cohort_routing.py and gated verbose logging behind TRACE_SIMILARITY flag; pushed new commits." 
- Sofia Martinez (reviewer): "Can you quantify memory footprint for the LRU cache under typical rollout sizes? Recommend a telemetry gauge." 
- Maya Chen: "Added telemetry gauge (rollout_similarity_cache_size) and documented sizing guidance in observability/metrics/rollout_metrics.md." 
- Ethan Green: "Approvals aside from minor nits in naming—suggest squash on merge to keep history small."

CI summary: rollout_e2e (passed), unit (passed), lint (passed after fix), integration (passed). One flaky test (tests/rollouts/test_cohort_routing.py::test_blend_transition) failed initially on CI due to timing assumptions; adjusted to wait for consistency and retried successfully.

Merge: Squash merge into main performed on 2026-02-24 by Maya Chen. Merge commit message notes ENG-11234 and includes brief rollout enabling steps.

Post-merge rollout notes: The feature is feature-flag gated; recommended rollout plan for customers: enable on canary selection only with conservative similarity thresholds (0.9) and monitor the new metrics rollout_similarity_decisions_total and rollout_similarity_cache_size for 48 hours before relaxing thresholds. Run the provided migration job to warm indices for historical cohorts if enabling on long-lived traffic rosters.

Related work: This PR complements previous staged rollout controllers by adding content-aware routing and deterministic drains; it intentionally avoids altering the core fallback routing logic and instead plugs into the existing decision pipeline.
Adds cohort-aware similarity routing to improve canary drains and reduce tail-latency regressions. Backwards compatible and feature-gated.

Motivation: Dedicated fleets occasionally suffer from two related problems: (1) tenants burn short bursts aggressively and then sit idle, causing transient overcommit and long-tail latency spikes; (2) global autoscalers lack fast, tenant-scoped signals to confidently grant short-term burst capacity without risking steady-state throughput guarantees. This change implements a per-tenant headroom estimator that tracks utilization with an exponentially decaying confidence window and pairs it with a burst credit redemption protocol to reclaim unused burst allocations safely.

What I changed (high-level):
- Introduced headroom estimator that maintains a decaying-weighted utilization summary and outputs a percentile-backed headroom recommendation (headroom_estimator.go). The estimator emits a confidence value (0..1) derived from effective sample count; low confidence widens safety margins.
- Implemented per-tenant ephemeral reservation layer that can grant small, time-limited burst credits based on estimator recommendations and global safety budget checks (ephemeral_reserver.go).
- Burst redemption protocol: unused or under-consumed burst allocations are redeemable by the pool after a grace window. Redemption is conservative and triggers soft notifications first (burst_redemption.go).
- Scheduler integration: autoscaler and slot-allocator consult the estimator confidence before committing reserved slots; low-confidence recommendations route through a conservative fallback path.
- Telemetry: new metrics and traces (pkg/telemetry/metrics.yaml) for headroom_estimate, headroom_confidence, burst_allocated, burst_redeemed, per_tenant_util_p95. Added label dimensions for pool, tenant_id, and region.
- Controls & rollout: feature flag (feature.flags.yml) to enable per-tenancy estimator; canary rollout configuration for two Dedicated pools (us-east-1-a, eu-west-1-b).

Implementation notes: estimator uses a simple EWMA over utilization buckets with a decaying effective sample count. Percentiles are approximated with a small hdr-like sketch to keep memory bounded per-tenant. The ephemeral reserver enforces two safety checks before granting bursts: (a) tenant daily commit headroom fraction must be below threshold, (b) global ephemeral budget must have slack. Both thresholds are tunable through runtime config.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests cover estimator edge cases (warmup, abrupt drop, long-tail idle).
- Integration tests simulate 1k tenants with synthetic burst patterns and assert that overall 99th token latency remains within SLO when bursts are enabled.
- Added a simulation harness job (ci/integration/sim-burst.yml) used in CI to run a nightly long-running test.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag disabled by default.
2) Enable in one small non-critical Dedicated pool (canary). Monitor new telemetry for 48 hours: headroom_confidence distribution, burst_allocated vs burst_redeemed ratio, and 99th latency.
3) If metrics look stable and no regressions, expand to two more pools; enable automated fallback for tenants whose burst_redeemed ratio exceeds configured limit.
4) After 2 weeks of stable signals, flip the global flag and enable for all Dedicated pools.

Related: Linear ENG-4821 (headroom estimator design), ENG-4897 (burst redemption protocol). Related PRs: internal autoscaler tuning in the past quarter.

Notes on safety: the design intentionally favors under-allocation when confidence is low. The redemption protocol uses a multi-step revoke (soft notify -> reclaim after grace -> force reclaim) to avoid tearing in-progress requests. All reclaim operations are idempotent.

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests for estimator and reserver
- [x] Integration simulation added to CI
- [x] Telemetry dashboards (draft) and alert recipes created
- [x] Feature flag and canary plan documented

If you want a deeper walkthrough I can demo the simulation traces and the headroom_confidence histogram in the next infra sync.
Samir Gupta: Nice design. One concern – how do we avoid oscillation when many tenants with similar patterns request bursts at the same cadence? Can the estimator coordinate?
Maya Patel: Answered: estimator is local to tenant and we introduced a short global damping window in the ephemeral_reserver (configurable) to add randomized jitter to grant timing; details in reserver docs. Added a TODO to explore coordinated smoothing in future (ENG-4930).
Elena Park: Please add clarity about what happens to in-flight KV cache entries when we reclaim a burst reservation.
Maya Patel: Added explicit handling: reclaim marks reservation as non-preemptive until active requests finish; scheduler frees slots only after active handle drain. See reservation_integration.go for comments.
Jonah Li: Request: add end-to-end test asserting that reclaimed bursts do not drop active requests and that latency stays within SLO.

Author: Added tests in tests/integration/burst_sim_test.go that assert no request failure and token-latency p99 within threshold in simulated reclaim scenarios.

Context: During regional failovers and policy-driven redirects, the gateway may respond with a redirect (307/308) to a different region. For non-streaming requests this is fine, but for streaming (SSE) we observed clients (and our SDK defaults) either (a) treating redirects as terminal errors, or (b) reconnecting but re-sending the request in a way that could duplicate generation if the original request had already been accepted by the upstream. This showed up in SUP-25322 and during rehearsals for the failover automation workstream (ENG-2422).

What this PR changes: (1) Adds explicit redirect handling to the streaming transport layer used by the API gateway → router → inference proxy path. For 307/308, we preserve method/body and re-issue the request to the Location target. For 301/302 (should not occur for API traffic), we treat as non-retryable and log at warn to surface misconfig. (2) Introduces/standardizes request idempotency for streaming: we now require a stable request identifier (request_id) to be forwarded end-to-end, and we attach it on redirect retries so the destination region can de-dupe. If client does not provide request_id, the gateway will generate one and return it in the initial response headers (x-redwood-request-id) so clients can correlate. (3) Improves partial-stream reconnect behavior: if the client disconnects mid-stream and reconnects (same request_id), the gateway will not attempt to resume token-by-token (not supported), but it will return a deterministic terminal event indicating the request is already in-progress/complete with guidance to fetch the final result via the non-streaming retrieval endpoint (where applicable) or to re-issue with a new request_id. (4) Tightens retry budget: redirect retries are now capped to 1 hop (to avoid loops) and share the existing per-request retry budget, with specific telemetry so we can see redirect-induced retries separately from upstream 5xx retries.

Implementation notes: - Added a RedirectPolicy to the streaming client used by the gateway proxy. It validates Location, prevents cross-scheme redirects (http→https allowed? we only allow https), and blocks redirects to non-allowlisted hostnames (regional ingress only). - Added de-dup on the inference proxy side keyed by (tenant_id, request_id). For now this is a short TTL cache (15m default) sufficient for failover windows; persistent de-dup is out of scope. - Added structured logs and metrics: streaming_redirect_count, streaming_redirect_retry_exhausted, streaming_idempotency_replay_detected, and streaming_reconnect_outcome (labels constrained per observability guidance).

Why this is safe: Redirect behavior is opt-in for streaming only and guarded by a feature flag (streaming_redirect_reconnect_enabled) default off in prod. When enabled, the code path only triggers on 307/308 with an allowlisted Location. If the redirect retry fails, we return the original error to the client with an explicit retry-after where available.

Tests: - Unit tests for redirect parsing/validation, loop detection, and allowlist enforcement. - Integration tests using a local fake router that issues 307 to a second test server and verifies the streamed event sequence. - Regression test for duplicate generation: first region accepts request then immediately redirects; second region sees same request_id and responds with a replay-detected terminal event (no second upstream invocation).

Rollout plan: - Land behind flag. - Enable in staging immediately; run through the controlled failover rehearsal scenario (us-east → eu-west redirect). - Enable for 1% of Hosted API streaming traffic for internal tenants, then expand by tier once metrics look clean (no unexpected redirect loops, replay rates near zero).

Follow-ups: - Coordinate with SDK teams to ensure request_id is consistently set for streaming by default (tracked separately). - Add documentation snippet to operator guide for interpreting streaming reconnect metrics during failover.

Checklist: - [x] Linked issue: ENG-2422 - [x] Added tests - [x] Added metrics/logs - [x] Flagged + safe defaults - [x] Verified no additional high-cardinality labels

Notes for reviewers: The main logic is in gateway/streaming/redirect.go and proxy/idempotency/cache.go. I tried to keep the redirect policy narrow to avoid surprising behavior; feedback welcome on whether we should allow 308 only (currently 307/308).
Mina Haddad: Can we guarantee we won't bounce across multiple regions if policy flaps? Also do we record the original region vs redirected region for debugging?
Vikram Singh: We hard-cap to a single redirect hop per request (and we track redirect_from_region/redirect_to_region in structured logs + a low-cardinality metric label set). If the second region also tries to redirect we fail closed and return an error with a clear message + request_id.
Ravi Menon: Request idempotency: what prevents a malicious client from forcing cache growth by spamming unique request_id?
Vikram Singh: TTL is short and cache is bounded (LRU, per-tenant quotas). Also we only store entries for requests that reach upstream acceptance; rejected requests don't create state. Added an explicit per-tenant max_entries guard and a metric when we evict due to pressure.
Peter Holtz: How does this interact with retry-after semantics and existing retry budgets? We don't want clients hammering both regions.
Vikram Singh: Redirect retry consumes the same request retry budget, and on overload we preserve retry-after from the target region. Added a test that ensures we do not perform redirect-follow when retry budget is already exhausted.
Miles Thornton: During game day, we saw clients reconnecting and duplicating streams. Does this fix the 'double invocation' path or just make it less likely?
Vikram Singh: It blocks double invocation when request_id is stable. If client doesn't send request_id, gateway generates one and uses it for redirect-follow, so we still get de-dup for the redirect scenario. Mid-stream client disconnect/reconnect still needs client behavior; we now provide deterministic guidance rather than silently re-issuing and duplicating.
Mina Haddad (request changes): Please ensure Location allowlist can't be bypassed via userinfo or punycode edge cases.
Vikram Singh: Good call. Added URL normalization + rejects userinfo, non-https, and hostnames failing strict match against allowlist. Also added tests for punycode + mixed-case hostnames.
Ravi Menon: Approving after the allowlist hardening changes.
Mina Haddad: Approved.
Peter Holtz: Approved.
Miles Thornton: Approved.
payload.title: Fix streaming reconnect on cross-region redirect + improve idempotency

Motivation: customers operating across regulated jurisdictions require deterministic tenant-level key routing and an auditable consent surface. This PR introduces a tenant "geo-locker" that pins KMS usage to region-asserted key anchors, a consent-forwarding bridge for operator workflows, and a tamper-evident audit signer to make audit records non-repudiable.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a tenant-scoped KMS routing layer that resolves preferred key endpoints based on tenant residency claims and policy overrides.
- Implements a consent bridge: when an operator or automated workflow needs cross-region key use, the bridge records consent assertions and attaches consent handles to requests.
- Adds an audit signer component that signs audit envelopes (ED25519) and includes signature metadata in the audit pipeline for downstream immutable storage.
- Wires new policy checks into RBAC v2 decision flow so cross-region key use is flagged and can be gated by consent.

Design notes:
- The geo-locker resolver is intentionally policy-driven: tenant residency metadata (provided at provisioning) + per-tenant allowlists produce an ordered preference list for KMS endpoints. The resolver is pluggable for future multi-provider mapping.
- Consent bridge maintains short-lived consent handles (opaque tokens) and an operator audit entry. Consent tokens are single-use and TTL-bound.
- Audit signer produces a compact signature header and a signature manifest that can be attached or stored alongside existing audit logs. The manifest includes key id, signer version, and canonicalized payload hash.

Compatibility and rollout:
- Default behavior preserves current KMS routing; geo-locker is opt-in per-tenant.
- Feature flag: features.geo_locker.enabled = false by default. We will enable in a staggered rollout: internal dogfood tenants -> opt-in customers -> enforced for regulated tenants.
- Backwards-compatible: when consent handles are absent, cross-region requests follow current fallback rules but are logged with reason=unconsented.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for resolver policy logic, consent token lifecycle, and signer output canonicalization.
- Integration test harness simulating cross-region request paths with a fake KMS endpoint and a signed-audit store.
- Load-tested signer at 10k/sec signing throughput in perf-canary cluster; signer adds ~2ms median latency when batched.

Security considerations:
- Signer keys are stored in HSM-backed KMS; the signer fetches a short-lived signing key via internal KMS assume role flow.
- Consent tokens are opaque and cannot be forged; they include a MAC tied to the tenant and operator id.
- RBAC v2 checks are extended; misconfiguration will log with metric rbac.geo_lock_denied to alert on accidental denies.

Checklist:
- [x] Add resolver and policy evaluation layer
- [x] Add consent bridge and token lifecycle
- [x] Add audit signer component and manifest format
- [x] Integrate RBAC v2 checks and metrics
- [x] Add unit + integration tests
- [x] Add feature flag and rollout plan

Related: Linear ENG-3127, ENG-3184. Jira: SUP-1429 (support case that drove TTL behavior).
Darren Liu: Can we avoid a hot-path call to KMS for signer key retrieval on every request? Suggest caching short-lived keys and adding retries with jitter.
Priya Menon: Answered - signer caches a 5m ephemeral key retrieved via internal KMS assume role flow; added tests and a backoff wrapper (see signer.go).
Sofia Martinez: RBAC change looks good, but we need clearer metric tags for multi-tenant alerting (added rbac.geo_lock_denied.{tenant,region}).
Ethan Park: Please add a doc note about operational recovery when consent-store DB is unavailable.

Motivation: Dedicated fleets occasionally experience 'fast-provision' oscillations where short-term demand spikes trigger aggressive provisioning followed by immediate scale-downs, which increases cost and leads to jitter for tail latency. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) a deferred provisioning contract (DPC) that encodes policy about how long a provisional allocation must survive before it becomes billable/reservable, and 2) a utilization surface calibrator (USC) that models observed utilization as a time‑smoothed surface instead of a single scalar, enabling the autoscaler to make provisioning decisions using shape-aware thresholds (ramp, slope, second derivative) rather than only percentiles. Design: - DPC is a lightweight state machine attached to warm-pool candidates: states {candidate, provisional, committed}. A candidate becomes provisional when predicted aggregated demand crosses a soft threshold; it is promoted to committed only after satisfying a configurable survival window. Promotion includes an idempotent ledger entry used by the reservation accounting service. - USC builds a compact time-series surface per tenant/model by aggregating min/median/max across rolling sub-windows (0–1s, 1–10s, 10–60s). The autoscaler consumes three derived signals: ramp_factor (first diff), curvature (second diff), and persistence_score (survival likelihood). These signals feed a ruleset that biases provisioning: prefer provisional allocations for short high-curvature spikes, commit when persistence_score > policy.threshold. Implementation highlights: - pkg/autoscaler/dpc.go: state machine, contract API, and ledger integration hooks. - pkg/autoscaler/util_surface.go: surface construction, smoothing kernels, sampling backfill for sparse tenants. - controllers/warmpool_controller.go: orchestration changes to prefer provisional -> staged promotion path. - telemetry/exporters/util_surface_prometheus.go: exposes ramp_factor/curvature/persistence_score per-tenant and aggregated 1h/24h histograms. - cmd/fleetctl/inspect-dpc: diagnostic CLI to inspect provisional commitments, useful for on-call and capacity planning. Backwards compatibility: DPC defaults to a conservative 30s survival window and disabled ledger promotion for accounts without committed reservations to avoid billing semantics changes. Feature is guarded behind config flag autoscaler.deferred_provisioning.enabled (off in existing clusters by default). Testing and validation: - Unit tests cover state transitions (candidate -> provisional -> committed), race windows for concurrent predictions, and failure recovery when promotion RPC fails and is retried. - Integration tests (kind/e2e) simulate synthetic workloads with deterministic spikes: low-frequency long spikes vs microbursts. - Perf microbenchmarks: measurement harness shows median decision latency increase of 120µs and a 6% reduction in cold-boot provisioning events under mixed workloads. Rollout plan: - Feature gated behind rollout flag. - Start canary on a small dedicated cluster and enable telemetry dashboards for ramp_factor/curvature. - Monitor commit rate vs provisional rate, p95 latency, and cost per token. - After 2 weeks of stable signals enable for 25% of fleets, then 100% with conservative defaults. Migration notes: No schema changes to reservation ledger. Operators wanting older behavior can set autoscaler.deferred_provisioning.enabled=false. Related work: complements tenant-weighting and headroom controllers; see ENG-1729 for historical demand forecasting improvements.
Liam Chen: Nice approach. Two asks: (1) add a unit test that simulates a flaky promotion RPC and ensures we don't double-commit; (2) can we avoid sampling at 100Hz for small tenants to limit memory?
Maya Patel: Added retry-idempotency and switched to adaptive sampling that drops to 10Hz for <10 concurrent shards. PTAL.
Sofia Martinez: Telemetry shape looks good but we need alerting guidance in the docs for 'provisional commit ratio' going >50%.
Maya Patel: Added docs section 'Observability and Alerts' with provisional/commit ratio dashboards and thresholds. Also added RBAC check to fleetctl to avoid leaking ledger info.
Arun Gupta: Approve after nits - prefer naming 'persistence_score' -> 'survival_score' for consistency with forecasting module.
Maya Patel: Renamed metric to survival_score across exports and tests.
CI Bot: integration tests flaky on linux-arm; re-ran and all checks passed.
Introduce Deferred Provisioning Contract (feature-flagged) and Utilization Surface Calibrator. Default: disabled. Improves provisioning stability and reduces cold-boot events for mixed workloads. Observability: new metrics ramp_factor, curvature, survival_score.
If provisional -> committed promotion spikes unexpectedly: check autoscaler.deferred_provisioning.enabled, inspect cmd/fleetctl inspect-dpc output, verify ledger RPC latencies, and look at survival_score time series for rapid curvature changes.

Title: Fix metrics cardinality for failover_reason/trigger_source labels

Context
During staging rehearsals for Regional Failover Automation (ENG-2418) we saw a sharp increase in time series for failover decision metrics. Root cause: we were emitting raw, free-form strings into failover_reason and trigger_source (e.g., concatenated signal names / error messages), and we also carried request- or policy-specific identifiers as labels in a few code paths. This becomes particularly painful during noisy/partial impairments where the controller evaluates frequently and produces many distinct label values.

This PR reduces label cardinality by (1) mapping reasons/sources to bounded enums, (2) removing high-cardinality labels from the exported series, and (3) adding guardrails that reject unexpected values and surface them via dedicated counters + structured logs.

What changed
- Bounded enums
  - Introduced FailoverReason enum: reachability | error_burn | latency_burn | capacity | operator | config_change | unknown
  - Introduced TriggerSource enum: region_health | perf_canary | gateway | controller | operator_cli | unknown
  - All call sites now translate internal signal identifiers to these enums via a single mapping table.
  - Unknown/unmapped inputs are coerced to "unknown" (not the raw string).

- Label set cleanup (cardinality reduction)
  - Removed labels: tenant_id, route_id, policy_id, model_id from exported metrics.
  - Kept bounded labels that are useful for SLO slicing without exploding series: environment, scope (hosted|dedicated), from_region, to_region, tenant_tier (free|pro|enterprise), action (recommend|execute|rollback).

- Aggregation safeguards
  - Added rw_failover_metric_label_reject_total{metric, label, scope} counter that increments when a value is rejected/coerced.
  - Added a small in-process LRU to rate-limit log spam for unknown label values (logs include the original value + call-site tag).
  - Added unit tests that fail if a new FailoverReason/TriggerSource is introduced without updating the mapping table.

- Backwards compatibility / rollout
  - The old metrics names remain, but their label sets are changed (same series name, fewer labels).
  - Dashboards/alerts PR will follow in observability-pack; this PR includes inline comments pointing to the new label names.
  - NOTE: anyone doing ad-hoc queries that group by tenant_id/route_id will need to switch to logs/audit events (see pr-19824-failover-event-audit-log).

Metric details
- rw_failover_decision_total{scope, action, failover_reason, trigger_source, from_region, to_region, tenant_tier, environment}
- rw_failover_metric_label_reject_total{metric, label, scope, environment}

Why this is safe
- The controller/auditing behavior is unchanged; this is strictly telemetry shaping.
- Unknown values are not dropped silently; they are coerced to "unknown" and we emit a reject counter + structured logs.

Testing
- Unit: metrics mapping + label guard tests (added).
- Integration: exercised controller decision loop in staging (dry-run) and verified series counts in Prometheus stayed flat under noisy signals.

Follow-ups
- Update dashboards/alerts to use new label set (tracked under ENG-2418 and handled in observability-pack).
- After game day, re-check rw_failover_metric_label_reject_total for unexpected spikes (indicates missing mapping or new signal names).

Links
- Related: pr-19816-add-multi-region-slo-metrics, pr-19818-alerts-failover-burn-rate, pr-19824-failover-event-audit-log
- Notes: engineering/observability/failover-metrics-cardinality-review
- Failover decision metrics now use bounded enums for failover_reason/trigger_source and drop high-cardinality labels (tenant_id, route_id). - Adds safeguards + telemetry for rejected/unknown label values to prevent silent cardinality regressions.
Allison Grant (review): Can we guarantee failover_reason/trigger_source are truly bounded (no accidental passthrough)? Also, removing tenant_id/route_id will break a couple internal Grafana panels—are we coordinating updates? 

Sergio Costa (author): Yep—mapping is centralized in signal_mapping.go and unknowns are coerced to "unknown" with a reject counter. I’ll open a follow-up in observability-pack to update dashboards/alerts; I added comments in docs/ops/metrics/failover-metrics.md with example queries.

Miles Thornton (review): +1 on coercing unknowns. Please add a test that fails when a new internal signal name is introduced without mapping. 

Sergio Costa (author): Added mapping coverage tests for both controller and policy engine call sites.

Benji Okafor (review): Any chance we still emit policy_id somewhere through tags? We’ve had this happen via helper wrappers. 

Sergio Costa (author): Good catch—there was one wrapper path in eval_metrics.go; removed and added a guard that rejects label keys outside the allowlist.

Aisha Bello (approval): Looks good. The reject counter is exactly what we need for early warning. Approved after the test addition.

Allison Grant (approval): Approved. Please post in #eng-sre once merged so on-call knows to update ad-hoc queries.

Context: Large monorepo presubmit lanes are a major contributor to slow feedback—full lint/test shards run even for small JS/TS changes. This PR introduces two coordinated changes: 1) a lightweight presubmit JS/TS transform that walks changed file lists, performs a focused AST transform to detect cross-file exports/imports that require wider test/lint scopes, and produces a deterministic file-affinity map so CI lanes only run the necessary shards; 2) a release-notes sanitizer CLI used by the release workflow to normalize entries, remove personal emails, and auto-reformat bullet styling to meet compliance and docs standards. Motivation: reduce developer waiting time, lower CI cost, and prevent leaking email addresses into release artifacts. Summary of changes and rationale: - New tool: tools/presubmit-js-transform/transformer.py (lightweight Python wrapper around esprima for fast parse-and-scan; intentionally minimal external deps). Purpose: compute minimal impacted file set given a git diff and package graph, emit a premerge.affinity file consumed by GH Actions. - New tool: tools/release-sanitizer/sanitize.js (Node script used in release workflows to rewrite release notes; configurable rules via .release-sanitizer.yaml). - CI: workflows/presubmit-light.yml added; this is a staged presubmit lane that runs quick file-affinity computation, then triggers targeted lint/test jobs; old heavy presubmit workflow is gated but still present as nightly fallback. - CI: workflows/release-sanity.yml modified to call release sanitizer before building release artifacts. - Build tooling: package.json updated with devDeps pinned (eslint-plugin-import@2.29.0, eslint@8.46.0) and a small helper script to call the transform in local dev. - Docs: docs/dev/presubmit.md and docs/release/release-notes-guidelines.md updated with usage and troubleshooting. - Tests: unit tests for both tools under tests/presubmit and tests/release-sanitizer; lightweight integration test that runs transform on a sample diff. Commits (high-level): - 3a7b9d5: initial presubmit transformer prototype, tests, and GH Action integration scaffold; - 5b2c1e1: add release-sanitizer, config schema, and formatter rules; - d4f1a7c: CI wiring, update package.json devDeps, small lint fixes; - e9c2b31: address reviewer feedback (improve error handling, adjust affinity heuristic), add docs; - 3a7b9d5efc2a4b8d6f1c9e2a: squash merge commit. Action: added a conservative fallback path that triggers full presubmit if the transformer encounters ambiguous dynamic imports or unresolvable package.json workspaces; updated README to document the fallback behavior. - Samir: safety suggestion to log the affinity results to build artifacts for 30 days to audit and tune heuristics; implemented as presubmit-affinity.json upload step with redaction of absolute paths. - Evan: asked for pinned devDeps to avoid CI surprises; package.json updated and lockfile refreshed. - Author replies: provided microbenchmarks and a short explainer in the PR body (transform step median runtime 220ms on local dev machine, full pipeline reduction ~35% in average presubmit time across sample runs). CI timeline and status: - Initial run: presubmit-light workflow failed due to a lint rule mismatch (eslint config expects plugin v2.X); author pinned eslint-plugin-import and reran. - Second run: unit tests passed, integration sample produced expected affinity file, release-sanity workflow initially warned about missing .release-sanitizer.yaml in release staging; author added example config and fallback default. - Final run: all checks passed (lint, unit tests, integration sample, GH Action artifact upload). Observability & rollout plan: - This will be enabled behind a feature flag in the presubmit GH Action; default for main is still full presubmit to avoid unexpected regressions. - After monitoring for 2 weeks with affinity logging enabled, plan to flip default to the targeted lane if no regressions in CI and no missed failures in staging. - Add a Canary tag to select repos that have historically had heavy JS changes to accelerate confidence. Backwards compatibility and risk: - No changes to production runtime code. Transformer is presubmit-only and conservative fallback ensures we never undertest when ambiguous. Release-sanitizer performs non-destructive reformatting but strips emails by default (configurable to preserve if a compliance exception is set). Dependency updates are pinned and contained to devDependencies. Post-merge actions performed by author: - Enabled presubmit-light on target repo for the CI testbed and uploaded affinity logs for future tuning. - Created Linear ticket ENG-2240 to evaluate heuristic improvements and gather telemetry. Merge outcome: merged via squash to main after approvals from Priya and Samir and CI green. Notes for reviewers/maintainers: - If you see unexpected test omissions, re-run the full presubmit via the UI or add the skip-affinity label to force full shards. - To extend the sanitizer rules add patterns to .release-sanitizer.yaml and a corresponding test under tests/release-sanitizer. Links: Linear ENG-2145, ENG-2198, ENG-2240; Support SUP-402 for a reported request to remove personal emails from release notes. 
Adds a lightweight JS/TS AST-based transformer that scopes lint/test runs to affected files and a release-notes sanitizer that normalizes changelog entries and strips personal emails. Improves CI feedback loop and reduces presubmit runtime for typical feature branches by ~35%. Includes minor eslint-plugin and devDependency updates.

Context: As part of the Regional Failover Automation Upgrade, we want the controller to be able to run in production with automation enabled while still requiring an explicit human ack (on-call) before it flips routing policies for certain tiers/routes. Today the controller either executes immediately (when enabled) or runs dry-run only; there is no first-class “pending approval” state, so teams have been relying on manual toggles/feature flags during game days and incidents.

What this PR does: Adds an optional approval gate to the failover controller execution path. When configured, the controller will (1) compute the recommended actions as usual, (2) emit an audit event with status=PENDING_APPROVAL containing the evidence signals and the exact policy changes, and (3) pause execution until it receives an approval decision (approve/deny) or times out. The gate is per-environment and per-scope (Hosted API vs Dedicated), so staging remains fully automated for testing while production can require an ack.

Design notes: The controller loop is now a small state machine. We persist pending approvals in the control-plane store with a TTL so we don’t block the reconciliation loop. The controller periodically re-checks pending items and applies them only once approved and still valid under the current signals (re-validate before execute to avoid acting on stale evidence). If the approval backend is unavailable, we fail closed (do not execute) and continue emitting recommendations/audit events.

Config/behavior: - New config: failover_controller.approval.mode = {"none","required","required_for_production"} - New config: failover_controller.approval.timeout = 5m (default) - New config: failover_controller.approval.scopes = [hosted_api,dedicated] (default: hosted_api only) - New config: failover_controller.approval.require_revalidation = true (default)

Interfaces: - Adds ApprovalProvider interface with NoopApprovalProvider and ControlPlaneApprovalProvider (decision written via internal API/CLI). This PR does not hard-depend on Slack/incident-bot; it exposes a stable API for Devon’s incident-bot follow-up to post buttons/commands.

Observability: - Metrics: failover_approval_pending_total, failover_approval_decision_total{decision=approve|deny|timeout}, failover_approval_wait_seconds (histogram) - Logs: structured log lines include approval_id, action_digest, tenant_tier, route_id, reason - Audit events: PENDING_APPROVAL, APPROVED, DENIED, TIMED_OUT

Testing: - Unit tests for state transitions and re-validation behavior - Integration test that simulates: recommendation -> pending -> approve -> execute (and a stale-signal reject) - Adds a small fake approval backend used by controller integration tests

Rollout: - Feature-flagged behind failover_controller.approval.enabled - Default mode remains “none” so existing staging/game-day configs are unaffected until explicitly enabled

Notes for on-call: There is a new internal endpoint to approve/deny a pending approval (see below). Runbook updates will be a separate doc-focused PR (ENG-2423) once the incident-bot UX lands.

Endpoints: - POST /internal/failover/approvals/{approval_id}: {decision: approve|deny, actor: <user>} - GET /internal/failover/approvals?state=pending

Screenshots: N/A (backend only)

Follow-ups: - incident-bot integration for posting pending approvals + one-click approve/deny - console banner behavior during “pending approval” state - add per-tenant safety limits to approval scope (max pending per tenant)

Refs: ADR-043 (rollback/anti-flap) and ongoing discussion in #eng-sre re: manual approval vs full automation in prod.
Miles Thornton: The controller loop can’t block waiting for approval; we’ll miss new signals and potentially queue up multiple flips. Please ensure pending approvals are persisted and the reconcile loop remains non-blocking.
Benji Okafor (author): Agree. Updated implementation to persist approval requests in control-plane store with TTL; reconcile loop only enqueues and returns. Added periodic poller for pending approvals with bounded concurrency. Added revalidation check before execute.

Rafael Mendes: On-call UX: what’s the minimum viable interface for approving? We need a deterministic audit trail with actor + timestamps and an easy way to deny.
Benji Okafor: Added internal endpoints for approve/deny and included actor field. Audit event now records actor + source. Follow-up will add incident-bot buttons; for now, failoverctl can call the internal endpoint.

Ethan Park: Please avoid putting approval state only in memory; controller restarts are common during incidents. Also, what’s the behavior if control plane is degraded?
Benji Okafor: State is stored in the control-plane store, keyed by approval_id and action_digest, TTL’d. If control plane is unavailable, we fail closed (no execution) but continue recommending actions + logging an explicit APPROVAL_BACKEND_UNAVAILABLE error.

Jordan Lee: Ensure the approval digest covers the exact policy mutations to avoid approving “one thing” and executing another.
Benji Okafor: Digest now hashes: route_id, from_region, to_region, policy_version, and normalized action list. Added a test that mutating any field invalidates the pending approval.

Tomáš Novák: Please add a clear annotation/log line so the on-call can tell “automation didn’t run because approval was required” vs “automation didn’t run because it was disabled.”
Benji Okafor: Added a distinct metric + log reason=approval_required and audit status=PENDING_APPROVAL; also added an alert annotation string (no alert rules added here).

Devon Price: This should be easy to integrate with incident-bot. Can you make the list endpoint filterable and include dashboard links?
Benji Okafor: Added filtering by state and scope; included an optional dashboard_url field in audit metadata (populated if configured).
High-level changes only (no large diffs):
- services/failover-controller/controller/reconcile.go (state machine, approval gating)
- services/failover-controller/controller/approval_provider.go (new interface + noop implementation)
- services/control-plane/approvals/store.go (persist pending approvals with TTL)
- services/control-plane/api/internal_failover_approvals.go (internal approve/deny endpoints)
- pkg/audit/events/failover.go (new audit event types/status)
- pkg/metrics/failover_approvals.go (new metrics)
- helm/redwood/values.yaml + charts/failover-controller/values.yaml (new config)
- services/failover-controller/controller/reconcile_test.go + integration/approval_flow_test.go
Adds optional approval gating for failover automation execution. When enabled, automated policy flips can require an explicit approve/deny decision with a persisted audit trail and revalidation before execution.
payload.title: Failover controller: add optional approval hooks before executing automation

Motivation: production clusters occasionally see short-lived, high-intensity request bursts from a small subset of tenants (outliers) that cause noisy autoscaler signals and suboptimal capacity allocation. This PR introduces an outlier-aware autoscaling component combined with a temporal capacity hedge that absorbs transient spikes while preserving throughput guarantees for steady tenants.

What this PR does: Adds an Outlier Detector that maintains lightweight per-tenant percentile sketches (latency + qps) and flags tenants with sudden delta > configurable threshold. When outliers are detected, the autoscaler engages a Temporal Hedge window (soft buffer of reserved ephemeral slots) and a SLO-fencing policy that temporarily isolates the outlier's burst from normal reservation accounting. The Hedge uses exponential decay of reserved capacity over a sliding window (configurable half-life) to avoid long tail reservation leaks.

Design highlights: - Outlier Detector: lightweight C++ component in runtime/allocator that updates P2/TDigest-like sketches and emits outlier events to the autoscaler controller. - Temporal Hedge: controller-managed soft reservoir scoped per-pool with leak (decay) and forgiveness window parameters. - SLO Fencing: a policy layer that enforces per-tenant in-flight concurrency caps during hedge engagement and triggers backoff advisories to gateway clients. - Telemetry: new utilization histogram series (per-pool and per-tenant sampled) and outlier event metrics, plus a tracer span for hedge lifecycle. - Safety: fails closed — if the detector crashes, autoscaler falls back to existing smoothing logic.

Checklist: [x] design doc referenced (Linear ENG-2314) [x] unit tests for detector logic [x] e2e sim in benchmark-lab harness [x] telemetry dashboards updated [x] rollout/feature-flag gating implemented

Related tickets: ENG-2314, ENG-2397, PM-412.

Implementation notes: - Runtime changes are confined to runtime/allocator/outlier_detector.{cc,h} and runtime/controller/hedge_controller.cc. - Controller exposes two new flags (hedge_window_ms, hedge_decay_half_life_ms) and a per-tenant manual override label. - Gateway side advisory implemented via an advisory header (x-redwood-hedge-suggested-backoff) for best-effort client guidance.

Testing: included unit tests in runtime/tests and controller/tests, plus an integration scenario in benchmark-lab that runs a 5k qps baseline with injected tenant spikes; validated hedge absorbs bursts with <3% SLO violations and reduces churn in scale events by ~48%.

Rollout plan: staged rollout behind feature flag outlier-hedge. Canary on two dedicated fleets for 48h -> expand to 25% of fleets for 72h -> global. Observability guardrails: increase histogram retention during rollouts; automatic rollback if 95th latency regression >10% over baseline for 3 consecutive windows.

Notes on operator UX: added a console page (redwood-console -> Capacity -> Temporal Hedges) with current hedges, their decay windows, and manual drain controls.
Zara Chen: Please add a note about memory overhead of per-tenant sketches.
Priya: Added a configurable sampling window and defaulted to 1% tenant sampling; memory delta ~6MB per 100k tenants (doc added).
Liam O'Connell: Can we tighten the rollback trigger? Suggested 95th latency regression >10% for 3 windows — implemented.
Mateo Alvarez: Approved after addressing telemetry labels and adding dashboard links.
Status: 3 approvals, 0 outstanding change requests.
