Motivation: Customers observed ambiguous 429/503 scenarios from the OpenAI-compatible bridge during tool/function streaming. Clients need machine-readable guidance to decide between immediate retries, exponential backoff, or moving to a degraded model. This PR introduces a compact, opaque backoff advice token (Retry-Advice-Token) and a unified, machine-friendly error frame for streamed tool/function failures. Goals: (1) provide deterministic retry guidance without exposing internal load heuristics, (2) unify error fields across HTTP and streaming frames, (3) maintain backward compatibility with existing Retry-After headers and OpenAI shim behavior.
Design summary:
- New header: Retry-Advice-Token (opaque string). Token encodes server-side lease for idempotency/retry window and a short advice TTL (server-signed). Clients that receive a 429/503 can include the token in the next request to opt-in to server-coordinated retry behavior.
- Error envelope: all error responses (HTTP and stream frames) include an error_code (string), user_message, and optional retry_advice_hint ("immediate", "backoff", "abort") and a numeric backoff_seconds when applicable. This is added to the streamed frame format as a single line frame with "type": "error" and a consistent schema to avoid ad-hoc parsing.
- Idempotency interplay: when tool/function calls are tied to idempotency keys, the server may attach a Retry-Advice-Token to allow replay without requiring the client to change keys. The token is short-lived and scoped to the idempotency key+route.
- OpenAI shim mapping: updates mapper to surface the new fields from internal errors into OpenAI-style JSON error.body and to preserve Retry-After for clients that only understand the legacy header.
Migration and compatibility:
- Clients not updated will still see legacy Retry-After and HTTP 429/503 with user-facing messages.
- New clients can take advantage of the header + structured frame for coordinated retries and improved backoff.
Security and privacy: tokens are server-signed and opaque; they do not reveal internal load or topology.
Implementation highlights:
- server/http/headers.go: new header parsing and validation.
- server/streaming/frame_writer.go: emit unified error frames on stream close and mid-stream failures.
- shims/openai/mapper.go: map internal error_code -> openai error fields, and attach Retry-After fallback when token is present.
- runtime/idempotency/lease_manager.go: short-lived leases for token validation and eviction.
- docs/api/retry-and-errors.md: detailed client guidance and examples.
Behavioural examples (text):
- HTTP 429 with token: Response includes Retry-Advice-Token: "radv_eyJ...", body contains {"error_code":"rate_limit_capacity","user_message":"Region capacity high","retry_advice_hint":"backoff","backoff_seconds":12}
- Streamed error frame: a single line JSON frame: {"type":"error","error_code":"tool_execution_failed","user_message":"upstream tool timed out","retry_advice_hint":"immediate"}
Testing: integration tests cover token roundtrip, lease expiration, and shim mapping. Load tests verify no measurable latency regression.
Checklist:
- [x] header parsing and validation
- [x] stream frame emission and consumers updated
- [x] OpenAI shim mapping
- [x] unit and integration tests
- [x] docs and SDK sample update
- [x] security review notes included
Backcompat notes: if both Retry-Advice-Token and Retry-After are present, clients should prefer structured token flow when supported. When absent, fall back to Retry-After seconds.
Relationship to other work: this complements ENG-1093 (stream framing refactor) and replaces ad-hoc backoff hints embedded in logs.
Ethan Zhao: Please add a short comment explaining why the token is opaque and what properties it encodes. Also verify that tokens are bounded in size.
Priya Menon: Added comment and enforced 256-byte limit on token in headers.go; updated lease tests to assert truncation behavior.
Lina Costa: The stream frame schema looks good; suggest adding a non-breaking feature flag for the streaming clients to opt-in.
Priya Menon: Added feature flag STREAM_ERROR_FRAME_V2 behind runtime config and documented migration steps in docs/api/retry-and-errors.md.
Marco Alvarez: CI flake on lease test reproduced locally; suggested pinning clock in tests. Priya updated tests accordingly.
Marco Alvarez: Approving after tests and docs updates.
Ethan Zhao: Approved. Left a follow-up note to iterate on observability labels for retry_token usage.
Merged via squash merge. Commit message consolidates token design, frame schema, and mapping notes. Post-merge tasks: backfill SDK examples across TS/Go, schedule a deprecation note for older clients that rely solely on Retry-After, and monitor prometheus metric retry_advice_token_issued for initial rollout.
Introduce Retry-Advice-Token header and unified error frame for streamed tool/function failures. Adds structured retry advice (immediate/backoff/abort) and a machine-friendly error_code field. Backward compatible with Retry-After. Clients may opt-in to coordinated retry flow for improved availability.

Motivation: Dedicated fleet decommits and short bursty drop-offs have caused frequent transient SLA slippage when many tenants simultaneously release reserved capacity. This PR introduces a lightweight rate-stabilizer controller that smooths sustained throughput commitments by sampling commitment deltas and maintaining a short-lived sustain pool, together with a deferred-decommit adapter that staggers decommit transactions to avoid synchronized capacity churn.

What this changes: single PR that touches the autoscaler control plane, scheduler decommit logic and telemetry so operators can observe the stabilization behavior. Key pieces: 
- autoscaler/rate_stabilizer.py: new controller that computes a per-tenant sustain budget based on recent commitment samples (EWMA + percentile guard).
- scheduler/decommit_adapter.go: replaces immediate batch decommit with a staggered commit queue that enqueues decommits and releases them in micro-batches by tenant weight and shard.
- telemetry/metrics_registry.yaml: new metrics (rate_stabilizer.sustain_headroom, decommit.stagger_delay_p50/p95, decommit.backpressure_events).
- tests/cluster_sim: synthetic workloads that validate stabilization under multi-tenant bursts.

Design notes and tradeoffs: The controller avoids long-lived reservations by favoring a short (30s-120s) sustain pool that reduces oscillation without blocking legitimate capacity reclamation. Deferred decommits use a deterministic jitter schedule keyed by tenant id + epoch to guarantee progress while preventing synchronized spikes. This is intentionally conservative: when cluster utilization is low, decommits proceed faster; when utilization is high or SLOs are at risk, stagger windows expand.

Rollout plan: deploy as opt-in feature flag (autoscaler.rateStabilizer.enabled=false by default). Canary on single Dedicated pool for two weeks, monitor new telemetry and existing SLA dashboards (error budget, p95 latency). If safe, enable for all Dedicated pools over 2 days using gradual ramp.

Testing: unit + integration tests added; cluster-sim demonstrates: 1) 12% reduction in tenants experiencing >3x transient queue growth in synthetic burst tests, 2) median decommit jitter ~150ms, p95 ~1.1s for busy pools, 3) ~4-7% decrease in spike-driven tail-latency cost.

Checklist:
- [x] Controller implementation with basic invariants and concurrency guards
- [x] Staggered decommit queue integrated with scheduler
- [x] Telemetry and dashboard patches
- [x] Unit and integration tests in CI
- [x] Canary rollout notes and feature flag

Related: ENG-7341 (stabilize reservation churn), ENG-7420 (telemetry for decommit pipeline).
Diego Martinez: Looks good overall. Main question: how do we ensure decommit progress in the pathological case where many tenants have identical jitter? Can you add a deterministic fallback that forces at least N decommits every Xs?
Evelyn Cho (author): Added deterministic epoch-based escalation (see decommit_adapter.go lines ~120-155). Fallback forces 2% of queued decommits per shard every 500ms when progress stalls.
Ravi Subramanian: Can the EWMA window be tuned per-tenant? Ops will want finer control for big customers. Suggest adding tenant-level override via annotation.
Evelyn Cho (author): Added tenant annotation support and documented safe values in docs/rate_stabilizer.md. Defaults remain cluster-safe.
Lina Chen: CI integration flake on cluster_sim; observed test timeout. Please add a retry and shorten wall-clock wait.


Evelyn Cho (author): Reduced wait in tests and added deterministic seed to avoid timing flakiness; re-ran CI.
Introduce Rate Stabilizer (opt-in) and deferred decommit adapter to reduce synchronized capacity churn in Dedicated pools; adds telemetry for sustain headroom and decommit staggering. Opt-in via autoscaler.rateStabilizer.enabled flag.

Motivation: Over the last two quarters customers reported subtle auth race conditions during stream reconnects and inconsistent ergonomics across the Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs. This PR consolidates the auth lifecycle surface, tightens retry defaults for streaming contexts, and harmonizes ergonomics (pause/resume, cancel semantics, typed async iterators) so client code can migrate with minimal friction.

What this changes (high-level): Introduces an AuthProfile abstraction shared conceptually across SDKs (not a new centralized package in this PR) to standardize token refresh windows, preflight checks, and telemetry tags emitted during refresh/fallback events; tightens streaming retry presets when a token refresh is in-flight to avoid double-inflight requests; adds pause()/resume() and graceful_cancel() helpers to stream handles with deterministic semantics; unifies method names and parameter order across SDKs for parity; adds end-to-end interop tests that exercise credential handoffs and stream resume across language bindings; bumps SDK minor versions to reflect ergonomic changes.

Commit summary: 1) Introduce auth lifecycle tests and fixtures (e2e harness) 2) Add stream ergonomics API to TS/Go/Python SDKs (pause/resume/graceful_cancel) 3) Implement latency-aware retry preset for streaming and guard against concurrent reauth races 4) Add telemetry tags (auth.stage, auth.reason) and instrumentation hooks for rollout analysis 5) Docs: migration guide and examples for common patterns 6) TS lint fixes and smaller follow-up commits to address CI failures.

Files of note changed: redwood-sdk-python/redwood/session.py (stream handle helpers + auth shim), redwood-sdk-typescript/src/stream/handle.ts (typed async iterator and pause/resume), redwood-sdk-go/auth/refresh.go (concurrency guard and backoff profile), docs/migration/sdk-auth-2.0.md (migration notes and examples), tests/e2e/sdk_interop/test_auth_stream.py (interop harness + docker compose config), examples/streaming-auth-examples/* (small samples).

Compatibility and migration: The surface-level renames are additive or aliased to previous names when possible. We provide a short migration guide (docs/migration/sdk-auth-2.0.md) and deprecation warnings at runtime for any renamed entry points. No breaking behavior introduced for synchronous API flows; streaming clients should follow the migration steps to adopt the new pause/resume helpers for deterministic reconnect behavior.

Testing and CI: Added ~12 new unit tests across the SDKs and 3 cross-language e2e tests that run in the CI matrix. Initial CI run failed TypeScript linting and a flaky go race in refresh.go; both were fixed in follow-up commits. All CI checks are green on merge. Local perf smoke tests show ~3–6% tail-latency reduction for reconnect-after-refresh scenarios due to reduced duplicate inflight token refreshes.

Risks and mitigation: The main risk is client-side misuse of pause/resume leading to blocked request loops; mitigations include: clear docs, runtime validation that resume cannot be called before pause, and telemetry to detect misused patterns. Another risk is telemetry / metric churn; added tags are opt-in behind a flag for hosted customers while we evaluate noise.

Related work: ENG-2034 (auth rollouts and telemetry), ENG-2110 (stream ergonomics research).

Release notes: Add SDK helpers for pause/resume and graceful stream cancel; unify auth refresh windows and add latency-aware streaming retry presets; e2e interop tests added; minor version bumps: python -> 2.1.0, typescript -> 1.6.3, go -> 1.8.0.

Merge: Squash-merged to main after approvals and green CI.
Ethan Park (requested_changes): Please add a metric for 'reauth_attempts' and make the concurrency guard opt-out for older servers. Also adjust the TS linter rule. — Sofia: added reauth_attempts metric and an env var REDWOOD_OLD_AUTH_COMPAT to relax the guard, updated CI config.
Marta Lopez (approved): Tests look good; small nit about error wording in session.py; resolved.
Julian Wu (comment): Curious about the runtime cost of telemetry tags. — Sofia: telemetry is behind a runtime flag and the tag emission path is low-overhead (fast path no-op when disabled).
Add pause/resume/graceful_cancel helpers for stream handles; unify auth refresh semantics across SDKs; introduce latency-aware streaming retry presets; add e2e interop tests and migration guide; bump SDK minor versions for py/ts/go.
Coordinate SDK releases: publish Python 2.1.0, TypeScript 1.6.3, Go 1.8.0. Alert integrators about optional telemetry flag REDWOOD_SDK_AUTH_TELEMETRY (off by default) and REDWOOD_OLD_AUTH_COMPAT for legacy servers.

Context and motivation: Customers asked for tighter operator delegation controls and stronger guarantees that tenant data encryption keys are used only in allowed regions. This PR implements three coordinated pieces: 1) RBACv2 delegation scopes (operator->service delegation with explicit allowed-action sets and TTLs), 2) a KMS region bind layer that asserts CMK region affinity at call time and provides soft-fallback telemetry, and 3) an audit snapshotter that periodically compacts residency-relevant audit events into attestable snapshots for offline compliance review.

What this PR changes (high level): - Add 'delegation_scope' primitives to RBACv2 policy model and enforcement paths. Delegation scopes can be minted by platform services and contain permitted role templates, permitted resource filters (by tenant, service, tag), and a TTL. - On the KMS client path add region-binding checks: when a request carries a tenant CMK reference, the region in the KMS metadata must match the tenant's pinned region; violations are rejected unless the tenant has an allowed-mpo (migration-permission) flag. - Audit snapshotter: new background component that streams filtered audit entries (kms operations, rbac delegation events, region-pin violations) and writes time-windowed, signed snapshots to the audit archive bucket for compliance teams. Snapshots include a compact SHA256 index and metadata for proof-of-origin.

Checklist: - [x] Policy model change and DB migration (+ backfill) - [x] Enforcement in auth dispatcher - [x] KMS client region validation with unit tests and a small integration test harness - [x] Audit snapshotter implementation with signing and retention headers - [x] Migration guide and rollout plan in docs/ - [x] E2E smoke in perf-canary for common request paths (no regression in p50/p95) - [x] Security review completed

Files changed (high level): - auth/policy/model.go (add DelegationScope struct, serialization) - auth/dispatcher.go (enforce scoped delegation at decision time) - db/migrations/20250115_add_delegation_scopes.sql (migration + index) - kms/region_bind.go (validation helper, soft-telemetry) - kms/client.go (integrate region check before Encrypt/Decrypt/Sign) - audit/snapshotter/snapshotter.go (streaming, signer) - audit/snapshotter/collector_test.go (tests + fake KMS events) - docs/security/delegation-scopes.md (usage + examples) - helm/values.yaml (feature flag rollout knobs)

Migration notes: - DB migration adds a new table 'delegation_scopes' and a small backfill job that converts historical operator grants into initial scopes with conservative TTLs. The backfill runs as a job that paginates; operator privileges are preserved if the backfill fails but the new enforcement path will treat absent scopes as denied until the backfill completes. - Feature gating: RBACV2_DELEGATION_SCOPES=off by default for 48 hours; helm chart exposes a gradual rollout percentage knob. - KMS region bind is opt-in via TENANT_REGION_BIND=true; customer-managed tenants are evaluated first. Operators can enable strict mode (reject on mismatch) or lax mode (record telemetry and attach an 'allowlist' bypass) during gradual rollout.

Motivation: Long-tail token-cost variance is causing noisy SLO alerts for enterprise tenants. Existing token sampling captures high-cost outliers but misses systematic epochal shifts when traffic shape changes (e.g., nightly batch jobs or A/B rollout cohorts). This PR introduces a lightweight heuristic cost sampler and an epochal workload dashboard to make attribution and alert tuning actionable. Summary of changes: 1) heuristic cost sampler: new sampler that combines token-cost weight, recent frequency sketch, and kernel-latency indicator to pick representative invocations for tracing and payload capture; sampler is pluggable into the existing invocation-sampler interface and defaults to a conservative 0.2% sample rate with adaptive bumping when epochal drift is detected; 2) epochal workload dashboard: Grafana dashboard (observability/epochal-cost.json) with epoch cohorting panels, cost delta waterfall, sampled invocation anchors, and a new 'epoch drift' sparkline; 3) alert tiling: alert rules updated to use epoch-aware baselines and an exponential smoothing parameter to reduce churn during planned rollouts (alert rules updated: alerts/token-cost-slo and alerts/long-tail-noise); 4) lightweight replay harness: add a synthetic epochal replay used in CI smoke to validate sampler bump behavior across 3 simulated epochs; 5) unit and integration tests: sampler logic covered with fuzzed distributions and deterministic replay tests; 6) docs: docs/observability/heuristic-sampler.md explains configuration knobs, tradeoffs, and migration steps. Checklist: - [x] Design review with ENG-obs (notes linked in Linear ENG-1428) - [x] Local unit tests - [x] Integration smoke test with synthetic replay - [x] Load-smoke on staging for 24h - [x] Dashboard review with SRE and Product Changes to runtime/config: - new config block observability.sampler.heuristic with fields: enabled (bool), base_rate (float), epoch_window_seconds (int), bump_policy (enum: conservative/aggressive), kernel_latency_threshold_ms (int). Backwards compatible: sampler defaults to disabled unless enabled via config; existing sampling paths unchanged until enabled in cluster config. Rollout plan: staged rollout via canary on dedicated capacity: enable sampler=false by default; enable on 1% of tenants for 48h, monitor drift detector, then ramp to 25% and 100% with SRE approval. Observability acceptance criteria: 1) no increase in error rates or CPU >2% on serving runtime in canary; 2) show reduction in alert noise (fewer distinct alert groups) for test tenants; 3) sampled traces should include high-fidelity kernel-latency and cost attribution tags for downstream debugging. Risks and mitigations: - Risk: additional I/O from sampled invocation capture. Mitigation: sampling rate conservative, sampler attaches only compact digest by default; full payload capture feature gated behind a tenant opt-in. - Risk: mis-calibrated bump policy causing alert suppression. Mitigation: bump policy has strict upper bound and can be overridden per-tenant. Related work: this complements existing epochal and cohort-based PRs (see ENG-1502, PRs linked in Linear).
Lucas Ortega: Can you explain why kernel-latency is included in the heuristic? Concerned about correlation with noisy GPU metrics.
Maya Patel: Kernel-latency is a proxy for backend contention; empirical tests on staging showed it identifies invocations where token-cost attribution spans are longer and more informative. Added comments and a unit test that simulates kernel spikes.
Priya Nair: Please add a safety cap to bump_policy to avoid sampling >5% automatically. Also request an e2e smoke run on dedicated-1.

Add heuristic invocation sampler (opt-in) and epochal workload dashboard to improve token-cost attribution and reduce alert noise. Configurable bump_policy and smoothing to tune alert churn. Backwards compatible; feature off by default.
Deployed to staging and canary. SRE to track ENG-1428 metric dashboard widgets for next two weeks. If alert noise does not improve after ramp, revert via feature flag.

payload.body:
Motivation: Continuous batcher fairness can degrade when a small number of KV-heavy or long-sequence requests occupy slots for extended periods, starving short requests and inflating tail latency. Previous fixes reduced individual timeouts or added static probes but did not jointly consider kernel selection characteristics, per-request KV pressure, and transient load patterns. This PR introduces two coordinated mechanisms: (1) Adaptive Timeout Corridor (ATC) — a dynamic timeout window per slot that adapts to observed service-time distributions and sequence-length/kernels hints; and (2) KV prefetch backoff — a per-request backoff policy that reduces aggressive KV prefetching for probed or long-running requests to give capacity back to the admission queue.

Design summary: ATC computes a rolling corridor [lower_ms, upper_ms] per scheduling cohort derived from percentile estimates (p50/p95) of serviced request durations, with additional headroom based on kernel hint (e.g., attention-optimized vs generic kernels) and whether the request used KV cache extensively. The scheduler uses the corridor to make two decisions: early release for requests exceeding upper_ms (attempt graceful slot preemption/fallback) and opportunistic coalescing for requests under lower_ms to maximize batch density. KV prefetch backoff adds an admission-time score that penalizes aggressive prefetch when KV pressure is high; the penalty scales down prefetch bandwidth and softens KV pin lifetime. Combined, the mechanisms aim to prevent starvation, reduce tail latency, and preserve throughput.

Implementation notes: - New metrics collected: cohort_p50_ms, cohort_p95_ms, kv_prefetch_tokens, kv_pin_lifetime_ms. - Kernel hints were surfaced from the kernel dispatcher via a small new flag on RequestContext (kernel_hint: "attn_fast" | "dense_basic" | "kv_heavy"). - ATC uses an exponential moving percentile estimator to stay robust to workload shifts. - Prefetch backoff uses a sliding-window admission score and a token-bucket limiter per GPU group. - Added a canary rollout flag (scheduler.atc_enabled) and a safety override that disables ATC on single-slot GPUs to avoid regressions.

Testing and benchmarks: - Microbenchmarks: p50 improved ~3-6% on mixed short/long workloads, p99 improved ~8-18% on synthetic KV-heavy tails. - End-to-end: internal perf harness (bench-lab) with same-model traffic saw 12% reduction in observed p99 latency for interactive workloads with ~20% KV request mix. - Load tests included adversarial sequences where 5% of requests were long (seq_len>4096); ATC prevented starvation and improved overall queue throughput. - Unit and integration tests added for percentile estimator edge cases and backoff state machine.

Rollout plan: 1) Deploy to canary pool (scheduler.atc_enabled=true) with telemetry gating for kernel_hint correctness. 2) Monitor cohort_violations and kv_backoff_suppressed metrics; if cohort_violations spike beyond threshold we will revert automatically via rollout controller. 3) Gradual ramp to 25% then 100% with 24h observation windows. Backport: will open a backport PR for the 2025.12 release branch after validation.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (Linear ENG-1829) - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Bench harness runs - [x] Canary flag and metrics - [x] Documentation snippets for ops console

Related: ENG-1974 (investigation into kernel hint accuracy), SUP-421 (customer incident citing KV-induced starvation).

Hotfix: add proportional SLO multiplexer to reduce circuit oscillation and transparent rejoin path to gradually restore tenants after regional failovers. Backwards-compatible. No config migration required.
Motivation: During a recent regional failover incident multiple high-throughput tenants repeatedly tripped their local circuits which caused aggressive global fallbacks and long tail recovery for low-rate tenants. The root cause was a binary routing decision in the SLO enforcer + fallback allocator: when a tenant exceeded its SLO bucket the system would immediately move 100% of requests to slowpath fallbacks which amplified upstream load and caused oscillation. This PR introduces a proportional SLO multiplexer that divides degraded traffic across fallback tiers in configurable proportions (fastfall, slowfall, degraded) and a transparent rejoin path that warms restored capacity with probe-driven ramping rather than abrupt reinstates. The changes are intended as a hotfix to stabilize production while preserving request-level SLAs.
1) add proportional multiplexer and configuration schema (slo/multiplexer.go + slo/config.go)
2) implement transparent rejoin probes and state machine (slo/rejoin.go)
3) integrate multiplexer into router and egress proxy (router/mux_integration.go, proxy/egress_shim.go)
4) add unit and integration tests + loadbench scenario (slo/multiplexer_test.go, perf/loadbench/proportional_slo.json)
5) update observability: new metrics and dashboard panels (telemetry/metrics.go, dashboards/proportional_slo.json)
6) small docs note and upgrade guidance (docs/release-notes/proportional-slo.md)
Ethan Cole: Nice approach, Priya. Can you clarify how the proportions are derived when multiple tenants are in partial degrade? Concerned about head-of-line inversion. Please add a short note in slo/config.go with the formula and a unit test for the multi-tenant case.

Motivation: customers on Dedicated want stronger guarantees for committed throughput while avoiding hard capacity preemption that causes large quality regressions. This PR introduces an SLO Contract Enforcer service that binds per-tenant SLO contracts (throughput floor, burst allowance, degradation band) to autoscaler decisioning and a new Granular Degradation Profile DSL to express staged shedding strategies. Design summary: the enforcer receives validated contracts from the control plane, exposes a per-pool enforcement API consumed by the autoscaler, and publishes a small set of signals (contracted_rps, available_headroom, degrade_hint) to the routing plane. The degradation profile DSL (YAML) lets operators declare ordered steps (soft-throttle, kv-cache-preserve, selective-model-fallback, queued-backpressure) with thresholds and cool-downs. Integration: the autoscaler consults the enforcer during scale-down and burst reconciliation to avoid violating contracts; the admission controller uses degrade_hint to switch to preconfigured fallback model variants. Telemetry: adds percentile utilization (p50/p95/p99) per-tenant and per-pool, a degradation_event counter with reason tags, and a headroom_time_series exported to existing telemetry pipeline. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is a no-op unless a contract is present or a feature flag is enabled; existing autoscaler heuristics remain intact. Migration: control plane will seed contracts for customers on Dedicated via a Linear task (ENG-3421) and ops will enable canary on a subset of pools. Testing: unit and integration tests mock contract lifecycle; end-to-end smoke runs against a local dedicated cluster using synthetic load. Rollout: canary 5% pools for 24h -> 25% for 48h -> full with rollback thresholds (error spike >2x baseline or contract violation rate >0.1%). Risks & mitigations: incorrect profiles can cause excessive shedding; mitigation includes safe-mode where first degradation step is always a soft-throttle and immediate rollback if tail latency increases beyond threshold. See release notes and docs for configuration examples.

Aisha Kapoor: Added p95/p99; limited dimension set to pool_id and slo_tier, recorded expected cardinality in docs.

Adds ops UI for configuring SLO tiers, telemetry for percentile utilization and degradation events, and autoscaler integration to honor contracts during scale decisions.

Motivation: teams frequently ask for a way to pick batching and quantization defaults that are tuned to their workload without trial-and-error. This PR introduces two orthogonal primitives: 1) Batch Journeys — a small DSL and set of presets that express workload 'journeys' (cold-heavy, chat-short-turns, long-completion) and map them to batching/cache defaults; 2) Quant Cost Maps — compact artifacts that capture per-model precision variants (fp16/int8/8+4/4bit) and their expected cost/latency/quality tradeoffs under common sequence length percentiles. Together these enable automated profile selection in Redwood Optimize and a safe CLI/console path for Dedicated/Private users to adopt conservative cost-saving defaults. Changes: single-string description of the user-visible changes and the implementation: - new CLI command: redwood cost-orch apply-profile --profile <journey> --cluster <id> --dry-run - batch-journey presets under internal/config/batch_journeys/{chat,api,long}.yaml - quant cost maps generated from webrtc-style microbench runs under telemetry/quant_maps/*.json - runtime adapter that consumes journey + quant map and emits a prioritized list of runtime hints (batch_size, max_latency_per_token_ms, kvcache_policy, quant_profile) - lightweight simulator that validates chosen profile against recent traffic samples before applying (CLI dry-run uses this) - telemetry: new metrics (rwi.batch_hint_applied, rwi.quant_profile_selected, rwi.profile_simulated_econ_delta) - canary rollout: console flag and api to apply profiles to 1%/10%/100% of traffic with automated rollback if latency/SLA regressions exceed thresholds Backwards compatibility and safety: profiles are always advisory; runtime will never lower per-request latency SLOs below the configured route level. We ship safe fallbacks: if quantized model variant fails to load, runtime falls back to the pinned canonical variant. Implementation notes: - batch journey DSL is intentionally small (3 top-level keys: selector, hints, thresholds) to make authoring predictable - quant maps are normalized to 95th/50th token-latency buckets and a small quality delta estimate (BLEU/ROUGE-like proxies for applicable models) - CLI leverages the existing orchestration API and introduces an idempotent apply operation with conservative defaults Testing and validation performed: - unit tests for YAML parsing and quant map ingestion - e2e simulator tests with synthetic workloads - benchmark runs on a small Dedicated pool (d-2-gpu-smoke) for each quant profile - integration smoke for console rollout UI - manual canary on a single customer cluster (log sanitized) Rollout plan: 1) behind feature flag (opt-in) for 2 weeks; 2) internal canary on non-prod clusters; 3) 10% Dedicated customers; 4) GA. Related: ENG-5227 (profiling pipeline), PM-118 (product spec), SUP-987 (support request for safer defaults).

payload.body:
Adds a telemetry-driven prefill synthesizer to generate tenant-specific warmup templates and a lightweight quantization escort that applies safe fallback rules. Improves cold-start cost by ~12% on benchmark suites. No breaking API changes.
Motivation: Cold-start and sparse-traffic tenants still account for a disproportionate share of per-token cost. Previous default prefill heuristics were static and required manual tuning per tenant. This PR implements a telemetry-driven "synthesizer" that ingests recent request traces, derives compact warmup templates, and surfaces tenant-specific prefill defaults to the autoscaler and runtime. It also introduces a small "quant escort" component: a rules layer that applies conservative quantization profiles with fallbacks when a risk signal is detected (loss spike, high perplexity, or regen rate).

What this changes: Adds a streaming telemetry transformer that computes per-tenant sample shapes, typical prompt prefixes, and cold-latency fingerprints. The synthesizer produces a prioritized list of warmup templates and target batch shapes that the runtime can use for speculative prefill or cache seeding. The quant escort registers safe quant profiles for each tenant and a graceful degradation path: if quality regressions are observed, requests route to the next-safe-variant and a rollback alert is raised.

Checklist: [x] telemetry ingestion pipeline and feature extractor implemented, [x] synthesizer scoring + prioritization, [x] runtime hooks to consume warmup templates (experimental opt-in), [x] quant escort policy and simple thresholds, [x] unit tests and end-to-end prefill integration test, [x] small docs and rollout guidance, [x] dashboard and alerting for regressions and cost delta.

Testing and results: Unit + integration test suite added. Local perf bench (small synthetic tenant mix) shows cold-start median latency improvement of 9–18% and a simulated unit-econ reduction ~12% across low-traffic tenants. Quant escort prevented three synthetic loss spikes during fault-injection runs by falling back to a higher-precision variant. CI runs passed except a transient flake in the telemetry ingestion test which was fixed in a follow-up commit.

Files touched summary: Key logic is in services/prefill/synthesizer.py (scoring, ranking, export API) and runtime/quant/escort.py (policy enforcement, fallback routing). Telemetry ingestion and extraction lives under telemetry/ingest with a small Go processor that emits tenant-level metrics. Observability changes include a Prefill Warmup dashboard and an alert (prefill.quant.regression) that triggers on repeated fallback events. Helm values include an opt-in flag for the synthesizer so we can canary on a subset of tenants.

Review notes and conversation: Reviewer Avery asked for clearer invariants around safety thresholds; added explicit circuit-breaker logic and integration tests demonstrating rollback within 5s. Samir requested an internal API for exporting synthesized templates to the Dedicated agent — added a compact JSON schema and versioning header. Laila signaled concern about telemetry cost; we added a lightweight sampling mode and a telemetry retention note in docs to mitigate. Approvals: Avery (approved), Samir (approved after changes), Laila (approved).

CI: All mandatory checks (unit, integration, lint, build) passed on final run. Perf benchmarks were run offline and recorded in the PR artifacts.

Rollout plan: Feature gated behind helm flag "prefill.telemetry.enabled". Suggested canary: enable on 3% of tenants for 48h, monitor prefill.cache.hitrate, cold-start p50/p95, and prefill.quant.regression alert. If regressions > 0.5% of requests, auto-disable and notify SRE.

Related work: builds on ENG-2041 (prefill API stabilization) and schema in ENG-2120 (quant profile format). Linear items linked above track follow-ups for wider tenant rollout and expanded quant heuristics.
This is opt-in and safe by default. The synthesizer writes artifacts to S3 under tenant-prefill/ and emits a versioned schema. If you observe any unexpected memory pressure in the runtime, disable prefill.telemetry.enabled and alert infra. We recommend enabling the sampling mode first to limit telemetry ingestion costs.

Verify warmup templates appear in runtime debug endpoint /_prefill/templates
Fault-inject a quant loss spike and confirm escort fallback triggers and alert is created
Run perf benchmark against cold-start suite and compare baseline

payload.body:
Context: We have three slightly divergent reauth and retry behaviors across the Python/TS/Go SDKs that cause intermittent session handoff bugs during long-lived pull/stream sessions. This PR introduces a small, explicit contract called 'reauth slices' (time-windowed credential refresh hints) plus an adaptive retry DSL that sits on top of existing retry primitives. It also adds a checkpointed pullstream abstraction (lightweight, opt-in) that gives consumers explicit resume points for streaming reconnects.

Motivation: Aim for behavioral parity across SDKs while keeping each SDK ergonomic for its language: minimal surface changes, explicit opt-in checkpointing for apps that need deterministic resume semantics, and clearer telemetry for auth failures to help SRE triage.

What this PR does: 
- Adds a reauth slice metadata header to outgoing streaming init requests and exposes a small ReauthSlice struct/class in each SDK binding.
- Implements an adaptive retry DSL: rules can express backoff floors, ceilings, jitter profiles, and a predicate for credential-refresh-triggered retries.
- Introduces checkpointed-pullstream helper APIs (pullstream.checkpoint() / PullStream.checkpoint() / PullStreamCheckpoint) in TS/Python/Go that serialize a resume token and last-ack offset.
- Upholds backward compatibility: existing streaming APIs continue to work; checkpointing is opt-in.
- Adds credential and auth telemetry tags emitted to the client-side metrics layer for troubleshooting (reauth_attempt, reauth_slice, refresh_latency_ms, retry_reason).
- Documents runtime safeguards: max reauth window, stale-slice rejection, retry budget accounting.

Checklist:
- [x] API surface defined for TS/Python/Go (minimal, idiomatic)
- [x] Unit tests for DSL evaluation and edge cases
- [x] Integration tests for stream reconnect+checkpoint resume
- [x] Telemetry emitted and validated in local metrics harness
- [x] Docs snippets and examples added to SDK guides
- [x] Version bumps for all three SDKs coordinated in monorepo release script

Testing & CI: Ran the TS and Py integration suites against the staging bridge that simulates intermittent token expiry; Go unit+integration ran in CI. Early CI run failed on a flaky TS e2e that exercised a timeout edge; root cause was a healthy timeout constant in tests that needed bumping — fixed and rerun. Final CI: linux-unit-tests ⬤ pass, ts-sdk-integration ⬤ pass (rerun once), py-sdk-integration ⬤ pass, go-sdk-integration ⬤ pass, lint ⬤ pass.

Rollout plan: Feature gated via SDK minor flags and server-side acceptance of reauth_slice header. Gradual ramp for production consumers: start with internal teams, then opt-in customers, then on-by-default in three weeks after metrics validate reduced auth-fallover errors.

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps retry semantics composable (the adaptive DSL composes onto the existing retry middleware) to avoid hard-breaking changes in customers' custom retry policies.
Diego Ruiz (2026-03-01): Nice surface. Two asks: (1) add a deterministic checksum to checkpoint payload so accidental corruption is detectable, (2) please ensure the Go serializer remains stable across minor releases.
Maya Thompson (2026-03-01): Added CRC32 checksum to checkpoint payload and tests that validate incompatible payloads fail to resume. Go serializer uses versioned envelope to keep stability; documented in reauth-slices.md.

Background and motivation: multiple teams reported hard-to-handle streaming cancellation + token rotation races in customer integrations. This PR implements a cross-SDK pattern ("flow-cancel + idempotent-retry shim") that: 1) lets callers cancel streams deterministically (Python context manager, TS AbortSignal, Go context.Context propagation), 2) ensures streaming reconnects are safe when auth tokens rotate mid-stream (lease-based token provider + idempotency keys), and 3) improves ergonomics for common patterns (with/using semantics and docs/examples).

What this PR contains (single string):
- Commits (high level):
  * introduce flow-aware stream context managers/abstractions in py/ts/go
  * implement lease-token provider to serialize token handoff with streaming kernel
  * add idempotent-retry shim to streaming runtime client, store per-chunk resume markers
  * ergonomics: Python context manager and async iterator helpers, TS AbortSignal adapter + AsyncIterable wrapper, Go StreamIterator convenience helpers and examples
  * unit/integration tests + e2e smoke for hosted streaming with simulated token rotation
  * docs + changelogs + version bumps across the three SDKs

- Files / areas touched (high level):
  * sdk/python/redwood/streaming.py (new ContextManagedStream, StreamResumeToken)
  * sdk/python/redwood/auth/lease_provider.py (new)
  * sdk/python/tests/test_stream_cancel_token_rotation.py
  * sdk/typescript/src/stream/abort-adapter.ts (AbortSignal -> stream adapter)
  * sdk/typescript/src/stream/iterable-wrapper.ts
  * sdk/typescript/__tests__/stream-reconnect.spec.ts
  * sdk/go/stream/iterator.go (context-aware iterator)
  * sdk/go/auth/leaseprovider.go
  * shared/proto/streaming.proto (minor resume token additions)
  * docs/sdk/streaming-cancellation.md
  * examples/streaming/stream-cancel-demo (py/ts/go)

- Short code snippets (illustrative):
  * Python: with client.open_stream(prompt) as s: s.send('...')
  * TypeScript: const controller = new AbortController(); client.stream(req, {signal: controller.signal})
  * Go: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 30*time.Second); defer cancel(); it := client.Stream(ctx, req)

Compatibility/migration notes:
- The public generation interfaces are unchanged. Streaming helpers are additive. The resume token field is optional and backward compatible in the wire proto. Consumers who currently rely on raw ws streams with custom token refresh may opt into the new lease provider or keep the existing behavior.

Testing and CI:
- Unit test coverage added across py/ts/go (~45 new tests). Integration harness simulates mid-stream token expiry and verifies reconnects resume from the last acked chunk.
- CI: initial run showed one flaky test in ts e2e (race on AbortSignal teardown). Fixed by explicit microtask drain in adapter. Final CI: pass.

Review conversation (condensed):

- Maya: "Addressed: added base64-stable encoding for resume tokens, updated proto comments, added server-rotation example and test harness."

- Final reviewers: Ravi (approved), Elena (approved), Samir (approved).

Merge and followups:

Notes on uniqueness: this PR combines flow-control cancellation primitives with an explicit auth lease + idempotent resume shim rather than changing the kernel. That separation is designed to keep serving runtime changes minimal while offering a safe application-level pattern for streaming resumes and token handoff.
- Added cancellable/flow-aware streaming contexts across Python/TS/Go SDKs.

Context and motivation: Some enterprise customers require strict per-request enforcement of data residency and KMS locality. Existing RBAC v2 evaluations computed policies and attribute checks on each request which increased p95 policy latencies and made per-request KMS-affinity checks expensive. This PR adds an explicit Location Assertor stage and a short-lived decision cache to reduce repeated policy work while preserving per-request residency guarantees.

What this PR does (high-level): Adds a small Location Assertor micro-component to the policy evaluation pipeline that: 1) resolves tenant geolocation claims (from tenant profile, VPC region, request headers) with precedence rules; 2) emits a signed "location-assertion" attribute used by RBAC v2 policy expressions for KMS region affinity; 3) records a compact audit envelope to the audit-proofs service. Introduces an in-process decision cache keyed by (tenant_id, route, assertion_hash, evaluation_version) that caches deterministic RBAC decisions for up to 30s to reduce repeated evaluation cost. Adds an Audit Archiver component that batches and signs audit envelopes and writes to the region-sticky immutable store with encryption context that includes the resolved location.

Design decisions and tradeoffs: The decision cache is intentionally conservative (short TTL, strict key includes evaluation_version) so that policy rollouts and canary changes don't create stale authorizations. Location resolution uses a deterministic precedence: explicit tenant override > VPC regional binding > request-region header. We do not trust free-form geo headers unless the tenant has "region_override" enabled. Audit envelopes are signed with the platform signing key and include a provenance bundle to support later attestation.

Rollout plan: Feature gated behind flag "rbac.v2.location_assertor". Default off for all customers. Rollout sequence: 1) enable in staging and run integration tests (automated), 2) canary on 3% of traffic in prod for tenants with a residency requirement annotation, 3) measure policy p95 and audit throughput; 4) enable wider after 72h if no regressions. In the rare event of a problem the feature flag allows immediate kill-switch.

Testing and benchmarks: Unit+integration tests added for resolution precedence, cache eviction, and audit envelope signing. End-to-end performance tests on benchlab show median policy eval time reduced from 2.1ms -> 1.6ms for high-frequency tenant routes and p95 reduced ~12%. Decision cache hit-rate observed ~37% during synthetic steady-state workloads for common tenant routes.

Files touched (high level): src/policy/location_assertor.go, src/policy/decision_cache.go, src/policy/audit_archiver.go, pkg/config/feature_flags.go, api/docs/rbac_v2.md (note: docs update adds a small section describing the assertion attribute), bench/bench_policy_eval_test.go, infra/helm/templates/audit-archiver.yaml, internal/keys/signing_key_rotation.md.

Commits summary: 6 commits including initial implementation, unit tests, bench harness updates, docs, and a follow-up tightening of TTL logic after reviewer feedback.

Security and compliance notes: Audit envelopes include minimal tenant identifiers and are encrypted with CMK scoped to the resolved region. The archiver validates destination store region matches the resolved location or fails closed. All storage writes go through the CMK-scoped write path and are audited. This change required a minor addition to RBAC policy grammar to expose the attribute attribute::location_assertion (documented).

Compatibility / migration: No breaking API changes. Operators will need to opt-in via the feature flag and provide a signing key in the cluster secret for audit envelopes. The default behavior when the feature is off is identical to current RBAC v2 behavior.

Known limitations: Decision cache does not cover non-deterministic policies (policies using request timestamps or external lookups). Location resolution currently supports AWS/GCP/Azure region formats; adding custom provider mappings is tracked in ENG-3470.

Follow-ups: ENG-3470 - provider mapping table for custom region strings; ENG-3501 - persistent audit-proofs backfill for pre-assertion events.

Checklist: [x] Unit tests added [x] Integration tests added [x] Benchmarks updated [x] Security review requested [x] Docs updated

Related tickets: Linear ENG-3421, ENG-3470; Jira SUP-1123.
Evan Chu: Please describe how we avoid cache poisoning if a tenant's policy references non-deterministic external data.
Aisha Martinez: Good point — the cache only accepts decisions for policies annotated deterministic=true or for routes explicitly marked cachable. Non-deterministic policies bypass the cache (added tests).
Priya Raman: Audit store writes need stronger failure semantics. If the archiver fails to write because region mismatch, what happens?
Aisha Martinez: The archiver fails closed and the evaluation returns denied if audit archiving is mandatory for tenant. For non-mandatory tenants we implement a retry/backoff and emit a critical metric. Documented in security notes and added unit tests.
Marco Silva: Can we add a small e2e smoke test that ensures assertion is present in the final policy trace?
Aisha Martinez: Added an integration smoke test in tests/integration/test_location_assertor.yaml that validates assertion presence and signed envelope.

SUMMARY: This PR instruments cohorted invocation latency and token-variance metrics, adds a correlation dashboard to surface cohort-level regressions, and implements a causal span->log join helper to make long-tail investigations easier. MOTIVATION: We keep seeing noisy p99 regressions driven by a small set of invocation archetypes (long sequences with cold KV cache or backfilled tool calls). Current per-route aggregates hide these cohorts and make alerting noisy. This change creates explicit cohorts and correlation surfaces so SREs and oncall can tune alerts and triage regressions with fewer false positives. WHAT'S INCLUDED: 1) Metrics: invocation_latency_ms_cohort{cohort,model,route,tenant}, invocation_token_variance_cohort{cohort,model,route}, kv_cache_hit_ratio_cohort{cohort}, invocation_cohort_sample_count. Cohort keys: model+route+sequence_length_bucket+kv_cache_hint+tool_invocation_flag. 2) Collector: new invocation_cohort_collector service that attaches cohort tags at ingest time and exposes aggregation-friendly labels for rollups. 3) Tracing: causal_span_joiner that links span IDs with sampled log anchors and provides a compact mapping for UI log fetches; supports late-arrival span hydration. 4) Dashboard: observability/dashboards/invocation-cohort-correlation.jsonnet containing cohort heatmaps (p50/p95/p99), token-variance violin panels, KV-cache correlation matrix, and a cohort-level traceback panel that surfaces representative traces. 5) Alerts: new alert rule invocation_cohort_p99_surge with dampening and a per-cohort suppression window to avoid alert storms from noisy tenants; added playbook notes in docs/observability/invocation-cohorting.md. 6) Backwards compatibility: metric names are additive; collector falls back to legacy metric labels if cohort tagging fails. CHECKLIST: - [x] Collector implementation and unit tests - [x] Dashboard panels and templating - [x] Alert rule and playbook - [x] Integration tests for span->log join - [x] Docs update and migration notes COMPATIBILITY & RISK: Low-risk additive metrics. The collector adds labels which increase cardinality for a controlled set of cohorts; cohort cardinality is bounded by sequence_length buckets to limit explosion. The causal join introduces a short-lived in-memory cache; instrumentation includes adaptive eviction to avoid memory spikes. OBSERVABILITY: Added metrics + traces for rollout 100% behind a feature flag telemetry.cohort_mode. Plan: enable in staging for 72h and monitor ingestion cost and SLOs before broad rollout.
Ethan Wu: Nice approach on cohort keying, can we limit sequence_length buckets to powers-of-two to reduce cardinality?
Sofia Martinez: Good call, switched to powers-of-two buckets and added unit tests to assert bucket boundaries.
Priya Nair: The alert dampening looks sensible but add a note in the playbook about when to escalate to chief oncall; also add a small synthetic test to validate suppressed flapping.
Sofia Martinez: Added escalation steps and a synthetic replay harness to the integration tests.
Luca Moretti: One nit: prefer explicit metric units in names (ms) for latency metrics to avoid confusion across teams.
Sofia Martinez: Renamed metrics to include _ms suffix where appropriate and updated dashboard panels.

Motivation: Customers running structured output with strict mode and tool-calls reported intermittent schema violation errors during streaming reconnections and partial tool-call handoffs. This PR introduces a lightweight runtime "contract enforcer" that validates the outgoing response against the requested response_format (JSON schema / shape hint), enforces a tool-call fence to prevent mid-call schema violations, and provides a controlled streaming fallback that can gracefully close and rewind the stream when the model produces unrecoverable schema drift. Design summary: - New runtime layer `contract_enforcer` sits between the generation runtime and the OpenAI-compatibility middleware. It receives the negotiated response_format schema (if any) and maintains a small validation state per-request to allow non-destructive streaming validation checks. - Tool-call fencing: when a function/tool call is declared in the response contract, the enforcer prevents interleaving partial JSON tokens from being interpreted as tool call boundaries; it emits clear failure codes when the model outputs data that would cause ambiguous tool invocation. - Streaming fallback: if validation fails mid-stream and cannot be fixed by coercion, the enforcer signals a controlled stream termination with a machine-readable error chunk and a short rewind token that clients and the OpenAI compat layer can use to request an immediate re-run or a non-streaming error payload. - OpenAI-compat changes: the middleware now maps contract enforcer error codes to OpenAI-style error responses (with improved error_message details) and supports `X-Redwood-Contract-Rewind` header for retries. Checklist: - [x] Implement core contract_enforcer runtime and attach to request pipeline - [x] Add schema coercion heuristics (soft coercion for permissive mode) - [x] Add tool-call fence with explicit error codes - [x] Emit streaming error chunk + rewind token on unrecoverable failures - [x] Update openai_compat middleware to map error codes and headers - [x] Unit tests for validator, tool-call fence, header mappings - [x] Integration tests for streaming rewind and non-stream fallback - [x] Update docs: API reference for response_format strict mode and error codes - [x] Benchmarked perf impact (micro-benchmark in perf-canary) Commits (high level): - feat(contract_enforcer): new runtime module + validation state machine - feat(openai_compat): map enforcer errors and add rewind header - fix(streaming): make buffer checkpoints reentrant and add a max-checkpoint cap - test: add unit/integration tests for tool-call fencing and streaming fallback - docs: API reference for error codes and usage examples Changed areas (high level): - runtime/contract_enforcer/{enforcer.py,validator.py,errors.py} (new) - middleware/openai_compat/contract_mapping.py (update) - serving/streaming/checkpoint.py (update to support rewind token) - api/docs/response_contracts.md (new section) - tests/{unit,test_integration_contracts}.py (new) Migration notes: This change is opt-in behind `response_contract_enforcer` feature flag in runtime config. Default behavior remains unchanged for customers not using response_format strict mode. Backwards compatibility: The OpenAI compatibility layer will translate enforcer errors to OpenAI-style errors so existing clients continue to receive familiar shapes, but with additional `x-redwood-*` headers and a new `contract_error_code` field in JSON error bodies. Operational notes: - Enforcer adds a small CPU cost and modest memory for per-request state; micro-benchmarks show ~4% median latency increase at p95 for strict mode on a <256 token sequence. We will start rollout to Dedicated customers only and monitor via perf-canary dashboards. - If regressions are observed, we can disable the feature flag per-cluster. CI: All checks passed on the final run (unit + integration + lint + mypy + perf-canary smoke). Merge: squash and merge.
Reviewer Marco Alvarez: 'Overall design looks good. Two concerns: 1) we need explicit limits on rewind token lifetime to avoid replay amplification, 2) please add more unit tests around nested tool-call sequences.' Author reply (Evelyn): 'Added limit config (max_rewind_ttl_seconds) and extended test coverage to nested tool-call cases.' Reviewer Priya Natarajan: 'Can we ensure we don't change existing response headers unless the feature flag is enabled?' Author: 'Yes — new headers are only emitted when the feature flag is on. Confirmed in middleware mapping.' Reviewer Jonas Becker: 'Benchmarks look acceptable; please add a canary dashboard alert if p95 climbs >10%.' Author: 'Added dashboard and alert rule in perf-canary.' Final status: Approved by all reviewers and passing CI.
Introduces an opt-in 'contract_enforcer' runtime to validate response_format schemas at runtime, tool-call fencing to prevent ambiguous tool invocations, and a controlled streaming fallback with machine-readable error chunks and a rewind token. Opt-in via runtime feature flag. OpenAI-compat layer maps new error codes to existing error shapes and exposes retry headers.

Adds a staged tenant surrender mechanism and ephemeral egress fuse to make regional failovers less noisy and reduce SLO oscillations. Exposes two new telemetry counters and a small config knob for surge-dribble window length.
Motivation: During regional overload and coordinated failovers we've observed cascading evictions where tenants are fully discharged then aggressively re-admitted causing SLO oscillations and KV cache churn. This change introduces a 'surge dribble' admission path and an epochal handoff protector that preserves short-term reservation credits and prevents immediate aggressive rejoin. Design: 1) Staged tenant surrender: when a node decides to shed tenant traffic it first enters a dribble phase where admission is throttled to a low steady rate while KV cache is preserved for a configurable window. 2) Epochal handoff protector: the node attaches an epoch token to surrendered tenants; downstream nodes defer hard-eviction for the token TTL and apply an exponentially decaying reservation credit to prioritize graceful rejoin. 3) Ephemeral egress fuse: a configurable per-region egress cap that will soft-deny new allocations when the region-wide egress budget is saturated; the fuse emits detailed telemetry that feeds the Console to explain soft-denies. Backwards compatibility: tokens are opt-in per deployment via runtime flags for Dedicated/Private. Metrics: tenant.surge.dribble_rate, tenant.surge.reservation_tokens_issued, tenant.surge.epoch_rejoins. Checklist: - [x] Design doc referenced in ENG-3145 - [x] Unit tests for reservation decay - [x] Integration test for dribble window - [x] Telemetry wired to Console dashboards - [x] Feature-flag gating for Private/Dedicated rollout Implementation summary: commits: see commits list. Files changed: high-level changes include new package pkg/slo/dribble.go that implements the dribble admission controller, runtime/egress/fuse.go to implement the ephemeral fuse and region coordinator hooks, pkg/slo/epoch_token.go for token lifecycle, telemetry/metrics.yaml to declare metrics, console/dashboards/surge-dribble.json to add a dashboard, integration/tests/regional_drain_test.go to exercise the flow, and small wiring changes in deploy/helm to expose flags. Why this is different: most prior solutions aggressively evict and rely on rebalancing; this PR creates a small, observable window that trades minimal additional latency for large reductions in repeated evictions and SLO churn. Rollout plan: feature-flag on main for 2 weeks in canary region, then staged ramp to 25%, 50%, global. Monitoring and alerting: added SLO regressions alert for 5xx increase during dribble window and an ops dashboard to inspect token churn. 
Priya Singh: Overall this looks good. Two requests: (1) add metric labels for customer tier on tenant.surge.* so we can compare free vs paid impact, (2) please document expected token TTL units in comments.
Diego Martinez: Added tier label to counters and clarified TTL docs in epoch_token.go comments in second commit f4c98e2.
Liam O'Connor: Integration test is solid but I saw a nondeterministic failure locally where the egress fuse didn't reset after simulated controller restart. Can you add a reconciliation pass on startup?
Diego Martinez: Good catch. Added a startup reconciliation pass in runtime/egress/fuse.go to reconcile outstanding tokens; pushed in commit a3b7c11. CI e2e flake caused one rerun but all tests green afterward.
Marta Kovacs: Approved after nits. Please make sure the Console dashboard has markdown explaining the dribble window semantics.
Diego Martinez: Dashboard description added and linked in docs commit d0c7b88.
Release Manager (automated): Merge prepared using squash. CI green. Merge method: squash_and_merge.
Initial CI run failed a flaky e2e test (integration/tests/regional_drain_test.go) due to timing assumptions. Adjusted test wait and re-ran CI which passed. No other regressions.
Enables opt-in staged rollout for Dedicated and Private with a small default dribble window (30s). No mandatory migrations. Ops should monitor tenant.surge.token_exhaustion and tenant.surge.epoch_rejoins to track behavior.

Context: Our repository still runs a number of ad-hoc shell build steps in CI that are hard to lint, test, and reason about. These scripts are the primary source of occasional flakiness in cross-platform runners and make dependency updates riskier because provenance metadata is not recorded. Motivation: Move build orchestration into a TypeScript composite GitHub Action so steps are typed, tested, and easier to debug; at the same time record dependency provenance (package manager, lockfile hash, container base image) to aid post-incident forensics and to provide an audit trail for Dedicated/Private customers. What this PR does: 1) Introduces actions/ts-build-composite, a lightweight TypeScript composite action that wraps the previous shell steps (install, generate-bindings, build, sanity-check). 2) Replaces inline shell usage in .github/workflows/ci.yml with the new action. 3) Adds a provenance reporter that emits a small JSON artifact to the run artifacts and logs a compact provenance line to the job log for quick glanceability. 4) Pins a small set of development dependencies and adds an audit script that runs in CI to remind engineers to stamp dependency updates to a provenance file. Checklist: [x] Compile and unit-test the TS action locally with act; [x] Add integration CI job to exercise the composite action in Umbrella repo; [x] Update developer docs (CONTRIBUTING.md) with how to run/iterate on the action; [x] Add a short-note release entry in internal changelog. Testing performed: local act runs, CI runs across ubuntu-latest and macos-latest (linux and mac runners exercised), added unit tests for the provenance reporter, manual validation of artifact contents. Rollout plan: merge to main, watch ci-build job for 48h; if any regression, feature flagging via using old shell action in a hotfix branch is possible. Risks and mitigations: The TS action adds node as a runtime in the runner; we ensured the action runs with node12+ compatibility shim and kept the action minimal to avoid heavy install overhead. Motivation: Customers need stricter proof that requests touching tenant data were evaluated against tenant residency constraints and that any KMS usage originates from approved provider endpoints. This PR introduces three coordinated pieces: 1) a Residency Attestor middleware that centralizes tenant residency checks and emits structured attestations into request context; 2) a compact, append-only Audit BloomFilter index to lower cost of residency/audit lookups while preserving strong tamper-evidence; and 3) a KMS Origin Whitelist enforcement layer that rejects KMS operations not matching tenant-approved origin attributes.

Summary of changes:
- residency attestor middleware at service/auth/rbacv2/residency_attestor.go which reads tenant metadata (preferred regions, geozone claims) and executes policy checks via the policy-engine facade; on success it attaches a signed residency attestation header (X-Residency-Attestation) to propagated requests and writes a small proof record to the audit index.
- audit bloomfilter index implemented under service/audit/bloom_index with a compact on-disk segment format and in-memory sliding window for recent writes; the structure is optimized for space and fast existence checks used by downstream compliance tools.
- kms origin whitelist at pkg/kms/origin_whitelist.go which validates incoming KMS provider claims (kms-provider, region, endpoint fingerprint) against tenant-scoped allowlists; integrates with operator-scoped overrides guarded by RBAC v2.
- new audit forwarder shim that batches BloomFilter delta writes and pushes compressed proof envelopes to the audit-backend.
- integration tests and unit tests added under test/integration/residency_attestor_test.go and service/audit/bloom_index_test.go.

Compatibility and rollout:
- Middleware is enabled behind a feature flag feature.residency_attestor (default off). We will enable for a small set of internal tenants first.
- BloomFilter index exposes a migration shim: existing audit-index consumers can query a compatibility endpoint (/audit/compat/exists) until they are migrated.
- KMS origin whitelist defaults to permissive mode unless tenant has an allowlist configured; enforcement is gated by feature.kms_origin_whitelist (default off) to avoid surprise failures.

Testing and validation:
- Local unit tests: 118 tests added/updated.
- Integration: simulated tenant with multi-region config validated attestation header round-trip and audit bloom index retention under 10k ops/min.
- Load impact: bloom index writer optimized with a background, sharded flush that keeps p99 write latency under 25ms for our canary dataset.

Checklist: 
- [x] Residency attestor implementation
- [x] Compact bloom index and on-disk format documented in comments
- [x] KMS origin whitelist enforcement hook
- [x] Integration tests and CI coverage
- [x] Feature flags for safe rollout

Notes: This PR focuses on enforcement primitives and a compact proof store. Follow-up PRs will: provide operator UI to manage KMS allowlists per tenant, add audit search adapters that map BloomFilter hits back to canonical records, and wire attestation signing to HSM for tenants requiring non-repudiation.
- Added Residency Attestor middleware that emits per-request attestations and performs tenant residency checks.
- Introduced a compact Audit BloomFilter index for efficient existence checks and lower storage costs.
- Added KMS Origin Whitelist enforcement to validate KMS provider origin attributes against tenant allowlists.
- All features are behind feature flags for staged rollout.
Miguel Torres: Can we avoid signing attestations with our main key until HSM wiring is ready?
Anika Rao: Yes — the attestation currently uses a short-lived signing key stored in KMS (development only). Follow-up PR will add HSM signing.
Linh Pham: The bloom index on-disk segment lacks a checksum field — this makes recovery brittle.
Anika Rao: Added segment checksum and test (see segment_writer.go update).
Evan Gallagher: Approve with minor comments on logging verbosity.
Anika Rao: Addressed logging comments; reduced info-level noise and added debug toggle.
CI bot: All checks green after re-run.

payload.body:
Context: Hot tenants and mixed-size shard allocations cause repeated micro-fragmentation in the KV cache and periodic spillstorms when eviction rounds converge on the same slab ranges. This PR introduces two coordinated mitigations: 1) microshard-aware slab striping that scatters allocations for small hot objects across independent slab lanes to reduce local fragmentation and contention; 2) an adaptive spill buffer and anticipatory spill gating that temporarily absorbs eviction candidates and spreads downstream spill writes to avoid IO bursts. Motivation: in production SLOs we observed 95th percentile token latencies spike during cluster-wide compaction/eviction windows and a sustained 2x increase in spill IOPS under churn. Goals: reduce fragmentation-induced memory loss, smooth spill volume, lower p95/p99 latency jitter, and keep changes additive to the existing evictor interface. Design summary: - Slab striping: the slab allocator uses a tenant-aware microshard hash to choose a stripe index for small-size allocations (<512B). Each stripe has its own freelist and local allocation counters. The allocator prefers the local stripe before borrowing from neighbors. This reduces per-stripe fragmentation and hot-spotting. - Adaptive spill buffer: Eviction candidates are first placed into an in-memory ring buffer (bounded by a per-tenant budget). The buffer exposes three consumption modes: immediate-pass-through, paced-flush (rate-limited writer), and fallback-compact (when memory pressure is high). The spill policy dynamically transitions based on cluster-wide IO pressure and active eviction backlog. - Anticipatory gating: when eviction heuristics detect converging eviction windows (multiple workers selecting similar slab ranges) we apply a short randomized backoff and increase buffer pacing to avoid synchronized spillstorms. - Metrics and safety: new metrics for stripe occupancy, buffer fill, spill-pacer rate, and stalled-evictor-count. Safety nets include a hard-cap on buffer size and a bypass path to force immediate spill under out-of-memory signals. Implementation notes: - Modified src/runtime/kv/slab_allocator.{cc,h} to add stripe bookkeeping and a small constant-cost hash function. - Added src/runtime/kv/spill_buffer.{cc,h} implementing the ring buffer and pacing logic. - Updated src/runtime/kv/evictor_scheduler.{cc} to add cooperative gating and to consult stripe occupancy when choosing victim ranges. - Added benchmarks/kv/bench_spill.md and tests/kv/evictor_integration_test.cc to validate correctness and measure behavior under synthetic churn. Outcomes: lab and cluster tests show meaningful improvements: - 95th percentile token latency reduced by ~18% on high-churn workloads (synthetic tenant mix). - Measured memory fragmentation (lost bytes due to unusable holes) reduced by ~30% in long-running stress runs. - Average spill write volume during eviction windows reduced by 2.4x and peak IOPS smoothed by 60%. Backwards compatibility: no ABI changes to public runtime interfaces; the allocator hooks are additive. Rollout plan: feature-flag gated (kv.microshard_slab = on/off) with canary in a single region, monitor stripe occupancy and spill pacing metrics for two weeks before broader rollout. Related: follows on work from ENG-1982 (evictor pacing prototype) and is intended to be complementary to later generational reclaimer designs.
Priya Rao: Can you quantify memory overhead for stripe metadata under 10k active tenants? Also please add a safety cap to avoid per-tenant blowups.
Author (Ethan): Added per-tenant stripe cap (configurable) and updated tests to include large-tenant allocation skew. Overhead measured ~1.4KB/tenant in our test harness (added to PR).
Lena Kaur: The pacing algorithm looks good, but we need a deterministic path in tests — please inject a fake clock or controllable pacer for unit tests.
Author (Ethan): Added a test pacer and deterministic tests that simulate ramp-up and force fallback-compact behavior.
Marco Diaz: Approve after addressing a minor concurrency note in borrow-from-neighbor logic (use atomic counters).
Author (Ethan): Fixed borrow path to use relaxed atomics where safe; added comment and microbenchmark validating no regression on allocation latency.
Unit + integration tests added. Bench harness shows p95 latency down ~18% on churny synthetic workloads. Long-running soak (72h) shows fragmentation improvements ~30% and reduced spill write peaks.
Improved KV cache behavior: microshard slab striping reduces small-object fragmentation and an adaptive spill buffer smooths spill writes to avoid eviction storms; feature is behind kv.microshard_slab feature flag.
Drafted with metrics and rollout guidance — canary enabled in us-west-2 for initial validation. Observability dashboards added under ops/kv/spill_pacer.
Backport to release/2024-11 with minimal changes: disable feature flag by default; port tests that rely on deterministic pacer.

payload.body:
Context
We’re rolling out FP8/INT8 kernel paths behind flags and gating via perf canary. Today, the runtime exports TTFT/TPOT/tokens-per-sec histograms without enough context to quickly localize regressions. During the last canary rollback we had to correlate node labels + routing logs by hand to infer which model/GPU/mode cohort was affected.

What
This PR adds low-cardinality dimensions to a small set of runtime perf metrics so canary comparisons can be sliced directly by:
- model_id (stable registry identifier; not the human display name)
- gpu_sku (coarse SKU string, e.g., H100-SXM/A100-80GB/L4)
- kernel_mode (baseline|fp8|int8)

Key points / guardrails
- Cardinality: model_id is allowlisted to “top hosted models” (config-driven); all other models emit model_id="other". gpu_sku is derived from the node’s GPU SKU label, normalized to a small set. kernel_mode is an enum from the kernel dispatch decision (after fallback).
- Scope: only the canary-relevant histograms/counters are tagged (TTFT, TPOT, tokens/s, request_error_total). We intentionally do NOT tag every internal metric.
- Correctness: kernel_mode is recorded after dispatch/fallback so a request that fell back from FP8 due to shape guardrails is labeled kernel_mode="baseline" (this is what we want for perf attribution).
- Rollout safety: tag emission is behind a runtime config flag metrics.enable_kernel_mode_tagging (default off). We plan to enable in perf-canary first.

Implementation notes
- Added KernelMode enum to dispatch context and plumbed it through to MetricsContext.
- Added GPU SKU normalization helper (maps a handful of known strings -> canonical SKU; unknown -> "unknown").
- Added model_id extraction from ModelHandle; uses registry id (e.g., "llama-3-70b") and redacts to "other" if not allowlisted.
- Updated metrics registration to include the new label set only when the config flag is enabled; otherwise preserves current series names/labels.

Illustrative snippet
Before:
  runtime_request_ttft_ms_bucket{route="/v1/chat/completions"} …
After (when enabled):
  runtime_request_ttft_ms_bucket{route="/v1/chat/completions",model_id="llama-3-70b",gpu_sku="H100-SXM",kernel_mode="fp8"} …

Testing
- Unit tests for GPU SKU normalization and model allowlist behavior.
- Added an integration test that exercises dispatch + fallback and asserts kernel_mode label reflects the final kernel mode.
- Verified locally against a dev Prometheus scrape; series count increase stays within expected bounds for the allowlisted model set.

Follow-ups
- Grafana dashboard updates are in observability-pack PR-377.
- Canary threshold profiles tuned for the new dimensions are in perf-canary PR-611.
Allison Grant (review): Concerned about Prometheus cardinality. Can we ensure model_id is stable + allowlisted and avoid tagging routes with high fanout? Also please add recommended queries for Grafana (grouping + fallback).
Julian Moore (author): Yep—model_id is registry id and gated by allowlist; non-allowlisted collapses to "other". Tagging is only on the 4 canary metrics. I added docs/examples (p95 TTFT by kernel_mode, and delta vs baseline) and a note to keep route label as-is for now (we already have it, and removing would be breaking).
Rafael Mendes (review): kernel_mode should reflect final behavior after fallback (e.g., FP8 attempted but fell back). Otherwise we’ll chase ghosts. Do we have a test for that?
Julian Moore (author): Agreed. Updated plumbing so we set kernel_mode after dispatch decision is finalized. Added integration test that triggers an FP8-ineligible shape and asserts kernel_mode="baseline".
Marcus Reed (review): Can we normalize GPU strings more aggressively? I’ve seen "NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3" vs "H100-SXM" across clusters. Also, please ensure unknown maps to a small set, not raw strings.
Julian Moore (author): Added gpu_sku normalization helper with explicit mappings and unknown->"unknown". It uses the node label (already normalized in most regions) but still defends against raw strings.
Irene Choi (review): For clusters with mixed driver images, GPU label might be missing. Should gpu_sku be required?
Julian Moore (author): If missing, gpu_sku="unknown". This keeps series stable and prevents accidental per-node cardinality.
Allison Grant (approval): Looks good with the allowlist + config flag. Please confirm default is off and we’ll enable only in canary first.
Julian Moore (author): Confirmed default off (values.yaml). Enablement will be via perf-canary config overlay.
Rafael Mendes (approval): Approved. This will make rollbacks far faster.
runtime/metrics: introduce MetricsContext labels (model_id/gpu_sku/kernel_mode)
runtime/dispatch: plumb KernelMode through selection + fallback paths
runtime/config: add metrics.enable_kernel_mode_tagging + model allowlist
tests: coverage for allowlist + fallback labeling correctness
docs: internal note on cardinality + recommended query patterns
Internal-only change (no customer-facing API impact): adds optional label dimensions (model_id/gpu_sku/kernel_mode) to select runtime perf metrics behind metrics.enable_kernel_mode_tagging (default off).
