payload.body:
Motivation: Production workloads with tight monthly budgets need a graceful way to trade cost vs latency without global policy churn. This PR adds a new batcher variant (Budgeted Swing) that targets a budget window rather than hard limits, plus a quantization gradualizer that applies conservative quant tiers on a ramp schedule. Goals: 1) provide safe defaults that improve unit economics for bursty, mid-tail workloads; 2) allow tenants to opt-in via a single flag; 3) ensure graceful fallbacks (no hard degradation) and telemetry to verify regressions.

What this contains (high-level):
- runtime/batcher/swing_batcher.go: new batcher implementing budget-windowed batching and swing lanes (fast/slow lanes that dynamically move requests based on short-term budget pressure).
- runtime/quant/gradualizer.go: conservative quant tier ramper that steps down precision on an exponential schedule when budget pressure persists for N consecutive windows.
- api/defaults/presets.yaml: pragmatic tenant default that enables the mode off-by-default; includes tuning knobs (window_ms, swing_threshold_pct, quant_step_ms).
- console/ui: read-only dashboard fragment for 'Budget Pressure' and 'Quant Ramp Progress' (observability hooks).
- e2e/test_prefill_budgeted_swing.py: integration smoke tests exercising canary L7 policy and fallback.

Design notes: Budgeted Swing uses a sliding window meter (configurable, default 60s) and computes a short-term spend delta relative to the assigned budget runway. When spend > threshold, new requests are preferentially steered to the slow lane which groups and prefetches prefixes (prefill-friendly) while the fast lane preserves SLOs for critical routes. The quantization gradualizer starts at a safe high-precision profile (fp16/int8-mixed) and after K windows steps toward more aggressive quant tiers. All steps are reversible and recorded in the telemetry trace.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implementation of swing batcher and gradualizer
- [x] Unit tests for lane assignment and reversal logic
- [x] Integration tests for fallback paths and no-data regressions
- [x] Console widgets + telemetry metrics (budget.pressure, quant.ramp_level)
- [x] Docs stub and changelog entry

Snippet: 
// simplified lane decision (pseudocode)
// if short_term_spend > budget * swing_threshold -> slow lane else fast lane

files changed (high level): runtime/batcher/swing_batcher.go, runtime/quant/gradualizer.go, runtime/metrics/metrics_defs.go, api/defaults/presets.yaml, console/partials/budget_pressure.html, tests/e2e/test_prefill_budgeted_swing.py, docs/whats-new/budgeted-swing.md, examples/tenant-optins/enable-budgeted-swing.yaml

Migration and opt-in: The feature is behind a tenant opt-in flag (defaults.yaml sets opt_in=false). No tenant will be affected unless they explicitly enable the preset. For Dedicated customers, the tenant-override CLI can flip the flag cluster-wide.

Risks and mitigations:
- Quality regression risk when quant steps are applied: mitigated by conservative default ramp (3 windows) and offline eval recommends sets based on heldout prompts. We also expose an immediate rollback endpoint.
- Latency SLO regressions for tail-sensitive routes: fast lane preserves low-latency routing and is only affected when budget pressure is severe. We also added a per-route override to keep specific routes immune.

Related: ENG-4678 tracks the long-running roadmap for budget-aware routing; SUP-1229 was a customer request for budget-graceful degradation.

Next steps after merge: run 2-week shadow rollout across 3 sandbox tenants, collect telemetry, and follow up with a policy shortpaper and recommended presets for common SaaS workloads.
Priya Srinivasan (review): Left a few nits on the ramp params + suggested increasing default window to 60s. Also requested stress-test results under seq_len=2048 workloads. (addressed)
Amira: Updated defaults and added stress bench notes to performance section.
Ethan Liu (review): Concerned about persistence TTL for ramp state causing stale decisions after host restart. Suggested storing epoch + TTL. (requested change)
Amira: Persisted ramp epoch + last_applied_ts, added TTL of 5 windows and recovery path. Added unit test covering restart path.
Sophie Chen (approval): Verified telemetry coverage and e2e smoke locally. Approves after minor doc tweak.
Adds an opt-in 'Budgeted Swing' batcher and a conservative quantization gradualizer to help tenants reduce short-term spend with safe, reversible defaults. Opt-in only. See docs/whats-new/budgeted-swing.md for details.
Shadow rollout recommended. Watch budget.pressure, quant.ramp_level, lane.swap_rate. Abort if quant.ramp_level increases >2 steps within first 24h for a tenant.
Run shadow rollout on 3 sandbox tenants for 14 days
Collect unit-econ delta report and perf benches
Add recommended presets to docs based on telemetry

Motivation: We observe a recurring source of slight double-counting and ambiguous phase attribution for long invocations where token cost/latency gets attributed to multiple phases (parse -> model -> postprocess). This PR introduces a lightweight 'fencepost' telemetry marker that explicitly bounds invocation phases, plus a contextual SLO clarifier that annotates alerts with burstiness-adjusted quiet-window recommendations.

What this changes (high level):
- Adds a fencepost marker API (server-side) that insertion points in the calling pipeline can emit to mark exact boundaries between phases; these markers are propagated to traces and metrics as fencepost_id and phase_boundary tags.
- Implements an SLO clarifier service that consumes rollups and recent invocation histograms to suggest per-tenant quiet-window and alert-weight overrides; suggestions are surfaced in the Console alerts UI and as annotation fields on SLO incidents.
- Dashboard: new compact panel (Observability > Invocation Boundaries) showing per-route fencepost hit-rates, phase-exclusive token distributions, and decile latency-by-phase.
- Alert tuning: the default SLO rule engine now consults clarifier suggestions (opt-in via feature flag) and can automatically apply a temporary quiet window when burstiness crosses configured thresholds.
- Sampling/tracing: small update to span enrichment to attach fencepost metadata; span sequence validation added to avoid stale fenceposts.

Checklist: 
- [x] fencepost API + server exporter (Go)
- [x] SLO clarifier (Python service) with feature flag gating
- [x] Console dashboard JSON and panel config
- [x] Unit + integration tests for fencepost logic and clarifier thresholds
- [x] Documentation updates and runbook snippet
- [x] Release notes entry

Commits (summary):
- feat(obsv): add fencepost marker interface and exporter (src/observability/fencepost.go)
- feat(slo-clarifier): initial clarifier service and decision API (services/slo_clarifier/main.py)
- perf(trace): attach fencepost tags during span emit and add sequence validation (pkg/tracing/enrich.go)
- ui(dashboards): invocation-boundaries panel and token-by-phase decile visualization (dashboards/invocation_boundaries.json)
- docs: observability/fencepost.md and runbook snippet
- test: unit + integration tests for clarifier heuristics (test/clarifier_test.py)

Files changed (high level):
- src/observability/fencepost.go: new API, exporter to telemetry pipeline
- pkg/tracing/enrich.go: span enrichment with fencepost tags + validation
- services/slo_clarifier/main.py: decision engine and HTTP suggestion API
- dashboards/invocation_boundaries.json: new dashboard panel (compact)
- docs/observability/fencepost.md: design doc and runbook
- test/clarifier_test.py: heuristics and integration mocks
- ci/integration/traces.yaml: added clarifier e2e job
- pkg/featureflags/flags.go: added gate for clarifier auto-apply

Behavioral notes: fencepost markers are intentionally lightweight (single key/value paired with a monotonic boundary sequence). The clarifier uses a short rolling window (default 10m) and computes a burstiness score based on Poisson-detrended token arrival variance; thresholds are conservative by default. All auto-apply behavior is opt-in per-tenant via a feature flag; we ship the suggestion-only mode by default.

Backward compatibility: all changes are additive. Existing tracing consumers ignore fencepost tags if unknown. The clarifier runs as a separate service and only affects alerting behavior when the feature flag is turned on per-tenant.

Deployment plan: feature-flagged rollout to canary tenants for 48h, monitor fencepost hit-rate and SLO suggestion churn; if stable, promote to 25% of tenants for 7d before full rollout.

Release notes (short): Add fencepost telemetry for precise phase attribution and a contextual SLO clarifier that proposes quiet-window and weight adjustments to reduce alert noise during bursts. Opt-in by default.

Related: ENG-2024 (observability long-tail attribution), ENG-2077 (alert-tuning playbook).

Motivation: intermittent corruption and dropped frames in the streaming proxy were causing tool/function-calling handshakes to fail for a subset of routes and large payloads. This PR introduces a strict stream framing protocol in the gateway proxy, a route-level shepherding policy that enforces payload size and framing invariants, and an OpenAI-compat shim update to make function_call/structured-output recoverable after partial frames. The change is gated behind a feature flag and rolled out as a canary; it also tightens per-route payload enforcement to prevent unbounded memory growth from malformed clients. Key changes include: 1) framing layer: add explicit 4-byte length prefix for framed proto/JSON chunks at the proxy boundary with CRC-8 validation; 2) backpressure metadata: attach per-chunk high-water signals to avoid excessive buffer accumulation while preserving low-latency streaming for small messages; 3) shepherd policy: route config additions to declare "shepherding" mode, max_payload_bytes, and strict_fncall_handshake; 4) OpenAI-compat shim: tolerate mid-stream JSON token boundaries by emitting incremental JSON-patch events and a final reconciled function_call object; 5) graceful fallback: when shepherding detects repeated malformed frames, requests are downgraded to non-streaming mode with an observability event and metric. Rollout is canary-scheduled and default-off for Dedicated/Private customers until helm values are available. This PR bundles proxy, gateway config schema, small changes to the openai-compat adapter, tests for race/partial-frame handling, and migration docs.
Improves streaming stability and function-calling reliability by adding strict framing and per-route shepherding. Introduces a new route config (shepherding + max_payload_bytes) and a feature flag gateway.strict_streaming. Notable behavior: malformed or repeated partial frames will now cause an automatic downgrade to non-streaming response and increment a metric gateway.stream.downgrades.
Private/Dedicated operators: upgrade gateway image and set helm value gateway.strict_streaming.enabled=false to retain previous behavior until you are ready to opt-in
If using ingress sidecars that terminate streaming connections, ensure they support length-prefixed frames or disable strict_streaming on the gateway
If you rely on unbounded route payloads, set route-level max_payload_bytes in gateway config to a suitable high value to avoid early truncation
OpenAI-compat adapter emits incremental json-patch events so clients that expect chunked function_call tokens will still reconstruct the final object. Legacy clients that assume raw token stream may see a change in framing; the gateway will fallback to non-stream mode for malformed frames to preserve correctness.
Risk: new framing could break non-compliant proxies -> Mitigation: feature flag default-off for Private/Dedicated and canary for hosted; detailed migration doc included
Risk: small increased latency from CRC check on tiny messages -> Mitigation: lightweight CRC8 and fast-path bypass for single-chunk responses
Risk: spike in downgrades confusing users -> Mitigation: dashboard + alerting and automatic rollback if downgrades exceed threshold

Motivation: Customers asked for finer-grained tenant assertions on requests that can be translated into RBAC v2 decisions and enforced at the KMS proxy layer so keys cannot be used outside of pinned regions. This PR implements a per-request claim translation layer (CLAIM-T) that normalizes heterogeneous tenant claims from different identity providers, emits canonical assertion headers, and drives a lightweight region-bound KMS proxy that rejects key usage when the request's canonical region does not match the key's allowed residency.

What this change does: CLAIM-T: - Introduces a request interceptor that runs before auth decision and normalizes claim inputs (OIDC sub/azp, custom tenant attributes, service principal annotations) into a canonical assertion map (x-rd-assertion-*) used by RBAC v2 policy evaluation. - Adds linear mapping rules (config-driven) so teams can plug in provider-specific claim keys without code changes. Region-bound KMS proxy: - Adds a sidecar-like proxy component (kms-region-proxy) that validates that the requested CMK region matches the tenant assertion or an allowed fallback list. - Proxy emits immutable audit headers (x-rd-audit-kms-origin, x-rd-audit-region-assertion) for downstream auditors and the central audit-collector. - Integrates with existing CMK metadata service to cache key residency and fallback policies to keep latency <6ms p50 on the proxy path.

Compatibility and rollout: - Backwards compatible by default: when CLAIM-T mapping is empty, request flow remains unchanged. - Feature gated via a runtime flag (feature.claim_translation=true) and a per-tenant annotation to opt-in. - Canary rollout plan: enable for internal-sandbox tenants -> 5% production -> 25% -> 100%.

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for mapping rules and assertion normalization. - Integration tests exercising proxy rejection/allow flows including cross-region failover. - Load test on benchmark-lab to verify proxy adds <5% p95 latency at 1k rps.

Checklist: - [x] Mapping engine + config docs - [x] Assertion header schema (RFC-like doc in repo) - [x] KMS proxy implementation + cache - [x] End-to-end tests and canary rollout config - [x] Updated operator playbook for incident response when proxy rejects legitimate traffic

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps policy evaluation out of the proxy — the proxy only enforces region residency gates and emits canonical assertion headers. Full RBAC v2 decisions continue to happen in the policy-evaluator component; CLAIM-T makes policy inputs consistent across identity providers.

--- a/services/auth/interceptor/claim_translation.go
+++ b/services/auth/interceptor/claim_translation.go
@@ -0,0 +1,45 @@
+// Normalize claims from OIDC/legacy tokens into canonical assertions
+func TranslateClaims(ctx context.Context, raw map[string]interface{}) map[string]string {
+    // mapping lookup and normalization logic
+}

--- a/services/kms-proxy/main.go
+++ b/services/kms-proxy/main.go
@@ -10,6 +10,24 @@
+// Reject when asserted region not allowed by key residency
+if !residencyCache.Allows(keyID, assertedRegion) {
+    writeAuditHeaders(w, "reject")
+    http.Error(w, "region mismatch for key", http.StatusForbidden)
+    return
+}

Akhil Rao: Can the mapping rules be reloaded without a full service restart? This matters for on-call when identity provider mappings change.
Maya Lin (author): Mapping rules are watched from S3/config-store and applied atomically; added a test and doc note in configs/claim_translation_rules.yaml.
Elena Petrova: The proxy adds an extra network hop. Have we measured tail latency impact for small payloads?
Maya Lin (author): Yes — benchmark-lab runs showed +4% p95 on 1k rps with local cache warm; p99 impact stays <10ms. Added results to docs and a dashboard panel in observability-pack for the canary.
Jonas Becker: What happens for customers that use multi-region CMKs (replicated)? We should allow an explicit fallback list on key metadata.
Maya Lin (author): Implemented key metadata fallback list and preference order; added unit tests and a migration note for key metadata service.

Motivation: We observed tail latency spikes under mixed interactive and streaming traffic during canary runs. Root cause analysis pointed to hard admission thresholds in the prefill stage that either over‑reserved KV memory and kernels or starved the decode stage under bursty arrivals. This PR introduces a predictive backpressure matrix and soft‑quota lane system that dynamically shapes admission and kernel allocation between prefill and decode to reduce stalls while preserving throughput.

Design summary: 1) Predictive backpressure matrix: a lightweight runtime component that consumes short history of per‑route arrival rate, batch sizes, and KV hit ratios to predict intra‑second demand. It computes an admission score per logical lane (latency‑sensitive, balanced, throughput) that ties into the scheduler. 2) Soft‑quota lanes: instead of hard segmented quotas, lanes have soft token buckets that allow transient overshoot with controlled decay; overshoots are reconciled by probabilistic throttling and KV admission demotion. 3) Kernel bucket scheduler: kernels are grouped into buckets by memory footprint and latency characteristics; scheduler assigns prefill and decode micro‑slices to kernel buckets based on lane scores and predicted contention. 4) KV stripe admission: KV cache admission now uses a stripe allocator that prefers admitting prefixes likely to be reused across lanes (LRU+reuse heuristic). 5) Continuous batching seam: micro‑slice boundaries are adjusted to allow cooperative coalescing across prefill→decode handoff when latency headroom exists.

Compatibility: Changes are backwards compatible at the API level. New runtime flags gate the behavior per deployment: --prefill-backpressure=adaptive and per‑route config options in the serving config to opt into soft‑quota lanes. Default is off on older clusters; enabled in canary clusters.

Checklist:
- [x] Predictive matrix proto, runtime telemetry hooks, and unit tests
- [x] Kernel bucket scheduler and integration tests
- [x] KV stripe admission and cache benchmarks
- [x] E2E canary with gradual rollout and metrics dashboard panels
- [x] Documentation updates (console and runtime flags)

Risk and mitigation: The predictive model uses only short window aggregated counters to avoid oscillation; we cap lane overshoot and enforce a global soft limit to prevent KV runaway. Rollout is staged by region and can be disabled via config.

How to validate: Follow canary playbook linked in the PR, check per‑route p50/p95/p99 latency, prefill/decode queue lengths, KV adoption ratio, and cost per 1k tokens. The PR includes Grafana dashboard diff and synthetic load scripts used in validation.
Sophie Chen: Could predictiveness introduce oscillations under diurnal patterns? Please add damping/decay tests.
Author (Anika Rao): Added exponential decay smoothing and a cap to overshoot; added unit tests in tests/prefill_backpressure_test.cc.
Marco Alvarez: Kernel buckets look good; consider exposing a per‑bucket headroom metric for ops to tune.
Author: Exposed kernel_bucket.headroom_gauge and added dashboard tile to canary panels.
Priya Nair: KV stripe allocator needs a config knob to prefer per‑tenant isolation in Dedicated mode.
Author: Added prefer_isolation boolean in the stripe allocator config; default preserved for shared modes.
Canary against mixed interactive+streaming synthetic workload: p95 end‑to‑end latency reduced 8.6% (from 320ms→292ms), p99 improved 6.9%. Average token throughput maintained within 1% of baseline. KV cache hit ratio improved ~4% on repeat conversational workloads. Observed cost per 1k tokens reduction ~11% due to fewer wasted prefill kernels and better batching coalescing.
Introduce runtime adaptive prefill backpressure with soft‑quota lanes and kernel bucket scheduler. Opt‑in via runtime flag --prefill-backpressure=adaptive; provides p95 latency and cost improvements for mixed workloads. Disabled by default for older clusters.
To enable in Dedicated: set serving.config.prefill_backpressure.mode=adaptive and adjust kernel_bucket.headroom per GPU class. Monitor metrics: backpressure.matrix.score, prefill.queue.length, decode.queue.length, kernel_bucket.headroom_gauge. Rollback: set mode=off and drain existing soft overshoots.

Context and motivation: We have several SDK ergonomics gaps that customers hit when they try to wire credentials together with streaming connectors and retry policies. This PR introduces a slim CredentialDelegator (language-agnostic contract with tiny implementations in py/ts/go) and consolidates generator/pullstream ergonomics so users get consistent cancel/resume/reauth behavior across SDKs.

Summary of changes:
1) Introduce CredentialDelegator abstraction and lightweight token fanout strategy to reduce hot-path allocations on high-throughput streaming.
2) Rework async-generator/pullstream helpers: add pause(), resume(), and graceful_close() helpers on generator wrappers and unify the backoff hooks used by the SDKs.
3) Tighten retry semantics for streaming reconnects (hedged retry floor + jitter) and expose a small set of retry presets.
4) Minor API surface alignment across Python, TypeScript, and Go; bump package versions (py 0.13.0 -> 0.14.0, ts 1.27.0 -> 1.28.0, go v1.5.2 -> v1.6.0).
5) Add telemetry hooks for credential exchange so we can measure stalled reauth events.

Checklist:
- [x] API proposal (linked Linear ENG-1893)
- [x] Implementation in Python SDK (py/sdk/connector.py, py/sdk/auth/delegator.py)
- [x] Implementation in TypeScript SDK (ts/src/connector.ts, ts/src/cred/delegator.ts)
- [x] Implementation in Go SDK (go/connector/connector.go, go/cred/delegator.go)
- [x] Unit tests added for reconnect/backoff and credential fallback
- [x] Integration test in benchmark-lab to validate latency impact
- [x] Docs snippet and migration notes added to README and changelogs

Design notes:
- CredentialDelegator provides two methods: GetToken(ctx) and Subscribe(ctx, channel) where Subscribe returns a small typed channel/iterator for token updates; implementations are intentionally minimal so embedding layers can add caching or pinning.
- Streaming helpers normalize close semantics: consumers can call graceful_close() to attempt flush then cancel; pause()/resume() allow user-controlled backpressure without tearing the session (useful for UI-driven consumers).
- Retry presets are defaults (conservative, balanced, aggressive) and can be overridden per-client or per-connector.

Backwards compatibility: Existing SDK surface remains supported; the delegator is additive and the default credential provider is a thin shim that wraps existing token providers.

Migration notes:
- Python: replace custom reconnect loops with the new generator_wrapper() helper (examples/py/migrate_streams.md).
- TypeScript: add a small adapter that calls credDelegator.subscribe() for long-lived pages; existing sync token flows still work.
- Go: use the NewCredDelegatorFromProvider(provider) helper to avoid refactor at call sites.

Problem: Tenants experiencing consecutive microbursts can cause large oscillations in their burst credit balance and aggressive reclaim which triggers backpressure and elevated latency tails. Existing burst accounting is reactive (hard drains / instant reclaim) and amplifies oscillation when multiple tenants alternate burst patterns. Goal: Introduce a controller that smooths per-tenant burst-credit accrual and reclaim signals using an EWMA + leaky-bucket hybrid, provide passive reclaim that prefers capacity backfill before hard drains, and expose observability hooks to measure credit oscillation and reclaim impact. The change is opt-in via feature flag `burst_smoother_v2` and is intended for Dedicated fleets and Private installs. What this PR does (high level): - Adds a new controller `BurstCreditSmootherController` in runtime/controller which maintains an EWMA-smoothed credit balance and a leaky reclaim window per tenant. - Implements passive reclaim logic: when the smoothed balance exceeds safe thresholds, the controller issues a reclaim with a configurable max rate instead of immediate hard drains; reclaim requests are eligible for backfill by idle capacity pools. - Introduces tenant-level safety caps and min-commit window to avoid starving long-running tenant workloads. - Adds feature flag gating, config knobs (smoothing_alpha, reclaim_rate_limit_qps, safety_cap_pct, min_commit_seconds) with sane defaults tuned from canary tests. - Adds and registers new telemetry metrics: `tenant_burst_credit_balance_gauge`, `tenant_burst_credit_smoothed_gauge`, `burst_reclaim_rate_counter`, `burst_reclaim_rate_histogram`, and `tenant_credit_oscillation_ratio` to quantify oscillation. - Updates Helm chart to include new RBAC and deployment manifest entries for the controller. - Adds unit tests and an e2e canary scenario (tests/e2e/burst_smoother_canary.yaml) used during staged rollout. Design notes: - Smoothing algorithm: EWMA on observed instantaneous balance with alpha default 0.15 (reduced from earlier 0.25 after reviewer feedback) to prioritize stability. Reclaim is enforced as a leaky token bucket where reclaim tokens are consumed at a bounded rate to avoid mass concurrent drains. - Backfill preference: reclaim requests are converted to low-priority backfill offers to warm pools and best-effort nodes; only if backfill is not accepted after a short window do we escalate to a hard drain. - Safety: tenants with active long-lived streams are exempted until min_commit_seconds elapses; safety_cap_pct provides a hard floor relative to contracted reservation. Rollout plan: 1) Feature flag rollout to 10% of Dedicated fleets (canary) with e2e scenario; monitor tenant_credit_oscillation_ratio and 95p latency. 2) If metrics stable after 48 hours, expand to 50% and run additional smoke tests. 3) Full rollout and mark feature flag default-on for new clusters in the next minor release. Testing and results: - Unit tests: new test coverage for controller logic, reclaim rate limiter, and edge cases (clock jumps, tenant churn). - Integration: initial integration run failed due to a race in config hot-reload (fixed in second commit). - Canary: synthetic microburst workload run on canary cluster shows reduced oscillation and latency improvements: 95th percentile tail latency down by ~8% and peak credit oscillation reduced by ~63% compared to baseline. CPU impact on controller pod ~+6% under sustained load. Backward compatibility & safety: - Opt-in via `burst_smoother_v2` feature flag. Default remains off for existing clusters until gradual rollout. - No user-facing API changes; config knobs are added to existing capacity/tenant config objects. - Breaking change: none. Related: ENG-2345 (autoscaler oscillation study), ENG-4048 (burst reclaim strategy doc), SUP-1123 (support ticket motivating urgent canary fix). Files of interest are summarized in changed_files.
Liam Chen: Please add an option to disable backfill -> hard-drain escalation (we shouldn't escalate in certain compliance clusters).
Aisha Patel: Added `escalate_to_drain` boolean flag with default=true; documented in charts/values and README.
Marcos Ruiz: Can you include more granular metrics for reclaim latency? Also, consider lowering smoothing alpha to reduce oscillation.
Aisha Patel: Added `burst_reclaim_latency_histogram` and reduced smoothing_alpha default to 0.15 (commit 3c4b5a).
Nora Ibrahim: Integration test failed on hot-reload initially — need deterministic test harness. Are we confident in concurrency model?
Aisha Patel: Fixed race in config watcher by serializing reloads with a mutex; added retry with jitter in test harness.
Introduce BurstCreditSmootherController (opt-in) to smooth tenant burst-credit oscillation and perform rate-limited passive reclaim with backfill preference. Adds observability metrics and new Helm flags. Expected to reduce latency tails during microbursts.
Enable feature flag `burst_smoother_v2` in charts/values.yaml, apply canary manifest in a dedicated test cluster, run tests/e2e/burst_smoother_canary.yaml, and monitor metrics tenant_credit_oscillation_ratio and tenant_burst_credit_smoothed_gauge for regressions.

Motivation: customers want a declarative way to express cost/performance goals (target p50 latency, cost-per-1k tokens, and quality guardrails) and have those translated into safe serving runtime configs (batching, cache TTLs, quant profiles, prefill strategies) without hand-tuning. This PR introduces an econ-policy-translator service + a lightweight CLI simulator so operators can validate the effects of a policy before applying it to production.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Implements econpolicy.v1 (YAML schema), a translator that maps high-level goals to runtime knobs, safety clamps to prevent regressions, a simulation harness (rw-econctl simulate) that runs synthetic workload traces against a cost/latency model, and a reconciler that emits controlled runtime deltas (no hot changes to quant profiles unless explicitly approved). Includes unit tests, integration simulations, and docs for the Console workflow.

Key design points: 1) Declarative policy schema (econpolicy.v1) exposes target_type: [latency, cost, quality], constraints (max_cost_per_1k, target_p50_ms, min_quality_score) and strategy hints (prefer_batching, prefer_cache, quant_tolerance). 2) Translator produces candidate runtime configs: batch_size, batch_timeout_ms, cache_ttl_ms, quant_profile (none, q4_0, q5_1), prefill_strategy, and a confidence score. 3) Safety layer: automatic clamps (max_token_multiplier, no_auto_quant_for_models_with_sensitive_tags), a simulated A/B check run, and manual approval gating for quant changes. 4) CLI simulator (rw-econctl) accepts traces or sample request shape distributions and shows projected unit economics, latency percentiles, and model-quality risk. 5) Reconciler: emits policy -> delta proposals to the runtime API (not applied automatically by default; can be toggled per-team).

Summary: Rework presubmit toolchain and introduce a dependency rollup action to reduce CI noise and speed developer feedback. Motivation: our presubmit lanes have grown fragile and slow due to fragmented toolchain bootstraps (legacy Makefiles + ad-hoc scripts + multiple container images) and an increasing tide of single-dep PRs from Dependabot. This PR consolidates the presubmit entrypoints, replaces the legacy make-based bootstrap with a lightweight Go runner (ci-helix), adds dep-rollup-action to batch low-risk dependency updates into weekly rollup PRs, and updates docs and release hooks. Changeset: 1) introduce ci/helix-runner: a small Go binary that coordinates staged presubmit shards, caches toolchains, and exposes a graceful shutdown for flaky runners; 2) migrate lint/test job definitions to use the new runner and remove duplicated shell bootstraps in .github/workflows; 3) add .github/actions/dep-rollup-action which aggregates Dependabot PRs, resolves version matrix conflicts using a curated allowlist, and opens a single weekly rollup PR per language ecosystem; 4) remove top-level Makefile bootstraps and translate targets into workspace scripts with explicit toolchain manifests; 5) update release automation to run an early artifact-sign step so that staging validation can use signed artifacts; 6) docs: presubmit-runner.md and dep-rollup.md with rollout notes and rollback instructions. Risk & rollout: feature guarded behind a repo-level opt-in flag (ci.presubmit.v2) and rollout device set to gradual: enable on non-critical repos for 48h, then full cutover. Summary: This PR introduces a new attestation-backed service (operator-attestor) that verifies proof-of-possession for operator sessions, enriches audit logs with attestation metadata and residency context, and plugs into a KMS usage leak detector to surface anomalous key consumption patterns. Motivation: After a recent operational postmortem (Linear ENG-4120) we found gaps in operator session validation and slow detection of abnormal KMS usage that complicated incident response. This change reduces blast radius from compromised operator credentials by requiring a short-lived attestation token and by flagging suspicious cross-region or high-throughput KMS activity.

What changed (high level):
- New service: /services/operator-attestor (Go)
  - Accepts attestation assertions from operator clients (TPM/secure element/YubiKey), verifies signatures and nonce freshness, and returns a signed ephemeral attestation token (1m TTL).
  - Exposes a gRPC health endpoint and a small admin UI to inspect recent attestation verdicts.
- RBAC v2 integration:
  - Added an authn hook that requires proof-of-possession attestation for operator-level roles when the feature flag 'attest.operator.enabled' is on.
  - Implemented a revocation path: the attestor can emit revocation events to the authz cache to immediately drop sessions tied to a failed attestation or leak signal.
- KMS Leak Detector (policy engine & telemetry):
  - New detector component subscribes to KMS usage stream and applies heuristics (geo-flux, entropy-of-callsites, sudden-rate-spike) to score suspicious activity.
  - When a score exceeds threshold, we emit an alert, attach the KMS evidence to an audit entry, notify the attestor to kick a revocation run, and surface findings in Console under Security -> KMS Incidents.
- Audit pipeline changes:
  - Audit entries gain new fields: attestation.subject, attestation.issuer, attestation.ttl, residency.region_hint (when present), and kms_detection.score.
  - Audit forwarder sanitizes attestation blobs for PII while retaining verification fingerprints for forensic replay.
- Data residency and region pinning:
  - KMS detector respects tenant residency constraints; cross-region usage is scored more aggressively and tagged for manual review.
- Feature flags & rollout:
  - All runtime hooks behind feature flags: attest.operator.enabled, kms.detector.mode (off | monitor | enforce).
  - Staged rollout plan: monitor-only for 1 week in us-west, then canary to 5% traffic, then full enforcement.

Implementation notes / commits (summary):
- commit 1: scaffolding for operator-attestor service, proto definitions, and CI jobs.
- commit 2: attestation verifier implementation (TPM + PKI chains + nonce replay protection).
- commit 3: RBAC hook and authz cache integration; small API change to authn middleware.
- commit 4: KMS leak detector module (stream consumer, scoring engine, alert adapter).
- commit 5: audit enrichment and forwarder changes (serializer and sanitizer).
- commit 6: console UI additions and docs and migration + tests and feature flag wiring.

Files changed (high level):
- services/operator-attestor/* (new)
- internal/authn/attestation_hook.go (new)
- internal/authz/cache_invalidator.go (mod)
- services/kms-detector/* (new)
- internal/audit/enricher.go (mod)
- telemetry/alerts/kms_alert_adapter.go (new)
- web/console/src/pages/security/kms-incidents.tsx (mod)
- docs/security/operator-attestation.md (new)
- deploy/helm/operator-attestor-values.yaml (new)
- test/integration/attestor_e2e_test.go (new)

Backward compatibility:
- All auth changes are behind feature flags; default behavior unchanged. Audit schema is additive and backwards compatible (new fields optional). KMS detector can be set to monitor mode which does not trigger revocations.

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests for verifier, detector scoring, and audit sanitizer added.
- Integration test runs that spin up attestor and a mock KMS telemetry stream were added; tests marked flaky on small runners and configured for retry (we observed one intermittent TPM simulator failure and added a 3s backoff in the harness).
- CI summary: initial pipeline failed on integration flakiness (test: TestAttestorNonceReplay) due to simulator timing; rerun succeeded. All checks green on final run. CI jobs added: attestor-lint, attestor-unit, attestor-integration (parallel), kms-detector-unit, audit-compat-check.

Review conversation (high level):
- Lucas Rivera: "Can the attestation token be rotated to a shorter TTL in enforcement mode? Also please ensure replay cache sharding scales with operator count." — Reply (Priya): "Yes, TTL is configurable via feature flag and the replay cache supports consistent hashing across shards; added comments and metrics (attestor.replay_cache.hit/miss)."
- Avery Nguyen: "KMS detector heuristics look promising, but are we generating too many false positives for tenants with bursty workloads?" — Reply (Priya): "Added tenant-level quiet windows and adaptive thresholds; detector operates in monitor mode by default and tracks false positive rate metric kms.detector.fpr to tune thresholds."
- Michael Chen: "Audit enrichment is good; ensure we scrub attestation blobs before external forwarding to log sinks to avoid leaking device identifiers." — Reply (Priya): "Scrubbing implemented with a whitelist of verification fingerprints; attestation.raw removed unless admin opt-in is set. Documented in docs/security/operator-attestation.md."
- Security review (SEC-89): Accept with minor tweaks; requested logging of why a revocation event fired (added kms_detector.reason field to audit).
- SRE: requested HPA and resource limits for operator-attestor; added helm values and autoscaling policy suggested in deploy/helm/*.

Rollout plan and mitigations:
- Phase 0: deploy operator-attestor in monitor-only mode (attest.operator.enabled = false) to gather telemetry and warm replay caches.
- Phase 1 (week 1): enable attest.operator.enabled true for us-west control plane with kms.detector.mode=monitor.
- Phase 2 (canary): enable detector enforce for small subset and set auto-revoke to false to validate false positives.
- Phase 3 (enforce): enable automatic revocation and scale to full fleet once FPR < 1% over 48h.
- Rollback: feature flag toggles allow immediate disable; revocation events are idempotent and carry tombstone markers for manual undo.

Operational runbooks (short):
- If kms.detector.alert spikes: set kms.detector.mode=monitor, investigate top KMS callers via Console KMS Incidents view, correlate with attestation.subject and residency.region_hint.
- If attestor fails health: fallback auth path allows short-term admin sessions (5m) with expedited logging and a PagerDuty alert to oncall.

Dependencies and follow-ups:
- Follow-up: integrate attestation-based session MFA into SDKs (ENG-4205).
- Follow-up: add long-term retention policy for attestation verification fingerprints tied to audits (COMPLIANCE-22).

Why this is different / not covered by previous work: Prior PRs focused on KMS scoping, residency tagging, and audit forwarding. This PR couples operator session proof-of-possession attestation with a KMS usage detector and a direct RBAC revocation hook to close the control loop between detection and mitigation. It also attempts to preserve privacy by scrubbing attestation material before export while retaining forensic fingerprints.

Merge: squash-and-merge. Merged after final sign-off from Security and SRE. Changelog and docs added.

Related: ENG-4120, SEC-89, ENG-4205.

Adds an attestation-based operator attestor service, RBAC revocation hook, KMS usage leak detector, and audit enrichment. Backwards-compatible rollout with staged canary and feature flag.

Motivation: customers with strict data residency and key custody requirements asked for an enforcement primitive that guarantees request-level jurisdictional constraints are evaluated and enforced before any KMS operation or model selection occurs. This PR implements a lightweight Jurisdictional Enforcement Gate (JEG) middleware that integrates with RBAC v2 policy expressions, enforces a KMS Usage Obligator (declared by tenant policy), and strengthens audit continuity by signing per-request audit envelopes. Design summary: 1) Introduce a new policy predicate namespace 'jurisdiction:' in RBAC v2 (examples in docs) allowing rules like 'jurisdiction:region == eu-west-1 and kms:provider in (aws, gcp)'. 2) Add JEG middleware in the front proxy path that resolves request claims (tenant, region_hint, operator_scope) and short-circuits requests that violate jurisdictional or KMS obligations. 3) KMS Usage Obligator enforces that certain tenants/routes must use pinned KMS providers/regions; the gate will inject a required_kms context or reject the request with 403 when not satisfied. 4) Audit continuity: every enforced decision produces a signed audit envelope (ed25519 over canonicalized envelope) and a monotonic audit sequence number per-tenant, forwarded to the audit-forwarder with delivery guarantees; envelopes include the jurisdiction assertion and KMS choice. Migration & rollout: feature-flagged behind 'jrg-2025' with three modes: monitor-only (log violations), enforce-soft (reject but allow operator override), enforce-strict. Default rollout plan is monitor-only for two weeks, canary to 10% of tenants, then full enforcement after SOC review. Backwards compatibility: legacy RBAC policies still work; the gate ignores jurisdiction predicates if absent. Operational controls: metrics (jrg.violation_count, jrg.enforced_count), a new Prometheus alert for spike in violations, and an installer flag for private deployments to provide HSM/KMS integration credentials. Security & threat model: keys used to sign envelopes are stored in tenant-scoped sealed secrets or customer-managed HSM when available; ephemeral signing keys rotate daily and are attested via our KMS attestor component. References: ENG-2045 (Linear), SUP-7890 (support ticket), design doc link: docs/compliance/jurisdictional-enforcement.md. Why this is different: unlike earlier region-pin middleware, JEG ties RBAC predicates, KMS obligations, and signed audit envelopes together so enforcement and non-repudiation are co-located in the decision path.
Diego Morales: Security review - please confirm private key lifecycle for envelope signing; prefer HSM when customer provides one.
Aria Chen (author): Added HSM integration and daily rotation, documented expected failure modes in audit forwarder.
Priya Patel: Ops - add metric for audit-forwarder failures; add clear rollback steps to installer.
Aria Chen: Added jrg.audit_forwarder_failures metric and installer 'jrg.rollback' flag; included rollback steps in docs.
Evan Rios: Code review - policy predicate parsing looks good but add unit for nested predicates; lgtm after tests.
CI Bot: compliance pipeline passed on re-run (flaky network test fixed).

payload.body:
Context and motivation:
Incidents over the last quarter (see ENG-7821) showed repeated oscillation where tenants that were briefly removed by the SLO enforcer re-entered traffic too aggressively and triggered cascading evictions. This led to repeated regional failovers and increased latency for steady-state tenants. The existing eviction policy is binary (evict / reinstate) and does not account for a gradual re-admission profile or a coordinated, staggered drain when capacity is constrained.

This PR implements two coordinated capabilities: (1) staged tenant warmup: when a tenant is reinstated after being shelved or moved, we gradually ramp its allowed admission rate over a configurable warmup window; and (2) gentle evacuation scheduler: when performing tenant evacuation (manual or automatic due to node/region pressure), we schedule staggered drain windows with small reservation slices for higher-priority tenants to avoid mass reconnect storms.

High-level changes (single-line summary):
- Add warmup state machine and admission token bucket per-tenant with decay schedules.
- Introduce evacuation scheduler that computes per-tenant drain windows and emits soft-deny decisions rather than immediate hard evictions.
- Tie warmup and scheduler into the SLO enforcer and circuit-breaker signals so tenants marked unhealthy take a slower path to rejoining.
- New telemetry: tenant_warmup_progress, evacuation_window_start, staged_evacuations_active, warmup_penalty_decay_seconds.
- Added feature flag (runtime with default OFF) and config knobs: warmup_window_seconds, step_increment_pct, reservation_slices, max_stagger_seconds.

Implementation notes:
The warmup implementation is in runtime/admission and uses the same admission-token framework as prior soft-doors but layered with a per-tenant timer and exponential decay on penalty ledger entries. Warmup applies only after a tenant exits a shelved or quarantined state; tenants that were preempted for SLA violations still go through the same process but with an initial lower admission cap. The evacuation scheduler is a lightweight orchestrator in controlplane/evac that receives the ordered list of tenants to drain and computes soft windows; it returns admit/soft-deny hints to the fronting admission layer so we can maintain short-circuit low-latency decisions at request time.

Compatibility and migration:
- Backwards compatible: when the feature flag is off, behavior is unchanged.
- Default values are conservative (warmup_window_seconds=120, step_increment_pct=20, reservation_slices=3, max_stagger_seconds=90) to ensure safe behavior in canaries.
- No database schema changes; state is kept in existing ephemeral tenant-lease store with a small additional key namespace.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests cover warmup state transitions, token refill math, and scheduler slot allocation.
- Integration test harness simulates a regional node drain and confirms staged rejoin avoids >30% oscillation compared to baseline.
- Added a small load canary on staging with 5% traffic for 24h before prod rollout.

Rollout plan:
- Feature flag default OFF in main.
- Canary in region-us-west-2 at 5% traffic for 24h (observability checklist attached).
- Gradual ramp to 25% then 50% if no anomalies in SLO delta, otherwise automatic rollback.

Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests added
- [x] Integration tests added
- [x] Telemetry events instrumented
- [x] Feature-flag gating and default-off config
- [x] Docs stub for runtime knobs and runbook updates

Related work and references:
- ENG-7821: incident writeup on oscillatory evictions
- SUP-4392: customer impact report (tenant X)

Notes to reviewers:
- The warmup math is intentionally conservative; if we want more aggressive re-admit we can expose step_increment_pct as a per-tenant override in a follow-up.
- The scheduler uses a best-effort time wheel; it's non-blocking and tolerates controller restarts by consulting the tenant-lease store.

Merge rationale:
Fixes a high-severity class of customer-visible instability and is behind a feature flag so we can iterate safely. The change is small enough to be rolled back quickly if needed.
Diego Morales: Can we make sure the warmup token refill uses a monotonic clock? There were subtle flakes in CI related to time.Now() vs monotonic. (requested change)
Maya Owens: Good catch — switched to runtime/clock package in the latest commit and added deterministic clock for tests. (reply)
Priya Singh: I want to see the canary dashboard panels for the new metrics before merging. Please add a link to the staging Grafana snapshot. (request)
Maya Owens: Grafana snapshot link added to observability/metrics/metrics.yaml and docs/runbooks/evacuation.md includes expected thresholds. (reply)
Ethan Burke: lgtm for runtime side; noted one minor naming nit in scheduler_test.go which I left inline. (approved)
Codeowner-bot: Approved by runtime/infra.

Introduce compact-on-access KV reclaimer and a bandwidth-aware spill controller to reduce memory fragmentation and smooth spill traffic under tenant hotspots. Improves memory efficiency and reduces tail latency during eviction-driven workloads.
Motivation: Production workloads with skewed tenant access patterns were triggering frequent full-segment compactions and heavy spill bursts that increased tail latency and egress IO costs. Existing eviction policies prioritized recency/size without accounting for fragmentation or downstream spill bandwidth. This change implements a compact-on-access reclaimer that opportunistically coalesces fragmented slots during normal access paths and a bandwidth-aware spill policy that rate-limits spills per-host and per-tenant to avoid I/O storming.

Summary of changes: Added a lightweight in-path compaction pass that runs when a page/slot is touched and fragmentation crosses a tenant-specific threshold; introduced a composite eviction score combining recency, fragmentation-penalty, and host-io-cost; implemented a SpillController that monitors host egress bandwidth and enforces tenant spill windows and backpressure signals; extended kernel_selector to prefer compact-friendly kernels when compact-on-access is enabled; added observability for fragmentation_score, spill_budget, and spill_backpressure events.

Checklist:
- [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-2147)
- [x] Unit + integration tests added
- [x] End-to-end perf benchmarked on benchmark-lab infra
- [x] Migration strategy for existing caches (toggle via runtime flag)
- [x] Metrics + dashboard tiles created in observability-pack

Design notes: The compact-on-access reclaimer is intentionally conservative: it attempts small coalesces limited to the current page neighborhood to avoid long pauses. It uses a lightweight fragmentation estimator (slot occupancy run-length analysis) to decide when to run. The eviction score is computed as: base_lru_score + alpha * fragmentation_penalty + beta * host_io_cost, where alpha/beta are runtime-tunable. The SpillController exposes soft and hard budgets: soft budgets throttle spills with delayed scheduling, hard budgets defer non-critical writebacks and escalate to tenant rate-limiters. To avoid cross-tenant interference, the controller tracks per-tenant recent spill bytes and enforces a fairness window.

Compatibility & rollout: Feature guarded behind runtime flag: runtime.kv.compact_on_access and runtime.kv.bandwidth_spill_controller. Default: disabled. We plan a staged rollout: opt-in on dedicated sandboxes, then enable with conservative alpha/beta on canary fleet, and finally enable on main with telemetry gating. Migration does not require on-disk changes.

Testing & perf: Benchmarks on benchmark-lab using a synthetic hotspot workload (90% of accesses to 8% of keys) show: median token-serve latency change: +1% (noise); 95th percentile latency: -9% to -14% depending on alpha; host spill egress bytes: -32% peak; resident fragmentation_score (aggregate): -18% after 30 minutes of steady state. Memory overhead: +0.8% for the compact-on-access metadata.

Files touched (high-level): kv/cache/reclaimer.cc, kv/cache/reclaimer.h, kv/evictor/score_calculator.cc, scheduler/spill_controller.go, runtime/kernel_selector.cc, runtime/config/runtime_flags.proto, tools/benchmark-lab/hotspot-sweep.yaml, observability/metrics/kv_fragmentation.prom, tests/kv/reclaimer_test.cc, tests/kv/spill_controller_integration.cc, docs/design/compact_on_access.md.

Operational considerations: SpillController emits backpressure events that are surfaced as a new alert (KVSpillBackpressureHigh) with severity P2. Owners can tune soft_budget_ms and tenant_window_bytes. We added dashboards for tenant spill windows, host egress utilization, and fragmentation heatmaps.

Related work: complements earlier eviction work (ENG-3378) by adding IO-budget awareness and in-path coalescing. This avoids the aggressive async compactions we observed in pr-xxxxxx patterns that caused large background IO spikes.

Implementation notes: The reclaimer integrates with existing KV lock-free structures; compaction operates on per-page runs and yields after a configurable cycle budget to prevent head-of-line blocking. The SpillController is implemented in Go in the scheduler plane and communicates via the placement RPC to runtime nodes to apply spill pacing tokens. Kernel selector was extended to set a compact-friendly kernel flag when the runtime option is enabled.

Rollout timeline: Feature branch created 2025-11-03. Initial prototype in integration tests 2025-12. Benchmarks and safety tests 2026-01. This PR finalizes the implementation and wiring for canary rollout (2026-02).

Why this is different: Prior PRs focused on large background compaction and eviction heuristics; this PR targets low-latency, incremental coalescing at access time and explicit spill budget control to smooth I/O without sacrificing tail latency.

Evan Wu: Can the compaction pass hold for long periods under pathological access patterns? Suggest adding a max_cycle_budget.
Priya Desai: Added cycle_budget with a default of 5ms and conservative defaults in runtime flags.
Marcus O'Neill: SpillController looks solid but we need a migration story for clusters without egress meters.
Priya Desai: Controller falls back to token-count heuristics when egress meters are unavailable; documented in design doc.
Sofia Klein: Please add more telemetry for per-tenant fairness and ensure we don't starve low-throughput tenants.
Priya Desai: Added tenant_window_bytes and fairness_ratio metric; integration tests simulate low-throughput tenants to verify no starvation.

Motivation: During a recent noisy-but-sustained tenant spike we observed repeated circuit flips and expensive rejoin churn that kept a small cohort of tenants from recovering while degrading tail latency for others. This PR introduces two coordinated controls: (1) a Tenant Sabbatical lease that temporarily quiesces admission for tenants that exceed sustained SLO violation thresholds, allowing KV/caches and routing to stabilize, and (2) a Predictive Circuit Quieting layer that smooths circuit reopen decisions using a short-term forecast (EWMA + trend dampener) so we avoid rapid reopen/close cycles. Design: The sabbatical lease is an admission-time token that marks a tenant as "sabbatical:pending" with a TTL derived from an adaptive backoff (base 30s, jittered, scales with repeat offenses). Sabbatical tenants are still responded to (503 with Retry-After + diagnostic headers) and get a lightweight health-check path so operators and SDKs can sample readiness without counting against normal throughput. The Predictive Circuit Quieting module augments the circuit state machine: instead of reopening immediately when healthy probes succeed, we compute a predicted error-rate window and require a low-confidence window before transition; this uses EWMA on error-rate and a sigmoid-based hysteresis to avoid stalls on borderline noise. Backwards compatibility: feature is behind two runtime flags (sabbatical.enabled, circuit_quieting.mode) and a per-tenant opt-out label so we can roll this out progressively. Checklist: - [x] Core sabbatical lease implementation (controller + admission hook) - [x] Predictive quieting circuit state machine changes - [x] Telemetry: new metrics (sabbatical_count, sabbatical_duration_bucket, circuit_predicted_error) - [x] API: Retry-After semantics and diagnostic response headers documented - [x] Integration tests that simulate repeated SLO violation - [x] Load tests to validate minimal overhead on fastpath - [x] Console annotations for sabbatical state and metrics wiring
Changeset summary: 3 commits touching controller, runtime, telemetry, docs and tests. See commits field for details.
Files changed (high-level): - controller/sabbatical_controller.go: new controller that observes tenant SLO metrics and issues sabbatical leases. - runtime/circuit/quieting.go: new predictive logic and state gating. - api/response_headers.go: standardized Retry-After + X-Redwood-Sabbatical reason header. - telemetry/metrics.yaml: metric definitions and dashboards wiring. - tests/integration/sabbatical_flow_test.go: integration test that simulates noisy tenant behavior. - docs/ops/sabbatical.md: runbook and rollback instructions. - examples/sdk/sabbatical-optout-snippet.md: example SDK usage for opt-out.
Testing notes: Unit tests for the state machine and controller logic are included. Integration test runs a synthetic tenant that alternates between high-error bursts and recovery; with quieting disabled the test reproduces circuit flapping, with quieting+sabbatical enabled the system converges and the tenant is temporarily placed in sabbatical then gracefully reintroduced.
Load impact: measured <0.6% median p95 CPU increase on control plane under Canary.
Rollout plan: gated rollout behind feature-flagging platform; start with canary set (5% of tenants), monitor sabbatical_rate and circuit_predicted_error, then ramp to 25% / 50% / 100% if no unexpected regressions.
Rollback: feature-flag off; controller removes active sabbatical leases within 30s TTL, circuits revert to legacy behavior.
Related work: follows patterns introduced by ENG-4390 (eviction smoothing) and compliments ENG-7721 (circuit telemetry uplift).
Liam O'Neill: Why a hard 30s base TTL? Can we tune that from runtime without redeploy?
Maya Chen: Answered: made TTL base configurable via sabbatical.base_ttl and added jitter; updated docs.
Priya Kapoor: Request change: add more granularity to telemetry buckets for sabbatical_duration.
Maya Chen: Added histogram buckets in metrics.yaml and added aggregation tests.
Diego Herrera: Noted potential race between lease expiration and circuit reopen; suggested a light probe hook.
Maya Chen: Added probe hook (sabbatical_probe) and test case covering race scenario; addressed in commit f9e7c2a.
Priya Kapoor: Approved after telemetry tweaks.
Liam O'Neill: Approved - looks safe for canary.
CI Bot: integration tests initially failed due to test flakiness (timing). Fixed by increasing test timeouts and using deterministic clock in controller.
Automation: perf smoke passed on canary cluster.
Introduces Tenant Sabbatical (experimental) to temporarily quiesce noisy tenants and a Predictive Circuit Quieting mechanism to reduce reopen/flap churn. Both features are behind runtime flags. Operators should monitor sabbatical_count and circuit_predicted_error metrics during rollout. See docs/ops/sabbatical.md for runbook and opt-out instructions.

payload.body:
Motivation: continuous-batcher workloads with a mix of tiny (chat) and large (long-context) requests were still suffering intermittent starvation and p99 spikes when KV cache pinning and kernel hotpaths competed for slots. This PR implements an intervalized 'slice throttle' which splits slot reservations into short time slices and applies a starvation sentinel that temporarily deprioritizes long-running KV-heavy slices while preserving grace for in-flight small requests. Summary of changes: 1) new scheduler policy 'intervalized-slice-throttle' with configurable slice_ms and sentinel_decay_ms; 2) starvation sentinel marker in the KV admission path (soft marker, non-destructive) that influences admission probability instead of hard eviction; 3) kernel hint export for short/long slice classification to help the runtime choose attention kernels and prefetch lanes; 4) KV cache pin aging and a probabilistic decay to avoid permanent pin monopolies; 5) telemetry and opt-in feature flag under deploy/feature_flags.yaml. Checklist: - [x] design doc linked (ENG-2147) - [x] unit and integration tests - [x] benchmark harness runs (mixed-small-large workload) - [x] safety review for KV semantics - [x] feature-flagged rollout plan Explanation of behavior: the scheduler now splits each slot reservation window into N intervals (default 4). Each incoming request is classified into a 'slice type' based on KV usage and estimated token length; long/kv-heavy slices are admitted into later intervals and are subject to a sentinel score which decays over time if they make progress. Small requests are preferred in early intervals to reduce tail latency. Sentinel score is recorded as a soft tag on admission metadata and is used by the admission sampler rather than being an eviction signal, so no extra cache churn is introduced. Kernel hints are emitted to the runtime via the existing kernel_hints API to switch to low-latency attention kernels for early-interval small requests. Testing and results: lab benchmarks show 15% reduction in p99 generation latency on mixed workloads, 7% higher aggregate throughput under steady-state, and 2x fewer KV-cache thrashing events in the replayed production trace. We ran a 48h canary with the feature flag enabled at 10% traffic and observed no regression in correctness or error-rate. Rollout plan: behind feature flag off by default; stage to 10% -> 50% -> 100% with monitoring alarms on p50/p95/p99, KV eviction rate, and allocation failures. Related: ENG-2210 contains the follow-up plan for heuristic tuning and adaptive slice sizing.
3 commits: initial implementation of intervalized throttle and sentinel (interval_throttle.go, kv_sentinel.go); add kernel hint plumbing and tests; docs and feature flag. Commit messages: feat(scheduler): add intervalized slice throttle; feat(kv): add starvation sentinel tagging; perf(runtime): emit kernel hints for slice classes; test: integration harness for mixed workloads; docs: interval throttle overview.
Liam: asked for clearer guardrails around sentinel decay and whether it could starve long running analytical jobs; response: sentinel is probabilistic and decays with progress, added extra unit tests and a knob sentinel_decay_ms and max_deprioritize_pct. Mateo: requested metrics for 'sentinel_hits' and an SLI proposal; added metrics and a dashboard template. Chen: asked to ensure kernel hint path is opt-in in case of future kernel churn; we added a runtime flag and a safe fallback path. Several small nit and style requests addressed. Final review approved after 2 iteration of changes.
Unit tests cover sentinel scoring and probabilistic admission; integration tests simulate mixed small/large request traces and verify fairness and non-starvation; benchmark harness run on m60 cluster with representative production trace; results captured in docs/engineering/batcher/benchmarks-2026-02-18.md.
Introduces an opt-in intervalized scheduling policy to reduce tail latency for mixed workloads. Default behavior is disabled; enabling may reduce p99 at the cost of slightly longer latency for very large KV-heavy requests. Provides knobs for slice duration, sentinel decay, and kernel-hinting. Backwards compatible when feature flag is off.
Feature-flagged rollout recommended. Watch metrics: batcher.p99_ms, batcher.p95_ms, kv.eviction_rate, scheduler.sentinal_hits, runtime.kernel_hint_switches. Suggested canary: 10% for 24h, then 50% for 24-48h, then full rollout if metrics stable. If regressions observed, toggle feature flag off and revert via rollout dashboard.
This PR is part of a broader effort to decouple admission pacing and kernel selection from pure slot accounting so that we can optimize for end-to-end latency rather than per-token throughput alone. Follow-ups include adaptive slice sizing and ML-powered sentinel thresholds (ENG-2210).
payload.title: Intervalized KV slice throttle with starvation sentinel for continuous batcher

Motivation: under multi-tenant bursty workloads we observed repeated small-page evictions caused by fragmentation and poor spill granularity. These evictions increase CPU and PCIe churn and spike tail latency. This PR introduces the 'Residence Reshaper' — a lightweight in-memory optimizer that periodically rebuckets resident KV pages to improve spatial locality and a selective spill-handoff protocol that prefers coalesced spill targets (cold-store or local fast-disk) when eviction is unavoidable. Changes are behind a runtime feature flag and include telemetry to validate safety. High level: 1) a low-overhead rebucketing pass that reassigns small scattered cache slots into contiguous slots within the same tenant working set, 2) a spill-handoff coordinator that defers single-page spills in favor of a coalesced spill window, 3) eviction scoring updates that penalize fragmentation contribution and favor hot-prefix retention, 4) scheduling changes so rebucketing runs opportunistically during idle cycles and cooperates with the continuous-batching scheduler to avoid interfering with latency SLOs. Implementation notes: the reshaper operates on 'page runs' (variable-length contiguous runs) and uses a lightweight bitmap snapshot to plan moves; moves are pread/pwrite-free within the KV arena (pointer updates) where possible and fall back to copy-on-write for shared pages. The spill-handoff uses a small write-behind buffer to coalesce victims for batch writes and a token-bucket to avoid saturating burst spill bandwidth. Testing: unit tests for allocator invariants and integrated simulation harness covering adversarial fragmentation patterns. Benchmarking: microbenchmarks and a 3-node canary under synthesized mixed-read/write workloads included below. Rollout plan: canary on 10% of traffic, monitor eviction_rate, 95p latency, and PCIe utilization; automatic rollback if eviction_rate increases or 95p latency regresses >5%. Related: builds on prior allocator refactors (ENG-3621) and eviction telemetry work (ENG-4102).
Introduce KV Residence Reshaper: reduces fragmentation-driven evictions and smooths spillover during load spikes. Feature gated; rollout via canary then 100% if metrics remain stable.
Microbenchmarks: adversarial fragmentation benchmark shows 34% fewer fragmentation-triggered evictions, 12% reduction in 95th percentile token-serving latency at 90% load. Canary (3 nodes, mixed read/write): eviction_rate down 28% and PCIe write bandwidth smoothed (peak reduced by 40%). End-to-end CPU overhead: +2.1% in steady-state, but avoided reserialize/copy cycles removed 7% CPU during spikes.
Arjun Patel: Nice design. Two questions: (1) can the reshaper starve the normal allocator during heavy loads? (2) what's the worst-case latency penalty for an in-flight move?
Maya Chen: Answered: reshaper is back-pressure aware and yields at bucket/granularity boundaries; worst-case single pointer-resolve move is O(1) pointer swap — copy fallback is async and limited by token-bucket. Added tests to assert allocator progress under load.
Sofia Martinez: Please add more conservative defaults for the canary. Suggest reducing canary traffic to 5% and longer warmup window.
Maya Chen: Updated ci/canary_pipeline.yaml to 5% initial canary and extended warmup to 15 minutes. Documented in docs/architecture/kv_residency.md.
Evan Lee: LGTM after a couple nit comments on metric names and a small cleanup in continuous_batcher integration.
Evan Lee: Approved
CI Bot: all checks green (unit, integration, benchmark smoke).
Maya Chen: Squashed and rebased, ready to merge.
Feature gated by KV_RESHAPER_ENABLED. Default: disabled on existing clusters. To enable: toggle via scripts/feature_flag_toggle.py for selected canary hosts and monitor telemetry names: kv_reshaper_evictions_reduced, kv_spill_coalesce_ratio, kv_fragmentation_score (per-tenant). Auto-rollback if kv_fragmentation_score increases or kv_eviction_rate increases by >10% over baseline.
Merged via squash-merge. Commit message: 'kv: residence reshaper + selective spill-handoff; reduce fragmentation-driven evictions (ENG-4726)'. Canary rollout started automatically after merge.
payload.title: KV residence reshaper and selective spill-handoff to reduce fragmentation-driven evictions

Introduce 'mosaic auth tiling' (credential tiling) and checkpointed streaming across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs. Motivation: high-concurrency streaming customers observed token-rotation contention and non-deterministic retry amplification when many streams concurrently triggered credential refresh. Mosaic auth tiling shards credential refresh responsibilities by request fingerprint to avoid global locks while preserving fallback semantics. Checkpointed streaming adds an opt-in resume token to streaming client surfaces so long-lived reads can be resumed idempotently after network failures or client restarts. This PR implements the runtime primitives, surface ergonomics changes, tests, example updates and coordinated version bumps. Checklist: - [x] core credential tiler implementation (py/ts/go) - [x] checkpoint/resume API on streaming clients (AsyncCheckpointIterator / StreamClient.checkpoint / StreamCheckpoint interface) - [x] feature gate and runtime flagging (enable_mosaic_auth default: false) - [x] unit + flaky-resiliency integration tests - [x] docs, examples and migration guide - [x] bump package versions for release Notes: Gate the new behavior behind a flag so we can stage rollout; older clients are unaffected. Migration notes included in docs_impacted and release_notes. Linked items: ENG-1420 ENG-1435
Reduce token refresh amplification under heavy concurrent streaming and provide an ergonomic, safe resume primitive for long-lived streams so production apps can recover without complex custom coordination.
Added deterministic unit tests for credential tiler sharding and a matrix of integration runs that injects transient network faults and simulated key rotations; smoke-tested examples against local staging streaming service.
- Introduced credential tiling (mosaic auth) to reduce refresh contention under high concurrency.
- Added opt-in checkpointed streaming API to allow idempotent resume of long-lived streams.
- Python SDK: AsyncCheckpointIterator and session credential_tiler available behind flag.
- TypeScript SDK: StreamClient.checkpoint() and iterator ergonomics.
- Go SDK: StreamCheckpoint interface and helpers.
Note: features are feature-gated (enable_mosaic_auth=false by default).
Ravi: Can we get a summary of fallback behavior when tiling is enabled and a tile hot-swap occurs? Requested a short table in docs.
Aisha: Reply: documented fallback paths and added deterministic backoff + bump counter per tile; added integration test that performs on-the-fly key rotation.
Sofia: Request: add explicit API doc for resume semantics (ordering guarantees and at-most-once vs at-least-once). Actioned by updating docs/sdk/migration/checkpointed-streams.md and tests.
