payload.body:
- All error responses (JSON + streaming SSE) now include a stable `request_id` field. - Gateway now guarantees a request_id is generated and propagated downstream, and echoed back to clients via `x-request-id`.
Context: SDK parity work (ENG-5120) and Support/Oncall feedback (INT-1182) highlighted that `request_id` is not reliably present across all failure modes. Specifically: (1) some gateway-generated errors returned `x-request-id` header but omitted `request_id` in JSON bodies, (2) upstream service errors sometimes used `requestId` or `trace_id` and the gateway passed them through inconsistently, and (3) streaming (SSE) error paths frequently dropped request_id entirely (disconnects, mid-stream 429/5xx, proxy-induced truncations), which made customer triage painful.

This PR standardizes request ID behavior end-to-end: the gateway guarantees a canonical request identifier exists for every request, propagates it to downstream services, and returns it consistently to the caller in both headers and error bodies/events.

What changed (high level):
- Canonicalization: adopt a single canonical field name `request_id` in all JSON error bodies and SSE error payloads.
- Header contract: gateway always sets `x-request-id` on responses (success + error). If a valid request id is already present in inbound `x-request-id`, we honor it; otherwise we generate one.
- Downstream propagation: gateway forwards `x-request-id` to downstream HTTP services and gRPC metadata so services can log it and (optionally) reflect it.
- Error normalization: map upstream variants (`requestId`, `trace_id`, `x-request-id`) into the canonical `request_id` field before returning to clients.
- Streaming: ensure the initial SSE metadata event includes `request_id`, and any SSE error event emitted by the gateway includes `request_id` even when the upstream stream fails mid-flight.

Why this is safe:
- No behavior change to success payload schemas.
- Adds fields/headers only; does not remove existing error fields (we keep legacy fields in internal logs only; client-facing remains canonicalized).
- Request IDs are non-secret; security review confirms they are safe to log and share with Support, and do not encode sensitive information.

Testing:
- Added unit tests for request-id selection/generation and upstream error normalization.
- Added integration tests for: JSON 429 with Retry-After, JSON 500, SSE mid-stream upstream 502, and gateway-generated 401/403 errors.

Follow-ups:
- SDKs will rely on this contract in their typed errors and conformance fixtures (ENG-5126 / ENG-5127).
Allison Grant (review): Can we ensure request_id is present on gateway-generated 401/403 as well? Those are the most common support escalations because customers can’t provide anything besides timestamps. Also please confirm we’re not generating a new request id when one is already present in inbound x-request-id; I want a single correlation id across proxies.

Ethan Park (author): Good call. Updated middleware so request_id is resolved before auth and attached to the response headers even for auth failures. Also made inbound x-request-id precedence explicit (we accept if it matches our validator; otherwise we generate). Added tests for 401 and malformed inbound header.

Kaitlyn Nguyen (review): For downstream propagation, we should forward x-request-id to the auth/policy service too; it’s the one we look at during incident debugging. Also, please align naming: we’ve used x-request-id historically (not x-redwood-request-id). Let’s keep x-request-id as the canonical header.

Ethan Park (author): Agreed — kept x-request-id canonical, removed x-redwood-request-id from earlier draft. Added propagation to auth/policy client and updated docs/internal/api-errors.md accordingly.

Ibrahim Khan (review): Streaming semantics: how do we guarantee request_id when the stream dies before the first chunk? The SDKs need a stable place to read it. If we only emit it in a meta event after the upstream yields, we’ll still miss some cases.

Ethan Park (author): Updated SSE writer to emit an immediate `event: meta` frame containing request_id as soon as headers are committed (before proxying upstream chunks). If the upstream fails before producing tokens, the client still receives meta + error with request_id. Added integration test simulating upstream connection failure before first token.

Sean Gallagher (review): Please consider rate-limit storms: does emitting meta before first byte change buffering/flush behavior? Also, confirm we don’t log request headers containing API keys.

Ethan Park (author): Meta event is a tiny frame (~60–90 bytes) and uses existing flush behavior; it doesn’t increase request fanout. No changes to header logging; request-id middleware only reads x-request-id and does not touch auth headers. Marcus also reviewed secret-handling implications below.

Marcus Lin (security review): Looks fine. Ensure request_id is randomly generated (no user-controlled concatenation), validate inbound request id characters/length to prevent log injection, and keep it out of any user-visible error messages besides the field itself.

Ethan Park (author): Implemented strict validator (UUIDv7 or 20–64 chars base62 with dashes/underscores), otherwise generate UUIDv7. Added test cases for newline/oversize inbound header. Client-visible output is only `request_id` field + x-request-id header.

Allison Grant (approval): Approved after tests. Please sync with observability-pack dashboards so request_id is extracted consistently from error payloads.

Ethan Park (author): Will follow up in observability-pack; for now, logs already include request_id and dashboards can join on it.

Result: Merged via squash. Gateway deploy scheduled with next weekday release window; coordinated with ENG-5130 rollout checklist.
payload.title: Gateway: standardize request_id propagation across streaming + non-streaming errors

payload.body:
Motivation: customer telemetry and internal canaries showed intermittent first-byte jitter in streaming responses under moderate bursty load. Root cause was interaction between instantaneous kernel dispatch (bursty GPU occupancy), KV cache contention on hot prefixes, and unbounded token emission when credits are returned immediately. This PR implements a lightweight controller ("stream shepherd") that shapes outbound token credits per-connection using a latency-budget-aware window and applies soft kernel throttling to avoid instant GPU occupancy spikes.

What this changes: 1) Credit shaping: per-stream credit windows are capped by a latency budget estimator and an adaptive refill timer. Credits returned from the generator are bucketed into a sliding token window (configurable, default 25ms) instead of being emitted immediately. 2) Kernel throttling: a soft rate limiter that hints to the scheduler to spread kernel launches across a small time jitter when the estimated tail pressure is above threshold. This avoids synchronous kernel spikes when many small streams finish KV lookups simultaneously. 3) KV prelock warm: add an opportunistic short-term KV lock for confirmed hot prefix hits to reduce high-contention stalls during window refill. This is conservative — it only applies when prefix hit rate > 70% and path latency < configured threshold. 4) Sizing controller: continuous-batching controller tweaks microbatch sizes up/down within a narrow band to keep latency within SLO while maximizing throughput.

Checklist: [x] Design doc + microbench plan (linked in Linear ENG-4921), [x] Unit tests for credit window logic, [x] End-to-end canary in benchmark-lab, [x] Safety flag gated behind feature flag `stream_shepherd_v1`, [x] Metrics and dashboard additions, [x] Rollout plan with staged percentage.

Testing and results: - Unit tests cover window arithmetic, refill cooldown, and kernel throttle heuristics. - Integration: ran a 48-hour canary against a mixed GPT-like 8k-seq workload (2.5k RPS emulator). Observed median TTFB improvement of 18% and p95 improvement of 12% for streaming routes under moderate burstiness. CPU/GPU utilization smoothed (less 99th-percentile GPU launch spikes). - Benchmarks: no regression on throughput for long-running steady-state throughput tests; microbatch controller increased average batch size by ~6% without SLO violations.

Rollout: feature gated; enable 5% traffic -> 25% -> 100% with checkpoints at each stage for regressions. Canary dashboards added: stream_shepherd.tokens_emitted, stream_shepherd.window_fill_latency_ms, scheduler.kernel_throttle_ratio.

Operational notes: feature can be disabled at runtime. Default behavior is unchanged when the flag is off. Initial default parameters are conservative (window=25ms, throttle_threshold=0.08 tail pressure). We will tighten after broader telemetry.

Related: ties to ENG-4980 (scheduler heuristics) and a follow-up ticket to explore making the latency-budget estimator cross-tenant (ENG-5050).
Omar: overall looks good; can we make the default window configurable via runtime config? (answered: added runtime flag, default 25ms)
Linnea: ensure this doesn't starve low-rate streams — suggested a minimum token allowance per stream (implemented)
Amit: questioned the KV prelock safety; added extra guard and TTL for the short-term lock to be conservative
Add an opt-in stream-shepherd controller that smooths token emission and reduces streaming first-byte jitter. Enabled behind feature flag. Improvements expected in median and tail TTFB for bursty workloads with minimal throughput impact.
payload.title: Introduce stream-shepherd credit shaping and kernel throttling to smooth token emission

payload.body:
Motivation: intermittent regional surges from a small set of tenants were causing sustained SLO violations despite existing static throttles. This PR introduces a runtime watermarking mechanism that computes per-tenant SLO watermarks from latency and token-usage histograms and a regional quarantine adapter that places manic tenants into a short probationary quarantine with progressive re-admit logic. The change is opt-in via feature flags and is compatible with existing admission and circuit-breaker flows. Key behaviors: dynamic watermarking emits a moving SLO threshold per tenant based on p50/p95 latency trends and recent KV-pressure; the quarantine adapter signals routing to standby pools and applies an exponential backoff for re-admit windows; telemetry emits watermark_offset, quarantine_state, and quarantine_retries metrics; rollout is staged with a canary and gradual ramp controlled by the feature flag. Implementation notes: watermark manager is a lightweight in-memory controller with a pluggable policy interface, quarantine adapter hooks into the scheduler admission path and defers to existing fallback policies when capacity is limited. Testing: unit tests for watermark computation and adapter decision logic, integration e2e that simulates tenant surge and validates graceful tenant re-admit. Docs and ops runbook added. Related Linear: ENG-3291.
Arjun: Can we bound memory usage for the watermark manager when tenant counts spike? Consider an LRU eviction for cold tenants.
Maya: Added LRU-based tenant cache and a configurable max_entries knob in config/defaults.yaml, default 50k.
Lena: We need clearer telemetry for re-admit failures and a tag for region to facilitate dashboards.
Maya: Emitted quarantine_retries and quarantine_region tags; updated metrics_definitions.yaml and docs.
Theo: Integration test flaky on CI due to timing; suggest reducing tight sleep and using event-driven wait.
Maya: Refactored e2e test to use a websocket signal from the scheduler test harness instead of fixed sleeps; re-run CI.
Unit coverage added for watermark math and adapter decision tree. Integration e2e simulates 100 tenants with synthetic latency spikes and validates that quarantined tenants are routed to standby pools and re-admit windows follow exponential backoff. CI initially surfaced a timing flake which was fixed by making e2e event-driven.
Step 1: merge to main behind feature flag off. Step 2: enable feature flag in canary cluster for 5% of traffic for 24 hours while monitoring watermark_offset and quarantine_state metrics. Step 3: incrementally ramp to 25% then 100% if no regressions. Step 4: emergency rollback path via feature flag toggle or configmap revert. Ops runbook included in docs/operations/slo-watermarking.md.
Introduce dynamic SLO watermarking and a regional quarantine adapter to improve graceful degradation during tenant surges. Opt-in via feature flag 'dynamic_slo_watermarking'. Emitted metrics: watermark_offset, quarantine_state, quarantine_retries. Rollout requires a staged canary and monitoring of p50/p95 and KV pressure.
If quarantine_state count for a region rises suddenly, consider pausing ramp and investigate tenant-level traffic patterns. Use the quarantine_region tag to scope dashboards. In emergency, toggle dynamic_slo_watermarking to false and run configmap rollback.
payload.title: Dynamic SLO watermarking and regional quarantine adapter

payload.body:
Motivation: Long-tail invocation latency and token-cost spikes are often caused by phase-localized regressions (initialization, kv-warm, model-emit/stream). Existing per-request metrics obscure phase structure because they aggregate end-to-end. This PR introduces a low-overhead "invocation prober" that periodically samples per-invocation phase timings and emits a compact phase-entropy gauge to our telemetry pipeline, plus a threshold-tuner service that suggests per-route alert thresholds based on historical phase percentiles and cost impact.

What this PR does (summary):
- Adds an invocation prober that attaches lightweight phase markers to a subset of invocations and emits phase-duration histograms and a computed phase-entropy gauge (how much time distribution across phases varies).
- Enriches OTLP spans with phase attributes (phase.start, phase.end, phase.name) for sampled spans and adds token-phase labels for streaming responses.
- Exposes new Prometheus metrics (invocation_phase_entropy, invocation_phase_pXX, invocation_phase_sample_rate) and a minimal aggregator that computes per-route percentile baselines used by the threshold-tuner.
- Adds a threshold-tuner microservice that computes adaptive alert bands per-route using a cost-weighted blend of p90/p95/p99 and suggests alert hysteresis values. The tuner can operate in passive-suggest mode (UI only) or active-suggest where it proposes changes to managed alert policies.
- Adds dashboards and panels under Observability -> Invocation Phase Insights (phase timeline heatmap, entropy sparkline, baseline bands) and a playbook for investigating high-phase-entropy incidents.
- Implements guardrails: probe sampling is bounded by tenant-configurable rate limits and prober includes a CPU/latency backoff to avoid perturbing hot paths.

Why this approach: Aggregates hide phase-specific regressions and make it hard to tune alerts without excessive noise. Phase-entropy provides a compact indicator that highlights when distribution of time across phases shifts (e.g., backend coldstart vs. slow kernel). The threshold-tuner reduces manual alert churn by recommending data-driven hysteresis tuned to cost impact.

Checklist: 
- [x] Prober core implementation (go): telemetry/prober.go, prober/worker.go
- [x] OTLP span enrichment and attribute docs: tracing/attrs.md
- [x] Prometheus metric exports and targets: metrics/invocation_phase_exporter.go
- [x] Threshold-tuner service (py): alerts/threshold_tuner.py, alerts/runner.py
- [x] Dashboard JSON and panels: observability/dashboards/invocation_phase_insights.json
- [x] Unit tests + integration e2e harness: prober_test.go, threshold_tuner_test.py, e2e/prober_harness.sh
- [x] Docs (Console playbook + runbook): docs/observability/invocation_phase_playbook.md
- [x] Backoff/guardrail implementation and feature flag: config/flags.yaml

Performance notes: The prober opportunistically samples ~0.5% of invocations by default (configurable) and adds ~120 bytes of span attribute payload for sampled requests. Benchmarks run in the PR show median overhead <0.25ms on hot paths at 0.5% sampling. Aggregation for entropy uses reservoir sketches to keep memory bounded.

Migration notes: No breaking API changes. New metrics are additive. Admins can toggle the prober via the observability toggle in Console or set sampling to 0 to disable. Threshold suggestions are opt-in before they modify alert policies.

Related work: This complements existing token-cost rollups and span-synthesis work (see ENG-2053, ENG-2310). Linear tickets included in linked_linear.

Testing: unit tests for metric exporters and tuner algorithm, local e2e harness that replays synthetic invocations with deterministic phase patterns, and a staged rollout in dev->staging->prod with gradual sampling increase.

Follow-ups planned: integrate tuner suggestions into rollout automation (A/B change), add tenant-aware cost simulation to the tuner, and add per-model phase profiles to the model registry for offline analysis.
Lena: Can the prober sampling be tenant-isolated so a noisy tenant can't affect cluster-wide metrics? -> Answer: yes, sampling key is per-tenant and the exporter enforces per-tenant rate caps (added notes in config).
Arjun: The OTLP attribute names collide with an older schema; suggest prefacing with rw.phase.* -> Action: renamed attributes to rw.phase.* and added attrs.md description (done).
Kofi: Threshold tuner needs a cost-sensitivity knob and opt-in before policy changes -> Action: added 'suggest_only' mode and cost_weight parameter; default is suggest_only (done).
Lena: Add a safety override if prober overhead rises above 1% on tail tests -> Action: added CPU/latency backoff and a hard disable flag (config/flags.yaml) (done).
Arjun (approval): Looks good after requested renames and safety guardrails.
Priya (author): Addressed comments, added tests and tightened defaults. Thanks for the reviews.
Kofi (approval): Approved — tuner suggestions look conservative and readable in the UI.
Add Invocation Prober (phase sampling + entropy gauge) and Threshold Tuner (adaptive alert suggestions). New metrics: invocation_phase_entropy, invocation_phase_pXX, invocation_phase_sample_rate. Dashboards: Invocation Phase Insights. Opt-in threshold automation; prober sampling is configurable and disabled by default.
If phase-entropy spikes appear after rollout, first toggle prober sampling to 0 for the affected tenant via Console feature flag. Use the playbook (docs/observability/invocation_phase_playbook.md) to correlate entropy spikes with kernel-queue/gpu-warm metrics. Threshold-tuner suggestions are non-destructive unless applied explicitly.
payload.title: invocation-prober-and-threshold-tuner-introduce-phase-sampling-and-alert-autocalibrate

payload.body:
Motivation:
Introduce stronger tenant-level guards around KMS usage and a managed lifecycle for audit records. Several incidents and compliance reviews flagged two gaps: (1) tenants could reference keys in regions that violate their residency controls, and (2) audit retention policy enforcement was manual and brittle. This PR adds an allowlist gate for KMS operations and an operator-configurable retention lifecycle controller for audit logs.

What this PR changes (high level):
- New runtime hook that enforces a per-tenant KMS allowlist. On key operation, we validate the tenant->key region and service allowlist. Cold-miss paths consult the policy store and cache the result with a TTL.
- A retention-lifecycle-controller daemon that reads tenant retention tags and moves/archives/purges audit segments according to configured schedules. Supports S3 archival and vaulting to long-term storage.
- RBAC v2 mappings for crypto roles: maps service accounts and platform roles to a minimal set of key operations (encrypt/decrypt/sign).
- Migration job to backfill missing tenant KMS-region metadata and to generate a default allowlist in permissive mode for operators.
- Operator docs and upgrade notes.

Implementation notes:
- KMS allowlist is driven by config/policy/kms_allowlist.yaml and exposed through a lightweight HTTP policy API for the runtime to query. The runtime uses an in-memory TTL cache to avoid per-request policy RPCs. Cache miss triggers a synchronous policy fetch to keep semantics strict for the first operation.
- Audit retention controller is implemented as a Kubernetes-deployable binary (cmd/retention-controller) that reconciles tenant CRs and applies lifecycle actions. It emits metrics and traces for each retention action.
- RBAC v2 role_mappings.yaml contains explicit bindings for new crypto roles and a helper to generate tenant-scoped grants.

Rollout and upgrade plan:
- Deploy controller and new policy API (read-only mode) alongside existing services.
- Run migration backfill in permissive mode for 48 hours to identify tenants without KMS metadata. Operators review the report and provide missing data or accept defaults.
- Enable hard enforcement in a canary (5% of traffic) for 72 hours, monitor key usage latency and audit retention metrics.
- Gradual ramp to 100% after signoff.

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests for policy evaluation, cache TTL, and migration job (tests/integration/kms_allowlist_test.go).
- Integration test against a fake KMS that exercises cross-region denies.
- CI initially failed on a race in the retention controller reconciliation loop; added a mutex and a retry backoff. All CI checks pass on the final push.

Caveats and operational considerations:
- Cold-cache policy evaluations add a small latency on the first key use; mitigated by TTL cache and recommended warmup strategy for heavy workloads.
- Operators must provide kms_allowlist configuration per-tenant prior to hard enforcement or accept the permissive fallback for the migration window.
- Retention controller requires credentials to archive to long-term storage; see docs/operators/audit-retention.md for required IAM roles.

Related items: linked linear tasks SEC-88 and ENG-4921 cover policy UX and migration automation.
Leah Kim: Please add unit tests covering multi-tenant allowlist behavior across regions.
Marco Alvarez: We should validate performance impact on hot-path -- consider async checks for cache miss.
Priya Nair: Add migration notes for existing tenants without KMS region tags; otherwise rollout could break keys.
Author (Anita Desai): Addressed comments; added cache-based check and migration job; expanded test coverage.
Implements tenant-level KMS usage allowlist and a pluggable audit retention lifecycle controller. Operators must provide kms_allowlist configuration for tenants to avoid service errors. Adds RBAC v2 mappings for crypto roles and a migration tool to backfill tenant KMS tags.
This PR introduces a small runtime check (cold-cache path) that may add latency on the first key usage; mitigated with TTL'd in-memory allowlist and an async backfill job. Rolling deploy recommended with canary on 5% traffic before full rollout.
payload.title: Enforce tenant KMS usage allowlist and audit retention lifecycle

payload.body:
Context: Customers have asked for a way to author RBAC v2 policy bundles declaratively and bind those to jurisdiction-aware KMS selection rules so that operator credentials and service requests automatically resolve to region-appropriate keys. This PR introduces a small, focused runtime component (policy-executor) that evaluates declarative policy templates at admission time and a lightweight kms-mapper library that annotates requests with KMS selection hints used by the routing layer. Motivation: reduce hand-edited role bindings, make operator scope deterministic, and improve audit signals so that KMS choices and RBAC decisions are traceable and reproducible. Changes: 1) Add policy-executor service that consumes policy-bundle.yaml and exposes an /evaluate endpoint used by operator-claim-webhook; 2) Implement kms-mapper library (go) to convert policy attributes (jurisdiction, zone, tenant-residency) into kms selection hints and canonical audit tags; 3) Extend audit enrichment pipeline to include kms_hint and policy_fingerprint fields; 4) Add feature-flag gate (rbac.declarative_executor) and staged rollout config for installer; 5) Migrate a small set of operator policies (operator-lease, operator-approval) to the new bundle format as examples; 6) Add end-to-end integration tests and CI job. Rollout plan: feature gated by default; after internal canary (10% of operator traffic) enable shadow evaluation in production to compare executor decisions against the legacy engine for 48h; if diffs < 0.1% and no behavioral regressions, flip executor to active for the canary cohort and gradually expand. Linear/Jira: ENG-8421 (policy executor), ENG-8450 (kms mapping), SUP-1294 (support ticket). Summary: Implements tier-aware LRU eviction for the serving runtime KV cache to make allocator behavior predictable under memory pressure and to reduce burst-driven tail latency caused by opportunistic/late evictions. The policy prefers evicting low-priority tiers first (e.g., free/trial) while preserving higher tiers (hosted paid / dedicated) and always respecting pinned sessions. This PR includes correctness-focused unit + integration tests and adds basic observability counters needed for rollout guardrails.

Motivation: During high churn with mixed sequence lengths, the KV arena frequently hits soft pressure and the existing eviction path behaves effectively FIFO-ish (depends on free-list ordering), which can evict recently-active sequences and trigger retries / cancellations at bad times. We also had a support report (SUP-28433) where pinned long-lived sessions were disproportionately impacted during bursts.

Design: 1) Tier-aware ordering: each active sequence is assigned an eviction tier based on request context (tier enum sourced from auth/customer routing). Eviction scans tiers from lowest to highest. Within a tier we evict LRU based on last_kv_access_step (monotonic scheduler step). 2) Pinned session guard: sequences marked pinned (explicit customer pin / long-lived session) are non-evictable unless we cross the hard OOM guardrail. In this PR we treat pinned as absolute non-evictable and let the allocator return PRESSURE_HARD -> scheduler backpressure (the follow-up compaction work will reduce how often we reach this). 3) Safety constraints: we never evict a sequence that is currently in an in-flight decode microbatch or mid-relocation; eviction operates only on sequences in a stable state. If a candidate becomes ineligible (state changes) we rescan with a bounded attempt budget.

Implementation notes: - Added EvictionIndex that maintains per-tier min-heaps keyed by last_access_step (LRU). Updates happen on decode step boundaries and on request state transitions (prefill->decode, end-of-sequence, cancellation). - Added configurable knobs (behind feature flag) in runtime_flags.yaml: kv_eviction_enabled, kv_eviction_scan_budget, kv_eviction_soft_pressure_bytes, kv_eviction_tier_weights (initially simple tier ordering; weights reserved for follow-up). - Integrated into kv_cache_arena pressure handling: on SOFT_PRESSURE we attempt eviction up to scan_budget candidates (bounded). If eviction frees enough pages, allocations proceed; otherwise we bubble PRESSURE_SOFT to scheduler for backpressure / admission control. - Observability: exported kv_evictions_total{tier,cause}, kv_eviction_scan_candidates_total, kv_eviction_pinned_skips_total, kv_eviction_ineligible_skips_total. Cause is one of: soft_pressure, hard_pressure, admin (future).

Tests: - Unit tests cover ordering (tier then LRU), monotonic step update behavior, pinned non-evictable behavior, and scan budget enforcement. - Integration test constructs a mixed-churn workload with a small arena and verifies: (a) pinned sequences remain alive, (b) low-tier sequences are preferentially evicted, (c) no token mismatch / stream corruption under repeated eviction, (d) allocator returns PRESSURE_SOFT (not crash/oom) when only pinned remain.

Perf impact: On microbench (single worker, 4k seqs), eviction index maintenance added ~0.15% CPU in scheduler loop; no measurable GPU throughput change. The eviction scan is bounded and only runs under pressure.

Rollout: Feature-flagged (kv_eviction_enabled default false). Intended to turn on first in internal canary after fragmentation metrics are live (see PR-19342) and before compaction is defaulted. This PR is a dependency for ENG-4826 kill-switch plumbing.

Known limitations / follow-ups: - Pinned-as-absolute may increase backpressure frequency in pathological workloads; compaction should reduce this, but we may also want a "pinned soft-evict" mode for internal tiers only (ADR discussion). - Prefix-cache interaction is limited to respecting pinned prefixes; we do not yet preferentially evict cold prefixes vs active decode sequences (follow-up ADR item).

Review discussion highlights (selected): Omar El-Sayed: "Please ensure pinned sequences are excluded before heap push, not after pop; otherwise scan_budget burns quickly." -> Updated EvictionIndex to avoid inserting pinned sequences and added kv_eviction_pinned_skips_total when encountering legacy registrations. Noah Patel: "I want an explicit invariant about not evicting in-flight decode." -> Added SequenceState::kEvictable check (covers not in batch, not relocating, not holding kv_write_lock) + unit tests for state transition race. Sofia Ivanova: "We should only update last_access_step at decode step boundary; per-token updates will be too hot." -> Changed update site to scheduler boundary (end of decode iteration) and added a perf-smoke guard in CI. Allison Grant: "Metric names need to match the standards draft; include tier label and cause label." -> Renamed counters to kv_evictions_total and added required labels.

CI: Initial integration run failed due to a flaky timeout in kv_cache_integration_eviction_test when GPU was heavily loaded. Adjusted the test harness to use deterministic step advancement and increased the per-test deadline from 5s to 12s; subsequent reruns passed.

Checklist: - [x] Feature-flagged, default off - [x] Metrics exported (prom + tracing hook points reserved) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Updated internal flags doc - [x] Linked Linear issues

Co-authored-by: Julian Moore (test harness adjustments) / Anika Gupta (integration test cases)
Adds tier-aware LRU eviction for KV cache under memory pressure; respects pinned sessions; exports eviction metrics by tier/cause.
Merged as part of KV cache compaction/eviction project; enablement requires runtime config rollout + dashboard wiring (ENG-4830).

Context: production users have intermittent latency spikes during multi-tenant bursts that correlate with GPU kernel queueing and priority inversion at the runtime scheduler. Existing metrics showed aggregate kernel latency but not contention by invocation priority, making alerts noisy and root-cause analysis slow.

This change introduces a small, low-overhead telemetry path that surfaces kernel contention and queue depth broken down by invocation priority class and model shard. It also wires a new SLO explainer endpoint that maps per-route SLA violations to the dominant contention signal (kernel-queue, kv-cache-miss, batching-delay) to help on-call narrow down remediation steps faster.

What I changed: instrumented runtime scheduler to emit: priority.queue_depth, priority.kernel_hold_time_ms, kernel.preempt_count, and kernel-contention-ratio (0-1) with labels: tenant_id (hashed), model, priority_class (P0/P1/P2), shard_id. Added a lightweight aggregation rollup that computes 1m/5m/1h contention percentiles and a per-route derived metric route.sla_attribution that surfaces the top-1 contributing resource for a given SLA breach.

Why this is safe: metrics are opt-in via a feature flag (observability.priority_kernels) and sampling defaults to 1 in 50 invocations for priority=P2 to avoid high-cardinality explosion. Tenant identifiers are hashed and truncated to 8 chars for privacy. No user payload is collected.

Rollout plan: behind feature flag for two weeks on canaries, 24h perf/telemetry spike window, then gradual ramp to 30% of edge traffic, then to all. Dashboards and alert rules are included in this PR and will be staged in the observability namespace; they are muted until the flag is enabled.

Checklist:
- [x] Scheduler instrumentation + protobuf change (backwards compatible)
- [x] Metrics exporter + aggregation rollup
- [x] Route-level SLA explainer service and README
- [x] Dashboards (contour and heatmap panels) and alert playbook
- [x] Unit + integration tests for exporter and attribution logic
- [x] Security review and PII audit

Testing and validation: unit tests and local integration run in CI; we exercised the feature on the perf-canary cluster with synthetic load that reproduces priority inversion and observed the contention ratio spike align with increased per-invocation kernel_hold_time_ms. The SLA explainer returned correct top contributors for 92% of synthetic failures in our end-to-end replay.

Notes: this PR intentionally avoids adding high-cardinality route tags to the base metrics. If customers opt into per-route attribution we emit a derived aggregated metric (route.sla_attribution) that is pre-aggregated server-side to reduce cardinality. Full docs for the feature flag lives in docs/observability/priority-kernels.md.

Motivation: Customers operating in regulated jurisdictions requested a mode where KMS usage is gated by explicit regional consent policies and audit logs are pseudonymized for privacy-preserving telemetry. This PR introduces a ConsentMediator component that centralizes region-based consent decisions for KMS operations, a region_resolver that deterministically maps tenant/context to a region affinity (with multi-provider fallback), and a PseudonymousAuditWriter which emits audit entries with stable pseudonyms and rotation hooks for downstream processors.

What this changes: Adds a new services/kms.ConsentMediator that is consulted by the KMS client before performing key operations. Consent decisions are logged (metrics + structured audit) and can be configured with per-tenant policy profiles (see internal/config/security.go). The region_resolver selects a primary region for routing and a fallback sequence; the ConsentMediator enforces policy delta (consent granted/denied/missing) and surfaces a machine-readable decision to callers. The PseudonymousAuditWriter implements a pluggable pseudonymization strategy: HMAC-based stable pseudonyms per-tenant+service with periodic key rotation and optional salt re-seeding for regulatory export.

Backwards compatibility: The default behavior is opt-in via helm values (deploy/helm/values-security.yaml). When disabled, KMS calls follow existing code paths. We added feature flags to enable staged rollout. No public API surface changes — the feature is internal and gated behind server-side config.

Security considerations: Consent decisions are authoritative for KMS access in this runtime; a denial results in aborting the KMS request with a structured error code (KMS_CONSENT_REQUIRED). PseudonymousAuditWriter ensures that raw identifiers are not present in logs/metrics; we retained enough context to support linking for forensic requests (via secure key escrow rotation records). The implementation is audited in code review and unit tests cover edge cases (rotation, missing keys, expired consent).

Testing and CI: Unit tests (pkg/kms, pkg/audit) added; an e2e job (integration/ci/kms-consent-e2e.yml) simulates tenant region profiles and verifies correct routing, consent enforcement, and audit output. CI summary: full test suite passing locally and on CI after two fixes (region_resolver edge-case + helm templating).

Operational notes & rollout: Start as disabled in staging, enable for a single compliance tenant using helm override values. Monitor new metrics: kms_consent_decisions_total{decision="granted|denied|missing"} and audit_pseudonym_rotate_count. If consent denials are high unexpectedly, abort rollout. There is a migration script (scripts/migrate/audit-pseudonymize-migration.sql) to seed pseudonym keys for historical entries if customers request backfilled pseudonymization.

Related work: ENG-4321 (region consent policy engine), SEC-128 (audit pseudonymization RFC). Jira SUP-7890 tracks a support request for tenant-specific consent profiles.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the ConsentMediator concurrency model (services/kms/consent_mediator.go), the deterministic nature and fallback strategy of region_resolver, and the pseudonym rotation surface in pseudonymous_writer.go. I included integration tests and a small e2e job for manual verification.

Context and motivation: We currently surface token-level cost and latency breakdowns but lack visibility into GPU kernel-level backpressure and how cost accumulates across batches. Teams were blind to 'hidden' latency introduced by kernel serialization and memory-pressure spikes during mixed-model workloads. This PR introduces kernel backpressure span linking, a deterministic per-batch cost attribution pipeline, and corresponding dashboard+alerting to help SREs and runtime engineers diagnose and cap cost/latency regressions.

What this PR does (high level):
- Add OTEL span enrichment for kernel events (attributes: kernel_name, kernel_queue_depth, kernel_queue_ms, gpu_active_ms, memory_bytes_reserved). Spans are linked to invocation batches via a new deterministic batch_id tag.
- Implement a lightweight span-linker in the serving runtime that emits a batch lifecycle span (batch.begin, batch.exec, batch.finish) and attaches kernel child spans with precise timestamps.
- Compute per-batch GPU-time cost and attribute it down to individual invocations in the batch using token-weighted attribution and a configurable per-GPU-cost-rate. This output is written to the telemetry pipeline as compact metrics and a rollup table for ad-hoc queries.
- New dashboards: "Batch Cost Waterfall", "Kernel Contention Timeline", "Per-model Memory Pressure sparkline" (Grafana). Dashboards include drilldowns that link directly to sampled traces for the offending batch_id.
- Alert tuning: add kernel-backpressure-high (SLO impact candidate) that triggers when kernel_queue_ms p50 > X for > 5min or when batch_gpu_cost p99 spikes by > 3x for same window. Alert suppressions added to avoid noisy short spikes (dampening with 5-minute evaluation).

Checklist (implementation & rollout):
- [x] Runtime: emit batch lifecycle spans and kernel attributes (C++ runtime change).
- [x] Telemetry: compact cost message schema and rollup ingestion (metrics pipeline).
- [x] Dashboards: Grafana panels + drilldown links.
- [x] Alerts: alert rules + dampening.
- [x] Tests: unit tests for batch attribution logic, integration test for span linkage, dashboard smoke test.
- [x] Docs: add short runbook and alert handling guide to observability runbooks.

Commits summary:
- commit 1: runtime: emit batch lifecycle spans and attach deterministic batch_id
- commit 2: tracing: add kernel attributes and link child spans to batch lifecycle
- commit 3: telemetry: batch-cost aggregator and token-weighted attribution mapper
- commit 4: metrics: compact schema, rollup ingestion job, and migration script
- commit 5: dashboards: add Grafana panels and sample dashboard JSON
- commit 6: alerts/docs: add alert rules and runbook/docs updates

Files/areas touched (high level):
- serving/runtime/batcher.cc (+ headers): batch lifecycle span emitter and batch_id generator
- serving/runtime/kernel_tracer.cc: kernel span attribute extraction and enqueue points
- tracing/otel_schema/README.md: document new attributes and conventions
- telemetry/aggregator/batch_cost_mapper.py: token-weighted attribution and per-batch cost computation
- telemetry/ingest/rollups/migrate_add_batch_cost.sql: migration to rollup table for batch cost time-series
- dashboards/grafana/batch_cost_waterfall.json: new dashboard panels and drilldown links
- alerting/rules/kernel_backpressure.yaml: new alert rule with dampening and runbook link
- docs/observability/batch-troubleshooting.md: runbook with triage steps and examples

Review conversation summary:
- Jonah Park: asked for defensiveness when batch_id cannot be generated (e.g., preflight failures). I added a fallback to a synthetic id and explicitly mark synthetic in span attribute so downstream can ignore if desired.
- Priya Natarajan: requested clarification on attribution when token counts are missing (e.g., streaming tool calls). We added a fallback proportional attribution by predicted output length and documented the bias in runbook.
- Leo Alvarez: flagged potential cardinality explosion from batch_id if we keep full string. We switched to a compact hex-encoded 8-byte batch_id and added a retention policy to drop raw span attributes in high-cardinality tenants; rollups keep aggregated numbers only.
- CI: initial lint failure (formatting), a small follow-up commit reformatted a header and fixed a flake8 complaint. Integration tests flagged a timing flake in test_batch_span_linking; increased test timeout and stabilized the test (added polling-based assertion). Final CI run: all checks passed.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests: attribution edge cases (zero-token fallback, zero-cost GPUs) covered.
- Integration: end-to-end trace generation registered in test harness and validated that batch spans and kernel spans are linkable and that rollup ingestion produced expected per-batch cost numbers.
- Staging rollout: deployed to staging traffic for 48 hours; compared per-batch GPU-time computed vs. GPU metrics (nvidia-smi derived) and observed <4% delta for stable models.

Operational considerations:
- Backfilling: migration script populates rollups for the last 7 days; long-term historical data will be sparse and is not a blocking issue.
- Cost namespaces: per-tenant config allows disabling per-batch rollups for low-volume tenants to avoid extra storage cost.
- Alert tuning: we opted for conservative thresholds initially and will adjust after 2 weeks of production telemetry.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged after approvals from Jonah and Priya. Post-merge actions: run telemetry migration job (ops runbook step included), schedule 1-week alert threshold review with SREs.

Docs/runbook excerpt (single-line sample included in this PR):
"If kernel_backpressure_high fires: identify offending batch_id from alert, open trace via Grafana drilldown, inspect kernel_queue_ms timeline and memory_bytes_reserved spikes. If contention is on a specific model, escalate to model-oncall and pin an alternative model or adjust autoscaler/kernel-affinity knobs per runbook."
Add kernel backpressure tracing attributes, batch-level GPU-cost attribution, new dashboards and tuned alerts. No user-facing API changes. Ops: run metrics-migration job to populate new rollup tables.
Jonah: please avoid exploding cardinality; use compact ids — addressed with hex-encoded 8b id and retention policy.
Priya: handle missing token counts gracefully — added proportional fallback and documented bias.
Leo: prefer adding a feature flag for per-tenant rollups — added tenant opt-out via config.
Author (Maya): fixed lint and test flakiness in follow-up commits; validated staging metrics match GPU telemetry within 4%.

Context and motivation: Teams onboarded to Redwood often need fast, low-risk ways to compress end-to-end unit economics for bursty tenants without impacting latency SLOs. Existing autotuners operate post-facto; this change introduces a small "costspector" agent that observes mini-batch lifecycle signals (warm windows, idle decay, burst patterns) and synthesizes batch/caching defaults plus conservative per-tenant quantization hints so ops and SREs can dry-run effects before rollout.

Summary of changes: Adds a runtime-side lightweight lifecycle sampler, a deterministic simulator/CLI (costspector simulate) for running dry-runs on traces, and a quant-hint advisor that emits ranked presets (safe/medium/aggressive) with expected delta to token-cost and expected p95 latency impact. New modules: runtime/sampler, tools/costspector-cli, optimizer/quant-hint. No protocol changes; everything is opt-in behind feature flag "costspector.v1".

Checklist: [x] design doc (ENG-1973) linked; [x] unit + integration tests; [x] small e2e smoke in perf-canary; [x] feature-flag gated; [x] docs snippet in console-guides.

Commits (high-level): - 9a7f1f2: initial lifecycle sampler and persistence schema - b3e4c5d: simulator harness + dry-run CLI - f2d8aa0: quant-hint advisor and ranking model (heuristic) - a4b6c90: integration with tenant defaults and feature-flag gate - 0f1e2b3: tests, docs and perf-canary config

Files changed (overview): - runtime/sampler/* : new sampler that emits windowed signals and compact histograms - tools/costspector-cli/* : dry-run simulator, CSV/JSON trace importer, CLI flags for target SLO and budget - optimizer/quant_hint/* : heuristic advisor and preset exporter - console-guides/docs/snippets.md : short instructions and example outputs - tests/* : unit tests + synthetic trace fixtures - ci/perf-canary.yaml : added a smoke job to validate no regression on main perf metric

Design notes: The sampler is intentionally lightweight — it stores compact delta-encoded histograms keyed by tenant+model+shape and emits TTL'd summaries. The simulator replays summaries deterministically to estimate batching gains and cache hit curves. Quant-hint advisor currently uses a conservative heuristic (loss thresholds derived from historical evals in ENG-1973) and outputs three ranked presets with expected cost/latency deltas and a confidence score. This is meant to be advisory: operators must review and can run the CLI dry-run which outputs a side-by-side delta table.

Review conversation (selected): 
- Asha Rao (review): "Nice and focused; main concern is accidental promotion of aggressive quant presets for low-volume tenants. Can we limit aggressive presets to tenants with >1000 daily tokens or explicit opt-in?"
  - Author reply: "Agree. Added a guard in optimizer/quant_hint/policy.go: aggressive presets only returned when recent_24h_tokens >= 1000 or tenant opt-in flag set. Updated tests to cover this."
- Miguel Hernandez (review): "Sampler persistence format looks fine but validate on cluster upgrade path? Need a migration path for older persisted summaries."
  - Author reply: "Added migration snippet (runtime/sampler/migrations.go) and schema versioning. Migration is no-op unless feature flag toggled; documented fallback behavior in console-guides."
- Dana Kline (review): "CI flake on canary smoke; re-run and ensure timeouts are robust for slow runners."
  - Author reply: "Increased the canary job timeout and added a retry wrapper in ci/perf-canary.yaml. Verified green on re-run."

CI summary: All CI checks passed on the final push. Build: pass, Unit tests: pass (coverage +0.7%), Integration tests: pass, Lint: pass, Perf-canary: pass. One failing test on the first run (simulator edge-case with empty traces) was fixed by a guard in simulate.go.

Testing and validation: Local unit + integration tests, a perf-canary smoke job against a synthetic 10k-request trace, and a dry-run with a real tenant trace (anonymized) showed expected cost delta estimations within 8% of observed baseline. Conservatively the advisor defaults to safe presets for tenants below thresholds.

Backward compatibility and rollout: No API contract changes. Feature gated behind "costspector.v1". Migration is additive and idempotent. Rollout plan: enable feature flag for internal staging, run costspector simulate for top-20 tenants, review suggested presets in UI, enable in canary and then staggered rollout with monitoring of token-cost and p95 latency.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main. Commit message: "mini-batch lifecycle costspector + quant-hint advisor: sampler, simulator, CLI, quant heuristics (ENG-1973)". Post-merge actions: schedule a short runbook for SREs describing how to run the dry-run and evaluate presets; will follow up with a short Console guide and a blog blurb for the PLG spotlight.

Notes for follow-ups: - Improve advisor by plugging in small supervised model once we have labeled degradation pairs; tracked in ENG-2022. - Add exported CSV format for bulk evaluation and RBAC controls for who can push presets. - Consider integrating tenant warmstart signals with Dedicated autoscaler for joint warmup + batch sizing.
Introduce a lightweight lifecycle-aware mini-batcher that tracks tenant warm/cold windows, a CLI for cost-sim dry-runs, and a quant-hint advisor that surfaces conservative quantization presets per workload.

payload.body:
Summary: Introduce a new orchestrator that evaluates candidate rollouts using a temporal-hedged, multi-metric decision process that hedges decisions across short-term spike signals and medium-term trends. Motivation: Existing canary detectors focus on single dominant signals (e.g., p95 latency) and trigger conservative rollbacks that either overreact to transient spikes or underreact to slow drifts. The new orchestrator combines several orthogonal signals (latency percentiles, throughput deltas, error-rate drift, and token-level tail latency) into a weighted decision surface that is temporally smoothed and hedged by probing sibling variants. It also adds a tenant-weighted rollback policy so multi-tenant deployments prioritize tenants with tighter SLOs when deciding cutover or throttle actions. Design: - Multi-metric fusion: normalized z-score fusion of configured metrics with configurable weights per feature flag. - Temporal hedging: short (1m), medium (10m), and long (60m) exponential smoothing windows; decisions require alignment across at least two windows or a hedged probe vote. - Hedged probing: when signals disagree, the orchestrator issues small, targeted probe traffic to candidate and baseline variants and computes a probe confidence. - Tenant weighting: rollback/quarantine budget is allocated proportionally to tenant SLO criticality and recent error exposure. - Rollout actions: allow staged cutover, pause, shrink, and immediate rollback with configurable quanta. Implementation: - New package: infra/canary/orchestrator with core engine, metric adapters, probe scheduler, and policy evaluators. - Integrations: metrics ingestion via observability/metrics-client; tracing hooks for attributions; console dashboards and per-route config UI. - Config surface: canary policies are expressed as YAML with fields: metrics, window_weights, probe_rate, tenant_priority_map, quorum_thresholds. Tests & results: - Local unit and integration tests added (canary engine, probe scheduler, policy evaluation). - Synthetic e2e runs against the perf-canary harness: 1200 simulated rollouts across three traffic shapes; true positive detection rate improved by 18% vs. existing canary, false positive reduced by 23% on bursty traffic. - Latency overhead: engine CPU < 2% tail at 50k checks/minute on a small sizing; probe traffic default limited to 0.5% of candidate traffic. Risk & mitigations: - Risk: miscalibrated tenant weights could bias decisions. Mitigation: safe defaults and a dry-run mode that logs decisions without enforcing actions. - Risk: probe-induced false negatives on very low-volume routes. Mitigation: minimum traffic floor and alternative passive heuristics. Rollout plan: - Stage 1 (dry-run): deploy orchestrator in dry-run to 10% of routes for 1 week. - Stage 2 (observability): enable dashboard panels and alerting for disagreement cases. - Stage 3 (gradual cutover): enable automatic actions for low-risk routes, keep manual approval for enterprise routes. Checklist: - [x] Core engine impl and unit tests - [x] Probe scheduler + rate limiter - [x] Tenant weighting + config mapping - [x] Console config UI and dashboard panels - [x] Integration tests in perf-canary harness - [x] Docs: design doc and runbook - [x] Linear ticket ENG-11472 updated with rollout dates Related: ENG-11499 (add tenant SLO metadata pipeline), SUP-8271 incident follow-up notes Examples: included in examples/canary-scenarios/hedged-configs.yaml with four canonical traffic shapes. Notes: this PR intentionally keeps the metric fusion layer extensible so future ML-based ranking can be swapped in behind the same policy API.

Maria Alvarez: The 1/10/60 windows were chosen from perf-harness grid search; documented in the design doc and exposed as per-route overrides in the YAML; added notes to runbook.
Priya Desai: Concern: probe traffic could skew billing on Dedicated customers. Suggest adding billing-tier probe caps.
Maria Alvarez: Added tenant_priority_map to cap probe_rate per tenant and a global probe_budget feature flag; included unit tests around probe budgeting.
Lukas Meyer: CI flaky test 'canary_engine_integration_test' failed once, rerun passed. Please add a brief comment in the test explaining the non-determinism and how we simulate clocks.
Maria Alvarez: Added test comment and tightened fake clock bounds; reran CI and green.
New orchestration mode: 'temporal-hedged' canary with multi-metric fusion, hedged probing, and tenant-weighted rollback policy. Default is dry-run. See docs/runbooks/canary-orchestrator.md for migration steps.

Motivation: MQA/GQA execution on some Qwen and Llama model variants showed transient memory spikes and tail-latency regressions when handling heterogeneous head widths and long-context KV cache prefetch. This PR introduces two complementary runtime optimizations: 1) head-wise padding to coalesce multi-head matmuls into head-groups with uniform width so kernels can use contiguous memory and avoid per-head shuffles; 2) layer-split prefetch that overlaps KV shard transfer with upstream attention computation by splitting the attention pipeline into a prefetch/compute schedule. Secondary changes include a conservative backpressure tweak for continuous batching so we don't accept batches that will blow peak GPU memory when prefetch is in-flight, and a Qwen-specific rotary offset fast-path to avoid expensive fallback for a known rotary encoding layout. Key outcomes: on internal perf harness (qwen-7b-mqa long-context synthetic traces) median latency down 8-18% depending on seqlen and batch mix, 95th percentile tail latency down 12-24%, and end-to-end token-cost reduction ~6-12% due to better packing and fewer fallback kernels. Implementation notes: head-wise padding is opt-in per-model via model config hint (model_config.runtime.head_pad_grouping); layer-split prefetch has a tunable window (runtime.scheduling.layer_prefetch_window_ms) and defaults conservatively to 8ms. See ENG-3241 and benchmark job links for raw data. Checklist: [x] perf microbench added, [x] unit tests for pad grouping and ordering, [x] e2e regression against existing KV cache testcases, [x] docs note and config defaults, [x] added canary flag for rollout. Follow-ups: automated quantile-based tuning for prefetch window (ENG-3308), expanded kernels to support dynamic head groups for mixed-precision models. Related PRs: ties into adaptive-kernel-routing work and the scheduler heuristics changes in previous releases.
Liam O'Connor: Nice approach — do we have any regressions on non-MQA models when head_pad_grouping is unset? Please add a guard so default is noop.
Maya Patel: Guard added; default path retains current behavior. Confirmed zero-regressions on Llama-2-13B baseline (unit+smoke).
Zoe Chen: The prefetch window looks promising but could overshoot GPU memory for small-instance Dedicated customers. Can we expose a per-pool override and document the safety knob?
Maya Patel: Added runtime.scheduling.layer_prefetch_window_ms per-pool override and documented in perf_tuning.md. Also added canary flag for staged rollout to Dedicated pools.

Runtime: Add optional head-wise padding and layer-split prefetch to reduce latency and memory spikes for MQA/GQA workloads. Conservative defaults; opt-in per-model and per-pool overrides available.

Motivation: High fragmentation and frequent spill events were observed on mixed OLTP/OLAP workloads where short-lived hot keys caused repeated eviction/promotion churn. Existing slab/segment allocators treat recency and frequency separately and are overly eager to evict recently touched but still-warm pages, causing unnecessary I/O and CPU during compaction/spill cycles. This change introduces a lightweight "warmth-map" overlay for the KV cache and an adaptive compact-probability mechanism driven by eviction feedback signals. The goal is to reduce spill frequency, lower fragmentation growth, and preserve low p99 latency for hot tails while keeping memory residency predictable.

Design summary: The warmth-map is a byte-per-segment probabilistic sketch that tracks short-term access warmth (a bounded decay counter per segment). The allocator uses the warmth score in three places: (1) compact probability, where cold segments are compacted more aggressively while warm ones are given deferral credit; (2) spill deferral window, which delays non-critical spills for segments that cross a warmth threshold; (3) eviction prioritization, where the effector integrates warmth with existing LRU/age heuristics to produce a combined score. An eviction feedback loop records when deferrals cause capacity pressure (spillback events); this telemetry reduces the deferral aggressiveness if we observe rising spill latencies or sustained OOMs. The feedback loop is rate-limited and uses exponential backoff to avoid oscillation.

Implementation notes: Changes touch: pkg/kv/allocator/warmth_map.go (new), pkg/kv/allocator/compact_prob.go (adaptive logic), pkg/kv/evictor/feedback_loop.go (feedback controller), pkg/kv/evictor/score_combiner.go (integrates warmth), internal/telemetry/metrics.go (new metrics: kv.warmth_score_histogram, kv.spill_deferred_count, kv.deferral_adjustments), cmd/benchmark-lab/kv_memory_workload.yaml (new perf scenario), and several unit/integration tests under test/kv. Warmth-map uses 8-bit decaying counters packed into a segment-aligned bitmap to bound memory overhead to ~0.5% of cache. The compact-probability function is deterministic given a segment's occupancy and warmth score and is exposed as a runtime-config knob (default conservative).

Commits (summary):
- Add warmth-map overlay and basic decay tick
- Integrate warmth into eviction scoring and compact probability
- Implement spill deferral window and interaction with spill scheduler
- Add feedback-loop controller with rate-limited adjustments
- Add telemetry + dashboards, tests, and benchmark config

Testing and results: Unit tests cover decay behavior, score combination, and adaptive backoff. Integration tests run kv-memory-suite with synthetic hot-spot, zipf, and mixed workloads. Benchmark-lab runs show: fragmentation index (measured by free-run histogram) decreased by ~22% at steady-state compared to baseline; spill events per minute reduced by ~35% on mixed workload; median eviction latency unchanged, p95 eviction latency improved from 9.4ms to 6.8ms in our staging cluster. Memory overhead measured at ~0.42% for 512GB cache. No regression in throughput for throughput-bound benchmarks.

Rollout plan: Feature behind runtime flag "kv.warmth_map.enabled" (defaults on for new tenants) and "kv.warmth_map.deferral_mode" with values conservative/normal/aggressive. We will enable conservative mode for Dedicated beta on Monday, monitor kv.spill_deferred_count and kv.deferral_adjustments, then scale to normal if no pressure. Revert path included via config toggles; scalar knobs also provided for compact probability floor/ceil.

Compatibility and migration: No on-disk format changes. Metrics and telemetry names are additive. For Private deployments, installer notes added to docs describing knob tuning and memory overhead.

Security: No new network surface. Warmth-map is local to allocator and uses existing memory safety patterns.

Notes for reviewers: Focus areas: correctness of decay semantics under concurrent access, performance of warmth-map reads in the hot path (lock-free read path implemented), and stability of feedback adjustments under synthetic thrash. Performance tests ran on GPU-backed serving nodes where applicable but the allocator is CPU-only.

Nadia Chen: Can you describe contention behavior when many goroutines touch the same segment? Arjun: warm-map reads are lock-free using atomic byte loads; increments are CAS-based with exponential backoff amortized per-segment.
Priya Singh: Telemetry names look fine but suggest kv.warmth_score_p50 in addition to histogram. Arjun: added p50 gauge in metrics.go and updated dashboards.
Tomás Alvarez: How does this interact with tenant throttles under Dedicated? Arjun: deferral reductions respect tenant quotas; added test to ensure tenant quota enforcement takes priority over deferral.
Nadia Chen (follow-up): We saw flaky TestEvictorFeedback in first CI run. Arjun: fixed race in feedback_loop.go by serializing adjustment state changes; re-ran CI.
unit: allocator and evictor (passed); integration: kv-memory-suite (passed); perf: benchmark-lab/kv_memory_workload (passed); manual staging ramp (observed improvements)
Introduce a low-overhead warmth-map overlay for KV cache to reduce fragmentation and spill frequency. Adds adaptive compact-probability and an eviction feedback loop with telemetry. Config knobs: kv.warmth_map.*. Improves steady-state fragmentation (~22% improvement) and reduces spill events (~35%) for mixed workloads.

Motivation: Customer audits and internal threat modeling highlighted two gaps: long-lived tenant keys increasing blast radius for operator compromise, and noisy audit streams that make user-level action correlation and deduplication expensive. This PR introduces two coordinated capabilities: 1) ephemeral tenant-scoped CMK wrapping (tenant-scoped ephemeral DEKs provisioned and rotated per-lease) and 2) an audit entropy aggregator that canonicalizes audit metadata and computes a compact entropy fingerprint to help downstream dedupe, sampling, and privacy-preserving indexing. Goals: minimize long-tail key exposure, provide a migration path for existing tenants, and reduce downstream audit volume while preserving provable non-repudiation. High level changes: - KMS subsystem: add tenant-scoped ephemeral key manager with lease TTLs, renewal logic, and fallbacks to tenant CMKs when configured. - Authz: RBACv2 hook extended to attach tenant lease claims to operator tokens; new policy predicate to require ephemeral lease for high-risk operations. - Audit pipeline: new aggregator service that computes an entropy fingerprint (sha256-based canonicalizer + salt per-tenant), supports rewrite rules for PII markers, and emits compact audit records to the main audit store. - Runtime: integration with request router to attach key provenance headers and to annotate traces. Backwards compatibility: feature gated by operator flags (feature.ephemeral-tenant-keys, feature/audit-entropy-agg) and default-off. Migration: opt-in per-tenant through Console or API; a rolling migration tool included (migration/ephemeral-key-adopter) that swaps token-binding for routes. Security considerations: TTL defaults to 12h for tenant DEKs, operator scopes cannot request leases longer than tenant policy allows. Checklist: - [x] KMS manager implementation + unit tests - [x] RBAC predicate + policy changes + unit tests - [x] Audit aggregator + integration tests - [x] Console API + docs updated - [x] E2E run in staging and perf baseline measured - [x] Feature flags and rollout playbook added Rollout plan: Stage behind feature flags; enable for internal tenants first, run audit-aggregator in parallel with current pipeline for 2 weeks, validate entropy collision rate and perf impact, then opt individual customers in. Risks and mitigations: potential increase in KMS calls -> added local caching and prefetch; audit aggregator may increase CPU load -> autoscale policy added. See linked linear tasks for acceptance criteria and perf SLOs.
Diego Alvarez: Flagged potential high QPS to KMS during rush traffic; asked for caching numbers and benchmarks. Response: added prefetch + batched Encrypt operations, included load test section in perf results.
Rina Sato: Asked for clarification on audit fingerprint salt rotation and storage. Response: salt is per-tenant, rotated on a 90-day schedule, and stored encrypted with tenant CMK; rotation triggers re-hash of incoming events only (no retroactive rewrite).
Samir Patel: Requested that lease TTL be configurable per-tenant and bounded by policy. Response: implemented tenant.metadata.max_lease_ttl and validation in lease_store, plus Console UI to surface limits.
Rina Sato: Security review requested adding a KMS usage quota metric and alert. Response: added ephemeral_kms_calls_total and an alert in deploy/charts/alerts.yaml; CI checks updated to include the alert rule linting.
Security: Add support for ephemeral tenant-scoped wrapping keys (opt-in) to reduce long-lived key exposure. Observability: New audit entropy aggregator to reduce noisy duplicate audit entries and enable privacy-preserving indexing. Rollout: feature flags default-off; opt-in per tenant via Console or API. See docs/security/ephemeral-keys.md and docs/security/audit-entropy-agg.md for migration instructions.
This PR intentionally keeps tenant lease default conservative (12h) to limit blast radius; security team to review TTLs after initial rollout. The audit fingerprint size is configurable; default uses 8 bytes (base64) to balance collision risk and storage.

Adds a new CLI tool (econ-lane-harmonizer) to generate tenant-aware batch/caching lane presets and a compact quantization threshold profile. Backwards-compatible defaults; non-breaking. Includes telemetry for lane selection and unit-econ deltas.
Summary: This PR adds a lightweight CLI (tools/econ-lane-harmonizer) plus runtime config glue to produce balanced 'lanes' for batching/caching defaults and a conservative compact quantization threshold profile that reduces unit cost while preserving edge-case quality.

Motivation: customers need deterministic, automated lane suggestions that respect both latency SLOs and tenant unit economics. Existing autotuners focus on throughput; this CLI provides a deterministic prescriptor for initial defaults and a safe quant threshold fallback path.

What is included: 1) tools/econ-lane-harmonizer: a Go-based CLI that consumes sampled workload histograms (token lengths, arrival rates, cold-start frequency) and outputs a manifest of lane presets (batch_size, max_latency_ms, cache_ttl_ms, quant_profile). The CLI supports dry-run and export-as-code (YAML) modes. 2) runtime integration: a small runtime adapter that can consume the YAML presets and translate them into the ServingRuntime's lane definitions (redwood/runtime/lanes_adapter.go). 3) quant profiles: introduces "compact-q" threshold set under models/quant-profiles/compact.json with conservative per-layer fallthrough rules and a runtime-safe degrade path that prefers latency-preserving quantization for short sequences. 4) telemetry: new events (telemetry/econ_lane_choice) and unit-econ delta metrics (unit_econ.delta.percent) to evaluate suggested lanes in canary. 5) tests and docs: unit tests for the CLI, e2e smoke tests that run generated lanes in the local benchmark lab, and a new docs page (docs/cli/econ-lane-harmonizer.md) with examples.

Commits (high-level): - a1b3f2e: initial CLI scaffold and histogram parser - 9c2d0b4: lane scoring algorithm (cost-latency tradeoff) - 4f7e8ab: YAML export + runtime adapter + tests - b3c2f11: compact quant profile + quant rollback hooks - e571ad9: telemetry events and dashboards + docs

Changes (high-level file list): - tools/econ-lane-harmonizer/main.go (new) - tools/econ-lane-harmonizer/README.md (new) - redwood/runtime/lanes_adapter.go (modified) - models/quant-profiles/compact.json (new) - telemetry/events/econ_lane_choice.yaml (new) - docs/cli/econ-lane-harmonizer.md (new) - integration-tests/cli/econ_lane_smoke_test.sh (new) - pkg/config/schema.yaml (minor addition: lane_presets export) - ci/workflows/econ-lane-ci.yml (new lightweight CI for CLI)

Testing & CI: CI run targeted CLI unit tests (go test ./tools/...), staticcheck, and a lightweight integration that runs the smoke script under a local fakeruntime. Initial CI run had a lint failure (go vet) which was fixed in commit 4f7e8ab. Final CI status: all checks passed (unit, lint, integration).

Review conversation (high-level): - Arjun: "Can the lane scoring be tuned per-tenant via feature flag?" Reply: "Yes — the CLI emits a 'tuneHint' field and the runtime adapter reads tenant overrides; documented in CLI README. We added a RFC-style flag --tenant-overrides to the CLI." - Sofia: "Telemetry looks noisy, can we aggregate at 1m buckets?" Reply: "Aggregated server-side by default, added config.telemetry.bucket_seconds=60 and updated event schema." - Liam: "Quant rollback path: please ensure there's an automatic safety net on quality regression." Reply: "Added a quality-check hook that compares canary responses against reference prompts; if regression > 2% we auto-disable compact-q for that tenant."

Approvals & merge: After addressal of comments, reviewers approved (Arjun, Sofia, Liam). Merge method: squash and merge.

Post-merge actions: - Run canary on limited tenants for 48 hours (QA ticket created) - Dashboard: added econ-lane-view to Console (telemetry dashboard) - Docs: publish CLI doc page to docs site.

Migration notes: No forced migration. Customers using existing defaults are unaffected; operators can run the CLI to generate lane presets and import them via the Console or CLI.

Security & privacy: No secret material in repo. Telemetry events contain only aggregated numeric counters and hashed tenant IDs; added consent note in telemetry schema.

Performance impact: Benchmarks on benchmark-lab showed median latency change <1% and unit cost reduction ~6% for medium token workloads with compact-q applied on warm lanes.

Rollout plan: Canary (10 tenants) -> Canary expansion (100 tenants) -> Global.

Related work items: ENG-2187 (lane prescriptor), ENG-2190 (quant fallback safety harness), SUP-4321 (support request: tenant cost nudges).

Notes for releases: algorithm is heuristic-based; we should track unit_econ.delta.percent in the 2-week sprint.

Contact: Maya Chen (author) for followups.

Motivation: tenants with bursty traffic and conservative defaults often burn budget during cold windows because prefill and quantization defaults are not tailored. This PR introduces the 'penny-jar' tenant saver: an orchestrator that generates safe slab-prefill defaults, a soft-quant fallback path, and a simple CLI for operators to preview and apply tenant-scoped suggestions. Implementation summary: added pkg/econ/pennyjar orchestrator implementing heatmap-driven slab sizing, sample-weighted prefill thresholds, unit-econ estimation (uCost per 1k tokens) and quality delta tracking hooks; introduced a soft-quant fallback in the serving runtime that can switch to a compatible lower-precision quant profile at variant boundaries with a configurable decay window; added cmd/pennyjarctl for dry-run previews, tenant-scoped apply, and a --simulate flag that runs a local cost/latency/quality projection; exposed telemetry: pennies.uCost, pennies.quality_delta, pennies.applied_tenants; added unit/integration tests and an e2e smoke test showing a 12-18% median token cost reduction on synthetic shopper workload. Safety & rollout: all suggestions are opt-in by default and behind a feature flag. The orchestrator emits a suggested config rather than auto-applying; when applied the system runs a shadow canary (5% traffic) and evaluates quality signals over the configured sample set; automatic rollback triggers if quality_delta > 0.5 (system-default) or if latency SLO degradation > 10%. Backwards compatibility: changes are additive and gated; default serving paths unchanged until explicit apply. Checklist: [x] unit tests, [x] integration smoke, [x] CLI help and man page, [x] docs/ops guide, [x] telemetry dashboard panels, [x] e2e smoke pass. Risks: quantized fallbacks can introduce subtle quality drift; mitigations include sample-based validation, canary windows, conservative default thresholds, and an immediate failover path to the pinned model variant. Motivation: Reproducing flaky regressions found during canary/A-B promotes is expensive. Teams need a deterministic way to capture and replay the exact cohort traffic used in a canary so debugging and postmortems are reliable. This PR introduces a small-footprint rehearsal traffic fabric and an "epochal rewind" snapshotter that together enable reproducible canaries, deterministic rollbacks, and on-demand replay for root cause analysis.

What this does (high level):
- Rehearsal traffic fabric: an in-process router that can shadow or rehearse traffic into isolated rehearsal lanes without impacting production routing. Supports fractional mirroring, session-affinity preservation, and lane-level quotas.
- Epochal snapshotter: captures a compact, deterministic snapshot for a cohort (user/session markers + normalized request events + metadata) at commit points. Snapshots are immutable epochs that can be pinned to a rollout.
- Rewind & replay harness: lightweight replay path that consumes an epoch, replays requests to a target model variant in a sandboxed lane, and emits parity diffs and telemetry. Designed to be low-cost and deterministic (time-normalization and KV-barriers).
- Telemetry and tie-ins: cohort markers, replay traces, and smoke assertions wired into Console and the rollouts API so a user can pin an epoch to a canary and run a replay from the web UI or CLI.

Design notes and constraints:
- Determinism: we avoid capturing external side-effects; the snapshotter records a normalized event stream and requires optional flush hooks for services with mutating side-effects. See docs/rehearsal-playbook.md for integration points.
- Storage: epochs are stored as append-only blobs with compact metadata index to support quick lookups and retention policies. Backing store is pluggable; this change adds a local S3-backed implementation.
- Safety: rehearsal lanes are opt-in behind "rehearsal.enabled" and require RBAC to execute replays in private deployments. Replays run in a sandbox and cannot mutate production caches by default.

Checklist: 
- [x] Fabric router and rehearsal lanes implemented
- [x] Epochal snapshot schema + store implementation
- [x] Replay harness with deterministic time-normalization
- [x] Telemetry markers and Console hooks
- [x] Feature flag + RBAC gating
- [x] Unit and integration tests (local)
- [x] Docs and playbook added

Commits summary: a1f3d9c adds the snapshotter and storage schema; b4c7e2f implements router and API routes; d2e9b11 wires telemetry markers; f6a2c38 adds the deterministic replay harness and tests; e8b7f55 author docs and playbook.

Files changed (high level): rollouts/rehearsal/fabric.go handles lane lifecycle and traffic mirroring; rollouts/snapshot/epochal_store.go defines snapshot format, flush hooks and S3 store; telemetry/cohort_markers.go adds markers tied to request lifecycle; simulators/replay/harness.py is the python harness for reproducible replays used in CI and by the debugging CLI; api/routes/rehearsal_routes.go exposes endpoints for creating epochs, listing, and triggering replays; docs/rehearsal-playbook.md describes integration patterns and known caveats.

Review convo highlights:
- Determinism concerns: added a KV-cache barrier and optional flush hook to ensure consistent snapshots.
- Time drift in replay: time-normalization added to harness and a long-session test to detect drift.
- Security gating: feature flag + RBAC checks added so private deployments keep control.

CI: Initial run had two flaky tests in the replay harness (time normalization mismatch) which failed on linux-ktest; I pushed a patch to normalize epoch timestamps and re-ran. Final CI: all checks passed (unit, integration, lint, e2e smoke profile).

How to use: See docs/rehearsal-playbook.md for the step-by-step guide. Quick flow: 1) create a rehearsal lane and enable rehearsal.enabled; 2) pin an epoch to a canary promote; 3) trigger a replay to the candidate variant in sandbox; 4) review parity diffs and telemetry in Console; 5) optionally promote epoch or rollback using the replay evidence.

Backward compatibility and rollout: This is fully backward compatible; rehearsal routes are opt-in. Storage schema includes a migration path for existing snapshot artifacts (migration is additive). Retention defaults are conservative (30d) and configurable per workspace.

Operational notes: Replays can be expensive for long epochs — the playbook recommends limiting epoch size and using sampling for long-running sessions. The retention policy and compact metadata index keep list operations fast.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged into main after approvals from Priya, Carlos and Samir. Merge commit: 7c3b1e4.

Related: ENG-7842 implements higher-level rollout integration planned for Q1; PM-1921 tracks UX work for pinning epochs in Console.
Adds a rehearsal traffic fabric and epochal rewind tooling to capture deterministic cohort snapshots for reproducible canaries; includes observability hooks and a lightweight replay harness for on-demand root-cause analysis.
Priya Shah: Can we guarantee deterministic ordering when snapshotting in presence of async side-effects? Suggested adding a lightweight flush hook before epoch commit.
Evelyn Tran: Added flush hook and explicit kv-cache barrier in epochal_store.go; documented caveats in playbook.
Carlos Mendes: Test for drift when replaying over long session lifetimes? Observed minor timestamp drift in one unit test.
Evelyn Tran: Tightened time-normalization in the harness and added a simulated long-session test (replay_edgecase_test).
Samir Patel: Please make sure rehearsal routes are guarded behind a feature flag and opt-in. Also add RBAC check for private deployments.
Evelyn Tran: Feature flag (rehearsal.enabled) gated routes and RBAC enforced; added e2e smoke that runs only when flag is on in CI profile.
payload.title: Rehearsal traffic fabric with epochal rewind for reproducible canaries
