Motivation: Teams keep hitting subtle auth edge-cases when swapping credential providers across SDKs (Python/TypeScript/Go). This patch introduces a credential-sanity linter, cross-SDK interop smoke tests, and a small set of streaming API ergonomics fixes and version bumps. The goal is to reduce incidents caused by mis-typed credential payloads and to make streaming helpers more uniform across languages. Summary of changes below with checklists and upgrade guidance.

What this PR does: Adds a new repo-level tool (tools/cred-lint) that validates credential payloads and common misconfigurations used in our SDK tests; standardizes streaming helper names and optional parameters across sdks/; adds interop smoke tests that call the same scripted scenarios from each SDK variant; bumps SDK packaged versions to pick up ergonomics helpers; fixes a handful of flaky reauth races visible in CI.

Checklist: [x] Add cred-lint CLI + JSON schema (tools/cred-lint) [x] Wire cred-lint into CI smoke-test job [x] Add interop smoke tests (tests/interop/) which run Py/TS/Go snippets against local test harness [x] Rename streaming helpers for parity (py: StreamReader->StreamHandle, ts: streamReader->streamHandle, go: StreamReader->StreamHandle) [x] Small API ergonomics: optional ctx param made last arg in all three SDKs [x] Patch flaky reauth path and telemetry hooks [x] Bump SDK package metadata (python v1.15.0, typescript v1.27.0, go v1.8.1) [x] Update docs snippets and quickstarts

Migration notes: Downstream users who relied on positional arg order for stream helpers will need to update call sites where an explicit context/opts object is supplied. The change is backwards-compatible for keyword/explicit arg usage; the linter will surface common cases and the SDK release notes include quick diffs.

Files of interest: tools/cred-lint/schema.json, tools/cred-lint/cli.py, sdks/python/redwood/stream.py, sdks/python/setup.cfg, sdks/typescript/src/stream.ts, sdks/typescript/package.json, sdks/go/stream.go, sdks/go/go.mod, tests/interop/python_scenario.py, tests/interop/ts_scenario.ts, tests/interop/go_scenario.go, ci/smoke-interoperability.yaml, docs/sdk-migration/stream-rename.md.

Related: ENG-1129 (reduce auth incidents), ENG-1144 (sdk ergonomics parity), SUP-872 (customer-reported streaming auth race).
Ava Chen (2026-02-22): Nice approach; can we make the linter non-blocking on CI initially so we don't break release branches?
Samir Patel (2026-02-22): Good call — added an allowlist and linter runs as warning on release/* and main remains green for feature branches.
Diego Morales (2026-02-24): The streaming rename in Python looks safe, but the public docs need an explicit migration snippet showing positional->keyword examples. Added a TODO.
Priya Nair (2026-02-26): I found a race when running the interop harness under heavy load — token refresh backoff was zero for a short window. I suggested a guarded atomic swap.
Samir Patel (2026-02-27): Addressed guarded swap; added unit that reproduces the race and fixed flaky test. CI rerun required.
Ava Chen (2026-03-02): CI passed on rerun, leaving LGTM — please squash and add an explicit entry in sdks/*/CHANGELOG.md about the ergonomics change.
Diego Morales (2026-03-03): Approved; small nit in Go docstring which I fixed in a follow-up commit.
Added credential-sanity linter (warns on malformed credential payloads); unified streaming helper names across SDKs (StreamHandle); small ergonomics change: optional ctx/opts parameter moved to last position. Bumped SDK versions: python->1.15.0, typescript->1.27.0, go->1.8.1. Added interop smoke tests to CI. Backwards-compatible except for positional-arg callsites (see migration guide).
Python before: StreamReader(client, opts, ctx)
Python after: StreamHandle(client, opts, ctx=None)  # ctx is now optional/last
TypeScript before: streamReader(client, opts, ctx)
TypeScript after: streamHandle(client, opts, ctx?)
Go before: NewStreamReader(client, opts, ctx)
Go after: NewStreamHandle(client, opts, ctx)
Backport to release/1.14.x only the reauth race fix and telemetry hooks (do not backport cred-lint as it changes CI).

payload.body:
Motivation: Engineering teams need faster root cause for token-level cost spikes that originate from cross-stage interactions (eg. prefetch warmups combined with streaming backpressure). Current observability surfaces show per-token cost and per-span latency but lack a joined view that surfaces correlated phase anomalies and a compact, time-aligned cost ribbon for an invocation.

What this PR does: Implements a lightweight crosswave span mesh that stitches spans from multiple pipeline stages into a single invocation graph, emits a new instrumented metric stream called invocation.cost_ribbon (time-series of compact per-segment cost deltas), and adds a dashboard and alert tuning knobs to detect cross-stage scarcity patterns. The change includes: 1) a server-side span enricher that attaches stage fingerprints and kernel-queue tags; 2) an on-path aggregator that produces an invocation-level cost ribbon (compact array encoded as proto text) and a set of per-segment cost histograms; 3) a Grafana dashboard with coordinated heatmaps (span mesh) + cost ribbon sparkline; 4) an alert rule that uses cohort-aware thresholds to reduce false positives during planned warmup windows.

Design notes: The span mesh preserves original span ids and emits a synthetic mesh_id for joinable spans; enrichment is best-effort and falls back to span-only mode when context is missing. Cost ribbon is intentionally compact: we store up to 12 equal-time buckets per invocation with normalized cost weights and a ring-index; this supports efficient indexing and low cardinality queries. Alerts run as a two-stage check: a short-window anomaly detector (30s) followed by a cohort stability verifier (10m) to avoid noisy triggers from transient bursts.

Rollout plan: feature flag "obs.crosswave_mesh" added with default off for prod. Start with 10% of invocations in canary, monitor ingestion and query costs for the new metric (linked Linear ENG-3421). If ingestion cost delta < 2% and query latency stable, increase to 50% and then enable alerts for SRE. Full rollout only after a 72h canary with no alert storms.

Checklist:
- [x] span enricher and mesh_id generation
- [x] invocation.cost_ribbon emitter with protobuf compatibility shim
- [x] per-segment histogram exporter (+ retention knob)
- [x] Grafana dashboard JSON + example links
- [x] cohort-aware alert rule + playbook notes
- [x] unit tests for encoder/decoder and sampler
- [x] e2e smoke that validates ribbon matches aggregated token-cost sample

Backward compatibility: All new fields are optional; services that don't understand cost_ribbon will ignore it. The encoder includes a version header for future changes.

Risks & mitigations: Higher cardinality if stage fingerprints are overly specific — mitigated by bucketing fingerprints to canonical kernel groups and a sampling cap. Dashboard panels are read-only and behind the feature flag to avoid confusing users.

Related work: Builds on token-cost-attribution groundwork (see ENG-2987) and complements existing prefix/KV cache telemetry. Helps RCA for incidents where model warmup + kernel contention cause sustained cost drift.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the mesh join semantics (span identity preservation), the compact ribbon encoding (we opted for a base64-compact proto text rather than JSON arrays), and the cohort threshold tuning logic (two-stage verifier). The dashboard JSON contains annotated example traces for offline replay.

Miguel Alvarez: Could the mesh_id collide across shards? Suggest prefixing with shard id or node id.
Aisha Kapoor (reply): We prefix mesh_id with the 16-bit node prefix where available; added test for cross-shard uniqueness.

Summary: Adds a budget-aware batching controller that enforces tenant-configured cost caps at request-routing time, a telemetry mapper that emits unit-econ events consumable by Optimize and Console, and a conservative quantization failsafe with canary gating. Motivation: Customers want automated defenses that reduce spend without silent regressions in quality. This PR combines three tightly-coupled pieces: 1) a runtime controller that clips dynamic batch sizes to tenant budget profiles and provides a soft fallback when budget pressure is detected, 2) a telemetry mapping layer that translates internal per-token cost/latency stats into unit-econ records and exposes a dry-run CLI for impact analysis, and 3) a quantization failsafe that only applies lower-precision variants when a canary sample shows no measurable quality drop.

What changed (high level): - runtime/batcher: new budgeted controller that annotates requests with budget_token and batch_priority; enforces per-tenant budget caps and reports decision reasons; implements a soft-reject flow that uses smaller batch shapes instead of hard failures. - telemetry/mappers: added budget_mapper (python) which converts internal metrics into unit-econ events (fields: tenant_id, token_cost, batch_shape, fallback_reason, timestamp) and forwards to the telemetry pipeline. - models/quant: added a lightweight quant-failsafe orchestrator that performs canary sampling and automatic rollback logic if quality thresholds are violated. - cli: new command redwood cost simulate-batch that runs a dry-run on historical traces and outputs projected cost delta and latency impact. - docs: operations runbook + rollout plan and troubleshooting guides. - tests: integration + load tests, plus a small offline evaluator for canary quality checks.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-1892) linked and reviewed - [x] Unit + integration tests added - [x] Load tests showing cost delta and SLO impact - [x] CLI dry-run implemented - [x] Rollout plan included

Behavior and rollout: Defaults: feature is disabled for all tenants. Behavioral controls: tenant flag budgeted_batching.enabled, budgeted_batching.daily_cap_usd, budgeted_batching.max_batch_pct (soft cap on batch size relative to baseline). Rollout: enable for internal / sandbox tenants -> 5% of production traffic -> 25% -> gradual to 100% after 2 weeks of monitoring. Canary quantization: quant-failsafe launches lower-precision variant only after canary sample (default 0.5% of requests) passes quality checks (WER/ROUGE heuristics depending on model). Automatic rollback on quality degradation or error rate increase.

Safety and failure modes: - If telemetry pipeline lag is detected, budgeted controller falls back to safe defaults (no budget clipping). - Soft-fallback ensures no hard 5xx path due to budget enforcement. - Quant failsafe includes a conservative conservative-tolerance (default 0.02 delta in quality metric) and a cooldown window before reattempt.

Testing and benchmarks: - Synthetic workload (mixed-seq) showed median cost reduction of 9% and 95th-percentile p99 latency increase of +18ms when budget caps engaged at 70% of baseline spend. - Canary runs with 10k requests showed no statistically significant quality drop when using the quant-failsafe on small LLM variants. - CI: unit + integration + an orchestrated smoke load (runs nightly) were green; a flaky integration test was re-run once and passed.

Commands: - redwood cost simulate-batch --tenant T-abc123 --trace traces/2026-01-28.json --dry-run - redwood tenant config set T-abc123 budgeted_batching.enabled true --canary-percent 5

Related: ENG-1892 (design), ENG-1976 (telemetry schemas), SUP-322 (customer ask for budget guardrails). Links: design doc https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1892/budgeted-batcher-design (internal), telemetry schema PR #1976 (internal).

Maya Patel: Split into evaluateBudget(), chooseBatchShape(), and emitDecisionLog() per Jonah's suggestion; added unit tests for each.
Priya Singh: Can we add a flag to force-enable quant canary in CI for a deterministic smoke run?
Maya Patel: Added --ci-canary flag to test harness and a short deterministic trace to exercise the quant path.
Anya Volkov: Approve after CI green — verify that the telemetry schema change is backward compatible with existing consumers.
Maya Patel: Confirmed backward compatibility: new fields are optional; updated telemetry docs and added a feature flag to gate schema rollout.
Adds an opt-in budgeted batching feature that enforces tenant-defined cost caps and produces unit-econ telemetry; includes a CLI dry-run for impact analysis and a conservative quantization failsafe with canary gating. Default disabled; see ops runbook for rollout steps.
Enable feature behind tenant flag; recommended canary progression: internal -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%. Monitor unit-econ events in Console and watch for quality signals from the quant canary. If telemetry lag > 30s, fallback to safe no-clip behavior.

Motivation: reduce CI image size and presubmit latency while improving dependency refresh hygiene. This PR introduces a slim build image for the majority of Lint/Test lanes, a small cache-warming helper that prefetches common dependency layers, and an automated weekly dep-refresh job that updates pinned devdeps and raises PRs for non-breaking upgrades. Key goals: 1) shorten cold CI worker startup and container pull times; 2) reduce transient network-induced flakiness by warming the remote cache for the most common toolchains; 3) keep dev dependency drift under control with an opt-in auto-PR flow. Changes are designed to be additive and guarded under a feature flag (CI_SLIM_BUILD=true) so rollout can be staged. See the checklist below and the related Linear cards.

Checklist: - [x] add slim Dockerfile and publish manifest to the internal registry - [x] implement cache-warm helper script with idempotent semantics - [x] wire slim image into GH Actions build matrix behind CI_SLIM_BUILD flag - [x] add weekly dep-refresh workflow and depbot fallback - [x] update docs: CONTRIBUTING.md and CI-runbook - [x] smoke test on staging runner and monitor DB of flakes for 72h

Context and links: Linear ENG-1728 (CI performance audit), ENG-1734 (dep hygiene initiative). Related infra doc: https://internal.redwood.ai/docs/ci-cache-strategy. This PR intentionally avoids changing production runtime images or release artifacts; it focuses on developer/CI ergonomics.
Aaron Patel: Nice direction. A couple questions: is the slim image missing any platform-specific deps needed for Linux-musl runners? Please add a short matrix in build.yml to validate musl vs glibc images.
Maya Chen: The slim image is intentionally glibc-based for now. I added a small validation job in build.yml and a TODO to extend to musl once we confirm libc compatibility across our toolchains.
Lina Gomez: cache-warm looks good but please make the helper tolerant to 429s and add exponential backoff. Also make TTL configurable via env var.
Maya Chen: Updated cache-warm to respect CACHE_WARM_TTL and added exponential backoff (up to 6 retries). Tests added to tools/dep-refresh/README.md to document behavior.

Maya Chen: Agreed. The job now opens a draft PR and tags it with 'dep-refresh'. We added a rule in the repo settings for human approval; auto-merge is disabled by default.

Introduce cache-warm helper to prefetch popular dependency layers and reduce flakiness
Add weekly dep-refresh workflow that opens draft PRs for devdep upgrades

payload.body:
Problem: Cost Model v1 needs stable, runtime-sourced inputs for (a) per-stage token accounting (prefill vs decode) and (b) KV cache behavior to correctly model cache hits, cache reuse, and batch efficiency. Today we only emit total tokens + ad-hoc cache counters in a couple of codepaths, which diverges from what Console/Optimize/billing need and makes drift analysis noisy.

This PR adds runtime-side instrumentation and export for KV cache stats and per-stage token accounting. The exported payload is designed to be: (1) low-cardinality, (2) deterministic for a given request execution, and (3) compatible with streaming + speculative decode disabled/enabled paths.

What changed: - Introduced a request-scoped "TokenAccounting" struct that accumulates tokens_processed_prefill and tokens_processed_decode. - Added KV cache counters captured at the scheduler boundary (before execution) and at completion: kv_cache_prompt_tokens_hit, kv_cache_prompt_tokens_miss, kv_cache_prefix_bytes_hit, kv_cache_prefix_bytes_miss, and kv_cache_evictions. - Emitted a single unified telemetry event "runtime.inference_accounting.v1" with stage token counts + KV cache stats, keyed by request_id and model_execution_id (NOT by prompt hash or cache key).

Semantics (v1): - Prefill tokens = tokens processed in the prefill phase for the chosen execution graph (includes prompt tokens after any truncation). - Decode tokens = tokens processed in decode iterations (includes all generated tokens, including EOS token if produced). - KV cache prompt token hit/miss are measured relative to the runtime's prefix-cache lookup result for the request (token-level units), and are emitted even when cache is disabled (0/total).

Bounds/perf: - No per-layer metrics, no per-head, no per-cache-entry output. - Event payload is bounded; no arrays. - Counters are computed from existing internal bookkeeping; no additional GPU sync points are introduced.

Testing: - Added unit tests for token accounting across streaming and non-streaming paths. - Added an integration test fixture that runs a tiny model with cache enabled and verifies hit/miss invariants (hits+misses == prefill tokens after truncation). - Added a debug-only assertion (guarded) to catch negative counters during development.

Rollout: - Gate emission behind feature flag RUNTIME_EXPORT_ACCOUNTING_V1 (default off). - Once telemetry pipeline is ready, we will enable in staging for 5% and validate drift dashboards before prod.

Notes / follow-ups: - This PR intentionally does not rename existing legacy metrics; Telemetry will map these new fields and then we can deprecate the old ones (see ENG-4823). - Speculative decode: we currently attribute speculative draft tokens to decode tokens_processed_decode; we do not emit a separate speculative bucket in v1.

Checklist: - [x] Metrics names reviewed with Telemetry - [x] Payload bounded (no high-cardinality tags) - [x] Backward compatible (flagged) - [x] Added tests + fixture

Risk: Moderate. Touches request execution accounting and telemetry emission; guarded by feature flag and includes invariants in tests.
Sofia Ivanova (review): Can we confirm the counters are taken post-truncation? Cost model needs consistency with what actually ran. Also, is the scheduler boundary the right place for cache hit/miss measurement given fallback paths?
Omar El-Sayed (author): Yes—prefill tokens are counted after truncation (same value used for the actual execution). For cache hit/miss: we record lookup result after routing picks the final execution plan, before running the graph. If we fall back (e.g., cache disabled for the run), counters emit 0/total and we set kv_cache_enabled=false in the event.
Nadia Rahman (review): Please explicitly define whether decode includes EOS. Billing currently includes it in generated tokens; Console expects same. Also, please avoid emitting prompt_hash or cache_key to keep this low-risk for PII.
Omar El-Sayed (author): Updated semantics: decode includes EOS if produced. Confirmed no prompt hash/cache key in the event; only request_id + model_execution_id which are already in telemetry.
Caleb Johnson (review): Telemetry pipeline prefers stable field names and units. Can we align token units (int) and bytes (int) and avoid floats? Also, name suggestion: kv_cache_prefix_bytes_hit/miss instead of just bytes_hit/miss.
Omar El-Sayed (author): Done. All counters are u64 serialized as int. Renamed to kv_cache_prefix_bytes_hit/miss and updated event schema + tests.
Grace Kim (review): How does this behave with quantized kernels where we may fuse prefill? Is stage detection reliable or will prefill/decode be ambiguous?
Omar El-Sayed (author): Stage is derived from the high-level execution loop (prefill call vs decode step calls). Even if kernels fuse internal ops, we still know which invocation is prefill vs decode. Added a comment in engine.rs clarifying this assumption.
Thomas Baird (review): Please double-check payload size and cardinality. No per-batch arrays. Also ensure we don't emit per-token timing in this event—Console hot path can't handle high volume of large events.
Omar El-Sayed (author): Payload is fixed fields only (no arrays). No timing fields included here; queue time remains in existing scheduler event. Added a size assertion in the schema test to catch accidental growth.
Sofia Ivanova (approve): Looks good with the rename and clarifications. Please keep speculative decode as-is for v1; we can add a separate bucket later if needed.
Nadia Rahman (approve): Approved. Thanks for documenting EOS behavior and ensuring no cache-key leakage.
Caleb Johnson (approve): Approved once staging flag default is OFF. Confirmed in flags.yaml.
Internal only: runtime now can emit bounded KV cache hit/miss + prefill/decode token accounting event (runtime.inference_accounting.v1) behind feature flag RUNTIME_EXPORT_ACCOUNTING_V1 for Standard Cost Model inputs.
payload.title: runtime: export KV cache stats + prefill/decode token accounting for cost model

Motivation: Many tenants run with overly conservative batching and wide quantization profiles, increasing per-token cost and GPU memory usage. This PR introduces a new component (Batchline Curator) that computes tenant-aware batching/caching defaults and a small deploy-time tool (Quant Slimmer) that suggests a minimal, safe quant profile per model family based on recent traffic and eval traces. The goal is to reduce unit economics by default while providing telemetry-driven rollback and safety checks.

What this PR does (high level):
- Add batchline-curator service (lightweight scheduler) that emits tenant default suggestions and a ranked list of safe batch shapes. Suggestions are written to configs/presets/batchline-defaults.yaml and exposed via the admin API.
- Add quant-slimmer CLI (rwprefill quant-slimmer) that runs during model onboarding or rollout to propose narrower quantization parameters; integrates with the existing model-registry/quality checks.
- Wire telemetry: new metrics (batchline.suggester.* and quant.slimmer.recommendation.*) and traces to Redwood Console to allow rollback if quality regressions are observed.
- Safety: multi-stage rollout — suggestion -> shadow-simulate -> canary -> apply. Automatic rollback triggers on eval set drift or QA alert counts.
- Docs: quickstart and a troubleshooting guide in redwood-docs/docs/ops/batching-and-quant.md.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc: Linear ENG-9407 (link: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-9407/batchline-curator-design)
- [x] Unit tests for core suggestion logic
- [x] Integration tests: perf-canary scenario added
- [x] E2E smoke on staging
- [x] Docs updated

Compatibility notes: The Batchline Curator writes opinions as tenant defaults that can be overridden by tenant config. Quant Slimmer outputs candidate profiles; we do not apply any quant changes automatically without explicit rollout approval.

Rollout plan: staged on staging -> internal dedicated tenants -> opt-in beta customers -> default for newly created tenants after 2 weeks of monitoring.

Related work: ties into ENG-8310 (tenant-prefill heuristics) and PRs that added telemetry-driven rollbacks.

2) feat(quant): implement quant-slimmer CLI and lightweight analyzer (pri: d4f3e89)

Reviewer: Samir Gupta — Can the quant-slimmer produce a conservative fallback automatically when an explicit profile is missing?

Reviewer: Elena Rossi — Tests flaked on CI twice (integration perf-canary).

Motivation: Over the last week we observed repeated SLO violations during regional failovers induced by an aggressive fast-reopen path in the fallback controller. Symptoms were rapid circuit flips, KV-cache drain collisions, and short-lived failovers that caused client retries and increased tail latency. This PR introduces a timeboxed fallback orchestrator that applies a short, configurable holdoff anchor when a region-level fallback is initiated. The goal is to reduce reopen flapping, give downstream systems (KV caches, routing tables) time to stabilize, and preserve the tenant SLOs while avoiding long hard-fail states.

What changed (high level):
- New orchestrator: src/runtime/fallback_orchestrator.go implements a timebox window (default 10s) during which reopen attempts are rate-limited and a soft circuit anchor is applied. The anchor prevents immediate reopen and coordinates with the SLO enforcer.
- Holdoff policy: pkg/slo/holdoff_policy.go introduces a small policy engine that selects a holdoff based on recent circuit history, tenant weight, and cross-region RTTs.
- KV cache drain sync: runtime/kv/drain_coordinator.go adds a two-phase drain handshake so we don't evict live KV entries during short failovers.
- Config toggle + feature-flag: config/defaults.yaml and infra/feature_flags/featureflags.go expose a canary flag (fallback_timebox_v2) so we can rollout per-region.
- Telemetry: observability/fallback_metrics.go emits new metrics (fallback_timebox_applied, fallback_anchor_duration_ms) and traces for the orchestrator's decision path.
- Tests: unit and integration tests + a small load canary harness under test/canary/fallback_timebox_test.go.

Checklist: [x] Unit tests added for policy branching; [x] Integration test for KV drain handshake; [x] Canary run in us-west-2 for 12 hours with synthetic spike; [x] Docs update in docs/ops/fallbacks.md; [x] Rollback plan documented.

Rollout and rollback: The rollout is behind an opt-in per-region flag. Default remains off. We performed a 12-hour canary in us-west-2 (see CI/canary logs) and then toggled additional regions sequentially with the console. Rollback is immediate: flip feature flag off and the orchestrator falls back to previous behavior; a short background reconciler drains anchors within 30s to avoid stale holds.

Backward compatibility & safety: No API changes. All behavior controlled by internal feature flags and a default conservative timebox. No tenant-visible config changes unless enterprise customers enable the flag.

Related linear/Jira: ENG-8743 tracks the broader SLO stabilization work; SUP-4421 was raised by on-call for a customer-facing incident.

Notes: This is marked as a hotfix because multiple incidents were traced to reopen flapping. The implementation prefers safety (slightly longer tail for some requests) to unstable reopen cycles that caused cascading retries.
Alicia: Can we make the default window configurable via config and not a compile-time const? (resolved: made configurable in defaults.yaml)
Diego: The KV drain handshake looks racy when multiple regions trigger simultaneously — added a jitter and leader election attempt to the handshake (resolved)
Priya: Please add an integration test for tenant-weighted holdoff selection (added test and adjusted policy thresholds)
Marisol: Responded to Diego with a note about the leader-election fallback path and included instrumentation to detect failed handshakes for SRE visibility
Hotfix: introduce timeboxed fallback orchestrator to reduce circuit reopen flapping during regional failovers. Default off behind feature flag. Improves SLO stability at the cost of a short holdoff during failovers. See docs/ops/fallbacks.md for runbook.
payload.title: Timeboxed fallback orchestrator and regional holdoff (hotfix)

payload.body:
Motivation: We observed intermittent warmup regressions when CUDA graph replays encounter small shape perturbations or partial KV-cache misalignment. Existing shape-guard heuristics either over-guard (preventing capture reuse) or under-guard (causing incorrect kernel replays). This PR implements a two-part runtime improvement: 1) persistent capture snapshots: lightweight, verifiable snapshots of the capture metadata (tensor shapes, stride hints, kernel signatures, KV cache root hashes) that can be persisted across ephemeral capture lifetimes and consulted during replay; 2) kernel reconciliation/stitching: a probe-driven reconciliation layer that attempts to reuse captured kernels by applying fast, safe transformations (axis-coercion, stride normalization, and small-kernel stitching) before falling back to full re-capture. Key design points: snapshots are compact (<=512B per capture) and opaque to backends; they include a TTL and monotonic version to avoid using stale captures after kernel migration. Reconciliation runs a prioritized sequence: (a) exact-match check, (b) stride/shape coercion with validation probe (dry-run on a small tile), (c) kernel-stitch attempt for fragmented batches (concatenate compatible kernel fragments), (d) safe fallback to non-graph execution or dynamic re-capture. Safety: every attempted reuse executes a validation probe which compares outputs on a small micro-batch under configured tolerances; if mismatch > epsilon or probe times out, the snapshot is retired and the request triggers re-capture. KV cache alignment: snapshot includes kv-root fingerprints allowing replay to fast-path only when prefix KV alignment is within bounds; otherwise reconciliation can realign keys for a limited window. Implementation: runtime/cudagraph/snapshot_manager.{h,cpp} manages lifecycle and persistence, runtime/cudagraph/reconciler.{h,cpp} implements probe logic and kernel-stitch primitives, scheduler/priming_coordinator.cpp integrates with continuous-batching to perform progressive priming using snapshots so common shapes receive validated captures earlier. Tests & validation: unit tests for snapshot serialization, reconciliation heuristics, and probe timeouts; integration tests that simulate shape jitter across batches; a synthetic perf harness measured P95 token latency and cold-start warmup times. Benchmarks: end-to-end text generation scenario with mixed sequence lengths (8/64/256 distribution) shows median P95 token latency improvement of ~18% across sustained load and a 60% reduction in observed warmup-induced latency spikes compared to baseline. Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag cudagraph.snapshot_reuse; staged rollout: canary on dedicated pools -> 25% -> 100% with automatic rollback on regression thresholds (3x error rate or 20% latency regression). Risk & mitigations: snapshot corruption detection causes safe retire & re-capture; reconciliation is deliberately conservative by default and can be made aggressive via tuning flags. Related work: follows ENG-3145 investigation into warmup flaps and complements prior shape-guard improvements by providing optimistic reuse with validation. Checklist: - [x] snapshot persistence and TTLs implemented - [x] reconciliation probe + kernel-stitch primitives - [x] KV fingerprinting and alignment checks - [x] unit/integration/perf tests - [x] feature-flag + rollout gating - [x] docs: runtime flags and observability metrics (cudagraph.snapshot.*)
Ethan Brooks: Nice approach to persist only metadata—did you consider including a versioned kernel ABI fingerprint to detect driver-level kernel mismatches?
Maya Patel: Good call. I added a kernel_abi_hash to the snapshot and a monotonic version field so we can invalidate snapshots on driver or kernel ABI upgrade.
Zara Novak: Probe wall-time could add latency on the hot path—can we amortize probes across the batch or run them on a small async tile?
Maya Patel: Probes run on a 16-token micro-batch inline but with a tight timeout; priming coordinator can run async priming for cold captures. Added config for probe_tile_size and probe_timeout.
Diego Ramos (requested changes): please add integration tests that simulate KV misalignment across interleaved requests and assert snapshot retirement logic.
Maya Patel: Added tests/integration/cudagraph_kv_misalignment.test and extended the shape_jitter test to include KV permutations. Ready for final review.
Ethan Brooks: Approving — results look good on canary, no regressions observed in nightly perf runs.
Introduce persistent CUDA-graph capture snapshots to enable safe replay across small shape perturbations.
Add probe-driven kernel reconciliation and stitching to increase capture reuse without sacrificing correctness.
KV-cache fingerprinting enables safe fast-path reuse when prefix alignment is preserved.
Feature-gated and rolled out gradually with observability exposed under cudagraph.snapshot.* metrics.
Observability: added metrics cudagraph.snapshot.used, cudagraph.snapshot.retired, cudagraph.reconcile.probe_latency and a debug log level for reconciliation decisions. Ops: can disable snapshot reuse per pool via pool config. Performance: measured safe reductions in warmup flaps during mixed-sequence traffic.
payload.title: add-capture-snapshotting-and-kernel-reconciliation-to-stabilize-replay-across-shape-perturbations

payload.body:
Motivation: Continuous batcher starvation and long-tail latency regressions have been observed in mixed KV-heavy workloads where small, low-cost requests repeatedly preempt larger requests, and where stalled requests with large KV pins can hold slots for long periods. Existing priority-decay heuristics reduced some cases but left pathological arrival patterns (bursts of tiny queries or very old requests) that caused tail SLO violations. This PR introduces a chronological debt-based throttling layer in the continuous batching path to (1) prevent starvation of older requests, (2) bound the time a request can hold active reservation without progress, and (3) provide a lightweight admission controller that cooperates with existing batching and KV pin heuristics. Design: - Each request entering the batching queue receives a monotonically increasing sequence timestamp and an initial debt score computed from estimated token work and KV pin cost. Debt accumulates linearly with wall-clock age and is reduced on successful kernel dispatch or when the request is partially serviced via prefix cache hits. - The scheduler computes an effective priority = base_priority + min(debt, debt_cap) - age_penalty_jitter. The debt_cap prevents single old requests from monopolizing throughput. - A soft-ejection timeout is applied per-request: if a request's wall-time in active reservation exceeds soft_timeout_without_progress, it is moved back to the waiting queue and its debt is increased to improve later admission odds; repeated ejections escalate to a hard backoff that defers the request for a short cooldown window to let the batch ecosystem clear. - KV-aware hints: the allocator tags reservations that pin large KV entries; such requests get a scaled debt boost but also a slightly longer soft_timeout to account for unavoidable kernel latency. - Kernel hinting: when multiple requests in a candidate batch share KV pages or overlapping attention windows, we tag the dispatch with a combined_kv_hint to prefer fused kernels (when available) and reduce redundant KV transfers. - Metrics and knobs: new metrics (queue_debt_histogram, eviction_reason_counter, avg_time_to_dispatch_by_age_bucket) and knobs (debt_growth_rate, debt_cap, soft_timeout_ms, hard_backoff_ms, kv_debt_scale) are exposed in the Console and as runtime flags for Dedicated/Private deployments. Implementation notes: - Changes are limited to continuous_batcher/scheduler.go, continuous_batcher/allocator.go, runtime/kv/hints.go and runtime/dispatch/dispatch_coordinator.go. Also added unit and e2e tests under continuous_batcher/test/ and a stress scenario in perf-canary/testvectors/kv_mixed_burst.yaml. - The debt and timeout logic is intentionally lightweight (O(1) per-request bookkeeping) to avoid adding scheduling overhead. - Added deterministic jitter to soft-timeouts to avoid synchronized ejection storms. Testing and results: - Microbenchmarks (local simulated workloads) show 2.8x reduction in 99.9th percentile latency for the mixed KV-small-burst scenario and <3% throughput regression for purely tiny-request workloads when defaults are enabled. - Canary in staging (10% traffic, Dedicated cluster) showed tail latency improvement with no observed increase in error budget; CI runs were adjusted to include the new perf tests. Rollout and migration: - Default knobs are conservative: debt_cap=1.5x, soft_timeout_ms=1200, kv_debt_scale=2.0. We recommend gradual ramp (10% -> 50% -> 100%) with the perf-canary testvector enabled. - No model or API surface changes. Operator notes include guidance for tuning knobs by workload type. Backwards compatibility: no breaking changes to the public API or storage formats. 
Jonas: 'Nice approach. Two concerns: 1) the debt growth params could starve tiny requests in extreme old-request scenarios; 2) how will this interact with the current slot-reservation preemption?' Asha: 'Added per-age-bucket caps and deterministic jitter to mitigate synchronized starvation; revised tests to include tiny-only workloads. Added note about preemption: soft-ejection returns reservation and does not preempt kernel once dispatch begins.' Priya: 'Please add a dashboard for eviction_reason_counter and an alert for sustained hard-backoff rates' -> Asha: 'Added dash and alert in docs and Console defaults; tweaked default debt_cap down from 2.0 to 1.5.' Markus: 'nit: move jitter code to util/time for reuse' -> addressed. Final approval from Jonas and Priya after CI perf runs passed.
Introduce chronological debt-based throttling for continuous batcher: improves tail latency in mixed KV and tiny-request workloads by bounding request holding time and prioritizing older stalled work. Exposes tuning knobs for debt growth, caps, and timeouts. Ships metrics for debugging ejection/backoff behavior.
payload.title: chronological-debt-based-throttling-for-continuous-batcher

payload.body:
Motivation: In production traffic patterns we've observed recurring tail-latency spikes when a small proportion of KV-heavy requests starve the continuous batcher queue. The existing continuous-batcher groups by sequence length and preferences but did not have a bounded 'spillover reservoir' for requests that cannot be immediately coalesced; long-lived KV-pinned requests could occupy soft slots and cause p95/p99 regressions for small, latency-sensitive requests. This PR introduces a spillover-reservoir mechanism + deadline-aware eviction to prevent starvation and jitter for low-latency request classes.

What this changes (single contiguous description): Adds a bounded spillover reservoir per batcher shard that temporarily holds requests that missed the active coalescing window and are KV-pin heavy. Reservoir entries have two timers: a short requeue deadline (for low-latency retries) and a soft eviction deadline (for graceful fallback to a compatible, slightly cheaper model variant or to a warmed-up hot-swap lane). We also add a small fairness faucet that enforces per-class admission caps so a single tenant or request class cannot flood the batcher. The scheduler changes include: (1) admission token accounting for reservoir + active queue, (2) deadline-aware dequeue policy that prioritizes small-latency classes when their requeue timer expires, (3) adaptive lease decay on long-running KV-pinned requests to release slots gradually, and (4) a config knob `spillover_reservoir_size` and `spillover_deadline_ms` with conservative defaults.

Benchmarks: Microbench marks run on a 4xA100 testbed with mixed workload (90% short chat, 10% KV-heavy long prefix). Compared to main at commit HEAD: p50 unchanged (~22ms), p95 improved from 240ms -> 175ms (-27%), p99 improved from 520ms -> 390ms (-25%), overall token throughput impacted -1.8% under synthetic mix. Under KV-heavy spikes (burst factor 3x), the main branch saw p99 climb above 1s; this branch keeps p99 <= 420ms in the same scenario due to bounded reservoir and prioritized dequeue.

Compatibility and rollout: Defaults are conservative; feature is off for Dedicated clusters by default and on for Hosted with a rollout config gating it behind release flag `continuous_batcher_spillover_v1`. We provide runtime knobs surfaced in the Console under batcher tuning. Operator guidance: start with spillover_reservoir_size=16 and spillover_deadline_ms=50 in high-latency sensitive workloads and increase reservoir for throughput-oriented workloads.

Testing: Unit tests for the reservoir lifecycle and deadline handling added; integration bench harness included in `runtime/bench/bench_spillover.py`. Manual soak on a shadow environment (24h) validating fairness caps and no token leakage.

Risks & mitigations: If misconfigured reservoir sizes may increase transient latency for throughput-optimized queues; mitigation: conservative defaults and a circuit-breaker metric (`batcher.reservoir_pressure`) that flips the feature off automatically when sustained pressure observed.

Related: ENG-4892 (KV-heavy tail investigation), PR #20512 (queue-timeout guard) for historical context.
Diego Ramos: Please add a metric that surfaces reservoir occupancy percent and make sure it's tagged by tenant and model_variant. We need this in the Console for rollout visibility.
Asha Menon (author): Added 'batcher.reservoir_occupancy' and tagged by tenant/model_variant. Also added alert runbook pointer in docs.
Priya Shah: The adaptive lease-decay math looks plausible but we need a short doc describing the decay curve and why we chose linear decay vs exponential. Could you add that to the config comments?
Asha Menon: Added detailed comments and a short appendix in docs/ops/continuous-batching.md explaining decay curves and trade-offs with empirical plots from the bench harness.
Liam O'Connor: CI failed on flake in TestContinuousBatcherRace; please ensure deterministic ordering in the test or add a small backoff.
Asha Menon: Fixed the flake by introducing a deterministic mock timer in the test; CI passes locally and in pipeline now.

Motivation: customer reports and internal canaries showed frequent small fragmented stream frames and noisy route selection changes under bursty traffic when OpenAI-compat mode is enabled. Small fragments increase CPU and connection churn for downstream clients and inflate billing token counts for short responses. Additionally, the router was oscillating between equivalent backends when experimental cost-based routing was active, causing intermittent tail-latency regressions. This PR introduces two coordinated changes: 1) a configurable coalescing window in the streaming proxy that aggregates small chunks into larger frames before forwarding (preserves order and streaming semantics, defaults to conservative 8ms/1KB thresholds), and 2) route weighting pins for compatible model variants so the router respects a sticky weight for short-lived requests to reduce flapping. Changes include lightweight metrics, a targeted rollout plan, and backwards-compatible feature flags. Rollout plan: enable feature flag for 10% traffic on dedicated, monitor 95/99 latencies and 'stream_frame_reassembly' metric for 48h, then widen to 50% before global release. Backwards compatibility: feature flag off maintains previous behavior; coalescing is bounded and disables for flagged routes that require strict per-token flushing (realtime voice, websocket low-latency flows). Monitoring/alerts: new alert 'gateway.coalesce.backpressure' when proxy queue depth exceeds threshold and 'router.weighting.flap' when route selection changes >20% within 5m. Motivation and summary:
This PR introduces a hybrid deadline-based scheduler combined with an anticipatory KV prefetch heuristic and a credit-smoothing replenishment algorithm to reduce streaming token-generation latency variance. Existing continuous-batching and emit/flush mechanisms reduce cost but still exhibit tail jitter when short-lived interactive streams contend with larger batched workloads. The goal is to smooth first-byte and inter-token latency without regressing throughput or increasing GPU stalls.

Design highlights (single-string description):
1) Hybrid deadline scheduler: requests carry a soft deadline derived from observed end-to-end SLOs and recent prefix latencies. The scheduler blends earliest-deadline-first for latency-sensitive lanes with throughput-oriented coalescing for bulk lanes. A short window (configurable, default 10ms) is reserved to let imminent short streams preempt larger microbatches.
2) Anticipatory KV prefetch: when a request's prefix matches a high-probability prefix (hot-token prefixes maintained by a lightweight LRU+freq estimator), we issue tentative KV prefetches into the local KV cache before kernel launch. Prefetches are conservative (max 2 per request) and cancelable to avoid evicting cold state.
3) Credit-smoothing replenishment: instead of refilling emission credits in large discrete jumps (which lead to microbursts), we use an exponential moving-average (EMA) based replenishment that paces token emission credit growth to steady-state. Combined with the scheduler, this reduces queue oscillation.
4) Fallback and feature gating: the behavior is behind two runtime feature flags (hybrid_deadline=true, kv_anticipation=true). If flags are disabled, system falls back to previous continuous-batching path.

Implementation notes:
- New files: runtime/scheduler/hybrid_deadline_scheduler.go, runtime/scheduler/deadline_policy_test.go, runtime/kv/anticipatory_prefetch.go, runtime/kv/prefetch_metrics.go, runtime/emitter/credit_smoother.go, and small wiring in runtime/service/stream_handler.go.
- The scheduler integrates with the existing batch coordinator: it exposes a scheduling hint API (softDeadline, laneHint) so we avoid deep coupling.
- Prefetch uses the existing KV async loader interface; added a cancel token so prefetched payloads are discarded if not used within 40ms.
- Credit smoother is lock-free for the hot path; uses atomic counters + timer-based lightweight tick on emit loop.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests added for deadline logic, prefetch cancellation, and credit smoothing edge cases.
- Microbench: streaming harness with 100 concurrent interactive connections and a background bulk workload. Observed changes relative to d0 (main): median TTFB -11%, p95 TTFB -28%, token stepping p99 reduced by 40% in tuned configs. Throughput loss: <1% on heavy batch workloads.
- Production canary: rolled out to canary pool (5 machines) for 48h; no increased GPU stall signals in telemetry and no cache thrashing alarms.

Checklist (implemented):

- [x] Anticipatory KV prefetch implementation + metrics
- [x] Credit smoother + unit tests
- [x] End-to-end streaming harness tests and perf numbers

Changed areas (high level):

Motivation: Dedicated fleets occasionally observe short-lived headroom starvation when many mid-sized tenants burst concurrently. The existing admission path provides per-tenant soft reservations and a simple first-fit burst allowance, but we see tail latency spikes and over-eager decommits under correlated bursts. This PR introduces a reservoir-based throttle arbiter that mediates burst grants across tenant groups and a lag mitigation controller that reduces reactive provisioning churn.

What this change does (summary): 1) reservoir/arbiter: adds a lightweight in-memory reservoir that tracks short-term burst budget across the fleet and issues proportional ephemeral grants based on recent utilization fingerprints and configured fairness weights; 2) lag mitigator: smooths autoscaler signals by detecting provisioning lag (nodes pending/booting) and temporarily biasing admission towards conservative allocations until capacity stabilizes; 3) telemetry: exports new metrics and sketches to diagnose burst contention and reservoir depletion; 4) safety: falls back to current behavior on misconfiguration and supports an opt-in feature-flag.

Design notes: - Reservoir state is sharded per-pool to avoid global lock contention. Each shard maintains a leaky-bucket style token pool with time-decay replenishment calibrated by pool commit size and historical burst frequency. - The arbiter issues ephemeral grants bounded by tenant-configured max-burst and global per-pool headroom. Grants are revocable and include a best-effort TTL. - The lag mitigator computes a provisioning gap metric (pending_nodes_weighted - expected_boot_capacity) and applies a sigmoid dampening to scale down ephemeral grants when gap > threshold. Dampening parameters are tunable via the autoscaler config map.

Checklist: - [x] Core reservoir implementation with unit tests and deterministic time control
- [x] Lag mitigator controller and integration tests (simulated provisioning delay)
- [x] Telemetry hooks (metrics, HDR sketches) + Grafana dashboard draft
- [x] Feature flag gate + config map defaults preserved
- [x] E2E scenario reproducing correlated two-tenant bursts
- [x] Docs: operator runbook and tuning guide

Why this is safe: The arbiter is opt-in per-pool and defaults to an inert mode that mirrors existing admission behavior. All grants are bounded and revocable; if the controller process crashes the system reverts to existing admission. We included a kill-switch and health-checks that force-drain the reservoir on mismatch.

How tested: Unit and integration tests included. The e2e suite simulates fleets with varying boot latencies (0s-120s) and shows 40-55% reduction in tail-99 latency for short bursts across our synthetic workload. Perf bench harness run on internal bench cluster (bench-01) shows median token allocation latency unchanged, and sustained throughput within 2% of baseline.

Rollout plan: 1) Canary on staging pools (opt-in) for 48h 2) Monitor reservoir_depletion_rate, provisioning_gap, tenant_throttle_events and tail latency 3) Gradual ramp to 30% production pools with daily checkpoints 4) Full rollout if no regressions after 7 days.

Related: ENG-1829 (throughput guarantees), ENG-1974 (eviction smoothing), SUP-412 (customer incident that motivated lag mitigator).
Jonas Park (2025-01-13): Nice approach. Two requests: (1) add a short doc comment on the mathematical properties of the replenishment decay so on-call can reason about parameters; (2) prefer context-aware cancellations in the arbiter grant path to avoid leaks. See inline.

Author (Aisha): Added comment and switched to context-aware grant workflows in the latest commit (b4c5d22).
Miguel Alvarez (2025-01-15): Can we add a safety unit test for controller crash + restart so we verify we don't double-credit the reservoir? Also the e2e seemed flaky once with a delayed API—I added a repro in the CI logs.

Author: Added TestReservoirIdempotentRecovery and extended e2e harness to tolerate API delay up to 5s. Fixed race in shard init. (commit 9f3a2d1).
Priya Singh (2025-01-17): From an SRE perspective, please expose an alert recipe for persistent reservoir_depletion_rate > 0.8 over a 10m window and add playbook steps. Docs updated.

Author: Added alert recommendations to docs and included grafana dashboard snapshot.
Introduces an opt-in reservoir-based burst arbiter and provisioning lag mitigator for Dedicated fleets. Adds telemetry for reservoir depletion and provisioning gap. Operators can tune decay and dampening parameters via the autoscaler config map.
If tail latency increases after enabling for a pool: 1) check reservoir_depletion_rate and provisioning_gap metrics; 2) toggle feature flag to revert to baseline admission; 3) consult docs/ops/dedicated/lag-mitigation.md for tuning parameters and playbook steps; 4) run TestReservoirIdempotentRecovery locally to reproduce restart semantics.
Risk: miscalibrated decay/dampening could starve legitimate bursts or over-issue grants. Mitigation: defaults are conservative, feature is opt-in, grants bounded and revocable, metrics and alerting added, rollback via feature flag. Runbook included.
Synthetic two-tenant correlated burst test: baseline tail-99 = 1.8s, with arbiter tail-99 = 0.95s (median of 5 runs); provisioning-gap > 0 scenario reduced oscillation in autoscaler decisions and reduced unnecessary decommits by ~33%.
This PR complements existing autoscaler work by focusing on short-term burst fairness and reducing reactive provisioning churn. It is intentionally orthogonal to long-window capacity planners; the reservoir only affects ephemeral granting and does not change reserved capacity commitments.

Motivation: reduce end-to-end cold-miss latency and lower tail p99 for KV lookups during bursty traffic while preserving throughput for steady-state workloads. This PR introduces a deferred-writeback allocator for paged KV blocks and a lightweight "fuzzy-pin" mechanism that biases reuse towards recently evicted pages without hard pinning. The deferred-writeback design batches dirty-page flushes to background worker threads so the fast-path allocation/eviction avoids synchronous disk/remote persist stalls; fuzzy-pin attaches a compact recency score to blocks to guide selection in the reuse path and helps avoid repeated thrashing on transient hot prefixes. Design highlights: 1) new deferred_writeback module implements a lock-free writeback queue per allocator shard with backpressure signals to avoid unbounded memory growth; writeback batches are coalesced by object-id and max latency bound (configurable). 2) allocator core refactor extracts a thin Policy trait; two implementations are provided: LRU-like baseline and FuzzyPin that tracks a 8-bit recency counter and a 1-bit soft-pin flag. 3) Eviction now exposes a try_reuse(path) fast-path that returns recently-deallocated blocks to the requester if the recency score exceeds a threshold; otherwise the block is enqueued for deferred writeback and made available after the writeback completes. 4) Integration with scheduler: allocation requests can mark priority; high-priority requests are allowed to preempt non-pinned candidates. 5) Telemetry: new metrics around writeback_batch_size, fuzzy_pin_hits, soft_pin_conflicts, and allocator_reuse_latency. Testing and validation: unit tests for race-free enqueue/dequeue in deferred writeback, fuzz tests for edge-case recency wraparound, and an integration harness that replays production KV traces (trace replay harness added under perf/trace-replays) to validate p50/p95/p99 improvements. Benchmarks: see bench_results field for numbers. Rollout plan: staged rollout - enable FuzzyPin behind runtime feature-flag in Canary and Dedicated, observe writeback latency and reuse-hit metrics for 48 hours, then flip default in 2.0.x branch. Rollback: feature flag and allocator policy knob allow immediate revert without data migration. Related: builds on discussions in ENG-5124 and complements earlier paged-kv reallocator work. This description intentionally keeps implementation detail high level; code comments explain invariants for concurrent writeback/shard ownership.
7 commits: initial refactor extracting Policy trait; add deferred_writeback worker and queue; implement fuzzy-pin policy; integrate try_reuse fast-path; add telemetry and unit tests; add perf replay harness and benchmarks; docs and changelog updates.
Ethan Cole: Can you clarify how the deferred writeback guarantees durability order for dependent objects? If object B references A we must ensure A's writeback is ordered first. Response: We keep intra-shard sequence numbers and coalesce by object group; background worker orders batches by smallest sequence number and emits per-group flushes, documented in code comments and covered by new unit test (ordered_writeback).
Marina Novak: The fuzzy-pin recency counter is 8-bit; how do we avoid pathological wraparound on long-lived workloads? Response: counters decay via periodic right-shift and aggressive decrement when memory pressure is detected; fuzz tests cover multiple wrap scenarios. Added configurable decay interval.
Owen Park: I see a 2% perf regression on steady-state throughput in perf CI when writeback batch size is small. Suggest an adaptive batch size. Response: added adaptive batch sizing based on queue latency and observed pending bytes; perf run after change shows regression resolved.
Marina Novak: approve after addressing adaptive batching and adding dashboard visuals for fuzzy_pin_hits and writeback_queue_depth. Author: thanks — pushed dashboard and updated metrics registry.

payload.body:
Motivation: In multi-GPU tensor-parallel serving workloads we observed repeated head-of-line stalls and higher-than-expected allgather volume for KV cache updates when the workload is dominated by many small microbatches (conversation turns, short generations). Small KV entries cause fragmented network payloads and prevent NCCL from issuing efficient vectorized collectives. Additionally, on NVLink-heavy topologies tight back-to-back kernel launches can create transient link congestion that amplifies latency spikes.

Summary: This PR introduces two complementary runtime optimizations: 1) a slab compaction layer for the KV cache that packs small key/value shards into contiguous "slabs" and exposes a vectorized buffer path to the collective layer; 2) an adaptive NCCL launch-rate throttler that probes topology (NVLink/PCIe) and dynamically inserts calibrated micro-delays between collective launches to avoid ring congestion on shared links. Both are gated behind runtime feature flags and conservative defaults.

Design highlights: - Slab compaction: lightweight on-GPU compaction allocator that groups variable-size KV entries into fixed-size slabs. Compaction is applied on eviction and warmup paths; a compacted slab produces a contiguous blob that the vector_coalesce collective will allgather/ allreduce in a single call instead of many small ops. The allocator exposes compact/expand primitives so we can fall back to the legacy path for downloads. Config knobs: TP_SLAB_SIZE (default 64KB), TP_COMPACT_THRESHOLD (default 12 entries). - Vectorized collectives: new vector_coalesce.cc implements gather/scatter helpers that prefer contiguous device buffers; falls back to existing shard path if entries are un-compacted. The implementation minimizes pinned-host staging and reuses persistent NCCL communicators allocated per peer-group. - NCCL throttler: runtime probe collects per-link utilization using NVML + lightweight counters and applies a token-bucket style micro-throttle (NCCL_THROTTLE_US) that spaces collective launches only when probe indicates link saturation. Probe runs during warmup and periodically. Throttle defaults are conservative and only enabled for topologies with shared NVLink links. - Scheduler changes: launch_policy.cc updated to prefer the coalesced-launch path for microbatches < 32 tokens and route large microbatches to the bulk path. Added heuristics to detect mixed-size workload and avoid oscillation.

Testing & Benchmarks: - Unit tests added for slab compactor invariants and expand/compact correctness. - Integration tests exercise mixed small/large token workloads in CI. - Perf harness: ran on 8xA100 NVLink ring and on 4xA40 PCIe nodes. Results (conversation workload, 8xA100 ring): throughput +9% (tokens/sec), p99 latency reduced 12-18% across load points, median latency stable. KV memory utilization decreased ~15% due to reduced fragmentation. On PCIe-only topologies gains are smaller (~3-5%) but p99 still improved due to reduced small-collective overhead. Detailed graphs are in docs/runtime/tp/slab_compaction.md.

Backward compatibility & rollout: - No public API changes; feature is behind two runtime flags (TP_SLAB_COMPACTION, NCCL_THROTTLE). Defaults off for dedicated/private customers; enabled by default in hosted perf lab rollout. - Added guardrails: conservative default throttle values, topology detection, and metrics/alerts (nccl_throttle_restarts, slab_compaction_rate). - Migration: no customer migration required; operators can opt-in or tune via config.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for compactor and expand/compact - [x] Integration tests for mixed microbatch paths - [x] Perf benchmarks collected and reviewed - [x] Feature flags and config knobs - [x] Documentation updated - [x] Added metrics and tracing points

Risks and mitigations: - Risk: compaction may increase CPU/GPU overhead during eviction causing small regressions for some workloads. Mitigation: compaction is asynchronous and bounded; can be disabled. - Risk: mis-calibrated throttle may increase latency for bursty traffic. Mitigation: conservative defaults + runtime metrics + quick rollback flag.

Context & related work: follows ENG-2387 (kvcache fragmentation) and ENG-2421 (tp collective failures on mixed microbatches). Builds on prior scheduler improvements and the persistent-communicator work in ENG-99501.

Next steps: expand topology-aware heuristics (cross-node NVLink islands), add a continuous learning step to tune NCCL_THROTTLE_US automatically from warmup traces, and expose a per-customer opt-in experiment in the console.
Arjun: Can you add a microbench that isolates the compaction cost vs collective savings? Requesting numbers for worst-case small-entry churn.
Maya: Added tp_slab_compaction_bench.py and included worst-case churn run in perf artifacts (see perf log). Compaction cost amortizes within 3-4 turns for our conversation workload.
Liam: Throttle looks plausible; default seems high for some PCIe setups. Can you make topology detection more conservative and add metric for throttle actions?
Maya: Adjusted probe to require two consecutive saturation samples before enabling throttle on PCIe topologies; added nccl_throttle_actions metric and logging.
Sofia: Please document feature flags and add guidance for tuning in the dedicated/private deploy docs. Also request a short rollback playbook.
Maya: Docs added at docs/runtime/tp/slab_compaction.md and included a rollback section. Added Linear tasks for follow-up tuning.
Improves multi-GPU tensor-parallel throughput and p99 latency by introducing KV cache slab compaction and an NCCL launch-rate throttler tuned for NVLink topologies. No API changes.
Merged PR introduces slab-based KV compaction and an adaptive NCCL throttler; measurable p99 improvements in NVLink rings and modest throughput wins. Feature gated and rolled out conservatively.
Perf artifacts uploaded to perf-bucket/redwood/pr-114512. QA: repro snippets, a quick injection test for throttle, and unit test checklist included.

Context and motivation: We observed two recurring issues in customer integrations that use long-lived streams: 1) mid-stream token refreshes could occasionally close the stream unexpectedly or cause duplicated events, and 2) ergonomics for consuming streamed responses across SDKs were inconsistent (async iterator vs event emitter patterns), which increased integration friction. This PR delivers coordinated fixes and parity improvements across the three SDKs.

What this PR does (single continuous description): Implements a safe token-rotation handshake that pauses the stream consumer loop while the auth token swap completes and resumes without losing in-flight chunks; introduces an opt-in 'resilientStream' wrapper across Python/TS/Go that standardizes backpressure-friendly async iteration, reconnection with idempotent resume tokens, and exponential jittered backoff on transient network errors; cleans up public ergonomics by adding a small helper API (stream.resume(), stream.pause(), stream.as_iterator()) to reduce integration boilerplate; fixes parity bugs noted in ENG-2143 (TS previously omitted final newline-preservation behavior), and ENG-2198 (Python had one-off cursor handling in the reattach path). Bumps SDK patch versions: python 0.14.3 -> 0.14.4, typescript 1.7.0 -> 1.7.1, go 0.8.9 -> 0.8.10. Adds end-to-end streaming tests and CI job permutations to run cross-SDK replay/resume scenarios.

Checklist:
- [x] Safe token swap handshake across SDKs
- [x] Resilient stream wrapper with backoff and resume token support
- [x] Unified ergonomic helpers (pause/resume/iterator)
- [x] Parity fixes for newline preservation and cursor handling
- [x] Added unit + e2e tests (simulated partial failures)
- [x] Updated changelogs and bumped patch versions
- [x] CI green on all SDK permutations

High-level commits summary (see commits field for detail): coordinated changes touching each SDK client, test harness additions (stream-fault-injector), and small doc snippets in SDK READMEs.

Notes/risks: The token-rotation protocol is opt-in behind the resilientStream flag to reduce blast radius. Default behavior remains backward compatible. Resume logic requires server support for resume tokens; for older servers the wrapper falls back to restart-on-failure behavior with a warning.

Related: Linear ENG-2143, ENG-2198. No linked Jira.

Improve streaming client resilience and safe token rotation across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs. Add ergonomic iterator helpers and bump patch versions. No breaking changes.
Leo Chen (reviewer): Nice cross-SDK approach. Two asks: add a short e2e assertion that validates no duplicate chunks after resume, and make the token-swap timeout configurable.

Aria Gomez (reviewer): TS impl looks good. Suggest tightening types on the iterator to avoid 'any' and add a small example in README showing pause/resume usage.

Motivation: intermittent partial-JSON emissions and out-of-order tool/function-call handoffs observed under backpressure for long-running SSE responses. This PR adds an explicit anchor-checkpointing approach to SSE fragment emission and rewrites delimiter handling to normalize mixed newline/\r sequences, while ensuring that function-call sentinel frames are fenced until the prior JSON span is fully committed. Key goals: 1) avoid emitting partial JSON slices that cannot be reassembled by OpenAI-compatible clients; 2) prevent toolcall tokens from leaking into earlier fragments during stream replay; 3) retain backwards compatibility with existing OpenAI-compat framing but make the reassembly deterministic under retries and replays. Implementation summary: (a) introduce an anchor sequence id (anchor_seq) embedded as a lightweight header on emitted SSE frames to allow receivers to latch reassembly windows and ignore stale fragments; (b) implement delimiter normalization and an escape-folding pass that collapses mixed CR/LF runs into a canonical \n boundary and preserves deliberate \r markers inside strings; (c) implement a "function-call fence" state in the SSE emitter so that function-call sentinel lines are only emitted once the emitter observes the anchor checkpoint acknowledged (or after a configurable flush timeout for best-effort clients); (d) add a replay-safe checksum tag for mid-json spans (optional) so clients can validate and request retransmit if available. Compatibility notes: behavior defaults to previous framing for clients that do not inspect anchor_seq but improves determinism for our OpenAI-compat layer and downstream SDKs. The PR includes unit and integration tests exercising backpressure, fragmentation, and replay scenarios, plus a short doc snippet explaining the anchor semantics for SDK consumers. Rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag sse_anchor_enable (off by default for 48 hours), will be enabled cluster-wide after canary verification. Related: ENG-2412 (stream-stability spike), SUP-9981 (customer incident resulting in partial JSON).
1) 9b1f2d3: add anchor_seq header to sse emitter and parser with tests; 2) a3c4f55: normalize delimiters and add escape-folding pass; 3) f7e8a90: introduce function-call fence and configurable flush timeout; 4) 2c3d444: add integration tests for replay and backpressure scenarios; 5) 7d9a1b0: docs and release-notes entry
Ethan Park: Can you explain how anchor_seq is exposed in the public wire format? Priya Desai: anchor_seq is an optional header line (e.g. "event: anchor_seq=12345") in the SSE envelope; it is benign for older clients and consumed by updated parsers. Marta Novak: I saw the integration flake on replays where the checksum mismatches; is that expected? Priya Desai: The checksum is optional and only emitted when runtime flag sse_anchor_checksum=true; tests were updated to cover both code paths. Liam Zhou: The function-call fence timeout default seems long (3s) — could we reduce? Priya Desai: Reduced default to 250ms after perf review; left configurable per-workload. Ethan Park: LGTM after nits. Marta Novak: approved. QA: flaky test removed; CI green on rerun.
stabilize SSE framing by adding anchor_seq header for deterministic fragment reassembly; normalize CR/LF delimiters; introduce function-call fencing to prevent toolcall token leakage across fragments; feature gated behind sse_anchor_enable.
Added unit tests for parser reassembly, emitter sequence semantics, and delimiter normalization. Integration harness simulates packet splits, backpressure and replay; added a deterministic test that reproduces the customer incident SUP-9981. e2e canary executed against a staging cluster with 10k simulated concurrent streams.
Enable sse_anchor_enable=false on prod prior to rollout; perform a 2-node canary with sse_anchor_enable=true and monitor streaming error-rate and function-call drop metrics (streaming.partial_json.error, streaming.toolcall.drop). Rollback by toggling feature flag and restarting the emitter pods if we observe regressions.

Context: mixed prompt-length workloads (short chat prompts interleaved with long-context requests) can produce head-of-line blocking in continuous batching, inflating p95/TTFT for latency-sensitive traffic. This PR introduces a two-queue dispatch policy (short/long classes) with explicit starvation prevention via aging + bounded skew, behind a feature flag, and adds basic correctness tests plus perf notes from local mixed-load runs. The classification logic lands in pr-24831; this PR assumes requests arrive with a class label and focuses on dispatch selection + guardrails.
What changed: implemented a class-based scheduler policy with two logical queues (SHORT, LONG) and a dispatch loop that chooses the next request to admit into the next prefill/decode iteration. The policy biases toward SHORT to reduce user-visible tail latency under mixed workloads, while guaranteeing progress for LONG via (1) aging that increases LONG priority as time-in-queue grows and (2) a max-skew guardrail to prevent unbounded short dominance. Design summary: The scheduler maintains per-class queues and per-class accounting over a rolling window. On each dispatch tick, we compute an effective priority for each class based on (base weight * backlog signal) plus an aging boost derived from the head-of-queue waiting time; we then select the class with higher effective priority, subject to a max-consecutive-short limit and a minimum long share floor when long backlog exists. The chosen request is then fed into existing batch formation, with minimal structural changes to avoid destabilizing kernel selection. Starvation prevention: (a) aging_half_life_ms controls how quickly LONG priority rises with wait time; (b) max_short_burst caps consecutive SHORT selections when LONG backlog is non-empty; (c) long_force_after_ms forces a LONG selection when the oldest LONG exceeds a hard wait threshold; and (d) queue-level invariants are asserted in debug builds and covered by unit tests. Feature flag/config: gated behind runtime.scheduler.policy = two_queue (default remains legacy), with knobs runtime.scheduler.two_queue.short_weight, long_weight, aging_half_life_ms, max_short_burst, long_force_after_ms, and max_dispatch_skew_ratio (validated and clamped to safe bounds). Tests: added deterministic scheduler unit tests for (1) no starvation under sustained short arrival (long eventually dispatches), (2) short preference when both queues non-empty and long age is low, (3) hard force trigger when oldest long exceeds threshold, and (4) stability of selection under jittery arrival patterns. Perf notes (local/dev bench): using a synthetic 80/20 short/long mix with long prompts ~8k context and short ~256 tokens on A100-80GB dev host, observed reduced p95 queue wait for short requests vs legacy policy with negligible throughput drift in steady state; results are directional only (real validation in benchmark-lab + perf-canary will follow in separate PRs). Follow-ups: token-budget guardrails and per-class metrics/tracing are intentionally not included here to keep review scope focused (see pr-24872 and pr-24888). Risk/rollback: fully gated; can revert to legacy by config. Known risks are parameter sensitivity and pathological mixes; addressed partially via bounded skew + hard force and covered by correctness tests. Pseudocode sketch (for reviewer orientation, not exact code): selectClass(): if longQ empty -> SHORT; if shortQ empty -> LONG; if oldestLongWait > long_force_after_ms -> LONG; if consecutiveShort >= max_short_burst -> LONG; scoreShort = short_weight * f(backlogShort); scoreLong = long_weight * f(backlogLong) + agingBoost(oldestLongWait, aging_half_life_ms); if scoreShort/scoreLong > max_dispatch_skew_ratio -> LONG else choose argmax(scoreShort, scoreLong).
Lena Fischer (review): Can you clarify the starvation guarantee? Specifically, what prevents long from starving if short arrival is sustained and short_weight is high? Also request: add a regression test that simulates a constant short stream with a single long enqueued at t=0 and asserts long dispatches within bounded steps/time.
Marcus Reed (author): Added long_force_after_ms + max_short_burst enforcement when long backlog is non-empty. Also added test_two_queue_policy.no_starvation_under_sustained_short to assert long dispatch occurs within N selections; wired test to virtual clock so it’s deterministic.
Sofia Ivanova (review): The max_dispatch_skew_ratio logic reads like it compares class scores directly, but scores can be near-zero when backlog is small. Please add comments/guards for divide-by-zero and document how f(backlog) behaves (linear vs log). Also: ensure legacy policy remains default for all pools until canary.
Marcus Reed (author): Updated scoring to avoid division by zero (epsilon floor) and added inline comment explaining backlog transform (log1p to reduce sensitivity). Confirmed default remains legacy; two_queue requires explicit config/flag.
Omar El-Sayed (review): Concern: picking class first and then letting batch formation run could still allow long-prefill to dominate if we admit a long with huge prefill cost. Are we separating prefill vs decode selection here?
Marcus Reed (author): This PR only gates the admission decision; prefill/decode separation hooks are being refactored in pr-24857 to avoid long-prefill dominating batch selection. Added a note in docs + TODO in dispatcher to keep reviewers aligned.
Hiro Tanaka (review): Please be careful with changes that might increase sequence-length variance within a batch and destabilize kernel selection. Any changes to batch composition beyond class selection?
Marcus Reed (author): No direct changes to batch composition; we select the next request class and then defer to existing batch builder constraints. Added debug counters to log when class selection results in large variance (guarded; metrics will come later).
Sean Gallagher (review): Add explicit rollback guidance in the PR description and ensure the policy can be toggled without restart (config reload path). Also: please link the SLO guardrails doc and call out canary-only usage.
Marcus Reed (author): Confirmed config reload supports policy knob changes at runtime; added note: rollback by setting runtime.scheduler.policy=legacy. Linked SUP-19387 context and referenced the SLO guardrails doc in internal notes.
Internal-only prototype behind feature flag/config. No default behavior change. Enables canary evaluation of mixed-workload tail-latency improvements with starvation prevention guardrails.
payload.title: runtime(scheduler): two-queue dispatch policy for mixed short/long prompts + aging guardrails
