payload.body:
Summary: Fixes incorrect cache hit/miss attribution in runtime metrics when multiple requests share a continuous batch prefill. Previously, the prefill stage could be executed as a single fused prefill for a set of requests (continuous batching). Our cache telemetry code was attributing prefill-derived cache outcomes (prefix reuse / KV reuse) to the batch as a whole, then fan-out incrementing per-request counters using the wrong join keys. This produced two bad effects in dashboards: (1) inflated hit counts for some routes/models (double-ish counting depending on batch shape), and (2) hit-rate distortions that correlated strongly with batch size and prefill coalescing rather than true cache behavior.

Context / why now: We saw a mismatch between span annotations (trace-level) and metrics breakdowns in the canary dashboard for the new cache telemetry. In workloads with high concurrency + similar prompt lengths, prefill batching increased and the hit-rate metrics drifted upward vs expected, while wasted-prefill was noisy. This blocks SRE/Telemetry from trusting the signals for alerts/recommendations.

Root cause: The metric instrumentation was keyed off PrefillBatchId and then tried to map back to RequestContext using the active scheduler queue snapshot. Under continuous batching, requests can enter/leave the fused prefill window, and the mapping is not stable across the entire prefill run. Additionally, the cache result object returned by the cache layer was “batch-aggregated” (reused_tokens_total, misses_by_reason) rather than per-request/per-segment. We were then distributing totals evenly (or per-token heuristic) which is wrong for partial reuse and causes incorrect per-route attribution.

Fix: 1) Introduce an explicit per-request CacheAttributionToken that is minted at request admission to the batch and passed through prefill execution. 2) Change the cache layer’s telemetry hook to emit an event per request segment (request_id + segment_index) with reused_tokens, attempted_tokens, and miss_reason (if any). 3) In the metrics layer, aggregate only along stable keys (request_id, model_version_id, route_id, deployment_mode, region, prompt_len_bucket) and increment counters/histograms exactly once per request segment. 4) Add guards to prevent fan-out duplication when a request spans multiple micro-batches (continuous batch “stitching”).

Implementation notes: - This PR does not change cache policy or scheduler behavior; it only changes how we attribute telemetry. - Event emission remains sampling-aware (respects existing cache telemetry sampling gates) and uses the same allowlisted tag set. - We keep batch-level debug stats behind a trace-only annotation (no new high-cardinality metric labels).

Illustrative snippet (simplified): Before: metrics.kv_cache_hits_total.add(batch.reused_tokens_total, tags=tags_for(requests[0])) // wrong: tags derived from an arbitrary request; fan-out adds again per request. After: for seg in prefill_result.request_segments: metrics.kv_cache_reused_tokens_total.add(seg.reused_tokens, tags=tags_for(seg.request_ctx)); metrics.kv_cache_attempted_tokens_total.add(seg.attempted_tokens, tags=tags_for(seg.request_ctx))

Tests: - Added integration test that drives two routes concurrently such that they fuse into a single prefill batch (forced by scheduler test harness). Asserts that attempted_tokens_total equals the sum of both requests, and reused_tokens_total matches only the request that should hit (based on seeded prefix cache). - Added regression test covering “stitching”: request A starts in batch1 and continues in batch2; ensures we don’t double-count attempted tokens. - Updated an existing unit test for the prefill metrics aggregator to validate segment-index semantics.

Performance/overhead: No measurable change in the perf-canary p95; the per-request event is emitted from already-available per-request prefill accounting. The new attribution token is an integer stored in RequestContext and passed by value.

Rollout: Safe to ship behind existing flags. No config changes required. Dashboards should show a small correction (downward) in hit counts for routes that heavily rely on continuous batching.

Related: ENG-4822 (KV cache hit/miss counters). This also unblocks dashboard correctness work in observability-pack (PR-612).

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration test for batched prefill attribution - [x] Verified tags comply with cardinality policy - [x] Verified trace annotations still line up with metrics on canary

Notes for reviewers: The key behavioral change is that hit-rate is now computed off per-request attempted/reused tokens, not batch totals. This should align with the ADR semantics for partial hits and avoid batch-size artifacts.
Omar El-Sayed: Can you clarify what exactly was getting double-counted? From the diff it looks like we were incrementing both tokens_total and requests_total multiple times, but the graphs I saw were mostly hit-rate inflation, not request volume inflation.
Samir Qureshi (author): Yep. request counters were usually OK because they were incremented on request completion, not in prefill. The inflation was primarily in token-based numerators/denominators: attempted_tokens_total and reused_tokens_total. We were taking a batch-level attempted/reused summary and then fanning out per request. For a batch of N, each request got credited with the full batch totals (or a heuristic split), which made hit-rate correlate with N. This PR changes attempted/reused accounting to be per-request segment so sums across requests equal the batch totals exactly once.
Sofia Ivanova: I’m concerned about the stability of the mapping. Continuous batching isn’t a single static list; requests can be admitted mid-prefill depending on the microbatch boundaries. How do we guarantee the attribution token stays correct if a request is “stitched” across two prefill microbatches?
Samir Qureshi (author): Good call. The token is minted at request admission to the scheduler and stored on RequestContext; it doesn’t rely on the batch snapshot. For stitching, the cache telemetry callback now emits (request_id, segment_index). The metrics aggregator dedupes by (request_id, segment_index, stage=prefill) so if a request is processed in multiple microbatches, we count each segment once. Added test_cache_metrics_batched_prefill_stitching to cover this.
Noah Patel: Why introduce segment_index rather than just request_id? Also, do we risk increasing event volume (one event per segment) beyond what sampling expects?
Samir Qureshi (author): segment_index is to model partial hits and partial attempts within a single request. With streaming + tool calls we can have multiple prefill segments per logical request; also, in continuous batching we can split prompt processing. Without segment_index, we either undercount (only first segment) or overcount (sum without dedupe). On volume: worst case events ~= prefill segments, which is already bounded by our internal segmentation logic. Sampling gate is still applied at request admission; if a request isn’t sampled, we emit no segment events. So we’re not multiplying sampled requests; we’re giving more accurate accounting within sampled requests.
Nadia Rahman: Please confirm labels don’t change. The metrics naming/cardinality policy explicitly forbids per-request labels and anything derived from prompt content. I see you mention request_id in the telemetry hook.
Samir Qureshi (author): Confirmed: request_id/segment_index only exist in the internal event struct used to aggregate; they never become metric labels. Exported labels remain model_version_id, route_id (allowlisted), deployment_mode, region, prompt_len_bucket, plus miss_reason enum where applicable. I added a comment in cache_metrics.cc and a unit test asserting the tag allowlist is unchanged.
Omar El-Sayed: One more: how does this interact with the fix in PR-18428 (stream retries double counting)? Any chance we’re reintroducing a retry path that counts twice because the same segment is retried?
Samir Qureshi (author): I audited the retry path. Retries now carry a new logical attempt_id but the same request_id; however, segment_index is assigned per attempt. In the retry case we want to count attempted_tokens (because we actually did work again) but we must avoid counting reused_tokens as a “hit” when the retry is due to transport. The existing guard from PR-18428 ensures we don’t treat retry-prefill as cache-hit attribution unless the cache layer explicitly reports reuse. I also ensured segment_index increments on a new prefill compute, so metrics reflect real work while staying consistent with hit semantics.
Sofia Ivanova: Can we add a note in the description that this is expected to lower hit-rate in workloads with big batches? SRE will get nervous if graphs change.
Samir Qureshi (author): Added to rollout section + pinged Allison/Sean to expect correction in canary dashboards.
Omar El-Sayed: Approved after test coverage + explanation. Thanks for the detailed breakdown.
Nadia Rahman: Approved. Please make sure downstream dashboards use attempted/reused tokens, not request counts, for hit-rate; otherwise this won’t fix their graphs.
Samir Qureshi (author): Ack. I linked this PR in the dashboard ticket notes and added a short note to the internal metrics README follow-up PR.
payload.title: Fix cache hit attribution for metrics under continuous batched prefill

payload.body:
Context and motivation: customers using Dedicated fleets reported intermittent P95 regressions during microbursts. Existing warm-pool and proportional allocators reduce long-term oversubscription but react too slowly to short surge windows. This PR introduces a headroom surge allocator: a short-lived, lease-based headroom slab that can be granted to tenants for fast, low-latency bursts without disrupting long-term capacity guarantees.

Goals: 1) Provide transient capacity that keeps P95 stable during sub-minute spikes. 2) Maintain fairness and overall throughput guarantees by ensuring surge slabs are ephemeral and reconciled with long-term reservations. 3) Surface decomposition telemetry so SRE/product can attribute utilization changes to sustained vs. transient activity.

What changed (high-level): - New controller redwood/fleet/surge_allocator that manages ephemeral "headroom slabs". Slabs are issued as short leases (default 45s) and tracked separately from reservations. - Lease smoothing: allocator applies an exponentially-weighted smoothing window and a reservoir cap to avoid oscillation when spikes are frequent. - Signal fusion: autoscaler now consumes a fused signal combining request rate, observed KV-cache-hit-adjusted token-rate, and sequence-length-weighted concurrency (seqlen-weighted RPS). This reduces false positives from large batch requests. - Fallbacks: when headroom exhausted allocator emits a soft-fail marker causing graceful degrade routes to opt for lower-cost model variants. - Telemetry: introduced exporter redwood.telemetry.util_decomp which reports per-tenant breakdown: sustained_alloc, transient_surge_alloc, cache_credits_used, and effective_concurrency. Also added histogram metrics for transient_alloc_duration and per-tenant surge_success_rate.

Design notes: - Lease semantics: slab leases are time-bound and replenished after a cooldown period. We avoid hard preemption; instead we prefer proportional dampening (reduce new lease grant rate) when global utilization > threshold. - Fairness: an allocation window enforces per-tenant caps that are a function of committed reservation * and a small transient multiplier (configurable via feature flag). - Safety: a global reservoir prevents uncontrolled total transient capacity; reservoir filling is controlled by long-term idle capacity and expected decommit timings.

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for allocator logic, lease expiry, and reservoir accounting. - Integration harness (perf-canary job) simulated microbursts across 500 tenants: observed P95 token latency reduction from baseline 372ms to 341ms (≈8.3%) while overall throughput unchanged. Transient capacity usage averaged 12% of cluster for 10s windows and returned to baseline within configured cooldown. - Load tests included failure scenarios (controller restart, partial partition) to validate idempotency and lease reconciliation.

Migration and rollout: - Feature flag: "surge_allocator_v1" off by default. Gradual rollout recommended: enable on 5% of fleets, monitor redwood.telemetry.util_decomp.surge_success_rate and p95 latency. - No client-facing API changes. Console: new per-tenant "transient utilization" chart added under Dedicated -> Pools (opt-in metric).

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Perf canary run - [x] Telemetry dashboards updated - [x] Docs entry (internal runbook)

Related work: ties into ENG-6421 (protect P95 during microbursts) and ENG-6498 (telemetry for tenant utilization).

Commit summary: see commits field for high-level descriptions.
Marta Lopez: Nice approach. Two asks: (1) please add a small e2e that simulates rapid repeated microbursts to validate smoothing won't starve tenants, (2) clarify the cooldown math in the runbook - current pseudocode is ambiguous.
Avery Chen: Added an e2e in canary harness and expanded runbook with explicit cooldown formula. See commit 09ab8c and docs update.
Jamal Rice: We should avoid wallet-like semantics where tenants can bank unused transient capacity; confirm reservoir prevents accumulation across longer windows.
Avery Chen: Reservoir explicitly decays at the long-term decommit cadence (configurable). Added unit tests that assert no cross-window carryover beyond configured expiry.
Priya Nair: Minor nit: metric naming should use 'redwood.fleet.headroom.*' prefix to align with naming conventions. Also add an alert for surge_success_rate dropping below 60%.
Avery Chen: Renamed metrics to redwood.fleet.headroom.* and added the suggested alert rule.
payload.title: Introduce headroom surge allocator and utilization decomposition exporter

payload.body:
Motivation: We see a class of small-to-medium tenants that oscillate between single-token spikes and short bursts. Existing tenant-level autoscalers skew heavy to throughput targets and end up overprovisioning GPU slots or forcing conservative batching that degrades unit economics. This change introduces a lightweight 'pocket-econ' autoscaler that targets per-tenant micro-bursts with compact batching defaults and a controlled quantization fallback path to reduce token cost during transient peaks without impacting tail latency SLAs.

Design summary: pocket-econ is a runtime-side controller that: (1) observes short-window sequence-length and inter-arrival distributions, (2) proposes compact-batcher templates (microbatch shapes tuned for single/short sequences), (3) toggles tenant-local KV prefill strategies for fast warmstarts, and (4) when safe, applies a graded quantization fallback (q8 -> q4 progressive) gated by quality checks and rollback timers. The system is conservative by default: presets are disabled except for tenants opted-in or evaluated via the /admin/econ-sim dry-run API.

What this PR changes: added controller implementation (src/econ/pocket_autoscaler.go), compact batcher templates and presets (configs/presets/pocket-defaults.yaml), a simulation harness and a dry-run CLI for tenant evaluation (tools/simulate_pocket_prefill.py), telemetry hooks and new metrics (src/telemetry/econ_metrics.go), and docs/ops/pocket-econ.md describing behavior and runbooks. Unit and integration tests exercise the rollout and safe-rollback semantics.

Checklist: - [x] Implementation of controller and compact batch templates - [x] Simulation harness and dry-run mode - [x] Telemetry and alerts for quality regressions - [x] Feature-flag gating for rollout - [x] Docs and runbook entries - [x] Load tests against the canary pool

Backward compatibility and rollout: By default pocket-econ is feature-flagged off for all tenants. The rollout plan is: 1) enable in staging and run the simulator against production traces (dry-run) 2) enable for a small set of budget-conscious tenants behind a canary flag 3) monitor econ.unit_cost and quality.* metrics for 48 hours 4) progressively widen the cohort. If quant fallback triggers a quality regression, the controller immediately reverts to the last safe quant profile and records a quality-alert event in telemetry.

Testing: Added unit tests for compact batch selection, simulated tenant traces and an integration test that spins up a minimal serving runtime and validates latency SLOs while applying the compact-batcher and quant fallback. CI includes a simulated workload run (tools/simulate_pocket_prefill.py --seed=42 --tenants=50) that completes in ~10 minutes on CI nodes.

Risks and mitigations: The primary risk is quality regressions from quant fallback. Mitigations include staged rollouts, automatic rollback timers, and an offline Monte Carlo evaluator (tools/quant_quality_probe.py referenced in docs) that runs nightly on stored eval prompts. The controller is limited to tenant-specified max_quant_tier and global opt-out.

Related: ENG-1458 (compact batcher templates), ENG-2102 (quant fallback safety harness).
Samir Patel: LGTM overall. A few questions on telemetry cardinality — storing tenant_id tags on the heatmap metrics could increase cardinality. Can we emit a sampled tenant tag or aggregate by tenant cohort instead?
Nora Chen: Good catch. Updated econ_metrics.go to emit tenant_cohort and a sampled_tenant tag (1%) for high-cardinality debugging. See commit d4f6c13.
Lena Cho: In integration tests I saw a nondeterministic 99.9th p99.9 spike when quant fallback flipped under load. Can we add a short (150ms) safety-delay before quant changes to avoid mid-inflight degradation?
Nora Chen: Added a gated safety_delay_ms config and adjusted the controller to apply quant changes only between batch windows; updated tests to account for the delay.
Diego Alvarez: CI failed once on the simulate prefills job due to a timeout on the CI runner. After splitting the workload into shards the job passed. Recommend we keep the sharding approach for CI to keep runtime reasonable.
Nora Chen: Sharded the CI simulation and added --ci-shards option to the script; also documented recommended timeout values in docs/ops/pocket-econ.md.
Adds a tenant-aware compact batching autoscaler (pocket-econ) with safe quantization fallback profiles; default presets are non-breaking and behind a feature flag.
Feature gated; ops teams should read docs/ops/pocket-econ.md before enabling. A follow-up will add a CLI 'pocket-econ audit' that summarizes decisions per tenant.
Create canary cohort via admin API (deployed by infra)
Add nightly quant quality probe to eval pipeline
payload.title: Introduce 'pocket-econ' autoscaler and compact-batcher with safe quant fallback

payload.body:
Motivation and summary: This PR instruments a new family of 'token-heatwave' metrics to detect sustained, high-intensity token activity (short-term bursts that persist across small windows) and introduces an alert-fanout-controller that routes observability alerts through tenant-aware dampening and escalation policies. The goal is to reduce noisy pager churn from transient multi-tenant bursts while providing clear visibility for true production regressions.

What this changes (high level):
- New metrics: token_heatwave_score{tenant,route,region,model_variant} (float), token_heatwave_window_count{tenant} (int), token_heatwave_phase{stage} (label). These are emitted from the serving runtime's telemetry hook and the edge proxy sampler.
- Lightweight tracing spans: heatwave.marker spans are attached to representative traces when score > threshold to allow quick drilldown into kernel queue and kv-cache pressure.
- Alert fanout controller: a small orchestration component in observability pipeline that applies tenant SLA and recent-noise-history to decide whether to forward, delay, or aggregate alert notifications. It integrates with the existing alerting backend and supports per-tenant silencing, exponential backoff, and safe-pass-through for high-severity SLO breaches.
- Dashboard: Heatwave Explorer (Grafana) with per-tenant calendar heatmap, per-route timeline, and correlated trace links.
- Tests and docs: unit tests for the score calc, e2e smoke in dev cluster, and docs/observability/heatwave.md with runbook guidance.

Design notes:
- Heatwave score is a weighted combination of short-window token rate, consecutive-window persistence, and kernel-queue occupancy. We intentionally keep the score bounded [0,1] for easy thresholding.

Context and motivation: Customers with mid-sized tenant fleets reported uneven unit economics across SKUs despite using the same model versions. We observed hot tenants driving microburst traffic that made fixed microbatch defaults suboptimal — increasing per-token cost or violating latency SLOs during spikes. This PR adds the "Cost Refinery": a lightweight runtime component that (1) profiles short-term shape distributions, (2) suggests microbatch lane shapes, and (3) autocalibrates per-tenant quantization slabs when safe. The goal is to reduce token cost without impacting tail latency or degrading model output quality.

What this PR does (high level):
- New runtime component: cost_refinery service that runs inside the shard-manager and exposes a local gRPC endpoint for policy suggestion. It samples request shapes and KV cache hit ratios and computes candidate microbatch lanes.
- Microbatch lane slimmer: a scoring module that chooses compact batch shapes (micro, mini, pooled) per-tenant with constraints for P95 latency and minimal throughput impact.
- Quant slab autocalibrator: safe heuristic that prefers lower precision lanes (int8/4) only after simulated smoke-checks against a small eval set (configured per-tenant). Calibration happens off the hot path and records rollback traces.
- CLI: redwood econ refine --dry-run to simulate suggested defaults and export JSON presets for Console.
- Console defaults: UI hooks to preview suggested lane profiles and toggle safe-rollback flags.
- Telemetry: adds metrics: refinery.suggested_lanes, refinery.applied_lanes, refinery.rollback_count and histograms for simulated_loss_delta.
- Tests and bench: unit tests for scoring logic, integration harness with synthetic shape generator, and perf bench results included in commits.

Checklist: 
- [x] Core algorithm and runtime integration
- [x] CLI + Console preview hook
- [x] Metrics + dashboards (telemetry definitions added)
- [x] Unit and integration tests
- [x] Simulated smoke checks + rollback paths
- [x] Docs stub in /docs/infra/cost_refinery.md (will be expanded in follow-up)

Changed areas (high level):

- runtime/batcher/microbatch_slimmer.go (modified): scoring integration and fallback rules
- runtime/quant/auto_calibrator.py (new): small python harness used by integration tests and CLI
- cli/redwood-econ/refine_cmd.go (new): dry-run and apply flow with export flags
- console/defaults/cost_refinery_preview.json (new): UI preview payloads
- telemetry/metrics.yaml (modified): new metric families and dashboards
- helm/charts/redwood/values.yaml (modified): feature flag toggle enabled by default in non-production clusters
- tests/integration/cost_refinery_sim_test.go (new) and tests/perf/refinery_bench.toml (new)
- docs/infra/cost_refinery.md (new)

Commits (summary):
- 9f7a2b: initial cost_refinery service prototype, sampling + scoring
- e3b4c1: integrate microbatch_lanes suggestions into batcher decision path (safe fallback implemented)
- d12f77: quant slab autocalibrator harness + smoke-check runner (python helper)
- 5b9da0: CLI and dry-run exporter implementation (with unit tests)
- 7f4c33: add telemetry metrics and dashboard templates
- ab11e2: integration tests and perf bench artifacts; fix race in sampler
- 2c9980: docs stub and helm toggle; final test fixes

Review conversation (condensed, chronological):
- Marco Diaz (2026-01-20): "Nice direction. Two asks: (1) ensure P95 SLAs are explicitly enforced in the scoring loop (not just as a heuristic), and (2) can we avoid an extra RPC hop in the hot path?"
- Author (Sana) reply: "Added hard constraint check before applying lane suggestions and moved suggestion lookup to a cached local endpoint within shard-manager to avoid cross-shard RPCs. See commit e3b4c1."
- Liam O'Connor (2026-01-22): "Concerned about quant rollouts — need clear observability and an emergency rollback switch. Also request additional unit tests for simulated_loss_delta thresholds."
- Author reply: "Added telemetry for simulated_loss_delta and a config flag `refinery.rollback_on_loss_threshold`. Added unit tests covering threshold edge cases. See tests/integration/cost_refinery_sim_test.go."
- Priya Rao (2026-01-28): "Bench results look promising, but can we gate apply-by-default behind a cluster feature flag for 2 weeks? Also add an admin note to Console with guidance."
- Author reply: "Feature flag added in helm values; Console preview includes admin note stub. We will follow up with rollout runbook (ENG-3321)."
- CI: initial run had intermittent test failure in bench harness (flake) — fixed in ab11e2 by adding deterministic seed and small retry logic. Final CI status: pass.

Risk and mitigation: 
- Risk: quant slab changes could degrade model output quality. Mitigation: autocalibrator performs offline smoke checks and records simulated_loss_delta; any positive degradation above configured threshold is prevented from auto-applying, and the system tags the tenant for manual review.
- Risk: unexpected latency regressions when switching lanes during microbursts. Mitigation: apply uses canary window (default 5 minutes) with rollback on P95 violation and opt-in conservative mode for enterprise tenants.

Release notes (short):
- Introduces Cost Refinery: automated microbatch lane suggestion and safe quant calibration per-tenant. Adds CLI `redwood econ refine` and Console preview. Metrics added for observability. Feature gated via helm flag for staged rollout.

Motivation: slow and noisy presubmit runs and fragile release hooks were causing developer friction and occasional post-release rollbacks. This PR introduces three coordinated changes: (1) contextual lint propagation: lint runners now inherit repository context so linters run only against affected packages and their transitive boundaries, dramatically reducing noisy failures and runtime; (2) incremental test harness: a lightweight, language-agnostic harness that runs a fast subset of unit and integration tests locally and in CI by reusing cached virtualenvs/venvs and a file-change test map; (3) guarded release hook: a release orchestration step that performs staged release checks and provides an automatic safe-rollback pathway if downstream release verification fails. Summary of changes: consolidated lint entrypoints into ./ci/lint/entrypoint.sh and introduced a small Go shim (ci/lint/context-propagator) that computes impacted packages using git changed files and stored dependency metadata; added an incremental test runner (ci/test/incremental-runner.py) and a caching layer (ci/cache/test-cache-proxy) used by CI templates; refactored GitHub Actions workflows to include a lightweight "fastpath" lane that runs contextual lint + incremental tests and a full lane for merge-to-main snapshots; added a release job guard (ci/release/guarded_release_runner.go) which triggers a canary publish and wait/verify stage then either finalizes or triggers a rollback playbook; bumped eslint from 8.29.0 to 8.37.0 and pytest from 7.1.3 to 7.3.2 to pick up flaky-test fixes and new performance flags; included migration script scripts/migrate-locks.sh to reconcile package-lock/yarn.lock discrepancies and a small helper to export the change-to-test mapping (tools/gen-test-map). Backwards compatibility and rollout: changes are opt-in via repository-level config in .github/ci-config.yaml with sane defaults that preserve the existing behavior until teams flip the "fastpath_enabled" flag. Rollout plan included canary on redwood/examples and redwood-sdk-python for two weeks, then org-wide opt-in. Testing and validation: unit tests for the context propagator and guarded-release runner, integration smoke for the incremental runner, and end-to-end dry-run in ephemeral CI envs. Migration steps for integrators are documented in docs/ci/incremental-harness.md. Risks and mitigations: potential mismatch in test mapping for very large repositories was mitigated by a fallback to full test set when the mapping confidence score is low; release rollback logic has a manual confirmation toggle to avoid accidental rollbacks in emergency windows. Checklist: [x] tests added/updated [x] documentation updated [x] linear tickets linked [x] dependency bumps reviewed [x] rollout plan added. Related work: builds on ENG-4250 (presubmit fastpath proposal) and complements the presubmit cache work in ENG-4718.

Maya Chen: Addressed nits, switched canary to FASTPATH_ENABLED env toggle and documented the change in docs/ci/incremental-harness.md
Luca Moretti: Verified guarded release runner handles partial canary failures and triggers the rollback playbook; approved after small logging improvement

Context and motivation: teams building long-lived streaming integrations were repeatedly re-implementing credential fallback/rotation logic and retry heuristics across SDKs. This PR introduces a small, deterministic orchestration layer for credential presets (ambient>project>explicit precedence) plus a single typed stream facade implemented in each SDK to reduce surface area and make retry behavior consistent across languages. High-level summary of what changed and why: 1) Credential Orchestrator: a lightweight, pluggable presets engine that composes credential sources (environment, file, delegated provider, token-cache) with a deterministic precedence matrix and optional prefetch hints. This lets clients opt into a single policy and avoid ad-hoc token fallback chains. 2) Unified retry profiles: we aligned default retry windows and backoff presets for streaming vs request endpoints and exposed a small retry-profile DSL so teams can pick deterministic patterns (fast-retry|sticky-backoff|circuit-like). 3) Typed stream facade: introduce a minimal stream cursor/pullstream interface with typed message envelopes and an ergonomic async iterator/async generator mapping for py/ts/go respectively. This facade normalizes chunking, resumability, and cancel semantics so higher-level apps can be language-agnostic in their logic. 4) Compatibility/adapters: added compact adapters that translate the new facade to the older push/pull shims to minimize migration friction. 5) Version bumps: python 0.9.3 -> 0.10.0, typescript 2.7.0 -> 2.8.0, go v1.6.0 -> v1.7.0. Commits (high-level): - Add credential orchestrator core, presets, and unit tests - Implement retry-profile DSL and apply to streaming client - Add typed stream facade interface and polyglot docs/examples - Python: async iterator mapping, token prefetch hooks, docs and tests - TypeScript: async generator bridge, typed envelopes, runtime guards - Go: slim pullstream cursor, context-friendly cancelation surface, examples - Adapter shims and migration guide - Bump versions and changelogs for py/ts/go - Minor CI fixes and linting updates Files/areas touched (high-level): sdk/python/redwood_sdk/credentials.py, sdk/python/redwood_sdk/streaming/facade.py, sdk/python/setup.cfg, sdk/python/CHANGELOG.md; sdk/typescript/src/credentials/orchestrator.ts, sdk/typescript/src/stream/facade.ts, sdk/typescript/package.json, docs/sdk/streaming.md; sdk/go/cred/orchestrator.go, sdk/go/stream/facade.go, examples/multi-sdk/streaming-presets; tests/* (unit + integration). Note: diffs kept intentionally small in each file; adapters centralize most of the logic. Review conversation summary: - Diego: asked for clarity on precedence rules and suggested making file-based creds opt-in rather than default. Reply: we made file-based credentials opt-in via an explicit preset and updated docs and tests to show the safer default (env->delegated provider->prefetch cache). - Priya: asked for benchmarks on latency/regression for the typed stream wrapper. Reply: added microbench harness and CI job; end-to-end median per-chunk latency unchanged (<5ms variance). - Liam: requested stronger typing and examples for cancellation semantics. Reply: added typed envelope interfaces in TS, Python docstrings, and Go context-aware examples. Edge cases and decisions captured in CHANGELOG and inline comments. CI and validation: initial CI run showed flaky integration test in TS stream adapter (timeout on Node 16). Patch: increased default jest timeout in the adapter integration and added a short retry in the CI harness. Final CI: all checks passed (unit, linters, microbench, integration matrix on py39/py310, node16/node18, go1.19/go1.20). Migration and compatibility notes: - Existing consumers will continue to work; adapters expose old push/pull surface with a deprecation notice and a 3-release grace window. - New consumers are encouraged to use the typed facade and credential presets for simpler semantics. - For Private/Dedicated deployments that use custom KMS/HSM credential providers, we added extension hooks and an opt-in prefetch policy to avoid leaking in-memory tokens across worker processes. Checklist (items completed): - [x] Design doc attached (ENG-2141 link) - [x] Unit tests for orchestrator and facade - [x] Integration tests exercising reauth and resume scenarios - [x] Perf microbench and CI job - [x] Migration guide and examples - [x] Version bumps and changelogs for all three SDKs Backwards-incompatible risks: none for normal usage; opt-in presets and adapters provided where behavior could change. Follow-ups tracked: ENG-3209 for telemetry (emit credential-source labels and retry-profile tags), and a post-release sweep to add e2e tests for enterprise Private installer flows. Merge notes: squash-merged on 2026-02-18 after approvals from reviewers. Rationale for merge method: many small commits with iterative tests and we wanted a single changelog-friendly commit for release. Contact: reach out to the author (Maya Chen) or reviewers for rollout coordination and to opt teams into the new presets during migration windows.
Introduce credential orchestration presets and a consolidated typed stream facade across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs. Includes ergonomic API improvements, aligned retry/profile defaults, and minor version bumps for each SDK. Backwards-compatible adapter shims provided for existing consumers.

payload.body: Motivation: customer tenants with spiky traffic were experiencing larger-than-expected unit cost due to conservative batching and lack of tenant-aware fallback routing. This PR implements a Tenant Fallback Cost Orchestrator: a runtime policy layer that (1) computes a lightweight tenant-level cost signal from recent per-token latency and batch-utilization telemetry, (2) applies tenant weighting to prefer cheaper compatible model variants and relaxed batching thresholds under budget constraints, and (3) integrates a safe fallback policy to preserve latency SLOs. High-level changes: added orchestrator shim that sits between request router and model selector; tenant cost signal aggregator using existing metrics streams; new policy DSL for weighted prefill and fallback rules; integration tests and end-to-end smoke tests; a small CLI to simulate tenant budget thresholds locally. Rollout plan: gated canary on 10 internal tenants, monitor unit cost and P95 latency for 48 hours, expand to 50% of production tenants, then full deploy. Context: We continue to see tail-latency spikes during tenant churn and bursty access patterns caused by KV cache fragmentation and hotspot reallocation. The existing slab allocator biases recently-written slots and can create micro-hotspots; when combined with spillover to disk the serving scheduler experiences jitter that propagates into continuous batching windows.

Motivation: Reduce fragmentation-driven stalls and smooth spillback to disk while preserving low-latency for hot prefixes. Provide a feedback signal (frag-score) into the request scheduler so batching and prefetch decisions are aware of memory health. This PR implements a new slot-rotor allocation strategy, a soft-spillback controller ("spill smoother"), and an adaptive pager that uses frag-score telemetry to proactively page cold segments.

What this changes (high level):
- slot-rotor allocator: rotates allocation hotspots across slab lanes per-tenant so long-lived writes don't permanently pin a small set of slots; reduces local fragmentation and evictor thrashing.
- frag-score telemetry: per-tenant fragmentation metric (0..100) computed from occupancy variance, free-run lengths, and eviction churn; exposed to runtime and scheduler.
- spill smoother: rate-limited, token-bucket-based soft spillback that prevents sudden mass-eviction waves; adds hysteresis to avoid oscillation.
- adaptive pager: background paging worker uses frag-score and access heat to proactively write cold pages to spill files under controlled IO budgets; includes paged-prefetch hints for the KV hot-path.
- scheduler integration: batching windows consult frag-score to bias small-window routing away from heavily fragmented shards and to trigger conservative batching when spill risk is high.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc and benchmarks attached (link in commits)
- [x] Unit tests for allocator rotations and frag-score calc
- [x] Integration tests for spill smoothing under synthetic churn
- [x] Benchmarks: steady-state throughput, cold-start churn, and end-to-end latency under synthetic tenant churn
- [x] Metrics & dashboards added

Motivation: When investigating cost spikes we frequently saw noisy, stage-local metrics (tokenization, model_forward, kv_fetch, decode) that were individually unhelpful. This PR introduces a cross-stage visualization ('Cost Flare') that aligns per-stage token-cost and latency signals to surface correlated flares across the inference pipeline and provides an SRE playbook with automated alert suggestions to speed triage. What changed: 1) A new dashboard JSON for the Cost Flare visualization that aggregates rollups from per-stage telemetry and renders a radial heat/flare view to highlight stages with simultaneous cost/latency deviations; 2) A lightweight cost-annotation agent (telemetry/cost_annotator.go) that tags spans with stage_cost_breakdown and emits compact provenance keys so the dashboard can do low-cardinality joins; 3) An auto-suggester (telemetry/thresholds/auto_suggester.py) that examines correlated anomalies across stages and proposes an alerting bundle (thresholds + priority) in the console; 4) A playbook runbook (observability/playbooks/cost_flare_playbook.md) with reproducible triage steps and recommended SLO actions. Backwards compatibility: All new fields are optional and safely ignored by older dashboards; the annotator falls back to emitting legacy token-cost labels if per-stage data is unavailable. Testing & rollout: Unit tests and integration tests added; deployed to staging with a 24h synthetic replay; gradual canary rollout to production with a kill-switch metric. Motivation: High-frequency SLO alerts from token-level cost spikes were noisy and hard to triage because surface metrics attributed cost/latency to endpoints only. This change introduces a causal token attribution matrix that attributes token-phase cost and latency back to callsite and prompt regions and a hysteresis-based alert attenuation layer to reduce alert churn without losing signal. Scope: 1) runtime telemetry: enrich spans with token-phase attribution and causal weights; 2) metrics pipeline: aggregate causal matrices into compact histograms and per-route rollups; 3) alerting: new hysteresis DAG that applies smoothing and minimum-stability windows before firing; 4) dashboards: attribution matrix panel, per-tenant token-fingerprint sparkline, and an alert-churn diagnostics page; 5) docs and runbook: guidance for tuning hysteresis knobs. Checklist: [x] runtime span enrichment implemented [x] pipeline aggregation and compact histogram schema added [x] dashboard panels and example queries [x] unit and integration tests [x] runbook and docs update [x] CI green Context and rationale: customers running bursty LLM workloads reported repeated alerts during ephemeral token-cost surges caused by a small number of high-entropy tokens in prompt templates. The causal matrix lets us correlate which token-phase (prompt, system, candidate, post-filter) and which prompt region is responsible for downstream token cost/latency while the hysteresis layer prevents transient spikes from immediately paging on-call. Backwards compatibility: all enriched span fields are optional at ingest time; older consumers ignore the new attributes. Implementation notes: - Runtime: added a lightweight token attribution hook in the serving runtime that emits a token-attrib span tag with a compact base64-encoded vector of 4 phase weights and a 32-bit fingerprint for prompt region. - Aggregation: new pipeline stage 'causal-matrix-compactify' that quantizes and reservoir-samples attribution vectors and increments multires histograms. - Metrics: two new metric families: redwood.token_attrib.rollup and redwood.token_attrib.heatmap_count with labels route, tenant, phase, quantile_bin. - Alerting: alert hysteresis introduced as an ordered policy chain (stability-window->decay-rate->coalesce) configurable per-tenant and per-route. - Dashboards: attribution matrix uses a density heatmap with reweighted color scale and an interactive token-fingerprint drilldown that joins samples to sparse logs. - Docs: added runbook with recommended knob defaults and debugging steps. Testing: unit tests for compactifier and histogram ingestion, integration test that replays synthetic invocations and verifies alert suppression behavior, and dashboard CI snapshots. Migration: rollout is opt-in via feature flag telemetry.token_attrib.v1; default off for private deployments for 2 weeks while we validate. Related work: follows up on ENG-4201 (kv-cache profiler) and SRE-220 regarding alert fatigue. See SUP-1021 for customer-reported incidents. Commits summary: 1) Add attribution hook and serializer 2) Add pipeline compactifier and metrics exporter 3) Add alert hysteresis policy and tests 4) Dashboard panels and queries 5) Docs and runbook Changes (high-level): - runtime/trace/attr_hook.go: new token attribution hook and deterministic fingerprinting - telemetry/pipeline/compactifier.py: quantization + reservoir sampler - telemetry/metrics/exporter.go: new metrics families and mapping - observability/dashboards/token_attribution.json: new panels and templating - alerts/alert_policies.go: hysteresis policy implementation and config knobs - tests/telemetry/test_compactifier.py: unit tests - tests/integration/test_hysteresis_replay.py: integration replay test Review summary: initial review requested improvement to knob names and default window sizes. Addressed by renaming stability_window_ms -> stability_window and lowering default from 60000ms to 20000ms after a small canary run showed latency to be safe. CI: initial run had one flaky dashboard snapshot mismatch on Windows runner; fixed by normalizing timezone and re-ran. Merge: squash and merge after approvals.
Adds a causal token attribution matrix to the telemetry pipeline and new alert hysteresis logic to reduce SLO alert churn. Includes dashboard panels and docs for on-call runbooks.

Motivation: Shadow traffic is an essential signal for validating new model variants without affecting production responses, but existing shadow capture leaves a gap: when worker lag increases (slow downstream KV writes, network backpressure), shadow frames are dropped or stored incompletely leading to noisy replay and misleading metrics. This PR introduces a transparent shadow capture pipeline with lag compaction and an atomic swap path for canary handoffs so that shadow replays are deterministic and can be used directly for automated A/B gating and rollback decisions. Summary of changes: 1) shadow capture layer: non-intrusive middleware that forks in-flight requests to a compacted write-ahead buffer; captures full request metadata, prompt prefixes, routing tags, and KV-cache deltas; uses schema-v2 envelope for forward/backward compatibility; 2) lag compactor: background compaction job that coalesces batches from slow backends, dropping/annotating only strictly redundant intermediate states (configurable TTL and tolerance); 3) atomic swap adapter: when a canary passes validation, the adapter can flip serving plane traffic via commit log pointer update (atomic pointer swap) rather than gradual rebinds, preserving session stickiness and avoiding double-processing; 4) observability & safety: new metrics (shadow_capture_lag_ms, compaction_coalesced_ops, swap_commit_latency_ms), distributed trace spans and per-request sampling hooks; 5) rollout integration: new rollout strategy type "shadow-verify-and-atomic-swap" for Console and API with default safety gates (latency SLO, quality delta threshold, error budget check); 6) tests & CI: unit coverage for compactor heuristics, integration harness that replays captured shadows into a canary instance and compares deterministic outputs against golden prompt sets. Migration notes: capture pipeline uses schema-v2 but falls back to schema-v1 if peer components not upgraded; compaction parameters default to conservative values (min_ttl=15s, max_coalesce=50) to avoid premature trimming in low-traffic environments. Rollout playbook: 1) enable shadow capture on a subset of routes; 2) run shadow-verify for 24h with session-affine sampling; 3) evaluate metrics dashboard produced by this PR's recorder; 4) on pass, invoke atomic swap via Console or API to commit canary. Safety: atomic swap is gated behind an explicit commit call and requires both latency and quality gates to be green; rollback is supported via swap-rewind which replays a snapshot of the previous commit pointer and issues a graceful drain. Backwards compatibility: changes are additive; older agents ignore the new envelope and compactor is no-op if not enabled. Related work: follows on ideas from ENG-4109 (shadow-replay-stability) and complements rollout-simulator work for deterministic playback. Checklist: - [x] design doc and API sketch attached - [x] unit & integration tests - [x] dashboards and alert rules - [x] migration + playbook - [x] docs for Console surface and SDK example - [x] staged canary run and observed stable metrics (internal test cluster)

Summary: Introduces a lightweight 'kms-consent-bridge' middleware and a configurable audit redaction layer to enforce jurisdictional KMS consent and remove PII from audit payloads for regulated tenants. Motivation: customers operating across jurisdictions requested a deterministic way to ensure KMS calls honor tenant residency constraints while preserving minimal, queryable audit telemetry. This PR implements the consent handshake, residency check cache, RBAC v2 operator-scope binding to limit who can bypass consent, and a redaction policy engine that runs before audit emission.

What changed (high level commits):
- feat: add kms-consent-bridge service and gRPC API (handles consent handshake, evidence caching, primary/secondary KMS selection)
- feat: residency-checker library with pluggable backends (cloud metadata, static config, remote attestor)
- feat: audit-redactor engine (yaml policy driven) and default PII rule set
- refactor: routing middleware to call consent-bridge in pre-invoke hook; added timeout and fallback path for legacy mode
- docs: operator guide and compliance playbook with examples for EU, APAC deployments
- test: unit + e2e harness updates including simulated multi-region KMS path and audit sink assertions

Files touched (representative):
- services/kms-consent-bridge/main.go
- services/kms-consent-bridge/consent/handshake.go
- libs/residency-checker/residency.go
- runtime/middleware/kms_consent_middleware.go
- runtime/audit/redactor/redactor.go
- infra/helm/kms-consent-bridge/values.yaml
- docs/ops/jurisdictional-kms.md
- tests/e2e/consent_bridge_multi_region_test.go
- examples/operator/policies/example-redaction.yaml

Design notes:
- Consent handshake is optimistic with a short TTL cache (30s by default) and proof-of-decision record emitted as 'consent.proof' in audit metadata; customers can configure longer caching per deployment.
- Fallback behavior: if consent-bridge is unreachable, middleware enforces a tenant-configurable fail-mode: 'deny' (default for strict deployments) or 'allow-with-warning' for permissive/dev environments.
- RBAC v2 changes: introduced a new operator scope claim 'rbac:region-bypass' that must be granted explicitly via policy templates; bypass audit logs are annotated and cannot be redacted by tenant-level redaction rules.
- Audit redaction engine: policy authored in YAML supports 'remove', 'mask', and 'hash' actions per JSONPath. Default rules target common PII keys but customers can supply their own policy via the console or helm.

Checklist: [x] Unit tests added and passing locally; [x] e2e harness updated with multi-region scenario; [x] Helm chart and infra config added; [x] Docs and runbook updated; [x] Feature gated behind runtime flag `enable_jurisdictional_kms` for staged rollout.

- Author (Ayesha): "Added backoff + a `fail_mode` flag exposed via helm; default remains 'deny' for strict compliance customers. Documented tradeoffs in ops runbook."
- Diego Rivera (security): "Ensure redaction policy cannot be overridden by tenant to remove operator bypass traces."

- Priya Singh (infra): "Helm values look fine but add readiness probe and resource requests for the bridge."

Motivation: our current telemetry fanout duplicates token-level metrics across many downstream consumers which increases ingestion cost and causes noisy long-tail cardinality. This PR implements a fanout optimizer that deduplicates and buckets token emission by 'token-slot' (a lightweight shape fingerprint) and provides a deterministic attribution map so dashboards and SLOs can show per-slot cost/latency breakdowns.

This is a single continuous description but includes: design, testing, rollout, and operational notes. Design summary: 1) Introduce a telemetry fanout optimizer (server-side component) that tracks active downstream consumers and merges redundant metric emissions when semantics permit. 2) Add a token-slot attribution layer that computes a compact 8-bit slot id per invocation prefix+model-shape and attaches it as telemetry.token_slot. 3) Expose a new set of aggregated dashboards (token-slot heatmap, slot-cost waterfall) and a lightweight query-time mapping so users can drill from slot->invocations. 4) Provide runtime config with per-route fanout tolerances and fallthrough rules to preserve critical tracing for SLO-sensitive flows.

Compatibility and safety: optimizer is opt-in per-tenant by default. For tenants with strict fidelity (enterprise tier) the feature defaults to pass-through. The token-slot is purely additive metadata and is separate from any PII or prompt content; hashing is salted per-tenant and non-reversible.

Testing: unit tests for optimizer logic and slot assignment (observability/fanout/optimizer_test.go), e2e against a reduced fanout topology using ci/test/telemetry-e2e.yaml, and a small synthetic replay harness to verify no statistical bias in SLO calculations.

Rollout plan: feature flag rollout across a canary cohort (5% of traffic) -> 25% -> 100% with metrics to monitor (slot cardinality, downstream ingestion delta, alert noise). If slot-cardinality grows > 2x expected baseline for a tenant, automatically revert for that tenant.

Related work: references Linear ENG-4201 (fanout-cost reduction) and ENG-4270 (token-cost decomposition). Also complements dashboards added in PRs that introduced token heatmaps; this PR adds attribution to make those panels actionable.

Checklist: - [x] Core optimizer implementation - [x] Token-slot assignment and hashing - [x] Unit tests and integration tests - [x] Dashboard JSON for Console - [x] Docs/playbook describing operational signals - [x] Linear links and instrumentation for rollback

Motivation: streaming instability and occasional toolcall stalls during bursty writes are caused by tight coupling between route credits and the proxy write buffer. This PR separates credit accounting from IO buffering, adds a small deterministic write buffer floor, and introduces per-route fncall_writer throttles (soft backpressure tokens) to avoid head-of-line blocking for other streams. Changes: refactor credit manager to expose a decoupled credit reservation API; add StreamBufferManager with configurable min_stream_buffer_bytes and per-route soft_limit_ms; implement FncallWriterThrottle that uses leaky-bucket smoothing and hedging for slow clients; route-level config flags to opt-in for aggressive buffering on legacy routes; compatibility shim for OpenAI-compat that preserves existing handshake semantics while using new buffering logic. Tests & validation: unit tests for credit edge-cases, integration tests simulating slow TCP drains, synthetic perf runs showing tail-latency improvements, and a gradual canary rollout plan. Checklist: [x] refactor credit model [x] implement buffer manager [x] fncall throttle + hedging [x] add metrics/traces [x] e2e tests + canary rollout. Rollout plan: staged rollout to 10% gateway nodes, monitor token-drop and stream-latency dashboards for 48h, expand to 50% if no regressions, full rollout after two successful expansion steps.
Decouple route credit accounting from proxy write buffers to improve streaming stability; introduce per-route fncall writer throttles and a minimal stream buffer configuration to reduce tail latency for streaming toolcalls. No user-facing API changes.

Aisha Patel: We picked 16KB after microbenchmarks on 4xV100 clusters; it balances kernel write overhead and latency. Added benchmark numbers to docs/gateway-buffering.md.
Sofia Alvarez: Concern: hedging opens additional concurrent downstream requests; how do we bound client-side amplification?
Aisha Patel: Hedging is limited to one extra speculative write per route and only triggers when the writer queue latency exceeds soft_limit_ms. Added a circuit-breaker that disables hedging if amplification > 1.5x over window.

Motivation: developers waste time iterating on CI workflows because reproducing GitHub Actions locally is slow and caches accumulate stale entries. This PR introduces a lightweight 'ci-dryrun' shim for local validation, standardizes Action inputs across repo workflows to reduce copy/paste and surprises, and adds a conservative cache-eviction policy + an automated pruning Action to reclaim buildup. High-level summary of changes and rollout: 1) ci-dryrun: a small CLI wrapper (tools/ci/dryrun) that validates workflow inputs, runs a fast smoke execution using containerless steps (node/go shims), and verifies cache-key calculations without network access. Intended for local dev and CI maintainers. 2) Action input standardization: reworked most .github/workflows/*.yml to accept a single standardized inputs file .github/ci/inputs.yml and added a reusable composite action .github/actions/inputs-guard to verify presence and types. 3) Cache eviction policy: added scripts/scripts/cache-evict.sh and a scheduled workflow .github/workflows/cache-prune.yml that prunes caches older than 30 days but keeps recent builds; eviction policy is conservative to avoid perf regressions. 4) Dep pinning helper: a small tool tools/dep/pin-checker that warns about floating devDeps and recommends lockfile updates; hooked into PR lint. 5) Docs and onboarding: docs/dev/ci.md and tools/ci/dryrun/README.md with examples and failure modes. Compatibility and safety: default behavior is opt-in via labels; scheduled cache pruning is limited to non-shared caches used only by CI jobs. Rollback: scheduled workflow is disabled behind a feature flag (repo setting) and can be reverted by flipping .github/ci/flags.yml. Testing: ran full CI on this branch, smoke-tested ci-dryrun on macOS/Linux, ran scheduled prune on a small sandbox org. Impact: faster developer iteration, fewer accidental cache misses, and a plan to keep cache growth in check. Follow-ups: a separate PR will add metrics to Console for cache reclaim and per-run cache hit ratios.

Motivation: We need safer, workload-aware defaults for quantization and caching that map to customer SKUs (hardware tiers and capacity classes) so teams get predictable unit economics without manual tuning. This PR introduces a SKU-to-quant preset catalog, a cache-fallback degradation matrix (safe degradation paths when a preferred preset is unavailable), and a lightweight unit-economics simulator that runs on representative traces to estimate per-token cost/latency impact for each SKU/preset. Summary: - Add configs/quant_presets/sku_catalog.yml that encodes hardware SKUs -> quant profiles + recommended batching/cache settings. - Introduce a degradation matrix (configs/cache_fallbacks.yml) which defines safe downgrade steps (e.g., 8bit -> 6bit fallback with KV-cache warmup heuristics) and associated quality checkpoints. - New CLI tool tools/cost_simulator (go) that ingests a request trace, applies cataloged presets, simulates batching/caching and outputs estimated latency, GPU-time, and token-cost deltas. - Integrate telemetry: econ.simulation.* metrics and an audit event when an automatic fallback is triggered at runtime. - Platform hooks: add a new routing option sku_based_defaults in the serving config; when enabled, the router will attach the appropriate preset to a request. Design decisions: - Catalog as YAML so SRE/solutions can patch presets per-customer without code changes. - Simulator is intentionally approximate (fast single-pass sim using empirical per-token kernels) — it is meant for comparative profiling, not absolute billing. - Degradation matrix includes explicit quality checkpoints (prompt tests) and a configurable safe_threshold to avoid silent regressions. Testing & rollout: - Unit tests for catalog parsing, fallback selector, and simulator core (fast-path and edge cases). - Integration tests: small end-to-end using a sampled trace and a local serving runtime (mocked kernels) to verify metrics emission and fallback path. - Canary rollout: default off; enable sku_based_defaults for Dedicated tier in canary region for 48h and monitor econ.simulation.delta and quality.regression.* alarms. Risks & mitigations: - Risk: quant fallbacks cause regressions in specific prompts. Mitigation: quality checkpoints and auto-disable if regression > safe_threshold. - Risk: incorrect catalog mapping for custom hardware SKUs. Mitigation: lifecycle hooks for operators to override mappings, and a validation command (tools/cost_simulator --validate-catalog). Related: builds on prior work for prefilling/batching heuristics (see ENG-1467) and compliments the economizer recommendations. Checklist: - [x] Catalog format defined - [x] Simulator CLI implemented - [x] Degradation matrix schema + validator - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Telemetry hooks - [x] Docs updated (docs/ops/sku-quant-presets.md)

Context: This PR implements two complementary compliance controls requested by Governance and several SRE customers: (1) a policy-ageing validator that enforces explicit freshness on RBAC v2 bindings (prevents accepting bindings older than a configurable TTL unless explicitly renewed), and (2) an audit-retention mapper that annotates outgoing audit events with retention metadata based on tenant residency claims and KMS key-region scoping.

Motivation: customers operating under varying residency regulations required both signal-level TTL for bindings (to limit blast radius of long-lived grants) and stronger audit retention metadata to drive downstream retention enforcement (on log storage and export pipelines).

What changed:
- core/policy/ageing_validator.go: new validator that plugs into the policy admission pipeline. It verifies the binding.issued_at and binding.last_renewed timestamps, applies per-namespace and per-tenant TTL policies, and emits structured policy.validation_reason tags for observability.
- core/policy/ageing_validator_test.go: unit tests covering edge cases (missing timestamps, future timestamps, renew-within-grace).
- core/policy/config/config_schema.yaml: added policy.ageing.ttl defaults and per-tenant override knobs.
- audit/retention/mapper.go: new component that maps tenancy/residency claims + KMS key-region to a retention_bucket label (short, medium, long, sovereign). Mapper exposes a stable TTL and retention_policy_id that the log-forwarder consumes.
- audit/retention/mapper_integration_test.go: integration tests simulating cross-region keys and tenant claims.
- infra/helm/templates/audit-config.yaml: template flags to turn on mapper or set defaults per-environment.
- docs/security/policy-ageing-and-retention.md: design doc and operator runbook (rollback, migration steps, FAQ).
- small changes in k8s/webhook/deployment.yaml and tests to wire the validator into the admission webhook ordering.

Migration and rollout:
- Default behaviour is OFF for existing customers; flagged on per-org via feature-flag and config override.
- When enabled, the admission webhook rejects RBAC bindings that fail the TTL check with a clear error and guidance on renewal.
- A migration tool (scripts/migrate/renewal-assist.sh) is added to surface potentially stale bindings and allow bulk renew in a controlled window.

Security/KMS interactions:
- Mapper consults KMS key metadata (region and provider) via the existing kms/metadata client; if key metadata is unavailable, mapper will conservatively tag events as "unknown-region" and put them into a short retention bucket until operator review.
- Validator requires secure time (NTP) on control-plane nodes; added note in docs and a liveness probe to alert if time skew exceeds threshold.

Testing:
- Local unit/integration tests added; CI runs the policy and audit test suites (some tests previously flakey were hardened).
- Load testing: added a small canary harness that exercises the admission path with bursts (~1k rps) to ensure latency regression <5ms median.

Backwards compatibility & risks:
- No breaking API changes to user-facing endpoints.
- There is risk of accidental mass-reject if TTL defaults are set too low; mitigation: defaults off, and migration tool + dry-run mode.
- Mapper adds a new top-level audit label (retention_bucket); downstream log processors must ignore unknown labels (we added compatibility shims in the forwarder).

Docs & operator runbook:
- docs/security/policy-ageing-and-retention.md contains rollout checklist, helm values, troubleshooting tips, and sample renewal commands.

Related: Linear ENG-4052 (policy-aged-binding UX) and ENG-4091 (audit retention mapping).

Checklist: [x] Unit tests added [x] Integration tests added [x] Docs updated [x] Feature-flag gating [x] Migration script included
Adds a policy-ageing validator to prevent stale RBAC bindings from being accepted and a configurable audit-retention mapper that annotates audit events with retention buckets based on data residency and regulatory profiles.

Validator enforces time-based rules; to avoid denial-of-service due to clock skew, nodes must run NTP. Mapper uses KMS metadata read-only; it does not alter keys. If KMS metadata fetch fails, mapper conservatively tags events as unknown-region rather than blocking audit writes. All new components are covered by existing RBAC for control-plane services.

Context: Customers frequently ask for safe, automated defaults to reduce per-token cost without regressing latency or accuracy. Existing heuristics (separate prefill and quant suggestion flows) required manual tuning and had limited visibility into unit economics across workloads. Motivation: Provide a single lightweight service (econ-advisor) that analyzes short workload samples, recommends a hybrid prefill strategy (mix of prefix-prefill and opportunistic microbatching) and a set of candidate quantization profiles with estimated unit-econ impact and a safety score. What this PR does (summary): 1) Introduces services/econ_advisor: analysis pipeline, candidate generator, safety evaluator and a lightweight REST endpoint used by the console and the runtime. 2) Adds runtime hooks in serving/batcher to accept advisory hints: suggested prefill ratios, preferred microbatch size, and quant profile id. 3) Adds quant-profile catalog integration and a cost-estimator module that emits per-request estimated delta cost and expected latency variance. 4) Adds observability: new metrics (econ.advisor.safety_score, econ.advisor.estimated_pct_cost_change, econ.advisor.recommendation_source), tracing spans and a small dashboard template. 5) Adds unit and integration tests and a canary rollout plan (feature flag + canary by tenant). Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-7123) - [x] Backend implementation of advisor pipeline - [x] Runtime hook and backward-compatible opt-in - [x] Unit tests for advisor sampling and safety evaluator - [x] Integration tests against a synthetic workload sampler - [x] Console integration (read-only recommendation endpoint) - [x] Basic dashboard panels and alerts - [x] Canary rollout config and migration notes - [x] Documentation snippets + quickstart example How to exercise locally: run services/econ_advisor locally (scripts/start_econ_advisor.sh) and use postman to POST sampled workload payloads to /v1/recommend. The runtime has an env flag REDWOOD_ECON_ADVISOR_URL to point to a local instance for canary testing. Migration/compatibility notes: All runtime changes are opt-in and default to existing behavior. The quant-profile registry is read-only by default; advisor outputs are suggestions stored in a tenant-scoped recommendations table. We included a dry-run mode that emits metrics but doesn't apply changes. Commits included below and a short list of changed files. CI: initial lint failure (unused import in serving/batcher) fixed in follow-up commit. All tests (unit+integration) are green on the final run. Merge: squashed and merged to main after 1 approval and one request-for-changes addressed.
Adds an automated econ-advisor service that recommends hybrid prefill and quant profiles with safety scoring and telemetry. Opt-in canary rollout, no default behavior changes.
Adds an automated cost advisor that synthesizes hybrid prefill heuristics and quantization profile selection based on workload samples. Backwards-compatible: disabled by default and gated behind feature flags and canary rollout.

Motivation: many tenants have bursty, shape-varying request patterns that are poorly served by single static minibatch configurations. This PR introduces two coordinated components: (1) Microshape Advisor, a runtime service that observes per-tenant sequence-length and concurrency distributions and recommends microbatch shapes (microbatch size, stride, KV split hints) optimized for latency/cost tradeoffs; (2) QuantBank, a small internal registry of validated quantization profiles annotated with compatibility fingerprints and safe-rollout constraints. Together they enable automated, tenant-aware recommendations and staged quant rollouts with guardrails. Summary of changes: added runtime Microshape Advisor + agent shim, QuantBank API and CLI, controller logic to join Advisor recommendations with existing autoscaling rules, recommendation serializer for the Console, a lightweight simulation harness for unit-econ impact estimation, docs and migration notes, and tests. Rollout plan: feature gated behind experimental.microshape and experimental.quantbank; start as read-only recommendations in console for selected tenants, then enable automated suggestions (opt-in) and finally enable auto-apply for low-risk profiles after 2 weeks of telemetry. Backwards compatibility: all public endpoints are additive and default to current behavior when the flags are off. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (Linear ENG-4321) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Simulation harness & example tenant profile - [x] Docs & Console wiring - [x] Feature flags - [x] Safety gates for quant rollouts Safety and testing: QuantBank entries require a signed compatibility fingerprint (model architecture, tokenizer hash, quant backend) and a staged rollout plan (canary percent, min-successful-requests). The Microshape Advisor runs with a conservative default that never raises microbatch size above tenant-configured max. Telemetry: new metrics microshape.recommendation.count, quantbank.rollout.progress, sim.unit_econ.delta; tracing spans for advisor decision points. Known limitations: advisor currently uses a sampling window of 10k requests and may be slow to converge for very small tenants; simulation assumes stationary arrival distributions. Future work: extend advisor to recommend KV caching windows and to feed batched kernel selection for FPGA/TPU profiles. Please see the Design doc link in Linear for simulation details.
Adds a Microshape Advisor service to recommend tenant-specific microbatch shapes and a QuantBank service to store vetted quantization profiles with safe rollout metadata; behind feature flag; no breaking API changes.

payload.body:
Context: Several customers and internal canaries reported intermittent failures when using the OpenAI-compatible streaming endpoint: partial JSON payloads or tool/function call sentinel events arriving out of order after network fragmentation or aggressive proxy chunking. The root cause is ambiguous fragment splice handling in the streaming parser: when a JSON boundary or toolcall sentinel sits on a chunk boundary, the previous reassembly logic would sometimes accept a premature end or delay a toolcall event, causing malformed JSON or function-call ordering regressions.

Motivation: Robustness of the streaming API is critical for downstream SDKs and tool call semantics. This change tightens the streaming reassembly window and introduces explicit boundary anchoring heuristics so event boundaries are preserved even when fragments arrive split or reordered by intermediate layers. It also avoids reconstructing partial JSON strings across non-deterministic chunk cuts without verification.

What I changed (high level):
- Introduced a FragmentAnchor table keyed by stream-id + monotonically-increasing span-id to detect and reconcile overlapping fragment ranges.
- Added an idempotent reassembly pass that validates JSON/bracket depth and string literal state before emitting a completed message. If ambiguity remains, we delay emission until a checksum or sentinel frames the span.
- Added sentinel-level ordering guarantees for tool/function-call handoff: toolcall events are now emitted only after their complete argument span is validated and reassembled; we add a short ack-window to ensure downstream router has accepted the previous fragment when applicable.
- Tightened delimiter handling: the parser no longer treats consecutive newlines as an atomic event boundary when inside a JSON string or unclosed brace/array; it now consults depth and escape-state to decide.
- Implemented end-to-end tests and a new fuzz harness simulating chunk reordering, CRLF/\n splits, and mid-utf8 boundary cuts.
- Added regression tests that reproduce customer canary failures and assert stable ordering of toolcall events.

Checklist: 
- [x] Unit tests for fragment reassembly and delimiter heuristics
- [x] Fuzz tests for chunk reordering and mid-codepoint splits
- [x] Integration tests covering function/tool call sequences over streaming API
- [x] Benchmarked (no measurable latency regression on typical workloads)
- [x] Docs note for compatibility layer changes (internal)

Commits (summary):
- 7f2c3d1: introduce FragmentAnchor and reassembly state machine; core parser hooks
- b3a1f5e: add checksum guard and sentinel ack window for toolcall handoff
- c4d2a9b: tighten delimiter logic to consult depth and escape state
- e8f7c11: integration tests reproducing reported canary failure; add fuzz harness
- 9aabb33: small refactor and error message improvements; add metrics for reassembly requeues

Files changed (high level):
- internal/streaming/parser/reassembly.go (new logic for fragment anchoring and checksum guards)
- internal/streaming/parser/delimiter.go (depth/escape-aware delimiter handling)
- internal/streaming/handshake/toolhandoff.go (ack-window and ordering guards for toolcall events)
- sdk/openai_compat/streaming_integration_test.go (integration reproduction tests)
- test/fuzz/chunk_reorder_fuzz.go (fuzz harness)
- telemetry/metrics/reassembly_metrics.yaml (new metrics)
- docs/internal/compat/streaming-frag-reassembly.md (design notes)
- Makefile / CI config tweaks to run fuzz target in nightly jobs

Small illustrative snippet (parser guard):
- Previously: emit on double-newline unconditionally
- Now: if depth != 0 or in_string == true then buffer until validated by checksum/sentinel

Review conversation (high level):
- Miguel: "Can we avoid increasing latency for small messages?"
  - Lina: "Microbenchmarked the common path; if fragments are complete the fast-path short-circuits and emission cost is unchanged. Only ambiguous cases hit the new verification window."
- Ravi: "What about proxies that re-chunk aggressively and reorder? Any state explosion risk?"
  - Lina: "FragmentAnchor coalesces adjacent spans and we cap anchor table size per-stream; we also emit a metric when we evict anchors to trigger investigation rather than silently failing."
- Aisha: "Add a test for a 3-way out-of-order reassembly where toolcall lands ahead of content."
  - Lina: "Added test 'TestToolcallOrderingThreeWay' to integration suite; it asserts stable ordering and that no toolcall is applied without its payload."

CI & Stability: Initial CI run surfaced a flaky fuzz target (timeout) that caused a rerun. After increasing the timeout and a small harness fix the full CI run passed (unit, integration, lint, format, fuzz-nightly). The changelist also adds a nightly fuzz job to track regressions.

Merge outcome: Merged to main via squash merge on 2025-02-13 after approval from reviewers and CI passing. No manual rollbacks required; canary rollout to hosted API showed no errors in 48h window.

Notes for SDK teams: The OpenAI-compat streaming semantics are preserved at the API level, but SDKs should observe the new ordering guarantees (toolcall events will not be emitted until validated). This is backward-compatible but may change the interleaving timing in pathological proxy cases; we've added notes to internal SDK release checklists.

Follow-ups (open items):
- Monitor new metrics (reassembly.evictions, reassembly.requeues) for two weeks and create alerts if rates climb above threshold.
- Consider exposing a diagnostic header in the streaming response for high-sensitivity customers to help debug reassembly failures in the field.

References: ENG-5432 (bug triage), ENG-5460 (streaming reliability epic), internal canary incident #INC-2025-01-28-07

Fixes an intermittent streaming parser bug where message fragments split across TCP/HTTP chunk boundaries could produce malformed JSON or reorder function/tool-call sentinel events. Improves reassembly heuristics and adds defensive checks to avoid toolcall misdelivery. No API contract changes.
Miguel Santos: Can we avoid increasing latency for small messages?
Lina Chen: Fast-path unchanged for complete fragments; only ambiguous cases hit verification window.
Ravi Kapoor: Any state explosion risk if proxies reorder?
Lina Chen: Anchor table capped per-stream; we emit eviction metrics to surface issues.
Aisha Karim: Add test for 3-way out-of-order toolcall ordering.
Lina Chen: Added TestToolcallOrderingThreeWay to integration suite.
