Context: Customers using the OpenAI-compatible invoke path observed two classes of failures when integrating third-party tool registries: (1) tooling ecosystems with variant names/aliases for the same logical tool (for example 'calendar.create' vs 'calendar.create_event') caused deterministic tool_choice mismatches; (2) streaming payload fragmentation could drop trailing schema fields resulting in invalid tool messages at the runtime boundary, which surfaced as hard failures for structured output. Motivation: Reduce customer friction when mapping external tool schemas into Redwood's canonical invoke model and improve streaming resilience without changing the existing OpenAI-compatible wire protocol. Goals: (A) provide a configurable alias map that normalizes incoming tool identifiers and signature metadata to canonical tool ids used by Redwood's router and executor; (B) add a lightweight fragment-repair heuristic that detects repeated partial fragments and attempts safe coalescing/repair before rejecting a tool invocation; (C) surface telemetry for alias mappings and repair decisions to help operators tune alias tables and detect problematic tool providers. Design summary: Alias resolution is implemented as a deterministic pre-dispatch step in openai_compat.invoke_adapter. A new optional config section openai_compat.alias_map allows key/value pairs where keys are external identifiers and values are canonical redwood tool ids. Aliasing also accepts glob-style patterns for common prefixes and an allowlist mode. The fragment repair logic lives in pkg/streaming/fragment_repair.go and runs in the streaming demux pipeline: when a tool invocation event arrives with a truncated JSON payload, the repairer will attempt four non-destructive fixes in order: 1) join with immediately preceding fragment(s) if timestamps indicate same logical chunk; 2) append closing braces/brackets if only syntactic closure is missing; 3) reconcile duplicate keys by preferring canonical tool signature fields; 4) fall back to invoking the tool with the original payload but attach a repair_hint header and emit a warning metric. All repairs are opt-in via openai_compat.enable_fragment_repair and limited by a per-request repair budget to avoid latency amplification. Implementation notes: - Introduced openai_compat.alias_resolver service with a small in-memory trie for fast lookup and pattern matching, with a periodic refresh hook to re-read alias config from the control plane without restart. - Kept the canonical tool signature canonicalization path intact to preserve existing provenance and telemetry; alias resolver returns both canonical_id and matched_key for provenance. - Added unit and integration tests covering exact matches, pattern matches, and ambiguous alias tiebreakers where the resolver emits a tie metric and uses longest-prefix. - Fragment repair includes deterministic invariants to ensure we never synthesize new typed fields; repairs only close structural tokens or coalesce fragments that share the same call_id and monotonic offsets. Rollout plan: Feature is behind two flags: openai_compat.enable_aliasing (default false) and openai_compat.enable_fragment_repair (default false). Plan is staged rollout: enable aliasing for a small set of customers first (canary group), monitor alias_hits, alias_mismatches, and any increased tool invocation latencies; then enable fragment_repair in a further canary where streaming truncation incidents were previously reported. Telemetry & observability: New metrics: openai_compat.alias.resolved_total, openai_compat.alias.tiebreak_total, openai_compat.fragment_repair.attempt_total, openai_compat.fragment_repair.success_total, and openai_compat.fragment_repair.fallback_total. Each repair emits a trace span with repair.kind and repair.cost_ms. A new per-request header X-OpenAI-Alias-Match carries matched_key for downstream auditing. Backwards compatibility: Default behavior unchanged when flags are off. Alias map is additive and never mutates incoming tool payloads. Fragment repair is limited by conservative heuristics to avoid changing semantics. Related work: aligns with ENG-3671 (tool schema normalization) and borrows the fragment coalescing approach from earlier streaming fixes in perf-canary. Security considerations: Alias configuration is treated as config plane data and requires admin role; repaired payloads are logged only at debug level to avoid leaking PII in production logs. Checklist: - [x] Alias resolver implementation and unit tests - [x] Fragment repair pipeline and integration tests - [x] Telemetry + dashboards - [x] Docs update and config examples - [x] Rollout playbook in PR description Tests and CI: All new unit tests added under tests/openai_compat and tests/streaming passed locally. E2E against the invoke harness showed no regressions on the happy path and reduced error rate for previously failing tool providers by ~86%. Gradle build and lint passed; some flaky e2e steps failed in the first CI run and were retried, final CI green. Merge notes: Squash-merged after a short reviewer thread and one follow-up hotfix commit to allow pattern precedence override.
Introduce configurable tool-alias mapping for OpenAI invoke compatibility and a heuristic stream fragment repair path to mitigate truncated tool payloads during streaming; opt-in via openai_compat.enable_aliasing
Ethan Miller (2025-11-13): Nice approach. Two asks: add a tie-break metric and allow explicit precedence for pattern keys. Can you also ensure alias resolution is O(1) for common prefixes?
Priya Shah (2025-11-13): Addressed both. Added openai_compat.alias.tiebreak_total and implemented longest-prefix with optional precedence override via pattern_precedence in config. Trie lookup now uses a shallow prefix cache for O(1) path in hot loops.
Sofia Alvarez (2025-11-14): Fragment repair looks safe but please add a test that ensures we never add new typed fields when repairing. Also document the repair budget behavior.
Priya Shah (2025-11-14): Added explicit test ensuring no new keys are synthesized and documented repair_budget semantics in the config docs.
Liam O'Connor (2025-11-15): CI flaked on one e2e, reran and green. Approving pending the small formatting nit in docs.
Priya Shah (2025-11-15): Fixed docs nit and pushed final test coverage report.

Motivation: Continuous batching scheduler occasionally starves small, latency-sensitive queues when KV-heavy or long-seq requests dominate. Prior fixes focused on static slot reservations and deadline nudging; those reduce starvation but either waste capacity or increase p50. This PR implements a proportional-share pacing allocator plus a stochastic probe escrow that injects small, jittered probe windows to detect under-served queues and re-balance without large reserved slots. Design: 1) Each queue is assigned a lightweight weight computed from a configurable priority + recent serviced tokens (EWMA). The allocator computes proportional token budgets per scheduling epoch which guide admission and slice sizes. 2) A probe escrow is maintained as a small fractional budget (configurable, default 3% of epoch tokens) split into jittered micro-windows that are opportunistically offered to candidate queues that have had low recent service. Probes are intentionally stochastic to avoid synchronized bursts across workers. 3) When a probe window uncovers backlog, the allocator temporarily bumps the queue weight for the next N epochs to allow draining; if the queue is empty, escrow is re-credited. 4) Integration with KV cache: probes are lightweight and attempt to warm the KV pin for the queue without triggering full model inflations; the KV-prefetch hint path was extended to be probe-aware and marked in traces. 5) Observability: new metrics: scheduler.queue_ewma_tokens, scheduler.probe_escrow_utilization, scheduler.probe_hits, scheduler.probe_misses. Implementation notes: - Runtime changes are limited to scheduler/core and scheduler/allocator modules. - Added a micro state machine for probes to avoid re-entrancy and races across worker threads. - Kept the continuous-batcher admission contract identical (no public API changes). Tests and performance: - Microbench: synthetic mix of 80% large KV-pin requests (seq len 2048, heavy KV accesses) + 20% small latency-sensitive requests (seq len 32). - Canary run in perf-canary harness across 8 GPUs, 10k rps sustained for 30 minutes. Results: p50 latency ~unchanged (-2ms), p95 improved by ~6ms, p99 improved by ~28ms in mixed load compared to baseline with static soft reservations; throughput unchanged within 1%. Starvation incidents detected by SLO checker dropped from 16 to 1 per hour in this workload. KV cache hit-rate remained within noise (+0.3%). Backwards compatibility and operational controls: - Feature gated behind runtime flag scheduler.proportional_pacing.enabled=false by default in older clusters; enabled in canary. - Two tuning knobs exposed: scheduler.proportional_pacing.escrow_fraction and scheduler.proportional_pacing.jitter_window_ms. - Default knobs selected after grid search described in the PR. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked in Linear ENG-3281 - [x] Unit tests for allocator math and EWMA updates - [x] Integration test in perf-canary - [x] Metrics and tracing added - [x] Feature flag + rollout plan Commits summary: - Add proportional pacing allocator and EWMA bookkeeping - Implement stochastic probe escrow and microstate machine - KV prefetch probe path and trace/span tagging - Add metrics, dashboards, and alerts - Tests: unit and perf harness integration - Fix race in probe state transitions (addressed during review) Changed files (high level): - scheduler/core/allocator.go - scheduler/core/allocator_test.go - scheduler/probes/probe_escrow.go - scheduler/probes/probe_escrow_test.go - scheduler/kv/probe_prefetch.go - runtime/config/schema.yaml - observability/metrics/scheduler.prom - docs/ops/scheduler-tuning.md - perf-canary/config/pacing-canary.yaml Small illustrative snippet: "func allocateEpoch(tokens int) map[string]int { // proportional share based on weight EWMA ... }" Review conversation: "Jordan Kim: Overall nice design. Please add a clear invariant comment about escrow re-crediting to avoid surprises during preemption.; Priya Rao: Added invariant comments and a unit test covering preemption and re-credit in probe_escrow_test.go.; Diego Martinez: Found a race when two workers try to claim the same probe window; could cause double-service of lightweight probes and corrupt EWMA counters.; Priya Rao: Fixed by introducing a CAS-backed probe lease and added test; also added an integration canary that reproduces the scenario.; Sofia Nguyen: Can we expose probe metrics at token granularity and add a dashboard tile?; Priya Rao: Metrics added and a Grafana tile in observability/dashboards/scheduler-probes.json; added alert scheduler.probe_escrow_utilization_high (warn) to ops runbook.; Jordan Kim: CI flaky on perf-canary step (timing-dependent) — reran and it passed.; Diego Martinez: Approved after fixes.; Jordan Kim: Approved and requested squash merge.; Release manager: Merged via squash and bumped runtime minor version.
Introduce proportional per-queue pacing and stochastic probe escrow to mitigate starvation and reduce p99 tail latency under mixed KV-heavy workloads. No API changes.
payload.title: Proportional fair pacing with stochastic probe escrow to reduce queue starvation

payload.body:
## Summary
This PR introduces the first cut of the **hardware tuning profile** schema (v1) and a strict JSON validation path for profile packs. The goal is to make profile changes safe-by-default: profiles are versioned, validated at load time, and unknown/invalid keys do not silently apply.

This is the foundation for the HW tuning profiles pack effort (H100/L40S first; B200 gated separately).

## Motivation
We’ve repeatedly seen (a) config drift between runtime defaults vs. tuned presets and (b) subtle mistakes in manually-edited JSON (typos, wrong types, missing required fields) that turn into tail latency regressions or OOMs during rollout.

We need:
- A stable, documented schema (what keys exist; what ranges are allowed)
- Clear compatibility rules (profile version vs runtime version)
- A safe failure mode (log + metric + fallback) rather than partial application
- Tests that pin the contract so downstream rollouts don’t break

## What’s included
### 1) Profile schema (v1)
- New file: `runtime/config/hardware_profiles/schema/hardware_profile.schema.json`
- Enforces:
  - `schema_version` (string, currently `"1"`)
  - `profile_id` (stable identifier; required)
  - `display_name` (human readable)
  - `target` block (GPU selector + optional qualifiers)
  - `compatibility` block (min/max runtime)
  - `knobs` block (scheduler/kernel/memory namespaces)
  - `defaults_behavior` (explicit handling of omitted fields)

### 2) Strict JSON validation + error messages
- Loader now validates against the schema before any knob application.
- Unknown keys are rejected **by default** (prevents silent typos).
- Validation errors include path + expected type/range.

Failure mode:
- If a profile fails validation, runtime:
  - emits `WARN` with error summary and profile_id
  - increments `runtime.profile.validation_failed_total{reason=...}`
  - falls back to runtime hard-coded defaults (no partial application)

### 3) In-code docs for supported keys + deprecation strategy
- Added a doc block in `runtime/config/hardware_profiles/README.md` describing:
  - Allowed keys in `knobs.*` namespaces
  - Range constraints and units
  - How new keys are introduced
  - How keys are deprecated (two-phase: warn-only -> reject)

Deprecation strategy (v1):
- Mark deprecated keys in schema via `"x-redwood-deprecated": true` (non-standard extension)
- Loader behavior:
  - Phase A: allow + warn (counts metric `runtime.profile.deprecated_key_used_total{key=...}`)
  - Phase B: reject (schema bump required)

### 4) Unit tests
- Golden tests for:
  - minimal valid profile
  - invalid type (string vs int)
  - out-of-range values
  - unknown keys
  - deprecated key warning behavior (Phase A)
- Snapshot-style output for validation error formatting.

## Non-goals / Not included
- No default profiles shipped in this PR.
- No runtime selection logic (that’s in follow-up PR ENG-4823 / pr-21991).
- No canary gates / dashboards changes here.

## Implementation details
### Supported namespaces (initial)
- `knobs.scheduler.*`
  - `continuous_batching.enabled` (bool)
  - `queue.max_depth` (int, 1..100000)
  - `prefill_decode_fairness.mode` (enum: `"auto"|"balanced"|"throughput"`)
  - `backpressure.target_p95_ms` (int, 50..20000)
- `knobs.kv_cache.*`
  - `budget.mode` (enum: `"auto"|"fixed"`)
  - `budget.fixed_gib` (number, 1..200)
  - `eviction.policy` (enum: `"none"|"lru"|"age"`)
- `knobs.kernels.*`
  - `autoselect.enabled` (bool)
  - `seq_len_buckets` (array of ints, sorted asc, 1..32768)

Note: We’re intentionally constraining keys early to reduce unsafe surface area. The schema can evolve once we’ve validated the rollout process.

### Compatibility
Profile includes:
- `compatibility.runtime_min` (e.g. `"1.18.0"`)
- `compatibility.runtime_max` (optional; use for breaking changes)

The loader checks compatibility and fails closed (log + metric + fallback) if runtime is out of range.

### Example profile (from tests)
```
{
  "schema_version": "1",
  "profile_id": "h100-balanced-v1",
  "display_name": "H100 balanced (v1)",
  "target": {"gpu": {"vendor": "nvidia", "sku": "H100"}},
  "compatibility": {"runtime_min": "1.18.0"},
  "knobs": {
    "scheduler": {"prefill_decode_fairness": {"mode": "balanced"}},
    "kv_cache": {"budget": {"mode": "auto"}},
    "kernels": {"autoselect": {"enabled": true}}
  }
}
```

## Testing
- `bazel test //runtime/config/hardware_profiles:all`
- `bazel test //runtime/config:config_validation_tests`
- Added CI job `runtime-config-validate` to run schema validation tests.

## Rollout / risk
Low-risk by itself since no profiles are enabled yet.
- Loader validation is only invoked when a profile pack is provided.
- When invoked, failures fallback to defaults (no partial application).

## Follow-ups
- ENG-4823 / pr-21991: hardware detection + profile selection + override precedence
- ENG-4824/4825/4826: ship H100/L40S presets + B200 experimental flag

---
### Commits
1. `add hardware profile json schema (v1)`
2. `runtime: validate profile pack against schema before applying knobs`
3. `config: add validation error formatting + metrics`
4. `tests: add golden fixtures for valid/invalid profile packs`
5. `docs: add supported keys + deprecation policy`
Benji Okafor: Can we ensure we never partially apply knobs when validation fails? The loader currently merges defaults then validates. I'd prefer validate first, then apply.
Ethan Park (author): Good call. Updated flow to: parse -> validate -> apply. Also added test to ensure no knobs are applied when validation fails.

Noah Patel: Please add a stable definition for unknown keys behavior. Today strict rejection is correct, but we’ll need a transition plan for older packs.
Ethan Park: Added `defaults_behavior` and documented the policy: strict by default. For future we can introduce `unknown_keys: warn` behind a schema bump, but not in v1.

Quentin Harris: Compatibility logic should handle runtime versions with pre-release tags. Are we parsing semver properly?
Ethan Park: Switched to our existing semver parser (`runtime/util/semver.h`). Added tests for `1.18.0-rc.1` comparisons.

Sofia Ivanova: For scheduler knobs, can we avoid freezing too many values per SKU? Please keep the initial schema minimal.
Ethan Park: Agreed; reduced scheduler surface area to 4 fields and removed a few candidate knobs (prefill chunk sizing, per-route queue weights) until we have more data.

Allison Grant: Metrics naming: prefer `runtime.profile.*` (singular) and add a label for `profile_id` where possible.
Ethan Park: Updated names + labels; added `profile_id` label to deprecated-key and validation-failed counters.

Approvals:
- Benji Okafor: Approved after flow change + tests
- Noah Patel: Approved
- Quentin Harris: Approved
- Allison Grant: Approved
Adds versioned hardware tuning profile schema + strict validation in runtime config loader. Invalid profiles fail closed with clear error and safe fallback to runtime defaults. Includes unit tests + docs for supported keys and deprecation process.

Motivation: production users reported long tail stalls when clients lost connectivity and reconnected immediately; the service would keep inflight resources for the previous session until server lease expired which increased latency and token waste. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: 1) a lightweight fast-fail reconnect probe that lets clients detect a stale server session lease and trigger a low-cost soft-abort locally, and 2) a small persistent commit-log per-stream (bounded to 64 entries) that records checkpoint metadata (prefix hash, last acked index, tool-call idempotency tokens) to allow deterministic client-led resume without server-side full session replay. Design constraints: keep OpenAI-compat streaming semantics intact, maintain idempotency for function/tool calls, and ensure no unbounded server memory growth. Implementation: added stream/commitlog service (inference/runtime/commitlog.go) implementing an append-only, ring-backed append with TTL eviction and metadata compaction; added probe handshake extension to the websocket/streaming protocol (api/compat/stream_probe.go) with two-phase probe: SYN (client) -> SYN-ACK (server lease + lease-version) -> FAST-ACK (client decision to continue or soft-abort). On soft-abort clients are instructed to issue a resume token against the commit-log rather than relying solely on server KV-cache. API compatibility: handshake extension is optional and backward compatible; servers that do not understand probe will continue to behave as today. Migration and rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag stream.fast_fail_probe (default off). QA & rollout plan: unit + e2e tests included, staged deploy to canary cluster for 48h, followed by region ramp. Checklist: [x] design doc linked (Linear ENG-2048) [x] unit tests [x] e2e stream recovery tests [x] SDK updates queued (Python/TS) [x] docs update (api/streaming.md) Related: addresses customer SUP-4821 and reduces incident recurrence for INC-2026. For reviewers: focus on (a) lease/version handling race conditions, (b) commit-log eviction semantics, (c) tool-call idempotency guarantees during resume.
Introduces a fast-fail reconnect probe to reduce client-observed stall windows; adds a small persistent commit-log for stream resume checkpoints; no API breaking changes; rollout: gradual 5%->50%->100% across regions; note: requires client SDK patch for best results.
Unit tests cover commitlog append/evict and token epoch semantics. E2E includes simulated client disconnects at random offsets with network partitioning; validated tool-call exactly-once constraints via idempotency tokens. Load tests show <1% additional p99 latency for handshake on warm sessions and 20-40ms improvement in median recovery time in tested scenarios.
Enable runtime flag stream.fast_fail_probe=false in canary, then enable true on 5% of nodes. Ensure SDKs are updated in client releases to include probe support; clients without SDK update will continue using legacy behavior. Operators: monitor metrics stream.probe.* and stream.resume.fail_rate and rollback if resume.fail_rate > 0.1%.
Arjun Patel: Left a couple of nits around the commit-log compaction window; main concern is what happens when a client holds on to a resume token past the ring wrap; suggestion: attach token generation epoch and validate against lease-version. Author (Maya): responded that tokens include epoch and the server validates token. Added tests for epoch mismatch.
Lena Ortiz: Asked for clarity on metrics - added counters for probe-sent, probe-accepted, probe-rejected, soft-aborts, resume-success/failure; please confirm labels and dashboards. Author: added metrics and dashboard PR pointer.
Tomás Rivera: Observed a potential race where server lease refresh could happen concurrently with probe SYN processing causing a false-reject and client unnecessary soft-abort. Requested a small retry window on the server side (100ms) and documented in code comments. Author: implemented and added integration test that simulates lease refresh race.
This PR is intentionally conservative: probe is opt-in and commit-log size is bounded. Follow-up tasks: SDK patches merge (PRs queued in redwood-sdk-python and redwood-sdk-typescript), add optional encrypted commit-log for Private deployments, and add diagnostic traces for lease-version mismatches.
payload.title: Stream resilience: fast-fail reconnect probe and persistent commit-log for client-led resumes

Motivation: long-tail latency and cost spikes are often concentrated in a small set of request cohorts (similar prompts, chains, or multi-turn patterns) but existing rollups blend them away. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) a 'latency cohorting' layer that buckets requests by a lightweight signature (prompt fingerprint + sequence-length class + model-variant) and produces cohort-level token latency/cost histograms; 2) a telemetry-bridge that correlates serving spans to billing units (model shards, quantization profile, and GPU type) so cost attribution can be broken down by both request cohort and infra dimension. What changed: added a cohorting aggregator that runs as an optional stage in the router pipeline; extended span tags to include cohort_id, billing_unit, quant_profile and hw_class; introduced a new compact histogram type (reservoir-slab) for cohorted token latency and cost; added a telemetry bridge service that enriches traces with billing metadata and emits cohort+billing rollups to metrics and to the observability events index. Included a new set of dashboards (Cohorts: latency & cost explorer, Cohort SLO decomposition) and a smaller alerting surface: dynamic per-cohort SLO scaling rules and adaptive suppression for noisy low-volume cohorts. Rollout plan: feature-gated behind rollout flag obs.cohorting.enabled=false by default; staged rollout to 10% traffic, then 50%, then 100% following perf validation. Checklist: - implement cohort id and deterministic fingerprinting - add span enrichment and telemetry bridge - add reservoir-slab histogram implementation and aggregation keys - expose metrics (cohort.token_latency.pXX,p50,p90,p99, cohort.token_cost.sum,count) - add dashboards and alert rules - tests (unit + e2e with synthetic replay) - documentation updates and migration notes for Query APIs Backwards compatibility: cohorting is opt-in; spans without cohort tags continue to be indexed normally. Performance: the cohorting stage uses a bounded in-memory LRU and is optimized to avoid per-token allocations; we ran local load tests with 5000 rps where CPU overhead stayed under 3% and memory within limits. Risks & mitigations: added a watchdog that disables cohorting if reservoir allocations exceed configured thresholds; billing correlation is best-effort and falls back to existing per-request cost tags. Related: follows up on ENG-5274 (cost-attribution proto) and complements ENG-7213 (slo decomposition).
Miguel Ortega: Can we make the fingerprint stable across restarts? Suggest storing the salt in config and falling back to a deterministic default.
Asha Iyer (author): replied: added persisted salt in router config (see aggregator.go) and documented migration implications.
Samantha Park: The reservoir implementation needs a deterministic seeding strategy for reproducible A/B comparisons.
Asha Iyer (author): replied: seeding is wired to cohort_id+namespace; added unit tests to validate determinism.
Daniel Kim: Alerting rules look noisy at low volume. Can we add an adaptive suppression window?
Asha Iyer (author): replied: added adaptive suppression and a configurable min_volume threshold; updated alert docs and dashboard annotations.
SRE Bot: CI initially failed on lint for logs—fix incoming.
Asha Iyer (author): pushed fix for logging format and re-ran CI. CI passed.
Added optional latency cohorting and a telemetry bridge for cohort+billing cost attribution. New dashboards and adaptive per-cohort SLO rules. Opt-in via obs.cohorting.enabled and rollout flags. Notes: cohort IDs are persisted; downstream consumers should tolerate missing cohort tags for older traces.
Unit tests added for fingerprinting and reservoir-slab determinism. E2E synthetic replay covers long-tail scenarios and validates that cohort SLOs trigger suppression as designed. Local load tests at 5k rps measured <3% CPU overhead when enabled. Observability team validated dashboard panels and alert suppression behavior.
Feature-flagged rollout: start with obs.cohorting.enabled=false. Canary: enable for 10% traffic in us-west for 48h, monitor cohort.rollup.latency and cohort.rollup.memory. If stable, expand to 50% for 72h then 100%. Watchdog will auto-disable if reservoir memory > 80% of configured budget or if trace enrichment latencies exceed 50ms p99.
Focus reviews on: (1) correctness and stability of fingerprinting across restarts; (2) reservoir memory/CPU characteristics under synthetic long-tail workloads; (3) alert suppression logic and the default thresholds; (4) SDK trace enrichment impact on client latency. I've included tests and dashboards to help validate these points.

Motivation: provide an operator-friendly way to validate RBAC v2 and KMS region constraints against real traffic patterns before rolling policy changes live, and to centralize consent gating for KMS operations. This PR ships three coordinated pieces: 1) a lightweight policy-simulator service that can ingest a sample of request events and evaluate RBAC v2 + KMS region rules to surface likely denials or silent fallbacks; 2) a KMS Consent Orchestrator that standardizes consent checks and short-circuiting for CMK operations (used by private deployments and Dedicated) and emits structured audit events; 3) an RBAC Safelist Scanner that runs periodically to detect overly permissive role bindings and suggests scoped replacements. Changes: added new services/policy-simulator (service, CLI, API), services/kms-consent-orchestrator (engine, adapters for AWS/GCP/Azure, tests), pkg/rbac/safelist_scanner.go and ruleset definitions, small infra updates (terraform module to grant simulator read-only event stream access), and docs/security/policy-simulator.md with runbook and examples. Checklist: - [x] Design doc: Linear ENG-4321 linked - [x] Unit tests for simulator rule evaluation - [x] Integration tests for orchestrator w/ mock KMS providers - [x] End-to-end smoke in staging - [x] Docs and runbook added - [x] Security review and threat model completed Key behaviors and notes: the simulator runs in dry-run mode by default and emits a per-request decision with reasons (missing role, region mismatch, consent-missing). The orchestrator exposes a consent API that returns a stable consent token used by downstream KMS adapters; tokens are short-lived and audited. The safelist scanner runs weekly and produces suggested remediations (JSON output) that can be consumed by infra teams. Backwards compatibility: all host-facing APIs are opt-in; no runtime changes to existing KMS flows unless the orchestrator is explicitly enabled in config. Rollout plan: feature flag behind release/tenant toggles, start with internal tenants, run simulator on 1% of traffic for two weeks, then increase to 25% while monitoring audit delta. Related: SUP-1123 (customer reported inconsistent region errors), ENG-4210 (observability hook for policy decisions). Risks & mitigations: increased audit volume — added batched audit forwarder and sampling config; potential latency in KMS path — orchestrator runs async consent validation for non-critical ops and provides fallback. Impact: improves compliance posture (clearer region pinning failures), reduces human error during RBAC updates, and enables safe rollout of stricter KMS scoping. Please see docs/security/policy-simulator.md and design/ENG-4321 for full details.

Introduce progressive pressure relief (soft per-route eviction and regional handoff); add `dampened-open` circuit state to reduce thrash; new runtime knobs: pressure_window_ms, handoff_fraction, dampen_backoff_ms; canary rollout to 5% of traffic; no API changes.
Motivation: During a recent maintenance window we observed tightly-coupled bursts across regions that triggered rapid circuit flips and cascading failovers. The consequence was unpredictable latency spikes for low-priority routes and unnecessary cross-region failover churn. This hotfix implements a progressive pressure relief strategy and a safer regional handoff path to reduce thrash while preserving SLOs.

What this PR does (single-line sections for compatibility): Implements a progressive pressure relief controller in the serving scheduler that: (1) applies a soft, per-route eviction curve instead of immediate hard drops; (2) introduces ephemeral capacity leases to allow short warm-up windows; (3) provides a regional handoff path that moves low-priority traffic to a neighboring region with backoff and telemetry; (4) adds a new circuit state `dampened-open` that waits an exponential dampen_backoff_ms before re-evaluating reopen; (5) exposes three runtime knobs: pressure_window_ms, handoff_fraction, dampen_backoff_ms for safe tuning.

Files changed: scheduler core, circuit state machine, config schema, unit + integration tests, runtime docs, canary rollout script.

Why this is safe: changes are additive and guarded by feature flags. Default behavior remains unchanged until the feature flag is enabled. Canary rollout plan included.

Testing and rollout: unit tests for eviction curve and lease expiry added; integration test simulates cross-region burst and verifies reduced handoff rate and fewer circuit flips; metrics and tracing added for pressure_events, handoff_decisions, dampened_open_count. Canary ran for 48h at 5% traffic in eu-west-1 with no increase in error-rate and a 42% reduction in circuit reopen events.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc attached (ENG-8421) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Canary script and dashboard queries - [x] Feature flag gating and default off - [x] Backwards-compatible config changes - [x] Ops runbook update (brief note in docs)

Rollout plan: 1) merge to main behind feature flag; 2) enable 5% canary in eu-west-1 for 24-48h; 3) monitor pressure_events, handoff_decisions, p95 latency for affected routes; 4) scale canary gradually to 25% and then 100% if stable.

Related: SUP-4123 (incident), ENG-8421 (design), follow-up task: ENG-8622 to add tenancy-aware handoff budgeting.
Arjun Patel: Great direction. Two quick asks — 1) add a metric that counts lease preemptions, 2) ensure the handoff path sets tracing tags for origin_region so we can filter traces. Without those it will be hard to debug post-rollout.
Author (Maya Chen): Added lease_preemptions counter and tracing tags in a follow-up commit (see b1f6c9a). Integration tests assert presence of tags.
Leah Romero: Race condition concern in controller.go line 218 where the lease expiry can collide with scheduler refill. Please add a mutex or document why it's safe.
Author (Maya Chen): Switched the lease map to use the existing scheduler lock (refactor commit d4e2a7f), added comment and unit that reproduces prior race locally.

payload.body:
## Context
Enterprise Private + Dedicated customers asked for verifiable, auditable runtime artifacts for the LTS channel (checksums, provenance, and a documented verification procedure). Today we publish images/tarballs but do not consistently ship machine-readable metadata that maps artifacts back to a commit + build environment.

This PR adds:
- SHA256 checksum generation for runtime artifacts (images + tarballs) with a stable manifest format
- Provenance metadata (build inputs + source commit + builder identity) emitted as a JSON sidecar per artifact
- A small verification guide aimed at enterprise distribution (how to validate checksums and map artifacts back to a git SHA/tag)

This is a prerequisite for Private installer pinning + "auditable release artifacts" in the LTS spec.

## What’s included
### 1) Checksum manifests
For each runtime release build we now produce:
- `<artifact>.sha256` (single-line sha256sum output)
- `runtime-artifacts-<version>.checksums.txt` (aggregate manifest)

Manifest format is intentionally compatible with standard tooling:
- generated via `sha256sum` style output (`<sha>  <filename>`)
- sorted by filename for stable diffs

### 2) Provenance JSON sidecars
Each artifact also gets a provenance sidecar:
- `<artifact>.provenance.json`

Fields included (v1):
- `source_repo`, `source_ref`, `source_commit`
- `build_id` (CI run id) + `builder` (workflow name)
- `created_at` (UTC)
- `dockerfile_digest` (when applicable)
- `toolchain` (compiler/tool versions we already pin in CI)

NOTE: This is not a full SLSA attestation yet; it’s a deterministic, auditable metadata block that we can evolve. (Follow-up will evaluate cosign/GitHub provenance once signing key management is finalized.)

### 3) Docs: verification procedure
Adds `docs/runtime/lts/artifact-verification.md` that covers:
- verifying aggregate checksum manifests
- verifying individual `.sha256` files
- validating provenance fields (commit/tag match, build id match)
- how Private customers can store manifests in their change-control/audit systems

## Implementation details
- New script: `tools/release/generate_artifact_metadata.py`
  - Inputs: artifact directory + release version + git commit
  - Outputs: `.sha256`, `.checksums.txt`, `.provenance.json`
- Updated release CI workflow for release branches to call metadata generation after packaging and before publish.
- Publish step now uploads metadata files alongside artifacts to the same release bucket/path.

## Example outputs
Aggregate checksum manifest snippet:
`e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855  runtime-1.18.1-lts-linux-amd64.tar.gz`

Provenance snippet:
`{"source_repo":"redwood","source_ref":"refs/tags/runtime-1.18.1-lts","source_commit":"3f2c9b1e...","builder":"release-ci/runtime-release","build_id":"12988421","created_at":"2025-03-02T18:44:10Z","toolchain":"cuda=12.4, gcc=11.4, python=3.11"}`

## Rollout / compatibility
- No runtime behavior changes.
- Hosted/Dedicated unaffected except improved artifacts.
- Private: installer/helm work will consume these manifests in follow-up PRs (ENG-4827 / ENG-4828).

## Security / threat model notes
- Checksums protect against accidental corruption and enable customer-side validation.
- Provenance is intended to support auditability and internal change control.
- This PR does not add signing. We will treat signing as a separate step once key custody / CI access controls are finalized.

## Checklist
- [x] Works for main + release/* branches
- [x] Metadata generation is deterministic for identical inputs
- [x] CI uploads metadata to the same destination as artifacts
- [x] Docs added for enterprise verification
- [x] Release eng reviewed

## Follow-ups
- Add optional signing of manifests (cosign or internal KMS-backed signing)
- Extend provenance schema to include SBOM pointer once SBOM generation lands for LTS builds
- Wire Private installer to enforce checksum verification by default

Links: ENG-4832, SUP-18506, INT-3302
Connor O'Brien (review): Can we ensure the checksum manifest is stable across runners? Sorting + consistent newline handling matters for diffs and for customer change-control.
Sahana Iyer (author): Yep. Updated generator to sort by filename and force LF newlines. Added a unit test that snapshots manifest output ordering.
Dr. Aisha Rahman (review): Please avoid claiming this is SLSA provenance in docs. Also add a note about trust boundaries (checksum != signature).
Sahana Iyer (author): Updated docs to call it "provenance metadata" and added a section clarifying checksum vs signing, plus a follow-up for signing once key custody is resolved.
Bruno Silva (review): For Private installer consumption, we’ll need a single URL we can embed. Can we keep the aggregate manifest name consistent across patches?
Sahana Iyer (author): Kept it versioned but stable: `runtime-artifacts-<version>.checksums.txt` plus per-artifact `.sha256`. We can also add a `latest.checksums.txt` alias later if needed; not doing that in this PR to avoid confusing caching behavior.
Sean Gallagher (review): CI incident: publish permissions. Confirm we’re not widening bucket write access for workflows beyond release branches.
Sahana Iyer (author): Confirmed. Token scope is restricted to the `runtime-releases/*` prefix and the workflow only runs on `release/*` and tag builds. Added a note in the workflow comments.

Title: Optimize scheduler knob defaults for mixed prefill/decode workloads

Context
During the FP8/INT8 benchmarking sprint we saw several cases where microbench wins (kernel runtime) did not translate cleanly to end-to-end improvements in the hosted runtime under mixed workloads (concurrent requests with a realistic prefill/decode mix). The main failure mode was scheduler-induced head-of-line effects: decode-heavy phases could keep the GPU busy, but TTFT (and TTFT p95 in particular) regressed because prefill admission and batching windows were tuned for "throughput-first" steady-state rather than mixed interactive traffic.

This PR updates the default scheduler knob set for the "mixed" workload profile to better realize kernel wins without paying a TTFT tail penalty. Changes were validated against the v3 top-hosted benchmark suite and compared to baseline scheduler defaults.

What changed (high level)
1) Batching window defaults (mixed profile)
- Reduce default batching_window_ms in the mixed profile (and enforce tighter min/max bounds) to reduce time spent accumulating batches when there is steady decode pressure.
- Add small jitter compensation in the batching window calculation to avoid oscillation when queue depth hovers around the batching threshold.

2) Backpressure defaults (mixed profile)
- Adjust backpressure to consider both queue depth and in-flight token budget, rather than queue depth alone.
- Increase sensitivity to decode saturation so prefill does not starve indefinitely behind decode microbatches.

3) Prefill admission / fairness tweaks
- Add a lightweight fairness guard for prefill admission when decode utilization is high, prioritizing at least one prefill "slot" per scheduling cycle (when safe) to keep TTFT p95 bounded.
- Keep the existing safety checks (OOM guardrails, max in-flight tokens) and preserve current behavior for pure prefill or pure decode profiles.

4) Observability additions
- Export scheduler window and queue depth stats needed to explain benchmark deltas and to tune canary thresholds (dimensions: model, gpu_sku, kernel_mode, scheduler_profile).

Rollout / safety
- This is gated behind a server-side flag: runtime.scheduler.profile=mixed_v2 (default remains mixed_v1 until canary results are green).
- Intended rollout sequence (aligned with ENG-7431): enable in perf canary first for top-hosted models on H100/A100 in one region cohort; monitor TTFT/TPOT + error rate; then expand regions.

Benchmark results (summary)
Bench suite: top-hosted-models-benchmark-suite-v3 mixed profile (prefill/decode mix, prompt length distribution, concurrency sweep). GPU: H100 and A100. Kernel modes: baseline / FP8 / INT8 where supported.
- Primary outcome: reduced TTFT p95 variance and recovered end-to-end gains from FP8/INT8 kernels in mixed scenarios.
- Typical improvements (mixed workloads, medium concurrency): TTFT p95 -6% to -14% vs mixed_v1 with negligible TPOT impact; in several cases TPOT improved slightly due to reduced scheduler oscillation.
- Guardrail outcome: no statistically significant regressions in error rate or GPU OOM incidence across runs; GPU utilization remained within expected bounds.
Notes: raw numbers and run IDs are linked from ENG-7428 artifacts; this PR intentionally does not embed benchmark tables to avoid drift.

Key files
- serving/runtime/scheduler/defaults.cc: introduce mixed_v2 defaults and bounds
- serving/runtime/scheduler/admission_control.cc: prefill fairness guard (mixed only)
- serving/runtime/scheduler/backpressure.cc: token-budget-aware backpressure thresholds
- serving/runtime/metrics/scheduler_metrics.cc: new histograms + tags
- benchmarks/e2e/configs/mixed_workload_v3/*.yaml: updated profiles used by benchmark-lab
- docs/internal/scheduler-knobs.md: definition + rationale + override guide

Review notes / discussion highlights
- Sofia requested we keep the fairness change narrowly scoped to mixed profile and add a kill-switch. Implemented: mixed_v2 only + flag-controlled.
- Omar asked for evidence that TPOT does not regress at higher concurrency. Added an additional concurrency sweep (64/96) in the benchmark config and updated expected ranges.
- Julian requested metric names and tags match the canary dashboards. Updated to use the standard kernel_mode/model/gpu_sku tags and added scheduler_profile.
- Rafael asked for explicit rollback triggers. Added to docs: revert to mixed_v1 via flag if TTFT p95 +8% sustained for 15m or if error rate +0.2% absolute.

Checklist
- [x] Benchmarked on H100 + A100 (mixed v3 scenarios)
- [x] No config-breaking changes (backward-compat aliases kept)
- [x] Added observability hooks needed for canary
- [x] Added docs + rollout notes

CI
Buildkite: runtime unit tests, scheduler tests, lint, benchmark config validation.

Co-authored-by: Marcus Reed (metrics tags + scheduler tests)

Merge
Squash merge into main; follow-up tracked in ENG-7431 to enable mixed_v2 in perf canary and expand cohorts after 24h stability.
Sofia Ivanova (review): The direction makes sense, but I want to avoid changing global defaults without a tight gate. Can we keep this scoped to a new mixed profile and make rollout flag-only initially?
Lena Fischer (author): Yep. I split the defaults into mixed_v2 and left mixed_v1 unchanged. Added runtime.scheduler.profile=mixed_v2 flag and documented rollback.
Omar El-Sayed (review): Any TPOT regressions at high concurrency? The earlier thread showed oscillation; want to ensure we’re not just shifting load.
Lena Fischer (author): Added 64/96 concurrency sweep to the benchmark config; TPOT is flat to slightly better. Linked run IDs in the PR description and added expected ranges to config validation.
Julian Moore (review): Metrics: can you tag by scheduler_profile and kernel_mode? The canary dashboard slices need that to attribute changes.
Marcus Reed (co-author): Updated metrics tagging (model/gpu_sku/kernel_mode/scheduler_profile) and added histograms for batching_window_ms and queue_depth to correlate.
Rafael Mendes (review): Please add explicit rollback triggers to docs so SRE can action quickly during canary.
Lena Fischer (author): Added rollback section (TTFT p95 +8% sustained 15m, or error rate +0.2% abs) and linked the runbook section we use for perf canary.

Motivation: Customers running Private deployments asked for a small, auditable control-plane tool to assert and prove per-operator residency decisions and to attribute KMS usage back to operator tokens. This PR introduces a lightweight CLI 'residency-guard' for operator-side residency checks and an audit-fanout adapter that tags and routes KMS usage events into the audit pipeline. The goal is minimal runtime footprint, clear audit trails, and compatibility with existing RBAC v2 enforcement and the private-installer flow.

Changes:
1) residency-guard CLI (Go): validates operator claims, enforces geozone mappings, consults residency policy cache, and emits signed proof blobs for downstream KMS allocation.
2) kms-usage-attributor (adapter): receives proof blobs and attaches operator-scoped attribution metadata to KMS request envelopes; forwards enriched audit events to audit-fanout (supports both Kafka and HTTP sink).
3) RBAC v2 shim updates: add an attribute matcher for operator.region_hint and operator_tier to allow conditional policy paths.
4) Tests and integration harness: unit tests for policy evaluation, e2e harness stubs for Private installer compatibility, CI job additions.
5) Docs: CLI quickstart and operator checklist.

Commits:

- b6d2a11: kms-usage-attributor adapter and audit-fanout integration (Kafka + HTTP)
- 3f1e00c: RBAC v2 attribute matcher and policy examples

- cmd/residency-guard/main.go (CLI entrypoint)

- Priya: flagged potential race in policy cache refresh during failover; asked for a short-term fix plus TODO for cache topology work. Author reply: implemented lock-free refresh with copy-on-write semantics and added integration test that simulates failover timing.
- Liam: asked to keep the CLI binary small and avoid importing heavy Kafka client into core binary. Author reply: split adapter as separate module and provided lightweight HTTP-only mode for operators that prefer it.
- Security review: Snyk scan indicated an indirect dep flagged; bumped the dep and re-ran tests.

CI summary: New CI job (ci-residency-guard) runs unit, lint, and a short e2e harness against a local mock KMS + audit sink. First run: lint error fixed in commit d2a7f9f; second run: all checks green.

Migration notes:

- Private-installer hook path added; operators must install the CLI on control-plane nodes and configure the residency-hook in the installer manifest.
- Backwards compatibility: adapters accept empty proof blobs but will mark events as unauthenticated (policy decision still enforced server-side).

Rollout plan:
1) Merge to main and deploy adapter in shadow mode to audit pipeline.
2) Ship CLI as beta on private-installer channel and notify enterprise customers.
3) Enable RBAC attribute matcher in a staged canary (10% traffic) then full rollout.

Release notes: Adds "residency-guard" CLI to assert operator residency and a kms-usage-attributor adapter that enriches audit events with operator-scoped KMS attribution. See docs/enterprise/operator-residency-quickstart.md for setup instructions.

Why this is different: Existing residency and KMS work focused on server-side decisioning and routing. This change introduces a small, auditable operator-side assertor and an explicit attribution path into the audit pipeline to aid forensic tracing and compliance reporting.
Diego: Please add explicit version header to proof blobs and ensure strict parsing to avoid silent failures.
Maya: Added header 'RGF-v1' and verification bounds in internal/proofs/signer.go; updated unit tests.
Priya: Policy cache refresh can race during leader failover; consider lock-free refresh.

Verify that audit events contain 'operator_id' and 'operator_region' attributes and that the signed_proof header validates.

payload.body:
Motivation: Large tensor-parallel (TP) workloads still show intermittent stalls due to uncoordinated KV prefetches and sharp NCCL allreduce bursts that perturb kernel scheduling. This PR introduces two complementary runtime mechanisms: a KV prefetch gating policy (prefetch gate) that smooths prefetch issuance across microbatches and a windowed reduce smoother that spaces and coalesces NCCL allreduce launches into a small time window to reduce peak peer load. The goals are lower tail latency, fewer NCCL retries/backoffs, and more consistent GPU utilization without changing model semantics.

Summary of changes: - Add a lightweight prefetch gate state machine in the TP runtime controlling KVCACHE prefetch issuance across continuous-batching microbatches. The gate uses a per-device token bucket and a microbatch-aware budget; when tokens are low it delays prefetches by up to one microbatch and marks the request as "gated" so the scheduler can reorder non-dependent launches. - Implement a windowed reduce smoother: reduces are enqueued into a short (configurable) window and coalesced if compatible (matching dtype, tensor size class, same comm group). The smoother then issues fewer, slightly larger NCCL allreduce ops with staggered offsets to limit instantaneous link saturation. - Introduce a soft NCCL submit jitterer to break pathological simultaneous launches from many ranks (tiny random seed per-GPU). Unlike previous coarse throttlers this jitter maintains throughput but flattens instantaneous concurrency spikes. - Add metrics, tracing spans, and assertion hooks: prefetch_gate.state, prefetch_gate.gated_count, reduce_smoother.coalesced_bytes, reduce_smoother.coalesced_ops, nccl.submit_jitter_ms distribution, and a new trace event when a prefetch is deferred. - Provide runtime knobs exposed via existing config system and Redwood Console: tp.prefetch_gate.enabled, tp.prefetch_gate.bucket_rate, tp.reduce_smoother.window_ms, tp.reduce_smoother.coalesce_threshold_bytes, tp.reduce_smoother.enabled, tp.nccl_jitter.enabled.

Design notes and rationale: - We observed bursts when many ranks with similar microbatch timing simultaneously issued KVCACHE prefetches and then launched compute kernels. The bursts pushed NCCL into busy-retry states and caused uneven stream scheduling. - Prefetch gating is intentionally conservative: it never blocks prefetches that are on the critical path (detected via dependency analysis), only delays best-effort prefetches and exposes that information to the scheduler so they can be interleaved. - The reduce smoother coalesces only when the tensors are in the same size "class" and the combined op remains within a safe NCCL payload size; we fall back to original allreduce otherwise. This avoids subtle numerical or ordering changes. - The jitterer is small (0..3ms default) and is applied only when the submit rate crossing a threshold is detected; it has negligible effect on throughput but measurably reduces simultaneous NCCL launches in stress tests.

Benchmark summary (internal perf lab): - Setup: 8xA100 per node, 4 nodes, TP world size 32, model: 25B decoder-only, sequence 2048, continuous batching microbatch=8, payload mix skewed to trailing-token KV reads. - Baseline: end-to-end 99th percentile step latency = 184ms, NCCL retries observed in 15% of steps, outlier GPU utilization oscillation +/- 12% across rank. - With this PR enabled (default config): 99th percentile step latency = 152ms (~17% tail reduction), NCCL retries reduced to 3% of steps, utilization oscillation +/- 5%. Average token throughput unchanged (<1% variance). - Ablation: turning off reduce_smoother but keeping gate removed 60% of tail improvement, indicating both components are important. Additional microbenchmarks show coalescing reduced number of distinct allreduce ops by ~28% and average coalesced op size increased by 1.4x.

Files changed (high level): - runtime/tp/prefetch_gate.{cc,h} new state machine and thin API hooks - runtime/tp/reduce_smoother.{cc,h} coalescer and window manager - runtime/tp/nccl_jitter.cc minor submission wrapper - runtime/tp/scheduler.cc scheduling policy changes to consider gated prefetches - runtime/metrics/metrics_registry.cc add metrics - tests/tp/prefetch_gate_test.cc new unit tests - bench/lab/tp_prefetch_windowed_reduce.yaml bench config in perf-lab - docs/ops/tp_runtime.md updated with knobs and rollout guidance

Commits (summary): - commit 1: initial prefetch_gate state machine and unit tests - commit 2: reduce_smoother coalescer implementation + compatibility checks - commit 3: nccl_jitter small submission wrapper and knobs - commit 4: scheduler integration and reorder heuristics - commit 5: metrics, tracing, docs, and perf config

Testing and CI: - Added unit tests covering gating semantics (gated vs critical prefetch), coalescing acceptance/rejection rules, and nccl_jitter boundaries. - Perf lab jobs (bench/tp_prefetch_windowed_reduce) were run nightly during validation. - CI: build and unit tests passed; one flaky integration test (tp_scheduler_reorder) was observed on older CUDA driver images and we added a retry in the harness.

Rollout plan: - Feature is behind tp.prefetch_gate.enabled and tp.reduce_smoother.enabled (both default on for dedicated/perf lab builds, off for older release branches). - Canary rollout on Dedicated pools in us-west-2 for customers running TP >= 1.12, ramp to 10% traffic for 48h, evaluate tail SLOs and NCCL error telemetry, then 100% if stable. - Console exposes the metrics and a built-in perf-dashboard linked to the bench config.

Risks and mitigation: - Coalescing could mask pathological tensor-size mixes that previously serialized differently; mitigated by compatibility checks and conservative thresholds. - Interaction with third-party NCCL versions: validated on NCCL 2.14/2.18 and Nvidia-driver 525/535; kept knob per-node to disable jitter/smoother. - If a customer observes degraded accuracy (unlikely due to no algorithmic changes), we provide an immediate config switch to restore prior behavior.

Related work: Builds on previous efforts to reduce comm spikes (see related PRs listed internally) but differs by combining a prefetch-aware scheduler signal with a light-weight coalescing window and low-latency jitter rather than bulk throttling.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests added - [x] Perf benchmarks ran and results attached - [x] Docs updated with runtime knobs - [x] Config gated and safe to rollback - [x] Reviewed by TP and SRE leads

If merged: Add a short runbook entry in docs/ops/rollback.md describing the two knobs and the path to disable them.
Arjun: Can the gate decision be made cheaper? Suggest inline fast-path for common case.
Author (Nina): added an inline fast-path in prefetch_gate.cc to avoid allocation on hot path.
Claire: Please add a console dashboard note and a guardrail for reduce coalescing in ops docs.
Author (Nina): docs updated and added 'coalesce_threshold_bytes' explanation.
Diego: observed a flake on tp_scheduler_reorder on older cuda images; added retry in test harness.
Arjun: LGTM after CI pass and perf numbers in bench job verified.
payload.title: Prefetch Gate and Windowed Reduce Smoother for TP runtime

Context: multiple consumer teams reported small inconsistencies between SDKs when migrating long-lived streaming integrations and when swapping credential sources. This PR harmonizes a small set of primitives: CredentialPreset (name + policy), default retry presets, and streaming consumer UX for pause/resume/peek. It also addresses a subtle token-rotation race in the Go connector discovered during dedicated capacity tests.

What this PR does (high level):
- Introduces CredentialPreset objects across Py/TS/Go with identical public fields and a stable serialization shape for config injection.
- Exposes a lightweight "preset" selection on client constructors (e.g. Client(preset="low-latency")).
- Normalizes retry preset names (fast, balanced, conservative) and aligns default backoff windows and jitter.
- Unifies streaming consumer primitives: async iterator resume(), peek(n) helper, and explicit close/abort semantics.
- Fixes token rotation race in Go connector when multiple goroutines refresh the same session token; added a central in-process lease map.
- Small ergonomics follow-ups: improved error types, more helpful docstrings, and parity test additions across SDKs.

Checklist: [x] API design doc (ENG-1128) referenced [x] Tests added across SDKs [x] Changelog entries [x] Version bump commits [x] CI green (flaky test retried once)

Risks / migration notes: all changes are additive or backwards-compatible; retry preset renames include mapping table for older names. Streaming consumer changes preserve previous semantics but add optional helpers—no forced migration.

Full change summary below and short notes for release engineering.
Aligned credential preset APIs across Python/TypeScript/Go, improved streaming consumer ergonomics (resume/peek semantics), clarified retry preset defaults and bumped SDK versions: py 1.12.0, ts 1.8.3, go v1.5.0. Non-breaking; migration notes included.
7 commits: initial credential-preset cross-SDK definitions; py/ts/go client constructors accept 'preset' param; retry preset normalization & mapping; streaming consumer API additions and tests; Go token lease implementation and unit tests; docs + changelogs; version bumps and release artifacts.
Reviewer feedback focused on naming consistency and tests covering token rotation under concurrency. Kenji requested a small refactor to the Go lease map for clearer invariants; addressed in commit 5 with additional unit tests. Motivation: Production SREs and customers asked for a compact dashboard widget that surfaces per-route and per-tenant cost signal trends alongside an explainability view for fat-tail latency/cost spikes. Large existing dashboards are useful for deep-dive but too noisy for paging UIs and small consoles. This PR introduces a lightweight 'cost-sparkline' panel plus a correlated 'fat-tail latency explainer' widget that links sampled traces and derived root-cause labels.

What changed (high level): Added derived metrics and dashboard assets, light-weight trace-tag propagation for sampled traces, and instrumented a tail-cause derivation that tags spans with a categorical label (kv_cache_miss|large_request|quant_tier|model_fallback). The UI panel shows a compact 7-day sparkline with min/median/p95/p99 overlaid and a small inline attribution summary (percent of tail events attributed to each cause). The explainer panel surfaces a sampled trace list and a heatmap correlating request size, kv cache hit rate, and quantization tier with tail latency.

Files and areas touched: telemetry/metrics/derived_cost.py (new): derives telemetry.cost_sparkline and telemetry.tail_cause_score; observability/grafana/panels/cost_sparkline.json (new): compact panel with sparkline + attribution summary; observability/grafana/panels/tail_explainer.json (new): explainer panel referencing trace links; otel/propagation/fast-sampling-propagator.patch: small change to attach sample tags for lightweight back-linking; tests/test_cost_sparkline.py: unit and integration snapshot tests; docs/observability/README.md: usage and dashboard placement guidance.

Commits summary: - 7 commits, squashed on merge. Key commits: 1) derive: add cost_sparkline and tail_cause_score metrics (unit-tested) 2) ui: add compact sparkline and explainer dashboard panels 3) infra: propagate sampling tags into trace headers 4) tests: dashboard snapshot + integration fixture for synthetic tenant workloads 5) docs: observability guidance and alert tuning notes.

Compatibility and performance: The derived metrics are computed in the metrics ingestion pipeline as a lightweight aggregation (rolling 1h->7d rollup); they add a small CPU footprint (benchmarked at ~0.4% additional CPU on ingestion workers for our internal test load). The trace propagation change is opt-in behind a feature toggle (observability.experimental.lightweight_tail_links) to avoid increasing cardinality by default.

Alerting and SLO ties: Updated rule suggestions in docs to use the new sparkline as a compact signal for oncall pages. Added guidance to switch from strict p99 thresholding to a probabilistic alert that combines p95 drift + tail attribution weight so teams only page when tail composition shifts toward KV misses or model fallback.

Testing and rollout: Unit tests added for metric derivation and attribution edge cases. Dashboard snapshots validated in CI (grafana-lint + JSON schema). Staged rollout: feature toggle off by default, enabled for internal dev orgs for 48h smoke, then ramped to staging tenants.

Backwards compatibility: No breaking API changes. Dashboard JSON is additive. Feature is off by default to prevent noisy signals for customers with high-cardinality labels.

Related: ENG-1998 (drive adoption of compact observability panels), SUP-721 (customer report about opaque cost spikes).
Evan Brooks (reviewer): Nice compact panel design; please double-check cardinality of new labels and ensure we aggregate by tenant_id to avoid high-cardinality blowup.
Maya Patel (author): Good catch — added aggregation by tenant_id and introduced a feature toggle to gate the sampling tags. See telemetry/metrics/derived_cost.py where we limit tag expansion.
Sofia Ortega (reviewer): Can we ensure behavior when KV cache is disabled (on-prem deployments)? Need a safe fallback for attribution scoring.
Maya Patel (author): Added unit test for kv cache disabled case and fallback to 'unknown_cache_state' label; documented behavior in README.
Ravi Kapoor (reviewer): Integration tests look good; one request: add a short blurb in release notes about oncall implications and suggested threshold defaults.
Maya Patel (author): Added release notes and default threshold guidance in docs and alert rule comments.
CI Bot: dashboard-snapshot validation initially failed due to a missing panel uid; fixed in commit 4 and re-ran — all checks passed.
Evan Brooks (approval): LGTM after the cardinality guard and kv-cache fallback. Approving for squash-merge.
Added a compact per-route cost-sparkline panel and a fat-tail latency explainer to help teams quickly surface and diagnose cost/latency spikes. Feature is behind a toggle and off by default. Suggested alert tuning guidance included in docs.

Motivation: We need a safer canary primitive that enforces session-coherent promotion and provides a forensic-backed automated rollback that can optionally rewind recent traffic for replay testing. The Turnstile gate implements a session-fence: during promotion the controller guarantees that sessions routed to the candidate model are isolated and can be rewound (replayed) against the golden variant for postmortem verification. The audit-rewind helper materializes compact, indexed per-cohort artifacts that let SREs and devs replay a timebox of requests deterministically.

What this PR does: implements a new rollout gate (turnstile), a compact on-disk audit store format, controller logic to fence sessions during canaries, a replay CLI for investigators, and operator docs/playbooks. Key behaviors: session affinity maintained while candidate is in the fenced lane; if the gate trips (latency/regression thresholds) the controller can trigger an automated rollback and optionally kick off an audit-rewind job to capture and replay affected sessions for debugging. The rewind job supports partial replays (sampling by cohort, developer tags, or explicit request IDs).

Checklist: 
- [x] Core controller implementation (turnstile_controller.go) 
- [x] Audit store writer + compact index (telemetry/audit_store.go) 
- [x] Replay CLI (tools/replay_cli.py) 
- [x] Unit tests for fencing and gated promotion logic (tests/turnstile_unit_test.py) 
- [x] Integration test that runs a small live canary, induces a latency spike, verifies rollback + rewind (tests/turnstile_integration_test.py) 
- [x] Runbook and operator docs (docs/runbooks/turnstile.md) 
- [x] Telemetry dashboards: added telemetry/turnstile_dashboard.json (skeleton) 

Testing notes: initial CI run flagged a flaky test in the sampling path (tests/turnstile_integration_test.py) due to timing assumptions; increased test harness timeouts and introduced deterministic pseudorandom seeds for sampling. Local integration: ran a 1k qps synthetic canary against the staging cluster with session stickiness and verified that scoreboard metrics (turnstile.active_sessions, turnstile.replay_candidates, turnstile.rollback_triggers) are emitted. Replayed a 5-minute window with replay_cli and confirmed parity for 98% of traced response hashes.

Backward compatibility and safety: the Turnstile gate plugs in as an optional gate in existing rollout policy YAMLs; if not referenced, there is zero behavioral change. The audit store expires by default after 72 hours and is configurable per-tenant to avoid storage blowup. The rewind path is read-only with a configurable dry-run mode so it can be used without automatically shadowing production traffic.

Operational concerns: 
- Storage: audit artifacts are compact (indexed delta blobs) but operators should monitor telemetry.audit_store_bytes; default retention is conservative. 
- Privacy: audit artifacts contain request metadata and user-cohort tags (no PII allowed). We added sanitization hooks in telemetry/audit_store.go and a KMS flag for encrypting on write. 

Related work: builds on ENG-1072 (session-anchored shadow bridge) and complements ENG-1624 (telemetry replay framework). This PR also references SUP-783 for a customer incident that motivated faster forensic replays.

How to review: focus on the controller invariants in turnstile_controller.go and tests/turnstile_unit_test.py. Replay CLI is small and intentionally opinionated — review for safety knobs. docs/runbooks/turnstile.md contains operator playbook and run examples.

Notes for release: enable behind feature flag rollout.turnstile_enabled=false by default for 2 weeks, then roll to opt-in tenants.

Introduces the Turnstile canary gate (session-fenced canary lane) and an audit-rewind helper for safer automated rollbacks. Backwards compatible with existing rollout policies. See docs/runbooks/turnstile.md for operator playbook.
Diego Martinez: overall this looks good — can we tighten the default retention from 72h to 48h for sandbox tenants?
Aisha Patel: replied: made retention configurable per-tenant and left default at 72h to match legal retention guidance; added config comment
Chen Li: nit: split large audit blobs into 64KB chunks for easier streaming — implemented in second commit
Marta Novak: request: add an SLO guard that prevents auto-rollback if less than X samples collected — added a gating check and test
Diego Martinez: approved after small comments; reran CI on last push
CI: initial run failed on tests/turnstile_integration_test.py (flaky sampling). Reran: all checks passed.

Context: perf-canary + SRE triage needs to quickly answer “what changed?” when p95 latency or tokens/sec regresses. Today we can see model/version + hardware, but we can’t reliably correlate to runtime build or kernel selection changes (especially when selection is dynamic). This PR adds low-cardinality tags to runtime telemetry (metrics + traces + request debug logs) to identify the runtime build and the kernel selection outcome for a request. These tags are explicitly designed for per-model aggregation and alert attribution and should be stable across rollouts. What’s included: (1) Runtime build tags: runtime.build_id (semver-ish build label from build pipeline), runtime.git_sha (short SHA), runtime.build_flavor (release|debug), runtime.feature_set (compile-time feature bitset exported as a short string; see below). (2) Kernel selection identifiers: kernel.bundle_version (version string for the kernel pack baked into the runtime image), kernel.selector_version (version for selection logic), kernel.policy (e.g. auto|pinned|compat), kernel.id (stable identifier for the chosen kernel impl), kernel.variant (e.g. fp16|bf16|int8 where applicable). (3) Guardrails to keep cardinality bounded: kernel.id is a curated stable name (NOT a per-build hash), kernel.variant is a small enum, runtime.feature_set is a fixed-format string with a bounded keyspace. We intentionally do NOT tag with full PTX/cubin hashes or per-host identifiers. (4) Backward compatibility: all tags are optional; exporters will omit on older runtimes. Dashboards/queries can use label_replace/defaults safely. (5) Tests: unit tests for tag formatting + allowed-value validation, and a golden telemetry test that asserts emitted label set for a representative request. Notes/decisions: - runtime.build_id source of truth is the build pipeline env var RUNTIME_BUILD_ID (already present in release builds but not previously emitted). We fall back to “unknown” in dev builds to avoid breaking local runs. - kernel.bundle_version is sourced from kernels/manifest.json embedded at build time; selector_version is incremented with changes to heuristics (documented in code). - For tracing, we add these as span attributes on the “runtime.decode” and “runtime.prefill” spans (not per-token spans) to avoid overhead. - For metrics, tags are applied only to the canary/perf aggregation metrics and a small set of existing runtime histograms that are already sampled/aggregated; we did not add tags to high-volume per-request counters. Rollout: safe to ship behind TELEMETRY_EMIT_RUNTIME_KERNEL_TAGS=true (default on in prod builds after this merges). We can flip it off quickly if there’s any telemetry cost surprise. Follow-ups: update perf-canary dashboard links and alert payload formatter to include these fields (separate PR in incident-bot/observability-pack).
Hiro Tanaka: Kernel.id needs to be stable across rebuilds; do not use hash of binary. Also, avoid tagging by “kernel_path” because that will explode. Omar El-Sayed: Agree. Updated to use a curated enum in kernel_ids.h and mapping in selector; removed path-based tag. Added allowlist test to prevent regressions. Sofia Ivanova: Please confirm these labels aren’t added to high-volume queueing metrics; we already have tight budgets there. Omar El-Sayed: Confirmed. Labels are only on perf histograms (sampled) and canary-focused series; queueing counters remain unchanged. Added comment in runtime_metrics.cc. Logan Wright: Two concerns: (1) runtime.feature_set string risks high cardinality if it changes frequently, (2) kernel.selector_version should be documented; otherwise people will assume bundle_version implies selection logic. Omar El-Sayed: Addressed by making feature_set a fixed-format bitset with bounded combinations (currently 7 flags), and by adding selector_version + inline docs. Also updated golden telemetry snapshot. Nadia Rahman: Baseline store will join on these values; can we ensure “unknown” doesn’t end up in prod? Omar El-Sayed: In release builds RUNTIME_BUILD_ID is always set (added assert + warning if missing). “unknown” only for dev/local builds. Added a unit test that release builds set build_id via env var injection in CI. Approvals: Hiro approved after enum change. Logan approved after sampling/label scope clarification. Sofia approved with note to watch telemetry cost. Nadia approved for baseline pipeline compatibility.
Runtime telemetry now includes runtime build identifiers and kernel selection identifiers (bounded labels) to improve attribution of performance regressions to releases/kernels (perf-canary + SRE triage).
payload.title: Runtime: emit build + kernel selection/version tags in telemetry

Motivation: large multi-tenant workloads expose two correlated but under-optimized behaviors in our KV cache: uneven occupancy causing high fragmentation, and eviction churn under transient load spikes. This PR introduces an occupancy-aware retention layer plus a stochastic, bounded-sample evictor that aims to reduce fragmentation, smooth eviction pressure during bursts, and preserve hot prefixes without heavy global compaction.

Summary of changes and rationale: implement a lightweight occupancy bucketing scheme that tracks hotness at segment granularity, add a lease-like soft-retention token to avoid immediately evicting recently-resurrected keys, and replace the deterministic LRU-scan used by the existing evictor with a probabilistic sampler that prioritizes underfilled buckets and respects per-tenant soft-quotas. The new algorithm reduces large contiguous free/used alternations, lowering fragmentation-induced memory amplification. We also add a cooperative compact hint channel so tenants can trigger low-priority compaction during idle cycles (scheduler-integrated).

Checklist: - [x] Core algorithm implemented (kv/retention + kv/evictor) - [x] Unit tests for eviction invariants and lease expiry - [x] Microbenchmarks (local and CI perf job) - [x] Node-level scheduler integration for low-priority compaction hints - [x] Documentation and rollout config flags

Operational notes: rollout gated behind feature flag KV_OCCUPANCY_RETENTION. Default is off for clusters < 8 GPUs to avoid unintended interactions with small-node packing heuristics. Telemetry exposes: eviction_cycles, sampled_bucket_hit_rate, retention_leases_active, tenant_eviction_pressure. Guidance: enable on a canary tenant first; monitor sampled_bucket_hit_rate and retention_leases_active to tune bucket granularity (default 128 slots).

Why different from previous work: unlike pure compaction or spill strategies, this approach focuses on reducing fragmentation at allocation-time by steering retention policy with occupancy signals and a low-cpu probabilistic evictor instead of expensive global scans or synchronous spill-to-disk paths. It complements, rather than replaces, the existing spill/overflow mechanisms.

Links: Linear ENG-2201 (design), supporting perf run artifacts: ci/perf/kv-occupancy-2025-11-18, internal doc: docs/kv-occupancy-retention.md
Diego Morales: The probabilistic sampler looks promising; can you quantify worst-case memory growth during a sudden spike?
Asha Rao: Added a burst-bound parameter (max_retention_leases) and a backoff path that forces immediate sampling under emergency pressure. See retention.rs:burst_control().
Priya Singh: Please add tenant isolation tests (one noisy tenant shouldn't evict another's retained keys).
Asha Rao: Added tenancy isolation unit tests and an integration scenario that simulates cross-tenant pressure. CI integration-tests included; added tenant_eviction_pressure metric.
Evan Li: Performance numbers look good but the integration test flaked once; can we stabilize the perf job?
Asha Rao: Tightened test timings and added deterministic seeds for sampler on CI. Re-ran perf job; results stable.
a1f3d9e  implement occupancy bucketing and lease tokens
b2c4e11  add stochastic sampler based evictor and priority heuristics
d5f7a9b  integration with scheduler: compaction hint channel
e3b2c44  unit tests + eviction invariants
f9d0a7c  docs and rollout config; add telemetry counters
Introduce occupancy-aware retention and a probabilistic evictor to reduce KV cache fragmentation and eviction churn.
Feature flag: KV_OCCUPANCY_RETENTION (off by default for small clusters).
New telemetry: sampled_bucket_hit_rate, retention_leases_active, tenant_eviction_pressure.
Recommended rollout: canary on a tenant and monitor eviction_churn and p99 latency before enabling org-wide.
