Context and motivation: The three SDKs diverged subtly in retry semantics and streaming ergonomics after the recent session/lease work. Downstream teams saw inconsistent behavior when switching languages in polyglot services (different retry floors, TTL handling, and backoff jitter application). This PR harmonizes retry preset names and timebound semantics, adds telemetry-ready hooks for observability, and introduces a small ergonomic PullGenerator pull-based streaming facade (py/ts/go) to make async pull consumption more consistent across languages.

What this PR does (summary): Consolidate retry profile names to a canonical set (fast, balanced, durable), unify timebound semantics (max_attempt_time applies to whole operation, not per-attempt), surface retry lifecycle telemetry events (retry_attempt, retry_backoff_ms, retry_final), and add PullGenerator facade which wraps existing async iterators/streams and exposes a small synchronous/pull-oriented consumer API useful for server integrations. Also bumps SDK minor versions and updates examples, docs, and changelogs.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc: ENG-1912 design notes linked in the Linear ticket - [x] Cross-SDK tests: smoke, handshake and session replay tests - [x] Telemetry hooks implemented and documented - [x] Examples updated (py/ts/go) - [x] README/changelog entries added - [x] Version bumps and packaging metadata updated

Commits (high-level): - 8a2f3d4: unify retry preset enum and rename presets across sdks - 1b7c9d2: implement timebound max_attempt_time logic in python sdk - c4d12fa: add PullGenerator facade (typescript) and tests - e1b9a77: add PullGenerator facade (go) and session glue - f2c3b9a: add PullGenerator facade (python) and examples - d9e6b2a: add telemetry hooks and adapters across sdks - a7b5c4e: bump versions, update changelogs and readme snippets

Files/areas changed (high level): - sdk/python/redwood/transport/retry.py: consolidate profiles, implement operation-level max_attempt_time and telemetry hooks. Added PullGenerator wrapper in sdk/python/redwood/streaming/pull_generator.py. - sdk/typescript/src/retry/presets.ts: renamed presets and exported canonical enum; add telemetry emitter interface. - sdk/typescript/src/stream/pullGenerator.ts: new small facade that consumes existing async iterators and exposes pull responses. - sdk/go/retry/presets.go: align names and timebound semantics; introduce RetryTelemetry interface. - sdk/go/stream/pull_generator.go: new pull-oriented facade for io-like consumer patterns. - docs/sdk/retries.md: explain presets and timebound semantics. - examples/pull-generator/: three short examples (py/ts/go) showing server integration patterns. - CHANGELOGs: bumped per-sdk.

Illustrative snippet (typescript PullGenerator usage): const pg = new PullGenerator(chatStream); while (true) { const chunk = await pg.pull(); if (!chunk) break; processChunk(chunk); }

Review conversation (highlights): Diego Ramos (reviewer): "Nice to see a single source of truth for preset names. Question: can we keep the old names as aliases for one release cycle to avoid breaking downstream code that references presets by string?" Mira Chen (author): "Added alias map in TS and PY for one release cycle; Go preserves typed enum compatibility by adding deprecated constants. Documented aliases in RELEASES.md." Lena Ho (reviewer): "Telemetry looks good, but payload size from retry events could be noisy in high-throughput services. Can we make emission configurable with a minimal default?" Mira Chen: "Telemetry emitter defaults to no-op unless user opts into sdk telemetry or provides an emitter; added opt-in config flag 'enableRetryTelemetry' with default off." Raj Patel (reviewer): "PullGenerator API looks ergonomic. A nit: synchronous-style pull() returning Promise<null> on completion is a little odd for Go consumers. Consider returning (chunk, ok) tuple semantics in Go." Mira Chen: "Adjusted Go PullGenerator to return (chunk, ok, err) style and updated examples. Thanks for catching that."

Requested changes and follow-ups: - Added alias map and documented deprecated names. - Exposed nullable telemetry config with opt-in default off. - Adjusted Go pull semantics to idiomatic (value, ok, err). - Add perf microbenchmark for PullGenerator layer (follow-up ticket ENG-1978).

CI and testing: Initial CI run showed one flaky test in sdk/python/test_stream_resume::test_resume_after_reauth (transient websocket timing). I rebased and added a small backoff jitter in the test harness; rerun passed. Full matrix: python unit tests (pass), typescript unit + integration (pass), go unit tests (pass), linting (pass), packaging checks (pass). E2E cross-sdk smoke (mainnet-like) run passed locally and on CI.

Compatibility notes: No breaking API changes were introduced; all renamed presets have one-release aliases for backward compatibility. PullGenerator is additive and opt-in. Version bumps are patch/minor: python 1.12.2 -> 1.12.3, typescript 2.7.0 -> 2.7.1, go 0.9.7 -> 0.9.8.

Docs and examples: Added docs/sdk/retries.md describing canonical presets (fast, balanced, durable) and their recommended use-cases and cost/latency tradeoffs. Added docs/streaming/pull_generator.md with code examples in three languages and a short note on telemetry configuration. Updated changelogs with highlights and migration notes.

Migration guidance for customers: - If you reference retry presets by string, use alias names for one release; prefer the canonical enum values moving forward. - PullGenerator is optional; server-side frameworks that expect pull-based reads (e.g., synchronous web frameworks) can adopt it for simpler integration. - Telemetry hooks are opt-in and should be enabled only in dev/observability environments to avoid high-cardinality metrics.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main on 2026-02-25 after approvals from Diego Ramos and Lena Ho and green CI. Release cuts scheduled by the release team: python/ts/go packages to be published within the next release window.

Post-merge follow-ups (open tasks): - ENG-1978: add microbenchmarks for PullGenerator overhead and confirm cost/latency numbers. - ENG-2009: add server-framework specific helper for fast server-side pull integration (express/fastapi/nethttp adapter). - Monitor telemetry opt-in adoption and adjust default if users request easier visibility.

If anything's unclear or you'd like a walk-through of the PullGenerator design (sync vs async tradeoffs) I'm happy to pair with reviewers to demo locally.
Aligned retry preset names and defaults across Python/TS/Go SDKs; introduce lightweight PullGenerator streaming facade for ergonomic pull-based consumption; minor SDK patch bumps (py 1.12.3, ts 2.7.1, go 0.9.8); telemetry hooks for retry events.

Context: customers with mixed workloads needed better defaults for batching, cache affinity, and quantization that respect tenant unit economics. This PR introduces 'Cost Alchemist', a profile compiler that ingests workload sketches, telemetry histograms, and pricing tiers and produces candidate presets for batching window, KV-cache retention, and quantization profiles. Motivation: reduce manual tuning and expensive rollout cycles while avoiding regressions in latency or quality. Summary of changes: 1) new service module redwood/econ/alchemist that implements candidate synthesis and scoring; 2) deterministic dry-run CLI (bin/cost-alchemist) to run on historical traces and export JSON presets; 3) an experimental readonly API route /v1/cost-alchemist/dryrun for internal tooling; 4) telemetry hooks and new unit-econ metrics (alchemist.score, preset.expected_tokens_saved); 5) quant profile generator that emits INT8/FP16 fallback chains and compatibility labels for runtime kernel selection; 6) safety gates: automatic canary selector and a revert plan on perf/quality regressions. Checklist: [x] implementation and unit tests; [x] integration tests against small synthetic traces; [x] perf microbenchmarks (no >2% p99 latency regression in our smoke harness); [x] docs: internal design doc linked; [x] added telemetry dashboards entries; [ ] cross-region rollout plan (follow-up). Related: ENG-2147 for preset format, ENG-2201 for unit-econ metrics. How to review: run bin/cost-alchemist --dry-run --trace samples/tenant_small.json to generate presets; CI provides example artifacts under ci/artifacts/cost-alchemist. Rollout notes: merged behind feature-flag econ.alchemist.enabled=false by default; ops will enable in staged clusters after monitoring 24h. Risk: low-medium; the generated presets are opt-in until we enable autosuggest. Links: design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/board/ENG/2147-cost-alchemist, perf results: ci/artifacts/cost-alchemist/perf-summary.html.
Adds a new profile compiler (Cost Alchemist) that synthesizes tenant-aware batching/caching defaults and emits compact quantization candidates; exposes a readonly /v1/cost-alchemist endpoint and a dry-run CLI; safe fallthrough to existing defaults preserved.
Samir Gupta: Overall nice direction. Please add a short doc that explains how the candidate scoring works (probabilistic token savings vs risk).
Ava Martinez: Added scoring breakdown in docs/internal/cost_alchemist_design.md and expanded telemetry naming for clarity.

payload.body:
Reduce client-visible 5xx spikes during regional failovers by persisting ephemeral connection state, restoring a consistent snapshot on rejoin, and applying a staged traffic wash/ramp with probe-driven holdoffs. No public API changes.
Context: In a recent multi-region failover test we observed brief client-facing error spikes (5xx) after nodes rejoined. Root cause analysis found two contributing factors: (1) ephemeral connection state (inflight KV and scheduler leases) was not consistently restored leading to transient backpressure and hot-path rejects, and (2) full traffic immediately flooded restored nodes before internal caches (KV/prefix) warmed, causing short-lived overloads.

Goal: Introduce a lightweight snapshot/restore for ephemeral connection metadata + an orchestrated, probe-driven traffic wash (staged-ramp) to give caches and rate controllers time to stabilize. This is a targeted reliability hotfix for regional soft recoveries; it is conservative and opt-in by feature-flag for initial rollout.

What changed (summary of commits):
- Add connection-snapshot store and restore glue (store ephemeral leases & inflight counts to local / tmp snapshot on drain) — small persisted snapshot lifecycle with TTL.
- Implement staged traffic-wash controller: probe-driven ramp with holdoff timers and per-tenant ramp factors.
- KV cache warm-checks and probe hook added to serving runtime; staged ramp consults warm-checks before advancing phases.
- Telemetry: new metrics (snapshot.restore.time, traffic_wash.phase, probe.warm_success_rate) and traces for restore paths.
- Feature flag + safe defaults: disabled by default for older clusters, enabled in canary via operator.

Files changed (high-level):
- runtime/connection/snapshot.go (new) — snapshot save/restore and TTL handling
- serving/wash/controller.go (new) — staged-ramp state machine and probe integration
- serving/wash/flags.go — feature flag + config knobs (ramp duration, probe window)
- telemetry/metrics.yaml — new metric definitions and dashboard hooks
- operator/canary-configs/redwood-canary.yaml — rollout toggle and default scaling policy updates
- tests/serving/wash_test.go — unit tests for ramp progression and failure modes
- docs/operational/traffic-wash.md — operator-facing runbook and recommended rollout steps

Review conversation (high-level excerpts):
- Miguel: "This looks sensible; can we ensure snapshot storage is local-only and never shipped to control plane? Also add a non-blocking path if snapshot fails."
- Author (Aisha): "Snapshot kept ephemeral and local; added non-blocking fallback — if snapshot write fails we fall back to cold-warm probe path and emit a metric (snapshot.write.failed)."
- Jordan: "Probe integration needs to avoid adding excess load; recommend exponential backoff on probe retries and cap probe concurrency per node."
- Author: "Added probe concurrency cap and backoff; unit tests updated."
- Sophie (approval): "Telemetry and runbook are clear. Approve subject to CI green and one more e2e validation in canary."

CI and validation: All checks passed on final push (unit tests, lint, integration smoke). We ran a canary in us-west-2 with 3% of traffic and observed no 5xx spikes during a simulated rejoin; metrics show snapshot.restore.time ~= 120-300ms and traffic_wash progressed across 3 phases with stable probe success rate > 95%.

Fallbacks and safety: If probe success rate remains low, controller stalls progression and moves nodes into a temporary warm-hold state with conservative rate limits. Snapshot failures are safe — the code falls back to existing slowpath recovery. Feature flag allows rollback without code revert.

Rollout plan: Enable as canary (3%) for 24h, monitor snapshot.restore.time and probe.warm_success_rate, then gradually increase to 25% and 100% in 48h windows. Operator runbook (docs/operational/traffic-wash.md) includes quick rollback steps and metrics to watch.

Motivation/Why unique: This PR stitches a short-lived persisted snapshot of ephemeral serving state with an orchestrated, probe-aware traffic ramp to avoid the classic "rejoin flood" problem where un-warmed caches + immediate load cause transient overloads. It targets production reliability without changing public APIs and keeps the change reversible and telemetry-rich for operational confidence.

Merge: Squash-merged after approvals and green CI.
payload.title: Connection snapshot + staged traffic wash orchestrator for regional soft-recoveries

Fix: Smooth egress throttle to prevent circuit flip loops; add slow-rejoin backoff and new telemetry for SLO breach investigation.
Context: During a regional egress saturation incident (SUP-8042) we observed repeatable circuit flips and tenant failovers when backend egress caps were hit. The symptom was a short storm of traffic (spike + uneven egress shaping) that caused rapid circuit open/close cycles and then a cascade of regional failovers. This PR implements a short, targeted hotfix: an egress throttle smoothing layer and a slow-rejoin backoff for circuits to avoid oscillation. Motivation: improve reliability under bursty egress constraints, reduce churn on the SLO enforcement path, and make regional failover events less noisy.

What I changed (high level):
- Introduced an egress_throttle_coordinator that performs exponential smoothing on instantaneous egress usage and emits an adjusted throttle target (new module: pkg/runtime/egress/throttle_coordinator.go).
- Added a slow_rejoin_backoff to the circuit manager so once a circuit transitions to OPEN it waits with an exponentially increasing probe interval before attempting to rejoin (pkg/runtime/circuit/manager.go).
- Hooked the smoothing signals into routing policy so the smart router can prefer spare capacity routes instead of immediately failing over (pkg/router/policy.go).
- Improved telemetry: new metrics and tags (slo.egress.smoothed_target, circuit.rejoin_delay_ms, circuit.rejoin_attempts) and a validation probe that stamps tenant id and region for postmortem (internal/telemetry/metrics.yaml + runtime/telemetry/instrumentation.py).
- Small docs and runbook update for incident responders (docs/runbooks/egress-throttle-surge.md).

Detailed commit summary:
- Commit 1: add throttle_coordinator with smoothing algorithm + unit tests (smoothing parameters configurable via env/runtime flags).
- Commit 2: integrate smoothing into router policy and add an adaptive margin to reduce unnecessary cross-region egress.
- Commit 3: add slow_rejoin_backoff to circuit manager with deterministic unit tests and simulation harness scenarios.
- Commit 4: add telemetry counters, tag propagation, and update Grafana dashboard JSON (telemetry changes are additive only).
- Commit 5: runbook and docs + minor lint fixes.

Files changed (high-level):
- pkg/runtime/egress/throttle_coordinator.go (new)
- pkg/runtime/circuit/manager.go (modified)
- pkg/router/policy.go (modified)
- runtime/telemetry/instrumentation.py (modified)
- docs/runbooks/egress-throttle-surge.md (new)
- observability/dashboards/egress-throttle-dashboard.json (modified)

Testing and CI: All unit tests and integration smoke tests passed in CI (linux/amd64, linux/arm64). Added a small simulation test in the existing harness to replay the incident pattern; simulation verifies no repeated immediate rejoin attempts and that smoothed target avoids cross-region panic. CI summary: build ✓, unit-tests ✓, integration-smoke ✓, lint ✓, e2e-sim (new) ✓. Post-merge we ran a staged canary in a low-traffic region for 2 hours before full rollout.

Backward compatibility and safety: The smoothing parameters are behind a runtime flag and default to conservative values (alpha=0.25, min_rejoin_ms=500, max_backoff_ms=60000). The telemetry additions are additive and do not change any existing metric names. No breaking changes.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Aisha Patel (reviewer): "This looks good overall; two requests: (1) add a small doc blurb explaining the tuning knobs and safe defaults; (2) ensure the backoff uses jitter to avoid thundering herd." 
- Author (Elena): "Added docs + jitter in commit 3. Jitter is triangular with a ±15% window; added unit test to assert jitter bounds in simulation harness." 
- Marco Li (reviewer): "Can we add an emergency override so ops can set throttle target to manual during maintenance?" 
- Author: "Added env var REDWOOD_EGRESS_THROTTLE_OVERRIDE in commit 5. It's gated by the ops role and logged as an audit event." 
- Claire Nguyen (approver): "Verified metrics in the staging run; behavior looks stable. Approving pending CI." 

CI reruns: one flaky test (router/policy_test) failed on first run due to a timing assertion; fixed by switching to condition-wait and re-run. All green after fix.

Risk and mitigation: The change touches routing and circuit manager paths which are sensitive. To mitigate: feature gated, rolled out to 10% of regions first, health check monitor (SLO delta > 0.5% triggers automatic rollback), and added an alert threshold on circuit.rejoin_attempts that will page SRE if spikes occur.

Merge & rollout: Merged via squash-merge after approvals. Rollout plan: 10% regions -> 50% -> global over 6 hours if no regressions. During canary we observed 27% reduction in immediate rejoin attempts and 12% reduction in cross-region failover events for the test tenant cohort.

Follow-ups: 
- ENG-1830: Tune smoothing alpha per-tenant workload profiles (tracking ticket created).
- Telemetry follow-up to add a correlation view on egress throttle vs token cost per request (low-priority).

Related tickets and references: SUP-8042 (support ticket), internal incident writeup: https://linear.app/redwood/incident/INC-2025-012-1, and the proposed SLO runbook change PR # (linked in runbook). 

If anything goes sideways during rollout, ops can flip REDWOOD_EGRESS_THROTTLE_OVERRIDE to set a static throttle target, or roll back the release using the rollback pipeline documented in docs/runbooks/rollback.md.

payload.body:
Summary: Adds a tenant-aware Rampdown Cost Advisor and a Mini-Batcher Coordinator. The advisor continuously scores tenants against budget and latency SLOs and emits short-lived 'rampdown' recommendations (temporary batch size reductions, cache TTL tightening, and conservative quantization levels). The coordinator receives those recommendations and applies tenant-scoped microbatch templates in the serving runtime with safe fallbacks to avoid SLO violations. Motivation: We see recurring short bursts of cost pressure from a small set of tenants that cause either sustained cost overruns or brittle manual interventions. Existing autotuners gestalt around long-lived defaults; this change provides an automated, low-latency control loop that (a) targets short-timescale budget smoothing, (b) reduces human toil, and (c) integrates safe fallbacks to prevent latency regressions. Design: - Rampdown Cost Advisor: a lightweight streaming analyzer in redwood/optimize that computes a time-decayed budget score per tenant using recent token spend, error rates, and latency percentiles. Outputs JSON recommendations with TTL (30–300s) and an action vector: {batch_delta, cache_ttl_delta, quant_profile}. - Mini-Batcher Coordinator: runtime component in redwood/runtime/batcher which can apply microbatch templates atomically for a tenant; templates include batch_size, max_wait_ms, and KV prefetch hints. Coordinator also negotiates with the kernel selector to prefer conservative quant profiles when recommended; all changes attach a correlation id and revert automatically at TTL expiry. - Safety model: each recommendation is simulated against a local cost/latency estimator; changes that predict >10% P95 latency increase are rejected locally. We ship a safety whitelist for latency-sensitive tenants. Backwards compatibility: changes are additive and disabled unless tenant-level advisor is enabled by config. Migration: config flag 'optimize.rampdown.enabled' defaults to false; rollout plan below. Implementation notes: - New infra: lightweight in-memory sliding windows for per-tenant metrics (time-decayed counters) persisted to redis for short-term coordination. - New RPC: coordinator exposes a small gRPC method ApplyTenantTemplate(tenant, template, ttl) used by the advisor. - Observability: added metrics optimizer.rampdown.recommendations_total, coordinator.applied_templates_total, coordinator.reverts_total and tracer spans on ApplyTenantTemplate. Testing: unit tests for advisor scoring, e2e sim harness that replays sampled tenant traffic and verifies no more than 5% regression in tail latency for safety-whitelisted tenants. Perf: bench harness shows ~3.9% median cost reduction for bursty tenants in our staging replay dataset with <1% median latency impact. Checklist: - [x] Advisor scoring algorithm implemented - [x] Coordinator apply/revert logic - [x] Safety simulator and whitelist - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Docs and config flags - [x] Telemetry and dashboards - [x] Rollout + kill switch Commits (summary): - feat(optimize): add rampdown advisor scoring engine and TTL recommendations - feat(runtime): implement mini-batcher coordinator and template application API - perf(kernel): conservative quant profile negotiation path - infra(redis): short-term tenant state persistence and TTL reconciliation - test: add replay sim and safety regression checks - docs: add operations guide and troubleshooting notes Files changed (high level): redwood/optimize/rampdown_advisor.py (new), redwood/runtime/batcher/mini_batch_coordinator.py (new), redwood/runtime/batcher/template_store.py (modified), redwood/runtime/kernel/quant_selector.py (hook added), redwood/infra/redis/tenant_state.py (new small shim), redwood/ops/docs/rampdown-advisor.md (new), tests/optimize/test_rampdown_scoring.py, tests/runtime/test_coordinator_revert.py, ci/workflows/e2e-sim.yaml (added sim job). Review notes and design rationale included inline. Rollout plan: stage feature off by default; enable for 5% of tenants in staging for 48h with monitoring alerts on optimizer.rampdown.recommendations_total and coordinator.reverts_total. If indicators are stable, increase to 25% canary for 72h, then 100% gradual rollout. Rollback: toggle config false or empty safety whitelist to prevent any new recommendations; coordinator will revert outstanding templates when TTLs expire. Backout patch provided for kernel quant hook if necessary.
Asha Patel (reviewer) on 2025-11-03: Overall nice work. Concern: how do we avoid continuous thrash if a tenant oscillates? Suggest adding exponential backoff on repeated recommendations.
Author (Jordan) on 2025-11-03: Added a cooldown counter and exponential backoff to the advisor; see rampdown_advisor.py cooldown_backoff() and unit tests.
Diego Ruiz (reviewer) on 2025-11-05: Please add smoke tests ensuring coordinator applies and reverts under TTL expiry even when Redis latency spikes.
Introduce Rampdown Cost Advisor (tenant-scoped temporary cost-smoothing recommendations) and Mini-Batcher Coordinator (tenant microbatch templates + safe quant fallbacks). Config-gated and off by default. Adds telemetry and an ops runbook.

payload.body:
Motivation: Customers asked for a transparent, auditable flow when service principals or operators request elevated RBAC v2 grants that also cause KMS key usage. Previously grants could be granted immediately by an admin or via automated policies which made compliance reviews and retroactive attribution hard. This PR introduces: 1) an approval queue service that records grant requests (who, why, TTL, requested roles, resource scope); 2) timebound provisional grants that can be auto-revoked after TTL if not escalated; 3) KMS usage attribution hooks so any KMS Encrypt/Decrypt/Sign operation performed while a provisional grant is active is annotated with an attestation token linking the KMS usage to the approval request; 4) an auditable hash chain persisted to the audit ledger topic to make tampering detectable; 5) a dual-signoff manual release flow in the Console for high-risk grants (requires two reviewers with distinct teams); and 6) migration tools to backfill existing short-lived grants into the queue to ensure consistent audit coverage. Checklist: - [x] Design doc: linear/ENG-5592 linked - [x] Approval queue service skeleton + API - [x] Console panel for reviewers with filtering by risk and region - [x] KMS attribution middleware and attestation token format - [x] Audit ledger hash-chain write + verification tool - [x] Dual-signoff UI and API gating - [x] E2E tests for provisional grant lifecycle - [x] Helm chart additions for deployment. Rollout plan: enabled by feature-flag (rbac.elevated_approval_queue) default off for existing clusters; opt-in per-tenant via Console or operator API. For Redwood Dedicated/Private, operators can enable in the installer values. Migration: a background migration scans for active grants created in the last 90 days and inserts them as "backfilled" requests with a small grace TTL; an operator must approve or reject backfilled items. Security considerations: attestation tokens are signed with the cluster KMS key and contain a minimal set of claims (request_id, principal, grant_scope, ttl, hash) to avoid leaking secrets. Audit ledger entries are append-only and include SHA256 over the canonical request blob; a verification utility is included to detect divergence. Backwards compatibility: the public inference API is unchanged; the RBAC decision point defers to approvals only for grants created via the new API path or flagged backfilled grants. Links: linear/ENG-5592, docs PR: docs/security/approval-queue.md, helm change: helm/charts/redwood/templates/approval-queue.yaml. Impact: expected slight latency increase for the initial grant path (synchronous persist + ledger write) but negligible for normal inference requests.
Lena Ortiz (reviewer): This looks solid; two concerns: (1) how do we ensure attestation token size doesn't escalate request headers, and (2) can we make the dual-signoff configurable per-tenant?
Author (Maya Chen): Attestation tokens are compacted and base64 url-safe; only the request_id is propagated in headers to keep per-request overhead minimal. Dual-signoff is gated by tenant feature flags and a cluster policy; updated docs include opt-in instructions.
Daniel Park (reviewer): Security scan reported a high entropy key usage pattern in tests — can we avoid committing test keys?
Author (Maya Chen): Removed embedded test keys and added mock signer interface; CI now runs with in-memory signer for unit tests and a dedicated test KMS instance for integration runs.
Priya Reddy (approver): Approving pending the small nit around log verbosity in the approval_queue worker.
New feature: Approval Queue for elevated RBAC grants with KMS usage attribution. Adds an auditable provisional grant flow, dual-signoff manual release, and migration/backfill tooling. Feature gated behind rbac.elevated_approval_queue. No breaking API changes.
For Dedicated/Private deployments: add 'approvalQueue.enabled=true' to helm values, ensure the cluster KMS key has sign permission for attestation tokens, and schedule the backfill job during a maintenance window. The ledger verifier should be run weekly as a cronjob.

- Runtime can now auto-select a hardware tuning profile by detected GPU SKU with explicit override precedence and safe fallbacks. - Adds startup logging for detection + selection source to reduce misconfig risk in Dedicated/Private.
Context: This PR wires up runtime-side hardware detection + profile selection for the hardware tuning profiles pack. The schema + validation landed in pr-21984; this change is the runtime integration layer that (a) detects GPU SKU at startup, (b) selects the best matching profile from the pack, (c) applies an explicit override order, and (d) fails safe when detection is ambiguous or unsupported. Motivation: We need predictable, supportable defaults across Hosted/Dedicated/Private without requiring per-pool manual configuration, while still allowing controlled overrides for canaries and customer environments. Summary of behavior (override order): 1) Explicit per-process override: REDWOOD_RUNTIME_HW_PROFILE (exact profile id). 2) Per-deployment override file: runtime_config.hardware_profile_id (e.g., set via Helm/values or local config). 3) Fleet/pool default: runtime_config.hardware_profile_family (e.g., "h100", "l40s") when ops wants a coarse pin without relying on SKU parsing. 4) Auto-detect: detect GPU SKU and map to family + variant using normalized device strings. 5) Safe fallback: if detection is unknown/ambiguous, select "generic" profile (conservative knobs) and emit a structured warning; runtime continues serving. Hardware detection details: - Uses NVML when available to fetch device name + PCI IDs; falls back to nvidia-smi parsing in minimal environments. - Normalizes common provider string variants (e.g., "NVIDIA H100 PCIe", "NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3", "NVIDIA H100 SXM") into canonical sku_family values (h100/b200/l40s) and sku_form_factor when available. - Handles MIG by treating the node as a family match but refusing to pick aggressive profiles that assume full device memory; we default to "family" profile unless an explicit profile id override is provided. - Multi-GPU nodes: selects one profile for the runtime process; if mixed families are detected (should not happen in prod pools), we warn and fall back to "generic" unless explicitly overridden. Guardrails / safety: - Any profile selected via auto-detect must pass schema validation + compatibility check (runtime min/max version) or we fall back to "generic". - We never hard-fail startup on detection errors; we fail open with conservative defaults and actionable logs. - Adds a metric label for selection_source (override_env, override_config, fleet_default, auto_detect, fallback) to enable rollout analysis (full dashboard work continues in pr-22027 / observability-pack). Logging: - On startup, logs a single-line summary: detected GPU info, normalized sku_family, selected profile id, selection_source, and fallback_reason when applicable. - In debug logs, prints the candidate matching path (exact match -> family match -> generic). Tests: - Unit tests for normalization against a table of real-world device strings from infra threads (PCIe vs SXM variants, cloud provider prefixes). - Integration test for override precedence (env > config > fleet default > auto-detect) with a fake NVML provider. - Regression test: unknown GPU string should not crash and should select generic with warning. Rollout plan: - Gate is runtime-only; actual tuned profiles remain controlled by pack versioning and per-pool enablement. - We will canary in a single H100 pool first; SRE asked that we ensure fallback remains silent-noisy (warn once) rather than spamming logs per request. Related: - pr-21984-add-hardware-profile-schema-and-json-validation (schema + validator) - ENG-4823 (loader + precedence) - SUP-29438 (Private customer request re: overriding profiles safely; this PR supports deterministic precedence and debuggability).
Changed areas/files (high level): - runtime/config/hardware_profiles/selector.ts: new selection module (override order + matching). - runtime/config/hardware_profiles/normalize_gpu.ts: GPU string normalization + MIG detection heuristics. - runtime/platform/nvml.ts: thin wrapper around NVML with safe fallbacks. - runtime/startup/logging.ts: startup log line for profile selection summary. - runtime/metrics/runtime_info.ts: adds selection_source label and selected_profile_id gauge (low-cardinality). - runtime/tests/hardware_profile_selector.test.ts: precedence + fallback tests. - runtime/tests/gpu_normalization_golden.test.ts: table-driven normalization coverage. Snippet (illustrative): selector precedence: if (envProfileId) return selectById(envProfileId, 'override_env'); if (config.profileId) return selectById(config.profileId, 'override_config'); if (config.profileFamily) return selectByFamily(config.profileFamily, 'fleet_default'); const detected = detectGpuFamily(); if (!detected) return selectGeneric('fallback', 'gpu_detection_failed'); return selectByDetectedSku(detected, 'auto_detect');
Ethan Park (review): Can you spell out precedence in-code and ensure we never throw on unknown GPUs? Also please avoid selecting an H100 variant profile on MIG by default; we’ve seen memory assumptions bite us. Benji Okafor (author): Added explicit precedence constants + comments in selector.ts and changed MIG path to family-only unless explicit profile id override is set. Unknown/ambiguous now always selects generic and logs a single warning. Irene Choi (review): The GPU name variants list is incomplete; we have at least 3 strings for H100 across providers. Please include the ones from the infra thread and add a unit test so we don’t regress. Benji Okafor (author): Added golden table cases for the provider variants we’ve observed and wired normalization to strip provider prefixes consistently. Sofia Ivanova (review): For mixed-family multi-GPU nodes: do we ever want to pick the “first device” and proceed? I’d rather fail safe. Benji Okafor (author): Agreed; mixed-family now triggers fallback to generic unless overridden. Sean Gallagher (SRE review): Logging looks good but please ensure the warning is once-per-startup, not per-request, and keep labels low cardinality. Benji Okafor (author): Confirmed: warning emitted at startup only; metrics are selected_profile_id (bounded by pack) + selection_source enum. Noah Patel (review): Please add a compatibility check hook so a new pack version can declare min runtime version. Benji Okafor (author): Added validator gate: incompatible profiles are rejected and we fall back to generic with reason 'incompatible_profile'. Approvals: Ethan Park approved; Irene Choi approved; Sean Gallagher approved after latest push.

Title: introduce-capacity-circuit-breaker-and-windowed-cooldown-for-dedicated-fleets

Description: This PR adds a capacity-level circuit breaker and a windowed cooldown policy to the Dedicated autoscaler. Motivation: during multi-tenant surges we've observed cascading scale-ups that drive temporary but significant cost and destabilize downstream provisioners. The circuit breaker prevents aggressive immediate scale-outs by limiting new allocation commits for a configurable short window when utilization growth exceeds a confidence threshold. The windowed cooldown provides a sliding observation window to progressively re-enable allocations as utilization stabilizes instead of a fixed cooldown timer.

Design summary: Implemented a light-weight circuit_breaker component used by the reservation allocator. The breaker tracks recent allocation decisions and a statistically smoothed utilization delta computed by the new windowed_cooldown component. It exposes a decision API Evaluate(requestContext) => {allow|throttle|fast_fail, reason}. Key behaviors: (1) short-circuit fast-fail for large concurrency spikes when downstream provisioning shows >90th percentile latency degradation; (2) throttle (soft deny) mode which returns allow=false but records a deferred request for backoff; (3) progressive re-open using an exponential-convergence window where allowance increases as rolling-utilization shows nominal behavior.

Telemetry and observability: added metrics for circuit_breaker_evaluations_total{decision}, circuit_breaker_open_duration_seconds, windowed_util_delta_percentile, and per-tenant throttled_allocations. Added metric registration and dashboards (docs/observability/capacity-circuit-breaker.md) with recommended alert rules for persistent open state.

Compatibility and defaults: Feature is off by default for all fleets. A Helm value redwood.dedicated.autoscaler.circuitBreaker.enabled=false controls rollout. The canary manifest deploys the component to a single small Dedicated pool for live experiments. Default thresholds are conservative (scale-out throttle at 25% sustained delta in the 60s window, open if combined with provisioning latencies above 95th pct).

Testing and CI: Unit tests for windowing math and breaker state transitions; integration test simulating step load with a fake provisioner. CI: initial run failed on lint (golangci-lint) which was fixed in a follow-up commit. Integration suite passed on rerun. Canary rollout was exercised in staging for 48 hours before merge.

Commits: init: add capacity circuit breaker core and windowing primitives; feat(autoscaler): integrate circuit breaker with reservation reconciler; chore(test): add integration tests; fix(lint): address go vet; docs: observability guide.

Files changed (high level):
- services/autoscaler/circuit_breaker.go: new state machine, evaluation API, unit tests in same package.
- services/autoscaler/windowed_cooldown.go: sliding-window util delta estimator (reservoir + EWMA hybrid).
- pkg/api/v1alpha/autoscaler.proto: added CRD fields for enabling circuit breaker and tuning knobs.
- cmd/observe/metrics/registration.go: register new metrics and export to prometheus client.
- helm/charts/redwood-dedicated/values.yaml: feature toggle and sane defaults.
- infra/k8s/manifests/dedicated-autoscaler-canary.yaml: canary deployment manifest and RBAC.
- docs/observability/capacity-circuit-breaker.md: operational guidance and dashboard links.
- tests/integration/test_circuit_breaker.py: integration flow that asserts stability under burst and slow-provision scenarios.
- README.md: short note on configuration and rollout plan.

Review conversation (high level):
- Evan: "We need clearer invariants around when the breaker moves to 'open' vs 'throttle'. Please add unit tests for corner cases and document the math."
- Maya(reply): "Added unit tests for the corner cases (zero baseline, negative deltas) and expanded comments in windowed_cooldown.go to spell out the math and invariants."
- Priya: "Telemetry looks good, but tie the open-duration metric to an alerting suggestion in docs."
- Maya: "Added recommended PromQL in docs and example alert rules; moved metric to top-level registry to avoid double-registration in short-lived test harnesses."
- Liam: "Suggest default thresholds be conservative; prefer feature off-by-default for existing customers."
- Maya: "Default set to off; documented canary and rollout steps."

CI summary: initial CI (lint) failed due to exported var name and a minor formatting issue. Fix applied and CI was re-run. Full test matrix passed (unit, integration, e2e canary smoke). PR merged via squash on 2026-03-04 after approving reviewers and green CI.

Merge outcome and rollout: Squash merge into main. Feature flag gated; chart values added so SRE can flip on per-fleet. Staging canary observed ~35% reduction in emergency scale-outs for a simulated noisy tenant with negligible impact to successful request admission. Next steps: gather two weeks of telemetry, tune heuristics, and expose a per-tenant override API for platform teams.
Add capacity circuit breaker and windowed cooldown policy for Dedicated autoscaler. Feature off by default; can be enabled per-fleet via Helm. Adds telemetry metrics and docs. Improves stability during transient multi-tenant surges.

Motivation: We continue to see rare incidents where SSE consumers receive partial JSON payloads that are syntactically valid individually but not reconstructible into the originally intended structured output due to delimiter coalescing and late-arriving fragments. These failures surface as missing tool/function call handoffs or JSON parse errors in downstream SDKs (notably in OpenAI compatibility layer consumers). This PR adds a lightweight 'SSE serde sanitizer' on both emitter and parser sides to ensure atomic span re-emission semantics and deterministic ordered handoff for tool/function calls.\n\nSummary of changes: Adds a boundary-collation pass during SSE emission that tags span segments with a stable span-id and an ordinal within-span index. On the parser side we use the span-id + ordinal to: 1) detect gaps (missing ordinal sequence), 2) temporarily stash out-of-order segments, 3) apply a short reassembly backoff window to allow late-arriving fragments to join the ordered stream, and 4) when backoff expires, emit a deterministic "reemit" envelope that contains an escape-wrapped partial JSON with a safe sentinel so downstream structured-output handlers can either attempt best-effort merge or surface a clear, actionable parse error.\n\nWhy this is different from previous work: Prior PRs focused on delimiter normalization and naive reassembly heuristics that attempted byte-level coalescing. This change introduces semantic span metadata (span-id + ordinal) and an explicit fallback reemit envelope rather than silent byte concatenation — helping SDKs make informed choices (retry, fallback model, or fail fast). It also introduces an ordered tool handoff marker (tool-ordinal) to guarantee function-call ordering even when chunks interleave across connections.\n\nHigh-level risk and rollout plan: The new span-id is opt-in on the emitter via a feature flag; readers treat untagged streams as pre-2026 format and use legacy heuristics. We will roll out on hosted API first behind the flag, run Canary for two days, then flip default-on after monitoring for a week. The parser includes a compact compatibility mode so older self-hosted Private deployments can accept the new envelopes without interface changes.\n\nBackwards-compat notes: SDKs that parse streaming structured output should be updated to recognize the reemit envelope and the tool-ordinal marker; fallbacks are documented in the release notes. The compatibility layer will continue emitting the plain SSE lines if the emitter configuration disables span tagging.
Mateo Alvarez: This looks promising. Question: how large can the span-id metadata be? We need to avoid inflating token sizes for tiny messages.
Ava Kim (reply): span-id is a 64-bit hex (8 byte) encoded; by default we attach the minimal base62 form. In practice it's ~6-8 bytes as an SSE attribute and we measured <0.2% token increase across sample workloads.
Rita Chang: The backoff window defaults to 50ms — is that sufficient for high-latency inter-region scenarios? Could that cause frequent reemit envelopes?
Ava Kim (reply): We added a per-route configurable backoff with a max cap via the canary config. For cross-region routes Canary shows ~0.6% reemit rate at 50ms; increasing to 200ms reduces that but increases tail latency. We tuned defaults to prioritize tail latency for interactive chat; we also expose this as a policy for Dedicated customers.
Ethan Brooks: Tests look good but add one more for multi-tool interleave where tool-ordinal wraps across spans (edge case).
Ava Kim (reply): Added test multi_tool_wrap_test.go and extended the integration harness to assert ordinal monotonicity across tool boundaries.

Motivation: reduce auth ceremony and improve streaming ergonomics across SDKs by introducing small, declarative credential annotations and a compact generator facade that provides typed streaming producers/consumers with backoff presets. This PR changes the auth surface in a backwards-compatible way while surfacing clearer retry metadata for observability. What I changed: 1) Python SDK: added redwood.credentials.annotations module, decorator-based credential hints (CredentialHint), a CompactGenerator class that wraps the existing streaming client into a Pythonic async generator with graceful reconnection hooks and a configurable retry preset DSL. Unit tests and examples updated. 2) TypeScript SDK: introduce CredentialAnnotations interface and a light-weight generator wrapper (createCompactStream) that returns an AsyncGenerator with typed payload envelopes, adds retry presets and explicit jitter-aware backoff profiles. 3) Go SDK: add credential tag parsing helpers, a CompactStreamIterator convenience type, and align retry options with the new declarative presets. 4) Cross-SDK: add telemetry fields for credential_source and retry_profile to stream events; updated examples and docs; bump versions (py 0.30.0 -> 0.31.0, ts 1.40.0 -> 1.41.0, go v1.8.0 -> v1.9.0). Migration: default behavior is unchanged; opt-in via new small imports or factory flags. For users who previously built custom stream wrappers, the CompactGenerator offers a drop-in ergonomic alternative and a migration guide is included in sdks/*/MIGRATING.md. Testing: unit tests for each SDK (python/ts/go), integration e2e run against staging inference with synthetic load, linting and type-checks. CI history: first run found a flaky Typescript e2e test (stream ordering) which was fixed by adding a short stabilization window; final CI green. Rollout: merged to main and cut SDK patch releases; followed up with a docs-only PR to amplify examples and a follow-up task to add an observability dashboard for retry_profile (ENG-3540). See linked Linear tickets for detailed acceptance criteria.

Context: our presubmit pipeline has grown heavy — a single monolithic lint entrypoint pulls in language toolchains and full dependency installs which increases timer-to-feedback and CI cost. This PR splits bootstrapping duties, adds a lightweight presubmit heuristic router to reduce unnecessary expensive checks, and introduces a small metadata change to dependency bumps (dep timestamping) to make automated dependency churn more traceable. Motivation: speed up developer feedback loops, reduce CI minutes by ~25% on average, and make dep PRs easier to triage. What this PR does (single continuous description): - Split lint/test bootstrap: introduce language-specific entrypoints (scripts/lint-entrypoint-{py,ts,go}.sh) and a minimal shared bootstrap that only downloads the toolchain for the languages touched by the PR. The presubmit manifest now declares per-language bootstraps so CI jobs only install what they need. - Presubmit heuristics: add tools/ci/presubmit_router.go that inspects the changed paths and routes to a slim, fast lane for docs/infra/README-only changes, a medium lane for small SDK changes (typechecks + unit tests), and a heavy lane for runtime/serving changes. Heuristics are configurable via .github/presubmit-config.yaml. - Dependency timestamping: add tools/dep/timestamp_updater.py which appends a machine-readable timestamp and source tag to package bump commits authored by the automation bot. This helps downstream alerts and reduces noisy “unknown origin” churn in the dep dashboards. - Backwards compatible: default behavior is unchanged unless the presubmit-config is present in the repo or a repo-specific override exists. Migration notes and rollout strategy: feature-flagged behind ci.feature.split-boot, gradually enabled for active contributors and then org-wide. We ran a canary for three weeks in redwood-examples and SDK repos. Observed impact: median presubmit wall-clock dropped from 6m45s -> 4m50s (roughly 28% faster) and average CI-minute consumption reduced by ~21% across sampled runs. Checklist: - [x] introduce split entrypoint scripts - [x] implement presubmit router and config - [x] add timestamping util and integrate with dep-bot workflow - [x] docs updated (docs/ci/presubmit.md) - [x] e2e smoke runs in redwood-examples - [x] add tests for presubmit router heuristics Related: Linear ENG-8427 (presubmit fast lanes), ENG-8431 (dep metadata and dashboards). Related PRs: #1584102 (dep-bot: add metadata support), #1579023 (ci: minor workflow refactor).
5 commits: split lint bootstraps and add per-language scripts; add presubmit router implementation + tests; add presubmit-config YAML and doc; dep timestamping tool + integration patch for dep-bot workflow; update CI workflows to call router and selective bootstraps.
Arjun Patel (review): Nice separation of concerns. Two requests: make the router config evaluate path globs before language heuristics (so docs-only PRs route even if a docs script touched a go file), and add a short-circuit in the bootstrap when TOOLCHAIN_LOCK is present to use cached toolchains.
Maya Chen (author reply): Good catches — reordered evaluation and added TOOLCHAIN_LOCK short-circuit in the 3rd commit. Also added a unit test covering the glob precedence case.
Liam O'Connor (review): Please ensure the timestamp format is RFC3339 and add a small consumer test in the dep dashboard parser. Also: confirm dep-bot workflow still signs commits correctly.
Maya Chen (author reply): Timestamp uses RFC3339 UTC; added parser test and validated dep-bot commit signing is unaffected (timestamp appended in commit message footer).
Sara Gupta (approval): Tests and docs look good. Observability changes (presubmit CI metrics) will require a follow-up dashboard PR but this is approved from the SRE side.
Reduce presubmit latency by splitting language bootstraps and add presubmit heuristics to avoid running expensive checks on low-risk PRs. Add dep timestamping to dependency-bump commits for better traceability.

Context and motivation: Customers requested safer migration from legacy service-role YAMLs to RBAC v2 while ensuring KMS usage remains constrained to validated zones and audit logs carry an immutable proof header. This PR implements a service-claim policy compiler (to generate least-privilege RBAC v2 roles from existing service claim manifests), a KMS zone attestor middleware that verifies incoming requests contain a short-lived zone attestation token, and an audit-seal generator that appends an HMAC-style seal to audit events derived from a transient CMK-wrapped nonce. Goals: 1) Make RBAC policy migration automated and auditable; 2) Ensure KMS operations are bound to declared zone attestations at the per-request level; 3) Provide an immutable, small footprint audit seal for downstream retention and tamper-evidence.

What changed (high level): Compiles service claim declarations into RBAC v2 RoleBindings + conditions; adds a new middleware path in the API gateway (authn/authz) for KMS zone attestation verification; introduces an audit-seal step in the audit pipeline that signs event envelopes using a short-lived nonce created by the customer CMK via the KMS proxy; includes end-to-end integration tests and a lightweight policy-lint tool to validate generated roles.

Single-line summary of commits: feat(compiler): add claim->rbacv2 compiler; feat(kms): implement zone attestation verifier; feat(audit): add sealed-audit-enveloper; test: integration tests for compiler+attestor+seal; docs: usage guide and migration notes; ci: add e2e job for sealed-audit.

Changed areas / files (high level): src/policy/compiler/* (compiler core, heuristics, test cases); api/gateway/middleware/kmz_attestor.go (attestor implementation + caching layer); audit/enveloper/seal.go (seal generator + verification helpers); tools/policy-lint/ (CLI to lint generated roles); docs/security/claim-migration.md (migration guide); tests/integration/claim_kms_seal_test.go (end-to-end scenarios); chart/templates/gateway-config.yaml (feature flag and config knobs).

Implementation notes and tradeoffs: The compiler uses a conservative heuristic to prefer deny-by-default and only emits allow conditions directly referenced by service claims. We intentionally avoid full semantic inference (too risky) and instead emit an annotated policy with a migration-warning section. The KMS zone attestor expects an attestation token signed by our attestation service; to keep latency low we cache attestation validation results for 30s and fall back to realtime verification on cache-miss. The audit-seal uses CMK-derived nonces (GenerateDataKey-like flow) to avoid exposing raw CMKs; the seal size is intentionally small (96 bytes) to keep event storage costs reasonable while preserving tamper-evidence when combined with the existing audit chain hash.

Security review summary: Diego performed threat modeling focusing on token replay, operator escalation, and KMS misuse. Mitigations include short TTLs for attestation tokens, nonce single-use checks at the audit ingress, and RBAC compiler warnings to disallow generating cluster-admin level bindings. Sophie validated policy generation against our test corpus of 300 internal services; none required manual widening of permissions beyond the compiler suggestions.

Testing and CI: Added unit tests for the compiler heuristics, property-based tests for attestation token parsing, and an integration job that provisions a test KMS key and runs a full request path (authn -> attestor -> kms proxy -> audit seal). CI summary: initial run had a flaky attestor cache race on linux-arm which was fixed in the second commit; final CI status green (all checks passed).

Migration and rollout plan: Feature gated behind security.feature.claim_policy_compiler. Rollout phases: canary (5% of requests) with compiler disabled (only emits dry-run diagnostics), opt-in for policy application via admin API, then automatic application for services that pass linting for two consecutive runs. KMS attestor gate defaults to off; enable only after attestation-key rollout and customer opt-in. Audit-seal enabled by default for new accounts, opt-in for existing accounts with retention considerations.

Review conversation (high level; truncated): "Diego: please confirm replay protection for attestation tokens; add tests." "Author (Maya): added nonce single-use check and e2e test." "Jasper: policy-lint CLI looks good — one nit on output formatting." "Sophie: approved after test refresh and docs updates." No outstanding changes requested at merge time.

Release notes: "Add service-claim to RBAC v2 policy compiler; optional KMS zone attestation middleware; audit-seal for tamper-evidence. See docs/security/claim-migration.md for migration steps and rollout options."

Operational impact: Adds a small in-memory cache in the gateway (default 30s) and an additional KMS GenerateDataKey call when seals are emitted (batched for high-throughput paths). Estimated cost impact: +0.6% per 1M requests when audit-seal enabled (based on KMS pricing model). Performance: median p95 increase for auth path ~8ms on canary; mitigations documented in the rollout guide.

Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main after approvals and green CI. Follow-ups: SEC-820 add attestation key rotation tooling; ENG-4898 make cache configurable per-tenant; DOC-901 expand migration examples for legacy YAMLs.
payload.title: Service-claim policy compiler, KMS zone attestor, and audit-seal

Motivation: Production rollouts that commit traffic swaps as soon as the control plane reports target replicas healthy still expose end users to transient regressions from cold KV cache, session affinity mismatches, or slow tail latency on a subset of cohorts. This change introduces a 'deferred consensus' adapter that requires affirmative acknowledgements from a configurable quorum of session-cohorts before finalizing a model swap, plus a heuristic-driven recovery path that can pause, degrade or automatically roll back a swap when post-swap signals indicate regression.

What this PR does (high level): Adds a new rollout adapter that sits in the orchestration plane and coordinates multi-cohort commit semantics: 1) cohort-level readiness probes (application + KV cache warm status + sample latency quantiles) 2) a consensus window where cohorts must report stable metrics for N consecutive intervals 3) an optional TTL fallback to avoid stalls 4) a heuristic recovery engine that applies graded responses (traffic hold, selective bleedback, or immediate rollback) when composite signals exceed thresholds. Also implements a lightweight KV-cache snapshot and prefetch handshake used during rollback to reduce cold-start noise.

Key user-visible behavior changes: Teams can opt into 'deferred_consensus' policy in rollout specs. When enabled, rollouts will not finalize until the configured quorum returns positive readiness within the consensus window. On failures the adapter will publish a named rollback reason and attach an anonymized snapshot fingerprint to the rollout event to help debugging (no raw model data or inputs are included).

Concrete changes in this PR: - orchestration/adapter/deferred_consensus.go: new adapter implementation + controller glue - orchestration/api/rollout_schema.yaml: new policy fields and validation - agent/cohort_probe: probe implementation that returns readiness + kv-snapshot-hash - runtime/kvcache/snapshot.go: compact snapshot + prefetch protocol (gRPC) - console/rollouts: added per-session trace link and rollout event details - tests: unit tests for consensus arithmetic, integration test stubbing 3 cohorts, e2e with simulated latency spikes - docs: rollout policy reference and migration notes

Migration notes and backward compatibility: Default behavior remains unchanged. The new policy is opt-in. For customers using session-affinity heavy workloads we recommend enabling the policy behind a canary rule with a single cohort before wider adoption. KV snapshotting requires the runtime to expose the prefetch gRPC endpoint; the change is backward compatible (adapter falls back to existing warmup behavior if endpoint not present).

Testing and validation: Local unit tests (100% for adapter core), simulated integration matrix with 3 cohorts on perf-canary harness, staged dogfood run on Dedicated cluster for 48 hours. The perf-canary run injected controlled tail-latency regressions to validate graded recovery actions. Metrics observed: reduced false-positive rollbacks by 34% vs immediate-swap baseline; rollback downtime reduced by median 23s due to snapshot prefetch during failover.

Rollout plan: merge -> enable behind feature-flag (redwood.rollout.deferred_consensus) -> enable for internal dogfood as 1-cohort canary on 2026-02-19 -> 7-day telemetry evaluation -> gradual expansion. Rollback window for first canary: 2 hours with automated alerting to oncall SRE.

Security & privacy: snapshot fingerprints contain only compact hashes and runtime metadata; no customer tokens or model parameters are serialized. All control-plane events are audited via existing audit-log exporter pipeline.
Ethan Park: Overall LGTM. Two requests: (1) make the consensus TTL configurable at rollout-level and document the default; (2) add a metric for 'consensus_wait_seconds' so we can alert on stuck rollouts.
Sofia Nguyen: Thanks Ethan — added rollout-level ttl field (rollout_schema.yaml) and emitted consensus_wait_seconds in controller metrics (orchestration/controller/metrics.go). Updated docs with default values.
Priya Menon: Concern about snapshot size on large KV caches — can we enforce a max snapshot byte-size and fall back to bloom-based fingerprint?
Sofia Nguyen: Added 64KB compact snapshot cap and bloom-fingerprint fallback in runtime/kvcache/snapshot.go. Integration tests include a large-kv case to validate fallback path.
Liam O'Connor: Question about multi-region rollouts — how do we treat cross-region latency skew?
Sofia Nguyen: Multi-region behavior remains the same; the adapter treats cohorts as independent voters. We added an optional policy field 'region_affinity_weight' to tune quorum contributions per cohort (documented).
Introduces an opt-in 'deferred_consensus' rollout policy that requires quorum-based cohort confirmations before finalizing swaps. Adds heuristic recovery actions and KV-cache snapshot/prefetch to reduce rollback impact. Opt-in behind feature flag; see docs/rollouts/deferred_consensus.md for migration steps.
payload.title: Deferred consensus rollout adapter with heuristic recovery

Context and motivation: Some tenants observe transient microbursts that briefly exceed their reserved capacity and cause tail latency spikes or opportunistic overcommit. Existing warm-pool and burst-token systems either over-provision for worst-case or throttle abruptly. This PR introduces a provisional reservation model plus a surge decomposition algorithm that (1) splits a detected surge into a short provisional tranche and a residual steady request, (2) applies conservative decommit windows for the provisional tranche to avoid long-lived over-allocations, and (3) coalesces provisional successes into steady reservations when sustained demand is observed.

Design summary: The provisionalizer lives in the fleet provisioning controller as a short-lived allocator layered above the existing reservation ledger. Key concepts: provisional tranche (TTL-limited allocation), decomposition score (based on recent seqlen/throughput/latency signals), coalescer (promotes provisional to steady when SUSTAIN_FACTOR threshold met), and harmonic decommit window (backoff schedule that increases TTL for repeated short surges to avoid oscillation).

Behavioral guarantees: Provisional allocations are strictly ephemeral and do not modify persistent reservation state until coalesced. The controller guarantees that at most PROVISION_FRACTION of a pool's spare capacity may be used for provisional tranches at any time, preserving throughput guarantees for steady reservations. On controller restart or split-brain scenarios provisional allocations expire and are retried conservatively.

Config and rollout: New flags and config: provisional.enabled (cluster-level), provisional.max_fraction (default 0.15), provisional.default_ttl_ms (default 120000), provisional.hysteresis_multiplier (default 1.5), decomposition.window_ms (60000). The feature is gated behind a feature flag and operator config; documentation added in docs/ops/dedicated-provisional.md. The console exposes provisional-utilization and provisional-failures as new metrics.

Implementation notes: Changes touch three core sub-systems: controller/fleet/provisionalizer (new package), pkg/ledger (provisional ledger view and expiry hooks), and observability (metrics + traces). The provisionalizer uses the existing rate-limiter and admission hooks; when decomposition_score > SCORED_THRESHOLD, requests are split and routed to provisional path first. Promotion is done via the coalescer in the background at a bounded rate to avoid sudden long-lived allocations.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for decomposition heuristics and TTL backoff; integration tests using the perf-canary harness to replay historical microburst traces (see benchmark traces added under benchmark-lab/cases/provisional). Canary run against a staging Dedicated cluster shows 42% reduction in tail latency for tenants with spiky workload, with provisional-utilization peaking under 9% (below max_fraction).

Safety and rollback: The provisional path is opt-in per cluster; metrics and canary gating must be observed for 1 week after rollout. If provisional failures or unexpected evictions exceed thresholds, ops can disable provisional.enabled to revert to prior behavior. The implementation includes aggressive logging for early debugging and alert rules (ops/alerts/provisional-oversubscribe.yaml) to catch misuse.
Introduce a provisional reservation agent that decomposes incoming surge requests into short-lived provisional allocations and a lower-risk steady reservation; adds new telemetry for provisional utilization and commit coalescing. Backwards compatible; enabled behind feature flag by default off for Dedicated clusters.
Avery Chen: Please clarify how provisional allocations affect billing and accounting.
Maya (author): Provisional tranches are billed as 'transient' at a discounted rate by default; accounting team will map them to a provisional bucket. Added note in docs and billing mapping in pkg/ledger/provisional_view.go header.
Diego Martinez: lgtm overall but requested an additional unit test for coalescer backoff behaviour.
Maya: Added test 'TestCoalescerHysteresis' and updated decomposition thresholds to be configurable via env for tests.
Ruth Alvarez: Raised concern about controller restart—what ensures provisional expiries are enforced after leader change?
Maya: expiry_worker persists last-run watermark and checks orphaned provisional leases on startup; added idempotent expiry reconciliation. See expiry_worker.go comments and integration test 'TestExpiryReconcileFromColdStart'.
Avery Chen: approved after changes. Diego Martinez: approved. Ruth Alvarez: approved.
CI: full suite passed; flaky e2e previously observed on unrelated docs build was fixed by caching in CI pipeline.

Operator steps: 1) set provisional.enabled=false by default in existing clusters; enable in canary clusters and watch metrics provisional-utilization and provisional-failures; 2) set provisional.max_fraction conservatively (0.05-0.15) for first rollout; 3) monitor ops/alerts/provisional-oversubscribe.yaml and latency dashboards for tenants. For rollback: set provisional.enabled=false and restart controller; provisional leases will expire within provisional.default_ttl_ms + jitter and expiry_worker will clean up any residual state.

Motivation: Tensor-parallel training/inference exhibits periods where NCCL ring progress stalls waiting on KV cache eviction and kernel readiness. This PR introduces an epochal ring ‘schism’ allocator plus a lazy KV handshake protocol to allow NCCL collectives to proceed opportunistically while KV cache eviction and slot reclamation complete asynchronously. The goal is to improve overlap of comm/compute in multi-GPU TP serving scenarios without increasing peak memory footprint.

Design summary: single-coherent change implemented in three parts: 1) epochal ring allocator: rings are versioned (epoch IDs) so peers can progress on a sovled subset of rings while others drain; 2) NCCL handoff path changes: lightweight per-ring state machine and a short-lived fallback ring to preserve forward progress when peers lag; 3) lazy KV handshake: on eviction path we introduce a two-phase handshake where eviction requests mark slots as reclaimable immediately while the actual data scrubbing runs asynchronously; requesters may speculatively launch collectives that only require reclaim-marked slots.

Why unique: differs from previous ‘staggered’ and ‘pipelined’ schedulers by versioning ring topology at runtime and decoupling KV slot lifetime from immediate data deletion — this reduces critical-path stalls and helps the kernel scheduler keep GPU SMs busy.

Performance: internal canary on a 16xA800 TP model (seq_len=2048, microbatch=8) shows median tail latency improvement of 18% and 99th percentile wall time improvement of 22% for end-to-end generation under sustained load. Throughput increased ~9% at 95th percentile. Memory overhead: <2% peak GPU memory increase due to short-lived fallback rings.

Testing & safety: added unit tests for ring epoch transitions, simulated multi-node integration test that injects artificial delays on one peer, and extended kvcache evictions tests to assert no double-free races. CI ran GPU-integration suite; an intermittent kernel-torch binding flake surfaced and was fixed in a follow-up commit.

Rollout plan: feature gated behind runtime flag TP_ENABLE_EPOCHAL_RING (off by default). Canary rollout on Dedicated capacity clusters for a week, monitor per-route tail-latency and kvcache drop rates. If metrics regress >5% in tail latency we will auto-disable and rollback.

Files of interest: runtime/scheduler/epochal_ring_allocator.cc, runtime/collectives/nccl_handoff.h/.cc, runtime/kvcache/lazy_handshake.{h,cc}, tests/integration/tp_epochal_ring_sim.py, docs/rfc/epochal-ring-kv-handshake.md.

Checklist: [x] design doc + perf numbers [x] unit tests [x] integration tests [x] gated runtime flag [x] metrics dashboard slice

Related: builds on ENG-1842 (comm/compute overlap initiative) and complements PRs that adjust kernel microbatching.
Evan Cho: Nice approach — can you clarify how epoch ids are garbage-collected across long-lived jobs?
Aisha Khan: Epoch IDs wrap with a small grace period tracked in the allocator; added detail and unit tests to ensure no reuse during grace window.
Lena Park: Did we consider impact on tracing/observability? we need to tag fallback-ring events as low-frequency to avoid alert noise.
Aisha Khan: Added tracing spans with ring.epoch and a debug-only histogram for fallback creation; dashboard updated to filter by tag.
Diego Ramos: The integration test failed CI once due to a CUDA allocator race — looks fixed in f11c3a0 but add a comment explaining the pin.
Aisha Khan: Added inline comment and reference to allocator bug in third-party upstream (issue #1043).

Background: During a transient regional egress saturation incident on 2026-02-17 we observed aggressive tenant-level circuit flips and abrupt global egress caps that caused long tail latency and tenant unfairness. This PR introduces two cooperating mitigations: 1) a deferred egress-smoothening algorithm that applies a short, topology-aware ramp to global egress caps instead of immediate hard clamps; and 2) a tenant-cohort sentry that groups noisy tenants into ephemeral cohorts and applies softer backpressure with a priority bias, preserving SLOs for unaffected tenants. Motivation: reduce oscillation and cascade restarts when SLO-budget-driven circuits trigger egress caps; reduce noisy-tenant blast radius; provide richer telemetry for post-incident diagnosis. This change is implemented as a targeted hotfix behind a feature flag (egress.smoothening_v2) and includes additional metrics, alerts, and a minimal change set to runtime admission and control-plane decision logic. The description below contains the full checklist, testing, and rollout plan. Checklist: - [x] Implement deferred ramp algorithm in controlplane/egress (bounded ramp over 5s by default, configurable) - [x] Add tenant-cohort classifier and priority bias policy in runtime/circuit - [x] Emit new telemetry: egress.ramp_rate, tenant.cohort_id, cohort.backpressure_applied - [x] Unit & integration tests covering ramp boundaries and cohort demotion - [x] Canary rollout config and abort criteria in deploy/rollouts - [x] Add a golden end-to-end test in perf-canary harness - [x] Feature flag gating and config defaults tuned to conservative behavior Risk summary: The change touches decision logic for egress caps and request admission; to limit blast radius the flag is off by default and defaults are conservative (short ramp, low bias). If misconfigured, SLOs could still be impacted; additional runbooks and alerts are included. Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main behind flag; 2) Canary in us-west with 2% of traffic for 30m; 3) If stable, increase to 20% for 2h while monitoring SLOs and ramp_rate distribution; 4) Gradual global rollout. Abort criteria: any sustained >1.5x tail latency on p99, or >5% increase in error rate for non-cohort tenants for >15m. Monitoring & alerts added: See telemetry section below. Related: Incident INC-3118 (support ticket SUP-4421), follow-up ENG-1960 for cohort tuning and long-term fairness work.
Marcus: Can you explain the cohort lifetime and how we avoid thrashing?
Asha: Cohorts are ephemeral (default 60s) and entry uses a hysteresis counter (3 consecutive exceed events) to avoid flapping; the classifier also requires a min-requests threshold per tenant. We appliestaggered demotion to avoid immediate eviction.
Sofia: The telemetry labels look good; please ensure cohort_id is indexed in our bigquery export.
Asha: Added cohort_id to telemetry export and a note in egress_events.md.
Daniel: I ran the canary test locally; looks good but please add a safety gate for negative ramp rates.
Asha: Added explicit clamp to ramp manager and tests for negative/zero rates.
Marcus: Approve after the perf-canary test finishes.
Sofia: Approved.
Merge-bot: All checks passed and branch protection satisfied.
Hotfix: introduce deferred egress smoothening (bounded ramp) and tenant-cohort sentry to reduce circuit oscillation and noisy-tenant blast radius. Feature-gated; disabled by default. Adds new telemetry: egress.ramp_rate, tenant.cohort_id, cohort.backpressure_applied.
1) Enable egress.smoothening_v2 for canary cluster via deploy/rollouts; 2) Run perf-canary job and monitor dashboards: telemetry/egress-smoothening and slo/tenant-fairness; 3) If stable, follow rollout plan; 4) Create ENG-1960 ticket for cohort tuning and fairness audit.

Motivation: In the last two incidents we observed transient connection failures cascade into retry storms that amplified regional load and caused SLO excursions for p95 latency. Existing circuit breakers were tripping but immediate client retries and aggressive controller rebalances created oscillation. This PR introduces a defense-in-depth change: a bounded-retry window on the gateway plus a connection_quarantine marker and 'circuit quiesce' behavior in the serving runtime to prevent retry amplification and give nodes time to recover.

What this PR does (summary): Add a bounded retry middleware to the gateway that tags requests with a retry-hash and enforces a per-hash retry window and max-attempts. When the runtime detects repeated failures for a connection or tenant it sets a connection_quarantine flag (short-lived) in the control-plane which causes the gateway middleware to fail-fast with a well-known error code instead of retrying. The runtime's circuit_quiesce routine introduces a staggered reopen schedule with exponential backoff and jitter to avoid synchronized reopen storms. We also add an SLO de-escalation gate: if the cluster-level SLO budget is low, the system reduces retry allowances for non-critical tenant tiers.

Why this is different: Prior fixes focused on shedding or increasing circuit thresholds. This change reduces amplification by stopping retries earlier, coordinating runtime-level quiesce windows and providing a small control-plane signal (connection_quarantine) that the gateway can act on. The approach minimizes user-visible 5xxs for low-priority traffic while preserving fast fallbacks for high-priority tiers.

Implementation notes: - Gateway: services/gateway/retry_middleware.go implements RetryWindow and reads connection_quarantine from control-plane cache. It attaches 'X-Retry-Hash' and increments attempt counters stored in Redis (short TTL). - Runtime: runtime/scheduler/circuit_quiesce.go observes repeated request failures and flips connection_quarantine via control-plane API with TTL and reopen schedule. - Control-plane: controlplane/flags/connection_quarantine_store.go stores markers and exposes read/write APIs. - Telemetry: telemetry/metrics_registry.yaml adds metrics: gateway.retry_window_hits, gateway.retry_window_denied, runtime.quiesce_set, controlplane.quarantine_count. - Docs: docs/operations/quarantine-playbook.md describes incident runbook and rollback steps.

Testing and verification: Unit tests added for middleware and runtime quiesce logic; e2e test under tests/e2e/connection_quarantine_test.go simulates transient failures and asserts no retry amplification and that high-priority tier still receives allowed retries. Canary rollout plan uses feature flag 'bounded_retry_v1' with default off and gradual rollout to 10% of traffic for 48h, monitor gateway.retry_window_denied and p95 latency. Rollback is feature-flag toggle + revert config in control-plane.

Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for gateway middleware - [x] Unit tests for runtime quiesce logic - [x] E2E simulation - [x] Telemetry instrumentation - [x] Runbook and doc update - [x] Feature flag gating - [x] Canary rollout plan

Backward compatibility and safety: All behavior is behind the 'bounded_retry_v1' feature flag; default remains current behavior. The connection_quarantine marker is advisory; if control-plane is unreachable the middleware falls back to the safer bounded-retry defaults.

Related: ENG-8742, SUP-2119.
Anya Patel (2026-02-19): Can we quantify the expected reduction in retry attempts per minute in staging? Please add a baseline+post metric from the e2e sim.
Maya Chen (2026-02-19): Added gateway.retry_window_denied and an e2e assertion. The e2e sim shows ~78% reduction in excessive retries under the simulated spike; added numbers to telemetry test case.
Liam O'Connor (2026-02-20): Looks good overall. Two nits: (1) prefer 10s minimum quiesce, not 5s; (2) add clarity on what happens if feature-flag control-plane is not reachable.
Maya Chen (2026-02-20): Bumped min quiesce to 10s and clarified fallback behavior in description and code comments. If control-plane unreachable gateway uses local fallback policy with conservative defaults.
Diego Ramos (2026-02-22): CI flaked on lint, re-ran and all green. Approving to merge after squash.
CI (2026-02-24): all checks passed (unit, integration, lint, e2e on small cluster).
