Motivation: tri-SDK ergonomics around streaming + auth have drifted: Python and TS expose slightly different async-generator ergonomics and Go uses a puller interface with inconsistent lifecycle signals. This PR simplifies credential wrapper shapes, clarifies retry semantics attached to credential refresh, and polishes the async-generator/pullstream surface so application authors have a consistent, minimal API across Python/TypeScript/Go. Changes are intentionally API-stable for most users; a small ergonomic rename in the Go iterator is called out below.

Summary of changes: - Introduce a lightweight CredentialWrapper abstraction (non-breaking) that standardizes token lookup + refresh hooks and an optional prefetch API used by streaming connectors. - Map credential retry presets to an explicit SDK-level RetryProfile enum so SDKs expose the same presets (fast-retry, steady, conservative). - Python: add an async generator adapter with consistent .aclose()/.__anext__() semantics and a convenience .resume(cursor) helper used by streaming examples. - TypeScript: normalize async iterator types to match the Python surface (AsyncGenerator<T, void, unknown>), and export RetryProfile and CredentialWrapper types in the top-level package index for ergonomic imports. - Go: add a small wrapper type PullIterator that implements io.Closer semantics and documents the rename from old StreamCursor -> PullCursor (compat shim included). - Tests/examples: update three quickstart examples (py/ts/go) to use the new shapes and add coverage for credential prefetch under jittered expiry.

Why this approach: SDKs previously relied on repo-specific helper shapes which caused surface mismatch in examples and led to subtle streaming edge cases on reauth + idempotent retries. The credential wrapper centralizes token TTL handling and exposes a concise prefetch hook that the runtime can call in advance without changing caller code. Making retry presets explicit prevents divergent presets across languages.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed (ENG-2149) - [x] API surface proposal reviewed by SDK leads - [x] Unit tests added for each SDK - [x] Quickstart examples updated - [x] Docs snippet for migration and Go rename added

Compatibility notes: This PR is backwards-compatible for existing call sites in Python and TypeScript. Go sees a small ergonomic name change: StreamCursor -> PullIterator. A thin compat shim preserves the old type at runtime and logs a deprecation warning for one release. No runtime behavior changes expected beyond clearer lifecycle semantics (Close becomes recommended for long-lived streams).

Testing and CI: Initial CI run had a flaky test in python/streaming/test_reauth.py (timeout on CI worker). I re-ran the job after adding a 200ms jitter tolerance in the test harness (see commit 4) and the full pipeline passed. Local manual smoke tests: hand-tested cross-lang quickstarts against staging hosted API with long-lived streams and simulated token expiry.

Rollout plan: Merge to main and ship SDK minor bumps: python v0.19.0, typescript v1.27.0, go v1.8.0. Publish docs migration guide in docs/sdk/auth-migration.md and link from release notes. Monitor streaming error rates and credential refresh telemetry for two weeks.

Related: references ENG-2149, SDK-132; follows work on session-lease and retry-presets in previous PRs.
Diego Morales: Left a minor suggestion around making the CredentialWrapper prefetch async optional to avoid forcing await in hot paths. See comment on sdks/typescript/src/credential/wrapper.ts:12
Maya Patel (author): Good catch — implemented a sync/async bifurcation so hot-path callers can opt-in to prefetch. Added unit test for the sync code path.
Elena Kuznetsova: Can we add one paragraph in the migration doc that explains the Go rename and recommended pattern for Close()?
Maya Patel (author): Added migration section and small code snippet for Go Close() pattern. Also included the compat shim which logs a deprecation warning.
Samir Rao: CI originally failed on python reauth test. After increasing jitter tolerance test is stable. Approving pending green CI.
Samir Rao: Approved on final run.
SDKs: introduce CredentialWrapper (standardized token lifecycle + optional prefetch), RetryProfile enums, and a harmonized async-generator/pullstream surface across Python/TypeScript/Go. Go rename StreamCursor -> PullIterator (compat shim + deprecation notice). Minor version bumps for py/ts/go. No breaking runtime changes expected.
Backwards compatible: compat shim for Go rename preserves runtime behavior and logs deprecation warning. Consumers who relied on internal StreamCursor internals should follow migration guide.

payload.body:
This PR adds a new set of multi-tenant integration tests for Dedicated Burst admission that exercise: (1) fairness enforcement across tenants under sustained contention, (2) cooldown window behavior after a tenant hits its configured burst cap, and (3) correctness/stability of denial reason codes returned to routing/gateway. Motivation: our existing unit tests cover token-bucket math and individual policy rules, but we were missing end-to-end coverage for the emergent behavior when multiple tenants are simultaneously bursting and the admission controller is combining policy + telemetry + fairness state. These tests are designed to be deterministic (fake clock + fixed seeds) and to fail with actionable diffs (snapshot of per-tenant admit/deny timelines + reason distributions). Scenarios included: (a) 3 equal-priority tenants contend for a shared pool: verify admitted share stays within tolerance and no tenant is starved; (b) mixed priority tiers (gold/silver) with anti-starvation floor: verify higher tier gets preference without driving lower tier to zero admits; (c) tenant cap reached then cooldown: verify immediate denials return TENANT_CAP_REACHED, subsequent requests during cooldown return COOLDOWN_ACTIVE, and requests after cooldown recover; (d) pool saturation with fleet safety guardrail: verify BURST_POOL_SATURATED vs FLEET_SAFETY_TRIPPED are mutually exclusive and stable under retries; (e) policy disabled / tenant not enabled: verify POLICY_DISABLED and that fairness state is not mutated for non-burst tenants. Notes: these tests depend on the denial code contract introduced in pr-23795 and the fairness state machine from pr-23777; they also align with determinism expectations from the admission semantics ADR (routing must not observe oscillating denial codes under identical inputs).
itest/burst: add multi-tenant harness with fake clock + deterministic scheduler
itest/burst: add fairness contention scenarios (equal priority + mixed tier)
itest/burst: add cooldown and cap transition assertions w/ reason code snapshots
admission: export redacted debug snapshot for tests only (build tag itest)
ci: wire burst integration tests into presubmit with bounded runtime
Jordan Lee: The fairness assertions look good, but can we avoid hardcoding exact admit counts? I’d prefer tolerances + clear failure output so we don’t break on minor scheduling changes.
Benji Okafor (author): Updated to assert ratios within +/-7% over a 2m simulated window and added a failure dump of (tenant -> admitted, denied_by_reason) + timeline sample. Also seeded the scheduler and removed a couple of time-based sleeps in favor of FakeClock.Advance().
Keiko Yamamoto: Cooldown scenario: please validate the transition between TENANT_CAP_REACHED and COOLDOWN_ACTIVE explicitly. We’ve had bugs where we returned CAP_REACHED throughout cooldown and it confused CS.
Benji Okafor (author): Added assertions for the exact sequence: first denial after crossing cap -> TENANT_CAP_REACHED; next N requests within cooldown -> COOLDOWN_ACTIVE; first request after cooldown expiry -> admitted (or if pool saturated, saturated reason only).
Mina Haddad: For routing determinism, do we test that retries with same request_id don’t flip denial reasons? That’s been a customer-visible pain point.
Benji Okafor (author): Added TestDenialReasons_StableUnderRetry with idempotency key held constant. It asserts reason codes and retry-after hints are stable unless telemetry epoch advances (we simulate that explicitly).
Sean Gallagher: Please keep runtime bounded. This will be on presubmit. Can we cap the number of iterations and still catch regressions?
Benji Okafor (author): Reduced iterations, switched to simulated time, and added -short behavior (skips the 20x flake loop). Presubmit runs the short suite; nightly runs the full suite.
Internal: Added deterministic multi-tenant integration coverage for burst admission fairness/cooldowns/denial code contracts; wired into presubmit as a bounded integration check.
The itest-only debug snapshot is guarded behind an itest build tag and returns redacted state (no tenant names; only opaque tenant IDs + counters). If this becomes a maintenance burden, we can migrate the snapshot to the existing internal debug endpoint introduced in the support tooling work (ENG-4881) and have tests call it via localhost.

Motivation and summary: Token-level observability is critical to understanding micro-latency and cost behavior during generation. This PR adds fine-grained per-token phase metrics, a lightweight entropy estimator to detect atypical token-phase variance, compact sparklines panels for Grafana, and a smoothing layer for alert thresholds that reduces noise from single-token spikes. Implementation highlights: 1) runtime: instrumented token phase boundaries (decode, kv-lookup, attention, kernel-run) and exposed a two-value histogram metric pattern (count+sum) to keep cardinality low; 2) telemetry: new OTLP metric names (redwood.inv.token_phase_duration_ms_count, redwood.inv.token_phase_duration_ms_sum, redwood.inv.token_phase_entropy) and Prometheus exposition hooks; 3) alerting: added a spike-smoothing transform that computes an entropy-weighted moving median over a short window before evaluating SLO rules to avoid alert churn; 4) dashboards: Grafana micro-sparkline row per-route and a compact per-invocation token timeline panel; 5) testing: unit tests for the entropy estimator and an integration smoke test that verifies metric emission under synthetic workloads. Backwards/compatibility notes: new metrics are additive and default to off for older exporters via feature flag TELEMETRY_TOKEN_PHASES=false. Security and perf: instrumentation is guarded and uses sampling; CPU overhead measured at ~0.4% P50 in internal load tests. See release notes for rollout guidance and opt-in knob details.
Luca Moretti (2026-02-11): Can you show CPU cost numbers for the estimator under heavy QPS? Also suggest histogram buckets tuned to 0-1ms/1-5ms/5-20ms/20-200ms.
Amrita Patel (2026-02-12): Added microbench numbers to token_phase_metrics.go comments and adjusted histogram buckets as suggested. CPU overhead measured in perf-canary: P50 ~0.4% across our 8k QPS workload.
Tiffany Chen (2026-02-13): Alert smoothing logic looks good but please make the smoothing window configurable per-tenant. Also add a unit test showing a noisy single-token spike is suppressed.
Amrita Patel (2026-02-14): Made smoothing window configurable via alerts.yaml per-route override and added a unit test in pkg/alerts. PTAL.
Ravi Suresh (2026-02-16): Found a small race in exporter when feature flag is toggled at runtime — added a guard and re-ran CI.
CI Bot (2026-02-17): CI passed after flakey/test-telemetry was retried once. All checks green.
Luca Moretti (2026-02-18): Approved. Merging with squash.

payload.body:
Problem: Streaming structured outputs (JSON schema) occasionally violate schema mid-stream (truncated arrays/objects, tokenization artifacts) and that causes downstream tool-calls to fail or clients to drop the connection. OpenAI-compat tool/function calling semantics also differ subtly (function_name vs tool_id metadata and argument shaping), which complicates using Redwood's structured output validation layer with OpenAI adapters. This PR introduces an opt-in protocol mode that attempts to repair schema violations at the stream layer and a compact shim to align OpenAI function_call semantics with Redwood's toolcall fencing.

Solution summary: add a new response_format mode named 'autorepair' (exposed as response_format.mode=\"autorepair\") that: 1) detects likely schema violations during streaming, 2) emits lightweight REPAIR frames (inline, out-of-band hints) so clients can patch partial JSON while the stream continues, 3) provides a schema_resume_token that clients can use to request a soft-resume if the repair cannot be applied locally. The mode is conservative by default and off behind a feature flag to avoid surprising existing clients. Additionally, this PR adds an OpenAI-compat adapter shim that maps function_call payloads into Redwood toolcall fences and back, preserving argument shaping and adding explicit tool_id metadata for clearer audits.

Key behaviors implemented: - REPAIR frame format: a compact, newline-delimited text frame prefixed with 'event:repair' that includes path (JSON Pointer), suggestion (stringified fragment), and confidence_score. These are transport frames and do not count as model tokens. - schema_resume_token: short opaque token returned when a repair cannot be auto-applied; clients can POST /responses/{id}/resume?token=... to attempt server-assisted reconstitution. - Error taxonomy: ERR_SCHEMA_VIOLATION (terminal if autorepair disabled), ERR_REPAIR_APPLIED (informational), ERR_REPAIR_DEFERRED (requires resume token), ERR_TOOLCALL_MISMATCH (openai shim mapping failure). - OpenAI shim: translates {\"function_call\": {\"name\": ..., \"arguments\": ...}} into Redwood toolcall fence with tool_id=name and normalized JSON args; when Redwood returns tool results, shim converts back into function_call-compatible structure for OpenAI-compat endpoints. - Telemetry: new metrics stream.schema.repairs.total, stream.schema.repairs.applied, stream.schema.repairs.deferred, stream.openai_shim.mapping_errors. These are low-cardinality and tied to namespace stream.schema.

Compatibility and rollout: - Feature flag: runtime.feature.flags.stream_autorepair default=false; rollout to canary clusters for 48h, then 10% of prod, with an opt-in console toggle per-tenant. - Backward compatibility: when mode is off, behavior is unchanged. Autorepair frames are additive and documented in the API changelog; clients ignoring unknown frames continue to work. - Clients using OpenAI-compat endpoints will be opt-in to the shim until we validate compatibility with third-party SDKs.

Tests and validation: - Unit tests for the repair heuristic and resume_token lifecycle. - Integration tests that simulate token-truncated JSON and validate the REPAIR frame + client-side apply flow. - End-to-end canary against redwood-examples/chatbot and redwood-quickstarts/sample-tool-runner. - Perf microbenchmark: extra median latency for streaming requests in autorepair mode is ~+7ms at p50 and +18ms at p99 in our synthetic harness (within SLA targets).

Rollout plan & rollback: - Canary (internal) for 48h; monitor metrics (repairs.applied ratio, mapping_errors, end-to-end error rate). - If repairs.applied < 10% or mapping_errors > 0.5% for 1h, rollback feature flag. - Full rollback is non-invasive (flag flip) — no DB migration required.

Checklist: - [x] Implementation of REPAIR frame emitter in streaming runtime - [x] Resume token lifecycle + endpoint - [x] OpenAI function_call shim and roundtrip tests - [x] Unit & integration tests - [x] Console feature flag and tenant toggle - [x] Metrics and dashboards - [x] Docs & changelog entry (docs PR linked) - [x] Canary run

Related: Linear ENG-3187 (streaming schema robustness), ENG-3224 (openai-compat toolcall mapping). Docs and quickstart updates live in redwood-docs and redwood-quickstarts (linked).
Marcus Li: Can you elaborate on how confident the repair heuristic is? I'm worried about it silently mutating outputs clients expect.
Aisha Patel: Good point — repair frames include confidence_score and we do not mutate the canonical model stream. The REPAIR is advisory: we emit repair frames and the canonical data stream remains unchanged. Clients can opt to apply the repair locally. Only when the client requests server resume do we produce a repaired canonical payload for downstream consumption.
Sofia Nguyen: How do we ensure the shim won't break SDKs that expect function_call to always be the terminal output?
Aisha Patel: The shim is opt-in. For OpenAI-compat endpoints the shim toggles only when the tenant enables the openai_shim feature. Also, the shim preserves all original fields and returns an additional metadata bridge header 'x-rw-openai-shim:1' to help SDKs detect the translation layer.
Diego Ramos: CI flaked on TestStreamResume initially — was that a real race?
Aisha Patel: Yes, it revealed a race in the resume token store TTL. Fixed with small synchronisation in resume_handler and added deterministic test harness; rerun CI and passed.
Marcus Li: Approving provided perf impact stays within SLA and we have dashboards.
Sofia Nguyen: Approved after docs and changelog are linked.
Introduced an opt-in response_format.mode=\"autorepair\" for streaming JSON schema results. When enabled, the runtime emits advisory REPAIR frames for mid-stream schema violations and provides a schema_resume_token for server-assisted reconstitution. Also adds an opt-in OpenAI-compat shim that maps function_call payloads to Redwood toolcall fences for safer tool integrations. Feature is off by default and gated behind a console flag.
payload.title: introduce-autorepairing-structured-output-protocol-and-openai-toolcall-shim

payload.body: Context: multiple teams requested a simpler, prescriptive set of credential profiles for common server and client flows plus a lightweight, pausable pullstream facade to simplify token priming and backpressure in long-lived streaming scenarios. Motivation: reduce app-level glue across Python/TS/Go SDKs, improve parity, and make retry/reauth interactions predictable when streams are paused/resumed. This PR implements a cross-SDK 'syncable' credential presets API (server, client, delegated) plus a pausable PullStream facade that unifies pause/resume semantics, heartbeats, and credential priming hooks. Changes are additive and opt-in; existing APIs are left intact. Compatibility notes: minor behavioral change when using the new pause() API (streams now buffer a single in-flight token batch by default); consumers that rely on exact timing should test with the new pause window. Linear items: ENG-3412 (credential presets), ENG-3599 (stream facade). Testing: comprehensive unit tests for each SDK, interop smoke tests (py<->ts loopback), and end-to-end Canary against the hosted runtime. Rollout: feature-flagged in SDKs, scheduled minor bumps for py/ts/go. Checklist: [x] design doc linked in Linear ENG-3412, [x] implement presets in py/ts/go, [x] pausable facade in all SDKs, [x] unit + integration tests, [x] docs snippets and examples, [x] release notes.

payload.body:
Motivation: a production incident (INT-5678) showed repeated region failover flapping when transient health probes overlapped with aggressive tenant-level shedding; this caused cascading KV cache drains and a spike in tail latency. Goal: implement a lightweight failover coalescer that groups committed failover decisions within a short soft-holdoff window, harmonize it with the per-tenant rate limiter to smooth backpressure bursts, and add safer KV-drain fencing so requests are not lost during rapid handoffs. This PR introduces a failover coalescer component in the controlplane, a coalescer-aware circuit state (sticky-with-decay), a coalesced rate-limiter hook to delay aggressive shedding when a coalesced event is in flight, and telemetry/alerts to detect coalescer-induced stalls. Changes are designed as a targeted hotfix (no public API changes) with opt-in rollout via a feature flag (feature.failover_coalescer=true) to allow staged enablement. Checklist: 1) implement coalescer state machine and holdoff timer; 2) wire into regional failover orchestration; 3) add backpressure harmonizer in rate-limiter path; 4) extend KV drain protocol with sequence fencing and graceful retry markers; 5) add unit + integration tests covering coalescer edge cases; 6) add observability events and a Grafana dashboard fragment; 7) add rollback plan and backport to release/2026-01 if needed. Testing summary: local unit tests + integration suite on canary infra covering failover flapping, simulated network partitions, and tenant surge scenarios; latency and throughput validated against typical PLG workload traces; manual soak for 48h on canary region. Rollout plan: enable on 1 canary region for 2 hours, monitor failover.coalescer.activated, coalescer.coalesced_events, and per-tenant tail latency; if stable, ramp to additional regions across 6 hours. Rollback: flip feature flag off and revert to prior controlplane snapshot; KV drain fencing is backward-compatible and will not block prior nodes. Mitigation during rollout: keep conservative default holdoff (500ms) and micro-backoff decay to avoid long stalls. Related: ENG-1945 summarizes incident postmortem, SUP-1023 is the customer support ticket.
Rohit: Can you explain why 500ms was chosen as the default holdoff? We should make it configurable per-region; response: Default chosen after running traces from canary workload; added region_override in flags.go and clarified in rollout docs.
Elena: KV drain fence looks correct but add a unit test for fence replay; response: added tests/drain_fence_replay and integration scenario to simulate clients retrying with markers.
Samir: Concern about coalescer state persistence across controlplane restarts; response: manager now persists active coalescer tombstones to the lightweight raft log and recovers on leader election.
Squashed and merged after 2 approvals. CI green after adding fence replay test and small linter fixes. Deployed to canary region within 30 minutes of merge.
Hotfix: introduce failover coalescer and backpressure harmonizer to reduce regional failover flapping and tail latency spikes. Opt-in via feature.failover_coalescer; default conservative settings applied. Backport candidate for release/2026-01.
Enable feature.failover_coalescer=false by default; to roll out, follow docs/rollout/feature-flags.md. Monitor metrics: failover.coalescer.coalesced_events (should increase briefly), failover.coalescer.rejected_events, telemetry.kv.drain_fence_replays, tenant.tail_latency_p95. If coalescer causes unexpected stalls, set feature.failover_coalescer=false and scale out failover orchestration replicas.
Integration scenarios included: rapid-probe-flap, network-partition-then-heal, tenant-surge-while-drain; added golden trace comparisons and p95/p99 latency assertions.
payload.title: Holistic Shepherding: Stable Failover Coalescer and Backpressure Harmonization (hotfix)

payload.body:
Context: We observed persistent tail latency spikes when prefill-heavy workloads interacted with decode burst traffic (especially for long-context and interactive chat flows). Existing handoff relies on ad-hoc queue draining which either starves decodes or causes prefill bursts to monopolize GPU kernels.
Motivation: Create a predictable, throughput-friendly handoff that preserves low median latency while reducing 95/99th percentile tail without changing model kernels.
Design summary:
- Introduces per-executor token-buckets that govern prefill admission into the decode-facing pipeline. Buckets accumulate credits based on dynamic rate estimates and available KV cache warmness.
- Implements a lightweight handshaking protocol between PrefillStage and DecodeStage: Prefill offers chunk tokens; Decode accepts when capacity exists; declined tokens are returned and trigger a short backoff.
- Adds a small in-memory ring buffer (handshake window) to smooth sudden bursts and allow continuous batching inside decode kernels.
- Scheduler updates: a new scheduling priority class prefill_handoff that the dispatcher uses to prefer short-prefill-chunks for low-latency paths while allowing larger chunked prefill on lower priority.
- KV cache policy: soft-evict thresholds extended to prefer retaining recently-handshaken prefixes; prefetch hints propagate through the handshake to warm KV entries for imminent decodes.
Backwards compatibility: All features are guarded behind runtime feature flags (runtime.prefill_token_bucket and runtime.prefill_handshake_window). Defaults are off for Private installs and enabled behind a gradual rollout on Hosted and Dedicated.
Performance: Benchmarked on benchlab with mixed chat trace (70% short queries, 30% long-context). Results:
- median latency for interactive decode path improved by ~18%
- p95 improved by ~27%
- overall tokens/sec increased by ~7% on p3-xlarge-equivalent clusters
- KV cache hit rate improved by ~5 percentage points for warmed conversational sessions
Implementation highlights:
- runtime/scheduler/token_bucket.h/cpp: token bucket implementation with cumulative fairness and dynamic refill based on measured decode drain rate.
- runtime/pipeline/handshake_manager.{cc,h}: handshake orchestration and ring buffer management.
- runtime/pipeline/prefill_executor.cpp: splits prefill into adjustable chunk sizes, attaches token IDs for traceability.
- runtime/pipeline/decode_executor.cpp: non-blocking accept/reject path for handshake tokens; integrates with continuous-batching loop.
- runtime/kvcache/soft_evict_policy.cpp: prioritizes entries tied to recent handshake tokens.
- tests/benchmark/bench_prefill_decode_integration.py: new workload harness and end-to-end perf assertions.
Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for token bucket corner cases (zero refill, burst pressure)
- Integration tests to assert no deadlocks during handshake failures
- Benchmarks with and without kernel coalescing to isolate scheduler effects
- Canary rollout to 5% Hosted and 2 Dedicated clusters with telemetry gating (latency + errors)
Observability and operations:
- New metrics: prefill.token_offer_rate, prefill.token_accept_rate, prefill.handshake_rejects, prefill.window_occupancy
- Tracing spans for handshake offer/accept paths (trace keys pref/handshake)
- Console flag controls for bucket refill weight and handshake window size
Rollout plan:
- Experimental in main behind flags
- Canary on low-traffic clusters for 48 hours, monitor p99/p95/p50, errors, backlog sizes
- Gradual ramp controlled by canary automation and manual checks
Potential risks and mitigations:
- Risk: mis-tuned buckets starve decodes. Mitigation: conservative defaults, auto-dial backoff on reject storms.
- Risk: additional locking in handshake manager introduces contention. Mitigation: lock-free ring buffer and optimistic accepts; measured contention <2% in benchlab.
Checklist:
- [x] Token bucket impl
- [x] Handshake protocol
- [x] Scheduler integration
- [x] KV soft-evict hints
- [x] Tests and bench harness
- [x] Telemetry and Console knobs
- [x] Docs snippet for ops

Introduce a token-bucket based pipelined handoff between prefill and decode stages to reduce tail latency and improve throughput. Backwards-compatible config flags allow staged rollout and tuning for Dedicated clusters. No user-facing API changes.
Arjun Patel: Can you add a short-circuit when bucket capacity is zero to avoid offering tokens and reduce cross-thread wakeups?
Author (Maya Chen): Added fast-path in token_bucket.cpp so offers are no-ops when capacity==0; included microbenchmark showing wakeup reduction.
Sofia Morales: The backoff multiplier looked aggressive during load tests; can we make it adaptive based on recent accept ratio?
Author (Maya Chen): Switched to an adaptive multiplier that decays toward 1.0 if accept ratio > 0.7; updated unit tests and bench results.
Liam O'Neal: Please ensure metrics include 'handshake_rejects' with tag reasons (capacity|kv_cold|policy).
Author (Maya Chen): Added tagged rejects and a small breaking-out in console to surface top reject reasons for ops.
payload.title: rearchitect-prefill-decode-handoff-with-token-bucket-pipelining

payload.body:
Motivation: presubmit setup time and noisy global virtualenvs are slowing local feedback and contributing to flaky CI. This PR refactors the presubmit bootstrap to create short-lived, per-language ephemeral virtual environments (venv/virtualenv for Python, isolated node_modules for JS) that are created on-demand and cached per-commit hash. It also introduces a release-preflight smoke-runner that validates signing artifacts, artifact metadata stamping, and the lightweight release path (used by release automation) before the full release pipeline is triggered.

What this changes: ephemeral per-language venv creation logic in tools/ci/bootstrap.py (faster, parallelizable, robust teardown), a small action wrapper that performs lazy dependency install only for changed language scopes, updates to .github/workflows/presubmit.yml to split fast local lint checks vs remote heavyweight lint runners, and a new tools/ci/release-preflight.py that performs a dry-run against release manifests and an artifact verification step. Also bumps two GitHub Actions that were causing provenance warnings.

Design notes: the venv agent uses a commit-hash keyed cache directory and a TTL of 48 hours; CI workers clear stale caches in nightly maintenance. The lazy installer detects changed files via git paths and installs only the minimal subset of devdeps (uses package-dev-manifests under each workspace). Release preflight focuses on deterministic steps: artifact hash validation, signature chain presence (when signing enabled), and version stamping consistency. This is intentionally conservative: the preflight will fail-fast on mismatches and provide deterministic diagnostics for on-call.

Testing and rollout: landed behind a toggle PRESUBMIT_EPHEMERAL=true so we can roll out to a fraction of CI lanes first. Smoke tests were added to the presubmit pipeline to exercise creation/teardown and cache hit/miss behavior. Release preflight is wired into the staging release lane and does not gate production releases until we've observed ~1 week of stable runs.

Notes: minimal surface changes to developers; CONTRIBUTING.md updated with a short troubleshooting section. Linear tickets ENG-2891 (speed up presubmit) and ENG-2905 (release safety) are linked.
Evan Morales: Can we make the cache TTL configurable per-repo? Some teams prefer longer-lived caches.
Aisha Turner: Added PRESUBMIT_CACHE_TTL env override (hours) and documented behavior in CONTRIBUTING.md.
Priya Nair: Release preflight looks good, but we should surface signature mismatch diagnostics as structured JSON for the on-call toolchain.
Aisha Turner: release-preflight now emits a compact JSON diagnostics blob when run with --emit-json; included examples in the unit tests.
Liam Chen: Flaky lint runner in the remote lane still failed once in CI rerun — was this investigated?
Aisha Turner: The failure was a transient network fetch to the remote runner. I added a retry and improved logs; reran CI and it passed. See CI checks below.
- Introduce ephemeral per-language presubmit venvs (faster local feedback, reduced global env pollution)
- Add release-preflight smoke-runner to validate artifact hashes and signatures
- Split presubmit into lightweight local checks and remote heavyweight lanes; add smoke tests
- Bump actions/setup-node and actions/cache (minor hygiene)
Nightly cache maintenance job should be monitored during the first week; a quick dashboard tile was added to infra -> ci to surface cache eviction rate and release-preflight failures. If release-preflight emits signature mismatch diagnostics, on-call should follow the signed-artifacts runbook (SEC-RELEASE-RUNBOOK).
payload.title: ephemeral-venv-presubmit-and-release-preflight-smoke-runner

payload.body:
Motivation: We observed a class of regressions during staged model swaps that affected long-lived user pathways (multi-request sessions, multi-call chains, and cross-service conversation handoffs). Existing canary and shadow flows validate per-request metrics but lose fidelity on session-level behavioral regressions. This PR introduces a pathway-preserving staged-swap controller plus an "oblique shadow" mode and a compact rollback playbook for operational teams. Design summary: (1) Pathway-preserver: attaches a transient pathway token to user sessions during promotion windows so we can deterministically route subsequent requests from the same logical pathway to the promoted variant for validation without permanently breaking session affinity. (2) Oblique shadow: a controlled, non-blocking shadower that replays a sampled fraction of ongoing session sequences to the candidate model asynchronously, preserving original timing and semantic annotations; responses are recorded but not surfaced to users. (3) Rollback playbook: a lightweight playbook and API to compute impact score from pathway-level deltas (latency tail, loss in intent fidelity, hallucination rate) and execute fast unwind with session handback. Implementation highlights (single-line): adds pathway token lifecycle and lease manager (rollout/pathway_preserver.go), extends orchestrator to support oblique shadow lanes with adaptive sampling (orchestrator/shadow_lane.rs), telemeters pathway traces and delta scoring hooks (telemetry/pathway_emitter.ts), and introduces an integration test harness that replays recorded session traces against old and candidate models to compute cohort-level deltas (tests/integration/pathway_replay_test.py). Backwards compatibility & safety: pathway tokens are optional and scoped; if downstream services don't recognize them, the token is ignored. All new control-plane flags default to off; rollout controller requires explicit enablement by operator via flag --enable-pathway-swap. Operational playbook: included docs/runbooks/pathway-preserve-rollout.md describing step-by-step canary, oblique shadow tuning, smoke thresholds, and automated rollback commands. Why this is different: instead of only looking at per-request aggregates we now validate sequence semantics and preserve user experience across short promotions, enabling earlier detection of regressions that manifest across request chains. Testing & validation: unit tests for token lifecycle, deterministic routing simulation harness, integration replay tests with 3 representative session bundles, and a synthetic smoke run on perf-canary cluster. Deployment plan: feature gated for 2 weeks behind a remote flag; initial rollout to internal tenants then staged to 10% external traffic, monitor pathway delta score for 48 hours, then progressive increase. Metrics to watch: pathway-delta-score, pathway-p99-latency-diff, intent-consistency-drop, model-edge-error-rate. Rollback criteria: automated rollback triggers when pathway-delta-score > 0.15 for two consecutive 30m windows OR intent-consistency-drop > 8% on custodial cohorts. Ops notes: small additional CPU on control plane for pathway lease management; oblique-shadows add async IO but are batched. Security/privacy: replayed requests are redacted according to existing PII pipeline before being stored in replay buckets. Migration notes: replays use anonymized trace ids so A/B experiments are not contaminated. Related work: builds on prior queued shadowing and cohort-aware rollouts but focuses on session-semantics preservation and oblique non-interfering shadow extraction.
Liam O'Connor: This design looks promising; can you clarify lease duration bounds and what happens if the pathway token expires mid-session?
Ayesha Khan: Lease defaults to 5 minutes and is renewable on activity; the preserver will prefer continuity but falls back to session-sticky routing if lease is missing (documented in runbook).
Priya Sharma: The oblique shadow replay could surface PII in stored traces — ensure redaction executes before write. Add an integration test that asserts no raw PII fields persisted.
Ayesha Khan: Added redaction pipeline hook and a test that asserts persisted trace samples are sanitized. See commit c311d55.
Diego Morales: CI flaked on the new integration test once — observed a timing race in the harness. Can we add a deterministic seed and make sleeps idempotent?
Ayesha Khan: Fixed race by moving to deterministic trace clock in harness and replaced nondeterministic sleeps with channel signaling. Re-ran CI.
Introduce pathway-preserving staged swap: optional pathway tokens, oblique shadow mode for session replay, pathway-level delta scoring, and an operator playbook for safe promotion and automated rollback. Feature gated behind --enable-pathway-swap.
payload.title: Pathway-preserving staged swap with oblique shadow and rollback playbook

payload.body:
Context: Multiple teams requested a small, composable way to declare retry/backoff behavior and streaming backpressure hints across our Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs. Current patterns are ad-hoc per-SDK and tests repeatedly exercise slightly different default configs which makes cross-language parity tests flaky. Motivation: provide ergonomic, named retry templates (RetryTemplate) and a compact backpressure hint envelope (StreamHint) that SDKs can map to native retry implementations, with minimal caller surface changes. Goals: 1) introduce RetryTemplate presets (optimistic, stable, failfast) with explicit jitter and deadline strategies; 2) add StreamHint metadata that servers and the console can consume to adjust batching and KV-cache warmup policies; 3) keep public client callsites backwards-compatible (optional new param bag) and increment SDKs' minor versions; 4) add cross-sdk interop test harness and CI jobs that validate parity on the presets. Summary of changes: - SDKs: python, typescript, go: add a small RetryTemplate shim and StreamHint type in each SDK; optional "retry_profile" and "stream_hints" params accepted on streaming and non-streaming call helpers; minor ergonomic helpers for building templates (builders in TS/Go, factory helpers in Python). - Runtime/client: add lightweight header mapping so upstream gateway can see StreamHint.x-batch-preference and x-retry-template (this is opt-in; defaults not sent). - Tests: new interop test harness that runs permutations of the three presets across languages and verifies behavior under synthetic latency/failure injected workloads. - Docs: consolidated SDK migration guide, examples for common presets, and release notes. Rollout: staged. 1) Merge SDK changes behind feature flag; 2) enable interop CI and run canary exercises; 3) unflag and bump minor versions (Py 0.22.0, TS 1.14.0, Go 1.8.0). Migration notes: callers may pass retry_profile="stable" or provide a RetryTemplate built from factory helpers; existing callers are unaffected. If callers want server-side batching adjustments they should set stream_hints.batch_preference. Testing & validation: local unit tests per SDK, new cross-language CI job (interop/retry-templates) passing against a synthetic server that injects 5–20% transient errors and randomized latencies. Checklist: - [x] SDK APIs added (Py/TS/Go) - [x] Gateway header mapping implemented - [x] Interop CI job added - [x] Docs and migration guide - [x] Version bump proposals filed Risks & mitigations: Risk: accidental overuse of aggressive retry presets leading to higher throughput and cost. Mitigation: templates include telemetry tags and guardrails; Console will show per-route retry-template usage. Production impact: none by default (feature flags off).
Avery Kim: Please ensure the default "stable" matches existing backoff windows in production. Reply: Maya Chen: confirmed, stable = current default (exp backoff with full jitter, base 50ms, max 2s, deadline 20s).
Priya Nair: Will console and metrics tag the templates? Reply: Maya Chen: yes, telemetry includes retry.template=stable|optimistic|failfast and stream.hint.batch_preference where present.
Luca Rossi: Can we avoid breaking changes to typed streaming function signatures? Reply: Maya Chen: API change is additive (options bag); samples updated in docs.
Add named RetryTemplate presets (optimistic/stable/failfast) and optional StreamHint metadata to SDKs. Backwards-compatible; feature off by default. SDK minor bumps after unflag: Python 0.22.0, TypeScript 1.14.0, Go 1.8.0.
Added unit tests in each SDK to validate template->native mapping and integration tests against a synthetic server that injects controlled failures/latency. New interop CI job executes permutations across languages and preset combinations.

Background and motivation: In a recent incident we observed cascading slowpaths during a multi-zone storm where a combination of aggressive admission and aggressive regional failover caused noisy eviction and repeated circuit flips for medium-priority tenants. This change introduces a tiered admission quarantine: lightweight per-tenant probation windows (soft quarantine) followed by a short, telemetry-backed hard quarantine, plus a geo-fence correction that prevents duplicate egress-forced failovers when AZ probes disagree. The goal is to reduce SLO oscillation, improve stability during brief regional storms, and make on-call recovery less noisy. Implementation summary: 1) Introduce kidnap-resistant admission tiers in pkg/shedder/tenancy_shedder.go. Tiers: new_requests -> probation -> restricted -> suspended. Probation windows are exponential-backoff per-tenant and decay with successful requests. 2) Add a geo-fence reconciler in pkg/circuit/geo_fence.go that remembers the last proven healthy region per-tenant for a short TTL and disallows automated cross-region egress-switching if the destination region has fewer live success probes than a threshold. 3) Add a new circuit state transition metric (circuit_transition_reason) and a lightweight counter to avoid repeated flips: circuit_manager.go includes a 60s sticky window with graded decay. 4) Add a short-lived oncall probe and runbook under cmd/oncall-probes/ to help SRE manually unstick tenants during rollouts. 5) Observer changes: observability/alerts/slo.yml adds an alert for "SLO-flutter-rate" (rate of tenant-level SLO regressions) and a dashboard panel for probation window occupancy. 6) Tests: tests/e2e/geo_quarantine_test.go simulates flapping AZ probe signals and verifies no more than one forced egress-redirection within a 3-minute window for a tenant; unit tests cover tier promotion/demotion logic. Rollout and migration plan: - Phase 1 (canary, 10% hosts, region A): enable the tiered admission default with probation windows set conservatively (min probation 6s, max 90s). Monitor SLO-flutter-rate and probation occupancy. - Phase 2 (regional ramp): expand to 50% of traffic; if SLO-flutter-rate drops by >25% and no increase in successful-request median latency >5ms, enable geo-fence enforcement. - Phase 3 (global): full rollout with current defaults. Feature flagging: all behavior gated behind feature flag service.feature.tiered_quarantine; geo-fence gated under service.feature.geo_fence_reconciler. Backout plan: flip flags off; circuit_manager sticky window will naturally decay. Observability and telemetry: added histogram for probation_duration_seconds, counter for probation_promotes and probation_demotes, gauge for probation_occupancy_by_tier. Alerts added for SLO-flutter-rate and geo-fence-mismatch-count. Related issues: links to incident notes and SUP-1284 and ENG-4521. Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed by SRE and Runtime teams - [x] Unit tests added (coverage +4%) - [x] E2E simulation added - [x] Feature flags in place - [x] Runbook + oncall probe included - [x] Dashboard + alert created - [x] Canary rollout plan documented Possible risks and mitigations: - Overly conservative probation windows could delay legitimate traffic: mitigated by conservative defaults and rapid toggle via feature flags. - Geo-fence may hide genuine multi-region failovers: reconciler tracks recent probe success ratios and logs decisions; we instrumented telemetry to surface suppressed failovers. Security and compliance: no secret or policy changes. No breaking API changes. Merge notes: squashed commits into a single logical change and added an expanded commit message for release notes.
Arjun Patel: Please explain the decay math for the probation window in more detail. Concern: exponential backoff could penalize bursty legitimate tenants.
Maya Chen (author): We use clipped exponential with a per-tenant success-based fast-path reset. If a tenant has 3 consecutive successful requests inside probation we reset to min_proba (6s). The decay factors and clips are in the comments of tenancy_shedder.go.
Diego Morales: The geo_fence TTL seems short (30s). On under-provisioned regions probes can bounce. Can we make it adaptive?
Maya Chen: Good call. I added an adaptive_ttl = min(max(30s, 2 * median_probe_rtt), 180s) — implementation in geo_fence.go. I also added unit tests to verify behavior across RTTs.
Sofia Alvarez: Integration test flaked once in CI (e2e simulated race). Did we stabilize it?
Maya Chen: The flake came from a time-based assertion; I adjusted the test to wait for a stable window and added a retry harness. CI re-run passed.
Arjun Patel: Please include a short note in runbook for manual unstick steps.
Maya Chen: Done — cmd/oncall-probes/runbook.md includes the commands to clear probation and force a safe egress redirect.
Diego Morales: Approving after CI green and docs update.
Review status: APPROVED by Diego Morales on 2026-03-03
Sofia Alvarez: Approved — small nits in comments fixed.
Review status: APPROVED by Sofia Alvarez on 2026-03-04

payload.body:
Adds parser-driven fallback for regex constraint backends and a tokenizer boundary coalescer to reduce fragmented tokens during constrained decoding; includes regression tests and OpenAI-compat streaming adjustments.
Context and motivation:
This change addresses a class of structured-output failures we saw in customer workloads where hybrid CFG/regex constraints interacted poorly with the tokenization boundary during streaming. Previously, when a regex backend rejected a candidate token fragment that spanned a grapheme or BPE split, the OpenAI-compat streaming layer sometimes emitted partial tool-call payloads or malformed JSON fragments. These issues surfaced in two ways: (1) streaming stability regressions for long, regex-constrained prefixes and (2) silent quality drops when token splits prevented the CFG parser from recovering parse state.

Summary of changes:
- New ParserFallback module: uses the internal CFG parse state to guide the regex backend when the backend reports a token-level rejection. If the parser indicates the fragment is part of a recoverable production, ParserFallback asks the regex adapter to retry with token-coalescing hints.
- TokenBoundaryCoalescer: a tokenizer-aware heuristic that detects when BPE/grapheme splits cross constraint boundaries and coalesces adjacent subtoken candidates during streaming emission. Coalescing is conservative by default and respects latency SLOs (configurable threshold).
- OpenAI-compat framing updates: when coalescing delays emission or rewrites bytes, the compatibility shim emits explicit framing hints so consumers (tooling/clients) can avoid interpreting partial payloads as final function-call arguments.
- Tests and docs: added targeted unit tests covering emoji/grapheme, CJK, and long-prefix regex scenarios; integration tests simulate streaming tool-call sequences. Updated docs with a migration note and tuning knobs.

Checklist:
- [x] ParserFallback implementation with clear public API on constraints module
- [x] TokenBoundaryCoalescer with opt-in config for Dedicated/Private deployments
- [x] OpenAI-compat framing hints and fallback behavior documented
- [x] Unit and integration tests added and passing
- [x] Benchmarks added to compare before/after token churn and latency impact

Files of note (high-level):
- serving/runtime/constraints/parser_fallback.rs: core algorithm that correlates parse stack with regex match windows and issues retry hints to regex_backend_adapter.
- serving/runtime/tokenizer/token_boundary_coalescer.rs: stateless coalescing helper used by the streaming emitter; exposes TuneTokenCoalesceThreshold.
- serving/runtime/openai_compat/stream_framing.rs: emits 'coalesce_hint' metadata in streaming chunks so clients can suppress early parse of partial JSON/toolcall payloads.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Miguel Ortega (reviewer): "Nice separation of concerns. Two asks: add a regression test for a multibyte emoji split and document the runtime cost tradeoffs. Also prefer explicit opt-in via config for Dedicated."
- Leah Kim (author): "Added test for U+1F9D0 sequence and a new config flag token_coalesce_threshold_ms with a safe default (10ms) — documented in docs/structured_output/constraints.md."
- Nina Shah (reviewer): "I hit a flaky test locally (test_parser_regex_integration) — looks like a race during async backpressure. Please add a retry hokey in the test harness."
- Leah Kim: "Added a deterministic backpressure stub in the test harness to remove flakiness; left a TODO to re-evaluate with the new concurrency scheduler."

CI and QA:
- First run: lint and unit tests passed, integration tests failed due to the flake noted by Nina.
- Second run: after adding backpressure stub and minor timing tweak, CI passed all checks. Performance microbenchmarks show ~1.8% median token latency increase under max-coalesce mode, but token churn reduced by ~32% for constrained workloads (benchmarks/decoder/regex_vs_parser_coalesce.md).

Risk assessment and rollout plan:
- Low user-visible breaking risk: coalescer is conservative and off by default for Hosted API; enabled with safe defaults for Dedicated and Private where customers can tune thresholds.
- Rollout: feature-flagged on main, enable in canary for 48h with real traffic and regression monitors (tokenization_error_rate, psi_constrained_failures). If stable, auto-release to 50% and then global.

Merge outcome:
- Approved by Miguel Ortega and Nina Shah after follow-ups. CI green on final run. Merged via squash on 2026-01-21.

Follow-ups and telemetry:
- ENG-4231: tie tokenization_error_rate alerts to the new coalescer telemetry flavors.
- ENG-4299: evaluate alternative coalescing heuristics (embedding-based merge) if users hit edge cases.

Notes for maintainers:
- The ParserFallback API is intentionally minimal; if adding new constraint backends, implement the ConstraintRetryHint trait so the parser can exchange structured hints with the backend.
- See docs/structured_output/constraints.md for recommended tuning values and example Linear tickets for customer migrations.

Motivation: We need a low-risk path to validate RBACv2 policy decision changes and a mitigation for KMS nonce reuse that impacted a recent support case (SUP-3314). This PR introduces three coordinated pieces: 1) a canary enforcement path for RBACv2 policies that allows simulated decisions to be compared against live decisions before forcing deny/allow; 2) KMS nonce isolation to ensure per-tenant nonces are scoped and never re-used across service proxies; 3) an audit assertion sanitizer that strips or pseudonymizes PII from assertion payloads before they are written to long-term audit storage. The goal is to improve safety, compliance, and our ability to validate policy changes without causing regressions. Implementation summary: - rbac/canary: new middleware rbacv2/canary_router.go and canary_decision_engine.go that fork policy evaluation into a safe sandbox (OPA evaluation with a readonly context) and compare results asynchronously. Decisions are emitted to a new metrics channel (rbac.canary.mismatch) and to a dedicated canary-audit stream. The canary path supports three modes via feature flag: off, simulated, enforce (default rollout uses simulated only). - kms/nonce: introduce kms/nonce_store with tenant-scoped nonce namespaces and a short-lived in-memory ledger backed by Redis. The nonce API guarantees monotonicity per-tenant and rejects reuse attempts with a clear error code (KMS_NONCE_REUSE). Changes touch the KMS client shim and the grpc sidecar that brokers key wrapping. - audit/sanitizer: add audit/sanitizer service (audit/sanitizer.go) applied as a pre-ingest hook. Sanitizer rules are definable via a policy bundle (yaml) with regex + replacement templates; defaults anonymize email addresses, partial account IDs, and SSH keys. The sanitizer emits a hash fingerprint to allow matching without retaining raw values. Rollout and migration plan: - Stage 0 (canary config off): merged to main behind feature flag. - Stage 1 (simulated only): enable canary.simulate=true for 5% of tenant traffic (region + tier sampling) for 7 days. Monitor rbac.canary.mismatch and canary.latency. - Stage 2 (expanded simulation): 25% traffic for 7 days; allow ops to review mismatch traces in the canary-audit stream. - Stage 3 (enforce): flip canary.mode=enforce for tenants that pass policy checks and manual signoff. KMS nonce isolation is enabled as a separate opt-in config per deployment and is safe by default (rejects only suspicious reuse events). The sanitizer is enabled in simulated mode first (it doesn't redact in the primary audit index, only in a secondary sanitized stream) until we validate false positive rates. Testing: - Unit tests: 86 new unit tests for canary router, nonce store and sanitizer rule matcher (coverage + mocks). - Integration tests: add end-to-end test harness that replays historical audit traces through the sanitizer to validate fingerprint stability. - Load tests: canary path uses an async comparator to keep tail latency impact <1ms; perf lab run shows 0.7ms median additional latency at 90th percentile with 1000 rps. Security review: Priya Nair audited KMS changes and confirmed nonce storage is ephemeral and encrypted in transit; Jordan Reyes validated policy-simulation doesn't leak secrets into metrics. Observability: - New metrics: rbac.canary.mismatch, rbac.canary.latency_ms, kms.nonce.rejected, audit.sanitizer.redacted_count - Traces: canary/eval spans, sanitizer/hook spans, kms/nonce span annotation - Dashboard: added RBAC Canary overview and KMS nonce telemetry to Redwood Console under Security > Canary. Migration concerns: - Some legacy tenants rely on raw audit payloads; we default to simulated sanitizer stream; ops will coordinate with customers before full sanitize. - KMS nonce change requires deploy of updated sidecar in Dedicated and Private; upgrade docs added. Related work: builds on policy simulation groundwork (ENG-2107) and addresses the SUP-3314 incident. See Linear SEC-4592 for acceptance criteria. Checklist: - [x] Implement canary router and comparator - [x] Add KMS nonce ledger and API changes - [x] Implement audit sanitizer + default rule set - [x] Unit and integration tests - [x] Console metrics/dashboards - [x] Docs: migrated examples and upgrade steps (docs/security/rbac-canary.md) - [x] Add feature flag gating and rollout playbook Notes on safety: by default canary is non-enforcing (simulate) so no change to policy outcomes unless explicitly switched. KMS nonce is opt-in per deployment to avoid accidental failures on older clients. The sanitizer defaults to a secondary sanitized stream to avoid loss of raw audit fidelity during validation. Please see the linked dashboards and canary-audit stream for examples of mismatches and sanitizer transformations. Merge strategy: squash-merge. This was validated in a staging rolling upgrade. See CI summaries for passing jobs.
Adds a staged RBACv2 canary path with non-disruptive enforcement by default; introduces KMS nonce isolation for cross-tenant key usage and an audit assertion sanitizer to remove sensitive PII from logs. Default behaviour is opt-in for tenants; rollout via config flag and canary scaled to 5% then 25% before full rollout.
Jordan Reyes: Overall looks good. Two asks: add a TTL metric for nonce_store and tighten the redis keyspace prefixing.
Maya Patel: Addressed TTL metric and namespacing; added unit test for prefix collision.
Priya Nair: Confirmed encryption in transit; request: add explicit handling for KMS_NONCE_REUSE in SDK errors.
Maya Patel: Added ECONONCEREUSE error mapping and documented fallback behavior in SDK changelog.
Samuel Ortiz: Can we ensure sanitizer rules are versioned? Suggest policy bundle versioning header.
Maya Patel: Added a simple semantic version field to default_rules.yaml and updated the pre-ingest hook to emit rule_version metric.
Jordan Reyes: Approved after minor nits fixed.
Priya Nair: Security approved.
Samuel Ortiz: UX reviewed dashboard layout.

Context: Customers reported intermittent token swap latency and client-side queueing spikes under high-throughput streaming workloads. Motivation: give SDKs a lightweight policy layer to route credential providers at call time and a small, opinionated backpressure adapter to prevent unbounded memory growth in long-lived pull/push streams. This PR introduces two orthogonal pieces: 1) CredentialRouter: a configurable router that maps request metadata (route, model, region, priority) to a credential provider chain. Router supports simple rules (prefix, exact, regex) and a fallback cascade so apps can express per-route ephemeral credentials without central orchestration. 2) BackpressureAdapter: a client-side stream operator for pull/push streaming that applies a bounded in-memory window, optional drop/slowdown policies, and a token-bucket throttler for outgoing requests to avoid overfilling the runtime queue. The changeset touches TypeScript/Go/Python SDKs and the redwood runtime test fixtures to validate multi-SDK interoperability. Key goals: - preserve existing public APIs where possible and add opt-in constructors - provide clear telemetry hooks (events emitted when router changes provider or when adapter drops/throttles) - ship pragmatic defaults that work for common server-side SLOs Checklist: [x] Spec and API doc in PR description [x] TypeScript implementation and tests [x] Python wrapper and tests [x] Go implementation and tests [x] Integration test against local runtime fixture [x] Docs and changelog entry Major user-facing notes: - Default behavior is opt-in; no change to existing credential lookup semantics unless app constructs a CredentialRouter. - BackpressureAdapter defaults to a 100-message window with drop-oldest behavior; configurable via constructor. - Added minor SDK version bumps: ts-sdk -> v1.31.0, py-sdk -> v1.22.3, go-sdk -> v1.9.7. Migration notes included in release_notes below.
feat(cred): add CredentialRouter core and rule engine
feat(stream): add BackpressureAdapter with token-bucket and drop/slow strategies
chore(py): expose router bindings in Python SDK and add integration tests
chore(go): implement router and adapter; add unit tests and examples
docs: add usage examples and migration notes to SDK changelogs
test: integration fixture against local runtime to exercise router+adapter
Marco Silva: Overall this looks sensible; can we avoid exposing regex-based rules by default? Security staff typically prefer exact/prefix rules. Asha: Agreed — restricted regex behind feature flag and documented the risk in docs.
Evelyn Chen: Test coverage looks good but add a case for heartbeat-heavy streams that exercise the token-bucket refill path. Asha: Added test test_backpressure_heartbeat and updated the integration fixture to simulate heartbeat bursts.
Jonah Wright: Go impl lgtm; nit: prefer context-aware constructor for adapter to support future cancellation. Asha: Updated adapter.NewWithOptions(ctx, ...) to accept context and documented backward-compatible helper NewDefault.
Security Bot (automated): flagged use of regexp package in credential_router.ts; ensure patterns are bounded. Asha: Added max-length check and safe_compile util; re-run CI.
QA: Ran integration against runtime fixture; observed expected throttling events and no memory growth for 1 hour run. QA: Approved for merge.
Added CredentialRouter (opt-in) to route per-request credential providers; Added BackpressureAdapter for client-side stream flow control; SDK version bumps: ts v1.31.0, py v1.22.3, go v1.9.7; Migration: if you plan to opt into CredentialRouter, review docs/sdk/credential-router.md for rule safety guidelines and rotate long-lived credentials to ephemeral providers where possible.
Low-risk changes to SDKs; BackpressureAdapter is safe to backport to the 1.x maintenance branches for each SDK. CredentialRouter uses new rule parsing helpers — recommend backport only after security review for regex support.

Adds a proportional surge diffuser for regional load spikes and a graceful rejoin orchestrator that staggers tenant reinstatement to avoid post-failover thundering. Backwards-compatible config flags and telemetry added.
Context: Recent incidents showed rapid post-failover rejoin (region -> global) causing concentrated bursts that trip local SLO enforcers and oscillate circuits. This PR introduces two cooperating pieces: 1) a proportional 'surge diffuser' which converts sudden regional capacity shortfalls into controlled, priority-weighted shedding over a configurable window; 2) a 'graceful rejoin orchestrator' that sequences tenant reinstatement (soft-reinstate) with adjustable ramp profiles to avoid thundering and allow KV-cache warmup.

Motivation: We want to reduce oscillation and repeat circuit flips after regional failover events, ensure higher-priority tenants regain capacity first, and give runtime subsystems (KV cache, batching warm pools) time to stabilize before full traffic is restored.

Summary of changes:
- New runtime controller: runtime/surge/diffuser.go — implements proportional falloff based on tenant weight, request histograms, and SLO headroom. Diffuser emits per-tenant allowance tokens over a sliding window rather than immediate binary shed decisions.
- Graceful rejoin orchestrator: orchestration/rejoin/orchestrator.go — coordinates tenant reinstatement across the cluster, supports linear and exponential ramp profiles, and integrates with the existing canary/rollout APIs.
- Config: config/defaults.yaml — new stanza 'surge_diffuser' and 'rejoin_orchestrator' with sensible defaults and feature gates.
- Telemetry: metrics/metering.go — adds diffuser_allowance_gauge, rejoin_phase_gauge, and rejoin_lag_histogram; also hooks for tracing rejoin cohorts.
- Tests: unit tests for diffuser logic and end-to-end integration in tests/e2e/rejoin_cohort_test.go.
- Docs: docs/operational/surge-diffuser.md — operational runbook and tuning guidance.

Checklist:\n- [x] Design review (SRE + Runtime)\n- [x] Unit tests (diffuser logic corner cases)\n- [x] E2E test simulating regional failover with 3 cohorts\n- [x] Telemetry validated in staging\n- [x] Rollout plan and feature flag gated

Implementation details and rationale: The diffuser uses a proportional algorithm so tenants with higher SLO priority receive a larger share of the limited allowance. The allowance is computed from: local capacity deficit, recent tail-latency breach rate, and tenant weight. This avoids strict priority cutoff which previously starved mid-tier tenants. The rejoin orchestrator groups tenants into cohorts (size configurable) and issues soft-reinstate tokens per cohort. Soft-reinstate means the router accepts the tenant's traffic but annotates requests with a cohort id and a short-lived 'rejoin token' so that downstream caches can warm with predictable traffic shaping. The orchestrator includes safety hooks: if tail latency or error rate worsens during a cohort ramp, the orchestrator pauses and backoffs using exponential cool-down.

Compatibility and ops: All behavior is behind two feature gates: feature.surge_diffuser and feature.rejoin_orchestrator. Default state in this PR is 'off' for dedicated clusters and 'on' for staging. Operators can tune cohort size, ramp window, and proportional weights in config. Metrics added are exposed to Prometheus and we added a Grafana dashboard (docs link) for observability.

Commits:\n- 1a2b3c4: runtime: initial surge diffuser core algorithm and interfaces\n- 2b3c4d5: orchestration: rejoin orchestrator and cohort model\n- 3c4d5e6: telemetry: expose allowance and phase gauges; add tracing hooks\n- 4d5e6f7: tests: unit and e2e for diffuser + rejoin interactions\n- 5e6f7g8: docs: operational runbook, rollout notes, dashboard links\n- 6f7g8h9: hotfix: adjust throttle threshold to prevent under-shedding on bursty embeddings

Files changed (high-level):\n- runtime/surge/diffuser.go\n- orchestration/rejoin/orchestrator.go\n- config/defaults.yaml\n- metrics/metering.go\n- tests/e2e/rejoin_cohort_test.go\n- docs/operational/surge-diffuser.md\n- dashboards/rejoin-diffuser.json (grafana template)
Marcus Liu (SRE): Left a couple of nits on the tracing tags. Asked for an additional e2e with cache-warmup verification. Marked as APPROVED after tests were added.
Ravi Menon (Runtime): Suggested proportional weighting instead of percentile thresholds — updated implementation accordingly. Verified concurrency safety for allowance counter.
Claire Novak (Eng Lead): Requested operational runbook and rollout gates; approved after runbook added and staging telemetry ok.
Marcus: The tracing span needs tenant.id and cohort.id (so we can correlate warmup).
Anika: Added cohort.id to the span and added a short-lived rejoin token annotation.
Ravi: computeAllowance may be expensive in hot paths; can we cache recent values per node?
Anika: Added an atomic snapshot per-100ms window to avoid recalculation on every request.
Claire: Rollout plan?
Anika: Feature flag gated; staged rollout over 48 hours with automated rollback on >2% tail-latency regression.
1) Enable feature in staging for 24h and validate rejoin metrics; 2) Canary on 5% of traffic in prod with cohort_size=4; 3) Full rollout over 48h if no regressions; auto-disable on >1.5% increase in 99th latency for any cohort.
Operators can tune 'default_cohort_size', 'window_seconds', and per-tenant weights. If unexpected backlog occurs, set feature.surge_diffuser=false to revert to legacy shedders. Dashboard 'Rejoin & Diffuser' added with cohort lag, allowance utilisation, and rejoin pause events.
1) Monitor staging and prod dashboards for 72h. 2) Run canary eviction drills to validate rejoin safety. 3) Follow-up PR to add runtime CLI knobs to dynamically adjust cohort size.

payload.body:
Motivation: production customers see a class of user-visible failures when clients abruptly cancel or disconnect during long tool/formatted calls. The server may hold a lease and the inflight toolcall can be replayed or double-executed after a client reconnect. This PR implements a lightweight stale-lease probe + tightened cancel semantics to reduce double-execution risk while preserving resumability for benign reconnects.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds a server-initiated stale-lease probe that differentiates abandoned sessions from short reconnect windows. The probe escalates timeouts conservatively before reclaiming KV/lease resources.
- Introduces a client-cancel token update path: clients can send a final-cancel marker which causes the server to tombstone the stream but preserve a resumable checkpoint for a short grace window.
- Adds tool-call reentrancy metadata and dedupe checks (idempotency-by-tool-call-id) for tool integrations invoked during streaming. Tool plugins opt into the check via a small SDK surface.
- Updates the OpenAI-compat adapter to map cancel semantics and expose the new probe/tombstone events over the streaming protocol.

Design notes and tradeoffs:
- Probe behavior favors availability: we lengthen the reclaim window by default (configurable) to avoid reclaiming during typical client reconnects (cellular/mobile). Operators can tighten this via the session.expiry_policy config.
- Idempotency is best-effort: tools must provide deterministic ids or be marked non-reentrant. For legacy tool integrations we fall back to at-most-once best-effort with explicit audit logs.
- No user-facing breaking changes to existing OpenAI-compat clients: old clients will see the same streaming messages, but will not emit the new cancel marker. They continue to be protected by the extended probe window.

Rollout plan:
1) Feature gated behind runtime flag stream.stale_lease_probe (off in canary).
2) Canary (10% traffic) with canary-specific probe windows and additional metrics.
3) 100% rollout after 48h of canary with no increase in tool double-execution alerts.

Testing:
- Unit tests for session manager, probe state machine, and idempotency table in go/service/session_manager_test.go.
- Integration test that simulates client disconnect -> reconnect within window and ensures no duplicated tool calls.
- Load tests replicate long-running tool calls with random client disconnects to validate latency/cost impact.
- Local sharp-failure test to reproduce early abort and ensure tombstone path cleans up correctly.

Notes: This PR intentionally keeps the probe state machine minimal (three states: active, probed, tombstoned) to avoid long-lived orchestration logic. Future follow-ups will add observability dashboards and per-tenant tuning UI.
Server: stale-lease probe and tombstone transition; Session manager adds client_cancel_marker and conservative reclaim. Adapter: OpenAI streaming mapping for new events. Tools SDK: reentrancy id header and dedupe table. Tests/docs/helm updates and rollout guide added.

SRE bot: CI smoke passed, one flaky test rerun passed.

Added a configurable stale-lease probe and client cancel marker to reduce tool double-execution on reconnects. Tool integrations can opt into reentrancy-id based deduping. No breaking changes for existing clients.

payload.body:
Context: During Hosted canary rollouts beta, we hit a failure mode where the rollout orchestrator could stall in a step transition if cohort metric evaluation timed out (telemetry query timeout / downstream lag). The UI would show the rollout as "Progressing" (or "Evaluating stop conditions") indefinitely, and subsequent actions (pause/rollback) were inconsistent depending on which region worker had the lock. This PR makes metric evaluation timeouts explicit and recoverable: we retry metric evaluation with bounded backoff, and if retries are exhausted we move the step into a terminal error state that is visible in Console and actionable (pause/rollback). Root cause: the orchestrator treated METRICS_EVAL_TIMEOUT as a transient internal error but did not update step state; the worker would release the lease without emitting a state transition, and subsequent runs would re-enter evaluation but keep hitting the same timeout due to identical query window, resulting in no forward progress and no clear operator signal. Fix: (1) Introduce an explicit evaluator result enum: OK | STOP_CONDITION_MET | INSUFFICIENT_DATA | TIMEOUT_RETRYABLE | TIMEOUT_EXHAUSTED | QUERY_ERROR. (2) Add retries for TIMEOUT_RETRYABLE with jittered backoff (default 3 attempts over ~90s) and a per-rollout "metrics_eval_deadline" so we don't retry forever across worker restarts. (3) On TIMEOUT_EXHAUSTED, transition the rollout step to ERROR with reason=METRICS_EVALUATION_TIMEOUT and include the last evaluator details (query window, service, attempt count). (4) Make the orchestrator action handlers (pause/rollback) tolerant of ERROR steps so customers can immediately rollback without needing an internal override. (5) Emit a telemetry/audit event when we enter this error state so SRE sees it and the customer sees it in the rollout timeline. UI/Console impact: Console now gets a stable error code to display: ROLLOUT_METRICS_TIMEOUT. In the activity panel, we record "Metric evaluation timed out" with retry attempts and a hint to adjust stop condition windows / check telemetry health. The workflow shows a primary CTA to rollback, and a secondary CTA to retry evaluation (manual "re-check"), which triggers a new evaluation window (now + lookback) rather than reusing the stuck window. Safety: No change to stop-condition semantics when metrics are available; only changes behavior when we cannot evaluate within the configured budget. We intentionally choose fail-closed for step progression: we do not automatically advance traffic if we cannot verify SLOs, but we also avoid indefinite stalls. Testing: Adds unit tests for evaluator retry behavior and state transitions; adds an integration test that simulates a telemetry query timeout and verifies we end in ERROR with an actionable message; updates one E2E test stub to accept the new error code. Rollout: This is a hotfix safe for beta tenants; gated behind existing rollouts orchestrator feature flag. After merge, we should deploy to staging, then enable for beta tenants in US-East first and monitor "rollout_step_error_total{reason=METRICS_EVALUATION_TIMEOUT}" and orchestrator loop latency. References: SUP-48302 (beta customer auto-paused after latency spike; investigation showed metric fetch timeouts under load) and incident thread 1740726110 (split mismatch follow-up highlighted need for clearer "stuck" states).
rollouts/orchestrator: plumb explicit metric evaluator result codes and details
telemetry/evaluator: add bounded retry w/ jitter for timeouts; add deadline
rollouts/state-machine: persist step ERROR state for metrics timeout; allow pause/rollback transitions from ERROR
console-contracts: surface ROLLOUT_METRICS_TIMEOUT error code + details
audit: emit rollout.activity METRICS_EVAL_TIMEOUT_EXHAUSTED event
tests: add evaluator retry unit tests + orchestrator integration test for timeout -> ERROR
Sean Gallagher (SRE): Can we ensure this doesn't retry forever across worker restarts? We've seen lease churn during deploys and don't want permanent "try again" loops.
Hannah Rivera (author): Yep — added metrics_eval_deadline persisted on the step (derived from first eval attempt + maxRetryDuration). On restart, we respect the deadline and move to TIMEOUT_EXHAUSTED once exceeded.
Aisha Bello: What alerts are we expecting off the new ERROR reason? We should page only if it's widespread; per-rollout errors should be visible but not pagey.
Hannah Rivera: Agreed. Emitting counter rollout_step_error_total{reason=METRICS_EVALUATION_TIMEOUT} + a rate-limited event. Paging is not part of this PR, but SRE can add a dashboard panel and an alert on sustained rate > threshold.
Jada Williams: State machine question: are pause/rollback allowed from ERROR? We need to ensure customers can always rollback without support.
Hannah Rivera: Yes. Updated transition guards to allow PauseRequested and RollbackRequested from ERROR steps. Also added a regression test for "rollback from ERROR".
Logan Wright: Any concern about changing telemetry query windows when user hits "re-check"? We should be explicit about which time range is used.
Hannah Rivera: Re-check starts a new evaluation window anchored at now with the configured lookback. We include the query window in evaluator details so UI can show it in the timeline.
Sean Gallagher: Requested change: please include attempt count + last error in the activity event for easier debugging.
Hannah Rivera: Done in 5th commit; activity payload includes attempts, last_error, and evaluator_deadline_ms. (Audit event remains minimal; activity timeline holds the verbose details.)
Sean Gallagher: LGTM after that, thanks.
Aisha Bello: LGTM.
Jada Williams: Approved.
Logan Wright: Approved.
Fixes a beta issue where Hosted canary rollouts could stall if cohort metrics evaluation timed out.
Adds bounded retries for metric evaluation timeouts and transitions to an explicit ERROR state when exhausted.
Improves Console-facing error messaging and rollout activity timeline for metrics evaluation failures.
Allows immediate pause/rollback actions even when a step enters ERROR due to metrics timeout.
