Context & motivation: Customers running low-latency chat/assistants observed tail and first-byte spikes under mixed workloads where long-running batch streams interfered with interactive requests. This PR introduces an emission-focused state machine and per-stream priority lanes to ensure interactive streams get earlier kernel dispatch and opportunistic KV prefetching. The goal is to decrease median and P95 TTFB for streaming tokens without harming aggregate throughput.

Design summary: 1) EmissionState: replace ad-hoc token loop with a small deterministic state machine (Idle -> Ready -> Emitting -> Paused -> Finished). Transitions are driven by credits, kernel readiness, and a new priority hint on each stream. 2) Priority lanes: streams are tagged as high/normal/low; scheduler maintains lightweight queues and enforces a short head-of-line preemption window so high-priority streams can steal upcoming microbatch slots. 3) Soft-credit backpressure: credits are now virtual (soft) so low-priority streams yield proactively under congestion instead of being forcefully stalled, reducing contention bursts. 4) Opportunistic KV prefetch: small prefetch window for predicted next-token KV keys when a stream enters Ready; prefetch is limited by a budget to avoid noisy eviction patterns. 5) Observability: token-level timers for state transitions, per-lane queue depths, and prefetch hit/miss counters were added to aid tuning.

What changed (high-level files): runtime/emitter.h, runtime/emitter.cpp (emission state machine + unit tests); runtime/scheduler.cpp (priority lanes and preemption window); runtime/kv_cache.cpp (budgeted prefetch + cache hints); runtime/continuous_batcher.cpp (minor integration to respect lanes); tests/streaming_latency_test.py (regression harness + synthetic mixed workload); docs/streaming-latency-notes.md (design rationale + tuning knobs); ci/flake8-rules.cfg (lint adjustments for new code). Small illustrative snippet (for reviewer context):

// state transition sketch
// Idle --(newRequest)-> Ready --(credits & kernel_ready)-> Emitting --(rate_limit)-> Paused --(resume)-> Emitting/Finished

Commits (summary):
- 0a1b2c3: Introduce EmissionState and basic loop replacement (emitter.*). Add unit tests for state transitions.
- 1d2e3f4: Scheduler priority lanes implementation and preemption window; integrate with continuous batcher.
- 2f3g4h5: KV prefetch budget implementation and observability counters; extend latency regression test scenarios.

Checklist: [x] Design doc linked in PR, [x] Unit + integration tests, [x] Metrics exposed for canary, [x] No semver-breaking API change, [x] Manual perf run (see notes below).

Performance results (local perf lab synthetic mixed workload, 8-GPU pool, baseline==main): Median streaming first-byte latency: 18ms -> 11ms (-39%). P95: 72ms -> 36ms (-50%). Overall tokens/sec throughput: -3% at extreme saturation (expected tradeoff); typical 10-20% tail improvements with negligible median throughput change. Results attached in CI artifacts and docs/streaming-latency-notes.md.

Testing & CI: Initial CI run: lint failed due to style in emitter tests (fixed in follow-up commit). Unit+integration tests: pass. Synthetic latency regression harness: included and green. Load runner noted minor increase in KV eviction under pathological synthetic low-memory test — we added prefetch budget to avoid regressions and document tuning.

Review conversation (high level):
- Marco Jensen: Suggested clearer invariants for Ready -> Emitting to avoid race with kernel handoffs. Asked for a stress test for rapid connect/disconnect. Action: added test covering 5000 short streams and explicit assertion for state cleanup.
- Priya Kapoor: Requested metrics for per-lane preemption counts and a flag to opt-out of priority lanes for Dedicated customers. Action: added per-lane counters and a runtime knob (enable_priority_lanes=false) that defaults to true.
- Ethan Cole: Raised concern about KV prefetch noise. Action: implemented budgeted prefetch and exposed prefetch_budget config; added hit/miss metrics.
- Author replies: Addressed all requested changes; included short tuning guide in docs/streaming-latency-notes.md.

Merge notes: After reviews and two CI reruns (lint fix + perf artifact inclusion), PR was approved by Marco and Priya and merged via squash on 2026-02-27. Commit message summarizes the state machine, priority lanes, soft-credit backpressure, and KV prefetch budget.

Operational guidance: For customers sensitive to throughput under extreme saturation, set enable_priority_lanes=false or tune prefetch_budget and preemption_window in runtime config. Default knobs are conservative and expected to help most interactive workloads.
Reduce first-byte latency for streaming generation by introducing an explicit emission state machine, priority lanes for low-latency streams, and soft-credit backpressure. Includes observability hooks and regression tests. No user-facing API changes.
If streaming regressions are reported after deploy: 1) check metrics emitter.state_transition_errors and per-lane queue_depth; 2) verify prefetch_hit_rate is non-zero and prefetch_budget not exceeded; 3) if throughput drop, consider toggling enable_priority_lanes temporarily and engage perf team. Linked Linear items track follow-ups: ENG-7891 (observability follow-ups), ENG-8032 (tuning defaults).
payload.title: Refactor emission state machine and priority lanes to reduce streaming TTFB

payload.body:
Context
We need strict, explainable fairness enforcement for Redwood-managed shared burst pools so that a single tenant (or a small set) cannot monopolize burst capacity and degrade neighbors. This PR implements the fairness mechanism selected in ADR: a token-bucket + WFQ hybrid suitable for admission-time decisions with deterministic outcomes, plus tests and a small simulation harness.

What this PR does
- Adds per-tenant burst fairness accounting in the Burst Admission Controller.
- Implements a weighted token bucket (WTB) for each tenant + pool, with:
  - refill_rate = weight * pool_fair_share (derived from configured priority tier + baseline)
  - burst_size = configurable max_credit_seconds (prevents long idle tenants from accumulating unbounded credit)
  - charge = admitted_burst_gpu_seconds (estimated) at decision time
- Adds a WFQ-style tie-breaker for queued requests when multiple tenants are simultaneously eligible:
  - each admitted request is assigned a virtual finish time based on tenant weight
  - scheduler selects the minimum virtual finish time among eligible tenants
  - ensures stable ordering under contention, reduces oscillation vs pure token bucket
- Introduces anti-starvation guardrails:
  - min_grant_interval (bounded waiting time for low-weight tenants when pool has any headroom)
  - max_consecutive_admits_per_tenant under saturation to avoid head-of-line domination
- Explicitly separates two signals:
  - fairness eligibility (this PR)
  - fleet safety / circuit breaker (out of scope here; tracked in ENG-4902)

Determinism notes
Admission decisions must be deterministic for a given snapshot to prevent routing thrash and retry storms. This PR:
- Computes all decisions using a single "decision_time" passed from the caller (gateway/router) and uses monotonic time only within the controller.
- Avoids reading "now" multiple times within the decision path.
- Makes refill a pure function of (last_update, decision_time).
- Adds rounding rules for charges/refills (ceil to 10ms) to keep floating point drift out of comparisons.

Implementation overview
- New package: services/burst-admission-controller/fairness
  - TokenBucket: credit_seconds, last_update, refill_rate_seconds_per_second, max_credit_seconds
  - FairnessStateStore: in-memory implementation for tests + interface for the production backing store (redis-like) used elsewhere in the service
  - WfqScheduler: maintains per-tenant virtual time and calculates finish times for each admitted request
- New config surface (wired through existing controller config struct; policy engine wiring in separate PR):
  - fairness.enabled (default false)
  - fairness.max_credit_seconds (default 30s)
  - fairness.min_grant_interval (default 2s)
  - fairness.max_consecutive_admits (default 8)
  - fairness.weight_map (tier -> weight; e.g., gold=4, silver=2, standard=1)

Illustrative snippet (fairness charge)
- Before: admission checked only pool-level saturation + per-tenant cap
- After: admission also requires sufficient tenant credit

Pseudo-code (actual code is Go; simplified here):
  bucket = loadBucket(tenant,pool)
  bucket.refill(decisionTime)
  cost = estimateBurstGpuSeconds(req)
  if bucket.credit < cost: deny(FairnessInsufficientCredit)
  if saturated: enqueueWithFinishTime(req, wfq.finishTime(tenant,cost))
  else: bucket.credit -= cost; admit()

Simulation harness
Adds tools/fairness-sim (Go) to run a discrete-event simulation over synthetic tenant traffic patterns:
- scenarios: 1 bully tenant + 9 normal, 3 gold tenants + 20 standard, thundering herd at top of minute
- outputs: per-tenant admitted share, avg wait, p95 wait, starvation events
- results (local, deterministic seed):
  - bully scenario: bully share capped at ~weight/(sum weights) within ~10s; no starvation events observed
  - herd scenario: lower p95 wait variance vs pure token bucket; fewer oscillations in admit/deny patterns

Tests
- Unit tests covering:
  - refill math + rounding invariants
  - max_credit_seconds cap
  - fairness denial reason codes
  - WFQ ordering stability under equal weights
  - anti-starvation: low-weight tenant gets admitted within min_grant_interval when pool has headroom
- Property-ish test (bounded randomized) asserting:
  - over N seconds under sustained contention, share error <= 8% from ideal weighted share

Observability (minimal in this PR)
- Adds internal debug counters (not yet exported as Prometheus metrics; those are in PR-23822):
  - fairness_admit_total
  - fairness_deny_insufficient_credit_total
  - fairness_enqueue_total
  - fairness_starvation_prevented_total

Rollout / safety
- Feature-gated behind fairness.enabled.
- No behavior change when fairness.enabled = false.
- Backward compatible with existing tenant configs.

Follow-ups
- Wire fairness config via policy engine rules (PR-24033).
- Export Prometheus metrics + dashboards (PR-23822 / observability-pack).
- Validate at scale with load test harness (ENG-4841).

Refs
- ADR: adr-fairness-model-for-shared-burst-pools
- Related: ENG-4810 (controller skeleton), ENG-4821 (fairness enforcement)

Release notes
- Dedicated Burst: admission controller can enforce weighted fairness across tenants sharing a burst pool (feature-flagged).
Keiko Yamamoto: Can we cap accumulated credits? Otherwise an idle tenant could come back and monopolize the pool for minutes. Also please add a test around the cap behavior.
Jordan Lee (author): +1. Added fairness.max_credit_seconds (default 30s) and tests (TokenBucket_CapsCredit).
Mina Haddad: Routing needs deterministic denials for retries. Please confirm we don’t call time.Now() multiple times and that rounding is stable across instances.
Jordan Lee (author): Updated decider to pass decision_time through the call chain; refill/charge are pure functions of that timestamp. Also added 10ms rounding to avoid drift; see Fairness_RoundingInvariant test.
Ethan Park: The WFQ piece worries me if we don’t persist virtual time across controller instances. What happens on restart?
Jordan Lee (author): We persist (per-tenant virtual_time, last_finish) in the same state store record as the bucket; in-memory store is for tests only. Added a restart test using store reload to ensure monotonicity.
Sean Gallagher: Please add an explicit anti-starvation knob and a metric/counter for when it triggers. We’ll want to alert on pathological cases in beta.
Jordan Lee (author): Added fairness.min_grant_interval + fairness_starvation_prevented_total counter; metrics export will land in PR-23822.
Allison Grant: Label/cardinality: please don’t include raw tenant_id in any exported metrics. OK to keep internal debug counters for now, but follow-up must be careful.
Jordan Lee (author): Agree. This PR only adds internal counters with tenant_id in structured logs (debug-level) behind redaction. Metrics export PR will use tier/pool only.
payload.title: Implement token-bucket fairness for shared burst pools (WFQ hybrid)

payload.body:
Summary: Fix a class of SSE streaming failures where an escape-like trailing byte sequence emitted at the end of a function/tool-call payload could be misinterpreted by the streaming lexer and produce truncated or syntactically invalid JSON frames for downstream OpenAI-compatible clients. This manifested as malformed partial JSON in long-running streaming responses, most often when the user-supplied tool payload ended with '\\' or when the runtime emitted a delimiter immediately after a binary/base64-encoded chunk.

Motivation: Customers reported intermittent errors during streaming tool calls where the client-side JSON parser would raise a parse error halfway through a function-call boundary. Root cause analysis showed the streaming FSM would sometimes drop a delimiter or fold a trailing escape into the following 'data:' line when fragments arrived in edge-sized TCP packets or when backpressure caused interleaving between model tokens and tool payload flushes.

Root cause: The sse stream lexer assumed delimiters ("\n\n" or a full 'data: ' event line) were always emitted atomically. In cases where the last byte of a payload looked like an escape/escape-like byte sequence (e.g. trailing backslash, CR without LF, or base64 chunk break), the lexer would transition into an escape-state that incorrectly consumed the next event's leading bytes as part of the payload rather than boundary markers. This was exacerbated when function-call sentinel markers (tool boundaries) were emitted back-to-back.

This change:
- Rework the small-state streaming lexer to introduce a "trailer buffer" that conservatively holds up to 8 bytes when a potential escape/trailer is detected. The buffer is validated against delimiter patterns before committing bytes to the active JSON span.
- Add an explicit handoff path for function/tool-call sentinel emission: when transitioning from token stream -> tool payload -> token stream, the emitter now inserts an idempotent sentinel marker with a hint header (x-sse-sentinel: toolcall) that the lexer recognizes to force boundary secures even if fragments split across packets.
- Normalize emitter behavior for trailing CR/\n and stray backslashes so the client-visible 'data:' lines are never produced in a way that can be stitched into the adjacent event.
- Tighten timeout-rescue semantics: if the trailer buffer doesn't resolve within 120ms (configurable) the lexer emits a safe-rescue marker and continues rather than stalling the stream. This trades a deterministic small marker for availability and avoids client-side hangs during network pathologies.
- Add integration tests that simulate packetized fragment arrival, deliberate backpressure, and tool payloads ending in escape-like bytes.

Files changed (high level):
- go/protocol/sse/stream_lexer.go — new trailer buffer and state transitions.
- go/protocol/sse/emitter.go — sentinel header injection and normalization of trailing bytes.
- go/protocol/sse/lexer_test.go — expanded unit tests including fuzz harness for edge packets.
- node/openai-compat/stream-adapter.ts — compatibility guard for idempotent sentinel markers and fallback parsing.
- integration/tests/toolcall_stream_fragments.yaml — end-to-end scenarios simulating interleaved fragments and delayed delimiters.
- docs/api/sse-boundaries.md — documented the new sentinel header and rescue behavior for users integrating low-level streaming clients.

Checklist: 
- [x] Reproduce issue deterministically in integration harness.
- [x] Fix lexer state machine and add unit+integration tests.
- [x] Add emitter-side guard to prevent ambiguous trailer emission.
- [x] Update OpenAI-compat adapter to accept sentinel hints.
- [x] Performance: ensure no measurable token-latency regression (microbench shows <0.5% median increase).
- [x] Security review (no new unsafe parsers or unbounded buffering).

Testing & QA:
- Unit tests added for deterministic fragment sequences (packet sizes: 5–64 bytes).
- Fuzz harness extended to generate boundary cases for trailing backslashes, CR-only endings, and base64 line-break placements.
- Integration E2E runs in CI that replay recorded incidents from SUP-2187 and validate stream JSON roundtrip for both native Redwood clients and the OpenAI-compat adapter.
- Canary rollout: behind feature-flag 'sse-trailer-buffer', staged to 10% of traffic for 48 hours before global flip.

Rollout plan: Merge to main, deploy emitter + lexer updates together as an atomic runtime release. Feature flag controls rescue timeout and may be dialed down while monitoring. Observe streaming-error-rate, client-parse-failures, and per-route latency.

Related: SUP-2187 incident report, ENG-4921 (streaming robustness epic), small followup planned to expose rescue-timeout to Dedicated configs.

Notes: This PR intentionally prefers conservative buffering and explicit sentinel markers over heuristics that guessed at delimiter boundaries. The approach reduces rare parse failures at the cost of a tiny deterministic marker in the pathological path and a small, bounded buffer on the lexer side.
Fixes rare stream corruption that could cause partial JSON fragments to be emitted during function/tool-call handoff, improving streaming stability and OpenAI-compat behavior.

Motivation:
Observability backends see large short-duration bursts from clients (prefetches, retries, synthetic tests) that cause alert storms and saturate trace ingestion. Existing burst-handling is coarse: we drop or sample traces at the ingestion tier which leads to blind spots when investigating incidents and frequent false-positive SLO alerts.

What this PR does (single-string description):
- Introduces a metric escrow service: a lightweight buffering/lease mechanism that holds short-lived high-cardinality metrics for up to a configurable window (default 30s) and emits aggregated summaries to long-term pipelines. The escrow preserves per-tenant attribution and a compact burst signature so we can reconstruct a burst without ingesting all raw samples.
- Adds an adaptive trace throttle that coordinates with the escrow service. During a surge the throttle: (1) temporarily reduces sampling of low-cost traces, (2) preserves traces flagged by the escrow as "burst anchors" (e.g., high token-cost or error-bearing), and (3) opens an on-demand trace-hydration path to fetch full payloads for selected anchors if investigators request them.
- Adds a new dashboard called "Burst Canvas" (dashboards/burst_canvas.json) that shows escrowed burst signatures, per-tenant escrow occupancy, and synthetic SLO playback overlays so SREs can replay how alert thresholds would behave under recorded bursts.
- Adds a synthetic SLO playback tool and harness (scripts/synthetic_slo_playback.py) to run recorded burst signatures against current alert rules to tune hysteresis/quiet windows without hitting production traffic.
- Adds per-tenant escrow quotas and a backpressure policy that factors token-cost and kernel-queue metrics so GPU-heavy tenants are backpressured earlier.

Background and motivation: In a recent incident we observed a tight loop of node rejoin attempts combined with aggressive regional probe logic that caused cascading KV-cache evictions and sharp SLO regressions for a small set of tenants. This PR adds three coordinated changes to make graceful degradation more stable: 1) a lightweight rejoin latch that enforces exponential backoff and a short jittered quiet window for nodes that recently left a healthy pool; 2) an anticipatory load-shed controller that uses a moving-window quantile of request latency + KV-pressure to pre-emptively throttle low-priority workloads before hard circuit trips; and 3) probe hysteresis to avoid false-positive regional evictions from spurious probe spikes. The goal is to reduce oscillation during transient congestion while keeping high-priority traffic flowing. Summary of changes: - runtime/scheduler/rejoin_latch.go: new latch with atomic state, per-node cooldown and jittered reopen function. - runtime/shed/anticipatory_shed.go: controller that computes a smoothed 95th latency quantile and a KV-pressure index, emits shed decisions via existing SLO-weighted admission API. - runtime/probe/hysteresis.go: probe smoothing layer with consecutive-success/failure counters and configurable grace window. - telemetry/tags.go: new tags added to request spans (rejoin_latch_state, shed_decision_reason, probe_hysteresis_window) for better post-incident triage. - config/defaults.yaml: conservative defaults for the grace windows and thresholds; documented in comments. - tests/*: unit tests for latch backoff, shed controller heuristics, and probe hysteresis. - docs/runbooks/graceful-degradation.md: runbook section describing operational knobs and how to interpret new telemetry. Implementation notes and tradeoffs: - The rejoin latch uses exponential backoff up to 2m with randomized jitter to prevent thundering; it intentionally favors conservative reopen behavior to avoid rapid reflows. - The anticipatory shed controller is advisory: it marks requests as LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH priority to the admission path instead of outright dropping HIGH priority traffic. This preserves SLA for premium tenants while protecting SLOs for the system. - Probe hysteresis is deliberately small (3 failures / 2 successes default) so it doesn't mask true outages, but reduces noise from flakey dataplane probes. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests added and passing locally - [x] Integration smoke run in staging (latency trace sanity, KV retention) - [x] Telemetry tags verified in staging traces - [x] Config defaults reviewed with SRE - [x] Runbook draft included Risks and mitigation: - Risk: miscalibrated thresholds could cause unnecessary shedding for medium-priority traffic. Mitigation: defaults are conservative; rollout is gated with a gradual config ramp and metric-backed alarms (SLO error budget burn and shed-rate alerts). - Risk: new telemetry increases span cardinality. Mitigation: tags are low-cardinality enums and opt-in via config for high-retention telemetry. Related work: this PR builds on prior adaptive-shed and soft-degradation efforts (see ENG-1987) and should be rolled out in tandem with the kv-preserve sticky lease fixes merged last quarter. Rollout plan: 1) Deploy to a single low-traffic region with shed controller in advisory mode. 2) Monitor shed_rate, 95p latency, and SLO error budget; escalate thresholds if excessive. 3) Enable enforced shedding for non-premium tranches and increase rejoin latch aggressiveness only if probe noise subsides. 4) Full rollout after two days of stable metrics. Links: runbook: docs/runbooks/graceful-degradation.md, incident: https://linear.app/redwood/incident/INC-2025-06-rejoin-thundering
Marco Chen (reviewer): Please add a comment clarifying when we escalate a shed from advisory to enforced. Asha: added rollout plan and conservative default values in config/defaults.yaml.
Lena Ortiz (reviewer): Tests look good; can we add a short integration scenario that runs a KV-pressured synthetic to ensure no regressions? Asha: added staging smoke run notes and test harness used for the integration smoke run.
Diego Morales (approver): Verified telemetry tags in staging traces and load test results showing reduced oscillation. Approve to merge once CI passes.

Context and motivation: Large customers on Dedicated reported transient SLA violations when microbursts from noisy tenants caused long tail latency and short-term throughput starvation for other tenants. Existing reservation and warm-pool mechanisms reduced tail events but lacked a graceful, low-latency enforcement layer that could (a) shape headroom at sub-second granularity, (b) preserve minimum throughput guarantees for committed tenants, and (c) surface utilization drift telemetry for capacity tuning. This PR implements a slot-throttle fabric plus a minimum-throughput guarantee adapter and a utilization-delta exporter to address these gaps.

Design summary: 1) Slot throttle fabric: a lightweight in-process controller that subdivides pool capacity into fixed-size "slots" and enforces per-tenant slot consumption rates. Slots are a logical unit (not pinned GPUs) that allow soft throttling with configurable window sizes and decay. The fabric exposes token-bucket semantics for short-term bursts while integrating with the existing warm-pool and reservation layers. 2) Minimum throughput guarantee adapter: an admission/time-slicing adapter that ensures tenants with committed throughput receive a best-effort minimum over a rolling SLA window, moving excess slots away from opportunistic tenants when necessary. Guarantees are expressed as a fractional throughput quota per pool and can be overridden per-tenant via fleet config. 3) Utilization-delta exporter: new telemetry that computes per-tenant utilization delta across configurable windows (100ms, 1s, 10s) and emits Prometheus metrics + an optional structured trace event. This helps ops tune slot sizing and decay policies.

API & config changes: - config/fleet/throughput_policy.yaml: new fields: slot_size, slot_window_ms, slot_decay_ms, min_throughput_fraction, guarantee_window_seconds, enforcement_mode (off/soft/hard) - scheduler/admission: new hook registerSlotThrottle() used by Dedicated autoscaler when pool_type == "slot-fabric" - observability: metrics new: redwood_slot_allocations_total, redwood_slot_reclaims_total, redwood_util_delta_seconds, redwood_min_throughput_violations_total

Files changed (high level): src/autoscaler/slot_throttle_fabric.go, pkg/scheduler/min_throughput_adapter.go, telemetry/util_delta_exporter.go, config/defaults/throughput_policy.yaml, cmd/operator/templates/throughput_policy_crd.yaml, tests/unit/slot_throttle_test.go, tests/integration/min_throughput_integration_test.go, docs/operator/throughput_guarantees.md, e2e/dedicated/slot_fabric_smoke.yaml

Compatibility & rollout: The new fabric is opt-in. No config is changed by default. Operators can enable per-pool by setting pool.metadata.policy = slot-fabric and tuning slot_window_ms. Rollout plan: 1) canary enable on a small warm-pool (non-critical customers) 2) monitor redwood_util_delta_seconds and redwood_min_throughput_violations_total for 48h 3) gradually expand, adjusting slot_size and decay. For fleets with strict guarantees, enforcement_mode: soft is recommended initially.

Testing: - Unit: slot allocation/reclaim, decay logic, adapter correctness (edge cases around fractional guarantees) - Integration: multi-tenant integration test where an opportunistic tenant surges and committed tenants maintain min throughput under enforced mode - E2E: smoke config in k8s with 2 small pools (canary) - Load test: synthetic burst harness validated a 62% reduction in 95th p99 latency amplification for non-committed tenants while committed tenants maintained >=99% of their min_throughput_fraction over 10s windows.

Observability / debugging: Added structured logging when slots are reclaimed or when a guarantee is degraded (log id includes pool, tenant_id, window_start, window_end, expected_vs_actual). Utilization-delta exporter includes labels: pool, tenant, region, enforcement_mode. Dashboards: docs include an example Grafana panel and an alert rule suggestion (Alert when redwood_min_throughput_violations_total > 5 in 5m).

Backward compat & migration notes: No migration required. Fleet managers must opt-in to slot-fabric. When disabling, system reverts to previous reservation/warm-pool behavior with no data loss.

Security: No new secrets. The exporter uses existing metrics plumbing; no elevated permissions required.

Related work: builds on top of prior warm-pool hedging and reservation controllers (ENG-1829 / pr-314653). This PR focuses on fine-grained short-window shaping and telemetry rather than long-window reservations.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc attached (docs/operator/throughput_guarantees.md) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Load test results (bench/load/slot_fabric/) - [x] Operator CRD template updated - [x] Release notes entry prepared

Adds slot-based soft-throttling fabric with minimum throughput guarantees and new utilization-delta exporter. Behavior is opt-in via fleet configuration. No breaking changes by default.

Ravi Srinivasan (review): What about tenant burst reclassification to opportunistic after sustained overshoot? Response: added reclassification thresholds; documented behavior in operator docs.
Marco Li (review): lint: prefer context-aware logging. Response: addressed and tweaked log fields; added unit for log formatting. Approved after fixes.

This PR brings the Redwood OpenAI-compat /v1/chat.completions surface closer to parity by standardizing the streaming handshake, introducing a compact structured 'annotation' envelope for token-level metadata, and normalizing stop/logprob behavior across streaming and non-streaming paths. Motivation: customers have reported mismatches between our streaming frames and OpenAI tooling (incorrect finish_reason, missing per-chunk logprob aggregates, and inconsistent stop enforcement) which complicate downstream tool integrations and evals. Key changes: 1) add a short handshake envelope at stream start ("handshake_v1") that negotiates toolcapabilities and role-hints so client-side tool routing can be deterministic; 2) replace ad-hoc delta fields with a single top-level "annotation" envelope added to stream fragments that can carry stop_mask, logprob_summary, role_hint, and structured_tool_output snippets; 3) enforce stop tokens at both prefix and streaming-fragment boundaries and emit normalized finish_reason values that match OpenAI semantics; 4) compute a per-chunk logprob_summary to avoid leaking huge per-token arrays in the stream while preserving enough info for reranking/eval; 5) add conversion layer for legacy clients via feature flag "compat.v1.streaming_annotations" and deprecation notes for older framed modes. Backwards compatibility and rollout: default remains backward-compatible for existing Redwood clients; the flag is enabled for the Redwood OpenAI-compat gateway and rolled out to 10% of traffic for one week before 100% migration. This PR also updates the Python and TypeScript SDKs to expose the handshake metadata in their streaming iterators. Testing: unit tests for frame serialization, integration test against a local OpenAI-compat harness, and production canary on a subset of customers. Related Linear: ENG-2219 (stream parity), ENG-2278 (stop behavior regression). Checklist: - [x] handshake envelope schema and parser implemented - [x] annotation envelope encoding/decoding in runtime and gateway - [x] SDK exposure for streaming handshake - [x] unit/integration tests - [x] canary rollout plan and monitoring dashboards created - [x] docs updated with migration guide and examples
Ethan Park: Please add a short note in the docs about the handshake version so support can correlate client reports.
Sofia Patel: Added handshake version and included a correlation ID in the top-level frame (see tests).
María Gómez: The logprob_summary shape needs to be stable across quantization modes. Can you add an explicit spec?
Sofia Patel: Expanded spec in docs and added unit tests that assert the summary shape under 8-bit/16-bit kernels.
Lina Zhou: Canary metrics look good but saw an increased 95p latency by ~2ms; is this expected?
Sofia Patel: That's the marshalling cost; added a micro-optimization to the encoder that reduced the 95p to baseline +0.4ms on our canary.
María Gómez: Approving pending one small nit in the TypeScript typedef (answered).

Context: During a recent regional maintenance window we observed a cascading spike in circuit transitions and an elevated error rate while nodes were draining KV caches. The root cause traced to two races: (1) circuits that were reopened immediately after a short cooldown when a partially drained KV cache still returned cache-miss latencies, causing rapid reopen/close churn; (2) eviction/drain signals were not coordinated with the scheduler's soft-eviction path, so requests were occasionally routed to nodes mid-drain leading to tail latency and increased 5xx counts.

What this PR does: Implements a staggered reopen backoff with tenant-scoped jitter and an eviction coordinator handshake to ensure KV cache drain completes before a node is re-advertised for normal traffic. The patch is deliberately narrow and labeled as a hotfix: it focuses on safe defaults and observability to reduce blast radius.

Design highlights: - Staggered reopen backoff: new backoff policy with exponential base, per-tenant seedable jitter, and a configurable max cap. This prevents synchronized reopen storms when many circuits flip at once. - Eviction coordinator: a lightweight gRPC control-plane signal that makes drains explicit. Nodes publish drain phase states (prepare -> draining -> complete). The scheduler honors 'draining' by avoiding routing new long-running requests and by triggering hard-prefetch of KV prefixes to minimize mid-request misses. - KV drain handshake: coordination between eviction_coordinator and kv_drain to ensure the cache flush/sync completes before node becomes schedulable again. - Observability: adds metric 'circuit.reopen_reason' (labels: tenant, region, reason) and tracing tag 'eviction.phase' to help root-cause future incidents. - Safe defaults: feature-gated at runtime with cluster-level opt-in; default settings are conservative for the hosted platform.

Why this is a hotfix: We saw this exact pattern during an ops-driven node drain where the combination of fast reopen and uncoordinated drains produced visible SLO regressions. The changes are backward-compatible (new handshake is optional/timeboxed) and guarded behind a single runtime flag so we can roll-forward or disable quickly.

Testing performed: - Unit tests for backoff math and jitter distribution (deterministic seeds). - Integration test simulating node drain + cross-region traffic with mock KV backend included in integration/tests/drain_e2e_test.go. - Canary rollout in staging with 3 customers reproduced previous failure mode and confirmed latency and 5xx rates stayed within SLO bounds. - Manual chaos run: concurrent tenant spikes while draining produced no reopen storm after the change.

CI history: initial push failed flaky TestSchedulerRace in integration; fixed by adding a deterministic drain timeout and re-ran CI. Final CI: all checks passing (unit, lint, integration).

Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main behind runtime flag. 2) Deploy to staging with flag enabled for 24 hours and run smoke + load tests. 3) Enable in a selected set of low-latency customers in hosted for 48h with enhanced monitoring dashboards. 4) Gradually enable globally if no regressions.

Rollback: disable runtime flag to revert behavior instantly. If deeper rollback required, revert the merge and redeploy; changes are isolated to runtime path and do not modify persisted schemas.

Notes / alternatives considered: - Full scheduler rewrite to make drains atomic (too large/risky for hotfix). - Global randomized reopen window (rejected because it lacks tenant granularity and makes debugging harder).

Related: ENG-5421 (SLO degradation investigation), ENG-5482 (regional drain postmortem).
Aisha Khatri (requested changes): please add a metric label for reopen_reason and make jitter seedable per-tenant. Also add a short comment explaining why max_backoff is capped at 30s.
Author response: added metric + seedable jitter, documented cap rationale in comments and docs.
Liam O'Connor (nit + approval): suggested renaming 'drain_phase' enum to 'eviction.phase' to align with tracing; verified tests run in CI after fix. Approves after small naming patch.
Marta Ruiz (comment): asked about interaction with Dedicated autoscaler; confirmed coordinator exposes opt-in hooks for external autoscalers. Author replied with usage example in docs.
Hotfix: reduce circuit flip storms during node drains by adding staggered reopen backoff and coordianted KV drain handshake; new observability to help diagnose reopen causes.

Motivation: production workloads showed persistent fragmentation in the paged KV block manager under mixed-generation traffic patterns. Fragmentation caused wasted memory, higher allocation latency and unexpectedly high tail latency during heavy continuous-batching workloads. This PR introduces a two-part approach: (1) a lightweight tiered fragmentation mitigator that separates small/short-lived allocation paths from large/sticky blocks, and (2) a compact reuse path that opportunistically coalesces adjacent free runs and exposes contiguous ranges back to the allocator without global pauses. Implementation details: added a 'fast lane' per-worker freelist for sub-page allocations with probabilistic reclaim to avoid long-lived freelist holds; large-block allocations use a separate set of arenas that prioritize locality and avoid interleaving with the fast lane. The compact reuse path runs at allocation-time and as a bounded background task: it attempts in-place fusion of adjacent free spans and rewires free lists with atomic compare-and-swap to keep lock contention low. Pinning behavior was softened via an exponential backoff with jitter on repeated pin failures, plus a short-lived 'lease' to let in-flight KV readers finish while still offering pages for reuse when safe. Scheduler integration: allocation hotpaths now emit lightweight hints used by the serving scheduler to prefer kernels with aligned physical ranges (reduces TLB/PCIe pressure), and prefetch hints for upcoming KV accesses are emitted for continuous-batching flows to reduce blocking during kv cache population. Testing & benchmarks: unit tests and stress harnesses added (kv_frag_stress_test.py and a Rust micro-benchmark). Microbenchmarks: mixed read/write continuous-batch workload shows 18-23% throughput improvement and tail latency drop of ~28th percentile under our internal bench profile. Safety & rollout: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and disabled by default on older Dedicated nodes. Linear/Jira: ENG-1254 tracked the mitigation strategy; SUP-3421 links an incident where fragmentation regressed a customer workload. Release notes attached. Continuous integration: added a stress job to the bench pool and a canary rollout plan for Dedicated customers.
Diego Morales (2026-02-20): Can we avoid holding global locks during coalesce? Please add a low-contention path and show latency microbenchmarks.
Asha Kapoor (2026-02-21): Updated to atomic splice and per-worker background coalescer, added latency microbench results to bench output (see commits c3d2e7a).
Lena Fischer (2026-02-24): Suggest reducing lease duration fallback for high-throughput frontends; could we make lease adaptive?
Asha Kapoor (2026-02-25): Implemented adaptive lease duration based on recent pin success rate; added tests for lease adaptivity.
Samir Patel (2026-02-28): Approval after CI green and stress run within SLAs.
Improves paged KV memory utilization and reduces allocation tail latency by introducing tiered arenas and a compact reuse path. Adds adaptive pin backoff to reduce contention and integrates scheduler hints to improve kernel locality. Rollout: gated behind runtime flag; safe canary for Dedicated customers. Impact: up to ~20% throughput improvement and significant tail-latency reductions for mixed continuous-batching workloads.
Run kv_frag_stress_test with mixed read/write profiles and continuous-batching generator. Confirm no regression in Dedicated low-memory configurations and verify runtime flag disables behavior. Verify telemetry: fragmentation_ratio metric and coalesce_count trend.
Added: tiered allocator arenas for small vs large blocks
Added: compact reuse path with atomic coalesce
Added: adaptive pin lease and backoff
Added: scheduler prefetch hints for continuous-batch flows
Docs: perf/kv_allocator.md and rollout guidance

payload.body:
Context: Private installs run customer-managed Prometheus with tighter TSDB/storage limits and stricter cardinality constraints than our hosted environments. We observed high series churn from per-request and per-route/model labels, especially when customers have many routes, frequently changing model versions, or multi-tenant traffic. This PR standardizes label names across control plane + data plane services and introduces bounded label strategies for Private (while keeping a compatibility path for existing dashboards/alerts). Scope: (1) Label normalization: unify common label keys across services (service/component/namespace/cluster), rename inconsistent keys (route vs endpoint, model vs model_name), and remove labels that should never exist on metrics (request_id, raw path). (2) Cardinality reduction for Private: replace unbounded labels with bounded dimensions: route_group (config-defined, limited set), model_family (derived, bounded), tenant_bucket (optional, hashed bucket count), and status_class (2xx/4xx/5xx). (3) Compatibility: dual-emit old + new metrics/labels for a deprecation window behind a feature flag, plus recording rules that map old queries to new series so dashboards/alerts keep working. (4) Documentation: add guidance in the Private metrics standards doc and inline comments explaining why certain labels are disallowed. Implementation details: - Added a shared metrics helper package used by gateway, policy/routing, and runtime sidecars to enforce label allowlists and cap label values. - Introduced `REDWOOD_PRIVATE_METRICS_MODE=bounded` (default on for Private Helm values; off by default in hosted/dev) to enable bounding behavior. - For route dimension: emit `route_group` (from route config; defaults to "default"; max 50 distinct values per cluster enforced with "other" overflow). - For model dimension: emit `model_family` (e.g., llama3, mistral, qwen; unknown -> "other") and `model_variant` (optional; capped to top-N by request volume per process; overflow -> "other"). - For tenant dimension: do not emit raw tenant_id; emit `tenant_bucket` only when enabled (default disabled) to support coarse multi-tenant skew debugging without exploding series. - Removed `path` label usage from HTTP metrics in gateway; replaced with `route_group` + `handler` (bounded). - Updated recording rules used by the minimum pack dashboards to prefer the new labels, while still supporting legacy selectors. Notes: This is a stepping stone for the Private observability minimum pack (dashboards/alerts). Keeping dual emission avoids a hard cutover, but we should schedule removal once the minimum pack GA branch is stable. Testing: - Unit tests assert label allowlist enforcement and overflow behavior. - Added a micro-benchmark for the label bounding map to ensure we don’t introduce hot-path locks. - Verified in the private smoke-test harness that series count stays within expected limits on a synthetic 200-route / 80-model workload. Rollout plan: - Enable bounded mode by default for Private Helm chart values (separate PR in charts). - Keep legacy labels available for 2 releases; emit a log warning in bounded mode when legacy selectors are detected (dashboard queries) only in debug builds (no customer-facing noise). - Document migration in `docs/private/observability/metrics-migrations.md` and link in alert annotations where relevant.
Allison Grant (review): Can we ensure we never emit raw tenant identifiers in labels? Even hashed labels can be risky if the hash is stable. Suggest bucketing only and keep default off.
Thomas Baird (author): Agreed. Updated to `tenant_bucket` (configurable bucket count) and default disabled. Removed stable hash emission; tests added to enforce no `tenant_id` label anywhere.
Nadia Rahman (review): Dual emission is good, but please confirm the recording rules don’t re-introduce high cardinality (e.g., by grouping over model_variant). Also want clarity on top-N cap semantics.
Thomas Baird (author): Recording rules group by `model_family` only; `model_variant` is only emitted when enabled and capped. Added doc comment + unit test verifying overflow -> "other" and max distinct variants per process.

Motivation: During a regional egress disruption we observed a recurring pattern where long-lived sticky route allocations would hold on to overloaded pools and cause cascading circuit flips and extended SLO violations for a subset of customers. This hotfix introduces an ephemeral route-rescue path and a conservative, adaptive rate-trim step to reduce tail latency and stabilize SLOs while a full rollout of the regional failover redesign is scheduled.

What this PR does:
- Introduces a Route Rescue controller that temporarily isolates and re-routes traffic for routes that repeatedly trigger circuit transitions in >3 attempts within a 30s window. The controller marks those routes as "ephemeral-rescue" and applies softer token-level rate trimming plus an accelerated cooldown to allow KV cache transfer.
- Adds an adaptive rate-trim heuristic to the request router that measures per-route token emission bursts and reduces token allotment (max_concurrent_tokens) by up to 30% under sustained tail pressure; trims are decayable and tracked per-tenant-route.
- Improves healthprobe hedging to probe alternate regions faster when a rescue is active to avoid sticky failback.
- Conservative telemetry: adds a new metric rescue_attempts_total and rescue_active_routes, plus tagging to existing slo_violation counters so we can correlate rescue activity with downstream SLO behavior.

Checklist: 
- [x] Implement route rescue controller and in-memory eviction guard
- [x] Add adaptive rate-trim algorithm and config flags
- [x] Add telemetry and dashboard panels (temporary)
- [x] Unit tests for rescue heuristics and rate trim decay
- [x] Integration test in perf-canary to validate CPU/latency impact
- [x] Manual canary run against staging cluster (passed)

Commits summary: single-squash for merge with the following logical commits:
- feat(router): add ephemeral route-rescue controller and state machine
- feat(router): adaptive rate-trim heuristic + config knobs
- perf(healthprobe): faster alternate-region probe when rescue active
- infra(metrics): expose rescue and trimmed_token metrics to statsd
- test: unit + integration coverage for rescue/trim behavior
- docs: brief runbook note in ops/incident-guides about rescue behavior

Files changed (high level):
- services/router/route_rescue.go -- controller and state machine with comments explaining decision thresholds
- services/router/rate_trim.go -- adaptive trim implementation and decay logic
- services/router/router_config.yaml -- new flags (rescue.enabled, rescue.window_seconds, rate_trim.max_pct)
- infra/metrics/rescue_metrics.go -- metrics + tagging
- pkg/healthprobe/hedged_probe.go -- alternate-region probe path when rescue active
- tests/router/rescue_test.go -- unit and table tests for edge cases
- docs/ops/route-rescue.md -- short runbook

Notes on approach and tradeoffs:
- This is intentionally conservative: rescue state duration is short (default 45s) and trims are capped at 30% to avoid harming throughput for stable heavy routes. We prefer a short-lived local mitigation that preserves client-perceived availability while we iterate on longer-term regional affinity fixes.
- Rescue is opt-in behind a feature flag (router.flags.rescue.enabled) to allow fast rollback if we see unintended regressions.

CI and validation:
- CI initially failed due to a flake in probe hedging UTs (race during test teardown). Fixed by adding deterministic clock and explicit probe cancellation.
- Full test matrix (unit + integration) ran in ~22m on CI; perf-canary integration against a staging cluster showed 45% reduction in 99.9th percentile tail latency for affected routes during synthetic cross-region spike. Memory/CPU increase <4% observed on serving nodes.

Merge: Squash-merged into main after approvals and green CI. Post-merge we kicked a staging canary and watched rescue_active_routes spike and slo_violation drop for the affected customers. Ops has the flag ready to toggle.

Follow-ups:
- ENG-10012: Integrate rescue signals into regional failover planner to make rescues trigger coordinated region handoffs instead of local isolation (medium term).
- Dashboard follow-up to create a permanent panel that cross-correlates rescue_sessions with slo_violation_by_tenant.

References: Linear ENG-9876, internal incident notes (INC-2026-02-24-route-stick), canary run links: https://perf-canary.internal/redwood/runs/112358 (internal)

Carlos Rivera: Can't we just increase the cooldown globally? Concern is cross-tenant impact if rescue misfires.
Maya Thompson: We considered a global cooldown but that adds latency for healthy tenants; rescue is per-route and opt-in so scope is limited. Added explanation and default limits in the PR description.
Anika Patel: Request: add an explicit metric for trims_by_tenant so SRE can attribute regressions quickly.
Maya Thompson: Added trimmed_token_count and labeled it by tenant and route. Also added tests that assert metric emission on trim events.
Liam O'Connor: Found a potential race in hedged_probe teardown. Reproducer attached.
Liam O'Connor: Approve after the deterministic clock fix and test update.
Maya Thompson: Addressed the race by injecting a cancellable context and deterministic clock in tests; pushed fix and re-ran CI.
Hotfix: add ephemeral route rescue to prevent long-lived sticky circuit flips under cross-region surge; adaptive per-route rate trimming reduces tail latency and reduces SLO violations during bursty regional failovers.

Context: We’ve seen intermittent TP hangs under memory pressure that correlate strongly with KV cache compaction activity. Root cause (repro’d in benchmark-lab mixed prefill/decode and in one Dedicated A100 cluster): KV compaction was being triggered based on rank-local allocator state and “best effort” heuristics. Under sustained load, ranks can make different compaction decisions (or compact different blocks) within the same decode step, leading to rank divergence: one rank proceeds to the next step with a different set of KV pages/handles while another rank is still relocating pages or waiting on a different stream dependency. In practice this shows up as a silent stall where one or more ranks block on a collective in the next iteration because a peer is stuck in compaction/copy, or worse, ranks enter different collective sequences due to early-return paths. Change summary: (1) Introduce a TP-synchronized compaction plan: rank0 computes a compact-or-skip decision and a deterministic move plan (block ids + destination ids + epoch), then broadcasts to all ranks before any relocation begins. All ranks execute the same plan or all skip. (2) Make compaction “epoch” explicit and monotonic (kv_compaction_epoch) and attach it to per-request decode steps; early exits/cancellation now still advance through a shared barrier to avoid leaving peers mid-epoch. (3) Ensure stream safety: relocation copies + frees now happen on a dedicated compaction stream, with explicit event handoff to the compute stream before the next decode iteration touches the relocated pages. This removes the previous implicit dependency on allocator-side synchronization (which was not consistent across ranks). (4) Harden against fragmentation edge-cases: if the move plan cannot be satisfied (e.g., insufficient contiguous destination pages after reservation), we fail the compaction attempt consistently across ranks for that epoch and continue without partial moves. (5) Observability: add structured logs and counters for compaction epochs, plan sizes, and “rank plan mismatch” (should remain zero), plus a trace annotation tying compaction epochs to decode step ids. Tests: Add a TP stress regression that forces compaction under decode by lowering KV reserve watermark and injecting fragmentation patterns; validate that (a) all ranks report identical compaction epoch + moved blocks, (b) no stalls/hangs over N iterations, and (c) post-compaction KV reads remain correct. The stress test is gated in CI on a 4-GPU TP runner and is also runnable via benchmark-lab harness. Risk/perf: Compaction now has one additional broadcast per epoch and an extra event sync between compaction and compute streams; microbench impact measured within noise (<0.3% tokens/s) on A100-80GB for our long-context decode profile, and the broadcast is amortized since compaction epochs are infrequent relative to decode iterations. This should substantially reduce stall probability in the pathological fragmentation regime. Rollout: Safe to ship behind existing TP stability flags; no API behavior changes. This is a correctness + reliability fix and is part of the ENG-4821 TP stability initiative.

runtime/kv: make compaction failure consistent across ranks; remove partial move early-return
runtime/tp: plumb rank/world info to KV compaction planner; add mismatch assertions (debug)

Omar El-Sayed (review): Can you clarify why we need both the broadcast plan and the event handoff? I want to make sure we’re not papering over an ordering bug elsewhere.
Samir Qureshi (author): The broadcast fixes decision divergence (whether/what to compact). The event handoff fixes stream visibility (when relocated pages are safe for compute). Previously ranks could agree on compaction but still observe different readiness because relocation ran on different streams with implicit deps. Added a comment in kv_cache_compaction.cc explaining the two failure modes + linked the repro signature from SUP-48377.
Noah Patel (review): Please make the failure path consistent across ranks. Right now if reservation fails mid-plan on one rank, it returns early and peers keep moving blocks. That’s still divergence.
Samir Qureshi (author): Good catch. Updated: reservation happens first, and if it fails we broadcast a compact=false for that epoch (plan_size=0). All ranks skip relocation. Added a test that simulates reservation failure by constraining destination pages.
Hiro Tanaka (review): Do we need a device-wide sync here? I’m worried about introducing perf cliffs with cudaDeviceSynchronize.
Samir Qureshi (author): No device sync. It’s per-stream: record event on compaction stream after relocation, then wait on compute stream before next decode step consumes KV. Verified via Nsight Systems that we don’t serialize unrelated streams.
Sofia Ivanova (review): Scheduler angle: decode loop can be cancelled; are we sure we won’t hold a barrier forever if the request is torn down mid-epoch?
Samir Qureshi (author): Added a cancellation-safe “epoch finalize” that always participates in the rank barrier once compaction is entered. If the request is cancelled, we mark the epoch aborted and proceed to finalize; watchdog/abort semantics are handled elsewhere (ENG-4826). Also added structured log kv_compaction_epoch_state=aborted.
Marcus Reed (review): Stress test looks good. Please add it to the tp_stress_suite YAML with a conservative runtime cap so it’s stable in CI.
Samir Qureshi (author): Done. Capped to 90s, 3 runs, and made fragmentation seed deterministic. Also added a skip if GPUs < 4.
Omar El-Sayed (approval): Approved. This aligns with the stall signature we saw in repro notes. Please keep the debug mismatch assertion under a debug-only flag.
Samir Qureshi (author): Ack; mismatch assertion is behind RUNTIME_DEBUG_TP_ASSERTS and logs a counter otherwise.
Runtime: Fix KV cache compaction under tensor-parallel load by making compaction decisions deterministic across ranks and adding a TP stress regression test. Reduces risk of rank divergence leading to stalls/timeouts under memory pressure.

Motivation: a recent incident (SUP-4421) exposed oscillations when regional slowpaths briefly breached tenant SLOs: circuits reopened on a single successful probe and traffic immediately shifted back causing a cycle of open/close with increased tail latency. This PR implements a two-part hotfix: 1) introduce a reopen_debounce window and persistent reopen backoff for the pulsebacker SLO mitigator so a single probe cannot re-open a circuit; 2) add a graceful diversion mode ("pulseback") that slowly reintroduces traffic to healthier replicas with controlled pacing and transient token-throttling instead of an all-or-nothing failover. Goals: stop oscillations, reduce tail latency amplification during recovery, and provide observability for future tuning. Changes include runtime logic and conservative default config so behavior is opt-in-per-tenant until a follow-up rollout. Checklist: - implement reopen_debounce and reopen_backoff counters in slo_mitigator runtime; - add pulseback diversion algorithm and token-shaper with configurable ramp-rate; - fix circuit state persistence bug where transient probe success cleared sticky_reopen flag; - add telemetry (slo_mitigator.latency_window, pulsebacker.divert_rate, pulsebacker.reopen_debounce_count) and dashboard snippets; - integration tests simulating steady-state and noisy probe flapping; - add runbook note under docs/operational for on-call steps and rollback. Testing: unit tests added for state machine paths; integration simulation that runs a 60s noisy-probe scenario shows circuits stay closed for configured debounce window and diversion ramps from 5% -> 50% over 30s without oscillation. CI history: initial CI run flagged a flaky probe unit test (probe_fuzzy_backoff_test) due to a timing assumption; updated test to use a deterministic clock and re-ran — CI passed. Rollout plan: merge hotfix to main, enable feature-flag to a small cohort of tenants for 48h, monitor new metrics and slowpath latencies, then widen. Rollback: revert feature-flag and configuration; state persistence changes include a migration-safe toggle. Risks: misconfigured ramp rates could increase median latency slightly during recovery; conservative defaults chosen to avoid impact. Related: ENG-2198 tracks the production rollout and param tuning; ENG-2320 is a follow-up to expose tenant-level control in Console. This is a non-breaking runtime patch but touches circuit persistence and routing; coordinated rollouts with SRE required.
Arjun Patel: Nice isolation of state machine changes; please add a short note in slo_mitigator.rs explaining why reopen_debounce is intentionally longer than typical probe interval.
Maya Chen (author): Added clarifying comment and unit test that demonstrates correct timeout behavior.
Liam O'Connor: I saw potential high-cardinality tags in the new metrics; can we ensure tenant_id is not added to every sample? Otherwise dashboards will explode.
Maya Chen (author): Good catch; metrics now include tenant-cohort tag instead of raw tenant_id and we added aggregation-friendly labels in the instrumentation layer.
Sofia Morales: Integration test looks robust but add an assertion verifying that divert_rate does not exceed configured max under repeated probe flapping.
Maya Chen (author): Added assertion and extended simulation period to 120s to cover long-tail scenarios.
CI: initial run failed: probe_fuzzy_backoff_test (timing race). Author updated tests to deterministic clock; CI re-run passed.
Fixes premature circuit re-open in pulsebacker SLO mitigator; adds safer fallback traffic shaping and additional telemetry for SLO breach windows.
payload.title: Graceful SLO breach mitigator and pulsebacker hotfix

Motivation: customers regularly ask for sensible defaults for batching, caching and quantization that map to clear unit-economic outcomes. We need a declarative way to encode tenant-level presets, a small telemetry adaptor to assign and evaluate those presets against live metrics, and tooling to safely preview and backfill assignments. This PR introduces: 1) a declarative presets format (YAML) and a lightweight parser in the control plane that exposes a /admin/unit-econ-presets endpoint; 2) a telemetry adaptor that consumes existing infra metrics and emits econ.assigned_profile, econ.estimated_savings, econ.confidence as meter-level metrics; 3) a dry-run CLI (redwood econ preview) that simulates applying presets to a tenant and produces an estimate report; 4) a backfill migration that assigns a best-effort preset to tenants missing explicit profiles (guarded behind a feature flag); 5) automated unit tests and integration smoke tests for the adaptor and CLI; 6) documentation and example presets in examples/unit-econ-presets/*. Why this shape: declarative YAML is easy for SRE/product to author and audit, the adaptor decouples ML inference of best-fit profile from enforcement, and the dry-run/backfill tooling reduces risk for gradual rollouts. Changes: - control plane: api/admin/unit_econ_presets.go (implements CRUD + validation + syntax errors with line numbers) - telemetry: services/telemetry/econ_adaptor.go (maps metrics, computes confidence, emits counters and histograms) - cli: tools/redwood-econ/cmd_preview.go (dry-run mode, CSV/JSON report) - migration: db/migrations/20260218_backfill_unit_econ.sql + migration runner changes with feature flag gating - examples and docs: docs/ops/econ-presets.md and examples/unit-econ-presets/* - tests: telemetry/*_test.go and cli/*_test.go Rollout plan: 1) merge behind feature flag; 2) enable adaptor in staging for 48h to validate metrics distribution and verify econ.estimated_savings is reasonable; 3) run redwood econ preview for top 10 tenants and manually inspect; 4) enable backfill for a small subset (10 tenants) with audit logging; 5) slowly expand. Backwards compatibility: control plane accepts both the new YAML presets and legacy JSON defaults; when both present explicit tenant config wins. Security/audit: CRUD requires platform-admin role, all changes recorded in audit log with diffs. Migration risks: backfill is best-effort and reversible — it writes assignments to a new table unit_econ_assignments with tenant_id and profile_id and a ttl column so it can be rolled back by deleting rows. Testing notes: - unit tests for parsing include malformed YAML cases and overlap/conflict semantics - integration test spins up telemetry mock and verifies econ.* metrics emitted - CLI dry-run compares estimated tokens and costs against a synthetic workload. Checklist: [x] API & validation [x] Telemetry adaptor [x] CLI dry-run [x] Backfill migration (feature flagged) [x] Unit + integration tests [x] Docs and examples [ ] Add end-to-end benchmark comparing inference costs (follow-up ticket).

Motivation: presubmit pipelines have become noisy and slow due to immediate CI triggers on rapid developer pushes and many dependency-chore PRs. This PR implements a debounce layer for push/branch events so rapid successive commits within a short window are coalesced into a single presubmit run, and adds an incremental linter cache keyed by tool version + file globs to avoid re-linting unmodified packages. We also add a small dependency-whitelist mechanism so authorized chore PRs (approved dep bumps from our depbot pipeline) can take a lightweight validation path rather than the full heavy presubmit. The changeset is intentionally incremental: 1) an event debounce service that runs as a lightweight GitHub Actions composite step and a small Go shim to translate webhooks into coalesced workflow_dispatch events 2) a disk-backed incremental linter cache used by existing golangci-lint and eslint invocations with fallthrough to fresh lint runs when cache versioning mismatches 3) a dep-whitelist JSON manifest and workflow guard to route chore PRs to a lightweight pipeline 4) small release-hook adjustment to avoid firing release workflows for chore-only merges. Checklist: - [x] add debounce composite action + shim - [x] implement incremental lint cache and integrate with existing lint jobs - [x] add dep-whitelist manifest + lightweight workflow - [x] updates to docs and contributing guide - [x] smoke run on staging repository Rollout plan: deploy debounce action to canary org for 48h, monitor presubmit queue and merge latency, then flip org-level flag for full rollout. If regressions observed rollback by removing webhook-forwarding secret and revert action inputs. Related: ENG-2145 tracks presubmit cost reduction, ENG-2210 tracks dep-routing. Notes: debouncing window defaults to 90s (configurable per-repo) to balance feedback latency and unnecessary runs. The linter cache is safe by versioning linter tool versions and cache schema; any mismatch triggers a cold lint. This PR focuses on developer experience and CI cost; it does not change production runtime or model-serving behavior.
Tomás Müller: Can we add unit tests for the debounce shim and a simple e2e smoke that simulates three rapid pushes? Please also document the window config default.
Aisha Banerjee: Added a small harness under tools/ci/webhook-debounce/testdata and a scripted smoke in docs. The window default is 90s and configurable via action input. See docs/ci/README.md.
Bradley Chen: The lint cache looks good but we should ensure cache invalidation is deterministic when toolchain updates land. Suggest adding a cache-schema version file to the cache key.
Aisha Banerjee: Added cache-schema versioning and included golangci-lint and eslint versions in the key. Also added a fallback to full lint run if the cache read fails.
Sofia Patel: Verified e2e on canary org, presubmit runs reduced 42% on average for burst pushes. LGTM pending CI.
CI Bot: Build passed on push, tests passed, lint job used cache hit rate 76%.
Tomás Müller: Approved (review)
1) Deploy tools/ci/webhook-debounce to a test repo and configure webhook-secret; push three commits within 30s and verify a single presubmit run is kicked. 2) Create a sample chore PR that only bumps dev deps and add it to ci/dep-whitelist.json; verify it executes lightweight-presubmit.yml instead of presubmit.yml. 3) Change a Go file and run the lint pipeline twice; second run should hit the cache if tool versions unchanged. Logs for cache hit/miss are written to /tmp/presubmit-cache-logs during local runs.
Adds CI debounce to reduce redundant presubmit runs, introduces incremental lint caching for faster feedback, and adds a dependency whitelist to route approved chore PRs to a lightweight validation pipeline. No runtime changes.

Context: Some operator-level actions (granting elevated operator roles, cross-region KMS wrap requests, and certain tenant-scoped key imports) require an additional approval/quarantine step for high-compliance customers. Motivation: Reduce blast radius from accidental or automated escalations, provide an auditable human consent trail for KMS operations, and give SRE/SEC teams an operator-friendly remediation path. Summary: This PR implements three coordinated pieces: 1) RBAC quarantine mode for operator grants: when a policy change matches configured quarantine predicates the decision is returned as 'quarantine' instead of allow/deny; the request is placed into a managed queue for review. 2) KMS consent queue: an internal queue that batches KMS grant/wrap requests requiring jurisdictional consent and records consent decisions as signed attestations. 3) Audit witness service: a lightweight append-only witness in the audit pipeline that links quarantined events, KMS queue entries, reviewer decisions, and evidence blobs. Changeset overview: - pkg/authorization/quarantine.go: new decision flow and predicate engine plus unit tests. - internal/kms/consent_queue/*: queue implementation, persistence adapter (sqlite-backed for local dev, Dynamo wrapper for prod), and metrics. - services/audit/witness/handler.go: witness recorder and integrity hash that is cross-referenced in tenant audit events. - api/handlers/operator_grants.go: integrates quarantine flow and surfaces queue IDs in API responses. - deploy/helm/redwood-operator/templates/quarantine-config.yaml: helm values to tune predicates, retention, and reviewer roster. - docs/security/quarantine-kms-consent.md: operator-facing runbook and migration guidance. Migration notes: This is opt-in per-tenant via a feature flag and helm values. Operators enabling this must provide KMS consent reviewers and set retention windows; rollout should be staged to a small set of tenants. Backwards compatibility: If the feature is disabled, decision behavior is unchanged. Checklist: - [x] predicate engine and unit tests - [x] end-to-end e2e test (k8s integration with sqlite persistence) - [x] metrics (queue length, time-to-approval, consent accept rate) - [x] audit witness cross-reference added to tenant audit log - [x] docs and runbook - [x] helm values and default disabled state Testing: Local unit tests and e2e suite executed. Initial CI run showed lint failures and one flaky e2e timing issue; fixes applied (formatting + extended timeout for sqlite-backed test). Security review: SEC review completed, notes addressed: non-repudiation of decisions via attestations, and KMS minimal-scope tokens used for queued operations. Observability: Added Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboard snippets in observability-pack. Future work: UI for reviewers and paged queue, RBAC policy editor suggestions based on predicate telemetry, and optional automatic fallback after configurable SLA.

Aisha Kumar: Added signed attestation proto and persistence; signatures are HMAC+KID and stored in the consent record.
Marina Varela: The sqlite-backed e2e test flakes under low-disk CI. Can we increase timeouts or switch to in-memory?
Aisha Kumar: Increased e2e timeouts and added an in-memory mode guarded by CI-only flag; will follow up with separate PR to refactor e2e fixtures.
Sreya Patel: Add metrics for average time-to-approval and stale-queue alerts. Also request an entry in the runbook for emergency 'force-approve' paths.
Aisha Kumar: Added metrics (quarantine_queue_time_seconds histogram) and an operator 'force-approve' CLI path that requires a secondary approval scope. Documented in runbook.
Marina Varela: Code looks good, approve once CI is green and docs updated.
Daniel Cho: Approved.

Adds an opt-in RBAC quarantine workflow for operator-level grants, a KMS consent queue to manage jurisdictional KMS operations requiring human consent, and an audit witness to link decisions to audit logs. Disabled by default; operators must enable via helm values and configure reviewers.

Context: We added new per-deployment scaling policy fields (min/max bounds, cooldowns, predictive mode). For existing Dedicated deployments we must not change autoscaling behavior until the feature flag is enabled per account/deployment. This PR adds DB migrations + a backfill job that (a) preserves legacy scaling semantics by default, (b) makes the new policy evaluation deterministic by ensuring all existing rows have explicit defaults where needed, and (c) adds safety checks/metrics to avoid accidental rollout impact.

What this PR does:
- Adds schema migration for scaling_policy columns on Dedicated deployments:
  - scaling_policy_mode: ENUM('legacy','policy_v1') (default: 'legacy')
  - scaling_policy_v1: JSONB (nullable)
  - scaling_policy_updated_at, scaling_policy_updated_by (nullable; populated only when policy_v1 is used)
  - scaling_policy_backfill_version: INT (for idempotency + audit)
- Introduces a backfill job (idempotent, resumable) that sets explicit legacy defaults for all existing Dedicated deployments:
  - scaling_policy_mode='legacy'
  - scaling_policy_v1 remains NULL (so control plane evaluation path continues to use legacy autoscaler config)
  - scaling_policy_backfill_version set to current migration version
- Adds safety checks to prevent unintended behavior changes:
  - Hard guard: if feature flag dedicated_scaling_policy_v1 is disabled, policy evaluation returns legacy config regardless of any JSONB contents
  - Validator rejects mixed states (e.g., policy_v1 JSON present while mode='legacy') unless initiated by the control plane "enable" endpoint
  - Migration includes a post-migration verification query that fails the deploy if any row violates invariants
- Adds rollout knobs:
  - Backfill runs in batches (default 2k rows) with adaptive sleep and can be stopped/restarted safely
  - Supports dry-run mode (logs counts + sample IDs only)
  - Emits metrics: dedicated_scaling_policy_backfill_rows_total, dedicated_scaling_policy_backfill_errors_total, dedicated_scaling_policy_invariant_violations_total

Why we need explicit backfill (vs relying on implicit DB defaults):
- We need deterministic behavior across regions and read replicas: older rows may have NULLs depending on write path.
- Control plane caching + policy evaluation requires stable "effective config" computation for auditability.
- We want to distinguish "legacy" deployments from "policy_v1" deployments without relying on presence/absence of JSON.

Safety invariants (enforced by migration + runtime):
- Existing Dedicated deployments remain on legacy path until opt-in.
- No deployment can enter policy_v1 without both (1) feature flag enabled for the account and (2) explicit mode switch.
- Backfill must be safe to rerun and safe during partial deploys (one region ahead).

Implementation notes:
- Backfill uses a WHERE clause on scaling_policy_backfill_version IS DISTINCT FROM <version> to avoid rewrites.
- Uses UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT N FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) to minimize lock contention.
- Adds a small helper in capacity-policy-service to compute effective mode with precedence: featureFlag -> mode -> legacy fallback.

Illustrative snippet (simplified):
- "WITH cte AS (SELECT id FROM dedicated_deployments WHERE scaling_policy_backfill_version IS DISTINCT FROM 3 ORDER BY id LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) UPDATE dedicated_deployments d SET scaling_policy_mode='legacy', scaling_policy_backfill_version=3, updated_at=NOW() FROM cte WHERE d.id=cte.id"

Test plan:
- Unit tests:
  - idempotent backfill does not change already-backfilled rows
  - invariant checks catch invalid mixed states
  - feature flag gate forces legacy behavior even if JSON is present
- Integration tests (sqlite + postgres in CI):
  - migration applies cleanly from prior schema
  - backfill runs in batches and completes
- Manual:
  - ran dry-run in staging; verified counts match expected Dedicated deployments; verified no changes in autoscaler desired replicas logs

Rollout plan:
- Land migrations + backfill tooling behind deploy-time toggle (runs after migration only in prod once).
- Canary in us-east-1 control plane first.
- Only after verification, enable account-level feature flag for pilot accounts via INT-9412 process.

Follow-ups:
- Once GA, consider setting scaling_policy_mode default to 'policy_v1' for new deployments created under eligible plans, but keep explicit creation-time semantics in the API.

Risk:
- Migration touches dedicated_deployments; risk of long-running updates. Mitigated via SKIP LOCKED batching + adaptive sleep + metrics/abort.

References:
- Linear: ENG-22153 (Migration defaults), ENG-22141 (Schema/API), PM-1842 (Epic)
- Related PRs: pr-48211 (schema fields), pr-48252 (Console endpoints)

Checklist:
- [x] Backward-compatible by default
- [x] Idempotent migrations/backfill
- [x] Metrics emitted for backfill progress/errors
- [x] Staging validation completed
- [x] SRE review requested for rollout safety
Ethan Park: Can we guarantee no behavior change if someone accidentally writes scaling_policy_v1 JSON directly to the DB? I want a hard runtime guard, not just migration defaults.
Michael Nguyen (author): Yep—added a feature-flag gate in effective mode computation. If dedicated_scaling_policy_v1 is off, we ignore policy_v1 entirely and always return legacy config. Also added invariant check to reject mixed states via API.
Vanessa Ortiz: Backfill UPDATE pattern—please avoid table-wide write amplification. Can we use SKIP LOCKED batches and emit progress metrics? Also ensure it won’t fight with autoscaler reads.
Michael Nguyen (author): Updated to SKIP LOCKED batching (2k default) with adaptive sleep. Autoscaler reads are unaffected since it’s control-plane only; we also only touch a few columns. Added metrics + dry-run.
Rafael Mendes: Post-migration verification query—what happens on violation? We should fail the deploy and page, not silently continue.
Michael Nguyen (author): Agreed. Verification runs as a deploy step; non-zero violations fail the release pipeline in that region. Metrics also emitted for alerting during canary.
Jordan Lee: The enum default 'legacy' is good, but make sure new deployment creation explicitly sets mode based on plan/flag. Don’t rely on DB defaults long term.
Michael Nguyen (author): Added TODO in service layer and left DB default as legacy specifically to preserve existing behavior. New deployment path will be handled in ENG-22141 follow-up wiring once feature flag is on.
Ethan Park: Please add one more test that simulates partial rollout (one region on new code, one on old) and ensures old readers don’t break when seeing the new columns.
Michael Nguyen (author): Added integration test that applies migration and runs legacy read path; verifies no deserialization issues for old payload shapes.
Rafael Mendes: Approved once CI passes and the runbook link is in the PR description.
Michael Nguyen (author): Added runbook link + rollout notes.
