Motivation: production tenants intermittently hit OOM spikes driven by long-lived fragmentation in the KV cache when background spill/compaction lags under bursty write workloads. Existing heuristics evict by simple LRU+priority and trigger spill-on-alloc failures, but observed tail OOMs during high tenant churn and work-stealing. This PR implements a multi-pronged approach: 1) a lightweight 'deflation' path that coalesces fragmented segments in-place or via fast migration to reduce footprint without full compaction scans, 2) a spill circuit breaker that detects allocation pressure patterns and applies proportional backpressure and rate-limited spill amplification, and 3) tenant-level pacing to prevent a single misbehaving tenant from consuming disproportionate spill bandwidth and causing global fragmentation. Design summary: - Deflation allocator: new code path in src/kv/deflator.rs that scans per-shard free lists for high-fragmentation buckets and either (a) coalesces adjacent free runs into larger spans when contiguous, or (b) migrates cold records to the spill file using a fast-copy API which preserves KV metadata and invalidates old slots atomically. Deflation runs are rate-limited and piggybacked on the existing maintenance worker to avoid CPU spikes. - Spill circuit breaker: a state machine in src/kv/spill_breaker.rs which samples allocation failure rates, page reclaim latencies, and resident set growth. When thresholds are exceeded, it trips and: (i) signals the scheduler to temporarily increase eviction aggressiveness, (ii) throttles incoming write-heavy RPCs by returning a soft-429 with Retry-After when tenant pacing is enabled, and (iii) scales spill workers up to a capped burst. Circuit breaker resets gradually using an exponential backoff with hysteresis to avoid oscillation. - Tenant pacing: scheduler-level token-bucket per-tenant implemented in runtime/scheduler.rs; when breaker is tripped, tenants above their fair-share are slowed and long-running KV mutations are prioritized for deflation-friendly migration. - Metrics & observability: added kv.deflation.{runs,bytes_freed,failed}, kv.spill_breaker.{state,trip_count,trip_reason}, and tenant.pacing.{violations,avg_delay_ms}. Instrumented in Grafana dashboards and SLO alerts. Implementation notes: - New config flags (config/kvcache.yaml): kv.deflation.enabled, kv.deflation.max_bytes_per_sec, kv.spill.breaker.threshold_fail_rate, kv.spill.breaker.window_ms, kv.tenant.pacing.window_ms. Defaults are conservative (deflation off in older clusters by default; breaker enabled). - Added unit/integration tests under tests/kv_deflation/* exercising edge cases (concurrent allocs, partial migration failure, cancellation). - Added end-to-end canary harness in perf-canary/kv-deflation-canary that simulates 1k tenants with churn patterns. Benchmarks: - Synthetic canary: tail resident set (99.9th) down 22% on write-heavy workload, median allocation latency unchanged. - Production canary (internal): 40% reduction in OOM incidents across two impacted clusters during a 7d window; spill IOPS increased 1.3x but CPU overhead <5%. Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main behind feature flag. 2) Enable deflation on canary clusters and keep breaker enabled cluster-wide. 3) Monitor kv.deflation.* and kv.spill_breaker.* for 72h; if regressions, revert deflation flag. 4) Progressive rollout to Dedicated and then Hosted. Backwards compatibility: deflation is safe across versions because migrations write to the canonical spill format; however cluster operators should ensure the spill store has >= 10% free capacity before enabling deflation aggressively. Migration/upgrade notes included in docs/upgrade-kv-deflation.md. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (ENG-1437) - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Canary harness - [x] Metrics + dashboards - [x] Config flags and defaults - [x] Release notes Draft - [x] Benchmarks attached (perf-canary report) Related work: builds on ENG-1024 (eviction priority refactor) and complements earlier compact-on-idle efforts (ENG-1310).
Aisha Patel: Can we bound worst-case CPU when many shards decide to run deflation simultaneously? Suggest adding a global budget metric and ensuring the maintenance worker respects it.
Marcus Chen (author): Added a global deflation_budget_bytes config and the maintenance worker marches shards round-robin; updated tests to cover concurrent runs.
Lena Rodriguez: The soft-429 path is useful, but we need to make sure SDKs surface a retry hint. Please add a machine-readable header and document it.
Marcus Chen (author): Added Retry-After and X-Redwood-Spill-Hint headers and documented behavior in docs/upgrade-kv-deflation.md.
Diego Morales: Observability looks good, but add a cumulative trip_reason histogram so we can debug root causes quickly.
Marcus Chen (author): Added trip_reason counter and annotated the Grafana panel.
kv: introduce deflation path to reduce in-memory fragmentation and tail OOMs (off by default)
kv: spill circuit breaker to apply proportional backpressure under allocation pressure
kv: tenant pacing to prevent noisy neighbors from overwhelming spill resources
observability: new kv.deflation and kv.spill_breaker metrics and dashboards

Context and motivation: In production we continue to see sporadic tail latency spikes on multi‑GPU TP workloads correlated with short windows of NCCL congestion and many small KV cache allocations from continuous batching. This PR introduces two coordinated runtime changes: (1) a drift‑resilient collective scheduler that perturbs and staggers NCCL launches to avoid pathological synchronization across tensor slices, and (2) a KV slab consolidation pass that reduces small allocation churn and improves L2/L3 locality for the KV cache allocator. The combined change targets multi‑GPU tensor‑parallel inference paths (TP runtime) and the continuous‑batching code path used by the API router.

What this PR does (high level): - Adds Scheduler::PerturbationWindow, a lightweight jittering layer that applies per‑peer launch offsets within a configurable window to break lockstep NCCL launches while preserving ordering and progress guarantees. The scheduler also tracks per‑peer outstanding credits and backs off launches when cumulative outstanding bytes exceed a runtime threshold. - Adds KVSlab::Consolidate and a consolidation task that merges hot small slabs into larger contiguous slabs at low priority, reducing per‑token allocation overhead and fragmentation. Consolidation is gated by memory pressure and configurable thresholds so it won’t interfere with SLOs. - Adds a small admission tweak to continuous batching: older requests receive a priority boost in the batch selector to reduce head‑of‑line latency under high QPS. - Benchmarks and regression tests: microbenchmarks for NCCL launch variance, end‑to‑end tp inference perf harness, and an integration test that exercises slab consolidation under load.

Design notes and rationale: - We intentionally avoid deterministic reordering. The perturbation window is randomized per launch but bounded; this prevents pathological worst‑case alignments while keeping collectives efficient. - Consolidation is incremental and infrequent; it uses a background worker with a budgeted runtime slice to avoid interfering with token service. - The NCCL perturbation is conservative: on rigs where we observe no contention, the perturbation window defaults to zero. Operators can tune the window via runtime flags and per‑cluster policies. - The combined effect reduces contention-caused retries and kernel stalls while also lowering memory allocation overhead that exacerbates NVLink traffic.

Commits (summary): - 1a2f3b4: Introduce perturbation scheduler hooks and config knobs; add unit tests for scheduling invariants. - 2b3c4d5: Implement KV slab consolidation pass, background worker, and new allocator stats. - 3c4d5e6: Integrate with continuous batching admission, add perf test harness and perf metrics, update docs and changelog.

Files changed (high level): - runtime/scheduler/perturbation_scheduler.{cc,h} - runtime/kv_cache/kv_slab_consolidator.{cc,h} - runtime/kv_cache/allocator_stats.{cc,h} - runtime/batching/batch_selector.{cc} (priority tweak) - tests/perf/tp_nccl_stress_test.py - ci/perf/benchmarks/launch_variance.yaml - docs/release_notes/2026-02-03-kv-nccl-optimization.md - examples/perf/tuning/README.md

Tiny illustrative snippet (informational only): "Scheduler::PerturbationWindow" accepts a window_ns and seed; when >0 it computes offset = rng.uniform(0, window_ns) and schedules NCCL launch at planned_time + offset. KVSlab::Consolidate scans slab list for contiguous small slabs with same owner and merges them under lock.

Review conversation (highlights): - Ethan Park (reviewer): "Nice isolation of perturbation logic. A few requests: make the default window configurable via env var, and add a per‑node debug metric for perturbed launches." Author reply: "Added RW_SCHED_PERTURB_NS env and metric runtime.scheduler.perturbed_launches_count; updated tests." - Lucia Ramirez: "Concern about consolidation causing a stop‑the‑world when merging many small slabs." Author reply: "Consolidation uses a background budgeted worker; added unit test and a runtime flag to disable consolidation during low latency SLO periods." - Owen Patel: "Can we get a perf comparison on a 8xA100 TP run?" Context: On production workloads we observed sporadic token-level tail latency during bursts where prefill and decode contend for kernel slots and KV cache priming causes thrashing. This PR introduces two cooperating runtime components: 1) an Adaptive Prefetch Regulator (APR) that uses short-horizon workload sampling to budget KV priming by request class and to assign prefetch priority; 2) a Decode-Fusion Orchestrator (DFO) that dynamically chooses when to fuse prefill and decode microstages versus when to strictly separate them. Design: APR maintains per-route exponential moving averages for prefix hit-rate, sequence-length distribution, and recent kernel occupancy. It computes a per-request prefetch_budget and a priority token used by the scheduler. Budget is consumed during prefill; excess budget allows speculative KV warmups up to a configurable window. DFO uses a lightweight confidence signal (based on APR budget, queue length, and GPU kernel contention) to decide for each microbatch whether to route it through a fused prefill+decode kernel path (better overall throughput when confidence high) or keep the two-stage handoff (better tail latency when contention high). Implementation notes: APR is implemented in server/runtime/prefetch/regulator.cpp and exposed via a small control API to the scheduler. DFO logic lives in server/runtime/scheduler.cpp with new kernel flags in server/runtime/kernel_params.h. We added unit tests and microbenchmarks under tests/bench and test/runtime. Backwards compatibility: default configuration keeps behavior identical to main until operator flips feature_gate "adaptive_prefetch_fuse". Results: microbenchmarks (see tests/bench/prefetch_bench.py) show median throughput +7% and 99th percentile token latency -18% on a mixed conversational workload (batch sizes 8-32). On our Canary cluster the feature reduced burst tail spikes by 35% during a controlled load test. Rollout plan: feature-gated, start on Dedicated pools with canary traffic for 48h, then gradual ramp to 25% fleet, monitor token-99 and KV-miss-rate. Motivation: reduce per-token cost for mixed workloads by adding a lightweight prefill filtering layer (prefill sieves) plus a conservative quant-pruning step that trims redundant weight blocks for inference on quantized variants. This PR implements a first-pass, tenant-scoped prefill sieve that quickly classifies requests by prefill utility score and applies three default policies: allow, coalesce, or defer to background warmup. We couple that with a pluggable quant pruning pipeline that runs as part of the model preparation step and produces compact quant profiles optimized for short-sequence chat workloads. The changes aim to improve unit economics for bursty traffic without sacrificing latency SLOs. Motivation: We observed increased tail latency and fragmented streaming sequences for long toolcall/structured-output sessions under mixed workloads. This surfaced as duplicate handshake attempts for OpenAI-compat clients and intermittent truncation when route-specific payloads exceeded transient buffer windows. The change introduces two complementary mitigations: (1) per-route size heuristics that dynamically clamp effective payload windows based on recent sequence-size histograms and route SLAs, and (2) an adaptive "slab" buffering layer in the streaming proxy that groups ingress fragments into sized slabs for more deterministic writer-side flushes.

Summary of changes: - Gateway: add RouteSizeHeuristic component that tracks per-route percentiles (p50/p95/p99) and exposes a lightweight decision API for the ingress path. - Gateway config: new route config flag `heuristic_window_ms` and `heuristic_max_payload_bytes` with sane defaults and ability to override per-route. - Streaming proxy: introduce slab buffer abstraction (slab size is adaptive based on moving average of fragment sizes and latency budget) and explicit slab-ack protocol to reduce partial fragment flushes. - OpenAI-compat shim: update tool/function call handshake to tolerate slab-ack delays and fall back to a legacy byte-stream when repeated handshakes fail. Adds exponential backoff and single-retry suppression to avoid thundering retries. - Observability: add metrics for slab_fill_rate, slab_ack_latency, route_size_percentiles, and compatibility_fallbacks; dashboards and alerts updated. - Tests: new unit tests for RouteSizeHeuristic, integration tests simulating mixed small/large payload mixes, and an end-to-end scenario validating OpenAI-compat handshake under load.

Checklist: [x] Unit tests added for heuristic logic and slab buffering [x] Integration tests for streaming proxy under stress [x] Updated docs for route config flags and compat behavior [x] Performance bench runs (internal) demonstrating 18-32% reduction in streaming tail fragmentation for tested workloads [x] Changelog/release notes drafted

Commits (high level): - feat(gateway): route size heuristic + config flags - feat(stream-proxy): adaptive slab buffer + slab-ack protocol - chore(metrics): add slab and heuristic metrics - fix(compat): handshake backoff + legacy fallback - test: add e2e toolcall stress test and unit coverage

Files changed (high level): - gateway/src/routing/route_size_heuristic.go (new) - gateway/config/route_schema.proto (schema bump) - stream-proxy/src/slab_buffer.rs (new) - stream-proxy/src/ack_protocol.rs (new) - compat/openai_shim/handshake.go (tolerate slab ACKs/backoff) - observability/dashboards/slab_buffer.json (dashboard) - tests/e2e/handshake_stress.test (integration fixture) and small build/test harness adjustments

Testing and CI: Initial CI run failed on a flaky integration that surfaced a race in the slab-ack timeout unit. The race was fixed in the second commit by tightening the cancelation ordering and adding a deterministic test hook. CI summary: initial run (fail on streaming-integration) -> fix commit -> full CI pass (unit/integration/e2e). Load tests run in benchmark-lab showed consistent decreases in fragment counts per session and a 25% lower incidence of handshake fallbacks at 95th percentile for our mixed small/large workload profile.

Review conversation (selected highlights): - Sofia Chen (reviewer): "RouteSizeHeuristic looks reasonable but we should ensure the memory footprint is bounded for high-cardinality routes." — Author reply: "Added a ring-sampled histogram with TTL per route and a hard cap on tracked routes; noted in comments and docs." - Marco Alvarez: "slab-ack protocol semantics need clear invariants around reordering and retransmit." — Author: "Added explicit sequence numbers to slab ACKs and a small retransmit window; included tests that simulate out-of-order ACKs." - Priya Subramanian: "Can we avoid changing existing route configs unless opted in?" — Author: "Defaults are zero-config: heuristic is opt-in per-route; when disabled the gateway behaves as before. Updated docs to call out opt-in migration path." - Follow-up from SRE: "Alert for compatibility_fallbacks spike should be moderate severity and tied to slab_ack_latency" — Action: added alert with 15-minute burn rate and notify SRE on escalation.

Backward compatibility and rollout: - Safe by default: heuristics are opt-in per-route (flag in route config). - Canary rollout plan: enable for a small set of internal routes behind feature flags, monitor slab_ack_latency and compatibility_fallbacks metrics, then widen. - Fallback: On repeated handshake failure, gateway transparently downgrades to legacy byte-stream fallback for that session and emits compatibility_fallbacks metric.

Performance notes: Benchmarks run against the benchmark-lab suite with mixed session profiles (chat-like short messages plus episodic toolcalls of 1-2MB total). Results: median latency change is +3% (due to slight extra buffering), p95/p99 streaming fragmentation and handshake failure rates decreased by 18-32% depending on workload, and overall consumed CPU per proxy decreased by ~5% because there are fewer small writes and retransmits.

Security/ops notes: - No new credentials or auth surface added. - RouteSizeHeuristic does not persist user payloads; only size histograms are recorded. - Observability exposes only aggregated percentiles. - Added a migration note for customers using strict per-route size enforcement: a small window exists during canary where heuristics might clamp transient large payloads; docs recommend increasing heuristic_max_payload_bytes if permitted.

Merge outcome: approved by reviewers after two rounds of iteration. CI green on final run. Merged via squash with a single commit containing the aggregated changes and test fixes.

Follow-ups and TODOs: - ENG-7198: expose an admin API to peek per-route heuristic stats for debugging (drafted) - ENG-7239: experiment with predictive slab sizing using model of recent session shapes - Docs PR to redwood-docs scheduled to land next week with config examples and rollout guidance

If you want to test locally: see tests/e2e/handshake_stress.test and run `./dev/bench --scenario=handshake_stress --duration=2m` against a local gateway+proxy compose. For immediate troubleshooting, the route metric `gateway.route_size_percentiles` and `proxy.slab_ack_latency` are the primary signals.

payload.body:
Problem: Current cohort rollouts occasionally leave a small fraction of users in an inconsistent state when an immediate rollback is triggered mid-phased-swap (observed in incidents SUP-4021 and ENG-1284). Root cause analysis showed race between drain fences and the traffic allocator, and lack of a resumable state for partially-evicted cohorts.

Goal: Introduce a sequential cohort escrow lane that provides: 1) deterministic eviction and resume semantics for cohort slices, 2) a small safety escrow budget that can be consumed to allow fast rollback without user-visible failure, and 3) telemetry hooks that annotate rollout timeline events to make post-mortem for partial rollbacks trivial.

What this PR does (high level): Adds a new rollout orchestration mode "sequential-cohort-escrow" that runs cohort slices one at a time in an escrowed lane. Each cohort slice commits when both health probes and telemetry anchor events pass. On failure, the controller can perform a resumable failover which drains cohorts deterministically and optionally consumes escrow capacity (configurable per-Linear ticket). The implementation is integrated with the router (servegraph) and the Console observability pipeline to emit annotations for tracing/alerts.

Key features implemented in this change: - CohortEscrow controller: state machine with states {Pending, Escrowed, Active, Draining, Evicted, ResumableFailover}. The controller persists minimal markers to rolloutmetadata so retries are idempotent. - Safety escrow budget: new per-rollout quota that is charged only when an accelerated rollback path is used; surfaced in Console and APIs. - Deterministic drain sequences: router changes traffic in a two-phase commit to avoid split-brain session affinity for session-affine cohorts. - Telemetry hooks and annotations: rollout events (escrow-granted, escrow-consumed, cohort-commit, cohort-evict, resumable-failover-start/end) are emitted as structured tags to tracing and metrics backends. - Resumable failover API: endpoint to resume a previously failed rollout after manual verification (or automated after alerts cleared).

Why this is different from other rollout modes: Existing progressive and canary controllers assume ephemeral, all-or-nothing commits. This PR introduces explicitly escrowed lanes and resume semantics for partial commits to support long-lived user sessions and regulated workflows where immediate global rollback is dangerous.

Compatibility and defaults: This mode is opt-in and off by default. Existing rollouts are unaffected unless admins select the "sequential-cohort-escrow" strategy. Backwards compatibility is ensured via compatibility shim in the scheduler that translates old rollout configs transparently.

Related work and references: Linear ENG-1284 and ENG-1285 track the design and follow-ups. Support ticket SUP-4021 provided incident traces used in testing. Design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-1284/sequential-cohort-escrow-design (internal).

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed by SRE/product - [x] Unit + integration tests added for controller state transitions - [x] End-to-end test in perf-canary sandbox (small traffic partition) - [x] Console surface and docs stubbed - [x] Feature gated and disabled by default
Diego Martins (reviewer): Left a note about potential race in drain_coordinator when a second eviction overlaps; requested explicit lock ordering.
Author (Aisha Kramer): Addressed by introducing coordinator.LockOrder() and added unit tests to assert no double-evict behavior.
Samir Patel (reviewer): Asked for clearer eviction telemetry to include cohort-id and request-sample for debugging.
Author: Added cohort-id tag and sampled request example to telemetry_emit.go; included an anonymized sample in the E2E test.
Lina Zhou (approver): Verified integration with Console and asked to gate safety-escrow toggles behind admin feature flag; requested docs for operators.
Author: Added admin gate and operator docs; included migration notes and recommended budget defaults.
Ran the escrow flow in perf-canary with synthetic session-affine traffic; validated resumable flow by injecting failure at commit; validated telemetry anchors in Console and traces. Recorded the incident replay artifacts in SUP-4021 for auditors.
Introduces an opt-in rollout strategy 'sequential-cohort-escrow' that provides deterministic cohort commit and resumable failover with safety escrow budgeting. Admins must opt-in and configure the escrow budget; see docs/rollouts/strategies/sequential-escrow.md for details.

Context and motivation: Over the past quarter we've seen CI presubmit latency regressions largely driven by two factors: long-running lint shards run on PRs that touch large scope, and false-positive failures triggered by stale transitive dependencies during deterministic dependency resolution. This PR introduces two coordinated features to reduce noise and improve feedback speed: 1) a CI Dependency Graph Sanitizer that runs in a presubmit gate and emits a compact sanitized-graph.json artifact when it detects stale/transitive anomalies; 2) a lightweight Lint Cost Estimator that computes an estimated lint-time score for a PR and short-circuits full lint shards when the estimate is below a safety threshold while still running fast linters and staged checks.

Summary of changes (single-line commits): commit 1: add ci/tooling/dep-sanitzer entrypoint and graph-normalizer; commit 2: add ci/tooling/lint-cost-estimator; commit 3: wire sanitizer into workflow .github/workflows/presubmit-deps.yml; commit 4: integrate estimator into staged-lint runner and update docs; commit 5: add unit tests + small e2e smoke script for workspace sampling.

Checklist: - [x] design doc linked ENG-4312 - [x] unit tests for graph normalizer - [x] integration tests for estimator fallback behavior - [x] small benchmark showing reduced lint runtime - [x] docs updated for dev onboarding

Files changed (high-level): - ci/tooling/dep_sanitizer.py (graph normalization, provenances) - ci/tooling/lint_cost.py (estimator heuristics & cache) - .github/workflows/presubmit-deps.yml (adds sanitizer job + artifact) - .github/workflows/staged-lint.yml (estimator fastpath hook) - docs/dev/ci.md (new section: presubmit fastpath & dep sanitization) - tests/ci/test_dep_sanitize.py - tests/ci/test_lint_cost.py

Small illustrative snippet (sanitizer summary JSON emitted as artifact): {"sanitized_nodes": 312, "removed_transitive": 14, "heuristic_note": "trimmed optional-node paths that resolve to duplicate hashes"}

Why this approach: The sanitizer is intentionally conservative: it never mutates build manifests; it only emits a sanitized graph and an advisory summary. CI policies can be configured to fail only on 'determinism' regressions (hash mismatches) not heuristic trims. The lint estimator uses a historical sample of lint shard runtimes driven by path-level fingerprints and a cached relic (sha -> percentile). On small diffs the estimator will allow a 'fastpath' that runs a curated, much lighter lint set (formatting, banned patterns, critical linters) while queuing full lint in an async job if the owner requests it.

Benchmarks (presubmit on redwood monorepo): - baseline median presubmit-lint wall-clock: 13m42s - with estimator fastpath applied to 60% of small PRs: median presubmit-lint wall-clock: 4m10s - sanitizer detected 28 presubmit-time transitive anomalies in trial window; triage reduced 4 flakey failures to advisory-only.

Review conversation (high level): - Marco Ruiz (reviewer): "This looks promising; can we ensure the estimator doesn't hide security-related linters?" - Author (Aisha): "Yes — estimator always includes security-critical checks; added a test fixture verifying that rule." - Elena Kim: "Consider exposing a toggle in console for teams to opt into strict sanitizer enforcement." - Author: "Good idea; added a small config block (ci.team_config.sanitizer.mode) and documented default 'advisory' mode." - Jonas Berg (approval): "LGTM after addressing flaky RNG seed in tests." - CI bot: initial presubmit fails on test/test_lint_cost intermittently; rerun passed.

CI summary and notable failures: - Unit tests: passed (local 8/8) - Integration: flaky on first run due to non-deterministic test in test_lint_cost.py (fixed: seed set) - Presubmit workflow: sanitizer job runs in ~12s for graph extraction, normalization added ~6s overhead to presubmit but prevented downstream 5–10min debug cycles.

Operational notes and migration: - Default behavior is opt-in via .github/ci_teams.yaml; repo-level default remains advisory. - Ops: added a lightweight monitor in console for 'sanitizer advisories' under CI -> Presubmit Issues. - Rollout plan: staged rollout to teams: infra (week 0), sdk (week 1), core redwood (week 2). - Backout plan: remove workflow hook or set ci.team_config.sanitizer.mode = "off".

Security and compliance: no new secrets; sanitizer runs with existing read-only dependency graph access. Estimator uses cached historical metrics stored in CI artifact store with read access limited to ci-agent service account.

Merge outcome: squash-merged into main on 2025-02-20 by Marco Ruiz. Follow-ups: ENG-4399 (add console toggles) and ENG-4421 (extend estimator to rust & go codepaths).

Contact: author Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.ai) for follow-up and rollout coordination.
Adds a CI-side dependency graph sanitizer and a presubmit lint cost estimator. Non-breaking. Improves presubmit latency and reduces noise from transient deps.

Motivation: We observed recurring tail-latency spikes and progressive KV cache fragmentation under mixed read/write workloads with long-lived cached prefixes. Existing eviction heuristics were too reactive to instantaneous occupancy signals and would thrash pages during short-lived write bursts, which amplified paging and spillover. This PR introduces three coordinated mechanisms: 1) a lightweight page-defrag timer that stages cold page candidates for low-priority in-place defragmentation during idle windows; 2) a spill-fuse limiter that gates concurrent spill operations to avoid I/O amplification during bursty reclaim; and 3) an eviction skyline probe that computes multi-horizon eviction scores (hotness over 1s/10s/60s) to prioritize items with sustained coldness. Summary of changes: - runtime/kv/defrag_timer.{cc,h}: new scheduler that marks candidate pages and attaches a low-priority work item to tenant cooperatives; supports max-defrag-ms and backoff-per-tenant. - runtime/kv/spill_fuse_limiter.{cc,h}: token-bucket style limiter with adaptive thresholds tied to async-io latency percentiles; includes metrics hooks. - runtime/kv/eviction_skyline.{cc,h}: computes composite eviction score using short/medium/long access histograms and residency age; compatible with existing LRU/BATTERY evictors. - runtime/kv/allocator_integration.{cc}: hooks that allow defrag timer to request migrations and the spill limiter to veto immediate async spill submissions. - tests/kv/bench_defrag_timer.sh: microbench bench harness for fragmentation-heavy workload. - docs/ops/kv-eviction-guides.md: operator-facing knobs and rollback steps. Performance: On staging runs with a 1k-concurrent clients mixed-readwrite workload (60/40 R/W, 6h run) we saw: - 42% reduction in 99.9th percentile latency for GETs under sustained traffic - 28% fewer background spill jobs during peak write bursts - 8-12% lower overall tokenized memory churn (measured as page rewrite bytes) Tradeoffs & rollout: The defrag timer performs best when tenants have modest idle windows; for extremely write-heavy tenants (sustained >90% writes) the system will fall back to current spill-first behavior. The spill-fuse limiter exposes two new operator knobs (max-concurrent-spills, spill-latency-threshold-ms) and includes a safe default that matches existing async-io concurrency on small instances. Checklist: - [x] unit tests for skyline scoring and limiter behavior - [x] integration test for staged defrag work - [x] perf harness runs and baseline comparison - [x] docs and operator runbook - [x] feature-flag gated behind runtime. Rollback plan: flip feature flag off to revert to prior evictor behavior; runtime will drain staged defrag work and abort pending spill submissions. Related: ENG-8421 (reduce KV churn), ENG-8490 (eviction telemetry), SUP-4092 (incident: spill storms).
Miguel Ortega: Can we avoid holder threads for the defrag work? Suggest using tenant cooperative polling instead to reduce thread pressure.
Author (Asha): Switched to cooperative task scheduling in latest commit (d6a7b9f), removed holder threads. Verified with microbench.
Sofie Nguyen: The skyline introduces extra per-access histogram maintenance; is memory overhead bounded? Please add accounting.
Author (Asha): Added bounded ring histograms with capped buckets and explicit accounting; added unit test that asserts peak metadata < 2MB/tenant.
Priya Raman: CI flaked on the async-io test (timeout). Reran and green. Please include a blurb in release notes about potential longer rollout on very large clusters.
Author (Asha): Added release note. CI now stable.
Introduce coordinated defragmentation and spill-rate limiting: page-defrag timer, spill-fuse limiter, and eviction skyline probe reduce tail latency and background spill amplification for mixed workloads. Feature gated; operator knobs provided. See docs/ops/kv-eviction-guides.md for tuning.

Motivation: Our presubmit and release bootstrap path currently relies on a heavy Node + Makefile flow that adds ~30s to every CI job and produces brittle caching behavior across runners. This PR replaces the fragile JS bootstrap with a tiny Rust CLI (tools/ci-bootstrap-rs) that performs deterministic toolchain installation, workspace snapshotting, and smart cache priming. The Rust tool is compiled into a single static binary used by CI images to shrink init time, reduce container layers, and centralize provenance checks.

Motivation: fragmentation and reactive spillovers continue to drive tail latency and unexpected OOMs on long-lived tenants with mixed-size keys. This PR introduces a hierarchical page-bank (HPB) allocator plus a lightweight eviction skyline planner to proactively reshape KV residency and smooth spill events. Summary: implement a page-granular bank that groups contiguous slab pages into hot/mid/cold lanes with fast in-place micro-compaction for small fragments; add a skyline-based eviction scorer that considers occupancy, write amplification risk, KV lifetime estimate, and downstream spill cost to prioritize candidates; integrate with the serving scheduler to allow preemptive async spill tasks and to mark lanes with temporary admission control. Design details: (1) HPB allocator: pages are tagged with lane metadata and a compacted-run map; allocation prefers hot lane for small sizes, cold lane for large allocations, and migrates low-touch fragments via bounded micro-compaction passes to coalesce free runs without full GC. The allocator exposes new metrics (lane_fill_pct, run_count, microcompact_ops/s). (2) Eviction skyline: a multi-dimensional score computed at eviction-time combining recency, per-key residency delta, estimated recompute cost (model KV warmup), and hypothetical downstream I/O latency; the skyline planner produces a ranked candidate list and supports batch evictions with spill hysteresis to avoid repeated small writes. (3) Scheduler integration: a low-priority async compaction worker pool that performs micro-compaction and coordinated spill with backoff; admission control can hold low-priority batches when lane_fill_pct exceeds configured thresholds. Backwards compatibility: all new behavior gated behind feature flag "hpbank_eviction_skyline" and defaulted off for existing Dedicated customers. Checklist: implement allocator core + API, skyline scorer, scheduler hooks, metrics, end-to-end integration tests, benchmark harness runs, docs and migration notes, feature-flag gating, and rollback switch. Testing: unit + fuzz for allocator invariants, stress tests with mixed-size synthetic workloads (zipf + large object injection), deterministic replay of an in-production incident trace that previously caused spill storms; stability verified across 72h soak on staging cluster. Benchmarks: p95 latency for small (<=64B) token fetches reduced by 18% under 20k qps steady workload with 40% large-object churn; sustained memory reclamation improved: average resident fragmentation dropped from 24% to 9% in high-churn tests; aggregate write bandwidth to spill storage fell 35% under the incident trace. Rollback plan: flip feature flag off, drain compaction workers, and run a light allocator compaction to restore pre-change placement; alert runbook updated to include expected metrics to observe (lane_fill_pct, skyline_rejects, spill_backlog). Related work: follows on ideas from ENG-1320 (adaptive slab) and borrows scoring heuristics from previous spillback dampener experiments. Files changed: allocator core, eviction planner, scheduler hooks, metrics, tests, and docs. Merge strategy: squash merge after green CI and 2 approvals.
Marcus Lee: Can you clarify the compaction work budget and how it interacts with CPU quotas on Dedicated nodes? The code looks safe but we need a throttle to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
Anika Sharma: Added a per-node compaction_budget_ms config, default 50ms per sweep, and tied it to the scheduler token bucket; documented in deploy notes.
Tessa Nguyen: The skyline score includes recompute cost—how do you estimate it for cold keys? Consider a cheaper default to avoid over-eviction.
Anika Sharma: Skyline uses a decayed histogram from access traces; for unknown keys we fall back to a conservative recompute estimate (10ms) and weight it low; added tests showing behavior on cold-key eviction.
Diego Alvarez: CI showed intermittent integration flakiness on macOS builders for the fuzz harness.
Anika Sharma: Adjusted harness to be deterministic on macOS by seeding RNG and widened timeouts; re-run CI and passed.
Add hierarchical page-bank allocator and skyline eviction planner to reduce fragmentation and spill events. Feature gated behind hpbank_eviction_skyline. Expected benefits: lower p95 latency for small fetches, reduced spill bandwidth, and lower fragmentation for mixed-size workloads.
Steady-state micro-benchmark: small-key p95 -18% at 20k qps; fragmentation median dropped from 24% to 9%; spill write throughput -35% on incident trace; compaction CPU overhead measured at ~2.1% of node CPU under default budget.

Motivation: CI cycle time has been steadily increasing as we add more integration and security checks. For small, low-risk changes (docs, single-file lint fixes, infra config tweaks) engineers should get feedback in under 5 minutes. At the same time we need an automated, conservative gate for dependency updates to catch transitive supply-chain regressions.

Summary: this PR introduces a small change detection tool and a staged CI workflow that routes PRs to a fast-feedback lane or a full-check lane based on change classification. It also adds a composite dependency-safety action that performs transitive dependency quarantine checks and configurable quarantine policies.

What changed: 1) .github/workflows/staged-ci.yml implements two lanes: fast-path (lint/units/docs + cached build) and full-path (integration, e2e, heavy flakiness-prone tests). 2) tools/change_detector: tiny Rust binary used in the CI to classify PRs by file globs and repo-scope rules. 3) .github/actions/dep-safety: composite action that runs our internal transitive-scan.sh, invokes Snyk for vulnerability context, and can attach a work item to Linear and block merging if policy thresholds are exceeded. 4) CI cache keying updates: finer-grained cache scopes keyed on workspace-subset to reduce invalidation blast radius. 5) docs/ci/fast-feedback.md describing developer experience, how to opt-out, and adding a quickci label to force fast-path or to bypass fast-path when requested.

Checklist: [x] change detector binary + unit tests, [x] staged-ci workflow, [x] dep-safety composite + integration test in CI, [x] docs and READMEs, [x] performance telemetry added to Console for CI latency.

Impact: default is conservative: most PRs still go to full path until the change-detector pool of rules grows. Fast-path is honored only for PRs that touch docs, shaders, README, comments, and single-package lint-only changes. Rolling rollout: feature flag via workflows/ci-config.yml to enable fast-path org-wide in phases.

Related: Linear ENG-15802 (ci-fast-feedback), ENG-16210 (dep-gate), and notes in #infra-ci slack for rollout planning.

How to validate locally: 1) cargo build --manifest-path=tools/change_detector/Cargo.toml 2) tools/change_detector --base main --head HEAD --rules-file .github/ci-rules.yaml 3) run actions locally via act or use GitHub UI to open a PR to a personal branch.

Priya Nair (security): The dep-safety composite runs Snyk which is fine, but we need to restrict token scopes and record an audit entry for every scan. Please add KMS usage for secret rotation.
Ava Chen (author): Dep-safety action updated to read SNYK_TOKEN from repository secrets and to call audit-log endpoint in the private control plane; added documentation for required secret scope.
Jonah Brooks (infra): CI caching keys look better but please avoid using the repo SHA for shared caches; use workspace-subset name instead to reduce churn.
Ava Chen (author): Switched to workspace-subset keying and added fallback cache hits metric for observability.

- Add fast-feedback CI lane to speed up feedback for docs/lint-only changes
- Introduce change-detector tool to classify PRs and route CI
- Add dependency safety composite action to quarantine risky transitive updates
- Improve cache keying to reduce invalidation blast radius

Motivation: We observe long-tail latency/cost regressions driven by small subsets of invocations (particular prompt shapes, streaming patterns, or large prefix KV cache misses). Current sampling is uniform and misses signal in those cohorts. This PR introduces a hierarchical token-sampling strategy plus a latency-tiling dashboard to make long-tail SLO analysis cheaper and more precise.

What this changes: 1) New runtime component (token_sampler) that maintains lightweight cohort sketches keyed by a stable invocation fingerprint, supports stratified sampling rates (global -> tenant -> cohort) and emits sample markers for traces/metrics. 2) Tiled latency model: latency is bucketted into sequence-length x prefix-warmth tiles so heatmaps and SLOs can be decomposed along both axes. 3) Dashboard artifacts: new latency_tiling panels and a sampler overview that link from tiles to sampled trace IDs. 4) Config surface: a config_schema.yaml mapping linear keys to sampling policy; rollout script for staged enablement. 5) Tests and docs.

Implementation notes: - Hierarchical sampler keeps in-memory count-min sketches (approximate) per tenant and global aggregate; sampling decisions are fast-path and annotated on request context. - Sampler emits tags: telemetry.sampled=true/false, telemetry.cohort=<cohort-id>, sampling.rate=<r>. - Latency tiling adds derived metrics: runtime.latency.tile.{len_bucket}.{warmth_bucket} and runtime.token_count.tile.{len_bucket}.{warmth_bucket}. - Dashboards are compatible with existing span IDs and link to trace viewer via sample anchors.

Migration & rollout: - Default sampler is disabled. Rollout is incremental: enable at 1% global -> 5% tenant cohort -> 50% targeted cohorts. scripts/rollout/telemetry-rollout.sh automates canary subsets and verifies metric continuity. - Backwards compatibility: absence of telemetry.sampled tag falls back to existing collectors.

Testing & CI: unit tests cover sampling logic and tile bucketing; integration test bootstraps the sampler with synthetic traffic and asserts trace anchoring and metric emission. CI had an initial flaky test (test_token_sampler::cohort_decay) which was fixed by adding a deterministic RNG seeding; full pipeline passed on rerun.

Checklist: - [x] Runtime sampling implementation
- [x] Metric emission & labeling
- [x] Latency-tiling dashboards + drilldowns
- [x] Rollout tooling and docs
- [x] Unit/integration tests

Fix: mitigate transient control-plane stalls caused by heartbeat drift and KV checkpoint leak; add telemetry and canary rollout for health-gate state changes.
Context and motivation: We observed intermittent regional stalls during high churn where control-plane health gates would hold requests open while a small subset of connections leaked KV cache checkpoints and failed to close cleanly. This manifested as a temporary spike in inflight slowpath requests and cascading per-tenant latency regressions despite available GPU capacity. The goal of this PR is to close the KV checkpoint leak, add a bounded stall mitigator on the health-gate path, and strengthen telemetry so SRE can detect recurrence quickly. Changes summary: 1) Introduce a lightweight stall mitigator state machine that limits per-connection slowpath retention with exponential backoff and a capped token budget; 2) Add a checkpoint-finalizer to runtime/kv to ensure in-flight KV checkpoints are reconciled on connection termination; 3) Harden the health_gate state transitions to tolerate transient heartbeat jitter and avoid sticky 'degraded' states; 4) Add telemetry tags and metrics (health_gate.state_changes, kv.checkpoint_finalized, stall_mitigator.evictions) and traces for the slowpath; 5) Add an integration test that simulates high-connection-churn and validates no stall persists beyond the configured quorum window; 6) Canary rollout plan via the helm values change to enable the mitigator by default in staging and 10% of production nodes. Commits (high-level): - 1a2b3c: initial refactor of health_gate to extract transition hooks and add unit tests - 2b3c4d: implement token-bucket stall mitigator and eviction logic - 3c4d5e: kv checkpoint finalizer and safe-reconcile flow with retry/backoff - 4d5e6f: telemetry and tracing annotations; update metric names and tag schema - 5e6f7g: integration test harness and canary helm values - 6f7g8h: fix for race condition found during CI run and test flake suppression Changed areas (high level): - services/controlplane/health_gate.go: refactor state machine, add transition hooks, integrate stall mitigator - runtime/kv/checkpoint_finalizer.go: ensure checkpoint is finalized on connection close - runtime/kv/persist.go: small reconciliation loop and retry policy - telemetry/metrics.go: new metrics and tag dimensions - tests/integration/ephemeral_stall_test.go: e2e simulation for churn - helm/values/staging.yaml: enable mitigator in staging - docs/operational/health-gate.md: operational notes and runbook (small doc additions) Checklist: - [x] Add unit tests for state transitions - [x] Integration test that simulates churn and verifies eviction within SLO window - [x] Telemetry + dashboard notes included - [x] Canary rollout values added - [x] Documentation and runbook updated Review conversation summary: - Marco Liu (SRE): "Observed pattern matches reported SUP-912; +1 on adding metrics but request to expose a percentile of stall duration and a labeled counter for evictions by reason." Author reply (Aisha): "Added stall_mitigator.duration_p50/p95 and stall_mitigator.eviction_reason tag in telemetry patch; included queries for the dashboard." - Sophie Kramer (Backend): "Refactor looks fine but please ensure the health_gate transition logging is not too verbose at scale." Author reply: "Switched to sampling logs at INFO for initial state changes and DEBUG for every transition; added a fail-safe to limit per-node transition logging to 5 events/sec." - Devon Brooks (Runtime): "Race on kv.persist noted in initial CI; suggest defensive nil-checks and a single reconcile goroutine per-connection." Author reply: "Applied single-goroutine reconcile and added an atomic guard; re-ran unit tests." CI summary: - Initial CI run: unit tests failed on a timing-sensitive test (race detected in kv persist); fixed in commit 6f7g8h. - Second CI run: all unit and integration tests passed. - E2E perf-canary job: passed with mitigator enabled in canary mode. Merge and rollout notes: - Merge method: squash and merge. - Merged to main and immediately deployed to staging via the helm/staging values update. - Production plan: progressive canary at 10% nodes for 24h with telemetry alerts (health_gate.state_flaps and stall_mitigator.evictions) and an automated rollback job if evictions exceed threshold for tenant fairness. Post-merge follow-ups: - Add a Grafana dashboard panel to surface eviction_reason breakdown (ENG-4821). - Run a 12-hour soak in staging and collect p50/p95 stall duration metrics (ENG-4873). - If any tenant sees >3 evictions/hour, trigger rollback and open an incident runbook (SUP-912). Rationale for this approach: The root cause is a combination of heartbeat jitter and unreconciled KV checkpoints; purely increasing timeouts hid the issue and allowed slowpath buildup. This mitigator restricts retention time, forces checkpoint finalization, and gives SRE the signals to act before customer-visible SLOs are impacted. Metrics added are intentionally low-cardinality with an eviction_reason tag to allow fast aggregation. Backwards compatibility and safety: The change is non-breaking; the mitigator is toggleable via helm values and defaults to off in legacy clusters. We validated the reconciler under load in the perf-canary harness and verified no regression in throughput. Merge outcome: merged via squash, closed associated Linear tickets as part of the merge commit message, and created a follow-up task to add an incident-runbook snippet to docs.

This PR introduces a language-agnostic stream-adapter registry and a pluggable token-provider abstraction to the SDK surface so that each SDK (Python/TypeScript/Go) can opt into a shared streaming handshake and reauth strategy without shipping duplicate logic. Motivation: persistent differences in stream handshake timing and token refresh semantics across SDKs were causing duplicate reauth attempts and subtle backpressure mismatches in production. The change packages three coordinated pieces: 1) a lightweight StreamAdapterRegistry in the core redwood library that maps protocol variants to SDK adapters; 2) a PluggableTokenProvider interface plus a default refresh provider used by hosted and dedicated customers; 3) thin ergonomic wrappers added to each SDK exposing the provider as an opt-in parameter and a compatibility shim for older code paths. Checklist: - [x] Core registry implementation and protocol contract - [x] Default token provider implementation and short-circuit for static tokens - [x] SDK wrappers: python client convenience function, TS builder option, Go functional option - [x] Cross-SDK integration tests for resume/reconnect and single-token refresh paths - [x] Documentation snippets and migration notes - [x] Version bumps for SDK packages (python/ts/go) Compatibility notes: the adapters are opt-in by default; existing call sites continue to work. To enable the new behavior set `stream_adapter: "registry-v1"` and pass `token_provider` in the client constructor. There is an opt-in migration guide in docs/sdk-migration/stream-adapter.md. Rollout plan: merge to main, cut a patch release for hosted clients who opt-in, coordinate SDK releases in the same week to avoid partial parity. Related work: ENG-4026 (streaming-reconnect stability), ENG-4041 (sdk-auth-resilience).

Context: We observe recurring noisy SLO alerts driven by rare, phase-specific token behavior (e.g. bursts when decoding long histories). Existing token-cost and latency metrics capture counts and percentiles but do not surface intra-invocation phase disorder. Motivation: Surface a lightweight per-token-phase entropy signal and compact invocation micro-digests so engineers can quickly identify whether a cost/latency spike is due to increased entropy (less predictable token distributions) versus kernel/backpressure issues. This PR introduces three parts: 1) token-phase entropy histogram metric emitted from the runtime; 2) compact invocation micro-digests (sharded, bounded summaries) attached to sampled traces for quick triage without full KV payloads; 3) an alert-slope auto-tuner that adjusts SLO thresholds dynamically based on short-term entropy baselines to reduce alert noise.

Changes: - Runtime: new runtime counter and histogram for per-token-phase Shannon entropy (phases: init, prefix, gen, postprocess). Exposes labels: model, route, tenant, device_pool, phase, seq_len_bucket. The histogram is coarse (8 buckets) to control cardinality. - Trace attachment: a new compact JSON micro-digest (<= 2KB) includes: token_count, entropy_estimate, avg_token_delay_ms, kernel_wait_ms, top3-token-shapes. Micro-digests are attached only to sampled traces (configurable sampling rate). - Alerting: add a new observability service module that consumes entropy rollups and computes short-window slope. When slope exceeds threshold, the module temporarily widens alert thresholds for affected routes to avoid immediate firing; it records decisions to an audit metric.

Checklist: - [x] Runtime metric emission and unit tests - [x] Micro-digest schema, serializer, and bounded size test - [x] Collector side aggregation and dashboard panels - [x] Alert-slope auto-tuner implementation + e2e integration tests - [x] Docs snippet in observability guide (short) - [x] QA: smoke runs on staging with 48h replay workload

High-level changed files: - runtime/src/metrics/entropy.rs (new) - runtime/tests/entropy_estimator_test.rs (new) - trace-exporter/src/microdigest.rs (new) - collector/rollups/entropy_roller.go (new) - observability/alerting/slope_tuner.py (new) - dashboards/entropy-and-microdigests.json (new panel) - docs/observability/token-entropy.md (docs) - e2e/replay/fixtures/entropy-replay.yaml (test fixture) - CI: update pipeline to include new e2e job

Review conversation: - Carlos Martinez (review): "Can we bound the cardinality here? labels like tenant+route+model can explode." - Author (Laura): "Bounded buckets (8) + seq_len bucketing implemented; micro-digests are sampled; added aggressive TTL on metric cardinality. See runtime/metrics/entropy.rs lines ~120 for bucket logic." - Rohit Nair (review): "How do we ensure this doesn't add CPU overhead in hot paths?" - Author: "Entropy estimator uses incremental one-pass estimator with tiny state per invocation; micro-digests are emitted asynchronously by the trace-exporter to avoid blocking inference threads. Benchmark added in entropy_estimator_test shows <2% CPU at p95 under load." - Priya Patel (review): "Operator controls for the alert-tuner? need explanation and safe defaults." - Author: "Added tunable knobs: enable_flag=false by default, slope_window=5m, cooldown=10m, max_widen_pct=25. Documented in docs/observability/token-entropy.md. Also feature-flagged for staged rollout." - Carlos: "Approved after clarifying cardinality and sampling defaults." - Rohit: "Approved after seeing microbenchmark results." - Priya: "Approved with request to land runbook note; added in PR." 

CI checks: - unit (linux): passed - lint: passed - integration (collector): passed - e2e entropy replay: passed (staging job) - docs build: passed - security scan: passed

payload.body:
Motivation: Production incidents showed correlated tenant spikes causing regional SLO thrashing when backend KV pressure and bursty fastpath requests coincide. This PR introduces a transient "load-shear gateway" that applies a soft, SLO-aware shedding curve for non-critical routes and a timeboxed "trickle-stop" mode for tenant cohorts when regional error/latency budgets are exhausted. The change is intentionally conservative: it never blocks high-priority customers, prefers shed decisions by route metadata and token-bucket scoring, and integrates with existing circuit state so we avoid double-enforcement. Changes include: 1) admission/gateway layer that computes a dynamic shear score combining region_slo_headroom, kv_pressure, and inflight_fastpath_ratio; 2) a thin token-bucket-based trickle-stop that paces retries and gracefully queues low-priority requests with a capped window (50ms per request additional latency budget by default); 3) integration points to the circuit-breaker state machine so shear is relaxed when circuits are open for lower-latency fallbacks; 4) Prometheus metrics and tracing spans for visibility; 5) a short rollback path and feature-flag gating for staged rollout. Test plan: unit tests for scoring logic, integration test harness simulating KV pressure + tenant spike, chaos run in perf-canary region, and a 48-hour canary with traffic shaping. Rollout plan: enable in perf-canary for 24h, staged ramp in us-west-2 and eu-west-1, enable global after 48h when error budgets stabilize. Rollback: flip feature flag or revert head branch; token-bucket state is ephemeral and drains within 60s. Related: Linear ENG-7261 tracks follow-ups (fine-tune thresholds per customer cohort); incident ref SUP-411 triggered this change. 
Add transient load-shear gateway module with scoring and admission APIs
Implement token-bucket trickle-stop and per-route priority classification
Wire shear decisions into circuit-breaker state machine (relax-on-open)
Export metrics: load_shear_score, trickle_stop_active, trickle_stop_shed_count
Add integration tests simulating kv pressure and tenant spike
Feature flag and rollout config; docs and release note draft

Introduce a conservative, feature-flagged regional load-shear gateway and token-bucket based trickle-stop to reduce correlated SLO violations during KV pressure spikes. Metrics and rollout instructions included. No breaking changes; gated behind feature flag and staged rollout.
New metrics: redwood_load_shear_score{region,route}, redwood_trickle_stop_active{region}, redwood_trickle_stop_shed_count_total. Tracing spans: load_shear.evaluate and load_shear.enforce. Alerting: add a temporary SLI to detect >5% shed rate in canary region.

If canary shows >2% customer-visible error increase for high-priority routes, roll back immediately. Observe metrics prefixed with redwood_trickle_stop_ and trace any requests with tag load_shear=1. Contact author Aisha Kumar or SRE pager for escalations.

+    score += clamp(stats.KVPressure, 0, 1) * 0.3
+    score += clamp(stats.InflightFastpathRatio, 0, 1) * 0.1

Adds a cached, hermetic toolchain wrapper to speed presubmit boot and a lightweight presubmit prober for faster feedback; no user-facing API changes.
Motivation: presubmit latency is a major drag on developer iteration. Cold presubmit setup (installing language toolchains, devdeps) adds minutes to feedback time and increases flakiness from transient network failures. Goal: provide a small, cacheable toolchain wrapper that produces deterministic build environments and a fast presubmit prober that exercises only the minimal smoke surface to detect obvious breakages quickly. This PR implements: 1) tools/toolchain-wrapper: a Go-based thin wrapper that normalizes tool versions, creates a local small cache image and exposes a simple wrapper CLI (redwood-tw) to run builds/tests hermetically; it supports a disk-backed cache artifact (tarball) and a lightweight HTTP cache server for CI runners. 2) .github/workflows/presubmit.yml: adds a presubmit fast-path job that uses the toolchain wrapper and runs the new prober job. 3) ci/presubmit-prober: a tiny Go binary that runs language-heuristic smoke checks (go vet, pytests targeted by quick tags, ts compile) and reports structured pass/fail to the checks API. 4) Scripts and Dockerfile.toolcache to build and snapshot a small toolcache image that can be reused across CI runners. Rollout plan: landing as opt-in under feature flag ci.fast-presubmit; we will run the new prober in parallel to existing presubmit for two weeks, collect failure-mode telemetry and then switch to fast-path by default. Backwards compatibility: the wrapper falls back to the legacy bootstrap when the toolcache is unavailable. Checklist: [x] unit tests for wrapper cache eviction [x] prober smoke tests [x] updated docs and README for wrapper usage [x] feature-flag gating and telemetry. Related: references ENG-4251 for presubmit SLO work and SUP-3112 for a recent customer incident caused by flaky devdep installs. See design notes at https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-4251/details.
Marcus: Can we avoid leaking registry auth into the cache snapshot? Added suggestion to use token vaulted via CI secrets.
Author reply: wrapped token exchange with ephemeral short-lived tokens; adjusted scripts to use CI secret projection.
Priya: Please add a Prometheus counter for cache hits/misses before merge.
Author reply: added cache_hit/cache_miss counters and a simple histogram for snapshot latency.
Evan: Noted a flaky test on macOS runner; requested we skip that probe for macOS until follow-up.
Author reply: added OS gating to prober and created follow-up ticket ENG-4295 to stabilize macOS probe.

Motivation: A recent incident showed short-lived global spike events could trigger aggressive SLO circuit breakers and immediate tenant preemption, causing cascading request failures for a subset of customers. This PR introduces a 'soft panic suppressor' layer that transiently dampens aggressive SLO reconfiguration during burst windows and adds a coordinated graceful queue-drain path for nodes that are being reprovisioned or taken out of service. The approach aims to avoid unnecessary tenant quarantines while preserving long-term SLO enforcement. Changes: 1) New controller softpanic.Suppressor that tracks ephemeral surge tokens and applies a short holdoff window before escalating to tenant-level circuit trip. 2) Queue drain orchestrator that transitions in-flight request queues into a draining state and coordinates KV-cache flush with a fast-path fallback. 3) Load-shedding policy update: introduce a tiered preemption score that prefers best-effort queues during soft panic windows and defers hard tenant eviction for a configurable grace period. 4) Small API surface: a runtime flag (ENABLE_SOFT_PANIC) and two config knobs (panic_holdoff_ms, drain_soft_ttl_ms). 5) Unit + e2e tests and a runbook section for on-call. Rollout plan: feature-gate off by default for 24h canary in us-east-1 (10% traffic), monitor token-eviction and SLO error-rate, then rollout to remaining regions with a 2-hour ramp. Backport: critical hotfixs to release/2026-02 recommended. payload.body:
Motivation: CI feedback time and noisy dependency churn are recurring pain points. This PR introduces a lightweight "premerge-sanity" lane that boots a minimal lint/test surface for changed paths and a new 'dep-pruner' helper that finds likely-unused devDeps to reduce transitive noise. The goals are: 1) reduce time-to-first-feedback for reviewers by running a fast, path-aware check on PRs; 2) avoid full test/lint runs unless the change touches relevant areas; 3) proactively reduce devDependency bloat and surface candidates for manual review or automatic pruning.

What this PR contains (high-level):
- A new CI lane: .github/workflows/premerge-sanity.yml. This is a fast GitHub Actions job which:
  - uses a small cached container image (node:20-slim-derived) that boots in ~4s on our runners;
  - computes changed paths with git --no-pager diff --name-only ${{ github.event.before }} ${{ github.sha }};
  - maps paths to test/lint selectors via .ci/path-map.yml;
  - runs eslint (subset config) and the unit-test smoke harness (jest --findRelatedTests) only for the affected packages;
  - publishes an annotation summary (warnings/errors) and exits non-zero if any error is found.
- A path mapping file: .ci/path-map.yml. This YAML maps repo globs to an ordered set of checks (lint, unit-smoke, build). The mapping is intentionally conservative and lives in-tree so teams can opt-in granularly.
- A small utility: tools/path-aware-runner.js (node). Responsible for selecting targets, reducing npm install surface via per-package node_modules caching, and invoking the appropriate commands.
- Dep-pruner: tools/dep-pruner.js. An AST-based analyzer (esbuild parse + a shallow graph walk) that reports devDependencies which appear unused across the workspace. It produces a human-reviewable report and an optional --apply flag that will open a draft PR removing candidates.
- CI integration: premerge-sanity job is enabled by default for PRs against main but resolves quickly for doc-only changes (skips when only markdown). Heavy lanes (integration, E2E, full lint) are only scheduled if path-aware-runner marks the change as broad-impact. There is also a weekly workflow .github/workflows/dep-pruner-weekly.yml that runs dep-pruner, creates a report artifact, and can open draft PRs for maintainers.

Checklist:
- [x] Add path-map and minimal runner
- [x] Add premerge-sanity workflow and cache config
- [x] Add dep-pruner analysis + report mode
- [x] E2E smoke run on a few internal packages (redwood-serving, redwood-api)
- [x] Add docs: docs/ci/premerge-sanity.md and docs/ci/dep-pruner.md
- [x] Tests: unit tests for path mapping logic and dep-pruner heuristics
- [x] Add reviewers and get approvals
Jonah Clark (reviewer): Nice approach. Two asks before merge: 1) make the path-map lookup deterministic when multiple globs match (prefer smallest scope); 2) add a way to opt-out per-package via package.json ci.skipPremerge=true. Aisha: addressed in commit 3f8b2c5 — deterministic ordering added and ci.skipPremerge honored.
Marta Silva (reviewer): dep-pruner looks useful, but I'm worried about false-positives for generated code. Can we exclude build output and .generated dirs by default? Aisha: added a default exclude list and configuration in dep-pruner.json; also added a test case for a generated file under packages/docs/.generated/.
Devon Lee (comment): CI cache key looks slightly broad (node-mods-{{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}). Could we squish it to per-package lock hashes to reduce cross-package invalidation? Aisha: updated cache key to include package path when running per-package installs; left monorepo-level cache for weekly jobs.
Unit test failure (CI, initial run): jest unit-tests/tools failed on dep-pruner heuristics — flake due to order of property enumeration. Aisha: fixed by canonicalizing import list in tools/dep-pruner.js and re-ran CI.
Performance note (Jonah): premerge-sanity median runtime on our runners is 18s for small PRs; good improvement.
- Add fast 'premerge-sanity' CI lane that runs lint and unit smoke tests only for changed paths to improve PR feedback time.
- Introduce 'dep-pruner' analysis tool to find likely-unused devDependencies and create draft PRs for maintainers.
- Add documentation for configuring path maps and dep-pruner behavior.
how to test locally:
1) npm ci && node tools/path-aware-runner.js --preview --changed "packages/runtime/src"
2) node tools/dep-pruner.js --report --out dep-pruner-report.json
3) act --workflow premerge-sanity.yml to emulate the GitHub Action locally (we have a small act preset in .github/act-config.yml)
Links: Linear: ENG-4102 (path-aware premerge) | ENG-4227 (dep-pruner prototype). Related: RFC: rfc/ci-path-aware.md. Security considerations: dep-pruner only inspects sources and package.json devDeps; it never touches production dependencies and when run with --apply it creates draft PRs rather than committing directly. Migration notes: teams that rely on our existing full-lint feedback should add their package globs to .ci/path-map.yml to ensure the minimal checks include their packages. This PR intentionally errs on the conservative side and preserves full-lint for changes flagged as broad-impact.

Context: a recent support incident (SUP-4123) exposed two risks: operator-initiated CMK usage without tight temporal scoping, and audit ingestion that lacked tamper-evident integrity markers across hops. This PR introduces two coordinated subsystems: (1) a KMS lease-warrant router that mints short-lived operator leases (warrants) for CMK operations and enforces operator identity + region affinity at the proxy layer; and (2) an audit chainproof generator that produces chained HMAC envelopes per request and surfaces integrity headers downstream so forwarders can detect injection or truncation. Design choices: operator warrants are GRPC-level tokens bound to service-account identity, TTL, and region claim; warrants are optional and enabled via helm flags for Dedicated/Private customers. The chainproof uses KMS-wrapped symmetric keys and rotates ephemeral signing keys per lease to avoid long-lived HMAC secrets. Rollout plan: disabled by default; staged canary enable in staging clusters followed by a 2-week canary in production; operators can opt-in per deployment via helm values. Checklist: - [x] design doc (Linear ENG-2289) and threat model attached - [x] KMS router + warrant store implementation with unit tests - [x] chainproof generator + verifier integrated into audit forwarder - [x] helm chart toggles and migration notes - [x] smoke e2e against local KMS emulator - [x] security review sign-off
Samir Patel (reviewer): Please add a negative test where a warrant is used from a different region to ensure rejection.
Author (Priya): Added router_test.go case simulating cross-region warrant misuse and fixed a timezone-related TTL bug.
Lina Gomez (security): Strongly prefer KMS-wrapped ephemeral keys for HMAC; do not persist raw symmetric keys in cluster storage.
Author (Priya): Updated generator to request ephemeral keys via the warranted KMS path and documented key lifecycle management.
CI Bot: unit test failure on lint rule gofmt; fixed formatting and re-ran CI.
Evan Wu (approver): LGTM pending a short migration note for customers using custom KMS proxies.
Release Manager: Approved for staged rollout. Will enable via helm override in staging on 2025-01-20.
