Summary: Introduces a headless SSR Rapid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) quickstart that demonstrates how to integrate Redwood hosted inference into server-side rendering flows. The intent is to give frontend and platform engineers a small, reproducible starter that: 1) runs in a devcontainer, 2) supports headless/server-side streaming for SSR responses, and 3) includes an optional lightweight browser debug proxy to inspect streaming events and KV cache behavior without changing production code.

Motivation and context: Teams building product features that render LLM responses server-side face subtle problems around streaming, tokenization differences between client and server, and debugging tools. Existing quickstarts cover in-browser RAG and agent tool-calling, but we lacked a concise example for headless SSR (Next-style, edge and node). This PR adds a minimal pattern to avoid anti-patterns we've seen in support cases (SUP-843) and provides guidance for safe timeouts, CSP headers, and caching semantics.

What this PR does (high level):
- Adds /templates/headless-ssr which contains a minimal Next-like server-rendering example (server-only route, streaming SSE and polyfilled fetch).
- Adds a devcontainer configuration (.devcontainer/) with lightweight GPU passthrough notes and reproducible tooling for local testing.
- Provides two runtime variants: node-express (standard) and edge-min (Deno/edge-compatible) with matching README docs and env examples.
- Adds a small browser debug proxy (tools/ssr-stream-proxy) that can optionally be mounted during development to open a websocket/UI for inspecting partial responses, KV cache hits, and latency traces. The proxy is intentionally small and opt-in (commented in the devcontainer).
- Adds docs/quickstarts/headless-ssr.md with best-practices, CSP suggestions, recommended Redwood SDK settings (batching=false for first token, streaming=true, kv_cache=prefix), and a checklist for production rollout.

Checklist (author):
- [x] Example server route and server-render template
- [x] Devcontainer and run instructions
- [x] Edge-compatible runtime example
- [x] Browser debug proxy and short guide
- [x] README and quickstart doc
- [x] Automated integration test for SSR endpoint (basic smoke test)

Commits (summary):
- Initial scaffold of templates/headless-ssr with Node and Edge examples
- Add .devcontainer and README with step-by-step runbook
- Implement tools/ssr-stream-proxy and lightweight UI for inspection
- Add docs/quickstarts/headless-ssr.md and internal checklist
- Fix lint/ESM import ordering and add CI workflow for quickstart smoke tests

Files changed (high-level):
- templates/headless-ssr/ (server.tsx, sse-handler.ts, edge-handler.ts, example-fetch.ts)
- tools/ssr-stream-proxy/ (proxy.js, ui.html, README.md)
- .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, .devcontainer/Dockerfile.dev
- docs/quickstarts/headless-ssr.md
- .github/workflows/quickstarts-smoke.yml (added a matrix job to validate Node/Edge smoke tests)
- tests/quickstarts/headless-ssr.test.ts (basic response streaming assertions)

Notes on security and production readiness: The proxy is explicitly disabled in the production README. The docs call out CSP header guidance and recommend setting the dev-only proxy behind an auth guard if used in shared environments. I added a short security checklist in the docs to ensure teams consider KMS for keys and HSTS/CSP when exposing endpoints.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Marco Liang (review): "Nice concise pattern — can we ensure server SSE closes correctly on client disconnect and that we don't buffer the entire response?"
  - Aisha: "Addressed in sse-handler: we now use response.flush() with a short keepalive and explicit abort on request 'close' event. Added test to assert no full-body buffering."
- Sofia Reyes (review): "Please add CSP examples and a note about X-Accel-Buffering in nginx fronting SSR endpoints. Also, the devcontainer Dockerfile had an unpinned base image."
  - Aisha: "Added CSP snippet in docs, mention of X-Accel-Buffering, and switched to pinned node:lts-slim@sha256 in the devcontainer Dockerfile."
- Luis Ortega (review): "CI failed once due to ESM import ordering; please run repo linting."
  - Aisha: "Fixed import order and added an ESLint override for the quickstarts folder. CI reran and passed."

CI summary: The new workflow quickstarts-smoke.yml runs a matrix for node/edge and includes lint/static checks and the smoke test. First run: lint failed (ESM imports). Second run: all checks passed. Final CI status: pass.

Testing: Added tests/quickstarts/headless-ssr.test.ts that starts the example server in a child process, establishes an SSE connection, and validates incremental chunks and final json metadata. The test is lightweight and runs in ~6s on CI.

Docs and examples: The README contains a minimal API key example and a short troubleshooting section with answers to common SSR pitfalls: 1) tokenization mismatches between client and server, 2) KV cache prefixing to avoid cross-route pollution, 3) recommended timeout values for server-side calls.

Backward compatibility and breaking changes: None. The quickstart is additive and opt-in. The only repo change that could affect other flows is the addition of an ESLint override file under .eslintrc.quickstarts.json; it is scoped and documented.

Merge: After two approvals (Marco, Sofia) and green CI, merged via squash to main on 2026-03-04.

Follow-ups (future work):
- Add an optional example that demonstrates server-side tool-calling with safe sandboxed execution (future PR).
- Add a short video walkthrough for the devcontainer flow and debugging proxy.

Related work and references: Linked Linear items ENG-2239 (headless-ssr quickstart epic), PM-118 (doc rollout), and support ticket SUP-843 with repro notes.

If you want to run this locally: clone the repo, cd templates/headless-ssr, cp .env.example .env (set REDWOOD_API_KEY), and:
  - docker compose up (devcontainer: open in container)
  - npm install && npm run dev:node (or npm run dev:edge)
  - optional: cd tools/ssr-stream-proxy && node proxy.js then open http://localhost:8080/ui to watch streaming frames.

This PR aims to be a compact, low-maintenance example teams can fork or reference when migrating server-side LLM rendering to Redwood.
Adds a minimal headless SSR RAG quickstart with devcontainer, two example runtimes (Node/Edge), and a lightweight browser debug proxy for streaming inspection.

payload.body:
Motivation: Engineers building retrieval-augmented agents need reproducible, offline workflows to author prompt/knowledge assertions and validate regressions without spinning up hosted infra. This quickstart provides a compact workshop that demonstrates assertion-driven evals, example agent tool-calling patterns, and telemetry probes that map errors to actionable traces.

What this PR adds: - a guided workshop README with hands-on tasks and expected outcomes - a tiny assertion DSL and runner (authorable JSON/YAML assertion files) to express functional and quality checks - an offline eval harness that spins a local retriever + lightweight model shim for fast iteration - telemetry probe presets (span names, tags, and sampling hints) and a small dashboard template - CI smoke job to run the assertion suite on PRs so regressions are caught early

Key usage notes: 1) Clone the quickstart and follow the README at quickstarts/rag-assertion-workshop/README.md for a 20-minute workshop. 2) To run locally: sh scripts/run-local-eval.sh --index ./data/small-corpus.json --assertions assertions/examples.yaml 3) To add assertions: author a new entry in assertions/ with description, input, expected retrieval top-k, and a fuzzy-match quality threshold. 4) Telemetry: add TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT to env and use the provided probes.yaml to map spans to workshop steps.

Checklist: - [x] Add README + step tasks - [x] Implement assertion runner and examples - [x] Add telemetry presets and dashboard skeleton - [x] Add CI smoke job and local run script - [x] Wire minimal example agent with tool-calling stub - [x] Tests: unit tests for assertion runner, end-to-end offline smoke run

Related: ENG-3921 (authoring-first evals), PM-684 (workshop materials), SUP-1205 (customer request for offline regression checks). Docs preview: https://docs.redwood.com/quickstarts/rag-assertion-workshop

Notes on scope: Designed to be small and local-first — it intentionally uses a model shim to keep costs low for teams onboarding. The toolkit is extensible and includes pointers for switching to a production-backed retriever or Redwood-hosted models.
Adds a compact, local-first RAG workshop and offline evaluation kit. Includes step-by-step authoring guide, assertion DSL, telemetry probe presets, and CI smoke job to validate regressions before release.

Adds an interactive RAG authoring sandbox (live-reload) with three kata scenarios, telemetry probes wired to the Redwood Console workbench, and e2e smoke tests and docs.
Context: New developer-onboarding quickstart to accelerate RAG authoring and telemetry adoption. The goal is to provide a compact, hands-on sandbox with stepwise exercises (katas) that teach: setting up a local index, wiring a retrieval tool, authoring prompts with structured output checks, and instrumenting telemetry probes for latency/cost/quality. This PR delivers the sandbox app, three kata scenarios, a telemetry probes package, docs site updates, and CI smoke tests.

Motivation: Engineering teams repeatedly ask for reproducible, minimal examples focused on both correctness (assertions/step checks) and observability. Existing quickstarts teach authoring but omit live telemetry wiring or stepwise kata-style learning. This PR fills that gap and provides a low-friction path to try telemetry workbench features paired with RAG.

Context: We have a Python RAG+agent quickstart scaffold landing first; this PR creates the matching TypeScript/Node scaffold so we can iterate on streaming stability, tool calling, retriever adapters, and OTel instrumentation in follow-on PRs.

What’s included (TS scaffold):
- New template directory: templates/rag-agent-ts/ mirroring the Python project structure (config, server entrypoint, agent loop placeholder, retrieval placeholder).
- Minimal HTTP server with a single chat endpoint and streaming support.
- Streaming robustness basics: abort handling + best-effort cleanup when the client disconnects.
- Environment/config parsing with explicit schema + .env.example.
- Repo-standard scripts and tooling: TypeScript build, lint/format, and a minimal “smoke” script that exercises streaming locally.

Design notes:
- This scaffold intentionally stays provider-light: it uses the Redwood TS SDK directly today (no extra abstraction layer yet). We’ll align provider abstraction/model pinning after the Python/TS templates converge on the same config surface.
- Observability is intentionally minimal here (log structure only). Full OTel spans/metrics will be added in the dedicated instrumentation PR to avoid mixing concerns.

Local run:
1) cd templates/rag-agent-ts
2) cp .env.example .env  (set REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_BASE_URL, REDWOOD_MODEL)
3) pnpm install
4) pnpm dev
5) curl -N http://localhost:3000/chat -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"message":"Explain continuous batching."}'

Illustrative snippet (streaming + abort):
- src/server.ts
  - Creates an AbortController per request
  - Hooks res.on('close') to abort upstream streaming
  - Streams tokens to the client as newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) for now; we can swap to SSE once docs settle on a single format.

Follow-ups (tracked in ENG-4183):
- Tool calling + structured output parsing (PR-109)
- OTel tracing/metrics + Redwood-specific conventions (ENG-4184)
- Retry/timeout defaults aligned with safe-defaults policy (ENG-4184/ENG-4186)

Checklist:
- [x] Template boots locally on Node 18/20
- [x] Streaming endpoint supports incremental output and handles client disconnect
- [x] .env.example included; no secrets committed
- [x] README skeleton + troubleshooting placeholders
- [ ] OTel instrumentation (separate PR)
- [ ] Retriever adapters + indexing flow (separate PR)

Notes for reviewers:
- Naming: I matched env var names with the Python scaffold where possible (REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_BASE_URL, REDWOOD_MODEL). If we want a different config surface for TS, I’d prefer we decide once and apply to both.

Refs:
- Linear: ENG-4183 (Ship RAG+agent quickstart - TypeScript)
- Related PRs: pr-101 (Python scaffold), pr-102 (OTel + log redaction), pr-103 (timeouts/retries defaults)

payload.body:
## Summary
This PR implements production-minded networking defaults for the Python RAG/agent quickstart scaffold:
- **Timeout defaults** for connect/read/overall request time
- **Retries with exponential backoff + jitter**, honoring `Retry-After` when present
- **Lightweight in-process circuit breaker** to avoid thundering herds during upstream instability
- **Streaming-specific policy** (SSE/chunked responses): retry only if the connection drops *before first token*; otherwise surface partial output and emit actionable logs/metrics

Motivation: internal beta users and early adopters hit a mix of streaming disconnects behind proxies (SUP-29410), 429s from bursty defaults, and "hung" requests due to missing read timeouts. We want templates to be resilient by default without being aggressive (avoid retrying non-idempotent work or multiplying token spend).

## Design notes
### Timeouts
Defaults (can be overridden via env):
- `RW_HTTP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_S=3.0`
- `RW_HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT_S=30.0` (time between bytes/chunks)
- `RW_HTTP_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_S=120.0`

Rationale:
- Connect timeout should fail fast in misconfigured networks.
- Read timeout for streaming is "between chunks" to detect dead connections without prematurely killing long generations.
- Total timeout prevents hanging requests when upstream/proxies keep sockets open.

### Retries
Retries are enabled by default for **transient failures** only:
- HTTP: `429`, `502`, `503`, `504`
- Network: connect resets, DNS failures, timeouts

Not retried:
- `401/403` (auth), `400/422` (bad request / schema), `404` (misconfig), `409` (conflict)

Defaults:
- `RW_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3` (non-streaming)
- `RW_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS_STREAMING=1` (only pre-first-byte)
- backoff: exponential with full jitter; base 0.5s, cap 8s; respects `Retry-After` if provided

### Circuit breaker
A minimal per-host circuit breaker is introduced to prevent overload loops when Redwood or an intermediate proxy is failing:
- Opens after `RW_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD=5` consecutive failures
- Remains open for `RW_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_OPEN_WINDOW_S=30`
- Half-open allows a single trial request; success closes, failure re-opens

Important: this is intentionally simple and in-process (template-safe). For multi-replica deployments we still recommend an L7 proxy / service mesh policy, but templates should degrade gracefully locally and in single-instance deployments.

### Streaming reconnect strategy
We cannot safely "resume" a generation mid-stream without explicit server support. Retrying after partial tokens risks duplicate output and unexpected token spend.
Policy implemented:
- If stream disconnects **before first token**: retry once (counts as a normal retry attempt)
- If disconnects **after some tokens**: do not retry; return partial output with a user-facing message and log an error with `stream_state=partial`

## What changed
- Added `networking.py` helper that wraps the Redwood client request path with:
  - standardized timeout config
  - retry policy
  - circuit breaker
  - streaming guardrails
- Updated template entrypoints to use the shared networking helper.
- Added unit tests for retry classification, `Retry-After` handling, and circuit breaker transitions.
- Updated README troubleshooting and "Safe defaults" sections with rationale + override env vars.

## Testing
- `pytest -q` (unit)
- Added a small "simulated flaky stream" test using a local stub server to validate pre-first-byte retry only.
- Manual sanity:
  - run app behind a local reverse proxy w/ idle timeouts
  - verify logs include retry attempt counts and final classification

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- TS template parity once the TS scaffold lands (Dana already tracking).
- Add explicit docs guidance on proxies that reject unknown headers; separate PR will make telemetry headers opt-in.

Co-authored-by: Sabrina James <sabrina.james@redwoodinference.com>
- Templates now use standardized timeouts, retries (w/ backoff + jitter), and a lightweight circuit breaker for Redwood API calls.
- Streaming requests get a conservative reconnect policy (retry only before first byte/token) to avoid duplicate generations.
- README includes rationale + env var overrides and guidance for proxies/429s.
Ibrahim Khan: Please make sure we do NOT retry on 401/403, and that 429 respects Retry-After if present. Also, can we cap total retry sleep so users don't think the app is frozen?
Monica Patel: Updated classification to explicitly exclude 401/403 and to honor Retry-After. Added cap via `RW_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_S` (default 8s) and ensured we log `retry_sleep_s` per attempt.
Christine Wong: Circuit breaker should be per-host and thread-safe. Also, be careful with streaming retries after partial output—I'd rather we never retry after the first token.
Monica Patel: Circuit breaker now keys on `base_url` and uses a lock. Streaming policy updated: retry only before first byte/token; after partial, return partial and log `stream_state=partial` with a remediation hint.
Brian Murphy: Please avoid retrying on 400/422. Also can we include the Redwood request id in the error logs so support can correlate?
Monica Patel: Confirmed 400/422 are non-retriable. Added log field `redwood_request_id` when present in response headers (best-effort). Follow-up PR will standardize propagation across templates once SDK helpers land.
Christine Wong (follow-up): Add a short README note explaining why we don't "resume" streaming.
Monica Patel: Added a paragraph under Troubleshooting > Streaming disconnects with the rationale and recommended proxy settings.

Context: Customers building lightweight clients for edge devices requested compact RAG playbooks that are small, deterministic, and instrumented for local telemetry and offline testing. ## Summary
This PR adds a containerized local-dev setup for the quickstart templates:
- A `Dockerfile` for the Python RAG+agent template so users can run the app consistently (and match deployment-like behavior).
- A `docker-compose.yml` that boots a local OpenTelemetry Collector and optional local backends, so users can validate traces/metrics/log correlation without needing a production observability stack.
- Example collector config with basic redaction safeguards and conservative defaults.
- README updates: setup steps, env vars, and a short “verify your telemetry” guide.

This is primarily meant to reduce onboarding friction for people who want to confirm observability quickly (and to make support/debugging easier by standardizing the local setup).

## Motivation
Internal beta feedback and early support cases show that many failures are “nothing is showing up in traces” or “exporter auth/endpoint is misconfigured”. Providing a known-good local collector + an app container helps:
- isolate issues to the exporter/collector path,
- minimize OS-specific Python dependency issues,
- give the docs a single canonical workflow.

## What’s included
### Dockerfile
- Multi-stage build with dependency install isolated from app runtime
- Runs the template app via `uvicorn` (same command as docs), binding to `0.0.0.0`
- Adds `.dockerignore` to keep images small and avoid leaking local artifacts

### docker-compose
- `otel-collector` with OTLP receiver enabled (gRPC + HTTP)
- Optional `jaeger` for local trace viewing (enabled by default in compose; can be disabled by profile)
- Optional `prometheus` scrape config for metrics (minimal, used mostly for smoke verification)
- Healthchecks so the app can depend on collector readiness

### Collector config
- Receivers: `otlp` (grpc/http)

Problem: Upgrading the private installer in environments that use an external KMS/HSM and a cluster-based TLS signer often required manual steps: draining signer keys, resealing/unsealing Vault, and coordinating certificate signer swaps. This caused support churn for on-prem upgrades and blocked some air-gapped installs.

Goal: Introduce a light-weight 'key-sink' operator that can absorb signer key handoffs, provide a predictable handover API during chart upgrades, and add upgrade/rollback hooks (Helm + Terraform) so the installer can perform non-disruptive TLS signer rotations and Vault unseal orchestration. The implementation must be idempotent and safe to re-run for interrupted upgrades.

What this PR does: Adds a Kubernetes operator (key-sink) into the private-installer distribution that watches for SignerHandOff custom resources and atomically persists ephemeral signer material to a sealed secret and optionally to an external KMS-backed sink. Adds Helm lifecycle hooks (pre-upgrade hook to stage the handoff, post-upgrade hook to reconcile live signer, pre-delete hook to safely drain ephemeral keys) and Terraform module updates to support idempotent provisioning of the KMS sink IAM roles and HSM partition bindings. Also includes: integration test harness updates for on-prem flows, example upgrade playbook in docs, and a small migration job to reconcile existing Vault sealed secret names.

Design notes and motivations: The operator intentionally keeps the handoff API narrow: a SignerHandOff resource contains a stable logical name, rotation intent (boolean), and a reference to a target sink (sealedsecret or kms). The reconcile loop performs a compare-and-swap using server-side apply and a small sequencer annotation to avoid race conditions during parallel upgrades. We avoid storing unencrypted keys in-cluster unless sealedsecret is enabled in the customer's namespace. For HSM-backed sinks we defer to the external KMS bridge module (updated Terraform) and only store metadata in-cluster.

Backward compatibility and safety: The Helm chart adds the operator as an opt-in subchart (enabled by default for new installs). Existing clusters without the operator continue to work because the pre-upgrade hooks are no-ops when the operator is not present. All hooks are written to be re-entrant: they check leader annotations and the presence of a completed marker before performing destructive actions.

Testing and validation: Unit tests for the operator reconciler and acceptance tests in the perf-canary job (k8s integration profile) were added. E2E smoke tests simulate a signer rotation during an in-progress upgrade and verify zero downtime TLS handoff for a sample control-plane microservice. CI initially failed on a flaky e2e; I isolated the race and added a wait-with-timeout in the test harness. CI now passes.

Migration notes: A migration script (bin/migrate-existing-signer.sh) attempts to find legacy sealedsecret names and create SignerHandOff resources to allow a smooth transition; a manual step is documented for privileged installs where operator cannot access existing sealed secrets.

Why unique from prior work: Existing rotation automation focused on Vault auto-unseal, HSM keywraps, and sealedsecret choreography. This change introduces a focused Kubernetes operator for signer handoffs and explicit upgrade hooks that are agnostic to Vault vs. external KMS, enabling safer control-plane certificate rotations across both on-prem and VPC private deployments.
Added a new key-sink operator and orchestrated TLS signer rotation hooks to make private installer upgrades safe for customers using external KMS/HSM. This includes Helm postinstall/predelete hooks and Terraform idempotency fixes.
Samir Zhou: Request changes - please add leader-election on the controller and a short explanation on how the sequence annotation prevents concurrent clobbering.
Priya Natarajan: Reply - added leader election and an inline comment in reconciler, and expanded design section in docs to describe sequencer behavior.
Elena Martinez: Request changes - Terraform role creation needs Least Privilege; reduce IAM permissions and document required permissions for offline installs.
Priya Natarajan: Reply - narrowed IAM policy scope and added an offline install doc block showing how to pre-seed the HSM partition binding; added unit tests for module input validation.
Jonah Park: Approved - tested chart upgrade against a local Kind cluster with a Vault dev instance; hooks behaved as expected and migration script recovered legacy sealed secrets.
CI Bot: e2e/perf-canary failed on first run due to timing race; rerun and passed after test harness fix.
payload.title: Introduce key-sink operator and upgrade-safe TLS signer orchestration for private installer

Context: Teams often need minimal, offline-capable RAG playbooks for rapid iteration and reproducible assertions. This PR introduces a compact 'sparkline' RAG quickstart that focuses on small indexed corpora, deterministic tool-calling examples, and an offline assertion runner for CI-free validation. Motivation: provide a tiny, copy-pasteable example that engineers can use in local dev loops, CI smoke tests, and sandboxed workshops without requiring a full vector DB or remote telemetry. What this PR delivers: 1) a new quickstart at quickstarts/sparkline-playbook with a README that includes step-by-step local setup (seeded index, minimal retriever, and tool stubs); 2) an offline assertion runner (playback/assert-runner.py) that replays an input sequence and validates structured outputs against JSON schemas and fuzzy-similarity thresholds; 3) a curated 50-document sample corpus in newline-delimited JSON format to keep indexing and runtime cheap; 4) compact examples of tool-calling patterns (weather lookup and calendar stubs) with deterministic, test-friendly stubs; 5) a docs.site nav entry and shortguide snippet to appear on the quickstarts index; 6) a lightweight telemetry sparklines reporter that surfaces per-step latency and token counts in the runner output (no external metrics backend). Migration notes: no breaking changes to public APIs. The quickstart uses the same SDK entrypoints as existing examples but pins versions in the README for deterministic boots. Checklist: • Add playbook skeleton and sample corpus ✓ • Implement assertion runner and schema checks ✓ • Add deterministic tool stubs and example traces ✓ • Add docs.site nav entry and quickstarts index blurb ✓ • Add CI smoke test for the runner and fix flakiness from initial run ✓ Usage summary: clone repo, cd quickstarts/sparkline-playbook, python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt, ./scripts/build_index.sh --source sample-corpus.jsonl, python playbook_runner.py --profile local --assertions assertions.jsonl. The README includes a minimal prompt template and tips for converting to Hosted/Dedicated flows. CI notes: initial run failed due to an asynchronous file handle in the indexer; fixed in commit 3 by switching to context-managed I/O and adding a small sleep in the smoke harness. Tests: added unit tests for the assertion runner and an integration smoke test that runs in ~18s on GitHub Actions. Review summary: reviewers requested clearer error messages for failed assertions and a shorter default corpus; both were addressed. Merge: squash and merge after approvals. Related: pairs well with ENG-1872 (mini-authoring kit) and PM-402 (quickstarts prioritization).
Samir Patel: Please add a smoke CI job and ensure the runner exits non-zero on assertion failures. Ava: added ci/smoke/sparkline-smoke.yml and updated runner exit codes.
Dana Brooks: The assertion errors are noisy; can we give a single-line summary and a verbose flag? Ava: added --verbose flag and condensed default output to one-line per failure.
Linus Chen: Consider shrinking the default corpus to reduce flakiness in CI. Ava: reduced sample corpus to 50 docs and added an explicit --seed option for reproducible indexing.
Introduce a compact RAG 'sparkline' quickstart with an offline assertion runner and deterministic tool stubs. Useful for local dev loops, smoke CI, and workshops. No breaking API changes.

## Summary
This adds a `doctor` command to the quickstart CLI to help users debug the top three categories of template setup failures we’ve seen in internal beta and support: (1) missing/malformed env vars, (2) can’t reach Redwood API / auth errors, and (3) OTel exporter/collector misconfig.

`doctor` runs a lightweight set of checks and prints a short, actionable remediation for each failure (e.g., which env var is missing, whether the key looks empty/whitespace, whether the collector endpoint is unreachable, etc.). The command is safe-by-default: it never prints secrets and it redacts header values.

## CLI UX
- `redwood-quickstart doctor` (human output)
- `redwood-quickstart doctor --json` (machine-readable output for CI / scripts)
- `redwood-quickstart doctor --timeout-ms 3000` (override network timeouts)
- `redwood-quickstart doctor --skip-otel` (skip OTel checks; helpful for users not running a collector)

Example output:
- ✅ Env vars: REDWOOD_API_KEY present (redacted), REDWOOD_MODEL set to `rw-verified/llama-3.1-8b-instruct`
- ✅ Redwood API: reachable (GET /v1/models, 200)
- ⚠️ OpenTelemetry: OTLP endpoint not reachable (http://localhost:4318) — start local collector via `docker compose up otel-collector` or set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT

## Checks implemented
### 1) Env/config validation
Validates presence/format of (template-agnostic) config keys:
- `REDWOOD_API_KEY` (required)
- `REDWOOD_BASE_URL` (optional; defaults to hosted)
- `REDWOOD_MODEL` (required for quickstarts; prints if unset)
- `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` (optional; if set, we validate it parses as a URL)
- `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` (optional; parsed but values redacted)

Notes:
- We treat empty-string and whitespace-only values as missing.
- We avoid suggesting shell commands that echo secrets back to stdout.

### 2) API connectivity / auth
Performs a short request to validate network connectivity and credentials:
- Uses the same client construction as `init` (same env var resolution path).
- Calls a low-cost endpoint to confirm auth and base URL correctness (currently `GET /v1/models`).
- Classifies common failures into user-facing messages:
  - 401/403: "API key missing/invalid or org not authorized"
  - 404: "Base URL looks wrong (did you set REDWOOD_BASE_URL to a non-API domain?)"
  - 429: "Rate limited; reduce concurrency or wait; verify template retry/backoff"
  - Timeout/DNS: "Network/proxy issues; check egress + corporate proxy rules"

### 3) Collector health (OTLP)
If `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set (or defaults to local dev when running from template scaffolds), `doctor` verifies we can reach the collector endpoint:
- For http(s) endpoints: performs a HEAD/GET probe to the base endpoint with a short timeout.
- Emits guidance aligned with the template docs: use docker-compose local collector + verify port mappings.
- Explicitly calls out the most common misconfig we’ve seen in SUP-29422: endpoint set but missing auth headers / incorrect scheme.

## Implementation notes
- Introduces `packages/cli/src/doctor/*` with a small check framework:
  - each check returns {status, summary, details, remediation}
  - `--json` prints a stable schema for downstream tooling
- Adds redaction helpers shared with the existing logging utilities.
- Adds unit tests around env parsing + redaction + error classification.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)
- Add a "send a test trace" option once we finalize the local collector pipeline (ENG-4184 follow-up).
- Expand model validation to optionally confirm configured model exists in the account (PM-913 alignment).

## Screenshots / output
(See CI artifacts: `doctor-output.txt`)

## Checklist
- [x] Doesn’t log secrets (API key, OTLP headers)
- [x] Network calls have bounded timeouts
- [x] `--json` output is stable and documented
- [x] Tests added
- [x] Docs blurb added to CLI README
Quickstart CLI: add `doctor` command to validate local environment (API key/config), Redwood API connectivity, and OpenTelemetry collector reachability with actionable remediation hints.
Human output format (example):

Doctor results
- ENV ................. OK
  - REDWOOD_API_KEY: set (redacted)
  - REDWOOD_MODEL: set (rw-verified/llama-3.1-8b-instruct)
- API ................. OK
  - GET /v1/models: 200 (latency=182ms)
- OTEL ................ WARN
  - OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4318 not reachable (ECONNREFUSED)
  Remediation: start local collector via `docker compose up otel-collector` or set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT to your collector URL.
Allison Grant: For the OTEL check, please make sure we don’t encourage users to add high-cardinality attributes in remediation text. Also confirm we never print OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS values (even in debug).
Monica Patel: Updated redaction to treat OTLP headers as secrets and only print header keys. Remediation text is now generic (no attribute suggestions), and `--json` details omit headers entirely.
Christine Wong: Can we bound all network calls with a default timeout and expose an override flag? Also ensure we don’t retry in doctor (we want deterministic + fast).
Monica Patel: Added `--timeout-ms` (default 3000) and removed any retry logic for doctor probes. API probe is single request only.
Ibrahim Khan: The API probe endpoint: /v1/models is fine but please confirm it’s cheap and doesn’t create side effects. Also classify 429 separately so we don’t tell users their key is wrong.
Monica Patel: Confirmed: GET /v1/models is read-only. Added explicit 429 handling with guidance to reduce concurrency and wait/backoff.
Sahana Iyer: Tests look good. One nit: JSON output should be stable; please include a version field so we can evolve later.
Monica Patel: Added `schema_version: 1` to the JSON formatter and documented it in README.
Allison Grant: Approved (thanks for the redaction fixes).
Christine Wong: Approved.
Sahana Iyer: Approved.

Motivation: internal teams and community contributors asked for a small, composable set of local RAG scenarios that can be used for iterative prompt authoring, deterministic replay, and offline evaluation without requiring a full production index or cloud infra. This PR adds 'RAG Labbook' — a quickstart that packages scenario templates, a lightweight offline eval runner, telemetry probes, and a set of seeded corpora to reproduce common authoring workflows locally.

What this PR includes (summary): labbook README with quickstart and devloop; three scenario templates (cli-assistant, voice-assistant, and research-summarizer) that show tool-calling and structured outputs; an offline-eval runner that executes scenarios deterministically against seeded indices and records structured eval outputs; telemetry probe hooks and example probes configuration; a small CI smoke workflow and basic unit/flow tests.

Why it matters: teams can iterate on prompts, tool bindings, and structured-output validators against a reproducible dataset and measure regressions locally before pushing to hosted evals. The offline runner is intentionally minimal (single-process, deterministic seed control, and optional replay mode) so it can be used in CI and by contributors on laptops.

Usage notes (short): clone the quickstart, run docker-compose up to start the lightweight index and mock tool server, then run 'python offline-runner/run_eval.py --scenario=cli-assistant --seed=42 --output=results/cli-seed42.json'. The README contains step-by-step guides for authoring, invoking the local telemetry dashboard, and converting runner outputs into Redwood eval artifacts.

Checklist (all completed): - [x] Add scenario templates and sample prompts - [x] Implement offline-eval runner with deterministic seeds and replay option - [x] Add telemetry probe examples and toggles - [x] Provide CI smoketest that runs one scenario end-to-end - [x] Write README and quickstart guide with local troubleshooting tips - [x] Add unit tests for runner harness and template loader

Compatibility and limits: The quickstart targets Redwood SDK v0.22+ APIs and includes a compatibility shim for older local dev SDK versions. This is not intended for production indexing or benchmarking at scale; use it for authoring and small-scale validation only.

Related work: builds on ENG-4921 (authoring UX improvements) and complements the existing 'rag-authoring-playbook' content by offering an executable local harness that outputs structured eval artifacts ready for Redwood Optimize ingestion.

Notes for reviewers: focus on the offline-runner deterministic behavior, safety of the mock tool server (no external calls), and clarity of the README steps. CI run included e2e smoke. If accepted, I will follow up with a small package that converts runner outputs to the formal eval JSON schema (separate PR).
Jonas Patel: Nice work — the deterministic seed behavior is exactly what the authoring team asked for. Two small asks: (1) please add a CLI flag to skip telemetry during CI runs; (2) include a short note in README about expected runtime on a dev laptop.
Maya Chen (author): Addressed both. Added --no-telemetry flag and noted typical runtimes in README (~30s for the example scenario with seed=42).
Leah Nguyen: CI looked flaky on first run (timeout on docker compose). Can we add a retry/wait strategy for the mock index service and a healthcheck?
Maya Chen (author): Added a healthcheck/wait loop in the CI smoke job and a more robust compose healthcheck for the index container. Reran CI — passing now.
Carlos Reyes: Suggest adding a small structured-output schema for the voice-assistant example so teams can test validators. Also OK to squash commits when merging.

Add a compact local-first RAG quickstart (Mini Authoring Lab) with devcontainer, example agent/tool stubs, telemetry probe presets and a smoke CI job. Recommended for onboarding engineers and product proto work.
Context and motivation: Small teams frequently ask for a reproducible, tiny RAG playground they can boot locally to iterate on retrieval + tool-calling patterns without the overhead of full demos. This quickstart (Mini Authoring Lab) is a compact authoring sandbox that demonstrates a minimal retrieval loop, an agent-style tool-calling stub, structured output linting, and lightweight telemetry probes wired to Redwood SDK calls. It is intended for onboarding, guided experiments, and authoring prompt/eval sets.

What this PR includes: - A new quickstarts/mini-authoring-lab directory with a short README, preseeded sample index, and a single-file example agent (node.js + typescript) that shows: retrieval -> candidate scoring -> tool call -> structured response. - Devcontainer and Dockerfile for consistent local environments. - A telemetry probes harness (telemetry/probes.yaml + example probe configs) that demonstrates token/cost sampling and a compact latency histogram export. - Structured-output linter config and a small set of stepwise assertions for local smoke runs. - A CI smoke job that runs the quickstart in headless mode using a small seeded index and validates the final JSON contract.

Checklist (author): [x] Add quickstart files and README; [x] Add devcontainer and runbook; [x] Add minimal telemetry probes and docs; [x] Add smoke CI workflow; [x] Add examples referencing Redwood SDK (TS).

Usage notes: The quickstart is intentionally constrained (small index, short sequence lengths) to make it feasible on a developer laptop. The README contains a 'development vs production' section describing where to swap in Redwood hosted API keys or Dedicated endpoints, how to pin model versions, and recommendations for batching/kv-cache profiles when scaling beyond the mini lab.

Related work and links: Linear ENG-2013 for authoring ergonomics, PM-98 for quickstart prioritization, and SUP-4421 for a customer ask that motivated the telemetry examples.

Testing and validation: Added a lightweight smoke test that uses the included seeded index and runs the agent in headless Node to assert structured JSON output. CI reproduces the smoke run on GitHub Actions.

Migration notes: This is additive; no breaking changes. The quickstart references consolidated SDK helper util functions placed under quickstarts/shared-utils for reuse by other quickstarts.

Contact: Maya Patel (author) for any follow-ups or iteration requests.
Ethan Li (reviewer): Nice compact layout. Two asks: add a short note on credentials handling in README (avoid committing keys) and can we make the telemetry sample_rate default to 0.01?
Maya Patel (author): Good catches — added a creds section to README and exposed TELEMETRY_SAMPLE_RATE as an env var with default 0.02 to balance noise and observability for local runs.
Santiago Cortez (reviewer): Can the smoke CI run in <3 mins? Current Docker build took ~7m on my run. Consider using node:alpine and caching the workspace to speed it up.

Motivation: Customers building agents with tool-calling asked for a small, security-first quickstart that demonstrates how to wire a connector (external API or internal microservice) into a RAG/agent workflow while preserving least-privilege access, auditability, and deterministic local testing. This PR adds a compact 'Secure Toolchain Connector Harness' quickstart that stitches together: ephemeral credential issuance, policy-based tool bindings, a local replay proxy for deterministic dev/eval, and examples for telemetry hooks and structured output checks.

What this includes (single continuous description): The quickstart contains a step-by-step README, a minimal connector adapter (TypeScript), a local proxy that records and replays connector invocations, example policy JSON schema and policy-enforcer middleware, CI smoke tests, and a short notebook demonstrating an agent flow that calls the connector for factual data augmentation. The narrative focuses on security trade-offs: short-lived tokens, scope-limited connector roles, and how to combine Redwood's function/tool-calling API with gateway-level RBAC.

Checklist: - [x] Add quickstart scaffold and README with architecture diagram and security guidance - [x] Implement connector adapter (ts) + auth shim - [x] Add local replay proxy and recorded fixtures for deterministic runs - [x] Instrument telemetry probes for connector latency and per-call cost - [x] Add end-to-end smoke tests to CI and a GitHub Actions job to validate replay fixtures - [x] Update docs index (quickstarts list) and link to the new page - [x] Add Linear references and basic release notes

Commits (high-level): ["init: add secure connector quickstart scaffold", "feat(connector): implement auth shim + ephemeral token flow", "test: add replay proxy and fixtures", "docs: quickstart README and security guidance", "ci: add smoke test job and matrix", "fix: tighten policy-enforcer error handling", "chore: small test flake fixes and formatting"]

Changed areas (high level): ["redwood-quickstarts/secure-connector-harness/README.md","redwood-quickstarts/secure-connector-harness/connector-adapter/src/index.ts","redwood-quickstarts/secure-connector-harness/replay-proxy/index.ts","redwood-quickstarts/secure-connector-harness/policies/example-policy.json","redwood-quickstarts/secure-connector-harness/tests/e2e/smoke.test.ts","redwood-quickstarts/secure-connector-harness/fixtures/recorded-calls.json","docs/quickstarts/index.yml",".github/workflows/quickstart-smoke.yml"]

Small snippets included in the PR: The adapter exports a single callConnector function that accepts an ephemeral token and an input payload; the policy-enforcer rejects requests with mismatched scopes. The replay proxy stores requests and responses in fixtures/ and exposes a --record flag for fresh captures.

Review conversation (summary): Marina Chen: "High level LGTM — the pattern here is useful. A couple of comments: (1) make the default token TTL shorter in the examples, (2) add a note in README about production KMS/HSM integration for signing ephemeral tokens, and (3) can we fail fast in the policy-enforcer when scopes are absent?" Samir (author): "Thanks Marina — reduced default TTL to 60s in the example, added KMS note, and updated enforcer to fail fast with an explicit 401 and audit log entry." Omar Delgado: "Two suggestions: include a sample of how to run the replay proxy with insecure-mode for local-only debugging, and add a check in CI that the recorded fixtures haven't drifted unexpectedly." Samir: "Added --insecure-dev flag and a CI job that runs the smoke test against recorded fixtures and fails on mismatch hashes." Lena Voss: "Please add one short paragraph to the README about how to adapt the connector to on-prem services that require mutual TLS." Samir: "Added mTLS guidance and an example curl command in the README."

CI summary and timeline: First run (Actions job quickstart-smoke) failed due to a flaky test around timing in the replay proxy. I pushed a small timing-lock fix and re-ran CI. Second run passed all jobs (unit, lint, smoke matrix) — logs are linked in the PR checks. A lightweight security review verified that no long-lived demo credentials are checked in.

Usage and testing notes for reviewers: - Quickstart can be launched with `yarn && yarn dev` inside the quickstart directory; the README has a three-step flow (issue ephemeral token -> run agent example -> inspect telemetry). - The replay proxy supports `--record` and `--replay` modes; the smoke CI runs in replay mode to ensure hermetic tests. - The connector adapter is intentionally minimal: production integrations should swap the in-memory token signer for a KMS-backed signer and replace demo policies with org-specific RBAC rules.

Why this is different from other quickstarts: Existing examples illustrate agent orchestration and tool-calling, but many assume connectors are trusted long-term or don't demonstrate secure credential exchange and dev-time replay. This quickstart fills that gap by showing end-to-end flows (dev -> CI -> prod) and surface-level telemetry to validate connector economics.

Follow-ups planned (linked ENG tickets): - ENG-8220: Add a Go adapter variant and a Python example for platform SDK parity - ENG-8221: Extend the policy-enforcer to support attribute-based access controls (ABAC) - PM-403: Collate quickstarts into an 'operational patterns' doc and add a short workshop

Merge: Squash and merge with a concise commit message "quickstarts: secure toolchain connector harness (ephemeral auth + replay)". The PR was merged after approvals from Marina and Omar and CI green.

Adds a new RAG playbook demonstrating branching/rollback semantics with a timebox simulator for tool calls. Useful for authoring resilient multi-tool agents; non-breaking.
Context and motivation: Teams building Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agents frequently need to express conditional branches (forking retrieval/toolflow) and safe rollback semantics when external tools are slow, fail, or return low-confidence responses. This quickstart introduces a compact playbook plus a lightweight timebox simulator to let engineers author branching flows, attach per-branch rollback policies, and validate behavior under latency/failure scenarios.

What this PR adds: 1) playbooks/branch-rollback/README.md - explains the branching model, timebox semantics, and suggested rollout patterns; 2) playbooks/branch-rollback/examples/{node,python} - runnable minimal agent examples that show branching by document-similarity score, fallback to shorter prompts, and automated rollback to a safe summary; 3) tools/timebox-sim - a small simulator service (TS) that can inject latency/failure modes to exercise circuit-breakers and rollbacks; 4) devcontainer and smoke CI job that runs the simulator and example smoke tests in headless mode; 5) docs/snippets/branching-playbook.adoc - a short docsite snippet intended for the RAG patterns gallery.

Checklist: - [x] Quickstart README with step-by-step run instructions and expected outputs - [x] Node + Python example agents (compact) - [x] Timebox simulator with config knobs (latency, error-rate, deterministic seeds) - [x] CI smoke job that runs examples against simulator - [x] Telemetry hooks (example tracing spans + metric names) - [x] Docs snippet ready for docsite inclusion

Guidance for maintainers: The simulator lives under quickstarts/tools/timebox-sim and is intentionally small (single-file TS server using express). It should not be considered production code; it is for local/e2e tests and authoring only. The branching model is implemented in a library-style example (playbooks/branch-rollback/lib) so teams can extract patterns into their own tool bindings. The README outlines trade-offs and recommended rollout (canary + stepwise increase of timebox windows).

Backwards compatibility: Non-breaking. Examples are additive; no runtime or API changes to Redwood runtime are required.

Security and privacy: Examples call a mocked retrieval endpoint and do not include real customer data. Guidance in README recommends using Private deployments or dedicated capacity for sensitive corpora.

Related work: Inspired by ENG-4219 (branching runner research spike) and PM-88 (authoring UX request). Also references the incident runbook from SUP-1023 which motivated clearer rollback semantics for tool calls.

Testing notes: Added smoke tests that start the timebox simulator and run both the Node and Python examples, asserting that rollback occurs within configured time windows and that telemetry spans are emitted. CI initially surfaced a flakiness in the smoke runner which was fixed by increasing simulator deterministic seeding and making the example tests tolerant of ordering on metric emission.

Diego Ramirez: Nice pattern. A few suggestions: make metric names consistent with /metrics/playbook/{name} so that dashboards can be templated.
Ava Thompson (author): Updated telemetry span names and added metrics prefix playbook.branching.timebox in latest commit.
Priya Nair: The README is great, but can we surface a short recommended canary config (percentages + timebox values) for teams migrating existing playbooks?
Ava Thompson: Added a "Recommended rollout" subsection with concrete example (5% -> 25% -> 100% with timebox 2s/5s/10s respectively).
Omar Chen: CI smoke failed on first run due to nondeterministic seed in simulator; tests were flaky. Please add deterministic seed and retry logic for smoke tests.
Ava Thompson: Fixed by adding deterministic seeding and a single-retry harness. Re-ran CI and green.
Priya Nair: Approving pending small wording nit in README (suggest replacing 'fallback summary' with 'safeguard summary')
Ava Thompson: Wording updated. Ready to merge.

Motivation: teams building RAG integrations often need a small, deterministic harness to assert retrieval and generation behavior against a fixed prompt set. This PR adds a compact 'assertion factory' quickstart that: 1) provides a collection of typed assertion templates for common RAG checks (presence, factuality, citation-to-source, and structured-schema validation), 2) ships a tiny local eval-runner that executes assertions against live or recorded model responses, and 3) integrates lightweight telemetry probes to make regression diagnostics actionable.

What changed (high level):
- New quickstart under quickstarts/rag-assertion-factory with README, step scripts, and examples.
- A small Node-based runner (bin/local-eval-runner.js) that can run assertion sets against a Redwood hosted API key or a recorded session (fixtures/).
- Typed assertion templates and example contract files (templates/), with schema examples for structured output checks.
- CI smoke job and a local dev script to generate a golden fixture for offline runs.

Checklist:
- [x] Quickstart README with step-by-step getting started and common troubleshooting notes.
- [x] Example assertion templates and sample fixtures.
- [x] Local runner with --record and --replay modes.
- [x] CI job that runs the runner in replay mode on commit.
- [x] Telemetry hooks added to surface failed assertions in traces.

Related work: ENG-4231 (RAG regression tooling), ENG-4287 (telemetry probes for quickstarts). See docs: https://docs.redwood.ai/quickstarts/rag-assertion-factory for the staged doc landing page.

Notes on design: the assertion DSL intentionally remains small and composable: checks are expressed as JSON objects with a type (contains/exact-match/schema/citation) and threshold fields. The runner performs deterministic normalization (whitespace, punctuation, unicode NFKC) before checks so fixtures are stable across model minor versions. Recorded fixtures are gzip-compressed JSONL to keep CI fast.

Upgrade notes: this quickstart is additive and opt-in; it does not change runtime behavior or SDKs. If teams later adopt the assertion templates, we recommend adding a replay-based smoke check to their PR pipelines.

David Kim (request changes): The runner should normalize Unicode (NFKC) and strip smart quotes — added normalization step and test. — @Maya replied: added unicode-normalize util and unit test (see commits).
Arjun Rao: Can we keep the assertion DSL agnostic to language? Suggest adding language tags to fixtures. — @Maya replied: added optional 'lang' field to fixtures and example templates.
Lina Ortega (approval): Docs are clear and the CI smoke covers replay mode. Approving after small README typo fix. — @Maya: fixed README typo and added troubleshooting note about API quotas.
Add compact RAG assertion factory quickstart: provides assertion templates, a local eval-runner, example fixtures, and a CI smoke job for replay-based acceptance checks. Useful for teams adding automated RAG regression tests.
Initial CI run failed due to missing gzip binary in the container; workflow updated to install 'gzip' in runner image. Final CI run passed (smoke replay).
1) Record: node bin/local-eval-runner.js --record --api-key=$REDWOOD_KEY --out=fixtures/my-session.jsonl.gz
2) Replay: node bin/local-eval-runner.js --replay=fixtures/my-session.jsonl.gz --assert=templates/assertion-presets.json
When authoring assertion templates, prefer small focused checks (one assertion per expected behavior). Use '--rebase-fixture' to update golden fixtures and commit only after review.

Motivation: teams repeatedly build slightly different RAG onboarding flows; this wizard codifies best-practice defaults (small-chunk overlap, vectordb options, incremental indexing, pipeline checkpoints, and smoke tests) to accelerate demos and reproducible quickstarts. Introduces a new quickstart that demonstrates typed tool contracts for RAG tool-chaining and includes a golden-path smoke harness (playbook + CI) for reproducible authoring and local replay.
Motivation: Teams authoring retrieval-augmented tool-chaining workflows repeatedly hit brittle tool schemas and unclear contracts between the agent and external tools. This quickstart provides a minimal, opinionated pattern for typed tool contracts (JSON Schema + examples), a small playbook that wires an agent to typed tools, and a golden-path smoke harness that runs a deterministic end-to-end scenario in CI so authors can validate regressions quickly.

What this PR does: - Adds a new quickstart at quickstarts/typed-tool-contract that contains a playbook.yaml, README, and sample index. - Adds a lightweight local runner (TS) that can deterministically replay a scenario with seeded embeddings and a fixed LLM stub. - Introduces JSON Schema tool contracts and example request/response fixtures for two sample tools (user_lookup and inventory_query). - Adds a CI smoke job (ci/smoke-goldenpath.yaml) that runs the playbook end-to-end and asserts structured outputs. - Adds docs page rag/typed-contracts.md that outlines the pattern and guidance for schema evolution and backward compatibility.

Commits (high level): - 1a2b3c4: scaffold quickstart layout and README - 5d6e7f8: add playbook.yaml and typed tool schemas - 9a0b1c2: implement local-replay TS runner and deterministic LLM stub - 3d4e5f6: add telemetry probes and golden-path CI job - 7a8b9c0: docs: add rag/typed-contracts.md and cross-links to console guides - f1e2d3c: polish: tweak timeouts and add more assertions for smoke test

Files changed (high level): - quickstarts/typed-tool-contract/README.md: quickstart overview, step-by-step authoring guide and expected outputs. - quickstarts/typed-tool-contract/playbook.yaml: compact playbook that wires prompt, retriever, and typed tools with contracts. - quickstarts/typed-tool-contract/fixtures/: example request/response JSON files used by the replay runner. - quickstarts/typed-tool-contract/local-replay.ts: deterministic runner for local dev and CI. - samples/tools/schemas/user_lookup.json & inventory_query.json: JSON Schemas for tool contracts plus examples. - docs/rag/typed-contracts.md: guidance on schema versioning and compatibility. - ci/smoke-goldenpath.yaml: CI job that boots the replay runner and asserts outputs. - examples/e2e/playwright/smoke.spec.ts: a small end-to-end smoke assertion harness for browser-based quickstart preview.

Notes on approach and reasoning: - We intentionally keep the playbook small and prefer explicit JSON Schemas over informal text docs. Schemas enable automatic structural validation and clearer migration paths when tool I/O changes. - The local replay runner uses a seeded PRNG and a deterministic LLM stub so CI failures reflect authoring regressions rather than model nondeterminism. - Telemetry probes emit a few structured events (playbook.start, tool.call, tool.response, playbook.assert) to demonstrate how Console dashboards can be wired to quickstarts.

Review conversation (selected): - Priya Nair (2026-02-16): "Nice pattern — can we shorten the default tool timeout in local-replay to 2s? Long timeouts make the CI job slow and mask downstream flakiness." - Maya Chen (2026-02-16): "Good call — lowered to 2s and pushed commit 3d4e5f6. Also added a retry wrapper around the inventory_query fixture so transient fetches are explicit in logs." - Owen Li (2026-02-17): "Suggest we add a brief migration note about schema bumping semantics in the docs page (major/minor mapping)." - Maya Chen (2026-02-17): "Added a 'Versioning and migrations' subsection in rag/typed-contracts.md with examples and recommended rollout steps (canary validation + fallback tool)." - Liam O'Connor (2026-02-18): "CI green on second run, smoke assertions look stable. Approving to merge."

Post-merge follow-ups: - ENG-4321: track expanding schemas to 5 more sample tools in a follow-up PR. - PM-88: create a short console walkthrough doc for the playbook and dashboard wiring.

How to try locally (summary): 1) cd quickstarts/typed-tool-contract 2) yarn && yarn start:replay --scenario=golden-path 3) open http://localhost:4000/preview to see structured events in the local trace UI (optional)

Context: Our presubmit pipeline has grown in runtime as test surface area increases. Teams want faster feedback without losing signal from critical slow tests. At the same time, dependency refreshes (automated bump PRs) are noisy and sometimes conflict with releases.

What this PR does: Adds two cooperating features: 1) a weighted test slicer that chooses a subset of tests to run on presubmit based on historical runtime, failure impact (test importance), and recent change area; and 2) a dependency refresh planner that schedules low-risk automated dependency updates into quiet windows and batches related bumps to reduce churn. Both are feature-flagged and opt-in per-repo by default.

Design notes: The test slicer lives under tools/test-slicer and exposes a small Go library and a CLI shim used by the presubmit runner. It computes a score per test: score = importance * (1 + alpha * normalized_runtime) * recent_relevance_factor. Importance is derived from historical knock-on failures (we count tests that preceded rollbacks), runtime from historical samples, and relevance from changed file ownership maps. There is a conservative default policy that preserves >95% probability of catching high-impact failures.

The dependency refresh planner (tools/dep-refresh/planner.py) coordinates Dependabot-like bots and internal schedulers. It queries our org calendar and release windows, groups minor bumps into batches, and delays non-critical major bumps until agreed maintenance ramps. It produces a planned calendar entry per repo and can annotate generated PRs with the expected rollout window.

Testing & QA: Unit tests added for slicer heuristics and planner logic (tools/test-slicer/*_test.go, tools/dep-refresh/tests/*.py). Integration test: presubmit runner executed against a staging repo with synthetic slow and fast tests to verify that conservative defaults keep critical tests. A canary rollout was executed on three low-risk repos for 48 hours; telemetry shows median presubmit runtime reduced by ~28% with no regression in post-merge incidents.

Migration & Rollout plan: Feature-flagged behind 'ci.weighted_slicing' and 'ci.dep_planner'. Default: disabled for top-level infra and disabled for repos with <200 test runs/day. Staged opt-in: 1) internal tools repos (2/2), 2) infra-adjacent and sdk repos (2/9), 3) open opt-in for product repos after 4 weeks. Dep planner: start as advisory mode (planner suggests windows; maintainers must approve), then auto-schedule after 6 weeks.

Operational safeguards: - Telemetry events added: ci.slice_applied, ci.slice_skipped_reason, dep_planner_suggestion, dep_planner_applied. - Fallback: if test infra error rate >10% or if slice_applied causes >2x post-merge failures in a 24h rolling window, automatically disable for the repo and open a diagnostic issue. - Planner respects blackout and release windows and exposes an emergency 'pause-refresh' label.

Files changed (high level): updated CI workflow to add slicer step and to gate on flags (.github/workflows/ci.yml), new picker implementation (tools/test-slicer/*), planner python module and small CLI used by the automation bot, docs describing config knobs and rollout, a small helper in release bridge to annotate refresh PRs.

Related work: follows work in ENG-9123 (test infra stability), and complements prior presubmit decomposition efforts (presubmit-profiles). Notable difference from earlier PRs: focuses on smart sampling with conservative defaults and pairs sampling with dependency churn reduction to preserve developer velocity.

Checklist: [x] unit tests added [x] integration testing in staging [x] telemetry instrumentation [x] docs updated [x] feature flags behind repo opt-in [x] reviewers approved

Merge outcome: Squash-merged to main after approvals and green CI on second run.

If you want to reproduce locally: see docs/ci/weighted-test-slicing.md for example config and tools/test-slicer/README.md for CLI usage.
Arjun Patel (2026-01-25): Nice work. Two asks: make the default slice weights conservative (we should not reduce coverage for slow but critical tests) and add a brief telemetry event for 'slice_applied' so we can monitor impact.
Maya Thompson (2026-01-26): Reply - updated default weights, added telemetry event 'ci.slice_applied' (count + bucket). Also wired in a feature flag 'ci.weighted_slicing' controlled via dev flags.
Carmen Li (2026-01-28): Please add a fallback to full-run if the presubmit runner detects more than 10% test infra errors in a day. Otherwise LGTM.
Maya Thompson (2026-01-29): Added infra-error rate guard and updated docs with a rollout plan. Pushed unit tests that simulate infra flakiness.
Ethan Morales (2026-02-01): Verified planner respects blackout windows in the organization calendar and avoids concurrent refreshes on major dependency groups. Approving.
CI Bot (2026-02-01): integration-tests rerun due to transient failure; second run passed.

Problem and motivation: teams keep copying monolithic RAG examples that mix retrieval, tool-calling, and telemetry. That makes it hard to swap components, add custom telemetry, or reuse parts across languages. This PR introduces a plugin-first quickstart layout and a short walkthrough doc that shows how to wire typed telemetry hooks into the Redwood Console ingestion pipeline.

What this PR does: adds a small, opinionated plugin architecture for RAG quickstarts (templates + runtime shims) that separates three concerns: retrieval adapters, tool-binding plugins, and telemetry hooks. Provides two concrete starter templates (TypeScript and Python) and a lightweight cross-language telemetry shim so teams can emit step-level events with a stable typed contract. Also updates the quickstarts docs page with a guided walkthrough and adds a smoke CI job and unit tests for the templates.

Highlights: - New layout under quickstarts/pluginified-rag with clear plugin boundaries - templates/ts-starter.yaml and templates/python-starter.yaml: minimal config-first starters you can deploy locally - examples/rag-plugin-adapter: canonical adapters showing how to implement retrieval/adapter/tool-binding/telemetry in TS and Python - docs/quickstarts/pluginified-rag.md: end-to-end walkthrough including migration notes and common pitfalls - typed-telemetry contract v1: small JSON schema and TypeScript types included as artifacts - small smoke test and CI job to catch basic runtime regressions

Checklist: - [x] add starter templates and examples - [x] add docs walkthrough and migration notes - [x] add CI smoke job and tests - [x] include typed telemetry contract + example ingestion snippet - [x] basic smoke runs pass on GHA (rerun after lint fixes)

Backward compatibility and migration: The starters are additive; they don't change existing quickstarts. Migration guidance is in the new docs page with an example diff that extracts a retrieval block into a retrieval plugin.

Notes for reviewers: pay particular attention to the typed telemetry contract (docs/quickstarts/pluginified-rag.md section) and the small Node worker implementation in examples/rag-plugin-adapter/ts/main.ts. I included a short raw payload example for Redwood Console ingestion; the Console team suggested this shape in ENG-2045.

Related: ENG-2045, PM-789.

Maya Chen (2026-02-20): Good call — added a small inlined adapter and a note in the README showing a vector DB swap (see templates/ts-starter.yaml and examples/rag-plugin-adapter/ts/main.ts).

Maya Chen (2026-02-21): Renamed event.type -> event.name and added schema comment. Updated docs with size guidance (100KB cap recommended).

New quickstart: compact RAG authoring cheatsheet with a local WASM adapter sandbox, stepwise assertion templates, and telemetry presets for scenario-driven debugging. No breaking changes.
Context and motivation: Teams repeatedly ask for a minimal, device-friendly authoring workflow that demonstrates writing RAG step assertions and debugging tool-calls locally without a heavy infra dependency. This PR introduces a compact cheatsheet for RAG authoring and a small WASM adapter scenario sandbox that runs in the browser or node-wasm runner to exercise tool-calling and step assertions deterministically. Goals: 1) provide a one-page cheatsheet for prompt/step design and failure modes, 2) include a runnable sandbox that can simulate tool responses (WASM + JSON fixtures) so authors can iterate locally, 3) wire lightweight telemetry presets to produce deterministic traces for QA and evals, and 4) add a smoke CI job so the quickstart remains runnable in CI.

What changed (single-string summary): Added docs/cheatsheets/rag-authoring-cheatsheet.md, quickstarts/wasm-sandbox/README.md, quickstarts/wasm-sandbox/adapter.wasm (small adapter stub), quickstarts/wasm-sandbox/fixtures/*.json, quickstarts/wasm-sandbox/playwright/smoke.spec.ts, examples/rag-step-assertions/sample.prompts, tooling/ci/quickstart-smoke.yml, and small updates to docs/site-sidebars.json to surface the cheatsheet.

Commits (high-level): 1) init: add cheatsheet and README with examples and step assertions, 2) wasm: add compiled adapter stub and fixture harness, 3) tests: add playwright smoke test and node-runner glue, 4) docs: hook cheatsheet into sidebars and add cross-links to telemetry presets, 5) ci: add quickstart-smoke workflow and fix lint issues from review.

Files of interest (illustrative): - docs/cheatsheets/rag-authoring-cheatsheet.md: compact rules, example sequence diagrams, failure-mode checklist and recommended telemetry probes (trace anchors and step IDs). - quickstarts/wasm-sandbox/README.md: local-run instructions for both browser preview and node-wasm runner, how to seed fixtures and assert steps. - quickstarts/wasm-sandbox/playwright/smoke.spec.ts: an end-to-end sanity runner that loads the wasm adapter, replays a fixture, and asserts final structured output. - examples/rag-step-assertions/sample.prompts: minimal set of prompt templates used by the cheatsheet.

Review conversation (highlights): Liam O'Connor: "Nice compact format, shippedable for first-time authors. Two minor nitpicks: 1) make telemetry anchors optional by default, 2) add an example showing tool-call fallback behavior." Priya Shah (author): "Addressed both: telemetry anchors guarded behind TELEMETRY=1 flag and added a fallback example in sample.prompts (commit 3)." Avery Kim: "Playwright smoke is flaky when run in parallel on small runners — can we pin to --retries=1 in workflow?" Priya Shah: "Updated quickstart-smoke.yml to run sequentially and added a comment explaining resource assumptions (commit 5)." Diego Martinez: "Docs cross-links look good; suggest adding a brief paragraph on how this ties into the Optimize recommendations." CI summary: quickstart-smoke workflow (node 20 + playwright) — passed on run #3 after rerunning flaky browser boot step; lint/job checks passed (prettier/markdownlint), unit tests for node-runner passed, smoke run completed in ~45s. Coverage not applicable for wasm stub.

Security and compliance: WASM adapter is a tiny stub with no external network access by default; README documents how to enable outbound connector stubbing and KMS usage for private keys. No secrets checked in.

How to use (short): 1) git clone && cd quickstarts/wasm-sandbox; 2) npm ci && npm run start:preview to open browser sandbox; 3) TELEMETRY=1 npm run replay -- --fixture=happy-path.json to collect trace anchors locally; 4) run playwright smoke locally with npm run smoke. The cheatsheet lives in docs/cheatsheets for quick reference.

Merge outcome: Merged via squash merge by Priya Shah on 2026-02-01. Changelog: documented in release_notes and top-level README updated to link the quickstart. Rollout: immediate; flagged on the docs site sidebar under "Authoring & Quickstarts".

Notes for maintainers: Keep the wasm adapter small — it exists to simulate tool behaviors rather than be production adapter code. If we later expand to real connectors, move under examples/connector-adapters and add explicit security review. Related tickets: ENG-1429 (authoring upgrade), PM-78 (docs prioritization), SUP-221 (customer asks for local debug tooling).

Add a compact interactive RAG playground called 'RAG Navigator' with a minimal CLI, browser devserver, and opinionated telemetry probes for quick local experimentation; targeted at developer onboarding and internal workshops.
Context and motivation: teams keep asking for a tiny, batteries-included RAG playground that lets new engineers run a retrieval+agent loop locally with minimal setup and observable telemetry. This PR adds 'RAG Navigator', a lightweight quickstart that combines: 1) a minimal Node-based CLI to scaffold an index and seed prompts; 2) a small devserver that serves a compact interactive UI for stepwise inspection of agent decisions and tool calls; 3) opinionated telemetry probes that emit structured traces (local file/console) for step-level assertions; 4) example prompt templates and a guided walkthrough README. Checklist: - [x] scaffold CLI and devserver - [x] add telemetry probes and sample assertions - [x] provide two example corpora (kb-small, kb-news) - [x] include CI smoke tests and offline index fixture - [x] add docs quickstart page and links to examples gallery Implementation notes: the CLI is intentionally minimal (no auth required) and targets local-first experimentation; it supports `nav init`, `nav index --corpus=kb-small`, `nav run --scenario=tutor`, and `nav export-session`. The devserver runs on :5173, serves a compact single-page authoring UI with stepwise trace view and a tool-call inspector. Telemetry format is newline-delimited JSON to simplify ingestion by local eval harnesses. Security: playground is explicitly for dev use; README warns about not exposing to public networks. Testing: added a CI job that runs `nav index` against a bundled offline fixture and executes a headless smoke-run that asserts the agent reaches an expected final step. Migration and rollout: non-destructive; added under examples with its own README and docsite quickstart. Links: linear/ENG-4821, support ticket SUP-7789.

Motivation: cold-start latency is a common pain for edge-deployed RAG microservices where first requests trigger model warming and index priming; this quickstart demonstrates an opinionated pattern (edge prefetch + lightweight WASM request preprocessor + adaptive prefix cache) to reduce first-request tail latency without changing server-side runtime. What this PR adds: a new quickstart 'rag-coldstart-warmup' with README, a small TypeScript edge worker example that prefetches likely context, a WASM preprocessor Dockerfile and build scaffold, sample Terraform module to deploy to an edge Lambda/edge VM, a small indexed sample corpus and manifest.yaml, and a GH Actions smoke job that validates end-to-end cold-start latency under controlled conditions. Checklist: [x] Quickstart README with architecture diagram and step-by-step run instructions; [x] Local dev script (scripts/run-local.sh) that runs the quickstart in Docker with sample index; [x] Example prefetch policy (heuristics.json) and adaptive prefix cache config; [x] WASM preprocessor build + simple JS shim demonstrating header-based routing and request normalization; [x] Smoke CI job to verify startup and a simple query baseline. Usage summary: follow README to run locally: cd quickstarts/rag-coldstart-warmup && yarn && make build && ./scripts/run-local.sh --index small; the quickstart launches a light HTTP shim (edge prefetcher), a local mini-indexer, and a Redwood dev-runner configured to use a pinned small model variant; sample queries and expected latency numbers are in README. Implementation notes: the edge worker demonstrates speculative fetch of up to three candidate passages using low-cost metadata heuristics before the first token is requested; the WASM preprocessor normalizes incoming tool-call payloads and enforces a size cap to avoid oversized first requests; the adaptive prefix cache is configured to hold the top-K prefix KV entries per session for 30s by default which reduces warm KV misses for repeated short-lived sessions. CI/QA: GH Actions smoke job 'rag-warmup-smoke' executes a cold-start timeline measurement and fails if 95th percentile first-token latency exceeds 1.2x baseline; unit tests cover the preprocessor and heuristic policy; integration test runs a headless scenario with synthetic traffic. Backwards compatibility: purely opt-in quickstart; server side expects no protocol changes. Related items: reference design doc in DOCS-198 and ENG-3456 for runtime knobs and perf targets; follows patterns in existing quickstarts but emphasizes an edge-first prefetch strategy and a WASM-based preprocessing shim. Migration notes: none for runtime, this is training material and sample configs only. Merge summary and outcome: 6 commits squashed into one merge, all CI green after a single re-run of flaky e2e, merged via squash. Links: internal linear ENG-3456 (https://linear.app/company/ENG-3456) and DOCS-198 (https://linear.app/company/DOCS-198).
Diego Alvarez: Nice pattern, can we make the prefetch heuristic pluggable? Please add config hooks for custom heuristics.
Maya Chen: Added a heuristics.json and documented extension points in README; kept a simple default for the quickstart.
Priya Natarajan: Tests look good but the WASM build step is heavy for CI; can we cache the toolchain?
Maya Chen: Added a GH Actions cache step and a lightweight wasm-opt fallback for the smoke job to keep CI fast.
Samir Patel: One nit: clarify expected cost tradeoffs in the README and call out when this is inappropriate (high churn workloads).
Maya Chen: Expanded README to include cost/benefit section and sample telemetry dashboards to monitor prefetch hit rate.
