Summary: Adds two complementary utilities to slo-toolkit: (1) callstack-minifier, a deterministic stack-frame compressor that collapses noisy library frames and normalizes addresses to produce stable, short signatures for alerts; and (2) heuristic-runbook-player, a lightweight replay harness that runs runbook steps against a sanitized, sampled telemetry snapshot to validate step applicability, estimate time-to-remediation (TTR), and surface brittle steps before an incident is handed off.
Motivation: On-call handoffs and post-incident reviews are frequently slowed by long, noisy traces and runbooks that assume instrumentation state. Ops teams want compact, stable artifacts to index incidents and a safe way to rehearse runbooks on representative data without exposing PII or high-cardinality secrets.
Design:
- callstack-minifier: walks structured stack traces (symbolized or raw) and applies a rule set: collapse known third-party prefixes, canonicalize inline frames, strip addresses beyond module offset, and emit a short signature string plus an interactive compressed trace for UI expansion. Configurable via TTL-based cache to preserve historical compression mapping for reproducible indexing. Implemented in Rust with a Python/TS thin wrapper for compatibility.
- heuristic-runbook-player: takes a runbook (YAML with sequenced steps expressed as CLI commands or query templates), a sanitized telemetry snapshot tarball, and executes steps in a sandboxed docker-like environment with resource/time caps. Steps run in dry-run mode by default; each step returns: applicability (bool), simulated-output-summary, execution-duration-estimate, and confidence score. The player includes a rules engine to map failed steps to remediation hints.
Privacy & security:
- Snapshot scrubber pipeline included: field allowlist/denylist, k-anonymization for high-cardinality fields, token replacement for secrets.
- All snapshot artifacts are encrypted at rest and ACL-protected.
- The player has a strict permission gate (requires the new slo-toolkit:sandbox-run permission) and runtime network policy to prevent egress.
Implementation notes & changed areas:
- rust/callstack_minifier/src/lib.rs (new): core compression algorithms, known-vendor patterns, and LRU cache hooks.
- bindings/python/slo_minifier.py (new): thin sync wrapper and CLI entrypoint.
- packages/ui/components/CompressedTraceView.tsx (mod): UI fold/unfold integration and copyable signature.
- tools/runbook_player/runner.go (new): orchestrates step execution in sandboxes, telemetry adapters, and the rules mapping table.
- tools/runbook_player/scrubber.py (new): scrubber utilities, default allow/deny lists, and anonymization heuristics.
- docs/runbook-player.md (new): user guide, security model, and runbook DSL reference.
- CI: add integration matrix for snapshot variants and permission gating.
Commits summary:
- 9e3b2f0 feat: initial callstack-minifier rust crate and tests
- a77bcfa feat: python bindings and CLI for minifier
- 5f4d310 feat: runbook-player runner skeleton and sandbox interface
- c231aab feat: snapshot scrubber and example allowlist
- d9a2f7b chore: docs for runbook DSL and security guidance
- e4f1c21 ci: add matrix for snapshot variants and policy gating
Testing & results:
- Unit tests: 94% coverage on minifier core, fuzzing harness for symbol tables.
- Integration tests: replayed 50 archived incidents (sanitized) across three snapshot shapes; the player correctly flagged 88% of steps as applicable and surfaced 12% brittle steps needing instrumentation updates.
- Performance: minifier median latency 1.3ms per trace on CI runner, tail 9ms.
Review conversation (high level):
- Jordan Li (reviewer): "This looks promising. Two asks: (A) Add explicit ACL checks before a player run to prevent accidental use in low-privilege repos; (B) document how compressed signatures map back to original frames for audit."
- Maya Rivera (author): "Added pre-run ACL gate enforced by tools/runbook_player/perm_check.go and documented reverse-mapping mechanism in docs/runbook-player.md section 4. Also added unit tests for mapping validity."
- Elliot Park (reviewer): "Concerned about anonymization edge-cases (IPs in nested fields). Can we assert scrubber test vectors cover major telemetry types?"
- Maya: "Expanded scrubber test matrix with nested-field vectors and added a sanitization log that reports fields redacted (hashed) without exposing values."
- Sanjay Rao (reviewer): "Please add a short rollback/kill-switch for the player in case of misconfiguration."
- Maya: "Added runtime killfile /var/run/slo_player_disable and a feature-flag controlled disable endpoint; CI verifies the kill-switch behaviour."
Approvals & CI:
- After two rounds of fixes the PR received approvals from Jordan and Elliot; Sanjay approved after the kill-switch patch.
- CI matrix: unit (pass), integration (pass), lint (pass), security static analysis (pass), sandbox smoke (pass).
Merge: Squash-merged into main on 2026-02-23 by Maya Rivera.
Migration / Rollout plan:
- Feature gated behind slo_toolkit.runbook_player opt-in flag; rollout to internal SRE alpha group for 2 weeks.
- Monitor: player run success rate, scrubber redaction counts, and any permission denial spikes.
- Post-rollout: enable on broader org after 2-week review and add per-team ACL templates.
Backwards compatibility & breaking changes:
- No breaking changes to existing APIs.
- New permission required to run player; docs updated.
Follow-ups:
- Add experimental preflight ranking model to prioritize which runbooks to rehearse automatically (ENG-2254).
- Integrate compressed signatures into alert index to improve deduplication (ENG-2210).
Known limitations:
- Player currently supports snapshots up to ~2GB; larger snapshots will be shard-and-stream in follow-up.
- Minifier ruleset will need periodic vendor updates.
Note to reviewers: logs and sanitized example snapshots are attached as artifacts in CI run 2026-02-22-774980 for reproducibility.
Checklist:
- [x] Unit tests
- [x] Integration tests with archived incidents
- [x] Security review (static + privacy)
- [x] Docs and migration notes
- [x] Backwards compatibility validated
Adds a compact stack trace normalizer and a rehearsal runner that can validate runbook steps against sampled telemetry snapshots; no behavior change to production alerting. Note: sampled telemetry is scrubbed and access-controlled.
Artifacts uploaded: ci/2026-02-22/774980/scrubber-test-vectors.tar.gz; security review stamped. Internal alpha rollout scheduled.

Motivation: our monolithic lint runner (tools/monolith-lint/) has become a maintenance bottleneck: adding new linters or adjusting staging semantics required touching a large Golang binary and CI glue. This PR replaces the monolith with a small, stable adapter and a plugin interface and migrates existing linters to the new plugin contract. Goals: 1) reduce CI startup surface, 2) enable per-repo plugin bundles, 3) allow non-Go linters to run as thin adapters (Python/JS), 4) simplify release automation by decoupling lint plugin lifecycle from the main runtime. Summary of changes: - Add docs/ci/lint-plugin-spec.md describing the plugin contract (manifest format, env, exit codes, caching hints). - Introduce tools/lint-adapter/ (minimal Go shim) that discovers plugins via repository .lint-plugins and executes them with sandboxed env. - Convert existing internal linters to plugin wrappers under tools/plugins/{golang-lint,rust-lint,js-lint}. These are thin shims that call existing linters but conform to the adapter API. - Update .github/workflows/lint.yml to call the adapter and add a staged fast-path for changed files only. - Add a migration script scripts/migrate-lint-manifest.py that translates old repo-level lint config to the new .lint-plugins manifest. - Update release automation hooks to include plugin-version checks in the release-smoke job (prevents shipping without compatible plugin manifests). Migration notes: - Repositories should add .lint-plugins at root. The PR includes migration script output for our monorepo root and the most common subpackages (examples/, sdk/). - For external repos, admins can opt-in by adding the manifest or continue using the legacy runner for 2 release cycles (legacy runner kept under tools/monolith-lint/compat/). Rollout plan: - Phase 1 (this PR): land adapter + plugin wrappers in monorepo; update monorepo CI to use adapter. - Phase 2: run repo-level migration across 50 high-activity repos using the migration script and the automation bot (Linear ENG-1982). - Phase 3: deprecate legacy runner and remove compat directory after 2 release cycles. Checklist: - [x] Spec for plugin contract - [x] Adapter implementation - [x] Existing linters migrated to plugin wrappers - [x] CI workflow updated with fast-path changed-files optimization - [x] Migration script added - [x] Release-smoke checks updated - [x] Documentation: docs/ci/lint-plugin-spec.md Tests and CI: initial run showed integration failures due to PATH differences in GitHub Actions; fixed by normalizing PATH in adapter and adding explicit tool cache restoration. Final CI matrix: unit-tests (pass), lint (pass via adapter), integration (pass), release-smoke (pass), dependency-bot (pass). Rollback plan: re-enable tools/monolith-lint/compat/entrypoint in the lint workflow and revert head_branch; compat entrypoint retained for two cycles. Related: ENG-2110 (release automation: validate plugin versions), RFC-2025 (lint plugin contract). Detailed rationale: consolidating the runner surface but modularizing plugins gives us improved iteration velocity (add a new linter by shipping a small plugin), better test isolation, and smaller hotfix blast radius for emergency lint fixes. The adapter is intentionally small and covered by unit tests and a lightweight integration test that runs in CI smoke. 
Evan Liu: Nice decomposition. Two asks: 1) add a strict schema for .lint-plugins so the adapter can validate early; 2) ensure plugin stderr scanning doesn't leak secrets.
Maya Patel (author): added docs/ci/lint-plugin-spec.md with JSON schema and implemented early validation in adapter. stderr now filtered by default; plugin authors can opt-in with an allowlist in the manifest.
Sofia Ramirez: CI speed looks good for changed-files path. Can we add a soft-fail flag for flaky third-party linters so repo owners can triage?
Maya Patel: added plugin manifest field 'soft_fail' and the adapter supports it; added notes in docs and tests.
Introduce plugin adapter for lint/test pipelines. No breaking runtime changes; repository owners must update .lint-plugins manifest. Rolling migration recommended.

Summary: This PR introduces the initial scaffold for the Python “RAG + agents” quickstart template. It focuses on a maintainable folder layout, environment/config parsing with safe defaults, and a README skeleton that gets users to a working local run quickly. Retrieval and agent loop are included as placeholders with clearly marked TODOs (functionality fleshed out in follow-up PRs). Motivation: We want a production-minded starting point that is easy to extend while keeping vendor lock-in minimal. This PR intentionally keeps scope tight (no OTel yet; no real vector store yet) to unblock iteration on conventions. What’s included: 1) Template folder layout with minimal “app” entrypoint. 2) Config management via env vars with validation and typed defaults. 3) README skeleton + troubleshooting placeholders. 4) Placeholder retriever interface + in-memory stub implementation. 5) Placeholder agent loop with tool registry shape and guardrails placeholders. Non-goals (for this PR): Real vector DB adapters, tool schema validation, tracing/metrics/logging, retries/timeouts defaults, CI smoke tests. Those land in subsequent PRs. Implementation details: - Python 3.11 baseline. - `pydantic-settings` used to define a single `Settings` object sourced from `.env` + process env; early validation fails fast with actionable error messages. - App is a small FastAPI server with one endpoint for now (`POST /query`) returning a simple JSON response; streaming is explicitly deferred. - Retrieval path is structured so we can drop in real adapters without rewriting the handler. - Agent loop is a minimal “planner/executor” skeleton with a max-iterations constant and a tool registry interface, but tool calling is stubbed. Files / structure: - `python/rag-agent/README.md`: Skeleton README with setup steps, env vars, and TODO placeholders for observability + deployment docs. - `python/rag-agent/pyproject.toml`: Template dependencies and entrypoints. - `python/rag-agent/.env.example`: Example env vars (no secrets) to guide setup. - `python/rag-agent/src/rag_agent_template/__init__.py` - `python/rag-agent/src/rag_agent_template/settings.py`: `Settings` model + env parsing. - `python/rag-agent/src/rag_agent_template/server.py`: FastAPI app + route wiring. - `python/rag-agent/src/rag_agent_template/retrieval/base.py`: `Retriever` protocol + return types. - `python/rag-agent/src/rag_agent_template/retrieval/inmemory.py`: Stub retriever returning hardcoded chunks. - `python/rag-agent/src/rag_agent_template/agent/loop.py`: Stub agent loop and tool registry interface. - `python/rag-agent/src/rag_agent_template/agent/tools.py`: Placeholder tool definitions and registry wiring. - `python/rag-agent/scripts/run_local.py`: Convenience script for local run. - `python/rag-agent/tests/test_settings.py`: Basic validation tests (missing env var, invalid values). Env vars (v0): - `REDWOOD_API_KEY` (required; fails fast if missing) - `REDWOOD_BASE_URL` (optional; defaults to hosted) - `REDWOOD_MODEL` (optional; placeholder value documented) - `APP_PORT` (optional; defaults to 8000) - `RAG_TOP_K` (optional; defaults to 4) Notes on safety: - `.env.example` explicitly excludes real keys and includes guidance to use local env only. - README warns not to log env vars and not to commit `.env`. - No request/response payload logging in this scaffold yet (to avoid accidental PII leakage before redaction conventions land). Screenshots / local test: - `uv run python scripts/run_local.py` and `curl -X POST localhost:8000/query -d '{"question":"..."}'` returns a stubbed answer with citations from the in-memory retriever. Follow-ups planned: - OTel instrumentation + structured logging + redaction defaults (ENG-4184). - Retry/timeout defaults and streaming robustness (ENG-4186 / SDK alignment). - Real retriever adapters + chunking defaults. - Agent tool calling + tool schema validation and guardrails. Checklist: - [x] Template layout matches proposed architecture conventions (retrieval/agent/config split). - [x] README skeleton created (setup, env vars, local run). - [x] `.env.example` provided (no secrets). - [x] Minimal tests added for settings validation. - [ ] Observability hooks (next PR). - [ ] Deployment recipes (later).
Sabrina James (review): The folder layout looks good and aligns with the architecture doc. Can we make it more obvious in the README what’s stubbed vs real? Also, please add a tiny smoke test that imports the app so we catch missing deps. Monica Patel (author): Good call. Updated README with a “What’s implemented in v0” section and added a minimal import test to ensure the server module imports cleanly. Wei Chen (review): README steps are clear. Request: add explicit note about not committing `.env` and where to put the API key. Also consider mentioning model pinning will come later. Monica Patel (author): Added a “Secrets & safety” callout and a short section on model configuration with a note that pinning/fallback guidance will be added in a follow-up. Ibrahim Khan (review): For settings, can we validate `APP_PORT` range and ensure `RAG_TOP_K` is >0? Also, please avoid defaults that encourage high concurrency (even if not implemented yet). Monica Patel (author): Added validation constraints for `APP_PORT` and `RAG_TOP_K`. No concurrency settings are introduced in this PR. Kaitlyn Nguyen (review): Thanks for keeping logging minimal. Ensure `.env` is in `.gitignore` for this template directory; also `.env.example` should not contain anything that looks like a real key. Monica Patel (author): Added `.gitignore` in the template directory and changed the example key format to `your_key_here` with an explicit warning.

Motivation: provide a compact, opinionated quickstart that demonstrates how to plug third-party indexers and tool adapters into a RAG flow while keeping the same Redwood API and telemetry contracts. What this includes: 1) quickstart/bridge-playground: a minimal Docker Compose playground that runs: - a local vector indexer (pgvector-backed demo), - a lightweight tool-adapter shim (HTTP adapter with OpenAPI contract), - a Redwood-compatible RAG runner stub that exercises tool-calling and structured outputs; 2) docs/site/walkthroughs/rag-bridge.md: step-by-step guided walkthrough for the docsite with screenshots and interactive code blocks; 3) tests/bridge-contracts: contract tests that validate request/response shapes for the indexer and tool-adapter (used by CI smoke); 4) examples/adapter-templates: two adapter templates (python-fastapi and ts-express) with README on auth, retries, and security practices; 5) telemetry/presets/bridge-presets.yaml: suggested probe configurations and metric names for teams integrating new adapters.

Summary: Adds a new interactive RAG playground quickstart that runs an embedded scenario simulator in the browser using WASM for deterministic tool stubs, plus lightweight instrumentation hooks for tracing token-level events and exporter snippets for the Redwood Console. Motivation: teams often need a fast, local-first way to prototype multi-tool RAG flows and reproduce user-session behaviors without standing up backend services. This quickstart provides a single-page dev experience that can run offline, replay recorded traces, and emit a minimal event stream compatible with Redwood Console's local debug mode.

What this PR contains (single-string sectioned description):
- Quickstart scaffold: a self-contained SPA (HTML+TS) under quickstarts/playground-sim that loads a pre-bundled WASM stub runtime and a tiny in-memory vector store. The page exposes a stepper UI to drive scenarios, capture prompts, and snapshot KV cache states.
- WASM tool stubs: wasm/tool-stub.wasm + TypeScript bindings. The stubs emulate external tool calls (search, code-exec, HTTP fetch) deterministically so replayed scenarios are identical across machines.
- Instrumentation SDK: quickstarts/playground-sim/instrumentation.ts introduces a small event API (emitEvent/flush) and an exporter shim that can push events to Redwood Console's local ingest endpoint or persist to localStorage for offline replay.
- Docs: docs/quickstarts/playground-sim.md with a step-by-step tutorial, screenshots, and a troubleshooting section. Also adds a short note to docs/CONTRIBUTING.md about including reproducible scenario data when opening quickstart PRs.
- Tests & CI: a tiny Jest scenario runner and snapshot tests (tests/scenario-runner.test.ts) to ensure WASM stubs produce stable outputs. CI updates add a job to build WASM with wasm-pack and run the scenario snapshots on Linux.

Motivation: debugging retrieval-augmented generations (RAG) end-to-end is hard when feedback loops span vector stores, model variants, and tool calls. This quickstart introduces a light-weight "step debugger" dev loop powered by Skaffold and a local replay proxy so authors can iterate on prompts, index snapshots, and tool mocks without heavy infra.

What this PR adds: a new quickstart at quickstarts/rag-skaffold-step-debugger that includes: a reproducible Docker devcontainer, skaffold.yaml for iterative rebuilds, a small replay server (node) that replays indexed documents and deterministic model stubs, telemetry probes that capture token-level timing and simulated KV-cache hits, and a short authoring guide (docs/rag/authoring/debugger.md). The replay harness supports an in-memory vector store and deterministic seeds for evals so test suites can assert exact agent decisions.

Key features / rationale: - Skaffold-based dev loop for fast rebuild+redeploy during prompt iteration. - Local replay proxy lets engineers record a session and replay scenarios for regression testing. - Telemetry scrubber included to remove tenant data from recorded sessions before sharing with product or SRE. - Lightweight deterministic model stubs allow CI to run smoke assertions without hitting hosted models.

Usage (quick start): - git checkout HEAD && ./quickstarts/rag-skaffold-step-debugger/scripts/bootstrap.sh - Start local replay server: ./examples/rag/replay-server/start.sh - Start Skaffold dev loop: skaffold dev - Open the authoring guide and follow the "record -> mutate -> replay -> assert" loop.

Adds a new quickstart demonstrating a finite-state-machine-driven RAG orchestration for stateful sessions, includes authoring guide, example code, and lightweight smoke CI.
Context & motivation: Many teams want RAG flows that maintain explicit conversational state across turns (session phases, latent tool state, multi-step confirmations) without shipping a heavyweight orchestrator. This PR introduces a compact Quickstart that wires a finite-state-machine (FSM) pattern to Redwood's tool-calling and incremental index APIs so developers can bootstrap stateful RAG sessions with clear guardrails and reproducible telemetry. Summary of changes: 1) new quickstart: quickstarts/stateful-fsm-rag/ containing a README, TypeScript sample runner, an auth-free local dev shim, and a test harness; 2) authoring doc: docs/authoring/stateful-rag-fsm.md with design rationale and recommended prompt templates; 3) telemetry presets: quickstarts/stateful-fsm-rag/telemetry-presets.json for Console probe ingestion; 4) smoke CI workflow: .github/workflows/qst-stateful-fsm-smoke.yml to validate local run in CI; 5) small SDK helper: packages/sdk-utils/src/fsm.ts (new lightweight FSM utilities) 6) tests: quickstarts/stateful-fsm-rag/__tests__/fsm-smoke.test.ts High-level commit summary: - Initial quickstart scaffold and README. - Add FSM runtime helpers and inline JSDoc + types. - Add authoring guide with example prompts and guardrails. - Add telemetry presets and console link example. - Add GitHub smoke workflow and a minimal unit test. Changed areas/files (high level): quickstarts/stateful-fsm-rag/{README.md,runner.ts,telemetry-presets.json,__tests__/fsm-smoke.test.ts}, docs/authoring/stateful-rag-fsm.md, packages/sdk-utils/src/fsm.ts, .github/workflows/qst-stateful-fsm-smoke.yml Notable design points: - FSM model: explicit states (INIT, RETRIEVE, TOOL_CALL, CONFIRM, FINALIZE) and deterministic transitions on structured outputs. - Tool binding: demonstrates idempotent tool wrappers and a replay-safe invocation pattern using request-scoped tokens. - Caching: shows prefix KV caching for retrieval tokens between RETRIEVE->TOOL_CALL transitions to reduce repeated embedding calls. - Telemetry: emits per-state timers and transition tags consumed by Redwood Console via provided presets. Single-line summary of example runner behavior: The TS runner seeds an in-memory index, starts a session in INIT, emits a retrieval request, enters RETRIEVE, chooses candidate passages, optionally enters TOOL_CALL (e.g., call external knowledge API or custom search tool), moves to CONFIRM when candidate requires human-in-loop confirmation, and then FINALIZE to return structured output; the runner includes a --simulate-human flag for deterministic CI. Review conversation (high-level): Diego: "Please add an example of error path transition when retrieval returns empty; show fallback to open-domain generation." Author (Maya): "Added fallback transition with explicit prompt template and covered in authoring doc." Priya: "Telemetry presets look good; please ensure tags use kebab-case." Author: "Fixed tags and added unit test asserting telemetry fields." Samir (approval): "Works for me, tests and CI pass." CI checks: lint (pass), unit-tests (pass), smoke-ci-run (pass after one rerun for environment flakiness), docs-build (pass). Testing notes: smoke CI uses node 18 and a lightweight in-memory vector index, tests assert deterministic outputs using seeded RNG. Migration/compat notes: SDK helper fsm.ts is additive and exported from packages/sdk-utils index without breaking existing APIs. Rollout plan: ship as a Quickstart under the Quickstarts landing page with a short blurb and a linked authoring guide. Merge outcome: merged via squash-merge after approvals. How to review locally: 1) cd quickstarts/stateful-fsm-rag 2) yarn install && yarn build 3) yarn run seed && yarn run start -- --simulate-human 4) run the smoke test: yarn test:fsm-smoke Why this is different from other RAG quickstarts: most quickstarts focus on tool-calling, debugging, or replay; this one centers an explicit FSM pattern and shows best practices for state transitions, telemetry tags per state, idempotent tool wrappers, and KV-backed retrieval caching. Motivation: interactive workloads show bimodal request shapes (short-turn chat vs long generation) which causes resource interference in the prefill->decode pipeline. Small/latency-sensitive requests stall behind large prefill kernels or large KV priming windows, increasing tail latency. This change introduces a lightweight lane scheduler that separates requests into short and long lanes, applies kernel smoothing to reduce variance in GPU kernel invocation times, and adds a speculative KV hedging slot for short-lane requests to opportunistically warm KV cache without impacting long-lane throughput.

What this PR does: 1) Adds a PrefillDecodeLaneScheduler that classifies requests at admission time into SHORT and LONG lanes based on token budget and historical service times. The scheduler enforces adaptive concurrency caps per lane and provides a fast-path for SHORT lane prefill (micro-chunking with prioritized KV micro-warmups). 2) Introduces KernelSmoother: a small runtime shim that aggregates small kernel launches into time-aligned waves to avoid high-frequency micro-kernel variance on A100/RTX instances. The smoother keeps latency SLOs for SHORT lane by dispatching at low-latency thresholds and amortizes overhead for LONG lane heavy prefill. 3) Implements a SpeculativeKVHedger: a guarded speculative prefetch that consumes a small token budget to prefetch likely KV entries for SHORT lane requests when GPU occupancy permits; hedging is no-op when cache pressure is high. 4) Runtime metrics and tracing hooks: per-lane p50/p95/p99, kernel-invocation variance, kv-hedge-hit-rate, admission-rejects. 5) Integration tests and perf benchmark harness extension to simulate mixed workload traffic profiles.

Design notes and trade-offs: - Classification uses an exponentially-weighted moving average of request service time and an explicit token limit heuristic to keep rules simple and deterministic. This avoids a full ML classifier in the hot path. - KernelSmoother adds small queuing (micro- to single-digit-ms) deliberate delay to reduce tail jitter; configurable via runtime flags and adaptive policy. - Speculative hedging is conservative: each worker has a per-second hedge budget to prevent KV eviction storms. Hedging disabled under kv_pressure > 0.75. - This is primarily a scheduling and runtime shim; no model changes required.

Testing & results: synthetic mixed-profile load (50% short chat 8-24 tokens, 50% long gen 512-1024 tokens) on a 4xA100 dedicated pool: - Baseline (main): short-lane p99 = 410ms, long-lane throughput = 820 samples/s - This PR: short-lane p99 = 260ms (-36%), long-lane throughput = 790 samples/s (-3.7%), overall GPU utilization improved 6% due to reduced kernel tail collisions. KV hedge hit-rate ~12% on short lane; when hedging budget increased we saw diminishing returns and slightly higher eviction churn.

Checklist: - [x] Implementation + unit tests for lane scheduler - [x] KernelSmoother runtime shim + tests - [x] SpeculativeKVHedger + integration tests - [x] Bench harness extension and perf artifacts uploaded - [x] Documentation (runtime flags, observability)

Related Linear items: ENG-1429, ENG-2034. Related PRs: none required but this complements earlier kernel coalescing work.
Miguel Santos: Can the SHORT/LONG thresholds be tuned per-customer? Suggest exposing as runtime flags and include safe defaults.
Leah Park: Responded — thresholds are runtime-configurable and we added an auto-tune mode that observes 1 minute of traffic to pick conservative defaults.
Anika Gupta: Nit — please add a guard in hedger to avoid prefetching for requests with disabled KV semantics.
Leah Park: Addressed — hedger checks request metadata and will skip hedging when kv_opt_out flag is set.
Rohit Mehta: Approval pending perf numbers stability. Can we get two more runs over 30 minutes?
Leah Park: Uploaded 2x30m runs to perf artifacts. Numbers stable; updated summary in PR description.

Summary: Introduces a compact quickstart that demonstrates a deterministic step-handoff pattern for RAG orchestrations and a set of small, lightweight tool shims (HTTP and KV) used during local development and CI smoke runs. Motivation: engineers frequently build RAG flows where the LLM decides to call external tools; we observed drift and brittle contracts between steps. This quickstart codifies a minimal contract (step-contract.yaml) and provides runnable shims to reduce friction when onboarding tool integrations and writing deterministic tests.

What changed (single-line description): added quickstart directory with templates, examples (TS), docs site page, CI smoke workflow, and lightweight shims to emulate common backend tools.

Why: Reduce iteration time when constructing tool-calling agents and increase reproducibility for evals/smoke tests. The step-contract schema helps teams define required input/outputs per step and enables lightweight validation in the orchestrator.

Key files: quickstarts/rag-step-handoff/README.md — quickstart instructions and local run steps; templates/step-contract.yaml — compact schema describing step boundaries and required fields; examples/*.ts — minimal agent runner and shims for HTTP and KV backends; docs/playbooks/rag-step-handoff.md — docs site guide and motivations; .github/workflows/rag-step-handoff-smoke.yml — CI job that boots the shims, runs the example agent, and validates a deterministic trace.

Implementation notes and design decisions: - Step contract: intentionally small (name, inputs schema, outputs schema, required_assertions). The contract is YAML first to be human-editable in authoring workflows. Teams can adopt a stricter JSON Schema if desired. - Shims: two shims included: http-shim.ts (mocks an external HTTP tool with configurable behaviors) and kv-shim.ts (in-memory key-value store used to emulate retrieval or caching tools). Both expose a minimal HTTP API used by the sample agent-runner.ts so the developer experience is "shellless"—no need for Docker or cloud services to run examples. - Determinism: CI smoke job runs with a fixed prompt/seed and verifies the step outputs against assertions in step-contract.yaml. This reduces flakiness in docs examples and simplifies troubleshooting for first-time users. - Compatibility: examples use the Redwood SDK pattern present in quickstarts (simple fetch/SDK wrapper); we avoid depending on internal runtime code so the quickstart stays runnable for external community contributors.

Testing and CI: Initial CI run flagged lint failures and a flaky timeout in the smoke job. Fixes applied: reduce timeouts in local shim startup, add explicit readiness probe, and run lint fixes across JS/TS files. Final CI: 1 workflow (smoke) passed, unit lint passed, integration smoke completed in ~45s using GitHub Actions hosted runner. CI logs are included in the PR checks.

Summary: Adds a compact RAG local debug prober quickstart intended for developer onboarding and iterative debugging. The quickstart bundles: 1) an HTTP adapter shim to emulate external tool calls; 2) an indexed-mock store for reproducible retrieval fixtures; 3) a lightweight prober CLI that can run trapped scenarios (offline) and produce traceable session artifacts; and 4) telemetry probe hooks for step-level timing and token accounting. Motivation: teams repeatedly requested a small reproducible devkit that mirrors production retrieval+tool-calling behavior but runs without remote infra. This quickstart targets contributor friction: zero cloud credentials to run, snapshotable mock indexes, and easy toggles for streaming vs non-streaming flows. Changeset overview: added quickstart scaffold under quickstarts/rag-local-prober, new prober CLI (node/ts), an HTTP adapter written in minimal express-style shim, two example retrieval index snapshots (small, 1k docs and tiny 10-doc), structured output validators, and a tracing exporter that writes compact JSON session traces for local replay. The description below is a continuous narrative (no separate files): Context and design: keep the runtime close to what Redwood serving expects (session tokens, step boundaries, tool-call hooks) while decoupling from the service control plane. The HTTP adapter accepts the same POST /call tool shape used in our agent samples and returns configurable canned responses or artifact echoes; it is purposefully minimal to be usable with Playwright or unit tests. The indexed-mock store implements a tiny on-disk inverted index with near-constant startup cost and supports incremental delta loading so developers can swap in new snapshots without rebuilding binaries. CLI and dev loop: prober run --scenario=browser-search --index=small creates a reproducible run, emits step traces to /tmp/rag-prober/traces, and prints a compact summary with token counts and latency percentiles. Integration with local authoring: the quickstart includes a devcontainer and npm scripts for one-command start (dev: up). The quickstart is intentionally opinionated about defaults (low-latency, small batch sizes, streaming off) but exposes configuration flags for batching, prefix-caching, and tool timeouts. Security and credentialing: the prober includes an optional credential injection step that accepts a local API token file; by default it runs in a credentialless mode and warns when tokens are present to avoid accidental leakage. Release rationale: this is developer tooling only (not for production) and reduces authoring iteration time for retrieval-and-tool workflows.
4 commits: 1) scaffold quickstart and README; 2) add prober CLI, HTTP adapter and index loader; 3) add example snapshots and structured-output lints; 4) test matrix and CI job updates (node 18/20). Each commit contains small, focused changes with unit tests for adapter and index loader.

Problem: Engineers often ask for compact, copy-pasteable guides for common RAG patterns (prefix caching, tool-calling fallbacks, progressive retrieval) that they can drop into a new repo or demo. Large quickstarts are useful but heavyweight for triage, onboarding, or offline workshops.

Proposal: Add a set of 'pocket playbooks' — intentionally small, single-page quickstarts focused on a single pattern each — plus a pair of minimal proxy tool-adapter examples that show how to safely surface third-party tool calls from a serverless environment (HTTP proxy and lightweight WebSocket bridge). The goals are: 1) tiny surface area so devs can read and run in <10 minutes; 2) explicit telemetry/ops hooks so these can be used in smoke suites; 3) clear license and security guidance for tool proxying.

What I changed: Introduced quickstarts/pocket-playbooks with 6 pocket playbooks (retrieval-warmup, prefix-cache-best-practice, progressive-retrieval, streaming-with-checkpoints, tool-fallback-pattern, structured-output-snippet). Each playbook is a README.md sized to fit a single screen with a runnable local docker-compose or Make target. Added examples/proxy-tool-adapters with two minimal adapters: http-proxy-adapter (Express-based, short-circuit auth, request signing) and ws-bridge-adapter (serverless-friendly WebSocket bridge with backpressure hints). Added lightweight telemetry probes and smoke tasks wired into the repo-level Makefile and a nav entry for the docs site.

Why this is different: There are many long-form quickstarts; these are deliberately scoped low-friction "pocket" recipes that pair example code with operational checklist and one-liner prompts. They reduce cognitive overhead for new teams and are targeted at SDK and examples consumers (browser, serverless, on-prem).

How to validate: Checkout branch, cd quickstarts/pocket-playbooks, run make smoke (requires Docker). Smoke runs: build tiny retrieval index, run sample worker, hit tool-proxy stub, and assert telemetry hooks emit expected metrics. Debugging section includes guidance for local port-forwarding into Redwood Private dev environments.

Motivation: debugging multi-turn RAG flows and reproducing regressions is hard without compact, versioned checkpoints. This quickstart introduces a chainable snapshot format and a tiny replay harness that makes deterministic debugging and contract checks trivial for engineers.

Summary: adds a new quickstart `rag-chain-snapshot` that demonstrates: 1) chainable session snapshots (versioned, minimal payloads capturing retrieval deltas, model token diffs, and tool-call envelopes); 2) a schema-enforced structured-output contract for tool calls and step records; 3) a deterministic replay runner that can pin a model variant or run against a local mock and performs token-precise diffs; 4) a devcontainer for reproducible local testing and a console-friendly telemetry probe that emits span-like events to stdout.

Highlights and rationale: The snapshot format is intentionally compact to encourage frequent checkpoints during iterative authoring. Each snapshot contains metadata (version, quickstart, seed), a `steps` array with `user`, `retrieval`, `model`, and `tools` subsections, and optional annotations for manually marking interesting frames. The replay harness validates the JSON Schema, replays prompts to a pinned model-id (or a stubbed mock) and reports regressions with a concise diff. This approach helps support teams reproduce SUP tickets and enables maintainers to run contract checks in CI.

How to try locally: copy .env.example to .env and add REDWOOD_API_KEY, start the devcontainer or run `docker compose up --build`, then `npm run dev` to open the small playground. Use `npm run record-session -- --example=payment-refund` to produce a snapshot in ./snapshots and `npm run replay -- --file=snapshots/payment-refund-1.json` to replay and run the contract linter.

CI: added a Jest-based smoke test that synthesizes a snapshot and runs the contract linter. A flake was observed on first run due to mock timing; I implemented a lightweight retry (3 attempts) around the mock server startup to stabilize CI. All checks are now passing.

Security/PII: quickstart purposely avoids shipping any real customer data. The SQLite seed is synthetic and the seeded DB is added to .gitignore if generated locally. No keys are committed.

Review notes: reviewers asked to keep the snapshot schema extensible (versioned) and to avoid heavy deps. I kept the runtime minimal (Node 18+, tiny dev UI) and added a clear migration path in docs.

Merge: squash-and-merge to keep the quickstart changes atomic.

Planned follow-ups: wire telemetry probe to Redwood Console exporter, contribute schema to redwood-model-registry, add a typed SDK helper in redwood-sdk-typescript to read/write snapshots.
Liam Chen: Can we keep the schema backward-compatible? — Answer: added version field and migration notes in README.
Maya Rodriguez: Please avoid heavy runtime deps in the quickstart UI. — Answer: replaced heavyweight UI library with a minimal web component and inlined CSS.
Thomas Nguyen: CI flaked on mock server startup. — Action: added a retry loop and a short backoff; observed stability after change.

Motivation: Customers increasingly ask for tenant-specific defaults that balance latency SLOs and unit economics without hand-tuning. This PR introduces two developer-facing tools: 1) a guided CLI (BatchSmith) that analyzes a tenant's request traces and proposes batching/caching presets (batch sizes, max wait, KV cache TTL suggestions, prefill hints); 2) an interactive 'Quant Tutor' assistant that runs a lightweight simulation over sampled requests and suggests quantization profiles (FP16/int8/4-bit mixes) with estimated token-cost and P50/P95 latency delta.

Summary of changes: Implemented a user-facing CLI binary (redwood-batchsmith) under cmd/ and a new internal package inference/econ/tutor that exposes the quant-suggestion API. Added a tenant sample analyzer that is conservative by default (prefers latency-safe presets) and a posterior score that estimates cost delta and quality risk. Instrumented telemetry: econ.batch.suggestion and econ.quant.tutor.* metrics, with tags for tenant_id/model/seq_dist. Included markdown docs and a quickstart in docs/cli/batchsmith.md.

Checklist: [x] tenant trace ingestion and sampling logic [x] heuristics engine + thresholds [x] quant simulation harness (fast, approximate) [x] telemetry metrics and dashboards links [x] unit + integration tests [x] docs and examples [x] canary rollout plan

Commits (high level): c1a2b3 entrypoint + command parsing; d4e5f6 sampling and heuristics; a7b8c9 quant tutor interactive flow; f0e1d2 perf harness and tests; 9a8b7c docs and examples.

Files changed (high level): cmd/batchsmith/main.go - new CLI entrypoint and flags; inference/econ/tenant_sampler.go - sampling and histogram helpers; inference/econ/heuristics.go - new rules and scoring; inference/econ/quant_tutor.go - quant simulation service; telemetry/metrics_registry.go - new metrics registered; docs/cli/batchsmith.md - usage and examples; scripts/canary_rollout.sh - deployment helper; tests/econ/* - unit and integration tests. Small illustrative snippet added to heuristics.go: if p95_latency > target && median_seq > prefill_threshold { suggest.prefill = true }

Review conversation excerpt: "Diego: Nice separation between sampling and scoring. Can you add an explicit lint check for max memory when simulating quant profiles?" "Asha: Added mem cap in a separate commit and updated tests to run the simulator with --max-mem flag." "Rina: Will the suggested presets be safe for low-traffic tenants? Add opt-out for automatic apply." "Asha: Defaults remain suggestions; CLI has --apply flag guarded by tenant admin scope. Documented in the quickstart." 

CI summary: unit tests 88 passed, integration smoke on staging passed, perf-run: simulated tenant sample (n=1000) shows median token-cost reduction of 9.4% and 95th latency increase of 1.9% on average for suggested quant profiles; end-to-end latency SLOs maintained for canary tenants. All checks green after two re-runs of the flaky e2e job.

Performance and safety notes: The quant simulator uses a sampled inference model and applies conservative error penalties; suggested profiles include an "estimated quality risk" tag (low/medium/high). For latency-sensitive tenants the default heuristic favors cache/prefill and FP16 over aggressive 4-bit quantization. We validated on three tenant canaries (tenant-a, tenant-b, tenant-c) with traffic shaping and rollback hooks. Cost win example: tenant-b sample estimated monthly token-cost savings of ~$18.2k on current usage with negligible change in observed quality metrics.

Canary and rollout: rolled to 5% of eligible tenants for 48h, monitored econ.batch.suggestion.accept_rate and customer reports. No regressions; proceeded to 25% on day 4. Merge includes a canary config and a safe rollback script (scripts/canary_rollout.sh). Operators should use the console dashboard link (dashboards/econ/batchsmith-suggestions) to monitor.

Backward compatibility: No API surface changes to existing inference endpoints. The CLI is additive. The quant tutor service is internal and behind a feature flag (econ.quant.tutor.enabled).

Follow-ups: automation to apply suggested presets as part of tenant onboarding (ENG-3590), and a telemetry privacy review for sampling windows (ENG-3421).

This PR adds the first slice of the quickstart scaffolding CLI: `init`. The goal is to let users scaffold a chosen quickstart template from a single command while we iterate on the template portfolio and release/versioning story. Scope intentionally stays minimal (no upgrades, no doctor, no deploy) but establishes the structure we’ll build on in follow-up PRs. What `init` does: (1) selects a template (via `--template` flag; if omitted, prints a short list + instructions), (2) copies the template directory into a target output folder, (3) applies light templating for project name/package name placeholders, (4) writes a version stamp file so support + docs can identify the originating CLI/template version, (5) prints next steps (env vars, install deps, run). Version stamping: writes `.redwood-template.json` with `template_id`, `template_version`, `cli_version`, and `generated_at` (no secrets; no user data). This is meant to support troubleshooting and future upgrade workflows (we can detect “generated by CLI vX”). Template resolution: for now, templates are sourced from the repo at build time (bundled in the published CLI package). This keeps UX simple and avoids needing network access during init. We can revisit remote template resolution once we have a stable registry/versioning policy. UX details: supports `--dir` (defaults to current directory), `--force` to allow non-empty dirs (with a loud warning), and `--yes` to skip confirmation. Error messages aim to be actionable (e.g., if target dir exists, if template ID is unknown, if placeholder substitution fails). Non-goals: do not attempt to install deps, do not validate API keys, do not configure OTel collector, and do not add telemetry. Follow-ups: `doctor` command (ENG-4185 follow-up / PR-111), docs updates to point to CLI install, and a release workflow to publish CLI versions alongside template releases.
The CLI is implemented in TypeScript (Node 18+) and published as a single package with a `bin` entry (current name: `@redwoodinference/quickstart-cli`, subject to final naming). Template copy uses a conservative allowlist approach: copies the selected template directory, excludes node_modules/.venv/.git, preserves executable bits, and avoids following symlinks. Placeholder replacement is intentionally small: `{{PROJECT_NAME}}`, `{{PACKAGE_NAME}}`, `{{APP_SLUG}}`. We avoid attempting to mutate arbitrary code beyond these markers to keep diffs predictable and maintenance low. Version stamp file example: `{ "template_id": "rag-agent-python", "template_version": "0.1.0", "cli_version": "0.1.0", "generated_at": "2025-02-24T18:12:03.221Z" }`.
Install (dev): `pnpm --filter @redwoodinference/quickstart-cli build` then `node cli/dist/index.js init --template rag-agent-python --dir ./my-app`.
Planned (published): `npx @redwoodinference/quickstart-cli init --template rag-agent-python --dir ./my-app`.
Flags: `--template <id>`, `--dir <path>`, `--force`, `--yes`.

Motivation: provide a small, copy-pasteable RAG example that demonstrates an end-to-end dev loop: a tiny React microfrontend that streams tokens from Redwood hosted inference, a lightweight serverless connector (AWS Lambda) that proxies the embedding + retrieval flow, and a local dev harness for iteration. This PR adds a new quickstart 'rag-microfrontend' aimed at frontend + platform engineers who want a simple integration with streaming responses and tool-calling patterns. What is included: a README with architecture diagrams and how to run locally; a React client (TypeScript, Vite) demonstrating streaming UI, partial-token rendering, and request batching recommendations; a Node.js Lambda handler that performs embeddings lookup against a sample SQLite vector index and calls Redwood for completion; CI workflow for preview deployments (GitHub Actions: build + test + deploy-preview to a static hosting action); example env templates and a small script to seed the local vector DB. Design notes: prefer a small move-fast example over full infra—using SQLite for portability and a minimal vector similarity function so users can experiment without cloud infra. The client demonstrates best-practice prompt shaping, streaming error handling, and a safe fallback that switches to a cheaper compatible model when the primary model returns a capacity error. Checklist: - [x] Add example scaffold and README with quickstart steps - [x] Add streaming client implementation with partial rendering and reconnect logic - [x] Add Lambda connector and local seed script - [x] Add CI preview workflow and basic tests - [x] Documentation links to Redwood Console routing and Dedicated autoscaling docs Testing: local dev run + unit test for the similarity function + integration smoke test using the seeded DB. Backwards-compat notes: compatible with Redwood API surface; no breaking changes. Related: ENG-7281 tracks a future follow-up for an opinionated production deployment guide.

Summary: Adds a new quickstart that combines a lightweight playbook visualizer, an inline "live" contract editor for tools, and a step inspector that surfaces telemetry/trace snippets. Motivation: authoring and debugging RAG playbooks is still split between static YAML/JSON and separate contract validators. This quickstart (playbook-visualizer) provides a single local development flow that speeds iteration: visual feedback for step ordering, simple drag-reorder, contract validation in-place, and an inspector pane showing the request/response, KV-cache usage, and telemetry markers emitted during a simulated run.

What this PR contains: single continuous description and checklist below. Files include a compact React-based visualizer (src/ui), a minimal TypeScript adapter that runs playbooks against a local light runner (src/runner), a devcontainer and docker-compose for local simulation, docs site quickstart page (docs/quickstarts/playbook-visualizer.md), CI smoke workflow ( .github/workflows/quickstart-smoke.yml ) to run the local runner in headless mode, and a small set of example playbooks and tool contracts (examples/). The UI is intentionally dependency-light to keep the quickstart fast to clone and run.

Checklist: - [x] Visualizer UI + step inspector implementation - [x] Live contract editor with inline linting & schema hints - [x] Local playbook runtime shim (no GPU required) - [x] Devcontainer and docker-compose quickstart - [x] Docs quickstart page and code snippets - [x] CI smoke workflow + unit tests for contract lint rules - [x] Telemetry samples and small synthetic run corpus for demos

How it works (high-level): The visualizer consumes a playbook JSON schema and renders steps as nodes. Each node has a contract editor that is backed by the same JSON-schema-based validator used in our production tool-contract linter. The runner simulates calls to tool adapters (stubbed network responses) and emits compact telemetry events. The step inspector subscribes to the runner over a websocket and shows the last 10 events for the selected step, KV cache hits/misses, and synthetic latency histograms. A local watch mode uses filesystem events to hot-reload playbooks and contracts in the browser for fast iteration.

Developer notes and usage: 1) Clone repo, cd quickstarts/playbook-visualizer 2) Start devcontainer (or run docker-compose up) to install and launch the UI and runner 3) Open http://localhost:3002 and pick an example playbook. Edit tool contracts inline and press "Validate". Validation errors appear in the contract panel and also as red badges on steps. 4) Press "Run (Simulate)" to execute a synthetic run; step inspector will stream events. 5) Use "Export" to generate a production-ready playbook.yaml that pins contract SHAs and a suggested rollout policy.

Testing and CI: The included workflow runs the runner in headless mode, executes a small set of example playbooks and asserts that exported playbooks pass the contract linter. Unit tests target contract validation rules (schema conformance, required fields, param typing) and the runner event semantics. CI output is lightweight to keep CI minutes low.

Changed areas / files (high level): src/ui/Visualizer.tsx - React visualizer and inspector; src/ui/ContractEditor.tsx - in-browser editor and lint integration; src/runner/sim-runner.ts - lightweight simulator; examples/sample-playbooks/*.json - three example playbooks demonstrating branching, tool-fallbacks and KV-cache reuse; docs/quickstarts/playbook-visualizer.md - step-by-step guide; .devcontainer/* and docker-compose.yml - local quickstart; .github/workflows/quickstart-smoke.yml - CI smoke flow.

Commits (summary): 1) initial scaffold of visualizer and minimal runner; 2) add contract editor + schema integration; 3) wire telemetry stream & step inspector; 4) add examples and docs; 5) CI workflow and unit tests; 6) polish UX, keyboard shortcuts, and accessibility tweaks.

Review thread highlights: - Miguel: requested clearer error mapping between contract lint messages and step nodes (addressed in commit 4; lint markers now include node id and line preview). - Lina: asked for a smaller devcontainer image to reduce onboarding time; switched base to node:18-slim and moved heavy deps to optional layer (commit 5). - Samir: suggested adding a demonstration of prefix/KV cache reuse; added sample-playbooks/cache-reuse.json and instrumented the runner to surface cache hit ratio in the inspector. All reviewers approved after the fixes.

CI checks: - quickstart-smoke (passed) - unit (passed) - lint (passed) - accessibility-scan (warn -> fixed in follow-up commit)

Merge outcome: squash and merge by Lina Chen. Changelog/release notes: Adds a new quickstart: "Playbook Visualizer + Live Contract Editor" (developer-facing tool to speed RAG playbook authoring, validation and debugging). This is non-breaking and intended as a local developer experience; no runtime or API surface changes to hosted Redwood product.

Follow-ups planned: (1) Add a compact rollout export that integrates with Redwood Console rollout API (ENG-2380). (2) Expand sample corpus with multi-tenant examples. (3) Post-merge: schedule a docs-site guided video walkthrough and short webinar for developer community.

If you'd like to run the quickstart locally and give UX feedback, see docs/quickstarts/playbook-visualizer.md for step-by-step commands and troubleshooting notes.

Motivation: Provide a concise quickstart for running Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) on constrained or intermittently-connected devices. This PR introduces an offline device proxy pattern that keeps a small, incremental vector index local to the device, uses a compressed index format, and falls back to Redwood Private when connectivity is available. It targets developers building on-device assistants or field apps where network is unreliable and latency must be bounded. Changes include a new quickstart under quickstarts/device-proxy, a lightweight local indexer binary (WASM/Go), example config for a device-side proxy shim that routes queries to the local store and gracefully escalates to cloud model endpoints, instrumentation probes for offline telemetry, and a devcontainer for easy iteration. Checklist: Implement local indexer wasm binary and fallback logic; Add quickstart README with step-by-step setup and validation; Provide sample dataset and incremental indexing script; Include smoke tests for cold start and offline-to-online failover; Add CI smoke job to run the quickstart end-to-end in containerized dev environment; Update docs nav to include the new quickstart. Backcompat: design is additive; no changes to Redwood API surface. How to try locally: 1) git clone && cd quickstarts/device-proxy; 2) make devcontainer to launch local indexer and device-proxy service; 3) ./scripts/index-local.sh --src sample-data/ --batch 64 to build a compressed incremental index; 4) start device-proxy: docker-compose up device-proxy; 5) run ./scripts/query-local.sh "What is the warranty period for product X?" to see cached-local hit and then network fallback when offline. Observability: added lightweight probes (Prometheus metrics and structured traces) to the proxy and indexer; quickstart shows example Grafana dashboard JSON and alerts for sync lag. Security: docs explain keys and a recommended short-lived token flow for devices, with KMS integration described for Private deployments. Test notes: CI runs devcontainer smoke to verify index build and a simulated offline failover; a lint step initially failed on markdown link style and was fixed in f6b2. Related work: follows design discussed in ENG-8421 and the DeviceEdge initiative; references the edge index format RFC.
Carlos: Nice end-to-end flow. Small request: make default proxy port 8081 to avoid colliding with other dev services. Please add a note about index size limits on devices.
Maya: Addressed; changed default port to 8081 and added a section 'Device constraints' with sample budgets for memory and disk. Added a note about using quantized embeddings to reduce index size.
Priya: CI failed on markdown lint (link style) and then passed after fixes. Also suggested including a short snippet showing Prometheus label conventions for device_id.
Maya: Added Prometheus label conventions and updated Grafana json example to use device_id query filters.
Ethan: Approved after verifying the smoke job reproduces offline-to-online failover in the devcontainer. Left a minor nit about a log line level change; not blocking.
Maya: Switched the log line to debug for the frequent sync message per Ethan's suggestion. Thanks!
CI: runs devcontainer build, index creation from sample-data, launches docker-compose, runs query scenarios for cache hit and offline failover. Locally: follow README steps; use ./scripts/simulate-network.sh to toggle online/offline modes.
Add device-focused offline RAG quickstart: local indexer, compressed vector format, device proxy shim and diagnostics. Includes devcontainer and CI smoke tests. Backwards compatible.
When deploying the quickstart in production or on fleet devices, ensure short-lived tokens are provisioned via your KMS and consider using delta sync schedules to minimize bandwidth. The quickstart uses a compact L2 quantized index by default to keep memory under 200MB on prototype devices.

Motivation: onboarding teams need a compact, opinionated RAG quickstart that teaches incremental debugging, deterministic turn-by-turn replay, and safe tool-calling patterns. This PR adds the 'RAG Scenario Tutor' quickstart: an interactive guided example that walks a developer through building a retrieval-augmented agent, instrumenting Redwood Console telemetry hooks, and swapping in local tool stubs (search, vector-store, web-scraper) across TypeScript and Python samples. The goal is to reduce time-to-first-success for engineers integrating RAG into product flows and to provide a reproducible debugging path for flaky outputs.

What this PR contains: checklist: - add quickstart scaffold and narrative README with step checkpoints and learning objectives - include a lightweight devcontainer and local runner to simulate streaming responses and tool calls - provide TypeScript and Python sample agents demonstrating structured tool output, function-style calls, and safe retries - add a small in-repo mock vector store and search tool for deterministic CI tests - instrument example telemetry hooks and a sample dashboard config for Redwood Console - add e2e smoke script for CI that runs through the guided scenario and verifies expected prompts/outputs - docs site metadata and sidebar entry so the quickstart shows up under "Quickstarts > RAG" - short demo gif (assets/demo-tutor.gif) and a screencast link in the README

Why this is different: unlike previous quickstarts that focus on microservices or single-language examples, the Scenario Tutor emphasizes stepwise pedagogy: checkpoints assert intermediate agent state, a replay file records turn-level events, and the devloop integration lets users iterate locally with the same telemetry surfaced in production. It also favors small deterministic tool stubs so CI can validate behavior without external networking.

Testing notes: ran the smoke e2e locally and in CI. The CI job uses a pinned node/python image, starts the mock tooling service, runs the guided scenario, records a replay file under /tmp/rag-tutor-replay.json and asserts 5 checkpoints passed. CI matrix: node 20 / python 3.11; both passed.

Docs/links: Linear: ENG-1421 contains the design notes and UX script. Demo screencast: https://internal.redwood.dev/screencasts/rag-tutor. Quickstart README: docs/quickstarts/rag-scenario-tutor/README.md.

Migration/rollout: adds a docs site sidebar entry; no runtime changes to the serving runtime. This is purely example/docs code that can be published immediately after merge.

Follow-ups: - extend the tutor with a 'failure injection' lesson for flaky retrievers (ENG-1503) - add a Go stub agent variant if adoption metrics warrant - bake the replay verifier into the eval-harness smoke kit
Liam O'Brien: Nice guided flow — can we shorten the demo gif to reduce repo bloat? Suggest 3s clip (done in last commit).
Sofia Martinez: Code looks good; please add a brief note explaining the replay format so teams can write custom verifiers (added in README).
Arjun Patel: CI flakes on linux-latest in first run due to ephemeral port collision; switched to fixed port range and added retry (see commit 4).
Maya Chen: replied: addressed gif size, added replay format section, pinned ports in CI job and added retry wrapper.
Add 'RAG Scenario Tutor' quickstart: interactive guided example with TypeScript and Python agents, replayable turn-level logs, mock tool stubs, and CI smoke tests. Useful for teams onboarding RAG flows and testing agent/tool integrations.

This PR introduces the 'RAG Fastboot' quickstart: a compact, opinionated playbook and minimal toolchain stubs designed to get engineers from zero to a reproducible RAG demo in under 10 minutes. Motivation: internal onboarding sessions and customer-run workshops were repeatedly slowed by heavy example repos; this lightweight starter unifies a small set of vetted patterns (structured output validation, a preseeded mini-index, tool-call stubs, and telemetry probes) so developers can iterate on prompt+index loops quickly.

What this includes (high level):
- README with step-by-step fastboot flow and explicit expectations for each step (devcontainer, index seed, run local agent, smoke CI).
- Minimal Python agent (sample_agent.py) with two tool-call stubs (search_tool, exec_tool) and a small harness to run deterministic scenarios.
- TypeScript playground runner (playground.ts) that mirrors the Python sample for browser-based experimentation (uses local shim connector).
- Preseeded index generator (small corpus + script) so examples are reproducible without external data.
- Structlinter config and a CI smoke workflow that validates structured output contract and basic policy checks.
- Telemetry probe presets (probes.yaml) to demonstrate key traces/metrics to instrument during early-stage testing.

Developer checklist (run before marking ready):
- [x] Confirm devcontainer snaps up and builds in under 3 minutes.
- [x] Smoke CI validates sample prompts produce expected structured JSON.
- [x] Telemetry probes emit to the local collector shim.
- [x] README contains troubleshooting tips and expected token/latency profiles for hosted vs. local inference.

Commits summary: single-feature branch with iterative commits for demo polish. Notable commits: initial skeleton and README, add python agent and preseed index, add TS playground and connector shim, add structlinter rules and CI, telemetry probes + documentation polish.

Changed areas (summary):
- quickstarts/rag-fastboot/: core quickstart materials (README, samples, devcontainer, probes).
- docs/: small cross-link to docs/rag-playbooks.md and an inter-doc anchor for quickstarts.
- .github/workflows/smoke.yml: lightweight smoke tests that run the structlinter and a headless agent scenario.

Review notes / rationale:
- We intentionally keep the tool stubs minimal: they return deterministic payloads so CI can assert structured output without flaky external dependencies.
- Structlinter rules exercise common failure modes (missing fields, type mismatches, extra unexpected fields) and point to remediation steps in the README.
- Telemetry probes are written as examples (not production configs); they show trace spans around 'retrieve', 'call_tool', and 'emit_response' with example metric names.

Migration/rollout: no migration needed. This is additive content intended for the quickstarts catalog and docs cross-links.

Notes for maintainers: keep the index small (<10 docs) and deterministic; avoid adding heavy dependencies to the quickstart. If adding a new sample, mirror both Python and TS runners to reduce cognitive load for users switching languages.

Ethan Gold: Left small nits on README clarity and suggested an explicit 'expected outputs' section for the smoke CI. Please add expected JSON snippets to make the CI assertions obvious.
Samira Ortiz: Added expected JSON snippets and an explanation of how the structlinter rule maps to each snippet. Also added troubleshooting tips for 'KV cache warmup' in the README.
Maya Chen: Asked to reduce reliance on external packages in the TS playbook; replaced the heavy http-client with our local connector shim. Verified build in devcontainer.
Diego Alvarez: Approved after CI green and one follow-up to rename a metric in probes.yaml for consistency with console dashboards. Metric name changed to 'fastboot.rag.latency_ms'.

payload.body: Adds a compact interactive quickstart called 'SinkPlay' that demonstrates a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) journey with a deterministic sink adapter and an embeddable local labshell runner. Motivation: give engineers a repeatable on-ramp for instrumenting tool-calling, failure-injection, and local structured-output debugging workflows without needing remote indexers or external services. Key deliverables: 1) quickstart package under quickstarts/sinkplay with a step-by-step codelab and preseeded mini-index, 2) labshell static runner (browser+worker) that can run the scenario locally, 3) deterministic sink adapter for instrumenting tool responses and failure modes, 4) CI smoke tests (GitHub Actions) that run the labshell headless scenario and validate structured output contracts, and 5) docs site snippets and a compact troubleshooting guide. Checklist: - [x] Add codelab markdown and step artifacts - quickstarts/sinkplay/README.md - [x] Include TypeScript adapter and Python shim for tool stubs - quickstarts/sinkplay/adapters/ - [x] Add labshell runner and headless integration test - .github/workflows/sinkplay-smoke.yml - [x] Add docsite snippet and recipe to docs/quickstarts.json - [x] Wire up telemetry probes and assertion hooks for evals This PR references ENG-4892 for the telemetry probes and PM-183 for the workshop agenda. How to try locally: 1) git checkout feature/sinkplay-labshell-quickstart 2) cd quickstarts/sinkplay 3) npm install && npm run dev to open the labshell at http://localhost:3000 4) follow the guided steps in README.md to seed the mini-index, run a RAG conversation, trigger deterministic sink failure, and inspect structured-output assertions. CI: added a headless runner job that launches the labshell in Playwright, fires the scripted RAG sequence, and verifies the output contract and telemetry events. Security: the quickstart runs locally and does not ship secrets; the CI job uses ephemeral tokens scoped to sandbox resources. Release notes: Adds a developer-facing interactive RAG quickstart (SinkPlay) to streamline learning and testing of tool calling and failure handling patterns.

payload.body:
Motivation: debugging RAG flows with tool-calling and adapters is hard because reproducing the exact sequence of model outputs, tool calls, and vector DB lookups is non-trivial. This quickstart introduces a lightweight 'session recorder' that captures full request/response traces (prompts, model outputs, tool calls, KV/cache events, and retrieval hits) and a local replay harness that deterministically replays sessions against a pinned model or a mocked runtime.

What this PR adds (single continuous description):
- session-recorder/README.md: developer quickstart that explains recorder architecture, replay modes (deterministic vs. stochastic), and privacy knobs.
- session-recorder/demo/: small Node/TS demo application that runs a RAG pipeline wired to the recorder. Shows tool-calling to a simple facts service and a mocked vector DB.
- session-recorder/docker-compose.yml: runs the demo + recorder + replay web UI locally for easier onboarding.
- session-recorder/.env.example: runtime switches (RECORD=true, REDWOOD_API_KEY=..., REPLAY_MODE=deterministic).
- session-recorder/test/playback.spec.ts: integration test that records a short session, replays it, and asserts identical event sequence and deterministic outputs when REPLAY_MODE=deterministic and model seed is pinned.
- docs/session-recorder.md: integrated docs for the docs site (how to install, security notes, retention policy and suggested evals).
- assets/session-recorder-diagram.svg: architecture diagram for the README and docs.

Checklist: [x] Demo runs locally via docker-compose [x] Unit/integration tests added [x] Docs and diagram included [x] Telemetry hooks instrumented but opt-in by default

How to try locally (short):
1) cp session-recorder/.env.example .env && fill REDWOOD_API_KEY and set RECORD=true
2) docker-compose up --build
3) Open http://localhost:8080 to start a demo conversation and then press "Record session"
4) Use the replay UI to load recorded session and choose "deterministic replay" to validate behavior

Security & privacy: recordings can include PII. Recorder defaults to redaction of fields matching a small patterns whitelist (emails, credit-card-like numbers) and exposes an opt-in retention TTL. The docs section shows how to plug in a KMS-backed encrypt-on-disk adapter before enabling long-term storage.

Motivation and scope notes: This quickstart is intentionally opinionated: it favors a developer ergonomics-first path (local run, Docker, deterministic replay) rather than a production-grade archival pipeline. It is meant as a developer tool to reproduce bugs, create ground-truth prompt/response pairs for regression tests, and to help SREs triage incidents involving tool-calling and retrieval mismatches.

Related: Linear ENG-8721 (session replay prototype), PM-342 (developer debugging UX), Support SUP-1124 (customer reproducer request).
Run tests: cd redwood-quickstarts/session-recorder && npm ci && npm test. To run e2e: docker-compose up --build then run npm run test:e2e. The integration test requires Docker to be available.
Diego Morales (reviewer): Nice ergonomics. A couple of nits: can we avoid using REDWOOD_API_KEY in .env.example and prefer a local-token file for the demo? Also the docker-compose exposes the recorder port on 0.0.0.0: consider limiting to 127.0.0.1 for safety.
Asha Patel (author): Good call — switched the example to use LOCAL_TOKEN_FILE and updated README. Docker compose now binds recorder to 127.0.0.1. Added note in docs about network exposure and experimental nature.
Katrina Liu (reviewer): Integration test is great. One request: add an explicit assertion that tool-call timing metadata is present, we've had bugs where timing gets dropped in the pipeline.
Asha Patel (author): Added timing assertion in playback.spec.ts and a small test fixture that simulates delayed tool responses to validate KV cache and timing capture.
Evan Brooks (approver): Verified demo runs locally, e2e passed in my run. Approving — small docs wording tweak suggested (see inline).
Katrina Liu (approver): Approved after timing assertion change.

payload.body:
Motivation: Our paging/block-manager was experiencing suboptimal reuse patterns when multi-tenant serving mixes short-lived hot prefixes with large cold ranges. This caused higher fragmentation and increased cache miss amplification under load, hurting p95 latency for streaming generation workloads. This PR implements a locality-aware allocator combined with a hierarchical reclamation (background scavenger) and a tenant-aware eviction score to prefer reclaiming blocks that minimize cross-tenant thrash.

Summary of changes (single-line sections intentionally concatenated into one string):
- New allocator heuristic: 'locality-first' allocation that biases new allocations toward blocks adjacent to recently used spans for the same tenant/route. This reduces KV cache relocation and preserves hot-prefix locality across re-rollouts.
- Hierarchical reclamation: background async scavenger that reclaims cold shards at multiple granularities (block -> span -> segment) to reduce fragmentation without blocking fast-path allocations. Scavenger runs at capped CPU budget and cooperates with existing GC windows.
- Tenant-aware eviction scoring: eviction score combines recency/frequency (weighted frecency), block contiguity (penalize isolated blocks), and tenant-traffic penalty to avoid evicting small hot regions from high-SLO tenants. Scores configurable via runtime flags and console.
- Integration with scheduler: allocation requests from continuous-batching pipeline now prefer nodes where the KV prefix is already cold/warm-cached; scheduler policy added to reduce cross-host cache misses for streaming prefixes.
- Benchmarks and tests: microbenchmarks for allocation hotpath, end-to-end workload bench harness (redistributed: chat-streaming, batch-embedding) and new unit tests covering reclamation invariants and scoring correctness.

Commits (high-level):
- 3bd4f1e: add locality-first allocation policy and public config knobs
- a2d77c9: implement hierarchical scavenger with budgeted worker
- e8f3b5a: tenant-aware eviction scoring and unit tests
- b12a9d0: scheduler integration and continuous-batching affinity policy
- c4e7e12: add benchmarks and docs (docs/alloc/hierarchical-reclaim.md)

Files changed (high level):
- src/kv/block_allocator.cpp (new heuristics, ~320 additions)
- src/kv/block_allocator.h (API for scoring and locality hints)
- src/kv/scavenger.cpp (new background reclamation worker)
- src/scheduler/locality_policy.cpp (affinity helpers, allocation hints)
- src/scheduler/locality_policy.h
- tests/kv/block_allocator_bench.cc (bench harness)
- tests/kv/block_allocator_unit_test.cc (new unit tests)
- docs/alloc/hierarchical-reclaim.md (design notes and tuning guide)
- ci/bench/workloads/chat_streaming.yaml (updated baseline)
- pkg/config/runtime_flags.yaml (added knobs)
- integration/kv_multi_tenant_e2e.yaml (tuned test scenario)
- go/metrics/allocator_metrics.go (added new metrics exporters)

Design notes: The allocator introduces a soft 'locality token' attached to each tenant-route that records recent allocation spans (2 recent ranges). When a new allocation request arrives, the allocator prefers free blocks adjacent to those ranges (same segment or nearby), using a score that trades off contiguity vs. absolute recency. If no suitable locality candidate exists, it falls back to fragmentation-aware first-fit. The hierarchical scavenger runs at three levels: block sweep (fast, frequent), span consolidation (medium), and segment defragment (slow, infrequent). Each tier has a separate budget to avoid noisy background work.

Benchmarks: All numbers are relative to main at commit HEAD before this PR. Measurements on Dedicated-local (4xA100-like) with mixed streaming/generation traffic for 30 minutes each.
- Chat streaming (100 tps, mixed prompt lengths): p95 token latency -11.7% (from 128ms -> 113ms), throughput +9.8% (measured tokens/s), memory fragmentation score -22%
- Embedding batch (large batch sizes): cold-start cache misses -14%, overall cost/sample -6.4%
- Continuous batching tail variance reduced by ~30% under synthetic tenant skew.

Backward compatibility: On-disk block format unchanged. Config knobs default to legacy-safe values; no operator action required.

Testing and CI: CI matrix run: unit tests, integration e2e, bench smoke. - Ayesha Khan 2026-02-16: "Approved"

Merge notes: Merged by squash (Leah Park) on 2026-02-18 after all approvals and green CI. Merge method: squash and merge.

Operational considerations and rollout plan:

- Gradual rollout: recommended canary 5% of traffic for 24h monitoring allocator.locality.hits and allocator.fragmentation.score before wider rollout. Dashboard add-on in Redwood Console is provided in docs.
- Observability: added exporter metrics for locality hits/misses, scavenger cycles/time, eviction_score distribution. Alerts suggested: scavenger_cpu > 20% for 10m and fragmentation_score increasing >20% in 30m.

Why this is different from prior allocator work: previous PRs focused on eviction/coalescing fastpaths or softpin behavior. This PR centers on tenant-locality and staged reclamation to reduce both micro-fragmentation and cross-tenant thrash while being workload-aware (streaming prefixes vs. bulk scans).

Introduces a locality-aware block allocator with hierarchical reclamation and tenant-aware eviction scoring. Improves tail latency and throughput for multi-tenant KV workloads; no API changes. Backwards compatible on-disk format.
