Context: The OpenAI-compat adapter has historically normalized vendor rate-limit headers in multiple ad-hoc places which led to inconsistent Retry-After handling across streaming and non-streaming endpoints and unreliable idempotency deduplication when requests were retried across internal proxies.
This PR centralizes header parsing and idempotency lifecycle handling in the compat adapter so downstream code (streaming, function/tool-calls, structured-output) can rely on a single set of semantics.
Motivation: Fix two production classes of issues we see in SLO alerts and incident postmortems: 1) streaming connections being closed prematurely when transient rate-limit headers were present but contained non-standard values (e.g. float seconds, comma lists, or vendor-specific names); 2) duplicate side-effects when idempotency keys were not deduplicated consistently across retries and replayed through the fallback routing layer.
Changes in this PR:
- Add a single RateLimitParser that canonicalizes common header shapes (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After, Retry-After-Milliseconds) and returns a deterministic object to the adapter. Parser implements tolerant parsing for floats, comma-separated values (takes first valid), and RFC 7231 date parsing.
- Introduce keyed idempotency policy in compat adapter: idempotency keys are normalized, hashed (SHA256 prefix), and stored in the internal dedupe cache with a configurable TTL that varies by route (default 60s for generation endpoints, 300s for tooling calls). The policy includes 'last-result' metadata to support deterministic replay for clients expecting the same completion when retrying.
- Streaming behavior: adaptors now surface rate-limit signals to the streaming mux layer instead of unilaterally closing streams. When a transient rate-limit is detected and the request is eligible for retry/fallback, the stream is paused and an idempotent retry is attempted (server-initiated), otherwise the stream sends a structured error event with our new error code "rate_limit" and a recommended "retry_after_ms" integer field.
- Error schema: add stable OpenAI-compat error codes: rate_limit, idempotency_failure, transient_backend_error. Each error includes message, type, code, and optionally retry_after_ms. This unifies behaviour across CLI/SDK and avoids ambiguous HTTP 429 handling.
- Backwards compatibility: old headers are still accepted, feature gated behind compat.features.new_rate_handling (default true for canary). Old adapter behavior is preserved when the flag is off.
- Tests: extensive unit tests for header permutations, idempotency TTL expiry, and streaming integration tests that simulate partial Retry-After formats and brokered fallback.
- Observability: add new metrics: compat.rate_limit_parsed.errors, compat.idempotency.hits, compat.idempotency.misses, compat.rate_limit.retry_attempts.
- Docs: update openai-compat README with the canonical header list and an SDK migration note.
Commits summary:
- 1a2b3c4: add RateLimitParser and unit tests
- 2b3c4d5: implement idempotency cache interface and TTL config
- 3c4d5e6: wire parser into adapter request path and expose canonical fields to stream mux
- 4d5e6f7: streaming integration tests and structured error payloads
- 5e6f7g8: docs and feature flag rollout config
Files changed (high level):
- src/openai_compat/adapter.py: central header parsing and idempotency orchestration (key logic)
- src/openai_compat/ratelimit.py: new tolerant parser and helpers
- src/openai_compat/idempotency.py: cache interface + hashing helpers
- src/openai_compat/stream_mux.py: pause/resume hooks and structured error emission
- tests/unit/test_ratelimit.py, tests/integration/test_streaming_rate_limit.py
- docs/openai_compat.md
Notes on behavior and edge cases:
- Retry-After parsing: we prefer numeric seconds when present, but support HTTP-date format; in ambiguous cases we return retry_after_ms=null to signal SDKs should apply client-side backoff heuristics.
- Comma lists are common in some vendors; parser will pick the first parsable token (documented).
- Idempotency collision risk is mitigated by storing a 16-byte prefix of SHA256 and the full last-result checksum; we log collisions at debug level and surface idempotency_failure when conflicting non-idempotent results are detected.
Rollout plan:
- Canary 5% on dedicated infra with feature flag enabled for 72h and close monitoring on new metrics.
- Expand to 50% if no elevated rate_limit_parsed.errors or idempotency_failure spikes.
- Full rollout targeted in next stable release after monitoring window.
Migration guidance for integrators:
- SDKs should prefer inspecting error.code rather than HTTP status for retry decisions.
- If you rely on custom Retry-After parsing, switch to the canonical fields once SDKs consume them.
- For deterministic replay across retries, include an idempotency key on generation and tooling endpoints; keys should be stable across retries.
Testing notes and CI:
- CI had an initial flaky test in streaming harness (mock timeouts) which was fixed by adding deterministic fake-clock in tests, see commit 4d5e6f7.
- All builds green on final run.
Related work: ENG-5123 (rate-limit standardization), ENG-5187 (idempotency cache interface), SUP-1247 (customer report about duplicate charge issue).
Priya Nair: Please verify RFC7231 date parsing edge cases — we saw an edge case with 'Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT' in integration harness. Can you add a test?
Ava Martinez: Added RFC7231 date parsing test and tolerant parser logic; extended integration harness to inject date-format Retry-After. See test_streaming_rate_limit.py:line 128.
Ethan Brooks: Suggest using a single metric namespace compat.idempotency.* and emit tag route=<name> for easier alerting.
Ava Martinez: Updated metrics to include route tag and consolidated metric names.
Liam O'Connor: Approve after addressing the tests and adding the canary rollout plan in the PR description.
CI Bot: pytest-3.11 build passed on run #4. One flaky streaming test fixed by deterministic fake-clock.
Priya Nair: Confirmed acceptance testing locally; LGTM.
Standardize OpenAI-compat rate-limit headers and idempotency semantics: SDKs and integrators should rely on X-RateLimit-* and Retry-After canonicalization. Add new consistent error codes for rate_limit and idempotency_failure. Rollout behind feature flag; no customer action required for most deployments.

Motivation: We see a class of user-reported flakiness and tail-latency regressions on the OpenAI-compat proxy when clients repeatedly negotiate schema versions on first call, especially for streaming + tool-calling flows. Negotiation involves schema validation and dynamic adapter selection which adds jitter to the streaming handshake and occasionally triggers incompatible fallback paths. This PR introduces a lightweight, opt-in client-directed schema prefetch shim that lets clients advertise and pre-warm their preferred request/response schema ahead of invocation, reducing per-request negotiation work and stabilizing streaming handoffs. The change also includes a conservative backward-compatibility path: if a client does not send the new header we fall back to the existing negotiation logic. Checklist: - [x] Add new header handler: X-Redwood-Prefer-Schema-Prefetch (values: schema:v2, schema:v1, auto) - [x] Server-side prefetch cache keyed by client_id (TTL 24h) with eviction heuristics - [x] Proxy change: avoid layered validation during streaming handshake when prefetch hits - [x] SDK opt-in helpers to set the header (TypeScript and Python) - [x] Validation tests and streaming e2e scenario that previously flaked - [x] Backward-compat shim to ensure older clients still negotiate normally - [x] Documentation and migration notes in openai-compat README Implementation notes: The header is advisory. When present and accepted the proxy records the preferred schema on the client prefetch cache and skips the heavier negotiation path for subsequent requests until TTL expiry. We added a fast-path in the streaming handshake that trusts the cached mapping and only performs a lightweight version check; if any validation mismatch occurs the proxy falls back to the full negotiation flow and emits a metric (openai.compat.prefetch.miss). To keep risk low the feature is gated behind an opt-in header and the proxy emits informational logs and metrics on acceptance, eviction, and mismatch. Testing: Unit tests cover header parsing, cache behavior, and mismatch fallbacks. We exercised streaming tool-calls using the flaky integration harness (see ENG-2399) and observed 45-65% reduction in handshake latency P95 across representative traces. A small load test confirmed no measurable regression in throughput with prefetch enabled. Security/compatibility: The prefetch cache respects tenant isolation. Prefetch values are validated against the server catalog; unrecognized values are rejected and logged. No sensitive data is stored. Rollout plan: - Stage 1: Merge behind a feature flag on the proxy, enable for internal clients only - Stage 2: Opt into TS/Python SDK helpers and experimental note in the public docs - Stage 3: Open beta for customer opt-in and monitor metrics for two weeks - Stage 4: Consider automatic suggestion by Redwood Optimize if stability gains are consistent Migration notes: Send X-Redwood-Prefer-Schema-Prefetch: schema:v2 to pre-warm v2 behavior. If you do not opt-in nothing changes. See release notes for more detail.
Diego Moreno (reviewer): The fast-path looks good but we need to be cautious about trusting cached schema with streaming where tool-calls can change mid-stream. Please ensure a fail-safe that re-runs full negotiation if the first token of structured output doesn't validate.
Aisha K. Patel (author): Good point — added a lightweight validation step that checks the first structured chunk and triggers a fallback negotiation if it fails. See handshake_stream.py delta. Also added a metric openai.compat.prefetch.invalid_first_chunk.
Ling Zhao (reviewer): Tests look solid. Please add a note about tenant isolation in the docs and ensure cache keys include region and tenant_id.
Aisha K. Patel (author): Done — cache now uses tenant_id+region as the key and the README notes tenant isolation.

payload.body:
Context and motivation: Several production customers reported spurious parsing errors when consuming streaming responses from our OpenAI-compatible SSE endpoint. Symptoms included JSON decode errors from partial object chunks, occasional scrambled tool/function_call payloads, and clients observing events out-of-order when network proxies split frames. Reproduction: 1) Simulate small MTU/slow connections that split SSE 'data:' payloads mid-JSON (e.g. '{"choices": [ {"delta": {"content": "hel' then 'lo"}} ] }'). 2) Proxy that injects an extra '
' delimiter between frames or merges small writes into a single TCP segment. Root cause: Our existing SSE chunking logic assumed that each 'data:' event contained a complete JSON payload or a single text delta. When the upstream runtime emitted partial token/text chunks, the OpenAI-compat layer attempted to decode the chunk immediately. Two related problems surfaced:  - Delimiter normalization bug: the handler sometimes emitted extra empty 'data:' lines (double newlines) which downstream clients treated as separators and attempted to parse an empty payload.  - Reassembly and ordering: without a lightweight sequence or stable buffer, clients could see function_call events interleaved with token-delta events if proxies re-ordered or coalesced writes. What I changed: 1) Robust chunk parser (openai_compat/sse/parser.py): Implemented a streaming JSON reassembly buffer that:   - Buffers partial 'data:' payloads until a valid JSON object can be parsed or until an explicit '[DONE]' sentinel is received.   - Uses a conservative brace/bracket balance scan first, then attempts a streaming json.loads() only when balance indicates a candidate complete object to avoid expensive trial parses on every fragment.   - Normalizes newline/delimiter sequences so we never emit empty 'data:' events. 2) Event sequencing (openai_compat/sse/handler.py):   - Added an optional per-event sequence counter (event_sequence) emitted as a header on each SSE event for internal compatibility clients. This is opt-in and defaults to off for strict OpenAI parity, but is enabled in our hosted deployments for safety.   - The handler will now preserve original upstream ordering and attach sequence metadata when reassembly spans multiple upstream writes. 3) Function-calls and structured output stability:   - Ensure function_call start/complete deltas are coalesced into a single function_call JSON payload before emitting to clients. 4) Tests and examples:   - Added integration test that simulates interleaved TCP/write fragmentation and proxy-induced delimiter insertion. 5) Observability:   - Expose a reassembly_latency histogram and a drop/retry counter so we can track regressions. Backwards compatibility and safety notes: - Clients that rely on strict OpenAI SSE formatting will see no semantic change to event shapes. The event_sequence header is optional and for robustness; we document it in the compatibility docs. - The parser is defensive and will time out/emit an error event if reassembly exceeds a configurable byte/time threshold. Commit summary: - 8b2f1c9: sse: add streaming brace-balance reassembler and delimiter normalizer - d4a7e12: sse: attach event_sequence and preserve upstream ordering when configured - c7f3b40: tests: simulate fragmented writes and proxy delimiter injection - 1a9e4d5: docs: add section on event_sequence and recommended client behavior - 9f0b2a1: examples: streaming_fragments.js client showing tolerant reassembly Failure modes considered: - Extremely pathological fragmentation (single-byte writes) will increase CPU work on parse attempts; mitigated with cheap balance-scan and configurable thresholds. - Clients that blindly parse every 'data:' event will still see transient errors; recommending clients adopt the documented reassembly behavior. How to validate locally: - Run tests: pytest openai_compat/tests/test_sse_reassembly.py - Run the example node client: node examples/openai/streaming_fragments.js and confirm it receives 3 complete JSON messages and one [DONE]. Related: ENG-3124 (customer incident), infra/mtu-proxy tickets. Checklists: - [x] Add parser and handler changes - [x] Add unit + integration tests - [x] Add docs and example client - [x] CI green + e2e passes - [x] Merge to main and bump changelog Links: - Design doc (internal): https://linear.app/redwood/issue/ENG-3124/sse-reassembly-design - Example reproduction harness commit: changes included in this PR
Aisha Patel: Nice catch — can you add a knob to disable event_sequence in case customers want exact OpenAI header parity?
Lina Moreno: Added config flag 'OPENAI_COMPAT_EVENT_SEQUENCE=false' in handler and documented it. Also kept default enabled in hosted envs.
Devon Liu: Can we avoid a second json.loads() pass when reassembling large objects? Benchmark the balance-scan approach.
Lina Moreno: Benchmarks added to parser module; balance-scan avoids repeated loads in >98% of fragments. Added microbenchmark to tests.
Marcus Reyes: Tests look good. One nit: increase the reassembly timeout to 2s in envs with high latency proxies.
Lina Moreno: Increased timeout and made it configurable via REDWOOD_SSE_REASSEMBLY_TIMEOUT_MS.
Aisha Patel: CI flakes earlier — rerunning workflows.
CI Bot: All checks passed after re-run. Artifacts: pytest (154 tests passed), lint (0 issues), mypy (no errors).
Devon Liu: Approved.
Aisha Patel: Approved and merged by squash.
Squashed and merged after approvals. Observability: added metrics for reassembly_latency_ms and sse_reassembly_timeouts_total. Rollout: feature gated event_sequence; enabled in hosted region us-west-2 for 48h canary before global flip. CHANGELOG updated.
Fix SSE streaming bug where partial JSON events could be mis-framed across network chunk boundaries causing client-side JSON parse errors; improved reassembly and ordering guarantees in the OpenAI compatibility SSE layer. Backwards-compatible: adds optional event_sequence header for robust client reordering.

payload.body:
Context: As part of Shadow Traffic (quality eval metrics) we need a repeatable way to quantify overhead from (a) request mirroring to shadow targets, (b) additional telemetry emission, and (c) backpressure/circuit breaker behavior under scoring/ingestion degradation. This suite is intended to run as a go/no-go gate for beta/GA (and as a nightly regression check).

What this PR does: 1) Adds a benchmark harness to perf-canary that drives realistic inference traffic (chat + streaming chat) through the Redwood gateway with shadowing enabled/disabled and varying sampling rates. 2) Captures user-path latency deltas and resource overhead while ensuring fail-open semantics (shadow path failures must not move user-path SLOs). 3) Emits a standardized results bundle (JSON + markdown) for consumption in rollout readiness docs and for CI gating.

Scenarios included: - Chat (non-streaming): 256 and 1024 token outputs, fixed prompt distribution; measures p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency, gateway CPU, and request error rates. - Streaming chat: measures time-to-first-token (TTFT), inter-chunk cadence, and tail latency; validates partial-chunk handling when shadow timeout trips. - Shadow sampling rates: 0% (baseline), 1%, 5%, 10%. - Shadow target behaviors: healthy, slow (adds 150ms), erroring (5xx), and unavailable (connection refused). - Telemetry modes: control-only vs control+shadow pair events (cardinality-safe dimensions only).

Go/no-go thresholds (current defaults; tunable via config): - User-path p99 delta <= +3ms at 1% sampling and <= +8ms at 10% sampling (non-streaming), measured at steady state (post-warmup). - Streaming TTFT p99 delta <= +5ms at 1% sampling and <= +12ms at 10% sampling. - Gateway CPU increase <= +5% absolute at 10% sampling under the reference load (see configs). - No statistically significant increase in user-path 5xx/timeout rate when shadow target is failing; circuit breaker should trip and shadow requests should be dropped while user path remains stable.

Outputs: - artifacts/shadow_overhead/<run_id>/results.json (machine-readable) - artifacts/shadow_overhead/<run_id>/summary.md (human-readable) - optional Prometheus snapshot export for deeper debugging

Notes: - This suite intentionally does not validate quality metrics correctness; it only measures performance/overhead and safety behavior. - Test prompts are synthetic and contain no customer data. - The benchmark defaults are aligned with the current routing implementation (mirroring inline with strict timeouts) and the SRE fail-open requirements.

Follow-ups: - Integrate this suite into the release-engineering feature flag plan as a required gate for enabling shadow traffic beyond internal tenants (tracked in ENG-5412). - Add an embeddings workload scenario once the shadow path supports embeddings consistently (out of scope for this PR).
Allison Grant (review): The headline metrics look right, but we need to be careful about label/cardinality in the exported results. Can you confirm we don’t include route_id/customer_id as raw strings? Also please add a section in README on how to compare runs (same prompt distribution + fixed seed).

Vikram Singh (author): Good call. Updated reporting to bucket route into {"route_class": "chat"|"streaming"} and to hash run_id only. Added fixed RNG seed + prompt distribution checksum and documented comparison steps in README.

Sean Gallagher (review): Two asks from SRE side: (1) warmup must be explicit (we’ve seen KV cache warmup skew p99 deltas) and (2) we should validate fail-open when shadow target is slow/erroring. Right now it measures but doesn’t assert.

Vikram Singh (author): Added a warmup phase (default 90s) that is excluded from results. Also added hard assertions: user-path timeout/5xx deltas must stay within configured bounds; if exceeded, the run fails and the summary highlights which gate failed. For fail-open, added fault injection modes and a circuit-breaker expectation check (shadow drop rate increases, user error rate stable).

Mina Haddad (review): Streaming: can we measure TTFT separately from completion? The routing change for streaming shadowing can impact TTFT even if overall completion is unchanged.

Vikram Singh (author): Yep—added TTFT histograms plus inter-chunk cadence percentiles. Summary now reports TTFT p50/p95/p99 deltas as the primary streaming gate.

Logan Wright (review): Please ensure we don’t rely on telemetry ingestion being healthy for benchmark correctness. The suite should still run if telemetry is lagging; we only measure overhead on user path.

Vikram Singh (author): Adjusted: telemetry collection is best-effort; benchmark uses gateway-side timers as source of truth. Telemetry export is optional and only included if available; it does not fail the run.

Cole Summers (review): For quotas/guardrails, add a note that the benchmark runs with elevated test tenant quotas, and link to the config field. Also confirm shadow requests are excluded from customer usage accounting in this setup.

Vikram Singh (author): Added README notes: suite uses the perf-canary tenant with separate accounting. Shadow requests are tagged with x-redwood-shadow: true and excluded from usage metering in the perf environment.

Final approvals: Allison ✅ Sean ✅ Mina ✅ Logan ✅
Adds a reproducible benchmark suite for measuring user-path overhead of shadow traffic mirroring across non-streaming + streaming workloads; produces gate-ready summaries (p50/p95/p99 delta, CPU/mem, telemetry overhead, and circuit-breaker behavior).

payload.body:
Motivation: Users reported intermittent broken JSON objects in streaming responses when the client receives tightly packed SSE fragments mixed with heartbeats and large binary token payloads. This caused structured output parsers and downstream function-call consumers to drop events or produce partial JSON parse errors. This PR introduces a small protocol-level improvement and deterministic reassembly behavior without changing the external API. Summary of changes: 1) ACK-window reassembly: maintain a bounded, per-stream ack-window (configurable, default 64 events) that accepts out-of-order fragments tagged with a lightweight event-seq id and defers emission until either the sequence fills the window or an explicit ack/timeout occurs; this prevents blind coalescing of fragments across unrelated events. 2) Delimiter normalization: introduce a normalization pass that collapses mixed CR/LF, zero-width whitespace, and doubled SSE delimiters into canonical single-delimiter tokens before JSON extraction; this prevents accidental splits when clients re-chunk network buffers. 3) Function-call and tool-call boundary preservation: allocate a small sentinel escape header for multi-part function-call payloads so that nested structured outputs do not get merged across event boundaries during coalescing. 4) Heartbeat & backpressure interaction: heartbeat frames are now treated as soft-acks (advance window by a single slot without forcing emission) to avoid premature sequence flushes under low-throughput clients; backpressure signals from the runtime will fast-forward the window for stalled streams. 5) Tests & telemetry: add exhaustive unit and integration tests covering interleaved heartbeats, high-frequency tiny chunks (1-8 bytes), and multi-tool-call streams; emit new metrics sse.reassembly.window_fill and sse.reassembly.dropped_out_of_window for observability. Compatibility and rollout: changes are backwards-compatible at the API level; existing clients will see fewer partial-JSON errors and unchanged event ids; rollout is staged: feature gated, enabled by default on canary for two weeks, then ramped to 100% with a re-run of canary tests. See linked Linear items for evaluation criteria and regression thresholds. Implementation notes: the reassembler is implemented in a small state machine in src/sse/reassembly.go with a normalization pipeline in src/sse/frame_normalizer.go; kept hot-path allocations minimal and added object pooling for fragment buffers. Performance: microbenchmarks show <4% median token latency increase at 1ms sequence windows and 0% p99 regression for typical chat workloads; load tests with bursty tiny-chunk clients show 28% reduction in parsed-json errors. Rollback plan: feature flag can be toggled per-cluster and we can disable ack-windows per-customer if any compatibility issue is detected. Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked in ENG-5042 - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Canary run results attached - [x] Docs updated (streaming guide)
+ func normalizeDelimiters(b []byte) []byte { /* collapse CRLF, ZWSP, repeated ':' markers */ }
+ type ackWindow struct { head uint64; buffer map[uint64][]byte; size int }
+ // heartbeat frames advance soft-ack: if backlog==0 { head++ }
- previous: coalesceAllFragments() -> new: coalesceWithinWindow()
Ethan Zhou (review): Can we guarantee that the ack-window won't grow unbounded if a client halts?
Asha Mehta (author): We bound the window and use a configurable timeout to force-forward; added metrics for dropped fragments and fast-forward counts.
Liam O'Connor (review): The function-call escape header looks ok but will downstream OpenAI compatibility clients need a parser update?
Asha Mehta (author): No client changes required for standard flows; only custom low-level integrations that parsed raw stream bytes will need to accept the new header; added compatibility note to streaming.md.
Priya Kapoor (approve): Verified canary results and integration tests, approving.
Fixes intermittent partial-JSON and structured-output corruption in SSE streaming by introducing ack-windowed reassembly and delimiter normalization; reduces parse errors for tiny-chunk and high-frequency streams; no API breaking changes.

Motivation: Customers using the new OpenAI Responses variants (v2b style payloads) reported gaps in compatibility when streaming tool/function calls and when propagating request-level metadata (seed/determinism flags and user-defined metadata) through the OpenAI adapter. This PR implements a compatibility shim that: 1) reliably reassembles structured streaming chunks (including toolcall boundaries and JSON-in-stream parts) into Redwood Response objects; 2) forwards seed/determinism and metadata passthrough to downstream runtime and to dedicated logging so we preserve determinism signals across retries/fallbacks; 3) hardens the streaming layer against mid-stream reconnects and duplicate chunk emission by adding idempotent fragment tracking and simple ACK semantics; 4) ensures tool/function calls are emitted as final structured events (not raw text) and include provenance metadata for RPC routing. The description below is one continuous string and includes checklist and testing notes. Checklist: - [x] Streaming reassembly with fragment-id dedupe (scoped to stream + seq) - [x] Toolcall event boundary detector + structured emission path - [x] Seed/determinism flag propagation end-to-end (normalized to response.metadata.seed) - [x] Metadata passthrough into Redwood audit logs and response.metadata (including request_id) - [x] Integration tests for reconnect / duplicate-chunk scenarios - [x] Docs (compatibility guide) - [x] Backcompat smoke with existing openai adapter flows Implementation notes: - new module openai_adapter/response_v2b/stream_handler.py implements a streaming parser that tracks (stream_id, fragment_seq, fragment_id) tuples emitted by the Responses v2b stream. When we see a duplicate tuple within the same stream we drop the second copy; this avoids incorrectly dropping legitimate same-id fragments that arrive with different seq after a reconnect. Reassembly happens in-memory with optional bounded buffering; if buffering would exceed configured limits we fallback to file-backed spill and mark the response with partial:true and an explanatory note in response.metadata. - updated runtime/stream_reassembly.py adds a small interface so other adapters can reuse the idempotent fragment tracking and ack callbacks. - api/compat/openai_mappings.py maps Responses v2b tool_call events into Redwood toolcall objects and preserves the original tool call tool_origin_id; seed is normalized to response.metadata.seed (previously seed_hint) and the request_id is forwarded for audit correlation. - telemetry: added metrics openai.compat.stream.reassembled_count and openai.compat.stream.duplicate_fragments; renamed the spill counter to openai.compat.stream.spill_bytes and traces annotate fragment counts and reconnections. - docs: docs/compat/responses_v2b.md describes expected wire shapes, streaming retry behavior, and recommended client-side idempotency keys. Testing and CI: - added tests/integration/test_responses_v2b_stream.py with simulated reconnects, duplicate fragments, and a long-running toolcall that is emitted as structured JSON. - CI matrix runs the new integration under both hosted and dedicated runtime mocks; rerun policy updated to reduce flake on slow runners. Rollback plan: revert the head branch; adapter registration is behind feature-flag OPENAI_RESPONSES_V2B_COMPAT so rollback is a config flip. Backcompat: default behavior unchanged for customers not enabling the feature flag. Release notes: "Adds an OpenAI Responses v2b compatibility adapter that improves streaming stability, preserves determinism seed flags, and forwards request metadata into Redwood responses and logs. Opt-in via OPENAI_RESPONSES_V2B_COMPAT."
Maya Rodriguez: Overall looks good. Two asks: add a unit test for fragment dedupe and make the backpressure spill-to-disk threshold configurable.
Liam Chen: Reply: added unit test for dedupe and introduced OPENAI_RESP_BUFFER_BYTES config with sane default. See tests/integration for the new case.
Arjun Mehta: Please add a brief note in docs about operational tradeoffs when enabling the feature for high-QPS routes.
Liam Chen: added docs/compat/responses_v2b.md section 'Operational guidance' with batching/backpressure notes.
Ellen Park: Verified CI flakiness was due to test timeouts; increased timeouts and re-ran. Approving for squash-merge.
Maya Rodriguez (post-merge follow-up): In release notes and docs, can we align on the final flag name? OPENAI_RESP_V2B_COMPAT vs OPENAI_RESPONSES_V2B_COMPAT is easy to fat-finger.
Liam Chen: Updated docs and release notes to use OPENAI_RESPONSES_V2B_COMPAT everywhere; kept the old name as an accepted alias in config parsing for one release cycle (handled in constants.py).
+ def handle_fragment(stream_id, fragment):
+     key = (stream_id, fragment['fragment_seq'], fragment['fragment_id'])
+     if key in self.seen: return
+     self.seen.add(key)
+     buffer.append(fragment['payload'])
+  # map Responses v2b tool_call -> Redwood ToolCall
+  toolcall = ToolCall(name=payload['tool'], args=payload.get('args', {}), origin_id=payload.get('tool_origin_id'), request_id=request_id)
+  response.metadata['seed'] = request_metadata.get('seed')
+  response.metadata['request_id'] = request_metadata.get('request_id')
Opt-in OpenAI Responses v2b compatibility adapter: streaming reassembly, deduplication of fragments (scoped by stream+seq), toolcall structured emission, and seed/request metadata passthrough. Feature is behind OPENAI_RESPONSES_V2B_COMPAT; OPENAI_RESP_V2B_COMPAT is supported as a deprecated alias for one release.
If customers report partial responses after enabling the adapter, check openai.compat.stream.reassembled_count vs stream.fragment_total and inspect for excessive spill_bytes. If duplicate toolcalls appear, confirm fragment keying includes fragment_seq (fix is in this PR) and verify clients send stable idempotency keys on reconnect. Flip OPENAI_RESPONSES_V2B_COMPAT=false to rollback immediately.

Motivation: Pager/notification fatigue during noisy rotations remains a major contributor to oncall burnout and missed actions. This PR introduces a lightweight orchestration layer for scheduled reminders that is rotation-aware and adaptive to recent alert noise. The feature provides per-rotation attenuation, smart backoff, and a simple opt-out path for individuals. Design summary: 1) A RemindOrchestrator service that consumes schedule snapshots and recent-alert-rate signals to compute a reminder cadence per oncall rotation slot. 2) A NoiseAttenuation policy module that applies exponential backoff, minimum/maximum cadence bounds, and a sliding-window noise score (persisted to Redis with TTL) so attenuation survives restarts but decays over time. 3) Slack + Email adapters that respect user-level opt-outs and per-rotation override flags. 4) Observability: new metrics (slo.reminders.sent, slo.reminders.attenuation_ratio, slo.reminders.opt_out_count) and traces for reminder decision paths. 5) Safety and rollout: default to conservative behavior (no reminders for rotations with >30 alerts/hour until attenuation decays), feature flag gating, and a canary rollout to 10% of rotations. This PR includes unit and integration tests, documentation updates, and a short runbook for oncall responders (see docs/runbooks/reminder-orchestrator.md). Backwards compatibility: existing reminder endpoints remain available; orchestrator runs as an opt-in feature. Rollback plan: flip feature flag off; orchestrator is stateless aside from Redis TTLs and can be disabled without disruption. Related: ENG-2314 (oncall fatigue reduction), ENG-2317 (reminder metrics), SUP-987 (support request about missed escalations).

Aisha: yes — using Redis with a configurable TTL; added tests that cover persistence and TTL decay.
Sofia Reyes: UX: need an explicit per-rotation opt-out and a global user-level opt-out surfaced in the Console.
Aisha: added user opt-out flag, CLI toggle, and Console hint to docs/runbooks. Updated metrics to count opt-outs.

Aisha: replaced sleep with fake clock in integration harness and reran tests.

Aisha: Added alert suggestion to docs and registered a default SLO dashboard panel.

Aisha: done in last commit.
Marco Li: Approved after CI green — left one suggestion to document the canary rollout steps.
Aisha: added a short canary checklist to docs/runbooks/reminder-orchestrator.md.
Adds a rotation-aware reminder orchestrator with noise attenuation, per-user opt-outs, Slack/Email adapters, new metrics (slo.reminders.*), and a canary rollout plan. Default behavior is conservative and gated by feature flag.

Motivation: We continue to see production anomalies where streamed SSE payloads emit partial JSON tokens for structured outputs (function calls / tool outputs) when the application layer triggers async flushes or when network segmentation coalesces small writes. This PR tightens segmentation logic in the OpenAI-compat SSE layer to ensure that emitted events are idempotent and reassemblable by downstream consumers even when mid-token boundaries are split or multiple producers race to flush.

Summary of changes: Atomic event framing tokens are introduced ("::sse-evt::") to delimit logical SSE events at the transport layer; an async boundary sanitizer defers boundary emission until the current UTF-8 token and JSON structural units are complete; a small in-memory reassembly window with sequence ids protects against out-of-order fragment delivery during concurrent flushes; and function-calling sentinel handling is hardened to avoid emitting partial function argument objects. The patch keeps backward compatibility with existing consumers by continuing to emit standard SSE event fields (event/data) but adds the optional framing marker to help fragile parsers.

Why this is different: Prior fixes focused on coalescing and delimiter ordering. This change targets the race between application flushes and network write coalescing by making the server-side emitter aware of async boundaries (goroutine/task flush contexts) and ensuring JSON token integrity across chunk boundaries. It also reduces reliance on heuristics (newline counts) and uses structurally-informed flush gating for structured outputs.

Testing and validation: Unit tests simulate 1000 randomized fragmentation patterns with both short and long sequences, including injected scheduler preemptions. Integration tests run the OpenAI-compat streaming harness with a reference client that deliberately splits UTF-8 codepoints and sends partial event fragments; metrics recorded include percent of reassembled valid JSON objects and percent of function-call sentinel errors. CI includes an interop job against the node and python SDK streaming parsers to ensure no regressions to legacy clients. Observability: added a per-request counter for "sse_reassembly_attempts" and histogram for "sse_fragment_latency_ms".

Deployment plan: staged rollout — Canary on Hosted (10% traffic) for 48h with automatic rollback on >0.1% rate of structured-output parse errors; then ramp to 50% for 24h, then full. Dedicated and Private customers will receive a config flag (compat.sse.strict_frame=true) to toggle the optional framing marker while we monitor client parsing compatibility.

Checklist: [x] Unit tests added and passing locally [x] Integration harness updates [x] Canary rollout plan documented [x] Release notes drafted

Related: ENG-2123 (streaming stability), ENG-2190 (function call robustness), SUP-4871 (customer-reported partial-json incidents).
Jordan Lee: Can we avoid adding a global mark that clients might echo back? Suggest making framing marker opt-in and backend-agnostic — implemented as a flag (see docs).
Marta Voss: Integration tests look good; observed a 2.3% reduction in malformed structured payloads in the harness. Please add a regression test for UTF-8 boundary splits — added in second commit.
Kenji Yamamoto: Suggest we expose the reassembly metrics as opentelemetry counters and add a low-overhead fast-path when no sanitization is required. Addressed in reassembly_window optimization.
Thanks — framed as opt-in by default; added docs section and rollout plan.
Added UTF-8 boundary randomized test and microbenchmark for reassembly window sizing.
Exposed metrics via OTEL and added fast-path checks when single-chunk emits detected.
Fixes an intermittent issue where SSE streaming could emit partial JSON for structured outputs when async flushes and network coalescing coincide. Adds optional idempotent framing marker for fragile parsers, improved reassembly window, telemetry, and rollout plan.
This is a backward-compatible change; framing marker is opt-in and controlled by compat.sse.strict_frame. We will monitor parse error rates closely during the canary. Private installers will get a patch release with the flag documented in the upgrader notes.

payload.body:
Motivation: Intermittent production incidents showed that when a model switch or function/tool-call injection occurs mid-stream, downstream SSE consumers occasionally saw truncated JSON objects or duplicate sentinel events. Root causes included: (1) partial-object chunks being flushed out-of-order by proxies during cutover, (2) ambiguous empty-event delimiters emitted by the compatibility shim, and (3) lack of an idempotent reassembly key for retries and reconnects.

This change introduces two coordinated primitives to make handoff deterministic and safe: a cutover-marker event and a sequenced fragment ID (sequence_id + fragment_index) attached to every SSE data event emitted by the compat layer. The cutover-marker is a dedicated SSE event emitted immediately before a model/variant switch or when the runtime needs to inject a tool/function-call sentinel mid-stream. Consumers can use the marker as a safe boundary: reassembly buffers must consider any fragments with sequence_id lower than the cutover as final and drop fragments that start after the cutover with missing earlier fragment_index values.

Implementation summary:
- sse/encoder: add fields sequence_id (monotonic per-stream) and fragment_index (per sequence) on the event meta header. This is opt-in for downstream parsers via the compat header X-Redwood-SSE-Seq.
- cutover-marker: a small, explicit SSE event type "cutover" is emitted synchronously before any model switch or tool-call injection. The payload is a tiny JSON blob {"seq":"<sequence_id>","reason":"variant-swap|tool-insert"}.
- parser reassembly: consumer-facing parser now uses sequence_id+fragment_index to reassemble event payloads deterministically and tolerantly; out-of-order or overlapping fragments are reconciled against the latest cutover marker. We limit reassembly buffer to 256KB per stream to avoid OOM during adversarial clients.
- delimiter normalization: shim now normalizes contiguous newline delimiters and treats 0-length events as no-op rather than emit empty JSON tokens. This avoids spurious empty payloads when intermediaries coalesce chunk boundaries.
- compat shim: older clients that do not opt into X-Redwood-SSE-Seq will receive cutover-marker events but no sequence headers; parser heuristics fall back to brace-completion heuristics for JSON fragments to preserve compatibility.
- tests: new deterministic integration harness simulates three failure modes: interleaved chunk delivery, delayed cutover marker, and proxy-rewrite that coalesces multiple chunk boundaries. Added fuzz tests that run 6k randomized fragment permutations to validate reconstruction invariants.

Backward compatibility and rollout: The changes are additive; non-stream clients and downstreams that do not parse the new fields are unaffected. We feature-flag sequence headers behind runtime config redwood.compat.sse.seqid.enabled (default true in staging, ramped to true in prod after 48h bake). Cutover-marker emission is enabled by default with a short TTL semantics and documented in the compatibility guide.

Testing and verification: Unit tests cover the encoder/decoder roundtrip, the buffer-limits, and the fallback brace heuristics. Integration tests run against the full compat stack and the webhook consumer emulator. We exercised the change during a canary rollout: three internal services (chat, codegen, and rerank) observed zero JSON truncation events versus ~0.12% observed pre-fix under synthetic adversarial chunking.

Operational notes: If downstream consumers implement strict ordering assumptions, they should parse sequence_id and respect cutover-marker boundaries. The compatibility page (docs/compat/sse-cutover.md) documents expected semantics and examples for popular client libraries. This PR also includes a migration note and a simple parser snippet for the Node & Python SDKs.
Ethan Park: requested changes - please add a unit test that validates the parser drops overlapping older fragments when a newer cutover arrives. Also prefer a smaller default reassembly buffer (256KB seems okay but add a constant to tunables).
Maya Chen: responded - added buffer constant and new unit test (parser: deterministic reassembly) in commit 3e8a2f9. Left a note in operational docs about tunables.
Lina Rodriguez: question - does cutover-marker order still hold if the proxy delays events? What guarantees do we make?
Maya Chen: reply - cutover-marker is emitted synchronously and should arrive before subsequent fragments from the new sequence, but proxies that reorder are covered by sequence_id reconciliation; documented fallback behavior in docs/compat/sse-cutover.md.
Arjun Patel: approved - tests look robust, CI green, and rollout plan is sensible. Recommend squash merge after final smoke in staging.
payload.title: introduce cutover-marker and sequence IDs to stabilize SSE handoff and JSON completion

payload.body:
Motivation and context: Several customers reported tool-calling failures when clients send legacy 'tool_call' envelopes without the newer 'toolInvocation' wrapper introduced in the v3 wire contract. We want a low-risk rollout path that avoids immediate breaking changes while steering clients to the new contract via opt-in and deprecation signals. This PR implements a gateway-side fallback middleware that accepts legacy envelopes, performs a deterministic coercion into the current runtime internal model, and emits deprecation telemetry. It also adds a prefer-contract header and a beta header so we can A/B test the stricter contract before turning off the fallback.

What this PR does (single-string summary): Adds client-contract-fallback middleware at the OpenAI-compat gateway, introduces two headers (X-Redwood-Contract: beta-v2 and Prefer-Redwood-Contract: v3), implements streaming-coercion for partial tool-call events to keep streaming stable, updates router and runtime adapter to accept the coerced shape, adds unit/integration tests for tool/function calling and stream reassembly, updates docs and migration guide, and wires deprecation signals into metrics and logs.

Checklist (automated + manual): - [x] Gateway middleware that recognizes legacy 'tool_call' envelopes and rewrites to internal 'toolInvocation' shape - [x] Streaming path handles partial frames and KV-cache passthrough during coercion - [x] Header handling: X-Redwood-Contract (for opt-in beta) and Prefer-Redwood-Contract (client preference) - [x] Emit deprecation.counter{client_version,route} and deprecation.event logs with sample payloads - [x] Unit tests for coercion edge cases (missing args, nested tools) - [x] Integration test against runtime adapter to validate tool call lifecycle - [x] Docs: migration guide + changelog entry - [x] E2E smoke in canary environment

High-level commits: - 'middleware: add contract fallback and header parsing' - 'streaming: support incremental tool-call coercion for partial frames' - 'adapter: accept coerced toolInvocation and preserve tool metadata' - 'tests: unit and integration coverage for legacy envelopes' - 'docs: migration guide and examples'

Changed areas (high level): - src/gateway/middleware/contract_fallback.rs (new) - src/gateway/headers.rs (parse X-Redwood-Contract and Prefer-Redwood-Contract) - src/runtime/adapter/compat_adapter.go (accept coerced shape) - src/streaming/frame_rewriter.py (handle partial tool-call frames) - tests/legacy_tool_calls.test.js (integration) - docs/migration/route-tool-calls.md (new) - metrics/emit_deprecation_metric.sh (new wrapper) - examples/client-examples/compat_headers.md (docs)

Review conversation (condensed): - Alessandra: "Please add a unit test for the case where args is a JSON string vs an object; coercion should preserve type and annotate source." - Priya (author): "Added tests and an annotation field 'coercion_source': 'legacy_tool_call' with enum values; kept it internal-only and not surfaced to users." - Dmitry: "I am concerned about latency added by coercion on hot paths — did you bench this?" - Priya: "Yes — microbenchmarks in middleware show median wall-clock +0.4ms per-request under synthetic load; added an opt-out via Prefer-Redwood-Contract header to bypass coercion for high-throughput partners." - Samir: "Streaming partial-frame handling looks good; please ensure backpressure semantics unchanged." - Priya: "Verified with E2E smoke and added comments documenting backpressure behavior; added an integration test that replays partial frames from old clients." - Alessandra: "Approved after addressing test and perf notes."

CI summary: - Initial push: CI lint failed (header parsing style) - Fixup push: lint & unit tests passed, one flaky streaming integration failed in CI on first run - Rerun CI: all checks green (unit/integration/e2e smoke) - Final status: pass

Migration and rollout plan captured in docs: - Step 1 (canary): Merge middleware behind feature-flag for canary region only; communicate opt-in header to partners - Step 2 (beta): Enable X-Redwood-Contract: beta-v2 to measure adoption and emit deprecation telemetry - Step 3 (prefer header): Add Prefer-Redwood-Contract to let clients opt out of coercion when they support v3 - Step 4 (decommission): After 90 days and adoption thresholds, flip default to strict parsing and remove fallback.

Telemetry and observability: - New metrics: deprecation.counter, coercion.latency.histogram, coerced.calls.total - Logs: structured deprecation.events with client.agent, route, and sample payload (sampled at 0.1%) - Dashboard: added 'Contract compatibility' panel to the API console showing legacy envelope rates by client version.

Security and correctness: - Coercion is sanitizing inputs: any ambiguous 'args' types are parsed but preserved as opaque strings when parsing fails; we do not execute or eval payloads. - Added unit tests to ensure maliciously shaped envelopes are rejected rather than silently accepted.

Docs and examples: - docs/migration/route-tool-calls.md explains headers, example curl commands (both legacy and new envelopes), and a recommended timeline for partners. - examples/client-examples/compat_headers.md shows how to set Prefer-Redwood-Contract and X-Redwood-Contract.

Merge notes: Squash-and-merge after approvals. This was merged to main on 2026-01-21 using squash. Release note added to changelog under 'compatibility'.

Why this is different from previous compat PRs: Instead of adding a server-side permanent mapping, this PR focuses on a time-limited, observable, header-driven fallback that keeps streaming semantics intact for partial frames and lets clients explicitly opt into strict parsing. The approach is intentionally conservative to avoid regressions in high-throughput production customers.
Adds gateway middleware that accepts legacy tool-call envelopes and a prefer-contract header for gradual client rollouts; introduces a beta header X-Redwood-Contract and docs on migration. Non-breaking by default; opt-in via header.
payload.title: introduce-client-contract-fallback-middleware-for-toolcall-headers-and-stream-fallback

payload.body:
Context: recurring seasonal traffic spikes have generated a large volume of low-actionability alert noise (false positives and transient SLO blips). This PR adds a forecast-driven alert suppressor that uses short-horizon per-route token-velocity forecasts and confidence buckets to temporarily mute non-actionable alerts, and a complementary token-cost decomposer that annotates spans with phase- and kernel-level cost attribution so finance and SRE teams can see where per-invocation cost is coming from. The description below contains the motivation, design, and rollout checklist. Motivation: reduce pager churn and signal fatigue while preserving incident coverage for genuine regressions; improve per-invocation cost explainability to prioritize optimization work. What changed: (1) lightweight forecast service (observability/forecast_service) that consumes existing token rollups and emits per-route forecast + confidence; (2) alerting policy adapter that applies suppression windows for alerts that match forecasted transient noise patterns and low confidence; (3) token-cost decomposer (observability/cost_decomposer) which enriches traces with per-token-phase tags (input, decode, kv-cache, kernel) and emits new rollups; (4) new dashboard and playbook entries showing forecasted window, suppressed alert counts, cost decomposition charts; (5) feature flag gating and an opt-in flow for Dedicated/Private tenants. Checklist: - [x] RFC reviewed and sign-off from SRE and Finance - [x] Unit/integration tests for forecast model thresholds - [x] Add e2e smoke that simulates predictable traffic spike - [x] Dashboard and playbook added - [x] Feature-flagged rollout plan in runbook Rollout plan: enable in staging behind flag for two weeks; run canary on low-impact tenant pool; monitor missed-alert count (must remain < 0.05% of baseline) and emergency unmute path. Risks and mitigations: forecast miscalibration could suppress real incidents; mitigated by confidence floors, trial-only auto-suppression (starts as suggestion), and an emergency override API. Backwards compatibility: fully gated, no API changes to public telemetry endpoints. Merge: squash-and-merge after CI green and final SRE ACK.
Ethan Chen: Please surface the calibration metric and the CI job that validates it (added a unit to validate forecast CRPS).
Diego Morales: Suggest adding integration for emergency-unmute API and a test that simulates a real regression during a forecasted spike (added).
Priya Nair: LGTM after CI flakes were addressed; asked to include a note about Dedicated tenant opt-in flows in the docs (done).
Author (Maya Patel): responded to calibration questions, tightened confidence bucket thresholds, added canary rollout instructions.
payload.title: Introduce forecast-driven alert suppressor and token-cost decomposer

payload.body:
Context and motivation: In heterogeneous client environments we observed two recurring modes of failure: 1) the stream terminator token sequence (what we call the 'terminus signature') could be split across TCP/HTTP/SSE chunks or obfuscated by heartbeat/keepalive padding, producing truncated JSON objects on reconnect; 2) tool/function-call handoffs that rely on implicit event ordering could race with reassembly heuristics and produce mis-ordered function-call metadata. Users hit this in a high-throughput private deployment and during an incident (SUP-5412) where third-party SSE proxies coalesced keepalives.

Goals: (a) unambiguously detect and recover a stream-level terminus even when split across chunks; (b) guarantee an atomic fence for tool/function-call frames so that downstream consumers never see a partial tool metadata payload without its accompanying content; (c) remain backward compatible with existing OpenAI-compat clients and proxies.

Changes in this PR: - Introduce a canonical "terminus signature" matcher that works across chunk boundaries and tolerates interleaved keepalive heartbeats; implemented in sse/parser.rs and exposed to the compatibility layer. The matcher uses a tiny rolling window scan and a short checksum to avoid false positives on long-lived streams. - Add a lightweight handshake coordinator (handshake_coordinator.go) co-located in the compat layer that sequences tool-call start/end fences and ensures the emitter flushes a terminus-adjacent checkpoint before yielding control to a tool runner. The coordinator exposes a small async API: BeginFence/EndFence but this remains internal to the compatibility layer (no public SDK change). - Update the Python and Go streaming compat adapters to use the coordinator: compatibility/stream_compat_layer.py and sse/handshake_coordinator.go. - Add deterministic end-to-end tests that simulate chunk splits, keepalives, and proxy coalescing (tests/test_stream_handshake.py + tests/fixtures/*). - Documentation: docs/streaming_behavior.md explains the terminus semantics and recommended proxy settings.

Implementation notes & rationale: - We intentionally avoided adding extra framing bytes to the wire to remain compatible with strict SSE proxies and clients. Instead the terminus signature is chosen to be a short, low-collision sequence plus a 8-bit rolling checksum when emitted by Redwood’s runtime. Clients that do not emit the checksum still interoperate: the parser will fallback to a conservative reassembly path with a small additional latency penalty. - The handshake coordinator is a best-effort sequencer: it prevents the compat layer from yielding a function/tool-call event until the emitter confirms the terminus checkpoint is durable. This prevents other consumers (e.g., proxy reconnections) from observing half-committed tool metadata. - Performance: microbenchmarks show an average 0.6ms median per-call overhead in the compat layer for typical 128-token responses (see bench notes in the PR commit).

Checklist: - [x] Parser roll-window matcher implemented and unit-tested - [x] Handshake coordinator implemented with Go and Python adapters - [x] Integration tests simulate proxy chunking and heartbeat interleaving - [x] Docs updated with guidance for proxies and SDKs - [x] Verified fallbacks for older clients - [x] Benchmarks added

Summary of commits: - 8c1f4a1: sse/parser.rs: add terminus signature rolling matcher and checksum fallback - 9b2d3f7: handshake_coordinator.go: implement BeginFence/EndFence + in-memory checkpoint - e4a7b2c: compatibility/stream_compat_layer.py: wire coordinator into streamer loop and add logging - f1d9c88: tests/test_stream_handshake.py: new integration harness w/ proxy simulation - a5b6c3d: docs/streaming_behavior.md: document terminus semantics and proxy guidance

Changed files (high level): - sse/parser.rs: new matcher + unit tests (parser/terminus_tests.rs) - sse/handshake_coordinator.go: coordinator and small in-memory checkpoint - compatibility/stream_compat_layer.py: adapters to call BeginFence/EndFence and emit checksum header - tests/test_stream_handshake.py and tests/fixtures/: end-to-end simulations - docs/streaming_behavior.md: guidance and migration notes

Review conversation (selected threads): - Devon Kim (reviewer): "Can we reduce the rolling checksum width? 8-bit seems sufficient but may still cause a tiny collision window on long-lived multiplexed streams." Author reply (Evelyn): "We started with 16-bit and iterated down; 8-bit gives acceptable safety vs. backwards compatibility. Added a comment and a small metric (terminus_checksum_collisions_count) so we can revisit if necessary." - Samir Patel (reviewer): "The coordinator feels like another point of coupling between runtime and compat. How will this behave under load and when the emitter is overloaded?" Author reply: "Coordinator is best-effort: timeouts are applied and we fallback to a conservative reassembly path emitting a recovery marker. Added integration test that simulates emitter overload (test simulates a stall and verifies the recovery marker is emitted)." - Arianna Park (approver): "Looks good — the tests exercise edge cases and the docs are clear. One nit: expand the migration note to call out nginx proxy config that caused the incident." Author reply: "Added nginx sample config and an ops note to docs/streaming_behavior.md per Arianna's suggestion."

CI and gating: - Initial CI run: build and unit tests passed; integration tests failed due to flaky proxy simulator on mac runners. - Second run after test harness fix: all checks passed (build: pass, unit-tests: pass, integration-tests: pass, lint: pass).

Merge notes: - Merge method: squash and merge - Merge commit: 7b3d2c9 - Post-merge follow-ups: ENG-2198 to instrument terminus_checksum_collisions_count in production dashboards; a small follow-up PR will add a graceful degradation metric and opt-in debug logging for private deployments.

Impact: This PR does not change the public API; it reduces incidence of partial JSON emissions and misordered tool/function-call events in the wild. Operators should review docs/streaming_behavior.md and evaluate proxy settings; recommend enabling the small checksum header in environments where proxies are known to coalesce SSE frames.
Fixes an ambiguous stream terminus encoding that could cause partial JSON to be emitted across reconnections; adds a small coordinator service to ensure function/tool-call frames are fenced atomically across chunk boundaries. No API surface change for end users; improves streaming robustness and compatibility with OpenAI-style SSE clients.

Summary: This PR harmonizes credential extension points and retry presets across the Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs and introduces a lightweight async-iterable facade to standardize streaming ergonomics. Motivation: teams have been implementing ad-hoc credential fallback and stream iteration logic per-language which causes subtle bugs during reauth, inconsistent backoff behavior, and doubles the maintenance surface. This change reduces duplication, improves cross-language parity, and makes migration to newer retry strategies straightforward.

What changed (high-level):
- Introduced a small, opinionated CredentialSynchronizer interface (language idioms: ContextManager for Python, CredentialAttendant for TS, CredentialOrchestrator for Go) and implementation hooks for delegated refresh, prefetch, and fanout.
- Added CompactAsyncIterable facade for streaming responses: provides a minimal, cancelable async iterator that supports pause/resume and a stable close/cleanup contract. Implemented in py/ts/go SDK entry points.
- Consolidated retry preset profiles into a single canonical set (fast_retries / balanced / conservative) and wired them into the SDK constructors and stream adapters. Presets are deterministic, test-covered, and documented.
- Small ergonomic API tweaks: clearer errors for credential failures, a single env var to opt-in to legacy vs new retry semantics (REDWOOD_SDK_RETRY_MODE), and explicit deprecation warnings for older credential hooks.
- Version bumps: python->1.9.0, typescript->2.6.0, go->v1.14.0; changelogs updated.

Checklist (done):
- [x] Design doc reviewed with SDK leads (ENG-8125)
- [x] Implementations for all three SDKs
- [x] Unit + integration tests for token rotation and stream cancellation
- [x] Basic interop e2e across hosted API (small script)
- [x] Migration notes in each SDK CHANGELOG

Testing and CI notes: All SDK builds pass on CI. The change required small parallelization tweaks in the python integration suite to avoid token-bus contention; CI workflow updated to use isolated fixtures when running interop tests. There is an additional flaky test (TS stream-reconnect) that was stabilized by increasing socket timeout; we've tracked the original flaky CI run in SUP-1478.

Backward compatibility and migration guidance: This PR aims to be non-breaking. Existing credential hooks will continue to work, but will emit a deprecation warning if they rely on the legacy reauth callback signature (old_signature: (ctx) -> token). Migration steps are documented in the CHANGELOGs and examples folder. For teams that cannot migrate immediately, set REDWOOD_SDK_RETRY_MODE=legacy to preserve prior retry timing.

Performance/behavior notes: Standardizing retry presets reduces end-to-end token refresh storms under burst load; internal perfbench across a simulated webhook workload showed a 18% reduction in auth-related request latency variance and a 12% reduction in token refresh RPCs per minute.

Files of interest (high-level): sdks/python/redwood_sdk/auth/synchronizer.py; sdks/python/redwood_sdk/stream/compact_iterable.py; sdks/typescript/src/auth/attendant.ts; sdks/typescript/src/stream/compactIterable.ts; sdks/go/credentials/orchestrator.go; sdks/go/stream/compact_iterable.go; ci/workflows/sdk-integration.yml; docs/sdks/migration/credential_and_retry.md

Release notes: Introduce CredentialSynchronizer and CompactAsyncIterable; align retry presets across SDKs; minor API ergonomics and version bumps (Python 1.9.0, TS 2.6.0, Go v1.14.0). No breaking changes by default; opt-in legacy mode available.

Why this is unique: Instead of a per-SDK one-off, this PR is a minimal cross-language contract + reference implementations approach — small surface area but high leverage for future SDK features (session caching, stream pooling, and observability hooks).
Diego Morales: Left a couple of nits in the TS attendant about edge-case cancellation; can we add an explicit unit test that calls .return() on the iterator path?
Priya Nair (author): Good catch, added ts test and clarified the return/cleanup contract in compactIterable.ts; included the test in the commit c8f1d55.
Ava Chen: The Go orchestrator looks good; one suggestion: rename StartPrefetch to Prime to match other orchestrator APIs. Not required for merge but would be nice for parity.
Priya Nair: Renamed StartPrefetch->Prime in a follow-up commit and added a tiny docstring, addressed the comment.
Liam O'Neill: Verified integration run locally with the hosted API; token rotation storm scenario behaved as expected and metrics improved. Approving.
Merged to main. SDK packages tagged and release pipelines triggered. Docs and examples updated. QA will run a canary for 48 hours on Dedicated customers before wider rollout.
See release notes: CredentialSynchronizer + CompactAsyncIterable + retry preset alignment; SDK version bumps; non-breaking by default (REDWOOD_SDK_RETRY_MODE to opt into legacy behavior).

Context: Production incidents showed a class of partial-json/structured-output failures when tiny, repeatable edge delays (sub-millisecond) caused the streamer to flush a chunk boundary that split a JSON object tail across two network frames. The OpenAI-compat adapter would then attempt to reconstruct and occasionally emit truncated JSON or mis-order function-call sentinel tokens when heartbeat/keepalive events interleaved.

Motivation: reduce user-visible malformed structured output and improve deterministic ordering guarantees for tool/function call handoff without trading off latency for steady-state traffic.

Summary:
- Add a short, bounded "edge-delay correction" window that waits for final byte drains for streams that look like they contain a JSON object tail (heuristic-based).
- Introduce a lightweight tail-coalescer that reorders late-arriving bytes within the window and keeps a small seq-anchored buffer to permit safe reassembly.
- Harden OpenAI-compat stream adapter to prefer function-call sentinel anchoring only after tail-rescue window expires or checksum verifies.
- Add deterministic ordering guard that ensures heartbeat events are treated as interleaving metadata (not JSON content) and do not close a pending structured-output span.

Checklist:
- [x] Add edge-delay window + buffer with bounded memory (50KB cap / per-stream)
- [x] Safeguard against unbounded buffering with immediate fallback to best-effort emit after timeout (25ms default)
- [x] Unit and integration tests covering split-json, heartbeat-interleave, and toolcall-ordering
- [x] CI matrix updated to include a stress test with synthetic microbursts
- [x] Docs note for behaviour change under extreme packet reordering

Commits summary:
- feat(stream): introduce edge window and tail-coalescer (main algorithm + config)
- fix(adapter): prefer seq-anchored function sentinel after tail verification
- test(stream): add fuzz/integration tests for split-json and heartbeat interleave
- ci: add stress matrix shard and timing tolerances

Changed areas (high-level):
- services/streaming/parser/edge_window_rescue.rs: implements the bounded window, voucher-based seq anchoring, and tail coalescing logic (main algorithm ~180 LOC).
- api/openai_compat/stream_adapter.go: updates to treat heartbeats as non-terminating events and to consult the rescue buffer before emitting function-call sentinels (~45 LOC).
- services/streaming/tests/test_partial_json.rs: new unit + integration scenarios exercising mid-json chunking, late-arrival bytes, and heartbeat interleaving.
- runtime/kv_cache/coalesce.py: minor change to avoid invalidating coalesced prefix when rescue buffer is active.
- docs/compatibility/streaming-edge-notes.md: operational notes and config knobs.
- ci/test-matrix.yml: stress shard added.

Small illustrative snippet (pseudo):
- before: flushOnDelimiter(chunk) -> could emit '..."content": "pa' + next frame 'rtial"}'
- now: if looksLikeJsonTail(chunk) holdFor(25ms) mergeLateBytes(seqWindow) -> emitWhenComplete or emitBestEffort

After implementation details:
- The rescue window uses a seq-anchored ledger to accept up to 3 late fragments; late fragments are only accepted if their seq id is contiguous and within the 25ms window.
- Memory bound enforced per stream; if buffer overrun occurs we fall back to immediate emit and metric to alert on overrun.
- Heartbeat frames are classified via stream metadata; classification is cheap and runs before tail heuristics.

Test plan:
- Unit tests added for heuristics and buffer edge cases.
- Integration tests with the openai-compat adapter in a real network simulator (packet reorder & microburst).
- End-to-end canary rollout to 5% of hosted API (monitor malformed-json/error-rate and function-call-order regressions).

Observability:
- Added metrics: stream.rescue.window_ms, stream.rescue.accepted_fragments, stream.rescue.fallback_emits, stream.rescue.buffer_overruns.
- Alert: stream.rescue.fallback_emits > 50/min triggers investigation.

Rollout:
- 0->5% canary with extended logging for 48h, then 5->50% if no regression, then full rollout.

Related: ENG-3284 (incident), ENG-3310 (follow-up quality gating).

Notes on tradeoffs:
- Adds a small tail latency (default 25ms) only when the heuristic detects a possible JSON tail; not applied to non-JSON streams.
- Bounded memory and timeout mitigate risk of head-of-line blocking.

Deployment: feature-gated behind feature.flag.stream_tail_rescue=false by default for immediate rollback if needed.
Fix partial JSON emit when stream chunks arrive with sub-ms edge delays; improve detection of function-call/structured-output tail boundaries when heartbeats interleave. No API changes.
Liam O'Connor: Algorithm looks good; please add a unit test for non-JSON binary streams to ensure no hold occurs.
Maya Gupta: Added test_non_json_no_hold() and updated heuristic to check content-type metadata. PTAL.
Ravi Menon: Can we reduce default window to 15ms? Production latency SLOs are tight. Also add metric for rescued-bytes.
Maya Gupta: Kept default at 25ms after measuring tail arrival distributions in canary; added configurable knob and metric stream.rescue.rescued_bytes.
Sofia Alvarez: Approving after tests and CI green. Left a minor nits request on doc wording.
Sofia Alvarez: APPROVED

Normalize incoming rate-limit headers from various providers into a single internal contract. Map vendor-specific 429 payloads to Redwood's standard error schema for predictable client handling. Backwards-compatible changes only.
Motivation: the OpenAI-compat adapter sees a wide variety of rate-limit headers and 429 error payloads from models/proxies in the wild. Clients (and our retry/fallback logic) need a single, predictable contract to make robust retry decisions and to emit consistent telemetry. This PR normalizes common rate-limit headers (Retry-After, X-RateLimit-Reset, RateLimit-Remaining variants) into a clear internal RateLimitInfo structure, and canonicalizes 429 and related error payloads into Redwood's error schema (code, reason, retry_after_seconds, scope). It also clarifies idempotency semantics for streaming/function-call requests: streaming responses that are aborted by client disconnect now surface a consistent retryable flag and a recommended backoff hint when we can infer a server-side retry-after. Changes: 1) openai_adapter/headers_normalizer.py: new utility that parses multiple header formats and returns RateLimitInfo. 2) openai_adapter/error_mapper.py: maps vendor error shapes into redwood error codes like RATE_LIMIT, THROTTLED, BAD_REQUEST and includes retry_after_seconds when available. 3) openai_adapter/streaming_guard.py: ensures idempotency-key and request fingerprint are included in logs and in the mapped error payload for streaming aborts and connection resets. 4) tests/*: unit and integration tests covering header permutations, streaming aborts, and adapter fallback to internal backoff logic. 5) docs/adapters/openai-rate-limits.md: short reference of header variants and recommended client behavior. Backwards compatibility: adapter emits the same HTTP responses to external callers but augments error JSON with standardized fields where possible; no public API contract change. Why not earlier approaches: previous heuristics were scattered and added flaky behavior in autoscaling canaries where transient 429s were misinterpreted. This centralization reduces duplicate parsing logic and yields cleaner metrics for rate-limit incidents. Rollout plan: feature gated via env var OPENAI_ADAPTER_NORMALIZE_HEADERS=false by default; flip on after staged canary for one week. See linked Linear tasks for SLO & dashboard updates.
Jonah Kim: Looks good overall, one request: can we add a unit test for the X-RateLimit-Reset header when it's a unix epoch in milliseconds? Observed in one proxy.
Ava Martinez: Added test for ms epoch and a fallback path that rounds to nearest second in the later commit c8f0e4d.
Priya Desai: How will this interact with our existing client-side retry middleware? We should ensure we don't double-backoff when both sides include Retry-After.
Ava Martinez: streaming_guard attaches source=adapter to the retry_hint so client middleware can detect adapter-origin hints and apply idempotency-aware backoff. Updated docs to call this out.
Lars Becker: CI flake on test_streaming_abort_behavior was due to a race; suggested increasing test hook timeout. Patch now increases timeout and replaces sleep-based assertion with event-based signal.
CI: failed on first run due to flaky integration test; rerun produced green results.
Priya Desai: Approved after test additions and a brief explanation of how this impacts metrics ingestion for rate-limit dashboards.
Jonah Kim: Approved and will follow up on dashboards update CL separately.
Merge Bot: Merged by squash on 2025-11-10.

Motivation: Product teams need a single, queryable surface to discover model capabilities, pricing tiers, and OpenAI-compatibility hints for routing and SDK fallbacks. Current model-listing endpoints scatter hints across several fields and duplicate logic in SDK shims. This PR introduces a unified /v1/models/capabilities endpoint (and corresponding openai-compat shim enhancements) to centralize capability flags (streaming, function_calling, structured_output), pricing/limits info, regional availability, and compatibility metadata.

Summary of changes: - New API: GET /v1/models/capabilities with query filters (capabilities, region, min_qps, openai_compatible=true|false, price_tier). Responses include a standardized capability set and price/limit objects. - Backwards compatibility: existing /v1/models and /v1/models/:id behavior unchanged; clients can opt-in to the new endpoint. The OpenAI-compat layer now consults the capabilities endpoint when resolving model choice for streaming and function-calling fallbacks. - Capability flags expanded: streaming_support (bool), streaming_latency_hint ("low"|"medium"|"best-effort"), function_calling (bool), structured_output_schema (optional JSON-schema URL string), kv_cache_supported (bool). - Pricing and limits: each model listing includes price_per_1k_tokens (float string in USD), max_tokens_supported (int string), recommended_batch_size (int string), and soft_qps_limit (int string). These are advisory and used by Redwood Optimize and routing decisions. - Query filters server-side: filter_by_capabilities (comma-separated), min_price_tier, region, and openai_compatible. Filtering is implemented efficiently using the existing catalog index and a new capability inverted index populated at model onboarding time.

Checklist:
- [x] API contract defined and documented in API spec.
- [x] Server implementation with pagination and filter validation.
- [x] OpenAI-compat shim updates to prefer models that advertise matching capabilities.
- [x] Unit tests for capability parsing, filter combinators, and price/limit format validation.
- [x] Integration tests covering streaming fallback and function-calling route selection.
- [x] Docs and SDK examples updated (Python and TS quickstarts).

Backward compatibility and rollout: This change is additive. Existing clients keep current behavior. The new endpoint is gated behind a feature flag (default on in staging, opt-in in prod for first 48h) and will be rolled to all regions after monitoring. The openai-compat shim will prefer models with matching flags but will fall back to previous selection logic if no capability match is found.

API contract (excerpt): GET /v1/models/capabilities?q=filter_by_capabilities=function_calling,streaming&region=us-west-2&openai_compatible=true&page_size=50
Response shape (fields): id, name, capabilities (csv flags), streaming_support, streaming_latency_hint, function_calling, structured_output_schema, price_per_1k_tokens_usd, max_tokens_supported, recommended_batch_size, soft_qps_limit, regions (list), openai_compatible_hint. All numeric values are returned as strings for stable parsing across SDKs.

Tests and CI: Initial CI run failed lint in api/specs (minor formatting); fixed in second commit. Unit test coverage added for catalog filter combinations and migration logic. Integration tests simulate a streaming-enabled model and validate that the openai shim reroutes requests to streaming-optimized endpoints when streaming_support=true and latency_hint=low.

Documentation and SDKs: API spec markdown added under docs/api/models-capabilities.md. Python and Typescript SDKs get a small helper (get_models_by_capabilities) that calls the new endpoint and normalizes returned fields into sdk-friendly types. Quickstart example demonstrates selecting a model capable of tool/function calling and streaming simultaneously.

Security and cost notes: Pricing fields are advisory; routing decisions should always respect tenant quotas. No sensitive data added to the catalog. All catalog writes are authenticated via existing model registry ACLs.

Related tickets: ENG-1289 (catalog capability indexing), PM-452 (product requirements for model discoverability), SUP-341 (support request for clearer streaming guarantees).

Rolling to production: staged feature flag, 48h telemetry window focusing on: 1) error rate for the new endpoint, 2) percent of requests using capability-driven routing, 3) latency P95 for streaming-handshake when routed via shim.

If merged: release notes will mention the new endpoint and the SDK helper. Migration: customers using custom model-selection logic should evaluate adopting the endpoint to simplify routing and to get advisory pricing/limits in a single call.
Diego Marquez: Can we ensure the streaming_latency_hint semantics are documented somewhere central? I want clear guidance for SDKs (low/medium/best-effort).
Amaya Chen: Added a section in docs/api/models-capabilities.md describing semantics and recommended client behavior; SDK helpers normalize the hint into enums.
Priya Nair: Tests look good. One request: validate price_per_1k_tokens format strictly (e.g. two decimals).
Amaya Chen: Tightened validation and added unit test for price format; server returns string but validation enforces decimal format with up to 4 places for future micro-pricing.
Samir Patel: Concern: capability index migration could be slow for customers with very large registries. Can we background this and expose a health indicator?
Amaya Chen: Migration runs as a background job with a shard-friendly cursor; added metrics and a /internal/catalog/migration-status endpoint (auth-protected) to monitor progress.
Diego Marquez: CI initially failed linting on api/specs. Fixed in m3n4o5 commit. Approving post-fix.
Priya Nair: Approve. Verified integration test that simulates function_calling routing and structured_output_schema handling.
Samir Patel: Approve after migration-run telemetry added.
Add new GET /v1/models/capabilities endpoint to expose centralized model capability flags, pricing hints, and regional availability; SDK helpers in Python and TS added. Backwards compatible and gated behind feature flag during rollout.
Feature flagged rollout: opt-in in prod for 48h, then enable by default if telemetry looks normal.
No breaking changes to existing /v1/models endpoints.
Telemetry dashboards added: Catalog > Capabilities Usage, Routing > OpenAI-compat selection.
Follow-up work: add UI filters in Console (ENG-1402), and add cost-aware routing examples in Redwood Optimize (PM-470).
