payload.body:
Context: Route-level experiments require deterministic assignment. The platform supports a stickiness key (preferred: stable per end-user or per tenant) that the router uses when bucketing a request into a variant. This PR adds an optional experimentStickyKey field to the TS SDK request options and includes small helpers to read the assigned {experiment_id, variant_id} from response headers so customers can log/debug assignments. Summary of changes: 1) New request option: experimentStickyKey?: string on chat/completions/embeddings/rerank request option types. When present, the SDK sends header X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key (exact casing handled by fetch). 2) New response metadata: the SDK now captures experiment assignment headers (x-redwood-experiment-id, x-redwood-experiment-variant, x-redwood-experiment-config-version) and exposes them via response.experimental?.assignment for non-streaming calls. 3) Streaming support: for stream responses, assignment headers are available immediately from the initial response; we surface them on the returned stream handle as stream.experimental.assignment and also provide an onResponse callback hook for callers that want to log headers before consuming tokens. 4) Ergonomics: add helper parseExperimentAssignment(headers) and type ExperimentAssignment to avoid callers hand-parsing header names. 5) Docs + examples: update README snippets for route experiments usage and add a troubleshooting note (stickiness key should be high-entropy; do not default to IP; prefer customer_user_id or customer_session_id). Backwards compatibility: option is fully optional and does not change behavior when omitted. No breaking changes to existing response shapes (new fields are additive under .experimental). Testing: unit tests for header injection + parsing, and one integration-style test with mocked fetch verifying streaming handle includes assignment. Notes: header names align with platform OTel conventions and ADR-047/048; the SDK intentionally does not attempt to generate a default stickiness key to avoid low-entropy skew (see recent beta issue).
Header contract: X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key is the only new request header added here. Response contract: SDK reads x-redwood-experiment-id, x-redwood-experiment-variant, and x-redwood-experiment-config-version. If headers are missing, assignment is undefined and the helper returns null. Streaming: because fetch exposes headers on the Response before reading the body, assignment is always available even if attribution later drops in telemetry; this is intended for client-side logging only and should not be used as a source of truth for analytics.
Jordan Lee: Can we confirm the stickiness header name matches what the policy engine expects? We recently standardized on X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key (not the older X-Redwood-Sticky-Key).
Dylan Brooks (author): Yep, using X-Redwood-Experiment-Sticky-Key. Added a small constant + tests to prevent regressions. Also updated README to match.
Logan Wright: Please make sure we don’t accidentally increase header cardinality in logs by default. Are we logging the stickiness key anywhere?
Dylan Brooks (author): SDK does not log headers. Also added note in docs: do not log raw stickiness keys; if needed, hash client-side.
Jada Williams: For streaming, how does a caller access the assigned variant? They won’t have the full response object.
Dylan Brooks (author): Added stream.experimental.assignment and an onResponse callback so they can log assignment before token iteration. Included a snippet in README.
Kaitlyn Nguyen: Any RBAC/security concerns with surfacing experiment_id/variant_id to customers? Should we gate it?
Dylan Brooks (author): Platform already sends these headers in beta/GA; this PR only makes them accessible. If an account isn’t enabled, headers won’t be present. No new sensitive data introduced.
Jordan Lee: Minor: parse helper should handle Header objects and plain records. Some frameworks provide a map-like interface.
Dylan Brooks (author): Updated parseExperimentAssignment to accept Headers | Record<string,string> | Array<[string,string]>. Added tests.
Jada Williams: Looks good after the streaming doc update. Approving.
Logan Wright: Approved. Thanks for keeping it additive under .experimental.

Title: Introduce frugality-mode runner and quant-drift watchdog. Summary: Adds an opt-in 'frugality' execution mode designed for cost-sensitive tenants. Frugality mode applies conservative batching and cache retention defaults, introduces a simulated shadow-runner to validate cheaper quant profiles before rollout, and a quant-drift watchdog that monitors eval/quality signals for regressions and triggers safe rollback policies. Motivation: customers requested stronger default guardrails for unit economics when enabling low-cost quantized variants. This change bundles deploy-time defaults, a dry-run validator, and runtime telemetry/alerts so teams can safely try tighter cost profiles without manual scaffolding. What changed (high level): 1) runtime/orchestrator: new frugality policy layer that adjusts batch sizing and kv-cache TTLs by tenant tier; 2) runtime/quant: shadow-runner that can run a sample percentage of requests with a candidate quant profile and compare quality metrics; 3) ops/cli: new `rwdctl frugality` subcommands for dry-run, promote, and rollback; 4) telemetry: new metrics and events (frugality.run.sampled, quant.cohort.regression, frugality.policy.applied) and dashboards; 5) safety: automated rollback hooks triggered by quant-drift watchdog when eval thresholds breach; 6) tests: end-to-end smoke harness and unit tests for policy application. Commits (summary): - a1b3c7d: initial frugality policy scaffolding and default profiles; - 9f4e2b1: shadow-runner implementation + sample scheduler; - 2c7d4f9: rwdctl CLI integration and docs; - c3a2f01: telemetry and dashboards; - f5b4a88: tests and CI fixes. Files touched (high-level): - runtime/policy/frugality_policy.go (new) - runtime/quant/shadow_runner.go (new) - cli/rwdctl/frugality_cmd.go (new) - config/defaults/frugality_profiles.yaml (new) - telemetry/metrics_registry.go (updated) - dashboards/cost_guardrails.json (new) - tests/e2e/frugality_smoke_test.go (new) - internal/rollback/quant_watchdog.go (new) - docs/frugality_mode.md (new) - CI: .github/workflows/frugality-ci.yaml (new) Change rationale: We observed several customer incidents where aggressive quant rollouts reduced cost but silently regressed quality for edge prompt families. Frugality mode is a defensive set of defaults and an automated validation loop to lower the blast radius of low-cost configurations while still enabling experimentation. Backwards compatibility: Mode is off by default. Existing tenants see no behavior change unless they opt in via the tenant profile API or CLI. Testing notes: Unit tests cover policy application, sample scheduling, and the watchdog threshold logic. E2E smoke runs a synthetic workload with a golden prompt set and verifies no regression for control vs candidate. CI flow: initial push failed unit tests due to a race in sample scheduler; fixed in commit f5b4a88. All CI checks green on final push. Documentation: Added docs/frugality_mode.md with configuration examples and recommended conservative defaults for small/medium/large tenants. Review conversation (high level and timeline): - Marina Lopez (reviewer) comment at 2026-02-19: "Nice encapsulation; need stronger typing on profile YAML and explicit schema validation to avoid silent misconfigs." Author reply 2026-02-19: "Added YAML schema validation and explicit error messages; see frugality_profiles.yaml and validation tests." - Ethan Brooks (reviewer) requested changes 2026-02-20: "Shadow-runner should not affect production latency; ensure sampling is entirely async and bounded CPU. Also add telemetry for sample throttles." Author reply 2026-02-21: "Made sampling strictly asynchronous, capped CPU/threads, and added telemetry events for throttles (frugality.sample.throttled)." - Chen Wang (reviewer) found an edge-case 2026-02-22: "Watchdog threshold config is per-tenant but fallback global exists — include clear precedence and docs." Author reply 2026-02-22: "Document precedence and implemented explicit merge order (tenant -> tenant-group -> global)." - CI initially: build: pass; unit: fail (flaky sample scheduler race) -> fixed; integration: pass; lint: pass. Final CI status: pass. Approvals: Marina Lopez approved 2026-02-24; Ethan Brooks approved 2026-02-24; Chen Wang approved 2026-02-25. Merge details: Squash merge performed on 2026-02-25 by Priya Shah with commit message "frugality: add runner, shadow validation, quant watchdog, CLI and telemetry (squash)". Deployment notes: Feature gated under runtime flag FRUGALITY_MODE and tenant opt-in API fields. Ops runbook: Added to docs/runbooks/cost-guardrails-runbook.md with steps to enable, monitor frugality.run.sampled, inspect quant.cohort.regression spikes, and how to trigger manual rollback via `rwdctl frugality rollback --tenant <id>`. Observability: Added dashboards/cost_guardrails.json and alerts: - critical if quant.cohort.regression > 0.05 over 5m -> auto rollback trigger (controlled) - warning if sample.throttled rate > 10% over 10m -> notify SRE. Performance expectations: Frugality defaults aim to reduce tail unit-cost by ~12-22% for quant-friendly workloads while targeting <3% quality delta on golden evals; numbers are workload dependent. Migration and compatibility: No migration necessary for existing tenants. New profile file contains sample conservative presets for nv4x, v100x, and aarch64 inference nodes. Security: Shadow-runner executes only on anonymized request copies; no PII retained; passes threat modeling review. Follow-ups and TODOs: - Add tenant-level UI in Console to enable frugality mode (tracked ENG-2040). - Add automated regression reporting per prompt family (ENG-2065). - Long-run telemetry retention policy discussion (SRE). Risk assessment: Low risk if kept opt-in; medium if enabled globally without careful rollout. Rollback and safety features implemented to mitigate regression risk. Tests included and CI passing. Release note blurb: "Introducing Frugality Mode — opt-in conservative batching/caching defaults, a shadow-runner for safe quant profile validation, and a quant-drift watchdog to protect quality during low-cost rollouts."
Add frugality-mode (opt-in) that provides conservative batching/caching defaults and a quantization drift detector; backward-compatible; new CLI helpers and telemetry added.

Motivation: Customers need clearer, actionable guidance when structured-output validation fails while preserving streaming availability and toolcall safety. This PR introduces an adaptive strictness layer for response_format validation, stream-anchor checkpoints to allow safe partial validation during streaming responses, and human-readable error hints that surface likely fixes and rollback options. It also tightens the OpenAI-compat adapter behavior to prefer soft-fallbacks unless the user requests strict=always. Summary of changes: 1) runtime: add response_format.strictness policy and adaptive mode that grades payloads 'per-checkpoint' and escalates to enforce only when confidence thresholds are met; 2) streaming: introduce stream anchor tokens and lightweight resumable checkpoints so validators can align partial JSON fragments without blocking byte-level streaming; 3) tool/function calling: add call-fence verification that ensures tool responses matched declared schema fields are validated before commit and includes a safe rollback hook; 4) openai adapter: change default negotiation to 'compat-soft' to reduce hard failures when clients don't opt into strict mode; 5) telemetry/docs: new telemetry counters for soft->hard escalation and a new docs guide with example prompts and remediation hints. Testing and rollout: unit tests for validator margins, e2e streaming harness tests to simulate truncated JSON and toolcall interleaving, staged rollout behind feature flag 'res_format_guidance_v2' with canary set to 10% on hosted API. Related work: ENG-8243 (schema UX), ENG-8290 (streaming stability). This description is a single continuous string and contains the context, the change list, and rollout notes.
Liam O'Connor: Nice approach minimizing hard failures. Question: how do we measure false-positive escalations? Please add an opt-out per-client config.
Maya Chen: Added client opt-out hook and telemetry counters in latest push, and documented the config in README.
Priya Kapoor: Request: make anchor token size configurable and document storage implications for private deployments.
Maya Chen: Ack. Anchor size is configurable via checkpoint.max_fragment_bytes and default retained in the feature flag docs.
Diego Ramos: Left a nit about log verbosity for soft failures; prefer warn-level with sampling.
Maya Chen: Reduced log rate and added sampling for warn-level entries in next commit.
payload.title: Introduce adaptive strictness and streaming anchors to improve structured-output validation UX while preserving streaming and toolcall safety

Context
We’re in the middle of the SDK parity initiative and TS currently differs from Python/Go in two customer-visible ways:
1) Retry classification: TS retry middleware has been overly permissive (observed retries on some terminal 4xx), which contributed to SUP-29438 (duplicate billing concern).
2) Error surfaces: request_id is inconsistently propagated (INT-1182), and error types differ between streaming/non-streaming paths.

This PR refactors the retry middleware and error construction so TS matches the standard taxonomy and aligns retryable status codes. Retry-After parsing/backoff tuning will be handled in follow-up PRs (see PR-1307).

What changed
- Introduced a single error normalization layer used by both streaming + non-streaming requests:
  - All thrown errors extend RedwoodError and include:
    - requestId (from x-redwood-request-id/x-request-id header, with body fallback)
    - statusCode (when available)
    - code (gateway error code when present)
    - retryable (computed)
- Refactored retry middleware to depend on the normalized error shape instead of ad-hoc checks.
- Updated retryable classification to match the SDK retry/timeout standard:
  - Retryable: 408, 409, 429, 500–599 (excluding 501 by default; see note below)
  - Non-retryable: other 4xx (400/401/403/404/etc)
  - Network/transport errors are retryable (DNS, connection reset, TLS handshake, fetch abort not initiated by user)
- Request ID propagation:
  - Successful responses: the Response wrapper exposes requestId.
  - Error responses: requestId is extracted from headers first, then JSON body fields (request_id/requestId) if present.
- Observability hooks:
  - Retry loop now increments a local attempt counter and attaches it to the error as metadata when we eventually give up.
  - Ensures we do NOT include the Authorization header or API key in any error message (Security review guidance).

Notes / decisions
- 501 handling: The standard doc calls out 5xx generally as retryable; SRE feedback was to treat 501 as non-retryable by default (usually indicates unsupported feature/method rather than transient). This PR implements that as a conservative default; we can revisit once gateway error codes are fully consistent.
- Abort semantics: When the caller’s AbortSignal triggers, we now classify it as non-retryable and preserve the original AbortError name/message.

Testing
- Added unit tests for shouldRetry(): verifies status code matrix and network error classification.
- Added tests ensuring request_id is extracted from:
  - response headers (preferred)
  - JSON error body (fallback)
- Updated existing integration tests to assert error.retryable and error.requestId are present.

Rollout
- This should be non-breaking for most customers: existing code catching Error will continue to work.
- Some customers may have relied on the previous (incorrect) retry-on-400 behavior; this change is intentional and documented in migration notes (tracked in ENG-5128).

Follow-ups
- Retry-After parsing + backoff jitter alignment (PR-1307)
- Timeout defaults + AbortController plumbing (PR-1302)
- Conformance suite fixtures (ENG-5127)

Screenshots/log samples
- Example error (sanitized):
  name=RedwoodAPIError statusCode=429 retryable=true requestId=req_01HR9Q6K9YQG3H2R9M4J7V0Z1A code=RATE_LIMITED
Ibrahim Khan (review) — 2026-01-30: “Thanks. Two asks for parity: (1) ensure request_id comes from headers first (gateway guarantees) and only fall back to body; (2) confirm we never retry 400/401/403/404. Also, can you align naming with other SDKs (requestId vs request_id)?”
Dana Lo (author) — 2026-01-30: “Ack. Updated extraction order to header-first; added tests. Keeping JS field as requestId but mapping both request_id/requestId from body; docstring calls out normalization.”

Allison Grant (review) — 2026-01-31: “On retryable codes: do we treat 409 as retryable? Standard says yes (conflicts can be transient with idempotency). Please add a note for customers and make sure retryable is surfaced on the error.”
Dana Lo — 2026-01-31: “Added 409 retryable and explicit test. error.retryable is now always defined for RedwoodError subclasses.”

Marcus Lin (security review) — 2026-02-01: “Please double-check no Authorization header contents end up in error.message or debug logs; also ensure requestId is safe to log.”
Dana Lo — 2026-02-01: “Removed inclusion of request headers from error messages. requestId is explicitly allowed (non-secret) and helps support triage.”

Ethan Park (platform) — 2026-02-02: “Gateway sometimes returns x-request-id vs x-redwood-request-id depending on path. Good that you check both. Can you also check body field request_id for OpenAI-compat?”
Dana Lo — 2026-02-02: “Yep, body fallback supports request_id/requestId. Added test for OpenAI-compat style payload.”

Ibrahim Khan (approval) — 2026-02-03: “Looks good. This closes the SUP-29438 class of retry misclassification for TS. Approved.”
payload.title: Unify retry middleware and error shapes (request_id + retryable) with SDK standard

Motivation: During a high-latency incident in eu-west we observed connection storms that caused abrupt circuit flips and large SLO oscillations for a subset of tenants. This PR introduces a connection-slice throttle mesh (lightweight admission layer that slices long-lived connections into bounded connection groups) and an emergency soft-rollback hook that can gracefully revert the throttle mesh state without restarting nodes.

Scope: The change adds a new connection-slice controller in the serving runtime, augments the SLO enforcer to observe slice-level load, and introduces an ops-facing hotpath to soft-rollback slice assignments when telemetry indicates regressions. The approach is designed to be conservative: slices limit concurrent fastpath reservations and favor evicting best-effort requests first. The controller is pluggable and toggled off by default for Dedicated clusters; rollout is controlled via feature flag and a short-lived config in the private installer manifest.

What this PR does (summary):
- Implement connection-slice controller with token-based slice quotas and soft-eviction policy.
- Wire slice metrics through the telemetry pipeline (slice.{utilization,evictions,avg_latency}).
- Extend the SLO enforcer to support slice-level budgets and to recommend per-tenant slice caps when backpressure triggers.
- Add an emergency soft-rollback API + ops CLI (no binary restart) to revert slice mappings and drain slices over a configurable grace window.
- Add unit + integration tests for controller invariants and a small e2e scenario that simulates a regional surge.

Checklist:
- [x] New controller implementation + tests
- [x] Telemetry hooks and dashboards updated (see docs path)
- [x] Ops hotfix manifest and CLI registered
- [x] Feature flag gating and default off for Dedicated
- [x] Canary rollout plan added to the PR description

Commits summary: squash of feature branch implementing controller and hotfix
- Add connection-slice controller scaffold and quota allocator
- Implement slice-level admission checks in serving runtime
- Telemetry: slice metrics + export
- SLO enforcer: slice budget integration
- Ops: soft-rollback API + CLI + hotfix manifest
- Tests: unit and conn-slice integration

Changed files (high-level):
- server/scheduler/connection_slice_controller.go: core controller + quota allocator
- server/scheduler/slice_admission.go: admission checks and eviction hooks
- server/slo/enforcer.go: slice-aware budget calculation and logging
- pkg/telemetry/slice_metrics_exporter.go: new metric exports
- ops/deploy/hotfix-manifest.yaml: emergency soft-rollback manifest for private installs
- tools/ops-cli/cmd/softrollback.go: CLI to trigger hot rollback
- tests/slo/conn_slice_integration_test.go: scenario tests
- docs/operations/connection-slice-throttle.md: runbook + canary plan
- proto/telemetry/slice.proto: metric proto definitions

CI summary: First run had a flaky integration test (integration/conn-slice/surge-sim) failing due to timing assumptions — adjusted the test harness to poll for drain completion instead of sleeping; rerun passed all checks.
- unit-tests: pass
- integration-tests: initial fail (timing) -> fix -> pass
- e2e-latency-smoke: pass
- lint: pass
- build: pass

Review conversation (high level):
- Priya Natarajan: "Controller looks reasonable; concerned about eviction fairness across tenants. Please add a unit that asserts eviction order when slice budget is saturated." — Author: "Added eviction-order unit and added comments explaining tenant fairness heuristic." (commit included)
- Marcus Lee: "Telemetry looks great, but slice export cardinality could be high for large clusters. Can we limit to top N hot slices?" — Author: "Implemented sampling cap and documented the cap; default is top 500 slices by evictions across window; configurable via telemetry config." (commit included)
- Jules Park: "Ops rollback API looks powerful; ensure RBAC and audit logs are present." — Author: "Added RBAC check in soft-rollback handler and audit log entry; updated ops manifest to require management ACL." (commit included)
- SRE acceptance: After canary in a single eu-west rack (observed no SLO regression), we ran a wider canary across eu-west region with throttled ramp; telemetry graphs in docs show reduced fastpath saturation and smoother SLO quantiles.

Rollout & rollback plan: Feature gated behind feature flag runtime.conn_slice.enabled=false by default. Rollout steps documented in docs/operations/connection-slice-throttle.md — initial canary on two noncritical racks, observe slice.* metrics for 30m, then scale to region. If SLO regressions detected, ops can trigger soft-rollback via ops-cli (softrollback --manifest ops/deploy/hotfix-manifest.yaml --grace-window 120s) which will replay previous mapping and drain slices over grace window; this API is non-blocking and returns a rollback_id for audit.

Release notes (for customers): Adds an experimental connection-slicing admission controller to help stabilize regional surges; disabled by default. An ops hotfix provides safe rollback without node restarts. See docs for canary and opt-in.
Experimental: connection-slice throttle mesh for mitigating regional connection storms. Disabled by default. Includes ops hotfix CLI for soft rollback that drains slice mappings without restarting nodes. See docs/operations/connection-slice-throttle.md for canary and rollback procedures.
payload.title: Introduce connection-slice throttle mesh and emergency soft-rollback hotfix

Motivation: multiple SDK teams requested a single source of truth for retry behavior and lightweight streaming ergonomics to reduce duplication and ensure parity across Python/TS/Go. This PR introduces a small, language-agnostic "retry DSL" and a compiler that emits typed bindings and compact runtime profiles for each SDK; it also ships a thin ergonomic pullstream helper in the TypeScript SDK plus compatibility shims for Python and Go. Work done: implemented a declarative retry policy language (backoff schedules, transient classifier predicates, idempotency hints); added a compiler tool (ts-node driven) that generates typed enums and presets for retries; extended the TS SDK with a new PullStream.peekable/resume helpers and a small AsyncCursor type that simplifies backpressure in user code; added a lease-based token provider interface to support short-lived rotating credentials and a small shim to make existing token providers backward-compatible; bumped SDK versions to publish the new artifacts. Scope: the changes are intentionally conservative at runtime: generated retry profiles are advisory to the SDKs, runtime fallback exists to previous behavior if a generated profile is incompatible. The change reduces boilerplate for customers implementing robust retries and makes streaming ergonomics more consistent across languages. Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed by ENG-1593 stakeholders; - [x] Compiler emits TS/Go/Python bindings; - [x] Unit tests for compiler and runtime adapters; - [x] Integration smoke tests against the hosted inference mock; - [x] Changelogs and upgrade notes included; - [x] Version bumps staged for TS@2.4.0, Py@1.9.0, Go@1.5.2 Notes on backwards compatibility: existing SDK consumers keep previous APIs; the new token lease provider is additive and can be gradually adopted. Release considerations: small window for ecosystem publishing required before client teams roll out. See linked Linear tickets ENG-1593 and ENG-1602 for rollout plan and gating criteria.
Asha Bhat: Nice approach using a tiny DSL; can we add a non-regression test that runs the generated Python bindings against the py-sdk CI container?
Rohan Patel (author): Added a quick integration check in tools/retry-dsl/tests/integration.py and wired it into the TS CI matrix so the generated Python stubs are validated. See updated commit c2d1e57.
Liam O'Connor: The lease token provider interface looks good, but we should clarify time skew handling when refreshing tokens under heavy load.
Rohan Patel (author): Added defensive checks and a jittered backoff to the lease provider adapter; documented expected clock skew behavior in docs/sdk/streaming-ergonomics.md.
Priya Reddy: Small nit on naming: AsyncCursor.peek() should be peekNext() for clarity; also please add a short example in the API doc.
Rohan Patel (author): Renamed to peekNext() and added an example snippet in streaming-ergonomics.md. PTAL.
Asha Bhat: CI flaked on a flaky integration test during the first run, reran and green now. Approving once CI is stable.
Liam O'Connor: Approved. I spot-checked generated Go bindings and runtime usage; looks fine.
Added a retry DSL and compiler that generates typed retry profiles for TS/Go/Python SDKs; TypeScript SDK gains ergonomic pullstream helpers (AsyncCursor, AsyncPeekable) and a lease-based token provider interface; minor version bumps: TypeScript SDK v2.4.0, Python SDK v1.9.0, Go SDK v1.5.2. No breaking changes; opt-in features only. See docs/sdk/retry-dsl.md for migration and examples.
Unit tests for compiler and adapters added. Integration verifies generated bindings by invoking a small harness in a python container. Manual smoke test run against hosted-mock validated streaming resume behavior and retry presets. QA checklist: publish artifacts to staging registry and run canary consumer (ENG-1602).

Context: During the Lifecycle Growth Experiments sprint we saw a non-trivial % of first-session failures caused by users attempting a first request without an API key, with the TS SDK surfacing a generic 401/403 or a low-signal fetch error. This PR adds clearer, action-oriented errors for missing/empty keys and invalid/unauthorized keys, including guidance that matches our current onboarding flow (create API key in Console, set env var, retry). What changed: (1) Validate apiKey at client construction time (and before first request) with a dedicated RedwoodAuthError, (2) map 401/403 responses to a RedwoodAuthError with a short remediation message + docs/console links, (3) improve default error text for "Bearer undefined" / empty string cases, (4) update README quickstart snippet to show recommended env var usage, and (5) add unit tests for key edge cases (undefined, empty string, whitespace, revoked key, malformed header). Notes: We intentionally do not log the API key and we avoid echoing request headers in error strings. This is meant to reduce early onboarding frustration and improve activation rate by making the "next best action" explicit. Related: PM-659 onboarding email/console CTA alignment; ENG-10492 activation funnel instrumentation (this reduces noise from accidental auth failures).
Marissa Cole (review): The message is much better. Can we make sure the guidance points to the Console path users actually see during onboarding ("API Keys" under Settings) and not an internal URL? Also please keep the copy short enough for in-console surfaced errors (some users paste errors into support).
Dylan Brooks (author): Good call. Updated links to /console/settings/api-keys and shortened the remediation text to 2 sentences + one docs link. Also ensured the error message is stable and doesn’t include request headers.
Nadia Rahman (review): Please double-check that we don’t accidentally emit a new error type that breaks downstream users catching by name/message. Do we expose a stable code property? Suggest adding error.code = "AUTH_MISSING_API_KEY" / "AUTH_INVALID_API_KEY". Also confirm we don’t include the apiKey value anywhere (even truncated).
Dylan Brooks (author): Added `code` field on RedwoodAuthError with `AUTH_MISSING_API_KEY` and `AUTH_INVALID_API_KEY`. Also added a regression test asserting the message does not contain `Authorization` or `Bearer`.
Nikhil Sharma (review): Love the onboarding alignment. One more suggestion: mention the env var name we recommend in docs. People copy/paste snippets. Also for 403 vs 401, the remediation is the same but the phrasing should avoid implying their key is "wrong" if it’s a permissions issue.
Dylan Brooks (author): Updated copy to say "API key is missing or not authorized" for 401/403, and the README snippet now shows `REDWOOD_API_KEY`. Split messages: missing key is explicit; unauthorized suggests checking key + org/project selection in Console.
Marissa Cole (approval): Approved after link/copy changes.
Nadia Rahman (approval): Approved with code field + no-secret assertions.
Nikhil Sharma (approval): Approved.
TypeScript SDK now provides actionable errors when API keys are missing/empty or unauthorized (401/403), with stable error codes and updated quickstart guidance.

Context and motivation: We need better tenant-level cost recommendations that combine realistic unit-econ projections with quantization safety margins. Current defaults are conservative and require manual tuning. This PR introduces 'econ-lighthouse' — an automation that (a) synthesizes simulated unit-econ projections for a tenant/profile using sampled telemetry, (b) annotates and proposes quantization profiles with estimated quality delta, and (c) exposes a dry-run CLI and telemetry so operators can validate before rollout. Goals: reduce manual tuning time, provide explainable projections, and allow safe opt-in profile suggestions.

What this PR does (single-line summary): Adds an economics projection pipeline + quant-profile annotator, a dry-run CLI, model/tenant feature-flag gating, new telemetry metrics, and a small runtime fallback for conservative application.

Implementation notes: The projection engine (pkg/econ/projection) consumes sampled traces and historical latency/cost buckets to simulate per-token cost under different batching and quant profiles. The quant-profile annotator (pkg/quant/annotator) runs lightweight fuzz tests against a golden subset (5 prompt families) and produces an annotated profile: {profile_id, expected_cost_delta, median_quality_delta, regression_risk_score}. All heavy simulation runs are CPU-bound and scheduled on the existing autoscaler job queue; a short-circuit fast-path returns approximations for interactive dry-runs.

CLI and operator UX: new command 'rw econ inspect --tenant <id> --dry-run --profile-candidates smallfp16,int8-q4' produces a JSON report and summary table. The report includes a deterministic seed so results are reproducible and an explain block that maps the dominant cost drivers (batch shape, prefix reuse, kv-hit-rate). The CLI also supports '--apply=preview' to annotate tenant defaults in the Console without activating them.

Telemetry & observability: Adds metrics 'econ.projection.cost_estimated', 'econ.projection.quality_delta_p50', 'econ.annotator.regression_risk' and a Console dashboard template under Observability -> Economics (prefill). Traces include sampling tags to correlate with existing 'prefill' and 'batching' spans.

Safety and rollout: Feature-gated by tenant flag 'econ_lighthouse_v1'. Default behavior for non-opted tenants is unchanged. For opt-in tenants we create a Console preview and a gradual rollout that starts as a suggestion (no auto-apply) and can be promoted after manual QA. We built a fallback so if the annotator reports regression_risk > 0.12 we keep the tenant on existing profile.

Testing: unit tests for projection math (pkg/econ/projection/*_test.go), integration test that runs a dry-run against a recorded tenant trace (ci/integration/econ_dryrun.sh), and a small E2E smoke test in perf-canary that verifies CLI output shape. Performance: simulated workloads (internal perf harness) show a median simulated per-token cost reduction of 9.7% when applying suggested profiles for high-prefill workloads; median quality delta stays within 1.8 BLEU-equivalent units on our evaluation prompts.

Checklist:
- [x] Projection engine implementation and API
- [x] Quant-profile annotator with golden prompt check
- [x] Dry-run CLI and JSON report output
- [x] Telemetry metrics and Console dashboard template
- [x] Unit/integration tests and CI job
- [x] Feature flag + safe fallback
- [ ] Long-running tenant canary (follow-up ticket created)

Backward compatibility and risk: No changes to existing runtime behavior unless tenant enables the feature. Annotated profiles are suggestions by default; the apply path is opt-in. The main risk is false-negative regression_risk estimates for rare prompt families; we mitigated by conservative thresholds and requiring manual promotion for now.

Follow-ups: ENG-2319 track canary rollout and long-running validation; ENG-2410 introduce automated A/B quality checks for promoted profiles.

Related: references to prior heuristics work and prefilling telemetry (internal docs link: https://intranet.redwood/econ-lighthouse)


Noah: 'Great shape — can we make the regression_risk scoring function pluggable? I want to iterate with SRE.'
Maya: 'Made the scoring strategy an interface, default implemented in annotator/strategy.go; added a TODO to experiment with ensemble scoring in follow-up.'
Sofia: 'CI integr test flaked once on the perf-canary; re-ran and passed.'
Ethan: 'Ensure dashboard contains links to trace IDs for failed dry-runs — added sample trace tags in telemetry.'
Author response: 'Addressed comments: made scoring pluggable, added extra trace tags, adjusted fallback threshold to 0.12 per discussion.'

Adds typed SDK support for model metadata + release notes/changelog endpoints (including pagination helpers) and an example showing how to render a simple customer-visible changelog feed.
Context: As part of the model metadata schema v1 + automated changelog work, we need first-class SDK affordances so customers can programmatically query: (1) model/version metadata (compatibility, deprecations, availability) and (2) generated release notes for a given model/version or time window. This PR adds TypeScript types that mirror the control plane responses, plus a small client wrapper (fetchers) and examples.

What’s included: 1) New public types (generated-by-hand for now, not OpenAPI-generated yet): ModelVersionMetadataV1, ModelArtifactRef, DeploymentAvailability, ReleaseNoteEntry, ReleaseNoteCategory, ReleaseNoteSeverity, and RedactionLevel (public-only; internal fields are not represented). 2) New client surface: changelog.getReleaseNotes({ model, after?, before?, limit?, cursor? }) and changelog.getModelVersionMetadata({ model, version }) with cursor-based pagination helper. 3) Error handling: maps 401/403/404 into existing RedwoodError types; adds a discriminated union for “not available in this deployment” vs “model/version not found”. 4) Docs/examples: adds examples/release-notes-feed.ts and updates README snippet for “Change visibility / Release notes”.

Notes/constraints: - This intentionally only models the public/customer-visible fields. Internal-only notes are not exposed in the SDK types even if a user is an admin in Console; the API’s redaction layer remains the source of truth. - Field names follow the API payloads (snake_case) but we expose camelCase accessors via a lightweight transform to keep the rest of the SDK consistent. - We did not add any dependency on the Console endpoints; this uses the control plane endpoints intended for SDK consumption.

Testing: - Unit tests for cursor pagination and response transforms. - Contract-ish tests using recorded fixtures from staging (sanitized). - Example runs in CI to ensure examples compile.

Rollout: Safe to ship as a minor version. No existing API behavior changes; only additive exports.

References: - ENG-9821 (schema) - ENG-9823 (changelog generator internal API) - Docs PR will reference the example in the “Release notes API” guide once endpoints are GA.

Nora Ahmed (author): Updated enum values to match the release note taxonomy (security, breaking, performance, quality, bugfix, deprecation). Also removed the internalNotes placeholder type and added a comment explaining why we intentionally omit internal fields.
Sahana Iyer: Pagination helper returns {items, nextCursor}. Could we standardize naming to match other list() calls in the SDK? Also please add a unit test for empty-page behavior.
Nora Ahmed (author): Renamed to {data, nextCursor} to match existing listResponses and added a test for empty page + missing cursor.
Wei Chen: Example is helpful. Please ensure wording in README doesn’t promise notifications/subscriptions yet. ‘Poll for updates’ is fine.
Nora Ahmed (author): Adjusted README to say customers can query/poll release notes; removed mention of webhooks/notifications.
Jada Williams: One concern: the client is doing snake->camel transform. Please keep raw response accessible for debugging.
Nora Ahmed (author): Added an optional { raw: true } flag to return the unmodified payload for both endpoints, documented in JSDoc, and added a test to ensure no transform occurs when raw=true.
Dylan Brooks: Looks ready. Please bump minor version and add changelog entry for the SDK release.
Nora Ahmed (author): Version bump + CHANGELOG.md entry added. Marked as minor since additive exports.
Coordinate with docs team to reference the example in public docs once release notes endpoints are GA.
After OpenAPI spec is finalized for metadata v1/changelog endpoints, revisit generating these types instead of hand-maintaining.

Motivation: teams using different Redwood SDKs observed small timing mismatches where near-expiry tokens caused sporadic 401s during stream reconnects and short-lived polling. This PR standardizes the refresh window semantics across TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs, and introduces a lightweight pull-stream adapter for iterator-style consumers to ease migration from callback-based streaming APIs. Changes are intentionally conservative: we keep the default refresh window behavior but expose a single cross-SDK configuration option (credentialRefreshMarginMs) and provide a compatibility shim for older consumer patterns. The PR also bumps the TypeScript SDK to v1.9.0, coordinates matching compatibility bumps in the Python and Go SDK packages, and adds migration notes.
feat: expose credentialRefreshMarginMs and centralize token refresh timing (types & runtime)
chore: add pull-stream adapter and iterator helper for streaming responses
fix: guard reconnect path for rapid reauth races during stream handoff
chore(release): bump ts sdk to v1.9.0 and pin compat notes for py/go
Jordan Patel: Nice consolidation. Can we add a short unit test that simulates near-expiry token and ensures stream reconnect doesn't throw?
Maya Chen: Added a new test in stream/reconnect.test.ts that fast-forwards the clock; it covers the race condition Jordan called out.
Samira Okafor: The public API change looks fine, but please surface the credentialRefreshMarginMs in the typed config docs and the examples.
Maya Chen: Updated docs/migrations and examples/streaming to show setting the new option; left default unchanged to preserve ergonomics.
Lucas Nguyen: LGTM after the e2e run re-pass. Ensure we call out the shim in the Go release notes so internal infra can coordinate.
Maya Chen: Noted; added a short paragraph in CHANGELOG and docs/migrations describing the Go shim and recommended upgrade path.
- SDK: TypeScript v1.9.0 - exposes credentialRefreshMarginMs (default preserved) and adds pull-stream adapter for iterator-style consumers.
- Fixes a reconnect race where near-expiry tokens could cause transient 401s during stream handoff.
- Coordinated minor bumps and a compatibility shim in Python and Go SDKs to align refresh semantics.
- Migration docs added: docs/migrations/2026-03-token-refresh.md
Backport not required; change is non-breaking by default. Teams using custom short refresh windows should validate their margin. The Go shim intentionally leaves behavior unchanged unless the new compat flag is enabled.

Summary: Aligns TS SDK authentication environment variables and resolution precedence with the Python and Go SDKs as part of the SDK parity initiative. This change also introduces deprecation warnings for legacy env var names to reduce "works in TS but not in Python" issues and to standardize support/debugging instructions. Motivation: Support + SE feedback shows customers frequently set different env vars per language and are surprised by which value wins when both are present. We’re standardizing on a single set of env var names and a single precedence order across SDKs, with security-reviewed guidance to avoid leaking secrets in logs/errors. New behavior (matches Python/Go): Precedence order: (1) explicit client option (apiKey / bearerToken) (2) environment variables (standard names) (3) none -> throw a typed auth error. Standard env vars supported: REDWOOD_API_KEY for API key auth; REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN for bearer token auth; REDWOOD_BASE_URL remains as-is for endpoint override. Legacy env vars (still accepted, now deprecated with a warning): RW_API_KEY, REDWOOD_API_TOKEN, REDWOOD_TOKEN. If multiple env vars are set: explicit client option always wins; between env vars we prefer REDWOOD_API_KEY over deprecated key vars; bearer token is only used when api key is not present (same as other SDKs). Deprecation warnings: Warnings are emitted once per process (guarded) and do not print secret values. We include guidance text pointing to the migration notes and the new standard names. Error handling: Missing credentials now throws RedwoodAuthError with message safe for logs; error includes "source" metadata (explicit/env/none) but never includes the credential string. Tests: Adds unit coverage for precedence, deprecation warning behavior, and non-leakage. Also updates the README auth snippet to reference REDWOOD_API_KEY / REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN consistently. Notes: This PR intentionally does not change header formats beyond existing behavior (Authorization: Bearer ...). This also keeps backwards compat: legacy env vars will continue to work for at least 2 minor versions; removal will be tracked separately after customers have had time to migrate. Related: ENG-5122 (env var alignment), INT-1182 (better error metadata / support triage).
High-level changes: packages/sdk/src/auth/resolveAuth.ts (new centralized resolver with explicit/env precedence); packages/sdk/src/client.ts (wire auth resolver into client construction and error surface); packages/sdk/src/errors.ts (add RedwoodAuthError w/ safe messaging + source metadata); packages/sdk/src/constants/env.ts (standard + legacy env var names and warning text); packages/sdk/test/auth/resolveAuth.test.ts (new tests); README.md (auth snippet + env var names). Small illustrative snippet (resolve order): `if (opts.apiKey || opts.bearerToken) return { kind: 'explicit', ... }; const apiKey = env('REDWOOD_API_KEY') ?? envLegacy('RW_API_KEY'); const bearer = env('REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN') ?? envLegacy('REDWOOD_TOKEN'); if (apiKey) return { kind: 'env', scheme: 'api_key' }; if (bearer) return { kind: 'env', scheme: 'bearer' }; throw new RedwoodAuthError('Missing Redwood credentials. Set REDWOOD_API_KEY or REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN, or pass apiKey/bearerToken explicitly.');`
Ibrahim Khan (requested changes): "Can we ensure the precedence matches the draft standard exactly? Specifically explicit param > env var, and within env vars prefer standard names over legacy. Also please make the deprecation warning one-time; we don't want spam in server logs." Dana Lo (author): "Updated resolver to prefer standard vars and added a `warnOnce()` guard keyed by env var name. Added tests for both." Marcus Lin (security): "Please confirm we never log the actual secret or include it in thrown errors, even in debug mode. Also avoid printing the full env var value in deprecation warnings." Dana Lo: "Confirmed; warnings reference only the env var name. Added regression test asserting error messages do not contain any provided credential string." Sabrina James (Python/examples): "Can you align naming with Python: REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN (not ACCESS_TOKEN)?" Dana Lo: "Yes, updated to REDWOOD_BEARER_TOKEN and marked older TS-only aliases deprecated." Mateusz Zielinski (Go): "In Go we treat bearer token as fallback if API key is present. This matches your current approach—thanks. One nit: can we include a short note in the warning pointing to migration notes?" Dana Lo: "Added link text to docs path and kept it generic for published docs." Final approvals: Ibrahim Khan (approved), Marcus Lin (approved after security nit), Sabrina James (approved), Mateusz Zielinski (approved).

Motivation: Customers repeatedly ask for clearer cancellation and credential semantics when writing streaming consumers across languages. Current SDKs each have partial support (Py: cancel via iterator.close(), TS: AbortSignal in some layers, Go: Context usage inconsistent). This PR harmonizes three ergonomics areas: 1) a first-class cancelable async iterable/iterator contract in Python and TypeScript and a context-aware stream receiver/sink in Go; 2) a prioritized credential fallback chain that makes token providers composable and deterministic across SDKs; 3) small ergonomic factory helpers and typed error classes to reduce surface area for application code. What this does (summary): - Python: introduces CancelableAsyncIterator and AsyncIterableCursor that accept an explicit CancellationToken (backwards-compatible default omitted). Adds improved SessionFactory.with_credential_chain(...) helper, typed sdk.errors.StreamCanceled and sdk.errors.AuthUnavailable. Bumps py SDK minor to 0.18.0 in packaging metadata. - TypeScript: adds AsyncIterable<T> helpers that accept AbortSignal at creation and expose a cancel() helper for ergonomic callers. Unifies credential fallback chain into CredentialCascade class with well-documented priority: explicit credential > env > metadata > delegate-providers. Bumps TS SDK to 2.7.0. - Go: makes StreamReceiver and StreamSink context-aware (Context passed to Open/Recv/Close) and introduces CredentialChain type mirroring behavior of other SDKs. Bumps go SDK module to v1.6.1. Cross-SDK notes: the credential chain is pluggable and exposes a simple interface (GetToken(ctx)) implemented in each SDK so teams writing multi-language clients can rely on the same semantics. Backoff/retry defaults: tune the default retry/backoff profile used by streaming reconnects to be slightly more conservative (lower retry attempts, longer exponential base) to reduce cascading load during infra flaps. Telemetry: adds a small heartbeat event for long-lived streaming sessions to help identifying leaked consumers. Migration notes: default behavior is backwards compatible; customers only see change if they explicitly opt into the new helpers or pass cancellation tokens/AbortSignals/Contexts. Linear references: ENG-1456 (sdk streaming ergonomics), ENG-1902 (credential fallback implementation).

Motivation: Consumers reported subtle incompatibilities between the TypeScript streaming API and the Python/Go SDKs when token refresh or credential handoff happened mid-stream. The root cause is duplicated token-refresh logic in streaming connectors and an ergonomic surface that exposes a low-level push/callback model that is hard to handle in some runtimes. This PR centralizes orchestration for streaming auth, introduces a light ergonomic downgrade path (async-generator wrapper) for older runtimes and establishes a cross-SDK compatibility contract. Scope: 1) Add a small 'AuthOrchestrator' in the TS SDK that owns token refresh logic for streaming connectors and exposes a consumer-friendly hook for credential handoff. 2) Provide an optional async-generator wrapper (streamToAsyncGenerator) that downgrades push-style streams to async generators for parity with Python's async iterator and Go's channel-based helpers. 3) Coordinate version bump and compatibility notes for Python/Go SDK teams (see linked linear tasks). 4) Add tests and update examples. Checklist: - [x] Implement AuthOrchestrator with pluggable token provider adapter - [x] Implement async-generator downgrade helper + docs - [x] Add unit + integration tests covering mid-stream token rotation and reattach semantics - [x] Update changelog and bump package version to 1.14.0 - [x] Coordinate companion PRs in python & go (ENG-1124, ENG-1188) Compatibility considerations: the orchestrator is opt-in; existing consumers keep current behavior unless they enable orchestration via the client config option 'streamAuth: { orchestrate: true }'. Default remains conservative (no behavioral change). When enabled, the orchestrator will: - serialize token refresh so only a single token refresh occurs concurrently for multi-connection use cases - expose an idempotent 'attachCredentials' hook called by the runtime before resume attempts - fallback to the async-generator wrapper if the consumer passed a legacy callback consumer or if runtime is Node 12 (older environments). Cross-SDK coordination: we worked with the Go and Python SDK owners to land companion adapters: python PR #533218 adds the generator-first helper; go PR #150412 exposes a channel shim; this TS change intentionally mirrors API ergonomics rather than copy implementation details to keep each SDK idiomatic. Risks & mitigations: - potential regressions in high-throughput streaming workloads: mitigated by a micro-benchmark and opt-in flag - complexity for custom credential providers: addressed by a documented adapter interface and two shipped adapters (default KMS adapter + in-memory token cache) - flakiness in CI: added test harness that can simulate mid-stream credential swap and network hiccups Notes for reviewers: please pay attention to the attachCredentials semantics in AuthOrchestrator.attachForResume; the idempotency guarantees are essential for safe retries. Also verify the async-generator wrapper properly passes back errors and final metadata in the same shape as the native push stream. Release notes: bump TS SDK to v1.14.0; add 'streamAuth.orchestrate' opt-in flag and 'streamToAsyncGenerator' helper; backwards compatible by default.

Summary: Introduces a compact 'AuthOrchestrator' surface for TypeScript SDK that centralizes credential rotation, telemetry tags, and a lightweight retry preset family optimized for streaming and low-latency token refresh patterns. This PR also adds explicit stream lifecycle hooks (warmup/drain) to the pullstream surface to improve ergonomic signal points for consumers. Motivation: customers integrate SDKs in long-lived streaming flows; token rotation, backoff tuning, and observability hooks were implemented ad-hoc across languages. This change standardizes behavior and provides small, backward-compatible ergonomics improvements across TS, with companion shims added to Go/Python to preserve parity. What changed (high level): - New AuthOrchestrator class (sdk/typescript/src/auth/orchestrator.ts): encapsulates credential chain, prefetch, and short-circuit fallback profiles. - New retry presets: "fast-fail", "balanced", "latency-optimized" and corresponding config schema in sdk/typescript/src/retry/presets.ts. - Pullstream lifecycle hooks: onWarmup(), onDrain(), and an optional healthHint() in sdk/typescript/src/stream/pullstream.ts. - Telemetry: SDK now attaches standardized tags (auth.source, auth.fallback_used, stream.warmup_ms) to internal spans and metrics. - Backcompat shims: minimal wrapper in sdk/typescript/src/auth/compat.ts to surface previous AuthManager API. - Cross-sdk parity: small adapter implementations added to redwood-sdk-go and redwood-sdk-python directories to keep behavior aligned while preserving idiomatic language surfaces. - Docs: docs/upgrade-auth.md + examples/polylang/ts/stream-warmup.ts updated. - Version bumps: typescript SDK -> 1.7.0, python SDK companion -> 0.9.3 (shim-only), go SDK companion -> 1.4.2 (shim-only). Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-2911) reviewed and linked - [x] TS unit + integration tests added - [x] Go/Python shims added and smoke-tested against staging runtime - [x] Telemetry fields documented - [x] CHANGELOG updated Migration notes: Consumers should: - Prefer AuthOrchestrator where long-lived streams use token rotation; short-lived calls can continue using legacy credential helpers. - Replace ad-hoc setImmediate warmups with onWarmup() when using pullstream helpers for better latency priming. - Use the new 'balanced' retry preset for most streaming workloads; 'latency-optimized' for p99-sensitive realtime routing. Compatibility: Existing APIs remain supported via compat.ts wrappers; calls that relied on internal AuthManager internals might need small refactors. Testing & CI: All CI jobs passed after 2 reruns (flaky e2e due to network emulator). Manual staging test: ran 10k short-lived and 50 long-lived streams concurrently against the staging runtime; observed ~12% fewer token refresh errors and 8% lower median stream warmup time when using orchestrator+balanced preset. Notes: kept the TS surface intentionally small and ergonomic; Go/Python change sets are shim-only and will be expanded in subsequent PRs dedicated to each repo.

Motivation: converge ergonomics and auth behavior across TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs while preserving backwards compatibility. This PR introduces a session-fusion pattern for credentialed streaming: a lightweight Session object that multiplexes token refreshes and heartbeat/lease renewals across parallel stream iterators, plus ergonomic typed-async-iterable sugar for JS consumers. The change addresses three recurring pain points: (1) repeated token fetches when consumers open many short-lived iterators, (2) awkward async iterator ergonomics for users that want pull semantics plus cancelation hooks, and (3) mismatch with the session/lease primitives shipped in Go/Python that caused subtle parity bugs in failover and canary rollouts. Key changes: new SessionFactory and SessionLease adapter (TS only public types), Session-aware StreamConnector that reuses a single in-flight refresh promise and exposes warmUp() for prefetching credentials, AsyncStream.from() convenience wrapper returning a typed AsyncIterable with built-in cancel() and pause() hints, and a compact fallback credential provider chain consistent with other SDKs. Backwards compatibility: consumers that pass a plain credential provider keep the same call signatures; new behavior is opt-in via passing SessionFactory or by bumping the ClientOptions.sessionConfig. Checklist: ensure cross-SDK tests green (done), add TypeScript doc examples (done), update changelog and bump package to v2.7.0 (done), add telemetry tags for session id and lease renewals (done).
Mariana: Nice design, can we avoid exposing lease internals on the top-level Session type? Asha: Updated — kept lease methods on an internal SessionLease but exposed warmUp()/id() on Session for observability. Ethan: Tests look good but add an integration test for rapid open/close of 50 iterators — discovered a race that caused double-refresh. Asha: Added test and fixed the race by centralizing the refresh promise and gating lease renewals behind a single compare-and-swap. Sofia: Please add a short note about telemetry cardinality; otherwise LGTM. Asha: Added telemetry tags and a short section in docs. Mariana: Approved. Ethan: Approved with comment resolved. Merge: squash and merge after CI passed.
v2.7.0: Introduces SessionFactory and session-fusion primitives for credential multiplexing across streaming iterators, ergonomic AsyncStream typed helpers (cancel/pause), improved cross-SDK parity for session/lease behavior, and telemetry tags for session id & lease renewals. Opt-in via ClientOptions.sessionConfig; no breaking changes expected.

payload.body: Summary: Introduces a small, extensible service (CostSmith) that generates tenant-aware prefill seed profiles and an online quantization autocalibrator that recommends safe quant profiles per-tenant and per-workload. Motivation: many customers see large variance in unit economics across tenants; one-size-fits-all batching/quant defaults either waste budget or regress quality. CostSmith uses lightweight workload fingerprinting + conservative RL-inspired annealing to propose batch/cache/quant presets that respect latency SLOs and a user-configurable cost budget. This PR wires CostSmith into the optimizer pipeline, adds a simple CLI for on-demand seeding, and exposes a telemetry contract for future offline analysis. Key capabilities: 1) seed profile generator: samples recent traces, computes latency/cost shape signatures, and emits 3 candidate prefill/batch templates (conservative, balanced, aggressive) with safety bands; 2) quant autocalibrator: runs short microbench sequences using shadow variants (int8/4-bit candidates) and uses a loss+latency penalty to pick the highest-compression profile that passes quality thresholds; 3) tenant warmstart: persists best-known profile per-tenant and uses it as a warmstart for new workloads; 4) rollback guards: automatic canary and fallback to base model if steady-state token-level regression is detected; 5) CLI: costsmith seed --tenant <id> --budget <tokens-per-hour> and costsmith apply --dry-run; 6) integratation points: optimizer pipeline hooks, Redwood Console feature flag, and a telemetry schema. Checklist: - [x] design doc attached (Linear ENG-2201) - [x] unit tests for profile generator and quant comparator - [x] integration smoke test with optimizer pipeline - [x] telemetry schema registered - [x] feature-flag gating and docs stub - [x] e2e canary run in benchmark-lab (green) Related work: builds on PrefillSampler (ENG-1210), econ-autotuner prototypes, and the quant-sentinels experiments (see linked linear items). Commits (summary): - Add CostSmith core service and CLI scaffold - Implement seed profile generator and workload fingerprinting - Add quant autocalibrator harness and shadow runner - Persist tenant profiles in lightweight key-value store - Hook CostSmith into optimizer pipeline via policy registry - Add unit and integration tests - Register telemetry schema and add console feature toggle Files changed (high level): - services/costsmith/* (new): core service, CLI, tests - optimizer/policy_registry.py: hook to call CostSmith for fresh tenants - infra/kvstore/tenant_profiles.py (new): small persistence shim - telemetry/schemas/costsmith.yaml (new) - console/feature_flags.yaml: register feature - benchmark-lab/playbooks/costsmith-smoke.yaml (new) - docs/operators/costsmith.md (new) Review thread summary: - Asha Ghosh (reviewer): requested clearer SLO reasoning and suggested adding a percentile-based rollback trigger. Response: updated quant comparator to include 95th/99th latency buckets and added a configurable percentile rollback guard. - Marco Rivera (reviewer): asked for more conservative default budgets and explicit per-tenant opt-out. Response: added tenant opt-out flag and lowered default aggressive template budget by 30%. - QA (Rina Patel): reported flaky microbench in CI on AMD instances; we added platform-guard to skip that bench on AMD runners and extended retries. - Security (Jude Okafor): reviewed persistence shim; requested encryption-at-rest note added to docs. CI summary: - unit (linux): pass - unit (macos): pass - integration (benchmark-lab): pass - lint: pass - e2e (smoke): pass - perf-regression: amber (one tokenization variance); investigated and accepted as noise; perf job re-run passed Merge outcome: merged via squash on 2026-02-25 after two approvals. Migration notes: consumers of optimizer policy registry should expect optional callbacks; the CLI and feature flag are off by default. Backwards compatibility: no breaking API changes; tenant_profiles storage uses a new keyspace but that is additive. Rollout plan: feature-flag gated rollout to 10% tenants for 48h, then 50% after smoke metrics OK. Monitoring: new dashboards added under Console -> Cost Optimization -> CostSmith (tokens saved, candidate profile acceptance rate, rollback events).

Motivation: Multiple SDKs had divergent token refresh/rotation helpers and different streaming consumer primitives (Iterator vs callback vs channel). This leads to duplication when implementing cross-language examples and causes subtle replay/ordering bugs in the Typescript consumer. This PR standardizes the credential lifecycle surface and introduces a compact, ergonomic stream consumer abstraction (StreamCursor) with consistent semantics across Python/TS/Go. Goals: 1) single TokenLifecycle contract that SDKs can implement or wrap around existing credential providers, enabling predictable refresh/backoff behavior and a single place for metrics; 2) a small, typed StreamCursor API that unifies 'resume' semantics, on-done/error hooks, and backpressure hints; 3) maintain backwards compatibility where feasible and provide clear migration paths for any unavoidable type renames in TS; 4) bump SDK minor versions and add telemetry counters for token refreshes and stream reconnects. Summary of changes: - Core: new TokenLifecycle interface and TokenManager adapter (handles refresh jitter, exponential backoff with max attempts, rotation handoff). TokenManager emits telemetry events (token_refresh.success, token_refresh.fail, token_rotation.count). - Streaming API: introduced StreamCursor<T> (sync/async variants where appropriate). Small runtime adapters added to keep old stream helpers working (deprecated wrappers that forward to StreamCursor). - Typescript: renamed public type StreamConsumer -> StreamCursor and introduced a compatibility shim exported as alias for two releases; however compiled types change is a breaking surface for strict TypeScript users. - Python: added token_manager.TokenLifecycle ABC, contextmanager helper (token_manager.refresh_context) and small change to StreamingClient.subscribe return type (iterator -> StreamCursor). Backwards-compat wrappers included. - Go: added credentials.TokenLifecycle interface and a thin ring-buffer based cursor implementation for channels. - Tests: added cross-SDK conformance tests (where possible in monorepo), unit tests for token backoff and stream resume, integration test emulating transient auth failures and forced reconnects. - Docs: migration guide added to SDK CHANGELOGs and a short example showing token rotation + stream resume. Related: references SUP-4921 (customer reported stream stalls after token rotation) and ENG-7321/ENG-7387 (design work).

Maya Patel (author): Good point — added an injectable Clock interface and defaulted to system monotonic time. Updated tests to use fake clock.

Maya Patel: Added a compatibility export (type alias + runtime shim) and marked it deprecated in CHANGELOG. Kept the core docs focused on StreamCursor.
Connor Blake: Observability looks great, one nit: use counter names with "sdk." prefix to match existing telemetry conventions.

Ethan Zhou: Approve after you add a short migration snippet to the top-level README and confirm type alias in TS exports.

- Introduced TokenLifecycle (TokenManager) to centralize credential refresh/rotation and emit telemetry.\n- Added StreamCursor as the unified streaming consumer primitive with resume/backpressure semantics.\n- Typescript: StreamConsumer renamed to StreamCursor (compat alias provided for one release). Strict TS users may need to update imports.\n- SDK version bumps: typescript -> 0.24.0, python -> 0.15.0, go -> v0.8.0.\n- Added integration tests that cover token rotation and stream resume scenarios.\nMigration: See docs/sdk-migration/streaming-token-rotation.md for examples. Motivation: customer incidents and internal integrations exposed inconsistencies in how the Python/TS/Go SDKs handle streaming cancellation and retry semantics. This PR introduces a small, explicit 'atomic stream cancel' API surface to avoid partial drain races, and harmonizes retry profile names and defaults across SDKs to make cross-language behavior predictable for production systems. The change set includes: 1) a language-agnostic contract for stream cancellation (CancelToken + finalizer hook) implemented in each SDK, 2) a compact retry-profile DSL (fast, balanced, conservative) with explicit idempotency tiers, 3) small ergonomic shims for async iterables/pull-stream consumers to prefer non-blocking cancel semantics, and 4) coordinated version bumps for the three SDKs. Backwards compatibility: the old cancel/abort helpers are retained as thin wrappers that emit a deprecation warning for one release cycle; retry profile aliases are accepted for backward compatibility by mapping legacy names to the new DSL. Migration notes: consumers who relied on synchronous stream close side-effects should switch to awaiting stream.cancel() in the next release; service-side semantics unchanged. Testing & rollout: feature flagged in runtime to allow staged rollouts; integration test matrix added for py/ts/go interop. Checklist: implement API in each SDK, add interop tests, document new retry profiles in release notes, add deprecation notices, verify CI stability across matrix. Impact: safer cancellation semantics reduce incidents from partial KV-cache flush races and make timeouts/retries consistent across client languages.

Motivation: onboarding throughput and reviewer bandwidth are limited during model intake bursts. We need a deterministic, explainable way to rank incoming model candidates so that profiling, human review, and compute-heavy sampling are allocated to models that maximize coverage and mitigate risk earlier. Additionally, onboarding currently emits multiple small changelog fragments (profiling notes, evaluation blips, policy checks) that are hard to consume. This PR introduces two coordinated features: (1) an affinity-aware onboarding scorer that computes a 'priority_score' for each intake based on resource affinity, expected sample cost, usage signal, and sensitivity heuristics; and (2) a release-threader service that stitches micro-changelog pieces into a concise, human-friendly release thread for the model record and for team-facing release notes. Implementation summary: added a new scoring module (src/onboard/affinity_scorer.py) implementing a configurable weighted scoring pipeline; introduced a DB migration to persist priority_score and score_metadata (migrations/20250210_add_priority_score.sql); new API endpoints (/onboard/priority, /release-threader/compose) and a background worker that enqueues prioritization jobs and composes threads; small changes to the intake pipeline to emit canonical micro-changelog fragments (src/onboard/micro_changelog_writer.py); release-threader templating and heuristics live in services/release_threader/ and include rules to collapse low-signal fragments into an "appendix" section. Observability: metrics onboarding.priority_seconds, onboarding.queue_wait_by_priority, threader.compose_duration, and a new tracing span for compose_thread; logs include deterministic score reasons for auditability. payload.body:
## Summary
Standardizes timeout behavior in the TS SDK and fixes AbortController wiring so cancellation/timeouts are applied correctly for both streaming and non-streaming requests. This brings TS into parity with the timeout model ADR and unblocks conformance tests around streaming idle hangs.

Primary changes:
- Introduce a single `timeouts` configuration block (`timeout_ms`, `connect_timeout_ms`, `read_timeout_ms`) at both client level and per-request override.
- Implement portable enforcement using `AbortController` for `timeout_ms` (overall per-attempt deadline).
- Implement streaming **idle** enforcement for `read_timeout_ms` by aborting the request if no bytes/events are observed for the configured period.
- Ensure we create a fresh AbortController/timers per retry attempt (no controller reuse across attempts).
- Document runtime limitations: granular connect/read enforcement is best-effort; browser fetch cannot reliably enforce connect timeouts, and non-streaming read timeout collapses to the overall timeout.

Refs:
- ADR: SDK Timeout Model (v1) — Overall + Connect/Read Timeouts (published 2026-01-24, updated 2026-02-18)
- ENG-5124: TypeScript retry/timeout refactor

## Motivation
Support + internal dogfooding found multiple edge cases where timeouts and cancellation were inconsistent:
- Streaming requests could remain open indefinitely when a corporate proxy half-opened the connection (no more events, no FIN).
- In Node, we were sometimes creating an AbortController but not consistently plumbing it through both request + stream reader.
- User-provided `signal` + SDK timeout signal were not combined, causing either (a) timeouts to be ignored or (b) user cancellation to be dropped depending on call path.

This PR implements the ADR semantics in TS and makes streaming timeout behavior predictable.

## Design / Behavior
### Public API
New standardized option names (client-level):
```ts
const client = new Redwood({
  apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY,
  timeouts: {
    timeout_ms: 60_000,
    connect_timeout_ms: 10_000,
    read_timeout_ms: 60_000,
  },
});
```
Per-request override (RequestOptions):
```ts
await client.responses.create(
  { model: "redwood/llama-3.1-70b", input: "..." },
  { timeouts: { timeout_ms: 30_000 } }
);
```
Legacy compatibility:
- `timeout` (number) is still accepted (client + request options) and maps to `timeouts.timeout_ms`.
- A deprecation warning is emitted once per process when `timeout` is used.

### Defaults (per ADR)
- Non-streaming default: `timeout_ms=60_000`, `connect_timeout_ms=10_000`, `read_timeout_ms=60_000`
- Streaming default: `timeout_ms=600_000`, `connect_timeout_ms=10_000`, `read_timeout_ms=60_000` (idle)

Disabling:
- `timeout_ms=0` disables overall deadline enforcement (no AbortController timer for overall timeout).
- `read_timeout_ms=0` disables streaming idle enforcement.

### Streaming semantics
- `timeout_ms` is the max wall-clock lifetime of the stream (per attempt).
- `read_timeout_ms` is an **idle timeout** between bytes/events. If we do not observe any bytes/events for `read_timeout_ms`, we abort the request and throw a typed TimeoutError (`phase=read`).
- We reset the idle timer on *any* received chunk, not just fully parsed SSE events, to be resilient to proxy buffering behavior.

### Per-attempt semantics (retries)
Timeouts are applied per attempt. The retry layer instantiates a new controller/timers per attempt to avoid accidental cancellation propagation to subsequent attempts. (Total elapsed time bounding remains the responsibility of retry configuration.)

## Implementation details
### Abort signal merging
We now consistently merge user cancellation with SDK timeout cancellation:
- If `AbortSignal.any` exists (Node 20+/modern runtimes), we use it.
- Otherwise we fall back to a small local `mergeAbortSignals()` helper that forwards abort and preserves a best-effort abort reason.

### Overall timeout timer
- For `timeout_ms > 0`, we create an AbortController and schedule a timer that aborts it with reason `{ type: "timeout", phase: "overall", timeout_ms }`.
- We always clear timers in `finally` blocks to avoid leaks.

### Streaming idle timeout
- For streaming responses we wrap the response body reader and maintain a “last activity” timer.
- When the timer fires we abort the controller with reason `{ type: "timeout", phase: "read", timeout_ms: read_timeout_ms }`.
- We capture `x-request-id` once headers are available and attach it to the TimeoutError when possible (idle timeouts happen after headers, so request_id is usually present).

### Error surface
This PR adds/extends `TimeoutError` (SDK error taxonomy work is ongoing in a separate PR, but we need a stable shape here):
- `name`: `TimeoutError`
- `message`: includes `phase` + `timeout_ms`
- `request_id`: included when available
- `phase`: `overall | read | connect` (connect is currently best-effort / not reliably detected in fetch; set only when we can infer)
- `retryable`: `true`

Non-timeout aborts:
- If the user signal aborts, we surface an `AbortError` mapped to our SDK error wrapper and do **not** label as TimeoutError.

### Runtime limitations (documented)
- Browser fetch cannot reliably implement `connect_timeout_ms` at the network layer; we accept the option for parity but do not enforce it.
- For non-streaming requests, `read_timeout_ms` is effectively equivalent to overall `timeout_ms` with fetch; we keep the knob for parity but document that enforcement is via overall deadline.

## Tests
- Unit tests:
  - Non-streaming request aborts after `timeout_ms`.
  - Streaming idle abort triggers after `read_timeout_ms` of inactivity and yields TimeoutError with `phase=read`.
  - Streaming overall abort triggers after `timeout_ms` even if bytes continue.
  - Merged signals: user abort wins and does not get classified as timeout.
  - Retry attempt isolation: first attempt timeout does not cancel subsequent attempt controller.
- Added fixtures for the conformance suite runner to simulate “no more bytes” on stream bodies (Node test harness).

## Docs / Developer notes
- Updated inline option docs + README snippet in this repo to use `timeouts.*` naming.
- Added a short “Timeouts & streaming” section to `docs/streaming.md` explaining idle vs overall and how to disable each.
- Follow-up docs-site PR will mirror these examples across languages (tracked in ENG-5128).

## Rollout / Compatibility
- No API removals in this PR.
- The only behavior change is the introduction of defaults for streaming overall timeout + idle timeout in cases where callers were relying on “infinite” streams. Callers can set `timeouts.timeout_ms=0` and/or `timeouts.read_timeout_ms=0` to preserve the previous behavior.

---

### Changed areas (high level)
- `src/core/requestOptions.ts`: introduce `Timeouts` type + normalization (legacy `timeout` -> `timeouts.timeout_ms`).
- `src/core/fetcher.ts`: consistent AbortController creation per attempt; signal merging; cleanup.
- `src/streaming/sse.ts`: add idle timer + activity reset on chunk reads; improved cancellation semantics.
- `src/errors.ts`: add `TimeoutError` fields + mapping from abort reason.
- `test/timeouts/*.test.ts`: new coverage for overall + idle timeouts and merged signals.

### Notable snippet (illustrative)
We now abort with a structured reason so we can differentiate user abort vs timeout abort:
```ts
controller.abort({ type: "timeout", phase: "read", timeout_ms: readTimeoutMs });
```
and later map to `TimeoutError` in a single place.

## Review conversation (highlights)
**Ibrahim Khan (requested changes)**: “Please align defaults + semantics exactly to the timeout ADR table (60s non-streaming / 10m streaming; idle=60s). Also confirm per-attempt controller creation under retries.”

**Dana Lo (author)**: “Updated defaults to match ADR; added an explicit `createAttemptSignals()` helper used by both non-streaming and streaming paths so retries always allocate a fresh controller + timers.”

**Allison Grant**: “For streaming idle timeout, reset on bytes read rather than parsed events; proxies can buffer SSE frames and we should treat any bytes as activity.”

**Dana Lo**: “Done. Idle timer now resets on each `reader.read()` chunk. Added a regression test where partial SSE frames arrive in multiple chunks.”

**Sahana Iyer**: “CI is running Node 18 in one workflow; `AbortSignal.any` isn’t available there.”

**Dana Lo**: “Added a polyfill merge helper with feature detection; Node 18 job is green now.”

**Henry Cho**: “Make sure the deprecation warning for `timeout` is non-spammy.”

**Dana Lo**: “Warning is once-per-process (guarded by a module-level flag). Also added a doc note showing the new `timeouts` block.”

### Approvals
- Ibrahim Khan: Approved
- Allison Grant: Approved
- Monica Patel: Approved

## CI
- lint: pass
- unit tests: pass
- integration (node fetch streaming): pass
- build: pass

## Follow-ups
- Wire conformance suite “timeout phase” expectations once error taxonomy PR lands (ENG-5126).
- Docs-site parity update (ENG-5128).
TypeScript SDK now supports a standardized `timeouts` config block: `timeout_ms`, `connect_timeout_ms`, `read_timeout_ms`.
Default timeouts are now consistent with the SDK timeout ADR (non-streaming: 60s overall; streaming: 10m overall + 60s idle).
Streaming now enforces an idle read timeout (no bytes/events) via AbortController to avoid hung streams behind proxies.
Legacy `timeout` option is still accepted but is deprecated; it maps to `timeouts.timeout_ms`.
payload.title: Standardize timeout defaults + AbortController plumbing (streaming vs non-streaming)
