Motivation: customers building low-latency streaming integrations reported occasional token churn and token-exchange hot paths that caused transient auth failures and increased first-byte latency for stream consumers. This PR adds a small, opt-in middleware called 'credential-waterfall' that tries credential sources in a staged order with progressive backoff and prefetch; it also introduces stream-prefetch helpers which warm KV cache and prime the runtime's small-batch path to reduce cold-start token latency. Summary of changes: (1) new src/auth/credential_waterfall.ts: an ergonomic middleware that composes multiple credential providers and exposes a lightweight lease/prefetch API; (2) new src/stream/prefetch.ts: helpers for warm-starting streaming requests including a prefetchWindow and jittered backoff policy; (3) compatibility shims: py-shim/credential_waterfall_adapter.py and go-adapter/cred_waterfall_adapter.go to make multi-lang examples show parity; (4) updated examples and tests and bumped package.json to v1.7.0. Compatibility: behavior is opt-in; existing SDK consumers are unaffected unless they enable the middleware via ClientConfig. Migration: documented usage in examples/ts/prefetch-quickstart.md; typical code change is single-line middleware registration. Testing & rollout: unit tests for middleware logic and integration e2e against local emulator added; canary release to 5% of package installs for one week recommended to measure error surface and median first-byte latency. Risks: overly-aggressive prefetch could increase token usage for idle clients; mitigated by default conservative prefetchWindow and telemetry-backed defaults. Related work: ENG-6217 (credential resiliency), SDK-203 (stream perf improvements).
Miguel Santos: Overall this looks good. A couple of small suggestions: use an explicit jitter function and add a diagnostic metric for 'prefetch_tokens_consumed' so we can monitor cost impact.
Asha Kapoor: Added jitter util and new metric in next commit. Kept prefetch defaults conservative (3s window, max 2 tokens) per offline experiment.
Claire Wu: Tests look thorough; can you add a short e2e that exercises a credential failure halfway through the waterfall to ensure fallback latencies stay bounded?
Asha Kapoor: Added e2e in integration harness and updated docs to call that out under 'testing'.
Evan Li: lgtm, please squash commits and update changelog. Verified that Go shim compiles with current adapter interface.
TS SDK v1.7.0: added credential-waterfall middleware for staged credential fallback, stream-prefetch helpers to reduce cold-start latency for streaming consumers, compatibility shims for Python/Go adapters. No breaking API changes; opt-in behavior behind flags.

Motivation: Developers repeatedly ask for a simple, declarative way to express retry semantics (backoff, idempotency predicates, circuit-breaker thresholds) that can be shared across SDKs and surfaced in the Console. At the same time, our streaming APIs are still awkward for generator-based consumers; this PR introduces a small ergonomic wrapper that exposes streams as async generators while preserving the existing pull/push semantics. This change unifies patterns we ship across TS/Python/Go and reduces boilerplate in app code.

What this PR includes: - A new declarative RetryProfile DSL (RetryProfile.fromSpec(spec)) that maps to runtime presets used by our agent/runtime. Profiles support: initial_delay_ms, max_delay_ms, multiplier, max_attempts, retryable_codes, idempotency_hint, and circuit_breaker (failure_threshold, recovery_ms). - An implementation of the retry engine used by the TS SDK that compiles the declarative profile into an execution plan (non-blocking, uses backoff timers tied to the SDK event loop). - A generator-based StreamFacade (createStreamGenerator) that yields chunk objects and handles resume/reauth transparently. The facade supports pause/resume, graceful drain, and an opt-in memory cap. - Cross-SDK compatibility notes and a small coordination shim used by the central session/credential orchestrator (this PR adds TypeScript types and a minimal contract used during coordinated release). - Tests for policy parsing, backoff timing behavior (fast simulated timers), stream resume semantics, and telemetry hooks for backoff/counts. - Docs: inline typed comments + a new short guide in docs/streams/retry-profiles.md (examples) and an updated CHANGELOG entry.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc linked (Linear ENG-4312) - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Cross-SDK coordination note updated - [x] Docs + changelog - [x] Version bump token (v3.7.0 -> v3.8.0)

Summary: This PR adds a lightweight credential fallback queue and a typed PushPull stream facade to the TypeScript SDK to improve streaming ergonomics across intermittent auth errors and to provide clearer backpressure signals for consumers. Motivation: real-world usage shows that transient auth failures (rotating tokens, short-lived KMS calls) cause noisy stream restarts that are hard to coordinate across consumer code. The credential fallback queue defers token refresh attempts, serializes credential handoffs, and exposes a compact retry policy hook. The PushPull stream facade provides a single ergonomic primitive for both push-based chunks from the server and pull-based iteration from the client with typed events and pause/resume hints.

Commits: 1) Add CredentialQueue dispatcher and tests; 2) Implement TypedPushPullStream facade + docs; 3) Wire credential queue into session manager and stream connector; 4) Add integration tests simulating token rollover; 5) Update package.json version to 1.7.0 and changelog.

Motivation: We observed gaps in late-arriving audit events and KMS consent state when services replayed historical data after cluster restarts or cross-region repairs. This PR introduces two coordinated components: 1) a retrospective audit stitcher that consumes audit event fragments, reconstructs canonical operation traces, and writes verified audit envelopes to the audit ledger; and 2) a tenant KMS consent synchronizer that reconciles consent assertions from external KMS providers and emits deterministic residency-aware consent events used by RBACv2 policy decisions. Together these address incidents where audit timelines diverged from KMS consent state and improve forensic completeness. || What this does: - Adds services/audit/retrospective_stitcher service (Go) with a pluggable input backend (Kafka/Blobstore) and deterministic envelope builder. - Adds services/kms/consent_synchronizer (Go) to perform periodic reconciliation, backfill missing consent events, and emit signed consent-assertions to the audit bus. - Extends rbac decision path with a lightweight consent cache and a new consent_verifier middleware used by policy-evaluator. - Adds migration tooling to reprocess a configurable lookback window and a one-off job to retroactively stitch the last 30 days of audit fragments. - Adds observability: new metrics, tracing spans, and labels for tenant/region pin provenance. || Notable implementation notes: - The stitcher uses HMAC-based chunk ordering to avoid reliance on eventual ordering guarantees from the input queues; integrity checks reject replays older than the configured watermark. - The synchronizer supports multiple KMS providers via a provider interface; the initial implementation includes AWS KMS and a noop shim for on-prem HSMs. - To avoid policy regressions during rollout, the consent cache is read-through and supports TTL-based soft-fallback while the synchronizer warms up. - Security: signed audit envelopes include a key-id header; consent events include residency evidence metadata (region-pin and telemetry hash). || Rollout plan: 1) Deploy stitcher and synchronizer in canary region with audit-only mode (no policy enforcement) for 48h. 2) Enable RBACv2 consent_verifier middleware in read-only mode to surface mismatches in tracing/metrics. 3) After validation, enable enforcement behind a kill-switch and gradual traffic ramp. 4) Run retro-stitch backfill job on production ledger with rate-limits; monitor ingestion backpressure and KMS API quotas. || Related: ENG-4921 (consent reconciliation), SEC-731 (audit completeness), SUP-2148 (customer incident: missing consent in cross-region failover).
Jonah Park: Please add an explicit proof of idempotency on the backfill job; replaying the same window should be a no-op. - Addressed in commit e4f7b66, added idempotency marker and dry-run flag.
Luis Romero: How does this interact with existing audit retention compaction? We should ensure we don't resurrect trimmed fragments. - Reply: stitcher skips fragments older than retention threshold and logs a soft-failure metric; added a WARN-level trace when fragments are missing.
Ellen Strauss: KMS quotas are a concern for large tenant fleets. Can we batch consent queries and add exponential backoff? - Reply: implemented batched provider lookups with per-tenant rate buckets and jittered backoff; see providers/aws_kms.go commit.
Security review (automated): Ensure envelope signatures are added and key rotation accounted for. - Action: envelope_builder signs with env-key and key-id header; key rotation handled via key registry lookup.
QA: Found a race in the consent cache TTL refresh under high concurrency; added sync.Once guard and a unit test covering concurrent refresh.
CI initially failed lint on envelope_builder.go (style) and a flaky e2e test; lint fixed and e2e retried — all checks pass (unit, integration, e2e in sandbox, security-scan: SCA ok).
Adds a retrospective audit stitcher to reconstruct and canonicalize fragmented audit events and a tenant KMS consent synchronizer to reconcile consent state across providers. Includes migration tooling to backfill recent history and new RBACv2 consent verification middleware. Rollout behind feature flags; non-breaking by default.
Operators: new Helm values (retrospectiveStitcher.enabled, consentSynchronizer.syncInterval, consentSynchronizer.batchSize). Backfill job cli: tools/migrations/audit_stitch_backfill --lookback=720h --dry-run. Watch metrics: audit.stitcher.missing_fragments, kms.consent.reconcile_errors, rbac.consent.cache_hit_rate.
1) Run dry-run backfill in staging and validate ledger diffs. 2) Schedule canary deployment for 48h. 3) Coordinate with SRE to monitor KMS quotas and set alert thresholds. 4) Add runbook entry under runbooks/audit-stitcher.md.

Motivation: There has been persistent cross-SDK divergence in how streaming consumers handle credential refresh and retries, resulting in token rotation races, duplicated refresh attempts, and awkward ergonomics when migrating examples between TypeScript, Go, and Python. This PR introduces a delegated token channel abstraction in the TypeScript SDK that matches the semantics we iterated on in Go/Python: single-flight refresh, lease-window proactive refresh, and explicit channel handoff for pull and push style streams. Summary of changes: 1) src/auth/delegated_channel.ts: new DelegatedTokenChannel class that accepts a user-provided async refresh handler and exposes a lightweight getToken()/invalidate() API optimized for streaming hot-paths. 2) src/stream/pullstream_adapter.ts and src/stream/pushstream_adapter.ts: adapters updated to consume DelegatedTokenChannel; removed inline refresh logic and consolidated retry logic into a shared stream/retry shim. 3) src/client/stream_client.ts: ergonomic convenience helpers StreamClient.openPullStreamWithDelegatedRefresh() and openPushStreamWithDelegatedRefresh() to reduce boilerplate for common patterns. 4) docs/auth/stream-credential-flow.md: documented the new pattern and migration notes. 5) tests/integration/stream_token_rotation.test.ts: deterministic test harness that simulates short-lived tokens and asserts single-flight refresh under concurrent consumers. 6) package.json bumped to 0.8.0 to reflect API additions. Compatibility and migration: The DelegatedTokenChannel is fully backward compatible with existing tokenProvider callback patterns but is recommended for streaming workloads. We maintained the legacy token callback wrapper (deprecated) and added deprecation warnings for one release cycle. Performance: stream hot-paths were benchmarked; added microbench in perf/bench_stream_token_hotpath.ts showing ~8% lower allocs and ~6% lower p95 latency when using delegated channel due to removed promise duplication. Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed with SDK owners (ENG-9345) - [x] Type-safe APIs with TS declarations and JSDoc - [x] Integration tests covering race conditions - [x] Docs and quickstart updated - [x] Version bump and changelog entry - [x] CI green after two reruns Test notes: initial CI run showed a flaky integration test that reproduced locally when environment timeouts were aggressive; adjusted harness timing and re-ran full suite. Observability: added telemetry events auth.refresh.requested/auth.refresh.completed for monitoring refresh count per-client to make regressions visible in Console. Rollout plan: merged to main behind feature-flag default-on for SDK 0.8.x; recommend library consumers to adopt DelegatedTokenChannel for streaming jobs and migrate examples. Related: aligns TypeScript behavior with redwood-sdk-go@v1.5.3 and redwood-sdk-python@0.12.4 token lease semantics.
Lars: Nice abstraction. A few nits: can we collapse internal single-flight into src/utils/single_flight.ts and add a small benchmark?
Maya: Moved single-flight into src/utils and added microbench; clarified JSDoc on edge cases where invalidate() should be used.
Priya: Integration test looks solid. Please add one assertion verifying no more than one refresh call for 30 concurrent consumers.
Maya: Added assertion and tightened timeouts; integration test now reproduces deterministically in CI harness.
Ethan: Docs are helpful. Consider adding a short migration snippet for existing tokenProvider users.

Motivation: high fragmentation and tenant-level contention in the KV cache continues to cause uneven memory utilization and spill storms during mixed workloads. This PR introduces a thermostat-based eviction strategy that adapts eviction 'temperature' per-tenant, a lightweight micro-tiering layout to reduce fragmentation, and a page-morpher that enables safe, concurrent page resizing to consolidate free space without global pauses. Goals: (1) smoother global memory usage across tenants, (2) predictable spill prioritization aligned with tenant SLAs, (3) reduce tail latency caused by background compaction and large spill batches. This description is intentionally a single continuous string and includes checklist, design notes, and rollout plan. Checklist: - [x] Design doc (ENG-5123) linked and reviewed - [x] Unit + integration tests - [x] Canary plan + feature flag - [x] Perf benchmarks (micro + system) - [x] Operational runbook and dashboard widgets Changes in this PR: - Implemented kv::evictor::ThermostatEvictor with per-tenant temperature curves derived from occupancy, fragmentation_score, and recent spill_rate. The thermostat exposes dynamic target_residency which the scheduler uses to shape eviction batches. - Added kv::layout::MicroTier to categorize pages into hot / soft-warm / cold bands and prefer in-place reuse within bands to avoid fragmentation churn. - Introduced page_morpher module that performs safe concurrent split/merge on page frames to coalesce small free fragments into larger contiguous pages (only on backgrounds threads; no mainline blocking). - Spill prioritizer: ties spill candidates to tenant SLA and throttle score; low-priority spills may be delayed short windows to favor high-SLA tenants and avoid simultaneous heavy IO. - Scheduler integration: background compaction now respects node load and keeps compaction windows aligned with continuous batching to avoid affecting token path latency. - Kernel hinting: allocator exposes small annotations so runtime kernel selector can prefer sub-page-aligned kernels when micro-tiering signals high fragmentation. Why different from prior work: prior PRs focused on eviction rate shaping or slab compaction. This PR combines an adaptive control-loop (thermostat) with structural page morphing and tenant-aware spill policies to minimize reactive global compactions and to provide SLA-aware degradation. Performance summary (canary/dev perf): - Memory reclaimed during mixed gen/embedding workload: 18-24% reduction in active page count (depends on workload skew). - P95 latency on small-request path: improved by ~7% in mixed tenant scenarios due to reduced background compaction spikes. - Spill IO bandwidth smoothing: peak spike amplitude reduced by ~32% in lab runs. - Unit test coverage: +24 tests added covering concurrent morph operations and thermostat hysteresis. Rollout plan: feature gated behind kv.thermostat_evictor boolean; starts in canary for 2 weeks with tenant_profile=conservative, then wider rollout with telemetry thresholds. Ops: added metrics kv.thermostat.temperature, kv.eviction.batch_size, kv.page_morpher.compactions, and a dashboard widget. Backwards compatibility: all behaviour behind feature flag; page format unchanged on-disk so safe for rollback.
Diego: Great direction — please add more telemetry on per-tenant hysteresis so we can reason about oscillation. Also call out worst-case IO amplification in the doc. Lina: Concern about morpher safety under high concurrent loads; request that you add an assertion to ensure no double-free and an integration test with simulated preemption. Omar: Asked for a clearer canary rollback path in the runbook and suggested an additional feature flag to disable page morphing only. Author replies: added kv.thermostat.hysteresis_alpha metric and a test harness that fuzzes concurrent morph ops; made page_morpher opt-in via kv.page_morpher.enabled and added explicit rollback steps in docs. Diego: Verified added metrics and gave a small nit on naming. Lina: Approved after the extra test. Omar: Approved after runbook update.
Introduces thermostat-based eviction for KV cache, micro-tier page layout to reduce fragmentation, and a concurrent page morpher to consolidate fragments. Exposed metrics and feature flags for controlled rollout. Expected memory and tail-latency improvements for mixed-tenant workloads.
Observability: dashboards added under 'KV / Eviction' and alerts for kv.eviction.throttle_rate > 0.2 sustained for 5m. Recommended tuning: start with tenant_profile=conservative and increase thermostat aggressiveness in 5% steps while monitoring kv.thermostat.temperature distribution. Canary ran on region-us-east-2 with 20 tenants and mixed RPS profile. No data plane format changes.

Motivation: Runtime peak GPU memory for long-context and multi-concurrent sessions is dominated by transient activation checkpoints and scratch buffers. Existing arena packing reduces fragmentation but still leaves worst-case peaks when large kernels and KV cache operations coincide. This PR introduces two complementary techniques: 1) a stripe-packed checkpoint layout that packs checkpointed activation fragments into tightly interleaved stripes to reduce per-kernel working set, and 2) a kernel-swap workspace scheduler that defers non-critical kernel workspace allocations and opportunistically swaps packed checkpoint stripes to a hotset buffer during safe epochs. The result is lower transient GPU footprint with negligible throughput impact for typical workloads.

Design summary: The changeset contains: - runtime/allocator/stripe_packer.{cpp,h}: new packing allocator that writes checkpoints as interleaved stripe pages and maintains a compact index. The layout is guided by per-layer size histograms so larger activations are split across stripes to avoid single large contiguous allocations. - runtime/scheduler/kernel_swap_scheduler.{cpp,h}: a lightweight scheduler that tracks upcoming kernel workspace needs (based on compiled kernel descriptors) and introduces micro-delays or pre-eviction of low-priority checkpoint stripes when a high-water mark is predicted. It integrates with existing continuous-batching signals to avoid affecting short-latency requests. - runtime/kv/cache_timing_adjuster.{cpp,h}: small heuristics that shift eager KV prefetchs slightly earlier or later (configurable window) to avoid simultaneous peaks with planned large kernel work. - runtime/config/runtime_flags.yaml: feature flag stripe_packed_ckpt + kernel_swap_mode with three modes (off, conservative, aggressive) to control rollout. - tests/benchmarks/stripe_packed_peak_mem.py: microbench harness used for the numbers below. - doc/ops/stripe_pack_notes.md: operator-facing notes and recommended knob settings.

Compatibility and safety: All new behavior is gated behind runtime flags and default to conservative mode in hosted. The stripe layout preserves on-disk and in-memory checkpoint semantics (index translates to original offsets) so no model changes are required. Kernel-swap scheduler only defers workspace allocations when allocation would otherwise fail the memory check; in conservative mode it only triggers for kernels > 32MB workspace.

Benchmarks and results: Measured on p4d.24xlarge with a long-context transformer (64k tokens synthetic) under mixed small/large batch traffic. Numbers are 95th percentile across runs: - peak GPU working-set: baseline 43.1GB -> stripe+swap 35.3GB (~18% reduction) - sustained throughput: baseline 112 seq/s -> stripe+swap 118 seq/s (+5%) due to reduced GC/evict churn in KV - 99p latency increase: +3ms in aggressive mode, <1ms in conservative mode - KV miss spikes reduced on concurrent load by ~40% (observed in trace samples)

Testing and QA: - Unit tests for stripe_packer allocation/compactness and index correctness. - Integration tests for kernel_swap_scheduler under synthetic batch traces. - End-to-end smoke runs against hosted canary with conservative flags enabled. - Load tests for KV timing behavior in the benchmark lab. CI includes unit + integration + e2e canary checks; initial CI run had a lint failure which was fixed in commit 3.

Rollout plan: 1) Merge to main behind flags. 2) Enable conservative mode in dedicated lab for 2 weeks and monitor peak memory and 95th latency. 3) Enable conservative for a small percentage of hosted traffic. 4) If metrics look good, enable aggressive mode in private clusters where customers opt-in.

Related work: follows on ideas from ENG-2170 (arena packing) but focuses on temporal co-location and ordering rather than raw fragmentation. Also complements KV windowed eviction work (see SUP-512) by smoothing timing interactions.

Checklist: - [x] Design doc reviewed - [x] Unit tests added - [x] Benchmarks present - [x] Feature flags added - [x] Docs for operators - [x] Security review N/A (no external surface change)

Notes: this PR intentionally keeps the stripe packer conservative in memory movement; a follow-up will add a compact-on-idle pass that further reduces fragmentation but requires pinned-memory staging to avoid host<->device thrash.
GPU peak working-set reduced (~18%) via stripe-packed checkpoint layout and dynamic kernel-swap scheduler; KV prefetch timing adjusted to avoid transient spikes; opt-in rollout behind runtime flag
Miguel Alvarez: Can you add more telemetry around stripe hotset residency? Right now we only report index compactions. -- author: added residency gauge and small dashboard in doc
Sofia Chen: Kernel-swap introduces micro-delays; do we have SLO regression risk? Please ensure conservative mode doesn't affect p95 for short contexts. -- author: conservative mode scoped to kernels >32MB and unit tests added
Daniel Park: Suggest making KV timing window configurable via per-tenant override instead of global flag. -- author: added runtime flag as well as per-tenant override config in runtime_flags.yaml

Motivation: client-side ungraceful disconnects (network flaps, browser tab kills, proxy resets) were causing partial-stream state to be dropped and tool/function-call side effects to be replayed or lost when clients reconnected. This PR implements a conservative lifecycle policy and an OpenAI-compat adapter for safer reconnect/resume semantics. Key ideas: 1) Deferred termination window (configurable grace period) where server retains ephemeral session state and outgoing event cache; 2) Idempotent stream tokens + sequence checkpoint published in final events to allow client resume without duplication; 3) Exponential reconnect backoff guidance surfaced via headers and adapter behavior; 4) Safe tool/function-call dedup marked by call-instance id and pre-commit acknowledgement; 5) Server-side fast-fail on stale resume attempts. This change touches runtime stream orchestration, the openai-compat shim, and a small addition to the client-visible headers. Checklist: - [x] implement deferred termination + retention cleanup - [x] add resume token and sequence metadata to streaming protocol - [x] add call-instance id plumbing for tool calls - [x] expose reconnect-backoff hints via X-Redwood-Retry header - [x] unit and integration tests for resume + duplicate suppression - [x] update docs and changelog. This description intentionally combines context and implementation notes in a single continuous string per repo convention.
Miguel Torres (2026-02-22): Nice isolation of the retention timer. Question: what happens if the tool-call had external side effects and the client never reconnects within the window? Should we make the call pre-commit optional?
Asha Patel (2026-02-23): We mark tool-calls with a call-instance-id and a pre-commit flag. By default pre-commit=false for potentially side-effecting calls; operator can opt-in. Added tests to cover post-window cleanup (deleted dedup entry and recorded as orphaned).
Rebecca Lin (2026-02-24): CI flaked on the integration test (sporadic fd leak). Please ensure the session eviction goroutine is bounded and context-cancel safe.
Asha Patel (2026-02-25): Addressed: eviction goroutine now uses time.AfterFunc with explicit cancel and test uses a test clock to avoid flakiness. Re-ran CI (see checks).
Samir Dutta (2026-02-27): Approve after small nits in doc wording. Consider a follow-up for telemetry counters for resume attempts.
Add server-side deferred termination window and resume-token support for streaming API. Improves safety for ungraceful client disconnects and reduces duplicate tool/function-call effects on reconnect. Exposes X-Redwood-Retry header to convey backoff guidance to clients.
Added deterministic tests using a test clock for eviction timing and a mocked upstream for tool-call dedup verification. Integration tests exercise browser-like reconnect (short disconnect + resume) and long disconnect eviction path.
docs/streaming/reconnect.md documents the new resume_token flow, recommended client backoff, and guidance on pre-commit tool-calls. Examples include a TypeScript reconnect client and notes for OpenAI-compatible consumers.

Motivation: CI currently gates prompt-set regressions using aggregate eval metrics which sometimes miss brittle regressions caused by small input perturbations or prompt paraphrases. This PR adds a perturbation-based smoke suite that generates lightweight synthetic variants of critical prompt sets (token-level shuffles, polite/impolite paraphrases, punctuation/noise insertion, and casing variants) and a progressive escalation policy that turns single-test failures into graduated CI outcomes: warn -> soft-fail -> hard-fail, depending on historical stability and threshold breaches. Design: 1) new module perturbation_suite that plugs into existing eval harness runner and exposes a declarative YAML to define perturbation families and generation ratios; 2) lightweight scoring adapter that computes delta-against-baseline using existing metrics (exact match, semantic-similarity embedding score, and response-structure checks) and emits a compact JSON report suitable for CI summaries; 3) escalation controller that consults cohort stability metadata (from the eval registry) and decides when to surface failures as warnings vs blocker failures; 4) CI integration hook that folds the report into GitHub checks UI and optionally annotates affected prompt IDs. Backwards compatibility: the perturbation suite is opt-in and disabled by default for existing repos; project-level config can enable it per-prompt-set and tune escalation thresholds. Rollout plan: enable on Canary projects for 2 weeks, monitor false-positive rate, adjust perturbation families. Docs & links: internal design doc https://linear.app/ENG/1123/perturbation-smoke-suite and example config in docs/perturbations.md. Checklist: - [x] unit tests for generator edge-cases - [x] integration test for CI annotation - [x] documentation and example config - [x] feature flagged in config schema - [x] Linear tasks linked. Impact: expected to catch ~65% of small-paraphrase regressions observed historically during retros, avoid noisy full-eval runs for low-severity regressions, and provide actionable prompt-level traces for owners.

Motivation: Reduce user-facing variance during incremental model swaps while preserving session consistency and enabling automated, telemetry-driven rollback decisions. Existing staged-swap controllers either (a) split traffic at coarse grain and cause session tear, or (b) delay swaps until quiescence which increases exposure time. This change introduces a minibatch-phased-swap controller that performs: (1) short-lived minibatch drains with session-affinity mapping to preserve in-flight conversations, (2) a stateful bisection probe that quickly identifies a problematic cohort via progressive sampling, and (3) an external rollback-oracle that synthesizes model telemetry and prompt-based regression checks to trigger safe immediate rollbacks. Summary of changes: - New controller: controllers/minibatch_phased_swap.go implements phased minibatch handoffs and a state store for session affinity mapping and drain tokens. - Rollback oracle: services/rollback_oracle/ evaluates metric deltas (latency, exact-match regression, hallucination score) and emits deterministic rollback recommendations. - Telemetry hooks: instrumentation added to runtime request traces and per-session tags for cohort bucketing. - E2E smoke harness: test/rollout_simulator introduces deterministic replay scenarios and a small simulated traffic generator for canaries and A/B experiments. - CLI flag and CRD: addons/k8s/crds/minibatchswap.yaml and cli flags to configure minibatch size, max-drift thresholds, and oracle confidence thresholds. Why this is different: mixes short minibatch drains (low blast radius) with session-affinity remapping so ongoing KV-cache-heavy sessions remain consistent, plus a lightweight bisection probe that accelerates failure localization within minutes. Rollback decisions can be automated via the oracle or gated for manual approval. Checklist: - [x] Unit tests for controller state transitions - [x] Integration tests with KV-cache warm/cold scenarios - [x] Canary simulation runs against historical traces - [x] Docs drafted in docs/rollouts/minibatch-swap.md - [x] Security review for session state store (RBAC limited) - [x] E2E run passed on staging CI (rerun after flaky test fix) Backwards compatibility: the controller is opt-in via new CRD; default behavior is off for existing clusters. Migration: no data migration required; sessions not pinned will fallback to default routing. Risk and mitigation: initial canaries run at 0.5% for 2 hours before increasing; rollback-oracle suggestions are logged and only executed automatically if confidence > 0.95 (configurable).
Ethan Liu: This looks promising. Can you explain how the session-affinity store scales? Maya: The store is sharded by ingress node and backed by an in-memory LRU with optional redis-backed persistence for very long sessions; the CRD controls retention TTL. Diego Fernández: We saw a flaky test failure in the first CI run — the simulator seed made a timing race. Can you add deterministic seeds? Maya: Fixed in commit d9f0ab3 and added retries for the timing-sensitive assertions. Priya Rao: Security ok, but add an RBAC note to docs. Maya: Added RBAC snippet and limited service account scope. Diego Fernández: Approved after test fixes. Priya Rao: Approved (security). Merge ready.
Initial pipeline failed due to simulator timing; rerun passed all e2e and unit suites. Lint and vet green. Load tests show <2% p99 latency regression at 1% canary traffic.
Squash-merged into main after approvals. Short release window scheduled; operator docs and quickstart added. Deployed to staging for a 0.5% canary followed by automated analysis from rollback-oracle.
Introduce an opt-in minibatch phased swap controller that preserves session affinity during incremental model swaps, plus a telemetry-driven rollback oracle. Configurable minibatch size, max-drift thresholds, and oracle confidence. Opt-in CRD; defaults disabled.
Default CRD disabled. To enable: apply addons/k8s/crds/minibatchswap.yaml and set controller flags --minibatch-size and --oracle-confidence. Start with minibatch-size=64 and oracle-confidence=0.95. Monitor metrics: rollout.swap.success, rollout.swap.rollback_suggestions, sessions.affinity_misses.
Staging run: first 2-hour 0.5% canary completed with no oracle-triggered rollbacks. The bisection probe isolated a transient cohort with higher hallucination_score and suggested rollback which was manually reviewed and then auto-applied on a subsequent failing run.
Session-affinity store runs under limited SA; no plaintext PII stored. Oracle only receives aggregated metrics and hashed prompt fingerprints. RBAC manifests included and reviewed by security.
1) Apply CRD and deploy controller in staging. 2) Start a small canary (0.5%), run simulator trace against historical traffic. 3) Verify session continuity for long-running conversations and KV cache reuse. 4) Force a regression signal in simulator and observe oracle suggestion and optional auto-rollback. 5) Review logs and metrics for rollback_suggestions and rollouts.swap.* metrics.
This implementation is intentionally conservative: controller is opt-in, oracle auto-actions require high confidence by default, and operator visibility is emphasized with opt-out gates. Future follow-ups: adaptive minibatch sizing, multi-tenant isolation, and a web console visualization for bisection probes.

Context: As part of the cross-SDK streaming/tool calling examples refresh, TS examples and types have drifted from the canonical pattern we’ve standardized in DevEx. This PR updates the TypeScript SDK tool calling types (request + response) and rewrites the examples to match the canonical semantics used across Python/Go/docs: (1) tool definitions live on the request, (2) the assistant can emit one or more tool calls (including parallel calls), (3) tool results are sent back as explicit tool_result messages keyed by tool_call_id, and (4) examples call out that streamed tool-call arguments may arrive incrementally and must be assembled before JSON parsing/validation. Motivation: reduce support load from type mismatches and broken copy/paste snippets (see SUP-18452), and improve parity so docs can share a single mental model. Summary of changes: - Refined TypeScript types: introduce explicit discriminated unions for tool call vs tool result message shapes; normalize tool call fields to canonical names (tool_call_id, name, arguments as string); tighten the response surface so users don’t accidentally treat partial tool args deltas as complete JSON. - Updated examples: rewrite tool-calling example to show a full agent loop: model -> tool_calls -> execute tools (including parallel) -> tool_result messages -> model final answer. - Migration note: previous examples used a simplified/older shape (e.g. tool_call.arguments as object, and “tool” role messages without explicit tool_call_id). Added a README section describing how to update existing code, including a small mapping table and guidance for runtime validation. - Minor ergonomic helpers in examples only (not exported API): helper to accumulate tool-call args across streamed events and a guard for JSON.parse with error messaging. Out of scope: any API redesign of the streaming protocol; this PR is example + typing alignment only. Testing: typecheck passes, examples compile, and tool-calling example runs against Hosted API with a Redwood-verified model. Follow-ups: golden transcript fixtures are tracked separately in ENG-4822; docs-site alignment in redwood-docs PRs will link to this once merged.

- TypeScript SDK: tighten tool-call typing for safer args/results handling in user code.

If you were using the older TS snippet shape: (1) tool call `arguments` should be treated as a string payload (often streamed incrementally), not an object; assemble before JSON.parse. (2) send tool results back as explicit `tool_result` messages containing `tool_call_id` so the model can correlate results (required for parallel tool calls). (3) tool definitions belong on the request (tools: [...]) rather than being implied by client-side code. See docs/migrations/tool-calling-2025-02.md for a mapping table and before/after example.

payload.body:
Motivation: Production streaming workloads showed intermittent first-byte spikes under mixed-latency clients and heterogeneous sequence lengths. Root cause analysis pointed to three interacting problems: (1) the emission window selection was too coarse for bursty arrivals leading to token batching tails, (2) a single-threshold backpressure policy caused under-utilization on GPUs with differing readiness, and (3) cold KV cache fills created transient latency cliffs during warmup. This PR introduces a reactive kernel window selector, a graded backpressure controller, and a KV warmup smoothing mechanism to reduce TTFB and tail latency without regressing throughput.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a reactive windowing layer that chooses kernel batch windows based on observed arrival distribution and per-kernel readiness signals (runtime/kernel/window_selector.*). The selector favors smaller windows when jitter is detected and grows windows adaptively for consistent high-throughput streams.
- Implements graded backpressure: instead of a binary credit/no-credit policy, we expose three levels (green/yellow/red) and allow partial admission for yellow requests to co-schedule low-cost kernels while preserving SLOs for green lanes (runtime/scheduler/graded_backpressure.*).
- Introduces KV warmup smoothing: when a request misses KV cache, we stamp a lightweight warmup hint and spread rewarm work across subsequent microbatches to avoid large synchronous stalls (runtime/cache/kv_warmup_smoother.*).
- Adds metrics, tracing tags, and a small observability dashboard to track window sizes, backpressure state transitions, and warmup amortization.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc and perf spikes reproduced locally (ENG-9123).
- [x] Unit tests for window selector heuristics and backpressure scoring.
- [x] Integration perf bench and canary run (benchmarks/perf/stream_latency_bench.py).
- [x] Added tracing tags and dashboard definitions.
- [x] Kept API backward compatible; no user-visible API changes.

Detailed notes on approach: The window selector uses a short sliding histogram of inter-arrival times and a per-kernel readiness probe (kernel readiness = scheduling queue depth + warm cache score) to compute an "aggressiveness" factor in [0.0, 1.0]. Aggressiveness < 0.35 forces micro-windows (min_batch), >0.7 allows expanded windows up to the kernel's fast path threshold. This reduces token tails by avoiding one-size-fits-all microbatching under bursty producers. The graded backpressure controller scores requests with a cost estimator (sequence length, model weight, kv-miss probability) and maps them to green/yellow/red lanes. Yellow lane requests are admitted opportunistically when kernel slack is detected; if a yellow request would delay guaranteed green requests beyond the SLO, it's buffered. KV warmup smoothing attaches a short-lived warmup token to the first miss and distributes prefetching work into the next N microbatches to turn large synchronous cache fills into smaller amortized work.

Performance: Canary results vs main (internal canary cluster, n=10 runs, mixed seq lengths 16/64/256):
- Median TTFB: -14%
- p95 TTFB: -22%
- Overall throughput at steady state: +1.8% (no regression beyond noise)
- Cold-start single long-seq case: p95 reduced by 30% due to warmup smoothing
These numbers represent typical regressions/improvements observed in our perf harness. We also ran the standard regression battery to ensure no throughput regressions on long-running saturated workloads.

Testing & validation: Unit tests added for scoring logic and warmup amortizer. End-to-end bench added and integrated into nightly CI. Canary deployment ran for 48h with traffic mirroring from prod during low risk window; we tracked per-route SLOs and found no increase in error rates.

Backward compatibility and migration: Changes are internal to the serving runtime; no config schema changes required. We added feature flags (runtime.feature.windowing and runtime.feature.graded_backpressure) guarded behind rollout flags for gradual enablement.

Rollout plan: 1) disable by default on main; 2) enable in dedicated canary; 3) enable progressively on Hosted API for low-traffic regions; 4) promote globally if metrics stable for 72h.

Related work: complements previous microbatch and flush cadence improvements (see linked PRs) but focuses on adaptive selection and cost-aware admission rather than only pacing.

Ethan Morales: Can you clarify how aggressiveness handles pathological oscillation? If arrival rate swings rapidly we risk oscillating window sizes and hurting throughput.
Priya Natarajan: We added a dampening factor and minimum hold time of 80ms for window changes. Commented the code and added a unit test simulating oscillation (see tests/unit/test_window_selector.cpp).
Sofia Kim: Graded lanes look good, but we should ensure metrics expose yellow->green preemptions for debugging. Would also like a tracing span when a yellow request is admitted opportunistically.
Priya Natarajan: Added metrics 'backpressure_lane' and 'opportunistic_admit' tracing span; updated dashboard to show preemptions.
Liam O'Connor: Small nit: use steady_clock in one place for timing. Also add a failure-mode test where KV warmup smoothing is disabled to ensure correctness.
Priya Natarajan: Fixed clock usage and added the failure-mode test. Thanks.
runtime: add adaptive kernel windowing, graded backpressure admission, and KV warmup amortization to reduce streaming TTFB and p95 latency. Feature gated, off by default. See docs/notes/kv-warmup.md for operational guidance.
payload.title: reactive kernel window, graded backpressure, and KV warmup smoothing

Motivation: CI boot time and repeated dependency installs are a significant part of our premerge latency (observed 35-55% of overall presubmit time across languages). This PR introduces two coordinated changes: 1) dep-snapshotter, a small Go service and packager that produces deterministic, compressed dependency artifacts (archives keyed by lockfile hash and platform tag) and a ci pipeline hook to publish them to the internal artifact cache; 2) lint-orchestra, a lightweight controller that coordinates linter runs across packages in a change-set so we avoid duplicate work (e.g., shared tsconfigs, monorepo packages) and allow staged language adapters to opt into fast-paths.

What changed (high level): Added a snapshotter binary (ci/snapshotter/*) that consumes lockfiles (pyproject.lock, package-lock.json, go.sum) and produces a signed tarball with a small manifest. CI pipeline ( .github/workflows/ci.yml and ci/pipeline.yaml ) now attempts to warm the runner workspace from a matching snapshot before running installs. We added a sparse-lock-importer script to only materialize install fragments needed for the changed files (reduces pip/npm churn). Lint-orchestra (tools/lint-orchestra/*) exposes an interface for adapters to report file-level ownership and run batches, and we wired Python and TypeScript adapters as prototypes. Tests include an end-to-end smoke that validates warm-path + fallback to normal installs and unit tests for the orchestra controller.

Checklist:
- [x] Implement dep-snapshotter + packager
- [x] Integrate warm-cache hook into CI pipeline
- [x] Add lint-orchestra controller and two adapters (py/ts)
- [x] Add e2e and unit tests
- [x] Document runbook and rollback
- [x] Feature-flag rollout plan for canary teams

Design notes: Snapshots are keyed by (lockfile_hash, platform, toolchain_stamp). The packager attests content using our CI signing key; snapshots are immutable and garbage-collected by an expiry policy. The sparse-lock importer maps changed paths to a minimal install set using heuristics and a small persisted index (built as part of nightly snapshots). Lint-orchestra uses a simple queue + lease model: a coordinator allocates owners to adapters and deduplicates file-level lint invocations; adapters can opt into parallelism hints.

Testing and validation: CI smoke runs were executed against dev and staging with a representative set of PRs. Observed median warm-path success 82% on staging (platform: ubuntu-22.04 images) and ~40-60% reduction in install time for cached PRs. Lint-orchestra reduced duplicate linter invocations in a 50-PR synthetic test by 38% and sped up average presubmit feedback by ~12s for multi-package changes.

Rollout plan: Feature-flag enabled in CI. Phase 1 (canary): opt-in for platform and infra teams for 2 weeks; Phase 2: enable for all presubmit jobs where a snapshot tag exists; Phase 3: default warm-path with monitoring guardrails. Lint-orchestra will be staged by repo and language adapter; default behavior is conservative (no skipping) and a telemetry-driven opt-in for teams.

Risks & mitigations: Broken snapshot keys could cause cache misses — mitigated by strong fallbacks to current install path and an automatic retry. Signing / verification errors are logged and cause a safe-fail to fallback. Lint-orchestra could introduce ordering/regression in linters; adapters run in a strict mode initially and the controller records a replayable trace for debugging. We included a rollback job to purge the pipeline hooks and a toggle to disable the warm path.

Follow-ups: 1) add Ruby/Go adapters for lint-orchestra; 2) increase cross-platform snapshot coverage (mac/linux/arm); 3) metrics exporter for snapshot hit/miss and per-adapter dedupe stats; 4) add artifact retention tuning to infra.

Operational notes: docs/ops/ci-snapshotter-runbook.md contains manual recovery commands for mis-signed artifacts and the steps to force a rebuild of nightly index. The CI team (Evan, Priya) will monitor snapshot-hit and installer duration dashboards for the first 4 weeks.
Adds a deterministic dependency snapshotter that produces lightweight archive artifacts for CI warmup; introduces a coordinated lint orchestration layer to reduce duplicate linter runs across languages and speed up presubmit feedback.
Evan: request_changes - Can we narrow the signer permissions? Priya: replied - moved signing to the CI agent and limited key access to the packager role, added audit logs. Marta: comment - need clearer failure-levels in pipeline to avoid noisy alerts; Priya: replied - introduced explicit metric tags and categorized logs as info/warn/critical. Diego: approved after small lint adapter refactor. CI: all checks passed after two reruns (one flaky npm cache issue), maintainer: squash-merged.
payload.title: Introduce dep-snapshotter and lint-orchestra to reduce CI boot latency and dep churn

Motivation: Customers building high-throughput agents asked for clearer failure behaviour when downstream model capacity degrades, and for an ergonomic way to cancel long-lived streaming responses from application code. This PR introduces two coordinated, backwards-compatible features across Python, TypeScript and Go SDKs: 1) a set of "fail-fast" circuit-style retry profiles (small, deterministic retry counts with early circuit open heuristics) that are safe for low-latency interactive workloads; 2) an explicit stream.abort/close API surface that signals the SDK to abort in-flight streams and emit a concise error shape for downstream apps to handle. The goal is parity across SDKs with minimal API churn and a single documented guidance doc for product teams.
This change is opt-in for most users: FailFast presets are not the default. To opt in: set retry_profile='failfast' in client options or use the FailFastRetryPolicy factory in Go. Stream abort APIs are additive: StreamHandle.abort() (py/ts) or AbortStream(ctx) (go) are available immediately. See docs/sdk/abort-and-retry-guidance.md for migration examples.
- Add fail-fast retry profiles (opt-in) to improve latency behavior for interactive apps.
- Add explicit stream abort APIs to Python (StreamHandle.abort), TypeScript (AbortableStream.abort), and Go (AbortStream(ctx)) to allow deterministic cancellation with a uniform error shape.
- SDK bumps: python 2.5.0, typescript 1.9.0, go 1.7.2.
Risk: customers might enable FailFast without understanding throughput tradeoffs. Mitigation: opt-in by default and clear decision table in docs; added telemetry to detect misuse. Risk: abort semantics could leak resources on older runtimes. Mitigation: added unit + integration tests and backfilled reader close paths in TS and finalizers in Python.
Priya Nair: Nice work. Please clarify which retry profile is the default for the hosted API consumer and add guidance for when customers should prefer FailFast vs Conservative.
Maya Chen (author): Added a short decision table to docs/sdk/abort-and-retry-guidance.md and set FailFast as an opt-in preset only; default remains Conservative for backwards compatibility.
Jonas Müller: In the TS implementation the AbortableStream still leaves a socket in some edge cases. I left an inline suggestion to close the reader on error path.
Maya Chen (author): Fixed TS reader close in the follow-up commit. Added a unit test that injects a flaky ReadableStream and asserts resources are released.
Liam O'Connor: Can we ensure the Go API follows Go idioms (context cancel semantics)? I left a suggestion to accept ctx on AbortStream and to return a typed error constant.
Maya Chen (author): Updated Go signature to AbortStream(ctx) and introduced ErrStreamAborted constant; added doc comment with migration note.
payload.title: polyglot-sdks: add fail-fast circuit retry profiles and explicit stream abort APIs

Motivation: customers running mixed-language integrations reported subtle behavior drift between Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs when short-lived credentials and long-lived streaming sessions are combined. This caused noisy retries and either token-exhausted stream failures or over-aggressive reauths. This PR unifies credential lease/refresh semantics, introduces a small "stream-swap" adapter that gracefully stitches a new stream instance during reauth, and applies ergonomic API surface polish across SDKs. Summary of changes: 1) Introduce a shared credential policy spec (TTL, prefetch jitter, backoff profile) and implement adapters in each SDK; 2) Add stream-swap adapter: a lightweight wrapper that allows an in-progress async iterator/stream consumer to transparently continue across credential rotation without forcing a reconnect from the application layer; 3) Align default backoff profiles and make them configurable via new RetryProfile type with presets (fast-retry, balanced, conservative); 4) Python: add AsyncStream.swap_on_auth(handler) method and small refactor to session manager to expose lease diagnostics; 5) TypeScript: add StreamHandle.swapOnAuth() and expose public RetryProfile enum; 6) Go: introduce StreamSwitcher interface and compact cred-cascade helper; 7) Update docs and examples (quickstart and streaming guides) and bump SDK versions: python 0.24.1, typescript 1.11.0, go 0.9.7. Backwards compatibility: default behaviours are preserved, migrations notes provided in release notes and in SDK CHANGELOGs. Testing: cross-language integration tests exercising token expiry during streaming; added unit tests for adapter swap semantics. Checklist: - [x] design doc (Linear ENG-8032) linked - [x] unit tests for each SDK - [x] e2e cross-language test harness run - [x] docs updated - [x] version bumps and package publish scripts updated Breaking changes: none expected; small API additions are additive and default runtime policy matches previous defaults. Rollout: feature gated by env var REDWOOD_SDK_STREAM_SWAP (off by default) for 2 weeks, then enabled by default after monitoring period.
Priya Shah: Great consolidation — can we add a small doc snippet showing how swap_on_auth behaves with partial message buffers?
Ava Martinez: Added section in streaming.md with a short code example and note about buffer semantics (we preserve existing in-flight buffer and replay only pending acknowledgements).
Diego Fernandez: In TS adapter, can we make the swap callback typed to accept an optional credentials object? Might help consumers avoid casting.
Ava Martinez: Updated StreamHandle.swapOnAuth signature to accept typed Cred object and added unit test for type safety.
Lina Chen: CI flaked initially in integration-crosslang on Windows runners, looks like a timing issue in token expiry harness. Suggest adding small jitter to the harness timeouts.
Ava Martinez: Increased harness sleep jitter and made the token expiry window configurable for CI; reran and all green.
Marcus Osei: Approving, left a nit about README ordering.
Add unified credential policy and stream-swap adapter across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs; introduce RetryProfile presets; add ergonomics for swap-on-auth APIs; minor SDK bumps: python 0.24.1, typescript 1.11.0, go 0.9.7. See docs/sdk/streaming.md for migration steps.
Gate rollout behind REDWOOD_SDK_STREAM_SWAP for two weeks to validate in production
Observability: added lease-age and reauth-count metrics to SDKs (see console metrics under sdk.session.*)
Follow-up: consider adding a C-based low-latency swap path for high-throughput Go consumers (ENG-8099)
Publish: packaging changes updated in ci/publish-sdks.yml to support triage cut for three SDKs simultaneously
payload.title: Trio SDK credential policy parity, stream-swap adapters, and ergonomic API polish

payload.body:
## Summary
This PR tightens up streaming behavior in the TS SDK to match the SDK parity standard work in-flight: (1) cancellation semantics are clarified and implemented consistently (AbortController / abort signal), and (2) partial output is surfaced deterministically when a stream disconnects mid-generation.

We have had multiple reports where customers see a stream stop (proxy FIN, connection reset, or local cancellation) and the SDK either (a) throws a generic error with no request_id and loses already-received text, or (b) treats abort errors as retryable in downstream middleware. Both create confusing behavior and make Support triage harder.

This PR is intentionally conservative: we do **not** automatically retry a partially-consumed stream because the server-side operation may not be safe to repeat. Instead, we (a) preserve and expose partial output and (b) make it obvious in the error surface what happened and what the caller should do.

## Behavior changes (intended)
- **User cancellation** (AbortController.abort(), or abort signal triggered):
  - We stop reading immediately, cancel the underlying reader, and close the iterator.
  - We throw a typed `RedwoodStreamCancelledError` (name bikeshedded below; see review) with `retryable=false`.
  - If we already parsed request metadata from SSE headers/events, we include `request_id`.
  - We do *not* increment retry counters or run retry middleware for cancellations.

- **Disconnect after partial output** (socket hang up, ECONNRESET, proxy closes, decode errors mid-chunk):
  - We continue to emit events up to the point we can parse them.
  - On failure, we throw `RedwoodStreamDisconnectedError` with:
    - `request_id` (if known)
    - `status_code` (if the response was received)
    - `streaming_disconnect_reason` (best-effort classification)
    - `partial_text` and `partial_events_count`
    - `retryable=false` by default (consistent with parity guidance)

- **Server-side errors prior to receiving any stream events** (e.g., 429/5xx with JSON error):
  - No change in classification here; this continues to flow through the standard error taxonomy and may be retryable depending on code.

## Why this is needed
- Support drivers: SUP-29505 (enterprise proxies causing mid-stream disconnects) and INT-1182 (request_id missing in SDK errors) repeatedly point to our streaming path as a gap.
- Parity: Python and Go are aligning on "don’t drop partial output" and "cancellation != retry". TS needed explicit plumbing because fetch/AbortController behavior differs across node/browsers.

## Implementation details
- Stream parsing now maintains a small accumulator with:
  - `partialText` (concatenated text deltas)
  - `eventCount`
  - `lastEventAt`
  - `requestId` (learned from initial response headers when available, and/or first metadata event)
- The streaming iterator wraps read/decode/parse errors into typed streaming errors and attaches partial output fields.
- Cancellation:
  - If the abort signal fires, we call `reader.cancel()` and stop iteration.
  - We normalize DOMException AbortError vs Node fetch abort variants to a single typed SDK error.
- Examples updated to demonstrate recommended usage:
  - call `controller.abort()` when user navigates away
  - log `request_id` on both normal completion and errors
  - do not retry the same stream automatically; instead, start a new request with user confirmation / idempotency guidance.

## Tests
- Unit tests for:
  - abort before first chunk => `RedwoodStreamCancelledError`
  - abort after N events => cancelled error includes partial_text
  - simulated disconnect mid-chunk => disconnected error includes partial_text + event count
  - request_id propagation (header + event)
- Adjusted existing streaming snapshot tests to reflect the new terminal error shapes.

## Docs / examples
- Updated `examples/stream-chat.ts` and `examples/stream-generate.ts` to use AbortController and handle partial output.

## Follow-ups
- Conformance suite will add a fixture for "disconnect after partial output" so Python/Go/TS all behave identically (tracked in ENG-5127).
- Once gateway request_id propagation PR lands everywhere, we should see request_id present earlier in the stream more reliably.

## Checklist
- [x] Typed errors include request_id where available
- [x] Cancellation is non-retryable and does not go through retry middleware
- [x] Partial output is surfaced on disconnect
- [x] Examples updated
- [x] Tests added

Refs: ENG-5124, ENG-5126, SUP-29505, INT-1182
- Streaming cancellation is now explicitly treated as user-initiated (non-retryable) and returns a typed cancellation error with request_id (when known).
- When a stream ends unexpectedly after some tokens/events were received, the SDK now surfaces partial output consistently via the streamed events and the terminal error includes partial_text/partial_events metadata.
- Examples updated to show AbortController usage and recommended logging fields (request_id, retry_count, streaming_disconnect_reason).
Ibrahim Khan (2026-01-29): We should be explicit in the docstring that cancellation is *never* retried, even if it happens after some tokens. Also, can we guarantee we cancel the reader to avoid hanging sockets in node/undici?
Dana Lo (2026-01-29): Yep—added `reader.cancel()` in both abort handler and finally block, and added a test that asserts we stop reading within 1 tick after abort. Updated docstrings to state: "user cancel => non-retryable".
Allison Grant (2026-01-30): Please add `streaming_disconnect_reason` as a stable string (for logging/telemetry parity). We can keep it best-effort but needs to be present on disconnected errors. Also ensure we don’t leak raw error messages that may include URLs w/ query params.
Dana Lo (2026-01-30): Added `streaming_disconnect_reason` with values: `abort`, `socket_hang_up`, `connection_reset`, `decode_error`, `unexpected_eof`, `unknown`. Also redacted underlying error to `cause` and we only surface sanitized message in the top-level error. Updated tests accordingly.
Monica Patel (2026-02-01): Minor naming: can we align error names with the taxonomy doc (Cancelled vs Aborted)? I think `StreamCancelled` is fine. Also: does `partial_text` exist for both disconnected + cancelled cases?
Dana Lo (2026-02-01): Renamed to `RedwoodStreamCancelledError` (kept alias for one release behind a deprecated export). `partial_text` is included when we have deltas parsed (both cancelled and disconnected). For cancellation before first chunk, it’s empty string and `partial_events_count=0`.
Wei Chen (2026-02-02): Example reads well. Please add one line: "don’t automatically retry a partially-consumed stream" and reference idempotency guidance. I’ll mirror this in docs PR later.
Dana Lo (2026-02-02): Added a short note in README + examples comment block; no new link added yet (will point to migration guide in ENG-5128).
Ibrahim Khan (2026-02-03): LGTM once CI is green on node18 (last run failed due to flaky timing).
Dana Lo (2026-02-03): Fixed the flaky test by waiting on a deterministic abort signal promise instead of setTimeout. Rerun green.
Ibrahim Khan (2026-02-03): Approved.
Monica Patel (2026-02-03): Approved.
payload.title: Streaming: clarify cancellation semantics + surface partial output consistently (AbortController)

Context and motivation: Multi-SDK teams continue to drift on small but breaking ergonomics around reauth metadata, session hints, and stream shutdown semantics. This PR standardizes the "reauth hint" metadata contract that the client SDK surfaces to the runtime and introduces a small, explicit ClosableAsyncIterator / StreamHandle API in the TypeScript SDK (mirrored in Go/Python in companion PRs) to make graceful stream teardown and in-flight token handoff deterministic. The goal is parity across TS/Py/Go for token hinting + a small ergonomic upgrade for consumers that need ordered shutdown (safely drain, optionally prefetch/prime next token) while preserving backwards compatibility.

This description contains the full change list, commits, CI summary, review conversation, and merge notes below.

What changed (high level): 1) Add a lightweight 'reauth-hint' header field in client requests and a typed ReauthHint interface in the SDKs so adapters and gateways can pick up a canonical hint (preferred expiry_offset_ms, preferred_credential_chain_id). 2) Introduce ClosableAsyncIterator and StreamHandle types in the TS SDK: close(reason?) returns a promise that resolves when the iterator drains and releases underlying resources; a gracefulClose option exists for draining vs abort. 3) Expose a new client config field 'credentialHinting: { enabled:true|false }' defaulting to true to allow gradual rollout. 4) Add integration tests across Node/Browser bundles that assert handshake includes reauth-hint and that close() triggers socket drain rather than immediate abort. 5) Bump package to v1.28.0 and add a short migration note.

Compatibility and migration notes: credentialHinting defaults to true so existing consumers see no behavioral change. The new types are additive; existing AsyncIterator consumers will continue to work. The reauth metadata keys are optional on the wire - runtime will ignore when missing. See release_notes for tips.

Checklist: - [x] Spec and Linear ticket (ENG-12291) linked - [x] TS SDK implementation - [x] E2E tests (Node + Browser) - [x] Companion PRs in redwood-sdk-go and redwood-sdk-python prepared - [x] Docs snippet and migration note - [x] Version bump and CHANGELOG entry

Related: Linear ENG-12291, ENG-12318; companion PRs: redwood-sdk-go#274590 (credential-dampener), redwood-sdk-python#381207 (session-lease-deterministic-retries).
Diego Alvarez: Nice small surface. One question: the reauth hint currently exposes expiry_offset_ms; how should SDKs compute that safely in low-resolution timers? Suggest we document recommended jitter/rounding.
Hannah Lee: Please add a short internal note explaining how this interacts with the Dedicated routing fallback: we need to ensure hints are stripped for customers who opt-out at the routing layer.
Marcus Chen: The StreamHandle API looks good. Can we add an optional onClose hook so applications can run a cleanup after drain?
Priya Menon: @Diego added explanation + code comment recommending Math.max(0, expiryMs - 1500) rounding in src/auth/reauth_hint.ts and an integration test to assert non-negative hint values.
Priya Menon: @Hannah noted in docs/migrations.md that routing layers may remove reauth meta; credentialHinting flag allows clients to opt out. Also added an internal-only flag to strip hints at gateway when configured.
Priya Menon: @Marcus added optional onClose hook to StreamHandle and unit tests that assert it is invoked after drain completes.
- Add ReauthHint metadata contract (optional).\n- Introduce ClosableAsyncIterator/StreamHandle to allow graceful drain and deterministic teardown.\n- Add credentialHinting config (default: enabled).\n- Bump TypeScript SDK to v1.28.0.\nMigration: Most consumers require no changes; see docs/migrations.md for examples on using StreamHandle.close() and opt-out configuration.

Fixes a bug where our SSE parser only consumed the first `data:` line per event. When proxies coalesce frames, Redwood may emit multiline `data:` segments that must be concatenated with `
` before JSON.parse. This manifested as missing deltas in streaming chat output (SUP-4835). Adds a dedicated SSE parse helper with unit tests for multiline data and mixed `event:` fields.

tests: add multiline data fixture
docs: clarify streaming transport assumptions

` per spec; JSON strings remain escaped; added a test.
Reviewer (Avery): Add changelog entry.

payload.body:
Motivation: onboarding often produces noisy changelogs; reviewers need a reproducible checklist to evaluate behavioral deltas. This PR adds two complementary pieces: (1) a provenance-diff playbook that composes deterministic artifacts (manifest fingerprints, sample probes, telemetry rollup) so reviewers can reproduce observed changes locally or in CI; (2) a weighted telemetry release-notes generator that synthesizes short, prioritized bullets from telemetry signals (quality regressions, latency deltas, token-cost impact) using configurable weights so PMs can tune what appears in the autogenerated draft.

What this changes: single continuous change set implemented in the model-registry service and the onboarding tooling: - new command `mrctl diff-playbook <model-version> --seed-sample` which outputs a compact tarball with manifest.json, probe-samples.ndjson, deterministic inference harness script, and a concise provenance graph; - a telemetry summarizer that consumes the sampling bucket and outputs a human-readable release snippet and an optional Linear draft; - safety sanitizer hook that removes high-confidence PII from probe samples and marks samples as scrubbed in the provenance manifest.

Checklist: - [x] provenance manifest schema v1 (manifest.json) added and validated in onboarding CI - [x] deterministic sample extractor (seeded RNG) - [x] release-note summarizer with tunable weights and markdown output - [x] sample sanitizer + opt-in scrubbed flag - [x] unit + integration tests for playbook generation - [x] telemetry aggregation hook and draft Linear creation (opt-in)

Compatibility and scope: This is backward-compatible for existing onboard flows; the `mrctl` command is opt-in and the summarizer only writes drafts unless `--publish-draft` is provided. The change adds metadata fields to the model registry DB (provenance_hash, scrubbed_samples) but the fields are optional for older entries. No runtime serving changes are included.

How reviewers can validate locally: 1) `./dev/mrctl build-playbook --model-id model:open-sample:1.2 --seed 42` 2) run `./dev/playbook-runner reproduce.tar.gz` inside a small pinned Python venv (requirements included) 3) assert that the outputs (log/histograms/nbest diffs) match the CI artifact.

Related work: ENG-7245 (onboard-sanity-probes), PM-331 (release-note prioritization), SUP-1982 (customer request for concise impact bullets).
Introduce a reproducible 'provenance-diff' playbook that captures model, dataset, and ingest-sample deltas; add a weighted-telemetry summarizer that drafts concise release notes and impact bullets for curators and SRE. No customer-facing API changes.
Diego: Please add more detail on how provenance_hash is computed — deterministic across infra? Maya: provenance_hash is SHA256 over ordered manifest entries (model-blob-hash, sample-seed, observed-metrics snapshot) and we added a helper to canonicalize the manifest. Diego: add unit test to ensure canonicalization stable across platforms — DONE in test_playbook_generation.py. Asha: telemetry weights should be configurable per-team; can we make a simple YAML override? Maya: YAML override supported via ~/.mrctl/config.yaml and CLI flags. Liam: small nit on docs wording about 'scrubbed' vs 'anonymized' — updated docs to prefer 'scrubbed' to reflect irreversible removal. Approvals: Diego approved after tests green; Asha approved after config change; Liam gave LGTM for docs.
Ops: this adds optional DB columns (provenance_hash, scrubbed_samples boolean). Migration is online and idempotent; run migrations in the normal deploy window. Telemetry summarizer writes drafts to a drafts bucket in staging by default; enable production by flipping mrctl.config.publish_drafts and granting the Linear webhook secret. Backfill: not required. If rollback needed, remove playbook artifacts and drop metadata columns carefully after pruning references.
payload.title: Add provenance-diff playbook and weighted telemetry release notes generator

payload.body:
Motivation: Onboarding new models currently requires manual triage to decide rollout priority and to draft release notes. That slows curator velocity and leads to inconsistent brief quality. This PR introduces an automated onboard priority scorer (onboard_score) that combines telemetry signals, compatibility checks, and profile stability heuristics, plus a generator that drafts compact release brief snippets for changelogs and release announcements. What this change does (single-continuous description): Implements a lightweight heuristic-based scorer that combines the following signals: 1) observed production traffic similarity (sampled usage match), 2) profile stability (sigma of latency/throughput across probes), 3) evaluation quality delta on our curated prompt set, and 4) compatibility surface area (number of dependent consumers flagged via manifest). The score is normalized 0-100 and persisted as metadata field model.metadata.onboard_score.
Adds a brief generator that creates a 1-2 sentence release snippet and a 1-3 bullet micro-summary of expected impact (tokens, latency, recommended rollout windows). The generator keeps output under a 280-character headline plus a 3-line body by default and redacts any example prompts or customer-identifying telemetry. Implementation notes: - Registry schema migration: adds onboard_score and onboard_brief snapshot fields (backward compatible; absent for older models). - New CLI command: `redwood model suggest-onboard --model-id ` which returns the score and brief in JSON or plain text. - Background job: `onboard-scorer-worker` samples recent telemetry (bounded window, default 72h, max 1000 samples) and computes score; runs at configurable cadence (default daily). - Release brief CI hook: `validate-release-brief` runs against any generated brief, flagging length/privacy/style rule violations. - Unit tests: scorer logic, normalization, and redaction rules covered; e2e integration test for the CLI against a test fixture. - Perf guardrails: the worker uses reservoir sampling and early-exit heuristics to bound compute and memory. Files changed (high level): registry/db/migrations/20260218_add_onboard_columns.sql, registry/services/onboard_scorer.py, registry/services/brief_gen.py, cli/commands/suggest_onboard.py, ci/validate_release_brief.sh, tests/test_onboard_scorer.py, tests/test_brief_gen.py, docs/onboarding/auto-briefs.md, examples/onboard-sample.yaml and small updates to api/serializers.py and web/ui components to display the score in the model detail page. Security & privacy: The brief generator strips prompt examples and any PII-like fields. Telemetry sampling uses only aggregated/prod-metric-level signals; raw request text is never pulled into brief generation. The CI rule enforces that generated briefs pass a privacy redaction check. For private/on-prem customers the worker is disabled by default; CLI works offline with local telemetry if enabled. Testing and CI: Initial CI run failed lint (flake8/black) and one unit test related to sampling edge-cases. Fixed in follow-up commit `fix: sampling bound and lint` and re-ran CI. Final status: all checks passed. Migration/rollout plan: - Deploy schema migration with nullable fields. - Enable background worker in canary region for 48h with telemetry throttles. - Surface score in UI behind a feature flag. - After 2 weeks of telemetry, enable automatic brief suggestions in PR templates but keep human approval required for final release note publish. Why not ML model-based scoring: We intentionally used heuristic composition to avoid adding a new training lifecycle and to keep determinism and auditability for release audits. Future work: pluggable ML-based ranker behind the same API (ENG-5012). Related work: ENG-4938 (onboard automation), ENG-4721 (profile stability telemetry), PM-127 (release note UX). Jared Klein: Good direction — please add a brief explainer of score composition and a reproducibility script so we can audit how a given score was derived. Maya Chopra (author): Added a reproducibility endpoint `/api/v1/models//onboard_score/explain` that returns component contributions and sample counts (no raw text). See new serializer and tests. Lina Morales: Need to ensure this is opt-in for Private customers; doc says disabled by default but please add a config flag and ensure worker doesn't attempt to call telemetry endpoints when disabled. Maya Chopra: Added `ONBOARD_SCORER_ENABLED` param and guard checks in worker; unit tests assert worker no-op when disabled. Aya Sato: CI hook looks fine but we should avoid failing PRs for minor style guidance — prefer warnings for suggested wording. Can we make length and privacy hard-fail but stylistic lint optional? Maya Chopra: CI now enforces privacy and length as hard-fail; style suggestions are reported as warnings and surfaced in the PR comment. See `ci/validate_release_brief.sh` changes. Lina Morales: Please add a small E2E job that runs the CLI suggestion against a representative model fixture to catch integration regressions. Maya Chopra: Added `tests/e2e/test_cli_suggest_onboard.sh` which is run in the integration CI matrix. Jared Klein: Approving after the fixes — nice work keeping this auditable and privacy-aware.
